weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A lot of rain in a short time can split ripe fruit. Pick anything that is nearly ready before it cracks, and check for soil splash on lower leaves which can spread disease.

germination.text_beginner: Bottom heat is the single biggest factor in germination speed. If you have a heat mat, use it; if not, the top of a refrigerator or any spot that stays around 75°F works well. Most roma tomato seeds sprout in 5 to 7 days with steady warmth.
germination.text_seasoned: Bottom heat is the single biggest factor in germination speed. A heat mat, the top of your refrigerator, or anywhere consistently warm works well. Most tomato seeds germinate in 5-7 days at 75°F.

germination.text_beginner: Cover your seed tray with a plastic dome or cling wrap until the first sprout appears, then remove it immediately. The dome traps humidity to keep the seed surface moist during germination, but once the shoot emerges, that same warm, still air is the ideal environment for damping off, a fungal problem that collapses the stem at the soil line and kills the seedling overnight with no recovery. Remove the dome at first sprout and give the seedlings fresh air; slightly drier conditions at the soil surface prevent it.
germination.text_seasoned: Cover your tray with a humidity dome or cling film until the first sprout appears, then remove it immediately. The dome holds humidity to prevent the seed surface from drying out during germination, but once the shoot emerges the same warm, still, humid air becomes the ideal environment for Pythium and Rhizoctonia, the soilborne fungi that cause damping off. Damping off collapses the stem at soil level; there is no recovery. Fresh air and slightly drier conditions at the soil surface after emergence are the primary prevention.

seedling.text_beginner: If your seedlings are tall and thin and look weak, they need more light, not less water. Move them right next to a bright window (but pull them back a few inches at night if the window gets cold), or set up a grow light to shine on them for 14-16 hours each day. Pale color is a sign of the same problem.
seedling.text_seasoned: Leggy, stretched seedlings almost always mean not enough light, not overwatering. Get them as close to a bright window as possible, or use a grow light 14-16 hours a day.

seedling.text_beginner: Once you have two sets of true leaves, move the seedling into its own small pot or 3-inch cell. Tomatoes root all along their stems, so plant it a little deeper than it was sitting, as the buried stem becomes more roots.
seedling.text_seasoned: Once you have two sets of true leaves, pot up into individual cells or small 3-inch pots. Tomatoes root all along their stems, so you can bury them deeper than they were, which builds a stronger plant.

established.text_beginner: Hardening off takes 7 to 10 days and is worth every day of it. The seedlings have been raised in still indoor air with no wind or direct sun, and their leaves aren't built for outdoor conditions yet. Start with 1 to 2 hours outside in a sheltered, partly shaded spot, then add more time and more sun each day. Plants that are hardened off gradually settle in within a week of transplanting; plants that skip it can take 3 weeks to recover.
established.text_seasoned: Harden off over 7-10 days, a gradual introduction to outdoor conditions rather than an abrupt move. Indoors, seedlings have thin cuticles, less concentrated chlorophyll, and stomata that have never experienced wind. Sudden outdoor exposure causes sunscald, wilting, and cold stress even on mild days. Start with 1-2 hours in a sheltered, partly shaded spot, adding time and sun exposure each day. Plants that skip hardening off sulk for 2-3 weeks after transplanting while they adapt.

established.text_beginner: Plant your tomatoes deeper than the pot they came in. Dig a hole deep enough to bury the stem right up to the lowest set of leaves, as every bit of buried stem grows roots, and more roots means a stronger, more drought-tolerant plant from day one.
established.text_seasoned: Plant your tomatoes deeper than they sit in the pot. Bury the stem right up to the lowest set of leaves. Every bit of buried stem becomes roots.

flowering.text_beginner: Give the flowering stems a gentle shake or tap in the morning to help with pollination. Tomato flowers release pollen when they vibrate, and bees do this naturally, but in sheltered gardens or when bee activity is low, giving the stems a quick shake does the same job. Without it, some flowers drop before setting fruit.
flowering.text_seasoned: A gentle shake or tap of the flowering stem in the morning helps pollen transfer. Tomato flowers are self-fertile, but pollen is released most efficiently by vibration: bumblebees accomplish this naturally through buzz pollination, where wing-beat frequency resonates the anthers and dislodges pollen. In sheltered gardens, polytunnels, or indoor growing environments without significant wind or bee activity, the plant depends on incidental vibration for pollination. Shaking the stem in the morning (when pollen is freshly released) is the practical substitute. Under-pollinated flowers drop without setting fruit.

flowering.text_beginner: Once flowers open, stop any high-nitrogen fertilizer and switch to a tomato fertilizer or one with a high third number (potassium). Nitrogen is what makes plants grow leaves, exactly right early on but exactly wrong once flowering starts. Potassium is what the plant needs to build good fruit.
flowering.text_seasoned: Stop high-nitrogen feeding when flowers appear and switch to a high-potassium, low-nitrogen feed. Nitrogen drives vegetative growth by stimulating cell division and chlorophyll synthesis, exactly what you want early in the season and exactly what you don't want once flowering starts; potassium plays a different role: it regulates stomatal opening, drives sugar transport from leaves into developing fruit, and is critical for cell wall formation in the fruit itself. A tomato-specific or high-K fertilizer (look for an NPK ratio with a high last number, such as 5-10-10 or 4-12-8) used from first flowering onward translates directly into heavier, better-flavored fruit.

harvest.text_beginner: With a determinate roma, most of the fruit ripens together, so plan on a few big harvests over a couple of weeks rather than picking every day. Gather the batch as it colors up for sauce or canning.
harvest.text_seasoned: Roma is determinate, so its crop ripens in a concentrated flush; harvest the main batch in a few large pickings rather than daily. Picking ripe fruit promptly limits cracking and lets you process the batch at once.

harvest.text_beginner: Try a few tomatoes at different stages to find what your palate likes. Some varieties are sweetest just at peak color; others improve with a few more days. Your own taste is the best harvest guide you have.
harvest.text_seasoned: Taste as you go. Different varieties peak at different moments: some are best just before fully ripe, others need a few more days. Your palate is the best harvest indicator you have.

end_of_season.text_beginner: When nights drop regularly below 50°F, pinch out the growing tips, the very top of each stem. Below 55°F, tomatoes stop setting new fruit reliably. By removing the growing tips, you redirect the plant's energy into ripening the fruit already on the vine rather than trying to grow new stems that won't produce before frost.
end_of_season.text_seasoned: When nights drop regularly below 50°F, pinch out all the growing tips. Below 55°F, pollen viability drops sharply and fruit set becomes unlikely even if flowers are still opening. At 50°F and below, the plant is physiologically in decline for new fruit production. Pinching the growing tips, the terminal bud at the top of each stem, removes the hormone sink that draws resources toward new vegetative growth, redirecting carbohydrates toward the fruit already on the vine. A plant with 10-15 near-ripe tomatoes will finish them faster once it has stopped trying to grow new stems.

end_of_season.text_beginner: Green tomatoes brought in before frost will ripen indoors. Lay them in a single layer somewhere cool (60 to 65°F) and dark, not the refrigerator. Refrigerator temperatures cause chilling injury, which produces the mealy, flavorless texture that makes people think they dislike tomatoes. Room temperature speeds ripening but hurts flavor; 60 to 65°F is the right balance.
end_of_season.text_seasoned: Green tomatoes left on the plant when frost threatens can be brought inside to ripen. Lay them in a single layer somewhere cool (60-65°F) and dark, not the refrigerator. Refrigerator temperatures (below 50°F) cause chilling injury: cell membranes in the fruit lose their selective permeability, releasing enzymes that break down cell walls, producing the mealy texture and muted flavor characteristic of cold-stored tomatoes. The damage is irreversible once it occurs. Ripening indoors at 60-65°F is slower than at room temperature but preserves flavor better than hurrying at 70°F+.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A determinate roma typically yields about 8 to 15 pounds of fruit per plant, set as a concentrated flush over two to four weeks rather than a season-long trickle. That batched harvest is the point for sauce and canning. Once the main flush finishes, a determinate plant produces little more, so growers who want a steady supply stagger two or three plantings a few weeks apart, or add a second planting where the season allows.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Expect roughly 8 to 15 pounds of tomatoes per plant, and here is the key difference from cherry tomatoes: a roma gives you most of that harvest in one big batch over a few weeks, then slows down. That is ideal if you want to make sauce all at once. If you would rather have a steady supply, plant two or three plants a couple of weeks apart so they ripen in sequence.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Production is front-loaded: a determinate roma ramps up quickly, peaks as most of the plant's fruit colors within a two to four week window, then tapers sharply. Plan canning or sauce-making for that peak.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: A roma plant does most of its work in a short burst: the fruit sizes up green, then a large share ripens within two to four weeks. Watch for that window and be ready to cook or can when it hits.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Your first year, expect to land in the lower part of the range while you learn what your spot needs. The four things that make the biggest difference are sun (at least 6 hours of direct sun daily), steady watering (which also prevents blossom-end rot), good soil, and catching problems early. Getting one solid batch of sauce tomatoes off a plant or two is a real first-season success.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: First-season plants often yield at the low end of the range as growers learn site-specific conditions. Soil organic matter, sun hours, consistent watering (the primary blossom-end-rot control), and timely disease response each move a plant within the 8 to 15 lb range. A single concentrated batch large enough to put up sauce is a genuine first-season success.
factors_seasoned: hours of direct sunlight
consistent watering (blossom-end rot control)
feeding schedule
caging and airflow

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: You'll see the leaves turn black or dark brown and go limp, sometimes overnight after a cold night. Tomatoes have no cold tolerance at all. Even without a hard freeze, temperatures below 50°F cause what's called chilling injury: the plant's cells start to break down, and young transplants are especially vulnerable because they haven't built up a protective waxy coating yet. It's tempting to think the plant just needs time to recover, but if it was hit by frost, it usually won't come back. For next time: wait until both your nighttime lows and your soil temperature are reliably above 60°F before transplanting.
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Frost or cold damage
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Wait until nighttime temperatures are reliably above 50°F AND your soil is above 60°F before transplanting, checking soil temperature 2 to 3 inches deep with an inexpensive probe thermometer. In Zones 3 to 5 this often means waiting until late May or early June no matter what the calendar says.
failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Frost or cold damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Tomatoes are warm-season crops with tropical origin and have no cold tolerance mechanism, unlike brassicas or root vegetables, they cannot harden or acclimate to cold. Chilling injury begins below 50°F and cell damage accelerates near freezing; a single frost event at the transplant stage usually kills the plant outright because young transplants have not yet developed the protective waxy cuticle layer that provides some buffer in established plants. Soil temperature is as important as air temperature: roots in cold soil (below 60°F) cannot take up water or nutrients efficiently even when air temperatures are acceptable, which causes transplant shock that looks like cold damage but persists for weeks after the weather improves.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait until both nighttime air temperatures are reliably above 50°F and soil temperature is above 60°F before transplanting. Check soil temperature with a probe thermometer 2-3 inches deep in the actual planting bed, as a south-facing raised bed can be 10°F warmer than a shaded in-ground bed on the same day. In zones 3-5, this means waiting until late May or even early June, regardless of calendar date.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Tomato plants can run into a few common problems. Blight is a leaf disease that shows up first on the bottom leaves and spreads fastest in wet, humid weather. Blossom end rot is the black or brown sunken spot on the bottom of the tomato, it looks like a nutrient problem, but it's almost always caused by uneven watering (dry one day, soaked the next). Adding calcium won't fix it. Steady moisture will.
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Water at the base of the plant (not from overhead) and stake the plant for good airflow, as leaves that dry quickly after rain are far harder for blight to infect. Move your tomatoes to a different bed each year; blight spores can persist in the soil and on old plant material. For blossom end rot: mulch heavily and water deeply and consistently rather than in small, frequent amounts.
failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Two of the most common problems, blight and blossom end rot, are frequently misdiagnosed and mistreated. Blight (early or late) is a fungal or oomycete disease that enters through wet leaf surfaces; spores splash up from soil and spread rapidly in warm, humid conditions, progressing from lower leaves upward. Removing affected leaves immediately slows but does not stop spread once established. Blossom end rot presents as a sunken, dark patch on the blossom end of developing fruit. Despite appearances, it is not a fungal disease and adding calcium to the soil rarely fixes it. The actual mechanism is calcium transport failure: calcium moves into developing fruit through the water stream in the xylem, and when watering is inconsistent, especially dry periods followed by heavy irrigation, the transpiration-driven flow to the blossom end is interrupted, and those cells die. Steady moisture at the root zone is the only reliable fix.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water at the base, never overhead, to eliminate the splash route that delivers blight spores to leaves. Stake and prune for airflow, as leaves that dry quickly after rain or dew are far less vulnerable. Rotate tomatoes to a different bed each year; blight spores persist in soil and on plant debris, and a fresh location breaks the inoculum cycle. For blossom end rot: mulch heavily to buffer moisture swings, and water deeply and consistently rather than shallowly and frequently.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Yellow lower leaves and wilting, even when the soil is wet, are the signs you've overwatered. Soggy soil pushes out the air the roots need to breathe; once roots suffocate, the plant can't take up water even though there's plenty of it, which is why it wilts. People often respond by watering more, which makes things worse. Cracked fruit is a related but separate problem: it happens when you water heavily after a dry stretch, the tomato swells fast and the skin splits. The fix is consistency: aim for steady moisture rather than long dry spells followed by big waterings.
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Too much water
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Water deeply and less often rather than a little every day. Deep watering encourages roots to grow down where the soil stays more stable; roots near the surface are the first to suffocate or dry out. A 2 to 3 inch layer of mulch around the base dramatically reduces moisture swings between waterings.
failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Too much water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Waterlogged soil drives out the oxygen roots need for cellular respiration, so roots in anaerobic conditions die back, and without functioning roots the plant cannot take up water or nutrients even as the soil stays wet. Yellowing lower leaves are the first visible sign, followed by generalized wilting that paradoxically looks like drought. Fruit cracking is a related but distinct problem: it happens when a sudden surge of water (heavy rain after a dry period, or a large irrigation after letting the plant get too dry) causes rapid fruit cell expansion in a skin that has already stopped stretching. The skin splits at the shoulders or develops concentric cracks. Both problems are rooted in inconsistency rather than sheer total volume, as a plant that receives consistent 1-2 inches per week rarely cracks or shows root oxygen stress.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water deeply and less frequently rather than a small amount every day. Deep watering (wetting the soil to 8-10 inches) encourages roots to grow down where soil moisture is more stable; shallow watering concentrates roots at the surface where they are most vulnerable to both drought and saturation. Mulching 2-3 inches around the base dramatically reduces moisture swings between waterings, which is the single most effective intervention against both fruit cracking and blossom end rot.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Flowers dropping before they form fruit and dark sunken patches on the bottom of tomatoes are the two big signs of insufficient or uneven watering. When water gets cut off during flowering, the plant sheds its flowers to conserve resources, physically cutting them loose at the stem. The dark patch on the fruit's base is called blossom end rot; it looks like a nutrient problem but it's almost always caused by uneven soil moisture, not a lack of calcium in your soil. People often add calcium supplements, but that won't fix it; steady, consistent watering will. Note that heat above 90°F causes the same flower-drop, so both can happen at the same time.
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Not enough water
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Aim for 1 to 2 inches of water per week, delivered consistently. Mulch around the base with straw or shredded leaves to slow the soil from drying out. In hot climates (Zones 8 to 11), a drip line on a timer is the most reliable way to keep moisture steady without thinking about it every day.
failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Too little water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Water stress during flowering triggers an abscission response: the plant activates an enzyme-driven separation layer at the base of each flower stem, dropping the flower before fruit can form. The same response is triggered by extreme heat (above 90°F daytime, below 55°F nighttime), which means during a heat wave, blossom drop can occur even if the soil seems adequately moist. During fruit development, inconsistent soil moisture is the primary cause of blossom end rot: calcium is transported to developing fruit through the transpiration stream, and interrupted water flow to the blossom end kills those cells. The external result is a sunken, darkened patch on the fruit's base.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Aim for 1-2 inches of water per week delivered consistently. Mulch heavily around the base to buffer the soil against rapid drying, as a 2-3 inch layer of straw or shredded leaves can halve moisture loss on a hot day. In zones 8-11, where summer heat makes consistent moisture especially difficult, a drip system on a timer is the most reliable tool. Water at the base of the plant, never the leaves.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: If your plant grows tall and leafy but produces very little fruit, or pale, flavorless tomatoes, sun is probably the problem. Tomatoes need at least 6 hours of direct sun per day; below that, the plant puts its energy into growing stems and leaves instead of fruit. What fruit does form tends to be bland because sugar development depends on sunlight. A secondary sign: shaded plants tend to stay wet longer and get more disease, because leaves don't dry out well in low light. If your spot gets 4-5 hours, you'll get some fruit, but manage expectations: fewer tomatoes, smaller, and less sweet than a full-sun plant.
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Not enough sun
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Tomatoes need at least 6 hours of direct sun per day, and this is not negotiable. If your current spot is borderline, walk your garden at different times of day and look for a spot a few feet over that gets more morning sun before something shades it. Compact roma tomato varieties like dwarf or patio types tolerate slightly less sun than full-size plants.
failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Not enough sun
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Tomatoes are among the most light-demanding vegetables: photosynthesis is the energy source for both vegetative growth and fruit sugar development, and fruit quality is directly proportional to the plant's photosynthetic output. Below 6 hours of direct sun, the plant redirects what energy it has toward survival, stem elongation and leaf area, rather than reproduction. Fruit set drops sharply, and what fruit does form is typically thin-skinned, pale, and bland. A secondary effect is increased disease: shaded plants stay wetter longer after rain or irrigation, and poor airflow through dense, etiolated growth creates the humid microclimate that blight and leaf mold need to establish.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Tomatoes are not negotiable on sun requirements. Below 6 hours of direct sun, expect significantly reduced yields and higher disease pressure regardless of everything else done correctly. If the current spot is marginal (6-7 hours), it is worth mapping sun across the garden before committing the bed again, as a spot that gets shade from a fence or tree in the afternoon may have 2-3 more hours of morning sun available just a few feet away. Dwarf or patio-type roma tomatoes tolerate slightly less sun than full-size plants.

crops.description_beginner: Roma tomatoes, also called paste or plum tomatoes, are the ones you grow to make sauce. They differ from cherry tomatoes in an important way: a roma is a determinate plant, which means it grows to a bushy, compact size and then ripens most of its tomatoes within a few weeks, instead of giving you a handful at a time all summer. That is actually the point: you get a big batch all at once, perfect for cooking down into sauce or canning in one go. The fruit is egg-shaped, thick-walled, and meaty, with few seeds and not much juice, so it cooks down fast. Because the plant stays short, it needs a sturdy cage rather than a tall stake, and it barely needs pruning. The main thing to watch for is blossom-end rot, a dark sunken spot on the bottom of the fruit. It looks like a disease, but it is caused by uneven watering, so water steadily and mulch around the base. If you are in a cold zone (3 to 5), pick an early variety so the crop finishes before frost; in a warm zone (9 to 11) you can plant a second batch in late summer for more sauce tomatoes in fall.

succession_policy.tip_beginner: A determinate roma ripens its crop in one concentrated flush, so a single planting gives you one big batch, ideal for a session of sauce or canning. If you want tomatoes coming in steadily, set out two or three plants a couple of weeks apart, or in warm zones (9 and up) add a second planting in late summer for a fall batch.
succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Determinate paste tomatoes fruit in a single concentrated flush rather than all season, so one planting yields one batch. For a staggered fresh supply, stagger plantings 2 to 3 weeks apart; in zone 9 and warmer a second late-summer planting extends into fall. Modeled here as discrete plantings, not continuous succession.
succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Determinate habit: one planting produces a concentrated flush, not continuous season-long fruit. Staggered or second plantings extend the supply.

crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Pick roma tomatoes when they are fully red all over and firm. Since you will most likely cook them, it is fine to let them ripen a little more on the vine and pick a big batch at once. A ripe roma twists off easily; if you have to tug, give it another day. Harvest in the morning when it is cooler.

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.source_quote: Plants started earlier are difficult to manage and do not necessarily lead to better or earlier harvests. (UMN)
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start tomatoes from seeds indoors, five to six weeks before planting outside. In most of Minnesota, this is mid-April. Roma is a determinate paste tomato, so a 6-week indoor start is appropriate. (UMN)

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: Many gardeners plant transplants the last week or two of May, after danger of frost has passed and air and soil temperatures warm. (MSU)
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start your warm season crops indoors for transplanting in mid-June, once the threat of frost has passed. Transplant outdoors after all danger of frost has passed and the soil has warmed. Don't be in a rush to transplant these tropical species. (UMaine, northern Maine Z3-4; UMN; NDSU)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.source_quote: Early varieties produce tomatoes from transplants in as little as 49 days. (MSU)
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Roma (paste) tomato varieties typically mature 70 to 80 days from transplant. (UGA Vegetable Garden Calendar; Clemson HGIC; MSU Extension)
harvest_start.design_note_seasoned: Conservative mid-point of 60 days used for cold zones.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.source_quote: Pick all the fruit and bring it indoors before the first frost at the end of summer. (UMN)
harvest_end.design_note_seasoned: Conservative policy: harvest_end = first_frost - 5 days to buffer against frost-risk week and to ensure notifications arrive before plants are killed.

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: For the fall crop in the warm end of the Northern Tier (zones 6-7), start seed indoors about six weeks before the early-to-mid-July transplant date, in late May to early June. Roma types (70 to 80 days from transplant) finish a fall crop before the first frost in these zones. (Virginia Cooperative Extension 426-331; Clemson HGIC)

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set the fall crop out in early-to-mid July so an early paste roma (70 to 80 days) matures before the first fall frost. VCE gives a zone-6 fall tomato transplant window of June 10-July 10; Clemson sets a fall tomato transplant deadline of about July 25 for the warmer zone-7 end. Back-timed from each zone's first-frost date. (Virginia Cooperative Extension 426-331; Clemson HGIC)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: First ripe fruit about 70 to 80 days after the July transplant, from mid-to-late September. (Clemson HGIC; Virginia Cooperative Extension 426-331)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest runs until the first fall frost cuts the plants short, late October in zone 6 and mid-November in zone 7. (Virginia Cooperative Extension 426-331)

3.notes: Short season: choose an early paste variety such as Plum Regal (early, blight resistant). Use black plastic mulch to warm soil.
3.zone_notes: Zone 3 is short-season but well-suited to roma tomatoes. Roma types (70 to 80 days) can still ripen before first frost in short seasons; choose an early paste variety in the coldest zones. Start seeds 6 weeks before last frost. Choose an early paste variety such as Plum Regal or Roma VF for a reliable, well-timed harvest.

4.notes: Start indoors 6 weeks before last frost. Wall-O-Waters can extend your season by 2-3 weeks.
4.zone_notes: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost. Choose an early, fast-maturing paste variety for best yield in a short season.

5.notes: Plant after soil hits 60°F. Mulch to retain moisture and prevent soil splash on lower leaves.
5.zone_notes: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost. Protect transplants if late frost threatens.

6.notes: Great zone for tomatoes. Two successions possible: plant again in early July for fall harvest.
6.zone_notes: Two crops possible: start first batch indoors in March, second batch indoors in late May for transplanting in July, as roma tomatoes ripen in about 70 to 80 days from transplant, still before first frost in these zones.

7.notes: Fruit set stops above 95°F, so time your planting so main harvest hits June and again in September.
7.zone_notes: Two crops possible: start first batch indoors in March, second batch indoors in late May for transplanting in July, as roma tomatoes ripen in about 70 to 80 days from transplant, still before first frost in these zones.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the cold northern states (zones 3 through 7) you grow roma tomatoes once a year, as a single summer crop. What limits the season here is frost on both ends, not summer heat: you plant after the last spring frost, pick all summer, and the plants are finished when the first fall frost arrives. There is no summer break the way hotter regions have, because northern summers usually are not hot enough to stop the plants from setting fruit. Wait to set out transplants until a week or two after your last frost, when nights stay warm and the soil has warmed up. Roma tomatoes ripen fast (about 55 to 65 days after transplanting), so they finish in time even where summers are short. In the coldest zones, pick quick varieties and warm the soil with black plastic mulch or season-extending covers; in the milder zones 6 and 7 you have time to plant a second batch in early summer for a fall crop.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: The Northern Tier (cold zones 3 through 7) grows roma tomatoes as a single frost-bracketed summer crop: the limiting factor on both ends is frost, not heat. Transplants go out a week or two after the last spring frost, once nights stay above the low 50s°F and soil warms past about 60°F, and a single planting then produces one continuous harvest through summer until plants are cut short by the first fall frost. There is no midsummer heat exclusion here: unlike the Southeast or the desert valleys, northern summers rarely sustain the high day and night temperatures that stop fruit set, so the winter gaps are frost pauses and the season is uninterrupted between them. Roma types (55 to 65 days from transplant) are well suited to short seasons and ripen before first frost even in zone 3. The cold end (zones 3 and 4) leans on fast-maturing varieties and season extension (black plastic mulch, Wall-O-Waters), while the warm end (zones 6 and 7) has room for a second transplanting in early-to-mid summer for a fall harvest. Frost dates shift sharply across the band, so confirm local last and first frost. (University of Minnesota Extension; North Dakota State University Extension; Michigan State University Extension; University of Maine Cooperative Extension)

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.source_quote: tomatoes will take 6 weeks
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start roma tomato seed indoors about six weeks before the spring transplant date. In the Southeast and Gulf region that places seeding in mid-to-late winter, roughly mid-February for the Georgia interior (zone 8) and two to three weeks earlier toward the warmer Gulf-coastal (zone 9) end. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: the last week of March or first week or two of April
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set roma tomato transplants out in spring once frost danger passes. UGA gives late March into the first half of April for middle Georgia (zone 8); the warmer zone 9 end runs two to three weeks earlier. Set out when soil is reliably above 60 degrees F. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Roma tomatoes begin ripening roughly two months after transplanting (about 70 to 80 days to maturity, mid near 75). The spring crop in this region comes in from late May into June, ahead of peak summer heat. (UF/IFAS VH021; UGA Cooperative Extension C943)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The spring crop winds down as summer heat sets in and night temperatures push fruit set toward blossom drop. Roma, a standard paste type, is no more heat tolerant than other large-fruited tomatoes and stops setting fruit as the summer heat arrives. (UF/IFAS VH021; UGA Cooperative Extension C943)

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.source_quote: tomatoes will take 6 weeks
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: For the fall crop, start seed indoors about six weeks before the late-summer transplant date, roughly late May into June across the region. For the fall window choose an early-maturing paste variety, since roma needs about 70 to 80 days to mature. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: Plant the following vegetables no later than July 20 ... tomatoes
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set the fall crop out in mid-to-late summer so plants establish through the back of the heat and produce into the cooler fall. UGA gives a fall tomato deadline of about July 20 for middle Georgia (zone 8); the warmer zone 9 end runs about two weeks later, into August, matching UF/IFAS North Florida's August tomato window. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall crop begins ripening about two months after the late-summer transplant, bringing first roma tomatoes in roughly September into October across the region. (UF/IFAS VH021; UGA Cooperative Extension C943)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.source_quote: Harvest mature green peppers and tomatoes before frost gets them
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall crop produces into the cooler autumn and is harvested up to first frost. Roma types, heat resistant and quick to mature, hold a longer productive tail here than large-fruited tomatoes. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer sowing gap is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: high day and especially night temperatures push tomato flowers to drop and fruit set to fail. Roma is a standard paste type and is no more heat tolerant than other large-fruited tomatoes, so this pause spans the full summer heat window for it. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

Summer sowing gap is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: high day and especially night temperatures push tomato flowers to drop and fruit set to fail. Roma is a standard paste type and is no more heat tolerant than other large-fruited tomatoes, so this pause spans the full summer heat window for it. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast and Gulf area you can grow roma tomatoes twice a year, once in spring and again in fall, with a summer break in between when it gets too hot for the plants to set fruit. Roma tomatoes are about as heat sensitive as other large tomatoes, so their summer break lasts the full hot season. Plant your spring crop early enough to pick before the worst heat, then plant again in mid-to-late summer for a fall crop.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: The Southeast and Gulf region runs two roma tomato seasons, spring and fall, split by a summer heat window when high day and night temperatures cause blossom drop and fruit set fails. Roma is a standard paste type and is no more heat tolerant than other large-fruited tomatoes, so its summer heat pause spans the full hot season, as for other large tomatoes. Time the spring crop to ripen before peak heat; set the fall crop out in mid-to-late summer to produce into the cooler autumn. The warmer zone 9 end of the region plants the spring crop earlier and the fall crop later than the zone 8 interior. Frost dates shift across the band, so confirm local last and first frost. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In California's interior valleys you plant roma tomatoes once, in spring (April or May), and then pick them all the way through summer and into fall until the first frost. You do not plant a second fall crop the way gardeners do in hotter, more humid places, because here roma tomatoes handle the summer heat well and just keep producing from that one planting. Wait to plant until the soil has warmed up, usually late April, even though the last frost is earlier.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: The interior valleys (Sacramento, San Joaquin, and similar) grow roma tomatoes as a single long season rather than the spring-and-fall split used in the humid Southeast. Transplants go out in April and May, after the mediterranean-climate last frost and once soil warms past about 65°F, and a single planting then produces one continuous harvest through the hot summer into fall up to first frost. Roma is a standard paste type without special heat tolerance, so fruit set slows in peak valley heat; there is still no separate fall crop, just a midsummer lull in set. Frost dates shift across the band, so confirm local last and first frost. (UC Master Gardener Program, Time of Planting / California Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC ANR)

In Marin and similar coastal counties early May is usually warm enough to transplant. (UC Master Gardener Program, Time of Planting / California Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Marin Master Gardeners)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.source_quote: North & North Coast: May
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Roma tomatoes begin ripening roughly two months after a May transplant (about 70 to 80 days to maturity, mid near 75), bringing the first North Coast fruit in around July. harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.source_quote: North & North Coast: May
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: From the single May planting the North Coast produces one warm-season harvest that carries through summer and tapers in October as the coast cools and days shorten. The season is bounded on the back end by falling temperatures and light rather than by a hard frost: coastal first frost comes late, but roma production winds down once the warm-season window closes. Microclimate varies sharply along the coast, so confirm locally. (UC Master Gardener Program; UC Marin Master Gardeners)

ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: On California's North Coast (the foggy coast from about Monterey north, including Marin), you plant roma tomatoes once, in May, and then pick them through summer into early fall. Here the thing holding tomatoes back is a lack of heat, not frost: the coast stays cool and foggy, and nights can drop below 55°F even in summer, so the plants need the warmer late-spring weather before they will really grow. Wait until May to set out transplants, give them the sunniest, most sheltered spot you have, and choose varieties that do well in cool summers. There is no second fall planting here, because the warm season is short.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: The North Coast (Monterey County north, including the cool marine-influenced counties such as Marin) grows roma tomatoes as a single short warm season set by heat availability rather than frost. Transplants go out in May, later than the interior valleys, because coastal summers are cool and nights can sit below 55°F in any month. A single planting then carries one harvest through summer and tapers in October as the coast cools and days shorten, ahead of the late coastal first frost. This is the cool-limited case: the limiting factor is insufficient summer heat, not a midsummer heat exclusion, so there is no summer planting pause and no separate fall crop. Cool-summer-adapted varieties and the warmest, most sheltered sites do best, and microclimate varies sharply along the coast, so confirm local conditions. (UC Master Gardener Program, Time of Planting / California Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Marin Master Gardeners)

plantings_provenance.window_structure_basis: UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2 (Time-of-Planting page) gives North & North Coast tomatoes as May (transplant), a single month with no semicolon and no fall window (contrast the table's genuine two-window crops such as snap beans 'July; May-June'). UC Marin Master Gardeners ('Tomato time!') independently confirms an early-May transplant and the cool-limit mechanism (Marin nights below 55F in any month; tomatoes need warmth). San Mateo/San Francisco MG and Monterey Bay MG corroborate cool coastal summers and a May start. Two independent T1 sources confirm single-window and the absence of a second window.
plantings_provenance.cool_limited_exception: ca_north_coast is the documented cool-limited exception to the warm-region heat-primary anchoring rule. The warm season is SHORT because summer never gets hot enough (marine layer, sub-55F nights), NOT because of a midsummer heat exclusion. No heat_pause is authored: there is no summer pause, the season is bounded by lack of heat at both shoulders. Contrast ca_desert / ca_interior summer behavior.
plantings_provenance.harvest_end_basis: Back-end boundary is production/temperature-limited (coast cools and days shorten in fall), not a hard frost cutoff. Coastal zone 9b/10a first frost is late (Nov-Dec or later), but roma production winds down in October as the warm-season window closes. harvest_end set to end of October; calendar fall months read 'wait' rather than 'cold_pause' because the season closes on heat/light, not frost. Table 13.2's own disclaimer (microclimate varies sharply) is surfaced in region_notes.

ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: On California's South Coast (the mild coast of San Diego and the Los Angeles basin), you plant roma tomatoes once, anytime from April through about mid-July, and then pick them through summer and fall. Right on the frost-free coast you can often harvest all the way to the end of the year. The weather here is gentle, so there is no summer break in planting the way hotter inland and southeastern areas have, and there is no separate fall crop, just one long season from a single planting. Plant when the soil has warmed and give the plants full sun.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: The South Coast (San Luis Obispo County south, including the San Diego and Los Angeles basin coast) grows roma tomatoes as a single long warm season. Transplants go out across a wide April through mid-July window, the longest planting window of the California regions, into a mild marine climate with no midsummer heat exclusion. A single planting then carries one continuous harvest: on the frost-free immediate coast (zone 10) fruit can be picked through the end of the year, while slightly cooler inland-edge sites (zone 9) taper a little earlier in late fall. The season is bounded by fall cooling and the late or absent coastal frost rather than by summer heat, so there is no summer planting pause and no separate fall crop. Roma sets fruit through the mild coastal warm season; coastal microclimate varies, so confirm local conditions. (UC Master Gardener Program, Time of Planting / California Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Master Gardeners of San Diego County)

plantings_provenance.window_structure_basis: UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2 (Time-of-Planting page) gives South Coast tomatoes as 'April - July 15' -- a single long continuous plant-out window with no semicolon (not a two-window split). The 'two-season' framing seen in some secondary sources is the OPTION to plant a later batch within this long window, not a forced spring-pause-fall split. Two T1 sources agree on single continuous window.

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: For the main desert crop, start roma tomato seed indoors in fall (about October into November) for the winter transplant. The desert calendar is inverted: the main planting goes out in the mild winter months, not spring, to beat the lethal summer heat. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Statewide IPM Program)

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: tomatoes ... Desert Valleys: Dec-March
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set the main roma tomato crop out in the desert valleys across the mild winter window, December through mid-March, so plants flower and set fruit before the summer heat arrives. This is the inverse of cold-climate timing: in Imperial and Coachella the winter is the growing season and the summer is the exclusion. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Statewide IPM Program)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: The main desert crop begins ripening roughly two months after the winter transplant (about 70 to 80 days to maturity, mid near 75), bringing spring fruit from around February into June before the heat shuts production down. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The main spring harvest runs into June and then ends as summer heat halts fruit set. A separate fall crop (see second planting) reopens the season after the heat breaks. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Statewide IPM Program)

start_indoors.label: fall
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: For the fall desert crop, start seed in mid-to-late summer (July into August) so transplants are ready to go out in September once the worst heat passes. The fall window is set by the break in the summer heat exclusion, not by the Time-of-Planting table (which lists only the Dec-March main desert window for tomatoes). (Mechanism: UC Statewide IPM Program; main-window table: UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2)

plant_out.label: fall

The September timing is taken from the end of the summer fruit-set-failure window rather than from the Time-of-Planting table, which lists only the Dec-March main desert window for tomatoes. (Mechanism: UC Statewide IPM Program; main-window table: UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2)

harvest_end.label: fall

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: The desert summer is a hard heat exclusion, not a frost gap. In the Imperial and Coachella Valleys, June through August daytime highs run well past 95°F and often above 110°F, and tomato flowers fail to set fruit once temperatures stay above about 95°F (high heat reduces viable pollen). This desert pause is climatic-absolute and wide: peak desert summer heat stops fruit set for roma as for any large-fruited tomato. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Statewide IPM Program)

ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: In California's desert valleys (Imperial and Coachella), the calendar is flipped: you grow roma tomatoes in the cool months and take the summer off, because summer here is too hot for tomatoes to make fruit. Plant your main crop in winter, from December through mid-March, so the plants can grow and set fruit before the heat. From about June through August it is too hot (often over 110°F), and tomato flowers will not set, so there is a summer break. Then plant a second crop in September for tomatoes through the mild late fall and winter. Even heat-loving roma tomatoes cannot handle the peak desert summer, so the summer break is not optional here.
ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: The desert valleys (Imperial and Coachella) grow roma tomatoes on an inverted, two-window calendar built around a hard summer heat exclusion. The main crop is transplanted in the mild winter window, December through mid-March, and harvested from spring into June; then June through August is too hot for fruit set (daytime highs past 95°F and often above 110°F, which collapses viable pollen), so planting pauses. A second, fall crop is set out in September as the heat breaks and produces through the mild desert winter into January. This summer pause is climatic-absolute: desert peak heat stops fruit set for roma as for any large-fruited tomato. Confirm local frost and heat timing, which vary across the desert. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Statewide IPM Program)

plantings_provenance.window_structure_basis: UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2 (Time-of-Planting page) gives Desert Valleys tomatoes as 'Dec-March' -- the mild-winter MAIN plant window (inverted calendar). UC Statewide IPM Program and UC ANR home-garden guidance anchor the summer heat-exclusion mechanism (desert summer daytime highs past 95-110F; fruit set fails above ~95F as viable pollen collapses). The two-window structure (winter-spring main + September fall crop bracketing a lethal summer) is the canonical desert pattern; UC Riverside County MG (Coachella low desert, read-not-cited, not catalogued) and University of Arizona Extension 'Growing Tomatoes' (low-desert two-season, read-not-cited, AZ source) independently corroborate. Two-window with structured summer heat_pause.
plantings_provenance.heat_inversion_note: Inverted calendar: winter is the growing season, summer is the exclusion. Main plant window Dec-Mar (mild winter), summer heat_pause Jun-Aug, fall replant Sep. This is the heat-inverted mirror of the cool-limited ca_north_coast and the mild ca_south_coast.
plantings_provenance.heat_pause_present: Jun-Aug (months 6,7,8). Climatic-absolute exclusion: Imperial/Coachella peak summer (>95-110F) stops fruit set. Mechanism anchored to UC IPM / UC ANR 8159 (>95F collapses viable pollen).
plantings_provenance.cherry_pause_not_narrowed: CONTRAST se_gulf (gs_exemplar_finding_001): there, extra heat tolerance narrowed the pause to a single month (month 7). HERE the desert pause is NOT narrowed by roma resistance -- peak desert summer heat is so extreme that even heat-tolerant roma types cannot set fruit. The Jun-Aug pause is the real lethal span regardless of roma resistance. This is a per-region roma judgment, not a universal narrowing.
plantings_provenance.second_planting_present: z9 + z10 both two-season. Discrete fall crop: start_indoors Jul15-Aug15, plant_out Sep, harvest_start Nov, harvest_end Jan. Structured as a discrete second_planting (NOT succession). Mild desert winter lets the fall crop run into January.

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start roma tomato seed indoors about six weeks before the spring transplant date. For a mid-to-late-March beginner transplant in Las Cruces (zone 8) that places seeding in early-to-mid February. The Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces chart starts seed earlier, in mid-January, to feed the experienced-grower early-March transplant. (NMSU Cooperative Extension Circular 457; Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces Vegetable Planting Chart)

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: Plant these after all danger of frost
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set roma tomato transplants out in spring once frost danger has passed. For Las Cruces and the Mesilla Valley (zone 8, Chihuahuan high desert) the average last frost is around March 19, so a beginner-safe transplant date is mid-to-late March. The Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces chart shows an earlier, early-March transplant (seed started indoors in mid-January); that earlier date reflects experienced-grower practice setting plants out right at or just before the frost-free point, often with frost protection. For a first season, waiting until after the last frost is the more reliable choice. (NMSU Cooperative Extension Circular 457; Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces Vegetable Planting Chart)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.source_quote: 55 to 70 days
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Roma tomatoes begin ripening roughly two months after transplanting. With a mid-to-late-March transplant the spring crop in Las Cruces begins coming in from about mid-to-late May, well ahead of the peak midsummer heat that suppresses fruit set. (NMSU Cooperative Extension Circular 457)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.source_quote: do not set fruit well ... when daytime temperatures exceed 95
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The spring crop winds down as peak midsummer heat sets in and daytime temperatures above about 95 degrees F push fruit set toward failure. Roma, a standard paste type, is no more heat tolerant than other large-fruited tomatoes and stops setting fruit as midsummer heat arrives. (NMSU Cooperative Extension Circular 457)

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.source_quote: start the seeds indoors 6 to 8 weeks before transplanting
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: For the fall crop, start seed indoors about six weeks before the midsummer transplant date, roughly early-to-mid June. For the fall window choose an early-maturing paste variety, since roma needs about 70 to 80 days to mature. (NMSU Cooperative Extension Circular 457; Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces Vegetable Planting Chart)

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: Tomatoes ... start ... transplant
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set the fall crop out after the peak of midsummer heat, in mid-to-late July, so plants establish as temperatures begin to ease and produce into the cooler fall. The local Las Cruces planting chart shows this second tomato transplant window; it is timed to follow the brief midsummer fruit-set pause. (Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces Vegetable Planting Chart; NMSU Cooperative Extension Circular 457)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.source_quote: 55 to 70 days
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall crop begins ripening about two months after the midsummer transplant, bringing first roma tomatoes in roughly late September into October. (NMSU Cooperative Extension Circular 457)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.source_quote: harvest ... before frost
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall crop produces into the cooler autumn and is harvested up to the first fall frost, which in Las Cruces (zone 8 high desert) arrives around mid-November. Roma types, heat resistant and quick to mature, make the most of the shorter fall window. (NMSU Cooperative Extension Circular 457; Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces Vegetable Planting Chart)

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer sowing gap is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap. In the warm arid Southwest, daytime temperatures above about 95°F at the peak of midsummer push tomato flowers to drop and fruit set to fail (NMSU Circular 457 gives 95°F day and 55°F night as the set thresholds). Roma types are heat resistant and the arid climate's cool nights aid recovery, so this pause is brief, roughly the single hottest month, and shorter for roma than for large-fruited tomatoes. (NMSU Cooperative Extension Circular 457)

warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: Where you live gets very hot in midsummer, so roma tomatoes grow best in two rounds. Plant the first round in mid to late March, after the last frost, and you will start picking tomatoes in mid to late May. When it gets hottest, around July, the plants stop setting new tomatoes for a few weeks because the flowers cannot set in the heat. Plant a second round in mid to late July for a fall crop that keeps going into November, until the first frost. Roma tomatoes handle heat well and your cool nights help, so they bounce back faster than big tomatoes.
warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: The warm arid Southwest, including Las Cruces and the Mesilla Valley in zone 8, gives roma tomatoes two planting windows around the peak of summer heat. Set the first crop out in mid to late March, once frost danger has passed (the average last frost is around March 19), for a harvest that begins in mid to late May, well before the most intense heat arrives. Through the hottest stretch of midsummer, daytime temperatures above about 95°F suppress fruit set, so production lulls for roughly the single hottest month, around July. Set a second crop out in mid to late July, transplanting through the heat so plants establish and then set as temperatures ease, for a fall harvest that runs into early November until the first frost. Roma varieties handle the heat better than large slicing tomatoes and the cool desert nights help them keep setting, so the summer lull is shorter for them. A note on sourcing: the spring window follows NMSU statewide guidance and Las Cruces frost data, while the second, midsummer planting comes from the Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces planting chart, a single regional Master Gardener source that we have not been able to corroborate independently. The Dona Ana chart also shows an earlier, early-March transplant for the spring crop, which reflects experienced-grower practice setting out right at the frost-free point; a mid-to-late-March transplant is the more reliable first-season choice.

plantings_provenance.structure_basis: Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces Vegetable Planting Chart shows two distinct tomato transplant windows (Path A chart read 2026-06-07: 1st transplant early March, 2nd transplant mid-July) separated by a midsummer set-failure window; NMSU Circular 457 fruit-set thresholds (>95F day) plus Mesilla Valley high-desert summer climate independently support a midsummer set-failure pause at month 7. Spring dates frost-anchored (arid_highland); fall dates single-source (MG chart, uncorroborated, disclosed).
plantings_provenance.spring_date_basis: Spring transplant timed to the zone-8 arid_highland last frost (Mar 19; Chihuahuan high desert, BSk; confirmed against NOAA 30% last-32F for Las Cruces = Mar 20). Beginner-safe plant-out mid-to-late March. The Dona Ana County MG chart's earlier early-March transplant (seed mid-Jan) is the seasoned/source anchor, reflecting experienced-grower practice at/just before frost-free. Beginner-safety divergence (hybrid ruling, same pattern as low_desert_az). CORRECTS the prior desert-analogy May transplant.
plantings_provenance.fall_window_basis: Fall transplant window (mid-to-late July; start indoors mid-June) taken from the Dona Ana County Master Gardeners Las Cruces chart (Path A chart read, 2026-06-07: tomato row shows 1st planting start mid-Jan -> transplant early March; 2nd planting start mid-June -> transplant mid-July). SINGLE-SOURCE, not independently corroborated; disclosed in region_notes_seasoned. Harvest re-derived to arid_highland first frost (Nov 12).
plantings_provenance.heat_pause_basis: Roma-narrowed to month 7 only (set-failure dip, not a plant/harvest exclusion). The chart transplants the fall crop IN mid-July, so July is not a do-not-plant month; it is the peak fruit-set-failure window (CR457: >95F day stops set). Calendar token at month 7 = heat_pause, mirroring the shipped se_gulf zone-8 roma cell (same biology: fall transplant into peak-heat July, plant action carried by second_planting{} on its own track). heat_pause.months=[7] kept coherent with calendar[Jul]=heat_pause for release_verify. Mesilla Valley zone 8 is hot but arid with strong nighttime recovery (nights into the 60s), unlike the zone-9 low deserts where the pause is climatic-absolute and not narrowed. Beefsteak re-derives independently and will likely hold a wider pause.
plantings_provenance.frost_basis: zone_frost_data zone-8 arid_highland variant (Southwest High Desert, Koppen BSk): last_spring Mar 19, first_fall Nov 12, 236 frost-free days. Selected over the generic zone-8 anchor (Feb 15 / Dec 1) because Las Cruces / Mesilla Valley is Chihuahuan high desert (BSk). Cross-checked against NOAA 1991-2020 30%-probability last-32F for Las Cruces (Mar 20) and first-32F (Nov 7-13 band). The prior cell's May transplant and Oct harvest_end were artifacts of the wrong (desert-analogy) anchor.

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.source_quote: start seeds indoors or in a greenhouse in January, six weeks before the last frost
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: For the spring crop, start roma tomato seed indoors in late fall to early winter so transplants are ready by February. The Arizona low desert runs an inverted, race-the-heat calendar: the spring crop must be in the ground early to set fruit before summer. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078; Maricopa County planting calendar az1005)

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: start in mid-March in Southern Arizona as soon as frost damage has ended
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set the spring roma tomato crop out in the low desert in February, right after the last frost, so plants flower and set fruit before the summer heat wall. In Phoenix and the Maricopa low desert that heat wall hits hard by late May, so early planting is essential. Choose short-season roma or plum types (45 to 80 days). (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078; Maricopa County planting calendar az1005)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.source_quote: Choose short-season varieties (less than 70 days)
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: The spring crop begins ripening about two months after the February transplant, bringing fruit in April and May before the heat shuts production down. Short-season roma types make the narrow spring window. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.source_quote: Poor fruit development during the heat of summer in southern Arizona (July - August) is expected
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The spring harvest ends in late May to June as summer heat halts fruit set. A separate fall crop (see second planting) reopens the season in September after the heat passes. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078)

start_indoors.label: fall
start_indoors.source_quote: Start new seeds for September planting in June
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: For the fall crop, start seed in June (or take cuttings from straggly spring plants in August) so transplants are ready for a September planting. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078)

plant_out.label: fall
plant_out.source_quote: Gardeners will get a second chance for healthy tomatoes in September, when summer heat has passed
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set the fall crop out in September as the summer heat passes. Without the hard deadline the spring crop faces, fall plants have time to grow and produce well into the mild low-desert winter. Many low-desert gardeners consider fall their better tomato season. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078)

harvest_start.label: fall
harvest_start.source_quote: hit peak production in October and November
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall crop reaches peak production in October and November, when low-desert weather is mild. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078)

harvest_end.label: fall
harvest_end.source_quote: fall plants can grow and produce well into December in the low desert
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall harvest runs into December in the low desert before winter frost ends the season. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078)

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: The low-desert summer is a hard heat exclusion. In the Phoenix and Maricopa low desert, poor fruit development is expected through the peak of summer (July and August), because daytime temperatures above 90°F reduce the number of viable pollen grains and stop fruit set. The main spring crop runs from a mid-March transplant through late June, then the July-August peak halts set; planting resumes in September once the heat passes. As in the California desert, this pause is climatic-absolute and is not narrowed by extra heat tolerance. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078)

low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: In the Arizona low desert (Phoenix, Yuma, and similar), the calendar is flipped and you get two short tomato seasons around a too-hot summer. Plant your spring crop early, in February right after the last frost, and pick fruit in April and May before the heat. From about June through August it is too hot (over 90°F) for tomatoes to set fruit, so there is a summer break. Then plant a second crop in September for tomatoes through fall and into December, which many desert gardeners think is the better season. Pick fast-maturing roma types (45 to 80 days) so they finish before the heat. Even heat-loving roma tomatoes cannot set fruit in peak desert summer.
low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: The Arizona low desert (Phoenix, Maricopa, Yuma) grows roma tomatoes on an inverted, two-window calendar around a hard summer heat exclusion. The spring crop is transplanted early, in February right after the last frost, and must set fruit before the heat wall arrives by late May; it harvests April into June. June through August is too hot for fruit set (daytime highs above 90°F collapse viable pollen), so planting pauses. A fall crop is set out in September once the heat passes and produces through the mild desert fall into December, often the more productive of the two seasons. Short-season roma and plum types (45 to 80 days) are essential to make the narrow spring window. As in the California desert, the summer pause is climatic-absolute and is not narrowed by extra heat tolerance. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078; Maricopa County planting calendar az1005)

plantings_provenance.window_structure_basis: University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078 'Growing Tomatoes' (peer-reviewed, Feb 2024) states the low desert allows two short growing seasons; poor fruit development in the heat of summer (July-August); a second chance in September when summer heat has passed; fall plants produce into December. Maricopa County planting calendar az1005 and the AZ1615 Yuma guide corroborate the spring (Feb) / fall (Sep) two-season structure. Spring transplant Feb (race the late-May heat wall); fall plant Sep. Two-window with structured summer heat_pause.
plantings_provenance.heat_inversion_note: Inverted two-window calendar like ca_desert, but with AZ-specific dates: spring window opens LATER (February transplant, racing the late-May Phoenix heat wall) than the CA desert's Dec-March winter window; fall replant September into December. Zone 9 only.
plantings_provenance.heat_pause_present: Jun-Aug (months 6,7,8). az2078: poor fruit development July-August; >90F reduces viable pollen and stops fruit set.
plantings_provenance.cherry_pause_not_narrowed: Same judgment as ca_desert: the desert summer pause is NOT narrowed by extra heat tolerance (contrast se_gulf month-7 single-month narrowing). Peak low-desert summer heat stops fruit set even for heat-tolerant roma types.
plantings_provenance.second_planting_present: Zone 9 two-season. Discrete fall crop: start_indoors Jun, plant_out Sep, harvest_start late Oct, harvest_end mid-Dec. az2078 notes fall is often the better season (no hard heat deadline). Discrete second_planting, not succession.
plantings_provenance.zone_9_only: low_desert_az is zone 9 ONLY per the region_source_map Phase B correction: U of Arizona (Yuma AZ1615) reaches ~10a but is thin there; zone-10 desert is well-served by ca_desert (UC ANR Desert Valleys, Imperial/Coachella). Did not extend low_desert_az to zone 10.
plantings_provenance.sourcing_note: uariz_ext carries both the dated windows and the heat mechanism (az2078 peer-reviewed + az1005 Maricopa calendar). Single-institution sufficient: az2078 is peer-reviewed and az1005 is the county planting calendar, two UofA documents agreeing. No CA or out-of-region source carried (climate-contamination guard).

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.source_quote: Start seeds of eggplant, okra, peppers, pumpkin, squashes, and tomatoes for the fall garden
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: On the Florida peninsula the roma tomato season is the cool, dry half of the year, so seed is started in late summer for fall transplanting. UF/IFAS South Florida starts tomato seed in August for the fall garden; counting back about six weeks from the September-October transplant window places indoor sowing in August. (UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar EP452; UF/IFAS VH021)

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: Easy crops that can be grown now include beans, broccoli, carrots, collards, lettuce, green onions, peppers, radishes, spinach, and tomatoes
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set roma tomato transplants out across the long cool-season window. The South Florida calendar opens the fall tomato transplant in September-October and keeps planting open through February, the last month to plant tomatoes for a late-spring harvest. Frost is rare on the peninsula, so this is one continuous cross-year window rather than separate spring and fall crops. (UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar EP452; UF/IFAS VH021)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Roma tomatoes begin ripening roughly two months after transplant (about 70 to 80 days to maturity). With fall transplanting from September into the fall, the peninsula's cool-season harvest begins in November and carries through the mild winter and spring. (UF/IFAS VH021; UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar EP452)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Peninsular roma tomato production runs through the mild winter and spring and winds down as peak-summer heat arrives. Larger-fruited tomatoes stop earlier and are grown as a cool-season crop only; roma types, being heat resistant, hold a productive tail into early summer before the July-August pause. (UF/IFAS VH021; UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar EP452)

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: On the Florida peninsula the summer gap is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap. In July and August, high day and especially night temperatures (sustained nights above about 78°F) push tomato flowers to drop and fruit set to fail. Larger-fruited tomatoes are grown as a cool-season crop only; roma types are heat resistant, so the exclusion is narrowed to the two peak months for them, and a few varieties keep setting through it. UF/IFAS South Florida lists roma tomatoes among the crops that can still be planted in June, and reopens tomato planting with August seed-starting for the fall garden. (UF/IFAS VH021; UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar EP452)

On the Florida peninsula the summer gap is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap. In July and August, high day and especially night temperatures (sustained nights above about 78°F) push tomato flowers to drop and fruit set to fail. Larger-fruited tomatoes are grown as a cool-season crop only; roma types are heat resistant, so the exclusion is narrowed to the two peak months for them, and a few varieties keep setting through it. UF/IFAS South Florida lists roma tomatoes among the crops that can still be planted in June, and reopens tomato planting with August seed-starting for the fall garden. (UF/IFAS VH021; UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar EP452)

fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: On the Florida peninsula (roughly Orlando south to Miami and the Keys), roma tomatoes are a cool-weather crop. Frost is rare here, so you plant in the fall, from about September through February, and pick through the mild winter and spring. The hard part is summer, not winter. In July and August it gets too hot, over about 78°F at night, for tomatoes to set fruit, so plants take a break then. Big slicing tomatoes only grow in the cool season here, but roma types handle the heat better, so they hold on a little into early summer and a few keep going. Pick fast-maturing roma varieties and start your seeds indoors in August for fall planting.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: The Florida peninsula (zones 10 and 11, south of about Orlando) grows roma tomatoes on a single long cool-season window rather than the spring-and-fall pattern of cooler regions. Because frost is rare, the planting window runs continuously from the fall transplant in September and October through February, the last month UF/IFAS lists for planting tomatoes for a late-spring harvest. Production carries through the mild winter and spring. The limiting season is summer: in July and August, high day and especially night temperatures (sustained nights above about 78°F) cause blossom drop and fruit-set failure. Larger-fruited tomatoes are grown as a cool-season crop only; roma types are heat resistant, so the exclusion narrows to those two peak months for them and a few varieties keep setting through it. Start seed indoors in August for fall transplanting, and choose fast-maturing roma types. (UF/IFAS VH021; UF/IFAS South Florida Gardening Calendar EP452)

plantings_provenance.window_structure_basis: UF/IFAS divides Florida into North, Central, and South planting regions; the Florida peninsula (zones 10-11) is South Florida, served by one calendar (ENH1191/EP452 South Florida Gardening Calendar) plus VH021's statewide guide. EP452 (rev. Oct 2024) opens the fall tomato transplant in September-October ('tomatoes' listed in the October planting list) and closes the cool-season planting in February ('last month to plant ... tomatoes for a late spring harvest'); August is tomato seed-start for the fall garden. Frost is rare in South Florida (VH021). This is ONE continuous cross-year cool-season window, NOT the desert two-window shape and NOT two discrete crops -> no second_planting band.
plantings_provenance.heat_pause_present: Jul-Aug (months 7,8). Roma-narrowed: the UF/IFAS Broward South Florida planting guide lists roma tomatoes among June-plantable crops (with okra, southern peas, tropical vegetables) while restricting 'tomatoes (larger fruit varieties)' to Sep-Mar; legacy zone-11 note: new fruit set fails above ~78°F nighttime. Peak fruit-set-failure months are July-August.
plantings_provenance.cherry_pause_narrowed: Yes -- same direction as se_gulf (extra heat tolerance narrows the summer pause), NOT the absolute desert pause. Distinct from se_gulf in that the peninsula has NO frost gap and NO spring crop: it is a single cool-season window with a two-month peak-summer exclusion, not two crops bracketing a one-month pause. Larger-fruited beefsteak will re-derive (wider; likely cool-season-only with a longer exclusion).
plantings_provenance.zone_split_decision: z10 and z11 carry IDENTICAL resolutions. VH021/EP452 do not separate zone 10 from zone 11 -- both are 'South Florida.' The legacy zones{} 10-vs-11 difference was a USCRN climate-data artifact and is NOT carried forward as verified (per Trevor 2026-06-06, source-decides).
