start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: In Hawaii (tropical, zone 11) roma tomato has no frost anchor and no seasonal no-sow window: CTAHR states tomato can be "grown throughout the year in most places in Hawaii by choosing varieties adapted" to the local area. Seed is started indoors in any month and transplanted about 3 to 5 weeks after sowing (CTAHR HGV-5); the plant-level baseline of six weeks indoors is the cooler-mainland figure. The year-round window rests on cultivar choice -- the locally bred, nematode- and disease-resistant UH cultivars (the determinate 'Anahu', 'Healani', 'Kewalo' and the indeterminate hybrids in the N-series) plus roma types -- rather than on hitting a particular season. (University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5)
start_indoors.from_year_round_note: Anchor from:'year_round'. Frost-independent: zone 11 has no last_frost/first_frost to offset against (frost_free_days 365). Resolver keys 'skip frost resolution, use authored windows as-is' off this named anchor; resolved_by_zone[11].year_round:true is derivable (region anchor = year_round <=> resolved-cell flag set). Mirrors lettuce hawaii_tropical (m15_na3g), adapted from direct_sow to the transplant (start_indoors + plant_out) shape because tomato is transplanted.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set roma tomato transplants out in any month of the year. CTAHR's home-garden tomato guidance gives a year-round planting capability for most of Hawaii contingent on adapted varieties, with no spring/fall bracketing and no summer exclusion stated; the limiting factors named are disease, insect, and rain pressure, not a season boundary. Keeping plants caged or staked and off the ground, and irrigating the soil rather than the foliage (in the morning when overhead water is used), are the management levers. (University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5)
plant_out.from_year_round_note: Region-constant plant_out uses a distinct from:'year_round' anchor (not a frost anchor overloaded with window_days:365), so the resolver keys 'use authored windows as-is' off a named anchor and resolved_by_zone[11].year_round:true is derivable. Verifier asserts: region plant_out anchor == 'year_round' <=> resolved-cell year_round flag set.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Roma tomatoes begin ripening about two months after transplant. CTAHR gives most tomato varieties 60 to 80 days to mature; roma types sit at the fast end, and the crop-level roma figure is roughly 70 to 80 days (about 62 mid). Because planting is year-round and the UH-bred hybrids are indeterminate -- producing continuously while healthy -- harvest is effectively continuous across the year from successive and overlapping plantings. (University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: There is no season-ending harvest boundary in tropical zone 11: roma tomato is planted and harvested continuously through the year. Production does not close at a frost or at a sustained-heat date; it is refreshed by successive plantings, which also helps stay ahead of the disease and pest pressure CTAHR flags as the real constraint in Hawaii. (University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5)
harvest_end.design_note_seasoned: Year-round cell: harvest_end mirrors the continuous window (from:'year_round', 365) rather than a frost or heat boundary, because the season does not close. The all-active calendar carries no season_over state by construction.

11.zone_notes: Hawaii tropical (USDA zone 11; frost-free, frost_free_days 365). No frost anchor and no seasonal no-sow window for roma tomato: CTAHR gives tomato a year-round planting capability for most of Hawaii, contingent on adapted varieties. The limiting factors are disease (tomato spotted wilt and tobacco mosaic viruses, and warm-wet leaf spots and blights), insect pests (whitefly, leafminer, fruit fly, thrips), and fruit cracking in heavy rain, managed with resistant locally-bred UH cultivars, staking or caging to keep fruit off the ground, morning soil-only irrigation, and successive plantings, rather than by pausing a season. Roma types and the compact determinates (for example 'Healani') also do well in 3 to 5 gallon containers here.
11.calendar_basis: Roma tomato is grown YEAR-ROUND in tropical zone 11; both heat_pause and cold_pause are intentionally absent. There is no winter cold to pause for (frost-free, frost_free_days 365) and no summer no-sow exclusion: CTAHR HGV-5 states tomato can be grown throughout the year in most places in Hawaii by choosing varieties adapted to the area, and names no seasonal fruit-set gap. This is the per-region source finding: the roma summer heat_pause documented for the Florida peninsula and the deserts does not universalize to Hawaii's oceanic lowland (guardrail: heat_pause is read from the source per region, never defaulted). Hawaii's challenge is disease, insect, and heavy-rain pressure, managed with resistant locally-bred cultivars and cultural practice, not a production stop. Absence of both pauses is intentional and carries this reason (standing principle: absence always carries a reason field); year_round:true makes the all-active calendar's intent machine-readable. (University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5)

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In Hawaii, roma tomatoes grow year-round, so you can start a few plants in any month rather than waiting for a season. There is no frost here, so the calendar is open all year. The hard part is not heat but pests and disease, which thrive in the warm, humid weather, plus heavy rain that can crack the fruit. Give yourself the best odds: pick varieties bred for Hawaii or tough roma types, keep plants up off the ground on a cage or stake, water the soil rather than the leaves (in the morning if you use a sprinkler), and start a fresh planting every few months so you always have healthy young plants coming on. Roma types and a few compact varieties also do well in 3 to 5 gallon pots.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: Hawaii's tropical calendar is aseasonal for roma tomato: plant and harvest year-round, with no frost anchor and no summer heat pause. University of Hawaii CTAHR states tomato can be grown throughout the year in most places in the state by choosing locally adapted varieties, and names no seasonal fruit-set exclusion. This is the per-region finding, not a default: the roma summer heat_pause documented for the Florida peninsula (zones 10 and 11) and for the low and high deserts does not carry to Hawaii's oceanic lowland, whose nights do not sustain the fruit-set-stopping highs of peninsular summer. The binding constraints here are disease and pests: tomato spotted wilt virus (thrips-vectored) and tobacco mosaic virus, plus warm-wet fungal and bacterial leaf spots and blights, whitefly, leafminer, and fruit fly, along with fruit cracking in heavy rain. CTAHR's primary lever is genetic: the locally bred, root-knot-nematode- and disease-tolerant UH cultivars, the determinate open-pollinated 'Anahu', 'Healani', and 'Kewalo' and the indeterminate N-series hybrids that fruit continuously while healthy; roma types and compact determinates such as 'Healani' suit 3 to 5 gallon containers. Cultural practice carries the rest: stake or cage to keep fruit off the ground, irrigate the soil (not the foliage; morning if overhead), and refresh with successive plantings. Most varieties mature in 60 to 80 days, roma types at the fast end. Windows verified against University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5 (Home Garden Tomato), with the 1943 bulletin B-91 (Home Gardening in Hawaii) as historical corroboration only.

crops.description_seasoned: Roma tomatoes, also called paste or plum tomatoes, are the workhorse of the sauce and canning garden. Unlike the cherry class, roma is determinate: the plant grows to a compact, bushy size, sets most of its fruit in a few heavy clusters, and ripens that crop over a concentrated two to four week window rather than trickling out fruit all season. That concentrated set is the whole point, giving you a batch large enough to cook down into sauce, paste, or canned tomatoes in one or two sessions. The fruit is egg to plum shaped, meaty and dense, with thick walls, few seeds, and little juice, which is exactly what you want for cooking because there is less water to boil off. A determinate plant stays short enough to hold up in a sturdy cage rather than a tall stake, and it needs little to no pruning: clear the suckers below the first flower cluster and otherwise leave the plant full. The disorder roma growers fight most is blossom-end rot, a dark sunken patch on the bottom of the fruit driven by uneven calcium delivery when soil moisture swings; steady watering and mulch are the fix, not calcium sprays. In warm zones (9 to 11) a second planting extends the canning season; in short-season zones (3 to 5) choose an early paste variety so the concentrated set finishes before first frost.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Pick when the fruit is fully and uniformly red and firm to the touch. Paste tomatoes are typically harvested a touch firmer than slicing types because they are destined for cooking, where dense, meaty flesh holds up. Full color indicates complete lycopene synthesis and peak flavor. The fruit should detach with a gentle twist. Because a determinate roma ripens much of its crop together, it is fine to let the fruit color up and pick in one or two large harvests for a canning batch. Harvest in the morning when cooler.

pet_safe.note: Ripe tomatoes are fine, but the leaves, stems, and unripe fruit are toxic to cats, dogs, and horses.

crops.name: Bell Pepper

soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Bell pepper wants a deep, fertile, well-drained loam or sandy loam rich in organic matter, and a soil that warms early and holds steady moisture. As a warm-season crop it sulks in cold, wet ground, so a sandy loam that warms quickly in spring suits it better than a heavy, slow-warming clay. Work 2 to 3 inches of compost into the bed before planting, and on heavy or cool soils many growers lay black plastic or fabric mulch to raise soil temperature and set transplants into warmer ground. Even soil moisture in a freely draining bed is the target, because the wide swings between dry and soaked that a poorly drained soil produces are the direct cause of the calcium-starved blossom-end rot bell peppers are prone to.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Bell peppers like rich, well-drained soil that warms up in the sun, since they are warm-season plants that dislike cold, soggy ground. Mix in 2 to 3 inches of compost before planting. If your soil is heavy clay or slow to warm, a sheet of black plastic or fabric mulch laid down before planting warms the soil and gives peppers the head start they want. Aim for soil that stays evenly moist but never waterlogged, because uneven watering is what causes the dark, sunken blossom-end rot on the bottom of the fruit.

ph.note_seasoned: Bell pepper grows best at a soil pH of about 6.0 to 6.8, with Clemson placing the sweet spot near 6.0 to 6.5 and Minnesota noting peppers do well up to about 7.0. In that band the nutrients peppers need, including the calcium that guards against blossom-end rot, stay most available. Peppers tolerate a somewhat wider range, roughly 5.5 to 7.5, but uptake of iron, manganese, and other micronutrients tightens as the soil turns alkaline, showing as yellowing between the veins of the youngest leaves. Alkaline soils common across the interior West often need sulfur worked in ahead of planting; most Eastern and Midwestern soils sit naturally near the target. A soil test from your local extension office settles it before you plant.
ph.note_beginner: Bell peppers like slightly acidic soil, about pH 6.0 to 6.8, and a lot of garden soil is already close. The pH scale runs from acidic to alkaline, and this range is where peppers take up nutrients best, including the calcium that prevents blossom-end rot. If your soil runs alkaline, common in the dry interior West, you may need to add sulfur before planting. An inexpensive soil test from your local extension office tells you where you stand.

fertilizer.frequency: At planting, then side-dress after fruit set
fertilizer.type: Balanced at planting, then calcium nitrate at fruit set
fertilizer.timing: Work into the bed before transplanting, then side-dress about three to four weeks after transplanting and again once fruit sets
fertilizer.example_product: 5-10-10 at planting, then calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0) as a side-dress
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Bell pepper is a moderate feeder that rewards restraint with nitrogen. Work a balanced fertilizer such as 5-10-10, or 2 to 3 pounds of it per 100 square feet, into the bed before transplanting, then side-dress with a nitrogen source such as calcium nitrate about three to four weeks after transplanting and again as the first fruits set. Hold nitrogen back early and never overdo it: too much drives a big, bushy, dark-green plant that flowers late and sets little fruit. The calcium nitrate side-dress does double duty, feeding the plant while supplying the calcium that, paired with even watering, heads off blossom-end rot.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Bell peppers like steady but modest feeding, and going heavy on nitrogen backfires. Mix a balanced fertilizer such as 5-10-10 into the soil before planting. Then, a few weeks after planting and again once the first peppers set, feed with a nitrogen fertilizer like calcium nitrate. Do not overdo it: too much nitrogen gives you a large leafy plant with few peppers. Calcium nitrate also supplies calcium, which, along with even watering, helps prevent blossom-end rot.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Your bell pepper is setting its first fruit, a good time to side-dress with a calcium nitrate source to feed the plant and supply calcium against blossom-end rot.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Your bell pepper is setting fruit. Feed it now with a nitrogen fertilizer such as calcium nitrate to keep it producing and to help prevent blossom-end rot.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced fertilizer such as 5-10-10 worked in at planting, then a calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0) side-dress three to four weeks after transplanting and again at fruit set. Avoid heavy nitrogen, which gives leaf at the expense of fruit.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer like 5-10-10 at planting, then a nitrogen feed such as calcium nitrate once the plant is growing well and setting fruit. Do not overdo the nitrogen or you get all leaves and few peppers.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A common rate is 2 to 3 pounds of 5-10-10 per 100 square feet worked into the bed before transplanting. For the side-dress, Clemson suggests about 5 pounds of calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0) per 1000 square feet or 300 feet of row, applied three to four weeks after transplanting and repeated three to four weeks later, placed a few inches out from the plants and watered in.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Mix 2 to 3 pounds of 5-10-10 per 100 square feet (or a few inches of compost) into the soil before planting. Then, a few weeks after planting and again at fruit set, scratch a small amount of calcium nitrate into the soil a few inches out from each plant and water it in.

companions.note_seasoned: Most pepper companion pairings are traditional rather than trial-tested. The aromatic-herb and flower companions (basil, marigold, nasturtium, alliums) are grown to deter or trap the aphids and thrips that trouble peppers and to draw beneficial insects, a plausible, habitat-based effect rather than an isolated one. The single firmest rule is a rotation one: keep peppers away from their Solanaceae relatives, tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplant, which share the full pepper pest and disease complex.
companions.note_beginner: The most useful pepper companions are strong-smelling herbs and flowers like basil, marigold, and nasturtium, which can help deter or lure away aphids and other pests. The one rule that really matters is to keep peppers away from tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplant, which are all close relatives and share the same pests and soil diseases.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Basil
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Basil is a classic pepper neighbor. Its strong scent is thought to help confuse soft-bodied pests like aphids and thrips, and it tucks neatly between young pepper plants. A pleasant, low-risk companion.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional interplanting with peppers; the aromatic foliage is thought to deter aphids and thrips and to draw pollinators and beneficial insects. The effect is habitat-based and traditional rather than trial-isolated for pepper.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Basil is a long-standing companion for peppers; aromatic-herb pest confusion is plausible and habitat-based, not trial-isolated for pepper.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Marigold
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Marigolds are a classic companion flower for peppers, grown to help keep pests down. Mostly tradition, but cheerful and low-risk.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A long-standing companion tradition near peppers; French marigold grown as a cover crop has documented nematode-suppressive effects, though the interplanted marigold-pepper pest benefit is traditional rather than trial-isolated.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: French marigold has documented nematode suppression as a cover crop; the interplanted marigold-pepper effect is traditional, not trial-isolated.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Nasturtium
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Nasturtiums are often planted near peppers to lure aphids away from the crop. A helpful, low-risk neighbor.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Planted as a trap and deterrent for aphids, drawing them off the peppers. Trap cropping is a documented principle, though the specific nasturtium-pepper effect is not formally isolated, so treat it as a plausible aid.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplant
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep peppers away from tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplant. They are all close relatives that share the same soil diseases and pests, so planting them together makes those problems worse.
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: All are Solanaceae and share pepper's pest and disease complex, including bacterial leaf spot, the mosaic viruses, Phytophthora blight, anthracnose, and aphids. Grouping them concentrates that pressure and lets soilborne problems build. A real epidemiology and rotation principle rather than a tested adjacency effect: spread the nightshades out and rotate them on at least a 3 year cycle.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Fennel
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Many gardeners keep fennel away from peppers and most other vegetables, since it is said to stunt their growth. This is more tradition than a proven rule.
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A widely repeated caution that fennel inhibits the growth of many garden vegetables and is best kept to its own corner. There is no strong T1 mechanism for a pepper-fennel antagonism, so it persists mostly as garden lore.
