A sound epidemiology and rotation principle, not a trial-tested adjacency.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Fennel
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Many gardeners keep fennel away from peppers and most other vegetables, since it is said to stunt their growth. This is more tradition than a proven rule.
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A widely repeated caution that fennel inhibits the growth of many garden vegetables and is best kept to its own corner. There is no strong T1 mechanism for a pepper-fennel antagonism, so it persists mostly as garden lore.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Fennel is a widely cautioned anti-companion said to inhibit many vegetables; the pepper-fennel antagonism is garden lore without a strong T1 mechanism.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Colonies of small soft-bodied insects, often green peach aphid, cluster on growing tips and leaf undersides, curling and yellowing the leaves, with sticky honeydew and sooty mold following. On peppers the greater damage is indirect: aphids are the main vectors of the mosaic viruses that mottle and distort pepper foliage and stunt the plant, so aphid control is largely virus prevention.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny soft green or black insects gather on new growth and the undersides of leaves, making them curl and yellow, often with a sticky film and black mold. Worse, aphids spread the viruses that stunt and mottle pepper plants.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several aphid species, predominantly green peach aphid (Myzus persicae), that suck sap and reproduce rapidly in warm weather, building up fast on soft, over-fertilized growth. As they probe plant to plant they transmit cucumber mosaic and other viruses, which is why they head the pepper pest list.
pests.cause_beginner: Small sap-sucking insects that multiply quickly in warm weather, especially on soft growth from too much nitrogen. As they move around they spread plant viruses.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong jet of water and spray insecticidal soap or horticultural oil with thorough coverage of leaf undersides, repeating every few days. Conserve lady beetles, lacewings, and parasitic wasps, which usually bring aphids under control; reflective mulch deters them from young plants.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water and treat the undersides of the leaves with insecticidal soap, repeating every few days. Ladybugs and other helpful insects eat aphids, so welcome them.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen, which drives the soft growth aphids favor, scout leaf undersides and growing tips, use reflective mulch on young plants, and support natural enemies rather than spraying broadly. Remove virus-infected plants promptly, since aphids spread the disease from them.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen, check the undersides of leaves regularly, use reflective mulch on young plants, and let helpful insects do their work. Pull out any badly virus-stunted plants so aphids do not carry the disease onward.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny shot-hole punctures riddle the leaves, a scatter of small round holes that is the classic flea-beetle signature. Damage is most severe on seedlings and young transplants, whose small leaf area a heavy infestation can shred; established plants tolerate considerable feeding. Brush a plant and the small dark beetles spring away like fleas.
pests.symptoms_beginner: The leaves are peppered with lots of tiny round holes, as if hit by birdshot. It hits young plants hardest. Touch the plant and you will see tiny dark beetles jump away.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several flea beetle species (potato, tobacco, and palestriped among them) that feed on pepper foliage, overwintering as adults in debris and emerging to attack the earliest, most vulnerable plants in spring. NC State rates them minor pests of pepper, but they can set back small transplants badly.
pests.cause_beginner: Small dark beetles that jump like fleas and chew tiny holes in the leaves. They are most active in spring and target young plants early in the season.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Protect transplants with floating row cover until they are large and vigorous, removing it at flowering so pollinators can reach the blooms. Set out stout, well-hardened transplants so plants can outgrow the damage, and treat heavy early infestations with spinosad or kaolin clay. Mature plants rarely need treatment.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover young plants with a light row cover until they are big and strong, then take it off when they flower. Setting out larger transplants helps them outgrow the damage. For heavy attacks on seedlings, an organic spray such as spinosad or a kaolin clay coating helps.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Use row cover from transplanting, delay setting plants out until the soil and air are warm so they grow away fast, and clean up crop debris and weeds that harbor overwintering adults. A nasturtium trap planting at the bed edge can draw beetles off the crop.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover plants early with row cover, set out larger transplants into warm soil so they grow quickly, and clear away weeds and old plant debris where the beetles hide over winter. A border of nasturtiums can lure them away.

pests.name: Pepper maggot
pests.symptoms_seasoned: A tiny white oviposition scar dimples the fruit surface where the fly laid an egg, and the maggot tunnels into the seed core inside; infested peppers often color up (turn red) prematurely and begin to rot from within. It is mainly a Northeastern and Mid-Atlantic pest, worst near tree lines. A useful jalapeno note: damage is negligible on slender, thin-walled peppers such as jalapeno and other hot types, which the maggot largely bypasses in favor of thick-walled bells.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Small pinprick scars appear on the pepper skin, and inside a maggot tunnels into the seed core, so the pepper ripens early and rots. It is mostly a problem in the Northeast. Good news for jalapeno: thin-walled hot peppers like it are rarely bothered, unlike thick bell peppers.
pests.cause_seasoned: The pepper maggot (Zonosemata electa), the larva of a striped fly that lays eggs in developing pepper fruit in July. Larvae feed inside the pod, then drop to the soil to pupate. Its host preference runs to thick-walled peppers, so hot, thin-walled types like jalapeno suffer little.
pests.cause_beginner: The larva of a small fly that lays eggs inside pepper fruit in midsummer, mostly in the Northeast. The maggot eats the seed core. It prefers thick bell peppers, so jalapeno is rarely a target.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Because eggs and larvae are protected inside the fruit, control targets the adult fly, and insecticides are the only reliable option where the pest is established. In a home garden, covering plants with insect netting during the mid-July egg-laying window and removing infested fruit are the practical non-chemical tools.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no easy fix once the maggot is inside the fruit, so the main tools are covering plants with insect netting in mid-July when the flies lay eggs and picking off any scarred, prematurely reddening fruit. Jalapeno is rarely affected, so most growers need no action.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Rotate peppers well away from last year's crop, control solanaceous weeds such as horsenettle that host the fly, cover the crop with insect netting during the mid-July egg-laying period, and disc or clear pepper residue promptly after harvest to kill larvae and pupae. Growing hot, thin-walled types like jalapeno is itself a strong cultural defense.
pests.prevention_beginner: Move peppers away from where they grew last year, clear weeds in the nightshade family nearby, and if pepper maggot is common where you live, cover plants with insect netting in mid-July. Growing jalapeno rather than thick bell peppers largely sidesteps this pest.

pests.name: Pepper weevil
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small buds and young fruit yellow and drop, and cut pods reveal a grub feeding at the seed core, the inside turned black and filled with frass. The adult is a small dark, brassy-lustered weevil about an eighth of an inch long. It is a serious pepper pest of the South and Southwest (including Florida, Texas, and southern California) and cannot overwinter where winters are cold.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Flower buds and small peppers turn yellow and fall off, and any pods that hang on are black and full of grubs and debris inside. The culprit is a tiny dark beetle. It is mainly a problem in the warm South and Southwest.
pests.cause_seasoned: The pepper weevil (Anthonomus eugenii), whose larvae develop inside buds and pods. Females lay eggs in flower buds and young fruit; the grubs feed at the seed core, causing bud and fruit drop and internal contamination. It breeds continuously in warm regions and reinvades from nightshade weeds and volunteer peppers.
pests.cause_beginner: A tiny beetle whose grubs grow up inside pepper buds and fruit, causing them to drop or rot from the inside. It lives year-round in warm areas and comes in from weeds and old pepper plants.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Field sanitation is the core tool: remove and destroy dropped and culled fruit through the season, since larvae mature inside them, and inspect transplants so you do not bring the weevil in. Pheromone-baited sticky traps detect it early. In a home garden, destroying spent plants right after harvest sharply reduces the next year's population.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: The main defense is cleanup: pick up and throw away every dropped or damaged pepper, since the grubs finish growing inside them, and check new plants before buying. Pull and destroy the plants as soon as harvest ends.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Rotate away from last year's peppers, remove nearby nightshade weeds and volunteer pepper and eggplant that harbor the weevil, monitor with pheromone traps, source clean transplants, and destroy the crop promptly at season's end to break the continuous breeding cycle.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not plant peppers where they grew last year, clear out nightshade weeds and any leftover pepper plants nearby, buy healthy transplants, and clean up the garden as soon as the season ends.

pests.name: Hornworms
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Large sections of leaf, and sometimes whole shoots or the odd fruit, are stripped overnight, with dark pellet droppings on the leaves below. The culprit is the big green tobacco (or tomato) hornworm, up to three and a half inches long, which blends into the stems and is easiest to find by its frass.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Leaves vanish overnight, leaving bare stems, with dark droppings on the leaves below. The cause is a large green caterpillar that hides against the stems, easier to spot by its droppings than by sight.
pests.cause_seasoned: Tobacco and tomato hornworms, the larvae of large sphinx moths, which feed on solanaceous foliage including pepper from midsummer on. A few caterpillars can do conspicuous damage given their size, though peppers are a secondary host to tomato.
pests.cause_beginner: Big green caterpillars, the young of large moths, that feed on pepper and tomato leaves mostly in mid to late summer. Even a few can strip a lot of foliage.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick the caterpillars, which is effective in a home garden, and apply Bacillus thuringiensis to younger larvae where numbers are high. Leave any hornworm studded with white parasitic-wasp cocoons in place, since the wasps will kill it and breed more.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick the caterpillars off by hand and drop them in soapy water. If you find one covered in small white capsules, leave it, those are parasitic wasps that will do the work for you. An organic Bt spray works on the smaller caterpillars.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Till the soil in fall to destroy overwintering pupae, scout for frass and stripped leaves from midsummer, and encourage the parasitic wasps and other natural enemies that keep hornworms in check.
pests.prevention_beginner: Turn the soil at the end of the season to destroy the pupae, watch for droppings and missing leaves from midsummer, and welcome the helpful wasps that attack hornworms.

diseases.name: Bacterial spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small, water-soaked spots on the leaves enlarge into brown, angular, sometimes scabby lesions with yellow halos, and heavy infection yellows and drops the foliage, exposing fruit to sunscald. Raised, scabby, cracked spots also form on the fruit, ruining it for use. It is the most common and damaging bacterial disease of peppers, worst in warm, wet, splashy weather.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The leaves get small dark, water-soaked spots that grow into brown patches with yellow edges, and badly spotted leaves yellow and fall, leaving fruit exposed. Rough, scabby spots also appear on the peppers. It is the most common serious pepper disease and spreads in warm, wet weather.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Xanthomonas bacteria, carried on seed and in crop debris and spread by splashing water and handling wet plants. Warm, humid, rainy conditions favor it, and once established in a planting it is very hard to stop, so control is built on clean seed, resistant varieties, and keeping foliage dry.
diseases.cause_beginner: A bacterium carried on seed and old plant debris that spreads in splashing water and on hands and tools when plants are wet. It thrives in warm, wet weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure for an infected plant; remove badly affected plants to slow spread, avoid working among wet plants, and where pressure is high, copper-based sprays can suppress it, though resistance to copper is common. Management is preventive.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot cure a plant that has it, so remove badly spotted plants and keep your hands and tools off wet foliage. Copper sprays can slow it a little, but prevention is what counts.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Start with certified, pathogen-free or hot-water-treated seed and disease-free transplants, choose resistant varieties, rotate peppers on a 2 to 3 year cycle out of solanaceous beds, water at the soil to keep foliage dry, mulch to limit splash, space for airflow, and remove crop debris at season's end.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Use clean seed and healthy transplants, look for resistant varieties, do not plant peppers in the same spot each year, water the soil rather than the leaves, and clean up old plants at the end of the season.

diseases.name: Mosaic viruses
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Leaves show a mottled light-and-dark-green mosaic, often puckered, narrowed, or distorted, and the plant stunts and sets fewer, smaller, sometimes misshapen or ringspotted fruit. Several viruses (cucumber mosaic, tobacco mosaic, and pepper-specific mottle viruses) cause the syndrome, most of them spread by aphids moving from plant to plant.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The leaves turn a patchy light-and-dark-green mosaic and may pucker or narrow, and the plant is stunted with fewer, smaller peppers. Several viruses cause this, mostly carried by aphids.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A group of plant viruses, chiefly cucumber mosaic virus and tobacco mosaic virus, transmitted by aphids and, for the tobamoviruses, mechanically on hands and tools and through infected seed and tobacco products. There is no cure once a plant is infected, so control is aimed at the aphid vectors and at clean seed and sanitation.
diseases.cause_beginner: Viruses spread mainly by aphids, and some by hands, tools, and even tobacco products. Once a plant is infected there is no cure.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no treatment for an infected plant; remove and destroy it promptly to cut the source of further spread, and control the aphids that move the virus. Wash hands and disinfect tools between plants, and do not handle peppers after using tobacco.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot cure an infected plant, so pull and destroy it so aphids do not carry the virus to healthy plants. Control aphids, wash your hands, and do not touch peppers right after handling tobacco.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Choose resistant varieties (many carry virus resistance), use clean seed, control aphids with reflective mulch and by conserving natural enemies, manage nearby weed reservoirs, wash hands and tools, and remove infected plants early. Avoid tobacco use around the plants.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Look for virus-resistant varieties, control aphids, keep weeds down, wash your hands before handling plants, and remove any stunted, mottled plants quickly. Do not use tobacco around peppers.

diseases.name: Phytophthora blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Plants wilt and collapse suddenly, often with a dark, water-soaked lesion girdling the stem at the soil line, and roots rot; dark, firm, sometimes white-cottony rot also strikes the fruit. Caused by Phytophthora capsici, it flares in warm, wet, poorly drained conditions and after heavy rain or flooding, and can move fast through a bed.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Plants suddenly wilt and die, often with a dark rotted patch on the stem at the soil line, and the fruit can rot too, sometimes with white fuzzy growth. It strikes in warm, soggy soil after heavy rain.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Phytophthora capsici, a soilborne water mold that thrives in saturated soil and spreads in splashing and running water. It survives in soil and debris for years and moves fast in warm, wet weather, especially on heavy or poorly drained ground, attacking roots, crown, and fruit.
diseases.cause_beginner: A mold-like disease that lives in wet soil and spreads in splashing and running water, attacking pepper roots, stems, and fruit in warm, soggy conditions. It moves fast once it starts.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy affected plants and fruit promptly, and improve drainage immediately. There is no effective home-garden cure once plants collapse, so control is preventive and drainage-based.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Pull and destroy affected plants and fruit, and fix the drainage. There is no good home cure once it takes hold, so prevention is what matters.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant on raised, well-drained beds, avoid low spots that stay wet, choose resistant varieties where available, water at the soil rather than overhead, mulch to limit splash, rotate away from solanaceous and cucurbit crops on a long cycle, and avoid overwatering, which is the single biggest trigger.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant on raised beds so water drains away, avoid wet low spots, do not overwater, water at the soil, and rotate peppers away from tomatoes, eggplant, and squash. Look for resistant varieties if this disease is common where you live.

diseases.name: Anthracnose
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Sunken, circular, water-soaked spots develop on the fruit, especially ripening red fruit, enlarging into dark lesions dotted with concentric rings of pink-to-black spore masses that rot the pepper. It is chiefly a fruit-rot disease, favored by warm, wet, humid weather, and can carry over on infected seed and debris.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Sunken dark spots appear on the peppers, especially ripe red ones, spreading into rotting patches flecked with tiny pink or black dots. It is worst in warm, wet, humid weather.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Colletotrichum fungi that infect the fruit and are spread by splashing water; the pathogen survives on infected seed, crop debris, and volunteer plants. Ripe and injured fruit are most susceptible, and long warm, wet spells drive outbreaks.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that rots pepper fruit, spread by splashing water and carried on seed and old plant debris. Ripe peppers are hit hardest, especially in wet weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy infected fruit promptly to reduce spore load, and keep foliage and fruit as dry as possible. Where the disease is active a labeled fungicide can protect healthy fruit, but rotted fruit cannot be saved. Pick ripening fruit promptly rather than letting it sit in warm, wet weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick off and throw away infected peppers right away, keep the fruit dry by watering at the soil, and harvest ripe peppers promptly instead of leaving them out in wet weather. Rotted fruit cannot be saved.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Start with clean or treated seed and healthy transplants, rotate peppers out of the bed for 2 to 3 years, water at the soil, mulch to limit splash, space for airflow, stake to keep fruit off the ground, and remove crop debris at season's end.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Use clean seed and healthy transplants, do not plant peppers in the same spot for a few years, water at the soil, keep fruit off the ground, and clean up old plants at the end of the season.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Aim for about 1 inch of water per week from rain plus irrigation, more in heat or on sandy soil, delivered deeply and less often rather than in light daily sprinkles. Peppers want steady, even moisture, and the water-critical stretch is flowering through fruit set: swings from dry to soaked drop blossoms and cause blossom-end rot on the developing pods. Container plants dry out far faster and need closer attention. A note peculiar to hot peppers: a mild, deliberate water pull as the fruit ripens tends to raise the heat, so a hot pepper grown slightly lean and dry late in the season is often the hottest.
watering.frequency_beginner: Give jalapeno about 1 inch of water a week, more when it is hot and dry. Water deeply rather than a little every day, and keep it even, since uneven watering while the plant is flowering drops the blossoms and causes rot on the bottom of the peppers. Plants in pots dry out much faster. Interestingly, letting a hot pepper run a little dry late in the season can make it hotter.
watering.amount_seasoned: Around 1 inch per week is the working range, leaning higher during flowering and fruit set, wetting the soil to a depth of at least 6 to 8 inches so the roots follow the moisture down. Even, deep watering sets and fills well-shaped pods; letting the soil swing from dry to saturated stresses the plant, drops blossoms, and invites blossom-end rot and root disease.
watering.amount_beginner: About 1 inch of water a week, soaking the soil down 6 to 8 inches so the roots grow deep. Keep it even: letting the soil go bone-dry and then flooding it stresses the plant, drops flowers, and causes rot on the bottom of the peppers.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base with a soaker hose or drip line, keeping the foliage as dry as possible, since wet leaves and splashing water spread the bacterial spot, anthracnose, and Phytophthora blight peppers are prone to. If overhead watering is unavoidable, do it in the morning so leaves dry before evening. A layer of mulch buffers soil moisture and warmth and blocks soil-borne spores from splashing onto the lower leaves and fruit.
watering.method_beginner: Water the soil, not the leaves, with a soaker hose or by holding the hose at the base. Keeping the leaves dry helps prevent disease. If you must use a sprinkler, do it in the morning so the leaves dry off by evening. Mulch helps keep the soil evenly moist and warm.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting even when the soil is wet, and soft, rotting stems or fruit point to overwatering or poor drainage. Saturated soil starves the roots of oxygen and is the single biggest trigger for Phytophthora blight, which collapses peppers quickly on heavy ground.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If the lower leaves yellow, the plant wilts even though the soil is wet, or stems and fruit go soft and rotten, it is getting too much water or the soil drains poorly. Overwatering is the main cause of the disease that suddenly kills peppers.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Midday wilting that recovers overnight is common in heat and not alarming, but leaves that stay limp and dull signal real drought. Sustained drought during flowering and fruit set drops blossoms and gives small pods and leathery, sunken blossom-end rot on the fruit. A brief, mild dry spell late in ripening, by contrast, tends to concentrate heat rather than harm the crop.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Some midday wilting in hot weather is normal and passes by evening. Leaves that stay wilted mean the plant is too dry. A long dry spell while it is flowering drops the flowers and causes rot on the bottom of the peppers, though a short dry stretch late on can make hot peppers hotter.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Base watering is the most useful habit for jalapeno, because the same plant that wants steady moisture is also prone to leaf and fruit diseases spread by wet foliage and splash. Keep water on the soil, air moving through the leaves, and the ripening fruit up off wet ground.
watering.method_note_beginner: Watering the soil instead of the leaves is the best thing you can do for jalapeno. It keeps the plant hydrated without spreading leaf and fruit disease.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The water-critical stretch runs from flowering through fruit set and sizing. Steady moisture here sets and fills well-shaped pods and prevents blossom-end rot, while swings between dry and saturated soil drop blossoms and give small, misshapen fruit. Keep it even once the plant is flowering and carrying fruit.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The most important time to keep jalapeno evenly watered is when it is flowering and setting fruit. Uneven water now causes dropped flowers and rot on the bottom of the peppers, so aim for steady moisture.

crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Jalapeno gives you a choice of when to pick, and the choice changes the pepper. For the familiar firm green jalapeno, harvest when the pods reach full size, roughly 2 to 3 inches long, and the skin is firm and deep, dark green, often shading toward black-green at the shoulders (Clemson's cue is that dark, black-green color). Left on the plant another two to three weeks, the same fruit ripens through to red, growing sweeter AND hotter as it matures. Two things surprise new growers and are worth knowing: heat rises with both maturity and stress, so a red pepper, or one grown hot and a little dry, is hotter than a well-watered green one; and corking, the fine tan or brown netting and stretch marks that appear on the skin, is a sign of a mature, fast-grown pepper prized in markets, not a defect or a disease. Cut fruit with shears or a knife leaving a short stem, rather than pulling, since a yanked branch tears easily, and pick regularly, since removing mature pods keeps the plant flowering and setting more. Wear gloves when picking and especially when cutting hot peppers: capsaicin, the compound that makes them hot, is an oil that clings to skin and burns painfully if it reaches your eyes, nose, or lips, so keep your hands away from your face and wash well afterward.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: You can pick jalapeno two ways. For the usual firm green pepper, harvest when it reaches full size, about 2 to 3 inches long, and the skin is firm and dark, deep green going toward black-green. Or leave it on the plant two to three more weeks and let it turn red, which makes it sweeter and hotter. Two things surprise first-timers: peppers get hotter as they ripen and when the plant is stressed by heat or dryness, and the fine tan lines or netting that show up on the skin, called corking, are a normal sign of a ripe, well-grown pepper, not damage. Cut the peppers off with scissors or a knife, leaving a bit of stem, instead of pulling, and keep picking so the plant makes more. Always wear gloves when handling and cutting hot peppers: the oil that makes them hot sticks to your skin and stings badly if it gets in your eyes, so keep your hands away from your face and wash them well after.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Harden off pepper transplants over 7 to 10 days, easing plants into sun and wind, and set them out only once nights stay reliably above 50°F and the soil is warm, at least 60 to 65°F. Peppers set into cold ground, as UMD puts it, just sit there and refuse to grow until it warms up, and an early cold check costs weeks of growth, so wait for real warmth rather than rushing the calendar.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: Harden pepper plants off over about a week to ten days, giving them more time outside each day, and do not set them out until nights stay above 50°F and the soil is warm. Planting too early into cold soil makes peppers stall and just sit there, so it pays to wait until it is truly warm.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Start jalapeno seeds indoors about 8 weeks before transplanting (6 to 8 weeks per Clemson and Iowa State, up to 8 to 10 per UMD), with bottom heat of 80 to 90°F for fast, even germination, since pepper seed is slow and erratic in cool mix. Grow sturdy transplants up to a foot tall in strong light, then set them out only after nights hold above 50°F and the soil has warmed to at least 60 to 65°F, typically around the tomato date or a touch later. Black plastic or fabric mulch warms the soil and gives this warmth-loving crop a head start. Jalapeno is a transplant crop across nearly all of the country; direct sowing is practical only in the longest, warmest regions.
start_method.notes_beginner: Start jalapeno seeds indoors about 8 weeks before you plan to plant out, keeping them warm (80 to 90°F on a heat mat) to sprout well, since pepper seeds are slow to come up in cool soil. Grow stocky plants up to a foot tall in bright light, then plant them outside only once nights stay above 50°F and the soil is warm, around when you would plant tomatoes. Black plastic mulch warms the soil and helps.

drainage.saucer_practice_seasoned: If you use a saucer, empty it within an hour of watering. Peppers will not tolerate sitting in standing water, which starves the roots of oxygen and invites the Phytophthora root rot they are prone to. A saucer is useful for holding warmth, which peppers like, but the roots must not stay submerged.
drainage.saucer_practice_beginner: Do not let the pot sit in a saucer of standing water. Empty it soon after watering. A saucer is fine for keeping the pot warm, which peppers enjoy, but the roots should never sit in pooled water.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Use a bag of potting mix made for containers, not soil dug from the garden, which packs down hard and drains poorly in a pot.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in compost and a slow-release fertilizer at planting. Pots need feeding more often than beds, because watering washes nutrients out.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: Use a rich, free-draining peat- or coir-based container potting mix, not garden soil, which compacts and drains poorly in a pot.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend in about 20 to 25 percent compost plus a slow-release balanced fertilizer at planting. Because frequent watering leaches nutrients, plan to feed a container jalapeno more regularly than one in the ground, shifting to a little nitrogen once fruit sets.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out much faster than garden beds, so in summer heat a potted jalapeno may need water every day. Check daily, and water until it runs from the bottom. Keep it even, since drying out and then flooding drops the flowers.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Feed a potted jalapeno a bit more often than a garden plant. Once it is growing strongly and especially once fruit sets, give a balanced liquid feed every week or two, but do not overdo the nitrogen.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Not usually done. Jalapeno is grown as an annual and is killed by frost. That said, peppers are actually tender perennials, so a potted plant can sometimes be cut back and kept alive over winter on a bright, warm windowsill, then set back out in spring. Most gardeners simply start fresh each year.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Not typically necessary. Jalapeno is grown as an annual and killed by the first frost, so most gardeners start fresh each spring. Botanically peppers are tender perennials, so an ambitious grower can overwinter a container plant indoors: cut it back hard, keep it in a bright, warm spot (above 55°F), water sparingly, and set it back out after frost for an earlier, larger second-year plant. This is optional and finicky, not standard practice.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Jalapeno is one of the best peppers for containers, compact, productive, and happy in the warm root zone of a pot in the sun. Use at least a 3-gallon pot, 10 inches deep, one plant per pot, in full sun. Keep it well watered (pots dry fast), feed lightly and regularly, and you will get a heavy crop from a small footprint on a patio or balcony. Compact types like Purple Jalapeño and the mild TAM are especially good in pots.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Jalapeno is an excellent container crop, arguably the best of the peppers for pots: it is naturally compact and very productive, and the warmer root zone of a dark pot in sun suits this heat-loving plant. Use a pot of at least 3 gallons (5 is better) and 10 inches deep, one plant per pot, in full sun. Water consistently, since a small soil volume dries fast and moisture swings drop blossoms and cause blossom-end rot, feed lightly and regularly because containers leach nutrients, and stake taller varieties carrying a heavy pod load. Compact cultivars such as Purple Jalapeño and the mild TAM are standouts in pots.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry far faster than beds, and a potted jalapeno can need water once or even twice a day in summer heat. Check daily by feeling the top inch of mix, and water until it runs from the drainage holes; even moisture prevents the blossom drop and blossom-end rot that water swings cause. A brief, mild dry-down late in ripening can raise the heat of the pods.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Feed container jalapeno a little more often than in-ground plants, since steady watering leaches nutrients. After the slow-release charge at planting, add a balanced liquid feed every 1 to 2 weeks, easing off heavy nitrogen so you get pods rather than all leaves.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering container suits jalapeno well, smoothing the moisture swings that drop blossoms and cause blossom-end rot. Keep the reservoir topped up in heat, water from below to keep the foliage dry, and occasionally water from the top to flush the salts that concentrate with constant sub-irrigation.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match for jalapeno because it keeps the water steady, which helps prevent dropped flowers and rot on the peppers. Keep the reservoir filled in hot weather, and every so often water from the top too, which rinses out built-up minerals.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: A container jalapeno wants a sturdy pot at least 10 inches deep and 3 gallons or more, with a base wide enough that a pod-laden plant does not tip. Depth for the roots matters more than width. The plant's naturally compact habit makes it well suited to the smaller pots that would not hold a tomato.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Give a container jalapeno a pot at least 10 inches deep and 3 gallons or more, so the roots have room and the plant does not tip over when loaded with peppers. Its small, bushy size makes it a great fit for pots too small for a tomato.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Tomatoes, eggplant, potatoes, and peppers, which share bacterial spot, anthracnose, Phytophthora blight, the aphid-borne mosaic viruses, and the flea beetle, pepper weevil, and hornworm. These seed-, soil-, and debris-borne diseases and overwintering pests build up wherever a nightshade has grown.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Do not plant jalapeno where you grew tomatoes, eggplant, potatoes, or peppers recently. They are all in the same family and share the same diseases and pests, which build up and carry over.
rotation.good_after: Legumes (beans, peas), brassicas, sweet corn, alliums (onions, garlic), and leafy greens make good preceding crops, since they do not share the nightshade pest and disease complex, and a legume leaves a little nitrogen behind for the moderately feeding pepper.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate jalapeno on at least a 3 year cycle, returning it to a given bed no sooner than the third or fourth year, to break the buildup of bacterial spot, anthracnose, and Phytophthora blight (all favored by warm, wet conditions and carried on debris or seed) and of the pepper weevil where it overwinters. The wider Solanaceae, tomato, eggplant, and potato, share that complex, so rotate them as a group and avoid following any of them. Clear and remove spent plants at season's end rather than tilling them in, which removes overwintering pest and disease sites, and is doubly important where pepper weevil or bacterial spot is present.
rotation.note_beginner: Move jalapeno to a different part of the garden each year, and do not return it, or its relatives tomato, eggplant, and potato, to the same spot for about three to four years. Diseases like bacterial spot and Phytophthora blight and pests like the pepper weevil build up where nightshades grow, and rotation is the main tool to keep them in check. Clean up old plants at the end of the season too.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Fresh jalapeno keeps a few days at cool room temperature, best out of direct sun. Green pods hold up somewhat better than fully red ones, which soften faster. For anything beyond a couple of days, refrigerate, and for real keeping, freeze or dry the crop rather than leaving pods on the counter.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Jalapeno keeps for a few days at cool room temperature, out of the sun. Green ones last a little longer than red. For longer than that, put them in the fridge or freeze or dry them.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Store jalapeno unwashed in the crisper, ideally around 45 to 50°F with moderate humidity, loosely bagged, for roughly 1 to 2 weeks. Peppers tolerate refrigeration better than eggplant but still suffer chilling pitting if held near freezing for long, so the warmest part of the fridge is best. Wash only just before use.
storage.fridge_beginner: Keep jalapeno unwashed in the crisper drawer, loosely bagged, and it will last about 1 to 2 weeks. The warmest part of the fridge is best, since very cold storage causes pitting. Wash the peppers only when you are ready to use them.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Jalapeno freezes exceptionally well and, unlike most vegetables, needs no blanching: simply wash, dry, stem, and chop or slice (or freeze whole), then spread on a tray to freeze and transfer to bags. Frozen peppers soften on thawing but keep their heat and flavor for cooking for many months. Wear gloves while prepping a large batch.
storage.freezer_beginner: Jalapeno is one of the easiest vegetables to freeze, and you do not even need to blanch it. Just wash, dry, and chop (or freeze whole), freeze on a tray, then bag. They go soft when thawed but keep their heat for cooking for months. Wear gloves when cutting a big batch.
storage.notes_seasoned: Jalapeno stores and preserves better than most fruiting vegetables. Use fresh pods within a week or two from the crisper; freeze the surplus (no blanching needed) for cooking; or dry it. A classic path for hot peppers is to let pods ripen fully red, then dry them, and smoke-dried red jalapenos are chipotles. Pickling is another easy route. Handle with gloves throughout, since capsaicin oil lingers on skin and cutting boards.
storage.notes_beginner: Jalapeno keeps well and is easy to preserve. Eat fresh peppers within a week or two, and freeze, dry, or pickle the extras. If you let the peppers ripen to red and then dry them, and especially if you smoke them, you get chipotles. Always wear gloves when cutting a lot, since the hot oil sticks to your hands and the cutting board.

recommended.name: Jalapeño M
recommended.recommended_note: The standard open-pollinated jalapeno and the benchmark for the type: firm, dark green pods about 3 inches long with medium heat around 2,500 to 8,000 Scoville, ripening red. Reliable, productive, and widely available, the default choice if you just want a jalapeno.

recommended.name: Early Jalapeño
recommended.recommended_note: An earlier, cold-tolerant strain that sets its first pods sooner, valuable in short-season and cool-summer gardens where a standard jalapeno runs late. Slightly smaller fruit, dependable medium heat, the best pick for the North.

recommended.name: Mucho Nacho
recommended.recommended_note: A vigorous hybrid bearing extra-large jalapeno pods up to 4 inches on a strong plant, heavy-yielding with full jalapeno heat. A good choice where you want big, meaty peppers for stuffing and poppers.

recommended.name: TAM Mild Jalapeño
recommended.recommended_note: A mild jalapeno bred by Texas A&M, with the classic look and flavor but far less heat, roughly 1,000 to 3,500 Scoville, plus useful disease resistance. The pepper to grow for jalapeno flavor without the burn, or for a family with mixed heat tolerance.

recommended.name: Biker Billy
recommended.recommended_note: A hybrid at the hot end of the jalapeno world, several times hotter than a standard jalapeno, on a tall, productive plant. For growers who want serious heat while keeping true jalapeno flavor.

recommended.name: Purple Jalapeño
recommended.recommended_note: A compact, ornamental-but-edible strain whose pods turn deep purple before ripening red, on a small tidy plant. Medium heat, striking in the garden, and one of the best jalapenos for containers and edging.

varieties.note_seasoned: Choose a jalapeno by heat, size, and season. Jalapeño M is the dependable standard; Early Jalapeño is the pick for short or cool seasons, setting sooner and tolerating cool nights; Mucho Nacho gives big, meaty pods for stuffing; the Texas A&M TAM Mild delivers jalapeno flavor with much less heat and good disease resistance, while Biker Billy runs to the hot end for chile-heads. Purple Jalapeño is compact and ornamental, excellent in a pot. Across all of them, remember the two levers on heat: let pods ripen red and grow the plant a little hot and lean for more burn, or pick green and keep it well watered for a milder pepper.
varieties.note_beginner: Pick a jalapeno to match how hot you like it and how long your season is. Jalapeño M is the reliable standard. In a short or cool-summer garden, choose Early Jalapeño, which ripens sooner. Mucho Nacho gives big peppers for stuffing. Want the flavor without much burn? Grow the mild TAM from Texas A&M. Want it really hot? Try Biker Billy. Short on space? Purple Jalapeño is compact and pretty in a pot. Remember: red, stressed peppers are hotter; green, well-watered ones are milder.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A healthy jalapeno is a heavy bearer, typically yielding 25 to 35 or more pods over the season, often more from a vigorous hybrid like Mucho Nacho, picked continuously. Steady warmth, even moisture, and regular harvesting carry a plant to the upper end; a cold start, heat that stalls fruit set, or letting pods over-ripen unpicked pulls it down.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Jalapeno is very productive: a single healthy plant usually gives you dozens of peppers over the season, picked a few at a time. Keeping it warm, evenly watered, and regularly picked makes the difference, and a couple of plants is plenty for most families.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Jalapeno bears continuously through the warm months once it starts, with production strongest from midsummer into early fall and tapering as nights cool. In the hottest regions fruit set stalls during the peak of summer heat and resumes as it eases, giving a spring and a fall flush. Picking pods promptly, green or red, keeps the plant flowering and setting; leaving mature fruit on the plant slows further set.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Once it gets going, jalapeno keeps producing through the warm months, heaviest from midsummer into fall. In very hot areas it pauses setting fruit during the worst of the summer heat and picks back up as it cools. Keep picking the peppers, green or red, since leaving them on the plant slows down new ones.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: First-season growers most often lose jalapeno to two things: setting plants out too early into cold soil, which stalls them for weeks, and over-feeding with nitrogen, which gives a big leafy plant with few pods. Wait for real warmth, go easy on nitrogen until fruit sets, keep water even, and this is one of the most rewarding, forgiving crops a beginner can grow.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: The two things that trip up first-year jalapeno growers are planting too early into cold soil and using too much fertilizer, which gives lots of leaves but few peppers. Wait until it is truly warm, go easy on the nitrogen until fruit sets, and keep the water steady. Jalapeno is otherwise easy and very rewarding.
factors_seasoned: Warmth: peppers need warm soil and air; a cold start or planting too early stalls the plant for weeks and cuts yield.
Restrained nitrogen: too much nitrogen before fruit set gives a lush, leafy plant with few pods.
Even moisture: steady water through flowering and fruit set prevents dropped blossoms and blossom-end rot.
Heat management: in the hottest regions, fruit set stalls above about 90°F days and 75°F nights and resumes as it cools, so timing catches a spring and a fall flush.
Regular harvest: picking pods promptly, green or red, keeps the plant flowering and setting more.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance places above-ground fruiting crops like peppers in the waxing (light) phase. This is folk tradition, not extension-backed; sow jalapeno by soil temperature and frost dates instead.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seeds sprout in about 8 to 14 days in warm conditions; bottom heat of 80 to 90°F is ideal, and cool soil delays or prevents germination. Two seed leaves emerge first. Pepper seed is notably slow and erratic without warmth.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: In warm conditions, seeds sprout in roughly one to two weeks, sending up two seed leaves first. Cool soil makes them slow or fail, so peppers need real warmth to come up.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Sow about a quarter inch deep in warm flats with bottom heat (80 to 90°F), keeping the mix evenly moist, not soggy. Give pepper seed heat and patience; it germinates slower than tomato.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Plant seeds about a quarter inch deep in a warm spot, ideally on a heat mat, and keep the soil damp until they sprout. Peppers like it warm to come up and take a bit longer than tomatoes.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Did your jalapeno seeds germinate, and how many days did it take?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your jalapeno seeds sprouted yet?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: After the seed leaves, true leaves appear and growth is steady but unhurried in warmth. Watch for flea-beetle shot-holes, which hit small plants hardest, and keep seedlings in strong light so they grow stocky rather than leggy.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: After the first two rounded leaves, true leaves appear and the plant grows slowly but steadily in warmth. Watch for tiny holes in the leaves from flea beetles, which hit young plants hardest.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep seedlings warm and in strong light to avoid legginess, pot up as needed, and protect from flea beetles. Grow stocky transplants and do not rush them outside before warmth arrives.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the seedlings warm and in bright light so they grow stocky, and protect them from flea beetles. Do not be in a hurry to plant them out; wait for warm weather.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How are your seedlings developing? Any flea-beetle shot-holes on the leaves?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How do your young jalapeno plants look?

growth_stages.name: Transplanting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Sturdy transplants up to a foot tall, ready to set out only once nights hold above 50°F and the soil has warmed to at least 60 to 65°F. Peppers set into cold ground just sit and sulk, the classic early setback.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Strong young plants up to a foot tall, ready to go outside only when nights stay above 50°F and the soil is warm. Planting too early into cold soil stalls them.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harden off over 7 to 10 days, then transplant into warm soil, 12 to 18 inches apart in rows 24 to 36 inches apart. Black plastic or fabric mulch warms the soil and gives a heat-loving crop a head start.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Harden the plants off over about a week, then plant them 12 to 18 inches apart into warm soil. A sheet of black plastic mulch warms the soil and helps.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have you transplanted? Were nights reliably above 50°F and the soil warm?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you planted your jalapeno outside yet?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small white star-shaped flowers open singly at the leaf and branch junctions. Pepper flowers are self-fertile and largely self-pollinating, so a single plant sets fruit; a small pod swells behind each successfully pollinated bloom. Blossom drop in extreme heat (above about 90°F days, 75°F nights) or a cold snap is normal and temporary.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Small white flowers appear where the leaves meet the stem. Pepper flowers pollinate themselves, so you do not need more than one plant. A tiny pepper forms behind each flower that sets. Some flowers drop in very hot or cold spells, which is normal.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture steady through flowering and side-dress with a little nitrogen as the first fruits set. If blossoms drop in a heat wave or cold snap, wait it out; set resumes as conditions moderate. A gentle tap can aid pollination on still days.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the plant evenly watered as it flowers, and feed it lightly with nitrogen once the first fruit sets. If flowers drop during a hot or cold spell, do not worry, it picks back up when the weather settles.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Is your jalapeno flowering and setting fruit? Any blossom drop in the heat?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Is your jalapeno flowering? Are any little peppers forming?

growth_stages.name: Fruiting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Set pods swell and firm up to a deep, dark green, and the plant carries fruit continuously through the warm months. Tan corking lines may appear on the skin as pods mature, a sign of vigor, not damage. Left on the plant, green pods ripen through to red, gaining heat and sweetness.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The little peppers grow and firm up to a dark green. The plant keeps making pods through the warm months. Fine tan lines (corking) on the skin are normal. Left on longer, green peppers turn red and get hotter and sweeter.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture even and feeding light through fruiting, support pod-laden branches, and begin harvesting once pods reach full size and firm dark green. Picking regularly keeps the plant setting; scout for aphids, hornworms, and, in the South, pepper weevil.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep watering evenly and feed lightly, hold up heavy branches if needed, and start picking once the peppers are full-sized and firm. Keep an eye out for aphids and hornworms.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How are the pods sizing and coloring? Are you picking them green or letting some ripen red?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are your jalapenos growing and firming up?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Firm, full-sized pods about 2 to 3 inches long at deep, dark green for the classic green jalapeno, or red for a sweeter, hotter pepper. Corking is a maturity sign, not a flaw. Pick green pods to keep the plant productive; leave some to redden for heat.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Firm, full-sized peppers about 2 to 3 inches long, dark green for the usual jalapeno or red for a sweeter, hotter one. Tan corking lines are normal. Pick green ones to keep the plant going; leave some to turn red for heat.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut pods with shears or a knife, leaving a short stem, rather than pulling. Wear gloves, since capsaicin oil burns skin and eyes. Harvest at least once or twice a week to keep the plant setting, and bring in the crop before the first frost ends the plant.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Cut the peppers off with scissors or a knife, leaving a bit of stem, and wear gloves so the hot oil does not burn your hands or eyes. Pick every few days, and bring in the last peppers before the first frost kills the plant.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have you harvested? Are you picking green, or letting some ripen red for heat?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you picked your first jalapeno yet?

notifications.title_seasoned: Plant jalapeno only when the soil is warm
notifications.title_beginner: Wait for warm weather to plant jalapeno
notifications.body_seasoned: Peppers set back badly in cold soil. Transplant only once nights hold above 50°F and the soil has warmed to 60 to 65°F, around the tomato date, and warm the soil first with black mulch.
notifications.body_beginner: Peppers hate cold soil. Wait to plant jalapeno out until nights stay above 50°F and the soil is warm, around when you would plant tomatoes.

notifications.title_seasoned: Side-dress your jalapeno at fruit set
notifications.body_seasoned: Your jalapeno is setting its first fruit, the moment to side-dress with a little nitrogen. Place it a few inches out from the plants and water it in. Go easy: too much nitrogen gives leaves, not pods.
notifications.body_beginner: Your jalapeno is starting to set fruit. Feed it lightly with a nitrogen fertilizer a few inches out from the stem, and water it in. Do not overdo it.

notifications.title_seasoned: Your jalapeno is ready to pick
notifications.body_seasoned: Your jalapeno pods are full-sized and firm dark green, ready to pick. Cut with shears leaving a short stem, wear gloves, and harvest regularly to keep the plant setting. Leave a few to ripen red for more heat.
notifications.body_beginner: Your jalapeno peppers are full-sized and firm, ready to pick. Cut them off with a little stem, wear gloves, and keep picking so the plant makes more. Leave a few to turn red for extra heat.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost is coming, harvest your jalapeno
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost warning for your jalapeno
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A frost is forecast. Jalapeno is frost-tender and the first frost ends the plant, so harvest all usable pods now, green and red alike, before the freeze.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Frost is coming, and it will kill your jalapeno. Pick all the usable peppers now, green and red, before the frost hits.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Extreme heat may stall your jalapeno's fruit set
weather_triggers.title_beginner: A heat wave may pause your jalapeno
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A stretch of extreme heat is forecast. Above about 90°F days and 75°F nights, pepper blossoms drop and fruit set pauses even though the plant is healthy. Keep it evenly watered and lightly shaded if you can; set resumes as the heat eases.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Very hot weather is coming. Above about 90°F in the day and 75°F at night, jalapeno flowers drop and it stops setting peppers for a while, then picks back up when it cools. Keep it well watered and give some afternoon shade if you can.

germination.text_seasoned: Pepper seed is slow and warmth-hungry. Give it bottom heat of 80 to 90°F and patience; cool flats sit and sulk. Start about 8 weeks before your warm transplant date.
germination.text_beginner: Jalapeno seeds like it warm and take a bit longer to sprout than tomatoes. A heat mat at 80 to 90°F helps a lot. Start them about 8 weeks before you will plant out.

seedling.text_seasoned: Grow stocky transplants in strong light, and guard seedlings from flea beetles, which can shred small plants. Do not rush them outside; peppers gain nothing from an early, cold start.
seedling.text_beginner: Keep seedlings in bright light so they grow stocky, and protect them from flea beetles. Do not hurry them outdoors; wait for warm weather.

transplanting.text_seasoned: Patience beats the calendar: a pepper set into cold soil just sits there and sulks for weeks. Wait until nights hold above 50°F and the soil is 60 to 65°F, around the tomato date, and warm the soil with black mulch.
transplanting.text_beginner: Do not rush jalapeno outside. Planting into cold soil stalls it. Wait until nights stay above 50°F and the soil is warm, around tomato time. Black plastic mulch warms the soil and helps.

flowering.text_seasoned: Pepper flowers are self-fertile and self-pollinating, so one plant sets fruit. Go easy on nitrogen now, since excess drives leaf over flowers. Blossom drop in a heat wave (above about 90°F days, 75°F nights) or cold snap is normal and temporary.
flowering.text_beginner: Jalapeno flowers pollinate themselves, so a single plant will fruit. Do not over-feed with nitrogen now, or you get leaves instead of peppers. If flowers fall off during very hot or cold spells, that is normal and it picks back up.

fruiting.text_seasoned: Keep water even to prevent blossom-end rot, feed lightly, and know your heat levers: pods get hotter as they ripen red and when the plant runs a little hot and dry, milder when picked green and kept well watered. Tan corking on the skin is a vigor sign, not damage.
fruiting.text_beginner: Keep the water steady so the peppers do not get rot on the bottom, and feed lightly. Peppers get hotter as they turn red and when the plant is a bit stressed, milder when green and well watered. The tan lines (corking) on the skin are normal.

harvest.text_seasoned: Pick pods full-sized and firm dark green for classic jalapenos, or let some ripen red for more heat and sweetness. Cut with shears leaving a short stem, and always wear gloves, since capsaicin oil clings to skin and burns eyes. Harvest regularly to keep the plant setting.
harvest.text_beginner: Pick peppers when they are full-sized and dark green, or leave some to turn red for more heat. Cut them off with a little stem, and wear gloves so the hot oil does not burn your hands or eyes. Keep picking so the plant makes more.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Lots of flowers but few or no peppers setting
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Flowers keep dropping and no peppers form
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Blossom drop, usually from temperature stress or excess nitrogen. Pepper flowers abort and fall when days run above about 90°F and nights above 75°F, or during a cold snap, and a plant pushed with too much nitrogen makes leaves instead of setting fruit. The plant looks healthy but sets little until conditions moderate.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The flowers are dropping instead of making peppers. This happens in very hot weather (above about 90°F days, 75°F nights), in a cold snap, or when the plant has had too much nitrogen and grows leaves instead of fruit.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Heat or cold stress on the blossoms, or over-fertilization with nitrogen driving vegetative growth over fruit set.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Too much heat or cold on the flowers, or too much nitrogen fertilizer.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Time planting so flowering avoids the worst midsummer heat, choose heat-tolerant or early varieties, keep moisture even, provide light afternoon shade in extreme heat, and hold nitrogen back until fruit sets. Set resumes on its own as the heat eases.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant so the flowering does not fall in the hottest weeks, keep the plant evenly watered, give it some afternoon shade in a heat wave, and go easy on nitrogen until fruit sets. It will set peppers again once it cools off.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Jalapenos came out much milder than expected
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The peppers were not very hot
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Low pungency, which comes down to variety, maturity, and growing conditions. Heat rises with ripeness (a red pepper is hotter than a green one) and with plant stress, especially heat and a controlled water pull, while a mild variety like TAM, a cool season, and generous watering all keep the burn down.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The peppers were mild. Heat depends on the variety, how ripe the pepper is, and how the plant was grown. Green, well-watered peppers from a mild variety in a cool summer are the mildest.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: A low-heat variety, picking green rather than red, a cool season, and abundant water all lower capsaicin; environmental stress and full ripeness raise it.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: A mild variety, picking green, cool weather, and lots of water make peppers milder.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: For more heat, grow a hotter variety (Biker Billy over TAM Mild), let pods ripen fully red, grow them in heat, and run the plant a touch lean and dry as the fruit matures. For less heat, do the opposite and pick green.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Want more heat next time? Grow a hotter variety, let the peppers turn red, and keep the plant a little drier late on. Want less heat? Pick them green and keep them well watered.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Tan, corky lines and netting on the pepper skin
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The peppers have tan lines or a rough netting
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Corking, and it is a good sign, not a problem. Those fine tan-to-brown stretch marks and netting form as a fast-growing, maturing jalapeno expands, and Mexican markets prize corked pods as a mark of quality and full flavor. It is not disease, insect damage, or a defect.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: That is corking, and it is completely normal, even a sign of a good pepper. The tan lines form as the jalapeno grows and matures. In Mexican markets, corked peppers are actually preferred. It is not a disease or damage.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Natural skin expansion during vigorous growth and maturation, characteristic of jalapeno.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: The skin stretching as the pepper grows fast and ripens. It is natural.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Nothing to fix, corking is desirable. If you prefer smooth green pods for appearance, pick a little earlier, but corked, mature pods generally have the fullest flavor.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Nothing to do, corking is a good thing. If you like smooth peppers, pick a bit earlier, but corked ones usually taste best.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Sunken, leathery brown patch on the bottom of the pods
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Dark leathery spots on the bottom of the peppers
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Blossom-end rot, a physiological disorder, not a disease. A sunken, leathery, tan-to-black patch at the blossom end comes from a local calcium shortage in the fruit, driven almost always by uneven watering (swings between dry and wet) rather than by a lack of calcium in the soil. It is worst on the first flush and in hot, dry spells.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: That is blossom-end rot. It is caused by uneven watering, which keeps the pepper from getting enough calcium to the tip, not by a bug or a fungus. It shows up most on the first peppers and in hot, dry weather.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Uneven soil moisture disrupting calcium delivery to the developing fruit; aggravated by heat, drought stress, and root damage.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Letting the soil swing from dry to wet, which stops calcium reaching the fruit.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Keep soil moisture even with mulch and steady watering, avoid drought and waterlogging, do not over-fertilize with nitrogen or damage roots by cultivating close, and the later flushes typically come in clean.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist with mulch and regular watering, and avoid letting it dry out and then soaking it. The later peppers usually come in fine.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Jalapeno is not a succession crop. One planting produces continuously through the whole warm season, so you set plants out once rather than at intervals. In most zones a later sowing would be caught by frost before its long warm season could finish. Only in the warmest, frost-free or near-frost-free zones, and in the hot desert where the planting splits around midsummer heat, is a second seasonal window viable, and that is a separate season rather than a true succession.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: You plant jalapeno once for the season. A single planting keeps producing all through the warm months, so there is no need to replant every few weeks. In most places a later planting would not have time to fruit before frost. Only in very warm, nearly frost-free areas, or the hot desert, can you fit a second planting, and that is really a separate season.
succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Jalapeno is a single long-season crop that bears continuously from one planting through the warm months, so interval succession sowing does not apply; a second sowing in most zones would not mature before frost. Warm frost-free zones and the hot desert support a separate seasonal planting window (spring and fall around the midsummer heat pause), which is a distinct season rather than a succession.

crops.description_seasoned: Jalapeno is a warm-season fruiting vegetable (Capsicum annuum), the most popular hot pepper in American gardens, grown for its firm, medium-hot pods. Its culture is that of any pepper, close to a bell: a heat-loving, self-fertile, transplant crop set into warm soil after frost, growing slowly until the ground is truly warm, then bearing continuously through the summer. What sets it apart is pungency. Jalapeno carries capsaicin, roughly 2,500 to 8,000 Scoville units, produced in glands on the placenta inside the pod, and its heat is not fixed: it rises as the fruit ripens from green to red and as the plant meets stress, especially heat and a controlled water pull, so the same variety can be mild or fiery depending on how and when it is grown and picked. Two jalapeno-specific points reassure new growers: corking, the fine tan netting on a mature pod's skin, is a prized sign of quality, not a defect; and pods can be picked firm and dark green (the usual harvest, around 70 to 80 days from transplant) or left to ripen red for more heat and sweetness. Like tomato, jalapeno drops its blossoms and pauses fruit set when days climb above about 90°F and nights above 75°F, so in the hottest regions the crop splits into a spring and a fall flush around the peak of summer. Its pests are aphids (and the mosaic viruses they carry), flea beetles on seedlings, the pepper maggot (which largely spares thin-walled hot types), the pepper weevil in the South, and hornworms; its main diseases are bacterial spot, mosaic viruses, Phytophthora blight, and anthracnose, all held off by clean seed, rotation, warm well-drained soil, and dry foliage. Handle the harvest with gloves: capsaicin is an oil that burns skin and eyes.
crops.description_beginner: Jalapeno is the most popular hot pepper for home gardens, a warm-season plant (Capsicum annuum) grown for its firm, medium-hot peppers. You grow it just like a bell pepper: start it indoors, then set it out into warm soil after the last frost, because peppers barely grow until it is truly warm. The special thing about jalapeno is its heat, which comes from capsaicin inside the pod. That heat is not fixed: peppers get hotter as they ripen from green to red and when the plant is stressed by heat or a little dryness, so the very same plant can give mild or fiery peppers depending on how you grow and pick them. Two things surprise beginners: the tan lines (corking) on a ripe jalapeno are a good sign, not damage, and you can pick the peppers firm and dark green (the usual way, about 70 to 80 days after planting out) or leave them to turn red for more heat. Like tomatoes, jalapeno drops its flowers and stops setting fruit in extreme heat, above about 90°F days and 75°F nights, then starts again when it cools. Watch for aphids, flea beetles on young plants, hornworms, and, in the South, the pepper weevil, and for diseases like bacterial spot and Phytophthora blight, which you head off with clean plants, crop rotation, and watering the soil rather than the leaves. Always wear gloves when cutting hot peppers, since the oil that makes them hot stings your skin and eyes.

northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In cold zones jalapeno is a single tight summer crop: start transplants indoors about 8 weeks early, then set them out only once nights hold above 50°F and the soil is warm, around the tomato date. Harvest continuously from midsummer, picking pods firm and green, until the first frost ends the plant. In the coldest zones (3 to 4) the season is short, so choose an early, cool-tolerant strain like Early Jalapeño, use black mulch and row cover, and expect fewer pods to ripen fully red before frost.
northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In cold areas jalapeno is a one-crop-a-summer plant. Start seeds indoors about 8 weeks early, and plant out only when nights stay above 50°F and the soil is warm, around tomato time. Pick peppers from midsummer until frost. In the very coldest zones, grow a fast variety like Early Jalapeño and warm the soil with black plastic, and do not count on many turning red before frost.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Like tomato, jalapeno drops its blossoms and stops setting fruit when daytime highs pass about 90°F and, especially, when nighttime lows stay above 75°F, which UMD notes will slow or stop pod production. Across the Gulf and coastal plain, July and August bring exactly that combination of heat and warm nights (compounded by humidity and disease pressure), so fruit set pauses through the peak of summer. Growers therefore run a spring crop that sets before the heat and a fall crop as it eases, leaving midsummer paused. This pause reflects reduced fruit set at high temperature, not frost or cold. The exact pause months are modeled from the regional warm-season pattern.

se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: Across the Gulf and coastal plain, jalapeno is planted in early spring for an early-summer crop, then paused through the July and August heat when warm nights above 75°F stall fruit set, and grown again as a fall crop set out in early September. Harvest is heaviest in early summer and again in fall. Watch for flea beetles on young plants, aphids and the viruses they carry, the pepper weevil, and in hot, wet soils the Phytophthora blight peppers are prone to.
se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast, plant jalapeno in early spring for an early-summer crop. The worst of the July and August heat makes it stop setting peppers, so there is a summer pause, then a fall crop planted in early September. Watch young plants for flea beetles, and keep beds well drained to avoid disease.

ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: In California's hot interior valleys, jalapeno is set out in spring once the soil is warm and harvested through the long, hot summer into fall. Unlike the true desert, the Central Valley usually stays just within reach of fruit set with steady irrigation, though a peak-summer heat wave can briefly stall set before it resumes, so a full midsummer pause is not modeled here. Keep water even and watch for the pepper weevil.
ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In California's hot inland valleys, jalapeno does well. Plant in spring once it warms up and harvest through the hot summer into fall. A short, very hot spell may pause fruit set, but with steady water it keeps producing. Keep the water even.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: Along California's cool, foggy north coast, jalapeno grows but sets and ripens slowly, since peppers want more heat than these cool summers provide. Choose the warmest, sunniest site, lean to an early variety like Early Jalapeño, use black mulch or a reflective wall for warmth, set plants out late once truly warm, and harvest into fall, picking mostly green since few pods redden.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: On California's cool, foggy north coast, jalapeno is a bit of a challenge because peppers want heat. Pick your sunniest, warmest spot, grow an early variety, warm the soil with black plastic, plant out late when it is truly warm, and harvest into fall. Most peppers will be picked green here.

ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: On California's mild south coast, jalapeno grows through a long, gentle warm season: set transplants out from spring into early summer and harvest continuously into late fall. The mild climate is forgiving and frost is rare, though the coolest coastal pockets favor faster varieties and a warm, sunny site, and rarely get hot enough to force a heat pause.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: On California's mild south coast, jalapeno grows over a long, easy season. Plant transplants from spring into early summer and harvest into late fall. The mild weather suits it, and it rarely gets hot enough to stop setting fruit.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Like tomato, jalapeno drops its blossoms and stops setting fruit above about 90°F days and 75°F nights (NMSU notes chile blossoms may fail to set above 90°F). In the California desert valleys, June through August routinely exceed 105 to 110°F by day with nights well above 75°F, far past the threshold, so even a well-watered pepper sets no fruit through those months. Desert growers run a late-winter planting for a late-spring crop and a September planting for a fall and early-winter crop, leaving the deep-summer weeks paused. This pause reflects blocked fruit set at extreme heat, not frost or cold. The exact pause months are modeled from the regional warm-season pattern.

ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: In the California desert valleys, jalapeno is planted in late winter for a late-spring crop and again in September for a fall and early-winter crop. June through August are simply too hot, routinely 105 to 110°F with warm nights, for a pepper to set fruit, so midsummer is paused. Steady irrigation is essential, and the spring and fall windows carry the crop.
ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: In the California desert, jalapeno is planted in late winter for a spring crop and again in September for a fall crop. Summer is far too hot for peppers to set fruit, so you skip June through August. Water steadily through the year.

warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: In the warm arid zones of southern New Mexico and West Texas, jalapeno is set out after frost once the soil warms. It carries an early-summer crop, pauses fruit set through the July and August heat, then resumes into fall from the same planting. Steady irrigation is essential in the dry heat, and a controlled late-season water pull can sharpen the pods' heat. This is classic chile country, and jalapeno thrives here.
warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: In the dry, warm zones of southern New Mexico and West Texas, plant jalapeno after the last frost once the soil warms. It gives an early-summer crop, pauses in the July and August heat, and picks back up in fall. Water steadily. This is chile country and jalapeno does great here.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Like tomato, jalapeno drops its blossoms and stops setting fruit above about 90°F days and 75°F nights (UMD notes evening temperatures above 75°F slow or stop pod production). In peninsular Florida the summer, roughly June through August, combines those warm nights with heavy rain, humidity, and pest and disease pressure, so peppers are grown in the cooler, drier halves of the year and midsummer is paused. This pause reflects blocked fruit set at high temperature (with wet-season disease compounding it), not frost or cold. The exact pause months are modeled from the regional warm-season pattern.

The long frost-free season makes jalapeno a strong Florida crop; watch for flea beetles, the pepper weevil, aphids and viruses, and the soilborne blights.

The hot, wet middle of summer stops fruit set and brings heavy disease and pest pressure, so it is skipped. Jalapeno does well in Florida's long warm season; watch for pepper weevil and disease.
