crops.description_seasoned: The slicing cucumber is the standard American salad cucumber, a fast warm-season cucurbit (Cucumis sativus) grown for long, smooth, dark-green fruit eaten fresh rather than pickled. Vines are vigorous and tendrilled, running long or forming compact bushes, and they crop heavily over a short summer window once soil and air warm. Slicers are picked young, at about 6 to 8 inches, while the skin is glossy and the seeds soft; a slicer left on the vine goes fat, seedy, and yellow, and new set slows. Most garden slicers are monoecious open-pollinated standards such as Marketmore 76 and Straight Eight, though gynoecious hybrids and seedless parthenocarpic types are widely sold. Grown up a trellis, the long fruit hangs straight and clean and the foliage stays drier against disease.
crops.description_beginner: The slicing cucumber is the classic salad cucumber you eat fresh, long, smooth, and dark green, rather than one you turn into pickles. It is an easy, fast summer vegetable that grows as a long vine or a compact bush and makes a lot of fruit in a short time. Pick the cucumbers while they are young and shiny, around 6 to 8 inches; if you leave one on too long it gets fat, yellow, and seedy, and the plant stops making more. Growing the vines up a trellis keeps the long fruit straight and clean and helps the plant stay healthy.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Pick slicing cucumbers young, while the skin is glossy and firm, the color deep green, and the seeds still soft, generally at about 6 to 8 inches for the variety. Earlier is more tender; a slicer left to over-size dulls, yellows at the tip, turns bitter and seedy, and tells the plant to stop setting. Cut or clip the stem rather than pulling, to spare the brittle vine. At peak in warm weather the fruit sizes up fast, so check every 1 to 2 days and pick often to keep new fruit coming.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Pick slicing cucumbers while they are young, firm, shiny, and deep green, usually around 6 to 8 inches long. The exact size is up to you, but younger cucumbers are more tender. Cut or clip the stem instead of pulling, so you do not tear the vine. Check every day or two, because cucumbers grow fast and one left too long turns yellow, seedy, and bitter while the plant slows down.
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Most slicing cucumbers are monoecious: each plant carries separate male and female flowers, so a single plant sets fruit with no second variety needed. The flowers are insect-pollinated, mostly by bees, and each female needs several bee visits to size a full slicing fruit. Poor pollination, common in cool, wet, or pollinator-scarce conditions, shows up as small fruit that yellow and shrivel at the tip, and early-season male flowers routinely open and drop before the first females appear, which is normal. Two variety types behave differently: gynoecious (nearly all-female) hybrids set heavily but usually want a pollenizer plant in the mix, and parthenocarpic types set seedless fruit with no pollination at all, which is why they suit greenhouses, row covers, and containers. Plant flowers nearby and avoid spraying open blooms to keep bees working, and hand-pollinate with a small brush in the morning if set stalls.
crops.pollinator_notes_beginner: Most slicing cucumber plants have both male and female flowers, so you only need one plant to get fruit. Bees carry the pollen between the flowers, and each cucumber needs several bee visits, so anything that brings bees to your garden helps. If your early cucumbers stay small and shrivel, the flowers usually were not pollinated well, often in cool or rainy weather. Some special varieties, called seedless or parthenocarpic, make cucumbers with no bees at all, which is handy for pots and covered beds.

crops.name: Kale

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Kale likes rich, loose soil that holds moisture but still drains well. Mix in plenty of compost before planting. It is not fussy and grows in most garden soils, but it does best when the soil is fertile and never bone dry or waterlogged.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Kale is forgiving about soil and grows in a wide range of textures, but it performs best in a fertile, well-drained loam or sandy loam high in organic matter. Work in compost before planting and keep moisture even; the plant is a leafy heavy feeder whose tenderness and color suffer in soil that either ponds water or dries out hard.

ph.note_beginner: Kale grows best in soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, around 6.0 to 7.0. A simple soil test tells you where you stand. If you have had clubroot, keeping the soil closer to neutral helps.
ph.note_seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0; kale still does fine across a wider 5.5 to 7.5 band. Holding the soil toward neutral, roughly 6.8 to 7.2, also helps suppress clubroot, a key brassica soil disease, so a grower with clubroot history should lean to the high end.

fertilizer.timing: starter at transplanting, then side-dress after cutting leaves
fertilizer.example_product: Blood meal, 21-0-0, or a balanced vegetable fertilizer
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Kale is a leafy crop that needs steady nitrogen for tender, dark green leaves. Use a starter fertilizer at transplanting, then side-dress with nitrogen about 4 weeks later, and feed again with a light dose of nitrogen after each heavy cutting of leaves to push new growth. Its nutrient demand is moderate rather than extreme, so avoid overdoing nitrogen, which softens growth and draws aphids.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Kale needs regular feeding to keep making tender leaves. Give it a feed when you plant it, again about 4 weeks later, and a light feed after each big harvest so it grows fresh leaves. Do not overdo it, since too much fertilizer makes soft growth that bugs love.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time to side-dress your kale with nitrogen.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Time to feed your kale.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: High N for leafy growth; e.g. 21-0-0 side-dress or blood meal. Starter feed at transplant, then a light nitrogen feed after each cutting.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a nitrogen-rich feed such as blood meal or a balanced vegetable fertilizer.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: Side-dress about half a cup of 21-0-0 per 10 feet of row roughly 4 weeks after transplanting, then a lighter feed after heavy cuttings.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Follow the label rate for a nitrogen-rich vegetable fertilizer.

companions.note_beginner: Kale does well next to aromatic herbs, onions, and quick cool-season crops like lettuce and beets. The main thing is to keep it away from other cabbage-family plants, which share its pests and diseases.
companions.note_seasoned: Most kale companion pairings are traditional rather than research-tested. The ones worth acting on are practical: aromatic herbs and alliums as scent-based deterrents against cabbage pests, and lettuce, spinach, or beets as cool-season interplants that use space and light while kale is small. The well-grounded caution is to separate kale from other brassicas, which share clubroot and the whole cabbage-family pest complex, a rotation and disease principle more than a tested adjacency effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Onions
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Onions are a traditional neighbor for kale; their strong smell is said to help confuse and deter cabbage pests.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: A UMN-cited Iowa study found a thyme/onion/nasturtium mix reduced cabbage looper and imported cabbageworm damage in brassicas, and aromatic alliums are widely advised as scent-based deterrents for cole crops. extension_backed/medium: the trial used onion within a multi-species mix on broccoli rather than onion alone on kale, so the effect is supported but not cleanly isolated.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Onions are one of the better-supported brassica companions. Their pungent allium scent helps mask the kale from cabbage-family pests, loopers, cabbageworms, and root maggots, that hunt partly by smell, and extension trial work including onion in a mix with cole crops showed reduced caterpillar damage. Alliums are shallow-rooted and undemanding, so they tuck around kale without competing for much.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Dill
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Dill is a classic friend for cabbage-family plants. Its strong smell is said to put off pests, and its flowers bring in helpful insects.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Umbel/aromatic plantings are extension-noted for attracting parasitoid wasps and predators that prey on brassica caterpillars and aphids; the specific dill-kale pairing is not trial-tested, so medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Dill works for kale mainly through beneficial insects. Its umbel flowers attract parasitoid wasps and predators like hoverflies and lady beetles that prey on the aphids and cabbage caterpillars kale draws, and extension work pairing aromatic umbels with brassicas has shown reduced caterpillar damage. Let some dill flower for the benefit, and site it nearby rather than crowding the kale.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Lettuce
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Lettuce grows fast and low, so you can tuck it between young kale plants to use the space while the kale fills in.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Rests on the complementary-root-depth / succession interplant logic extensions endorse generally (a quick short crop under a slower one). Sound and widely taught, but a space/timing benefit rather than a measured kale-specific effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Lettuce and kale interplant well on structure and timing rather than chemistry. Lettuce is shallow-rooted and quick, kale taller and slower, so the lettuce uses the open ground and light between young kale plants and is harvested before the kale spreads. Expect an efficient use of the bed, not pest protection.

good_seasoned.name: Onions
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Alliums are a traditional companion for brassicas, their scent thought to deter cabbage pests, and an extension-cited trial including onion in a mix with cole crops showed reduced caterpillar damage. A practical, low-risk pairing that shares no major pest with kale.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: UMN-cited Iowa study included onion in a mix that reduced cabbage looper/imported cabbageworm on brassicas; isolated onion-on-kale effect not cleanly quantified.

good_seasoned.name: Dill
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Aromatic umbels like dill draw parasitoid wasps and predators that attack brassica caterpillars and aphids; extension work pairing umbels with cole crops has shown reduced damage. Let some flower, and keep it from crowding the kale.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Umbel/aromatic predator-recruitment for brassicas is extension-supported; specific dill-kale pairing not trial-tested.

good_seasoned.name: Lettuce
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A shallow, quick cool-season crop that shares kale's season and tucks along the bed edge, using space and light while the kale is still small. Space-driven and traditional, not a documented growth effect, and the two share no serious pest.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Space-use intercropping lore; no T1 source documents a lettuce-kale benefit.

good_seasoned.name: Beets
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A cool-season root that shares kale's window and works the lower soil while kale feeds higher up. A traditional, space-efficient pairing rather than a tested effect.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Cool-season interplant lore; no T1 source documents a beet-kale benefit.

good_seasoned.name: Nasturtiums
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Often planted as a trap crop for cabbage aphids near brassicas. Trap cropping is a documented principle but works best for moderately mobile pests and is not a tested kale-nasturtium pairing, so treat it as a plausible aid rather than a proven control.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Trap cropping for aphids is a documented mechanism, but the specific nasturtium-kale pairing is not formally tested.

good_seasoned.name: Aromatic herbs (thyme, mint, sage)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Strongly scented herbs are a long-standing brassica companion, thought to mask the crop from cabbage moths and aphids that locate hosts by smell. Folk practice with partial mechanistic support rather than a measured kale-specific benefit.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Aromatic-herb pest confusion is well-documented companion tradition for brassicas; no kale-specific T1 trial.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Other brassicas
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep kale away from other cabbage-family plants like broccoli, cabbage, collards, and cauliflower. They share the same pests and diseases, so planting them together makes problems worse.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Same-family crops share pests and pathogens, so clustering raises pest/disease pressure, and successive brassica planting builds soil-borne clubroot. A sound epidemiological/rotation mechanism rather than a measured antagonism.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Planting kale cheek-by-jowl with its brassica relatives, broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, collards, Brussels sprouts, concentrates the whole family's shared pests (cabbage worms, loopers, flea beetles, harlequin bugs, root maggots) and shared diseases in one spot, and repeated same-family planting lets soil-borne clubroot build up. Spread brassicas out and rotate where they grow each year.

bad_seasoned.name: Other brassicas
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, collards, and the other cole crops share kale's clubroot and cabbage-family pests, so grouping them concentrates disease and pest pressure. A real rotation and disease principle rather than a tested adjacency effect; the practical rule is to spread brassicas out and rotate them.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Shared clubroot and shared cabbage-family pests are extension-documented; the bad-adjacency claim is a known agronomic principle, not formally pair-tested.

bad_seasoned.name: Strawberries
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional caution that brassicas and strawberries inhibit each other. There is no documented mechanism or T1 support; it persists as folklore.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Folk anti-companion claim with no pattern match or T1 support.

pests.name: Cabbageworms and cabbage loopers
pests.symptoms_beginner: You'll see ragged holes eaten in the leaves, green caterpillars on the plant, and little dark droppings. Some caterpillars loop up in the middle as they crawl.
pests.cause_beginner: These are caterpillars that hatch from eggs laid by white butterflies and small moths. They love cabbage-family plants like kale and chew the leaves, which are the part you eat.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray a product called Bt, which is safe and targets only caterpillars, or pick the caterpillars and eggs off by hand from under the leaves. Spray again after rain, since it washes off.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover plants with a light fabric row cover right after planting to keep the butterflies and moths from laying eggs. Clear away old cabbage-family plants, and watch for the first white butterflies as your signal to act.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Ragged holes chewed through the leaves, with green caterpillars and dark frass on the foliage. Imported cabbageworms are velvety green; cabbage loopers move in a looping arch; diamondback larvae are small and wriggle when disturbed.
pests.cause_seasoned: The larvae of the imported cabbageworm, cabbage looper, and diamondback moth feed on brassica foliage; the adults are white or brownish butterflies and moths that lay eggs on the leaves. Because kale is harvested as leaves, even modest feeding damages the crop.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Spray Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) or spinosad, which target caterpillars, and hand-pick larvae and eggs from leaf undersides. Repeat after rain, since Bt breaks down.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Use floating row cover from transplanting to exclude the egg-laying adults, clean up brassica debris that shelters pupae, and scout for the first white butterflies as a spray cue.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_beginner: You'll see clusters of tiny soft insects on the new growth and tucked into the curled leaves, often a waxy gray-green kind. Leaves curl and pucker, and there may be a sticky coating.
pests.cause_beginner: Aphids are tiny insects that suck juice from the plant. They breed fast and hide deep in kale's crinkled leaves, where they are hard to wash out.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water, or use insecticidal soap or neem oil, making sure to hit under the leaves and into the crinkles where they hide. Repeat every few days.
pests.prevention_beginner: Welcome helpful bugs like ladybugs and lacewings that eat aphids, don't overdo the nitrogen fertilizer (lush growth attracts them), and check the new growth often.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of small soft-bodied insects on growing tips and leaf undersides; the waxy gray-green cabbage aphid is especially troublesome because it lodges in the crinkles and curls of kale leaves and is very hard to wash out at harvest.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several aphid species, notably the cabbage aphid, suck sap from kale; they multiply quickly and their feeding distorts growth and contaminates the harvested leaves.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong jet of water, or spray insecticidal soap or neem, covering leaf undersides and the leaf crinkles; repeat every few days. Curly-leaf varieties are hardest to clear, so catch infestations early.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Encourage natural enemies like lady beetles and lacewings, avoid overfeeding nitrogen (which spurs the soft growth aphids favor), and inspect growing tips early so colonies do not lodge in the leaves.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms_beginner: Lots of tiny round holes in the leaves of young plants, made by small dark beetles that jump away like fleas when you get close. Bad damage can stunt seedlings.
pests.cause_beginner: Flea beetles are small jumping beetles that chew on young cabbage-family leaves. They hurt seedlings most, because a tiny plant can't grow fast enough to recover.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover young plants with a row cover, and if there are a lot of beetles, use a spray such as spinosad or a kaolin clay coating. The main goal is to get the seedlings big enough to handle it.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover seedlings with row cover from the start, keep them strong with steady water and food so they grow past the damage, and pull nearby weeds in the cabbage family.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny round shot-hole pits chewed in the leaves of young plants; the small dark beetles jump like fleas when disturbed. Heavy feeding stunts or kills seedlings and scars the leaves of a leaf crop.
pests.cause_seasoned: Flea beetles chew the foliage of young brassicas and are most damaging at the seedling stage; on kale they also leave cosmetic shot-holes in the harvested leaves.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Protect seedlings with row cover, and spray spinosad or apply kaolin clay if pressure is high; the goal is getting plants past the vulnerable seedling stage.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Use row cover from sowing or transplanting, keep seedlings vigorous with even water and feeding so they grow through the damage, and clean up weedy brassica relatives nearby.

pests.name: Cabbage root maggot
pests.symptoms_beginner: New transplants wilt and grow badly or fall over. If you pull one up, you'll find small white maggots eating the roots. It's worst in cool, wet spring soil.
pests.cause_beginner: A small fly lays eggs at the base of the plant, and the maggots that hatch burrow down and eat the roots. The fly is most active in cool spring weather.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Once the maggots are in the roots you can't save that plant, so pull and throw away the badly damaged ones. Put your effort into protecting the rest from new eggs.
pests.prevention_beginner: Put a small collar or disk around the base of each transplant to stop the fly from laying eggs there, or use a row cover. Don't plant into cold, soggy soil, and avoid spots where you grew cabbage-family plants last year.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Transplants wilt, grow poorly, and may collapse; pulling a plant reveals small white maggots tunneling in the roots and lower stem. Damage is worst in cool, wet spring soil.
pests.cause_seasoned: The larvae of the cabbage root fly tunnel into brassica roots; the adult lays eggs at the stem base, and the maggots feed on the roots below, sometimes killing young plants.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no effective rescue once maggots are in the roots; remove and destroy badly affected plants and protect the rest from further egg-laying.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Place a collar or disk around the stem base at transplanting to block egg-laying, or use row cover; avoid planting into cold, wet soil and rotate away from where brassicas grew.

pests.name: Harlequin bug
pests.symptoms_beginner: Shield-shaped black-and-orange (or black-and-red) bugs on the leaves, which develop white or yellow spots, then brown and look tattered. It's mostly a warm-region problem and loves kale.
pests.cause_beginner: The harlequin bug is a colorful stink-bug relative that pierces the leaves and sucks the juices, leaving pale blotches. It strongly prefers cabbage-family plants like kale, mustard, and collards, especially in the South.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Search out and crush the bugs, their eggs (little barrel-shaped eggs in rows), and young ones by hand. Use a row cover to keep them off, pull out badly infested plants, and clear away weeds and old plants where they hide over winter.
pests.prevention_beginner: Clean up garden debris and cabbage-family weeds where the adults overwinter, use row cover, and consider a trap crop of mustard or an early kale planting to lure them away from the main crop, then destroy it.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Shield-shaped bugs up to about 3/8 inch, brightly black-and-yellow or black-and-red, feeding with piercing-sucking mouthparts that leave white stipples; affected leaves brown and look tattered, and heavy feeding wilts and deforms plants. A warm-region pest that prefers kale, mustard, and collards over other cole crops.
pests.cause_seasoned: The harlequin bug (Murgantia histrionica) is a brassica-specialist stink bug, most damaging in the southern United States, where it completes two to four generations a year and overwinters as an adult in debris and weeds.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick and crush adults, nymphs, and the barrel-shaped egg rows; exclude with floating row cover; remove heavily infested plants. Pyrethrins are permitted in organic production if pressure is severe.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Eliminate overwintering sites by removing crop debris and crucifer weeds, use row cover, and deploy an early trap crop of mustard, kale, or rapeseed to divert overwintering adults, then destroy it before the main crop is set out.

diseases.name: Clubroot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Plants wilt in the afternoon, stay small and yellowish, and don't bounce back. If you dig one up, the roots are swollen into lumpy, club-shaped knobs.
diseases.cause_beginner: A germ that lives in the soil infects the roots of cabbage-family plants and makes them swell, which stops the plant from taking up water and food. It stays in the soil for years.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There's no cure once a plant has it, so pull and destroy infected plants. Adding lime to make the soil less acidic (closer to neutral) helps hold it back, and growing cabbage-family plants only rarely in that spot starves the germ out.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Don't grow kale or its cabbage-family relatives in the same spot more than once every 3 years, or longer if you've had clubroot. Keep the soil from being too acidic, improve drainage, and clean soil off your tools.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Plants wilt in the heat of the day, grow stunted and yellowed, and recover poorly; roots are swollen into distorted clubs and galls instead of normal fine roots.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A soilborne organism (Plasmodiophora brassicae) infects brassica roots and causes the galls, which block water and nutrient uptake. It persists in soil for many years and spreads in contaminated soil and water.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once plants are infected; remove and destroy them. Raising soil pH toward 7.0 or above with lime can suppress the disease, and long rotations starve it out over time.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate brassicas on a cycle of at least 3 years, and longer where clubroot is known; keep soil pH up, improve drainage, and avoid moving infested soil on tools and boots.

diseases.name: Black rot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Yellow patches shaped like the letter V appear at the leaf edges, pointing inward, with black veins inside them. It can spread through the plant and rot the leaves you want to eat.
diseases.cause_beginner: A bacteria that often comes in on infected seeds or transplants. It gets into the leaves and travels through the plant's veins, spreading fastest in warm, wet weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There's no real cure, so remove and destroy infected plants to keep it from spreading. Don't handle or brush against the plants while they're wet, because that spreads the bacteria.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Begin with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants, don't plant where cabbage-family crops grew recently, space plants for good airflow, and avoid overhead watering.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellow, V-shaped lesions spread inward from the leaf margins, with the veins inside the V turning black; the disease moves through the vascular system and can blacken and rot the harvested leaves.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A seedborne bacterium (Xanthomonas campestris) that enters through leaf pores and wounds and moves through the plant's veins; it spreads in warm, wet conditions and on infected seed or transplants.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no effective cure; remove and destroy infected plants. Avoid working among plants when foliage is wet, since that moves the bacteria.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Start with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants, rotate away from brassicas, give plants room for airflow, and avoid overhead watering and handling wet foliage.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Pale yellow blotches on top of the leaves, with fuzzy grayish growth on the underside, mostly in cool, damp weather. Bad cases discolor the leaves.
diseases.cause_beginner: A mold-like disease that loves cool, wet, humid weather and spreads through the air and water. Wet leaves and crowded plants make it worse.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Open up the airflow so leaves can dry, remove the worst leaves, and use a copper spray if it's spreading. It's hard to stop once the weather stays damp.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Space plants so air moves between them, water at the soil instead of from above, and pick resistant varieties if downy mildew is common where you live.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Pale yellow patches form on the upper leaf surface with a fuzzy gray-white growth underneath, mainly in cool, damp weather; severe infection discolors and downgrades the leaves.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A fungus-like organism that thrives in cool, wet, humid conditions and spreads by spores in water and air; long leaf wetness and crowded plantings favor it. Kale's cool-season window overlaps the weather it likes.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Improve airflow and let foliage dry, remove badly affected leaves, and apply a copper-based fungicide if pressure is high; the disease is hard to stop once humidity stays high.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants for good air movement, water at the soil line rather than overhead, and choose resistant varieties where downy mildew is common.

diseases.name: Alternaria leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small dark spots on the leaves that grow into round patches with concentric rings, like a tiny target. Bad cases make the leaves yellow and unusable.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that spreads in warm, wet weather and infects the leaves, leaving target-like spots. It's worse on stressed plants and in crowded, damp plantings.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove and destroy badly spotted leaves, improve airflow so leaves dry quickly, and use a copper spray if it spreads. Avoid wetting the leaves when you water.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Start with clean seed, rotate away from brassicas, space plants for airflow, water at the soil line, and keep plants healthy so they resist infection.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small dark lesions enlarge into circular spots with characteristic concentric rings (a target-spot look) and a yellow halo; because the leaves are the crop, even moderate spotting reduces the harvest. Favored by warm, wet conditions.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Fungi in the genus Alternaria (with Cercospora causing a similar leaf spot) infect brassica foliage, spreading by spores in wind and splashing water; infected seed, crop debris, and long leaf wetness drive it.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy spotted leaves and debris, improve airflow, avoid overhead watering, and apply a copper-based fungicide if pressure is high.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Use clean, disease-free seed, rotate away from brassicas, space for airflow, water at the soil line, and clear crop debris that harbors spores.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Give about 1 to 1.5 inches weekly, kept even through the season.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly 1 to 1.5 inches a week.
watering.amount_seasoned: About 1 to 1.5 inches per week, a little more in hot, dry spells.
watering.amount_beginner: Aim for roughly 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose where possible.
watering.method_beginner: Water at the base of the plant rather than over the leaves.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves and limp, soft growth; kale dislikes waterlogged soil and can rot at the crown.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Lower leaves yellow and the plant looks soggy and limp.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting, slowed growth, and tough, bitter leaves; drought stress hurts leaf quality and invites pests.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Wilting leaves that turn tough and bitter.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Even moisture keeps the leaves tender and mild; dry spells make kale tougher and more bitter.
watering.method_note_beginner: Keep the water steady so the leaves stay tender, not tough.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Even moisture through the main leaf-production weeks matters most for tender, mild leaves.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Water steadily while the plant is making lots of leaves.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Kale can be direct sown or transplanted. For a spring crop, start seeds indoors about 4 to 5 weeks before set-out and transplant around 4 to 5 weeks before the last frost, or direct sow as soon as the soil is workable; kale tolerates frost. For a fall and overwintering crop, sow in midsummer (often direct in the garden) so plants size up before cold, then harvest through fall and, in milder zones, winter. Harden transplants off over 7 to 10 days.
start_method.notes_beginner: You can sow kale seeds right in the garden or start them indoors. For spring, start seeds about a month before planting out, and set plants in the garden a few weeks before your last frost, or just sow seeds once the soil can be worked. For a fall crop, sow in mid to late summer so it is ready before winter. If you grow your own transplants, let them get used to the outdoors over a week before planting.

drainage.saucer_practice: Empty the saucer after watering so roots never sit in water; kale dislikes waterlogged soil.

soil_mix.type_beginner: A good-quality potting mix, not garden soil.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in some compost for a steady supply of nutrients.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: A light, well-drained commercial potting mix high in organic matter.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend in compost and a slow-release nitrogen source; container kale still feeds steadily.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out faster than the ground, so check daily in warm weather.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Feed a bit more often than in the ground, since watering washes nutrients out of pots.

overwintering.approach_beginner: In mild-winter areas, kale in a pot keeps going through winter; just move it to a sheltered, sunny spot. In cold areas, pull the pot against the house or into an unheated garage during hard freezes, or grow a fast variety and enjoy it before deep winter.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Kale is cold-hardy enough to overwinter in a container in mild zones, where it keeps producing through winter in a sheltered, sunny spot. In colder zones the limited root volume of a pot freezes harder than open ground, so move containers against a wall or into an unheated structure during hard freezes, or treat the potted crop as a single fall-into-early-winter planting.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Kale grows well in a pot of at least 3 gallons that is 10 inches or more deep, one or two plants per pot. Keep it watered and fed, and pick the outer leaves as you need them. In hot areas, give it some afternoon shade.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Kale is a good container crop because it is compact and harvested as leaves over a long period. Use a container of at least 3 gallons and 10 inches deep, one or two plants per pot, and keep moisture even since pots dry quickly. Pick outer leaves and leave the growing point, and in warm regions give afternoon shade and avoid heat-absorbing dark pots.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry faster than beds; check moisture daily in heat and water before the mix dries out.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Container kale needs more frequent feeding than in-ground plants because watering leaches nutrients.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering container suits kale well, since it smooths out the steady moisture that keeps the leaves tender and mild.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match because it keeps the water steady, which keeps kale leaves tender.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: Kale stays relatively compact but builds a substantial root system over a long season, so choose a container at least 3 gallons and 10 inches deep. Width matters more than height: a broad pot gives room to grow one or two plants and buffers the fast drying that narrow pots suffer.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Kale does not get huge, but it grows for a long time, so give it a pot that holds at least 3 gallons and is about 10 inches deep. A wider pot is better than a tall skinny one because it holds moisture better and gives the roots room.

recommended.name: Lacinato (Dinosaur / Tuscan)
recommended.note: Flat, strap-like dark blue-green leaves with a heavily savoyed texture; a popular gourmet type. The least cold-hardy of the common kales, so give it row cover at the cold end of the season.

recommended.name: Winterbor
recommended.note: A very cold-hardy curly blue-green hybrid; a top pick for fall and overwintering because it holds up through hard freezes.

recommended.name: Red Russian
recommended.note: Tender, flat, oak-leaf-shaped leaves with purple veins; fast and very cold-hardy, good for baby leaf and salads. A favorite of swede midge, so watch for it in the North.

recommended.name: Dwarf Blue Curled Scotch (Vates)
recommended.note: A compact, hardy curly heirloom that holds well in cold and is a dependable, space-saving garden standard.

recommended.name: Redbor
recommended.note: A striking deep-purple curly hybrid, ornamental as well as edible, and cold-hardy with color that deepens in the cold.

recommended.name: Improved Dwarf Siberian
recommended.note: Broad, mildly frilled blue-green leaves on a hardy, vigorous, heat- and cold-tolerant plant; one of the most forgiving kales for beginners.

varieties.note_seasoned: Match the variety to the slot and the climate. For fall and overwintering, lean on the hardiest types: Winterbor, Improved Dwarf Siberian, and Red Russian shrug off hard frost, while Lacinato is the least cold-hardy and wants protection. Curly types (Winterbor, Vates, Redbor) hold texture and color in cold; flat types (Lacinato, Red Russian) are more tender for fresh eating. Where clubroot or other brassica diseases are a concern, look for resistant cultivars.
varieties.note_beginner: Winterbor and Dwarf Siberian are easy, very hardy choices, great for a fall or winter crop. Red Russian is tender and fast, nice for salads. Lacinato (Dinosaur kale) is popular for cooking but is the least cold-hardy, so cover it when it gets really cold.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Other brassicas (broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, collards, Brussels sprouts, kohlrabi, turnip, radish, mustard), which share clubroot and cabbage-family pests.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Other cabbage-family crops like broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, collards, and turnips.
rotation.good_after: Legumes such as beans and peas, or unrelated crops like tomatoes, squash, or onions.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate so kale and its brassica relatives do not return to the same ground for at least 3 years, and longer where clubroot is present, since the clubroot organism persists in soil for years. The University of Minnesota advises not growing cole crops in the same spot for the past four years. Keeping soil pH near neutral also helps suppress clubroot.
rotation.note_beginner: Do not plant kale or other cabbage-family crops in the same spot year after year. Waiting at least 3 years between them, and longer if you have had clubroot, helps avoid soil diseases.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Kale wilts and toughens at room temperature and its leaves yellow within a day or two, so do not leave it out. Refrigerate as soon as possible after cutting; if it must sit out briefly, stand the stems in water like cut flowers.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Do not leave kale out on the counter. It wilts and yellows fast in the warmth, so get it into the fridge soon after picking.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerate unwashed in a loose or perforated bag in the crisper; kale holds its quality for roughly 1 week, and up to about 2 weeks held near 32°F at high humidity. Washing before storage traps moisture and speeds spoilage.
storage.fridge_beginner: Store kale unwashed in a loose bag in the fridge's crisper drawer, where it stays good for about a week, sometimes up to 2 weeks if very cold. Wait to wash it until you are ready to cook.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Kale freezes well once blanched: strip the leaves from the stems, blanch about 2 to 3 minutes in boiling water, cool quickly in ice water, drain, and freeze. Blanching halts the enzymes that otherwise cause off-flavors and loss of color in storage.
storage.freezer_beginner: Kale freezes well if you blanch it first. Strip the leaves off the stems, boil them for 2 to 3 minutes, cool them right away in ice water, drain, and freeze.
storage.notes_seasoned: Quality is highest straight from the garden, and a key kale advantage is that the plant itself is the best storage: leaves keep on the plant for weeks in cool weather and sweeten after frost, so harvest close to when you will use it rather than stockpiling. Chilling promptly after cutting keeps the leaves crisp and mild.
storage.notes_beginner: Kale is best right after you pick it, and the plant is its own best storage: in cool weather the leaves keep on the plant for weeks and even get sweeter after frost. So pick what you need when you need it, and chill it quickly after cutting.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: In about 5 to 10 days, your seeds sprout and push up their first two little leaves (the seed leaves).
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil damp. Once the first real kale leaves appear after the seed leaves, thin crowded seedlings.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your seeds come up yet?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seeds sprout in about 5 to 10 days at soil temperatures of roughly 45 to 85°F, pushing up two seed leaves (cotyledons).
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep the seedbed or starting mix evenly moist; thin or pot up once the first true leaves appear.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Did your kale seeds sprout?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The seedlings grow their real, slightly frilly leaves and a stronger stem. They are ready to move outside at about 4 to 5 weeks old.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: If you grew transplants, harden them off over about a week before planting out. Watch for flea beetle shot-holes on the young leaves.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How many real leaves do your seedlings have?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Young plants develop true leaves and a sturdy stem; kale transplants are ready at about 4 to 5 weeks. Flea beetles are the main seedling threat.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harden off over 7 to 10 days before setting out; protect seedlings from flea beetles with row cover.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How many true leaves does your seedling have?

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant grows into an upright rosette of big leaves. This is when it builds the frame that you will harvest from for months.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Feed with nitrogen and keep it evenly watered so the leaves stay tender. Check for aphids in the leaf crinkles and caterpillars on the undersides.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Is your plant growing lots of healthy leaves?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The plant builds an upright rosette of large leaves over several weeks, laying down the productive frame.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Side-dress with nitrogen, keep moisture even for tender leaves, and scout for aphids and cabbageworms while the frame fills out.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Is your kale putting on healthy leafy growth?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Once the outer leaves are about hand-sized, start picking. Take the lowest, outside leaves and leave the center to keep growing, so the plant gives leaves for months.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pick the outer leaves regularly, never stripping more than about a third at once. Feed lightly after a big harvest. The leaves taste sweeter after frost.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you started picking outer leaves?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Outer leaves reach usable size at about 50 to 65 days (baby leaf around 25 to 30 days); harvest cut-and-come-again, taking the lowest leaves and leaving the growing point.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Crop the outer leaves regularly to keep new growth coming, side-dress lightly after heavy picking, and expect the best flavor after a frost.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are you harvesting outer leaves?

growth_stages.name: Overwintering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: As cold sets in, kale keeps going. In mild areas you harvest right through winter; in cold areas the plant may rest under snow or cover and may regrow, then send up a flower stalk (bolt) in spring.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: In mild zones, keep picking through winter. In cold zones, protect plants with a row cover or low tunnel. When spring warmth makes the plant bolt, harvest what is left, since the leaves turn bitter once it flowers.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Is your kale still producing in the cold?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Kale is among the hardiest garden vegetables: mature plants tolerate hard frost and into the low-to-mid 20s°F, sweetening as starch converts to sugar. In mild zones it crops through winter; in cold zones it overwinters under cover and resumes, then bolts as spring warms and days lengthen.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest through winter in mild zones; use row cover or low tunnels in cold zones. Once the plant bolts in spring, harvest remaining leaves promptly, as flavor turns bitter, and pull it to make room.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Is your kale overwintering or starting to bolt?

notifications.title_beginner: Time to start picking kale leaves
notifications.body_seasoned: Your kale's outer leaves should be about hand-sized now. Begin cropping the lowest, outermost leaves and leave the central growing point so the plant keeps producing for months.
notifications.body_beginner: Your kale's outside leaves should be big enough to pick. Take the lowest, outer ones and leave the middle growing, so it keeps making more.

notifications.body_seasoned: Kale needs steady nitrogen for tender leaves. Side-dress now and again after heavy cuttings, placing the feed near the plant and watering it in.
notifications.body_beginner: Kale likes regular feeding. Give it some nitrogen now, and again after big harvests, to keep tender leaves coming.

notifications.title_seasoned: Frost is coming: expect sweeter kale
notifications.title_beginner: Frost ahead, your kale will sweeten
notifications.body_seasoned: A frost is on the way. Kale takes light and hard frost in stride and the cold actually sweetens the leaves, so there is no need to cover it for a normal frost; just keep harvesting.
notifications.body_beginner: Frost is coming, but that is good news for kale: the cold makes the leaves sweeter. You do not need to cover it for a normal frost. Keep picking.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot weather warning for your kale
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Sustained heat above about 80°F to 85°F makes kale leaves tough and bitter and can trigger bolting. Keep moisture even, harvest in the cool morning, and in hot regions give afternoon shade; treat summer as off-season where it stays hot.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Hot weather makes kale leaves tough and bitter and can make it flower early. Water evenly, pick in the cool morning, and give it some afternoon shade. In hot areas, kale is really a fall-to-spring crop.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hard freeze coming
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Kale is very cold-hardy and a freeze sweetens the leaves; mature plants tolerate hard frost and into the low-to-mid 20s°F. In the coldest zones a deep freeze below about 20°F may damage exposed leaves, so a row cover or low tunnel extends the harvest, but for most freezes simply keep picking.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Kale handles hard freezes well, and the cold makes it taste sweeter, so you usually do not need to do anything. In very cold areas, a row cover or low tunnel helps it keep going through the worst cold.

germination.text_seasoned: Sow about 0.25 to 0.5 inch deep into a moist seedbed or starting mix; kale germinates reliably across 45 to 85°F in about 5 to 10 days.
germination.text_beginner: Plant the seeds about a quarter to half an inch deep in damp soil, and keep it evenly moist while they sprout in 5 to 10 days.

germination.text_seasoned: For a spring crop start indoors about 4 to 5 weeks before set-out, or direct sow as soon as the soil is workable; kale tolerates cool soil.
germination.text_beginner: Start seeds indoors about a month before planting out, or just sow them in the garden once the soil can be worked.

seedling.text_seasoned: Transplant or thin to about 12 to 18 inches apart for full plants, or 4 inches for baby-leaf harvest; harden transplants off over 7 to 10 days.
seedling.text_beginner: Space plants about 12 to 18 inches apart for big plants, or about 4 inches apart if you only want baby leaves.

seedling.text_seasoned: Protect seedlings from flea beetles with row cover; a vigorous, well-watered seedling outgrows light feeding damage.
seedling.text_beginner: Cover young plants with a light row cover to stop flea beetles from peppering the leaves with holes.

established.text_seasoned: Side-dress nitrogen as the rosette builds and keep moisture even at roughly 1 to 1.5 inches per week; drought stress toughens and embitters the leaves.
established.text_beginner: Feed with nitrogen and water steadily, about 1 to 1.5 inches a week, so the leaves stay tender and mild.

established.text_seasoned: Scout the leaf crinkles and growing tips for cabbage aphids and the undersides for caterpillars; catching them early keeps the harvested leaves clean.
established.text_beginner: Check inside the curled leaves for aphids and under the leaves for green caterpillars, and deal with them early.

harvest.text_seasoned: Crop the outer leaves once they reach usable size, taking no more than about a third of the plant so the central growing point keeps producing for months.
harvest.text_beginner: Pick the outside leaves when they are big enough, and leave the center growing, so the same plant keeps making leaves for a long time.

harvest.text_seasoned: Leaves are sweetest after a frost or two; in cool weather you can keep harvesting straight from the garden even after the foliage has frozen.
harvest.text_beginner: Kale tastes sweeter after frost, and you can keep picking even after the leaves have frozen in cool weather.

overwintering.text_seasoned: In mild zones keep cropping through winter; in cold zones a low tunnel or row cover extends the harvest, and the hardiest curly and Siberian types take the most cold.
overwintering.text_beginner: In mild areas keep picking all winter. In cold areas, cover the plants to keep harvesting longer, and grow hardy kinds like Winterbor or Siberian.

overwintering.text_seasoned: Watch for spring bolting as warmth and long days return: harvest remaining leaves before the flower stalk elongates, since the leaves turn bitter once the plant flowers.
overwintering.text_beginner: In spring, kale that lived through winter will send up a flower stalk and turn bitter, so pick the last good leaves before that happens.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A single kale plant yields a steady run of outer leaves over a long season rather than one harvest, roughly 0.5 to 1 pound or more per plant depending on variety, season length, and how often you crop it. Extension yields run about 5 to 10 pounds per 10 feet of row.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Each kale plant gives you a steady supply of leaves over months, not one big harvest. How much you get depends on the variety and how long your season is, but a row of plants keeps producing for a long time.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Production climbs as the plant sizes up and then holds for weeks to months as you crop the outer leaves, peaking in the cool weeks of fall and, in mild zones, through winter. Output slows in summer heat (where the crop is even grown then) and ends when the plant bolts in spring or a deep freeze kills it.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Kale produces the most once the plant is full-sized, and it keeps going strongest in cool fall weather and, in mild areas, through winter. It slows down in summer heat and stops once it flowers in spring or a hard winter freeze finishes it.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: The key to total yield is cropping the outer leaves regularly while leaving the central growing point: frequent, moderate picking keeps a plant productive for months, whereas stripping a plant bare or letting old leaves yellow checks it. New growers often pick too timidly or harvest the center, which stalls the plant.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Here is the trick: pick the outer leaves often, but always leave the small center leaves to keep growing. Regular picking keeps a plant making leaves for months. Do not take the middle of the plant, and do not let old leaves just yellow and rot.
factors_seasoned: Harvest method: regular cut-and-come-again cropping of outer leaves (leaving the growing point) sustains months of production; taking the center or stripping the plant ends it.
Temperature: cool weather through fall and mild winters gives the highest-quality, sweetest leaves; summer heat toughens and embitters them and can cause bolting.
Variety: hardy curly and Siberian types crop longest into cold and overwinter best; tender flat types are faster but less cold-durable.
Nitrogen and even moisture: steady nitrogen and consistent water keep new leaves tender; stress makes them tough, bitter, and aphid-prone.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No reliable extension or peer-reviewed evidence supports timing kale planting or harvest by moon phase. Plant by soil temperature, frost dates, and the seasonal windows instead.

failure_diagnostics.label: Bolting (flower stalk and bitter leaves)
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Summer heat and long days, or a plant that lived through winter and is now flowering in spring.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your kale shot up a tall stalk with buds or yellow flowers and the leaves turned bitter. Kale bolts (runs to flower) when heat and long days, or a spring after overwintering, tell it to make seed, and once it bolts the leaves go bitter and tough. People often blame the plant, but it is just its life cycle or the heat. Next time, plan the main crop for cool weather (fall is ideal), and treat an overwintered plant as a spring bonus you harvest before it flowers.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Grow kale to mature in cool weather, lean on fall and winter crops, and harvest overwintered plants before they bolt in spring.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The plant elongated a flowering stalk and the leaves turned bitter and tough. Bolting is driven by heat and lengthening days, or by vernalized overwintered plants flowering in spring; once it bolts, leaf quality is lost. Growers often plant too late into spring heat. Next time time the main crop for the cool side of the season, favor fall and overwintering crops, and crop overwintered plants out before the stalk elongates.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Heat and long days, or spring bolting of a vernalized overwintered plant.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Time the crop for cool weather, favor fall and overwintering plantings, and harvest overwintered kale before it bolts.

failure_diagnostics.label: Tough, bitter leaves
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Hot weather, drought stress, or leaves left on the plant too long.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your kale leaves are tough, leathery, and bitter instead of tender. This usually comes from summer heat, from the plant drying out, or from leaving leaves on too long so they age. It is tempting to think the variety is bad, but conditions are almost always the cause. Next time, keep the soil evenly moist, grow kale in the cool seasons, pick leaves while they are young to medium-sized, and remember that frost actually sweetens them.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep moisture steady, grow in cool weather, pick leaves young, and enjoy the post-frost sweetening.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Leaves are tough and bitter rather than tender. Heat, drought stress, and over-mature leaves are the usual causes; kale's flavor is best in cool weather and is sweetened by frost. Next time hold even moisture, schedule the crop for cool conditions, crop leaves at a young-to-medium size, and lean on the fall/winter window.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Heat, drought stress, or over-mature leaves.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Hold even moisture, grow in cool weather, crop leaves young, and use the fall and winter window for the sweetest leaves.

failure_diagnostics.label: Aphids packed into the leaves
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Cabbage aphids settling into the curled leaves, often worse on soft, over-fed growth.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: You found dense clusters of small gray-green insects tucked deep in the crinkles of the leaves, hard to wash out. Cabbage aphids love kale and hide in the leaf folds, and they breed fastest on soft growth from too much nitrogen. People often miss them until harvest. Next time, scout the growing tips and leaf crinkles weekly, blast or wash colonies off early, avoid overfeeding nitrogen, and welcome lady beetles and lacewings.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Scout weekly, knock off colonies early, go easy on nitrogen, and encourage beneficial insects.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Dense cabbage-aphid colonies lodged in the leaf crinkles, very hard to clean at harvest. The waxy gray-green cabbage aphid specializes on brassicas and favors the soft growth that excess nitrogen produces. Next time scout tips and crinkles weekly, dislodge colonies early with a water jet or insecticidal soap, avoid overfeeding nitrogen, and conserve natural enemies; curly types are the hardest to clean, so stay ahead of them.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Cabbage aphids colonizing the leaf folds, worsened by soft, over-fertilized growth.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Scout weekly, dislodge colonies early, moderate nitrogen, conserve beneficials, and prefer flatter leaves where aphids are chronic.

failure_diagnostics.label: Stunted, yellow plants with clubbed roots
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Clubroot, a soil disease of cabbage-family plants, or planting brassicas in the same spot too often.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your kale stayed small and yellowish, wilted in the afternoon, and when you dug it up the roots were swollen into lumps. That is clubroot, a soil disease that infects cabbage-family roots and lasts for years in the soil. It usually builds up when brassicas are grown in the same spot repeatedly. Next time, rotate so cabbage-family crops do not return to that bed for at least 3 years, keep the soil pH near neutral, and improve drainage.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Rotate brassicas out of that bed for at least 3 years, keep soil pH near neutral, and improve drainage.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Plants were stunted and chlorotic, wilted by day, and showed galled, clubbed roots, the signature of clubroot (Plasmodiophora brassicae). The soilborne organism persists for years and builds under repeated brassica cropping and acidic, poorly drained soil. Next time rotate cabbage-family crops out for at least 3 years (longer where known), lime toward a neutral-to-slightly-alkaline pH, and improve drainage; there is no in-season cure.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Clubroot building in soil cropped to brassicas too frequently, favored by acidic, wet soil.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Use a 3-year-plus brassica rotation, raise pH toward neutral, and improve drainage; remove and destroy infected plants.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Kale crops over a long window, so rather than one big planting, sow small batches every 2 to 3 weeks through the cool stretches of spring and again from late summer for a fall and overwintering crop. Because each plant is cut over many weeks, you need fewer sowings than for a fast crop, but staggering them keeps a supply of tender young leaves coming. In hot regions skip the summer heat and plant for fall and winter instead.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: Plant kale in small batches a couple of weeks apart, in spring and again in late summer for fall, rather than all at once. Each plant keeps giving leaves for a long time, so you do not need many. In hot-summer areas, skip the summer and plant for fall and winter.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: kale_author_fresh_pilot (Claude Code lane authoring test, 2026-06-29). Authored from the kale shell, modeled structurally on the broccoli certified template, with kale biology re-derived from live T1 extension sources (UMN/USU/NCSU/Clemson/UMD/Iowa State for biology; per-region planting calendars from UC ANR/UC MG, UF/IFAS, UGA/Clemson/LSU/MSU State/Alabama, UArizona/NMSU/TAMU, CTAHR, plus UMN/Iowa State/Cornell/UMaine/UNH/MSU for the northern tier). DRAFT for review, not certified: launch flags false. Key kale-vs-broccoli refits: leafy non-heading continuous cut-and-come-again harvest (no head_forming/side_shoots stages; added overwintering stage); much greater cold-hardiness (survives hard frost, sweetens after frost, overwinters in mild zones); NO summer heat_pause in the northern tier (kale crops through northern summers, unlike heading broccoli); summer heat_pause only in genuinely hot regions (SE/Gulf, FL, Hawaii low-elevation, CA interior/south-coast/desert, low desert AZ, warm arid), each backed at the cell; Brassicaceae rotation (shared with broccoli) but kale-specific pest (harlequin bug) and disease (Alternaria leaf spot) emphasis. successions_realized intentionally NOT hand-authored (deriver-filled). See kale_NOTES.md for flags and modeled values.

open_findings.summary: hawaii_tropical z11 uses a bounded low-elevation winter window with a summer heat_pause and notes high-elevation year-round; CTAHR B-91 is a 1943 scanned PDF that did not parse via WebFetch (text extracted locally) and does not table kale's planting months directly (inferred from its cole-crop / leafy-green guidance). Corroborate against a parseable modern CTAHR source at review.
open_findings.basis: B-91 explicitly frames kale as preferring cooler temperatures than low-elevation Hawaii summers and cole crops as low-elevation winter / high-elevation year-round crops, so the bounded window is honest; only the PDF parse and bulletin age are gaps. Same pattern as broccoli's hawaii open finding.

open_findings.summary: germination_temp_f [45, 85] is the standard cole-crop germination envelope; the kale-specific T1 pages state 5 to 10 day germination but not an explicit min/max soil temperature, so the range is modeled on the brassica germination envelope.
open_findings.basis: Consistent with broccoli's germination_temp_f and the 5 to 10 day germination the kale sources report; flagged in kale_NOTES.md.

3.zone_notes: In the coldest zone, kale crops from midsummer through the fall frosts; deep winter usually kills or fully dormants unprotected plants, so harvest is a single long season.

4.zone_notes: Plant in spring once the soil is workable and again in midsummer for fall; harvest runs through the fall frosts that sweeten the leaves, then deep winter ends it.

5.zone_notes: A long season from spring through the fall frosts; under a low tunnel or row cover, harvest can extend into winter, since kale is very cold-hardy.

6.zone_notes: Kale crops spring through fall and into early winter and often overwinters with simple protection, resuming growth before it bolts in spring.

7.zone_notes: At the mild end of the cold zones kale overwinters reliably and is often harvestable nearly year-round, with only a brief midwinter slowdown; summer leaves run a little tougher.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: Up north, grow kale as one long crop. Plant it around your last spring frost, or sow seeds once the soil can be worked, and sow again in midsummer for a fall crop. Kale keeps making leaves all summer here, so you can pick the outer leaves from midsummer right through fall, and the leaves get sweeter after frost. In the coldest areas, winter finally stops it, but a row cover helps it last longer; in milder cold areas it often lives through winter and keeps going. Pick tough, cold-hardy types like Winterbor or Siberian where winters are harsh.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In the cold zones kale is one long cool-season crop rather than a split one. Direct sow or set transplants out around the last frost (often April into May), and sow again in midsummer for fall. Unlike heading broccoli, kale keeps producing leaves right through the northern summer, so there is no midseason heat gap; quality is simply best in the cool ends of the season. Harvest the outer leaves cut-and-come-again from roughly midsummer, straight through the fall frosts that sweeten the leaves. In zones 3 to 5 deep winter ends the crop, though a low tunnel extends it; in zones 6 to 7 kale frequently overwinters with simple protection and resumes before bolting in spring. Lean on the hardiest curly and Siberian types in the coldest zones.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: kale is a cool-season brassica that grows and tastes best when average temperatures stay around 55°F to 75°F. Through the hot months its leaves turn tough and bitter, plants are prone to bolting (running to flower), and pressure from aphids and harlequin bugs peaks, so kale is grown as a fall-through-spring crop here and the summer is left out of the planting calendar. In the inland coastal plain, hot, humid summers run kale tough, bitter, and pest-prone, so it is grown fall through spring. (Clemson Cooperative Extension; University of Georgia Extension)

9.zone_notes: A long cool-season window: plant from late summer into fall, harvest through a mild winter into spring. Summer is too hot.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast, grow kale in fall, winter, and spring, not summer. Plant in late summer or fall, pick the outer leaves through the mild winter, and plant again in late winter for spring. Frost makes the leaves sweeter and does not hurt them. Skip the hot summer, when the leaves get tough and bitter and bugs are bad, especially the colorful harlequin bug. Keep the garden clean to cut down on pests.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: Across the Southeast kale is a fall, winter, and spring crop. Set out transplants or sow from about August into fall (a touch later toward the coast), harvest the outer leaves cut-and-come-again through a mild winter, and add a late-winter planting for spring. Frost sweetens the leaves and rarely harms them. The hot, humid summer is the off-season, when leaves turn tough and bitter and harlequin bugs, aphids, and caterpillars peak, so the planting calendar leaves roughly June through August out. Choose heat-tolerant types for the shoulders and clean up debris to blunt the harlequin-bug pressure this region is known for.

Pick the outer leaves over a long season, and enjoy that the cool winter makes them sweeter. Skip the heat of summer, when kale turns bitter and tries to flower.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: In the interior valleys kale is a cool-season crop grown from fall through spring. Sow or set transplants in late summer (around August into September) for a fall and winter harvest, and again in February for a spring crop before the heat. Harvest the outer leaves cut-and-come-again; the leaves are sweetest through the cool, sometimes frosty winter. The hot Central Valley summer is left out of the calendar, since heat makes the leaves bitter and pushes plants to bolt. Keep moisture even and give afternoon shade at the warm shoulders.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: On the cool, foggy coast, kale grows almost all year. Plant in spring and again in fall, and pick the outer leaves whenever you need them, even through the mild winter, when frost makes them sweeter. Right by the coast you can grow it through summer too; a bit inland, summer leaves may taste a little bitter, so it is best in the cooler months there.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: The cool maritime climate of the north coast suits kale nearly year-round. Plant in spring (start indoors in February, set out March into May) and again in early fall, and harvest the outer leaves cut-and-come-again across the seasons, including a mild, frost-sweetened winter. Right on the coast the cool summers let kale keep producing through summer; a little inland, summer heat can bring some bitterness, so favor the cool ends of the season there. This is the one region where kale runs without a real summer gap.

ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: On the south coast kale runs from fall through spring. Plant from about September into fall and again in late winter to early spring, and harvest the outer leaves cut-and-come-again, including right through the mild winter, when the occasional frost sweetens them. ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: In the low desert valleys kale is strictly a cool-season crop. Plant as the extreme heat breaks in fall (October is ideal) and harvest the outer leaves cut-and-come-again through the mild, sometimes frosty winter into early spring. The long, intensely hot summer, roughly May through September, is left entirely out of the calendar. Keep moisture steady and use afternoon shade at the start and end of the season.

Plant in late summer (around August into September) for a fall and winter harvest, and again in February into March for spring. Harvest the outer leaves cut-and-come-again; the cool, frosty winter gives the sweetest leaves. The hot, dry midsummer is the gap, since heat makes the leaves bitter and bolts the plants. Keep moisture even in the dry air and watch for harlequin bugs and aphids.
