fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: On the Florida peninsula kale is a cool-season crop. UF/IFAS lists the planting window from about September into February in central Florida and September into January in the far south, with harvest peaking December through February. Pick the outer leaves cut-and-come-again; the cool, frost-free-to-light-frost winter gives the best quality, and a rare frost only sweetens the leaves. The hot, humid summer, roughly May into September, is the off-season, when only tropical crops thrive. Watch for caterpillars and aphids in the warm shoulders.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: At low elevation plant kale in the cooler months; at higher elevation it grows year-round.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Kale crops cut-and-come-again from about 50 to 65 days after sowing.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest continues for months and through frosts, sweetening in the cold.

11.zone_notes: At low elevation kale is a cool-season crop, roughly planted September through winter and harvested into spring; at higher, cooler elevations it can be grown year-round.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: kale is a cool-season brassica that grows and tastes best when average temperatures stay around 55°F to 75°F. Through the hot months its leaves turn tough and bitter, plants are prone to bolting (running to flower), and pressure from aphids and harlequin bugs peaks, so kale is grown as a fall-through-spring crop here and the summer is left out of the planting calendar. At low elevation the warm season is too hot for kale, which prefers cooler temperatures than prevail in the islands' lowlands; at higher, cooler elevations it grows year-round. (UH Manoa CTAHR Bulletin B-91)

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In Hawaii, where you garden matters more than the month. Down low and warm, grow kale in the cooler months, from about September into spring, and skip the hot summer. Up higher where it is cooler, you can grow kale all year. Pick the leaves while they are young for the best flavor.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: In Hawaii kale follows elevation more than the calendar. At low elevations it is a cool-season crop: CTAHR frames cole crops as low-elevation winter crops, so plant from about September through the cooler months and harvest the outer leaves cut-and-come-again into spring, with the warm summer left out because kale prefers cooler temperatures than the lowlands provide. At higher, cooler elevations kale grows essentially year-round. There is no frost to sweeten the leaves at low elevation, so harvest young for the mildest flavor.

crops.description_seasoned: Kale is a hardy, non-heading cole crop grown for its nutritious leaves, which are harvested continuously rather than as a single head. A cool-season brassica, it produces the best quality in the cool weather of spring and fall and is one of the most cold-hardy vegetables in the garden: mature plants shrug off hard frost, and a touch of cold actually sweetens the leaves as the plant converts starch to sugar. In mild-winter regions it grows right through winter, and in colder zones it overwinters with simple protection, making it one of the longest-cropping plants a gardener can grow.
crops.description_beginner: Kale is a leafy cabbage-family plant you grow for its leaves, picking a few at a time over a long season instead of harvesting it all at once. It loves cool weather and is one of the toughest vegetables you can grow: it survives hard frost, and the cold actually makes the leaves taste sweeter. In mild areas it keeps going all winter, and in cold areas it can survive winter with a little cover, so one planting can feed you for months.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Start picking once the outer leaves reach a usable size, about hand-length: baby leaves in roughly 25 to 30 days, full-size leaves in about 50 to 65 days. Harvest with the cut-and-come-again method, snapping or cutting the lowest, outermost leaves and leaving the central growing point and young inner leaves to keep producing. Avoid stripping more than about a third of the plant at once. Picking continues for months and runs right through fall frosts; the leaves are sweetest after a frost or two, so in cool weather you can harvest straight from the garden even after the leaves have frozen.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Begin picking when the outer leaves are big enough to use, about the length of your hand: small baby leaves in about a month, full leaves in roughly 2 months. Take the lowest, outside leaves first and leave the small center leaves to keep growing, so the same plant feeds you for months. Do not strip the whole plant at once. Keep picking right through fall, and know that the leaves taste sweetest after frost, so you can harvest even when it is cold out.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Work in 1 to 2 inches of compost before planting to build a fertile, moisture-retentive but well-drained bed; kale is a leafy heavy feeder that rewards organic matter. Loosen the soil well, and aim for a pH near 6.0 to 7.0. Because brassica diseases like clubroot build in the soil, choose a bed where no cabbage-family crop has grown for at least 3 years.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Mix a couple of inches of compost into the bed before planting so the soil is rich and holds moisture but still drains. Loosen it well. Try not to plant kale where you grew other cabbage-family crops (broccoli, cabbage, collards) in the last few years, since that spreads soil diseases.

crops.name: Spinach

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Spinach likes rich, loose soil that holds moisture but drains well, with lots of compost mixed in. The one thing it really cares about is not-too-acidic soil, so if your ground is very acidic, add a little lime to bring it closer to neutral. A quick soil test tells you where you stand.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Spinach does best in a fertile, well-drained sandy loam or loam high in organic matter, kept evenly moist. Its defining soil need is a near-neutral pH: spinach is notably sensitive to acidic soil and grows poorly below about 6.0, so lime an acid plot up toward 6.5 to 7.5 before sowing. Work in compost to feed the fast leafy growth and hold steady moisture, which delays bolting and keeps the leaves tender.

ph.note_beginner: Spinach grows best in soil that is close to neutral, about 6.5 to 7.5. It does not like acidic soil, so if a soil test reads below 6.0, mix in some lime before planting.
ph.note_seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.5 to 7.5; spinach is one of the more acid-sensitive vegetables and yields drop on soils below roughly 6.0, where manganese can become available enough to injure the plant. Clemson advises a 6.0 to 7.0 minimum and the University of Minnesota up to about 8, so lean to the neutral-to-slightly-alkaline side and lime an acid plot the season before.

fertilizer.timing: a light feed at thinning, then side-dress 3 to 4 weeks after sowing
fertilizer.example_product: Calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0), blood meal, or 21-0-0
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Spinach is a fast leafy crop that runs on nitrogen, but the season is short, so one or two feedings are usually enough. Work compost or a balanced fertilizer in before sowing, then side-dress with nitrogen about 3 to 4 weeks after planting (or at thinning) to push tender, dark-green leaves. Utah State suggests about a quarter cup of 21-0-0 per 10 feet of row; Clemson uses calcium nitrate. Avoid heavy late feeding, since spinach readily takes up nitrate and lush growth draws aphids and leafminers.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Spinach grows fast and likes nitrogen for big green leaves. Mix some compost or fertilizer into the soil before planting, then give it one feeding of a nitrogen fertilizer about 3 to 4 weeks after the seeds come up. Because the crop is quick, you usually do not need to feed it more than that.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time to side-dress your spinach with nitrogen.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Time to give your spinach a feeding.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: High N for leafy growth; e.g. a quarter cup of 21-0-0 per 10 ft of row, or calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0), side-dressed 3 to 4 weeks after sowing. No phosphorus or potassium needed beyond a soil-test baseline.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a nitrogen-rich feed such as blood meal or a 21-0-0 fertilizer once the plants are a few weeks old.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: About a quarter cup of 21-0-0 (or 1 pound of calcium nitrate per 100 square feet) side-dressed once, 3 to 4 weeks after sowing.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Follow the label rate for a nitrogen-rich vegetable fertilizer, one feeding a few weeks after the seeds sprout.

companions.note_beginner: Spinach is small, fast, and shade-tolerant, so it tucks in well between slower, taller crops. It grows happily next to peas and beans, strawberries, and members of the cabbage family, and it does not get along badly with much. Just keep it away from its close relatives beets and chard, which share its leafminer pest.
companions.note_seasoned: Most spinach companion pairings rest on space, timing, and tradition rather than measured effects. The practical ones are structural: spinach is shallow-rooted, quick, and tolerates light shade, so it interplants under or beside taller, slower crops (peas, beans, brassicas) and is harvested before they crowd it. The one well-grounded caution is to separate spinach from beets and Swiss chard, its close relatives in the goosefoot family, which share the spinach leafminer and several diseases, a rotation and pest principle more than a tested adjacency effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Peas
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Peas grow up while spinach stays low, so they share a bed without competing, and both love the same cool weather. Peas also add a little nitrogen to the soil that the leafy spinach can use.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: A classic cool-season interplant: peas climb and fix nitrogen while spinach occupies the shaded ground below. Sound space/timing and legume-nitrogen logic that extensions teach generally, but not a measured spinach-specific yield effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Peas and spinach are a traditional cool-season pairing on structure and timing: peas trellis upward and cast light shade that suits spinach, both thrive in the same early-spring and fall windows, and the legume fixes a little nitrogen the leafy spinach can draw on. Expect efficient use of the bed and season rather than a documented growth boost.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Strawberries
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Strawberries and spinach are a long-standing garden pairing. The low spinach fills space between strawberry plants early in the season and is picked before the berries take over.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: A traditional companion pairing with no T1-documented mechanism; rests on complementary habit and timing.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Strawberries and spinach are a traditional pairing that works mainly on habit and timing: low, quick spinach uses the open ground between young strawberry plants in the cool of spring and is harvested before the berries spread. A space-use tradition, not a measured effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Brassicas (cabbage, broccoli)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Tall cabbage-family plants give spinach a bit of light shade in warm spells, which helps it last longer before bolting, and the quick spinach is gone before the brassicas need the room.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Interplanting a quick shade-tolerant green beneath slower brassicas is widely taught space-use lore; the shade-delays-bolting benefit is plausible but not a tested spinach-brassica trial.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Spinach interplants beneath cabbage-family crops on a space-and-light basis: it tolerates the partial shade taller brassicas cast, which can buy a little time against bolting in warm spells, and it matures and is cleared before the brassicas fill out. Traditional and practical rather than a documented adjacency effect; the two do not share a major pest.

good_seasoned.name: Peas
good_seasoned.timing: interplant in the same cool window
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional cool-season interplant: peas climb and lightly shade the low spinach, both share the early-spring and fall windows, and the legume fixes a little nitrogen for the leafy crop. Space and timing, not a tested effect.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Cool-season legume interplant logic extensions teach generally; no spinach-specific T1 trial.

good_seasoned.name: Strawberries
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Low, quick spinach uses the open ground between young strawberry plants in spring and is cleared before the berries spread. A traditional, space-efficient pairing rather than a measured benefit.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Folk companion pairing; no documented mechanism or T1 source.

good_seasoned.name: Brassicas (cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Shade-tolerant spinach grows in the partial shade of taller cole crops, which can slow bolting in warm spells, and matures before the brassicas need the room. Space-and-light tradition; the two share no major pest.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Space-use intercropping lore; the shade-delays-bolting effect is plausible but untested for the pairing.

good_seasoned.name: Radishes
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A fast cool-season root often sown with spinach to mark rows and use space; both are quick and frost-tolerant. Traditional and space-driven, not a documented effect.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Quick-crop interplant tradition; no T1 spinach-radish trial.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Beets and Swiss chard
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep spinach away from beets and Swiss chard. They are close relatives and share the same leafminer pest and some diseases, so planting them together helps those problems build up.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Beets, chard, and spinach are all goosefoot-family hosts of the spinach leafminer (Pegomya hyoscyami) and share leaf diseases; clustering them concentrates the shared pest and pathogen load. A sound epidemiological/rotation mechanism rather than a measured antagonism.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Beets, Swiss chard, and spinach all belong to the goosefoot family and are the favored hosts of the spinach leafminer, whose maggots blister and ruin the leaves; they also share several leaf diseases. Planting them side by side or in succession concentrates the leafminer and disease pressure and lets the soil-overwintering leafminer build. Separate them in space and rotate so goosefoot crops do not follow one another.

bad_seasoned.name: Beets and Swiss chard
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Spinach, beets, and chard are goosefoot-family relatives and the shared hosts of the spinach leafminer plus several leaf diseases, so grouping them concentrates the pest and disease load and feeds the soil-overwintering leafminer. Separate them and rotate goosefoot crops apart.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Shared leafminer host range and shared diseases are extension-documented; the bad-adjacency claim is a sound agronomic principle, not a formally pair-tested effect.

pests.name: Spinach leafminer
pests.symptoms_beginner: You'll see pale, winding tunnels in the leaves that widen into large tan blisters or blotches. If you hold a leaf up to the light, you can sometimes see the tiny maggot inside. The damaged parts are not good to eat.
pests.cause_beginner: A small fly lays eggs on the underside of the leaves, and the maggots that hatch tunnel inside the leaf between the top and bottom layers, eating as they go. Spinach, beets, and chard are its favorites.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Once a maggot is inside a leaf, sprays do not reach it well, so pick off and destroy mined leaves as soon as you see them, before the maggots drop to the soil. Crushing the maggot inside the leaf works too.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover the plants with a light row cover right after sowing so the flies cannot lay eggs, and pull nearby weeds like lambsquarters that host the pest. Rotating where you grow spinach, beets, and chard each year also helps.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Slender, winding mines in the foliage enlarge into translucent tan blotches; heavily mined leaves are unmarketable and the crop is the leaf, so even light feeding matters. The pale legless maggots are visible inside the leaf against the light.
pests.cause_seasoned: The spinach leafminer (Pegomya hyoscyami) overwinters as pupae in the soil and emerges around mid-May; females lay rows of white eggs on leaf undersides, and the maggots tunnel between the leaf surfaces. There are three to four overlapping generations a season on spinach, beets, chard, and goosefoot weeds.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Insecticides poorly reach larvae inside the leaf, so rely on cultural control: pick and destroy mined leaves before larvae drop to pupate, and crush maggots in the leaf. Spinosad has some activity on young larvae; abamectin is a conventional option.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Exclude the egg-laying flies with floating row cover or insect netting from sowing, control goosefoot weeds (lambsquarters, chickweed, nightshade) that host the pest, rotate away from where spinach, beets, or chard grew, and deep-cultivate in spring to bury overwintering pupae.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_beginner: Clusters of tiny soft green or gray insects on the undersides of leaves and on new growth, sometimes with curled, puckered leaves and a sticky coating. They are hard to wash out of crinkled savoy leaves.
pests.cause_beginner: Aphids are small insects that suck sap from the plant. They breed quickly, especially on soft growth from too much fertilizer, and they can spread plant viruses.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water, or use insecticidal soap or neem oil, making sure to hit the undersides of the leaves. Repeat every few days until they are gone.
pests.prevention_beginner: Welcome helpful bugs like ladybugs and lacewings, go easy on nitrogen fertilizer, and check the new growth often so you catch them early.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Colonies of green peach or other aphids on leaf undersides and growing tips distort and pucker the foliage; honeydew and sooty mold downgrade the crop, and curly savoy leaves are hard to clean. Aphids also transmit cucumber mosaic and other viruses.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several aphid species feed on spinach; they reproduce rapidly, favor the soft growth that excess nitrogen produces, and are most damaging as virus vectors.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Dislodge colonies with a strong water jet or spray insecticidal soap or neem, covering leaf undersides; repeat every few days. Conserve lady beetles, lacewings, and parasitoid wasps.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Scout growing tips early, avoid overfeeding nitrogen, conserve natural enemies, and use row cover, which doubles as leafminer exclusion.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms_beginner: Lots of tiny round holes peppering the leaves of young plants, made by small dark beetles that jump like fleas when you come near. Heavy damage can stunt seedlings.
pests.cause_beginner: Flea beetles are small jumping beetles that chew little holes in young leaves. They hurt small seedlings the most, since a tiny plant cannot outgrow the damage.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover young plants with a row cover, and if there are many beetles use a spinosad spray or a kaolin clay coating. The main goal is to get the seedlings big enough to shrug it off.
pests.prevention_beginner: Use row cover from sowing, keep seedlings strong with steady water and food so they grow past the damage, and clear weeds nearby.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small round shot-holes pepper the leaves of young plants; the tiny dark beetles jump when disturbed. Damage is mostly cosmetic on a leaf crop but can stunt or kill seedlings at high pressure.
pests.cause_seasoned: Flea beetles chew the foliage of young spinach and are most damaging at the seedling stage; the holes mar the harvested leaves.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Protect seedlings with row cover and spray spinosad or apply kaolin clay if pressure is high; the aim is getting plants past the vulnerable seedling stage.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Row cover from sowing, vigorous seedlings kept evenly watered and fed, and clean cultivation of nearby weeds.

pests.name: Caterpillars (loopers and armyworms)
pests.symptoms_beginner: Ragged chewed holes in the leaves, green or striped caterpillars on the plants, and dark droppings. They are mostly a warm-season and southern problem.
pests.cause_beginner: Several moths lay eggs on the leaves, and the caterpillars that hatch chew the foliage. Because you eat the leaves, even a little chewing is a problem.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray Bt, which is safe and targets only caterpillars, or pick them off by hand. Spray again after rain since it washes off.
pests.prevention_beginner: Use a row cover, clean up old plants and weeds where moths shelter, and check the undersides of leaves for eggs and small caterpillars.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Ragged feeding holes with green or striped larvae and frass; cabbage loopers, beet armyworms, and corn earworms feed on spinach, mostly in warm-season and southern plantings.
pests.cause_seasoned: The larvae of several moths feed on spinach foliage; on a leaf crop even modest defoliation reduces the harvest.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) or spinosad targeting young larvae, and hand-pick where practical; repeat after rain.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Use row cover, clean up crop debris and weed hosts, and scout leaf undersides for eggs and early instars.

diseases.name: Downy mildew (blue mold)
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Pale yellow patches on the tops of the leaves with a fuzzy gray-purple mold on the undersides, mostly in cool, damp, crowded conditions. Bad cases yellow and collapse the leaves.
diseases.cause_beginner: A mold-like disease that loves the same cool, wet weather spinach grows in, and spreads through wet leaves and splashing water. Crowded plants and long leaf wetness make it worse.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove the worst leaves, open up the airflow so leaves dry faster, and water at the soil instead of over the plants. It is hard to stop once it gets going, so prevention matters most.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Grow resistant varieties (this is the main defense), space plants for good airflow, water at the base, and rotate where you plant spinach each year.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Irregular pale-yellow lesions on the upper leaf surface with grayish-purple sporulation beneath (the blue mold), spreading in cool, wet, humid weather; lesions brown and the leaves collapse. It is the most important spinach disease.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Peronospora effusa, an oomycete favored by cool temperatures, long leaf wetness, and high humidity; it spreads by wind- and splash-borne spores and survives on debris and as oospores, with many physiological races that overcome resistance.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Cultural control dominates: improve airflow, avoid overhead irrigation, remove infected leaves and debris; copper has limited efficacy. There is no rescue once it is established in humid weather.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant resistant cultivars (the primary tool, choosing the broadest race resistance available), widen spacing for airflow, use drip rather than overhead water, and rotate away from spinach for several years.

diseases.name: White rust
diseases.symptoms_beginner: White, blister-like bumps on the undersides of leaves, with yellow spots on top. Badly spotted leaves are not good to eat.
diseases.cause_beginner: A different mold-like disease, not a true rust, that makes white pustules on the leaves and spreads in cool, moist weather. It can ruin a crop quickly.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove and destroy infected leaves, improve airflow, and water at the soil line. As with downy mildew, prevention works better than trying to cure it.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Choose resistant varieties where it is common, space plants out, avoid wetting the leaves, and rotate your planting spot.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: White, blister-like pustules on leaf undersides with chlorotic spotting above; severe infection distorts and downgrades the foliage. A serious disease in the southern and south-central states.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The oomycete Albugo occidentalis, favored by cool nights, warm days, and leaf wetness; it spreads by splash- and wind-dispersed spores and survives on debris.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove infected leaves and debris, improve airflow, and avoid overhead irrigation; chemical options are limited for the home garden.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Grow resistant cultivars where white rust is endemic, space for airflow, use drip irrigation, and rotate away from spinach.

diseases.name: Damping-off
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Seeds that never come up, or seedlings that flop over at the soil line with a pinched, rotted stem and then die. It strikes in cold, wet soil.
diseases.cause_beginner: Soil fungi attack the seeds and tiny seedlings, especially when the soil is cold and soggy and the seeds are slow to come up. Spinach sown in cold wet ground is at risk.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure for an affected seedling, so focus on prevention. Pull and discard collapsed seedlings.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Do not sow into cold, soggy soil, plant at the right depth in well-drained ground, do not overwater, and use fresh seed so it comes up fast.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Poor stands from seed and pre- or post-emergence collapse of seedlings with water-soaked, pinched stems at the soil line, worst in cold, wet, poorly drained soil where germination is slow.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Soilborne Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Fusarium species attack germinating seed and seedlings; cold, saturated soil that slows emergence favors them.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No cure once seedlings collapse; manage by prevention and remove affected plants.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Sow into well-drained soil when temperatures favor quick emergence, avoid overwatering, use fresh viable seed, and consider treated seed where damping-off is chronic.

diseases.name: Fusarium wilt
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Older leaves yellow and wilt even though the soil is moist, and the wilting spreads up the plant, which is stunted and may die. It is worse in warm soil.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soil fungus infects the roots and clogs the plant's water pipes, so it wilts and yellows. It lives in the soil for years and is worse when the soil warms up.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure once a plant is infected, so pull and destroy wilted plants. Put your effort into rotation and timing for next time.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant spinach in the cooler parts of the season, keep the soil near neutral (not acidic), and do not grow spinach in the same spot year after year. Resistant varieties help where it is a problem.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Progressive yellowing and wilting from the lower leaves upward despite adequate soil moisture, with stunting and plant death; symptoms intensify as soil warms through the season.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. spinaciae, a soilborne vascular pathogen that persists for years and is favored by warm soil and acidic conditions; once established it limits where spinach can be grown.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No effective cure; remove and destroy infected plants and manage the soilborne population by rotation and timing.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Schedule the crop for the cool side of the season when soils are cooler, maintain a near-neutral pH, use long rotations away from spinach, and choose resistant cultivars where the wilt is established.

watering.frequency_seasoned: About 1 to 1.5 inches per week, kept even; spinach is shallow-rooted and bolts faster under drought stress.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly 1 to 1.5 inches a week.
watering.amount_seasoned: Roughly 1 to 1.5 inches per week (Utah State cites 1 to 2 inches), more in warm, dry spells.
watering.amount_beginner: Aim for about 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week, a bit more when it is warm.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose; keeping the foliage dry checks downy mildew and white rust.
watering.method_beginner: Water at the base of the plants rather than over the leaves, which helps prevent leaf diseases.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, damping-off in seedlings, and downy mildew in crowded, constantly wet plantings.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Lower leaves yellow, seedlings rot at the base, and leaves get moldy in soggy, crowded beds.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting, slowed growth, and faster bolting; drought stress is a direct bolt trigger in spinach.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Wilting leaves and a plant that bolts (flowers) sooner than it should.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Even moisture keeps spinach growing fast and tender and delays bolting; dry spells push it to flower and turn the leaves bitter.
watering.method_note_beginner: Keep the water steady so the plants grow fast and tender and do not bolt early.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Steady moisture through the leaf-bulking weeks and during any warm, lengthening-day spell matters most for delaying bolt.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Water steadily while the plants are filling out and whenever the weather warms up.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Spinach is almost always direct-sown, since it grows fast and resents root disturbance. Sow seed about 0.5 inch deep as soon as the soil can be worked in spring (it germinates in soil as cool as 40°F), and again in late summer for the main fall crop. Transplanting is possible from cells or soil blocks for an early start or to place an overwintering crop, but handle the roots gently. Germination is poor in soil above about 75 to 85°F, so summer sowings in warm regions wait for cooling soil.
start_method.notes_beginner: Spinach is best planted straight in the garden from seed, because it grows quickly and does not like having its roots disturbed. Sow the seeds about half an inch deep as soon as the soil can be worked in spring, and again in late summer for a fall crop. The seeds sprout even in cold soil, but they will not come up well in hot soil, so do not sow in the heat of summer.

drainage.saucer_practice: Empty the saucer after watering so roots never sit in water, which invites damping-off and root rot.

soil_mix.type_beginner: A good-quality potting mix, not garden soil.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in some compost for steady nutrients, and a little lime if your mix is acidic.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: A light, well-drained potting mix high in organic matter.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend in compost and a starter nitrogen source; spinach dislikes acidity, so a pinch of lime helps if the mix is peat-heavy and acidic.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Shallow pots dry out fast, so check daily in warm weather and keep the mix evenly moist.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Feed a little more often than in the ground, since watering washes nutrients out of pots.

overwintering.approach_beginner: In mild areas, a pot of fall-sown spinach can keep going through winter in a sheltered, sunny spot. In cold areas, move the pot against the house or into a cold frame, or cover it during hard freezes, and it will often resume in spring.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Spinach is very cold-hardy, so a fall-sown container can overwinter in mild zones, holding through winter in a sheltered spot and resuming growth in spring. In cold zones the limited root volume of a pot freezes harder than open ground, so sink it, move it to a cold frame or unheated structure, or cover it during hard freezes; an overwintered pot then yields the earliest spring picking.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Spinach grows well in a wide, shallow pot at least 6 inches deep, sown thickly and thinned for baby leaves or spaced for full plants. Keep it watered and in the cool seasons, and give it some afternoon shade in warm weather.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Spinach is a good container crop because it is shallow-rooted, compact, and quick. Use a broad container at least 6 inches deep, one gallon or more, sown densely for cut baby leaves or thinned to 3 to 4 inches for full plants, and keep moisture even since shallow pots dry fast. Grow it in the cool seasons and give afternoon shade in warm spells to slow bolting.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Shallow containers dry faster than beds; check moisture daily in warmth and water before the mix dries, since drought stress triggers bolting.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Container spinach needs slightly more frequent light feeding than in-ground plants because watering leaches nutrients.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering container suits spinach well, since it smooths out the steady moisture that keeps the leaves tender and delays bolting.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match because it keeps the water steady, which keeps spinach tender and slow to bolt.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: Spinach is shallow-rooted, so depth matters less than surface area: a wide, shallow container at least 6 inches deep gives more sowing area for cut-and-come-again leaves and buffers the fast drying narrow pots suffer.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Spinach has shallow roots, so a wide, shallow pot is better than a tall narrow one. Aim for at least 6 inches deep and as much width as you can give it.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Spinach wilts and yellows within a day at room temperature, so refrigerate it promptly after cutting; if it must sit briefly, keep it cool and out of the sun.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Do not leave spinach out on the counter. It wilts fast in the warmth, so get it into the fridge soon after picking.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerate unwashed in a loose or perforated bag in the crisper; spinach holds about 1 to 2 weeks near 32°F at high humidity. Washing before storage traps moisture and speeds breakdown, so wait to wash until use.
storage.fridge_beginner: Store spinach unwashed in a loose bag in the fridge's crisper drawer, where it keeps for 1 to 2 weeks if kept very cold. Wash it only when you are ready to use it.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Spinach freezes well once blanched: dunk leaves in boiling water about 2 minutes, cool quickly in ice water, drain well, and freeze. Blanching halts the enzymes that otherwise cause off-flavors and color loss.
storage.freezer_beginner: Spinach freezes well if you blanch it first. Boil the leaves for about 2 minutes, cool them right away in ice water, drain, and freeze.
storage.notes_seasoned: Quality is highest straight from the garden. Spinach is more perishable than sturdier greens like kale, so chill it fast and use it within a week or so fresh; freezing is the best way to hold a glut from a fast spring or fall crop.
storage.notes_beginner: Spinach is best right after you pick it and does not keep as long as tougher greens. Chill it quickly, use it within a week or so, and freeze any extra.

bolting.triggers: lengthening days (over about 13 to 14 hours) and warm temperatures, accelerated by heat and drought stress
bolting.prevention_seasoned: Spinach bolts primarily in response to long days, so the spring window is short: sow as early as the soil can be worked, choose slow-bolting (long-standing) varieties, keep moisture and nitrogen steady, and harvest before the longest days of June. The fall crop, grown under shortening days, rarely bolts and is the main season; overwintered plants bolt in spring as days lengthen, so crop them before the flower stalk elongates.
bolting.prevention_beginner: Spinach flowers (bolts) when the days get long and warm in late spring, and then the leaves turn bitter. To avoid it, plant as early as you can in spring, pick slow-bolting varieties, water steadily, and harvest before midsummer. The fall crop hardly bolts at all, which is why fall is the best time to grow spinach.
bolting.note_seasoned: Bolting in spinach is mainly a long-day (photoperiod) response, with heat and drought speeding it; once the plant sends up a seed stalk the leaves turn bitter and tough. This is why spinach is grown as a fall, winter, and very-early-spring crop and the summer is left out across most regions.
bolting.note_beginner: Spinach bolts (sends up a flower stalk and turns bitter) when days get long and warm. It is a normal part of its life cycle, not something you did wrong. The trick is to grow it in the cool, short-day parts of the year, especially fall.

recommended.name: Bloomsdale Long Standing
recommended.note: A classic heavily-savoyed heirloom with thick, crinkled dark leaves and good cold-hardiness; slower to bolt than plain Bloomsdale, a dependable spring and overwintering type. The crinkles hold grit, so wash well.

recommended.name: Tyee
recommended.note: A vigorous semi-savoy hybrid, slow to bolt and resistant to downy mildew; an upright plant that stays clean, good for spring and fall.

recommended.name: Melody
recommended.note: An All-America Selections semi-savoy with disease resistance and broad adaptability; a reliable, productive beginner choice.

recommended.name: Space
recommended.note: A fast, smooth-leaved hybrid with downy mildew resistance and slow bolting; smooth leaves are easy to wash and good for baby-leaf and containers.

recommended.name: Olympia
recommended.note: A smooth-leaved, slow-bolting type that holds in spring heat better than many; good for a longer spring window.

recommended.name: Giant Winter (Winter Bloomsdale)
recommended.note: An extra-hardy savoy bred for fall sowing and overwintering; sized up before winter, it survives under snow or row cover and gives the earliest spring picking.

varieties.note_seasoned: Match the variety to the slot. For the short spring window and any warm stretch, lean on slow-bolting (long-standing) types like Bloomsdale Long Standing, Tyee, and Olympia. Where downy mildew is a concern, choose resistant cultivars (Tyee, Melody, Space, and newer race-resistant hybrids). For fall and overwintering, the hardiest savoys (Giant Winter, Bloomsdale) take the most cold. Smooth-leaf types (Space, Olympia) wash easily and suit baby-leaf and containers; savoys are hardiest but trap grit; semi-savoys split the difference.
varieties.note_beginner: For spring, pick slow-bolting kinds like Bloomsdale Long Standing or Tyee so the plants last longer before flowering. Melody and Space are easy, disease-resistant choices. For a fall or winter crop, grow a hardy type like Giant Winter. Smooth-leaf varieties are easiest to wash; the crinkly savoy types are the most cold-hardy but hold more grit.

thinning.when: when seedlings have 3 to 4 true leaves
thinning.method: snip or pull extra seedlings; the thinnings are edible as baby leaves
thinning.tip_seasoned: Sow a little thick and thin to 3 to 4 inches once plants have 3 to 4 true leaves; eat the thinnings as baby spinach. Crowded plants compete, stay small, and bolt sooner, and poor airflow invites downy mildew.
thinning.tip_beginner: Spinach is often sown a bit thick, then thinned so plants stand about 3 to 4 inches apart. Do not waste the thinnings, they are tender baby spinach. Thinning gives each plant room to grow full leaves.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Beets, Swiss chard, and spinach itself (all goosefoot-family hosts of the spinach leafminer, Fusarium wilt, and the leaf-mold diseases).
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Beets, Swiss chard, and spinach, which are all close relatives that share its pests and diseases.
rotation.good_after: Legumes (peas, beans), brassicas, alliums (onion, garlic), cucurbits, or nightshades such as tomatoes.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate so spinach and its goosefoot relatives (beets, chard) do not return to the same ground for at least 3 years. The spinach leafminer overwinters as pupae in the soil and Fusarium wilt persists for years, so a long rotation away from the whole family is the core defense; deep spring cultivation also helps bury leafminer pupae.
rotation.note_beginner: Do not plant spinach, beets, or chard in the same spot year after year. Waiting at least 3 years between these related crops helps avoid the leafminer and soil diseases that build up in the ground.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: In about 5 to 14 days the seeds sprout and push up two narrow seed leaves. Spinach comes up even in cold soil, but slowly.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil damp and do not let it crust over. Cold soil means slower sprouting, which is normal.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your spinach seeds come up yet?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seeds germinate in about 5 to 14 days, faster as soil warms toward 60 to 70°F and poorly above 75 to 85°F; two narrow cotyledons emerge.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep the seedbed evenly moist and uncrusted; expect slow but reliable emergence in cool soil and erratic germination in warm soil.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Did your spinach germinate, and how even is the stand?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The seedlings grow their first real spinach leaves. When they have 3 to 4 true leaves, it is time to thin them.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Thin to about 3 to 4 inches apart and eat the thinnings. Watch for flea beetle holes and the first leafminer tunnels.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How many true leaves do your seedlings have?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Young plants form a low rosette; thin at the 3-to-4-true-leaf stage. Flea beetles and the first leafminer mines appear now.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin to 3 to 4 inches, keep moisture even, and set or check row cover to exclude leafminer flies.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have you thinned, and is the row cover on?

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plants form a rosette of full-sized leaves. This is the main growing stage, when they build the leaves you will eat.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep them evenly watered and give one nitrogen feeding. Check the undersides of leaves for aphids and pick off any mined leaves.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Is your spinach making lots of healthy leaves?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Plants bulk a rosette of leaves over a few weeks; this is the productive window before bolt.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Side-dress nitrogen once, hold even moisture to delay bolt, and scout for aphids, leafminer, and downy mildew.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Is the rosette filling out cleanly?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The leaves reach a usable size, about 3 to 6 inches long, dark green and tender. Pick before the plant starts to stretch upward.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pick the outer leaves, or cut the whole plant about an inch above the soil and let it regrow. Harvest in the cool morning.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you started picking spinach?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves reach 3 to 6 inches at about 37 to 50 days (baby leaf earlier); harvest outer leaves cut-and-come-again or cut the whole rosette above the crown for regrowth.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Crop frequently in the cool morning, taking outer leaves or whole-plant cuts; pick faster as days lengthen and warm to beat the bolt.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are you harvesting, and is the plant still flat (not bolting)?

growth_stages.name: Bolting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The center of the plant stretches up and starts to form a flower stalk, and the leaves turn bitter and arrow-shaped. This happens as the days get long and warm.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Harvest everything usable right away, because the leaves only get more bitter. Then pull the plant and use the space for something else.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Is your spinach starting to bolt (stretch up)?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The rosette elongates into a flowering stalk as days pass about 13 to 14 hours and warm; leaf flavor turns bitter and texture coarsens.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Strip the remaining usable leaves immediately, then pull the plant; an overwintered crop bolts in spring, so clear it before the stalk elongates.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Has it bolted, and have you cleared the bed?

notifications.body_seasoned: Your spinach should have 3 to 4 true leaves now. Thin to 3 to 4 inches apart for full plants and eat the thinnings as baby spinach.
notifications.body_beginner: Your spinach seedlings should be big enough to thin. Space them about 3 to 4 inches apart and eat the little ones you pull.

notifications.body_seasoned: Your spinach leaves should be 3 to 6 inches and tender. Crop the outer leaves or cut the whole rosette above the crown, and pick in the cool morning.
notifications.body_beginner: Your spinach leaves should be big enough to pick. Take the outer leaves or cut the whole plant about an inch above the soil so it can regrow.

notifications.title_beginner: Warm, long days ahead: pick your spinach
notifications.body_seasoned: Days are lengthening and warming, which triggers bolting in spinach. Harvest the spring crop promptly and clear bolting plants, since the leaves turn bitter once the stalk forms.
notifications.body_beginner: The days are getting long and warm, which makes spinach flower and turn bitter. Pick your spring spinach now while it is still good.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot weather warning for your spinach
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Sustained heat above about 75 to 80°F, especially with long days, pushes spinach to bolt and turns the leaves bitter. Keep moisture even, harvest promptly in the cool morning, and treat summer as off-season; in hot regions spinach is a fall-through-spring crop.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Hot weather makes spinach flower early and turn bitter. Water evenly, pick everything usable in the cool morning, and remember spinach is really a cool-season, fall-to-spring crop.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hard freeze coming
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Spinach is very cold-hardy and tolerates frost; mature plants survive into the low 20s°F and overwinter under snow or row cover. For most freezes simply keep harvesting; in the coldest zones a low tunnel or row cover carries the crop through winter for an early-spring picking.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Spinach handles frost and even hard freezes well, so you usually do not need to do anything. In very cold areas, a row cover or low tunnel helps it survive winter and start up again in early spring.

germination.text_seasoned: Sow about 0.5 inch deep into a moist, uncrusted seedbed; spinach germinates from about 40°F and reliably at 60 to 70°F, but poorly above 75 to 85°F.
germination.text_beginner: Plant seeds about half an inch deep in damp soil. Spinach sprouts even in cold soil, so you can sow it very early.

germination.text_seasoned: For the fall crop, pre-sprout or water the furrow to cool it, or wait for soil to drop below 75°F, since warm soil is the main cause of poor late-summer stands.
germination.text_beginner: If you sow in late summer for fall, wait until the soil cools down, because spinach seeds will not come up well in hot soil.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin to 3 to 4 inches at the 3-to-4-true-leaf stage and eat the thinnings; crowding stunts plants and speeds bolting.
seedling.text_beginner: Thin seedlings to about 3 to 4 inches apart once they have a few real leaves, and eat the ones you pull.

seedling.text_seasoned: Set floating row cover at sowing to exclude leafminer flies and flea beetles, the two main seedling pests.
seedling.text_beginner: Cover young plants with a light row cover to keep leafminer flies and flea beetles off.

established.text_seasoned: Hold even moisture at roughly 1 to 1.5 inches per week and side-dress nitrogen once; drought and heat both trigger bolt.
established.text_beginner: Water steadily and give one feeding of nitrogen so the plants grow fast and tender and do not bolt early.

established.text_seasoned: Scout leaf undersides for aphids and the first leafminer mines; pick and destroy mined leaves before larvae drop to pupate.
established.text_beginner: Check under the leaves for aphids and pick off any leaves with pale tunnels (leafminer) before the bugs spread.

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest at 3 to 6 inch leaf size, either outer leaves cut-and-come-again or the whole rosette cut about an inch above the crown for regrowth; pick in the cool morning.
harvest.text_beginner: Pick spinach when the leaves are 3 to 6 inches. Take outer leaves, or cut the whole plant an inch above the soil and let it regrow.

harvest.text_seasoned: As days lengthen and warm, harvest faster and watch for the central stalk; once it elongates, the leaves turn bitter, so clear the crop.
harvest.text_beginner: When the weather warms and the plant starts to stretch up, pick everything quickly, because the leaves turn bitter once it flowers.

bolting.text_seasoned: Spinach bolts mainly on long days (over about 13 to 14 hours), sped by heat and drought; there is no reversing it, so harvest and replace the planting.
bolting.text_beginner: Once spinach starts to flower it will not stop, so pick what you can and pull the plant. It bolts when days get long and warm.

bolting.text_seasoned: Favor the fall and overwintering crop, which grows under shortening days and rarely bolts; clear overwintered plants in spring before the stalk forms.
bolting.text_beginner: Fall is the best time to grow spinach because the short days keep it from bolting. Spinach that lives through winter will bolt in spring, so pick it before that.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A single spinach plant yields a modest rosette of leaves, roughly 0.25 pound, over a few weeks; the crop is grown in quantity rather than per plant. Utah State cites about 4 to 6 pounds per 10-foot row.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Each spinach plant gives a small bunch of leaves, so it is grown in rows or patches rather than one big plant. A short row of plants gives several pickings before they bolt.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Production peaks in the cool weeks of fall and early spring; a spring crop produces hard for a few weeks and then ends abruptly at bolt, while the fall crop holds longer under shortening days and, with cover, into winter.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Spinach produces the most in the cool weather of fall and early spring. A spring crop gives a few good weeks and then bolts, but a fall crop lasts longer and can carry into winter under a cover.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: The key to total yield is timing and frequent picking: get the crop in early enough to mature before the bolt-triggering long days, harvest often once leaves size up, and lean on the fall and overwintering crops for the longest harvest. New growers usually sow too late in spring and lose the crop to bolt.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: The trick with spinach is timing. Plant early in spring or in late summer for fall, and pick often once the leaves are big enough. Most beginners plant too late in spring and the plants flower before giving much, so try fall, which is easier.
factors_seasoned: Timing: a crop that matures before the long, warm days of late spring yields well; one sown too late bolts before producing. Fall and overwintering crops yield longest.
Variety: slow-bolting (long-standing) and disease-resistant types extend the productive window.
Even moisture and nitrogen: steady water and one nitrogen feed keep leaves tender and delay bolt; stress cuts yield and quality.
Spacing and airflow: thinning to 3 to 4 inches prevents crowding and the downy mildew that crowded, wet plantings invite.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No reliable extension or peer-reviewed evidence supports timing spinach planting or harvest by moon phase. Plant by soil temperature, day length, and frost dates instead.

failure_diagnostics.label: Bolting (flower stalk and bitter leaves)
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Long, warm days of late spring, or an overwintered plant flowering in spring.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your spinach shot up a central stalk and the leaves turned bitter and arrow-shaped. Spinach bolts (runs to flower) when the days get long and warm, which tells it to make seed, and once it bolts the leaves are no good. People often blame themselves, but it is the plant's normal response to day length. Next time, sow as early as you can in spring, choose slow-bolting varieties, and lean on a fall crop, which grows under short days and rarely bolts.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Sow very early in spring, use slow-bolting varieties, and grow a fall crop for the easiest, longest harvest.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The rosette elongated into a seed stalk and leaf quality collapsed. Bolting is driven mainly by lengthening days (over about 13 to 14 hours), accelerated by heat and drought; an overwintered crop bolts as spring warms. Growers most often sow too late in spring. Next time sow at first workable soil, use long-standing cultivars, hold even moisture, and favor the fall and overwintering window.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Long-day photoperiod, accelerated by heat and drought, or spring bolt of an overwintered plant.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sow at first workable soil, choose long-standing cultivars, keep moisture even, and lean on fall and overwintering crops.

failure_diagnostics.label: Tunnels and tan blisters in the leaves
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Spinach leafminer, whose maggots tunnel inside the leaves.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: You found pale winding tunnels that widened into tan blisters on the leaves, with no good way to wash them off. That is the spinach leafminer, a fly whose maggots eat inside the leaf. Because you eat the leaves, the damage ruins them. Next time, cover the plants with a row cover from the day you sow so the flies cannot lay eggs, pull weeds like lambsquarters that host them, and pick off mined leaves early.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Use a row cover from sowing, pull host weeds, and remove mined leaves before the maggots spread.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Leaves showed serpentine mines opening into translucent blotches, the signature of the spinach leafminer (Pegomya hyoscyami), which has three to four generations and overwinters as soil pupae. Sprays reach larvae inside the leaf poorly. Next time exclude the adult flies with row cover from sowing, control goosefoot weeds, rotate away from spinach, beets, and chard, and remove mined leaves before pupation.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Spinach leafminer larvae mining the leaves, with soil-overwintering pupae and multiple generations.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Row-cover from sowing, control host weeds, rotate the goosefoot crops, and strip mined leaves before larvae drop.

failure_diagnostics.label: Yellow patches with gray mold underneath
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Downy mildew (blue mold), the main spinach disease, in cool, damp, crowded conditions.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your spinach got pale yellow patches on top with fuzzy gray-purple mold underneath, and the leaves yellowed and collapsed. That is downy mildew, which thrives in the same cool, wet weather spinach likes, especially when plants are crowded and stay wet. Next time, grow resistant varieties, thin the plants for airflow, water at the soil line, and rotate where you plant.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Grow resistant varieties, thin for airflow, water at the base, and rotate your spinach bed.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Chlorotic upper-surface lesions with grayish-purple sporulation beneath indicate downy mildew (Peronospora effusa), the most important spinach disease, favored by cool temperatures and long leaf wetness, with races that defeat resistance. Next time choose the broadest available race resistance, widen spacing, switch to drip, and lengthen the rotation.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Peronospora effusa under cool, wet, humid, crowded conditions.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Use broadly race-resistant cultivars, widen spacing for airflow, irrigate by drip, and rotate away from spinach.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor or patchy germination
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Soil too warm, old seed, or crusted soil.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your spinach came up thin and patchy, or barely at all. Spinach seed will not sprout well in warm soil (above about 75 to 85°F), loses its vigor quickly with age, and can be blocked by a hard soil crust. Next time, sow in cool soil (early spring or once late-summer soil cools), use fresh seed each year, and keep the surface moist so it does not crust.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Sow in cool soil, use fresh seed, and keep the surface moist so it does not crust over.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Stand was thin and uneven. Spinach germination is inhibited above roughly 75 to 85°F, the seed is short-lived and drops in vigor within a year or two, and a crust blocks the weak shoots. Next time sow into cool soil (or pre-sprout for late-summer sowings), buy fresh seed yearly, and keep the seedbed moist and uncrusted.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Warm soil inhibiting germination, low-vigor or old seed, or a soil crust.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sow into cool soil (pre-sprout in late summer), use fresh seed yearly, and keep the bed moist to prevent crusting.

3.zone_notes: The coldest zone: a short spring crop sown at snowmelt is cut in June before the long days of midsummer bolt it, then the bed sits out the high-summer heat and long days; the dependable crop is a late-summer sowing harvested through fall. Overwintering is possible only under heavy mulch or a low tunnel.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer heat-and-daylength exclusion (July): spinach grows best below about 75°F and bolts to seed and turns bitter once long summer days and heat arrive, with seed germinating poorly above 75 to 85°F. Midsummer here is too warm, so the calendar pauses and the crop resumes as a fall sowing. (Clemson HGIC; USU Extension)

4.zone_notes: A short spring crop is harvested in June before the lengthening days bolt it; the main crop is sown in August for a fall harvest that runs through the frosts spinach shrugs off. Overwintering works under a row cover in milder spots.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer heat-and-daylength exclusion (July): spinach grows best below about 75°F and bolts to seed and turns bitter once long summer days and heat arrive, with seed germinating poorly above 75 to 85°F. Midsummer here is too warm, so the calendar pauses and the crop resumes as a fall sowing. (Clemson HGIC; USU Extension)

5.zone_notes: Sow as soon as the soil is workable in late March for a spring crop cut in May and June, before midsummer long days bolt it; sow again in August for the main fall crop. Under a low tunnel an overwintered sowing gives the earliest spring picking.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer heat-and-daylength exclusion (July): spinach grows best below about 75°F and bolts to seed and turns bitter once long summer days and heat arrive, with seed germinating poorly above 75 to 85°F. Midsummer here is too warm, so the calendar pauses and the crop resumes as a fall sowing. (Clemson HGIC; USU Extension)

6.zone_notes: A short early-spring sowing is harvested in April and May; the summer is too long-dayed and warm, so the bed rests; the main fall sowing is harvested October into November. Fall-sown spinach reliably overwinters under cover here for the earliest spring harvest.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer heat-and-daylength exclusion (June through August): spinach grows best below about 75°F and bolts to seed and turns bitter once long summer days and heat arrive, with seed germinating poorly above 75 to 85°F. Midsummer here is too warm, so the calendar pauses and the crop resumes as a fall sowing. (Clemson HGIC; USU Extension)

7.zone_notes: Overwintering is the headline crop: spinach sown September into November sizes up, holds through a mild winter, and gives a heavy late-winter and early-spring harvest under a row cover. Summer is left out for heat and long-day bolting; an early-spring sowing is also possible for a quick April cut.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer heat-and-daylength exclusion (May through August): spinach grows best below about 75°F and bolts to seed and turns bitter once long summer days and heat arrive, with seed germinating poorly above 75 to 85°F. Midsummer here is too warm, so the calendar pauses and the crop resumes as a fall sowing. (Clemson HGIC; USU Extension)

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In cold regions, grow spinach in spring and especially in fall. Sow as soon as the soil can be worked in spring for a quick crop before summer, then sow again in late summer for fall. In the milder cold zones, a fall sowing covered with a row cover lives through winter and gives you the earliest spring spinach.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Across the northern tier spinach is a spring-and-fall crop bracketing a summer it cannot grow through: the region's rapidly lengthening days (to 15 or 16 hours by mid-June) bolt even slow-standing varieties, so the spring window is short and the summer is left out. Fall, grown under shortening days, is the main and most reliable season, and from zone 6 southward a fall sowing overwinters under a row cover or low tunnel for the earliest spring harvest. There is no summer heat_pause object here: the exclusion is a long-day bolt and end-of-cool-season effect, not the thermal exclusion the hot regions carry.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: On California's cool, foggy north coast you can grow spinach for most of the year. Plant in late winter through spring and again in late summer; the mild summers mean it only pauses briefly at midsummer.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: The cool maritime north coast supports spinach over a long, nearly year-round window, sown late winter into spring and again from late summer. 9.zone_notes: The mild south coast grows spinach fall through spring, with a long cool-winter harvest and a short spring sowing. The warm, dry summer (June through August) is excluded.

ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: The mild south coast grows spinach fall through spring, anchored by the long cool-winter harvest, with a short spring sowing. 9.zone_notes: In the low desert valleys spinach is a fall-sown winter crop: plant October into November and harvest December through April. The brutal summer, May through September, is entirely excluded.

ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: In California's desert valleys, spinach is a winter crop. Plant in fall (October to November) and harvest through the cool winter and into spring. Do not try it in the hot summer.
ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: The desert valleys grow spinach as a fall-sown winter crop, harvested December through April; the long, extreme summer (May through September) is a hard heat exclusion. It is one short cool window each year rather than the two-cycle pattern of milder zones.

9.zone_notes: In the Arizona low desert spinach is a cool-season winter crop. The University of Arizona Maricopa calendar sows it from mid-September into January once highs drop below about 100°F, for a harvest from late fall through April. The long summer (May through September) is excluded.

low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: The Arizona low desert grows spinach as a fall-into-winter crop sown September through January per the UA Maricopa calendar, harvested late fall through April. 8.zone_notes: Around Las Cruces and El Paso spinach is a spring and fall crop: direct sow in late winter (about late February to March) for a spring harvest and again from late summer for fall. The hot summer is excluded and the brief cold winter brackets the season.

fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: On the Florida peninsula spinach is a marginal cool-season crop, sown October into November for a short winter harvest; true spinach struggles in the subtropical heat and humidity, and many gardeners substitute heat-tolerant New Zealand or Malabar spinach in the warm season. The long hot season is a hard heat exclusion, longer in south-Florida zone 11.

11.zone_notes: True spinach is marginal in lowland Hawaii: it grows only in the cooler months (a winter sowing) and does far better at higher elevations. At low elevation the warm season excludes it, and many gardeners grow heat-tolerant substitutes year-round instead. Window modeled on CTAHR cool-season / upland guidance.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In Hawaii, true spinach is hard to grow in the warm lowlands and does best in the cooler months or up in the cooler highlands. Many gardeners grow heat-loving substitutes instead.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: In tropical Hawaii true spinach is a marginal cool-season or upland crop: at low elevation it manages only a winter sowing and bolts in the warm season, while cooler highlands extend it. The window is modeled on CTAHR cool-season and elevation guidance (the relevant CTAHR bulletin is an older scanned publication that did not parse cleanly); heat-tolerant New Zealand and Malabar spinach are the common warm-season substitutes.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Spinach matures fast and bolts hard, so sow small batches every 1 to 2 weeks through the cool windows rather than all at once: across spring until days lengthen and warm, and again from late summer through fall, which is the longer, more reliable run. In hot regions skip summer entirely and succession-sow through the cool fall, winter, and spring.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: Plant a little spinach every week or two instead of all at once, so you get a steady supply before it bolts. Do this in early spring and again in late summer for fall. In hot areas, skip summer and keep sowing through the cool months.

crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Spinach is ready when the leaves are 3 to 6 inches long, dark green, and tender, usually 37 to 50 days from sowing (baby leaf sooner). Harvest the outer leaves cut-and-come-again, or cut the whole rosette about an inch above the crown and let it regrow; pick in the cool morning and crop faster as days lengthen, since the leaves turn bitter once the plant bolts.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Spinach is ready to pick when the leaves are about 3 to 6 inches long and tender, around 37 to 50 days after planting. Take the outer leaves a few at a time, or cut the whole plant an inch above the soil so it grows back. Pick in the cool morning, and harvest it all before it starts to flower (bolt), because the leaves get bitter then.
crops.description_seasoned: Spinach (Spinacia oleracea) is a fast, very cold-hardy leafy annual in the goosefoot family, grown for its tender, nutrient-dense leaves in the cool halves of the year. It is one of the hardiest garden vegetables, surviving hard frost into the low 20s°F and overwintering under snow or a row cover for the earliest spring harvest, yet it is also one of the quickest to bolt: lengthening days past about 13 to 14 hours, sped by heat and drought, send it to seed and turn the leaves bitter. That combination makes fall the main season nearly everywhere, with a short early-spring window and, in hot regions, a fall-through-spring winter crop. Spinach comes in three leaf types, smooth (flat), semi-savoy, and savoy (heavily crinkled), and is sensitive to acidic soil, preferring a near-neutral, fertile, evenly moist bed.
crops.description_beginner: Spinach is a fast-growing, very cold-hardy leafy green grown in the cool parts of the year. It handles frost better than almost any other vegetable and can even live through winter under a cover to give you the first greens of spring. But it does not like heat and long summer days, which make it bolt (send up a flower stalk) and turn bitter quickly. That is why spinach grows best in fall and early spring, and why in hot places it is a winter crop. It comes in smooth-leaf types that are easy to wash and crinkly savoy types that are extra hardy, and it likes rich, moist soil that is not too acidic.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: spinach_author_fresh_pilot (Claude Code lane authoring, 2026-06-29). Authored from the spinach shell, modeled structurally on the lettuce-leaf certified template and the kale/brussels CC gate-clean examples, with spinach biology re-derived from live T1 extension sources. DRAFT for daily biology-fidelity review, not certified: launch flags false. Key spinach-vs-lettuce refits: far greater cold-hardiness (survives into the low 20s°F, overwinters under snow/row cover for an early-spring harvest, the headline calendar feature); FASTER (37 to 50 days); a LONG-DAY (photoperiod) bolting trigger that makes the spring window short and fall the main season; goosefoot-family (Amaranthaceae) rotation with the signature spinach LEAFMINER and the downy mildew (blue mold) / white rust / damping-off / Fusarium wilt disease set; near-neutral pH 6.5 to 7.5 (acid-sensitive); 2 to 4 inch spacing; direct-sown. crops.name: Carrot

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Carrots want deep, loose soil with no rocks or hard clumps, the looser the better. This matters more for carrots than for most vegetables: a carrot growing down into heavy clay or packed soil will come out short, forked, or twisted instead of long and straight. Loosen the soil at least 8 inches down before you plant, and mix in some compost. Go easy on fertilizer that is high in nitrogen (the first number on the bag), because too much makes big leafy tops but small roots. If your soil is heavy clay, a raised bed or a deep container filled with loose mix is the easiest fix.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Carrots need deep, loose, friable soil free of stones, clods, and debris, ideally a light sandy loam or loam worked to at least 8 inches deep (deeper for long Imperator types). The texture matters more for carrots than for almost any other vegetable: roots grown in heavy clay or compacted ground grow poorly and come out forked, stunted, or misshapen. Work in well-rotted compost or manure before planting, but go easy on nitrogen, since excess nitrogen drives leafy top growth at the expense of root development and can cause forking and splitting. Moderate organic matter improves both moisture retention and friability; the goal is an open, stone-free root channel, not a rich heavy bed.

ph.note_beginner: Soil pH measures how acidic or alkaline your soil is, on a scale from 1 to 14 where 7 is neutral. Carrots like it right around 6.0 to 6.8, slightly acidic. They are not very fussy about it, so do not stress over pH if your roots are coming out fine, getting the soil loose and stone-free matters more. If you want to know your number for certain, a cheap soil test from your local extension office will tell you, and let you know whether to add anything before planting.
ph.note_seasoned: Carrots grow best in neutral to slightly acidic soil, roughly pH 6.0 to 6.8, with extension sources placing the optimum band between about 5.8 and 6.8. Below 5.5, phosphorus, calcium, and molybdenum availability drops; above 7.5, micronutrients including boron, manganese, and iron become less available. pH is rarely the first thing that limits a home carrot crop (soil texture and even moisture matter more), but a $10 to $15 soil test from your local extension office removes the guesswork and tells you whether lime or sulfur is warranted before sowing.

fertilizer.timing: Work compost into the bed before sowing; optional single light side-dressing once tops are established.
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: In decent garden soil amended with compost, carrots often need no supplemental feeding at all. If growth is weak, a single light side-dressing of a low-nitrogen fertilizer once the tops are established is enough. Avoid fresh manure and high-nitrogen lawn-type feeds entirely, since they cause the forking and excessive top growth carrots are prone to.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: If your soil has compost mixed in, carrots usually need no extra feeding. If they look weak and pale, you can give one light feeding of a low-nitrogen fertilizer after the leafy tops fill in. Never use fresh manure or high-nitrogen lawn fertilizer, because that is exactly what causes forked roots and too many leaves.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: Carrots are light feeders, and excess nitrogen is the classic mistake: it grows lush tops and forked, hairy roots at the expense of a clean taproot. Favor a low-nitrogen blend with adequate phosphorus and potassium to support root development, such as a 5-10-10. Most of the feeding is done by working modest, well-finished compost into the bed before sowing.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: The three numbers on a fertilizer bag are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium (N-P-K). Carrots do not want much of the first one: too much nitrogen makes big leafy tops but forked, hairy roots. Pick a fertilizer that is low in the first number with more of the other two, like a 5-10-10, and mostly just mix compost into the soil before planting.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: Carrots are light feeders. Work 1 to 2 pounds of a low-nitrogen complete fertilizer such as 5-10-10 per 100 feet of row into the bed before sowing (UC IPM), then, only if the tops pale, side-dress nitrogen lightly once plants are 3 to 4 inches tall, on the order of 0.1 to 0.5 pound of actual nitrogen per 100 feet of row. Excess nitrogen produces forked, hairy roots and lush tops, so err low.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Carrots do not need much feeding. Mix a little low-nitrogen vegetable fertilizer into the bed before you plant, following the label rate. Only feed again, lightly, if the tops look pale and growth stalls. Going heavy on fertilizer, especially nitrogen, gives you leafy tops and forked, hairy roots instead of clean ones.

companions.note_beginner: Carrots are easygoing about neighbors. The most reliable trick is sowing a few fast radishes in the carrot row to mark it and save space. Onions and chives are a popular choice to help fend off the carrot fly, though they do not always work. The main plants to keep away are carrot's close relatives, dill, parsnip, and fennel, since they share the same pests. Do not trust every companion-planting chart online; many of their claims have not held up when tested.
companions.note_seasoned: Carrots fit easily into mixed beds. The best-supported pairing is the radish row-marker trick, which extension research presents as a genuine space-saver. Allium pairings (onion, chives) for carrot rust fly are popular and mechanistically plausible but not firmly proven, useful, not guaranteed. The clearest avoids are carrot's own family, dill, parsnip, and fennel, which share its pests and diseases. Treat most other companion-chart claims with skepticism: university reviews find many are not backed by evidence.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Radishes
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Radishes sprout in just a few days, while carrots can take 2 to 3 weeks. Sow a few radishes in the same row and they show you where the carrot row is; pull and eat them before they crowd the carrots. This is a proven space-saving trick from university gardening guides.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: UMN Extension names radish-and-carrot as the canonical space-saving interplant (a soil-use and succession benefit, not a pest mechanism). The space/timing rationale is mechanistically sound and extension-endorsed; the broader pest-deterrence folklore is not. Labeled traditional/medium: the practice is well-founded and widely taught, but its real value is the agronomic timing trick rather than a measured pest effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Radishes earn their spot mostly through timing, not chemistry. They germinate in days while carrots can take two to three weeks, so a light scatter of radish seed down the carrot row marks the line, lets you cultivate and weed before the carrots are even up, and is pulled out well before the carrots need the room. The pest-deterrence claims are thinner, so treat the benefit as row-marking and space-sharing rather than protection.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Onions and other alliums
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Onions, chives, leeks, and garlic have a strong smell that many gardeners use to help hide carrots from the carrot fly, a pest whose larvae tunnel into the roots. It is a popular pairing, though the evidence for it is mixed rather than ironclad.

provenance.label: research_backed
provenance.reason: The carrot/onion intercrop is one of the few companion claims with direct intercropping trial support: the scent-masking mechanism against carrot rust fly (Psila/Chamaepsila rosae) is well documented and classic mixed-cropping studies report substantial fly-damage reductions at small scale. research_backed is earned by the mechanism + trial literature. confidence is medium, not high, for two reasons: (1) a 2022 organic-ag intercropping paper notes the small-scale benefit is difficult to replicate at larger scale, and (2) I could not open a single measured carrot-fly-reduction figure to a directly-verified T1 source in this session (ResearchGate 429), so I am declining to treat a specific percentage as confirmed. Density and arrangement materially affect whether the effect shows up.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: This is the carrot pairing with the most real evidence behind it. Onions, leeks, chives, and garlic give off sulfur volatiles that mask the carrot's scent and make it harder for the carrot rust fly to find the row and lay eggs; classic intercropping trials have measured meaningful reductions in fly damage where the two are grown together. Two practical catches: you need enough allium density relative to carrots for the masking to matter (roughly one allium per two carrots, in alternating rows), and the strongest results come from small mixed plantings rather than large blocks. Alliums are shallow-rooted and slow, so they share the bed without crowding the carrot's taproot.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Lettuce and other leafy greens
