crops.description_seasoned: Carrot (Daucus carota) is a cool-season root crop grown for its swollen taproot, which forms best in loose, stone-free, deeply worked soil that lets the root drive straight down. It is direct-sown only: the taproot extends almost immediately, so transplanting forks or stunts it. Seed is slow and erratic to germinate, often 2 to 3 weeks, and the fine seedlings cannot push through a crusted surface, so the seedbed must stay evenly moist from sowing until emergence. Roots size up over roughly 60 to 75 days and hold flavor and texture best when they finish in cool weather; sustained air temperatures above about 75°F push roots toward coarse texture, fibrousness, and strong or bitter flavor rather than killing the plant. Carrots tolerate light frost and sweeten after it as the root converts stored starch to sugar, which is why fall crops in cold climates and winter crops in mild ones are often the sweetest. The crop succeeds across a wide range of zones, but the planting season inverts by climate: a spring-through-early-summer and fall window where summers are cool, and a fall-through-early-spring window where summers are hot.
crops.description_beginner: Carrots are a cool-weather root vegetable. The part you eat is one long root that grows straight down, so they need loose, rock-free soil and plenty of depth to grow well. Always plant carrot seeds right where they will grow, because moving a young carrot bends or splits that root. The seeds are slow, often taking 2 to 3 weeks to come up, and the tiny sprouts cannot break through a hard, dried-out crust, so keep the soil surface damp until they appear. Roots are usually ready in about 60 to 75 days and taste best when they finish growing in cool weather. In heat above about 75°F they turn tough and can taste bitter, though the plant itself keeps growing. A light frost actually makes carrots sweeter, which is why fall and winter carrots are often the best tasting. When you plant depends on your climate: spring and fall where summers are cool, and fall through early spring where summers are hot.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Carrots are ready when the root has reached usable size, judged by the shoulder rather than the calendar: brush soil from the crown and look for a shoulder roughly 1/2 to 3/4 inch or more across, which for most varieties lands around 60 to 75 days from sowing. Size, not a fixed date, is the cue, and pulling a test carrot is the surest check. Flavor improves in cool weather and after light frost, so there is no rush to lift them; in mild soil they hold well in the ground for weeks, and in cold regions a heavy straw mulch lets them overwinter for pull-as-needed harvest until the ground freezes hard. Loosen the soil beside the row with a fork before pulling, especially in heavier ground, so the roots lift cleanly instead of snapping. Do not leave mature roots in hot soil, where they grow coarse and woody and may split.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Carrots are ready based on their size, not a set date. Gently scrape the soil away from the top of a root and look at the shoulder, the widest part where the leaves meet the root. When it looks about 1/2 to 3/4 inch across or bigger, pull one to check. For most kinds this is around 60 to 75 days after planting. There is no rush: carrots taste even better after a light frost, and they keep well right in the ground for weeks. In cold areas you can pile straw over the row and dig them as needed into winter until the ground freezes solid. Before pulling, loosen the soil next to the row with a fork so the roots come out whole instead of breaking off. Just do not leave fully grown carrots sitting in hot summer soil, where they get tough and may crack.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Carrot quality is set in the seedbed more than anywhere else, so the soil is worked deeply and finely before sowing. Loosen and remove stones, clods, and debris to at least 8 inches, and deeper for long-rooted types, since any obstruction the taproot meets makes it fork, kink, or grow stubby. A loose sandy loam gives the straightest, longest roots; heavy clay and compacted ground produce short, forked, or misshapen carrots and are best improved with compost or worked into raised beds for depth and drainage. Avoid fresh manure and heavy nitrogen before planting: excess nitrogen drives forked, hairy roots and lush tops at the expense of the root, so use only well-finished compost and a modest, balanced feeding. Rake the surface smooth and fine, because the small seeds need close contact with soil and an even, crust-free surface to emerge. Aim for a slightly acidic to neutral pH, roughly 6.0 to 6.8.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: With carrots, getting the bed right before you plant matters more than almost anything else you do later. Dig and loosen the soil at least 8 inches down (deeper for long types) and pull out rocks, hard clumps, and roots, because anything the carrot hits as it grows down makes it fork or come out stubby. Loose, sandy soil grows the straightest carrots; heavy clay grows short, twisted ones, so mix in compost or use a raised bed or deep container. Do not add fresh manure or lots of high-nitrogen fertilizer before planting (nitrogen is the first number on the bag), since too much grows big leafy tops but small, forked roots. Rake the top smooth and fine so the little seeds sit snug against the soil, and aim for a soil pH around 6.0 to 6.8, which is slightly acidic.

heat_threshold_temp_f.basis_seasoned: Air-temperature ceiling for carrot root quality. UF/IFAS AE588 gives 61 to 75°F as the optimum air-temperature range for growth and root color; sustained air temperatures above this range degrade root quality (forking, coarse texture, strong flavor). The mechanism is soil-driven, but the cited T1 evidence and the WeatherKit-resolvable signal are air temperature; germination retains its soil anchor (soil_temp_40f).

crops.name: Basil

soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Fertile, well-drained loam or sandy loam with good air circulation is the ideal. Basil prioritizes drainage strongly: waterlogged roots are prone to root rot, and soils with persistently high moisture also favor Fusarium wilt. Amending heavy soils with compost improves both drainage and fertility. Rich, organically active soils support the rapid vegetative growth that keeps leaf yield high.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Basil prefers loose, well-draining soil that has been improved with compost. Avoid heavy clay that stays wet, which can rot roots and encourage disease.

ph.note_seasoned: Basil is tolerant across a wide pH range compared to most vegetables. The 6.0-7.5 optimum reflects nutrient availability across the typical mineral spectrum; very acidic soils (below 5.5) can impair uptake of calcium and magnesium, which may increase susceptibility to physiological disorders and disease.
ph.note_beginner: Aim for a pH of 6.0-7.5. Most garden soil is fine for basil without any adjustment.

fertilizer.timing: At transplant and every 3-4 weeks through active growth; more frequently in containers
fertilizer.example_product: 5-10-5 granular or balanced liquid (fish emulsion or all-purpose at half-strength for containers)
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Basil is a moderate feeder that responds well to consistent modest nitrogen supply, which supports the rapid vegetative growth that produces tender, flavorful leaves. Overfertilizing with high nitrogen produces lush growth but can reduce essential oil concentration and flavor intensity, and may attract aphids. A 5-10-5 balanced granular applied once or twice per season is sufficient in average garden soil; containers require more frequent supplementation (every 2-3 weeks at half-strength) because nutrients leach with regular watering. Liquid fertilizer applied at the base, not foliarly, reduces disease pressure.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Feed basil with a balanced liquid fertilizer once a month in the garden, or every 2-3 weeks if it is in a pot. Do not overdo it: too much fertilizer makes the leaves less flavorful.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time to feed your basil. Use a balanced fertilizer at moderate strength; a 5-10-5 granular at 3 oz per 10 ft of row, or a liquid fish emulsion at half-label dilution for containers. Avoid high-nitrogen products during peak harvest to preserve essential oil concentration and flavor.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Your basil could use a feed. Mix a liquid fertilizer at half the label strength and water it in at the base of the plant. Once a month in the garden, every 2-3 weeks in a pot.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: 5-10-5 balanced to modest nitrogen-forward; avoid high-nitrogen formulations during peak harvest
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Any balanced fertilizer works well
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: 3 oz per 10 feet of row (granular), or half-label-strength liquid every 2-3 weeks in containers
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Follow the product label at the recommended rate, or half-strength for liquid in pots

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Marigolds
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Not a direct basil partner, but it shares the same warm-season bed and helps keep pests down across the whole planting.

provenance.label: research_backed
provenance.reason: UMN Extension pairs marigolds (with basil) for reduced thrips on tomato in field and greenhouse; the marigold strand has independent peer-reviewed backing in Conboy et al. 2019 (PLOS ONE), where French marigold limonene emission protected tomato from glasshouse whitefly — a directly measured volatile mechanism. With basil as the host the same nematode-suppression and beneficial-attracting roles apply at the bed scale. research_backed earned by the measured volatile/whitefly work; medium because the cleanest trials are glasshouse and marigold field results are mixed across the literature (UMN debunks marigold vs Colorado potato beetle in the same review), so not high.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Marigolds are an easy, cheerful flower to tuck in beside basil. Their roots release a natural compound that helps keep soil pests called nematodes down, and their bright blooms pull in helpful insects. Drop a few around the edge of your basil and let them flower.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Tomatoes
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: The most-studied pairing in the kitchen garden: basil grown among tomatoes can reduce thrips, may help the tomatoes along, and flags powdery mildew early because it shows symptoms before the tomatoes do. Sow it early and harvest before the tomato canopy fills in, and you get two crops from the same space.

provenance.label: research_backed
provenance.reason: UMN Extension states basil reduces thrip populations on tomato in both field and greenhouse conditions and may promote tomato growth, anchored to peer-reviewed work (Ahmad et al. 2020, on Lamiaceae companions and tomato). The basil-tomato pairing is the mirror of beefsteak's basil entry. research_backed earned by the underlying trials; medium because UMN hedges ('a few studies', 'may even') and the effect is thrips-specific rather than broad pest protection, so not high.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Basil and tomatoes are the classic garden pair, and not just in the kitchen. Studies show basil can help cut down on thrips, a common tomato pest, and tomato plants often grow a little better with basil nearby. They like the same sun and watering, so they are easy to grow side by side.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Peppers
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Peppers want the same heat, full sun, and steady moisture as basil, so the two share a bed easily and come ready to pick on a similar schedule.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Peppers and tomatoes are both Solanaceae with near-identical cultural needs to basil, and the basil scent/pollinator-attraction and shared-conditions rationale transfers cleanly. But the measured basil-companion evidence (UMN thrips work, Ahmad 2020) is tomato-specific; I found no direct basil-pepper trial. So this is 'likely' (sound by close analogy to a research-backed pairing + shared biology) rather than research_backed (no pepper-specific measurement). It is also genuinely low-risk, which is why beginners are pointed to it confidently.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Peppers want the same things basil does, lots of sun and steady water, so they make comfortable neighbors. Basil's scent helps draw in pollinators and confuse some pests, and the pepper plants give your basil a little afternoon shade. An easy, low-risk pairing.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Sage
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Sage likes lean, dry soil while basil wants rich ground and steady moisture, so they work against each other in one spot. Give them separate beds.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Unlike most 'bad herb pairing' folklore, the basil/sage caution has a sound horticultural mechanism: a cultural-conditions conflict. Basil requires rich, evenly moist soil; sage (a Mediterranean herb) prefers lean, well-drained, drier soil. Co-planting forces a watering/soil compromise that disadvantages one. Secondary (thinner) claims exist that sage releases growth-suppressing compounds affecting basil. Labeled mechanistic/medium: the conditions-conflict reason is real and physiologically grounded, but it is a management incompatibility rather than a measured antagonism, and the allelopathy-style claim is unverified.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Sage and basil want opposite things from the soil. Basil likes it rich and evenly moist; sage and other Mediterranean herbs like it lean and on the dry side. Keeping them together means one of them is always unhappy, so it is easier to give sage its own pot or a separate dry corner.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Fennel
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Fennel releases compounds that hold back many herbs and vegetables, basil included, so keep it in its own corner away from the kitchen-herb bed.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Same call as beefsteak-tomato and carrot Fennel entries (precedent 2026-06-25). Near-universal folk rule, not contested; real allelopathic mechanism (fennel EO suppresses germination/seedling growth in weed bioassays) but never measured on basil at garden spacing — and at least one source explicitly notes the evidence that fennel harms basil specifically is thin. Dominant traditional rule, mechanism-backed, unmeasured on this pairing -> traditional/medium. Confidence stays medium (not low) on the strength of the general mechanism, but this is arguably the weakest of the Fennel 'bad' pairings; flagging in case you'd prefer low here.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Fennel is a poor neighbor for almost everything in the garden, basil included. It is said to release substances from its roots that can slow nearby plants down. The simple fix most gardeners use is to grow fennel off on its own, in a separate bed or a large pot.

companions.note_seasoned: The basil-tomato pairing is the most-studied companion combination in the kitchen garden. University of Minnesota research cites replicated field studies showing basil intercropping reduces thrip populations on tomatoes in both field and greenhouse conditions, and may promote tomato growth. Texas A&M notes basil as a useful disease indicator plant for tomatoes, as basil shows powdery mildew and other diseases earlier than tomatoes, providing an early-warning function. The pairing also serves as a space-efficiency strategy: basil planted early in a tomato bed can be harvested before tomato canopy fill-in, maximizing yield per square foot. Marigolds are not a direct basil companion but share the warm-season frame and contribute to pest management in the broader bed. Fennel is a general allelopath suppressing many vegetable crops; keep basil and other kitchen herbs away from fennel plantings.
companions.note_beginner: Basil and tomatoes are classic garden companions. Plant basil near your tomatoes for a traditional combination that may also help deter some insects. Keep basil away from fennel, which inhibits many herbs and vegetables.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of soft-bodied insects, often green or black, on new growth and leaf undersides. Infested leaves curl downward or pucker. Honeydew excretion leads to sooty mold growth on leaf surfaces, reducing photosynthesis. Aphid feeding also vectors mosaic viruses in basil.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Look for clusters of tiny insects on new growth or under leaves. Leaves may curl or feel sticky.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species, including Myzus persicae (green peach aphid) and Aphis spp. Populations explode in warm conditions and when plants are overfertilized with nitrogen, which produces the soft, sweet growth aphids prefer.
pests.cause_beginner: Aphids are tiny insects that suck sap from new growth. They multiply quickly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: A strong jet of water dislodges colonies effectively without pesticides; repeat over several days. Insecticidal soap or neem oil applied directly to colonies (including undersides) is effective; avoid application in full sun or when temperatures exceed 90 °F. Introduce or encourage beneficial insects (ladybugs, parasitic wasps).
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Blast aphids off with a strong stream of water from a hose. Insecticidal soap spray also works.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen fertilization, which produces the lush soft growth aphids favor. Plant flowering herbs and companion flowers nearby to attract beneficial predators. Inspect transplants before purchase.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not over-fertilize. Check plants regularly for aphids so you can catch them early.

pests.name: Japanese beetle
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Skeletonized leaves with only the veins remaining, appearing to be eaten from the inside out. Metallic green and copper-brown beetles, about 0.5 inches long, visible on the plant in summer.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Leaves have holes or look skeletonized with only the veins left. Look for shiny green-brown beetles.
pests.cause_seasoned: Popillia japonica. Adults emerge in early to mid-summer and feed on foliage of many plants. Basil is a preferred host in regions where Japanese beetles are established (primarily eastern US).
pests.cause_beginner: Japanese beetles are shiny green and brown bugs that feed on leaves in summer.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick beetles into soapy water in the early morning when they are sluggish and temperatures are cool. Neem oil spray applied directly has some deterrent effect. Avoid pheromone traps near the garden; they attract more beetles than they catch.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Hand-pick beetles into a jar of soapy water in the morning while they are slow. Do not use beetle traps near the garden.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Row covers during peak beetle season (July-August) provide physical exclusion. Milky spore disease (Bacillus popilliae) applied to lawn areas reduces larval populations over multiple seasons.
pests.prevention_beginner: Row covers can protect plants during July and August when beetles are active.

pests.name: Slugs and snails
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Irregular, ragged holes in leaves, particularly toward the plant base; seedlings may be severed at soil level. Silvery slime trails visible on foliage and surrounding soil in the morning.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Holes in leaves with silvery slime trails nearby. Worst on seedlings.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple slug and snail species. Active at night and in cool, moist conditions; populations are highest in spring and fall, or any time following heavy rain or overhead irrigation.
pests.cause_beginner: Slugs and snails feed on basil at night, especially when it is wet.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Beer traps set at soil level are effective. Diatomaceous earth applied around plant bases acts as a physical barrier. Hand-pick at night. Iron phosphate-based slug pellets are organic-approved and low-risk to non-target organisms.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Set out beer traps at ground level. Iron phosphate slug pellets are safe to use around food plants.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid overhead watering and mulching heavily around basil stems, as both create the moist conditions slugs require. Eliminate debris and board piles that serve as daytime refuge. Transplants are most vulnerable; maintain tighter spacing so the canopy shades the soil and dries it faster.
pests.prevention_beginner: Water at the base of plants, not overhead. Remove debris from around basil where slugs hide during the day.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellowing of leaves in irregular patches beginning on the upper leaf surface; affected areas turn uniformly yellow before browning. The diagnostic symptom is a gray-to-dark-purple fuzzy sporulation on the undersides of infected leaves, visible in humid conditions or in the morning. In warm, humid weather the disease spreads rapidly across a planting within days. Infected plants decline quickly once systemic.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Yellow patches on the tops of leaves, and a grayish-purple fuzzy growth on the undersides. This is the most serious basil disease and spreads fast in humid weather.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Peronospora belbahrii, an oomycete (a water mold, not a true fungus). First documented in the US in Florida in 2007, it has since become the dominant disease threat to sweet basil across North America. Obligate biotrophic parasite; sporangia spread via wind and water splash. Sweet Ocimum basilicum is the most susceptible basil type; spice and citrus basil types show greater resistance. Fungicide classes effective against true fungi are often ineffective against oomycetes.
diseases.cause_beginner: A disease called basil downy mildew, caused by a water mold first found in the US in 2007. Sweet basil is the most susceptible type. Resistant varieties now exist.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No organic curative once systemic infection is established. Remove and destroy infected plants or heavily infected stems promptly to reduce spore load. Copper-based fungicides applied preventively at label rates have moderate efficacy; timing before infection is critical. Improve air circulation immediately. Resistant varieties are the most effective management tool.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove infected plants immediately to stop spread. Copper fungicide spray can help prevent it in future plantings, but the best defense is choosing resistant varieties.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Selecting downy-mildew-resistant (DMR) varieties is the single most effective control. Rutgers University breeding program varieties (Devotion, Obsession, Passion, Thunderstruck) and Prospera (organic-approved) showed strong resistance in replicated field trials. Avoid overhead irrigation; sporangia require leaf wetness for germination. Space plants for air circulation. Start with certified disease-free seed, which may include steam-treated lots.
diseases.prevention_beginner: The best prevention is growing resistant varieties. Look for names like Devotion, Obsession, Prospera, or anything labeled DMR. Avoid watering from above and give plants room to breathe.

diseases.name: Fusarium wilt
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Sudden wilting of one or more stems, initially resembling drought stress but not recovering when watered. Leaves yellow from the bottom up; affected stems may show brown streaking in vascular tissue when cut. Plants die rapidly. The disease can appear days after transplanting if infected nursery stock is planted.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Basil suddenly wilts and does not recover even after watering. Stems may turn brown inside. Plants die quickly.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. basilici, a soil-borne fungus that persists in soil and infects through roots. Can be seed-borne or introduced via infected transplants. Warm soils (above 70 °F) and wet conditions accelerate symptom development. Rotating basil breaks the soil reservoir.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soil fungus that infects roots and rapidly kills the plant. It can be in the soil or in infected transplants or seeds.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No effective organic curative once a plant is infected. Remove and destroy infected plants immediately; do not compost. Do not replant basil in the same location for 2-3 years. Improve soil drainage.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove and throw away any infected plants right away. Do not plant basil in that spot again for a few years.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Purchase certified disease-free seed or transplants; inspect transplants at the nursery before purchase. Rotate basil planting locations. Improve soil drainage. Some varieties carry Fusarium wilt resistance; check seed catalog disease-resistance notation.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Buy certified disease-free seed or transplants, and rotate where you plant basil each year.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Every 5-7 days in garden beds; more frequently in containers (check daily in heat)
watering.frequency_beginner: Water every 5-7 days or when the top inch of soil feels dry. Container basil may need water every 1-2 days in summer.
watering.amount_seasoned: 1-1.5 inches per week, adjusted for temperature and container vs. in-ground
watering.amount_beginner: About 1 inch per week in the garden. In pots, water until it drains from the bottom.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at soil level to keep foliage dry; overhead watering promotes Fusarium wilt and downy mildew. Drip irrigation is preferred at scale. In containers, avoid standing water in saucers.
watering.method_beginner: Water at the base of the plant, not over the leaves. Wet leaves can cause disease, especially in humid conditions.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves; soft, dark stem bases; wilting despite wet soil (root rot); Fusarium wilt progression accelerated in waterlogged soil.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Yellow lower leaves or a soft, dark base on the stem are signs of too much water.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting in the morning heat that does not recover by evening; leaf edges curling or browning; stunted growth and early bolting under water stress.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Basil wilts dramatically when thirsty but usually recovers quickly once watered. If it's wilting in the evening when it's cool, it needs water.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Seeds need consistent surface moisture for the 5-14 day germination window; drying out during germination causes uneven emergence.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep the soil damp but not soggy until you see sprouts.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Roots are shallow; water more frequently but in smaller amounts. Avoid overhead watering to reduce damping-off risk.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Young seedlings are sensitive; keep soil moist but never waterlogged.

schedule_by_stage.frequency: every 5-7 days in-ground; more often in containers
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: The main production phase. Consistent moisture supports rapid leaf growth and delays bolting.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Water regularly during the main growing season.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Maintain consistent moisture through the harvest period. Water stress accelerates bolting.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep watering regularly even while harvesting. Dry stress causes basil to flower and stop making new leaves.

watering.method_note_seasoned: Basil is one of the herbs most sensitive to foliar wetness. Wet-leaf conditions are the primary environment for both Fusarium wilt spore germination and downy mildew (Peronospora belbahrii) sporulation. Consistent drip or base watering and morning-only irrigation if overhead is unavoidable are the two most effective cultural disease controls.
watering.method_note_beginner: Always water basil at the base, not from above. This simple habit prevents the two most common basil diseases.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Germination (soil must stay moist for 5-14 days); the first 2 weeks post-transplant (establishing roots); and during hot dry spells when water stress rapidly accelerates bolting.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Keep soil moist when seeds are germinating and for the first 2 weeks after you transplant seedlings into the garden.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Start seeds indoors 6 weeks before last frost date for an early harvest. Transplant out when night temperatures stay consistently above 50 °F and all frost risk has passed. Direct sowing is equally effective once soil reaches 70 °F, typically 1-2 weeks after last frost. In zones 7 and warmer, direct sowing is the standard approach. Harden transplants off over 7-10 days by gradually increasing outdoor exposure before planting out.
start_method.notes_beginner: You have two options: start seeds indoors 6 weeks before your last frost, or wait and plant seeds directly in the garden after your last frost when the soil feels warm. Basil is very cold-sensitive, so do not rush it outside. If night temperatures are still dropping below 50 °F, wait.

drainage.saucer_practice_seasoned: Empty saucers after each watering to prevent standing water; basil roots rot quickly in waterlogged conditions.
drainage.saucer_practice_beginner: After watering, empty the saucer under the pot so the roots do not sit in standing water. Basil roots rot quickly if left wet.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Standard potting mix or herb potting mix
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: No amendment needed with a good potting mix
soil_mix.type_seasoned: Well-draining potting mix with added perlite for improved drainage
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Add 10-15% perlite to standard potting mix to ensure drainage; avoid mixes with heavy peat that retain too much moisture around roots

container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Container basil needs more frequent watering than in-ground plants. Check the pot daily in summer heat and water when the top inch is dry.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Water pot basil more often than garden basil. Check it every day in hot weather.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Container basil needs more frequent fertilization than in-ground plants because nutrients leach with each watering. Apply a balanced liquid fertilizer at half-label strength every 2-3 weeks during active growth.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Feed pot basil with liquid fertilizer every 2-3 weeks through summer, since watering flushes out nutrients.

overwintering.approach_seasoned: Basil is a true annual and will eventually flower and decline even indoors, but a container plant can be brought inside before first frost and kept productive through winter with adequate light. A south-facing window providing at least 6 hours of direct light, or 12 hours of supplemental grow light, is required. Indoor plants should be watered less frequently and fertilized at half the summer rate. Plan on starting fresh seeds in late winter for the following season.
overwintering.approach_beginner: You can bring pot basil inside before the first frost to extend your harvest. Give it the sunniest window you have. It will slow down but stay alive. Start fresh seeds in late winter for next year.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Basil is one of the best herbs for container growing. A single 2-gallon pot on a sunny patio or south-facing sill can produce more leaves than most households use fresh. The container advantage is heat: pots warm faster than soil, extending the growing season at both ends, and allow placement in a microclimate that avoids frost risk. Self-watering containers perform well for basil, allowing the gardener to manage the reservoir rather than the soil moisture surface directly.
container_notes.notes_beginner: Basil is one of the best herbs to grow in a pot. A single pot on a sunny windowsill can supply all the fresh basil a family needs. Just make sure the pot drains well and gets plenty of sun.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering containers work well for basil when the reservoir is managed to keep the wicking medium moist but not saturated. Basil root rot is the main risk if the reservoir is kept consistently full; allow it to partially dry between refills.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: Self-watering pots work for basil. Let the reservoir get partly empty before refilling to avoid overwatering.

recommended: Genovese (classic sweet basil, the pizza and pesto standard; susceptible to downy mildew; pair with a DMR variety if disease pressure is high in your region)
Devotion / Obsession / Prospera (downy-mildew-resistant Genovese types from Rutgers University breeding program; same culinary use as Genovese; first line of defense in humid regions)
Thai basil (Ocimum basilicum var. thyrsiflora; distinct anise and clove flavor; more heat-tolerant and slower to bolt than sweet; purple stems and flowers; essential for southeast Asian cooking)
Lemon basil (O. x citriodorum; distinct lemon fragrance and lighter flavor; excellent in salads, iced teas, and desserts; 12-18 inches; slower to bolt than Genovese)

Purple / Dark Opal basil (O. basilicum 'Purpurascens'; striking red-purple foliage; ornamental and culinary; basil vinegars and garnish; fully edible with a similar but slightly spicier flavor than Genovese)
Spicy Globe / Greek dwarf basil (compact 8-10 inch mounding habit; excellent for containers and pot culture; slower to bolt; slightly spicier flavor; the windowsill variety of choice)
varieties.note_seasoned: The variety decision for basil has two primary axes: culinary use and disease resistance. Genovese remains the standard for pesto, Italian cooking, and fresh eating, but it is highly susceptible to basil downy mildew (Peronospora belbahrii). In regions with humid summers or a history of downy mildew, the Rutgers DMR program varieties (Devotion, Obsession, Prospera) offer equivalent culinary quality with significantly reduced disease risk. Thai basil and lemon basil are distinct culinary herbs rather than substitutes for Genovese; growing one of each fills different kitchen roles. For container or windowsill production, dwarf/Greek types outperform full-size varieties in limited space.
varieties.note_beginner: Start with Genovese basil for classic Italian flavor or, if you're in a humid area, choose a disease-resistant variety like Devotion or Prospera. Thai basil is a completely different herb with an anise flavor, great for Asian cooking.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: 1-2 weeks in a jar of water at room temperature, out of direct sun, like cut flowers. Change the water every 2 days. Do not refrigerate (chilling injury begins below 50 °F, causing blackening within hours).
storage.room_temp_beginner: Store fresh basil like flowers in a small jar of water on the counter, not in the fridge. It will blacken in the refrigerator.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Not recommended for fresh leaves; refrigerator temperatures cause rapid chilling injury and blackening. If refrigeration is necessary, wrap loosely in a dry paper towel, place in a zip-close bag, and use within 1-2 days. Store in the warmest part of the refrigerator (door shelf).
storage.fridge_beginner: Avoid refrigerating fresh basil if possible. If you must, wrap it in a dry paper towel and use within 1-2 days.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Blanching is not recommended; direct freezing in oil or as a puree preserves flavor best. Blend fresh basil with olive oil (approximately 2:1 oil-to-herb by volume) and freeze in ice cube trays, then transfer to bags. Frozen pesto-base cubes keep 3-6 months. Alternatively, freeze whole leaves on a tray and transfer to bags; texture is lost but flavor is retained for cooking.
storage.freezer_beginner: Blend basil with a little olive oil and freeze in an ice cube tray. These cubes are great to add to pasta sauces later.
storage.notes_seasoned: Basil is one of the most chilling-sensitive herbs; even brief refrigerator exposure degrades appearance and flavor. For growers with large harvests, making pesto, infused oils, or drying (though fresh-frozen retains flavor better than drying) are the primary preservation approaches.
storage.notes_beginner: Fresh basil is best used same-day. The counter-in-water method works for a few days. Freeze the rest in oil cubes.

bolting.prevention_seasoned: Pinch out the central growing tip and any emerging flower spikes as soon as they appear, cutting back to just above a pair of leaves. This redirects the plant's energy from reproduction back to vegetative leaf production and can extend productive harvest by 4-6 weeks. Consistent, complete flower removal is the primary management lever. Successive plantings also guarantee a supply of young, pre-bolt plants throughout the season. Providing afternoon shade in zones 8-11 during peak summer reduces heat-induced bolting.
bolting.prevention_beginner: The key trick with basil is pinching off any flower buds as soon as you see them. This keeps the plant focused on making leaves. Once it flowers fully, the leaves taste different and the plant winds down.
bolting.note_seasoned: Bolting in basil is triggered by long day lengths (daylength is actually the primary driver, though heat accelerates it) combined with high temperatures. This is why warm-climate gardeners find basil bolts faster in midsummer regardless of consistent pinching: the photoperiodic trigger is stronger. Planting successions through late June keeps a fresh, vegetative cohort available even as earlier plantings reach reproductive maturity.
bolting.note_beginner: Basil starts to flower as summer gets longer and hotter. This is normal, not a mistake. Your job is to pinch those flowers off before they open.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Avoid planting basil where basil or other Lamiaceae herbs (mint, oregano, thyme) grew the previous year, as Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. basilici can persist in soil. In beds with a known Fusarium wilt history, extend the rotation to 3 years.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Do not plant basil where you grew basil (or other mints) last year, to avoid soil diseases.
rotation.good_after: Legumes (nitrogen-improving), brassicas, root vegetables
rotation.note_seasoned: Basil's rotation driver is primarily Fusarium wilt, which is soil-persistent and also seed-borne. Because basil is typically grown in a small bed or container, rotation is easy to execute even in a small garden. The 2-year gap is sufficient for most gardens without a disease history.
rotation.note_beginner: Just move your basil to a different spot each year to keep the soil healthy.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: First seed leaves (cotyledons) emerging, pale yellow-green initially then deepening to dark green within 1-2 days of light exposure. Basil cotyledons are oval and relatively large for a herb. At soil temperature below 65 °F, emergence is delayed or absent.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Small pale green seedlings pushing up through the soil. Basil seeds germinate in 5-14 days when warm. If nothing appears after 14 days, soil was likely too cold.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Maintain soil temperature at 70-85 °F and consistent surface moisture. Remove any humidity dome or plastic cover at first emergence to prevent damping off. Do not let the seedbed surface dry out during this window.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil moist but not soggy and make sure it is warm. Remove any plastic cover the moment you see seedlings coming up.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Germination confirmed?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are seedlings showing?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: True leaves developing above the cotyledons; true basil leaves are distinctly aromatic, ovate, and show the characteristic glossy surface. Seedlings should be compact, deep green, and upright; leggy, pale seedlings indicate light deficit.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Real basil leaves (not the first rounded seed leaves) appearing above the base. The new leaves will smell like basil. Tall, floppy seedlings mean they need more light.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin to the correct spacing once two sets of true leaves are present. Ensure maximum light exposure; supplement with a grow light if natural light is under 6 hours. Harden off 7-10 days before transplanting outdoors.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Thin seedlings to one plant every 12 inches. Give them as much sun as possible. If they are getting leggy, move them closer to the window or under a light.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: True leaves developing?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Seedlings looking healthy?

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Plant has 3-4 pairs of true leaves; main stem is sturdy and self-supporting; root system is established and the plant recovers quickly from watering gaps. This is the trigger point for first pinching.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant looks full and healthy with several sets of leaves. It stands up on its own and is growing noticeably. This is the time to start pinching.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Begin pinching above the third or fourth leaf pair. Initiate regular watering-at-base habit. Apply first fertilizer dose if not already done at transplant.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pinch off the very top of each stem above a spot where two leaves meet it. Two new branches will grow from there instead of one, making the plant bushy. This single technique gives you far more basil all season long.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Ready to begin pinching?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Plant looking established?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Actively branching, multi-stemmed plant producing multiple harvestable shoot tips. Leaves large, fragrant, and deeply green. No flower buds visible or immediately emerging. The plant is in the peak productive window.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A bushy plant with lots of leafy tips. Good basil at this stage smells strongly when you brush the leaves. No white or purple flowers visible yet.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest on a regular 7-10 day schedule, cutting above a node each time and removing no more than one-third of the plant. Conduct a flower-bud scan at each harvest visit. Harvest in the morning for peak essential oil concentration.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Cut the tops of stems every week or two, always above where two leaves meet the stem. Check for any flower buds and pinch them off immediately. Pick in the morning for the best flavor.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Harvesting regularly?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Getting regular harvests?

growth_stages.name: Bolting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Central elongating flower spike with small, opposite leaves and visible flower buds at the tip. Basil flowers are small, white or pale purple, in whorls on the spike. Leaves on the flowering stem become smaller and more pointed. On Genovese-type basil, a sharp increase in clove-like aroma may accompany early bolting.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A tall spike growing from the center of the plant with small leaves and what will become flowers at the tip. This is the bolt. Pinch or cut it off now.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Remove all flower spikes immediately, cutting back to just above a healthy leaf pair. Increase pinching frequency to every 5-7 days during the peak bolt risk period (midsummer in most zones). Consider planting a succession start if the main planting is approaching full bolt.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Cut off any flower spikes as soon as you see them. Then keep an eye out and remove new ones every few days. If the plant is covered in flowers, pull it out and replace it with a fresh young plant from a new sowing.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Flower spikes appearing?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Seeing flower buds?

notifications.title_beginner: Time to start basil seeds indoors
notifications.body_seasoned: Start basil indoors 4 weeks before last frost. Use a seedling heat mat to maintain soil temperature at 75-80 °F. Basil sown in cold conditions germinates slowly or not at all, and seedlings from cold starts tend to damp off. Do not transplant outdoors until night temperatures are reliably above 50 °F.
notifications.body_beginner: Plant basil seeds indoors now, about 4 weeks before your last frost. Use a warm spot or a heat mat set to around 75 °F. Keep the soil moist. Do not put the plants outside until nights stay above 50 °F.

notifications.title_seasoned: Last frost passed: harden off basil before transplanting
notifications.title_beginner: Last frost has passed: get basil ready for outdoors
notifications.body_seasoned: Last frost date reached. Begin hardening off basil transplants over 7-10 days: start with 1-2 hours of outdoor shade, then gradually increase sun and duration. Transplant only when night temperatures are consistently above 50 °F and seedlings are showing 3-4 true leaf pairs.
notifications.body_beginner: Your last frost date has passed. Start introducing your basil seedlings to the outdoors gradually over 7-10 days: a little time outside each day, starting in shade. Transplant to the garden once nights are reliably above 50 °F.

notifications.title_beginner: Time to start pinching your basil
notifications.body_seasoned: Your basil has reached 3-4 leaf pairs: start pinching the central growing tip above the third or fourth pair. This is the most impactful single action for basil productivity. Repeat every 7-10 days to suppress bolting and stimulate branching.
notifications.body_beginner: Your basil is ready for its first pinch. Snip or pinch off the very top of the main stem just above where two leaves meet it. This makes the plant branch and grow bushy. Keep doing this every week or two all summer.

notifications.title_beginner: Basil flowers appearing: remove them now
notifications.body_seasoned: Basil flower spikes detected. Remove all visible spikes now by cutting back to just above a healthy leaf pair. A basil plant allowed to set seed redirects energy from leaf production and the flavor profile shifts. Check every 5-7 days for new spikes during the peak bolt window.
notifications.body_beginner: Your basil is trying to flower. Pinch off all the flower spikes you can see. Once basil flowers fully, the leaves get smaller and the flavor changes. Removing flowers early extends your harvest by weeks.

notifications.title_seasoned: Harvest all basil before first frost
notifications.title_beginner: Harvest all your basil before frost
notifications.body_seasoned: First frost is approximately one week away. Basil blackens and dies at the first frost with no recovery. Harvest everything harvestable now: make pesto, blend leaves with oil and freeze in ice cube trays, or dry stems. Nothing from the basil plant should be left exposed to frost.
notifications.body_beginner: Frost is coming in about a week and basil will be killed by it. Harvest everything now. Make pesto, freeze leaves in an ice cube tray with a little oil, or use them fresh. After frost, basil is gone until next year.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning: protect or harvest basil
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost coming: protect or pick all basil tonight
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Basil is killed by frost with no recovery. Bring all containers indoors immediately. Cover in-ground plants with frost cloth if you have it; this buys 3-5 °F of protection and may save the plant for another week. If frost is at or below 32 °F, harvest everything harvestable before tonight.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Basil dies in a frost. Bring any pots inside tonight. If your basil is in the ground, cover it with a sheet or frost cloth. If it is close to the end of the season anyway, just pick everything edible now before the frost gets it.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Cold night ahead: protect young basil
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Temperatures forecast below 50 °F. Basil experiences chilling injury below this threshold even without ice formation: membrane damage leads to water-soaked patches and blackening within hours. Bring containers inside or cover with frost cloth. Avoid transplanting into outdoor conditions until night minimums are reliably above 50 °F.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Temperatures below 50 °F can damage basil even without frost. Bring pot basil inside or cover in-ground plants with a sheet tonight. Wait for consistently warm nights before leaving basil unprotected.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity: foliar wetness and disease risk elevated
weather_triggers.title_beginner: High humidity: check basil leaves for disease
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Sustained high humidity (above 85% RH) combined with wet foliage significantly increases downy mildew (Peronospora belbahrii) sporulation and spread. Avoid overhead watering during humid periods. If the plant was watered or rained on, do not harvest or handle foliage while wet, as this can spread spores. Check leaf undersides for gray-purple sporulation.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: When it is hot and very humid, check your basil leaves for signs of downy mildew: yellow patches on top of the leaf and a gray or purple fuzz underneath. Water only at the base, never over the leaves, especially during humid weather.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat wave: monitor bolting and water stress
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot weather: check basil for flowers and wilting
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Extended temperatures above 90 °F accelerate the daylength-triggered bolting response in basil. Increase pinching frequency to every 5-7 days during heat waves. Basil does not have a true heat-pause like cool-season crops; it actively grows in heat but the bolt risk spikes. Ensure consistent watering during heat; water stress under high temperatures accelerates bolting.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Hot weather makes basil want to flower faster. Check more often during heat waves and pinch off any flower buds you see. Make sure the plant is getting enough water: heat plus drought causes basil to bolt quickly.

germination.text_seasoned: Soil temperature is the controlling variable at germination. Basil germinates reliably and quickly at 70-85 °F soil temperature; below 65 °F germination becomes erratic and slow, and seedlings from cold sowings often damp off before establishing. A seedling heat mat set to 75-80 °F is the most reliable method indoors. Direct-sow timing outdoors should be calibrated to soil temperature, not calendar date.
germination.text_beginner: Basil needs warm soil to sprout well. Wait until soil temperatures are at least 70 °F before sowing outdoors, or use a heat mat indoors set to around 75 °F. Cold soil leads to poor, uneven germination. A basic soil thermometer (a probe you push into the ground) tells you when conditions are right.

germination.text_seasoned: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep and keep the seedbed or flat consistently moist but not saturated for the 5-14 day germination window. Surface drying is the most common cause of failed germination indoors; a humidity dome or plastic wrap over the flat maintains moisture without overwatering. Remove the dome the moment you see the first seedling to prevent damping off.
germination.text_beginner: Plant basil seeds about 1/4 inch deep and keep the soil moist until they sprout (5-14 days). If starting indoors, cover the pot with plastic wrap to hold moisture in, and remove it as soon as you see green shoots appearing. Leaving the cover on after sprouting can cause seedlings to rot at the base.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin seedlings to one plant per 12-18 inches once they have their first true leaves. Crowded basil seedlings compete for light and air circulation, accelerating the damping-off conditions that kill seedlings at the base. The thinnings are edible; add them to salads or use as a first harvest.
seedling.text_beginner: Once basil seedlings have their first real leaves (not the rounded seed leaves), thin them to one plant every 12 inches. Crowded seedlings are weaker. The ones you pull are edible and taste great in salads.

seedling.text_seasoned: Leggy, pale seedlings signal light deficit, not overwatering. Basil needs bright light from day one; on a windowsill, turn seedlings daily to prevent lean and supplement with a grow light if the windowsill receives fewer than 6 hours of direct sun. Leggy transplants can be buried deeper at transplant to compensate, but deep planting does not work for basil the way it does for tomatoes; addressing light is the root fix.
seedling.text_beginner: If your basil seedlings grow tall and floppy, they need more light, not less water. Move them to a sunnier spot or closer to a grow light. Basil is a sun-loving herb and gets stretched out when light is low.

established.text_seasoned: Begin pinching the central growing tip as soon as the plant has 3-4 sets of true leaves. Cut directly above a node (where a pair of leaves meets the stem); the plant will branch at that node, producing two new shoots instead of one. Repeat every 7-10 days throughout the productive season. Consistent pinching is the single most effective yield-management technique for basil and is the primary mechanism for extending harvest by suppressing the bolt.
established.text_beginner: Start pinching basil as soon as it has 3-4 sets of leaves. Pinch means snipping or pinching off the top of the stem just above where two leaves meet the stem. The plant then grows two new branches instead of one, becoming bushy instead of tall. Do this every week or two all summer.

established.text_seasoned: Water at soil level, never overhead. The foliar wetness nexus is the primary environmental driver of both downy mildew (Peronospora belbahrii) and Fusarium wilt: wet leaf surfaces and high humidity provide the conditions for sporulation and infection. Drip irrigation or hand watering at the stem base is the simplest preventive measure and carries more disease-prevention leverage than any fungicide.
established.text_beginner: Always water basil at the base, not over the top. Wet leaves are the main way basil gets its two most serious diseases: downy mildew (a fast-spreading leaf disease) and Fusarium wilt. Keeping leaves dry is your best prevention.

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest in the morning after the dew dries but before midday heat, when essential oil concentration in the leaves is at its peak. Always cut above a leaf node rather than stripping individual leaves from the base; node-cuts cause branching that increases future yield, while leaf-stripping exposes woody stem and reduces plant productivity. Never remove more than one-third of the plant in a single harvest.
harvest.text_beginner: Pick basil in the morning before it gets hot for the best flavor. Snip the stem above a point where two leaves meet the main stem, and new branches grow there. Never pull single leaves from the base of the plant. Harvest no more than a third of the plant at any one time to keep it healthy and productive.

harvest.text_seasoned: Never refrigerate fresh basil. Chilling injury begins below 50 °F: cellular membranes are disrupted, releasing enzymes that oxidize chlorophyll and produce the characteristic blackening within hours. Store harvested stems like cut flowers in a glass of water at room temperature; they keep 1-2 weeks this way. For longer preservation, blend with olive oil and freeze in ice cube trays: the oil coating prevents oxidation and preserves volatile flavor compounds better than blanching.
harvest.text_beginner: Do not put fresh basil in the refrigerator. It turns black quickly when cold, because basil is a warm-climate plant that is damaged by low temperatures. Instead, stand the cut stems in a small glass of water on the counter like a bouquet. To preserve a bigger harvest, puree the leaves with oil and pour into ice cube trays to freeze for winter cooking.

bolting.text_seasoned: Bolting in basil is triggered primarily by increasing day length (photoperiod) combined with accumulating heat. The plant perceives long days as a signal to shift from vegetative to reproductive growth; warm nights accelerate the transition. Pinching suppresses bolting by removing the apical meristem (the growing tip that carries the flower initiation signal), redirecting the plant's hormone balance back toward vegetative branching. In practice, basil grown under consistent harvest pressure bolts 2-4 weeks later than unpinched plants of the same variety.
bolting.text_beginner: Basil starts trying to flower as summer days get longer and hotter. This is normal but you want to delay it as long as possible, because once the plant flowers the leaves become smaller and the flavor changes. The way to delay flowering is to pinch off any flower buds the moment you see them. Regular harvesting helps too.

bolting.text_seasoned: When a plant enters full flower, flavor character shifts but the plant is not finished. For culinary herbs, the shift in essential oil profile after flowering is variety-dependent: Genovese-type sweet basil develops a clove-like and sometimes anise character as eugenol increases relative to linalool during flowering. Some growers harvest at this stage for pesto. Aggressive deadheading of spent flowers can squeeze 1-2 more weeks of usable leaf production from a flowering plant. If the plant is fully committed to seed production, pull it and start a fresh succession rather than managing an exhausted plant.
bolting.text_beginner: Once basil flowers fully, you can still use the leaves but the flavor is stronger and a bit different. Some people like it; some do not. Keep pinching off spent flowers to extend harvest. When the plant looks tired and woody, pull it out and plant a fresh one from your succession starts.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A single Genovese basil plant in full sun, regularly pinched and succession-planted, yields 1/4 to 1/2 cup of fresh leaves per week at peak production, or roughly 2-4 oz of fresh leaves per harvest over a 10-14 week productive season. Container yields are proportional to pot size and sun exposure; a 2-gallon pot in full sun performs comparably to an in-ground plant.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: One basil plant can supply a family with fresh leaves all summer if you pick from it regularly. Expect a generous handful of leaves every week or two once the plant is established.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Basil is one of the few herbs where the first-season yield equals or exceeds subsequent years; it is a fast-maturing annual with no establishment lag. The main first-season variable is how quickly the grower develops the pinching habit; growers who pinch consistently from the fourth leaf pair onward produce significantly more usable leaf than those who let the plant grow unchecked.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Your first year growing basil can be just as productive as any year after, since basil is an annual that grows fresh each season. The key is learning to pinch the tips early: that one habit makes the difference between a lush plant and a tall, woody one.
factors_seasoned: Pinching frequency: the single largest yield driver; plants pinched every 7-10 days produce 2-3x more usable leaf than unpinched plants over the season
Flower removal: immediate removal of any flower bud that escapes pinching prevents leaf quality decline and seed-energy diversion
Sunlight: basil is a high-light crop; below 6 hours of direct sun daily, yield drops substantially and plants become leggy

Soil nitrogen: modest, consistent nitrogen supply drives the tender leaf production basil needs for high yield; excessive nitrogen is counterproductive, reducing the concentration of essential oils that determine flavor quality
Succession planting: staggering new plantings every 3 weeks provides a constant cohort of young, productive plants as older ones bolt
Zone and season length: zones 9-11 can produce 2-3 successive basil crops per year; zones 3-5 have a compressed 10-12 week productive window

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Moon-phase planting guidance assigns leaf crops and herbs to the waxing phase between new and full moon, when sap flow is traditionally believed to be rising. No peer-reviewed or Land Grant extension literature supports a yield or quality benefit from moon-phase timing for basil specifically. The recommendation reflects traditional agricultural folklore that has not been subjected to controlled trial. Growers who use biodynamic calendars will naturally apply this phase; it carries no evidence-based advantage over planting within the verified temperature and frost windows.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Cold or frost damage
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Plant killed or blackened by cold
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Basil blackens and dies at or below 32 °F frost; chilling injury (cellular membrane disruption without ice crystal formation) begins below 50 °F and is visible as dark water-soaked patches within hours. This is the most abrupt and total failure mode in basil: there is no recovery from a frost event. The common misconception is that a mild frost will cause the plant to bounce back after warming; basil does not recover from frost-level temperatures.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Basil blackens and dies very quickly when it gets too cold. A frost will kill it overnight with no recovery. Even temperatures just above freezing (below 50 °F) can cause dark blotchy patches on the leaves. Basil is one of the most frost-sensitive crops you can grow. The mistake most beginners make is planting too early in spring before nights are consistently warm.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant after last frost date when night temperatures are reliably above 50 °F. In zones 3-5, this is typically late May to early June. Use a soil thermometer to confirm soil temperature is above 60 °F at transplant. If you must plant early, use row covers or a cold frame that can maintain 50 °F+ overnight.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Wait until your last frost date has passed and nights stay above 50 °F before planting basil outside. When in doubt, wait another week. Basil planted in warm conditions will grow fast and catch up to an early-planted but cold-stressed plant.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Leggy, tall plant with few leaves
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Plant is tall and spindly instead of bushy
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Etiolation (excessive internode elongation) is caused by two independent mechanisms that are often conflated: (1) light deficit, where photoreceptors trigger elongation as the plant 'reaches' toward light; and (2) failure to pinch, where the intact apical meristem produces auxin that suppresses lateral bud development (apical dominance). In basil, both mechanisms are usually operating simultaneously. A plant getting only 3-4 hours of sun that has never been pinched will be the leggiest; one in full sun with consistent pinching will be the bushiest.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Basil gets tall and spindly for two reasons: not enough sun, and not being pinched. Both make the plant grow upward instead of outward. If your basil is leggy, check that it is getting at least 6 hours of direct sun, and start pinching the tips.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site basil in the location with maximum direct sun exposure (minimum 6 hours, ideally 8). Begin pinching above the third leaf pair, and continue on a 7-10 day schedule. If the seedling stage was the leggy period, ensure maximum light from day one after emergence.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant basil in your sunniest spot and start pinching the top of each stem as soon as the plant has 3-4 sets of leaves. These two habits produce a bushy, productive plant.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Downy mildew (Peronospora belbahrii)
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Yellow leaves with fuzzy gray growth underneath
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Peronospora belbahrii, an oomycete, produces irregular yellow patches on the upper leaf surface; the diagnostic sign is gray-purple sporulation on the lower leaf surface visible under magnification or in bright light. The pathogen requires free moisture on leaf surfaces (from overhead watering, rain, or dew) to sporulate and spread. Sweet Genovese basil is highly susceptible; the disease has become the dominant foliar threat to basil in the eastern US since its introduction in 2007. No curative organic option exists once systemic infection is established.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Basil downy mildew appears as uneven yellowing across leaf surfaces followed by a gray or purple coating on the underside. It is caused by a water mold that needs wet foliage to spread. Sweet basil varieties are especially susceptible. Once the plant is seriously infected, it usually cannot be saved. The best defense is choosing resistant varieties and never watering over the top of the leaves.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant downy-mildew-resistant varieties (labeled DMR): Devotion, Obsession, Prospera, Thunderstruck, or Amazel. Never water overhead; use drip or base watering. Ensure good air circulation through correct plant spacing (12-18 inches). In high-humidity regions, siting basil in a spot with afternoon airflow materially reduces risk.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Look for basil varieties labeled DMR (downy mildew resistant) such as Devotion, Prospera, or Obsession. These are much harder to kill with this disease. Always water at the base, not over the leaves.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Fusarium wilt (Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. basilici)
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Plant suddenly wilts and does not recover
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. basilici is a soil-borne and seed-borne vascular pathogen that colonizes the xylem, blocking water transport. Plants wilt suddenly and one-sidedly, initially resembling drought stress but not recovering after watering. Internal stem browning (visible when stem is cut) is diagnostic. The pathogen can persist in soil for years and be introduced via infected transplants, contaminated seed lots, or infected soil. There is no curative treatment; infected plants should be removed and not composted.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Fusarium wilt is a soil disease that attacks basil roots and stems. The plant suddenly wilts, does not recover when you water it, and often turns brown inside the stem. It can spread in the soil and in transplants bought from nurseries. Once a plant is infected, it cannot be saved. Remove it immediately.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Purchase certified disease-free seed or transplants from reputable suppliers; inspect nursery transplants for wilted or yellowing lower leaves before buying. Rotate basil planting location by at least 2 years. Avoid overhead watering and waterlogged soil. Improve drainage if the bed stays wet.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Move your basil to a different spot next year and buy seeds or transplants from a reputable source. Do not plant basil in the same spot if it had Fusarium wilt this year. Good drainage and base watering help prevent it.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Poor or uneven germination
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Seeds did not sprout or germinated patchily
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Basil germination failure has two primary causes: soil temperature below 65 °F (most common in spring), and surface drying of the seedbed during the 5-14 day germination window. At temperatures below 60 °F, germination may be zero; seeds sit dormant and often rot rather than germinate as soil warms. The misconception is that seed failure is the cause of poor germination; in practice, viable commercial basil seed has high germination rates and fresh seed from reputable sources rarely fails under correct conditions.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Basil seeds usually fail to sprout for one of two reasons: the soil was too cold, or it dried out before they could germinate. Basil needs warm, moist soil to sprout. Cold conditions are the main culprit in spring. The seeds themselves are usually fine.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Calibrate outdoor direct-sow timing to soil temperature (minimum 65 °F, ideally 70+ °F) rather than calendar date. Use a seedling heat mat for indoor starts. Keep the seedbed or flat consistently moist during the germination window; a humidity dome or mist-spray schedule prevents surface drying.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Check soil temperature before sowing basil outdoors: use a soil thermometer and wait for at least 65 °F. Indoors, a heat mat greatly improves success. Keep the seedbed moist every day until sprouts appear.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Sow a new batch of seeds every 3 weeks from last frost through midsummer for a continuous supply of young, tender leaves. Older plants become woodier and more prone to bolting; fresh successions always outperform aged plants for leaf quality.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: Plant a new set of basil seeds every 3 weeks through summer for a continuous harvest. Basil plants get woody and start flowering after a couple of months, but a fresh start nearby stays productive.

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.source_quote: Sow seeds indoors six to eight weeks before planting outside to get a head start on the growing season.
start_indoors.synthesis_note: UMN Extension recommends starting basil indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost date and transplanting after all frost risk has passed. 6-week lead (42 days) used as the primary offset, consistent with basil weeks_indoors=6.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: Sow seeds directly into the ground after danger of spring frosts has passed.
plant_out.synthesis_note: Plant out after last frost once soil has warmed above 65°F, typically 1-2 weeks post-frost. Basil is frost-tender; no rushing. Applies to both transplants and direct sowing.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note: First harvest possible approximately 30 days after transplanting out (60-90 day DTM; pinching from top begins earlier at ~4 weeks). Leaf harvest can begin whenever plants have multiple true-leaf sets.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Basil is killed by first frost in cold zones. Harvest all remaining leaves before the first fall frost arrives. UMN: basil will not survive winter in the region.

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.synthesis_note: Succession plantings: start new batches indoors every 3 weeks from the first start-indoors date through midsummer. Stop when a new transplant would not have 60+ days to harvest before first frost.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note: Succession transplants go out every 3 weeks through midsummer. Stop planting when there is insufficient time to harvest before first frost (60-day minimum).

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note: Each succession batch begins harvest ~30 days after plant-out.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note: All successions end at first frost. Final succession should have at least 60 days to reach harvest before first frost.

plantings_provenance.note: Northern_tier cells derived from last_frost offsets per UMN Extension (plant after frost, 6-8 wk indoors lead). From-scratch authoring per Step 3.5 protocol (no verified zones{} warm data to promote). Zone-specific dates derive from frost offsets at apply time.

3.zone_notes: Zone 3 has the shortest frost-free window (~90 days). One planting only; prioritize transplants over direct sowing to maximize harvest time.

4.zone_notes: Zone 4 supports 1-2 successions. Start a second round of seeds 3 weeks after the first transplant-out date for extended harvest.

5.zone_notes: Zone 5 supports 2 successions comfortably. Frost-free window of approximately 150 days allows for fresh basil from early June through late September.

6.zone_notes: Zone 6 supports 2-3 successions. With a frost-free window near 180 days, a May-through-late-summer basil supply is achievable with staggered starts every 3 weeks.

7.zone_notes: Zone 7 has the longest northern_tier season (approximately 210 frost-free days). Three to four successions are achievable from early April through July, keeping fresh basil on hand all summer and well into fall.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: Basil needs warm weather to thrive, so timing matters more here than almost any other herb. Do not plant outside until after your last frost and the soil feels warm to the touch (at least 65°F at 2 inches). Starting seeds indoors 6 weeks before that date gives you a head start. Once plants are outside, pick leaves regularly from the top down to keep the plant bushy and prevent flowering. When you see a flower bud forming, snap it off right away. Your growing window ends at the first fall frost, so keep an eye on the forecast in September and October and harvest everything you want before a frost hits.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Basil is strictly frost-bounded in northern zones: plant transplants a week or two after your last spring frost once soil temperatures exceed 65°F, and plan to harvest everything before the first fall frost. Starting seeds indoors 6 weeks early (mid-February in zone 7, mid-April in zone 3) gives you the longest possible season. In zones 3-4, where the frost-free window runs only 90-120 days, plan one main planting plus one succession started 3 weeks later. In zones 5-7 you can fit 2-3 successions through midsummer for a continuous leaf supply, since basil has no heat pause in this region. Pinch off any flower buds as they form to keep the plant producing tender leaves; once basil bolts, leaf quality drops quickly.

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.source_quote: Seed herbs for April planting.
start_indoors.synthesis_note: UGA C943: Plant tender herbs in April for Middle Georgia (last frost ~Mar 15-31). Start transplants indoors 6 weeks prior. South GA (z9) 2-3 weeks earlier; North GA 1-3 weeks later.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: Plant tender herbs.
plant_out.synthesis_note: Plant out tender herbs after last frost. Middle GA = April. South GA (z9) = late March-April. UF/IFAS EP451 North FL: Plant heat-loving herbs, including basil in April-May.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note: First harvest approximately 30 days after transplanting.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note: UGA C943: Spring plantings are harvested in June and July. No hard heat-end for basil (pause_in_heat=false), but peak productivity diminishes as summer progresses; succession plantings maintain quality. Conservative harvest_end = mid-July before peak heat stalls growth, but plant keeps producing.

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.synthesis_note: UGA C943: fall planting period is mid-July to September. Start basil indoors 6 weeks before fall plant-out (mid-July = Jun 1 start; Sep = Jul 20 start). Yields a fall crop harvested October-December.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: The two major planting periods, however, are spring (March to May) and fall (mid-July to September).
plant_out.synthesis_note: UGA C943 fall planting: mid-July to September for Middle Georgia. Basil transplants go out in this window. South GA (z9): 2 weeks later on fall side (Sep extension); fall harvest extends to December.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note: Fall arm harvest begins approximately 30 days after plant-out (September-October).

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.source_quote: The fall plantings are harvested from October to December.
harvest_end.synthesis_note: UGA C943: fall harvest October-December. Harvest to first frost. In z9 South GA, first frost can be Dec or later, extending the fall arm further.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note: Succession plantings in the spring arm every 3 weeks from first plant-out through mid-May (z8) or late May (z9) keep fresh leaf quality high as early plants begin to bolt in summer heat.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast, you can grow basil twice a year: once in spring (plant after your last frost, usually March in south Georgia or April in the Panhandle) and once in fall (plant again in August). Basil keeps growing through summer heat here, but older plants tend to flower and get bitter, so starting a new set of seeds every few weeks keeps a steady supply of young, flavorful leaves coming. Pinch off any flower buds as soon as you see them. The biggest challenge in this region is a disease called basil downy mildew, which spreads when leaves stay wet, so always water at the base of the plant rather than overhead.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: Basil in the Southeast has two distinct planting arms: a spring arm (late March through April in zone 9, April through May in zone 8) and a fall arm (August through September). Between the two arms, summer heat continues to support basil growth but leaf quality often declines in older plants, making succession plantings every 3 weeks the key to keeping tender, flavorful leaves available. The spring arm yields its best harvest in May-June before peak summer; the fall arm produces through October-December. UGA Extension recommends starting warm-season herb seeds indoors for the spring arm and transplanting after last frost. High humidity in this region makes foliar disease, particularly basil downy mildew, the primary management challenge; water at the base and ensure good airflow between plants. Pinch flower buds consistently to extend productive leaf yield.

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.synthesis_note: UC ANR: start basil indoors in spring before transplanting. Central Valley LF: z8 ~Feb 15-Mar 1, z9 ~Jan 15-Feb 1. 6-week lead brings start indoors to mid-January (z9) through mid-February (z8). Transplant when soil > 65°F.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: a sun-loving annual that thrives during summer months in the Inland Valley and Desert. Start indoor in pots in spring.
plant_out.synthesis_note: UCANR: basil thrives in Inland Valley summer; start in spring. Central Valley soil warms to 65°F typically late March (z9) or mid-April (z8). Plant out 3 weeks after last frost once soil is warm.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note: First harvest approximately 30 days after plant-out. Continuous harvest through summer.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Central Valley first frost: z8 ~Dec 1, z9 ~Nov 15. Harvest to first frost. Basil can keep producing into early November in zone 9.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note: Central Valley supports 3-4 succession plantings across April-July. Long hot summer means even late-June transplants have ample season.
