hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In Hawaii, grow broccoli in the cooler months rather than all year round, especially at lower elevations. Plant transplants from about November into December, and harvest from January into March, the coolest part of the year. It rarely if ever frosts here, so the challenge is heat, not cold: the steady warmth at low elevation can keep broccoli from forming a tight head, so plant in the cool season and choose heat-tolerant varieties. Up at higher, cooler elevations the season runs longer.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: In Hawaii broccoli is grown at the cooler, higher-elevation end of the year rather than as a true year-round crop. In the lowlands the practical window is the cooler months: transplants go out from about November into December, heads form through the coolest part of the year, and harvest runs from January into March. Persistent warmth at low elevation pushes against tight heading, so timing the crop into the cool season and choosing heat-tolerant varieties matters more here than frost, which is essentially absent. At higher elevations the cool season stretches longer, but the lowland default is this bounded winter window.

crops.description_seasoned: Broccoli is a cool-season brassica grown for its tight head of immature flower buds, harvested before the buds open. It performs best in the cool shoulders of spring and fall, bolts or fails to head in summer heat, and rewards a steady supply of moisture and nitrogen. After the central head is cut, most types keep producing smaller side shoots.
crops.description_beginner: Broccoli is a cool-weather vegetable grown for its green head, which is really a cluster of flower buds you pick before they open. It grows best in spring and fall, not summer heat, and keeps making smaller side shoots after you cut the main head.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Cut the central head while the buds are tight, blue-green, and still closed, before any yellow flowers show, taking about 6 inches of stem. Side shoots then form for later picking.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Cut the main head while it is firm, green, and tight, before the little buds open into yellow flowers. More small shoots grow afterward.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Work plenty of compost into a fertile, well-drained bed before planting and confirm pH is around 6.0 to 6.5. Broccoli feeds heavily and roots shallowly, so a rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil pays off.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Before planting, mix plenty of compost into loose, well-drained soil. Broccoli is a hungry plant and likes rich ground.

crops.name: Garlic

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Garlic likes loose, rich soil that drains well but still holds some moisture, with plenty of compost worked in. Loosen the bed deeply before planting so the roots and bulbs have room. The thing it cannot stand is soggy, waterlogged ground, which rots the cloves over winter, so avoid heavy clay and any low spot where water sits.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Garlic grows in most soils but does best in a loose, fertile, well-drained loam or sandy loam rich in organic matter. Because the crop sits in the ground from fall through the next summer, drainage over winter is the make-or-break factor: cloves in cold, saturated soil rot before spring. Work in generous compost and loosen the bed deeply before planting, and on heavy ground plant in raised beds or rows so the bulb zone never stays waterlogged.

ph.note_beginner: Garlic grows best in soil close to neutral, about 6.0 to 7.0. It is not very fussy, but very acidic ground holds it back, so if a soil test reads below about 6.0, mix in some garden lime before you plant in fall.
ph.note_seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0; garlic tolerates a slightly wider band, roughly 5.5 to 7.5, but yields fall off on strongly acidic soils. Test the bed the season before and lime an acid plot up toward neutral, since fall is your one planting window and there is no second chance to adjust mid-season.

fertilizer.timing: Work fertilizer in at fall planting, then side-dress nitrogen as shoots grow in early spring; stop by early May
fertilizer.example_product: ammonium sulfate (21-0-0), blood meal, or a balanced vegetable fertilizer
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Garlic has a moderate to high nitrogen demand and builds its bulb on the leaves it grows in spring, so feeding is front-loaded onto the spring vegetative push. Mix a complete fertilizer or compost into the bed at fall planting, then side-dress nitrogen as the shoots resume growth in early spring and again two to three weeks later. The exact cutoff tracks your season rather than a fixed calendar date. In cold-winter regions with a later crop, the last feedings run later: Utah State suggests about half a pound of 21-0-0 per 100 square feet in mid-April with a quarter pound in late May, and the University of Minnesota feeds through spring growth before bulbing. In the warm Southeast, where the crop runs weeks earlier, UGA advises no nitrogen after the first week of April. The unifying rule is to stop nitrogen several weeks before bulbing begins, since late feeding delays bulbing, thickens necks, and worsens storage.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Garlic is a hungry plant that makes its bulb from the leaves it grows in spring, so feed it then. Mix some compost or fertilizer into the soil when you plant in fall, then give it a nitrogen feeding once the green shoots are growing well in early spring, and again a few weeks later. Stop feeding before the bulbs start sizing up, which falls around April in warm regions and into May where winters are cold. Feeding late makes leafy plants with thick necks and small bulbs that do not keep well.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Side-dress your garlic with nitrogen now to drive spring leaf growth before bulbing.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Feed your garlic some nitrogen now, while it is growing leaves in spring.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: Higher first-number (N) feeds in spring, e.g. ammonium sulfate (21-0-0) or blood meal; taper off and stop by early May so bulbing is not delayed.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a feed higher in the first number (nitrogen) such as blood meal or a 21-0-0 fertilizer in spring, then stop by early May.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: About half a pound of ammonium sulfate (21-0-0) per 100 square feet as shoots resume in spring, with a lighter follow-up two to three weeks later; finish before early May.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: About half a pound of a nitrogen fertilizer such as ammonium sulfate per 100 square feet in early spring, then a lighter feeding a few weeks later, following the package directions.

companions.note_beginner: Garlic is famous as a good-neighbor plant, mostly because its strong smell is thought to keep aphids and some other pests away, so it is often tucked among roses, fruit trees, tomatoes, and cabbage-family plants. The one thing to keep it away from is beans and peas, since garlic and its onion relatives are believed to slow those down. These are helpful traditions, not sure things, so do not worry if your garden does a little differently.
companions.note_seasoned: Garlic's companion reputation rests almost entirely on its sulfur scent, traditionally credited with deterring aphids, spider mites, and some borers, which is why it is interplanted among roses, fruit trees, tomatoes, and brassicas. The one firm caution is the legume conflict: alliums are widely held to inhibit beans and peas, so keep garlic away from them. Most of these pairings are traditional rather than trial-proven, and garlic's long fall-to-summer occupancy means it shares the bed with whatever overwinters or goes in around it; treat the pairings as low-risk suggestions, not guarantees.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Tomatoes
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Garlic's strong smell is thought to help keep aphids and spider mites off tomatoes, and the two fit together in the bed because garlic is finishing up in early summer as tomatoes take off.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: A popular folk pairing resting on the general allium pest-repel reputation; no measured garlic-tomato trial. The timing fit (garlic clears in early summer) is real and practical.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Tomatoes are a traditional garlic companion on the allium pest-repel reputation, the scent said to discourage aphids and spider mites, plus a tidy timing fit: fall-planted garlic is sizing and harvested in early summer just as tomatoes need the room. The pest claim is folk wisdom rather than a tested effect, but the pairing is low-risk and space-efficient.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Roses and fruit trees
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Garlic is a classic underplanting for roses and fruit trees, where its smell is believed to help fend off aphids and borers. It takes little room and is harvested before midsummer.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Long-standing ornamental/orchard companion tradition; the aphid/borer deterrence is widely repeated but not well documented in trials.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Underplanting roses and fruit trees with garlic is a long-standing tradition, the pungent foliage credited with deterring aphids and some borers. It is a space-and-scent pairing rather than a demonstrated effect; garlic's small footprint and early-summer harvest make it an easy, low-competition neighbor for perennials.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Brassicas (cabbage, broccoli)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Cabbage-family plants share garlic's cool-season liking, and the strong garlic smell is thought to bother some of their pests like aphids and cabbage worms.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Mirror of the broad allium-brassica scent-deterrence tradition; plausible but not isolated for garlic specifically.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Brassicas are interplanted with garlic on the same allium-scent logic used for onions: the sulfur smell is traditionally credited with masking the cabbage family from aphids and caterpillars. Garlic is shallow and undemanding, so it tucks between cole crops without competing, though the pest benefit is traditional rather than trial-proven for garlic.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Carrots and beets
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Garlic grows alongside carrots and beets without crowding them, and its smell is said to help confuse pests like the carrot rust fly. They use different space above and below ground.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Carries the better-evidenced allium scent-masking-of-carrot-rust-fly tradition (strongest on the onion side) plus sound non-competition; garlic-specific data is thin, so medium at best.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Carrots and beets pair with garlic on complementary form and the allium scent-masking tradition, the same logic behind the well-known carrot-and-onion pairing against carrot rust fly. Garlic sends a narrow bulb down with little leafy spread, so it shares space efficiently. The scent-masking effect is best evidenced for onions; for garlic treat it as a reasonable, low-risk extension.

good_seasoned.name: Tomatoes
good_seasoned.timing: interplant; garlic clears in early summer
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional pairing on the allium pest-repel reputation plus a timing fit: garlic is harvested in early summer as tomatoes expand. The aphid and mite deterrence is folk wisdom, not a measured effect.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Folk allium-repel pairing; no garlic-tomato trial.

good_seasoned.name: Roses and fruit trees
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A classic ornamental and orchard underplanting; the pungent foliage is credited with deterring aphids and borers. Space-and-scent tradition rather than a documented effect.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Long-standing companion tradition, not trial-proven.

good_seasoned.name: Brassicas (cabbage, broccoli)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Cool-season cabbage crops share garlic's window, and the allium scent is traditionally said to discourage their aphids and caterpillars. Anecdotal for garlic specifically.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Allium-brassica scent tradition; not isolated for garlic.

good_seasoned.name: Carrots and beets
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Complementary root habit and the allium scent-masking tradition (strongest for the carrot-and-onion pairing against carrot rust fly) make these easy, space-efficient neighbors for garlic.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Extends the better-evidenced onion-carrot scent-masking; thin for garlic itself.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Beans and peas
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep garlic away from beans and peas. Garlic and its onion relatives are long believed to slow the growth of these legumes, so plant them in separate parts of the garden.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: The allium-legume antagonism is one of the oldest and most consistently repeated companion cautions; mechanism is debated but the tradition is strong and widely taught.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Beans and peas are the standard allium caution: garlic, like onion, is traditionally held to inhibit legume growth, so the two are kept apart. The mechanism is not firmly established, but the recommendation is consistent across companion guidance, so separate garlic from beans and peas as a low-cost precaution.

bad_seasoned.name: Beans and peas
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Alliums including garlic are traditionally held to inhibit beans and peas, so keep them in separate parts of the garden. The mechanism is debated, but the caution is long-standing and consistent.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Classic, widely repeated allium-legume antagonism; not mechanistically pinned down.

pests.name: Onion thrips
pests.identification_seasoned: Tiny slender insects rasping silvery streaks and flecks into the leaves and down in the leaf folds; heavy feeding in warm, dry spells reduces bulb size.
pests.identification_beginner: Very small insects that leave silvery streaks and specks on the leaves, often hiding in the tight folds where leaves meet. Bad infestations shrink the bulbs.
pests.cause_seasoned: Onion thrips (Thrips tabaci) build through warm, dry weather and shelter in the leaf axils where sprays miss them; they move readily between alliums.
pests.cause_beginner: A tiny insect called onion thrips. It multiplies fast in warm, dry weather and hides in the tight folds of the leaves.
pests.management_seasoned: Keep plants vigorous and watered, hose off light infestations, use reflective mulch, and rotate away from alliums; treat persistent outbreaks per local extension guidance.
pests.management_beginner: Keep the plants healthy and watered, spray them off with water if thrips are light, and do not plant garlic where onions or garlic grew last year. For heavy infestations, ask your local extension office what to use.

pests.name: Onion maggot
pests.identification_seasoned: Wilting, yellowing plants and rotting bulbs riddled by small white larvae; stand loss is worst in cool, wet conditions and where allium debris carries the pest over.
pests.identification_beginner: Plants wilt and yellow, and bulbs rot with small white grubs inside. Worst in cool, wet weather.
pests.cause_seasoned: Larvae of the onion maggot fly (Delia antiqua), whose eggs are laid at the plant base; populations carry over in allium residue and cull bulbs.
pests.cause_beginner: The larvae (maggots) of a small fly that lays eggs at the base of the plants. They survive in leftover onion and garlic debris.
pests.management_seasoned: Rotate away from alliums, remove cull bulbs and crop residue, and avoid planting into fresh manure; cultural sanitation is the main home-garden tool.
pests.management_beginner: Do not plant garlic in the same place each year, and clean up old onion and garlic scraps where the fly breeds.

pests.name: Stem and bulb nematode (garlic bloat nematode)
pests.identification_seasoned: Stunting, distortion, yellowing, and premature dieback of leaves, with swollen, distorted stems and bulbs; infected bulbs turn brown, shrivel, go lightweight, and the wrapper layers crack and detach from the basal plate, with damage progressing in storage.
pests.identification_beginner: Plants are stunted and yellow and die back early. The bulbs turn brown, shrivel, feel light, and their papery skins crack and peel away from the base. The damage keeps getting worse in storage.
pests.cause_seasoned: The stem and bulb nematode (Ditylenchus dipsaci), the garlic bloat nematode, a microscopic worm that feeds inside the leaves, stems, and bulbs. It rides in on infected planting cloves and survives dried in soil and debris for at least four years, favored by cool, moist conditions.
pests.cause_beginner: A microscopic worm that lives and feeds inside the leaves, stems, and bulbs. It usually arrives on infected cloves you plant and can survive dried in the soil for years.
pests.management_seasoned: Plant only clean, tested, nematode-free seed stock, the single most important practice; rotate garlic out for four years with poor-host crops (carrots, potatoes, spinach, corn, wheat); remove and destroy infected plants and debris. Hot-water seed dips are no longer recommended because they only reduce, not eliminate, the nematode.
pests.management_beginner: Start with clean, healthy cloves from a trusted source, since this is how the worm usually arrives. Do not grow garlic or onions in that spot for four years, and pull and throw away any infected plants. Crops like carrots, potatoes, and corn are safe to grow there in between.

diseases.name: White rot
diseases.identification_seasoned: Leaves decay at the base, yellow, wilt, and topple, and the plant pulls up easily; a fluffy white mold and tiny black sclerotia about the size of a poppy seed form on the rotting roots and bulb. It is the most serious soilborne disease of garlic.
diseases.identification_beginner: The plant yellows and wilts from the bottom and pulls out of the ground easily. You find white fuzzy mold and tiny black specks on the rotting roots and bulb.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Sclerotium cepivorum, which produces hardy sclerotia that survive in soil for many years and germinate in the cool soils garlic grows in (activity is restricted above about 75°F). It spreads on contaminated soil, tools, and infected cloves.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soil fungus that makes tiny long-lived resting bodies that can sit in the ground for years and attack in cool weather. It spreads on dirty tools, soil, and infected cloves.
diseases.management_seasoned: There is no cure once soil is infested. Plant only disease-free cloves in clean soil, never move contaminated soil into new ground, remove and destroy infected plants, and use long allium-free rotations; the fungus persists for years, so prevention is everything.
diseases.management_beginner: There is no fix once it is in the soil, so prevention is key. Plant only clean cloves in clean ground, do not move soil from an infected bed, pull and destroy sick plants, and keep alliums out of that spot for years.

diseases.name: Fusarium basal rot
diseases.identification_seasoned: Yellowing and dieback of leaves, stunting, and a brown dry rot that starts at the basal plate (the root end) and spreads up into the bulb, which becomes pitted; roots die back and bulbs rot in the field and in storage.
diseases.identification_beginner: Leaves yellow and die back and the plant is stunted. The bottom of the bulb turns brown and rots, and the decay works its way up into the bulb.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Soilborne Fusarium oxysporum (including f. sp. cepae) and related species that persist in soil for years and progress fastest in warm soils (about 77 to 82°F); wounds, maggot feeding, and infected cloves open the door.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soil fungus that lives in the ground for years and does the most damage in warm soil. Injuries and infected cloves let it in.
diseases.management_seasoned: Plant clean, tested cloves, rotate out of alliums for several years, avoid wounding bulbs, store cured bulbs cool (below about 39°F) and dry, and choose less-susceptible stock where available.
diseases.management_beginner: Plant healthy cloves, do not grow garlic in the same spot for several years, handle the bulbs gently so they are not injured, and store them cool and dry.

diseases.name: Botrytis neck rot
diseases.identification_seasoned: A soft, water-soaked rot starting at the neck after harvest, with a gray mold on or between the scales and later small black sclerotia; poorly cured, thick-necked, or immature bulbs are most affected.
diseases.identification_beginner: Garlic goes soft and rotten at the neck after harvest, often with a gray mold. It mostly hits bulbs that were not dried well or were picked too green.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Botrytis species that overwinter on debris and infected bulbs and as sclerotia in soil; excess late nitrogen, rain or irrigation late in the season, and inadequate curing or storage all worsen it.
diseases.cause_beginner: A mold that gets into the necks of garlic that was harvested too green or dried poorly. Too much late fertilizer and wet weather near harvest make it worse.
diseases.management_seasoned: Stop nitrogen by early May, cut water before harvest, cure thoroughly until necks are tight and dry, handle gently, and store cool and dry with good airflow.
diseases.management_beginner: Stop feeding by early May, stop watering before harvest, dry (cure) the garlic well until the necks are tight, and store it cool, dry, and airy.

diseases.name: Garlic rust
diseases.identification_seasoned: Small orange to rust-colored pustules scattered on the leaves, which in heavy cases yellow and die back early and reduce bulb size; usually a minor problem but worse in cool, humid, crowded plantings, notably in coastal and mild-winter areas.
diseases.identification_beginner: Little orange or rusty spots and bumps on the leaves. Usually minor, but a bad case yellows the leaves early and makes smaller bulbs. It likes cool, damp, crowded plantings.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A Puccinia rust fungus favored by cool temperatures, leaf wetness, and high humidity; spores spread on wind and splashing water and overwinter on volunteer alliums.
diseases.cause_beginner: A rust fungus that spreads in cool, damp weather through wet leaves and splashing water.
diseases.management_seasoned: Space for airflow, avoid overhead watering and excess nitrogen, remove volunteer alliums and badly infected leaves, and rotate; rust is usually minor enough that cultural steps suffice in the home garden.
diseases.management_beginner: Give plants room for air to move, water at the base, do not over-fertilize, and pull out badly spotted leaves and any volunteer onions or garlic nearby. It is usually minor.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Keep the soil evenly moist through spring leaf growth and bulbing, about an inch of water per week including rain. Then taper and stop watering about two weeks before harvest so the bulbs firm up and the wrappers cure clean.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water garlic regularly in spring so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly an inch a week. Then stop watering a couple of weeks before harvest so the bulbs can dry down and the skins set.
watering.amount_seasoned: Roughly one inch of water per week from rain plus irrigation through the spring growing season; more in warm, dry, or sandy conditions, delivered steadily rather than in swings.
watering.amount_beginner: About one inch of water a week while the plants are growing in spring, and a bit more in warm, dry weather. Steady is better than a flood one week and nothing the next.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base with drip or a soaker to keep the foliage dry; wet leaves and standing water feed the leaf and bulb rots garlic is prone to.
watering.method_beginner: Water the soil at the base of the plants, not over the leaves. Keeping the tops dry helps prevent disease.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing, soft lower leaves and a sour smell signal waterlogging; saturated soil over winter and at bulbing drives white rot, basal rot, and neck rot.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If the soil stays soggy and the bottoms of the plants turn yellow and soft, that is too much water. Garlic sitting in wet soil rots.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Bluish, tip-burned, or prematurely dying leaves and stalled growth mean the bulbs are short of water during the spring sizing window, which caps final bulb size.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Wilting, blue-tinged, or brown-tipped leaves in spring mean the garlic is too dry. Garlic that dries out while sizing makes smaller bulbs.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Base or drip watering keeps the foliage dry, which matters for garlic because lingering leaf wetness and saturated soil feed the storage rots that spoil bulbs after harvest.
watering.method_note_beginner: Watering at the base instead of over the leaves keeps the tops dry, and dry tops are less likely to catch the diseases that make garlic rot in storage.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Spring leaf growth and bulb sizing are the water-sensitive weeks; never let the bed dry out then. Equally important is cutting water off about two weeks before harvest so the wrappers cure tight.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The most important time to water is during spring growth and while the bulbs are sizing up. Then stop about two weeks before harvest so the bulbs dry down properly.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Not applicable. Garlic is planted directly in the ground from cloves in fall, not raised as transplants, so there is no indoor start or hardening-off step. Break a bulb into cloves just before planting and set the largest ones, papery wrappers intact, pointed end up.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: Not needed. You plant garlic straight in the garden from cloves in fall, so there are no seedlings to harden off. Just split a bulb into individual cloves right before planting and put the biggest ones in pointy side up.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Garlic is grown from cloves, not seed. Break apart firm, healthy bulbs into individual cloves just before planting, keep the papery skins on, and plant the largest cloves pointed end up about 2 to 3 inches deep and 4 to 6 inches apart in fall. Bigger cloves make bigger bulbs, so save the largest for planting and eat the small inner ones. Use clean, disease-free seed stock from a reputable source, since white rot and bloat nematode ride in on infected cloves.
start_method.notes_beginner: Garlic does not grow from seed, you plant the cloves. Just before planting in fall, break a bulb into separate cloves and leave the papery skin on each one. Plant the biggest cloves pointy side up, about 2 to 3 inches deep and 4 to 6 inches apart. Big cloves grow big bulbs, so plant the largest and cook with the little ones. Start with healthy cloves from a trusted source so you do not bring in disease.

drainage.saucer_practice_seasoned: Empty the saucer after each watering; garlic must never sit in standing water, which saturates the bulb zone over winter and rots the cloves.
drainage.saucer_practice_beginner: After you water, pour out any water that collects in the saucer. Garlic should never sit in standing water, because soggy soil rots the cloves, especially over winter.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Use a bag of potting mix with some compost stirred in.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in compost, and a little slow-release fertilizer at planting helps.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: A free-draining potting mix blended with compost.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Work in compost for fertility and a slow-release balanced feed at planting; keep the mix free-draining for the long overwinter.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out faster than the ground, so check often in spring growth, but do not keep the mix soggy over winter or the cloves rot.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Because watering washes food out of pots, feed container garlic a little more often through spring, then stop by early May.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Garlic in a pot is meant to overwinter, since you plant it in fall and harvest the next summer. In cold areas the roots in a pot freeze harder than in the ground, so sink the pot, move it against the house or into an unheated shed or cold frame, or mulch it well, and let it freeze and rest rather than trying to keep it growing.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Overwintering is the whole point of a garlic container: fall-planted, it sits dormant through winter and finishes the next summer. The limited root volume of a pot freezes colder than open ground, so in cold zones sink the pot, move it to a cold frame or unheated structure, or heap mulch around it; the goal is to carry the cloves safely through the cold, not to force winter growth.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Garlic grows fine in a deep pot because its roots are not huge. Use a container at least 8 inches deep with drainage holes, plant cloves 4 to 6 inches apart in fall, and plan to leave it out all winter. Keep it watered in spring and stop a couple of weeks before harvest.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Garlic is workable in containers given depth and drainage. Use a pot at least 8 inches deep, 3 gallons or more, set cloves 4 to 6 inches apart in fall, and treat it as a year-long resident: it overwinters in the pot and matures the next summer. Containers dry fast in spring, so water steadily through bulbing, then cut water two weeks before harvest. The main risk is winter waterlogging in a pot that drains poorly.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Expect to water more often than in-ground during spring growth; the shallow pot volume dries quickly and a drought check at sizing shrinks bulbs. Keep the mix on the dry side over winter to avoid clove rot.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Frequent spring watering leaches nutrients, so feed container garlic lightly but regularly through leaf growth, then stop by early May as in the ground.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering containers are a poor match for garlic: the constantly moist reservoir keeps the bulb zone too wet over the long overwinter and during the curing-down before harvest, both of which invite clove and bulb rot. A free-draining pot you water on demand is safer.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: Skip a self-watering pot for garlic. It keeps the soil too wet for a crop that sits all winter and needs to dry out before harvest, which can rot the bulbs. A regular pot with drainage holes that you water yourself is better.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Do not follow garlic or other alliums (onion, leek, shallot, chives) in the same ground. Garlic's worst soilborne problems, white rot and bloat nematode, persist for years and build up under continuous alliums; extension guidance is to rotate garlic out for about 4 years.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Do not plant garlic where you grew garlic, onions, or leeks recently. The diseases and the nematode that hit garlic live in the soil for years and build up, so wait about 4 years before alliums return to the same spot.
rotation.good_after: legumes, leafy greens, or other non-alliums such as carrots, potatoes, corn
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate so garlic and its allium relatives do not return to the same bed for about 4 years. White rot sclerotia survive in soil for years and bloat nematode persists in debris, so a long rotation away from the whole family is the core defense. Carrots, potatoes, spinach, corn, and grains are good rotation crops because they are poor hosts for the bloat nematode.
rotation.note_beginner: Keep moving garlic around the garden. Wait about 4 years before planting garlic, onions, or leeks in the same spot, because soil diseases and the nematode build up there. Following garlic with crops like carrots, potatoes, or corn, which the nematode does not feed on, helps clean the ground.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: After curing, store cured bulbs in a cool, dry, airy place. The classic storage range is cool and dry, around 32 to 40°F for long holding, though many cooks simply keep braids or bulbs at a cool room temperature out of light. Warm, humid spots and the 40 to 60°F range encourage sprouting.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Once the garlic is cured (dried), keep the bulbs somewhere cool, dry, and airy, out of the light. A cool pantry works for a while; a steady cool spot keeps them longest. Damp or warm places make garlic sprout and soften.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Whole cured bulbs store poorly in the refrigerator: the 40 to 50°F, humid environment is exactly what triggers sprouting, so keep them cool and dry instead. Peeled cloves can be refrigerated briefly for convenience.
storage.fridge_beginner: Do not store whole garlic bulbs in the fridge. The cold, damp air actually makes them sprout. Keep cured bulbs in a cool, dry cupboard instead. You can refrigerate a few peeled cloves for a day or two if it is handy.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Garlic freezes well peeled and chopped, or as a puree, for cooking; texture softens, so use frozen garlic in cooked dishes rather than raw.
storage.freezer_beginner: You can peel and chop garlic and freeze it for cooking. It goes soft after thawing, so use frozen garlic in cooked food, not raw.
storage.notes_seasoned: Storage life tracks type and curing. Well-cured softneck types (artichoke, silverskin) keep the longest, commonly six to nine months or more, which is why they are the braiding and grocery-store garlics. Hardneck types are richer-flavored but shorter-keeping, often about four to six months. Good curing, dry necks and papery wrappers, is the single biggest lever on how long any garlic keeps.
storage.notes_beginner: How long garlic keeps depends on the type and how well you dried it. Softneck garlics (the braiding kinds) keep longest, often six to nine months. Hardneck garlics taste stronger but keep a shorter time, often four to six months, so eat those first. Drying the bulbs well is the most important thing for good storage.

recommended.name: Music
recommended.recommended_note: A Porcelain hardneck prized in the cold North: very winter-hardy, large easy-to-peel cloves, strong flavor, and produces scapes. A reliable first hardneck. Stores well for a hardneck, roughly six months.

recommended.name: German White (German Extra Hardy)
recommended.recommended_note: Another hardy Porcelain hardneck with big cloves and a robust flavor, well suited to cold-winter gardens. Produces scapes; moderate storage.

recommended.name: Spanish Roja
recommended.recommended_note: A classic Rocambole hardneck with rich, complex flavor and easy-peel cloves, a favorite in the cooler North and Pacific Northwest. Needs a real cold winter and stores only a few months, so use it first.

recommended.name: Chesnok Red
recommended.recommended_note: A Purple Stripe hardneck that holds its flavor when cooked and roasts beautifully; attractive purple-streaked wrappers, scape-producing, hardy.

recommended.name: Inchelium Red
recommended.recommended_note: A widely adaptable Artichoke softneck that performs from the South to the North, with a mild flavor, many cloves, and long storage. A safe, forgiving pick if you are unsure of your climate, and braidable.

recommended.name: California Early / California Late
recommended.recommended_note: The standard Artichoke softneck supermarket garlics, well adapted to mild-winter and warm regions; mild flavor, heavy yields, and long storage. California Late keeps a little longer than California Early.

recommended.name: Creole and Silverskin types
recommended.recommended_note: Softneck groups suited to the warm South and low desert, where hardnecks fail for lack of winter cold. Silverskins are the longest-storing and best braiders; Creoles tolerate mild winters and heat. Elephant garlic, often sold as garlic, is actually a leek relative with mild, large cloves and poor storage.

varieties.note_seasoned: Choose by winter cold first, then by use. Hardneck garlics (Rocambole, Porcelain, Purple Stripe groups, such as Music, German White, Spanish Roja, Chesnok Red) need a genuine cold winter to vernalize and bulb, produce edible scapes, have fewer larger cloves, and store a shorter time, so they shine in the North. Softneck garlics (Artichoke and Silverskin groups, such as Inchelium Red, California Early and Late, Creole and Silverskin types) tolerate mild winters, yield more smaller cloves, braid well, and store the longest, so they are the choice for the South and warm regions. Where winters are mild, lean softneck; where winters are cold, hardnecks reward you with flavor. Elephant garlic is a leek relative, not true garlic.
varieties.note_beginner: Pick the type that matches your winters first. In cold-winter areas, grow hardneck garlic (like Music, Spanish Roja, or Chesnok Red), which needs real cold, makes big cloves, and gives you edible scapes, but does not store as long. In mild-winter and southern areas, grow softneck garlic (like Inchelium Red or California Early), which handles warm winters, makes lots of cloves, braids nicely, and keeps the longest. If you are not sure, Inchelium Red is forgiving in many climates. Elephant garlic is not really garlic, it is a mild leek relative.

growth_stages.name: Planting & Rooting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: In fall you set cloves pointed end up, 2 to 3 inches deep and 4 to 6 inches apart. Over the next few weeks roots grow and a small shoot may push up before cold sets in; the cloves are anchoring and beginning to vernalize, not yet making top growth.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: After you plant the cloves in fall, they grow roots underground and may send up a small green shoot before winter. This is normal. The garlic is settling in and starting to feel the cold it needs, not making big leaves yet.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Plant on time for your zone, water in, and once the ground starts to freeze in cold regions cover the bed with 3 to 4 inches of straw or shredded-leaf mulch to buffer the soil through winter and prevent freeze-thaw heaving.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Plant the cloves at the right time for your area and water them in. In cold regions, once the ground begins to freeze, cover the bed with a few inches of straw or chopped leaves to protect the cloves over winter.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record your planting date, variety, and clove size; over seasons this is the best predictor of bulb size and timing for your site.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Write down when you planted, which kind of garlic, and how big the cloves were. It helps you do better next year.

growth_stages.name: Overwintering & Spring Shoots
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Through winter the plant is largely dormant under mulch in cold regions, or grows slowly in mild ones. As soil warms in late winter to early spring, green shoots emerge or resume and the plant begins building leaves, the leaves that will become bulb wrappers.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: In cold areas the garlic mostly rests under its mulch all winter. In mild areas it keeps growing slowly. When spring arrives, green shoots come up and the plant starts making leaves.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: In spring, pull mulch back if it is matting wet over the crowns, begin nitrogen feeding as shoots resume, and keep the bed weed-free; garlic competes poorly with weeds and early weed control protects yield.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: In spring, loosen the winter mulch if it is soggy, start feeding nitrogen as the shoots grow, and keep weeds pulled, because weeds easily crowd out young garlic.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Note when shoots emerged or resumed and your first spring feeding; emergence timing tracks how your winter ran.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Write down when the green shoots came up in spring and when you first fed the plants.

growth_stages.name: Spring Leaf Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The plant adds upright leaves through spring. This is the size-setting stage: each leaf corresponds to a bulb wrapper, so vigorous, uninterrupted leaf growth now sets the bulb-size ceiling. You want steady moisture and feeding, not a check from drought, weeds, or starvation.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The garlic grows lots of upright leaves in spring. This stage matters most for bulb size, because the leaves now turn into the layers of the bulb later. The more healthy leaves it grows, the bigger the bulb can be.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Push leaf growth: keep moisture even, finish nitrogen feeding by early May, and stay on top of weeds. Front-load feeding so the canopy is built before bulbing; nitrogen applied late delays bulbing and worsens storage.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Help it grow leaves now: keep the soil evenly moist, finish feeding nitrogen by early May, and keep weeds out. Feed early, because feeding late leads to soft necks that do not store.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Track leaf count and feeding dates; leaf count going into bulbing is the best in-season predictor of final bulb size.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Count the leaves and note when you fed. More leaves now usually means bigger bulbs later.

growth_stages.name: Scaping & Bulbing
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: On hardneck types a curling flower stalk (the scape) rises from the center in late spring; the base then begins to swell into a bulb as the plant shifts from leaves to filling cloves. Lower leaves start to age. This is the fast-fill window, when steady moisture translates directly into bulb size.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: On hardneck garlic a curling stalk called a scape grows up from the middle in late spring. Around then the bulb starts to swell underground and the plant stops making new leaves. This is when the bulb puts on most of its size.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: On hardnecks, snip the scape off once it curls to redirect energy into the bulb (and eat it, it is a delicacy). Hold even moisture through sizing and keep nitrogen off; do not bend or knock down the tops to force maturity.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: If you grow hardneck garlic, cut off the curly scape when it appears so the plant puts its energy into the bulb, and cook with the scape. Keep watering evenly while the bulb sizes up, and do not add more fertilizer now.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Note the scape date (hardnecks) and any dry spells during sizing; matching these to final size tunes your timing.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Write down when the scapes appeared and any times the bed dried out while bulbs were sizing.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The lower leaves brown and die back while several upper leaves stay green; the cue is when about a third to half of the leaves have turned, with roughly the lower half browning and five or so green leaves remaining (each green leaf is an intact wrapper). Pull a test bulb: if the cloves fill the skins and the wrappers are intact, it is ready.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The lower leaves turn brown and die back while the top leaves are still green. Garlic is ready when about a third to a half of the leaves have browned. Dig one bulb to check: if the cloves fill out the skins, it is time.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Stop watering about two weeks ahead, then lift, do not pull, the bulbs gently with a fork on a dry day to avoid bruising. Do not wait for all the leaves to brown, which over-matures the bulbs and splits the wrappers and storage.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Stop watering about two weeks before, then loosen the bulbs out of the ground with a fork on a dry day, handling them gently. Do not wait until all the leaves are brown, or the bulbs split open and store poorly.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record the harvest date and how many green leaves remained; green-leaf count at harvest is the cleanest maturity gauge to repeat.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Write down when you harvested and how many green leaves were left. It helps you judge timing next year.

growth_stages.name: Curing & Storage
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Freshly lifted bulbs are not storage-ready until cured: hung or laid out with tops attached in a warm, dry, airy, shaded place for two to four weeks, the necks dry tight and the outer wrappers turn papery, sealing the bulb against rot.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Just-dug garlic needs to dry before storing. Keep the bulbs with their tops on in a warm, dry, airy, shady spot for two to four weeks until the necks dry shut and the skins go papery.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cure with good airflow out of direct sun, keeping tops and roots on until dry. Then trim tops to about an inch and roots close, brush off loose dirt (do not wash), and store cool and dry; save the biggest bulbs as next year's seed.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Dry the garlic in a shady, breezy place out of the sun, leaving the tops and roots on until it is fully dry. Then trim the tops and roots, brush off the dirt (do not wash it), and store it cool and dry. Keep your biggest bulbs to replant.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Log the curing length and how the bulbs stored; curing time versus storage life is the feedback that pays off all season.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Write down how long you dried the garlic and how well it kept, so you know how long to cure next time.

notifications.body_seasoned: Plant cloves in fall, generally a few weeks before to just after your first hard frost, so they root before the ground freezes. Set the largest cloves pointed end up, 2 to 3 inches deep and 4 to 6 inches apart. In mild and southern regions, choose softneck types.
notifications.body_beginner: Plant garlic cloves in fall, around the time of your first hard frost, so they grow roots before winter. Put the biggest cloves in pointy side up, 2 to 3 inches deep and 4 to 6 inches apart. In mild or southern areas, use softneck garlic.

notifications.body_seasoned: In cold regions, once the ground begins to freeze, cover the bed with 3 to 4 inches of straw or shredded-leaf mulch. It buffers soil temperature swings and prevents freeze-thaw heaving that can push cloves out of the ground over winter.
notifications.body_beginner: In cold areas, once the ground starts to freeze, cover the garlic with a few inches of straw or chopped leaves. This protects the cloves through winter and keeps the freezing and thawing soil from pushing them up.

notifications.title_seasoned: Feed garlic as spring shoots resume
notifications.body_seasoned: As shoots resume growth in early spring, side-dress nitrogen to drive the leaf growth that sets bulb size, and repeat in two to three weeks. Stop nitrogen by early May; late feeding delays bulbing and worsens storage.
notifications.body_beginner: When green shoots start growing in early spring, feed your garlic a nitrogen fertilizer to grow lots of leaves, and feed again a couple of weeks later. Stop feeding by early May.

notifications.title_beginner: Cut off the curly stalks (hardneck garlic)
notifications.body_seasoned: If you grow hardneck garlic, a curling scape will rise in late spring. Snip it off once it curls so the plant puts energy into the bulb rather than the flower, and cook the scape, it is a delicacy. Softneck garlic usually makes none.
notifications.body_beginner: If you grow hardneck garlic, a curly stalk (a scape) grows up in late spring. Cut it off when it curls so the plant feeds the bulb instead, and cook the scape, it is tasty. Softneck garlic usually does not make one.

notifications.title_beginner: Time to harvest and dry garlic
notifications.body_seasoned: When about a third to half the leaves have browned and several upper leaves stay green, stop watering, then lift gently with a fork on a dry day. Cure two to four weeks in a warm, airy, shaded spot until necks are tight and wrappers papery, then trim and store cool and dry.
notifications.body_beginner: When about a third to half the leaves have turned brown but the top ones are still green, stop watering, then dig the bulbs gently with a fork on a dry day. Dry them two to four weeks in a shady, airy spot until the necks are tight, then trim and store cool and dry.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Cover garlic before a hard freeze
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Fall-planted garlic is cold-hardy and needs winter cold, but bare beds in cold regions suffer freeze-thaw heaving that lifts cloves out of the soil. Cover with 3 to 4 inches of straw or leaf mulch before hard freezes set in; the goal is to steady the soil, not to keep the plants growing.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Garlic needs winter cold, but in cold areas the freezing and thawing of bare soil can push the cloves up out of the ground. Cover the bed with a few inches of straw or leaves before hard freezes to keep the soil steady.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat and dry stress while bulbs size
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot, dry weather while bulbs grow
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A hot, dry spell during spring leaf growth and bulb sizing checks the swell and caps final size, since any drought interruption costs bulb weight. Water deeply and evenly through the spell, and mulch helps hold moisture in the shallow root zone; ease off only as harvest approaches.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Hot, dry weather while the garlic is growing leaves and sizing bulbs makes smaller bulbs. Water deeply and evenly during the spell, and a layer of mulch helps keep the soil from drying out. Only stop watering as harvest gets close.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Wet weather at harvest and curing
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Rain while harvesting or drying garlic
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Rain and humidity during harvest and curing invite neck rot and white-mold staining, since bulbs cure only when necks dry tight. If a wet stretch hits before harvest, wait for dry soil to lift, and move curing under cover with strong airflow out of direct sun.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Rain and damp air while you harvest or dry garlic can cause rot at the neck, because garlic only dries properly when the necks dry out. If it turns wet before harvest, wait for a dry day to dig, and dry the bulbs under cover where air moves well.

planting.text_seasoned: Plant the largest cloves, pointed end up, 2 to 3 inches deep and 4 to 6 inches apart in fall; big cloves make big bulbs, so save the largest for seed and cook the small inner ones. Use clean, healthy stock to keep white rot and bloat nematode out.
planting.text_beginner: Plant your biggest cloves, pointy side up, 2 to 3 inches deep and 4 to 6 inches apart in fall. Big cloves grow big bulbs. Use healthy cloves from a good source so you do not bring in disease.

early_growth.text_seasoned: In cold regions mulch the bed with 3 to 4 inches of straw or leaves after the ground starts to freeze to prevent winter heaving, then pull it back in spring if it mats wet over the crowns. Start nitrogen as shoots resume and keep weeds out early.
early_growth.text_beginner: In cold areas, cover the bed with a few inches of straw or chopped leaves once the ground starts to freeze, to protect the garlic over winter. In spring, loosen soggy mulch, start feeding, and keep weeds pulled.

established.text_seasoned: Garlic builds its bulb from the leaves it grows in spring, so push steady leaf growth with even moisture and nitrogen, and finish feeding by early May. Late nitrogen delays bulbing and gives thick necks that store poorly.
established.text_beginner: The leaves garlic grows in spring become the layers of the bulb, so keep it watered and fed for strong leaf growth, but stop feeding nitrogen by early May so the bulbs form well.

bulb_forming.text_seasoned: On hardneck garlic, cut the scape once it curls to send energy into the bulb, and enjoy the scape in the kitchen. Keep moisture even through sizing and stop adding nitrogen.
bulb_forming.text_beginner: If you grow hardneck garlic, snip off the curly scape when it appears so the plant feeds the bulb instead, and cook with the scape. Keep watering evenly and stop fertilizing.

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest when about a third to half the leaves have browned and several upper leaves are still green, after stopping water for about two weeks. Lift gently with a fork on a dry day; harvesting too late splits the wrappers and ruins storage.
harvest.text_beginner: Harvest when about a third to half of the leaves have turned brown but the top ones are still green. Stop watering about two weeks before, then dig the bulbs gently with a fork on a dry day.

curing.text_seasoned: Cure bulbs with tops on in a warm, dry, airy, shaded place for two to four weeks until necks are tight and wrappers papery, then trim and store cool and dry. Poor curing is the main cause of garlic rotting in storage.
curing.text_beginner: Dry the garlic with the tops still on in a warm, airy, shady spot for two to four weeks until the necks dry shut and the skins are papery. Then trim and store it cool and dry. Garlic that is not dried well rots.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: One bulb per planted clove, and each bulb typically holds 10 to 15 cloves (fewer, larger on hardnecks; more, smaller on softnecks). A 10-foot row at about 5-inch spacing yields roughly 24 bulbs.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Each clove you plant grows into one whole bulb, and each bulb has about 10 to 15 cloves inside. So a handful of cloves planted in fall becomes a basket of garlic the next summer.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Garlic of a given variety matures together in one main flush in early to mid summer, so the harvest comes all at once rather than over a long window; it is then cured and stored for months.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: All your garlic of one kind finishes around the same time in summer, so you harvest it together, then cure it and store it to use over the following months.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Matching type to your winter (hardneck where winters are cold, softneck where mild) and planting good-sized cloves in fall are the biggest first-year levers; the wrong type for your climate, or spring planting, gives small or split bulbs.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: The most important things for a good first harvest are choosing the right type for your winters and planting big cloves in fall. The wrong type, or planting in spring, gives small bulbs.
factors_seasoned: variety type matched to winter cold
clove size at planting
fall planting and vernalization
spring leaf growth before bulbing
early nitrogen then stop
steady moisture then cut water before harvest

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No verified evidence ties garlic bulbing or yield to moon phase; bulbing is driven by winter cold (vernalization), spring leaf growth, and lengthening days. Plant in fall by soil readiness and your frost timing, not lunar phase.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Bulbs stay small, or the plant makes one round undivided bulb instead of cloves.
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: The garlic bulbs are tiny, or you get one small round ball instead of a bulb with cloves.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Almost always too little vernalization: garlic needs several weeks of cold (roughly 32 to 50°F for a month or two) to divide into cloves and bulb properly. Spring planting, a too-warm winter, a softneck pushed into the deep South without pre-chilling, or planting too late all under-vernalize the crop. Small cloves and late nitrogen also cap size.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Usually not enough cold. Garlic needs several weeks of winter chill to split into cloves and make a real bulb. Planting in spring, a mild winter, or planting too late means it never gets enough cold, so you get a small round bulb. Tiny cloves and late feeding also keep bulbs small.
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Plant in fall, not spring, so the cloves get winter cold; choose hardnecks for cold winters and softnecks for mild ones; in warm regions pre-chill cloves about 6 to 8 weeks at 40°F before planting; plant large cloves and finish nitrogen by early May.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Plant in fall, not spring, so the garlic gets winter cold. Use hardneck types where winters are cold and softneck where they are mild. In warm areas, chill the cloves in the fridge for about 6 to 8 weeks before planting. Plant big cloves and stop feeding by early May.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Bulbs rot at the neck or base in storage, or wrappers stain and mold.
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Garlic rots at the top or bottom after you store it, or the skins get moldy.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Harvesting too late or too wet, poor curing, excess late nitrogen, and bruising drive neck rot, basal rot, and white-mold staining. Thick necks never seal, and bulbs put away before the necks dry tight rot from the inside.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Picking garlic too late or in wet weather, not drying it well, too much late fertilizer, and bruising all cause storage rot. Bulbs stored before the necks dry shut rot from the inside.
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Stop watering about two weeks before harvest, lift on a dry day and handle gently, cure two to four weeks until necks are tight and wrappers papery, finish nitrogen by early May, and store cool and dry with airflow.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Stop watering about two weeks before harvest, dig gently on a dry day, and dry the garlic two to four weeks until the necks are tight. Stop feeding by early May and store the bulbs cool, dry, and airy.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Cloves push up out of the soil over winter, or plants emerge poorly in spring.
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Cloves work their way up out of the ground in winter, or few come up in spring.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Freeze-thaw heaving in unmulched beds lifts shallow cloves, and very cold bare ground can kill marginally hardy or shallowly set cloves; planting too shallow or too late (insufficient rooting before freeze-up) makes both worse.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: When bare soil freezes and thaws over and over, it pushes the cloves up. Very cold bare ground can also kill cloves that were planted too shallow or too late to root well before winter.
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Plant at the right depth (2 to 3 inches) early enough to root before freeze-up, and mulch with 3 to 4 inches of straw or leaves once the ground starts to freeze; press any heaved cloves back down and re-cover.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Plant the cloves 2 to 3 inches deep, early enough to grow roots before winter, and cover the bed with a few inches of straw or leaves once it starts to freeze. Push any cloves that pop up back down and re-cover them.

UF/IFAS Northwest District Horticulture Vegetable Garden Planting Dates (Florida Panhandle)
UF/IFAS SP 103/VH021 Florida Vegetable Gardening Guide
UGA Extension Bulletin 577 (Vegetable Garden Planting Chart)

succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Garlic is a single, once-a-year crop. It is planted in one fall window, vernalizes over winter, and matures the following summer, so there is no staggering it within a season; every clove of a variety reaches harvest together. The next planting waits a full year, after a multi-year rotation away from the bed.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: garlic_author_fresh_pilot 2026-06-29 (scale batch, overwinter/vernalization stretch crop). Authored by FILLING the garlic shell, modeled structurally on the certified onion allium template. Calendar_basis=frost_anchored, archetype=cool_season_annual. Region fill complete across all 10 regions / 20 cells with non-empty 12-token overwinter calendars (fall plant -> winter dormancy or slow growth -> spring growth -> mid-summer harvest, spanning the year boundary). DEPARTURE FROM TEMPLATE: gating_factors set to [] (NOT onion's [photoperiod]) -- see open_findings; garlic's variety axis is hardneck/softneck driven by VERNALIZATION, not day-length cultivar class, and the A9 window-fit check (long-day=spring-planted) structurally contradicts a fall-planted, long-day-bulbing crop. Sources: 11 catalogued T1 ids, all WebFetch/WebSearch-read 2026-06-29 except low_desert_az (uariz PDF) and hawaii_tropical (CTAHR PDF), which are search-surfaced and flagged modeled. whole_crop_gate self-run to PASS; status author_fresh_pilot, launch flags false, NOT certified.

open_findings.summary: gating_factors set to [] rather than onion's [photoperiod]. Garlic IS photoperiod-responsive for bulbing (long days induce bulbing), but its varieties are classified hardneck vs softneck by VERNALIZATION (cold need), not by short/intermediate/long-day cultivar class, so there is no honest day_length_type to assign. The A9 window-fit gate (B4) also encodes onion's assumption that long_day = spring-planted; garlic is a fall-planted, long-day-bulbing crop, which that rule structurally rejects. Choosing [photoperiod] would force either biologically false day_length_type labels or an A9 failure. Flagged for Trevor: confirm [] (vernalization-driven, like the strawberry photoperiod-INVERSE precedent), or rule a garlic-specific gating model.

In cold regions the deep-winter overwintering months are modeled as cold_pause (the frost-bracketed dormant token). For garlic this means crop-in-ground-but-dormant, which differs from a warm-season annual's cold_pause (no crop planted). The app may render both identically, so a grower could read cold_pause as 'nothing to do' when garlic is actually overwintering in the bed and needs mulch. Flagged as a possible token-semantics gap for the overwinter lifecycle; no dedicated dormant-resident token exists today.

lifecycle set to 'perennial' (garlic is botanically a vegetatively propagated perennial, mirroring onion's biological 'biennial') while perennial:false marks it as grown as a single-cycle crop (not a standing perennial in the planner). Flagged in case the project prefers lifecycle 'annual' to reflect cultivation; chose the biology token to mirror onion's convention.

low_desert_az planting/harvest windows and the 4-to-6-week-below-40F vernalization figure are drawn from University of Arizona Maricopa County extension material (az1005 calendar + garlic factsheet) that is PDF-only and was read via WebSearch snippets, not a clean WebFetch. Cited to uariz_ext_az1005 (nearest catalog id). Modeled; verify against the live PDF in the daily review.

hawaii_tropical (elevation >500ft / Kula, pre-chilled cloves, Oct-Nov plant -> Mar-Apr harvest) is drawn from CTAHR garlic material (VC-8 and a CTAHR news article) that is PDF/article-only, read via WebSearch snippets, not a clean WebFetch. Cited to uhawaii_ctahr. Garlic is genuinely marginal in Hawaii (no natural winter chill); modeled, verify in the daily review.

fl_peninsula is modeled from UF/IFAS qualitative guidance (warm winters require pre-chilling cloves about two months; softneck/Creole or elephant garlic only; hardnecks fail). The specific month windows (plant Nov-Dec, harvest Mar-May) are inferred from that guidance plus the regional climate, not a dated FL garlic planting chart. Modeled; the daily review should confirm against a FL-specific source if one is catalogued.

warm_arid (zone 8 interior Southwest, e.g. New Mexico, west Texas) windows are modeled from neighboring continental T1 (USU garlic, Texas A&M garlic); no New-Mexico-specific garlic page was catalogued/read. The cold-winter, fall-plant, early-to-mid-summer-harvest shape is well supported, but verify NM timing against an NMSU source in review.

days_to_maturity set to [180, 270] (mid 240). Sources span the climate range: UGA gives 180-210 days (warm South, later plant), UMD gives 250-270 days (fall-planted, cold North). The wide range reflects the genuine region spread of an overwintered crop rather than a single figure.

germination_temp_f left empty: garlic is propagated vegetatively from cloves, not seed, so there is no seed germination temperature. Clove root growth and the cold vernalization requirement (about 32-50F for several weeks) are covered in prose and failure_diagnostics instead.

plant_out.label: main
plant_out.source_quote: Plant cloves in the fall, usually one or two weeks after the first killing frost
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Fall-planted in the cold North, garlic roots before freeze-up, overwinters dormant under mulch, resumes growth in spring, and is harvested the following mid summer. A single planting spanning the year; no spring planting (it under-vernalizes and bulbs poorly).

harvest_start.label: main
harvest_start.source_quote: harvest garlic between late June and late July
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Bulbs mature in mid summer as lower leaves brown.

harvest_end.label: main
harvest_end.source_quote: harvest when half or slightly more than half of the upper leaves remain green
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest window closes by late summer; lift before over-maturity splits the wrappers.

plantings_provenance.basis: Built from northern_tier cold-zone T1 (UMN growing-garlic, UMD growing-garlic, USU garlic-in-the-garden), verified live 2026-06-29. Fall plant -> overwinter dormant (mulched) -> spring growth -> mid-summer harvest, spanning the year boundary.

3.zone_notes: Coldest northern zone: plant in early-to-mid October so cloves root before hard freeze, mulch heavily for winter, growth resumes in spring, harvest in August. Lean on hardy hardneck (Porcelain) types.

4.zone_notes: Plant in October, mulch for winter, harvest mid-to-late summer. Hardneck types thrive on the cold winter here.

5.zone_notes: Plant in October, overwinter under mulch, harvest in July. Both hardneck and softneck succeed.

6.zone_notes: Plant October into November, mulch lightly, harvest early-to-mid summer.

7.zone_notes: Mild end of the cold tier: plant October-November, winter dormancy is short, harvest by June. Softnecks do well alongside hardnecks.

northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In the cold-winter North (zones 3 to 7), garlic is a fall-planted, overwintering crop. Set cloves October into November so they root before the ground freezes, mulch the bed once it begins to freeze to prevent heaving, and let the plants go dormant through winter. Growth resumes in spring and bulbs mature in early-to-mid summer. The reliable winter cold favors hardneck (Rocambole, Porcelain, Purple Stripe) types, which need it to vernalize and reward you with scapes and rich flavor.
northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the cold North, plant garlic in fall, around October. The cloves grow roots, then rest under a blanket of mulch all winter, and finish the next summer. Cover the bed with straw or leaves once the ground starts to freeze so the cloves are not pushed out. This cold-winter region is perfect for hardneck garlic, which needs real cold and gives you edible scapes.

se_gulf.region_label: Southeast and Gulf (humid subtropical South, zones 8-9)

plant_out.label: main
plant_out.source_quote: Late September through November is the time to plant garlic in Georgia
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Mild-winter South: fall-planted softneck garlic grows slowly through winter rather than going fully dormant, and is harvested in late spring. Hardnecks usually fail here for lack of winter cold.

harvest_start.label: main
harvest_start.source_quote: garlic will be ready to harvest from late May to mid-July
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Bulbs finish in late spring to early summer as a third to half the leaves brown.

harvest_end.label: main
harvest_end.source_quote: Harvest the garlic when one-third to one-half of the leaves have died back
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest before summer heat and humidity drive neck rot.

plantings_provenance.basis: Built from se_gulf T1 (UGA C854 garlic, Texas A&M Bexar County garlic, UMN), verified 2026-06-29. Softneck-led, fall plant -> slow winter growth -> late-spring harvest.

8.zone_notes: Plant October-November, grow slowly through the mild winter, harvest May-June. Choose softneck (Artichoke, Silverskin) or Creole types; hardnecks rarely get enough cold.

9.zone_notes: Warm end: plant October-November, harvest by May before heat sets in. Softneck and Creole types only.

se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: Across the humid subtropical South (zones 8 to 9), garlic is fall-planted and grows slowly through the mild winter rather than going dormant, maturing in late spring before summer heat and humidity bring on rot. Winters here are often too warm to fully vernalize hardneck types, so lean on softneck (Artichoke, Silverskin) and Creole garlics, which tolerate mild winters, and harvest promptly when a third to half the leaves brown.
se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the warm, humid South, plant garlic in fall (October-November). It grows slowly through the mild winter and is ready in late spring. Grow softneck garlic here, not hardneck, because the winters are usually too warm for hardneck types to make good bulbs. Harvest before the hot, muggy summer arrives.

plant_out.label: main
plant_out.source_quote: Plant in late fall, at least two weeks before the first frost (mid-October through the end of November)
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Interior California: fall-planted, grows through the cool winter, harvested in early summer. The mnemonic: plant by Thanksgiving, feed by St. Patrick's Day, stop water by Mother's Day, harvest by Father's Day.

harvest_start.label: main
harvest_start.source_quote: After the tops turn brown, around mid-June, dig them up
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Bulbs mature in early summer; lower leaves brown while upper leaves stay green.

harvest_end.label: main
harvest_end.source_quote: harvest when one-third to one-half of the leaves have died back
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest before the dry heat of high summer.

plantings_provenance.basis: Built from California T1 (UC Master Gardeners garlic, UMN), verified 2026-06-29. Fall plant -> cool-winter growth -> early-summer harvest.

8.zone_notes: Central Valley: plant mid-October to November, grow through the cool winter, harvest June-July. Both softneck and intermediate types do well.

9.zone_notes: Warmer valley floor: plant October-November, harvest by June. Softneck types preferred.

ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: In California's interior valleys (zones 8 to 9), garlic is planted in late fall, at least a couple of weeks before the first frost, grows through the cool, wet winter, and is harvested in early summer. A handy local rhythm is to plant by Thanksgiving, feed in March, stop watering by early May, and harvest around mid-June. Softneck and intermediate types suit the mild winters; the hottest valley floors are marginal for cold-demanding hardnecks.
ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In California's inland valleys, plant garlic in fall (mid-October to November), let it grow through the cool winter, and harvest in early summer. An easy way to remember it: plant by Thanksgiving, feed in March, stop watering in early May, and harvest in June. Softneck garlic does best here.

plant_out.label: main
plant_out.source_quote: Plant in late fall, at least two weeks before the first frost (mid-October through the end of November)
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Cool coastal California: fall-planted, grows through the mild, moist winter, harvested early-to-mid summer once tops brown.

harvest_start.label: main
harvest_start.source_quote: After the tops turn brown, around mid-June, dig them up
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Bulbs mature early-to-mid summer in the cool coastal climate.

harvest_end.label: main
harvest_end.source_quote: Stop watering in May when the garlic tops begin to turn yellow

low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: In the Arizona low desert, plant garlic in fall (September to November) and harvest in late spring or early summer, before the extreme heat. Garlic needs a few weeks of cool weather after planting to form a good bulb, so grow softneck types, and chilling the cloves in the fridge first helps in warm winters.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: Hawaii's tropical climate does not naturally provide the winter cold garlic needs, so production is limited to higher elevations (above about 500 feet, such as Kula on Maui and the Waimea uplands) where cool nights supply partial vernalization, or to gardeners who pre-chill their cloves. Where it works, garlic is fall-planted for a late-winter to spring harvest. At low elevations expect small, single-clove rounds rather than full bulbs.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: Hawaii is a very hard place for garlic because it never really gets cold. It works best up in the cooler highlands (like Kula on Maui), or if you chill the cloves in the fridge first. Plant in fall and harvest in late winter or spring. Down at sea level, garlic usually makes only small round bulbs, not full heads.

crops.description_seasoned: Garlic (Allium sativum) is a hardy allium grown from individual cloves planted in fall. It roots before winter, overwinters in the ground (mulched in cold regions), then resumes growth in spring and matures the following summer, an eight to nine month crop that spans the year. Winter cold is essential: cloves must be vernalized to divide and bulb properly, which is why fall planting beats spring. Hardneck types suit cold winters, produce edible scapes, and store a few months; softneck types suit mild climates, braid well, and store the longest.
crops.description_beginner: Garlic is one of the easiest crops to grow, but it works on an unusual schedule. You plant the cloves in fall, they rest through winter (under a mulch blanket where it is cold), and they finish growing the next summer, so a single planting takes most of a year. Garlic needs that winter cold to form a proper bulb, which is why you plant in fall rather than spring. Grow hardneck garlic where winters are cold and softneck garlic where they are mild.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Garlic is ready in early to mid summer (late spring in warm regions) when the lower leaves have browned and died back while several upper leaves stay green, about a third to half the foliage turned. Each green leaf is an intact wrapper, so do not wait for all the leaves to brown. Confirm by lifting a test bulb: ready bulbs have cloves that fill the skins.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Garlic is ready in early summer (or late spring in warm areas) when the lower leaves have turned brown but the top leaves are still green, about a third to half of them browned. Do not wait for all the leaves to die. Dig one bulb to check: if the cloves fill out the skins, it is time to harvest.

pet_safe.note: In the onion (allium) family and toxic to cats, dogs, and horses; it damages their red blood cells.

crops.name: Peach

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Peach likes a deep soil that drains well and lets air reach the roots. Good drainage is the one rule you cannot bend with stone fruit, because peach roots will not stand being wet. A sandy loam (a loose soil that drains easily) is a great fit, and a lighter sandy soil works if you stay on top of watering and feeding. Heavy clay that holds water is the trouble spot, since it can bring on crown and root rot; on clay, plant the tree on a raised mound so the roots sit above the soggy soil. A soil of average richness with some compost worked in suits it well.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Peach wants a deep, well-drained loam with good aeration; drainage is the non-negotiable for stone fruit, which will not tolerate wet feet. A sandy loam is well suited and a lighter sandy soil is workable with attention to water and feeding. Heavy clay that holds water is the problem texture, raising the risk of crown and root rot; on such ground, plant on a raised mound or berm to lift the roots above standing water. Moderate fertility and a modest amount of organic matter suit it well.

ph.note_beginner: Peach grows best in slightly acidic soil, around pH 6.0 to 6.5, and is fine up to about 7.0 (pH is just a measure of how acidic or alkaline the soil is). Test your soil before planting and adjust slowly if you need to: garden lime raises the pH if the soil is too acidic, and elemental sulfur lowers it if the soil is too alkaline. Mix any of this in before you plant, because pH changes slowly and is much easier to fix before the permanent tree goes in.
ph.note_seasoned: Peach does best in a slightly acidic soil, roughly pH 6.0 to 6.5, and tolerates up to about 7.0. Test the soil before planting and adjust gradually if needed: lime raises a too-acidic pH, while elemental sulfur lowers one that is too alkaline. Work amendments in ahead of planting, since pH shifts slowly and is far easier to correct before the permanent tree is in the ground.

fertilizer.timing: spring at bloom to petal fall; optional light postharvest
fertilizer.example_product: 10-10-10 balanced fertilizer
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Broadcast the fertilizer evenly around the root zone out to the drip line, keeping it off the trunk, and water it in. Split timing (the bulk in spring, a lighter touch after harvest) suits sandy soils; never feed late in the season, since late nitrogen delays dormancy and invites winter injury and short-life problems.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Scatter the fertilizer evenly on the soil around the tree out to where the branches reach, keep it off the trunk, and water it in. On sandy soil it helps to split it, most in spring and a little after harvest. Never feed late in the year, because late feeding keeps the tree growing when it should be going dormant and makes winter damage more likely.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 suits backyard peaches; mature trees draw most heavily on nitrogen (N) and potassium (K). Avoid high-nitrogen feeding, which pushes soft, disease-prone growth at the expense of fruit.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: A balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 (the three numbers are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium) works well for backyard peaches. Do not overdo nitrogen, the first number, because too much pushes leafy growth and more disease instead of fruit.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A common home-garden rate is about 1 cup of 10-10-10 per year of tree age, applied in spring from bloom to petal fall, up to roughly 10 cups for a mature tree (about 1/2 to 1 pound of fertilizer per year of age, to a maximum near 10 pounds). Do not fertilize at planting or place fertilizer in the hole; wait until growth begins. If a late frost takes the crop, skip the postharvest feeding that year.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A simple rule is about 1 cup of 10-10-10 for each year of the tree's age, spread in spring as the tree blooms, up to about 10 cups for a full-grown tree. Do not put fertilizer in the planting hole or feed right at planting; wait until the tree starts growing.
