failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Switch to an acid-forming, ammonium-form fertilizer made for blueberries or azaleas, and feed lightly, especially on young plants. Stop using anything with lime or nitrate nitrogen. Mulch with an acidic mulch and keep the pH in the 4.5 to 5.5 range.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Use an acid (azalea or blueberry) fertilizer and feed lightly, especially on young plants. Never use anything with lime. Keep the soil acidic with pine bark or pine straw mulch.

sources_summary.note: T1 university-extension blueberry guides spanning the type-by-region split: cold-zone unis (UMaine 2253, Penn State home-fruit variety guide, OSU PNW-656, MSU E3490, UMass NE Small Fruit Guide) for northern highbush; warm-zone unis (Clemson HGIC 1401, UGA C1278/C946, UF/IFAS MG359 Blueberry Gardener's Guide) for rabbiteye and southern highbush. MS State Establishment & Maintenance corroborates per-type chill bands; flag for Claude Code to mint msstate_ext at release if cited as evidence.

succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Not applicable. A blueberry is a long-lived woody shrub planted once and kept for decades, not a crop sown in succession. There is no replanting cycle and no renovation; the bush is maintained in place through annual pruning.

3.type_note_seasoned: Northern highbush is the cold-climate type. It needs the high winter chill your zones provide (about 800 to 1000 hours) and a true dormancy, and it is the most cold-hardy of the cultivated blueberries; the half-high cultivars in the set push hardiness even farther north.
3.type_note_beginner: Northern highbush is the type bred for cold winters, and it is the one to plant here. It needs a long, cold rest each winter to fruit well, which your area provides, and it tolerates hard freezes better than the southern types.
3.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Northern highbush blooms relatively late, which helps, but in the coldest zones a late spring freeze can still catch open bloom in a cold year. Favor the hardiest, latest-blooming cultivars and plant on a slope where cold air drains away.
3.grown_as_note_seasoned: Northern highbush is a permanent deciduous shrub built for your long, cold winter; planted once, it fruits for decades. It rests fully dormant and leafless through the deep cold, then breaks bud and blooms in spring, when an open flower can still be caught by a late freeze. Fruit sets and ripens across summer, roughly July into early September, latest in the coldest zones. After leaf drop you prune late in the dormant season, just before bud break, to shape the bush and keep it productive.
3.grown_as_note_beginner: Your northern highbush blueberry is a long-lived bush you plant once and keep for many years, and it needs the real winter your area gives it. It loses its leaves and rests all winter (this rest is called dormancy), then leafs out and flowers in spring, where a late frost can still catch the open blooms in a cold year. Berries ripen through summer, from about midsummer into early fall. After the leaves fall you prune it late in its winter rest, just before the buds open, to keep it strong.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: Northern highbush is the classic blueberry for cold-winter gardens, and it is the right choice here. It drops its leaves each fall and needs a real winter to fruit well, which your area gives it. Plant young bushes in early spring in very acidic soil, and you will pick berries from about midsummer into early fall. Always plant two or more different varieties near each other so they pollinate and you get a bigger crop.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Up here the blueberry to grow is northern highbush, a fully deciduous shrub that wants the long, cold winter your zones deliver (commonly 800 to 1000 or more chill hours). Set 2 to 3-year-old plants in early spring, give them strongly acidic soil (pH 4.5 to 5.5), and expect ripening from roughly July into early September, latest in the coldest zones. Plant at least two cultivars for better fruit set, and lean on the hardiest varieties and a slope with good air drainage in zones 3 and 4.

8.type_note_seasoned: Rabbiteye is gated in by your moderate chill (about 350 to 650 hours) and long, hot summers. It is native to the region, the most heat-tolerant type, and blooms late enough to dodge most spring freezes; northern highbush gets too little chill here and resents the summer heat.
8.type_note_beginner: Rabbiteye is the type that loves the warm Southeast. Your winters are not cold enough for northern types, but they are just cold enough for rabbiteye, which also handles the summer heat and flowers late enough to usually avoid frost damage.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Rabbiteye blooms later than southern highbush and usually escapes spring freezes, but a warm late-winter spell can push bloom early, and a hard freeze on open flowers can cut the crop sharply. Later-blooming cultivars are the safer bet.
8.grown_as_note_seasoned: Rabbiteye is a permanent evergreen shrub in the Gulf South, planted once and productive for decades; it holds its leaves through the mild winter and stays in leaf year round. The year runs from a late, frost-dodging bloom to harvest from roughly late May into July, then a quieter care period of light shaping and feeding. Rabbiteye needs a second, different rabbiteye nearby to cross-pollinate and set a crop.
8.grown_as_note_beginner: Your rabbiteye blueberry is a long-lived bush you plant once and keep for many years, and here it stays green all year. It flowers late enough to usually miss spring frosts, ripens berries from late spring into summer, then moves into a calmer stretch of light tidying and feeding. One key point: it must have a second, different rabbiteye variety planted nearby so the two can pollinate each other and make fruit.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast, rabbiteye blueberries are the easy, dependable choice. They are native to the region, handle the heat, and flower late enough to usually miss spring frosts. They keep their leaves through the warm winter and ripen from late spring into summer. One important rule: rabbiteye must have a second, different rabbiteye variety planted nearby to produce fruit, so always plant at least two.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: Rabbiteye is the Gulf-South home blueberry: native, heat- and humidity-tolerant, and late enough in bloom to dodge most spring freezes. It holds its leaves through the mild winter (evergreen here) and ripens from roughly late May into July. Plant a few different varieties so they pollinate each other, keep an eye out for a leaf disease called rust in cool, damp spots, and enjoy it as a fun specialty crop.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: Blueberries are a niche crop in Hawaii: only low-chill and no-chill southern highbush cultivars fruit here, grown as evergreen shrubs from roughly 250 to 4000 feet, almost always in containers with an acidic peat-perlite mix at pH 4.0 to 5.0. UH trials have fruited southern highbush as low as Hilo. Plant several cultivars for cross-pollination, watch for blueberry rust in cool, wet sites, and treat it as a rewarding specialty rather than a default backyard crop.

crops.description_seasoned: Blueberries are long-lived, acid-loving woody shrubs that reward patience: a well-sited bush can produce for decades. Success turns on three things most growers underestimate: matching the type to your winter chill, getting the soil acidic enough, and planting more than one cultivar for cross-pollination.
crops.description_beginner: Blueberries are bushes, not annual plants, and a healthy one can fruit for decades. They are easy to grow once you nail two things: very acidic soil and the right type for your climate. Plant at least two different varieties so they pollinate each other, and you are set for years.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Ripe berries turn fully blue and develop a dusty bloom, and they detach with a light roll of the thumb. Color comes a few days before full sweetness, so wait until they part easily from the cluster. Pick every 5 to 10 days through the ripening window; rabbiteye flavor improves with a slightly longer interval.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: A blueberry is ready when it is completely blue and falls off into your hand with a gentle roll of the thumb. Berries turn blue a few days before they are truly sweet, so give them a little longer, then taste one. Pick over the bush every several days as more ripen.
crops.bloom_time_seasoned: Blueberries bloom in spring, with the exact timing set by type, cultivar chill, and region. Low-chill southern highbush flowers earliest, which is why late frost is its main risk; rabbiteye flowers later, dodging more spring freezes. Each flower cluster opens over a one-to-two-week window.
crops.bloom_time_beginner: Blueberries flower in spring. Earlier-blooming types can get caught by late frosts, while later-blooming ones usually escape them. The white or pink bell-shaped flowers open over a week or two before the berries begin to form.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Cold-hardiness depends on the type. Northern highbush handles deep cold (cold-hardy cultivars and half-high types reach the coldest zones); southern highbush and rabbiteye are less cold-tolerant and are matched to mild-winter regions. A plant that survives a winter is not the same as one that fruits reliably through it, so the region recommendation targets dependable fruiting, not bare survival.
crops.hardiness_notes_beginner: How much cold a blueberry can take depends on its type. The northern types are very cold-hardy; the southern types are not and belong in milder climates. Surviving the winter and actually producing berries are two different things, so follow the type the app recommends for where you live.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Chill hours are the hours of winter temperature below 45°F a blueberry needs to break dormancy and bloom normally. The requirement varies sharply by type: northern highbush wants roughly 800 to 1000 hours, rabbiteye about 350 to 650, and southern highbush as little as 150 to 600. Too little chill for the type gives weak, erratic bloom and little fruit; the figure is the single best predictor of whether a given cultivar will crop where you live.
crops.chill_hours_note_beginner: Blueberries need a stretch of cold winter weather before they will flower and fruit, measured in chill hours (time below 45°F). Each type needs a different amount: northern highbush needs a lot of cold, southern highbush very little, rabbiteye somewhere in between. This is why choosing the type that matches your climate matters so much.
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Plant at least two different cultivars of the same type with overlapping bloom. Rabbiteye is self-incompatible and needs a second rabbiteye to set a crop at all. Highbush, both northern and southern, is partially self-fertile but yields noticeably larger, earlier, more abundant fruit with a cross-pollinating partner. Cross types do not pollinate each other reliably, so pair rabbiteye with rabbiteye and highbush with highbush.
crops.pollinator_notes_beginner: Plant two or more different blueberry varieties of the same type so they can pollinate each other. Some types, like rabbiteye, will barely fruit without a partner. Others fruit a little on their own but do far better with a second variety nearby. Just make sure both plants are the same type, since types do not cross well.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: Focus the first year or two on root and shoot growth, not fruit. Pick off the flower buds so the bush builds structure; this sacrifices an early handful of berries for far better long-term yields. Keep the soil evenly moist through the establishment season and mulch heavily to protect the shallow roots.
crops.year_one_notes_beginner: In the first year or two, pinch off the flowers so the plant puts its energy into growing strong instead of making a few berries. It feels wrong, but it pays off with much bigger harvests later. Water steadily and keep a thick mulch around the base while the plant settles in.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Test the soil the season before planting. If pH is above 5.5, work in elemental sulfur at the soil-test rate several months ahead, since sulfur needs time to acidify. Blend generous peat moss or aged pine bark into the planting zone for acidity, organic matter, and drainage. Where native soil is unsuitable or alkaline, a raised bed of acidic mix or a large container is the more reliable route.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Prepare the soil before you plant. Do a soil test, and if it is not acidic enough, mix in garden sulfur a few months ahead following the test's directions. Work plenty of peat moss or pine bark into the spot where the plant will go. If your soil just will not get acidic, grow your blueberry in a pot of acidic mix instead.
crops.planting_method_notes_seasoned: Set the plant at the depth it grew in the nursery, in acidic, well-drained soil amended with peat or pine bark. On heavy or wet ground, plant on a raised mound or ridge at least 6 inches high to keep the shallow roots out of standing water. Space plants by type: about 4 to 5 feet apart for highbush, 5 to 6 feet for the larger rabbiteye.
crops.planting_method_notes_beginner: Dig a hole and set the plant so it sits at the same depth it was in its pot, then backfill with soil mixed with peat moss or pine bark. If your ground stays wet, plant on a raised mound instead. Give each bush room: about 4 to 5 feet between highbush plants, a bit more for the bigger rabbiteye types.

pollination.notes_seasoned: See pollinator_notes for the full guidance. In short, blueberry uses a simple model: plant two or more different cultivars of the same type with overlapping bloom. There is no apple-style specific pollinizer pairing to chart; any two compatible cultivars of the same type cross-pollinate. Rabbiteye requires a second rabbiteye to set a crop; highbush is partially self-fertile but yields far better with a partner.
pollination.notes_beginner: See the pollination notes above for details. The short version: plant at least two different kinds of blueberry of the same type so they can pollinate each other. You do not need to match specific varieties, just grow two that bloom at the same time.

crops.establishment_note: Pick off the flower buds the first year or two after planting so the bush spends its energy building roots and wood instead of fruit. It pays off in far better yields once the plant is established.
crops.cane_management_seasoned: Not applicable in the cane-fruit sense. Blueberry is a crown-forming bush, not a cane fruit like raspberry or blackberry. Its pruning is old-wood renewal: once the bush is established, remove the oldest, least productive stems at ground level each dormant season to keep a balance of young and mature wood. This rides the dormant-season prune beat in the care calendar rather than a cane-by-cane training structure.
crops.cane_management_beginner: Not applicable the way it is for raspberries. Blueberries grow as a bush, not on canes you tie up. Once the plant is a few years old, cut out the oldest, woodiest stems at the base each winter to make room for fresh growth. That is the whole job.
crops.type_selection_seasoned: Which type you grow is decided by your winter chill, not preference. Northern highbush (about 800 to 1000 chill hours) is the cold-climate type, deciduous and truly cold-hardy. Southern highbush (roughly 150 to 600 hours) and rabbiteye (about 350 to 650 hours) are the warm-climate types for mild winters; in the warmest zones they hold their leaves year-round. Plant a high-chill type where winters are too mild and it never breaks dormancy properly, so it barely fruits; plant a low-chill type where winters are cold and it blooms too early and loses the crop to frost. Match the chill, and pick the type the page recommends for your region.
crops.type_selection_beginner: There are different kinds of blueberry, and the right one depends on how cold your winters get, not which you like best. In cold-winter areas, grow northern highbush. In mild-winter areas, grow southern highbush or rabbiteye. The plant tag usually says which type it is. If you plant the wrong one for your climate, it may grow fine but produce almost no berries. The app will point you to the type that fits your region.

crops.name: Heirloom Tomato

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Heirloom tomatoes do best in loose, well-draining soil rich in organic matter: think compost-improved garden beds rather than hard clay. Good drainage matters even more for heirlooms than for hybrids, because most heirlooms have no built-in resistance to the soilborne wilt diseases that thrive in wet, compacted soil. Work in 2 to 3 inches of compost before planting. If water pools after rain and takes more than an hour to soak in, improve the bed or use a raised bed filled with a topsoil-and-compost mix before planting.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Heirloom tomatoes perform best in well-drained loam or sandy loam with high organic matter. Because heirlooms generally lack the VFN resistance bred into hybrids, drainage is doubly important: waterlogged, compacted soil favors Fusarium and Verticillium wilt and Pythium root rot, to which heirlooms are fully susceptible. The indeterminate, heavily fruiting habit also places sustained calcium and phosphorus demand on the soil, and large-fruited types strain calcium uptake, which is why blossom-end rot tracks moisture consistency. Working in 2 to 3 inches of compost before planting builds structure and fertility and moderates the calcium-availability swings that drive blossom-end rot in big heirloom fruit.

ph.note_beginner: Heirlooms want slightly acidic soil: a pH between 6.0 and 6.8. Outside that range, nutrients the plant needs get locked up in the soil even if they're there. Blossom-end rot (the dark sunken spot on the bottom of the fruit) is often triggered by pH problems limiting how much calcium the plant can absorb. If you've never tested your soil, an inexpensive test kit from a garden center is worth doing before your first season. Many extension offices also offer low-cost testing.
ph.note_seasoned: Tomatoes are particularly sensitive to pH because it governs the solubility of phosphorus, calcium, and magnesium, three nutrients they consume in large quantities. At pH below 5.5, manganese and aluminum become increasingly available at phytotoxic levels; blossom-end rot risk rises as calcium uptake is impaired. Above 7.0, iron and manganese deficiencies drive interveinal chlorosis on younger leaves. In the alkaline soils common across the interior West and alkaline-irrigation regions, growers routinely need to acidify before planting. Eastern soils often run naturally in the preferred range; Pacific Northwest soils vary widely by parent material.

fertilizer.notes_beginner: Heirloom tomatoes are heavy feeders and need regular fertilizing throughout the season. Start with a balanced fertilizer at transplant time, then switch to a fertilizer higher in potassium once flowers appear: look for 'tomato fertilizer' or a formula where the third number on the bag (potassium) is the largest. Feed every two weeks through the fruiting period.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Time to feed your tomatoes
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Look for a high-potassium formula, often labeled 'tomato food' or showing a higher third number on the bag (like 5-10-10). That third number is the potassium, which supports fruit development.
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Heavy feeder. Start with balanced feed at transplant, switch to high-potassium once flowering begins.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time to feed your tomatoes
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: high K, e.g. 5-10-10
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: About 1 pound of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet side-dressed once the first fruits reach about the size of a quarter, repeated every 3 to 4 weeks through harvest, per UGA Extension; absent a soil test, incorporate about 1.5 pounds of a complete fertilizer per 100 square feet before planting. Use the high-potassium formula from the hint above at this rate.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A common rate is about 1 to 2 tablespoons of fertilizer worked into the soil around each plant, 6 to 8 inches from the stem, beginning when the first fruits form and repeating every 3 to 4 weeks. Water it in each time and keep it off the stem and leaves. A big heirloom plant is a heavier feeder than a cherry type.

companions.note_beginner: The most reliable companion for heirloom tomatoes is marigolds: plant them around the edges of the bed, not between the tomatoes, since heirloom plants get large and will shade out anything too close. Nasturtiums at the bed perimeter draw aphids away from your tomatoes (aphids prefer the nasturtiums). Keep heirlooms away from fennel, which stunts many neighboring plants, and away from potatoes and eggplant, which share the same diseases and pests. Basil is a popular choice to plant nearby and does well in the same sun and water conditions.
companions.note_seasoned: Heirloom tomato companions follow the same species-level lore as other tomatoes, with two heirloom-specific nuances. First, heirloom's large plant footprint (24-36 inch spacing, 6-foot cages) shades out many traditional companion candidates; prioritize companions that tolerate partial shade or position them at the drip-line edge rather than between plants. Second, the marigold/nematode connection is the best-documented pairing in this crop's companion set, effective as a dense pre-season cover crop, not as scattered concurrent interplanting. For most growers the practical guidance is: avoid fennel, avoid planting near potatoes or eggplant if disease pressure has been a problem, and consider nasturtiums as an aphid trap crop at the bed perimeter where they won't be shaded.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Long-established pairing; flavor-improvement claims are traditional. Basil's aromatic compounds may deter some pest insects, though not extension-documented for this specific pair, but widely practiced and low risk.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Basil is a classic tomato partner. Gardeners have grown the two together for generations, and basil's strong scent may put off some pest insects. It is not a proven effect for this exact pair, but it is harmless and worth trying.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Marigolds
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: French marigolds suppress root-knot nematodes, most effectively as a dense cover crop planted 2+ months before tomatoes, not as concurrent interplanting. Extension-documented mechanism.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Iowa State University Extension's 'Growing Marigolds in the Home Garden' page documents that French marigolds release alpha-terthienyl which suppresses root-knot nematodes. Oklahoma State University Extension confirms the mechanism but notes that reduction occurs only in the marigold's immediate root zone. Extension consensus (ISU, UF/IFAS ENY-056, UH CTAHR PD-35, NC State, Mississippi State) is that marigolds work best as a dense cover crop for 2+ months BEFORE the vegetable crop, not as concurrent interplanting. This claim's nematode component aligns with the extension-documented mechanism, but the 'concurrent companion' application pattern reflects popular gardening practice rather than extension protocol.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: French marigolds help fight root-knot nematodes (tiny soil worms that attack roots). They work best when grown as a thick patch a couple of months before you plant tomatoes, rather than just tucked in alongside them at the same time.

good_seasoned.name: Nasturtiums
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Nasturtiums function as a trap crop for aphids, since aphids preferentially colonize nasturtiums, drawing them away from tomatoes. UC IPM documents trap-crop use of nasturtiums in vegetable gardens. Particularly useful for heirloom plants, which are large and difficult to spray thoroughly once fully grown.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap-crop principle is documented in IPM literature. UC IPM references nasturtiums as aphid attractors. The specific nasturtium-tomato trap-crop pairing is referenced in extension-adjacent IPM guidance; strongest evidence is for brassica pests, but aphid trap-crop mechanism applies broadly.

good_seasoned.name: Borage
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Borage flowers attract pollinators over an extended bloom period, coinciding with heirloom's long indeterminate fruiting season. Heirloom's larger flowers benefit from robust pollinator activity during the extended set window. Hornworm repellence is a traditional claim without T1 backing.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Borage as pollinator attractor is plausible and consistent with floral-resource literature. The hornworm-repellence claim is traditional companion-planting lore without T1 extension backing.

good_seasoned.name: Carrots
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Carrots' deep taproot partitions the root zone differently from heirloom's fibrous roots, theoretically reducing below-ground competition. This is a plausible root-zone partitioning inference, not an extension-tested pairing. Note: give carrots adequate distance from heirloom's cage footprint (24-36 inch spacing), or they will be shaded out.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Root-zone partitioning between taprooted and fibrous-rooted crops is a real ecology concept. The specific carrot-tomato pairing benefit is a plausible inference that has not been directly studied in extension research.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Fennel
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Fennel is broadly allelopathic and suppresses growth of many neighboring plants. Extension literature documents fennel as a poor companion for most vegetables; the specific tomato interaction is traditional but consistent with fennel's known allelopathic properties.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: 'Fennel suppresses neighbors' is a common gardening-book claim. Limited research; allelopathy is real but specific claim pattern is traditional.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Fennel gives off natural chemicals that stunt the growth of many plants around it, so it is a poor neighbor for most vegetables, including tomatoes. It is best kept in its own spot away from the garden beds.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Brassicas
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Both brassicas and tomatoes are heavy feeders; close interplanting creates real competition for nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. Not a toxic pairing, but productivity of both crops is reduced under competition.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Both brassicas and tomatoes are heavy feeders; close interplanting creates real competition for nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. Not a toxic pairing, but productivity of both crops is reduced under competition.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Cabbage-family plants (like broccoli, kale, and cabbage) and tomatoes are both hungry feeders, so planting them close together makes them fight over nutrients in the soil. It will not poison either one, but both end up less productive.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Corn
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Both crops host the tomato fruit worm / corn earworm (Helicoverpa zea, same species). Planting together creates a concentrated host reservoir that amplifies pest pressure on both crops.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Both crops host the tomato fruit worm / corn earworm (Helicoverpa zea, same species). UC IPM and Cornell document H. zea as a shared host pest across Solanaceae and Poaceae. Planting together creates a concentrated host reservoir that amplifies pest pressure on both crops.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Corn and tomatoes are attacked by the very same caterpillar (the tomato fruitworm, also called the corn earworm). Planting them side by side gives that pest two favorite foods in one place and makes the problem worse for both crops.

bad_seasoned.name: Potatoes
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Both are Solanaceae and share primary diseases (late blight, Phytophthora infestans; early blight, Alternaria solani) and several pests. Planting together creates a continuous host bridge that sustains inoculum across the season and into following years. Crop rotation separating Solanaceae is the standard extension recommendation for disease management.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Extension literature (UMN, Cornell, Clemson HGIC) documents shared disease and pest pressure within Solanaceae and recommends rotation to break disease cycles.

bad_seasoned.name: Eggplant
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Same family (Solanaceae), shares Colorado potato beetle pressure and early blight. Interplanting concentrates beetle and disease pressure; separating Solanaceae crops, even within a season, reduces crossover pest load.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Colorado potato beetle and early blight are documented shared pests/pathogens across Solanaceae in extension IPM literature.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_beginner: Clusters of tiny soft green or black insects on the growing tips and the undersides of leaves, often so small they look like dots. Leaves may start to curl or feel sticky. You might notice ants walking up the stems; ants actually farm aphids for the sweet liquid they produce, so ants are a good early warning sign.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray the clusters directly with a strong jet of water from a hose; this dislodges most of them. For a persistent infestation, apply insecticidal soap or neem oil spray, making sure to coat the leaf undersides where the aphids cluster.
pests.prevention_beginner: Plant marigolds or nasturtiums near your tomatoes; both attract beneficial insects that feed on aphids. Avoid over-fertilizing with high-nitrogen fertilizer, which produces the soft, fast-growing shoots that aphids prefer.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several aphid species (most often green peach and potato aphids) colonize tomatoes. They reproduce asexually and explosively in warm weather, so a few founders become dense colonies on tender new growth within days. Soft, nitrogen-flush growth from over-fertilizing is especially attractive, which is why feeding history drives outbreak severity as much as weather.
pests.cause_beginner: Aphids are tiny soft-bodied insects that breed very fast in warm weather, so a few quickly turn into crowds on the soft new growth at the tips. Too much fertilizer makes that soft growth they love, so going easy on feeding helps keep them down.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Tomato hornworm
pests.symptoms_beginner: Large sections of leaves or whole stems stripped very quickly, sometimes overnight. Look for fat green caterpillars up to 4 inches long that blend almost perfectly into the stems and leaves. The easiest way to find them is to look for the dark green or black droppings they leave on leaves below.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Hand-pick and drop them in a bucket of soapy water; it's simple but effective. If you find any with small white oval capsules stuck to their backs, leave those alone; parasitic wasps have already laid eggs on them and the wasps will take care of the rest.
pests.prevention_beginner: Turn or till the soil in autumn to expose and kill overwintering pupae. Planting dill or fennel nearby attracts predatory wasps that prey on hornworms.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Large green caterpillars (up to 4 inches) stripping foliage. Leaves disappear rapidly. Black droppings on leaves.
pests.cause_seasoned: Larvae of the five-spotted hawk moth (Manduca quinquemaculata). Adult moths lay eggs on tomato foliage from early summer; the caterpillars feed and grow through mid-to-late summer, reaching up to about four inches and defoliating fast because a single large larva eats a great deal. They pupate in the soil over winter, so the prior season's population carries forward in an unworked bed.
pests.cause_beginner: These are the caterpillars of a large moth. The moth lays eggs on the leaves in early summer, and the caterpillars grow big (up to about four inches) through mid and late summer, eating a lot of leaves fast. They spend the winter in the soil, so a bed left undug can carry them into next year.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick; they are well camouflaged but easy to remove. Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) spray. If white cocoons visible on back, leave them; parasitic wasps are doing the work.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Till soil in autumn to kill overwintering pupae. Plant dill and basil nearby to attract predatory wasps.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms_beginner: Lots of tiny round holes in the leaves, making them look like they've been peppered with a hole punch, most noticeable on seedlings and young plants. The beetles themselves are tiny, shiny, and black; they jump when disturbed, which is how they got their name.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover seedlings with row cover fabric to keep beetles off young plants. Sprinkle diatomaceous earth (a fine powder made from fossilized algae) around the base and on the leaves; it damages soft-bodied insects on contact. Neem oil spray also works.
pests.prevention_beginner: Wait to transplant until plants are large and well-established; flea beetles cause the most damage to small seedlings. Larger, established plants can usually tolerate some feeding without major harm.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny round shot-holes in leaves, especially on seedlings and young plants. Small shiny black beetles jump when disturbed.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several flea beetle species. They overwinter as adults and emerge in spring, so pressure is heaviest early, on seedlings and freshly set transplants whose small leaf area makes the shot-hole feeding proportionally damaging. Established plants with ample foliage tolerate the same beetle numbers easily, which is why the timing of the attack matters more than its size.
pests.cause_beginner: Flea beetles are tiny black beetles that jump when you disturb them and chew small round holes in leaves. They come out in spring and hit young seedlings hardest, because small plants do not have many leaves to spare. Bigger, established plants shrug off the same chewing.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Use row covers on seedlings. Apply diatomaceous earth. Neem oil spray.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Delay transplanting until plants are large. Use transplants rather than seeds.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms_beginner: A fine stippling or scattering of tiny yellow or white dots across the upper surface of leaves, making them look dull and washed out. In heavier infestations you may see fine webbing on the undersides of leaves. Spider mites are barely visible to the naked eye; hold a white sheet of paper under a leaf and tap; if you see tiny dots moving, that's them. Worst in hot, dry weather.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray the plant, especially the leaf undersides, with a strong jet of water repeatedly over several days to knock off mites and disrupt their colonies. Follow up with neem oil or insecticidal soap applied to the undersides of leaves.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep plants well-watered in hot weather; water-stressed plants are far more vulnerable. Avoid dusty, dry conditions around the garden if possible.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine stippling or yellow dots on leaves. Fine webbing on leaf undersides. Leaves may bronze, dry out, and drop. Worst in hot dry weather.
pests.cause_seasoned: Twospotted spider mite (Tetranychus urticae) and relatives. They thrive in hot, dry, dusty conditions and complete a generation in under a week in summer heat, so populations explode late in the season. Drought-stressed plants are far more vulnerable, which makes consistent watering and dust suppression the primary cultural controls rather than an afterthought.
pests.cause_beginner: Spider mites are tiny mites (so small they look like moving dust) that love hot, dry, dusty weather and multiply incredibly fast, so they tend to flare up late in summer. Plants that are short on water suffer the most, so keeping plants watered and dust down is the best defense.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast with water repeatedly. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap to leaf undersides. Increase humidity around plants.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep plants well-watered in hot weather. Avoid dusty conditions. Introduce predatory mites.

diseases.name: Early blight
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Dark brown spots with a target-ring pattern (concentric rings, like a bullseye) appear on the lowest leaves first. Those leaves yellow and drop, and the disease works its way up the plant over the season.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove affected leaves as soon as you see them and bag them for the trash, not the compost. A copper-based fungicide slows the spread. Mulch around the base to stop soil splash, which is how the fungal spores travel from the ground up onto the leaves.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Move your tomatoes to a new spot each year, because the spores persist in the soil. Water at the base, never overhead. Stake or cage plants so leaves stay off the ground with good airflow. Heirlooms lack the blight resistance some hybrids carry, so these habits matter more.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark brown spots with concentric rings on lower leaves first; affected leaves yellow and drop, and the disease spreads upward through the plant.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Alternaria solani. It overwinters on infected debris and in the soil, then splashes up onto the lowest leaves in warm, wet weather, so infection starts low and climbs. Repeated tomato plantings build soil inoculum. Most heirlooms lack the partial early-blight tolerance bred into some modern hybrids, so unmanaged heirlooms tend to defoliate faster; rotation and mulch to block soil splash are the core preventions.
diseases.cause_beginner: Early blight is a fungus that lives in old plant debris and soil and splashes up onto the lowest leaves in warm, wet weather, which is why it starts at the bottom and climbs. Planting tomatoes in the same spot builds it up. Heirlooms are not bred to resist it, so moving the planting and mulching the soil are the main defenses.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves immediately. Apply copper-based fungicide preventively. Mulch soil to prevent splash-up.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate tomatoes every 3 to 4 years. Water at soil level. Space plants for airflow and prune to open the canopy. Stake to keep foliage off the ground.

diseases.name: Late blight
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Water-soaked patches that turn brown and expand fast on leaves and stems; this disease moves very quickly and can destroy a plant in a matter of days. In humid weather you may see white fuzzy growth on the leaf undersides. It is the most serious tomato disease in the garden.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove and immediately bag and bin all affected plant material; do not compost any of it. A copper-based fungicide can help as a preventive in wet spells. If a plant is badly affected, pull it entirely so it cannot spread to neighbors.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Good airflow is your best defense: stake and space plants so air moves through. Never leave tomato debris in the garden over winter. Because heirlooms rarely carry late-blight resistance, choose a resistant variety only if this disease has hit your area before, and watch closely in cool, wet weather.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Water-soaked, rapidly expanding brown patches on leaves and stems; white fuzzy growth on undersides in humid conditions. Can destroy plants in days.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The oomycete Phytophthora infestans, the pathogen behind the Irish potato famine. Its spores travel on wind and rain over long distances and infect leaves, stems, and fruit directly, spreading explosively in cool, wet weather. Because the inoculum arrives airborne, rotation helps little; resistant varieties and immediate removal of infected plants matter most, and heirlooms almost never carry the late-blight resistance genes bred into a few modern hybrids.
diseases.cause_beginner: Late blight is a fast, destructive disease whose spores blow in on wind and rain rather than starting from the soil. In cool, wet weather it can kill a plant in a few days. Because it arrives through the air, the best protection is pulling out any infected plant right away; heirlooms are not bred to resist it.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy all affected material immediately; do not compost. Apply copper fungicide preventively in wet conditions.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Ensure excellent airflow. Never leave tomato debris in the garden over winter. Choose a resistant variety where late blight recurs, since heirlooms rarely carry resistance.

diseases.name: Septoria leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small circular spots with a dark brown border and a pale gray or tan center, appearing first on the lower leaves, sometimes with a faint yellow ring. Over time the spotted leaves yellow and drop.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove and discard affected leaves right away; do not compost them. Apply a copper-based fungicide. Keep the plant staked and prune very dense growth so air moves through.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Rotate your tomatoes to a new spot each year. Water only at the base, never overhead. Mulch around the base to prevent soil splash. Heirlooms are not bred to resist leaf-spot diseases, so airflow and sanitation carry the load.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small circular spots with dark borders and pale gray centers, starting on lower leaves; spots may carry yellow halos.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Septoria lycopersici, one of the most common tomato leaf diseases. Like early blight it carries over on debris and infected soil and spreads by water splash onto lower foliage in warm, wet, humid weather, defoliating from the bottom up. Heirlooms carry no bred resistance, so the same moisture-management and sanitation practices, rather than a single spray, are the fix.
diseases.cause_beginner: Septoria leaf spot is a very common tomato fungus. Like early blight it overwinters in old debris and soil and splashes onto the lower leaves in warm, humid weather, working up the plant. The same habits that slow early blight, moving the planting, watering low, and mulching, keep it in check.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves. Apply copper fungicide. Ensure good air circulation through spacing and pruning.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate crops. Water at soil level. Mulch around plants. Open the canopy for airflow.

diseases.name: Fusarium and Verticillium wilt
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The plant wilts on hot afternoons and recovers at night at first, then whole branches yellow and wilt for good, often on just one side of the plant or one side of a leaf. Cut a wilted stem lengthwise near the base and you may see brown streaking inside. There is no cure once a plant is infected.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no spray that cures a wilted plant; remove and bag badly affected plants so they do not seed the soil further. Focus on protecting the rest: keep plants watered evenly and avoid wounding the roots. Next year, plant into a fresh bed and choose resistant varieties if you can.
diseases.prevention_beginner: This is the big one for heirlooms: most heirlooms have little or no resistance to these two soil fungi, while many hybrids are bred to resist them (look for V and F on a hybrid's tag). Rotate tomatoes out of a bed for several years, keep soil well drained, and if wilt has struck before, grow heirlooms in containers of fresh mix or graft them onto resistant rootstock.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Non-uniform yellowing and wilting, frequently on one side of the plant or one half of a compound leaf; early on the plant wilts in the heat of the day and recovers overnight, then collapses. Vascular browning is visible in a split lower stem.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Two soilborne fungi, Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lycopersici and Verticillium dahliae, which invade through the roots and plug the water-conducting vascular tissue. Both survive in soil as resting structures for many years (Fusarium favors warm soils, Verticillium cooler ones). This is the defining heirloom vulnerability: most heirlooms lack the V and F resistance genes bred into modern hybrids (the VFN codes), so they are fully susceptible where the pathogens are established. Cherokee Purple is a notable heirloom exception with some tolerance.
diseases.cause_beginner: These are two soil fungi that get in through the roots and clog the plant's water pipes, so it wilts and dies. They live in the soil for years. Modern hybrids are often bred to resist them (the V and F on the tag), but heirlooms usually are not, which is why heirlooms are more likely to wilt.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No curative treatment exists; rogue out and destroy infected plants. Manage by prevention: long rotation, good drainage, resistant rootstock for grafting, or container culture in fresh medium.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Long rotation (4 to 6 years out of the bed). Maintain drainage and avoid root injury. Where wilt is established, use resistant (VF) rootstock for grafting or grow heirlooms in containers of pathogen-free mix; heirlooms carry no bred resistance.

diseases.name: Blossom end rot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: A dark, sunken, leathery patch on the bottom (the blossom end) of the tomato, opposite the stem. It hits the first fruits of the season most and is not contagious.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Mulch around the plant and water deeply and consistently; blossom end rot comes from uneven moisture, not a nutrient shortage, so steady watering is the real fix. Remove affected fruit so the plant can put energy into the next ones.
diseases.prevention_beginner: The single most important prevention is consistent watering. Avoid disturbing the roots at the base of the plant, and do not over-fertilize with high-nitrogen fertilizer. Large heirloom fruit is especially prone, so keep moisture even once fruit sets.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark, sunken, leathery patch at the blossom end of the fruit; affects the first fruits most and is not contagious.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Not an infection but a calcium-delivery failure in the developing fruit. Calcium moves with water, so when soil moisture swings between wet and dry (or roots are damaged), the fast-growing blossom end is starved of calcium and its cells break down. It tracks watering consistency, not soil calcium levels, and large-fruited heirlooms show it more severely than small types.
diseases.cause_beginner: Blossom end rot is not a bug or an infection. It happens when the fruit cannot get enough calcium, almost always because watering swung from wet to dry and back. Calcium travels with water, so steady, even watering, not adding calcium, is what prevents it. Even calcium-rich soil gets it when watering is uneven.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Mulch to maintain even soil moisture. Water consistently. Remove affected fruit.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Consistent watering is the key prevention. Avoid root disturbance. Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen.

diseases.name: Fruit cracking
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Splits in the skin of ripening fruit, either rings around the stem end (concentric) or lines running down the sides (radial). Cracks often appear after a heavy rain that follows a dry spell.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Cracks cannot be undone, so pick cracked fruit promptly and use it quickly before it rots or attracts insects. The real work is prevention through even watering. Fruit that is close to ripe can be picked just before a big rain to beat the cracking.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Keep soil moisture as even as you can: water deeply and regularly during dry spells, and mulch to buffer the swings. Many heirlooms have thin skins and crack easily, so pick ripe fruit right away, especially before heavy rain.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Radial (vertical, down the sides) or concentric (rings at the stem end) splits in the skin of ripening fruit, typically after rapid water uptake such as heavy rain following a dry period.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Cracking occurs when rapid changes in soil moisture make the fruit interior expand faster than the skin can grow. Radial cracking is the more serious form and worsens in hot, humid weather. Variety matters: many heirlooms are thin-skinned and large-fruited and split more readily than crack-resistant hybrids, so heirlooms are among the more crack-prone tomatoes.
diseases.cause_beginner: Cracking happens when the inside of the fruit swells faster than the skin can stretch, usually after a big drink of water following a dry stretch. Thin-skinned heirlooms split more easily than tougher-skinned hybrids.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No treatment reverses a crack; harvest promptly to avoid secondary rot and insect entry. Manage by keeping moisture even.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Maintain even soil moisture through deep, regular watering during drought and mulch to buffer fluctuations. Harvest near-ripe fruit ahead of heavy rain; heirlooms are more crack-prone, so pick promptly.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Every 2-3 days in peak summer heat; weekly or less when temperatures are moderate. The correct interval is driven by soil moisture at 2-3 inch depth, not a fixed schedule, as evapotranspiration rates in a heirloom at full canopy can pull 1+ inch per week in hot weather.
watering.frequency_beginner: In the hottest part of summer, water about every 2 to 3 days; when it is cooler, once a week or less is plenty. Rather than following a strict schedule, check the soil a few inches down and water when it is starting to dry out.
watering.amount_seasoned: 1-2 inches per week, delivered to depth. Heirloom roots extend 18-24 inches in good soil; shallow frequent watering keeps roots near the surface where they are more vulnerable to heat and drought stress. Deep, infrequent watering drives root development downward.
watering.amount_beginner: Aim for about 1 to 2 inches of water a week, and water deeply so it soaks well down. Heirloom roots go quite deep, and deep watering pulls them down where they handle heat and dry spells better; quick shallow sprinkles keep roots near the surface where they dry out fast.
watering.method_seasoned: At soil level: drip, soaker hose, or hand-water at the base. Overhead irrigation wets foliage and creates the leaf-surface moisture that Septoria leaf spot and early blight require for spore germination. Morning is preferred over evening: any foliage wetted accidentally dries before nightfall, narrowing the infection window.
watering.method_beginner: Water at the base of the plant, not over the top, using a drip line, soaker hose, or just the hose at the soil. Wet leaves invite leaf-spot diseases, so keeping the foliage dry helps. Watering in the morning is best, so any leaves that do get splashed dry off before night.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Yellow leaves on the lower part of the plant, especially if the soil stays wet for days at a time. Cracked fruit is another sign: the plant drinks unevenly when soil stays wet, then surges when it dries out, which splits the skin. If the soil feels wet to your finger 2 inches down and the plant still looks unhappy, too much water is the likely cause, not too little.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Leaves wilting in the morning and not recovering overnight; afternoon wilt on a hot day is normal and not a reliable indicator, but wilt that's still there at sunrise means the plant is stressed. Flowers dropping off before making fruit is the other big warning sign; water stress at flower time cuts your harvest. Dry, cracked soil that pulls away from the container or bed edge confirms the problem.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellow lower leaves (nitrogen displaced from anaerobic root zone), cracked fruit (surge uptake after dry spell), and persistently soggy soil. In waterlogged soil, roots shift from aerobic respiration to fermentation, which impairs calcium and potassium uptake and accelerates the blossom-end rot cycle even when soil calcium is adequate.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting in morning that does not fully recover overnight, blossom drop, dry cracked soil. Flower abscission is triggered by water stress at the abscission zone at the base of each pedicel; once flowers drop, that fruit set opportunity is gone for the season. Prolonged drought stress followed by heavy watering also causes fruit cracking and blossom-end rot via the same calcium-uptake disruption as overwatering.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Keep water off the foliage: overhead irrigation creates the leaf-surface wetness Septoria leaf spot and early blight need to infect. If overhead watering is unavoidable, do it in the morning so foliage dries before nightfall. Mulch to steady soil moisture, which also limits the blossom-end rot that large-fruited types are especially prone to.
watering.method_note_beginner: Water the soil and not the leaves. Wet leaves invite leaf-spot diseases, so if you do use a sprinkler, water in the morning. A layer of mulch keeps the soil evenly moist, which matters even more for big heirloom fruit that crack and rot on the bottom when watering is erratic.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The moisture-critical window runs from transplant establishment through flowering, fruit set, and the long fruit-sizing period that large-fruited heirlooms demand. Inconsistent moisture during fruit development is the direct cause of blossom-end rot and cracking, which show up more severely on big fruit than on small-fruited types.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The time to be most careful about even watering is from flowering through the weeks the big fruit are sizing up. Large heirloom tomatoes are the most prone to cracking and to dark sunken spots on the bottom when the soil dries out and then gets flooded, so keep moisture steady once fruit has set.

start_method.hardening_off_beginner: Hardening off means gradually introducing your seedlings to outdoor conditions before transplanting. Start about a week before your planned transplant date: put the plants outside for a couple of hours in a sheltered, partly shaded spot, then bring them back in. Add more time and more direct sun each day. This helps the plant build up its waxy leaf coating and adjust to outdoor wind and temperature swings. Plants that skip this step often struggle for two to three weeks after transplanting.
start_method.notes_beginner: Start seeds 8 weeks before your last frost date; heirloom tomatoes need a long season, so starting on time is important. Plant two seeds per cell about a quarter inch deep in seed-starting mix, somewhere warm (a heat mat helps a lot). At transplant time, bury the stem deeper than it sat in the pot: right up to the lowest set of leaves. New roots will form along the buried stem and give the plant a stronger, more drought-tolerant foundation.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Start 8 weeks before last frost; heirlooms need a long season. Harden off carefully. Bury stem deep at transplant.

container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: Minimum 18-inch depth. Wide containers (15+ inches diameter) preferred to accommodate the root spread of large indeterminate plants. Standard 20-gallon nursery containers work for compact varieties; full-size indeterminates will struggle even in 20+ gallon containers without aggressive pruning.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Use a pot at least 18 inches deep, and a wide one (15 inches across or more) so the big roots have room. A 20-gallon pot works for smaller varieties, but full-size heirloom plants will struggle even in a 20-gallon pot unless you prune them back hard.

drainage.saucer_practice_seasoned: Empty any standing water from the saucer within an hour of watering. Heirloom's high water demand means containers are often watered daily in heat, but roots left sitting in pooled water lose oxygen and begin to rot, so the saucer must catch overflow without becoming a reservoir.
drainage.saucer_practice_beginner: Pour out any water that collects in the saucer within an hour of watering. In hot weather you may water a pot every day, but the roots should never sit in standing water or they start to rot.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Use a potting mix made for containers (look for bags labeled 'potting mix' or 'container mix', not garden soil or topsoil, which gets too dense in pots and doesn't drain well).
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in about 20-25% perlite (those small white volcanic pellets sometimes pre-mixed into potting soil) to keep the mix from compacting around the roots as the season progresses. Heirloom plants get heavy and their roots fill the container fast, so good drainage matters. Stir in a slow-release granular fertilizer at planting following the label rate, then add liquid fertilizer every 1-2 weeks once flowers appear.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: container_potting_mix
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Incorporate 20-25% perlite by volume to compensate for compaction under a heavy plant. Add slow-release balanced fertilizer at planting; supplement with liquid balanced fertilizer every 1-2 weeks once flowering begins. Heirloom's heavy fruit load makes nutrient buffering especially important in containers.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Container heirlooms dry out much faster than in-ground plants. In hot weather, check the soil every day and water when the top 2 inches feel dry; daily watering is normal during summer heat. Don't let the container dry out completely between waterings; uneven moisture is the main cause of blossom-end rot in containers. Large 20-gallon containers hold moisture better than smaller ones, but even these need checking frequently during heat waves.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Container soil runs out of nutrients faster than garden beds. Once the first flowers open, feed with a liquid tomato fertilizer every 1 to 2 weeks through the rest of the season. If the bottom of the fruit develops a dark sunken spot (blossom-end rot), it's almost always a calcium and watering issue, not a fertilizer deficiency; keep moisture consistent rather than adding more fertilizer.
container_notes.notes_beginner: Heirloom tomatoes are a tough fit for containers; they're not well-suited to pot growing. The plants get very large, the roots need a lot of space, and you need a sturdy cage that's hard to anchor in a pot. If you want to try, use at least a 15-gallon container (20 gallons is better) and look for compact varieties like Stupice or Stupice, which stay smaller than standard indeterminate heirlooms. A raised bed is a much better option if you have any outdoor space at all.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Heirloom tomatoes are generally not well-suited to container growing. Indeterminate varieties develop extensive root systems that are cramped even in 20-gallon containers, and the large fruit load requires very robust staking that is difficult to anchor in a pot. If container growing is necessary, use compact or determinate heirloom-type varieties (Stupice, Bloody Butcher) in 15-20 gallon containers with heavy-duty caging. Raised beds are strongly preferred for full-size indeterminate varieties.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry significantly faster than in-ground soil; daily watering is common during summer heat for a large plant drawing heavily on a limited root volume. Check moisture 2 inches below the surface daily. Consistent moisture is critical; irregular watering drives blossom-end rot, which is more severe in containers than in-ground. Large containers (20+ gallons) provide some buffer but heirloom's demand typically exceeds that buffer in peak heat.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Container medium has limited nutrient buffering capacity, and heirloom's fruit load is higher than most tomato types. Supplement with liquid balanced fertilizer every 1-2 weeks once flowering begins, or apply slow-release granular at planting plus a liquid mid-season boost. Calcium deficiency (blossom-end rot) is common in containers; consider a calcium supplement if symptoms appear.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering container helps a heirloom hold the steady moisture that prevents blossom-end rot, but match the pot to the plant: these are large, thirsty vines that need a big reservoir and a big soil volume, so undersized self-watering pots run dry fast in heat. Keep the reservoir filled in peak summer, let the mix draw down between fills rather than sitting saturated, and top-water occasionally to flush accumulated salts.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot can work for a heirloom tomato and keeps the water steady, which helps prevent rot on the bottom of the fruit. Use the largest one you can, because these are big, thirsty plants. Keep the reservoir full in hot weather, and now and then water from the top to rinse out built-up minerals.

recommended: Brandywine (large pink slicer)
Cherokee Purple (dusky red-purple)
Mortgage Lifter (large pink, mild)
Black Krim (dark, rich flavor)
Green Zebra (green-striped, tangy)
Hillbilly (large bicolor)
San Marzano (paste)
Amish Paste (paste)
varieties.note_beginner: Heirlooms are open-pollinated, so you can save seed from your best fruit and grow the same variety again next year. Good starting choices: Brandywine and Mortgage Lifter for classic big pink slicers, Cherokee Purple and Black Krim for deep, rich flavor, Green Zebra for something tangy and different, and San Marzano or Amish Paste for sauce. If disease has been a problem in your garden, Cherokee Purple tends to hold up a little better than most heirlooms. Brandywine is delicious but slower and a bit fussier, so it makes a great second-season variety once you have the basics down.
varieties.note_seasoned: Heirlooms are open-pollinated cultivars, so seed saved from a healthy fruit grows true to type; that is what lets named heirlooms persist across generations. The class spans the full range of the species: large pink slicers (Brandywine, Mortgage Lifter, Hillbilly), dark or dusky varieties (Cherokee Purple, Black Krim), green-when-ripe types (Green Zebra), and open-pollinated paste tomatoes (San Marzano, Amish Paste). Days to maturity vary widely, roughly 70 to 90 days, with the big pink slicers at the long end. Because almost all heirlooms lack the VFN (Verticillium, Fusarium, nematode) resistance bred into hybrids, expect more disease pressure and lean on rotation, sanitation, and airflow; Cherokee Purple is a notable heirloom with some wilt tolerance.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, and potatoes. All four are nightshades and share the same soilborne diseases, chiefly early blight and the Fusarium and Verticillium wilts, whose spores persist in the soil for several years. Following one nightshade with another lets that inoculum build, so heirloom does best on a bed that has been out of the family for about three years.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Do not plant heirloom where tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, or potatoes grew recently. They are all in the same family and share the same soil diseases (mainly early blight and the wilt diseases), which build up in the soil over several years. Give the bed about three years off from this family before planting tomatoes there again.
rotation.good_after: Brassicas, legumes, corn, root vegetables
rotation.note_beginner: Don't plant tomatoes in the same bed two years in a row. Move them to a fresh spot every year if you can, and wait at least 3 years before coming back to the same location. The same rule applies to peppers, eggplant, and potatoes; they're all in the same family and share the same soil diseases, so rotating one without rotating the others doesn't help much. If you've had plants wilt and die even with good watering, look for disease-resistant varieties: a 'V' or 'F' on the seed packet means the variety is bred to resist the most common soilborne wilts.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate nightshades to a fresh bed every 3 years. Fusarium oxysporum and Verticillium dahliae, the two primary soilborne wilts in tomatoes, persist as chlamydospores in soil for 4-6 years and infect through root wounds. Rotation delays pathogen buildup but does not eliminate it; in beds with confirmed wilt history, resistant varieties (coded VF or VFN on seed packets) are the stronger intervention.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Up to 1 week at room temperature, stem-scar side down. Ethylene continues to drive sugar development after harvest; room temperature keeps ethylene-sensitive receptors active, allowing flavor to continue developing. The stem scar is the primary permeability site for moisture loss; resting it downward reduces desiccation.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Keep tomatoes on the counter for up to a week, stem-scar side down. They actually keep getting sweeter and tastier at room temperature, and resting them scar-side down helps them lose less moisture.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Avoid refrigeration for any tomato intended for fresh eating. Below 50-55°F, chilling injury disrupts membrane integrity in mesocarp cells; the damage is irreversible and converts firm flesh to mealy, waterlogged texture. Flavor compounds (volatile esters and aldehydes) are also suppressed by cold and do not recover when the fruit warms. Even a few hours below the threshold causes detectable texture loss in large heirloom fruit.
storage.fridge_beginner: Do not refrigerate tomatoes you plan to eat fresh. Cold below about 50 to 55°F permanently damages them, turning the flesh mealy and watery and dulling the flavor for good, even after they warm back up. Just a few hours in the fridge can leave a big heirloom slice noticeably worse.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Core and slice before freezing; freeze on parchment-lined trays until firm, then bag. Cell walls rupture at freezing temperatures; thawed heirloom will be soft and collapsed. This makes frozen heirloom unsuitable for fresh eating but fully functional for sauces, soups, and roasting where texture is cooked out anyway. Large heirloom slices freeze well and are convenient for winter sauce use.
storage.freezer_beginner: To freeze, core and slice the tomatoes, freeze the slices on a parchment-lined tray until firm, then bag them up. Freezing makes them soft, so they are not good for fresh eating, but they are perfect for sauces, soups, and roasting where they get cooked down anyway.
storage.notes_beginner: Keep tomatoes on the counter, never in the refrigerator. Cold temperatures break down the texture permanently and kill the flavor; even a few hours in the fridge makes a noticeable difference in a large heirloom. Store stem-scar side down to slow moisture loss. If a big fruit is starting to soften unevenly, use the softest sections first. Over-ripe heirlooms that are too soft to eat fresh make excellent sauce; don't throw them away.
storage.notes_seasoned: Never refrigerate a heirloom you intend to eat fresh; cold breaks down cell structure and kills flavor compounds irreversibly. Room-temperature storage extends eating quality. If the fruit is very large and beginning to soften unevenly, prioritize the softest sections first and use firmer sections later. Over-ripe large heirlooms are still excellent for sauce.

det_indet.detail_beginner: Indeterminate means the plant keeps growing and producing all season until frost; it will not stop at a set height. Most heirloom tomatoes are indeterminate and can reach 6 feet or more, so they need a strong cage or stakes put in at planting time. Unlike determinate types that ripen one big batch and stop, an indeterminate heirloom keeps setting new fruit as long as you keep picking and the weather holds.
det_indet.detail_seasoned: Most heirloom tomatoes are indeterminate: the vine keeps growing and setting fruit until frost and can reach 6 to 8 feet, so it needs sturdy staking or caging and continuous support. Prune to one or two main stems for larger fruit and better airflow, which also helps limit the foliar diseases heirlooms are prone to. A few heirlooms are compact or semi-determinate (the open-pollinated Stupice runs early and bushy; paste types like Amish Paste are often semi-determinate), but the classic large slicers (Brandywine, Cherokee Purple, Mortgage Lifter) are strongly indeterminate.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A tiny white root emerging from the seed, then a pale curved shoot pushing upward through the soil. The shoot will straighten and the first two small leaves will unfold at the top.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Tomato seeds need warm soil to sprout: around 75 to 85°F is ideal. A heat mat under the seed tray is the easiest way to get there; without one, try the top of your refrigerator or any consistently warm spot. Cover the tray with a clear plastic lid or cling wrap until the first sprout appears, then take it off right away.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tiny white root emerging from the seed, then a pale shoot pushing upward through the soil.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep soil temperature in the 70-85°F range. A heat mat makes a real difference for staying in the optimal zone. Cover with a humidity dome until sprouts appear.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have you seen any sprouts yet?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Any little sprouts poking up yet?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Two small flat leaves open first; those are the seed leaves. Then the first true leaves emerge between them; they'll have the distinctive jagged edges and tomato-leaf smell.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Take off the plastic cover the moment you see the first green sprouts; leaving it on after emergence creates the warm, still, humid conditions that cause damping off, a fungal problem that collapses seedling stems at the soil line and kills them fast. Move the tray as close to your brightest light as possible. If seedlings grow tall and floppy instead of short and stocky, they need more light, not more water; that stretched-out look (called etiolation) means the seedling is reaching toward brighter light.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Two seed leaves open flat, then the first true leaves emerging between them; they will look distinctly tomato-shaped.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Remove the humidity dome the moment sprouts appear; trapped moisture after emergence drives damping off (Pythium/Rhizoctonia fungal complex attacking the hypocotyl). Get seedlings as close to your brightest light source as possible. Leggy, etiolated growth is caused by light deficiency, not overwatering; the seedling is elongating its internode lengths to search for brighter light.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How are your seedlings looking?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How do your young seedlings look so far?

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A strong, thick stem, 3 to 4 sets of true leaves, and a deep green color. The plant looks sturdy and compact rather than tall and floppy.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Start hardening off about a week before you plan to transplant: put the plant outside for a couple of hours in a sheltered spot, then bring it back in. Add more time and more direct sun each day. This gradual process thickens the plant's waxy leaf coating and helps it adjust to outdoor wind and temperature swings; plants that skip it tend to struggle for weeks after transplanting. When you plant, bury the stem deeper than it sits in the pot, right up to the lowest set of leaves; new roots will form all along the buried stem.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong stem, 3-4 sets of true leaves, deep green color. Ready to pot up or transplant.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Begin hardening off 7-10 days before transplant date: short outdoor exposures starting in a sheltered spot, progressively longer and less sheltered. Hardening triggers thicker cuticular wax deposition and stomatal adaptation to outdoor vapor pressure deficit; plants that skip this step show photoinhibition and sulk for 2-3 weeks post-transplant. Plant deep: bury the stem right up to the lowest leaves. Adventitious roots form all along buried stem tissue, building a substantially larger root system than transplanting at pot depth alone would produce.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are they outside yet, or still hardening off?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are your plants outside in the garden yet, or still getting used to outdoor air?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Small yellow flowers appearing in clusters. Each flower is a potential tomato.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Switch from a general fertilizer to one higher in potassium once flowers appear: look for 'tomato fertilizer' or a formula like 5-10-10. Too much nitrogen at this stage (the first number on the fertilizer bag) pushes the plant into producing more leaves instead of fruit. Give the flowering stems a gentle shake each morning to help pollen release and improve fruit set; heirloom flowers are self-pollinating, but a little movement makes a real difference, especially in calm weather.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small yellow flowers in clusters. Each flower is a potential fruit.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Switch from a balanced feed to a high-potassium fertilizer when flowers appear. Nitrogen drives vegetative (leaf) growth via chlorophyll and cell division pathways; excess nitrogen at flower set pushes resources back into the canopy rather than into fruit development. Potassium supports sugar loading, cell turgor, and the hydraulic pressure that drives fruit fill. Gently tap or shake the flowering stems in the morning to assist pollination; heirloom flowers are self-fertile but buzz pollination (vibration dislodging pollen from anthers) substantially improves fruit set, especially in still air.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Flowers open yet?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have any flowers opened up yet?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Fully colored fruit that gives slightly to a gentle squeeze. The skin may start to lose its shine when perfectly ripe.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pick every ripe tomato at each visit to the plant. Harvesting regularly signals the plant to keep producing; leaving ripe fruit on the vine slows that process down. Heirloom tomatoes keep producing until frost on a healthy plant, so staying on top of harvesting is the single biggest thing you can do to keep production going.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fully colored fruit that gives slightly to a gentle squeeze. The skin may start to lose its sheen when perfectly ripe.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick every ripe tomato at each visit; the plant is an indeterminate sink that routes photosynthate toward existing fruit. Ripe fruit remaining on the vine is an energy sink that competes with new fruit development and reduces total yield. Harvest also removes the ethylene-producing ripe fruit that can accelerate ripening of nearby fruit faster than you want.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: First tomatoes picked? Log your harvest.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Picked your first tomatoes? Add them to your log.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant slows down: fewer new flowers, yellowing on the lower leaves, and nights cooling consistently below 50°F.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: When nights are reliably below 50°F, pinch out all the growing tips at the top of each stem. This stops the plant from putting energy into new growth and directs what's left into ripening the fruit already on the vine. Heirloom tomatoes won't fully color below 50°F, so bring any threatened green tomatoes inside and let them ripen at room temperature, never in the refrigerator, which ruins the flavor.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Slowing production, yellowing lower leaves, nights cooling below 50°F.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: When nights drop regularly below 50°F, pinch out all growing tips (apical meristems). Removing the apical meristem ends auxin-driven vegetative extension and concentrates the remaining photosynthate into ripening existing fruit. Heirloom fruit needs temperatures above 50°F to complete lycopene synthesis; fruit that stays on the vine below this threshold will not fully color. Bring threatened green tomatoes inside to ripen at room temperature; chilling injury below 50°F is irreversible.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How was your season? Worth logging what worked.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How did the season go? It helps to jot down what worked and what did not.

notifications.title_beginner: Time to start your heirloom tomatoes indoors
notifications.body_beginner: Your last frost date is about {{weeks_until_anchor}} weeks away, the right window to get heirloom tomato seeds started. Fill small trays or cells with seed-starting mix, plant one or two seeds per cell about a quarter inch deep, and put them somewhere warm (70 to 80°F is ideal). Cover with a plastic dome or cling wrap until you see sprouts, then remove it right away. Heirloom tomatoes need a long season, so starting on time really matters.
notifications.title_seasoned: Time to start your tomatoes indoors
notifications.body_seasoned: Your last frost date is about {{weeks_until_anchor}} weeks away, the perfect window to get tomato seeds into trays. Find somewhere warm (70-80°F), keep the soil consistently moist, and cover with a dome until you see sprouts. This is where your season begins.

notifications.title_beginner: Start introducing your tomatoes to the outdoors
notifications.body_beginner: Your last frost is {{days_until_anchor}} days away: time to start hardening off your seedlings. Put them outside for a couple of hours today in a sheltered, partly shaded spot, then bring them back in. Add more time and more direct sun each day over the next week. This gradual process helps the plant adjust to outdoor wind, temperature swings, and stronger sun before it goes out for good.
notifications.body_seasoned: Your last frost is {{days_until_anchor}} days away. Begin putting your plants outside for a few hours each day; start sheltered, increase exposure gradually. This week of adjustment makes a real difference to how they settle in after transplanting.
