notifications.title_beginner: Last frost has passed: time to transplant
notifications.body_beginner: Your heirloom tomatoes are ready to go outside for good. Plant them deeper than they sit in the pot: bury the stem right up to the lowest set of leaves. New roots will form all along the buried stem, which gives the plant a larger, stronger root system and makes it more drought-tolerant through the season.
notifications.title_seasoned: Last frost has passed: time to transplant
notifications.body_seasoned: Your tomatoes are ready to go outside for good. Plant them deep: bury the stem right up to the lowest set of leaves. Roots will form all along the buried stem and give you a stronger, more drought-tolerant plant.

notifications.title_beginner: Your tomatoes should be flowering soon
notifications.body_beginner: Small yellow flowers appearing means fruit is on the way. Switch to a fertilizer higher in potassium now (look for 'tomato fertilizer' or something labeled for fruiting). Give the flowering stems a gentle shake each morning to help pollen release and improve fruit set. Each flower is a potential tomato.
notifications.title_seasoned: Your tomatoes should be flowering soon
notifications.body_seasoned: Small yellow flowers appearing means fruit is on the way. Switch to a high-potassium feed now, and give the flowering stems a gentle shake in the morning to help pollination. Each flower is a potential tomato.

notifications.title_beginner: First tomatoes should be nearly ready
notifications.body_beginner: Based on when you planted, you should be seeing ripe or nearly-ripe fruit about now. Heirloom tomatoes are ready when fully colored and give just slightly to a gentle squeeze. Pick ripe ones regularly; the more you harvest, the more the plant produces.
notifications.title_seasoned: First tomatoes should be nearly ready
notifications.body_seasoned: Based on when you planted, you should be seeing ripe or nearly-ripe fruit about now. Pick when fully colored and slightly soft to the touch. The more you pick, the more the plant produces; stay on top of it.

notifications.title_beginner: First frost in {{weeks_until_anchor}} weeks: finish strong
notifications.body_beginner: Your season is almost done. Pinch out the growing tips at the top of each stem now; this stops the plant from putting energy into new growth and sends it all into the fruit already on the vine. Harvest everything you can and bring green tomatoes inside to ripen on a cool windowsill.
notifications.title_seasoned: First frost in {{weeks_until_anchor}} weeks: finish strong
notifications.body_seasoned: Your growing season is almost done. Pinch out the growing tips now so the plant puts all its remaining energy into the fruit already on the vine. Harvest anything you can and bring green tomatoes inside to ripen on a windowsill.

notifications.body_beginner: You haven't logged anything in a couple of weeks. How's the plant looking? Any flowers, fruit, or pests worth noting? Checking in regularly helps you catch problems before they get serious.
notifications.body_seasoned: You have not logged anything in a couple of weeks. How is the plant looking? Any flowers, fruit, or pests worth noting? Regular check-ins help you catch problems early.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost tonight: cover your tomatoes
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Freezing temperatures are forecast tonight. Tomatoes are frost-tender and one hard freeze can kill the plant. Cover them with an old bedsheet, a bucket, or frost cloth before dark, and uncover in the morning once temperatures are back above freezing. Container plants can be moved inside.
weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning: protect your tomatoes tonight
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Temperatures are dropping close to freezing tonight. Cover plants with fleece or old bedsheets, or bring containers inside. Tomatoes are frost-tender and one cold night can end your season early.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Very hot days ahead: help your tomatoes through
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Several very hot days are forecast. Above about 95°F, tomato flowers tend to drop without setting fruit; this is heat stress, not a disease. Water deeply in the early morning so the soil stays moist through the day, and add a layer of mulch around the base to hold that moisture. Shade cloth draped over the plant during the hottest part of the afternoon can help if you have it.
weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat stress warning for your tomatoes
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Several very hot days ahead. Tomato flowers can drop when temperatures stay above 95°F. Water deeply in the early morning, add mulch around the base to retain moisture, and consider shade cloth during the hottest part of the day.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: It's been dry: water your tomatoes deeply
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Dry conditions have been building. Uneven watering right now can cause blossom end rot (dark patches on the fruit bottom) and cracked fruit. Water deeply at the base of the plant; aim for 1 to 2 inches this week. A thick layer of mulch around the stem helps hold moisture between watering sessions.
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: It has been dry. Inconsistent watering at this stage causes blossom end rot and cracked fruit. Water deeply at the base; aim for 1-2 inches this week. Mulching around the stem helps hold moisture.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: High humidity: check your tomato leaves
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Humid weather creates ideal conditions for fungal diseases like early and late blight. Take a few minutes to check the lower leaves for brown spots, yellow patches, or anything unusual. If you spot affected leaves, remove them right away and don't put them in your compost. Keeping the plant staked and open for airflow is your best prevention.
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Humid conditions are ideal for early and late blight. Check lower leaves for dark spots with yellow halos. Remove any affected leaves immediately and do not compost them. Good airflow around the plant is your best defense.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Heavy rain coming: harvest ripe tomatoes now
weather_triggers.body_beginner: A lot of rain in a short period can cause ripe tomatoes to split; heirlooms are especially prone to cracking because of their size. Pick anything that looks close to ready before the rain arrives. After the rain, check the lower leaves; soil splashed up by heavy rain can spread disease spores onto the plant.
weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heavy rain: harvest ripe tomatoes now
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A lot of rain in a short time can split ripe fruit. Pick anything that is nearly ready before it cracks, and check for soil splash on lower leaves which can spread disease.

germination.text_beginner: Bottom heat is the single biggest factor in germination speed. If you have a heat mat, use it; if not, the top of a refrigerator or any spot that stays consistently around 75°F works well. Most heirloom tomato seeds sprout within 5 to 7 days with steady warmth.
germination.text_seasoned: Bottom heat is the single biggest factor in germination speed. A heat mat, the top of your refrigerator, or anywhere consistently warm works well. Most tomato seeds germinate in 5-7 days at 75°F.

germination.text_beginner: Cover your seed tray with a plastic dome or cling wrap until the first sprout appears, then remove it right away. The dome traps humidity to keep the seed surface moist during germination; but once the shoot emerges, that same warm, still air is the ideal environment for damping off, a fungal problem that collapses the seedling stem at the soil line and kills it overnight with no recovery.
germination.text_seasoned: Cover your tray with a humidity dome or cling film until the first sprout appears. Remove it immediately when you see growth; leaving it on causes damping off.

seedling.text_beginner: If your seedlings are tall and thin and look weak, they need more light, not less water. Move the tray right next to your brightest window, or set up a grow light to shine on them for 14 to 16 hours each day. Pale color is a sign of the same problem.
seedling.text_seasoned: Leggy, stretched seedlings almost always mean not enough light, not overwatering. Get them as close to a bright window as possible, or use a grow light 14-16 hours a day.

seedling.text_beginner: Once you have two sets of true leaves, pot up into individual cells or small 3-inch pots. You can bury the stem deeper than it was sitting; tomatoes form roots all along any buried stem tissue, so a deeper pot-up now means a stronger root system later.
seedling.text_seasoned: Once you have two sets of true leaves, pot up into individual cells or small 3-inch pots. Tomatoes root all along their stems, so you can bury them deeper than they were; it builds a stronger plant.

established.text_beginner: Harden off properly: a week of outdoor time before transplanting, starting with just a couple of hours in a sheltered spot. Plants that skip this step often struggle for two to three weeks after transplanting, which eats into the long season heirloom tomatoes need.
established.text_seasoned: Harden off properly: a week of outdoor time before transplanting, starting with just a couple of hours in a sheltered spot. Plants that skip this step sulk for weeks after transplanting.

established.text_beginner: Plant your tomatoes deeper than they sit in the pot: bury the stem right up to the lowest set of leaves. Every bit of buried stem becomes roots, and a larger root system means a more drought-tolerant, productive plant.
established.text_seasoned: Plant your tomatoes deeper than they sit in the pot. Bury the stem right up to the lowest set of leaves. Every bit of buried stem becomes roots.

flowering.text_beginner: Give the flowering stems a gentle shake each morning to help pollen transfer and improve fruit set. It sounds fussy, but it genuinely makes a difference, especially in a sheltered spot without much natural breeze. Each flower is a potential tomato.
flowering.text_seasoned: A gentle shake of the flowering stem in the morning helps pollen transfer and improves fruit set. It sounds fussy but it genuinely makes a difference, especially in a sheltered spot without much breeze.

flowering.text_beginner: Stop high-nitrogen fertilizing the moment flowers appear. Nitrogen drives leafy growth; what you want now is potassium. Switch to a tomato-specific feed or any formula with a higher third number; that third number on the fertilizer bag is the potassium.
flowering.text_seasoned: Stop high-nitrogen feeding the moment flowers appear. Nitrogen pushes leafy growth. What you want now is potassium: switch to a tomato-specific or high-K feed.

harvest.text_beginner: Pick every ripe tomato every time you visit the plant. The more you harvest, the more the plant produces. Leaving ripe fruit on the vine is the most common reason production slows mid-season; the plant has less reason to keep setting new fruit.
harvest.text_seasoned: Pick every ripe tomato you can find, every time you check the plant. The more you harvest, the more the plant produces. Leaving ripe fruit on the vine is the most common reason production slows mid-season.

harvest.text_beginner: Taste as you go. Heirloom tomatoes peak at slightly different moments depending on the variety and the weather; some are best when just fully colored, others benefit from another day or two. Your palate is the best harvest indicator you have.
harvest.text_seasoned: Taste as you go. Different varieties peak at different moments; some are best just before fully ripe, others need a few more days. Your palate is the best harvest indicator you have.

end_of_season.text_beginner: When nights drop below 50°F regularly, pinch out all the growing tips at the top of each stem. This stops the plant from putting energy into new growth and channels everything into ripening the fruit already on the vine.
end_of_season.text_seasoned: When nights drop below 50°F regularly, pinch out all the growing tips. The plant will stop trying to set new fruit and put everything into ripening what is already there.

end_of_season.text_beginner: Green tomatoes left on the plant when frost threatens can be brought inside to ripen. Lay them in a single layer somewhere cool and dark, not the refrigerator, which damages the texture and kills the flavor.
end_of_season.text_seasoned: Green tomatoes left on the plant when frost threatens can be brought inside to ripen. Lay them in a single layer somewhere cool and dark, not the refrigerator, which kills flavor.

end_of_season.text_beginner: Because heirlooms are open-pollinated, you can save seed from your best fruit and grow the same variety again next year. Scoop the seeds and pulp from a fully ripe tomato into a jar with a little water, let it ferment 3 to 4 days until a film forms on top, then rinse the seeds clean, dry them on a plate or screen somewhere warm and airy, and store them cool and dark. Seed saved from a hybrid will not come back true, but heirloom seed will.
end_of_season.text_seasoned: Heirlooms are open-pollinated, so seed saved from a healthy, ripe fruit grows true to type. Ferment the seed and gel in water for 3 to 4 days to break down the gel coat and suppress seedborne pathogens, then rinse, dry, and store cool and dark. Save from your best plants; hybrid seed segregates and will not reproduce the parent.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Highly variety-dependent: an indeterminate heirloom typically yields 8 to 20 lbs over the season, but fruit size ranges enormously, from 2 to 4 oz Green Zebra and paste types to 1 to 2 lb Brandywine and Hillbilly slicers, so per-fruit counts vary widely. In short-season zones (3 to 5) total yield is limited by season length; in zones 7 to 9 a well-managed vine often exceeds 20 lbs. Heirlooms frequently yield somewhat less than disease-resistant hybrids because foliar and wilt disease shortens the productive window, which is the main yield tradeoff for the flavor.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Expect roughly 8 to 20 pounds of tomatoes per plant over the season, though it depends a lot on the variety: a big Brandywine plant makes fewer, huge fruit, while a paste or Green Zebra plant makes many smaller ones. Heirlooms often yield a bit less than modern hybrids because they catch disease more easily, but most gardeners grow them for the flavor rather than the weight.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: A healthy indeterminate heirloom at peak produces a steady flow of fruit for roughly 4 to 8 weeks in mid-season, then tapers as fall cools and, for many heirlooms, as foliar disease advances. Weekly counts depend on fruit size: a few large slicers, or many small paste and salad types. Fruit set is most reliable when night temperatures stay between about 55 and 75°F; below 55°F pollen viability drops, and above about 70 to 75°F pollen becomes non-viable and flowers drop.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: At its peak a healthy plant produces steadily for about 4 to 8 weeks in midsummer, then slows as fall arrives. Big-fruited heirlooms give you a few large tomatoes a week; smaller paste or salad types give you many. Fruit sets best when nights stay between about 55 and 75°F; much colder or hotter than that and the flowers often drop without setting.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Your first heirloom season will probably feel slow. The plant spends the first half of summer building its root system and vine structure before it really starts setting fruit. Getting 3 to 5 large tomatoes in your first season is a real success; don't measure yourself against experienced gardeners who know every trick. Focus on two things: get a strong cage or stake in place early (before you think you need it), and keep the watering consistent when the plant starts flowering.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: First-season heirlooms frequently disappoint on yield, not because of mistakes, but because the plant architecture is building for the first half of the season. Getting 3-5 large fruit in a first season is a genuine success. Focus on getting the support structure right early and on consistent watering at fruit set; those two factors drive the difference between a partial and a full-season harvest.
factors_seasoned: hours of direct sunlight
consistent watering
feeding schedule
staking and airflow

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Frost or cold damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: You'll see the leaves turn black or dark brown and go limp, sometimes overnight after a single cold night. Tomatoes are tropical plants with no cold tolerance at all. Even without a hard freeze, temperatures below 50°F cause what's called chilling injury: the plant's cells start to break down, and young transplants are especially vulnerable because they haven't yet built up a protective waxy coating on their leaves. A plant hit hard by frost usually won't recover. For next time: both your nighttime air temperature AND your soil temperature need to be reliably above 60°F before you transplant.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Wait until nighttime temperatures are reliably above 50°F AND your soil is above 60°F before transplanting; check soil temperature 2 to 3 inches deep with an inexpensive probe thermometer. In Zones 3 to 5 this often means waiting until late May or early June regardless of what the calendar says.
failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Frost or cold damage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Tomatoes are tropical plants and suffer the moment temperatures drop near freezing. Even a brief cold night can blacken leaves and kill young plants. If it happened at transplant, the plant was likely moved out too early; soil temperature matters as much as air temperature.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait until both night temperatures are reliably above 50°F and soil temperature is above 60°F before transplanting. A cheap soil thermometer removes the guesswork.

failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Heirloom tomatoes can run into a few common problems. Blight is a leaf disease that starts on the lower leaves first and spreads fastest in wet, humid weather. Blossom end rot shows up as a dark, sunken patch on the bottom of the fruit; it looks like a nutrient problem, but it's almost always caused by uneven watering (dry for a stretch, then suddenly soaked). Adding extra calcium won't fix it. Consistent moisture will.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Water at the base of the plant, not from overhead, and stake the plant for good airflow. Leaves that dry quickly after rain are much harder for blight to infect. Move your tomatoes to a different bed each year; blight spores can survive in the soil over winter. For blossom end rot: mulch heavily and water deeply and consistently rather than in small frequent amounts.
failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Pests or disease
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Tomatoes are susceptible to blight, blossom end rot, and several common pests. Blight spreads fast in wet, humid conditions and usually starts at the lower leaves. Blossom end rot is caused by calcium deficiency triggered by irregular watering, not a nutrient problem.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water consistently at the base, not overhead. Remove any affected leaves immediately. Rotate tomatoes to a different bed each year and stake plants to improve airflow.

failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Too much water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Overwatered tomatoes show yellowing leaves starting at the bottom of the plant, and roots that can't get oxygen; waterlogged soil suffocates them. Inconsistent watering is actually more damaging than steady overwatering: if the soil dries out and then you flood it, the sudden change in moisture causes the fruit skin to expand faster than the inside, and the tomatoes crack. Blossom end rot (dark patches on the fruit bottom) can follow the same pattern.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Water deeply two or three times a week rather than a small amount every day. Deep watering encourages roots to grow down into the soil rather than staying shallow near the surface. A thick layer of mulch around the base of the plant evens out moisture and dramatically reduces the wet-dry swings that cause cracking.
failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Too much water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Overwatered tomatoes show yellowing lower leaves, cracked fruit, and roots that cannot get oxygen. Inconsistent watering, dry then suddenly wet, causes fruit splitting and blossom end rot.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water deeply twice a week rather than a little every day. Mulching around the base dramatically improves moisture consistency.

failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Too little water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Drought stress during flowering causes blossom drop; the flowers fall off before fruit can set, and those potential tomatoes are gone for good. During fruiting, inconsistent moisture (dry spells followed by heavy watering) causes blossom end rot and cracked skin. Heirloom tomatoes are large-fruited and especially water-hungry; they need steady moisture throughout the whole season.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Heirloom tomatoes need about 1 to 2 inches of water per week. Mulch heavily around the base to hold moisture in the soil between waterings. Always water at the base of the plant, not the leaves; wet leaves in the evening invite disease.
failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Too little water
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Drought stress during flowering causes blossom drop; no flowers, no fruit. During fruiting, inconsistent moisture causes blossom end rot and cracked skin.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Tomatoes need 1-2 inches of water per week. Mulch heavily to retain moisture, and water at the base never the leaves.

failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Not enough sun
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Tomatoes need at least 6 to 8 hours of direct sun each day to produce fruit well. In a shady spot the plant will grow, sometimes quite lushly, but will set little or no fruit, and will be much more prone to fungal disease because the leaves stay damp instead of drying out. Heirloom types in particular need full sun to develop their large, dense fruit properly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Tomatoes are one of the most sun-hungry vegetables in the garden. If your current spot is getting less than 6 hours of direct sun, move the tomatoes to your sunniest bed next season and plant something more shade-tolerant, like lettuce or spinach, in the shadier spot.
failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Not enough sun
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Tomatoes need a minimum of 6-8 hours of direct sun to produce well. In shade they grow leafy but set little or no fruit, and are much more prone to disease.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Tomatoes are one of the most sun-hungry vegetables. If your current spot is marginal, prioritize this bed for tomatoes next season and move something more shade-tolerant elsewhere.

succession_policy.tip_beginner: You only need to plant heirloom tomatoes once; the same plant will keep producing fruit all summer until frost kills it. No need to replant partway through the season. If you live in a very warm climate (think Southern California, Phoenix, or South Florida, Zone 9 or warmer,), you can start a second planting in late summer for a fall and winter harvest.
succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Not a true succession crop; one indeterminate plant produces all season until frost. A second planting started mid-season in most zones would be killed by frost before its 75-100 day maturity window closes. In zones 9-11 a late-summer planting (July-August) is viable as a separate fall crop, not a succession.
succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Heirloom is an indeterminate crop that continues setting new flower clusters until frost. A single plant produces continuously through the season, making succession planting unnecessary and impractical, since a second planting started weeks later would simply be frost-killed before reaching its long (75-100 day) maturity window in most zones. In zones 9-11 where a fall planting is common, that is a separate season, not a succession.

crops.description_beginner: Heirloom tomatoes are open-pollinated varieties, which means you can save their seed and grow the same tomato again next year (hybrid tomatoes do not do this; their saved seed comes up as a mix). They come in an amazing range of colors, shapes, and sizes: deep purple-brown Cherokee Purple and Black Krim, green-striped Green Zebra, huge pink Brandywine and Mortgage Lifter slicers, and slender paste types like San Marzano. Most heirlooms are indeterminate, meaning the plant keeps growing and setting new fruit until frost, so it needs a strong cage or stake from the start; plan for a plant 5 to 6 feet tall or more. The main catch is that heirlooms usually do not have the built-in disease resistance that modern hybrids are bred for, so they are more likely to run into wilt diseases, leaf blights, and cracked fruit. You keep ahead of that with good spacing and airflow, watering at the base, moving your tomatoes to a fresh spot each year, and steady, even watering. The flavor is why people grow them: many gardeners think heirlooms are the best-tasting tomatoes there are.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: The tricky part with heirlooms is that many of them are not red when ripe. Cherokee Purple and Black Krim ripen to a dusky purple-brown and keep green shoulders, Green Zebra stays green with a yellow blush, and Brandywine turns deep pink. Learn what your variety looks like ripe, then pick when it has full color, gives a little to a gentle squeeze without being mushy, and the skin looks slightly less shiny than before. Big heirlooms take a few extra days than small ones. Heirlooms split easily, so pick them as soon as they are ripe, especially right after rain.

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.source_quote: It is possible to start tomatoes from seeds indoors about six to eight weeks before you'll want to move them outside. (MSU)
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Heirloom (larger-fruited, slower-maturing) varieties require the 8-week end of this range to reach transplant size.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: Many gardeners plant transplants the last week or two of May, after danger of frost has passed and air and soil temperatures warm. (MSU)
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start your warm season crops indoors for transplanting in mid-June, once the threat of frost has passed. Transplant outdoors after all danger of frost has passed and the soil has warmed. Don't be in a rush to transplant these tropical species. (UMaine, northern Maine Z3-4; UMN; NDSU)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Most traditional tomato varieties take 70 to 85 days from the time plants are placed in the ground to the time fruits are ready to harvest; heirloom varieties sit at the upper end of this range (80-85 days). (UMN Extension; MSU Extension)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.source_quote: Pick all the fruit and bring it indoors before the first frost at the end of summer. (UMN)
harvest_end.design_note_seasoned: Conservative policy: harvest_end = first_frost - 5 days to buffer against frost-risk week and to ensure notifications arrive before plants are killed.

northern_tier.plantings_provenance: Zone-promoted and re-verified from cold zones 3-7 (m16_heirloom_step3_5_region_shells, 2026-06-07). Supersedes the Phase A verbatim lift.

3.notes: Very challenging in Zone 3: 80+ day maturity leaves little margin. Choose Fast varieties like Stupice. Use season extenders.
3.zone_notes: Zone 3 is marginal for large heirloom varieties (80-100 day maturity). Choose a faster 75-day variety (Stupice, Bloody Butcher) or consider cherry tomatoes for more reliable harvest. Start 8 weeks before last frost.

4.notes: Start 8 weeks early. Choose varieties under 85 days. Heavy mulching and black plastic help.
4.zone_notes: Start indoors 8 weeks early. Heirlooms push the limits of Zone 4, so choose carefully.

5.notes: Plant after last frost. Stake heavily, as heirlooms get large and heavy. Consistent watering prevents blossom end rot.
5.zone_notes: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost.

6.notes: Excellent zone for heirlooms. Long season allows full flavor development. Remove suckers to focus energy on fruit.
6.zone_notes: Heirlooms need 80+ days, so plant by mid-May at latest for harvest before first frost.

7.notes: Heat stress above 95°F can cause blossom drop. Shade cloth and deep watering help through July to August peak.
7.zone_notes: Plant by late May. Too late to do a second planting, so focus on one great crop.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the cold northern states (zones 3 through 7) you grow heirloom tomatoes once a year, as a single summer crop. What limits the season here is frost on both ends, not summer heat. Because big heirloom tomatoes are slow to ripen (about 75 to 90 days after transplanting), start the seeds indoors well before your last frost, then set the plants out a week or two after that last frost, once nights stay warm and the soil has warmed up. That single planting gives you one long harvest until the first fall frost ends it. There is no summer break the way hotter regions have, because northern summers usually are not hot enough to stop the plants from setting fruit. Unlike cherry tomatoes, heirlooms take too long to fit in a second crop, so plan on one well-timed planting and choose faster varieties. In the coldest zones, start seed early indoors, pick quick-maturing varieties, and warm the soil with black plastic mulch or season-extending covers so the fruit ripens before frost returns.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: The Northern Tier (cold zones 3 through 7) grows heirloom tomatoes as a single frost-bracketed summer crop: the limiting factor on both ends is frost, not heat. Because large-fruited heirloom types are slow (about 75 to 90 days from transplant), the season is started indoors well ahead of the last frost, transplants go out a week or two after that last spring frost once nights hold above the low 50s°F and soil warms past about 60°F, and that one planting then produces a single continuous harvest until plants are cut short by the first fall frost. There is no midsummer heat exclusion here: northern summers rarely sustain the high day and night temperatures that stop fruit set, so the only gaps are the winter cold pauses and the season between them is uninterrupted. Unlike cherry types, heirloom's longer days-to-maturity leaves no room for a second crop even at the warm end of the band, so the whole region runs on one well-timed planting; the short-season north strongly favors the faster large-fruited varieties and starting seed indoors. The coldest zones (3 and 4) depend on early indoor starts, fast-maturing varieties, and season extension (black plastic mulch, Wall-O-Waters) to ripen fruit before frost. Frost dates shift sharply across the band, so confirm your local last and first frost. (University of Minnesota Extension; North Dakota State University Extension; Michigan State University Extension; University of Maine Cooperative Extension)

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.source_quote: tomatoes will take 6 weeks
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start heirloom seed indoors about six weeks before the spring transplant date. In the Southeast and Gulf region that is roughly mid-February for the Georgia interior (zone 8) and two to three weeks earlier toward the warmer Gulf-coastal zone 9 end. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: the last week of March or first week or two of April
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set heirloom transplants out in spring once frost danger passes. UGA gives late March into the first half of April for middle Georgia (zone 8); the warmer zone 9 end runs two to three weeks earlier. Heirloom is large-fruited and slower to mature than cherry types, so time it to set fruit before peak summer heat arrives. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Heirloom begins ripening roughly three months after transplanting (about 75 to 90 days to maturity, longer than cherry types). The spring crop comes in from late June, just as the summer heat begins to shut fruit set down. (UF/IFAS VH021; UGA Cooperative Extension C943)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The spring crop ends as summer heat sets in. Large-fruited tomatoes are more sensitive to high day and night temperatures than cherry types, so blossom drop and fruit-set failure begin earlier for heirloom, by about June. (UF/IFAS VH021; UGA Cooperative Extension C943)

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.source_quote: tomatoes will take 6 weeks
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: For the fall crop, start seed indoors about six weeks before the late-summer transplant date, roughly mid-to-late spring across the region. Because heirloom needs 75 to 90 days to mature, start early enough that the fall transplant can go out as soon as the summer heat-pause lifts. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: Plant the following vegetables no later than July 20 ... tomatoes
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set the fall crop out as the worst summer heat eases so plants establish and produce into the cooler fall. UGA gives a fall tomato deadline of about July 20 for middle Georgia (zone 8) so the crop matures before frost; large-fruited heirloom, being slower than cherry, should hit the early end of the fall window. The warmer zone 9 end runs about two weeks later, into early August. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall crop begins ripening about three months after the late-summer transplant, bringing heirloom tomatoes in from roughly October across the region. (UF/IFAS VH021; UGA Cooperative Extension C943)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.source_quote: Harvest mature green peppers and tomatoes before frost gets them
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall crop produces into the cooler autumn and is harvested up to first frost. Large-fruited heirloom has a shorter productive fall tail here than quick-maturing cherry types. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer fruit set fails from heat, not frost: like all tomatoes, heirloom flowers abort and drop once daytime highs pass the upper 80s to 90s°F and nights stay above about 70°F, when pollen turns non-viable. Large-fruited heirlooms are as heat-sensitive as any large tomato, so Jun through Aug is a set-failure window rather than a growing gap. (Penn State Extension, Heat Stress and Tomatoes; University of Missouri IPM, Understanding Tomato Fruit Set)

Summer fruit set fails from heat, not frost: like all tomatoes, heirloom flowers abort and drop once daytime highs pass the upper 80s to 90s°F and nights stay above about 70°F, when pollen turns non-viable. Large-fruited heirlooms are as heat-sensitive as any large tomato, so Jun through Aug is a set-failure window rather than a growing gap. (Penn State Extension, Heat Stress and Tomatoes; University of Missouri IPM, Understanding Tomato Fruit Set)

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast and Gulf area you can grow heirloom tomatoes twice a year, once in spring and again in fall, with a summer break in between when it gets too hot for the plants to set fruit. Big heirloom tomatoes handle the heat less well than small cherry tomatoes, so their summer break is longer, running through most of the summer. Plant your spring crop early enough to pick before the heat, then plant again in late summer once the worst heat passes for a fall crop.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: The Southeast and Gulf region runs two heirloom seasons, spring and fall, split by a summer heat window when high day and night temperatures cause blossom drop and fruit set fails. Large-fruited heirloom is more heat-sensitive than cherry types, so its summer pause is wider, spanning roughly June through August rather than a single midsummer month. Heirloom also needs 75 to 90 days to mature, longer than cherry, so time the spring crop to set fruit before peak heat and set the fall crop out promptly once the heat eases (UGA gives a July 20 fall deadline for middle Georgia so the crop beats frost). The warmer zone 9 end plants the spring crop earlier and the fall crop later than the zone 8 interior. Frost dates shift across the band, so confirm local last and first frost. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

plantings_provenance.window_structure_basis: UGA Cooperative Extension C943 gives two major planting periods (spring March-May, fall mid-July-September) with an explicit fall tomato deadline (no later than July 20 for middle Georgia), corroborated by UF/IFAS VH021 (North FL tomato Late Mar-Apr + Aug). Two-window is the source grammar, not analogy.
plantings_provenance.heat_pause_basis: WIDER than cherry (Jun-Aug vs single Jul). Large-fruited tomatoes are not heat-set-bred and abort flowers at lower thresholds (UF/IFAS VH021: 'Cherry types are heat resistant' -- large-fruited not; Alabama Coop Ext and U.Missouri IPM: day >85 / night >72 deg-F abort). SE/Gulf high summer breaches this June through August.

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In California's interior valleys you plant heirloom tomatoes once, in spring (April into May), and the same plant produces all summer into fall. You do not need a second planting. Big heirloom tomatoes may slow down and set fewer fruit during the hottest weeks of summer, then pick back up as the nights cool in late summer and fall.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: California's interior valleys (Sacramento, San Joaquin) grow heirloom as a single long warm season: set transplants out April into May and harvest from midsummer into fall up to first frost. UC ANR lists one April-May tomato window with no separate fall planting, so this is one continuous crop, not a spring-and-fall split. Large-fruited heirloom sets fewer fruit through the peak-heat weeks of the valley summer (it is more heat-sensitive than cherry types), with set resuming as nights cool; the plant stays in the ground through the dip. Cages suit the valley heat. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2)

Large-fruited heirloom needs warm days to ripen and can be slow in the coolest coastal pockets, so choose a variety matched to your season length and give it the warmest, most sheltered exposure. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2)

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer fruit set fails from heat, not frost: like all tomatoes, heirloom flowers abort and drop once daytime highs pass the upper 80s to 90s°F and nights stay above about 70°F, when pollen turns non-viable. Large-fruited heirlooms are as heat-sensitive as any large tomato, so Jun through Aug is a set-failure window rather than a growing gap. (Penn State Extension, Heat Stress and Tomatoes; University of Missouri IPM, Understanding Tomato Fruit Set)

ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: In California's low desert (Imperial and Coachella valleys) you grow heirloom tomatoes in the cool months, not the summer. Plant the main crop from December through March so it makes fruit before the extreme heat, and plant a second crop in early fall (around September) once the worst heat breaks. Summer (June through August) is simply too hot for any tomato to set fruit, so the plants rest then.
ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: California's desert valleys (Imperial, Coachella) grow heirloom on an inverted, two-window calendar driven by extreme summer heat. The main crop is set out across the cool season, December through March, to mature and set fruit before summer; a second fall crop goes out in early fall (about September) as the heat breaks and produces into the mild winter. June through August is a climatic-absolute fruit-set exclusion: complete blossom drop for every tomato type, not narrowed for heirloom, which is at least as heat-sensitive as cherry. Confirm local frost for the winter harvest tail. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC IPM)

plantings_provenance.window_structure_basis: UC ANR Table 13.2 (Desert Valleys) gives tomatoes as Dec-March (cool-season main); the early-fall second window and the Jun-Aug heat exclusion are the established low-desert grammar (cf. UA AZ1005 for the adjacent AZ low desert). Two-window.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Peak summer heat is a fruit-set exclusion, not a frost gap: like all tomatoes, heirloom flowers drop and fail to set once daytime highs pass the upper 80s to 90s°F and nights stay above about 70°F, when pollen turns non-viable. In this high-desert band July is the hottest set-failure month, though arid nights recover enough that the shoulders of summer still set. Large-fruited heirlooms are as heat-sensitive as any large tomato. (Penn State Extension, Heat Stress and Tomatoes; University of Missouri IPM, Understanding Tomato Fruit Set)

warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: In the southern high desert (around Las Cruces, New Mexico) you can grow heirloom tomatoes in spring and again in fall, with a hot-summer gap. Plant the spring crop in late March or early April so it makes fruit before the July heat. You can try a fall crop planted in mid-July, but big heirloom tomatoes set fruit poorly in the July and August heat and are slow to ripen, so the fall crop is a bit of a gamble before the November frost. Pick fast-maturing, heat-tolerant varieties.
warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: The southern high desert (Las Cruces, Mesilla Valley; Chihuahuan high desert, zone 8) runs two heirloom windows split by peak summer heat. Set the spring crop out in late March to early April, after the local last frost (about March 19), so it sets fruit before July. A fall crop can be transplanted in mid-July per the Dona Ana County Master Gardener chart, but for large-fruited heirloom this is marginal: fruit set is poor once day temperatures exceed 95 °F through July and August, and a 75-90 day plant only just matures before the November frost (about November 12). Favor fast-maturing, heat-tolerant cultivars for the fall attempt. The fall window and two-window structure rest on the single Las Cruces Master Gardener chart, a regional source; the spring dates are anchored to the high-desert frost data with NOAA cross-check. (NMSU Circular 457; Dona Ana County Master Gardener Las Cruces planting chart)

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set heirloom transplants out in any month of the year. CTAHR gives year-round tomato planting for most of Hawaii contingent on choosing adapted varieties, with no spring/fall bracketing and no summer no-sow exclusion. Note that large-fruited heirloom sets fruit poorly under Hawaii's warm lowland nights, so cooler-elevation siting, cooler-season timing, and heat-tolerant or locally bred cultivars give the best results. (University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5; CTAHR Field Tomato Production Guidelines for Hawaii)

11.calendar_basis: Heirloom tomato can be planted YEAR-ROUND in tropical zone 11; both heat_pause and cold_pause are intentionally absent. There is no winter cold to pause for (frost-free) and no documented summer no-sow exclusion: CTAHR HGV-5 states tomato can be grown throughout the year in most places in Hawaii by choosing adapted varieties, and names no seasonal fruit-set gap. UNLIKE cherry (which CTAHR treats as cleanly heat resistant), CTAHR's Field Tomato Production Guidelines specifically warn that large-fruited varieties set fruit poorly under Hawaii's warm lowland nights (optimum fruit set 60-70 deg-F). This is a fruit-set-QUALITY caveat, disclosed in the seasoned region_note, not an absolute no-sow month, so the year-round structure holds (guardrail: heat_pause is read from the source per region, never defaulted; HGV-5 documents no exclusion month). Hawaii's dominant challenge is disease, insect, and heavy-rain pressure, managed with resistant locally bred cultivars (Kewalo, Anahu, Healani, N-series) and cultural practice. Absence of both pauses is intentional and carries this reason; year_round:true makes the all-active calendar machine-readable. hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In Hawaii's tropical lowlands you can plant heirloom tomatoes any month of the year; there is no cold winter and no planting season to wait for. The catch is that big heirloom tomatoes do not set fruit well in the warm tropical nights, so they do best at cooler elevations and in the cooler parts of the year, and you will have the most luck with heat-tolerant or locally bred varieties. The bigger day-to-day challenges are disease, bugs, and heavy rain.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: Hawaii's tropical zone 11 grows heirloom year-round: CTAHR gives a year-round planting capability for most of the islands contingent on adapted varieties, with no winter cold pause and no documented summer no-sow exclusion. The important caveat for heirloom specifically is fruit-set quality, not timing: CTAHR's field production guidance notes that large-fruited varieties are sensitive to high night temperatures and set fruit poorly in the warm lowland (optimum set 60-70 °F), unlike heat-resistant cherry types. Favor cooler-elevation siting, the cooler part of the year, and heat-tolerant or locally bred wilt-resistant cultivars (Kewalo, Anahu, Healani, the N-series). The dominant production challenges here are disease, insect, and heavy-rain pressure, managed with resistant varieties and cultural practice rather than a seasonal stop. (University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5; CTAHR Field Tomato Production Guidelines for Hawaii)

crops.description_seasoned: Open-pollinated, mostly indeterminate tomatoes grown for flavor and diversity. The defining trait of an heirloom is that it is open-pollinated: it breeds true from saved seed, so a Brandywine grown from last year's seed comes back as Brandywine, unlike an F1 hybrid whose saved seed segregates into a mix of the parent traits. Heirlooms span an enormous range of size, color, and shape, from the dusky Cherokee Purple and Black Krim, to the green-when-ripe Green Zebra, to two-pound pink Brandywine and Hillbilly slicers, to open-pollinated paste types like San Marzano and Amish Paste. Most classic heirlooms are indeterminate: the vine keeps extending and setting fruit until frost, so it needs strong staking or caging and benefits from pruning to one or two main stems. Days to maturity vary widely by variety, roughly 70 to 90 days from transplant. The main tradeoff is disease: heirlooms generally lack the Verticillium, Fusarium, and nematode resistance (the VFN codes) bred into modern hybrids, so they are more prone to the soilborne wilts, to early and late blight and Septoria leaf spot, and to fruit cracking, and they reward attentive rotation, sanitation, and even watering. Like all tomatoes they need a long frost-free window and set fruit poorly once day temperatures pass the upper 80s°F or nights stay above about 70°F.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: The ripeness cue depends on the variety's ripe color, which for heirlooms is often not red: Cherokee Purple and Black Krim ripen to a dusky brick-purple with shoulders that stay green, Green Zebra ripens green with a yellow blush and softens rather than reddens, and pink types like Brandywine deepen to rose. Across types, pick when the fruit has reached its full variety color, yields to gentle pressure without feeling mushy, and the skin shifts from a hard glossy sheen to a softer, slightly matte surface. Learn each variety's ripe look rather than waiting for red. Large heirloom slicers (12 oz and up) take a few extra days than small types; mass slows the ripening front. Heirlooms crack readily, so pick promptly when ripe, especially after rain.

pet_safe.note: Ripe tomatoes are fine, but the leaves, stems, and unripe fruit are toxic to cats, dogs, and horses.

crops.name: Grape Tomato

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Grape tomatoes want soil that drains well and is rich in organic matter. If water sits on top of your bed after rain or stays soggy for more than a day, drainage is a problem, soggy roots will rot even if the soil is otherwise good. The easiest fix for most soils is to work in 2 to 3 inches of compost before planting, which improves both drainage and fertility at once. Tomatoes are heavy feeders, so starting with rich soil means less fertilizing mid-season.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Grape tomatoes perform best in well-drained loam or sandy loam with high organic matter content. Adequate drainage is non-negotiable, waterlogged roots invite both Pythium root rot and nutrient lockout even in otherwise fertile soil. Working in 2 to 3 inches of compost before planting addresses both texture and fertility in one amendment. Tomatoes are heavy feeders, and organically rich soil reduces the mid-season fertilizer burden considerably.

ph.note_beginner: Soil pH is a measure of acidity on a scale from 1 to 14, where 7 is neutral. Grape tomatoes do best at a soil pH of 6.2 to 6.8, the slightly acidic range where the nutrients they need are most available. Soils in the interior West (Arizona, Nevada, Utah, Colorado) often run alkaline (above 7), which can lock up nutrients even when you fertilize; growers there often add sulfur before planting. Eastern and Midwestern soils are frequently already in range, but an inexpensive soil test from your local extension office tells you for sure.
ph.note_seasoned: Grape tomatoes, like all tomatoes, are sensitive to pH because it governs the solubility of phosphorus, calcium, and magnesium, the three nutrients they draw down most heavily. The target band is 6.2 to 6.8. Below about 5.5, manganese and aluminum climb toward phytotoxic levels and calcium uptake falters, raising blossom-end rot risk; above 7.0, iron and manganese deficiencies drive interveinal chlorosis on younger leaves. In the alkaline soils common across the interior West and alkaline-irrigation districts, growers routinely acidify before planting. Eastern soils often sit naturally in range; Pacific Northwest soils vary widely by parent material.
