crops.description_seasoned: Grape tomatoes are small, oblong, grape-shaped fruit on vigorous indeterminate plants, and they are one of the most rewarding small tomatoes for a first-season grower. Like cherry tomatoes they are sweet and produce continuously from first flowering until frost, but the fruit is a different animal: the skin is noticeably thicker and the flesh is meatier and less watery. That gives grape types two practical advantages over round cherries. First, they crack far less, both on the vine after rain and in the bowl, because the tougher skin resists the sudden swelling that splits a thin-skinned cherry. Second, they hold much longer after picking, often a week or more at room temperature. The plants are almost always indeterminate and set fruit in long, heavy clusters over a 10 to 14 week season, so a single plant is highly productive. Most modern hybrids (Santa, Juliet, Sweet Hearts, Five Star Grape) also carry disease tolerance. In warm climates (zones 9 to 11), a second late-summer planting can extend harvest into winter; in the coldest zones (3 to 5), choose the faster grape hybrids, around 65 days, and warm the soil before transplanting.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Pick when the fruit is fully and evenly colored, usually deep red, and firm with just a slight give. Grape tomatoes hold their quality on the vine longer than round cherries because the thicker skin resists cracking, so an extra day or two of hang time to deepen color and sugar is lower risk here than with a thin-skinned cherry. Full color indicates that lycopene synthesis and sugar accumulation are complete. Ripe fruit detaches with a gentle twist; if it resists, the abscission zone has not fully formed, so give it another day. The fruit is borne in long clusters, and the individual grapes within a cluster ripen in sequence rather than all at once, so plan to pick a cluster over several visits. Harvest in the morning when temperatures are cooler, as fruit held at 90°F and above deteriorates faster.

pet_safe.note: Ripe tomatoes are fine, but the leaves, stems, and unripe fruit are toxic to cats, dogs, and horses.

crops.name: Banana Pepper

soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Banana pepper wants a deep, fertile, well-drained loam or sandy loam rich in organic matter, and a soil that warms early and holds steady moisture. As a warm-season pepper it sulks in cold, wet ground, so a sandy loam that warms quickly in spring suits it better than a heavy, slow-warming clay. Work 2 to 3 inches of compost into the bed before planting, and on heavy or cool soils many growers lay black plastic or fabric mulch to raise soil temperature and set transplants into warmer ground. Even soil moisture in a freely draining bed is the target, because the wide swings between dry and soaked that a poorly drained soil produces are the direct cause of the calcium-starved blossom-end rot peppers are prone to.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Banana peppers like rich, well-drained soil that warms up in the sun, since they are warm-season plants that dislike cold, soggy ground. Mix in 2 to 3 inches of compost before planting. If your soil is heavy clay or slow to warm, a sheet of black plastic or fabric mulch laid down before planting warms the soil and gives peppers the head start they want. Aim for soil that stays evenly moist but never waterlogged, because uneven watering is what causes the dark, sunken blossom-end rot on the bottom of the fruit.

ph.note_seasoned: Banana pepper grows best at a soil pH of about 6.0 to 6.8, with Georgia and Clemson both placing the target near 6.0 to 6.5. In that band the nutrients peppers need, including the calcium that guards against blossom-end rot, stay most available. Peppers tolerate a somewhat wider range, roughly 5.5 to 7.5, but uptake of iron, manganese, and other micronutrients tightens as the soil turns alkaline, showing as yellowing between the veins of the youngest leaves. Alkaline soils common across the interior West often need sulfur worked in ahead of planting; most Eastern and Midwestern soils sit naturally near the target. A soil test from your local extension office settles it before you plant.
ph.note_beginner: Banana peppers like slightly acidic soil, about pH 6.0 to 6.8, and a lot of garden soil is already close. The pH scale runs from acidic to alkaline, and this range is where peppers take up nutrients best, including the calcium that prevents blossom-end rot. If your soil runs alkaline, common in the dry interior West, you may need to add sulfur before planting. An inexpensive soil test from your local extension office tells you where you stand.

fertilizer.frequency: At planting, then side-dress after fruit set
fertilizer.type: Balanced at planting, then calcium nitrate at fruit set
fertilizer.timing: Work into the bed before transplanting, then side-dress about three to four weeks after transplanting and again once fruit sets
fertilizer.example_product: 10-10-10 at planting, then calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0) as a side-dress
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Banana pepper is a moderate feeder that rewards restraint with nitrogen. Work a balanced fertilizer such as 10-10-10 or 13-13-13, about 2 pounds per 100 square feet, into the bed before transplanting, then side-dress with a nitrogen source such as calcium nitrate about three to four weeks after transplanting and again as the first fruits set. Hold nitrogen back early and never overdo it: too much drives a big, bushy, dark-green plant that flowers late and sets little fruit. The calcium nitrate side-dress does double duty, feeding the plant while supplying the calcium that, paired with even watering, heads off blossom-end rot.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Banana peppers like steady but modest feeding, and going heavy on nitrogen backfires. Mix a balanced fertilizer such as 10-10-10 into the soil before planting. Then, a few weeks after planting and again once the first peppers set, feed with a nitrogen fertilizer like calcium nitrate. Do not overdo it: too much nitrogen gives you a large leafy plant with few peppers. Calcium nitrate also supplies calcium, which, along with even watering, helps prevent blossom-end rot.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Your banana pepper is setting its first fruit, a good time to side-dress with a calcium nitrate source to feed the plant and supply calcium against blossom-end rot.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Your banana pepper is setting fruit. Feed it now with a nitrogen fertilizer such as calcium nitrate to keep it producing and to help prevent blossom-end rot.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced fertilizer such as 10-10-10 worked in at planting, then a calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0) side-dress three to four weeks after transplanting and again at fruit set. Avoid heavy nitrogen, which gives leaf at the expense of fruit.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 at planting, then a nitrogen feed such as calcium nitrate once the plant is growing well and setting fruit. Do not overdo the nitrogen or you get all leaves and few peppers.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A common rate is about 2 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet worked into the bed before transplanting. For the side-dress, Clemson suggests about 5 pounds of calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0) per 1000 square feet, or roughly half a pound per 100 square feet, applied three to four weeks after transplanting and repeated three to four weeks later, placed a few inches out from the plants and watered in.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Mix about 2 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet (or a few inches of compost) into the soil before planting. Then, a few weeks after planting and again at fruit set, scratch a small amount of calcium nitrate into the soil a few inches out from each plant and water it in.

companions.note_seasoned: Most pepper companion pairings are traditional rather than trial-tested. The aromatic-herb and flower companions (basil, marigold, nasturtium, alliums) are grown to deter or trap the aphids and thrips that trouble peppers and to draw beneficial insects, a plausible, habitat-based effect rather than an isolated one. The single firmest rule is a rotation one: keep banana peppers away from their Solanaceae relatives, tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplant, which share the full pepper pest and disease complex.
companions.note_beginner: The most useful pepper companions are strong-smelling herbs and flowers like basil, marigold, and nasturtium, which can help deter or lure away aphids and other pests. The one rule that really matters is to keep banana peppers away from tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplant, which are all close relatives and share the same pests and soil diseases.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Basil
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Basil is a classic pepper neighbor. Its strong scent is thought to help confuse soft-bodied pests like aphids and thrips, and it tucks neatly between young pepper plants. A pleasant, low-risk companion.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional interplanting with peppers; the aromatic foliage is thought to deter aphids and thrips and to draw pollinators and beneficial insects. The effect is habitat-based and traditional rather than trial-isolated for pepper.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Basil is a long-standing companion for peppers; aromatic-herb pest confusion is plausible and habitat-based, not trial-isolated for pepper.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Marigold
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Marigolds are a classic companion flower for peppers, grown to help keep pests down. Mostly tradition, but cheerful and low-risk.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A long-standing companion tradition near peppers; French marigold grown as a cover crop has documented nematode-suppressive effects, though the interplanted marigold-pepper pest benefit is traditional rather than trial-isolated.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: French marigold has documented nematode suppression as a cover crop; the interplanted marigold-pepper effect is traditional, not trial-isolated.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Nasturtium
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Nasturtiums are often planted near peppers to lure aphids away from the crop. A helpful, low-risk neighbor.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Planted as a trap and deterrent for aphids, drawing them off the peppers. Trap cropping is a documented principle, though the specific nasturtium-pepper effect is not formally isolated, so treat it as a plausible aid.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Trap cropping and aphid attraction by nasturtium is documented in principle; the nasturtium-pepper pairing is not trial-isolated.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplant
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep peppers away from tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplant. They are all close relatives that share the same soil diseases and pests, so planting them together makes those problems worse.
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: All are Solanaceae and share pepper's pest and disease complex, including bacterial leaf spot, the mosaic viruses, Phytophthora blight, anthracnose, and aphids. Grouping them concentrates that pressure and lets soilborne problems build. A real epidemiology and rotation principle rather than a tested adjacency effect: spread the nightshades out and rotate them on at least a 3 year cycle.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplant are all Solanaceae and share pepper's pest and disease complex; grouping them concentrates that pressure. A sound epidemiology and rotation principle, not a trial-tested adjacency.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Fennel
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Many gardeners keep fennel away from peppers and most other vegetables, since it is said to stunt their growth. This is more tradition than a proven rule.
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A widely repeated caution that fennel inhibits the growth of many garden vegetables and is best kept to its own corner. There is no strong T1 mechanism for a pepper-fennel antagonism, so it persists mostly as garden lore.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Fennel is a widely cautioned anti-companion said to inhibit many vegetables; the pepper-fennel antagonism is garden lore without a strong T1 mechanism.
