crops.name: Cayenne Pepper

soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Cayenne wants a deep, fertile, well-drained loam or sandy loam that warms early in spring, since like all peppers it is a warm-season crop that sulks in cold, wet ground. Work 2 to 3 inches of compost into the bed before planting to feed a long season and improve moisture holding. On heavy or slow-warming soil, a raised bed or a sheet of black plastic or fabric mulch lifts the soil temperature and gives transplants the warm start they need. Above all the soil must drain freely: saturated ground stalls the roots, invites the Phytophthora blight and root rots peppers are prone to, and the uneven moisture it causes drives blossom-end rot on the developing pods. Steady moisture in freely draining soil is the target.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Cayenne likes rich, well-drained soil that warms up nicely in the sun, because peppers are warm-season plants that dislike cold, soggy ground. Mix 2 to 3 inches of compost into the bed before planting. If your soil is heavy clay or slow to warm, a raised bed or a sheet of black plastic mulch warms it up and helps peppers get going. The most important thing is drainage: soggy soil stalls the plant, causes root and fruit rots, and the uneven watering that comes with it leads to blossom-end rot on the pods.

ph.note_seasoned: Cayenne grows best at a soil pH of about 6.0 to 6.8, the range where the nutrients peppers need stay most available; Penn State reports best yields in the 6.0 to 6.8 band, and Clemson and UGA center a slightly tighter 6.0 to 6.5. It tolerates a little either side of this, but as the soil turns strongly acidic or above about 7.0 the uptake of several nutrients tightens and growth suffers. Most Eastern and Midwestern garden soils sit naturally near the target; alkaline soils common across the interior West often need sulfur worked in before planting. A simple soil test from your local extension office settles it before you plant.
ph.note_beginner: Cayenne likes soil that is slightly acidic, about pH 6.0 to 6.8, and a lot of garden soil is already close. The pH scale runs from acidic to alkaline, and this range is where peppers take up nutrients best. If your soil runs alkaline, common in the dry interior West, you may need to add sulfur before planting. An inexpensive soil test from your local extension office tells you where you stand.

fertilizer.frequency: At planting, then side-dress after fruit set
fertilizer.type: Balanced at planting, then a light nitrogen side-dress at fruit set
fertilizer.timing: Work into the bed before transplanting, then side-dress 3 to 4 weeks after planting and again once the first pods set
fertilizer.example_product: 10-10-10 at planting, then calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0) as a light side-dress
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Cayenne is a moderate feeder rather than a heavy one, and the timing matters more than the amount. Work a complete fertilizer such as 1 to 2 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet, or a few inches of compost, into the bed before transplanting. Then side-dress lightly with nitrogen about 3 to 4 weeks after planting and again once the first pods have set. The cardinal rule is to go easy on nitrogen: too much gives a big, bushy, leafy plant with plenty of foliage but few blooms and little fruit, the single most common pepper-feeding mistake. Pair modest feeding with steady moisture, since even watering, not extra fertilizer, is what fills clean pods and heads off blossom-end rot.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Cayenne does not need heavy feeding, and the timing matters more than the amount. Mix a balanced fertilizer such as 10-10-10, or a few inches of compost, into the soil before you plant. Then feed lightly with nitrogen about 3 to 4 weeks after planting and again once the first pods set. The big rule: go easy on nitrogen. Too much gives you a large, leafy plant with lots of leaves but hardly any peppers. Steady watering matters more than extra fertilizer for a good crop.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Your cayenne has set its first pods, a good time for a light nitrogen side-dress to keep it producing. Go easy: too much nitrogen gives leaves, not peppers.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Your cayenne is setting its first peppers. Give it a light nitrogen feed to keep it going, but do not overdo it or you will get all leaves.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A complete fertilizer such as 10-10-10 worked in at planting, then a light nitrogen side-dress (for example calcium nitrate, 15.5-0-0) 3 to 4 weeks after planting and again at fruit set. Avoid heavy nitrogen, which gives foliage at the expense of pods.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 at planting, then a light nitrogen feed once pods set. Do not overdo the nitrogen, or you get all leaves and few peppers.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A common rate is 1 to 2 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet worked into the bed before transplanting, then a light side-dress of about 0.5 pound of calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0) per 100 square feet 3 to 4 weeks after planting and again once the first pods set, placed a few inches out from the plants and watered in. Skip further nitrogen if the plants are lush and leafy but not fruiting.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Mix 1 to 2 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet, or a few inches of compost, into the soil before planting. Then, 3 to 4 weeks after planting and again once pods set, scratch a little nitrogen fertilizer into the soil a few inches out from each plant and water it in. If the plant is big and leafy but not fruiting, hold off on more nitrogen.

companions.note_seasoned: Most cayenne companion pairings are traditional rather than trial-tested. The useful ones share the warm, sunny, evenly watered culture peppers want and help deflect their pests: basil and a border of nasturtium or marigold are the classic aphid and flea-beetle deflectors, alliums such as onions and chives are traditional pungent deterrents, and low root or leaf crops like carrots and lettuce use different space without sharing pepper problems. The single firmest rule is a rotation one: keep cayenne away from its Solanaceae relatives, tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplant, which share its aphid-vectored viruses, flea beetle, bacterial spot, and the soilborne Phytophthora and verticillium.
companions.note_beginner: Most cayenne companions are more tradition than proven science, but the sensible ones share the warm, sunny, well-watered conditions peppers like and help with pests. Basil, and a ring of nasturtiums or marigolds, can lure aphids and flea beetles away, onions and chives are traditional pest deterrents, and low crops like carrots and lettuce fit around peppers without competing. The one rule that really matters is to keep cayenne away from tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplant, which are close relatives that share the same pests and soil diseases.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Basil is a classic partner for peppers, thought to keep aphids and other pests away, and it likes the same warm, sunny, well-watered spot. A pleasant, low-risk companion.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional pepper companion said to repel aphids and thrips, and a good match because it wants the same warm, sunny, evenly watered conditions cayenne does. The pest effect is folklore rather than trial-isolated, but the shared culture makes it a natural, low-risk neighbor.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplant
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep cayenne away from tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplant. They are all close relatives that share the same pests, viruses, and soil diseases, so planting them together makes those problems worse.
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: All are Solanaceae and share cayenne's pest and disease complex: aphids and the mosaic and other viruses they vector, the flea beetle, bacterial leaf spot, and the soilborne Phytophthora blight and verticillium wilt. Grouping them concentrates that pressure and lets soilborne problems build. A real epidemiology and rotation principle rather than a tested adjacency effect: spread the nightshades out and rotate them on at least a 3 to 4 year cycle.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Fennel
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Many gardeners keep fennel away from peppers and most other vegetables, since it is said to stunt their growth. This is more tradition than a proven rule.
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A widely repeated caution that fennel inhibits the growth of many garden vegetables and is best kept to its own corner. There is no strong Tier-1 mechanism for a pepper-fennel antagonism, so it persists mostly as garden lore.
