succession_policy.tip_seasoned: A single-stem English cucumber cordon crops for a long stretch, but plants eventually tire or succumb to mildew, so a staggered succession keeps a protected house or tunnel in steady supply. Under cover the season is long, spring through fall, so a second planting started while the first is in full production takes over cleanly as the first fades. Space and expense argue for a few well-tended plants in succession rather than many at once.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: English cucumbers crop for a long time on a single stem, but plants slow down and can get mildew, so start a second planting while the first is still producing to keep a steady supply. Under cover the season is long, so you can stagger plantings from spring into fall.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: Batch-2 Wave-1 cert (2026-07-05): source-truth review (CC agent, WebFetch). The parthenocarpic + gynoecious + seedless + POLLINATION-MUST-BE-EXCLUDED crux VERIFIED verbatim on two independent T1 pages (UF/IFAS CV268: 'If pollination does occur, the fruit will form seeds, the shape of the fruit will be distorted and a bitter tasting fruit will develop ... essential to prevent bees and other pollinators'; Penn State high-tunnels corroborates 'If pollination does occur fruit can be seeded, bitter, and misshapen'). open_findings.summary: Per-zone resolved_by_zone planting/harvest windows are the shared Cucumis sativus frost-anchored windows carried from the certified cucumber twin: extension planting charts list 'cucumber' without distinguishing English/greenhouse type, and the two share days-to-maturity, so the OUTDOOR windows are physiologically the same. Protected culture (greenhouse/high tunnel) extends both ends well beyond these dates. Individual per-zone dates are not each source-verified against an English-cucumber-specific regional chart.

days_to_maturity [55,65] (mid 60) is modeled from the type: T1 greenhouse sources give about 10 to 11 days from fruit set to picking size but not a total seed-to-harvest figure; the parthenocarpic English/Beit Alpha hybrids run roughly 48 to 65 days by catalog norms (e.g. Socrates ~52, Tyria ~56). Tighten at the variety-delta pass.

pH: preferred soil range [6.0,6.8] is the standard Cucumis sativus soil band (UMN, Clemson); the greenhouse nutrient-solution target of about 5.5 to 6.0 (UF/IFAS CV268; ACES gives 5.5 to 6.5) is a hydroponic figure carried in the note, not the in-ground preferred. Soilless-substrate culture figures are modeled.

Container figures (min_pot_gallons 5, recommended 10, depth 12 in) follow general container-vegetable guidance (UW-Madison Horticulture) rather than an English-cucumber-specific container source. Parthenocarpic types are especially container/balcony-suited since they need no pollinators, so the numbers are reasonable but modeled.

Telegraph Improved is included as the classic long English glasshouse heirloom on general horticultural knowledge; no US T1 extension page read this session names it or confirms its (older, not reliably all-female/parthenocarpic) pollination behavior, and the note flags that its male flowers are traditionally removed. The all-female parthenocarpic hybrids (Tyria/Socrates/Corinto/Katrina/Diva/Picolino) are T1-anchored (CSU, Penn State, Purdue, Illinois).

hawaii_tropical z11 authored bounded-continuous (carried from the twin); CTAHR Bulletin B-91 is a scanned/image PDF that did not parse this session (deny rule: not extracted). z11 frost-free alone is insufficient to upgrade to year_round, so the honest bounded-continuous default stands. Corroborate against a parseable CTAHR source at display-readiness.

The recommended greenhouse cultivars split into two groups: Tyria, Socrates, and Diva are named as parthenocarpic/gynoecious all-female types on the cited Colorado State greenhouse-cucumber page, while Corinto, Katrina, and Picolino are widely-sold parthenocarpic greenhouse and high-tunnel cultivars whose names are not printed on the specifically cited CSU/PSU/Purdue pages (they trace to seed-trade catalogs and PSU high-tunnel trial reports). All six are genuine all-female parthenocarpic types and their descriptions are horticulturally standard; no data is fabricated. Likewise, the powdery-mildew tolerance of Tyria is a widely-reported cultivar trait not stated on the cited extension pages, so that specific claim was removed from the prose. Re-anchor individual cultivar names/attributes to a per-cultivar source at the biology review if desired.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the colder northern states (zones 3 to 7), cucumber is a summer crop. Plant after your last frost once the soil is warm, and in the coldest areas start a few seedlings indoors about three weeks early for a head start. Plant a second batch about three weeks after the first so the harvest keeps coming, since the first plants tire by late summer.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Across the northern tier (zones 3 to 7) cucumber is a single warm-season crop. Direct-sow after the last frost once the soil reaches 70°F, or set out transplants started about three weeks earlier in the shortest-season zones to gain time. One continuous summer window runs until the fall-frost runway closes, and a second sowing about three weeks after the first spreads the harvest and replaces the first planting as beetles and mildew wear it down. The exact dates shift later toward the colder northern edge and earlier in the milder south of the region.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer sowing gap is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap. Above about 90°F cucumber suffers reproductive failure: flowers and young fruit set poorly or drop, and set resumes once temperatures fall below the 90s. Heat builds fast under cover, so even protected plantings pause or lean on hard venting and shade through the hottest weeks, which is why these hot regions split into a spring and a fall crop rather than running through summer. (Penn State Extension, growing cucumbers in high tunnels; regional extension planting chart)

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast and Gulf, cucumber grows in two seasons, spring and fall, with a break in the hottest part of summer. Plant in spring once frost has passed, then plant again in late summer for a fall crop. Skip the peak of summer, when heat and pests make cucumbers struggle and turn bitter.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: In the Southeast and Gulf (zones 8 to 9) cucumber is a true spring-and-fall crop with a hot midsummer gap. Sow in spring from about April, making a second sowing two to three weeks later, then stop: heat, humidity, beetle-vectored wilt, and mildew curtail production and turn fruit bitter through the worst of summer. Sow again for fall by mid to late August so plants establish before cooling weather. The exact dates shift earlier in spring and later in fall toward the Gulf, and the reverse toward the cooler northern edge. The midsummer stretch is a deliberate no-plant gap, not a growing month.

crops.description_seasoned: English cucumber is the long, thin-skinned, seedless form of Cucumis sativus grown mainly under cover, in a greenhouse or high tunnel or trellised outdoors in warm regions. Its defining trait is genetic: these types are parthenocarpic, so they set fruit without any pollination, and most are gynoecious, carrying nearly all female flowers for a heavy, early crop. Because the fruit forms without fertilization it is seedless, mild, and burpless, with a tender skin that needs no peeling, and it sizes up to roughly 12 to 14 inches on the standard Dutch or English type (the Beit Alpha and mini types run shorter, about 5 to 8 inches). The catch is that pollination is unwelcome: if bees carry pollen to a parthenocarpic plant, the fruit turns seedy, misshapen, and bitter, so growers exclude pollinators and isolate these plants from ordinary cucumbers. Plants are trained up a string or trellis as a single stem with the side shoots removed, and they want warmth, full light, steady moisture, and regular feeding over a long, productive season.
crops.description_beginner: English cucumbers are the long, smooth, seedless cucumbers usually sold wrapped in plastic, and they are grown mostly in a greenhouse, a high tunnel, or up a trellis in a warm spot. The special thing about them is that they make cucumbers all by themselves, without needing bees, and the fruit has no seeds, a thin skin you do not peel, and a mild taste that is easy on the stomach. Because they do not need pollinating, you actually want to keep bees away: if a bee pollinates one, the cucumber comes out seedy, crooked, and bitter. Grow them up a string or trellis as a single stem, give them warmth, sun, steady water, and regular feeding, and they will crop heavily for a long time.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Harvest English cucumbers young and often, while the skin is glossy and firm. Pick the long Dutch or English types at about 12 to 14 inches (the USDA fresh-market minimum is 11 inches) and the shorter Beit Alpha and mini types at about 5 to 8 inches, cutting or clipping the stem rather than pulling, since the thin-skinned fruit and brittle vine bruise easily. Fruit sizes up fast, often reaching pickable size within about 10 to 11 days of set, so check every 1 to 2 days at peak. The thin, tender skin needs no peeling. Pick promptly, because an overheld fruit stops the plant setting new ones and the crop keeps best when cut young.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Pick English cucumbers while they are firm and glossy. The long ones are usually picked at about 12 to 14 inches and the short Beit Alpha types at about 5 to 8 inches. Cut or clip the stem instead of pulling, because the skin and vine are tender. They grow fast, ready in a couple of weeks once they set, so check every day or two. The thin skin does not need peeling, and picking often keeps more cucumbers coming.
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: English cucumbers turn the usual cucumber pollination advice on its head. These types are parthenocarpic, meaning they set fruit with no pollination at all, and gynoecious, carrying almost entirely female flowers, so a single plant crops heavily on its own, which is exactly why they suit greenhouses, high tunnels, screened spaces, and containers where bees are absent. The critical rule is to keep pollen away: if bees pollinate a parthenocarpic plant, the fruit develops seeds, distorts in shape, and turns bitter. So growers exclude pollinators under cover with insect screening, keep bee-drawing flowers away outdoors, and isolate these plants from ordinary seeded cucumbers whose pollen bees would carry over. There is no hand-pollinating and no pollenizer needed; the plant does it all without help.
crops.pollinator_notes_beginner: English cucumbers are the opposite of ordinary cucumbers when it comes to bees. They make seedless cucumbers all by themselves, without any pollination, and they carry almost all female flowers, so one plant produces a lot on its own. The important thing is to keep bees away: if a bee pollinates one, the cucumber turns seedy, crooked, and bitter. So growers screen bees out under cover, keep bee-attracting flowers away, and keep these plants apart from ordinary cucumbers. You never need to hand-pollinate them.

crops.name: Yellow Summer Squash

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Plant summer squash in rich, well-drained soil. Mix a few inches of compost into the bed before you plant, and use raised beds or low mounds if your soil is heavy or stays wet. Good drainage plus plenty of compost gives you healthy, productive plants.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Summer squash grows best in deep, fertile loam that holds steady moisture yet drains freely. Work several inches of compost or well-rotted manure into the bed before planting, since these are organic-matter-hungry plants. Raised beds or mounded hills improve drainage and warm the soil faster in spring. Sandy loams warm early and suit the earliest sowings, while heavy clay holds water and invites root and crown rot, so amend it generously or grow in raised beds.

ph.note_beginner: Summer squash likes soil close to neutral, around pH 6.0 to 6.5, and most garden soil is already in range. If you have never tested your soil, an inexpensive test kit tells you whether you need to adjust it.
ph.note_seasoned: Summer squash does best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, around pH 6.0 to 6.5. It tolerates a wider band, roughly 5.8 to 7.5, and still produces in mildly alkaline soil, though uptake of iron and manganese tightens as pH climbs. A soil test is the only reliable guide before adding lime or sulfur.

fertilizer.timing: Work into the bed before planting, then side-dress from vining to flowering
fertilizer.example_product: balanced 10-10-10 or compost plus a nitrogen source
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Summer squash is a moderate feeder, hungrier than a light crop like beans but well short of a heavy feeder. The main pitfall is too much nitrogen, which drives lush leaves and shy fruiting, sometimes with poor set. A bed enriched with compost plus one balanced side-dressing as the plant comes into flower is usually all it needs. Pair feeding with steady, even moisture, since the nutrients only help if the plant is not also drought-stressed.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Summer squash needs a moderate amount of feeding, not a lot. The biggest mistake is too much nitrogen, which gives you big leafy plants but fewer squash. Good compost in the soil plus one feeding when flowers appear is usually enough. Keep the plant evenly watered too, since feeding only helps a well-watered plant.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Your summer squash is coming into flower, time for a single balanced side-dressing. Keep nitrogen moderate so the plant sets fruit instead of running to leaf.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Your summer squash is starting to flower. Give it one feeding of balanced fertilizer now.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 suits summer squash. Avoid high-nitrogen lawn-type fertilizers, which push foliage at the expense of fruit.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer with equal numbers, like 10-10-10. Avoid high-nitrogen lawn fertilizer.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: Work a balanced fertilizer or 1 to 2 inches of compost into the bed before planting, then side-dress once as plants begin to run and flower, roughly 4 to 6 weeks after sowing. A common rate is about 1 tablespoon of 10-10-10 per plant worked into the soil a few inches away from the stem, or a comparable scoop of compost or balanced organic fertilizer.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Mix some compost or a balanced fertilizer into the soil before planting. Then feed once more when the plants start to flower, about a month after sowing. A spoonful of balanced fertilizer per plant, scratched into the soil a few inches from the stem, is plenty.

companions.note_beginner: Good companions for squash do one of three things: draw pests away, bring in bees, or feed the soil. Plant a few nasturtiums or marigolds nearby to lure squash bugs off your plants, add flowers like borage to attract the bees that pollinate your squash, and let beans share the bed to enrich the soil. Just give your squash plenty of room, since the plants get big.
companions.note_seasoned: Squash benefits most from companions that pull pests away, feed beneficial insects, or fix nitrogen, rather than from plants packed in tight. Give sprawling vines their room and use companions as a border or light interplanting. The strongest evidence is for nasturtium, with marigold close behind, reducing squash bug and cucumber beetle pressure, while the Three Sisters trio (corn, beans, squash) earns its place through nitrogen, support, and pest confusion. Pollinator flowers like borage and sweet alyssum matter because squash is insect-pollinated, so anything that keeps bees working improves fruit set. Several herb and flower pairings here are traditional rather than trial-proven, and are labeled accordingly.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Corn
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Part of the classic Three Sisters planting. The tall stalks support climbing beans, and growing corn, beans, and squash together can confuse squash pests.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: The three-sisters corn/squash/beans polyculture is the best-documented historical companion arrangement (Indigenous practice 1000+ years; USDA confirms the polyculture out-yields the monocultures per area). But the corn/squash benefit is a structural and space/soil-use relationship, not a measured corn-protects-summer squash pest effect, and the two are competing heavy feeders. traditional/medium: well-grounded, widely taught, structural rather than a crop-specific measured antagonism or protection.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Corn is summer squash's partner in the three-sisters planting, and the benefit is structural rather than chemical: the corn gives vertical height and light shade, the sprawling squash shades the soil to hold moisture and suppress weeds beneath it. The catch is that both are heavy feeders, so on a small bed they compete for nitrogen unless you feed well and space them properly; the trio works best with the beans in the mix to offset that draw.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Pole beans
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Beans pull nitrogen from the air and feed the soil, which hungry squash appreciate. Let them climb the corn in a Three Sisters bed.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Legume N-fixation via Rhizobium symbiosis is established plant biology, not folklore, and the soil-nitrogen benefit to neighboring heavy feeders is real. mechanistic/medium rather than research_backed because the in-season transfer of fixed nitrogen to an adjacent summer squash specifically is modest and timing-dependent (much is released on decomposition), so the mechanism is sound but its direct same-season benefit to the squash is limited.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Pole beans earn their place through nitrogen fixation. Working with Rhizobium bacteria on their roots, legumes convert atmospheric nitrogen into a plant-available form, which offsets some of the heavy nitrogen demand a vigorous summer squash puts on the bed. In the three-sisters arrangement they also climb the corn rather than the squash. Practical note: the nitrogen benefit largely reaches neighbors after the beans are spent and their roots break down, so treat it as season-long soil-building, not an instant feed.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Nasturtium
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: These easy flowers lure squash bugs and beetles away from your squash, and research backs it up. Bonus: the flowers are edible.

provenance.label: research_backed
provenance.reason: UMN Extension cites nasturtium-with-squash as research-supported for reducing squash bug populations, plus an Iowa study (nasturtium + marigold vs squash bugs and cucumber beetles). research_backed earned by the extension-cited trial basis. medium not high: effect sizes vary by pest (aphid trap effect most consistent; squash-bug effect more variable in real gardens), and timing/placement matter.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Nasturtium is the best-evidenced flower companion for squash. Extension trial work shows it reduces squash bug pressure (and aphids and cucumber beetles in mixed plantings), partly as a trap crop drawing pests onto itself and partly by adding the foliage complexity that disrupts pest host-finding. Plant it around the perimeter or at the base of the hills. One honest caveat from growers: the aphid trap-crop effect is the most reliably observed; the squash-bug effect is real in the literature but more variable in practice.

good_seasoned.name: Corn
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: The structural backbone of the Three Sisters. Tall corn gives pole beans a living trellis, and interplanting corn, beans, and squash makes it harder for squash pests to zero in on the planting.

provenance.label: research_backed
provenance.reason: Three Sisters polyculture; corn-as-support and squash-as-groundcover are well established in extension guidance.

good_seasoned.name: Pole beans
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Beans fix atmospheric nitrogen and ease the fertilizer demand of hungry squash, and in a Three Sisters bed they climb the corn while squash shades the soil below.

provenance.label: research_backed
provenance.reason: Legume nitrogen fixation and Three Sisters companion structure are extension-supported.

good_seasoned.name: Nasturtium
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: The strongest flower pairing for squash: research shows nasturtium can pull squash bugs off the crop, and an Iowa study found it reduced squash bug and cucumber beetle damage. The flowers are also edible.

provenance.label: research_backed
provenance.reason: UMN states the practice is supported by research; cites an Iowa study on squash bug and cucumber beetle damage.

good_seasoned.name: Marigold
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Often planted with squash to deter pests. The evidence is mixed overall, but the same Iowa study that backs nasturtium also found marigolds reduced squash bug and cucumber beetle damage, so it earns a likely rating here.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: UMN reports an Iowa study showing marigolds reduced squash bug and cucumber beetle damage, while noting marigold results are inconsistent generally.

good_seasoned.name: Sweet alyssum
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A low carpet of sweet alyssum draws hoverflies and other beneficial insects. A Florida study found alyssum increased natural enemies of aphids on squash, and the blooms also feed pollinators.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: UMN cites a Florida study in which sweet alyssum increased natural enemies of aphids on squash.

good_seasoned.name: Borage
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A classic pollinator magnet. Its bee-friendly blue flowers help keep pollinators working the squash blooms, which matters because summer squash is insect-pollinated. The pairing is traditional rather than trial-proven.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Well-documented traditional pollinator companion; squash-specific benefit not from a controlled trial.

good_seasoned.name: Sage
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: An aromatic herb long planted near squash to discourage squash bugs. Treat this as traditional garden lore rather than a tested effect for squash.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Aromatic-herb pest-deterrence is widely repeated folk practice; no squash-specific trial support.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Potatoes
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep potatoes in a separate bed. Both plants are big and hungry and will compete for food and space.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: The summer squash/potato caution rests on a sound resource-competition mechanism: two large heavy feeders competing for nutrients and root space, with some shared soil-borne disease risk. mechanistic/medium: the competition reasoning is physiologically grounded (not folklore), but it is a management/competition issue rather than a measured allelopathic or pest antagonism specific to the pairing.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Potatoes and summer squash are both large, hungry plants that pull heavily on the same nutrients and fight for the same ground and root space, so neither does its best when they share a bed. There is also some shared susceptibility to soil-borne trouble. This is a resource-competition call rather than a chemical antagonism: if space is tight, give them separate beds and rotate.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Fennel
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Plant fennel on its own, away from squash. It grows large and may crowd or stunt nearby vegetables.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Same precedent as beefsteak/carrot/basil Fennel entries (2026-06-25). Near-universal folk rule, not contested; real allelopathic mechanism (fennel EO suppresses germination/seedling growth in weed bioassays) but never measured on summer squash at garden spacing. traditional/medium.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Fennel is a poor neighbor across the garden, and summer squash is no exception. It is reputed to release allelopathic compounds from its roots that can suppress nearby plants. As elsewhere, the standard handling is to isolate fennel in its own bed or a large container rather than work it into the squash patch.

bad_seasoned.name: Potatoes
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Both potatoes and squash are vigorous, hungry plants that compete hard for the same water, nutrients, and ground space, so most growers keep them in separate beds. The caution is traditional rather than trial-proven.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Widely repeated competition-based caution; not from a controlled companion trial.

bad_seasoned.name: Fennel
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Fennel is the classic give-it-its-own-bed plant. It is reputed to release compounds that can suppress nearby vegetables, and it grows large enough to crowd sprawling squash. The allelopathy evidence is mostly observational, so treat this as traditional caution.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Fennel allelopathy toward garden vegetables is largely observational; squash-specific effect uncertain.

pests.name: Squash vine borer
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Sudden wilting of the whole plant or individual vines in midsummer, often after looking healthy. A telltale ring of yellow-orange frass (sawdust-like waste) sits at the base of the stem near a small entry hole.
pests.symptoms_beginner: The plant suddenly wilts in midsummer, even with wet soil. Look for sawdust-like specks at the base of the stem, a sign the borer is inside.
pests.cause_seasoned: Larvae of a clearwing moth tunnel inside the stem, cutting off water flow. The adult lays eggs at the stem base from early to midsummer; the hatching larva bores in and feeds, collapsing the plant.
pests.cause_beginner: A moth lays eggs at the base of the plant in summer. The larvae hatch and tunnel inside the stem, blocking water and killing the plant.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: At the first frass, slit the stem lengthwise with a knife, remove the larva, and mound moist soil over the wound so it can re-root. Promptly remove and destroy plants too far gone.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: If you catch it early, carefully cut a slit in the stem, remove the grub inside, and cover the spot with damp soil. Remove plants that are too damaged.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Time a fall succession to crop after the borer's main flight. Row cover until flowering excludes the egg-laying moth. Wrap the lower stem with foil, scout for eggs from early summer, and remove spent vines to break the cycle.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover young plants until they flower to keep the moth away, and plant a second crop in summer that grows after the borer is gone. Clean up old plants at season's end.

pests.name: Squash bug
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Leaves develop yellow then brown speckling and wilt; heavy infestations cause whole-vine collapse. Look for clusters of bronze, oval eggs on leaf undersides and fast-moving gray-brown nymphs.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Leaves get yellow or brown spots and wilt. Check leaf undersides for shiny bronze eggs in clusters and gray bugs that scatter when disturbed.
pests.cause_seasoned: A shield-shaped true bug that feeds by sucking sap from leaves and stems, injecting toxic saliva. Adults overwinter in garden debris and emerge to lay eggs on cucurbits in early summer.
pests.cause_beginner: A flat, gray bug that sucks sap from the plant and injects damaging saliva. It hides in old plant debris over winter and comes out to lay eggs in summer.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Crush egg clusters by hand and drop adults and nymphs into soapy water. Lay a board near plants overnight; bugs gather under it and can be collected at dawn. Insecticidal soap works on young nymphs only.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Squash the egg clusters and knock bugs into soapy water. A board left out overnight gives them a hiding spot you can check and clear each morning.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Remove garden debris where adults overwinter, rotate cucurbits, and use row cover until flowering. Scout leaf undersides for eggs from early summer, before populations explode.
pests.prevention_beginner: Clean up old plant debris, move squash to a new spot each year, and check leaf undersides for eggs through the summer so you can remove them early.

pests.name: Cucumber beetle
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Striped or spotted yellow-and-black beetles chewing leaves, flowers, and young fruit. Seedling damage can be severe, and the beetles transmit bacterial wilt as they feed.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Small yellow beetles with stripes or spots chewing the leaves and flowers. They are most damaging to young plants and can spread disease.
pests.cause_seasoned: Striped and spotted cucumber beetles feed on cucurbits and vector the bacterium that causes bacterial wilt. They overwinter nearby and move onto plants from emergence onward.
pests.cause_beginner: These beetles feed on squash plants and carry bacterial wilt disease, which they pass on as they chew.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick or vacuum beetles in the cool morning, and use yellow sticky traps to monitor. Kaolin clay deters feeding. Protecting seedlings matters most, since young plants and wilt transmission are the real risks.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick beetles off by hand in the morning when they are slow. Yellow sticky traps help you track them. Protecting young plants is the most important step.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Row cover until flowering keeps beetles off vulnerable seedlings (remove for pollination). Rotate cucurbits and clear debris. Wilt-resistant practices matter more than killing every beetle.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover young plants until they flower to keep beetles off, then remove the cover for the bees. Rotate crops and clean up debris.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: White, powdery patches on leaf surfaces, usually starting on older leaves in mid- to late season, spreading until leaves yellow, brown, and die. Severe defoliation exposes fruit and cuts yield.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: White powdery spots on the leaves, usually later in the season, that spread until leaves dry up and die.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A fungal disease favored by warm days, cool nights, and high humidity. Unlike most leaf diseases it does not need leaf wetness to infect, but crowded, poorly ventilated plantings worsen it.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that thrives in warm, humid weather. It spreads fastest on crowded plants with poor air flow.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: At first spots, treat with a labeled fungicide such as potassium bicarbonate, neem, or sulfur (not in high heat), repeating per label. Remove the worst leaves. Treatment slows spread but does not cure infected tissue.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Treat early spots with an approved fungicide like neem or potassium bicarbonate, and remove the worst leaves. Catching it early works best.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Choose resistant varieties, space plants for airflow, and water at the base to keep humidity around foliage down. Full sun and good spacing matter more than spraying.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Pick mildew-resistant varieties, give plants room to breathe, and water the soil instead of the leaves. Good air flow is the best prevention.

diseases.name: Bacterial wilt
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Individual leaves or runners wilt and the whole plant collapses, often with leaves still green. A diagnostic test: cut a wilted stem, press the cut ends together and slowly pull apart, and a sticky white ooze strings between them.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The plant wilts and dies even though the soil is moist and the leaves still look green. It is caused by a disease beetles carry.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A bacterium that clogs the plant's water-conducting tissue, transmitted by cucumber beetles as they feed. The bacterium overwinters in the beetles, not the soil, so beetle control is disease control.
diseases.cause_beginner: A disease spread by cucumber beetles. It clogs the plant's water system, so controlling the beetles is the way to prevent it.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once a plant is infected. Remove and destroy wilting plants promptly to limit beetle spread to healthy ones.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure once a plant has it. Pull out and remove affected plants quickly so the disease does not spread.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Control cucumber beetles, especially on seedlings: row cover until flowering, scouting, and prompt removal of infected plants. Resistant cucurbit types help where available.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Prevent it by controlling cucumber beetles. Cover young plants until they flower, and remove any plant that wilts and dies suddenly.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Aim for about 1 inch of water per week, more in heat or sandy soil, delivered deeply and less often rather than in light daily sprinkles. Container plants dry out faster and often need water every day or two at peak.
watering.frequency_beginner: Give summer squash about 1 inch of water a week, more when it is hot. Water deeply rather than a little every day. Plants in pots dry out fast and may need water daily in summer.
watering.amount_seasoned: Around 1 inch per week is the baseline, equivalent to roughly two-thirds of a gallon per square foot. Push toward the higher end during fruit set and through hot, dry spells, when uneven water shows up directly in the fruit.
watering.amount_beginner: About 1 inch of water a week is a good target. Water more during hot weather and while the plant is setting and growing fruit.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base of the plant with a soaker hose, drip line, or a wand aimed at the soil, keeping the leaves as dry as possible. Wet foliage, especially overhead watering late in the day, invites powdery mildew on a plant already prone to it. A 2 to 3 inch mulch holds soil moisture even and keeps splashing down.
watering.method_beginner: Water the soil, not the leaves. Use a soaker hose or aim a watering wand at the base of the plant. Keeping the leaves dry helps prevent powdery mildew, a common summer squash problem. A layer of mulch keeps the soil evenly moist.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting even when the soil is wet, and soft or rotting stems at the base point to overwatering or poor drainage. Constantly saturated soil invites root and crown rot, particularly in heavy ground.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If lower leaves turn yellow, the plant wilts even though the soil is wet, or the base gets soft and mushy, it is getting too much water or the soil drains poorly.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Midday wilting that recovers overnight is normal in heat, but leaves that stay limp, dull, and curled signal real drought. The clearest fruit-stage tell is misshapen or pinched squash, often narrow at the blossom end, which traces directly to inadequate or uneven water during sizing.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Some midday wilting in hot weather is normal and passes by evening. Leaves that stay wilted mean the plant is too dry. Uneven watering can also make the squash come out misshapen.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Base watering is the single most useful habit for summer squash, because the same plant that wants steady moisture is also one of the most mildew-prone in the garden. Keep water on the soil and air moving through the leaves.
watering.method_note_beginner: Watering the soil instead of the leaves is the best thing you can do for summer squash. It keeps the plant hydrated without encouraging leaf disease.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The water-critical stretch is flowering through fruit set and sizing. Steady moisture here is what produces well-formed fruit; let it swing dry and you get poor set and pinched, misshapen squash even with good pollination.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The most important time to keep summer squash watered is when it is flowering and forming fruit. Even watering then gives you well-shaped squash.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Harden off indoor-started squash over 7 to 10 days, easing them into direct sun and wind before transplanting. Handle the rootball gently at planting, because squash resents root disturbance and a checked seedling can sulk for weeks.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: If you started seedlings indoors, set them outside for a little longer each day over about a week so they adjust to sun and wind. Be gentle with the roots when you plant, since squash does not like having its roots disturbed.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Because squash resents root disturbance, direct sowing once the soil warms past 60°F, ideally 70°F, is the simplest and most reliable method, and direct-sown plants quickly catch up to transplants. Start seeds indoors only to gain two to three weeks in a short season, using larger cells (3 inch or bigger) and setting plants out before the roots circle the pot.
start_method.notes_beginner: The easiest way to grow summer squash is to sow seeds right where they will grow, once the soil is warm (about 70°F). Squash grows fast and does not transplant happily, so direct sowing usually works best. Start seeds indoors only if your season is short, and move them outside while they are still small.

drainage.saucer_practice: If you use a saucer, empty it after watering. Summer squash will not tolerate sitting in standing water, which invites root and crown rot.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Use a good bagged potting mix, not soil from the garden. Garden soil packs down too hard in a pot.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in some compost, and add a slow-release fertilizer when you plant. Pots need feeding more often than garden beds because watering washes nutrients out.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: Use a high-quality peat- or coir-based potting mix, not garden soil, which compacts and drains poorly in a container. The mix should be rich but free-draining.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend in about a third compost for fertility and a handful of a slow-release balanced fertilizer at planting. Because frequent watering flushes nutrients from a pot, plan to feed more regularly than you would in the ground.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out much faster than garden beds. In summer you may need to water a potted summer squash every day, sometimes twice. Check daily and water until it drains from the bottom.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Feed potted summer squash more often than garden plants. After planting, give a balanced liquid feed every couple of weeks once it starts flowering.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Not applicable. Summer squash lives for one season and dies with the first frost, so you cannot overwinter it. Just plant new seeds next year.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Not applicable. Summer squash is a frost-tender annual that completes its life in a single season and is killed by the first hard frost, so there is nothing to overwinter. Pull spent plants at season's end and start fresh from seed the following year.

container_notes.notes_beginner: You can grow summer squash in a container, but it needs a big pot, at least 10 gallons and 12 inches deep, and a compact variety works best. Put it in full sun, keep it well watered (pots dry out fast), and feed it regularly. Water the soil, not the leaves, to help avoid mildew.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Yellow summer squash is growable in containers but demands a big one: a 10 gallon or larger pot at least 12 inches deep, and ideally a compact or bush variety such as Saffron, Goldbar, Sundance, or Early Prolific Straightneck rather than a large spreading type. The main container challenges are water and feeding, since pots dry and deplete fast, plus the same powdery mildew and pollination issues as in the ground. Give it full sun, water at the base daily in heat, and feed regularly.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry out far faster than beds, and a large summer squash in a pot can need water once or even twice a day in summer heat. Check daily by feeling the top inch of mix, and water until it runs from the drainage holes. Self-watering or larger pots buffer the swings that cause misshapen fruit.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Feed container plants more often than in-ground ones, since watering steadily leaches nutrients. After the slow-release charge at planting, add a balanced liquid feed every 2 to 3 weeks once flowering begins, keeping nitrogen moderate.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Summer squash does well in self-watering containers, which smooth out the moisture swings this thirsty, mildew-prone plant dislikes. Keep the reservoir topped up in heat and still water from below, leaving the foliage dry, and use a large enough planter that the root mass is not constantly waterlogged.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: Self-watering pots work well for summer squash because they keep moisture steady. Keep the water reservoir filled, especially in hot weather, and use a good-sized pot.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: Summer squash is a big, sprawling plant with a deep root system, so it needs a wide, deep container, at least 12 inches deep and a 10 gallon or larger pot for a full-size variety. Wide and sturdy beats tall and narrow, since a top-heavy plant in a small pot tips and dries out fast. Compact and bush varieties are far happier in containers than sprawling heirlooms.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Summer squash plants grow big with deep roots, so give them a large, deep pot: at least 12 inches deep and 10 gallons or more for a full-size plant. Pick a wide, heavy pot rather than a tall, narrow one, because a big plant in a small pot tips over and dries out quickly. If you only have room for a container, choose a compact or bush variety, which stays happier in a pot than the large spreading kinds.

recommended.name: Early Prolific Straightneck
recommended.recommended_note: All-America Selections heirloom straightneck; smooth, buttery-yellow, and reliably heavy-yielding on a compact bush.

recommended.name: Early Summer Crookneck
recommended.recommended_note: Classic heirloom crookneck with a curved, bumpy neck and rich, old-fashioned flavor.

recommended.name: Sundance
recommended.recommended_note: Early, uniform hybrid crookneck that sets fruit quickly and holds quality on an open plant.

recommended.name: Goldbar
recommended.recommended_note: Vigorous hybrid straightneck with smooth, deep-gold fruit on an easy-to-pick bush.

recommended.name: Saffron
recommended.recommended_note: Compact bush crookneck that suits small beds and containers.

recommended.name: Zephyr
recommended.recommended_note: Slender bicolor hybrid, bright yellow with a pale green tip, prized for firm texture and flavor.

varieties.note_seasoned: Yellow summer squash comes in crookneck and straightneck forms, and for a first garden almost any of them succeeds, so choose by shape and space. Straightneck types like Early Prolific Straightneck and Goldbar are smooth and easy to clean; crookneck types like Early Summer Crookneck and Sundance carry the curved, bumpy neck and a fuller old-fashioned flavor but bruise a little more easily. Compact bush habits such as Saffron fit small beds and containers and keep airflow open to slow powdery mildew. The bright gold color makes fruit easy to spot before it oversizes, and if you also grow zucchini, the two read clearly apart in the basket.
varieties.note_beginner: Yellow summer squash is forgiving, so pick a variety by shape and space. Straightneck kinds like Early Prolific Straightneck are smooth and simple to grow, while crookneck kinds have a curved, bumpy neck and lots of flavor. Bush types like Saffron stay compact and do well in pots. The bright yellow color makes the squash easy to spot at picking size before it gets too big.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Avoid planting summer squash where another cucurbit grew last year, including cucumber, melon, pumpkin, winter squash, and other summer squash. They share squash bug, squash vine borer, cucumber beetle, and soilborne diseases that build up in the soil and on debris.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Do not plant summer squash where you grew cucumbers, melons, pumpkins, or other squash last year. They get the same pests and diseases, which build up in the soil.
rotation.good_after: Legumes (beans and peas), leafy greens, or alliums (onions and garlic) make good preceding crops, since they do not share the cucurbit pest and disease complex; a legume also leaves nitrogen behind.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate cucurbits on a 2 to 3 year cycle, returning summer squash to a given bed no sooner than the third year. The point is to break the buildup of squash bug, vine borer, and soilborne disease. Clearing spent vines at season's end, rather than tilling them in, removes overwintering sites and makes rotation more effective.
rotation.note_beginner: Try not to grow summer squash or its relatives in the same spot more than once every 3 years. Moving it around the garden each year helps avoid a buildup of pests and disease. Clean up old plants at the end of the season too.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Summer squash is tender and short-lived off the plant. At room temperature it keeps only a couple of days before softening, so refrigerate soon after picking unless you will use it right away.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Summer squash does not keep long at room temperature, just a day or two. Put it in the fridge if you are not using it right away.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Stored unwashed in a perforated or loosely closed bag in the crisper, summer squash keeps about 1 week, sometimes a few days more. It is chilling-sensitive below about 41°F, where prolonged cold causes pitting and soft spots, so it does not store as long or as cold as hardy vegetables.
storage.fridge_beginner: Keep summer squash in the fridge in a loosely closed bag for about a week. Do not wash it until you are ready to use it.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Summer squash does not freeze well raw, turning watery and limp, but freezes fine for cooking when shredded or sliced and blanched briefly first. Shredded summer squash, drained and frozen in measured portions, is ideal for breads and soups later.
storage.freezer_beginner: Summer squash freezes best shredded or sliced and quickly blanched first, then frozen for cooking later. Frozen raw, it turns watery, so it is best used in cooked dishes, not eaten fresh.
storage.notes_seasoned: Treat summer squash as a use-it-soon vegetable rather than a keeper. The practical answer to a glut is not long storage but cooking, giving it away, and freezing shredded squash for winter baking.
storage.notes_beginner: Summer squash is best used fresh and soon after picking. If you have too much, the best options are to cook it, share it, or freeze it shredded for later.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seeds sprout in about 5 to 10 days in warm soil (70 to 95°F is ideal); cold soil below 60°F rots seed rather than germinating it.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: In warm soil, seeds sprout in about a week. Two seed leaves push up first. If the soil is cold, seeds rot instead of sprouting.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Sow 1 inch deep in warm soil. Keep evenly moist, not soggy. If you sowed several seeds per spot, thin to the strongest seedling once true leaves appear.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Plant seeds 1 inch deep once the soil is warm. Keep the soil damp until they sprout. If several come up together, keep the strongest one.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Did your summer squash seeds germinate, and how many days did it take?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your seeds sprouted yet?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Cotyledons followed by the first true leaves; growth is fast once warm. Watch for cucumber beetles, which target young plants and can transmit bacterial wilt.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: After the first two rounded leaves, true leaves appear and the plant grows quickly. Watch for beetles chewing the young leaves.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Protect from cucumber beetles, with row cover if needed (remove it at flowering for pollination). Keep evenly watered and free of weeds.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep an eye out for beetles on young plants. Water regularly and keep weeds down. A light row cover can protect seedlings, but remove it once flowers form.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How are your seedlings developing? Any sign of beetle damage?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How do your young plants look?

growth_stages.name: Established and vining
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Rapid leafy growth and a thickening main stem as the plant bulks up before flowering. This is the window to side-dress and the time squash vine borer moths begin laying eggs at the stem base.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant grows fast, with big leaves and a thick stem, getting ready to flower. This is when you feed it.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Side-dress once with balanced fertilizer. Mulch to hold moisture. Begin scouting the stem base for squash vine borer eggs and frass, especially from early summer.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Give the plant one feeding of balanced fertilizer now. Add mulch to keep the soil moist. Start checking the base of the stem for pests.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Has your summer squash been side-dressed? Any pests at the stem base?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Is your plant growing well?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Large yellow flowers. Male flowers (on thin stalks) usually open first and may drop before females appear, which is normal; female flowers carry a tiny squash behind the bloom.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Big yellow flowers open. The first flowers are usually male and fall off, which is normal. Female flowers have a tiny squash at their base.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Encourage pollinators and avoid spraying open blooms. If small fruit yellow and rot at the tip, pollination is poor, hand-pollinate with a small brush in the morning. Keep moisture steady now.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Let the bees do their work and do not spray the flowers. If tiny squash turn yellow and rot, the flowers were not pollinated, you can hand-pollinate with a small brush. Keep watering steadily.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are you seeing female flowers and fruit set? Any blossom-end rot on small fruit?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Is your plant flowering? Are any little squash forming?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Glossy fruit reaching pickable size (4 to 6 inches for standard types), sizing up fast, often an inch or more per day at peak.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Shiny squash reaching about 4 to 6 inches. They grow fast, so they are ready before you expect.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick every 1 to 2 days, cutting the stem with a knife. Harvest young for tenderness and to keep the plant producing; remove any oversized fruit you missed.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Check every day or two and pick the squash while they are still small and shiny. Cut the stem with a knife. Picking often keeps more coming.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How much are you harvesting, and how often are you picking?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you started picking summer squash?

growth_stages.name: End of season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Declining production, increasing powdery mildew, or sudden wilting from squash vine borer or bacterial wilt. The first frost kills the plant outright.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant slows down and leaves may get powdery and white, or it wilts suddenly from pests. Frost kills it.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pull and remove spent plants rather than tilling them in, to cut overwintering pest and disease sites. A summer-sown succession often crops cleanly after the first planting fades.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pull out finished plants and clear them away at the end of the season. This helps prevent pests next year. A second planting made in summer often keeps producing after the first one is done.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Is this planting winding down? Did you remove the spent plants?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Is your plant finished for the season?

notifications.title_seasoned: Start scouting for squash vine borer
notifications.title_beginner: Time to watch for stem pests
notifications.body_seasoned: Your summer squash is bulking up, which is when squash vine borer moths lay eggs at the stem base. Check the base of the stem for sawdust-like frass from now through midsummer, and act early if you see it.
notifications.body_beginner: Your summer squash is growing fast now. Check the bottom of the stem for sawdust-like specks, an early sign of a borer, and keep checking through summer.

notifications.title_beginner: Plant a second summer squash now
notifications.body_seasoned: Time to sow a succession planting. A fresh sowing now, counted back from your first fall frost, often outproduces the spring crop on cleaner plants once borer and mildew wear the first planting down.
notifications.body_beginner: Now is a good time to plant a second summer squash as a backup. Pests often wear out the first plants by late summer, so a fresh planting keeps squash coming.

notifications.title_seasoned: Check your summer squash, it sizes up fast
notifications.body_seasoned: Your summer squash is fruiting. At peak it can gain an inch a day, so check every 1 to 2 days and pick young at 4 to 6 inches. Frequent picking keeps the plant producing.
notifications.body_beginner: Your summer squash is making fruit. Check every day or two and pick them while small and shiny, they grow fast.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost is coming, summer squash will not survive it
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost warning for your summer squash
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A frost is forecast. Summer squash is frost-tender and the first frost ends the plant, so pick everything usable now. There is no covering that reliably carries a large squash plant through a freeze.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Frost is coming, and it will kill your summer squash. Pick all the squash you can use before it hits.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Extreme heat may stall fruit set
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot spell may slow your squash
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A stretch of extreme heat is forecast. Very hot days can reduce pollination and fruit set temporarily, sometimes dropping young fruit. Keep moisture steady; set usually resumes when the heat eases.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Very hot weather is coming. Your summer squash may slow down or drop small fruit for a while. Keep it well watered, it usually picks back up when it cools.

germination.text_seasoned: Soil temperature, not the calendar, governs summer squash germination. Wait until soil is at least 70°F at 2 inches; seed sown in cold ground rots before it sprouts.
germination.text_beginner: Wait for warm soil before sowing. Summer squash seeds rot in cold ground but sprout fast once it warms up.

seedling.text_seasoned: Cucumber beetles swarm young squash and can spread bacterial wilt. A floating row cover protects seedlings, but pull it off at flowering so bees can pollinate.
seedling.text_beginner: Protect young plants from beetles. A light cover helps, but take it off once flowers appear so bees can reach them.

established.text_seasoned: This is the one feeding summer squash needs: a single balanced side-dressing as the plant bulks up and starts to run. Resist piling on nitrogen, which gives leaves at the expense of fruit.
established.text_beginner: Feed the plant once now, as it gets big and starts to flower. Do not overdo the fertilizer, too much makes leaves instead of squash.

established.text_seasoned: Start scouting the stem base for squash vine borer from early summer. A ring of frass (sawdust-like waste) at the base is the early warning before the wilt.
established.text_beginner: Check the bottom of the stem for pests starting in early summer. Look for sawdust-like specks, an early sign of a borer.

flowering.text_seasoned: Early male flowers opening and dropping with no fruit is normal; females come a little later. Judge pollination by whether small fruit size up or yellow and rot at the blossom end.
flowering.text_beginner: The first flowers often fall off without making squash, that is normal. Real trouble is when tiny squash turn yellow and rot, which means poor pollination.

flowering.text_seasoned: If set is poor in cool or pollinator-scarce conditions, hand-pollinate in the morning: pick a male flower, strip the petals, and dab pollen onto the center of each open female.
flowering.text_beginner: If squash are not forming, you can hand-pollinate. In the morning, pick a male flower, peel off the petals, and gently touch it to the center of a female flower.

harvest.text_seasoned: Pick young and pick often. At peak, fruit can gain an inch a day, so check every 1 to 2 days, and harvesting promptly keeps the plant setting new fruit instead of slowing down.
harvest.text_beginner: Pick summer squash while small and check every day or two, they grow fast. Picking often keeps more squash coming.

harvest.text_seasoned: Missed a fruit and it turned into a big, seedy squash? Cut it off and compost or use it anyway; leaving mature, seedy fruit on the plant suppresses further production.
harvest.text_beginner: If a squash got huge, pick it off anyway, even if you do not use it. Leaving big squash on the plant makes it stop producing.

end_of_season.text_seasoned: Pull spent vines and remove them rather than tilling them under, which buries overwintering squash bugs and disease. Clean beds now mean fewer pests next season.
end_of_season.text_beginner: At the end of the season, pull up old plants and clear them away. This cuts down on pests and disease next year.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A healthy plant yields heavily, commonly 6 to 10 pounds of fruit over a season, often more in a long, warm climate. Two plants are plenty for most households, and a single plant at peak can produce more than one family can eat.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: One summer squash plant produces a lot, usually several pounds over the season. One or two plants are plenty for most families.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: At peak in warm weather a plant can set new fruit daily, and squash sizes up so fast that picking every 1 to 2 days is essential. Frequent harvest at this stage actually keeps the plant producing; leaving mature fruit on the vine signals it to slow down.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: At its peak, a summer squash plant makes squash incredibly fast. Pick every day or two, picking often actually keeps more squash coming.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Summer squash is forgiving and productive even for a first-time grower; the usual first-year surprise is not too little but too much. Plant only one or two, and be ready to pick constantly once it gets going.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Summer squash is one of the easiest crops for beginners, and the usual surprise is how much you get. Start with just one or two plants.
factors_seasoned: Pollination: poor pollination in cool or pollinator-scarce conditions cuts yield and causes blossom-end rot of small fruit.
Harvest frequency: picking young and often keeps a plant productive; letting fruit mature slows new set.
Pest and disease pressure: squash vine borer and powdery mildew commonly end the first planting by midsummer.
Even moisture: steady water through fruit set drives well-formed fruit and sustained production.
Season length and heat: long warm seasons extend the productive window; a frost ends it.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No T1 source supports timing summer squash planting by moon phase. We do not make a recommendation here; sow by soil temperature and frost dates instead.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Small fruit yellowed and rotted at the blossom end
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Tiny squash turned yellow and rotted
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Poor pollination. The female flower was not adequately pollinated, so the young fruit aborts, yellowing and rotting at the blossom end instead of sizing up. Common in cool, wet, or pollinator-scarce conditions.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The flower was not pollinated well, so the little squash died instead of growing. This often happens in cool or rainy weather, or when there are few bees.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Inadequate transfer of pollen to the female flower, often compounded by early-season timing before pollinator activity peaks.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Not enough pollination of the flower.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant flowers to draw pollinators, avoid spraying open blooms, and hand-pollinate in the morning if early set is poor. It usually improves as more flowers open and bees get active.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Grow some flowers nearby for the bees, and hand-pollinate early squash if needed. It usually gets better as the season goes on.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Squash hidden under leaves until it was a giant squash
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Found a giant summer squash you missed
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Fruit grows fast and hides under the large leaves, so a missed squash becomes an oversized, seedy, tough-skinned squash within days. Mature fruit left on the plant also slows new production.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Summer squash grows so fast it hides under the leaves and gets huge in just a few days. Big squash are tough and seedy, and leaving them on slows the plant down.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Infrequent harvest combined with dense foliage; fruit can gain an inch or more a day at peak.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Not picking often enough while squash grow very fast.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Check plants every 1 to 2 days at peak, lifting leaves to find hidden fruit, and pick young. Remove any oversized squash you find to keep the plant cropping.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Check every day or two and look under the leaves. Pick squash small, and remove any big ones to keep more coming.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Healthy plant wilted and collapsed in midsummer
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Plant suddenly wilted and died
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Most likely squash vine borer: a larva tunneled into the stem and cut off water, collapsing a previously vigorous plant in mid- to late summer. Look for frass at the stem base. Bacterial wilt (beetle-vectored) causes similar sudden collapse.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Usually a squash vine borer, a grub that tunnels into the stem and kills the plant in summer. Look for sawdust-like specks at the base. Beetle-spread bacterial wilt can look similar.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Squash vine borer larva inside the stem, or bacterial wilt clogging the water-conducting tissue.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: A borer inside the stem, or a disease spread by beetles.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Use row cover until flowering, scout the stem base for frass from early summer, and time a fall succession to crop after the borer's flight. Remove spent vines at season's end.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Cover plants until they flower, check the stem base for pests, and plant a second crop in summer as a backup. Clean up old plants at the end of the season.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Leaves turned white and powdery, then the plant faded early
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Leaves got white and powdery and the plant died back
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Powdery mildew defoliated the plant ahead of schedule. The white fungal coating spread across the leaves until they browned and died, cutting the productive season short and exposing fruit to sunscald.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Powdery mildew, a white coating on the leaves, spread until the leaves died and the plant stopped early.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Powdery mildew fungus, worsened by crowding, poor airflow, and high humidity around the foliage.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: A fungus that spreads on crowded plants with poor air flow.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Choose resistant varieties, space plants generously, water at the base, and treat at the first spots. A summer-sown succession can carry harvest past the worst of it.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Pick resistant varieties, give plants more room, water the soil not the leaves, and treat early spots. A second planting helps too.

primary.name: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center
UF/IFAS Northwest District Horticulture Vegetable Garden Planting Dates (Florida Panhandle)
UF/IFAS SP 103/VH021 Florida Vegetable Gardening Guide
UGA Extension Bulletin 577 (Vegetable Garden Planting Chart)

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Summer squash is famous for overwhelming a garden, so resist sowing the whole crop at once. A first sowing after your last frost, then a second about three weeks later, spreads the harvest and keeps vigorous plants coming as the originals tire. The real payoff is late season: squash vine borer and powdery mildew often take down the first planting by midsummer, so a replacement sown in early to midsummer, counting back from your first fall frost so it has time to mature, frequently outproduces the spring crop on cleaner, less stressed plants.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: You rarely need more than one or two summer squash plants at a time, and a single planting can feed you for weeks. For a steadier supply, sow a few seeds now and a few more about three weeks later. A second planting in summer is a smart backup, since pests and disease often wear out the first plants by late summer.

northern_tier.plantings_provenance: Author-fresh from T1 (no legacy zones{} to de-multiplex). Direct-sow-dominant cucurbit: plant_out is the after-frost direct-sow window once soil >=70F at 2 in (UMN); start_indoors is the 3-week transplant-early lead used at the short-season cold end (z3-z5) to gain time. Single continuous summer window capped by the fall-frost runway; succession is the 3-week cadence (UMD/UMN), not a spring/fall split. Fall replacement (squash vine borer / powdery mildew) sits inside the same continuous window, counted back from first frost. Region-specific window per A5; not analogized from another region.
northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In cold northern areas, summer squash is a summer crop. Wait until after your last frost and the soil has warmed before sowing seeds outside, usually late spring to early summer. If your summers are short, you can start a few seeds indoors about 3 weeks early and move them out gently. For a steady supply, sow a few seeds, then a few more about 3 weeks later. A second planting in summer is a good backup since pests often slow the first plants by late summer.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Across the cold northern tier (zones 3 to 7) summer squash is a single continuous summer crop, bracketed by frost on both ends. Direct sow after the last frost once the soil reaches about 70°F at 2 inches, which is the reliable trigger here; in the shortest-season zones (3 to 5) you can start seeds indoors roughly 3 weeks ahead and transplant carefully to gain time. There is no spring-and-fall split, just one warm window, so space sowings about 3 weeks apart through early summer for a steady supply. Count any midsummer replacement planting back from your first fall frost so it has time to mature, since squash vine borer and powdery mildew often wear out the first planting by then.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer sowing gap is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: summer squash flowers and young fruit drop in deep-summer heat. When daytime highs run in the 90s degrees F with warm nights, heat injures the flowers and reduces or kills pollen, so plants abort fruit or set misshapen squash; set recovers as temperatures ease. (UGA Cooperative Extension B577; UF/IFAS VH021)

Summer sowing gap is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: summer squash flowers and young fruit drop in deep-summer heat. When daytime highs run in the 90s degrees F with warm nights, heat injures the flowers and reduces or kills pollen, so plants abort fruit or set misshapen squash; set recovers as temperatures ease. (UGA Cooperative Extension B577; UF/IFAS VH021)

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast and Gulf, summer squash grows in two seasons: spring and fall, with a break in the hottest part of summer. Plant in spring once frost has passed, then plant again in late summer for a fall crop. Skip the peak of summer, when heat and pests make squash struggle. A spring sowing plus a second one a couple of weeks later gives you a good early supply.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: In the Southeast and Gulf (zones 8 to 9) summer squash is a true spring-and-fall crop with a hot midsummer gap. Sow in spring from about April, making a second sowing 2 to 3 weeks later, then stop: virus pressure, squash vine borer, and heat curtail production through the worst of summer. Sow again for fall by late August so plants establish before cooling weather. The exact dates shift within the region, earlier in spring and later in fall toward south Georgia, the reverse toward the cooler northern edge. The midsummer stretch is a deliberate no-plant gap, not a growing month.
se_gulf.plantings_provenance: UGA Extension Bulletin 577 home-garden planting chart (Squash, bush, 50-55 days: spring Apr 1-May 15, fall Aug 1-20, middle Georgia) plus Circular 943 (make a second planting 2-3 weeks after the first in spring; plant cucumbers and squash for fall no later than Aug 31). The Southeast/Gulf is a true SPRING + FALL split: virus pressure, squash vine borer, and mid-summer heat curtail production in late summer, leaving a no-plant gap between the spring crop's heat-driven end and the fall sowing. The chart's own zone notes shift the dates (south Georgia ~ z9 earlier in spring/later in fall; north-Georgia edge ~ z8 later in spring/earlier in fall). succession_spring + succession_fall per second_planting spec v1.1; the mid-summer no-plant month renders heat_pause. Region-specific per A5; the fall window is a SE finding and is NOT carried to ca_interior or warm_arid.

9.succession_continuous: Mar 15, Apr 5, Apr 26, May 17, Jun 7, Jun 28

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In California's inland valleys, summer squash grows right through the warm season in one long stretch. Sow seeds once the soil is warm, from around mid-March into early summer. Hot summer weather is fine, summer squash loves the heat. Production slows in fall as pests build up. Sow a few seeds every few weeks for a steady supply.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: In California's interior valleys (zones 8 to 9) summer squash runs as one long, continuous warm-season crop rather than a spring-and-fall split. Direct sow once the soil warms to about 70°F, safely from roughly mid-March, with set-out continuing into July. Because summer squash is heat-loving, peak summer is the productive core here, not a pause, though production tapers in fall as aphid-transmitted virus and whitefly build up. Space sowings about 3 weeks apart for a steady run, and favor a later planting to carry harvest into the cleaner fall weather.
ca_interior.plantings_provenance: UC ANR Pub 7245 (Summer Squash Production in California) plus Sacramento and Santa Clara/Marin County Master Gardener charts: Central Valley squash is direct-sown once soil reaches ~70 degrees F (Mar 15 safe without protection; soil-warm late Mar through July set-out), producing through summer and tapering in fall on aphid-transmitted virus and whitefly pressure. This is one continuous warm-season window, not a spring/fall split: no mid-summer no-plant gap is documented, and summer squash is heat-loving, so peak heat is a window edge, not a heat_pause. succession_continuous per second_planting spec v1.1 (window_type continuous). Region-specific per A5.

9.succession_continuous: May 1, May 22, Jun 12, Jul 3

ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: On California's cool north coast, summer squash grows all season in one stretch, but it gets going later than in hotter areas because of the cool ocean air. Start seeds indoors in March and plant out once nights are reliably mild, from mid-April into June. Harvest continues well into fall. Give plants a warm, sunny spot to make the most of the cooler climate.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: On California's cool north coast (zones 9 to 10) the marine layer makes summer squash heat-limited rather than heat-stalled: it grows in one continuous window but starts later and blooms more slowly than inland. Start seeds indoors in March and set plants out from mid-April through June, or even July, once nights stay above about 55°F. Harvest carries late, into fall, as the season cools gradually. There is no midsummer gap here; the limit is cool air, not heat.
ca_north_coast.plantings_provenance: UC Marin Master Gardener squash guide plus UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2 (North/North Coast column): on the cool maritime coast squash is seeded indoors in March and set out from mid-April through June (some to July), once nights are above 55 degrees F, and bears until weather cools in fall. The marine layer makes this region heat-LIMITED (a later start, a slower bloom), not heat-stalled, so there is no heat_pause and the window is one continuous run. succession_continuous. Region-specific per A5; the coastal behavior is the inverse of ca_interior at the same hardiness band.

9.succession_continuous: Apr 15, May 6, May 27, Jun 17

ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: On California's mild south coast, summer squash grows in one long warm-season stretch from spring into late fall. Wait until the soil is warm, around late April, before planting out. Harvest continues until the weather cools. Even with mild winters, summer squash is killed by frost and slows in the cool season, so it is a warm-weather crop, not year-round.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: California's mild south coast (zones 9 to 10) supports one long continuous warm-season window from spring set-out into late fall. Wait for warm soil, roughly late April, before setting plants out, and harvest can run until weather cools. The marine influence limits peak heat rather than forcing a midsummer pause, so this is a single run, not a spring-and-fall split. Despite the mild winters summer squash is still a frost-tender annual with a clear cool-season slowdown; it is not a year-round crop here.
ca_south_coast.plantings_provenance: UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2 (South Coast column) plus Los Angeles County Master Gardener guidance (wait until warm soil, roughly end of April, to set out squash): the mild South Coast supports one long continuous warm-season window from spring set-out into late fall, heat-limited by the marine layer rather than stalled. No heat_pause; not year_round (a frost-tender annual with a cool-season slowdown). succession_continuous. Region-specific per A5.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer sowing gap is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: summer squash flowers and young fruit drop in deep-summer heat. When daytime highs run in the 90s degrees F with warm nights, heat injures the flowers and reduces or kills pollen, so plants abort fruit or set misshapen squash; set recovers as temperatures ease. (UC ANR; University of Arizona Cooperative Extension AZ1005)
