succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Acorn squash is not a succession crop. It is a single, warm-season planting that sets fruit through summer and matures together for one fall harvest, so you sow once per season rather than at intervals. In most zones a second sowing would be killed by frost before its 80 to 100 day crop could ripen. Only in the warmest, frost-free or near-frost-free zones, or the low desert where a summer sowing is the fall crop, is a second seasonal window viable, and that is a separate season, not a succession.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: You plant acorn squash once for the season. It grows through summer and ripens together in the fall for a single harvest, so there is no need to replant every few weeks. In most places a later planting would be caught by frost before the squash could ripen. Only in very warm, nearly frost-free areas can you fit a second planting, and that is really a separate season.
succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Acorn squash is a single warm-season crop (80 to 100 days) harvested once at full maturity, so succession sowing does not apply; a second sowing in most zones would not mature before frost. Warm frost-free zones and the low desert support a separate seasonal planting window, which is a distinct season rather than a succession.

crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Acorn squash is monoecious: each plant carries separate male and female flowers, so a single plant sets fruit with no second variety needed. The flowers are insect-pollinated, mostly by bees, and pollen must move from the male to the female blooms. Acorn squash is strongly pollinator-dependent: each female flower needs several bee visits to set a full fruit, and poor pollination shows up as young fruit that yellow and rot at the blossom end, or as small, misshapen squash. Early-season male flowers often open and drop for a week or more before the first females appear, which is normal. Plant flowers nearby, avoid spraying open blooms, and hand-pollinate with a male flower or small brush in the morning if set stalls.
crops.pollinator_notes_beginner: Each acorn squash plant has both male and female flowers, so you only need one plant to get fruit. Bees move the pollen between the flowers, and the plant needs a lot of bee visits to set each fruit, so anything that brings bees to your garden helps. The first flowers are usually male and fall off, which is normal. If your little squash stay small and rot at the tip, the flowers were not pollinated well, so hand-pollinate in the morning and grow some flowers nearby for the bees.
crops.description_seasoned: Acorn squash is a warm-season winter squash (Cucurbita pepo, the same species as zucchini and spaghetti squash) grown for its small, hard-rind, deeply ribbed, heart-shaped fruit with sweet, fine-grained flesh, ideal halved and roasted by the single serving. Unlike its summer-squash cousin zucchini, it is harvested once, at full maturity in fall, when the rind is hard and the pale ground spot where the fruit rests on the soil has turned deep orange. It is the shortest keeper of the common winter squashes, storing only about 1 to 2 months, and, unlike a butternut, it is not cured: curing at high heat actually reduces its quality. Acorn squash comes in both true bush and vining forms, so it suits small gardens as readily as large ones, with vining types running roughly 4 to 8 feet and compact bush types like Table King and Honey Bear staying tidy. It is monoecious, carrying separate male and female flowers on one plant, and fruit set is strongly pollinator-dependent. As a pepo, it is susceptible to the squash vine borer, so managing that pest is part of growing it. The season's shape is set by three things: a warm runway of 80 to 100 frost-free days to mature the crop, moderate pest and disease pressure (squash bug, squash vine borer, cucumber beetle and the bacterial wilt it spreads, plus powdery and downy mildew), and the single fall harvest, timed at a hard rind with an orange ground spot, before frost.
crops.description_beginner: Acorn squash is a warm-season squash grown for small, ribbed, heart-shaped fruit with sweet flesh that is perfect halved and roasted. You harvest it once in the fall, when the rind is hard and the pale patch where it sits on the ground turns orange, unlike summer squash that you pick young all season. It grows in both bush and vining forms, so it fits gardens of any size: vining types spread about 4 to 8 feet, while bush types like Table King and Honey Bear stay small enough for pots. Each plant has both male and female flowers and needs plenty of bee visits to set fruit. The main things to know: give it a warm season of about 80 to 100 days, water steadily while the fruit grows, watch for squash bugs, squash vine borers, beetles, and mildew, and pick when the skin is hard and dull and the underside spot has turned orange, before frost. Do not cure acorn squash the way you would a butternut; just store it in a cool, dry spot, where it keeps for about a month or two, less than most other winter squash but far longer than summer squash.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Prepare a fertile, well-drained bed in full sun, working several inches of compost or rotted manure into the soil before planting, since acorn squash is a hungry, warm-season plant. Many growers set plants in low hills or mounds about a foot across, which warm faster in spring, drain better, and give the plants a clear starting point. Space to the type: bush and semi-bush acorn squash can go about 18 to 24 inches apart, while vining types want 24 to 36 inches in the row with 3 to 6 feet between rows, since the vines run 4 to 8 feet. On heavy or wet ground, build the mounds up for drainage to head off crown and fruit rot.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Pick a sunny spot with rich, well-drained soil and mix in plenty of compost before planting, since acorn squash is a hungry plant. Plant it on low hills or mounds, which warm up and drain better. Space it to the type: bush kinds like Table King can go about a foot and a half to two feet apart, while vining kinds need more room, about 2 to 3 feet apart in rows 3 to 6 feet apart. If your soil is heavy or wet, build the mounds up higher so water drains away from the roots and fruit.

northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In cold zones the acorn squash season is a single tight summer window: plant after the last frost once soil is warm, and harvest the mature crop in early fall before the first frost. Short-season zones (3 to 4) do well with a fast-maturing, often bush variety such as Table Ace, started about three weeks early where needed; warmer zones (6 to 7) have room for full-size vining Table Queen.
northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In cold areas you get one acorn squash crop a summer: plant after the last frost and harvest in early fall before frost returns. In the coldest zones, grow a fast variety like Table Ace, and start transplants indoors so the squash ripen in time.

se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: Across the Gulf and coastal plain, acorn squash is a late-spring-into-fall crop, planted as the soil warms and timed so the fruit matures in fall ahead of the first frost. Summer heat and humidity drive mildew and pest pressure, and the squash vine borer is active, so give plants room, use row cover on young plants, choose tougher varieties, and scout closely.
se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast, plant acorn squash in late spring to early summer so it ripens in fall before frost. The hot, humid summers bring mildew, squash vine borers, and other pests, so give plants room and watch them closely.

ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: In California's hot interior valleys, acorn squash is a warm summer crop: plant from spring into early summer and harvest in fall. The dry heat suits it well as long as irrigation is steady; time the planting so fruit matures in the warm, dry fall, and scout for squash vine borer through midsummer.
ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In California's hot inland valleys, plant acorn squash from spring into early summer and harvest in fall. It handles the dry heat well as long as you water steadily.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: Along California's cooler north coast, plant acorn squash after the spring chill passes and the soil warms, and harvest in fall. Cool, foggy summers can slow ripening and favor mildew, so choose a sunny site, give airflow, and lean toward earlier-maturing varieties like Table Ace.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: On California's cool north coast, plant acorn squash in late spring once it warms up and harvest in fall. Foggy, cool summers can slow it down, so pick a sunny spot and an earlier variety.

ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: On California's mild south coast, acorn squash grows through a long, gentle warm season: plant from spring into early summer and harvest in fall. The mild climate is forgiving, though coastal humidity favors mildew, so prioritize airflow and full sun.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: On California's mild south coast, plant acorn squash from spring into early summer and harvest in fall. The mild weather is easy on it, but watch for mildew in the coastal damp.

ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: In the California desert valleys, acorn squash grows as two plantings: a late-winter to spring sowing that matures before peak heat, and a midsummer (around July) sowing that grows into a fall harvest. Steady irrigation is essential, and the fall timing is the reliable one.
ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: In the California desert, plant acorn squash in late winter to spring for an early crop, and again around July for a fall crop. Water steadily.

warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: In the warm arid zones of southern New Mexico and West Texas, plant acorn squash after frost once the soil warms and harvest in fall. The dry heat is manageable with steady irrigation; intense early-summer heat can briefly stall fruit set, which usually resumes as conditions ease.
warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: In the dry, warm zones of southern New Mexico and West Texas, plant acorn squash after the last frost and harvest in fall. Water steadily through the heat, and do not worry if fruit set pauses briefly during the hottest spells.

low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: In Arizona's low desert, acorn squash is planted in late winter for an early-summer crop before peak heat, and again in midsummer (around July) for a fall harvest that uses the long, hot autumn. Either way, steady irrigation matters, and the fall timing is the reliable one.
low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: In Arizona's low desert, plant acorn squash in late winter for an early-summer crop, and again in July for a fall harvest. Water steadily through the heat.

fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: In peninsular Florida, acorn squash is grown in the cooler halves of the year, planted in late winter to spring and again in late summer for a fall crop, avoiding the wettest, most disease-prone midsummer. Expect mildew, squash vine borer, and other pest pressure, so use row cover on young plants and scout closely.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: In Florida, plant acorn squash in late winter to spring and again in late summer, avoiding the wet, buggy middle of summer. Watch closely for mildew and pests.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: In Hawaii and tropical zones there is no frost, so acorn squash can be planted across much of the year, with timing driven by rainfall and pest pressure rather than cold. Choose the drier, sunnier windows to limit mildew and fruit rot. Specific local timing is modeled pending a parseable CTAHR source.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In Hawaii and the tropics there is no frost, so you can plant acorn squash through much of the year. Aim for the drier, sunnier stretches to avoid mildew and rot.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: Wave-5 cucurbit cert (2026-07-02): parallel per-crop source-truth review (CC agents, WebFetch of cited T1 pages). cantaloupe CERTIFY_CLEAN (bacterial-wilt susceptibility near-verbatim on UMD/UMN). honeydew does-not-slip/multi-cue ripeness triple-sourced (ISU/USU/Clemson); andromonoecious wording kept (more precise than 'monoecious' for Cucumis melo). acorn's 3 flips (do-not-cure verbatim on Iowa State/UMass, SVB-susceptible on UIUC, shortest-keeper) all honestly sourced. spaghetti curing/storage/pests strongly sourced. yellow harvest-young + pest complex verified; 2 dead UMN URLs re-pointed live (bacterial-wilt, cucumber-beetle), harvest_ready anchored. Systemic dead-URL items (yellow iastate /encyclopedia/squash 404s; honeydew 404 UMN log URL) flagged for the post-123 URL-liveness sweep.

open_findings.summary: Per-zone resolved_by_zone planting/harvest windows are MODELED from days-to-maturity (80-100) + the shared frost anchors + representative extension planting dates, and parallel the butternut/spaghetti/pumpkin pilots' windows (all share a near-identical warm cucurbit calendar; acorn's slightly shorter season does not shift the monthly-token calendar). Individual per-zone dates are not each source-verified against a live regional planting calendar.
open_findings.basis: Warm-season frost-anchored windows derived deterministically from DTM + crop-invariant frost anchors; calendars are internally coherent (A5/A24/A37 PASS). Daily biology review + a per-region source-truth sample should confirm the regional dates before flip.

open_findings.summary: spacing_inches is [24,48]. Acorn squash is spaced about 18-24 in for bush types and 24-36 in in the row with 3-6 ft between rows for vining types, and vining plants run 4-8 ft; the structured field spans in-row plant spacing (24 in) to about a 4 ft row (48 in), and the full row/sprawl and bush-vs-vine figures are carried in prose (soil_prep, description, yield).
open_findings.basis: The placeability number spans in-row plant spacing to row spacing; the full habit range is described in consumer prose. Well within the numeric-sanity non-tree bound of 72 in.

open_findings.summary: The variety days_to_maturity values (Table Queen 80, Table Ace 78, Table King 80, Honey Bear 95, Celebration 95) are modeled from widely published breeder / seed-catalog norms and AAS standing (Table King, Honey Bear AAS), not pinned to a per-variety T1 extension page. Table Queen as the OP standard and the bush Table King / Honey Bear are well established.

crops.name: Spaghetti Squash

soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Spaghetti squash wants deep, fertile, well-drained loam rich in organic matter, with steady moisture but no waterlogging. It is a big, long-season vine with hungry roots, so work several inches of compost or rotted manure into the bed before planting. Many growers set plants in low hills or mounds, which warm faster in spring, improve drainage, and give the sprawling vines a clear starting point. Sandy loams warm early and suit the earliest sowings, while heavy clay holds water and invites crown and fruit rot, so amend it generously or build raised mounds.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Plant spaghetti squash in rich, well-drained soil with plenty of compost mixed in. It is a large, long-season plant, so give it a generous, fertile bed. Many gardeners plant on low hills or mounds, which warm up faster and drain better. If your soil is heavy or stays wet, build up mounds or use raised beds so the roots and developing fruit do not sit in water.

ph.note_seasoned: Spaghetti squash does best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, around pH 6.0 to 6.8, with a sweet spot near 6.0 to 6.5. It still grows across a wider band, roughly 5.8 to 7.5, but uptake of some nutrients tightens as the soil turns alkaline. Test before planting and lime or add sulfur only on the test's advice rather than by guess.
ph.note_beginner: Spaghetti squash likes soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, about pH 6.0 to 6.8, and most garden soil is already close. An inexpensive soil test tells you where you stand and whether you need to adjust it before planting.

fertilizer.frequency: At planting, then side-dress once or twice
fertilizer.type: balanced at planting, then nitrogen side-dress
fertilizer.timing: Work into the bed before planting, then side-dress about 3 to 4 weeks after planting and again at flowering
fertilizer.example_product: balanced 10-10-10 at planting, then a nitrogen source such as blood meal or 46-0-0
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Spaghetti squash is a moderate feeder over a long season. Work a complete fertilizer such as 10-10-10 into the bed before planting, then side-dress with nitrogen about three to four weeks after planting as the vines begin to run, and again as flowering starts. Ease off heavy nitrogen once fruit has set, since late, lush vine growth comes at the expense of fruit and draws pests. Pair feeding with even moisture, because the nutrients only help a plant that is not also drought-stressed.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Spaghetti squash grows for a long time and likes steady feeding. Mix a balanced fertilizer into the soil before planting, then feed with a little extra nitrogen about three to four weeks later as the vines start to run, and again when flowers appear. Once the squash begin to form, go easy on the nitrogen, because too much makes leafy vines instead of fruit.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Your spaghetti squash vines are running, time to side-dress with nitrogen. Keep feeding moderate once fruit sets so the plant builds squash, not just leaves.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Your spaghetti squash vines are spreading. Give them a feeding of nitrogen now.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A complete fertilizer such as 10-10-10 worked in at planting, then a nitrogen side-dress while vines run, easing off once fruit sets. Avoid pushing high nitrogen late, which gives vine at the expense of fruit.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 at planting, then a little nitrogen as the vines spread. Do not overdo the nitrogen once fruit forms.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A common rate is a complete fertilizer such as 10-10-10 worked into the bed before planting (roughly 1.5 pounds per 100 square feet, or a balanced scoop per hill), then a nitrogen side-dress about three to four weeks after planting placed a few inches out from the plants and watered in, repeated lightly at flowering.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Mix a balanced fertilizer or a few inches of compost into the soil before planting. Then feed with a nitrogen fertilizer about three to four weeks later, scratched into the soil a few inches away from the plants, and once more when flowers appear.

companions.note_seasoned: Most spaghetti squash companion pairings are traditional rather than trial-tested, and the ones worth acting on serve two practical ends: pollination and pest pressure. Because cucurbit fruit set is pollinator-limited, with each female flower needing many bee visits, flowering insectary plants like borage near the patch are a genuine help. The Three Sisters partners, corn and beans, give the sprawling vines structure and a nitrogen boost while sharing none of spaghetti squash's pests, and a trap planting of nasturtium can divert squash bugs and beetles. The firmest rule is a rotation one: keep spaghetti squash away from other cucurbits, which share the full squash pest and disease complex, including the squash vine borer this pepo squash is prone to.
companions.note_beginner: The most useful spaghetti squash companions are flowers that bring in bees, since spaghetti squash needs lots of bee visits to set fruit, and the traditional Three Sisters partners, corn and beans. Nasturtiums can lure pests away. The one rule that really matters is to keep spaghetti squash away from other squash, cucumbers, and melons, which all share the same pests and diseases.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Corn
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Corn and spaghetti squash are the traditional Three Sisters pairing. The corn stands tall while the squash vines spread along the ground, and the big leaves shade out weeds. It is a time-tested combination more than a proven boost.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: The classic Three Sisters partner: tall corn gives sprawling spaghetti squash vines structure and light shade in high heat, while the broad squash leaves shade the soil and suppress weeds beneath the corn. A long-standing intercropping tradition with a sound space-and-shade rationale, not a measured yield effect for this exact pair.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Three Sisters intercropping is a documented traditional system; the corn-squash benefit is space-and-shade, not a trial-isolated pair effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Beans
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Beans are the third Three Sisters plant. They pull nitrogen from the air into the soil, which the hungry squash appreciates, and they do not share spaghetti squash's pests. A good, traditional neighbor.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: The third of the Three Sisters: pole or bush beans fix nitrogen that benefits the long-feeding spaghetti squash, and they share none of the cucurbit pests. A traditional, mechanistically plausible pairing rather than a trial-isolated one.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Legume nitrogen fixation is a documented mechanism; the bean-squash adjacency benefit is traditional, not pair-isolated.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Nasturtium
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Nasturtiums are often grown near squash to lure squash bugs and beetles away, and their flowers bring in bees, which spaghetti squash needs to set fruit. A helpful, low-risk neighbor.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Often planted near cucurbits as a trap and deterrent for squash bugs and cucumber beetles, and its flowers also draw the bees spaghetti squash depends on for fruit set. Trap cropping is a documented principle, but the specific nasturtium-spaghetti squash effect is not formally isolated, so treat it as a plausible aid.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Trap-cropping for cucurbit beetles/bugs is documented in principle; the nasturtium-spaghetti squash pairing is not trial-isolated.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Borage
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Borage flowers are loved by bees, and spaghetti squash needs lots of bee visits to set fruit, so a few borage plants nearby can help with pollination. Mainly grown to bring in bees.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A strong bee magnet whose flowers recruit the pollinators that spaghetti squash fruit set depends on, since each female flower needs many bee visits to size a fruit. Pollinator-habitat value is well grounded; the specific borage-spaghetti squash pairing is traditional rather than trial-tested.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Spaghetti squash fruit set is pollinator-limited; flowering insectary plants like borage draw the bees needed for fruit set. Pairing is habitat-based, not pair-isolated.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Other cucurbits
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep spaghetti squash away from other squash, cucumbers, and melons. They share most of the same pests and diseases, including the squash vine borer, so planting them together makes those problems worse.
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Cucumber, melon, summer squash, and other winter squash share spaghetti squash's pest and disease complex, including squash bug, the squash vine borer that readily attacks this pepo squash, cucumber beetle with the bacterial wilt it spreads, and powdery and downy mildew. Grouping them concentrates that pressure and lets soilborne problems build. A real epidemiology and rotation principle rather than a tested adjacency effect: spread cucurbits out and rotate them.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Shared cucurbit pests/pathogens and cucumber-beetle wilt vectoring are extension-documented; the bad-adjacency claim is a sound epidemiological principle, not pair-tested.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Potatoes
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Some gardeners keep potatoes and squash apart, since both are big, hungry plants and potatoes can bring their own diseases. This is more tradition than a proven rule.
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional caution that potatoes and cucurbits compete heavily and that potatoes can harbor disease and attract pests near squash. There is no strong T1 mechanism for the specific pairing, so it persists mostly as garden lore.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: A folk anti-companion caution; competition is plausible but there is no T1 source isolating a potato-squash antagonism.

pests.name: Squash bug
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Leaves develop yellow specks that brown and wilt, and heavily fed vines wilt rapidly and turn brittle, a damage pattern sometimes called anasa wilt. Flat bronze egg clusters appear on leaf undersides along the veins, and gray-brown adults and pale nymphs cluster near the crown and under debris.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Leaves get yellow spots, then brown and wilt, and you find clusters of shield-shaped gray-brown bugs and their bronze eggs on the undersides of leaves near the base of the plant.
pests.cause_seasoned: The squash bug, a true bug that feeds with piercing-sucking mouthparts on cucurbit foliage and stems, injecting saliva that wilts and browns the vines. Populations build through the season and are hardest to control once nymphs are large; the bugs overwinter as adults in garden debris.
pests.cause_beginner: Squash bugs pierce the leaves and stems and suck out the juices, which makes the vines wilt. They breed through the summer and hide in plant debris over winter.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick adults, crush the egg masses on leaf undersides, and trap bugs by laying a board near the plants overnight, then lifting it in the morning and destroying the cluster underneath. Target young nymphs with insecticidal soap, since large nymphs and adults are tough to kill.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick the bugs off by hand and scrape off the egg clusters under the leaves. A board laid on the ground overnight draws them underneath, then lift it in the morning and destroy them. Treat the young bugs with insecticidal soap.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Use row cover on young plants until flowering, clean up vines and debris at season's end to cut overwintering sites, and rotate cucurbits. Scout leaf undersides for the bronze egg clusters from early in the season and act before nymphs mature.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover young plants until they flower, check under the leaves for eggs early in the season, and clean up old vines after harvest so the bugs have nowhere to overwinter.

pests.name: Cucumber beetles
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small yellow beetles, striped or spotted, chew young leaves, stems, and flowers, and can scar developing fruit. The bigger threat is indirect: striped and spotted cucumber beetles transmit bacterial wilt, so beetle feeding on seedlings can be followed weeks later by sudden vine wilt.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Small yellow beetles with stripes or spots chew on the leaves and flowers, especially of young plants. Worse, they can spread a disease called bacterial wilt that makes the vines collapse later.
pests.cause_seasoned: Striped and spotted cucumber beetles feed on cucurbits and carry the bacterium that causes bacterial wilt in their gut, infecting plants as they feed. Seedlings are most vulnerable; once plants have several leaves they tolerate some feeding, and bacterial wilt is generally less severe in winter squash like spaghetti squash than in cucumber and melon.
pests.cause_beginner: Cucumber beetles feed on spaghetti squash plants and carry the germ that causes bacterial wilt, infecting the plant as they chew. Young seedlings are most at risk.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Protect seedlings with row cover removed at flowering, hand-pick beetles, and use yellow sticky traps to monitor and reduce numbers. Where bacterial wilt is a known problem, controlling the beetles is the most effective control of the disease, since there is no cure once a plant is infected.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover young plants with row cover (remove it when flowers open), pick the beetles off, and use yellow sticky traps. Keeping the beetles down is the best way to avoid the wilt disease they spread.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Exclude beetles from seedlings with row cover, keep young plants vigorous so they grow past the vulnerable stage, clear weeds and debris, and rotate away from where cucurbits grew. Aim control at the early-season colonizers that vector wilt.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover seedlings until they flower, keep them growing strong, clear away weeds and old plants, and do not plant where squash-family crops grew last year.

pests.name: Squash vine borer
pests.symptoms_seasoned: A vigorous vine wilts suddenly in mid to late summer, often one runner at a time, with sawdust-like frass oozing from a small hole low on the stem and a fat white caterpillar tunneling inside. As a Cucurbita pepo, spaghetti squash is a preferred, susceptible host, so a healthy plant can collapse within days once a borer is inside.
pests.symptoms_beginner: A healthy plant wilts all at once in summer, with what looks like wet sawdust at a hole near the base of the stem and a fat white grub inside. Spaghetti squash is one of the squashes borers love, so watch for this.
pests.cause_seasoned: The larva of the squash vine borer moth, which lays eggs at the stem base in early summer; the hatching larvae bore into the stem and cut off the plant's water. The moth strongly prefers thin-stemmed Cucurbita pepo squash, which includes spaghetti squash along with zucchini, acorn, and summer squash, so this is a pest to plan for rather than hope to avoid.
pests.cause_beginner: A moth lays eggs at the base of the stem in early summer, and the grubs tunnel inside and kill the vine. The moth likes thin-stemmed squash such as spaghetti squash and zucchini, so this squash is a common target.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Catch it early: scout the stem base for frass from early summer. If a borer has entered, slit the stem lengthwise with a knife, remove the larva, and mound moist soil over that node to encourage re-rooting. Burying vine joints as they run so a damaged plant can survive on secondary roots, and removing and destroying infested vines at season's end, both reduce next year's brood.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Check the base of the stems often in summer. If you find a borer, slit the stem with a knife, dig out the grub, and cover the spot with damp soil so the vine can re-root. Pull and destroy badly damaged vines so the pest does not come back next year.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Row cover from planting until flowering excludes the egg-laying moths and is the most reliable defense; remove it at bloom so bees can pollinate. Time a planting to dodge the main moth flight where its timing is known, wrap or mound soil over the lower stem, and choose semi-bush types, which some growers find recover better. Scout the stem base for frass from early summer and act at the first sign.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover young plants with a light row cover until they flower, then take it off so bees can reach the blooms. Check the base of the stems for the sawdust-like frass starting in early summer, and clean up old vines after harvest so borers cannot overwinter.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Colonies of small soft-bodied insects, often melon aphids, cluster on leaf undersides and growing tips, causing leaves to curl, pucker, and yellow, with sticky honeydew and sooty mold following. Beyond direct feeding, aphids transmit mosaic viruses that mottle and distort the foliage.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny soft insects gather on the undersides of leaves and on new growth, making leaves curl and turn yellow, often with a sticky film. They can also spread viruses.
pests.cause_seasoned: Melon and other aphids suck sap and reproduce rapidly in warm weather, building up quickly on stressed or over-fertilized plants. The honeydew they excrete fosters sooty mold, and several aphid species spread cucurbit mosaic viruses.
pests.cause_beginner: Aphids are small insects that suck the plant's juices and multiply fast, especially on soft, over-fed growth. The sticky honeydew they leave behind grows black mold.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong jet of water and spray insecticidal soap or horticultural oil with thorough coverage of leaf undersides, repeating every few days. Conserve lady beetles, lacewings, and parasitic wasps, which usually bring aphids under control.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water and treat the undersides of the leaves with insecticidal soap, repeating every few days. Ladybugs and other helpful insects eat aphids, so welcome them.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen, which drives the soft growth aphids favor, scout leaf undersides and growing tips, and support natural enemies rather than spraying broadly. Reflective mulch deters aphids from young plants.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen, check the undersides of leaves regularly, and let helpful insects do their work instead of spraying everything.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: White, powdery patches appear first on the upper and lower leaf surfaces and stems, spreading until leaves yellow, brown, and die back ahead of schedule. Early defoliation cuts the season short, reduces fruit size and the sugars that make spaghetti squash sweet, and exposes fruit to sunscald.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: A white, powdery coating spreads over the leaves until they turn yellow and brown and die. The plant fades early, and the squash may not size up or sweeten well.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Powdery mildew fungi that thrive in warm conditions with high humidity but do not need leaf wetness, spreading by wind-blown spores. Crowded plantings, poor airflow, and shade worsen it, and it is one of the most common late-season winter-squash diseases.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that spreads on warm, humid days, especially where plants are crowded and air does not move well. It does not need wet leaves to take hold.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Treat at the first spots, before it spreads, with a labeled fungicide such as sulfur or a horticultural oil or biofungicide, covering both leaf surfaces, and remove the worst leaves. Avoid overhead watering. Once it is widespread, control is mostly damage limitation.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Treat early, at the first white spots, with a labeled fungicide like sulfur or horticultural oil, and remove badly affected leaves. Water the soil, not the leaves. Once it covers the plant it is hard to stop.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Choose mildew-tolerant varieties where available (some spaghetti squash hybrids such as Stripetti hold up better), space plants generously for airflow, plant in full sun, and avoid excess nitrogen and overhead watering. Scout from midsummer and treat at the first sign, since prevention and early action beat rescue.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Pick mildew-tolerant varieties if you can, give plants plenty of room so air moves between them, plant in full sun, and water at the base. Start checking in midsummer and act at the first white spots.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Angular yellow blotches, bounded by the leaf veins, appear on the upper leaf surface, with a grayish or purplish fuzzy growth on the underside in humid weather. Spots brown and coalesce, and severe infection rapidly defoliates the vines.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Yellow patches show on top of the leaves with fuzzy gray growth underneath, mostly in damp, humid weather. The spots brown and spread until the leaves die.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A fungus-like water mold that spreads on wind-borne spores and needs leaf wetness and humidity to infect, so it flares in wet, humid spells and dewy conditions. It moves fast once established and is favored by crowding and prolonged leaf wetness.
diseases.cause_beginner: A mold-like disease that spreads in wet, humid weather and needs wet leaves to infect. It can move through a planting quickly.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Improve airflow, let foliage dry, remove badly affected leaves, and apply a labeled fungicide, covering leaf undersides, when conditions favor the disease. Avoid overhead irrigation, which keeps leaves wet and feeds the infection.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Open up the planting so leaves dry faster, remove the worst leaves, and use a labeled fungicide when wet weather sets in. Do not water over the leaves.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space for airflow, water at the soil line rather than overhead, choose resistant varieties where available, and avoid working among wet vines. Scout closely in humid weather, when the disease can appear and spread quickly.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Give plants room so air moves between them, water at the base, and watch closely in humid weather. Choose resistant varieties if downy mildew is common where you live.

diseases.name: Bacterial wilt
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Individual leaves, then whole vines, wilt and collapse even though the soil is moist, often spreading until the plant dies. A field test helps confirm it: cut a wilted stem and slowly draw the cut ends apart, and infected sap pulls into thin, sticky white strands.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Vines wilt and die even though the soil is wet. If you cut a wilted stem and pull the two ends apart slowly, infected sap stretches into sticky white strings.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A bacterium spread by striped and spotted cucumber beetles, which carry it in their gut and infect plants as they feed. It clogs the water-conducting tissue, so the plant wilts despite adequate water. Winter squash like spaghetti squash are generally less susceptible than cucumber and melon, but losses still occur.
diseases.cause_beginner: A germ spread by cucumber beetles as they feed. It blocks the plant's water pipes, so the vine wilts even when watered. Spaghetti squash is somewhat less prone than cucumbers or melons.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once a plant is infected; remove and destroy wilting plants to limit spread. Control is really beetle control, so management aims at keeping cucumber beetle numbers down, especially early in the season.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure once a plant has it, so pull and destroy infected plants. The real fix is keeping cucumber beetles down, since they spread it.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Manage cucumber beetles from seedling stage with row cover removed at flowering, keep young plants vigorous, and remove infected plants promptly. Controlling the beetle vector is the most effective control of the disease.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Keep cucumber beetles under control, since they spread the disease. Cover young plants until they flower, and pull any plant that wilts and tests positive.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Aim for at least 1 inch of water per week, leaning to 1.5 inches in heat or sandy soil, delivered deeply and less often rather than in light daily sprinkles. The long-season, big-leaved vine transpires heavily through summer.
watering.frequency_beginner: Give spaghetti squash about 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week, more when it is hot and dry. Water deeply rather than a little every day.
watering.amount_seasoned: Around 1 to 1.5 inches per week is the working range, leaning higher during flowering and fruit sizing and through hot, dry spells. Even, deep watering builds well-formed fruit; let it swing dry and you get poor set and small, uneven squash.
watering.amount_beginner: About 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week is a good target, more while the plant is flowering and the squash are growing.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base of the plant with drip or a soaker hose, keeping the foliage as dry as possible, since wet leaves invite powdery and downy mildew. Taper watering as the fruit nears maturity and the rind hardens, which helps the squash cure and store, and keep ripening fruit off saturated soil.
watering.method_beginner: Water the soil, not the leaves, using a soaker hose or watering wand at the base. Keeping the leaves dry helps prevent mildew. As the squash ripen and the skin hardens, ease off the water so they cure well.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting even when the soil is wet, and soft, rotting stems or fruit at the base point to overwatering or poor drainage. Saturated soil invites crown and fruit rot, especially on heavy ground.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If lower leaves yellow, the plant wilts even though the soil is wet, or fruit and stems go soft and rotten, it is getting too much water or the soil drains poorly.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Midday wilting that recovers overnight is normal in heat, but leaves that stay limp and dull signal real drought. Dry spells during fruit sizing show up as small, poorly filled squash and aborted young fruit.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Some midday wilting in hot weather is normal and passes by evening. Leaves that stay wilted mean the plant is too dry, and drought while fruit is forming gives small, poorly filled squash.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Base watering is the most useful habit for spaghetti squash, because the same plant that wants steady moisture is also mildew-prone. Keep water on the soil, air moving through the leaves, and the ripening fruit up off wet ground.
watering.method_note_beginner: Watering the soil instead of the leaves is the best thing you can do for spaghetti squash. It keeps the plant hydrated without encouraging leaf disease.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The water-critical stretch is flowering through fruit set and sizing. Steady moisture here drives well-formed, well-filled squash; uneven water gives poor set and small, misshapen fruit. Ease off near maturity to help the rind harden and the fruit cure.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The most important time to keep spaghetti squash watered is when it is flowering and the fruit is growing. Ease off near the end so the skin hardens for storage.

crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Harvest spaghetti squash once at full maturity, not young: wait for a deep, even golden-yellow rind with no green or cream tint, a hard rind a thumbnail cannot dent, and a dried, corky stem. The skin turns from glossy to dull at ripeness, and the ground spot where the fruit rests turns from white to a deep yellow. A mature spaghetti squash is what strands well when cooked; picked immature it stays pale and cooks up mushy rather than into distinct strands. Cut the fruit from the vine with shears or a knife, leaving a 1 to 2 inch handle of stem, and avoid carrying it by the stem. Get the crop in before a hard frost, which damages the rind and shortens storage. A short cure of about 10 days in a warm, dry spot hardens the skin, though as a Cucurbita pepo it is also fine to eat straight from the vine.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Unlike summer squash, you pick spaghetti squash once, when it is fully ripe. Look for a deep, even yellow color with no green, a hard rind you cannot dent with a thumbnail, and a dry, woody stem. The skin also goes from shiny to dull when ready, and the pale spot where it sits on the ground turns yellow. A ripe squash is what makes those nice spaghetti-like strands; picked too early it comes out mushy instead. Cut the squash off the vine with a knife, leaving a short piece of stem attached. Bring them in before a hard frost. You can eat it right away, or let it cure in a warm, dry place for about 10 days so the skin toughens for storage.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Harden off indoor-started spaghetti squash over 7 to 10 days, easing the plants into direct sun and wind before transplanting. Handle the rootball gently, because cucurbits resent root disturbance and a checked seedling sulks for weeks; use larger cells and set plants out young, before the roots circle the pot.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: If you started seedlings indoors, set them outside for a little longer each day over about a week so they get used to sun and wind. Be gentle with the roots when you plant, since squash do not like having their roots disturbed.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Because cucurbits resent root disturbance, direct sowing once the soil is reliably warm (at least 65°F, ideally 70°F, at 2 inches) is the simplest, most reliable method, and direct-sown plants quickly catch up. Sow several seeds about 1 inch deep per hill and thin to the strongest. Start seeds indoors only to gain two to three weeks in a short season, sowing in large cells and setting plants out before they outgrow the pot. In the coldest zones, transplants and an early-maturing variety such as Small Wonder are what make a fall crop possible.
start_method.notes_beginner: The easiest way to grow spaghetti squash is to sow seeds right where they will grow, once the soil is warm (about 70°F). Plant a few seeds 1 inch deep in each hill and keep the strongest. Start seeds indoors only if your season is short, about three weeks before planting out, and move them outside while they are still small. In cold areas, use transplants and a fast-maturing variety like Small Wonder so the fruit ripens before frost.

thinning.when: when seedlings have one or two true leaves
thinning.tip_seasoned: Sow three to four seeds per hill and thin to the one or two strongest once they have a true leaf or two. Snip the extras off at soil line rather than pulling, so you do not disturb the roots of the keepers. In rows, thin to one plant every 24 to 36 inches.
thinning.tip_beginner: Plant three or four seeds in each hill, then keep the one or two strongest seedlings once they grow their first real leaves. Cut the extra ones off at the ground instead of pulling them, so you do not hurt the roots of the ones you keep.

drainage.saucer_practice: If you use a saucer, empty it after watering. Spaghetti squash will not tolerate sitting in standing water, which invites crown and fruit rot.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Use a good bagged potting mix, not garden soil, which packs down too hard in a pot.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in compost and a slow-release fertilizer at planting. Pots need feeding more often than beds because watering washes nutrients out.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: Use a rich, free-draining peat- or coir-based potting mix, not garden soil, which compacts and drains poorly in a container.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend in about a third compost plus a slow-release balanced fertilizer at planting. Because frequent watering flushes nutrients, plan to feed a container spaghetti squash more regularly than one in the ground.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out much faster than garden beds. In summer a potted spaghetti squash may need water every day. Check daily and water until it drains from the bottom.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Feed a potted spaghetti squash more often than a garden plant, with a balanced liquid feed every couple of weeks once it is growing strongly.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Not applicable. Spaghetti squash lives for one season and dies with the first frost, so there is nothing to overwinter. Plant new seeds next year.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Not applicable. Spaghetti squash is a frost-tender annual that completes its life in a single season and is killed by the first hard frost, so there is nothing to overwinter. Pull spent vines at season's end and start fresh from seed the following year.

container_notes.notes_beginner: You can grow spaghetti squash in a container, but choose a compact or bush type like Tivoli or Small Wonder, since full-size vining spaghetti squash is too big for a pot. Use a large container, at least 10 gallons and 12 inches deep, put it in full sun, keep it well watered (pots dry out fast), and feed it regularly. Give the vines room to trail out of the pot, and water the soil, not the leaves, to help avoid mildew.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Spaghetti squash is a marginal container crop because it is a long-season vine, but the bush and semi-bush varieties make it workable. Choose a compact type (Tivoli, Small Wonder, or Orangetti) and give it a big pot: at least 10 gallons and 12 inches deep, larger is better. Give it full sun, let the vines trail out over the rim or up a sturdy support, water at the base daily in heat, and feed regularly, since a small soil volume dries and depletes fast over a long season. The container figures here follow general container-vegetable guidance; spaghetti-squash-specific container numbers are modeled.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry far faster than beds, and a spaghetti squash in a pot can need water once or even twice a day in summer heat. Check daily by feeling the top inch of mix, and water until it runs from the drainage holes; even moisture prevents the small, poorly filled fruit that water swings cause.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Feed container spaghetti squash more often than in-ground ones, since steady watering leaches nutrients. After the slow-release charge at planting, add a balanced liquid feed every 2 to 3 weeks, easing off nitrogen once fruit sets.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering container suits a potted spaghetti squash well, smoothing the moisture swings this thirsty, mildew-prone plant dislikes. Keep the reservoir topped up in heat, still water from below to keep foliage dry, and use a large enough planter that the roots are not constantly waterlogged.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match because it keeps the water steady, which spaghetti squash likes. Keep the reservoir filled, especially in hot weather, and use a big pot.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: A container spaghetti squash needs a wide, deep, heavy pot, at least 12 inches deep and 10 gallons or more, even for a compact variety, with room for the vines to trail out over the edge or up a trellis. Wide and sturdy beats tall and narrow, since a vining plant in a small pot dries out and tips. Choose bush or semi-bush types such as Tivoli or Small Wonder for containers, never full-size vining spaghetti squash.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Give a container spaghetti squash a large, deep, heavy pot, at least 12 inches deep and 10 gallons or more, and let the vines trail out of it or climb a small trellis. A wide, sturdy pot is better than a tall, narrow one. Only grow small or bush varieties in pots, such as Tivoli or Small Wonder, not the big vining kinds.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Avoid planting spaghetti squash where another cucurbit grew in the last few years, including cucumber, melon, summer squash, and other winter squash. They share squash bug, cucumber beetle, bacterial wilt, the mildews, and soilborne rots, all of which build up in the soil and on debris.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Do not plant spaghetti squash where you grew cucumbers, melons, or other squash in the last few years. They get the same pests and diseases, which build up in the soil.
rotation.good_after: Legumes such as beans and peas, sweet corn, leafy greens, or alliums like onions and garlic make good preceding crops, since they do not share the cucurbit pest and disease complex, and a legume leaves nitrogen behind for the long-feeding spaghetti squash.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate cucurbits on a 3 year cycle, returning spaghetti squash to a given bed no sooner than the third or fourth year, to break the buildup of squash bug, beetle-vectored wilt, and soilborne disease. Clear and remove spent vines at season's end rather than tilling them in, which removes overwintering pest and disease sites and makes rotation more effective.
rotation.note_beginner: Try not to grow spaghetti squash or its relatives in the same spot more than once every 3 years or so. Moving them around the garden each year helps avoid a buildup of pests and disease. Clean up old vines at the end of the season too.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: A sound spaghetti squash is a good keeper at room temperature, the opposite of tender summer squash, though a moderate one: figure a couple of months in a cool room out of direct sun, not the half-year a butternut manages. Warm indoor heat shortens that. It keeps best sitting on a shelf with airflow rather than on a cold or damp floor.
storage.room_temp_beginner: A spaghetti squash keeps well at room temperature, often for a couple of months in a cool spot out of the sun, much longer than summer squash but not as long as a butternut. Keep it off cold, damp floors so the bottom does not rot.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Whole spaghetti squash is not refrigerated; cold storage below about 50°F causes chilling injury and faster breakdown. Cut squash and cooked or pureed flesh, however, should be refrigerated and used within a few days, or frozen.
storage.fridge_beginner: Do not put a whole spaghetti squash in the fridge, it is too cold and makes it break down faster. Once it is cut, wrap the pieces and keep them in the fridge for a few days, or freeze them.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Spaghetti squash freezes well as cooked strands: roast or steam the halves, fork the flesh into strands, cool, and freeze in measured portions, draining off excess water when you reheat. Frozen cooked spaghetti squash keeps about a year.
storage.freezer_beginner: Spaghetti squash freezes well once cooked. Roast or steam it, scrape the flesh into strands with a fork, cool it, and freeze it in portions. It keeps about a year; drain off any extra water when you reheat it.
storage.notes_seasoned: Spaghetti squash is a moderate keeper, which is why it is harvested once at full maturity: as a Cucurbita pepo it stores about 1 to 3 months, longer than acorn but well short of a butternut's 4 to 6. Being a pepo, it is edible right off the vine and does not strictly need curing; a short cure of about 10 days at 80 to 85°F with good airflow hardens the rind and heals small wounds for longer storage, though holding it too warm too long can shorten its keeping. Then store cool but not cold, ideally 50 to 60°F with 50 to 70 percent humidity and good airflow. Store only blemish-free fruit with the stem intact, and check periodically, removing any that begin to soften.
storage.notes_beginner: Spaghetti squash keeps for a couple of months, which is why you pick it once when fully ripe. You can eat it straight from the vine, or toughen the skin for storage with a short cure of about 10 days in a warm spot (around 80 to 85°F). Then keep it somewhere cool but not cold, about 50 to 60°F, with some air movement, where good squash last about 1 to 3 months. Store only perfect squash with the stem still on, and check now and then for any starting to go soft.

recommended.name: Vegetable Spaghetti
recommended.recommended_note: The classic open-pollinated spaghetti squash and the standard by which the rest are judged. Oblong, creamy-to-golden-yellow fruit about 8 to 9 inches long and 3 to 5 pounds, with pale flesh that strands cleanly when cooked. The dependable, seed-saveable choice.

recommended.name: Tivoli
recommended.recommended_note: An All-America Selections winner with a compact bush habit rather than long vines, making it the pick for small beds and large containers. Uniform yellow fruit about 3 to 4 pounds with good strand quality on a space-saving plant.

recommended.name: Small Wonder
recommended.recommended_note: A compact semi-bush type bred for single-serving fruit, about 1 to 2 pounds, that ripen earlier than full-size spaghetti squash. The go-to for short seasons, small gardens, and pots, and productive for its size.

recommended.name: Orangetti
recommended.recommended_note: A semi-bush hybrid with orange, higher-beta-carotene flesh that is a bit sweeter and denser than standard spaghetti squash while still stranding. A compact, productive choice for smaller gardens.

recommended.name: Stripetti
recommended.recommended_note: A striped hybrid (a spaghetti-and-delicata cross) prized among the spaghetti types as a good keeper and for holding up better against powdery mildew. Sweeter flesh and a longer storage life where mildew or storage is a concern.

varieties.note_seasoned: Choose by season length and space. Where there is room, the open-pollinated Vegetable Spaghetti is the dependable full-size standard. For small beds or containers, the bush Tivoli and the compact semi-bush Small Wonder stay tidy, and Small Wonder ripens earliest for short seasons. Orangetti offers sweeter, orange flesh on a semi-bush plant, and where powdery mildew or a long storage life matters, the striped Stripetti keeps best and holds up better to mildew.
varieties.note_beginner: Pick a spaghetti squash variety by your season and space. For a full-size, reliable squash, grow Vegetable Spaghetti. If your garden or season is small or short, grow the compact Tivoli or Small Wonder. Orangetti has sweeter, orange flesh on a smaller plant, and Stripetti stores the longest and stands up to mildew better if those are problems where you live.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A healthy spaghetti squash vine typically yields 4 to 5 oblong fruit of 2 to 4 pounds each; compact and bush types set fewer, smaller fruit on far less space. Vining types need plenty of room per plant, and even moisture and feeding through sizing build full, well-formed squash that strand cleanly.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: A spaghetti squash plant usually gives you several squash, often 4 to 5, each 2 to 4 pounds. Bush types like Tivoli make fewer but take much less room. Plan on one or two plants going a long way, since each one spreads widely.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Spaghetti squash does not produce continuously; the plant sets fruit through summer and then the crop matures together in fall for a single harvest. Once several fruit have set, removing the latest small fruit and pinching vine tips channels energy into sizing and ripening the keepers before frost.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Unlike summer squash, spaghetti squash does not keep producing all season. The plant sets its fruit over the summer and they all ripen together in fall, when you harvest once. Removing the latest tiny fruit helps the rest grow bigger before frost.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: The usual first-year surprises are how much room the vines take (6 to 8 feet) and how pollinator-dependent fruit set is. Give plants more space than seems necessary, and grow some flowers nearby to draw bees.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: The big first-year surprise is how far spaghetti squash vines spread, often 6 to 8 feet. Give them more room than you think, and grow flowers nearby to bring in bees, since the plant needs lots of bee visits to set fruit.
factors_seasoned: Pollination: fruit set is pollinator-limited, with each female flower needing many bee visits; poor pollination in cool or pollinator-scarce conditions drops young fruit.
Season length: spaghetti squash needs a warm season of 90 to 100 days to mature before frost; a short season limits variety choice and yield.
Space and vine vigor: vines sprawl 6 to 8 feet and need room; crowding cuts yield and worsens disease.
Pest and disease pressure: squash bug, the squash vine borer that readily attacks this pepo squash, beetle-vectored bacterial wilt, and powdery and downy mildew can all end a planting early.
Even moisture and feeding: steady water and moderate feeding through fruit sizing build full, well-formed squash.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No T1 source supports timing spaghetti squash planting by moon phase. We do not make a recommendation here; sow by soil temperature and frost dates instead.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seeds sprout in about 5 to 10 days in warm soil (70 to 95°F is ideal); soil below about 65°F rots seed rather than germinating it. Two seed leaves push up first.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: In warm soil, seeds sprout in about a week to ten days, sending up two seed leaves first. In cold soil, seeds rot instead of sprouting.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Sow about 1 inch deep in warm soil, three to four seeds per hill. Keep evenly moist, not soggy. Thin to the one or two strongest seedlings once true leaves appear.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Plant seeds 1 inch deep once the soil is warm, a few per hill. Keep the soil damp until they sprout, then keep the strongest one or two.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Did your spaghetti squash seeds germinate, and how many days did it take?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your seeds sprouted yet?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Cotyledons followed by the first true leaves; growth is fast once warm. Watch for cucumber beetles, which target young plants and transmit bacterial wilt, and for squash bug eggs on leaf undersides.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: After the first two rounded leaves, true leaves appear and the plant grows quickly. Watch for beetles chewing the young leaves.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Protect from cucumber beetles and squash bugs with row cover if needed, removing it at flowering for pollination. Keep evenly watered and free of weeds.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep an eye out for beetles on young plants and use a light row cover if needed, but remove it once flowers form. Water regularly and keep weeds down.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How are your seedlings developing? Any sign of beetle or squash bug damage?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How do your young plants look?

growth_stages.name: Vining
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The plant sends out long runners and bulks up its leaves, often growing a foot or more of vine per day in warm weather. This is the window to side-dress. It is also when squash vine borer moths are laying at the stem base, so this pepo squash needs its lower stems scouted for frass now.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant sends out long vines that spread fast across the ground, with big leaves. This is when you feed it, give it room to run, and start checking the base of the stems for signs of squash vine borer.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Side-dress with nitrogen as the vines run, mulch to hold moisture, and give the runners room to spread, 6 to 8 feet. Bury vine joints to encourage secondary rooting, which helps a plant survive a squash vine borer hit, and keep scouting the stem base for frass.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Feed the vines as they start to run and give them room to spread. Add mulch to keep the soil moist, and check the base of the stems for the sawdust-like frass that means squash vine borer.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are the vines running well? Have you side-dressed?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are your spaghetti squash vines spreading out?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Large yellow-orange flowers. Male flowers on thin stalks usually open first, often for a week or more before females appear, which is normal; female flowers carry a tiny squash behind the bloom. Each female needs many bee visits to set a full fruit.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Big yellow-orange flowers open. The first ones are usually male and fall off, which is normal. Female flowers have a tiny squash at their base, and bees need to visit them many times to set fruit.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Encourage pollinators and avoid spraying open blooms. If small fruit yellow and rot at the tip, pollination is poor, so hand-pollinate in the morning with a male flower or small brush. Keep moisture steady now.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Let the bees do their work and do not spray the flowers. If tiny squash turn yellow and rot, the flowers were not pollinated, so you can hand-pollinate in the morning. Keep watering steadily.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are you seeing female flowers and fruit set? Any young fruit yellowing and dropping?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Is your plant flowering? Are any little squash forming?

growth_stages.name: Fruit development
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Set fruit swell and gradually turn from pale green or cream to the mature deep yellow over several weeks, while the rind hardens. The plant is sizing and ripening its crop for a single fall harvest rather than setting new fruit continuously.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The little squash grow bigger and slowly change color, going from pale green or cream to deep yellow as they ripen over several weeks.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture even through sizing, then taper as fruit nears maturity. Remove the latest small fruit and pinch vine tips to channel energy into the keepers, set ripening fruit on a board or mulch to keep it off wet soil, and keep scouting for mildew.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep watering steadily while the squash grow, then ease off as they ripen. Slip a board or some straw under each fruit so it is not sitting on damp ground, and watch the leaves for powdery mildew.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How are the fruit sizing and coloring up? Any rot where fruit meets the soil?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are your squash growing and changing color?

growth_stages.name: Harvest and cure
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Full, deep yellow color with no green, a hard rind a thumbnail cannot dent, a dried corky stem, and dull rather than glossy skin. Harvest the whole crop at maturity before a hard frost.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The squash are fully yellow, the skin is hard and dull, and the stem has dried and gone woody. They are ready to pick, all around the same time in fall.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut each squash with shears leaving a 1 to 2 inch handle, and get the crop in before a hard frost. It is fine to eat right away, or cure about 10 days in a warm, dry, airy spot (80 to 85°F) and then store cool (50 to 60°F) for a couple of months.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Cut the squash off the vine with a knife, leaving a short piece of stem, and bring them in before a hard frost. Eat them fresh, or cure them in a warm, dry place for about 10 days, then store somewhere cool.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have you harvested? How is the cure and storage going?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you picked your spaghetti squash yet?

notifications.title_seasoned: Side-dress your spaghetti squash as the vines run
notifications.title_beginner: Time to feed your spaghetti squash
notifications.body_seasoned: Your spaghetti squash vines are running, the window to side-dress with nitrogen. Place it a few inches out from the plants and water it in, then ease off nitrogen once fruit sets so the plant builds squash, not just leaves.
notifications.body_beginner: Your spaghetti squash vines are spreading fast now. Give them a feeding of nitrogen a few inches away from the stems, and water it in.

notifications.body_seasoned: Your spaghetti squash is flowering. Fruit set depends on many bee visits per female flower, so if small fruit yellow and drop, hand-pollinate in the morning and keep blooms unsprayed.
notifications.body_beginner: Your spaghetti squash is flowering. If the tiny squash turn yellow and fall off, the flowers were not pollinated, so try hand-pollinating in the morning.

notifications.title_seasoned: Harvest at full maturity, then store or cure
notifications.title_beginner: Time to harvest your spaghetti squash
notifications.body_seasoned: Your spaghetti squash should be reaching full, deep yellow color with a hard, dull rind and dry stem. Harvest the crop before a hard frost, leaving a short handle. Eat it fresh, or cure it about 10 days in a warm, dry spot before storing cool for a couple of months.
notifications.body_beginner: Your spaghetti squash should be fully yellow with hard skin. Pick them before a hard frost, leaving some stem on. You can eat them right away, or let them cure in a warm, dry place for about 10 days and then store them somewhere cool.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost is coming, harvest your spaghetti squash
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost warning for your spaghetti squash
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A frost is forecast. Spaghetti squash is frost-tender, and a hard frost damages the rind and ends the vines, so harvest any mature or near-mature fruit now, leaving a short handle, and bring them in to cure.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Frost is coming, and it will damage your spaghetti squash and kill the vines. Pick any ripe or nearly ripe squash now and bring them inside.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Extreme heat may stall fruit set
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot spell may slow fruit set
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A stretch of extreme heat is forecast. Very hot days can reduce pollination and drop young fruit on cucurbits like spaghetti squash. Keep moisture steady; set usually resumes when the heat eases.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Very hot weather is coming. Your spaghetti squash may drop small fruit or slow down for a while. Keep it well watered, it usually picks back up when it cools.

germination.text_seasoned: Soil temperature, not the calendar, governs spaghetti squash germination. Wait until soil is at least 65°F, ideally 70°F, at 2 inches; seed sown in cold ground rots before it sprouts.
germination.text_beginner: Wait for warm soil before sowing. Spaghetti squash seeds rot in cold ground but sprout fast once it warms up.

seedling.text_seasoned: Cucumber beetles swarm young cucurbits and can spread bacterial wilt. A floating row cover protects seedlings, but pull it off at flowering so bees can pollinate.
seedling.text_beginner: Protect young plants from beetles. A light cover helps, but take it off once flowers appear so bees can reach them.

vining.text_seasoned: Feed the vines as they run, then ease off nitrogen once fruit sets, or you get vine at the expense of squash. Give vining types 6 to 8 feet to sprawl.
vining.text_beginner: Feed the vines as they spread, but do not overdo the nitrogen once fruit forms, or you get lots of leaves and few squash. Give them plenty of room.

vining.text_seasoned: As a Cucurbita pepo, spaghetti squash is a favorite of the squash vine borer. Scout the stem base for sawdust-like frass from early summer, keep row cover on until flowering where pressure is high, and bury vine joints so a hit plant can survive on secondary roots.
vining.text_beginner: Spaghetti squash is one of the squashes the squash vine borer attacks, so check the base of the stems for what looks like wet sawdust starting in early summer, and cover young plants until they flower if borers are bad where you live.

flowering.text_seasoned: Early male flowers opening and dropping with no fruit is normal; females come later. Judge pollination by whether small fruit size up or yellow and rot at the blossom end.
flowering.text_beginner: The first flowers often fall off without making squash, that is normal. Trouble is when tiny squash turn yellow and rot, which means poor pollination.

flowering.text_seasoned: Spaghetti squash fruit set is pollinator-limited, each female needing many bee visits. If set is poor, hand-pollinate in the morning: pick a male flower, strip the petals, and dab pollen onto the center of each open female.
flowering.text_beginner: Spaghetti squash needs lots of bee visits to set fruit. If fruit is not forming, hand-pollinate in the morning by touching a male flower to the center of a female flower.

fruit_development.text_seasoned: Slip a board or straw under sizing fruit to keep it off wet soil and prevent rot. To push size, remove the latest small fruit and pinch vine tips so energy goes to the keepers before frost.
fruit_development.text_beginner: Put a board or some straw under each squash so it is not on damp ground. To get bigger squash, remove the latest tiny fruit so the plant feeds the rest.

fruit_development.text_seasoned: Ripeness is full, deep yellow color with no green, a hard rind a thumbnail cannot dent, and a dry, corky stem. A fully mature squash is what strands well; taper watering near maturity to harden the rind for storage.
fruit_development.text_beginner: A spaghetti squash is ripe when it is fully yellow, the skin is hard and dull, and the stem has dried out. Ripe squash makes the best strands, so do not rush it, and ease off watering near the end.

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest the whole crop at maturity before a hard frost, cutting with shears and leaving a 1 to 2 inch handle. As a pepo it is good to eat right away; to store, cure about 10 days in a warm, dry, airy spot (80 to 85°F), then store cool near 50 to 60°F, where spaghetti squash keeps about 1 to 3 months.
harvest.text_beginner: Pick all your spaghetti squash when ripe, before a hard frost, leaving a short stem on. Eat them fresh, or cure them in a warm, dry place for about 10 days and then store somewhere cool, where they keep for a couple of months.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Small fruit yellowed and rotted at the blossom end
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Tiny squash turned yellow and rotted
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Poor pollination. The female flower was not adequately pollinated, so the young fruit aborts, yellowing and rotting at the blossom end instead of sizing up. Common in cool, wet, or pollinator-scarce conditions, and spaghetti squash is strongly pollinator-dependent.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The flower was not pollinated well, so the little squash died instead of growing. This often happens in cool or rainy weather, or when there are few bees.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Inadequate transfer of pollen to the female flower; each fruit needs many bee visits, so set fails when pollinators are scarce.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Not enough pollination of the flower, since spaghetti squash needs lots of bee visits.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant flowers to draw bees, avoid spraying open blooms, and hand-pollinate in the morning if set is poor. It usually improves as more flowers open and bees get active.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Grow some flowers nearby for the bees, and hand-pollinate early flowers if needed. It usually gets better as more flowers open.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Squash sat on wet soil and rotted on the bottom
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Squash rotted on its underside
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Fruit rot, typically from a wet underside in contact with damp soil, often a soilborne rot in poorly drained, rainy conditions. A soft, sometimes molded patch develops where the fruit sits, and can spread in storage.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The squash sat on wet ground and rotted on the bottom. Damp soil and poor drainage let a soil disease soften the fruit where it touched the ground.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Prolonged contact between fruit and saturated soil, favoring soilborne fruit rots in wet, poorly drained beds.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: The squash sitting on wet soil, which lets rot set in on the underside.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant on raised hills for drainage, avoid low wet spots, and set each sizing fruit on a board or thick mulch to lift it off the soil. Harvest promptly and cure before storing.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant on raised hills so water drains away, and slip a board or straw under each squash so it is not on wet ground. Pick and cure them before storing.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Leaves turned white and powdery, then the plant faded early
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Leaves got white and powdery and the plant died back
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Powdery mildew defoliated the plant ahead of schedule. The white fungal coating spread across the leaves until they browned and died, cutting the season short and reducing fruit size, fill, and sweetness.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Powdery mildew, a white coating on the leaves, spread until the leaves died and the plant stopped early, so the squash did not finish well.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Powdery mildew fungus, worsened by crowding, poor airflow, shade, and high humidity around the foliage.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: A fungus that spreads on crowded plants with poor air flow.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Choose mildew-tolerant varieties such as Stripetti, space plants generously, plant in full sun, water at the base, and treat at the first spots from midsummer rather than waiting.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Pick mildew-tolerant varieties, give plants more room and full sun, water the soil not the leaves, and treat the first white spots early.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Cut a pale spaghetti squash that cooked up mushy instead of stranding
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Spaghetti squash was mushy and would not strand
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Harvested before full maturity. Spaghetti squash needs to ripen fully on the vine to a deep, even yellow with a hard rind; a fruit picked while still pale, cream, or green-tinged has flesh that cooks down soft and watery instead of separating into distinct strands. Pale color or a still-white ground spot is the tell.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The squash was picked too early. Spaghetti squash has to ripen all the way to deep yellow with a hard skin, or the flesh cooks up mushy instead of pulling apart into strands.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Immaturity at harvest; the rind and flesh finish developing on the vine, and only a fully mature, hard-rinded, deep-yellow fruit strands the way spaghetti squash is grown for.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Picking before the squash was fully ripe, while it was still pale and soft-skinned.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait for a hard, dull, fully deep-yellow rind with no green and a dry stem, and a ground spot that has turned from white to yellow, before cutting. Roast the halves cut-side down and fork the flesh into strands while hot.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Wait until the squash is fully yellow with no green, the skin is hard, and the stem is dry. Then roast it and scrape the flesh with a fork to get the strands.
