succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Spaghetti squash is not a succession crop. It is a single, long-season planting that sets fruit through summer and matures together for one fall harvest, so you sow once per season rather than at intervals. In most zones a second sowing would be killed by frost before its 90 to 100 day crop could ripen. Only in the warmest, frost-free or near-frost-free zones, or the low desert where a summer sowing is the fall crop, is a second seasonal window viable, and that is a separate season, not a succession.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: You plant spaghetti squash once for the season. It grows all summer and ripens together in the fall for a single harvest, so there is no need to replant every few weeks. In most places a later planting would be caught by frost before the squash could ripen. Only in very warm, nearly frost-free areas can you fit a second planting, and that is really a separate season.
succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Spaghetti squash is a single long-season crop (90 to 100 days) harvested once at full maturity, so succession sowing does not apply; a second sowing in most zones would not mature before frost. Warm frost-free zones and the low desert support a separate seasonal planting window, which is a distinct season rather than a succession.

crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Spaghetti squash is monoecious: each plant carries separate male and female flowers, so a single plant sets fruit with no second variety needed. The flowers are insect-pollinated, mostly by bees, and pollen must move from the male to the female blooms. Spaghetti squash is strongly pollinator-dependent: each female flower needs several bee visits to set a full fruit, and poor pollination shows up as young fruit that yellow and rot at the blossom end, or as small, misshapen squash. Early-season male flowers often open and drop for a week or more before the first females appear, which is normal. Plant flowers nearby, avoid spraying open blooms, and hand-pollinate with a male flower or small brush in the morning if set stalls.
crops.pollinator_notes_beginner: Each spaghetti squash plant has both male and female flowers, so you only need one plant to get fruit. Bees move the pollen between the flowers, and the plant needs a lot of bee visits to set each fruit, so anything that brings bees to your garden helps. The first flowers are usually male and fall off, which is normal. If your little squash stay small and rot at the tip, the flowers were not pollinated well, so hand-pollinate in the morning and grow some flowers nearby for the bees.
crops.description_seasoned: Spaghetti squash is a warm-season winter squash (Cucurbita pepo, the same species as zucchini and acorn) grown for its mature, hard-rind fruit, whose cooked flesh separates into long, pale strands like spaghetti, which is the whole point of growing it. Unlike its summer-squash cousin zucchini, it is harvested once, at full maturity in fall, when the oblong rind turns a deep, even yellow and a thumbnail cannot dent it. It is a moderate keeper: after an optional short cure it stores about 1 to 3 months, not as long as a butternut but far longer than any summer squash. Plants are moderately vigorous vines that run roughly 6 to 8 feet, so they need real room, though compact bush and semi-bush types like Tivoli and Small Wonder suit small gardens and containers. Spaghetti squash is monoecious, carrying separate male and female flowers on one plant, and fruit set is strongly pollinator-dependent. As a pepo, it is susceptible to the squash vine borer, so managing that pest is part of growing it. The season's shape is set by three things: a warm runway of 90 to 100 frost-free days to mature the crop, moderate pest and disease pressure (squash bug, squash vine borer, cucumber beetle and the bacterial wilt it spreads, plus powdery and downy mildew), and the single fall harvest, timed at a hard, fully yellow rind, before frost.
crops.description_beginner: Spaghetti squash is a warm-season squash grown for its unusual flesh: once cooked, it pulls apart into long strands like spaghetti. You harvest it once in the fall, when the oblong fruit turns a deep, even yellow and the skin is too hard to dent with a thumbnail, unlike summer squash that you pick young all season. It grows on vines that spread about 6 to 8 feet, so it needs a good amount of room, though compact bush types like Tivoli and Small Wonder fit smaller gardens and pots. Each plant has both male and female flowers and needs plenty of bee visits to set fruit. The main things to know: give it a warm season of about 90 to 100 days and space to run, water steadily while the fruit grows, watch for squash bugs, squash vine borers, beetles, and mildew, and harvest when the squash are fully yellow with hard, dull skin and a dry stem, before frost. Stored in a cool, dry spot it keeps for a couple of months, much longer than summer squash.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Prepare a fertile, well-drained bed in full sun, working several inches of compost or rotted manure into the soil before planting, since spaghetti squash is a hungry, long-season plant. Many growers set plants in low hills or mounds about a foot across, which warm faster in spring, drain better, and give the vines a clear starting point. Space generously: roughly 24 to 36 inches between plants in the row with 3 to 5 feet between rows for vining types (closer for bush types like Tivoli), because the vines can run 6 to 8 feet. On heavy or wet ground, build the mounds up for drainage to head off crown and fruit rot.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Pick a sunny spot with rich, well-drained soil and mix in plenty of compost before planting, since spaghetti squash is a large, hungry plant. Plant it on low hills or mounds, which warm up and drain better. Give it room: space plants about 2 to 3 feet apart in rows 3 to 5 feet apart, since the vines can spread 6 to 8 feet (bush types like Tivoli need less). If your soil is heavy or wet, build the mounds up higher so water drains away from the roots and fruit.

northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In cold zones the spaghetti squash season is a single tight summer window: plant after the last frost once soil is warm, and harvest the mature crop in early fall before the first frost. Short-season zones (3 to 4) need transplants started about three weeks early and a fast-maturing variety such as Small Wonder to ripen a crop in time; warmer zones (6 to 7) have room for full-size Vegetable Spaghetti.
northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In cold areas you get one spaghetti squash crop a summer: plant after the last frost and harvest in early fall before frost returns. In the coldest zones, start transplants indoors and grow a fast variety like Small Wonder so the squash ripen in time.

se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: Across the Gulf and coastal plain, spaghetti squash is a late-spring-into-fall crop, planted as the soil warms and timed so the fruit matures in fall ahead of the first frost. Summer heat and humidity drive mildew and pest pressure, and the squash vine borer is active, so give plants room, use row cover on young plants, choose tougher varieties, and scout closely.
se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast, plant spaghetti squash in late spring to early summer so it ripens in fall before frost. The hot, humid summers bring mildew, squash vine borers, and other pests, so give plants room and watch them closely.

ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: In California's hot interior valleys, spaghetti squash is a long, warm summer crop: plant from spring into early summer and harvest in fall. The dry heat suits it well as long as irrigation is steady; time the planting so fruit matures in the warm, dry fall, and scout for squash vine borer through midsummer.
ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In California's hot inland valleys, plant spaghetti squash from spring into early summer and harvest in fall. It handles the dry heat well as long as you water steadily.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: Along California's cooler north coast, plant spaghetti squash after the spring chill passes and the soil warms, and harvest in fall. Cool, foggy summers can slow ripening and favor mildew, so choose a sunny site, give airflow, and lean toward earlier-maturing varieties like Small Wonder.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: On California's cool north coast, plant spaghetti squash in late spring once it warms up and harvest in fall. Foggy, cool summers can slow it down, so pick a sunny spot and an earlier variety.

ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: On California's mild south coast, spaghetti squash grows through a long, gentle warm season: plant from spring into early summer and harvest in fall. The mild climate is forgiving, though coastal humidity favors mildew, so prioritize airflow and full sun.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: On California's mild south coast, plant spaghetti squash from spring into early summer and harvest in fall. The mild weather is easy on it, but watch for mildew in the coastal damp.

ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: In the California desert valleys, spaghetti squash grows as two plantings: a late-winter to spring sowing that matures before peak heat, and a midsummer (around July) sowing that grows into a fall harvest. Steady irrigation is essential, and the fall timing is the reliable one.
ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: In the California desert, plant spaghetti squash in late winter to spring for an early crop, and again around July for a fall crop. Water steadily.

warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: In the warm arid zones of southern New Mexico and West Texas, plant spaghetti squash after frost once the soil warms and harvest in fall. The dry heat is manageable with steady irrigation; intense early-summer heat can briefly stall fruit set, which usually resumes as conditions ease.
warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: In the dry, warm zones of southern New Mexico and West Texas, plant spaghetti squash after the last frost and harvest in fall. Water steadily through the heat, and do not worry if fruit set pauses briefly during the hottest spells.

low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: In Arizona's low desert, spaghetti squash is planted in late winter for an early-summer crop before peak heat, and again in midsummer (around July) for a fall harvest that uses the long, hot autumn. Either way, steady irrigation matters, and the fall timing is the reliable one.
low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: In Arizona's low desert, plant spaghetti squash in late winter for an early-summer crop, and again in July for a fall harvest. Water steadily through the heat.

fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: In peninsular Florida, spaghetti squash is grown in the cooler halves of the year, planted in late winter to spring and again in late summer for a fall crop, avoiding the wettest, most disease-prone midsummer. Expect mildew, squash vine borer, and other pest pressure, so use row cover on young plants and scout closely.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: In Florida, plant spaghetti squash in late winter to spring and again in late summer, avoiding the wet, buggy middle of summer. Watch closely for mildew and pests.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: In Hawaii and tropical zones there is no frost, so spaghetti squash can be planted across much of the year, with timing driven by rainfall and pest pressure rather than cold. Choose the drier, sunnier windows to limit mildew and fruit rot. Specific local timing is modeled pending a parseable CTAHR source.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In Hawaii and the tropics there is no frost, so you can plant spaghetti squash through much of the year. Aim for the drier, sunnier stretches to avoid mildew and rot.

Spaghetti squash is spaced 24-36 in in the row with 3-5 ft (36-60 in) between rows, and vines run 6-8 ft; the structured field spans in-row plant spacing (24 in) to about a 4 ft row (48 in), and the full row/sprawl figures are carried in prose (soil_prep, description, yield).
