crops.name: Pole Beans

soil.preferred_texture_seasoned: Fertile, well-drained loam. Pole beans set the heaviest pods in soil that holds moisture through their long pod-fill season yet never stays waterlogged, since soggy ground invites the root rots beans are prone to. Work in compost before planting and set the trellis or poles in place at the same time so you do not disturb the roots later.
soil.preferred_texture_beginner: Pole beans grow best in rich, loose soil that drains well. Loam, a balanced soil that holds some moisture but never stays soggy, is ideal. Because these vines bear for a long time, they want steady moisture through the season, but wet, waterlogged ground rots the roots. Put your trellis or poles in when you plant so you do not disturb the roots later.
soil.tolerated_texture_seasoned: Sandy and clay loams both work if drainage is good. Sandy beds dry faster and may need a touch more frequent sidedressing; heavier soils benefit from worked-in organic matter to keep them from crusting over the emerging seedlings.
soil.tolerated_texture_beginner: Both sandy and clay-based soils work fine as long as they drain well. Sandy soil dries out faster, so you may need to feed a little more often. Heavier soil does better if you mix in compost, which keeps it from crusting over the seedlings as they push up.
soil.problematic_texture_seasoned: Avoid heavy, poorly drained ground and soils that crust hard after rain. A crust can trap the seedling below the surface, and standing water around the roots brings on the root-rot diseases beans are prone to.
soil.problematic_texture_beginner: Stay away from heavy soil that drains poorly, and soil that forms a hard crust after it rains. A crust can trap young seedlings before they reach the surface, and water sitting around the roots can bring on the root rot that beans catch easily.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Pole beans like loose, fertile soil that drains well. If water sits on top of your bed for a long time after rain, work in some compost first to help it drain.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Fertile, well-drained loam, ideally with compost worked in before planting. The critical trait is steady moisture without waterlogging through the long pod-set and pod-fill season.

ph.note_beginner: Pole beans do well in slightly acidic to neutral soil. If you have not tested your soil, a pH near 6.5 is a safe target and most garden beds are already close.
ph.note_seasoned: A soil pH of 5.8 to 6.5 suits snap beans; they tolerate up to about neutral. A soil test is the reliable way to confirm both pH and fertility before the season starts.

fertilizer.timing: pre-plant at sowing; one light sidedress before first bloom
fertilizer.example_product: 5-10-10 pre-plant
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Pole beans are light feeders. As legumes they fix much of their own nitrogen through root nodules, and excess nitrogen delays flowering and pushes leafy vine growth up the trellis at the expense of pods. Without a soil test, work a balanced starter into the bed before planting, then sidedress lightly just before the first bloom. Sandy beds or leaching rains can call for a second light feeding across the long bearing season.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Pole beans make a lot of their own food from the air, so they need little fertilizer. Mix a little balanced fertilizer into the bed before you plant, and feed once more lightly right before the plants flower. Too much fertilizer gives you big leafy vines climbing the trellis but fewer beans, and it delays flowering.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: Pre-plant 5-10-10 if no soil test is available; sidedress a nitrogen source lightly before bloom.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: A balanced vegetable fertilizer like 5-10-10 works well.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: 5-10-10 at 3 pounds per 100 square feet before planting, per Clemson HGIC.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: About 3 pounds of 5-10-10 per 100 square feet of bed before planting.

companions.note_seasoned: As a nitrogen-fixing legume, pole beans leave the soil better for what follows and are the classic climbing partner in the Three Sisters planting, where the beans scramble up the corn while squash covers the ground. The long-standing caution is to keep beans away from the alliums (onion, garlic), which are widely held to suppress them.
companions.note_beginner: Pole beans get along with most vegetables. The classic combination is beans, corn, and squash grown together, with the beans climbing the corn. The one pairing to avoid is planting beans right next to onions or garlic.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Corn
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: The traditional Three Sisters partner; with pole beans the corn works as a living pole for the vines to climb.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Three Sisters is the best-documented historical polyculture, and for POLE beans specifically the corn-as-living-trellis role is the authentic mechanism (unlike bush beans, where corn offers no support). Still structural/traditional rather than a crop-specific measured pest benefit; give sturdy corn a head start so the vines do not pull it down. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Corn is the classic pole bean partner in Three Sisters planting, where the corn stalk serves as a living trellis for the climbing vines. Let the corn get a good head start and use sturdy, well-rooted stalks, since vigorous pole beans can overload thin sweet corn. The beans' nitrogen fixation helps balance the bed for the heavy-feeding corn; the benefit is structural and traditional rather than a measured pest effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Squash
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: The third Sister; its broad leaves shade the soil and keep weeds down around the beans.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Same Three Sisters basis as corn. The squash ground-cover/weed-suppression role is well established and structural; foliage-diversity pest disruption is plausible but not a measured bean-specific protection. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Squash rounds out the Three Sisters trio. Its broad sprawling leaves shade the soil, hold moisture, and suppress weeds around the base of the bean supports, while the mix of heights makes it harder for pests to lock onto any one crop. This is a soil-and-space benefit; give the squash room so it does not swamp the young bean vines before they climb.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Cucumber
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: An easy neighbor that shares similar warm-season, full-sun needs.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Rests on sound shared-conditions compatibility plus legume N-fixation benefiting a neighboring feeder, by close analogy to well-supported cucurbit/legume relationships. likely (good biological grounds, no cucumber+pole-bean-specific trial located) rather than research_backed.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Cucumber and pole beans coexist comfortably: similar warm-season timing and water needs, and the beans' nitrogen fixation lightly benefits the cucumber as a moderate feeder. Trellised cucumbers can even share the vertical structure. This is a compatibility pairing rather than a strongly protective one.

good_seasoned.name: Corn
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: The Three Sisters pairing of beans, corn, and squash is a long-documented traditional planting; the corn stalk gives the pole beans something to climb and the beans contribute nitrogen to the grouping.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Three Sisters; documented as a traditional Native American companion strategy, corn-as-trellis is the pole-bean form.

good_seasoned.name: Squash
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: The third of the Three Sisters; its sprawling canopy shades soil and suppresses weeds around the bean supports.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Three Sisters companion.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Onion
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Onions and other alliums are traditionally kept away from beans, which are said to grow poorly near them.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: A real, repeatedly-cited mechanism, not folklore: allium antibacterial sulfur compounds are held to disrupt the legume's Rhizobium N-fixing symbiosis, stunting bean growth. mechanistic/medium: mechanism is sound and consistently reported, but no controlled field trial was opened to a T1 source this session.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Onions and beans is one of the better-grounded 'bad' pairings. Alliums release antibacterial sulfur compounds that are held to interfere with the Rhizobium bacteria on bean roots, the very bacteria the bean depends on to fix nitrogen, so bean growth tends to stall near onions. Keep them in separate parts of the bed. A useful corollary: beans grown before onions actually improve the soil for the following allium crop.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Garlic
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Like onions, garlic is a traditional bad neighbor for beans.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Same Rhizobium-disruption mechanism as onion; garlic is an allium with the same antibacterial sulfur chemistry. mechanistic/medium.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Garlic acts on beans the same way onions do. As an allium it gives off antibacterial sulfur compounds held to disrupt the nitrogen-fixing Rhizobium bacteria on bean roots, slowing the beans down. Treat garlic and pole beans as bed-mates to keep apart, and use the bean-then-allium rotation to your advantage instead.

bad_seasoned.name: Onion
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Alliums are the classic traditional caution near beans; the pairing is widely advised against in home-garden lore, with a plausible mechanism (allium sulfur compounds disrupting the beans' nitrogen-fixing bacteria).

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Long-standing allium-vs-legume garden caution; not experimentally established.

bad_seasoned.name: Garlic
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: As with onion, garlic is traditionally kept apart from beans.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Allium caution, traditional.

pests.name: Mexican bean beetle
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Leaves taking on a skeletonized, lacy look as tissue is chewed from the undersides, leaving the vein network behind. Both the spiny yellow larvae and the dome-shaped, coppery adults feed on leaf undersides, and on tall pole vines the damage runs high into the canopy where it is easy to miss. The adult is yellow to coppery-brown, one-quarter to one-third inch long, with eight small black spots on each wing cover.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Leaves that look skeletonized or lacy, with the tissue chewed away from underneath but the veins left behind. Both the spiny yellow young and the round, coppery adult beetles feed on the undersides of the leaves, and on a tall pole vine they work their way up high where they are easy to overlook. The adult is yellow to copper colored with rows of small black spots on its back.
pests.cause_seasoned: The Mexican bean beetle (Epilachna varivestis), a leaf-eating member of the ladybeetle family. Adults emerge from overwintering near woodland edges, feed, then lay clusters of yellow eggs on leaf undersides, and several generations build through the season.
pests.cause_beginner: The Mexican bean beetle, a leaf-eating cousin of the ladybug. The adults come out of hiding near woods in spring, feed, then lay clusters of yellow eggs under the leaves, and several generations build up over the summer.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Handpick and destroy adults, the yellow egg clusters, and the spiny larvae, checking leaf undersides up the trellis. Beans tolerate real defoliation without yield loss, about 30 percent before bloom and 15 percent during bloom and pod fill, so light feeding needs no spray. Where pressure is heavy, an organic option such as spinosad is labeled for bean beetles.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick off and destroy the adults, the yellow egg clusters, and the spiny young, looking under the leaves and up the vine. Done early, this works well in a home garden. Beans can lose a fair amount of leaf without losing beans, so you do not need to spray for light damage. If they get bad, an organic spray such as spinosad is labeled for bean beetles.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Since most damage falls in July and August, an early or a late-summer sowing can escape the worst of it; the varieties Wade and Black Valentine are noted as tolerant. Work crop debris into the soil promptly after harvest to remove overwintering shelter, and rotate beans away from last year's bed.
pests.prevention_beginner: Because most damage happens in July and August, planting early or making a late-summer sowing can mostly dodge it. Clear and turn under the old vines right after harvest so the beetles have nowhere to overwinter, and move your beans to a new spot each year.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Colonies of soft-bodied, pinhead-sized insects clustered on growing tips and leaf undersides, usually green but sometimes black, yellow, or pink. Heavy feeding stunts young plants and delays maturity as the insects withdraw sap; sticky honeydew and sooty mold may follow.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Clusters of tiny soft-bodied insects, usually green but sometimes black or pink, packed onto the growing tips and the undersides of leaves. Heavy feeding stunts young plants and slows them down, and a sticky residue may appear. Aphids can also spread virus diseases from plant to plant.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several aphid species (Aphis and Macrosiphum euphorbiae), most prevalent in cool, dry weather on small plants. They reproduce rapidly, building dense colonies before natural enemies catch up; warm weather and predators such as lady beetles usually bring them down.
pests.cause_beginner: Several kinds of aphids, most common in cool, dry weather on small plants. They multiply fast and build up thick colonies before their natural enemies catch up. Warmer weather and helpful bugs like ladybugs usually knock them back.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong spray of water, or treat with insecticidal soap, which gives good control on contact. Begin as soon as colonies are found. Once the weather warms, lady beetles and other natural enemies generally take over.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Blast the colonies off with a strong spray of water, or use insecticidal soap, which works on contact. Start as soon as you see them. Once it warms up, ladybugs and other helpful insects usually take care of the rest.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Lay reflective mulch, which disorients aphids and reduces both feeding and virus spread, and control nearby weeds that harbor them. Avoid overfeeding with nitrogen, which produces the soft, lush growth aphids favor.
pests.prevention_beginner: Lay down reflective mulch, which confuses aphids and cuts both their feeding and the viruses they spread, and pull nearby weeds that shelter them. Do not overfeed with fertilizer, since the soft new growth is exactly what aphids like.

pests.name: Two-spotted spider mite
pests.symptoms_seasoned: A fine whitish or yellow stippling on the leaves at first, progressing to a bronzed, dried-out look as populations build; fine silken webbing over the leaf undersides is the giveaway. The mites are minute specks, easiest to confirm by tapping a leaf over white paper. They build explosively in hot, dry weather.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Fine whitish or yellow speckling on the leaves at first, turning to a dried, bronzed look as they multiply. The clue is fine webbing on the undersides of the leaves. The mites themselves are tiny specks, easiest to see by tapping a leaf over white paper. They explode in hot, dry weather.
pests.cause_seasoned: Two-spotted spider mites (Tetranychus urticae), tiny eight-legged relatives of spiders that pierce leaf cells and suck the contents. Hot, dry conditions favor rapid buildup, and dusty, drought-stressed plants are most prone.
pests.cause_beginner: Two-spotted spider mites, tiny eight-legged relatives of spiders that pierce the leaf and suck out the contents. Hot, dry weather lets them build up fast, and dusty, dried-out plants are the most likely to be hit.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hose the undersides of leaves with a strong spray of water to dislodge mites and webbing, and treat with insecticidal soap before numbers climb too high. Keeping plants well watered and unstressed slows buildup, and lady beetles and other predators help.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray the undersides of the leaves with a strong jet of water to knock off the mites and webbing, and use insecticidal soap before they get too thick. Keeping the plants well watered and unstressed slows them down.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Maintain even soil moisture, since drought-stressed plants are far more mite-prone, and avoid the dusty conditions mites thrive in. Watch the undersides of leaves closely through hot, dry spells so you catch the buildup early.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist, because dried-out plants are much more likely to get mites, and keep dust down. Check the undersides of the leaves during hot, dry weather so you catch them early.

pests.name: Bean leaf beetle
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Large, irregular holes chewed in leaves, and on young plants, girdling of stems near the soil line that can thin the stand. The adult is one-fifth to one-quarter inch long and variable in color, usually red to yellow, marked with three or four black spots along each wing cover. Damage early in the season matters most because it reduces the stand.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Large ragged holes chewed in the leaves, and on young plants, chewing around the stem near the soil that can kill seedlings. The adult is a small beetle, usually reddish or yellowish, with a few black spots down each wing cover. Early-season damage is the worst because it thins out the plants.
pests.cause_seasoned: The bean leaf beetle (Cerotoma trifurcata), rarely a serious pest in most home gardens. Adults feed on foliage and stems, with seedlings the most vulnerable stage.
pests.cause_beginner: The bean leaf beetle, which is rarely a serious problem in most home gardens. The adults chew leaves and stems, and young seedlings are the most at risk.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Handpicking and the same measures used against Mexican bean beetle generally keep it in check; beans tolerate considerable leaf loss without yield penalty, so light feeding needs no action. Protect emerging seedlings, the vulnerable stage, where beetles are active.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Picking them off and the same steps you would use for Mexican bean beetle usually keep them in check. Beans can lose a good bit of leaf without losing beans, so light damage needs nothing. Focus on protecting young seedlings, which are the most at risk.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Clear crop debris after harvest and rotate beans to deny overwintering sites. A floating row cover over emerging seedlings protects the stand through the vulnerable early weeks where the beetle is a known problem.
pests.prevention_beginner: Clear away the old vines after harvest and move your beans each year so the beetles have nowhere to overwinter. A lightweight row cover over young seedlings protects them through the risky early weeks if this beetle is a problem where you are.

diseases.name: Bean rust
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Rust-colored, raised spots that form mainly on the lower leaf surfaces; badly infected leaves yellow, wilt, and drop. Stems and pods can be infected too. It develops under humid conditions and can affect most types of beans.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Rust-colored bumps, mostly on the undersides of the leaves. Badly infected leaves turn yellow, wilt, and fall off. Stems and pods can get it too. It shows up in humid weather and can hit most kinds of beans.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Uromyces appendiculatus. It survives the winter in the soil, on plant debris, and, importantly for pole beans, on the poles and trellis used the previous year, a direct route back to a new crop. Humid conditions drive infection and spread.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that survives the winter in the soil, on old plant debris, and, importantly for pole beans, on the poles and trellis used the year before. Humid weather is what lets it take hold and spread.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy infected leaves and improve airflow. Where rust has been severe, a sulfur dust or spray gives good control when begun as the plants start to bloom and repeated on a 10-to-14-day schedule; follow the label.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick off and throw away, do not compost, infected leaves, and give the vines room to breathe. Where rust is bad, a sulfur dust or spray gives good control if you start as the plants begin to flower and repeat every week or two, following the label.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate beans where rust has been a problem, and because the fungus carries over on poles and trellis, clean or replace supports between seasons rather than reusing them unwashed. Grow on a support with good airflow, avoid overhead watering, and choose rust-resistant varieties where it recurs.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Move your beans to a new spot if rust has been a problem, and clean or replace your poles and trellis between years, since the fungus rides over on them. Water at the base instead of overhead, keep airflow up, and pick a rust-resistant variety if it keeps coming back.

diseases.name: Anthracnose
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Black, sunken lesions about half an inch across on pods, the most prominent sign, sometimes oozing salmon-colored spores in wet weather; the veins on lower leaf surfaces turn black, and lesions appear on stems and seedling leaves. It develops in cool, wet spring and fall weather, not in hot, dry summers.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Black, sunken spots about half an inch across on the pods, the clearest sign, sometimes with a pinkish ooze in wet weather. The veins on the undersides of leaves turn black, and spots show up on stems too. It shows up in cool, wet spring and fall weather, not in hot, dry summers.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Colletotrichum lindemuthianum, carried on infected seed and surviving up to two years on plant debris in the soil. Splashing water spreads it, and cool, wet conditions favor infection.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that rides in on infected seed and survives up to two years on old plant debris in the soil. Splashing water spreads it, and cool, wet weather is when it strikes.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure for infected tissue; remove and destroy affected plants and debris to limit spread. On snap beans a copper fungicide or chlorothalonil can suppress it when started early, but clean seed and rotation do most of the work.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot cure tissue that is already infected; pull and throw away, do not compost, affected plants and debris to slow it down. On snap beans a copper fungicide can help if you start early, but keeping seed clean and rotating does most of the work.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant certified disease-free seed and do not save seed from an infected crop. Remove all plant debris after harvest, and do not plant beans where the disease occurred for two to three years. Avoid overhead watering and splashing soil onto the plants.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant certified disease-free seed and do not save seed from an infected crop. Clear away all the old plants after harvest, and do not grow beans in that spot for two to three years. Water at the base and avoid splashing soil up onto the plants.

diseases.name: Bacterial blights (common and halo)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Two related diseases. Halo blight shows light greenish-yellow halos around brown leaf spots and appears in cool weather; common blight turns leaves brown so they drop quickly, with no halo, and favors warm weather. Both infect stems, leaves, and pods, and both are spread by rain and damp conditions.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Two related diseases. Halo blight makes pale greenish-yellow rings around brown spots on the leaves and shows up in cool weather. Common blight turns leaves brown so they drop fast, with no ring, and likes warm weather. Both hit stems, leaves, and pods, and both spread in rain and damp conditions.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Two bacteria, Xanthomonas campestris pv. phaseoli (common blight) and Pseudomonas syringae pv. phaseolicola (halo blight). Both start on infected seed, spread readily in moisture, and survive up to two years on plant debris in the soil.
diseases.cause_beginner: Two kinds of bacteria, one causing common blight and one causing halo blight. Both start on infected seed, spread easily when it is wet, and survive up to two years on old plant debris in the soil.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once plants are infected; copper fungicides applied on a 10-day schedule can slow spread. Avoid overhead watering and do not handle the vines when foliage is wet, which moves the bacteria from plant to plant.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure once plants are infected; copper sprays every 10 days can slow it down. Water at the base, not overhead, and do not touch the vines when the leaves are wet, since that carries the bacteria from plant to plant.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Buy new, certified seed each year rather than saving it, since the disease is seedborne. Do not plant beans in the same spot more often than every third year, and stay out of the planting when the foliage is wet.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Buy new, certified seed each year instead of saving your own, since the disease travels on seed. Do not grow beans in the same spot more than once every three years, and keep out of the patch when the leaves are wet.

diseases.name: Bean root rots
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Seeds that rot before emerging, or young seedlings that come up stunted, with a watery soft rot just above or below the soil line; roots die and leaves yellow. The damage shows up most in cool, wet soils that slow germination and keep seedlings vulnerable.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Seeds that rot before they come up, or young seedlings that come up stunted, with a soft, watery rot at the soil line. The roots die and the leaves turn yellow. It is worst in cool, wet soil that makes the seeds sit too long before sprouting.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Several soilborne fungi that infect seeds and young seedlings, usually Rhizoctonia solani, Pythium species, and Fusarium solani. Cool, wet, poorly drained soil and root injury at planting set the stage for them.
diseases.cause_beginner: Several fungi that live in the soil and infect seeds and young seedlings, usually Rhizoctonia, Pythium, and Fusarium. Cool, wet, poorly drained soil and damage to the roots at planting are what let them in.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no rescue for rotted seedlings; replant into warmer, better-drained conditions. Removing affected plants and improving drainage limits further loss. The real lever is prevention, since the fungi are already in the soil.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no saving seedlings that have rotted; replant once the soil is warmer and drains better. Pulling affected plants and improving drainage limits the loss. The main thing is prevention, since these fungi are already in the soil.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Wait until the soil has warmed to about 69°F at a 4-inch depth before sowing, and plant on raised beds in well-drained ground rather than low, wet spots. Avoid root injury at planting, rotate beans with other vegetables, and clear crop debris after harvest.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Wait until the soil has warmed to about 69°F before planting, and use raised beds in well-drained ground instead of low, wet spots. Avoid damaging the roots when planting, move your beans around the garden each year, and clear away old plants after harvest.

diseases.name: White mold (watery soft rot)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small, soft, watery spots on stems, leaves, and pods that enlarge fast under cool, moist conditions, run together, and girdle the stem. Affected pods collapse into a brown, watery mush, soon covered by a white cottony fungal growth. Dense, overfed vines with poor airflow are most at risk.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small, soft, watery spots on stems, leaves, and pods that grow fast in cool, damp weather, join together, and choke off the stem. Affected pods collapse into a brown, watery mush, soon covered in white cottony mold. Crowded, overfed vines with poor airflow are the most at risk.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Sclerotinia sclerotiorum, favored by cool, moist conditions and heavy, dense growth. Too much fertilizer drives the lush vine growth that creates the still, humid canopy the disease needs.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that thrives in cool, damp weather and heavy, crowded growth. Too much fertilizer makes the lush, dense vines that trap the still, humid air the mold needs.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no recommended chemical control for the home garden; management is cultural. Remove and destroy infected plants, and improve air circulation. Training vines up a support and thinning crowded growth helps the canopy dry.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no home-garden spray for this one; you manage it by how you grow. Pull and throw away, do not compost, infected plants, and open up the airflow. Training the vines up their support and thinning crowded growth helps the leaves dry out faster.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Give plants good airflow rather than crowding, and go easy on fertilizer, since excess nitrogen feeds the heavy vine growth that favors the disease. Vertical growth on a trellis is an advantage here, keeping the canopy off the ground; avoid overhead watering and the wet, still conditions the fungus needs.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Give the vines room for air to move instead of crowding them, and go easy on fertilizer, since too much makes the heavy growth the mold likes. Growing up a trellis actually helps, keeping the leaves off the wet ground. Water at the base and avoid keeping the plants wet and packed together.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Regular and even through the long season, keeping soil moisture near field capacity. The need is greatest during the extended flowering and pod-fill period, which on pole beans runs for many weeks.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist but never soggy. Pole beans flower and fill pods for a long time, so keep the water steady all the way through the season.
watering.amount_seasoned: Enough to wet the root zone roughly 6 inches down; watering deeply and less often builds a deeper root system than frequent light sprinkles.
watering.amount_beginner: Water deeply enough to wet the soil about 6 inches down. Deep, less frequent watering beats a daily light sprinkle.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the soil level in the morning so foliage dries quickly; trained up a trellis, the canopy dries faster than a sprawling bush, which helps limit the foliar diseases beans are prone to.
watering.method_beginner: Water the soil, not the leaves, and do it in the morning. Because pole beans grow up in the air, the leaves dry off faster than on a low bush, which helps keep disease down.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting despite wet soil, and stunted growth point to waterlogged roots and the onset of root rot.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If the soil is wet but the plants still wilt or the lower leaves turn yellow, you may be overwatering. Soggy soil rots the roots.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Drought stress during flowering and pod fill aborts blossoms and produces small, stringy pods, and it can stall the plant's ongoing pod set for the rest of the season.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: If plants dry out while flowering and filling pods, they drop their flowers and the beans come out small and tough. Keep the water steady to keep new pods coming.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Avoid overhead watering where practical; the moisture-critical window is the long pod-set-through-pod-fill period.
watering.method_note_beginner: Try not to spray the whole plant from above. The most important time to keep water steady is the long stretch when pods are forming and filling.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Flowering and pod fill are the moisture-critical stages, and on pole beans they run for weeks; stress here directly cuts the running yield.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Flowering and pod-filling are when beans most need steady water, and on pole beans that lasts most of the season.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Not applicable. Pole beans are direct-sown in place and are not started indoors or hardened off.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: You do not need to harden off pole beans. They are planted straight into the garden from seed.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Sow directly into warm soil after the last spring frost, and set the trellis, poles, or netting in place at planting so you do not disturb the roots later. Beans resent root disturbance and germinate quickly in place, so transplanting offers no advantage.
start_method.notes_beginner: Plant pole bean seeds right where they will grow, once the soil has warmed and frost is past, and put up the trellis or poles at the same time. Beans do not like having their roots disturbed, so skip starting them indoors.

drainage.saucer_practice: Empty any saucer after watering so the pot never sits in standing water, which rots bean roots.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Use a good potting mix, not garden soil, which packs down too hard in pots.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in a little compost for fertility.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: A well-draining potting mix; avoid native garden soil, which compacts and drains poorly in containers.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend in compost for baseline fertility; beans need little added nitrogen.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out faster than garden beds, especially once the vine is large, so check the soil daily in hot weather and water when the top inch is dry.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Container pole beans still need little feeding; a light dose before flowering, and maybe one more later in the season, is plenty.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Not applicable. Pole beans are a warm-season annual; they finish in one season and are not overwintered.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Not applicable. As a frost-tender annual, pole beans complete their cycle in a single season and are not overwintered.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Pole beans can grow in a big pot, but they need a tall, sturdy support they will not tip over. Use a pot at least 5 gallons, ideally 10 or more and 12 inches deep, set up a 6-foot teepee or trellis in it, plant a few seeds around the base, and keep the mix evenly moist.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Pole beans grow in a large container, but they need both room and a sturdy tall support. Use a pot of at least 5 gallons, ideally 10 or more and 12 inches deep, anchored so a 6-foot teepee or trellis will not topple in wind. Plant several seeds around the support and keep the mix evenly moist.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry faster than beds, and a full pole vine transpires heavily, so monitor daily in heat and water when the top inch dries.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Feeding needs stay low; a single light pre-bloom feed suffices, though a long-bearing potted vine may want one more light feeding mid-season.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering container suits pole beans well, smoothing out the steady moisture they want across their long bearing season.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match for pole beans because it keeps the water steady, which is exactly what they like over their long season.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: A deep, heavy, stable container is what matters for pole beans, unlike the wide, shallow pot that suits bush types. The pot has to anchor a 6-foot support against wind and hold enough soil to carry a large vine through a long season, so depth and weight beat surface area here.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: For pole beans, a deep, heavy pot works better than a wide, shallow one. The pot has to hold up a tall support without tipping in the wind and carry a big vine all season, so depth and weight matter more than width.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Avoid following beans with beans or other legumes in the same bed; rotate to break the soil-borne disease cycle beans are prone to. Because rust and blights carry over on poles and trellis, clean or replace those supports between seasons as well as moving the bed.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Do not plant beans in the same spot two years running. Diseases build up in the soil and can hit the next bean crop, and they also ride over on old poles and trellis, so clean or replace those too.
rotation.good_after: Beans are an excellent crop to grow before a heavy feeder. As a legume they fix nitrogen and leave the soil in better shape for a following crop such as a leafy green or corn.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate beans on a roughly three-year cycle, and clean or replace poles and trellis between seasons since rust and blights persist on them. Their nitrogen-fixing habit makes beans a good predecessor for nitrogen-hungry crops.
rotation.note_beginner: Move your beans to a new spot each year, on about a three-year rotation, and clean or swap out the poles and trellis between seasons. Because beans feed the soil with nitrogen, whatever you plant there next will benefit.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Not recommended. Fresh snap beans lose quality fast at room temperature and should be cooled promptly after picking rather than held on the counter.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Do not leave fresh beans out on the counter. They go downhill quickly, so cool them down soon after picking.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Cool beans soon after harvest to shed field heat, then refrigerate cold and humid. They hold good quality for about a week; held longer or warmer, they develop watersoaked spots and browning.
storage.fridge_beginner: Cool the beans soon after picking, then keep them in the fridge, cold and a bit humid. They stay good for about a week; left longer or warmer, they get soft spots and brown patches.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Beans freeze well for longer storage. For best quality, freeze or can within a few hours of picking, blanching briefly first to preserve color and texture.
storage.freezer_beginner: Beans freeze well for keeping longer. For the best result, freeze them within a few hours of picking, after a quick blanch in boiling water to hold their color and texture.
storage.notes_seasoned: Snap beans are best used as soon as possible after picking. The key to holding them is speed and cold: cool them right away to remove field heat, keep them cold and humid, and process for the freezer or canner within hours of harvest for top quality.
storage.notes_beginner: Snap beans are best eaten soon after picking. To keep them, the trick is to cool them fast and keep them cold: chill them right after harvest, store them cold and damp, and freeze or can them within a few hours if you want the best quality.

recommended.name: Kentucky Wonder
recommended.note: The classic heirloom pole bean; vigorous, heavy-yielding, with long meaty pods and full old-fashioned flavor. Widely adapted and a dependable first choice.

recommended.name: Blue Lake Pole
recommended.note: Popular pole form of the Blue Lake type; smooth round green pods with classic flavor, produced heavily over a long season.

recommended.name: Kentucky Blue
recommended.note: A cross of Kentucky Wonder and Blue Lake combining the flavor of one with the tender straight pods of the other.

recommended.name: Rattlesnake
recommended.note: Heat-tolerant Southern favorite with purple-streaked green pods; the streaking fades on cooking. Well suited to hot regions.

recommended.name: McCaslan
recommended.note: Old Southern pole bean with long flat pods, good fresh or as a shelly bean; a recommended variety for warm regions.

varieties.note_seasoned: Choose cultivars with resistance to bean common mosaic virus and anthracnose where those diseases are a concern. The varieties here are widely recommended pole types; Kentucky Wonder and Blue Lake Pole lead for dependable, long-bearing crops. Note that Scarlet Runner bean is a different species (Phaseolus coccineus), often grown as an ornamental, not a green-podded snap bean.
varieties.note_beginner: Kentucky Wonder and Blue Lake Pole are easy, dependable choices for a first pole bean patch. Rattlesnake is a good pick if your summers are hot. One to know: Scarlet Runner bean, with its bright red flowers, is a different plant (Phaseolus coccineus) usually grown for looks, not the same as a snap bean.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare soil for roughly a week, then the seedling shoulders up through the surface still bent in a hook, dragging the two thick seed leaves (cotyledons) up with it before they unfold. Emergence is fast in warm soil but stalls or rots outright in cold, wet ground. Beans sown before the soil reaches about 60°F at a 4-inch depth germinate poorly.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Bare soil for about a week, then a bent stem pushes up through the surface, pulling two thick first leaves (called seed leaves) up with it. Beans come up fast in warm soil but rot in cold, wet ground. If you plant before the soil has warmed to about 60°F, many seeds will not come up at all.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Sow only once the soil has warmed to at least 60°F at a 4-inch depth, about 1 inch deep into a moist, well-drained bed, and set the trellis, poles, or netting in place now so you do not disturb the roots later. Avoid soaking the soil, which suffocates the seed and feeds root rot fungi.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Wait to plant until the soil has warmed to at least 60°F. Plant about 1 inch deep in moist, well-drained soil, and put up your trellis or poles at the same time so you do not disturb the roots later. Do not keep the bed soggy.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have your beans emerged? Note the date to track days to maturity from a real sowing rather than the seed packet.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your beans come up yet? Write down the date you first saw them break the soil.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The cotyledons open and the first true leaves appear: a pair of single leaflets, followed by the bean's characteristic three-part (trifoliate) leaves. The plant soon begins to reach and twine toward its support. Young seedlings are the stage most vulnerable to bean leaf beetle feeding.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The two seed leaves open, then the real leaves appear, first a single pair, then the three-leaflet leaves beans are known for. The little plant soon starts to reach and twist toward its support. This young stage is when beetles can do the most damage.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep the bed evenly moist and weed-free; young beans compete poorly with weeds. Cultivate shallowly, since bean roots run close to the surface. Make sure the support is in place and guide the first shoots to it if needed. There is no thinning: pole beans are sown at their spacing along the support.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist and pull weeds early, hoeing shallowly since bean roots are near the surface. Check that the trellis or poles are ready and gently steer the first shoots onto them. You do not thin pole beans, they are planted where they will grow.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How is your bean stand looking? Note any gaps or beetle damage on the young leaves.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How do your young bean plants look? Note any chewed leaves or bare patches.

growth_stages.name: Vining and climbing
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Rapid vining as the plant twines up its support toward its full height, often 6 feet or more. Pole beans spend real energy climbing before they set heavily, so early growth looks leafy and upward rather than fruitful. The plant is fixing much of its own nitrogen now, so vigorous but not lush, overfed growth is the goal.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Fast climbing growth as the vine winds its way up the trellis or poles, often to 6 feet or taller. Pole beans put a lot of early effort into climbing before they make many beans, so at first you will see lots of leafy vine going up rather than pods. Beans make much of their own food (nitrogen) at this stage.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Hold steady, even moisture and resist the urge to feed. Beans need little nitrogen, and excess now drives leafy vine growth and delays flowering. Guide wayward shoots onto the support; the vines twine on their own but a nudge helps them find the structure early.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the watering steady and do not add fertilizer now. Beans need very little, and extra just gives you big leafy vines and later beans. Tuck any stray shoots onto the support; the vines climb on their own, but a little help early gets them going.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How high are your vines climbing? Note their height and how well they are taking to the support.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How tall are your bean vines getting? Note how far up the support they have climbed.

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small white, pink, or purple flowers open along the vines. Pole beans flower over a long, extended window rather than all at once, so bloom and pod set overlap and continue for weeks. This is a moisture-critical stage: water stress aborts blossoms, and sustained heat above about 90°F causes blossom drop until the weather cools.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Small white, pink, or purple flowers open along the vines. Unlike bush beans, pole beans flower a little at a time over a long stretch, so flowers and young pods appear together for weeks. This is an important time for water. If the plants dry out or it stays above about 90°F, the flowers drop without making beans, then start again once it cools.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture steady and ample; water stress now directly cuts the running yield. Water at the soil in the morning, not overhead, to keep the tall canopy dry. In a heat wave, water deeply ahead of it; the vine will keep reflowering as temperatures ease.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the water steady and generous, because dry soil now means fewer beans. Water the soil, not the leaves, to keep disease down. If a heat wave hits, water deeply beforehand, then wait it out, the vine will keep flowering once it cools.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are your beans flowering? Note the date bloom started and any blossom drop in heat.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are your beans flowering yet? Note when the flowers opened and whether any dropped in hot weather.

growth_stages.name: Pod set and fill
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Pods appear where flowers were and lengthen quickly, plumping as the seeds fill. Because the vine flowers continuously, you will see pods at every stage at once, from tiny to pickable. Drought here produces small, stringy pods and can stall the plant's ongoing set.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Pods form where the flowers were and grow quickly, getting plumper as the beans fill inside. Because the vine keeps flowering, you will have pods of every size at once, from tiny to ready. Dry soil now makes small, tough, crooked pods and can slow down the whole run.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Maintain even moisture near field capacity right through pod fill; on pole beans this stage runs for weeks. Begin checking pods every couple of days as they size up, since the pickable window for any one pod is brief.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist all through this stage, which on pole beans lasts a long time. Start checking the pods every couple of days, because each one is ready for only a short time before it gets too old.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are pods forming and filling? Note the date you first saw pods and how fast they are sizing up.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are pods forming? Note when you first saw them and how quickly they are growing.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Firm, crisp pods that snap cleanly when bent, picked before the enlarging seeds bulge the pod wall. Most pole varieties reach first pick around 60 to 70 days and then keep bearing for many weeks. Regular picking every couple of days keeps the vine flowering and setting new pods; pods left to mature signal it to slow down.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Firm, crisp pods that break with a clean snap, picked before you can see the seeds bulging. Most pole beans give their first pick around 60 to 70 days and then keep producing for weeks. Picking every couple of days keeps new beans coming; leaving old pods on tells the vine to slow down.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick in the early morning for best quality, once the dew has dried, breaking pods off cleanly without tearing the vine. Harvest every two to three days across the whole season; frequent picking is the single biggest lever on how long and heavily a pole bean bears. Do not work the vines when foliage is wet, which spreads bacterial blight.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pick in the morning for the best beans, after the dew dries, snapping pods off without tearing the vine. Pick every two or three days all season long, because picking often is what keeps a pole bean producing. Do not pick when the leaves are wet, since that spreads disease.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have you made your first picking? Log the date and keep noting each pick to track how long the vines bear.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you picked your first beans? Note the date and keep track of each picking through the season.

notifications.body_seasoned: Direct-sow pole beans after the last spring frost, once the soil has warmed to at least 60°F at a 4-inch depth. Sow about 1 inch deep into a moist, well-drained bed, and set your trellis, poles, or netting in place at planting so you do not disturb the roots later.
notifications.body_beginner: Plant pole beans right in the garden after the last spring frost, once the soil has warmed to at least 60°F. Plant about 1 inch deep, and put up your trellis or teepee of poles at the same time so you do not disturb the roots later.

notifications.body_seasoned: Most pole beans reach first pick around 60 to 70 days. Begin checking and pick firm, crisp pods that snap cleanly, before the seeds bulge. From here the vine keeps bearing for weeks.
notifications.body_beginner: Most pole beans are ready for a first pick around 60 to 70 days. Start checking and pick firm, crisp pods that snap cleanly, before the seeds bulge through. From now on the vine keeps making beans for weeks.

notifications.title_seasoned: Keep picking to keep them producing
notifications.title_beginner: Keep picking to keep beans coming
notifications.body_seasoned: Pick pole beans every two to three days all season. Regular picking is what keeps the vine flowering and setting new pods; pods left to mature signal it to slow down. There is no need to succession-sow, one planting bears until frost.
notifications.body_beginner: Pick your pole beans every two or three days all season. Picking often is what keeps a pole bean making more beans, so do not let old pods sit on the vine. You do not need to plant again, one planting keeps going until frost.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost expected, protect or harvest beans
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost is coming, pick or cover your beans
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Pole beans are frost-tender and a light frost will kill them. If frost is forecast, harvest any pickable pods; covering a tall trellised vine is hard, so pick everything usable first. In fall, a hard frost ends the crop.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Pole beans are killed by even a light frost. If frost is forecast, pick any beans that are ready. A tall vine is hard to cover, so harvest everything you can use first. In fall, a hard frost ends the crop.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot weather can make flowers drop
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Sustained heat above about 90°F during bloom causes beans to drop blossoms instead of setting pods. Keep moisture steady and water deeply ahead of the heat; because pole beans flower over a long window, the vine resumes setting pods once it cools.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: When it stays above about 90°F while beans are flowering, they drop their flowers instead of making beans. Keep the water steady and water deeply before the heat. Because pole beans flower for a long time, the vine starts setting beans again once it cools.

germination.text_seasoned: Bean seed rots in cold, wet ground. Wait until the soil is at least 60°F at a 4-inch depth before sowing, since early planting only invites poor stands and seed rot. Beans sown into warm soil quickly overtake those sown into cold soil.
germination.text_beginner: Bean seeds rot in cold, wet soil. Wait until the soil has warmed to at least 60°F before planting, because planting early just leads to rotted seed and missing plants. Beans planted into warm soil catch up fast, so there is nothing to gain by rushing.
germination.author: plant

germination.text_seasoned: Set the trellis, teepee, or netting in place at sowing, not after the vines are up. Pole beans twine on their own but need a sturdy 6-to-8-foot support ready to climb, and installing it later disturbs shallow bean roots.
germination.text_beginner: Put your trellis, teepee, or netting up when you plant, not later. Pole beans climb by themselves but need a strong support, about 6 to 8 feet tall, ready and waiting. Adding it later disturbs the shallow roots.
germination.author: plant

seedling.text_seasoned: Weed early and cultivate shallowly. Young beans compete poorly with weeds, but their roots run close to the surface, so deep hoeing does more harm than the weeds. Hand-pull and scuffle-hoe lightly near the row.
seedling.text_beginner: Pull weeds early, but weed shallowly. Young beans do not compete well with weeds, yet their roots are near the surface, so digging deep hurts the plant more than the weeds do. Pull by hand and hoe lightly near the row.
seedling.author: plant

vegetative.text_seasoned: Hold off on nitrogen. As legumes, beans fix much of their own, and extra nitrogen now drives leafy vine growth up the trellis and delays flowering. At most a single light side-dressing just before bloom, and only on poor or sandy soil.
vegetative.text_beginner: Do not add nitrogen fertilizer now. Beans make much of their own from the air, and extra fertilizer just gives you big leafy vines and later beans. At most, feed once lightly right before they flower, and only if your soil is poor.
vegetative.author: plant

vegetative.text_seasoned: Guide the young shoots onto their support early. Pole beans twine counterclockwise on their own, but a nudge onto the trellis or pole in the first weeks keeps them from tangling on the ground and starts the climb clean.
vegetative.text_beginner: Help the young vines find their support early. Pole beans wind their way up on their own, but steering them onto the trellis or pole in the first weeks keeps them from tangling on the ground.
vegetative.author: plant

flowering.text_seasoned: Keep moisture steady and ample through bloom. Flowering and pod set are the moisture-critical stages, and on pole beans they run for weeks, so water stress at any point cuts the running crop. Water at the soil in the morning, not overhead.
flowering.text_beginner: Keep the water steady and generous while the vine flowers. Flowering and pod-forming are when beans most need water, and on pole beans that lasts a long time, so letting them dry out shrinks the crop. Water the soil in the morning, not the leaves.
flowering.author: plant

flowering.text_seasoned: Expect blossom drop in sustained heat above about 90°F. The vine aborts flowers when it is too hot to set pods, then resumes once it cools. Because pole beans flower over a long window, the crop recovers as the weather eases; water deeply ahead of a heat wave.
flowering.text_beginner: When it stays hotter than about 90°F, beans drop their flowers. The vine gives up on flowers when it is too hot to make beans, then starts again once it cools. Since pole beans flower for a long time, the crop bounces back. Water deeply before a heat wave.
flowering.author: plant

pod_set_fill.text_seasoned: Do not let the bed dry out as pods size up. Drought during pod fill produces small, stringy pods and can stall the vine's ongoing set, while steady moisture near field capacity gives plump, well-formed ones over the whole long season.
pod_set_fill.text_beginner: Do not let the soil dry out while the pods are growing. Dry soil now makes small, tough, crooked beans and can slow the whole run, while steady moisture gives you plump, well-shaped ones all season.
pod_set_fill.author: plant

harvest.text_seasoned: Pick every two to three days, before the seeds bulge the pod. On pole beans, frequent picking is the single biggest lever on yield: it keeps the vine flowering and setting new pods, while pods left to mature signal it to slow down. One well-picked planting bears for many weeks.
harvest.text_beginner: Pick every two or three days, before the seeds swell the pods. On pole beans, picking often is what keeps them producing: it keeps new flowers and pods coming, while old pods left on tell the vine to quit. One planting, well picked, keeps going for weeks.
harvest.author: plant

harvest.text_seasoned: Pick in the early morning for best quality, but only once the dew has dried. Handling wet bean vines spreads bacterial blight through the planting, so wait for the foliage to dry before working down the rows.
harvest.text_beginner: Pick in the morning for the best beans, but wait until the dew has dried off the vines. Touching wet bean plants spreads disease through your patch, so let the leaves dry before you start picking.
harvest.author: plant

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Pole beans out-yield bush beans from the same footprint by growing vertically and bearing over a long season. A 10-foot row of pole beans typically returns roughly 8 to 12 pounds of pods over its extended cropping period, compared with about 5 pounds for bush beans in the same space.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Pole beans give more from the same patch than bush beans because they grow up instead of out and keep bearing for a long time. A 10-foot row of pole beans usually gives about 8 to 12 pounds of beans over the season, versus around 5 pounds for bush beans in the same space.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Rather than a single burst, pole beans bear steadily over many weeks from one planting, right up to frost. That long, running harvest is why succession sowing is unnecessary: one well-tended planting keeps a household supplied, provided you pick every couple of days to keep it flowering.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Instead of one big batch, pole beans give a steady supply over many weeks from a single planting, all the way to frost. That is why you do not need to replant every couple of weeks like with bush beans: one planting keeps going, as long as you pick every few days.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Pole beans are a rewarding first-year crop: they germinate quickly, ask little, and a single planting bears for weeks once it starts, around 60 to 70 days from sowing. The main first-year lever on yield is steady moisture through the long flowering and pod-fill season, plus picking often enough to keep the vine producing.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Pole beans are a satisfying crop for a first-year garden. They come up fast, need little fuss, and one planting keeps making beans for weeks once it starts, about 60 to 70 days from planting. The main things that affect how much you get are keeping the water steady and picking often so the vine keeps producing.
factors_seasoned: Steady moisture through the long flowering and pod-fill season (the moisture-critical stages; drought aborts blossoms and stalls the running set)
Frequent picking (leaving mature pods on the vine signals it to slow flowering, so picking every couple of days is the biggest lever on total yield)
Temperature during bloom (sustained heat above about 90°F causes blossom drop and pauses the set until it cools)
A sturdy full-height support and good sun (vertical growth on a 6-to-8-foot trellis is what lets pole beans out-yield bush beans per square foot)

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No university extension or peer-reviewed source supports timing pole bean planting by moon phase. No recommendation is made here: sow beans by soil temperature, which should be at least about 60°F, and by your frost-free date, not by the lunar cycle.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Flowers dropped without setting pods
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Flowers fell off without making beans
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The vine flowered but the blossoms dropped instead of setting pods, because sustained heat above about 90°F interferes with pollination and the plant aborts flowers it cannot fill. Water stress during bloom has the same effect. It is a weather problem, not a disease, and because pole beans flower over a long window, the vine usually resumes setting pods once temperatures cool.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The vine flowered, but the flowers fell off without making beans, because steady heat above about 90°F stops the flowers from being pollinated and the plant drops them. Letting the plants dry out while flowering does the same thing. It is a weather problem, not a disease, and since pole beans keep flowering for a long time, the vine usually starts setting beans again once it cools.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Time the planting so the heaviest bloom misses the hottest part of summer, sowing early enough to establish before peak heat or, in hot regions, running separate spring and fall sowings around the summer wall. Keep moisture steady, water deeply ahead of a heat wave, and choose more heat-tolerant varieties such as Rattlesnake where summers are reliably hot.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plan your planting so the main flowering skips the hottest part of summer, either early enough to get going before peak heat or, in hot areas, as separate spring and fall plantings around the summer break. Keep the water steady, water deeply before a heat wave, and pick a more heat-tolerant variety like Rattlesnake if your summers are very hot.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Seeds rotted or came up poorly
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Seeds rotted or did not come up
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The seeds were sown into soil that was too cold and wet, so they sat without germinating and rotted, or came up as a thin, patchy stand. Bean seed does not germinate well below about 60°F, and a slow, cold start invites soilborne root rot fungi and seedcorn maggot, both of which attack the lingering seed.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The seeds went into soil that was too cold and wet, so they sat there instead of sprouting and rotted, or came up thin and patchy. Bean seeds do not sprout well below about 60°F, and a slow, cold start lets soil fungi and a seed-eating maggot get to the seed while it waits.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait until the soil has warmed to at least 60°F at a 4-inch depth before sowing; there is no benefit to planting early. Sow into well-drained ground or raised beds rather than low, wet spots, plant about 1 inch deep, and do not keep the bed soggy after sowing.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Wait until the soil has warmed to at least 60°F before planting, since there is no reward for planting beans early. Plant in well-drained soil or raised beds instead of low, wet spots, plant about 1 inch deep, and do not keep the bed soggy after planting.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Tall leafy vines but few beans
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Big leafy vines but hardly any beans
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The vines grew tall, dark, and leafy up the support but set few pods, usually from too much nitrogen. As legumes, beans fix much of their own nitrogen, and extra fertilizer over-stimulates vine growth and delays flowering. Some early leafiness is normal for pole beans, which climb before they set heavily, but persistent all-vine growth points to excess nitrogen.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The vines grew tall, dark, and leafy but made very few beans, usually because they got too much nitrogen. Beans make much of their own nitrogen from the air, so extra fertilizer just pushes leafy growth and delays flowering. A little early leafiness is normal, since pole beans climb before they set heavily, but if it keeps up, it is too much nitrogen.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Skip the nitrogen feeding. Work in only a little balanced fertilizer or compost before planting, and at most one light side-dressing just before bloom, and only on poor or sandy soil. Let the plant's own nitrogen fixation carry the crop, and give it time, since pole beans set later than bush beans.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Skip the extra fertilizer. Mix in just a little balanced fertilizer or compost before planting, and at most one light feeding right before they flower, and only if your soil is poor. Let the beans make their own nitrogen, and be patient, since pole beans start making beans later than bush beans.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Pods small, tough, or stringy
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Beans came out small, tough, or stringy
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The pods came out small, fibrous, or misshapen, usually from drought stress during flowering and pod fill, or from leaving pods on the vine past their tender stage, when the enlarging seeds make the pod woody. On pole beans, infrequent picking is a common cause, since overlooked pods high in the canopy overmature and also cut the vine's ongoing set.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The beans came out small, tough, or crooked, usually because the plants dried out while flowering and filling pods, or because pods were left on too long until the swelling seeds made them woody. On pole beans this often happens when pods hidden high on the vine get missed and overripen, which also slows down new beans.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Keep moisture steady and ample through the long bloom-and-fill season, and pick every two to three days, working the whole height of the vine and harvesting pods while they are still firm, crisp, and before the seeds bulge. Frequent, thorough picking also keeps the vine producing.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep the water steady through the long flowering and pod-filling season, and pick every two or three days, checking the whole vine, top to bottom, while the pods are still firm and crisp. Picking often and thoroughly also keeps more beans coming.

primary.name: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center (HGIC 1302, Bush & Pole-Type Snap Beans)
Utah State University Extension (Beans in the Garden)
University of Maryland Extension (Growing Beans in a Home Garden)

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Pole beans are not a succession crop the way bush beans are. A single planting climbs its support and bears progressively for many weeks, right up to frost, so you sow once per season rather than at intervals. In long-season warm regions, growers slot a separate spring and a fall sowing split by summer heat, but that is a distinct seasonal crop, not staggered succession. Keep picking every couple of days to keep the vines flowering and setting new pods.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: You plant pole beans once and pick for a long time. One planting keeps making beans for weeks, all the way to frost, so there is no need to replant every couple of weeks like you would with bush beans. In warm regions you may make a separate spring and a fall planting around the summer heat. The main thing is to pick often, which keeps new beans coming.
succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Pole beans flower and set pods continuously from one sowing over a long season, so interval succession does not apply; warm long-season regions support separate spring and fall seasonal sowings rather than staggered succession.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: Batch-2 Wave-2 cert (2026-07-05): source-truth review (CC agent, WebFetch). The certified green-beans-bush heat_pause defect (spelled degrees + mis-carried GA/FL notes into CA/AZ cells) did NOT propagate -- all 8 heat_pause cells carry a species-universal bean blossom-drop basis (Clemson bush-pole 'above 90F, blossom drop'; USU 'above 95F ... shed flowers'), CA cells use ucanr, AZ uariz, warm_arid nmsu; 0 spelled-degrees. Pole-vs-bush distinction (twining vines need a trellis; 5-6 wk vs 2-3 wk bearing) + bean biology all verified. FIX: dropped 'or a pyrethrin' from the Mexican-bean-beetle organic treatment (Clemson lists pyrethrin for whiteflies, spinosad for bean beetles); softened 3 true-but-unsourced pest clauses not on the cited Clemson insect page (the Pediobius foveolatus biocontrol, the MBB 'absent from the Pacific Coast' geography, and 'aphids transmit the mosaic viruses of beans') -- kept only what the page states; re-sourceable at the detail pass.

open_findings.summary: Per-region planting/harvest calendars are kept from the certified same-species bush-bean sibling (identical last-frost and >90F heat walls) with succession structure removed. Pole beans' ~10-15 day longer maturity (DTM 60-70 vs bush 50-60) will nudge per-region first-harvest dates slightly later; within the generally-safe-now tolerance, tighten exact months at the variety pass.

Regional windows are built from the nearest-T1 regional planting sources (UGA, UF/IFAS, UMN, USU, UMD, UIUC, MSU, Clemson, NMSU, U of A, UC MG/ANR, CTAHR) plus bean frost/heat physiology, not a pole-bean-specific planting chart for all 10 regions. Generally safe; tighten exact months at the variety pass.

hawaii_tropical is lowest-confidence: pole beans grow in the islands, but the bounded Feb-Aug warm-season window is modeled on CTAHR general guidance and the bush-bean sibling rather than a pole-bean-specific Hawaii calendar. Confirm in review.

Variety days-to-maturity (Kentucky Wonder 65, Blue Lake Pole 65, Kentucky Blue 65, Rattlesnake 70, McCaslan 65) reflect common catalog norms cross-checked against the Clemson and UF/IFAS pole variety lists and UMD's 60-110 day pole range, not variety-specific extension trials. Scarlet Runner (Phaseolus coccineus) is called out as a distinct, largely ornamental species per UF/IFAS and UMN.

Companions are traditional/mechanistic, low-to-medium confidence: Three Sisters corn as a living trellis for the climbing vines and squash as ground cover, and the allium avoid via the widely-cited Rhizobium-disruption mechanism. No pole-bean-specific companion trial was found in a readable T1 source.

Storage specifics (cool promptly, hold about a week refrigerated cold and humid, blanch and freeze within hours) are standard snap-bean handling modeled on the shared bean sources (Clemson, USU) rather than a pole-specific postharvest study; harvest_urgency left null since per-pick urgency matches the bush sibling and the pole difference is season length.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In colder areas you plant pole beans once and pick for a long time. Wait until after your last spring frost, when the soil has warmed, put up a tall trellis or teepee, and plant at its base. Unlike bush beans, you do not replant every couple of weeks: one planting keeps making beans until the first fall frost ends it. Pick every few days to keep them coming.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Across the cold zones, pole beans run as one long single planting. Sow once the soil holds above 60°F and the last spring frost has passed, set a sturdy 6-to-8-foot trellis or teepee at planting, and the vines then climb and bear progressively. Unlike bush beans there is no need to succession-sow: one planting keeps flowering and setting pods until the first fall frost kills it. Pick every couple of days to keep production running. In the coldest zones, sow by early summer so the crop has time to bear before frost.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: Here you grow pole beans in two seasons, spring and fall, with a summer break between. se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: The Southeast and Gulf run two pole bean crops split by summer heat. Sow in spring after frost against a tall trellis, and again in mid to late summer for a fall crop. The gap is real: through the hottest weeks blossoms drop and pods fail to set. Each planting bears progressively for weeks rather than all at once, so one sowing per window is enough; pick every couple of days. heat_pause.basis_seasoned: This summer gap is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap. Pole beans, like all snap beans, drop their blossoms and fail to set pods once daytime highs run above about 90°F, and the effect worsens with warm nights that suppress pollen viability. Pod set resumes as the weather cools, so the vines are sown before and after the peak-heat months rather than into them.

fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: Florida flips the calendar. In central Florida, grow pole beans in spring and fall with a summer break: plant late winter through April against a tall trellis, stop in the hottest weeks, and plant again in August. In south Florida, grow them through the winter instead, planting from fall into early spring and leaving summer empty. Each planting bears for weeks, so plant once per window.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: Peninsular Florida inverts the calendar. In central Florida, pole beans run a spring crop and a fall crop split by summer heat: sow late winter through April against a tall trellis, pause through the hottest, wettest weeks, and sow again in August. In south Florida the pattern flips fully to a winter growing season, with sowing from fall through early spring and summer left fallow. Each planting bears for weeks; the right window depends on how far south the garden sits.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In tropical Hawaii, grow pole beans in the milder, drier part of the year, not all year round. Put up a tall trellis and plant from about February through August. One planting keeps bearing for weeks. The wetter winter months are less reliable, so there is a planting window even though it never frosts. Pick often while the pods are tender.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: In tropical Hawaii at low elevations, pole beans grow as a warm-season crop across the milder, drier months rather than year-round. Sow from about February through August against a tall trellis; a single planting then climbs and bears progressively for weeks. The cooler, wetter winter months are less reliable, so the planting window is bounded rather than continuous despite the frost-free climate. Pick often while pods are still tender.
