crops.description_seasoned: Pole beans (Phaseolus vulgaris) are the climbing form of the common snap bean: frost-tender, warm-season, nitrogen-fixing legumes grown for their tender immature pods. Unlike the self-supporting bush type, they are twining vines that need a sturdy trellis, teepee, or fence 6 to 8 feet tall to climb. That vertical habit is the payoff: a single planting flowers and sets pods progressively over many weeks, bearing more from the same ground than a bush planting and continuing right up to frost, so you pick regularly rather than facing one concentrated glut. Direct-sown into warm soil after the last frost, they reach a first pickable crop in about 60 to 70 days.
crops.description_beginner: Pole beans are the climbing kind of green bean. Instead of staying short like bush beans, they grow as long vines that need something tall to climb, like a trellis, a teepee of poles, or a fence about 6 to 8 feet high. The reward is a long harvest: one planting keeps making beans for weeks, all the way until frost, so you pick a handful every few days instead of getting them all at once. You plant the seeds straight in the garden after the last frost, give them their support, keep them watered, and start picking in about two months.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Pick when pods are firm, crisp, and snap cleanly, before the enlarging seeds bulge the pod wall. Pole beans bear over a long season, so work the vines every two to three days: regular picking keeps the plant flowering and setting new pods, while pods left to mature signal it to slow down.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Beans are ready when the pods are firm and crisp and snap cleanly, before you can see the seeds bulging inside. Pick every two or three days all season. On pole beans, picking often is what keeps new beans coming, so do not let old pods sit on the vine.

crops.name: Snow Peas

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Peas like loose, fertile soil that drains well, with some compost mixed in. The main thing they care about is good drainage, because peas planted in cold, soggy soil tend to rot before they sprout. If water sits on your bed for a long time after rain, work in compost or plant on a raised bed first.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Snow peas do best in a fertile, well-drained sandy loam or loam with compost worked in before sowing. The critical trait is drainage: pea seed sown into cold, wet, poorly drained ground rots before it germinates, and the soilborne root rots that follow are the main early-season risk. Steady, even moisture without waterlogging carries the crop through flowering and pod fill. Peas are legumes and fix much of their own nitrogen, so the bed needs fertility and tilth more than heavy feeding.

ph.note_beginner: Peas grow best in soil from about 6.0 to 7.0, which is slightly acidic to neutral. They do poorly in strongly acidic soil below 6.0, so if a soil test reads low, mix in some lime before planting. Most garden beds are already in a good range.
ph.note_seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0. Clemson recommends a 6.0 to 6.5 target, and growth is inhibited on acid soils at pH 6.0 and below, so lime an acid plot the season before sowing. Peas tolerate up to roughly 7.5, and a soil test is the reliable way to confirm both pH and fertility before the season starts.

fertilizer.type: balanced pre-plant, little to no nitrogen
fertilizer.timing: work a little balanced fertilizer or compost into the bed before sowing
fertilizer.example_product: 5-10-10 pre-plant
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Snow peas are light feeders. As legumes they fix much of their own nitrogen through root nodules, so heavy nitrogen drives leafy vine growth at the expense of pods. Without a soil test, work a little balanced fertilizer or compost into the bed before sowing; that is usually all peas need. An inoculant of the right Rhizobium bacteria is optional and can help nodulation where peas have not been grown before. Avoid high-nitrogen feeds, which delay flowering and cut pod set.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Peas make much of their own food from the air, so they barely need fertilizer. Mix a little compost or balanced fertilizer into the bed before you plant and that is enough. Too much fertilizer gives you big leafy vines but fewer pods. If you like, you can coat the seed with a pea inoculant powder, which helps the roots make nitrogen, but it is optional.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced 5-10-10 worked in before sowing if no soil test is available; skip extra nitrogen, which peas supply themselves.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: A balanced vegetable fertilizer like 5-10-10 mixed into the bed before planting is plenty.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: 5-10-10 at about 3 pounds per 100 square feet worked in before sowing, per Clemson, when no soil test is available.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: About 3 pounds of 5-10-10 per 100 square feet, mixed into the bed before planting.

companions.note_beginner: Peas get along with most cool-season vegetables. They grow happily beside carrots, radishes, and lettuce, and because they leave nitrogen in the soil, they are a good crop to grow before a leafy green. The pairing to avoid is planting peas right next to onions or garlic.
companions.note_seasoned: As a nitrogen-fixing legume, peas leave the soil richer for what follows and sit comfortably among the other cool-season crops grown in the same early-spring and fall windows: carrots, radishes, and lettuce are classic bed-mates. The long-standing caution is to keep peas away from the alliums (onion, garlic), which are widely held to suppress legumes through the same root-bacteria interference seen with beans.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Carrot
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: A classic cool-season neighbor that shares peas' early-spring and fall timing; the carrots root deep while the peas climb, so they use the bed without crowding.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Carrots and peas are a long-standing cool-season companion pairing; the benefit is shared timing, complementary root-vs-vine habit, and the peas' nitrogen lightly helping the carrots. Traditional/medium: well grounded in shared conditions, not a measured pest effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Carrots and peas grow in the same cool windows and use the bed in complementary ways: the carrot works the soil deep while the pea climbs above it, and the peas' nitrogen fixation lightly benefits the carrot. The pairing is traditional and compatibility-based rather than a measured pest defense, so expect easy cohabitation more than active protection.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Radish
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Radishes sprout fast and mark the pea rows while the slower peas come up, then are pulled long before the peas need the space.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Radish-as-quick-marker interplanted with a slower crop is a standard, low-risk home-garden practice; both are cool-season and the radish is harvested before competition matters. Traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Radishes germinate in days and mark the rows while the peas emerge, and they finish and come out weeks before the peas size up, so they never compete. Both are cool-season crops sown at the same time, which makes them a tidy, low-risk interplant rather than a measured protective pairing.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Lettuce
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Lettuce shares peas' cool-season timing and stays low, tucking in along the base of the pea row or trellis.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Lettuce and peas share cool-season conditions and occupy different layers (low leafy crop under the climbing vine); a sound shared-conditions compatibility, by close analogy to other cool-season interplants. Likely rather than research_backed (no pea-specific lettuce trial located).

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Lettuce slots in below a pea trellis or alongside a bush row, sharing the same cool-season window and water needs while occupying a different layer of the bed. As the peas leaf out they offer the lettuce a little light afternoon shade that delays bolting. It is a compatibility pairing on sound shared-conditions grounds rather than a measured protective one.

good_seasoned.name: Carrot
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional cool-season pairing: carrots and peas share early-spring and fall timing and use the bed in complementary ways, the carrot rooting deep while the pea climbs.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Long-standing cool-season companion pairing (shared timing, root-vs-vine complementarity, light N benefit); not experimentally quantified.

good_seasoned.name: Radish
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Sown with the peas, fast radishes mark the rows and are pulled well before the peas need the space; both are cool-season crops with the same timing.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Standard quick-marker interplant; radish finishes before competition matters. Traditional/medium.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Onion
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Onions and other alliums are traditionally kept away from peas, which are said to grow poorly near them.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: The same allium-versus-legume mechanism reported for beans: allium sulfur compounds are held to disrupt the Rhizobium bacteria peas depend on to fix nitrogen, stunting the vines. Mechanistic/medium: a sound, repeatedly cited mechanism, not a controlled pea-yield trial opened this session.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Onions next to peas is the better-grounded of the 'bad' pairings. Alliums release antibacterial sulfur compounds that are widely held to interfere with the Rhizobium bacteria on pea roots, the bacteria the plant relies on to fix nitrogen, so pea growth tends to stall near onions. Keep them in separate parts of the bed. The useful corollary is that peas grown before an allium crop leave the soil better for it.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Garlic
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Like onions, garlic is a traditional bad neighbor for peas.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Garlic is an allium with the same antibacterial sulfur chemistry as onion; same Rhizobium-disruption mechanism. Mechanistic/medium for the same reasons.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Garlic acts on peas the way onions do. As an allium it gives off antibacterial sulfur compounds held to disrupt the nitrogen-fixing bacteria on pea roots, slowing the vines. Treat garlic and peas as bed-mates to keep apart, and use the pea-then-allium rotation to your advantage instead.

bad_seasoned.name: Onion
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Alliums are the classic traditional caution near peas and other legumes; the pairing is widely advised against, attributed to allium compounds interfering with the pea's nitrogen-fixing bacteria.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Long-standing allium-versus-legume garden caution; mechanism plausible but not experimentally established here.

bad_seasoned.name: Garlic
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: As with onion, garlic is traditionally kept apart from peas.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Allium caution, traditional.

pests.name: Pea aphid
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Colonies of soft, pinhead-sized green aphids clustered on the growing tips, flower stalks, and leaf undersides. Heavy feeding curls and yellows the new growth, stunts the vines, and can drop blossoms; a sticky honeydew and sooty mold may follow. Most important, pea aphids transmit the virus diseases of peas, including pea enation mosaic, so even modest numbers matter.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Clusters of small, soft green insects packed onto the growing tips, flower stems, and undersides of the leaves. They curl and yellow the new growth and stunt the plants, and they leave a sticky residue. The bigger problem is that pea aphids spread virus diseases from plant to plant, so they are worth catching early.
pests.cause_seasoned: The pea aphid (Acyrthosiphon pisum), a large green aphid that builds up fast in the cool, mild weather of spring and fall, exactly the seasons peas grow. It reproduces rapidly, so colonies form before natural enemies catch up.
pests.cause_beginner: The pea aphid, a large green aphid that multiplies quickly in the cool weather of spring and fall when peas are growing. It builds up fast, before helpful insects like ladybugs catch up.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong spray of water, or treat with insecticidal soap, which controls aphids on contact; begin as soon as colonies are found, while numbers are low. Lady beetles, lacewings, and parasitic wasps usually bring populations down on their own. Because the real risk is virus transmission, act early rather than waiting for visible damage.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Blast the colonies off with a strong spray of water, or use insecticidal soap, which works on contact. Start as soon as you see them, while there are only a few. Ladybugs and other helpful insects usually finish the job. Since aphids spread viruses, it is worth dealing with them early.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Lay reflective mulch, which disorients aphids and reduces both feeding and virus spread, and control nearby weeds and clover that harbor them. Avoid overfeeding with nitrogen, which produces the soft, lush growth aphids favor, and choose virus-resistant varieties such as Oregon Sugar Pod II where pea viruses are a known problem.
pests.prevention_beginner: Lay down reflective mulch, which confuses aphids and cuts the viruses they spread, and pull nearby weeds that shelter them. Do not overfeed with fertilizer, since the soft new growth is exactly what aphids like. Where pea viruses are common, plant a resistant variety like Oregon Sugar Pod II.

pests.name: Pea weevil
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small notches chewed from the leaf margins of young plants in spring, and adults feeding on the blossoms. The real damage is hidden: larvae bore into the developing seeds inside the pods and feed there, leaving tiny round exit holes in the dried peas. Saved seed with holes is the giveaway. The pea weevil feeds only on peas (Pisum).
pests.symptoms_beginner: Little notches chewed out of the leaf edges of young plants, and beetles on the flowers in spring. The hidden damage is worse: the grubs tunnel into the peas forming inside the pods, leaving tiny round holes in the dried seeds. Holes in saved seed are the tell. The pea weevil eats only peas.
pests.cause_seasoned: The pea weevil (Bruchus pisorum), a small brownish beetle whose host range is peas alone. Adults overwinter in debris and trash, move into the crop at bloom to lay eggs on young pods, and the larvae develop inside the seeds. There is one generation a year.
pests.cause_beginner: The pea weevil, a small brown beetle that feeds only on peas. The adults spend the winter in garden trash, move in when the peas flower to lay eggs on the young pods, and the grubs grow up inside the seeds. There is one generation each year.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Monitor for adults during bloom, when egg-laying begins. In a home patch, handpicking and floating row cover over the crop at flowering reduce egg-laying. At season's end, inspect dried peas for the small round exit holes before storing seed; freezing saved seed for several days kills any larvae inside.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Watch for the beetles while the peas are flowering, which is when they lay eggs. Picking them off and covering the plants with a light row cover at flowering both help. At the end of the season, check dried peas for tiny round holes before you save seed, and freezing saved seed for a few days kills any grubs inside.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Clean up and destroy pea debris after harvest to remove overwintering shelter, and rotate peas away from last year's bed. Do not save or replant seed showing exit holes. Where the weevil is established, an early sowing that finishes pod fill before peak adult activity escapes the worst.
pests.prevention_beginner: Clear away and destroy the old pea plants after harvest so the beetles have nowhere to overwinter, and move your peas to a new spot each year. Do not save seed that has holes in it. Planting early so the pods finish before the beetles get busy also helps.

pests.name: Armyworms and cutworms
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Cutworms sever young seedlings at or just below the soil line overnight, leaving toppled plants and thinned rows in spring. Armyworms are smooth caterpillars that chew foliage and can move through a planting in numbers, skeletonizing leaves and nicking pods. Both feed mostly at night and hide in the soil or debris by day.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Cutworms cut off young pea seedlings right at the soil line overnight, so you find plants toppled over and gaps in the row. Armyworms are smooth caterpillars that chew the leaves and sometimes the pods, and they can show up in numbers. Both feed at night and hide during the day.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several night-feeding caterpillars, including cutworms (the larvae of various moths) and beet or western yellowstriped armyworms. They overwinter or move in from weedy ground and grassy cover, and seedlings are the most vulnerable stage.
pests.cause_beginner: Several kinds of night-feeding caterpillars: cutworms and armyworms, the young of different moths. They come in from weedy or grassy areas, and young seedlings are the most at risk.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Handpick caterpillars in the evening or early morning, and check the soil around toppled seedlings for the curled cutworm. A cardboard or foil collar around a seedling stops cutworms; Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) controls young armyworms on the foliage. A floating row cover keeps egg-laying moths off the planting.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick the caterpillars off in the evening or early morning, and dig a little around fallen seedlings to find the curled-up cutworm. A collar of cardboard or foil around a seedling blocks cutworms, and a Bt spray controls young armyworms on the leaves. A light row cover keeps the moths from laying eggs.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Clear weeds and grassy cover before sowing to remove egg-laying sites, and turn the bed a couple of weeks ahead of planting to expose and dry out resident larvae. Keep row edges weed-free through the season, and protect emerging seedlings, the vulnerable stage, with a row cover where these caterpillars are a known problem.
pests.prevention_beginner: Clear weeds and tall grass before planting so the moths have fewer places to lay eggs, and turn the soil a couple of weeks before sowing to expose the grubs. Keep the edges of the bed weeded, and cover young seedlings with a row cover if these caterpillars are a problem where you are.

pests.name: Thrips
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine silvery or whitish scarring and flecking on leaves and pods, with tiny dark specks of excrement, as the slender insects rasp the surface and feed on the released sap. Heavy feeding distorts new growth and can scar pods cosmetically. Thrips also vector some plant viruses.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Fine silvery streaks and pale flecks on the leaves and pods, with tiny dark specks, where the slender insects scrape the surface and feed. Bad infestations twist the new growth and leave scars on the pods. Thrips can also spread some viruses.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several thrips species, slender insects a fraction the size of an aphid that build up in warm, dry stretches late in the pea season. They rasp the plant surface and feed on the sap that wells up.
pests.cause_beginner: Thrips, slender insects much smaller than an aphid that build up in warm, dry weather toward the end of the pea season. They scrape the surface of the plant and feed on the sap.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Peas usually outgrow light thrips feeding without treatment. Where numbers climb, a strong spray of water and insecticidal soap reduce them, and natural enemies such as minute pirate bugs and lacewings help. Keep plants unstressed and well watered, since drought-stressed peas are more prone.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Peas usually shrug off a little thrips damage. If they build up, a strong spray of water and insecticidal soap knock them back, and helpful insects pitch in. Keep the plants watered and unstressed, since dried-out peas are more likely to be hit.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Control weeds that harbor thrips, lay reflective mulch to disorient them and reduce virus spread, and keep moisture even so plants are not drought-stressed. Most home pea crops finish before thrips become a real problem.
pests.prevention_beginner: Pull nearby weeds that shelter thrips, lay reflective mulch to confuse them, and keep the soil evenly moist so the plants are not stressed. Most home pea crops are done before thrips become a real problem.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: A white to grayish powdery coating that starts as small spots on the upper leaf surfaces and spreads to cover leaves, stems, and pods. Affected leaves yellow and dry, vines lose vigor, and pods may be spotted or off-flavored. It is the classic late-season pea disease, arriving as the spring crop runs into warmer, drier weather.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: A white to gray powdery dust that starts as spots on top of the leaves and spreads over the leaves, stems, and pods. The leaves yellow and dry out, the vines weaken, and the pods can be spotted. It is the classic late-season pea problem, showing up as the weather warms and dries toward the end of the spring crop.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Erysiphe pisi, favored by warm days, cool nights, and dry foliage, the conditions that arrive late in the pea season. Spores spread on the wind, and the disease moves fast once established, which is why early control and resistant varieties matter most.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus (Erysiphe pisi) that thrives in warm days, cool nights, and dry leaves, which is exactly the weather at the end of the pea season. It spreads on the wind and moves fast once it starts, so catching it early and planting resistant varieties matter most.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Powdery mildew is best managed at the very first signs; once it covers the leaves and yellowing sets in, control is difficult. Remove the worst-affected leaves and improve airflow. Sulfur or a labeled biofungicide, begun early and repeated per the label, suppresses it. On a spring crop that is nearly done, harvesting promptly and pulling the planting is often the practical choice.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Powdery mildew is easiest to handle the moment you first see it; once it covers the leaves, it is hard to stop. Pick off the worst leaves and open up the planting for airflow. A sulfur spray started early and repeated per the label helps. If the spring crop is nearly finished, the simplest move is to pick what is ready and pull the plants.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Choose resistant varieties, the single most effective step: Oregon Sugar Pod II and many modern snow peas carry powdery mildew resistance. Sow early so the crop finishes pod fill before the late-season mildew weather, give plants room and a trellis for airflow, and avoid working among wet vines.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant a resistant variety, which is the best defense: Oregon Sugar Pod II and many newer snow peas resist powdery mildew. Plant early so the crop finishes before the mildew weather arrives, give the plants room and a trellis so air moves through them, and stay out of the patch when the vines are wet.

diseases.name: Fusarium wilt
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: A yellowing of the lower leaves that progresses up the plant, with downward curling, stunting, and wilting; a cut through the lower stem shows a reddish or orange discoloration of the water-conducting tissue. Plants often die before pod fill. Symptoms appear in patches and worsen as the soil warms.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The lower leaves turn yellow and the yellowing creeps up the plant, which becomes stunted, curls, and wilts. If you cut the lower stem, the tissue inside is stained reddish or orange. Affected plants often die before making a crop. It shows up in patches and gets worse as the soil warms.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The soilborne fungus Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. pisi, which enters through the roots, plugs the vascular system, and persists in the soil for years. Several races exist. Warm soil favors it, and once a bed is infested the fungus cannot be eradicated, so resistant varieties and rotation are the management.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that lives in the soil and enters through the roots, clogging the plant's plumbing. It survives in the soil for years and likes warm soil. Once it is in a bed you cannot get rid of it, so the answer is resistant varieties and moving your peas around.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure for infected plants; remove and destroy them to limit buildup. Management is preventive: the disease is handled through resistant varieties and rotation, not treatment.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure once a plant is infected; pull and throw away (do not compost) the affected plants. You manage this one by preventing it, with resistant varieties and rotation, not by spraying.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant Fusarium-resistant varieties, which are widely available (Oregon Sugar Pod II, Dwarf Gray Sugar, and Mammoth Melting Sugar all carry wilt resistance). Rotate peas on a three-to-four-year cycle away from infested ground, improve drainage, and avoid moving infested soil between beds.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant a wilt-resistant variety, which most modern snow peas are (Oregon Sugar Pod II, Dwarf Gray Sugar, Mammoth Melting Sugar all resist it). Move your peas to a new spot on a three-to-four-year cycle, improve drainage, and avoid carrying infected soil from bed to bed.

diseases.name: Root rots and damping-off
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Seed that rots before emerging, and seedlings that damp off, collapsing at a water-soaked, pinched stem base. On older plants the root rot complex stunts the vines, yellows and kills the lower leaves, and rots the roots and lower stem brown. Damage is worst in cold, wet, poorly drained soil that slows germination and keeps seedlings vulnerable.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Seeds that rot before they come up, and seedlings that flop over at a pinched, water-soaked spot near the soil. On bigger plants the roots rot, the vines stunt, and the lower leaves yellow and die. It is worst in cold, wet, poorly drained soil that makes the seed sit too long before sprouting.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A complex of soilborne fungi and water molds, chiefly Pythium, Rhizoctonia, Fusarium solani, and Aphanomyces euteiches. Cold, saturated soil and root injury at planting set the stage; Aphanomyces in particular builds up in beds cropped to peas too often and severe infections kill plants outright.
diseases.cause_beginner: A group of soil fungi and water molds (including Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Aphanomyces) that attack seeds, roots, and seedlings. Cold, soggy soil and damaged roots at planting let them in, and they build up where peas are grown too often in the same spot.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no rescue for rotted seed or collapsed seedlings; replant into warmer, better-drained conditions once the soil has dried. Removing affected plants and improving drainage limits further loss, but prevention is the real lever since the organisms are already in the soil.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no saving seed or seedlings that have rotted; replant once the soil is warmer and drains better. Pulling affected plants and improving drainage help, but the main thing is preventing it, since these organisms live in the soil.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Sow into well-drained ground or raised beds rather than cold, low, wet spots, and do not sow peas into waterlogged soil. Avoid root injury at planting, rotate peas on a three-to-four-year cycle to keep Aphanomyces down, and clear crop debris after harvest. Some varieties offer partial root-rot tolerance.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant in well-drained soil or raised beds instead of cold, wet, low spots, and never sow peas into soggy ground. Avoid damaging the roots when planting, move your peas around the garden on a three-to-four-year cycle, and clear away the old plants after harvest.

diseases.name: Ascochyta blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Brown to purplish-black spots and streaks on leaves, stems, and pods, often with darker margins; a blackening at the base of the stem (foot rot) in one form, and sunken lesions on the pods that can carry the fungus into the seed. It develops in cool, wet spring and fall weather and is carried on infected seed and debris.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Brown to purple-black spots and streaks on the leaves, stems, and pods, sometimes with a blackened stem base. Sunken spots on the pods can carry the disease into the seed. It shows up in cool, wet spring and fall weather and rides in on infected seed and old plant debris.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A complex of related fungi (the Ascochyta blight complex, including Ascochyta pisi and Mycosphaerella pinodes). The fungi survive on infected seed and on pea debris in the soil, and cool, wet conditions with splashing water drive infection and spread.
diseases.cause_beginner: A group of related fungi that survive on infected seed and on old pea plants left in the soil. Cool, wet weather and splashing water spread them. Once they are on the seed, they travel with it to the next planting.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure for infected tissue; remove and destroy affected plants and all debris to limit spread. Cultural control is the mainstay for a home crop, since the disease is seed- and debris-borne.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot cure tissue that is already infected; pull and throw away (do not compost) affected plants and all the old debris to slow it down. For a home garden, prevention does most of the work, since the disease travels on seed and old plants.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant certified disease-free seed and do not save seed from an infected crop. Remove all pea debris after harvest and rotate peas off the ground for a minimum of three to four years before returning. Avoid overhead watering and working among wet vines, which splash and carry the fungus.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant certified disease-free seed and do not save seed from an infected crop. Clear away all the old pea plants after harvest, and do not grow peas in that spot for at least three to four years. Water at the base, not overhead, and stay out of the patch when the vines are wet.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Regular and even through the season, keeping the soil moist but never waterlogged. The need peaks during flowering and pod fill; before that, established vines in cool weather ask relatively little.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist but not soggy. Pay closest attention while the plants are flowering and the pods are filling out.
watering.amount_seasoned: Enough to wet the root zone roughly 6 inches down; watering deeply and less often builds deeper roots than frequent light sprinkles. Clemson advises watering to moisten the soil to a depth of 6 inches.
watering.amount_beginner: Water deeply enough to wet the soil about 6 inches down. Deep, less frequent watering beats a daily light sprinkle.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the soil level in the morning so the foliage dries before evening; this limits the powdery mildew and Ascochyta the crop is prone to. Avoid overhead watering on a trellised crop in particular.
watering.method_beginner: Water the soil, not the leaves, and do it in the morning so the plants dry off during the day. Wet leaves, especially overnight, help spread disease.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting despite wet soil, and stunted vines point to waterlogged roots and the onset of the root rots peas are prone to in cold, wet ground.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If the soil is wet but the plants still wilt or the lower leaves turn yellow, you may be overwatering. Soggy soil rots pea roots.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Drought stress during and after flowering aborts blossoms and produces small, tough, stringy pods, and it hastens the late-season decline as heat arrives.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: If plants dry out while flowering, they drop their flowers and the pods come out small and tough. Keep the water steady at that stage.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Avoid overhead watering where practical; the critical moisture window is flowering through pod fill.
watering.method_note_beginner: Try not to spray the whole plant from above. The most important time to keep water steady is when the plants are flowering and forming pods.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Flowering and pod fill are the moisture-critical stages; stress here directly cuts the crop and toughens the pods.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Flowering and pod-filling are the times peas most need steady water.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Not applicable. Peas are direct-sown in place and are not started indoors or hardened off.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: You do not need to harden off peas. They are planted straight into the garden from seed.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Direct-sow into cool, workable soil as early as the ground can be prepared in spring, and again for a fall crop. Peas resent root disturbance and germinate readily in cool soil, so transplanting offers no advantage. Sow about 1 to 1.5 inches deep; some growers presoak seed overnight to speed emergence.
start_method.notes_beginner: Plant pea seeds right where they will grow, as soon as the soil can be worked in spring and again in late summer for fall. Peas do not like their roots disturbed, so skip starting them indoors. Plant about 1 to 1.5 inches deep.

drainage.saucer_practice: Empty any saucer after watering so the pot never sits in standing water, which brings on the root rots peas are prone to in cool, wet conditions.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Use a good potting mix, not garden soil, which packs down too hard in pots.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in a little compost for fertility.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: A well-draining potting mix; avoid native garden soil, which compacts and drains poorly in containers and worsens root rot.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend in compost for baseline fertility and tilth; peas need little added nitrogen.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out faster than garden beds, so check the soil daily in warm weather and water when the top inch is dry.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Container peas still need little feeding; a little compost in the mix is usually enough.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Not applicable. Peas are a cool-season annual; they finish in one season and are not overwintered as a plant.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Not applicable. As a single-season annual, peas complete their cycle and are pulled; in mild regions a fall sowing is grown over winter in the ground, but a container crop is grown and finished within a season.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Bush and dwarf snow peas grow well in a pot at least 5 gallons and 8 inches deep. Push a few short twiggy branches or a small trellis into the pot for the tendrils to climb, plant several seeds, and keep the mix evenly moist.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Dwarf and bush snow pea types suit containers well; tall climbing varieties are awkward in pots because of their trellis height. A pot of at least 5 gallons and 8 inches deep, planted with several seeds and given a few twiggy branches or a small trellis for support, performs well with even moisture.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry faster than beds; monitor daily in warm spells and water when the top inch dries.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Feeding needs stay low in containers; compost blended into the mix usually suffices.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering container suits peas well, smoothing out the steady moisture they want through pod fill while avoiding the soggy roots they dislike.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match for peas because it keeps the water steady, which is what they like, without leaving the roots soggy.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: Match the container to the variety: a wide, shallow pot suits low bush types grown several together, while a tall climbing variety needs a deep, stable pot that will not tip under a loaded trellis. For most container growers a dwarf or bush snow pea in a broad pot is the easier choice.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Pick the pot to fit the variety. Low bush peas do well in a wide pot with several plants together; tall climbing peas need a deep, heavy pot that will not tip over once the trellis is loaded with vines. For a pot, a short bush variety is usually the easier pick.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Avoid following peas with peas or other legumes in the same bed; rotate to break the soilborne disease cycle (root rots, Fusarium, Ascochyta) that peas are prone to. Where Ascochyta or Aphanomyces root rot have appeared, extend the rotation toward four years.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Do not plant peas where peas or beans grew last year. Diseases build up in the soil and hit the next crop. If you have had root rot or blight, wait even longer, up to four years, before peas return.
rotation.good_after: Peas are an excellent crop to grow before a heavy feeder. As a legume they fix nitrogen and leave the soil in better shape for a following crop such as a leafy green, a brassica, or corn.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate peas on a roughly three-year cycle, longer where Ascochyta blight or root rot have shown up. Their nitrogen-fixing habit makes them a good predecessor for nitrogen-hungry crops.
rotation.note_beginner: Move your peas to a new spot each year, on about a three-year rotation, and longer if you have had disease trouble. Because peas feed the soil with nitrogen, whatever you plant there next will benefit.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Not recommended. Snow peas lose sweetness and crispness fast at room temperature and should be cooled promptly after picking rather than held on the counter.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Do not leave snow peas out on the counter. They go limp and lose their sweetness quickly, so cool them soon after picking.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Cool snow peas immediately after harvest to shed field heat, then refrigerate in a perforated bag. They hold good quality for about five days kept cold and humid, near 32 to 40°F at high humidity; the sugars convert to starch over time, so use them sooner rather than later.
storage.fridge_beginner: Cool the pods right after picking, then keep them in the fridge in a loosely closed bag. They stay good for about five days when kept cold and slightly damp; the longer they sit, the less sweet they get.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Snow peas freeze well for longer storage. Blanch briefly to set the color and texture, cool, and freeze within a few hours of picking for the best quality.
storage.freezer_beginner: Snow peas freeze well for keeping longer. Give them a quick dip in boiling water (blanch), cool them, and freeze within a few hours of picking for the best result.
storage.notes_seasoned: Snow peas are at their sweetest within hours of picking and are best used promptly. To hold them, cool them fast to remove field heat, keep them cold and humid, and blanch and freeze within a few hours if you want to store them beyond a few days.
storage.notes_beginner: Snow peas taste best soon after picking. To keep them, cool them fast, store them cold and slightly damp, and freeze (after a quick blanch) within a few hours if you want them to last beyond a few days.

recommended.name: Oregon Sugar Pod II
recommended.note: The standard home-garden snow pea: semi-dwarf vines around 30 inches, heavy yields of large flat pods, and broad disease resistance including powdery mildew and Fusarium wilt. The most widely recommended choice.

recommended.name: Dwarf Gray Sugar
recommended.note: Compact heirloom around 24 to 30 inches with attractive purple flowers; an early, space-saving snow pea that resists Fusarium wilt and suits containers and small beds.

recommended.name: Mammoth Melting Sugar
recommended.note: Tall climbing snow pea to 4 or 5 feet that needs a trellis; large, sweet, tender pods and Fusarium wilt resistance. Productive where there is room to support it.

recommended.name: Snowbird
recommended.note: Early, bush-type snow pea around 18 inches that bears pods in clusters of two or three for easy picking; a good quick, self-supporting choice.

recommended.name: Avalanche
recommended.note: Productive snow pea with large, sweet pods on semi-vining plants; appreciated for flavor and a reliable set.

varieties.note_seasoned: These are flat-podded snow (mangetout) peas, picked young while the pods are flat and the seeds barely formed. Do not confuse them with sugar snap peas, a separate edible-pod type bred for plump, rounded pods eaten whole once filled. Lean to powdery-mildew- and wilt-resistant varieties such as Oregon Sugar Pod II where those diseases recur, and match the variety's height to your support: bush types stand alone, tall types need a trellis.
varieties.note_beginner: These are snow peas, the flat kind you eat pod and all while the pods are still flat and the peas inside are tiny. They are different from sugar snap peas, which are plump and rounded and eaten when filled out. Oregon Sugar Pod II and Dwarf Gray Sugar are easy, dependable choices; pick a short bush type if you do not want to build a tall trellis.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare soil for about a week to ten days, then the seedling pushes up through the surface. Peas germinate in cool soil and can be sown as soon as the ground is workable, but seed sown into cold, saturated ground rots before it emerges. Emergence is quickest in soil around 55 to 65°F and slows below that; the lower limit for germination is about 40°F.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Bare soil for a week or so, then the little plants push up. Peas come up in cool soil and can go in very early, but seed planted in cold, soggy ground rots instead of sprouting. They come up fastest when the soil is around 55 to 65°F.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Sow as early as the soil can be worked, about 1 to 1.5 inches deep, into a moist but well-drained bed; do not sow into waterlogged ground. There is no benefit to soaking the bed afterward, which suffocates the seed and feeds root rot. An optional overnight presoak of the seed speeds emergence, and a pea inoculant helps nodulation where peas are new to the bed.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Plant as soon as you can work the soil, about 1 to 1.5 inches deep, in moist but well-drained ground. Do not keep the bed soggy after planting, since that rots the seed. Soaking the seeds overnight before planting can speed things up.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have your peas emerged? Note the date to track days to maturity from a real sowing rather than the seed packet.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your peas come up yet? Write down the date you first saw them break the soil.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Young plants a few inches tall putting out their first leaves and, soon, the curling tendrils that mark a climbing crop. Pea seedlings are cold-hardy and shrug off light spring frost, but they are the stage most vulnerable to cutworms, which sever them at the soil line, and to slugs in wet weather.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Small plants a few inches tall with their first leaves and the little curling tendrils that peas use to climb. Young peas handle light frost fine, but this is when cutworms can cut them off at the ground and slugs can chew them in wet weather.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Set up support now, before the vines flop: push twiggy branches or a trellis or netting in alongside even bush types, which crop better held up. Keep the bed evenly moist and weed-free, cultivate shallowly since pea roots run near the surface, and watch for toppled seedlings that signal cutworms.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Put up the support now, before the vines sprawl: a trellis, netting, or twiggy branches alongside the row, even for short types. Keep the soil evenly moist, pull weeds early, and weed shallowly so you do not damage the roots. Check for plants cut off at the ground, which means cutworms.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How is your pea stand looking? Note any gaps, cutworm damage, or the first tendrils reaching for support.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How do your young pea plants look? Note any chewed or toppled plants and whether the tendrils are reaching for the trellis.

growth_stages.name: Vine growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Steady growth as the vines climb and fill the trellis, tendrils gripping as they go. Bush types reach two to three feet and stand together; tall types climb to four or five feet. The plants are fixing much of their own nitrogen now through root nodules, so vigorous green growth, not dark, overfed lushness, is the goal.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The vines climb and fill in, their tendrils grabbing the support as they go. Short types reach two to three feet, tall types four to five. Peas make much of their own food (nitrogen) at this stage, so you want healthy green growth, not huge dark leafy vines, which usually mean too much fertilizer and fewer pods.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture steady and resist the urge to feed; peas need little nitrogen and extra now pushes foliage at the expense of pods. Guide the first tendrils onto the support, and keep the rows open for airflow to hold off powdery mildew as the weather warms.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the watering steady and do not add fertilizer now. Peas need very little, and extra just gives you big leafy vines with fewer pods. Help the first tendrils find the trellis, and keep the plants from getting crowded so air moves through them.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How are your pea vines filling in? Note their height and whether they are climbing the support cleanly.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How tall are your pea vines getting? Note how well they are climbing the trellis.

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small white (sometimes pink or purple) pea flowers open along the vines. This is a moisture-critical stage: water stress now aborts blossoms, and sustained heat above about 80°F causes the plant to drop flowers instead of setting pods. The flowers and tiny pods are far more frost-tender than the hardy seedlings were.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Small white (sometimes pink or purple) flowers open along the vines. This is an important time for water: if the plants dry out or it stays hotter than about 80°F, the flowers drop without making pods. The flowers and tiny pods are much more sensitive to frost than the young plants were.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture steady and ample through bloom; this is where water stress directly cuts the crop. Avoid overhead watering on the dense canopy. If a late frost threatens open flowers, cover the planting overnight, and in a heat wave water deeply ahead of time; the plant will set again when it cools, but the spring crop is racing the heat at this point.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the water steady and generous while the plants flower, because dry soil now means fewer peas. Water the soil, not the leaves. Cover the plants overnight if a frost threatens the open flowers, and water deeply before a heat wave. The plants set pods again once it cools, but the spring crop is running out of cool weather by now.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are your peas flowering? Note the date bloom started and any blossom drop in heat.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are your peas flowering yet? Note when the flowers opened and whether any dropped in hot weather.

growth_stages.name: Pod development
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flat pods form where the flowers were and lengthen quickly. For snow peas the pickable window is brief and early: harvest while the pods are still flat, bright, and tender, before the seeds inside begin to swell and round out the pod. Snow peas reach this stage about a week after flowering. Left on the vine they turn tough, fibrous, and starchy fast.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Flat pods form where the flowers were and grow quickly. With snow peas you want to pick them while they are still flat, bright green, and tender, before the little peas inside start to swell. They are ready about a week after the flowers open, and they get tough and stringy fast if you leave them.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Maintain even moisture right through pod fill, the payoff stage for steady watering. Begin checking the vines daily as the first pods size up, since the snow-pea window is short and the pods go from tender to tough in a few days.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist while the pods grow. Start checking the vines every day once the first pods appear, because snow peas are tender for only a short time before they get tough.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are pods forming? Note the date you first saw flat pods and how fast they are sizing up.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are pods forming? Note when you first saw them and how quickly they are growing.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flat, bright, crisp pods snapped from the vine while the seeds inside are still tiny, about 7 days after flowering. Picking every couple of days is essential: regular harvest keeps the vines flowering and producing, while pods left to mature signal the plant to stop. Most snow peas crop over a few weeks, then decline as the heat builds.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Flat, bright, crisp pods picked while the peas inside are still tiny, about a week after flowering. Pick every couple of days: regular picking keeps more pods coming, while pods left to fill up tell the plant to quit. Snow peas crop for a few weeks, then fade as it warms up.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick in the cool of the morning, holding the vine with one hand and the pod with the other so you do not tear the brittle stems. Harvest every two to three days; leaving overmature pods on the vine ends the crop early. Pull the planting once it declines in the heat and add the vines to the compost, roots left to return their nitrogen.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pick in the cool morning, holding the vine with one hand and pulling the pod with the other so you do not tear the stem. Pick every two or three days, because old pods left on the plant make it stop producing. When the vines fade in the heat, pull them up and compost them.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have you made your first picking? Log the date and how the pods sized up.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you picked your first snow peas? Note the date and how they turned out.

notifications.body_seasoned: Direct-sow snow peas as early as the soil can be worked in spring, well before the last frost; pea seedlings are cold-hardy. Sow about 1 to 1.5 inches deep into a moist, well-drained bed, and set up support at sowing.
notifications.body_beginner: Plant snow peas as soon as you can work the soil in spring, even weeks before the last frost, since young peas handle cold. Plant about 1 to 1.5 inches deep in moist, well-drained soil, and put up a trellis when you plant.

notifications.title_seasoned: Sow your next short row of peas
notifications.title_beginner: Plant your next row of peas
notifications.body_seasoned: Snow peas crop over a few weeks, then decline as the weather warms. Sow a fresh short row now, about two weeks after the last, to stretch the spring harvest. Stop in time for the crop to finish before summer heat sets in.
notifications.body_beginner: Snow peas give a crop over a few weeks, then slow down in the heat. Plant a new short row now, about two weeks after the last one, to keep peas coming. Stop early enough that the last batch finishes before it gets hot.

notifications.title_seasoned: Start checking your snow peas daily
notifications.title_beginner: Start checking your snow peas every day
notifications.body_seasoned: Most snow peas are ready about 55 to 70 days from sowing, roughly a week after flowering. Begin checking daily and pick the pods while they are flat, bright, and tender, before the seeds swell. Harvest every two to three days to keep the vines producing.
notifications.body_beginner: Most snow peas are ready about 55 to 70 days from planting, about a week after they flower. Start checking every day and pick the pods while they are flat and tender, before the peas inside swell. Pick every two or three days to keep more coming.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost is coming, protect flowering peas
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Pea seedlings shrug off light frost, but open flowers and young pods are tender and a hard frost will damage them. If frost is forecast while the vines are flowering or podding, cover the planting with row cover or sheets overnight, and pick any usable pods first.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Young pea plants handle light frost fine, but the flowers and small pods are tender and a hard frost can damage them. If frost is forecast while the plants are flowering or making pods, cover them with row cover or sheets overnight, and pick any pods that are ready first.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat will stop your peas setting pods
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot weather will stop your peas
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Sustained heat above about 80°F during bloom causes peas to drop blossoms instead of setting pods, toughens the pods that do form, and brings on powdery mildew. Keep moisture steady and water deeply ahead of a heat wave, harvest promptly, and treat the arrival of summer heat as the end of the spring crop.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: When it stays above about 80°F while peas are flowering, they drop their flowers instead of making pods, the pods that form turn tough, and powdery mildew sets in. Keep the water steady, water deeply before the heat, pick what is ready, and treat the first real heat as the end of the spring crop.

germination.text_seasoned: Sow peas as soon as the soil can be worked, but into moist, well-drained ground, not cold mud. Pea seed germinates from about 40°F up and fastest at 55 to 65°F, yet it rots in cold, saturated soil, the most common cause of a thin stand. Raised beds and good drainage matter more than calendar date.
germination.text_beginner: Plant peas as early as you can work the soil, but make sure it drains well and is not soggy. Pea seeds sprout in cool soil but rot in cold, wet mud, which is the usual reason for gaps in the row. Good drainage matters more than planting on an exact date.
germination.author: plant

germination.text_seasoned: Peas fix their own nitrogen with Rhizobium bacteria on their roots. Where peas or beans have grown before, those bacteria are already present; in a new bed, an inexpensive seed inoculant can improve nodulation. It is optional, not required, and no substitute for good drainage and tilth.
germination.text_beginner: Peas make their own nitrogen with the help of tiny bacteria on their roots. If peas or beans have grown in your bed before, the bacteria are already there. In a brand-new bed you can coat the seed with a pea inoculant powder to help, but it is optional.
germination.author: plant

seedling.text_seasoned: Put the support in early, at or just after sowing. Even bush peas crop better and stay cleaner held up off the ground, and tall types must have a trellis or netting before the vines start to sprawl. Setting it up later risks tearing the brittle vines and damaging shallow roots.
seedling.text_beginner: Put up the trellis or netting early, when you plant or right after. Even short peas do better held up off the ground, and tall ones need support before they start to flop. If you wait too long you can tear the vines or hurt the roots putting it in.
seedling.author: plant

vegetative.text_seasoned: Hold off on nitrogen. As legumes, peas fix much of their own through root nodules, and extra nitrogen now drives leafy vine growth at the expense of flowers and pods. A little compost or balanced fertilizer worked in before sowing is all peas need.
vegetative.text_beginner: Do not add nitrogen fertilizer now. Peas make much of their own from the air, and extra fertilizer just gives you big leafy vines with fewer peas. A little compost mixed into the bed before planting is all they need.
vegetative.author: plant

flowering.text_seasoned: Keep moisture steady and ample through bloom. Flowering and pod fill are the moisture-critical stages, and water stress now aborts blossoms and shrinks the crop. Water at the soil in the morning, not overhead, to keep the canopy dry and slow powdery mildew.
flowering.text_beginner: Keep the water steady and generous while the plants flower. Flowering and pod-filling are when peas most need water, and letting them dry out now means fewer peas. Water the soil in the morning, not the leaves, to keep disease down.
flowering.author: plant

flowering.text_seasoned: The spring crop is racing the heat. Once sustained temperatures pass about 80°F, peas drop blossoms instead of setting pods, so a planting that flowers into early summer heat sets poorly. Sow early, and where summers come on fast, lean to the earliest, shortest-season snow peas.
flowering.text_beginner: The spring crop is in a race with the heat. Once it stays above about 80°F, peas drop their flowers instead of making pods, so a planting that flowers as summer arrives makes few peas. Plant early, and where summer comes fast, pick the earliest, quickest snow peas.
flowering.author: plant

pod_development.text_seasoned: Pick snow peas while the pods are still flat, before the seeds swell. The whole point of a snow pea is the tender flat pod; once the peas inside round out, the pod turns tough and starchy. They reach pickable size about a week after flowering, so start checking early.
pod_development.text_beginner: Pick snow peas while the pods are still flat, before the peas inside fill out. That flat, tender pod is the whole point; once the peas swell, the pod gets tough. They are ready about a week after flowering, so start checking early.
pod_development.author: plant

harvest.text_seasoned: Pick every two to three days. Snow peas crop over a short window, and leaving mature pods on the vine signals the plant to stop flowering and ends the crop early. Frequent picking keeps the vines producing and catches the pods at their flat, sweet, tender best.
harvest.text_beginner: Pick every two or three days. Snow peas crop for a short time, and leaving old pods on the vine tells the plant to quit. Picking often keeps more pods coming and catches them while they are flat, sweet, and tender.
harvest.author: plant

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Snow peas yield modestly per plant, so they are grown in rows or blocks rather than singly. Utah State puts a snow or snap pea crop at about 3 to 4 pounds of pods per 10 feet of row over its cropping window; a trellised double row in a small bed gives a steady picking for several weeks.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Each pea plant gives only a modest amount, so peas are grown in rows, not one at a time. A 10-foot row of snow peas gives about 3 to 4 pounds of pods over its picking weeks.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Snow peas come on over a few weeks and then decline as the weather warms. Most of a sowing's crop arrives in that window, which is why a couple of succession sowings a week or two apart, and a separate fall crop where summers allow, are the way to stretch the supply.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Snow peas crop for a few weeks, then slow down as it heats up. Most of the harvest comes in that stretch, so planting a second short row a week or two later, and a fall crop where it works, keeps peas coming longer.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Snow peas are a rewarding first-year crop: cold-hardy seed sown straight into early-spring soil, quick to a flat, sweet pod in about 55 to 70 days, and forgiving of cool weather. The main levers on yield are sowing early enough to beat the heat, giving the vines support, and picking often while the pods are flat.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Snow peas are a great first-year crop. You plant the seed straight into cool spring soil, and in about two months you are picking flat, sweet pods. The main things that affect your harvest are planting early before the heat, giving the vines a trellis, and picking often while the pods are flat.
factors_seasoned: Sowing early enough to flower and fill pods before summer heat (the spring crop is racing the heat; pods do not set above about 80°F)
Steady moisture through flowering and pod fill (drought here aborts blossoms and toughens pods)
Support for the vines (held up, peas crop better, stay cleaner, and resist mildew through better airflow)
Regular picking (leaving mature pods on the vine signals the plant to stop flowering and ends the crop early)

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No reliable extension or peer-reviewed evidence supports timing pea planting or harvest by moon phase. Sow peas by soil workability and temperature, by day length, and by your frost dates instead, not by the lunar cycle.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Flowers dropped or no pods set
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Flowers fell off without making pods
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The vines flowered but set few or no pods, because the weather turned too warm. Once sustained temperatures pass about 80°F, peas abort their blossoms instead of setting pods, and any pods that form are tough and stringy. It is the classic fate of a spring crop sown too late, caught by early-summer heat, and it is a weather problem, not a disease.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The plants flowered but made few or no pods, because it got too hot. Once it stays above about 80°F, peas drop their flowers instead of making pods, and the few that form are tough. This usually happens to a spring crop planted too late that runs into summer heat. It is a weather problem, not a disease.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sow as early as the soil can be worked so the crop flowers and fills pods in cool weather, well before summer heat. Where summers come on fast, choose the earliest short-season snow peas, and add a fall sowing timed so the crop matures in cooling weather.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant as early as you can work the soil so the peas flower and fill in cool weather, before the heat. Where summer comes fast, pick the quickest snow peas, and try a fall planting timed to finish as it cools down.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Seed rotted or came up poorly
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Seeds rotted or did not come up
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The seed was sown into cold, saturated soil and rotted before emerging, or came up as a thin, patchy stand. Peas tolerate cool soil, but waterlogged ground starves the seed of oxygen and feeds the soilborne root rots, so a too-early sowing into a wet, poorly drained bed is the usual cause of gaps.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The seed went into cold, soggy soil and rotted instead of sprouting, or came up thin and patchy. Peas like cool soil, but wet, poorly drained ground rots the seed and lets soil fungi get to it. Planting too early into a wet bed is the usual reason for gaps.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sow into well-drained ground or raised beds rather than cold, low, wet spots, and wait for the surface to be workable rather than muddy. Plant about 1 to 1.5 inches deep, do not keep the bed soggy, and an overnight presoak helps the seed get up and out of harm's way faster.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant in well-drained soil or raised beds instead of cold, wet, low spots, and wait until the soil is workable, not muddy. Plant about 1 to 1.5 inches deep, do not keep the bed soggy, and soaking the seeds overnight helps them come up faster.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: White powdery coating late in the crop
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: White powdery dust on the leaves and pods
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: A white to gray powdery film spread over the leaves, stems, and pods as the crop ran into warm days and cool nights, the conditions that favor powdery mildew. It is the classic end-of-season pea disease; it weakens the vines, taints the pods, and is hard to stop once it has covered the foliage.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: A white to gray powdery dust spread over the leaves and pods as the weather warmed up and the nights stayed cool. This is powdery mildew, the classic late-season pea disease. It weakens the plants and spoils the pods, and it is hard to stop once it has spread.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant powdery-mildew-resistant varieties, the most effective step (Oregon Sugar Pod II and many modern snow peas resist it), and sow early so the crop finishes before the mildew weather. Give the vines a trellis and room for airflow, water at the soil, and pull a spent spring planting promptly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant a resistant variety, which works best (Oregon Sugar Pod II and many newer snow peas resist mildew), and plant early so the crop finishes before mildew weather arrives. Give the vines a trellis and room to breathe, water at the soil, and pull the old plants once the spring crop is done.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Pods tough, stringy, or starchy
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Pods came out tough and stringy
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The snow pods came out fibrous and starchy rather than flat and tender, usually because they were left on the vine past their brief pickable window, when the swelling seeds toughen the pod, or because heat and drought stress hit during pod fill. Snow peas are a pick-young crop and go from tender to tough in a few days.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The pods came out tough and stringy instead of flat and tender, usually because they were left on the vine too long, until the peas inside swelled, or because heat and dry soil hit while the pods were filling. Snow peas need to be picked young and go from tender to tough in just a few days.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Pick every two to three days while the pods are still flat and bright, before the seeds round out, starting about a week after flowering. Keep moisture steady through pod fill, and sow early so the pods size up in cool rather than hot weather.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Pick every two or three days while the pods are still flat, before the peas swell, starting about a week after the flowers open. Keep the water steady while the pods fill, and plant early so they grow in cool weather, not heat.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Snow peas crop over a short window and then decline in the heat, so sow small batches a week or two apart through the cool spring window rather than all at once, and again for fall where summers allow. In hot regions skip summer entirely and succession-sow through the cool fall, winter, and early spring.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: Plant a little patch of snow peas every week or two instead of all at once, so you get a steady supply before the heat ends them. Do this through cool spring, and again in late summer for fall where it works. In hot areas, skip summer and keep sowing through the cool months.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: snow_peas_author_fresh_pilot (Claude Code lane authoring, 2026-06-29). Authored from the snow-peas shell, modeled STRUCTURALLY on the certified green-beans-bush legume template, with the calendar INVERTED to a cool-season pattern (spinach gate-clean skeleton). All pea biology re-derived from live T1 extension sources (Clemson Garden Peas, USU Peas in the Garden, UMN Growing peas, UMD Peas, UC IPM Peas, WSU PNW Pea, Cornell disease-resistant pea varieties). DRAFT for daily biology-fidelity review, NOT certified: launch flags false. Key snow-peas-vs-green-beans refits: COOL-season not warm (the calendar inverts; sown early spring as soon as soil is workable and again in fall, NOT summer); cold-hardy seedlings but frost-tender flowers/pods; pods stop setting above about 80F so summer is the hot exclusion (heat_pause where hot, season_over in cool maritime CA); DTM 55-70; pH 6.0-7.0; spacing 1-3 in; germination from 40F, optimal 55-65F; climbing types need a trellis; edible flat immature pods (snow/mangetout) picked young about 7 days after flowering, distinct from the sugar-snap cousin; pea-specific pests (pea aphid, pea weevil, armyworms/cutworms, thrips) and diseases (powdery mildew, Fusarium wilt, root rot complex, Ascochyta blight). archetype cool_season_annual (matches the certified broccoli anchor + the gate-clean cabbage/spinach examples, NOT green-beans' warm_season_fruiting; see NOTES flag). successions_realized is CC-derived (not hand-authored). See snow_peas_NOTES.md for modeled values and flags.

open_findings.summary: archetype set to cool_season_annual, NOT green-beans-bush's warm_season_fruiting. The task modeled snow peas structurally on the green-beans legume template but the dataset's archetype encodes SEASON, not botanical family. Snow peas are cool-season, so cool_season_annual is the correct, gate-proven value.
open_findings.basis: Matches the certified broccoli anchor (cool_season_annual / frost_anchored) and the gate-clean cabbage and spinach examples, and matches the value already declared in the snow-peas shell. The gate dispatches on calendar_basis (frost_anchored, same for both); archetype only drives the numeric_sanity spacing bound (annual, correct here). whole_crop_gate PASS confirms.

open_findings.summary: germination_temp_f [40, 75] is modeled. USU gives a 40F minimum and 55 to 65F optimal emergence and states soil should stay below 80F for best germination; UMD and UMN give a 40F floor. No single T1 page tables an explicit min and max, so [40, 75] was synthesized with the decline toward 75 to 80F stated in prose.
open_findings.basis: Consistent with the cited USU, UMD, and UMN figures; the operative facts (sowable from about 40F, fastest at 55 to 65F, declining as soil warms) are sourced.

open_findings.summary: days_to_maturity [55, 70] (mid 62), spacing_inches [1, 3], and pH preferred [6.0, 7.0] / tolerated [6.0, 7.5] were chosen from a spread of T1 figures: DTM Clemson 55 to 70, USU 60 to 70, UMD 50 to 70; spacing USU and Clemson 1 to 2 in, UMD 1 to 3 in; pH Clemson 6.0 to 6.5, UMD and UMN up to 7.5.
open_findings.basis: Every endpoint sits within at least one cited T1 source's range; pH prose leads with 6.0 to 7.0 to satisfy the A34 cross-consistency check against preferred_range.

open_findings.summary: Per-region planting windows are modeled on the cool-season regional planting calendars and corroborated against the directly-read pea sources (Clemson southern timing Feb to Mar + Aug to Nov, UC IPM California fall and spring, USU and UMN northern spring, UF Florida and UAriz desert winter). At monthly granularity the gate-clean spinach cool-season skeleton (same 10 regions and zones, same summer heat exclusion) was reused for the calendar token shapes, plant_out, harvest, and heat_pause months.
open_findings.basis: Peas and spinach share the cool-season climate logic (sow early spring and fall, excluded by summer heat), and the independently-read pea windows match the spinach windows. Calendar/heat_pause values are crop-specific (release_verify G confirms none byte-identical to the reference).

open_findings.summary: Regional HARVEST months are DERIVED, not directly tabled per region: plant windows are sourced, and harvest spans were computed from the plant window plus the 55 to 70 day maturity, pea frost tolerance, and the summer heat ceiling. Peas mature about two weeks later than spinach, usually within the same calendar month at this granularity.
open_findings.basis: Conservative monthly rounding; the daily review's source-truth sample is the backstop for the exact per-region harvest boundaries.

open_findings.summary: The summer gap is a BACKED heat_pause object in the northern tier and all genuinely-hot regions (peas stop setting pods above about 80F, a true thermal exclusion), and season_over only in cool-maritime ca_north_coast (foggy summers stay cool, no heat exclusion). This mirrors the gate-clean spinach token choices and the task's instruction to back the heat where hot.
open_findings.basis: Each heat_pause carries months + a pea-physiology basis_seasoned (about 80F ceiling + powdery mildew) + USU and UMN sources with live anchoring URLs (A28 PASS). ca_north_coast's season_over is the documented cool-maritime exception.

Three are PDFs that are unreadable under the no-pdftotext sourcing rule and were cited from their catalog URLs without parsing: uariz_ext_az1005, tamu_agrilife_fall_veg, uhawaii_ctahr_b91. Pest detail (pea aphid, pea weevil, armyworms/cutworms, thrips) was instead sourced from UC IPM Peas, USU Peas in the Garden, WSU PNW Pea, and Clemson Garden Peas, all directly read.

open_findings.summary: UMD's Garden Peas page states peas are 'heavy users of nitrogen (peas fix little nitrogen),' which conflicts with the consensus (USU, UMN, Clemson, general legume biology): peas fix much of their own nitrogen and need little feeding. The record follows the consensus low-nitrogen legume framing and cites USU and Clemson (5-10-10 at 3 lb/100 sq ft pre-plant, avoid excess N) for fertilizer.
open_findings.basis: The low-N legume framing is the dominant, better-supported position and matches the green-beans legume template; flagged for the biology-fidelity review to confirm the call.

3.zone_notes: The coldest zone: sow peas as soon as the ground can be worked in spring, around late April, for a harvest in June before midsummer heat stops the vines; July is too hot, so the bed rests, and a late-summer sowing gives a fall crop the frost-hardy plants carry into October.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion for peas, not a frost gap. Snow peas grow and set pods best between about 55 and 70°F and stop producing once midsummer heat pushes past roughly 80°F, when the vines fade and powdery mildew moves in. The spring sowing is harvested before the heat arrives, the bed then rests through the hottest weeks, and a fresh sowing goes in as the weather cools for a fall crop, so summer is left out of the planting calendar.

4.zone_notes: Sow at snowmelt in spring for a June harvest before the heat, leave the hot midsummer out, then sow again in late summer for a fall crop that ripens as the weather cools and shrugs off the first light frosts.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In cold regions, grow snow peas in spring, and again in fall where you can. Plant as soon as you can work the soil in spring, even before the last frost, because young peas handle cold. You harvest in early summer, then the heat ends the crop. Plant again in late summer for a fall crop, since peas take the first light frosts. In the mildest cold zones a fall planting can grow through the cool months for a winter and spring harvest.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Across the cold northern tier snow peas are a spring crop, with a second fall crop where the season allows. Sow as soon as the ground can be worked, even weeks before the last frost, since pea seedlings are cold-hardy; the spring crop is harvested in late spring to early summer and then ends as midsummer heat stops the vines and brings on powdery mildew. The hot weeks are left out, and a late-summer sowing gives a fall crop the frost-tolerant plants carry into autumn. From the milder end of the region (zone 7) a fall sowing can be grown through the cool months for a winter-into-spring harvest. The summer gap here is a true heat exclusion for peas, backed at each cell.

8.zone_notes: Peas are a cool-season crop on the Gulf and coastal plain: sow in February for a spring harvest and again from September into October for a fall and early-winter crop. The hot, humid summer is left out, when peas will not flower or set pods.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap. Snow peas are a cool-season legume that sets pods best between about 55 and 70°F and stops producing once daytime temperatures climb past about 80°F. Through this region's hot months the vines quit flowering, any pods that form turn tough and stringy, and powdery mildew takes hold, so peas are grown in the cool season here and the summer is left out of the planting calendar.

9.zone_notes: In the warm coastal zone 9 the productive window is the cool fall through spring, with only a short February sowing for spring; the long hot season from May through August excludes peas entirely.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a long heat exclusion, not a frost gap. Snow peas grow and set pods best between about 55 and 70°F and shut down above about 80°F. Through the long, intense heat of this region's summer the vines cannot flower or set pods and quickly succumb to mildew and stress, so peas are grown as a cool-season crop from fall into spring and the whole hot half of the year is left out of the planting calendar.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: Along the Gulf and coastal plain, grow snow peas in the cool months, fall through spring, not in summer. Plant in fall for a fall and winter harvest, and again in February for spring. Summer is too hot, the plants stop making pods.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: On the Gulf and southeastern coastal plain snow peas are a cool-season crop grown fall through spring. Sow from September into October for a fall and winter harvest and again in February for spring; the hot, humid summer is a true heat exclusion, when peas drop their flowers and powdery mildew takes hold, so summer is left out of the calendar in both zones.

8.zone_notes: In the interior valleys peas are a cool-season crop sown in late winter (February to March) and again in fall (September to October), bracketing the hot summer when the vines cannot set pods.
