ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In the inland valleys, grow snow peas in late winter and in fall, not summer. Plant in February or March for spring, and again in fall for a winter crop. The hot summer is left out, since peas stop making pods in the heat.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: In California's interior valleys snow peas are grown in the cool seasons that bracket the hot summer: a late-winter sowing (February to March) for a spring harvest, and a fall sowing (September to October) for a harvest through the mild winter. The long, hot summer from June into September excludes peas, which will not set pods above about 80°F.

9.zone_notes: Cool, foggy summers let peas grow over most of the year on the north coast: sow late winter through spring and again in late summer, for harvests spring into early summer and again fall into winter. The brief warm transition in midsummer is the only real gap, and there is no hot exclusion.

10.zone_notes: The mild maritime climate keeps peas going through much of the year: plant late winter through spring and again in late summer, harvesting spring and early summer, then fall through winter. Summers stay cool enough that peas are limited more by the turn of the season than by heat.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: On the cool north coast, you can grow snow peas through much of the year. Plant from late winter into spring and again in late summer. The foggy summers stay cool enough that peas keep going, so there is no hot-summer gap here, just a short warm break.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: On the cool, foggy north coast snow peas can be grown over most of the year. Sow from late winter through spring and again in late summer, for harvests spring into early summer and again from fall through winter. Summers stay cool enough here that peas are limited more by the turn of the season than by heat, so this region carries no summer heat exclusion, only a brief warm transition.

ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: In California's desert valleys snow peas are a winter crop. Sow in October and November for a harvest from December through April, and leave out the long, intense heat from May into September, a true heat exclusion when peas cannot flower or set pods.

Through this region's hot months the vines quit flowering, any pods that form turn tough and stringy, and powdery mildew takes hold, so peas are grown in the cool season here and the summer is left out of the planting calendar.

warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: In this warm, dry region, grow snow peas in two short cool windows. Plant in late winter for a spring harvest and again in early fall for an autumn crop. The hot summer and the cold of deep winter are both left out.
warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: In southern New Mexico and West Texas snow peas are squeezed into two short cool windows that dodge both the cold winter and the hot summer: a late-winter sowing (February to March) for an April and May harvest, and an early-fall sowing for an October and November crop. The hot midsummer is a heat exclusion and the deep winter is frost-bracketed.

A fall sowing can give a winter-into-early-spring harvest, while the warm lowland weather excludes them most of the year. This window is modeled on cool-season and elevation guidance and is honestly low-confidence in the tropics; New Zealand spinach-style heat-tolerant substitutes are more dependable in the warm lowlands.

crops.description_seasoned: Snow peas (Pisum sativum) are a cool-season, frost-hardy legume grown for their flat, edible immature pods, picked young before the seeds swell (the mangetout type). Unlike warm-season beans, peas are sown as early as the soil can be worked in spring and again in fall, and they decline once summer heat passes about 80°F, so the season runs opposite a bean's. Climbing types need a trellis while bush types stand together; as a legume the crop fixes much of its own nitrogen and asks little feeding, reaching a flat, sweet pod in about 55 to 70 days. They are distinct from the sugar-snap pea, a cousin grown for plump, rounded pods eaten whole when filled.
crops.description_beginner: Snow peas are the flat, tender peas you eat pod and all, stir-fried or raw, picked while the pods are still flat and the peas inside are tiny. They are a cool-weather crop: you plant the seeds straight in the garden as soon as the soil can be worked in spring, and again in late summer for fall, not in the heat of summer. Young plants handle frost, but the vines fade once it gets hot. Tall kinds need a trellis to climb; short kinds hold each other up. They go from seed to harvest in about two months and, like all peas, feed the soil with nitrogen. They are a close cousin of the plumper sugar snap pea.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Pick snow peas while the pods are flat, bright, and tender, before the seeds inside begin to swell, about a week after flowering. Harvesting every couple of days keeps the vines producing and catches the pods at peak sweetness.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Snow peas are ready when the pods are flat, bright green, and tender, before you can see the peas swelling inside, about a week after the flowers open. Pick every few days to keep more pods coming.

crops.name: Broad Beans / Fava

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Fava beans grow in most garden soil as long as it drains well. They like a fertile loam with some compost worked in, but they are not fussy and will handle heavier clay loam or lighter sandy soil. The one thing to avoid is cold, soggy ground, because the large seeds rot easily when they sit in wet soil before sprouting. If your bed stays wet after rain, add compost or plant on a raised bed.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Fava beans do best on a well-drained silt loam or loam with compost worked in, but they are adaptable and tolerate clay, loam, and sand, and they are salt tolerant once established. Good drainage is the priority: the big flat seeds are slow to germinate in cool soil and rot readily if sown into cold, saturated ground. As a legume, fava fixes much of its own nitrogen through root nodules, so the bed needs tilth and fertility more than heavy feeding. Because favas are often used as a cover crop and green manure, they in turn leave the soil looser and richer for what follows.

ph.note_beginner: Fava beans grow best in soil from about 6.0 to 6.8, which is slightly acidic to neutral, and they tolerate up to about 7.5. Most garden beds are already in a good range. If a soil test reads strongly acidic, mix in a little lime before planting.
ph.note_seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 6.8, slightly acidic to neutral, with tolerance up to roughly 7.5. Fava beans are not demanding about pH, but like other legumes they nodulate and fix nitrogen best in this near-neutral range. A soil test is the reliable way to confirm pH and baseline fertility before sowing; lime an overly acidic plot the season before.

fertilizer.type: balanced pre-plant, little to no nitrogen
fertilizer.timing: work a little compost or balanced fertilizer into the bed before sowing
fertilizer.example_product: 5-10-10 pre-plant
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Fava beans are light feeders. As a legume, fava fixes much of its own nitrogen through Rhizobium nodules on the roots, so heavy nitrogen drives leafy stalk growth at the expense of pods and can make plants more prone to aphids and disease. Without a soil test, work a little compost or balanced fertilizer into the bed before sowing and leave it at that. Adequate potassium supports the plant against chocolate spot. An inoculant of the correct Rhizobium can help nodulation where favas or vetch have not grown before, but it is optional.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Fava beans make much of their own food from the air, so they barely need fertilizer. Mix a little compost or a balanced fertilizer into the bed before you plant and that is enough. Too much fertilizer gives you tall leafy plants but fewer pods, and it can attract aphids. You can coat the seed with a bean or pea inoculant powder to help the roots make nitrogen, but it is optional.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced 5-10-10 worked in before sowing if no soil test is available; skip added nitrogen, which favas supply themselves.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: A balanced fertilizer like 5-10-10 mixed into the bed before planting is plenty; skip extra nitrogen.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A modest pre-plant application of a balanced fertilizer such as 5-10-10, worked into the bed before sowing when no soil test is available; favas need no nitrogen side-dressing.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A small amount of balanced fertilizer such as 5-10-10 mixed into the bed before planting; no need to feed again during the season.

companions.note_beginner: Fava beans get along with most cool-season vegetables and, because they leave nitrogen in the soil, they make a good crop to grow before a leafy green or a brassica. Many growers plant summer savory nearby, which is the traditional herb partner for favas. As with peas, the pairing to be cautious about is planting favas right next to onions or garlic.
companions.note_seasoned: As a nitrogen-fixing legume and a common cover crop, favas leave the bed richer for what follows and pair naturally with the other cool-season crops that share their spring and fall windows: brassicas, potatoes, lettuce, and spinach are traditional bed-mates that benefit from the nitrogen. Summer savory is the classic herb companion, long grown alongside broad beans and said by many growers to help deter the black bean aphid. The traditional caution, as with all legumes, is to keep favas away from the alliums (onion, garlic), which are widely held to interfere with the root bacteria the plant depends on to fix nitrogen.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Potato
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: A classic cool-season neighbor; the favas add nitrogen the potatoes can use, and the two share the same early season.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Long-standing cool-season companion pairing; favas fix nitrogen that benefits a following or neighboring heavy feeder like potato. Traditional/medium: grounded in shared conditions and the legume nitrogen benefit, not a measured pest trial.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Potatoes and favas are a traditional pairing that share the cool early season, and the favas' nitrogen fixation lightly benefits the potato, a heavier feeder. It is a compatibility and soil-benefit pairing rather than a measured pest defense.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Summer savory
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: The traditional herb partner for broad beans; many growers plant it alongside and say it helps keep black bean aphids down.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Summer savory is the classic culinary and companion herb for broad beans in long-standing garden tradition, often credited with deterring black bean aphid; the deterrent effect is traditional, not experimentally established here.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Summer savory is the classic companion herb for broad beans, grown alongside them for centuries as both a culinary match and, by tradition, a deterrent for the black bean aphid that plagues favas. Treat the aphid-deterrent claim as hedged garden tradition rather than a measured effect, but the pairing is harmless and useful in the kitchen.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Lettuce
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Lettuce shares favas' cool-season timing and stays low, tucking in along the base of the taller bean plants.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Lettuce and favas share cool-season conditions and occupy different layers (low leafy crop under the upright bean); a sound shared-conditions compatibility by close analogy to other cool-season interplants. Likely rather than research_backed.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Lettuce slots in below the upright fava plants, sharing the same cool-season window and even moisture while occupying a lower layer of the bed. As the favas fill out they cast light shade that can delay lettuce bolting into spring. It is a compatibility pairing on shared-conditions grounds.

good_seasoned.name: Potato
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional cool-season pairing: favas fix nitrogen that benefits the heavier-feeding potato, and both share the early season.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Long-standing companion pairing; legume nitrogen benefit to a neighboring heavy feeder. Not experimentally quantified here.

good_seasoned.name: Summer savory
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: The historic companion herb for broad beans, traditionally credited with helping deter the black bean aphid; a harmless, useful pairing framed as tradition.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Centuries-old broad-bean companion herb; aphid-deterrent effect is traditional, not established here.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Onion
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Onions and other alliums are traditionally kept away from beans and favas, which are said to grow poorly near them.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: The allium-versus-legume mechanism reported for beans and peas: allium sulfur compounds are held to disrupt the Rhizobium bacteria the legume depends on to fix nitrogen. Mechanistic/medium: a repeatedly cited mechanism, not a controlled fava-yield trial opened this session.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Onions next to favas is the better-grounded of the traditional 'bad' pairings. Alliums release antibacterial sulfur compounds widely held to interfere with the Rhizobium bacteria on legume roots, the bacteria favas rely on to fix nitrogen, so keep them in separate parts of the bed. The useful corollary is that favas grown before an allium crop leave the soil better for it.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Garlic
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Like onions, garlic is a traditional bad neighbor for favas and other legumes.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Garlic is an allium with the same antibacterial sulfur chemistry as onion; same Rhizobium-disruption mechanism. Mechanistic/medium for the same reasons.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Garlic acts on favas the way onions do. As an allium it gives off antibacterial sulfur compounds held to disrupt the nitrogen-fixing bacteria on the roots, so treat garlic and favas as bed-mates to keep apart, and use the fava-then-allium rotation to your advantage instead.

bad_seasoned.name: Onion
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Alliums are the classic traditional caution near legumes; the pairing is widely advised against, attributed to allium compounds interfering with the plant's nitrogen-fixing bacteria.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Long-standing allium-versus-legume caution; mechanism plausible but not experimentally established here.

bad_seasoned.name: Garlic
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: As with onion, garlic is traditionally kept apart from favas and other legumes.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Allium caution, traditional.

pests.name: Black bean aphid
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Dense colonies of small, matte-black aphids packed onto the growing tips, flower trusses, and the undersides of the upper leaves, arriving as the weather warms. Heavy feeding curls and stunts the new growth, drops blossoms, and coats the plant in sticky honeydew that turns to black sooty mold. The black bean aphid is the signature pest of favas, and beyond direct damage it spreads bean and legume viruses.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Thick clusters of tiny black insects packed onto the growing tips, flower stalks, and undersides of the top leaves, showing up as it warms up in spring. They curl and stunt the new growth, knock off flowers, and leave a sticky coating that turns black and moldy. This is the classic fava pest, and it also spreads plant viruses, so catch it early.
pests.cause_seasoned: The black bean aphid (Aphis fabae), a dark green to black, soft-bodied aphid with a dark head and cornicles that builds up explosively on favas as spring warms. It reproduces very fast, so colonies form on the succulent growing tips before natural enemies catch up, which is why favas are its namesake host.
pests.cause_beginner: The black bean aphid, a dark, soft-bodied aphid that multiplies very fast on favas as the weather warms. It swarms the tender growing tips before helpful insects like ladybugs can catch up, and favas are its favorite host.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Once the lower pods have set, pinch out the soft growing tip of each plant: this removes the tender shoot the aphids concentrate on and the bulk of the colony with it, a standard broad-bean tactic. Knock remaining colonies off with a strong spray of water or treat with insecticidal soap on contact. Lady beetles, lacewings, and parasitic wasps usually finish the job; act early, since the real risk is virus spread.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Once the lowest pods have set, pinch off the soft growing tip of each plant, which is where the aphids gather, and you remove most of the colony at once. Blast the rest off with a strong spray of water or use insecticidal soap. Ladybugs and other helpers usually clean up the rest. Deal with them early, because they spread viruses.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Sow early so the crop is well grown and podding before the spring aphid flights peak, and grow summer savory nearby by tradition. Avoid overfeeding with nitrogen, which produces the soft, lush growth aphids favor, and lay reflective mulch to disorient them. Conserve natural enemies by not spraying broadly, and pinch the tips promptly once pods have set.
pests.prevention_beginner: Plant early so the favas are strong and podding before the aphids peak, and try planting summer savory alongside as tradition suggests. Do not overfeed with fertilizer, since soft new growth is exactly what aphids like, and lay reflective mulch to confuse them. Pinch off the growing tips once the lower pods have set to take away their favorite spot.

pests.name: Pea and bean weevil
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Neat, half-moon notches chewed from the leaf margins of young plants, which line up into a scalloped edge as the small weevils feed. The above-ground notching is mostly cosmetic on established plants, but the hidden damage matters: the larvae feed underground on the root nodules, which inhibits nitrogen fixation and can set back a young, cool-soil crop.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Neat half-circle notches chewed out of the edges of the leaves on young plants, lining up into a scalloped look. The leaf notching alone does not hurt a strong plant much, but the grubs feed underground on the root nodules, which cuts the plant's own nitrogen supply and can slow a young crop.
pests.cause_seasoned: The pea and bean weevil (Sitona lineatus), an elongate light-brown weevil with pale stripes down its back and a short snout. Adults overwinter and move onto favas and peas as they emerge; the larvae develop on the root nodules. In mild-winter regions the adults do not fully diapause, so they are present as soon as the crop comes up, and larval feeding is worst from spring into early summer.
pests.cause_beginner: The pea and bean weevil (Sitona lineatus), a small brown striped weevil. The adults spend the winter nearby and move onto young favas and peas, and their grubs feed on the root nodules underground. Where winters are mild they are around as soon as the plants come up.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Vigorous plants outgrow the leaf notching, so a strong, well-fed stand is the main defense; keep young plants growing steadily. A floating row cover over emerging seedlings keeps adults off during the vulnerable stage. Handpicking is impractical, but conserving ground beetles and other natural enemies helps hold numbers down.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Healthy, fast-growing plants shrug off the leaf notching, so keep young favas growing well. A light row cover over the seedlings keeps the weevils off while the plants are small and most at risk. Encouraging beneficial ground insects helps keep them in check.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Sow into warm-enough soil so seedlings grow away quickly past the vulnerable stage, and rotate favas and peas away from last year's ground. Clear crop debris that shelters overwintering adults, and protect emerging seedlings with a row cover where the weevil is established.
pests.prevention_beginner: Plant so the seedlings come up and grow quickly past the tender stage, and move your favas and peas to a new spot each year. Clear away old plant debris where the weevils hide over winter, and cover young seedlings with a row cover if these weevils are a problem where you are.

pests.name: Bean seed fly
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Poor, patchy emergence with gaps in the row, and seeds that rot in the ground before sprouting; digging up a gap turns up a hollowed, rotting seed with small, pale maggots inside. Seedlings that do emerge may be weak or damaged. The damage is worst in cold, wet soil rich in fresh organic matter, exactly the conditions favas are often sown into after a cover crop.
pests.symptoms_beginner: The seed comes up thin and patchy, with gaps in the row, and if you dig into a gap you find a rotted seed with small pale maggots in it. Any seedlings that do come up may be weak. It is worst when the seed is sown into cold, wet soil that has a lot of fresh compost or crop residue in it.
pests.cause_seasoned: The bean seed fly, or seedcorn maggot (Delia platura), a small gray fly whose maggots burrow into germinating bean seed and prevent it from emerging. The flies are drawn to decaying organic matter and lay eggs in cool, moist, recently worked soil; cold, wet conditions that slow germination leave the seed exposed to attack for longer and are the main risk factor.
pests.cause_beginner: The bean seed fly (also called seedcorn maggot), a small gray fly whose maggots tunnel into the sprouting seed. The flies are attracted to rotting compost and manure, and they attack most when cold, wet soil makes the seed sit for a long time before it sprouts.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no rescue for a seed already hollowed out; replant the gaps once the soil is warmer and drier so the new seed germinates fast and outruns attack. Sowing shallowly into well-drained, workable soil, and waiting for the ground to warm before sowing where the fly is a known problem, is the practical control.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot save a seed that has already been eaten out, so replant the gaps once the soil is warmer and drains better and the new seed can sprout quickly. Planting into workable, warmer soil rather than cold mud is the main way to avoid it.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Sow into a firm, well-drained seedbed once the soil is workable rather than cold and saturated, and let coarse fresh residue or manure break down well before sowing rather than turning it in just ahead of the crop. Shallow sowing that speeds emergence, and warmer soil, both shorten the window when the seed is vulnerable.
pests.prevention_beginner: Plant into workable, well-drained soil, not cold soggy ground, and let any fresh compost or manure rot down well before you sow rather than digging it in right before planting. Getting the seed to sprout quickly is the best protection, so favor warmer soil and shallow planting.

diseases.name: Chocolate spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small, round, red-brown (chocolate-colored) spots scattered over the leaves, stems, and flowers. In dry spells the spots stay small and discrete, but in prolonged wet weather they enlarge, merge, and darken, killing whole leaves, shedding blossoms, and in severe attacks collapsing the entire plant. It is the signature and most damaging disease of favas, and it is worst on dense, overwintered crops from late winter on.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small round reddish-brown spots, the color of chocolate, scattered over the leaves, stems, and flowers. In dry weather they stay as small spots, but in a wet spell they spread and darken, killing leaves, dropping the flowers, and in bad cases collapsing the whole plant. It is the most serious fava disease and hits hardest on crowded, overwintered plants in late winter and spring.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Botrytis fabae (with Botrytis cinerea also involved), favored by cool, damp, overcrowded conditions and long leaf wetness. Spores are airborne and the fungus can carry over on infected debris and on the seed, so a wet spring on a dense autumn-sown stand is the classic setup for a damaging outbreak.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus (Botrytis fabae) that thrives in cool, damp, crowded conditions when the leaves stay wet for a long time. It spreads on the wind and can carry over on old plant debris and infected seed, so a wet spring on a thick, overwintered stand is when it does the most harm.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There are no fungicides available to home gardeners for chocolate spot, so management is cultural. At the first spots, improve airflow by thinning crowded growth and pulling weeds, remove the worst-affected leaves, and avoid working among wet plants. On a badly hit overwintered stand, harvesting what is usable and clearing the crop is often the practical choice.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no home garden spray for chocolate spot, so you manage it by keeping plants open and dry. At the first spots, thin crowded growth and pull weeds to move air through the planting, pick off the worst leaves, and stay out of the patch when the plants are wet. If an overwintered stand is badly hit, pick what you can and pull the plants.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Give plants plenty of room and maximize airflow with wider spacing; avoid damp, sheltered sites and dense stands, the conditions the disease needs. Ensure good drainage, sow at a sensible rate rather than thickly, do not save seed from an infected crop, and remove crop debris and nearby common vetch that can harbor it. Rotate favas on a three-to-four-year cycle.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Space plants well and keep the planting open so air moves through it, and avoid damp, shady, crowded spots, which are exactly what the disease likes. Plant into well-drained soil, do not sow too thickly, do not save seed from an infected crop, and clear away old plant debris after harvest. Move your favas to a new spot on a three-to-four-year cycle.

diseases.name: Broad bean rust
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small, dusty, dark-brown pustules scattered over the leaves and stems, each often ringed by a faint yellow halo; rubbing them leaves a rusty smudge. It usually appears later in the season, in warmer weather from around midsummer, and while it is less destructive than chocolate spot, a severe attack can defoliate plants and sap their vigor as they finish.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small, dusty, dark-brown spots (pustules) scattered over the leaves and stems, often with a faint yellow ring around each, that leave a rusty smudge when rubbed. It usually turns up later, in the warmer weather of mid to late season. It is less serious than chocolate spot, but a heavy attack can strip the leaves and weaken plants as they finish up.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The rust fungus Uromyces viciae-fabae, which completes its life cycle on favas and spreads by airborne spores in warm conditions. It keeps the infected leaf tissue alive to feed on, and its end-of-season spores survive in crop debris and on the seed, so it returns where favas are grown repeatedly without a break.
diseases.cause_beginner: A rust fungus (Uromyces viciae-fabae) that lives on favas and spreads on the wind in warm weather. Its spores survive on old plant debris and seed over winter, so it comes back where favas are grown in the same spot year after year.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There are no fungicides available to home gardeners for broad bean rust, so cultural control is the mainstay. Improve airflow with wider spacing, avoid humid, sheltered sites, and remove badly affected leaves. Because rust arrives late, an early-sown crop often finishes its pods before rust does real harm; clear and destroy the debris at the end.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no home garden spray for broad bean rust, so keep the plants open and airy with wider spacing and avoid damp, sheltered spots. Pull off badly spotted leaves. Since rust shows up late, an early planting usually finishes its pods before it matters, and clearing away the old plants at the end helps.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Sow early so the crop matures before the warm midsummer weather that drives rust, space plants for airflow, and avoid humid, crowded sites. Destroy infected plant material at the end of the season, since the spores overwinter in residue and on seed, and rotate favas so the disease does not build up in one bed.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant early so the crop finishes before the warm weather that brings on rust, give plants room for air to move, and avoid damp, crowded spots. Clear away and destroy the old plants at season's end, since the spores survive on debris and seed, and move your favas to a new spot each year.

diseases.name: Root rots and seed decay
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Large seed that rots before emerging and seedlings that damp off at a pinched, water-soaked stem base, leaving gaps in the row; on older plants a root-rot complex yellows and stunts the vines and rots the lower stem and roots. Damage is worst in cold, wet, poorly drained soil that slows germination and keeps seedlings vulnerable, and it overlaps with bean seed fly injury in the same conditions.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The big seeds rot before they come up, or seedlings flop over at a pinched, water-soaked spot near the soil, leaving gaps in the row. On older plants the roots rot, the lower leaves yellow, and growth stalls. It is worst in cold, wet, poorly drained soil that makes the seed sit too long before sprouting.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A complex of soilborne fungi and water molds (Pythium, Rhizoctonia, Fusarium, and others) that attack seeds, roots, and seedlings. Cold, saturated soil and injured roots at sowing set the stage, and the organisms build up in ground cropped to legumes too often, so drainage and rotation are the levers rather than treatment.
diseases.cause_beginner: A group of soil fungi and water molds that attack the seed, roots, and seedlings. Cold, soggy soil and damaged roots let them in, and they build up where beans and favas are grown too often in the same place. You manage this by preventing it, not by spraying.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no rescue for rotted seed or collapsed seedlings; replant the gaps into warmer, better-drained conditions once the soil has dried. Removing affected plants and improving drainage limits further loss, but because the organisms are already in the soil, prevention is the real control.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no saving seed or seedlings that have already rotted, so replant the gaps once the soil is warmer and drains better. Pulling affected plants and improving drainage help, but the main thing is preventing it, since these organisms live in the soil.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Sow into well-drained ground or raised beds rather than cold, low, wet spots, and do not sow into waterlogged soil. Avoid root injury at planting, keep beds in a three-to-four-year rotation away from legumes to limit buildup, and clear crop debris after harvest.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant in well-drained soil or raised beds instead of cold, wet, low spots, and never sow into soggy ground. Avoid damaging the roots when planting, move your favas and beans around the garden on a three-to-four-year cycle, and clear away the old plants after harvest.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Pale, blurry patches on the upper surface of the leaves, with a grayish to mauve, velvety mold on the corresponding underside in damp weather. Growing points can become distorted and discolored, and heavy infection reduces pod set. It develops in cool, humid conditions and tends to be more of a problem on the spring crop.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Pale, fuzzy patches on the top of the leaves, with a grayish, velvety mold on the underside in damp weather. The growing tips can twist and discolor, and a bad case means fewer pods. It shows up in cool, humid weather and is more of a spring problem.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The downy mildew fungus, which favors cool, humid conditions and long leaf wetness and can persist in the soil and on seed for years. Crowded, damp plantings and repeated cropping in the same ground favor it.
diseases.cause_beginner: A downy mildew fungus that likes cool, humid weather and wet leaves, and that can survive in the soil and on the seed for years. Crowded, damp plantings and growing favas in the same spot repeatedly make it worse.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Home management is cultural: improve airflow by thinning and wider spacing, remove affected leaves and growing tips early, avoid overhead watering, and stay out of the planting when wet. Clear infected debris at the end of the season.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Manage it by keeping plants open and dry: thin crowded growth, pull off affected leaves and tips early, water at the soil rather than overhead, and stay out of the patch when it is wet. Clear away the old plants at the end of the season.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants for airflow, avoid damp, sheltered sites, and water at the soil rather than overhead. Do not save seed from an infected crop, rotate favas on a three-to-four-year cycle, and remove crop debris, since the fungus can persist in soil and on seed.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Give plants room so air moves through, avoid damp, shady spots, and water the soil rather than the leaves. Do not save seed from an infected crop, move your favas around the garden on a three-to-four-year cycle, and clear away debris, since the fungus can live on in the soil and seed.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Moderate and even through the season. Favas are fairly drought tolerant once established, but the moisture-critical window is flowering through pod fill, when steady water sets and sizes the pods; before that, an established cool-season stand asks relatively little.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water moderately and evenly. Favas handle some dryness once they are growing well, but keep the water steady while they are flowering and filling pods, which is when it matters most.
watering.amount_seasoned: Enough to wet the root zone several inches down; deep, less frequent watering builds a stronger root system than frequent light sprinkles. In cool weather favas need little; step it up through flowering and pod fill.
watering.amount_beginner: Water deeply enough to wet the soil several inches down, and water less often but more thoroughly rather than a daily splash. Give more while the plants are flowering and podding.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the soil in the morning so the foliage dries quickly; wet, crowded foliage is what chocolate spot, rust, and downy mildew need. Avoid overhead watering on a dense stand in particular.
watering.method_beginner: Water the soil, not the leaves, and do it in the morning so the plants dry off during the day. Wet leaves, especially in a crowded planting, help spread disease.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting despite wet soil, and stunted plants point to waterlogged roots and the onset of the root rots favas are prone to in cold, wet ground.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If the soil is wet but the plants still wilt or the lower leaves yellow, you may be overwatering. Soggy soil rots fava roots.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Drought stress during and after flowering aborts blossoms and produces small, poorly filled pods, and it hastens the decline as heat arrives.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: If plants dry out while flowering, they drop their flowers and the pods come out small and poorly filled. Keep the water steady at that stage.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Avoid overhead watering where practical; the critical moisture window is flowering through pod fill.
watering.method_note_beginner: Try not to spray the whole plant from above. The most important time to keep water steady is when the plants are flowering and forming pods.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Flowering and pod fill are the moisture-critical stages; stress here directly cuts the pod set and yield.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Flowering and pod-filling are the times favas most need steady water.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Not applicable. Favas are direct-sown in place from their large seed and are not started indoors or hardened off; they resent root disturbance and germinate well in cool soil.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: You do not need to harden off favas. They are planted straight into the garden from seed.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Direct-sow the large flat seed about 1 to 2 inches deep and 4 to 6 inches apart, thinning to stand 8 to 10 inches apart, in rows 18 to 30 inches apart. In mild-winter regions sow in fall (roughly October to November) to overwinter; in cold regions sow as early as the soil can be worked in late winter or early spring. Germination is slow in cool soil and can take up to three weeks; there is no benefit to starting favas indoors.
start_method.notes_beginner: Plant the big flat fava seeds right where they will grow, about 1 to 2 inches deep and 4 to 6 inches apart, then thin to about 8 to 10 inches apart. Where winters are mild, plant in fall so the crop grows over winter; where winters are cold, plant as early as you can work the soil in late winter or spring. The seeds are slow to sprout, sometimes taking up to three weeks, and there is no need to start them indoors.

drainage.saucer_practice: Empty any saucer after watering so the pot never sits in standing water, which brings on the root rots favas are prone to in cool, wet conditions.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Use a good potting mix, not garden soil, which packs down too hard in pots.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in a little compost for fertility.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: A well-draining potting mix; avoid native garden soil, which compacts and drains poorly in containers and worsens root rot.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend in compost for baseline fertility and tilth; favas need little added nitrogen.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out faster than garden beds, so check the soil regularly and water when the top inch is dry, especially as the plants grow tall.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Container favas still need little feeding; a little compost in the mix is usually enough.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Not applicable as a container practice. Favas are a cool-season annual grown and finished within a season; in mild regions a fall sowing is overwintered in the ground rather than in a pot.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Not applicable as a container practice. As a single-season annual, favas complete their cycle and are pulled; the fall-sown overwintering that defines the crop in mild regions is done in the ground, not in a container.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Favas can be grown in a large pot, but most varieties are tall, 2 to 4 feet, so pick a big, deep, stable pot at least 5 gallons and 10 inches deep, or choose a dwarf variety like Robin Hood. Plant several seeds, keep the mix evenly moist, and stake or corral the plants if they lean.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Dwarf fava varieties such as Robin Hood suit containers best; the common tall types (2 to 4 feet, sometimes taller) are workable in a large, deep, stable pot but tend to lean and need staking. Use a pot of at least 5 to 7 gallons and 10 inches deep, plant several seeds, keep moisture even, and support the plants so they do not topple.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry faster than beds; monitor regularly and water when the top inch dries, and more as the plants size up.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Feeding needs stay low in containers; compost blended into the mix usually suffices.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering container suits favas well, smoothing out the even moisture they want through pod fill while avoiding the soggy roots they dislike.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match for favas because it keeps the water steady, which is what they like, without leaving the roots soggy.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: Favas need a deep, heavy, stable pot: the plants are tall and top-heavy and a light or shallow container tips once they are grown and loaded with pods. A dwarf variety in a broad pot is the easier choice for most container growers.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Pick a deep, heavy pot that will not tip over, because favas grow tall and top-heavy. A short dwarf variety in a wide pot is the easiest choice for a container.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Avoid following favas with favas, peas, or beans in the same bed. Favas are prone to soilborne diseases (chocolate spot, downy mildew, and root rots) and to the pea and bean weevil, all of which build up where legumes crop the same ground repeatedly. A three-to-four-year break is the standard guidance, and four years is advised where chocolate spot has appeared.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Do not plant favas where favas, peas, or beans grew recently. Diseases and pests build up in the soil and hit the next legume crop. Wait three to four years before favas return, and closer to four if you have had chocolate spot.
rotation.good_after: Favas are one of the best crops to grow before a heavy feeder. As a nitrogen-fixing legume, and a widely used cover crop and green manure, favas leave the soil looser and richer, so follow them with a nitrogen-hungry crop such as a brassica, a leafy green, corn, or squash.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate favas on a three-to-four-year cycle away from all legumes, leaning to four years where chocolate spot has shown up. Their nitrogen-fixing habit and their common use as a cover crop make them an excellent predecessor for nitrogen-hungry crops.
rotation.note_beginner: Move your favas to a new spot on a three-to-four-year cycle, and do not plant them where any beans or peas grew recently. Because favas feed the soil with nitrogen, whatever heavy feeder you plant there next will benefit.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Not recommended for fresh green favas, which lose quality at room temperature and should be cooled soon after picking. Fully dried fava beans, by contrast, store for months in a cool, dry, airtight container.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Do not leave fresh green favas out on the counter; cool them soon after picking. Dried favas, though, keep for months in a cool, dry, sealed jar.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Cool fresh green favas promptly after harvest and refrigerate them in the pod in a perforated bag; they hold good quality for about a week kept cold. Shelled beans keep a few days. Always cook favas before eating, since some people react badly to raw or undercooked beans.
storage.fridge_beginner: Cool fresh green favas right after picking and keep them in the fridge in the pod in a loosely closed bag, where they stay good for about a week. Shelled beans keep a few days. Always cook favas before eating them, because raw or undercooked favas make some people ill.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Green favas freeze well. Shell them, blanch briefly to set color and texture, cool, and freeze. For dried favas, let the pods dry fully on the plant, then shell and store the hard beans airtight.
storage.freezer_beginner: Green favas freeze well: shell them, give them a quick dip in boiling water (blanch), cool, and freeze. To dry favas, leave the pods on the plant until they are papery, then shell out the hard beans and store them in a sealed jar.
storage.notes_seasoned: Favas keep two ways. Fresh green beans are best used soon after picking: cool them fast, refrigerate in the pod for about a week, or shell, blanch, and freeze. Left on the plant to dry fully, the beans store for months as a dried pulse. In all cases, cook favas before eating, since raw or undercooked beans can cause a reaction in sensitive people.
storage.notes_beginner: You can keep favas two ways. Use fresh green beans soon after picking, storing them in the fridge in the pod for about a week or freezing them shelled and blanched. Or leave the pods to dry fully on the plant and store the hard dried beans in a sealed jar for months. Either way, always cook favas before eating them.

recommended.name: Windsor (Broad Windsor)
recommended.note: The classic large-seeded broad bean: tall, sturdy plants bearing short pods of big, flat, buttery beans. A standard spring-sown variety for fresh green favas and shelling.

recommended.name: Aquadulce
recommended.note: The go-to overwintering fava (often sold as Aquadulce Claudia). Exceptionally cold hardy, to roughly 15°F, so it is the variety of choice for fall sowing and overwintering; long pods with smooth white beans.

recommended.name: Sweet Lorane
recommended.note: A small-seeded, very cold-hardy fava favored in the Pacific Northwest for fall sowing and as a cover crop and green manure; heavy nitrogen fixation and good flavor for eating too.

recommended.name: Ianto's Return
recommended.note: A hardy, small-to-medium-seeded overwintering fava selected for cold tolerance and reliable fall sowing; productive and good as both a food and cover crop.

recommended.name: Vroma
recommended.note: A productive, adaptable fava noted for high nitrogen fixation as a cover crop; a dependable choice for both eating and green manure that can be sown fall or spring.

recommended.name: Robin Hood
recommended.note: A dwarf fava around 12 to 18 inches, good for containers and small beds and for growing under cover; earlier and more compact than the tall standards.

varieties.note_seasoned: Fava beans (Vicia faba) come in a tall broad-bean form (Windsor and most named types, 2 to 4 feet, big flat seeds for shelling) and a shorter, small-seeded form grown for cover cropping and overwintering. The single most important variety choice is timing: for a fall-sown, overwintered crop pick a cold-hardy overwintering type such as Aquadulce, Sweet Lorane, or Ianto's Return; for a spring crop the large-seeded Windsor types shine. Vroma is a versatile all-rounder, and Robin Hood is the dwarf choice for containers.
varieties.note_beginner: Fava beans, also called broad beans, come in tall big-seeded types like Windsor and shorter small-seeded types used for overwintering and cover cropping. The key is to match the variety to when you plant: for a fall planting that grows over winter, choose a hardy overwintering type like Aquadulce or Sweet Lorane; for a spring planting, the big Windsor types are excellent. Robin Hood is a short variety that suits pots.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare soil for one to three weeks, then the seedling pushes up. Favas germinate in cool soil, from about 40°F and best around 50 to 65°F, and the large seed is slow to emerge, sometimes taking up to three weeks. Seed sown into cold, saturated ground rots before it emerges, and the bean seed fly attacks slow-germinating seed, so drainage and workable soil matter more than an early calendar date.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Bare soil for one to three weeks, then the seedlings push up. Favas sprout in cool soil but the big seeds are slow, so be patient. Seed planted in cold, soggy ground rots instead of coming up, so wait for workable soil rather than muddy ground.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Sow the large flat seed about 1 to 2 inches deep and 4 to 6 inches apart into a moist but well-drained bed; do not sow into waterlogged ground. Where winters are mild, sow in fall to overwinter; where cold, sow as early as the soil can be worked. A bean or pea inoculant helps nodulation where favas or vetch are new to the bed.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Plant the big seeds about 1 to 2 inches deep and 4 to 6 inches apart in moist but well-drained ground. Plant in fall where winters are mild, or as early as you can work the soil where winters are cold. Do not keep the bed soggy after planting, since that rots the seed.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have your favas emerged? Note the date to track days to maturity from a real sowing rather than the seed packet.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your favas come up yet? Write down the date you first saw them break the soil.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Sturdy young plants a few inches tall with their first pairs of leaves on square, upright stems. Fava seedlings are exceptionally cold-hardy and shrug off frost, which is what lets a fall-sown crop overwinter, but they are the stage most vulnerable to the pea and bean weevil (scalloped leaf notches) and to slugs in wet weather.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Sturdy little plants a few inches tall with their first leaves on upright stems. Young favas are very cold-hardy and handle frost well, which is how a fall planting survives the winter, but this is when the pea and bean weevil notches the leaf edges and slugs can chew them in wet weather.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep the bed evenly moist and weed-free and cultivate shallowly, since fava roots run near the surface. Watch for weevil notching on the margins; a vigorous stand outgrows it. On an overwintered crop, avoid overcrowding, which invites chocolate spot later.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist, pull weeds early, and weed shallowly so you do not damage the roots. Watch for half-circle notches on the leaf edges from the weevil; healthy plants grow past it. If the crop is overwintering, do not let it get too crowded.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How is your fava stand looking? Note any gaps, weevil notching, or frost the seedlings came through.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How do your young fava plants look? Note any chewed leaves and how they handled any frost.

growth_stages.name: Plant growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Steady upward growth on stiff, square stems to 2 to 4 feet (dwarf types much shorter, some tall types to 5 or 6 feet). Unlike peas, favas stand on their own sturdy stalks and do not climb or need a trellis, though a tall stand may lean and benefit from a stake and string corral. The plants are fixing much of their own nitrogen now through root nodules, so aim for vigorous green growth, not overfed lushness that draws aphids.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Steady upward growth on stiff, upright stems to 2 to 4 feet. Unlike peas, favas stand up on their own sturdy stalks and do not climb or need a trellis, though a tall row may lean and can be corralled with stakes and string. The plants make much of their own nitrogen now, so you want healthy green growth, not big soft leafy stems, which draw aphids.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture steady and resist feeding; favas need little nitrogen and extra now pushes foliage and aphids over pods. Stake or string a tall row so it does not lodge. Keep the stand open for airflow to hold off chocolate spot, and watch the growing tips for the first black bean aphids.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the watering steady and do not add fertilizer now. Favas need very little, and extra just gives you soft leafy plants and more aphids. Stake or corral a tall row so it does not fall over, keep the plants from crowding so air moves through, and check the tips for black aphids.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How are your favas filling in? Note their height, whether they are leaning, and any aphids on the tips.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How tall are your fava plants getting? Note whether they are leaning and if you see aphids on the tips.

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Clusters of white flowers with striking black blotches (a few varieties are all-white or crimson) open along the upper stems, often fragrant. This is a moisture-critical stage: water stress now aborts blossoms, and sustained heat above about 75 to 80°F causes the plant to drop flowers instead of setting pods. Pinch out the soft growing tip once the lowest trusses have set to remove the black bean aphids that concentrate there.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Clusters of white flowers marked with black blotches open along the upper stems, often sweetly scented. This is an important time for water: if the plants dry out, or if it stays hotter than about 75 to 80°F, the flowers drop without making pods. Once the lowest flowers have set little pods, pinch off the soft growing tip, which is where the black aphids gather.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture steady and ample through bloom, where water stress directly cuts the crop. Once the bottom flower clusters have set pods, pinch out the growing tips: this both removes the aphid-prone shoot and steers energy into pod fill. Avoid overhead watering on the dense canopy, and in a heat wave water deeply ahead of time, though a crop flowering into real heat is nearing its end.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the water steady and generous while the plants flower, because dry soil now means fewer beans. Once the lowest flowers have turned into small pods, pinch off the soft growing tips to remove the aphids and push the plant into podding. Water the soil, not the leaves, and water deeply before a heat wave, but a crop flowering in real heat is running out of season.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are your favas flowering? Note the date bloom started, whether you pinched the tips, and any blossom drop in heat.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are your favas flowering yet? Note when the flowers opened and whether any dropped in hot weather.

growth_stages.name: Pod development
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Pods form where the flowers were and at first point upward, then lengthen and begin to droop as the beans inside swell. For fresh green favas, the target is a plump, glossy, well-filled pod with beans the size you want but still tender; for dried beans, leave the pods to mature and dry on the plant. Watch for chocolate spot in wet weather and for rust as the season warms.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Pods form where the flowers were, standing up at first, then getting longer and drooping as the beans inside swell. For fresh green favas, wait until the pods are plump and glossy and the beans have filled out but are still tender. For dried beans, leave the pods on the plant to dry. Watch for chocolate-brown spots (chocolate spot) in wet weather.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Maintain even moisture right through pod fill, the payoff stage for steady watering. Begin checking the pods as they plump up, and keep the stand open and dry to slow chocolate spot and rust. If the plants have not been tipped yet and aphids are building, pinch the tops now.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist while the pods fill. Start checking the pods as they plump up, and keep the plants open and dry to slow disease. If you have not pinched the tops yet and aphids are building up, do it now.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are pods forming? Note the date you first saw pods and whether you are growing them for fresh or dried beans.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are pods forming? Note when you first saw them and whether you want fresh green favas or dried beans.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: For fresh green favas, plump, glossy, well-filled pods picked while the beans are tender and bright, before the seed coats toughen; pick from the bottom of the plant up as the lower pods fill first. Very young, finger-sized pods can be eaten whole. For dried beans, wait until the pods turn dark and papery on the plant. The green harvest runs over a few weeks, then the crop ends as heat arrives.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: For fresh green favas, pick the pods when they are plump and glossy and the beans inside have filled out but are still tender, starting from the bottom of the plant where the pods fill first. Small young pods can be eaten whole. For dried beans, wait until the pods go dark and papery on the plant. The fresh harvest lasts a few weeks, then the heat ends it.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick fresh favas regularly as the pods fill, holding the stem and snapping or cutting the pod so you do not tear the plant. Shell the beans and cook them; the tender inner beans are often peeled after a quick blanch. Always cook favas before eating. Pull the spent plants once the crop finishes or the heat sets in; leave the roots to return their nitrogen, or turn the whole crop under as green manure.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pick fresh favas regularly as the pods fill, snapping or cutting them off so you do not tear the plant. Shell out the beans and cook them before eating; the tender beans inside are often peeled after a quick dip in boiling water. When the crop finishes or the heat arrives, pull the plants and compost them, or dig them in to feed the soil.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have you made your first picking? Log the date and whether you went for fresh green favas or let some dry.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you picked your first favas? Note the date and how they turned out.

notifications.body_seasoned: Direct-sow favas now. In mild-winter regions this is a fall sowing (about October to November) to overwinter; in cold regions sow as early as the soil can be worked in late winter or early spring, since fava seedlings are very cold-hardy. Sow the large seed 1 to 2 inches deep and 4 to 6 inches apart in a moist, well-drained bed.
notifications.body_beginner: Plant favas now. Where winters are mild, plant in fall so the crop grows over winter; where winters are cold, plant as soon as you can work the soil, because young favas handle cold well. Plant the big seeds 1 to 2 inches deep and 4 to 6 inches apart in moist, well-drained soil.

notifications.title_seasoned: Pinch out the tops to beat black bean aphid
notifications.title_beginner: Pinch off the tops to stop black aphids
notifications.body_seasoned: Once the lowest flower clusters have set pods, pinch out the soft growing tip of each fava plant. This removes the tender shoot where black bean aphids concentrate, taking most of the colony with it, and steers the plant's energy into filling pods. It is the classic broad-bean tactic against the crop's signature pest.
notifications.body_beginner: Once the bottom flowers have turned into small pods, pinch off the soft growing tip of each fava plant. That is where the black aphids gather, so you remove most of them at once, and it also helps the plant put energy into making beans.

notifications.body_seasoned: A spring-sown fava crop is usually ready about 80 to 100 days from sowing (an overwintered fall crop matures in spring). For fresh green favas, pick the pods when they are plump and glossy and the beans are filled but still tender, working from the bottom of the plant up. Cook favas before eating.
notifications.body_beginner: A spring-planted fava crop is usually ready about 80 to 100 days from planting; a fall-planted crop matures in spring. For fresh green favas, pick the pods when they are plump and glossy and the beans have filled out but are still tender, starting at the bottom of the plant. Always cook favas before eating.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost expected: plants are hardy, flowers less so
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost is coming: plants are tough, flowers less so
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Fava plants are among the most cold-hardy of vegetables and shrug off frost, tolerating hard freezes to roughly 10 to 15°F, which is what lets a fall-sown crop overwinter. Open flowers and young pods are more tender than the foliage, so if a hard frost threatens a flowering crop, cover it overnight and pick any usable pods first.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Fava plants are very cold-hardy and handle frost well, down to about 10 to 15°F, which is how a fall planting survives winter. The flowers and small pods are more tender than the leaves, so if a hard frost is coming while the plants are flowering, cover them overnight and pick any pods that are ready first.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat will stop your favas setting pods
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot weather will stop your favas
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Favas are heat-intolerant. Sustained daytime temperatures above about 75 to 80°F during bloom cause the plants to drop blossoms instead of setting pods, and the heat also brings on rust and black bean aphids. Keep moisture steady, harvest promptly, and treat the arrival of summer heat as the end of the crop; there is no watering your way through it.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Favas do not like heat. When it stays above about 75 to 80°F while they are flowering, they drop their flowers instead of making pods, and the heat also brings rust and aphids. Keep the water steady, pick what is ready, and treat the first real heat as the end of the crop.

germination.text_seasoned: Sow favas into moist, well-drained ground, not cold mud. The large seed germinates from about 40°F and best around 50 to 65°F, but it is slow, up to three weeks, and rots in cold, saturated soil, the most common cause of a thin stand. Good drainage matters more than the calendar.
germination.text_beginner: Plant favas in moist, well-drained soil, not soggy mud. The big seeds sprout in cool soil but are slow, sometimes taking up to three weeks, and they rot in cold, wet ground, which is the usual reason for gaps in the row. Good drainage matters more than an exact date.
germination.author: plant

germination.text_seasoned: The defining choice is when to sow. In mild-winter regions favas are fall-sown (about October to November) and overwintered for an early crop, since the plants are exceptionally cold-hardy; in cold regions they go in as early as the soil can be worked in late winter or spring. Either way, the aim is to flower and fill pods before summer heat.
germination.text_beginner: The big decision with favas is when to plant. Where winters are mild, plant in fall so the crop grows over winter; where winters are cold, plant as early as you can work the soil in late winter or spring. Either way, you want the plants to flower and make pods before the summer heat.
germination.author: plant

seedling.text_seasoned: Fava seedlings are among the most cold-hardy of any vegetable, tolerating hard frost to roughly 10 to 15°F, which is exactly why a fall sowing can overwinter. Do not rush to protect them from ordinary frost; keep them growing steadily instead, and watch the leaf margins for the scalloped notches of the pea and bean weevil.
seedling.text_beginner: Fava seedlings are very cold-hardy, handling frost down to about 10 to 15°F, which is how a fall planting survives winter. You do not need to protect them from normal frost. Just keep them growing well, and watch the leaf edges for the half-circle notches of the pea and bean weevil.
seedling.author: plant

vegetative.text_seasoned: Unlike peas, favas stand on their own stiff, upright stalks and do not climb or need a trellis. Tall types (2 to 4 feet, some to 5 or 6) can lean or lodge in wind or rain, so run a stake at each end of the row with string down both sides to corral them. Keep the stand open for airflow to hold off chocolate spot.
vegetative.text_beginner: Unlike peas, favas stand up on their own sturdy stalks and do not need a trellis. Tall types can lean over in wind or rain, so put a stake at each end of the row and run string down both sides to hold them up. Keep the plants from crowding so air moves through and disease stays down.
vegetative.author: plant

vegetative.text_seasoned: Hold off on nitrogen. As a legume, fava fixes much of its own through root nodules, and extra nitrogen now drives soft, leafy growth that draws black bean aphids and gives fewer pods. A little compost worked in before sowing is all favas need, and they leave the soil richer for the next crop.
vegetative.text_beginner: Do not add nitrogen fertilizer now. Favas make much of their own from the air, and extra fertilizer just gives you soft leafy plants that attract aphids and set fewer beans. A little compost mixed in before planting is all they need, and they feed the soil for the next crop.
vegetative.author: plant

flowering.text_seasoned: Once the lowest flower clusters have set pods, pinch out the soft growing tip of each plant. The tender tip is where black bean aphids, the signature fava pest, concentrate, so removing it takes most of the colony with it and channels energy into pod fill. It is the standard broad-bean tactic and worth doing before aphids build up.
flowering.text_beginner: Once the bottom flowers have turned into little pods, pinch off the soft growing tip of each fava plant. That tender tip is where the black aphids gather, so you remove most of them at once, and it also helps the plant put its energy into making beans.
flowering.author: plant

flowering.text_seasoned: The crop is racing the heat. Favas set pods best around 60 to 65°F and drop their blossoms once sustained temperatures pass about 75 to 80°F, so a planting that flowers into early summer heat sets poorly. This is why favas are sown early or overwintered: the goal is to flower and fill pods in cool weather.
flowering.text_beginner: The crop is in a race with the heat. Favas make pods best in cool weather and drop their flowers once it stays above about 75 to 80°F, so a planting that flowers as summer arrives makes few beans. That is why favas are planted early or over winter: to flower and fill pods while it is still cool.
flowering.author: plant

pod_development.text_seasoned: Keep the stand open and dry as the pods fill. Chocolate spot (chocolate-brown blotches in wet weather) is the crop's most damaging disease and thrives on crowded, damp plantings, and rust follows as the weather warms. Wider spacing, good drainage, soil-level morning watering, and removing the worst leaves are the home controls, since no fungicides are available to gardeners.
pod_development.text_beginner: Keep the plants open and dry while the pods fill. Chocolate spot (brown blotches in wet weather) is the worst fava disease and loves crowded, damp plantings, and rust comes on as it warms up. Space plants well, water the soil in the morning not the leaves, and pull off the worst leaves, since there is no home spray for these.
pod_development.author: plant

harvest.text_seasoned: Decide fresh or dried and pick accordingly. For fresh green favas, harvest when the pods are plump and glossy and the beans are filled but still tender, working from the bottom of the plant up; the shelled beans are often peeled after a quick blanch. For dried beans, leave the pods to turn papery on the plant. In all cases, cook favas before eating.
harvest.text_beginner: Decide whether you want fresh or dried favas. For fresh green favas, pick when the pods are plump and glossy and the beans have filled out but are still tender, starting at the bottom of the plant. For dried beans, leave the pods on the plant until they are papery. Always cook favas before eating them.
harvest.author: plant

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Favas yield modestly per plant and are grown in rows or blocks rather than singly. A well-grown plant carries roughly a dozen to two dozen pods up its sturdy stalks; a short double row gives a steady picking of fresh green favas over a few weeks, or a batch of dried beans if left to mature.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Each fava plant gives a modest handful of pods, so favas are grown in rows, not one at a time. A short row gives a steady picking of fresh green favas over a few weeks, or a batch of dried beans if you let them mature on the plant.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: The fresh green harvest comes on over a few weeks from the bottom of the plant up, then the crop ends as summer heat stops pod set. Because favas are a single main sowing rather than a succession crop, most of the yield arrives in that window; growing several plants and picking regularly is how to make the most of it.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: The fresh harvest comes over a few weeks, from the bottom of the plant up, then ends as the heat arrives. Favas are a one-sowing crop, not something you replant every couple of weeks, so grow several plants and pick regularly to get the most from them.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Favas are a rewarding and forgiving first-year crop: hardy seed sown straight into cool soil, plants that stand on their own without a trellis, and real cold tolerance that lets a fall sowing overwinter. The main levers on yield are sowing at the right time for your winters, pinching the tops to beat black bean aphid, and picking fresh favas while the beans are tender.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Favas are a great, forgiving first-year crop. You plant the big seeds straight into cool soil, the plants stand up on their own without a trellis, and they are tough enough that a fall planting can grow over winter. The main things that affect your harvest are planting at the right time for your climate, pinching the tops to control aphids, and picking while the beans are tender.
factors_seasoned: Sowing at the right time for your winters so the crop flowers and fills pods before summer heat (favas set pods poorly above about 75 to 80°F)
Steady moisture through flowering and pod fill (drought here aborts blossoms and shrinks the beans)
Pinching out the growing tips once the lower pods set, to remove black bean aphid and steer energy into pods
Open spacing and good airflow to hold off chocolate spot, the crop's most damaging disease

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No reliable extension or peer-reviewed evidence supports timing fava planting or harvest by moon phase. Sow favas by soil workability and temperature, by your winters, and by your frost dates instead, not by the lunar cycle.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Flowers dropped or few pods set
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Flowers fell off without making beans
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The plants flowered but set few or no pods because the weather turned too warm. Favas are heat-intolerant: once sustained temperatures pass about 75 to 80°F, they abort their blossoms instead of setting pods. It is the classic fate of a spring crop sown too late, or grown where summer arrives fast, and it is a weather problem, not a disease.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The plants flowered but made few or no beans because it got too hot. Favas do not like heat: once it stays above about 75 to 80°F, they drop their flowers instead of making pods. This usually happens to a spring crop planted too late, or grown where summer comes on fast. It is a weather problem, not a disease.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sow at the right time for your climate so the crop flowers in cool weather: fall-sow and overwinter a cold-hardy variety in mild regions, or sow as early as the soil can be worked in cold regions. Choose an early variety where summers come on fast, and keep moisture steady through bloom.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant at the right time so the favas flower while it is cool: plant in fall and overwinter a hardy variety where winters are mild, or plant as early as you can work the soil where winters are cold. Pick an early variety where summer comes fast, and keep the water steady while they flower.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Black aphids swarming the tips
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Black aphids all over the tops
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Dense colonies of black bean aphid built up on the soft growing tips and flower trusses, curling growth, dropping blossoms, and coating the plant in honeydew and sooty mold. It is the signature fava pest and it arrives fast as spring warms, and beyond direct damage it spreads legume viruses.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Clusters of black aphids built up on the soft tops and flower stalks, curling the growth, knocking off flowers, and leaving a sticky, moldy coating. This is the classic fava pest, it comes on fast as it warms up, and it also spreads plant viruses.
failure_diagnostics.cause: black bean aphid colonizing the growing tips
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Pinch out the growing tips as soon as the lowest pods set, removing the shoot the aphids concentrate on. Sow early so the crop is podding before the aphid flights peak, avoid excess nitrogen that softens growth, grow summer savory nearby by tradition, and conserve the lady beetles and wasps that control them.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Pinch off the growing tips as soon as the bottom pods set, since that is where the aphids gather. Plant early so the crop is podding before the aphids peak, do not overfeed, try planting summer savory alongside, and leave the ladybugs and other helpers to do their work.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Chocolate-brown spots spreading over the plants
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Brown spots spreading over the leaves and stems
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Red-brown, chocolate-colored spots spread over the leaves, stems, and flowers, merging and darkening in wet weather until leaves died and, in severe cases, plants collapsed. This is chocolate spot (Botrytis fabae), the most damaging fava disease, favored by cool, damp, overcrowded conditions and worst on dense, overwintered stands in late winter and spring.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Reddish-brown spots the color of chocolate spread over the leaves, stems, and flowers, joining up and darkening in wet weather until leaves died and, in bad cases, whole plants collapsed. This is chocolate spot, the worst fava disease, which loves cool, damp, crowded plantings and hits overwintered stands hardest.
failure_diagnostics.cause: Botrytis fabae in cool, damp, crowded conditions
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: There is no home fungicide, so prevent it culturally: space plants wide for airflow, avoid damp, sheltered sites and dense stands, ensure good drainage and adequate potassium, sow at a sensible rate, do not save seed from an infected crop, clear debris, and rotate favas on a three-to-four-year cycle.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: There is no home garden spray, so prevent it: space plants well so air moves through, avoid damp, shady, crowded spots, plant in well-drained soil, do not sow too thickly, do not save seed from a sick crop, clear away old plants, and move your favas on a three-to-four-year cycle.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Seed rotted or came up patchy
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Seeds rotted or did not come up
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The large seed was sown into cold, saturated soil and rotted before emerging, or came up as a thin, patchy stand. Favas germinate slowly in cool soil and the seed is exposed for a long time; waterlogged ground starves it of oxygen, feeds the soilborne root rots, and invites the bean seed fly, so a too-early sowing into a wet, poorly drained bed is the usual cause of gaps.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The big seeds went into cold, soggy soil and rotted instead of sprouting, or came up thin and patchy. Favas are slow to sprout, so the seed sits in the ground a long time; wet, poorly drained soil rots it and invites soil fungi and the bean seed fly. Planting too early into a wet bed is the usual reason for gaps.
failure_diagnostics.cause: cold, waterlogged soil rotting slow-germinating seed
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sow into well-drained ground or raised beds rather than cold, low, wet spots, and wait for the surface to be workable rather than muddy. Sow about 1 to 2 inches deep, do not keep the bed soggy, and let coarse fresh residue break down before sowing to reduce bean seed fly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant in well-drained soil or raised beds instead of cold, wet, low spots, and wait until the soil is workable, not muddy. Plant about 1 to 2 inches deep, do not keep the bed soggy, and let any fresh compost break down before planting to cut down the bean seed fly.
