succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Fava beans are grown as one main cool-season sowing per window, not as a rapid-succession crop: a fall sowing to overwinter in mild regions, or an early spring sowing in cold regions. The crop crops over a few weeks from the bottom of the plant up, then ends with the heat. A second sowing two to three weeks after the first can lengthen the fresh window a little, but favas take up space and are usually sown once.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: You plant favas once per season, not every couple of weeks like some crops. In mild-winter areas that is a fall planting that grows over winter; in cold areas it is an early spring planting. The plants crop for a few weeks and then the heat ends them. You can plant a second batch two to three weeks after the first to stretch the harvest a bit, but usually one planting is enough.

3.zone_notes: In the coldest zones favas are a single early-spring crop and a marginal one: sow as soon as the ground can be worked in May, harvest fresh green favas in July and August, and expect the summer heat and short season to limit the yield, since favas set only a few pods once it turns hot. Fall sowing is not viable here; the winters are too cold for the plants to overwinter.

4.zone_notes: Sow as early as the soil can be worked in April or May for a July and August harvest of fresh green favas before the heat ends the crop. Favas are cold-hardy enough to go in well before the last frost, but this is a heat-limited northern crop that sets its best pods in the cool of early summer; overwintering is unreliable at these winter lows.

5.zone_notes: Sow in late March or April, as soon as the soil is workable, for a June and July harvest before midsummer heat stops pod set. Fava seedlings shrug off spring frost, so an early sowing is safe and lets the crop flower and fill in cool weather. Winters are generally too cold here to overwinter a fall sowing.

6.zone_notes: An early sowing in February or March gives a May and June harvest before the summer heat shuts favas down; the hot months are left out. In milder parts of the zone a fall sowing in September can be overwintered with the plants' strong frost tolerance for an earlier crop the following spring.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion for fava beans, not a frost gap. Fava beans are a cool-season legume that grows best around 60 to 65°F and sets pods poorly once daytime temperatures climb past about 75 to 80°F, so a crop caught by summer heat drops its blossoms, forms few pods, and declines as rust and black bean aphids build up. The cool-season sowing is timed to flower and fill pods before the heat, the bed then rests through the hottest weeks, and the calendar leaves summer out.

7.zone_notes: Mild winters make fall sowing the headline here: favas sown in October or November are hardy enough to overwinter, resuming growth in early spring for an April and May harvest, well before the summer heat that excludes the crop. A very early spring sowing is also possible where a fall sowing was missed.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion for fava beans, not a frost gap. Fava beans are a cool-season legume that grows best around 60 to 65°F and sets pods poorly once daytime temperatures climb past about 75 to 80°F, so a crop caught by summer heat drops its blossoms, forms few pods, and declines as rust and black bean aphids build up. The cool-season sowing is timed to flower and fill pods before the heat, the bed then rests through the hottest weeks, and the calendar leaves summer out.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In cold regions favas are mostly an early-spring crop: plant as soon as you can work the soil, even before the last frost, since young favas are very cold-hardy, and harvest fresh green favas in early to midsummer before the heat ends the crop. In the far north the summer heat comes on fast and limits the yield. In the milder end of the region (zones 6 and 7) you can plant in fall and let the hardy plants overwinter for an earlier crop the next spring.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Across the cold northern tier favas are grown mainly as a very early spring crop, sown as soon as the ground can be worked since the seedlings are exceptionally frost-hardy, and harvested for fresh green favas in late spring to midsummer before the heat stops pod set. In the coldest zones the crop is genuinely heat-limited and sets only a modest yield before summer arrives. From the milder end of the region (zones 6 and 7) the plants' strong cold tolerance allows a fall sowing to overwinter for an earlier spring harvest, the fava signature. The summer gap in zones 6 and 7 is a true heat exclusion, backed at each cell.

8.zone_notes: On the Gulf and coastal plain favas are a cool-season crop: sow in October and November, let the hardy plants grow through the mild winter, and harvest fresh green favas from March into May. The hot, humid summer is left out, when favas will not flower or set pods.

The cool-season sowing is timed to flower and fill pods before the heat, the bed then rests through the hottest weeks, and the calendar leaves summer out.

9.zone_notes: In the warm coastal zone 9 favas are sown in fall (October to November), grow through the mild winter, and are harvested February into April; the long, hot season from May through September excludes the crop entirely.

The cool-season sowing is timed to flower and fill pods before the heat, the bed then rests through the hottest weeks, and the calendar leaves summer out.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: Along the Gulf and coastal plain, grow favas in the cool months, fall through spring, not in summer. Plant in fall and the hardy plants grow through the mild winter for a late-winter and spring harvest. Summer is too hot; the plants stop making pods.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: On the Gulf and southeastern coastal plain favas are a cool-season crop sown in fall and grown through the mild winter, taking advantage of their exceptional cold tolerance. Sow October into November for a harvest that runs late winter into spring; the hot, humid summer is a true heat exclusion, when favas drop their flowers and rust and aphids take hold, so summer is left out of the calendar in both zones.

8.zone_notes: In the interior valleys favas are a cool-season crop: sow in fall (October to November), grow through the mild winter, and harvest March into May. A late-winter sowing is also workable, but the hot summer excludes the crop, when the plants cannot set pods.

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In California's interior valleys, plant favas in fall so they grow through the mild winter, and harvest in late winter and spring. The hot summer is too much for them, so leave it out.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: In the interior valleys favas are a cool-season crop grown fall through spring: sow October into November and take advantage of the plants' cold tolerance to carry them through the mild winter for a late-winter to spring harvest. The hot valley summer is a true heat exclusion and is left out of the calendar.

9.zone_notes: On the cool north coast favas do well over a long mild season: a late-winter sowing in February gives a spring and early-summer harvest, and a fall sowing in August and September grows on for an early crop. The foggy summer is cool rather than hot, so it registers as a brief season lull, not a heat exclusion.

10.zone_notes: The mildest north-coast zone grows favas over a long season: sow in late winter for a spring and early-summer harvest and again in late summer for a fall-established crop. Cool, foggy summers mean the short summer gap is a season lull rather than a heat exclusion.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: On California's cool, foggy north coast favas grow through much of the year. Plant in fall and again in late winter, and harvest in spring and early summer. The mild coastal summer is not hot enough to force the plants out, but there is a short summer lull before fall planting begins again.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: The cool, foggy north coast is close to ideal for favas: the plants' cold tolerance and dislike of heat both suit the long, mild season. Sow in fall (August to September) and again in late winter (February) for harvests through spring and early summer. Unlike the hot interior, the maritime summer is not a heat exclusion, so the brief summer gap is marked as a season lull rather than a backed heat pause.

9.zone_notes: On the south coast favas are sown in fall (October to November), grow through the mild winter, and are harvested March into May. The warm coastal summer is enough to stop pod set, so the summer months are left out of the calendar.

The cool-season sowing is timed to flower and fill pods before the heat, the bed then rests through the hottest weeks, and the calendar leaves summer out.

10.zone_notes: In the mildest south-coast zone favas are a fall-sown, overwintered crop harvested March into May; the warm summer excludes pod set, so summer is left out of the calendar.

The cool-season sowing is timed to flower and fill pods before the heat, the bed then rests through the hottest weeks, and the calendar leaves summer out.

ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: On the southern California coast, plant favas in fall so they grow through the mild winter, and harvest in spring. The warm summer stops them from making pods, so leave it out.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: On the south coast favas are a fall-sown, overwintered cool-season crop, taking advantage of the mild winter for a spring harvest. The warmer coastal summer, unlike the foggy north coast, does reach the point where favas stop setting pods, so it is treated as a true heat exclusion and left out of the calendar.

9.zone_notes: In the desert valleys favas are strictly a cool-season crop: sow in fall (October to November), grow through the mild winter, and harvest February into April. The long, intense heat from May through September excludes the crop entirely.

10.zone_notes: In the mildest desert zone favas are sown in fall, grow through the warm-mild winter, and are harvested February into April; the fierce summer heat is a long exclusion when the plants cannot flower or set pods.

ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: In the California desert, favas are a winter crop only. Plant in fall, grow them through the mild winter, and harvest in late winter and early spring. The long, hot summer is far too much for them.
ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: In the desert valleys favas are a fall-sown winter crop harvested late winter into spring; their cold tolerance carries them easily through the mild desert winter, while the long, intense summer heat from May through September is a hard exclusion left out of the calendar.

9.zone_notes: In the Arizona low desert favas are a cool-season winter crop: sow from October into December, grow through the mild winter, and harvest February into April. The long, extreme summer heat from May through September excludes the crop.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion for fava beans, not a frost gap. Fava beans are a cool-season legume that grows best around 60 to 65°F and sets pods poorly once daytime temperatures climb past about 75 to 80°F, so a crop caught by summer heat drops its blossoms, forms few pods, and declines as rust and black bean aphids build up. The cool-season sowing is timed to flower and fill pods before the heat, the bed then rests through the hottest weeks, and the calendar leaves summer out.

low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: In the Arizona low desert, plant favas in fall or early winter and harvest in late winter and spring. The summer is far too hot for them.
low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: In the Arizona low desert favas are grown as a winter vegetable, sown October into December and harvested late winter into spring, with the plants easily handling the mild desert winter. The extreme summer heat is a long, hard exclusion left out of the calendar.

warm_arid.region_label: Warm Arid: Southern New Mexico & West Texas

8.zone_notes: In the warm arid Southwest favas are a cool-season crop bracketing the hot summer: sow in February for an April and May harvest, and again in September for a fall-established, overwintered crop. The hot early summer stops pod set, and the cold desert-winter nights bracket the season.

warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: In southern New Mexico and west Texas, plant favas in late winter for a spring harvest, and again in fall for an overwintered crop. The hot early summer and the cold winter nights bracket the season.
warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: In the warm arid Southwest favas are grown in the cool shoulders of the year: a February sowing for an April and May harvest before the heat, and a September sowing that overwinters for an early spring crop, using the plants' cold tolerance against the sharp desert-winter nights. The hot early summer is a true heat exclusion left out of the calendar.

Even the mild winter is on the warm edge for favas, and the long hot season from April through October excludes the crop. Where favas struggle, heat-tolerant southern peas are the better fit.

The window here is modeled on general cool-season and elevation guidance rather than a Hawaii-specific fava calendar, and it is the lowest-confidence region in the record; warm-adapted legumes are the practical lowland choice.

crops.description_seasoned: Broad beans, also called fava beans (Vicia faba), are a cool-season legume grown for their large, flat, buttery seeds, eaten as tender green favas shelled from the pod or dried as a pulse. They are a different plant from the garden pea, in a different genus (Vicia, not Pisum): the seeds are large and flat, and the plants are stiff, upright stalks 2 to 4 feet tall that stand on their own and need no trellis, unlike climbing peas. Two traits define how favas are grown. They are among the most cold-hardy of all vegetables, tolerating hard frost to roughly 10 to 15°F, so in mild-winter regions they are fall-sown and overwintered for an early crop, and in cold regions they are one of the first crops sown in late winter or spring. And they are heat-intolerant: they set pods best around 60 to 65°F and stop podding once daytime temperatures pass about 75 to 80°F, so the crop must flower and fill before summer heat. As a nitrogen-fixing legume, fava is also a favorite cover crop and green manure that leaves the soil richer. One honest caution: favas can trigger a serious reaction, called favism, in the minority of people with an inherited G6PD enzyme deficiency, so they should always be cooked before eating.
crops.description_beginner: Broad beans, better known as fava beans, are a cool-weather crop grown for their big, flat, buttery beans, eaten fresh and green shelled from the pod or dried. They are not the same as garden peas: the seeds are large and flat, and the plants are sturdy, upright stalks 2 to 4 feet tall that stand up on their own and do not need a trellis. Two things make favas special. They are extremely cold-hardy, handling frost down to about 10 to 15°F, so where winters are mild you plant them in fall to grow over winter, and where winters are cold they are one of the first things you plant in late winter or spring. And they dislike heat: they stop making pods once it stays above about 75 to 80°F, so they have to flower and fill before summer arrives. Favas also feed the soil with nitrogen and make a great cover crop. One important note: fava beans can cause a serious reaction, called favism, in people who have an inherited enzyme deficiency (G6PD), so they should always be cooked before you eat them.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: For fresh green favas, pick the pods when they are plump, glossy, and well filled but the beans are still tender, before the seed coats toughen, working from the bottom of the plant up as the lower pods fill first. Very young, finger-sized pods can be eaten whole. For dried beans, leave the pods to turn dark and papery on the plant. Always cook favas before eating.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Fresh green favas are ready when the pods are plump and glossy and the beans inside have filled out but are still tender, starting with the lower pods on the plant. Small young pods can be eaten whole. For dried beans, leave the pods on the plant until they are dark and papery. Always cook favas before eating them.

crops.name: Lettuce (Leaf)

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Lettuce likes loose, rich soil that drains well but never dries out completely. Because its roots are shallow and delicate, soggy or packed-down soil hurts lettuce more than it would a tomato, and letting the bed dry out even briefly makes the leaves turn bitter and the plant go to seed early. The simplest fix for almost any soil is to mix 2 to 3 inches of compost into the top few inches before you plant, which helps sandy soil hold water and helps heavy soil drain. Try to avoid thick clay, it forms a hard crust that small seedlings struggle to push through and stays wet around the roots.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Lettuce is widely adaptable on the texture front, and although it produces well in almost any soil that drains freely, a fertile loam or sandy loam that stays high in organic matter and holds moisture well is where it does best. Its root system is shallow and fine, so it is far less forgiving of compaction and waterlogging than deeper-rooted crops, and consistent moisture is essential because even brief drought stress checks vegetative growth and pushes the plant toward bolting. Working 2 to 3 inches of compost into the bed before sowing improves both drainage on heavier soils and water retention on sandy ones. Heavy clay is the main texture to avoid, it crusts as seedlings emerge and holds water around the roots.

ph.note_beginner: Soil pH measures acidity on a scale from 0 to 14, where 7 is neutral and lower numbers are more acidic. Lettuce does best between 6.0 and 6.8, slightly acidic, because that is where the nutrients it needs are easiest for the roots to take up. If your soil is more acidic than 6.0 or more alkaline than 7.0, lettuce can show yellowing leaves or browning edges even when fertilizer is present. The only way to know your number is to test, so get an inexpensive soil test from your local extension office before adding lime to raise pH or sulfur to lower it.
ph.note_seasoned: Soil pH governs nutrient availability, and lettuce is most productive in the slightly acidic 6.0 to 6.8 band where phosphorus, calcium, and magnesium stay soluble. Below about 6.0, calcium uptake falls off and aluminum and manganese grow more available, which can scorch leaf margins and stunt the fine root system. Above 7.0, iron and manganese begin to lock up and drive interveinal yellowing on new growth. Across the alkaline interior West and in alkaline-irrigation districts, growers often acidify before planting, while the naturally acidic soils of the forested East more often need lime to reach the target band.

direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Cool season crops such as spinach, leaf lettuce, peas, onions, and root crops can germinate at minimum soil temperatures of 35-40 degrees F. harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Leaf lettuce can begin harvest 40–60 days after direct sowing under spring conditions, depending on variety and growing conditions; leaf types are at the fast end of this range. harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Fall lettuce in cold zones is grown from fast-maturing looseleaf varieties, with the first leaves ready about 45 days after sowing. harvest_end.design_note_seasoned: Harvest extends to approximately first_frost + 5 days for hardy greens; first_frost - 5 days for tender greens like lettuce.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Spring succession arm: sow looseleaf lettuce every 2 weeks from when soil reaches 40 degrees F through the bolt-driven close of the spring window. Leafy greens germinate at 35-40 degrees F minimum and mature in 40-60 days, so sequential plantings give consistent production; the arm ends as rising heat (above ~75 degrees F) triggers bolting and bitterness. 3.safe_sowing_note_seasoned: Safest sowings: around Apr 29 in spring and Jul 1 for the fall crop. The earliest possible spring date risks slow germination in cold soil, and late-spring sowings run into bolting heat; a mid-spring sowing after the soil has warmed is the most reliable. The first fall sowing, once peak summer heat eases, establishes most dependably.

fertilizer.timing: throughout growing season
fertilizer.example_product: Fish emulsion or liquid seaweed
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Leafy crops run on nitrogen, which directly drives the tender leaf growth you're harvesting, so feed a balanced or nitrogen-forward liquid fertilizer every 2 to 3 weeks. Keep it steady rather than heavy: a sudden surge of nitrogen pushes fast, lush growth that can worsen tipburn by outrunning calcium delivery to the inner leaves. No amount of feeding prevents bolting once heat and long days arrive, since that is hormonal, not nutritional.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Leafy crops run on nitrogen, the nutrient that drives the leaf growth you are harvesting, so feed a balanced or nitrogen-forward liquid fertilizer every 2 to 3 weeks. Keep it steady rather than heavy: a sudden big dose of nitrogen pushes fast, soft growth that can make tipburn worse (brown, dried edges on the inner leaves). And no amount of feeding stops bolting once heat and long days arrive, because that is driven by the plant's hormones, not by nutrients.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time to feed your lettuce, a balanced liquid feed keeps leaves tender
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Time to feed your lettuce. A balanced liquid feed keeps the leaves tender.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: higher N, e.g. 10-5-5 or a balanced 10-10-10
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a fertilizer with more nitrogen (the first number), such as 10-5-5, or a balanced 10-10-10. Those three numbers on the label are the amounts of nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: Lettuce responds to nitrogen for fast, tender growth. Work in a complete fertilizer such as 10-10-10 at about 2 pounds per 100 square feet before planting, then side-dress nitrogen once plants are 3 to 4 inches tall, about 1 pound per 25 feet of row of 10-10-10 (UMN), or roughly a quarter cup of 21-0-0 per 10 feet of row (USU). For tipburn-prone conditions favor a calcium-nitrate source over an ammonium-based one.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Lettuce likes a bit more nitrogen for quick, tender leaves. Mix a balanced fertilizer into the bed before planting at the label rate, then feed once more when the plants are a few inches tall. A small side-dressing of a nitrogen fertilizer, following the package rate for your row length, is plenty. Keep the fertilizer off the leaves and water it in.

companions.note_beginner: For lettuce, companion planting is mostly about sharing space well, not about one plant protecting another. Its best neighbors are crops that do not compete with it for the same room: fast radishes and deep-rooted carrots, plus chives, whose oniony smell helps hide lettuce from aphids. A lot of the popular "never plant these together" pairings for lettuce are old garden lore with mixed or no real evidence, so we keep those out of the way in the seasoned view. Get sun, water, and spacing right first. Companions are a small bonus on top.
companions.note_seasoned: Lettuce companions are mostly about sharing space, not chemistry. Its best partners are fast or deep-rooted crops it does not compete with (radishes, carrots) and scent plants that help mask it from aphids (chives). Many popular 'avoid' pairings for lettuce are traditional lore with conflicting evidence rather than documented harm, so we keep those in the seasoned view with honest framing. Get sun, water, and spacing right first, companions are a small bonus on top.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Radishes
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Fast-maturing relay crop: radishes are harvested before lettuce fills the bed, and their taproots loosen surface compaction for lettuce's shallow roots. A space-saving pairing, not a pest control one.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Relay/space-saving interplanting of fast root crops with leafy greens is extension-documented. University of Minnesota Extension ('Companion planting in home gardens') frames radish/carrot side-by-side and early greens under a later canopy as research-backed space-saving; West Virginia University Extension ('Companion Planting') documents taproots of radishes/carrots alleviating soil compaction and names lettuce as a cool-season interplant; UF/IFAS ('Companion Planting') describes long- and short-season pairings (carrots/radishes) to make best use of space. The structural/space-saving mechanism is what is extension-backed; the popular 'radish as flea-beetle trap crop' and 'row marker' sub-claims are NOT T1-supported and are deliberately omitted from the why.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Radishes grow fast and come out of the bed before the lettuce needs the room, so the two share space well. Their roots also loosen the soil a little for the lettuce. This is about saving space, not keeping pests away.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Carrots
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Different root zones: lettuce is a shallow-rooted light feeder and carrots send a taproot deep, so the two share a bed without competing underground.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Pairing plants with different root structures to reduce below-ground competition and use the soil profile efficiently is extension-documented. University of Minnesota Extension ('Companion planting in home gardens') and West Virginia University Extension ('Companion Planting') both describe taproot crops (carrots) interplanted with shallow-rooted greens, with carrots breaking compaction while greens occupy the surface layer. Lettuce as a light, shallow-rooted feeder is the well-supported half of the claim; the narrower 'carrots specifically improve lettuce' direction is not separately T1-validated.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Lettuce roots stay near the surface and carrots root deep, so the two do not fight for the same space underground and can grow side by side.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Chives
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Allium scent compounds help mask lettuce from aphids that locate hosts by smell. A supporting deterrent, not a standalone fix, plant chives as a border row.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Allium sulfur-based volatile organic compounds have a documented aphid-repellent mechanism in the peer-reviewed literature (Durenne & Gosset, Insects 2018; leek/Myzus persicae masking, Scientific Reports 2021). The companion application is described at home-gardening rigor by Utah State University Extension (Mohr et al., 'Creating Sustainable School and Home Gardens: Companion Planting'), which lists alliums among pest-repelling companions, and by UC ANR Master Gardener material ('Best Friends in the Garden' and the Fresno County 'Winter companion planting to repel insects' page, which names chives among aphid repellents for lettuce specifically). These describe the pairing at plausible-mechanism rigor rather than as a validated lettuce-specific protocol; the mechanism is peer-reviewed, the lettuce pairing is extension-named. Honest framing in the why reflects 'supporting deterrent, not standalone.'

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: The oniony smell of chives can help hide lettuce from aphids, which find plants by scent. It helps a little rather than solving the problem on its own, so plant chives as a border around the bed.

good_seasoned.name: Nasturtiums
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Often grown as an aphid trap crop, but the evidence is weaker than it sounds: trap cropping works best for moderately mobile pests, and aphids disperse passively on wind, so treat this as a supplementary tactic rather than reliable aphid protection.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap cropping is an extension-documented IPM tactic, and nasturtiums are specifically named as an aphid/flea-beetle trap crop by WSU Skagit County Extension Master Gardeners (Wolfe, 2020) and Utah State University Extension (Mohr et al.). The confidence is LOW and the entry is seasoned-only because the named application has a protocol mismatch the sources themselves flag: UConn IPM notes trap cropping works best for insects of intermediate mobility rather than those, like aphids, passively dispersed by air currents. So the companion is extension-named but the aphid use is not reliable for a first-season grower. Moved from good_core to good_seasoned on this basis (M13 companions walk).

bad_seasoned.name: Celery
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Traditional companion lore advises against pairing celery with lettuce, often citing shared pests (aphids, whiteflies) or competition in close quarters. This is widely repeated guidance, not extension-documented, and some sources consider the pairing fine.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Celery-as-poor-lettuce-neighbor is a stable, widely-repeated entry in companion lore with a coherent stated basis (shared aphid/whitefly pressure; water/nutrient competition when crowded), but no T1 extension source documents it and other lists treat celery+lettuce as acceptable. Classified traditional (real lore, no documented harm), confidence low, seasoned-only so an unverified anti-companion claim does not steer a first-season grower away from a planting that may be fine.

bad_seasoned.name: Parsley
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: You may see parsley listed as a lettuce antagonist, sometimes blamed for crowding and sometimes for triggering bolting. The evidence conflicts: the bolting claim is unsupported even by the sources that repeat it, and other guides list parsley as a fine or beneficial lettuce neighbor.

provenance.label: disputed
provenance.reason: Two distinct parsley claims circulate. (1) 'Parsley causes lettuce to bolt' is hedged or disclaimed even in the seed-catalog/blog tier that repeats it ('unclear whether there's a direct connection') and has no mechanism or T1 backing. (2) 'Parsley competes/crowds' is a generic spacing concern true of any bushy neighbor, not parsley-specific. Multiple lists name parsley as a GOOD lettuce companion. Net evidence conflicts, so labeled disputed (not traditional), confidence low, seasoned-only. Honest why acknowledges the conflict rather than asserting inhibition.

bad_seasoned.name: Brassicas
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Cabbage-family crops (cabbage, broccoli, kale, etc.) are often called poor lettuce neighbors, but for lettuce specifically the evidence is genuinely mixed, and some field trials show lettuce intercropped with broccoli yielding more, not less.

provenance.label: disputed
provenance.reason: Two competing mechanisms are claimed and neither is T1-settled for lettuce: (a) nutrient competition (the 'both heavy feeders' framing, which fits tomato better than lettuce since lettuce is a light feeder), and (b) brassica root exudates inhibiting lettuce seed germination (an allelopathy claim repeated at seed-catalog/blog rigor). At least one source cites field intercropping of lettuce with broccoli producing higher yields. Labeled disputed, confidence low, seasoned-only. WATCH: the 'heavy feeder competition' language is lifted from the tomato anchor and does not transfer cleanly to lettuce; honest why flags the conflicting field evidence.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_beginner: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and the undersides of leaves. The leaves may curl, yellow, or turn sticky with a substance called honeydew. A black, sooty mold sometimes grows on that stickiness.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: First knock the colonies off with a strong jet of water, which dislodges most of them, and they rarely find their way back. For any that remain, spray insecticidal soap or neem oil directly onto the aphids, covering the leaf undersides, since both only work when they hit the insect, not by being eaten. Encourage helpful insects like ladybugs, lacewings, and tiny parasitic wasps, which keep small infestations in check on their own.
pests.prevention_beginner: Go easy on nitrogen fertilizer. The fast, soft growth that lots of nitrogen produces is exactly what aphids feed on, so an over-fed plant attracts far more of them. Plant flowers like marigolds and nasturtiums nearby, and grow some dill or cilantro too, whose flowers feed the helpful wasps and predators that do most of the real control.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several aphid species feed on leafy greens, most commonly the green peach aphid. Through the growing season they reproduce asexually, so a few founders become dense colonies within days once temperatures warm and growth is soft and lush.
pests.cause_beginner: Several kinds of aphid feed on leafy greens, most often the green peach aphid. During the growing season they reproduce without mating, so a few can become a dense colony within days once it warms up and the growth is soft and lush.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong jet of water first, which dislodges most of them and they rarely find their way back. For what remains, spray insecticidal soap or neem oil directly onto the aphids, covering leaf undersides, since both work only on contact and kill by disrupting the insect's outer membrane rather than by being eaten. Encourage ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps, which keep light infestations in check on their own.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Go easy on nitrogen fertilizer. The fast, soft growth that high nitrogen pushes is exactly what aphids feed on, so a lush over-fed plant attracts far more of them. Interplant flowers such as marigolds and nasturtiums, and grow some umbellifers like dill or cilantro nearby, whose flowers feed the parasitic wasps and predators that do most of the real control.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms_beginner: Ragged holes appearing in leaves overnight, with shiny slime trails visible in the morning. Seedlings may be cut off right at the soil line.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Set beer traps with the rim level with the soil so the slugs fall in and cannot climb out, and refresh them every couple of days. Sprinkle diatomaceous earth in a ring around vulnerable plants, but remember it stops working once it gets wet and needs reapplying after rain or watering. Hand-pick them after dark with a flashlight, when they are out feeding. An iron-phosphate bait (sold as Sluggo and similar) is approved for organic gardens and safe around pets and wildlife; it stops the slugs feeding so they die within a few days. Scatter it in the evening after watering, when slugs are most active, for the best results.
pests.prevention_beginner: Pull mulch back from around seedlings and clear away the boards, pots, and leaf litter near the bed that give slugs a daytime hiding spot. A bare, raked strip around the planting slows them down on their way in. Encourage ground beetles, and hedgehogs if you have them, since both hunt slugs through the night.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause_seasoned: Slugs and snails feed mostly at night and in the cool, damp hours, rasping irregular holes through tender leaves and shearing off young seedlings entirely. Damage is heaviest in wet spells and in beds with damp mulch or debris that give them daytime shelter.
pests.cause_beginner: Slugs and snails feed mostly at night and in cool, damp weather, rasping ragged holes in tender leaves and shearing off young seedlings completely. The damage is worst in wet spells and in beds with damp mulch or debris that give them somewhere to hide during the day.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Set beer traps with the rim at soil level so they fall in and cannot climb back out, and refresh them every couple of days. Ring vulnerable plants with diatomaceous earth, remembering it stops working once wet and needs reapplying after rain or irrigation. Hand-pick after dark with a flashlight, when they are out feeding. Iron phosphate bait (sold as Sluggo and similar) is approved for organic use and safe around pets and wildlife; it disrupts their gut so they stop feeding and die within a few days. Scatter it in the evening after watering, when slugs are most active, for the best effect.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Pull mulch back from around seedlings and clear the boards, pots, and leaf litter that give slugs a daytime hiding place close to the bed. A bare, cultivated strip around the planting slows their approach. Encourage ground beetles and, if you have them, hedgehogs, which prey on slugs through the night.

pests.name: Lettuce root aphid
pests.symptoms_beginner: Plants wilt in the heat of the day and just fail to thrive even though you are watering steadily, then slowly decline with no obvious cause above ground. Lift a struggling plant and you find clusters of aphids on the roots under a mass of white, woolly wax. It is easy to mistake for drought or a root disease until you look below the soil.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Once the aphids are on the roots, no spray will rescue the crop, so the fix is about how you manage the planting rather than treating it. Pull up and remove badly affected plants. Where it has happened, dig the soil over deeply and let it dry out thoroughly before planting lettuce there again, and keep your plants unstressed and well watered so a fast-growing crop can often still finish acceptably.
pests.prevention_beginner: Move lettuce around so it does not come back to the same ground each season, and avoid planting it close to Lombardy poplar trees, which are where the aphid spends the winter. Some lettuce varieties are bred to resist root aphid and are worth looking for if this pest keeps showing up in your garden.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Plants wilt during the heat of the day and fail to thrive despite steady watering, then decline with no obvious cause above ground. Lift a suspect plant and you find clusters of the aphids on the roots under masses of white, woolly wax. The damage is easy to mistake for drought or root disease until you look below the soil.
pests.cause_seasoned: The lettuce root aphid, Pemphigus bursarius, feeds on lettuce roots out of sight. It spends winter as eggs on Lombardy poplar, then winged forms migrate to lettuce in early summer, which is why infestations are worst where lettuce grows near those trees.
pests.cause_beginner: The lettuce root aphid feeds on lettuce roots out of sight. It spends winter as eggs on Lombardy poplar trees, then winged ones fly to lettuce in early summer, which is why the problem is worst where lettuce grows near those trees.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no spray that rescues an infested crop once the aphids are on the roots, so control is cultural. Pull and remove badly affected plants. Where the problem has occurred, work the soil deeply and let it dry thoroughly before replanting lettuce there, and keep plants unstressed and well watered so a fast-growing crop can often still finish acceptably.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Rotate lettuce so it does not return to the same ground each season, and avoid planting it close to Lombardy poplars, the aphid's overwintering host. Some lettuce varieties carry resistance to root aphid and are worth seeking out if the pest is a recurring problem in your garden.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Pale yellow patches show up on the upper side of the older leaves first, with a downy gray-purple mold underneath them. In cool, wet weather it spreads fast, and the affected areas turn brown and die as it moves up the plant.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove and throw away affected leaves right away, and open the planting up so air moves through and the leaves dry faster. A copper-based spray can help if you use it before the disease takes hold, as a preventive, rather than trying to cure it once it has spread.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Water at the soil and early in the day so the leaves are not wet overnight, since wet leaves are what this disease needs. Space plants well apart for airflow, and choose resistant varieties, which extension programs rate as the single most effective control. Avoid growing lettuce under cover through fall and winter without good airflow, where the cool, still, humid air is just what the disease likes.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Pale yellow patches appear on the upper surface of older leaves first, matched underneath by a downy gray-purple mold. In cool, wet weather it spreads fast, and affected areas brown and die as the infection moves up the plant.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Downy mildew is caused by Bremia lactucae, an oomycete (a water mold, not a true fungus). It needs cool, damp conditions and water sitting on the leaves to take hold, and its wind-borne spores spread quickly during moist spells. It does not survive in the soil, and because it is not a true fungus, ordinary fungicides aimed at fungi may not touch it.
diseases.cause_beginner: Downy mildew is caused by an organism called Bremia lactucae, a water mold rather than a true fungus. It needs cool, damp conditions and water sitting on the leaves to take hold, and its spores blow on the wind and spread quickly during wet spells. It does not survive in the soil, and because it is not a true fungus, ordinary fungus sprays may not work against it.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and dispose of affected leaves promptly, and open the planting up to improve airflow so leaves dry faster. A copper-based fungicide can help when used preventively, before the disease takes hold, rather than as a cure once it has spread.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Water at soil level and early in the day so leaves are not wet overnight, since leaf wetness is what the pathogen needs. Space plants generously for airflow, and choose resistant varieties, which extension programs rate as the single most effective control. Avoid growing under cover through autumn and winter without good ventilation, where the cool, still, humid air is ideal for it.

diseases.name: Tipburn
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Brown, papery scorch appears along the edges of the inner leaves, down in the heart of the plant rather than on the outer leaves. It does not spread from plant to plant, and it shows up most in romaine types and in hot weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no fix for leaves that are already scorched. Keep your watering consistent to steady the plant's calcium uptake, and improve airflow around the planting so the inner leaves can release a little more water.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Avoid forcing soft, fast growth with heavy nitrogen, which outruns the plant's ability to move calcium into the new leaves. Keep moisture even, harvest before heads are fully tight and mature in hot weather, and choose heat-tolerant varieties if summer tipburn keeps being a problem for you.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Brown, papery scorch appears along the edges of the inner leaves, down in the heart of the plant rather than the outer leaves. It does not spread from plant to plant, and it shows up most in cos and romaine types and in hot weather.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Tipburn is a physiological disorder, not a disease, and it is rarely about low calcium in the soil. Calcium travels through the plant in the stream of water it pulls up and transpires, so it collects in the fast-transpiring outer leaves. The young inner leaves are enclosed in the head where the air is still and humid and they transpire very little, so during rapid growth they cannot draw enough calcium and their edges collapse. Heat and lush, fast growth make it worse.
diseases.cause_beginner: Tipburn is a growing problem rather than a disease, and it is rarely about a lack of calcium in the soil. Calcium moves through the plant in the stream of water it pulls up and releases through its leaves, so it ends up in the outer leaves that release the most water. The young inner leaves are tucked inside the head where the air is still and humid, so they release very little water and, during fast growth, cannot pull in enough calcium, and their edges collapse. Heat and lush, fast growth make it worse.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no fix for leaves already scorched. Keep watering consistent to steady the plant's calcium uptake, and improve air movement around the planting so the inner leaves can transpire a little more.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Avoid pushing soft, rapid growth with heavy nitrogen, which outruns the plant's ability to move calcium into the new leaves. Keep moisture even, harvest before heads are fully tight and mature in hot weather, and choose heat-tolerant varieties where summer tipburn is a recurring problem.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Every 2 to 3 days in mild weather, more often in heat or in containers. The shallow root mass dries out faster than deeper-rooted crops, so the topsoil it depends on loses moisture quickly. Irregular watering is the real risk: a dry-then-flooded cycle stresses the plant, and water stress both reduces calcium transport to the leaf tips, which drives tipburn, and pushes the plant toward bolting.
watering.frequency_beginner: Every 2 to 3 days in mild weather, and more often in heat or in containers. The shallow roots dry out faster than those of deeper-rooted crops, so the topsoil they rely on loses moisture quickly. Uneven watering is the real risk: letting the soil go dry and then soaking it stresses the plant, which both causes tipburn (brown inner-leaf edges) and pushes the plant to bolt.
watering.amount_seasoned: 1 inch of water per week, but consistency matters more than volume for lettuce. Because the root system is shallow and concentrated in the top few inches of soil, lettuce has little buffer against drying out, and brief dry spells translate quickly into stress. Even, frequent moisture also supports the steady calcium uptake that prevents tipburn in fast-growing inner leaves.
watering.amount_beginner: About 1 inch of water per week, but for lettuce being consistent matters more than the exact amount. Because the roots are shallow and sit in just the top few inches of soil, lettuce dries out easily, and even short dry spells stress it quickly. Steady, even moisture also helps the plant move calcium to the fast-growing inner leaves, which prevents tipburn (the brown, dried leaf edges).
watering.method_seasoned: Water at soil level rather than overhead where practical. Lettuce sits low with leaves close to the soil, so overhead watering leaves moisture trapped in the crown and on leaf surfaces, where it invites downy mildew, bottom rot, and gray mold. If you do water overhead, do it in the morning so the foliage dries before the cool, damp evening hours when fungal infection is most likely.
watering.method_beginner: Water at the soil rather than over the top of the plants where you can. Lettuce sits low with its leaves close to the ground, so overhead watering leaves moisture trapped in the center and on the leaves, where it invites diseases like downy mildew and rot. If you do water from above, do it in the morning so the leaves dry off before the cool, damp evening, when leaf diseases are most likely to take hold.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Slimy or rotting leaf bases, yellowing outer leaves, and persistently wet soil. The slime at the base is bottom rot or gray mold taking hold in a crown that stays too wet, and yellowing lower leaves signal roots sitting in oxygen-starved, waterlogged soil. Because lettuce roots are shallow, soil that drains poorly keeps them waterlogged longer than it would a deeper-rooted plant.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Slimy or rotting leaf bases, yellowing outer leaves, and soil that stays wet. The slime at the base is rot taking hold in a crown that is too wet, and the yellowing lower leaves mean the roots are sitting in soggy, airless soil. Because lettuce roots are shallow, soil that drains poorly keeps them waterlogged longer than it would a deeper-rooted plant.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting in the afternoon heat, brown crisping along the edges of the inner leaves (tipburn), and bitterness. Tipburn is the diagnostic one: when the plant grows fast but cannot move enough calcium to the rapidly expanding inner leaves, often because water stress has slowed the transpiration that carries calcium upward, the leaf margins die back. Drought stress also accelerates bolting, after which leaves turn bitter as the plant floods them with defensive compounds.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Wilting in the afternoon heat, brown crisping along the edges of the inner leaves (this is called tipburn), and a bitter taste. Tipburn is the clearest sign: when the plant grows fast but cannot move enough calcium to the quickly expanding inner leaves, often because dry conditions have slowed the plant down, the leaf edges die back. Dry stress also makes the plant bolt sooner, and once it bolts the leaves turn bitter.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Water at soil level rather than overhead where practical: lettuce sits low with leaves near the ground, so overhead watering traps moisture in the crown and invites downy mildew, bottom rot, and gray mold. If overhead is unavoidable, water in the morning so foliage dries before the cool, damp evening. Even, frequent moisture also supports the steady calcium uptake that prevents tipburn.
watering.method_note_beginner: Water the soil rather than the leaves where you can. Lettuce grows low to the ground, so water sitting on the leaves can lead to mildew and rot. If you do water from above, do it in the morning so the leaves dry off before evening. Keeping the water even and steady also helps prevent the brown, crispy leaf edges called tipburn.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Lettuce has a shallow root mass with little drought buffer, so it wants consistent moisture across its whole short cycle rather than one critical stage. The highest-stakes window is the final rapid leaf expansion before harvest: water stress here both reduces calcium transport to the inner leaf tips, driving tipburn, and pushes the plant toward bolting.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Because lettuce roots are shallow, it needs steady, even moisture for its whole short life rather than at one particular moment. The riskiest time to let it dry out is the last stretch of fast leaf growth before you pick it: dry spells then cause brown leaf edges (tipburn) and can make the plant bolt, turning bitter and going to seed.

start_method.hardening_off_beginner: You do not need to harden off leaf lettuce when you direct sow it. Seeds go straight into the garden. If you instead buy or raise transplants, give them a few days to adjust to outdoor conditions before planting out.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Direct sow outdoors about 3 to 4 weeks before your last spring frost, as soon as the soil is workable, since lettuce tolerates light frost and germinates in cool soil. To get an earlier harvest, start seeds indoors roughly 4 weeks ahead and set out 3 to 4 week old transplants, which also skips the thinning step. Lettuce transplants easily because its shallow roots re-establish quickly, just harden plants off before moving them outside.
start_method.notes_beginner: Sow seed straight into the garden about 3 to 4 weeks before your last spring frost, as soon as you can work the soil, since lettuce handles light frost and sprouts in cool ground. For an earlier harvest, start seeds indoors about 4 weeks ahead and set out the young plants when they are 3 to 4 weeks old, which also lets you skip thinning. Lettuce moves outdoors easily because its shallow roots settle in fast, just harden the plants off first (let them get used to outdoor conditions over several days before planting them out).

container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: Depth matters far more than width for lettuce. The roots are shallow, so about 6 to 8 inches of soil depth is plenty, which is why window boxes, grow bags, shallow troughs, and salad tables all work well. Width drives how many plants you can fit rather than whether they will thrive: give leaf types a few inches apart and head types more room. Wider, shallower vessels usually out-produce a tall narrow pot of the same volume because they expose more surface for cut-and-come-again leaves.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: For lettuce, depth matters far less than you might think and width matters more. The roots are shallow, so about 6 to 8 inches of soil depth is plenty, which is why window boxes, grow bags, shallow troughs, and salad planters all work well. Width mainly decides how many plants you can fit, not whether they will do well: give leaf types a few inches apart and head types more room. A wide, shallow container usually produces more than a tall narrow pot holding the same amount of soil, because it gives you more surface for cut-and-come-again leaves.

drainage.saucer_practice_seasoned: Drainage holes are non-negotiable, and the roots must never sit in standing water: waterlogged soil leaves no air for the roots and invites root rot, which lettuce rarely recovers from. If you use a saucer, empty it after each watering and after rain, or raise the pot on feet, bricks, or slats so it is not sitting in a pool or flat on concrete; a detachable saucer is far safer than a built-in one you cannot drain. There is a real tradeoff, since a saucer does help hold moisture and humidity in hot, dry conditions, but the standing-water risk outweighs that benefit, so the rule is empty-or-elevate rather than going without drainage.
drainage.saucer_practice_beginner: Drainage holes are a must, and the roots must never sit in standing water: waterlogged soil leaves no air for the roots and invites root rot, which lettuce rarely recovers from. If you use a saucer under the pot, empty it after each watering and after rain, or raise the pot up on feet, bricks, or slats so it is not sitting in a puddle or flat on concrete. A removable saucer is much safer than a built-in one you cannot drain. There is a real trade-off, since a saucer does help hold moisture in hot, dry weather, but the risk of standing water outweighs that, so the rule is empty it or raise it rather than skipping drainage.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Use a potting mix made for containers (sometimes labeled potting soil), not soil dug from the garden.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Start with a good container or potting mix rather than garden soil, which packs down in a pot and drains poorly; if you do reuse garden soil, keep it to no more than a third of the total. A good blend balances drainage with holding moisture: a peat or coir base to hold water, perlite (the little white specks) for air and drainage, and compost for richness. Mixing in roughly a quarter perlite by volume lightens a mix that feels heavy, and a slow-release balanced fertilizer added at planting gives the plants an even start.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: container_potting_mix
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Start from a quality container or potting mix rather than garden soil, which compacts in a pot and drains poorly; if you do reuse garden soil, keep it to no more than a third of the total. A good blend balances drainage and moisture retention: a peat or coir base for water-holding, perlite for air and drainage, and compost for fertility and structure. Working in roughly 20 to 25 percent perlite by volume lightens a mix that feels dense, and a slow-release balanced fertilizer added at planting gives the crop an even start.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Containers dry out much faster than garden beds because they hold less soil and the sides and top are exposed to sun and air, so there is little moisture to fall back on. In summer heat, especially on a sunny patio or balcony, you will often need to water daily, and sometimes twice a day during hot, dry spells. Water until it runs out the drainage holes so the whole root zone gets wet, and do not let the mix dry out completely: once a peat or coir potting mix fully dries it pulls away from the pot wall, and water then runs straight down that gap and leaves the middle dry. Even moisture is the real goal, because the dry-then-wet swings of a small pot stress lettuce's shallow roots and push it toward bitterness and bolting.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Lettuce in a container needs feeding more often, and more lightly, than lettuce in the ground. A pot holds only a small amount of nutrients, the plant uses them up quickly, and every watering washes a little out the drainage holes, so the supply does not last the way garden soil does. A good rhythm is a balanced liquid feed every 1 to 3 weeks during the growing season, or a slow-release granular fertilizer mixed in at planting with a top-up check mid-season. Lettuce is a leafy crop that likes nitrogen but grows fast and finishes quickly, so steady light feeding works better than heavy doses, which can force soft growth and, in warm weather, speed up bolting.
container_notes.notes_beginner: Lettuce is one of the best crops for containers. The roots are shallow, so any pot about 6 inches deep or more works fine, including window boxes, grow bags, and shallow salad planters.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: One of the best container crops. The roots are shallow, so any container about 6 inches deep or more works, including window boxes, grow bags, and salad tables.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry out much faster than in-ground beds because the soil volume is limited and the sides and top are exposed to air and sun, so the moisture buffer is small. In summer heat, and especially on a sunny patio or balcony, daily watering is often necessary and twice a day is not unusual during hot, dry spells. Water until it runs from the drainage holes so the whole root zone wets through, and do not let the mix dry out completely: once a peat or coir mix fully dries it shrinks from the pot wall and water channels straight down the gap, leaving the center dry. Even moisture is the real goal, since the swings that come with under-watering a small pot stress shallow lettuce roots and push the plant toward bitterness and bolting.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Container lettuce needs feeding more often, and more lightly, than lettuce in the ground. The medium holds only a small nutrient reserve, plant uptake draws it down quickly, and every watering leaches some nutrients out the drainage holes, so the supply does not last the way garden soil does. A practical rhythm is a balanced water-soluble feed every 1 to 3 weeks through the growing season, or a slow-release granular worked into the mix at planting with a check mid-season. Lettuce is a leafy, nitrogen-responsive crop but a short one, so steady modest feeding beats heavy doses, which can force soft growth and, in warm spells, hasten bolting.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering container suits lettuce especially well, since the shallow, drought-sensitive root system benefits directly from the even moisture that wicking sub-irrigation provides, and keeping water off the foliage limits the leaf diseases lettuce is prone to. Keep the reservoir filled in warm weather, when the small soil volume dries fast, and top-water occasionally to flush salts.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot is a great match for lettuce because it keeps the water steady, which is exactly what these shallow-rooted plants want, and it keeps the leaves dry so they are less likely to get diseases. Keep the bottom reservoir filled in warm weather since small pots dry out quickly, and water from the top now and then to rinse out built-up minerals.

recommended: Black Seeded Simpson (classic loose-leaf)
Buttercrunch (butterhead)
Romaine/Cos
Salad Bowl (heat tolerant)
varieties.note_seasoned: Buttercrunch is among the most forgiving varieties for beginners, a butterhead type that is more heat tolerant and slower to bolt than crisphead lettuces, with a longer productive window in warm weather.
varieties.note_beginner: Buttercrunch is one of the easiest varieties for beginners. It is a butterhead type, which handles heat better and is slower to go to seed (bolt) than the crisphead lettuces you see as supermarket iceberg, so it keeps producing longer when the weather warms up.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: A few hours at most. Lettuce has a high respiration rate and loses water rapidly at room temperature, so it wilts within hours of being left out. Unlike fruit, it gains nothing from sitting on the counter, so get it into the cold as soon as possible after harvest or purchase to preserve crispness.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Only a few hours. Lettuce loses water very quickly at room temperature, so it wilts within hours if left out. Unlike fruit, it does not improve by sitting on the counter, so get it into the fridge as soon as you can after picking or buying it to keep it crisp.
storage.fridge_seasoned: 7 to 10 days, wrapped loosely in a dry paper towel inside a partly open bag. Lettuce loses water and wilts quickly because its thin, high-surface-area leaves transpire fast, so the towel absorbs excess surface moisture while the bag slows drying. Keep it in the crisper, the coldest and most humid part of the fridge, and away from the freezer wall, since lettuce is easily damaged by freezing.
storage.fridge_beginner: About 7 to 10 days, wrapped loosely in a dry paper towel inside a partly open bag. Lettuce wilts quickly because its thin leaves lose water fast, so the towel soaks up extra surface moisture while the bag slows the drying. Keep it in the crisper drawer, which is the coldest and most humid part of the fridge, and away from the back wall, since lettuce is easily damaged if it freezes.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Not suitable. Freezing forms ice crystals inside the leaf cells that rupture the cell walls, so thawed lettuce collapses into darkened, water-soaked tissue that quickly turns slimy. There is no cooked use that recovers it the way frozen tomatoes work for sauce; the high water content and delicate structure leave nothing usable. Lettuce is a fresh-only crop.
storage.freezer_beginner: Lettuce does not freeze well. Freezing forms tiny ice crystals inside the leaves that break the cells apart, so once thawed the lettuce turns dark, soggy, and quickly slimy. There is no cooked use that brings it back the way frozen tomatoes still work for sauce, because lettuce is too watery and delicate. It is a fresh-only crop.
storage.notes_seasoned: Don't wash until you're ready to eat, since surface moisture speeds rot in storage. Keep lettuce away from apples, pears, and other ethylene-producing fruit: lettuce is highly sensitive to ethylene gas, which triggers russet spotting, the small rusty-brown spots that appear along the leaf ribs. Store loosely in the crisper drawer so leaves aren't crushed and air can move around them.
storage.notes_beginner: Do not wash lettuce until you are ready to eat it, because surface water speeds up rotting in the fridge. Keep it away from apples, pears, and other ripening fruit: those fruits give off a natural gas called ethylene, and lettuce is very sensitive to it. The gas causes russet spotting, small rusty-brown spots along the leaf ribs. Store the leaves loosely in the crisper drawer so they are not crushed and air can move around them.

bolting.triggers: Heat above 75°F, long days (>14 hours), stress
bolting.prevention_seasoned: Choose slow-bolt varieties (Buttercrunch, Batavian types, heat-tolerant romaines like Jericho). Give afternoon shade in summer, or site lettuce where taller crops shade it during peak heat. Succession sow every 2 to 3 weeks rather than one large planting, so a bolted batch is quickly replaced. Harvesting the outer leaves regularly also delays bolting by keeping the plant in vegetative growth.
bolting.prevention_beginner: Choose slow-to-bolt varieties (Buttercrunch, Batavian types, and heat-tolerant romaines like Jericho). Give the plants afternoon shade in summer, or grow them where taller crops shade them during the hottest part of the day. Sow a new small batch every 2 to 3 weeks instead of one big planting, so a batch that bolts is quickly replaced. Picking the outer leaves regularly also delays bolting by keeping the plant focused on leaf growth.
bolting.note_seasoned: Bolting is the plant switching from leaf growth to flowering, and it's irreversible once it starts. The trigger is primarily long days, lengthening past about 14 hours, with heat and water stress accelerating it; it is not heat alone. As the plant bolts it floods its leaves with sesquiterpene lactones, bitter defensive compounds, so harvest promptly at the first sign, since the central leaves are still usable before bitterness fully sets in.
bolting.note_beginner: Bolting is when the plant switches from growing leaves to making flowers, and once it starts there is no reversing it. The main trigger is long days, when daylight stretches past about 14 hours, with heat and dry stress speeding it up. It is not heat alone. As the plant bolts it fills its leaves with bitter compounds, so harvest right away at the first sign, while the inner leaves are still good to eat before the bitterness fully sets in.

thinning.to_spacing: 6-8 inches for leaf lettuce, 10-12 for heads
thinning.method: Snip extras at soil level; thinnings are edible as salad.
thinning.tip_seasoned: Thin in stages rather than all at once. Thin loosely on the first pass to give seedlings room, then as plants crowd again pull every other one and eat the pulls as baby salad, leaving the rest more space to size up. Successive thinning turns a necessary chore into extra early harvests and avoids wasting any plants.
thinning.tip_beginner: Thin in stages rather than all at once. On the first pass, thin loosely to give the seedlings some room. Then, as the plants crowd together again, pull every other one and eat those pulls as baby salad, leaving the rest more space to grow. Thinning this way turns a necessary chore into extra early harvests and means no plant goes to waste.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Other daisy-family crops, endive, radicchio, chicory, and artichoke. They host the same soilborne diseases as lettuce (the fungi behind lettuce drop, bottom rot, and downy mildew build up where these hosts return year after year), and they also share lettuce root aphid, so following one with another keeps the same pests and pathogens in the bed.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Avoid planting lettuce where its daisy-family relatives grew last: endive, radicchio, chicory, and artichoke. They get the same soil diseases as lettuce (the organisms behind lettuce drop, bottom rot, and downy mildew build up in the soil when these plants keep returning to the same spot), and they share the same root-feeding aphid, so following one with another just keeps the same pests and diseases going in that bed.
rotation.good_after: Legumes, brassicas, root vegetables
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate lettuce out of the same bed for about 3 years, and avoid following other daisy-family crops (endive, radicchio, chicory, artichoke) in the same spot. The main reason is soilborne disease: the fungi behind lettuce drop (Sclerotinia), bottom rot, and downy mildew build up in soil and on debris when hosts return year after year. Lettuce root aphid, which can carry over in soil as well as cycling through nearby poplars, is a secondary reason to move the crop.
rotation.note_beginner: Try not to grow lettuce in the same spot more than about once every 3 years, and avoid planting it where its close relatives in the daisy family grew last (endive, radicchio, chicory, artichoke). The main reason is soil disease: the organisms behind common lettuce problems like lettuce drop, bottom rot, and downy mildew build up in the soil when the same kind of plant keeps coming back to that spot. A root-feeding insect called lettuce root aphid, which can survive in the soil, is a second reason to keep moving the crop around.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The first pair of rounded seed leaves pushing up through the soil. Leafy greens come up readily in cool, moist ground, often in well under a week, and germination is usually even if the surface has not been allowed to dry out.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The first pair of rounded seed leaves pushing up through the soil. Leafy greens come up readily in cool, moist ground, often in well under a week, and they usually come up evenly as long as you have not let the surface dry out.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep the soil surface consistently moist but never waterlogged until seedlings are up. Most leafy greens germinate best between about 50 and 65°F and actually prefer cooler soil than warm-season crops like tomatoes; in real heat, germination drops off and seed can go dormant, so early sowings tend to come up better than late-spring ones.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil surface evenly moist but never soggy until the seedlings are up. Most leafy greens sprout best between about 50 and 65°F and actually prefer cooler soil than warm-season crops like tomatoes. In real heat, fewer seeds sprout and some go dormant, so early sowings tend to come up better than late-spring ones.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The first true leaves, which look like miniature versions of the crop rather than the plain oval seed leaves. At this point you can tell the seedlings apart from any weeds coming up alongside them.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The first true leaves, which look like miniature versions of the grown-up plant rather than the plain oval seed leaves. At this point you can tell your seedlings apart from any weeds coming up next to them.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin to the recommended spacing now, even though pulling healthy seedlings feels wasteful. Crowded leafy greens get less airflow, compete for water, and bolt sooner while producing smaller plants. The thinnings are completely edible, so use them as baby leaves or microgreens in a salad.

growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Leaves reaching a useful size and the plant looking full and healthy, well before any stalk starts to rise from the center. This is the long, productive stretch for a leafy crop.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Start picking the outer leaves now rather than waiting for the plant to look finished. Taking the outer leaves signals the plant to keep pushing new growth from the center, so regular light harvesting gives you more over a longer period than a single cut. Leave the growing point and inner leaves intact.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Start picking the outer leaves now rather than waiting for the plant to look finished. Taking the outer leaves tells the plant to keep pushing new growth from the center, so regular light picking gives you more over a longer time than one big cut. growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves at full, good size and still tender, with no yellowing and no sign of a flowering stem forming in the center. Once a stalk appears the eating window is closing.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Leaves at full, good size and still tender, with no yellowing and no sign of a flower stalk forming in the center. Once a stalk appears, the eating window is starting to close.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest cut-and-come-again: take the outer leaves and let the center keep growing for repeat pickings over weeks. Take no more than about half the plant at once so it can recover. For butterhead and other heading types, cut the whole head once it has formed rather than picking leaf by leaf.

growth_stages.name: Bolting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A central stalk shooting up from the middle of the plant, with the newer leaves turning smaller, narrower, and noticeably more bitter. This is bolting, the plant shifting from leaf growth to flowering and seed.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A stalk shooting up from the middle of the plant, with the newer leaves turning smaller, narrower, and noticeably more bitter. This is bolting, the plant switching from growing leaves to making flowers and seed.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Once bolting starts the flavor turns and there is no reversing it, so harvest everything worth eating right away. Bolted leaves are still safe to eat but get increasingly bitter, so use them quickly. Then pull the plant and either resow for a later crop or give the space to a warm-season vegetable, and consider leaving one plant to flower for the pollinators or to save seed.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to sow your leafy greens
notifications.title_beginner: Time to sow your leafy greens
notifications.body_seasoned: Leafy greens thrive in cool weather and can go out 4 to 6 weeks before your last frost, earlier than most crops. Sow them straight into prepared soil, or start them indoors to transplant. Sow a short row every couple of weeks rather than all at once, so you get a steady supply of young, tender leaves instead of everything maturing together.
notifications.body_beginner: Leafy greens love cool weather and can go out 4 to 6 weeks before your last frost, earlier than most crops. Sow them straight into prepared soil, or start them indoors to plant out later. Sow a short row every couple of weeks instead of all at once, so you get a steady supply of young, tender leaves rather than everything coming ready together.

notifications.title_seasoned: Your greens should be ready to start picking
notifications.title_beginner: Your greens should be ready to start picking
notifications.body_seasoned: Begin picking the outer leaves now, even if the plant still looks small. Regular harvesting is what drives more growth from the center, so frequent light picking gives you far more over the season than waiting for a finished plant. Leafy greens are a harvest-as-you-go crop, not a one-time cut.

notifications.title_seasoned: Heat incoming: watch your greens for bolting
notifications.title_beginner: Heat incoming, watch your greens for bolting
notifications.body_seasoned: Hot weather pushes leafy greens to bolt, sending up a flower stalk and turning the leaves bitter. Harvest everything you can now, before the heat sets in. Steady watering and a bit of afternoon shade buy a little time, and a fresh sowing in late summer will give you a tender fall crop once temperatures ease.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to sow your fall leafy greens
notifications.title_beginner: Time to sow your fall leafy greens
notifications.body_seasoned: About eight weeks before your first frost is the window for a second sowing of leafy greens. A fall crop often outdoes spring: the cooling temperatures mean slower bolting and sweeter leaves, and many greens, kale especially, actually taste better after a light frost.
