pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick them off after dark by flashlight, set out shallow dishes of beer to trap them, or scatter an iron-phosphate slug bait, which is safe around pets and wildlife. Remove hiding spots like boards and dense debris near the plants.
pests.prevention_beginner: Water in the morning so the surface dries by night, give plants room for airflow, and clear leaf litter, boards, and weeds where slugs hide during the day. A ring of coarse, scratchy material around plants can slow them down.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Irregular ragged holes with smooth edges in the foliage, concentrated on the large lower leaves and any leaf resting on damp soil, accompanied by silvery slime trails. Feeding is nocturnal and worst in cool, wet, shaded conditions and under dense canopy.
pests.cause_seasoned: Slugs and land snails that shelter in moist debris by day and feed on tender foliage at night; chard's broad, low leaves and the humid microclimate beneath a full stand favor them, particularly in wet weather and irrigated beds.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick after dark, trap with shallow beer dishes or boards used as daytime refuges to collect under, and apply an iron-phosphate bait where pressure is high. Reduce the moist daytime harborage that sustains them.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Irrigate in the morning so surfaces dry by nightfall, space plants for airflow, and clear boards, litter, and weeds that harbor slugs. Remove the lowest leaves resting on soil to cut humidity at the crown.

diseases.name: Cercospora leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The leaves get many small round spots, about an eighth of an inch wide, with a pale tan or gray center and a darker reddish-purple or brown ring around each one. They start on the older outer leaves and spread inward, and when there are lots of them the leaves brown and die. It spoils the leaves you want to eat.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that lives on old chard and beet debris and on related weeds, and gets splashed onto the plant by rain or overhead watering. It loves warm, humid weather and wet leaves, so it is worst in warm, wet areas and rainy spells.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot cure leaves that are already spotted, only slow it down. Pick off and throw away the worst leaves, water at the soil in the morning so the leaves dry fast, and give plants room so air moves through. In a very wet year a copper fungicide labeled for vegetables can help if you start early.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Do not grow chard (or beets and spinach) in the same spot two or three years running, clean up old leaves and debris where the fungus lives, water at the base instead of overhead, and give plants room so the leaves dry quickly.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Numerous small round spots about an eighth of an inch across, each with a tan to gray center and a darker reddish-purple to brown margin, appear first on the older outer leaves and spread inward; when numerous they merge and the leaf withers. Because the crop is the leaf, even moderate spotting downgrades the harvest, and severe leaf loss reduces overall yield.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Cercospora beticola, which survives on infected chard and beet debris and on related weeds and is splashed onto the leaves by rain and overhead irrigation. It is favored by warm, humid weather and prolonged leaf wetness, so it is most damaging in warm, wet regions and seasons, including the long southern harvest.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure for spotted tissue; management slows spread. Remove and destroy badly infected leaves, water at the base in the morning so foliage dries quickly, and thin or space plants for airflow. In a wet season a copper-based fungicide labeled for vegetables can suppress spread if started early, but cultural control carries most of the load.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate chard and its relatives (beet, spinach) out of the bed for two to three years, clear and destroy crop debris, avoid overhead watering, and space and thin for airflow. Choose tolerant varieties where the disease recurs.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Pale yellow patches show on top of the leaves, with a grayish or purplish fuzzy growth underneath in damp weather. The young leaves in the center can be twisted, thick, and curled. It is worst in cool, wet weather and mainly hurts the leaves.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus-like water mold that infects in cool, wet weather and spreads in damp air and splashing water. It survives on old plant debris and on chard's relatives beets and spinach.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot cure infected leaves, so pick off and throw away the worst ones and help the plants dry out by giving them room. Keeping the leaves dry does most of the work; a copper fungicide is a last resort in a very wet stretch.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Water at the soil instead of overhead, give plants room so air moves through, and stay out of the bed when the leaves are wet. Move chard away from where you grew chard, beets, or spinach, and pick a tolerant variety if it keeps showing up.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Pale yellow, indistinct blotches on the upper leaf surface with a grayish to purplish downy growth on the corresponding undersides in damp weather; young central leaves are often distorted, thickened, and curled. It is most damaging in cool, wet conditions and chiefly disfigures the foliage.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The water mold Peronospora farinosa (P. betae), which infects in cool, moist conditions and survives on crop debris and related goosefoot hosts, spreading in moist air and splashing water. Chard shares it with beet and spinach.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No cure for infected tissue; remove and destroy affected leaves to reduce spread and improve airflow and drying. Cultural control is the mainstay, with copper fungicides a last resort in a persistently wet season.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Water at the base, space and thin for airflow, and avoid working among wet plants. Rotate away from chard, beet, and spinach, clear crop debris, and choose tolerant varieties where it recurs.

diseases.name: Damping-off
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Seeds that never come up, or tiny seedlings that flop over and die just after sprouting, with a dark, pinched, wet-looking spot on the stem right at the soil line. You see it as bare gaps in the row. Cool, soggy soil and the slow-sprouting chard seedball make it more likely.
diseases.cause_beginner: Soil organisms attack sprouting seeds and baby seedlings, especially when the soil is cold and soggy and the seeds are slow to come up. Chard sown in cold, wet ground is at risk.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Seedlings that have flopped will not recover. If it shows up, stop watering for a bit and let the soil surface dry out some, and clear away the fallen seedlings. There is no good home cure once it starts, so this one is mostly about prevention.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Wait until the soil is warm enough and not cold and soggy, keep the seedbed damp without keeping it soaking, plant at the right depth in well-drained soil, and use fresh seed. Soaking the seedballs for a day before sowing helps them come up faster.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Poor stands from seed and pre- or post-emergence collapse of seedlings with a dark, water-soaked, pinched lesion at the stem base at the soil line, worst in cold, wet, poorly drained soil where the slow chard seedball prolongs the vulnerable window. Losses show as bare gaps in the row.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Soilborne Pythium and Rhizoctonia species that attack germinating seed and young seedlings, favored by cool, wet, poorly drained soil and overwatering; old or weak seed and a crusted seedbed increase losses.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Affected seedlings cannot be saved. Stop watering and let the surface dry to slow the pathogens, and clear collapsed seedlings; there is no effective home cure once it takes hold, so prevention is the lever.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Sow into warm-enough, well-drained soil rather than cold, wet ground, keep the seedbed evenly moist without saturating it, use fresh seed, and do not sow too deep. Soaking the seedball for a day speeds emergence and shortens the risk window.

diseases.name: Root-knot nematode
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The plants grow slowly and wilt in the heat of the day even when the soil is moist, and the leaves yellow and stay stunted. If you dig up a plant, the roots have small knots or swellings (galls) on them. It is worst in warm, sandy soils, which is why it matters most in places like Florida.
diseases.cause_beginner: Tiny worms in the soil, too small to see, invade the roots and make the galls that block the plant from taking up water and food. They build up where chard or other host crops are grown over and over in warm soil.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no spray that cures an infected plant, so pull and destroy badly affected plants at the end of the season. The fix is for next time: rotate to a different bed, add lots of compost, and keep plants well watered to help them cope.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Rotate chard to a fresh spot, add plenty of organic matter, and avoid following other host crops in warm, sandy beds. In bad spots, plant in containers with fresh mix, or grow chard in the cooler months when nematodes are less active.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Stunting, midday wilting despite adequate soil moisture, chlorosis, and reduced vigor aboveground, with characteristic root galls (knots) belowground. UF/IFAS notes chard is very susceptible. Damage is heaviest in warm, sandy soils and where host crops are grown repeatedly, so it is chiefly a southern and warm-region concern.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne species), microscopic soilborne roundworms that invade roots and induce galls that impair water and nutrient uptake; populations build under warm soil and continuous host cropping.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No rescue for an infected plant; remove and destroy heavily galled plants. Management is preventive and cultural: build organic matter, keep plants watered to tolerate the stress, and break the host cycle for future crops.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate with non-host or resistant crops, incorporate ample organic matter, avoid following susceptible hosts in warm sandy beds, and consider container culture with fresh mix or cool-season scheduling where nematodes are established.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Even, consistent moisture is the rule, most critical during the slow germination window and through the long cutting season. Aim for about 1 to 1.5 inches of water per week including rain once established, delivered in deeper, less frequent soakings; chard is shallow-rooted and steady moisture keeps the leaves and stalks tender.
watering.frequency_beginner: Keep the soil evenly damp, paying closest attention while the seeds are sprouting and while you are harvesting. Once the plants are growing, give about 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week, counting rain, in fewer but deeper waterings.
watering.amount_seasoned: Roughly 1 to 1.5 inches per week including rainfall once established, more in heat or sandy soil and less in cool or heavy soil. During germination the seedbed needs only enough to stay evenly moist near the surface.
watering.amount_beginner: About 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week, including rain, once the plants are growing. Give more in hot, dry weather and less in cool weather. While the seeds are sprouting, just keep the top of the soil damp.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base with a soaker hose or drip line to keep the surface evenly moist without crusting the bed or washing out the shallow-sown seedballs, and to keep the foliage dry, which checks Cercospora and downy mildew. Avoid hard overhead bursts on a fresh seedbed.
watering.method_beginner: Water gently at soil level, using a soaker hose or drip line. A hard blast from the hose can wash out the shallow seeds or pack the soil into a crust the sprouts cannot push through, and wet leaves invite disease, so keep it gentle and low.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Constantly saturated soil invites damping-off in seedlings and the leaf diseases, and yellowing lower leaves, soft growth, and a sour, waterlogged bed are signs to back off. Poor drainage is the usual cause.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If the soil stays soaking wet, seedlings can damp off and the leaves can get moldy. Watch for yellow lower leaves and a constantly wet, sour-smelling bed. If you see these, water less and make sure the soil drains well.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Dull, wilting leaves, slowed growth, and toughened, stringy stalks signal too little water. Chard is heat-tolerant but only with steady moisture; drought in heat is what stalls it, so keep water even through warm spells.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Droopy, dull leaves, slow growth, and tough, stringy stems mean the chard needs more water. Chard handles heat well, but only if you keep it watered, so do not let the bed dry out in summer.
watering.method_note_seasoned: On a fresh seedbed, keep the surface evenly moist without crusting or dislodging the shallow seedballs. After establishment, shift to deeper, less frequent soakings; steady moisture is what lets chard keep producing through summer heat that would bolt or scorch lettuce and spinach.
watering.method_note_beginner: While the seeds are sprouting, water gently so you do not wash them out or make a hard crust. Once the chard is growing, water more deeply but less often. Keeping the water steady is the secret to harvesting chard right through the summer.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Two windows matter most: germination through emergence, when the surface must stay continuously moist and uncrusted or the slow stand fails, and any sustained summer heat, when even moisture is what keeps the heat-tolerant crop growing tender leaves instead of stalling.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The two most important times to keep the soil moist are while the seeds are sprouting and during hot summer weather. Steady water in the heat is what lets chard keep going when other greens give up.

start_method.hardening_off_beginner: You do not need to harden off chard when you direct-sow it. If you start a few plants indoors to transplant, harden them off over about a week before setting them out.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Chard is usually direct-sown, since it grows quickly and, like its relative the beet, transplants best when young; it can be started indoors for an early plant or set out as transplants spaced 4 to 6 inches apart (UMN), but most gardeners sow in place. Sow about half an inch deep once the soil is workable and at least 50°F, from about 2 to 3 weeks before the last spring frost. The key chard-specific point is that each chard seed is a multigerm seedball, a dried fruit containing several embryos, so a single seed sprouts a small cluster of seedlings and the stand must be thinned. Avoid sowing into cold soil, which can vernalize young plants and trigger premature bolting. Keep the surface moist and uncrusted until emergence, often 1 to 2 weeks.
start_method.notes_beginner: Plant chard seeds right in the garden where they will grow. Sow them about half an inch deep once the soil is no longer frozen or soggy, about 2 to 3 weeks before your last spring frost. Here is the chard surprise: each seed is really a little dried fruit holding several seeds, so one seed grows a small clump of seedlings, which is why you have to thin them later. You can also start a few indoors and transplant them. Do not plant too early into cold soil, which can make young plants flower (bolt) prematurely. Keep the soil surface damp until the sprouts appear, often 1 to 2 weeks.

drainage.saucer_practice_seasoned: Do not let the pot stand in a saucer of water. Chard needs even moisture, but a waterlogged mix rots the crown and invites disease; empty the saucer within an hour of watering.
drainage.saucer_practice_beginner: Do not let the pot sit in a saucer of water. Chard likes steady moisture, but soil that stays soggy will rot the plant, so empty the saucer within an hour of watering.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Use a bag of loose potting mix made for containers, not garden soil.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in some compost so the soil holds water evenly and feeds the long harvest.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: container_potting_mix
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Use a light, loose potting mix high in organic matter; blend in compost and a starter nitrogen source for the sustained leafy harvest. Avoid garden soil, which compacts in a pot.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out much faster than the ground, so check daily in warm weather. Chard needs steady moisture to keep making tender leaves, so do not let the mix dry out, especially in summer heat.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Feed a little more often than in the ground, since watering washes nutrients out of pots. A light liquid feed every couple of weeks keeps the leaves coming.

overwintering.approach_beginner: In mild areas, a pot of chard can keep producing through winter in a sheltered, sunny spot. In cold areas, move the pot against the house or into a cold frame, or cover it during hard freezes, and it will often resume in spring.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Chard is frost-tolerant, so a container can overwinter in mild zones, holding through winter in a sheltered spot and resuming growth in spring. In cold zones the limited root volume of a pot freezes harder than open ground, so sink it, move it to a cold frame or unheated structure, or cover it during hard freezes. Note that an overwintered plant has been vernalized and will bolt as spring warms, so plan to crop it before the stalk forms.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Chard is a great container crop and a pretty one, especially the rainbow-stemmed types. Use a pot at least 10 inches deep with drainage holes and loose potting mix, give one plant a 5-gallon pot or space several in a larger one, keep the soil evenly moist, and pick the outer leaves so it keeps regrowing all season.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Chard suits containers well and the colorful-stemmed cultivars double as ornamentals. Use a container at least 10 inches deep with drainage holes and a loose, organic potting mix; a single plant fills a 5-gallon pot, or space several in a larger trough. Keep moisture even to keep leaves and stalks tender, feed regularly for the long harvest, and crop the outer leaves cut-and-come-again. It carries well from a sunny patio through much of the year.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry far faster than beds, and chard stalls and toughens under drought stress, so check the top inch or two daily in warm weather and water before the mix dries. Aim for consistently moist but never soggy.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Chard is a sustained leafy feeder. Mix a balanced slow-release fertilizer into the potting mix at sowing and supplement with a half-strength liquid nitrogen feed every couple of weeks through the cutting season, since frequent watering leaches pots.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering container suits chard well once it is growing, because steady sub-irrigation delivers the even moisture that keeps the leaves and stalks tender through heat. It does not help germination, though: the seedball sits at the dry surface above the wicking zone, so keep the top inch moist by hand until the stand is up.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot works well for chard once it is growing, because it keeps the water steady, and steady water means tender leaves through summer. It will not keep the seeds moist while they sprout, though, so water the surface gently by hand until the seedlings come up.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: Chard makes a substantial leafy plant, so give it depth and room: a container at least 10 inches deep with enough width to space plants 6 inches or more apart. A 5-gallon pot suits one full plant; wider troughs hold several for a steady cut-and-come-again supply.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Chard grows into a good-sized plant, so use a roomy pot at least 10 inches deep. One plant is happy in a 5-gallon bucket, or space a few out in a wider container.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Poor for more than a day or two. At room temperature chard leaves wilt and yellow quickly; cut leaves should be refrigerated promptly. The sturdy stalks hold a little better than the blades but are still best chilled.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Do not leave chard out on the counter. The leaves wilt fast in the warmth, so get it into the fridge soon after picking.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerate unwashed in a loose or perforated bag in the crisper; chard holds about 1 to 2 weeks near 32°F at high humidity, a bit longer than spinach thanks to the sturdier leaves and stalks. Washing before storage traps moisture and speeds breakdown, so wait to wash until use.
storage.fridge_beginner: Store chard unwashed in a loose bag in the fridge's crisper drawer, where it keeps for 1 to 2 weeks if kept very cold. Wash it only when you are ready to cook it.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Chard freezes well once blanched: separate the stalks from the leaves (the stalks need a minute or two longer), blanch about 2 minutes, cool quickly in ice water, drain well, and freeze. Blanching halts the enzymes that otherwise cause off-flavors and color loss.
storage.freezer_beginner: Chard freezes well if you blanch it first. Cut the leaves from the stalks, boil the leaves about 2 minutes (the stalks a little longer), cool them right away in ice water, drain, and freeze.
storage.notes_seasoned: Quality is highest straight from the garden, which is one of the joys of a cut-and-come-again crop: pick what you need and the plant keeps making more. The colorful stalks can be stored and cooked separately from the leaves, like a vegetable in their own right. Chill promptly and use fresh within a week or so, or blanch and freeze a glut.
storage.notes_beginner: Chard is best right after you pick it, and since you cut it leaf by leaf you can pick just what you need and let the plant keep growing. Save the colorful stalks to cook on their own. Chill it quickly, use it within a week or so, and freeze any extra after blanching.

bolting.triggers: winter cold or a hard cold snap on young plants (vernalization), not summer heat or long days
bolting.prevention_seasoned: Chard is a biennial and, unlike spinach and lettuce, does not bolt from summer heat or long days; it flowers only after it has lived through a winter, so a spring planting crops cleanly into fall without running to seed. The two ways to trigger premature bolting in the first year are sowing too early into cold soil, which can vernalize the young plants, and an unusually cold spring snap; avoid both by sowing once the soil has warmed past about 50°F. Overwintered plants will bolt as spring warms, so crop them before the stalk elongates and start a fresh sowing.
bolting.prevention_beginner: Good news: chard does not bolt (run to flower) in summer heat the way lettuce and spinach do. It is a biennial, which means it only flowers after living through a winter, so a plant you set out in spring keeps making leaves all season. The one thing to avoid is planting too early into cold soil, which can trick a young plant into flowering. If a plant lives through winter, it will flower in spring, so harvest it and plant a new one.
bolting.note_seasoned: Bolting resistance is a defining chard advantage. As a biennial it requires vernalization (a winter, or a sustained cold snap on a young plant) to flower, so first-year plants set out after the soil warms run straight through summer and fall, the basis for chard's long single-planting harvest. The failure mode is premature vernalization from a too-early cold-soil sowing, the same mechanism that bolts beets.
bolting.note_beginner: Chard bolts (sends up a flower stalk and turns bitter) only after it has gone through a winter, not because of summer heat. That is why one spring planting can feed you for months. If you plant too early into cold soil, a young plant can be fooled into flowering, so wait until the soil warms a little.

recommended.name: Fordhook Giant
recommended.note: The classic heirloom: large, dark-green, heavily crinkled (savoyed) leaves on broad white stalks. Heavy-yielding, dependable, and notably heat-tolerant, a good first chard.

recommended.name: Bright Lights
recommended.note: An All-America Selections rainbow mix with stems in gold, pink, orange, red, and white; ornamental as well as edible, with milder flavor. The most popular colorful type.

recommended.name: Ruby Red (Rhubarb Chard)
recommended.note: Deep crimson stalks and veins against dark-green leaves; vivid in the garden and on the plate, though red types can bolt a touch more readily than the whites.

recommended.name: Lucullus
recommended.note: A pale-green, lightly crumpled heirloom with white stalks, prized for heat tolerance and a long, productive harvest in warm regions.

recommended.name: El Dorado / Bright Yellow
recommended.note: Vivid yellow or gold petioles with smooth to lightly savoyed green leaves; a bright single-color alternative to the rainbow mixes.

recommended.name: Perpetual Spinach (leaf beet)
recommended.note: A chard type grown for thin-stemmed, spinach-like leaves rather than wide stalks; very slow to bolt and an excellent heat-season spinach substitute.

varieties.note_seasoned: Chard varieties differ mainly in stalk color and leaf texture rather than growing needs. Fordhook Giant is the dependable white-stemmed standard and one of the most heat-tolerant; Lucullus and the leaf-beet type Perpetual Spinach are the choices for the hottest regions and the longest harvest. For color, Bright Lights gives the full rainbow, Ruby Red the deep crimson, and El Dorado or Bright Yellow the gold tones; the colorful types are as ornamental as they are edible, though some red strains bolt slightly sooner. Most cultivars mature in about 50 to 60 days, with baby leaves much sooner.
varieties.note_beginner: Chard varieties are mostly about color. Fordhook Giant is the reliable white-stemmed classic and takes heat well. For a rainbow of stems, grow Bright Lights; for deep red, Ruby Red; for yellow, Bright Yellow or El Dorado. If you garden somewhere hot, Lucullus and Perpetual Spinach hold up especially well. They all grow the same way and are ready in about 50 to 60 days, with small leaves sooner.

thinning.when: when seedlings have 2 to 3 true leaves
thinning.method: snip or pull extra seedlings from each seedball cluster; the thinnings are edible as baby chard
thinning.tip_seasoned: Because each chard seed is a multigerm seedball, a single seed sprouts a cluster of seedlings, so thinning is mandatory, not optional. Thin to one strong seedling every 6 inches (or to 12 inches for the largest plants) once they have 2 to 3 true leaves, snipping rather than pulling to avoid disturbing the keeper's roots; eat the thinnings as baby chard. Crowded clumps stay small and stringy.
thinning.tip_beginner: Each chard seed is really a little fruit with several seeds inside, so you get a clump of seedlings from one seed and you must thin them. When they have a few real leaves, keep the strongest one every 6 inches (up to 12 inches for big plants) and snip off the rest at the soil line. Do not waste the thinnings, they are tender baby chard.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Do not plant chard where another goosefoot-family (Amaranthaceae) crop grew the previous season, including Swiss chard, beet, and spinach. They are close relatives (chard and beet are the same species) and share leaf pests such as the leafminer and flea beetle and leaf diseases such as Cercospora leaf spot and downy mildew, which build up where the family is grown repeatedly. A two-to-three-year gap breaks that cycle.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Do not grow chard where you grew chard, beets, or spinach last year. These are all in the same plant family and share the same leaf pests (leafminers, flea beetles) and diseases (leaf spot, downy mildew), which build up in the soil and on debris. Wait about two to three years before chard or its relatives go back into the same bed.
good_after: Legumes such as beans and peas that have added nitrogen
Alliums such as onions and garlic
Fruiting crops such as tomatoes and squash
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate chard on a roughly three-year cycle, keeping it and its close relatives beet and spinach out of a bed for two to three seasons. This breaks the buildup of the leafminers, flea beetles, and leaf diseases the goosefoot family shares, and in warm sandy soils it also helps with root-knot nematode. Following a legume that has added nitrogen, or an allium, suits the leafy crop well.
rotation.note_beginner: Move your chard to a different spot each year, and do not put it (or its relatives beets and spinach) back in the same bed for about three years. This keeps shared pests and diseases from piling up. Chard does well following beans or peas, which add nitrogen, or onions and garlic.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: In about 1 to 2 weeks the seedballs sprout, and because each one holds several seeds you will often see a little clump of seedlings come up together.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil damp and do not let it crust over. Do not worry if you see clusters of seedlings, that is normal for chard and you will thin them soon.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your chard seeds come up yet?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seedballs germinate in about 7 to 14 days at 55 to 75°F soil; each multigerm fruit yields a small cluster of seedlings, so emergence looks bunched.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep the seedbed evenly moist and uncrusted; expect clustered emergence from the seedballs and plan to thin.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Did your chard germinate, and how even is the stand?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The seedlings grow their first real chard leaves. When they have 2 to 3 true leaves, it is time to thin the clumps.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Thin to one strong plant every 6 inches and eat the thinnings. Watch for flea beetle holes, slug trails, and the first leafminer tunnels.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How many true leaves do your seedlings have?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Young plants form a low rosette; thin the seedball clusters to one plant every 6 to 12 inches at the 2-to-3-true-leaf stage. Flea beetles, slugs, and the first leafminer mines appear now.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin by snipping, keep moisture even, and set or check row cover to exclude leafminer flies and flea beetles.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have you thinned the clusters, and is the row cover on?

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plants form an upright rosette of large leaves on colorful or white stalks. This is the main growing stage, when they build the leaves you will cut for months.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep them evenly watered, feed with nitrogen every few weeks, and check the undersides of leaves and the stalks for aphids. Chard keeps growing right through summer if you keep it watered.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Is your chard making lots of healthy leaves?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Plants build an upright rosette of large leaves on white or colored petioles; this is the long productive window, which in chard runs through summer rather than ending at a bolt.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Side-dress nitrogen every 4 to 6 weeks, hold even moisture through heat, and scout for aphids, leafminer, slugs, and Cercospora. Begin cutting outer leaves as they size up.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Is the rosette filling out and producing cuttable leaves?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The outer leaves reach a usable size, about 8 to 12 inches long (or smaller for baby leaves), on firm stalks. New leaves keep pushing up from the center.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Cut or snap off the outer leaves an inch or two above the crown, leaving the center to keep growing. Pick a few from each plant and it will produce for months.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you started picking chard?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Outer leaves reach 8 to 12 inches (baby leaf much sooner) at about 50 to 60 days; the central crown keeps generating new leaves for a cut-and-come-again harvest that runs for months.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest the outer leaves cut-and-come-again, snapping or cutting an inch or two above the crown and leaving the growing point intact; keep cutting regularly to keep new growth tender. The colorful stalks cook as a separate vegetable.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are you cropping outer leaves, and is the crown still producing?

growth_stages.name: Bolting (second year)
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: After living through a winter, an overwintered plant stretches up a tall flower stalk in spring and the leaves turn tough and bitter. This does not happen to a first-year plant in summer.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Harvest everything usable right away, then pull the plant and start a fresh sowing. A plant that has flowered will not go back to making good leaves.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Has an overwintered chard plant started to flower?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: An overwintered (vernalized) plant elongates a flowering stalk as spring warms and leaf quality collapses; first-year summer plants do not bolt, the chard advantage.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Strip the remaining usable leaves from a bolting overwintered plant, then pull it and replace with a fresh sowing; do not rely on a bolted plant to resume production.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Has an overwintered plant bolted, and have you replaced it?

notifications.body_seasoned: Your chard should have 2 to 3 true leaves now. Because each seedball sprouts a cluster, thin to one strong plant every 6 to 12 inches and eat the thinnings as baby chard.
notifications.body_beginner: Your chard seedlings should be big enough to thin. Each seed grew a little clump, so keep the strongest plant every 6 inches and eat the little ones you pull.

notifications.body_seasoned: Your chard's outer leaves should be 8 to 12 inches and firm. Cut them an inch or two above the crown and leave the center to regrow; keep cutting regularly for months of harvest.
notifications.body_beginner: Your chard leaves should be big enough to pick. Cut the outer leaves and leave the middle to keep growing, and you will harvest from the same plants for months.

notifications.title_seasoned: Feed your chard for sustained growth
notifications.body_seasoned: Chard is cut over a long season and runs on nitrogen, so side-dress every 4 to 6 weeks and keep moisture even, especially through summer heat, to keep the leaves large and tender.
notifications.body_beginner: Because you pick chard for months, give it a nitrogen feeding every 4 to 6 weeks and keep it watered, and it will keep making tender leaves all season.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot weather and your chard
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Chard is one of the most heat-tolerant greens and, unlike lettuce or spinach, does not bolt in summer heat. In sustained heat above about 85 to 90°F its growth slows and leaves can scorch at the edges, so keep moisture even, mulch the bed, and provide afternoon shade in the hottest regions; it will keep producing where other greens fail.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Chard handles heat better than almost any other leafy green and will not flower in summer the way lettuce and spinach do. In very hot weather it just slows down, so keep it well watered, mulch around it, and give it afternoon shade if your summers are extreme, and it will keep making leaves.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hard freeze coming
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Chard is frost-tolerant: young plants shrug off temperatures down to about 32°F and established plants take light frosts, often sweetening a little. It is less hardy than spinach or kale, though, so a hard freeze into the low 20s°F can damage or kill unprotected plants. Harvest ahead of a hard freeze, or cover plants with a row cover or low tunnel; in mild zones it overwinters.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Chard takes light frosts well and even tastes a little sweeter after one, but it is not as tough as kale or spinach in a hard freeze. Before a hard freeze into the low 20s°F, pick what you can or cover the plants with a row cover. In mild-winter areas chard often lives right through winter.

germination.text_seasoned: Sow seedballs about half an inch deep into a moist, uncrusted seedbed; they germinate in 7 to 14 days at 55 to 75°F soil, slower and riskier in cold, wet ground.
germination.text_beginner: Plant chard seeds about half an inch deep in damp soil. They take 1 to 2 weeks to come up, and each seed makes a little clump of seedlings.

germination.text_seasoned: Soak the seedballs in water for several hours to a day before sowing to speed the slow germination, and avoid sowing into cold soil, which can vernalize and bolt young plants.
germination.text_beginner: Soak the seeds for a few hours before planting to help them sprout faster, and do not plant too early into cold soil, which can make plants flower too soon.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin each seedball cluster to one strong plant every 6 to 12 inches at the 2-to-3-true-leaf stage; snip rather than pull to spare the keeper's roots, and eat the thinnings.
seedling.text_beginner: Thin the clumps so one strong plant stands every 6 inches, snipping off the extras at the soil line. Eat the little ones you remove.

seedling.text_seasoned: Set floating row cover at sowing to exclude leafminer flies and flea beetles, the two main seedling pests, and watch for slug trails on the lowest leaves.
seedling.text_beginner: Cover young plants with a light row cover to keep leafminer flies and flea beetles off, and look for slug trails on the low leaves.

established.text_seasoned: Hold even moisture and side-dress nitrogen every 4 to 6 weeks; this is what carries chard through summer heat that would bolt lettuce and spinach.
established.text_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist and feed with nitrogen every few weeks. Steady water and food are what let chard keep growing all summer.

established.text_seasoned: Scout leaf undersides and petioles for aphids and the first leafminer mines, and pick and destroy mined leaves before larvae drop to pupate.
established.text_beginner: Check under the leaves and along the stalks for aphids, and pick off any leaves with pale tunnels (leafminer) before the pests spread.

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest the outer leaves cut-and-come-again at 8 to 12 inches (or baby size), snapping or cutting an inch or two above the crown and leaving the growing point; crop regularly to keep new leaves tender.
harvest.text_beginner: Pick chard by cutting the outer leaves and leaving the middle to grow. Take a few from each plant often, and it will keep producing for months.

harvest.text_seasoned: Cook the colorful stalks as a separate vegetable, sliced and given a head start over the quicker-cooking leaves; the stems are crisp like a mild celery or asparagus.
harvest.text_beginner: Do not throw away the bright stalks. Slice them and cook them a little before the leaves, since they take longer, and enjoy them like a mild vegetable on their own.

bolting.text_seasoned: A first-year chard plant will not bolt in summer; only an overwintered, vernalized plant flowers in spring. Crop a bolting overwintered plant out and resow rather than waiting for it to recover.
bolting.text_beginner: Chard only flowers after a winter, not in summer heat, so a spring plant keeps going. If a plant that lived through winter starts to flower, pick it and plant a new one.

bolting.text_seasoned: To avoid premature first-year bolting, do not sow into cold soil; wait until it warms past about 50°F so a cold snap cannot vernalize the seedlings.
bolting.text_beginner: To keep young plants from flowering too soon, wait to plant until the soil warms up a little instead of sowing into cold ground.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A single chard plant is highly productive over a long season, yielding repeated cuttings of leaves and stalks for months from one sowing. Utah State cites about 8 to 12 pounds from a 10-foot row over the season.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: One chard plant gives you leaves again and again over months, not just a single harvest. A short row of a few plants keeps a household in greens for much of the year.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Production builds through the warm months and holds longest where winters are mild; a spring planting peaks across summer and fall, and in mild zones the same plants carry into and through winter. Because the plant does not bolt in its first year, there is no abrupt early end as there is with spinach or lettuce.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Chard produces steadily from early summer right through fall, and in mild-winter areas it keeps going into winter. Unlike lettuce and spinach, it does not flower and quit in the heat, so the harvest just keeps coming.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: The key to total yield is steady care and frequent cutting: keep moisture and nitrogen even, crop the outer leaves regularly so the crown keeps generating new ones, and let a single healthy planting run for months rather than replanting. New growers often underestimate how long one chard sowing produces.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: The trick with chard is to keep picking. Cut the outer leaves often, keep it watered and fed, and one planting will feed you for months. Most beginners are surprised how long a few chard plants keep going.
factors_seasoned: Frequent harvest: cropping outer leaves regularly keeps the crown producing tender new growth; letting leaves over-mature slows the plant.
Even moisture and nitrogen: steady water and periodic feeding sustain large, tender leaves through heat and a long season.
Heat handling: chard keeps producing in summer where other greens bolt, but only with even moisture, mulch, and afternoon shade in extreme heat.
Thinning: thinning the seedball clusters to proper spacing prevents the small, stringy plants that crowding produces.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No reliable extension or peer-reviewed evidence supports timing Swiss chard planting or harvest by moon phase. Sow by soil temperature and frost dates and harvest by leaf size instead.

failure_diagnostics.label: Tunnels and tan blisters in the leaves
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: The beet and spinach leafminer, whose maggots tunnel inside the leaves.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: You found pale winding tunnels that widened into tan blisters on the leaves, with no good way to wash them off. That is the leafminer, a fly whose maggots eat inside the leaf, and because you eat chard leaves it ruins them. Next time, cover the plants with a row cover from the day you sow so the flies cannot lay eggs, pull weeds like lambsquarters that host them, keep chard away from beets and spinach, and pick off mined leaves early.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Use a row cover from sowing, keep chard away from beets and spinach, and remove mined leaves before the maggots spread.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Leaves showed serpentine mines opening into translucent tan blotches, the signature of the beet and spinach leafminer, which has several generations and overwinters as soil pupae. Sprays reach larvae inside the leaf poorly. Next time exclude the adult flies with row cover from sowing, control goosefoot weeds, rotate away from chard, beets, and spinach, and remove mined leaves before pupation.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Leafminer larvae mining the leaves, with soil-overwintering pupae and multiple generations across the goosefoot family.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Row-cover from sowing, control host weeds, rotate the goosefoot crops apart, and strip mined leaves before larvae drop.

failure_diagnostics.label: Round spots with dark rings on the leaves
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Cercospora leaf spot, a fungus that spreads in warm, wet weather.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your chard leaves got many small round spots with pale centers and dark reddish rings, and badly spotted leaves browned and died. That is Cercospora leaf spot, a fungus that lives on old debris and splashes up onto the leaves in warm, humid weather. Next time, water at the soil in the morning, space the plants for airflow, clean up old leaves, and do not plant chard where beets or spinach just grew.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Water at the base in the morning, space for airflow, clean up debris, and rotate away from beets and spinach.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Round tan-centered spots with reddish-purple margins coalesced on the older leaves, the signature of Cercospora beticola, favored by warm, humid weather and prolonged leaf wetness. Next time water at the base early in the day, widen spacing, destroy infected debris, lengthen the goosefoot rotation, and choose tolerant varieties where it recurs.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Cercospora beticola under warm, humid, leaf-wet conditions, surviving on chard and beet debris and goosefoot weeds.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Base-water early, space for airflow, destroy debris, rotate the goosefoot crops, and use tolerant varieties.

failure_diagnostics.label: Tall flower stalk and bitter leaves (bolting)
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: An overwintered plant flowering in spring, or a too-early cold-soil planting that vernalized a young plant.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your chard shot up a tall central stalk and the leaves turned tough and bitter. Chard is a biennial, so it normally flowers only after a winter; a plant that lived through winter will bolt in spring. The other cause is planting too early into cold soil, which can fool a young plant into flowering. It does not bolt from summer heat. Next time, wait to sow until the soil warms, and treat an overwintered plant as a spring crop to harvest before it flowers.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Sow once the soil warms past about 50°F, and harvest overwintered plants before they flower in spring.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The plant elongated a seed stalk and leaf quality collapsed. In chard this is vernalization-driven, an overwintered plant bolting in spring, or premature bolting from a too-early cold-soil sowing or a hard spring cold snap on young plants. It is not a heat or long-day response. Next time delay sowing until soil passes about 50°F and crop overwintered plants before the stalk elongates.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Vernalization: an overwintered plant, or a young plant chilled by cold soil or a hard snap, not summer heat or photoperiod.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sow into warmed soil, avoid cold-snap vernalization of seedlings, and harvest overwintered plants before bolt.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor, patchy, or crowded stand
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Slow or weak germination, a soil crust, or unthinned seedball clumps.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your chard came up thin and patchy, or in crowded clumps that stayed small. Chard seed is slow, can be blocked by a hard soil crust, and each seedball sprouts several seedlings that must be thinned or they choke each other. Next time, soak the seed before sowing, keep the surface moist so it does not crust, use fresh seed, and thin the clumps to one plant every 6 inches.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Soak the seed, keep the surface moist so it does not crust, use fresh seed, and thin the clumps early.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Stand was thin and uneven or crowded. The multigerm seedball germinates slowly and unevenly, a crust blocks the weak shoots, and unthinned clusters compete to small, stringy plants. Next time pre-soak the seedballs, keep the bed moist and uncrusted, sow fresh seed, and thin clusters to one plant every 6 to 12 inches at the 2-to-3-leaf stage.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Slow multigerm-seedball germination, surface crusting, low-vigor seed, or failure to thin the seedball clusters.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Pre-soak seedballs, prevent crusting, use fresh seed, and thin the clusters promptly.

3.zone_notes: In the coldest zone chard is a single long-season crop: sow once the soil warms in May (early enough to avoid a cold snap that could bolt seedlings is the only timing trap), and cut outer leaves from July until a hard freeze ends the season around October. It runs straight through the short northern summer that bolts spinach. Killed by deep winter cold.

4.zone_notes: A single spring sowing in late April or May crops from June through fall, running through the summer heat that stops spinach. Light fall frosts only sweeten it; a hard freeze ends the season. Overwintering is unreliable this cold without a low tunnel.

5.zone_notes: Sow once the soil warms in spring for one long crop cut from June through fall and, with a row cover, into November. Chard carries through midsummer here while spinach bolts; a hard freeze finally ends it.

6.zone_notes: A single spring planting produces from early summer through fall and into late autumn under a row cover, straight through the summer. In milder parts of the zone a covered plant overwinters for an early-spring cut before it bolts.

7.zone_notes: The mildest northern zone grows chard nearly all year from one spring sowing: cut from May through fall and, under a row cover, into early winter. A fall sowing overwinters for an early-spring harvest, bolting only as spring warms. Summer runs uninterrupted.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In cold regions, chard is an easy single-planting crop. Sow once the soil warms in spring and cut the outer leaves from early summer until a hard freeze, right through the summer when spinach and lettuce give up. It is killed by deep winter cold, though in the milder cold zones a row cover can carry it later or even overwinter it.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Across the northern tier chard is one long spring-to-frost crop rather than the two cool cycles spinach needs. A single sowing made once the soil warms (early enough to dodge a cold snap that could vernalize and bolt seedlings) crops from early summer through fall, running straight through the midsummer heat and long days that bolt spinach. There is no summer pause; the season ends at a hard freeze, with row cover extending it and, from zone 6 southward, overwintering a fall sowing for an early-spring cut.

9.zone_notes: The cool, foggy coast grows chard nearly year-round: sow in late winter through spring and again in late summer, and cut outer leaves continuously. The mild maritime summer holds it without bolting and the mild winter rarely stops it, so a single planting can run for the better part of a year.

10.zone_notes: The mildest north-coast stretch grows chard essentially year-round in the cool maritime climate, with no summer bolt and no winter stop; plant any cool spell and crop the outer leaves for months.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: On California's cool, foggy north coast you can grow chard almost all year. Plant in late winter through spring and again in late summer, and keep cutting the outer leaves. The mild summers and winters mean a single planting keeps going for months.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: The cool maritime north coast supports chard nearly year-round: the fog keeps summers cool enough that the heat-tolerant crop never pauses, and winters are mild enough that it rarely stops. Sow late winter into spring and again from late summer and crop cut-and-come-again. No heat_pause and no winter cold_pause apply.

9.zone_notes: The mild south coast grows chard nearly year-round. Sow in fall and again in late winter to early spring and cut outer leaves continuously; the heat-tolerant crop holds through the warm, dry summer with steady water and the mild winter rarely stops it.

10.zone_notes: The warmest south-coast zone still grows chard year-round near the coast, where the marine influence tempers summer; inland pockets get hot, so give afternoon shade and steady water through the peak, and the crop keeps producing.

ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: On California's south coast, grow chard nearly year-round. Plant in fall and again in late winter or early spring and keep picking the outer leaves. It handles the warm, dry summers well if you keep it watered, and the winters are mild.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: The mild south coast grows chard nearly year-round. Unlike spinach, which is excluded all summer here, chard carries through the warm, dry season with even moisture and some afternoon shade inland, and the mild winters let a single planting run for months. No heat_pause or winter cold_pause is applied near the coast.

8.zone_notes: In the interior valleys chard runs a long season. Sow in late winter and again in early fall and cut outer leaves through spring, summer, and fall; the hot valley summer slows it but does not stop it if you give afternoon shade and steady water. In a mild winter it carries through, and a hard freeze only sets it back.

9.zone_notes: The warmer interior zone 9 grows chard nearly year-round, through a hot summer that bolts spinach and lettuce. Keep moisture even and give afternoon shade in the peak heat, and the heat-tolerant crop keeps producing; mild winters let one planting run for months.

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In California's hot inland valleys, chard is one of the few greens you can grow nearly all year. It slows in the worst summer heat but keeps making leaves if you give it afternoon shade and steady water, and it does not bolt in the heat the way spinach and lettuce do.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: California's interior valleys grow chard over a long, nearly year-round season. Where spinach is excluded all summer, chard pushes through the hot, dry valley summer with even moisture and afternoon shade, slowing but not bolting, and mild winters let a single planting run for months. No heat_pause is applied; the summer is a quality slowdown, not an exclusion.

8.zone_notes: On the coastal plain chard is a long-season green. South Carolina's calendar sows it February through June and again in late summer; cut outer leaves through spring, summer, and fall. It tolerates the humid summer heat better than most greens, slowing but producing with afternoon shade and steady water, and in mild winters it carries through, set back only by a hard freeze.

9.zone_notes: The warm coastal zone 9 grows chard nearly year-round. UF and the Gulf calendars treat it as an excellent warm-weather green: it produces through the long warm season with even moisture and some shade, and the mild winter keeps it going, so one planting runs for months.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: Along the Gulf and the coastal plain, chard is one of the best greens for the long warm season. It keeps producing through the hot, humid summer when spinach and lettuce cannot, especially with afternoon shade and steady water, and the mild winters let it run for months.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: On the Gulf and southeastern coastal plain chard is a long-season green grown nearly year-round, the heat-tolerant alternative to spinach. Clemson's South Carolina window runs February through June and again from late summer, and UF calls chard an excellent warm-weather green; it carries through the humid summer with shade and even moisture, slowing but not bolting, while watching for Cercospora and downy mildew in the wet heat. No heat_pause is applied; disease pressure, not heat exclusion, is the summer concern.

warm_arid.region_label: Warm Arid: Southern New Mexico & West Texas

8.zone_notes: Around Las Cruces and El Paso chard runs a long season from a late-winter sowing, cut spring through fall, with a late-summer sowing extending it. The hot, dry summer slows but does not stop it given afternoon shade and steady water, so it produces where spinach is paused; the brief but real cold winter ends the season until spring.

warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: In southern New Mexico and West Texas, chard grows from late winter through fall. The dry summer heat slows it but it keeps making leaves with afternoon shade and steady water, unlike spinach, which has to skip summer here. The cold winter ends the season until spring.
warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: The warm arid valleys grow chard as a long spring-through-fall crop, direct sown in late winter and again in late summer. Unlike spinach, which carries a summer heat_pause here, the more heat-tolerant chard pushes through the dry summer with afternoon shade and even moisture, slowing rather than stopping; only the genuine winter cold brackets the season, so a cold_pause winter applies but no heat_pause.

9.zone_notes: In the low desert valleys chard is a fall-through-spring crop. Sow from September and harvest October into May; even this heat-tolerant green cannot hold the genuinely extreme peak summer, so June through August is excluded, though the shoulder months can be pushed with heavy afternoon shade.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Swiss chard is one of the most heat-tolerant leafy greens and, unlike lettuce or spinach, it does not bolt in summer; across most regions it runs straight through the warm months. This cell is the exception: in the genuinely extreme summer of the desert valleys, sustained highs around and above 105 to 110°F push even chard past what it can hold, germination fails above about 85°F, and leaves scorch and stall, so the peak summer is left out of the planting calendar and the crop resumes in fall. The shoulder months can sometimes be pushed with heavy afternoon shade, mulch, and steady water, which chard tolerates better than spinach.

10.zone_notes: The hottest desert zone grows chard in the cool fall, winter, and spring, sown from September for a harvest October into May. The extreme peak summer, June through August, is excluded even for this heat-tolerant crop; the rest of the year is productive.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Swiss chard is one of the most heat-tolerant leafy greens and, unlike lettuce or spinach, it does not bolt in summer; across most regions it runs straight through the warm months. This cell is the exception: in the genuinely extreme summer of the extreme desert, sustained highs around and above 110°F push even chard past what it can hold, germination fails above about 85°F, and leaves scorch and stall, so the peak summer is left out of the planting calendar and the crop resumes in fall. The shoulder months can sometimes be pushed with heavy afternoon shade, mulch, and steady water, which chard tolerates better than spinach.

ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: In California's desert valleys, chard grows in the cool fall, winter, and spring. It is more heat-tolerant than spinach, so its summer break is shorter, but the extreme peak summer is still too much; plant from September and harvest into May.
ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: The desert valleys grow chard fall through spring, harvested October into May. Chard's greater heat tolerance shortens its summer exclusion to the genuinely extreme peak, June through August (versus spinach's longer pause here); the shoulder months are pushable with heavy shade and water. One long cool window each year rather than the two-cycle pattern of milder zones.

9.zone_notes: In the Arizona low desert chard is a cool-season crop sown from September, once highs ease, for a harvest October into May. The University of Arizona Maricopa calendar groups it with the cool-season greens; the extreme peak summer, June through August, is excluded even for this heat-tolerant crop, though it outlasts spinach into late spring.

This cell is the exception: in the genuinely extreme summer of the low desert, sustained highs around and above 110°F push even chard past what it can hold, germination fails above about 85°F, and leaves scorch and stall, so the peak summer is left out of the planting calendar and the crop resumes in fall. The shoulder months can sometimes be pushed with heavy afternoon shade, mulch, and steady water, which chard tolerates better than spinach.

low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: In the Arizona low desert, grow chard in the cool season, from fall through spring. It holds the heat better than spinach and lasts later into spring, but the extreme peak summer is too hot even for chard.
low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: The Arizona low desert grows chard as a fall-into-spring crop sown from September per the UA Maricopa calendar, harvested October into May. Its heat tolerance lets it outlast spinach into late spring, but the genuinely extreme peak summer, June through August, is a hard exclusion; the shoulder months are marginal and pushable only with heavy shade.

10.zone_notes: On the central Florida peninsula chard is a strong cool-season green, sown September through fall (and again in February) for a harvest October into May. UF lists it as an excellent warm-weather alternative green, so it runs longer than spinach; only the deep, humid peak summer, June through August, is excluded, when heat, disease, and root-knot nematode pressure all peak.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Swiss chard is one of the most heat-tolerant leafy greens and, unlike lettuce or spinach, it does not bolt in summer; across most regions it runs straight through the warm months. This cell is the exception: in the genuinely extreme summer and humidity of the Florida peninsula, sustained highs in the 90s°F with extreme humidity push even chard past what it can hold, germination fails above about 85°F, and leaves scorch and stall, so the peak summer is left out of the planting calendar and the crop resumes in fall. The shoulder months can sometimes be pushed with heavy afternoon shade, mulch, and steady water, which chard tolerates better than spinach.

11.zone_notes: South Florida is the warmest zone: chard is a cool-season crop sown October into January for a harvest November into May, longer than spinach manages here. The hot, humid summer, June through September, is excluded, with heat, disease, and nematode pressure heaviest; many gardeners grow heat-loving substitutes in the off months.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Swiss chard is one of the most heat-tolerant leafy greens and, unlike lettuce or spinach, it does not bolt in summer; across most regions it runs straight through the warm months. This cell is the exception: in the genuinely extreme summer and humidity of subtropical south Florida, sustained highs in the 90s°F with extreme humidity push even chard past what it can hold, germination fails above about 85°F, and leaves scorch and stall, so the peak summer is left out of the planting calendar and the crop resumes in fall. The shoulder months can sometimes be pushed with heavy afternoon shade, mulch, and steady water, which chard tolerates better than spinach.

fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: In peninsular Florida, chard is one of the better cool-season greens and a good warm-weather alternative to spinach, lasting later into spring. Plant from fall and harvest through the cool months; the deep, humid summer is too hot, and watch for root-knot nematodes in sandy soil.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: On the Florida peninsula chard is a productive cool-season green that UF lists as an excellent warm-weather alternative, running later into spring than spinach. The exclusion is the deep, humid peak summer (June through August in central, June through September in the hotter south), when heat, leaf disease, and root-knot nematode pressure all peak. Sandy-soil nematode susceptibility is the key local caution.

11.zone_notes: In lowland Hawaii chard grows best in the cooler months, sown October into January for a harvest November into May; it tolerates the warm climate better than spinach and at cooler elevations grows year-round. The hot, humid lowland summer, June through September, is excluded at low elevation. Window modeled on CTAHR cool-season and elevation guidance.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Swiss chard is one of the most heat-tolerant leafy greens and, unlike lettuce or spinach, it does not bolt in summer; across most regions it runs straight through the warm months. This cell is the exception: in the genuinely extreme summer of the tropical lowlands, sustained highs warm and humid year-round at low elevation push even chard past what it can hold, germination fails above about 85°F, and leaves scorch and stall, so the peak summer is left out of the planting calendar and the crop resumes in fall. The shoulder months can sometimes be pushed with heavy afternoon shade, mulch, and steady water, which chard tolerates better than spinach.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In Hawaii, chard grows well in the cooler months and at cooler elevations can grow year-round. It takes the warmth better than spinach, but the hot, humid lowland summer is still too much, so plant from fall through winter at low elevation.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: In tropical Hawaii chard is a cool-season or upland crop that handles the warmth better than spinach: at low elevation it grows from fall through spring and is excluded in the hot, humid summer, while cooler highlands extend it year-round. The window is modeled on CTAHR cool-season and elevation guidance (the relevant CTAHR bulletin is an older scanned publication that did not parse cleanly).

succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Swiss chard is a cut-and-come-again crop, not a succession crop. A single planting is cut leaf by leaf and regrows from the same crown for months (a full season, or most of the year in mild climates), so staggered sowings are unnecessary; you harvest continuously from one stand rather than from a series of plantings. A spring and a separate late-summer or fall sowing are the most anyone typically makes, and even those overlap in production. The successioned analog is a quick leafy green like lettuce or arugula, a separate crop.

crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Swiss chard is ready to start cutting when the outer leaves reach a usable size, roughly 8 to 12 inches long (or smaller for tender baby leaves), usually about 50 to 60 days from sowing. Harvest cut-and-come-again: snap or cut the outer leaves an inch or two above the crown and leave the central growing point, and the plant keeps generating new leaves for months. Crop regularly to keep new growth tender, and cook the colorful stalks as a separate vegetable, giving them a head start over the quicker leaves.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Swiss chard is ready to pick when the outer leaves are about 8 to 12 inches long (or smaller for baby leaves), around 50 to 60 days after planting. Cut or snap off the outer leaves and leave the middle of the plant to keep growing, and it will produce for months from the same plant. Pick a few leaves from each plant regularly, and save the bright stalks to cook on their own, since they take a little longer than the leaves.
crops.description_seasoned: Swiss chard (Beta vulgaris) is a leafy member of the goosefoot family grown for its large, tender leaves and its broad, often vividly colored edible stalks. It is the same species as the beet, selected for leaf and stem rather than root, and it shares the beet's pests, diseases, and multigerm seedball. Its defining trait is an unusual tolerance of both heat and cold: unlike lettuce and spinach, chard does not bolt in summer heat or long days (as a biennial it flowers only after a winter), so a single spring planting crops straight through the summer and well into fall, and in mild zones it overwinters for a harvest that spans much of the year. Harvested cut-and-come-again, the outer leaves picked while the crown keeps producing, one chard plant yields for months. The colorful-stemmed types such as Bright Lights are as ornamental as they are useful, and the stalks cook as a vegetable in their own right.
crops.description_beginner: Swiss chard is a leafy green grown for both its big, tender leaves and its colorful, edible stalks, which come in white, gold, pink, orange, and red. It is actually the same plant species as the beet, just grown for the leaves and stems instead of a root. What makes chard special is that it handles both heat and cold better than most greens: it does not flower and turn bitter in summer the way lettuce and spinach do, so one spring planting keeps producing right through summer and fall, and in mild-winter areas it lives nearly all year. You harvest it cut-and-come-again, picking the outer leaves while the center keeps growing, so a few plants feed you for months. The rainbow-stemmed kinds are pretty enough for a flower bed, and you can cook the bright stalks like a vegetable on their own.

Key chard-vs-lettuce/spinach refits: chard tolerates BOTH heat and cold and, as a biennial, does NOT bolt in summer heat or long days (it flowers only after a winter), so a single spring planting runs straight through summer and fall and a heat_pause is reserved ONLY for genuinely extreme desert/tropical peak summer (6 cells), where spinach pauses in 13; cut-and-come-again long harvest (harvest_urgency low; succession_policy.suitable=False, plant-once); colorful edible stems; multigerm seedball -> thinning mandatory; goosefoot-family (Amaranthaceae) rotation with the beet/spinach leafminer + Cercospora/downy mildew/damping-off set plus UF's root-knot-nematode caution; pH 6.0 to 7.0 (more acid-tolerant than spinach); 6 to 12 inch spacing; direct-sown. See swiss_chard_NOTES.md for modeled values and flags.

open_findings.summary: days_to_maturity [50, 60] (mid 55) is synthesized: Clemson states 40 to 45 days direct-sown, UF/IFAS states 45 to 60 days to harvest, USU implies roughly 50 to 60 to full size; baby leaves come much sooner. The [50, 60] full-size span is a defensible midpoint of the sourced ranges, with the earlier baby-leaf and Clemson figures stated in prose.
open_findings.basis: Within the cited Clemson/UF/USU ranges; per-variety days (50 to 55) corroborate.

open_findings.summary: The central modeling decision: chard RUNS THROUGH summer (no heat_pause) in the northern tier, both coastal CA regions, the CA interior, the SE/Gulf, and the warm arid valleys, and carries a heat_pause ONLY in the genuinely extreme desert and subtropical cells (ca_desert, low_desert_az, fl_peninsula, hawaii_tropical: 6 heat_pause cells). This follows the sourced fact that chard is unusually heat-tolerant and biennial (does not bolt in summer): USU notes it grows past 75F with reduced quality but keeps producing with moisture; UMN notes summer growth slows but continues; UF lists chard as an excellent warm-weather alternative green. The summer in hot-but-survivable regions (CA interior, SE/Gulf, warm arid) is modeled as a quality slowdown, not an exclusion, which is the chard-vs-spinach distinctive.
open_findings.basis: Sourced heat tolerance + biennial (vernalization-only) bolt; spinach by contrast carries 13 heat_pause cells. The hottest-region judgment calls (CA interior z8/z9, SE/Gulf z9, warm arid z8 running through summer) are flagged for the daily biology review to confirm against local practice.

open_findings.summary: The desert/tropical heat_pause month boundaries are MODELED to the genuinely-extreme peak (Jun-Aug in ca_desert/low_desert_az/fl_peninsula z10; Jun-Sep in fl_peninsula z11 and hawaii z11). Chard's greater heat tolerance shortens its pause relative to spinach (which paused May-Sep in these cells); the shoulder months are stated as marginal and pushable with heavy shade. No chart prints explicit chard no-plant months, so these are inferred from the cool-season planting windows and chard's documented heat tolerance. Each is backed at the cell per A28.
open_findings.basis: Consistent with the cool-season planting windows in the cited UA/UF/UC calendars and chard's sourced heat tolerance; the exact peak-month cutoffs are a modeled judgment.

open_findings.summary: Regional HARVEST months are partly DERIVED across all regions. Extension planting charts give planting windows (sourced); the long cut-and-come-again harvest spans were computed from the plant window plus the 50-to-60-day first cut plus the continuous-regrowth and frost behavior. Plant-out windows are directly sourced; harvest months are sourced approximations.
open_findings.basis: Plant windows sourced; harvest spans derived from maturity, cut-and-come-again behavior, and frost dates.

open_findings.summary: The growth_stages 'bolting' stage and the bolting block are reframed as a SECOND-YEAR / vernalization event, not a summer-heat or long-day event, per UMN ('will not flower until the plant has lived through a winter') and the beet vernalization-bolting mechanism. First-year summer plants do not bolt; premature first-year bolting is attributed to too-early cold-soil sowing or a hard cold snap. bolting.risk = low.
open_findings.basis: UMN explicitly; chard is the same biennial species as beet. This is the basis for the long single-planting harvest and the run-through-summer calendars.
