crops.name: Arugula

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Arugula likes loose, rich soil with plenty of compost that holds moisture but still drains well. It is not fussy and grows in most garden soils, but steady moisture keeps the leaves mild and tender; dry, hard soil makes them hot and tough and pushes the plant to flower.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Arugula grows in a wide range of soils but does best in a fertile, well-drained loam or sandy loam high in organic matter, kept evenly moist. As a fast leafy brassica it responds to compost worked in before sowing, which feeds quick growth and buffers the steady moisture that keeps the leaves tender and mild. It tolerates a fairly broad pH but leans toward 6.0 to 7.0, and keeping the soil out of the strongly acidic range also helps hold down clubroot, the brassica-family soil disease.

ph.note_beginner: Arugula grows best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, about 6.0 to 7.0. A simple soil test tells you where you stand. Keeping the soil from getting too acidic also helps prevent clubroot, a cabbage-family soil disease.
ph.note_seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0; arugula is forgiving and still does fine across roughly 5.5 to 7.5. Clemson lists 6.0 to 6.5 for the leafy greens in its arugula fact sheet. As with other brassicas, holding the soil toward neutral rather than strongly acidic also helps suppress clubroot, so a grower with clubroot history should lean to the high end.

fertilizer.timing: a little at sowing, then a light side-dress 2 to 3 weeks after the seedlings are up
fertilizer.example_product: Blood meal, 21-0-0, or a balanced vegetable fertilizer
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Arugula is a fast leafy brassica that runs on nitrogen, but the crop is so quick that one light feeding is usually plenty. Work compost or a balanced fertilizer in before sowing, then side-dress lightly with nitrogen about 2 to 3 weeks after the seedlings emerge to push tender, mild leaves. Avoid heavy nitrogen late, since lush growth draws aphids and flea beetles and does not improve a crop you will cut within a few weeks.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Arugula grows fast and likes a little nitrogen for tender green leaves. Mix some compost or fertilizer into the soil before planting, then give it one light feeding a couple of weeks after the seeds come up. Because the crop is so quick, you usually do not need to feed it again.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time to side-dress your arugula with a little nitrogen.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Time to give your arugula a light feeding.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: High N for fast leafy growth; a light side-dress of 21-0-0 or blood meal 2 to 3 weeks after emergence. No phosphorus or potassium needed beyond a soil-test baseline; do not overfeed a 3-to-4-week crop.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a nitrogen-rich feed such as blood meal or a 21-0-0 fertilizer once, when the plants are a couple of weeks old.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: About a quarter cup of 21-0-0 per 10 feet of row, side-dressed once a few weeks after emergence; for baby-leaf patches a single compost-rich bed often needs no extra feed at all.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Follow the label rate for a nitrogen-rich vegetable fertilizer, one light feeding a few weeks after the seeds sprout.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms_beginner: Lots of tiny round shot holes peppering the leaves, made by tiny dark beetles that jump like fleas when you come near. Arugula is one of their favorites, and heavy damage can riddle or kill young seedlings.
pests.cause_beginner: Flea beetles are small jumping beetles that chew little pits and holes in cabbage-family leaves. They are drawn strongly to arugula and mustard and hit small seedlings hardest, since a tiny plant cannot outgrow the damage.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover young plants with a light row cover from the day you sow, and if beetles are heavy use a spinosad spray or a kaolin clay coating. The main goal is to get the seedlings up and big fast, before the beetles riddle them.
pests.prevention_beginner: Use row cover from sowing (the single best defense), keep seedlings growing fast with steady water, sow when beetles are less active, and clear nearby cabbage-family weeds. Some growers plant a sacrificial arugula patch as a trap crop.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small round shot-holes pepper the foliage and the tiny dark beetles jump when disturbed. Arugula and other mustards are highly preferred hosts, so pressure is often intense; seedlings can be stunted or killed and the holes mar the harvested leaves of a crop eaten raw.
pests.cause_seasoned: Crucifer and striped flea beetles (Phyllotreta species) chew the foliage of brassicas and strongly prefer arugula and mustard; adults overwinter in debris and emerge to attack the earliest, smallest plants. Multiple generations occur through the season.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Floating row cover from sowing is the most effective tool; spinosad or kaolin clay help under heavy pressure. The aim is rapid establishment past the vulnerable seedling stage, so push fast growth.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Exclude beetles with row cover from sowing, keep seedlings vigorous with even water and a light feed, clean up crucifer weeds and crop debris, and consider an early trap planting of arugula or mustard to divert beetles from the main crop.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_beginner: Clusters of tiny soft green or gray insects on the undersides of leaves and on new growth, sometimes with curled, sticky leaves. The waxy gray-green cabbage aphid hides deep in the crinkles and is hard to wash out.
pests.cause_beginner: Aphids are small insects that suck sap from the plant. They breed quickly, especially on soft growth from too much fertilizer, and they can spread plant viruses; the cabbage aphid in particular loves brassicas like arugula.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water, or use insecticidal soap or neem oil, hitting the undersides of the leaves. Repeat every few days until they are gone, and pick before a colony lodges in the leaves.
pests.prevention_beginner: Welcome helpful bugs like ladybugs and lacewings, go easy on nitrogen, check new growth often, and use row cover, which also keeps out flea beetles.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Colonies of green peach aphids and the waxy gray-green cabbage aphid (Brevicoryne brassicae) on leaf undersides and tips distort the foliage; honeydew and the aphids lodged in the leaves contaminate a raw-eaten crop, and several aphids vector viruses.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several aphid species feed on arugula; they reproduce rapidly, favor the soft growth excess nitrogen produces, and the cabbage aphid is especially hard to dislodge from sheltered leaf folds.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Dislodge colonies with a strong water jet or spray insecticidal soap or neem, covering leaf undersides; repeat every few days. Conserve lady beetles, lacewings, and parasitoid wasps.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Scout growing tips early, avoid overfeeding nitrogen, conserve natural enemies, and exclude with row cover; harvest the quick crop before colonies build.

pests.name: Cabbage caterpillars
pests.symptoms_beginner: Ragged chewed holes in the leaves, green caterpillars on the plants, and dark droppings. Because you eat the leaves, even a little chewing is a problem.
pests.cause_beginner: Several moths and white butterflies lay eggs on cabbage-family leaves, and the caterpillars that hatch (imported cabbageworms, loopers, and small wriggling diamondback larvae) chew the foliage.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray Bt, which is safe and targets only caterpillars, or pick them and their eggs off by hand from the undersides of leaves. Spray again after rain, since it washes off.
pests.prevention_beginner: Use a row cover to keep the adults from laying eggs, clean up old cabbage-family plants and weeds, and check leaf undersides for eggs and small caterpillars.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Ragged feeding holes with green or striped larvae and frass; imported cabbageworm, cabbage looper, and diamondback moth larvae feed on arugula, and on a fast leaf crop even light feeding downgrades the harvest.
pests.cause_seasoned: The larvae of several brassica moths and butterflies feed on the foliage; the adults lay eggs on the leaves, and warm-region plantings see the most pressure.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) or spinosad targeting young larvae and hand-pick where practical; repeat after rain.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Exclude egg-laying adults with row cover, clean up brassica debris and weed hosts, and scout leaf undersides for eggs and early instars.

pests.name: Slugs and snails
pests.symptoms_beginner: Ragged holes with smooth edges chewed in low leaves, slimy trails on the leaves and soil, and worst damage in cool, damp, shady spots and after rain.
pests.cause_beginner: Slugs and snails are soft, moisture-loving mollusks that feed at night and rasp holes in tender low greens like arugula. They thrive in damp mulch and dense, shaded plantings.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Hand-pick at night or after rain, set out shallow traps, and use an iron-phosphate slug bait, which is pet-safe. Reduce damp hiding places and water in the morning so the surface dries by night.
pests.prevention_beginner: Thin and space plants for airflow, keep mulch light near the plants, clear damp debris, and water early in the day rather than at dusk.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Smooth-edged holes in low foliage with silvery slime trails, worst in cool, wet, densely planted or heavily mulched beds; a tender low salad green like arugula is highly susceptible.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several slug and snail species feed nocturnally, rasping the foliage; they shelter in moist debris and mulch by day and build up in cool, wet conditions.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick after dark or rain, use shallow traps and iron-phosphate baits (pet-safe), and remove daytime shelter; morning watering lets the surface dry before they feed.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Reduce moisture and shelter near the plants: thin for airflow, keep mulch off the crowns, clear debris, and irrigate in the morning rather than the evening.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Pale yellow or angular patches on the tops of the leaves with a fuzzy grayish-white mold on the undersides, mostly in cool, damp, crowded conditions. Bad cases discolor and collapse the leaves.
diseases.cause_beginner: A mold-like disease that loves the same cool, wet weather arugula grows in, spreading through wet leaves and splashing water. Crowded plants and long leaf wetness make it worse.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove the worst leaves, open up the airflow so leaves dry faster, and water at the soil instead of over the plants. It is hard to stop once it gets going, so prevention matters most.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Space plants for good airflow, water at the base, choose resistant varieties where available, and rotate where you plant arugula and other brassicas.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Angular yellow-to-brown lesions on the upper leaf surface with grayish-white sporulation beneath, spreading in cool, wet, humid weather; lesions brown and the leaves collapse. It is a leading arugula disease.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Hyaloperonospora parasitica (the brassica downy mildew oomycete), favored by cool temperatures, long leaf wetness, and high humidity; it spreads by wind- and splash-borne spores and survives on debris.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Cultural control dominates: improve airflow, avoid overhead irrigation, and remove infected leaves and debris; there is no rescue once it is established in humid weather.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Widen spacing for airflow, use drip rather than overhead water, choose resistant cultivars where offered, and rotate away from brassicas for several years.

diseases.name: White rust
diseases.symptoms_beginner: White, blister-like bumps on the undersides of the leaves, with yellow spots on top. Badly spotted leaves are not good to eat.
diseases.cause_beginner: A different mold-like disease, not a true rust, that makes white pustules on cabbage-family leaves and spreads in cool, moist weather. It can ruin a leafy crop quickly.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove and destroy infected leaves, improve airflow, and water at the soil line. As with downy mildew, prevention works better than trying to cure it.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Space plants out, avoid wetting the leaves, choose resistant varieties where it is common, and rotate your planting spot.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: White, blister-like pustules on leaf undersides with chlorotic spotting above; severe infection distorts and downgrades the foliage. A common brassica-greens disease, worse in the South.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The oomycete Albugo candida, favored by cool nights, mild days, and leaf wetness; it spreads by splash- and wind-dispersed spores and survives on debris and as oospores.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove infected leaves and debris, improve airflow, and avoid overhead irrigation; chemical options are limited for the home garden.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Grow resistant cultivars where white rust is endemic, space for airflow, use drip irrigation, and rotate away from brassicas.

diseases.name: Damping-off
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Seeds that never come up, or seedlings that flop over at the soil line with a pinched, rotted stem and then die. It strikes in cold, wet soil.
diseases.cause_beginner: Soil fungi attack the seeds and tiny seedlings, especially when the soil is cold and soggy and the seeds are slow to come up.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure for an affected seedling, so focus on prevention. Pull and discard collapsed seedlings.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Do not sow into cold, soggy soil, plant shallowly in well-drained ground, do not overwater, and use fresh seed so it comes up fast.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Poor stands from seed and pre- or post-emergence collapse of seedlings with water-soaked, pinched stems at the soil line, worst in cold, wet, poorly drained soil where germination is slow.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Soilborne Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Fusarium species attack germinating seed and seedlings; cold, saturated soil that slows emergence favors them.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No cure once seedlings collapse; manage by prevention and remove affected plants.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Sow shallowly into well-drained soil when temperatures favor quick emergence, avoid overwatering, and use fresh viable seed.

diseases.name: Alternaria and Cercospora leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small dark spots on the leaves that grow into round patches, sometimes with rings like a tiny target or a pale halo. Spotted leaves are not good to eat.
diseases.cause_beginner: Fungi that spread in warm, wet weather and infect the leaves, leaving spots. They are worse on stressed plants and in crowded, damp plantings.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove and destroy spotted leaves, improve airflow so leaves dry quickly, and avoid wetting the leaves when you water. Start with clean seed.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Use clean seed, rotate away from brassicas, space plants for airflow, water at the soil line, and clear crop debris.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small dark lesions enlarge into circular spots, Alternaria often with concentric rings (a target look) and Cercospora as gray-brown spots with a halo; on a leaf crop even moderate spotting reduces the harvest. Favored by warm, wet conditions.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Alternaria (A. brassicae, A. brassicicola) and Cercospora fungi infect brassica foliage, spreading by spores in wind and splashing water; infected seed, crop debris, and long leaf wetness drive them.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove spotted leaves and debris, improve airflow, and avoid overhead watering; a copper-based fungicide can help under heavy pressure.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Use clean, disease-free seed, rotate away from brassicas, space for airflow, water at the soil line, and clear crop debris that harbors spores.

watering.frequency_seasoned: About 1 to 1.5 inches per week, kept even; arugula is shallow-rooted and bolts faster and turns hotter under drought stress.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly 1 to 1.5 inches a week.
watering.amount_seasoned: Roughly 1 to 1.5 inches per week, more in warm, dry spells.
watering.amount_beginner: Aim for about 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week, a bit more when it is warm.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose; keeping the foliage dry checks downy mildew and white rust on a crop you eat raw.
watering.method_beginner: Water at the base of the plants rather than over the leaves, which helps prevent leaf diseases.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, damping-off in seedlings, and downy mildew in crowded, constantly wet stands.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Lower leaves yellow, seedlings rot at the base, and leaves get moldy in soggy, crowded beds.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting, slowed growth, hotter and tougher leaves, and faster bolting; drought stress both sharpens the flavor and triggers the seedstalk.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Wilting leaves that turn extra spicy and tough, and a plant that bolts (flowers) sooner than it should.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Even moisture keeps arugula growing fast, tender, and mild; dry, hot spells push it to flower and make the leaves harshly pungent.
watering.method_note_beginner: Keep the water steady so the leaves stay mild and tender and the plant does not bolt early.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Steady moisture through the few weeks of leaf growth, and during any warm or lengthening-day spell, matters most for delaying bolt and keeping the bite mild.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Water steadily while the plants are growing their leaves, and especially as the weather warms up.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Arugula is almost always direct-sown, since it grows fast and resents root disturbance. Sow seed about 0.25 to 0.5 inch deep as soon as the soil can be worked in spring; it germinates readily even in cool soil, often in 5 to 7 days, and tolerates frost, so it can go in several weeks before the last frost. Sow a little more thickly than the final stand and thin to taste, eating the thinnings. In hot regions, shift sowing to fall through spring, since warm soil above about 80°F cuts germination and lengthening warm days bolt the crop.
start_method.notes_beginner: Arugula is best planted straight in the garden from seed, because it grows so fast and does not like having its roots disturbed. Sow the seeds about a quarter to half an inch deep as soon as the soil can be worked in spring, since they sprout even in cold soil and the plants handle frost. Sow again every couple of weeks, and in hot areas plant in fall through spring instead of summer, because heat keeps the seeds from sprouting well and makes the plants bolt.

drainage.saucer_practice: Empty the saucer after watering so roots never sit in water, which invites damping-off and root rot.

soil_mix.type_beginner: A good-quality potting mix, not garden soil.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in some compost for steady nutrients.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: A light, well-drained potting mix high in organic matter.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend in compost and a little starter nitrogen; arugula is a quick feeder but needs only a light charge for its short life.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Shallow pots dry out fast, so check daily in warm weather and keep the mix evenly moist, since drought makes arugula bolt and turn hot.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Feed a little, since watering washes nutrients out of pots, but the crop is so fast it rarely needs more than a starter charge.

overwintering.approach_beginner: In mild areas, a pot of fall-sown arugula can keep going through winter in a sheltered, sunny spot. In cold areas, move the pot against the house or into a cold frame, or cover it during hard freezes, and it will often resume in spring.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Arugula is cold-hardy, so a fall-sown container can overwinter in mild zones, holding through winter in a sheltered spot and resuming in spring. In cold zones the limited root volume freezes harder than open ground, so sink the pot, move it to a cold frame or unheated structure, or cover it during hard freezes; an overwintered pot then yields the earliest spring picking.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Arugula is an easy, fast container crop. Use a wide, shallow pot at least 6 inches deep, sow the seed thickly, and snip baby leaves cut-and-come-again. Keep it watered and in the cool seasons, and give it some afternoon shade in warm weather to slow bolting.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Arugula is one of the best container salad crops: shallow-rooted, fast, and happy sown densely for cut-and-come-again baby leaf in a broad container at least 6 inches deep. Keep moisture even, since shallow pots dry fast and drought triggers bolting, grow it in the cool seasons, and give afternoon shade in warm spells. A pot is also the easiest way to move the crop into shade or shelter as the weather turns.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Shallow containers dry faster than beds; check moisture daily in warmth and water before the mix dries, since drought stress bolts arugula and sharpens its flavor.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Container arugula needs only a light starter feed; frequent watering leaches nutrients, but the crop is harvested before heavy feeding would matter.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering container suits arugula well, since it smooths out the steady moisture that keeps the leaves mild and slow to bolt.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match because it keeps the water steady, which keeps arugula tender and slow to bolt.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: Arugula is shallow-rooted, so depth matters less than surface area: a wide, shallow container at least 6 inches deep gives more sowing area for cut-and-come-again leaves and buffers the fast drying narrow pots suffer.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Arugula has shallow roots, so a wide, shallow pot beats a tall narrow one. Aim for at least 6 inches deep and as much width as you can give it.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Other brassicas: cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kale, collards, mustard, radish, turnip, and arugula itself. They share the cabbage-family pests (flea beetles, cabbage caterpillars, aphids) and the soilborne clubroot, so following one brassica with another concentrates and builds that pressure.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Other cabbage-family plants like broccoli, cabbage, kale, mustard, radishes, and arugula itself, because they share the same pests and diseases.
rotation.good_after: Legumes (peas, beans), alliums (onion, garlic), cucurbits, or nightshades such as tomatoes.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate arugula and its brassica relatives so they do not return to the same ground for about 3 years. The cabbage-family pest complex (flea beetles above all, plus cabbage caterpillars and aphids) and the soilborne clubroot organism build up where brassicas repeat, and arugula's quick succession plantings make it easy to keep flea beetles cycling in one bed. Follow brassicas with legumes, alliums, cucurbits, or nightshades, and keep the soil near neutral to help suppress clubroot.
rotation.note_beginner: Try not to grow arugula or other cabbage-family plants (broccoli, kale, cabbage, mustard, radishes) in the same spot more than about once every 3 years. They share pests like flea beetles and a soil disease called clubroot that build up when these crops keep coming back. Plant arugula after peas, beans, onions, squash, or tomatoes instead.

bolting.triggers: heat above about 75°F and lengthening days, accelerated by drought and crowding
bolting.prevention_seasoned: Arugula bolts fast once it is warm and the days lengthen, and the leaves turn sharply hot and bitter as it does. Keep the productive window in the cool shoulders of the year: sow early in spring and crop quickly, lean on the fall crop, choose slower-bolting types or wild (Diplotaxis) rocket where heat is a problem, give light afternoon shade in warm spells, and keep moisture steady. Succession sow every 2 to 3 weeks so a bolted batch is quickly replaced, and harvest promptly at the first sign of a central stalk.
bolting.prevention_beginner: Arugula flowers (bolts) quickly when it gets warm and the days get long, and the leaves turn harshly spicy and bitter. To avoid it, grow arugula in the cool parts of the year, especially fall, sow a fresh little batch every 2 to 3 weeks, water steadily, and give it some afternoon shade when it is warm. Pick it promptly, and as soon as you see a flower stalk in the middle, harvest the whole plant.
bolting.note_seasoned: Bolting in arugula is driven by heat and lengthening days, sped by drought and crowding, and it comes on fast because the plant is so quick. Once a central seedstalk rises the leaves narrow and flood with the mustard-oil compounds that make a sharp, almost acrid pungency, so the eating window closes quickly. The flowers are edible and peppery, and one plant left to bloom feeds pollinators and self-sows readily.
bolting.note_beginner: Arugula bolts (sends up a flower stalk and turns very sharp and bitter) when it gets warm and the days are long. It happens fast and is just the plant's natural cycle, not a mistake. Grow it in cool weather, pick it young, and enjoy the flowers too, which are edible and peppery. Left alone, arugula often drops seed and comes up again on its own.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Arugula wilts and yellows within a day at room temperature, so refrigerate it promptly after cutting; if it must sit briefly, keep it cool and out of the sun.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Do not leave arugula out on the counter. It wilts fast in the warmth, so get it into the fridge soon after picking.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerate unwashed in a loose or perforated bag in the crisper; arugula holds about 5 to 10 days near 32°F at high humidity. It is more perishable than sturdy greens like kale, so use it promptly, and wash only at use, since trapped moisture speeds breakdown.
storage.fridge_beginner: Store arugula unwashed in a loose bag in the fridge crisper drawer, where it keeps about a week if kept very cold. Wash it only when you are ready to use it.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Arugula is a salad green and does not freeze well for raw use, losing its texture; if you have a glut, blanch briefly and freeze for cooking, or make pesto and freeze that, where its peppery bite holds up.
storage.freezer_beginner: Arugula is best fresh and does not freeze well for salads. If you have extra, turn it into pesto and freeze that, or blanch it briefly and freeze it to cook later.
storage.notes_seasoned: Quality is highest straight from the garden. Arugula is delicate and short-lived once cut, so chill it fast and use it within a week or so fresh; its peppery flavor also turns stronger and harsher in storage, another reason to eat it young and soon.
storage.notes_beginner: Arugula is best right after you pick it and does not keep long. Chill it quickly and use it within a week or so, and remember the flavor gets stronger the longer it sits.

recommended.name: Astro
recommended.note: A fast, broad-leaved salad rocket with a milder, less aggressive bite and good cold tolerance; quick to baby leaf and a dependable beginner choice.

recommended.name: Roquette (Rocket)
recommended.note: The classic standard Eruca sativa salad rocket: deeply lobed leaves with the full nutty-peppery pungency; fast but bolts readily in heat.

recommended.name: Sylvetta (wild rocket)
recommended.note: Wild or perennial rocket, a different species (Diplotaxis tenuifolia) with small, finely cut leaves, an intense pungent flavor, slower growth, and much slower bolting; short-lived perennial in mild climates and the best pick for heat and longevity.

recommended.name: Surrey
recommended.note: A uniform cut-leaf salad rocket selected for baby-leaf production, with good regrowth for repeated cuttings.

recommended.name: Esmee
recommended.note: A fast oak-leaf-type rocket with deeply lobed, tender leaves and a clean peppery flavor; quick for cut-and-come-again baby leaf.

varieties.note_seasoned: Match the type to the slot. Standard salad rocket (Eruca sativa, Roquette and the like) is fastest and most pungent but bolts quickly in heat, so it suits the cool shoulders and baby-leaf cutting. Milder, broad-leaf selections like Astro give a gentler bite and quick baby leaf. For warm weather and a longer stand, wild or perennial rocket (Diplotaxis tenuifolia, sold as Sylvetta or wild arugula) is slower-growing, far slower to bolt, and more intensely flavored, and it can persist as a short-lived perennial in mild climates. Cut-leaf types like Surrey and Esmee are bred for tidy, regrowing baby-leaf patches.
varieties.note_beginner: For a quick, peppery salad green, grow standard salad arugula like Roquette or the milder Astro, which are fast but flower quickly in heat. For hot weather or a longer-lasting patch, try wild arugula (sold as Sylvetta), which is slower to bolt, more intense in flavor, and can come back year after year in mild areas. Cut-leaf kinds like Surrey are great for snipping baby leaves again and again.

companions.note_beginner: Arugula is small, fast, and easygoing, so it tucks in between slower crops. It grows well next to lettuce and other quick greens, bush beans, and aromatic herbs like dill, and alliums such as onions. The main thing is to keep it away from other cabbage-family plants, which share its pests and diseases, and to watch for flea beetles, which love it.
companions.note_seasoned: Most arugula companion pairings rest on space, timing, and tradition rather than measured effects. The practical ones are structural: arugula is quick and shallow-rooted, so it interplants with lettuce and other fast greens and tucks beside legumes and aromatic herbs. Aromatic herbs and alliums are the traditional scent-based deterrents for the cabbage-family pests arugula shares. The well-grounded caution is to separate arugula from other brassicas, which share clubroot and the whole cole-crop pest complex, a rotation and disease principle more than a tested adjacency effect; arugula is also a flea-beetle magnet, sometimes deliberately used as a trap crop near choicer brassicas.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Bush beans
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Beans add a little nitrogen to the soil that the leafy arugula can use, and the two share a cool-to-mild season without competing much.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Legume nitrogen and complementary habit are widely taught; no arugula-specific trial.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A legume interplant on nitrogen and structure: beans fix a little nitrogen the leafy arugula draws on, and the quick arugula uses the ground between young bean plants. Sound space and timing logic rather than a measured arugula effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Lettuce and other quick greens
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Lettuce grows fast and low like arugula, so you can sow them together to fill a salad bed, and both like the same cool weather.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Quick cool-season interplant logic extensions endorse generally; not an arugula-specific measured effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Arugula and lettuce share a cool season, a shallow root zone, and a salad bed, so they interplant efficiently and are cut young together. A space-and-timing pairing, not a documented growth boost; the two share no major pest.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Dill and aromatic herbs
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Strong-smelling herbs like dill are a classic neighbor for cabbage-family plants; their scent is said to confuse pests, and their flowers bring in helpful insects.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Aromatic umbels are extension-noted for recruiting parasitoids/predators of brassica pests; the dill-arugula pairing itself is not trial-tested.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Aromatic umbels like dill draw the parasitoid wasps and predators that attack brassica aphids and caterpillars, and extension work pairing umbels with cole crops has shown reduced damage. Let some flower nearby; a partial-mechanism aid, not a measured arugula-specific effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Onions and other alliums
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Onions are a traditional neighbor for cabbage-family plants; their strong smell is thought to help put off the pests that hunt by scent.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Allium scent-masking for brassicas is widely taught companion lore; no arugula-specific trial.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Alliums are the classic scent-based brassica companion, their pungency thought to mask the crop from cabbage pests that locate hosts partly by smell. Shallow-rooted and undemanding, they tuck around arugula without competing. Traditional with partial mechanistic support, not an arugula-specific measured effect.

good_seasoned.name: Bush beans
good_seasoned.timing: interplant in the same cool window
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A legume interplant on nitrogen and structure: beans fix a little nitrogen for the leafy arugula and the quick arugula uses the open ground between them. Space and timing, not a tested effect.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Legume nitrogen + complementary habit; no arugula-specific trial.

good_seasoned.name: Lettuce and other quick greens
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A quick, shallow cool-season green that shares arugula's season and salad bed; the two interplant and are cut young together. Space-driven and traditional, with no shared major pest.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Quick-green interplant lore; no arugula-specific measured effect.

good_seasoned.name: Dill and aromatic herbs
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Aromatic umbels draw parasitoids and predators of brassica aphids and caterpillars; extension work pairing umbels with cole crops has shown reduced damage. A plausible aid, not an arugula-specific trial.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Umbel predator-recruitment for brassicas is extension-supported; the dill-arugula pairing is not trial-tested.

good_seasoned.name: Onions and other alliums
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: The classic scent-based brassica companion, thought to mask the crop from cabbage pests that hunt by smell; shallow-rooted and low-competition. Traditional with partial mechanistic support.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Allium scent-masking lore for brassicas; no arugula-specific trial.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Other brassicas
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep arugula away from other cabbage-family plants like broccoli, cabbage, kale, mustard, and radishes. They share the same pests and diseases, so planting them together makes flea beetles and clubroot worse.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Same-family crops share pests and clubroot; clustering raises pressure and builds soil-borne disease. A sound rotation/epidemiology mechanism, not a measured antagonism.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Planting arugula shoulder to shoulder with its brassica relatives, broccoli, cabbage, kale, mustard, radish, concentrates the shared cabbage-family pests, flea beetles above all, plus cabbage caterpillars and aphids, and repeated same-family planting builds soilborne clubroot. Spread brassicas out and rotate where they grow. Because arugula is a strong flea-beetle draw, some growers exploit this and use it as a sacrificial trap crop away from choicer brassicas.

bad_seasoned.name: Other brassicas
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Broccoli, cabbage, kale, mustard, and radish share arugula's clubroot and cabbage-family pests, so grouping them concentrates disease and pest pressure, especially flea beetles. A real rotation and disease principle; the practical rule is to spread brassicas out and rotate them. Arugula's strong flea-beetle appeal also makes it a deliberate trap crop in some plantings.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Shared clubroot and cabbage-family pests are extension-documented; the bad-adjacency claim is a known agronomic principle, not a pair-tested effect.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The first pair of rounded seed leaves pushing up through the soil. Arugula comes up fast, often in 3 to 7 days, even in cool soil, and germination is usually even if the surface has not dried out.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The first pair of little rounded leaves poking up. Arugula sprouts fast, often in under a week, even in cool soil.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep the soil surface consistently moist but never waterlogged until seedlings are up. Arugula germinates well in cool soil but poorly in warm soil above about 80°F, so early-spring and fall sowings come up best.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil surface evenly moist but not soggy until the seedlings are up. Arugula sprouts well in cool soil but badly in hot soil, so sow in spring or fall, not the heat of summer.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Any sprouts yet?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Any sprouts yet?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The first true leaves, lobed little versions of the grown leaf. Now you can tell seedlings from weeds and start thinning.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The first true leaves, which look like tiny versions of the grown arugula leaf. Now you can thin them.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin to taste, dense at 1 to 3 inches for baby leaf or 4 to 6 inches for full plants, and eat the thinnings. Watch for flea beetles, which hit small seedlings hardest; row cover from sowing is the best defense.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Thin the seedlings, leaving them close for baby leaves or farther apart for bigger plants, and eat the ones you pull. Watch for tiny holes from flea beetles, and use a row cover if they are bad.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How are they coming along?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How are they coming along?

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves reaching a useful size and the patch looking full, well before any central stalk rises. This is the short, productive window for a fast leaf crop.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Leaves big enough to use and the patch looking full, before any flower stalk appears. This is the productive stretch.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Start cutting outer leaves or shearing baby leaf now rather than waiting; regular light cutting keeps new growth coming. Keep moisture even to hold off bolt, and crop faster as the weather warms.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Start picking the outer leaves or snipping baby leaves now. Picking often keeps new leaves coming. Keep the water steady so it does not bolt, and pick faster when it warms up.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Ready to start cutting?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Ready to start cutting?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Full, tender leaves with no central flower stalk forming. Once a stalk appears the eating window is closing fast, since arugula bolts quickly.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Full, tender leaves and no flower stalk in the middle yet. Once a stalk appears the good window is closing fast.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut-and-come-again: take outer leaves or shear the patch an inch above the crown for a second or third cutting. Pick young and in the cool morning, and clear a patch as soon as it shows a stalk.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Take the outer leaves, or cut the whole patch about an inch above the soil so it regrows. Pick young and in the cool morning, and clear it as soon as you see a flower stalk.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Harvesting regularly?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Harvesting regularly?

growth_stages.name: Bolting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A central stalk shooting up, the newer leaves narrowing and turning sharply hot and bitter. This is bolting, the plant shifting to flower and seed; it comes on fast in arugula.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A stalk shooting up from the middle, with the new leaves turning very sharp and bitter. This is bolting, and in arugula it happens fast.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest everything worth eating at once, since the flavor turns quickly. The flowers are edible and peppery; leave one plant to bloom for pollinators or to self-sow, then pull the rest and resow or give the space to a warm-season crop.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pick everything good right away, since the leaves get sharper by the day. The flowers are edible and peppery, so you can enjoy them, and arugula often drops seed and comes back on its own.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Seen a flower stalk yet?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Seen a flower stalk yet?

notifications.body_seasoned: Your arugula should have 2 to 3 true leaves now. Thin to 1 to 3 inches for baby leaf or 4 to 6 inches for full plants, and eat the thinnings.
notifications.body_beginner: Your arugula seedlings should be big enough to thin. Space them out and eat the little ones you pull as baby arugula.

notifications.body_seasoned: Your arugula leaves should be usable now. Cut outer leaves or shear baby leaf an inch above the crown, pick young for the mildest flavor, and refrigerate at once.
notifications.body_beginner: Your arugula should be big enough to pick. Take the outer leaves or cut the patch about an inch above the soil so it regrows. Pick it young while it is mild.

notifications.title_seasoned: Warm, long days ahead: beat the bolt
notifications.title_beginner: Warm weather ahead: pick your arugula
notifications.body_seasoned: Warming, lengthening days bolt arugula fast and turn the leaves sharply hot. Harvest the patch promptly, and lean on a fall sowing, which bolts far less.
notifications.body_beginner: Warm, long days make arugula flower and turn very spicy and bitter fast. Pick your arugula now while it is still good, and plan a fall crop, which lasts longer.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot weather warning for your arugula
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Sustained heat above about 75°F, especially with long days, bolts arugula fast and turns the leaves harshly hot and bitter. Keep moisture even, give afternoon shade, harvest promptly in the cool morning, and treat summer as off-season in hot regions.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Hot weather makes arugula flower early and turn very sharp and bitter. Water evenly, give it afternoon shade, pick everything usable in the cool morning, and remember arugula is a cool-season crop.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hard freeze coming
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Arugula is cold-hardy and tolerates frost; mature plants take light freezes and overwinter under a row cover in mild zones. For most freezes simply keep harvesting; in cold zones a low tunnel or cover carries the crop for an early-spring picking.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Arugula handles frost well, so you usually do not need to do anything. In cold areas, a row cover or low tunnel helps it survive winter and start up again in early spring.

germination.text_seasoned: Arugula germinates fast and in cool soil, but germination drops off sharply above about 80°F, which is why midsummer sowings fail. Sow shallowly, a little thicker than your final stand, and thin to taste.
germination.text_beginner: Arugula sprouts quickly, even in cold soil, but not in hot soil, so do not sow in the heat of summer. Sow it shallow and a bit thick, then thin the seedlings out, eating the ones you pull.

seedling.text_seasoned: Flea beetles target young arugula hard, riddling seedlings with shot-holes. A floating row cover from the day you sow is the single most effective defense; keep seedlings growing fast so they outrun the damage.
seedling.text_beginner: Flea beetles love young arugula and chew tiny holes all over it. Covering the bed with a light row cover from the day you sow is the best way to stop them, and keeping the plants growing fast helps too.

established.text_seasoned: Cut arugula young for the mildest flavor: leaves picked small are nutty and gentle, while older leaves and any heat stress turn them sharply pungent. Steady moisture keeps the bite mild and delays bolt.
established.text_beginner: Pick arugula young for the mildest taste. Bigger or heat-stressed leaves get a lot spicier. Keep the water steady so the leaves stay mild and the plants do not bolt as fast.

harvest.text_seasoned: Shear a baby-leaf patch about an inch above the crown and it will regrow for a second and often third cutting; pick in the cool morning and refrigerate at once, since arugula wilts fast.
harvest.text_beginner: Cut a baby-leaf patch about an inch above the soil and it grows back for another cutting or two. Pick in the cool morning and get it in the fridge right away, because it wilts quickly.

bolting.text_seasoned: Bolting arrives fast in arugula and the leaves turn harshly hot, so do not fight it: harvest the patch at the first stalk, enjoy the edible peppery flowers, and let one plant self-sow. A fall sowing bolts far less than spring.
bolting.text_beginner: Arugula bolts fast and the leaves get very sharp, so just pick the patch when you see a flower stalk. The flowers are edible and peppery, and the plant often reseeds itself. A fall crop bolts much less than a spring one.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A single arugula plant yields a small rosette of leaves over a few weeks, so the crop is grown in dense patches or rows rather than per plant. Cut as baby leaf or cut-and-come-again, a bed gives two or three cuttings before heat or bolt ends it; the productive window is bounded by temperature, not a fixed calendar.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Each arugula plant gives a small bunch of leaves, so it is grown in patches or rows rather than as one big plant. A patch gives a few cuttings before it bolts, so sow more every couple of weeks.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Production peaks in the cool weeks of fall and early spring. A spring patch produces hard for a couple of weeks and then ends abruptly at bolt, while the fall crop, under cooling weather and shortening days, holds longer and, with cover, into winter.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Arugula produces the most in the cool weather of fall and early spring. A spring patch gives a couple of good weeks and then bolts, but a fall crop lasts longer and can carry into winter under a cover.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Arugula is one of the fastest, most forgiving crops for a first season: baby leaves in about 3 weeks from sowing and almost nothing to go wrong if you sow into cool weather. The key to total yield is frequent succession sowing and picking young, and leaning on the fall crop, since a spring patch sown too late bolts before it produces much.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Arugula is one of the easiest, fastest crops for a beginner, with baby leaves in about 3 weeks. The trick is to sow a little every couple of weeks, pick it young, and grow it in cool weather, especially fall, so it does not bolt before you get to eat it.
factors_seasoned: Timing: a crop grown in the cool shoulders yields well; one caught by heat and long days bolts before producing. Fall is the most reliable.
Variety: slower-bolting selections and wild (Diplotaxis) rocket extend the productive window in warmth.
Even moisture: steady water keeps leaves mild, tender, and slow to bolt; drought sharpens the flavor and triggers the seedstalk.
Frequent cutting: picking young and often, and succession sowing every 2 to 3 weeks, keeps tender leaves coming.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No reliable extension or peer-reviewed evidence supports timing arugula planting or harvest by moon phase. Sow by soil temperature, day length, and frost dates instead.

failure_diagnostics.label: Bolting (flower stalk and harsh, bitter leaves)
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Heat and long days, sped by drought, telling the fast-growing plant to flower.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your arugula shot up a central stalk and the leaves turned sharply hot and bitter. Arugula bolts fast in heat and long days, which is its normal cycle, not a mistake. Next time, grow it in cool weather, especially fall, sow a fresh batch every couple of weeks, pick it young, and try wild (Sylvetta) arugula, which bolts much slower.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Grow it in cool weather, sow every couple of weeks, pick young, and try slow-bolting wild arugula for warmth.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The plant elongated into a seedstalk and leaf quality collapsed, with mustard-oil pungency spiking. Bolting is driven by heat above about 75°F and lengthening days, accelerated by drought and crowding, and is rapid in arugula. Growers most often sow too late into warming weather. Next time sow into the cool shoulders, succession-sow, favor fall, and use slower-bolting or Diplotaxis types.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Heat and long-day photoperiod, accelerated by drought and crowding; rapid in a fast brassica.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sow into cool weather, succession-sow every 2 to 3 weeks, lean on fall, and choose slow-bolting or wild (Diplotaxis) rocket.

failure_diagnostics.label: Tiny shot-holes all over the leaves
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Flea beetles, arugula's signature pest, chewing pits and holes in the leaves.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your arugula leaves got peppered with tiny round holes, made by little dark beetles that jump when disturbed. Those are flea beetles, and they love arugula, hitting seedlings hardest. Next time, cover the bed with a light row cover from the day you sow, keep the plants growing fast, and clear nearby cabbage-family weeds.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Cover the bed with row cover from sowing, keep plants growing fast, and clear cabbage-family weeds.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Foliage was riddled with shot-holes from crucifer and striped flea beetles (Phyllotreta), which strongly prefer arugula and overwhelm seedlings. Sprays are a stopgap. Next time exclude beetles with floating row cover from sowing, push rapid establishment, clean up crucifer weeds and debris, and consider a sacrificial trap planting.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Crucifer and striped flea beetles, a strongly preferred host in arugula, attacking small plants.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Use floating row cover from sowing, keep seedlings vigorous, clean up crucifer weeds, and consider a trap crop.

failure_diagnostics.label: Yellow patches with gray mold underneath
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Downy mildew, a leading arugula disease, in cool, damp, crowded conditions.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your arugula got pale yellow patches on top with a fuzzy gray-white mold underneath, and the leaves discolored. That is downy mildew, which thrives in the same cool, wet weather arugula likes, especially when plants are crowded and stay wet. Next time, space the plants for airflow, water at the soil line, choose resistant varieties where you can, and rotate the bed.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Thin for airflow, water at the base, choose resistant varieties, and rotate your arugula and brassicas.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Angular chlorotic lesions with grayish-white sporulation beneath indicate downy mildew (Hyaloperonospora parasitica), favored by cool temperatures and long leaf wetness. Next time widen spacing, switch to drip, choose resistant cultivars where offered, and lengthen the brassica rotation.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Hyaloperonospora parasitica under cool, wet, humid, crowded conditions.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Widen spacing for airflow, irrigate by drip, use resistant cultivars where offered, and rotate away from brassicas.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor or patchy germination
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Soil too warm, old seed, or a soil crust.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your arugula came up thin and patchy, or barely at all. Arugula seed sprouts poorly in warm soil above about 80°F and can be blocked by a hard crust. Next time, sow in cool soil (early spring or once late-summer soil cools), keep the surface moist so it does not crust, and use fresh seed.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Sow in cool soil, keep the surface moist so it does not crust, and use fresh seed.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Stand was thin and uneven. Arugula germination is inhibited by warm soil above roughly 80°F, and a surface crust blocks the shallow-sown shoots. Next time sow into cool soil, keep the seedbed moist and uncrusted, and sow shallowly with fresh seed.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Warm soil inhibiting germination, or a soil crust over shallow-sown seed.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sow into cool soil, keep the bed moist to prevent crusting, and sow shallowly with fresh seed.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Arugula is one of the best succession crops: it matures so fast and bolts so readily that one sowing is gone in a few weeks. Sow a short row every 2 to 3 weeks through the cool windows, spring until heat and long days set in, and again from late summer through fall, which is the longer, more reliable run. In hot regions skip summer and succession-sow through the cool fall, winter, and spring.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: Sow a little arugula every 2 to 3 weeks instead of all at once, so you always have fresh, mild leaves before it bolts. Do this in spring and again in late summer for fall. In hot areas, skip summer and keep sowing through the cool months.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: arugula_author_fresh_pilot (Claude Code lane authoring, 2026-06-29). Authored from the arugula shell, modeled structurally on the lettuce-leaf certified template and the spinach/kale CC gate-clean examples, with arugula (Eruca sativa) biology re-derived from live T1 extension sources (Clemson arugula fact sheet, Wisconsin Horticulture, Cornell, UMass brassicas). DRAFT for daily biology-fidelity review, not certified: launch flags false. Key arugula-vs-lettuce refits: a fast COOL-SEASON BRASSICA (mustard family, Brassicaceae) rather than a composite-family lettuce, so a brassica rotation/pest/disease set replaces lettuce's; VERY FAST (baby leaf ~3 weeks, full leaf ~30 to 40 days, DTM 20 to 40); bolts even harder than lettuce, on HEAT plus long days, and the leaves turn sharply hot and bitter, so the spring window is short and fall is the main crop; frost-hardy and overwinters in mild zones; the SIGNATURE pest is the flea beetle (shot-hole damage), with downy mildew / white rust / damping-off / Alternaria the disease set; pH 6.0 to 7.0; broadcast/baby-leaf spacing 1 to 3 inches; direct-sown; wild/perennial rocket (Diplotaxis tenuifolia, 'Sylvetta') noted as a slower, more pungent, slower-bolting relative. The cool northern zones 3 to 5 run through summer (no heat_pause); 15 genuinely-hot region cells carry backed heat_pause objects. successions_realized is CC-derived (deriver), not hand-authored. See arugula_NOTES.md for modeled values and flags.

open_findings.basis: Within the cited Cornell/Wisconsin ranges; the operative fact (very fast, baby leaf ~3 weeks) is sourced and surfaced in prose. Clemson's longer figure is for the largest mature leaves.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: Up North (zones 3 through 7), arugula is a quick spring-and-fall crop. Start sowing in early spring as soon as you can work the soil, since arugula shrugs off frost, and sow a little every 2 to 3 weeks. In the coldest zones the cool summer lets it keep going, but in the milder zones 6 and 7 the hottest weeks make it bolt and turn harsh, so take a break in midsummer and sow again for fall, which is the best crop. A last sowing under a row cover can live through winter for super-early spring greens.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In the cold-winter North (zones 3 through 7), arugula is a fast spring-and-fall succession green built around frost. Sow as soon as the soil can be worked in spring, since arugula tolerates frost and even germinates in cool soil, and sow a short row every 2 to 3 weeks for a steady supply. In the coolest zones the cool summer often carries a continuous crop straight through, while in the warmer end of this band (zones 6 and 7) midsummer heat and long days bolt it, so the calendar pauses through the hottest weeks and resumes for the main fall crop. A late-summer sowing run into fall is the most reliable, and a final sowing under a row cover can overwinter for the earliest spring picking.

The long, intensely hot season bolts and scorches it, so plant from October into winter and harvest through early spring. Sow every 2 to 3 weeks across the cool window.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Arugula is direct-sown shallowly as soon as the soil can be worked, tolerates frost, and is succession-sown every 2 to 3 weeks through the cool windows; the hot months are excluded where summer heat bolts it. (Cornell; Wisconsin Horticulture; Clemson)

fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: In peninsular Florida (zones 10 and 11), grow arugula in winter. It is too hot most of the year, so plant in fall and pick through the cool months. Sow a little every 2 to 3 weeks while it is cool. The farther south you are, the shorter that window.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: On the Florida peninsula (zones 10 and 11), arugula is a winter crop. The long subtropical heat bolts it, so plant in fall and harvest through the cool months, with the hot two-thirds of the year off-season. Sow every 2 to 3 weeks across the short cool window; the deeper south (zone 11) has the shortest window of all.
