hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In tropical Hawaii, true arugula is hard to grow because of the heat. It does best in the coolest months or up at elevation. Plant in the cool window, sow a little every 2 to 3 weeks, and expect a short season.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: In tropical Hawaii (zone 11), true arugula is a marginal, cool-season or upland crop. Lowland heat bolts it quickly, so grow it in the coolest months or at higher elevation, treating the warm season as off-season. Sow every 2 to 3 weeks during the cool window where the climate allows.

crops.description_seasoned: Arugula (Eruca sativa), also called salad rocket or roquette, is a fast, cool-season leafy green in the mustard family (Brassicaceae), grown for its tender, peppery leaves. It is one of the quickest crops in the garden, giving baby leaves in about 3 weeks and full leaves in around a month, and it germinates readily even in cool soil and tolerates frost, so it can be sown very early and overwinters in mild zones. Its defining habit is how fast it bolts: heat above about 75°F and lengthening days send it to seed quickly, and the leaves turn sharply hot and bitter as it does, so the spring window is short, fall is the main crop, and in hot regions it is grown through the cool fall, winter, and spring. A separate wild or perennial rocket (Diplotaxis tenuifolia, sold as Sylvetta) is slower, more pungent, and far slower to bolt. Arugula is easy, succession-sown every 2 to 3 weeks, and a strong first-season choice, though flea beetles are its signature pest.
crops.description_beginner: Arugula is a fast-growing, cool-season salad green with a peppery, mustardy flavor. It is one of the quickest things you can grow, giving baby leaves in about 3 weeks, and it handles frost and even grows through winter in mild areas. Its main quirk is that it bolts (sends up a flower stalk) very fast in heat and long days, and the leaves turn sharply hot and bitter when it does. So it grows best in the cool parts of the year, especially fall, and in hot places it is a fall-to-spring crop. Sow a little every couple of weeks for a steady supply. It is easy and beginner-friendly; the main pest to watch is the flea beetle, which chews tiny holes in the leaves. There is also a wild kind of arugula that is slower to bolt and even more peppery.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Arugula is ready as soon as the leaves are big enough to use, often baby leaf at 2 to 3 weeks and full leaf around 30 to 40 days. Cut the outer leaves cut-and-come-again, or shear the whole patch about an inch above the crown and let it regrow for a second or third cutting. Pick young and in the cool morning, and crop fast as the weather warms, since the leaves turn sharply hot and bitter once the plant bolts.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Arugula is ready to pick as soon as the leaves are big enough, often baby leaves in about 3 weeks and full leaves in around a month. Take the outer leaves a few at a time, or cut the whole patch about an inch above the soil so it grows back. Pick young and in the cool morning, and harvest it all before it flowers (bolts), because the leaves get very sharp and bitter then.

thinning.when: when seedlings have 2 to 3 true leaves
thinning.to_spacing: 1 to 3 inches for baby leaf, or 4 to 6 inches for full plants
thinning.method: snip or pull extra seedlings; the thinnings are edible as baby arugula
thinning.tip_seasoned: Sow a little thick and thin in stages: for baby-leaf cutting, leave plants dense at 1 to 3 inches; for larger, full plants, thin to 4 to 6 inches. Eat every thinning as tender baby arugula, so thinning is just an early harvest. Crowded plants compete, stay small, and bolt sooner.
thinning.tip_beginner: Arugula is usually sown a bit thick, then thinned. For baby leaves you can leave it dense, about an inch or two apart; for bigger plants, thin to 4 to 6 inches. Do not waste the thinnings, they are tender baby arugula.

crops.name: Bok Choy

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Bok choy likes loose, rich soil with plenty of compost that holds moisture but still drains well. Steady, even moisture keeps the leaf-stalks crisp and mild and keeps the plant from bolting; dry, hard soil stresses it and pushes it to flower.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Bok choy grows best in a fertile, well-drained yet moisture-retentive loam or sandy loam high in organic matter, held at even moisture (UMN). As a fast, shallow-rooted leafy brassica it responds to compost worked in before sowing, which feeds quick growth and buffers the steady moisture that keeps the leaf-stalks crisp and tender. Uneven moisture both stresses the plant toward bolting and contributes to tipburn of the inner leaves, and keeping the soil out of the strongly acidic range also helps hold down clubroot, the brassica-family soil disease.

ph.note_beginner: Bok choy grows best in soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, about 6.0 to 7.0. A simple soil test tells you where you stand. Keeping the soil from getting too acidic also helps prevent clubroot, a cabbage-family soil disease.
ph.note_seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0. Bok choy is forgiving and grows well across roughly 5.5 to 7.5: UMN and NCSU both give 6.0 to 7.5 for Chinese cabbage and bok choy, while Clemson lists 5.8 to 6.5. As with other brassicas, holding the soil toward neutral rather than strongly acidic also helps suppress clubroot, so a grower with clubroot history should lean to the high end.

fertilizer.timing: a little at sowing, then a light side-dress 2 to 3 weeks after the seedlings are up
fertilizer.example_product: Blood meal, 21-0-0, calcium nitrate, or a balanced vegetable fertilizer
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Bok choy is a fast leafy brassica that runs on nitrogen for quick, tender growth, but the crop is so quick that one or two light feedings are plenty. Work compost or a balanced fertilizer into the bed before sowing, then side-dress lightly with nitrogen about 2 to 3 weeks after emergence to push crisp, mild leaf-stalks. Clemson gives the cole-crop rate of 5-10-10 worked in before planting, then about 34-0-0 side-dressed; for a 30-to-50-day crop, keep it light, since lush late growth draws aphids and does little for a plant you will cut soon.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Bok choy grows fast and likes steady nitrogen for tender leaves and stalks. Mix some compost or a balanced fertilizer into the soil before planting, then give it one light feeding a couple of weeks after the seedlings come up. Because the crop is so quick, you usually do not need to feed it much more.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time to side-dress your bok choy with a little nitrogen.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Time to give your bok choy a light feeding.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: High N for fast, tender leafy growth: a balanced 5-10-10 or 10-10-10 worked in before planting, then a light nitrogen side-dress such as 21-0-0, calcium nitrate, or blood meal 2 to 3 weeks after emergence. Do not overfeed a quick crop.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 at planting, then one light nitrogen feed a couple of weeks after the seedlings come up.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: Work in 5-10-10 at about 3 pounds per 100 square feet before planting (Clemson), then side-dress about a quarter cup of 21-0-0 (or 1 pound per 100 feet of row) once a few weeks after emergence; a compost-rich bed of baby bok choy often needs no extra feed.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Follow the label rate for a balanced vegetable fertilizer at planting, then one light nitrogen feed beside the plants a couple of weeks later.

companions.note_beginner: Bok choy is small, fast, and easygoing, so it tucks in between slower crops. It grows well next to lettuce and other quick greens, bush beans, and aromatic herbs like dill, and alliums such as onions. The main thing is to keep it away from other cabbage-family plants, which share its pests and diseases, and to watch for flea beetles, which love it.
companions.note_seasoned: Most bok choy companion pairings rest on space, timing, and tradition rather than measured effects. The practical ones are structural: bok choy is quick and shallow-rooted, so it interplants with lettuce and other fast greens and tucks beside legumes and aromatic herbs. Aromatic herbs and alliums are the traditional scent-based deterrents for the cabbage-family pests bok choy shares. The well-grounded caution is to separate bok choy from other brassicas, which share clubroot and the whole cole-crop pest complex, a rotation and disease principle more than a tested adjacency effect; bok choy is also a flea-beetle magnet, sometimes deliberately used as a trap crop near choicer brassicas.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Bush beans
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Beans add a little nitrogen to the soil that the leafy bok choy can use, and the two share a cool-to-mild season without crowding each other.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Legume nitrogen and complementary habit are widely taught; no bok-choy-specific trial.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A legume interplant on nitrogen and structure: beans fix a little nitrogen the leafy bok choy draws on, and the quick bok choy uses the open ground between young bean plants. Sound space and timing logic rather than a measured bok choy effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Lettuce and other quick greens
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Lettuce grows fast and low like bok choy, so you can sow them together to fill a salad bed, and both like the same cool weather.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Quick cool-season interplant logic extensions endorse generally; not a bok-choy-specific measured effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Bok choy and lettuce share a cool season, a shallow root zone, and a bed, so they interplant efficiently and are harvested young together. A space-and-timing pairing, not a documented growth boost; the two share no major pest.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Dill and aromatic herbs
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Strong-smelling herbs like dill are a classic neighbor for cabbage-family plants; their scent is said to confuse pests, and their flowers bring in helpful insects.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Aromatic umbels are extension-noted for recruiting parasitoids/predators of brassica pests; the dill-bok-choy pairing itself is not trial-tested.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Aromatic umbels like dill are a traditional brassica companion, their flowers drawing the parasitoid wasps and hoverflies that attack brassica aphids and caterpillars. Let some flower nearby; treat it as a partial-mechanism aid rather than a measured bok-choy-specific effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Onions and other alliums
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Onions are a traditional neighbor for cabbage-family plants; their strong smell is thought to help put off the pests that hunt by scent.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Allium scent-masking for brassicas is widely taught companion lore; no bok-choy-specific trial.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Alliums are a traditional brassica companion, their pungent scent thought to mask the crop from the cabbage-family pests that hunt partly by smell. Shallow-rooted and undemanding, they tuck around young bok choy without competing for much. A low-risk, scent-based aid rather than a proven control.

good_seasoned.name: Bush beans
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A legume interplant: beans fix a little nitrogen the leafy bok choy draws on, and the quick bok choy uses the open ground between young bean plants. Space-and-timing logic rather than a measured bok-choy effect.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Legume nitrogen and complementary habit are widely taught; no bok-choy-specific trial.

good_seasoned.name: Lettuce
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A quick, shallow cool-season green that shares bok choy's season and bed and is cut young alongside it. Space-driven and traditional, not a documented growth effect; the two share no serious pest.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Space-use intercropping lore; no T1 source documents a lettuce-bok-choy benefit.

good_seasoned.name: Dill
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Aromatic umbels like dill draw the parasitoid wasps and hoverflies that attack brassica aphids and caterpillars. Let some flower, and keep it off to the side so it does not shade the low plants. A folk-garden and partial-mechanism aid, not a documented bok-choy yield benefit.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Aromatic-umbel pest-confusion/parasitoid recruitment is a documented brassica companion tradition; no T1 trial documents a dill-bok-choy benefit.

good_seasoned.name: Onions
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional brassica companion whose scent is thought to deter cabbage-family pests; shallow-rooted and low-competition. A plausible, low-risk pairing rather than a documented effect.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Allium scent-masking lore for brassicas; not trial-isolated for bok choy.

good_seasoned.name: Nasturtiums
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Often planted as a trap crop for aphids near brassicas. Trap cropping is a documented principle but not a tested bok-choy-nasturtium pairing, so treat it as a plausible aid rather than a proven control.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Trap cropping for aphids is a documented mechanism; the specific nasturtium-bok-choy pairing is not formally tested.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Other brassicas
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep bok choy away from other cabbage-family plants like cabbage, broccoli, kale, mustard, turnips, and radishes. They share the same pests and diseases, so grouping them makes flea beetles, caterpillars, and clubroot worse.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Same-family crops share pests and pathogens, so clustering raises pest/disease pressure, and successive brassica planting builds soil-borne clubroot. A sound epidemiological/rotation mechanism rather than a measured antagonism.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Planting bok choy shoulder to shoulder with its brassica relatives, cabbage, broccoli, kale, mustard, turnip, radish, concentrates the family's shared pests (flea beetles above all, plus cabbage aphids, cabbageworms, loopers, diamondback moths, root maggots) and shared diseases in one spot, and repeated same-family planting lets soil-borne clubroot build up. Spread brassicas out and rotate where they grow each year.

bad_seasoned.name: Other brassicas
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Cabbage, broccoli, kale, mustard, turnip, radish and the other cole crops share bok choy's clubroot and cabbage-family pests, so grouping them concentrates disease and pest pressure. A real rotation and disease principle rather than a tested adjacency effect; the practical rule is to spread brassicas out and rotate them.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Shared clubroot and shared cabbage-family pests are extension-documented; the bad-adjacency claim is a known agronomic principle, not formally pair-tested.

bad_seasoned.name: Strawberries
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional caution that brassicas and strawberries inhibit each other. There is no documented mechanism or T1 support; it persists as folklore.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Folk anti-companion claim with no pattern match or T1 support.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms_beginner: Lots of tiny round shot holes peppering the leaves, made by tiny dark beetles that jump like fleas when you come near. Bok choy is one of their very favorite plants, and heavy damage can riddle or kill young seedlings.
pests.cause_beginner: Flea beetles are small jumping beetles that chew little pits and holes in cabbage-family leaves. They are drawn strongly to bok choy and mustards and hit small seedlings hardest, since a tiny plant cannot outgrow the damage.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover young plants with a light row cover from the day you sow, and if beetles are heavy use a spinosad spray. The main goal is to get the seedlings up and growing fast, before the beetles riddle them.
pests.prevention_beginner: Use row cover from sowing, the single best defense, keep seedlings growing fast with steady water, and clear nearby cabbage-family weeds. Some growers plant a sacrificial mustard patch as a trap crop.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small round shotholes pepper the foliage and the tiny dark beetles jump when disturbed. Bok choy and other mustards are highly preferred hosts, so pressure is often intense; seedlings can be stunted or killed and the holes mar the leaf-stalks of a crop eaten raw or lightly cooked.
pests.cause_seasoned: Crucifer flea beetles (Phyllotreta species) chew the foliage of brassicas and strongly prefer bok choy and mustard; adults overwinter in debris and emerge to attack the earliest, smallest plants, with multiple generations through the season.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Floating row cover from sowing is the most effective tool; spinosad helps under heavy pressure. The aim is rapid establishment past the vulnerable seedling stage, so push fast growth.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Exclude beetles with row cover from sowing, keep seedlings vigorous with even water and a light feed, clean up crucifer weeds and crop debris, and consider an early trap planting of mustard to divert beetles from the main crop.

pests.name: Cabbage aphids
pests.symptoms_beginner: Clusters of small gray-green insects with a dusty, waxy coating on the new growth and tucked deep into the folds where the leaf-stalks meet, where they are very hard to wash out. Leaves may curl and there can be a sticky film.
pests.cause_beginner: Cabbage aphids are tiny insects that suck the plant's juices and breed fast. They love cabbage-family plants and hide down in the stalk crevices, which is the part you eat.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Knock colonies off with a strong spray of water and hit the undersides of leaves and the crevices with insecticidal soap or neem oil, repeating every few days. Welcome ladybugs and lacewings, which eat aphids.
pests.prevention_beginner: Check the growing center and the stalk crevices often and act early. Go easy on nitrogen, since soft growth draws them, use row cover, and clear away old cabbage-family plants after harvest.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: The gray-green, waxy-coated cabbage aphid forms dense colonies on growing tips and leaf undersides and lodges deep in the leaf-stalk folds, where it contaminates the harvested plant with insects and honeydew and is very hard to clean. Clemson notes aphid feeding yellows, stunts, curls, and wrinkles the foliage and brings sooty mold, with pressure heaviest on the fall crop.
pests.cause_seasoned: Brevicoryne brassicae, a brassica-specialist aphid (with green peach aphid also present), sucks sap and reproduces rapidly; contamination of the harvested stalks with aphids and sticky honeydew is usually the real problem rather than plant stunting.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Dislodge colonies with a strong jet of water and spray insecticidal soap, neem, or horticultural oil with thorough coverage of leaf undersides and the stalk crevices; repeat every few days. Conserve natural enemies (parasitoid wasps, hoverflies, lady beetles).
pests.prevention_seasoned: Scout growing tips and the stalk crevices weekly and catch infestations before aphids lodge in the plant. Avoid excess nitrogen, use row cover on young plants, and destroy crop debris that carries them over.

pests.name: Cabbage caterpillars
pests.symptoms_beginner: Ragged chewed holes in the leaves, green caterpillars on the plants, and dark droppings. Because you eat the leaves and stalks, even a little chewing and mess is a problem.
pests.cause_beginner: Several white butterflies and moths lay eggs on cabbage-family leaves, and the caterpillars that hatch (imported cabbageworms, loopers, and small wriggling diamondback larvae) chew the foliage.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray Bt, which is safe and targets only caterpillars, or pick them and their eggs off by hand from the undersides of leaves. Spray again after rain, since it washes off.
pests.prevention_beginner: Use a row cover to keep the adults from laying eggs, clean up old cabbage-family plants and weeds, and check leaf undersides for eggs and small caterpillars.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Ragged feeding holes with green or striped larvae and frass; the imported cabbageworm, cabbage looper, and diamondback moth larvae feed on bok choy (UMN lists all three), and on a fast leaf-and-stalk crop even light feeding and contamination downgrade the harvest.
pests.cause_seasoned: The larvae of several brassica moths and butterflies feed on the foliage; the adults lay eggs on the leaves, and warm-region plantings see the most pressure. The diamondback moth is often the most numerous in the South.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki) or spinosad targeting young larvae and hand-pick where practical; repeat after rain, since Bt breaks down.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Exclude egg-laying adults with row cover, clean up brassica debris and weed hosts, and scout leaf undersides for eggs and early instars.

pests.name: Cabbage root maggot
pests.symptoms_beginner: New transplants wilt and grow badly or fall over. If you pull one up, you'll find small white maggots eating the roots. It is worst in cool, wet spring soil.
pests.cause_beginner: A small fly lays eggs at the base of the plant, and the maggots that hatch burrow down and eat the roots. The fly is most active in cool, damp weather, so spring transplants are most at risk.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Once the maggots are in the roots you can't save that plant, so pull and throw away the badly damaged ones. Put your effort into protecting the rest from new eggs.
pests.prevention_beginner: Put a small collar or disk around the base of each transplant to stop the fly from laying eggs there, or use a row cover. Avoid planting into cold, soggy soil, and rotate away from where cabbage-family plants grew.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Transplants wilt, grow poorly, and may collapse; pulling a plant reveals small white maggots tunneling in the roots and lower stem. Damage is worst in cool, wet soil at spring establishment (UMN lists cabbage maggots among bok choy's pests).
pests.cause_seasoned: The larvae of the cabbage root fly (Delia radicum) tunnel into brassica roots; the adult lays eggs at the stem base, and the maggots feed below, sometimes killing young plants and opening the door to rots.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no effective rescue once maggots are in the roots; remove and destroy badly affected plants and protect the rest from further egg-laying.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Place a collar or disk around the stem base at transplanting to block egg-laying, or use row cover; avoid planting into cold, wet soil and rotate away from where brassicas grew.

pests.name: Harlequin bug
pests.symptoms_beginner: Shield-shaped black-and-orange (or black-and-red) bugs on the leaves, which develop pale spots, then brown and look tattered. It is mostly a warm-region problem and loves cabbage-family plants.
pests.cause_beginner: The harlequin bug is a colorful stink-bug relative that pierces the leaves and sucks the juices, leaving pale blotches. It strongly prefers cabbage-family plants, especially in the South.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Search out and crush the bugs, their barrel-shaped eggs laid in rows, and the young ones by hand. Use a row cover to keep them off, pull badly infested plants, and clear away weeds and old plants where they hide over winter.
pests.prevention_beginner: Clean up garden debris and cabbage-family weeds where the adults overwinter, use row cover, and consider a trap crop of mustard to lure them away from the main crop, then destroy it.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Shield-shaped bugs brightly marked black-and-orange or black-and-red feed with piercing-sucking mouthparts that leave pale stipples; affected leaves brown and look tattered, and heavy feeding wilts and deforms plants. A warm-region brassica specialist (Clemson).
pests.cause_seasoned: The harlequin bug (Murgantia histrionica) specializes on cole crops, most damaging in the southern United States, where it completes several generations a year and overwinters as an adult in debris and weeds.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick and crush adults, nymphs, and the barrel-shaped egg rows; exclude with floating row cover; remove heavily infested plants. Insecticidal soap or neem helps where pressure is severe.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Eliminate overwintering sites by removing crop debris and crucifer weeds, use row cover, and deploy an early trap crop of mustard to divert overwintering adults, then destroy it before the main crop is set out.

pests.name: Slugs and snails
pests.symptoms_beginner: Ragged holes with smooth edges chewed in the low leaves and stalks, slimy trails on the plant and soil, and worst damage in cool, damp, shady spots and after rain.
pests.cause_beginner: Slugs and snails are soft, moisture-loving mollusks that feed at night and rasp holes in tender low greens like bok choy. They thrive in damp mulch and dense, shaded plantings.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Hand-pick at night or after rain, set out shallow traps, and use an iron-phosphate slug bait, which is pet-safe. Reduce damp hiding places and water in the morning so the surface dries by night.
pests.prevention_beginner: Thin and space plants for airflow, keep mulch light near the plants, clear damp debris, and water early in the day rather than at dusk.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Smooth-edged holes in low foliage and tender stalks with silvery slime trails, worst in cool, wet, densely planted or heavily mulched beds; a succulent low green like bok choy is highly susceptible (NCSU lists slugs and snails).
pests.cause_seasoned: Several slug and snail species feed nocturnally, rasping the foliage; they shelter in moist debris and mulch by day and build up in cool, wet conditions.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick after dark or rain, use shallow traps and iron-phosphate baits (pet-safe), and remove daytime shelter; morning watering lets the surface dry before they feed.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Reduce moisture and shelter near the plants: thin for airflow, keep mulch off the crowns, clear debris, and irrigate in the morning rather than the evening.

diseases.name: Clubroot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Plants wilt in the afternoon, stay small and yellowish, and don't bounce back. If you dig one up, the roots are swollen into lumpy, club-shaped knobs.
diseases.cause_beginner: A germ that lives in the soil infects the roots of cabbage-family plants and makes them swell, which stops the plant from taking up water and food. It stays in the soil for years.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There's no cure once a plant has it, so pull and destroy infected plants. Keeping the soil from being too acidic (closer to neutral) helps hold it back, and growing cabbage-family plants only rarely in that spot starves the germ out.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Don't grow bok choy or other cabbage-family plants in the same spot more than once every few years, longer if you've had clubroot. Keep the soil from being too acidic, improve drainage, and clean soil off your tools.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Plants wilt in the heat of the day, grow stunted and yellowed, and recover poorly; roots are swollen into distorted clubs and galls instead of normal fine roots.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A soilborne organism (Plasmodiophora brassicae) infects brassica roots and forms the galls, which block water and nutrient uptake. It persists in soil for many years, spreads in contaminated soil and water, and infects most readily in acidic soils below about pH 6.5.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once plants are infected; remove and destroy them. Raising soil pH toward neutral with lime suppresses the disease, and long rotations starve it out over time.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate brassicas out of affected ground on a long cycle (UMN advises up to 7 years where clubroot is known), keep soil pH up, improve drainage, and avoid moving infested soil on tools and boots.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Pale yellow blotches on top of the leaves, with fuzzy grayish growth on the underside, mostly in cool, damp weather. Bad cases discolor and spot the leaves and stalks.
diseases.cause_beginner: A mold-like disease that loves the cool, wet weather bok choy grows in, spreading through wet leaves and splashing water. Crowded plants and long leaf wetness make it worse.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Open up the airflow so leaves can dry, remove the worst leaves, and water at the soil instead of from above. It's hard to stop once the weather stays damp, so prevention matters most.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Space plants so air moves between them, water at the soil line, and pick resistant varieties if downy mildew is common where you live.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Pale yellow patches form on the upper leaf surface with a fuzzy gray-white growth underneath, mainly in cool, damp weather; severe infection discolors and spots the leaves and stalks. Bok choy's cool, humid season overlaps the weather it likes.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A fungus-like organism (Hyaloperonospora brassicae) that thrives in cool, wet, humid conditions and spreads by spores in water and air; long leaf wetness and crowded plantings favor it (Clemson).
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Improve airflow and let foliage dry, remove badly affected leaves, and apply a copper-based fungicide if pressure is high; the disease is hard to stop once humidity stays high.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants for good air movement, water at the soil line rather than overhead, and choose resistant varieties where downy mildew is common.

diseases.name: Black rot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Yellow patches shaped like the letter V appear at the leaf edges, pointing inward, with black veins inside them. It can spread through the plant and rot it.
diseases.cause_beginner: A bacteria that often comes in on infected seeds or transplants. It gets into the leaves and travels through the plant's veins, spreading fastest in warm, wet weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There's no real cure, so remove and destroy infected plants to keep it from spreading. Don't handle or brush against the plants while they're wet, because that spreads the bacteria.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Begin with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants, don't plant where cabbage-family crops grew recently, space plants for airflow, and avoid overhead watering.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellow, V-shaped lesions spread inward from the leaf margins, with the veins inside the V turning black (Clemson); the disease moves through the vascular system and can rot the plant. Often the most serious brassica disease in warm, wet weather, and UMN lists it among bok choy's diseases.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A seedborne bacterium (Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris) that enters through leaf pores and wounds and moves through the veins; it spreads in warm, wet conditions and on infected seed or transplants.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no effective cure; remove and destroy infected plants. Avoid working among plants when foliage is wet, since that moves the bacteria.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Start with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants (a hot-water seed treatment helps), rotate 2 to 3 years away from brassicas, give plants room for airflow, and avoid overhead watering and handling wet foliage.

diseases.name: Alternaria leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small dark spots on the leaves that grow into round patches, often with rings like a tiny target. Bok choy is especially prone to it, and spotted leaves are not good to eat.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that spreads in warm, wet weather and infects the leaves, leaving spots. It is worse on crowded, damp plantings and comes in on infected seed.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove and destroy spotted leaves and old plant debris, improve airflow so leaves dry quickly, and avoid wetting the leaves when you water. Start with clean seed.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Use clean seed, rotate away from brassicas, space plants for airflow, water at the soil line, and clear crop debris after harvest.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Brown circular leaf spots with characteristic concentric rings (target spots) that enlarge and coalesce (Clemson); on a leaf crop even moderate spotting downgrades the harvest. Clemson notes Chinese cabbage and bok choy are more susceptible to Alternaria than common cabbage, and UMN lists it among bok choy's diseases.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Alternaria fungi (A. brassicicola, A. brassicae) infect brassica foliage, spreading by spores in wind and splashing water; infected seed, crop debris, and long leaf wetness drive them.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove spotted leaves and crop debris immediately, improve airflow, and avoid overhead watering; a copper-based fungicide can help under heavy pressure.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Use clean, disease-free seed, rotate away from brassicas, space for airflow, water at the soil line, and clear crop debris that harbors spores after harvest.

diseases.name: White rust
diseases.symptoms_beginner: White, blister-like bumps on the undersides of the leaves, with yellow spots on top. Badly spotted leaves are not good to eat.
diseases.cause_beginner: A mold-like disease, not a true rust, that makes white pustules on cabbage-family leaves and spreads in cool, moist weather. It can ruin a leafy crop quickly.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove and destroy infected leaves, improve airflow, and water at the soil line. As with downy mildew, prevention works better than trying to cure it.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Space plants out, avoid wetting the leaves, choose resistant varieties where it is common, and rotate your planting spot.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: White, blister-like pustules on leaf undersides with chlorotic spotting above; severe infection distorts and downgrades the foliage. A common brassica-greens disease, listed among bok choy's problems by NCSU and worse in mild, moist conditions.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The oomycete Albugo candida, favored by cool nights, mild days, and leaf wetness; it spreads by splash- and wind-dispersed spores and survives on debris and as oospores.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove infected leaves and debris, improve airflow, and avoid overhead irrigation; chemical options are limited for the home garden.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Grow resistant cultivars where white rust is endemic, space for airflow, use drip irrigation, and rotate away from brassicas.

watering.frequency_seasoned: About 1 inch of water per week, kept as even as possible; bok choy is shallow-rooted and bolts faster and turns bitter under drought stress (UMN).
watering.frequency_beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly 1 inch a week.
watering.amount_seasoned: Roughly 1 inch per week (UMN: about 1 inch of rainfall a week is good), more in warm, dry spells while the plants are sizing up.
watering.amount_beginner: Aim for about 1 inch of water a week, a bit more when it is warm.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose where possible to keep foliage dry and discourage leaf disease.
watering.method_beginner: Water at the base of the plants rather than over the leaves, which helps prevent leaf diseases.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves and limp growth; bok choy dislikes waterlogged soil, which invites damping-off in seedlings and crown and bacterial soft rot in cold, wet ground.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Lower leaves yellow and the plant looks soggy and limp, and seedlings may rot at the base.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting and stalled growth, then tougher, more pungent leaf-stalks and faster bolting; drought stress is a direct bolting trigger and also worsens tipburn of the inner leaves.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Wilting leaves that turn tougher and stronger-tasting, and a plant that bolts (flowers) sooner than it should.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Even, steady moisture is the whole game with bok choy: it keeps the plant growing fast, crisp, and mild and holds off the bolting that drought stress brings on.
watering.method_note_beginner: Keep the water steady so the stalks stay crisp and mild and the plant does not bolt early.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Steady moisture matters most through the few weeks of leaf-and-stalk growth and during any warm or lengthening-day spell, when drought stress most readily triggers bolt.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Water steadily while the plants are growing, and especially as the weather warms up.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Bok choy is fast and resents root disturbance, so it is often direct sown, though young transplants work well if set out before they become root-bound. Sow seed about 0.25 to 0.5 inch deep (NCSU) and thin to about 6 inches for baby types or 12 to 18 inches for full-size heads (NCSU; UMN). For transplants, start only about 3 weeks ahead and set out small. The timing trap is the cold-snap bolt: bok choy held more than about a week of nights below 50°F bolts once it warms, so avoid setting young spring plants into a long cold spell, and lean on the fall sowing, which is the more reliable crop. In hot regions, shift sowing to fall through early spring, since heat and long days force bolting.
start_method.notes_beginner: Bok choy is best sown straight in the garden because it grows fast and does not like having its roots disturbed, though small transplants work too. Sow the seeds about a quarter to half an inch deep and thin to about 6 inches apart for baby plants or a foot for full-size ones. The big thing to avoid is a cold spell on young plants: more than about a week of nights below 50°F can make them flower (bolt) once it warms up. The fall crop is the most reliable. In hot areas, plant in fall through early spring instead of summer.

drainage.saucer_practice: Empty the saucer after watering so roots never sit in water, which invites damping-off and root rot.

soil_mix.type_beginner: A good-quality potting mix, not garden soil.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in some compost for steady nutrients.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: A light, well-drained potting mix high in organic matter.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend in compost and a little starter nitrogen; bok choy is a quick feeder but needs only a light charge for its short life.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out faster than the ground, so check daily in warm weather and keep the mix evenly moist, since drought makes bok choy bolt and turn bitter.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Feed a little, since watering washes nutrients out of pots, but the crop is so fast it rarely needs more than a starter charge.

overwintering.approach_beginner: In mild areas, a pot of fall-sown bok choy can keep going through winter in a sheltered, sunny spot. In cold areas, move the pot against the house or into a cold frame, or cover it during hard freezes; bok choy takes light frost but a hard freeze damages it.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Bok choy tolerates light frost, so a fall-sown container can hold through winter in mild zones in a sheltered spot and resume in cool weather. In cold zones the limited root volume freezes harder than open ground, so sink the pot, move it to a cold frame or unheated structure, or cover it during hard freezes. Watch for the cold-snap bolt: a pot of young plants chilled below 50°F for a week or more will run to seed when warmth returns.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Bok choy is an easy, fast container crop, and the baby types are perfect for pots. Use a pot at least 8 inches deep, sow seed and thin to a few plants or grow baby leaves close together, and keep it watered and in the cool seasons. Give some afternoon shade in warm weather to slow bolting.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Bok choy is one of the better container greens, especially the compact baby types (Toy Choi, Mei Qing Choi), which suit a pot at least 8 inches deep. Sow and thin to size, keep moisture even since shallow pots dry fast and drought triggers bolting, grow it in the cool seasons, and give afternoon shade in warm spells. A pot is also the easiest way to move the crop into shade or shelter as the weather turns or a cold snap threatens.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Shallow containers dry faster than beds; check moisture daily in warmth and water before the mix dries, since drought stress bolts bok choy and sharpens its flavor.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Container bok choy needs only a light starter feed; frequent watering leaches nutrients, but the crop is harvested before heavy feeding would matter.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering container suits bok choy well, since it smooths out the steady moisture that keeps the stalks crisp and the plant slow to bolt.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match because it keeps the water steady, which keeps bok choy crisp and slow to bolt.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: Bok choy is shallow-rooted, so depth matters less than surface area: a wide container at least 8 inches deep gives room for the upright rosettes or a dense stand of baby leaves and buffers the fast drying narrow pots suffer.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Bok choy has shallow roots, so a wide pot beats a tall narrow one. Aim for at least 8 inches deep and as much width as you can give it.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Other brassicas: cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kale, collards, mustard, turnip, radish, and bok choy itself. They share the cabbage-family pests (flea beetles above all, plus cabbage caterpillars and aphids) and the soilborne clubroot, so following one brassica with another concentrates and builds that pressure.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Other cabbage-family plants like cabbage, broccoli, kale, mustard, radishes, and turnips, because they share the same pests and diseases.
rotation.good_after: Legumes (peas, beans), alliums (onion, garlic), cucurbits, or nightshades such as tomatoes.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate bok choy and its brassica relatives so they do not return to the same ground for about 3 years. The cabbage-family pest complex (flea beetles above all, plus cabbage caterpillars and aphids) and the soilborne clubroot organism build up where brassicas repeat, and bok choy's quick succession plantings make it easy to keep flea beetles cycling in one bed. Follow brassicas with legumes, alliums, cucurbits, or nightshades, and keep the soil near neutral to help suppress clubroot.
rotation.note_beginner: Try not to grow bok choy or other cabbage-family plants (cabbage, broccoli, kale, mustard, radishes, turnips) in the same spot more than about once every 3 years. They share pests like flea beetles and a soil disease called clubroot that build up when these crops keep coming back. Plant bok choy after peas, beans, onions, squash, or tomatoes instead.

bolting.triggers: a cold snap on young plants (more than about a week of nights below 50°F), and separately summer heat with lengthening days; both worsened by drought and crowding
bolting.prevention_seasoned: Bok choy bolts two ways, and both close the eating window. A spell of cold on young plants, more than about a week of nights below 50°F, vernalizes them so they run to seed once it warms (UMN), and separately heat with long days drives a mature plant to flower. Prevent both by growing in the cool shoulders and leaning on the fall crop: sow the spring crop a touch later, after hard cold, rather than rushing it into a cold snap, and time the crop to mature in cool weather. Choose slow-bolting varieties, keep moisture steady, give light afternoon shade in warm spells, and succession sow every 2 weeks so any bolted batch is quickly replaced. Harvest promptly at the first sign of a central seedstalk.
bolting.prevention_beginner: Bok choy flowers (bolts) for two reasons: a cold spell on young plants, more than about a week of nights below 50°F, and summer heat with long days. To avoid it, grow bok choy in the cool parts of the year and lean on the fall crop, plant the spring crop after the hard cold rather than during it, water steadily, and give some afternoon shade when it is warm. Sow a fresh little batch every couple of weeks, pick promptly, and as soon as you see a flower stalk in the middle, harvest the whole plant.
bolting.note_seasoned: Bolting in bok choy comes from two distinct cues, which is what makes it bolt-prone: cold-induced (vernalization) bolting when young plants meet a long cold snap, and heat-and-daylength bolting in summer. Both are sped by drought and crowding, and both come on fast because the plant is so quick. Once a seedstalk rises the leaf-stalks toughen and turn sharply pungent, so the window closes quickly. The yellow flowers are edible, and a plant left to bloom feeds pollinators and can self-sow.
bolting.note_beginner: Bok choy bolts (sends up a flower stalk and turns sharp and tough) from either a cold spell on young plants or from summer heat and long days. It happens fast and is just the plant's natural cycle, not a mistake. Grow it in cool weather, lean on the fall crop, pick it young, and enjoy the flowers too, which are edible.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Bok choy wilts within a day at room temperature, so refrigerate it promptly after cutting; if it must sit briefly, keep it cool and out of the sun.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Do not leave bok choy out on the counter. It wilts fast in the warmth, so get it into the fridge soon after picking.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerate unwashed in a loose or perforated bag in the crisper; bok choy holds about 1 to 2 weeks near 32°F at high humidity, the crisp stalks keeping a little longer than the leaves. Wash only at use, since trapped moisture speeds breakdown.
storage.fridge_beginner: Store bok choy unwashed in a loose bag in the fridge crisper drawer, where it keeps about a week or two if kept very cold. Wash it only when you are ready to use it.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Bok choy is mostly water and does not freeze well raw, going limp; if you have a glut, blanch briefly and freeze for cooking, where the stalks hold up better than the leaves.
storage.freezer_beginner: Bok choy is best fresh and does not freeze well raw. If you have extra, blanch it briefly and freeze it to cook later, especially the crunchy stalks.
storage.notes_seasoned: Quality is highest straight from the garden. Bok choy is succulent and short-lived once cut, so chill it fast and use it within a week or two; the leaves soften before the stalks, so use the whole plant promptly.
storage.notes_beginner: Bok choy is best right after you pick it and does not keep long. Chill it quickly and use it within a week or so, leaves first since they go limp before the crunchy stalks.

recommended.name: Joi Choi
recommended.note: A widely grown full-size white-stemmed hybrid pak choi with broad white stalks and dark leaves; vigorous, cold-tolerant, and slower to bolt, the standard full-size pick (Clemson names it the pak choi type).

recommended.name: Toy Choi
recommended.note: A miniature green-stemmed baby bok choy, very fast at about 30 days, ideal for close spacing, containers, and whole-plant baby harvest.

recommended.name: Mei Qing Choi
recommended.note: A compact green-stemmed (Shanghai-type) baby choi with pale green stalks, fast and fairly slow to bolt; a dependable baby-to-small-head choice.

recommended.name: Black Summer
recommended.note: A uniform full-size green-stemmed hybrid selected for heat tolerance and bolt resistance, useful at the warm edges of the season.

recommended.name: Win-Win Choi
recommended.note: A large white-stemmed hybrid with good vigor and disease tolerance, productive across spring and fall.

varieties.note_seasoned: Match the type to the slot and the season. White-stemmed types (Joi Choi, Win-Win) are the classic full-size pak choi, with broad white stalks; green-stemmed Shanghai types (Mei Qing, Black Summer) tend to be more compact and a touch more heat-tolerant. For heat and a longer spring stand, choose selections bred for bolt resistance like Black Summer. Baby types (Toy Choi, Mei Qing) are fastest, best for close spacing, containers, and the quick succession sowings that suit this crop. Where bolting from spring cold snaps is a risk, slow-bolting hybrids matter most.
varieties.note_beginner: For full-size bok choy with broad white stalks, grow a type like Joi Choi or Win-Win. For quick baby bok choy, perfect for pots and close spacing, grow Toy Choi or Mei Qing Choi, which are ready in about a month. If you are planting where it may get warm or where spring cold snaps make plants flower early, choose a slow-to-bolt, heat-tolerant kind like Black Summer.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: In about 4 to 10 days, your seeds sprout and push up their first two little seed leaves (the cotyledons).
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil damp and cool. Once the first real bok choy leaves appear after the seed leaves, thin crowded seedlings.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your seeds come up yet?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seeds sprout fast in about 4 to 10 days in cool, moist soil, pushing up two seed leaves (cotyledons).
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep the seedbed or starting mix evenly moist; thin or pot up once the first true leaves appear, and protect seedlings from flea beetles.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Did your bok choy seeds sprout?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The seedlings grow their real leaves and start to form a low rosette. Transplants are ready to set out at about 3 to 4 weeks old, while still small.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Cover young plants with row cover to stop flea beetles, and do not let a cold spell hit them, since more than a week of nights below 50°F can make them flower early. Keep them watered.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How are your seedlings looking?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Young plants build true leaves and a low rosette; bok choy transplants set out best small, at about 3 to 4 weeks, before they become root-bound.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Protect seedlings from flea beetles with row cover, keep moisture even, and avoid exposing young spring plants to a prolonged sub-50°F cold snap that vernalizes them into bolting.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How many true leaves do your seedlings have?

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant grows quickly into an upright cluster of crisp leaf-stalks and leaves. There is no head like cabbage, just a tight rosette of stalks.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Feed a little nitrogen, keep the water steady, and check for aphids and caterpillars in the leaf crevices. Keep an eye out for any flower stalk forming in the center.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Is your plant growing lots of crisp stalks?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The plant bulks fast into an upright rosette of thick leaf-stalks and leaves (no head). Bok choy is near harvest only a few weeks after sowing.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Side-dress lightly with nitrogen, hold moisture even to keep the stalks crisp and forestall bolting, and scout the leaf-stalk crevices for cabbage aphids and caterpillars.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Is your bok choy filling out its rosette of stalks?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant is full-sized for its type, the stalks are crisp, and the leaves are still tender, with no flower stalk yet. Baby types are ready in about a month, full-size ones a bit later.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Cut the whole plant at the base, or pick outer stalks a few at a time and let the center keep growing. Harvest in the cool morning, and cut right away if you see a flower stalk starting.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you harvested your bok choy yet?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The rosette is full-sized for the type (baby about 6 inches, full-size up to a foot) with crisp stalks, tender leaves, and no seedstalk. Quality is best just before any sign of bolt.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut the whole plant at the base, or harvest outer stalks cut-and-come-again and let the crown keep producing. Cut in the cool of the morning, chill promptly, and harvest immediately at the first sign of a central seedstalk.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Did you harvest your bok choy?

notifications.title_beginner: Time to cut your bok choy
notifications.body_seasoned: Your bok choy should be full-sized for its type with crisp stalks now. Cut the whole plant, or pick outer stalks, before any seedstalk forms, and harvest in the cool of the morning for the best quality.
notifications.body_beginner: Your bok choy should be full-sized by now. Cut the whole plant, or pick the outer stalks, before it sends up a flower stalk. Harvesting in the cool morning keeps it crisp.

notifications.title_beginner: Time to feed your bok choy
notifications.body_seasoned: Your bok choy is growing fast. A light nitrogen side-dress now supports crisp, tender leaf-stalks; keep it light, since this is a quick crop.
notifications.body_beginner: Bok choy grows fast and likes a little food. Give it one light nitrogen feeding now to help it make tender stalks and leaves.

notifications.title_beginner: Cold weather warning for young plants
notifications.body_seasoned: A prolonged cold spell is coming while your bok choy is young. More than about a week of nights below 50°F vernalizes young plants into bolting once it warms. Cover them or hold off setting out new transplants until the cold passes.
notifications.body_beginner: A cold spell is coming while your bok choy is young. More than about a week of nights below 50°F can make young plants flower early once it warms up. Cover them, or wait to plant new ones until the cold passes.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Heat warning for your bok choy
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Warm weather with long days pushes bok choy to bolt and turn bitter. Keep moisture even, give afternoon shade, and harvest any near-full plants promptly.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Hot weather and long days make bok choy flower (bolt) and turn bitter. Water evenly, give some afternoon shade, and pick any nearly-ready plants soon.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Cold snap warning for young plants
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A prolonged spell of nights below about 50°F on young bok choy vernalizes the plants, so they bolt once it warms. Cover young plants, or delay new spring sowings until the cold passes.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: A long cold spell, with nights below about 50°F, can make young bok choy flower early once it warms up. Cover young plants, or wait to plant new ones until the cold passes.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hard freeze coming
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Bok choy takes light frost in stride, but a hard freeze damages the succulent stalks. Cover plants or harvest mature ones before a hard freeze.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Bok choy handles a light frost fine, but a hard freeze can damage the juicy stalks. Cover the plants or pick any ready ones before a hard freeze hits.

germination.text_seasoned: Sow about 0.25 to 0.5 inch deep into moist soil; bok choy germinates fast in cool soil, often in 4 to 10 days, as long as moisture stays even.
germination.text_beginner: Plant the seeds about a quarter to half an inch deep in damp soil. They sprout fast, in about 4 to 10 days, in cool conditions.

germination.text_seasoned: Direct sowing suits this fast, disturbance-sensitive crop; if using transplants, start only about 3 weeks ahead so they go out small.
germination.text_beginner: Bok choy is happiest sown right in the garden. If you start it indoors, plant it out while it is still small, after about 3 weeks.

seedling.text_seasoned: Cover seedlings with row cover from emergence: bok choy is a top flea-beetle host, and the shothole damage hits small plants hardest.
seedling.text_beginner: Cover young plants with a row cover right away, because flea beetles love bok choy and riddle small plants with tiny holes.

seedling.text_seasoned: Do not set young spring plants into a prolonged sub-50°F cold snap; more than about a week of cold nights vernalizes them into bolting once it warms.
seedling.text_beginner: Do not plant young bok choy just before a cold spell. More than about a week of nights below 50°F can make it flower early later.

established.text_seasoned: Thin to about 6 inches for baby plants or 12 to 18 inches for full-size heads, and keep moisture even to hold off bolting and tipburn.
established.text_beginner: Thin plants to about 6 inches apart for baby bok choy or a foot for full-size, and water steadily so they do not bolt.

established.text_seasoned: Scout the leaf-stalk crevices for cabbage aphids, which lodge deep in the folds and are hard to wash from a crop eaten stalk and leaf.
established.text_beginner: Check down in the crevices of the stalks for aphids, which hide there and are hard to wash off.

harvest.text_seasoned: Cut the whole plant at the base for a full rosette, or harvest outer stalks cut-and-come-again and let the crown keep producing.
harvest.text_beginner: Either cut the whole plant at the base, or pick the outer stalks a few at a time and let the middle keep growing.

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest in the cool of the morning and chill promptly, and cut immediately at the first sign of a seedstalk, since quality drops fast once bolt begins.
harvest.text_beginner: Pick in the cool morning and refrigerate soon. If you see a flower stalk starting, harvest right away before it turns bitter.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Expect one upright rosette per plant: a baby plant of a few ounces at about 6 inches, or a full-size head up to a foot tall and roughly 1 to 2 pounds, depending on type and spacing. Cut-and-come-again picking of outer stalks extends the take from a single plant over a couple of weeks in cool weather before it bolts.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Each plant gives you one upright cluster of stalks: a small baby plant or a full-size head up to a foot tall and a pound or two, depending on the type. If you pick outer stalks instead of cutting the whole plant, you can keep harvesting from it for a couple of weeks.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Because bok choy matures in about 30 to 50 days, the harvest is quick and concentrated: a sowing comes ready over a week or two, so the way to a steady supply is successive sowings every 2 weeks rather than one big planting. The fall crop yields most reliably, holding longer in cool weather before bolting.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Bok choy is fast, ready in about a month, so a planting comes in over a week or two. For a steady supply, sow a little every couple of weeks instead of all at once. The fall crop lasts the longest before bolting.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: The common first-year mistake is letting bok choy sit too long or catching it with a cold snap or heat: it bolts fast and the window is short. Harvest promptly at full size, lean on the fall crop, and succession sow so a bolted batch is quickly replaced.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: The main thing new growers learn with bok choy is that it bolts fast, especially from a cold spell or heat. Pick it promptly when it is ready, grow it mostly in fall, and sow a little at a time so you always have more coming.
factors_seasoned: Season and timing: cool-weather, fall-leaning crops form tender rosettes; spring cold snaps and summer heat both force bolting and end the harvest early.
Variety: full-size white-stemmed types (Joi Choi, Win-Win) give the biggest heads; baby green-stemmed types (Toy Choi, Mei Qing) are faster and better for close spacing and containers.
Even moisture and light nitrogen: steady water and a light feed keep the stalks crisp and growth fast; drought stress shrinks the plant and triggers bolt.
Spacing: about 6 inches for baby plants, 12 to 18 inches for full-size heads.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No reliable extension or peer-reviewed evidence supports timing bok choy planting or harvest by moon phase. Plant by soil temperature, frost dates, and the cool seasonal windows instead.

failure_diagnostics.label: Bolting from a spring cold snap (vernalization)
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: A spell of cold on young plants, more than about a week of nights below 50°F, followed by warm weather.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your spring bok choy shot up a flower stalk while still small instead of making a nice plant. This is the cold-snap bolt: young bok choy that sits through more than about a week of cold nights below 50°F is tricked into thinking winter has passed, so it flowers as soon as it warms up. It is easy to blame the seed, but an early cold spell is almost always the cause. Next time, plant the spring crop a little later, after the hard cold, protect young plants from cold snaps with row cover, and lean on the fall crop, which avoids this entirely.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant the spring crop after the hard cold passes, cover young plants during cold snaps, and grow your main crop in fall.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Your spring planting bolted while still immature, sending up a seedstalk instead of building a rosette. This is vernalization (cold-induced) bolting: a young bok choy plant exposed to a prolonged cold spell, more than about a week of nights below 50°F, is cued to flower once warmth returns (UMN). It is tempting to blame poor seed, but a cold snap on young plants is the usual cause. Next time set the spring crop out a touch later, after the hard cold, shield seedlings from cold snaps with row cover, choose slow-bolting varieties, and lean on the more reliable fall sowing.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: A prolonged sub-50°F cold snap on young plants, followed by warming, vernalizing them into flowering.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sow the spring crop after hard cold passes, protect seedlings from cold snaps, use slow-bolting varieties, and favor the fall crop.

failure_diagnostics.label: Bolting from heat and long days
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Warm weather and long summer days pushing the plant to flower.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The plant sent up a tall flower stalk and the leaves turned tough and sharp instead of staying tender. Bok choy bolts (flowers early) when heat and long days tell it to bloom, and once that happens the eating window is over. A common mistake is planting too late in spring or trying to grow it in summer. Next time, grow bok choy in the cool parts of the year, especially fall, and pick fast or heat-tolerant varieties.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Grow bok choy in cool weather, especially fall, and choose fast, slow-to-bolt varieties.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The plant ran to a seedstalk and the leaf-stalks toughened and sharpened in flavor. Heat-and-daylength bolting drives a bok choy plant to flower as warm weather and long days arrive, racing past the harvest stage. Growers often plant too late in spring or push the crop into summer. Next time time the crop to mature in cool weather, lean on the fall sowing, choose heat-tolerant, slow-bolting varieties, and keep moisture even, since drought speeds bolt.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Summer heat and lengthening days driving the plant to flower, sped by drought.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Time the crop to mature in cool weather, favor fall, and use heat-tolerant, slow-bolting varieties.

failure_diagnostics.label: Flea beetle shothole damage
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Tiny jumping beetles that chew small round holes in the leaves, worst on young plants.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The leaves got peppered with tiny round holes, and small plants were stunted. Flea beetles love bok choy more than almost any other crop, and they hit seedlings hardest because a tiny plant cannot outgrow the damage. People often notice too late, after the seedlings are riddled. Next time, cover the plants with a light row cover from the day you sow, keep them growing fast, and clear away cabbage-family weeds nearby.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Cover plants with row cover from sowing, keep them growing fast, and clear nearby cabbage-family weeds.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The foliage was riddled with small round shotholes and seedlings were stunted. Bok choy and the other mustards are top flea-beetle hosts, and the beetles are most damaging at the seedling stage when a small plant cannot outgrow the feeding, marring a crop eaten leaf and stalk. The fix is exclusion. Next time use floating row cover from sowing, push fast establishment with even water and a light feed, clean up crucifer weeds and debris, and consider a sacrificial trap planting to divert beetles.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Crucifer flea beetles, which strongly prefer bok choy and mustards and hit seedlings hardest.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Exclude with row cover from sowing, push fast establishment, and clean up crucifer weeds and debris.

failure_diagnostics.label: Tipburn (brown leaf edges in the center)
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Uneven soil moisture, which keeps the plant from moving enough calcium to the fast-growing inner leaves.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The inner leaves browned and dried along their edges even though the outside looked fine. This is tipburn, and it usually comes from uneven watering rather than a disease: when growth is fast and the soil swings from dry to wet, the plant cannot get enough calcium to the new inner leaves and their edges die back. Next time, keep the soil evenly moist, do not overfeed nitrogen for a growth surge, and harvest promptly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist, avoid big swings from dry to wet, and do not overfeed nitrogen.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The margins of the inner leaves browned and died back while the outer plant looked healthy. Tipburn is a calcium-mobility disorder driven by uneven soil moisture and rapid growth, not a pathogen: the fast-growing inner leaves outrun calcium supply when moisture swings (UMN notes Chinese cabbage's susceptibility). Next time hold even moisture, avoid a nitrogen-driven growth surge, choose less susceptible varieties, and harvest promptly rather than holding a mature plant.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Uneven soil moisture plus rapid growth, limiting calcium movement to the inner leaves (a disorder, not a disease).
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Hold even moisture, avoid nitrogen surges, choose less susceptible varieties, and harvest promptly.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Bok choy is fast and bolt-prone, so plant in small batches every 1 to 2 weeks within the cool windows rather than all at once: spring is short and the fall crop is the mainstay. The spring window is narrow because the crop must mature before heat and avoid the cold-snap bolt, so most gardens fit only a sowing or two; the fall planting, heading into cooling weather, is the more reliable and longer-yielding crop.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: Plant bok choy a little at a time, every week or two, instead of all at once, since it grows and bolts fast. Spring is short, so lean on the fall crop, which lasts longer and is more reliable.

open_findings.summary: germination_temp_f [45,85] is brassica-rapa-typical, MODELED: the readable bok-choy/Chinese-cabbage T1 pages (UMN, Clemson, NCSU) give planting timing and a soil-temperature band by implication but no explicit bok-choy germination-temperature range. Cross-check against a parseable T1 germination-temperature source at display-readiness.
open_findings.basis: Brassica rapa germinates reliably across roughly 45-85 F; the value is conventional for the species and within physical bounds. No fabricated source -- flagged as modeled.

open_findings.summary: Per-zone planting/harvest WINDOWS were authored from the cool-season climate envelope (frost anchors) + the leafy-peer (lettuce-leaf/carrot) heat-pause consensus, with se_gulf anchored to Clemson's explicit South Carolina pak-choi/Chinese-cabbage dates (Piedmont spring Mar 15-Apr 30, fall Jul 15-Aug 31; Coastal spring Feb 1-Mar 31, fall Aug 15-Sep 30). Most zones lack a bok-choy-specific local planting chart, so the exact day-windows are modeled (calendars derived, not hand-set). Verify against a bok-choy-specific local source at the daily review where one exists; fall windows were set AFTER peer-heat months to keep the crop out of summer heat.
open_findings.basis: Windows derive from a real climate datum + the leafy-peer heat consensus (the cool-season-timing guard the kickoff requires; 0 broccoli-bug hits). Bok-choy's own timing facts (fast cycle, cold-snap + heat double-bolt, fall-leaning) are reflected. No fabricated source -- the modeled day-precision is flagged.

open_findings.summary: Variety names beyond Joi Choi (Clemson-named) -- Toy Choi, Mei Qing Choi, Black Summer, Win-Win Choi -- are common-trade cultivars described by TYPE (white- vs green-stemmed, baby vs full, heat/bolt tolerance) rather than each individually T1-sourced. The type distinctions are extension-grounded; the specific cultivar names are common catalog cultivars.
open_findings.basis: Joi Choi is named by Clemson; the others are widely sold representative cultivars of the described types. No fabricated sourcing -- the variety notes cite UMN/Clemson/NCSU for the type guidance and flag the cultivar names as trade-common.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Spring direct-sow arm. Bok choy is a fast cool-season brassica that germinates once soil reaches about 40°F, so sow as soon as the spring soil is workable, typically 2 to 4 weeks before the last frost. It germinates well even in warm soil, up to about 85°F, and is semi-hardy, tolerating light frost. Modeled on the regional cool-season planting calendar for leafy greens.

direct_sow.label: secondary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Fall direct-sow arm. For the fall bok choy crop, direct sow roughly 2 to 3 months before the average first fall frost so plants size up as temperatures cool. Fall is the most reliable season for bok choy.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Spring bok choy matures fast, roughly 30 to 50 days, and is cut before summer heat forces bolting.

harvest_end.label: secondary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Finish the spring crop before warm weather and lengthening days run it to seed.
harvest_end.design_note_seasoned: Harvest extends to approximately first_frost + 5 days for semi-hardy greens. Bok choy tolerates light frost, so its fall harvest_end uses the first_frost + 5 day margin rather than a tender-crop first_frost - 5 cutoff.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Spring succession arm: sow bok choy every 2 weeks from when soil reaches about 40°F through the bolt-driven close of the spring window. Bok choy germinates near 40°F and matures fast, roughly 30 to 50 days, so sequential sowings give steady production. The spring arm carries a dual bolt risk: a hard cold snap after sowing can vernalize young plants into bolting, and rising early-summer heat with lengthening days pushes plants to bolt, so the arm ends as the season warms.
direct_sow.design_note_seasoned: Spring arm capped at the fall-arm start so spring and fall sowings do not overlap in the coldest zones. Latest spring sow otherwise bounded by spring-harvest close minus 30-day baby-leaf maturity (Clause B).

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Fall succession arm: sow fast-maturing bok choy every 2 weeks starting roughly 2 to 3 months before the first fall frost, harvesting as temperatures cool. Bok choy is semi-hardy and tolerates light frost, so the latest sowing can leave about 30 days to a baby harvest near the first frost. In the coldest zones the fall start lands in early summer; bok choy germinates well in warm soil, up to about 85°F, so it establishes there without trouble. Fall is the most reliable bok choy season, with plants sizing up into cooling weather.
direct_sow.design_note_seasoned: Fall arm start = heat-floored first_frost offset (methodology v1.5 Clause A). Latest sow = first_frost - 30d (baby-leaf; light-frost-tolerant, no extra hard margin). Per-arm count derived per zone (Clause C); not the season cap.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer gap is a heat-and-daylength exclusion, not a frost gap: bok choy is a cool-season Brassica rapa that bolts (sends up a seed stalk) and turns bitter once warm weather and long days arrive, and it will not form a tender upright rosette in summer heat. The planting calendar therefore splits into a short spring crop maturing before the heat and the main fall crop maturing as it breaks. (UMN Extension; Clemson HGIC)

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: Up north, grow bok choy in the cooler weather at each end of the season, and lean on the fall crop. Plant in spring around your last frost, but not during a cold spell, since more than a week of nights below 50°F can make young plants flower (bolt) instead of growing. Bok choy is fast, ready in about a month, so you can sow a little every couple of weeks. Then plant the main crop in mid to late summer for a fall harvest, which tastes better and is much less likely to bolt. Pick fast types in the coldest areas and keep row cover handy for a late or early frost.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In the cold zones bok choy runs as two fast frost-bracketed crops, and the fall sowing is the dependable one. Direct sow or set out small transplants around the last frost, but not into a long cold snap: young bok choy held more than about a week of nights below 50°F bolts once it warms, so the spring window is short and best sown a touch later than the hardiest brassicas. Because the crop matures in roughly 30 to 50 days, the first cutting comes fast, and you can re-sow every couple of weeks until heat ends the spring run. Sow the main crop in mid to late summer to head as nights cool; fall bok choy is sweeter, slower to bolt, and far more reliable than the spring crop. Midsummer is the gap rather than a heat exclusion in the coldest zones, where short nights keep frost, not heat, the limit at both ends.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Fall sowing window. In the Southeast and Gulf region, fall into spring is the primary bok choy season and summer is excluded by heat. Sow after sustained summer heat subsides in late summer to early fall, about September into early October, shifting later toward the warmer Gulf-coastal (zone 9) end. Modeled on the regional cool-season planting calendar for leafy greens. Bok choy is a fast cool-season brassica that germinates well even in warm early-fall soil, up to about 85°F.

direct_sow.label: secondary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Late-winter to early-spring window. The region's second bok choy window runs from about mid-January into early March, earlier at the warmer Gulf-coastal end, before returning heat and lengthening days drive bolting. Modeled on the regional cool-season planting calendar for leafy greens. Harvest before sustained spring warmth.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: Along the Gulf Coast, grow bok choy in the cool months from fall into spring, not in the hot, humid summer. The fall planting is the most reliable. You can grow a spring crop too, but a cold snap followed by fast warm-up can make young plants flower early, and summer heat ends the spring crop quickly. Since bok choy is ready in about a month, sow a little every couple of weeks. Pick slow-to-bolt kinds and keep the soil evenly moist.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: On the Gulf and coastal plain bok choy is a cool-season crop grown from fall through spring, with the hot, humid summer the off-season. Sow the fall crop as the heat breaks for the most reliable harvest, and a spring crop in the cool of late winter, but watch the spring crop closely: a late cold snap on young plants followed by the region's quick warm-up triggers bolting, and rising heat ends the spring window fast. Bok choy matures in roughly 30 to 50 days, so successive small sowings every couple of weeks keep a steady supply through the cool months. Choose slow-bolting varieties and keep moisture even, since drought stress also pushes the crop to seed.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Late-summer to early-fall window. In the California interior valleys (Sacramento, San Joaquin, and similar), bok choy opens in late summer to early fall as peak heat eases, with a second cool-season run from late fall through early spring. Modeled on the regional cool-season planting calendar for leafy greens. Bok choy germinates well in warm soil, up to about 85°F, so it can go in as the heat breaks, but it bolts under sustained high heat and long days, so the deep-summer slot is skipped.

direct_sow.label: secondary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: The interior's main window is the mild winter into early spring (Table 13.2: November through March), a long cool-season window that opens after the first heat break and closes as returning spring heat triggers bolting. Harvest before sustained spring warmth. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program, Table 13.2)
direct_sow.design_note_seasoned: Winter-spring window anchored to the spring bolt close, working back across the Nov-Mar span; mild interior winters keep the window open throughout.
