For a steady supply, plant a new short row every week or so instead of one big batch.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Radishes are an annual grown fresh from seed every season, so there is no first-year-versus-later distinction as there is with perennials; the first sowing performs as well as any, provided the soil is loose and moisture stays even and the crop grows fast in cool weather.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Radishes are grown fresh from seed each time, so your very first planting can do just as well as any later one. The main things that decide your results are loose soil, steady moisture, and growing them fast in cool weather.
factors_seasoned: Temperature and timing: heat and lengthening days cause bolting and hot, woody roots, so the cool windows matter most.
Final spacing after thinning: crowded radishes fail to form usable roots and grow only tops.
Even moisture: drought-then-flood cycles split roots and sharpen flavor.
Soil looseness: compaction and heavy clay cause small or misshapen roots, especially for long types.
Harvest timing: radishes over-mature fast, turning pithy and strong if left in the ground too long.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting assigns root crops like radishes to the waning moon, the period after the full moon, on the folk principle that the changing lunar pull favors root growth. This is long-standing gardening folklore with no controlled scientific evidence of an effect on radish germination or yield. Plant radishes by soil temperature and your cool-season window, not the moon; this is recorded only for growers who follow the tradition.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Bolting (flower stalk, no root)
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Bolting (flower stalk instead of a radish)
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The plant sent up a flower stalk instead of sizing a root, because warm temperatures and lengthening spring days triggered bolting. The root stays small, woody, and sharply hot once the plant shifts to flowering.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The radish shot up a tall flower stalk instead of making a good root, because the weather warmed up and the days got longer. Once it bolts, the root stays small, woody, and very hot.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Grow radishes in the cool windows and stop spring sowings before sustained heat and long days; favor fall plantings. Keep plants growing fast with even moisture, and choose heat-tolerant or slow-bolt varieties for late-spring sowings.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant radishes in the cool parts of the year and stop spring planting before it gets hot; fall is easier. Keep them growing fast with steady water, and pick heat-tolerant or slow-to-bolt kinds if you plant late in spring.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Pithy, woody, or sharply hot roots
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Hollow, woody, or super-hot radishes
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The roots grew slowly or sat too long, becoming pithy (spongy and hollow), woody, and strongly pungent. The usual causes are heat, drought stress, crowding, or simply leaving mature radishes in the ground past their short window.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The radishes came out spongy and hollow inside, woody, or so hot they are hard to eat. This usually means they grew too slowly or sat too long, from heat, dry soil, crowding, or being left in the ground too long.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Grow them fast in cool weather with even moisture and correct spacing, and harvest on time, since radishes over-mature quickly. Pull round types at about 1 inch and do not hold them in warm soil.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Grow them fast in cool weather, water evenly, give them room, and harvest on time, because radishes go downhill fast. Pull round radishes at about an inch and do not leave them in warm soil.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Cracked or split roots
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Cracked or split radishes
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The roots split because soil moisture swung from dry to wet: after a dry spell, heavy watering or rain made the root take up water fast and crack. Over-mature roots crack more readily.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The radishes split open because the soil went dry and then got soaked. After a dry spell, a big watering or rain makes the radish drink fast and crack. Old, over-ready radishes crack more easily too.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Keep moisture even through the short cycle rather than letting the bed swing dry-then-wet, and harvest on time. If a heavy rain is coming and radishes are near size, pull them first.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep the soil evenly damp the whole time instead of letting it dry out and then soaking it, and harvest on time. If a big rain is coming and the radishes are nearly ready, pull them first.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: All tops, no root (failure to bulb)
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: All leaves, no radish
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The plants grew lush leaves but never formed a usable root. The most common causes are crowding (seedlings not thinned), excess nitrogen, and heat or stress that pushes top growth over root development.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: You got plenty of leaves but no radish underneath. This usually means the seedlings were too crowded and not thinned, or there was too much nitrogen fertilizer, or heat and stress pushed leaf growth instead of a root.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Thin promptly to a final 2 inches (4 to 6 for daikons), go easy on nitrogen and fresh manure, and grow in cool weather with even moisture so the plant puts energy into the root.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Thin the seedlings to about 2 inches apart (4 to 6 for daikons), go easy on fertilizer and skip fresh manure, and grow them in cool weather with steady water so they make a root instead of just leaves.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Forked or branched roots
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Forked or branched radishes
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The root split into prongs because it met an obstruction (a stone, clod, or hardpan) as it swelled, or because fresh manure or concentrated nitrogen stimulated branching. Long daikon types are most affected in heavy or compacted soil.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The radish split into several prongs because it hit something hard as it grew (a rock, clod, or packed soil), or because fresh manure or strong fertilizer made it branch. The long daikon kinds fork most in heavy soil.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Work the bed loose and stone-free to an appropriate depth for the type, avoid fresh manure and heavy nitrogen, and use short round types or a deep loose container in heavy or rocky ground.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Loosen the soil and pull out rocks and clumps before planting, skip fresh manure and heavy fertilizer, and grow short round kinds or use a deep pot of loose mix if your soil is heavy or rocky.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Shot-hole leaf damage (flea beetles)
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Tiny holes all over the leaves
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The leaves are riddled with small round holes from flea beetles, worst on young spring seedlings. On a fast, vigorous radish the root is usually fine, but a heavily fed-on seedling slows down.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The leaves are full of tiny round holes from flea beetles, worst on young spring seedlings. A healthy fast radish usually still makes a fine root, but badly chewed seedlings slow down.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Cover early spring sowings with a floating row cover at planting, clean up crop debris to cut overwintering, and keep the stand growing fast; a trap crop of arugula or mustard can pull beetles away.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Cover early spring plantings with a light row cover at planting, clean up old plants so fewer beetles survive winter, and keep the radishes growing fast; planting a little arugula or mustard nearby as bait helps too.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Radishes are the textbook succession crop: sow a short row every week to ten days through the cool window rather than one large planting, so roots mature in sequence instead of all at once and none over-mature waiting to be pulled. In cool-summer climates that means spring through early summer, then a late-summer-into-fall run; in hot-summer climates it means fall through early spring, skipping the heat. Stop spring sowings before sustained heat and long days arrive, since radishes bolt and turn pithy and hot in warm weather. The number of sowings per season is set by the length of your cool window, not a fixed cap.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: Instead of planting all your radishes at once, sow a short row every week or so. That way they are ready a few at a time over several weeks rather than all on the same day, and none sit too long and turn hollow. In places with cool summers, start in spring and keep going, then sow again in late summer for fall. In places with hot summers, grow them in fall, winter, and early spring and skip the summer heat, since radishes bolt and turn hot in warm weather. Stop spring sowings before the hottest part of the year.

plantings.label: spring

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: In the northern tier, radish is an early cool-season crop. Direct-sow as soon as the soil can be worked and reaches about 40 °F; UMN places this in roughly mid to late April for most of the region, earlier at the warm (zone 7) end and later at the cold (zone 3) end. Radish germinates fast in cool soil (3 to 7 days) and tolerates light frost, so it goes in well before the last frost. Make small repeat sowings every 7 to 10 days through spring for a steady supply. (UMN Extension; University of Maryland Extension)

plantings.plantings_note_seasoned: Spring window runs from workable soil (~40°F) until heat and lengthening days push plants to bolt; the colder zones start later as soils warm slowly.

plantings.label: fall

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall sowing is the easier, higher-quality crop in the North. UMN direct-seeds fall radish from about August 1 into early September, sizing roots in cooling weather before hard freeze. Garden radish matures in 3 to 5 weeks, so a sowing 4 to 6 weeks before the first fall frost finishes before the ground freezes; the stored offset of -45 days sits inside that window and runs earlier in the colder zones as frost advances. Daikon and other winter types are sown at the early edge of this window because they need 50 to 60 days. (UMN Extension)
direct_sow.design_note_seasoned: Fall sow anchored to first_frost - 45 days (radish 3-5 wk maturity + buffer); earlier edge applies in the colder zones as first frost advances.

plantings.plantings_note_seasoned: Fall window is the marquee radish season in the North: cooler days mean milder, crisper roots and far less bolting than spring.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the cold-winter North, grow radishes in two waves around the hot middle of summer. Plant the first seeds in spring as soon as the soil is soft and not frozen, usually around mid to late April, and keep sowing a few more every week or so. Stop in the heat of summer, because radishes turn bitter and go to flower (bolt) when it is hot. Start again in late summer for a fall crop, which is usually the best-tasting one. Radishes are fast, often ready in just 3 to 5 weeks, so you get several rounds. Plant in full sun in loose soil, keep it evenly moist so the roots do not crack, and pull them as soon as they size up so they do not get woody.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Northern-tier radish runs two sowings around a summer that is too hot for quality. The spring window opens at workable, ~40 °F soil (UMN: roughly mid-to-late April, earlier in zone 7, later in zone 3) and closes as heat and long days drive bolting; sow every 7 to 10 days through it. Skip high summer, then reopen in late summer (UMN: about August 1 into early September) for the higher-quality fall crop, which finishes before hard freeze. Garden types mature in 3 to 5 weeks; sow daikon and winter types at the early edge of the fall window for their 50-to-60-day needs. Keep moisture even to prevent cracking and pull promptly to avoid pithiness.

UGA's Georgia calendar plants radish in January and February; Clemson gives February for the Central zone and January 1 to March 1 for the Coastal zone. Radish tolerates frost and germinates in 3 to 7 days, so it goes in ahead of the last frost; sow every 7 to 10 days until daytime heat (and lengthening days) start to push bolting. (UGA Extension; Clemson HGIC)

UGA plants fall radish in August and September; Clemson gives September 1 to October 25 for the Central zone and September 1 to November 1 for the Coastal zone, where mild winters let radish run nearly until the new year. Sow every 7 to 10 days through the window; garden types finish in 3 to 5 weeks, so the latest Coastal sowings still mature before any hard freeze. (UGA Extension; Clemson HGIC)

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast and along the Gulf, radishes grow in the cooler parts of the year, not the hot, humid summer. Plant in late winter and early spring (often January and February) and keep sowing every week or so until it turns hot. Take a break in summer, when radishes bolt and turn sharp. Plant again from late summer through fall, which is the longest and best window here, especially near the coast where mild winters let you keep going almost to the new year. Radishes are fast (about 3 to 5 weeks), so plant a little at a time. Give them full sun, keep the soil evenly moist, and pull them as soon as they are ready.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: Southeastern and Gulf radish is a two-window cool-season crop. UGA sows radish in January-February and again August-September; Clemson gives Central February and September 1 to October 25, and Coastal January 1 to March 1 and September 1 to November 1. Spring closes early as heat and humidity build; fall through early winter is the marquee window, and zone-9 coastal sites run it nearly continuously from September into late winter. Sow every 7 to 10 days; keep moisture even in sandy coastal soils to prevent cracking, and pull promptly because heat-stressed roots turn pithy and pungent fast.
