crops.description_seasoned: Radish (Raphanus sativus) is a fast cool-season root crop in the cabbage family (Brassicaceae), grown for its crisp, peppery root. It is one of the quickest vegetables in the garden: small round and oval garden types size up in roughly 22 to 30 days from sowing, while the large Asian and winter types (daikon) take longer, around 50 to 60 days. Radishes are direct-sown, germinate fast (often in 3 to 7 days, far quicker than carrots), and grow best in loose, well-drained, slightly acidic soil at cool temperatures, roughly 50 to 65 °F. Quality is set by speed: radishes that grow quickly and without stress stay mild, crisp, and tender, while heat, crowding, or uneven moisture turn them woody, pithy, cracked, and sharply hot. As days lengthen and temperatures rise in late spring, radishes bolt, sending up a flower stalk and turning strong-flavored, so the crop is grown in the cool windows on either side of summer. They tolerate cool weather and light frost but are not a frost-sweetened storage crop the way carrots are. The planting season inverts by climate: spring and fall where summers are warm, and fall through early spring where summers are hot.
crops.description_beginner: Radishes are a fast cool-weather root vegetable in the cabbage family. The part you eat is the crisp, peppery root. They are one of the quickest crops you can grow: the small round kinds are ready in about 22 to 30 days, while the big Asian or winter kinds (daikon) take longer. Plant the seeds right where they will grow, and they sprout fast, often in just 3 to 7 days. Radishes like loose, well-drained soil and cool weather, around 50 to 65 °F. The trick is to grow them fast and steadily: radishes that grow quickly stay mild and crunchy, while heat, crowding, or uneven watering make them tough, hollow, cracked, and very hot-tasting. When the weather warms up and days get longer in late spring, radishes bolt, meaning they send up a flower stalk and turn strong and woody, so they are grown in the cool parts of the year. They handle cool weather and a light frost, but unlike carrots they do not get sweeter after frost. When you plant depends on your climate: spring and fall where summers are warm, and fall through early spring where summers are hot.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Radishes are ready fast and over-mature even faster, so check by size and on time rather than by a fixed date. Small round garden types are usually ready about 22 to 30 days from sowing, when the root is roughly 1 inch across at the shoulder; the shoulders often push up out of the soil, so you can see the width. Pull a test radish to judge. Do not leave mature radishes in the ground: held too long, or in warm weather, they turn pithy, woody, and sharply hot, and can crack. Round red types are best pulled before they exceed about an inch, white types before about three-quarters of an inch. Long daikon and winter types take longer, around 50 to 60 days; lift them with a fork to avoid snapping the long root.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Radishes are ready quickly and then go downhill fast, so check by size and pull them on time. The small round kinds are usually ready about 22 to 30 days after planting, when the radish is about an inch across. The tops of the radishes often poke up out of the soil, so you can see how big they are; pull one to check. Do not leave ready radishes sitting in the ground, especially in warm weather, or they turn hollow, woody, and very hot, and may crack. Pull round red radishes before they get bigger than about an inch, and white ones a little smaller. The long daikon kinds take longer, around 50 to 60 days; loosen the soil with a fork before pulling so the long root does not snap.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Radishes reward a loose, fine seedbed, though they are far more forgiving than carrots. Loosen the soil at least 6 inches deep for small garden types, and a foot or more for long daikon and winter types, removing stones and clods so the root can swell quickly and evenly. A loose sandy loam grows the cleanest radishes; heavy clay and compacted ground give small or misshapen roots and are best improved with compost or worked into raised beds. Avoid fresh manure and heavy nitrogen before planting, since excess nitrogen drives leafy tops and can cause the roots to branch while the radish stays small. Rake the surface smooth and fine for good seed-to-soil contact, and aim for a slightly acidic to neutral pH, roughly 6.0 to 6.8.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Radishes like loose, crumbly soil, but they are much more forgiving than carrots. Loosen the soil about 6 inches deep for the small round kinds, and a foot or more for long daikon types, pulling out rocks and hard clumps so the radish can swell fast and evenly. Loose, sandy soil grows the cleanest radishes; heavy clay grows small, twisted ones, so mix in compost or use a raised bed. Do not add fresh manure or lots of high-nitrogen fertilizer before planting, since too much grows big leafy tops and can make the roots branch. Rake the top smooth so the little seeds sit snug against the soil, and aim for a soil pH around 6.0 to 6.8, which is slightly acidic.

heat_threshold_temp_f.basis_seasoned: Air-temperature ceiling for radish root quality. Clemson gives 50 to 65 °F as the optimum growing range and notes that high temperatures make radishes crack, turn pithy, and develop a strong, hot flavor, while warming late-spring temperatures drive bolting. Sustained air above roughly 70 °F degrades quality and pushes the crop toward bolting rather than killing the plant; germination retains its own soil-temperature window (radish seed germinates from about 45 to 85 °F).

crops.name: Potato

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Potatoes want loose, well-drained soil that the growing tubers can swell into easily. Light, sandy or loamy soil with plenty of compost works best. Heavy, soggy clay is the main thing to avoid: it holds water and rots the seed pieces and tubers, and it makes the potatoes come out knobby. If your soil is heavy clay, a raised bed or a deep container of loose mix is the easy fix. Keep the soil on the acidic side (pH about 5.0 to 6.0), which also helps prevent scab, the rough corky patches on the skin. Do not add fresh manure, because it makes scab worse.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Potatoes need loose, friable, well-drained soil so the developing tubers can expand without resistance and the seed pieces do not rot. A light sandy loam or loam worked deep and amended with compost gives the best yields and the cleanest skin; cold, wet, heavy clay rots seed pieces, restricts tuber growth, and produces knobby, misshapen potatoes, and is best improved with organic matter or replaced with a raised bed. Keep the soil acidic, roughly pH 5.0 to 6.0, which suppresses common scab. Avoid fresh manure and excess nitrogen: manure encourages scab, and too much nitrogen drives leafy top growth at the expense of tubers. Steady, even moisture in well-drained soil is the goal, never waterlogged ground.

ph.note_beginner: Soil pH measures how acidic or alkaline your soil is, on a scale from 1 to 14 where 7 is neutral. Potatoes like it on the acidic side, about 5.0 to 6.0, which is lower (more acidic) than most vegetables. There is a good reason: keeping the soil acidic helps prevent scab, the rough corky patches that form on the potato skin. Scab gets worse when the soil is less acidic and dry, so if scab is a problem, aim toward the low end (around 5.0 to 5.3) and keep the soil evenly moist while the tubers are forming. A cheap soil test from your local extension office tells you your number.
ph.note_seasoned: Potatoes grow best in acidic soil, roughly pH 5.0 to 6.0, lower than most garden vegetables. The acidity is deliberate disease management: common scab (Streptomyces scabies) is suppressed in acidic soil and worsens as pH rises above about 5.5, especially in dry soil. Where scab is a recurring problem, hold the pH between about 5.0 and 5.3 and keep the soil evenly moist for the 4 to 9 weeks after planting when tubers are forming. Potatoes tolerate a wider band (down to about 4.8 and up to 6.5), and they will grow at neutral pH, but scab pressure climbs with pH, so do not lime a potato bed. A soil test removes the guesswork before planting.

fertilizer.timing: Work a balanced fertilizer into the row at planting; side-dress once about 4 weeks after planting as the plants establish.
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Potatoes are moderate feeders. Work a balanced fertilizer such as 10-10-10 into the row at planting (UGA suggests about 1.5 pounds per 100 square feet), then side-dress lightly about 4 weeks later as the tops fill in and again as the vines spread. Favor balanced feeding over heavy nitrogen: excess nitrogen grows lush vines and delays tuber formation, and fresh manure encourages scab, so use only well-finished compost. Adequate potassium supports tuber quality.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Potatoes need a moderate amount of food. Mix a balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 into the row when you plant, then feed lightly again about a month later as the plants grow. Do not pile on high-nitrogen fertilizer or fresh manure: too much nitrogen grows big leafy tops but fewer potatoes, and manure makes scab worse. Compost mixed into the bed is the safe way to enrich the soil.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: Potatoes are moderate feeders that want balanced nutrition with good potassium and only modest nitrogen. A balanced blend such as 10-10-10 worked into the row at planting covers most home soils. Too much nitrogen drives vines instead of tubers, and fresh manure encourages scab, so lean on compost and a balanced fertilizer rather than a high-nitrogen feed.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: The three numbers on a fertilizer bag are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium (N-P-K). Potatoes do best with a balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10, not a high-nitrogen one. Too much of the first number grows leaves instead of potatoes, and fresh manure brings on scab, so use compost and a balanced feed.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: Work about 1.5 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet into the row at planting (UGA), and side-dress a similar light amount about 4 weeks later and again as the vines spread. Keep nitrogen modest; excess nitrogen delays tuberization and grows vines at the expense of tubers.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Mix in about 1.5 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet when you plant, then feed lightly again about a month later. Go easy: more fertilizer does not mean more potatoes, and too much nitrogen just grows leaves.

companions.note_beginner: Potatoes are easygoing with most neighbors. Beans and peas are a classic match because they add nitrogen to the soil, and bush beans are said to help keep the Colorado potato beetle down. The plants to keep well away are potato's nightshade relatives, tomato, pepper, and eggplant, because they share the same diseases, especially late blight, and the same soil pests. Do not trust every companion chart online; many of their claims have never been tested.
companions.note_seasoned: Potatoes mix easily into the garden. The best-grounded pairings are with legumes (beans, peas), which fix nitrogen and are traditionally credited with deterring the Colorado potato beetle. The clearest avoids are potato's own family, the nightshades: tomato, pepper, and eggplant share late blight and other soilborne diseases and pests, so keep them apart and rotate among them on a multi-year cycle. Most other companion-chart claims for potato are folklore; treat them with healthy skepticism, since university reviews find little evidence behind most of them.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Bush beans
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Beans are legumes that pull nitrogen from the air and leave some in the soil, and many gardeners plant bush beans near potatoes to help fend off the Colorado potato beetle. It is a popular, sensible pairing, though the pest-deterrent part is traditional rather than proven.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Bean-and-potato is a long-standing reciprocal interplant: the legume fixes nitrogen, and bush beans are widely said to repel Colorado potato beetle while potatoes are said to repel the Mexican bean beetle. The nitrogen benefit is sound; the mutual pest-repellence is folk-level, not measured in a controlled potato trial. Near-universal, undisputed tradition with a partly sound mechanism.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Beans and potatoes are a classic reciprocal pairing. As legumes, beans fix nitrogen and undemanding bush beans share a bed without competing hard, and tradition holds that beans deter Colorado potato beetle while potatoes deter Mexican bean beetle. The nitrogen contribution is real; treat the mutual pest-repellence as traditional rather than proven.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Cabbage-family greens
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Leafy brassicas like cabbage, kale, and lettuce-style greens grow in the same cool season as potatoes and use the bed without fighting for the same below-ground space, a handy way to fit more into a spring garden.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Cool-season co-cropping rationale: brassica greens share potato's cool-season window and root at a different depth, an efficient space/timing interplant rather than a measured pest or yield effect. Extension-aligned in principle, not a studied potato-specific pairing.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Cool-season leafy crops (cabbage-family greens, lettuce) overlap potato's spring window and root shallowly, so they share the bed efficiently while the potato builds tubers below. This is a space-and-timing interplant, not a measured pest benefit, but it is a reliable way to use a spring bed.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Horseradish
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: An old tradition is to plant horseradish at the corner of the potato patch, where some gardeners believe it helps keep the potatoes healthier. It spreads aggressively, so keep it contained or in its own spot.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: A long-standing folk pairing (horseradish at the corners of the potato patch, reputed to improve potato vigor and resistance). No controlled evidence; horseradish is also invasively spreading, so the practical advice is to contain it. Recorded as tradition for growers who follow it.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Planting horseradish at the edge of the potato patch is traditional lore said to improve potato health. There is no controlled evidence for it, and horseradish spreads aggressively, so contain it. Recorded for growers who keep the tradition, not as a proven tactic.

good_seasoned.name: Bush beans
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Legume that fixes nitrogen and shares the bed without heavy competition; tradition also credits bush beans with deterring Colorado potato beetle (and potatoes with deterring Mexican bean beetle). Nitrogen benefit real, mutual pest-repellence traditional.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Reciprocal legume interplant: nitrogen fixation is the sound mechanism; the mutual beetle-repellence is folk tradition, not a controlled potato trial.

good_seasoned.name: Cabbage-family greens and lettuce
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Cool-season, shallow-rooted greens overlap potato's spring window and use the surface layer while the potato builds tubers below, an efficient space-and-timing interplant rather than a tested pest pairing.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Complementary cool-season timing and root depth; a space/soil-use rationale, not a measured potato-specific effect.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Tomatoes
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Tomatoes are potato's close cousin (both nightshades) and catch the same diseases, especially late blight, which can wipe out both. Keep them well apart, and do not plant potatoes where tomatoes, peppers, or eggplant grew last year.

provenance.label: research_backed
provenance.reason: Potato and tomato are both Solanaceae and share Phytophthora infestans (late blight), early blight, and soilborne pests; late blight readily moves between them. The shared-disease risk is well documented by extension. research_backed/high.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Tomatoes and potatoes are both Solanaceae and share their worst diseases, including late blight (Phytophthora infestans) and early blight, plus soilborne pests. Grown together they form a disease bridge that can destroy both crops, so keep them apart and rotate so potatoes never follow tomato, pepper, or eggplant.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Peppers and eggplant
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Peppers and eggplant are also nightshades, like potatoes, so they share the same soil diseases and pests. Grow them in a different part of the garden and rotate where each goes each year.

provenance.label: research_backed
provenance.reason: Peppers and eggplant are Solanaceae and share potato's soilborne disease and pest spectrum (Verticillium, early blight, flea beetles); co-planting and short rotations concentrate that pressure. Extension rotation guidance is explicit. research_backed/high.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Peppers and eggplant are nightshade relatives that share potato's soilborne diseases (Verticillium, early blight) and pests (flea beetles). Clustering the family or following one with another sustains that pressure, which is why extension guidance rotates potatoes well away from all Solanaceae.

bad_seasoned.name: Tomatoes and other nightshades
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Tomato, pepper, and eggplant are all Solanaceae and share potato's key diseases, above all late blight, and its soil pests. Keep them apart and rotate so potatoes never follow another nightshade; the shared late-blight risk is the best-documented reason to separate them.

provenance.label: research_backed
provenance.reason: Shared Solanaceae diseases (late blight, early blight, Verticillium) and pests are well documented; late blight moves between potato and tomato. The rotation-away rule is standard extension guidance.

pests.name: Colorado potato beetle
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Ragged, chewed foliage that can be stripped to the stems in a bad outbreak. Look for oval, 3/8-inch adults with yellow and black lengthwise stripes, plump pink-to-salmon larvae with black heads and two rows of dark spots, and bright yellowish-orange egg clusters on the undersides of leaves. The last-stage larvae do most of the damage. Potatoes tolerate up to about 30 percent defoliation before flowering but only about 10 percent once tubers are sizing.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Leaves chewed ragged, sometimes stripped to the stems. The beetles are oval, about 3/8 inch, with yellow and black stripes; the larvae are fat, pinkish-orange grubs with black heads; and the eggs are clusters of bright orange ovals on the undersides of leaves. The big grubs do most of the eating, and damage hurts most once the potatoes are forming underneath.
pests.cause_seasoned: Larvae and adults of the Colorado potato beetle (Leptinotarsa decemlineata), which overwinter 5 to 10 inches deep in soil in and around last year's potatoes and emerge in spring to feed and lay eggs. Each female lays up to 350 eggs, and there is often a second generation by midsummer in central and southern areas. It also attacks eggplant and other nightshades.
pests.cause_beginner: The Colorado potato beetle, a striped beetle that spends winter in the soil near old potato patches and comes out in spring to feed and lay eggs. Each female lays hundreds of eggs and there can be two rounds in a summer, so numbers build fast. It also goes after eggplant and other nightshades.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Handpicking is effective in a home garden: knock adults and larvae into a pail of soapy water and crush the orange egg clusters on the leaf undersides; check every few days. There is no quick spray cure, and the beetle has developed resistance to many insecticides, so persistence with handpicking and removal does most of the work.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick the beetles, grubs, and orange egg clusters off by hand and drop them in soapy water; check the plants every couple of days. There is no easy spray fix, because the beetles have grown resistant to many of them, so hand-removal is the most reliable home control.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Rotate potatoes well away from last year's bed, since the overwintered adults emerge where potatoes grew before. Floating row cover laid over the bed at emergence keeps the beetles off until you need to remove it for the developing plants, and a thick straw mulch can slow the adults walking in. Crush early egg clusters before they hatch to break the first generation.
pests.prevention_beginner: Move potatoes to a new spot each year, away from where they (or eggplant) grew last year, because the beetles wake up right there in spring. A row cover over the bed early keeps them off, straw mulch slows them down, and crushing the first egg clusters stops a generation before it starts.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny dark beetles that jump when disturbed and chew many small round shot-holes in the leaves. Heavy early feeding on young plants stunts growth; the larvae feed on roots and can leave small tracks or pits on tubers. Established, vigorous plants usually outgrow light feeding.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Lots of tiny holes in the leaves, as if peppered with shot, made by little dark beetles that hop away when you come near. Young plants are hurt most; big healthy plants shrug it off. The grubs can also nibble the tubers.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several species of small flea beetles, including the tuber flea beetle, that overwinter nearby and move onto young potato foliage in spring. They are worst on small, slow plants and in warm, dry weather.
pests.cause_beginner: Small beetles called flea beetles that spend winter nearby and jump onto young potato plants in spring. They do the most harm to little plants and in warm, dry spells.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Healthy, well-watered plants usually outgrow flea beetle damage. Floating row cover protects young plants during the vulnerable early weeks; remove it once the plants are established. Clearing weeds and old crop debris reduces the shelter they overwinter in.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Keep young plants growing strong with steady water and they usually outgrow the damage. A row cover protects seedlings early on, and clearing weeds and old plant debris takes away their winter hiding spots.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Rotate away from last year's nightshade beds, keep the area weed-free, and protect young plants with row cover until they are large enough to tolerate feeding. Vigorous, evenly watered plants are far more tolerant than stressed ones.
pests.prevention_beginner: Move the potatoes to a new spot, pull weeds, and cover the young plants until they are big and strong. Plants that are well fed and watered handle flea beetles much better than struggling ones.

pests.name: Aphids and the viruses they spread
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small soft-bodied insects, often green or pink, clustered on growing tips and leaf undersides, sometimes with sticky honeydew and sooty mold. The bigger problem is not their feeding but the viruses they transmit (such as potato virus Y and leafroll), which cause mottled, curled, or rolled leaves and reduce yield; virus-infected plants do not recover.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny soft insects, usually green or pink, crowded on the new growth and the undersides of leaves, sometimes leaving a sticky film. Their feeding is minor, but they can pass on plant viruses that make the leaves mottle, curl, or roll and cut your harvest. A plant that catches a virus will not get better.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several aphid species colonize potato foliage, and as they move plant to plant they spread potato viruses. Virus pressure, not the feeding itself, is the main reason to manage them, and it is the reason gardeners are advised to start from certified disease-free seed potatoes rather than saved tubers.
pests.cause_beginner: Aphids are small sap-sucking insects, and as they move from plant to plant they carry potato viruses. The viruses, more than the bugs, are the real concern, which is why it is best to plant certified disease-free seed potatoes instead of saving your own.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Start with certified seed potatoes to keep virus out of the patch. Tolerate light aphid numbers, since beneficial insects (lady beetles, lacewings, parasitic wasps) often control them; a strong spray of water or insecticidal soap knocks down heavy colonies. Remove and destroy any plant showing clear virus symptoms.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Plant certified disease-free seed potatoes so the patch starts clean. A little aphid activity is fine, because ladybugs and other helpers usually keep them in check; for heavy clusters, spray them off with water or use insecticidal soap. Pull and throw away any plant that clearly has a virus.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Use certified seed potatoes, encourage beneficial insects by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays, control nearby weeds that host aphids and virus, and rogue out virus-symptomatic plants promptly so they do not seed an outbreak.
pests.prevention_beginner: Buy certified seed potatoes, avoid harsh sprays that kill the helpful bugs, keep weeds down, and pull out any virus-looking plant right away so it does not spread.

pests.name: Wireworms
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Slender, shiny, yellow-brown, hard-bodied larvae in the soil that bore narrow holes straight into the tubers, leaving clean round tunnels that downgrade quality and invite rot in storage. There are no useful aboveground symptoms; the damage is found at harvest.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Hard, shiny, tan-colored worms in the soil that drill narrow holes into the potatoes. You usually do not notice anything above ground; you find the little tunnels when you dig the crop. Tunneled potatoes do not store well.
pests.cause_seasoned: The larvae of click beetles, which live in the soil for several years and are most common in ground recently in sod or grass. They feed on many roots and tubers and are hard to detect until harvest.
pests.cause_beginner: The larvae of click beetles. They live in the soil for years and are most common in beds that were lawn or grass not long ago. You tend to find them only when you dig.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no rescue for tunneled tubers; trim damaged areas and use them first rather than storing them. Harvest promptly once the crop matures rather than leaving tubers in infested soil, where damage accumulates.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot fix potatoes that are already tunneled, so cut out the bad parts and eat those first instead of storing them. Dig the crop on time rather than leaving it in the ground, where the worms keep boring.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid planting potatoes in ground that was recently lawn or pasture, since wireworm numbers are highest there. Rotate, keep the soil well worked, and harvest on time. Where wireworm history is bad, grow elsewhere or in clean raised-bed soil.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not plant potatoes in a bed that was grass or lawn in the last year or two, where wireworms are worst. Rotate your crops, work the soil, and dig on time. If wireworms keep ruining a bed, use a raised bed with clean soil.

diseases.name: Late blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark, water-soaked spots that appear on leaves and stems and enlarge rapidly, often with a downy white mold on the leaf undersides in cool, wet weather. The foliage can collapse within days, and the disease moves into the tubers, which develop a firm, reddish-brown, dry, corky rot beneath the skin. This is the disease behind the Irish potato famine and the most serious threat to a potato crop.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Dark, wet-looking spots on the leaves and stems that spread fast, with a fuzzy white mold underneath in cool, damp weather. The plants can collapse in just a few days, and the rot moves down into the potatoes, leaving firm reddish-brown corky patches inside. This is the famous, most dangerous potato disease, the one behind the Irish famine.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The water mold Phytophthora infestans, favored by cool, wet, humid weather and spread on wind and splashing water. It infects both potato and tomato, so a nearby infected tomato is a real risk, and it survives between seasons in infected tubers and cull piles.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus-like organism (Phytophthora infestans) that thrives in cool, wet, humid weather and blows in on the wind. It attacks tomatoes too, so an infected tomato nearby is a danger, and it survives in leftover infected potatoes.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no home cure once a plant is badly infected. Remove and destroy infected plants quickly to slow spread, and do not compost them. In wet seasons a copper-based fungicide applied early and repeated can suppress it, but the real defenses are cultural. Destroy all infected tubers so they cannot carry it over.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot cure a badly infected plant, so pull and destroy infected plants fast (do not compost them) to slow it down. In a wet year a copper fungicide started early can help, but mostly it is about prevention. Throw away every infected potato so it does not bring the disease back next year.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Start with certified disease-free seed, choose resistant varieties (such as Kennebec or Sebago), keep foliage dry by watering at the base in the morning, space for airflow, and never plant near tomatoes. Remove volunteer potatoes and cull piles that harbor the pathogen, and destroy any infected vines before harvest so spores do not reach the tubers.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant certified disease-free seed potatoes and a resistant variety like Kennebec, water at the soil in the morning so the leaves stay dry, give plants room for air to move, and keep them away from tomatoes. Clean up any leftover or volunteer potatoes, and cut and remove infected vines before you dig so the disease does not reach the potatoes.

diseases.name: Early blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small dark brown to black lesions on the older, lower leaves, each with concentric rings that give a target or bull's-eye look, often ringed by a yellow halo. Spots multiply and merge and the lower canopy dies back; severe infection causes defoliation and brown, corky, dry spots on the tubers. Stressed and aging plants are hit hardest.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Dark spots with rings inside them, like a little target or bull's-eye, on the older lower leaves, often with a yellow edge. The spots spread and the lower leaves die off; in a bad case the plant loses its leaves and the potatoes get brown corky patches. Tired, stressed plants get it worst.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Alternaria solani, which survives on crop debris and in the soil and spreads in warm, humid weather with wet foliage. It is more of a slow, stress-related decline than the explosive collapse of late blight.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus (Alternaria solani) that lives on old plant debris and in the soil and spreads in warm, damp weather. It comes on gradually, especially on stressed plants, rather than wiping a plant out overnight like late blight.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove badly spotted lower leaves, keep plants vigorous with steady water and feeding (stress worsens it), and water at the base in the morning. A copper or other labeled fungicide can slow spread in a wet season if started early, but cultural care carries most of the load.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick off the worst spotted lower leaves, keep the plants healthy with even water and feeding, and water at the soil so the leaves dry fast. A copper fungicide can help if you start early in a wet spell, but keeping plants strong and the leaves dry does most of the work.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate potatoes and other nightshades out of the bed for several years, start with clean seed and resistant varieties, clear crop debris, space and hill for airflow, avoid overhead watering, and keep plants well nourished so they resist the slow decline.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Do not grow potatoes (or tomatoes and peppers) in the same spot for a few years, use clean seed and a resistant variety, clear away old plant debris, give plants room, water at the base, and keep them well fed so they stay strong.

diseases.name: Common scab
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Rough, brown, corky scabs or pits on the tuber skin that can merge into larger patches; sometimes raised, sometimes sunken. The leaves and stems are not affected, so it is found only at harvest. It is a skin-quality problem rather than a rot, and the potatoes are fine to eat after peeling, but it downgrades appearance and storage.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Rough, brown, corky patches or pits on the potato skin, sometimes spreading into larger areas. The leaves look fine, so you only see it when you dig the potatoes. It does not rot them, it just roughens the skin, and they are fine to eat once peeled, but they do not store or sell as well.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The soil bacterium Streptomyces scabies, which is favored by less-acidic soil (pH above about 5.5), dry conditions while tubers are forming, and fresh manure. It persists for years in the soil and on many hosts, so rotation alone does not eliminate it.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soil germ (Streptomyces scabies) that gets worse when the soil is not acidic enough (above about pH 5.5), when it is dry while the potatoes are forming, and when fresh manure is used. It lives in the soil for years, so just rotating crops does not get rid of it.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no rescue once tubers are scabbed; the potatoes are still edible after peeling. Management is preventive: it is controlled by soil conditions, not a spray.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot fix scabbed potatoes, but they are fine to eat after peeling. There is no spray for it; you prevent it by managing the soil instead.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Keep soil acidic, around pH 5.0 to 5.3 where scab is a problem, and never lime a potato bed. Keep the soil evenly moist for the 4 to 9 weeks after planting when tubers form, avoid fresh manure, and grow scab-resistant varieties (such as Russet Burbank or Superior) where the disease recurs. Rotate on a 3 to 4 year cycle.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Keep the soil acidic (about pH 5.0 to 5.3 if scab is a problem) and never add lime to a potato bed. Keep the soil evenly moist while the potatoes are forming, skip fresh manure, plant a scab-resistant variety if it keeps happening, and rotate the bed every few years.

diseases.name: Blackleg and bacterial soft rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Blackleg shows as an inky-black, slimy rot at the base of the stem with yellowed, wilting, stunted tops, often from infected seed; bacterial soft rot turns tubers into a soft, wet, foul-smelling mush, in the ground or in storage, and can rot a tuber completely within days. The bacteria enter through wounds and spread in wet conditions.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Blackleg makes the bottom of the stem turn black and slimy while the top of the plant yellows, wilts, and stays small, usually from a bad seed piece. Soft rot turns the potatoes themselves into a soft, wet, smelly mush, in the ground or in storage. Both get into the potato through cuts and bruises and spread in wet conditions.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Bacteria in the Pectobacterium and related groups, which are favored by wet soil, poor drainage, and warm conditions, and which spread on cutting knives and through wounds. They often arrive on infected or poorly cured seed pieces and are worst in waterlogged ground and in bruised, wet-stored tubers.
diseases.cause_beginner: Bacteria that thrive in wet, poorly drained, warm soil and spread through cuts. They often come in on a bad seed piece, and they are worst when the soil is waterlogged or when bruised potatoes are stored damp.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure for an infected plant or tuber; remove and discard affected plants and do not store blemished or soft potatoes. Management is preventive: handle tubers gently and keep them dry.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure once a plant or potato is infected, so pull out affected plants and never store soft or damaged potatoes. The fix is prevention: be gentle with the tubers and keep them dry.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant certified, well-cured seed pieces (or whole small seed potatoes) in warm, well-drained soil, let cut seed suberize before planting, avoid overwatering and waterlogged beds, harvest in dry conditions, cure the crop, and avoid bruising. Do not store damaged or wet tubers.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Use certified, well-cured seed pieces and plant them in warm, well-drained soil, not cold mud. Let cut seed pieces heal before planting, do not overwater, dig in dry weather, and handle the potatoes gently. Never store bruised or wet potatoes.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Potatoes want steady, even moisture, especially from the time tubers begin forming (around flowering) through bulking. Aim for about 1 inch of water per week including rain, delivered in deeper, less frequent soakings. Even moisture is what produces smooth, well-shaped tubers; a dry-then-wet swing causes knobby growth, growth cracks, and hollow heart, and it worsens scab.
watering.frequency_beginner: Keep the soil evenly damp, especially once the plants flower and the potatoes start forming underneath. Give about 1 inch of water a week, counting rain, in fewer but deeper waterings. Steady water makes smooth potatoes; letting the soil go dry and then soaking it makes them knobby and cracked and brings on more scab.
watering.amount_seasoned: About 1 inch per week including rainfall, increased in heat or sandy soil. The critical window is from tuber initiation through bulking; do not let the bed dry out then. Taper off as the vines yellow and die so the crop can cure and the skins set before harvest.
watering.amount_beginner: About 1 inch of water a week, counting rain, and a bit more in hot or sandy conditions. Do not let the bed dry out while the potatoes are sizing up. Ease off on water once the tops start to yellow and die back, so the skins toughen before you dig.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base with a soaker hose or drip line to keep foliage dry, since wet leaves favor late and early blight. Mulch helps hold even moisture and keeps the soil cooler over the developing tubers.
watering.method_beginner: Water at the soil with a soaker hose or drip line instead of overhead, because wet leaves bring on blight. A layer of mulch helps keep the moisture steady and the soil cooler around the potatoes.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Constantly saturated soil rots seed pieces and tubers and drives soft rot and blackleg; yellowing, wilting from the base, a sour waterlogged bed, and soft tubers are signs to back off and improve drainage.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If the soil stays soaking wet, the seed pieces and potatoes rot. Watch for yellowing, wilting from the bottom, a sour-smelling soggy bed, and soft potatoes; if you see these, water less and fix the drainage.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting in the heat of the day, dull foliage, and slow growth signal too little water; the sharper risk is an irregular dry-then-soaked cycle during tuber sizing, which causes knobs, growth cracks, and hollow heart.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Droopy leaves in the afternoon, dull color, and slow growth mean the plants are thirsty. The bigger problem is letting the soil go dry and then flooding it while the potatoes are sizing, which makes them knobby and cracked.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Keep water off the foliage and even at the root zone. Wet leaves favor blight, while uneven soil moisture during tuber formation drives knobby, cracked, and hollow tubers, so steady base watering plus mulch is the goal.
watering.method_note_beginner: Water at the soil, not over the leaves, and keep it steady. Wet leaves bring disease, and on-again off-again watering while the potatoes form makes them lumpy and cracked, so even moisture and a little mulch help a lot.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The make-or-break window is tuber initiation through bulking, from about flowering onward: even moisture here sets tuber number, size, and shape and limits scab. Ease watering as the vines die back so skins set for storage.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The most important time to keep the soil evenly moist is from flowering on, while the potatoes are forming and sizing up, because that decides how many, how big, and how smooth they are. Then water less as the tops die down so the skins toughen for storage.

start_method.hardening_off_beginner: You do not harden off potatoes. They are grown from seed pieces planted straight into the ground, not from indoor-raised seedlings, so there is no transplant step.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Plant potatoes from certified seed potatoes, not grocery-store tubers (which may carry disease or be sprout-inhibited) and not true seed. Cut larger seed potatoes into blocky pieces of about 1.5 to 2 ounces, each with at least one or two eyes, and let the cut surfaces heal (suberize) for a few days in a warm, humid spot before planting; small egg-sized tubers can be planted whole. Plant pieces cut-side down about 3 to 5 inches deep in rows 30 to 36 inches apart, spacing the pieces 10 to 12 inches apart, once the soil reaches about 50°F. There is no indoor-start or hardening-off step.
start_method.notes_beginner: Grow potatoes from seed potatoes, which are small whole potatoes or cut pieces, bought as certified disease-free stock (not from the grocery store, and not from packets of seed). Cut bigger ones into chunky pieces about the size of an egg, each with one or two eyes (the little dimples that sprout), and let the cut sides dry and heal for a few days before planting. Plant the pieces cut-side down about 3 to 5 inches deep, 10 to 12 inches apart, in rows about 3 feet apart, once the soil has warmed to about 50°F. There is nothing to start indoors and nothing to harden off.

container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: Depth and volume matter more than width: the container must give room to hill soil over the developing tubers. Use a grow bag or tub of at least 10 gallons (15 or more is better) and at least 14 inches deep, filling it part way at planting and adding soil as the plants grow. Fabric grow bags drain and aerate well and make harvest easy.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Use a deep, roomy container so you can mound soil up over the plants as they grow. A grow bag or tub of at least 10 gallons (bigger is better) and at least 14 inches deep works well. Start with soil partway up and add more as the plants get taller. Fabric grow bags are easy and drain well.

drainage.saucer_practice_seasoned: Do not let the container stand in a saucer of water. Potatoes rot in waterlogged mix, so ensure free drainage and empty any saucer after watering.
drainage.saucer_practice_beginner: Do not let the pot sit in a tray of water. Soggy soil rots potatoes, so make sure the water drains out and empty the saucer after you water.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Use a loose, well-drained potting mix, not heavy garden soil, which packs down and stays too wet in a container.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in some compost for nutrition and a little balanced fertilizer. Keep it loose so the tubers can swell and the mix drains freely.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: container_potting_mix
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Use a light, free-draining potting mix amended with compost and a modest balanced fertilizer. Avoid heavy garden soil, which compacts and waterlogs in a container and rots tubers.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Containers dry out faster than the ground, so check daily in warm weather and keep the mix evenly moist while the potatoes are forming. Do not let it swing between bone-dry and soaked, which makes knobby potatoes.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Potted potatoes need a little regular feeding because watering washes nutrients out. Mix balanced fertilizer in at planting and feed lightly every few weeks, but do not overdo nitrogen or you will get all leaves.
container_notes.notes_beginner: Potatoes grow well in containers, which is great if your soil is heavy clay or you are short on space. Use a deep grow bag or tub with drainage holes, start with a few inches of loose mix, set the seed pieces in, and add more soil over the stems as they grow (this is container hilling). Keep the mix evenly moist and tip the bag out to harvest when the tops die back.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Potatoes are well suited to containers and a good option on heavy clay or in small spaces. Use a 10 gallon or larger grow bag or tub at least 14 inches deep with drainage holes; start with several inches of loose mix, plant the seed pieces, and add soil over the stems as they grow to mimic hilling and keep tubers covered. Keep moisture even and harvest by tipping out the bag once the foliage dies back.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry far faster than beds, and potatoes are unforgiving of moisture swings while tubers form. Check the top inch or two daily in warm weather and water to keep the mix evenly moist but never waterlogged.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Frequent watering leaches nutrients from a container, so incorporate a balanced fertilizer at planting and feed lightly every 2 to 3 weeks during active growth, keeping nitrogen modest to favor tubers over foliage.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering container can help hold the even moisture potatoes want during tuber bulking, but it must drain freely: potatoes rot in a constantly saturated reservoir, so use it carefully and never let the mix stay waterlogged, and choose a deep container so there is room to hill.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot can keep the moisture steady while the potatoes are forming, which helps, but it must not keep the soil soaking wet or the potatoes rot. Use a deep container so you still have room to mound soil over the plants.

recommended: Yukon Gold: yellow-fleshed, all-purpose early-to-mid main crop, widely adapted and a reliable first choice
Red Pontiac: red-skinned, vigorous, tolerant of heavier soils, a strong pick in the South
Kennebec: high-yielding mid-to-late white, with useful late blight tolerance
Russet Burbank: classic late russet for baking and frying, with some scab tolerance
Irish Cobbler: heirloom early white, quick to a first dig of new potatoes
varieties.note_seasoned: Choose by maturity and your climate. Early varieties (Irish Cobbler, Yukon Gold) finish fastest and suit short seasons and hot-summer regions where the crop must beat the heat; mid and late varieties (Kennebec, Russet Burbank) yield more and store better where the season is long. In the South, thin-skinned reds and whites (Red Pontiac, Yukon Gold) outperform thick russets, which size up poorly there. Where scab or late blight recurs, lean on resistant or tolerant varieties (Russet Burbank or Superior for scab; Kennebec or Sebago for late blight). Always start from certified disease-free seed potatoes.
varieties.note_beginner: Pick a variety for your area and how soon you want potatoes. Early kinds like Yukon Gold and Irish Cobbler are ready fastest and are good where summers turn hot. Later kinds like Kennebec and Russet Burbank give bigger harvests and store longer. In the South, grow thin-skinned reds and golds (Red Pontiac, Yukon Gold) rather than thick brown russets. If scab or blight is a problem in your garden, choose a resistant variety. Always buy certified disease-free seed potatoes, not grocery-store ones.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Do not plant potatoes where another nightshade (Solanaceae) grew recently: potato, tomato, pepper, or eggplant. They share soilborne diseases (late blight, early blight, Verticillium wilt) and pests that build up where the family is grown repeatedly. Avoid beds freshly amended with manure, which encourages scab. The standard guideline is a 3 to 4 year gap before potatoes or their relatives return to a bed.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Do not grow potatoes where you grew potatoes, tomatoes, peppers, or eggplant in the last few years. They are all in the same family and share the same soil diseases and pests, which pile up over time. Also avoid beds that just got fresh manure, because that brings on scab. Wait about 3 to 4 years before potatoes or their cousins go back in a bed.
good_after: Legumes such as beans and peas
Brassicas such as cabbage and broccoli
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate potatoes on a 3 to 4 year cycle, keeping them and all other nightshades out of a bed for several seasons. This breaks the buildup of late blight, early blight, scab, Verticillium, and nightshade pests. Following a legume (which adds nitrogen) or a non-host crop is ideal; following a heavily manured crop is not, because residual conditions favor scab.
rotation.note_beginner: Move your potatoes to a different spot each year and do not put them (or tomatoes, peppers, and eggplant) back in the same bed for about 3 to 4 years. This keeps diseases and pests from building up. Planting potatoes after beans or peas is great, since those add nitrogen.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Short term only. At room temperature potatoes sprout, soften, and shrivel within a couple of weeks, and light exposure greens them. Keep only what you will use soon on the counter, in the dark, and store the rest cool.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Only for a short while. Left out warm and in the light, potatoes sprout, go soft, and turn green. Keep a few days' worth in a dark cupboard and store the rest somewhere cool.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Not ideal for raw potatoes. Below about 40°F the starch converts to sugar, making them overly sweet and prone to darkening when cooked. A cool cellar or garage near 40 to 50°F is better than the refrigerator for raw storage; if you must refrigerate, let them warm at room temperature for a day or two before frying.
storage.fridge_beginner: The fridge is not the best place for raw potatoes. When they get colder than about 40°F, their starch turns to sugar and they taste sweet and brown too fast when cooked. A cool spot like a cellar or unheated garage around 40 to 50°F is better. If you do refrigerate them, let them sit out a day or two before frying.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Raw potatoes do not freeze well and turn watery and dark. Freeze only after cooking (blanched, mashed, or as prepared dishes), where they keep for several months.
storage.freezer_beginner: Do not freeze raw potatoes, which go mushy and dark. Freeze them only after cooking, like mashed or par-cooked, and they keep for several months.
storage.notes_seasoned: Cure the crop before storing: hold freshly dug potatoes in the dark at about 50 to 60°F with high humidity for about two weeks to toughen the skins and heal small wounds. Then store in the dark in a cool, humid place near 40 to 50°F with good ventilation, where a well-cured main crop keeps for months. Keep them dark at all times to prevent greening, do not wash until use, and do not store bruised, cut, or diseased tubers. New potatoes have thin skins and do not store; use them fresh.
storage.notes_beginner: Cure potatoes before storing them: keep the just-dug crop in the dark somewhere warm and humid (about 50 to 60°F) for about two weeks so the skins toughen and small nicks heal. Then move them to a cool, dark, humid spot around 40 to 50°F with some airflow, where they keep for months. Always keep them in the dark so they do not turn green, do not wash them until you use them, and never store damaged ones. New (baby) potatoes do not keep, so eat those fresh.

growth_stages.name: Sprouting and emergence
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare soil for two to four weeks, then sprouts pushing up from the buried seed pieces. Emergence is slower in cold soil and faster as it warms. A late frost can blacken the first leaves, but the plants regrow from the protected seed piece.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Nothing for a couple of weeks, then green shoots poking up from the buried seed pieces. They come up slower in cold soil. If frost nips the first leaves, do not worry, the plants grow back from the seed piece below.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep the soil evenly moist but not soggy while sprouts emerge. If a hard frost threatens after emergence, mound a little soil or mulch over the young shoots or cover them overnight.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil damp but not soaking while the shoots come up. If a hard frost is coming after they sprout, mound a little soil over them or cover them for the night.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have your potatoes sprouted? Note the emergence date to track maturity from a real start.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your potato shoots come up yet? Jot down the date.

growth_stages.name: Vegetative growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leafy stems growing quickly. This is when the plant builds the canopy that will feed the tubers, and when the first hilling is usually done as the stems reach 6 to 12 inches.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Bushy, leafy plants growing fast. This is the time for the first hilling, mounding soil up around the stems once they are about 6 to 12 inches tall.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Begin hilling: draw soil up around the stems when they reach 6 to 12 inches, leaving the top few inches exposed. Keep the bed weed-free and evenly watered, and side-dress lightly if growth is weak.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Start hilling: mound soil up around the stems once they are 6 to 12 inches tall, leaving the leafy tops sticking out. Keep weeds down and water evenly, and feed lightly if the plants look weak.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How are your potato plants growing? Have you done the first hilling?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How are your potato plants doing? Have you mounded soil up around them yet?

growth_stages.name: Tuber initiation
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Plants reaching full size and often flowering, which roughly coincides with the start of tuber formation underground. Hill again to keep the developing tubers covered and out of the light.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Big, full plants, often with flowers, which is about when the little potatoes start forming underground. Hill again to keep them covered so they do not turn green.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Hill a second time to keep tubers covered, and hold steady, even moisture now that tubers are forming, since this window sets tuber number and shape. Watch for Colorado potato beetle and remove egg clusters.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Mound up soil again to keep the potatoes covered, and keep the watering steady now that they are forming, because this is when the number and shape of your potatoes is decided. Watch for potato beetles and squash their egg clusters.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are your potatoes flowering? Have you hilled a second time?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are your potato plants flowering? Have you mounded soil up again?

growth_stages.name: Tuber bulking
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tubers sizing up underground while the tops stay green and full. You can dig a few thin-skinned new potatoes now, about 7 to 8 weeks after planting, without disturbing the rest.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The potatoes are growing bigger underground while the plants stay green and leafy. You can sneak a few small new potatoes now, about 7 to 8 weeks after planting, by digging gently at the edge.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture even and steady while tubers bulk, which is the critical period for size and quality. Keep shoulders covered. For new potatoes, dig carefully at the edge of a hill and re-cover.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the water steady while the potatoes are sizing up, which is the most important time. Keep them covered with soil. For a few new potatoes, dig gently at the side of a plant and cover it back up.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have you dug any new potatoes? How is the size?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you tried digging a few new potatoes yet?

growth_stages.name: Maturity and harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tops yellowing and dying back, the signal that the main crop is mature and the skins are setting. For storage potatoes, wait about two weeks after the vines die before digging so the skins toughen.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The tops turn yellow and die down, which means the potatoes are full grown and the skins are toughening up. For potatoes you want to store, wait about two weeks after the tops die before digging.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Ease off watering as the vines die back. Dig on a dry day, lifting carefully with a fork well outside the hill to avoid spearing tubers. Let them dry briefly, then cure in the dark before storage.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Stop watering as the tops die back. Dig on a dry day, pushing a fork in well away from the plant so you do not stab the potatoes. Let them dry off, then cure them in the dark before storing.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have you harvested your potatoes? Note the date and the yield.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you dug your potatoes yet? Write down the date and how many you got.

sprouting.text_seasoned: Plant certified seed potatoes, not grocery-store tubers: certified stock is disease-free, while store potatoes may carry late blight or scab or be treated to resist sprouting. Cut large pieces to about 1.5 to 2 ounces with one or two eyes and let them suberize a few days before planting.
sprouting.text_beginner: Use certified seed potatoes from a garden store, not ones from the grocery, which can carry disease or be treated not to sprout. Cut big ones into egg-sized chunks with an eye or two, and let the cut sides dry for a few days before planting.
sprouting.author: plant

sprouting.text_seasoned: Plant once the soil reaches about 50°F, roughly 2 to 4 weeks before the last frost; the seed underground tolerates cold, but cold, wet soil rots seed pieces, so do not rush into mud.
sprouting.text_beginner: Plant when the soil has warmed to about 50°F, about 2 to 4 weeks before your last frost. The seed underground can take the cold, but planting into cold, soggy mud rots the pieces, so wait for the soil to warm a bit.
sprouting.author: plant

vegetative.text_seasoned: Start hilling when stems reach 6 to 12 inches: draw loose soil up around them, leaving the top few inches of leaves exposed. Hilling builds the zone where tubers form and keeps them covered.
vegetative.text_beginner: Begin mounding (hilling) soil up around the plants when they are 6 to 12 inches tall, leaving the leafy tops out. This gives the potatoes room to form and keeps them covered.
vegetative.author: plant

vegetative.text_seasoned: Feed modestly: a light side-dressing as the tops fill in is plenty. Skip heavy nitrogen and fresh manure, which grow vines instead of tubers and encourage scab.
vegetative.text_beginner: Feed lightly as the plants fill in. Do not pile on high-nitrogen fertilizer or fresh manure, which grow leaves instead of potatoes and bring on scab.
vegetative.author: plant

tuber_initiation.text_seasoned: Hill again around flowering as tubers begin forming, keeping every tuber covered with soil. Exposed tubers turn green and develop bitter, toxic solanine, so covering them is both a quality and a safety step.
tuber_initiation.text_beginner: Mound up soil again around flowering, when the potatoes start forming, so none are uncovered. Potatoes left in the light turn green and form a bitter, mildly poisonous substance, so keeping them covered matters for safety too.
tuber_initiation.author: plant

tuber_initiation.text_seasoned: Scout for Colorado potato beetle now: handpick adults and larvae into soapy water and crush the orange egg clusters on leaf undersides. The beetle resists many sprays, so steady handpicking is the home grower's best tool.
tuber_initiation.text_beginner: Watch for the Colorado potato beetle: pick the striped beetles and orange grubs off into soapy water and crush their orange egg clusters under the leaves. They resist many sprays, so hand-picking is your best bet.
tuber_initiation.author: plant

bulking.text_seasoned: Keep moisture steady and even while tubers bulk, about 1 inch per week. Swings from dry to soaked now cause knobby growth, growth cracks, and hollow heart, so consistency matters more than volume.
bulking.text_beginner: Keep the watering steady while the potatoes size up, about 1 inch a week. Letting the soil go dry and then soaking it now makes the potatoes lumpy and cracked, so being even matters more than giving a lot at once.
bulking.author: plant

bulking.text_seasoned: For new potatoes, dig carefully at the edge of a hill about 7 to 8 weeks after planting and re-cover the plant; the rest keep bulking. Use new potatoes fresh, since their thin skins do not store.
bulking.text_beginner: For baby new potatoes, dig gently at the side of a plant about 7 to 8 weeks after planting, then cover it back up so the rest keep growing. Eat new potatoes fresh, because their thin skins do not store.
bulking.author: plant

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest the main crop when the tops yellow and die back. For storage, wait about two weeks after the vines die so the skins set, then dig on a dry day, lifting with a fork well outside the hill.
harvest.text_beginner: Dig the main crop when the tops turn yellow and die down. For storing, wait about two weeks after the tops die so the skins toughen, then dig on a dry day with a fork, pushing it in well away from the plant.
harvest.author: plant

harvest.text_seasoned: Cure dug potatoes in the dark at about 50 to 60°F and high humidity for roughly two weeks before storage to toughen skins and heal wounds, then store cool, dark, and humid. Keep them out of the light always to prevent greening.
harvest.text_beginner: Cure the dug potatoes in the dark somewhere around 50 to 60°F and humid for about two weeks so the skins toughen, then store them cool, dark, and humid. Always keep potatoes out of the light so they do not turn green.
harvest.author: plant

notifications.body_seasoned: Plant certified seed pieces about 2 to 4 weeks before your last frost, once the soil reaches about 50°F. Plant cut-side down 3 to 5 inches deep, 10 to 12 inches apart.
notifications.body_beginner: Plant your seed potatoes about 2 to 4 weeks before your last frost, when the soil has warmed to about 50°F. Set the pieces cut-side down, a few inches deep and about a foot apart.

notifications.title_beginner: Potatoes take a while to come up
notifications.body_seasoned: Sprouts often take 2 to 4 weeks, longer in cold soil. Keep the bed evenly moist, and if a hard frost threatens after emergence, mound soil or cover the shoots.
notifications.body_beginner: Potato shoots can take 2 to 4 weeks to appear, longer when it is cold. Keep the soil damp, and cover the shoots if a hard frost is coming.

notifications.title_beginner: Time to mound up your potatoes
notifications.body_seasoned: Once stems reach 6 to 12 inches, draw soil up around them, leaving the top few inches exposed. Hill again around flowering to keep tubers covered and prevent greening.
notifications.body_beginner: When the plants are 6 to 12 inches tall, mound soil up around them, leaving the tops out. Do it again at flowering so the potatoes stay covered and do not turn green.

notifications.body_seasoned: As tubers bulk, hold even moisture (about 1 inch per week). A dry-then-soaked cycle now causes knobby, cracked, and hollow tubers.
notifications.body_beginner: While the potatoes are sizing up, water evenly (about 1 inch a week). Letting the soil dry out and then soaking it makes the potatoes lumpy and cracked.

notifications.title_beginner: Check if your potatoes are ready
notifications.body_seasoned: When the tops yellow and die back, the crop is mature. Dig new potatoes earlier (about 7 to 8 weeks); for storage, wait about two weeks after the vines die.
notifications.body_beginner: When the tops turn yellow and die down, the potatoes are ready. You can dig small new potatoes earlier (about 7 to 8 weeks); for storing, wait about two weeks after the tops die.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost can hurt potato leaves
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Potato foliage is frost tender. A hard frost blackens the tops, though plants usually regrow from the seed piece. Mound soil over young shoots or cover the bed overnight when frost threatens.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Potato leaves are tender to frost. A hard frost can blacken the tops, but the plants usually grow back from the seed below. Mound soil over young shoots or cover the bed for the night when frost is coming.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot weather slows potato growth
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Tubers form best in cool soil, roughly 60 to 70°F, and tuber set falls off in sustained heat. Mulch to cool the soil, keep moisture even, and in hot regions time the crop to finish before peak heat.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Potatoes make tubers best in cool soil (about 60 to 70°F) and slow down in heat. Mulch to keep the soil cool, water evenly, and in hot areas plan the crop so it finishes before the worst heat.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Dry weather, keep potatoes watered
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Even moisture during tuber bulking sets size and shape and limits scab. Do not let the soil go bone dry and then flood it, which causes knobs, cracks, and hollow heart.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Steady water while the potatoes are forming makes them smooth and limits scab. Do not let the soil go bone dry and then soak it, which makes the potatoes lumpy and cracked.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Heavy rain can rot potatoes
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Waterlogged soil rots tubers and drives soft rot and blackleg, and a heavy soaking on a near-mature crop can split tubers. Ensure drainage, and if the crop is mature, harvest before a prolonged wet spell.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Soggy soil rots potatoes and brings on rot diseases, and a big rain on a ready crop can crack them. Make sure the bed drains, and if the potatoes are ready, dig them before a long wet spell.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Cool, wet weather favors late blight
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Damp weather can bring late blight
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Cool, wet, humid weather with prolonged leaf wetness drives late blight, the most serious potato disease. Water at the base, space for airflow, scout daily, and remove infected plants immediately.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Cool, damp, humid weather with wet leaves brings on late blight, the most dangerous potato disease. Water at the soil, give plants room, check daily, and pull out any infected plant right away.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Green potatoes
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Green potatoes
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Tubers developed green patches because they were exposed to light, either pushing out of the soil while growing or sitting in the light after harvest. The green tissue contains solanine, a bitter, mildly toxic alkaloid, so green portions should be cut away and discarded, or the tuber discarded if heavily greened.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Some potatoes turned green because they got light, either by poking out of the soil or by sitting out in the light after you dug them. The green part contains solanine, which is bitter and mildly poisonous, so cut the green parts off and throw them away (or toss the whole potato if it is very green).
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Hill thoroughly and keep every tuber covered through the season, and store the crop in the dark. Re-cover any shoulders that heave up, and never leave dug potatoes in the sun.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Mound soil up well so no potatoes are uncovered, and store them in the dark. Cover any that push up to the surface, and do not leave dug potatoes sitting in the light.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Hollow center in the tuber
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Hollow middle in the potato
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Large tubers showed a star-shaped or irregular hollow cavity in the center, a physiological disorder, not a disease. It comes from uneven, rapid growth, often a checked-then-surging pattern from irregular water or very wide spacing that lets individual tubers grow too fast.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Big potatoes had a hollow space in the middle. This is not a disease; it comes from uneven, fast growth, usually from on-again off-again watering or plants spaced too far apart so the potatoes grow too quickly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Keep moisture even through bulking and avoid feast-or-famine watering, and do not space plants too widely, which encourages oversized, fast-growing tubers prone to hollowing.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Water steadily while the potatoes size up instead of letting them dry out and then soaking them, and do not space the plants too far apart, which makes a few oversized potatoes that hollow out.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Rough, scabby skin
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Rough, scabby skin
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Tubers came up with rough, corky brown scabs or pits on the skin. This is common scab, a soil bacterium favored by less-acidic soil (pH above about 5.5), dry conditions during tuber formation, and fresh manure. The potatoes are still edible after peeling.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The potatoes had rough, corky brown patches on the skin. That is scab, caused by a soil germ that gets worse when the soil is not acidic enough, when it is dry while the potatoes form, and when fresh manure is used. The potatoes are fine to eat once peeled.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Keep the soil acidic (around pH 5.0 to 5.3 where scab recurs) and never lime a potato bed, keep the soil evenly moist for the weeks after planting, avoid fresh manure, and grow scab-resistant varieties.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep the soil acidic (do not add lime), keep it evenly moist while the potatoes are forming, skip fresh manure, and grow a scab-resistant variety if it keeps happening.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Knobby, misshapen tubers
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Lumpy, oddly shaped potatoes
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Tubers grew knobby, with secondary lumps or growth cracks, from a stop-and-start growth pattern: a dry spell or heat check followed by a surge of moisture and growth, or heavy clay soil that resists smooth expansion.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The potatoes came out lumpy or cracked because their growth started and stopped, usually from the soil going dry and then wet again, or from heavy clay that the potatoes could not grow through smoothly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Hold even moisture through bulking, mulch to buffer soil temperature and moisture, and loosen heavy soil with organic matter or use raised beds so tubers can expand evenly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep the watering steady while the potatoes grow, mulch to even out the soil, and loosen heavy soil with compost or use a raised bed so the potatoes can grow smoothly.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Lots of vines but few potatoes
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Big plants but few potatoes
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The plants grew lush, leafy tops but set few tubers. The usual causes are too much nitrogen (which favors foliage over tubers), sustained heat during tuber formation (tubers set poorly above the cool optimum), or planting too late so bulking ran into summer heat.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The plants were big and leafy but made few potatoes. This usually comes from too much nitrogen (which grows leaves not potatoes), heat while the potatoes were trying to form, or planting too late so they were sizing up in the summer heat.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Cut back nitrogen and use balanced feeding, and time the crop so tubers form and bulk in cool weather rather than summer heat: plant earlier in spring, or grow in the cool season in hot regions.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Use less nitrogen and a balanced fertilizer, and time the crop so the potatoes form in cool weather, not summer heat: plant earlier in spring, or grow them in the cool season where summers are hot.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Roughly 5 to 10 tubers, about 1 to 2 pounds, per plant in good conditions, varying widely with variety, season length, and care. Yield is best thought of by row: Iowa State puts a home crop at about 20 to 30 pounds per 10 feet of row.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: About 5 to 10 potatoes, roughly 1 to 2 pounds, from each plant when things go well, though it varies a lot. By the row, expect something like 20 to 30 pounds from a 10-foot row.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: A potato planting matures over a single window, about 90 to 120 days, and is dug once when the vines die back, with optional earlier new-potato digs from about 7 to 8 weeks. It is not a repeat-harvest crop; for a longer supply, stagger plantings where the season allows, or store the cured main crop.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: A potato planting is ready all at once, about 3 to 4 months after planting, and you dig it when the tops die back (with a few early new potatoes from about 7 to 8 weeks). It does not keep producing after that, so store the cured crop for a longer supply.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Potatoes are grown fresh from seed pieces each season, so there is no first-year-versus-later difference as with perennials; results depend on certified seed, loose well-drained soil, even moisture, and finishing in cool weather.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Potatoes are grown fresh each year from seed pieces, so your first crop can do as well as any later one. What matters is good seed, loose well-drained soil, steady water, and finishing in cool weather.
factors_seasoned: Certified disease-free seed: virus or blight carried on saved seed caps yield from the start.
Even moisture during bulking: drought-then-flood cycles cut yield and cause knobs, cracks, and hollow heart.
Temperature at tuber formation: sustained heat above the cool 60 to 70°F optimum reduces tuber set.
Nitrogen balance: excess nitrogen grows vines at the expense of tubers.
Hilling and depth: thorough hilling expands the tuber zone and prevents greening losses.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting assigns root and tuber crops like potatoes to the waning moon, the period after the full moon, on the folk principle that the changing lunar pull favors below-ground growth. This is long-standing gardening folklore with no controlled scientific evidence of an effect on potato yield. Plant potatoes by soil temperature and your cool-season window, not the moon; this is recorded only for growers who follow the tradition.

NMSU Extension Circular CR-457-B -- Home vegetable garden planting (warm zones)
