succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Potatoes are not a succession crop. They are planted once per growing window from seed pieces and dug as a single main crop when the tops die back, not sown in repeated short intervals. In mild and hot regions a separate spring and fall planting is possible, but each is a discrete crop rather than a staggered succession, so no per-zone succession count applies.

open_findings.summary: Modeled regional planting windows: warm_arid (NM), low_desert_az, and hawaii_tropical month windows are modeled on the regional cool-season pattern plus potato's tuber physiology, not lifted from a machine-readable T1 calendar. The Arizona (UA IrishPotatoes.pdf) and Hawaii (CTAHR B-91) sources are image/PDF-only and were not machine-read; NMSU CR457B confirms 102-day maturity and 4-inch depth but not the month windows. Flagged for source-truth review.

Page-level pest citation: the aphid/virus-vector pest entry and the flea beetle, wireworm entries are cited to the comprehensive UMN and Clemson potato pages (which name these pests) rather than to a pest-specific factsheet. CPB is sourced to the dedicated UMN Colorado potato beetle page. Recommend a source-truth sample of the aphid/virus entry.

The cool-season / heat-pause thermal framing was RE-ANCHORED from uc_ipm to clemson_hgic at Wave-6 cert: the cited UC IPM cultural-tips page actually calls potato a 'warm-weather plant' and carries no soil-temperature numbers, so it did not back the cool-season 60-70F optimum it was anchored to. Clemson ('potatoes prefer a cool spring') now anchors the cool-season basis; the 60 to 70F optimum and ~80F ceiling are standard, well-established tuber physiology, modeled here rather than lifted from a single numeric T1 figure. Per-region heat-month boundaries remain modeled on that physiology plus each region's planting source.

DTM range low bound [70,...] is modeled (early / new-potato digging). The cited DTM sources give ~90-120 days for the mature crop (Iowa State 90-120, Clemson 100-120), and Clemson/UMN put new potatoes at ~7-8 weeks; mid=100 is source-backed. Pin the early-harvest low bound at the variety pass.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: Wave-6 cert (2026-07-02): CC source-truth review. CONSUMER-SAFETY greening/solanine chain PROPERLY T1-SOURCED and airtight -- light->green->toxic-bitter-alkaloid->cut-away/discard->don't-eat-heavily-greened->hill-to-prevent->store-dark is backed verbatim (Clemson + UMN, UC IPM corroboration); 'solanine' kept as the standard textbook alkaloid name (uncontroversial, though not printed on the two cited pages). Late blight (Phytophthora infestans) + Colorado potato beetle backed VERBATIM (Clemson/UMN; CPB 3/8 in, 10 stripes, 350 eggs, 5-10 in overwinter). Seed-potato culture backed (Iowa State: 1-2 eyes, callus/suberize, hill). FIX: re-anchored the cool-season/heat cells (heat_threshold + 12 heat_pause) from uc_ipm -> clemson_hgic because the UC IPM page says 'warm-weather plants' and carries no soil-temp numbers; OF003 elevated to medium; DTM low-bound-modeled -> open_finding. cold_pause rides on the sourced frost-tender-foliage claim (decision-3, kept).

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer heat gap (Jul, Aug). Potato is a cool-season crop: tubers set and bulk best in cool soil, roughly 60 to 70°F, and tuber formation falls off sharply as the soil warms through summer, so the tops may keep growing while few usable tubers form. In the upper South edge of the cold-winter North the hot months sit outside the plant and harvest windows, which is why the extension planting calendars place potatoes in the cool season and skip the heat. (cool-season basis per Clemson; the 60 to 70°F optimum and ~80°F ceiling are modeled, not from a single T1 figure)

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the cold-winter North, grow potatoes once, in spring. Plant the cut seed pieces 2 to 4 weeks before your last frost, when the soil has warmed to about 50°F, usually early to mid April in the middle of the region (a little earlier in the warmest parts, later in the coldest). The leafy tops can be hurt by a hard frost, but the plants bounce back and the seed underground is safe. As the plants grow, mound (hill) soil over the row so the new potatoes stay covered and do not turn green. You can sneak a few new potatoes about 7 to 8 weeks after planting, and dig the main crop when the tops turn yellow and die down, usually 3 to 4 months after planting, in late summer. Skip a fall crop here: it gets cold too soon.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Northern-tier potatoes are a single spring crop. Plant seed pieces 2 to 4 weeks before the last spring frost, once the soil reaches about 50°F: University of Minnesota places this in early April in the Twin Cities (zone 4), Iowa State in early to mid April (zone 5), earlier toward zone 7 and later in zone 3 where the soil warms slowly. The tops are frost tender, so a hard late frost can nip emerged foliage, but the plants recover and the seed underground is protected. Hill soil over the row as the plants grow to keep developing tubers covered and out of the light. Dig new potatoes about 7 to 8 weeks after planting and the main crop when the tops yellow and die back, roughly 90 to 120 days, in late summer across most of the region. There is no fall crop: the season is too short and the foliage will not survive frost. Windows from UMN, Iowa State, and University of Maine; maturity 90 to 120 days.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast and along the Gulf, plant potatoes in late winter to early spring, when the soil has warmed to about 45 to 50°F. In the coastal South that is around February, and a bit later (March into April) in the cooler Piedmont. Dig them in late spring before the hot, muggy summer arrives, because heat stops potatoes from making tubers and damp heat brings on disease. The bed then rests through the hot summer, and winter is too frosty for the tender tops. Folks right on the Gulf Coast can sometimes try a second crop planted in late summer, but spring is the dependable time here.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: Across the Southeast and Gulf, potatoes are mainly an early-spring crop. Plant seed pieces once the soil reaches about 45 to 50°F, which Clemson places at February 1 to March 31 on the coast and March 15 to April 30 in the Piedmont, and University of Georgia puts in mid to late February in middle Georgia. The crop is dug in late spring, before the hot, humid summer that favors late blight and stalls tuber formation. Summer is too hot for tubers to set, so the bed rests through the heat, and winter is a cold, frost-prone off-season for this frost-tender crop. Gardeners on the lower Gulf Coast can sometimes add a fall crop planted in late summer, but the reliable home crop here is spring. Spring windows from Clemson and UGA; the summer heat gap reflects potato's cool-season tuber physiology (cool-season basis per Clemson; regional windows modeled per open findings).

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In the hot inland valleys of California, plant potatoes twice: once in late winter to early spring (February to March) and again in August for a fall crop. Skip the hottest part of summer, because potatoes cannot make tubers in that heat. The spring crop is dug in late spring and the fall crop in late fall. Winters are mild with only a short frosty spell.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: In California's interior valleys (Sacramento and San Joaquin), UC IPM gives two potato windows: a spring planting in February to March and a fall planting in August. The spring crop is dug in late spring before peak heat, the fall crop grows on into the cool, mild fall and is dug toward year's end. Midsummer is set aside: valley heat is too high for tubers to bulk, and the brief winter cold snap is the only frost risk this frost-tender crop sees. (cool-season basis per Clemson; regional windows modeled per open findings)

ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: On California's cool, foggy north and central coast, potatoes are happy. Plant seed pieces in February and again in April or May, and harvest through the summer. The mild ocean air keeps things cool enough that potatoes make tubers steadily without a hot-weather break. Just rest the bed over the cool winter.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: Along California's cool north and central coast (Monterey County and north), UC IPM plants potatoes in February and again in April to May, harvesting through summer. The marine climate is close to ideal for potatoes: cool, even temperatures let tubers bulk steadily with no real summer heat gap, so the planting window simply runs through spring. Winter is the mild off-season. (cool-season basis per Clemson; regional windows modeled per open findings)

ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: On the mild southern California coast, you have a long potato season. Plant from February all the way through August, and harvest from late spring into fall. The weather stays mild enough that even summer plantings do fine, and hard frost is rare.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: On California's mild south coast (San Luis Obispo County south), UC IPM gives a long potato window: February to May, then June to August. The coastal climate stays mild enough that summer planting is workable, so the season runs from late winter through summer with harvest into fall. Frost is rare, and there is no real summer heat shutdown the way there is inland. (cool-season basis per Clemson; regional windows modeled per open findings)

ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: In California's low desert, potatoes are a cool-season crop. Plant the seed pieces from December through February and dig the crop in spring. The blazing desert summer is no time for potatoes, so the whole hot stretch is skipped. Winters are mild with only light frost.
ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: In California's low desert valleys (Imperial and Coachella), UC IPM plants potatoes in the cool window of December to February for a late-winter-to-spring harvest. The desert summer is far too hot for tubers to form, so the long hot stretch from late spring through fall is left out entirely and the crop is grown only in the cool months. Frost is brief and light. (cool-season basis per Clemson; regional windows modeled per open findings)

warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: In the dry inland Southwest, grow potatoes in two cooler stretches with a break for the hot summer. Plant a spring crop in late winter once the cold eases and the soil warms to about 50°F, and a fall crop in late summer as it starts to cool. Skip the hottest part of summer, when potatoes will not form tubers, and rest the bed over the frosty winter. Potatoes take about 3 to 4 months from planting here.
warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: Across the inland Southwest, potatoes run two cool-season windows around a hot, dry summer. Plant a spring crop in late winter once frost danger eases and the soil reaches about 50°F, and a fall crop in late summer as the heat begins to break. New Mexico State University lists potato at about 102 days to harvest, planted 4 inches deep. Midsummer is left out: tubers do not bulk in the heat. Winter brings the only hard frost for this frost-tender crop. Maturity and depth from NMSU; the precise spring and fall month windows are modeled on the region's cool-season planting pattern and flagged for review.

low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: In the Arizona low desert, grow potatoes in the cool months and skip the brutal summer. Plant a spring crop in January or February and a fall crop in September. Winters are mild, so there is no real cold-weather break, just the long hot summer when potatoes cannot make tubers.
low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: In Arizona's low desert, potatoes are grown in the cool months around an unworkable summer. Plant a spring crop in January to February for a spring harvest, and a fall crop in September for a winter harvest, with the long, extreme summer left out because tubers cannot set in that heat. Winters are mild, so the calendar runs nearly year-round apart from the summer gap. The month windows are modeled on University of Arizona low-desert planting guidance (the source PDF could not be machine-read) plus potato's cool-season tuber physiology (cool-season basis per Clemson; regional windows modeled per open findings), and are flagged for source-truth review.

fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: In peninsular Florida, potatoes grow in the cool season, planted from fall into winter. Across most of the state that means January (and into February up north), while in south Florida you can plant any time from October through January. Harvest from midwinter into spring. Skip the hot, rainy summer, which is too warm for tubers and brings disease.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: On the Florida peninsula, potatoes are a cool-season crop planted from fall through winter. UF/IFAS plants potatoes statewide in January, still into February in north and central Florida, and from October to January in south Florida, with harvest from midwinter into spring. The hot, wet summer is left out: it is far too warm for tubers and it favors disease. Light winter frost is the only cold risk. (UF/IFAS)

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In Hawaii, potatoes do best in the cooler months and at higher elevations, where it is not so warm. The hot, wet lowlands are a tough spot for them, and damp heat brings leaf disease. This calendar plants in the cool season (about October to December) for a winter-to-spring harvest and leaves out the warm summer. The exact local timing is an estimate here and is flagged for a closer look.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: In Hawaii, potatoes are a cooler-season and higher-elevation crop. They grow best in the cool, drier months and at elevation (the Kula and Volcano uplands), where temperatures are mild enough for tubers to form. The warm tropical lowland is marginal, and leaf diseases are serious in warm, wet weather. This calendar models a cool-season planting (about October through December) with a winter-to-spring harvest, with the warm lowland summer set aside. The University of Hawaii CTAHR home-garden bulletin (B-91) is the nearest cataloged source; it is PDF-only and was not machine-read, so the Hawaii window is modeled and flagged.

crops.description_seasoned: Potato (Solanum tuberosum) is a cool-season member of the nightshade family (Solanaceae) grown for its starchy underground tubers. It is planted not from seed but from seed potatoes: small whole tubers or cut pieces, each carrying one or more eyes, set directly in the ground. The foliage is frost tender, so the tops are killed by hard frost even though the crop is grown in the cool season; in cold climates it is a single spring crop, and in mild and hot climates a fall-through-winter crop. The signature practice is hilling: soil is mounded over the row as the plants grow, which expands the zone where tubers form and, critically, keeps them covered and out of the light, since exposed tubers turn green and develop bitter, mildly toxic solanine. Tubers set and bulk best in cool soil, roughly 60 to 70°F, and tuber formation falls off in sustained heat. The crop is ready when the tops yellow and die back, about 90 to 120 days from planting, with thin-skinned new potatoes dug a few weeks earlier. Potatoes prefer loose, well-drained, acidic soil (pH about 5.0 to 6.0, lower than most vegetables) which suppresses common scab, and they are rotated away from their nightshade relatives (tomato, pepper, eggplant) to limit shared disease, above all late blight, the water mold behind the historic Irish potato famine.
crops.description_beginner: Potatoes are a cool-weather crop grown for the starchy tubers that form underground. You do not grow them from seed: you plant seed potatoes, which are small whole potatoes or cut chunks, each with an eye or two, set right in the soil. The leafy tops are tender and killed by hard frost, so in cold places potatoes are a spring crop, and in warm places they are grown through fall and winter. The key trick is hilling: as the plants grow, you mound soil up over the row. This gives the potatoes room to form and, most importantly, keeps them covered so they do not turn green, because green potatoes are bitter and mildly poisonous. Potatoes grow best in loose, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and they like cool soil to make tubers, so heat slows them down. They are ready when the tops turn yellow and die back, about 3 to 4 months after planting, and you can dig a few small new potatoes a bit earlier. Keep potatoes away from their cousins (tomatoes, peppers, eggplant), which share the same diseases, especially late blight, the famous one behind the Irish potato famine.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Potatoes are ready to harvest based on the foliage, not a fixed date. New potatoes, thin-skinned and best used fresh, can be dug carefully at the edge of a hill from about 7 to 8 weeks after planting. The main crop is mature when the tops yellow and die back, roughly 90 to 120 days from planting. For storage potatoes, leave them in the ground about two weeks after the vines die so the skins set and toughen, then dig on a dry day, pushing a fork in well outside the hill so you do not spear tubers. Lift, let them dry briefly out of direct sun, brush off soil (do not wash), and cure in the dark at about 50 to 60°F for two weeks before storing. Keep tubers covered and shaded at every stage, since light greens them and produces bitter, mildly toxic solanine.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: You can tell potatoes are ready by the plants, not a set date. Small new potatoes can be dug gently at the side of a plant from about 7 to 8 weeks after planting, and are best eaten fresh. The main crop is ready when the tops turn yellow and die down, about 3 to 4 months after planting. If you want to store them, leave them in the ground about two weeks after the tops die so the skins toughen, then dig on a dry day with a fork, pushing it in well away from the plant so you do not stab the potatoes. Let them dry off out of the sun, brush off the dirt (do not wash them), and keep them in the dark. Always keep potatoes covered and out of the light, because light turns them green and bitter, and green potatoes are mildly poisonous.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Potato quality starts in loose, well-drained, acidic soil. Work the bed deep and incorporate compost, breaking up clods so the tubers can expand smoothly; heavy clay rots seed pieces and produces knobby, misshapen tubers and is best improved with organic matter or replaced with a raised bed. Aim for an acidic pH, roughly 5.0 to 6.0, to suppress common scab, and do not lime a potato bed. Avoid fresh manure (which encourages scab) and heavy nitrogen (which grows vines over tubers); use well-finished compost and a balanced fertilizer instead. Plant cut, suberized seed pieces 3 to 5 inches deep, 10 to 12 inches apart in rows 30 to 36 inches apart, once the soil reaches about 50°F, and plan to hill soil over the row as the plants grow.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Getting the soil right matters for potatoes. Loosen the bed deep and mix in compost so the soil is light and drains well, which lets the potatoes grow smoothly; heavy, soggy clay rots the seed and makes lumpy potatoes, so use a raised bed or deep container if your soil is clay. Keep the soil on the acidic side (pH about 5.0 to 6.0) to prevent scab, and do not add lime. Skip fresh manure and heavy fertilizer, which bring scab and grow leaves instead of potatoes; use compost and a balanced fertilizer. Plant the cut, healed seed pieces a few inches deep and about a foot apart, in rows about 3 feet apart, once the soil has warmed to about 50°F, and remember you will mound (hill) soil over the row as they grow.

heat_threshold_temp_f.basis_seasoned: Soil-temperature ceiling for potato tuber formation. Tubers initiate and bulk best in cool soil, roughly 60 to 70°F, and tuber set falls off sharply as soil warms through summer, which is why potato is grown in the cool season and why cool-region calendars place it in spring while hot-region calendars place it in fall and winter and omit the summer (cool-season basis per Clemson; the 60 to 70°F optimum and ~80°F ceiling are modeled, not from a single T1 figure). The ~80°F figure marks where tuber formation is strongly suppressed; the exact ceiling is variety-dependent and modeled here rather than lifted from a single numeric T1 statement.

pet_safe.toxic_parts: green parts, sprouts, leaves, and stems
pet_safe.note: The tuber is fine when cooked, but the green parts, sprouts, leaves, and stems are toxic to cats, dogs, and horses (solanine).

crops.name: Sweet Potato

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Sweet potatoes want loose, well-drained, sandy or loamy soil that the swelling storage roots can push through easily. Light soil on raised ridges or mounds is ideal, because it drains well and gives the roots room to grow smooth and long. Heavy, wet clay is the thing to avoid: it stays soggy, rots the roots, and forces them into short, knobby shapes. If your soil is heavy, build up a ridge or a raised bed of loose mix, which also warms up faster in spring. Keep the soil slightly acidic, about pH 5.8 to 6.5. Go easy on nitrogen and fresh manure, which grow lots of leafy vine and few roots.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Sweet potatoes yield best in loose, friable, well-drained sandy loam worked into raised ridges or mounds, which give the developing storage roots room to expand and keep them out of standing water. A light, warm soil produces the longest, smoothest roots; cold, heavy, poorly drained clay stays wet, rots roots, and produces short and misshapen ones, and is best improved with organic matter or replaced with a built-up ridge or raised bed. Hold the soil slightly acidic, roughly pH 5.8 to 6.5. Keep nitrogen modest and avoid fresh manure: rich, high-nitrogen ground drives rampant vine growth at the expense of roots. Even, moderate moisture in free-draining soil is the goal, never waterlogged ground.

ph.note_beginner: Soil pH measures how acidic or alkaline your soil is, on a scale from 1 to 14 where 7 is neutral. Sweet potatoes like it slightly acidic, about 5.8 to 6.5, which is close to what most vegetables want. They are not fussy and will grow from about 5.0 up to nearly neutral, so you rarely need to change your soil much. A cheap soil test from your local extension office tells you your number, and if your soil is very alkaline, mixing in compost helps. Do not overdo lime.
ph.note_seasoned: Sweet potatoes grow best in slightly acidic soil, roughly pH 5.8 to 6.5 (University of Georgia gives 6.0 to 6.5). They are adaptable and will crop from about 5.0 up toward neutral, so pH is rarely the limiting factor. Where soil pox and Streptomyces soil rot are a problem on susceptible varieties, growers avoid pushing the pH high and lean on resistant cultivars rather than heavy liming. Amend very alkaline ground with organic matter and confirm your starting point with a soil test before planting.

fertilizer.timing: Work a low-nitrogen fertilizer into the ridge before planting; side-dress once about 4 to 6 weeks after setting slips, as the vines begin to run.
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Sweet potatoes are light feeders and specifically want restrained nitrogen. University of Georgia suggests working in about 30 pounds of 5-10-10 per 1,000 square feet before planting, then side-dressing roughly 4 pounds of 5-10-10 per 100 feet of row about 4 to 6 weeks after transplanting. Favor a low-nitrogen, higher-potassium ratio: too much nitrogen (and fresh manure) grows lush, sprawling vine and few storage roots, while adequate potassium supports root sizing and quality.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Sweet potatoes do not need much feeding, and too much of the wrong kind backfires. Mix a low-nitrogen fertilizer like 5-10-10 into the ridge before you plant, then feed once more about a month after setting the slips. Do not pile on high-nitrogen fertilizer or fresh manure: that grows a jungle of leafy vine and hardly any sweet potatoes underneath. A little compost worked into the bed is the safe way to enrich it.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: Sweet potatoes are light feeders that want low nitrogen and good potassium. A blend such as 5-10-10 worked into the ridge before planting covers most home soils. Excess nitrogen drives vine at the expense of roots, and fresh manure has the same effect, so lean on a low-nitrogen fertilizer and compost rather than a balanced or high-nitrogen feed.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: The three numbers on a fertilizer bag are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium (N-P-K). Sweet potatoes do best with a low first number, like 5-10-10, not a high-nitrogen feed. Too much nitrogen grows leaves and vines instead of sweet potatoes, so use a low-nitrogen fertilizer and some compost.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: Work about 30 pounds of 5-10-10 per 1,000 square feet into the ridge before planting (UGA), then side-dress about 4 pounds of 5-10-10 per 100 feet of row roughly 4 to 6 weeks after transplanting. Keep nitrogen low; excess nitrogen grows vine at the expense of storage roots.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Mix in about 30 pounds of 5-10-10 per 1,000 square feet before planting, then side-dress lightly about a month later. Go easy: more fertilizer, especially nitrogen, grows more leaves, not more sweet potatoes.

companions.note_beginner: Sweet potatoes are easygoing and take up a lot of ground with their sprawling vines, so companions are mostly about using the edges of the bed. Bush beans and other legumes are a sensible neighbor because they add nitrogen to the soil. The main thing to avoid is crowding them next to other sprawling vine crops like squash and pumpkins, which fight for the same space and sunlight. Do not trust every companion chart online; many of their claims have never been tested.
companions.note_seasoned: Sweet potatoes are undemanding neighbors but greedy for space, since a single plant can run vines many feet in every direction. The best-grounded pairing is with legumes (bush beans, southern peas), which fix nitrogen and share the bed without heavy competition. Aromatic herbs are a traditional edge planting. The clearest practical avoids are other rampant vine crops, squash, pumpkins, and melons, which compete for the same ground and light. Most companion-chart claims for sweet potato are folklore; treat them with healthy skepticism, since university reviews find little evidence behind most of them.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Bush beans
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Beans are legumes that pull nitrogen from the air and leave some in the soil, which suits sweet potatoes since they want only modest nitrogen. Bush beans stay compact and can share the edge of the bed without fighting the vines for space.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Legume interplant: the nitrogen-fixing benefit is a sound, general mechanism, and compact bush beans do not compete hard with sweet potato's ground-running vines. Not a controlled sweet-potato-specific trial, so recorded as sound-mechanism tradition.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Bush beans and other legumes are a sensible sweet potato neighbor: they fix nitrogen and, being compact and upright, do not compete hard with the ground-running vines. The nitrogen contribution is a real mechanism; treat the pairing as a grounded tradition rather than a measured yield effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Aromatic herbs (dill, summer savory)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Some gardeners plant strong-smelling herbs around the edge of the sweet potato patch in the hope of confusing pests. It is a traditional idea rather than a proven one, but the herbs use the border space the vines do not need early on.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Aromatic-herb pest confusion is widespread folk tradition with no controlled evidence for sweet potato specifically. Recorded, hedged, for growers who follow it; the practical benefit is efficient use of border space.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Aromatic herbs at the border are a traditional pest-confusion planting with no controlled evidence behind it for sweet potato. Recorded as hedged tradition; the concrete value is filling edge space the vines reach only later in the season.

good_seasoned.name: Bush beans and southern peas
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Legumes fix nitrogen, which suits a light-nitrogen feeder, and stay compact enough not to compete with the running vines. Nitrogen benefit sound; recorded as grounded tradition, not a measured sweet-potato trial.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Nitrogen fixation is the sound mechanism; the pairing is a grounded space-and-soil interplant, not a controlled sweet-potato yield study.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Squash, pumpkins, and melons
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: These are all big, sprawling vine crops, just like sweet potatoes. Grown side by side they smother each other and fight for the same sunlight and ground, so give each its own space in the garden.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: A space-and-light competition avoid, not a shared-disease one: two rampant ground-running vine crops in the same bed shade and crowd each other. Grounded in growth habit rather than a controlled trial.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Cucurbits (squash, pumpkins, melons) are rampant ground-running vines like sweet potato, so interplanting them means two sprawling crops competing for the same ground and light. This is a habit-based space conflict, not a shared-disease risk, and the fix is simply separate beds.

bad_seasoned.name: Other sprawling vine crops
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Squash, pumpkins, and melons run vigorous ground vines that collide with sweet potato's own sprawl, shading and crowding both. Keep rampant vine crops in separate beds; this is a space-and-light conflict rather than a shared pest or disease problem.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Growth-habit competition (two ground-running vine crops) rather than a documented disease bridge. Grounded in habit, hedged as tradition.

pests.name: Sweet potato weevil
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small holes and dark, spongy tunnels running through the storage roots, found when you dig or cut them. Even light feeding triggers a chemical reaction that gives the roots a bitter taste and an off, turpentine-like odor, ruining them for eating. The adult is a slender, ant-like weevil, about a quarter inch long, with a dark head and snout, reddish legs, and a metallic blue-black body; you may see chewing on stems and leaves. This is the single most serious pest of sweet potato, worst in the Deep South and Gulf.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Small holes and dark, spongy tunnels inside the sweet potatoes, which you usually find only when you dig or slice them. Even a little feeding makes the roots taste bitter and smell off, so they are no longer good to eat. The beetle itself is a slim, ant-like weevil with a long snout, reddish legs, and a shiny blue-black body. It is the worst sweet potato pest, especially in the Deep South.
pests.cause_seasoned: The sweet potato weevil (Cylas formicarius, family Brentidae). Larvae do the principal damage by mining tunnels through the storage roots (and stems), leaving them riddled with cavities, spongy, and darkened; the feeding induces bitter terpenes even at low levels. It breeds continuously in warm climates, spreads mainly on infested slips and in leftover roots, and continues to damage the crop in storage.
pests.cause_beginner: A small weevil called the sweet potato weevil. Its grubs tunnel through the sweet potatoes and stems, and the plant reacts by turning bitter, so even lightly damaged roots are ruined. It rides in on infested slips and survives in leftover sweet potatoes in the ground, and it keeps damaging the crop even after harvest in storage.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no rescue for tunneled roots; discard them. Control is prevention: start only with certified weevil-free slips, and practice strict sanitation, removing and destroying every leftover, cull, and volunteer root that can harbor the weevil between crops. Harvest promptly once the crop matures rather than leaving roots in infested soil, and keep new plantings away from last year's beds and from stored roots.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot fix sweet potatoes that are already tunneled, so throw them out. The whole game is prevention: plant only certified weevil-free slips, and clean up every leftover or volunteer sweet potato in the ground after harvest, because the weevil lives on in them. Dig your crop on time instead of leaving it in the soil, and do not plant next to last year's bed.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Buy certified, weevil-free slips rather than saving your own or using field-run roots. Rotate sweet potatoes well away from last year's beds and from any sweet potato storage, since the weevil moves only short distances. Remove all volunteer and cull roots after harvest, harvest promptly, and in badly infested areas grow on a strict rotation with a fallow break. Certified slips plus sanitation carry nearly all of the control.
pests.prevention_beginner: Start with certified weevil-free slips, not saved sweet potatoes. Move the patch to a new spot each year, well away from where sweet potatoes grew before and away from where you store them. After you dig, clean up every leftover and volunteer root, because the weevil survives in them. Harvest on time rather than leaving the crop in the ground.

pests.name: Wireworms and root-feeding beetle larvae
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Narrow holes and shallow, winding grooves bored straight into the storage roots, leaving pinhole punctures and tracks that downgrade quality and open the door to storage rots. The culprits are slender, shiny, hard-bodied wireworms (click beetle larvae) plus the larvae of cucumber beetles and flea beetles (the wireworm, Diabrotica, Systena complex). There are no useful aboveground signs; the damage is found at harvest.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Narrow holes and shallow tracks drilled into the sweet potatoes, found when you dig them. They are made by hard, shiny soil worms (wireworms) and the grubs of cucumber and flea beetles. You do not see anything above ground; you find the little tunnels and pits at harvest, and damaged roots do not store as well.
pests.cause_seasoned: Wireworms are click beetle larvae that live in the soil for several years and are most numerous in ground recently in sod, grass, or corn. The same root-scarring complex includes larvae of spotted and banded cucumber beetles (Diabrotica) and flea beetles (Systena), which move into the soil to feed on the developing roots through the season.
pests.cause_beginner: Wireworms are the larvae of click beetles; they live in the soil for years and are worst in beds that were lawn, grass, or corn not long ago. The larvae of cucumber beetles and flea beetles do similar damage, moving into the soil to nibble the sweet potatoes as they grow.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no rescue for scarred roots; trim damaged areas and use those roots first rather than storing them. Harvest promptly once the crop matures rather than leaving roots in infested soil, where feeding accumulates. Keeping the ground worked and free of grassy weeds reduces the habitat these larvae favor.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot fix roots that are already tunneled, so cut out the bad spots and eat those first instead of storing them. Dig the crop on time rather than leaving it in the ground, where the worms keep boring, and keep grassy weeds down.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid planting sweet potatoes in ground that was recently pasture, lawn, or corn, where wireworm numbers peak; extend the interval between grass and a root crop. Rotate, keep the soil well worked, control grassy weeds, and harvest on time. Where wireworm history is bad, grow elsewhere or in clean raised-bed soil.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not plant sweet potatoes in a bed that was grass, lawn, or corn in the last year or two, where wireworms are worst. Rotate your crops, work the soil, pull grassy weeds, and dig on time. If wireworms keep ruining a bed, use a raised bed with clean soil.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny dark beetles that jump when disturbed and chew many small round shot-holes in the leaves. Heavy early feeding on young transplants stunts growth; the soil-dwelling larvae also scar the developing storage roots. Established, vigorously running plants usually outgrow light foliage feeding.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Lots of tiny holes in the leaves, as if peppered with shot, made by little dark beetles that hop away when you come near. Young slips are hurt most; big, healthy vines shrug it off. The grubs in the soil can also scar the sweet potatoes.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several species of small flea beetles that overwinter nearby and move onto young sweet potato foliage in spring and early summer. They are worst on small, slow transplants and in warm, dry weather; their larvae contribute to the root-scarring complex below ground.
pests.cause_beginner: Small beetles called flea beetles that spend winter nearby and jump onto young sweet potato plants. They do the most harm to freshly set slips and in warm, dry spells, and their grubs can scar the roots underground.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Healthy, well-watered transplants usually outgrow flea beetle feeding once the vines run. Floating row cover protects young plants during the vulnerable first weeks; remove it as the vines begin to sprawl. Clearing weeds and old crop debris reduces the shelter they overwinter in.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Keep young slips growing strong with steady water and they usually outgrow the damage as the vines take off. A row cover protects them early on, and clearing weeds and old plant debris takes away their winter hiding spots.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Rotate away from last year's beds, keep the area weed-free, and protect freshly set slips with row cover until they are established and running. Vigorous, evenly watered transplants tolerate feeding far better than stressed ones.
pests.prevention_beginner: Move the patch to a new spot, pull weeds, and cover the young slips until they are established and the vines start to run. Plants that are well watered handle flea beetles much better than struggling ones.

pests.name: Whiteflies and the viruses they spread
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clouds of tiny white, moth-like insects that lift off the foliage when disturbed, clustered on leaf undersides with sticky honeydew and sooty mold. The bigger problem is not their feeding but the viruses they transmit (such as sweet potato feathery mottle virus and sweet potato leaf curl virus), which mottle, curl, and stunt the foliage and erode yield over time; virus-infected plants do not recover.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny white flying insects that scatter in a cloud when you brush the leaves, clustered underneath with a sticky film. Their feeding is minor, but they can pass on plant viruses that mottle and curl the leaves and cut your harvest. A plant that catches a virus will not get better.
pests.cause_seasoned: Whiteflies colonize sweet potato foliage and, as they move plant to plant, transmit sweet potato viruses. Virus pressure, not the feeding itself, is the main reason to manage them, and it is the reason growers are advised to start from certified, virus-tested slips rather than saved or field-run material.
pests.cause_beginner: Whiteflies are tiny sap-sucking insects, and as they move from plant to plant they carry sweet potato viruses. The viruses, more than the bugs, are the real concern, which is why it is best to plant certified, disease-tested slips instead of saving your own.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Start with certified, virus-tested slips to keep virus out of the patch. Tolerate light whitefly numbers, since beneficial insects often control them; a strong spray of water or insecticidal soap knocks down heavy colonies on the leaf undersides. Remove and destroy any plant showing clear virus symptoms.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Plant certified, disease-tested slips so the patch starts clean. A few whiteflies are fine, because helpful bugs usually keep them in check; for heavy clusters, spray them off with water or use insecticidal soap. Pull and throw away any plant that clearly has a virus.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Use certified slips, encourage beneficial insects by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays, control nearby weeds that host whiteflies and virus, and rogue out virus-symptomatic plants promptly. Do not save and replant slips from a patch that showed virus, since it carries over.
pests.prevention_beginner: Buy certified slips, avoid harsh sprays that kill the helpful bugs, keep weeds down, and pull out any virus-looking plant right away. Do not save slips from a patch that had virus, because it comes back with them.

diseases.name: Fusarium wilt (stem rot)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellowing and wilting that starts on the lower leaves and progresses up the vine, often on one side, with stunting; a lengthwise cut of the stem near the base shows a brown, discolored streak in the water-conducting tissue. Plants may collapse before making a crop. It moves up from infected slips or through the soil.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Lower leaves yellow and wilt, often on one side of the plant, and the vine is stunted; if you slit a stem near the base you see brown streaks inside. Badly affected plants wilt and die before making sweet potatoes. It usually comes in on infected slips or from the soil.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The soilborne fungus Fusarium oxysporum, which enters through the roots and stem base and plugs the vascular tissue. It survives for years in the soil and is carried on infected slips, so it builds up where sweet potatoes are grown repeatedly in the same ground.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soil fungus (Fusarium oxysporum) that gets into the roots and stem and clogs the plant's plumbing. It lives in the soil for years and rides in on infected slips, and it builds up if you grow sweet potatoes in the same spot again and again.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure for an infected plant; remove and destroy it. Management is preventive and variety-based: it is controlled by clean slips, resistant cultivars, and rotation, not by a spray.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot cure an infected plant, so pull it and throw it away (do not compost it). There is no spray fix; you prevent it with clean slips, resistant varieties, and rotating the bed.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Start with certified, disease-free slips and grow Fusarium-resistant varieties (such as Sumor or other wilt-resistant releases) where the disease occurs. Rotate sweet potatoes out of an infected bed for several years, and do not save slips from a patch that showed wilt.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant certified, disease-free slips and choose a wilt-resistant variety if this has been a problem. Do not grow sweet potatoes in the same bed year after year, and never save slips from a patch that wilted.

diseases.name: Root-knot nematode
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Stunted, off-color, wilt-prone vines above ground, and below ground storage roots that are cracked, bumpy, and galled, with small knots and rough, split skin that downgrade quality and storage. The southern root-knot nematode is the main species, and damage is worst in sandy soils and warm regions.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Plants that are stunted and wilt easily even with water, and sweet potatoes that come up cracked, bumpy, and rough-skinned with little knots on them. The damage is worst in sandy soil and hot regions. You usually see it clearly only when you dig the roots.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The southern root-knot nematode (Meloidogyne incognita), a microscopic soil roundworm that invades the roots, causing galling and the cracked, bumpy roots that grade out. It persists in the soil and on many hosts, so it builds up where susceptible crops are grown repeatedly.
diseases.cause_beginner: A microscopic soil roundworm (the southern root-knot nematode) that attacks the roots and makes them crack and knot. It lives in the soil and feeds on many crops, so it builds up when you grow the same kinds of plants in one spot over and over.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no rescue for galled, cracked roots. Management is preventive: grow nematode-resistant varieties, rotate to non-host or less-susceptible crops, and keep the soil high in organic matter. Solarizing the bed in the hot months and cover cropping can lower populations over time.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot fix roots that are already cracked and knotted. Instead, prevent it: grow a nematode-resistant variety, rotate the bed to different crops, and build up the soil with compost. In hot climates, covering moist soil with clear plastic through the summer can knock the numbers down.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Choose root-knot-resistant varieties (such as Centennial, Covington, or other resistant releases), rotate away from susceptible hosts on a multi-year cycle, and raise soil organic matter. Start with certified, clean slips so you do not introduce new populations.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Grow a nematode-resistant variety like Centennial or Covington, rotate your crops so sweet potatoes and their susceptible cousins are not in the same bed each year, and add plenty of compost. Start with certified, clean slips.

diseases.name: Black rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Round, dark, sunken lesions on the storage roots that are firm and greenish-black to dark brown, sometimes with a bitter taste in the affected tissue; on the lower stems it shows as dark cankers. It spreads in storage and in the field from infected slips and contaminated soil, and it is a major cause of cull and storage loss.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Dark, sunken, round spots on the sweet potatoes, firm and greenish-black to brown, and the affected part can taste bitter. It also shows as dark patches on the lower stems. It gets worse in storage and comes in on infected slips or from the soil.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Ceratocystis fimbriata, which infects roots and stems through wounds, survives in soil and crop debris, and is spread on infected slips and by handling. Warmth and moisture favor it, and it continues to develop on stored roots.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus (Ceratocystis fimbriata) that gets into the roots and stems through cuts and bruises, lives in the soil and on old plant debris, and rides in on infected slips. It likes warm, damp conditions and keeps spreading on stored sweet potatoes.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure for infected roots; discard them and do not store blemished ones. Management is preventive: clean slips, careful handling to avoid wounds, prompt curing, and sanitation.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot cure an infected sweet potato, so throw out affected ones and never store damaged roots. The fix is prevention: clean slips, gentle handling, curing right after harvest, and keeping tools and bins clean.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Start with certified, disease-free slips from clean stock, rotate out of infected beds, handle roots gently to avoid the wounds the fungus enters through, and cure the crop promptly after harvest. Discard cull and volunteer roots that carry the fungus over.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Use certified, disease-free slips, rotate the bed, and handle the sweet potatoes gently so you do not bruise them, since the fungus enters through cuts. Cure the crop right after digging and clean up leftover roots.

diseases.name: Scurf and storage soft rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Scurf shows as brown to blackish blotches on the skin surface that do not penetrate the flesh; it is a cosmetic, skin-quality problem that also increases moisture loss and shrinkage in storage. Bacterial and fungal soft rots turn wounded or chilled roots into a soft, wet, sometimes foul mush in storage. Both are worst on bruised, poorly cured, or improperly stored roots.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Scurf is dark brown to black blotches on the skin of the sweet potato; it does not rot the inside, but it makes the roots look poor and dry out faster in storage. Soft rot turns bruised or too-cold roots into a soft, wet, smelly mush in the bin. Both are worst on damaged roots that were not cured or were stored wrong.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Scurf is caused by the fungus Monilochaetes infuscans, carried on infected slips and in soil, and confined to the skin. Storage soft rots are caused by bacteria and fungi (including Rhizopus) that enter through wounds and are favored by bruising, poor curing, and cold or damp storage.
diseases.cause_beginner: Scurf is a skin fungus that comes in on infected slips and lives in the soil. Soft rot is caused by bacteria and fungi that get into bruised roots, especially when the sweet potatoes were not cured or were stored too cold or too wet.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no rescue for scurfed or rotting roots; scurfed ones are safe to eat after peeling, but soft-rotted ones are discarded. Management is preventive: clean slips, careful handling, prompt curing, and correct warm storage.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot fix scurf or soft rot. Scurfy sweet potatoes are still fine to eat once peeled, but soft, rotting ones should be thrown out. Prevent both with clean slips, gentle handling, curing, and proper warm storage.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Use certified, scurf-free slips, rotate out of infected beds, and handle roots gently to avoid wounds. Cure the crop warm and humid right after harvest to heal skins, then store warm (never cold or wet), and do not store bruised or diseased roots.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant certified, clean slips, rotate the bed, and be gentle with the sweet potatoes so you do not bruise them. Cure them warm and humid right after digging so the skins heal, then store them warm (not in the fridge), and never store damaged roots.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Sweet potatoes want even, moderate moisture, especially while the slips establish and again while the storage roots are sizing. Aim for about 1 inch of water per week including rain, delivered in deeper, less frequent soakings. Once well established the deep root system makes them fairly drought tolerant, but a prolonged dry-then-wet swing during root bulking causes cracked and misshapen roots. Ease off water in the last few weeks before harvest so the roots do not split and the skins firm up.
watering.frequency_beginner: Keep the soil evenly, moderately damp, especially right after planting the slips and later while the sweet potatoes are sizing up. Give about 1 inch of water a week, counting rain, in fewer but deeper waterings. Once the vines are growing well the plants handle dry spells fairly well, but letting the soil go dry and then soaking it while the roots form makes them crack. Cut back on water in the last few weeks before you dig.
watering.amount_seasoned: About 1 inch per week including rainfall, more in heat or sandy soil, concentrated at establishment and during root bulking. Do not keep the ridge waterlogged. Taper off in the last 2 to 3 weeks before harvest to reduce cracking and let the skins set.
watering.amount_beginner: About 1 inch of water a week, counting rain, and a bit more in hot or sandy conditions. Water most attentively right after planting and while the roots are sizing. Ease off in the last couple of weeks before harvest so the sweet potatoes do not split.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base with a soaker hose or drip line where practical, and keep the raised ridge moist but never waterlogged. A mulch helps hold even moisture and smother weeds while the vines fill in, though the sprawling canopy soon shades the ground itself.
watering.method_beginner: Water at the soil, keeping the ridge damp but not soggy. A layer of mulch early on helps hold steady moisture and keep weeds down until the vines spread out and shade the ground themselves.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Constantly saturated soil rots the roots and drives soft rot and black rot; yellowing, wilting despite wet soil, a sour waterlogged ridge, and soft or cracked roots are signs to back off and improve drainage. Waterlogging is worse than short drought for this crop.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If the soil stays soaking wet, the sweet potatoes rot. Watch for yellowing, wilting even though the soil is wet, a sour-smelling soggy bed, and soft or split roots; if you see these, water less and fix the drainage.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting in the heat of the day, dull, small foliage, and slow vine growth signal too little water, most critical during establishment and root sizing. The sharper risk is an irregular dry-then-soaked cycle during bulking, which cracks and misshapes the roots.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Droopy leaves in the afternoon, dull color, and slow growth mean the plants are thirsty, which matters most just after planting and while the roots size up. The bigger problem is letting the soil go dry and then flooding it, which cracks the sweet potatoes.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Keep moisture even at the root zone and avoid waterlogging the ridge. Established sweet potatoes tolerate some drought, but uneven soil moisture during root formation drives cracked and knobby roots, so steady base watering plus a well-drained ridge is the goal.
watering.method_note_beginner: Water the ridge evenly and never let it stay soggy. Grown-in sweet potatoes handle dry spells fairly well, but on-again off-again watering while the roots form makes them crack, so aim for even moisture and good drainage.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The two make-or-break windows are establishment (the first 2 to 3 weeks, while slips root in) and root bulking (from about mid-season on), when even moisture sets root number, size, and shape. Then ease watering in the final weeks so skins set and roots do not split for storage.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The most important times to keep the soil evenly moist are the first couple of weeks after planting the slips, and later while the sweet potatoes are sizing up. Then water less in the last few weeks before harvest so the roots firm up and do not crack.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Sweet potatoes are set out as slips (rooted sprouts), not seed-raised seedlings, so there is little to harden off. Field-pulled or bought slips are already acclimated; greenhouse-grown slips benefit from a day or two in shade before planting. Set slips out only once all frost danger has passed and the soil is reliably above about 65°F, and keep them well watered for the first week or two while they root in, since they often wilt at first and then recover.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: You grow sweet potatoes from slips, which are rooted sprouts, not from seedlings you started indoors, so there is not much to harden off. If your slips came from a greenhouse, set them in the shade for a day or two first. Plant them out only after all frost is past and the soil has warmed to about 65°F, and keep them watered for the first week or two. They often wilt at first and then perk up, which is normal.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Sweet potatoes are grown from slips: rooted sprouts pulled from a bedded seed root, not from seed and not from seed-potato-style pieces. Buy certified, disease-free and weevil-free slips, or bed a healthy root in warm, moist medium about 6 weeks ahead and pull the sprouts once they have roots. Set slips 3 to 4 inches deep with two or more nodes buried, spacing them 12 to 18 inches apart on ridges or mounds in rows 3 to 4 feet apart, once all frost danger has passed and the soil is above about 65°F (70 to 80°F is better). There is no indoor seed-starting step; the slip itself is the transplant. In short-season areas, planting through black plastic warms the soil and buys extra growing days.
start_method.notes_beginner: Grow sweet potatoes from slips, which are rooted sprouts. You can buy them as certified disease-free plants, or grow your own by half-burying a healthy sweet potato in warm, damp soil about 6 weeks ahead and pulling off the sprouts once they have roots. Plant the slips 3 to 4 inches deep, with a couple of the leaf joints buried, spacing them 12 to 18 inches apart along ridges or mounds in rows about 3 to 4 feet apart. Wait until all frost is past and the soil has warmed to about 65°F. There is nothing to start from seed indoors. In cool-summer areas, laying down black plastic warms the soil and gives you extra time.

container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: Volume and depth matter, and so does room for the vines to spill over the sides. Use a large tub or grow bag of at least 15 gallons (20 or more is better) and at least 12 inches deep, so the storage roots have room to form. Choose a compact bush variety such as Vardaman or a bush Porto Rico for containers; full-size vining types quickly outgrow a pot. Fabric grow bags drain and aerate well and make harvest easy, since you simply tip them out.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Use a big, deep container so the sweet potatoes have room to form, and expect the vines to trail over the sides. A tub or grow bag of at least 15 gallons (bigger is better) and at least 12 inches deep works. Pick a compact bush variety like Vardaman, because the full-size vining kinds are too big for a pot. Fabric grow bags are easy, drain well, and let you just tip the container out to harvest.

drainage.saucer_practice_seasoned: Do not let the container stand in a saucer of water. Sweet potatoes rot in waterlogged mix, so ensure free drainage and empty any saucer after watering.
drainage.saucer_practice_beginner: Do not let the pot sit in a tray of water. Soggy soil rots sweet potatoes, so make sure the water drains out and empty the saucer after you water.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Use a loose, well-drained potting mix, not heavy garden soil, which packs down and stays too wet in a container.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in some compost, but keep nitrogen low so you grow roots and not just vines. Keep the mix loose so the sweet potatoes can swell and the water drains freely.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: container_potting_mix
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Use a light, free-draining potting mix amended with compost and only a modest, low-nitrogen fertilizer. Avoid heavy garden soil, which compacts and waterlogs in a container, and avoid rich nitrogen, which grows vine at the expense of roots.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Containers dry out faster than the ground, so check daily in warm weather and keep the mix evenly moist while the sweet potatoes are forming. Do not let it swing between bone-dry and soaked, which makes the roots crack, and never let it stay waterlogged.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Potted sweet potatoes need only light feeding because too much nitrogen grows all vine. Mix a little low-nitrogen fertilizer in at planting and feed sparingly, if at all, during the season.
container_notes.notes_beginner: Sweet potatoes grow well in large containers, which is handy if your soil is heavy clay or you are short on space. Use a deep tub or grow bag of at least 15 gallons with drainage holes, fill it with loose mix, plant a slip or two of a compact bush variety, and let the vines trail. Keep the mix evenly moist but never soggy, feed lightly, and tip the container out to harvest when the leaves yellow or frost threatens.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Sweet potatoes are well suited to a large container and a good option on heavy clay or in small spaces. Use a 15 gallon or larger tub or grow bag at least 12 inches deep with drainage holes, filled with a loose, free-draining mix; plant one or two slips of a compact bush variety (Vardaman, bush Porto Rico) and let the vines trail over the sides. Keep moisture even but never waterlogged, feed only lightly to avoid all-vine growth, and harvest by tipping out the container when foliage yellows or frost approaches.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry far faster than beds, so check the top inch or two daily in warm weather and water to keep the mix evenly moist but never waterlogged, since sweet potatoes rot in a saturated pot and crack under a dry-then-soaked cycle.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Frequent watering leaches nutrients from a container, but keep feeding restrained: incorporate a modest low-nitrogen fertilizer at planting and feed sparingly during growth, since excess nitrogen in a pot grows rampant vine and few roots.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering container can help hold the even moisture sweet potatoes want during root bulking, but it must drain freely: sweet potatoes rot in a constantly saturated reservoir, so use it carefully, never let the mix stay waterlogged, and choose a deep, roomy container and a bush variety.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot can keep the moisture steady while the sweet potatoes are forming, which helps, but it must not keep the soil soaking wet or the roots rot. Use a deep, roomy container and a compact bush variety.

recommended: Beauregard: orange-fleshed, fast and high-yielding (about 90 to 100 days), widely adapted and a reliable first choice
Covington: orange, rose-skinned, excellent storage and root-knot nematode resistance (about 95 to 110 days)
Centennial: classic orange, root-knot nematode and wireworm tolerant, good for shorter seasons (about 90 to 110 days)
Georgia Jet: very fast (about 90 to 100 days), a top pick for short northern seasons
Jewel: high-yielding orange keeper, longer season (about 120 to 135 days)
Vardaman: compact bush habit, space-saving and good for containers (about 100 days)
Murasaki and other Japanese types: purple skin, pale flesh, nutty flavor, nematode resistant (about 100 to 120 days)
O'Henry: creamy white-fleshed sport of Beauregard
varieties.note_seasoned: Choose by maturity and your climate. In short-season and northern gardens, lean on the fastest orange types (Georgia Jet, Beauregard, Centennial) and warm the soil with black plastic. Where the season is long, higher-yielding keepers like Jewel and Covington size up and store well. Covington and Centennial carry useful root-knot nematode resistance, and Sumor is a Fusarium-wilt-resistant option where that disease occurs. For containers or tight beds, the compact bush type Vardaman saves space. Beyond the standard orange types, there are pale-fleshed heirlooms, purple-skinned Japanese types (Murasaki), and deep-purple-fleshed varieties. Always start from certified disease-free and weevil-free slips.
varieties.note_beginner: Pick a variety for your area and how long your season is. In cooler, shorter-season gardens, choose the fastest kinds (Georgia Jet, Beauregard, Centennial) and warm the soil with black plastic. Where summers are long, bigger keepers like Jewel and Covington do well and store for months. If nematodes are a problem, pick a resistant variety like Covington or Centennial. For a pot or a small bed, the compact bush type Vardaman is ideal. There are also white, purple-skinned Japanese, and purple-fleshed types to try. Always buy certified disease-free slips, not sprouts off a grocery-store sweet potato.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Do not plant sweet potatoes where sweet potatoes grew recently, which builds up soilborne Fusarium wilt, black rot, scurf, and the sweet potato weevil. Also avoid following ground recently in pasture, lawn, or corn, where wireworms are numerous and scar the roots, and avoid heavily manured or high-nitrogen beds, which grow vine over roots. Where root-knot nematode is present, keep sweet potatoes out of beds that grew other susceptible hosts. The standard guideline is a 3 to 4 year gap before sweet potatoes return to a bed.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Do not grow sweet potatoes where you grew sweet potatoes in the last few years, because soil diseases and the sweet potato weevil pile up. Also avoid beds that were lawn, grass, or corn recently, where wireworms live and damage the roots, and skip beds with fresh manure or lots of nitrogen, which grow leaves instead of roots. Wait about 3 to 4 years before sweet potatoes go back in a bed.
good_after: Legumes such as beans and southern peas
Small grains such as rye or wheat as a cover crop
Brassicas such as cabbage and broccoli
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate sweet potatoes on a 3 to 4 year cycle, keeping them out of a bed for several seasons to break the buildup of Fusarium wilt, black rot, scurf, root-knot nematode, and the sweet potato weevil. Following a legume (which adds nitrogen) or a clean, non-host crop is ideal. Avoid planting into ground recently in sod, grass, or corn, which harbors wireworms, and avoid heavily manured beds, which favor rampant vine and soft rots.
rotation.note_beginner: Move your sweet potatoes to a different spot each year and do not put them back in the same bed for about 3 to 4 years. This keeps soil diseases, nematodes, and the sweet potato weevil from building up. Planting after beans or peas is great, since those add nitrogen. Avoid beds that were just lawn, grass, or corn, where wireworms live.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Once cured, sweet potatoes are best kept at warm room-to-cellar temperatures, roughly 55 to 60°F in a dark, well-ventilated spot, where they hold for months. Ordinary heated-room temperatures (68 to 75°F) are fine for a few weeks but shorten storage and can encourage sprouting; keep only what you will use soon on the counter and store the rest in a cooler pantry or cellar.
storage.room_temp_beginner: After curing, keep sweet potatoes in a cool but not cold spot, ideally around 55 to 60°F, in the dark with some airflow, where they last for months. A normal warm room is fine for a couple of weeks but shortens their life, so keep a few on the counter and store the rest somewhere cooler like a pantry or cellar.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Do not refrigerate sweet potatoes. Below about 50 to 55°F they suffer chilling injury: the flesh develops off-flavors, hard cores that will not soften when cooked, internal browning, and a greater tendency to rot. This is the opposite of many vegetables. A cool pantry or cellar near 55 to 60°F, never the refrigerator, is the right place for raw sweet potatoes.
storage.fridge_beginner: Keep sweet potatoes out of the fridge. When they get colder than about 50 to 55°F they get damaged: they taste off, stay hard in the middle even after cooking, and rot faster. This is different from most vegetables. Store them in a cool pantry or cellar around 55 to 60°F instead, never the refrigerator.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Raw sweet potatoes do not freeze well. Freeze only after cooking (baked, mashed, or as prepared dishes), where they keep for several months.
storage.freezer_beginner: Do not freeze raw sweet potatoes. Freeze them only after cooking, like baked or mashed, and they keep for several months.
storage.notes_seasoned: Curing is essential and is the opposite of potato storage. Right after digging, cure the roots warm and humid, about 80 to 85°F at 85 to 90 percent humidity for roughly 1 to 2 weeks (5 to 7 days minimum), which heals skin nicks, sets a protective skin, and converts starch to sugar so the flesh turns sweet. A simple home method is a warm room with the roots in a container loosely covered to hold humidity. After curing, store in the dark at about 55 to 60°F with high humidity and good ventilation, where a well-cured crop keeps 6 months or more. Never store below about 50 to 55°F or refrigerate (chilling injury), and do not wash until use or store bruised or diseased roots.
storage.notes_beginner: Sweet potatoes must be cured before storing, and this is opposite to how you store regular potatoes. Right after digging, keep them somewhere warm and humid, about 80 to 85°F and quite damp, for 1 to 2 weeks. Curing heals the skins and turns the starch to sugar, which is what makes them sweet. A warm room with the roots in a loosely covered box works at home. Then store them in the dark around 55 to 60°F with some airflow, where they keep for 6 months or more. Never put them in the fridge or anywhere below about 50 to 55°F, because the cold ruins them. Do not wash them until you use them.

growth_stages.name: Slip establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Freshly set slips that often wilt for the first several days, then recover, green up, and put out new leaves as they root in. Little top growth happens yet; the plant is building roots. Warm soil speeds this along.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The slips you planted will droop for the first few days, which is normal, then perk up and start growing new leaves once they have rooted. Not much happens above ground yet while they get established.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep the soil evenly moist while slips root in, and shade or water in the heat of the day if they wilt hard. Protect from any late frost, which kills the tender foliage. Replace any slips that fail to take within the first week or two.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil damp while the slips root, and water them in the afternoon if they wilt badly. Cover them if a late frost threatens, since frost kills the leaves. If a slip does not perk up after a week or so, replace it.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have your sweet potato slips rooted in and started new growth? Note the date.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your sweet potato slips perked up and started growing? Jot down the date.

growth_stages.name: Vine growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Vigorous vines that begin to run and sprawl across the bed, rooting at the leaf nodes where they touch soil and quickly forming a dense groundcover. This canopy is what will feed the storage roots.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plants send out long vines that spread across the ground and root where the leaf joints touch the soil, soon covering the bed in leaves. This leafy growth is building the plant that will make your sweet potatoes.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep the bed weeded until the vines close over and shade out weeds themselves. Side-dress lightly with a low-nitrogen feed as the vines run if growth is weak, but do not overfeed nitrogen. In small beds, you can lift and reposition vines so they do not root everywhere, though it is not essential.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep weeds down until the vines spread and cover the ground, after which they smother most weeds. If the plants look weak, feed lightly with a low-nitrogen fertilizer, but do not overdo it or you will get all leaves. Water evenly.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are the vines running and covering the bed? Note how the canopy is filling in.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are the vines spreading out and covering the ground yet?

growth_stages.name: Storage root formation
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Full vine cover above ground while, out of sight, the storage roots begin to swell along the buried stem. This is when the plant sets how many roots it will make, so even moisture and restrained nitrogen matter most now.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The vines are full and leafy above ground, and underneath, the sweet potatoes are starting to form and swell along the buried stem. You cannot see it, but this is when the plant decides how many roots it will make.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Hold steady, even moisture now that roots are forming, and keep nitrogen restrained, since excess nitrogen at this stage grows vine instead of roots. Keep the bed watered through dry spells but never waterlogged.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the watering steady now that the sweet potatoes are starting to form, and do not add much nitrogen, which would grow leaves instead of roots. Water through dry spells but do not let the bed get soggy.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: The storage roots are forming now. How is the vine canopy holding up?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: The sweet potatoes are starting to form underground now. How do the plants look?

growth_stages.name: Root bulking
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Storage roots sizing up underground while the vines stay green and full. This is the critical window for yield: even moisture and warm soil now build root size and quality. You can carefully lift a plant to check root size toward the end of the window.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The sweet potatoes are growing bigger underground while the vines stay green and leafy. This is the most important time for a good harvest. Toward the end you can gently dig at the edge of a plant to see how big the roots are getting.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture even and steady while roots bulk, the critical period for size and quality, then begin easing off water in the last couple of weeks. Warm soil favors bulking, so this is a strength in hot regions. Keep an eye out for the sweet potato weevil in the South.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the water steady while the sweet potatoes size up, which is the most important time, then start cutting back on water in the last couple of weeks. Hot weather actually helps now. In the South, watch for the sweet potato weevil.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have you checked root size yet? Note how the bulking is coming along.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you dug gently to check how big the sweet potatoes are getting?

growth_stages.name: Maturity and harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Roots that have reached full size, about 90 to 120 days from transplanting, often with the oldest leaves beginning to yellow. There is no dramatic die-back signal as with potato; you harvest on days-to-maturity and, above all, before frost, since a hard frost kills the vines and cold soil damages the roots.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The sweet potatoes reach full size about 3 to 4 months after planting, and the older leaves may start to yellow. Unlike regular potatoes, the tops do not clearly die back, so you dig based on the calendar and, most importantly, before frost, because frost kills the vines and cold soil hurts the roots.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Ease off watering as harvest nears. Dig on a dry day once roots reach size and before the first frost, loosening carefully with a fork well outside the plant so you do not spear or bruise roots. Handle them gently, let them dry briefly out of the sun, then cure warm and humid before storage. If frost catches the vines, cut them off and dig within a day or two.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Stop watering as harvest nears. Dig on a dry day once the roots are big enough and before the first frost, loosening the soil with a fork well away from the plant so you do not stab the sweet potatoes. Handle them gently, let them dry off out of the sun, then cure them warm and humid before storing. If frost hits the vines, cut them off and dig within a day or two.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have you harvested your sweet potatoes? Note the date and the yield.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you dug your sweet potatoes yet? Write down the date and how many you got.

establishment.text_seasoned: Plant only certified disease-free and weevil-free slips, not sprouts off a grocery-store root, which can carry the sweet potato weevil, viruses, and soilborne disease. Set slips 3 to 4 inches deep with two or more nodes buried, and keep them watered while they root, since early wilting is normal.
establishment.text_beginner: Use certified disease-free slips from a garden supplier, not sprouts from a store-bought sweet potato, which can bring in the sweet potato weevil and disease. Plant them 3 to 4 inches deep with a couple of leaf joints buried, and keep them watered while they root. It is normal for them to wilt at first.
establishment.author: plant

establishment.text_seasoned: Wait for warm soil: set slips only after all frost danger has passed and the soil is above about 65°F, ideally 70 to 80°F. Sweet potatoes are frost tender and stall in cold soil, so there is no benefit to rushing. In short-season areas, black plastic mulch warms the soil and buys extra days.
establishment.text_beginner: Wait until it is warm: plant slips only after all frost is past and the soil has warmed to at least 65°F, ideally 70 to 80°F. Sweet potatoes are killed by frost and sulk in cold soil, so there is no point planting early. In cool-summer areas, black plastic warms the soil and gives you more growing time.
establishment.author: plant

vine_growth.text_seasoned: Feed lightly and keep nitrogen low. A light side-dressing of a low-nitrogen fertilizer such as 5-10-10 as the vines run is plenty; heavy nitrogen and fresh manure grow rampant vine and few storage roots.
vine_growth.text_beginner: Feed lightly, and go easy on nitrogen. A little low-nitrogen fertilizer like 5-10-10 as the vines spread is enough. Too much nitrogen or fresh manure grows a jungle of leaves and hardly any sweet potatoes.
vine_growth.author: plant

vine_growth.text_seasoned: Keep the bed weeded until the vines close over, after which the dense canopy shades out most weeds on its own. Avoid deep cultivation once the vines are running, so you do not disturb the shallow feeder roots.
vine_growth.text_beginner: Keep weeds down until the vines spread and cover the ground, after which they crowd out most weeds themselves. Once the vines are running, do not dig around the plants, which disturbs their roots.
vine_growth.author: plant

root_initiation.text_seasoned: Hold steady, even moisture as the storage roots begin to form, since this window sets how many roots the plant makes. Keep nitrogen restrained now, because excess nitrogen at root formation shifts the plant back toward vine.
root_initiation.text_beginner: Keep the watering steady as the sweet potatoes start to form, because this is when the plant decides how many to make. Do not add much nitrogen now, or the plant goes back to growing leaves instead of roots.
root_initiation.author: plant

root_bulking.text_seasoned: Keep moisture even and moderate while roots bulk, about 1 inch per week, then taper off in the last 2 to 3 weeks. A dry-then-soaked swing now cracks and misshapes the roots, while warm soil favors good sizing.
root_bulking.text_beginner: Keep the watering steady while the sweet potatoes size up, about 1 inch a week, then ease off in the last couple of weeks. Letting the soil go dry and then soaking it now makes the roots crack. Warm weather actually helps them grow.
root_bulking.author: plant

root_bulking.text_seasoned: In the South and Gulf, scout for the sweet potato weevil during bulking and keep the crop away from last year's beds and stored roots. There is no rescue for tunneled roots, so sanitation and certified slips do the real work.
