root_bulking.text_beginner: In the South, watch for the sweet potato weevil while the roots are sizing, and keep the patch away from last year's bed and from stored sweet potatoes. You cannot fix tunneled roots, so clean slips and cleanup are what protect the crop.
root_bulking.author: plant

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest on days-to-maturity (about 90 to 120 days) and before the first frost, since frost kills the vines and cold soil damages the roots and shortens storage. Dig on a dry day with a fork well outside the plant to avoid spearing roots. If frost catches the vines, cut them off and dig within a day or two.
harvest.text_beginner: Dig your sweet potatoes about 3 to 4 months after planting and before the first frost, because frost kills the vines and cold soil hurts the roots. Dig on a dry day with a fork, pushing it in well away from the plant so you do not stab them. If frost hits the vines, cut them off and dig within a day or two.
harvest.author: plant

harvest.text_seasoned: Cure the dug roots warm and humid, about 80 to 85°F at 85 to 90 percent humidity for 1 to 2 weeks, to heal the skins and convert starch to sugar (the step that makes them sweet), then store warm at about 55 to 60°F. Never refrigerate or store below about 50 to 55°F, which causes chilling injury.
harvest.text_beginner: Cure the sweet potatoes warm and humid, about 80 to 85°F and damp, for 1 to 2 weeks so the skins heal and the flesh turns sweet, then store them warm at about 55 to 60°F. Never put them in the fridge or anywhere below about 50 to 55°F, which ruins them.
harvest.author: plant

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to plant sweet potato slips
notifications.title_beginner: Time to plant sweet potato slips
notifications.body_seasoned: Set certified slips out once all frost danger is past and the soil is above about 65°F, usually a few weeks after your last frost. Plant 3 to 4 inches deep, 12 to 18 inches apart on ridges, rows 3 to 4 feet apart.
notifications.body_beginner: Plant your sweet potato slips once all frost is past and the soil has warmed to about 65°F, usually a few weeks after your last frost. Set them 3 to 4 inches deep and about a foot apart on ridges or mounds.

notifications.body_seasoned: Newly set slips often wilt for several days, then recover as they root. Keep the soil evenly moist for the first week or two, and replace any slip that fails to take.
notifications.body_beginner: Sweet potato slips droop for the first few days, which is normal, then perk up as they root. Keep the soil damp for the first week or two, and replace any slip that does not recover.

notifications.title_seasoned: Vines are running, ease off nitrogen
notifications.body_seasoned: As the vines run and cover the bed, keep weeds down until the canopy closes and feed only lightly with a low-nitrogen fertilizer. Too much nitrogen now grows vine at the expense of roots.
notifications.body_beginner: As the vines spread and cover the ground, keep weeds down until they take over, and feed only a little, with a low-nitrogen fertilizer. Too much nitrogen now grows leaves instead of sweet potatoes.

notifications.title_seasoned: Keep watering even as roots bulk
notifications.title_beginner: Water evenly while roots size up
notifications.body_seasoned: As the storage roots bulk, hold even moisture (about 1 inch per week). A dry-then-soaked cycle now cracks and misshapes the roots; taper off water in the final couple of weeks.
notifications.body_beginner: While the sweet potatoes are sizing up, water evenly (about 1 inch a week). Letting the soil dry out and then soaking it makes the roots crack. Ease off water in the last couple of weeks.

notifications.title_seasoned: Your sweet potatoes may be ready
notifications.title_beginner: Check if your sweet potatoes are ready
notifications.body_seasoned: Roots are usually ready about 90 to 120 days after planting. Dig before the first frost, since frost kills the vines and cold soil damages the roots, then cure warm and humid before storage.
notifications.body_beginner: Sweet potatoes are usually ready about 3 to 4 months after planting. Dig them before the first frost, because frost kills the vines and cold soil hurts the roots, then cure them warm before storing.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost kills sweet potato vines
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Sweet potato foliage is frost tender and killed by frost, and cold soil damages the roots. Protect newly set slips from a late spring frost, and in fall, dig before the first frost. If frost catches the vines, cut them off and dig within a day or two.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Sweet potato vines are tender and killed by frost, and cold soil hurts the roots. Cover young slips if a late spring frost threatens, and in fall, dig before the first frost. If frost hits the vines, cut them off and dig within a day or two.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Dry spell, water at establishment and bulking
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Dry weather, keep sweet potatoes watered
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Established sweet potatoes are fairly drought tolerant, but even moisture during slip establishment and root bulking sets root number and size. Do not let the soil go bone dry and then flood it, which cracks the roots.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Grown-in sweet potatoes handle dry spells fairly well, but steady water while the slips establish and while the roots size up makes for a good crop. Do not let the soil go bone dry and then soak it, which cracks the roots.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heavy rain can rot and split roots
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Heavy rain can rot and crack roots
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Waterlogged soil rots the storage roots and drives soft rot and black rot, and a heavy soaking on a near-mature crop can split the roots. Ensure the ridge drains freely, and if the crop is mature, harvest before a prolonged wet spell.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Soggy soil rots sweet potatoes and brings on rot diseases, and a big rain on a ready crop can crack them. Make sure the ridge drains well, and if the roots are ready, dig them before a long wet spell.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Warm, wet weather favors foliar disease
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Warm, damp weather can bring leaf disease
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Prolonged warm, wet, humid weather with leaf wetness favors fungal leaf spots and, in the roots, storage rots. Space and site for airflow, avoid overhead watering late in the day, and start with certified, disease-free slips.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Long spells of warm, damp, humid weather can bring on leaf spots and root rots. Give the plants a sunny, airy spot, avoid wetting the leaves late in the day, and start with certified, disease-free slips.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Lots of vine but few sweet potatoes
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Big vines but few sweet potatoes
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The plants grew lush, sprawling vine but set few or small storage roots. The usual causes are too much nitrogen (which favors foliage over roots), overly rich or heavily manured soil, too much shade, or a season too short and cool for roots to bulk.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The plants made a jungle of leafy vine but few sweet potatoes. This usually comes from too much nitrogen, over-rich soil, too much shade, or a season too short and cool for the roots to size up.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Cut nitrogen and use a low-nitrogen feed such as 5-10-10, avoid fresh manure, give full sun, and grow on ridges. In short-season areas, warm the soil with black plastic and choose a fast variety so roots have time to bulk.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Use less nitrogen and a low-nitrogen fertilizer like 5-10-10, skip fresh manure, give full sun, and grow on ridges. In cooler areas, warm the soil with black plastic and pick a fast variety so the roots have time to grow.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Cracked, knobby, misshapen roots
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Cracked or lumpy sweet potatoes
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Roots grew cracked, knobby, or misshapen from a stop-and-start growth pattern: a dry spell followed by a surge of water, heavy clay soil that resists smooth expansion, or root-knot nematode galling. Uneven moisture during bulking is the most common cause.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The sweet potatoes came out cracked or lumpy because their growth started and stopped, usually from the soil going dry and then wet again, from heavy clay they could not grow through smoothly, or from root-knot nematodes.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Hold even moisture through bulking and taper off before harvest, loosen heavy soil with organic matter or grow on ridges and raised beds, and use nematode-resistant varieties where galling is the cause.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep the watering steady while the roots grow and ease off before harvest, loosen heavy soil with compost or grow on ridges, and use a nematode-resistant variety if knots and cracks keep happening.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Off-flavor, hard core, or rot in storage
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Sweet potatoes went bad in storage
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Stored roots developed off-flavors, hard cores that would not soften when cooked, internal browning, or rot. The usual cause is chilling injury from storing (or refrigerating) below about 50 to 55°F, or skipping the warm, humid curing step that heals skins and sets a protective layer.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The sweet potatoes tasted off, stayed hard in the middle even after cooking, or rotted in storage. This usually happens when they were kept too cold (like in the fridge) below about 50 to 55°F, or were not cured warm and humid first.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Cure warm and humid (about 80 to 85°F, 85 to 90 percent humidity) for 1 to 2 weeks right after harvest, then store at about 55 to 60°F in the dark. Never refrigerate or store below about 50 to 55°F, and do not store bruised or diseased roots.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Cure the roots warm and humid (about 80 to 85°F) for 1 to 2 weeks right after digging, then store them around 55 to 60°F in the dark. Never put them in the fridge or anywhere below about 50 to 55°F, and do not store damaged ones.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Tunneled, bitter roots (sweet potato weevil)
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Tunneled, bitter sweet potatoes
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Roots came up riddled with small holes and dark, spongy tunnels, with a bitter taste and off odor even where damage looked light. This is the sweet potato weevil, whose larvae mine the roots and induce bitter terpenes; it is the most serious sweet potato pest, worst in the South and Gulf.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The sweet potatoes were full of small holes and dark tunnels and tasted bitter, even the parts that looked okay. That is the sweet potato weevil, whose grubs tunnel the roots and make them bitter. It is the worst sweet potato pest, especially in the South.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Start with certified weevil-free slips, rotate well away from last year's beds and from stored roots, and remove every cull and volunteer root after harvest, since the weevil survives in them. Harvest promptly rather than leaving roots in infested soil.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant certified weevil-free slips, move the patch far from last year's bed and from where you store sweet potatoes, and clean up every leftover root after digging, because the weevil lives on in them. Harvest on time.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Small roots from too short a season
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Sweet potatoes stayed small
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Roots stayed small because the warm-season window was too short: slips set into cold soil, a late start, a cool summer, or an early frost cut the growing period below the 90 or more warm days the crop needs to bulk. This is the common outcome in marginal northern and cool-coastal gardens.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The sweet potatoes stayed small because the warm season was too short: cold soil at planting, a late start, a cool summer, or an early frost gave them too little time to size up. This is common in cooler northern and coastal gardens.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Choose the fastest varieties (Georgia Jet, Beauregard, Centennial), warm the soil with black plastic, plant as soon as the soil is reliably warm, and give the sunniest, most sheltered spot to stretch the effective season.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Pick the fastest varieties (Georgia Jet, Beauregard, Centennial), warm the soil with black plastic, plant as soon as the soil is truly warm, and use the sunniest, most sheltered spot to give them the longest possible season.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Roughly 3 to 6 storage roots, about 1 to 2 pounds, per plant in good conditions, varying widely with variety, season length, and care. By the row, a home crop often runs about 1 to 1.5 pounds per foot of row on a good site.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: About 3 to 6 sweet potatoes, roughly 1 to 2 pounds, from each plant when things go well, though it varies a lot with the variety and the season. A row gives you something like a pound or more per foot on a good site.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: A sweet potato planting matures over a single window, about 90 to 120 days, and is dug once when the roots reach size and before frost. It is not a repeat-harvest crop; for a longer supply, cure and store the crop, which keeps for months, or in frost-free regions stagger plantings.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: A sweet potato planting is ready all at once, about 3 to 4 months after planting, and you dig it when the roots are sized and before frost. It does not keep producing after that, so cure and store the crop, which lasts for months.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Sweet potatoes are grown fresh from slips each season, so there is no first-year-versus-later difference as with perennials; results depend on certified slips, a long warm season, loose well-drained ridges, even moisture, and restrained nitrogen.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Sweet potatoes are grown fresh each year from slips, so your first crop can do as well as any later one. What matters is good slips, a long warm season, loose well-drained ridges, steady water, and going easy on nitrogen.
factors_seasoned: Season length and warmth: sweet potatoes need about 90 or more warm, frost-free days, and a short or cool season caps yield.
Nitrogen balance: excess nitrogen grows vine at the expense of storage roots.
Even moisture during bulking: drought-then-flood cycles cut yield and crack the roots.
Certified, disease-free and weevil-free slips: virus or weevil brought in on slips undercuts the crop from the start.
Well-drained ridges: waterlogged, heavy soil rots roots and forces short, knobby shapes.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting assigns root crops like sweet potatoes to the waning moon, the period after the full moon, on the folk principle that the changing lunar pull favors below-ground growth. This is long-standing gardening folklore with no controlled scientific evidence of an effect on sweet potato yield. Plant sweet potatoes by soil temperature and your warm-season window, not the moon; this is recorded only for growers who follow the tradition.

primary.name: UGA Extension Home Garden Sweet Potatoes (Circular 1014)
UH Manoa CTAHR Bulletin B-91 (home-garden vegetables for Hawaii)

succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Sweet potatoes are not a succession crop. They are planted once per warm-season window from slips and dug as a single crop when the roots reach size and before frost, not sown in repeated short intervals. In long-season and frost-free regions a grower can stagger plantings, but each is a discrete seasonal crop rather than a staggered succession, so no per-zone succession count applies.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the cold-winter North, sweet potatoes are a stretch but doable in the warmer zones. Wait until all frost is past and the soil is warm (usually late May into June), then plant slips. Warm the soil first with black plastic, which also gives you extra time, and choose the fastest varieties like Georgia Jet, Beauregard, or Centennial. The vines grow through the summer, and you dig the crop in early fall before the first frost, since frost kills the vines. In the coldest zones (3 and 4) the season is short, so expect a lighter, smaller crop; zones 6 and 7 do better.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Sweet potatoes are marginal in the cold-winter North and depend on stretching the warm season. Set slips only after all frost danger passes and the soil is reliably above about 65°F, generally late May into June, and warm the soil with black plastic to add growing days (USU). Choose the fastest-maturing varieties (Georgia Jet, Beauregard, Centennial), since the crop needs about 90 or more warm, frost-free days. The frost-tender vines run through summer, and the crop is dug in early fall before the first frost. Zones 3 to 4 are the tightest and may not reliably size a full crop; zones 6 to 7 are more dependable. Windows modeled on USU short-season guidance + the frost anchors and flagged for review.

Plant slips after the last frost once the soil is warm, from mid-April into June, and the vines run happily through the hot, humid summer that sweet potatoes love. Dig the crop in late summer through fall, before the first frost. Watch for the sweet potato weevil, the main pest here, by starting with certified weevil-free slips and cleaning up leftover roots. Cure the crop warm and humid before storing.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: The Southeast and Gulf are sweet potato's stronghold. Plant slips once frost is past and the soil is above about 65°F: Clemson gives coastal South Carolina April 15 to June 15 and the Piedmont May 1 to June 15, University of Georgia mid-April in south Georgia to early May farther north, and NC State plants May 1 to July 15. The heat-loving vines run straight through the hot, humid summer with no midseason pause, and the crop is dug from late summer into fall before the first frost. The sweet potato weevil is the key pest, so certified weevil-free slips and strict sanitation matter here. ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: California's hot inland valleys suit sweet potatoes well, since they love the dry summer heat. Plant slips in mid to late spring once frost is past and the soil is warm, and the vines grow right through the hot summer with no break. Dig the crop in late summer into fall before the first frost. Just keep the plants watered while the roots size up.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: California's hot interior valleys (Sacramento and San Joaquin) are well suited to sweet potato, which thrives in the dry summer heat that stalls other crops. Plant slips from mid to late spring once the soil warms, and the heat-loving vines run through summer with no midseason pause, with harvest from late summer into fall before the first frost. Keep irrigation even during root bulking, since the dry heat dries the soil fast. The exact month windows are modeled on sweet potato's warm-season physiology (Clemson, USU) plus the frost anchors and flagged for review.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: The cool, foggy north and central California coast is a hard place for sweet potatoes, which really want heat the coast often lacks. Plant slips in the warmest, sunniest, most sheltered spot in late spring or early summer, use a fast variety, and warm the soil with black plastic. Expect a smaller, later crop than inland gardeners get, and in a very cool, foggy summer the roots may stay small.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: California's cool, foggy north and central coast is marginal for sweet potato, which needs the heat the marine climate often withholds. Plant slips in the warmest stretch of the year (late spring into early summer) in the sunniest, most sheltered site, warm the soil with black plastic, and choose the fastest varieties. Harvest in fall before the first frost. Where summers stay cool and foggy, roots may barely size up. Windows modeled on sweet potato's warm-season physiology (Clemson, USU) plus the frost anchors and flagged for review.

ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: The California desert valleys (Imperial and Coachella) are excellent for sweet potato, which thrives in the extreme heat that forces a midsummer pause on cucurbits and tomatoes. fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: In peninsular Florida, sweet potatoes grow over the long warm season. Plant slips from spring through June, and the vines run through the hot, humid summer that sweet potatoes love. Harvest from summer into fall. In frost-free South Florida you can plant over a long stretch and harvest much of the year. Watch for the sweet potato weevil and root-knot nematodes, and start with certified slips.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: On the Florida peninsula, sweet potato is a warm-season crop planted from spring through June (UF/IFAS: anytime after frost through the end of June; about 120 to 150 days), with the heat-loving vines running through the hot, humid summer and harvest from summer into fall. In frost-free deep South Florida, plantings can be staggered over a long window for a harvest across much of the year. The sweet potato weevil and root-knot nematode are the key concerns, so certified slips and rotation matter.
