crops.description_seasoned: Sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas) is a warm-season, frost-tender member of the morning glory family (Convolvulaceae), not a nightshade and unrelated to the ordinary potato despite the shared name. It is grown for its swollen storage roots and planted not from seed or tubers but from slips: rooted sprouts pulled from a bedded seed root and set out only after all frost danger has passed and the soil is warm, above about 65°F. The plant is a vigorous, sprawling groundcover, running long vines that root at the nodes, and it is grown on raised ridges or mounds that drain well and give the roots room to expand. The crop needs a long, hot season, roughly 90 to 120 frost-free days, and it relishes the summer heat that stalls many other vegetables, so the warm South, Gulf, Florida, and the low deserts are its stronghold while short-season northern gardens are marginal and lean on black plastic and fast varieties. Feed sparingly and keep nitrogen low, since rich ground grows rampant vine and few roots. The crop is dug before the first frost, which kills the vines, then cured warm and humid (about 80 to 85°F at high humidity for one to two weeks) to heal the skins and turn starch to sugar, and stored warm, near 55 to 60°F. Sweet potatoes are damaged by cold and must never be refrigerated or stored below about 50 to 55°F, the opposite of white potato storage. The young leaves and shoots are also edible as a cooked green.
crops.description_beginner: Sweet potatoes are a warm-weather crop grown for the sweet, starchy roots that form underground. Despite the name, they are not related to regular potatoes; they belong to the morning glory family. You do not grow them from seed or from tubers. Instead you plant slips, which are rooted sprouts, set out only after all frost is past and the soil is warm. The plants send out long, trailing vines that cover the ground, so they are grown on ridges or mounds with plenty of room. Sweet potatoes need a long, hot summer (about 3 to 4 months of warm, frost-free weather) and they love heat, so the warm South, Gulf, Florida, and the desert Southwest are the best places to grow them, while cooler northern gardens are a stretch and use black plastic and fast varieties. Go easy on fertilizer, especially nitrogen, or you get lots of vine and few sweet potatoes. Dig the crop before the first frost, which kills the vines, then cure the roots somewhere warm and humid for a week or two, which heals the skins and makes them sweet, and store them warm, around 55 to 60°F. Never put sweet potatoes in the fridge or anywhere cold, which ruins them. This is the opposite of how you store regular potatoes. The young leaves are also good to eat as a cooked green.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Sweet potatoes are harvested by days-to-maturity and, above all, before frost, not by a die-back signal. The crop is usually ready about 90 to 120 days from transplanting slips, when the roots have reached full size; the oldest leaves may yellow, but the vines do not clearly die back the way potato tops do. Dig before the first fall frost, since frost kills the vines and cold soil damages the roots and shortens storage. Loosen the soil with a fork well outside the plant so you do not spear or bruise the roots, lift them gently, and handle them carefully, since sweet potatoes bruise easily and skins are thin at harvest. Let them dry briefly out of direct sun, do not wash them, then cure warm and humid, about 80 to 85°F for one to two weeks, before storing. If a frost catches the vines, cut them off and dig within a day or two so rot does not travel down into the roots.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: You harvest sweet potatoes by the calendar and, most importantly, before frost, not by watching the tops die back. They are usually ready about 3 to 4 months after planting, when the roots are full size; the older leaves may yellow, but unlike regular potatoes the vines do not obviously die down. Dig before the first fall frost, because frost kills the vines and cold soil hurts the roots. Loosen the soil with a fork well away from the plant so you do not stab the sweet potatoes, lift them gently, and handle them carefully because they bruise easily and the skins are thin at first. Let them dry off out of the sun, do not wash them, then cure them somewhere warm and humid for a week or two before storing. If frost hits the vines, cut them off and dig within a day or two.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Sweet potato quality starts with loose, warm, well-drained soil built up into ridges or mounds. Work the bed deep, incorporate compost, and form ridges 8 to 10 inches high, which drain well, warm quickly, and give the storage roots room to expand smoothly; heavy clay stays cold and wet, rots roots, and forces short, knobby shapes, and is best improved with organic matter or grown in raised ridges. Aim for a slightly acidic pH, roughly 5.8 to 6.5. Keep nitrogen low and avoid fresh manure, which drive rampant vine at the expense of roots; use a low-nitrogen fertilizer such as 5-10-10 and modest compost. Set slips 3 to 4 inches deep, 12 to 18 inches apart along the ridge in rows 3 to 4 feet apart, once all frost is past and the soil is above about 65°F. In short-season areas, lay black plastic to warm the soil and add growing days.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Getting the soil right matters for sweet potatoes. Loosen the bed deep, mix in compost, and mound the soil up into ridges about 8 to 10 inches high, which drain well, warm up faster, and give the roots room to grow long and smooth. Heavy, cold, soggy clay rots the roots and makes them lumpy, so use ridges or a raised bed if your soil is clay. Keep the soil slightly acidic (pH about 5.8 to 6.5). Go easy on fertilizer and skip fresh manure, which grow leaves instead of roots; use a low-nitrogen fertilizer like 5-10-10 and a little compost. Plant the slips 3 to 4 inches deep and 12 to 18 inches apart along the ridge, in rows about 3 to 4 feet apart, once all frost is past and the soil has warmed to about 65°F. In cooler areas, lay down black plastic to warm the soil and buy extra time.

crops.name: Cauliflower

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Cauliflower grows best in rich, well-drained soil with lots of compost worked in, and it needs steady, even moisture the whole way. More than most vegetables, cauliflower hates being stressed: if it dries out or runs short on food even briefly, it can quit growing and form a tiny, useless head early (called buttoning). Soil that holds moisture but still drains well is ideal.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Cauliflower is a heavy feeder that demands a fertile, well-drained loam high in organic matter held at steady, even moisture. It is the fussiest of the cole crops: any check to growth from drought, low fertility, or a stalled transplant can trigger buttoning (premature, undersized curds), so the goal is uninterrupted, vigorous growth from set-out to harvest. Work in compost before planting and aim for a moisture-retentive but well-draining bed, since waterlogging invites root maggots and rots while drought stress ruins the curd. Clubroot, the key brassica soil disease, is far more likely in acidic, poorly drained ground.

ph.note_beginner: Cauliflower grows best in soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, about 6.0 to 7.0. A simple soil test tells you where you stand. If you have had clubroot, a soil disease, keeping the soil closer to neutral (up toward 7.0) helps hold it back.
ph.note_seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0 (UMN and Iowa State both give 6 to 7; Clemson lists 5.8 to 6.5). Cauliflower tolerates a wider 5.5 to 7.5 band. Clubroot, the major brassica soil disease, is far more likely in acidic soil below about 6.5, so where it is a concern lime acidic ground well ahead of planting and hold the pH toward neutral.

fertilizer.frequency: once or twice during the season
fertilizer.timing: starter at transplanting, then side-dress about 3 to 4 weeks later as the plant builds its frame
fertilizer.example_product: Blood meal, 33-0-0, calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0), or a balanced 10-10-10 vegetable fertilizer
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Cauliflower is a heavy feeder, and steady fertility matters even more than with other cole crops because a hungry plant buttons, forming a tiny premature curd instead of a full one. Work a balanced fertilizer such as 5-10-10 or 10-10-10 into the bed before planting (Clemson: 5-10-10 at 3 pounds per 100 square feet), then side-dress with nitrogen about 3 to 4 weeks after transplanting, using roughly 33-0-0 or calcium nitrate. Keep the plant growing vigorously and without interruption right up to curd formation; the most common cause of failed curds is any stall in growth from low fertility or uneven water. On acid or sandy soils, a boron and molybdenum deficiency can cause hollow stem and whiptail, so a soil rich in organic matter at a near-neutral pH is the best insurance.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Cauliflower needs rich soil and regular feeding to grow a good head. The big rule is to never let it get hungry or stressed: a plant that runs short on food or water stops growing and makes a tiny, useless head early. Mix a balanced fertilizer into the soil before planting, then feed with a nitrogen fertilizer about 3 to 4 weeks after planting out. Keep it growing steadily the whole way.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time to side-dress your cauliflower with nitrogen to keep it growing without a stall.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Time to feed your cauliflower.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: High N to drive steady, uninterrupted growth to a full curd: a 5-10-10 or 10-10-10 starter worked in before planting, then a nitrogen side-dress such as 33-0-0 or calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0) about 3 to 4 weeks after transplanting.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 at planting, then a nitrogen feed a few weeks after planting out to keep it growing strong.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: Work in 5-10-10 at about 3 pounds per 100 square feet before planting, then side-dress with about 1 pound of 33-0-0 (or roughly a half cup of 21-0-0 per 10 feet of row) about 3 to 4 weeks after transplanting, watered in alongside the plants.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Follow the label rate for a balanced vegetable fertilizer at planting, then a nitrogen feed beside the plants a few weeks after they go out.

companions.note_beginner: Cauliflower does well next to aromatic herbs, onions, and quick crops you can tuck in while the plants are small. The most important rule is to keep it away from other cabbage-family plants, which share the same pests and diseases.
companions.note_seasoned: Most cauliflower companion pairings are traditional rather than trial-tested. The ones worth acting on are practical: aromatic herbs and alliums as scent-based deterrents for cabbage-family pests, small flowering plants such as sweet alyssum and dill to draw the parasitic wasps and hoverflies that attack cabbage aphids and caterpillars (a habitat tactic Clemson recommends for cole crops), and quick crops like lettuce that use the open ground while the cauliflower fills in. The well-grounded caution is to separate cauliflower from other brassicas, which share clubroot and the whole cabbage-family pest complex, a rotation and disease principle more than a tested adjacency effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Sweet alyssum
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Sweet alyssum makes lots of tiny flowers that bring in helpful insects which eat aphids and caterpillars, two major cauliflower pests.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Clemson recommends planting small flowers like sweet alyssum and dill near cole crops to attract beneficial parasites and predators; the specific alyssum-cauliflower pairing is not trial-isolated, so medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Sweet alyssum is one of the better-supported cole-crop companions. Its low mats of tiny flowers are a classic insectary plant, drawing the hoverflies, lacewings, and parasitic wasps that prey on cabbage aphids and the cabbage-family caterpillars, and Clemson specifically advises small flowers like alyssum near cole crops for biological control. Let it self-sow along the bed edge.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Dill
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Dill's flowers attract helpful insects that hunt the aphids and caterpillars that bother cauliflower.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Clemson names dill among the small flowers that attract beneficial parasites to cole crops; aromatic umbels are widely extension-noted for recruiting parasitoid wasps and hoverflies. Dill-cauliflower not trial-isolated, so medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Dill works for cauliflower mainly through beneficial insects. Its umbel flowers draw the parasitoid wasps and hoverflies that attack cabbage aphids and cabbageworms, and Clemson lists dill among the flowers to plant near cole crops for natural control. Let some flower, and keep it off to the side so it does not shade the plants.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Onions
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Onions are a traditional neighbor for cole crops; their strong smell is said to help confuse and deter cabbage pests.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Allium scent-masking of brassica pests is a long-standing companion tradition with partial mechanistic support; not trial-isolated for cauliflower, so low.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Alliums are a traditional brassica companion, their pungent scent thought to mask the crop from the cabbage pests that hunt partly by smell. Shallow-rooted and undemanding, onions tuck around young cauliflower without competing for much. Treat it as a low-risk, scent-based aid rather than a proven control.

good_seasoned.name: Sweet alyssum
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A classic insectary plant whose tiny flowers recruit hoverflies, lacewings, and parasitic wasps against cabbage aphids and caterpillars. Clemson recommends small flowers like alyssum near cole crops for biological control.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Clemson advises alyssum/dill near cole crops to attract beneficial parasites; not isolated for cauliflower.

good_seasoned.name: Dill
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Aromatic umbels like dill draw parasitoid wasps and hoverflies that attack cabbage aphids and caterpillars; Clemson lists dill among the flowers to plant near cole crops. Let some flower, and keep it from shading the plants.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Clemson cole-crop beneficial-habitat recommendation; specific dill-cauliflower pairing not trial-isolated.

good_seasoned.name: Onions
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional brassica companion whose scent is thought to deter cabbage pests; shallow-rooted and low-competition. A plausible, low-risk pairing rather than a documented effect.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Allium scent-masking lore for brassicas; not trial-isolated.

good_seasoned.name: Lettuce
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A quick, shallow cool-season crop that uses the open ground and light between young cauliflower plants and is harvested long before they fill in. Space-driven and traditional, not a documented growth effect; the two share no serious pest.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Space-use intercropping lore; no T1 source documents a lettuce-cauliflower benefit.

good_seasoned.name: Nasturtiums
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Often planted as a trap crop for cabbage aphids near brassicas. Trap cropping is a documented principle but is not a tested cauliflower-nasturtium pairing, so treat it as a plausible aid rather than a proven control.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Trap cropping for aphids is a documented mechanism; the specific nasturtium-cauliflower pairing is not formally tested.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Other brassicas
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep cauliflower away from other cabbage-family plants like broccoli, cabbage, brussels sprouts, and kale. They share the same pests and diseases, so grouping them makes problems worse.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Same-family crops share pests and pathogens, so clustering raises pest/disease pressure, and successive brassica planting builds soil-borne clubroot. A sound epidemiological/rotation mechanism rather than a measured antagonism.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Planting cauliflower shoulder to shoulder with its brassica relatives, broccoli, cabbage, brussels sprouts, kale, collards, concentrates the family's shared pests (cabbage aphids, cabbageworms, loopers, harlequin bugs, root maggots) and shared diseases in one spot, and repeated same-family planting lets soil-borne clubroot build up. Spread brassicas out and rotate where they grow each year.

bad_seasoned.name: Other brassicas
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Broccoli, cabbage, brussels sprouts, kale, and the other cole crops share cauliflower's clubroot and cabbage-family pests, so grouping them concentrates disease and pest pressure. A real rotation and disease principle rather than a tested adjacency effect; the practical rule is to spread brassicas out and rotate them.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Shared clubroot and shared cabbage-family pests are extension-documented; the bad-adjacency claim is a known agronomic principle, not formally pair-tested.

bad_seasoned.name: Strawberries
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional caution that brassicas and strawberries inhibit each other. There is no documented mechanism or T1 support; it persists as folklore.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Folk anti-companion claim with no pattern match or T1 support.

pests.name: Cabbageworms, loopers, and diamondback moths
pests.symptoms_beginner: You'll see ragged holes chewed in the leaves, green caterpillars on the plant, and dark droppings, and worst of all, caterpillars and their mess tucked down into the curd, where they are very hard to wash out.
pests.cause_beginner: These are caterpillars that hatch from eggs laid by white butterflies and small moths. They love cabbage-family plants, chew the leaves, and crawl into the head you want to eat.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray Bt, which is safe and targets only caterpillars, or spinosad, and pick caterpillars and eggs off by hand from under the leaves. Spray again after rain, since it washes off.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover plants with a light fabric row cover after planting to keep the butterflies and moths from laying eggs, clear away old cabbage-family plants, and watch for the first white butterflies as your signal to act.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Ragged holes chewed in the leaves with green caterpillars and dark frass; as the curd forms, larvae crawl into it and foul it, the costly damage that is very hard to clean from a tight white curd. Imported cabbageworms are velvety green; cabbage loopers move in a looping arch; diamondback larvae are small and wriggle when disturbed (Clemson rates the diamondback the most numerous cole-crop caterpillar in home gardens).
pests.cause_seasoned: The larvae of the imported cabbageworm, cabbage looper, and diamondback moth feed on brassica foliage and contaminate the curd; the adults are white or brownish butterflies and moths that lay eggs on the leaves. Cauliflower is a primary host for all three.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Spray Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki) or spinosad, which target caterpillars and spare beneficials, and hand-pick larvae and eggs from leaf undersides. Repeat after rain, since Bt breaks down. Tighten control as the curd forms, when contamination of the head is the expensive kind.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Use floating row cover or fine mesh from transplanting to exclude the egg-laying adults, clean up brassica debris that shelters pupae, and scout for the first white butterflies as a spray cue.

pests.name: Cabbage aphids
pests.symptoms_beginner: You'll see clusters of small gray-green insects with a dusty, waxy coating on the new growth and tucked into the curd, where they are very hard to wash out. Leaves may curl and there can be a sticky film.
pests.cause_beginner: Cabbage aphids are tiny insects that suck the plant's juices and breed fast. They love cabbage-family plants and hide down in the curd, which is the part you eat.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Knock colonies off with a strong spray of water and hit the undersides of leaves with insecticidal soap or neem oil, repeating every few days. Welcome ladybugs and lacewings, which eat aphids.
pests.prevention_beginner: Check the growing tips and the developing curd often and act early. Go easy on nitrogen once the curd forms, since soft growth draws them, and clear away old cabbage-family plants after harvest.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: The gray-green, waxy-coated cabbage aphid forms dense colonies on growing tips and leaf undersides and then lodges in the curd, where it contaminates the marketable product with insects and honeydew and is nearly impossible to clean from the tight florets. Curling and distortion of young leaves is common.
pests.cause_seasoned: Brevicoryne brassicae, a brassica-specialist aphid, sucks sap and reproduces rapidly; contamination of the harvested curd with aphids and sticky honeydew is usually the real problem rather than plant stunting. Pressure is heaviest on the long-season fall crop.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Dislodge colonies with a strong jet of water and spray insecticidal soap, neem, or horticultural oil with thorough coverage of leaf undersides; repeat every few days. Conserve natural enemies (the parasitoid Diaeretiella rapae, hoverflies, lady beetles) that suppress this aphid.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Scout growing tips and the curd weekly and catch infestations before aphids colonize the head. Avoid excess nitrogen once the curd sets, use row cover on young plants, and destroy crop debris that carries them over.

pests.name: Cabbage root maggot
pests.symptoms_beginner: New transplants wilt and grow badly or fall over. If you pull one up, you'll find small white maggots eating the roots. It is worst in cool, wet soil.
pests.cause_beginner: A small fly lays eggs at the base of the plant, and the maggots that hatch burrow down and eat the roots. The fly is most active in cool, damp weather, so spring transplants are most at risk.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Once the maggots are in the roots you can't save that plant, so pull and throw away the badly damaged ones. Put your effort into protecting the rest from new eggs.
pests.prevention_beginner: Put a small collar or disk around the base of each transplant to stop the fly from laying eggs there, or use a row cover. Avoid planting into cold, soggy soil, and rotate away from where cabbage-family plants grew.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Transplants wilt, grow poorly, and may collapse; pulling a plant reveals small white maggots tunneling in the roots and lower stem. Damage is worst in cool, wet soil at spring establishment, and a root-checked plant is also far likelier to button.
pests.cause_seasoned: The larvae of the cabbage root fly (Delia radicum) tunnel into brassica roots; the adult lays eggs at the stem base, and the maggots feed below, sometimes killing young plants and opening the door to rots.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no effective rescue once maggots are in the roots; remove and destroy badly affected plants and protect the rest from further egg-laying.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Place a collar or disk around the stem base at transplanting to block egg-laying, or use row cover; avoid planting into cold, wet soil and rotate away from where brassicas grew.

pests.name: Harlequin bug
pests.symptoms_beginner: Shield-shaped black-and-orange (or black-and-red) bugs on the leaves, which develop white or yellow spots, then brown and look tattered. It is mostly a warm-region problem and loves cabbage-family plants.
pests.cause_beginner: The harlequin bug is a colorful stink-bug relative that pierces the leaves and sucks the juices, leaving pale blotches. It strongly prefers cabbage-family plants, especially in the South.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Search out and crush the bugs, their barrel-shaped eggs laid in rows, and the young ones by hand. Use a row cover to keep them off, pull badly infested plants, and clear away weeds and old plants where they hide over winter.
pests.prevention_beginner: Clean up garden debris and cabbage-family weeds where the adults overwinter, use row cover, and consider a trap crop of mustard to lure them away from the main crop, then destroy it.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Shield-shaped bugs up to about 3/8 inch, brightly black-and-yellow or black-and-red, feeding with piercing-sucking mouthparts that leave white stipples; affected leaves brown and look tattered, and heavy feeding wilts and deforms plants. A warm-region brassica specialist.
pests.cause_seasoned: The harlequin bug (Murgantia histrionica) is a true bug that specializes on cole crops, most damaging in the southern United States, where it completes several generations a year and overwinters as an adult in debris and weeds.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick and crush adults, nymphs, and the barrel-shaped egg rows; exclude with floating row cover; remove heavily infested plants. Insecticidal soap, pyrethrum, or neem help where pressure is severe.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Eliminate overwintering sites by removing crop debris and crucifer weeds, use row cover, and deploy an early trap crop of mustard to divert overwintering adults, then destroy it before the main crop is set out.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms_beginner: Lots of tiny round holes in the leaves of young plants, made by small dark beetles that jump away like fleas when you get close. Bad damage can stunt seedlings.
pests.cause_beginner: Flea beetles are small jumping beetles that chew on young cabbage-family leaves. They hurt seedlings most, because a tiny plant can't grow fast enough to recover, and a stunted cauliflower seedling often heads early and badly.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover young plants with a row cover, and if there are a lot of beetles, use a spray such as spinosad. The main goal is to get the seedlings big enough to handle the damage.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover seedlings with row cover from the start, keep them strong with steady water and food so they grow past the damage, and pull nearby weeds in the cabbage family.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny round shot-hole pits chewed in the leaves of young plants; the small dark beetles jump like fleas when disturbed. Heavy feeding stunts or kills seedlings and slows establishment, and a checked cauliflower seedling is prone to buttoning.
pests.cause_seasoned: Flea beetles chew the foliage of young brassicas and are most damaging at the seedling stage; a vigorous transplant generally outgrows them, but a stalled seedling can be set back badly.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Protect seedlings with row cover and spray spinosad if pressure is high; the goal is getting plants past the vulnerable seedling stage without a growth check.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Use row cover from transplanting, keep seedlings vigorous with even water and feeding so they grow through the damage, and clean up weedy brassica relatives nearby.

diseases.name: Clubroot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Plants wilt in the afternoon, stay small and yellowish, and don't bounce back. If you dig one up, the roots are swollen into lumpy, club-shaped knobs.
diseases.cause_beginner: A germ that lives in the soil infects the roots of cabbage-family plants and makes them swell, which stops the plant from taking up water and food. It stays in the soil for years.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There's no cure once a plant has it, so pull and destroy infected plants. Keeping the soil from being too acidic (closer to neutral) helps hold it back, and growing cabbage-family plants only rarely in that spot starves the germ out.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Don't grow cauliflower or other cabbage-family plants in the same spot more than once every few years, longer if you've had clubroot. Keep the soil from being too acidic, improve drainage, and clean soil off your tools.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Plants wilt in the heat of the day, grow stunted and yellowed, and recover poorly; roots are swollen into distorted clubs and galls instead of normal fine roots. A clubroot-checked plant rarely makes a usable curd.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A soilborne organism (Plasmodiophora brassicae) infects brassica roots and forms the galls, which block water and nutrient uptake. It persists in soil for many years, spreads in contaminated soil and water, and infects most readily in acidic soils below pH 6.5.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once plants are infected; remove and destroy them. Raising soil pH toward neutral with lime suppresses the disease, and long rotations starve it out over time.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate brassicas out of affected ground on a long cycle (UMN advises up to 7 years where clubroot is known), keep soil pH up, improve drainage, and avoid moving infested soil on tools and boots.

diseases.name: Black rot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Yellow patches shaped like the letter V appear at the leaf edges, pointing inward, with black veins inside them. It can spread through the plant and rot the curd.
diseases.cause_beginner: A bacteria that often comes in on infected seeds or transplants. It gets into the leaves and travels through the plant's veins, spreading fastest in warm, wet weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There's no real cure, so remove and destroy infected plants to keep it from spreading. Don't handle or brush against the plants while they're wet, because that spreads the bacteria.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Begin with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants, don't plant where cabbage-family crops grew recently, space plants for good airflow, and avoid overhead watering.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellow, V-shaped lesions spread inward from the leaf margins, with the veins inside the V turning black; the disease moves through the vascular system and can blacken and rot the curd. Often the most serious cole-crop disease in warm, wet weather.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A seedborne bacterium (Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris) that enters through leaf pores and wounds and moves through the veins; it spreads in warm, wet conditions and on infected seed or transplants.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no effective cure; remove and destroy infected plants. Avoid working among plants when foliage is wet, since that moves the bacteria.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Start with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants (a hot-water seed treatment helps), rotate 2 to 3 years away from brassicas, give plants room for airflow, and avoid overhead watering and handling wet foliage.

diseases.name: Alternaria leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small dark spots with rings like a target appear on the leaves and can spread onto the curd as brown, fuzzy patches that ruin it. It is worse in warm, wet weather.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that spreads by spores in wet weather and on infected seed. It spots the leaves and, on cauliflower, can blemish the white curd, which makes it unsellable.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove badly spotted leaves, improve airflow so leaves dry, and use a copper spray if it is spreading onto the curd. Keep water off the leaves.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Start with clean seed, space plants for airflow, water at the soil rather than overhead, rotate away from cabbage-family crops, and clear away old plants where the fungus survives.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small dark leaf spots with concentric target-like rings and a yellow halo; in wet weather the spots enlarge, and on cauliflower the fungus can spread onto the curd as a brown, sometimes fuzzy discoloration that ruins its market quality. Clemson lists Alternaria brown spot among the main cauliflower diseases.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Alternaria species (A. brassicae / A. brassicicola), fungi that spread by airborne and splashed spores and on infected seed; long leaf wetness and warm, humid weather favor them, and they survive in crop debris and on seed.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves, improve airflow and let foliage dry, and apply a copper-based fungicide if the disease threatens the curd; control is largely preventive.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Use clean, certified, hot-water-treated seed, space for airflow, water at the soil line, rotate away from brassicas, and bury or remove crop debris that carries the fungus over.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Pale yellow blotches on top of the leaves, with fuzzy grayish growth on the underside, mostly in cool, damp weather. Bad cases discolor the leaves and can spot the curd.
diseases.cause_beginner: A mold-like disease that loves cool, wet, humid weather and spreads through the air and water. Wet leaves and crowded plants make it worse.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Open up the airflow so leaves can dry, remove the worst leaves, and use a copper spray if it's spreading. It's hard to stop once the weather stays damp.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Space plants so air moves between them, water at the soil instead of from above, and pick resistant varieties if downy mildew is common where you live.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Pale yellow patches form on the upper leaf surface with a fuzzy gray-white growth underneath, mainly in cool, damp weather; severe infection discolors the leaves and can spot and darken the curd. Cauliflower's cool, humid season overlaps the weather it likes.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A fungus-like organism (Hyaloperonospora parasitica) that thrives in cool, wet, humid conditions and spreads by spores in water and air; long leaf wetness and crowded plantings favor it.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Improve airflow and let foliage dry, remove badly affected leaves, and apply a copper-based fungicide if pressure is high; the disease is hard to stop once humidity stays high.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants for good air movement, water at the soil line rather than overhead, and choose resistant varieties where downy mildew is common.

diseases.name: Bacterial soft rot (head rot)
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The curd develops soft, watery, brown or black mushy patches that quickly turn slimy and smell bad. It usually shows up in warm, wet weather on a curd that stayed wet.
diseases.cause_beginner: Bacteria get into the curd through small wounds or where water sits in the head, then rot it from the inside, especially in warm, humid weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There's no cure for a rotting curd, so remove affected heads. The fix is prevention: keep the curd dry and harvest promptly.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Keep water off the curd, give plants room so heads dry quickly after rain, blanch (tie the leaves) loosely so water doesn't pool, harvest promptly, and avoid bruising the heads.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Soft, water-soaked brown to black lesions on the curd that rapidly become slimy and foul-smelling, the bacterial head rot Clemson lists for cauliflower; it spreads fastest in warm, wet weather and where water sits in a tied (blanched) head.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Soft-rot bacteria (Pectobacterium / Pseudomonas species) enter through wounds and natural openings and macerate the curd tissue; free moisture in the head and warm, humid conditions drive it, and a tightly tied blanch that traps water raises the risk.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure for a rotting curd; remove and discard affected heads. Management is cultural and preventive.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Keep the curd dry: space for airflow, blanch loosely so water drains rather than pools, avoid overhead watering and handling wet heads, harvest promptly once the curd is full, and do not bruise the heads.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Give about 1 to 1.5 inches weekly, kept as even as possible; cauliflower must never go through a dry check, which triggers buttoning.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly 1 to 1.5 inches a week. Never let it dry out and wilt, since stress makes it head early and badly.
watering.amount_seasoned: About 1 to 1.5 inches per week (UMN: roughly 1 inch a week; USU: 1 to 2 inches, deep and infrequent), more in warm, dry spells while the plant is sizing up.
watering.amount_beginner: Aim for roughly 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose where possible to keep foliage dry and discourage leaf disease.
watering.method_beginner: Water at the base of the plant rather than over the leaves.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves and limp growth; cauliflower dislikes waterlogged soil, which invites root maggots, clubroot, and crown rot in cold, wet ground.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Lower leaves yellow and the plant looks soggy and limp.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting and stalled growth, then the classic failure: a stressed plant buttons, forming a tiny, premature curd instead of a full head. Drought stress is the single most common cause of a ruined cauliflower crop.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Wilting leaves and stalled growth, and worst of all, a tiny head forms way too early (buttoning) because the dry spell stressed the plant.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Even, uninterrupted moisture is the whole game with cauliflower: more than any other cole crop it punishes a dry check by buttoning, so the goal is steady, vigorous growth with no stress from transplant to harvest.
watering.method_note_beginner: Keep the water steady so the plant never gets stressed. A cauliflower that dries out even once can make a tiny, premature head, so do not let it wilt.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Even moisture matters from transplanting all the way through curd formation; a single drought stress at any point, but especially on a young plant, can trigger buttoning.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Keep the water steady the whole time, especially when the plant is young, so it never gets stressed into heading early.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Cauliflower is almost always transplanted, since precise timing and an unstressed start matter so much. For spring, start seeds indoors about 4 to 6 weeks before set-out and transplant sturdy young plants out around 2 weeks before the last frost; cauliflower transplants are less cold-hardy than cabbage or broccoli, so do not rush them into hard cold. For fall, start indoors or direct sow in early-to-mid summer and set out so the curd matures in cool fall weather. The single biggest transplant mistake is setting out an old, root-bound, or cold-checked plant: that stress triggers buttoning, where the plant forms a tiny premature curd. Set out stocky plants with 4 to 6 true leaves, harden them off over 7 to 10 days, and keep them growing without a stall.
start_method.notes_beginner: Cauliflower is best grown from transplants, since timing and a smooth, unstressed start are so important. For spring, start seeds indoors about a month before planting out and set the plants out around 2 weeks before your last frost; do not rush them into hard cold, since young cauliflower is touchier than cabbage. For fall, start them in early-to-mid summer. The key is to never let the seedlings get old, root-bound, or chilled, because that stress makes them head early. Let homegrown seedlings get used to the outdoors over a week before planting.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Other brassicas (broccoli, cabbage, brussels sprouts, kale, collards, kohlrabi, turnip, radish, mustard), which share clubroot and the cabbage-family pests.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Other cabbage-family crops like broccoli, cabbage, brussels sprouts, kale, and turnips.
rotation.good_after: Legumes such as beans and peas, or unrelated crops like tomatoes, squash, cucumbers, or onions.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate so cauliflower and its brassica relatives do not return to the same ground for at least 3 years, and longer where clubroot is present (UMN advises up to a 7-year break where clubroot is known). Repeated same-family cropping builds soil-borne clubroot, and holding soil pH near neutral also helps suppress it.
rotation.note_beginner: Don't plant cauliflower or other cabbage-family crops in the same spot year after year. Waiting at least 3 years between them, and longer if you have had clubroot, helps avoid soil diseases.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Cauliflower is a poor keeper at room temperature, holding only a day or two before the curd softens and discolors. Unlike cabbage, it is not a storage vegetable: plan to use it fresh or freeze it.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Cauliflower does not keep well at room temperature, only a day or two. It is best eaten soon after cutting or frozen.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerate the head unwashed, with a few wrapper leaves on, stem side down. It holds about a week in the crisper, and no more than 2 to 3 weeks even at an ideal 32°F and high humidity (Clemson; USU). The curd yellows and develops off odors as it ages, so use it promptly.
storage.fridge_beginner: Store the head unwashed in the fridge crisper, where it keeps about a week (up to 2 to 3 weeks if very cold). Use it soon, since the curd yellows and starts to smell as it sits.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Cauliflower freezes well after blanching: cut into florets, blanch about 3 minutes, cool quickly in ice water, drain, and freeze. Blanching (the boiling step) halts the enzymes that cause off-flavors; frozen cauliflower is best used cooked. Note this freezer blanch is unrelated to the in-garden leaf-tying also called blanching.
storage.freezer_beginner: You can freeze cauliflower if you boil the florets briefly first (about 3 minutes), cool them in ice water, drain, and freeze; use them cooked. This freezer step is a different thing from the leaf-tying also called blanching out in the garden.
storage.notes_seasoned: Cauliflower is for fresh use or the freezer, not long storage; this is a real difference from cabbage, which keeps for months. Cut the head with a few wrapper leaves to protect the curd, keep it cold, and use it within a week or so. The curd discolors fastest in light and warmth, so refrigerate promptly.
storage.notes_beginner: Cauliflower is not a keeper like cabbage. Cut it with a few leaves around the head to protect it, keep it cold, and use it within about a week, or freeze it for longer.

recommended.name: Snow Crown
recommended.note: An early, dependable white hybrid (about 50 to 60 days) and the standard beginner pick; vigorous, fairly forgiving, and quick enough for spring before the heat. Some leaf wrap, but blanching (tying the leaves) gives the whitest curd.

recommended.name: Amazing
recommended.note: A mid-season white hybrid (about 65 to 70 days) noted for self-wrapping leaves and tolerance of a wider weather range, which makes it one of the more reliable types for the fall crop and for less-than-perfect conditions.

recommended.name: Early Snowball / Snowball Y Improved
recommended.note: Open-pollinated white heirloom types (about 60 to 70 days) with compact white curds; seed-saveable garden standards, though less self-wrapping than the hybrids, so plan to blanch them.

recommended.name: Self Blanche
recommended.note: A self-blanching white variety (about 65 to 70 days) whose inner leaves curl up over the curd on their own, so it needs little or no tying; a good fall choice and an easy one for new growers. Days approximate.

recommended.name: Cheddar (orange)
recommended.note: An orange-curded hybrid (about 58 to 70 days) high in beta-carotene; do NOT tie the leaves, since the color needs sun. Holds its color when cooked. Days approximate.

recommended.name: Graffiti / Purple of Sicily (purple)
recommended.note: Purple-curded types (about 70 to 85 days) colored by anthocyanins; grown unblanched in full sun for the deepest color. Purple of Sicily is a large open-pollinated Italian heirloom. Days approximate.

recommended.name: Veronica / Romanesco (green)
recommended.note: Lime-green Romanesco types (about 75 to 85 days) with a striking spiraled, pointed curd; grown unblanched and best as a long-season fall crop, since they want a steady cool finish. Days approximate.

varieties.note_seasoned: Match the variety to the season and your tolerance for fuss. For a first try, the early self-wrapping or self-blanching hybrids (Snow Crown, Amazing, Self Blanche) are the most forgiving and need the least leaf-tying. Open-pollinated whites (Early Snowball, Snowball Y Improved) are seed-saveable but want blanching. The colored types are the fun ones and skip blanching entirely: orange (Cheddar) and purple (Graffiti, Purple of Sicily) are grown in full sun for their color, and lime-green Romanesco (Veronica) brings a spiraled curd but wants a long, steady cool fall. Days-to-maturity figures are approximate and run from transplanting.
varieties.note_beginner: Pick the type that fits your patience. For a first try, choose an easy self-blanching or self-wrapping kind like Snow Crown, Amazing, or Self Blanche, which need little or no leaf-tying. The colored kinds are fun and skip blanching completely: orange (Cheddar) and purple (Graffiti) just need full sun, and green Romanesco makes a beautiful spiraled head but takes a long, cool fall to do well.

drainage.saucer_practice: Empty the saucer after watering so roots never sit in water; cauliflower resents waterlogged soil but must never dry out.

soil_mix.type_beginner: A good-quality potting mix, not garden soil.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in compost and a slow-release fertilizer for steady feeding.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: A rich, well-drained commercial potting mix high in organic matter.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend in compost and a slow-release balanced fertilizer; a single cauliflower in a pot is a heavy feeder in a small soil volume, and starving it is the fast track to buttoning.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out faster than the ground, so check daily in warm weather and keep the water steady. Cauliflower buttons (heads early) if it ever dries out, so this matters more than for most pot crops.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Feed a bit more often than in the ground, since watering washes nutrients out of pots, and a hungry cauliflower heads early.
container_notes.notes_beginner: Cauliflower grows in a large pot, but it is one of the harder vegetables to get right in a container because it cannot take any stress. Use a pot of at least 5 gallons, one plant per pot, and keep it watered and fed without fail. Easy early varieties like Snow Crown are the best fit. If it ever dries out or runs low on food, it will make a tiny head early.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Cauliflower is a workable but demanding container crop, since the small soil volume makes it harder to deliver the unbroken moisture and fertility it needs to avoid buttoning. Use a pot of at least 5 gallons (10 is better) at least 12 inches deep, one plant per pot, in a rich, well-drained mix, and keep moisture and feeding relentlessly steady. Choose easy, quick types (Snow Crown, Self Blanche, Amazing). Container-specific figures are modeled on general container-vegetable guidance plus the plant's size.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry faster than beds; check moisture daily in heat and water before the mix dries, since any dry check can trigger buttoning.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Container plants need more frequent feeding than in-ground ones because watering leaches nutrients, and a starved plant buttons.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering container suits cauliflower especially well, since it smooths out the unbroken moisture that prevents buttoning, the crop's biggest container risk.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot is a great match because it keeps the water steady, which is exactly what cauliflower needs to avoid heading early.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: Cauliflower has a shallow, wide root system and a broad leaf spread, so choose a wide pot of at least 5 gallons and about 12 inches deep for one plant; a broad, stable container holds moisture more evenly than a narrow one, which matters for avoiding the dry checks that cause buttoning.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Give one cauliflower a wide pot that holds at least 5 gallons and is about 12 inches deep. A broad, sturdy pot holds water more evenly than a tall skinny one, which helps keep the plant from getting stressed.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: In about 5 to 10 days, your seeds sprout and push up their first two little leaves (the seed leaves).
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the starting mix damp. Once the first real leaves appear, give the seedlings strong light so they do not get leggy.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your seeds come up yet?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seeds sprout in about 5 to 10 days, pushing up two seed leaves (cotyledons). Cauliflower is started indoors for transplanting in nearly all regions.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep the starting mix evenly moist and give bright light from emergence to avoid stretch; pot up before plants crowd, since a root-bound cauliflower seedling is prone to buttoning.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Did your cauliflower seeds sprout?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The seedlings grow their real leaves and a stronger stem. They are ready to plant out at about 4 to 6 weeks old, with several true leaves.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Harden the seedlings off over about a week before planting out, and plant them before they get old or root-bound. Watch for flea beetle holes and use a row cover.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How many real leaves do your seedlings have?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Young plants build true leaves and a sturdy stem; transplants are ready at about 4 to 6 true leaves, roughly 4 to 6 weeks from sowing. Set out stocky young plants, never oversized or root-bound ones.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harden off over 7 to 10 days, then transplant at 18-to-24-inch spacing without a growth check; protect from flea beetles with row cover and from cabbage root maggot with stem collars. An old, root-bound, or cold-shocked transplant is the classic cause of buttoning.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are your transplants stocky and ready to go out?

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant grows a big rosette of spreading leaves before it forms a curd. This leafy frame is what feeds the head, so you want lots of strong growth now.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Feed with nitrogen and keep it evenly watered so it never stalls. A cauliflower that gets stressed now will head early and badly, so steady growth is everything.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Is your plant growing a big rosette of leaves?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The plant builds a broad rosette of frame leaves over several weeks before initiating a curd. Vigorous, uninterrupted growth now sets the eventual curd size; any stall risks buttoning.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Side-dress with nitrogen, hold moisture dead even, and scout for cabbageworms, loopers, cabbage aphids, and (in the South) harlequin bugs. The whole job at this stage is to prevent any check to growth from drought, low fertility, heat, or cold.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Is your plant putting on steady, unchecked leafy growth?

growth_stages.name: Curd forming
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A small white head (the curd) appears in the center of the plant and grows bigger and rounder. For white types, this is when you blanch it by tying the outer leaves over the head.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: When the curd is about the size of an egg or a tennis ball, gather the outer leaves up over it and tie them loosely with twine or a rubber band to keep it white. Skip this for orange, purple, or green types, which need sun. Keep watering steady.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Has a small white head started to form?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A small curd initiates in the center and enlarges over 1 to 3 weeks. White types need blanching: when the curd reaches roughly silver-dollar to tennis-ball size, tie the outer leaves up over it with twine or rubber bands to shade it white (self-blanching types wrap on their own). Colored and Romanesco types are left unblanched in full sun.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Blanch white curds at silver-dollar to tennis-ball size and keep moisture even; tie loosely so water drains rather than pools (a wet, tied head invites bacterial rot). Tighten caterpillar and aphid control, since contamination of the curd is the costly damage, and watch the weather, since heat now causes ricing and discoloration.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Is the curd forming, and have you blanched the white types?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The head is full size (about 6 to 8 inches across), firm, and still tight and smooth. That is the moment to cut it, before the head loosens or discolors.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Cut the whole head off with a few leaves attached while it is still compact, usually about a week or two after you tied the leaves. Don't wait, since a cauliflower head goes from perfect to loose and grainy quickly.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Is your cauliflower head full-sized and still tight?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Curds are ready when full-sized (about 6 to 8 inches across), firm, compact, and still smooth, typically 1 to 2 weeks after blanching. A curd left too long rices (separates into a loose, grainy texture), discolors, and begins to open toward flower, so the harvest window is short.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut the head at the base with a few wrapper leaves while it is still tight, before the curd rices or yellows; this window is only a few days to a week, shorter in warm weather. Cauliflower does not hold in the garden the way cabbage does, so harvest promptly and refrigerate.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are you cutting firm, tight, still-white curds on time?

notifications.title_beginner: Time to tie the leaves over the head
notifications.body_seasoned: Your cauliflower's curd is reaching silver-dollar to tennis-ball size. For white types, gather the outer leaves up over it and tie loosely with twine or a rubber band to blanch it white; tie loosely so water drains rather than pools. Skip this for orange, purple, and green types, which need sun for their color. Keep moisture even.
notifications.body_beginner: A small white head has started. For white cauliflower, gather the big outer leaves up over it and tie them loosely so the head stays white. Skip this for orange, purple, or green types. Keep watering steady.

notifications.title_seasoned: Harvest the curd before it rices
notifications.title_beginner: Your cauliflower looks ready, cut it now
notifications.body_seasoned: The curd should be full-sized (about 6 to 8 inches), firm, compact, and still smooth, usually 1 to 2 weeks after blanching. Cut it at the base with a few wrapper leaves now: left too long it rices (turns loose and grainy), discolors, and opens toward flower. The window is only a few days, shorter in warm weather.
notifications.body_beginner: Your cauliflower head should be full-sized and still tight and smooth. Cut it off with a few leaves attached now, since the head goes from perfect to loose and grainy quickly. Don't wait.

notifications.title_seasoned: Keep it growing without a stall
notifications.title_beginner: Don't let your cauliflower get stressed
notifications.body_seasoned: Cauliflower buttons (forms a tiny premature curd) whenever growth is checked by drought, low fertility, heat, or cold. Keep moisture dead even, feed it so it never goes hungry, and protect young plants from cold snaps and heat. Steady, unbroken growth from transplant to harvest is the whole job.
notifications.body_beginner: Cauliflower makes a tiny, useless head early if it ever gets stressed. Keep the water steady, feed it so it never gets hungry, and shield young plants from sudden cold or heat. The trick is to keep it growing smoothly the whole time.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot weather warning for your cauliflower
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Cauliflower forms a firm white curd only in steady cool weather, roughly 60°F to 65°F. Sustained heat above about 75°F to 80°F (and hot nights above about 70°F to 77°F) stops the plant from forming a proper curd and causes buttoning, ricing (a loose, grainy curd), and yellow-brown discoloration. Keep moisture even and shade if you can, and recognize that in hot regions cauliflower is timed to mature in cool spring or fall, never summer.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Cauliflower needs steady cool weather to make a good head. In a heat wave it may make a tiny premature head (buttoning), a loose grainy head (ricing), or discolor, so keep it watered and shaded. In warm areas, cauliflower is really a fall, winter, and early-spring crop, not a summer one.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hard freeze coming
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Cauliflower is less cold-hardy than cabbage or broccoli. The plants take light frost, but a developing or mature curd is damaged by a hard freeze (much below about 28°F), turning brown and water-soaked. Cover plants with a curd nearby, or cut mature heads ahead of a deep freeze. Note also that a prolonged cold spell on a young plant can trigger buttoning, so do not rush transplants into hard cold.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Cauliflower is not as tough as cabbage. The leaves handle a light frost, but a hard freeze damages the white head, turning it brown. If a hard freeze is coming, cover the plants or cut any ready heads first. Also, do not plant young plants out into hard cold, since a long cold spell can make them head early.

germination.text_seasoned: Start seeds indoors about 4 to 6 weeks before set-out; cauliflower is transplanted in nearly all regions for timing and an unstressed start.
germination.text_beginner: Start seeds indoors about a month before you plan to plant them out.

germination.text_seasoned: Sow about 0.25 to 0.5 inch deep into a moist starting mix, give bright light from emergence, and pot up before roots crowd, since a root-bound start invites buttoning.
germination.text_beginner: Plant the seeds about a quarter to half an inch deep, keep them damp, and give them strong light so they do not get leggy.

seedling.text_seasoned: Transplant stocky young plants (4 to 6 true leaves) at 18 to 24 inches apart without a growth check; harden off over 7 to 10 days first and do not set out old or root-bound plants.
seedling.text_beginner: Space plants about 18 to 24 inches apart and plant them while they are still young and stocky, never old or root-bound. Harden them off over about a week first.

seedling.text_seasoned: Protect transplants from flea beetles with row cover and from cabbage root maggot with stem collars, especially in cool, wet spring soil; a checked seedling is prone to buttoning.
seedling.text_beginner: Cover young plants with a row cover to stop flea beetles, and put a collar around the stem to keep root maggots out.

established.text_seasoned: Side-dress nitrogen and hold moisture dead even at about 1 to 1.5 inches per week; the entire job now is to prevent any stall in growth, which causes buttoning.
established.text_beginner: Feed with nitrogen and water steadily so the plant never stalls. Any stress now can make it head early.

established.text_seasoned: Scout for cabbageworms and loopers on the leaves and cabbage aphids on the growing tips; getting ahead of them now keeps them out of the curd later.
established.text_beginner: Check the leaves for green caterpillars and the new growth for aphids, and deal with them early before the head forms.

curd_forming.text_seasoned: Blanch white curds at silver-dollar to tennis-ball size by tying the outer leaves up over them with twine or rubber bands; tie loosely so water drains. Leave colored and Romanesco types unblanched in full sun.
curd_forming.text_beginner: When the white head is about the size of an egg or tennis ball, tie the big outer leaves up over it to keep it white. Skip this for orange, purple, or green types, which need sun.

curd_forming.text_seasoned: Keep moisture even and watch the weather as the curd fills; heat causes ricing and discoloration, and a wet, tightly tied head invites bacterial rot, so tie loosely.
curd_forming.text_beginner: Keep watering steady while the head forms. Heat can make it loose and discolored, so shade it in hot spells, and tie the leaves loosely so water does not pool in the head.

harvest.text_seasoned: Cut curds while full-sized (about 6 to 8 inches), firm, compact, and still smooth, usually 1 to 2 weeks after blanching; left too long they rice and discolor, so the window is short.
harvest.text_beginner: Cut the head while it is full-sized and still tight and smooth. Don't wait, since it quickly turns loose and grainy.

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest with a few wrapper leaves to protect the curd and refrigerate promptly; cauliflower does not hold in the garden the way cabbage does.
harvest.text_beginner: Cut the head with a few leaves around it to protect it, and put it in the fridge soon. Cauliflower does not keep well, so use it within about a week.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: One curd per plant, typically about 1 to 3 pounds and 6 to 8 inches across depending on variety, spacing, and how steadily the plant grew. Unlike broccoli, cauliflower does not produce useful side shoots after the main curd is cut, so it is strictly a single harvest.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Each plant gives you one head, usually about 1 to 3 pounds. There are no side shoots afterward like broccoli has, so it is one head per plant.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Each curd matures over a short window in cool spring or fall weather and must be cut promptly before it rices; the crop is a one-time cut per plant. In hot regions the spring crop must beat the summer heat and the fall crop is usually the more reliable one.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Each cauliflower makes one head over a few weeks and is cut once, while it is still tight. The best heads form in the cool weather of fall and spring.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Cauliflower is the most demanding of the common cole crops, and almost every failure traces to one cause: a check to growth. Buttoning (a tiny premature curd) comes from any stress, drought, low fertility, heat, cold, or a root-bound transplant, on a young plant; ricing and discoloration come from heat or harvesting late. The two keys are steady, unbroken growth (even water, steady feeding, no transplant shock) and tight timing so the curd matures in cool weather. Blanch white types by tying the leaves, and harvest the instant the curd is full and still smooth.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Cauliflower is the fussiest of the cabbage family, and almost all of its problems come from getting stressed. If it dries out, runs low on food, or hits heat or cold while young, it makes a tiny useless head early (buttoning). The two tricks are to keep it growing smoothly with even water and feeding, and to time it so the head forms in cool weather. Tie the leaves over white heads to keep them white, and cut the head as soon as it is full and still tight.
factors_seasoned: No growth checks: drought, low fertility, heat, cold, or a root-bound transplant all cause buttoning (tiny premature curds), the signature cauliflower failure.
Timing and temperature: curds form best in steady cool weather (about 60°F to 65°F); heat above roughly 75°F to 80°F causes ricing and discoloration, so time maturity for cool spring or fall.
Blanching: white types need the outer leaves tied over the curd to stay white; colored and Romanesco types are grown unblanched in sun.
Even moisture and steady feeding: cauliflower is a heavy feeder that must never go hungry or dry, more so than other cole crops.
Harvest timing: the curd holds only a short window before it rices and discolors, so cut promptly.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No reliable extension or peer-reviewed evidence supports timing cauliflower planting or harvest by moon phase. Plant by soil temperature, frost dates, and the seasonal windows instead, and harvest by curd firmness and size.

failure_diagnostics.label: Tiny premature head (buttoning)
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: The plant got stressed, usually by drying out, running low on food, hitting cold or heat, or being planted as an old, root-bound seedling, so it made a tiny head far too early.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your cauliflower formed a tiny, button-sized head while the plant was still small. This is called buttoning, and it is the most common cauliflower problem. It happens when a young plant gets stressed, most often by drying out, going hungry, sitting too long as a root-bound transplant, or hitting a cold spell or heat. Once it buttons, that plant will not recover. Next time, set out young, stocky transplants without a check, keep them watered and fed without fail, and time the crop for cool weather.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Set out young, unstressed plants, keep them watered and fed without fail, and time the crop for cool weather.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The plant buttoned, forming a tiny premature curd on an undersized plant. Buttoning is triggered by any check to growth that pushes the plant to head before it has built a leafy frame: drought, low fertility, an old or root-bound transplant, a cold spell (Iowa State: prolonged temperatures below 50°F), or heat. Next time transplant young, stocky plants without a stall, hold moisture and fertility dead even, protect from cold and heat, and avoid setting out root-bound starts.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Any growth check on a young plant: drought, low fertility, an old or root-bound transplant, prolonged cold (below ~50°F), or heat stress.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Transplant young, stocky, unchecked plants; keep moisture and fertility even; protect from cold and heat; never set out root-bound starts.

failure_diagnostics.label: Loose, grainy, or discolored head (ricing and browning)
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Heat, or leaving the head too long, made the curd separate into a loose, ricey texture and turn yellow or brown instead of staying tight and white.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your cauliflower head turned loose and grainy (called ricing) or yellowed and browned instead of staying tight and white. This usually means it ran into warm weather or was left on the plant too long, and for white types it can also mean the head was not blanched (the leaves were not tied over it to shade it). Next time, time the crop for cool weather, blanch white types by tying the leaves, and cut the head the moment it is full and still smooth.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Time the crop for cool weather, tie the leaves over white heads, and cut as soon as the head is full and tight.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The curd riced (the buds separated into a loose, grainy surface) or discolored. This comes from heat (sustained temperatures above about 75°F to 80°F), from leaving the curd past its short prime, or, for the yellow-brown sun discoloration of white types, from failing to blanch. Next time time maturity for cool weather, blanch white curds at silver-dollar size by tying the outer leaves, and harvest promptly while the curd is firm, compact, and smooth.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Heat above ~75 to 80°F, over-mature curds left past prime, and (sun yellowing of white types) failure to blanch.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Time maturity for cool weather, blanch white curds, and harvest promptly at firm, compact, smooth stage.

failure_diagnostics.label: Caterpillars or aphids in the curd
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Cabbageworms or cabbage aphids that crawled into the head as it formed, often missed until you cut it.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: When you cut the head you found green caterpillars and droppings, or clusters of gray-green aphids, tucked down in the curd. These pests love cabbage-family plants and hide right in the head, which is the part you eat, and they are very hard to wash out of a tight white curd. Next time, cover plants with a row cover, scout the leaves and growing tips weekly, and treat caterpillars with Bt before the curd forms.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Use a row cover, scout weekly, and treat caterpillars with Bt before the head forms.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Cabbageworms, loopers, or diamondback larvae crawled into the curd, or cabbage aphids colonized it, contaminating the head and proving nearly impossible to clean from the tight florets. The window to act is before and during early curding. Next time exclude egg-laying adults with row cover from transplanting, scout leaves and tips weekly, apply Bt or spinosad for caterpillars, and dislodge aphid colonies early; taper nitrogen as the curd sets, since soft growth favors aphids.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Cabbageworm-complex larvae and cabbage aphids penetrating the curd, worsened by late detection and soft, over-fed growth.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Exclude adults with row cover, scout weekly, treat caterpillars early with Bt, and knock aphids back before the curd closes.

failure_diagnostics.label: Stunted, yellow plants with clubbed roots
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Clubroot, a soil disease of cabbage-family plants, or planting brassicas in the same spot too often.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your plants stayed small and yellowish, wilted in the afternoon, and when you dug one up the roots were swollen into lumps. That is clubroot, a soil disease that infects cabbage-family roots and lasts for years in the soil. It builds up when brassicas are grown in the same spot repeatedly and in acidic soil. Next time, rotate so cabbage-family crops do not return to that bed for several years, keep the soil pH near neutral, and improve drainage.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Rotate brassicas out of that bed for several years, keep soil pH near neutral, and improve drainage.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Plants were stunted and chlorotic, wilted by day, and showed galled, clubbed roots, the signature of clubroot (Plasmodiophora brassicae). The soilborne organism persists for years and builds under repeated brassica cropping and acidic, poorly drained soil. A clubroot-checked plant also tends to button. Next time rotate cole crops out for at least 3 years (up to 7 where clubroot is known), lime toward a neutral pH, and improve drainage.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Clubroot building in soil cropped to brassicas too frequently, favored by acidic, wet soil.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Use a long brassica rotation, raise pH toward neutral, and improve drainage.
