succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Cauliflower crops in the cool shoulders of the year, so plant in small batches within the spring window and again in late summer for fall, rather than all at once. Because it is so tightly tied to cool weather and so prone to buttoning in heat, the spring window is short and unforgiving: most gardens fit only a sowing or two before midsummer heat shuts it down. The fall planting, with the curd maturing into cooling weather, is usually the more reliable crop. Mixing early and late varieties in one planting also spreads the harvest.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: Plant cauliflower in spring and again in late summer for fall, in small batches a couple of weeks apart, instead of all at one time. The fall crop, with the head forming in cool weather, is usually the easier and more reliable one. Skip the hottest part of summer, since cauliflower will not form a good head in the heat.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: cauliflower_author_fresh_pilot (Claude Code lane authoring, 2026-06-29). Authored by FILLING the cauliflower shell, modeled STRUCTURALLY on the broccoli certified template (heading double-crop), mirroring the gate-clean cabbage and brussels-sprouts CC pilots for field shapes, with biology RE-DERIVED from live T1 extension sources (UMN/Clemson/USU/Iowa State for core biology; UMass + UMN for cabbage aphid; Clemson cole-crop insect and disease factsheets for the pest/disease complex; UMN clubroot). Per-region planting calendars from the same regional extension cole-crop/vegetable calendars the cabbage pilot cites (UMN/Iowa State/MSU/Penn State/UMaine/NDSU northern; Clemson/UGA/LSU/Alabama/Mississippi State SE Gulf; UC IPM/UC MG/UC Marin/UC San Diego California; U Arizona AZ1005 low desert AZ; NMSU/Texas A&M warm arid modeled; UF/IFAS VH021+EP450+EP452 Florida; CTAHR B-91 Hawaii modeled). DRAFT for review, not certified: launch flags false. Key cauliflower-vs-broccoli refits: forms a SINGLE white CURD with NO side shoots (curd_forming stage replaces broccoli's head + side_shoots, single harvest per plant); FUSSIER and LESS cold-hardy than broccoli or cabbage; the signature failures are BUTTONING (tiny premature curd from any growth check, the central theme of soil/water/fertilizer/transplant copy) and RICING/discoloration (heat or over-mature curd); BLANCHING (tying outer leaves over white curds) plus self-blanching and colored (orange/purple/green Romanesco, grown unblanched) types added throughout; harvest_urgency HIGH (short window before ricing); storage SHORT (about a week, not a keeper like cabbage); difficulty HARD (the most demanding cole crop); DTM 50 to 100; spacing 18 to 24 in; pH 6.0 to 7.0; diseases swap to clubroot/black rot/Alternaria leaf spot/downy mildew/bacterial head rot. Heat backing per cell only in genuinely hot regions/zones (northern z6/z7, se_gulf z8/z9, ca_interior, ca_south_coast, warm_arid), season_over for the dead summer in the single-winter-crop desert/Florida/Hawaii regions; cool northern z3 to z5 and the fog-belt north coast carry NO heat_pause. successions_realized CC-DERIVED (not authored). See cauliflower_NOTES.md for all flags and modeled values.

open_findings.summary: germination_temp_f [45, 85] is the standard cole-crop germination envelope; the cauliflower T1 pages report 5 to 10 day germination but do not state an explicit min/max soil temperature, so the range is modeled on the brassica germination envelope (consistent with cabbage/brussels [45, 85] and broccoli [40, 86]).
open_findings.basis: Consistent with the sibling cole-crop pilots and the germination the sources report; flagged in NOTES.

open_findings.summary: days_to_maturity [50, 100] uses a directly sourced lower/common end (Snow Crown 50, Amazing/Early Snowball/White Contessa ~60 to 70, Denali 80 per USU/Iowa State/Clemson) and extends the upper bound to ~100 to cover long-season and overwintering/Romanesco types; the highest single sourced figure found was ~80 to 85 days, so the 80-to-100 tail is a modeled allowance for specialty long types.
open_findings.basis: Common types are T1-sourced at 50 to 80; the upper tail is labeled approximate and flagged in NOTES.

open_findings.summary: Regional HARVEST month windows are DERIVED from the sourced PLANT windows plus the crop's ~50 to 100 day maturity, since the extension calendars give planting windows, not explicit harvest months. Plant windows are taken from the regional cole-crop/vegetable calendars (or flagged modeled).
open_findings.basis: Standard derivation; same pattern accepted in the cabbage/kale/brussels pilots. Sourced approximations surfaced for review.

open_findings.summary: Per-region planting windows are grounded in the same regional extension vegetable/cole-crop planting calendars the cabbage pilot cites; several list cauliflower together with broccoli and cabbage rather than as a standalone table, so cauliflower windows are taken as the cole-crop window for the region, tightened where cauliflower's narrower heat and cold tolerance demands. Windows judged too warm for cauliflower's curd were trimmed relative to cabbage (e.g. May harvest dropped on the Gulf coast and in the interior valleys; deep-cold December harvest trimmed in northern z4/z6).
open_findings.basis: Cole-crop calendars are the standard regional source for cauliflower; the cauliflower-specific tightening is a conservative judgment call, surfaced for the daily biology review.

open_findings.summary: Cauliflower is treated as LESS cold-hardy than cabbage and broccoli: plants take light frost but a developing or mature curd is damaged by a hard freeze below about 28°F, and young plants button from prolonged cold. USU states transplants can go out 1 to 2 weeks before last frost; the specific curd hard-freeze damage threshold (~28°F) is a modeled, widely held figure rather than a single quoted T1 number.
open_findings.basis: Cold sensitivity and buttoning-from-cold are T1-sourced (USU/Iowa State/Clemson); the exact curd damage temperature is modeled and flagged.

open_findings.summary: warm_arid (El Paso/high desert z8) planting window is MODELED on NMSU's hardy-crop rule and Texas A&M's relative spring/fall rules; the exact zone-8 month tables live in PDF/complex sources that did not parse. Cauliflower is treated as a spring-and-fall crop bracketing a backed summer heat pause.
open_findings.basis: Cauliflower is sourced as a cool-season spring-and-fall crop for the region; only the exact month table is modeled. Harvest months derived.

open_findings.summary: hawaii_tropical z11 uses a modeled low-elevation cool-season window with a high-elevation year-round caveat; CTAHR B-91 is a scanned PDF that did not parse via WebFetch and does not table cauliflower months. Cauliflower is flagged marginal at low elevation in the lowland tropics.
open_findings.basis: Same pattern as the broccoli/cabbage/kale/brussels hawaii open finding; only the PDF parse and month precision are gaps.

open_findings.summary: Cauliflower is flagged MARGINAL in south Florida (UF/IFAS lists cole crops only for the coolest months) and in lowland tropical Hawaii; its tight cool-weather requirement and heat intolerance make it a low-confidence, coolest-months-only crop there. Cells carry the marginal note.
open_findings.basis: Sourced caveat plus the crop's documented heat intolerance; cells carry the marginal note explicitly.

open_findings.summary: container_notes figures (5+ gallon, 12 inch depth, one plant per pot, container_recommended false) are modeled on general container-vegetable guidance (uwi_hort) plus the plant's size and shallow, wide root habit; no cauliflower-specific container source was found. The uwi_hort anchor is the live Wisconsin cole-crops landing page.
open_findings.basis: Honest modeling consistent with the plant's habit; flagged in NOTES.

open_findings.summary: Variety days-to-maturity are exact where sourced (Snow Crown 50, Amazing 65, White Contessa 65, Self Blanche 60, Denali 80 per USU) and APPROXIMATE for the grouped open-pollinated and colored/Romanesco types (Early Snowball/Snowball Y, Cheddar, Graffiti/Purple of Sicily, Veronica/Romanesco), where catalogs give names and color but a varietal days range rather than a single sourced figure.
open_findings.basis: Approximate values sit within the sourced 50 to 85 day varietal span and are labeled approximate in the variety notes.

open_findings.summary: successions_realized intentionally left unauthored; the CC deriver fills it and reconciles succession_policy.successions / max_successions_per_season to the max over zones. open_findings.basis: Authoring boundary: the per-zone realized count is a derived metric, not a sourced claim (radish/kale/cabbage/brussels pilot lesson).

3.zone_notes: In the coldest zones cauliflower is a tricky, short-season crop. Start indoors in April and set out sturdy (not root-bound) transplants in May for a late-summer harvest; a quick early variety set out in early July gives a fall harvest by September. Cauliflower buttons easily from cold checks and water or nutrient stress, so keep young plants growing without a stall. Harvest months derived from the sourced planting windows and maturity.

4.zone_notes: Start indoors in April and transplant in May for a late-summer harvest; set a fall crop out in July for a September-October harvest. Iowa State sets spring transplants early-to-mid April in central counties and fall transplants early-to-mid July. Cut the fall curd before a hard freeze, since the curd is less cold-hardy than cabbage. Harvest months derived.

5.zone_notes: Transplant in April for a June harvest and set a fall crop out in early-to-mid July, which grows through the warm late summer to curd in the cool of October. Iowa State harvests spring cauliflower as early as June and fall cauliflower mid-September to mid-October. The hottest weeks of midsummer are too warm to curd, so nothing is timed to mature then. Harvest months derived.

6.zone_notes: Transplant in March for a late-spring harvest, then again in August for a fall harvest into November; the peak of midsummer (July) is too hot to curd, so it is left out of the planting calendar. Penn State gives fall last-planting dates in mid-summer for the warmer zones. The December curd of cabbage is trimmed here, since cauliflower's curd is damaged by hard freeze. Harvest months derived.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: cauliflower is a cool-season brassica that forms a firm white curd only in steady cool weather, roughly 60°F to 65°F. Sustained heat above about 75°F to 80°F (and hot nights above about 70°F) stops the plant from forming a proper curd and instead causes buttoning (tiny premature curds), ricing (a loose, grainy curd), and yellow-brown discoloration, so the crop is grown to mature in cool spring and fall and the hottest months are left out of the planting calendar. In the warmer northern zones the peak of midsummer (July) runs too hot for cauliflower to curd, so it is grown as a spring planting and a late-summer planting bracketing a short heat gap. (Penn State Extension, Iowa State University Extension)

7.zone_notes: In the mild end of the cold tier (Clemson Piedmont and similar), transplant about mid-March for a late-spring harvest, then set fall transplants in September as the heat breaks for a fall-into-early-winter harvest; June through August is too hot to curd. Clemson gives Piedmont fall planting in late summer. Harvest months derived.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: cauliflower is a cool-season brassica that forms a firm white curd only in steady cool weather, roughly 60°F to 65°F. In the mild Piedmont end of the northern tier the summer (June through August) is distinctly too hot to curd cauliflower, so the spring crop must mature before the heat and the more reliable crop is the fall planting. northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In cold regions, cauliflower is a spring crop and a fall crop. Start seeds indoors and set young plants out in spring for a summer harvest, and start a second batch in early-to-mid summer for a fall harvest, when the cool weather makes the best heads. Cauliflower is fussier than cabbage: keep it growing steadily with even water and food so it does not head early, and protect young plants from sudden cold.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Across the cold northern tier cauliflower is a spring-and-fall double crop, and the fall crop is usually the more reliable one. Start transplants under cover and set them out from April-May (cold zones) to March (mild end) for a late-spring to late-summer harvest, then set a second crop in mid-to-late summer for a fall harvest. The coolest zones (3 to 5) crop through a moderate summer with no formal heat gap, though midsummer is too hot to curd; the warmer zones (6 to 7) carry a backed summer pause. Cauliflower is less cold-hardy than cabbage, so the deep-cold harvest tail is trimmed and fall curds are cut before a hard freeze. Steady, unbroken growth is essential to avoid buttoning. Harvest months are derived from the sourced planting windows plus the crop's 50-to-100-day maturity.

The spring planting cabbage tolerates is dropped here, since cauliflower's curd will not size up before the Gulf heat arrives. LSU lists cole-crop transplants in fall. Summer is the off-season. Harvest months derived.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast, cauliflower is a fall, winter, and early-spring crop, not a summer one. Set transplants out in late summer or fall for a harvest through the mild winter. Skip the hot, humid summer, when cauliflower will not form a head.
