Steady moisture is essential against the dry heat to prevent buttoning. Harvest months are derived from the sourced planting windows plus maturity.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set spring transplants out about 2 weeks before the last frost (cauliflower is less cold-hardy than cabbage, so do not rush it into hard cold), and a second crop in late summer for fall; in mild-winter regions cauliflower is planted in fall and winter. Resolved per-zone windows are authored from the regional extension cole-crop calendars.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Curds firm up about 50 to 80 days after transplanting for early-to-mid types; later and Romanesco types take 80 to 100 days.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest runs as curds firm; a curd left too long rices and discolors, so harvest promptly. Cauliflower does not hold the way cabbage does.

10.zone_notes: In central Florida (zone 10), cauliflower is a cool-season winter crop set out October through December for a harvest January through March. UF/IFAS lists cole crops for the cool months (roughly September-February statewide). The warm months are too hot for cauliflower. Harvest months derived; cauliflower is a marginal, coolest-months-only crop this far south.

11.zone_notes: In south Florida (zone 11), cauliflower is marginal and grown only in the coolest months: set transplants October through December for a short January-February harvest. UF/IFAS South Florida lists cole crops only for the coolest part of winter. Most of the year is far too warm. Harvest months derived; a low-confidence crop fit here.

fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: In Florida, cauliflower is a winter-only crop, and it is on the edge of what the climate allows. Set plants out in fall for a harvest in the coolest months, roughly January through March in central Florida and only January-February in the far south. The rest of the year is too hot.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: In peninsular Florida cauliflower is a marginal cool-season winter crop, set out in fall for a midwinter harvest (January-March in central, only January-February in the far south). UF/IFAS lists cole crops for the coolest months only, and cauliflower's tight cool requirement makes it a low-confidence fit this far south. The warm season is off entirely. Harvest months are derived from the sourced planting windows plus maturity.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set spring transplants out about 2 weeks before the last frost (cauliflower is less cold-hardy than cabbage, so do not rush it into hard cold), and a second crop in late summer for fall; in mild-winter regions cauliflower is planted in fall and winter. Resolved per-zone windows are authored from the regional extension cole-crop calendars.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Curds firm up about 50 to 80 days after transplanting for early-to-mid types; later and Romanesco types take 80 to 100 days.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest runs as curds firm; a curd left too long rices and discolors, so harvest promptly. Cauliflower does not hold the way cabbage does.

11.zone_notes: In tropical Hawaii, cauliflower is marginal at low elevation and grown in the coolest months (a winter planting for a January-February harvest), while cool high-elevation areas can grow it more of the year. CTAHR Bulletin B-91 notes cole crops do best at cooler elevations; it is a scanned PDF that did not parse for exact months, so the low-elevation window is modeled. Harvest months derived.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In Hawaii, cauliflower is hard to grow in the warm lowlands and is best in the cool months or up at higher, cooler elevations. Set plants out in fall for a winter harvest near the coast. The heat is the limiting factor.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: In tropical Hawaii cauliflower is marginal at low elevation, grown in the coolest months for a midwinter harvest, while cool high-elevation sites can grow it through more of the year. CTAHR B-91 indicates cole crops favor cooler elevations; the low-elevation month window is modeled (the bulletin is a scanned PDF that did not parse). Harvest months are derived.

crops.description_seasoned: Cauliflower is a cool-season brassica grown for the single dense white curd, the immature flower head, that forms at the center of the plant. It comes in white types plus orange, purple, and lime-green spiraled Romanesco forms, maturing from about 50 to 100 days, and is grown as a spring crop and a fall crop, timed to mature in cool weather. It is the fussiest of the common cole crops and less cold-hardy than cabbage or broccoli: the curd forms well only in steady cool weather around 60°F to 65°F, and almost any stress (heat, cold, drought, or a checked transplant) causes buttoning (a tiny premature curd) or ricing and discoloration of the head. Many white varieties need blanching, tying the outer leaves over the curd to keep it white, while self-blanching and colored types skip that step. Unlike broccoli it forms no side shoots, so it is a single harvest per plant, and unlike cabbage it does not store, so it is used fresh or frozen.
crops.description_beginner: Cauliflower grows one dense, round head (the curd) in the center of the plant. There are white kinds plus fun orange, purple, and spiraled green Romanesco types, taking about 2 to 3 months to mature. It likes steady cool weather, so it is grown in spring and fall, not summer heat. Cauliflower is the trickiest of the cabbage family: it needs to grow without any stress, or it makes a tiny head early (buttoning) or a loose, discolored one. Many white types need blanching, where you tie the outer leaves over the head to keep it white. There are no side shoots like broccoli, so it is one head per plant, and it does not store like cabbage, so use it fresh or freeze it.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Cut the curd when it is full-sized (about 6 to 8 inches across), firm, compact, and still smooth and white, usually 1 to 2 weeks after blanching and roughly 50 to 100 days from transplanting depending on the variety. Slice the whole head off at the base with a few wrapper leaves to protect it. Harvest promptly: a curd left too long rices (separates into a loose, grainy surface), discolors, and starts to open toward flower, and that window is only a few days, shorter in warm weather. Refrigerate soon, since cauliflower does not hold in the garden the way cabbage does.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Your cauliflower is ready when the head is full-sized (about 6 to 8 inches), firm, and still tight, smooth, and white, usually a week or two after you tied the leaves over it. Cut the whole head off with a few leaves attached. Don't wait, because the head quickly goes loose and grainy and yellows. Use it within about a week, since it does not keep like cabbage.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Work plenty of compost into a fertile, well-drained but moisture-retentive bed before planting and confirm pH is near 6.0 to 7.0, liming acidic ground well ahead where clubroot is a concern. Because clubroot builds in the soil, choose a bed where no cole crop has grown for at least 3 years. Set up to water evenly and plan for steady feeding, since the whole secret to cauliflower is uninterrupted growth with no stress, which is what prevents buttoning.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Before planting, mix plenty of compost into a rich, well-drained bed and check that the soil is not too acidic. Try not to plant where you grew other cabbage-family crops in the last few years, since that spreads soil diseases. Plan to water evenly and feed steadily, because cauliflower needs to grow without any stress or it heads early and badly.

crops.name: Cabbage

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Cabbage grows best in rich, well-drained soil with plenty of compost mixed in, and it likes steady, even moisture. Keep the water consistent: a big swing from dry to soaking wet near harvest makes the heads split. Soil that holds moisture but drains well is ideal.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Cabbage is a heavy feeder that rewards a fertile, well-drained loam high in organic matter held at even moisture. Work in compost before planting, and aim for a moisture-retentive but well-draining bed, since both waterlogging (which invites root maggot and rots) and drought stress hurt heading. The signature cabbage soil issue is uneven water near maturity: a sudden flush of water into a firm head bursts it, so steady moisture matters most as the heads fill. Clubroot, the key brassica soil disease, is far more likely in acidic, poorly drained ground.

ph.note_beginner: Cabbage grows best in soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, about 6.0 to 7.0. A simple soil test tells you where you stand. If you have had clubroot, a soil disease, keeping the soil closer to neutral (up toward 7.0 or a bit above) helps hold it back.
ph.note_seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0 (UMN and Iowa State both give 6 to 7; Clemson lists 5.8 to 6.5). Cabbage tolerates a wider 5.5 to 7.5 band. Clubroot, the major brassica soil disease, is far more likely in acidic soil below about 6.5, so where it is a concern lime acidic ground well ahead of planting and hold the pH toward neutral or slightly above.

fertilizer.frequency: once or twice during the season
fertilizer.timing: starter at transplanting, then side-dress about 3 to 4 weeks later as heads begin to form
fertilizer.example_product: Blood meal, 34-0-0, calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0), or a balanced 10-10-10 vegetable fertilizer
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Cabbage is a heavy feeder that needs steady nitrogen to build a large, solid head. Work a balanced fertilizer such as 5-10-10 or 10-10-10 into the bed before planting (Clemson: 5-10-10 at 3 pounds per 100 square feet), then side-dress with nitrogen once the plants are established and again as heads begin to cup, using about 34-0-0 or calcium nitrate. Keep nitrogen steady through heading, but pair it with even moisture: a late surge of growth from heavy feeding plus a sudden drink of water is what splits heads.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Cabbage needs rich soil and regular feeding to grow a big, solid head. Mix a balanced fertilizer into the soil before planting, then feed with a nitrogen fertilizer once the plants take off and again as the heads start to form. Keep the watering even, because a lot of fertilizer plus a sudden soaking can crack the heads.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time to side-dress your cabbage with nitrogen as the heads begin to form.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Time to feed your cabbage.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: High N to build a large, solid head: a 5-10-10 or 10-10-10 starter worked in before planting, then a nitrogen side-dress such as 34-0-0 or calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0) as the plants establish and begin to head.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 at planting, then a nitrogen feed once the plants take off and again as heads form.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: Work in 5-10-10 at about 3 pounds per 100 square feet before planting, then side-dress with about 1 pound of 34-0-0 (or 2 pounds of calcium nitrate) per 100 feet of row as heads begin to form, watered in alongside the plants.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Follow the label rate for a balanced vegetable fertilizer at planting, then a nitrogen feed beside the plants as heads start.

companions.note_beginner: Cabbage does well next to aromatic herbs, onions, and quick crops you can tuck in while the plants are small. The most important rule is to keep it away from other cabbage-family plants, which share the same pests and diseases.
companions.note_seasoned: Most cabbage companion pairings are traditional rather than trial-tested. The ones worth acting on are practical: aromatic herbs and alliums as scent-based deterrents for cabbage pests, small flowering plants such as sweet alyssum and dill to draw the parasitic wasps and hoverflies that attack cabbage aphids and caterpillars (a habitat tactic Clemson recommends for cole crops), and quick crops like lettuce that use the open ground while the cabbage fills in. The well-grounded caution is to separate cabbage from other brassicas, which share clubroot and the whole cabbage-family pest complex, a rotation and disease principle more than a tested adjacency effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Sweet alyssum
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Sweet alyssum makes lots of tiny flowers that bring in helpful insects which eat aphids and caterpillars, two major cabbage pests.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Clemson recommends planting small flowers like sweet alyssum and dill near cole crops to attract beneficial parasites and predators; the specific alyssum-cabbage pairing is not trial-isolated, so medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Sweet alyssum is one of the better-supported cabbage companions. Its low mats of tiny flowers are a classic insectary plant, drawing the hoverflies, lacewings, and parasitic wasps that prey on cabbage aphids and the cabbage-family caterpillars, and Clemson specifically advises small flowers like alyssum near cole crops for biological control. Let it self-sow along the bed edge.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Dill
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Dill's flowers attract helpful insects that hunt the aphids and caterpillars that bother cabbage.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Clemson names dill among the small flowers that attract beneficial parasites to cole crops; aromatic umbels are widely extension-noted for recruiting parasitoid wasps and hoverflies. Dill-cabbage not trial-isolated, so medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Dill works for cabbage mainly through beneficial insects. Its umbel flowers draw the parasitoid wasps and hoverflies that attack cabbage aphids and cabbageworms, and Clemson lists dill among the flowers to plant near cole crops for natural control. Let some flower, and keep it off to the side so it does not shade the heads.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Onions
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Onions are a traditional neighbor for cabbage; their strong smell is said to help confuse and deter cabbage pests.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Allium scent-masking of brassica pests is a long-standing companion tradition with partial mechanistic support; not trial-isolated for cabbage, so low.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Alliums are a traditional brassica companion, their pungent scent thought to mask the crop from the cabbage pests that hunt partly by smell. Shallow-rooted and undemanding, onions tuck around young cabbage without competing for much. Treat it as a low-risk, scent-based aid rather than a proven control.

good_seasoned.name: Sweet alyssum
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A classic insectary plant whose tiny flowers recruit hoverflies, lacewings, and parasitic wasps against cabbage aphids and caterpillars. Clemson recommends small flowers like alyssum near cole crops for biological control.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Clemson advises alyssum/dill near cole crops to attract beneficial parasites; not isolated for cabbage.

good_seasoned.name: Dill
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Aromatic umbels like dill draw parasitoid wasps and hoverflies that attack cabbage aphids and caterpillars; Clemson lists dill among the flowers to plant near cole crops. Let some flower, and keep it from shading the heads.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Clemson cole-crop beneficial-habitat recommendation; specific dill-cabbage pairing not trial-isolated.

good_seasoned.name: Onions
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional brassica companion whose scent is thought to deter cabbage pests; shallow-rooted and low-competition. A plausible, low-risk pairing rather than a documented effect.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Allium scent-masking lore for brassicas; not trial-isolated.

good_seasoned.name: Lettuce
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A quick, shallow cool-season crop that uses the open ground and light between young cabbage plants and is harvested long before they fill in. Space-driven and traditional, not a documented growth effect; the two share no serious pest.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Space-use intercropping lore; no T1 source documents a lettuce-cabbage benefit.

good_seasoned.name: Nasturtiums
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Often planted as a trap crop for cabbage aphids near brassicas. Trap cropping is a documented principle but is not a tested cabbage-nasturtium pairing, so treat it as a plausible aid rather than a proven control.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Trap cropping for aphids is a documented mechanism; the specific nasturtium-cabbage pairing is not formally tested.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Other brassicas
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep cabbage away from other cabbage-family plants like broccoli, brussels sprouts, kale, and cauliflower. They share the same pests and diseases, so grouping them makes problems worse.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Same-family crops share pests and pathogens, so clustering raises pest/disease pressure, and successive brassica planting builds soil-borne clubroot and Fusarium yellows. A sound epidemiological/rotation mechanism rather than a measured antagonism.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Planting cabbage shoulder to shoulder with its brassica relatives, broccoli, brussels sprouts, cauliflower, kale, collards, concentrates the family's shared pests (cabbage aphids, cabbageworms, loopers, harlequin bugs, root maggots) and shared diseases in one spot, and repeated same-family planting lets soil-borne clubroot and Fusarium yellows build up. Spread brassicas out and rotate where they grow each year.

bad_seasoned.name: Other brassicas
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Broccoli, brussels sprouts, cauliflower, kale, and the other cole crops share cabbage's clubroot, Fusarium yellows, and cabbage-family pests, so grouping them concentrates disease and pest pressure. A real rotation and disease principle rather than a tested adjacency effect; the practical rule is to spread brassicas out and rotate them.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Shared clubroot and shared cabbage-family pests are extension-documented; the bad-adjacency claim is a known agronomic principle, not formally pair-tested.

bad_seasoned.name: Strawberries
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional caution that brassicas and strawberries inhibit each other. There is no documented mechanism or T1 support; it persists as folklore.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Folk anti-companion claim with no pattern match or T1 support.

pests.name: Cabbageworms, loopers, and diamondback moths
pests.symptoms_beginner: You'll see ragged holes chewed in the leaves, green caterpillars on the plant, and dark droppings, and worst of all, caterpillars and their mess tunneled down inside the head where they are hard to wash out.
pests.cause_beginner: These are caterpillars that hatch from eggs laid by white butterflies and small moths. They love cabbage-family plants, chew the leaves, and bore into the head you want to eat.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray Bt, which is safe and targets only caterpillars, or spinosad, and pick caterpillars and eggs off by hand from under the leaves. Spray again after rain, since it washes off.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover plants with a light fabric row cover after planting to keep the butterflies and moths from laying eggs, clear away old cabbage-family plants, and watch for the first white butterflies as your signal to act.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Ragged holes chewed in the wrapper leaves with green caterpillars and dark frass; as heads form, larvae bore inside and foul them, the costly damage. Imported cabbageworms are velvety green; cabbage loopers move in a looping arch; diamondback larvae are small and wriggle when disturbed (Clemson rates the diamondback the most numerous cole-crop caterpillar in home gardens).
pests.cause_seasoned: The larvae of the imported cabbageworm, cabbage looper, and diamondback moth feed on brassica foliage and penetrate the head; the adults are white or brownish butterflies and moths that lay eggs on the leaves. Cabbage is a primary host for all three.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Spray Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki) or spinosad, which target caterpillars and spare beneficials, and hand-pick larvae and eggs from leaf undersides. Repeat after rain, since Bt breaks down. Tighten control as heads cup, when damage to the head is the expensive kind.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Use floating row cover or fine mesh from transplanting to exclude the egg-laying adults, clean up brassica debris that shelters pupae, and scout for the first white butterflies as a spray cue.

pests.name: Cabbage aphids
pests.symptoms_beginner: You'll see clusters of small gray-green insects with a dusty, waxy coating on the new growth and tucked into the folds of the head, where they are very hard to wash out. Leaves may curl and there can be a sticky film.
pests.cause_beginner: Cabbage aphids are tiny insects that suck the plant's juices and breed fast. They love cabbage and hide down in the head, which is the part you eat.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Knock colonies off with a strong spray of water and hit the undersides of leaves with insecticidal soap or neem oil, repeating every few days. Welcome ladybugs and lacewings, which eat aphids.
pests.prevention_beginner: Check the growing tips and the developing head often and act early. Go easy on nitrogen once heads form, since soft growth draws them, and clear away old cabbage-family plants after harvest.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: The gray-green, waxy-coated cabbage aphid forms dense colonies on growing tips and leaf undersides and then lodges in the folds of the developing head, where it contaminates the marketable product with insects and honeydew and is very hard to clean at harvest. Curling and distortion of young leaves is common.
pests.cause_seasoned: Brevicoryne brassicae, a brassica-specialist aphid, sucks sap and reproduces rapidly; contamination of the harvested head with aphids and sticky honeydew is usually the real problem rather than plant stunting. Pressure is heaviest on the long-season fall crop.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Dislodge colonies with a strong jet of water and spray insecticidal soap, neem, or horticultural oil with thorough coverage of leaf undersides; repeat every few days. Conserve natural enemies (the parasitoid Diaeretiella rapae, hoverflies, lady beetles) that suppress this aphid.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Scout growing tips and the head weekly and catch infestations before aphids colonize the head. Avoid excess nitrogen once heads set, use row cover on young plants, and destroy crop debris that carries them over.

pests.name: Cabbage root maggot
pests.symptoms_beginner: New transplants wilt and grow badly or fall over. If you pull one up, you'll find small white maggots eating the roots. It is worst in cool, wet soil.
pests.cause_beginner: A small fly lays eggs at the base of the plant, and the maggots that hatch burrow down and eat the roots. The fly is most active in cool, damp weather, so spring transplants are most at risk.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Once the maggots are in the roots you can't save that plant, so pull and throw away the badly damaged ones. Put your effort into protecting the rest from new eggs.
pests.prevention_beginner: Put a small collar or disk around the base of each transplant to stop the fly from laying eggs there, or use a row cover. Avoid planting into cold, soggy soil, and rotate away from where cabbage-family plants grew.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Transplants wilt, grow poorly, and may collapse; pulling a plant reveals small white maggots tunneling in the roots and lower stem. Damage is worst in cool, wet soil at spring establishment.
pests.cause_seasoned: The larvae of the cabbage root fly (Delia radicum) tunnel into brassica roots; the adult lays eggs at the stem base, and the maggots feed below, sometimes killing young plants and opening the door to rots.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no effective rescue once maggots are in the roots; remove and destroy badly affected plants and protect the rest from further egg-laying.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Place a collar or disk around the stem base at transplanting to block egg-laying, or use row cover; avoid planting into cold, wet soil and rotate away from where brassicas grew.

pests.name: Harlequin bug
pests.symptoms_beginner: Shield-shaped black-and-orange (or black-and-red) bugs on the leaves, which develop white or yellow spots, then brown and look tattered. It is mostly a warm-region problem and loves cabbage-family plants.
pests.cause_beginner: The harlequin bug is a colorful stink-bug relative that pierces the leaves and sucks the juices, leaving pale blotches. It strongly prefers cabbage-family plants, especially in the South.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Search out and crush the bugs, their barrel-shaped eggs laid in rows, and the young ones by hand. Use a row cover to keep them off, pull badly infested plants, and clear away weeds and old plants where they hide over winter.
pests.prevention_beginner: Clean up garden debris and cabbage-family weeds where the adults overwinter, use row cover, and consider a trap crop of mustard to lure them away from the main crop, then destroy it.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Shield-shaped bugs up to about 3/8 inch, brightly black-and-yellow or black-and-red, feeding with piercing-sucking mouthparts that leave white stipples; affected leaves brown and look tattered, and heavy feeding wilts and deforms plants. A warm-region brassica specialist.
pests.cause_seasoned: The harlequin bug (Murgantia histrionica) is a true bug that specializes on cole crops, most damaging in the southern United States, where it completes several generations a year and overwinters as an adult in debris and weeds.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick and crush adults, nymphs, and the barrel-shaped egg rows; exclude with floating row cover; remove heavily infested plants. Insecticidal soap, pyrethrum, or neem help where pressure is severe.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Eliminate overwintering sites by removing crop debris and crucifer weeds, use row cover, and deploy an early trap crop of mustard to divert overwintering adults, then destroy it before the main crop is set out.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms_beginner: Lots of tiny round holes in the leaves of young plants, made by small dark beetles that jump away like fleas when you get close. Bad damage can stunt seedlings.
pests.cause_beginner: Flea beetles are small jumping beetles that chew on young cabbage-family leaves. They hurt seedlings most, because a tiny plant can't grow fast enough to recover.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover young plants with a row cover, and if there are a lot of beetles, use a spray such as spinosad. The main goal is to get the seedlings big enough to handle the damage.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover seedlings with row cover from the start, keep them strong with steady water and food so they grow past the damage, and pull nearby weeds in the cabbage family.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny round shot-hole pits chewed in the leaves of young plants; the small dark beetles jump like fleas when disturbed. Heavy feeding stunts or kills seedlings and slows establishment.
pests.cause_seasoned: Flea beetles chew the foliage of young brassicas and are most damaging at the seedling stage; a vigorous transplant generally outgrows them, but a stalled seedling can be set back badly.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Protect seedlings with row cover and spray spinosad if pressure is high; the goal is getting plants past the vulnerable seedling stage.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Use row cover from transplanting, keep seedlings vigorous with even water and feeding so they grow through the damage, and clean up weedy brassica relatives nearby.

diseases.name: Clubroot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Plants wilt in the afternoon, stay small and yellowish, and don't bounce back. If you dig one up, the roots are swollen into lumpy, club-shaped knobs.
diseases.cause_beginner: A germ that lives in the soil infects the roots of cabbage-family plants and makes them swell, which stops the plant from taking up water and food. It stays in the soil for years.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There's no cure once a plant has it, so pull and destroy infected plants. Keeping the soil from being too acidic (closer to neutral) helps hold it back, and growing cabbage-family plants only rarely in that spot starves the germ out.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Don't grow cabbage or other cabbage-family plants in the same spot more than once every few years, longer if you've had clubroot. Keep the soil from being too acidic, improve drainage, and clean soil off your tools.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Plants wilt in the heat of the day, grow stunted and yellowed, and recover poorly; roots are swollen into distorted clubs and galls instead of normal fine roots.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A soilborne organism (Plasmodiophora brassicae) infects brassica roots and forms the galls, which block water and nutrient uptake. It persists in soil for many years, spreads in contaminated soil and water, and infects most readily in acidic soils below pH 6.5.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once plants are infected; remove and destroy them. Raising soil pH toward neutral with lime suppresses the disease, and long rotations starve it out over time.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate brassicas out of affected ground on a long cycle (UMN advises up to 7 years where clubroot is known), keep soil pH up, improve drainage, and avoid moving infested soil on tools and boots.

diseases.name: Black rot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Yellow patches shaped like the letter V appear at the leaf edges, pointing inward, with black veins inside them. It can spread through the plant and rot the head.
diseases.cause_beginner: A bacteria that often comes in on infected seeds or transplants. It gets into the leaves and travels through the plant's veins, spreading fastest in warm, wet weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There's no real cure, so remove and destroy infected plants to keep it from spreading. Don't handle or brush against the plants while they're wet, because that spreads the bacteria.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Begin with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants, don't plant where cabbage-family crops grew recently, space plants for good airflow, and avoid overhead watering.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellow, V-shaped lesions spread inward from the leaf margins, with the veins inside the V turning black; the disease moves through the vascular system and can blacken and rot the head. Often the most serious cabbage disease in warm, wet weather.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A seedborne bacterium (Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris) that enters through leaf pores and wounds and moves through the veins; it spreads in warm, wet conditions and on infected seed or transplants.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no effective cure; remove and destroy infected plants. Avoid working among plants when foliage is wet, since that moves the bacteria.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Start with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants (a hot-water seed treatment helps), rotate 2 to 3 years away from brassicas, give plants room for airflow, and avoid overhead watering and handling wet foliage.

diseases.name: Blackleg
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Pale, sunken spots dotted with tiny black specks appear on the stem and leaves, and the base of the stem darkens and rots, so the plant may girdle and topple. It often arrives on infected seed.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that comes in on infected seed or plants and attacks the stem and leaves of cabbage-family crops. It spreads in wet weather and lingers in old plant debris.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There's no cure, so pull and destroy infected plants. The real fix is prevention: clean seed, rotation, and clearing away old cabbage-family debris.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Start with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants, rotate away from cabbage-family crops for a few years, and clear away old brassica plants where the fungus survives.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Pale, sunken lesions peppered with small black fruiting bodies (pycnidia) form on stems and leaves, and a dark, girdling canker at the stem base can rot the crown and lodge the plant; cankers may extend into the head.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Phoma lingam (Leptosphaeria maculans) is chiefly seedborne and also survives in brassica debris; it spreads in cool, wet weather by splashing water and infects through wounds and pores.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no effective cure; remove and destroy infected plants. Management is preventive, since the pathogen is carried on seed and in residue.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Use clean, certified, hot-water-treated seed and disease-free transplants, rotate 3 years away from brassicas, and bury or remove crop debris that carries the fungus over.

diseases.name: Fusarium yellows
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Whole plants turn a dull yellow-green, often more on one side, with leaves curling and dropping from the bottom up. Cut a stem and the water-carrying tissue inside is browned. It is worst in warm soil.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soil fungus that gets into the roots and plugs the plant's plumbing, so it yellows and wilts. It lives in the soil for years and is most active when the soil is warm, so it hits summer-grown cabbage hardest.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There's no cure once a plant is infected, so pull and destroy it. The reliable answer is to plant resistant (yellows-resistant) varieties.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant yellows-resistant varieties, which are widely available and the main control. Rotate away from cabbage-family crops, and avoid planting cabbage to mature in the hottest soil.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: A warm-season wilt: plants turn dull yellow-green (often one-sided), leaves curl, cup, and drop from the base up, and the vascular tissue in the stem browns. Stunting and death follow in susceptible varieties; symptoms resemble black rot but without the V-shaped marginal lesions.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The soilborne fungus Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. conglutinans invades the roots and vascular system; it persists in soil for years and is most active in warm soil (roughly 80°F and up), so it most damages spring cabbage maturing into summer heat.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure for infected plants; remove and destroy them. Resistant varieties are the practical control, since the fungus is long-lived in soil.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Grow yellows-resistant (YR) varieties, which provide durable, effective resistance and are the standard control; rotate away from brassicas and avoid timing the crop to mature in the hottest soil.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Pale yellow blotches on top of the leaves, with fuzzy grayish growth on the underside, mostly in cool, damp weather. Bad cases discolor the leaves and can spot the head.
diseases.cause_beginner: A mold-like disease that loves cool, wet, humid weather and spreads through the air and water. Wet leaves and crowded plants make it worse.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Open up the airflow so leaves can dry, remove the worst leaves, and use a copper spray if it's spreading. It's hard to stop once the weather stays damp.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Space plants so air moves between them, water at the soil instead of from above, and pick resistant varieties if downy mildew is common where you live.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Pale yellow patches form on the upper leaf surface with a fuzzy gray-white growth underneath, mainly in cool, damp weather; severe infection discolors the wrapper leaves and can blemish the head. Cabbage's cool, humid season overlaps the weather it likes.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A fungus-like organism (Hyaloperonospora parasitica) that thrives in cool, wet, humid conditions and spreads by spores in water and air; long leaf wetness and crowded plantings favor it.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Improve airflow and let foliage dry, remove badly affected leaves, and apply a copper-based fungicide if pressure is high; the disease is hard to stop once humidity stays high.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants for good air movement, water at the soil line rather than overhead, and choose resistant varieties where downy mildew is common.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Give about 1 to 1.5 inches weekly, kept as even as possible, and ease off slightly right at maturity to avoid splitting.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly 1 to 1.5 inches a week. Try to keep it steady, not dry-then-soaked.
watering.amount_seasoned: About 1 to 1.5 inches per week (UMN: roughly 1 inch of rainfall a week is enough), more in hot, dry spells while heads are sizing up.
watering.amount_beginner: Aim for roughly 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose where possible to keep foliage dry and discourage leaf disease.
watering.method_beginner: Water at the base of the plant rather than over the leaves.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves and limp growth; cabbage dislikes waterlogged soil, which invites root maggots, clubroot, and crown rot in cold, wet ground.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Lower leaves yellow and the plant looks soggy and limp.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting and stalled growth, then small, loose heads; and worst of all, a heavy watering or rain after a dry spell near maturity bursts the heads.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Wilting leaves and small heads, and cracked, split heads if a dry spell is followed by a big drink of water.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Even, steady moisture is the whole game with cabbage: it builds firm, solid heads and, just as important, prevents the splitting that a sudden flush of water causes near maturity.
watering.method_note_beginner: Keep the water steady so the heads grow firm and do not crack. Big swings from dry to wet are what split cabbage.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Even moisture matters most while heads are forming and filling; this is also when a sudden change in watering will split a nearly mature head.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Water steadily while the heads are forming and filling, and do not suddenly soak a nearly ripe head.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Cabbage is usually transplanted but can also be direct sown, especially for the fall crop. For spring, start seeds indoors about 4 to 6 weeks before set-out and transplant sturdy young plants out 2 to 4 weeks before the last frost, since cabbage transplants are cold-hardy. For fall, sow indoors or direct seed in early-to-mid summer and set out in mid-to-late summer to mature in cool fall weather. Set out stocky plants with 4 to 6 true leaves and harden them off over 7 to 10 days. Avoid setting out overly large or root-bound transplants into a cold spell, which can trigger bolting.
start_method.notes_beginner: You can grow cabbage from transplants or sow the seeds right in the garden, especially for a fall crop. For spring, start seeds indoors about a month before planting out and set the plants out a few weeks before your last frost, since young cabbage handles cold well. For fall, start them in early to mid summer. Let homegrown seedlings get used to the outdoors over a week before planting.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Other brassicas (broccoli, brussels sprouts, cauliflower, kale, collards, kohlrabi, turnip, radish, mustard), which share clubroot and the cabbage-family pests.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Other cabbage-family crops like broccoli, brussels sprouts, cauliflower, kale, and turnips.
rotation.good_after: Legumes such as beans and peas, or unrelated crops like tomatoes, squash, cucumbers, or onions.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate so cabbage and its brassica relatives do not return to the same ground for at least 3 years, and longer where clubroot is present (UMN advises a 7-year break where clubroot is known). Repeated same-family cropping builds soil-borne clubroot and Fusarium yellows, and holding soil pH near neutral also helps suppress clubroot.
rotation.note_beginner: Don't plant cabbage or other cabbage-family crops in the same spot year after year. Waiting at least 3 years between them, and longer if you have had clubroot, helps avoid soil diseases.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: A solid cabbage head keeps for a week or two in a cool room, but quality is best cold. Cabbage is one of the great storage vegetables: late, dense storage types keep for months near freezing, which is the real advantage of the crop.
storage.room_temp_beginner: A firm cabbage head will keep a week or two at room temperature, but it lasts far longer in the cold. Late storage types are made to keep for months.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerate whole, unwashed heads with the wrapper leaves on; a solid head holds for several weeks to a couple of months in the crisper. For long storage, hold at 32°F to 34°F and 95% to 98% humidity, where dense late types keep 2 to 6 months (USU; Clemson up to 5 months). Keep cabbage away from ethylene-producing fruit, which yellows the leaves faster.
storage.fridge_beginner: Store whole, unwashed heads in the fridge crisper, where a firm head keeps for several weeks. In a very cold, humid spot (right around freezing) late storage cabbage keeps for months. Keep it away from apples and other ripening fruit, which make it go off sooner.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Cabbage freezes after blanching: cut into wedges or shred, blanch about 1.5 minutes (shreds) to 3 minutes (wedges), cool quickly in ice water, drain, and freeze. Blanching halts the enzymes that cause off-flavors; frozen cabbage is best used cooked. Fresh cabbage is also the basis of fermented sauerkraut and kimchi for long keeping.
storage.freezer_beginner: You can freeze cabbage if you blanch it first. Cut it up, boil it briefly (1 to 3 minutes), cool it in ice water, drain, and freeze; use it cooked. Cabbage is also great for making sauerkraut or kimchi, which keep a long time.
storage.notes_seasoned: Storage life depends heavily on type: dense, late storage varieties (Danish Ballhead, late flat Dutch types) are bred to hold for months in a root cellar or cold, humid fridge, while early, looser types are for fresh use within weeks. For cellar storage, harvest with a few wrapper leaves and the stem on, keep cold and humid, and check periodically for soft outer leaves.
storage.notes_beginner: How long cabbage keeps depends on the type: late storage varieties are made to last for months somewhere cold and humid, while early types are for eating fresh within a few weeks. For long storage, leave a few outer leaves on, keep it cold and damp, and check now and then.

recommended.name: Golden Acre
recommended.note: A classic early green variety (about 65 days) with small, round, solid 3-to-4-pound heads; quick and dependable for spring. Good for small gardens and early eating, but does not hold or store as long as late types.

recommended.name: Early Jersey Wakefield
recommended.note: An heirloom early variety (about 63 days) with pointed, compact heads, cold-hardy and a longtime garden standard; open-pollinated and seed-saveable.

recommended.name: Stonehead
recommended.note: An early-mid hybrid (about 70 days) with very firm, dense 3-to-4-pound heads that resist splitting and hold well in the garden; carries Fusarium yellows resistance. A reliable all-around pick.

recommended.name: Bravo / Market Prize / Rio Verde
recommended.note: Mid-season hybrids (about 75 to 85 days) recommended by Clemson for the Southeast; productive, uniform, and yellows-resistant, useful where Fusarium yellows or warm-season disease is a concern. Days approximate.

recommended.name: Ruby Ball / Red Acre (red types)
recommended.note: Red or purple cabbages (about 70 to 80 days) with firm, colorful heads that hold well and add color to the garden and plate. Ruby Ball is an AAS-winning hybrid; Red Acre is an open-pollinated standard.

recommended.name: Savoy Ace / Savoy Express (savoy types)
recommended.note: Crinkle-leaved savoy cabbages (about 80 days; Savoy Express is earlier and an AAS winner) with tender, mild leaves prized for cooking; very cold-hardy and good for fall. Days approximate.

recommended.name: Danish Ballhead (late storage)
recommended.note: A late storage variety (about 100 days) with dense, heavy, round heads bred to keep for months in cold storage; the type to grow for a fall crop you want to hold through winter. Late and slow, so give it a long cool season.

varieties.note_seasoned: Match the variety to the season and the purpose. Early types (Golden Acre, Early Jersey Wakefield, Stonehead) finish fast for spring and small heads; mid-season hybrids (Bravo, Market Prize, Rio Verde) give uniform, often yellows-resistant heads; late storage types (Danish Ballhead and late flat Dutch types) are the ones to grow for fall and long winter keeping. Where Fusarium yellows is a problem, choose a yellows-resistant (YR) variety, the main control for that disease. Savoy types are tender and cold-hardy for cooking; red types add color and hold well. Days-to-maturity figures are approximate and run from transplanting.
varieties.note_beginner: Pick the type that fits your season. Early kinds like Golden Acre and Stonehead grow quickly for spring; later, denser kinds like Danish Ballhead are made to store for months in fall and winter. If you have had trouble with cabbage yellows (a soil disease), choose a yellows-resistant variety. Savoy cabbages have pretty crinkled leaves and are very cold-hardy, and red cabbages add color.

drainage.saucer_practice: Empty the saucer after watering so roots never sit in water; cabbage resents waterlogged soil.

soil_mix.type_beginner: A good-quality potting mix, not garden soil.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in compost and a slow-release fertilizer for steady feeding.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: A rich, well-drained commercial potting mix high in organic matter.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend in compost and a slow-release balanced fertilizer; a single cabbage in a pot is a heavy feeder in a small soil volume.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out faster than the ground, so check daily in warm weather and keep the water steady, since uneven watering cracks the heads.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Feed a bit more often than in the ground, since watering washes nutrients out of pots.
container_notes.notes_beginner: Cabbage grows fine in a large pot. Use a container of at least 5 gallons, one plant per pot, and keep it well watered and fed. Compact early varieties like Golden Acre are the best fit. The main trick is steady watering so the head does not crack.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Cabbage is a workable container crop, especially the compact early varieties. Use a pot of at least 5 gallons (10 is better) at least 10 inches deep, one plant per pot, in a rich, well-drained mix, and keep moisture and feeding steady, since a small soil volume runs out and uneven watering splits the head. Choose small, fast types (Golden Acre, Early Jersey Wakefield, Stonehead) over the big late storage kinds. Container-specific figures are modeled on general container-vegetable guidance plus the plant's size.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry faster than beds; check moisture daily in heat and water before the mix dries, keeping it even to avoid splitting the head.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Container plants need more frequent feeding than in-ground ones because watering leaches nutrients.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering container suits cabbage well, since it smooths out the even moisture that keeps the head solid and uncracked.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match because it keeps the water steady, which keeps the head from cracking.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: Cabbage has a shallow, wide root system and a broad leaf spread, so choose a wide pot of at least 5 gallons and about 10 inches deep for one plant; a broad, stable container holds moisture more evenly than a narrow one, which matters for split-free heads.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Give one cabbage a wide pot that holds at least 5 gallons and is about 10 inches deep. A broad, sturdy pot holds water more evenly than a tall skinny one, which helps keep the head from cracking.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: In about 5 to 10 days, your seeds sprout and push up their first two little leaves (the seed leaves).
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the starting mix damp. Once the first real leaves appear, give the seedlings strong light so they do not get leggy.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your seeds come up yet?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seeds sprout in about 5 to 10 days, pushing up two seed leaves (cotyledons). Cabbage is usually started indoors for transplanting, though the fall crop can be direct sown.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep the starting mix evenly moist and give bright light from emergence to avoid stretch; thin or pot up once the first true leaves appear.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Did your cabbage seeds sprout?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The seedlings grow their real leaves and a stronger stem. They are ready to plant out at about 4 to 6 weeks old, with several true leaves.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Harden the seedlings off over about a week before planting out. Watch for flea beetle holes on the young leaves and use a row cover.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How many real leaves do your seedlings have?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Young plants build true leaves and a sturdy stem; transplants are ready at about 4 to 6 true leaves, roughly 4 to 6 weeks from sowing. Set out stocky young plants rather than oversized, root-bound ones.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harden off over 7 to 10 days before setting out at 12-to-24-inch spacing; protect seedlings from flea beetles with row cover and from cabbage root maggot with stem collars. Avoid exposing large transplants to a prolonged cold spell, which can trigger bolting.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are your transplants ready to go out?

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant grows a rosette of big, spreading leaves before it starts to form a head. This is when it builds the frame that wraps into the head.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Feed with nitrogen and keep it evenly watered so it grows steadily. Check for caterpillars and aphids, and keep the row cover on if you can.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Is your plant growing a big rosette of leaves?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The plant builds a broad rosette of frame leaves over several weeks before cupping into a head. Steady, vigorous growth now sets the eventual head size.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Side-dress with nitrogen, keep moisture even, and scout for cabbageworms, loopers, cabbage aphids, and (in the South) harlequin bugs as the frame fills out. Even watering from here on is the key to a solid, split-free head.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Is your plant putting on steady leafy growth before heading?

growth_stages.name: Head forming
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The center leaves start to cup and fold inward, forming a tight ball in the middle of the plant. The head firms up as it fills.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the watering steady and even now, because big swings from dry to wet make the head crack. Watch for caterpillars and aphids getting into the head.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Has a head started to form in the center?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The central leaves cup and wrap into a head that firms and fills from the inside; this is the crop forming. Even moisture now builds a solid head and prevents the late splitting a sudden flush of water causes.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Hold moisture even and taper heavy nitrogen as the head fills; tighten caterpillar and aphid control, since damage inside the head is the costly kind. Pick varieties and timing so heads mature in cool weather, not summer heat.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Is the head cupping and firming up?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The head is full size, firm, and solid when you squeeze it. That is the signal to cut it, before it sits too long and splits.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Cut the head off at the base with a sharp knife once it is firm. If you are not ready to pick, give the plant a quarter turn or tug to slow it down so it does not split.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Is your cabbage head firm and ready to cut?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Heads are ready when full-sized, firm, and solid to a squeeze (about 60 to 120 days from transplanting depending on type). A mature head left in the ground will split, especially after rain, so harvest on time.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut firm heads at the base with a sharp knife, leaving a few wrapper leaves for protection. To hold mature heads in the garden, give the plant a quarter turn or pull it up slightly to shear some roots and slow water uptake. Late storage types can be cut with the stem and cellar-stored cold and humid for months.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are you cutting firm, solid heads?

notifications.title_seasoned: Keep watering even as heads form
notifications.title_beginner: Water steadily now so heads don't crack
notifications.body_seasoned: Your cabbage is cupping into a head. Keep moisture as even as possible from here on and taper heavy nitrogen: a sudden flush of water into a firming head is exactly what splits it. Tighten caterpillar and aphid control, since damage inside the head is the costly kind.
notifications.body_beginner: Your cabbage is starting to form a head. Keep the watering steady, not dry-then-soaked, so the head does not crack, and watch for caterpillars and aphids getting inside.

notifications.title_beginner: Your cabbage looks ready to cut
notifications.body_seasoned: The head should be full-sized, firm, and solid to a squeeze. Cut it at the base with a sharp knife, leaving a few wrapper leaves. A mature head left in the ground will split, especially after rain, so harvest on time.
notifications.body_beginner: Your cabbage head should be firm and solid. Cut it off at the base with a sharp knife. Don't leave a ripe head sitting too long, or it may crack.

notifications.title_seasoned: Hold a ripe head to prevent splitting
notifications.title_beginner: Not ready to pick? Slow the head down
notifications.body_seasoned: If a head is mature but you are not ready to use it, give the plant a quarter turn or pull it up slightly to shear some roots and slow water uptake. This buys you a week or two before splitting; storage types can be cut and cellar-stored cold and humid for months.
notifications.body_beginner: If your cabbage is ripe but you are not ready to use it, give the plant a quarter turn or a gentle tug to break some roots. That slows it down so the head does not split.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot weather warning for your cabbage
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Cabbage forms solid heads best in cool weather, roughly 60°F to 65°F. Sustained heat above about 80°F slows or stops heading, encourages loose heads and bolting, and worsens Fusarium yellows and aphid pressure. Keep moisture even, and recognize that in hot regions cabbage is timed to mature in cool spring or fall, not midsummer.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Cabbage likes cool weather to form a good head. In a heat wave it can make loose heads or bolt (send up a flower stalk), so keep it watered. In warm areas, cabbage is really a spring and fall crop, not a summer one.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hard freeze coming
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Cabbage is very cold-hardy: mature heads take frost in stride and tolerate temperatures down to about 18°F to 20°F (Clemson; USU notes little damage to 25°F), and many growers find fall heads sweeter after cool weather. A solid head holds well in the cold. Below the high teens, the head can be damaged, so harvest before a deep freeze; seedlings are more frost-sensitive than mature plants.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Cabbage handles frost well, and mature heads are fine down to about 20°F, so you usually do not need to do anything. Fall cabbage often tastes a little sweeter after cool weather. Before a really hard, deep freeze, cut and store the heads, since extreme cold can damage them.

germination.text_seasoned: Start seeds indoors about 4 to 6 weeks before set-out for spring; the fall crop can be started indoors or direct sown in early-to-mid summer.
germination.text_beginner: Start seeds indoors about a month before you plan to plant them out, or sow them right in the garden for a fall crop.

germination.text_seasoned: Sow about 0.25 to 0.5 inch deep into a moist starting mix and give bright light from emergence to keep seedlings stocky.
germination.text_beginner: Plant the seeds about a quarter to half an inch deep, keep them damp, and give them strong light so they do not get leggy.

seedling.text_seasoned: Transplant stocky young plants with 4 to 6 true leaves at 12 to 24 inches apart (closer spacing gives smaller heads, wider spacing larger ones); harden off over 7 to 10 days first.
seedling.text_beginner: Space plants about 12 to 24 inches apart. Closer together gives smaller heads, farther apart gives bigger ones. Harden the seedlings off over about a week before planting out.

seedling.text_seasoned: Protect transplants from flea beetles with row cover and from cabbage root maggot with stem collars, especially in cool, wet spring soil.
seedling.text_beginner: Cover young plants with a row cover to stop flea beetles, and put a collar around the stem to keep root maggots out.

established.text_seasoned: Side-dress nitrogen as the rosette builds and keep moisture even at about 1 to 1.5 inches per week; steady water now is what builds a solid head later.
established.text_beginner: Feed with nitrogen and water steadily while the plant grows its big leaves. Even watering is the secret to a firm, crack-free head.

established.text_seasoned: Scout for cabbageworms and loopers on the leaves and cabbage aphids on the growing tips; getting ahead of them now keeps them out of the head later.
established.text_beginner: Check the leaves for green caterpillars and the new growth for aphids, and deal with them early before the head forms.

head_forming.text_seasoned: Hold moisture as even as you can as the head fills, and taper heavy nitrogen; a sudden flush of water into a firm head is what splits it.
head_forming.text_beginner: Keep the watering steady as the head forms, and do not suddenly soak a nearly ripe head, or it will crack.

head_forming.text_seasoned: Tighten caterpillar and aphid control as the head cups, since damage inside the head is the expensive kind, and use Bt or spinosad for caterpillars.
head_forming.text_beginner: Watch closely for caterpillars and aphids getting into the head and treat them, because that is the part you eat.

harvest.text_seasoned: Cut heads when full-sized, firm, and solid; a mature head left too long splits, especially after rain, so harvest on time.
harvest.text_beginner: Cut the head when it feels firm and solid. Don't leave a ripe head sitting, or it may crack, especially after rain.

harvest.text_seasoned: To hold mature heads in the garden, give the plant a quarter turn or pull it up slightly to break some roots and slow water uptake; cellar late storage types cold and humid for months.
harvest.text_beginner: If you can't pick a ripe head yet, give the plant a quarter turn or a gentle tug to slow it down so it does not split. Late storage cabbage keeps for months somewhere cold and damp.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: One head per plant, typically about 2 to 5 pounds depending on variety and spacing (early types and close spacing give smaller 2-to-3-pound heads; late and widely spaced plants give larger ones). Some varieties resprout small secondary heads after the main head is cut.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Each plant gives you one head, usually about 2 to 5 pounds. Smaller, closer-spaced plants make smaller heads; bigger spacing and late varieties make bigger ones.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Heads mature over a few weeks in cool spring or fall weather; the crop is a one-time cut per plant rather than a long picking season. In hot regions the spring crop must beat the summer heat and the main crop is the fall planting.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Each cabbage makes its head over a few weeks and is cut once when firm. The best heads form in the cool weather of spring and fall.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: The two keys to good cabbage are even watering and timing. Steady moisture builds a solid head and prevents the splitting that a sudden drink of water causes near maturity, and timing the crop to head up in cool spring or fall weather avoids the heat that gives loose heads, bolting, and yellows. New growers most often lose heads to splitting (let it sit too long or watered unevenly) or to summer heat.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Here are the two tricks: water evenly so the head grows solid and does not crack, and plant so the head forms in cool spring or fall weather, not summer heat. Cut the head as soon as it is firm, and if you can't, give the plant a quarter turn to slow it down so it does not split.
factors_seasoned: Even moisture: steady watering builds a solid head, while a dry spell followed by heavy water splits a nearly mature head.
Timing and temperature: heads form best in cool weather (about 60°F to 65°F); heat gives loose heads, bolting, and Fusarium yellows.
Spacing: closer spacing gives smaller heads, wider spacing larger ones, so space to the head size you want.
Variety and purpose: early types for quick small heads, mid-season hybrids for uniform yellows-resistant heads, late storage types for big heads that keep for months.
Nitrogen and soil fertility: cabbage is a heavy feeder, but excess late nitrogen plus uneven water worsens splitting.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No reliable extension or peer-reviewed evidence supports timing cabbage planting or harvest by moon phase. Plant by soil temperature, frost dates, and the seasonal windows instead, and harvest by head firmness.

failure_diagnostics.label: Split or cracked heads
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Uneven watering near maturity (a dry spell then a big soaking or rain), or leaving a ripe head in the ground too long.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your cabbage head cracked open. This almost always means the head took up water too fast near maturity, usually a heavy rain or watering after a dry spell, or it simply sat ripe in the garden too long. People often blame the variety, but watering and timing are the cause. Next time, keep the water as even as you can, harvest heads as soon as they are firm, and if you can't pick a ripe one, give the plant a quarter turn to slow it down.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Water evenly, pick heads as soon as they are firm, and give a ripe head a quarter turn if you can't harvest it yet.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Heads split from a rapid late surge in water uptake, classically a heavy rain or irrigation after a dry interval, or from leaving a mature head in the field past firmness. Excess late nitrogen compounds it by pushing fast interior growth. Next time hold moisture even through heading, taper late nitrogen, harvest promptly at firmness, and root-prune (quarter turn or a slight lift) to hold mature heads.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Rapid water uptake near maturity (uneven irrigation or rain after drought), over-mature heads, and excess late nitrogen.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Keep moisture even, taper late nitrogen, harvest at firmness, and root-prune to hold ripe heads.

failure_diagnostics.label: Plant bolted (sent up a flower stalk) instead of heading
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Young plants exposed to a cold spell, or hot weather, so the plant flowered instead of forming a head.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your cabbage shot up a flower stalk instead of making a head. This usually happens when transplants get chilled by a long cold spell after they are set out, or when the plant runs into heat. Big, older transplants are most at risk. Next time, set out younger, stocky plants after the worst cold, and time the crop so it heads in cool (not cold, not hot) weather.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Set out younger plants after hard cold passes, and time the crop to head in mild weather.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The plant bolted rather than heading. Cabbage vernalizes: a prolonged cold period (Clemson: about 10 or more days between 35°F and 50°F) on a plant past the juvenile stage triggers flowering, and heat stress also pushes bolting. Oversized transplants exposed to spring cold are the classic cause. Next time set out younger, stocky transplants after hard cold, avoid stalling seedlings, and time maturity for mild weather.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Vernalization of past-juvenile plants by a prolonged cold spell (or heat stress), worst on oversized spring transplants.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Set out younger transplants after hard cold, avoid checks to growth, and time heading for mild weather.

failure_diagnostics.label: Caterpillars or aphids inside the head
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Cabbageworms or cabbage aphids that got into the head as it formed, often missed until harvest.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: When you cut the head you found caterpillars and droppings, or clusters of gray-green aphids, tucked down inside. These pests love cabbage and hide right in the head, which is the part you eat. People often miss them until it is too late. Next time, cover plants with a row cover, scout the leaves and growing tips weekly, and treat caterpillars with Bt before heads form.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Use a row cover, scout weekly, and treat caterpillars with Bt before the head forms.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Cabbageworms, loopers, or diamondback larvae bored into the head, or cabbage aphids colonized its folds, contaminating the product and very hard to clean. The window to act is before heading. Next time exclude egg-laying adults with row cover from transplanting, scout leaves and tips weekly, apply Bt or spinosad for caterpillars, and dislodge aphid colonies early; taper nitrogen, since soft growth favors aphids.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Cabbageworm-complex larvae and cabbage aphids penetrating the head, worsened by late detection and soft, over-fed growth.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Exclude adults with row cover, scout weekly, treat caterpillars early with Bt, and knock aphids back before heading.

failure_diagnostics.label: Stunted, yellow plants with clubbed roots
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Clubroot, a soil disease of cabbage-family plants, or planting brassicas in the same spot too often.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your plants stayed small and yellowish, wilted in the afternoon, and when you dug one up the roots were swollen into lumps. That is clubroot, a soil disease that infects cabbage-family roots and lasts for years in the soil. It builds up when brassicas are grown in the same spot repeatedly and in acidic soil. Next time, rotate so cabbage-family crops do not return to that bed for several years, keep the soil pH near neutral, and improve drainage.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Rotate brassicas out of that bed for several years, keep soil pH near neutral, and improve drainage.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Plants were stunted and chlorotic, wilted by day, and showed galled, clubbed roots, the signature of clubroot (Plasmodiophora brassicae). The soilborne organism persists for years and builds under repeated brassica cropping and acidic, poorly drained soil. (A one-sided yellowing with browned stem vessels but normal roots instead points to Fusarium yellows, a warm-soil wilt; grow resistant varieties.) Next time rotate cole crops out for at least 3 years (up to 7 where clubroot is known), lime toward a neutral pH, and improve drainage.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Clubroot building in soil cropped to brassicas too frequently, favored by acidic, wet soil (distinguish from Fusarium yellows).
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Use a long brassica rotation, raise pH toward neutral, improve drainage, and grow yellows-resistant varieties for the Fusarium look-alike.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Cabbage crops in the cool shoulders of the year, so plant in small batches within the spring window and again in late summer for fall, rather than all at once. Mixing early, mid, and late varieties in one planting also spreads the harvest, since they mature at different times. The spring window is short because heads must size up before summer heat, so most gardens fit only a sowing or two before the midsummer gap; the fall planting, heading into cooling weather, is often the more reliable crop and the one to grow for storage.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: Plant cabbage in spring and again in late summer for fall, in small batches a couple of weeks apart, instead of all at one time. Planting a few different varieties that ripen at different times also spreads out the harvest. Skip the hottest part of summer, since cabbage will not form good heads in the heat.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: cabbage_author_fresh_pilot (Claude Code lane authoring, 2026-06-29). Authored by FILLING the cabbage shell, modeled STRUCTURALLY on the broccoli certified template (heading double-crop) with brussels-sprouts field shapes, biology RE-DERIVED from live T1 extension sources (UMN/Iowa State/Clemson/USU/UMD for core biology; UMass + UMN for cabbage aphid; Clemson cole-crop disease factsheet for blackleg/Fusarium yellows/downy mildew; UMN clubroot). Per-region planting calendars from UMN/Iowa State/MSU/Penn State/UMaine/NDSU (northern), Clemson/UGA/LSU/Alabama/Mississippi State (SE Gulf), UC IPM/UC MG/UC Marin/UC San Diego (California), U Arizona AZ1005 (low desert AZ), NMSU/Texas A&M (warm arid, modeled), UF/IFAS VH021+EP450+EP452 (Florida), CTAHR B-91 (Hawaii, modeled). DRAFT for review, not certified: launch flags false. Key cabbage-vs-broccoli refits: forms a SOLID LEAFY HEAD (head_forming stage kept, broccoli's side_shoots dropped); longer/variable maturity 60 to 120 days (early/mid/late types) vs broccoli's 55 to 75; harvest_urgency MODERATE because a mature head SPLITS if left, holdable by root-twisting/pruning (vs broccoli's high); strong STORAGE emphasis (late storage types keep months at 32 to 34 degrees F); even-moisture/splitting is the signature challenge; very cold-hardy (mature heads to about 20 degrees F); spacing 12 to 24 in drives head size; pests add diamondback moth + harlequin bug, diseases add blackleg + Fusarium yellows (yellows-resistant varieties as control). Spring AND fall double crop (like broccoli) with backed heat_pause only in genuinely hot double-crop regions (northern z6/z7, se_gulf z8/z9, ca_interior, ca_south_coast, warm_arid) and season_over for the dead summer in the single-winter-crop desert/Florida/Hawaii regions; cool northern z3 to z5 and the fog-belt north coast carry NO heat_pause. successions_realized CC-DERIVED (not authored). See cabbage_NOTES.md for all flags and modeled values.

open_findings.summary: germination_temp_f [45, 85] is the standard cole-crop germination envelope; the cabbage T1 pages report 5 to 10 day germination and a 60 to 65 degrees F optimum but do not state an explicit min/max soil temperature, so the range is modeled on the brassica germination envelope (consistent with broccoli's [40, 86]).
open_findings.basis: Consistent with broccoli/brussels germination_temp_f and the germination the sources report; flagged in NOTES.

open_findings.summary: The claim that cool weather and light frost improve cabbage flavor is stated mildly. Cold-hardiness is well sourced (Clemson: mature heads to 18 to 20 degrees F; USU: little damage to 25 degrees F), but UMN explicitly notes no flavor improvement, so frost-sweetening is framed as a softer, less-pronounced effect than in kale or brussels sprouts.
open_findings.basis: Cold-hardiness is T1-sourced; the sweetening nuance is widely held but not uniformly stated by T1, so it is hedged in the prose and weather copy.

open_findings.summary: Regional HARVEST month windows are DERIVED from the sourced PLANT windows plus the crop's 60 to 120 day maturity (early/mid/late types), since the extension calendars give planting windows, not explicit harvest months. Plant windows are directly sourced (or flagged modeled).
open_findings.basis: Standard derivation; same pattern accepted in the kale/brussels pilots. Sourced approximations surfaced for review.

open_findings.summary: warm_arid (El Paso/high desert z8) planting window is MODELED on NMSU's hardy-crop rule (plant as soon as the ground can be worked in spring, or midsummer for fall) and Texas A&M's relative spring/fall rules; the exact zone-8 month tables live in PDF/complex sources that did not parse.
open_findings.basis: Cabbage is sourced as a hardy spring-and-fall crop for the region; only the exact month table is modeled. Harvest months derived.

open_findings.summary: hawaii_tropical z11 uses a modeled low-elevation cool-season window with a high-elevation year-round caveat; CTAHR B-91 is a scanned PDF that did not parse via WebFetch and does not table cabbage months. The qualitative season/elevation rule (cabbages excellent at low elevation in winter, year-round at cool high elevation) is sourced via CTAHR's indexed text.
open_findings.basis: Same pattern as the broccoli/kale/brussels hawaii open finding; only the PDF parse and month precision are gaps.

open_findings.summary: Cabbage is flagged MARGINAL in south Florida (UF/IFAS lists it only for the coolest months; the South Florida calendar names it only in January as the last month to plant) and in lowland tropical Hawaii. Honest but low-confidence crop fits, noted in the cells.
open_findings.basis: Sourced caveat (UF/IFAS) plus the crop's documented heat intolerance; cells carry the marginal note explicitly.

open_findings.summary: container_notes figures (5+ gallon, 10 inch depth, one plant per pot, container_recommended false) are modeled on general container-vegetable guidance (uwi_hort) plus the plant's size and shallow, wide root habit; no cabbage-specific container source was found. The uwi_hort anchor uses the live cole-crops article (the edible-cabbage page 404s).
open_findings.basis: Honest modeling consistent with the plant's habit; flagged in NOTES.

open_findings.summary: Variety days-to-maturity are exact where sourced (Golden Acre 65, Ruby Ball 55 to 70, Savoy Ace 80, Danish Ballhead 100 per USU; Clemson 60 to 80 from transplants) and APPROXIMATE for the grouped mid-season hybrids (Bravo/Market Prize/Rio Verde) and savoy/red groupings, where the lists give names and resistance traits but not a single days figure.
open_findings.basis: Approximate values sit within the sourced 55 to 120 day varietal span and are labeled approximate in the variety notes.

open_findings.summary: The northern-tier heat_pause is placed only in the WARMER zones (z6 July; z7 June-August) where midsummer genuinely excludes heading (Clemson Piedmont, Penn State fall-planting dates); cool z3 to z5 carry no heat_pause because cabbage crops through their moderate summers (Iowa State harvests spring cabbage into August and sets fall transplants mid-June to mid-July).
open_findings.basis: Mirrors broccoli's region heat-pause pattern; each heat_pause is backed at the cell with a degrees-F basis and sources (A28).

open_findings.summary: successions_realized intentionally left unauthored; the CC deriver fills it and reconciles succession_policy.successions / max_successions_per_season to the max over zones. Cabbage is a spring-and-fall double crop, so realized counts reflect the staggering each region's windows support at a 3-week cadence.

3.zone_notes: In the coldest zones, start indoors in April and transplant in May; the spring crop heads through summer for a late-summer harvest, and a quick early type direct sown in early July gives a fall crop by October. 6.zone_notes: Transplant in March for a late-spring harvest, then again in August for a fall-into-early-winter harvest; the hottest part of midsummer is too warm for solid heads, so July is left out of the planting calendar. heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: cabbage is a cool-season brassica that forms firm, solid heads only in cool weather, roughly 60°F to 65°F. Sustained heat above about 80°F gives loose, open heads, triggers bolting, and worsens Fusarium yellows and cabbage aphid pressure, so the crop is grown to mature in cool spring and fall and the hottest months are left out of the planting calendar. In the warmer northern zones the peak of midsummer (July) runs too hot for cabbage to head well, so the crop is grown as a spring planting and a late-summer planting bracketing a short heat gap. (Penn State Extension, Iowa State University Extension)

7.zone_notes: In the mild end of the cold tier (Clemson Piedmont and similar), transplant about mid-March through April for a late-spring harvest, then set fall transplants mid-July through August for a fall-into-winter harvest; June through August is too hot for heading. Clemson gives Piedmont spring March 15-April 30 and fall July 15-August 31. Harvest months derived.
