northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In cold regions, cabbage is a spring crop and a fall crop. Start seeds indoors and set plants out in spring for a summer harvest, and start a second batch in early-to-mid summer for a fall harvest, when the cool weather makes especially good heads. In the very coldest zones the season is short, so lean on quick early varieties. Keep the watering even so the heads do not crack.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Across the cold northern tier cabbage is a spring-and-fall double crop. Start transplants under cover and set them out from April (cold zones) to March (mild end) for a late-spring to midsummer harvest, then set a second crop in mid-to-late summer for a fall harvest that runs into November and, at the mild end, December. The coolest zones (3 to 5) crop through a moderate summer with no real heat gap; the warmer zones (6 to 7) reach genuine midsummer heat that excludes heading, so those calendars carry a backed summer pause. Quick early varieties suit short seasons and the fall crop; late storage types want the long fall window. Harvest months are derived from the sourced planting windows plus the crop's 60-to-120-day maturity.

Inland, early varieties struggle in the still-warm early fall, so mid and late types are preferred for fall transplants. The warm midsummer is excluded and carries a backed heat pause. Harvest months are derived from the sourced planting windows plus maturity.

8.zone_notes: In the warm-arid high desert (El Paso and similar zone-8 areas), grow cabbage as a late-winter spring crop and a late-summer fall crop. NMSU lists cabbage as hardy, planted as soon as the ground can be worked in spring or in midsummer for the fall garden; Texas A&M gives spring 4 to 6 weeks before the frost-free date and fall 10 to 16 weeks before the first freeze. The exact month tables are in PDF/complex sources that did not parse, so the planting window is modeled on those rules. Harvest months derived.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: cabbage is a cool-season brassica that forms firm, solid heads only in cool weather, roughly 60°F to 65°F. Sustained heat above about 80°F gives loose, open heads, triggers bolting, and worsens Fusarium yellows and cabbage aphid pressure, so the crop is grown to mature in cool spring and fall and the hottest months are left out of the planting calendar. In the hot, arid Southwest the late-spring and summer heat (June and July) excludes heading, so cabbage is grown as a late-winter spring crop and a late-summer fall crop bracketing the heat. (NMSU Cooperative Extension, Texas A&M AgriLife Extension)

warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: In the warm, dry Southwest around El Paso, grow cabbage in late winter for a spring crop and in late summer for a fall crop. Skip the hot early summer. Keep it watered so the heads do not crack.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: Cabbage is a hard crop in lowland Hawaii because it is usually too warm. At low elevation, grow it in the coolest months of winter; cooler upland areas do much better and can grow it year-round. Expect looser heads in the warm lowlands.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: Cabbage is marginal in tropical lowland Hawaii: CTAHR frames the cabbages as excellent garden crops at low elevations during winter and as year-round crops at cool high elevations, where leaf diseases become the main concern. The low-elevation cool-season window is modeled on that qualitative guidance, since the cited CTAHR Bulletin B-91 is a scanned PDF that did not parse and does not list cabbage months directly. Treat the window and the derived harvest as a modeled estimate pending a parseable modern CTAHR source.

crops.description_seasoned: Cabbage is a cool-season brassica grown for the large, solid head of tightly wrapped leaves that forms at the center of the plant. It comes in early, mid, and late types maturing from about 60 to 120 days, in green, red, and crinkled savoy forms, and is grown as a spring crop and again as a fall crop in most regions, timed to head up in cool weather since heat gives loose heads and bolting. It is very cold-hardy, with mature heads tolerating frost down to about 20°F, and dense late storage types are among the best-keeping garden vegetables, holding for months in cold, humid storage. The crop's signature challenge is splitting: a solid head bursts if it takes up water too fast near maturity or is left standing too long.
crops.description_beginner: Cabbage grows one big, round, solid head of tightly wrapped leaves at the center of the plant. There are green, red, and crinkly savoy types, some quick (about 2 months) and some late storage kinds (about 4 months). It likes cool weather, so it is grown in spring and again in fall, not in summer heat. Cabbage handles frost well, and late storage types keep for months somewhere cold. The main thing to watch is splitting: keep the watering even and pick the head as soon as it is firm so it does not crack.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Cut the head when it is full-sized, firm, and solid to a squeeze, about 60 to 120 days from transplanting depending on the type. Slice it off at the base with a sharp knife, leaving a few wrapper leaves for protection. Harvest promptly, since a mature head left in the ground will split, especially after rain; to hold a ripe head, give the plant a quarter turn or a slight lift to shear roots and slow water uptake.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Your cabbage is ready when the head is full-sized and firm and solid when you squeeze it. Cut it off at the base with a sharp knife. Pick it as soon as it is firm, because a ripe head left sitting will crack, especially after rain. If you are not ready, give the plant a quarter turn to slow it down.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Work plenty of compost into a fertile, well-drained but moisture-retentive bed before planting and confirm pH is near 6.0 to 7.0, liming acidic ground well ahead where clubroot is a concern. Because clubroot and Fusarium yellows build in the soil, choose a bed where no cole crop has grown for at least 3 years, and set up to water evenly, since steady moisture is what builds a solid, split-free head.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Before planting, mix plenty of compost into a rich, well-drained bed and check that the soil is not too acidic. Try not to plant where you grew other cabbage-family crops in the last few years, since that spreads soil diseases. Plan to water evenly, which keeps the heads firm and crack-free.

crops.name: Onion

soil.preferred_texture_seasoned: Loose, fertile loam or sandy loam with good moisture-holding capacity grows the cleanest bulbs.
soil.preferred_texture_beginner: Onions grow the cleanest bulbs in loose, rich soil that holds moisture well. Loam or sandy loam is ideal.
soil.tolerated_texture_seasoned: Tolerates a wide range of soils, including silt loam and sandier ground, if drainage and fertility are good.
soil.tolerated_texture_beginner: Onions handle a wide range of soils, including silty and sandier ones, as long as the soil drains well and is rich enough to feed the plants.
soil.problematic_texture_seasoned: Avoid heavy, tight clay and soils that crust or cap; shallow onion roots and emerging seedlings struggle in them, and poor internal drainage invites bulb rots.
soil.problematic_texture_beginner: Avoid heavy, tight clay and soil that forms a hard crust on top. Onions have shallow roots, and their seedlings and bulbs struggle in those conditions. Soil that drains poorly on the inside can also rot the bulbs.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Onions like loose, rich, well-drained soil. Mix in compost before you plant. They do not do well in heavy clay or in soil that forms a hard crust on top, because their roots stay shallow and need air and steady moisture right near the surface.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Work in generous organic matter before planting and aim for a loose, fertile, well-drained bed; onions are heavy feeders with small root systems, so the soil has to carry both water and nutrients close to the surface.

ph.note_beginner: Onions like soil that is close to neutral, about pH 6.0 to 7.0. They do not like sour (acidic) soil. If a soil test comes back below 6.0, adding garden lime helps. A simple soil test takes the guesswork out of it.
ph.note_seasoned: Onions grow best near neutral, roughly pH 6.0 to 7.0, and tolerate up to about 7.8. They dislike acid soil; below pH 6.0 a liming amendment helps. Confirm with a soil test before adjusting.

fertilizer.timing: Side-dress through leaf growth, then taper off as bulbs form
fertilizer.example_product: ammonium sulfate or a balanced vegetable fertilizer
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Onions are heavy feeders. Drive leaf growth early with nitrogen, side-dressing twice while the leaves build, with a first feeding by the middle of May and a second toward the end of June, because every leaf at bulb initiation becomes a bulb scale and sets the size ceiling. Then stop: hold off on nitrogen past about mid-July. Late, excess nitrogen delays maturity and produces thick necks, soft bulbs, and poor storage.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Onions are hungry plants. Feed them nitrogen while the leaves are growing, because more healthy leaves mean a bigger bulb later. Feed twice: once by the middle of May, then again near the end of June. Stop feeding after about mid-July. Feeding late makes thick necks and soft onions that do not keep well.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time to side-dress your onions with nitrogen to push leaf growth before bulbing.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Feed your onions some nitrogen now to grow lots of leaves before the bulbs form.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: Higher first-number (N) feeds early; ease off nitrogen at bulb initiation.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a feed higher in the first number (nitrogen) early on, then stop the nitrogen once bulbs start.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: About half a pound of ammonium sulfate (21-0-0) per 100 square feet at each side-dressing, or the label rate of a balanced fertilizer.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: About half a pound of a nitrogen fertilizer such as ammonium sulfate for every 100 square feet each time you feed, or follow the package directions.

pests.name: Onion thrips
pests.identification_seasoned: Tiny slender insects rasping silvery streaks and flecks into the leaf necks and folds; heavy feeding reduces bulb size and invites disease.
pests.identification_beginner: Very small insects that leave silvery streaks and specks on the leaves, often down in the crease where leaves meet. Bad infestations shrink the bulbs.
pests.cause_seasoned: Onion thrips (Thrips tabaci) build through warm, dry spells, sheltering in the leaf axils where sprays miss them.
pests.cause_beginner: A tiny insect called onion thrips. It multiplies fast in warm, dry weather and hides in the tight folds of the leaves.
pests.management_seasoned: Keep plants vigorous and watered, hose off light infestations, use reflective mulch, and rotate away from alliums; treat persistent outbreaks per local extension guidance.
pests.management_beginner: Keep the plants healthy and watered, spray them off with water if thrips are light, and do not plant onions in the same spot every year. For heavy infestations, ask your local extension office what to use.

pests.name: Onion maggot
pests.identification_seasoned: Wilting, yellowing seedlings and rotting bulbs riddled by small white larvae; stand loss is worst in cool, wet springs.
pests.identification_beginner: Young plants wilt and yellow, and bulbs rot with small white grubs inside. Worst in cool, wet spring weather.
pests.cause_seasoned: Larvae of the onion maggot fly (Delia antiqua), whose eggs are laid at the plant base; populations carry over in allium residue.
pests.cause_beginner: The larvae (maggots) of a small fly that lays eggs at the base of onion plants. They survive in leftover onion debris.
pests.management_seasoned: Rotate away from alliums, remove cull bulbs and crop residue, and use floating row cover at emergence to block egg-laying.
pests.management_beginner: Do not plant onions in the same place each year, clean up old onion scraps, and cover young plants with row-cover fabric so the fly cannot lay eggs on them.

diseases.name: Botrytis neck rot
diseases.identification_seasoned: A soft, sunken rot starting at the neck in storage, often with gray mold; white-skinned and immature or poorly cured bulbs are most susceptible.
diseases.identification_beginner: Onions go soft and rotten at the neck after harvest, sometimes with gray mold. It mostly hits white onions and bulbs that were not dried well.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Botrytis infection of immature or insufficiently cured necks; excess nitrogen and bent-over green tops worsen it.
diseases.cause_beginner: A mold that gets into the neck of onions that were harvested too green or not dried properly. Too much fertilizer and bending the tops down make it worse.
diseases.management_seasoned: Let tops mature naturally, do not knock down green tops to force bulbing, cure thoroughly, and store cool and dry.
diseases.management_beginner: Let the tops fall on their own, do not bend them over, dry (cure) the onions well, and store them somewhere cool and dry.

diseases.name: Fusarium basal rot
diseases.identification_seasoned: Browning, decay, and pink-to-brown discoloration at the basal plate, with roots dying back; bulbs rot from the bottom in the field and in storage.
diseases.identification_beginner: The bottom of the bulb (the root end) turns brown and rots, and the roots die. The bulb decays from the base.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Soilborne Fusarium that persists for years and is favored by warm soil; wounds and maggot damage open the door.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soil fungus that stays in the ground for years and likes warm soil. Injuries and insect damage let it in.
diseases.management_seasoned: Choose resistant varieties where available, rotate out of alliums for several years, and avoid wounding bulbs.
diseases.management_beginner: Pick resistant varieties if you can, do not grow onions in the same spot for several years, and handle the bulbs gently so they are not injured.

diseases.name: Pink root
diseases.identification_seasoned: Roots turn pink then red and shrivel, stunting plants and shrinking bulbs; common where alliums are grown repeatedly and in warm soils.
diseases.identification_beginner: The roots turn pink, then red, then shrivel up. Plants stay small and make small bulbs. Common when onions are grown in the same place often.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A soilborne fungus (Setophoma terrestris) that builds in continuous allium ground; stressed plants show it worst.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soil fungus that builds up when onions and their relatives are grown in the same ground year after year. Stressed plants get it worst.
diseases.management_seasoned: Rotate away from alliums for several years, start with clean, disease-free transplants, and keep plants unstressed.
diseases.management_beginner: Rotate where you plant onions, start with clean, healthy transplants, and keep the plants well cared for so they are not stressed.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Keep the soil consistently moist throughout leaf growth and bulbing; onions have small, shallow root systems and any drought check directly reduces yield and bulb size. Then stop watering once the tops begin to fall, to start the bulbs curing.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water onions regularly so the soil stays evenly moist while they grow. Their roots are shallow, so they cannot find water deep down, and dry spells make the bulbs smaller. Stop watering when the tops start to flop over, so the bulbs can begin to dry.
watering.amount_seasoned: Aim for roughly an inch of water per week from rain plus irrigation, more in heat or sandy soil, delivered steadily rather than in swings.
watering.amount_beginner: About an inch of water a week is a good target, and more during hot, dry weather. Steady is better than a flood one week and nothing the next.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base with drip or a soaker to keep the foliage dry; wet tops invite leaf and neck diseases.
watering.method_beginner: Water the soil at the base of the plants, not over the leaves. Keeping the tops dry helps prevent disease.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Waterlogged soil and yellowing, mushy bases signal overwatering; standing moisture around the bulb encourages basal and neck rots.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If the soil stays soggy and the bottoms of the plants turn yellow and soft, that is too much water. Sitting in wet soil makes onions rot.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Bluish, wilting, or tip-burned leaves and stalled growth indicate the bulbs are running short of water; under-watered bulbs stay small and turn more pungent.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Wilting, bluish, or brown-tipped leaves mean the onions are too dry. Onions that do not get enough water stay small and taste sharper.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Base or drip watering keeps the foliage dry, which matters for onions because lingering leaf wetness feeds the neck and leaf diseases that spoil bulbs in storage.
watering.method_note_beginner: Watering at the base instead of over the leaves keeps the tops dry, and dry tops are less likely to get the diseases that make onions rot later.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Bulb enlargement is the most water-sensitive phase; never let the bed dry out between leaf growth and bulb sizing.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The most important time to keep onions watered is while the bulbs are getting bigger. Do not let them dry out then.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Greenhouse or windowsill transplants need a week of gradual outdoor exposure before set-out. Keep transplants pencil-thick or smaller at planting; if tops top about 5 inches, trim them back so the seedling does not topple.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: If you grew your own seedlings indoors, set them outside for a few hours a day for a week before planting so they get used to sun and wind. Plant them while they are still thin, about the thickness of a pencil.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Three entry points: direct-seed in early spring for the largest, longest-storing bulbs; set out field-grown or homegrown transplants for an earlier harvest in short-season areas; or push small sets into workable spring soil for the fastest, easiest start. Choose set or transplant size deliberately: small sets (smaller than a dime, under about half an inch) resist bolting, while oversized sets are primed to flower instead of bulbing. Bulbs from seed tend to run larger than bulbs from transplants of the same variety.
start_method.notes_beginner: You can start onions three ways. Seeds give the biggest bulbs but take the longest. Transplants (young plants) are a faster, reliable choice. Sets (tiny dried bulbs) are the easiest of all. If you buy sets, pick the smallest ones, smaller than a dime, because big sets tend to flower (bolt) instead of forming a good bulb.

drainage.saucer_practice_seasoned: Empty the saucer after each watering; onions must never sit in standing water, which saturates the shallow bulb zone and invites rot.
drainage.saucer_practice_beginner: After you water, pour out any water that collects in the saucer under the pot. Onions should never sit in standing water, because soggy soil around the bulbs leads to rot.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Use a bag of potting mix with some compost stirred in.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in compost, and a slow-release fertilizer at planting helps.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: A free-draining potting mix blended with compost.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Work in compost for fertility and a slow-release balanced feed at planting.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Water container onions more often than garden onions. The soil in a pot dries out fast, and dry spells make the bulbs small.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Because you water pots often, the food washes out faster. Give container onions a little fertilizer regularly while the leaves are growing, then ease off once bulbs start to form.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Where winters are mild, you can plant onions in pots in fall and let them grow over winter for a spring harvest. Move or cover the pots during hard freezes, because roots in a container get colder than roots in the ground.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: In mild-winter zones, fall-set container onions can overwinter for a spring bulb; protect pots from hard freezes since roots in a container chill faster than in open ground.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Onions grow well in pots because their roots stay shallow. Use a wide container at least 10 inches deep with drainage holes, and space the plants 4 inches apart. Pots dry out faster than garden beds, so check the soil often and do not let it stay dry, or the bulbs will be small.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Onions are shallow-rooted and container-friendly. A wide, well-drained pot at least 10 inches deep, roughly 5 gallons or more, holds a small cluster spaced 4 inches apart. Containers dry fast, so water before the surface crusts and feed a touch more often than in the ground; interrupted growth shrinks bulbs.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Expect to water more frequently than in-ground; the shallow root zone in a pot dries quickly and any drought check reduces final bulb size.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Frequent watering leaches nutrients, so feed container onions lightly but regularly through leaf growth, tapering as bulbing begins.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering containers suit onions well, smoothing out the steady moisture they need; keep the mix free-draining so the bulb zone never stays saturated.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: Self-watering pots work nicely for onions because they keep the soil evenly moist. Just use a mix that drains well so the bulbs are not sitting in water.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Avoid following onions or other alliums (garlic, leeks, shallots) in the same ground; several onion diseases, including pink root and white rot, persist in soil. Commercial guidance runs as long as 5 to 7 years between allium crops; a home garden can target at least 3 to 4.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Do not plant onions where you grew onions, garlic, or leeks recently. Some onion diseases live in the soil and build up. Wait at least 3 to 4 years before growing onions in the same spot again.
rotation.good_after: leafy greens or legumes
rotation.note_seasoned: Onions follow well after a leafy or legume crop and pair poorly before beans and peas, which alliums tend to inhibit.
rotation.note_beginner: Onions do well planted after leafy greens or beans and peas. Just do not plant beans or peas right next to onions, since onions can slow them down.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: After curing, store cured bulbs in a cool, dry, well-ventilated spot near 32 to 40°F; warmer than about 40°F encourages sprouting. Use thick-necked bulbs first; they do not keep.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Once the onions are cured (dried), keep them somewhere cool, dry, and airy. They keep best just above freezing; a warm spot makes them sprout. Eat any thick-necked ones first, since those do not store well.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Whole cured onions do not need refrigeration and can sweat in the crisper; sweet short-day types, which store poorly, are the exception and keep longer chilled.
storage.fridge_beginner: You do not need to refrigerate whole cured onions, and the fridge can make them damp. Sweet onions are the exception, since they do not keep long, so the fridge helps them last.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Onions freeze well chopped for cooking; texture softens, so use frozen onion in cooked dishes rather than raw.
storage.freezer_beginner: You can chop onions and freeze them for cooking. They go soft after thawing, so use frozen onions in cooked food, not in salads.
storage.notes_seasoned: Storage life tracks type: pungent long-day storage onions hold for months, while sweet short-day types are thin-skinned and best used fresh. Good curing is the single biggest lever on how long any onion keeps.
storage.notes_beginner: How long an onion keeps depends on its type. Strong-flavored storage onions last for months; sweet onions do not last long and should be eaten first. Drying (curing) them well is the most important thing for good storage.

recommended.name: Walla Walla
recommended.recommended_note: The Pacific Northwest long-day standard: very mild and sweet, but thin-skinned and a poor keeper, so eat it fresh. In mild-winter areas it is often fall-set and overwintered for an early-summer harvest.

recommended.name: Yellow Sweet Spanish
recommended.recommended_note: A large, dependable long-day yellow for northern gardens; more pungent than the sweet types and a better keeper for winter storage.

recommended.name: Super Star
recommended.recommended_note: A widely adaptable intermediate-day white that bulbs across most of the country, which is why it is a safe pick if you are unsure of your latitude. Mild and sweet; like most whites, not for long storage.

recommended.name: Cimarron
recommended.recommended_note: An intermediate-day type suited to the central latitudes between the long-day North and short-day South.

recommended.name: Texas 1015Y SuperSweet
recommended.recommended_note: Bred by Texas A&M and named for its ideal Rio Grande Valley seeding date, October 15. A large, very sweet short-day onion for the South; set transplants in fall to winter for a spring harvest. Sweet, so it stores only a couple of months.

recommended.name: Yellow Granex
recommended.recommended_note: The classic flat sweet short-day onion, the Vidalia type, for southern gardens; mild and juicy, with a short storage life.

varieties.note_seasoned: Choose by day-length class first, then by use. The set below spans all three classes so a grower at any latitude has a fit: long-day (Walla Walla, Yellow Sweet Spanish) for the North, intermediate-day (Super Star, Cimarron) for the central band, and short-day (Texas 1015Y, Yellow Granex) for the South. As a rule, sweet onions store poorly and pungent storage onions keep for months. When in doubt about your latitude, an intermediate type is the safest bet.
varieties.note_beginner: Pick the type that matches where you live first, then pick a flavor. Northern gardeners want long-day onions like Walla Walla or Yellow Sweet Spanish. Southern gardeners want short-day onions like Texas 1015Y or Yellow Granex. In the middle of the country, or if you are not sure, choose an intermediate one like Super Star. Remember that sweet onions do not keep long, and stronger onions store for months.

thinning.tip_seasoned: Sow or set on the close side, then thin to 4 to 6 inches in the row before plants compete or begin to bulb. Thin early; crowding after bulb initiation costs size. Eat the thinnings as green onions.
thinning.tip_beginner: Plant onions a bit close together, then pull out the extras so the ones you keep stand 4 to 6 inches apart. Do this early. The little plants you pull are perfectly good green onions for the kitchen.

companions.note_beginner: Onions are good neighbors for carrots, beets, lettuce, and cabbage-family plants, mostly because their strong smell is thought to keep some pests away. The main thing to avoid is planting onions next to beans or peas, since onions can slow those down. These are helpful traditions, not sure things, so do not worry if your garden does a little differently.
companions.note_seasoned: Onions earn their companion reputation mostly through their scent, which is traditionally credited with deterring aphids and the carrot rust fly, so they pair well with carrots, beets, lettuce, and brassicas. The one firm caution is the legume conflict: alliums are widely held to inhibit beans and peas, so keep onions away from them. Most of these claims are traditional rather than trial-proven; treat them as low-risk suggestions, not guarantees.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Carrots
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Onions and carrots are a classic garden pair. Their strong smell is said to help hide carrots from the carrot rust fly, and the two plants do not crowd each other's roots.

provenance.label: research_backed
provenance.reason: Same call as the carrot/onion entry from the carrot session: scent-masking vs carrot rust fly is the best-evidenced companion mechanism, with classic intercropping trials showing substantial fly-damage reduction at small scale; the reciprocal onion-side benefit (reduced thrips on onions grown with carrots) is extension-reported (HGTV/UC-aligned). research_backed earned; medium because the small-scale effect is hard to replicate at larger scale and I have not opened a single quantified figure to a T1 source. Density/arrangement dependent.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Carrots and onions are the textbook reciprocal pairing. Your onions' sulfur scent helps mask the carrots from the carrot rust fly, and in return carrots interplanted with onions tend to carry less onion thrips damage, so each crop disrupts the other's main pest. Intercropping trials have measured real reductions in carrot fly where the two grow together. Plant in alternating rows with enough onion density for the scent-masking to register, and note the strongest results come from small mixed plantings rather than large solid blocks.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Beets
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Beets and onions grow well side by side. They like the same cool weather and stay out of each other's way.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Rests on the general allium pest-repel reputation plus non-competition (different root/canopy profiles). Widely recommended and sound on space grounds, but no beet-specific measured effect; the pest-repel benefit is the general allium-scent claim rather than a measured beet trial. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Beets and onions share a bed comfortably. The onion's pungency helps deter pests that bother beets, and because onions bulb shallowly with sparse upright foliage while beets put their energy into a single root, the two do not crowd each other above or below ground. This is mostly a good-neighbor, efficient-space pairing with a modest pest-repel bonus.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Lettuce
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Fast little lettuce plants fit nicely in the gaps between onions and like the same cool season, so you get two crops from one spot.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Complementary root/canopy space efficiency (extension-endorsed interplant logic) plus a modest allium aphid-repel bonus. Sound and widely taught but a space/timing benefit rather than a measured lettuce-specific effect. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Lettuce and onions interplant efficiently. Lettuce is shallow-rooted and quick while onions send a narrow bulb down with little leafy spread, so they occupy different space and the lettuce fills in between onion rows. The onion scent offers a little aphid deterrence over the lettuce as a bonus. Treat it as a space-and-timing pairing first, mild pest help second.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Brassicas (cabbage, broccoli)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Cabbage and broccoli like the same cool weather as onions, and the strong onion smell is thought to bother some of their pests.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Mirror of the broccoli<-onion call this batch: UMN-cited Iowa study included onion in the thyme/onion/nasturtium mix that reduced cabbage looper and imported cabbageworm in broccoli, plus marigold/onion/nasturtium vs cabbage worms in cabbage. extension_backed/medium: the trial used onion within a multi-species mix rather than alone, so supported but not cleanly isolated, hence medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Onions are a well-supported brassica companion. Their sulfur scent helps mask the cabbage family and deter its signature pests, cabbage loopers, worms, and root maggots, and extension trial work including onion in a mix with broccoli showed reduced caterpillar damage. Alliums are shallow and undemanding, so they tuck between brassicas without competing for the heavy feeding those crops want.

good_seasoned.name: Carrots
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: The pungent foliage of onions is widely cited as masking the scent cues carrot rust fly uses to find carrots, and the two have complementary root habits. The pairing is traditional and intuitive but not cleanly demonstrated at the bed scale.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Long-standing interplanting tradition with a plausible scent-masking mechanism; specific-pair field evidence is thin.

good_seasoned.name: Beets
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional bed companion: similar cool-season culture and shallow, non-competing form make beets an easy neighbor that uses space efficiently alongside onions.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Compatible culture and spacing; a conventional pairing rather than a research-demonstrated benefit.

good_seasoned.name: Lettuce
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Quick, shallow-rooted lettuce fills the row between slow upright onions and shares their cool-season window, a space-efficient and traditional intercrop.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Spacing- and season-compatible intercrop; conventional companion advice without pair-specific trial evidence.

good_seasoned.name: Brassicas (cabbage, broccoli)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Cabbage-family crops share onions' cool-season timing, and the strong allium scent is traditionally credited with discouraging some brassica pests; the pest effect is anecdotal rather than demonstrated.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Shared season plus a folk pest-deterrence claim; not verified for the specific pairing.

growth_stages.name: Germination & Emergence
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A single looped seed leaf pushes up bent like a hairpin, then straightens into the first slender tube. Stands are sparse and uneven at first; onion germinates slowly and unevenly over a wide soil range (about 48 to 90°F), fastest in the middle of that band.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Look for thin grass-like shoots coming up. Each one starts bent over in a little loop, like a hairpin, then stands up straight. Onions sprout slowly and not all at once, so do not worry if they come up over a week or two rather than all together.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep the surface evenly moist so the fine seed never dries mid-germination, and keep the bed weed-free from the start; onion seedlings are weak competitors. If you set transplants or sets instead of sowing seed, this stage is already behind you.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the top of the soil damp so the tiny seeds do not dry out while sprouting, and pull weeds early, because young onions lose out to weeds easily. If you planted young plants or sets instead of seeds, you can skip this stage.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Note your sowing or set-out date and the first emergence; the gap tells you your soil's germination pace for next season.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Write down when you planted and when the first shoots appeared. That tells you how fast your soil sprouts onions next time.

growth_stages.name: Leaf & Canopy Building
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The plant adds upright tubular leaves one after another. This is the stage that decides bulb size: each leaf becomes a bulb ring, so the number of leaves a plant builds before bulbing sets its size ceiling. You want vigorous, uninterrupted leaf growth, not a check from drought, weeds, or cold.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant grows more and more upright leaves. This stage matters most for how big your onions get, because each leaf turns into a layer of the bulb later. The more healthy leaves the plant grows now, the bigger the onion can be, so you want steady, unbroken growth.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Push leaf growth: side-dress nitrogen, hold moisture steady, and stay ruthless about weeds. Front-load the feeding so the canopy is built before day length triggers bulbing; nitrogen applied late goes to soft necks instead of rings.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Help the plant grow lots of leaves now. Feed it with a nitrogen fertilizer, keep the soil evenly moist, and keep weeds out. Do most of the feeding early, while it is making leaves, because feeding too late leads to soft necks that do not store well.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Track leaf count and feeding dates; counting leaves at bulbing start is the best in-season predictor of final bulb size.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Count the leaves and note when you fed the plants. The number of leaves when bulbs start forming is a good clue to how big they will be.

growth_stages.name: Bulb Initiation
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Once day length crosses your cultivar's threshold (long, intermediate, or short day per the variety you planted), the plant stops adding leaves and the base begins to thicken. This is the photoperiod switch: the trigger is day length, set by your latitude and the season, not the calendar date or anything you do. Bulbing starts on whatever leaf count the plant reached, which is why the leaf stage mattered.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Day length is how long the daylight lasts. When the days reach the right length for your kind of onion, the plant stops making new leaves and the bottom starts to swell into a bulb. This switch is set by how long the days are where you live, not by the calendar, so you cannot speed it up. The bulb forms using however many leaves the plant already grew.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: There is no action that moves this trigger; the work was done in the leaf stage. Keep moisture steady so the swell starts without a check, and confirm you planted the right day-length class for your latitude (a mismatch shows up now as no bulbing or premature bulbing).
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: You cannot make this happen faster, so just keep watering steadily as the bulb starts to form. If nothing swells, or it swells when the plants are still tiny, you probably planted the wrong type of onion for your area, which is the thing to fix next year.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Note the date bulbing visibly began and the leaf count at that point; over seasons this confirms whether your variety's day-length class fits your site.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Write down when the bulbs started to swell and how many leaves the plants had. Over time this shows whether your onion type suits where you live.

growth_stages.name: Bulb Sizing
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tops stay green and upright while the bulb swells underneath and shoulders begin to show at the soil surface. This is the fast-fill window; steady, even moisture now translates directly into size, while any drought check costs you final bulb weight.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The leaves stay green and standing up while the bulb gets bigger below them, and you start to see the tops of the bulbs at the soil surface. This is when onions put on most of their size, so keep the watering steady; letting them dry out now makes smaller onions.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Hold even moisture through the swell and taper nitrogen off; late nitrogen now thickens necks and works against storage. Do not pull soil up over the bulbs or bend the tops to force them, an old trick that backfires because the standing leaves are still feeding the bulb.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep watering evenly and stop adding nitrogen fertilizer, because feeding now leads to thick necks that do not store. Do not pile soil over the bulbs or bend the green tops down to hurry them, an old trick that actually makes onions smaller, since those leaves are still feeding the bulb.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Log when you stopped feeding and any dry spells; matching those against final size tells you how tight your moisture needs to be.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you stopped feeding and any times the bed dried out. Comparing that to your harvest size shows how steady the watering needs to be.

growth_stages.name: Maturity & Curing
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The neck softens and the tops fall over on their own; about half the tops down is the harvest cue. After lifting, the bulb is not storage-ready until it is cured: outer scales turn papery and the neck dries tight, which seals the bulb against rot.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The necks get soft and the green tops flop over by themselves. When about half of them have fallen, it is time to harvest. After you pull the onions, they still are not ready to store until they have dried out: the outer skin turns papery and the neck dries shut, which keeps them from rotting.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Loosen and lift on a dry day, handling gently to avoid the bruises that seed storage rot. Cure two to four weeks in a warm, airy, shaded spot until scales rustle and necks are tight, then cut tops to leave roughly an inch of stem before storing cool and dry.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: On a dry day, loosen the soil and lift the onions, handling them carefully so they do not get bruised (bruised spots tend to rot). Then dry, or cure, them for two to four weeks somewhere warm, shaded, and breezy until the skins go papery and the necks dry shut. Snip the tops to leave about an inch of stem, and keep them somewhere cool and dry.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record the lift date, curing length, and how the bulbs stored; curing time versus storage life is the feedback that pays off all season.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Write down when you harvested, how long you dried the onions, and how well they kept. That tells you next year how long to dry them.

notifications.title_beginner: Time to start onion seeds inside
notifications.body_seasoned: If you are growing from seed, sow indoors now, roughly 10 to 12 weeks before set-out. The long lead lets plants build a full leaf canopy before day length triggers bulbing. Growing from sets or bought transplants instead? Skip this one.
notifications.body_beginner: If you are growing onions from seed, plant them in trays indoors now, about 10 to 12 weeks before they go outside. Onions need this long head start to grow lots of leaves first. If you are using sets or young plants from a store, you can ignore this reminder.

notifications.body_seasoned: Plant sets or transplants once soil is workable and has warmed past the cold-snap window. Set them shallow, pencil-thick or smaller, and use small sets; oversized sets and a hard cold spell after planting drive bolting.
notifications.body_beginner: Plant your sets or young onions outside now, once the soil is workable and not ice-cold. Set them shallow and use small, thin ones. Big sets, or a cold snap right after planting, can make onions bolt (shoot up a flower stalk instead of making a bulb).

notifications.body_seasoned: Side-dress nitrogen during leaf building and repeat every few weeks until bulbing starts. Front-loaded feeding grows the canopy that sets bulb size; feeding is wasted, even harmful, once bulbs begin to swell.
notifications.body_beginner: Give your onions a nitrogen fertilizer now, while they are growing leaves, and again every few weeks until the bulbs start forming. Feeding early builds the leaves that decide bulb size. Once bulbs start to swell, stop feeding, because it does more harm than good then.

notifications.title_seasoned: Your onions are switching to bulbs
notifications.title_beginner: Onions are starting to make bulbs
notifications.body_seasoned: Around now, lengthening days cross your variety's threshold and plants shift from making leaves to filling a bulb. You cannot speed this; just hold moisture steady and stop adding nitrogen so the swell runs uninterrupted.
notifications.body_beginner: About now, the days have gotten long enough that your onions stop growing new leaves and start growing a bulb instead. You cannot make this go faster. Just keep watering steadily and stop feeding, so the bulbs can swell without interruption.

notifications.title_seasoned: Ease off water as tops fall
notifications.title_beginner: Stop watering as tops flop over
notifications.body_seasoned: As necks soften and tops begin to fall, taper off watering so the bulbs firm up and the necks start to dry. Lifting into dry soil and dry weather sets up clean curing and better storage.
notifications.body_beginner: When the necks get soft and the tops start to flop over, stop watering. Letting the soil and the onions dry out now helps the bulbs firm up and keeps them from rotting later.

notifications.title_beginner: Time to harvest and dry onions
notifications.body_seasoned: When about half the tops have fallen, lift on a dry day and handle gently. Cure two to four weeks in a warm, airy, shaded spot until scales are papery and necks are tight, then trim and store cool and dry.
notifications.body_beginner: Once roughly half the tops have fallen on their own, pull the onions on a dry day, handling them carefully to avoid bruising. Cure them for two to four weeks in a warm, shaded, breezy spot until the skins are papery and the necks dry shut. Trim the tops and store the bulbs somewhere cool and dry.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: A cold spell could make onions bolt
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A warm stretch followed by several weeks below about 50°F can vernalize young plants: they misread that swing into and out of cold as a completed winter and switch to flowering rather than bulbing. Cover young plants through an unseasonable cold spell, especially oversized sets or transplants, which are already primed to bolt.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Onions can bolt (send up a flower stalk instead of making a bulb) when warm weather is followed by a few weeks of cold and then it warms again, because the plant thinks a winter has passed. If a cold spell is coming, cover young plants, especially if you used big sets or large transplants, which bolt the easiest.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Cover young fall-planted onions
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Established onions are cold-hardy, but young fall-set transplants in the South want protection through a hard freeze. Cover them with row cover or mulch when a hard freeze is forecast; the goal is to carry them through, not to push growth.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Grown onions handle cold well, but young onions planted in fall in the South should be protected during a hard freeze. Cover them with a row cover or some mulch when a hard freeze is coming, just to help them get through it.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat and dry stress at sizing
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot, dry weather while bulbs size up
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Hot, dry spells during bulb sizing check the swell and cap final size, since any drought interruption costs bulb weight. Water deeply and evenly through a heat spell to keep the fill running; mulch helps hold moisture in the shallow root zone.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Hot, dry weather while the bulbs are sizing up makes smaller onions, because letting them dry out interrupts their growth. Water deeply and evenly during a heat spell, and a layer of mulch helps keep the soil from drying out so fast.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Rain while you are drying onions
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Rain and humidity during the harvest and curing window invite neck rot and Botrytis, since bulbs cure only when necks dry tight. Move curing under cover with good airflow, and if a wet stretch hits before harvest, wait for dry weather to lift.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Rain and damp air while you are harvesting or drying onions can cause rot at the neck, because onions only dry properly when the necks dry out fully. Move the drying onions under cover where air moves well, and if it turns wet before harvest, wait for a dry day to pull them.

germination_emergence.text_seasoned: Set out at the right size and time: small sets and pencil-thick transplants into soil that has warmed past the cold-snap window resist bolting. Plant shallow; deep planting and hilling soil over the bulb damage shallow roots and shrink bulbs.
germination_emergence.text_beginner: Plant small sets or thin transplants once the soil has warmed up a bit, so they do not bolt. Set them shallow and do not pile soil over the bulbs, because the roots are shallow and that hurts them.

leaf_canopy_building.text_seasoned: Push leaf growth now: this is a leaf crop until day length flips it to a bulb crop, and every leaf becomes a ring. Side-dress nitrogen, keep moisture steady, and stay ruthless about weeds, which onions compete with poorly.
leaf_canopy_building.text_beginner: Focus on growing lots of healthy leaves now, because each leaf becomes a layer in the bulb later. Feed with nitrogen, keep the soil moist, and pull weeds, since onions do not compete with weeds well.

leaf_canopy_building.text_seasoned: Keep the bed weed-free and evenly watered through canopy build; uninterrupted growth before bulbing sets your maximum bulb size.
leaf_canopy_building.text_beginner: Keep weeding and watering steadily while the leaves fill in. The more uninterrupted growth the plants get now, the bigger the bulbs can be.

bulb_sizing.text_seasoned: As bulbs swell, taper off nitrogen and let the necks mature; do not bend or break the green tops to force bulbing, since the leaves are still feeding the bulb and knocking them down reduces final size.
bulb_sizing.text_beginner: When the bulbs start to swell, stop adding nitrogen. Do not bend over the green tops to try to hurry things along, an old trick that actually backfires, because the leaves are still feeding the bulb and breaking them makes the onion smaller.

maturity_curing.text_seasoned: Harvest when about half the tops have naturally fallen and necks have softened. Loosen and lift on a dry day; careful handling avoids the bruises that seed storage rot.
maturity_curing.text_beginner: Harvest when about half the tops have flopped over on their own and the necks feel soft. Lift the bulbs gently on a dry day, and try not to bruise them, since bruises lead to rot in storage.

maturity_curing.text_seasoned: Cure in a warm, airy, shaded spot (about 75 to 90°F) for two to four weeks until outer scales are papery and the neck is tight and dry, then trim tops about an inch above the bulb. Poor curing is the main cause of storage loss.
maturity_curing.text_beginner: Dry (cure) the onions in a warm, airy, shaded place for two to four weeks until the outer skins are papery and the neck is tight and dry. Then cut the tops about an inch above the bulb. Onions that are not dried well are the ones that rot in storage.

bulb_initiation.text_seasoned: Bulbing is triggered by day length crossing your cultivar's threshold, not by anything you do, so there is no action that moves it; the leaf count the plant reaches before the switch sets the bulb size. Keep moisture and nitrogen steady so the swell starts without a check, and confirm you planted the right day-length class for your latitude, since a mismatch shows up now as no bulbing or premature bulbing.
bulb_initiation.text_beginner: When the days reach the right length for your kind of onion, the plant stops making leaves and the bottom starts to swell. You cannot speed this up, so just keep watering steadily as it begins. If nothing swells, or it swells while the plants are still tiny, you likely planted the wrong onion type for your area, which is the thing to fix next year.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: One bulb per plant. A 10-foot row at 4-inch spacing yields roughly 20 to 25 pounds of bulbs in a good season.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Each onion plant makes one bulb. A 10-foot row can give you about 20 to 25 pounds of onions in a good year.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: All bulbs of a variety size up and mature together as day length triggers bulbing, so the harvest comes in one main flush rather than over a long window.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Onions of the same kind all finish around the same time, so you harvest most of them together rather than a few at a time.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Matching variety day-length type to your latitude is the biggest first-year yield lever; a mismatched type bulbs too early (small) or never bulbs at all.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: The most important thing for a good first harvest is picking the right type for where you live. The wrong type will make tiny bulbs or no bulbs.
factors_seasoned: variety day-length type matched to latitude
leaf count at bulb initiation
consistent moisture
early nitrogen then taper
spacing
freedom from bolting

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No verified evidence ties onion bulbing or yield to moon phase; bulbing is driven by day length and temperature. Planting timing follows soil readiness and the cold-snap window, not lunar phase.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Plants send up a hollow flower stalk (bolt) instead of sizing a bulb.
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: An onion shoots up a tall round flower stalk instead of growing a good bulb.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Bolting is vernalization, not day length: a young plant that experiences several weeks below about 50°F and then warms reads the cold-then-warm sequence as a passed winter and switches to flowering. Oversized sets and transplants are already part-vernalized, so they bolt readily; planting too early into cold soil does the same. Once a stalk forms, the bulb stops enlarging and stores poorly.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: This is called bolting. It is triggered by cold, not by day length. If young plants sit through a few weeks of cold weather and then it warms up, they think a winter has passed and try to make seeds. Big sets and plants set out too early into cold soil are the usual cause. Once an onion bolts, the bulb stops growing and will not keep.
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Prevention is the only fix. Use small sets (under about half an inch), set transplants pencil-thick or smaller, and wait until soil has warmed past the cold window for your area before planting. If a few bolt, pull and eat them soon; removing the stalk does not restore the bulb.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: You cannot reverse bolting, so prevent it: plant small sets, use thin transplants, and do not plant too early into cold soil. If a few onions bolt anyway, pull them and use them right away, because they will not store.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Tops grow well but bulbs stay small or never form.
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Lots of green leaves, but the bulbs stay tiny or do not form at all.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: The commonest cause is a day-length mismatch: a long-day variety grown too far south never reaches its trigger, while a short-day variety grown too far north bulbs almost immediately on few leaves and makes a small bulb. Late nitrogen, crowding, and weed competition also cap size.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Usually the wrong type for your area. A northern (long-day) onion grown in the South never gets long-enough days to bulb, and a southern (short-day) onion grown in the North bulbs too soon and stays small. Feeding too late, crowding, and weeds also keep bulbs small.
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Match the variety's day-length type to your latitude, front-load nitrogen so the plant builds leaves before bulbing, thin to spacing, and keep the bed weed-free.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Choose the right type for where you live, feed early so the plant makes plenty of leaves first, give the plants room, and keep weeds out.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Bulbs rot at the neck or base in storage.
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Onions rot at the top or bottom after you store them.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Harvesting too green, poor curing, excess late nitrogen, and bruising all drive storage rots (neck rot, basal rot). Thick necks never seal properly.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Picking onions too early, not drying them enough, too much late fertilizer, and bruising all cause storage rot. Thick-necked onions never seal up.
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Let about half the tops fall before harvest, cure two to four weeks until necks are tight and scales rustle, handle gently, taper nitrogen at bulbing, and store cool and dry.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Wait until about half the tops have flopped, then dry the onions two to four weeks until the necks are tight, handle them gently, stop fertilizing once bulbs form, and store them cool and dry.

succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Bulb onions are a single main planting per season. Bulbing is gated by day length, so every plant of a given variety reaches its trigger and matures on roughly the same schedule regardless of when within the planting window it went in; staggered sowings do not yield a staggered bulb harvest. The successioned allium is the green onion or scallion, which is a separate crop.

start_indoors.label: main
start_indoors.source_quote: raise your own transplants by starting seed indoors 10 to 12 weeks before planting outside
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Long-day onion in the North is a single spring crop. Start seed indoors about 10 weeks before the plant-out window (UMN: sow in February for a May transplant), so the indoor sow sits roughly 12 weeks before the last frost. The long lead is deliberate: the plant must build a large leaf canopy before lengthening summer days trigger bulbing, since each leaf becomes a bulb ring.

plant_out.label: main
plant_out.source_quote: plant your transplants 2 to 4 weeks before your average last frost date, as soon as the soil is workable
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Onion is cold-hardy: transplants tolerate light frost and go out as soon as the soil is workable, about two weeks before the last frost (Cornell: 2 to 4 weeks before; UMN: when temperatures reach 50°F). Sets follow the same as-soon-as-workable rule. The window opens the cool-season planting early so the crop banks leaf growth before the bulbing trigger; it does not wait for warm soil the way a tender summer crop does.

harvest_start.label: main
harvest_start.source_quote: Harvest onions when about half the tops are falling over and dry
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Bulbs size up across early-to-mid summer as days reach 14 to 16 hours, then mature when about half the tops fall over (UMN). At a 90 to 120 day maturity from transplant, the first bulbs pull in mid-to-late summer; the date is back-derived from the plant-out window plus the fast end of maturity, not a calendar fixed point.

harvest_end.label: main
harvest_end.source_quote: Keep the onions in a warm, well-ventilated area for two to four weeks, until outer bulb scales are dry
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The pull window closes at the slow end of maturity, after which bulbs are lifted and cured two to four weeks before storage (UMN). Curing is a post-harvest step, not a separate growing phase, so it folds into the tail of the harvest window rather than extending the calendar.

3.zone_notes: Coldest northern zone: a tight single spring window. Start seed indoors in late February, transplant in early May once soil is workable, harvest late summer before the mid-September frost. Lean on faster-maturing long-day varieties.
3.day_length_note_seasoned: At this latitude (roughly 43 degrees N and up) grow long-day onions, which bulb at 14 to 16 hours of daylight. Long summer days here let the plant build a large canopy before the bulbing trigger. A short-day variety planted here bulbs far too early, on too few leaves, and yields only small bulbs.
3.day_length_note_beginner: Where you live, pick long-day onions. Day length is just how many hours of sunlight a day brings, and long-day onions wait until days are very long (14 to 16 hours) before making a bulb, which is exactly what northern summers give them. A southern (short-day) onion planted here would make a bulb too soon and stay tiny.

4.zone_notes: Start seed indoors in February, transplant mid-April to early May as soon as soil is workable, harvest mid-summer to mid-August. Onion is among the first crops out in spring here.
4.day_length_note_seasoned: Long-day onions are the type for this latitude: they bulb at 14 to 16 hours of daylight, which the northern summer provides. The long pre-solstice canopy here builds large bulbs. A short-day variety would bulb prematurely and stay small.
4.day_length_note_beginner: Choose long-day onions here. They only start a bulb when days get very long (14 to 16 hours), which your summer delivers. A southern short-day onion would form its bulb too early and end up small.

5.zone_notes: Start seed indoors in late January to early February, transplant in early April once soil is workable, harvest late June into July. A slightly longer spring runway than the colder zones.
5.day_length_note_seasoned: This latitude calls for long-day onions, which bulb at 14 to 16 hours of daylight. Summer days here are long enough to trigger bulbing on a well-built canopy. Short-day types bulb too early and stay small.
5.day_length_note_beginner: Go with long-day onions. They wait for long summer days (14 to 16 hours) before forming a bulb, which suits where you live. A short-day onion would make its bulb too soon and stay small.

6.zone_notes: Milder northern zone: start seed indoors in early January, transplant mid-March into early April, harvest from mid-June. The longest spring runway of the northern tier.
6.day_length_note_seasoned: Long-day onions suit this latitude, bulbing at 14 to 16 hours of daylight. At the warm edge of the long-day band (around 39 to 40°N N), choose faster-maturing long-day varieties so bulbing completes before high summer soil temperatures push the crop. Intermediate-day types also perform here and are a reasonable hedge if you are near the band boundary.
6.day_length_note_beginner: Long-day onions work where you live. They form a bulb once days are long (14 to 16 hours). You are near the southern edge of long-day country, so pick faster-maturing kinds. Intermediate-day onions are also a safe choice if you are unsure.

7.zone_notes: Warm edge of the northern tier: start seed indoors in late December, transplant in March, harvest from late May into June. The indoor start straddles year-end here. Near the long-day and intermediate-day boundary, so either type can work.
7.day_length_note_seasoned: This zone sits near the long-day and intermediate-day boundary (roughly 37 to 39°N N). Long-day onions bulb here at 14 to 16 hours, and intermediate-day types (12 to 14 hours) also bulb well, so both are viable; choose by variety availability and storage goals. Avoid short-day types, which would bulb prematurely at this latitude.
7.day_length_note_beginner: You are on the line between long-day and intermediate-day onions, so both will work. Long-day onions bulb on the longest summer days; intermediate-day onions bulb a bit sooner. Either is fine here. Just avoid southern short-day onions, which would bulb too early and stay small.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: If you live in the colder northern states (zones 3 to 7), onions are a one-time spring crop. Buy or grow "long-day" onions. Day length means how many hours of sunlight there are each day, and long-day onions only start forming a bulb once days reach 14 to 16 hours, which happens in northern summers. A long-day type is the kind that will actually make a full-size bulb where you live. Start seeds indoors about 10 weeks early (around February if your spring is cold), then plant the young onions, or small bulbs called sets, outside as soon as the ground can be worked, about two weeks before your last frost. Onions handle light frost, so you do not wait for warm weather. They are ready in mid-to-late summer when about half the leafy tops flop over and dry. Pull them, then let them dry in a warm airy spot for two to four weeks before storing. The day length only controls when the bulb forms, not when you plant, so you still go by frost and soil.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In the cold-winter North (zones 3 to 7), onion is a single spring-planted crop. Grow long-day cultivars: they need 14 to 16 hours of daylight to bulb, which northern summers deliver, and they build a full leaf canopy before the solstice trigger so bulbs size up large. Start seed indoors about 10 weeks ahead (sow in February for a May transplant in the coldest zones), then set cold-hardy transplants or sets out as soon as the soil is workable, roughly two weeks before the last frost. Bulbs mature in mid-to-late summer when about half the tops fall over; lift and cure them two to four weeks before storage. Day length gates which cultivar bulbs here, not when you plant: planting stays anchored to frost and workable soil. The bolting trap here is cold-driven, not day-length driven, so it stays minor for a spring crop set as a small transplant, but oversized sets exposed to a cold snap can run to seed instead of bulbing.

start_indoors.label: main
start_indoors.source_quote: Transplants can be planted November through February
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Short-day onion in the Southeast and Gulf is a fall-planted overwintering crop. Seed is started in early-to-mid fall (TAMU: October seeding in the Rio Grande Valley; UGA commercial Vidalia seed late September) to raise transplants for late-fall setting.

plant_out.label: main
plant_out.source_quote: Transplants can be planted November through February
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set transplants (or sets) from November through February (TAMU; UGA Vidalia transplanting November-December), overwintering the small plant so it builds leaves before short winter days trigger bulbing. Use pencil-sized or smaller transplants and sets under half an inch: a too-large plant exposed to winter cold vernalizes and bolts to seed instead of bulbing, the South's central failure mode (it is cold-driven, not day-length driven).

harvest_start.label: main
harvest_start.source_quote: harvested in April/May
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Bulbs mature in mid-spring as days lengthen to the 10-to-12-hour short-day trigger; the Vidalia harvest opens mid-to-late April (UGA), with the home-garden window running April into May.

harvest_end.label: main
harvest_end.source_quote: You just have to wait until April or May before harvest
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The pull window closes in May before summer heat; bulbs are lifted when about half the tops fall, then cured before storage (short-day sweet types keep only one to two months).

8.zone_notes: Set transplants November through February; the panhandle/inland zone 8 leans to the later end. Harvest April into May. Use small transplants to avoid winter-cold bolting.
8.day_length_note_seasoned: At this latitude (below about 35 degrees N) grow short-day onions, which begin bulbing at just 10 to 12 hours of daylight. They are planted in fall or winter and bulb as days lengthen toward spring. A long-day variety here never reaches its longer daylength trigger and stays a leafy scallion that never forms a bulb.
8.day_length_note_beginner: Where you live, plant short-day onions. Day length means how many hours of sunlight there are in a day, and short-day onions make a bulb once days reach only 10 to 12 hours, which happens in your mild fall and winter. A northern (long-day) onion planted here would never make a bulb at all, just leaves.

9.zone_notes: Mild zone 9: transplant November through February, the prime Vidalia-belt window; harvest April into May. Small transplants and sets resist bolting.
9.day_length_note_seasoned: At this latitude (below about 35 degrees N) grow short-day onions, which begin bulbing at just 10 to 12 hours of daylight. They are planted in fall or winter and bulb as days lengthen toward spring. A long-day variety here never reaches its longer daylength trigger and stays a leafy scallion that never forms a bulb.
9.day_length_note_beginner: Where you live, plant short-day onions. Day length means how many hours of sunlight there are in a day, and short-day onions make a bulb once days reach only 10 to 12 hours, which happens in your mild fall and winter. A northern (long-day) onion planted here would never make a bulb at all, just leaves.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast and along the Gulf (zones 8 to 9), onions are planted in fall and grow through winter. Use "short-day" onions. Day length means how many hours of sunlight a day brings, and short-day onions make a bulb once days are only 10 to 12 hours long, which fits your mild fall and winter. Start seeds in early fall, then plant young onions, or small bulbs called sets, anytime from November through February. They grow leaves all winter and form bulbs as spring days lengthen, ready to harvest in April or May before it gets hot. One key tip: plant small. A transplant or set that is too big when winter cold hits will flower and go to seed instead of making a bulb, so choose pencil-thin transplants and sets smaller than half an inch.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: In the Southeast and Gulf (zones 8 to 9), onion is a fall-planted, overwintering short-day crop. Grow short-day cultivars: they bulb at only 10 to 12 hours of daylight, which the region's mild fall and winter provide. Start seed in early-to-mid fall, then set transplants or sets from November through February so the plant builds a strong leaf canopy over winter before short days trigger bulbing. Bulbs mature in mid-spring, harvested April into May before summer heat; lift when about half the tops fall and cure before storage. Day length gates which cultivar bulbs here, not when you plant. The central pitfall is bolting: a transplant or set that is too large going into winter cold vernalizes and runs to seed instead of bulbing, so use pencil-sized or smaller transplants and sets under half an inch.

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In California's interior valleys (zones 8 to 9, around Sacramento and the San Joaquin) onions are a cool-season crop you can plant in two windows. Use "intermediate-day" onions. Day length is how many daylight hours a day brings, and intermediate-day onions make a bulb at about 12 to 14 hours, the reliable middle-of-the-state choice. Plant in October-November or in January-March. The plants are cold-hardy, grow through winter, and bulb in late spring or summer. Growing your own transplants gives the most choices and the least flowering. Just do not plant too early, since cold can make them flower instead of bulb.

Do not plant too early, or cold can make them flower instead of bulb.
