crops.description_seasoned: Onion (Allium cepa) is a cool-season biennial grown as an annual for its bulb, which is a stack of swollen leaf bases rather than a root. Each green leaf builds one bulb scale, so leaf count at the moment bulbing starts sets the ceiling on bulb size. What triggers bulbing is day length, not the calendar: a cultivar switches from making leaves to filling a bulb only once daylight crosses its threshold. That threshold is what splits onions into long-day (14 to 16 hours), intermediate-day (12 to 14 hours), and short-day (10 to 12 hours) types, and it is why the right variety depends on your latitude. Grow a heavy-feeding, shallow-rooted plant in loose fertile soil, keep moisture steady so growth never stalls, then ease off water as the tops fall to begin curing.
crops.description_beginner: An onion is the swollen base of the plant's leaves, packed into the layered bulb you cook with. Here is the part that surprises most first-time growers: an onion decides to start forming its bulb based on how long the days are, not on a date. Because of that, onions are sold by "day length" instead of by the usual hardiness zone. Long-day kinds need very long summer days and suit the North, short-day kinds need only short days and suit the South, and intermediate kinds sit in the middle and grow well across much of the country. Pick the type that matches where you live, give the plants rich loose soil, water them steadily, and they are not hard to grow.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Bulb onions are ready when about half the tops have naturally fallen over and the necks have begun to soften and dry. Pinch a neck to judge maturity: a stiff neck is immature, a soft, limber neck is ripe, and a collapsed neck means over-mature. Lift on a dry day, then cure.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Your onions are ready to dig when about half the tops have flopped over on their own and the necks feel soft. A simple test: gently pinch the neck just above the bulb. If it is stiff, wait; if it is soft and floppy, it is time. Pull them on a dry day, then dry (cure) them.

photoperiod.explainer_seasoned: Onion is photoperiodic: a bulb forms only once day length crosses a cultivar-specific threshold, at which point the plant stops adding leaves and starts filling a bulb. Cultivars fall into three classes by that threshold, long-day at 14 to 16 hours, intermediate-day at 12 to 14 hours, and short-day at 10 to 12 hours, so the suitable class depends on your latitude. Long-day types fit northern latitudes (roughly above 38 to 39°N), where summer days run long enough that plants build a large leaf canopy before the trigger; short-day types fit southern latitudes (roughly below 35°N), where they are planted in fall or winter and bulb as days lengthen; intermediate types span the middle (roughly 32 to 42°N) and grow well across much of the country. Plant the wrong class and a long-day onion in the South may never bulb, while a short-day onion in the North bulbs too early on few leaves and stays small. Day length triggers bulbing only; it never moves your planting date, which stays anchored to frost and soil temperature.
photoperiod.explainer_beginner: Onions are unusual: they start making a bulb based on how long the days are, not on the calendar. Each kind of onion needs a certain number of daylight hours before it will switch from growing leaves to growing a bulb. That is why onions are sold by "day length" instead of by hardiness zone. There are three kinds. Long-day onions need very long summer days (14 to 16 hours) and grow best in the North. Short-day onions need only short days (10 to 12 hours) and grow best in the South, where they are planted in fall or winter. Intermediate onions need about 12 to 14 hours and grow well across the middle of the country. Pick the kind that matches where you live: a northern onion planted in the South may never make a bulb, and a southern onion planted in the North makes only a tiny one. Day length decides when the bulb forms, but it does not change when you plant, which still depends on frost and soil temperature.

pet_safe.note: Toxic to cats, dogs, and horses; onions and the whole allium family damage their red blood cells.

crops.name: Spring Onion / Scallion

soil.preferred_texture_seasoned: A loose, fertile loam or sandy loam high in organic matter grows the cleanest, fastest scallions.
soil.preferred_texture_beginner: Scallions grow best in loose, rich soil that drains well. A loam or sandy loam with plenty of compost is ideal.
soil.tolerated_texture_seasoned: Tolerates a range of soils, including silt loam and sandier ground, where drainage and fertility are good.
soil.tolerated_texture_beginner: Handles a range of soils, including silty and sandier ones, as long as the soil drains well and is rich enough.
soil.problematic_texture_seasoned: Avoid heavy, tight clay and soils that crust; shallow scallion roots and fine seedlings struggle to push through a capped surface.
soil.problematic_texture_beginner: Avoid heavy, tight clay and soil that forms a hard crust on top. Scallions have shallow roots and their seedlings struggle in those conditions.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Scallions like loose, rich, well-drained soil. Mix in compost before you plant. They do not do well in heavy clay or in soil that crusts over, because their roots stay shallow and need air and steady moisture near the surface.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Work organic matter into a loose, fertile, well-drained bed before sowing. Scallions have small, shallow root systems, so the soil has to carry steady moisture and nutrients close to the surface; Clemson recommends a fertile, well-drained loam with plenty of organic matter.

ph.note_beginner: Scallions like soil close to neutral, about pH 6.0 to 7.0. Clemson lists an ideal of 6.2 to 6.5. They do not like sour (acidic) soil; a simple soil test takes the guesswork out of it.
ph.note_seasoned: Scallions grow best near neutral, roughly pH 6.0 to 7.0, with Clemson giving an ideal band of 6.2 to 6.5. They tolerate up to about 7.5 and dislike acid soil; confirm with a soil test before adjusting.

fertilizer.timing: Work in compost or a balanced feed before planting, then side-dress lightly as the tops grow
fertilizer.example_product: compost plus a balanced 10-10-10 vegetable fertilizer
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Scallions are light-to-moderate feeders. Unlike bulb onions there is no bulb to size, so feeding aims only at steady, tender leaf growth. Mix a balanced fertilizer into the bed before sowing, around 9 pounds of 10-10-10 per 1,000 square feet per Clemson, and side-dress lightly once or twice during leaf growth if the soil is lean. Avoid heavy nitrogen, which makes floppy, disease-prone tops.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Scallions do not need much feeding. Mix some compost or a balanced fertilizer into the soil before you plant, then give a light feeding once or twice while the tops are growing if the soil is poor. Do not overdo the nitrogen, or you get floppy, weak tops.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Side-dress your scallions lightly to keep the tops growing tender.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Give your scallions a light feeding now to keep the tops growing.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced feed worked in before planting carries scallions through; side-dress lightly only if growth stalls.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Mix a balanced fertilizer into the soil before planting; feed lightly later only if the plants look pale or slow.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: About 9 pounds of 10-10-10 per 1,000 square feet worked into the bed before planting (Clemson), plus a light side-dressing during leaf growth if needed.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Roughly 9 pounds of a balanced 10-10-10 fertilizer per 1,000 square feet mixed in before planting, or follow the package directions, with a light feeding later only if needed.

pests.name: Onion thrips
pests.identification_seasoned: Tiny slender insects that rasp silvery streaks and flecks into the leaf folds; heavy feeding stunts the tops and can spread disease.
pests.identification_beginner: Very small insects that leave silvery streaks and specks on the leaves, often in the crease where leaves meet. Heavy feeding stunts the plants.
pests.cause_seasoned: Onion thrips (Thrips tabaci) build through warm, dry spells, sheltering in the leaf axils where sprays miss them.
pests.cause_beginner: A tiny insect called onion thrips. It multiplies fast in warm, dry weather and hides in the tight folds of the leaves.
pests.management_seasoned: Keep plants vigorous and watered, hose off light infestations, and rotate away from alliums; treat persistent outbreaks per local extension guidance.
pests.management_beginner: Keep the plants healthy and watered, spray them off with water if thrips are light, and do not plant alliums in the same spot every year. For heavy infestations, ask your local extension office what to use.

pests.name: Onion maggot
pests.identification_seasoned: Wilting, yellowing seedlings and rotting shanks riddled by small white larvae; stand loss is worst in cool, wet springs.
pests.identification_beginner: Young plants wilt and yellow, and the white bottoms rot with small white grubs inside. Worst in cool, wet spring weather.
pests.cause_seasoned: Larvae of the onion maggot fly (Delia antiqua), whose eggs are laid at the plant base; populations carry over in allium residue.
pests.cause_beginner: The larvae (maggots) of a small fly that lays eggs at the base of the plants. They survive in leftover onion debris.
pests.management_seasoned: Rotate away from alliums, remove crop residue, and use floating row cover at emergence to block egg-laying.
pests.management_beginner: Do not plant alliums in the same place each year, clean up old onion scraps, and cover young plants with row-cover fabric so the fly cannot lay eggs on them.

pests.name: Allium leafminer
pests.identification_seasoned: Rows of white dots punched down the leaf where adults feed, then larvae mining inside the leaves and shank, leaving distorted, scarred tops.
pests.identification_beginner: Lines of small white dots on the leaves, then little grubs tunneling inside, leaving twisted, scarred leaves.
pests.cause_seasoned: The allium leafminer (Phytomyza gymnostoma), active in spring and fall, lays eggs in the leaves; larvae mine down toward the base.
pests.cause_beginner: A small fly whose grubs tunnel inside allium leaves. It is active in spring and fall.
pests.management_seasoned: Cover plants with insect netting during the spring and fall flights, rotate away from alliums, and remove infested debris.
pests.management_beginner: Cover the plants with fine netting in spring and fall when the fly is active, rotate where you plant alliums, and clear away infested leaves.

diseases.name: Botrytis neck rot
diseases.identification_seasoned: A soft, sunken rot at the neck and leaf bases, often with gray mold; favored by lingering leaf wetness and crowding.
diseases.identification_beginner: Soft, rotten spots at the base of the leaves, sometimes with gray mold. It is worse when the tops stay wet and the plants are crowded.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Botrytis infection of wet, crowded foliage; overhead watering and excess nitrogen worsen it.
diseases.cause_beginner: A mold that gets into wet, crowded leaves. Watering over the top and too much fertilizer make it worse.
diseases.management_seasoned: Water at the base, space for airflow, avoid excess nitrogen, and harvest on dry days.
diseases.management_beginner: Water at the base, do not crowd the plants, go easy on fertilizer, and harvest when the leaves are dry.

diseases.name: Fusarium basal rot
diseases.identification_seasoned: Browning and decay at the basal plate with roots dying back; plants yellow, wilt, and pull up easily.
diseases.identification_beginner: The very bottom of the plant turns brown and rots and the roots die, so the plant yellows and pulls up easily.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Soilborne Fusarium that persists for years and is favored by warm soil; wounds and maggot damage open the door.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soil fungus that stays in the ground for years and likes warm soil. Injuries and insect damage let it in.
diseases.management_seasoned: Rotate out of alliums for several years, choose resistant stock where available, and avoid wounding the plants.
diseases.management_beginner: Do not grow alliums in the same spot for several years, pick resistant varieties if you can, and handle the plants gently.

diseases.name: White rot
diseases.identification_seasoned: Yellowing, wilting plants with a fluffy white fungal mat and small black sclerotia at the base; the root system rots away.
diseases.identification_beginner: Plants turn yellow and wilt, and you find a fluffy white mold with tiny black specks at the base. The roots rot.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The soilborne fungus Sclerotium cepivorum, whose sclerotia survive in soil for many years; cool, moist conditions favor it.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soil fungus whose tough resting bodies survive in the ground for many years. Cool, damp conditions make it worse.
diseases.management_seasoned: There is no cure once soil is infested; use clean transplants, never move infested soil, and rotate alliums far away for many years.
diseases.management_beginner: Once the soil has it, there is no cure, so start with clean plants, avoid moving infested soil, and keep alliums far from that spot for many years.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Keep the soil consistently moist through the whole short crop; scallions have small, shallow roots and any drought check slows growth and toughens the tops. If rain does not supply about an inch a week, soak the bed thoroughly once a week.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water scallions so the soil stays evenly moist the whole time they grow. Their roots are shallow, so dry spells slow them down and make the tops tough. If it does not rain about an inch a week, give the bed a good soak once a week.
watering.amount_seasoned: Aim for roughly an inch of water per week from rain plus irrigation, more in heat or sandy soil, delivered steadily rather than in swings.
watering.amount_beginner: About an inch of water a week is a good target, and more in hot, dry weather. Steady is better than a flood one week and nothing the next.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base with drip or a soaker to keep the foliage dry; wet tops invite leaf and neck diseases.
watering.method_beginner: Water the soil at the base of the plants, not over the leaves. Keeping the tops dry helps prevent disease.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Waterlogged soil and yellowing, mushy bases signal overwatering; standing moisture around the shank encourages basal and neck rots.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If the soil stays soggy and the bottoms of the plants turn yellow and soft, that is too much water. Sitting in wet soil makes scallions rot.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Bluish, wilting, or tip-burned leaves and stalled growth indicate the plants are short of water; under-watered scallions stay thin and turn sharply pungent.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Wilting, bluish, or brown-tipped leaves mean the scallions are too dry. Plants that do not get enough water stay thin and taste sharper.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Base or drip watering keeps the foliage dry, which matters because lingering leaf wetness feeds the leaf and neck diseases that spoil alliums.
watering.method_note_beginner: Watering at the base instead of over the leaves keeps the tops dry, and dry tops are less likely to get disease.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Steady moisture during the first few weeks of stand establishment and leaf growth matters most; a fine seedbed must not dry out mid-germination.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The most important time to keep scallions watered is right after sowing and while the tops are growing. Do not let the seedbed dry out while the seeds are sprouting.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Indoor-grown transplants need about a week of gradual outdoor exposure before set-out. Keep seedlings slender at transplanting and trim the tops to a few inches so they do not topple.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: If you grow your own seedlings indoors, set them outside for a few hours a day for a week before planting so they get used to sun and wind. Trim the tops to a few inches so they stand up.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Two easy routes. Direct-sow seed in a two-inch-wide band, a quarter to a half inch deep, in rows 12 to 18 inches apart, then thin to about one plant per inch (UMN); this is the simplest method and suits succession sowing. Or start seed indoors about four weeks before set-out for an earlier first cutting, transplanting seedlings an inch apart. Bunching types can also be multiplied by dividing established clumps.
start_method.notes_beginner: There are two easy ways. The simplest is to sow seed right in the garden, a quarter to a half inch deep, then thin the seedlings to about one per inch. Or start seeds indoors about four weeks before planting out for an earlier harvest, then set the little plants an inch apart. Bunching kinds can also be split from an existing clump.

drainage.saucer_practice_seasoned: Empty the saucer after watering; scallions should never sit in standing water, which saturates the shallow root zone and invites rot.
drainage.saucer_practice_beginner: After you water, pour out any water that collects in the saucer under the pot. Scallions should not sit in standing water, because soggy soil leads to rot.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Use a bag of potting mix with some compost stirred in.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in compost, and a little balanced fertilizer at planting helps.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: A free-draining potting mix blended with compost.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Work in compost for fertility and a little balanced feed at planting.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Water container scallions more often than garden ones. The soil in a pot dries out fast, and dry spells make the tops thin and tough.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Because you water pots often, the food washes out faster. Give container scallions a little balanced fertilizer every few weeks while they grow.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Bunching types are very cold hardy, so where winters are mild you can leave a pot of scallions out over winter and keep cutting. In cold areas, move the pot to a sheltered spot or mulch it during hard freezes, since roots in a container get colder than roots in the ground.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Cold-hardy bunching types overwinter readily in containers in mild zones for cut-and-come-again use; in colder zones shelter or mulch pots through hard freezes, since container roots chill faster than open ground.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Scallions are excellent in pots because their roots stay shallow. Use a wide container at least 6 inches deep with drainage holes, sow or set them about an inch apart, and you can keep cutting bunching types for weeks. Pots dry out fast, so check the soil often.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Scallions are shallow-rooted and ideal for containers. A wide, well-drained pot at least 6 inches deep holds a dense stand sown about an inch apart. Containers dry fast, so water before the surface crusts and feed lightly every few weeks; bunching types regrow after cutting for repeat harvests.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Expect to water more frequently than in-ground; the shallow root zone in a pot dries quickly and any drought check thins the tops.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Frequent watering leaches nutrients, so feed container scallions lightly but regularly through leaf growth.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering containers suit scallions well, smoothing out the steady moisture they need; keep the mix free-draining so the root zone never stays saturated.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: Self-watering pots work nicely for scallions because they keep the soil evenly moist. Just use a mix that drains well so the roots are not sitting in water.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Avoid following onions or other alliums (garlic, leeks, shallots) in the same ground; allium diseases such as pink root and white rot persist in soil. A home garden can target at least 3 years between allium crops.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Do not plant scallions where you grew onions, garlic, or leeks recently. Some allium diseases live in the soil and build up. Wait at least 3 years before growing alliums in the same spot again.
rotation.good_after: leafy greens or legumes
rotation.note_seasoned: Scallions follow well after a leafy or legume crop and pair poorly before beans and peas, which alliums tend to inhibit.
rotation.note_beginner: Scallions do well planted after leafy greens or beans and peas. Just do not plant beans or peas right next to scallions, since onions can slow those down.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Scallions are not a room-temperature storage crop; they wilt within a day or two on the counter. Harvest close to use, or refrigerate promptly.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Scallions do not keep on the counter, they go limp within a day. Pick them close to when you will use them, or put them in the fridge right away.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Stand trimmed scallions in a little water or wrap them in a damp towel in a plastic bag in the crisper; they hold about one to two weeks (Clemson).
storage.fridge_beginner: Keep scallions in a plastic bag in the fridge, or stand them in a glass with a little water. They last about one to two weeks.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Scallions freeze well chopped; texture softens, so use frozen scallion in cooked dishes rather than raw.
storage.freezer_beginner: You can chop scallions and freeze them for cooking. They go soft after thawing, so use them in cooked food, not raw in salads.
storage.notes_seasoned: Best fresh. Because there is no cured bulb, scallions do not store for months the way bulb onions do; the bunching habit makes the garden the best storage, cutting what you need and leaving the rest growing.
storage.notes_beginner: Scallions are best used fresh. They do not keep for months like big onions. The easiest way to store them is to leave them growing in the garden and cut what you need.

recommended.name: Evergreen Hardy White
recommended.recommended_note: A perennial Allium fistulosum bunching type that clumps and is exceptionally cold hardy, so it overwinters and gives cut-and-come-again scallions in most regions. The classic choice for a permanent scallion patch.

recommended.name: White Lisbon
recommended.recommended_note: A quick, mild Allium cepa scallion, one of the most widely grown for an early straight white stem in roughly 60 days. Best for repeat spring and fall sowings rather than as a perennial clump.

recommended.name: Tokyo Long White
recommended.recommended_note: A bunching type prized for long, thick white shanks and heat tolerance; a dependable warm-shoulder-season scallion.

recommended.name: Beltsville Bunching
recommended.recommended_note: A bunching onion bred for heat and drought tolerance, named by Clemson among the types specifically bred for green-onion use.

recommended.name: Parade
recommended.recommended_note: A vigorous, uniform non-bulbing bunching onion that holds in the garden without forming a bulb, good for staggered harvests.

varieties.note_seasoned: Choose between two habits. True bunching types (Allium fistulosum) such as Evergreen Hardy White, Tokyo Long White, Beltsville Bunching, and Parade never form a bulb and many are perennial and very cold hardy, ideal for cut-and-come-again clumps. Regular bulb onions sown thickly and pulled young, such as White Lisbon, give a quick straight scallion but are pulled once, not divided. Clemson names Beltsville Bunching and Evergreen Bunching among types bred specifically for green-onion use.
varieties.note_beginner: There are two kinds. Bunching onions like Evergreen Hardy White or Tokyo Long White never make a bulb, grow back after cutting, and many survive winter, so they are great for a patch you keep cutting. Regular onions like White Lisbon, sown close together and pulled young, give a fast scallion but you pull the whole plant once. Either works for the kitchen.

companions.note_beginner: Scallions are good neighbors for carrots, beets, lettuce, and cabbage-family plants, mostly because their strong smell is thought to keep some pests away, and they are small enough to slip between other crops. The main thing to avoid is planting them next to beans or peas, since onions can slow those down. These are helpful traditions, not sure things, so do not worry if your garden does a little differently.
companions.note_seasoned: Scallions earn their companion reputation mostly through their allium scent, traditionally credited with deterring aphids and the carrot rust fly, so they pair well with carrots, beets, lettuce, and brassicas, and tuck neatly between slower crops. The one firm caution is the legume conflict: alliums are widely held to inhibit beans and peas, so keep scallions away from them. Most of these claims are traditional rather than trial-proven; treat them as low-risk suggestions, not guarantees.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Carrots
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Scallions and carrots are a classic garden pair. Their strong smell is said to help hide carrots from the carrot rust fly, and the two plants do not crowd each other's roots.

provenance.label: research_backed
provenance.reason: Same call as the carrot/onion entry from the carrot session: scent-masking vs carrot rust fly is the best-evidenced companion mechanism, with classic intercropping trials showing substantial fly-damage reduction at small scale; the reciprocal onion-side benefit (reduced thrips on onions grown with carrots) is extension-reported (HGTV/UC-aligned). research_backed earned; medium because the small-scale effect is hard to replicate at larger scale and I have not opened a single quantified figure to a T1 source. Density/arrangement dependent.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Carrots and scallions are the textbook reciprocal pairing. Your scallions' sulfur scent helps mask the carrots from the carrot rust fly, and in return carrots interplanted with scallions tend to carry less scallion thrips damage, so each crop disrupts the other's main pest. Intercropping trials have measured real reductions in carrot fly where the two grow together. Plant in alternating rows with enough scallion density for the scent-masking to register, and note the strongest results come from small mixed plantings rather than large solid blocks.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Beets
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Beets and scallions grow well side by side. They like the same cool weather and stay out of each other's way.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Rests on the general allium pest-repel reputation plus non-competition (different root/canopy profiles). Widely recommended and sound on space grounds, but no beet-specific measured effect; the pest-repel benefit is the general allium-scent claim rather than a measured beet trial. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Beets and scallions share a bed comfortably. The onion's pungency helps deter pests that bother beets, and because scallions shank shallowly with sparse upright foliage while beets put their energy into a single root, the two do not crowd each other above or below ground. This is mostly a good-neighbor, efficient-space pairing with a modest pest-repel bonus.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Lettuce
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Fast little lettuce plants fit nicely in the gaps between scallions and like the same cool season, so you get two crops from one spot.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Complementary root/canopy space efficiency (extension-endorsed interplant logic) plus a modest allium aphid-repel bonus. Sound and widely taught but a space/timing benefit rather than a measured lettuce-specific effect. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Lettuce and scallions interplant efficiently. Lettuce is shallow-rooted and quick while scallions send a narrow shank down with little leafy spread, so they occupy different space and the lettuce fills in between scallion rows. The scallion scent offers a little aphid deterrence over the lettuce as a bonus. Treat it as a space-and-timing pairing first, mild pest help second.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Brassicas (cabbage, broccoli)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Cabbage and broccoli like the same cool weather as scallions, and the strong scallion smell is thought to bother some of their pests.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Mirror of the broccoli<-onion call this batch: UMN-cited Iowa study included onion in the thyme/onion/nasturtium mix that reduced cabbage looper and imported cabbageworm in broccoli, plus marigold/onion/nasturtium vs cabbage worms in cabbage. extension_backed/medium: the trial used onion within a multi-species mix rather than alone, so supported but not cleanly isolated, hence medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Scallions are a well-supported brassica companion. Their sulfur scent helps mask the cabbage family and deter its signature pests, cabbage loopers, worms, and root maggots, and extension trial work including scallion in a mix with broccoli showed reduced caterpillar damage. Alliums are shallow and undemanding, so they tuck between brassicas without competing for the heavy feeding those crops want.

good_seasoned.name: Carrots
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: The pungent foliage of scallions is widely cited as masking the scent cues carrot rust fly uses to find carrots, and the two have complementary root habits. The pairing is traditional and intuitive but not cleanly demonstrated at the bed scale.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Long-standing interplanting tradition with a plausible scent-masking mechanism; specific-pair field evidence is thin.

good_seasoned.name: Beets
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional bed companion: similar cool-season culture and shallow, non-competing form make beets an easy neighbor that uses space efficiently alongside scallions.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Compatible culture and spacing; a conventional pairing rather than a research-demonstrated benefit.

good_seasoned.name: Lettuce
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Quick, shallow-rooted lettuce fills the row between slow upright scallions and shares their cool-season window, a space-efficient and traditional intercrop.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Spacing- and season-compatible intercrop; conventional companion advice without pair-specific trial evidence.

good_seasoned.name: Brassicas (cabbage, broccoli)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Cabbage-family crops share scallions' cool-season timing, and the strong allium scent is traditionally credited with discouraging some brassica pests; the pest effect is anecdotal rather than demonstrated.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Shared season plus a folk pest-deterrence claim; not verified for the specific pairing.

growth_stages.name: Germination & Emergence
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Thin, looped seed leaves push up bent like a hairpin, then straighten into the first slender tubes. Alliums germinate slowly and unevenly over a wide soil range (about 50 to 75 °F), so a sparse, gradual stand over a week or two is normal.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Look for thin, grass-like shoots coming up, each starting bent over in a little loop like a hairpin, then standing straight. Scallions sprout slowly and not all at once, so do not worry if they come up over a week or two.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep the surface evenly moist so the fine seed never dries mid-germination, and keep the bed weed-free from the start; allium seedlings are weak competitors. If you set transplants instead, this stage is already behind you.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the top of the soil damp so the tiny seeds do not dry out while sprouting, and pull weeds early, because young scallions lose out to weeds easily. If you planted young plants instead of seeds, you can skip this stage.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Note your sowing date and first emergence; the gap tells you your soil's germination pace for next time.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Write down when you planted and when the first shoots appeared. That tells you how fast your soil sprouts scallions.

growth_stages.name: Leaf Development
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Upright tubular leaves stack up one after another and the white shank lengthens and slowly thickens. Steady, uninterrupted growth here is what makes tender, full-flavored tops; a drought or weed check thins and toughens them.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plants grow more and more upright green leaves, and the white bottom gets longer and a little thicker. Steady growth now is what makes nice tender scallions, so keep them watered and weeded.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin to about one plant per inch before the seedlings crowd, hold moisture steady, and stay on top of weeds. A light side-dress of nitrogen helps lean soil.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Thin the seedlings to about one per inch so they are not crowded, keep the soil evenly moist, and pull weeds. If the soil is poor, a little fertilizer helps.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Track thinning and feeding dates and roughly how tall the tops are; it helps you time the next succession sowing.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you thinned and fed the plants and how tall the tops are getting.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Sturdy upright tops 6 inches and taller with a clean, pencil-thick white shank. Bunching types form a clump of several shoots; the planting is approaching usable size and will hold a while in cool weather.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Strong upright tops about 6 inches or taller, with a white bottom about as thick as a pencil. Bunching kinds make a little clump of several stems. They are getting close to ready.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture even and begin pulling the largest plants as you need them; harvesting thins the stand and lets the rest size up. Sow the next short succession now if you have not.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep watering, and start pulling the biggest ones as you need them, which gives the others room. Sow your next short row now for a steady supply.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Note the first usable-size date against your sowing date to learn your real days-to-harvest.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Write down when the first ones reached usable size, so you know how long they take for you.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tops 6 to 8 inches, shank pencil-thick to about half an inch, base still straight and unswollen. Pull or cut before a bulb forms and before summer heat or long-held plants push a hollow flower stalk.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Green tops 6 to 8 inches tall and a white bottom about as thick as a pencil, still straight with no round bulb. Pick them before a bulb forms or before they shoot up a flower stalk in heat.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Lift whole plants, or cut bunching types about an inch above the crown to let them regrow. Harvest on the young side for mildness; do not let plants over-mature or bolt.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pull the whole plant, or with bunching kinds cut the tops about an inch above the soil so they grow back. Younger is milder, and do not let them get old and woody.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record harvest dates and which succession they came from to fine-tune your sowing interval.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Write down when you harvested so you can plan your next sowings.

notifications.body_seasoned: Direct-sow scallion seed as soon as the soil is workable; the crop is cold hardy and does not wait for warm weather. Sow shallowly and plan to thin to about an inch.
notifications.body_beginner: Plant scallion seeds outside as soon as you can work the soil. They handle cold, so you do not need to wait for warm weather. Plant shallow and thin them later to about an inch apart.

notifications.body_seasoned: Sow another short row now, about two to three weeks after the last, so scallions keep coming in sequence through the cool season rather than all at once.
notifications.body_beginner: Plant another short row of scallions now, a couple of weeks after the last one, so you always have some coming along.

notifications.body_seasoned: Around 50 to 70 days from sowing, start pulling scallions once the tops reach 6 to 8 inches. Harvesting the largest first gives the rest room to size up.
notifications.body_beginner: About 50 to 70 days after planting, start picking scallions when the tops are 6 to 8 inches tall. Pull the biggest ones first to give the others room.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Cover young fall scallions
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Established scallions and bunching types are very cold hardy, but newly emerged fall seedlings appreciate a row cover or light mulch through a hard freeze until they toughen up.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Grown scallions handle cold well, but tiny fall seedlings do better with a row cover or a little mulch during a hard freeze until they get bigger.

germination_emergence.text_seasoned: Sow scallion seed shallowly, a quarter to a half inch deep, in a two-inch-wide band so the seedlings support each other, and keep the surface evenly moist until they emerge (UMN).
germination_emergence.text_beginner: Plant scallion seeds shallow, a quarter to a half inch deep, in a little two-inch-wide band, and keep the soil damp until they sprout.
germination_emergence.author: plant

leaf_development.text_seasoned: Thin seedlings to about one plant per inch once they are up; crowded scallions stay thin and tough, while thinned plants make clean, pencil-thick shanks.
leaf_development.text_beginner: Thin the little seedlings to about one per inch after they come up. Crowded scallions stay skinny, so give them room.
leaf_development.author: plant

established.text_seasoned: Sow a short row every two to three weeks through the cool season instead of one big planting, so scallions mature in sequence and none over-mature waiting to be pulled.
established.text_beginner: Plant a short new row every couple of weeks instead of all at once, so you get scallions a few at a time over many weeks.
established.author: plant

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest scallions when the tops reach 6 to 8 inches; lift whole plants, or cut bunching types about an inch above the crown to let them regrow for a second cutting (Clemson).
harvest.text_beginner: Pick scallions when the green tops are 6 to 8 inches tall. Pull the whole plant, or with bunching kinds cut the tops about an inch above the soil so they grow back.
harvest.author: plant

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: One scallion per plant for bulb-onion types pulled young; bunching types regrow after cutting for repeat harvests. A densely sown foot of row yields a generous handful.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Each regular onion plant gives one scallion when pulled young, while bunching kinds grow back after you cut them, so you keep harvesting from the same clump.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: With succession sowing the harvest is continuous through the cool season rather than a single flush; bunching clumps deliver over many weeks.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: If you sow a little at a time, you get scallions steadily for weeks instead of all at once, and bunching clumps keep producing.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Thinning to about an inch and keeping steady moisture are the biggest levers on tender, pencil-thick shanks in the first crop.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: The two things that matter most for good scallions are thinning them to about an inch apart and keeping the soil evenly moist.
factors_seasoned: thinning to about an inch
steady moisture
succession sowing
harvesting before over-maturity
cool-season timing

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No verified evidence ties scallion growth or yield to moon phase. Planting timing follows soil readiness and the every-two-weeks succession cadence, not lunar phase.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Plants send up a round, hollow flower stalk instead of staying as tender scallions.
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: A scallion shoots up a tall round flower stalk and the center goes hard.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Bolting. It is driven by a cold-then-warm swing (vernalization) in overwintered or oversized plants, and pushed along by summer heat and long-held plants. Once a stalk forms, the shank toughens and the flavor sharpens.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: This is called bolting. It happens after a cold spell followed by warmth, or when plants sit too long or get hot. Once a flower stalk forms, the scallion gets tough and strong.
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Harvest before plants over-mature, sow in succession so you always have young stock, and do not hold a spring sowing into summer heat. The tops are still usable young; cut and use them before the stalk hardens.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Pick scallions while they are young and keep planting small new batches so you always have tender ones. Do not let a spring planting sit into the summer heat. You can still eat bolting plants if you catch them early.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Tops are thin, spindly, and tough, with pale color.
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: The scallions are skinny and tough with pale leaves.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Usually crowding, drought, or low fertility: an unthinned stand and dry or lean soil all stall leaf growth and toughen the tops.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Usually the plants are too crowded, too dry, or the soil is too poor, which keeps the tops thin and tough.
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Thin to about an inch, keep the soil evenly moist, and side-dress lightly on lean ground. Thinnings are perfectly usable as baby scallions.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Thin the plants to about an inch apart, keep the soil damp, and give a light feeding if the soil is poor. The little ones you pull are good baby scallions.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Seedlings wilt and yellow and the shanks rot with small white larvae inside.
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Young plants wilt and yellow and the white bottoms rot with little white grubs inside.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Onion maggot, the larva of a fly that lays eggs at the plant base, worst in cool, wet springs and where allium debris carries it over.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Onion maggot, the grub of a small fly. It is worst in cool, wet spring weather and where old onion scraps are left around.
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Cover plants with row cover at emergence to block egg-laying, rotate away from alliums, and clear crop residue; pull and discard affected plants.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Cover young plants with row-cover fabric so the fly cannot lay eggs, rotate where you plant alliums, and clean up old onion scraps. Pull and throw out affected plants.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Scallions are a natural succession crop: sow a short row every two to three weeks through the cool season rather than one big planting, so they mature in sequence and none over-mature. In cool-summer regions that means spring through fall; in hot-summer regions it means fall through spring, skipping peak summer heat; in mild regions it runs nearly year-round. The number of sowings is set by the length of your cool window, not a fixed cap.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: Instead of planting all your scallions at once, sow a short row every couple of weeks. That way they are ready a few at a time over many weeks. In places with cool summers, plant spring through fall. In hot places, grow them fall through spring and skip the summer heat. Where winters are mild, you can plant nearly all year.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: Up North, scallions are easy to grow from spring through fall. Since you pick them young, you do not worry about bulbs or day length. Plant the seeds as soon as you can work the soil, since they handle light frost, and sow a short new row every couple of weeks for a steady supply. They handle the northern summer fine, so you can keep going until the ground freezes. Tough bunching kinds can even survive the winter under mulch for an early start.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In the cold-winter North, scallions are an easy cool-season crop you can grow from spring right through fall. Because you harvest them young and green, day length and bulbing never enter into it. Direct-sow as soon as the soil is workable, the crop shrugs off light frost, and keep sowing a short row every two to three weeks for a steady supply. They tolerate the northern summer better than most cool-season crops, so there is no real summer gap; the season simply closes when the ground freezes. Very cold-hardy bunching types can even overwinter under mulch for an extra-early spring cutting.

crops.description_seasoned: Spring onion, or scallion, is a fast cool-season allium grown for its slender white shank and green tops rather than a mature bulb. It is harvested young, before bulbing, so the day-length trigger that governs bulb onions is irrelevant here: you pull the plant while it is still a straight stem. Two routes give the same kitchen result, true bunching types (Allium fistulosum) that never form a bulb, or regular bulb onions (Allium cepa) sown thickly and pulled at the green stage. Sow seed shallowly, thin to about an inch, keep the soil evenly moist, and harvest in roughly 50 to 70 days when the tops stand 6 to 8 inches. Because the crop is quick and very cold hardy, sow a short row every two to three weeks through the cool season for a steady supply, year-round in mild regions.
crops.description_beginner: A spring onion, also called a scallion or green onion, is a young onion you eat whole: the long white base and the green tops. You harvest it before it makes a round bulb, so it grows fast and is easy. Some kinds (called bunching onions) never make a bulb at all, and you can also just sow regular onions close together and pull them young as scallions. Plant the seeds shallow, thin the seedlings to about an inch apart, keep the soil damp, and they are usually ready in about 50 to 70 days, when the green tops are 6 to 8 inches tall. They handle cold well, so plant a short row every couple of weeks through the cool season for a steady supply, and nearly year-round where winters are mild.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Pull scallions once the green tops reach about 6 to 8 inches and the white shank is roughly pencil thick. There is no need to wait for a bulb: harvest at the straight-stem stage, before the base swells. Lift the whole plant, or cut bunching types about an inch above the crown and let them regrow. Younger is milder, so harvest on the small side for salads and a bit larger for cooking.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Your scallions are ready when the green tops are about 6 to 8 inches tall and the white bottom is roughly as thick as a pencil. Do not wait for a round bulb to form, pull them while the base is still straight. Lift the whole plant, or with bunching types snip the tops about an inch above the soil and let them grow back. Smaller ones taste milder, bigger ones are a little stronger.

pet_safe.note: An onion-family allium, toxic to cats, dogs, and horses; scallions damage their red blood cells.
