crops.name: Edamame

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Edamame likes loose, fertile soil that drains well, with some compost worked in. It grows best in full sun and warm soil. Like other beans, edamame seed rots in cold, soggy ground, so good drainage matters and you wait for the soil to warm before planting. If water sits on your bed a long time after rain, mix in compost or plant on a raised bed first.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Edamame does best in a deep, fertile, well-drained loam or sandy loam with compost worked in before sowing. As a warm-season soybean it wants full sun and warm soil; the seed is large and rots readily in cold, wet ground, so drainage and soil warmth carry the crop through a clean stand. Steady, even moisture without waterlogging matters most through flowering and pod fill. Edamame is a legume that fixes much of its own nitrogen, so the bed needs fertility and tilth more than heavy feeding.

ph.note_beginner: Edamame grows best in soil from about 6.0 to 6.8, which is slightly acidic to neutral. It does poorly in strongly acidic soil, so if a soil test reads low, mix in some lime before planting. Most garden beds are already in a good range.
ph.note_seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 6.8, the band where soybean nodulates and yields best. Rutgers gives an ideal of 6.0 to 6.5 for edamame; below about 6.0 nitrogen fixation falls off, and above roughly 7.0 the crop is more prone to iron and manganese problems. A soil test is the reliable way to confirm pH and fertility before the season starts, and lime an acid plot the season before sowing.

fertilizer.type: balanced pre-plant, soybean inoculant, little to no nitrogen
fertilizer.timing: work a little balanced fertilizer or compost into the bed before sowing; inoculate the seed
fertilizer.example_product: 5-10-10 pre-plant
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Edamame is a light feeder. As a legume it fixes much of its own nitrogen through root nodules, so heavy nitrogen drives leafy growth at the expense of pods. Without a soil test, work a little balanced fertilizer or compost into the bed before sowing; that is usually all edamame needs. The one feeding step that matters is the inoculant: edamame needs the SOYBEAN-specific bacterium Bradyrhizobium japonicum, not the all-purpose bean and pea inoculant, to nodulate and fix nitrogen, and it helps most where soybeans have not grown before. Avoid high-nitrogen feeds, which delay flowering and cut pod set.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Edamame makes much of its own food from the air, so it barely needs fertilizer. Mix a little compost or balanced fertilizer into the bed before you plant and that is enough. The useful step is to coat the seed with an inoculant, but it must be the soybean kind (Bradyrhizobium japonicum), not the regular bean and pea inoculant, since soybeans use a different bacteria. Too much fertilizer gives you big leafy plants but fewer pods.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced 5-10-10 worked in before sowing if no soil test is available; skip extra nitrogen, which edamame supplies itself, and inoculate the seed with a soybean-type inoculant.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: A balanced vegetable fertilizer like 5-10-10 mixed into the bed before planting is plenty.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: 5-10-10 at about 3 pounds per 100 square feet worked in before sowing when no soil test is available; the priority input is a soybean inoculant on the seed, not nitrogen.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: About 3 pounds of 5-10-10 per 100 square feet, mixed into the bed before planting.

companions.note_beginner: Edamame gets along with most warm-season vegetables and, like other beans, leaves nitrogen in the soil for the next crop. It is a classic Three Sisters partner with corn and squash, and a good neighbor to cucumbers and potatoes. The pairing to avoid is planting edamame right next to onions or garlic.
companions.note_seasoned: As a nitrogen-fixing legume, edamame leaves the soil richer for what follows and sits comfortably among the warm-season crops grown in the same window. It is a traditional Three Sisters partner with corn and squash and a compatible neighbor for cucumbers and potatoes. The long-standing caution is to keep edamame away from the alliums (onion, garlic), which are widely held to suppress legumes by interfering with the root bacteria they depend on to fix nitrogen.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Corn
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: The traditional Three Sisters partner; the planting has been grown together for generations and the edamame's nitrogen helps the hungry corn.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Three Sisters is the best-documented historical legume polyculture; for edamame the corn relationship is foliage diversity plus the legume nitrogen benefiting a heavy feeder, structural rather than a measured crop-specific effect. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Corn is the classic Three Sisters partner for a bushy soybean like edamame. Edamame does not climb the corn the way pole beans do, so the benefit is mostly foliage diversity and the legume nitrogen helping the heavy-feeding corn over the season. Give the corn room so it does not shade the lower edamame, which needs full sun to fill its pods.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Squash
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: The third Sister; its broad leaves shade the soil and keep weeds down around the edamame.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Same Three Sisters basis; the squash ground-cover and weed-suppression role is well established and structural; foliage-diversity pest disruption is plausible but not a measured edamame-specific protection. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Squash rounds out the Three Sisters trio. Its sprawling leaves shade the soil, hold moisture, and suppress weeds around the edamame, while the varied foliage heights make it harder for pests to lock onto one crop. This is a soil-and-space benefit; give the squash room so it does not swamp the lower edamame.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Cucumber
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: An easy warm-season neighbor that shares edamame's sun, warmth, and water needs.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Rests on sound shared warm-season conditions plus legume nitrogen lightly benefiting a neighboring feeder, by close analogy to cucurbit and legume relationships. likely rather than research_backed; no edamame-specific cucumber trial located.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Cucumber and edamame coexist comfortably: similar warm-season timing, sun, and water needs, with complementary growth habits, and the edamame's nitrogen fixation lightly benefits the cucumber as a moderate feeder. It is a compatibility pairing rather than a strongly protective one, so expect easy cohabitation more than active pest control.

good_seasoned.name: Corn
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: The Three Sisters pairing of beans, corn, and squash is a long-documented traditional planting; the legume contributes nitrogen to the hungry corn.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Three Sisters; documented traditional companion strategy.

good_seasoned.name: Squash
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: The third of the Three Sisters; its sprawling canopy shades soil and suppresses weeds, complementing the upright edamame.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Three Sisters companion.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Onion
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Onions and other alliums are traditionally kept away from beans and soybeans, which are said to grow poorly near them.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: The allium-versus-legume mechanism reported for beans: allium sulfur compounds are held to disrupt the Rhizobium-type bacteria the legume depends on to fix nitrogen. mechanistic/medium: a sound, repeatedly cited mechanism, not a controlled edamame-yield trial opened this session.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Onions next to edamame is the better-grounded of the 'bad' pairings. Alliums release antibacterial sulfur compounds widely held to interfere with the nitrogen-fixing bacteria on legume roots, the bacteria edamame relies on, so growth tends to stall near onions. Keep them in separate parts of the bed. The useful corollary is that a legume grown before an allium crop leaves the soil better for it.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Garlic
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Like onions, garlic is a traditional bad neighbor for beans and soybeans.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Garlic is an allium with the same antibacterial sulfur chemistry as onion; same root-bacteria disruption mechanism. mechanistic/medium for the same reasons.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Garlic acts on edamame the way onions do. As an allium it gives off antibacterial sulfur compounds held to disrupt the nitrogen-fixing bacteria on legume roots, slowing the plants. Treat garlic and edamame as bed-mates to keep apart, and use the legume-then-allium rotation to your advantage instead.

bad_seasoned.name: Onion
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Alliums are the classic traditional caution near legumes; the pairing is widely advised against, attributed to allium compounds interfering with the legume's nitrogen-fixing bacteria.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Long-standing allium-versus-legume garden caution; mechanism plausible but not experimentally established here.

bad_seasoned.name: Garlic
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: As with onion, garlic is traditionally kept apart from beans and soybeans.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Allium caution, traditional.

pests.name: Bean leaf beetle
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Round to irregular holes chewed through the leaves, and on the pods the more damaging sign: chewing on the pod wall and, late in the season, clipping at the base of the pod that drops it entirely. The adult is a small reddish to yellowish beetle with a black triangle behind the head and usually a row of black spots along each wing cover.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Round holes chewed in the leaves, and worse, chewing on the pods themselves and even pods clipped off at the stem late in the season. The adult is a small reddish or yellowish beetle with a little black triangle behind its head and rows of black spots on its back.
pests.cause_seasoned: The bean leaf beetle (Cerotoma trifurcata), the most important leaf-feeding beetle of soybeans. Overwintered adults move into seedlings in spring, and a later summer generation feeds on the pods, which is the costly stage. It also transmits bean pod mottle virus.
pests.cause_beginner: The bean leaf beetle, the main leaf-eating beetle of soybeans. The adults move into young plants in spring, and a summer generation feeds on the pods, which is the worst damage. It can also spread a virus from plant to plant.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Edamame tolerates a lot of early leaf feeding without losing yield, so light damage on the foliage needs nothing. Handpick adults in a small patch, and protect the pods later in the season, when pod feeding and clipping matter; a floating row cover keeps beetles off, and an organic option such as spinosad or pyrethrin is labeled where pressure is heavy.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Edamame can lose a fair amount of leaf early without losing beans, so light leaf damage needs nothing. Pick beetles off in a small patch, and focus on protecting the pods later in the season, when the beetles do the real harm. A light row cover keeps them off, and an organic spray such as spinosad helps if they get bad.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Since pod feeding is the costly damage, an early sowing that fills pods before the summer beetle generation peaks helps. Clear crop debris after harvest and rotate edamame away from last year's bed to remove overwintering shelter; a row cover protects emerging seedlings where the beetle is a known problem.
pests.prevention_beginner: Because the pod damage is the worst part, planting early so the pods finish before the summer beetles build up helps. Clear away the old plants after harvest and move your edamame each year, and cover young seedlings with a row cover if this beetle is a problem where you are.

pests.name: Stink bugs
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Pods that look intact from outside but hold flat, shriveled, or discolored beans, because the bugs pierce the pod wall and feed on the developing seeds. Green and brown stink bugs are shield-shaped insects about half an inch long; their feeding scars the seed and can stop it filling.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Pods that look fine on the outside but hold flat, shrunken, or stained beans inside, because the bugs poke through the pod and feed on the seeds. Stink bugs are shield-shaped insects about half an inch long, green or brown.
pests.cause_seasoned: The stink bug complex (green stink bug, brown stink bug, and the invasive brown marmorated stink bug). They are among the most damaging soybean pests because they feed directly on the seed during pod fill, exactly the part of edamame you eat.
pests.cause_beginner: Several kinds of stink bugs, including the green, brown, and brown marmorated stink bugs. They matter because they feed straight on the beans inside the pods while the pods are filling, which is the part you eat.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Handpick the shield-shaped adults and the barrel-shaped egg clusters in a home patch, checking through pod fill. Keep weeds down around the bed, since stink bugs move in from weedy edges, and treat with an organic option such as spinosad or pyrethrin only where feeding on the pods is heavy.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick the shield-shaped bugs and their barrel-shaped egg clusters off by hand, checking while the pods fill. Keep weeds down around the bed, since the bugs come in from weedy edges, and use an organic spray only if they are really feeding on the pods.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Watch the pods closely from pod set through fill, the window stink bugs damage. Mow or clear weedy borders that harbor them ahead of the season, rotate the bed, and clean up debris after harvest. An early-maturing crop can finish before peak late-summer pressure.
pests.prevention_beginner: Check the pods from the time they set through filling, which is when stink bugs do harm. Clear weedy edges that shelter them before the season, move your edamame each year, and clean up old plants after harvest. An early variety can finish before the bugs peak in late summer.

pests.name: Soybean aphid
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Colonies of small, soft, pale-yellow aphids on the growing tips, undersides of upper leaves, and stems, often tended by ants. Heavy feeding puckers and yellows the leaves, stunts the plant, and leaves a sticky honeydew that blackens with sooty mold; the aphids also transmit several plant viruses.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Clusters of tiny, soft, pale-yellow insects on the growing tips and undersides of the upper leaves, sometimes with ants around them. Heavy feeding curls and yellows the leaves and leaves a sticky residue, and the aphids can spread viruses.
pests.cause_seasoned: The soybean aphid (Aphis glycines), an invasive aphid specific to soybeans that can build explosively in midsummer. Cool to warm, calm weather favors rapid buildup; lady beetles and other natural enemies usually catch up.
pests.cause_beginner: The soybean aphid, an invasive aphid that feeds only on soybeans and can multiply fast in midsummer. Mild weather lets it build up quickly, and ladybugs and other helpers usually bring it down.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong spray of water or treat with insecticidal soap, beginning while numbers are low. Lady beetles, lacewings, and parasitic wasps usually control soybean aphid in a garden, so avoid broad sprays that kill those helpers. Act early, since the aphids also move viruses.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray the colonies off with a strong jet of water or use insecticidal soap, starting while there are only a few. Ladybugs and other helpful insects usually finish the job, so avoid sprays that kill them too. Deal with aphids early since they can spread viruses.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid overfeeding with nitrogen, which produces the soft growth aphids favor, and keep nearby weeds and buckthorn (the aphid's overwintering host) in check. Reflective mulch disorients them and reduces virus spread, and natural enemies do most of the work in a home garden.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not overfeed with fertilizer, since the soft new growth is what aphids like, and keep weeds down nearby. Reflective mulch confuses them and cuts the viruses they spread, and helpful insects do most of the work in a home garden.

pests.name: Japanese beetle
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Leaves skeletonized to a lacy network of veins, the classic Japanese beetle signature, as the metallic green-and-copper adults feed in groups on the upper canopy in midsummer. Heavy feeding can strip the foliage, though edamame tolerates a good deal of leaf loss before yield suffers.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Leaves chewed down to a lacy skeleton of veins, the classic Japanese beetle damage, as the shiny green-and-copper beetles feed in groups on top of the plants in midsummer. They can strip a lot of leaf, but edamame handles a fair amount of leaf loss.
pests.cause_seasoned: The Japanese beetle (Popillia japonica), a metallic green beetle with coppery wing covers whose grubs develop in lawns and whose adults feed on many garden plants, soybeans included, through midsummer.
pests.cause_beginner: The Japanese beetle, a shiny green beetle with copper wings whose grubs live in lawns and whose adults feed on many plants, including soybeans, in midsummer.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Handpick the beetles in the early morning when they are sluggish, knocking them into soapy water; this is effective in a home patch and avoids the traps, which draw in more beetles than they catch. Because edamame tolerates real defoliation, light to moderate feeding on the leaves needs no spray.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick the beetles off in the early morning when they are slow, dropping them into soapy water; this works well in a garden. Skip the beetle traps, which often attract more beetles than they catch. Since edamame handles a lot of leaf loss, light damage needs no spray.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Watch through midsummer, the adult-feeding window, and protect plants with a floating row cover during a heavy flight if needed. Healthy lawns kept on the dry side in midsummer support fewer grubs; tolerate light leaf feeding rather than spraying.
pests.prevention_beginner: Watch through midsummer, when the adults feed, and cover plants with a row cover during a heavy beetle flight if needed. Keeping the lawn a bit drier in midsummer means fewer grubs, and light leaf damage is better tolerated than sprayed.

pests.name: Two-spotted spider mite
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine whitish or yellow stippling on the leaves that progresses to a bronzed, dried-out look, with fine silken webbing on the undersides; the mites are minute specks, easiest to confirm by tapping a leaf over white paper. They build explosively in hot, dry weather.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Fine whitish or yellow speckling on the leaves, turning to a dried, bronzed look, with fine webbing on the undersides. The mites are tiny specks, easiest to see by tapping a leaf over white paper. They explode in hot, dry weather.
pests.cause_seasoned: Two-spotted spider mites (Tetranychus urticae), tiny relatives of spiders that pierce leaf cells and suck the contents. Hot, dry, dusty conditions and drought-stressed plants favor rapid buildup, so they flare in dry midsummer spells.
pests.cause_beginner: Two-spotted spider mites, tiny relatives of spiders that pierce the leaf and suck out the contents. Hot, dry, dusty weather and dried-out plants let them build up fast, so they flare in dry midsummer.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hose the undersides of leaves with a strong spray of water to dislodge mites and webbing, and treat with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil before numbers climb. Keeping plants well watered and unstressed slows buildup, and natural predators help.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray the undersides of the leaves with a strong jet of water to knock off the mites and webbing, and use insecticidal soap before they get thick. Keeping the plants well watered and unstressed slows them down, and helpful bugs pitch in.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Maintain even soil moisture, since drought-stressed plants are far more mite-prone, and keep dust down around the bed. Watch the undersides of leaves through hot, dry spells so you catch the buildup early.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist, because dried-out plants are much more likely to get mites, and keep dust down. Check the undersides of the leaves during hot, dry weather so you catch them early.

diseases.name: White mold (Sclerotinia stem rot)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Water-soaked lesions on the stems at the nodes that turn into a white, cottony fungal growth, often with hard black resting bodies (sclerotia) inside or on the stems; affected stems bleach, wilt, and die above the lesion. It develops in cool, wet weather in dense, lush canopies with poor airflow.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Stems with a white, cottony mold at the joints, sometimes with hard black lumps in them; the stem above bleaches, wilts, and dies. It shows up in cool, wet weather where the plants are crowded and the air does not move.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Sclerotinia sclerotiorum, the same white mold that hits beans. Its hard black sclerotia survive years in the soil and germinate in cool, moist conditions to infect flowering plants, especially where dense, overfed growth keeps the canopy humid.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus, the same white mold that hits beans. Hard black survival bodies live for years in the soil and sprout in cool, damp weather to infect the plants, especially where crowded, overfed growth keeps the leaves humid.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no home-garden cure once plants are infected; management is cultural. Remove and destroy infected plants (do not compost them, since the sclerotia survive), and open up spacing and airflow to dry the canopy.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no home spray that cures it; you manage it by how you grow. Pull and throw away (do not compost) infected plants, since the black lumps survive, and space the plants out so the leaves dry faster.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants and rows for good airflow rather than crowding, and go easy on nitrogen, since excess feeding drives the dense growth the mold needs. Rotate away from beans and other susceptible crops on a long cycle, avoid overhead watering, and do not plant where white mold has been severe.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Give plants room so air moves through them, and go easy on fertilizer, since heavy growth feeds the mold. Move edamame away from beans on a long rotation, water at the base instead of overhead, and avoid spots where white mold has been bad.

diseases.name: Bacterial blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small, angular, water-soaked spots on the leaves that turn brown to black with a yellow-green halo, the spots often dropping out to leave a ragged, tattered look; it favors cool, wet weather and spreads in wind-driven rain. The most common foliar disease of soybeans.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small angular spots on the leaves that turn brown to black with a yellowish ring, often falling out to leave the leaves looking torn. It likes cool, wet weather and spreads in blowing rain. It is the most common leaf disease of soybeans.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The bacterium Pseudomonas savastanoi pv. glycinea. It overwinters on infected residue and seed, and splashing rain and handling wet plants move it from leaf to leaf; cool, wet conditions favor infection.
diseases.cause_beginner: A bacterium that survives the winter on old plant debris and seed. Splashing rain and touching wet plants carry it from leaf to leaf, and cool, wet weather is when it strikes.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once plants are infected; the disease rarely causes real yield loss in a garden. Avoid overhead watering and do not handle plants when the foliage is wet, which moves the bacteria from plant to plant.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure once plants are infected, but it rarely costs much in a garden. Water at the base, not overhead, and stay out of the patch when the leaves are wet, since that spreads the bacteria.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant clean seed and do not save seed from an infected crop, since the disease is seedborne. Rotate away from soybeans and beans, clear residue after harvest, give plants room for airflow, and keep out of the bed when the foliage is wet.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant clean seed and do not save seed from infected plants, since the disease travels on seed. Move your edamame each year, clear away old plants after harvest, give the plants room, and keep out of the patch when the leaves are wet.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Pale green to yellow spots on the upper leaf surface with a matching grayish, downy fungal growth on the underside in humid weather; spots enlarge and brown. It is common but usually minor, and seed from infected plants can carry a white crust.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Pale green to yellow blotches on top of the leaves with a grayish, fuzzy growth underneath in humid weather; the spots grow and turn brown. It is common but usually mild, and infected seed can have a white coating.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus-like organism Peronospora manshurica, favored by warm, humid weather and frequent leaf wetness. It survives on residue and seed and spreads on wind and splashing in humid spells.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus-like organism that likes warm, humid weather and wet leaves. It survives on old plant debris and seed and spreads in damp, humid spells.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Downy mildew seldom needs treatment in a home garden; edamame outgrows light infection. Improve airflow and avoid wetting the foliage to slow it, and remove badly spotted leaves where practical.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Downy mildew rarely needs treatment in a garden; the plants usually grow through it. Give the plants room and avoid wetting the leaves to slow it, and pull badly spotted leaves if you like.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants for airflow, water at the soil rather than overhead, and rotate away from soybeans. Clean up residue after harvest and use clean seed, since the organism carries over on debris and seed.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Give plants room so the leaves dry, water at the base, and move your edamame each year. Clear away old plants after harvest and use clean seed, since it carries over on debris and seed.

diseases.name: Soybean cyst nematode
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Patches of stunted, yellowed, slow-growing plants, often in spots rather than uniformly, with few nodules and tiny lemon-shaped white to yellow females (cysts) just visible on the roots in summer. Above-ground symptoms are easy to miss, but the cysts on the roots are the giveaway.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Patches of stunted, yellow, slow plants, usually in spots rather than all over, with very few of the normal root nodules. The clue is tiny lemon-shaped white or yellow specks (cysts) on the roots in summer.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The soybean cyst nematode (Heterodera glycines), a microscopic roundworm that is the most damaging soybean pest in much of the country. Its cysts hold eggs that survive in the soil for years, and they build up where soybeans are grown repeatedly.
diseases.cause_beginner: The soybean cyst nematode, a microscopic worm that is the most damaging soybean pest in much of the country. Its egg-filled cysts survive in the soil for years and build up where soybeans grow in the same spot again and again.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no rescue treatment in a home garden; management is preventive. Where plants are stunted in patches, check the roots for cysts in summer and avoid moving soil from that bed to clean ground on tools or shoes.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no home treatment once it is established; you manage it by prevention. If plants are stunted in patches, check the roots for the tiny cysts in summer, and avoid carrying soil from that bed to clean ground on tools or shoes.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate edamame with non-host crops (anything but soybeans and dry beans) on a long cycle, the main control, and do not grow soybeans in the same bed year after year. Where the nematode is established, grow resistant soybean varieties and keep the soil clean of weed hosts.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Rotate edamame with crops other than soybeans and dry beans on a long cycle, which is the main control, and never grow soybeans in the same spot every year. Where it is a known problem, plant resistant varieties and keep weeds down.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Regular and even through the season, about an inch of water a week from rain or irrigation, keeping the soil moist but never waterlogged. The need peaks during flowering and pod fill, when moisture stress directly cuts the set.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water regularly, about an inch a week, so the soil stays evenly moist but not soggy. Pay closest attention while the plants are flowering and the pods are filling out.
watering.amount_seasoned: Enough to wet the root zone roughly 6 inches down; watering deeply and less often builds deeper roots than frequent light sprinkles.
watering.amount_beginner: Water deeply enough to wet the soil about 6 inches down. Deep, less frequent watering beats a daily light sprinkle.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the soil level in the morning so the foliage dries before evening; this limits the foliar diseases edamame is prone to in humid weather.
watering.method_beginner: Water the soil, not the leaves, and do it in the morning so the plants dry off during the day. Wet leaves, especially overnight, help spread disease.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting despite wet soil, and stunted growth point to waterlogged roots and the root rots edamame is prone to in cold, wet ground.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If the soil is wet but the plants still wilt or the lower leaves turn yellow, you may be overwatering. Soggy soil rots the roots.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Drought stress during and after flowering aborts blossoms and produces small, poorly filled pods, the single biggest avoidable hit to an edamame crop.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: If plants dry out while flowering, they drop their flowers and the pods fill poorly. Keep the water steady at that stage.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Avoid overhead watering where practical; the critical moisture window is flowering through pod fill.
watering.method_note_beginner: Try not to spray the whole plant from above. The most important time to keep water steady is when the plants are flowering and forming pods.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Flowering and pod fill are the moisture-critical stages; drought here aborts blossoms and shrinks the beans.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Flowering and pod-filling are the times edamame most needs steady water.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Not applicable. Edamame is direct-sown in place and is not started indoors or hardened off.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: You do not need to harden off edamame. It is planted straight into the garden from seed.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Direct-sow after the last spring frost, once the soil has warmed to at least 60 to 65°F. Edamame resents root disturbance and germinates quickly in warm soil, so transplanting offers no advantage. Sow about 1 to 1.5 inches deep, and inoculate the seed with a soybean-type (Bradyrhizobium japonicum) inoculant, especially where soybeans have not grown before.
start_method.notes_beginner: Plant edamame seeds right where they will grow, after the last frost once the soil has warmed to at least 60 to 65°F. Edamame does not like its roots disturbed, so skip starting it indoors. Plant about 1 to 1.5 inches deep, and coat the seed with a soybean inoculant if you have it.

drainage.saucer_practice: Empty any saucer after watering so the pot never sits in standing water, which rots edamame roots.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Use a good potting mix, not garden soil, which packs down too hard in pots.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in a little compost for fertility.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: A well-draining potting mix; avoid native garden soil, which compacts and drains poorly in containers.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend in compost for baseline fertility and tilth; edamame needs little added nitrogen but does want a soybean inoculant on the seed.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out faster than garden beds, so check the soil daily in warm weather and water when the top inch is dry.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Container edamame still needs little feeding; a little compost in the mix is usually enough.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Not applicable. Edamame is a warm-season annual; it finishes in one season and is not overwintered.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Not applicable. As a frost-tender annual, edamame completes its cycle in a single season and is not overwintered.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Edamame grows in a pot at least 5 gallons and 8 inches deep, but one plant gives only a handful of pods, so plant several seeds across a wide container and expect a small harvest. A big bed gives a far better return than pots.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Edamame will grow in a container of at least 5 gallons and 8 inches deep, but it is a low-yielding-per-plant crop (about a pound of pods per foot of row) that matures all at once, so a pot returns only a small one-time pick. Plant several seeds across a wide container for a worthwhile handful; growers who want a real harvest are better served by an in-ground block.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry faster than beds; monitor daily in heat and water when the top inch dries.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Feeding needs stay low in containers; compost in the mix plus a seed inoculant usually suffices.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering container suits edamame well, smoothing out the steady moisture it wants through pod fill while avoiding the soggy roots it dislikes.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match for edamame because it keeps the water steady, which is what it likes, without leaving the roots soggy.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: A wide container suits edamame better than a deep, narrow one. The plants are bushy and shallow-rooted and crop best grown several together, so surface area matters more than depth. A broad pot lets you space several plants for a worthwhile one-time pick.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: A wide pot works better for edamame than a deep, narrow one. The plants stay bushy with roots near the surface and do best grown several together, so width matters more than depth. A broad pot lets you plant several across the top for a worthwhile handful.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Avoid following edamame with soybeans, dry beans, or other legumes in the same bed; rotate to break the soilborne disease cycle and, above all, to keep soybean cyst nematode and white mold from building up. Where the nematode is present, extend the rotation and grow only non-host crops there for several years.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Do not plant edamame where soybeans or beans grew last year. Diseases and especially the soybean cyst nematode build up in the soil and hit the next crop. If you have had nematode or white mold trouble, wait several years before soybeans return.
rotation.good_after: Edamame is an excellent crop to grow before a heavy feeder. As a legume it fixes nitrogen and leaves the soil in better shape for a following crop such as a leafy green, a brassica, or corn.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate edamame on at least a three-year cycle, longer where soybean cyst nematode or white mold have appeared. Its nitrogen-fixing habit makes it a good predecessor for nitrogen-hungry crops.
rotation.note_beginner: Move your edamame to a new spot each year, on about a three-year rotation, and longer if you have had nematode or mold trouble. Because edamame feeds the soil with nitrogen, whatever you plant there next will benefit.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Not recommended. Edamame loses sweetness fast at room temperature as the sugars convert to starch, so cool it promptly after picking rather than holding it on the counter. Soybeans must be cooked before eating and are not eaten raw.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Do not leave edamame out on the counter. It loses its sweetness quickly, so cool it soon after picking. Always cook edamame before eating it; do not eat the beans raw.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Cool edamame immediately after harvest to shed field heat, then refrigerate in a perforated bag. It holds good quality for only a few days, near 32 to 40°F at high humidity; the sugars convert to starch over time, so use it sooner rather than later. Many growers cook or blanch it the day it is picked.
storage.fridge_beginner: Cool the pods right after picking, then keep them in the fridge in a loosely closed bag. They stay good for only a few days and get less sweet the longer they sit, so use them soon.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Edamame freezes very well for longer storage and is the usual way to keep a one-time harvest. Blanch the pods in boiling water for three to four minutes, cool them, and freeze within a few hours of picking for the best quality; shell after cooking.
storage.freezer_beginner: Edamame freezes very well, which is the usual way to keep a big harvest. Blanch the pods in boiling water for three to four minutes, cool them, and freeze within a few hours of picking. Shell the beans out after cooking.
storage.notes_seasoned: Edamame is at its sweetest within hours of picking and is best cooked or frozen the same day. Because the whole crop matures at once, most gardeners blanch and freeze the surplus: a three-to-four-minute blanch in the pod sets the color and texture, then freeze promptly. Always cook edamame before eating; raw soybeans are not eaten.
storage.notes_beginner: Edamame tastes best soon after picking and is best cooked or frozen the same day. Since the whole crop comes at once, most gardeners blanch and freeze what they cannot eat fresh: boil the pods three to four minutes, cool, and freeze. Always cook edamame before eating it.

recommended.name: Envy
recommended.note: An early, short-season green edamame on compact two-foot plants; a dependable choice for northern gardens and short summers where a later variety would not finish before frost.

recommended.name: Midori Giant
recommended.note: A popular large-podded green edamame with big, sweet beans and good yields; widely grown and a reliable mid-season standard.

recommended.name: BeSweet 2032
recommended.note: A sweet, productive green edamame valued for flavor and a concentrated set that makes the single harvest easy to time.

recommended.name: Tohya
recommended.note: An early, tender Japanese-type edamame with good flavor and a uniform set; suits cooler and shorter seasons.

recommended.name: Chiba Green
recommended.note: A vigorous green-seeded edamame with large pods and a clean, nutty flavor; a well-regarded mid-season pick.

varieties.note_seasoned: These are vegetable soybean (edamame) cultivars, eaten as immature green pods, not the small dry grain soybean. The single most important choice is matching the variety's maturity to your latitude: soybean is a short-day plant, so a variety bred for the South will flower late and may not fill pods before frost in the North, while a northern early type rushed in the South may flower and mature too soon and yield little. Pick an early, short-season type (Envy, Tohya) in cold and short-summer regions and a mid-season type farther south, and lean on adapted regional recommendations.
varieties.note_beginner: These are edamame, the kind of soybean you eat as green pods, not the dry grain soybean. The key is to pick a variety that matures in your area: soybeans flower based on day length, so a variety from the wrong region may not make pods before frost. Choose an early type like Envy or Tohya in cool or short-summer areas, and a mid-season type in warmer regions. A local garden center or extension office can point you to a good match.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare soil for about a week, then the seedling shoulders up through the surface, dragging its two thick seed leaves (cotyledons) up with it. Edamame seed is large and needs warm soil: it germinates well only once the soil has warmed to about 60 to 65°F, and it rots in cold, wet ground. A slow, cold start invites seed rot and seedcorn maggot.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Bare soil for about a week, then a stem pushes up through the surface, pulling two thick first leaves up with it. Edamame seed is large and needs warm soil; it comes up well only once the soil has warmed to about 60 to 65°F and rots in cold, wet ground.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Sow only once the soil has warmed to at least 60 to 65°F, after the last frost; there is no advantage to planting early. Sow about 1 to 1.5 inches deep into a moist, well-drained bed, inoculate the seed with a soybean-type inoculant where soybeans are new to the ground, and avoid soaking the bed, which suffocates the seed and feeds root rot.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Wait to plant until the soil has warmed to at least 60 to 65°F, after the last frost. There is no reward for planting edamame early, only rotted seed. Plant about 1 to 1.5 inches deep in moist, well-drained soil, coat the seed with a soybean inoculant if you have it, and do not keep the bed soggy.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have your edamame plants emerged? Note the date to track days to maturity from a real sowing rather than the seed packet.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Has your edamame come up yet? Write down the date you first saw it break the soil.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The cotyledons open and the first true leaves appear: a pair of single leaflets, then the soybean's characteristic three-part (trifoliate) leaves. Growth is quick once the plant is up and the weather is warm. Young seedlings are the stage most vulnerable to cutworms, bean leaf beetle, and rabbits.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The two seed leaves open, then the real leaves appear, first a single pair, then the three-leaflet leaves soybeans are known for. Once they are up and the weather is warm, they grow fast. This young stage is when cutworms, beetles, and rabbits can do the most damage.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep the bed evenly moist and weed-free; young edamame competes poorly with weeds. Cultivate shallowly, since the roots run near the surface. There is no thinning if sown at final spacing of 2 to 4 inches; protect the stand from rabbits and cutworms, which can clip seedlings overnight.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist and pull weeds early, since small plants do not compete well with them. Weed and hoe shallowly, since the roots are close to the surface. You do not need to thin if you planted at the right spacing, but watch for rabbits and cutworms that can chew off seedlings.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How is your edamame stand looking? Note any gaps, beetle damage, or seedlings clipped at the soil line.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How do your young edamame plants look? Note any chewed leaves or bare patches in the row.

growth_stages.name: Leafy growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Steady, bushy growth as the plant fills out to its full two to three feet, sturdy and upright with no need for support, building the canopy that will carry the pods. The plant is fixing much of its own nitrogen now through root nodules, so vigorous green growth, not dark, overfed lushness, is the goal.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant grows bushy and fills out to its full size, usually two to three feet tall and standing on its own without support. Edamame makes much of its own food (nitrogen) at this stage, so you want healthy green growth, not huge dark leafy plants, which usually mean too much fertilizer and fewer pods.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Hold steady, even moisture and resist the urge to feed. Edamame needs little nitrogen, and adding more now pushes leafy growth at the expense of pods. Keep the rows open for airflow to hold off the foliar diseases that come on in humid weather.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the watering steady and do not add fertilizer now. Edamame needs very little, and extra just gives you big leafy plants with fewer pods. Keep the plants from getting crowded so air moves through them.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How are your edamame plants filling in? Note their height and how bushy they look.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How big are your edamame plants getting? Note how tall and full they look.

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small white or purple flowers open in the leaf axils along the stems. Soybean is a short-day plant, so flowering is triggered by shortening days as much as by age, which is why matching the variety's maturity to your latitude matters. This is a moisture-critical stage: drought now aborts blossoms, and sustained extreme heat above roughly 95 to 100°F can drop flowers and small pods.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Small white or purple flowers open along the stems. Soybeans flower partly in response to the shortening days of late summer, which is why the right variety for your area matters. This is an important time for water: if the plants dry out, or in extreme heat above about 95 to 100°F, the flowers can drop without setting pods.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture steady and ample through bloom; water stress here directly cuts the crop. Avoid overhead watering on the dense canopy. In an extreme heat wave, water deeply ahead of time; edamame tolerates ordinary summer heat far better than snap beans, but sustained extremes still abort some flowers.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the water steady and generous while the plants flower, because dry soil now means fewer pods. Water the soil, not the leaves. In a serious heat wave water deeply beforehand; edamame handles normal summer heat well, but extreme heat can still drop some flowers.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are your edamame plants flowering? Note the date bloom started and any blossom drop in extreme heat.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are your edamame plants flowering yet? Note when the flowers opened.

growth_stages.name: Pod fill
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flat young pods form where the flowers were, then plump rapidly as the seeds swell to fill them. Edamame is picked at the R6 stage, when the bright green pods are plump and the beans inside nearly touch but are still tender and sweet, not yet hard or yellowing. This and flowering are the moisture-critical stages; drought here gives thin, poorly filled pods.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Flat young pods form where the flowers were and then plump up fast as the beans inside swell. You pick edamame when the pods are bright green and plump and the beans nearly touch inside but are still tender, before they get hard or start to yellow. Steady water matters most now.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Maintain even moisture right through pod fill, the payoff stage for steady watering. Watch the pods closely as they plump: because the whole plant matures together, the crop comes ready over just a few days, so this is when you decide the timing of a single concentrated harvest.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist while the pods fill, since this is what the steady watering was for. Watch the pods as they plump up, because the whole plant ripens together and the crop will be ready all at once over just a few days.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are the pods filling? Note the date you first saw plump pods and how fast they are sizing up toward the picking stage.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are the pods filling out? Note when you first saw plump green pods.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Plump, bright green pods with the beans filling about 80 to 90 percent of the pod and nearly touching inside, still tender and sweet. The whole plant ripens together, so most pods reach this stage within a few days of one another, and the prime window is short, roughly four to ten days before the pods toughen, the beans turn starchy, and the color dulls toward yellow.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Plump, bright green pods with the beans nearly filling them and almost touching inside, still tender and sweet. The whole plant ripens at the same time, so the pods are ready together, and the best window is short, about four to ten days, before they get tough and starchy and start to yellow.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest the whole plant at once when most pods are plump and green: pull or cut the plant and strip the pods, or pick all the ready pods in one or two passes. Pick in the cool morning. Because the window is short and the quality drops fast once the beans pass their peak, check daily as the pods plump and do not wait. Cook or freeze the same day for the best flavor.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Harvest the whole plant at once when most of the pods are plump and green: pull up the plant and strip off the pods, or pick all the ready pods in one go. Pick in the cool morning. The window is short, so check every day as the pods fill and do not wait too long. Cook or freeze them the same day for the best flavor.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have you harvested? Log the date and how full and green the pods were when you picked.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you picked your edamame? Note the date and how the pods turned out.

notifications.body_seasoned: Direct-sow edamame after the last spring frost, once the soil has warmed to at least 60 to 65°F. Sow about 1 to 1.5 inches deep into a moist, well-drained bed, and inoculate the seed with a soybean-type (Bradyrhizobium japonicum) inoculant where soybeans are new to the ground.
notifications.body_beginner: Plant edamame after the last spring frost, once the soil has warmed to at least 60 to 65°F. Plant about 1 to 1.5 inches deep in moist, well-drained soil, and coat the seed with a soybean inoculant if you have it. There is no benefit to planting earlier.

notifications.title_seasoned: Sow your next short row of edamame
notifications.title_beginner: Plant your next row of edamame
notifications.body_seasoned: Because each edamame plant matures all at once, the way to spread the harvest is to sow a fresh short row every week or two rather than picking over a long window. Sow again now, about two weeks after the last, and stop early enough that the final sowing matures before your first fall frost.
notifications.body_beginner: Because the whole edamame plant ripens at once, the way to get a steady supply is to plant a new short row every week or two instead of all at once. Plant again now, about two weeks after the last row, and stop in time for the last batch to finish before your first fall frost.

notifications.title_beginner: Start checking your edamame every day
notifications.body_seasoned: Most edamame is ready about 75 to 100 days from sowing. Begin checking daily as the pods plump: harvest when they are bright green and plump with the beans nearly touching inside. The whole plant ripens together and the prime window is only about four to ten days, so do not wait.
notifications.body_beginner: Most edamame is ready about 75 to 100 days from planting. Start checking every day as the pods fill, and pick when they are bright green and plump with the beans nearly touching inside. The whole plant ripens at once and the best window is only about four to ten days, so do not wait too long.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost expected, protect or harvest edamame
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost is coming, cover or pick your edamame
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Edamame is frost-tender and a light frost will kill it. If frost is forecast, harvest any plants whose pods are plump and green, and cover younger plants with row cover or sheets overnight. In fall, a hard frost ends the crop, so pick everything usable first.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Edamame is killed by even a light frost. If frost is forecast, pick any plants with plump green pods and cover younger plants with row cover or sheets overnight. In fall, a hard frost ends the crop, so pick everything you can use first.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Extreme heat may cause flower and pod drop
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Extreme heat can make flowers and pods drop
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Edamame tolerates ordinary summer heat far better than snap beans, but sustained extremes above roughly 95 to 100°F during bloom and pod set can drop flowers and young pods. Keep moisture steady and water deeply ahead of a heat wave; the plant resumes setting once the worst heat eases.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Edamame handles normal summer heat much better than snap beans, but very hot spells above about 95 to 100°F while it is flowering can make it drop flowers and small pods. Keep the water steady and water deeply before the heat. The plant sets pods again once the worst heat passes.

germination.text_seasoned: Edamame seed is large and rots in cold, wet ground. Wait until the soil is at least 60 to 65°F after the last frost before sowing, since early planting only invites poor stands, seed rot, and seedcorn maggot. There is no head start to be had: seed sown into warm soil quickly overtakes seed sown into cold soil.
germination.text_beginner: Edamame seeds are big and rot in cold, wet soil. Wait until the soil has warmed to at least 60 to 65°F after the last frost, because planting early just leads to rotted seed and missing plants. Seed planted in warm soil catches up fast, so there is nothing to gain by rushing.
germination.author: plant

germination.text_seasoned: Edamame fixes its own nitrogen, but only with the SOYBEAN bacterium Bradyrhizobium japonicum, which is a different species from the all-purpose bean and pea inoculant. Where soybeans have not grown before, coating the seed with a soybean-specific inoculant improves nodulation; the generic legume inoculant will not work for soybeans.
germination.text_beginner: Edamame makes its own nitrogen, but it needs the soybean kind of inoculant (called Bradyrhizobium japonicum), not the regular bean and pea inoculant, which is a different bacteria. If soybeans have never grown in your bed, coat the seed with a soybean inoculant to help. The regular bean inoculant will not do the job.
germination.author: plant

seedling.text_seasoned: Weed early and cultivate shallowly. Young edamame competes poorly with weeds, but the roots run close to the surface, so deep hoeing does more harm than the weeds. Hand-pull and scuffle-hoe lightly near the row through the first few weeks, and watch for rabbits and cutworms on the tender seedlings.
seedling.text_beginner: Pull weeds early, but weed shallowly. Young edamame does not compete well with weeds, yet the roots are near the surface, so digging deep hurts the plant more than the weeds. Pull by hand and hoe lightly near the row, and watch for rabbits and cutworms on the young plants.
seedling.author: plant

vegetative.text_seasoned: Hold off on nitrogen. As a legume, edamame fixes much of its own through root nodules, and extra nitrogen now drives leafy growth at the expense of pods. A little balanced fertilizer or compost worked in before sowing, plus a soybean inoculant on the seed, is all the crop needs.
vegetative.text_beginner: Do not add nitrogen fertilizer now. Edamame makes much of its own from the air, and extra fertilizer just gives you big leafy plants with fewer pods. A little balanced fertilizer or compost mixed in before planting, plus a soybean inoculant on the seed, is all it needs.
vegetative.author: plant

flowering.text_seasoned: Keep moisture steady and ample through bloom and pod set. Flowering and pod fill are the moisture-critical stages, and water stress now aborts blossoms and thins the set. Water at the soil in the morning, not overhead, to keep the dense canopy dry and limit foliar disease.
flowering.text_beginner: Keep the water steady and generous while the plants flower and set pods. Flowering and pod-filling are the times edamame most needs water, and letting it dry out now means fewer pods. Water the soil in the morning, not the leaves, to keep disease down.
flowering.author: plant

pod_fill.text_seasoned: Start watching the pods daily as they plump. Because the whole plant matures together, edamame does not give a long, forgiving pick like green beans: the prime window is only about four to ten days, when the pods are plump and green and the beans nearly touch but are still tender. Picked past that, the beans turn starchy and the color dulls.
pod_fill.text_beginner: Start checking the pods every day as they fill out. Unlike green beans, edamame ripens all at once, so the best picking window is short, only about four to ten days, when the pods are plump and green and the beans nearly touch inside but are still tender. Left longer, the beans get starchy and dull.
pod_fill.author: plant

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest the whole plant in one go. Because edamame ripens together, the easiest method is to pull or cut the plant when most pods are plump and green and strip the pods off, rather than picking over many times. Cook or freeze the same day, and remember the beans must be cooked, since soybeans are not eaten raw.
harvest.text_beginner: Harvest the whole plant at once. Since edamame ripens all together, the easiest way is to pull up the plant when most pods are plump and green and strip off the pods, instead of picking many times. Cook or freeze them the same day, and remember edamame must be cooked, never eaten raw.
harvest.author: plant

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Edamame yields modestly per plant, which is why it is grown in blocks or rows rather than singly. Missouri Extension puts a home crop at roughly a pound of pods per foot of row, and notes a dozen plants will supply more than enough pods for a family of four. A single plant gives only a handful, all at once.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Each edamame plant gives only a handful of pods, all at once, which is why it is grown in rows or blocks rather than one at a time. A rough guide is about a pound of pods per foot of row, and a dozen plants is plenty for a family of four.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Unlike green beans, edamame ripens all at once: the whole plant, and most of a planting, comes ready over just a few days, so there is no long picking season. The way to stretch the supply is to make several small succession sowings a week or two apart, each maturing in turn, and to freeze the surplus from each one-time harvest.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Unlike green beans, edamame ripens all at once, so a planting gives one big harvest over just a few days rather than picking for weeks. To spread it out, plant several small batches a week or two apart so they ripen in turn, and freeze what you cannot eat fresh.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Edamame is a rewarding and forgiving first-year crop: large seed that comes up strongly in warm soil, sturdy self-supporting plants that need no trellis, and few demands beyond steady water. The main levers on yield are matching the variety's maturity to your latitude, sowing into warm soil, keeping moisture steady through flowering and pod fill, and catching the short harvest window.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Edamame is a great first-year crop. The seed is big and comes up strongly in warm soil, the plants stand on their own without a trellis, and they ask little beyond steady water. The main things that affect your harvest are choosing the right variety for your area, planting in warm soil, keeping the water steady while it flowers and fills pods, and picking in the short window when the pods are plump.
factors_seasoned: Variety maturity matched to latitude (soybean is short-day; a mismatched variety flowers too early or too late and yields poorly)
Warm soil at sowing (edamame germinates poorly below about 60 to 65°F and the seed rots in cold, wet ground)
Steady moisture through flowering and pod fill (the moisture-critical stages; drought here aborts blossoms and thins pods)
Catching the short harvest window (the whole plant ripens together, and pods pass from prime to starchy in a few days)

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No reliable extension or peer-reviewed evidence supports timing edamame planting or harvest by moon phase. Sow edamame by soil temperature, which should be at least about 60 to 65°F, and by your frost-free date, and harvest by the pods, not by the lunar cycle.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Pods tough, starchy, or yellowing
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Pods came out tough and starchy
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The pods were picked past their brief prime window, so the beans turned starchy and tough and the pods dulled from bright green toward yellow. This is the signature edamame mistake: unlike green beans, the whole plant ripens together over just a few days, and a crop left even a week too long passes from sweet and tender to mealy. It is a timing problem, not a disease.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The pods were picked too late, so the beans turned starchy and tough and the pods went from bright green to yellowish. This is the classic edamame mistake: the whole plant ripens at once over just a few days, and waiting even a week too long makes the beans mealy instead of sweet. It is a timing problem, not a disease.
failure_diagnostics.cause: harvested past the short prime window
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Start checking daily once the pods plump, and harvest the whole plant as soon as most pods are full and green with the beans nearly touching, before any yellowing. Stagger several small sowings a week or two apart so the crop does not all peak at once, and freeze the surplus the day you pick.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Start checking every day once the pods fill out, and harvest the whole plant as soon as most pods are plump and green, before they yellow. Plant a few small batches a week or two apart so they do not all ripen together, and freeze what you cannot eat the day you pick.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Seeds rotted or came up poorly
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Seeds rotted or did not come up
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The seed was sown into soil that was too cold and wet, so it sat without germinating and rotted, or came up as a thin, patchy stand. Edamame seed is large and germinates well only once the soil reaches about 60 to 65°F, and a slow, cold start invites soilborne root rots and seedcorn maggot.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The seed went into soil that was too cold and wet, so it sat there instead of sprouting and rotted, or came up thin and patchy. Edamame seed is big and sprouts well only once the soil warms to about 60 to 65°F, and a slow, cold start lets soil fungi and a seed-eating maggot get to it.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait until the soil has warmed to at least 60 to 65°F after the last frost before sowing; there is no benefit to planting early. Sow into well-drained ground or raised beds rather than low, wet spots, plant about 1 to 1.5 inches deep, and do not keep the bed soggy after sowing.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Wait until the soil has warmed to at least 60 to 65°F after the last frost before planting, since there is no reward for planting edamame early. Plant in well-drained soil or raised beds instead of low, wet spots, plant about 1 to 1.5 inches deep, and do not keep the bed soggy.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Big leafy plants but few pods
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Big leafy plants but hardly any pods
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The plants grew large, dark, and leafy but set few pods, usually from too much nitrogen, or because the variety was a poor match for your latitude. As a legume, edamame fixes its own nitrogen, and extra fertilizer over-stimulates leaves and delays pod set; a soybean variety bred for a different latitude also flowers at the wrong time and yields poorly.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The plants grew big, dark, and leafy but made few pods, usually from too much nitrogen, or because the variety was wrong for your area. Edamame makes its own nitrogen, so extra fertilizer just pushes leaves and delays pods, and a variety bred for a different region flowers at the wrong time and makes few pods.
failure_diagnostics.cause: excess nitrogen or a mismatched variety
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Skip the nitrogen feeding: work in only a little balanced fertilizer or compost before planting, inoculate the seed with a soybean inoculant, and let the plant's own nitrogen fixation carry the crop. Choose a variety whose maturity is recommended for your latitude.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Skip the extra fertilizer: mix in just a little balanced fertilizer or compost before planting, coat the seed with a soybean inoculant, and let the plant make its own nitrogen. Pick a variety that is recommended for your area.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Flowers dropped or pods stayed flat
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Flowers fell off or pods did not fill
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The plants flowered but set few pods, or the pods stayed flat and empty, usually from drought stress or a spell of extreme heat during bloom and pod set. Edamame tolerates ordinary summer heat well, but sustained temperatures above roughly 95 to 100°F, or dry soil at flowering, cause the plant to abort blossoms and small pods.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The plants flowered but made few pods, or the pods stayed flat and empty, usually because the soil dried out or it got extremely hot while the plants were flowering. Edamame handles normal summer heat, but very hot spells above about 95 to 100°F, or dry soil at flowering, make it drop its flowers and small pods.
failure_diagnostics.cause: drought or extreme heat at flowering
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Keep moisture steady and ample from first flower through pod fill, and water deeply ahead of a heat wave. In the hottest regions, time the crop so flowering misses the peak of summer, sowing for a late-spring or a fall set rather than flowering in midsummer extremes.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep the water steady from the first flowers through pod-filling, and water deeply before a heat wave. In very hot areas, time the planting so the flowering misses the hottest part of summer, aiming for a late-spring or a fall crop instead.
