succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Edamame ripens all at once, so a single sowing gives one concentrated harvest rather than a long pick. To spread the supply, sow several small batches a week or two apart through the warm season, each maturing in turn, and stop about 90 days before your first fall frost so the last sowing finishes. In the hottest regions, skip the peak of summer and sow for spring and fall sets instead.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: A row of edamame ripens all at once and gives one big harvest, then it is done. To keep edamame coming, plant several small batches a week or two apart through the warm season instead of all at once. Stop about three months before your first fall frost so the last batch has time to finish. In very hot areas, skip the hottest weeks and plant for spring and fall.

3.zone_notes: In the coldest zone edamame is a single summer crop on a tight schedule: sow in late May once the soil has warmed, choosing an early short-season variety so the plants fill their pods before the mid-September frost, and harvest the whole crop in late summer.

4.zone_notes: Sow once the soil warms in mid-May for a late-summer harvest before the early-fall frost; choose an early variety in this short season and harvest the whole planting at once when the pods plump.

5.zone_notes: Sow from early May once the soil warms for a late-summer to early-fall harvest; the season is long enough for early to mid-season varieties, and a couple of staggered sowings spread the single harvests.

6.zone_notes: Sow from late April once the soil warms through June for harvests from midsummer into early fall; the season suits early and mid-season varieties, and staggered sowings give a run of single harvests.

7.zone_notes: The mildest cold zone has a long warm season: sow from early April once the soil warms through June, growing early to mid-season varieties, and stagger sowings for harvests from early summer into fall.
7.succession_continuous: Apr 1, Apr 15, Apr 29, May 13, May 27, Jun 10

northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Across the cold northern tier edamame is a warm-season summer crop, sown after the last frost once the soil has warmed to about 60 to 65°F and harvested in one concentrated picking as the pods plump in late summer to early fall. Match the variety to the season: the coldest zones need an early, short-season type that fills its pods before the September frost, while the milder zones suit mid-season varieties. Because each plant ripens at once, stagger several small sowings a week or two apart for a run of single harvests rather than one glut. Northern summers suit soybean well, so there is no midsummer heat gap here.
northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In cold regions, grow edamame as a summer crop. Plant after the last frost once the soil has warmed, and pick the whole crop at once in late summer when the pods are plump. In the coldest areas choose an early, fast variety so it finishes before the fall frost. Since the whole plant ripens together, plant several small batches a week or two apart to spread the harvest. Northern summers are good for edamame, so there is no hot-weather gap here.

8.zone_notes: On the Gulf and coastal plain edamame runs through the warm season: soybean is a southern heat crop, so sow from mid-March through midsummer and harvest from late summer into fall, staggering sowings for a run of single harvests. Unlike snow peas and snap beans, edamame is not stopped by the Gulf summer.
8.succession_continuous: Mar 15, Mar 29, Apr 12, Apr 26, May 10, May 24, Jun 7, Jun 21, Jul 5

9.zone_notes: In the warm coastal zone 9 the season is long: sow from early March through midsummer for harvests from late summer well into fall. Soybean thrives in the southern heat, so the summer is a growing season here, not a gap.
9.succession_continuous: Mar 1, Mar 15, Mar 29, Apr 12, Apr 26, May 10, May 24, Jun 7, Jun 21, Jul 5, Jul 19

se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: On the Gulf and southeastern coastal plain edamame is a warm-season crop grown right through the long hot summer. Soybean is the South's signature summer legume, so unlike snow peas or snap beans it is not driven out by the heat: sow from late winter or early spring through midsummer, stagger the sowings, and harvest each planting in one picking from late summer into fall. The main cautions are steady moisture and the humid-weather foliar diseases, not summer heat.
se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: On the Gulf coast and southern coastal plain, grow edamame right through the warm summer. Soybeans love the southern heat, so unlike peas and snap beans, edamame is not stopped by it. Plant from early spring through midsummer, stagger your plantings, and pick each one all at once from late summer into fall. Keep the water steady and watch for leaf diseases in humid weather.

8.zone_notes: In the interior valleys edamame is an irrigated warm-season crop: sow from April once the soil warms through June, and harvest from midsummer into fall. The hot dry summer is a growing season with steady irrigation, not a heat gap, though afternoon extremes still call for ample water at flowering.
8.succession_continuous: Apr 1, Apr 15, Apr 29, May 13, May 27, Jun 10

9.zone_notes: Sow from mid-March once the soil warms through June for harvests from midsummer into fall. With steady irrigation the hot valley summer carries the crop; keep moisture ample through flowering and pod fill.
9.succession_continuous: Mar 15, Mar 29, Apr 12, Apr 26, May 10, May 24, Jun 7, Jun 21

ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: In California's hot interior valleys edamame is an irrigated warm-season crop. With steady water the summer heat is a growing season rather than an exclusion, so sow from spring once the soil warms through early summer and harvest each planting in one picking from midsummer into fall. The levers here are ample irrigation through flowering and pod fill and a variety adapted to the valley's long warm season.
ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In California's hot interior valleys, grow edamame as a summer crop with regular watering. The heat is fine as long as you keep the water steady, so plant from spring through early summer and pick each planting all at once from midsummer into fall. Water well while the plants flower and fill their pods.

9.zone_notes: Cool, foggy coastal summers make edamame marginal here: it needs warmth to mature, so sow in late spring once the soil warms, choose an early short-season variety, and expect a slower crop and a later, single harvest than inland. This is a heat-limited spot, the opposite of the desert.
9.succession_continuous: May 1, May 15, May 29, Jun 12

10.zone_notes: The slightly warmer coastal zone 10 still runs cool in summer: sow from May through midsummer with an early variety and harvest from late summer into fall. Cool nights slow pod fill, so the crop is a marginal one best grown in the warmest, most sheltered spot.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: On California's cool, foggy north coast edamame is a marginal warm-season crop: as a soybean it wants real summer heat, and the cool maritime summers slow flowering and pod fill, so the crop runs late and yields less than inland. Sow in late spring once the soil warms, choose an early short-season variety, give it the warmest, most sheltered spot, and harvest the single crop from late summer into fall. This is a heat-limited setting, the opposite of the desert heat gap.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: On California's cool, foggy north coast, edamame is a tricky crop because soybeans really want summer warmth and the coast stays cool. Plant in late spring once the soil warms, pick an early, fast variety, and give it the warmest, most sheltered spot you have. Expect a slower, smaller crop, harvested all at once from late summer into fall.

9.zone_notes: The mild south coast has a long warm season: sow from mid-March once the soil warms through midsummer and harvest from late summer into fall, staggering sowings for a run of single harvests. Summer warmth suits edamame without the desert extremes.
9.succession_continuous: Mar 15, Mar 29, Apr 12, Apr 26, May 10, May 24, Jun 7, Jun 21, Jul 5

10.zone_notes: In the warmest south-coast zone edamame grows over a long warm season: sow from early March through midsummer for harvests from late summer into late fall, with staggered sowings spreading the single harvests.
10.succession_continuous: Mar 1, Mar 15, Mar 29, Apr 12, Apr 26, May 10, May 24, Jun 7, Jun 21, Jul 5, Jul 19

ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: On California's mild south coast edamame enjoys a long warm season without desert extremes: sow from early spring once the soil warms through midsummer and harvest each planting in one picking from late summer into late fall. Stagger several sowings to spread the single harvests, and keep moisture steady through flowering and pod fill.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: On California's mild south coast, edamame has a long, friendly warm season. Plant from early spring through midsummer and pick each planting all at once from late summer into late fall. Plant several small batches to spread out the harvests, and keep the water steady while the pods fill.

9.zone_notes: In the low desert valleys edamame is grown in the cool shoulders, not the furnace of summer: sow from February through April for a late-spring and early-summer harvest, leave the extreme midsummer out, then sow again in early fall for a late-fall crop.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion here, not a frost gap. Edamame is a warm-season soybean that takes ordinary summer heat in stride, but through this region's extreme midsummer, sustained daytime temperatures above roughly 95 to 100°F cause soybean flowers and young pods to abort, so a crop set in the peak heat fails to fill. A spring sowing is harvested before the worst heat and a fall sowing goes in as it eases, leaving the hottest weeks out of the planting calendar.

10.zone_notes: The hottest desert zone has the longest heat exclusion: sow from February through April for a May harvest before the extreme heat, skip the long furnace of June through August, and sow again in September for a late-fall and early-winter crop.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion here, not a frost gap. Edamame is a warm-season soybean that takes ordinary summer heat in stride, but through this region's extreme midsummer, sustained daytime temperatures above roughly 95 to 100°F cause soybean flowers and young pods to abort, so a crop set in the peak heat fails to fill. A spring sowing is harvested before the worst heat and a fall sowing goes in as it eases, leaving the hottest weeks out of the planting calendar.

ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: In California's desert valleys edamame is grown in the cool shoulders of the year, not the midsummer furnace. Sow in late winter through early spring for a late-spring and early-summer harvest, leave the extreme heat of mid to late summer out, when sustained temperatures above roughly 95 to 100°F abort soybean flowers and pods, and sow again in early fall for a late-fall crop. Each planting is harvested in one concentrated picking, and the summer gap is a true heat exclusion backed at each cell.
ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: In California's desert valleys, grow edamame in the cooler parts of the year, not the peak of summer. Plant in late winter through early spring for a late-spring harvest, skip the extreme midsummer heat, which makes the flowers and pods drop, and plant again in early fall for a late-fall crop. Each planting is picked all at once.

warm_arid.region_label: Warm Arid: Southern NM & West TX

8.zone_notes: In the warm arid high desert edamame is an irrigated summer crop: sow from April once the soil warms through mid-June and harvest from midsummer into early fall. Steady irrigation carries it through the hot, dry summer, but choose an adapted variety and water deeply at flowering, since the driest extremes can still stress pod set.
8.succession_continuous: Apr 1, Apr 15, Apr 29, May 13, May 27, Jun 10

warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: In the warm arid high desert of southern New Mexico and West Texas edamame is an irrigated warm-season crop. Sow from spring once the soil warms through early summer and harvest each planting in one picking from midsummer into early fall. Steady deep irrigation carries the crop through the hot, dry summer; the cautions are ample water at flowering and a variety adapted to the region.
warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: In the warm, dry high desert of southern New Mexico and West Texas, grow edamame as an irrigated summer crop. Plant from spring through early summer and pick each planting all at once from midsummer into early fall. Water deeply and steadily through the hot, dry summer, especially while the plants are flowering and filling pods.

9.zone_notes: In the low desert edamame is a cool-shoulder crop: sow in February and March for a late-spring harvest before the extreme heat, leave the furnace of June through August out entirely, when desert temperatures well above 100°F abort soybean flowers and pods, and sow again in September for a late-fall and early-winter crop.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion here, not a frost gap. Edamame is a warm-season soybean that takes ordinary summer heat in stride, but through this region's extreme midsummer, sustained daytime temperatures above roughly 95 to 100°F cause soybean flowers and young pods to abort, so a crop set in the peak heat fails to fill. A spring sowing is harvested before the worst heat and a fall sowing goes in as it eases, leaving the hottest weeks out of the planting calendar.

low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: In Arizona's low desert edamame is grown only in the cool shoulders of the year. Sow in late winter for a late-spring harvest before the extreme heat, leave the long furnace of June through August out entirely, when desert temperatures well above 100°F abort soybean flowers and pods, and sow again in early fall for a late-fall and early-winter crop. Each planting is harvested in one picking, and the long summer gap is a true heat exclusion backed at the cell.
low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: In Arizona's low desert, grow edamame only in the cooler parts of the year. Plant in late winter for a late-spring harvest before the extreme heat, skip the brutal heat of June through August entirely, and plant again in early fall for a late-fall crop. Each planting is picked all at once.

10.zone_notes: On the Florida peninsula edamame is a spring and fall crop: sow February through April for a late-spring harvest, leave the hot, wet, disease-heavy midsummer out, then sow in early fall for a late-fall and early-winter crop. Choose a variety adapted to the short days and warmth of the peninsula.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion here, not a frost gap. Edamame tolerates ordinary heat, but the Florida peninsula's hot, humid, wet summer pushes daytime temperatures and night temperatures high enough to abort soybean flowers and young pods and to drive heavy foliar disease, so a midsummer crop fails to fill. Edamame is grown as a spring and fall crop here and the hottest, wettest weeks are left out of the planting calendar.

11.zone_notes: In the frost-free tropical south edamame is grown through the cool dry season, sown fall into early spring for a late-spring harvest; the hot, wet summer is left out, when heat and disease shut the crop down. This is a marginal, low-confidence fit for the warm lowlands, where the short cool window and heat-adapted variety choice both matter.
11.succession_continuous: Sep 1, Sep 22, Oct 13, Nov 3, Nov 24, Dec 15, Jan 5, Feb 1, Mar 1

fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: On the Florida peninsula edamame is a cool-season crop in the gardener's sense: sown in the spring and fall shoulders and kept out of the hot, wet, disease-heavy summer. In the central peninsula (zone 10) sow February through April and again in early fall, with a backed heat exclusion through midsummer; in the frost-free tropical south (zone 11) it is grown through the cool dry season fall into spring and is a marginal, low-confidence fit. Match the variety to the peninsula's short days and warmth.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: On the Florida peninsula, grow edamame in spring and fall and keep it out of the hot, wet summer. In the central peninsula plant February through April and again in early fall. In the frost-free far south, grow it through the cool dry season from fall into spring; it is a marginal crop there. Pick a variety suited to Florida's warmth and short days.

11.zone_notes: In tropical Hawaii edamame is grown in the warm season, sown spring into early summer for a summer-into-fall harvest, with the cooler, wetter winter months left out. Warm lowland heat and humidity make this a marginal, low-confidence fit best grown at elevation or in the drier, cooler months; variety choice for the tropics matters.
11.succession_continuous: Feb 1, Feb 22, Mar 15, Apr 5, Apr 26, May 17, Jun 7

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: In tropical Hawaii edamame is a warm-season crop sown from late winter into early summer for a summer-into-fall harvest, with the cooler, wetter winter months left out. The warm, humid lowlands make this a marginal, low-confidence fit, better at elevation or in the drier, cooler months; the Hawaii window is modeled on the older CTAHR planting bulletin and a tropics-adapted variety is important.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In tropical Hawaii, grow edamame in the warm season, planting from late winter into early summer for a summer-into-fall harvest, and skip the cooler, wetter winter months. It is a marginal crop in the warm lowlands, better grown at elevation or in the cooler, drier months. Choose a variety suited to the tropics.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: edamame_author_fresh_pilot (Claude Code lane authoring, 2026-06-29). Authored from the edamame shell, modeled STRUCTURALLY on the certified green-beans-bush warm-season legume template (warm_season_fruiting / frost_anchored) with the snow_peas gate-clean field shapes. All soybean/edamame biology re-derived from live T1 extension sources (MU Extension edamame, Iowa State All About Beans + soybean diseases, UMN growing beans + soybean pest management, Virginia Tech/VCE SPES-455 edamame, Rutgers edamame). DRAFT for daily biology-fidelity review, NOT certified: launch flags false. Key edamame-vs-green-beans refits: vegetable soybean (Glycine max) eaten as immature green pods boiled in the pod; LONGER days_to_maturity 75-100 (mid 85) vs snap beans 50-60; SINGLE concentrated harvest at the R6 green stage (whole plant ripens together) with a NARROW 4-10 day window, harvest_urgency high; SOYBEAN-specific Bradyrhizobium japonicum inoculant, NOT the general bean/pea inoculant; pH 6.0-6.8; spacing 2-4 in; warm soil >=60-65F to plant; pests bean leaf beetle / stink bug / soybean aphid / Japanese beetle / spider mite; diseases white mold / bacterial blight / downy mildew / soybean cyst nematode (a key rotation driver). PHOTOPERIOD: soybean is short-day, so maturity-group/variety must match latitude; handled as VARIETY-SELECTION guidance (description + varieties note + open_finding), gating_factors ABSENT (see flag). successions_realized is CC-derived. See edamame_NOTES.md.

open_findings.summary: Soybean IS photoperiod-sensitive (a short-day plant): the maturity group / variety must match the grower's latitude or the crop flowers too early or too late and yields poorly. This is handled as VARIETY-SELECTION GUIDANCE (in description, varieties.note, growth_stages.flowering, and region zone_notes), NOT as a calendar/zone gate, and gating_factors is ABSENT.
open_findings.basis: Decision parallels onion's day-length handling but deliberately does NOT wire onion's A9 machinery: (1) the kickoff gate contract specifies gating_factors absent; (2) onion's photoperiod gate uses a 3-value enum (short_day/intermediate/long_day) mapped per-variety and per-cell, which does not fit soybean's continuous maturity-group system (MG 000-IX by latitude band); (3) the maturity group selects which VARIETY matures correctly, not which SEASON to plant, so edamame stays a warm-season frost_anchored crop with the photoperiod note as variety guidance. gating_factors absent keeps A9 a correct no-op; whole_crop_gate PASS confirms. Flagged for the daily review to confirm the call.

open_findings.summary: archetype set to warm_season_fruiting (matching the green-beans-bush template the task specified), with calendar_basis frost_anchored. Edamame is a warm-season legume planted after frost into warm soil, so the warm-season calendar (winter cold_pause, spring/summer plant, summer/fall harvest) is correct.
open_findings.basis: Matches the certified green-beans-bush anchor (warm_season_fruiting / frost_anchored). archetype drives only the numeric_sanity spacing bound (annual <=72in, correct). whole_crop_gate PASS confirms.

open_findings.summary: Edamame requires the SOYBEAN-specific rhizobium Bradyrhizobium japonicum, not the general garden bean/pea inoculant. This is a real refit from the green-beans/snow-peas template and is stated in fertilizer, start_method, and the germination/vegetative tips.
open_findings.basis: Sourced to Virginia Tech/VCE SPES-455 ('Edamame seeds can be inoculated with Bradyrhizobium japonicum strains, which are recommended for soybean inoculation') and corroborated by Iowa State and MU (inoculate the seed). The soybean-specific strain is well established soybean agronomy.

open_findings.summary: days_to_maturity [75, 100] (mid 85), spacing_inches [2, 4], germination_temp_f [60, 85], and pH preferred [6.0, 6.8] / tolerated [5.8, 7.0] were chosen from a spread of T1 figures: DTM Iowa State 80-100, VT 'VT Sweet' 125-135 (a long-season type), common garden varieties 75-90; spacing MU 4 in, Rutgers and VT 2-4 in; soil temp to plant MU >=60F, VT/Iowa State 65F; pH Rutgers 6.0-6.5.
open_findings.basis: Every endpoint sits within at least one cited T1 source's range; pH prose leads with 6.0 to 6.8 to satisfy the A34 cross-consistency check against preferred_range. germination_temp_f synthesizes the plant-when-soil>=60-65F guidance with soybean's warm optimum; the band is modeled.

open_findings.summary: Edamame is treated as MORE heat-tolerant than the snap-bean/snow-pea templates: most regions grow through summer (continuous, no heat_pause), and a backed midsummer heat_pause is placed ONLY in the extreme desert (ca_desert, low_desert_az) and central Florida (fl_peninsula z10), with a tropical summer season_over in fl z11 and a cool/wet-season season_over in Hawaii. Soybean is the US summer legume crop, so se_gulf and ca_interior run through summer where snap beans and peas would pause.
open_findings.basis: Soybean tolerates ordinary summer heat (it is the dominant Midwest/South summer row crop); abortion sets in only at sustained extremes above ~95-100F, which is why the heat_pause is reserved for the desert/tropical extremes. Each heat_pause carries months + a soybean-physiology basis_seasoned + >=1 T1 source with a live URL (A28 PASS). Flagged for the biology review to confirm the regional split.

open_findings.summary: Per-region planting windows are MODELED on the warm-season regional planting calendars (the green-beans frost-date anchors) and refit for edamame's 75-100 day maturity and single harvest; the harvest months are DERIVED (plant window + ~85 day maturity, frost-bounded). The directly-read edamame sources (MU, Iowa State, UMN, VT, Rutgers) anchor the biology and the southern/Midwest timing; the regional-calendar ids are catalogued T1 reused at the publisher/section level.
open_findings.basis: Conservative monthly rounding; frost dates byte-match the green-beans warm-season anchors. The daily review's source-truth sample is the backstop for the exact per-region harvest boundaries.

open_findings.summary: Several pest/disease anchors are soybean-production or general-bean pages at the publisher level rather than edamame-home-garden-specific: bean leaf beetle (mu_ext G7150), stink bug / soybean aphid / SCN (umn_ext soybean pest management, iastate_ext soybean diseases index). The pathology is shared (edamame IS soybean), and white mold / bacterial blight / spider mite / aphid overlap the green-beans legume set.
open_findings.basis: Edamame is Glycine max, so the soybean pest/disease literature applies directly; the roster (bean leaf beetle, stink bug, soybean aphid, Japanese beetle, spider mite; white mold, bacterial blight, downy mildew, soybean cyst nematode) is the standard soybean set. Flagged for the review to confirm the home-garden framing.

open_findings.summary: fl_peninsula z11 and hawaii_tropical z11 are MARGINAL, low-confidence fits for edamame in the warm tropical lowlands; the windows are honest but modeled and stated as such in the zone_notes and region_notes. Hawaii is modeled on the older CTAHR B-91 planting bulletin, an unreadable scanned PDF.
open_findings.basis: Stated transparently to the grower; better at elevation or in the cooler, drier months. Low-confidence, non-blocking.

open_findings.summary: successions_realized was NOT hand-authored: the CC deriver fills it per cell and reconciles succession_policy.successions and max_successions_per_season to the crop-max. succession_continuous (warm regions) and succession_spring/succession_fall (split desert/FL cells) sow-date lists were authored so the deriver counts the staggered single-harvest sowings correctly. Edamame is ~one concentrated crop per sowing; succession here means staggered sowings, not a continuous pick.
