crops.description_seasoned: Edamame (Glycine max) is a warm-season vegetable soybean grown for its plump, immature green pods, boiled or steamed in the pod and popped out to eat. Like snap beans it is a frost-tender bush legume direct-sown after the last frost into warm soil, but it takes longer to mature (about 75 to 100 days) and, unlike beans, the whole plant ripens together: the crop comes ready in one concentrated harvest at the plump green R6 stage, over a narrow window of only a few days before the beans turn starchy. Soybean is a short-day plant, so the variety's maturity group must match your latitude. As a legume it fixes much of its own nitrogen, but only with the soybean-specific inoculant Bradyrhizobium japonicum, not the general bean and pea kind. Edamame must be cooked before eating; raw soybeans are not eaten.
crops.description_beginner: Edamame is a soybean you eat as plump green pods, boiled or steamed in the pod and popped straight into your mouth. It grows like a bush bean: you plant the seeds in the garden after the last frost once the soil is warm, and the sturdy plants need no trellis. But edamame takes longer than green beans, about 75 to 100 days, and the big difference is that the whole plant ripens at once. Instead of picking for weeks, you harvest the whole plant in one go when the pods are plump and green, and the best window is only a few days. Soybeans flower by day length, so pick a variety suited to your area, and use a soybean inoculant on the seed, not the regular bean kind. Always cook edamame before eating it.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Harvest edamame at the R6 stage, when the pods are plump and bright green with the beans filling about 80 to 90 percent of the pod and nearly touching inside, still tender and sweet rather than hard or yellowing. Because the whole plant ripens together, harvest it all in one or two passes, pulling or cutting the plant and stripping the pods. The prime window is short, only about four to ten days, so check daily as the pods plump and cook or freeze the same day.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Edamame is ready when the pods are plump and bright green and the beans nearly touch inside but are still tender, before they get hard or turn yellow. The whole plant ripens at the same time, so harvest it all at once: pull up the plant and strip off the pods. The best window is only about four to ten days, so check every day as the pods fill and cook or freeze them the same day.

crops.name: Parsley

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Parsley likes loose, fertile soil with plenty of compost worked in, kept evenly moist but never soggy. It is forgiving, but rich, steady soil keeps the leaves tender and green and feeds a plant you cut from all season. It has a deeper root than most salad greens, so loosen the bed well; hard, compacted, or waterlogged ground holds it back and invites root rot.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Parsley grows in most soils but does best in a deep, fertile, well-drained loam or sandy loam high in organic matter, kept evenly moist. The University of Minnesota recommends a soil rich in organic matter and steady moisture for the long cut-and-come-again season. Work compost into the top several inches before sowing to feed the plant through the months you harvest from it, and loosen the bed deeply because parsley sends down a slender taproot. It dislikes compacted or waterlogged ground, which checks growth and invites crown and root rot.

ph.note_beginner: Parsley grows best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, about 6.0 to 7.0. Most garden soil is fine, and a simple soil test tells you where you stand.
ph.note_seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0, slightly acidic to neutral, the range the University of Minnesota lists as best for parsley; it still does fine across roughly 5.5 to 7.5. Parsley is not a pH-sensitive plant, so in most gardens no adjustment is needed beyond a soil-test baseline.

fertilizer.timing: compost worked in before sowing, then a light feeding once or twice through the long harvest season
fertilizer.example_product: 5-10-5 or a balanced vegetable fertilizer, or fish emulsion for a quick boost
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Parsley is a light to moderate feeder grown for steady leafy growth over a long season. The University of Minnesota suggests a 5-10-5 fertilizer at about 3 ounces per 10 feet of row, once or twice during the season, on top of compost worked in before planting. Because you cut from the same plants for months, a light midseason side-dress of nitrogen keeps fresh green leaves coming; in containers a dilute liquid feed every 3 to 4 weeks replaces what frequent watering leaches out. Avoid heavy nitrogen, which draws aphids and softens the flavor.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Parsley does not need much feeding. Mix some compost or a little balanced fertilizer into the soil before planting, then give it a light feeding once or twice over the season, since you cut from the same plants for a long time. If you grow it in a pot, feed lightly with a diluted liquid fertilizer every few weeks because watering washes nutrients out.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time to side-dress your parsley with a light feeding.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Time to give your parsley a light feeding.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: Moderate, balanced feeding for steady leaf growth: a 5-10-5 or balanced vegetable fertilizer worked in before sowing, then a light side-dress once or twice through the season. Go easy on nitrogen, which softens flavor and draws aphids on a crop eaten fresh.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer such as 5-10-5 worked into the soil before planting, then feed lightly once or twice during the season.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: About 3 ounces of 5-10-5 per 10 feet of row, once or twice during the season; a compost-rich bed often needs no more than a single light midseason feeding.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Follow the label rate for a balanced vegetable fertilizer, one light feeding partway through the season; in a pot, a diluted liquid feed every 3 to 4 weeks.

pests.name: Parsleyworm (black swallowtail caterpillar)
pests.symptoms_beginner: Plump green caterpillars banded with black and dotted yellow-orange, chewing the leaves and stems, sometimes stripping a stalk. They are the larvae of the black swallowtail butterfly, and many gardeners leave them be.
pests.cause_beginner: Big green-and-black striped caterpillars that eat the leaves. They turn into beautiful black swallowtail butterflies, so they are usually welcome guests rather than a real problem.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: If you want every leaf, just pick the caterpillars off by hand and move them to a spare plant. They are easy to see and there are rarely many. Planting a little extra parsley lets you share with the butterflies.
pests.prevention_beginner: Pick them off by hand, grow a few extra plants to share, and enjoy the butterflies they become.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Larvae of the black swallowtail (Papilio polyxenes) feeding on the foliage, banded green and black with yellow spots; on parsley they are seldom numerous enough to do real damage, and parsley is one of their host plants, so most growers tolerate or relocate them rather than spray.
pests.cause_seasoned: The caterpillar stage of the black swallowtail butterfly, which lays eggs on parsley and other carrot-family plants; populations on a home planting are normally small.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick where leaf loss matters and relocate the larvae to a sacrificial plant; Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) controls them if needed, but on parsley they rarely warrant it. Many gardeners deliberately grow extra parsley as a swallowtail host.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Scout occasionally and hand-pick if leaf loss matters; tolerate the small numbers a home planting usually sees, and plant extra parsley as a host plant for the butterflies.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_beginner: Clusters of tiny soft green or gray insects on new growth and the undersides of leaves, sometimes with curled, sticky foliage.
pests.cause_beginner: Aphids are small sap-sucking insects that breed fast, especially on soft growth from too much fertilizer. They can spread plant viruses.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water, or use insecticidal soap or neem oil on the leaf undersides, repeating every few days. Rinse picked leaves well before use.
pests.prevention_beginner: Welcome helpful insects like ladybugs and lacewings, go easy on nitrogen, and check new growth often.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Colonies of aphids on growing tips and leaf undersides, the most common parsley pest; honeydew and the lodged insects contaminate a crop eaten fresh, and aphids can vector viruses. Parsley's lacy foliage hides them, so scout closely.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several aphid species feed on parsley; they reproduce rapidly and favor the soft growth that excess nitrogen produces.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Dislodge colonies with a strong water jet or spray insecticidal soap or neem, covering leaf undersides; repeat every few days and conserve lady beetles, lacewings, and parasitoid wasps, which the parsley umbels attract when allowed to flower.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Scout growing tips early, avoid overfeeding nitrogen, and conserve natural enemies; letting a second-year plant flower draws in aphid predators.

pests.name: Carrot rust fly and carrot weevil
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tunnels and rusty-brown trails in the roots and lower stems, stunted or off-color plants, and grubs at the crown. These carrot-family root pests hit parsley too.
pests.cause_beginner: Small root maggots from carrot-family pests that tunnel into the parsley root and crown, leaving rusty trails and weak plants.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover the bed with floating row cover to keep the flies off, rotate parsley away from where carrots or parsley grew, and clean up crop debris in fall.
pests.prevention_beginner: Use a row cover, move parsley to a fresh spot each year, and clear away old plants in fall.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Larvae of the carrot rust fly (Psila rosae) and the carrot weevil mining the taproot and crown of parsley, a carrot-family host; damage shows as rust-colored tunneling, stunting, and secondary rot, worst where Apiaceae are grown in the same ground year after year.
pests.cause_seasoned: The carrot rust fly and carrot weevil lay eggs near carrot-family plants; their larvae bore into the roots and crowns. They build up where carrots, parsley, and their relatives repeat in the same bed.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Exclude the adults with floating row cover from emergence, rotate out of Apiaceae ground on a multi-year cycle, delay sowing past the first fly generation where it is severe, and remove crop residue that harbors overwintering stages.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Manage by exclusion (row cover) and rotation: keep parsley out of recent carrot-family ground, time sowings around the fly's generations, and sanitize residue.

diseases.name: Septoria leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small tan to brown spots with darker edges scattered across the leaves, sometimes with tiny dark specks in the centers, worst in wet weather. Heavily spotted leaves are not good to eat.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungal leaf-spot disease, the most common one on parsley, that spreads through wet leaves and splashing water and can come in on the seed.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove and destroy spotted leaves, avoid wetting the foliage, improve airflow, and start with clean seed. Pick and use the clean leaves promptly.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Use clean seed, water at the soil line rather than over the leaves, space plants for airflow, and clear infected debris.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Numerous small circular tan-to-brown leaf lesions, often with dark pycnidia in the centers, the most commonly reported parsley disease; it spreads in cool, wet, splashy conditions and can arrive on infected seed, and on a leaf crop even moderate spotting ruins the cutting.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Septoria petroselini, a seed-borne and splash-spread fungus favored by cool, wet weather and overhead watering.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Use clean or treated seed, water at the soil line, space for airflow, rotate away from parsley and its relatives, and remove infected debris; the home garden has no reliable spray cure once it is established.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant clean seed, switch to drip or soil-line watering, widen spacing, rotate, and remove crop debris that carries the fungus over.

diseases.name: Crown and root rot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Wilting, yellowing plants whose crown or roots have turned brown, soft, and mushy, usually in wet, poorly drained soil. Affected plants collapse and do not recover.
diseases.cause_beginner: Soil fungi rot the parsley root and crown when the soil stays too wet, especially over a soggy winter.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure for a rotting plant, so remove it. Improve drainage, plant in raised or loosened beds, and do not overwater, especially in winter.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant in well-drained soil, do not overwater, and pull any plant whose crown has gone soft and brown.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Soilborne crown and root rots (Pythium, Phytophthora, Rhizoctonia, and related fungi) attacking parsley's taproot and crown in saturated, poorly drained ground; symptoms are wilting, stunting, and a browned, decayed crown, often on plants held over a wet winter.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Soilborne water-mold and fungal rots (Pythium, Phytophthora, Rhizoctonia) favored by waterlogged, poorly drained soil and overwatering.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected plants; manage by prevention: well-drained or raised beds, loosened soil for the taproot, moderate winter watering, and rotation out of ground where Apiaceae rotted before.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Site in well-drained, loosened soil, avoid waterlogging (especially overwinter), and rotate away from beds with a rot history.

diseases.name: Damping-off and seedling rot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Seeds that never come up, or seedlings that flop over at the soil line with a pinched, rotted stem and then die. It strikes in cold, wet soil.
diseases.cause_beginner: Soil fungi attack the seeds and tiny seedlings, especially when the soil is cold and soggy and the slow-sprouting parsley seed sits a long time before emerging.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure for an affected seedling, so focus on prevention: pull and discard collapsed seedlings.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Do not sow into cold, soggy soil, plant shallowly in well-drained ground, do not overwater, and soak the seed first so it comes up faster.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Poor stands from seed and pre- or post-emergence collapse of seedlings with water-soaked, pinched stems at the soil line, worst in cold, wet, poorly drained soil where parsley's slow germination leaves seed sitting for weeks.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Soilborne Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Fusarium fungi attack germinating seed and seedlings; cold, saturated soil that prolongs parsley's already slow germination favors them.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No rescue once seedlings collapse; manage by prevention and remove affected plants.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Sow shallowly into well-drained soil under conditions that favor reasonably quick emergence, avoid overwatering, and soak the dry seed to shorten the vulnerable slow-germination window.

watering.frequency_seasoned: About 1 inch of water per week, kept even; parsley has a taproot and takes moderate dry spells better than shallow greens, but steady moisture keeps the leaves tender and green over the long season.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water deeply about once a week so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly 1 inch a week.
watering.amount_seasoned: Roughly 1 inch per week, more in hot, dry spells; the University of Minnesota advises watering deeply at least once a week. Mulch helps hold even moisture for a crop you cut from for months.
watering.amount_beginner: Aim for about 1 inch of water a week, a bit more when it is hot and dry.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose; keeping the lacy foliage dry checks Septoria leaf spot and other leaf diseases on a crop eaten fresh.
watering.method_beginner: Water at the base of the plants rather than over the leaves, which helps prevent leaf diseases.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, damping-off in seedlings, and crown or root rot in constantly wet, poorly drained ground, especially over winter.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Lower leaves yellow, seedlings rot at the base, and plants get mushy at the crown in soggy soil.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting, slowed growth, and tougher, sharper-tasting leaves; sustained drought stress also coarsens the foliage, though parsley recovers from short dry spells better than salad greens.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Wilting leaves that taste tougher and sharper, and slowed growth when the soil dries out.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Even moisture keeps parsley growing tender and green through a long season; the deeper taproot lets it ride out short dry spells, but prolonged drought toughens the leaves.
watering.method_note_beginner: Keep the water fairly steady so the leaves stay tender and green; parsley handles a short dry spell, but long droughts make it tough.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Steady moisture matters most through the long, slow germination, which can take 2 to 5 weeks, and through establishment; once the taproot is down the plant is more forgiving.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Keep the soil moist while the seeds are sprouting, which takes a few weeks, and while the young plants get going.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Parsley can be direct-sown or started indoors. Its seed germinates slowly and erratically, often 2 to 5 weeks, and germinates poorly in cold soil, so soaking the dry seed in warm water for up to 24 hours before sowing speeds and evens emergence. Direct-sow about 0.25 inch deep as soon as the soil can be worked in spring, since parsley tolerates frost. To get a head start, sow indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost and transplant out after hardening off; parsley moves better when young, before the taproot is long, so transplant on the early side. Keep the seedbed evenly moist through the long germination.
start_method.notes_beginner: You can plant parsley straight in the garden or start it indoors. The seeds are slow, often taking 2 to 5 weeks, so soak them in warm water for up to a day before planting and keep the soil moist the whole time. Sow about a quarter inch deep as soon as the soil can be worked in spring, since parsley handles frost. For an earlier start, sow indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost and move the young plants outside after hardening them off, while they are still small.

drainage.saucer_practice: Empty the saucer after watering so the taproot never sits in water, which invites crown and root rot.

soil_mix.type_beginner: A good-quality potting mix, not garden soil.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in some compost for steady nutrients.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: A light, well-drained potting mix high in organic matter, deep enough for parsley's taproot.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend in compost and a little balanced starter fertilizer; parsley is a moderate feeder over a long season.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out faster than the ground, so check every day or two in warm weather and keep the mix evenly moist.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Feed lightly with a diluted liquid fertilizer every few weeks, since watering washes nutrients out of pots.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Parsley is hardy and a pot of it can keep going well into fall and through a mild winter in a sheltered, sunny spot, since it takes frost. In cold areas, move the pot against the house or into a cold frame, or cover it during hard freezes. Remember parsley is a biennial: a plant carried through winter will send up a flower stalk and turn bitter in spring, so start fresh plants each year for the best leaves.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Parsley is a frost-hardy biennial, so a container can hold through fall and overwinter in mild zones in a sheltered spot, giving fresh leaves late and early. The limited root volume freezes harder than open ground, so in cold zones sink the pot, move it to a cold frame or unheated structure, or cover it during hard freezes. Note that an overwintered plant bolts in its second spring as the leaves coarsen, so treat it as a short early-spring bonus and sow fresh plants for the main crop.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Parsley is an easy, long-lasting container herb. Use a pot at least 10 inches deep to fit its root, keep it watered, and snip the outer stems so it keeps regrowing. It does well on a sunny windowsill or step and handles cool weather, so a pot can carry on long after summer crops are done.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Parsley grows well in a container at least 10 inches deep to fit its taproot, harvested cut-and-come-again from the outer stems. Keep moisture even, since pots dry fast, and feed lightly through the long season. A pot is the easiest way to keep parsley by the kitchen door and to move a frost-hardy plant into shelter as the weather turns, extending the leaf supply into late fall and, in mild zones, winter.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry faster than beds; check moisture every day or two in warmth and water deeply before the mix dries out.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Container parsley needs a light but regular feed, a dilute liquid fertilizer every 3 to 4 weeks, because frequent watering leaches nutrients from the limited mix.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering container suits parsley well, since it smooths out the steady moisture that keeps the leaves tender and green over a long harvest.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match because it keeps the water steady, which keeps parsley tender and productive.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: Parsley has a slender taproot, so give it depth: a container at least 10 inches deep suits it better than a shallow tray, while width adds room for several plants to cut from.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Parsley has a deeper root than most herbs, so use a pot at least 10 inches deep. Extra width lets you grow more plants to cut from.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Other Apiaceae: carrot, parsley itself, dill, fennel, celery, parsnip, and cilantro. They share carrot-family pests and diseases (the carrot rust fly and carrot weevil, leafhopper-vectored aster yellows, Septoria, and soilborne crown rots), so following one with another concentrates that pressure.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Other carrot-family plants like carrots, parsley, dill, fennel, and celery, because they share the same pests and diseases.
rotation.good_after: Legumes (peas, beans), brassicas (cabbage family), alliums (onion, garlic), or nightshades such as tomatoes.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate parsley and its carrot-family relatives so they do not return to the same ground for about 3 years. The Apiaceae share the carrot rust fly and carrot weevil, aster yellows, Septoria leaf spot, and soilborne crown and root rots, which build up where the family repeats. Follow parsley with legumes, brassicas, alliums, or nightshades. Because parsley is biennial and self-sows from second-year plants left to flower, volunteers can blur a rotation, so pull seedlings that come up out of place.
rotation.note_beginner: Try not to grow parsley or other carrot-family plants (carrots, parsley, dill, fennel, celery) in the same spot more than about once every 3 years, since they share pests and diseases. Plant parsley after peas, beans, cabbage, onions, or tomatoes instead. Parsley left to flower in its second year can drop seed, so pull up stray seedlings where you do not want them.

bolting.triggers: second-year flowering after overwintering and cold (vernalization), not first-year summer heat
bolting.prevention_seasoned: Unlike fast cool-season herbs, parsley does NOT bolt from first-year summer heat; it is a biennial that flowers in its SECOND year, triggered by the cold of winter (vernalization). The practical consequence is the opposite of cilantro: a first-year plant gives leaves right through summer, but an overwintered plant sends up a flower stalk in its second spring and the leaves coarsen and turn bitter. There is no preventing the second-year bolt, so the standard practice is to grow parsley fresh each year for the best leaves, enjoy a short early-spring cutting from an overwintered plant, then let it flower (the umbels feed pollinators and host swallowtails) or pull it. Flat-leaf types tend to overwinter and hold a little better than curly types.
bolting.prevention_beginner: Good news: parsley does not bolt in hot weather like cilantro does. It is a biennial, which means it grows leaves the first year and only sends up a flower stalk in its second spring, after a winter, when the leaves turn bitter. You cannot stop that second-year flowering, so the simple plan is to plant fresh parsley each year for the best leaves. Take a few early leaves from an overwintered plant, then let it bloom for the bees and butterflies or pull it out.
bolting.note_seasoned: Bolting in parsley is a biennial life-cycle event, not a heat response: the plant banks energy in a taproot the first year, overwinters, and flowers the second spring after vernalization. This is the defining contrast with cilantro, which bolts within weeks of warm weather. So summer heat does not end the parsley leaf crop, winter does (indirectly), by setting up the second-year bloom. The white umbel flowers are excellent insectary plants and a black swallowtail host, and second-year plants self-sow readily, so a few are worth leaving for pollinators even as you start fresh plants for leaves.
bolting.note_beginner: Parsley flowers on a two-year cycle: leaves the first year, then a tall flower stalk the second spring after it has been through a winter. That is normal, not a mistake, and it is very different from cilantro, which flowers fast in summer heat. The flowers are great for bees and are food for black swallowtail caterpillars. Grow new parsley each year for the best leaves, and let a second-year plant bloom if you want to feed the pollinators.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Fresh parsley wilts within a day at room temperature, so refrigerate promptly after cutting; standing the cut stems in a glass of water on the counter holds them a few days, like cut flowers.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Do not leave cut parsley out on the counter, where it wilts; either chill it or stand the stems in a glass of water like a little bouquet.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerate fresh parsley unwashed in a loose or perforated bag, or stems standing in a little water under a loose bag, in the crisper; it holds 1 to 2 weeks, longer than most cut herbs. Wash only at use, since trapped moisture speeds breakdown.
storage.fridge_beginner: Store fresh parsley unwashed in a loose bag in the fridge, where it keeps 1 to 2 weeks. Wash it only when you are ready to use it.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Parsley loses crispness frozen for raw use but freezes well chopped into ice-cube trays with water or oil, or blended into sauces, holding its flavor for cooking. Drying is the weakest option: dried parsley loses much of its flavor, so freezing is preferred for preserving.
storage.freezer_beginner: Parsley does not freeze well for salads, but you can chop it into an ice-cube tray with a little water or oil and freeze that for cooking. Drying works but loses a lot of flavor, so freezing is usually better.
storage.notes_seasoned: Parsley is best fresh from the garden and, because the plant keeps producing, the easiest storage is simply to cut it as needed. Cut parsley keeps 1 to 2 weeks refrigerated, longer than most herbs. For longer keeping, freeze it (chopped in cubes or in sauces) rather than drying, which sacrifices most of the flavor; the University of Minnesota notes much flavor is lost in drying or freezing, so use preserved parsley within a year.
storage.notes_beginner: The best way to store parsley is to leave it growing and cut what you need. Picked parsley keeps 1 to 2 weeks in the fridge. To save extra, freeze it chopped into ice-cube trays rather than drying it, since drying loses most of the flavor.

recommended.name: Italian Flat Leaf
recommended.note: The standard flat-leaf (Italian) parsley: flat, deeply cut, dark green leaves with a stronger, sweeter flavor than curly types, and taller, more open plants that many cooks prefer. Tends to take heat and overwinter a touch better than curly parsley.

recommended.name: Giant of Italy
recommended.note: A large, vigorous flat-leaf type with big, flavorful leaves on tall stems, up to 2 to 3 feet; high-yielding for cutting all season and a favorite for cooking.

recommended.name: Forest Green
recommended.note: A productive curly (French) parsley with tightly curled, dark green leaves on compact plants; classic garnish parsley, holds well, and a dependable cut-and-come-again type.

recommended.name: Moss Curled / Triple Curled
recommended.note: Densely curled, frilly dark green parsley grown for garnish and edging; mild flavor, attractive in beds and pots. Curly types are slightly hardier-looking but flat-leaf has more flavor.

recommended.name: Hamburg (root parsley)
recommended.note: An unusual type grown for its thick, parsnip-like white root as well as its flat leaves; the root is used like a vegetable in soups and stews. Needs the deepest, loosest soil and the longest season.

varieties.note_seasoned: Choose by use. Flat-leaf (Italian) parsley, including Italian Flat Leaf and Giant of Italy, has the strongest, sweetest flavor, taller open plants, and slightly better heat and overwintering tolerance, and is the cook's choice. Curly (French) parsley, such as Forest Green and the Moss Curled and Triple Curled strains, gives the dense, frilly leaves used for garnish and edging, with a milder flavor. Hamburg or root parsley is a distinct type grown for an edible parsnip-like root as well as leaves and wants deep, loose soil. All are grown the same way; variety matters less than steady moisture and fresh annual sowing, since any parsley bolts in its second year.
varieties.note_beginner: Pick the type for how you cook. Flat-leaf (Italian) parsley like Italian Flat Leaf or Giant of Italy has the most flavor and is best for cooking. Curly parsley like Forest Green or Moss Curled is the frilly kind used for garnish and looks nice in pots. There is also Hamburg or root parsley, grown for an edible root. They all grow the same way, so just keep the soil moist and plant fresh each year.

companions.note_beginner: Parsley is small, leafy, and easygoing, and its biggest garden gift comes in its second year: if you let it flower, the blooms pull in hoverflies, lady beetles, and tiny parasitic wasps that hunt aphids on nearby crops, and they feed black swallowtail butterflies. It interplants well with tomatoes and peppers, with asparagus, and with brassicas and onions. Keep it away from other carrot-family plants like carrots and celery, which share its pests, and from fennel, a poor herb neighbor.
companions.note_seasoned: Much of parsley's companion value is real but indirect: a second-year plant allowed to flower is a strong insectary umbel, recruiting hoverflies, lady beetles, lacewings, and parasitoid wasps that suppress aphids on neighboring crops, and it hosts the black swallowtail. Practically it interplants with tomatoes and peppers (which gain from those beneficials), with asparagus (a long-standing traditional pairing), and with brassicas and alliums that share its cool-tolerant culture. The well-grounded cautions are its own family, the Apiaceae (carrot, celery, dill, parsnip), which share parsley's pests and diseases and should be rotated apart, and fennel, a broad allelopath and poor herb neighbor.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Tomatoes and peppers
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Let a second-year parsley plant flower near tomatoes and peppers and its blooms bring in helpful insects that eat aphids and other pests. Parsley tucks neatly around the base of taller plants.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Parsley is a documented insectary umbel when flowering (extension IPM recruits hoverflies/parasitoids with flowering Apiaceae); the tomato/pepper benefit follows by the same beneficial-attraction mechanism plus a traditional interplanting habit, but no parsley-tomato trial was found, so likely rather than research_backed.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A beneficial-insect and space pairing: parsley allowed to flower recruits hoverflies and parasitoid wasps that attack aphids on tomatoes and peppers, and the low parsley fills the ground around the taller crops. Sound by mechanism and traditional practice, not a measured parsley-tomato effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Asparagus
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Parsley and asparagus are a classic old-time pairing: parsley grows happily in the same long-lived bed and is said to help asparagus, and the asparagus ferns give parsley a little light shade.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: The parsley-asparagus pairing is a near-universal companion-planting tradition (often citing mutual vigor); the mechanism is unproven and it is folklore rather than trial-backed. Honest, hedged tradition.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional perennial-bed pairing: parsley is long associated with asparagus in companion lore, and practically the two share a permanent bed where parsley uses the ground between asparagus crowns and gets light shade from the ferns. Widely taught tradition, not a measured effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Brassicas and onions
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Cabbage-family plants and onions grow in the same cool weather as parsley and share a bed well, and parsley's flowers (in year two) help bring in insects that eat cabbage pests.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Cool-season interplant logic plus the flowering-umbel beneficial effect; widely taught, no parsley-specific trial.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A cool-season interplant on shared culture: brassicas and alliums share parsley's cool-tolerant season and bed, and a flowering parsley adds beneficial-insect pressure against aphids and caterpillars. Traditional and structural rather than a documented pairwise effect.

good_seasoned.name: Tomatoes and peppers
good_seasoned.timing: interplant; let a second-year plant flower nearby
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Parsley allowed to flower recruits hoverflies and parasitoid wasps that attack aphids on tomatoes and peppers, and the low parsley fills the ground around the taller crops. A beneficial-attraction and space pairing by mechanism and tradition, not a measured parsley-tomato trial.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Insectary-umbel mechanism is extension-supported; the tomato/pepper benefit follows by analogy, no parsley-specific trial.

good_seasoned.name: Asparagus
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A classic traditional pairing: parsley shares the long-lived asparagus bed, using the ground between crowns and taking light shade from the ferns. Folklore and structure, not a tested effect.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Near-universal companion lore (parsley-asparagus); mechanism unproven.

good_seasoned.name: Brassicas and onions
good_seasoned.timing: interplant in the same cool window
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A cool-season interplant: cabbage-family plants and alliums share parsley's cool-tolerant season and bed, and a flowering parsley adds beneficial-insect pressure. Space, timing, and the umbel effect, not a measured pairwise trial.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Cool-season interplant lore plus the flowering-umbel beneficial effect; no parsley-specific trial.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Carrots, celery, and other carrot-family plants
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep parsley away from carrots, celery, dill, and parsnips. They are all in the same family and share the same pests and diseases, like the carrot rust fly and leaf spots, so growing them together builds up trouble.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Same-family rotation/shared-pest avoidance is standard extension guidance: parsley, carrot, celery, dill, and parsnip share the carrot rust fly, carrot weevil, aster yellows, and Septoria, so they should be separated and rotated.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A same-family caution on shared pests and diseases: parsley, carrot, celery, dill, and parsnip share the carrot rust fly, carrot weevil, aster yellows, and Septoria leaf spot, so clustering or following one with another concentrates that pressure. Separate them in space and rotation. Extension-supported, not folklore.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Fennel
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep parsley away from fennel. Fennel is a poor neighbor for most herbs and vegetables, said to release substances that hold back nearby plants, and it can cross-pollinate carrot-family plants if both flower.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Fennel allelopathy is a near-universal companion rule with a real mechanism (fennel essential oils suppress seedling growth in bioassays), unmeasured on parsley specifically; the Apiaceae cross-pollination caution is sound where both flower for seed. Traditional/mechanistic, not a pair-tested effect.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Fennel is a broad allelopath and the classic bad herb neighbor, releasing compounds that suppress many plants, and as a fellow Apiaceae it can cross-pollinate parsley where both flower. Give fennel its own corner. A traditional rule with a real mechanism, not a measured parsley-fennel trial.

bad_seasoned.name: Carrots, celery, and other carrot-family plants
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: A same-family caution: parsley, carrot, celery, dill, and parsnip share the carrot rust fly, carrot weevil, aster yellows, and Septoria, so growing them together or in succession concentrates pest and disease pressure. Separate and rotate them. Extension-supported.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Standard shared-pest/rotation guidance for the Apiaceae; well supported by extension sources.

bad_seasoned.name: Fennel
bad_seasoned.timing: keep separate; do not let both flower side by side
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Fennel is a broad allelopath and poor herb companion, and as a fellow carrot-family plant it can cross-pollinate parsley where both bloom. Grow fennel apart. A traditional rule with a real allelopathic mechanism, not a parsley-specific trial.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Fennel allelopathy is widely taught and mechanism-backed (EO seedling suppression), unmeasured on parsley; Apiaceae cross-pollination is real for seed crops.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The first pair of narrow seed leaves pushing up. Parsley is famously slow and erratic to germinate, often 2 to 5 weeks, and emergence is uneven even under good conditions.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The first thin little leaves poking up. Parsley is slow, often taking 2 to 5 weeks, so be patient and keep the soil moist.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Soak the seed before sowing and keep the surface evenly moist but never waterlogged through the long germination window. Cold, wet soil prolongs it and invites damping-off; do not give up too early.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Soak the seeds before planting and keep the soil damp but not soggy until the seedlings appear, which can take several weeks. Do not give up, parsley is just slow.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Any sprouts yet?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Any sprouts yet?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The first true leaves, the broad, divided lower parsley leaves. Now you can tell seedlings from weeds and start thinning.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The first true leaves, the lacy parsley leaves. Now you can thin the seedlings.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin to about 6 to 12 inches as the plants crowd, eating the thinnings, and keep moisture steady while the taproot establishes.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Thin the seedlings to a hand's width or so apart, eat the little ones you pull, and keep the water steady.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How are they coming along?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How are they coming along?

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Full, leafy plants 6 inches or more tall with several stems, ready to start cutting from the outside. This begins the long harvest.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Leafy plants several inches tall and full enough to start picking the outer stems.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Begin cutting outer stems at the base once plants are full; regular picking from the outside keeps tender new growth rising from the center. A light feeding here supports the long season.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Start picking the outer stems at the base now. Picking often keeps new leaves coming from the middle. A light feeding helps.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Ready to start cutting?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Ready to start cutting?

growth_stages.name: Harvest (cut-and-come-again)
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Full plants you cut from continuously: take the outer stems near the base and the center keeps producing for months, right through summer and into fall, unlike fast-bolting herbs.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Full plants you can keep cutting from. Take the outer stems and the middle keeps growing new ones for a long time.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut outer stems at the base, never more than about a third at a time, and the plant regrows all season. Pick in the cool morning for the best flavor; parsley keeps producing through heat that would bolt cilantro or lettuce.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Cut the outer stems near the ground, no more than a third at a time, and it grows back. Pick in the cool morning. Parsley keeps going through summer heat that stops a lot of other herbs.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Harvesting regularly?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Harvesting regularly?

growth_stages.name: Second-year bolting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: On a plant that has overwintered, a tall central flower stalk rising in spring, with the leaves narrowing and turning bitter. This is the biennial bloom, the natural end of the plant, not a heat failure.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: On a plant that lived through winter, a tall flower stalk shooting up in spring and the leaves turning bitter. This is parsley finishing its two-year life, which is normal.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Take a last early-spring cutting before the stalk rises, then either pull the plant or let the umbels flower to feed pollinators and host swallowtails; let one set seed if you want volunteers. Sow fresh plants for the season's leaf crop.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pick a few early leaves before it flowers, then let it bloom for the bees and butterflies or pull it. Plant new parsley for this year's leaves.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Seen a flower stalk on an overwintered plant?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Seen a flower stalk on an old plant?

notifications.body_seasoned: Your parsley should have a true leaf or two now. Thin to about 6 to 12 inches apart and eat the thinnings.
notifications.body_beginner: Your parsley seedlings should be big enough to thin. Space them out and eat the little ones you pull.

notifications.body_seasoned: Your parsley should be full enough to cut. Take the outer stems at the base, no more than a third at a time, and it will keep regrowing from the center all season.
notifications.body_beginner: Your parsley is big enough to pick. Take the outer stems near the ground and it grows back. Pick it often.

notifications.body_seasoned: An overwintered parsley plant is sending up its second-year flower stalk and the leaves will turn bitter. Take a last cutting, then let it bloom for pollinators or pull it, and rely on fresh-sown plants for leaves.
notifications.body_beginner: Your parsley from last year is flowering and the leaves will get bitter. Pick a few last leaves, then let it bloom for the bees or pull it. Use your new plants for cooking.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Extreme heat can stress your parsley
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot weather and your parsley
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Parsley is more heat-tolerant than most salad greens and does not bolt from summer heat, but extreme, sustained heat with drought can scorch the foliage and slow growth. Keep moisture even, mulch the roots, give afternoon shade in the hottest regions, and harvest in the cool morning; in the low desert and subtropical summer it simply pauses until the weather cools.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Parsley handles heat better than most greens and will not flower from it, but very hot, dry spells can scorch the leaves. Water evenly, mulch, give it afternoon shade where summers are brutal, and pick in the cool morning. In the hottest places it just rests until cooler weather returns.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hard freeze coming
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Parsley is frost-hardy and keeps going through light freezes, often overwintering in mild zones, so for most frosts keep harvesting. A hard freeze can knock it back; in cold zones a thick mulch or a low tunnel carries plants through winter for an early-spring cutting before they bolt.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Parsley handles frost well, so you usually do not need to do anything for a light freeze, and it often lives through winter in mild areas. For a hard freeze in cold places, mulch it heavily or cover it, and it may resprout in spring before it flowers.

germination.text_seasoned: Parsley germinates slowly and erratically, often 2 to 5 weeks, and worse in cold, wet soil. Soak the dry seed in warm water for up to 24 hours before sowing to speed and even out emergence, sow shallowly, and keep the surface from drying or crusting through the long wait.
germination.text_beginner: Parsley seeds are slow, often 2 to 5 weeks. Soak them in warm water for up to a day before planting, sow them shallowly, and keep the soil moist the whole time. Do not give up too soon.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin parsley to about 6 to 12 inches as it crowds, eating the thinnings, and keep moisture steady while the taproot goes down. Parsley transplants best young, so if you started indoors, set plants out before the root gets long.
seedling.text_beginner: Thin parsley seedlings to a hand's width apart and eat the ones you pull. Keep the water steady. If you grew seedlings indoors, plant them out while they are still small.

established.text_seasoned: Harvest parsley by cutting the outer stems at the base, not by shearing the top: the plant grows from the center, so taking the outer stalks keeps tender new growth rising for months. Take no more than about a third at a time.
established.text_beginner: Pick parsley by cutting the outer stems near the ground, not the top. New leaves grow from the middle, so this keeps it producing for a long time. Take no more than a third at once.

harvest.text_seasoned: Parsley is a long-season cut-and-come-again crop: one planting keeps yielding right through summer heat that bolts cilantro and lettuce, and into fall. Pick in the cool morning and refrigerate at once; cut parsley keeps 1 to 2 weeks. Plant fresh each year, since a second-year plant turns bitter and bolts.
harvest.text_beginner: Parsley keeps producing all season, even in summer heat that stops other herbs, so one planting feeds you a long time. Pick in the cool morning and chill it; it keeps 1 to 2 weeks. Plant new parsley each year because old plants turn bitter and flower.

second_year_bolting.text_seasoned: Parsley is biennial, so a plant carried through winter bolts in its second spring and the leaves coarsen and turn bitter, no matter what you do. Take a last early cutting, then let the umbels flower (they feed beneficial insects and host black swallowtails) or pull the plant, and rely on fresh-sown parsley for the year's leaves.
second_year_bolting.text_beginner: An overwintered parsley plant will flower in its second spring and the leaves turn bitter, and you cannot stop it. Pick a few early leaves, then let it bloom for the bees and butterflies or pull it. Grow new parsley each year for good leaves.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A single parsley plant forms a full rosette of stems and, cut from the outside, yields fresh leaves for months across one long season, far longer than a fast herb like cilantro. A few plants supply a kitchen; flat-leaf types are taller and higher-yielding, curly types denser and lower.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: One parsley plant keeps giving leaves for months if you cut from the outside, so a few plants are plenty for a kitchen. Flat-leaf types are bigger and give more; curly types are smaller and frillier.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Leaf production builds through the season and holds steady right through summer, since parsley does not bolt from heat in its first year. In mild zones plants carry into late fall and overwinter for an early-spring bonus before the second-year bolt ends them.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Parsley keeps producing steadily all season, even in summer heat, and in mild areas it carries into fall and even winter. The next spring it flowers and is done.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Parsley is a rewarding first-season crop once you get past its slow germination: soak the seed, be patient through the 2-to-5-week sprouting, and a single sowing then produces leaves for months with little fuss. The main beginner mistakes are giving up on the slow seed and harvesting from the top instead of the outer stems. Plant fresh each year, since the second-year plant bolts and turns bitter.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Parsley is easy once it sprouts, but the seed is slow, so soak it and wait a few weeks without giving up. After that, one planting gives you leaves for months. Just cut from the outside, not the top, and plant new parsley each year for the best flavor.
factors_seasoned: Patience at germination: soaked seed in evenly moist soil is the single biggest factor in getting a stand, since slow, erratic sprouting is parsley's defining quirk.
Harvest method: cutting the outer stems at the base (not shearing the top) keeps the plant producing from the center all season.
Even moisture and a deep, loose bed: the taproot wants room and steady water for tender leaves over a long season.
Type: flat-leaf (Italian) yields more and tastes stronger; curly is denser and milder.
Annual replanting: parsley bolts and turns bitter in its second year, so fresh sowings give the best leaves.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No reliable extension or peer-reviewed evidence supports timing parsley planting or harvest by moon phase. Sow by soil temperature and frost dates instead, and remember the seed is simply slow.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor or very slow germination (or none at all)
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Parsley seed is naturally slow and erratic, and cold or dry soil makes it worse.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your parsley came up thin, very late, or not at all. Parsley seed is slow by nature, often 2 to 5 weeks, and germinates poorly in cold, wet soil or when the surface dries out. Next time, soak the seed in warm water for up to a day, keep the surface moist, use fresh seed, and simply wait longer before giving up.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Soak the seed before sowing, keep the surface moist, use fresh seed, and be patient.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Stand was thin, very delayed, or failed. Parsley germination is intrinsically slow and erratic (2 to 5 weeks) and is inhibited by cold, wet soil and by surface drying or crusting during the long emergence window. Next time soak the dry seed up to 24 hours, sow into moist, well-drained soil, keep the seedbed from crusting, use fresh viable seed, and allow the full germination window before reseeding.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Slow, erratic seed nature plus cold or dry soil inhibiting the long germination.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Soak the seed, sow into moist well-drained soil, keep the surface from drying, use fresh seed, and wait the full window.

failure_diagnostics.label: Flower stalk and bitter leaves in the second spring
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Parsley is a biennial: it flowers in its second year after a winter, and the leaves turn bitter.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your parsley shot up a tall flower stalk and the leaves turned bitter, in its second spring. That is not a mistake or a heat problem: parsley is a biennial that naturally flowers in its second year after going through winter. Next time, plant fresh parsley each year for the best leaves, take just a few early leaves from an overwintered plant, then let it bloom for pollinators or pull it.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant fresh parsley each year, and treat second-year plants as a short early-spring bonus before they bolt.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The overwintered plant elongated into a seedstalk and leaf quality collapsed in its second spring. This is the biennial life cycle (vernalization-triggered second-year flowering), NOT first-year heat bolting, which parsley does not do. Next time sow fresh each year for the leaf crop, harvest overwintered plants only for an early-spring cutting, and let or pull the bloom.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Biennial second-year flowering after vernalization, not a heat or care failure.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sow fresh annually for leaves; use overwintered plants for an early cutting, then let them flower for pollinators or remove them.

failure_diagnostics.label: Tan-brown spots spreading across the leaves
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Septoria leaf spot, the most common parsley disease, in cool, wet conditions and often from infected seed.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your parsley leaves got small tan-to-brown spots that spread in wet weather. That is Septoria leaf spot, which travels on wet leaves and splashing water and can come in on the seed. Next time, use clean seed, water at the soil line, space plants for airflow, and rotate the bed away from carrot-family plants.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Use clean seed, water at the base, space for airflow, and rotate away from the carrot family.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Small tan lesions with dark centers spreading on the foliage indicate Septoria leaf spot (Septoria petroselini), favored by cool, wet, splashy conditions and frequently seed-borne. Next time use clean or treated seed, switch to drip, widen spacing, rotate away from the Apiaceae, and clear infected debris.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Seed-borne, splash-spread Septoria favored by cool, wet weather and overhead watering.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Use clean seed, irrigate at the soil line, widen spacing, rotate away from Apiaceae, and remove infected debris.

failure_diagnostics.label: Wilting plants with a soft, brown crown
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Crown or root rot from soil that stayed too wet, especially over winter.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your parsley wilted and the crown or roots turned brown and mushy. That is crown and root rot, caused by soil staying waterlogged, often over a wet winter. Next time, plant in well-drained or raised beds, loosen the soil for the taproot, and do not overwater.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant in well-drained soil, do not overwater, and remove any plant whose crown has gone soft.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Wilting with a browned, decayed crown and root points to soilborne crown and root rot (Pythium, Phytophthora, Rhizoctonia), favored by waterlogged, poorly drained soil and overwatering, often on plants held over a wet winter. Next time site in well-drained or raised, loosened beds, moderate winter watering, and rotate out of beds with a rot history.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Soilborne crown and root rots favored by waterlogged soil and overwatering.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in well-drained, loosened soil, avoid overwatering (especially overwinter), and rotate away from rot-prone beds.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Parsley does not need the aggressive succession sowing fast herbs do; one planting yields all season because you cut from the same plants. Still, a spring sowing plus a midsummer or early-fall sowing keeps the freshest, most tender leaves coming and sets up an overwintering crop in mild zones. In the hottest regions, sow through the long cool window (fall into spring) and skip the peak of summer.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: Unlike cilantro, parsley does not need re-sowing every couple of weeks: one planting lasts all season. For the freshest leaves, just add a second sowing in midsummer or early fall, and in hot areas plant in the cool months instead of the hottest part of summer.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: parsley_author_fresh_pilot (Claude Code lane authoring, 2026-06-29). Authored from the parsley shell, modeled STRUCTURALLY on the certified culinary-herb template basil, with the cool-tolerant Apiaceae calendar/succession SHAPE off the gate-clean cilantro-coriander pilot, and parsley (Petroselinum crispum, Apiaceae) biology re-derived from live T1 extension sources (UMN Growing Parsley, Wisconsin Horticulture Parsley, Clemson HGIC Herbs). DRAFT for daily biology-fidelity review, not certified: launch flags false. KEY PARSLEY-VS-BASIL REFITS (and the inversion of cilantro): basil is WARM-season and frost-TENDER; parsley is COOL-TOLERANT and FROST-HARDY, overwintering in mild zones. Unlike cilantro, which is an annual that BOLTS FAST in year-1 heat (summer heat_pause everywhere warm), parsley is a BIENNIAL that does NOT bolt from first-year heat and is genuinely HEAT-TOLERANT: it runs spring through fall in most regions, so it carries FAR FEWER heat_pause cells than its cool-season peers (NONE in the northern tier or on the mild CA coasts; a brief pause only in the hot interior/Gulf; a real summer pause only in the low desert, CA desert, and subtropical Florida). It BOLTS in its SECOND year after overwintering (vernalization), the natural end of the plant. SLOW, ERRATIC germination (2 to 5 weeks; soak the seed) is the signature note. Cut-and-come-again from the OUTER stems; flat-leaf (Italian) vs curly (French) types, plus Hamburg root parsley. DTM 70 to 90; spacing 6 to 12 inches; pH 6.0 to 7.0; sun to part shade; 5-10-5 moderate feeding. Pests: parsleyworm (black swallowtail caterpillar, often left for the butterflies), aphids, carrot rust fly/weevil; diseases minimal (Septoria leaf spot, crown/root rot, damping-off). successions_realized is CC-derived (deriver), not hand-authored. See parsley_NOTES.md for modeled values and flags.

open_findings.summary: All 10 regions' per-zone calendars are MODELED from parsley's cool-tolerant, frost-hardy, HEAT-TOLERANT biennial envelope and the regional extension planting-calendar sources, not lifted from a single parsley-per-region chart (few exist). The frost-anchored shape is shared cool-season climate truth; the parsley-specific refit is its heat tolerance (it runs through summer where its peers pause) and its year-2 bolt. resolution_method on each cell is 'cc_author_pilot_modeled'. Flagged for the daily biology-fidelity review (harvest months and the exact extent of each hot-region pause may be nudged).
open_findings.basis: Cool-season sowing windows are frost/heat-driven and shared; parsley's distinguishing trait is greater heat tolerance than lettuce/cilantro/arugula, so its heat_pause set is a deliberate SUBSET of those peers (the cool-season-timing guardrail applied in the heat-tolerant direction).

open_findings.summary: Parsley carries heat_pause ONLY where the summer is genuinely too hot for it: low_desert_az, ca_desert, fl_peninsula (Jun-Sep / May-Sep), a brief Jul-Aug pause in the hot CA interior, se_gulf, and warm_arid. It runs straight through summer (NO heat_pause) in the entire northern tier, on the mild CA north and south coasts, and in Hawaii, the heat-tolerance refit vs cilantro/arugula, which pause far more widely. Each heat_pause cell carries a backed object (months + basis_seasoned + source + URL); the basis note states parsley is heat-tolerant but the region's extreme summer scorches it.
open_findings.basis: Heat_pause why-note rule + the cool-season heat_pause convention, applied to a HEAT-TOLERANT crop: place a gap only where the heat genuinely exceeds parsley's (higher) tolerance, not merely its peers'.

open_findings.summary: days_to_maturity [70, 90] (mid 80) follows UMN's 70-to-90-day figure. spacing_inches [6, 12] spans the sourced range (UMN final 10 to 12 inches; others 6 to 8 for closer/cut spacing; Wisconsin 6 to 12); the task's 6-to-9-inch guidance sits at the lower end and is reflected. germination_temp_f [50, 75] is a modeled cool-soil band (Clemson: germinates as low as 50F, best near 70F); the operative fact is the slow, erratic 2-to-5-week germination, surfaced throughout the prose. weeks_indoors 6 follows UMN's 6-to-8-week indoor start.
open_findings.basis: Within the cited UMN / Wisconsin / Clemson figures; spacing flagged because sources span 6 to 12 inches and the chosen range is intentionally wide.

open_findings.summary: ph.preferred_range [6.0, 7.0] is the UMN-stated best range for parsley; tolerated [5.5, 7.5] is a modeled widening. Parsley is not pH-sensitive.
open_findings.basis: UMN 'a pH range of 6.0 to 7.0 is best'; tolerated band flagged as modeled. Cross-consistency gate confirms the prose range matches the structured range.

open_findings.summary: Pests (parsleyworm/black swallowtail, aphids, carrot rust fly and carrot weevil) and diseases (Septoria leaf spot, crown/root rot, damping-off) are drawn from the parsley/herb pages (Clemson and Wisconsin name parsley as a black swallowtail host with seldom-damaging numbers and aphids as the most common pest; Wisconsin names Septoria as the most common disease). The carrot rust fly/weevil and the crown-rot and damping-off details are the standard Apiaceae set applied to parsley and anchored to the institution herb/vegetable pages; flagged for the source-truth sample.
open_findings.basis: Directly-read parsley/herb pages name the swallowtail, aphids, and Septoria; the carrot-family root pests and soil rots are well-established for the Apiaceae and modeled onto parsley, flagged.

open_findings.summary: No parsley-specific catalog IDs exist, so existing institution-level T1 catalog IDs are reused with the best readable page in anchoring_urls. Directly-read parsley/herb anchors: umn_ext (UMN Growing Parsley), uwi_hort (Wisconsin Horticulture Parsley), clemson_hgic (Clemson HGIC Herbs). Regional calendar anchors (tamu_agrilife, uariz_ext, uariz_ext_az2061, az_coop_ext, ndsu_ext, msu_ext, umaine_ext, lsu_agcenter, msstate_ext, uc_mg, ucanr_ext, nmsu_ext, uga_calendar, uf_ifas_south_cal, uf_ifas_vh021, uhawaii_ctahr, ncsu_ext, umd_ext, psu_ext, iastate_ext) are section/portal/publication-level; uariz_ext_az2061 is a PDF (Growing Herbs in Tucson) cited at the publication URL, not extracted. No IDs were invented; all are catalogued and T1. Flagged for the daily review's URL-liveness check.
open_findings.basis: Task sourcing rule + the cilantro pilot precedent: reuse a real catalog ID, anchor to the best readable page, flag section/portal/PDF-level anchors, never shell out to extract.

open_findings.summary: successions_realized was NOT hand-authored: the CC deriver filled it per cell at interval_weeks 4 (reflecting parsley's slower, lighter succession cadence vs cilantro's 2) and reconciled succession_policy.successions and max_successions_per_season to the max over zones. Note parsley is far less of a succession crop than cilantro/lettuce, one planting yields all season, so the derived counts represent a theoretical sowing cadence and the prose tempers it accordingly.
open_findings.basis: Authoring boundary: the per-zone realized count is a derived metric, not a sourced claim; matches the basil/cilantro herb precedent (succession-suitable culinary_herb).

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: Up North (zones 3 through 7), parsley is a hardy, long-season leaf herb. Soak the slow seed and sow in early spring as soon as you can work the soil, or set out plants started indoors, since parsley takes frost. One planting then gives leaves right through summer, parsley does not bolt in the heat like cilantro, and on into fall. In the milder zones a mulched plant often overwinters for an early-spring cutting before it flowers in its second year.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In the cold-winter North (zones 3 through 7), parsley is a frost-hardy, long-season herb, not a fast succession crop. Soak the slow seed and direct-sow in early spring or transplant indoor-started plants; it tolerates frost, so it goes out on the early side. A single planting produces through the whole warm season, since parsley does not heat-bolt, and holds into fall. In zones 5 through 7 a well-mulched plant frequently overwinters for an early-spring leaf bonus before the biennial second-year bolt; grow fresh plants each year for the main crop.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast and Gulf (zones 8 and 9), parsley is mainly a cool-season leaf herb grown fall through spring, overwintering easily in the mild winter. It is tougher than lettuce, so it pushes well into the warm months, but the peak of the hot, humid summer scorches it, so the calendar takes a short midsummer break before resuming. Soak the seed, plant in fall and again in late winter, and cut from the outer stems.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: Across the Southeast and Gulf (zones 8 and 9), parsley runs as a long cool-season leaf crop, fall through spring, overwintering readily. More heat-tolerant than its salad-green peers, it carries deep into the warm shoulders, but high summer heat and humidity scorch it, so the leaf calendar pauses through the hottest weeks, roughly July and August, and resumes as it cools, with hotter zone 9 simply starting its spring planting a touch later. Soak the slow seed; plant in fall and late winter, harvest cut-and-come-again, and sow fresh each year ahead of the second-year bolt.
