hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In tropical Hawaii (zone 11), parsley grows for leaves year-round in the mild climate, best in the cooler season or at upland elevations; unlike cilantro it does not bolt in the warmth, so it just slows a little in the lowland heat. Soak the seed, plant any time, give afternoon shade where it is hot, and cut from the outer stems.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: In tropical Hawaii (zone 11), parsley is a year-round leaf crop in the mild climate, since it does not heat-bolt like cilantro; it is most productive in the cooler season and at higher elevations, and merely slows in lowland heat rather than stopping. Soak the slow seed, plant across the year, give afternoon shade and steady water in the warm lowlands, and harvest cut-and-come-again. A genuinely year-round fit, with upland plantings the most reliable.

crops.description_seasoned: Parsley (Petroselinum crispum) is a hardy biennial herb in the carrot family (Apiaceae), grown for its flavorful, vitamin-rich leaves. Its biology is the mirror image of warm-season herbs like basil and the opposite of fast cool-season herbs like cilantro. Parsley is COOL-TOLERANT and FROST-HARDY, taking light freezes and overwintering in mild zones, yet it is also genuinely HEAT-TOLERANT: because it is a biennial that does not flower until its second year, it does NOT bolt from first-year summer heat the way cilantro does, so a single planting yields leaves spring through fall, and only the most extreme desert and subtropical summers slow it. That long, flexible season is the headline. The signature challenge is at the start: parsley seed germinates slowly and erratically, often 2 to 5 weeks, so growers soak it and wait. It is harvested cut-and-come-again from the OUTER stems, leaving the center to regrow for months. It comes in flat-leaf (Italian) types, with the stronger, sweeter flavor cooks prefer, and curly (French) types grown for garnish, plus Hamburg root parsley grown for an edible root. The one catch is the biennial cycle: an overwintered plant bolts in its second spring and the leaves turn bitter, so parsley is sown fresh each year for the best leaves. Pests are few, chiefly the parsleyworm (the handsome black swallowtail caterpillar, often left for the butterflies) and aphids, and disease is minimal.
crops.description_beginner: Parsley is a hardy herb in the carrot family, grown for its tasty, healthy leaves. It is easygoing once it gets started, and very different from both basil and cilantro: it handles frost and cool weather, but it also takes summer heat without flooding into flower the way cilantro does, so one planting gives you leaves from spring all the way through fall. The one tricky part is the beginning: parsley seed is slow, often taking 2 to 5 weeks to sprout, so soak it in warm water first and be patient. You harvest it by cutting the outer stems near the base, and the middle keeps growing new leaves for months. There are two main kinds, flat-leaf (Italian), which has the best flavor for cooking, and curly, the frilly kind used for garnish. One thing to know: parsley lives two years, and in its second spring it sends up a flower stalk and the leaves turn bitter, so plant fresh parsley each year for the best leaves. It has few pests, mainly the big green-and-black parsleyworm caterpillar, which turns into a black swallowtail butterfly and is usually welcome.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Begin cutting parsley once plants are full and about 6 inches tall, roughly 70 to 90 days from sowing. Harvest by cutting the OUTER stems at the base, taking no more than about a third at a time, and the plant keeps producing fresh leaves from the center for months, right through summer heat that would bolt cilantro or lettuce, and into fall. Pick in the cool morning for the best flavor and refrigerate at once; cut parsley keeps 1 to 2 weeks. In mild zones a mulched plant overwinters for an early-spring cutting, but take that as a bonus: an overwintered plant bolts in its second spring and the leaves turn bitter, so sow fresh plants each year for the main leaf crop.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Start picking parsley when the plants are full and about 6 inches tall, a couple of months after sowing. Cut the OUTER stems near the base, no more than a third at a time, and the middle keeps growing new leaves for months, even through summer heat. Pick in the cool morning for the best flavor and put it in the fridge, where it keeps 1 to 2 weeks. In mild areas a mulched plant can live through winter and give you a few early leaves, but it will flower and turn bitter that second spring, so plant new parsley each year for the best leaves.

pet_safe.note: Large amounts contain furanocoumarins that can make skin sun-sensitive in cats, dogs, and horses.

crops.name: Cilantro / Coriander

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Cilantro likes loose, fertile soil with plenty of compost mixed in that holds moisture but still drains well. It is not fussy, but steady moisture and rich soil keep the leaves tender and mild and put off bolting a little; hot, dry, hard soil makes it rush to flower and turn the foliage bitter.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Cilantro grows in most soils but does best in a fertile, well-drained loam or sandy loam high in organic matter, kept evenly moist. Utah State University suggests working 2 to 4 inches of well-rotted compost into the top 4 to 6 inches before sowing, which feeds the fast leaf growth and buffers the steady moisture that keeps the leaves tender and slow to bolt. It dislikes damp, humid, poorly drained ground, which invites damping-off and leaf disease. The plant has a slender taproot and resents transplanting, so it is best direct-sown into loosened soil.

ph.note_beginner: Cilantro grows best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, about 6.2 to 6.8. Most garden soil is fine, and a simple soil test tells you where you stand.
ph.note_seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.2 to 6.8, slightly acidic to neutral; cilantro is forgiving and still does fine across roughly 6.0 to 7.5. Clemson lists a working range of 6 to 7 for the crop. It is not a pH-sensitive plant, so in most gardens no adjustment is needed beyond a soil-test baseline.

fertilizer.timing: a little worked in before sowing, then a light side-dress once or twice during the few weeks of leaf growth
fertilizer.example_product: 21-0-0 or blood meal, or a balanced vegetable fertilizer
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Cilantro is a fast leafy herb that runs on nitrogen, but the crop is so quick that a modest charge is plenty. Utah State University suggests about a quarter cup of 21-0-0 per 25 square feet, one to two times during the season. Work compost or a balanced fertilizer in before sowing, then side-dress lightly with nitrogen once the seedlings are established to push tender, mild leaves. Avoid heavy late nitrogen, which draws aphids and does little for a crop you cut within a few weeks; a plant grown on for coriander seed needs no extra feeding once it bolts.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Cilantro grows fast and likes a little nitrogen for tender green leaves. Mix some compost or fertilizer into the soil before planting, then give it one light feeding once the seedlings are up and growing. Because the crop is so quick, you usually do not need to feed it again, and a plant left to make coriander seed needs nothing more.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time to side-dress your cilantro with a little nitrogen.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Time to give your cilantro a light feeding.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: High N for fast leafy growth; a light side-dress of 21-0-0 or blood meal once or twice during the crop. No extra phosphorus or potassium needed beyond a soil-test baseline; do not overfeed a 4-to-6-week leaf crop.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a nitrogen-rich feed such as blood meal or a 21-0-0 fertilizer once or twice while the plants are young.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: About a quarter cup of 21-0-0 per 25 square feet, side-dressed once or twice during the crop; a compost-rich bed often needs no extra feed at all.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Follow the label rate for a nitrogen-rich vegetable fertilizer, one light feeding while the plants are young.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_beginner: Clusters of tiny soft green or gray insects on new growth and the undersides of leaves, sometimes with curled, sticky foliage.
pests.cause_beginner: Aphids are small sap-sucking insects that breed fast, especially on soft growth from too much fertilizer. They can spread plant viruses.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water, or use insecticidal soap or neem oil on the leaf undersides, repeating every few days. Pick the leaves before a colony settles in.
pests.prevention_beginner: Welcome helpful insects like ladybugs and lacewings, go easy on nitrogen, check new growth often, and pick the quick crop young.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Colonies of green peach and other aphids gather on growing tips and leaf undersides; honeydew and the lodged insects contaminate a crop eaten fresh, and aphids can vector viruses. Cilantro's lacy foliage hides them, so scout closely.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several aphid species feed on cilantro; they reproduce rapidly and favor the soft growth that excess nitrogen produces.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Dislodge colonies with a strong water jet or spray insecticidal soap or neem, covering leaf undersides; repeat every few days and conserve lady beetles, lacewings, and parasitoid wasps, which cilantro's own flowers attract.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Scout growing tips early, avoid overfeeding nitrogen, conserve natural enemies, and harvest the fast crop before colonies build; letting a few plants flower draws in aphid predators.

pests.name: Leafhoppers (and aster yellows / curly top)
pests.symptoms_beginner: Small wedge-shaped insects that hop or fly up when disturbed, plus yellowed, twisted, or stunted plants. The leafhoppers themselves do little chewing damage, but they can carry diseases that deform the plant.
pests.cause_beginner: Tiny jumping insects that suck sap and, more seriously, spread diseases (aster yellows and curly top) that twist and yellow the plants.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover plants with a light row cover to keep leafhoppers off, pull and discard any yellowed, distorted plants right away, and clear nearby weeds that harbor the insects and the diseases.
pests.prevention_beginner: Use row cover, clear weedy hosts around the garden, and remove infected plants early so they do not seed disease into the planting.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: The beet leafhopper and aster leafhoppers feed on cilantro and, more importantly, transmit aster yellows and beet curly top virus, which yellow, distort, and stunt the plants. Infected plants do not recover and should be removed.
pests.cause_seasoned: Leafhoppers (including the beet leafhopper, Circulifer tenellus) feed on the foliage and vector aster yellows and beet curly top virus; the disease damage far outweighs the feeding.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Exclude leafhoppers with floating row cover, rogue out symptomatic plants promptly since there is no cure for the viral diseases, and control weed reservoirs; insecticides give poor control of a mobile vector.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Manage leafhoppers mainly by exclusion (row cover) and sanitation: remove weed reservoirs and rogue symptomatic plants, since spraying rarely stops a mobile virus vector.

diseases.name: Bacterial leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small dark, angular, water-soaked spots on the leaves that run along the veins and can merge into larger blotches, worst in cool, wet weather. Spotted leaves are not good to eat.
diseases.cause_beginner: A bacterial disease, the most common one reported on cilantro, that spreads through wet leaves and splashing water and often arrives on infected seed.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove and destroy spotted leaves, avoid wetting the foliage, improve airflow, and start with clean seed. There is no spray cure in the home garden, so prevention matters most.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Use clean seed, water at the soil line rather than over the leaves, space plants for airflow, and clear infected debris.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Angular, vein-limited dark lesions on the foliage, sometimes with a yellow halo, spreading in cool, wet, splashy conditions; on a leaf crop even moderate spotting ruins the harvest. It is the most-reported cilantro disease.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Pseudomonas syringae pv. coriandricola, a seed-borne and splash-spread bacterium favored by cool, wet weather and overhead watering.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Use clean, disease-free or hot-water-treated seed, avoid overhead irrigation, space for airflow, rotate away from cilantro and its relatives, and remove infected debris; copper has limited effect once it is established.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant clean seed, switch to drip or soil-line watering, widen spacing, rotate, and remove crop debris that carries the bacterium over.

diseases.name: Damping-off and seedling rot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Seeds that never come up, or seedlings that flop over at the soil line with a pinched, rotted stem and then die. It strikes in cold, wet soil.
diseases.cause_beginner: Soil fungi attack the seeds and tiny seedlings, especially when the soil is cold and soggy and the slow-sprouting cilantro seed sits a long time before emerging.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure for an affected seedling, so focus on prevention: pull and discard collapsed seedlings.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Do not sow into cold, soggy soil, plant shallowly in well-drained ground, do not overwater, and use fresh seed so it comes up faster.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Poor stands from seed and pre- or post-emergence collapse of seedlings with water-soaked, pinched stems at the soil line, worst in cold, wet, poorly drained soil where cilantro's slow germination leaves seed sitting.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Soilborne Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Fusarium fungi attack germinating seed and seedlings; cold, saturated soil that slows cilantro's already slow germination favors them.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No rescue once seedlings collapse; manage by prevention and remove affected plants.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Sow shallowly into well-drained soil under conditions that favor reasonably quick emergence, avoid overwatering, and use fresh, viable seed; some growers soak the dry seed to speed emergence past the vulnerable window.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_beginner: A white, powdery coating on the leaves and stems, usually later in the crop and in warm, dry-day weather. Heavily coated leaves yellow and are unpleasant to eat.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungal disease (Erysiphe heraclei) that coats the leaves in white powder, favored by warm days, cool nights, and crowding.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove the worst leaves, open up the planting for airflow, and avoid crowding. Most home crops are harvested before it does much harm.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Space plants for airflow, avoid crowding and overfeeding, and pick the leaf crop young before mildew builds.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: A white, talc-like fungal growth on the foliage and stems, the most common fungal disease of cilantro, that builds in warm days with cool nights and crowded plantings; coated leaves lose quality.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Erysiphe heraclei, favored by warm days and cool humid nights and by dense stands with poor airflow.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Improve airflow with wider spacing, remove affected leaves, and avoid excess nitrogen; the fast leaf crop is usually cut before mildew matters, but a plant grown on for seed is more exposed.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Widen spacing for airflow, avoid heavy nitrogen, and harvest the leaf crop promptly; remove infected foliage on plants held for coriander seed.

diseases.name: Soft rot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Mushy, slimy, foul-smelling collapse of the crown or stems, usually in warm, wet conditions or after the foliage has been damaged. Affected plants rot quickly.
diseases.cause_beginner: Bacterial soft rot that enters through wounds and rots the tissue in warm, wet, poorly drained soil.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove and discard rotted plants, improve drainage, avoid injuring the plants, and do not overwater. There is no cure once a plant is rotting.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant in well-drained soil, avoid overwatering and injury, and keep the planting open so foliage dries.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Wet, mushy breakdown of the crown and stems with a bad smell, caused by soft-rot bacteria entering through wounds in warm, wet, poorly drained conditions; the plant collapses fast.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Soft-rot bacteria (such as Pectobacterium species) invade through wounds and bruises and dissolve the tissue, favored by warm temperatures, wet soil, and poor drainage.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy affected plants, improve drainage and airflow, avoid wounding and overwatering, and do not work the bed when wet; no rescue once rot sets in.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Site in well-drained soil, avoid waterlogging and mechanical injury, space for drying airflow, and clear infected debris.

watering.frequency_seasoned: About 1 inch of water per week, kept even; cilantro is shallow-rooted and bolts faster and turns harsher under drought stress.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly 1 inch a week.
watering.amount_seasoned: Roughly 1 inch per week, more in warm, dry spells; Texas A&M notes an inch a week suffices once established unless it turns very hot.
watering.amount_beginner: Aim for about 1 inch of water a week, a bit more when it is warm and dry.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose; keeping the lacy foliage dry checks bacterial leaf spot and other leaf diseases on a crop eaten fresh.
watering.method_beginner: Water at the base of the plants rather than over the leaves, which helps prevent leaf diseases.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, damping-off in seedlings, and soft rot or leaf disease in constantly wet, poorly drained ground.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Lower leaves yellow, seedlings rot at the base, and plants get mushy or diseased in soggy soil.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting, slowed growth, harsher-tasting leaves, and faster bolting; drought stress hurries the plant toward its coriander seedstalk.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Wilting leaves that taste sharper, and a plant that bolts (flowers) sooner than you want.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Even moisture keeps cilantro growing fast, tender, and mild; dry, hot spells push it straight to flower and coriander seed and coarsen the leaves.
watering.method_note_beginner: Keep the water steady so the leaves stay mild and tender and the plant does not bolt early.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Steady moisture through germination, which is slow in cilantro, and through the few weeks of leaf growth, especially as the weather warms, matters most for delaying bolt.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Keep the soil moist while the seeds are sprouting (which takes a while) and through the leaf-growing weeks, especially as it warms up.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Cilantro is almost always direct-sown, since it has a slender taproot and resents transplanting. Sow seed about 0.25 to 0.5 inch deep as soon as the soil can be worked in spring; it tolerates frost, so it can go in several weeks before the last frost, and it germinates slowly, often 7 to 21 days. The round seed is actually two seeds fused, so growers sometimes gently crack it to speed and even out germination. Sow a little thicker than the final stand and thin to taste. In hot regions, shift sowing to fall through spring, since heat both slows germination and bolts the crop almost at once; midsummer sowings are grown for coriander seed rather than leaves.
start_method.notes_beginner: Plant cilantro straight in the garden from seed, because it has a deep little root and does not like being moved. Sow the seeds about a quarter to half an inch deep as soon as the soil can be worked in spring, since the plants handle frost. The seeds are slow, often taking one to three weeks, so keep the soil moist. Sow again every couple of weeks, and in hot areas plant in fall through spring instead of summer, because heat makes it bolt almost right away. A summer crop is really for the coriander seed.

drainage.saucer_practice: Empty the saucer after watering so roots never sit in water, which invites damping-off and root rot.

soil_mix.type_beginner: A good-quality potting mix, not garden soil.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in some compost for steady nutrients.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: A light, well-drained potting mix high in organic matter, deep enough for cilantro's taproot.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend in compost and a little starter nitrogen; cilantro is a quick feeder but needs only a light charge for its short leaf life.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out fast, so check daily in warm weather and keep the mix evenly moist, since drought makes cilantro bolt.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Feed a little, since watering washes nutrients out of pots, but the crop is so fast it rarely needs more than a starter charge.

overwintering.approach_beginner: In mild areas, a pot of fall-sown cilantro can keep going through winter in a sheltered, sunny spot, since cilantro takes frost. In cold areas, move the pot against the house or into a cold frame, or cover it during hard freezes, and it will often resume in spring before bolting.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Cilantro is frost-hardy, so a fall-sown container can overwinter in mild zones, holding through winter in a sheltered spot and giving the earliest, longest leaf run before spring heat bolts it. In cold zones the limited root volume freezes harder than open ground, so sink the pot, move it to a cold frame or unheated structure, or cover it during hard freezes; a hard freeze will still kill it.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Cilantro is an easy, fast container herb. Use a pot at least 8 inches deep to fit its root, sow the seed thickly, and snip leaves cut-and-come-again. Keep it watered and in the cool seasons, and give it afternoon shade in warm weather to slow bolting.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Cilantro grows well in a container at least 8 inches deep to fit its taproot, sown densely for cut-and-come-again leaves. Keep moisture even, since pots dry fast and drought triggers bolting, grow it in the cool seasons, and give afternoon shade in warm spells. A pot is also the easiest way to move the crop into shade or shelter as the weather turns, and to keep a fresh succession by the kitchen door.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry faster than beds; check moisture daily in warmth and water before the mix dries, since drought stress bolts cilantro.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Container cilantro needs only a light starter feed; frequent watering leaches nutrients, but the crop is harvested before heavy feeding would matter.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering container suits cilantro well, since it smooths out the steady moisture that keeps the leaves mild and slow to bolt.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match because it keeps the water steady, which keeps cilantro tender and slow to bolt.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: Cilantro has a slender taproot, so give it depth: a container at least 8 inches deep suits it better than a shallow tray, while width adds sowing area for cut-and-come-again leaves.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Cilantro has a deeper root than most salad greens, so use a pot at least 8 inches deep. Extra width gives you more leaves to cut.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Other Apiaceae: carrot, parsley, dill, fennel, celery, parsnip, and cilantro itself. They share carrot-family pests and diseases (leafhopper-vectored aster yellows, the carrot motley dwarf complex, and soilborne rots), so following one with another concentrates that pressure.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Other carrot-family plants like carrots, parsley, dill, fennel, and celery, because they share the same pests and diseases.
rotation.good_after: Legumes (peas, beans), brassicas (cabbage family), alliums (onion, garlic), or nightshades such as tomatoes.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate cilantro and its carrot-family relatives so they do not return to the same ground for about 3 years. The Apiaceae share aster yellows (spread by leafhoppers), the carrot motley dwarf complex, and soilborne rots, which build up where the family repeats. Follow cilantro with legumes, brassicas, alliums, or nightshades. Because cilantro readily self-sows from bolted plants, volunteers can blur a rotation, so pull seedlings that come up out of place.
rotation.note_beginner: Try not to grow cilantro or other carrot-family plants (carrots, parsley, dill, fennel, celery) in the same spot more than about once every 3 years, since they share pests and diseases. Plant cilantro after peas, beans, cabbage, onions, or tomatoes instead. Cilantro often self-sows, so pull up stray seedlings that pop up where you do not want them.

bolting.triggers: heat above about 75°F and lengthening days, accelerated by drought and crowding
bolting.prevention_seasoned: Cilantro bolts fast once it is warm and the days lengthen, and the leaves coarsen and turn bitter as it shifts to its coriander seedstalk. Keep the leaf window in the cool shoulders of the year: sow early in spring and crop quickly, lean on the fall crop, which is the longer and more reliable leaf season, choose slow-bolting types (Santo, Calypso, Leisure, Slow Bolting) where heat is a problem, give light afternoon shade in warm spells, and keep moisture steady. Succession-sow every 2 to 3 weeks so a bolted batch is quickly replaced. There is no real fix once it bolts, so the productive answer in heat is to stop fighting it and grow the plant on for coriander seed.
bolting.prevention_beginner: Cilantro flowers (bolts) quickly when it gets warm and the days get long, and the leaves turn bitter. To keep the leaves coming, grow it in the cool parts of the year, especially fall, sow a fresh little batch every 2 to 3 weeks, water steadily, give afternoon shade when it is warm, and try slow-bolting types like Santo or Calypso. When it does bolt, do not fight it: let the plant flower and make coriander seed, which is the spice.
bolting.note_seasoned: Bolting in cilantro is driven by heat above roughly 75°F and lengthening days, sped by drought and crowding, and it comes on fast because the plant is so quick. This is the defining fact of the crop: the same bolt that ends the cilantro leaf harvest begins the coriander seed crop, so the plant is not failing, it is changing product. The white flowers feed pollinators and beneficial insects strongly, and bolted plants self-sow readily. In hot regions the leaf window is short and growers deliberately let summer plantings run to coriander seed.
bolting.note_beginner: Cilantro bolts (sends up a flower stalk) when it gets warm and the days are long. It happens fast, but it is not a mistake: the very same flowering that ends the leafy cilantro gives you coriander seed, the spice. The flowers are great for bees and helpful insects, and the plant often drops seed and comes up again on its own. Grow it in cool weather for leaves, and let it bloom in summer for seed.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Fresh cilantro leaves wilt within a day at room temperature, so refrigerate promptly after cutting; standing the cut stems in a glass of water on the counter holds them a few days. Coriander seed, by contrast, is shelf-stable for months once dried.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Do not leave cut cilantro out on the counter, where it wilts fast; either chill it or stand the stems in a glass of water. Dried coriander seed keeps for months at room temperature.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerate fresh leaves unwashed in a loose or perforated bag, or stems standing in a little water under a loose bag, in the crisper; cilantro holds about a week. Wash only at use, since trapped moisture speeds breakdown.
storage.fridge_beginner: Store fresh cilantro unwashed in a loose bag in the fridge, where it keeps about a week. Wash it only when you are ready to use it.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Fresh cilantro loses its texture frozen for raw use, but freezes well chopped into ice-cube trays with water or oil, or blended into sauces, where the flavor holds for cooking. Coriander seed is dried, not frozen: cut seed heads as they brown, dry them, then thresh and store the seed airtight.
storage.freezer_beginner: Cilantro does not freeze well for salads, but you can chop it into an ice-cube tray with a little water or oil and freeze that for cooking. For coriander, let the seeds dry on the plant, then store them in a jar.
storage.notes_seasoned: Cilantro is best straight from the garden, delicate and short-lived once cut, so chill it fast and use it within a week; its flavor is also strongest fresh. The seed is the keeper: harvest coriander when the seed heads turn tan but before they shatter, dry them in a paper bag, and the threshed seed stores airtight for months to a year.
storage.notes_beginner: Use fresh cilantro within a week or so of picking, since it does not keep long. Coriander seed is the opposite: dry the brown seed heads, shake out the seeds, and store them in a sealed jar for many months.

recommended.name: Santo
recommended.note: A widely grown standard cilantro noted by extensions as slower to bolt than average; dependable, full cilantro flavor, and a common slow-bolt choice for spring and warm-shoulder sowing.

recommended.name: Calypso
recommended.note: One of the slowest-bolting cilantros, with full, frilly leaves and strong regrowth for repeated cut-and-come-again leaf harvests; a top pick where heat shortens the window.

recommended.name: Leisure
recommended.note: A Utah State University-listed slow-bolting type with full leaves and good leaf yield before flowering.

recommended.name: Caribe
recommended.note: Noted by Clemson, along with Santo, as less prone to bolting; a reliable leaf cilantro for the cool shoulders.

recommended.name: Slow Bolting / Long Standing
recommended.note: Selections sold specifically for delayed bolting (also Slo-Bolt, California Long Standing); the best general choice when you want the longest leaf window. For coriander seed instead, any standard cilantro left to flower works, and Moroccan is grown for large seed.

varieties.note_seasoned: Match the type to the goal. For leaves, choose slow-bolting selections, Santo, Calypso, Leisure, Caribe, and the various Slow Bolting and Long Standing strains, which hold in leaf longer before the seedstalk rises; none truly resist heat and long days, but they buy time. Specialty leaf types include Delfino, a feathery cut-leaf cilantro, and Lemon. For coriander seed, any standard cilantro left to bolt sets seed readily, and large-seeded types like Moroccan are grown specifically for the spice. Because the bolt is inevitable, succession sowing matters more than variety for a steady leaf supply.
varieties.note_beginner: If you want leaves, pick a slow-bolting cilantro like Santo, Calypso, Leisure, or one labeled Slow Bolting or Long Standing, which take a bit longer to flower. None of them stop flowering in heat, so sow a fresh batch every couple of weeks too. If you want coriander seed, just let any cilantro flower and go to seed.

companions.note_beginner: Cilantro is small, fast, and easygoing, and its biggest garden gift comes when it flowers: the blooms pull in hoverflies, lady beetles, and tiny parasitic wasps that hunt aphids and caterpillars on nearby crops. It interplants well with tomatoes and peppers, with quick cool-season greens like lettuce and spinach, and with legumes. Keep it away from fennel, a poor neighbor for most herbs that can also cross-pollinate carrot-family plants.
companions.note_seasoned: Most cilantro companion value is real but indirect: allowed to flower, cilantro (an Apiaceae umbel) is a strong insectary plant, recruiting hoverflies, lady beetles, lacewings, and parasitoid wasps that suppress aphids and caterpillars on neighboring crops, an effect extension IPM guidance leans on. Practically it interplants with tomatoes and peppers (which benefit from those beneficials and lend the cool-season cilantro a little afternoon shade), with quick cool greens that share its season, and with legumes. The well-grounded caution is fennel, a broad allelopath and poor herb neighbor that also crosses with carrot-family plants. Avoid clustering cilantro with its Apiaceae relatives (carrot, dill, parsley) on rotation and shared-pest grounds.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Tomatoes and peppers
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Let some cilantro flower near tomatoes and peppers and its blooms bring in helpful insects that eat aphids and caterpillars. The taller plants also give cilantro a little cooling shade in warm weather.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Cilantro is a documented insectary umbel (extension IPM recruits hoverflies/parasitoids with flowering Apiaceae); the tomato/pepper benefit follows by the same beneficial-attraction mechanism plus shared culture, but no cilantro-tomato trial was found, so likely rather than research_backed.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A beneficial-insect pairing: cilantro left to flower recruits hoverflies and parasitoid wasps that attack aphids and hornworms on tomatoes and peppers, and the taller crops shade the cool-season cilantro to slow its bolt. Sound by mechanism and shared culture, not a measured cilantro-tomato effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Lettuce and other quick cool greens
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Lettuce and spinach grow fast and low in the same cool weather as cilantro, so you can sow them together to fill a salad bed.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Quick cool-season interplant logic; shared season and shallow rooting. No cilantro-specific trial.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A cool-season interplant on space and timing: cilantro, lettuce, and spinach share a cool window and a salad bed and are cut young together, with no shared major pest. Traditional and structural rather than a documented effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Beans and peas
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Legumes add a little nitrogen to the soil that the leafy cilantro can use, and they share a cool-to-mild season without crowding it.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Legume nitrogen and complementary habit are widely taught; no cilantro-specific trial.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A legume interplant on nitrogen and structure: beans and peas fix a little nitrogen the leafy cilantro draws on, and the quick cilantro uses the open ground between them. Sound space-and-timing logic, not a measured cilantro effect.

good_seasoned.name: Tomatoes and peppers
good_seasoned.timing: interplant; let some cilantro flower nearby
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Cilantro left to flower recruits hoverflies and parasitoid wasps that attack aphids and hornworms on tomatoes and peppers, and the taller crops shade the cool-season cilantro. A beneficial-attraction pairing by mechanism and shared culture, not a measured cilantro-tomato effect.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Insectary-umbel mechanism is extension-supported; the tomato/pepper benefit follows by analogy, no cilantro-specific trial.

good_seasoned.name: Lettuce and other quick cool greens
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A quick, shallow cool-season green that shares cilantro's season and salad bed; the two interplant and are cut young together. Space-driven and traditional, with no shared major pest.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Quick cool-season interplant lore; no cilantro-specific measured effect.

good_seasoned.name: Beans and peas
good_seasoned.timing: interplant in the same cool window
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A legume interplant: beans and peas fix a little nitrogen for the leafy cilantro and the quick cilantro uses the open ground between them. Space and timing, not a tested effect.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Legume nitrogen plus complementary habit; no cilantro-specific trial.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Fennel
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep cilantro away from fennel. Fennel is a poor neighbor for most herbs and vegetables, said to release substances that hold back nearby plants, and it can also cross-pollinate carrot-family plants like cilantro if both flower.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Fennel allelopathy is a near-universal companion rule with a real mechanism (fennel essential oils suppress seedling growth in bioassays), unmeasured on cilantro specifically; the Apiaceae cross-pollination caution is sound where both are allowed to flower for seed. Traditional/mechanistic, not a pair-tested effect.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Fennel is a broad allelopath and the classic bad herb neighbor, releasing compounds that suppress many plants, and as a fellow Apiaceae it can cross-pollinate cilantro where both flower for seed. Give fennel its own corner. A traditional rule with a real mechanism, not a measured cilantro-fennel trial.

bad_seasoned.name: Fennel
bad_seasoned.timing: keep separate; do not let both flower side by side
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Fennel is a broad allelopath and poor herb companion, and as a fellow carrot-family plant it can cross-pollinate cilantro where both bloom for seed. Grow fennel apart. A traditional rule with a real allelopathic mechanism, not a cilantro-specific trial.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Fennel allelopathy is widely taught and mechanism-backed (EO seedling suppression), unmeasured on cilantro; Apiaceae cross-pollination is real for seed crops.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The first pair of narrow seed leaves pushing up. Cilantro is slow to germinate, often 7 to 21 days, and emergence can be uneven because each round fruit holds two seeds.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The first thin little leaves poking up. Cilantro is slow, often taking one to three weeks, so be patient and keep the soil moist.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep the soil surface evenly moist but never waterlogged through the long germination window. Sow into cool soil; warm soil above about 75°F slows germination and primes early bolting.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil damp but not soggy until the seedlings are up, which can take a couple of weeks. Sow in cool weather, not summer heat.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Any sprouts yet?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Any sprouts yet?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The first true leaves, the broad, scalloped lower cilantro leaves. Now you can tell seedlings from weeds and start thinning.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The first true leaves, the broad lacy cilantro leaves. Now you can thin the seedlings.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin to taste, dense at 2 to 4 inches for cut leaf or 6 to 8 inches for fuller plants, and eat the thinnings. Keep moisture steady to delay the bolt.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Thin the seedlings, leaving them close for cutting leaves or farther apart for bigger plants, and eat the ones you pull. Keep the water steady.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How are they coming along?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How are they coming along?

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leafy plants 4 to 6 inches tall and the patch looking full, well before any central stalk rises. This is the short, productive leaf window.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Leafy plants a few inches tall and full enough to start picking, before any flower stalk appears.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Start cutting outer leaves or shearing now rather than waiting; regular light cutting keeps tender new growth coming. Keep moisture even to hold off bolt, and crop faster as the weather warms.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Start picking the outer leaves now. Picking often keeps new leaves coming. Keep the water steady so it does not bolt, and pick faster when it warms up.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Ready to start cutting?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Ready to start cutting?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Full, tender leaves with no central flower stalk yet. Once a feathery stalk rises the leaf window is closing fast and the lower leaves coarsen.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Full, tender leaves and no flower stalk in the middle yet. Once a stalk appears the good leaf window is closing fast.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut outer leaves or shear the patch a couple of inches above the crown for regrowth. Pick young and in the cool morning, and clear or convert a patch to seed as soon as it shows a stalk.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Take the outer leaves, or cut the patch a couple of inches above the soil so it regrows. Pick young in the cool morning, and once you see a flower stalk either clear it or let it go to coriander seed.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Harvesting regularly?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Harvesting regularly?

growth_stages.name: Bolting (to coriander)
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A feathery central stalk shooting up, the new leaves narrowing into thread-like fronds, then white umbel flowers and green seed. This is the shift from cilantro leaf to coriander seed, and it is rapid.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A tall feathery stalk from the middle, then white flowers and round green seeds. This is cilantro turning into coriander, and it happens fast.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: For leaves, harvest everything worth eating at once. To make coriander, leave the plant: let the flowers feed pollinators, then cut the seed heads as they turn tan but before they shatter, and dry them. Let one plant self-sow if you want volunteers.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: If you want leaves, pick everything good right away. If you want coriander seed, leave the plant to flower and set seed, then cut and dry the brown seed heads. Cilantro often reseeds itself too.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Seen a flower stalk yet?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Seen a flower stalk yet?

notifications.body_seasoned: Your cilantro should have a true leaf or two now. Thin to 2 to 4 inches for cut leaf or 6 to 8 inches for fuller plants, and eat the thinnings.
notifications.body_beginner: Your cilantro seedlings should be big enough to thin. Space them out and eat the little ones you pull.

notifications.body_seasoned: Your cilantro leaves should be usable now. Cut outer leaves or shear a couple of inches above the crown, pick young for the mildest flavor, and refrigerate at once.
notifications.body_beginner: Your cilantro should be big enough to pick. Take the outer leaves or cut the patch a couple of inches above the soil so it regrows. Pick it young.

notifications.title_seasoned: Warm, long days ahead: beat the bolt (or make coriander)
notifications.title_beginner: Warm weather ahead: pick your cilantro
notifications.body_seasoned: Warming, lengthening days bolt cilantro fast. Harvest the leaf patch promptly and lean on a fall sowing; or let the bolted plants flower and set coriander seed.
notifications.body_beginner: Warm, long days make cilantro flower fast. Pick your cilantro leaves now, plan a fall crop, and let the plants that bolt make coriander seed.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot weather warning for your cilantro
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Sustained heat above about 75°F, especially with long days, bolts cilantro fast and coarsens the leaves. Keep moisture even, give afternoon shade, harvest promptly in the cool morning, and in hot regions treat summer as the coriander-seed season rather than the leaf season.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Hot weather makes cilantro flower early and the leaves turn bitter. Water evenly, give it afternoon shade, pick the leaves in the cool morning, and remember a summer plant is really for coriander seed.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hard freeze coming
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Cilantro tolerates frost and light freezes and overwinters under cover in mild zones, but it will not survive a hard freeze. For most frosts keep harvesting; in cold zones a low tunnel or row cover carries an overwintered crop to the earliest spring leaves.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Cilantro handles frost well, so you usually do not need to do anything for a light freeze. A hard freeze will kill it, so in cold areas cover it, and a row cover can help it overwinter and start again in early spring.

germination.text_seasoned: Cilantro germinates slowly, often 7 to 21 days, partly because each round fruit holds two seeds; some growers gently crack the seed to speed and even out emergence. Sow shallowly into cool, moist soil, since warm soil above about 75°F slows germination and pushes early bolting.
germination.text_beginner: Cilantro seeds are slow, often one to three weeks. Keep the soil moist the whole time. The round seed is really two seeds, so cracking it gently can help it sprout faster. Sow in cool weather, not summer heat.

seedling.text_seasoned: Watch for leafhoppers on young plants: their feeding matters less than the aster yellows and curly top viruses they carry, which yellow and twist the plants. A light row cover excludes them; pull any distorted seedlings, since the viral diseases have no cure.
seedling.text_beginner: Watch young cilantro for tiny jumping leafhoppers. They can spread diseases that twist and yellow the plants, so cover the bed with a light row cover and pull out any seedlings that look distorted.

established.text_seasoned: Cut cilantro young for the mildest flavor and cut often: shearing outer leaves or the whole patch a couple of inches above the crown keeps tender new growth coming. Steady moisture keeps the leaves mild and delays the bolt.
established.text_beginner: Pick cilantro young and often for the best flavor. Cut the outer leaves or shear the patch a couple of inches above the soil and it grows back. Keep the water steady so the leaves stay mild and it does not bolt as fast.

harvest.text_seasoned: Shear a cilantro patch a couple of inches above the crown and it regrows for a second cutting; pick in the cool morning and refrigerate at once, since cut cilantro wilts fast. Use the lower, broad leaves for cilantro and let the upper feathery growth signal the coming bolt.
harvest.text_beginner: Cut a cilantro patch a couple of inches above the soil and it grows back for another cutting. Pick in the cool morning and get it in the fridge right away, because it wilts quickly. The broad lower leaves are the best cilantro.

bolting.text_seasoned: Bolting arrives fast and is the whole point of the plant's second act: once the feathery stalk rises, stop fighting it. Harvest the last good leaves, then let the umbels flower for pollinators and set seed. Cut the seed heads as they turn tan but before they shatter, dry them, and thresh out coriander. One plant left to drop seed reliably self-sows.
bolting.text_beginner: Cilantro bolts fast, and that is how you get coriander. When you see the flower stalk, pick the last good leaves, then let it bloom and make seed. Cut the seed heads when they turn tan, dry them, and shake out the coriander. A plant left alone often reseeds itself.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A single cilantro plant yields a small rosette of leaves over a few weeks before bolting, so the crop is grown in dense patches or rows rather than per plant. Cut young or cut-and-come-again, a bed gives one to three cuttings before heat or bolt ends the leaf phase; a plant then left to flower yields a head of coriander seed.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Each cilantro plant gives a small bunch of leaves before it flowers, so it is grown in patches rather than as one big plant. A patch gives a couple of cuttings, then bolts, so sow more every couple of weeks. A bolted plant gives you coriander seed.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Leaf production peaks in the cool weeks of fall and early spring. A spring patch produces for a couple of weeks and then ends abruptly at bolt, while the fall crop, under cooling weather and shortening days, holds far longer and, with cover, into winter. The coriander seed crop peaks from summer-bolted plants.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Cilantro makes the most leaves in the cool weather of fall and early spring. A spring patch gives a couple of good weeks and then bolts, but a fall crop lasts much longer. Summer plants are best left to make coriander seed.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Cilantro is a fast, forgiving first-season crop: leaves in about 4 to 6 weeks from a cool-weather sowing and almost nothing to go wrong if you do not sow into heat. The key to total yield is frequent succession sowing, picking young, and leaning on the fall crop, since a spring patch sown too late bolts before it produces much. The bonus is that even a bolted crop is not wasted, it becomes coriander.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Cilantro is one of the easier, faster herbs for a beginner, with leaves in about a month from a cool-weather sowing. The trick is to sow a little every couple of weeks, pick it young, and grow it in cool weather, especially fall, so it does not bolt before you can eat it. And if it does bolt, you get coriander seed.
factors_seasoned: Timing: a crop grown in the cool shoulders yields leaves well; one caught by heat and long days bolts before producing much. Fall is the most reliable leaf season.
Variety: slow-bolting selections (Santo, Calypso, Leisure, Slow Bolting) extend the leaf window in warmth, though none stop the bolt.
Even moisture: steady water keeps leaves mild, tender, and slower to bolt; drought sharpens the flavor and hurries the seedstalk.
Frequent cutting and succession: picking young and sowing every 2 to 3 weeks keeps tender leaves coming.
Goal: in heat, shift the goal from leaf to coriander seed rather than fighting the bolt.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No reliable extension or peer-reviewed evidence supports timing cilantro planting or harvest by moon phase. Sow by soil temperature, day length, and frost dates instead.

failure_diagnostics.label: Bolting (flower stalk; leaves turn bitter)
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Heat and long days, sped by drought, telling the fast plant to flower and make coriander seed.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your cilantro shot up a feathery stalk and the leaves turned bitter. Cilantro bolts fast in heat and long days, which is its normal shift from leaf to coriander seed, not a mistake. Next time, grow it in cool weather, especially fall, sow a fresh batch every couple of weeks, pick it young, and try slow-bolting types like Santo or Calypso. And let the bolted plant make coriander seed.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Grow it in cool weather, sow every couple of weeks, pick young, choose slow-bolting types, and harvest the bolted plant for coriander.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The plant elongated into a seedstalk and leaf quality collapsed as the foliage narrowed and turned bitter. Bolting is driven by heat above about 75°F and lengthening days, accelerated by drought, and is rapid in cilantro. Growers most often sow too late into warming weather. Next time sow into the cool shoulders, succession-sow, favor fall, use slow-bolting selections, and treat warm-season plantings as a coriander seed crop.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Heat and long-day photoperiod, accelerated by drought; the rapid leaf-to-seed shift that defines the crop.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sow into cool weather, succession-sow every 2 to 3 weeks, lean on fall, choose slow-bolting types, and grow summer plantings for coriander seed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor or very slow germination
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Cilantro seed is naturally slow, and warm soil or dry conditions make it worse.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your cilantro came up thin, patchy, or very slowly. Cilantro seed is slow by nature, often one to three weeks, and germinates poorly in warm soil above about 75°F or when the surface dries out. Next time, sow in cool soil, keep the surface moist, crack the round seed gently to help it along, and use fresh seed.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Sow in cool, moist soil, keep the surface from drying, crack the seed gently, and use fresh seed.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Stand was thin and slow. Cilantro germination is intrinsically slow (the schizocarp holds two seeds) and is further inhibited by warm soil above roughly 75°F and by surface drying. Next time sow into cool, moist soil, consider gently cracking the fruit, keep the seedbed from crusting, and use fresh viable seed.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Slow seed nature plus warm or dry soil inhibiting germination.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sow into cool, moist soil, keep the bed from drying or crusting, crack the seed to even out emergence, and use fresh seed.

failure_diagnostics.label: Dark angular spots on the leaves
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Bacterial leaf spot, the most common cilantro disease, in cool, wet conditions and often from infected seed.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your cilantro leaves got dark, angular, water-soaked spots, worst in cool, wet weather. That is bacterial leaf spot, which spreads on wet leaves and splashing water and often comes in on the seed. Next time, use clean seed, water at the soil line, space plants for airflow, and rotate the bed.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Use clean seed, water at the base, space for airflow, and rotate where you grow cilantro.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Angular, vein-limited lesions indicate bacterial leaf spot (Pseudomonas syringae pv. coriandricola), favored by cool, wet, splashy conditions and frequently seed-borne. Next time use clean or hot-water-treated seed, switch to drip, widen spacing, rotate away from the carrot family, and clear infected debris.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Seed-borne, splash-spread bacterium favored by cool, wet weather and overhead watering.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Use clean seed, irrigate at the soil line, widen spacing, rotate away from Apiaceae, and remove infected debris.

failure_diagnostics.label: Yellowed, twisted, stunted plants
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Aster yellows or curly top, virus-like diseases spread by leafhoppers.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your cilantro turned yellow, twisted, and stunted and did not recover. That is usually aster yellows or curly top, diseases that leafhoppers carry into the plant; there is no cure. Next time, cover plants with a light row cover to keep leafhoppers off, clear nearby weeds that harbor them, and pull infected plants right away.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Use row cover against leafhoppers, clear weedy hosts, and remove infected plants promptly.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Yellowing, distortion, and stunting point to leafhopper-vectored aster yellows or beet curly top virus; infected plants do not recover. Next time exclude leafhoppers with row cover, manage weed reservoirs that host the pathogens and vectors, and rogue symptomatic plants early.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Leafhopper-vectored aster yellows / beet curly top virus, with no cure once infected.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Exclude leafhoppers with row cover, control weed reservoirs, and remove symptomatic plants early.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Cilantro is a classic succession crop: it matures fast and bolts faster, so one sowing is gone in a few weeks. Sow a short row every 2 to 3 weeks through the cool windows, spring until heat and long days set in, and again from late summer through fall, which is the longer, more reliable leaf run. In hot regions skip summer for leaves and succession-sow through the cool fall, winter, and spring, while letting any summer plants run to coriander seed.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: Sow a little cilantro every 2 to 3 weeks instead of all at once, so you always have fresh leaves before it bolts. Do this in spring and again in late summer for fall. In hot areas, skip summer for leaves and keep sowing through the cool months, and let summer plants make coriander seed.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: cilantro_coriander_author_fresh_pilot (Claude Code lane authoring, 2026-06-29). Authored from the cilantro-coriander shell, modeled STRUCTURALLY on the certified culinary-herb template basil, with the cool-season calendar/heat_pause/succession SHAPE modeled on the gate-clean arugula/spinach cool-season pilots (shared cool-season frost/heat climate envelope), and cilantro (Coriandrum sativum, Apiaceae) biology re-derived from live T1 extension sources (USU cilantro/coriander page, Wisconsin Horticulture, Clemson, Texas A&M, WSU PNW vegetable problems). DRAFT for daily biology-fidelity review, not certified: launch flags false. Key cilantro-vs-basil refits, the BIG inversion: basil is a WARM-season frost-TENDER herb grown through summer, while cilantro is a COOL-season FROST-TOLERANT herb whose calendar INVERTS, spring + fall leaf windows with a SUMMER heat_pause bolt gap and overwintering in mild zones. ONE plant, TWO products: the leaf is CILANTRO, the seed is CORIANDER, so the bolt that ends the leaf crop begins the seed crop. Very fast (baby leaf ~3 to 4 weeks, bolts ~45 to 60 days) and succession-sown every 2 to 3 weeks because it bolts; slow-bolt cultivars (Santo, Calypso, Leisure) exist. Apiaceae rotation/pest/disease set replaces basil's Lamiaceae one: aphids and leafhoppers (aster yellows / curly top), and bacterial leaf spot / damping-off / powdery mildew / soft rot. pH 6.2 to 6.8; spacing 2 to 4 inches (baby leaf / broadcast); direct-sown. successions_realized is CC-derived (deriver), not hand-authored. See cilantro_coriander_NOTES.md for modeled values and flags.

open_findings.summary: All 10 regions' per-zone calendars are MODELED from cilantro's cool-season frost/heat envelope and the regional extension planting-calendar sources, reusing the gate-clean arugula/spinach cool-season calendar SHAPE (spring + fall plant windows, summer heat_pause in warm regions, cold_pause in winter, overwinter in mild zones). Few cilantro-per-region charts exist; the frost-anchored cool-season shape is shared climate truth across cool-season leafy crops, and the cilantro-specific refit is its dual leaf/seed use and rapid heat bolt. resolution_method on each cell is 'cc_author_pilot_modeled'. Flagged for the daily biology-fidelity review.
open_findings.basis: Cool-season sowing windows are frost/heat-driven and shared across cool-season crops; cilantro shares arugula's bolt-at-~75F, frost-tolerant, overwinter-mild envelope. Harvest months may run ~2 to 4 weeks later than arugula's given cilantro's slower maturity (DTM 45 to 80 vs 20 to 40); the review may nudge harvest tokens.

open_findings.summary: Each genuinely-hot region cell carries a backed heat_pause object (months + basis_seasoned + source + URL). The basis note frames the pause honestly for cilantro: leaf production stops because the crop bolts to coriander seed almost at once above ~75F, so the summer is the coriander-seed season rather than the leaf season. Cool northern zones 3 to 5 are modeled as running through summer (no heat_pause).
open_findings.basis: Task heat_pause why-note rule + the locked cool-season heat_pause convention (a summer leaf gap with a fall crop after = backed heat_pause, not season_over).

open_findings.summary: days_to_maturity [45, 80] (mid 60) is the Wisconsin Horticulture leaf figure (seed crop needs 100+ days, stated in prose). spacing_inches [2, 4] reflects the baby-leaf / broadcast and cut-leaf practice (USU 2 inches for leaf); fuller plants at 6 to 8 inches and seed plants at 8 to 12 inches are stated in the thinning/variety prose. germination_temp_f [55, 70] is a modeled cool-soil band (USU/TAMU give cool-season growth 50 to 85F and slow 7 to 21 day germination; no single T1 page tables an explicit min/max).
open_findings.basis: Within the cited USU / Wisconsin / Texas A&M figures; the operative facts (fast leaf, slow seed, baby-leaf spacing, warm-soil-inhibited slow germination) are sourced and surfaced in prose.

open_findings.summary: ph.preferred_range [6.2, 6.8] follows the commonly cited cilantro optimum (slightly acidic to neutral); Clemson states a working range of 6 to 7, used as the tolerated band [6.0, 7.5]. Cilantro is not pH-sensitive.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: Up North (zones 3 through 7), cilantro is a quick spring-and-fall leaf herb. Start sowing in early spring as soon as you can work the soil, since cilantro takes frost, and sow a little every 2 to 3 weeks. In the coldest zones the cool summer lets it keep making leaves, but in the milder zones the hottest weeks bolt it, so take a break in midsummer and sow again for fall, the best leaf season. A last sowing under a row cover can overwinter for super-early spring greens, and any summer plant that bolts gives you coriander seed.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In the cold-winter North (zones 3 through 7), cilantro is a fast spring-and-fall succession herb built around frost. Sow as soon as the soil can be worked, since cilantro tolerates frost, and sow a short row every 2 to 3 weeks. In the coolest zones the cool summer often carries leaf production through, while in the warmer end of the band midsummer heat and long days bolt it, so the leaf calendar pauses through the hottest weeks and resumes for the main fall crop. A late sowing under a row cover can overwinter for the earliest spring picking, and bolted summer plants are left for coriander seed.
