crops.description_seasoned: Cilantro and coriander are one plant, Coriandrum sativum, an annual herb in the carrot family (Apiaceae) grown for two products: the leaf is the herb cilantro and the dried seed is the spice coriander. Its defining biology is the mirror image of warm-season herbs like basil: cilantro is a COOL-season, frost-tolerant crop that bolts almost the moment the weather warms, sending up a flower stalk above roughly 75°F and with lengthening days. That single fact shapes everything. The spring leaf window is short, fall is the main and most reliable leaf season, and in mild zones a fall sowing overwinters for the earliest, longest spring run; in hot regions and the heat of summer the leaf crop is brief and growers instead let the plant bolt and harvest coriander seed. Because the bolt is fast and inevitable, cilantro is a succession crop above all, sown in small batches every 2 to 3 weeks so a fresh, pre-bolt cohort is always coming on. It is direct-sown (a slender taproot resents transplanting), fast (baby leaf in about 3 to 4 weeks, bolting by 45 to 60 days), and easy, with few serious pests. The grower's real skill is timing the crop into the cool shoulders of the year and accepting the bolt as the start of the coriander harvest rather than a failure.
crops.description_beginner: Cilantro and coriander come from the very same plant: the leaves are cilantro and the dried seeds are the spice coriander. Unlike warm-season herbs such as basil, cilantro is a cool-weather plant that handles frost but bolts (flowers) very fast once it gets warm, above about 75°F, and the leaves turn bitter. So the trick is to grow it in the cool parts of the year: a short spring window, a longer and better fall crop, and overwintering in mild areas. Sow a little every 2 to 3 weeks, since each plant bolts after a few weeks, and plant the seeds right in the garden because cilantro does not like being moved. It is fast and easy, with baby leaves in about 3 to 4 weeks. And when summer heat finally makes it bolt, do not be discouraged: let it flower and you get coriander seed.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Begin cutting cilantro leaves once plants are about 4 to 6 inches tall, roughly 3 to 6 weeks from sowing, well before any central stalk rises. Cut the broad lower leaves, or shear the whole patch a couple of inches above the crown for a second cutting, taking no more than a third at a time and picking in the cool morning for the mildest flavor. Pick promptly and often as the weather warms, since the leaf window closes fast at bolt. For coriander, stop cutting and let the plant flower and set seed; harvest the seed heads as they turn from green to tan but before they shatter, dry them in a paper bag, then thresh and store the seed airtight.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Start picking cilantro when the plants are about 4 to 6 inches tall, a few weeks after sowing and before you see a flower stalk. Take the outer leaves or cut the whole patch a couple of inches above the soil so it regrows, and pick in the cool morning for the best flavor. Pick often, because once it bolts the leaves turn bitter fast. To get coriander, let the plant flower and form seeds, then cut the seed heads when they turn tan, dry them, and shake out the round seeds to store.

crops.name: Chives

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Chives are not fussy about soil and grow in almost any kind, but they do best in loose, fertile ground with some compost mixed in, kept evenly moist but never soggy. Good drainage matters most: an established clump handles a short dry spell, but ground that stays wet through winter can rot the roots and crown.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Chives tolerate a wide range of soils but grow best in a well-drained loam rich in organic matter, kept evenly moist. The University of Minnesota recommends well-drained soil rich in organic matter, and Michigan State notes chives grow best in soils high in organic matter while adapting to most soil types. Work compost into the bed before planting to feed a clump you cut from for years, and site it where water does not stand, since a waterlogged crown, especially over winter, invites rot on this otherwise trouble-free perennial.

ph.note_beginner: Chives grow best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, about 6.0 to 7.0. Most garden soil is fine, and a simple soil test tells you where you stand.
ph.note_seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0, slightly acidic to neutral, the range the University of Minnesota and Michigan State both list as best for chives; they still do fine across roughly 5.5 to 7.5. Chives are not pH-sensitive, so in most gardens no adjustment is needed beyond a soil-test baseline.

fertilizer.frequency: light, once or twice per season
fertilizer.timing: compost worked in before planting, then an optional light feeding in spring or after a heavy cutting
fertilizer.example_product: 5-10-5 or a balanced vegetable fertilizer, or fish emulsion for a gentle boost
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Chives are light feeders with low nutrient needs and rarely need regular fertilizer. The University of Minnesota suggests only a very light application of a 5-10-5 fertilizer once each spring if a clump looks weak, on top of compost worked in before planting. A clump you cut from repeatedly benefits from a light feeding after a hard shearing to push fresh tender regrowth; in containers, where frequent watering leaches nutrients, a dilute liquid feed every four to six weeks keeps leaves green. Avoid heavy nitrogen, which softens the flavor.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Chives do not need much feeding. Mix some compost into the soil before planting, and that is often enough. If a clump looks weak or you cut it hard, give it a light feeding to bring back fresh green leaves. In a pot, feed lightly with a diluted liquid fertilizer every few weeks, since watering washes nutrients out.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time to give your chives a light feeding if they look weak.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Time to give your chives a light feeding.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: Light, balanced feeding for a low-demand perennial: a little 5-10-5 or balanced fertilizer worked in before planting, then an optional light feed in spring or after a hard cutting. Go easy on nitrogen, which softens flavor on a crop eaten fresh.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer such as 5-10-5, a little worked into the soil before planting, then feed lightly only if the plant looks weak or after you cut it hard.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A very light application of 5-10-5 once in spring is plenty for an established clump; a compost-rich bed often needs no feeding at all, with a light feed only after a hard shearing.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: One light feeding in spring is plenty, or none at all if your soil is good; in a pot, a diluted liquid feed every four to six weeks.

pests.name: Onion thrips
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny, slender pale-yellow to brown insects hiding down in the leaf folds, leaving silvery or whitish streaks and flecks on the green blades. Bad infestations make the foliage look bleached and papery.
pests.cause_beginner: Thrips are minute sap-sucking insects, common on onion-family plants, that rasp the leaves and are worst in hot, dry weather. Chives usually shrug them off, but a heavy year can mark the leaves.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Hose the plants down to knock thrips off, shear a badly streaked clump to the base so it regrows clean, and use insecticidal soap on the leaves if needed. Rinse cut leaves before use.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep plants watered in hot spells, welcome helpful insects like lacewings and pirate bugs, and cut a marked-up clump back to force fresh leaves.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Onion thrips (Thrips tabaci) feeding in the leaf axils and folds, producing silvery-white stippling, streaking, and a bleached, papery look on heavy pressure; they favor hot, dry weather. On chives the damage is usually cosmetic, but a severe year degrades a leaf crop.
pests.cause_seasoned: Thrips tabaci, the principal allium thrips, rasps leaf surfaces and feeds on the sap; populations build fast in hot, dry conditions and on stressed plants.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Dislodge with a strong water jet, shear a heavily infested clump to the base to remove the population and force clean regrowth, and spray insecticidal soap or spinosad if warranted; conserve natural enemies (minute pirate bugs, lacewings). Keeping plants unstressed and watered blunts outbreaks.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid drought stress, conserve natural enemies, cut back streaked foliage to reset the clump, and avoid siting chives beside heavily thrips-pressured onion or garlic plantings.

pests.name: Allium leafminer
pests.symptoms_beginner: Rows of white dots punched down a leaf where the adult fly fed, then wavy pale mines inside the leaves, with small maggots or brown seed-like pupae tucked into the leaf bases. It shows up in spring and again in fall.
pests.cause_beginner: The allium leafminer is a small fly whose larvae tunnel inside onion-family leaves, including chives, and burrow toward the base. It is a newer pest in parts of the eastern United States.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover plants with floating row cover in early spring and again in fall to keep the flies off, cut off and destroy mined leaves, and clean up plant debris.
pests.prevention_beginner: Use row cover during the spring and fall flights, remove mined leaves, and keep the bed clean.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Allium leafminer (Phytomyza gymnostoma): lines of white oviposition punctures down the distal leaf, followed by larval mines and brown puparia lodged in leaf sheaths and bulbs. The University of Maryland lists chive (A. schoenoprasum) among its hosts; wounds open the door to secondary bacterial and fungal rots.
pests.cause_seasoned: Phytomyza gymnostoma, an invasive allium-specific fly with a spring flight (roughly March into May) and a fall flight (September into October); larvae mine toward the leaf base and bulb, with up to dozens of pupae per plant in severe cases.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Exclude the adults with floating row cover timed to the spring and fall flights, remove and destroy mined foliage, and sanitize crop debris; spinosad or azadirachtin can help where pressure is high. Rotation away from recently infested allium ground reduces carryover.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Row-cover through both flight periods, remove infested leaves, sanitize residue, and separate new plantings from pressured allium beds.

pests.name: Onion maggot
pests.symptoms_beginner: Yellowing, wilting, and stunted growth as small white maggots tunnel into the base of the plant and the bulbs below the soil, sometimes rotting the crown. Worst in cool, wet springs.
pests.cause_beginner: Onion maggots are the larvae of a fly that lays eggs at the base of onion-family plants; the maggots eat into the roots and bulbs. Chives are rarely hit hard, but a clump can be damaged.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no rescue for a maggot-riddled crown, so remove badly affected plants. Use row cover to keep the flies off, and clean up debris and culls that attract them.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover plants with row cover in spring, avoid leaving old bulbs and debris around, and do not crowd alliums together.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Onion maggot (Delia antiqua) larvae mining into the basal plate, roots, and bulbs, causing wilting, yellowing, stunting, and crown rot; damage is worst in cool, moist springs and where allium debris accumulates. Established chive clumps are seldom destroyed but can be set back.
pests.cause_seasoned: Delia antiqua overwinters as pupae in the soil; spring flies lay eggs at plant bases and successive generations attack roots and bulbs, favored by cool wet weather and by cull and debris that lure egg-laying.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy infested plants, exclude flies with floating row cover, and sanitize debris and culls; rotation and avoiding dense allium plantings limit buildup. No effective organic rescue exists once larvae are in the crown.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Row-cover early, sanitize allium residue, rotate, and avoid clustering chives with other alliums that concentrate the fly.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_beginner: Clusters of tiny soft green or gray insects on the leaves and flower stalks, sometimes with sticky residue. Chives rarely get them badly, and their scent even helps keep aphids off nearby plants.
pests.cause_beginner: Aphids are small sap-sucking insects that breed fast on soft growth. They are an occasional, minor visitor on chives.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water or use insecticidal soap, and rinse cut leaves before use. It is seldom needed.
pests.prevention_beginner: Welcome ladybugs and lacewings, go easy on nitrogen, and check flower stalks now and then.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Occasional aphid colonies on foliage and scapes; chives are among the most aphid-free herbs (their odor is credited with repelling aphids from neighbors), so infestations are minor and sporadic rather than a standing threat.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several aphid species may alight on chives in flushes of soft growth, but the plant's sulfur compounds make it an inhospitable host, so colonies rarely persist.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: A water jet or insecticidal soap handles the rare colony; conserve lady beetles, lacewings, and hoverflies, which the chive umbels also feed when in bloom.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen, conserve natural enemies, and monitor scapes; control is seldom warranted on chives.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Pale, fuzzy gray-violet patches on the leaves in cool, damp weather, with the blades yellowing and collapsing. It spreads fastest in wet, crowded, poorly drained plantings.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus-like disease of the onion family, favored by cool, humid, wet conditions, that can affect chives along with onions, garlic, and leeks.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove affected leaves, improve airflow by dividing crowded clumps, water at the base rather than over the leaves, and cut a badly hit clump back so it regrows in drier weather.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Space and divide plants for airflow, water at the soil line, and avoid soggy, shaded, crowded spots.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Downy mildew (Peronospora destructor) producing pale oval patches that turn violet-gray with sporulation under moisture, with leaves paling, yellowing, and collapsing; it is favored by cool (below about 75°F), humid, wet conditions and affects chives among many alliums.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Peronospora destructor, an oomycete spread by wind and splashing water and favored by cool, moist weather and long leaf-wetness periods; crowded, poorly drained plantings hold it.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Manage culturally: divide crowded clumps and space for airflow, irrigate at the soil line, remove infected foliage, and shear a heavily affected clump to regrow under drier conditions. The home garden has no reliable cure once it is established.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Open the canopy by dividing, water at the base, site in well-drained sun, and avoid the cool, wet, crowded conditions the pathogen needs.

diseases.name: Rust
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Bright orange raised spots or streaks (pustules) scattered on the leaves. Heavily rusted blades yellow and dry up. It is more common in wet seasons and on crowded, over-fed plants.
diseases.cause_beginner: Rust is a fungal disease of the onion family, including chives, that shows as orange pustules on the leaves and spreads by airborne spores in damp weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Cut off and destroy rusty leaves or shear the clump to the base to regrow clean, thin crowded plantings for airflow, and avoid overhead watering and heavy nitrogen.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Give plants room and airflow, water at the base, go easy on nitrogen, and remove rusty foliage promptly.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Allium rust (Puccinia species) forming bright orange to rusty raised pustules on leaves and scapes, with chlorosis and dieback of heavily infected foliage; it is favored by moist conditions, crowding, and lush high-nitrogen growth, and affects chives along with garlic, leeks, and onions.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Puccinia rust fungi spread by airborne urediniospores in humid weather; dense stands and excess nitrogen worsen it.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Shear infected foliage (a hard cut to the base removes the pustules and regrows clean), divide to open crowded clumps, avoid overhead irrigation and heavy nitrogen, and remove debris. Fungicides are rarely warranted in a home planting.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Divide for airflow, moderate nitrogen, irrigate at the soil line, and cut out rust early before it spreads.

diseases.name: White rot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Yellowing, wilting plants whose roots and crown rot, with a fluffy white mold and tiny black specks (like poppy seeds) at the base. Affected plants do not recover, and the disease stays in the soil for many years.
diseases.cause_beginner: White rot is a serious soil fungus of the onion family that rots the roots and crown. Once it is in the soil it lasts a very long time, so keeping it out is the whole game.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure. Remove and destroy affected plants along with the soil around the roots, and do not plant chives, onions, or garlic in that spot again. Never move infected soil or plants to a clean bed.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Start with clean plants, do not bring in soil from an infected garden, and rotate onion-family plants to fresh ground.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: White rot (Sclerotium cepivorum) causing yellowing, wilting, and a soft rot of roots and crown, with a fluffy white mycelium and abundant tiny black sclerotia at the base; the sclerotia persist in soil for many years, and the disease affects chives with onions, garlic, and leeks.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Sclerotium cepivorum, a soilborne fungus favored by cool, moist soil; its long-lived sclerotia make an infested site unusable for alliums for a decade or more, so exclusion and sanitation are the only real controls.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No rescue: rogue out affected plants with surrounding soil, avoid spreading infested soil on tools or transplants, and do not replant alliums in the site. Long rotation is the standing management.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant clean, sclerotia-free stock, quarantine infested ground from alliums, sanitize tools, and never import garden soil of unknown history.

diseases.name: Botrytis (leaf blight and neck rot)
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small whitish sunken spots on the leaves in cool, wet weather that can run together and brown out the tops, sometimes with a gray fuzzy mold. It is worst in humid, crowded plantings.
diseases.cause_beginner: Botrytis is a gray-mold fungus of the onion family that spots and blights the leaves in cool, damp, crowded conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove spotted leaves or shear the clump to regrow, open up crowded plantings for airflow, and water at the base instead of over the leaves.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Space and divide for airflow, water at the soil line, and clean up dead foliage.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Botrytis leaf blight and neck rot (Botrytis species) producing small white sunken leaf spots that coalesce into blast and tip dieback under cool, moist conditions, sometimes with gray sporulation; humid, crowded stands favor it, and it affects chives among the alliums.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Botrytis fungi favored by cool, wet, humid weather and dense canopies; splashing water and leaf wetness spread the spores.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Cull spotted foliage or shear the clump to regrow, divide to open the stand, irrigate at the soil line, and remove senescing debris. Fungicides are seldom needed on a home chive planting.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Divide for airflow, water low and early, and sanitize dead foliage to cut inoculum.

watering.frequency_seasoned: About 1 inch of water per week, kept even; chives are drought tolerant once the clump is established, but steady moisture keeps the leaves tender and green over the long cutting season. Do not let established plants sit in constantly wet soil.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water about once a week so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly 1 inch a week. Established chives handle a dry spell, but even water keeps the leaves tender.
watering.amount_seasoned: Roughly 1 inch per week, more in hot, dry spells; the University of Minnesota advises watering deeply when rainfall is sparse so the soil does not dry out around the roots. A mulch helps hold even moisture for a clump you cut from for years.
watering.amount_beginner: Aim for about 1 inch of water a week, a bit more when it is hot and dry. Mulch helps keep the soil evenly moist.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose; keeping the foliage dry checks the leaf diseases (downy mildew, rust, botrytis) chives can catch in cool, wet, crowded conditions.
watering.method_beginner: Water at the base of the plants rather than over the leaves, which helps prevent leaf diseases.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing, floppy foliage and crown or root rot in constantly wet, poorly drained ground, especially over winter; downy mildew and botrytis also flare in cool, saturated, crowded conditions.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Leaves go yellow and floppy and the base can rot in soggy soil, especially over winter.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting, slowed growth, and tougher, sharper foliage in prolonged drought; established clumps recover quickly once watered, but a dry, hot spell can push them toward summer dormancy.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Wilting leaves that taste sharper and tougher, and slowed growth when the soil dries out for too long.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Even moisture keeps chives growing tender and green; an established clump tolerates short dry spells, but prolonged drought toughens the leaves and can trigger early summer dormancy in hot regions.
watering.method_note_beginner: Keep the water fairly steady so the leaves stay tender; chives handle a short dry spell once established, but long droughts make them tough.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Steady moisture matters most through the slow germination (2 to 3 weeks) and while a new clump establishes; once the root system is down the plant is forgiving.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Keep the soil moist while the seeds are sprouting, which takes a couple of weeks, and while a new plant gets going.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Chives are easiest to establish from a division or a nursery clump, which gives a cuttable plant in weeks, but they also grow readily from seed. The seed is slow, germinating over about 2 to 3 weeks (up to 4 to 6 in cool soil), so start it indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost and transplant the young clumps out after hardening off, or direct-sow once the soil warms. Plant outdoors in spring after hard-frost danger passes in cold regions, or in fall through late winter in mild and hot regions. Set clumps 8 to 12 inches apart; they widen over the years and are the easiest herb to propagate by simply lifting and splitting an established clump.
start_method.notes_beginner: The easiest way to start chives is to buy a small pot or split a clump from a friend, which is ready to cut almost right away. You can also grow them from seed, but the seed is slow, taking a couple of weeks or more, so start it indoors about 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost, or sow it outside once the soil is warm. Plant outside in spring in cold areas, or in fall through winter where summers are hot. Space plants about 8 to 12 inches apart, and remember one clump can be split into many.

drainage.saucer_practice: Empty the saucer after watering so the roots never sit in water, which invites crown and root rot.

soil_mix.type_beginner: A good-quality potting mix, not garden soil.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in a little compost for steady nutrients.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: A light, well-drained potting mix with some organic matter.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend in compost; chives are light feeders, so no heavy starter fertilizer is needed.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out faster than the ground, so check every day or two in warm weather and keep the mix evenly moist.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Feed lightly with a diluted liquid fertilizer every four to six weeks, since watering washes nutrients out of pots.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Chives are very hardy, so a pot can stay outside through fall and winter in most areas; the leaves die back and the plant regrows in spring. In the coldest zones the small amount of soil in a pot freezes harder than the ground, so sink the pot in the garden, move it against the house, or mulch it heavily. You can also dig up a small clump in fall, pot it, and grow it on a bright windowsill for winter snipping.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Chives are frost-hardy to roughly zone 3 and go dormant over winter, so an outdoor pot simply dies back and returns in spring. Container root volume freezes harder than open ground, so in cold zones sink the pot, cluster pots against a wall, or mulch to buffer the roots. A classic trick is to lift a small divided clump in fall, pot it, give it a few weeks of cold to satisfy dormancy, then bring it to a sunny window for fresh winter leaves.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Chives are one of the best herbs for a pot. Use a container at least 6 inches deep with drainage holes, keep it watered, and snip leaves as you need them. A pot does well on a sunny windowsill or step, and because chives are so hardy it can carry on outdoors long after tender herbs are done.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Chives grow very well in a container at least 6 inches deep, harvested cut-and-come-again. Keep moisture even, since pots dry fast, and feed only lightly. A pot is the easiest way to keep chives by the kitchen door, to move a small clump indoors for winter cutting, and to contain a plant that self-sows in the open garden.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry faster than beds; check moisture every day or two in warmth and water deeply before the mix dries out.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Container chives need only a light feed, a dilute liquid fertilizer every four to six weeks, because frequent watering leaches the limited mix.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering container suits chives well, smoothing out the steady moisture that keeps the leaves tender over a long cutting season.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match because it keeps the water steady, which keeps chives tender and productive.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: Chives have a shallow, fibrous root system and do not need depth; a pot 6 inches or deeper is plenty, and extra width lets the clump widen and lets you grow more to cut from.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Chives have shallow roots, so a pot at least 6 inches deep is fine. Extra width lets the clump spread and gives you more to cut.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Avoid establishing chives where onions, garlic, leeks, shallots, or other chives grew recently: the alliums share soilborne troubles, above all white rot (whose sclerotia persist for years), plus pink root, onion maggot, and thrips. Because chives are a long-lived perennial planted once and left in place, rotation matters mainly when you first site a clump or replace an old one; keep new plantings out of recently cropped allium ground.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Do not plant chives where you recently grew onions, garlic, or leeks, since onion-family plants share soil diseases and pests that build up. Because chives stay put for years, this mainly matters when you first choose the spot.
rotation.good_after: Leafy greens or legumes (peas, beans).
rotation.note_seasoned: Chives are an allium, so they share the onion family's soilborne diseases (white rot, pink root) and pests (onion maggot, thrips, allium leafminer). Standard allium guidance keeps the family off the same ground for several years, but chives are a permanent perennial, so the practical rule is to establish a new clump in ground that has not recently grown onions, garlic, or leeks, and to follow a leafy or legume crop rather than another allium. A clump left to flower self-sows freely, so pull stray seedlings that come up out of place.
rotation.note_beginner: Chives are in the onion family, so they can pick up the same soil diseases as onions and garlic. Since a chive clump stays in one place for years, just choose a spot where you have not grown onion-family plants recently, ideally after leafy greens or beans. Chives that flower drop seed, so pull up stray seedlings where you do not want them.

bolting.triggers: natural flowering in late spring to early summer, not heat-bolting; leaves near the scapes turn tough and hollow-woody
bolting.prevention_seasoned: Chives do not bolt-and-quit the way lettuce or cilantro do; flowering is a normal, even desirable, part of a perennial allium's year. In late spring to early summer the clump sends up round pink to pale purple flower scapes above the leaves, and the flowers are edible and good for pollinators. The catch is twofold: the foliage around the scapes turns tougher and more hollow, and a clump left to set seed self-sows prolifically (garlic chives especially). The standard practice is to enjoy some flowers, then shear the whole clump down to about 1 to 2 inches after bloom, which removes the spent scapes before they seed and forces a fresh flush of tender leaves. Removing flower stalks at the soil line as they fade also prevents unwanted volunteer seedlings.
bolting.prevention_beginner: Chives are not like cilantro; flowering is normal and the flowers are pretty and edible. But two things happen when they bloom: the leaves get tougher, and if the flowers go to seed you get lots of surprise seedlings. So enjoy some flowers, then cut the whole clump back to about 1 to 2 inches. That takes off the old flower stalks before they seed and brings back fresh, tender leaves.
bolting.note_seasoned: Flowering in chives is a perennial life-cycle event in late spring to early summer, not a heat response, and it is partly a feature: the pink-purple umbels are edible and strong insectary plants. Its practical downside is coarsened, hollow foliage and prolific self-seeding, both fixed by shearing the clump hard after bloom to renew tender leaves and cut off seed set. Garlic chives (Allium tuberosum) flower later, in late summer, are white, and self-sow so freely they can become weedy if the scapes are not removed.
bolting.note_beginner: Chives flower in late spring or early summer with round pink-purple blooms, and that is normal, not a mistake. The flowers taste good and feed the bees. Just know the leaves get tougher around the flowers, and the seeds can sprout all over, so cutting the clump back after it blooms keeps the leaves tender and the plant tidy.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Fresh chives wilt quickly at room temperature, so refrigerate promptly after cutting; the leaves lose their delicate onion aroma fast once cut, so use them soon.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Do not leave cut chives out on the counter, where they wilt fast. Chill them and use them soon after cutting.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerate fresh chives unwashed in a loose or perforated bag, or wrapped in a slightly damp paper towel, in the crisper; they hold about 1 week. Wash only at use, since trapped moisture speeds breakdown.
storage.fridge_beginner: Store fresh chives unwashed in a loose bag in the fridge, where they keep about a week. Wash them only when you are ready to use them.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Chives freeze better than they dry: snip the washed leaves and freeze them loose or in ice-cube trays with a little water; the University of Minnesota notes you can use the frozen pieces straight from the freezer without thawing. Drying is the weakest option, since dried chives lose most of their delicate flavor, so freezing is preferred for keeping.
storage.freezer_beginner: Chives are best frozen rather than dried. Chop the clean leaves and freeze them loose or in an ice-cube tray with a little water, then use them straight from the freezer without thawing. Drying works but loses most of the flavor.
storage.notes_seasoned: Chives are best fresh, and because the clump keeps producing, the easiest storage is to cut what you need as you need it. Cut chives keep about a week refrigerated. For longer keeping, freeze them chopped (loose or in cubes) rather than drying, which sacrifices most of the flavor; frozen chives go straight into cooking without thawing.
storage.notes_beginner: The best way to store chives is to leave them growing and cut what you need. Picked chives keep about a week in the fridge. To save extra, freeze them chopped rather than drying them, since drying loses most of the flavor.

recommended.name: Common Chives
recommended.note: The standard Allium schoenoprasum: fine, hollow, grass-like leaves in tidy clumps 8 to 14 inches tall, with edible pink to pale purple pom-pom flowers in late spring. Mild onion flavor, extremely hardy, and the workhorse kitchen chive.

recommended.name: Fine Leaf (Grolau types)
recommended.note: Selections with especially fine, slender, dark green leaves and vigorous regrowth; a favorite for forcing and for growing in pots on a windowsill because it recovers quickly from cutting.

recommended.name: Staro
recommended.note: A thicker-leaved Swiss selection bred for uniform, upright, easily cut blades that hold their form; prized for kitchen cutting and for freezing, since the sturdier leaves handle handling well.

recommended.name: Forescate
recommended.note: A taller ornamental-leaning selection, roughly 18 to 20 inches, with showy rosy-pink flowers; grown as much for the bloom and pollinators as for the kitchen.

recommended.name: Garlic Chives (Allium tuberosum)
recommended.note: A distinct species, not a variety of common chives: flat, strap-like gray-green leaves with a mild garlic flavor and white star-shaped flowers in late summer to early fall. Hardy in roughly zones 3 to 9 and very heat, cold, and drought tolerant once established, but it self-seeds prolifically and can become weedy, so remove spent flower stalks.

varieties.note_seasoned: Chives come in two distinct plants. Common chives (Allium schoenoprasum) are the familiar fine, hollow-leaved clump with pink-purple spring flowers and a mild onion taste; named selections differ mostly in leaf fineness and vigor, from the slender Fine Leaf and Grolau strains favored for pots and forcing, to the thick, easy-cutting Staro, to taller showy-flowered Forescate. Garlic chives (Allium tuberosum) are a separate species with flat leaves, a garlic flavor, and white late-summer flowers; they are tougher in heat and drought but self-sow aggressively. All are grown much the same way, so choice comes down to flavor (onion versus garlic), leaf form, and how much you value the flowers, while any chive self-seeds if you let the blooms set seed.
varieties.note_beginner: There are really two kinds. Common chives have thin, hollow leaves and pink-purple flowers and taste mildly of onion; the named types just vary in how fine or sturdy the leaves are. Garlic chives are a different plant with flat leaves, a mild garlic taste, and white flowers in late summer, and they take heat well but spread by seed a lot. They all grow the same way, so pick by flavor and looks, and cut off the flowers if you do not want seedlings everywhere.

companions.note_beginner: Chives are a classic companion herb: their oniony scent is said to help keep aphids and some other pests off nearby plants, and their early flowers feed pollinators and helpful insects. Gardeners traditionally tuck them at the base of roses (for black spot and aphids) and apple trees (for scab), and near carrots and tomatoes. The one plant to keep them away from is beans and peas, which onion-family plants can slow down.
companions.note_seasoned: Much of the chive companion tradition rests on two real mechanisms: allium sulfur compounds that deter aphids and some fungal problems, and the flowering umbels' pull on hoverflies, lady beetles, and parasitoid wasps. Michigan State, citing Penn State, passes along the traditional pairings of chives at the base of apple trees (to help suppress apple scab) and roses (black spot), plus a reputed boost to carrots. These are hedged tradition with a plausible mechanism, not measured trials. The one well-grounded caution is the allium-legume antagonism: onions and their relatives are widely documented to inhibit beans and peas, so keep chives away from legumes.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: From seed, the first thin, grassy blades pushing up. Chive seed is slow and can take 2 to 3 weeks, up to 4 to 6 in cool soil, and emergence is uneven. A division or nursery clump skips this stage entirely.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: If you sowed seed, the first thin little green blades. Chive seed is slow, often a couple of weeks or more, so be patient. A bought or divided clump skips this step.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep the surface evenly moist through the long germination and do not let it crust or dry. If you want a faster start, set out a division or nursery clump instead of sowing seed.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil damp but not soggy until the seedlings appear, which can take a few weeks. For a quicker start, plant a small pot or a split clump instead of seed.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Any sprouts yet?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Any sprouts yet?

growth_stages.name: Establishment (first year)
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A young clump filling out with several upright blades. In the first year it is building the root and bulblet reserves it needs to overwinter and return.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A small clump of grassy leaves getting fuller. In its first year the plant is putting energy into its roots so it comes back next spring.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest sparingly the first year and keep moisture steady so the clump can bank strength for winter; a light feeding helps a weak plant. Thin or space seedlings to about 8 to 12 inches.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Go easy on cutting the first year and keep the soil moist so the plant gets strong for winter. Space plants about 8 to 12 inches apart.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How is the clump filling in?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How is it filling in?

growth_stages.name: Harvest (cut-and-come-again)
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Full clumps 6 inches or more tall that you cut from repeatedly: shear the outer blades to about 1 to 2 inches and the clump regrows for months, spring through fall in cold regions and through the cool season where summers are hot.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Full clumps about 6 inches tall you can keep cutting from. Snip the leaves to about 1 to 2 inches above the soil and they grow back again and again.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut blades near the base, leaving some green so the clump keeps feeding itself, and never shear it fully bare. Regular cutting keeps tender new growth coming; shear the whole clump hard after flowering to renew it.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Cut the leaves to about 1 to 2 inches, leaving some green behind, and they grow back. Cutting often keeps them tender. After the flowers fade, cut the whole clump back to freshen it.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Harvesting regularly?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Harvesting regularly?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Round pink to pale purple flower globes rising above the leaves in late spring to early summer (white in late summer for garlic chives). The blooms are edible, but foliage near the scapes coarsens.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Round pink-purple flowers on stalks above the leaves in late spring or early summer. They are pretty and edible, but the leaves near them get tougher.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Enjoy or harvest some flowers just as they open, then shear the clump to about 1 to 2 inches to remove spent scapes before they seed and to force a fresh flush of tender leaves. Deadhead to prevent prolific self-seeding.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pick a few flowers to eat, then cut the whole clump back to about 1 to 2 inches. This stops it from seeding everywhere and brings back fresh, tender leaves.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Flowering yet?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Any flowers yet?

growth_stages.name: Winter dormancy and spring return
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: In cold regions the foliage yellows and dies back to the ground with hard frost, and the clump rests dormant over winter, pushing up fresh blades as one of the first herbs of spring. In mild regions it may stay semi-evergreen.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: In cold areas the leaves die back and the plant rests over winter, then greens up again very early in spring. In mild areas it may stay green most of the year.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Let the clump die back naturally; tidy old remains in late winter and mulch in the coldest zones. Do nothing to force it; it returns on its own. Divide overgrown clumps in early spring as growth resumes.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Leave the plant alone as it dies back; clean up the old leaves in late winter. It will come back on its own in spring. Split crowded clumps in early spring.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Died back or greening up?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Resting or coming back up?

notifications.body_seasoned: Your chive clump is establishing. Harvest only lightly this first year and keep moisture steady so it banks strength to overwinter and return.
notifications.body_beginner: Your chives are young. Cut only a little this first year so the plant gets strong for winter.

notifications.body_seasoned: Your chives are full enough to cut. Shear the outer blades to about 1 to 2 inches, leave some green, and the clump keeps regrowing all season.
notifications.body_beginner: Your chives are big enough to snip. Cut the leaves to about 1 to 2 inches and leave some green, and they grow back.

notifications.body_seasoned: Your chives are sending up pink-purple flowers. Enjoy some, then shear the clump to about 1 to 2 inches to prevent self-seeding and force fresh tender leaves.
notifications.body_beginner: Your chives have flowers. Eat a few, then cut the whole clump back to about 1 to 2 inches so it does not seed everywhere and grows back tender.

notifications.body_seasoned: In cold regions your chives will die back with frost and rest over winter. Tidy the old remains in late winter; they return on their own in spring.
notifications.body_beginner: Your chives will die back for winter and come back on their own in spring. Just clean up the old leaves in late winter.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Extreme heat can stall your chives
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot weather and your chives
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Chives are cool-preferring and, unlike heat-tolerant herbs, can slow, scorch, and go semi-dormant in extreme sustained heat. Keep moisture even, mulch the roots, give afternoon shade in the hottest regions, and shear a scorched clump to the base to regrow when it cools. In the low desert and subtropical summer, chives simply rest until the weather eases.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Chives like cool weather and can wilt or rest in very hot spells. Water evenly, mulch, give them afternoon shade where summers are brutal, and cut a scorched clump back so it regrows when it cools. In the hottest places they just rest until cooler weather returns.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hard freeze coming
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Chives are extremely frost-hardy (roughly zone 3) and a hard freeze simply pushes them into their normal winter dormancy; no protection is needed. The foliage dies back and the clump returns on its own in spring. A late-fall pot can be mulched or moved to keep cutting a little longer.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Chives are very hardy, so a hard freeze just sends them into their normal winter rest and you do not need to do anything. The leaves die back and the plant comes back in spring on its own.

germination.text_seasoned: Chive seed is slow, germinating over about 2 to 3 weeks (4 to 6 in cool soil) and unevenly. Sow shallowly, keep the surface from drying or crusting, and be patient, or skip the wait entirely by planting a division or nursery clump.
germination.text_beginner: Chive seeds are slow, often taking a couple of weeks or more. Sow them shallowly, keep the soil moist, and do not give up too soon. For a fast start, plant a small pot or a split clump instead.

establishment.text_seasoned: Do not over-harvest first-year chives: taking too many leaves weakens a young clump and hurts its ability to overwinter. Cut lightly, keep moisture steady, and space plants about 8 to 12 inches so the clumps have room to widen.
establishment.text_beginner: Go easy cutting chives the first year, since taking too much weakens the young plant before winter. Keep the soil moist and space plants about 8 to 12 inches apart.

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest chives by shearing blades near the base, down to about 1 to 2 inches, taking some from each clump rather than shearing it bare; leaving green keeps the plant feeding itself. Cutting low, not just tipping, keeps leaves tender and pushes fresh bulblets and regrowth.
harvest.text_beginner: Cut chives down to about 1 to 2 inches above the soil, not just the tips, and leave some green behind. This keeps the leaves tender and the plant grows right back for more cutting.

flowering.text_seasoned: When chives bloom, harvest a few flowers to eat, then shear the whole clump to about 1 to 2 inches to remove the scapes before they set seed and to force a fresh flush of tender leaves. Deadheading also prevents prolific self-seeding, which is heaviest in garlic chives.
flowering.text_beginner: When chives flower, eat a few blooms, then cut the whole clump back to about 1 to 2 inches. That stops the seeds from spreading everywhere and brings back fresh, tender leaves.

dormancy.text_seasoned: Chives are a hardy perennial: let the foliage die back on its own in fall, remove old remains in late winter, and mulch in the coldest zones. The clump returns each spring for years. Lift and divide an overgrown or hollow-centered clump in early spring to keep it vigorous.
dormancy.text_beginner: Chives come back every year. Let the leaves die back in fall, clean them up in late winter, and the plant returns in spring. Every few years, dig up a big or thinning clump in early spring and split it to keep it healthy.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A single established chive clump yields fresh leaves for years, cut repeatedly through each season; one clump supplies a kitchen, and it multiplies into many as you divide it. Yield builds as the clump widens, so a two- or three-year-old plant gives far more than a first-year one.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: One chive clump gives you leaves for years and only gets bigger, so a plant or two is plenty for a kitchen. You can split a big clump into several new ones for free.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Production peaks in the cool of spring and again in fall. In cold regions chives run through the northern summer; in hot regions they slow or rest in peak heat and rebound as it cools. Cutting the clump back after flowering renews a flush of tender leaves.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Chives are most productive in cool spring and fall weather. In cold areas they keep going through summer; in hot areas they slow down in the worst heat and pick back up when it cools.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Chives are a rewarding, low-effort perennial, but the first year is about establishment: harvest sparingly so the young clump banks strength to overwinter, and expect the big yields from year two on. The main beginner mistakes are over-cutting a new clump, shearing only the tips instead of cutting low, and letting the flowers seed a lawn of volunteers.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: In its first year, go easy on cutting chives so the plant gets strong for winter; the big harvests come in later years. Cut low, not just the tips, and snip off flowers before they seed so you do not get seedlings everywhere.
factors_seasoned: Age and division: a clump yields more as it widens, and dividing every 2 to 3 years keeps it vigorous and prevents a dead, hollow center.
Harvest method: shearing low (to 1 to 2 inches), not tipping, keeps leaves tender and pushes fresh regrowth and bulblets.
Cool weather and even moisture: chives crop hardest in the cool of spring and fall and with steady water; extreme heat slows them.
Post-bloom shearing: cutting the whole clump back after flowering renews a flush of tender leaves and prevents self-seeding.
Type: common chives for onion flavor and fine leaves; garlic chives for garlic flavor and greater heat and drought tolerance.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No reliable extension or peer-reviewed evidence supports timing chive planting or harvest by moon phase. Establish plants by soil temperature and frost dates, and simply cut the leaves as you need them.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor or very slow germination from seed
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Chive seed is naturally slow, and cold or dry soil makes it worse.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your chive seed came up thin, very late, or not at all. Chive seed is slow by nature, often 2 to 3 weeks or more, and does poorly in cold, dry soil. Next time, keep the surface moist, use fresh seed, and wait longer, or just start with a division or a nursery pot, which is much faster.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep the surface moist, use fresh seed, be patient, or plant a division instead of seed.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Stand was thin, delayed, or failed. Chive germination is intrinsically slow (2 to 3 weeks, up to 4 to 6 in cool soil) and is inhibited by cold, dry, or crusted soil. Next time sow into warm, evenly moist soil, keep the surface from crusting, use fresh viable seed, and allow the full window, or bypass seed with a division or nursery clump.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Slow seed nature plus cold, dry, or crusted soil inhibiting the long germination.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sow into warm moist soil, keep the surface from crusting, use fresh seed and the full window, or establish from divisions.

failure_diagnostics.label: Tough, hollow leaves and flower stalks in early summer
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: The clump is flowering, which is normal for a perennial; the leaves near the flowers turn tough.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your chives sent up flower stalks and the leaves got tough and hollow. That is normal: chives flower in late spring or early summer. Next time, enjoy some flowers, then cut the whole clump back to about 1 to 2 inches to bring back fresh, tender leaves and to stop it from seeding everywhere.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Shear the whole clump back to 1 to 2 inches after it flowers to renew tender leaves.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The clump bolted into flower scapes and the surrounding foliage coarsened and turned hollow. This is the normal late-spring to early-summer bloom of a perennial allium, not a heat or care failure. Next time harvest some flowers, then shear the clump hard (to 1 to 2 inches) to remove scapes before seed set and force a fresh flush of tender leaves.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Normal perennial flowering; foliage near the scapes coarsens as the plant blooms.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Shear the whole clump to 1 to 2 inches after bloom to renew tender leaves and prevent self-seeding.

failure_diagnostics.label: Silvery streaks, orange spots, or leaf mines
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: One of the onion-family pests or diseases: thrips (silvery streaks), rust (orange spots), or leafminer (pale mines).
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your chive leaves showed silvery streaks, orange spots, or wavy pale tunnels. Those are onion-family troubles: thrips, rust, or allium leafminer. Chives usually shrug them off. Next time, shear a marked-up clump to the base to regrow clean, give plants airflow and even water, and use row cover in spring and fall against the leafminer.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Shear the clump to regrow clean, space plants for airflow, and use row cover against the leafminer.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Silvery stippling (onion thrips), bright orange pustules (rust), or white oviposition dots and mines (allium leafminer) marked the foliage. Chives are usually trouble-free, so these are occasional. Next time reset the clump by shearing to the base, open crowded stands by dividing, water at the soil line, moderate nitrogen (rust), and row-cover through the leafminer's spring and fall flights.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Occasional allium pests and diseases: onion thrips, allium rust, or allium leafminer, favored by stress, crowding, or their seasonal flights.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Shear to reset the clump, divide for airflow, water low, moderate nitrogen, and row-cover against the leafminer.

failure_diagnostics.label: Clump thinning or dying out in the center
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: The clump has grown too crowded and needs dividing, which perennials need every few years.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your chive clump got crowded and the middle went thin or died out, with weaker growth. That is a sign it is overdue for dividing. Next spring, dig up the whole clump, pull or cut it into several smaller pieces (each with a handful of little bulbs), and replant them with fresh spacing.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Dig and divide the clump in early spring every 2 to 3 years to keep it vigorous.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The clump crowded itself, vigor fell, and the center thinned or died out, a classic sign an established perennial chive is overdue for division. Next spring lift the clump and split it into divisions of at least several bulblets each, discarding a dead center, and replant at 8 to 12 inch spacing in refreshed soil.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Overcrowding: chives should be divided every 2 to 3 years, or the clump loses vigor and dies out in the middle.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Lift and divide every 2 to 3 years in early spring, discarding the dead center and replanting vigorous divisions.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Chives, pets, and the kitchen
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Are chives safe for pets and cooking
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Important safety note: chives are in the onion (allium) family, and all alliums are toxic to cats, dogs, and horses. They contain organosulfur compounds (N-propyl disulfide) that damage red blood cells and can cause hemolytic anemia, with cats the most sensitive, and raw, cooked, and dried parts are all toxic. Chives are safe for people in normal culinary amounts, but unlike a pet-safe herb such as rosemary, keep the plant and its trimmings away from pets. NC State lists Allium schoenoprasum as a problem for cats, dogs, and horses.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Chives are in the onion family, which is toxic to cats and dogs (and horses), even though it is perfectly fine for people to eat. Keep the plants and any trimmings away from pets.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Grow chives where pets do not graze, and dispose of clippings where cats and dogs cannot reach them; if a pet eats a significant amount, contact a veterinarian.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep chives and their clippings away from cats and dogs, and call a vet if your pet eats a lot.

succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Chives are a perennial planted once, not a succession crop. A single clump returns every year and is cut repeatedly, so there is nothing to stagger by re-sowing; you increase supply by dividing an established clump, not by successive plantings. The clump should be lifted and divided every 2 to 3 years to keep it vigorous.

Edible flowers triple-sourced (UMN/UWI/NCSU); allium leafminer fully verified (UMD, chives the named host); spring division + zone-3 hardiness confirmed. FIXES: re-anchored the disease trio -- downy mildew (Peronospora destructor), rust (Puccinia allii), white rot (Sclerotium cepivorum) -- to the UC IPM Onion-and-Garlic pages (the prior UMN/USU onion anchors do NOT name them), and corrected the downy-mildew temp 72->75F to match UC IPM; dropped umn_ext from onion thrips (USU carries it); DOWNGRADED the beans/peas antagonism provenance from extension_backed / confidence-high / verified-true to traditional / low / not-verified (the antagonism is not on the cited UMN page). open_findings.summary: MODELING CHOICE flagged for certify: chives is a HARDY HERBACEOUS PERENNIAL modeled in the frost_anchored culinary_herb lane (inherited from the parsley template and the chives shell), NOT in perennial_herbaceous (fitted to strawberry) or a woody lane. The perennial nature is represented honestly WITHIN frost_anchored: perennial=true, lifecycle=perennial, succession_policy.suitable=false (plant once, divide every 2 to 3 years), winter cold_pause dormancy + spring regrowth in cold zones, season-long cut-and-come-again harvest, and a dedicated dormancy growth stage + failure_diagnostic for dividing. A37 coherence is satisfied by placing a spring establishment 'plant' token ahead of regrowth. Confirm this lane choice is acceptable vs promoting chives (and the sibling perennial herb shells mint/thyme/sage/oregano/rosemary/lemongrass) to a dedicated perennial-herb basis.

All 10 regions' per-zone calendars are MODELED from chives' cold-hardy, cool-preferring, clump-forming perennial envelope and the regional extension planting-calendar sources, not lifted from a single chives-per-region chart (few exist). Establishment windows (spring in cold zones; fall through late winter in mild/hot zones), harvest spans, and the exact extent of each hot-region pause may be nudged at review. resolution_method on each cell is cc_author_pilot_modeled.

Chives carry a summer heat_pause where a cool-preferring perennial genuinely struggles: se_gulf, ca_interior, ca_desert, low_desert_az, fl_peninsula (and a brief Jul-Aug pause in warm_arid). They run straight through summer (NO heat_pause) in the northern tier and on the mild CA north/south coasts, and near year-round on the coasts and Hawaii. Each heat_pause cell carries a backed object (months + chives-specific basis_seasoned + sources with URLs), anchored to UF/IFAS (chives as a cool-season herb needing afternoon shade) + UMN; the exact pause months per region are modeled from the regional summer heat pattern, not a chives-specific regional chart. Chives is LESS heat-tolerant than parsley, so its heat_pause set is broader than parsley's.

days_to_maturity [60, 90] (mid 75) is modeled: T1 sources give slow 2-to-3-week (up to 4-to-6) germination and a full first establishment season, with divisions cuttable in weeks; no crisp DTM is published, so the range spans seed-to-first-cutting. spacing_inches [8, 12] sits within the sourced span (UMN 6 to 12 in; Wisconsin 12 to 20 in for widening landscape clumps). germination_temp_f [60, 70] is a modeled cool-soil band. weeks_indoors 6 follows the standard 6-to-8-week indoor start. Flagged for the variety-delta pass.

The directly-read chives pages (Wisconsin, UMN, MSU) state chives have FEW pest/disease problems. The pest/disease entries are therefore the ALLIUM family set modeled onto chives and framed honestly as occasional: onion thrips and onion maggot (UMN onion page), allium leafminer (UMd explicitly names chive A. schoenoprasum as a host), aphids (minor; chives repel them); downy mildew, rust, white rot (Sclerotium cepivorum), and botrytis (allium disease overviews; UVM, uncatalogued, corroborated chives as a host for several). Rust and white rot are anchored to the UMN garlic page + USU; downy mildew/botrytis to the UMN onion page + USU. Flagged for the source-truth sample.

hawaii_tropical is the lowest-confidence cell: common chives is cool-preferring and marginal in tropical lowland heat, reliable mainly at elevation or as a cool-season/container plant. Modeled as a near-year-round grower with NO heat_pause, cited generally to UH CTAHR rather than a chives-specific Hawaii calendar. Confirm in review. Garlic chives would tolerate the heat better.

No chives-specific catalog IDs exist, so existing institution-level T1 catalog IDs are reused. Directly-read chives/allium anchors: umn_ext (UMN Growing Chives), uwi_hort (Wisconsin Horticulture chives + garlic-chives), msu_ext (MSU Growing Chives), uiuc_ext (Illinois chives), umd_ext (UMd Allium Leafminer, names chive), uf_ifas (UF/IFAS Pasco chives, cool-season/afternoon-shade). Regional calendar anchors (tamu_agrilife, uariz_ext, uariz_ext_az2061, nmsu_ext, ndsu_ext, umaine_ext, lsu_agcenter, msstate_ext, uc_mg, ucanr_ext, uga_calendar, uf_ifas_vh021, uhawaii_ctahr, ncsu_ext, clemson_hgic, usu_ext) are section/portal/publication-level; uariz_ext_az2061 is a PDF cited at the publication URL, not extracted. Allium pest/disease claims anchored to the umn_ext onion/garlic pages and usu_ext (per-entry URL overrides). No IDs invented; all catalogued and T1. Flagged for the URL-liveness check.

Companions are TRADITIONAL/low-to-medium except the beans-and-peas avoid. The chives-under-roses (aphids/black spot), chives-around-apple (scab), and chives-with-carrots/tomatoes pairings are relayed by MSU citing Penn State as tradition with a plausible allium-volatile mechanism, not measured trials. The one extension-backed, high-confidence call is the allium-legume antagonism (alliums inhibit beans and peas). No chives-specific companion trial found in a readable T1 source.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: Up North (zones 3 through 7), chives are one of the hardiest, easiest herbs you can grow. Plant a clump once in spring after hard frost, or start slow seed indoors, and it returns on its own every year: it dies back over winter, then greens up as one of the very first herbs of spring. One planting gives leaves right through the mild northern summer and into fall. Cut low, leave some green, and split the clump every few years.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In the cold-winter North (zones 3 through 7), chives are a frost-hardy perennial, reliable to roughly zone 3. Establish a clump in spring after hard-frost danger, from a division or an indoor-started seedling, and it overwinters dormant and regrows early each spring. A single planting produces through the whole mild northern summer, since chives are cool-tolerant and not heat-stressed here, and holds into fall until hard frost. Shear low to keep leaves tender, shear the clump after flowering, and divide every 2 to 3 years.

Give it afternoon shade and steady water in the heat, cut low, and it returns year after year.
