hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In Hawaii, thyme does not grow well in the hot, humid lowlands where most people garden, because the wet heat rots it. It only succeeds in cool, dry, higher-elevation places with cool nights. If you live somewhere cool and dry like that, you can grow thyme as a low fragrant perennial in a sunny spot with fast-draining soil and little water. Otherwise, it is best to skip it.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: In Hawaii, thyme is marginal, and the honest answer is that it is not a crop for the humid lowlands where most islanders garden. Thyme is a cool-and-dry Mediterranean herb, and the warm, wet lowlands drive rot. The one workable niche is microclimatic: at cool, dry, higher elevations with hot days and cool nights, thyme grows as a low fragrant perennial. If you garden in such an upcountry microclimate, give thyme full sun, very sharp drainage, and lean, infrequent water. In the warm, humid lowlands it is not a sound choice, and no reliable planting calendar exists for those conditions.

crops.description_seasoned: Thyme is a low, woody Mediterranean perennial in the mint family, grown for its tiny aromatic leaves that flavor soups, stews, sauces, meats, and fish. It forms a low, spreading, mat-like mound only about 6 to 12 inches tall and thrives on neglect in full sun and lean, sharply drained soil; wet, rich soil rots it and dulls its flavor. Frequent harvesting and a light shear after its summer bloom keep it bushy, though it goes woody with age and is best divided or replaced every few years. It is hardy and pest-resistant, and its small pink, lavender, or white flowers are a strong bee draw.
crops.description_beginner: Thyme is a low, spreading herb with tiny fragrant leaves you cook with. It comes from the dry Mediterranean, so it wants full sun, poor dry soil, and very little water, and it actually does worse if you pamper it. It grows only about 6 to 12 inches tall and spreads into a low mat. Snip it often and give it a light trim after it flowers to keep it bushy; it gets woody as it ages, so replace or divide it every few years. It is tough and rarely bothered by pests, and bees love its little flowers.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Harvest thyme sprigs anytime once the plant is established: snip the top few inches of leafy growth, taking no more than about a third of the plant at once. Flavor is most concentrated just before and as the plant flowers, so cut for drying then, on a dry morning after the dew has lifted. Regular harvesting also keeps the plant from going woody.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: You can snip thyme anytime once it is established: cut the top few inches of leafy stems, taking no more than about a third at once. The flavor is strongest just before and as it flowers, so that is the best time to cut thyme to dry. Cut in the morning after the dew dries. Snipping it often also keeps it from getting woody.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Thyme is a hardy perennial. Common, English, French, German Winter, and lemon thymes are reliably perennial in roughly zones 5 to 9, and creeping thyme is hardier still, to about zone 4. With sharp drainage and a sheltered spot, hardy types push into zone 4, while zone 3 usually calls for growing thyme as an annual or a bring-in container plant. Good drainage matters as much as cold: thyme rots in wet winter soil before cold alone kills it, and it also struggles in hot, humid climates.
crops.hardiness_notes_beginner: Thyme is tough and comes back year after year in most of the country (about zones 5 to 9, and zone 4 for the hardiest types like creeping and German Winter thyme if drainage is good). In the very coldest areas (zone 3), grow it for one season or in a pot you bring inside. Just as important as cold: thyme hates wet feet and will rot in soggy soil, and it also struggles in hot, humid places.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: In the first year, focus on root establishment: water regularly until the plant is settled, then taper off, and harvest only lightly. Thyme grows slowly the first season and reaches full size by about the second year, after which it produces steadily for several years before it should be divided or replaced.
crops.year_one_notes_beginner: The first year is about getting the roots going. Water it fairly regularly until it is established, then cut back, and only pick a little. Thyme grows slowly at first and fills out by about year two, then produces well for several years before you replace or divide it.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Choose the sunniest, best-draining spot you have. Work only a little coarse compost into lean soil, and on heavy clay improve drainage with a raised bed or mound rather than digging in sand, which can worsen clay. Aim for lean, gritty, neutral to slightly alkaline ground; thyme does not want rich soil.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Pick the sunniest spot with the best drainage. Mix only a little coarse compost into the soil. If your ground is heavy clay, plant thyme in a raised bed or mound instead, because that drains better. The goal is poor, gritty soil, not rich soil.
crops.bloom_time_beginner: Thyme flowers in summer, with tiny lavender, pink, or white flowers that bees love. The flavor is strongest just before it blooms. When yours flowers depends on where you live.
crops.bloom_time_seasoned: Thyme blooms in early to mid summer, carrying small clusters of lavender, pink, or white flowers that are a strong pollinator draw. Leaf flavor peaks just before and as the flowers open. Exact timing shifts with your region and is set per zone.

dormancy_window.note_seasoned: In zones with freezing winters, thyme slows or goes semi-dormant. Hold off on watering and feeding, leave any hard shaping for spring, and protect less hardy types or move container plants under cover. A resting plant needs almost no water, and it is wet soil or a late-fall hard cut, not the cold itself, that most often kills thyme over winter.
dormancy_window.note_beginner: Where winters freeze, thyme mostly rests through the cold months. Stop watering and feeding it, save any big trim for spring, and in cold areas shelter the less hardy types or bring potted plants somewhere protected. A resting plant barely needs water, and it is usually soggy soil or a late-fall haircut, not the cold, that kills thyme over winter.

pollination.notes_seasoned: Thyme is grown for its leaves, not for fruit, so no cross-pollination planning is needed and a single plant is fine. Its small summer flowers are self-fertile and are a strong draw for bees, butterflies, and small beneficial insects, a bonus for the garden rather than something the plant needs.
pollination.notes_beginner: You only need one thyme plant, and you do not need a partner plant, because thyme is grown for its leaves rather than fruit. Bees and butterflies love its little flowers, but that is a bonus for your garden, not something the plant needs.

pruning_window.note_seasoned: After the summer flowers fade, shear off the spent flower stems and lightly reduce the plant, cutting into leafy growth only and never into the bare woody base, which resprouts poorly. Frequent harvesting through the season plus this post-bloom shear keeps thyme compact; even so, plants go woody with age and are best divided or replaced every few years.
pruning_window.note_beginner: Once the summer flowers fade, trim off the old flower stems and neaten the plant, cutting only into the leafy parts and not into the hard woody stems, which do not grow back well. Snipping thyme often plus this trim keeps it bushy, but it still gets woody with age, so replace or divide it every few years.

crops.name: Dill

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Dill likes loose, well-drained soil and is not fussy about richness; it actually does fine in lean ground. Mix in a little compost so the soil holds some moisture but still drains freely. Heavy, soggy, or compacted soil is the main thing to avoid, since it rots the slow-sprouting seed and the deep little taproot. Steady moisture keeps the feathery leaves tender.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Dill grows in most soils but does best in a loose, well-drained loam or sandy loam, and it tolerates poorer, leaner ground than most herbs. Utah State University describes it as a plant for well-drained, low-fertility to moderately fertile soil, so heavy feeding and very rich beds are unnecessary and can leave it lank. Work a little compost into the top few inches before sowing to hold even moisture, but do not overdo richness. It dislikes damp, poorly drained ground, which invites damping-off of the slow-germinating seed and leaf disease. Dill forms a slender taproot and resents transplanting, so it is best direct-sown into loosened soil.

ph.note_beginner: Dill grows best in slightly acidic soil, about 5.5 to 6.5. Most garden soil is fine, and a simple soil test tells you where you stand.
ph.note_seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 5.5 to 6.5, slightly acidic; Utah State University gives this as dill's ideal range. It is forgiving and still does fine up to neutral, roughly 5.5 to 7.0. Dill is not a pH-sensitive plant, so in most gardens no adjustment is needed beyond a soil-test baseline.

fertilizer.timing: a little compost worked in before sowing, then at most one light feeding during leaf growth
fertilizer.example_product: compost, or a light balanced vegetable fertilizer
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Dill is a light feeder and one of the few herbs that prefers lean soil; Utah State University notes that no additional nutrients are needed if the soil is amended at planting. Work a little compost in before sowing and, in poor ground, give one light feeding once the plants are growing. Avoid heavy nitrogen, which makes dill lank and floppy and can dull the aromatic oils that give the leaves and seed their flavor. A plant grown on for seed or pickling heads needs no extra feeding once it bolts.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Dill does not need much fertilizer and even grows well in poor soil. Mix a little compost into the bed before planting, and that is usually all it needs. If the soil is poor, you can give one light feeding while the plants are young. Too much fertilizer makes dill floppy and weakens the flavor, so go easy.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: If your dill is in poor soil, you can give it one light feeding now.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Your dill can take one light feeding now if the soil is poor.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: Dill is a light feeder that prefers lean soil; compost worked in at planting usually covers it, with at most one light, balanced feeding in poor ground. Avoid heavy nitrogen, which makes the plant floppy and weakens the aromatic oils.
fertilizer.npk_tag: Light feeder: little to no supplemental fertilizer needed
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Dill needs very little feeding. Mix compost into the soil at planting, and only feed lightly if the soil is poor.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: Compost worked in at planting is usually enough; in poor soil, one light side-dress of a balanced fertilizer at the label rate while the plants are young.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Usually just compost at planting. If you feed, use a light all-purpose fertilizer once, at the label rate.

pests.name: Parsleyworm (black swallowtail caterpillar)
pests.symptoms_beginner: Plump green caterpillars banded with black and yellow-orange dots, chewing the feathery leaves. They can strip a young plant, but on an established dill they usually do only light damage.
pests.cause_beginner: These are the caterpillars of the black swallowtail butterfly, which lays eggs on dill and other carrot-family plants. They are also a welcome garden visitor, since they turn into a beautiful butterfly.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: On a big plant, just leave them; the damage is minor and you get butterflies. If they threaten a small planting, pick them off by hand and move them to a spare dill plant.
pests.prevention_beginner: Grow a little extra dill so there is enough to share with the caterpillars, and simply relocate them rather than spraying.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Larvae of the black swallowtail (Papilio polyxenes), banded green, black, and yellow, feed on the foliage. On an established dill the defoliation is usually light and cosmetic; a heavy load can strip a seedling.
pests.cause_seasoned: Dill is a larval host plant for the black swallowtail butterfly. The caterpillars are a feature as much as a pest, so dill is often planted deliberately to support them.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: On established plants, tolerate them, the feeding is minor and the butterflies are a benefit; on small plantings, handpick and relocate to a sacrificial dill. Bt is effective if control is truly needed, but is rarely warranted on a host plant grown partly for the butterflies.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Manage by tolerance and a little surplus planting rather than control: grow enough dill to share, relocate larvae from plants you want to protect, and reserve sprays for genuine seedling threats.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_beginner: Clusters of tiny soft green or gray insects on new growth and the undersides of the feathery leaves, sometimes with curled, sticky foliage.
pests.cause_beginner: Aphids are small sap-sucking insects that breed fast, especially on soft growth from too much fertilizer. They can spread plant viruses.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water, or use insecticidal soap on the leaf undersides, repeating every few days. Dill's own flowers also draw in ladybugs and lacewings that eat aphids.
pests.prevention_beginner: Welcome helpful insects like ladybugs and lacewings, go easy on nitrogen, and check new growth often.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Colonies of aphids gather on growing tips and leaf undersides; honeydew and the lodged insects contaminate a crop used fresh, and aphids can vector viruses. Dill's lacy foliage hides them, so scout closely.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several aphid species feed on dill; they reproduce rapidly and favor the soft growth that excess nitrogen produces. Dill itself, allowed to flower, is a strong insectary that recruits aphid predators.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Dislodge colonies with a strong water jet or spray insecticidal soap, covering leaf undersides; repeat every few days and conserve lady beetles, lacewings, and parasitoid wasps, which dill's own umbel flowers attract.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Scout growing tips early, avoid overfeeding nitrogen, and conserve natural enemies; letting some dill flower draws in the aphid predators it is famous for hosting.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_beginner: A white, powdery coating on the leaves and flower stalks, usually later in the crop and in warm, dry-day weather. Heavily coated leaves yellow and are unpleasant to eat.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungal disease that coats the leaves in white powder, favored by warm days, cool nights, crowding, and overwatering.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove the worst leaves, open up the planting for airflow, and avoid crowding and overhead watering. Most home crops are picked before it does much harm.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Space plants for airflow, avoid crowding and overfeeding, and water at the base rather than over the leaves.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: A white, talc-like fungal growth on the foliage and stems, the most commonly noted fungal disease of dill, that builds in warm days with cool humid nights, in crowded stands, and where plants are overwatered; coated leaves lose quality.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Powdery mildew (Erysiphe heraclei on Apiaceae), favored by warm days, cool humid nights, dense stands with poor airflow, and excess moisture. Utah State University notes dill mildews when overwatered.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Improve airflow with wider spacing, remove affected leaves, avoid excess nitrogen and overhead watering; the leaf crop is usually cut before mildew matters, but a tall plant held for seed is more exposed.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Widen spacing for airflow, avoid heavy nitrogen and overwatering, and harvest the leaf crop promptly; remove infected foliage on plants held for seed.

diseases.name: Leaf spot / leaf blight
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small tan to brown spots, sometimes with a yellow halo, that spread on the leaves and can merge until the leaflets wilt and die back, worst in wet weather.
diseases.cause_beginner: Fungal leaf diseases that spread on wet leaves and splashing water and can arrive on infected seed. Spotted, blighted leaves are not good to eat.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove and destroy spotted leaves, avoid wetting the foliage, improve airflow, and start with clean seed. There is no spray cure in the home garden, so prevention matters most.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Use clean seed, water at the soil line rather than over the leaves, space plants for airflow, rotate the bed, and clear infected debris.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small tan-brown leaf lesions, sometimes yellow-haloed, that expand and coalesce until leaflets blight and die; favored by wet, splashy conditions and prolonged leaf wetness. Cercospora leaf blight (Cercosporidium punctum) and Alternaria leaf spot are the documented agents on dill.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Foliar fungi, chiefly Cercosporidium punctum (Cercospora blight) and Alternaria spp., spread by splash, wind, and infected seed and favored by warm, wet weather and overhead irrigation.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Use clean, disease-free seed, avoid overhead irrigation, space for airflow, rotate away from the carrot family, and remove infected debris; there is no effective home-garden cure once it is established.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant clean seed, switch to drip or soil-line watering, widen spacing, rotate, and remove crop debris that carries the fungi over.

diseases.name: Damping-off and seedling rot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Seeds that never come up, or seedlings that flop over at the soil line with a pinched, rotted stem and then die. It strikes in cold, wet soil.
diseases.cause_beginner: Soil fungi attack the seeds and tiny seedlings, especially when the soil is cold and soggy and the slow-sprouting dill seed sits a long time before emerging.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure for an affected seedling, so focus on prevention: pull and discard collapsed seedlings.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Do not sow into cold, soggy soil, plant shallowly in well-drained ground, do not overwater, and use fresh seed so it comes up faster.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Poor stands from seed and pre- or post-emergence collapse of seedlings with water-soaked, pinched stems at the soil line, worst in cold, wet, poorly drained soil where dill's slow germination leaves seed sitting in the danger zone.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Soilborne Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Fusarium fungi attack germinating seed and seedlings; cold, saturated soil that slows dill's already slow germination favors them.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No rescue once seedlings collapse; manage by prevention and remove affected plants.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Sow shallowly into well-drained soil under conditions that favor reasonably quick emergence, avoid overwatering, and use fresh, viable seed.

watering.frequency_seasoned: About 1 inch of water per week, kept reasonably even; dill is fairly drought-tolerant once established but bolts faster and grows lank under heat and dry stress.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly 1 inch a week, especially while the plants are young.
watering.amount_seasoned: Roughly 1 inch per week, more in warm, dry spells; once established dill takes some drought, but steady moisture keeps the leaves tender and slows the bolt.
watering.amount_beginner: Aim for about 1 inch of water a week, a bit more when it is warm and dry.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose; keeping the lacy foliage dry checks powdery mildew and leaf spot on a crop used fresh.
watering.method_beginner: Water at the base of the plants rather than over the leaves, which helps prevent leaf diseases.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, damping-off in seedlings, and powdery mildew or root rot in constantly wet, poorly drained ground.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Lower leaves yellow, seedlings rot at the base, and plants get mildewed or mushy in soggy soil.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting, slowed growth, and faster bolting; drought stress hurries the plant toward its flower stalk and seed.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Wilting leaves and a plant that bolts (flowers) sooner than you want.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Even moisture keeps dill growing tender and slows the bolt; hot, dry spells push it to flower and set seed sooner and coarsen the foliage.
watering.method_note_beginner: Keep the water fairly steady so the leaves stay tender and the plant does not bolt as early.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Steady moisture through germination, which is slow in dill, and through the first weeks of leaf growth matters most; an established plant tolerates more drought.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Keep the soil moist while the seeds are sprouting, which takes a while, and through the early leaf-growing weeks.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Dill is almost always direct-sown, since it forms a slender taproot and resents transplanting. Sow seed about 0.25 inch deep as soon as the soil can be worked in spring; young dill tolerates light frost, so Wisconsin Horticulture suggests sowing a week or two before the last hard frost, and it germinates slowly, often 10 to 21 days. Sow a little thicker than the final stand and thin to 8 to 12 inches for full plants, or 4 to 6 inches for cut leaf. Succession-sow every 2 to 3 weeks for a steady leaf supply. In hot regions, shift sowing to fall through spring, since summer heat and long days bolt the crop to seed; midsummer plantings are grown for seed and pickling heads rather than leaves.
start_method.notes_beginner: Plant dill straight in the garden from seed, because it has a deep little root and does not like being moved. Sow the seeds about a quarter inch deep as soon as the soil can be worked in spring, since young plants handle light frost. The seeds are slow, often taking two to three weeks, so keep the soil moist. Thin the plants to about 8 to 12 inches apart, and sow again every couple of weeks for a steady supply. In hot areas plant in fall through spring instead of summer, because heat makes it bolt; a summer crop is really for the seed and pickling heads.

drainage.saucer_practice: Empty the saucer after watering so roots never sit in water, which invites damping-off and root rot.

soil_mix.type_beginner: A good-quality potting mix, not garden soil.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in a little compost for steady moisture; dill does not need rich soil.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: A light, well-drained potting mix, deep enough for dill's taproot.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend in a little compost; dill is a light feeder, so avoid heavy fertilizer that leaves it lank in a pot.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out fast, so check daily in warm weather and keep the mix evenly moist, since drought makes dill bolt.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Feed only lightly, since dill prefers lean soil and too much fertilizer makes potted dill floppy.

overwintering.approach_beginner: In mild areas, a pot of fall-sown dill can keep growing through winter in a sheltered, sunny spot, since young dill takes light frost. In cold areas dill is not very cold-hardy, so a hard freeze will kill it; bring a small pot indoors to a bright window or simply let a plant drop seed, since dill reseeds itself readily.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Dill tolerates light frost when young, so a fall-sown container can carry a leaf crop through winter in mild zones. It is less cold-hardy than the hardiest greens, and a hard freeze kills it, so in cold zones move a small pot to a bright indoor window or an unheated but protected spot, or simply rely on its heavy self-seeding to return plants in spring rather than overwintering the parent.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Dwarf dill makes an easy container herb. Use a pot at least 10 inches deep to fit its root, choose a compact variety like Fernleaf so it does not get too tall and tippy, and snip the feathery leaves as you need them. Keep it watered, grow it in the cool seasons, and give afternoon shade in hot weather to slow bolting.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Dill grows well in a container at least 10 inches deep to fit its taproot. Standard dill reaches 3 to 5 feet and gets top-heavy, so choose a dwarf, slow-bolting variety such as Fernleaf for pots. Keep moisture even, since pots dry fast and drought triggers bolting, grow it in the cool seasons, and give afternoon shade in warm spells. A pot is also the easiest way to move the crop into shade or shelter as the weather turns.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry faster than beds; check moisture daily in warmth and water before the mix dries, since drought stress bolts dill.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Container dill needs only a light feed, if any; it prefers lean soil and overfeeding in a pot makes it floppy and weakens the flavor.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering container suits dill well, since it smooths out the steady moisture that keeps the leaves tender and slow to bolt.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match because it keeps the water steady, which keeps dill tender and slow to bolt.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: Dill has a slender taproot and grows tall, so give it depth and stability: a container at least 10 inches deep suits it, and a dwarf variety stays short enough not to topple. Width adds sowing area for cut leaf.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Dill has a deeper root than most herbs and grows tall, so use a pot at least 10 inches deep and pick a short, compact variety so it does not tip over.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Other Apiaceae: carrot, parsley, cilantro, fennel, celery, parsnip, and dill itself. They share carrot-family pests and diseases (leaf blights, the carrot motley dwarf complex, and soilborne rots), so following one with another concentrates that pressure.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Other carrot-family plants like carrots, parsley, cilantro, fennel, and celery, because they share the same pests and diseases.
rotation.good_after: Legumes (peas, beans), brassicas (cabbage family), alliums (onion, garlic), or nightshades such as tomatoes.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate dill and its carrot-family relatives so they do not return to the same ground for about 3 years. The Apiaceae share foliar blights, the carrot motley dwarf complex, and soilborne rots, which build up where the family repeats. Follow dill with legumes, brassicas, alliums, or nightshades. Because dill self-sows heavily from bolted plants, volunteers can blur a rotation, so pull seedlings that come up out of place if you are managing the family carefully.
rotation.note_beginner: Try not to grow dill or other carrot-family plants (carrots, parsley, cilantro, fennel, celery) in the same spot more than about once every 3 years, since they share pests and diseases. Plant dill after peas, beans, cabbage, onions, or tomatoes instead. Dill self-sows a lot, so pull up stray seedlings that pop up where you do not want them.

bolting.triggers: summer heat above roughly 75 to 80°F and lengthening days, accelerated by drought and crowding
bolting.prevention_seasoned: Dill bolts once summer heat and long days set in, sending up a tall flower stalk, and the leafy growth narrows and slows as the plant shifts to seed and pickling heads. Keep the leaf window in the cool shoulders of the year: sow early in spring and crop steadily, lean on a late-summer sowing for a fall leaf crop, choose slow-bolting or dwarf types (Fernleaf, Dukat, Hera) where heat is a problem, give light afternoon shade in warm spells, and keep moisture steady. Succession-sow every 2 to 3 weeks so a bolted batch is quickly replaced. There is no real fix once it bolts, so the productive answer in heat is to stop fighting it and grow the plant on for seed heads and dried dill seed.
bolting.prevention_beginner: Dill flowers (bolts) when it gets hot and the days are long, sending up a tall stalk, and leaf growth slows. To keep the leaves coming, grow it in the cool parts of the year, sow a fresh little batch every 2 to 3 weeks, water steadily, give afternoon shade when it is hot, and try slow-bolting or dwarf types like Fernleaf or Dukat. When it does bolt, do not fight it: let the plant flower and make seed heads for pickling and dried dill seed.
bolting.note_seasoned: Bolting in dill is driven by summer heat above roughly 75 to 80°F and lengthening days, sped by drought and crowding. This is the defining rhythm of the crop: the same bolt that slows the leafy dill weed produces the flower heads and seed used for pickling and as the spice, so the plant is not failing, it is changing product. The yellow umbel flowers feed pollinators and beneficial insects strongly, and unharvested plants self-sow readily, often returning as volunteers the next spring. In hot regions the leaf window is short and growers deliberately let summer plantings run to seed and heads.
bolting.note_beginner: Dill bolts (sends up a tall flower stalk) when it gets hot and the days are long. It is not a mistake: the very same flowering gives you the seed heads for pickling and the dried dill seed used as a spice. The flowers are great for bees and helpful insects, and the plant often drops seed and comes up again on its own the next year. Grow it in cool weather for leaves, and let it bloom in summer for seed.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Fresh dill leaves wilt within a day or two at room temperature, so refrigerate promptly after cutting; standing the cut stems in a glass of water on the counter holds them a few days. Dried dill seed, by contrast, is shelf-stable for months once dried.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Do not leave cut dill out on the counter, where it wilts fast; either chill it or stand the stems in a glass of water. Dried dill seed keeps for months at room temperature.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerate fresh dill leaves unwashed in a loose or perforated bag, or stems standing in a little water under a loose bag, in the crisper; dill holds about a week. Wash only at use, since trapped moisture speeds breakdown.
storage.fridge_beginner: Store fresh dill unwashed in a loose bag in the fridge, where it keeps about a week. Wash it only when you are ready to use it.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Dill freezes well for cooking: chop the fronds into ice-cube trays with water or oil, or freeze them flat in bags, where the flavor holds better than dried. Dill seed is dried, not frozen: cut the seed heads as they turn tan, dry them, then thresh and store the seed airtight.
storage.freezer_beginner: Dill freezes well for cooking. Chop it into an ice-cube tray with a little water or oil and freeze. For dill seed, let the seed heads dry on the plant, then store the seeds in a jar.
storage.notes_seasoned: Fresh dill weed is delicate and short-lived once cut, so chill it fast and use it within a week, or freeze it for cooking. The seed and heads are the keepers: harvest seed heads as they turn from green to tan but before they shatter, dry them in a paper bag, and the threshed dill seed stores airtight for months. Green seed heads are used fresh for pickling.
storage.notes_beginner: Use fresh dill within a week or so of picking, or freeze it. Dill seed is the opposite: dry the tan seed heads, shake out the seeds, and store them in a sealed jar for many months. Green seed heads are picked fresh for pickling.

recommended.name: Bouquet
recommended.note: The most widely grown garden dill, productive of both leafy dill weed and large seed heads, good for pickling; reaches about 2 to 3 feet. A reliable all-purpose standard.

recommended.name: Long Island Mammoth
recommended.note: A tall heirloom, 3 to 5 feet, grown above all for big seed heads and pickling; the classic dill for putting up cucumbers. Bolts sooner, so less suited to long leaf harvest.

recommended.name: Fernleaf
recommended.note: A compact, slow-bolting dwarf, about 18 inches, an All-America Selections winner and the best choice for containers and small spaces, with a longer leaf window before flowering.

recommended.name: Dukat
recommended.note: A leafy, slow-bolting type prized for high essential-oil content and sweet, strong flavor; an excellent dill-weed variety for fresh leaf harvest.

recommended.name: Hera
recommended.note: A slow-bolting bunching dill bred for uniform, upright leaf production, holding in leaf longer before the seedstalk rises; a good cut-leaf choice where heat shortens the window.

varieties.note_seasoned: Match the type to the goal. For leafy dill weed, choose slow-bolting selections, Fernleaf (dwarf, for pots), Dukat, Hera, and Bouquet, which hold in leaf longer before the seedstalk rises; none truly stop the bolt in heat and long days, but they buy time. For seed and pickling heads, the tall heirlooms Long Island Mammoth and Mammoth set big heads fast and are the classic pickling dills. Because the bolt is inevitable in warmth, succession sowing matters as much as variety for a steady leaf supply.
varieties.note_beginner: If you want leafy dill weed, pick a slow-bolting or dwarf variety like Fernleaf, Dukat, Hera, or Bouquet, which take a bit longer to flower. None of them stop flowering in heat, so sow a fresh batch every couple of weeks too. If you mainly want seed heads for pickling, grow a tall type like Long Island Mammoth.

companions.note_beginner: Dill is one of the great companion herbs, mostly because of what it does when it flowers: the yellow blooms pull in hoverflies, lady beetles, lacewings, and tiny parasitic wasps that hunt aphids and caterpillars on nearby crops. It is a traditional partner for the cabbage family, where it is said to help against cabbageworms, and it interplants well with cucumbers, onions, lettuce, and corn. Keep it away from fennel, which can cross-pollinate it, and from carrots, its close relative.
companions.note_seasoned: Most of dill's companion value is real but indirect: allowed to flower, dill (an Apiaceae umbel) is a strong insectary plant, recruiting hoverflies, lady beetles, lacewings, and parasitoid wasps that suppress aphids and caterpillars on neighboring crops, an effect extension IPM guidance leans on. It is a traditional companion for brassicas (cabbage, broccoli, kale), where folklore credits it with deterring cabbageworms, plausible via the beneficials it draws but not measured as a direct effect; it also interplants with cucumbers, onions, lettuce, and corn. The well-grounded cautions are its own carrot-family relatives: fennel and carrots, which can cross-pollinate dill where they flower together, and which share Apiaceae pests on rotation grounds.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Cabbage family (cabbage, broccoli, kale)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Dill is a classic partner for the cabbage family. Let some dill flower nearby and its blooms bring in helpful insects that eat aphids and cabbageworm caterpillars, and gardeners have long planted the two together.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Dill-with-brassicas is a near-universal companion tradition; the mechanism (flowering dill as an insectary recruiting parasitoids and predators of cabbage pests) is extension-supported, but a direct measured dill-protects-cabbage trial was not found, so traditional/mechanistic rather than research_backed.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional brassica pairing with a real mechanism: dill left to flower recruits hoverflies, lacewings, and parasitoid wasps that attack aphids and caterpillars, including cabbageworms, on cole crops. Sound by the insectary mechanism and long tradition, not a measured dill-on-cabbage effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Cucumbers
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Dill and cucumbers are a kitchen and garden match, since you pickle cucumbers with dill, and they grow in an overlapping season; the flowering dill also draws in insects that help the cucumbers.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: A widely taught interplant with shared culinary use and the insectary mechanism; no cucumber-specific dill trial found.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional culinary-and-garden pairing: cucumbers and dill share the pickling jar and an overlapping season, and flowering dill recruits beneficials that help cucumbers. Tradition plus the insectary mechanism, not a measured pair effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Onions, lettuce, and corn
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: These grow alongside dill without crowding it, and the helpful insects dill's flowers attract spill over onto them. A simple, easygoing interplant.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Complementary-habit interplant lore plus the insectary mechanism; no dill-specific trials.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Complementary-habit interplants: onions, lettuce, and corn share space and season with dill without strong competition, and benefit from the beneficials its flowers draw. Structural and traditional, not a tested effect.

good_seasoned.name: Cabbage family (cabbage, broccoli, kale)
good_seasoned.timing: interplant; let some dill flower nearby
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Dill left to flower recruits hoverflies, lacewings, and parasitoid wasps that attack aphids and caterpillars, including cabbageworms, on cole crops. A traditional brassica pairing sound by the insectary mechanism, not a measured dill-on-cabbage trial.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Near-universal companion tradition; insectary mechanism is extension-supported, direct trial not found.

good_seasoned.name: Cucumbers
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A culinary-and-garden pairing: cucumbers and dill share the pickling jar and an overlapping season, and flowering dill recruits beneficials. Tradition plus mechanism, not a measured pair effect.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Widely taught interplant and shared culinary use; no cucumber-specific dill trial.

good_seasoned.name: Onions, lettuce, and corn
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Complementary-habit interplants that share space and season with dill without strong competition and benefit from the beneficials its flowers draw. Structural and traditional, not a tested effect.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Complementary-habit lore plus insectary mechanism; no dill-specific trials.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Carrots
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep dill away from carrots. They are close relatives, so if both flower they can cross-pollinate, and they share carrot-family pests and diseases.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Carrot-dill cross-pollination is real where both flower (same family); the shared-pest caution is sound. The stronger folklore claim that mature dill stunts carrots is largely untested, so traditional/mechanistic rather than measured.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Dill and carrots are both Apiaceae and can cross-pollinate where both are allowed to flower for seed, and they share carrot-family pests and diseases on rotation grounds. The classic folklore that mature dill suppresses carrot growth is largely untested; keep them apart mainly for the cross-pollination and shared-pest reasons.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Fennel
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep dill away from fennel. They are carrot-family cousins that can cross-pollinate if both flower, muddling the flavor of saved seed, and fennel is a poor neighbor for many plants.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Apiaceae cross-pollination between dill and fennel is sound where both flower; fennel allelopathy is a near-universal companion rule with a real mechanism (essential oils suppress seedling growth in bioassays), unmeasured on dill specifically.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Fennel is a fellow Apiaceae that can cross-pollinate dill where both bloom for seed, and it is a broad allelopath and classic poor herb neighbor that suppresses many plants. Give fennel its own corner. A traditional rule with a real mechanism, not a measured dill-fennel trial.

bad_seasoned.name: Carrots
bad_seasoned.timing: keep separate; do not let both flower side by side
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: A fellow Apiaceae that can cross-pollinate dill where both flower for seed, and that shares carrot-family pests and diseases. The folklore that mature dill stunts carrots is largely untested; separate them mainly for cross-pollination and shared pests.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Cross-pollination and shared Apiaceae pests are sound; the growth-suppression claim is untested.

bad_seasoned.name: Fennel
bad_seasoned.timing: keep separate; do not let both flower side by side
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: A fellow carrot-family plant that can cross-pollinate dill where both bloom for seed, and a broad allelopath and poor herb companion. Grow fennel apart. A traditional rule with a real allelopathic mechanism, not a dill-specific trial.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Fennel allelopathy is widely taught and mechanism-backed; Apiaceae cross-pollination is real for seed crops.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The first pair of narrow, thread-like seed leaves pushing up. Dill is slow to germinate, often 10 to 21 days, and emergence can be uneven, so be patient.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The first thin, grassy little leaves poking up. Dill is slow, often taking two to three weeks, so be patient and keep the soil moist.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep the soil surface evenly moist but never waterlogged through the long germination window. Sow shallowly into cool soil, about 60 to 70°F; cold, soggy soil rots the slow seed.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil damp but not soggy until the seedlings are up, which can take a couple of weeks. Sow shallowly in cool weather.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Any sprouts yet?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Any sprouts yet?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The first true leaves, finely divided and feathery. Now you can tell seedlings from weeds and start thinning.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The first true feathery leaves. Now you can thin the seedlings.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin to 8 to 12 inches for full plants, or 4 to 6 inches for cut leaf, and use the thinnings in the kitchen. Keep moisture steady to delay the bolt.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Thin the seedlings to about 8 to 12 inches apart, and use the ones you pull. Keep the water steady.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How are they coming along?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How are they coming along?

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bushy, feathery plants 8 to 12 inches tall, well before any central stalk rises. This is the productive dill-weed window.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Bushy, feathery plants several inches tall, before any flower stalk appears.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Start cutting feathery fronds now rather than waiting; regular cutting keeps tender new growth coming. Keep moisture even to hold off the bolt, and crop faster as the weather warms.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Start picking the feathery leaves now. Picking often keeps new leaves coming. Keep the water steady so it does not bolt, and pick faster when it warms up.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Ready to start cutting?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Ready to start cutting?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Full, tender feathery foliage with no central flower stalk yet. Once a thick stalk rises the leaf window narrows and the plant turns to flowering.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Full, feathery leaves and no flower stalk in the middle yet. Once a tall stalk appears the leafy stage is ending.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut whole fronds from the outside or shear the upper plant for fresh dill weed. Pick young and in the cool morning, and as a plant shows a stalk, decide whether to keep it for seed heads.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Snip the feathery leaves from the outside. Pick young in the cool morning, and once you see a flower stalk, either pick the last leaves or let it go to seed heads for pickling.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Harvesting regularly?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Harvesting regularly?

growth_stages.name: Bolting (to seed and heads)
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A tall central stalk shooting up, the foliage thinning, then flat yellow umbel flowers and green seed. This is the shift from leafy dill weed to flower heads and dill seed.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A tall stalk from the middle, then flat yellow flowers and green seeds. This is dill turning to seed heads, which you use for pickling.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: For leaves, cut everything worth using before quality fades. For pickling heads, cut the umbels as the flowers open; for dried seed, let the heads turn tan but cut before they shatter, then dry them. Leave one plant to self-sow if you want volunteers.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: If you want leaves, pick everything good now. For pickling, cut the flower heads as they open; for dill seed, let the heads turn tan, then cut and dry them. Leave a plant alone and it often reseeds itself.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Seen a flower stalk yet?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Seen a flower stalk yet?

notifications.body_seasoned: Your dill should have a true leaf or two now. Thin to 8 to 12 inches for full plants or 4 to 6 inches for cut leaf, and use the thinnings.
notifications.body_beginner: Your dill seedlings should be big enough to thin. Space them out and use the little ones you pull.

notifications.body_seasoned: Your dill should be bushy enough to harvest. Snip whole feathery fronds from the outside, pick young for the best flavor, and refrigerate or freeze at once.
notifications.body_beginner: Your dill should be big enough to pick. Snip the feathery leaves from the outside, and pick it young.

notifications.title_seasoned: Warm, long days ahead: beat the bolt (or make seed heads)
notifications.title_beginner: Warm weather ahead: pick your dill
notifications.body_seasoned: Warming, lengthening days bolt dill. Harvest the leaf crop promptly and plan a late-summer sowing for fall; or let bolted plants flower and set seed heads for pickling.
notifications.body_beginner: Warm, long days make dill flower. Pick your dill leaves now, plan a fall crop, and let the plants that bolt make seed heads for pickling.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot weather warning for your dill
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Sustained heat above roughly 75 to 80°F, especially with long days, bolts dill and slows leafy growth. Keep moisture even, give afternoon shade, harvest leaves promptly in the cool morning, and in hot regions treat summer as the seed-and-pickling season rather than the leaf season.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Hot weather makes dill flower early and stop making soft leaves. Water evenly, give it afternoon shade, pick the leaves in the cool morning, and remember a summer plant is really for seed heads and pickling.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hard freeze coming
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Young dill tolerates light frost, but it is less cold-hardy than the toughest greens and a hard freeze kills it. Harvest what you can before a hard freeze; in cold zones cover plants for a light frost, and rely on dill's heavy self-seeding to return plants in spring rather than overwintering the parent.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Young dill handles a light frost, but a hard freeze will kill it. Pick what you can before a hard freeze, cover plants for a light frost, and remember dill usually reseeds itself and comes back in spring.

germination.text_seasoned: Dill germinates slowly, often 10 to 21 days. Sow it shallowly, only about a quarter inch deep, directly where it will grow, since the taproot resents transplanting, and keep the surface evenly moist. Cool soil around 60 to 70°F suits it; young plants tolerate light frost, so you can sow a week or two before the last hard frost.
germination.text_beginner: Dill seeds are slow, often two to three weeks. Keep the soil moist the whole time and sow them shallowly, right where they will grow, because dill does not like being moved. You can sow early, since young dill takes a light frost.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin dill seedlings to 8 to 12 inches for full plants or 4 to 6 inches for cut leaf, and use the thinnings. Crowded plants bolt sooner and mildew more, so give them room. Keep moisture steady to delay the bolt.
seedling.text_beginner: Thin the little dill plants so they are not crowded, about 8 to 12 inches apart, and use the ones you pull. Crowded dill flowers sooner, so giving it room keeps the leaves coming.

established.text_seasoned: Cut dill young and often: snip whole feathery fronds from the outside and the plant keeps producing tender new growth. Steady moisture keeps the leaves tender and delays the bolt, and a little afternoon shade helps in warm spells.
established.text_beginner: Pick dill young and often. Snip the feathery leaves from the outside and more grow back. Keep the water steady so the leaves stay tender and it does not bolt as fast.

harvest.text_seasoned: Pick dill leaves in the cool morning and refrigerate or freeze at once, since cut dill wilts fast; the flavor is strongest just before the plant flowers. As plants begin to bolt, start cutting green umbels for pickling rather than fighting the change.
harvest.text_beginner: Cut dill leaves in the cool morning and get them in the fridge or freezer right away, because they wilt quickly. The flavor is best just before it flowers. When it starts to bolt, cut the flower heads for pickling.

bolting.text_seasoned: Bolting is the plant's second act: once the tall stalk rises, stop fighting it. Cut the green umbels for fresh pickling, or let the heads flower and set seed, then cut them as they turn tan but before they shatter, dry them, and thresh out dill seed. One plant left to drop seed reliably self-sows for next year.
bolting.text_beginner: Dill bolts fast, and that is how you get pickling heads and seed. When you see the tall stalk, cut the green flower heads for pickling, or let them turn tan, dry them, and shake out the dill seed. A plant left alone often reseeds itself.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A single dill plant gives a flush of feathery leaves over several weeks, then a tall flowering stalk topped with seed heads, so it yields on two timelines: leaves early and seed later. For steady dill weed, grow several plants in a patch and cut often; for pickling, a few tall plants supply plenty of heads and seed.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Each dill plant gives you feathery leaves for a few weeks, then sends up a tall stalk with flower heads and seeds. Grow a small patch and cut the leaves often, and let a few plants make seed heads for pickling.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Leaf production peaks in the cool weeks of late spring and fall. A spring patch produces leaves until heat and long days bolt it, while a late-summer sowing gives a strong fall leaf crop. The seed and pickling-head crop peaks from summer-bolted plants.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Dill makes the most leaves in the cooler weeks of spring and fall. Once summer heat hits, plants bolt and make flower heads and seed instead. So the leaves come in the cool seasons and the seed heads come in summer.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Dill is a fast, forgiving first-season crop: leafy dill weed in about 6 to 8 weeks from a cool-weather sowing, and seed heads later in the same season. The key to a steady leaf supply is frequent succession sowing and picking young, since a single plant soon turns to making seed. The bonus is that a bolted plant is not wasted, it gives you pickling heads and dried dill seed.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Dill is one of the easier, faster herbs for a beginner, with leaves in about 6 to 8 weeks from a cool-weather sowing. The trick is to sow a little every couple of weeks and pick it young so you keep getting tender leaves. And when it bolts, you get seed heads for pickling and dried dill seed.
factors_seasoned: Timing: a crop grown in the cool shoulders yields leaves well; one caught by summer heat and long days bolts to seed sooner. Spring and fall are the leaf seasons.
Variety: slow-bolting and dwarf selections (Fernleaf, Dukat, Hera) extend the leaf window, while tall types (Long Island Mammoth) maximize seed and pickling heads.
Even moisture: steady water keeps leaves tender and slows the bolt; drought hurries the seedstalk.
Frequent cutting and succession: picking young and sowing every 2 to 3 weeks keeps tender leaves coming.
Goal: in heat, shift the goal from leaf to seed and pickling heads rather than fighting the bolt.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No reliable extension or peer-reviewed evidence supports timing dill planting or harvest by moon phase. Sow by soil temperature, day length, and frost dates instead.

failure_diagnostics.label: Bolting (tall flower stalk; leaf growth slows)
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Summer heat and long days, sped by drought, telling the plant to flower and make seed heads.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your dill shot up a tall stalk and stopped making soft leaves. Dill bolts in summer heat and long days, which is its normal shift from leafy dill weed to flower heads and seed, not a mistake. Next time, grow it for leaves in cooler weather, sow a fresh batch every couple of weeks, pick it young, and try slow-bolting or dwarf types like Fernleaf or Dukat. And let the bolted plant make seed heads for pickling.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Grow it in cool weather, sow every couple of weeks, pick young, choose slow-bolting types, and harvest the bolted plant for seed heads.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The plant elongated into a seedstalk and leafy growth slowed as the foliage thinned. Bolting is driven by summer heat above roughly 75 to 80°F and lengthening days, accelerated by drought. Growers most often sow too late into warming weather. Next time sow into the cool shoulders, succession-sow, lean on a late-summer sowing for fall, use slow-bolting or dwarf selections, and treat warm-season plantings as a seed-and-pickling crop.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Summer heat and long-day photoperiod, accelerated by drought; the leaf-to-seed shift that defines the crop.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sow into cool weather, succession-sow every 2 to 3 weeks, lean on a late-summer sowing, choose slow-bolting types, and grow summer plantings for seed and pickling heads.

failure_diagnostics.label: Poor or very slow germination
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Dill seed is naturally slow, and cold wet soil or a dried-out surface make it worse.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your dill came up thin, patchy, or very slowly. Dill seed is slow by nature, often two to three weeks, and germinates poorly in cold, soggy soil or when the surface dries out. Next time, sow shallowly into warm-enough, moist soil, keep the surface from drying, and use fresh seed.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Sow shallowly into moist soil that is not cold and soggy, keep the surface from drying, and use fresh seed.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Stand was thin and slow. Dill germination is intrinsically slow, often 10 to 21 days, and is worsened by cold, wet soil that rots the seed and by surface drying or crusting. Next time sow shallowly into well-drained soil around 60 to 70°F, keep the seedbed evenly moist, and use fresh viable seed.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Slow seed nature plus cold, wet, or dry soil inhibiting germination.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sow shallowly into moist, well-drained, warm-enough soil, keep the bed from drying or crusting, and use fresh seed.

failure_diagnostics.label: White powdery coating on the leaves
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Powdery mildew, a fungus favored by crowding, warm days with cool nights, and overwatering.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your dill leaves got a white, powdery coating and yellowed. That is powdery mildew, which builds in crowded, overwatered plantings. Next time, space plants for airflow, water at the soil line, and pick the leaf crop young before mildew builds.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Space plants for airflow, water at the base, and pick the leaves young.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: A white, talc-like growth on the foliage indicates powdery mildew (Erysiphe heraclei), favored by crowding, warm days with cool humid nights, and overwatering. Next time widen spacing, avoid overhead watering and excess nitrogen, and harvest the leaf crop promptly; remove infected foliage on plants held for seed.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Erysiphe heraclei, favored by dense stands, warm-day cool-night weather, and excess moisture.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Widen spacing, water at the soil line, avoid heavy nitrogen, and harvest promptly.

failure_diagnostics.label: Tan-brown spots spreading on the leaves
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: A fungal leaf spot or blight, spread by wet leaves and splashing water and sometimes carried on the seed.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your dill leaves got tan-brown spots that spread and blighted the foliage, worst in wet weather. That is a fungal leaf spot. Next time, use clean seed, water at the soil line, space plants for airflow, and rotate the bed.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Use clean seed, water at the base, space for airflow, and rotate where you grow dill.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Spreading tan-brown leaf lesions that blight the foliage indicate Cercospora leaf blight or Alternaria leaf spot, favored by warm, wet, splashy conditions and sometimes seed-borne. Next time use clean seed, switch to drip, widen spacing, rotate away from the carrot family, and clear infected debris.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Cercosporidium punctum or Alternaria spp., splash- and seed-spread and favored by wet weather.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Use clean seed, irrigate at the soil line, widen spacing, rotate away from Apiaceae, and remove infected debris.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Dill is a natural succession crop: it matures fast and bolts once summer heat and long days arrive, so one sowing fades in a few weeks. Sow a short row every 2 to 3 weeks through the cool windows, spring until heat sets in, and again from late summer through fall, which gives a strong second leaf crop. In hot regions skip high summer for leaves and succession-sow through the cool fall, winter, and spring, letting any summer plants run to seed and pickling heads.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: Sow a little dill every 2 to 3 weeks instead of all at once, so you always have fresh leaves before it bolts. Do this in spring and again in late summer for fall. In hot areas, skip high summer for leaves and keep sowing through the cool months, and let summer plants make seed heads.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: dill_author_fresh_pilot (Claude Code lane authoring, 2026-06-29). Authored from the dill shell, modeled STRUCTURALLY on the certified culinary-herb template basil, with the cool-season calendar / heat_pause / succession SHAPE modeled on the gate-clean cilantro-coriander pilot (the closest analog: a cool-season, bolt-prone Apiaceae herb with a dual leaf/seed use) and the arugula/spinach cool-season pilots (shared cool-season frost/heat climate envelope). Dill (Anethum graveolens, Apiaceae) biology re-derived from live T1 extension sources: USU 'Dill in the Garden', Wisconsin Horticulture dill page, and Clemson herbs. DRAFT for daily biology-fidelity review, not certified: launch flags false. Key dill-vs-basil refits: basil is a WARM-season frost-TENDER herb grown through summer, while dill is a COOL-leaning herb whose leaf crop favors the cool shoulders and which BOLTS to a tall (3 to 5 ft) flower stalk in summer heat and long days. ONE plant, TWO products like cilantro: the leaf is dill weed, the flower heads and dried seed are for pickling and the spice dill seed, so the bolt that slows the leaf crop begins the seed/head crop. Direct-sown (slender taproot resents transplant), succession-sown every 2 to 3 weeks, and SELF-SOWS readily so it often returns as volunteers. Apiaceae rotation/pest/disease set: pests are the parsleyworm (black swallowtail caterpillar, a welcome visitor) and aphids; diseases are minimal (powdery mildew, leaf spot/blight, damping-off). pH 5.5 to 6.5; spacing 8 to 12 inches; full sun; germination ~60 to 70°F. successions_realized is CC-derived (deriver), not hand-authored. See dill_NOTES.md for modeled values and flags.

open_findings.summary: All 10 regions' per-zone calendars are MODELED from dill's cool-season frost/heat envelope and the regional extension planting-calendar sources, reusing the gate-clean cilantro/arugula/spinach cool-season calendar SHAPE (spring + fall plant windows, summer heat_pause in warm regions, cold_pause in winter). Few dill-per-region charts exist; the frost-anchored cool-season shape is shared climate truth across cool-season bolt-prone herbs, and the dill-specific refit is its dual leaf/seed use and summer bolt. resolution_method on each cell is 'cc_author_pilot_modeled'. Flagged for the daily biology-fidelity review.
open_findings.basis: Cool-season sowing windows are frost/heat-driven and shared across cool-season crops; dill shares cilantro's bolt-in-heat, frost-tolerant-when-young envelope. Dill is less cold-hardy than cilantro and self-sows rather than reliably overwintering, so the review may temper any overwinter framing and nudge harvest tokens for dill's ~40 to 70 day leaf maturity.

open_findings.summary: Each genuinely-hot region cell carries a backed heat_pause object (months + basis_seasoned + source + URL). The basis frames the pause honestly for dill: leaf (dill weed) production stops because the crop bolts to seed and pickling heads once summer heat and long days set in, so summer is the seed/head season rather than the leaf season. Cool northern zones 3 to 5 and the mild CA north coast are modeled as running through summer (no heat_pause).
open_findings.basis: Task heat_pause why-note rule + the locked cool-season heat_pause convention (a summer leaf gap with a fall crop after = backed heat_pause, not season_over). All heat_pause cells anchored to the USU dill page.

open_findings.summary: days_to_maturity [40, 70] (mid 55) brackets the leaf figures of USU (6 to 8 weeks) and harvest-to-table (~70 days leaf); seed/heads run ~90 to 100 days, stated in prose. spacing_inches [8, 12] follows USU (thin to 9 inches) and harvest-to-table (10 to 12 inches), with 4 to 6 inch cut-leaf spacing in prose. germination_temp_f [60, 70] follows the commonly cited dill germination band (USU gives 7 to 21 day emergence by soil temperature; no single T1 page tables an explicit min/max).
open_findings.basis: Within the cited USU / Wisconsin figures; the operative facts (slow germination, fast leaf, tall seed plant, 8 to 12 inch spacing) are sourced and surfaced in prose.

open_findings.summary: ph.preferred_range [5.5, 6.5] is Utah State University's stated ideal range for dill; the tolerated band [5.5, 7.0] reflects dill's forgiving, not-pH-sensitive nature (harvest-to-table gives 5.5 to 6.7).
open_findings.basis: USU 5.5 to 6.5 ideal; flagged for the daily review's source-truth sample.

open_findings.summary: The bolt threshold stated as 'roughly 75 to 80°F and lengthening days' is MODELED. The readable T1 dill pages state that dill bolts in 'hot weather' and long days and that heat reduces seed production (USU notes +95°F decreases seed; Wisconsin: hot or dry triggers the flower stalk), but none table a precise bolt temperature. The ~75 to 80°F figure follows the cool-season bolt convention (cilantro ~75°F) and is surfaced consistently in the heat_pause basis, bolting, and weather-trigger prose.
open_findings.basis: Sources confirm heat-and-long-day bolting qualitatively; the exact threshold is a modeled convention, flagged for the daily review.

open_findings.summary: Powdery mildew is directly sourced (USU and Wisconsin both name it on dill). The leaf-spot/blight and damping-off entries are anchored to the same readable T1 dill pages, but the specific pathogen IDs (Cercosporidium punctum / Alternaria for leaf blight; Pythium/Rhizoctonia/Fusarium for damping-off) are MODELED from general Apiaceae disease knowledge: the Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks document dill Alternaria leaf spot and damping-off but returned HTTP 403 and were not WebFetch-readable, so per the sourcing rule they are flagged rather than extracted.
open_findings.basis: Powdery mildew sourced; leaf spot + damping-off are real for dill (PNW handbooks) but the catalogued source was unreadable, so the pathogen specifics are flagged for the daily review's source-truth check.

open_findings.summary: fertilizer.npk_ratio is the explicit-null sentinel with npk_tag 'Light feeder: little to no supplemental fertilizer needed', because dill is a genuinely lean-soil, light-feeding herb: USU states no additional nutrients are needed if the soil is amended at planting, and heavy nitrogen makes dill lank and weakens its aromatic oils. No fabricated N-P-K ratio.
open_findings.basis: USU: dill needs no extra feeding if amended at planting; the npk pill renders the qualitative tag rather than an invented ratio.

open_findings.summary: No dill-specific catalog IDs exist, so existing institution-level catalog IDs are reused with the best readable page in anchoring_urls. Directly-read dill anchors: usu_ext (USU 'Dill in the Garden'), uwi_hort (Wisconsin Horticulture dill page), clemson_hgic (Clemson herbs, dill section). Regional calendar anchors (uc_mg, ucanr_ext, ndsu_ext, msu_ext, umaine_ext, uga_ext_c943_calendar, msstate_ext, lsu_agcenter, uariz_ext, az_coop_ext, nmsu_ext, uf_ifas_south_cal, uf_ifas_vh021, uhawaii_ctahr) are section/portal/calendar-level, carried over from the cilantro pilot's regional model. No IDs were invented; all are catalogued and T1. Flagged for the daily review's URL-liveness check.
open_findings.basis: Task sourcing rule + the cilantro/arugula/spinach pilot precedent: reuse a real catalog ID, anchor to the best readable page, flag section/portal-level anchors.

open_findings.summary: successions_realized was NOT hand-authored: the CC deriver filled it per cell (rule 3, day-precise sow window split on the calendar's heat_pause/cold_pause months) at interval_weeks 2, and reconciled succession_policy.successions and max_successions_per_season to the max over zones.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: Up North (zones 3 through 7), dill is a quick spring-and-fall leaf herb. Start sowing in early spring as soon as you can work the soil, since young dill takes a light frost, and sow a little every 2 to 3 weeks. In the coldest zones the cool summer lets it keep making leaves, but in the milder zones the hottest weeks bolt it, so take a break in midsummer and sow again for fall. Dill reseeds itself, so it often comes back on its own, and any summer plant that bolts gives you seed heads for pickling.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In the cold-winter North (zones 3 through 7), dill is a fast spring-and-fall succession herb built around frost. Sow as soon as the soil can be worked, since young dill tolerates light frost, and sow a short row every 2 to 3 weeks. In the coolest zones the cool summer often carries leaf production through, while in the warmer end of the band midsummer heat and long days bolt it, so the leaf calendar pauses through the hottest weeks and resumes for a fall crop. Dill self-sows heavily, so volunteers often return in spring, and bolted summer plants are left for seed and pickling heads.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast and Gulf (zones 8 and 9), grow dill for leaves in the cool months, fall through spring. The hot, humid summer bolts it, so skip summer for leaves and let any summer plants make seed heads. Sow every 2 to 3 weeks across the long cool window, and watch for volunteers, since dill reseeds itself.
