pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny shot-hole punctures riddle the leaves, a scatter of small round holes that is the classic flea-beetle signature on eggplant. Damage is by far most severe on seedlings and young transplants, whose small leaf area a heavy infestation can shred or kill outright; established plants tolerate considerable feeding. Brush a plant and the small dark beetles spring away like fleas.
pests.symptoms_beginner: The leaves are peppered with lots of tiny round holes, as if hit by birdshot. It hits young plants hardest and can devastate seedlings. Touch the plant and you will see tiny dark beetles jump away.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several Epitrix flea beetle species that feed on eggplant foliage, overwintering as adults in debris and emerging to attack the earliest, most vulnerable plants in spring. Eggplant is a strongly preferred host, and the beetles concentrate on it, which is why flea beetles are the defining early-season eggplant pest.
pests.cause_beginner: Small dark beetles that jump like fleas and chew tiny holes in the leaves. They are most active in spring and love eggplant, so they target young plants early in the season.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Protect transplants with floating row cover until they are large and vigorous, removing it at flowering. Set out stout, well-hardened transplants rather than tiny seedlings so plants can outgrow the damage, and treat heavy early infestations with spinosad or kaolin clay. Mature plants rarely need treatment.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover young plants with a light row cover until they are big and strong, then take it off when they flower. Setting out larger transplants helps them outgrow the damage. For heavy attacks on seedlings, an organic spray such as spinosad or a kaolin clay coating helps.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Use row cover from transplanting, delay setting plants out until the soil and air are warm so they grow away fast, and clean up crop debris and weeds that harbor overwintering adults. A nasturtium or other trap planting at the bed edge can draw beetles off the crop.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover plants early with row cover, set out larger transplants into warm soil so they grow quickly, and clear away weeds and old plant debris where the beetles hide over winter. A border of nasturtiums can lure them away.

pests.name: Colorado potato beetle
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Rounded yellow-and-black-striped adults and humpbacked, brick-red larvae with rows of black spots chew the leaves, and eggplant is a favorite host. Both stages feed voraciously and populations build fast, so an unmanaged infestation can defoliate plants and cut yield sharply. Look for clusters of orange-yellow eggs on leaf undersides.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Striped yellow-and-black beetles and plump red larvae with black spots eat the leaves, sometimes stripping a plant bare. Eggplant is one of their favorite foods. Check the undersides of leaves for clusters of orange-yellow eggs.
pests.cause_seasoned: Leptinotarsa decemlineata, a Solanaceae specialist that prefers potato and eggplant. Adults overwinter in the soil and nearby debris and move in as plants establish; left alone they go through multiple generations a season and quickly resist many insecticides, making non-chemical control important.
pests.cause_beginner: A striped beetle whose larvae and adults both feed on eggplant and potato leaves. They overwinter in the soil, show up as plants get going, and multiply quickly through the summer.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: In a home garden, hand-pick adults, larvae, and egg clusters daily into soapy water, which keeps small plantings clean. Crush egg masses on leaf undersides, and where pressure is high apply spinosad or Bacillus thuringiensis var. tenebrionis to young larvae. Rotating away from last year's nightshade bed cuts the overwintered population.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick the beetles, larvae, and egg clusters off by hand and drop them in soapy water, checking every day or two. Squash the orange egg clusters under the leaves. For heavy infestations, an organic spray such as spinosad or Bt (the tenebrionis strain) works on the young larvae.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Rotate eggplant well away from where potatoes, tomatoes, or eggplant grew last year, since the overwintered adults emerge near old hosts. Row cover on young plants excludes the colonizers, and a thick straw mulch hinders the adults that walk in from the soil.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not plant eggplant where potatoes, tomatoes, or eggplant grew last year, since the beetles come up from the soil there. Cover young plants with row cover, and a thick straw mulch makes it harder for the beetles to reach them.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Colonies of small soft-bodied insects, often green peach aphid, cluster on growing tips and leaf undersides, causing leaves to curl, pucker, and yellow, with sticky honeydew and sooty mold following. Beyond direct feeding, aphids transmit mosaic and other viruses that mottle and distort the foliage.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny soft green or black insects gather on new growth and the undersides of leaves, making them curl and yellow, often with a sticky film and black mold. They can also spread plant viruses.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several aphid species, predominantly green peach aphid, that suck sap and reproduce rapidly in warm weather, building up fast on soft, over-fertilized growth. The honeydew they excrete fosters sooty mold that shades the leaves.
pests.cause_beginner: Small sap-sucking insects that multiply quickly in warm weather, especially on soft growth from too much fertilizer. The sticky honeydew they leave grows black mold.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong jet of water and spray insecticidal soap or horticultural oil with thorough coverage of leaf undersides, repeating every few days. Conserve lady beetles, lacewings, and parasitic wasps, which usually bring aphids under control.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water and treat the undersides of the leaves with insecticidal soap, repeating every few days. Ladybugs and other helpful insects eat aphids, so welcome them.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen, which drives the soft growth aphids favor, scout leaf undersides and growing tips, and support natural enemies rather than spraying broadly. Reflective mulch deters aphids from young plants.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen, check the undersides of leaves regularly, and let helpful insects do their work instead of spraying everything.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine yellow stippling speckles the leaves, which may bronze, dry, and drop, and in bad infestations fine webbing appears on leaf undersides. Two-spotted spider mites thrive in hot, dry weather, exactly the conditions eggplant is grown in, so mite pressure often peaks in midsummer.
pests.symptoms_beginner: The leaves look dusty or speckled with tiny yellow dots, and in bad cases you see fine webbing underneath. The leaves can bronze and dry out. Mites love hot, dry weather.
pests.cause_seasoned: Tetranychus urticae and related mites that feed on the lower leaf surfaces with piercing mouthparts. Populations explode in heat and drought and on dusty, water-stressed plants, and can build quickly on eggplant in summer.
pests.cause_beginner: Tiny mites, almost too small to see, that feed on the undersides of leaves and thrive in hot, dry, dusty conditions. They build up fast in summer.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Spray the leaf undersides with a strong jet of water repeatedly to disrupt colonies, then apply insecticidal soap or horticultural oil to the undersides, repeating every few days. Keeping plants well watered and raising humidity discourages mites; predatory mites help under heavy pressure.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray the undersides of the leaves with a strong jet of water every day for a week, then follow up with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil if needed. Keeping plants well watered helps, since stressed plants are hit hardest.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep plants well watered in hot weather, since drought-stressed plants are most vulnerable, avoid dusty conditions, and avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that kill the predators holding mites in check.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep plants well watered in hot weather, hose dust off the leaves now and then, and avoid spraying broad insecticides that kill the helpful bugs that eat mites.

pests.name: Eggplant lace bug
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Leaves develop a pale, yellow-stippled or bleached look on top, while the undersides carry dark, varnish-like specks of excrement and the small, lacy-winged adults and spiny nymphs. Heavy feeding browns and curls the foliage and can stunt the plant, and lace bugs are fairly eggplant-specific.
pests.symptoms_beginner: The tops of the leaves look pale and stippled, and underneath you find dark sticky specks and small insects with lacy-looking wings. Bad infestations brown and curl the leaves.
pests.cause_seasoned: The eggplant lace bug (Gargaphia solani), a true bug that feeds in colonies on leaf undersides with piercing-sucking mouthparts. It overwinters in debris and is most damaging in warm weather, with several generations a season.
pests.cause_beginner: A small flat insect with lacy wings that feeds in groups on the undersides of eggplant leaves, sucking out the juices. It is most active in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Scout leaf undersides early and treat colonies directly with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil, which reach the soft nymphs, covering the undersides thoroughly and repeating as needed. Remove and destroy the worst-infested leaves.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Check the undersides of the leaves and spray any colonies directly with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil, making sure to coat underneath. Pick off and destroy the most badly affected leaves.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Clean up crop debris at season's end to remove overwintering sites, rotate eggplant, and scout the undersides of lower leaves from early in the season so colonies are caught while small.
pests.prevention_beginner: Clear away old plants at the end of the season, move eggplant to a new spot each year, and check the undersides of the lower leaves early so you catch the bugs before they spread.

pests.name: Hornworms
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Large sections of leaf, and sometimes whole shoots, are stripped down to the veins overnight, with dark pellet droppings on the leaves below. The culprits are big green tomato or tobacco hornworms, up to four inches long, that blend into the stems and are easiest to find by their frass.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Whole leaves vanish overnight, leaving just the veins, with dark droppings on the leaves below. The cause is a large green caterpillar that hides against the stems, easier to spot by its droppings than by sight.
pests.cause_seasoned: Tomato and tobacco hornworms, the larvae of large sphinx moths, which feed on solanaceous foliage including eggplant from midsummer on. A few caterpillars can do conspicuous damage given their size.
pests.cause_beginner: Big green caterpillars, the young of large moths, that feed on eggplant and tomato leaves mostly in mid to late summer. Even a few can strip a lot of foliage.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick the caterpillars, which is effective in a home garden, and apply Bacillus thuringiensis to younger larvae where numbers are high. Leave any hornworm studded with white parasitic-wasp cocoons in place, since the wasps will kill it and breed more.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick the caterpillars off by hand and drop them in soapy water. If you find one covered in small white capsules, leave it, those are parasitic wasps that will do the work for you. An organic Bt spray works on the smaller caterpillars.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Till the soil in fall to destroy overwintering pupae, scout for frass and stripped leaves from midsummer, and encourage the parasitic wasps and other natural enemies that keep hornworms in check.
pests.prevention_beginner: Turn the soil at the end of the season to destroy the pupae, watch for droppings and missing leaves from midsummer, and welcome the helpful wasps that attack hornworms.

diseases.name: Verticillium wilt
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Lower and outer leaves yellow, often in a wedge or one-sided pattern, then wilt, brown, and drop, working upward as the plant stunts and fails to size its fruit. A cut through a wilting stem shows tan-to-brown streaking in the water-conducting tissue. It is the most common and damaging eggplant disease in much of the country.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Leaves turn yellow and wilt, often on one side of the plant first, then brown and drop while the plant stunts. Cut a wilting stem and you may see brown streaks inside. It is the most common serious eggplant disease.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Verticillium dahliae, a soilborne fungus that infects the roots and clogs the vascular system, so the plant wilts despite moist soil. It persists in soil for years as resting structures, has a wide host range across the Solanaceae and many other crops, and is favored by cool-to-moderate soil temperatures.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soil fungus that infects the roots and blocks the plant's water pipes, so it wilts even when watered. It lives in the soil for years and attacks many crops, especially the nightshade family.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once a plant is infected; remove and destroy affected plants. Management is preventive and centered on rotation and resistant or grafted plants, since the fungus cannot be eradicated from infested soil by home-garden means.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure once a plant has it, so pull and destroy infected plants. The real answer is prevention: rotate your crops and choose resistant or grafted plants next time.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Do not plant eggplant where verticillium-susceptible crops (tomato, pepper, potato, eggplant, and many others) have grown, rotate on a long cycle, choose tolerant varieties or grafted plants on resistant rootstock, and keep plants vigorous with steady water and balanced feeding. Solarizing infested beds can lower inoculum.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant eggplant in soil with no recent history of the disease, rotate away from tomatoes, peppers, and potatoes, and look for resistant or grafted plants. Keeping plants healthy with steady water and feeding helps them cope.

diseases.name: Phomopsis blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Pale, sunken spots appear on the fruit that rapidly enlarge to soft, spongy, rotting areas, sometimes shrinking the fruit into a dry mummy; the disease also causes grayish leaf spots and a collar rot that can break young stems an inch or two above the soil line. It is most damaging in warm, wet weather and toward fall.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Pale sunken spots on the fruit spread quickly into soft, rotting patches, and the disease can also spot the leaves and rot the stem near the base. It is worst in warm, wet weather and later in the season.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Phomopsis vexans, a fungus that is both soil- and seedborne and overwinters on crop debris. Warm, humid conditions and splashing water spread it, and infected seed or volunteer debris often starts an outbreak, so clean seed and rotation are central to control.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus carried on seed and in old plant debris that spreads in warm, wet weather. It can come in on infected seed, so starting clean matters.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy infected fruit and plants promptly to limit spread, and where the disease is active apply a labeled fungicide, keeping foliage and fruit as dry as possible. There is no rescue for badly rotted fruit.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick off and throw away infected fruit and plants right away. Keep the leaves and fruit dry by watering at the soil, and use a labeled fungicide if it is spreading. Rotted fruit cannot be saved.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Start with clean, treated, or resistant seed and disease-free transplants, rotate eggplant out of the bed for about four years, water at the soil rather than overhead, mulch to limit splash, space for airflow, and remove crop debris at season's end.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Use clean seed and healthy transplants, do not plant eggplant in the same spot for about four years, water at the soil instead of over the leaves, and clean up old plants at the end of the season.

diseases.name: Bacterial wilt
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Individual leaves, then whole plants, wilt and collapse suddenly even though the soil is moist, with little of the yellowing that precedes verticillium. Cut low on the stem and the pith is discolored reddish-brown; suspended in clear water, a cut stem streams milky bacterial ooze. It is most serious in hot, wet soils of the South.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The plant wilts and collapses suddenly even though the soil is wet, without much yellowing first. If you cut the stem near the base, the inside looks brown, and a cut stem held in a glass of water gives off milky strands. It is mainly a problem in the hot, wet South.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Ralstonia solanacearum, a soilborne bacterium that invades the roots and plugs the vascular tissue. It survives in soil and infected debris, spreads in water and on tools, and is favored by high soil temperature and moisture, so it is most damaging in warm, wet regions.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soil bacterium that gets into the roots and blocks the plant's water flow, so it wilts fast. It lives in warm, wet soil and spreads in water and on tools.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure; remove and destroy wilted plants promptly to limit spread, and disinfect tools. Because it persists in soil, management is preventive, through rotation, resistant or grafted plants, and improved drainage.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure, so pull and destroy any plant that wilts from it, and clean your tools. The real fix is prevention next season.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Avoid planting eggplant where tomato, potato, or eggplant grew in the previous three years, choose resistant varieties or graft onto resistant rootstock in problem areas, improve drainage, and avoid moving infested soil or working among wet plants.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Do not plant eggplant where tomatoes, potatoes, or eggplant grew in the last three years, improve drainage in wet spots, and look for resistant or grafted plants if this disease is common where you live.

diseases.name: Phytophthora blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark, water-soaked lesions and streaking develop on stems, leaves, or fruit, and a plant can collapse and die rapidly once the stem is girdled. Fruit rots with a firm, sometimes white-cottony decay. It flares in warm, wet, poorly drained conditions and after heavy rain or flooding.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Dark, wet-looking patches appear on the stems, leaves, or fruit, and the plant can wilt and die quickly. The fruit can rot, sometimes with white fuzzy growth. It strikes in warm, wet, poorly drained ground.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Phytophthora species (such as P. capsici and P. nicotianae), water molds that thrive in saturated soil and spread in splashing and running water. They survive in soil and debris and move fast in warm, wet weather, especially on heavy or poorly drained ground.
diseases.cause_beginner: A mold-like disease that lives in wet soil and spreads in splashing water, attacking plants in warm, soggy conditions. It moves fast once it starts.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy affected plants and fruit promptly, and improve drainage immediately. There is no effective home-garden cure once plants collapse, so control is preventive and drainage-based.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Pull and destroy affected plants and fruit, and fix the drainage. There is no good home cure once it takes hold, so prevention is what matters.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant on raised, well-drained beds or hills, avoid low spots that stay wet, water at the soil rather than overhead, mulch to limit splash, rotate away from solanaceous and cucurbit crops, and keep fruit up off saturated soil.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant on raised beds or mounds so water drains away, avoid wet low spots, water at the soil, and keep fruit off soggy ground. Rotate away from peppers, tomatoes, and squash.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Aim for about 1 inch of water per week from rain plus irrigation, more in heat or on sandy soil, delivered deeply and less often rather than in light daily sprinkles. As a heat-loving plant grown through the hottest part of the year, eggplant transpires heavily in summer, and container plants dry out far faster still.
watering.frequency_beginner: Give eggplant about 1 inch of water a week, more when it is hot and dry. Water deeply rather than a little every day. Plants in pots dry out much faster and may need checking daily in summer.
watering.amount_seasoned: Around 1 inch per week is the working range, leaning higher during flowering and fruit set, wetting the soil to a depth of at least 6 to 8 inches so the roots follow the moisture down. Even, deep watering is what sizes well-shaped fruit; letting the soil swing from dry to soaked stresses the plant and drops blossoms.
watering.amount_beginner: About 1 inch of water a week, soaking the soil down 6 to 8 inches so the roots grow deep. Keep it even: letting the soil go bone-dry and then flooding it stresses the plant and makes flowers drop.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base with a soaker hose or drip line, keeping the foliage as dry as possible, since wet leaves favor the leaf spots and fruit rots eggplant is prone to. If overhead watering is unavoidable, do it in the morning so leaves dry before evening. A layer of mulch buffers soil moisture and warmth and blocks soil-borne spores from splashing onto the lower leaves.
watering.method_beginner: Water the soil, not the leaves, with a soaker hose or by holding the hose at the base. Keeping the leaves dry helps prevent disease. If you must use a sprinkler, do it in the morning so the leaves dry off by evening. Mulch helps keep the soil evenly moist and warm.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting even when the soil is wet, and soft, rotting stems or fruit point to overwatering or poor drainage. Saturated soil starves the roots of oxygen and invites the Phytophthora and bacterial wilts eggplant is susceptible to, especially on heavy ground.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If the lower leaves yellow, the plant wilts even though the soil is wet, or stems and fruit go soft and rotten, it is getting too much water or the soil drains poorly.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Midday wilting that recovers overnight is common in heat and not alarming, but leaves that stay limp and dull signal real drought. Drought stress during flowering and fruit set shows up as dropped blossoms and small, misshapen, sometimes bitter fruit.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Some midday wilting in hot weather is normal and passes by evening. Leaves that stay wilted mean the plant is too dry, and drought while it is flowering causes dropped blossoms and small, bitter fruit.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Base watering is the most useful habit for eggplant, because the same plant that wants steady moisture is also prone to leaf spots and fruit and root rots. Keep water on the soil, air moving through the leaves, and the ripening fruit up off wet ground.
watering.method_note_beginner: Watering the soil instead of the leaves is the best thing you can do for eggplant. It keeps the plant hydrated without encouraging leaf and fruit disease.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The water-critical stretch runs from flowering through fruit set and sizing. Steady moisture here sets and fills well-shaped fruit, while swings between dry and saturated soil drop blossoms and give small, bitter, misshapen fruit. Keep it even once the plant is carrying fruit.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The most important time to keep eggplant evenly watered is when it is flowering and setting fruit. Uneven water now causes dropped flowers and small, bitter fruit, so aim for steady moisture.

crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Harvest eggplant YOUNG and GLOSSY, while the fruit is immature, not at full size. The single best cue is the skin: a ripe eggplant is firm and has a high, mirror-like gloss, and press the side gently with a thumbnail and the dent springs back. Once the skin turns dull or bronzed, the flesh has gone seedy, spongy, and bitter and the dent stays, the sign you waited too long. Pick large oval types from about 2 inches across up to two-thirds of their mature size, and slender Asian types at finger-to-hot-dog size. Cut the fruit with shears or a knife leaving a short piece of the stem and the green calyx attached, rather than pulling, since the stems are tough and often spiny. Harvest regularly, at least once or twice a week, because picking fruit while immature keeps the plant setting more; fruit left to over-ripen shuts down further production.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Pick eggplant while it is young and shiny, not when it is biggest. A ready eggplant has firm flesh and a bright, glossy skin, and when you press the side with your thumb the dent springs back. If the skin looks dull instead of shiny, you waited too long: the inside will be seedy, spongy, and bitter. Harvest large oval types when they are firm and glossy and slimmer Asian types at finger or hot-dog size. Cut the fruit off with scissors or a knife, leaving a little stem on, instead of pulling, because the stems are tough and sometimes prickly. Keep picking every few days, since taking the fruit young keeps the plant making more.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Eggplant transplants are especially sensitive to a cold check, so harden off carefully over 7 to 10 days, easing plants into sun and wind, and set them out only once nights stay reliably above 50°F and the soil is thoroughly warm. A transplant chilled below about 50°F sulks for weeks and yields poorly, so it is better to wait a week or two past the tomato date than to plant into cold ground.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: Eggplant hates the cold, so harden plants off over about a week to ten days, giving them more time outside each day, and do not set them out until nights stay above 50°F and the soil is warm. Planting too early into cold ground stalls eggplant badly, so it pays to wait until it is truly warm, a couple of weeks after you would plant tomatoes.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Start eggplant seeds indoors about 8 weeks before transplanting (UMD uses 8 to 10 week old transplants), with bottom heat of 75 to 85°F for fast, even germination. Eggplant needs a longer, warmer start than tomato and is set out later, once nights hold above 50°F and the soil has warmed to at least 60 to 65°F. Choose sturdy transplants up to a foot tall with stems about pencil thick, and set plant supports at planting. Direct sowing is practical only in the longest, warmest regions; everywhere else this is a transplant crop.
start_method.notes_beginner: Start eggplant seeds indoors about 8 weeks before you plan to plant out, keeping them warm (75 to 85°F) to sprout well. Eggplant needs more warmth and a longer head start than tomatoes, and it goes outside later, only once nights stay above 50°F and the soil is warm. Use stocky transplants up to a foot tall, and put a stake or cage in at planting time.

drainage.saucer_practice_seasoned: If you use a saucer, empty it within an hour of watering. Eggplant will not tolerate sitting in standing water, which starves the roots of oxygen and invites root rot. A saucer is useful for holding warmth, which eggplant likes, but the roots must not stay submerged.
drainage.saucer_practice_beginner: Do not let the pot sit in a saucer of standing water. Empty it soon after watering. A saucer is fine for keeping the pot warm, which eggplant enjoys, but the roots should never sit in pooled water.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Use a bag of potting mix made for containers, not soil dug from the garden, which packs down hard and drains poorly in a pot.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in compost and a slow-release fertilizer at planting. Pots need feeding more often than beds, because watering washes nutrients out.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: Use a rich, free-draining peat- or coir-based container potting mix, not garden soil, which compacts and drains poorly in a pot.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend in about 20 to 25 percent compost plus a slow-release balanced fertilizer at planting. Because frequent watering leaches nutrients, plan to feed a container eggplant more regularly than one in the ground, shifting to nitrogen once fruit sets.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out much faster than garden beds, so in summer heat a potted eggplant may need water every day. Check daily, and water until it runs from the bottom. Keep it even, since drying out and then flooding drops the flowers.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Feed a potted eggplant more often than a garden plant. Once it is growing strongly and especially once fruit sets, give a balanced liquid feed every week or two.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Not applicable. Eggplant lives for one season and is killed by frost, so there is nothing to overwinter. Plant fresh from seed or transplants next year.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Not applicable. Eggplant is a frost-tender annual that completes its life in a single season and is killed by the first frost, so there is nothing to overwinter. Pull spent plants at season's end and start fresh the following year.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Eggplant is a great container plant, and pots even help by warming the roots, which this heat-lover enjoys. Use at least a 5-gallon pot, 12 inches deep, one plant per pot, in full sun. Compact varieties like Patio Baby and Fairy Tale are bred for containers, and slim Asian types like Ichiban also do well. Keep it well watered (pots dry fast), feed regularly, and stake or cage the plant so a fruit-laden stem does not topple.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Eggplant is an excellent container crop, and the warmer root zone of a dark pot in sun suits this heat-loving plant. Use a pot of at least 5 gallons (7 is better) and 12 inches deep, one plant per pot, in full sun. Compact, container-bred varieties such as Patio Baby and Fairy Tale, and slender Asian types such as Ichiban, perform best; full-size globe types need the larger pot and a stake. Water consistently, since a small soil volume dries fast and moisture swings drop blossoms, feed regularly because containers leach nutrients, and cage or stake plants to carry the fruit.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry far faster than beds, and a potted eggplant can need water once or even twice a day in summer heat. Check daily by feeling the top inch of mix, and water until it runs from the drainage holes; even moisture prevents the blossom drop and misshapen fruit that water swings cause.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Feed container eggplant more often than in-ground plants, since steady watering leaches nutrients. After the slow-release charge at planting, add a balanced liquid feed every 1 to 2 weeks, shifting toward nitrogen once fruit sets.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering container suits eggplant well, smoothing the moisture swings that drop blossoms on this thirsty summer crop. Keep the reservoir topped up in heat, water from below to keep the foliage dry, and occasionally water from the top to flush the salts that concentrate with constant sub-irrigation.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match for eggplant because it keeps the water steady, which helps prevent dropped flowers. Keep the reservoir filled in hot weather, and every so often water from the top too, which rinses out built-up minerals.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: A container eggplant wants a deep, sturdy pot, at least 12 inches deep and 5 gallons or more, with a wide enough base that a fruit-laden plant does not tip. Depth for the roots matters more than width. Choose compact or Asian varieties for the smallest pots and give full-size globe types a larger container and a stake.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Give a container eggplant a deep, heavy pot, at least 12 inches deep and 5 gallons or more, so the roots have room and the plant does not tip over when loaded with fruit. A deep, sturdy pot beats a shallow, light one. Use small or Asian varieties in the smallest pots.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Tomatoes, peppers, potatoes, and eggplant, which share verticillium and bacterial wilt, phomopsis, the flea beetle, and the Colorado potato beetle. These soilborne diseases and overwintering pests build up wherever a nightshade has grown.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Do not plant eggplant where you grew tomatoes, peppers, potatoes, or eggplant recently. They are all in the same family and share the same soil diseases and pests, which build up and carry over.
rotation.good_after: Legumes (beans, peas), brassicas, sweet corn, alliums (onions, garlic), and leafy greens make good preceding crops, since they do not share the nightshade pest and disease complex, and a legume leaves nitrogen behind for the long-feeding eggplant.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate eggplant on a long cycle, returning it to a given bed no sooner than the fourth year, to break the buildup of verticillium and bacterial wilt, phomopsis (which is also seedborne), and the flea and Colorado potato beetles. The wider Solanaceae, tomato, pepper, and potato, share that complex, so rotate as a group and avoid following any of them. Clear and remove spent plants at season's end rather than tilling them in, which removes overwintering pest and disease sites.
rotation.note_beginner: Move eggplant to a different part of the garden each year, and do not return it, or its relatives tomato, pepper, and potato, to the same spot for about four years. Soil diseases like verticillium wilt and the pests that bother eggplant build up where nightshades grow, and rotation is the main tool to keep them in check. Clean up old plants at the end of the season too.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Eggplant is a poor keeper and is best used within a day or two of picking, when its texture and mild flavor are at their best. Held at warm room temperature it softens and shrivels quickly, so a cool spot out of direct sun is better for a short hold. Unlike a winter squash, it does not cure or store, so harvest close to when you will cook it.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Eggplant does not keep well, so use it within a day or two for the best texture and flavor. At warm room temperature it goes soft and wrinkled fast, so keep it somewhere cool and out of the sun if you are not cooking it right away.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Eggplant is chilling-sensitive: store it at a medium-cool 45 to 54°F with high humidity for up to about a week, not in the coldest part of the fridge. Below about 50°F for long it develops chilling injury, surface pitting, bronzing, and browning of the seeds and flesh, so a cool pantry or the warmest part of the refrigerator, loosely bagged to hold humidity, beats deep cold. Use within a week.
storage.fridge_beginner: Eggplant does not like the cold. Keep it in the warmest part of the fridge, ideally around 45 to 50°F, loosely bagged so it does not dry out, and use it within a week. Stored too cold for too long it develops pitting and brown spots.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Eggplant does not freeze well raw; the texture turns mushy. To freeze, slice and blanch it or, better, cook it first, for example roast or grill and puree it, then cool and freeze in portions for later dishes. Cooked or breaded-and-cooked eggplant freezes acceptably for a few months.
storage.freezer_beginner: Do not freeze raw eggplant, as it turns mushy. Instead cook it first, by roasting or grilling, then cool it and freeze it in portions to use in cooked dishes later. It keeps a few months that way.
storage.notes_seasoned: Treat eggplant as a fresh-use crop, not a storage one. Pick it young and glossy and cook it within a few days. For a short hold, keep it at a medium-cool temperature (about 45 to 54°F) and high humidity, away from the coldest part of the refrigerator, since prolonged cold below 50°F causes chilling injury. Handle gently, as the skin bruises, and keep it away from ethylene-producing fruit, which hastens softening.
storage.notes_beginner: Eggplant is for eating fresh, not storing. Pick it shiny and young and cook it within a few days. If you need to keep it a little while, put it somewhere cool but not cold, around 45 to 50°F, loosely bagged. It bruises easily, so handle it gently, and keep it away from apples and other fruit that make it soften faster.

recommended.name: Black Beauty
recommended.recommended_note: The classic large, glossy, deep-purple-black globe eggplant and a dependable open-pollinated standard. Big, meaty, teardrop fruit on a sturdy plant; the benchmark American type for slicing and grilling, though slower than the hybrids.

recommended.name: Ichiban
recommended.recommended_note: A productive Asian hybrid with long, slender, glossy purple fruit and tender, mild, low-seed flesh. Early and heavy-bearing on a tall plant; excellent for containers and small gardens and quick to a first pick.

recommended.name: Rosa Bianca
recommended.recommended_note: An Italian heirloom with rounded, lavender-and-white streaked fruit and creamy, mild, non-bitter flesh prized for cooking. Beautiful and delicious, somewhat slower and less productive than hybrids, and best where the season is warm and long.

recommended.name: Fairy Tale
recommended.recommended_note: An All-America Selections dwarf hybrid bred for containers, with small, slender, purple-and-white striped fruit on a compact plant. Very early, sweet, and tender, and productive in a pot or small bed.

recommended.name: Casper
recommended.recommended_note: A white-skinned variety with elongated, ivory fruit and mild, tender flesh that some find less bitter. The white types are eye-catching and good for cooking; protect the pale fruit from sunscald in intense sun.

recommended.name: Patio Baby
recommended.recommended_note: An All-America Selections miniature hybrid for containers, bearing many small, deep-purple, egg-sized fruit on a compact, spineless plant. Extremely early and well suited to pots, balconies, and short seasons.

varieties.note_seasoned: Choose by type, season, and space. The large globe types (Black Beauty and the many hybrids) give the familiar meaty slicing fruit but need a long, warm season; slender Asian types (Ichiban and kin) are earlier, more productive, tender, and less seedy; Italian heirlooms such as Rosa Bianca offer creamy, mild flesh prized for cooking but are slower. White types (Casper) are mild and striking but want sunscald protection. For containers, short seasons, or cool summers, the early dwarf hybrids Fairy Tale and Patio Baby ripen a crop fast on a compact plant, the safest choice where the warm season is short.
varieties.note_beginner: Pick an eggplant variety to match your space and season. For the classic big purple eggplant, grow Black Beauty, but give it a long, warm summer. Slim Asian types like Ichiban are easier, earlier, and very productive. Italian heirlooms like Rosa Bianca are beautiful and mild but slower. White types like Casper are eye-catching. If you have a short or cool season, or you are growing in a pot, choose a fast dwarf variety like Fairy Tale or Patio Baby.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A healthy full-size eggplant typically yields about 4 to 8 fruit over the season for large globe types, and many more for the slender Asian and small-fruited types, which set heavily and continuously. Steady warmth, even moisture, and regular picking are what carry a plant to the upper end; a single cold check or a flea-beetle-ravaged seedling pulls it down.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: A healthy eggplant usually gives you several fruit over the season, around 4 to 8 for the big globe types and many more for slim Asian and baby types. Keeping it warm, evenly watered, and regularly picked makes the difference.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Eggplant bears continuously through the warm months once it starts, with production accelerating in midsummer heat (its strength relative to tomato) and slowing as nights cool in fall. Picking fruit while it is still immature and glossy keeps the plant flowering and setting; leaving fruit to over-ripen on the plant shuts down further set.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Once it gets going, eggplant keeps producing through the warm months, picking up in the heat of summer and slowing as fall cools down. Keep picking the fruit while it is young and shiny, since leaving big fruit on the plant makes it stop setting new ones.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: First-season growers most often lose eggplant to two things: setting plants out too early into cold soil, which stalls them for weeks, and flea beetles shredding unprotected seedlings. Wait for real warmth, protect young plants with row cover, and the rest is steady water, sun, and regular picking.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: The two things that trip up first-year eggplant growers are planting too early into cold soil and letting flea beetles destroy the young plants. Wait until it is truly warm, cover the seedlings, and then just keep the plant watered, sunny, and picked.
factors_seasoned: Warmth: eggplant needs a long, warm season and warm soil; cold checks stall it and cut yield, while it thrives in summer heat that stalls tomato.
Flea-beetle protection of seedlings: unprotected young plants can be devastated, slashing the season's yield.
Even moisture: steady water through flowering and fruit set prevents dropped blossoms and small, bitter fruit.
Regular harvest: picking fruit young and glossy keeps the plant setting more.
Sun and feeding: full sun and a nitrogen side-dress after fruit set drive continuous production.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance places above-ground fruiting crops like eggplant in the waxing (light) phase. This is folk tradition, not extension-backed; sow eggplant by soil temperature and frost dates instead.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seeds sprout in about 7 to 14 days in warm conditions; bottom heat of 75 to 85°F is ideal, and cool soil delays or prevents germination. Two seed leaves emerge first.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: In warm conditions, seeds sprout in roughly one to two weeks, sending up two seed leaves first. Cool soil makes them slow or fail.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Sow about a quarter inch deep in warm flats with bottom heat (75 to 85°F), keeping the mix evenly moist, not soggy. Eggplant germinates slower and warmer than tomato, so give it heat and patience.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Plant seeds about a quarter inch deep in a warm spot, ideally on a heat mat, and keep the soil damp until they sprout. Eggplant likes it warmer than tomatoes to come up.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Did your eggplant seeds germinate, and how many days did it take?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your eggplant seeds sprouted yet?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: After the seed leaves, true leaves appear and growth is steady but unhurried in warmth. This is the most vulnerable stage to flea beetles, which can shred small plants, so watch the leaves closely.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: After the first two rounded leaves, true leaves appear and the plant grows slowly but steadily in warmth. Watch for tiny holes in the leaves from flea beetles, which hit young plants hardest.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep seedlings warm and in strong light to avoid legginess, pot up as needed, and protect from flea beetles. Grow stocky, pencil-thick transplants and do not rush them outside before warmth arrives.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the seedlings warm and in bright light so they grow stocky, and protect them from flea beetles. Do not be in a hurry to plant them out; wait for warm weather.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How are your seedlings developing? Any flea-beetle shot-holes on the leaves?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How do your young eggplant plants look?

growth_stages.name: Transplanting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Sturdy transplants up to a foot tall with pencil-thick stems, ready to set out only once nights hold above 50°F and the soil has warmed to at least 60 to 65°F. Planting into cold ground is the classic eggplant setback.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Strong young plants up to a foot tall, ready to go outside only when nights stay above 50°F and the soil is warm. Planting too early into cold soil stalls them.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harden off over 7 to 10 days, then transplant into warm soil, 18 to 24 inches apart in rows 30 to 36 inches apart, and set a stake or cage at planting. Black plastic or fabric mulch warms the soil and gives a heat-loving crop a head start.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Harden the plants off over about a week, then plant them 18 to 24 inches apart into warm soil, and put a stake or cage in right away. A sheet of black plastic mulch warms the soil and helps.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have you transplanted? Were nights reliably above 50°F and the soil warm?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you planted your eggplant outside yet?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Star-shaped purple (or white) flowers open singly or in small clusters. Eggplant flowers are self-fertile and largely self-pollinating, so a single plant sets fruit; a small fruit swells behind a successfully pollinated bloom. Blossom drop in cold snaps or extreme heat is normal and temporary.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Pretty star-shaped purple or white flowers appear. Eggplant flowers pollinate themselves, so you do not need more than one plant. A tiny eggplant forms behind each flower that sets. Some flowers drop in very hot or cold spells, which is normal.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture steady through flowering and side-dress with nitrogen as the first fruits set. If blossoms drop in a heat wave or cold snap, wait it out; set resumes as conditions moderate. A gentle tap or shake can aid pollination on still days.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the plant evenly watered as it flowers, and feed it with nitrogen once the first fruit sets. If flowers drop during a hot or cold spell, do not worry, it picks back up when the weather settles.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Is your eggplant flowering and setting fruit? Any blossom drop?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Is your eggplant flowering? Are any little fruit forming?

growth_stages.name: Fruiting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Set fruit swell and color up with a high gloss. Eggplant carries fruit continuously through the warm months, often accelerating in midsummer heat. Watch the skin: peak quality is firm and glossy, well before the fruit reaches full size.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The little eggplants grow and turn shiny. The plant keeps making fruit through the warm months, often fastest in the heat of summer. The fruit is best while it is firm and glossy, before it gets really big.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture even and feeding steady through fruiting, support fruit-laden stems, and begin harvesting while fruit is immature and glossy. Picking regularly keeps the plant setting; scout for mites and lace bugs in the heat.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep watering evenly and feeding, hold up heavy stems with stakes or a cage, and start picking the fruit while it is young and shiny. Keep an eye out for spider mites in hot, dry weather.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How are the fruit sizing and coloring? Are you picking them young and glossy?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are your eggplants growing and turning shiny?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Firm fruit with a high, mirror-like gloss, picked from about 2 inches across up to two-thirds of mature size for globe types, or finger-to-hot-dog size for Asian types. A dull skin and a dent that stays when pressed mean the fruit is over-mature, seedy, and bitter.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Firm, shiny fruit, picked while it is young rather than at its biggest. Dull skin and a dent that stays when you press it mean it is past its best, seedy and bitter.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut fruit with shears or a knife, leaving a short stem and the green calyx, and harvest at least once or twice a week. Wear care around the often-spiny calyx. Keep picking through the season until frost; bring the harvest in before the first frost ends the plant.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Cut the eggplant off with scissors or a knife, leaving a bit of stem on (watch for prickles on the cap), and pick every few days. Keep harvesting until frost, and bring in the last fruit before the first frost kills the plant.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have you harvested? Are you picking the fruit young and glossy?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you picked your first eggplant yet?

notifications.title_seasoned: Plant eggplant only when it is truly warm
notifications.title_beginner: Wait for warm weather to plant eggplant
notifications.body_seasoned: Eggplant is heat-loving and sets back badly in cold soil. Transplant only once nights hold above 50°F and the soil has warmed to 60 to 65°F, a week or two after the tomato date, and set a stake at planting.
notifications.body_beginner: Eggplant hates the cold. Wait to plant it out until nights stay above 50°F and the soil is warm, a couple of weeks after you would plant tomatoes. Put a stake in when you plant.

notifications.title_seasoned: Side-dress your eggplant at fruit set
notifications.body_seasoned: Your eggplant is setting its first fruit, the moment to side-dress with nitrogen. Place it a few inches out from the plants and water it in, then repeat every 3 to 4 weeks through harvest.
notifications.body_beginner: Your eggplant is starting to set fruit. Feed it with a nitrogen fertilizer a few inches out from the stem, and water it in.

notifications.title_beginner: Pick your eggplant while it is shiny
notifications.body_seasoned: Your eggplant is ready to pick while firm and glossy, before full size. Cut with shears leaving a short stem, and harvest at least once or twice a week to keep the plant setting more fruit.
notifications.body_beginner: Your eggplant is ready to pick while it is firm and shiny, not at its biggest. Cut it off with a little stem on, and keep picking every few days so the plant makes more.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost is coming, harvest your eggplant
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost warning for your eggplant
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A frost is forecast. Eggplant is frost-tender and the first frost ends the plant, so harvest all usable fruit now, even slightly immature ones, and cut your losses on the plant.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Frost is coming, and it will kill your eggplant. Pick all the usable fruit now, even the smaller ones, before the frost hits.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Cold nights may stall your eggplant
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Cold snap may set back your eggplant
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A cold spell is forecast. Nights below 50°F chill eggplant, stalling growth and dropping blossoms even though the plant survives. If you can, protect young plants with row cover or cloches; set usually resumes as warmth returns.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Cold nights are coming. Eggplant does not like temperatures below 50°F and may stop growing and drop flowers for a while. Cover young plants if you can; they usually bounce back when it warms up.

germination.text_seasoned: Eggplant germinates slower and warmer than tomato. Give it bottom heat of 75 to 85°F and patience; cool flats sit and sulk. Start about 8 weeks before your warm transplant date.
germination.text_beginner: Eggplant seeds like it warmer than tomatoes and take a bit longer to sprout. A heat mat at 75 to 85°F helps a lot. Start them about 8 weeks before you will plant out.

seedling.text_seasoned: Grow stocky transplants in strong light, and guard seedlings from flea beetles, the signature early eggplant pest, which can shred small plants. Row cover or a screened cold frame protects them until they are large.
seedling.text_beginner: Keep seedlings in bright light so they grow stocky, and protect them from flea beetles, which chew tiny holes and can destroy young eggplant. A light cover keeps them off.

transplanting.text_seasoned: Patience beats the calendar: eggplant set out into cold soil sulks for weeks and never fully recovers. Wait until nights hold above 50°F and the soil is 60 to 65°F, a week or two past the tomato date, and warm the soil with black mulch.
transplanting.text_beginner: Do not rush eggplant outside. Planting into cold soil stalls it badly. Wait until nights stay above 50°F and the soil is warm, a couple of weeks after tomato time. Black plastic mulch warms the soil and helps.

flowering.text_seasoned: Eggplant flowers are self-fertile and self-pollinating, so one plant sets fruit. Blossom drop during a heat wave or a cold snap is normal and temporary; keep moisture steady and let set resume as conditions moderate.
flowering.text_beginner: Eggplant flowers pollinate themselves, so a single plant will fruit. If flowers fall off during very hot or cold spells, that is normal and it picks back up. Just keep the plant evenly watered.

fruiting.text_seasoned: This is eggplant's advantage over tomato: it keeps setting fruit through midsummer heat that stalls tomato. Feed with nitrogen at fruit set, keep water even to avoid bitter, misshapen fruit, and support fruit-laden stems.
fruiting.text_beginner: Unlike tomatoes, eggplant keeps going strong in summer heat. Feed it with nitrogen once fruit sets, keep the water steady so the fruit is not bitter, and stake the plant so heavy fruit does not snap it.

harvest.text_seasoned: Pick eggplant immature and glossy, not at full size: firm fruit with a mirror gloss is at its peak, while a dull skin and a dent that stays means seedy, bitter flesh. Cut with shears leaving a short stem, and harvest at least once or twice a week to keep production going.
harvest.text_beginner: Pick eggplant while it is young and shiny, not when it is biggest. Shiny and firm is perfect; dull skin means it is past its best and bitter. Cut it off with a little stem on, and keep picking every few days.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Seedlings shredded with tiny round holes
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Young leaves full of tiny holes
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Flea beetles, the signature early eggplant pest. The small beetles riddle the leaves with shot-hole punctures, and on a young transplant with little leaf area the damage can stunt or kill the plant. Mature plants tolerate the same feeding easily.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Flea beetles. These tiny beetles chew lots of little holes in the leaves and can devastate young eggplant, though big plants shrug it off.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Epitrix flea beetles concentrating on a strongly preferred host, worst on small spring transplants.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Tiny jumping beetles that love eggplant and hit young plants hardest.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Protect transplants with floating row cover from planting until they are large, set out bigger, well-hardened plants into warm soil so they grow away fast, and use a nasturtium trap planting at the edge.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Cover young plants with row cover until they are big and strong, plant larger transplants into warm soil, and grow a few nasturtiums nearby to lure the beetles away.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Plant set out early then stalled and sat for weeks
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Eggplant stopped growing after planting
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: A cold check from transplanting too early. Eggplant is highly cold-sensitive, and exposure to soil and nights below about 50°F stalls growth, drops blossoms, and leaves the plant sulking for weeks even after warmth returns; yield never fully recovers.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The plant was set out too early into cold conditions. Eggplant hates the cold, and a chilly start makes it sit and sulk for weeks instead of growing.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Transplanting before nights reliably held above 50°F and the soil had warmed, exposing a chill-sensitive crop to cold stress.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Planting before it was truly warm, which chilled a heat-loving plant.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait until nights hold above 50°F and the soil is 60 to 65°F, a week or two past the tomato date, harden off fully, and warm the soil with black plastic or fabric mulch before planting.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Wait to plant until nights stay above 50°F and the soil is warm, a couple of weeks after tomatoes. Warming the soil first with black plastic mulch helps a lot.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Cut a dull eggplant that was seedy, spongy, and bitter
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Eggplant was bitter and full of seeds
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Harvested over-mature. Eggplant is picked immature; once the skin loses its gloss and turns dull, the flesh has gone seedy and spongy and the bitter compounds have built up. A thumbnail dent that stays rather than springing back is the tell.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The eggplant was left on the plant too long. Picked past its prime, when the skin is dull instead of shiny, the inside turns seedy, spongy, and bitter.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Delayed harvest past the glossy-immature stage, plus any drought stress, which intensifies bitterness.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Picking too late, after the skin went dull, sometimes made worse by uneven watering.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Pick while the skin is firm and glossy and the dent springs back, well before full size, and harvest at least once or twice a week. Keep moisture even, since drought stress adds bitterness.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Pick eggplant while it is shiny and firm, before it gets big, and harvest every few days. Keep it evenly watered, since dry spells make it more bitter.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Leaves yellowed and wilted one side, plant stunted
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Leaves wilted and yellowed and the plant stunted
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Most likely verticillium wilt, the most common serious eggplant disease. The soilborne fungus clogs the vascular system, so leaves yellow (often one-sided), wilt, and drop while the plant stunts and fails to size fruit; a cut stem shows brown streaking. There is no cure.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Probably verticillium wilt, a common soil disease of eggplant. It blocks the plant's water flow, so leaves yellow and wilt and the plant stunts. There is no cure once a plant has it.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Verticillium dahliae in the soil, often built up by growing nightshades in the same bed, and favored where eggplant follows tomato, pepper, or potato.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: A soil fungus that builds up where eggplant, tomatoes, peppers, or potatoes have grown before.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Rotate to a bed with no recent nightshade history, choose tolerant varieties or grafted plants on resistant rootstock, keep plants vigorous with steady water and feeding, and consider soil solarization where the disease is established.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant in a spot where eggplant, tomatoes, peppers, and potatoes have not grown for several years, and look for resistant or grafted plants. Keeping plants healthy helps them cope.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Eggplant is not a succession crop. One planting produces continuously through the whole warm season, so you set plants out once rather than at intervals. In most zones a later sowing would be caught by frost before its long warm season could finish. Only in the warmest, frost-free or near-frost-free zones, and in the low desert where the planting splits around midsummer heat, is a second seasonal window viable, and that is a separate season rather than a true succession.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: You plant eggplant once for the season. A single planting keeps producing all through the warm months, so there is no need to replant every few weeks. In most places a later planting would not have time to fruit before frost. Only in very warm, nearly frost-free areas, or the hot desert, can you fit a second planting, and that is really a separate season.
succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Eggplant is a single long-season crop that bears continuously from one planting through the warm months, so interval succession sowing does not apply; a second sowing in most zones would not mature before frost. Warm frost-free zones and the low desert support a separate seasonal planting window, which is a distinct season rather than a succession.

crops.description_seasoned: Eggplant is a warm-season fruiting vegetable (Solanum melongena) in the nightshade family, a close relative of tomato and pepper grown for its glossy, immature fruit. Where it differs from tomato is instructive: eggplant is markedly more heat-loving, thriving and setting fruit through summer heat that makes tomato sulk and drop blossoms, while it is the more cold-sensitive of the two, stalling badly if set out before the soil and nights are reliably warm. It is also slower, wanting a long, warm season (roughly 100 to 120 days from seed, about 65 to 85 from transplant), so it is grown from transplants set into warm soil a week or two after tomatoes. Plants are bushy and often need staking once loaded with fruit. The crop is harvested young and glossy and picked continuously; a dull skin signals an over-mature, seedy, bitter fruit. Types span the large purple-black globes (Black Beauty), slender Asian fruit (Ichiban), Italian heirlooms (Rosa Bianca), white-skinned (Casper), and compact container varieties (Patio Baby, Fairy Tale). The season's shape is set by three things: a long warm runway with no cold checks, the signature early pest pressure of flea beetles on seedlings (plus the Colorado potato beetle later), and the soilborne wilts (verticillium, bacterial wilt) and fruit rots (phomopsis) that rotation and warm, well-drained soil hold off.
crops.description_beginner: Eggplant is a warm-season vegetable in the same family as tomatoes and peppers, grown for its shiny, smooth fruit. The big thing to know is that eggplant loves heat: it keeps producing through hot summer weather that makes tomatoes struggle, but it really dislikes the cold and will sulk for weeks if planted out too early. It is also slower than a tomato and needs a long, warm season, so you grow it from transplants set into warm soil a week or two after you would plant tomatoes, and you usually stake the plant once it is carrying fruit. You pick eggplant while it is young and glossy, not at its biggest, because once the skin goes dull the inside turns seedy and bitter. There are many kinds: big purple globes like Black Beauty, slim Asian types like Ichiban, beautiful Italian heirlooms like Rosa Bianca, white ones like Casper, and small container types like Patio Baby and Fairy Tale. The main things to get right are warmth (never rush it into cold soil), protecting young plants from flea beetles, watering steadily, and rotating it away from where tomatoes, peppers, or potatoes grew.

northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In cold zones eggplant is a single tight summer crop and is the most demanding of the warm-season fruiting vegetables here: start transplants indoors about 8 weeks early, then set them out only once nights hold above 50°F and the soil is warm, a week or two after tomatoes. Harvest continuously from midsummer until the first frost ends the plant. In the coldest zones (3 to 4) the season is marginal for eggplant, so choose fast dwarf or Asian varieties (Fairy Tale, Patio Baby, Ichiban), use black mulch and row cover, and treat a good crop as an achievement.
northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In cold areas eggplant is a one-crop-a-summer plant and the fussiest of the warm-season vegetables. Start seeds indoors about 8 weeks early, and plant out only when nights stay above 50°F and the soil is warm, after tomato time. Pick from midsummer until frost. In the very coldest zones it is a stretch, so grow fast varieties like Fairy Tale or Ichiban and warm the soil with black plastic.

se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: Across the Gulf and coastal plain, eggplant thrives: set transplants out in early spring once the soil warms and harvest continuously from early summer well into fall, with no midsummer pause, since this heat-lover relishes the hot, humid summers that stall tomato. Watch for flea beetles on young plants, the Colorado potato beetle, and in hot, wet soils the bacterial wilt eggplant is prone to.
se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast, eggplant loves the long, hot summers and keeps producing right through them, unlike tomatoes. Plant transplants in early spring and harvest from early summer into fall. Watch young plants for flea beetles and the Colorado potato beetle, and keep beds well drained to avoid wilt diseases.

ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: In California's hot interior valleys, eggplant is in its element: set transplants out in spring once the soil is warm and harvest continuously through the long, hot summer into fall. The dry heat suits it well as long as irrigation is steady; unlike tomato, eggplant keeps setting fruit through the midsummer heat.
ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In California's hot inland valleys, eggplant does great. Plant transplants in spring once it warms up and harvest all through the hot summer into fall. Just keep the water steady, and it will keep producing through heat that slows tomatoes down.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Eggplant is far more heat-tolerant than tomato or pepper and is one of the few fruiting crops that keeps setting through a hot summer, so it runs straight through the heat in nearly every region. The exception is the absolute extreme of the California desert valleys: in July and August, daytime highs reach well into the 110s°F with nights above 80°F, hot enough that even eggplant's pollen loses viability and fruit set stalls. Desert growers therefore run a spring crop that matures before peak heat and a fall crop set out in September as the heat eases, leaving midsummer paused. This pause reflects reduced fruit set at extreme heat, not frost or cold. The exact pause months are modeled from the regional warm-season pattern.
