Heat-tolerant single continuous season except the low desert and South Florida, which split spring/fall around a backed heat_pause.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: Hawaii's tropical calendar is essentially aseasonal for tomatillo: with no frost anchor and mild year-round temperatures, plant and harvest across the year on a representative two-cycle schedule. Plant two or more for pollination. (Window modeled; see open findings.)
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In Hawaii's mild climate, tomatillos can grow year-round. There is no frost, so you can plant in roughly two cycles and harvest across the year. Grow at least two plants.

crops.description_seasoned: The tomatillo (Physalis philadelphica) is a warm-season Solanaceae grown for its tart, husk-covered fruit, the green base of salsa verde. Culture mirrors tomato, started indoors and transplanted after frost, with three differences worth knowing. First, it is self-incompatible: a single plant sets almost no fruit, so grow at least two for cross-pollination. Second, the plant is large, sprawling, and vigorous, reaching 3 to 4 feet tall and wide, so it needs a sturdy cage or stake and wide spacing. Third, it tolerates summer heat and drought better than tomato and is notably less disease-prone, which makes it forgiving across hot regions. Fruit is ready when it swells to fill, and often split, its papery husk. Plants are heavy bearers and self-seed readily from dropped fruit, so expect volunteers the following spring.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Pick when the fruit swells to fill its papery husk and the husk begins to split, turning from green toward tan. For bright, tart fruit (the classic salsa-verde flavor) harvest while the fruit is still firm and green; left longer it turns yellow, soft, and blandly sweet. Ripe fruit detaches easily and often drops to the ground on its own, where it keeps for days inside the protective husk. Harvest over the whole season as fruit fills out, roughly weekly at peak.
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Tomatillo is functionally self-incompatible: a flower will not set fruit with its own pollen, so a lone plant flowers heavily and produces almost nothing, just a few empty husks. Grow at least two plants, ideally two different varieties, close together so insects can move pollen between them. Bees and other pollinators do the work, so keep the planting open to insect traffic and avoid spraying during bloom. This is the single most common reason a tomatillo crop fails. (Utah State University Extension; SDSU Extension; University of Minnesota Extension)
crops.pollinator_notes_beginner: Here is the one thing that trips up most first-time tomatillo growers: a single plant will hardly set any fruit, no matter how healthy it looks. Tomatillos cannot pollinate themselves, so you have to grow at least two plants near each other, and two different kinds is even better. Bees carry the pollen from one plant to the other, so plant them within a few feet and let the bees visit. Plant two and you will be giving tomatillos away by late summer.
crops.disease_resistance_notes_default_seasone: Tomatillo is notably less disease-prone than tomato. It can develop early blight, powdery mildew, mosaic viruses, and root rots, but typically at lower incidence and severity. A sunny, well-drained, well-spaced site plus a 3-year rotation away from Solanaceae prevents most problems; few home growers ever need to spray.
crops.disease_resistance_notes_default_beginne: Good news: tomatillos get sick far less often than tomatoes. They can catch the same things (leaf blights, powdery mildew, viruses, root rot), but usually only mildly. Full sun, well-drained soil, room between plants, and keeping them away from other nightshades head off most trouble, you rarely need to spray.

pet_safe.note: Ripe tomatillos are fine, but the unripe fruit, leaves, and stems contain solanine and are toxic to cats, dogs, and horses.

crops.name: Watermelon

soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Watermelon does best in deep, well-drained, light soil, with sandy loams and loamy sands the classic choice because they warm quickly in spring and drain freely, which this heat-loving, deep-rooted crop rewards. Work a few inches of compost into the bed before planting, but go easier on nitrogen-rich amendments than you would for leafy crops, since too much nitrogen pushes vine at the expense of fruit and sugar. Many growers plant on low, wide hills or raised mounds, which warm faster, drain better, and lift the crown and developing fruit off wet ground. Heavy clay holds water and stays cold, slowing growth and inviting Fusarium wilt and fruit rot, so amend it generously and build mounds, or grow on sandier ground.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Plant watermelon in light, well-drained soil that warms up fast, like a sandy loam, with some compost mixed in. Avoid going overboard on rich, high-nitrogen material, because that gives you lots of leaves and vine but less fruit. Many gardeners plant on low hills or raised mounds, which warm up and drain better and keep the fruit off soggy ground. If your soil is heavy clay, it stays cold and wet and can bring on disease, so mix in compost and build the soil up into mounds, or pick the sandiest, best-draining spot you have.

ph.note_seasoned: Watermelon grows best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, around pH 6.0 to 6.8, and tolerates a wider band of roughly 5.5 to 7.5. It is a little more forgiving of mildly acidic ground than many vegetables, but strongly acidic or strongly alkaline soil tightens nutrient uptake. Test before planting and lime or add sulfur only on the test's advice rather than by guess.
ph.note_beginner: Watermelon likes soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, about pH 6.0 to 6.8, and most garden soil is already close. An inexpensive soil test tells you where you stand and whether you need to adjust it before planting.

fertilizer.frequency: At planting, then side-dress once or twice
fertilizer.type: lower-nitrogen at planting, then nitrogen side-dress
fertilizer.timing: Work into the bed before planting, then side-dress when vines begin to run and again at flowering
fertilizer.example_product: 5-10-10 at planting, then a nitrogen source such as calcium nitrate or blood meal
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Watermelon is a moderate feeder that wants more phosphorus and potassium than nitrogen, since excess nitrogen drives leafy vine at the expense of fruit set and sugar. Work a lower-nitrogen complete fertilizer such as 5-10-10 into the bed before planting (Clemson suggests about 30 pounds per 1,000 square feet), then side-dress with a nitrogen source as the vines begin to run, and again lightly at flowering. Ease off nitrogen once fruit has set so the plant pours its energy into sizing and sweetening the melons rather than growing more vine. Pair feeding with even moisture, because the nutrients only help a plant that is not also drought-stressed.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Watermelon does not need a lot of nitrogen, and too much gives you big leafy vines but fewer, less sweet melons. Mix a fertilizer that is lower in nitrogen, like a 5-10-10, into the soil before planting, then give the plants a little nitrogen when the vines start to run and again when flowers appear. Once the melons start to form, stop pushing nitrogen so the plant puts its energy into growing sweet fruit instead of more leaves.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Your watermelon vines are running, time to side-dress with a little nitrogen. Then keep feeding light and ease off nitrogen once fruit sets, so the plant builds sweet melons rather than vine.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Your watermelon vines are spreading. Give them a light feeding of nitrogen now.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A lower-nitrogen complete fertilizer such as 5-10-10 worked in at planting, then a nitrogen side-dress as the vines run and again lightly at flowering, easing off nitrogen once fruit sets. Too much nitrogen gives vine and leaf at the expense of fruit and sweetness.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a lower-nitrogen fertilizer like 5-10-10 at planting, then a little nitrogen as the vines spread. Do not overdo the nitrogen once melons form, or you get leaves instead of fruit.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A common approach is a lower-nitrogen complete fertilizer such as 5-10-10 worked into the bed before planting (Clemson cites about 30 pounds per 1,000 square feet, or a balanced scoop per hill), then a nitrogen side-dress about three to four weeks after planting as vines run, placed a few inches out from the plants and watered in, repeated lightly at flowering.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Mix a lower-nitrogen fertilizer or a few inches of compost into the soil before planting. Then feed with a little nitrogen about three to four weeks later, scratched into the soil a few inches away from the plants, and once more when flowers appear.

companions.note_seasoned: Most watermelon companion pairings are traditional rather than trial-tested, and the ones worth acting on serve two practical ends: pollination and pest pressure. Because watermelon fruit set is strongly pollinator-limited, flowering insectary plants like borage near the patch are a genuine help, and that help is doubly important if you grow seedless types, which lean entirely on bees moving pollen from a seeded pollinizer. Bush beans fix nitrogen the crop can use without the heavy feeding that would otherwise grow vine over fruit, and a trap planting of nasturtium can divert cucumber beetles and other pests. The firmest rule is a rotation one: keep watermelon away from other cucurbits, which share its pest and disease complex, including the soilborne Fusarium wilt and the foliar anthracnose and gummy stem blight that build up where melons follow melons.
companions.note_beginner: The most useful watermelon companions are flowers that bring in bees, since watermelon needs lots of bee visits to set fruit (especially seedless kinds, which depend on bees carrying pollen from a seeded variety). Bush beans add a little nitrogen, and nasturtiums can lure pests away. The one rule that really matters is to keep watermelon away from other melons, cucumbers, and squash, which all share the same pests and diseases.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Borage
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Borage flowers are loved by bees, and watermelon needs lots of bee visits to set fruit, so a few borage plants nearby can help with pollination. This matters most for seedless watermelon, which depends on bees.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A strong bee magnet whose flowers recruit the pollinators watermelon fruit set depends on, which is especially valuable for seedless types that rely on bees moving pollen from a seeded pollinizer. Pollinator-habitat value is well grounded; the specific borage-watermelon pairing is traditional rather than trial-tested.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Watermelon fruit set is pollinator-limited; flowering insectary plants like borage draw bees. Pairing is habitat-based, not pair-isolated.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Bush beans
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Beans pull nitrogen from the air into the soil, which watermelon can use, and they do not share watermelon's pests. A good, traditional neighbor.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Bush beans fix nitrogen that lightly benefits the crop without the heavy nitrogen that would push vine over fruit, and they share none of the cucurbit pests. A traditional, mechanistically plausible pairing rather than a trial-isolated one.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Legume nitrogen fixation is a documented mechanism; the bean-watermelon adjacency benefit is traditional, not pair-isolated.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Nasturtium
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Nasturtiums are often grown near melons and squash to lure cucumber beetles and other pests away, and their flowers bring in bees. A helpful, low-risk neighbor.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Often planted near cucurbits as a trap and deterrent for cucumber beetles, and its flowers also draw the bees watermelon depends on for fruit set. Trap cropping is a documented principle, but the specific nasturtium-watermelon effect is not formally isolated, so treat it as a plausible aid.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Trap-cropping for cucurbit beetles is documented in principle; the nasturtium-watermelon pairing is not trial-isolated.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Corn
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Corn is the traditional Three Sisters partner that gives sprawling vines something to grow among. With watermelon it is more tradition than a proven boost, and watermelon's full-sun need means you should not let corn shade it much.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: The classic Three Sisters partner, though the fit is looser for watermelon than for shade-tolerant squash: tall corn can give the trailing vines structure, but watermelon wants full sun to sweeten, so keep corn from shading the patch. A long-standing intercropping tradition with a space rationale, not a measured yield effect for this pair.

provenance.label: traditional

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Other cucurbits
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep watermelon away from other melons, cucumbers, and squash. They share most of the same pests and diseases, so planting them together makes those problems worse.
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Cucumber, muskmelon, squash, and pumpkin share watermelon's pest and disease complex, including cucumber beetle, aphid-spread mosaic viruses, the mildews, and the soilborne Fusarium wilt and foliar anthracnose and gummy stem blight that build up where cucurbits repeat. Grouping them concentrates that pressure. A real epidemiology and rotation principle rather than a tested adjacency effect: spread cucurbits out and rotate them on a long cycle.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Shared cucurbit pests/pathogens (Fusarium wilt, anthracnose, gummy stem blight, mildews, cucumber beetles) are extension-documented; the bad-adjacency claim is a sound epidemiological principle, not pair-tested.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Potatoes
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Some gardeners keep potatoes and melons apart, since both are hungry plants and potatoes can bring their own diseases. This is more tradition than a proven rule.
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional caution that potatoes and cucurbits compete heavily and that potatoes can harbor disease and attract pests near melons. There is no strong T1 mechanism for the specific pairing, so it persists mostly as garden lore.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: A folk anti-companion caution; competition is plausible but there is no T1 source isolating a potato-watermelon antagonism.

pests.name: Cucumber beetles
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small striped or spotted yellow beetles chew young leaves, stems, flowers, and the rind of developing fruit, and can enter the soil to feed on seedlings below ground. The bigger threat is indirect: cucumber beetles can transmit bacterial wilt and spread mosaic viruses, though watermelon is far less prone to bacterial wilt collapse than cucumber and muskmelon.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Small yellow beetles with stripes or spots chew on the leaves and flowers of young plants and can scar the fruit. They can also spread disease, though watermelon handles the wilt disease better than cucumbers or cantaloupe.
pests.cause_seasoned: Striped and spotted cucumber beetles feed on cucurbits and overwinter as adults, colonizing plants early in the season. They carry the bacterial wilt organism in their gut and spread mosaic viruses as they feed; seedlings are most vulnerable.
pests.cause_beginner: Cucumber beetles spend the winter as adults and move onto young plants early. They feed on the leaves and can carry diseases from plant to plant, and seedlings are most at risk.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Protect seedlings with floating row cover removed at flowering for pollination, hand-pick beetles, and clear weeds that shelter them. Yellow sticky traps help monitor and reduce numbers; keep young plants vigorous so they grow past the most vulnerable stage.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover young plants with a light row cover (take it off when flowers open so bees can reach them), pick beetles off by hand, and clear away weeds. Yellow sticky traps help, and strong young plants shrug off some feeding.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Exclude beetles from seedlings with row cover, keep plants growing fast, clear weeds and debris, and rotate away from where cucurbits grew. Aim control at the early-season colonizers.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover seedlings until they flower, keep them growing strong, clear away weeds and old plants, and do not plant where melons or squash grew last year.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Colonies of small soft-bodied insects, often melon aphids, cluster on leaf undersides and growing tips, curling and yellowing the leaves and coating them in sticky honeydew that grows sooty mold. Beyond direct feeding, melon aphids transmit mosaic viruses that mottle and distort the foliage and can ruin a crop.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny soft insects gather under the leaves and on new growth, making leaves curl and yellow, often with a sticky film. They can also spread viruses that damage the plant.
pests.cause_seasoned: Melon and other aphids suck sap and multiply rapidly in warm weather, building up fast on stressed or over-fertilized plants, and typically colonize once the vines begin to run. The honeydew they excrete fosters sooty mold, and several species spread cucurbit mosaic viruses.
pests.cause_beginner: Aphids are small insects that suck the plant's juices and multiply quickly, especially on soft, over-fed growth. The sticky honeydew they leave grows black mold, and they can carry plant viruses.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong jet of water and spray insecticidal soap or horticultural oil with thorough coverage of leaf undersides, repeating every few days. Conserve lady beetles, lacewings, and parasitic wasps, which usually bring aphids under control; reflective mulch deters them from young plants.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water and treat the undersides of the leaves with insecticidal soap, repeating every few days. Ladybugs and other helpful insects eat aphids, so welcome them.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen, which drives the soft growth aphids favor, scout leaf undersides and growing tips, and support natural enemies rather than spraying broadly. Reflective or aluminum-foil mulch deters aphids from young plants.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen, check the undersides of leaves regularly, and let helpful insects do their work. A reflective mulch around young plants helps keep aphids away.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Pale yellow and reddish-brown stippling appears on the upper sides of leaves, ranging from small specks to large whitish, stippled areas, and fine webbing shows on leaf undersides in bad infestations. Two-spotted spider mites explode in hot, dry weather, exactly watermelon's season, and heavy feeding bronzes and dries the foliage, cutting fruit size and sugar.
pests.symptoms_beginner: The leaves get a fine yellow or bronze speckling, and in bad cases you see tiny webs underneath. Spider mites love hot, dry weather and can build up fast on watermelon in summer.
pests.cause_seasoned: Two-spotted spider mites are tiny sap-feeders that proliferate during hot, dry weather and whose populations explode rapidly when their natural enemies are killed off by broad-spectrum sprays. They feed mostly on leaf undersides.
pests.cause_beginner: Tiny mites that thrive in hot, dry summers and multiply fast, especially after broad insecticide sprays kill the helpful bugs that normally keep them down. They feed on the undersides of the leaves.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Spray plants with a strong jet of water to dislodge mites and raise humidity, and apply insecticidal soap or horticultural oil with thorough leaf-underside coverage before populations peak, repeating as needed. Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides, which kill the predatory mites and insects that control them.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray the plants, especially the undersides of the leaves, with a strong stream of water, and treat with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil if needed. Avoid spraying broad insecticides, which kill the good bugs that eat mites.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep plants well watered and not heat-stressed, since drought-stressed plants are hit hardest, and avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that wipe out natural enemies. Scout leaf undersides through hot, dry spells and act early.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep plants watered so they are not stressed in the heat, and avoid spraying strong insecticides that kill helpful bugs. Check under the leaves during hot, dry weather and treat early if you see speckling.

pests.name: Squash bug
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Leaves develop yellow specks that brown and wilt, and heavily fed runners can wilt and turn brittle. Flat bronze egg clusters appear on leaf undersides along the veins, and gray-brown adults and pale nymphs cluster near the crown and under debris. Watermelon is less affected than winter squash, but young plants can still be hurt.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Leaves get yellow spots, then brown and wilt, and you find clusters of shield-shaped gray-brown bugs and their bronze eggs under the leaves. Watermelon is not their favorite, but they can still bother young plants.
pests.cause_seasoned: The squash bug feeds with piercing-sucking mouthparts on cucurbit foliage and stems, injecting saliva that wilts and browns the tissue. There is one generation a year in much of the South, and adults overwinter in garden debris. It prefers squash and pumpkin to watermelon.
pests.cause_beginner: Squash bugs pierce the leaves and stems and suck out the juices, which makes the vines wilt. They hide in plant debris over winter and prefer squash to watermelon, but can still attack young plants.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick adults, crush the bronze egg masses on leaf undersides, and trap bugs by laying a board near the plants overnight, then lifting it in the morning and destroying the cluster underneath. Target young nymphs with insecticidal soap, since adults are tough to kill.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick the bugs off by hand and scrape off the egg clusters under the leaves. A board laid on the ground overnight draws them underneath, then lift it in the morning and destroy them. Treat the young bugs with insecticidal soap.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Clean up vines and debris at season's end to cut overwintering sites, rotate cucurbits, and scout leaf undersides for the bronze egg clusters from early in the season, acting before nymphs mature.
pests.prevention_beginner: Clean up old vines after harvest so the bugs have nowhere to overwinter, move your melons around the garden each year, and check under the leaves for eggs early in the season.

pests.name: Squash vine borer
pests.symptoms_seasoned: On susceptible squash a vine wilts suddenly in midsummer with sawdust-like frass oozing from a hole low on the stem and a fat white caterpillar inside. Watermelon is the fortunate exception: the borer rarely attacks watermelon or cucumber, so this collapse is uncommon, though heavy local pressure can occasionally produce damage.
pests.symptoms_beginner: On many squash, a healthy plant suddenly wilts in summer with sawdust-like specks at a hole near the base of the stem, and a fat white grub inside. Watermelon rarely gets this, since the borer mostly leaves it alone, but it is still worth a look.
pests.cause_seasoned: The larva of the squash vine borer moth bores into thin-stemmed Cucurbita pepo squash; it largely avoids watermelon and cucumber, so watermelon planted near a borer-ravaged zucchini usually sails through untouched. Where pressure is severe, an occasional larva may still enter.
pests.cause_beginner: A moth lays eggs at the base of squash stems in early summer and the grubs tunnel inside, but the moth strongly prefers thin-stemmed squash like zucchini and mostly leaves watermelon alone.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rarely needed on watermelon. If a borer does enter, slit the stem lengthwise, remove the larva, and bury that node under moist soil to re-root; remove badly damaged vines.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Watermelon seldom needs treatment. If you do find a borer, slit the stem with a knife, dig out the grub, and cover the spot with damp soil so it can re-root.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Choosing watermelon is itself most of the prevention, since the borer mostly avoids it. Where pressure is severe, row cover from planting until flowering excludes the egg-laying moths, and tilling in late winter and rotating disrupts overwintering pupae.
pests.prevention_beginner: Growing watermelon is half the battle, since the borer mostly skips it. If borers are bad where you live, cover young plants with a light row cover until they flower, then take it off so bees can pollinate.

diseases.name: Anthracnose
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small brown-black spots appear first on the older crown leaves, expanding into ragged, sometimes water-soaked lesions; in damp weather the spots carry orange-pink spore masses that turn gray as it dries. On fruit it causes sunken, dark spots on the rind that can keep developing in transit and storage, and severe infection defoliates the vines.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Dark brown-black spots show up on the older leaves and grow into ragged patches, and the fruit can get sunken dark spots on the rind. In wet weather the spots may look pink-orange. Bad cases strip the leaves off the vine.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Anthracnose is caused by the seed-borne fungus Colletotrichum, favored by warm, damp weather and prolonged leaf wetness, and it hits late plantings especially hard. It overwinters on infected debris and seed.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that thrives in warm, wet weather and spreads from infected seed and old plant debris. It is worse on late plantings and in rainy spells.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Treat at the first spots with a labeled fungicide such as chlorothalonil or mancozeb, covering both leaf surfaces, and remove the worst-affected leaves and fruit. Avoid overhead watering and working among wet vines. Once it is widespread, control is mostly damage limitation.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Treat early, at the first spots, with a labeled fungicide and remove badly affected leaves and fruit. Water the soil, not the leaves, and stay out of the patch when the vines are wet.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant resistant varieties and disease-free seed, do not soak seed before planting, rotate watermelon and other cucurbits out of the bed for several years, water at the base, and start a protective spray schedule before the disease appears in wet seasons.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Choose resistant varieties and clean seed, rotate where you grow melons so they are not in the same spot every year, water at the base, and remove sick leaves and fruit early.

diseases.name: Gummy stem blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Round, black, wrinkled spots form on young leaves and dark, sunken, sometimes girdling lesions develop on the stems, often with a brown gummy ooze on the surface. Brownish circular leaf spots expand rapidly into large tan lesions, and a brown streak can appear at the blossom end of the fruit. In warm, wet weather the foliage and vines can collapse quickly.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: You see round black spots on the leaves and dark sunken patches on the stems, sometimes with a brown gummy ooze. The leaf spots grow fast into big tan blotches, and in warm, wet weather the vines can collapse.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Gummy stem blight is caused by the seed-borne fungus Didymella bryoniae (Stagonosporopsis), a warm-weather, southern cucurbit disease driven by prolonged rainy periods and leaf wetness. It survives on seed and infected debris.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that spreads in warm, wet weather, especially in the South, and survives on seed and old plant debris. Long rainy spells make it move fast.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Start a protective fungicide schedule at the first sign, covering leaf undersides, and remove and destroy badly affected vines. Improve airflow, avoid overhead irrigation, and keep the foliage as dry as possible.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Use a labeled fungicide at the first sign and remove the worst vines. Give plants room so air moves between them, and water at the base to keep the leaves dry.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant resistant varieties and clean seed, rotate cucurbits out of the bed for several years, space plants for airflow, water at the soil line, and avoid working among wet vines. Scout closely in warm, humid weather.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Pick resistant varieties and clean seed, rotate where you grow melons, give plants room, water at the base, and keep an eye out in warm, humid weather.

diseases.name: Fusarium wilt
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Foliage turns yellow and wilts, often starting on one side or one runner, and infected plants decline and die soon after symptoms appear even though the soil is moist. A pinkish-white cottony growth can show near the soil line on dying stems, and a cut stem reveals browned, discolored vascular tissue. It is the most damaging soilborne disease of watermelon.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The leaves turn yellow and wilt, often on just one runner at first, and the plant dies even though the soil is wet. You may see a pinkish mold near the base of a dying stem. It is the most serious soil disease of watermelon.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Fusarium wilt is caused by the soilborne fungus Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. niveum, which is specific to watermelon and clogs the water-conducting tissue. It thrives in warm, sandy soils typical of watermelon ground and persists in soil for many years; several races exist, and resistance covers only some of them.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soil fungus that only attacks watermelon, blocking the plant's water pipes so it wilts. It builds up in warm, sandy soil and survives for years, which is why long rotations matter.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once a plant is infected; remove and destroy wilting plants. Management is preventive and cultural, since fungicides do not control a soilborne vascular wilt.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure once a plant has it, so pull and destroy infected plants. You cannot spray it away, so prevention is everything.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant resistant varieties, follow a long rotation of at least five years out of watermelon and related cucurbits, and consider grafting onto resistant rootstock where the disease is established. Avoid moving infested soil, and keep plants vigorous but not over-watered.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Choose resistant varieties, do not grow watermelon in the same ground for at least five years, and where the disease is bad, look into grafted plants on resistant roots. Keep plants healthy and do not overwater.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: White, powdery patches appear on the upper and lower leaf surfaces and stems, spreading until leaves yellow, brown, and die back ahead of schedule. Early defoliation cuts the season short, reduces fruit size and sugar, and exposes melons to sunscald.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: A white, powdery coating spreads over the leaves until they yellow, brown, and die. The plant fades early, and the melons may not size up or sweeten well.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Powdery mildew fungi thrive in warm conditions with high humidity but do not need leaf wetness, spreading by wind-blown spores. Crowded plantings, poor airflow, and shade worsen it, and it is a common late-season cucurbit disease.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that spreads on warm, humid days, especially where plants are crowded and air does not move well. It does not need wet leaves to take hold.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Treat at the first spots with a labeled fungicide such as sulfur or a horticultural oil or biofungicide, covering both leaf surfaces, and remove the worst leaves. Avoid overhead watering. Once it is widespread, control is mostly damage limitation.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Treat early, at the first white spots, with a labeled fungicide like sulfur or horticultural oil, and remove badly affected leaves. Water the soil, not the leaves.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Choose resistant varieties, space plants for airflow, plant in full sun, and avoid excess nitrogen and overhead watering. Scout from midsummer and treat at the first sign.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Pick resistant varieties, give plants plenty of room and full sun, water at the base, and start checking in midsummer, treating the first white spots early.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small yellowish, angular areas bounded by the leaf veins appear on the upper leaf surface, water-soaked underneath with a grayish or purplish fuzzy spore growth in humid weather. Lesions turn from yellow to brown and several infected leaves can die within 10 to 14 days, rapidly defoliating the vines.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Yellow, angular patches show on top of the leaves with fuzzy gray-purple growth underneath, mostly in damp, humid weather. The spots brown and spread, and badly hit leaves can die within a couple of weeks.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Downy mildew is caused by the air-borne, fungus-like water mold Pseudoperonospora cubensis, which needs leaf wetness and humidity to infect and arrives on wind currents during mild, rainy stretches, often spreading north through the season from overwintering sites in the far South.
diseases.cause_beginner: A mold-like disease that blows in on the wind during mild, rainy weather and needs wet leaves to infect. It can move through a planting quickly.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Improve airflow, let foliage dry, remove badly affected leaves, and apply a labeled fungicide covering leaf undersides when conditions favor the disease. Avoid overhead irrigation, which keeps leaves wet.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Open up the planting so leaves dry faster, remove the worst leaves, and use a labeled fungicide when wet weather sets in. Do not water over the leaves.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space for airflow, water at the soil line rather than overhead, choose resistant varieties where available, and start protective sprays when the disease is reported moving into your area. Scout closely in humid weather.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Give plants room so air moves between them, water at the base, choose resistant varieties if downy mildew is common where you live, and watch closely in humid weather.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Aim for about 1 to 2 inches of water per week, more in heat or on sandy soil, delivered deeply and less often rather than in light daily sprinkles. Watermelon is deep-rooted, with the bulk of its roots in the top 12 inches, and the fruit is about 92 percent water, so steady moisture through fruit sizing is essential.
watering.frequency_beginner: Give watermelon about 1 to 2 inches of water a week, more when it is hot and dry. Water deeply rather than a little every day, since the plant roots deep and the fruit is almost all water.
watering.amount_seasoned: Around 1 to 2 inches per week is the working range, leaning higher during flowering and fruit sizing and through hot, dry spells. Even, deep watering builds large, well-filled melons; let the plant swing dry and you get poor set, small fruit, and blossom-end and hollow-heart problems.
watering.amount_beginner: About 1 to 2 inches of water a week is a good target, more while the plant is flowering and the melons are growing.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base with drip or a soaker hose, keeping the foliage as dry as possible, since wet leaves invite anthracnose, gummy stem blight, and the mildews that watermelon is prone to. The key move unique to watermelon is to taper watering as the fruit approaches ripeness, which concentrates the sugars and sweetens the flesh, while over-watering near harvest dilutes flavor and can split fruit.
watering.method_beginner: Water the soil, not the leaves, using a soaker hose or watering wand at the base, which helps prevent leaf disease. As the melons get close to ripe, ease off the water. That last step is what makes watermelon sweet, since too much water near harvest waters down the flavor and can crack the fruit.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting even when the soil is wet, soft or rotting stems, and split or bland, watery fruit point to overwatering or poor drainage. Saturated soil also favors Fusarium wilt and fruit rot, especially on heavy ground.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If lower leaves yellow, the plant wilts even though the soil is wet, stems go soft, or the melons split or taste watery, it is getting too much water or the soil drains poorly.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Midday wilting that recovers overnight is normal in heat, but leaves that stay limp and dull signal real drought. Dry spells during fruit sizing show up as small, misshapen melons, aborted young fruit, and blossom-end problems.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Some midday wilting in hot weather is normal and passes by evening. Leaves that stay wilted mean the plant is too dry, and drought while fruit is forming gives small, misshapen melons.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Base watering is the most useful habit for watermelon, because the same plant that wants steady moisture through sizing is also disease-prone when its leaves stay wet. Keep water on the soil and air moving through the leaves, then ease off as the fruit nears ripeness to concentrate the sugars.
watering.method_note_beginner: Watering the soil instead of the leaves is the best thing you can do for watermelon. It keeps the plant healthy without encouraging leaf disease, and easing off near harvest makes the fruit sweeter.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The water-critical stretch is flowering through fruit set and sizing. Steady moisture here drives large, well-filled melons; uneven water gives poor set, small fruit, and hollow heart. Then deliberately taper watering in the last week or two before harvest to sweeten the flesh.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The most important time to keep watermelon watered is when it is flowering and the fruit is growing. Then ease off in the last week or two before harvest so the melon turns sweet.

crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Watermelon is harvested once, at full ripeness, and does not ripen further after cutting, so reading the plant correctly is everything. No single sign is perfect, so use several together: the curly tendril nearest the fruit dries up and turns brown; the ground spot where the melon rests on the soil turns from white or pale green to a creamy, buttery yellow; the skin loses its gloss and dulls to a matte finish; and a ripe melon gives a deep, dull, hollow thump when tapped (an unripe one rings tight and high). The melon should also have reached full size and color for its variety. Cut the fruit from the vine with shears or a knife leaving a short stub of stem rather than pulling it, since watermelon does not slip from the vine. When in doubt, the browning tendril plus a yellow ground spot is the most reliable pair.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: You pick a watermelon once, when it is fully ripe, and it will not get any riper after you cut it, so timing matters. Look for several signs together: the little curly tendril closest to the melon dries up and turns brown; the pale spot where the melon sits on the ground turns creamy yellow instead of white; the skin goes from shiny to dull; and the melon makes a deep, dull thump when you tap it, instead of a tight, high ring. Cut it off the vine with a knife, leaving a short piece of stem, rather than pulling it. The browning tendril and the yellow ground spot together are the most reliable check.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Harden off indoor-started watermelon over 7 to 10 days, easing the plants into direct sun and wind before transplanting. Handle the rootball gently, because cucurbits resent root disturbance and a checked seedling sulks for weeks; use larger cells or pots and set plants out young, before the roots circle the container, and only once the soil is reliably warm.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: If you started seedlings indoors, set them outside for a little longer each day over about a week so they get used to sun and wind. Be gentle with the roots when you plant, since watermelon does not like having its roots disturbed, and only plant out once the soil is good and warm.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Watermelon needs warm soil and a long, hot season. Direct sow once the soil at 2 inches is reliably 70°F or more (it will not germinate well below about 65°F), sowing several seeds about 1 inch deep per hill and thinning to the strongest two. In short-season or cooler areas, start transplants indoors about 3 weeks ahead in large cells and set them out after the soil warms, using black plastic mulch to warm the ground and gain time, and lean on early-maturing icebox varieties. Seedless (triploid) types germinate best in warm conditions and must be grown alongside a seeded pollinizer variety, since they make no viable pollen of their own.
start_method.notes_beginner: Watermelon loves heat, so wait for warm soil (about 70°F) before planting. The easiest way is to sow seeds right where they will grow, a few seeds 1 inch deep per hill, then keep the strongest two. If your summers are short or cool, start seeds indoors about 3 weeks early and move them out once it warms up, and use black plastic mulch to warm the soil. If you grow a seedless kind, remember it needs a regular seeded watermelon planted nearby to pollinate it.

thinning.when: when seedlings have one or two true leaves
thinning.tip_seasoned: Sow three to four seeds per hill and thin to the strongest two once they have a true leaf or two. Snip the extras off at soil line rather than pulling, so you do not disturb the roots of the keepers. In rows, thin to one plant every 24 to 36 inches for icebox types and wider for full-size vines.
thinning.tip_beginner: Plant three or four seeds in each hill, then keep the two strongest seedlings once they grow their first real leaves. Cut the extra ones off at the ground instead of pulling them, so you do not hurt the roots of the ones you keep.

drainage.saucer_practice: If you use a saucer, empty it after watering. Watermelon will not tolerate sitting in standing water, which invites wilt and fruit rot.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Use a good bagged potting mix, not garden soil, which packs down too hard in a pot.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in compost and a slow-release fertilizer at planting. Pots need feeding more often than beds because watering washes nutrients out.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: Use a rich, free-draining peat- or coir-based potting mix, not garden soil, which compacts and drains poorly in a container.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend in some compost plus a slow-release lower-nitrogen fertilizer at planting. Because frequent watering flushes nutrients, plan to feed a container watermelon more regularly than one in the ground, easing off nitrogen once fruit sets.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out much faster than garden beds. In summer a potted watermelon may need water every day. Check daily and water until it drains from the bottom, but ease off near harvest so the fruit sweetens.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Feed a potted watermelon more often than a garden plant, with a balanced-to-low-nitrogen liquid feed every couple of weeks once it is growing strongly, stopping the heavy nitrogen once melons form.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Not applicable. Watermelon lives for one season and dies with the first frost, so there is nothing to overwinter. Plant new seeds next year.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Not applicable. Watermelon is a frost-tender annual that completes its life in a single season and is killed by the first hard frost, so there is nothing to overwinter. Pull spent vines at season's end and start fresh from seed the following year.

container_notes.notes_beginner: You can grow a watermelon in a container, but only the small icebox or bush kinds like Sugar Baby or Bush Sugar Baby, since full-size vining watermelons are far too big. Use a large pot, at least 15 gallons and 12 inches deep, put it in full sun, keep it well watered (pots dry out fast), and feed it regularly. Give the vines room to trail out of the pot or up a sturdy trellis, support any fruit on a sling, and water the soil, not the leaves, to help avoid disease.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Watermelon is a marginal container crop because it is a large, long-season, sprawling, heat-hungry vine, but a compact icebox or bush variety such as Sugar Baby or Bush Sugar Baby makes it workable. Choose a small-fruited type and give it a big pot: at least 15 gallons and 12 inches deep, larger is better. Give it full sun and all-day warmth, let the vines trail out over the rim or climb a sturdy trellis with each fruit cradled in a cloth sling, water at the base daily in heat, and feed regularly while easing off nitrogen once fruit sets. The container figures here follow general container-vegetable guidance; watermelon-specific container numbers are modeled.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry far faster than beds, and a watermelon in a pot can need water once or even twice a day in summer heat. Check daily by feeling the top inch of mix, and water until it runs from the drainage holes; even moisture prevents the small, misshapen fruit that water swings cause, but taper in the final week or two before harvest to concentrate sweetness.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Feed container watermelon more often than in-ground ones, since steady watering leaches nutrients. After the slow-release charge at planting, add a balanced-to-low-nitrogen liquid feed every 2 to 3 weeks, easing off nitrogen once fruit sets so the plant builds sweet fruit rather than vine.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering container suits a potted watermelon well during vining and sizing, smoothing the moisture swings that cause small, cracked, or hollow fruit. Keep the reservoir topped up in heat and water from below to keep foliage dry. The one caveat is unique to watermelon: in the last week or two before harvest, let it run drier to sweeten the flesh rather than keeping the reservoir full.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot helps while the plant is growing and the fruit is sizing, because it keeps the water steady. Keep the reservoir filled in hot weather. Just let it run a bit dry in the last week or two before you pick, so the melon turns sweet.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: A container watermelon needs a wide, deep, heavy pot, at least 12 inches deep and 15 gallons or more, even for a compact icebox variety, with room for the vines to trail out over the edge or climb a sturdy trellis. Wide and stable beats tall and narrow, since a vining plant in a small pot dries out and tips, and any fruit grown up a trellis needs a cloth sling for support. Choose icebox or bush types for containers, never full-size vining watermelons.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Give a container watermelon a large, deep, heavy pot, at least 12 inches deep and 15 gallons or more, and let the vines trail out of it or climb a small trellis with each melon held in a sling. A wide, sturdy pot is better than a tall, narrow one. Only grow small icebox or bush watermelon varieties in pots, not the big vining kinds.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Avoid planting watermelon where any cucurbit grew in the last few years, including cucumber, muskmelon, squash, and pumpkin. They share cucumber beetle, the mildews, and especially the soilborne Fusarium wilt and seed- and debris-borne anthracnose and gummy stem blight, which build up in the soil and on residue.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Do not plant watermelon where you grew cucumbers, melons, squash, or pumpkins in the last few years. They get the same pests and diseases, which build up in the soil.
rotation.good_after: Legumes such as beans and peas, sweet corn, leafy greens, or alliums like onions and garlic make good preceding crops, since they do not share the cucurbit pest and disease complex, and a legume leaves a little nitrogen behind.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate watermelon and its cucurbit relatives on at least a 3 year cycle, and stretch it to five years where Fusarium wilt or anthracnose are established, since the watermelon wilt fungus persists in soil for years and anthracnose and gummy stem blight carry over on debris and seed. A long rotation is the single most important cultural defense against the diseases that limit this crop. Clear and remove spent vines at season's end rather than tilling them in, which removes overwintering disease sites.
rotation.note_beginner: Try not to grow watermelon or its relatives (cucumbers, melons, squash) in the same spot more than once every 3 years, and wait longer, up to five years, if you have had wilt or anthracnose. Moving them around the garden is the best way to avoid a buildup of disease. Clean up old vines at the end of the season too.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: An uncut, ripe watermelon holds at room temperature for about a week, or 7 to 10 days, kept out of direct sun. Unlike winter squash, it does not improve or keep for months, so plan to eat it within a week or so of picking. Whole melons hold a bit longer in a cool room than a warm one.
storage.room_temp_beginner: A whole, ripe watermelon keeps at room temperature for about a week. It does not store for months like a pumpkin, so eat it within a week or so of picking, and keep it out of direct sun.
storage.fridge_seasoned: A whole watermelon keeps about 2 weeks held cool at around 50 to 60°F, the practical limit before flavor and texture decline; do not store it very cold for long, as watermelon is subject to chilling injury below about 50°F. Once cut, wrap the pieces tightly and refrigerate, using them within 3 to 5 days.
storage.fridge_beginner: A whole watermelon keeps for up to about 2 weeks if held cool, around 50 to 60°F. Do not keep it very cold for a long time, since that harms the flesh. Once you cut it, wrap the pieces and keep them in the fridge, using them within a few days.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Watermelon does not freeze well as chunks, since freezing collapses the crisp texture into mush, but it freezes nicely as puree or juice: blend the flesh, strain if you like, and freeze in portions for slushies, granita, or agua fresca. Frozen cubes also work for chilling drinks.
storage.freezer_beginner: Watermelon turns mushy if you freeze it in chunks, so it is best frozen as juice or puree. Blend the flesh and freeze it in portions for slushies and drinks, or freeze cubes to drop into a glass like ice.
storage.notes_seasoned: Watermelon is an eat-fresh crop, not a keeper, which is why you harvest it only at full ripeness and use it promptly. A whole, sound melon holds about a week at room temperature or up to two weeks held cool near 50 to 60°F, but it will not ripen or sweeten any further off the vine, and very cold storage causes chilling injury. Refrigerate cut pieces wrapped and use within a few days. There is no curing step as there is for winter squash.
storage.notes_beginner: Watermelon is best eaten soon after picking, not stored for the long haul, which is why you wait and harvest it fully ripe. A whole melon keeps about a week at room temperature, or up to two weeks somewhere cool but not cold. It will not get any riper after picking. Once cut, wrap it and keep it in the fridge for a few days.

recommended.name: Sugar Baby
recommended.recommended_note: A classic early icebox watermelon, round and dark green with sweet red flesh, about 8 to 10 pounds. Quick to mature, which makes it the go-to for shorter or cooler-summer gardens and the North. Open-pollinated and seed-saveable.

recommended.name: Crimson Sweet
recommended.recommended_note: The dependable home-garden standard: round-oval, light-and-dark green striped, 15 to 25 pounds, with very sweet red flesh. Carries resistance to anthracnose and Fusarium wilt, which makes it forgiving in the Southeast. Open-pollinated.

recommended.name: Charleston Gray
recommended.recommended_note: The classic long, oblong gray-green watermelon, 20 to 30 pounds, with sweet red flesh, a tough rind, and good heat and drought tolerance plus anthracnose and Fusarium wilt resistance. A strong choice for hot regions and long seasons.

recommended.name: Jubilee
recommended.recommended_note: A large oblong striped watermelon, 25 pounds or more, with crisp, sweet red flesh and Fusarium wilt and anthracnose resistance. A long-season Southern favorite where there is room and heat to finish it.

recommended.name: Yellow Doll
recommended.recommended_note: An early yellow-fleshed icebox hybrid, small at around 5 to 8 pounds, very sweet, and fast to ripen. A good pick for short seasons, small gardens, and gardeners who want something different.

recommended.name: Seedless (triploid) types
recommended.recommended_note: Seedless hybrids such as the Crimson-type triploids ripen in roughly 85 to 90 days and produce no viable pollen of their own, so they must be planted alongside a seeded pollinizer variety (commonly one seeded plant per two to three seedless). Sweet and convenient, but they need warm conditions to germinate and a longer, hotter season.

varieties.note_seasoned: Choose by season length, space, and use. Where summers are short or cool, lean on the fast icebox types such as Sugar Baby and Yellow Doll, which ripen in 70 to 80 days; in long, hot regions the full-size Crimson Sweet, Charleston Gray, and Jubilee reward the heat with big, sweet melons. In the disease-prone Southeast, prioritize varieties with anthracnose and Fusarium wilt resistance such as Crimson Sweet, Charleston Gray, and Jubilee. Seedless types are popular and sweet but add a real requirement: a seeded pollinizer must be grown alongside, and they want the warmest conditions to germinate and finish.
varieties.note_beginner: Pick a watermelon by your summer and your space. If your season is short or cool, grow a fast small type like Sugar Baby or Yellow Doll. If you have a long, hot summer and room to spread, grow a big one like Crimson Sweet, Charleston Gray, or Jubilee. In the South, choose disease-resistant varieties like Crimson Sweet. Seedless watermelons are sweet and convenient, but remember they need a regular seeded variety planted nearby to pollinate them, and they like it extra warm.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A healthy full-size watermelon vine typically yields 2 to 4 marketable melons, while icebox and bush types set more, smaller fruit. Limiting fruit to two or three per vine on full-size types channels energy into larger, better-filled melons. Plants need plenty of room, roughly 24 square feet each for full-size types, and even moisture and modest feeding through sizing build sweet fruit.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: A full-size watermelon plant usually gives you 2 to 4 melons, while small icebox types make more, smaller ones. Each plant needs a lot of room. If you want bigger melons, keep just two or three fruit per vine so the plant can size them up.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Watermelon does not produce continuously; the plant sets fruit over a few weeks and then sizes and ripens that crop, with the melons coming ready over a window in mid to late summer rather than all at once or all season long. Each melon is harvested once, at full ripeness.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Unlike summer squash, watermelon does not keep producing all season. The plant sets its fruit over a few weeks and the melons ripen over a stretch in mid to late summer, and you pick each one once when it is ripe.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: The usual first-year surprises are how much room the vines take (8 to 12 feet for full-size types), how pollinator-dependent fruit set is, and how much ripeness judgment matters, since the melon does not finish off the vine. Give plants far more space than seems necessary, grow flowers nearby for bees, and learn the tendril-and-ground-spot check before you cut.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: The big first-year surprises are how far watermelon vines spread, how much they depend on bees, and how tricky it is to tell when a melon is ripe (it will not ripen after you pick it). Give them lots of room, grow some flowers for the bees, and learn the ripeness signs before cutting.
factors_seasoned: Heat and season length: watermelon needs a long, hot season (70 to 95 days) with warm nights to ripen and sweeten; cool-summer northern and coastal areas are marginal and need early icebox types, transplants, and black plastic mulch.

Pollination: fruit set is pollinator-limited, each female flower needing many bee visits, and seedless types additionally need a seeded pollinizer nearby; poor pollination drops or deforms young fruit.
Space and vine vigor: full-size vines sprawl 8 to 12 feet and need about 24 square feet each; crowding cuts yield and worsens disease.
Disease pressure: Fusarium wilt, anthracnose, gummy stem blight, and the mildews can end a planting early, so resistant varieties and long rotations matter.
Even moisture, then a dry finish: steady water through sizing builds full melons, but tapering water near ripeness is what concentrates the sugars and makes them sweet.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No T1 source supports timing watermelon planting by moon phase. We do not make a recommendation here; sow by soil temperature (70°F and warm) and frost dates instead.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seeds sprout in about 5 to 10 days in warm soil (70 to 95°F is ideal); soil below about 65°F rots seed rather than germinating it. Two seed leaves push up first.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: In warm soil, seeds sprout in about a week to ten days, sending up two seed leaves first. In cold soil, seeds rot instead of sprouting.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Wait for warm soil (70°F at 2 inches) and sow about 1 inch deep, three to four seeds per hill. Keep evenly moist, not soggy. Thin to the strongest two seedlings once true leaves appear.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Plant seeds 1 inch deep once the soil is warm, a few per hill. Keep the soil damp until they sprout, then keep the strongest two seedlings.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Did your watermelon seeds germinate, and how many days did it take?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your seeds sprouted yet?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Cotyledons followed by the first true leaves; growth is fast once warm. Watch for cucumber beetles, which target young plants, and for aphids on leaf undersides.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: After the first two rounded leaves, true leaves appear and the plant grows quickly once it is warm. Watch for beetles chewing the young leaves.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Protect from cucumber beetles with row cover if needed, removing it at flowering for pollination. Keep evenly watered and free of weeds, and use black plastic mulch in cooler areas to keep the soil warm.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep an eye out for beetles on young plants and use a light row cover if needed, but remove it once flowers form. Water regularly and keep weeds down.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How are your seedlings developing? Any sign of beetle damage?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How do your young plants look?

growth_stages.name: Vining
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The plant sends out long runners and bulks up its leaves, growing fast in warm weather. This is the window to side-dress lightly with nitrogen and the time to start watching for spider mites in hot, dry spells.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant sends out long vines that spread across the ground, with big leaves. This is when you feed it a little and give it room to run.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Side-dress with a little nitrogen as the vines run, then ease off, mulch to hold moisture, and give the runners room to spread, 8 to 12 feet for full-size types. Scout for spider mites and aphids on leaf undersides.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Feed the vines a little as they start to run, then go easy on nitrogen, add mulch to keep the soil moist, and give them plenty of room to spread. Check under the leaves for tiny pests.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are the vines running well? Have you side-dressed, and any pests on the leaf undersides?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are your watermelon vines spreading out?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Yellow flowers open. Male flowers on thin stalks usually open first, often for a week before females, which is normal; female flowers carry a tiny melon behind the bloom. Each female needs many bee visits to set, and seedless types need a seeded pollinizer nearby to supply pollen.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Yellow flowers open. The first ones are usually male and fall off, which is normal. Female flowers have a tiny melon at their base, and bees need to visit them many times to set fruit.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Encourage pollinators and avoid spraying open blooms. If small fruit yellow and abort, pollination is poor, so hand-pollinate in the morning with a male flower or small brush. Make sure a seeded pollinizer is flowering near any seedless plants. Keep moisture steady.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Let the bees do their work and do not spray the flowers. If tiny melons turn yellow and drop, the flowers were not pollinated, so you can hand-pollinate in the morning. Keep watering steadily.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are you seeing female flowers and fruit set? Any young fruit yellowing and dropping?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Is your plant flowering? Are any little melons forming?

growth_stages.name: Fruit development
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Set fruit swell quickly over several weeks, reaching full size before the rind dulls and the ripeness signs appear. The plant is sizing and ripening its crop rather than setting new fruit continuously, and it takes roughly 35 to 45 days from fruit set to ripeness.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The little melons grow bigger fast over several weeks. The plant is busy growing and ripening the melons it has set, which takes about five to six weeks from when the fruit forms.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture even through sizing, then taper in the last week or two to concentrate sugars. Set each melon on a board, tile, or mulch to keep it off wet soil, limit fruit per vine for bigger melons, and keep scouting for mildew and spider mites.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep watering steadily while the melons grow, then ease off near the end to sweeten them. Slip a board or some straw under each melon so it is not sitting on damp ground, and watch the leaves for disease.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How are the fruit sizing? Are you keeping them off wet soil and easing off water as they near ripeness?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are your watermelons growing bigger?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Full size and color for the variety, a browned tendril nearest the fruit, a creamy-yellow ground spot, a dull (not glossy) skin, and a deep, dull thump. Harvest each melon once at full ripeness, since it will not ripen further off the vine.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The melon is full size, the little tendril next to it has dried brown, the spot on the bottom has turned creamy yellow, the skin is dull, and it thumps deep and dull. That is ripe, and it will not get riper after picking.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Check the ripeness signs together, then cut each melon from the vine with shears leaving a short stub of stem, rather than pulling it. Use the browning tendril plus the yellow ground spot as your most reliable pair, and eat or refrigerate promptly, since watermelon does not store long.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: When the signs line up, cut the melon off the vine with a knife, leaving a short piece of stem. Do not pull it off. Eat it within a week or so, since watermelon does not keep for long.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have you harvested? How did the ripeness signs line up, and how was the flavor?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you picked your watermelon yet?

notifications.title_seasoned: Watch for spider mites in the heat
notifications.title_beginner: Time to watch for tiny pests in hot weather
notifications.body_seasoned: Your watermelon vines are running in summer heat, which is exactly when two-spotted spider mites build up. Check leaf undersides for fine yellow stippling and webbing, and treat early with a water blast or insecticidal soap before they peak.
notifications.body_beginner: Your watermelon is growing fast in the summer heat, which is when spider mites show up. Check under the leaves for fine yellow speckling, and treat early if you see it.

notifications.body_seasoned: Your watermelon is flowering. Fruit set depends on many bee visits per female flower, and seedless types need a seeded pollinizer nearby, so if small fruit yellow and drop, hand-pollinate in the morning and keep blooms unsprayed.
notifications.body_beginner: Your watermelon is flowering. If the tiny melons turn yellow and fall off, the flowers were not pollinated, so try hand-pollinating in the morning.

notifications.title_beginner: Time to check if your watermelons are ripe
notifications.body_seasoned: Your watermelons should be nearing ripeness. Look for a browned tendril nearest the fruit, a creamy-yellow ground spot, a dull skin, and a deep, dull thump, then cut at full ripeness, since watermelon does not ripen off the vine.
notifications.body_beginner: Your watermelons should be getting close. Check for the dried brown tendril, the creamy-yellow spot on the bottom, a dull skin, and a deep thump, then pick when ripe, since it will not ripen after you cut it.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost is coming, harvest your watermelons
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost warning for your watermelons
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A frost is forecast. Watermelon is frost-tender, and frost ends the vines, so harvest any ripe or near-ripe melons now. Note that under-ripe melons will not finish off the vine, so pick what is closest to ready.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Frost is coming, and it will kill the vines. Pick any ripe or nearly ripe watermelons now, since they will not ripen any further once frost hits.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Extreme heat may briefly stall fruit set
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot spell may slow fruit set
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A stretch of extreme heat is forecast. Watermelon thrives in heat, but very hot days with hot nights can briefly reduce pollination and drop young fruit. Keep moisture steady; set usually resumes as the worst heat eases.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Very hot weather is coming. Watermelon loves heat, but the most extreme days may slow fruit set for a while. Keep it well watered, it usually picks back up when it cools a little.

germination.text_seasoned: Soil temperature, not the calendar, governs watermelon germination. Wait until soil is at least 70°F at 2 inches; seed sown in cold ground below 65°F rots before it sprouts.
germination.text_beginner: Wait for warm soil before sowing. Watermelon seeds rot in cold ground but sprout fast once it is warm, around 70°F.

seedling.text_seasoned: Cucumber beetles swarm young cucurbits. A floating row cover protects seedlings, but pull it off at flowering so bees can pollinate. In cooler areas, black plastic mulch warms the soil and speeds growth.
seedling.text_beginner: Protect young plants from beetles with a light cover, but take it off once flowers appear so bees can reach them. Black plastic mulch helps in cooler spots.

vining.text_seasoned: Go easy on nitrogen once the vines run. Too much gives lush vine at the expense of fruit and sugar, which is the classic watermelon mistake. Give full-size types 8 to 12 feet to sprawl.
vining.text_beginner: Do not overdo the nitrogen once the vines spread, or you get lots of leaves and few melons. Give them plenty of room.

vining.text_seasoned: Spider mites explode in hot, dry weather, exactly watermelon's season. Scout leaf undersides for fine stippling and webbing, keep plants watered so they are not heat-stressed, and avoid broad-spectrum sprays that kill the mites' natural enemies.
vining.text_beginner: Watch for spider mites in hot, dry weather. Check under the leaves for fine speckling, keep the plants watered, and do not spray strong insecticides that kill the good bugs.

flowering.text_seasoned: Early male flowers opening and dropping with no fruit is normal; females come later. Judge pollination by whether small fruit size up or yellow and abort.
flowering.text_beginner: The first flowers often fall off without making melons, that is normal. Trouble is when tiny melons turn yellow and drop, which means poor pollination.

flowering.text_seasoned: If you grow seedless watermelon, a seeded pollinizer variety must be flowering nearby, since seedless plants make no viable pollen. Without it, seedless plants flower but set no fruit no matter how many bees visit.
flowering.text_beginner: Seedless watermelon needs a regular seeded watermelon planted nearby to pollinate it. Without that partner, a seedless plant will flower but never make fruit.

fruit_development.text_seasoned: Slip a board, tile, or straw under each sizing melon to keep it off wet soil and prevent rot, and limit the number of fruit per vine if you want larger melons. It takes roughly 35 to 45 days from fruit set to ripeness.
fruit_development.text_beginner: Put a board or some straw under each melon so it is not on damp ground. For bigger melons, keep just a few fruit per vine. They take about five to six weeks to ripen after they form.

fruit_development.text_seasoned: Taper watering in the last week or two before harvest to concentrate the sugars. Over-watering near ripeness dilutes the flavor and can split the fruit, the single biggest cause of a bland homegrown melon.
fruit_development.text_beginner: Ease off the water in the last week or two before picking, so the melon turns sweet. Too much water near the end makes it watery and can crack it.

harvest.text_seasoned: No single ripeness sign is perfect, so use several: the browned tendril nearest the fruit, a creamy-yellow ground spot, a dull skin, and a deep, dull thump. The browning tendril plus the yellow ground spot is the most reliable pair. Cut, do not pull, and remember it will not ripen off the vine.
harvest.text_beginner: Check several signs together: the dried brown tendril, the creamy-yellow spot on the bottom, a dull skin, and a deep thump. Cut the melon off with a knife, do not pull it, and pick it ripe since it will not ripen after.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Cut the melon open and it was bland, pale, or watery
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The watermelon was not sweet inside
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The melon was harvested under-ripe, or it was over-watered near harvest. Watermelon does not sweeten off the vine, so a melon picked early stays bland, and heavy watering in the final week dilutes the sugars and can leave the flesh watery.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The melon was picked too early, or it got too much water right before harvest. Watermelon does not get sweeter after you cut it, and too much late water makes it watery.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Harvesting before full ripeness, or over-watering in the final week or two before harvest.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Picking too soon, or watering too much right before harvest.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Learn the ripeness signs and use several together (browned tendril, creamy-yellow ground spot, dull skin, dull thump), and taper watering in the last week or two before harvest to concentrate the sugars.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Wait for the ripeness signs to line up before picking, and ease off the water in the last week or two so the melon sweetens.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Vine yellowed and wilted on one side and died
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The vine wilted and died even though it was watered
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Most likely Fusarium wilt, the watermelon-specific soilborne fungus that clogs the water-conducting tissue, often killing one runner first, then the plant, even in moist soil. A pinkish mold near the soil line and browned vascular tissue in a cut stem confirm it. It builds up where watermelon repeats on the same ground.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Usually Fusarium wilt, a soil disease that only attacks watermelon and blocks the plant's water pipes, so it wilts and dies even when watered. It builds up in soil where you grow watermelon too often.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. niveum in the soil, favored by warm sandy ground and short rotations.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: A soil fungus specific to watermelon that survives for years in the ground.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant resistant varieties, rotate out of watermelon and cucurbits for at least five years, and consider grafted plants on resistant rootstock where the disease is established.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Grow resistant varieties, do not plant watermelon in the same spot for at least five years, and look into grafted plants if the disease keeps coming back.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Tiny fruit yellowed and dropped after flowering
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Little melons turned yellow and fell off
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Poor pollination. The female flower was not adequately pollinated, so the young fruit aborts. Watermelon needs many bee visits per flower, and seedless types fail entirely without a seeded pollinizer nearby. Common in cool, wet, or pollinator-scarce conditions and during extreme heat.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The flowers were not pollinated well, so the little melons died instead of growing. Watermelon needs lots of bee visits, and seedless kinds need a seeded variety planted nearby.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Inadequate pollen transfer to the female flower; with seedless types, a missing or non-flowering seeded pollinizer.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Not enough pollination, or no seeded pollinizer near a seedless plant.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant flowers to draw bees, avoid spraying open blooms, hand-pollinate in the morning if set is poor, and always grow a seeded pollinizer alongside seedless types.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Grow some flowers nearby for the bees, hand-pollinate early flowers if needed, and always plant a seeded watermelon next to any seedless ones.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Melon rotted on the bottom where it touched the soil
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The melon rotted on its underside
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Fruit rot, typically from a wet underside in prolonged contact with damp soil, favored by poorly drained, rainy conditions and the cucurbit fruit-rot fungi. A soft, sometimes molded patch develops where the melon sits.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The melon sat on wet ground and rotted on the bottom. Damp soil and poor drainage let rot soften the fruit where it touched the ground.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Prolonged contact between fruit and saturated soil, favoring soilborne fruit rots in wet, poorly drained beds.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: The melon sitting on wet soil, which lets rot set in on the underside.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant on raised hills for drainage, avoid low wet spots, and set each sizing melon on a board, tile, or thick mulch to lift it off the soil.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant on raised hills so water drains away, and slip a board or straw under each melon so it is not on wet ground.
