crops.name: Strawberry

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Strawberries grow best in loose, rich soil that drains well, like a sandy loam. Their roots are shallow, so they rot if the ground stays soggy. If your soil is heavy clay or puddles after rain, build a raised bed or a mounded row about 12 inches tall and plant into that. Mixing 1 to 2 inches of compost into the bed before planting gives the roots a good start.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Strawberries want a fertile, well-drained sandy loam or loam with steady but not excessive moisture. The roots are shallow and fibrous, so they suffocate in soil that stays waterlogged for more than a day or two, and root rots follow. On heavy or slow-draining ground, plant into a raised bed or mounded row about 12 inches high so water drains away from the crowns. Work 1 to 2 inches of compost or aged organic matter into the bed before planting to lift organic matter above 3 percent.

ph.note_beginner: Strawberries prefer soil on the slightly acidic side, roughly pH 5.6 to 6.5. A cheap test kit shows where you are. Garden sulfur lowers a too-high number; garden lime raises a too-low one. Both take a few months to take effect, so test and adjust the season before you plant.
ph.note_seasoned: Aim for slightly acidic soil in the range of pH 5.6 to 6.5. Test the bed a season ahead so there is time to adjust: elemental sulfur brings a high reading down, and ground dolomitic limestone raises a low one. Both amendments take months to move the soil, so apply them well before the crowns go in.

fertilizer.frequency: At planting and through the first season for new plantings; for established June-bearing beds, once a year at renovation.
fertilizer.timing: renovation
fertilizer.example_product: 16-16-16 balanced fertilizer (or a comparable all-purpose granular)
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Strawberry feeding is nitrogen-driven and timed to the planting model. In the first year, apply a total of about 0.5 to 0.8 ounces of actual nitrogen per 10 feet of row, split across the season: a small dose one to two weeks after planting, a second about a month later, and a third roughly two months after planting. On established June-bearing beds, do not feed in spring; spring nitrogen drives leaf growth, not fruit, and a dense canopy traps moisture and promotes gray mold. Instead, fertilize once at renovation, just after harvest, to build the flower buds for next year. Established day-neutral and everbearing plants, which fruit all season, take the same total split into monthly doses through summer with an optional August feeding. On sandy soil, divide every rate into more frequent, lighter applications.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Strawberries mainly need nitrogen, and when you feed depends on the type. The first year, give a little fertilizer two or three times spread across the season rather than one big dose. After that, the rule for June-bearing plants is simple: do not feed in spring, because it grows lots of leaves but not more berries, and the thick leaves trap dampness that causes mold. Feed them once instead, right after harvest when you cut the plants back. Day-neutral and everbearing plants, which fruit all summer, get small amounts spread across the months instead. If your soil is sandy, feed smaller amounts more often.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time to renovate and feed your June-bearing strawberries. Mow the old leaves, narrow the row, then apply about 0.4 to 0.6 ounces of nitrogen per 10 feet of row and water it in to set next year's crop.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Your June-bearing strawberries are ready for their after-harvest cutback and feeding. Mow the old leaves, then give the plants a balanced fertilizer and water it in to help next year's berries.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced analysis such as 16-16-16 works well. Rates are given as actual nitrogen per length of row, so divide the nitrogen you need by the decimal nitrogen fraction of your product: about 0.4 to 0.6 ounces of nitrogen per 10 feet at renovation works out to roughly 2.5 to 3.75 ounces of 16-16-16 per 10-foot row.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: A balanced fertilizer like 16-16-16 (the three numbers are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium) is a good all-purpose choice. Follow the label rate for the row length you are feeding, and water it in after spreading.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: First year: about 0.5 to 0.8 ounces of nitrogen per 10 feet of row total, in two to three splits. Established June-bearers: about 0.4 to 0.6 ounces of nitrogen per 10 feet of row, all at once at renovation. Day-neutral and everbearing: about 0.1 to 0.2 ounces of nitrogen per 10 feet each month after spring growth begins, with an optional August dose.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A rough guide: feed a new bed lightly two or three times the first year. Feed an established June-bearing bed once, after harvest. Feed day-neutral or everbearing plants a little each month through summer. Use the label rate on your fertilizer for the length of your row.

companions.note_beginner: The most important placement rule for strawberries is about what grew there before, not what you plant beside them. Do not put strawberries where tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes, raspberries, or blackberries grew recently. Those plants can leave a soil disease called Verticillium wilt behind, and it attacks strawberries too and stays in the soil for years. Also keep weeds out, since strawberries have shallow roots and lose out to weeds easily. The companion plants listed above are nice, low-risk neighbors, but they are garden tradition rather than a proven way to grow more fruit.
companions.note_seasoned: The one firm rule for strawberry placement is rotation, not companionship: do not plant strawberries where tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes, raspberries, or blackberries have recently grown, because all of them host Verticillium wilt, a soilborne fungus that also attacks strawberries and lingers in the ground for years. Keep the same crops out of the bed for several years afterward. Beyond that, strawberries compete poorly with weeds because their roots are shallow, so the most valuable neighbor is bare, weed-free soil rather than any particular plant. The good-companion pairings above are traditional and low-risk, not documented yield boosters.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Bush beans
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Beans are an easy, friendly neighbor for strawberries. They do not compete much and add a little nitrogen to the soil, though do not expect them to make your berries bigger.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Legume Rhizobium N-fixation is established biology and benefits a neighboring moderate feeder; bush beans also do not compete heavily with low strawberry crowns. mechanistic/medium: sound mechanism, but the same-season transfer to strawberries specifically is modest and timing-dependent (much released on decomposition), so not research_backed.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Bush beans bring nitrogen fixation to the strawberry bed. Working with Rhizobium bacteria on their roots, they pull atmospheric nitrogen into a plant-available form that lightly benefits strawberries as moderate feeders, and their upright, shallow habit does not compete much with low-running strawberry crowns. As with most legume pairings, the nitrogen mostly reaches neighbors as the bean roots break down, so treat it as gentle soil-building across the season rather than an immediate feed.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Lettuce
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Lettuce fits nicely along the edge of a strawberry bed while the berries are still small, using space the strawberries are not using yet.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Shallow-root quick interplant using space between strawberry crowns / first-year beds; extension-aligned interplant logic. Space/timing benefit, not a measured strawberry-specific effect. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Lettuce makes good use of the open space in a strawberry planting, especially in the first season before the strawberries fill in and run. It is shallow-rooted and quick, so it crops and clears before the strawberries need the room, and its low canopy helps shade soil and suppress weeds between crowns. A space-and-timing pairing rather than a pest or flavor one.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Borage
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Borage is a herb with blue flowers that bees love. A few plants near your strawberries can bring in more bees, which helps the flowers turn into well-shaped berries.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Split call recorded honestly. The pollinator-attraction benefit is grounded (borage is a strong bee attractant; strawberry fruit set/shape improves with better pollination) and would justify likely/mechanistic on its own. But the headline traditional claim ('strawberry farmers set borage to enhance flavor and yield') is the folk part - Farmers' Almanac's science-based guide explicitly flags the analogous borage-vs-hornworm claim as often-repeated-but-unsupported, and no controlled study backs borage->strawberry flavor/yield. Net label traditional (the pairing's headline status is folk) at medium confidence on the strength of the real pollinator component. Flagging in case you'd prefer to split into two entries or relabel the pollinator basis as likely.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Borage is the traditional strawberry companion, and it is worth separating what it reliably does from what is folklore. Reliably: borage is a powerful bee magnet, and better pollinator visitation gives strawberries more complete fruit set and fewer misshapen berries, a real, mechanism-backed benefit. The older claim that borage directly improves strawberry flavor and yield through the soil is widely repeated but unsupported by controlled study, so lean on borage for pollination, not as a flavor additive.

good_seasoned.name: Bush beans
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional strawberry companion: as a legume, beans fix nitrogen and occupy a different root zone, and they share no major strawberry pest. The benefit is a folk-garden one rather than a documented yield effect, so treat it as a low-risk neighbor, not a proven booster.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Classic interplanting practice; no T1 extension study documents a strawberry yield or pest benefit from the pairing.

good_seasoned.name: Lettuce
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Lettuce is a shallow, quick, cool-season crop often tucked along a strawberry bed edge while the berries fill in. It uses space and light the young strawberries are not yet using and shares no serious pest. The pairing is traditional and space-driven, not a documented growth benefit.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Space-use interplanting lore; no T1 source documents a strawberry benefit.

good_seasoned.name: Borage
good_seasoned.timing: interplant a few plants near the bed
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Borage is a long-standing strawberry companion said to draw pollinators and improve fruit set. The pollinator-attraction half is mechanistically plausible, since more bee visits do mean better-shaped berries, but the specific borage-strawberry pairing has not been tested in T1 extension trials, so it stays a traditional claim.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Pollinator-draw mechanism is plausible but the borage-strawberry pairing is untested in T1 literature.

pests.name: Slugs
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Ragged holes chewed in ripe fruit and leaves, with slime trails, worst in damp, heavily mulched beds and wet weather.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Ragged holes eaten in the berries and leaves, with shiny slime trails. Worst in damp, mulchy beds and wet weather.
pests.cause_seasoned: Slugs, which shelter in deep or wet mulch and feed at night on soft ripe fruit.
pests.cause_beginner: Slugs, which hide in damp mulch and eat the soft ripe berries at night.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick in the evening, set out shallow traps, and remove damp hiding places. Keep ripening fruit off wet mulch.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick them off in the evening, use simple traps, and clear away damp hiding spots. Keep berries off wet mulch.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid deep straw mulch during the growing season, keep the bed tidy, and harvest ripe fruit promptly.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not pile on thick straw in summer, keep the bed clean, and pick ripe berries quickly.

pests.name: Spotted wing drosophila
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Soft, collapsing spots on ripening and ripe fruit; tiny larvae feed inside berries. Populations build through the season, so later fruit is hit hardest.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Soft, sunken spots on ripening berries, with tiny maggots inside. It gets worse later in the season.
pests.cause_seasoned: A vinegar fly that lays eggs in coloring fruit; the larvae feed inside as the berry ripens.
pests.cause_beginner: A small fruit fly that lays eggs in the berries as they start to color, and the maggots eat the fruit from inside.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Pick fruit frequently and completely, remove and destroy overripe and culled berries, and use fine exclusion netting on susceptible later crops.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick all the ripe berries often, throw away overripe and damaged ones, and cover later crops with fine netting.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Harvest on a tight schedule, never leave overripe fruit on the plant, and exclude adults with fine netting where pressure is high.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep up with picking, never leave overripe berries on the plant, and use fine netting if the flies are bad.

pests.name: Tarnished plant bug (lygus)
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Catfaced fruit, dimpled and pinched at the tip with seedy, woody patches; most noticeable on day-neutrals in summer.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Lumpy, dented berries with a pinched, seedy tip. Most common on day-neutral plants in summer.
pests.cause_seasoned: Lygus bugs feeding on developing flowers and fruit, which disrupts seed and berry development at the tip.
pests.cause_beginner: A small bug that feeds on the flowers and young fruit, which makes the berry tip grow lumpy.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Keep the bed and surrounding area weed-free to remove alternate hosts, and monitor flowers during fruiting.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Keep weeds down in and around the bed, since the bugs live on them, and watch the flowers while fruiting.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Control broadleaf weeds that host lygus near the planting and keep the bed clean through the season.
pests.prevention_beginner: Pull broadleaf weeds near the bed, since the bugs breed on them, and keep the area tidy.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of small soft-bodied insects on new growth and leaf undersides, with sticky honeydew and sometimes sooty mold; aphids can also transmit strawberry viruses.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Groups of tiny soft bugs on new leaves and leaf undersides, leaving a sticky film. They can also spread plant viruses.
pests.cause_seasoned: Aphids feeding on plant sap, building up quickly on tender new growth.
pests.cause_beginner: Aphids, tiny bugs that suck plant juices and multiply fast on new leaves.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Knock populations back with a strong spray of water, encourage natural predators such as lady beetles, and use insecticidal soap on heavy infestations.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray them off with water, let helpful bugs like ladybugs do their work, and use insecticidal soap if there are a lot.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Start with clean, certified plants to limit virus introduction, and avoid excess nitrogen that flushes soft, aphid-prone growth.
pests.prevention_beginner: Start with clean plants, and do not over-feed, since lots of soft new growth attracts aphids.

pests.name: Two-spotted spider mite
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine stippling and bronzing of leaves with faint webbing on undersides, worst in hot, dry, dusty conditions; heavy infestations weaken plants and reduce yield.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Leaves look speckled and bronzed, with fine webbing underneath. Worst in hot, dry, dusty weather, and bad cases weaken the plants.
pests.cause_seasoned: Tiny mites that feed on the underside of leaves and multiply rapidly in hot, dry weather.
pests.cause_beginner: Tiny mites under the leaves that multiply fast when it is hot and dry.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rinse foliage to raise humidity and dislodge mites, encourage predatory mites, and treat severe cases with horticultural oil or insecticidal soap.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray the leaves with water to knock mites off and raise humidity, and use horticultural oil or soap for bad cases.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid drought stress and dusty conditions, and keep plants well watered in heat.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep plants watered in hot weather and avoid letting them get dusty and dry.

pests.name: Root and crown weevils (black vine weevil)
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Notched leaf margins from night-feeding adults, and stunted, wilting, or collapsing plants whose roots and crowns have been eaten by larvae.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Leaf edges notched as if cut with pinking shears, and plants that wilt or collapse because grubs have eaten the roots and crown.
pests.cause_seasoned: Weevils whose adults notch leaves at night and whose larvae feed underground on roots and crowns.
pests.cause_beginner: Beetles whose adults chew the leaf edges at night and whose grubs eat the roots underground.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Inspect on warm evenings and remove adults; beneficial nematodes can target soil-dwelling larvae. Remove and destroy heavily infested plants in fall.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Look for the beetles on warm evenings and remove them. Beneficial nematodes can attack the grubs in the soil. Pull badly infested plants in fall.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Rotate to a fresh site when starting a new bed, since larvae build up in older plantings, and start with clean stock.
pests.prevention_beginner: Start new beds in a fresh spot, since the grubs build up in old beds, and use clean plants.

pests.name: Birds
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Pecked and partly eaten ripe berries, often the first fully colored fruit taken just before you would pick it.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Ripe berries pecked or half-eaten, often the best red ones taken right before you pick them.
pests.cause_seasoned: Birds attracted to ripening red fruit.
pests.cause_beginner: Birds that go for the ripe red berries.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Drape bird netting over the bed as fruit colors, or use floating row cover, keeping it secured at the edges.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover the bed with bird netting or a light cloth as the berries turn red, tucking the edges down.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Net the planting before the first fruit ripens rather than after birds find it.
pests.prevention_beginner: Put netting on before the first berries ripen, not after the birds have already found them.

diseases.name: Gray mold (Botrytis fruit rot)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: A soft, tan rot of green and ripe fruit that quickly becomes a fuzzy gray mold, often starting where berries touch soil, mulch, or another berry. It spreads fast through a picked basket.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Berries turn soft and rot, then grow a gray fuzz. It often starts where a berry touches the ground or another berry, and spreads quickly.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Botrytis cinerea, which overwinters on dead leaves and thrives when it rains during bloom and fruit development.
diseases.cause_beginner: A mold that lives on old dead leaves and takes hold when it is wet while the plants are flowering and fruiting.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy infected berries the moment you see them. Keep an open, airy canopy, keep ripening fruit off wet soil, and clean out old leaves at renovation and in early spring.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick off and throw away any moldy berries right away. Keep the plants from getting crowded, keep berries off wet ground, and clear away old dead leaves.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Avoid spring nitrogen on June-bearers, which thickens the canopy and traps moisture. Water at the base rather than overhead, space plants for airflow, and pick fruit promptly and often.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Do not feed June-bearing plants in spring, since extra leaves trap dampness. Water at the soil, give plants room to breathe, and pick ripe berries often.

diseases.name: Anthracnose fruit rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark, sunken, circular lesions on fruit; the fungus can also infect crowns and runners, causing wilting and plant death in warm, wet spells.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Dark, sunken round spots on the berries. The disease can also rot the crown and runners, making plants wilt and die in warm, wet weather.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Colletotrichum fungi, favored by warm, humid, rainy conditions during fruit development and spread by splashing water.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that thrives in warm, wet, humid weather and splashes around in the rain.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy diseased fruit and plants promptly. Reduce splash by watering at the base and mulching, and improve airflow.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Pull off and throw away diseased berries and plants. Water at the soil instead of overhead, and give plants room.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Start with certified disease-free plants, avoid overhead watering, and do not plant into ground with a recent history of the disease.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Buy clean, certified plants, water at the base, and avoid spots where this disease has been a problem before.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Upward cupping and purpling of leaf edges with a white powdery film; in some cultivars infected fruit tastes bitter.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Leaf edges curl upward and turn purple, with a white dusty coating. In some varieties the berries taste bitter.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A fungus that, unlike most strawberry diseases, spreads in dry conditions with high humidity and moderate temperatures.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that spreads when the air is humid but the leaves are dry.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove badly affected leaves and improve airflow. Choose resistant cultivars where mildew is a recurring problem.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick off the worst leaves and give plants more room. Grow varieties known to resist mildew if it keeps coming back.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants well, avoid dense canopies, and select tolerant cultivars.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Give plants room, keep them from getting crowded, and choose mildew-resistant varieties.

diseases.name: Red stele (Phytophthora root rot)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Stunted, wilting plants that collapse in spring; roots are rotted and, when sliced lengthwise, show a reddish-brown core. Worst in heavy, wet, poorly drained soil.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Plants are stunted and wilt, then collapse in spring. If you cut a root open, the center is reddish-brown. It is worst in heavy, wet soil that drains poorly.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Soilborne Phytophthora fungi that thrive in cold, saturated soils and persist for years.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soil fungus that builds up in cold, soggy ground and stays in the soil for years.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once plants are infected; remove and destroy affected plants. Improve drainage with raised beds and choose resistant cultivars.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure once a plant has it, so pull and destroy sick plants. Build raised beds for better drainage and grow resistant varieties.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant only in well-drained soil or raised beds, start with certified plants, and choose red-stele-resistant cultivars on wet sites.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant in well-drained soil or raised beds, buy certified plants, and pick resistant varieties if your ground stays wet.

diseases.name: Verticillium wilt
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Outer leaves wilt, dry at the margins, and collapse while inner leaves may stay upright; plants are stunted and may die. Symptoms often appear as fruit load increases.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The outer leaves wilt, dry at the edges, and flop down while the middle leaves stay up. Plants are stunted and may die, often as the berries are forming.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The soilborne fungus Verticillium, which also infects tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes, and brambles and persists in soil for years.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soil fungus that also attacks tomatoes, peppers, potatoes, and other berries, and stays in the soil for years.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no rescue treatment; remove affected plants. Manage it through rotation and resistant cultivars rather than cure.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure, so remove sick plants. The real fix is where you plant and which variety you choose.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Do not plant strawberries after or near tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes, raspberries, or blackberries, and start with certified disease-free stock on a clean site.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Do not plant strawberries where you recently grew tomatoes, peppers, potatoes, or other berries, and start with certified clean plants.

watering.frequency_seasoned: About 1 to 1.5 inches of water per week through the growing season, adjusted for vigor, growth stage, soil, and weather. On sandy soil and in heat, water more often and more lightly. Newly set plants have undeveloped roots and stress easily, so irrigate several times a week until established.
watering.frequency_beginner: Give strawberries about 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week while they are growing. Water more often in hot weather or sandy soil, and keep new plants well watered since their roots are still small.
watering.amount_seasoned: Wet the soil to a depth of about 6 inches to 1 foot with each irrigation, enough that the shallow root zone does not fully dry between waterings, but never so much that water stands. Standing water harms strawberries even for a day or two.
watering.amount_beginner: Water enough to wet the soil about 6 inches to a foot deep, so the roots stay moist but never soggy. Strawberry roots are shallow and rot if they sit in water, so do not overdo it.
watering.method_seasoned: Drip irrigation is ideal: it keeps water off the foliage and fruit, which reduces gray mold and weeds. Run a single drip line per row with half-gallon emitters spaced about every 12 inches, or use a soaker hose while monitoring soil moisture.
watering.method_beginner: The best way to water strawberries is at the base, not over the leaves, because wet leaves and fruit lead to mold. A drip line or soaker hose along the row works well; if you water by hand, water the soil rather than the plants.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Wilting despite wet soil, yellowing lower leaves, and soft or collapsing crowns signal waterlogging and the root and crown rots that follow. Standing water and slow-draining ground are the usual causes.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If the soil is wet but the plants still wilt, the leaves yellow, or the crowns turn soft and mushy, you are watering too much or the ground drains poorly. Soggy soil rots strawberry roots.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Dull, wilting leaves in dry soil and small, soft berries point to drought stress. Because fruit is mostly water, under-watering during fruit development directly cuts size and yield.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Drooping, dull leaves with dry soil, and small berries, mean the plants need more water. Strawberries especially need water while the fruit is filling out, or the berries stay small.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Keep new plantings evenly moist; shallow, undeveloped roots stress quickly.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep new plants evenly watered so they do not dry out.

schedule_by_stage.frequency: as needed to keep soil evenly moist
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Even moisture during fruit sizing drives berry size and quality; keep fruit off wet soil.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Water evenly while berries are filling out, and keep the fruit off wet ground.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Irrigate right after renovation to push fresh leaf and runner growth.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Water right after you cut the plants back and feed them, to help them regrow.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Dormant beds need little water; avoid waterlogged soil over winter.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Dormant plants need almost no water; just do not let them sit in soggy soil.

watering.method_note_seasoned: Keep water off ripening fruit and foliage where possible. Overhead watering wets the canopy and raises gray mold pressure, so if you must use it, water early in the day so leaves and fruit dry quickly.
watering.method_note_beginner: Try to keep water off the berries and leaves. If you can only water from above, do it in the morning so everything dries out during the day and does not stay damp.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: On established beds, two periods matter most: from just after bloom through harvest, when fruit is sizing, and from late summer into early fall, when next year's flower buds form. Do not let plants stress for water in either window.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Two times are most important for watering: while the berries are forming and ripening, and again in late summer to early fall when the plant is setting up next year's crop. Keep the soil from drying out during both.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Not applicable. Strawberries are set as dormant bare-root crowns (or as potted plugs), not as tender indoor-raised seedlings, so there is no hardening-off step. Dormant crowns go straight into the ground in their planting window; potted plugs from a garden center are already acclimated and can be set out the same way.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: There is no hardening-off step for strawberries. You plant them either as dormant bare-root crowns, which look like a clump of roots with a small bud, or as small potted plants from a garden center. Neither one was raised soft indoors, so you can plant them straight out without the week of gradual exposure that tender seedlings need.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Planting depth is the make-or-break detail: position each crown with its midpoint at soil height, roots just beneath the surface and the growing tip exposed to light. Set too deep, the bud smothers and rots; set too shallow, the roots dry out. Spread the roots in the hole without bending them, firm the soil, and water in. Bare-root crowns are the cold-region norm in early spring; potted plugs are common for fall and warm-region planting. June-bearers fill a matted row from runners over the first season, so give them room.
start_method.notes_beginner: The most important thing is planting depth. A strawberry has a thick short stem called the crown. Set it so the middle of the crown sits right at soil height: roots just under the surface, the little growing bud sitting on top in the light. Plant it too deep and the bud rots; too shallow and the roots dry out. Spread the roots out without bending them, firm the soil down, and water. Bare-root crowns are usual in early spring; small potted plants are easy to set out in fall or in mild climates.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Use a potting mix that drains well so the plants never sit in soggy soil. An easy homemade version is two scoops of potting soil mixed with one scoop of perlite and one scoop of fine bark.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix a little slow-release fertilizer into the soil when you plant, and add fresh mix and fertilizer each spring if you keep the plants past the first year.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: Fast drainage is essential, because strawberry crowns rot in standing moisture. A blend that works is two parts potting or garden soil to one part perlite and one part fine bark: enough to hold some moisture while still shedding excess water quickly.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend a slow-release fertilizer into the mix at planting, and refresh the top inch of mix and feed each spring for plants kept more than one season.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Strawberries in pots dry out fast, so check every day in warm weather and water when the top of the soil feels dry. Empty the saucer after watering so the roots are not sitting in water.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Because watering washes food out of the pot, give container strawberries a small amount of fertilizer often instead of one large feeding. A weak liquid feed added when you water is easy.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Roots in a pot get much colder in winter than roots in the ground. In cold areas, move your strawberry pots into an unheated garage or shed for the winter, or bury the pot up to its rim in the garden and cover it with mulch. Set them back out when they start growing in spring.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: A potted root ball freezes harder than the same plant in the ground, so in cold-winter regions move pots into an unheated garage, shed, or against a sheltered wall for winter, or sink the pot to its rim in a garden bed and mulch over it. Bring containers back out as growth resumes in spring.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Strawberries do great in pots, and the day-neutral kind is the best choice because it gives berries all season and does not spread much. Pick a pot at least 10 inches deep and a foot or more wide; up to four plants fit in a 12-inch pot. Snip off any runners the plants send out, since they cannot take root in a pot and just weaken the main plant. The little strawberry jars with side pockets usually only work for one year.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Strawberries grow well in containers, and day-neutral cultivars are the best fit because they fruit all season and throw few runners. Choose a pot no less than 10 inches deep and at least a foot across; a 12-inch pot holds up to four plants. Remove any runners that form, since daughter plants cannot root over the pot edge and only drain the mother. The small pocketed strawberry jars sold at garden centers usually last just one season.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Pots dry far faster than ground beds, especially in summer heat, so check daily and water whenever the top inch is dry. Do not let a pot sit in a full saucer, which keeps the lower roots waterlogged and invites crown rot.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Frequent watering flushes nutrients out of a pot quickly, so feed lightly and often through the growing season rather than in one big dose. A diluted soluble fertilizer applied with watering works well.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering containers are risky for strawberries. The constant-moisture reservoir keeps the lower root zone and crown wet, which is exactly the condition that drives crown and root rot. If you use one, run it on the dry side and make sure the mix drains freely.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: Self-watering pots are not a good match for strawberries. They keep the soil wet all the time, and wet soil rots strawberry roots and crowns. If you already have one, keep it on the drier side and use a mix that drains well.

recommended.name: Honeoye
recommended.recommended_note: A hardy, productive early June-bearer that does well in cold-winter matted rows. Bright, firm, slightly tart fruit.

recommended.name: Earliglow
recommended.recommended_note: The flavor standard among early June-bearers. Small to medium deep-red berries; modest yield but excellent taste.

recommended.name: Jewel
recommended.recommended_note: Large, glossy, firm berries on a vigorous plant. Productive, though prone to red stele and verticillium on poorly drained sites.

recommended.name: Allstar
recommended.recommended_note: Very large, light-colored, sweet berries with a long mid- to late-season harvest. A reliable, disease-tolerant garden choice.

recommended.name: Albion
recommended.recommended_note: A day-neutral that fruits the first season and bears steadily into fall. Large, conical, firm, sweet-tart berries; excellent in raised beds and containers.

recommended.name: Seascape
recommended.recommended_note: A widely adapted day-neutral with large, good-quality fruit across the season. Forgiving and well suited to containers.

recommended.name: Tristar
recommended.recommended_note: A disease-resistant day-neutral, sweet and dependable. A long-standing home-garden standard for season-long picking.

recommended.name: Ozark Beauty
recommended.recommended_note: A classic everbearer giving two lighter crops, one in early summer and one in late summer. Good flavor; less total yield than a day-neutral.

recommended.name: Quinault
recommended.recommended_note: A soft, sweet everbearer that produces some fruit its first year. Tender berries best eaten fresh; can be grown without winter cover in milder areas.

varieties.note_seasoned: Choose by type first, then by season and local adaptation. Match cold hardiness to your winters and pick a fruiting pattern that fits how you want to harvest: one big flush from a June-bearer for preserving, or a steady trickle from a day-neutral for fresh eating. Within a type, cultivars differ in flavor, size, firmness, and disease tolerance, so trying two or three is the fastest way to find what thrives at your site. Always start from certified disease-free stock rather than runners off an old patch.
varieties.note_beginner: Pick the type that matches how you want to eat your berries first: a June-bearer if you want a big batch all at once for jam or freezing, a day-neutral if you want a few fresh berries at a time over a long season. After that, choose a variety known to grow well in your area, and feel free to plant two or three to see which you like best. Buy fresh plants labeled disease-free rather than digging up runners from an old bed.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Strawberries are highly perishable and do not ripen further after picking, so hold them at room temperature only if eating within a day. For anything longer, refrigerate promptly; cool freshly picked fruit as soon as possible after harvest.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Strawberries do not get sweeter after picking and spoil fast, so only leave them out if you will eat them that day. Otherwise, get them into the fridge soon after picking.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerate unwashed in the crisper drawer, kept in a closed clamshell or a partially open plastic bag to hold humidity near 90 to 95 percent. Do not wash until just before use, since surface moisture speeds spoilage. Under good conditions berries keep up to about a week, depending on ripeness at picking.
storage.fridge_beginner: Put the berries in the fridge unwashed, in their container or a loosely closed bag, and wash them only right before you eat them. Washing too early makes them mushy. Stored this way they last up to about a week, depending on how ripe they were.
storage.freezer_seasoned: For long-term storage, hull the berries, spread them on a tray to flash-freeze, then transfer to airtight containers or bags. Held at 0 °F they keep good quality for up to about a year.
storage.freezer_beginner: To keep strawberries for months, remove the green tops, freeze them spread out on a tray first so they do not clump, then pack them into airtight bags. In the freezer they keep for up to about a year.
storage.notes_seasoned: Sort before storing and discard any bruised or molding fruit, since gray mold spreads quickly from one berry to the next. Pick and store fruit with the cap on for the longest shelf life.
storage.notes_beginner: Before storing, pick out and toss any soft or moldy berries, because mold jumps quickly from one to another. Berries keep best with their green caps left on.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Do not plant strawberries after tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes, raspberries, or blackberries. All host Verticillium wilt, a soilborne fungus that infects strawberries and persists in soil for years; a strawberry bed following them is at real risk. Avoid replanting strawberries into ground where strawberries recently grew, too, since soilborne pests and viruses build up.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Do not plant strawberries in a spot where you recently grew tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes, raspberries, or blackberries. Those crops can leave behind a soil disease (Verticillium wilt) that also harms strawberries and stays in the soil for years. It is also best not to replant strawberries right where old strawberries were.
rotation.good_after: legumes, leafy greens, alliums, or a cover crop
rotation.note_seasoned: Strawberries are a multi-year planting, so the rotation decision is mostly made once, at bed establishment: choose ground that has not grown a Verticillium host recently, and plan to move the next bed to fresh ground when this one declines after three to four fruiting seasons. Starting the replacement bed in a new spot during the old bed's last productive year keeps production continuous and breaks the soilborne pest cycle.
rotation.note_beginner: Because a strawberry bed lasts a few years, the main thing is choosing a good spot at the start: somewhere that has not grown tomatoes, peppers, potatoes, or berries lately. When the bed slows down after three or four years, start a fresh one in a different part of the garden rather than replanting the same ground.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Set dormant bare-root crowns or potted plugs in the planting window, crown midpoint level with the soil surface. In matted rows, space plants about 15 inches apart in rows 3 to 4 feet apart.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Plant your strawberry crowns or small potted plants, setting each so the middle of the crown sits right at soil height. In a wide row, leave about 15 inches between plants.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Newly set plants with the growing tip exposed and roots just below the surface; no top growth yet on bare-root crowns.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A small bud at the top of each crown sitting in the light, with roots tucked just under the soil.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Firm the soil around the roots and water in to settle it. Check that the crown is still at the right depth after watering and adjust if it has sunk or heaved.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Press the soil down around the roots and water. Make sure the little bud on top is not buried and the roots are not poking out.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Planted: variety, type, and number of crowns set, with the date.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Wrote down what you planted and when.

growth_stages.name: Establishment
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: The first season after planting. June-bearing plants pour energy into roots, crown, and runners rather than fruit; all flowers are pinned off to build a strong matted row for year two.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: The first growing season. The plants are building roots and spreading, not making a real crop yet.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New leaves unfurling from the crown and the first flower stems emerging. On June-bearers these flowers are removed, not kept.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Fresh leaves growing and small flower stalks appearing. On June-bearing plants you pick these flowers off.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pinch off every flower on June-bearers through the first season so the plant invests in establishment. On day-neutral and everbearing plants, remove flowers only for the first four to six weeks, then allow fruiting. Keep the bed evenly watered and weed-free; strawberries have shallow roots and lose out to weeds quickly.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: On June-bearing plants, pinch off all the flowers the first year so the plant grows strong. On day-neutral or everbearing plants, only pick off flowers for the first month or so. Water often and pull weeds. The roots are shallow, so weeds crowd them out fast.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Establishment: leaf-out date and, for June-bearers, that flowers are being pinched.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Noted that leaves are growing and, for June-bearers, that you are picking off flowers.

growth_stages.name: Runner and daughter-plant growth
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: June-bearers send out runners (stolons) bearing daughter plants from early summer. Early runners (rooted before September) are the productive ones; sweep strays back into the row so they root in the bed, not the aisle.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Through summer the plants send out long stems called runners, with baby plants on the ends. These fill in your row.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Above-ground stems arching out from the mother plant with small plantlets that root where they touch soil.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Long stems creeping out sideways with little new plants on them that take root when they reach the ground.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Guide early runners into the row to build the matted bed. In containers or a hill system, remove runners instead, since daughter plants cannot root over a pot edge and only drain the mother. Direct early runners into the row before they root in the aisle; remove late runners that will not fruit next year.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Let the runners root in your row to fill it in. If you are growing in a pot, snip the runners off, because they cannot root in a pot and just weaken the plant. Tuck the runners into your row so they root there, not in the path.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Runners: that daughter plants are rooting in the row (or being removed in containers).
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Noted that runners are filling in the row, or that you removed them from a pot.

growth_stages.name: Bloom
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: On an established bed (year two and later), June-bearing plants flower in mid-spring near the last-frost date. Open blossoms are frost-sensitive, so a late frost during bloom can cut the crop.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: In the second year and after, the plants flower in mid-spring. These open flowers can be killed by a late frost.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: White five-petaled flowers opening across the bed, with yellow centers that become the fruit.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: White flowers with yellow centers opening up. Each one can turn into a berry.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Watch the forecast during bloom. Cover open flowers with row cover in the late afternoon when frost is predicted and remove it the next morning once the danger has passed. If row cover is over the bed, pull it back as bloom opens so bees can reach the flowers and set well-shaped fruit.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep an eye on the weather while the plants flower. If frost is coming, cover the flowers in the evening with a light cloth and take it off in the morning. If you covered the plants, open them up while they flower so bees can get to them.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Bloom: first-flower date and any frost protection used.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Noted when flowers opened and whether you covered them for frost.

growth_stages.name: Green fruit and ripening
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Pollinated flowers form green fruit that swells and colors over roughly four weeks. Fruit is mostly water, so steady moisture through this period drives size and quality.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: After the flowers are pollinated, small green berries form and slowly ripen over about four weeks. The berries need steady water now.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Green berries enlarging and beginning to blush red. Well-pollinated fruit is plump and even; poorly pollinated fruit is grooved or pinched.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Green berries getting bigger and starting to turn red. Good berries are plump and even; lumpy ones did not get pollinated well.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture steady and even, about 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week, and keep ripening fruit off wet soil to limit gray mold. Maintain even watering and watch for the first blush of color to time your first picking.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Water evenly, about 1 to 1.5 inches a week. Try to keep the ripening berries off wet ground so they do not rot. Keep watering and watch for the first berries to turn red.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Fruit set: that green fruit has formed and is beginning to color.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Noted that green berries formed and are starting to ripen.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: June-bearing strawberries ripen about four weeks after flowering, giving one concentrated flush over roughly four weeks. Pick every one to three days; fruit is sweetest fully red and ripened on the plant.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: About four weeks after flowering, the berries ripen all at once over roughly four weeks. Pick every couple of days, and let them turn fully red for the best flavor.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fully red, fragrant berries that pull free easily. Color deepens after picking, so fruit picked at 75 percent red stores a little longer.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Bright red, sweet-smelling berries that come off easily. If you need them to last longer, pick when they are about three-quarters red.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest in the cool of the morning and refrigerate promptly. If a long rain is forecast, pick fruit that is 75 percent to fully red, since rain dilutes flavor and invites rot. Pick ripe fruit every one to three days, checking more often in warm weather; remove any rotting berries to protect the rest.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pick in the morning when it is cool and get the berries into the fridge soon. If a lot of rain is coming, pick the riper berries first so they do not rot. Pick ripe berries every day or two, more often when it is hot. Toss any moldy ones so they do not spread.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Harvest: first-pick date and a rough running weight if you want to track yield.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Noted when you started picking and how the harvest is going.

growth_stages.name: Renovation
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: June-bearing matted rows only. Within one to two weeks of the last picking, mow leaves to about 2 inches above the crowns, rake debris, narrow the row to 10 to 12 inches, then fertilize and irrigate to push fresh growth. Day-neutral and everbearing plants are not renovated.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: For June-bearing wide rows only. A week or two after the last berries, mow the old leaves to about 2 inches above the crowns, rake them away, narrow the row, then feed and water. Leave day-neutral and everbearing plants alone.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tired, spotted foliage after the four-week harvest. After renovation the crowns regrow fresh leaves and new runners within a few weeks.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Worn-out leaves after harvest. Once you cut them back, the plants grow fresh leaves again in a few weeks.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Mow without cutting into the crowns, remove the clippings to reduce next spring's fruit rot, narrow the matted row, and fertilize at the renovation rate to drive flower-bud development for next year. Renovate within one to two weeks of the final harvest; fertilize and water right after to encourage regrowth.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Cut the leaves but not the crowns, rake the cut leaves away, narrow the row, and feed the plants so they set up next year's crop. Renovate a week or two after the last berries, then feed and water.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Renovation: the date you mowed and renovated the bed.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Noted the day you cut back and tidied the bed.

growth_stages.name: Dormancy and winter
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: In cold regions the bed goes dormant in late fall. Crowns are injured between about 10 and 20 °F at the crown, so a 2 to 3 inch loose straw mulch is applied after the first hard freeze and raked off in early spring. In wet-winter regions, straw over the crowns invites rot and is skipped.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: In cold areas the plants go dormant for winter. Cover them with 2 to 3 inches of loose straw after the first hard freeze to protect the crowns, then rake it off in early spring. In mild, rainy areas, skip the straw because it makes the crowns rot.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Plants stop growing and leaves die back where winters are cold. In mild regions the plants may hold some green leaves through winter.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plants stop growing and the leaves die back in cold places. In mild places they may stay a little green.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Apply straw after plants harden off and the first hard freeze arrives, not earlier, which would smother the crowns. Remove it as growth resumes in spring. Move containers to an unheated garage or sink them to the rim and mulch. Mulch cold-region beds for winter and plan to remove it promptly in spring; protect container roots, which freeze harder than in-ground beds.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Put straw on after the first hard freeze, not before, or it will smother the plants. Take it off when growth starts in spring. Move pots into an unheated garage or bury them to the rim and cover with mulch. Cover the bed with straw for winter in cold areas and uncover it in spring. Protect pots, since roots in pots get colder than roots in the ground.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Dormancy: the date you mulched for winter (cold regions).
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Noted when you covered the plants for winter.

notifications.body_seasoned: Your strawberry planting window is open. Set dormant bare-root crowns or potted plugs with the crown midpoint level with the soil surface.
notifications.body_beginner: It is time to plant your strawberries. Set each plant so the middle of the crown sits right at soil height.

notifications.title_beginner: Pick off the flowers this year
notifications.body_seasoned: On June-bearing plants, pinch off flowers through the first season so the plant builds roots, crown, and runners for a full year-two crop.
notifications.body_beginner: On June-bearing plants, pick off the flowers this first year so the plant grows strong and gives a big crop next year.

notifications.title_beginner: Frost coming while plants are flowering
notifications.body_seasoned: Frost is forecast during bloom. Open blossoms are injured at about 30 °F. Cover the bed with row cover in the late afternoon and remove it in the morning once the danger passes.
notifications.body_beginner: Frost is coming while your strawberries are flowering. Cover the plants with a light cloth in the evening and take it off in the morning.

notifications.title_beginner: Your strawberries are ready to pick
notifications.body_seasoned: Fruit is ripening. Pick fully red berries every one to three days, more often in warm weather, and refrigerate promptly.
notifications.body_beginner: Your strawberries are starting to ripen. Pick the fully red ones every day or two and get them into the fridge.

notifications.title_beginner: Time to cut back your June-bearing bed
notifications.body_seasoned: Within one to two weeks of your last picking, mow the old leaves to about 2 inches above the crowns, narrow the row, then fertilize and water to set next year's crop.
notifications.body_beginner: A week or two after your last berries, mow the old leaves to about 2 inches above the crowns, narrow the row, then feed and water the plants.

notifications.title_beginner: Cover the plants for winter (cold areas)
notifications.body_seasoned: In cold regions, after the first hard freeze, cover the bed with 2 to 3 inches of loose straw to protect the crowns. Skip this in wet-winter regions, where straw causes crown rot.
notifications.body_beginner: In cold areas, after the first hard freeze, cover the plants with 2 to 3 inches of loose straw to protect them. Skip this if your winters are mild and rainy.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost while flowering
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A frost is forecast while plants are in bloom. Open flowers are injured at about 30 °F and closed flowers at about 28 °F. Apply row cover in the late afternoon and remove it after the morning thaw.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Frost is coming while your plants are flowering. Cover them with a light cloth in the late afternoon and uncover them once it warms up in the morning.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot weather pauses the berries
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Sustained temperatures of 90 °F or higher pause flower formation on day-neutral plants until it cools. Keep soil evenly moist and consider afternoon shade in extreme heat.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: When it stays 90 °F or hotter, day-neutral plants stop setting new flowers until it cools down. Keep the soil evenly watered and give some afternoon shade in extreme heat.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Rain coming while berries ripen
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: An extended rain is forecast during ripening. Rain dilutes flavor and promotes gray mold, so pick fruit that is 75 percent to fully red before it arrives.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: A lot of rain is coming while your berries ripen. Rain makes them watery and moldy, so pick the riper berries before it hits.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hard freeze coming (cold areas)
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A hard freeze is forecast. Strawberry crowns are injured between about 10 and 20 °F. In cold regions, ensure winter straw mulch is in place; protect or relocate containers, whose roots freeze harder than in-ground beds.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: A hard freeze is coming. In cold areas, make sure your straw winter cover is on. Move or protect pots, since roots in pots get colder than roots in the ground.

plant.text_seasoned: Set each crown so the midpoint sits right at the soil line: roots fully buried, the growing tip fully exposed. Plant too deep and the crown rots, too shallow and the roots dry out, and this one detail decides whether a bare-root plant takes.
plant.text_beginner: Plant so the crown, the spot where leaves meet roots, sits level with the soil. Bury the roots but leave that crown on top. Too deep rots it, too shallow dries it out.

plant.text_seasoned: Soak bare-root crowns and keep them shaded and damp until they are in the ground, planting on a cool or overcast day if you can. Exposed strawberry roots dry out fast, and a crown that desiccates before planting often never establishes.
plant.text_beginner: Keep bare-root plants damp and in the shade until you plant them, and plant on a cool or cloudy day if possible. Dried-out roots may not survive.

establishment.text_seasoned: On a matted-row or June-bearing planting, pinch off all the first-year flowers. Letting a new plant fruit in year one starves root and runner growth, and removing those blossoms is what builds the crown that carries a full crop the next season.
establishment.text_beginner: In the first year, pick off the flowers on June-bearing plants. Letting them fruit too early weakens the plant. Removing the blooms now gives you a much bigger crop next year.

establishment.text_seasoned: Keep new plantings consistently moist while they root in. Strawberries are shallow-rooted and dry out quickly, so even, frequent watering through establishment is what gets crowns anchored before they have to support runners or fruit.
establishment.text_beginner: Water new plants often so they stay moist while they take root. Strawberries have shallow roots and dry out fast.

runner.text_seasoned: Space the daughter plants as runners root in, keeping the strongest and removing the crowded extras to hold roughly the matted-row density your source recommends. A bed left to fill in solid yields small, hard-to-pick berries and traps the moisture that feeds fruit rot.
runner.text_beginner: As runners take root and make new little plants, keep the strongest and pull out crowded extras. A bed packed too tight gives small berries and more rot.

runner.text_seasoned: On day-neutral or everbearing types, remove early runners instead of letting them root. These types fruit on the mother plant through the season, so energy spent on runners is energy taken from the berries you actually want.
runner.text_beginner: If you have everbearing or day-neutral strawberries, snip off the runners. These kinds fruit on the main plant, so runners just steal energy from the berries.

bloom.text_seasoned: Cover blooming plants when a late frost threatens; open strawberry flowers are killed at right around freezing, and the giveaway is a blackened center in the flower the next morning. A row cover or even a sheet over the bed saves that first set.
bloom.text_beginner: Cover the plants if a late frost is coming while they are flowering. Open blooms are killed by frost, leaving a black center. A row cover or sheet protects them.

bloom.text_seasoned: Keep water steady and keep pollinators welcome through bloom. Each berry is built from many fertilized seeds on the flower, so poor pollination is what gives you small, lopsided, misshapen fruit even when the plant looks healthy.
bloom.text_beginner: Water evenly and let bees visit while the plants flower. Each strawberry forms from many pollinated seeds, so poor pollination makes small, lumpy berries.

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Tuck clean straw or mulch under the developing berries to keep fruit off bare soil. Berries resting on damp ground are where gray mold and rot start, and that simple barrier is where the name strawberry comes from.
fruit_set.text_beginner: Slip straw or mulch under the growing berries so they do not sit on bare dirt. Fruit touching wet soil rots, and the straw keeps it clean and dry.

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Water at the base and in the morning as fruit ripens, keeping the berries themselves dry. Wet fruit and wet foliage going into the night drive the gray mold that turns ripening berries fuzzy overnight.
fruit_set.text_beginner: Water the soil, not the berries, and do it in the morning so plants dry by night. Wet berries overnight grow gray mold.

harvest.text_seasoned: Pick fully red, ripe berries every two to three days, pinching the stem rather than tugging the fruit. Strawberries do not sweeten further once picked, so color-up on the plant is the whole game, and frequent picking keeps the plant setting and keeps mold from spreading off overripe fruit.
harvest.text_beginner: Pick the fully red berries every couple of days, snapping the stem instead of pulling. Strawberries do not get sweeter after picking, so let them ripen on the plant.

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest into a shallow container in the cool of the morning and chill the berries promptly; leave them unwashed until you eat them. Strawberries are fragile and short-lived, and warmth plus surface moisture is what collapses them within a day.
harvest.text_beginner: Pick in the cool morning into a shallow tray, then refrigerate soon. Wash only right before eating, since wet berries spoil fast.

renovation.text_seasoned: Renovate a June-bearing matted row right after the last harvest: mow the old foliage about an inch above the crowns, then narrow and thin the rows. The planting fruits on new growth, so clearing the tired leaves now is what drives a vigorous, productive bed next year.
renovation.text_beginner: After the last berries on June-bearing plants, mow the leaves to about an inch above the crowns and thin the rows. This refreshes the bed for next year.

renovation.text_seasoned: Feed and water right after renovating to push the regrowth that sets next year's flower buds. The new runners and leaves coming up now are forming the crowns you will harvest from, so do not let the bed coast through late summer.
renovation.text_beginner: Right after cutting back, feed and water the bed so it grows back strong. That late-summer regrowth is what makes next year's berries.

dormancy.text_seasoned: Mulch over the crowns with straw once plants have gone dormant and the ground starts to freeze, not before. The mulch guards against winter cold and the freeze-thaw heaving that lifts shallow crowns out of the soil, but applied too early it can smother plants still trying to grow.
dormancy.text_beginner: Once plants are dormant and the ground begins to freeze, cover the crowns with straw. It protects them from cold and from being pushed out of the soil by freezing and thawing. Do not mulch too early.

dormancy.text_seasoned: Pull the winter mulch back off the crowns in early spring as growth resumes, raking it into the paths to keep fruit clean later. Leaving it piled on the crowns once they want to grow slows green-up and traps dampness against the plant.
dormancy.text_beginner: In early spring, rake the winter straw off the crowns and into the paths. Leaving it on top slows new growth, and it still keeps berries clean later.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: About 1 to 2 pounds per plant, or roughly 7 to 15 pounds per 10-foot row, varying with cultivar and planting age.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Expect roughly 1 to 2 pounds of berries per plant, depending on the variety and how old the bed is.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Yield peaks the year after planting (year two). It is often similar or slightly lower in year three, and both berry size and total yield decline from years two to four.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: You will get the most berries the second year, the year after planting. After that the crop slowly tapers off in size and amount.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Expect little or no crop in the planting year. On June-bearers the flowers are pinned off the first season by design, so a missing first-year harvest is the plan working, not a failure.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Do not expect berries the first year. On June-bearing plants you pick the flowers off on purpose, so no first-year crop is exactly what should happen.
factors_seasoned: Cultivar and type: June-bearers concentrate yield in one flush; day-neutrals spread a similar or smaller total across the season.
Planting age: highest in year two, declining through year four as the bed ages.
Pollination: cold or wet bloom weather and few bees give small, grooved, or pinched berries.
Water during fruiting: fruit is mostly water, so moisture stress during sizing cuts yield and berry size directly.
Renovation and weed control on June-bearers: timely renovation and a weed-free, well-spaced row sustain yield across seasons.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No T1 extension or peer-reviewed source supports a lunar-phase planting preference for strawberries. Plant by soil readiness and frost timing, not the moon.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Lots of runners and leaves, but little or no fruit
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Big leafy plants and lots of runners, but hardly any berries
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Heavy leaf and runner growth at the expense of fruit usually means too much nitrogen, spring feeding on an established June-bearing bed, or, in year one, the normal result of pinching flowers to establish the plant.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Too much nitrogen, or feeding a June-bearing bed in spring, pushes leaves and runners instead of berries. In the first year, no fruit is normal because you pinch the flowers off on purpose.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Feed June-bearers only at renovation, not in spring, and keep total nitrogen modest. Remember that a fruitless first year on a June-bearing bed is the plan, with the real crop coming in year two.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Feed June-bearing plants only after harvest, not in spring, and do not overdo the fertilizer. And remember the first year is supposed to be fruitless, with the big crop the second year.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Small, lumpy, or pinched-tip berries
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Small, lumpy, or pinched berries
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Misshapen or grooved fruit comes from poor pollination during cold or wet bloom weather, or from tarnished plant bug feeding that pinches the berry tip (catfacing).
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Lumpy or pinched berries usually mean the flowers were not pollinated well in cold or wet weather, or a small bug fed on them and deformed the tip.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Protect bloom from frost, pull row covers back so bees can work the flowers, and control broadleaf weeds that host tarnished plant bug.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Cover flowers only when frost threatens and open them up for bees otherwise, and keep weeds down to reduce the bugs that deform the tips.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Berries rotting with gray fuzz
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Berries rotting with gray fuzz
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Soft fruit covered in gray fuzz is gray mold (Botrytis), driven by wet conditions, a dense canopy, fruit resting on wet soil, and rain during bloom and ripening.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Gray fuzzy rot on the berries is a mold that takes hold when things stay wet, the plants are crowded, or berries sit on damp ground.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Open up the canopy by skipping spring nitrogen on June-bearers, water at the base, keep fruit off wet soil, clean out old leaves, and pick ripe fruit promptly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Give the plants more air by not feeding June-bearers in spring, water at the soil, keep berries off wet ground, clear old leaves, and pick ripe berries quickly.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: No fruit at all in the first year
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: No berries the first year
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: On a June-bearing bed this is expected and correct: flowers are pinned off the first season so the plant builds roots, crown, and a matted row, with the first real crop in year two.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: On June-bearing plants this is normal. You pick the flowers off the first year so the plant gets strong, and the first real crop comes the second year.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Stay the course: pinch first-year flowers on June-bearers and let runners fill the row. For fruit the first year, grow a day-neutral type, which fruits in its planting season.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep pinching the flowers off June-bearing plants the first year and let the runners fill in. If you want berries the first year, grow a day-neutral type instead.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Plants dead or stunted after winter, with blackened crowns
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Plants dead or weak after winter, with dark mushy crowns
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Winter cold injury: strawberry crowns are damaged between about 10 and 20 °F at the crown, especially without snow cover or winter mulch in cold regions, or with a poorly cold-hardy cultivar.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Winter cold killed the crowns. This happens in cold areas when there is no snow or straw cover, or when the variety is not hardy enough for your winters.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: In cold regions, apply 2 to 3 inches of loose straw after the first hard freeze and remove it in early spring, and choose cultivars rated for your hardiness zone. Skip straw in wet-winter regions, where it causes crown rot instead.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: In cold places, cover the plants with 2 to 3 inches of straw after the first hard freeze and uncover them in spring, and pick a variety hardy for your area. In mild, rainy places, skip the straw, since it makes the crowns rot.

succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Strawberries are not a succession crop. A June-bearing bed is a perennial planting that runs on a yearly cycle of bloom, fruit, renovation, and dormancy; in hot-summer regions strawberries are grown as a single fall-planted annual that is pulled and replaced once a year. Neither model stacks staggered sowings within a season the way lettuce or beans do, so there is no succession interval to set.
