plant_out.label: establishment
plant_out.synthesis_note: Set dormant bare-root crowns about two weeks before the last spring frost, as soon as the soil can be worked. The plants are dormant, so there is no need to wait until frost danger has passed (USU). Plant so the middle of the crown sits level with the soil surface. In matted rows, space plants 18 to 24 inches apart in rows 3 to 4 feet apart (UMN, OSU EC1307).

bloom.label: establishment
bloom.synthesis_note: On an established bed, June-bearing plants begin flowering around mid-spring, near the last-frost date. UMN reports flowering begins about mid-May in southern Minnesota. Open blossoms are frost-sensitive, so a late frost during bloom can reduce the crop (OSU EC1307).

harvest_start.label: establishment
harvest_start.synthesis_note: June-bearing strawberries ripen about four weeks after flowering (UMN), giving one concentrated early-summer flush. This is the established-bed (year 2 and later) cycle; in the planting year all flowers are removed so no crop is taken (year_one_notes).

harvest_end.label: establishment
harvest_end.synthesis_note: The June-bearing flush runs roughly four weeks. After the last picking, renovate the matted row within about two weeks: mow the leaves two inches above the crowns, narrow the row, and fertilize (UMN, OSU EC1307).

northern_tier.plantings_provenance: Region-constant June-bearing matted-row establishment window, frost-relative. Dormant bare-root crowns are set early, around two weeks before the last spring frost, because they are dormant stock and can go in as soon as the soil can be worked. Window dates resolve per zone from zone_frost_data.json last_spring frost. Sourced to UMN, OSU EC1307, and USU home-garden guides.

3.grown_as_note_seasoned: Zone 3 grows strawberries as a perennial matted row, but it is the cold edge: crowns are damaged near 10 to 20°F at the crown, so without dependable snow cover apply two to three inches of straw mulch in late fall and rake it off as growth resumes in spring.
3.grown_as_note_beginner: In zone 3 your strawberry bed comes back each year, but winters are harsh, so cover the plants with a few inches of straw in late fall and pull it back when they start growing again in spring.
3.frost_risk_note_seasoned: A late spring frost can damage open blossoms (late May to mid-June here); cover the bed with row cover or straw on frosty nights during bloom to protect the crop.

4.grown_as_note_seasoned: Zone 4 is the reliable cold floor for perennial matted-row strawberries. Mulched June-bearing varieties such as Honeoye, Jewel, and Earliglow overwinter well here; apply straw mulch after several hard frosts in late fall and rake it off as growth resumes.
4.grown_as_note_beginner: Zone 4 is a great fit for a come-back-every-year strawberry bed. Pick winter-hardy June-bearing types, mulch with straw in late fall, and uncover the plants in spring.
4.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Open blossoms in mid-May to early June are frost-sensitive; cover the bed with row cover or straw on frosty nights during bloom to protect the crop.

5.grown_as_note_seasoned: Zone 5 grows strawberries as a dependable perennial matted row. A light straw mulch over winter protects the crowns and reduces frost heaving; rake it off as growth resumes in spring.
5.grown_as_note_beginner: Zone 5 is a comfortable fit for a strawberry bed that returns each year. A layer of straw over winter keeps the plants safe; pull it back in spring.
5.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Blossoms opening in late April to mid-May are frost-sensitive; cover the bed on frosty nights during bloom to protect the crop.

6.grown_as_note_seasoned: Zone 6 grows strawberries as a perennial matted row with a longer, milder season than the colder zones. Light winter mulch is still worthwhile to limit frost heaving and protect crowns in open winters.
6.grown_as_note_beginner: Zone 6 strawberries come back every year and enjoy a longer growing season. A thin layer of straw over winter still helps in cold snaps.
6.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Blossoms opening in mid-April to early May can be caught by a late frost; cover the bed on frosty nights during bloom to protect the crop.

7.grown_as_note_seasoned: Zone 7 grows strawberries as a perennial matted row with the earliest bloom and harvest in the northern tier. Winters are mild enough that heavy mulch is usually unnecessary, though a light cover helps in a hard freeze; summer heat is not yet severe enough to force an annual system here.
7.grown_as_note_beginner: Zone 7 strawberries return each year and ripen earliest in this group. Winters are mild, so you usually do not need heavy winter cover.
7.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Early bloom in late March to mid-April can still meet a late frost; cover the bed on frosty nights during bloom to protect the crop.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the north (zones 3 to 7), strawberries are a perennial: you plant them once and the same bed comes back and fruits for several years. Plant the small brown dormant crowns in early spring, as soon as you can dig the soil, even if frost is still possible. June-bearing kinds give one big batch of berries in late spring or early summer, about a month after they bloom, then grow runners that root into new plants and fill the row. After the berries finish, cut the leaves back and thin the plants to keep the bed healthy, and start a fresh bed every three or four years. In zone 3, cover plants with straw over winter for protection; berries are most reliable from zone 4 and warmer.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Across the northern tier (zones 3 to 7), strawberries are grown as a perennial matted-row bed, the dominant US backyard system. Set dormant bare-root crowns in early spring, about two weeks before the last frost, as soon as the soil can be worked. June-bearing types give one concentrated flush about four weeks after they flower in late spring to early summer, then send runners to fill the row. Renovate the bed within two weeks of the last harvest, mow tops two inches above the crowns, narrow the row, and fertilize, and replace the planting after three or four fruiting years. In zone 3, and in colder pockets of zone 4 without reliable snow cover, give plants extra winter protection; reliable fruiting starts at zone 4.

plant_out.label: establishment
plant_out.synthesis_note: Set bare-root or plug transplants in the fall, from early October through mid November, the LSU AgCenter window for the Gulf Coast (mid to late October is ideal in southeast Louisiana). Strawberries are grown here as a fall-planted annual: plants are set in fall, fruited through winter and spring, then removed in early summer because humid-summer disease pressure is extreme; fresh plants are set the following fall. Grow on raised rows with plastic mulch or a thick pine-straw layer for drainage and clean fruit. This is an absolute, month-resolved window driven by the cool fall-to-spring season, not anchored to a last spring frost.

bloom.label: establishment
bloom.synthesis_note: Short-day varieties initiate flowers during the short days and cool temperatures of fall and winter, and fruit appears in late winter and early spring when conditions favor good-quality berries. Open flowers are damaged below 32 degrees Fahrenheit even though the plants themselves are cold-hardy.

harvest_start.label: establishment
harvest_start.synthesis_note: Production can begin as early as late November when plug plants are used, with the harvest running through winter and building in spring. Louisiana berries appear as early as November, December, and January.

harvest_end.label: establishment
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Fruiting continues into spring and can run to the beginning of June; after June the plants stop fruiting and turn to vegetative growth, so the planting is removed in early summer and replaced the following fall (the nine-month strawberry season). The cell harvest window is scoped to this late-fall-to-spring span.

8.grown_as_note_seasoned: The Gulf Coast grows strawberries as a fall-planted annual, not a perennial bed. Set transplants from early October through mid November, fruit them from late fall into spring, then remove the planting in early summer because humid-summer disease pressure is severe, and replant fresh each fall. Grow on raised rows with plastic mulch or a thick pine-straw layer to keep the heavy rains drained and the fruit clean. Choose short-day varieties suited to the South.
8.grown_as_note_beginner: On the Gulf Coast, strawberries are a cool-season crop you grow over the winter and then replace, not a bed that lives for years. Plant in October or early November, pick from late fall into spring, then pull the plants out when summer arrives and start fresh next fall. Grow them on raised rows covered with plastic or pine straw so the rain drains and the berries stay clean.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Gulf Coast strawberry plants are hardy to about 17°F, but the flowers are damaged below 32°F. Whenever a freeze is forecast and there are open blossoms, cover the bed with a lightweight row-cover cloth and anchor the edges; remove or vent it once the freeze passes.

9.grown_as_note_seasoned: In the warmer Gulf Coast zone 9, strawberries are grown on the same fall-planted annual system: set transplants from early October through mid November, with production starting as early as late November from plugs and running through spring into early summer, then remove the planting before the humid summer and replant the next fall. Raised rows with plastic or pine-straw mulch handle the heavy rain and keep fruit clean.
9.grown_as_note_beginner: In the warmer Gulf Coast areas, strawberries are still a winter crop you grow and then replace. Plant in October or early November, start picking as early as late fall, keep going through spring, then pull the plants before the humid summer and replant next fall. Use raised rows with plastic or pine straw for drainage.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Zone 9 on the Gulf Coast sees occasional freezes; the plants are hardy to about 17°F but the open flowers are damaged below 32°F. Cover the bed with row-cover cloth when a freeze is forecast during bloom and anchor the edges.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: On the Gulf Coast, strawberries are a cool-season crop you grow over the winter and then replace, not a bed that lives for years. Plant transplants in October or early November on raised rows covered with plastic or pine straw so the heavy rain drains and the berries stay clean. You will pick berries from late fall through spring, into early summer. When summer arrives, pull the plants out, because the heat and humidity bring disease, and plant fresh ones the next fall. The plants handle cold well, but the flowers do not, so cover them when a freeze is coming. Feed them in winter and again in spring.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: On the Southeast and Gulf Coast (zones 8 and 9), strawberries are grown as a fall-planted annual, not a perennial bed. Set bare-root or plug transplants from early October through mid November (mid to late October is ideal in southeast Louisiana), on raised rows covered with plastic mulch or a thick layer of pine straw for drainage and clean fruit. Short-day varieties initiate flowers in the cool, short days of fall and winter; expect fruit from late fall (as early as late November from plugs) through winter and spring, running to about early June. After June the plants stop fruiting and the planting is removed, because humid-summer disease pressure is extreme; replant fresh each fall. The plants are cold-hardy to roughly 17°F, but open flowers are damaged below 32, so cover the bed with row-cover cloth on forecast freezes during bloom. Side-dress with nitrogen in January and again in mid-to-late spring, and rotate away from recent tomato, pepper, or eggplant beds.

plant_out.label: establishment
plant_out.synthesis_note: Set short-day (June-bearing) plants in the interior valley in August; this is the UC home-garden planting window for the San Joaquin Valley (UC IPM home-and-landscape strawberry guidance), corroborated by UC Cooperative Extension San Joaquin Valley production guidance, which plants in August. Winter planting is not used here. Space plants about 12 inches apart in two-row beds, keeping the crown at the soil surface. This is an absolute, month-resolved window driven by the summer to early-fall planting season, not anchored to the last spring frost.

bloom.label: establishment
bloom.synthesis_note: After the small fall crop, flowering for the main spring flush builds in late winter into early spring ahead of the May to June harvest peak. Open blossoms are frost-sensitive, so a hard or late freeze during bloom can reduce the crop.

harvest_start.label: establishment
harvest_start.synthesis_note: First harvest in the interior valley begins in mid-April; UC Cooperative Extension San Joaquin Valley production guidance gives a harvest window of mid-April through mid-June, with heaviest production in May and June (UC IPM). The cell harvest window is scoped to this main spring crop. A small first crop also comes the fall of the planting year from August-set short-day plants (UC IPM); that fall set is carried as optional prose, not a separate calendar block, and is normally removed to strengthen the spring crop.

harvest_end.label: establishment
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Harvest ends in mid-June; UC Cooperative Extension San Joaquin Valley production guidance states the crop is harvested through mid-June and is severely limited by hot weather, and its irrigation schedule runs three-day intervals through June until final harvest with no July fruiting line. Valley heat ends the crop in June; there is no meaningful July or August harvest for short-day plants here. After the spring crop the planting is carried for at most two to three years before replacement, since summer heat and soilborne pests drive decline (UC IPM).

8.grown_as_note_seasoned: The interior valley grows strawberries as a spring-cropping annual rather than a perennial bed, since summer heat and soilborne disease pressure cut productive life to one or two seasons. Short-day varieties planted in August do most of their fruiting the following spring, with harvest running from mid-April through mid-June and heaviest picking in May and June. Plants set in August may put out a small flush of blossoms the first fall, but removing those fall blossoms channels energy into crown development and produces a heavier spring crop. Replace the bed with fresh nursery stock every two to three years as heat and disease pressure accumulate. White mulch over the bed in summer keeps the soil cooler and reduces fruit burn once temperatures climb above 90°F.
8.grown_as_note_beginner: Here in the Central Valley, strawberries are planted as an annual, meaning you replace the bed every couple of years rather than keeping the same plants going, because summer heat and soil diseases shorten their productive life. You set plants out in August. The main thing to know: your big harvest comes the following spring, from about mid-April through mid-June, not in the fall. Short-day varieties (the most common type in nurseries here, bred to flower when days get shorter in fall) may set a few berries in October or November, but if you pinch off those early blossoms, removing the flower buds before they open, the plant puts that energy into its roots and crown instead, and you get a bigger spring harvest. It feels counterintuitive to remove fruit, but it is the standard UC advice for home growers in the valley.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Valley winters are mild but not frost-free, so a hard or late freeze in winter or early spring can damage open blossoms on the overwintering crop; cover the bed on freezing nights during bloom.

9.grown_as_note_seasoned: The interior valley grows strawberries as a spring-cropping annual rather than a perennial bed, since summer heat and soilborne disease pressure cut productive life to one or two seasons. Short-day varieties planted in August do most of their fruiting the following spring, with harvest running from mid-April through mid-June and heaviest picking in May and June. White mulch over the bed in summer keeps the soil cooler and reduces fruit burn once temperatures climb above 90°F.

You set plants out in August. The main thing to know: your big harvest comes the following spring, from about mid-April through mid-June, not in the fall. Short-day varieties (the most common type in nurseries here, bred to flower when days get shorter in fall) may set a few berries in October or November, but if you pinch off those early blossoms, removing the flower buds before they open, the plant puts that energy into its roots and crown instead, and you get a bigger spring harvest. It feels counterintuitive to remove fruit, but it is the standard UC advice for home growers in the valley.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Zone 9 valley winters rarely freeze hard, but an occasional cold snap during late-winter bloom can injure open blossoms; protect the bed on the rare freezing night.

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: Your summers are too hot for a strawberry bed that lasts for years, so treat strawberries as a yearly crop here. Plant in August. You may get a few berries that fall, but pinching those off gives a bigger harvest the next spring, from about mid-April through mid-June. Plan to start over with new plants every couple of years when the old ones slow down. A light-colored mulch over the soil in summer helps keep the roots cool.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: In the interior valley, summer heat is the limit, so strawberries are grown as a spring-cropping annual rather than a long-lived bed. Set short-day (June-bearing) plants in August. They may set a small crop the first fall, but pinching off those fall blossoms strengthens the main spring flush, which is harvested from mid-April through mid-June, with heaviest picking in May and June. Replace the planting with fresh nursery stock every two to three years, or sooner if vigor or fruit quality drops, since heat and soilborne pests build up over time. White mulch laid over the bed in summer keeps the soil cooler and reduces fruit burn once temperatures climb above 90°F.

In the hot interior valley strawberries are grown as a spring-cropping annual that is set in August, takes a small fall crop that is normally pinched off, then carries its main flush into the following spring, harvested mid-April through mid-June, before summer heat exhausts the planting; the cycle is driven by heat avoidance and the summer planting window, not by the last spring frost. Windows resolve from UC IPM home-and-landscape strawberry guidance and the UC Cooperative Extension San Joaquin Valley cost study (short-day cultivars, summer plantings in August; harvest mid-April through mid-June); winter planting is not used in the valley. resolved_from is null per cell. Sourced to UC IPM home-garden strawberry guidance. plant_out.label: establishment
plant_out.synthesis_note: Set transplants from mid August into fall, the UC window for the California coast; mid to late August is a good time in all coastal locations, and day-neutral types can also go in during the fall. Strawberries are grown on the mild coast as a fall-planted annual system: fruit production is highest in the first full season after planting and then declines, so the bed is replaced rather than carried for years. Space plants about 12 inches apart in two-row beds. This is an absolute, month-resolved window driven by the mild coastal season, not anchored to a last spring frost.

bloom.label: establishment
bloom.synthesis_note: Flowering builds from late winter into spring on the mild coast. Short-day types flower as the cool, short days of late winter give way to spring; day-neutral types flower across a longer span. The cool, foggy coastal climate suits berries well, with little heat stress on fruit set.

harvest_start.label: establishment
harvest_start.synthesis_note: Harvest begins in spring and builds toward the heaviest production in May and June (UC IPM: heaviest production for both short-day and day-neutral plantings is in May and June).

harvest_end.label: establishment
harvest_end.synthesis_note: On the mild coast, harvest of day-neutral plantings can extend through summer into fall, but the main flush ends by midsummer and production declines after the first full season, so beds are typically replaced. The cell harvest window is scoped to the main spring-to-early-summer flush.

9.grown_as_note_seasoned: The cool, foggy north and central coast grows strawberries as a fall-planted annual system rather than a long-lived perennial bed. Set short-day (June-bearing) transplants from mid August to early September, or in the fall, and day-neutral types from late September into November; production peaks the first full spring and then declines, so replace the bed rather than carrying it for years. The mild climate means little heat stress, and day-neutral varieties can fruit across much of the year here.
9.grown_as_note_beginner: On the cool, foggy coast, strawberries grow best when you plant them in late summer or fall and replace them rather than keeping the same bed for years. Plant transplants from about mid August into fall, and you will get the most berries the following spring. The mild weather is easy on the plants, and some types keep fruiting much of the year.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: The mild coast rarely sees a hard freeze, but an inland cold pocket or an early cold snap can nip open blossoms, which are damaged below 32°F. On a forecast frosty night during bloom, cover the bed with frost cloth.

10.grown_as_note_seasoned: The warmest north-coast pockets (zone 10) grow strawberries on the same fall-planted annual system: set transplants from mid August into fall, take the main crop the following spring, and replace the bed as production declines. Zone 10 here is essentially frost-free, so the season is bounded by the mild climate rather than cold, and day-neutral types can fruit across much of the year.
10.grown_as_note_beginner: In the mildest, nearly frost-free coastal spots, strawberries are still best planted in late summer or fall and replaced rather than kept for years. Plant from about mid August into fall for the biggest crop the next spring. With no real frost, some types keep producing much of the year.
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: These mild coastal zone 10 areas are essentially frost-free, so freeze injury to blossoms is rarely a concern; the season is shaped by the cool maritime climate rather than cold.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: On the cool, foggy California coast, strawberries grow best when you plant them in late summer or fall and replace them rather than keeping the same bed for years. Plant transplants from about mid August into fall, and you will pick the most berries the following spring, with the heaviest picking in May and June. The mild weather is easy on the plants, and some types keep fruiting much of the year. Grow them on raised beds so water drains away, and try to keep the leaves and flowers dry to avoid rot. Hard frost is rare here, but cover the flowers if a cold night is forecast inland.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: On California's cool, foggy north and central coast (zones 9 and 10, Monterey County north), strawberries are grown as a fall-planted annual system rather than a long-lived perennial bed. Set short-day (June-bearing) transplants from mid August to early September, or in the fall, and day-neutral types from late September into November; mid to late August is a good planting time in all coastal locations. Production is highest in the first full season after planting and declines after that, so replace the bed rather than carrying it for years. The cool maritime climate puts little heat stress on fruit set, the main flush builds to heaviest production in May and June, and day-neutral varieties can fruit across much of the year on the mild coast. Hard frost is rare, but protect open blossoms in any inland cold pocket. Grow on raised, well-drained beds and keep moisture off the flowers to limit fruit rot in the damp coastal air.

harvest_start.label: establishment
harvest_start.synthesis_note: Harvest begins in late winter to early spring as temperatures warm into the fruiting range. In the low desert the first berries typically ripen around March. The nearly frost-free zone 10 pockets can start a few weeks earlier than zone 9.

harvest_end.label: establishment

Set dormant, pre-chilled plants in fall, fruit them through winter and spring, then pull and discard the planting before the summer heat, which is too stressful to carry a bed over. Use well-drained beds and provide afternoon shade to reduce heat and water stress; strawberries are sensitive to salts in desert soil and water.
9.grown_as_note_beginner: In the California low desert, strawberries are a winter crop you grow and then replace, not a bed that comes back for years. plant_out.label: establishment
plant_out.synthesis_note: Set dormant bare-root crowns in early spring, after the danger of hard frost has passed and as soon as the soil can be worked. New Mexico State recommends spring planting because the cool weather gives the plants the best chance to establish. Plant so the middle of the crown is level with the soil surface. In a matted-row system, space plants about 18 inches apart in rows 36 to 42 inches apart and let runners fill the row to 12 to 18 inches wide; a plastic- or fabric-covered perennial bed is an alternative for day-neutral types.

bloom.label: establishment
bloom.synthesis_note: On an established bed, June-bearing plants flower in early spring from buds that formed the previous fall under short days. Those early blossoms produce the largest berries and are frost-sensitive, so frost protection during bloom is strongly recommended (NMSU).

harvest_start.label: establishment
harvest_start.synthesis_note: The single concentrated June-bearing harvest begins in late spring. In the planting year, flowers are pinched off so no crop is taken, which strengthens the plants for a full crop the following spring (year_one_notes).

harvest_end.label: establishment
harvest_end.synthesis_note: The spring flush finishes by early summer; matted-row beds are renovated immediately after harvest (mow old foliage above the crowns, narrow the row, weed, and fertilize), and should not be renovated after July 15. Beds remain productive for about three to four years before replanting (NMSU).

8.grown_as_note_seasoned: Interior arid New Mexico and similar high-desert zone 8 areas grow strawberries as a perennial matted row, planted in early spring after hard frost. June-bearers set flower buds the previous fall and crop once in late spring; renovate the bed right after harvest and expect three to four productive years. In the warmer, lower areas, afternoon shade (a fence, wall, or 65 percent shade cloth) reduces summer heat and water stress, and a winter straw mulch protects crowns. High-pH desert soils cause iron chlorosis, so choose tolerant cultivars and treat with iron chelate as needed.
8.grown_as_note_beginner: In the high desert of New Mexico (zone 8), a strawberry bed comes back each year. Plant dormant crowns in early spring once hard frost is past, and you will get one big crop in late spring. After picking, mow and tidy the bed so it stays healthy, and replant every three to four years. Shade the plants from harsh afternoon sun, mulch with straw over winter, and watch for yellowing leaves, which iron treatment fixes.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Late spring frosts are the main risk: open blossoms in April and May are frost-sensitive and the earliest blossoms produce the largest berries, so cover the bed with a frost blanket or straw on frosty nights during bloom. Siting the bed on a gentle slope so cold air drains away, or using a northern exposure to delay bloom, reduces frost loss.

Shade the plants from harsh afternoon sun, cover them with straw over winter, and protect the flowers on frosty spring nights. If the leaves turn yellow, an iron treatment usually fixes it.

Renovate the bed right after harvest (mow the old foliage above the crowns, narrow the row, weed, and fertilize) and expect about three to four productive years before replanting. In warmer, lower spots, afternoon shade reduces summer heat and water stress. High-pH desert soils cause iron chlorosis, so choose tolerant cultivars and apply an iron chelate when leaves yellow. Late spring frosts are the main threat to the crop, so protect open blossoms, and mulch crowns with straw over winter.

plant_out.label: establishment

Commercial Maui farms extend supply year-round only by moving harvest higher up the mountain in summer and lower in winter, which a home garden at one site cannot do.

11.grown_as_note_seasoned: In Hawaii (zone 11), strawberries are a cool-elevation niche crop, not a warm-lowland year-round one. They are grown upcountry, on the cool slopes of Haleakala (around Kula) and at Waimea on Hawaii Island, where conditions stay mild. At a fixed upcountry site, treat the bed as a short-lived perennial: set plants in the cool fall months for a main crop through winter and spring. Year-round supply exists in Hawaii only because commercial farms move harvest up and down the mountain with the seasons, which a single home garden cannot replicate. In the warm lowlands strawberries perform poorly.
11.grown_as_note_beginner: In Hawaii, strawberries grow best up in the cool higher country, like Kula on Maui, not down in the warm lowlands. Plant in the cool fall months and you will get berries through winter and spring. The big farms have berries all year because they move up and down the mountain with the seasons, but in a home garden at one spot you will get a cool-season crop, not year-round fruit.
11.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Upcountry Hawaii (zone 11) is frost-free, so freeze injury to blossoms is not a concern. The practical season is set by the mild upcountry temperatures and elevation rather than by cold; warm spells, not frost, end the crop at a given site.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In Hawaii, strawberries grow best up in the cool higher country, like Kula on Maui or Waimea on the Big Island, not down in the warm lowlands. Plant in the cool fall months and you will pick berries through winter and spring, roughly February through June. There is no frost to worry about up there. You may have heard Hawaii has strawberries year-round, but that is because big farms move up and down the mountain with the seasons. In your own garden at one spot, expect a cool-season crop, not fruit all year. Grow them where water drains away well.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: In Hawaii (zone 11), strawberries are a cool-elevation niche crop, not a warm-lowland year-round one. They are grown upcountry, on the cool slopes of Haleakala around Kula on Maui and at Waimea on Hawaii Island, where the climate stays mild; in the warm lowlands they perform poorly. At a fixed upcountry site, treat the planting as a short-lived perennial: set plants in the cool fall months for a main crop that builds through winter into spring, with the upcountry season running roughly February through June. Hawaii's day length barely changes across the year, so temperature and elevation, not day length, set the practical season at a given site. The year-round Hawaiian strawberry supply you see at markets comes from commercial farms shifting harvest up and down the mountain with the seasons, which a single home garden cannot replicate. Grow on well-drained beds; the zone is frost-free, so cold protection is not needed.

crops.description_seasoned: The garden strawberry is a low-growing herbaceous perennial with a short, compressed stem called the crown, from which leaves, flowers, and runners arise. It is grown in three types: June-bearing (one concentrated early-summer flush, the matted-row backbone of US backyard growing), day-neutral (fruiting through the season, compact, ideal for containers), and everbearing (two lighter flushes). Plants are self-fertile, set from dormant bare-root crowns or potted plugs, and a bed stays productive for about three to four fruiting seasons before it is replaced.
crops.description_beginner: Strawberries are low, leafy plants that come back year after year. There are three kinds: June-bearing, which gives one big batch of berries in early summer; day-neutral, which gives a few berries at a time all season and does great in pots; and everbearing, which gives two smaller batches. One plant makes fruit on its own, and a strawberry patch keeps producing for about three to four years before you start a fresh one.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Fruit is ready when it is fully red and fragrant and pulls free easily; flavor is best when berries ripen on the plant. Color deepens after picking, so fruit picked at about 75 percent red stores slightly longer. Pick every one to three days, more often in warm weather, and pick before forecast rain to protect flavor and limit rot.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: A strawberry is ready when it is bright red all over, smells sweet, and comes off the plant easily. Berries taste best left to ripen on the plant. Pick every day or two, more often when it is hot, and pick before heavy rain so the berries do not get watery or moldy.
crops.bloom_time_seasoned: On established beds, June-bearing plants flower in mid-spring, near the last-frost date, and fruit ripens about four weeks later. Day-neutral plants flower and fruit through the season whenever temperatures sit between about 40 and 90 °F. Open blossoms are frost-sensitive, so bloom timing and late frosts together set the crop.
crops.bloom_time_beginner: June-bearing strawberries flower in mid-spring, around the last frost, and the berries ripen about four weeks after that. Day-neutral plants flower on and off all season as long as it is not too cold or too hot. Open flowers can be killed by a late frost, so watch the weather while they bloom.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Strawberries grow across USDA zones 3 through 11, but how they are grown shifts with climate. In cold-winter regions they are a perennial matted-row bed that needs winter straw mulch, since crowns are injured between about 10 and 20 °F at the crown. In hot-summer regions, summer heat exhausts the planting, so strawberries are grown as a fall-set annual that is pulled and replaced each year. Choose cultivars matched to your winters; cold-hardy types and heat-adapted types are not interchangeable.
crops.hardiness_notes_beginner: Strawberries grow in most of the country, from cold zone 3 to warm zone 11, but the way you grow them changes with your climate. Where winters are cold, they live for years as a bed and need a straw cover in winter to protect the crowns. Where summers are hot, the heat wears the plants out, so people plant fresh ones each fall and pull them after one season. Pick a variety suited to your area.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Strawberries need only modest winter chill, and chilling is not a limiting factor for the home grower the way it is for tree fruit. It is informational here, not a hardiness gate. Cultivar cold-hardiness and summer heat, not chill accumulation, decide where and how strawberries are grown.
crops.chill_hours_note_beginner: Strawberries do not need a set amount of winter cold to fruit, unlike apples or peaches. You do not have to count chill hours for them. What matters instead is choosing a variety that suits your winters and summers.
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Strawberries are self-fertile, so a single cultivar fruits on its own with no pollinizer needed. Each flower still relies on bees, wind, and its own structure to set fully: a thoroughly pollinated flower produces the largest, best-shaped berry, while poor pollination from cold or wet bloom weather leaves small, grooved, or pinched fruit. If plants are under a row cover, pull it back as bloom opens so bees can reach the flowers.
crops.pollinator_notes_beginner: You only need one kind of strawberry to get fruit, because each plant pollinates itself. Bees still help a lot: a flower that gets plenty of bee visits makes a big, even berry, while one that does not can make a small or lumpy one. If you cover your plants to protect them from frost, take the cover off once the flowers open so bees can get in.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: For June-bearers, pinch off every flower the entire first season so the plant pours its energy into roots, crown, and runners instead of a small early crop; the payoff is a strong matted row and a full harvest in year two. Let the early runners root in the row to build the bed, and sweep stray runners back into the row before they root in the aisles. Day-neutral and everbearing plants are pinched only for the first four to six weeks after planting, then allowed to fruit the same season.
crops.year_one_notes_beginner: In the first year, June-bearing strawberries do best if you pinch off all their flowers as they appear. It feels wrong to remove flowers, but it lets the plant build strong roots and send out runners that fill the bed, so you get a big crop the next year instead of a few berries now. Let those runners take root to fill in the row. Day-neutral and everbearing plants only need their flowers pinched for the first month or so, and then you let them fruit.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Strawberries want a fertile, well-drained sandy loam or loam rich in organic matter. Because the roots are shallow and rot in waterlogged soil, plant into a raised bed or mounded row about 12 inches high on heavy or slow-draining ground. Work 1 to 2 inches of compost into the bed before planting and adjust pH to 5.6 to 6.5 a season ahead, since sulfur or lime take months to act. Avoid ground that recently grew tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes, raspberries, or blackberries, which leave Verticillium wilt in the soil.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Strawberries like loose, rich soil that drains well. Their roots are shallow and rot in soggy ground, so if your soil is heavy clay or puddles after rain, build a raised bed or mound about 12 inches tall and plant into that. Mix in an inch or two of compost before planting. Strawberries prefer slightly acidic soil, so test it the season before and adjust if needed. Do not plant where tomatoes, peppers, potatoes, or other berries grew recently, because they leave behind a soil disease that attacks strawberries.
crops.establishment_note: Strawberries are planted one year and reach full production the next. A June-bearing matted-row bed stays productive for about three to four fruiting seasons before yield and berry size decline and it is time to start a fresh bed in a new spot.
crops.renovation_seasoned: Renovation applies to June-bearing matted rows. Do it within a week or two of picking the final berries, while the plants still have time to regrow before fall. Mow or shear the old leaves to roughly 2 inches above the crowns without cutting into the crowns themselves, rake out the debris to cut next spring's fruit rot, narrow the row back to about 10 to 12 inches by tilling or hoeing the edges, then fertilize and water to push fresh leaf and runner growth. Leave day-neutral and everbearing plants alone, since they are still fruiting in late summer.
crops.renovation_beginner: Renovation is a once-a-year tidy-up for June-bearing strawberries, done a week or two after the last berries are picked. Mow or cut the old leaves down to about 2 inches above the crowns (the thick stems at soil level), being careful not to cut into the crowns. Rake away the cut leaves, narrow the row back to about a hand's width by removing plants from the edges, then feed and water so the plants put out fresh leaves before winter. Skip this for day-neutral and everbearing types, since they are still making fruit in late summer.
crops.type_selection_seasoned: Strawberries come in three types, and the choice shapes your whole season. June-bearing cultivars set flower buds in the short days of fall and deliver one concentrated crop over about four weeks in late spring or early summer; they throw the most runners, so they suit a matted row and give a large flush ideal for freezing and jam. Their first real crop comes the season after planting. Day-neutral cultivars flower regardless of day length whenever temperatures sit between about 40 and 90°F, so they fruit from late spring through fall, bear in their first season, and throw few runners, which makes them the pick for containers, raised beds, and a steady supply of fresh berries. Everbearing cultivars give two lighter crops, one in early summer and one in late summer, and are generally less productive than day-neutrals. This guide follows the June-bearing matted-row model because it is the backbone of US backyard strawberry growing; the day-neutral notes throughout tell you where the care diverges. In mild-winter coastal regions, day-neutral plantings can fruit across much of the year and are often grown as a fall-set annual rather than a long-lived bed, which is why the warm-region notes treat them differently from the cold-region matted row.
crops.type_selection_beginner: There are three kinds of strawberries, and picking the right one matters more than picking a fancy variety. June-bearing types give you one big harvest over about four weeks in late spring or early summer, perfect if you want a pile of berries at once for jam or the freezer. They spread by sending out runners that fill in a wide row, and they give their first real crop the year after you plant them. Day-neutral types fruit a little at a time from late spring all the way to fall, give berries the first year, and stay compact, so they are the best choice for pots and small raised beds. Everbearing types fall in between, with one crop in early summer and another in late summer. This guide is built around the June-bearing kind grown in a wide row, since that is how most home gardeners grow strawberries, and it points out along the way where day-neutrals are handled differently. In mild coastal areas with gentle winters, day-neutral plants can give berries through much of the year, and gardeners there often plant fresh ones each year instead of keeping a bed for years.

crops.name: Pumpkin

soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Pumpkins want deep, fertile, well-drained loam rich in organic matter, with steady moisture but no waterlogging. They are big plants with hungry roots and a long season, so work several inches of compost or rotted manure into the bed before planting. Most growers plant in low hills or mounds, which warm faster in spring, improve drainage, and give the sprawling vines a clear starting point. Sandy loams warm early and suit the earliest sowings, while heavy clay holds water and invites crown and fruit rot, so amend it generously or build raised mounds.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Plant pumpkins in rich, well-drained soil with plenty of compost mixed in. They are large, long-season plants, so give them a generous, fertile bed. Many gardeners plant them on low hills or mounds, which warm up faster and drain better. If your soil is heavy or stays wet, build up mounds or use raised beds so the roots and developing fruit do not sit in water.

ph.note_seasoned: Pumpkins do best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, around pH 6.0 to 6.8, with a sweet spot near 6.2 to 6.5. They still grow across a wider band, roughly 5.8 to 7.5, but uptake of some nutrients tightens as the soil turns alkaline. Test before planting and lime or add sulfur only on the test's advice rather than by guess.
ph.note_beginner: Pumpkins like soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, about pH 6.0 to 6.8, and most garden soil is already close. An inexpensive soil test tells you where you stand and whether you need to adjust it before planting.

fertilizer.frequency: At planting, then side-dress once or twice
fertilizer.type: balanced at planting, then nitrogen side-dress
fertilizer.timing: Work into the bed before planting, then side-dress about 3 to 4 weeks after planting and again at flowering
fertilizer.example_product: balanced 13-13-13 or 10-10-10 at planting, then a nitrogen source such as blood meal
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Pumpkins are moderately heavy feeders over a long season. Work a complete fertilizer such as 13-13-13 into the bed before planting, then side-dress with nitrogen about three to four weeks after planting as the vines begin to run, and again as flowering starts. Ease off heavy nitrogen once fruit has set, since late, lush vine growth comes at the expense of fruit and draws pests. Pair feeding with even moisture, because the nutrients only help a plant that is not also drought-stressed.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Pumpkins grow for a long time and need steady feeding. Mix a balanced fertilizer into the soil before planting, then feed with a little extra nitrogen about three to four weeks later as the vines start to run, and again when flowers appear. Once the pumpkins begin to form, go easy on the nitrogen, because too much makes leafy vines instead of fruit.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Your pumpkin vines are running, time to side-dress with nitrogen. Keep feeding moderate once fruit sets so the plant builds pumpkins, not just leaves.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Your pumpkin vines are spreading. Give them a feeding of nitrogen now.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A complete fertilizer such as 13-13-13 or 10-10-10 worked in at planting, then a nitrogen side-dress while vines run, easing off once fruit sets. Avoid pushing high nitrogen late, which gives vine at the expense of fruit.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer like 13-13-13 or 10-10-10 at planting, then a little nitrogen as the vines spread. Do not overdo the nitrogen once fruit forms.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A common rate is a complete fertilizer such as 13-13-13 worked into the bed before planting (roughly 20 pounds per 1,000 square feet, or a balanced scoop per hill), then a nitrogen side-dress about three to four weeks after planting placed a few inches out from the plants and watered in, repeated lightly at flowering.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Mix a balanced fertilizer or a few inches of compost into the soil before planting. Then feed with a nitrogen fertilizer about three to four weeks later, scratched into the soil a few inches away from the plants, and once more when flowers appear.

companions.note_seasoned: Most pumpkin companion pairings are traditional rather than trial-tested, and the ones worth acting on serve two practical ends: pollination and pest pressure. Because pumpkin fruit set is pollinator-limited, with each female flower needing many bee visits, flowering insectary plants like borage near the patch are a genuine help. The Three Sisters partners, corn and beans, give the sprawling vines structure and a nitrogen boost while sharing none of pumpkin's pests, and a trap planting of nasturtium can divert squash bugs and beetles. The firmest rule is a rotation one: keep pumpkins away from other cucurbits, which share the entire squash pest and disease complex.
companions.note_beginner: The most useful pumpkin companions are flowers that bring in bees, since pumpkins need lots of bee visits to set fruit, and the traditional Three Sisters partners, corn and beans. Nasturtiums can lure pests away. The one rule that really matters is to keep pumpkins away from other squash, cucumbers, and melons, which all share the same pests and diseases.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Corn
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Corn and pumpkin are the traditional Three Sisters pairing. The corn stands tall while the pumpkin vines spread along the ground, and the big pumpkin leaves shade out weeds. It is a time-tested combination more than a proven boost.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: The classic Three Sisters partner: tall corn gives sprawling pumpkin vines structure and light shade in high heat, while the broad pumpkin leaves shade the soil and suppress weeds beneath the corn. A long-standing intercropping tradition with a sound space-and-shade rationale, not a measured yield effect for this exact pair.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Three Sisters intercropping is a documented traditional system; the corn-pumpkin benefit is space-and-shade, not a trial-isolated pair effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Beans
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Beans are the third Three Sisters plant. They pull nitrogen from the air into the soil, which the hungry pumpkin appreciates, and they do not share pumpkin's pests. A good, traditional neighbor.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: The third of the Three Sisters: pole or bush beans fix nitrogen that benefits the heavy-feeding pumpkin, and they share none of the cucurbit pests. A traditional, mechanistically plausible pairing rather than a trial-isolated one.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Legume nitrogen fixation is a documented mechanism; the bean-pumpkin adjacency benefit is traditional, not pair-isolated.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Nasturtium
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Nasturtiums are often grown near squash and pumpkins to lure squash bugs and beetles away, and their flowers bring in bees, which pumpkins need to set fruit. A helpful, low-risk neighbor.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Often planted near cucurbits as a trap and deterrent for squash bugs and cucumber beetles, and its flowers also draw the bees pumpkins depend on for fruit set. Trap cropping is a documented principle, but the specific nasturtium-pumpkin effect is not formally isolated, so treat it as a plausible aid.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Trap-cropping for cucurbit beetles/bugs is documented in principle; the nasturtium-pumpkin pairing is not trial-isolated.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Borage
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Borage flowers are loved by bees, and pumpkins need lots of bee visits to set fruit, so a few borage plants nearby can help with pollination. Mainly grown to bring in bees.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A strong bee magnet whose flowers recruit the pollinators that pumpkin fruit set depends on, since each female flower needs many bee visits to size a fruit. Pollinator-habitat value is well grounded; the specific borage-pumpkin pairing is traditional rather than trial-tested.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Other cucurbits
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep pumpkins away from other squash, cucumbers, and melons. They all get the same pests and diseases, so planting them together makes those problems worse.
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Cucumber, melon, summer squash, and other winter squash share pumpkin's whole pest and disease complex, including squash bug, squash vine borer, cucumber beetle with the bacterial wilt it spreads, and powdery and downy mildew. Grouping them concentrates that pressure and lets soilborne problems build. A real epidemiology and rotation principle rather than a tested adjacency effect: spread cucurbits out and rotate them.

provenance.reason: Shared cucurbit pests/pathogens and squash-bug/vine-borer/cucumber-beetle vectoring are extension-documented; the bad-adjacency claim is a sound epidemiological principle, not pair-tested.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Potatoes
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Some gardeners keep potatoes and pumpkins apart, since both are big, hungry plants and potatoes can bring their own diseases. This is more tradition than a proven rule.
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional caution that potatoes and cucurbits compete heavily and that potatoes can harbor blight and attract pests near squash. There is no strong T1 mechanism for the specific pairing, so it persists mostly as garden lore.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: A folk anti-companion caution; competition is plausible but there is no T1 source isolating a potato-pumpkin antagonism.
