pests.name: Squash vine borer
pests.symptoms_seasoned: A previously vigorous vine wilts suddenly in mid to late summer, often near the base, and you find sawdust-like frass oozing from a hole low on the main stem. Cutting the stem open reveals a fat white caterpillar tunneling inside. Whole plants can collapse once the borer severs the stem's water flow.
pests.symptoms_beginner: A healthy pumpkin plant wilts all at once in summer, and you see sawdust-like specks coming out of a hole near the base of the stem. Inside the stem is a fat white grub.
pests.cause_seasoned: The larva of the squash vine borer moth, which lays eggs at the stem base in early summer. The hatching larvae bore into the main stem and feed inside for several weeks, cutting off the plant's water and collapsing the vine. There can be two generations in the South.
pests.cause_beginner: A moth lays eggs at the base of the stem in early summer, and the grubs that hatch tunnel inside and kill the vine from within.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Once a borer is inside, slit the stem lengthwise with a knife, remove the larva, and bury that node under moist soil to re-root. Bury vines at the joints as they run so a damaged plant can survive on secondary roots. Removing and destroying infested vines reduces next year's brood.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: If you catch it early, slit the stem with a knife, dig out the grub, and cover that spot with damp soil so it can re-root. Pull and destroy badly damaged vines.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Use floating row cover from planting until flowering to exclude the egg-laying moths, then remove it for pollination. Plant early or time a planting after the main flight, scout the stem base for frass from early summer, and grow more tolerant cucurbits where pressure is severe. Till in late winter and rotate to disrupt overwintering pupae.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover young plants with a light fabric row cover until they flower to keep the moths out, then take it off so bees can reach the flowers. Check the base of the stem for sawdust-like specks starting in early summer, and clean up old vines at the end of the season.

pests.name: Squash bug
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Leaves develop yellow specks that brown and wilt, and heavily fed vines wilt rapidly and turn brittle, a damage pattern sometimes called anasa wilt. Flat bronze egg clusters appear on leaf undersides along the veins, and gray-brown adults and pale nymphs cluster near the crown and under debris.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Leaves get yellow spots, then brown and wilt, and you find clusters of shield-shaped gray-brown bugs and their bronze eggs on the undersides of leaves near the base of the plant.
pests.cause_seasoned: The squash bug, a true bug that feeds with piercing-sucking mouthparts on cucurbit foliage and stems, injecting saliva that wilts and browns the vines. Populations build through the season and are hardest to control once nymphs are large; the bugs overwinter as adults in garden debris.
pests.cause_beginner: Squash bugs pierce the leaves and stems and suck out the juices, which makes the vines wilt. They breed through the summer and hide in plant debris over winter.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick adults, crush the egg masses on leaf undersides, and trap bugs by laying a board near the plants overnight, then lifting it in the morning and destroying the cluster underneath. Target young nymphs with insecticidal soap, since large nymphs and adults are tough to kill.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick the bugs off by hand and scrape off the egg clusters under the leaves. A board laid on the ground overnight draws them underneath, then lift it in the morning and destroy them. Treat the young bugs with insecticidal soap.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Use row cover on young plants until flowering, clean up vines and debris at season's end to cut overwintering sites, and rotate cucurbits. Scout leaf undersides for the bronze egg clusters from early in the season and act before nymphs mature.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover young plants until they flower, check under the leaves for eggs early in the season, and clean up old vines after harvest so the bugs have nowhere to overwinter.

pests.name: Cucumber beetles
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small yellow beetles, striped or spotted, chew young leaves, stems, and flowers, and can scar developing fruit. The bigger threat is indirect: striped and spotted cucumber beetles transmit bacterial wilt, so beetle feeding on seedlings can be followed weeks later by sudden, runaway vine wilt.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Small yellow beetles with stripes or spots chew on the leaves and flowers, especially of young plants. Worse, they can spread a disease called bacterial wilt that makes the vines collapse later.
pests.cause_seasoned: Striped and spotted cucumber beetles feed on cucurbits and carry the bacterium that causes bacterial wilt in their gut, infecting plants as they feed. Seedlings are most vulnerable; once pumpkin plants have four or more leaves they tolerate some feeding, and bacterial wilt is generally less severe in pumpkin and squash than in cucumber and melon.
pests.cause_beginner: Cucumber beetles feed on pumpkin plants and carry the germ that causes bacterial wilt, infecting the plant as they chew. Young seedlings are most at risk.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Protect seedlings with row cover removed at flowering, hand-pick beetles, and use yellow sticky traps to monitor and reduce numbers. Where bacterial wilt is a known problem, controlling the beetles is the most effective control of the disease, since there is no cure once a plant is infected.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover young plants with row cover (remove it when flowers open), pick the beetles off, and use yellow sticky traps. Keeping the beetles down is the best way to avoid the wilt disease they spread.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Exclude beetles from seedlings with row cover, keep young plants vigorous so they grow past the vulnerable stage, clear weeds and debris, and rotate away from where cucurbits grew. Aim control at the early-season colonizers that vector wilt.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover seedlings until they flower, keep them growing strong, clear away weeds and old plants, and do not plant where squash-family crops grew last year.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Colonies of small soft-bodied insects, often melon aphids, cluster on leaf undersides and growing tips, causing leaves to curl, pucker, and yellow, with sticky honeydew and sooty mold following. Beyond direct feeding, aphids transmit mosaic viruses that mottle and distort the foliage.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny soft insects gather on the undersides of leaves and on new growth, making leaves curl and turn yellow, often with a sticky film. They can also spread viruses.
pests.cause_seasoned: Melon and other aphids suck sap and reproduce rapidly in warm weather, building up quickly on stressed or over-fertilized plants. The honeydew they excrete fosters sooty mold, and several aphid species spread cucurbit mosaic viruses.
pests.cause_beginner: Aphids are small insects that suck the plant's juices and multiply fast, especially on soft, over-fed growth. The sticky honeydew they leave behind grows black mold.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong jet of water and spray insecticidal soap or horticultural oil with thorough coverage of leaf undersides, repeating every few days. Conserve lady beetles, lacewings, and parasitic wasps, which usually bring aphids under control.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water and treat the undersides of the leaves with insecticidal soap, repeating every few days. Ladybugs and other helpful insects eat aphids, so welcome them.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen, which drives the soft growth aphids favor, scout leaf undersides and growing tips, and support natural enemies rather than spraying broadly. Reflective mulch deters aphids from young plants.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen, check the undersides of leaves regularly, and let helpful insects do their work instead of spraying everything.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: White, powdery patches appear first on the upper and lower leaf surfaces and stems, spreading until leaves yellow, brown, and die back ahead of schedule. Early defoliation cuts the season short, reduces fruit size and sugars, and exposes pumpkins to sunscald.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: A white, powdery coating spreads over the leaves until they turn yellow and brown and die. The plant fades early, and the pumpkins may not size up well.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Powdery mildew fungi that thrive in warm conditions with high humidity but do not need leaf wetness, spreading by wind-blown spores. Crowded plantings, poor airflow, and shade worsen it, and it is one of the most common late-season pumpkin diseases.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that spreads on warm, humid days, especially where plants are crowded and air does not move well. It does not need wet leaves to take hold.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Treat at the first spots, before it spreads, with a labeled fungicide such as sulfur or a horticultural oil or biofungicide, covering both leaf surfaces, and remove the worst leaves. Avoid overhead watering. Once it is widespread, control is mostly damage limitation.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Treat early, at the first white spots, with a labeled fungicide like sulfur or horticultural oil, and remove badly affected leaves. Water the soil, not the leaves. Once it covers the plant it is hard to stop.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Choose resistant varieties, space plants generously for airflow, plant in full sun, and avoid excess nitrogen and overhead watering. Scout from midsummer and treat at the first sign, since prevention and early action beat rescue.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Pick resistant varieties, give plants plenty of room so air moves between them, plant in full sun, and water at the base. Start checking in midsummer and act at the first white spots.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Angular yellow blotches, bounded by the leaf veins, appear on the upper leaf surface, with a grayish or purplish fuzzy growth on the underside in humid weather. Spots brown and coalesce, and severe infection rapidly defoliates the vines.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Yellow patches show on top of the leaves with fuzzy gray growth underneath, mostly in damp, humid weather. The spots brown and spread until the leaves die.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A fungus-like water mold that spreads on wind-borne spores and needs leaf wetness and humidity to infect, so it flares in wet, humid spells and dewy conditions. It moves fast once established and is favored by crowding and prolonged leaf wetness.
diseases.cause_beginner: A mold-like disease that spreads in wet, humid weather and needs wet leaves to infect. It can move through a planting quickly.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Improve airflow, let foliage dry, remove badly affected leaves, and apply a labeled fungicide, covering leaf undersides, when conditions favor the disease. Avoid overhead irrigation, which keeps leaves wet and feeds the infection.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Open up the planting so leaves dry faster, remove the worst leaves, and use a labeled fungicide when wet weather sets in. Do not water over the leaves.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space for airflow, water at the soil line rather than overhead, choose resistant varieties where available, and avoid working among wet vines. Scout closely in humid weather, when the disease can appear and spread quickly.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Give plants room so air moves between them, water at the base, and watch closely in humid weather. Choose resistant varieties if downy mildew is common where you live.

diseases.name: Bacterial wilt
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Individual leaves, then whole vines, wilt and collapse even though the soil is moist, often spreading until the plant dies. A field test helps confirm it: cut a wilted stem and slowly draw the cut ends apart, and infected sap pulls into thin, sticky white strands.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Vines wilt and die even though the soil is wet. If you cut a wilted stem and pull the two ends apart slowly, infected sap stretches into sticky white strings.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A bacterium spread by striped and spotted cucumber beetles, which carry it in their gut and infect plants as they feed. It clogs the water-conducting tissue, so the plant wilts despite adequate water. Pumpkin and squash are generally less susceptible than cucumber and melon, but losses still occur.
diseases.cause_beginner: A germ spread by cucumber beetles as they feed. It blocks the plant's water pipes, so the vine wilts even when watered.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once a plant is infected; remove and destroy wilting plants to limit spread. Control is really beetle control, so management aims at keeping cucumber beetle numbers down, especially early in the season.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure once a plant has it, so pull and destroy infected plants. The real fix is keeping cucumber beetles down, since they spread it.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Manage cucumber beetles from seedling stage with row cover removed at flowering, keep young plants vigorous, and remove infected plants promptly. Controlling the beetle vector is the most effective control of the disease.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Keep cucumber beetles under control, since they spread the disease. Cover young plants until they flower, and pull any plant that wilts and tests positive.

diseases.name: Phytophthora blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Water-soaked, collapsing crowns and a soft, white-mold fruit rot, especially on fruit resting on wet soil, with vines wilting in low, poorly drained spots after heavy rain. It can rot fruit in the field and in storage and persists in the soil for years.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Pumpkins resting on wet ground develop a soft, white, moldy rot, and vines collapse in low, soggy spots after heavy rain. It can spread to fruit in storage.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A soilborne water mold (Phytophthora) that thrives in saturated soil and standing water, spreading by spores in splashing and running water. Wet, poorly drained ground and fruit in direct contact with soaked soil drive it; the pathogen survives in soil for years.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soilborne disease that loves wet, poorly drained ground and standing water. It spreads in splashing water and rots fruit that sits on wet soil.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no rescue for infected plants; remove and destroy them and affected fruit. Management is cultural: improve drainage, never let water stand, and harvest fruit promptly off wet ground.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure, so remove infected plants and rotted fruit. The main thing is to fix drainage and keep water from standing around the plants.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant on raised beds or hills for drainage, avoid low or poorly drained ground, do not overwater, rotate out of cucurbits and other hosts on a long cycle, and lift ripening fruit onto a board or mulch to keep it off wet soil.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant on raised hills so water drains away, avoid soggy spots, and do not overwater. Set ripening pumpkins on a board or thick mulch so they are not sitting on wet ground.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Aim for about 1 to 2 inches of water per week, more in heat or sandy soil, delivered deeply and less often rather than in light daily sprinkles. The long-season, big-leaved plant transpires heavily through summer.
watering.frequency_beginner: Give pumpkins about 1 to 2 inches of water a week, more when it is hot and dry. Water deeply rather than a little every day.
watering.amount_seasoned: Around 1 to 2 inches per week is the working range, leaning to the higher end during flowering and fruit sizing and through hot, dry spells. Even, deep watering builds well-formed fruit; let it swing dry and you get poor set and small, uneven pumpkins.
watering.amount_beginner: About 1 to 2 inches of water a week is a good target, more while the plant is flowering and the pumpkins are growing.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base of the plant with drip or a soaker hose, keeping the foliage as dry as possible, since wet leaves invite powdery and downy mildew on an already mildew-prone crop. Taper watering as the fruit nears maturity and the rind hardens, which helps the pumpkins cure and store, and keep ripening fruit off saturated soil.
watering.method_beginner: Water the soil, not the leaves, using a soaker hose or watering wand at the base. Keeping the leaves dry helps prevent mildew. As the pumpkins ripen and the skin hardens, ease off the water so they cure well.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting even when the soil is wet, and soft, rotting stems or fruit at the base point to overwatering or poor drainage. Saturated soil invites crown and Phytophthora fruit rot, especially on heavy ground.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If lower leaves yellow, the plant wilts even though the soil is wet, or fruit and stems go soft and rotten, it is getting too much water or the soil drains poorly.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Midday wilting that recovers overnight is normal in heat, but leaves that stay limp and dull signal real drought. Dry spells during fruit sizing show up as small, misshapen pumpkins and aborted young fruit.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Some midday wilting in hot weather is normal and passes by evening. Leaves that stay wilted mean the plant is too dry, and drought while fruit is forming gives small, misshapen pumpkins.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Base watering is the most useful habit for pumpkins, because the same plant that wants steady moisture is also highly mildew-prone. Keep water on the soil, air moving through the leaves, and the ripening fruit up off wet ground.
watering.method_note_beginner: Watering the soil instead of the leaves is the best thing you can do for pumpkins. It keeps them hydrated without encouraging leaf disease.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The water-critical stretch is flowering through fruit set and sizing. Steady moisture here drives well-formed pumpkins; uneven water gives poor set and small, lopsided fruit. Ease off near maturity to help the rind harden and the fruit cure.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The most important time to keep pumpkins watered is when they are flowering and the fruit is growing. Ease off near the end so the skin hardens for storage.

crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Harvest pumpkins once at full maturity, not young: wait for full, deep color for the variety, a hard rind a thumbnail cannot dent, and a dried, corky stem. Tapping a ripe pumpkin gives a hollow sound. Cut the fruit from the vine with shears or a knife, leaving a 3 to 4 inch handle of stem (never carry a pumpkin by the stem, since a broken stem invites rot). Get the crop in before a hard frost, which damages the rind and shortens storage. Then cure the pumpkins about 10 days in a warm, dry spot to toughen the skin before storing.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Unlike summer squash, you pick pumpkins once, when they are fully ripe. Look for full color all over, a hard rind you cannot dent with a thumbnail, and a dry, woody stem. Cut the pumpkin off the vine with a knife or shears, leaving a 3 to 4 inch piece of stem attached, but do not carry it by the stem. Bring them in before a hard frost. Then let them cure in a warm, dry place for about 10 days so the skin toughens for storage.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Harden off indoor-started pumpkins over 7 to 10 days, easing them into direct sun and wind before transplanting. Handle the rootball gently, because cucurbits resent root disturbance and a checked seedling sulks for weeks; use larger cells and set plants out young, before the roots circle the pot.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: If you started seedlings indoors, set them outside for a little longer each day over about a week so they get used to sun and wind. Be gentle with the roots when you plant, since pumpkins do not like having their roots disturbed.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Because cucurbits resent root disturbance, direct sowing once the soil is reliably warm (at least 65°F, ideally 70°F, at 2 inches) is the simplest, most reliable method, and direct-sown plants quickly catch up. Sow several seeds about 1 inch deep per hill and thin to the strongest. Start seeds indoors only to gain two to three weeks in a short season, sowing in large cells and setting plants out before they outgrow the pot. In the coldest zones, transplants and early-maturing varieties are what make a fall pumpkin possible.
start_method.notes_beginner: The easiest way to grow pumpkins is to sow seeds right where they will grow, once the soil is warm (about 70°F). Plant a few seeds 1 inch deep in each hill and keep the strongest. Start seeds indoors only if your season is short, about three weeks before planting out, and move them outside while they are still small. In cold areas, use transplants and a fast-maturing variety so the fruit ripens before frost.

thinning.when: when seedlings have one or two true leaves
thinning.tip_seasoned: Sow four to five seeds per hill and thin to the two or three strongest once they have a true leaf or two. Snip the extras off at soil line rather than pulling, so you do not disturb the roots of the keepers. In rows, thin to one plant every 24 to 36 inches for bush types and wider for the big vining kinds.
thinning.tip_beginner: Plant four or five seeds in each hill, then keep the two or three strongest seedlings once they grow their first real leaves. Cut the extra ones off at the ground instead of pulling them, so you do not hurt the roots of the ones you keep.

drainage.saucer_practice: If you use a saucer, empty it after watering. Pumpkins will not tolerate sitting in standing water, which invites crown and fruit rot.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Use a good bagged potting mix, not garden soil, which packs down too hard in a pot.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in compost and a slow-release fertilizer at planting. Pots need feeding more often than beds because watering washes nutrients out.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: Use a rich, free-draining peat- or coir-based potting mix, not garden soil, which compacts and drains poorly in a container.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend in about a third compost plus a slow-release balanced fertilizer at planting. Because frequent watering flushes nutrients, plan to feed a container pumpkin more regularly than one in the ground.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out much faster than garden beds. In summer a potted pumpkin may need water every day. Check daily and water until it drains from the bottom.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Feed a potted pumpkin more often than a garden plant, with a balanced liquid feed every couple of weeks once it is growing strongly.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Not applicable. Pumpkins live for one season and die with the first frost, so there is nothing to overwinter. Plant new seeds next year.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Not applicable. Pumpkin is a frost-tender annual that completes its life in a single season and is killed by the first hard frost, so there is nothing to overwinter. Pull spent vines at season's end and start fresh from seed the following year.

container_notes.notes_beginner: You can grow a pumpkin in a container, but only the small, compact, or bush kinds, since full-size vining pumpkins are far too big. Use a large pot, at least 10 gallons and 12 inches deep, put it in full sun, keep it well watered (pots dry out fast), and feed it regularly. Give the vines room to trail out of the pot, and water the soil, not the leaves, to help avoid mildew.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Pumpkins are a marginal container crop because they are large, long-season, sprawling plants. Only miniature, pie, or bush varieties such as Jack Be Little, Baby Bear, or Small Sugar are realistic in a pot, and they still want a big one: at least 10 gallons and 12 inches deep, larger is better. Give it full sun, let the vines trail out over the rim or up a sturdy support, water at the base daily in heat, and feed regularly, since a small soil volume dries and depletes fast over a long season. The container figures here follow general container-vegetable guidance; pumpkin-specific container numbers are modeled.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry far faster than beds, and a pumpkin in a pot can need water once or even twice a day in summer heat. Check daily by feeling the top inch of mix, and water until it runs from the drainage holes; even moisture prevents the small, misshapen fruit that water swings cause.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Feed container pumpkins more often than in-ground ones, since steady watering leaches nutrients. After the slow-release charge at planting, add a balanced liquid feed every 2 to 3 weeks, easing off nitrogen once fruit sets.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering container suits a potted pumpkin well, smoothing the moisture swings this thirsty, mildew-prone plant dislikes. Keep the reservoir topped up in heat, still water from below to keep foliage dry, and use a large enough planter that the roots are not constantly waterlogged.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match because it keeps the water steady, which pumpkins like. Keep the reservoir filled, especially in hot weather, and use a big pot.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: A container pumpkin needs a wide, deep, heavy pot, at least 12 inches deep and 10 gallons or more, even for a compact variety, with room for the vines to trail out over the edge or up a trellis. Wide and sturdy beats tall and narrow, since a vining plant in a small pot dries out and tips. Choose miniature or bush types for containers, never full-size vining pumpkins.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Give a container pumpkin a large, deep, heavy pot, at least 12 inches deep and 10 gallons or more, and let the vines trail out of it or climb a small trellis. A wide, sturdy pot is better than a tall, narrow one. Only grow small or bush pumpkin varieties in pots, not the big vining kinds.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Avoid planting pumpkins where another cucurbit grew in the last few years, including cucumber, melon, summer squash, and other winter squash. They share squash bug, squash vine borer, cucumber beetle, bacterial wilt, the mildews, and soilborne Phytophthora, all of which build up in the soil and on debris.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Do not plant pumpkins where you grew cucumbers, melons, or other squash in the last few years. They get the same pests and diseases, which build up in the soil.
rotation.good_after: Legumes such as beans and peas, sweet corn, leafy greens, or alliums like onions and garlic make good preceding crops, since they do not share the cucurbit pest and disease complex, and a legume leaves nitrogen behind for the hungry pumpkin.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate cucurbits on a 3 year cycle, returning pumpkins to a given bed no sooner than the third or fourth year, longer where Phytophthora is known, since it persists in soil for years. The point is to break the buildup of squash bug, vine borer, beetle-vectored wilt, and soilborne disease. Clear and remove spent vines at season's end rather than tilling them in, which removes overwintering pest and disease sites and makes rotation more effective.
rotation.note_beginner: Try not to grow pumpkins or their relatives in the same spot more than once every 3 years or so. Moving them around the garden each year helps avoid a buildup of pests and disease. Clean up old vines at the end of the season too.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: A well-cured, sound pumpkin is a keeper at room temperature, the opposite of tender summer squash. After curing, it holds for weeks to a few months in a cool room out of direct sun, though warm indoor heat shortens that. Display pumpkins last longest sitting on a shelf rather than on cold or damp ground.
storage.room_temp_beginner: A cured pumpkin keeps well at room temperature, often for weeks to a couple of months in a cool spot out of the sun. Keep it off cold, damp floors so the bottom does not rot.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Whole pumpkins are not refrigerated; cold storage below about 50°F causes chilling injury and faster breakdown. Cut pumpkin and cooked or pureed flesh, however, should be refrigerated and used within a few days, or frozen.
storage.fridge_beginner: Do not put a whole pumpkin in the fridge, it is too cold and makes them break down faster. Once a pumpkin is cut, wrap the pieces and keep them in the fridge for a few days, or freeze them.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Pumpkin freezes well as cooked, mashed, or pureed flesh: bake or steam, scoop and puree, cool, and freeze in measured portions for pies and soups. Raw cubes can also be frozen for cooking. Frozen pumpkin keeps about a year.
storage.freezer_beginner: Pumpkin freezes well once cooked. Bake or steam it, scoop out and mash the flesh, cool it, and freeze it in portions for baking and soup later. It keeps about a year.
storage.notes_seasoned: Storage is a real pumpkin advantage and the reason the crop is harvested once, at full maturity. Cure the fruit first, about 10 days in a warm, humid, airy spot, ideally near 80°F (cure indoors if the weather turns cold or wet), to harden the rind and heal small wounds. Then store cool but not cold, ideally around 50 to 55°F with good airflow and moderate humidity, where sound pumpkins keep for two to three months or more. Store only blemish-free fruit with the stem intact, and check periodically, removing any that begin to soften.
storage.notes_beginner: Pumpkins are made for storing, which is why you pick them once when fully ripe. First cure them for about 10 days in a warm, humid place to toughen the skin. Then keep them somewhere cool but not cold, around 50 to 55°F, with some air movement, where good ones last two to three months or more. Store only perfect pumpkins with the stem still on, and check now and then for any starting to go soft.

recommended.name: Howden
recommended.recommended_note: The classic large jack-o'-lantern: tall, ribbed, deep-orange carving pumpkin around 15 to 25 pounds. A market and home-garden standard, and a top pick in the South per UF/IFAS.

recommended.name: Connecticut Field
recommended.recommended_note: Old open-pollinated field pumpkin for carving, 15 to 25 pounds; dependable, seed-saveable, and widely adapted.

recommended.name: Small Sugar / New England Pie
recommended.recommended_note: The classic pie pumpkin: small, 5 to 8 pounds, sweet, fine-grained flesh for cooking. Open-pollinated and seed-saveable.

recommended.name: Baby Bear
recommended.recommended_note: Small, semi-flat pie pumpkin around 1.5 to 2.5 pounds with a long handle; an All-America Selections winner good for cooking and decorating.

recommended.name: Jack Be Little
recommended.recommended_note: Miniature palm-sized ornamental pumpkin on shorter vines; productive and well suited to small gardens and large containers.

recommended.name: Atlantic Giant
recommended.recommended_note: The giant competition pumpkin, capable of hundreds of pounds with rich soil, heavy feeding, water, and a long season. Grow one fruit per plant for size.

varieties.note_seasoned: Choose by use and by season length. For carving, the big jack-o'-lantern types like Howden and Connecticut Field want a long, warm season; for cooking, the smaller, sweeter pie pumpkins such as Small Sugar and Baby Bear have finer, less stringy flesh; for small spaces or containers, miniatures like Jack Be Little stay compact. Giant types like Atlantic Giant are a long-season project needing rich soil and one fruit per plant. Where the season is short, lean on the earlier-maturing pie and miniature types, and where mildew is chronic, look for resistant varieties.
varieties.note_beginner: Pick a pumpkin variety by what you want it for. For carving, grow a big type like Howden or Connecticut Field. For pies and cooking, grow a small, sweet pie pumpkin like Small Sugar or Baby Bear. For small gardens or pots, grow a miniature like Jack Be Little. Giant pumpkins like Atlantic Giant are a fun, long-season challenge. In a short season, choose a faster-maturing pie or mini type.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A healthy full-size vine typically yields 2 to 5 carving pumpkins, while pie and miniature types set more, smaller fruit. Big jack-o'-lantern plants need plenty of room per plant; giant-pumpkin growers deliberately keep one fruit per plant to channel everything into size.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: A full-size pumpkin plant usually gives you a few pumpkins, often 2 to 5, while small and mini types make more. Plan on one or two plants going a long way, since each one sprawls widely.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Pumpkins do not produce continuously; the plant sets fruit through summer and then the crop matures together in fall for a single harvest. Once a few fruit have set on a vine, removing the latest small fruit and pinching vine tips channels energy into sizing and ripening the keepers before frost.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Unlike summer squash, pumpkins do not keep producing all season. The plant sets its fruit over the summer and they all ripen together in fall, when you harvest once. Removing the latest tiny fruit helps the rest grow bigger before frost.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: The usual first-year surprises are how much room the vines take (10 to 20 feet is common for full-size types) and how pollinator-dependent fruit set is. Give plants far more space than seems necessary, and grow some flowers nearby to draw bees.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: The big first-year surprise is how far pumpkin vines spread, often 10 to 20 feet. Give them much more room than you think, and grow flowers nearby to bring in bees, since pumpkins need lots of bee visits to set fruit.
factors_seasoned: Pollination: fruit set is pollinator-limited, with each female flower needing many bee visits; poor pollination in cool or pollinator-scarce conditions drops young fruit.
Season length and heat: pumpkins need a long warm season (90 to 120 days) to mature before frost; a short season limits variety choice and yield.
Space and vine vigor: full-size vines sprawl 10 to 20 feet and need room; crowding cuts yield and worsens disease.
Pest and disease pressure: squash vine borer, squash bug, beetle-vectored bacterial wilt, and powdery and downy mildew can end a planting early.
Even moisture and feeding: steady water and moderate feeding through fruit sizing build full, well-formed pumpkins.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No T1 source supports timing pumpkin planting by moon phase. We do not make a recommendation here; sow by soil temperature and frost dates instead.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seeds sprout in about 5 to 10 days in warm soil (70 to 95°F is ideal); soil below about 65°F rots seed rather than germinating it. Two seed leaves push up first.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: In warm soil, seeds sprout in about a week to ten days, sending up two seed leaves first. In cold soil, seeds rot instead of sprouting.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Sow about 1 inch deep in warm soil, four to five seeds per hill. Keep evenly moist, not soggy. Thin to the two or three strongest seedlings once true leaves appear.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Plant seeds 1 inch deep once the soil is warm, a few per hill. Keep the soil damp until they sprout, then keep the strongest two or three seedlings.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Did your pumpkin seeds germinate, and how many days did it take?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your seeds sprouted yet?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Cotyledons followed by the first true leaves; growth is fast once warm. Watch for cucumber beetles, which target young plants and transmit bacterial wilt, and for squash bug eggs on leaf undersides.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: After the first two rounded leaves, true leaves appear and the plant grows quickly. Watch for beetles chewing the young leaves.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Protect from cucumber beetles and squash bugs with row cover if needed, removing it at flowering for pollination. Keep evenly watered and free of weeds.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep an eye out for beetles on young plants and use a light row cover if needed, but remove it once flowers form. Water regularly and keep weeds down.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How are your seedlings developing? Any sign of beetle or squash bug damage?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How do your young plants look?

growth_stages.name: Vining
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The plant sends out long runners and bulks up its leaves, often growing a foot or more of vine per day in warm weather. This is the window to side-dress and the time squash vine borer moths begin laying eggs at the stem base.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant sends out long vines that spread fast across the ground, with big leaves. This is when you feed it and give it room to run.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Side-dress with nitrogen as the vines run, mulch to hold moisture, and give the runners room to spread, 10 to 20 feet for full-size types. Begin scouting the stem base for squash vine borer frass from early summer, and bury vine joints to encourage secondary rooting.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Feed the vines as they start to run and give them plenty of room to spread. Add mulch to keep the soil moist, and start checking the base of the stem for sawdust-like specks from a borer.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are the vines running well? Have you side-dressed, and any pests at the stem base?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are your pumpkin vines spreading out?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Large yellow-orange flowers. Male flowers on thin stalks usually open first, often for a week or more before females appear, which is normal; female flowers carry a tiny pumpkin behind the bloom. Each female needs many bee visits to set a full fruit.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Big yellow-orange flowers open. The first ones are usually male and fall off, which is normal. Female flowers have a tiny pumpkin at their base, and bees need to visit them many times to set fruit.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Encourage pollinators and avoid spraying open blooms. If small fruit yellow and rot at the tip, pollination is poor, so hand-pollinate in the morning with a male flower or small brush. Keep moisture steady now.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Let the bees do their work and do not spray the flowers. If tiny pumpkins turn yellow and rot, the flowers were not pollinated, so you can hand-pollinate in the morning. Keep watering steadily.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are you seeing female flowers and fruit set? Any young fruit yellowing and dropping?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Is your plant flowering? Are any little pumpkins forming?

growth_stages.name: Fruit development
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Set fruit swell and gradually turn from green to the variety's mature color over several weeks, while the rind hardens. The plant is sizing and ripening its crop for a single fall harvest rather than setting new fruit continuously.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The little pumpkins grow bigger and slowly change color, going from green to orange (or the variety's color) as they ripen over several weeks.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture even through sizing, then taper as fruit nears maturity. Remove the latest small fruit and pinch vine tips to channel energy into the keepers, set ripening fruit on a board or mulch to keep it off wet soil, and keep scouting for mildew.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep watering steadily while the pumpkins grow, then ease off as they ripen. Slip a board or some straw under each pumpkin so it is not sitting on damp ground, and watch the leaves for powdery mildew.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How are the fruit sizing and coloring up? Any rot where fruit meets the soil?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are your pumpkins growing and changing color?

growth_stages.name: Harvest and cure
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Full mature color, a hard rind a thumbnail cannot dent, a dried corky stem, and a hollow sound when tapped. Harvest the whole crop at maturity before a hard frost, then cure to toughen the rind for storage.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The pumpkins are fully colored, the skin is hard, and the stem has dried and gone woody. They are ready to pick, all around the same time in fall.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut each pumpkin with shears leaving a 3 to 4 inch handle, never carrying it by the stem, and get the crop in before a hard frost. Cure about 10 days in a warm, humid, airy spot, then store cool (around 50 to 55°F) for the months ahead.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Cut the pumpkins off the vine with a knife, leaving a few inches of stem, and bring them in before a hard frost. Let them cure in a warm, humid place for about 10 days, then store them somewhere cool.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have you harvested? How is the cure and storage going?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you picked your pumpkins yet?

notifications.title_seasoned: Start scouting for squash vine borer
notifications.title_beginner: Time to watch for stem pests
notifications.body_seasoned: Your pumpkin vines are running, which is when squash vine borer moths lay eggs at the stem base. Check the base of the main stem for sawdust-like frass from now through midsummer, and act early if you see it.
notifications.body_beginner: Your pumpkin vines are growing fast now. Check the bottom of the main stem for sawdust-like specks, an early sign of a borer, and keep checking through summer.

notifications.body_seasoned: Your pumpkins are flowering. Fruit set depends on many bee visits per female flower, so if small fruit yellow and drop, hand-pollinate in the morning and keep blooms unsprayed.
notifications.body_beginner: Your pumpkins are flowering. If the tiny pumpkins turn yellow and fall off, the flowers were not pollinated, so try hand-pollinating in the morning.

notifications.title_seasoned: Harvest at full maturity, then cure
notifications.title_beginner: Time to harvest and cure your pumpkins
notifications.body_seasoned: Your pumpkins should be reaching full color with a hard rind and dry stem. Harvest the crop before a hard frost, leaving a 3 to 4 inch handle, then cure about 10 days in a warm, humid spot before storing.
notifications.body_beginner: Your pumpkins should be fully colored with hard skin. Pick them before a hard frost, leaving some stem on, then let them cure in a warm, humid place for about 10 days.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost is coming, harvest your pumpkins
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost warning for your pumpkins
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A frost is forecast. Pumpkins are frost-tender, and a hard frost damages the rind and ends the vines, so harvest any mature or near-mature fruit now, leaving a handle of stem, and bring them in to cure.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Frost is coming, and it will damage your pumpkins and kill the vines. Pick any ripe or nearly ripe pumpkins now and bring them inside.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Extreme heat may stall fruit set
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot spell may slow fruit set
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A stretch of extreme heat is forecast. Very hot days can reduce pollination and drop young fruit. Keep moisture steady; set usually resumes when the heat eases.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Very hot weather is coming. Your pumpkins may drop small fruit or slow down for a while. Keep them well watered, it usually picks back up when it cools.

germination.text_seasoned: Soil temperature, not the calendar, governs pumpkin germination. Wait until soil is at least 65°F, ideally 70°F, at 2 inches; seed sown in cold ground rots before it sprouts.
germination.text_beginner: Wait for warm soil before sowing. Pumpkin seeds rot in cold ground but sprout fast once it warms up.

seedling.text_seasoned: Cucumber beetles swarm young cucurbits and can spread bacterial wilt. A floating row cover protects seedlings, but pull it off at flowering so bees can pollinate.
seedling.text_beginner: Protect young plants from beetles. A light cover helps, but take it off once flowers appear so bees can reach them.

vining.text_seasoned: Feed the vines as they run, then ease off nitrogen once fruit sets, or you get vine at the expense of pumpkins. Give full-size types 10 to 20 feet to sprawl.
vining.text_beginner: Feed the vines as they spread, but do not overdo the nitrogen once fruit forms, or you get lots of leaves and few pumpkins. Give them plenty of room.

vining.text_seasoned: Start scouting the stem base for squash vine borer from early summer. A ring of sawdust-like frass at the base is the early warning before the wilt. Burying vine joints lets a damaged plant survive on secondary roots.
vining.text_beginner: Check the bottom of the main stem for sawdust-like specks starting in early summer, an early sign of a borer.

flowering.text_seasoned: Early male flowers opening and dropping with no fruit is normal; females come later. Judge pollination by whether small fruit size up or yellow and rot at the blossom end.
flowering.text_beginner: The first flowers often fall off without making pumpkins, that is normal. Trouble is when tiny pumpkins turn yellow and rot, which means poor pollination.

flowering.text_seasoned: Pumpkin fruit set is pollinator-limited, each female needing many bee visits. If set is poor, hand-pollinate in the morning: pick a male flower, strip the petals, and dab pollen onto the center of each open female.
flowering.text_beginner: Pumpkins need lots of bee visits to set fruit. If fruit is not forming, hand-pollinate in the morning by touching a male flower to the center of a female flower.

fruit_development.text_seasoned: Slip a board or straw under sizing fruit to keep it off wet soil and prevent rot. To push size, remove the latest small fruit and pinch vine tips so energy goes to the keepers before frost.
fruit_development.text_beginner: Put a board or some straw under each pumpkin so it is not on damp ground. To get bigger pumpkins, remove the latest tiny fruit so the plant feeds the rest.

fruit_development.text_seasoned: Ripeness is full color, a hard rind a thumbnail cannot dent, and a dry, corky stem. Taper watering near maturity to help the rind harden for storage.
fruit_development.text_beginner: A pumpkin is ripe when it is fully colored, the skin is hard, and the stem has dried out. Ease off watering near the end so the skin toughens.

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest the whole crop at maturity before a hard frost, cutting with shears and leaving a 3 to 4 inch handle (never carry by the stem). Cure about 10 days in a warm, humid, airy spot, then store cool near 50 to 55°F for months.
harvest.text_beginner: Pick all your pumpkins when ripe, before a hard frost, leaving some stem on but not carrying them by it. Cure them in a warm, humid place for about 10 days, then store somewhere cool.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Small fruit yellowed and rotted at the blossom end
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Tiny pumpkins turned yellow and rotted
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Poor pollination. The female flower was not adequately pollinated, so the young fruit aborts, yellowing and rotting at the blossom end instead of sizing up. Common in cool, wet, or pollinator-scarce conditions, and pumpkins are especially pollinator-dependent.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The flower was not pollinated well, so the little pumpkin died instead of growing. This often happens in cool or rainy weather, or when there are few bees.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Inadequate transfer of pollen to the female flower; each pumpkin needs many bee visits, so set fails when pollinators are scarce.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Not enough pollination of the flower, since pumpkins need lots of bee visits.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant flowers to draw bees, avoid spraying open blooms, and hand-pollinate in the morning if set is poor. It usually improves as more flowers open and bees get active.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Grow some flowers nearby for the bees, and hand-pollinate early flowers if needed. It usually gets better as more flowers open.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Healthy vine wilted and collapsed in midsummer
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Vine suddenly wilted and died
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Most likely squash vine borer: a larva tunneled into the main stem and cut off water, collapsing a previously vigorous plant in mid to late summer. Look for sawdust-like frass at the stem base. Beetle-vectored bacterial wilt causes a similar sudden collapse, confirmed by sticky white strands in a cut stem.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Usually a squash vine borer, a grub that tunnels into the stem and kills the vine in summer. Look for sawdust-like specks at the base. Beetle-spread bacterial wilt can look similar.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: A squash vine borer larva inside the stem, or bacterial wilt clogging the water-conducting tissue.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: A borer inside the stem, or a disease spread by cucumber beetles.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Use row cover until flowering, scout the stem base for frass from early summer, bury vine joints so a damaged plant can re-root, and control cucumber beetles to limit wilt. Remove spent vines at season's end.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Cover plants until they flower, check the stem base for pests, and keep cucumber beetles down. Clean up old vines at the end of the season.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Leaves turned white and powdery, then the plant faded early
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Leaves got white and powdery and the plant died back
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Powdery mildew defoliated the plant ahead of schedule. The white fungal coating spread across the leaves until they browned and died, cutting the season short, reducing fruit size and color, and exposing pumpkins to sunscald.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Powdery mildew, a white coating on the leaves, spread until the leaves died and the plant stopped early, so the pumpkins did not finish well.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Powdery mildew fungus, worsened by crowding, poor airflow, shade, and high humidity around the foliage.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: A fungus that spreads on crowded plants with poor air flow.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Choose resistant varieties, space plants generously, plant in full sun, water at the base, and treat at the first spots from midsummer rather than waiting.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Pick resistant varieties, give plants more room and full sun, water the soil not the leaves, and treat the first white spots early.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Pumpkin rotted on the bottom where it touched the soil
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Pumpkin rotted on its underside
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Fruit rot, typically from a wet underside in contact with damp soil, often Phytophthora or other soil rots in poorly drained, rainy conditions. A soft, sometimes white-molded patch develops where the pumpkin sits, and can spread in storage.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The pumpkin sat on wet ground and rotted on the bottom. Damp soil and poor drainage let a soil disease soften the fruit where it touched the ground.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Prolonged contact between fruit and saturated soil, favoring Phytophthora and other soilborne fruit rots in wet, poorly drained beds.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: The pumpkin sitting on wet soil, which lets rot set in on the underside.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant on raised hills for drainage, avoid low wet spots, and set each sizing fruit on a board or thick mulch to lift it off the soil. Harvest promptly and cure before storing.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant on raised hills so water drains away, and slip a board or straw under each pumpkin so it is not on wet ground. Pick and cure them before storing.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Pumpkins are not a succession crop. They are a single, long-season planting that sets fruit through summer and matures together for one fall harvest, so you sow once per season rather than at intervals. In most zones a second sowing would be killed by frost before its 90 to 120 day crop could ripen. Only in the warmest, frost-free or near-frost-free zones, or the low desert where a July sowing is the Halloween crop, is a second seasonal window viable, and that is a separate season, not a succession.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: You plant pumpkins once for the season. They grow all summer and ripen together in the fall for a single harvest, so there is no need to replant every few weeks. In most places a later planting would be caught by frost before the pumpkins could ripen. Only in very warm, nearly frost-free areas can you fit a second planting, and that is really a separate season.
succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Pumpkin is a single long-season crop (90 to 120 days) harvested once at full maturity, so succession sowing does not apply; a second sowing in most zones would not mature before frost. Warm frost-free zones and the low desert support a separate seasonal planting window, which is a distinct season rather than a succession.

crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Pumpkin is monoecious: each plant carries separate male and female flowers, so a single plant sets fruit with no second variety needed. The flowers are insect-pollinated, mostly by bees, and pollen must move from the male to the female blooms. Pumpkins are strongly pollinator-dependent: each female flower needs several bee visits (UGA notes seven to ten) to set a full, well-shaped fruit, and poor pollination shows up as young fruit that yellow and rot at the blossom end, or as small, lopsided pumpkins. Early-season male flowers often open and drop for a week or more before the first females appear, which is normal. Plant flowers nearby, avoid spraying open blooms, and hand-pollinate with a male flower or small brush in the morning if set stalls.
crops.pollinator_notes_beginner: Each pumpkin plant has both male and female flowers, so you only need one plant to get fruit. Bees move the pollen between the flowers, and pumpkins need a lot of bee visits to set each fruit, so anything that brings bees to your garden helps. The first flowers are usually male and fall off, which is normal. If your little pumpkins stay small and rot at the tip, the flowers were not pollinated well, so hand-pollinate in the morning and grow some flowers nearby for the bees.
crops.description_seasoned: Pumpkin is a warm-season winter squash grown for its mature, hard-rind fruit, the long-season cousin of summer squash like zucchini. Unlike zucchini, it is harvested once, at full maturity in fall, then cured and stored for months. Plants are vigorous, sprawling vines that can run 10 to 20 feet for full-size carving types, so they need far more room than a bush squash. Pumpkin is monoecious, carrying separate male and female flowers on one plant, and fruit set is strongly pollinator-dependent, with each female flower needing many bee visits. The season's shape is set by three things: a long warm runway (90 to 120 frost-free days) to mature the crop, heavy pollinator and pest pressure (squash vine borer, squash bug, cucumber beetle and the bacterial wilt it spreads, plus powdery and downy mildew), and the single fall harvest, timed at full color and hard rind, before frost and followed by a curing period for storage.
crops.description_beginner: Pumpkins are a warm-season squash grown for big, hard-skinned fruit you harvest once in the fall, unlike summer squash that you pick young all season. They grow on long, sprawling vines that can spread 10 to 20 feet, so they need a lot of room. Each plant has both male and female flowers and needs lots of bee visits to set fruit. The main things to know: give them a long, warm season and plenty of space, water steadily while the fruit grows, watch for squash bugs, vine borers, beetles, and mildew, and harvest when the pumpkins are fully colored with hard skin and a dry stem, before frost. Then cure them in a warm, dry place so they store for months.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Prepare a deep, fertile, well-drained bed in full sun, working several inches of compost or rotted manure into the soil before planting, since pumpkins are big, hungry, long-season plants. Most growers plant in low hills or mounds about a foot across, which warm faster, drain better, and give the sprawling vines a starting point. Space hills generously: roughly 4 to 8 feet apart with 6 to 12 feet between rows for full-size vining types (closer for bush and miniature kinds), because a full-size vine can run 10 to 20 feet. On heavy or wet ground, build the mounds up for drainage to head off crown and Phytophthora fruit rot.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Pick a sunny spot with rich, well-drained soil and mix in plenty of compost before planting, since pumpkins are large, hungry plants. Plant them on low hills or mounds, which warm up and drain better. Give them lots of room: space hills about 4 to 8 feet apart for full-size pumpkins, since the vines can spread 10 to 20 feet (small and bush types need less). If your soil is heavy or wet, build the mounds up higher so water drains away from the roots and fruit.

northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In cold zones the pumpkin season is a single tight summer window: plant after the last frost once soil is warm, and harvest the mature crop in early fall before the first frost. Short-season zones (3 to 4) need transplants started about three weeks early and fast-maturing pie or miniature varieties to ripen a crop in time; warmer zones (6 to 7) have room for full-size carving types.
northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In cold areas you get one pumpkin crop a summer: plant after the last frost and harvest in early fall before frost returns. In the coldest zones, start transplants indoors and grow a fast variety so the pumpkins ripen in time.

Warm-season single fall harvest; hot-desert cells split spring/fall around a backed heat_pause.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: Across the Gulf and coastal plain, pumpkins are a late-spring-into-fall crop, planted as the soil warms and timed so the fruit matures in fall for Halloween, ahead of the first frost. Summer heat and humidity drive heavy mildew and pest pressure, so airflow, resistant varieties, and scouting matter; some growers also try an early planting for a summer crop.
se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast, plant pumpkins in late spring to early summer so they ripen in fall for Halloween, before frost. The hot, humid summers bring lots of mildew and pests, so give plants room and watch them closely.

ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: In California's hot interior valleys, pumpkins are a long, warm summer crop: plant from spring into early summer and harvest in fall. The dry heat suits pumpkins as long as irrigation is steady; time the planting so fruit matures and cures in the warm, dry fall.
ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In California's hot inland valleys, plant pumpkins from spring into early summer and harvest in fall. They handle the dry heat well as long as you water steadily.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: Along California's cooler north coast, plant pumpkins after the spring chill passes and the soil warms, and harvest in fall. Cool, foggy summers can slow ripening and favor mildew, so choose a sunny site, give airflow, and lean toward earlier-maturing varieties.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: On California's cool north coast, plant pumpkins in late spring once it warms up and harvest in fall. Foggy, cool summers can slow them down, so pick a sunny spot and an earlier variety.

ca_south_coast.plantings_provenance: Author-fresh pumpkin windows, MODELED from days-to-maturity (90 to 120) + the shared frost anchors + representative extension planting dates; per-zone dates not individually source-verified (flagged in verification_status.open_findings). Warm-season single fall harvest; hot-desert cells split spring/fall around a backed heat_pause.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: On California's mild south coast, pumpkins grow through a long, gentle warm season: plant from spring into early summer and harvest in fall. The mild climate is forgiving, though coastal humidity favors mildew, so prioritize airflow and full sun.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: On California's mild south coast, plant pumpkins from spring into early summer and harvest in fall. The mild weather is easy on them, but watch for mildew in the coastal damp.

ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: In the California desert valleys, pumpkins grow as two plantings with no midsummer pause: a late-winter to spring sowing that matures before peak heat, and a midsummer (around July) sowing that grows through the heat for a fall harvest. Steady irrigation is essential, and the fall timing is the reliable one.
ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: In the California desert, plant pumpkins in late winter to spring for an early crop, and again around July for a fall crop that grows right through the summer heat. Water steadily.

warm_arid.region_label: Warm Arid: Southern New Mexico & West Texas
warm_arid.plantings_provenance: Author-fresh pumpkin windows, MODELED from days-to-maturity (90 to 120) + the shared frost anchors + representative extension planting dates; per-zone dates not individually source-verified (flagged in verification_status.open_findings). warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: In the warm arid zones of southern New Mexico and West Texas, plant pumpkins after frost once the soil warms and harvest in fall. The dry heat is manageable with steady irrigation; intense early-summer heat can briefly stall fruit set, which usually resumes as conditions ease.
warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: In the dry, warm zones of southern New Mexico and West Texas, plant pumpkins after the last frost and harvest in fall. Water steadily through the heat, and do not worry if fruit set pauses briefly during the hottest spells.

low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: In Arizona's low desert, the signature pumpkin window is a July sowing for an October Halloween harvest, which uses the long, hot fall; an earlier late-winter planting can give an early-summer crop before peak heat. Either way, steady irrigation and afternoon resilience matter, and the fall timing is the reliable one.
low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: In Arizona's low desert, the classic move is to plant pumpkins in July so they ripen in October for Halloween. You can also plant in late winter for an early-summer crop. Water steadily through the heat.

fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: In peninsular Florida, pumpkins are grown in the cooler halves of the year, planted in late winter to spring and again in late summer for a fall crop, avoiding the wettest, most disease-prone midsummer. Seed the fall crop by about early July to be ready for Halloween, and expect heavy mildew and pest pressure.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: In Florida, plant pumpkins in late winter to spring and again in late summer, avoiding the wet, buggy middle of summer. For Halloween pumpkins, plant by about early July. Watch closely for mildew and pests.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: In Hawaii and tropical zones there is no frost, so pumpkins can be planted across much of the year, with timing driven by rainfall and pest pressure rather than cold. Pumpkins and tropical pumpkin types grow well; choose the drier, sunnier windows to limit mildew and fruit rot. Specific local timing is modeled pending a parseable CTAHR source.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In Hawaii and the tropics there is no frost, so you can plant pumpkins through much of the year. Aim for the drier, sunnier stretches to avoid mildew and rot, since heat and rain are the main challenges, not cold.

crops.name: Plum

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Plum likes a deep soil that drains well, from a sandy loam to a sandy clay loam. Good drainage matters most, because plum roots do not like sitting in wet ground and can rot if they stay soggy. Of the common home fruit trees, plum is a little more forgiving of heavier ground than peach is, especially European types on a tolerant rootstock, but standing water is still the thing to avoid. If your soil is heavy clay that holds water, plant the tree on a raised mound so the roots sit above the wettest layer. A soil of average richness with some compost worked in suits it well.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Plum wants a deep, well-drained soil ranging from a sandy loam to a sandy clay loam; drainage is the priority, since Prunus roots will not tolerate prolonged wet feet. Plum is somewhat more tolerant of heavier ground than peach, particularly European cultivars on a heavy-soil-tolerant rootstock such as Marianna or Myrobalan, but chronically saturated soil still invites crown and root rot. On heavy clay, plant on a raised berm to lift the roots above the perched water table. Moderate fertility and a modest amount of organic matter suit it well.

ph.note_beginner: Plum grows best in slightly acidic soil, around pH 6.0 to 6.5, and is fine up to about 7.0 (pH is just a measure of how acidic or alkaline the soil is). Test your soil before planting and adjust slowly if you need to: garden lime raises the pH if the soil is too acidic, and elemental sulfur lowers it if the soil is too alkaline. Mix any of this in before you plant, because pH changes slowly and is much easier to fix before the permanent tree goes in.
ph.note_seasoned: Plum does best in a slightly acidic soil, roughly pH 6.0 to 6.5, and tolerates up to about 7.0. Test the soil before planting and adjust gradually if needed: lime raises a too-acidic pH, while elemental sulfur lowers one that is too alkaline. Work amendments in ahead of planting, since pH shifts slowly and is far easier to correct before the permanent tree is in the ground.

fertilizer.timing: spring at bloom to petal fall; optional light postharvest
fertilizer.example_product: 10-10-10 balanced fertilizer
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Broadcast the fertilizer evenly around the root zone out to the drip line, keeping it off the trunk, and water it in. Split timing (the bulk in spring, a lighter touch after harvest) suits sandy soils. Go easy on nitrogen: plums push vigorous shoots readily, and lush, succulent growth is more prone to aphids, bacterial canker, and black knot, and never feed late in the season, since late nitrogen delays dormancy and invites winter injury.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Scatter the fertilizer evenly on the soil around the tree out to where the branches reach, keep it off the trunk, and water it in. On sandy soil it helps to split it, most in spring and a little after harvest. Do not overdo the nitrogen (the first number on the bag), because too much pushes soft, leafy growth that draws aphids and disease. Never feed late in the year, because late feeding keeps the tree growing when it should be going dormant and makes winter damage more likely.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 suits backyard plums; a young tree that is not making about a foot of new growth a year can take a spring nitrogen boost, but a vigorous tree needs little. Avoid high-nitrogen feeding, which pushes soft, disease-prone growth at the expense of fruit.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: A balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 (the three numbers are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium) works well for backyard plums. Do not overdo nitrogen, the first number, because too much pushes leafy growth and more disease instead of fruit.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A common home-garden rate is about 1 cup of 10-10-10 per year of tree age, applied in spring from bloom to petal fall, up to roughly 8 to 10 cups for a mature tree. Do not fertilize at planting or place fertilizer in the hole; wait until growth begins. Judge by shoot growth: a bearing tree making 8 to 15 inches of new wood a year is fed about right, and one growing faster than that needs less nitrogen, not more.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A simple rule is about 1 cup of 10-10-10 for each year of the tree's age, spread in spring as the tree blooms, up to about 8 to 10 cups for a full-grown tree. Do not put fertilizer in the planting hole or feed right at planting; wait until the tree starts growing. If the tree is already growing strongly, with lots of long new shoots, give it less, not more.

companions.note_beginner: Whether a plum needs a companion tree is really a pollination question, and it depends on the type. European plums (like Stanley, Italian prune, and damson) are mostly self-fruitful, so one tree makes fruit on its own. Japanese plums (like Santa Rosa and Methley) usually need a second, different Japanese variety blooming nearby to set a good crop. Beyond that, the things that matter for a tree are not the usual vegetable-garden pairings but what grows around the roots: keep grass and weeds pulled back from under the branches, because lawn competes hard with a young tree, and a mulched, weed-free area helps the tree settle in. One thing to avoid is planting a plum near other wild or neglected plums and cherries, because those spread black knot, the black warty branch disease, to your tree.
companions.note_seasoned: For a plum, the key interaction is pollination, and it splits by type: European plums (Stanley, Italian prune, damson) are largely self-fruitful and fruit alone, while Japanese plums (Santa Rosa, Methley, and most others) are self-unfruitful and need a second compatible Japanese cultivar blooming at the same time. The other interactions that matter are about the root zone, not classic vegetable companions: keep turf and weeds cleared back from under the canopy, since a young tree competes poorly with grass for water and nitrogen. The site rule to respect is inoculum: do not plant near wild, ornamental, or neglected Prunus (chokecherry, wild plum, purple-leaf plum), which are reservoirs of black knot and brown rot.

good_seasoned.name: A second compatible plum for cross-pollination
good_seasoned.label: research_backed

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: The strongest 'good pairing' for plum is a pollenizer, and it is squarely extension-documented. MU Extension G6001 states European plums such as Stanley and Damson are self-fruitful while all Japanese varieties (Santa Rosa, Burbank, Shiro, Methley) need cross-pollination from another Japanese or American-Japanese hybrid; Clemson concurs that many plums are self-unfruitful and that fruit set improves with a compatible pollenizer. extension_backed/HIGH.

good_seasoned.why_seasoned: For Japanese plums, and for the many European cultivars that set more heavily with a partner, the single most useful companion is a second compatible plum. Match type to type: a Japanese cultivar needs another Japanese (or an American-Japanese hybrid) blooming at the same time, since European and Japanese plums bloom weeks apart and will not pollinate each other. Santa Rosa and Methley are widely used pollenizers for other Japanese plums; a self-fruitful European such as Stanley or Damson can stand alone but still crops more reliably with a second European nearby. Plant the pollenizer within about 100 feet so bees move freely between the trees.

bad_seasoned.name: Wild, ornamental, or neglected plums and cherries nearby
bad_seasoned.label: research_backed

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Multiple extensions (UMN, UMaine) identify unmanaged Prunus as the reservoir that sustains black knot: the fungus overwinters in galls on wild plum, chokecherry, purple-leaf plum, and neglected trees and re-infects nearby plums each spring. Removing or scouting nearby wild hosts is a standard cultural control. extension_backed/HIGH.

bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: A plum's worst neighbors are other Prunus you do not manage. Wild plum, chokecherry, ornamental purple-leaf plum, and abandoned plum or cherry trees are reservoirs of black knot and brown rot: the black-knot fungus overwinters in galls on those hosts and releases spores that infect your tree every wet spring, so an unmanaged thicket downwind undoes your own pruning. Where practical, remove or prune the black knot out of nearby wild hosts, or at least scout them, and site a new plum away from them.

pests.name: Plum curculio
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small developing fruit carries a distinctive crescent-shaped scar where the female cut a slit to lay an egg. Infested fruit often drops early; fruit that hangs on may be gnarled or have a grub tunneling inside. Damage appears shortly after petal fall and is one of the most common causes of wormy backyard plums.
pests.symptoms_beginner: On small developing plums, look for a curved, crescent-shaped scar, the mark the beetle leaves when it lays an egg. Damaged fruit often drops early, and some that stays on the tree ends up misshapen or has a grub inside. You see this soon after the petals fall, and it is the usual reason for wormy plums.
pests.cause_seasoned: The plum curculio (Conotrachelus nenuphar), a small snout beetle and a signature pest of its namesake crop. Adults emerge around bloom and attack fruit from petal fall onward, laying eggs in the developing fruit; the larvae feed inside, then drop to pupate in the soil.
pests.cause_beginner: A small beetle with a long snout called the plum curculio, which is named for this very crop. The adults show up around bloom and start damaging the little fruits right after the petals drop, laying eggs inside them. The larvae then feed within the fruit and later drop to the ground.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: For a backyard tree, jarring the limbs over a sheet in the cool early morning when the beetles are sluggish, then destroying what drops, reduces the population. Promptly gather and dispose of dropped infested fruit to break the cycle. Kaolin clay applied from petal fall is an organic deterrent.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Early in the morning the beetles are slow. Spread a sheet under the tree, tap the branches so the beetles fall, and destroy them. Pick up and throw away any dropped fruit promptly so the larvae inside do not mature. A kaolin clay spray (a fine white mineral coating) starting at petal fall helps keep them off.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Sanitation is the backbone: remove dropped fruit through the season so larvae cannot complete development in the soil beneath the tree. A clean orchard floor and prompt fruit pickup steadily lower pressure year over year.
pests.prevention_beginner: The main thing is cleanup. Pick up fallen fruit all season so the larvae inside cannot finish growing in the soil under the tree. Keeping the ground clear lowers the number of beetles the next year.

pests.name: Aphids (leaf curl plum aphid and mealy plum aphid)
pests.symptoms_seasoned: In spring, new leaves at the shoot tips pucker and curl tightly around colonies of small soft-bodied aphids (leaf curl plum aphid), while the pale, wax-dusted mealy plum aphid clusters on the undersides of leaves. Both excrete honeydew that turns leaves shiny and sticky and grows black sooty mold; heavy early infestations stunt shoots and can distort young fruit.
pests.symptoms_beginner: In spring the new leaves at the shoot tips curl up tightly, and if you unroll one you find little green or waxy-gray insects, aphids, packed inside. They leave a sticky shine (called honeydew) that turns black with sooty mold. A bad early attack curls the leaves and slows the new growth.
pests.cause_seasoned: Two aphids specific to plum: the leaf curl plum aphid (Brachycaudus helichrysi), which curls the spring foliage, and the mealy plum aphid (Hyalopterus pruni), whitish with a mealy wax coat. Both overwinter as eggs near the buds, build up on new spring growth, then migrate to summer hosts (leaf curl plum aphid to plants in the aster family, mealy plum aphid to reeds and cattails).
pests.cause_beginner: Two kinds of aphids that live on plum: one curls the new leaves, and the other is a pale, waxy gray one. They spend the winter as eggs near the buds, then multiply fast on the tender spring growth before flying off to other summer plants.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Natural enemies (ladybugs, lacewings, syrphid larvae, parasitic wasps) usually bring aphids under control by early summer, so protect them by not spraying broad insecticides. A strong jet of water knocks colonies off, and narrow-range horticultural oil or insecticidal soap on the affected shoots helps in a heavy infestation. A dormant or delayed-dormant oil spray targets the overwintering eggs.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Ladybugs and other helpful bugs usually clean aphids up by early summer, so avoid harsh sprays that kill those helpers too. Blast the colonies off with a hard spray of water, and for a bad case use insecticidal soap or a light horticultural oil on the curled shoots. A dormant oil spray in late winter kills the overwintering eggs.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid heavy spring nitrogen, which pushes the soft flush aphids favor. Keep ants (which farm aphids for honeydew and drive off predators) off the trunk with a sticky band, and preserve natural enemies. A late-fall or dormant oil where aphids are a chronic problem is the most effective single measure.
pests.prevention_beginner: Go easy on spring feeding, since lush new growth attracts aphids. Keep ants off the trunk (they protect aphids) with a sticky band, and leave the helpful bugs alone. If aphids come back every year, a dormant oil spray in late fall or winter is the best prevention.

pests.name: Peachtree borer
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Gummy ooze mixed with sawdust-like frass at the base of the trunk, right around the soil line, often with a mounded look where the bark meets the ground. Plums, like other stone fruit, are a host. A heavily infested young tree loses vigor as the larvae girdle the inner bark; several borers in one trunk can kill a newly planted tree in a season.
