pests.symptoms_beginner: Look at the very bottom of the trunk where it meets the soil. The peachtree borer, which also attacks plums, leaves a sticky, gummy ooze mixed with what looks like wet sawdust (frass). You may see a small mound of gum and frass at the base. A young tree with several borers can be killed in one season, so catch this early.
pests.cause_seasoned: Larvae of the peachtree borer (Synanthedon exitiosa), a clearwing moth whose day-flying adults are wasp-like. Eggs are laid on the lower trunk in summer; larvae tunnel in the inner bark at and just below the soil line. Trees stressed by winter injury, mechanical wounds, or bacterial canker are attacked first.
pests.cause_beginner: The larvae (young grub stage) of the peachtree borer, a moth whose adults look like wasps and fly by day. The adults lay eggs on the lower trunk in summer, and the larvae burrow into the bark at and below the soil line. Trees with existing wounds are hit hardest.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no rescue spray once larvae are tunneling inside. The practical home control is to expose the crown in late summer or fall, find the entry holes by the gum and frass, and kill larvae by hand with a thin wire. Keep the trunk base free of wounds.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Once the larvae are tunneling inside, no spray reaches them. The backyard fix is to scrape soil away from the base in late summer or fall, find the holes marked by gum and frass, and kill the larvae with a thin, stiff wire pushed into each hole. Then smooth the soil back.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Protect the lower trunk from mechanical injury (the wounds that draw egg-laying females), keep the tree vigorous, and clear weeds and tall grass from the base so the crown stays open and easy to inspect. Check the soil line each late summer for fresh gum.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep mowers and string trimmers away from the trunk; the wounds they leave attract the egg-laying moths. Keep grass and weeds cleared from the base so you can see the soil line, and check it every late summer for fresh gummy ooze.

pests.name: San Jose scale
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny gray, circular, hard-shelled scales encrust the bark of twigs and branches, sometimes so densely the bark looks ashy; feeding sites on fruit show as small red-purple haloed spots. Heavy infestations kill twigs and whole limbs from the top down and weaken the tree over a few seasons.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Little gray, round, hard bumps crust over the bark of twigs and branches, and the fruit can get small reddish spots where the scales feed. A bad infestation makes the bark look ashy and can kill off twigs and branches, weakening the tree.
pests.cause_seasoned: San Jose scale (Diaspidiotus perniciosus), an armored scale insect. Immobile once settled, it feeds on sap under a waxy shell and passes several overlapping generations a year; crawlers (the mobile young stage) are the only vulnerable window and spread the infestation along the branches.
pests.cause_beginner: An armored scale insect called San Jose scale. After the tiny young 'crawlers' settle down, they stay put under a hard shell and suck sap, with several generations a year. Only the crawler stage moves around and can be targeted.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: A thorough dormant or delayed-dormant application of horticultural oil, wetting all the bark, smothers overwintering scales and is the mainstay of home control. In-season, natural enemies (tiny parasitic wasps, predatory beetles) suppress light infestations; prune out and destroy heavily encrusted wood.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: The main control is a thorough spray of horticultural oil in late winter while the tree is leafless, coating all the bark to smother the scales. During the season, helpful insects keep light infestations down. Prune out and destroy branches that are heavily crusted with scale.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep the tree vigorous and well pruned so airflow is good, apply dormant oil where scale has appeared before, and inspect incoming nursery stock, since scale often arrives on new trees. Preserve natural enemies by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays.
pests.prevention_beginner: Prune for good airflow, use a dormant oil spray in areas where scale has shown up before, and check any new trees you buy, since scale often hitches in on nursery stock. Avoid harsh sprays that kill the helpful insects.

diseases.name: Black knot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Hard, black, elongated, warty swellings (knots) grow along twigs and branches, from an inch to six inches or more long, girdling and eventually killing the wood beyond them. A new gall starts as an inconspicuous olive-green, corky swelling one year, then hardens and turns coal-black by the second. Leaves on knotted branches may wilt and die, and a heavily infected tree becomes stunted and misshapen. This is the signature disease of plum.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Hard, black, warty lumps (called knots) grow along the twigs and branches, anywhere from an inch to six inches or more long. They start as a soft olive-green swelling one year and turn coal-black and hard the next. The branch beyond a knot often wilts and dies, and a badly infected tree gets stunted and gnarled. Black knot is the classic plum disease, the one to learn to recognize.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Apiosporina morbosa (formerly Dibotryon morbosum). It overwinters in the galls on the tree and on nearby wild or ornamental Prunus, and in cool, wet spring weather releases spores that infect the new green shoots. Infection is invisible the first season; the gall swells the following year and blackens the year after, so the disease runs on a roughly two-year cycle.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus (Apiosporina morbosa) that lives in the black knots over winter, on your tree and on any wild plums or cherries nearby. In cool, wet spring weather it shoots out spores that infect the new green shoots. You will not see anything the first year; the knot swells the next year and turns black the year after.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Pruning is the core control, and timing is everything: in the dormant season, before growth resumes (before about April 1), cut out every knot, making the cut 3 to 4 inches below the visible gall into clean wood, since the fungus extends beyond what you can see. Remove the prunings from the area and burn, bury, or bag them, and disinfect tools between cuts. On a scaffold too valuable to remove, cut the gall out to healthy wood. A protective fungicide on the new shoots in early spring supports the pruning where pressure is high.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Cutting the knots out is the main fix, and when you do it matters: prune in late winter while the tree is bare, before it starts growing in spring. Cut each knot off 3 to 4 inches below the black lump, into clean wood, because the fungus reaches farther than you can see. Carry the cut pieces away and burn, bury, or bag them so they cannot re-infect the tree, and wipe your pruners with rubbing alcohol between cuts.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Scout and prune out knots every dormant season before they can release spores, and deal with the reservoir: remove or clean up wild plum, chokecherry, and neglected ornamental Prunus within range, which sustain the disease. Choosing a less-susceptible cultivar and keeping the tree open and vigorous both help, but annual knot removal is the non-negotiable habit.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Check the tree every winter and cut out any knots before spring, when they spread. Just as important, clean up or remove wild plums, chokecherries, and neglected ornamental plums nearby, because they keep re-infecting your tree. Some plum varieties resist black knot better than others, so ask when you buy, but cutting the knots out each year is the habit that matters most.

diseases.name: Brown rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: At bloom, infected blossoms wilt and turn brown, and the infection can run back into the twig to form a small gummy canker. As fruit ripens, brown circular spots appear and spread fast, sometimes rotting a whole plum within a day or two in warm, wet weather, with a dusty tan spore mass on the surface. Rotted fruit dries into a mummy that clings to the tree or drops.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: At bloom, infected flowers go limp and brown, and small gummy dead patches can form on the nearby twigs. As the plums ripen, brown spots appear and spread quickly, sometimes rotting a whole fruit in a day or two in warm, wet weather, with a dusty tan fuzz on the surface. Rotted fruit shrivels into a hard, dried mummy that hangs on the tree.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Monilinia fructicola. It overwinters in mummified fruit (whether hanging in the canopy or fallen) and in twig cankers; spores released at bloom infect flowers, and those infections later seed the fruit rot. Warm, humid, wet conditions drive rapid spread, and any skin break (curculio scar, hail, cracking) is an entry point.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus called Monilinia fructicola. It survives the winter in dried mummy fruit and in dead twig patches, then releases spores at bloom that infect the flowers. Those flower infections later cause the fruit to rot. Warm, humid, wet weather makes it spread fast, and any break in the skin lets it in.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Sanitation is the core control: remove and destroy every mummy from the tree and the ground, and prune out gummy twig cankers, because these are the spore sources. During a wet bloom, an organic-approved bloom-time fungicide reduces blossom blight. Once fruit is rotting, pick and dispose of it promptly, and thin fruit so plums do not touch, which slows spread through a cluster.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: The main control is cleanup: take off and destroy every dried mummy from the tree and the ground, and prune out the gummy dead twig patches, since these hold the spores. If the weather is wet during bloom, an organic-approved spray at bloom helps protect the flowers. As soon as you see a plum rotting, pick it and throw it away, and thin the fruit so plums are not touching.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Year-round sanitation prevents most loss: never leave mummies on the tree over winter, remove dropped and thinned fruit, and keep the canopy open with good pruning so fruit dries quickly after rain. Control plum curculio and other pests whose wounds open the door, harvest promptly, handle fruit gently, and cool it soon after picking.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Cleanup all year prevents most of the damage: never leave dried mummies on the tree over winter, pick up dropped fruit, and prune so the tree is open and the plums dry fast after rain. Keep pests like plum curculio in check, since their wounds let rot in. Pick fruit on time, handle it gently, and chill it soon after picking.

diseases.name: Bacterial spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small angular, water-soaked spots on leaves turn brown to purple-black and drop out, leaving a shot-hole look; heavy infection yellows and thins the canopy. On fruit, small sunken spots, pits, and cracks develop on the skin, downgrading the crop. Susceptibility varies sharply by cultivar, and Japanese plums are often hit harder than European.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Leaves get small angular water-soaked spots that turn dark and fall out, leaving little holes, called a shot-hole look. Bad cases turn leaves yellow and thin out the tree. On the fruit, small sunken spots, pits, and cracks form. How badly a tree is hit depends a lot on the variety, and Japanese plums are often more affected than European ones.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The bacterium Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni. It spreads in warm, wet, windy weather and builds up where susceptible plum, peach, and related trees grow nearby. Symptoms are sometimes mistaken for spray injury or nutrient problems.
diseases.cause_beginner: A bacterium (a microscopic organism, not a fungus) called Xanthomonas. It spreads in warm, wet, windy weather and builds up when there are other susceptible plum or peach trees close by. The spots can look like spray damage.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Home options are limited once symptoms appear: copper sprays help more as prevention than cure and can injure the tree if overused, so they are not a reliable home fix. Keeping the tree vigorous and the canopy open and dry helps it tolerate the disease.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no good home cure once it shows up. Copper sprays help a little as prevention but can hurt the tree if overused, so they are not a dependable fix. The best you can do is keep the tree healthy and the canopy open so it shrugs off the damage.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: The most effective measure is choosing a resistant or tolerant cultivar at planting; this is largely a variety decision made before the tree goes in. Good airflow, avoiding excess nitrogen, and tree vigor reduce severity.
diseases.prevention_beginner: The best prevention is the variety you pick. Choosing a plum known to resist or tolerate bacterial spot avoids most of the trouble, so it is a decision to make before planting. Good airflow, going easy on nitrogen, and a healthy tree also help.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Water on a deep-and-infrequent rhythm rather than a little every day: about once or twice a week while a young tree establishes, easing to roughly weekly for a bearing tree in the heat of summer, always adjusted for rain and soil type. A sandy soil dries faster and needs more frequent soaks; a heavier soil holds longer. Through winter dormancy, water need drops sharply and rainfall usually suffices.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water deeply now and then instead of a little every day. Plan on about once or twice a week while a young tree is getting established, easing to about once a week for a fruiting tree in summer heat, adjusting for rain and your soil. Sandy soil dries out faster and needs watering more often; heavier soil stays wet longer. In winter, when the tree is resting, it needs very little and rain usually covers it.
watering.amount_seasoned: Water deeply each time so the moisture reaches the full depth of the root zone, rather than wetting only the surface. For an establishing tree, that is on the order of 5 gallons per soak; for a bearing tree, aim for roughly the equivalent of an inch of water per week through the growing season, more in heat. Deep, thorough soaks drive the deep rooting that carries the tree through dry spells.
watering.amount_beginner: Each time you water, give the tree a deep soak that reaches all the way down to the roots, not just a quick splash on top. A young tree wants about 5 gallons per soak. An older, fruiting tree wants roughly an inch of water a week through the growing season, and more when it is hot. Deep soaks help the tree grow deep roots that handle dry spells.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the root zone with drip or a soaker hose, and keep the canopy and fruit dry. Overhead watering that wets the leaves and fruit prolongs leaf wetness and feeds brown rot and bacterial spot, so deliver water to the soil, not the tree. Apply it across the root area out toward the drip line rather than only at the trunk.
watering.method_beginner: Water at the ground around the roots using a drip line or a soaker hose, and keep the leaves and fruit dry. Spraying water over the top wets the leaves and fruit and helps diseases like brown rot take hold, so put the water on the soil, not on the tree. Spread it across the root area out to the edge of the branches, not just right at the trunk.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Overwatering and poor drainage show as yellowing leaves, wilting that persists even in wet soil, and a generally declining tree, since waterlogged roots suffocate and rot. In stone fruit, chronically wet soil also invites crown and root rot, which is often fatal and rarely reversible once advanced. Soggy soil that never dries between waterings is the warning sign to act on.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Too much water, or soil that drains poorly, shows up as yellowing leaves, wilting that does not go away even when the soil is wet, and a tree that slowly goes downhill. That is because waterlogged roots cannot breathe and start to rot. In plum, soil that stays wet can also bring on crown and root rot, which often kills the tree. Soil that never dries out between waterings is your warning to back off.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Underwatering shows as wilting and dull, curling leaves, slowed shoot growth, and early leaf drop in a prolonged dry spell. The most telling symptom is on the fruit: a tree short of water during the final swell sizes its plums poorly, leaving them small and prone to shriveling even though the tree itself survives. Catch the dry stress before the fruit pays for it.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Too little water shows as wilting and dull, curling leaves, slower growth, and leaves dropping early in a long dry spell. The clearest sign is in the fruit: a tree that runs short of water while the plums are sizing up makes small, shriveled fruit, even though the tree itself lives through it. Try to catch the dry stress before the fruit suffers for it.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Through establishment, keep the root ball and surrounding soil consistently moist, never waterlogged. Deep soaks of about 5 gallons once or twice a week, adjusted for rain and heat, build the deep root system the tree relies on later.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: While the tree is getting established, keep the soil around the roots evenly moist but not soggy. A deep soak of about 5 gallons once or twice a week, more in heat and less after rain, helps the tree grow the deep roots it needs.

schedule_by_stage.rate: deep soak, ~1 in per week equivalent
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: From fruit set through the final swell, do not let the tree dry out. Aim for the equivalent of about an inch of water per week, more in heat, delivered as deep soaks. Steady moisture now translates directly into larger, better-filled fruit and helps prevent the shriveling that dry stress causes.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: While the plums are setting and sizing up, keep the water steady. Aim for about an inch of water a week, more when it is hot, given as deep soaks. This is exactly when steady watering pays off in bigger, better plums.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Once the tree is dormant and leafless, water need drops sharply; rely mostly on rainfall and water only during prolonged dry spells to keep roots from desiccating. Avoid keeping dormant soil saturated.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: After the leaves drop and the tree is resting for winter, it needs very little water. Let rain do most of the work and only water during long dry stretches so the roots do not dry out. Do not keep the soil soaked in winter.

watering.method_note_seasoned: Water deeply and infrequently at the root zone, ideally by drip or soaker, to encourage deep rooting; avoid wetting the canopy, which feeds brown rot and bacterial spot. Young trees need consistent moisture through their first two seasons to establish; mature trees are moderately drought-tolerant but size fruit poorly under stress.
watering.method_note_beginner: Give the tree a deep soak now and then rather than a little every day, and water at the ground (a drip line or soaker hose is ideal) instead of spraying the leaves, since wet leaves and fruit lead to disease. Young trees need steady moisture for their first couple of years to get established. Older trees can handle some dry spells, but the plums come out small if the tree gets too dry.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The make-or-break window is the final swell, roughly the last 3 to 5 weeks before harvest, when cell expansion adds most of the fruit's final size. Water stress then causes irreversible loss of size and can leave plums small and prone to shriveling. Early rapid growth just after bloom is also sensitive; mild stress during pit hardening (mid-season) is the most tolerable time to ease off if water is limited.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The most important time to keep the tree watered is the last few weeks before harvest, when the plums do most of their growing. If the tree runs dry then, the fruit stays small and watering later will not fix it. The few weeks right after bloom matter too. If you ever have to cut back on water, the safest time is the middle of the season, when the pits are hardening.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Hardening off does not apply to plum. It arrives as a dormant, bare-root tree and goes in the ground in late winter or early spring, not raised from a seedling indoors, so there is no tender transplant to acclimate to the outdoors.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: Hardening off (slowly getting an indoor-grown seedling used to outdoor conditions) does not apply to plum. You plant it bare-root and dormant, in late winter or early spring, rather than as a seedling started inside, so there is no tender young plant to ease outdoors.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Plant the bare-root tree while it is still dormant in late winter to early spring, before bud break, once the ground has thawed enough to dig. Soak the roots in water for an hour or two beforehand to rehydrate them. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots without bending them and set the tree so the graft union (that swollen joint near the base of the trunk) sits 2 to 3 inches above the final soil line. Do not add fertilizer to the planting hole; backfill with native soil, water in well, and stake only if the site is windy.
start_method.notes_beginner: Plant the bare-root tree while it is still dormant (resting, with no leaves) in late winter to early spring, before the buds open, once the ground has thawed enough to dig. Soak the roots in a bucket of water for an hour or two first so they do not stay dried out. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots out without bending them, and set the tree so the graft union (that bumpy joint near the base, where the fruiting variety meets the rootstock) sits 2 to 3 inches above the soil. Do not put fertilizer in the hole. Refill with the same soil you removed, water it in well, and add a stake only if the spot is windy.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Fill the pot with a chunky, fast-draining mix made for shrubs and trees, not a soft peat-based potting soil that stays soggy. A bark-based mix (composted bark with perlite or pumice mixed in for drainage) holds the air the roots need. Do not use soil dug from the yard in a pot, because it packs down and drains badly when you water often.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Keep it simple and aim for drainage. If the mix seems to hold water, stir in more perlite or pumice, and lay a thin layer of compost on top instead of mixing a lot of rich material all through the pot. Stay away from water-holding crystals or a lot of peat, since plum roots need the mix to drain, not stay wet.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: Use a coarse, fast-draining soilless mix built for woody plants, not a peat-heavy potting soil that stays wet. A bark-based mix (composted pine bark with perlite or pumice) gives the air-filled porosity stone-fruit roots demand; plum will not tolerate a mix that holds water against the crown. Skip native garden soil in a pot, which compacts and drains poorly under irrigation.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Keep amendments minimal and drainage-first: blend in extra perlite or pumice if the base mix feels water-retentive, and top-dress with a thin layer of compost rather than mixing heavy organics throughout. Avoid water-holding additives such as moisture-retentive crystals or large peat fractions, which work against the fast-draining root zone plum needs.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: A plum in a pot dries out much faster than one in the ground, since there is no deep soil for the roots to reach. In summer heat, check it every day and water when the top inch or two feels dry, until water runs out the bottom. Water more often than a ground tree, but never let the pot sit in a saucer full of water, because roots left wet will rot. In winter, when the tree is resting, give it just enough to keep the root ball from drying out completely.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Watering often washes food out of the pot, so feed a little at a time instead of one big dose. Use a diluted balanced liquid fertilizer every few weeks from spring into midsummer, then stop by late summer so the tree does not push out tender new growth that winter cold can kill. Do not fertilize when you first plant it, and stop feeding once the tree drops its leaves for winter.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Roots in a pot get much colder than roots in the ground, because cold air reaches the soil from every side. A plum that survives winter fine in your yard can still have its roots freeze in a pot. Before hard freezes come, either bury the pot up to its rim in a garden bed, or move it into an unheated but protected spot like an attached garage or shed that stays cold but not deep-freezing. The tree still needs the cold to rest, so do not bring it into a warm, heated room.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Roots in a pot sit several zones colder than roots in the ground, because the soil ball is exposed to the air on all sides, so a plum that is hardy in your ground may still freeze its roots in a container. Before hard freezes, either sink the pot to its rim in a garden bed or move it to an unheated but sheltered space (an attached garage or shed) that stays cold enough to hold dormancy but buffers the deep freezes. The tree still needs its winter chill, so do not bring it into a heated room.

container_notes.notes_beginner: A plum really wants to grow in the ground, and a pot is the workaround if you do not have the space. It can be done, especially with a semi-dwarfing rootstock like St. Julien or Marianna, but plan on more hands-on care and smaller, less dependable crops than a tree in the ground. Use the biggest pot you can that drains really well, and know that watering, feeding, and winter protection all need closer attention than they would in open ground.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Plum is fundamentally a ground tree, and a container is the compromise for growers who lack the space or the soil for an in-ground tree. It can work, best on a size-limiting rootstock such as St. Julien or Marianna, but expect more hands-on management and lighter, less reliable crops than the same tree in the ground. Give it the largest practical pot with excellent drainage, and accept that watering, feeding, and winter protection all demand closer attention than they would in open soil.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: A potted plum dries far faster than one in the ground and has no deep soil to draw on, so check moisture daily in the heat of summer and water when the top inch or two is dry, until it runs from the drainage holes. The discipline is the opposite of the in-ground tree: water more often, but never leave the pot standing in a full saucer, because continuously wet roots rot. Through dormancy the tree needs only enough water to keep the root ball from drying out completely.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Frequent watering flushes nutrients out of a pot quickly, so feed lightly and often rather than in one heavy dose: a dilute balanced liquid feed every few weeks through the spring-to-midsummer growth flush, then stop by late summer so no soft growth is pushed into fall and caught by frost. Do not feed at planting, and ease off entirely once the tree goes dormant.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering or sub-irrigated planter is not recommended for plum. Its reservoir keeps the lower root zone continuously moist, which is exactly the condition that triggers root and crown rot in stone fruit. Plum needs a pot that drains freely and a wet-then-dry cycle, not a constant water table held against the roots.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot (one with a water tank in the bottom) is not a good choice for plum. The tank keeps the lower roots wet all the time, and that constant wetness is just what causes plum roots and the crown to rot. Plum needs a pot that drains freely and soil that dries out a bit between waterings, not water sitting against the roots.
container_notes.container_overwintering_seasoned: Cold protection in a pot is about more than the roots: the exposed trunk and the graft union (the low swollen joint where the fruiting variety sits on its rootstock) are also vulnerable to freeze and to winter sun-scald. Wrap or shade the lower trunk in exposed sites, and bank mulch or pack the sunk pot to insulate the root zone. The goal is a cold, stable dormancy without the deep lows that kill exposed roots and bark; a too-warm shelter that breaks dormancy early is its own hazard, leaving the tree to bloom into frost.
container_notes.container_overwintering_beginner: Protecting a potted plum in winter is not just about the roots. The bare trunk and the graft union (the low swollen joint where the fruiting top sits on its rootstock) can also be hurt by freezing and by winter sun on cold bark. In open, exposed spots, wrap or shade the lower trunk, and pile mulch around a sunk pot to keep the roots insulated. You want a cold, steady rest without the deep freezes that kill exposed roots and bark. Be careful too that a shelter that is too warm can wake the tree up early and leave it blooming right into a frost.

recommended.name: Methley
recommended.recommended_note: A low-chill Japanese plum and one of the few that is partially self-fruitful; reddish-purple, very sweet, ripens early. A good pollenizer for other Japanese plums; suited to mild-winter and southern gardens.

recommended.name: Santa Rosa
recommended.recommended_note: The classic Japanese plum: reddish-purple skin, amber flesh, heat-tolerant and low-chill. Partially self-fruitful but crops much better with a second Japanese variety, and is itself an excellent pollenizer.

recommended.name: Burbank
recommended.recommended_note: A vigorous, productive Japanese plum with sweet red-fleshed fruit; self-unfruitful, so plant a second Japanese cultivar such as Santa Rosa or Methley nearby.

recommended.name: Green Gage (Reine Claude)
recommended.recommended_note: An old-world European dessert plum, greenish-gold and richly sweet; partially self-fruitful and crops best with another European variety. Prized for flavor over looks.

recommended.name: Stanley
recommended.recommended_note: The standard European prune-plum: self-fruitful, cold-hardy, blue-black oval fruit good fresh, canned, or dried. A dependable single-tree choice for most northern gardens.

recommended.name: Italian Prune (Fellenberg)
recommended.recommended_note: A European prune-plum with deep-purple freestone fruit and high sugar; largely self-fruitful, the classic drying and canning plum, ripening in late summer.

recommended.name: Damson
recommended.recommended_note: A small, tart, high-chill European (P. insititia) plum, self-fruitful and very cold-hardy; too astringent for fresh eating but unmatched for jam, jelly, and preserves.

varieties.note_seasoned: Choose first by TYPE, because it decides both hardiness and pollination. European plums (Stanley, Italian prune, damson, Green Gage) are the northern default: more cold-hardy, higher chill (roughly 700 to 1,000 hours), later-blooming so they dodge frost, and mostly self-fruitful, so a single tree bears. Japanese plums (Santa Rosa, Methley, Burbank) are lower-chill (about 400 to 800 hours), better for mild-winter and southern gardens, but bloom early (more frost-exposed) and are usually self-unfruitful, needing a second compatible Japanese cultivar. Then match chill hours to your winters, weigh bloom timing and disease resistance (bacterial spot, black knot), and pick freestone versus clingstone for your use.
varieties.note_beginner: The first choice is the TYPE of plum, because it sets both how cold-hardy the tree is and whether it needs a partner. European plums (like Stanley, Italian prune, and damson) are the usual pick in cold areas: hardy, they bloom later so frost is less of a risk, and most make fruit on their own. Japanese plums (like Santa Rosa and Methley) suit warmer, milder-winter areas, but they bloom early (more frost risk) and usually need a second, different Japanese plum nearby to set fruit. After type, match the variety's chill needs to your winters and think about disease resistance.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Hold firm-picked plums at room temperature out of direct sun to finish ripening, typically 2 to 4 days, until they yield to gentle pressure and smell fragrant. Tree-ripe fruit picked soft lasts only a day or two on the counter, so plan to eat or refrigerate it promptly.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Leave firm plums on the counter, out of direct sun, to ripen the rest of the way, usually 2 to 4 days, until they give to a gentle squeeze and smell sweet. Plums you picked already soft will only keep a day or two out, so eat or refrigerate them soon.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerate plums once they are ripe or nearly so, then eat within about a week. Unlike peaches, plums tolerate refrigeration well and are less prone to mealy chilling injury, so the fridge is a good holding place for ripe fruit. Bring them back to room temperature before eating for the fullest flavor.
storage.fridge_beginner: Put plums in the fridge once they are ripe or almost ripe, and eat them within about a week. Plums keep in the fridge better than peaches do, so it is a good spot for ripe fruit. For the best taste, let cold plums warm back to room temperature before you eat them.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Plums freeze well halved and pitted. Cut ripe fruit in half, remove the pits, and freeze on a tray in a single layer, then transfer to freezer bags; freestone European prune-plums are easiest since the pit pulls free. Frozen plums keep their quality for several months and are best used for cooking, baking, and sauces rather than fresh eating.
storage.freezer_beginner: Plums freeze nicely if you halve and pit them first. Cut ripe plums in half, take out the pits, spread them on a tray to freeze, then pack them into freezer bags. Freestone types (where the pit pulls free) are easiest. They keep for several months and are best for cooking, baking, and sauces instead of eating fresh.
storage.notes_seasoned: Plums are climacteric and finish ripening off the tree, so firm-picked fruit counter-ripens well; store ripe fruit cold and use within a week. Freestone European prune types are the best keepers and freezers, while soft, juicy Japanese plums are more perishable and best eaten fresh.
storage.notes_beginner: Plums keep ripening after they are picked, so firm plums soften nicely on the counter. Once ripe, store them in the fridge and use within a week. The firmer European prune plums keep and freeze best; the soft, juicy Japanese plums spoil faster and are best eaten fresh.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Annual crop rotation does not apply to a plum: the tree holds its site for decades. The real concern is replant disease. Do not plant a new plum (or other stone fruit) where a plum, peach, cherry, apricot, or nectarine was recently growing, since Prunus-after-Prunus replanting causes stunting and poor establishment, and old sites can carry ring nematodes and soilborne carryover.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: You do not rotate a plum tree the way you rotate vegetables, because it stays in one spot for many years. What matters instead is replant disease: do not plant a new plum where a plum, peach, cherry, apricot, or nectarine just came out. Planting a stone fruit right back where another stone fruit grew leads to weak, stunted trees, and old spots can hold pests that hold the new tree back.
rotation.good_after: a fresh site with no recent stone-fruit history (no plum, peach, cherry, apricot, or nectarine)
rotation.note_seasoned: If a plum must go where a stone fruit was removed, replace a generous volume of soil, choose a vigorous, tolerant rootstock such as Myrobalan or Marianna, and expect slower establishment. Best practice is simply to pick a new location well away from wild Prunus that harbor black knot.
rotation.note_beginner: If you have no choice but to replant where a stone fruit was, dig out and replace a big area of soil, pick a tough rootstock like Myrobalan or Marianna, and expect the tree to start slower. The simplest fix is to plant in a new spot instead, away from any wild plums or cherries that carry black knot.

growth_stages.name: Planting (bare-root, dormant)
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Late winter to early spring, while the tree is dormant and leafless, as soon as the soil can be worked.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Late winter or early spring, while the young tree is still bare and leafless and the ground can be dug.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A dormant bare-root whip or branched tree with firm, plump buds and healthy, unbroken roots. The graft union (the swollen joint where the variety meets the rootstock) should sit a couple of inches above the final soil line.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A leafless young tree with firm buds and healthy roots. Find the graft union, the swollen joint low on the trunk where your plum variety was joined to its rootstock, and keep that joint a couple of inches above the soil when you plant.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Dig a hole as wide as the roots spread and no deeper than they sat in the nursery, spread the roots, and set the tree at the same depth with the graft union above grade. Backfill with native soil, water in well to settle it, and do not bury the trunk. If you are planting a Japanese variety, plant its pollenizer at the same time.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Dig a hole wide enough for the roots to spread and only as deep as they were growing before. Set the tree at that same depth, keeping the graft joint above the soil. Fill in with the soil you dug out, water well to settle it, and never pile soil up the trunk. If it is a Japanese plum, plant its partner tree now too.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record the planting date and the cultivar, type, and rootstock you set.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note the day you planted, and which plum variety, type, and rootstock it is.

growth_stages.name: Year-one establishment
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: The first full growing season after planting.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: The first whole growing season after you plant the tree.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Steady new shoot growth and a strengthening root system. Any blossoms that form in the first year should be removed so the tree spends its energy on roots and framework rather than fruit.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Healthy new shoots and a tree settling in. If it tries to flower in this first year, pick the flowers off so the tree puts its energy into roots and branches instead of fruit.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply and regularly through the first season so the roots establish, keep a weed-free, mulched circle around the trunk without piling mulch against the bark, and remove first-year flowers. Begin training the framework with light formative pruning.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Water deeply and often this first season, since a new tree needs steady water to get its roots going. Keep a mulched, weed-free circle around the trunk, but keep the mulch off the bark. Remove any flowers this year, and begin shaping the branches with light pruning.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Log first-season watering and the date you removed first-year blossoms.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note your watering and the day you removed the first-year flowers.

growth_stages.name: Framework training (years one to three)
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: The first three years, the framework-building phase before reliable bearing.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: The first three years, while you are building the tree's main branches and before it fruits much.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The training system depends on type: Japanese plums are trained to an open-center (vase) form of three to five main scaffolds for light and air, while the more upright European plums take a modified central leader. Either way, watch for crossing, inward, or overly upright shoots to remove, and for the fruiting spurs that will carry the crop.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: How you shape the tree depends on the type. Japanese plums are usually trained to an open, vase shape with three to five main branches; the more upright European plums keep a central trunk with branches spaced up it (a modified central leader). Look for branches that cross, crowd, or shoot straight up to remove.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Each late dormant season, select and keep the best-placed scaffolds and remove competing, crossing, and inward growth. Plums are pruned more lightly than peaches, since they bear largely on long-lived spurs rather than only one-year wood; thin to open the canopy and spread the upright form rather than heading everything back hard.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Each year in late winter, keep the best-placed main branches and cut away ones that cross, crowd, or grow inward. Plums need lighter pruning than peaches, because they fruit on short spurs that live several years, so thin to open up the tree rather than cutting everything back hard.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record each dormant-season pruning, the training form, and the scaffolds retained.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you prune each winter and which main branches you kept.

growth_stages.name: Winter dormancy
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Roughly December through February, the leafless months when the tree banks chill.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: About December through February, the leafless winter months.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A leafless tree at rest. During these cold months the tree accumulates chill hours (time between about 32 and 45°F) that it needs to break dormancy and bloom evenly. This is also the clearest time to spot black knot: the hard black galls stand out on the bare branches.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A bare, resting tree. Through these cold months the tree is collecting chill hours, the cold time it needs before it will bloom properly in spring. It is also the easiest time to see black knot, since the hard black lumps show up clearly on the bare branches.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Little is required beyond the dormant-season tasks: scout the bare branches for black knot and remove any galls (see dormant pruning), and clear mummified fruit and fallen debris that harbor brown rot. Established trees need minimal water now.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Not much to do beyond the winter tasks: look the bare branches over for black knot and cut out any lumps, and clear away dried mummy fruit and fallen debris that carry disease. An established tree needs very little water now.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Note any black knot found and removed, and any winter sanitation.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note any black knot you cut out and any winter cleanup.

growth_stages.name: Dormant pruning and black knot removal
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Late dormancy, roughly February into March, before growth resumes (and before about April 1 for black knot).
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Late winter, around February into March, just before the tree wakes up.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare branches that show the tree's structure clearly, and any black knot galls, which must come out now before they release spores. Read the framework and the balance of fruiting spurs before the buds swell.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Bare branches, so you can see the whole shape of the tree and spot any black knot lumps, which must be cut out now before spring. This is the easiest time to judge the framework before the buds swell.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Prune in late dormancy: thin to keep the canopy open, remove dead, diseased, crossing, and downward wood, and preserve fruiting spurs (plums are pruned more lightly than peaches). Cut out every black knot gall 3 to 4 inches below the visible swelling into clean wood, remove the prunings from the area and destroy them, and disinfect tools between cuts. Make clean cuts to avoid the wounds that invite borers and canker.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Prune in late winter: thin to keep the center open, cut out dead, diseased, crossing, and downward branches, and keep the short fruiting spurs (plums need lighter pruning than peaches). Cut out any black knot 3 to 4 inches below the black lump, carry the pieces away and destroy them, and wipe your pruners with rubbing alcohol between cuts. Make clean cuts, because ragged wounds invite borers and canker.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record the pruning date, how much you removed, and any black knot cut out.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note the day you pruned, how much you took off, and any black knot you removed.

growth_stages.name: Bloom
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Early spring; Japanese plums open first (often late February to March), European plums a few weeks later.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Early spring. Japanese plums flower earliest, European plums a bit later. The exact week depends on where you live.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: White blossoms opening across the tree. This is where pollination type shows: a self-fruitful European plum sets on its own, while a Japanese plum needs its compatible pollenizer blooming at the same time and bees moving between them. It is also the most frost-vulnerable moment of the year, and early-blooming Japanese plums are the most exposed.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: White flowers opening all over the tree. This is when pollination matters: a European plum can set fruit by itself, but a Japanese plum needs its partner tree flowering at the same time, with bees visiting both. It is also the riskiest time for frost, and the early-blooming Japanese plums are most at risk.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Watch the frost forecast closely; if a hard frost threatens open bloom, a backyard tree can sometimes be covered overnight. In a wet bloom, this is the window for a brown-rot blossom spray. Make sure a Japanese variety has its pollenizer flowering nearby; otherwise let the tree set its own crop.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep an eye on the frost forecast. If a hard frost is coming while the tree is in bloom, you can sometimes protect a small tree by covering it overnight. If bloom is wet, this is the time for a brown-rot spray. For a Japanese plum, make sure its partner tree is flowering nearby.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record the bloom date, whether the pollenizer overlapped, and any frost protection or bloom spray.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when bloom started, whether the partner tree was flowering too, and anything you did for frost or spray.

growth_stages.name: Fruit set and thinning
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Spring, after petal fall and the natural June drop, once young fruit has sized to about marble stage.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Spring, after the petals drop and the tree sheds some small fruit on its own, once the little plums are about marble-sized.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Clusters of small green fruit, often heaviest on Japanese plums, which overset badly. An unthinned tree produces many small plums, risks limb breakage, and tends toward biennial (alternate-year) bearing.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Lots of small green plums, often crowded, especially on Japanese types. Without thinning you get many small plums, branches can break under the weight, and the tree may swing into bearing heavily only every other year.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin the young fruit to roughly one plum every 4 to 6 inches along the branch, removing the rest while they are small. Thinning is the biggest lever on fruit size, protects the limbs, evens out alternate-year bearing, and spaces fruit so they do not touch (which slows brown rot). Japanese plums need heavier thinning than European.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Thin the little fruits so about one plum is left every 4 to 6 inches along each branch, picking off the extras while they are small. This does more for fruit size than anything else, keeps branches from breaking, evens out the crop from year to year, and spaces the plums so they do not touch and spread rot. Japanese plums need more thinning than European ones.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record the thinning date and the spacing you thinned to.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you thinned and how far apart you left the plums.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Summer; Japanese plums ripen earlier (June to August), European prune types later (August to September). First reliable crop around years three to five.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Summer. Japanese plums ripen earlier and European plums later. Most trees give their first real crop around years three to five.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Ripe plums take on full variety color, develop a dusty bloom on the skin, give slightly to gentle pressure, and pull free easily. European prune types are ripe when soft and sweet all the way to the pit. A tree ripens over one to two weeks, so it is picked in several passes.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A ripe plum shows full color, has a dusty coating on the skin (that is natural), gives a little when gently squeezed, and comes off with an easy pull. European prune plums are ready when soft and sweet through to the pit. The tree ripens over one to two weeks, so pick it a few times.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick in several passes as fruit ripens, handling gently to avoid bruises that invite brown rot. Eat or use tree-ripe fruit quickly, or chill promptly. Clear any rotted or dropped fruit as you go so it does not seed disease.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pick over several days as the plums ripen, handling them gently so they do not bruise (bruises invite brown rot). Eat or use ripe fruit quickly, or put it in the fridge. Pick up any rotted or dropped fruit so it does not spread disease.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record harvest dates and a rough yield.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you picked and roughly how much you got.

notifications.title_beginner: Time to plant your plum tree
notifications.body_seasoned: Set a dormant bare-root tree now, while it is still leafless and the ground is workable. Keep the graft union (the swollen knuckle where the top variety joins the root) two to three inches above the final soil line, pick a full-sun, well-drained spot away from frost pockets and away from wild plums that carry black knot, and if you planted a Japanese variety, set its pollenizer at the same time.
notifications.body_beginner: Now is the time to plant a bare-root plum, while it is still dormant (leafless and resting) and the soil can be dug. Keep the graft union, the swollen bump low on the trunk, about two to three inches above the soil, and choose a sunny spot with good drainage away from low frosty dips and away from wild plums. If it is a Japanese plum, plant its partner tree now too.

notifications.title_seasoned: Dormant pruning and black knot check
notifications.title_beginner: Time to prune and check for black knot
notifications.body_seasoned: Prune now, in late dormancy before buds swell, and while the branches are bare, scout hard for black knot. Plums are pruned more lightly than peaches, so thin to open the canopy and keep the fruiting spurs. Cut any black knot gall 3 to 4 inches below the black swelling into clean wood, carry the prunings off and destroy them, and disinfect tools between cuts.
notifications.body_beginner: Prune now, in late winter before the buds swell, and look the bare branches over for black knot, the hard black lumps. Plums need lighter pruning than peaches, so just thin to open the tree and keep the short fruiting spurs. Cut out any black knot 3 to 4 inches below the lump, carry the pieces away and destroy them, and wipe your pruners between cuts.

notifications.title_seasoned: Bloom is open: watch frost and pollination
notifications.title_beginner: Flowers are open: frost and pollination
notifications.body_seasoned: Your tree is flowering, the year's highest-risk stretch for the crop: a hard freeze on open blossoms or just-set fruit can take all of it, and early-blooming Japanese plums are the most exposed. Watch the overnight lows and cover a small tree if a hard frost is forecast. Pollination splits by type: a European plum (Stanley, damson) sets on its own, but a Japanese plum needs its compatible pollenizer flowering nearby with bees working both trees.
notifications.body_beginner: Open flowers are when a plum crop is most at risk from frost, and early-blooming Japanese plums are the most exposed. Watch the overnight forecast and drape a cover over a small tree if a hard frost is coming. Remember the pollination rule: a European plum can fruit on its own, but a Japanese plum needs its partner tree flowering nearby so bees can carry pollen between them.

notifications.body_seasoned: Once the tree has finished its natural early-summer drop, thin the remaining fruit to about one plum every four to six inches. Thinning is the biggest lever on fruit size, protects limbs from an overset crop (Japanese plums overset heavily), evens out alternate-year bearing, and spaces the fruit so brown rot cannot jump between touching plums.
notifications.body_beginner: After the tree drops some small fruit on its own in early summer, thin what is left to about one plum every four to six inches (roughly a hand's width). Removing extra fruit grows bigger plums, keeps branches from snapping, evens the crop out from year to year, and keeps the plums from touching so rot does not spread.

notifications.body_seasoned: Through its first two seasons a plum is at its most water-sensitive while roots establish. Water deeply and regularly at the root zone, by drip or soaker, and avoid wetting the canopy, which feeds brown rot and bacterial spot. Keep a weed-free, mulched circle around the trunk so the tree is not competing for moisture.
notifications.body_beginner: For its first couple of years, a young plum needs steady water while its roots get going. Give it a deep soak at the ground every week or so (a drip line or soaker hose is ideal) rather than spraying the leaves, since wet leaves invite disease. Keep a mulched, weed-free ring around the trunk so weeds are not stealing the water.

notifications.title_beginner: Plums are sizing up: harvest soon
notifications.body_seasoned: The last few weeks before harvest are the make-or-break window: most of the fruit's final size is added now, and water stress causes irreversible loss. Keep moisture steady. A plum is ready when it reaches full variety color, wears a dusty bloom, gives slightly, and pulls free easily; European prune types are ripe when soft and sweet to the pit. A tree ripens over one to two weeks, so pick in several passes.
notifications.body_beginner: Plums gain most of their size in the final few weeks, so keep the watering steady right up to harvest. A plum is ripe when it shows full color, has a dusty coating, gives a little, and pulls off easily; European prune plums are ready when soft and sweet through to the pit. The tree ripens over a week or two, so pick a few at a time.

notifications.body_seasoned: As the tree drops its leaves, clear every mummified fruit from the branches and the ground and rake up fallen debris, the overwintering source of brown rot. Once the branches are bare, scan them for black knot so you know what to cut out at dormant pruning. Late summer through fall is also the window to check the trunk base for fresh gum and frass that signal borers.
notifications.body_beginner: As the leaves fall, pick off any shriveled dried-up fruit still hanging on the tree, gather what dropped, and rake up the litter, since that old fruit carries brown rot into next year. With the branches bare, look them over for black knot so you know what to cut out when you prune. It is also a good time to check the bottom of the trunk for sap or sawdust, which can mean borers.

notifications.title_seasoned: Anything to log on the plum?
notifications.title_beginner: How is your plum tree doing?
notifications.body_seasoned: It has been a while since your last note. A quick check pays off on a tree: scan the branches for black knot, look for fresh gum or frass at the trunk base, confirm any mummified fruit is gone, and note where bloom and harvest landed this year. Logging the dates now makes your tree's pattern clearer over time.
notifications.body_beginner: It has been a while since you logged anything. A quick look at the tree is worth it: check the branches for black knot, look at the base of the trunk for sap or sawdust, make sure no old dried fruit is left hanging, and jot down when the tree bloomed and when you picked. Writing the dates down helps you see the tree's rhythm year to year.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost warning while flowering
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A hard freeze on open bloom or newly set fruit is the single most common way a plum crop is lost, and early-blooming Japanese plums are hit hardest. If a frost is forecast tonight, cover a small tree before evening to trap ground warmth, and water the soil beforehand, since moist ground holds and releases more heat overnight. A frost-aware site and, in cold areas, a later-blooming European variety matter most.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: A hard frost on open flowers or tiny new fruit is the most common reason a plum crop fails, and early-blooming Japanese plums are most at risk. If frost is forecast tonight, cover a small tree before dark to hold in the ground's warmth, and water the soil first, since damp ground stays warmer overnight. In cold areas, a later-blooming European plum is the safer choice.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Muggy weather: watch for rot
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Warm, humid conditions drive brown rot, which browns blossoms at bloom and can rot a ripening plum within a day or two. There is no spraying it away mid-spell: keep the canopy open and dry, water only at the root zone, remove any rotting fruit promptly, thin so plums do not touch, and harvest ripe fruit without delay so it is off the tree before the rot reaches it.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Warm, muggy weather is what brown rot loves, the disease that turns blossoms brown and can rot a ripe plum in a day or two. You cannot spray it away once it is muggy, so keep the tree open and the leaves dry, water only at the ground, pick off any rotting fruit right away, keep plums from touching, and harvest ripe ones promptly.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Heavy rain: watch ripe fruit
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A wet canopy feeds brown rot and bacterial spot, and rain on nearly ripe fruit can crack and rot it on the tree, especially thin-skinned Japanese plums. After a soaking rain, check ripening plums and pick any that are ready rather than leaving them to split. An open canopy that dries fast after rain is your best standing defense.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Wet leaves and fruit invite disease, and rain on almost-ripe plums can split and rot them right on the branch, especially the thin-skinned Japanese kinds. After a heavy rain, look over the ripening fruit and pick anything that is ready instead of leaving it to crack. Keeping the tree open so it dries quickly after rain is the best ongoing protection.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Dry stretch: keep up deep watering
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Dry spell: do not let the tree run dry
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: During a dry stretch, deep, regular watering matters most in two windows: a first-year tree establishing its roots, and the final few weeks of swell before harvest, when most of the fruit's size is set. Water stress in that final swell causes irreversible loss of size and can shrivel the fruit, so soak deeply at the root zone and let the surface dry between waterings rather than sprinkling lightly.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: In a dry spell, deep and steady watering matters most at two times: a young tree in its first year putting down roots, and the final stretch as the fruit fills out before harvest. Let the tree go dry while the plums are sizing and they will stay small or shrivel, so give a deep soak at the ground and let the top dry out between waterings instead of watering a little every day.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot spell: shade exposed plums
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Plums take summer heat well, but fruit on the sun-exposed side of the tree can sunburn during an extreme heat spell, showing as tan, sunken patches that later rot. Keep the tree well watered so it is not also drought-stressed, and avoid stripping interior leaves that shade fruit when you thin. A little canopy over the fruit is protection, not crowding.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Plums handle summer heat well, but during an extreme hot spell the fruit on the sunny side can sunburn, showing as tan, sunken spots that may rot later. Keep the tree watered so heat and dryness are not hitting it at once, and when you thin, leave the leaves that shade the fruit. A bit of leaf cover over the plums protects them.

planting.text_seasoned: Set the graft union two to three inches above the final soil line. Burying it lets the scion root and defeats the rootstock you chose.
planting.text_beginner: Keep the graft joint (where your variety meets its rootstock) two to three inches above the soil. If you bury it, the top can grow its own roots and you lose the benefit of the rootstock.
planting.author: claude_code_scale_perennial

planting.text_seasoned: Decide pollination at planting: a Japanese variety needs a second compatible Japanese cultivar, so plant the pollenizer at the same time; a self-fruitful European can stand alone.
planting.text_beginner: Sort out pollination when you plant. A Japanese plum needs a second, different Japanese plum, so put both in together. A European plum like Stanley can fruit on its own.
planting.author: claude_code_scale_perennial

establishment.text_seasoned: Remove every blossom the first year. A first-year tree that fruits diverts energy from root and framework development it cannot get back.
establishment.text_beginner: Pick off all the flowers the first year. If a brand-new tree fruits, it spends energy it needs for roots and branches, and it cannot make that up.
establishment.author: claude_code_scale_perennial

establishment.text_seasoned: The first season is the tree's most water-sensitive period; water deeply and regularly so roots establish before the tree is left to rainfall.
establishment.text_beginner: Water deeply and often all through the first season. A new tree needs steady water to get its roots going before you can rely on rain.
establishment.author: claude_code_scale_perennial

scaffold_formation.text_seasoned: Match the training form to the type: an open center for the spreading Japanese plums, a modified central leader for the more upright Europeans. Prune more lightly than a peach.
scaffold_formation.text_beginner: Shape the tree to its type: an open, vase shape for the spreading Japanese plums, and a central trunk with spaced branches for the upright European ones. Prune more lightly than you would a peach.
scaffold_formation.author: claude_code_scale_perennial

dormancy.text_seasoned: Winter chill banks next year's bloom. Match your variety to your winters: a high-chill European in a mild winter blooms poorly, a low-chill Japanese in a cold zone blooms too early into frost.
dormancy.text_beginner: The cold of winter sets up next spring's flowers. Pick a variety that fits your winters: a high-chill European plum barely blooms in a mild area, and a low-chill Japanese plum blooms too early into frost in a cold area.
dormancy.author: claude_code_scale_perennial

dormancy.text_seasoned: Bare branches make black knot obvious. Scout for the hard black galls now so you know exactly what to cut out at dormant pruning.
dormancy.text_beginner: You can see black knot best on bare branches. Look for the hard black lumps now so you know what to cut out when you prune.
dormancy.author: claude_code_scale_perennial

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Cut every black knot gall 3 to 4 inches below the visible swelling into clean wood, during the dormant season before the fungus sporulates, and destroy the prunings off site.
dormant_prune.text_beginner: Cut out any black knot 3 to 4 inches below the black lump, into clean wood, while the tree is dormant and before spring. Carry the cut pieces away and burn, bury, or bag them.
dormant_prune.author: claude_code_scale_perennial

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Prune plums more lightly than peaches and preserve the fruiting spurs; plums bear largely on long-lived spurs, so thin to open the canopy rather than heading everything back hard.
dormant_prune.text_beginner: Prune plums more gently than peaches, and keep the short fruiting spurs. Plums fruit on spurs that live several years, so just thin to open the tree instead of cutting everything back hard.
dormant_prune.author: claude_code_scale_perennial

blossom.text_seasoned: Open bloom is the most frost-vulnerable moment of the year, and early-blooming Japanese plums are the most exposed. Track the forecast and cover a small tree if a hard late frost threatens.
blossom.text_beginner: When the tree is in full bloom it is most at risk from frost, and Japanese plums bloom earliest. Watch the forecast, and cover a small tree overnight if a hard late frost is coming.
blossom.author: claude_code_scale_perennial

blossom.text_seasoned: Pollination splits by type: European plums (Stanley, damson) are mostly self-fruitful and set alone, while Japanese plums (Santa Rosa, Methley) are self-unfruitful and need a second compatible Japanese cultivar blooming at the same time.
blossom.text_beginner: European plums like Stanley and damson usually make fruit on their own. Japanese plums like Santa Rosa and Methley almost always need a second, different Japanese plum blooming nearby to set fruit.
blossom.author: claude_code_scale_perennial

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Thin young fruit to one plum every 4 to 6 inches. Thinning is the biggest lever on fruit size, protects limbs, and helps prevent alternate-year bearing; Japanese plums need heavier thinning than European.
fruit_set.text_beginner: Thin the little plums to about one every 4 to 6 inches. Thinning does more for fruit size than anything else, keeps branches from breaking, and evens out the crop year to year. Japanese plums need more thinning than European ones.
fruit_set.author: claude_code_scale_perennial

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Space fruit so plums do not touch. Touching fruit lets brown rot spread from one plum to the next through a cluster.
fruit_set.text_beginner: Leave space between the plums so they do not touch. When plums touch, brown rot spreads from one to the next.
fruit_set.author: claude_code_scale_perennial

harvest.text_seasoned: A tree ripens over one to two weeks; pick in several passes. Ripe plums show full color, wear a dusty bloom, give slightly, and pull free easily; European prunes are ripe when soft to the pit.
harvest.text_beginner: The tree ripens over one to two weeks, so pick it a few times. A ripe plum shows full color, has a dusty coating, gives a little, and pulls off easily; European prune plums are ready when soft to the pit.
harvest.author: claude_code_scale_perennial

harvest.text_seasoned: Handle gently and clear dropped fruit. Bruises are entry points for brown rot, and fruit left to mummify on the tree or ground is next year's inoculum.
harvest.text_beginner: Handle the fruit gently and pick up any that drops. Bruises let brown rot in, and plums left to dry into mummies on the tree or ground spread rot next year.
harvest.author: claude_code_scale_perennial

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A mature standard plum (roughly years 5 and up) commonly yields about 2 to 3 bushels per tree, on the order of 60 to 150 pounds, depending on type, variety, pruning, thinning, pollination, and season. Japanese plums tend to overset and can out-yield European types when well thinned; crop is limited far more by thinning, frost, and pollination than by feeding.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: A grown plum tree (about year 5 onward) usually gives roughly 2 to 3 bushels a year, which is 60 to 150 pounds of fruit. The exact amount depends on the type and variety, how you prune and thin, whether it is well pollinated, and the weather. Japanese plums often set the heaviest, but only if you thin them so the fruit sizes up.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Trees reach full bearing around years 5 to 6 and stay productive for many years after, given annual pruning, thinning, black knot removal, and disease control. Thinning each year also evens out the alternate-year (biennial) bearing plums are prone to.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: A plum tree hits its full production around years 5 to 6 and keeps producing for years after, as long as you prune, thin, cut out black knot, and manage disease each year. Thinning every year also helps keep the tree from swinging between a huge crop one year and almost none the next.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Expect no crop in the planting year and little to none in year 2. Remove any fruit that sets early so the tree puts its energy into roots and framework; the first meaningful harvest typically comes in years 3 to 5, with full bearing by years 5 to 6.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Do not expect plums the first year, or really the second. If a few fruit form early, pick them off so the young tree can build roots and strong branches. Your first real harvest usually comes in years 3 to 5, with full crops by years 5 to 6.
factors_seasoned: type and variety
pollination (European self-fruitful vs Japanese cross-pollination)
fruit thinning
annual pruning and black knot removal
winter chill accumulation
late-frost damage at bloom
disease and insect control
tree age and establishment

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No moon-phase planting preference is asserted. Extension sources do not support timing plum planting or care by lunar phase; site, chill matching, pollination pairing, and frost avoidance govern outcomes.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Tree bloomed well but set little or no fruit
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The tree flowered but I got almost no plums
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The tree flowered heavily but few or no plums formed. On plum the first thing to check is pollination, because it splits by type: a Japanese plum (Santa Rosa, Methley, Burbank) is usually self-unfruitful and needs a second compatible Japanese cultivar blooming at the same time, so a lone Japanese tree, or one whose partner bloomed at a different time, sets almost nothing. European plums (Stanley, Italian prune, damson) are mostly self-fruitful and should set alone. The other common cause is a late frost on the early bloom (Japanese plums are especially exposed), and in mild-winter areas too few chill hours give a weak, uneven bloom. The fixes are a matched pollenizer, a frost-aware site, and a variety whose chill suits your winters.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The tree bloomed but barely fruited. On plums the first thing to check is pollination, and it depends on the type. A Japanese plum (like Santa Rosa or Methley) usually needs a second, different Japanese plum flowering at the same time, so a single Japanese tree sets almost nothing on its own. European plums (like Stanley and damson) usually fruit by themselves. The other common causes are a late frost on the early flowers and, in mild-winter areas, too little winter cold. The fixes are a matching partner tree, a spot less prone to frost, and a variety whose chill fits your winters.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: If it is a Japanese plum, add a compatible Japanese pollenizer that blooms at the same time (Santa Rosa and Methley are reliable); confirm bloom overlap, keep a frost cover ready, and check the variety's chill requirement fits your region.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: If it is a Japanese plum, plant a second Japanese variety that blooms at the same time (Santa Rosa or Methley work well); make sure both flower together, keep a cover handy for frost, and check the variety suits your winters.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Hard black warty galls on the branches
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Black lumpy growths on the branches
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Hard, black, elongated warty galls have appeared along twigs and branches, girdling and killing the wood beyond them. This is black knot, the signature disease of plum, caused by the fungus Apiosporina morbosa. Growers often reach for a spray, but the galls are already established; the effective action is to cut them out. Prune each gall 3 to 4 inches below the visible swelling into clean wood during the dormant season before the fungus sporulates, remove and destroy the prunings, and deal with any wild or neglected Prunus nearby that re-infect the tree each spring.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Hard, black, warty lumps have grown along the branches, and the branch beyond them is dying. This is black knot, the classic plum disease, caused by a fungus. Spraying will not fix the lumps that are already there; the fix is to cut them out. Prune each one 3 to 4 inches below the black lump while the tree is bare in winter, carry the pieces away and destroy them, and clean up or remove any wild plums and cherries nearby that keep re-infecting your tree.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Scout the bare branches every dormant season and remove every knot 3 to 4 inches into clean wood before growth resumes; clean up nearby wild Prunus and consider a less-susceptible cultivar when you replant.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Check the bare branches every winter and cut out every knot before spring, cutting well below the lump; clean up nearby wild plums and cherries, and choose a more resistant variety next time.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Many small, poor-quality plums (and alternate-year bearing)
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Lots of tiny plums, or a big crop only every other year
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The tree carried a heavy crop of small, poorly sized fruit, or it swings between a huge crop one year and almost none the next. Plums, especially Japanese types, overset badly, and an unthinned tree divides its resources among too many fruit and locks into alternate-year (biennial) bearing. It is easy to assume the tree needs more feeding, but the limiting factor is fruit number, not inputs. The corrective action is thinning: remove young fruit early to about one plum every 4 to 6 inches so the remainder size properly and the tree bears more evenly year to year.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The tree had lots of small plums, or it gives a big crop one year and almost nothing the next. Plums, especially Japanese ones, set far more fruit than they can size, and a tree that is not thinned splits its energy among too many and falls into bearing only every other year. More food will not fix it; the problem is too many plums. The fix is thinning: remove the small fruit early to about one every 4 to 6 inches so the rest grow large and the crop evens out.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Thin young fruit early and firmly to one plum every 4 to 6 inches, heaviest on Japanese types; this does more for size and for evening out the crop than any feeding.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Thin the small fruit early to about one every 4 to 6 inches, more on Japanese plums. This one step does more for size and for evening out the crop than extra feeding.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Gummy ooze and frass at the base of the trunk
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Sticky gum and sawdust at the bottom of the trunk
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Gummy ooze mixed with sawdust-like frass has appeared at the soil line, sometimes mounded. This is the signature of peachtree borer, which also attacks plum; the larvae tunnel in the inner bark at the crown. Plums gum in response to many stresses, so the ooze alone is sometimes dismissed as sap, but the frass is the tell that larvae are inside, and a young tree can be girdled and killed. Expose the crown, locate the entry holes, and kill the larvae by hand, then protect the trunk base from the wounds that attract egg-laying.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Sticky gum mixed with what looks like wet sawdust (frass) has shown up where the trunk meets the soil, sometimes in a little mound. This is the sign of the peachtree borer, which also attacks plums; the larvae tunnel in the bark at the base. Plums ooze gum for many reasons, so it is easy to shrug off as sap, but the sawdusty frass means larvae are inside, and they can kill a young tree. Scrape away the soil, find the holes, and kill the larvae with a wire, then keep the trunk base free of wounds.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Inspect the soil line each late summer for fresh gum and frass, keep mowers and trimmers off the trunk base, and worm out any larvae promptly before they girdle the tree.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Check the base of the trunk every late summer for fresh gum and frass, keep mowers and trimmers away from it, and dig out any larvae right away before they ring the trunk.

succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Succession planting does not apply to plum. It is a permanent tree that occupies its site for many years and bears once each season as the fruit ripens, so there is no staggered re-sowing to schedule the way there is for a short-season annual crop.

open_findings.summary: crop-level self_fertile=true / needs_pollinizer=false defaults to the EUROPEAN case; the pollination prose + varieties table carry the full European-self / Japanese-needs-pollinizer split. A type-aware pollination flag is owed at the variety-delta pass so a consumer reading only the boolean is not misled for Japanese plums.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: Wave-1 stone-fruit cert (2026-07-02): parallel per-crop source-truth review (CC agents, WebFetch of the cited T1 pages) confirmed the pollination call + chill + signature disease; pollination pinned to its cited page under A38; open_findings record the modeled/deferred items.

crops.description_seasoned: Plum is a deciduous stone-fruit tree grown in two main types that behave quite differently.
