failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Pick mature but FIRM (upward-twist detachment, lightening ground color), cool-store to satisfy post-harvest chilling, then ripen at room temperature and eat promptly once the neck softens.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Next time pick the pears while still firm and green, give them a cold rest, then ripen them on the counter and eat them soon after they soften.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Sparse, delayed, or straggly bloom
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Few flowers, or flowers very late
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: A high-chill variety grown in a warm-winter zone did not accumulate enough chill to break dormancy normally, giving delayed, uneven, weak bloom and poor set. European pears need more chill than apples, so the mismatch is easy to make.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The tree barely flowered, or flowered oddly late and patchy. This usually means the variety needs more winter cold than your area gives, and pears need more cold than apples.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Match variety chill to your winters: in warm zones choose low-chill cultivars (Hood, Kieffer, Orient).
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Pick a low-chill pear variety suited to mild winters, like Hood, Kieffer, or Orient. The right variety for your climate flowers normally.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Sticky leaves with black sooty mold
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Sticky, blackened leaves and shoots
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Pear psylla nymphs fed heavily and exuded honeydew that grew black sooty mold, scorching leaves and russeting fruit. Outbreaks often follow broad-spectrum sprays that kill the psylla's natural enemies.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The leaves and young pears got coated in sticky goo that turned black and grimy. That is pear psylla, a pear-specific insect; it gets worse if harsh sprays have killed the helpful bugs.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Apply dormant oil in late winter, use insecticidal soap or summer oil in season, and conserve natural enemies by avoiding broad-spectrum insecticides.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Spray dormant oil in late winter to smother the overwintering insects, use insecticidal soap during the season, and avoid harsh sprays that kill the good bugs.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Heavy crop one year, almost none the next
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: A huge year, then a bare year
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The tree fell into biennial bearing: a heavy crop suppressed next year's flower buds, giving an off year. Some pear varieties are naturally prone to it.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: One year the tree was loaded, the next it had almost none. Pears can get into this on-and-off rhythm when they over-crop.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Thin fruit consistently every year (about one per cluster) so the tree sets flower buds for the following season and crops more evenly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Thin the young pears every single year, even in a big year. Leaving fewer pears helps the tree make flower buds for next year and evens out the crops.

succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Not applicable. Succession planting (re-sowing in waves for a continuous harvest) is an annual-vegetable practice. Pear is a perennial tree that holds its site for decades and bears once a year, so there is no succession to schedule; continuity comes from variety choice (summer through winter pears) and storage, not replanting.

3.suitability_note_seasoned: Hardy pears survive zone 3 winters, but the standard roster here (hardy to zone 4) makes a dependable crop unlikely, and pear blooms early into late frosts. Chill is abundant, so the tree blooms each spring; reliable fruit takes ultra-hardy cultivars (Ure, Summercrisp) outside this guide.
3.suitability_note_beginner: A pear tree of these varieties can live here, but reliable fruit is a stretch; the tree will still flower each spring. For real fruit this cold, choose an ultra-hardy variety not in this guide.
3.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Bloom often coincides with the last hard frosts, and pear blooms early, so a freeze during open bloom can wipe out the season. Site trees away from low frost pockets.

4.suitability_note_seasoned: The hardiest varieties (Warren) fruit in good years. Late spring frost on the early bloom is the main risk, and the short season favors earlier-ripening summer pears over late winter keepers.
4.suitability_note_beginner: Tough pear varieties produce here in most years. A late frost during flowering is the thing to watch.
4.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Late frost can damage open bloom, and pears bloom early; choose later-blooming hardy varieties and avoid frost pockets.

5.suitability_note_seasoned: Dependable pear country. The full hardy roster fruits well, with ample chill and a long enough season for mid and late varieties.
5.suitability_note_beginner: Pears grow well here. Most varieties will give you a good crop.
5.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Occasional late frost on early bloom in colder years; generally low risk for mid to late bloomers.

6.suitability_note_seasoned: Prime pear growing. Every variety in this guide fruits dependably, with strong chill and a full season for late keepers.
6.suitability_note_beginner: Excellent pear country. Any variety here should do well.
6.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Low frost risk on bloom in most years.

7.suitability_note_seasoned: Reliable pear country. Chill comfortably exceeds every variety's need and the long season ripens late keepers like Bosc and Anjou; mind fire blight in humid pockets.
7.suitability_note_beginner: Pears do well here, including later-ripening kinds. Keep an eye out for fire blight in damp spells.
7.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Late frost on bloom is uncommon at this latitude.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: Good pear country. From the middle of the region south, most pear varieties do well. In the coldest spots, pick the toughest varieties and know that a late frost can sometimes take the early blossoms.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Pear's strong cold-climate range, and a region where the cooler air keeps fire blight and Fabraea lighter than in the South. The full hardy roster fruits dependably from zone 5 south; in zones 3 and 4, lean on the hardiest varieties (Warren, plus the ultra-hardy Ure/Summercrisp outside this roster) and expect frost to cost some early-blooming crops. Plant bare-root dormant trees in early spring once the soil thaws.
northern_tier.chill_basis_seasoned: Cold northern winters bank roughly 700 to 1,600 chill hours, far more than any European pear needs, so chill is never the limiter here. The constraints are growing-season length, winter hardiness, and late spring frost on early bloom.
northern_tier.chill_basis_beginner: Winters here are plenty cold for pears. The challenge is the short summer, winter hardiness, and late spring frosts, not the cold itself.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Cooler Piedmont winters bank ample chill, and fire-blight-resistant varieties (Kieffer, Orient, Moonglow, Ayers) fruit dependably. Disease management through the humid summer is the work, not climate fit; avoid the blight-prone dessert pears.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Pears fruit well in this cooler part of the region IF you choose disease-resistant varieties. Plan on steady care for diseases in summer.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Some risk to early bloomers from a late frost; favor mid-season bloom groups.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Warmer coastal-plain winters meet low and mid chill, fire-blight-resistant varieties (Kieffer, Orient, Hood). Heavy summer fire blight and leaf disease make this the harder end of the region; only resistant varieties succeed.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Lower, warmer parts of the region can grow low-chill, disease-resistant pears, but it takes work. Fire blight is a real challenge in the humid summer.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Mild winters can leave high-chill varieties blooming unevenly, and early bloom risks late frost; choose low-chill, blight-resistant types.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: Pears grow well here if, and only if, you choose disease-resistant varieties like Kieffer, Orient, or Moonglow. The famous dessert pears (Bartlett, Bosc) tend to die of fire blight. Plan on care for diseases through the humid summer.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: Pears are one of the more reliable tree fruits for the humid Southeast, but ONLY with fire-blight-resistant varieties (Kieffer, Orient, Moonglow, Ayers, Warren). Bartlett, Bosc, and Comice usually fail here to blight. Disease management through the warm, humid season is the real work, not climate fit; chill is adequate across most of the region.
se_gulf.chill_basis_seasoned: Southeastern winters bank roughly 350 to 1,000 chill hours, enough for most pear varieties; the binding constraint is fire blight and summer leaf disease, not chill. Match variety chill to your local winter and prioritize blight resistance.
se_gulf.chill_basis_beginner: Winters here give enough cold for most pear varieties. The real challenge is disease, especially fire blight, so resistant varieties matter most.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Classic Bartlett country. Northern valley winters bank enough chill for most of the roster, and long, hot, dry summers ripen the crop and keep disease low.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Pears grow very well in the cooler, northern part of the valley, this is prime pear ground.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Late frost is an occasional risk for early bloomers in the colder northern valley.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Southern valley winters meet mid and low chill varieties (Bartlett, Hood, Kieffer) dependably; the hot, dry season favors early to mid ripening and keeps fire blight low.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Pears fruit well here. In the warmer south valley, pick mid- and lower-chill varieties for the most reliable crops.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Generally low frost risk; protect the earliest blooms in colder pockets.

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: Excellent pear country. Hot, dry summers mean fewer disease problems than in wetter climates. In the southern valley, lean toward lower-chill varieties.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: Prime European pear country: the Sacramento River delta and interior valleys are among the most productive pear regions in the country (Bartlett above all). Long, hot, dry summers keep disease low and ripen the crop; the full roster fruits in the cooler north valley, and low to mid chill varieties carry the warmer south valley.
ca_interior.chill_basis_seasoned: Central Valley winters bank roughly 300 to 1,100 chill hours, higher in the Sacramento north than the southern San Joaquin. Most of the roster fruits, with the southern valley favoring lower-chill selections as winter chill trends down.
ca_interior.chill_basis_beginner: Valley winters give a moderate to good amount of cold, enough for most pear varieties, with more in the north than the south.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Strong inland pear country (Lake County, inland Mendocino) with a long Bartlett history. Enough chill for low and mid chill varieties; cool, relatively dry summers suit pears well.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Pears grow well a little inland from the coast, this region has a long pear history. Choose low- to mid-chill varieties and a sunnier, less foggy spot.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Spring frost is a minor risk inland; the earliest blooms are most exposed.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: The immediate, fog-cooled coast banks too little winter chill for even low-chill European pears in most years. Trees survive and may bloom in cold winters, but fruit set is unreliable; move inland for a dependable crop.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Pear trees live and sometimes flower right on the coast, but a real crop is unreliable because winters are so mild. Move a little inland for fruit.
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: The limiter is too little winter chill, not frost. In most years the immediate coast does not chill even low-chill pears enough to crop.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: Pears grow well a little inland from the coast. Right at the foggy coast, winters are too mild for a dependable crop, so stay inland and choose low-chill varieties.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: A strong coastal pear region inland (Lake County and Mendocino have a long Bartlett history) where chill, not winter survival, sets the variety list. Right at the fog-cooled coast, winter chill barely clears even low-chill pears, so the immediate coast is a survive-but-rarely-fruit edge.
ca_north_coast.chill_basis_seasoned: North-coast winters bank roughly 150 to 800 chill hours, with cooler inland valleys at the high end and the immediate, fog-cooled coast at the low end. Inland sites fruit the roster; the coast itself sits below even low-chill pear needs in many years.
ca_north_coast.chill_basis_beginner: Winters near the coast are mild, so cold can be limited. Inland valleys get more chill than the immediate coast.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Inland south-coast valleys bank just enough chill for the lowest-chill varieties (Hood, Kieffer). Workable with the right variety; standard high-chill pears never break dormancy properly here.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Low-chill pear varieties like Hood and Kieffer grow in the inland valleys here. Standard pears will not fruit.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is a minor concern; too little chill is the real limit, so choose the lowest-chill varieties first.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: The immediate coast banks only about 50 to 350 chill hours, below even the lowest-chill European pear in most years. Trees survive and may bloom, but do not set a dependable crop; this is past the warm edge of the species.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Pear trees can live right on the coast but will not fruit dependably, winters are simply too mild even for low-chill kinds.
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: The limiter is too little winter chill, not frost. The immediate coast sits below even the lowest-chill pear's need.

ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: A little inland, low-chill pears like Hood and Kieffer can fruit. Right by the ocean, winters are too mild for a dependable crop. Pick the lowest-chill varieties and a spot away from the immediate coast.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: Inland valleys grow low-chill pears (Hood, Kieffer) acceptably; the immediate coast is below even low-chill needs and does not earn a dependable crop. This is the warm-and-mild edge of European pear's range, where variety choice is narrow and tied to your exact distance from the coast.
ca_south_coast.chill_basis_seasoned: South-coast winters bank as little as 50 to 350 chill hours at the coast and 200 to 550 inland. Only low-chill varieties (near 200 to 350 hours) are workable, and the immediate coast sits below even those.
ca_south_coast.chill_basis_beginner: Winters here are mild, and cold is the main limit on pears. Inland is colder than the coast. Choose low-chill varieties, and know the immediate coast is too mild.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Desert valley floors bank only about 150 to 400 chill hours, below even low-chill European pears in most years, and summer heat plus fire-blight pressure compound it. Trees may survive and bloom but rarely fruit.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Only the lowest-chill pears even attempt this, and most years they will not fruit. Winters are too mild and summers too harsh.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Too little winter chill plus extreme summer heat make a crop unreliable; this is past European pear's warm edge.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: The hottest, lowest desert banks only about 100 to 300 chill hours, below even the lowest-chill European pear. Trees may survive but set no dependable fruit, and extreme heat further stresses any crop.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Pear trees can survive in the lowest desert but essentially never produce a real crop. Winters are too mild and summers too extreme.
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Too little winter chill plus extreme summer heat make a crop unreliable; this is the hottest, mildest-winter edge.

ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: Pears are a poor fit for the California desert. Winters are too mild to give enough chill, and summers are brutally hot. A tree may live but will rarely fruit.
ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: European pear is essentially out of range in the low California desert: winter chill is too short for even the lowest-chill cultivars in most years, and extreme summer heat plus fire-blight pressure compound it. Trees may survive and bloom in mild years but do not set a dependable crop.
ca_desert.chill_basis_seasoned: Low-desert winters (Coachella, Imperial) bank only about 100 to 400 chill hours, below the requirement of even low-chill European pears in most years; intense summer heat further stresses any crop.
ca_desert.chill_basis_beginner: Desert winters are too short and mild to give pears the cold they need, so they rarely fruit here.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Elevation banks enough chill for mid-chill varieties (Bartlett, Bosc, Comice) plus low-chill types, and dry air keeps fire blight and Fabraea low. Late spring frost and summer sun on young bark are the practical constraints.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Pears fruit well in these higher, drier areas, where the dry air keeps disease down. Water steadily and guard against late frosts.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Late spring frost at elevation can damage early bloom; favor mid to late bloom groups and avoid frost pockets.

warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: Pears grow well in these higher, drier areas, where the dry air keeps disease down. Watch for late spring frosts, water regularly, and protect young trees from strong sun.
warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: Elevation gives this arid region enough chill for a solid variety list, and the dry air keeps fire blight and Fabraea low, a genuinely good pear climate (much of New Mexico, west Texas, the inland intermountain west). The key risks are late spring frost on early bloom and intense sun on young bark; irrigation is essential.
warm_arid.chill_basis_seasoned: High-desert and inland arid winters bank roughly 450 to 850 chill hours, more than the low deserts because of elevation, enough for mid-chill varieties alongside low-chill types.
warm_arid.chill_basis_beginner: Higher, drier areas get a fair amount of winter cold, enough for many pear varieties. A late frost in spring is the thing to watch.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Low-desert winters bank only about 100 to 400 chill hours, below even low-chill European pears in most years, and extreme summer heat plus fire blight finish the case. Trees may survive but rarely crop; choose low-chill apples or other fruit instead.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Pears rarely fruit in the Arizona low desert, winters are too mild for the chill they need and summers are too hot.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Heat and sunburn, not frost, are the hazards, but too little chill is the binding limit on fruit.

low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: Pears are a poor choice for the Arizona low desert. Winters are too mild to give enough chill and summers are too hot, so trees rarely fruit.
low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: European pear does not fruit dependably in the Arizona low desert: winter chill (around 100 to 400 hours) falls below even low-chill pear needs in most years, and extreme summer heat plus fire blight finish the case. Trees may survive but rarely crop; the desert is far better suited to low-chill apples or other fruit.
low_desert_az.chill_basis_seasoned: Arizona low-desert winters (Phoenix, Tucson) average about 100 to 400 chill hours, below the requirement of even low-chill European pears in most years.
low_desert_az.chill_basis_beginner: Desert winters here give too little cold for European pears to fruit reliably.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: Central-peninsula winters bank only about 50 to 150 chill hours, below the roughly 200-hour floor of even the lowest-chill European pears in most years. A tree may survive but does not fruit dependably, so no growing calendar is shown.
10.suitability_note_beginner: A pear tree might survive here, but it will not fruit. Winters are too warm to wake the tree properly. North Florida, outside this zone, can grow a few low-chill pears.

11.suitability_note_seasoned: The southern peninsula banks essentially no winter chill. European pears cannot complete dormancy or set fruit here.
11.suitability_note_beginner: Pears do not grow on the southern Florida peninsula. There is no winter chill to wake the tree.

fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: Pears are not a good fit for the Florida peninsula. The winters are too warm for the tree to fruit. North Florida can grow a few low-chill pears, but the peninsula proper cannot.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: Outside European pear's range. UF/IFAS limits pear growing to north and north-central Florida (with low-chill, blight-resistant selections); the central-to-southern peninsula does not bank enough winter chill for dependable bloom or fruit set, and the southern tip none at all.
fl_peninsula.chill_basis_seasoned: The Florida peninsula banks well under 150 chill hours, dropping to near zero in the south, below the requirement of even low-chill European pears.
fl_peninsula.chill_basis_beginner: Winters on the Florida peninsula are too mild for pears, even the lowest-chill kinds need more cold than this region provides.

11.suitability_note_seasoned: No appreciable winter chill at reachable elevations. European pears cannot break dormancy here, so the tree neither blooms reliably nor fruits.
11.suitability_note_beginner: Pears will not fruit in Hawaii. There is no cold winter to wake the tree.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: Pears are not suited to Hawaii. The climate never gets cold enough in winter for the tree to fruit. Tropical fruits are the right choice here.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: Outside European pear's range. With no meaningful winter chill at reachable elevations, pears cannot complete dormancy or set fruit. The verdict below is honest rather than a fabricated planting window; tropical fruits are the right choice here.
hawaii_tropical.chill_basis_seasoned: Hawaii's tropical lowlands bank essentially no winter chill. Pears require a cold dormant period to bloom, which this climate does not supply at any reachable elevation.
hawaii_tropical.chill_basis_beginner: Hawaii does not get cold enough in winter for pears. They need a real cold season to fruit, and this climate stays warm year round.

crops.description_seasoned: A long-lived deciduous fruit tree (Pyrus communis) grown for fresh-eating, dessert, and storage fruit. European pear is a cross-pollination crop: most cultivars are self-unfruitful, so you plant two different varieties whose bloom periods overlap and rely on bees to move pollen between them (a few, like Bartlett and Anjou, are partially self-fruitful in mild climates but still crop better with a pollinizer). The signature difference from apple is at harvest: European pears ripen OFF the tree. Pick them mature but firm and green, give them a cool rest, then ripen at room temperature; a pear left to ripen on the branch goes mealy and rotten at the core. Fire blight is the major disease, worst in warm, humid regions, so cultivar and rootstock resistance matter. Chill requirement is variety-set, and rootstock choice sets mature size and how soon the tree bears.
crops.description_beginner: Pear is a fruit tree that lives for decades, often longer than an apple. Two things make pears special. First, most pear trees cannot make fruit from their own flowers, so you need a second, different pear variety nearby that blooms at the same time, with bees to carry the pollen. Second, and this surprises people: you do NOT let pears ripen on the tree. You pick them while they are still firm and green but full-sized, then let them finish ripening on the counter. A pear left on the tree turns brown and mushy in the middle while the outside still looks fine. The biggest disease to know about is fire blight, which is worst in warm, damp places, so picking a resistant variety helps a lot.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: European pears are picked MATURE BUT FIRM, not tree-ripe: full varietal size with the ground color shifting from grass-green toward a lighter yellow-green, lenticels turning corky and tan, and the fruit detaching when lifted and twisted upward to horizontal. Tree-ripening ruins them, the flesh browns and breaks down at the core (stone-cell grittiness) while the skin still looks sound. After picking, most varieties need a cool rest (near 30 to 40°F) before they will ripen evenly at room temperature. First meaningful crop typically comes around year 4 to 6, rootstock-dependent.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: A pear is ready to PICK, not eat, when it has reached full size, its green has started to lighten, and it snaps off the branch easily when you lift it and twist it up to horizontal. It will still be hard, and that is correct. Do not wait for it to soften on the tree, a tree-ripened pear rots from the inside out and turns gritty and brown at the core. Bring the firm pears indoors, give them a week or two somewhere cool, then let them finish on the counter until the neck gives slightly to a gentle press. Do not expect a real crop until about the fourth to sixth year after planting.
crops.bloom_time_seasoned: European pears bloom in early spring after their chill requirement is met, generally a few days BEFORE apples, which makes the open bloom more exposed to late frost. Cultivars are staggered from early to late over roughly two weeks; bloom timing governs cross-pollination, since only varieties whose windows overlap can pollinate each other. Pear blossoms are less attractive to bees than many fruits (low nectar), so good pollination depends on warm, calm bloom weather and strong bee activity.
crops.bloom_time_beginner: Pear trees flower in early spring, usually a little earlier than apples, which means a late frost is more likely to catch the open blossoms. Different varieties bloom a few days apart, spread over about two weeks, and two trees can only pollinate each other if they bloom at the same time. Pear flowers are not a bee favorite, so warm, calm weather during bloom really helps the bees do their work and set a good crop.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: As a species European pear is reliably cold-hardy through USDA zone 4 (a touch less hardy than apple), and this guide's roster fruits dependably zones 5 to 8. In zone 4 the roster survives and fruits in good years; in zone 3 it survives but is not rated for reliable fruit, which there takes ultra-hardy cultivars (Ure, Summercrisp, Golden Spice, Patten) outside this roster. At the warm edge, zones 9 and warmer succeed only with low-chill, fire-blight-resistant cultivars (Hood, Kieffer, Orient), and the frost-free low desert and tropics bank too little chill for any European pear to fruit. Across the humid Southeast, fire blight, not cold, is the binding constraint.
crops.hardiness_notes_beginner: Pear trees handle cold winters well, down to about zone 4, though they are slightly less tough than apples. The varieties in this guide give reliable fruit in zones 5 through 8. In zone 4 they will live and fruit in good years; in colder zone 3 you would want a special extra-hardy variety not listed here (like Ure or Summercrisp). In warm zones (9 and up) choose a low-chill, disease-resistant variety like Hood, Kieffer, or Orient, and know that the frost-free deep South and tropics simply do not get cold enough for pears to fruit.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Chill hours are the accumulated hours between about 32 and 45°F during winter dormancy that a tree must bank before it breaks bud and flowers normally in spring. European pear's requirement is set by the cultivar: this guide's roster runs from about 200 hours (low-chill Hood) through the classic 600 to 800 hours (Bartlett, Bosc, Anjou, Comice). As a group European pears need MORE chill than apples, which is why they are less at home in the warm-winter South than apples or Asian pears. Match the variety's chill need to what your winters reliably deliver: too little chill gives delayed, straggly bloom and poor fruit set.
crops.chill_hours_note_beginner: Pear trees need a stretch of winter cold before they will flower well in spring, measured in 'chill hours' (hours between about 32 and 45°F). Different pear varieties need different amounts: a low-chill kind like Hood needs only about 200 hours, while the familiar Bartlett and Bosc need 600 to 800. As a rule, pears want a bit more winter cold than apples do. Pick a variety whose chill need matches your winters; in a mild-winter area, choose a low-chill variety or the tree will bloom poorly and set little fruit.
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: European pear is largely self-unfruitful: a lone tree, or two trees of the same cultivar, sets little or no fruit. Plant a second, genetically different European pear whose bloom overlaps, within about 50 to 100 ft, with bees to move pollen between them (pear flowers are low in nectar, so strong bee activity matters more than for apples). A few cultivars (Bartlett, Anjou) are PARTIALLY self-fruitful and will set a light crop alone in mild climates, but all of them yield heavier, more regular crops with a pollinizer. Bloom groups must overlap to cross. Mind the known incompatibilities: Bartlett and Seckel will not pollinate each other, so pair each with a third variety (Bosc, Comice, or Moonglow). One caution: a few cultivars (Magness) produce sterile pollen, cannot serve as a pollinizer, and themselves need two other compatible varieties nearby. European and Asian pears can cross only when their bloom genuinely overlaps, which is often unreliable.
crops.pollinator_notes_beginner: This is the most important thing about growing pears: one pear tree alone usually will not make fruit. Pear flowers need pollen from a DIFFERENT pear variety, carried by bees. So plan to plant two different kinds of European pear, not two of the same, within about 50 to 100 ft of each other, and make sure they bloom at the same time. A couple of varieties (Bartlett, Anjou) can set a small crop on their own in mild areas, but even they do much better with a partner. Watch out for one famous mismatch: Bartlett and Seckel cannot pollinate each other, so give each of them a different partner like Bosc or Comice. And a few varieties (like Magness) cannot pollinate anything and need two partners themselves, so ask the nursery before you rely on one as your second tree.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: In the planting year, prioritize root and scaffold establishment over fruit. Remove any blossoms that open the first spring so the tree spends its energy on roots and framework rather than a few pears. Keep the young tree evenly watered through its first summer and stake it if it is on a dwarfing or quince rootstock. Prune lightly and only in dry weather, fresh cuts on a young pear are an entry point for fire blight, and go easy on nitrogen for the same reason. Expect no crop in year 1; a first meaningful harvest comes around year 4 to 6, rootstock-dependent.
crops.year_one_notes_beginner: Do not let your pear tree fruit in its first year. If flowers open that first spring, pinch them off. It feels wrong, but a young tree that skips fruiting puts its energy into roots and branches and becomes much stronger. Water it steadily through the first summer, and stake it if it is a small (dwarf or quince) tree. Prune only a little, and only when the weather is dry, because cuts in damp weather invite fire blight. Go easy on fertilizer too, since lots of soft growth catches that disease. You will not get pears the first year, and that is normal. Your first real crop is usually around the fourth to sixth year.

pollination.notes_seasoned: European pear is largely self-unfruitful: a lone tree, or two trees of the same cultivar, sets little or no fruit. Plant a second, genetically different European pear whose bloom overlaps, within about 50 to 100 ft, with bees to move pollen between them (pear flowers are low in nectar, so strong bee activity matters more than for apples). A few cultivars (Bartlett, Anjou) are PARTIALLY self-fruitful and will set a light crop alone in mild climates, but all of them yield heavier, more regular crops with a pollinizer. Bloom groups must overlap to cross. Mind the known incompatibilities: Bartlett and Seckel will not pollinate each other, so pair each with a third variety (Bosc, Comice, or Moonglow). One caution: a few cultivars (Magness) produce sterile pollen, cannot serve as a pollinizer, and themselves need two other compatible varieties nearby. European and Asian pears can cross only when their bloom genuinely overlaps, which is often unreliable.

Pear flowers need pollen from a DIFFERENT pear variety, carried by bees. So plan to plant two different kinds of European pear, not two of the same, within about 50 to 100 ft of each other, and make sure they bloom at the same time. A couple of varieties (Bartlett, Anjou) can set a small crop on their own in mild areas, but even they do much better with a partner. Watch out for one famous mismatch: Bartlett and Seckel cannot pollinate each other, so give each of them a different partner like Bosc or Comice. And a few varieties (like Magness) cannot pollinate anything and need two partners themselves, so ask the nursery before you rely on one as your second tree.

crops.establishment_note: Roughly the first four years are establishment: the tree builds roots and a scaffold of main branches before it carries a real crop. Remove first-year blossoms, train the framework with light annual dormant pruning (pear is prone to fire blight, so prune conservatively and only in dry weather), and do not expect meaningful yield until bearing begins (around year 4 to 6, rootstock-dependent and later than apple).
crops.recommended_rootstock_note: OHxF 87 (semi-dwarf) is the default backyard pick for European pear: it makes a manageable tree slightly smaller than a Bartlett seedling, bears reasonably young, and is one of the most productive of the fire-blight-tolerant Old Home x Farmingdale series, which also resists pear decline. For the smallest patio or container tree choose a quince stock or OHxF 333 (but note quince is graft-incompatible with Bartlett, Bosc, Seckel, and others without an Old Home interstem, and is not winter-hardy in cold regions); for a large, low-maintenance standard, choose Bartlett or Winter Nelis seedling, accepting a longer wait to bear.

rootstock_options.name: Quince (with interstem)
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask which rootstock the tree is on, and if it is quince, whether your variety is grafted with an Old Home interstem (Bartlett, Bosc, and Seckel are graft-incompatible with quince directly).
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: Quince (e.g., Provence/Quince A or C) is the dwarfing pear rootstock, about 8 to 12 ft, precocious and container-suitable, and induces early, heavy bearing. Two real cautions: it is graft-incompatible with several major cultivars (Bartlett, Bosc, Seckel) unless an Old Home interstem is used, and it is poorly cold-hardy, so it is a mild-climate or container choice, not for the cold North.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: Quince makes the smallest pear tree, about 8 to 12 ft, and gives fruit soonest. Two catches: several popular varieties (Bartlett, Bosc, Seckel) will not graft directly onto quince and need a middle 'bridge' piece, and quince roots are not very cold-hardy, so it suits mild climates or pots best.

rootstock_options.name: OHxF 333
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask which rootstock the tree is on and whether it needs staking.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: OHxF 333 is a semi-dwarfing Old Home x Farmingdale stock, about half to two-thirds standard size, with strong resistance to fire blight, collar rot, woolly pear aphid, and pear decline. Productivity and fruit size run a touch lower than OHxF 87, but it is the best size-controlled, disease-tolerant choice and works in a large container.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: OHxF 333 makes a medium-small tree, about 10 to 14 ft, and resists fire blight and pear decline. It fruits a bit lighter than OHxF 87 but is a great disease-tolerant pick for a smaller yard or a big pot.

rootstock_options.name: OHxF 87
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask which rootstock the tree is on and whether it needs staking.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: OHxF 87 is the workhorse backyard pear rootstock: semi-dwarf at slightly smaller than a Bartlett seedling, precocious for the series, and one of its best producers, with strong fire-blight and pear-decline resistance. The common default for a home European pear.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: OHxF 87 makes a medium tree, the usual backyard choice. It fruits fairly young for a pear, produces well, and resists fire blight and pear decline. A reliable all-rounder.

rootstock_options.name: OHxF 97
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask which rootstock the tree is on and whether it needs staking.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: OHxF 97 is a larger, semi-vigorous to near-standard Old Home x Farmingdale stock, hardy and cold-resilient, with strong resistance to fire blight and pear decline, but less precocious than OHxF 87. A durable choice for a bigger in-ground tree, especially in colder regions.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: OHxF 97 makes a larger tree, about 16 to 22 ft, and is tough and cold-hardy with good disease resistance. It is slower to start fruiting than OHxF 87, but a solid pick if you have the room, especially up North.

rootstock_options.name: Bartlett / Winter Nelis seedling
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask which rootstock the tree is on (seedling makes a full-size tree) and whether it needs staking (usually not).
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: Seedling pear rootstock (Bartlett or Winter Nelis, or vigorous Pyrus species) makes a full-size, deeply anchored, long-lived standard tree, about 25 to 40 ft, needing no staking but the slowest to bear (around year 6 to 10) and large to spray, prune, and harvest. Vigorous and adaptable, but it offers less of the OHxF disease tolerance. Choose it for a permanent landscape tree where ultimate size is acceptable.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: A 'standard' seedling rootstock makes a big, classic pear tree, about 25 to 40 ft, that stands on its own and lives a very long time. The downsides: it takes the longest to fruit (around year 6 to 10) and is tall to reach. Pick it only if you want a large tree and have the space.

pet_safe.note: The flesh is fine, but the seeds contain the same cyanide compounds as apple seeds and are best kept from cats, dogs, and horses.

crops.name: Pear (Asian)

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Asian pear trees grow best in deep, fertile soil that drains well but holds some moisture, a loam or clay-loam is ideal. Like other pears they tolerate heavier, wetter ground better than most fruit trees, including some clay, but they still will not stand in water, so avoid a spot where puddles linger. If your soil is very sandy and dries out fast, work in compost and plan to water more, since a thirsty tree drops fruit.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Asian pear wants a deep, fertile loam to clay-loam with steady moisture and moderate organic matter. It is more forgiving of heavy, moisture-retentive soils than apple or stone fruit and tolerates a fairly wide pH band, but it still will not accept standing water, which drives crown and root rots. On a wet site, plant on a low berm. One important trade-off: rich soil and heavy nitrogen push the soft, succulent growth that fire blight colonizes, so feed Asian pears lean and favor a fire-blight-tolerant rootstock on any site with disease history.

ph.note_beginner: Asian pear trees like soil that runs from slightly acidic to neutral, a pH around 6.0 to 7.0 (pH just measures how acidic or alkaline soil is, where 7.0 is neutral). Test your soil before planting, since it is much easier to adjust the pH now than after the tree is in the ground. Garden lime raises a low pH; garden sulfur lowers a high one. Your local extension office can test a sample for you.
ph.note_seasoned: Asian pear does best at a pH of about 6.0 to 7.0 and tolerates roughly 5.5 to 7.5. Test the soil before planting and adjust the whole root zone, not just the hole, because correcting pH around an established tree is slow. Lime raises a low pH; elemental sulfur lowers a high one. Well outside this band, iron and manganese availability falls and new growth yellows between the veins.

fertilizer.timing: early spring before bud break
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Feed lightly in early spring before bud break, guided by shoot growth: a healthy young pear makes about 12 to 18 inches of new shoot growth a year, so feed to reach that and no more. Excess nitrogen is the classic pear mistake, it drives soft, succulent growth that fire blight runs straight through, and it delays fruiting. Mature trees on fertile soil often need no nitrogen at all. If anything, err on the side of underfeeding a pear.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Feed pear trees once a year, in early spring before the buds open, with a balanced fertilizer, and go light. Too much feeding is the number-one pear mistake: it makes lots of soft new growth that the disease fire blight loves, and it pushes the tree to grow leaves instead of fruit. If the tree is growing well and putting out healthy new branches each year, it may need no feeding at all. When in doubt, use less.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced N-P-K ratio (the three numbers on the bag, nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium) such as 10-10-10 at a modest rate, leaning toward the low end on any vigorous tree to limit fire-blight-prone growth. On fertile ground a pear often wants none.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: The three numbers on a fertilizer bag are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. A balanced one like 10-10-10 is fine for pears, used sparingly. The first number (nitrogen) is the one to keep low, because too much makes soft growth that catches fire blight.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A common home rule is about 1/8 lb of actual nitrogen per year of tree age, capped near 1/2 to 3/4 lb actual N for a mature tree, noticeably leaner than the apple rule because of fire blight. Always follow the label and skip nitrogen entirely in a year of strong shoot growth.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A simple guideline is a small amount that grows a little with the tree's age, following the directions on the bag, and using even less than you would for an apple. When in doubt, feed less, an underfed pear is far healthier than an overfed one.

companions.note_beginner: Pears do not pair with other plants the way vegetables do. For an Asian pear, the neighbor that counts is a second, different Asian pear variety that blooms at the same time, within about 50 to 100 ft, because most Asian pears need another Asian pear nearby to make fruit. Right around the trunk, do the opposite of planting companions: keep grass and other plants away from the base out to the edge of the branches, because they steal water and food from the young tree. Use mulch there instead, and never plant an Asian pear near a black walnut tree, which poisons the soil for it.
companions.note_seasoned: Pear does not companion-plant in the vegetable sense; the interactions that matter are pollination and root competition. The single most important neighbor is a second, bloom-overlapping Asian pear variety (the pollinizer) within about 50 to 100 ft, since most Asian pears are self-unfruitful. At the trunk, the rule reverses: keep turf and aggressive perennials out of the root zone, where grass competes hard with a young tree for water and nitrogen. Maintain a mulched, vegetation-free circle to the dripline, and avoid siting near black walnut, whose juglone is toxic to Asian pear.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: spring bulbs (daffodil)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A ring of daffodils at the drip line is a traditional fruit-tree-guild move with two intended jobs: the early foliage forms a band that helps hold back creeping grass, the tree's main competitor, and daffodils are toxic enough that voles and deer tend to avoid grazing through them to the trunk. They emerge and feed before the canopy leafs out, then go dormant, so they do not compete in summer. Treat this as a useful cultural barrier rather than a measured yield booster.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: The daffodil-ring (grass suppression + rodent/deer deterrence via toxicity) is a well-established permaculture fruit-tree-guild practice grounded in daffodils' real toxicity and spring-ephemeral timing, applied to pear the same way it is to apple; not a measured pear yield/health effect. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Plant a ring of daffodils around your pear tree, out where the branches reach. They come up early in spring, help keep grass from creeping toward the trunk, and because they are poisonous to nibble, they discourage mice and deer. They die back in summer, so they stay out of the tree's way.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: comfrey
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Comfrey is a workhorse of the fruit-tree guild. Its deep taproot pulls from well below the tree's surface feeder roots, so it does not compete for the same water and nutrients, and it shades out grass along the row. Chopped two or three times a season and dropped under the tree, its lush leaves break down into a mineral-rich mulch, and the flowers feed pollinators. The dynamic-accumulator framing is more tradition than proven chemistry, but the practical value as non-competing mulch and grass suppression is real.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Comfrey as chop-and-drop mulch / grass suppressor with a deep non-competing taproot is widely practiced and partly grounded (deep taproot, vigorous biomass); the 'dynamic accumulator' mineral claims are permaculture tradition, not peer-reviewed. Same mechanism whether under apple or pear. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Comfrey is a leafy plant that grows well around fruit trees. Its roots reach deep down, so it does not steal water from the tree, and it crowds out grass. A few times each summer you can cut the big leaves and lay them on the soil under the tree, where they rot down into natural food for it. Its flowers also bring in helpful bees.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: clover (living mulch)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Dutch white clover makes a strong living mulch under pears. As a legume it fixes atmospheric nitrogen through its root symbiosis, feeding the tree slowly while staying low and tolerating harvest foot traffic. It covers the ground to suppress weeds and hold moisture without the aggressive grass competition bare turf brings. Keep it back from the immediate trunk zone, and note it does draw some moisture, so manage it on dry sites. Because pears want lean nitrogen, treat the clover's slow trickle as a feature, not a reason to also fertilize.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Dutch white clover living mulch = legume N-fixation + weed suppression + walkable cover; mechanistically sound and supported by extension/NRCS orchard legume cover-crop work. mechanistic/medium: real mechanism, held at medium because clover-to-tree N transfer magnitude and net water effect vary by site.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: White clover is a low, soft plant you can grow as a living carpet under your pear tree. It pulls nitrogen from the air and feeds it slowly into the soil, while covering the ground to keep weeds down and hold in moisture. It is tough enough to walk on at picking time. Just keep it from growing right against the trunk.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: black walnut
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Black walnut is a definitive bad neighbor for pear. Its roots, hulls, and leaf litter release juglone, an allelopathic compound toxic to many sensitive plants, and pear (like apple) is among those affected, showing decline and dieback within the walnut's root zone. The effect extends well beyond the visible canopy, roughly to the full root spread (commonly cited at fifty-plus feet from a mature tree), so siting matters more than spacing tweaks: keep pears entirely out of a black walnut's root zone.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Juglone allelopathy is a real, well-characterized chemical mechanism; pome fruit including pear is documented as juglone-sensitive across extension sources. mechanistic/high: the mechanism and pome-fruit sensitivity are well established and uncontested.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep pear trees far away from black walnut trees. Black walnuts release a natural chemical called juglone from their roots and leaves that is poisonous to pears and can make them sicken and die. The chemical spreads through the soil well past the walnut's branches, so give them a very wide berth, at least 50 feet from a big walnut.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: turfgrass to the trunk
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Letting turfgrass grow right up to a pear trunk is a quiet but real drag on the tree, especially when young. Grass competes directly for water and nitrogen in the surface zone where the feeder roots sit, slowing growth and delaying bearing, and dense grass and mulch against the trunk harbor voles that girdle bark over winter. Maintain a vegetation-free or mulched strip about two feet out from the trunk (mulch pulled back a few inches off the bark itself).

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Extension guidance consistently prescribes a vegetation-free/mulched zone around young fruit trees and warns of rodent bark damage from grass/mulch at the trunk; the grass-competition effect on young tree growth is well documented for pome fruit. extension_backed/high.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Do not let lawn grass grow right up against your pear tree's trunk. The grass competes with the young tree for water and food, so it grows slower and fruits later. Grass at the trunk also hides mice that can chew the bark in winter. Keep a clear or mulched circle about two feet around the trunk, with the mulch pulled back slightly so it does not touch the bark.

pests.name: Codling moth
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Larvae tunnel into the fruit core, leaving a frass-filled entry hole (often at the calyx end) and brown trails; infested Asian pears drop early or are inedible.
pests.symptoms_beginner: This is the classic 'worm in the fruit.' You find a small hole with brown crumbly stuff (frass) around it, and a tunnel into the core when you cut it open. Bad pears drop early.
pests.cause_seasoned: Cydia pomonella; female moths lay eggs on developing fruit and young leaves near bloom, and hatching larvae bore into the pear. Two or more generations per season in most regions. The same pest attacks apple.
pests.cause_beginner: A small moth lays eggs on the tiny pears in spring; the eggs hatch into caterpillars that crawl into the fruit. There can be two batches a summer, so the problem repeats.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Monitor with pheromone traps to time control; remove and destroy dropped and infested fruit; bag individual fruit; spinosad or kaolin clay on a degree-day/petal-fall schedule. Mating disruption works at larger scale.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick up and throw away every pear that drops, do not leave them under the tree. You can slip paper bags over young pears to keep moths out, and scent traps help you know when to act. Sprays like spinosad work if timed right.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Orchard sanitation (clear dropped fruit and debris), keep nearby abandoned pear or apple trees pruned or removed, and band trunks to catch larvae seeking pupation sites.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep the ground under the tree clean of fallen pears, and wrap a band of cardboard around the trunk to trap crawling caterpillars. Nearby neglected pear or apple trees make it worse.

pests.name: Pear psylla
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Nymphs feed in clusters on shoots and leaves and exude copious sticky honeydew that blackens with sooty mold; heavy feeding causes leaf scorch, premature drop, fruit russeting, and tree decline. The signature pear pest.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Leaves and young pears get coated in a sticky, shiny film that turns black and grimy (sooty mold), and the leaves may scorch and drop. Tiny insects cluster on the new shoots.
pests.cause_seasoned: Cacopsylla pyricola; a small psyllid specific to pear that overwinters as an adult and builds several overlapping generations through the season. Outbreaks follow broad-spectrum sprays that kill its natural enemies.
pests.cause_beginner: A tiny pear-specific insect (a kind of jumping plant louse) that sucks sap and oozes sticky stuff. It can build up fast, especially if bug sprays have wiped out the good bugs that normally keep it down.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Dormant-season horticultural oil to smother overwintering adults and eggs; in-season insecticidal soap or summer oil; conserve natural enemies (anthocorid bugs, lacewings) by avoiding broad-spectrum insecticides; kaolin clay deters egg-laying.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray horticultural oil while the tree is dormant in late winter to smother the overwintering insects, and use insecticidal soap in the growing season. Avoid harsh sprays, which kill the helpful bugs that eat psylla.
pests.prevention_seasoned: A well-timed dormant oil program plus a natural-enemy-friendly spray regime is the backbone of psylla management; avoid the lush nitrogen-pushed growth psylla favors.
pests.prevention_beginner: A good dormant oil spray in late winter and going easy on harsh sprays and fertilizer keep this pear-specific pest in check.

pests.name: Stink bug
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Stink bugs, including the invasive brown marmorated stink bug, pierce developing fruit to feed, leaving dimpled, catfaced pears with hard, corky, pithy brown patches in the flesh under each feeding site. The skin often looks nearly normal while the interior is pitted. Worst near weedy field and woodland borders.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Stink bugs poke the growing pears to feed, leaving dented, lumpy fruit with hard brown corky spots inside. The outside can look mostly fine while the flesh underneath is pitted and dry.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several native stink bugs plus the invasive brown marmorated stink bug (Halyomorpha halys); adults and nymphs feed on fruit from petal fall through harvest, moving in from surrounding weeds, crops, and woodland edges.
pests.cause_beginner: Shield-shaped bugs, including an invasive kind called the brown marmorated stink bug, that suck on the fruit through the season. They move in from nearby weeds, fields, and woods.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Kaolin clay deters feeding; clear weedy and brushy borders that harbor them; hand-pick or trap adults; bagging individual fruit excludes them. Where pressure is high, use a labeled product timed to nymph emergence and conserve natural enemies.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Coating the fruit with kaolin clay (a fine white clay spray) helps keep them off, and clearing weeds and brush around the tree removes their hideouts. You can also slip bags over young fruit to protect them.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Cut back weedy borders and brush piles, monitor with traps from bloom on, and bag fruit where damage recurs. Avoid broad-spectrum sprays so predators keep populations down.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep the area around the tree tidy, since weeds and brush are where they live, watch for them from bloom onward, and bag the fruit if they are a yearly problem.

pests.name: Pear scab
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Olive-green to black velvety spots on leaves, shoots, and fruit; fruit lesions become corky and cracked, and severe infection causes leaf yellowing and early defoliation. The pear analog of apple scab.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Dark, fuzzy olive-to-black spots appear on the leaves and the pears get rough, scabby, cracked patches. In a bad year the tree drops its leaves early.
pests.cause_seasoned: Venturia pyrina; spores overwinter in fallen leaves and infect during wet spring weather, with infection periods driven by leaf wetness and temperature. Distinct from the apple-scab fungus but managed the same way.
pests.cause_beginner: A fungus that survives winter in last year's fallen leaves and spreads in cool, wet spring weather onto the new leaves and fruit.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Apply sulfur or other labeled fungicide on a protective schedule keyed to spring infection periods; far easier to prevent than to cure once established.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Sulfur spray in spring, applied before infection takes hold, is the organic option. Once the spots are everywhere it is too late for that year, so prevention is the game.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Rake and remove fallen leaves in autumn (destroys the overwintering source), prune for airflow, and choose less-susceptible varieties.
pests.prevention_beginner: The single best move is to rake up and remove fallen leaves every autumn, that is where the fungus hides over winter. Prune for good airflow too.

diseases.name: Fire blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Blossoms and shoot tips suddenly wilt, blacken, and die, bending into a characteristic shepherd's-crook; affected branches look scorched, and sunken, oozing cankers form on wood. Asian pear is highly susceptible (20th Century and Niitaka among the worst), and a single warm, wet bloom can kill whole limbs or a young tree.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Branch tips and flower clusters suddenly turn black and look burned, as if scorched by fire, and the tip bends over into a hook. It can kill whole branches or the whole tree. Asian pears catch it easily.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Erwinia amylovora; bacteria infect through open blossoms and tender shoot tips in warm, wet spring weather and spread fastest on lush, nitrogen-pushed growth. It is the single biggest reason European pears fail in the humid South and East.
diseases.cause_beginner: Bacteria that infect through the flowers and soft new shoots in warm, wet spring weather. Fast, soft growth from too much fertilizer makes it much worse. It is the main reason pears struggle in warm, damp climates.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Prune out infected wood at least 8 to 12 inches below visible symptoms, disinfecting tools between cuts, in dry weather; remove badly affected trees. There is no cure once established, management is prevention plus cutting it out.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Cut off the blackened branches well below the damage (about a hand's length past it), wiping your pruners with disinfectant between every cut so you do not spread it, and only in dry weather. There is no spray that cures it.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: The decisive moves are cultivar and rootstock choice: plant more fire-blight-tolerant Asian pears (Shinko, Chojuro) on a tolerant rootstock (the OHxF series, or Pyrus calleryana). Then avoid excess nitrogen, prune only in dry weather, and follow a bloom-time forecast model where available.
diseases.prevention_beginner: The best defense is to choose a more resistant variety (Shinko, Chojuro) on a resistant rootstock, especially where summers are warm and humid. Then go easy on fertilizer (soft growth catches it) and prune only in dry weather.

diseases.name: Pear scab
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Olive to black velvety lesions on leaves and fruit that turn corky and cracked; severe infection yellows leaves and causes early defoliation and scabby, misshapen fruit.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Dark, fuzzy spots on the leaves and rough, scabby, cracked patches on the pears. In a bad year the tree drops its leaves early.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Venturia pyrina; overwinters in fallen leaves and infects during wet spring weather, infection periods set by leaf wetness and temperature.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that overwinters in last year's fallen leaves and spreads onto new leaves and fruit in cool, wet spring weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Sulfur or a labeled fungicide on a protective spring schedule keyed to infection periods; prevention beats cure.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Sulfur spray in spring before the spots appear is the organic route. Once it is widespread it is too late for that year.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rake and remove fallen leaves each autumn, prune for airflow, and choose less-susceptible varieties.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Rake up fallen leaves every fall and prune for good airflow. Resistant varieties rarely need spraying.

diseases.name: Pear decline
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Slow decline, weak growth, small leaves with reddish autumn color, and reduced yield, or in acute cases sudden collapse; driven by a phytoplasma transmitted by pear psylla and expressed through a sensitive rootstock.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The tree slowly weakens over years, with small leaves that redden early in fall and a shrinking crop, or sometimes a sudden collapse. It is tied to the pear psylla insect and to certain rootstocks.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A phytoplasma (a bacteria-like organism) spread by pear psylla; severity depends heavily on rootstock sensitivity, which is why decline-resistant rootstocks (OHxF series) matter.
diseases.cause_beginner: A tiny disease organism carried by the pear psylla insect. How badly a tree is hit depends on its rootstock, so a resistant rootstock is the main protection.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No cure; manage by controlling pear psylla (the vector) and, at planting, choosing a tolerant rootstock (OHxF). Remove severely declining trees.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure once a tree has it. Keep pear psylla under control and, most importantly, start with a resistant rootstock when you plant.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant on a decline-tolerant rootstock (OHxF 87/97/333) and keep psylla populations low; avoid highly sensitive rootstocks.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Buy a tree grown on a resistant rootstock (the OHxF series) and keep pear psylla in check. That is the whole prevention.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Deep, infrequent irrigation: about 1 inch of water per week through the growing season, more in heat and during fruit sizing, tapering off as the tree goes dormant.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water deeply but not too often, aim for about 1 inch a week while the tree is growing and making fruit. Water more in hot, dry spells and less once the leaves drop in fall.
watering.amount_seasoned: Roughly 1 inch per week as a baseline (a deep soak that wets the full root zone), increasing during fruit sizing in mid to late summer; pears drop fruit when droughted at sizing.
watering.amount_beginner: About 1 inch a week. The easiest way is one long, slow soak that gets the water down deep, rather than a quick daily sprinkle.
watering.method_seasoned: Drip or a slow soak at the dripline; keep water off the trunk and crown to avoid collar rot, and mulch to hold moisture (pulled back a few inches from the trunk).
watering.method_beginner: Use a soaker hose or drip line, or let a hose trickle slowly at the edge of the branches. Keep water off the trunk itself, and mulch around the tree (not touching the trunk) to hold moisture in.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing leaves, persistently soggy soil, and root or collar rot at the trunk base signal too much water or poor drainage; pear tolerates wet ground better than most fruit trees but not standing water.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If the leaves yellow and the ground stays soggy, the tree is getting too much water or the soil drains poorly. Rot at the base of the trunk is a warning sign.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting or scorched leaf margins and premature fruit drop in summer indicate drought stress, especially during fruit sizing.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Wilting or dry, brown leaf edges, and small fruit that drops early, mean the tree is too dry, especially in mid to late summer when the pears are filling out.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Establishment: deep-soak 1 to 2 times per week through the first summer to drive root growth; do not let the root ball dry out.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: First-year tree: give it a deep soak once or twice a week all summer so the roots get established. Do not let it dry out.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Fruit sizing: water weekly and consistently as pears bulk up; steady moisture now prevents premature drop and cracking.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: While the pears are growing bigger, water once a week and keep it steady, this is when uneven watering makes fruit drop.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Dormant: minimal irrigation; rely on natural precipitation unless soils are unusually dry over a mild winter.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: In winter, when the tree is bare and resting, you barely need to water at all, rain usually covers it.

watering.method_note_seasoned: Consistent soil moisture during fruit sizing prevents premature drop and cracking; a young tree in its establishment year needs the most attention to even watering.
watering.method_note_beginner: Steady, even watering matters most in the first year and while the pears are growing. Big swings between bone-dry and soaked make fruit drop.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Establishment year (root development) and fruit sizing (mid to late summer) are the critical irrigation windows; dormant-season water needs are minimal.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Two times matter most for watering: the first year after planting, and mid-to-late summer when the pears are filling out. In winter the tree needs almost no water.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Not applicable. Pear is planted as a bare-root dormant tree or a potted nursery tree, not started from seed indoors, so there is no tender seedling to harden off. Plant during dormancy (late winter to early spring) and the tree breaks bud already acclimated to outdoor conditions.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: This step does not apply to pears. Hardening off means slowly getting an indoor-grown seedling used to the outdoors, but you do not start a pear from seed. You buy a young tree, either bare-root (no soil on the roots) or in a pot, and plant it straight into the ground, so there is nothing to harden off.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Plant a bare-root tree while fully dormant, late winter to early spring, as soon as the ground is workable. Soak the roots in water for an hour or two before planting, dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots without bending, and set the tree so the graft union (the swollen knob where the variety meets the rootstock) sits 2 to 3 in above the final soil line, burying it lets the variety root over and defeats the rootstock. Backfill with native soil, water in to settle, and stake dwarf and size-controlled stocks. A potted tree follows the same depth rule but can go in through spring.
start_method.notes_beginner: If your tree comes bare-root (bare roots, no pot), plant it in late winter or early spring while it is still leafless and dormant, as soon as you can dig the soil. Soak the roots in a bucket of water for an hour or two first. Dig a hole wide enough that the roots spread out without folding. The key thing: find the graft union (the bumpy spot low on the trunk where the top variety was joined to the roots) and keep it about 2 to 3 in above the soil, never bury it. Fill the hole with the same soil you dug out, water well, and tie small trees to a stake. A potted tree is planted the same way and can go in anytime through spring.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Fill the pot with bagged potting mix from a garden center, not soil dug from your yard. Garden soil packs down hard in a pot and holds too much water, which rots the roots. Potting mix stays loose and drains well.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in some compost (about a quarter of the pot) to feed the tree, plus a few handfuls of perlite (the little white pellets) or bark to help water drain through. Do not add water-holding crystals, a potted pear is more likely to be harmed by soggy roots than by dry ones.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: Use a high-quality bagged potting mix (a soilless peat- or coir-based medium), not native garden soil or topsoil, which compacts and drains poorly in a container. The mix must be free-draining and stay open over several seasons in the same pot.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend in roughly 20 to 30 percent compost for nutrition and moisture buffering, and a handful of coarse material such as perlite or fine bark to keep drainage open. Avoid water-holding gels; a potted pear is far more often lost to wet roots than to drought.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: A tree in a pot dries out much faster than one in the ground, so check it every day when it is warm. Stick a finger an inch into the mix; if it feels dry, water until it runs out the holes in the bottom. Empty the saucer so the pot is not sitting in water. The goal is moist mix, never dust-dry and never swampy.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Because you water a pot so often, the water washes the food out of the soil, so a potted pear needs feeding a bit more than one in the ground, but still go light because of fire blight. Add a slow-release fertilizer in early spring, and stop feeding by midsummer so the tree is not pushing soft new shoots when cold weather arrives.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Winter is the hard part for a potted pear. In a pot, the roots sit above ground and get cold from every side, so they freeze much more easily than roots in the ground. After the leaves drop and the tree is dormant (resting for winter), move the pot somewhere cold but protected, like an unheated garage or shed, or up against the north side of the house. It still needs the cold to rest, but the shelter keeps the roots from freezing solid. Give it a little water now and then so the soil never dries out completely.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: A potted pear is the winter-vulnerable case: roots in an above-ground pot are exposed to cold from all sides and run several zones less hardy than the same tree in the ground. Once dormant, move the pot to an unheated but sheltered spot (an unheated garage, shed, or against a north wall) where it stays cold enough to hold dormancy but is buffered from the deep-freeze and freeze-thaw swings that kill container roots. Water occasionally so the rootball never fully dries.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Only the smallest Asian pear trees do well in pots, the ones grown on a size-controlling rootstock such as OHxF 333 (ask the nursery). A tree on a vigorous betulifolia or calleryana stock quickly gets too big for any pot. Every 2 to 3 years, trim some roots and replace the top few inches of mix. And remember the pollination rule still applies: even a potted Asian pear needs a second, different Asian pear variety blooming nearby to make fruit.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Containers suit Asian pear only on a genuinely size-controlling rootstock such as OHxF 333; a betulifolia or calleryana standard tree will outgrow any practical pot. Expect to root-prune and refresh the top few inches of mix every 2 to 3 years to keep the tree productive, and remember a potted Asian pear still needs a bloom-overlapping pollinizer nearby. Containers are the realistic route to pears on a patio without space for two full trees, paired with a second potted variety.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Container roots dry out far faster than ground roots, so check moisture daily in warm weather; a 20-gallon pot in summer sun can need water every day or two. Water until it runs from the drainage holes, then let the top inch begin to dry before the next watering. Never let the pot go bone-dry (it drops fruit) and never leave it standing in a full saucer.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Frequent watering flushes nutrients from a pot, so a container pear needs feeding somewhat more often than one in the ground, but keep nitrogen modest because of fire blight. Use a balanced slow-release fertilizer at the start of the season and stop by midsummer so the tree hardens off and does not push tender growth into fall.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering (sub-irrigated) containers are not the first choice for pear. They keep the lower rootball continuously moist, and while pear tolerates damp ground better than apple, a permanently wet pot still risks crown rot. Use a free-draining pot with open drainage holes and water from the top.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: Skip self-watering pots (the kind with a water reservoir in the bottom) for pears. They keep the lower roots wet all the time, which can rot the crown. Use a regular pot with holes in the bottom and water it from the top.
container_notes.container_overwintering_seasoned: Plan winter protection in from the start in cold zones: a pear hardy to zone 4 in the ground may only survive zone 6 or 7 winters in an exposed pot, because the root zone has no insulating soil mass. In order of protection, sink the pot to its rim in the ground for winter, cluster and wrap pots, or move to an unheated sheltered structure. Do not bring a dormant pear into a heated room, warmth breaks dormancy and the tree misses its winter chill.
container_notes.container_overwintering_beginner: If you live where winters are cold, plan for winter before you even plant. A potted pear is much less cold-hardy than the same tree in the ground, because the roots have no surrounding soil to keep them warm. To protect them, sink the whole pot into a hole in the ground for winter, group pots together and wrap them, or move the pot into an unheated garage or shed. Do not bring the tree indoors where it is warm, the warmth wakes it up too early and it misses the cold it needs to fruit.

recommended.name: Ya Li
recommended.recommended_note: A pale-green, slightly pear-shaped Chinese type, crisp and mild. Very low chill and very early bloom; pair it with another early Chinese pear such as Tsu Li, since it usually finishes before the Japanese types open.

recommended.name: Tsu Li
recommended.recommended_note: Large, firm, long-keeping Chinese pear with very early bloom; a good pollinizer for Ya Li. Like Ya Li it blooms too early to reliably cross the round Japanese cultivars.

recommended.name: Shinseiki
recommended.recommended_note: The low-chill workhorse (about 250 hours) and the key to fruiting in mild-winter zones. Round, yellow, crisp and sweet, stores well, and is partially self-fruitful, though it still crops far better with a pollinizer.

recommended.name: 20th Century
recommended.recommended_note: Nijisseiki, the benchmark Asian pear: round, yellow-green, exceptionally juicy and crisp. Partially self-fruitful but heavier with a pollinizer, and notably fire-blight susceptible, so best where summers are drier.

recommended.name: Kosui
recommended.recommended_note: An early-ripening, russet-skinned Japanese pear, small and very sweet with low acid. A reliable, high-flavor choice; needs a pollinizer.

recommended.name: Hosui
recommended.recommended_note: A golden-brown russet type, among the sweetest and most popular home Asian pears. Vigorous and productive; needs a pollinizer and benefits from hard thinning.

recommended.name: Chojuro
recommended.recommended_note: A bronze-russet Japanese pear with a distinctive butterscotch note; firm, stores for months, and carries better fire-blight tolerance than 20th Century.

recommended.name: Shinko
recommended.recommended_note: A bronze-russet late-mid pear and one of the more fire-blight-tolerant cultivars, making it a strong pick for the humid Southeast. Sweet and stores well.

recommended.name: Niitaka
recommended.use: fresh eating (very large russet; needs pollinizer)
recommended.recommended_note: A very large brown-russet pear, mild and crisp. Its pollen is a weak pollinizer, so give it TWO good partners and do not rely on it to pollinate others.

recommended.name: Olympic
recommended.recommended_note: Korean Giant (Olympic, Dan Bae): a huge brown-russet pear that ripens very late, keeps for months in the fridge, and holds its crunch. Needs a pollinizer and heavy thinning.

recommended.name: Seuri
recommended.recommended_note: A large, orange-russet, aromatic late pear. Blooms late, so pair it with another late cultivar such as Olympic or Niitaka for overlapping bloom.

varieties.note_seasoned: Eleven cultivars sequenced very early to very late by bloom so you can pair overlapping bloom groups for cross-pollination. Chill spans about 250 hours (low-chill Shinseiki) to roughly 500 (the late russets); match it to your winters. The round yellow types (Shinseiki, 20th Century) are smooth-skinned and tart-sweet; the russet types (Kosui, Hosui, Chojuro, Shinko, Olympic) are brown-skinned and richer. For the humid Southeast lean on the more fire-blight-tolerant Shinko and Chojuro. Two pairing rules: the Chinese pears (Ya Li, Tsu Li) bloom too early to cross the Japanese types, so pair them together, and Niitaka is a weak pollen source, so do not use it as a pollinizer.
varieties.note_beginner: Pick at least two different varieties that bloom around the same time so they can pollinate each other. Where winters are mild, choose a low-chill kind like Shinseiki or Ya Li. Where summers are warm and humid, choose a more fire-blight-resistant kind like Shinko or Chojuro. The smooth yellow ones (Shinseiki, 20th Century) are crisp and tart-sweet; the brown russet ones (Hosui, Chojuro, Olympic) are sweeter and richer. Two gotchas: the Chinese kinds (Ya Li, Tsu Li) bloom too early to match the Japanese kinds, and Niitaka cannot pollinate well, so do not rely on it as a partner.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Asian pears are picked tree-ripe and eaten crisp, so unlike European pears they need no ripening rest. At room temperature a ripe Asian pear holds about a week, staying firm and juicy; eat the softest first.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Asian pears are ready to eat straight off the tree, crisp and sweet. On the counter they keep about a week.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerated near 32 to 34°F at high humidity, Asian pears store unusually well for a pear: most cultivars keep 1 to 3 months and stay crisp, and the late russet keepers (Chojuro, Shinko, Olympic) hold longest. They are ready to eat cold, with no ripening step needed.
storage.fridge_beginner: In the fridge, Asian pears last a long time, often 1 to 3 months, and stay crisp. Take one out and eat it cold whenever you like, no waiting for it to soften.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Asian pears are watery and lose their signature crunch when frozen whole; freeze them as slices in light syrup or as sauce for cooking use up to about a year.
