storage.freezer_beginner: Frozen whole, Asian pears go mushy and lose their crunch. Slice them into a little light syrup or cook them down first, then freeze; they keep about a year.
storage.notes_seasoned: The Asian-pear rule is the reverse of the European pear: RIPEN ON THE TREE and pick tree-ripe. The fruit sweetens only on the branch, so a pear picked early stays hard and bland and will not finish indoors. Pick when the skin has turned full varietal color and a taste test is sweet and crisp, then eat fresh or refrigerate. Handle gently, the thin skin bruises easily, which is why market fruit ships in foam nets.
storage.notes_beginner: Here is the Asian-pear secret, and it is the opposite of European pears: let them ripen ON the tree. They only get sweet on the branch, so a pear picked too soon stays hard and flavorless and will not improve on the counter. Pick when it has turned full color and tastes sweet and crisp. Handle them gently, they bruise easily.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Not applicable as annual rotation: pear is a permanent tree that holds its site for decades. The real concern is replant disease, avoid planting a new pear where an old pear or apple stood, or replace the soil in the planting hole and choose a vigorous rootstock.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Crop rotation is for annual vegetables, not pear trees, a pear stays in one spot for many years. The one thing to know: do not plant a new pear exactly where an old pear (or apple) used to be, because leftover soil problems can stunt the new tree. Pick a fresh spot, or dig out and replace the old soil.
rotation.note_seasoned: Site selection, not rotation, is the lever: full sun, well-drained soil (pear tolerates heavier ground than most fruit), good air movement to limit fire blight and Fabraea, and fresh ground free of replant issues.
rotation.note_beginner: Instead of rotating, just choose a good permanent spot: full sun, soil that drains (pears handle heavier soil than most fruit trees), and open air around the tree to keep disease down.

growth_stages.name: Planting (bare-root, dormant)
growth_stages.timing: late winter to early spring, while dormant
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A dormant, leafless bare-root or potted young tree with a visible graft union; buds tight and not yet swelling. Roots should be moist and pliable, not dried out.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: You are planting a small, leafless tree, often sold bare-root (no pot, roots wrapped). Look for a bump low on the trunk, that is the graft where your pear variety joins the rootstock, and keep it above the soil line.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Plant while dormant in well-drained full sun; keep the graft union 2 to 3 inches above the soil line; water in deeply; stake if on a dwarfing or quince rootstock. Do not fertilize at planting.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Plant it in early spring in a sunny, well-drained spot, before the buds open. Keep that graft bump above the ground, water it in well, and stake it if it is a small tree. Hold off on fertilizer for now.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record planting date, variety, rootstock, and pollinizer planted nearby.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note the date you planted, which pear variety, and which second variety you planted nearby to pollinate it.

growth_stages.name: Year-1 establishment (remove blossoms)
growth_stages.timing: first spring and summer after planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: First leaves and shoots emerge; the tree may attempt to flower. Watch for steady new shoot growth (the sign roots are taking) and for any blackened shoot tips (early fire blight).
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The tree leafs out and grows its first new shoots. It may even try to flower, do not let it. Watch for any branch tips that suddenly turn black and bend over.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Remove any blossoms that open this first year so energy goes to roots and scaffold. Keep soil evenly moist (deep-soak 1 to 2 times per week), mulch, protect the trunk from rodents and sunscald, and prune only lightly and only in dry weather to limit fire blight.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: If flowers open this first year, pinch them off, the tree is too young to fruit. Water deeply once or twice a week, mulch (not touching the trunk), and let it build roots. No pears this year is exactly right.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Note first-year shoot growth, whether blossoms were removed, and any fire-blight strikes cut out.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Jot down how much the tree grew and that you removed the first flowers.

growth_stages.name: Scaffold formation (years 1 to 4)
growth_stages.timing: first few dormant seasons
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The permanent branch framework develops. Pears grow naturally upright and narrow, so look for well-spaced scaffolds and work to widen their crotch angles with spreaders.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Over the first few years the tree builds its main branches. Pears want to grow tall and narrow, so you want to encourage a few strong branches that spread outward.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Each winter, prune lightly in dry weather to train structure: keep a central leader, select well-spaced scaffolds, and use limb spreaders to widen the naturally narrow crotch angles. Prune conservatively, heavy cuts force the succulent regrowth fire blight exploits.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Each winter while the tree is bare and the weather is dry, do some light shaping: keep one main upright stem and a few evenly spaced side branches, and gently spread upright branches outward with small spacers. Go easy, hard pruning makes soft growth that catches disease.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record dormant-pruning date, branches removed, and spreaders placed.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you pruned and what you shaped.

growth_stages.name: Annual winter dormant prune
growth_stages.timing: late winter (about February to March), before bud break, in dry weather
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A leafless, dormant canopy, the time to shape structure. Note water sprouts, crossing limbs, and any blackened fire-blight wood or cankers to remove.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: In late winter the tree is bare, the best time to prune because you can see the branches. Look for any black, scorched-looking wood from fire blight.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Prune annually in late winter, in dry weather: thin for light and air, remove water sprouts, crossing, and dead wood, and cut out fire-blight cankers 8 to 12 inches below the damage, disinfecting tools between cuts. Keep cuts moderate.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Once a year, in late winter and only when it is dry out, thin the branches so sunlight and air get in, and remove dead or crossing wood. If you see any fire-blight-burned branch, cut well below it and wipe your tools with disinfectant between cuts.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record annual prune date and any disease wood removed.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note the date you pruned and anything diseased you took out.

growth_stages.name: Bloom and pollination
growth_stages.timing: early spring, after chill is satisfied (often just before apples)
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Buds open to white blossoms, generally a few days before apples. Watch for bee activity (pear nectar is low, so bees can be sparse) and check that a compatible pollinizer is blooming at the same time. Warm, wet bloom weather is the fire-blight danger window.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The tree covers itself in white flowers, a bit earlier than apples. Bees should be visiting. Check that your second pear variety is flowering too, and watch the weather, warm and wet during bloom is when fire blight spreads.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Do not apply insecticide during bloom (it kills pollinators). Watch the frost forecast and protect open bloom from late frost. Ensure a compatible pollinizer is in bloom within about 50 to 100 ft. In warm, wet weather, follow a fire-blight forecast and avoid pruning.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Never spray bug killer while the tree is in bloom, you would kill the bees you need. Cover small trees if a hard frost is coming, since frost on open flowers means no pears. Make sure your second pear variety is blooming too, and do not prune in warm, wet weather.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record bloom start, overlap with pollinizer, frost events, and bloom-time weather.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when blooming started, whether your two trees overlapped, and any frosts.

growth_stages.name: Fruit set and thinning
growth_stages.timing: late spring to early summer, after petal fall
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small fruitlets form in dense clusters after petals drop, and Asian pears set very heavily, far more than the tree can size. A natural drop sheds a few, but the crop is almost always badly overloaded. Petal fall is also a codling-moth timing window.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: After the flowers fall, lots of little pears appear in tight clusters. Asian pears set way more fruit than they can grow well, so the tree is almost always overloaded.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin HARD within 4 to 6 weeks of bloom, down to one fruit per cluster and roughly 6 inches apart. Asian pears over-set, so aggressive thinning is essential for good size, to prevent limb breakage, and to curb biennial bearing. Target codling moth at petal fall, and watch for the first sticky signs of pear psylla and for stink-bug feeding.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Thin the young pears hard: snap off extras so you leave about one per cluster, spaced roughly a hand-width apart. Asian pears set way too much fruit, so you will remove a lot, and that is exactly right for big, good pears and unbroken branches. Petal fall is also the time to deal with the codling moth (the worm in the fruit).
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record thinning date, pest treatments at petal fall, and any psylla activity.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you thinned and any pest treatment after the petals dropped.

growth_stages.name: Harvest tree-ripe (around year 3 to 5+)
growth_stages.timing: late summer to fall, variety-dependent
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Full varietal color (green to yellow on smooth types, green to golden-brown on russet types), easy detachment on a gentle upward twist, and above all a sweet, crisp, juicy taste. Asian pears ripen ON the tree, so taste is the surest guide, and they hold on the tree for a few weeks. Different varieties ripen weeks apart.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The pears reach full color and come off easily on a gentle upward twist, and, most important, they taste sweet and crisp. Asian pears ripen on the tree, so taste a couple to be sure before picking the rest.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick tree-ripe as each variety comes ready (first real crop usually around year 3 to 5, rootstock-dependent). Sample test fruit for sweetness before stripping the tree, handle gently to avoid bruising, and refrigerate; Asian pears keep for weeks to months and stay crisp. Do not pick early expecting them to ripen indoors, they will not.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pick the pears tree-ripe as each kind comes ready (your first real harvest is usually around the third to fifth year). Taste one first, then pick, handling them gently so they do not bruise. Store them in the fridge, where they last for weeks and stay crisp. Do not pick them early, they will not sweeten off the tree.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record harvest dates, taste/sweetness at picking, yield, and fruit quality by variety.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you picked (tree-ripe), roughly how many, and how they tasted.

growth_stages.name: Post-harvest and fall sanitation
growth_stages.timing: fall, after harvest into leaf drop
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves yellow and drop as the tree re-enters dormancy. Note dropped fruit and fallen leaves (carryover sources for codling moth, scab, and Fabraea leaf spot).
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: After harvest the leaves turn and fall, and the tree goes to sleep for winter. Look at what is left on the ground.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Rake and remove fallen leaves (breaks pear scab and Fabraea cycles) and clear dropped fruit (breaks codling moth). A late-fall or dormant horticultural oil sets up pear-psylla control. Do not prune now, wait for late-winter dormancy and dry weather.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Rake up and remove the fallen leaves and any pears on the ground, this one chore prevents a lot of next-year disease and pests. Do not prune yet, save that for late winter when it is dry.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record fall sanitation done and tree condition going into dormancy.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note that you cleaned up leaves and fruit, and how the tree looks heading into winter.

notifications.title_beginner: Pinch off the flowers this year
notifications.body_seasoned: Your tree is in its establishment year. Remove the blossoms now so energy goes to roots and scaffold, not fruit.
notifications.body_beginner: It is your tree's first year. Pinch off any flowers that open, no pears yet. This builds a much stronger tree.

notifications.body_seasoned: Through the first summer, deep-soak 1 to 2 times per week to establish roots. Do not let the root ball dry out.
notifications.body_beginner: All this first summer, give your tree a deep soak once or twice a week so the roots get going. Do not let it dry out.

notifications.title_beginner: Late-winter oil spray for pear psylla
notifications.body_seasoned: Apply dormant horticultural oil in late winter to smother overwintering pear psylla adults and eggs before bud break, the backbone of psylla control.
notifications.body_beginner: While the tree is bare in late winter, spray horticultural oil to smother the overwintering pear psylla (a sticky-honeydew pest specific to pears) before the buds open.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time for the annual dormant prune
notifications.body_seasoned: Prune now in late winter before bud break, in dry weather: thin for light and air, remove dead, crossing, and water-sprout wood, and cut out fire-blight cankers.
notifications.body_beginner: It is late winter and the tree is bare, the right time to prune, but only when it is dry out. Thin out branches so light gets in, and cut dead, crossing, or fire-blight-burned wood.

notifications.title_beginner: Frost can kill the flowers now
notifications.body_seasoned: The tree is blooming, often a few days before apples, so the bloom is more frost-exposed. A hard late frost on open blossoms can eliminate this year's crop, watch the forecast and protect small trees.
notifications.body_beginner: Your tree is flowering, a bit earlier than apples, so frost is a real risk. A hard frost right now can wipe out this year's pears. Watch the forecast and cover a small tree if frost is coming.

notifications.title_seasoned: Thin fruit and target petal-fall pests
notifications.title_beginner: Thin pears and check for pests
notifications.body_seasoned: Within 4 to 6 weeks of bloom, thin HARD to about one fruit per cluster, roughly 6 inches apart, Asian pears over-set and need aggressive thinning. Petal fall is the codling-moth timing window; also scout for pear psylla honeydew and stink-bug feeding.
notifications.body_beginner: Now that petals have dropped, snap off lots of the extra little pears so you leave about one per cluster. Asian pears set way too much fruit, so thin hard. This is also the time to deal with the codling moth (the worm in the fruit).

notifications.body_seasoned: Check ripeness by full varietal color, easy upward-twist detachment, and a sweet, crisp taste, then pick tree-ripe. Asian pears ripen on the tree and do not sweeten off it, so taste before you pick. Varieties ripen weeks apart.
notifications.body_beginner: Start checking your pears: full color, they snap off on a gentle upward twist, and they taste sweet and crisp. Pick them tree-ripe and eat them fresh, they will not sweeten indoors.

notifications.title_seasoned: Fall cleanup: rake leaves and clear drops
notifications.title_beginner: Rake up leaves and fallen pears
notifications.body_seasoned: After harvest, rake and remove fallen leaves (breaks pear scab and Fabraea leaf spot) and clear dropped fruit (breaks codling moth).
notifications.body_beginner: After picking, rake up the fallen leaves and any pears on the ground. This one chore prevents a lot of next-year disease and pests.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost coming while your tree flowers
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A hard frost is forecast while the tree is in bloom. Pear blooms early and its open blossoms and young fruitlets are frost-tender, protect small trees with covers or run sprinklers through the frost.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Frost is on the way while your pear tree is flowering. The flowers can be killed by cold, which means no pears this year. Cover a small tree, or run a sprinkler over it through the cold night.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Warm, wet weather raises a serious disease risk
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Warm, wet conditions during bloom strongly favor fire blight infection through pear blossoms, which are highly susceptible. Do not prune in the wet, and follow a fire-blight forecast model if available.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Warm and wet while the tree is blooming is exactly when fire blight (a serious disease that pears catch easily) spreads. Do not prune in wet weather right now, and watch for blackened branch tips.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot spell while pears are growing
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Sustained heat during fruit sizing increases water demand and the risk of premature fruit drop and sunscald. Keep soil moisture even with a weekly deep soak.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: A hot stretch while the pears are filling out means the tree needs more water. Keep watering steady so the fruit does not drop early.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Strong winds expected
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: High wind can drop fruit and break fruit-laden limbs, especially on size-controlled trees. Check stakes and supports; harvest tree-ripe fruit ahead of a major blow.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Strong wind can knock pears down and snap branches loaded with fruit. Check that your tree's stake is solid, and pick any tree-ripe pears before a big storm.

planting.text_seasoned: Keep the graft union 2 to 3 inches above the soil line, burying it lets the variety root and lose the rootstock's size and disease benefits.
planting.text_beginner: Keep the graft union (the bumpy spot low on the trunk where the variety was joined to the roots) 2 to 3 in above the soil. If you bury it, the top variety grows its own roots and the tree loses the size control and disease resistance the rootstock gives it.

planting.text_seasoned: Plant a compatible, bloom-overlapping pollinizer at the same time, a lone pear (or an incompatible pair like Bartlett with Seckel) wastes years.
planting.text_beginner: Plant a second, different pear variety at the same time so they can pollinate each other, and check they are compatible (Bartlett and Seckel are not). A single pear, or a mismatched pair, usually makes no fruit.

establishment.text_seasoned: Pinch off every blossom the first spring, a fruitless year 1 builds a stronger tree for the decades pear lives.
establishment.text_beginner: Pinch off all the flowers the first spring. Going without fruit in year 1 lets the tree put its energy into roots and branches, which makes it much stronger for the long life ahead.

establishment.text_seasoned: Mulch a wide ring but keep it a few inches off the trunk to avoid rot and rodent cover.
establishment.text_beginner: Spread mulch in a wide circle around the tree, but keep it a few inches away from the trunk. Mulch against the trunk holds rot-causing moisture and hides mice that chew bark.

establishment.text_seasoned: Aim for about 12 to 18 inches of new shoot growth a year, much more means too much nitrogen, which on a pear directly feeds fire blight.
establishment.text_beginner: A young pear should grow about 12 to 18 in of new branch each year. A lot more than that means too much nitrogen (the leafy-growth nutrient), which on pears feeds the disease fire blight, so ease off feeding.

establishment.text_seasoned: Protect the young trunk from sunscald and voles with a light-colored guard over the first winters.
establishment.text_beginner: Protect the young trunk through its first few winters with a light-colored tree guard. This prevents sunscald (bark damage from winter sun) and stops voles from chewing the bark.

scaffold_formation.text_seasoned: Pears grow naturally upright and narrow, so train the framework with limb spreaders to widen crotch angles while the wood is young, and prune conservatively in dry weather, heavy cuts force the succulent regrowth fire blight exploits. The shape you set in the first few years is the shape the tree keeps for decades.
scaffold_formation.text_beginner: Pears want to grow tall and narrow, so in the first few winters gently push the upright branches outward with small spreaders to build a strong, open shape. Prune only a little, and only when it is dry, because hard pruning makes soft growth that catches fire blight. The shape you set now is the shape the tree keeps for life.

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Prune in late winter before bud break and only in dry weather; pruning a pear in humid conditions opens cuts to fire blight.
dormant_prune.text_beginner: Do your pruning in late winter, before the buds open, and only when the weather is dry. Cuts made in damp weather let in fire blight, a serious disease that blackens and kills pear branches.

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Disinfect pruners between cuts whenever fire blight may be present, and cut cankers 8 to 12 inches below visible damage.
dormant_prune.text_beginner: If fire blight might be around, wipe your pruners with disinfectant between each cut, and when you remove a burnt-looking branch, cut well below the damage (about a hand's length past it).

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Dormancy is when the tree banks its chill hours, the cold is doing necessary work, not harm.
dormant_prune.text_beginner: In winter the leafless tree is resting and collecting its chill hours (the cold it needs in order to flower and fruit later). The cold is helping the tree, not hurting it.

bloom.text_seasoned: Never spray insecticide during bloom, and remember pear nectar is low, so you need every bee that visits.
bloom.text_beginner: Never spray bug killer while the tree is in bloom. Pear flowers do not attract many bees to begin with, and insecticide kills the few you are counting on to set fruit.

bloom.text_seasoned: Watch the frost forecast: pear blooms early, so a hard frost on open blossoms can cost the whole crop.
bloom.text_beginner: Keep an eye on the frost forecast while the tree is flowering. Pears bloom early, so a hard frost can destroy the whole year's crop, cover the tree if a freeze is coming.

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Thin HARD within about a month of bloom, to one fruit per cluster and roughly 6 inches apart. Asian pears over-set, so heavy thinning is the single biggest lever for fruit size and for steadier annual crops.
fruit_set.text_beginner: About a month after bloom, thin the tiny pears hard, down to one per cluster, spaced roughly a hand-width apart. Asian pears make far too much fruit, so you will remove a lot, and that is what gives you big pears and an even crop year to year.

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Petal fall is the codling-moth timing window; also scout the new shoots for the first sticky honeydew of pear psylla and for stink-bug feeding on the young fruit.
fruit_set.text_beginner: The time right after petals fall is the key window to control codling moth (the worm in the fruit). Also check the new shoots for sticky, shiny goo (pear psylla) and the fruit for dimpling from stink bugs.

harvest.text_seasoned: Asian pears ripen ON the tree, the reverse of European pears: pick tree-ripe by full color, easy upward-twist release, and above all a sweet, crisp taste. A pear picked early stays hard and bland, it will not finish indoors.
harvest.text_beginner: Let Asian pears ripen on the tree and pick them ready to eat: full color, they snap off with a gentle twist, and they taste sweet and crisp. Picked early, they stay hard and bland, because they do not sweeten on the counter.

harvest.text_seasoned: Asian pears store unusually well: refrigerated, most keep 1 to 3 months and stay crisp, with the late russets (Chojuro, Shinko, Olympic) holding longest. Handle gently, the thin skin bruises easily.
harvest.text_beginner: Keep Asian pears in the fridge and they last a long time, often 1 to 3 months, staying crisp. Handle them gently, the skin bruises easily.

post_harvest.text_seasoned: Rake and remove fallen leaves, this single chore breaks the pear-scab and Fabraea-leaf-spot cycles for next year.
post_harvest.text_beginner: Rake up and remove the fallen leaves in autumn. This one chore breaks the cycle of pear scab and Fabraea leaf spot (two leaf-spotting fungi that overwinter in old leaves) for next year.

post_harvest.text_seasoned: Clear dropped fruit to break the codling-moth cycle, and apply a dormant oil to set up pear-psylla control.
post_harvest.text_beginner: Pick up every dropped pear to break the codling-moth cycle, and a late-fall or winter spray of horticultural oil helps knock back pear psylla for next year.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Mature yield is rootstock-driven and Asian pears crop heavily: a size-controlled tree (OHxF 333 or 87) carries roughly 1 to 3 bushels (about 40 to 120 lb) per year, and a vigorous betulifolia or calleryana standard can far exceed that at full maturity. The heavy natural set is the reason aggressive thinning is essential, unthinned trees make many small, gritty fruit and break limbs.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Asian pears set a lot of fruit. A smaller tree gives roughly 1 to 3 bushels a year (a bushel is about 40 lb), and a full-size tree gives much more. Because they set so heavily, you must thin off a lot of the young fruit, or you get many tiny, gritty pears and broken branches.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Trees reach full bearing several years after first crop, roughly years 5 to 8, sooner than a European pear and sooner still on a size-controlling rootstock. Many cultivars tend toward biennial bearing (a heavy year then a light one); consistent hard thinning evens it out.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: An Asian pear builds up to full production over several years after its first crop, a bit faster than a European pear. Some varieties swing between a big year and a small year; thinning the young fruit hard every year helps keep crops steadier.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: No crop in the planting year (blossoms are removed). First meaningful fruit around year 3 to 5, rootstock-dependent and a bit earlier than a European pear.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Expect zero pears the first year, that is normal and intended. Your first real handful of fruit usually comes around year 3 to 5, a little sooner than a European pear.
factors_seasoned: rootstock (sets tree size, bearing age, and fire-blight/decline tolerance)
cross-pollination success (a compatible, overlapping pollinizer within ~50 ft)
hard fruit thinning (Asian pears over-set; thinning drives size and curbs biennial bearing)
late-frost damage to the early bloom
fire blight, pear psylla, and stink bug pressure

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No research-backed lunar planting preference applies to pear; dormant bare-root planting timing is driven by soil workability and the dormant window, not moon phase.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Tree flowered but set no fruit
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Lots of flowers, but no pears
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Without a compatible pollinizer in overlapping bloom within about 50 ft, Asian pear blossoms are not fertilized and drop. Common traps: two of the same cultivar, a Chinese pear (Ya Li, Tsu Li) whose early bloom never overlaps the Japanese types, or relying on Niitaka, whose pollen is a weak partner.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your tree flowered but the blossoms fell without making pears. Usually there was no second, compatible Asian pear variety blooming nearby. Watch for two traps: the Chinese kinds (Ya Li, Tsu Li) bloom too early to match the Japanese kinds, and Niitaka cannot pollinate well.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Add a second, genetically different, COMPATIBLE Asian pear whose bloom overlaps, within about 50 ft (pair Chinese with Chinese, Japanese with Japanese). A European pear like Bartlett can also pollinate Japanese types where bloom overlaps.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant a second, different Asian pear that blooms at the same time and is a compatible match, within about 50 ft. Pair Chinese kinds together and Japanese kinds together, or use a Bartlett pear that blooms at the same time.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Branch tips blackened and scorched
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Branches turned black, as if burned
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Fire blight (Erwinia amylovora) infected through blossoms or tender shoots in warm, wet weather, blackening shoots into shepherd's crooks and forming cankers. Asian pear is highly susceptible (20th Century and Niitaka worst), and lush nitrogen-pushed growth made it worse.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Branch tips suddenly turned black and bent into a hook, as if scorched. This is fire blight, the main pear disease, which spreads in warm, wet weather and loves the soft growth from too much fertilizer.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Cut out infected wood 8 to 12 inches below symptoms in dry weather, disinfecting between cuts; going forward plant more resistant cultivars (Shinko, Chojuro) on a tolerant rootstock (OHxF or calleryana) and keep nitrogen lean.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Cut the blackened branches well below the damage in dry weather, wiping tools between cuts. Next time choose a more resistant variety (Shinko, Chojuro), go easy on fertilizer, and only prune when it is dry.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Pears hard, starchy, and bland
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Pears hard and flavorless, never sweetened
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The fruit was picked before it was tree-ripe. Unlike European pears, Asian pears sweeten only on the tree and do not finish ripening off it, so an early-picked pear stays hard, low-sugar, and starchy no matter how long it sits on the counter.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: You picked the pears too early and they never got sweet. Asian pears only ripen on the tree, so once they are picked hard, they stay hard and bland indoors.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Let them ripen on the tree and pick tree-ripe: wait for full varietal color and taste-test for sweetness and crispness before harvesting. They hold on the tree for a few weeks, so there is time to get it right.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Leave them on the tree until they are fully colored and taste sweet and crisp, then pick. There is no rush, they hang on the tree for weeks.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Many small, gritty pears and sagging limbs
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Lots of tiny, gritty fruit
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Asian pears set very heavily, and the fruit was not thinned, so the tree carried a huge number of small, stone-celled (gritty) pears and risked breaking limbs. Over-cropping also pushes the tree toward biennial bearing (a heavy year then a bare one).
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The tree made a huge number of tiny, gritty pears, and the branches sagged or broke. Asian pears set far too much fruit on their own and were not thinned.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Thin hard within 4 to 6 weeks of bloom, to one fruit per cluster and roughly 6 inches apart. Fewer fruit means larger, less gritty pears, less limb breakage, and steadier annual bearing.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Thin the young pears hard, about a month after bloom: leave just one per cluster, spaced roughly a hand-width apart. You lose a lot of little fruit but get big, good ones and protect the branches.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Sparse, delayed, or straggly bloom
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Few flowers, or flowers very late
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: A higher-chill cultivar grown in a warm-winter zone did not accumulate enough chill to break dormancy normally, giving delayed, uneven, weak bloom and poor set. Asian pears need only moderate chill, so the mismatch is easy to avoid with the right variety.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The tree barely flowered, or flowered oddly late and patchy. This usually means the variety needs more winter cold than your area gives, and pears need more cold than apples.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Match variety chill to your winters: in warm zones choose low-chill cultivars (Shinseiki, Ya Li).
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Pick a low-chill Asian pear suited to mild winters, like Shinseiki or Ya Li. The right variety for your climate flowers normally.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Sticky leaves with black sooty mold
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Sticky, blackened leaves and shoots
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Pear psylla nymphs fed heavily and exuded honeydew that grew black sooty mold, scorching leaves and russeting fruit. Outbreaks often follow broad-spectrum sprays that kill the psylla's natural enemies.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The leaves and young pears got coated in sticky goo that turned black and grimy. That is pear psylla, a pear-specific insect; it gets worse if harsh sprays have killed the helpful bugs.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Apply dormant oil in late winter, use insecticidal soap or summer oil in season, and conserve natural enemies by avoiding broad-spectrum insecticides.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Spray dormant oil in late winter to smother the overwintering insects, use insecticidal soap during the season, and avoid harsh sprays that kill the good bugs.

primary.name: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center
UF/IFAS Northwest District Horticulture Vegetable Garden Planting Dates (Florida Panhandle)
UF/IFAS SP 103/VH021 Florida Vegetable Gardening Guide
UGA Extension Bulletin 577 (Vegetable Garden Planting Chart)

succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Not applicable. Succession planting (re-sowing in waves for a continuous harvest) is an annual-vegetable practice. Asian pear is a perennial tree that holds its site for decades and bears once a year, so there is no succession to schedule; continuity comes from variety choice (early through late cultivars) and cold storage, which Asian pears take unusually well, not replanting.

open_findings.summary: chill_hours_range [250,600] is modeled: the cited ucd_fruitnut chilling page 403s; values (Shinseiki ~250, 20th Century 300-400) are nursery/corroborated, not lifted from a live cited page. Refine at the variety-delta pass.

3.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 3 winters, often below -30°F, are too cold for reliable survival of Asian pear (Pyrus pyrifolia), which is rated hardy to about zone 5. Even where a tree survives a mild winter in a sheltered spot, cold damage and late frost on the early bloom prevent a dependable crop. For fruit this far north, grow an ultra-hardy European or Ussurian-hybrid pear outside this guide.
3.suitability_note_beginner: This far north is too cold for an Asian pear, which is hardy only to about zone 5. For pears in a cold-winter area like this, choose an extra-hardy Asian pear instead.

4.suitability_note_seasoned: At the zone-4 cold edge, an Asian pear survives in favorable, sheltered sites and blooms each spring on ample chill, but winter cold damage and late frost on the early bloom make a dependable crop unlikely. The hardiest, earliest-ripening cultivars (Shinseiki, Chojuro) are the best bets; for reliable fruit this cold, consider a hardier European pear.
4.suitability_note_beginner: Right at the cold edge of where Asian pears can grow. A tree can survive and flower in a protected spot, but reliable fruit is a stretch because of winter cold and late frosts.
4.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Late frost can damage the early open bloom, and cold winters test hardiness at this edge; choose the hardiest, earliest cultivars and avoid frost pockets.

5.suitability_note_seasoned: Dependable pear country. The full hardy roster fruits well, with ample chill and a long enough season for mid and late varieties.
5.suitability_note_beginner: Pears grow well here. Most varieties will give you a good crop.
5.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Occasional late frost on early bloom in colder years; generally low risk for mid to late bloomers.

6.suitability_note_seasoned: Prime pear growing. Every variety in this guide fruits dependably, with strong chill and a full season for late keepers.
6.suitability_note_beginner: Excellent pear country. Any variety here should do well.
6.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Low frost risk on bloom in most years.

7.suitability_note_seasoned: Reliable Asian pear country. Chill comfortably exceeds every variety's need, and the long season ripens the late russet keepers (Chojuro, Shinko, Olympic).
7.suitability_note_beginner: Pears do well here, including later-ripening kinds. Keep an eye out for fire blight in damp spells.
7.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Late frost on bloom is uncommon at this latitude.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: Good Asian pear country from zone 5 south, where most varieties fruit well. In the coldest spots (zone 4) a tree can live and flower but rarely crops, and zone 3 is too cold for these varieties. Plant in early spring, and remember to thin off a lot of the young fruit.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Asian pear's cool, dependable range. The full mid to high chill roster fruits reliably from zone 5 south, with abundant chill and a long enough season for the late russets. In zone 4 the tree survives in sheltered sites and blooms, but cold and late frost make a dependable crop unlikely; zone 3 is too cold for Asian pear (Pyrus pyrifolia, hardy to about zone 5). Plant bare-root dormant trees in early spring, once the soil thaws enough to dig, and thin the heavy set hard.
northern_tier.chill_basis_seasoned: Cold northern winters bank roughly 700 to 1,600 chill hours, far more than any Asian pear needs, so winter chill is never the limiter here. The constraints are cold-hardiness at the zone-4 and colder edge, growing-season length, and late spring frost on the early bloom. From zone 5 south, variety choice and the season decide the crop, not chill.
northern_tier.chill_basis_beginner: Winters here are far more than cold enough for Asian pears. The challenge is surviving the deepest cold at the northern edge, plus the short summer and late spring frosts, not a lack of chill.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Cooler Piedmont winters bank enough chill for the full Asian pear roster. Fire-blight management through the humid summer is the real work, not climate fit; favor the more resistant cultivars (Shinko, Chojuro).
8.suitability_note_beginner: Pears fruit well in this cooler part of the region IF you choose disease-resistant varieties. Plan on steady care for diseases in summer.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Some risk to early bloomers from a late frost; favor mid-season bloom groups.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Warmer coastal-plain winters meet the low-chill cultivars (Shinseiki, Ya Li) reliably and mid-chill types in colder years. Heavy summer fire-blight pressure makes this the harder end of the region.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Lower, warmer parts of the region can grow low-chill, disease-resistant pears, but it takes work. Fire blight is a real challenge in the humid summer.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Mild winters can leave high-chill varieties blooming unevenly, and early bloom risks late frost; choose low-chill, blight-resistant types.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: Asian pears do well here, often better than Asian pears, because they take the heat and need less winter cold. The main job is managing fire blight through the humid summer, so pick a resistant variety like Shinko or Chojuro.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: Asian pears grow well across the Southeast, and their heat tolerance and lower chill need make them a better fit here than Asian pears. Fire blight is the binding constraint, so lean on the more resistant cultivars (Shinko, Chojuro) and a consistent spray and sanitation routine, and match variety chill to your local winter.
se_gulf.chill_basis_seasoned: Southeastern winters bank roughly 350 to 1,000 chill hours, declining toward the coast. That meets most Asian pears in the cooler Piedmont and the low-chill cultivars (Shinseiki, Ya Li) near the coast. Summer humidity drives heavy fire-blight and disease pressure during the season.
se_gulf.chill_basis_beginner: Winters here give enough cold for many Asian pears, more in the upper part of the region than near the coast. Expect to manage fire blight and other diseases through the humid summer.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Dependable Asian pear country. Chill and season suit the full roster, and the dry summers keep fire blight lighter than in the humid Southeast.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Pears grow very well in the cooler, northern part of the valley, this is prime pear ground.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Late frost is an occasional risk for early bloomers in the colder northern valley.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: The warmer valleys still bank enough chill for most Asian pears, with the low-chill cultivars (Shinseiki, Ya Li) the safest picks in the mildest winters.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Pears fruit well here. In the warmer south valley, pick mid- and lower-chill varieties for the most reliable crops.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Generally low frost risk; protect the earliest blooms in colder pockets.

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: Excellent pear country. Hot, dry summers mean fewer disease problems than in wetter climates. In the southern valley, lean toward lower-chill varieties.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: Prime Asian pear country. The warm, dry-summer interior suits Asian pears especially well, with strong fruit quality and lighter disease pressure than the humid East. The full roster fruits, and low-chill cultivars extend the range into the mildest-winter valleys.
ca_interior.chill_basis_seasoned: Central Valley winters bank roughly 300 to 1,100 chill hours, higher in the Sacramento north than the southern San Joaquin. Most of the roster fruits, with the southern valley favoring lower-chill selections as winter chill trends down.
ca_interior.chill_basis_beginner: Valley winters give a moderate to good amount of cold, enough for most pear varieties, with more in the north than the south.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Cooler inland North Coast valleys bank enough chill for most Asian pears, and the low-chill cultivars (Shinseiki, Ya Li) are reliable. Mild, damp springs can raise fire blight, so favor resistant types.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Pears grow well a little inland from the coast, this region has a long pear history. Choose low- to mid-chill varieties and a sunnier, less foggy spot.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Spring frost is a minor risk inland; the earliest blooms are most exposed.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: The immediate, fog-cooled coast banks too little winter chill for even low-chill Asian pears in most years. Trees survive and may bloom in cold winters, but fruit set is unreliable; move inland for a dependable crop.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Pear trees live and sometimes flower right on the coast, but a real crop is unreliable because winters are so mild. Move a little inland for fruit.
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: The limiter is too little winter chill, not frost. In most years the immediate coast does not chill even low-chill pears enough to crop.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: Pears grow well a little inland from the coast. Right at the foggy coast, winters are too mild for a dependable crop, so stay inland and choose low-chill varieties.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: Asian pears fruit well in the cooler inland valleys of the North Coast, where winters chill even mid-chill cultivars. On the immediate fog-cooled coast, chill runs short for a dependable crop; move a little inland or choose the lowest-chill cultivars.
ca_north_coast.chill_basis_seasoned: North-coast winters bank roughly 150 to 800 chill hours, with cooler inland valleys at the high end and the immediate, fog-cooled coast at the low end. Inland sites fruit the roster; the coast itself sits below even low-chill pear needs in many years.
ca_north_coast.chill_basis_beginner: Winters near the coast are mild, so cold can be limited. Inland valleys get more chill than the immediate coast.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: At the low-chill edge, only the lowest-chill cultivars (Shinseiki, Ya Li) fruit, and only in colder-than-average winters or cooler inland pockets. Treat any crop as a bonus.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Right at the edge for Asian pears. In a colder-than-usual winter a low-chill kind (Shinseiki, Ya Li) may fruit, but do not count on a crop every year.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is a minor concern; too little chill is the real limit, so choose the lowest-chill varieties first.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: The immediate coast banks only about 50 to 350 chill hours, below even the lowest-chill Asian pear in most years. Trees survive and may bloom, but do not set a dependable crop; this is past the warm edge of the species.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Pear trees can live right on the coast but will not fruit dependably, winters are simply too mild even for low-chill kinds.
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: The limiter is too little winter chill, not frost. The immediate coast sits below even the lowest-chill pear's need.

ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: Winters here are mild, near the edge for Asian pears. Only the lowest-chill kinds (Shinseiki, Ya Li) will fruit, and only in colder years. A cooler inland spot helps.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: The mild-winter South Coast is at the low-chill edge for Asian pears. Only the lowest-chill cultivars (Shinseiki, Ya Li) fruit here, and only in colder years or cooler inland pockets; the immediate coast rarely chills enough for a dependable crop.
ca_south_coast.chill_basis_seasoned: South-coast winters bank as little as 50 to 350 chill hours at the coast and 200 to 550 inland. Only low-chill varieties (near 200 to 350 hours) are workable, and the immediate coast sits below even those.
ca_south_coast.chill_basis_beginner: Winters here are mild, and cold is the main limit on pears. Inland is colder than the coast. Choose low-chill varieties, and know the immediate coast is too mild.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Desert valley floors bank only about 150 to 400 chill hours, below even low-chill Asian pears in most years, and summer heat plus fire-blight pressure compound it. Trees may survive and bloom but rarely fruit.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Only the lowest-chill pears even attempt this, and most years they will not fruit. Winters are too mild and summers too harsh.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Too little winter chill plus extreme summer heat make a crop unreliable; this is past Asian pear's warm edge.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: The hottest, lowest desert banks only about 100 to 300 chill hours, below even the lowest-chill Asian pear. Trees may survive but set no dependable fruit, and extreme heat further stresses any crop.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Pear trees can survive in the lowest desert but essentially never produce a real crop. Winters are too mild and summers too extreme.
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Too little winter chill plus extreme summer heat make a crop unreliable; this is the hottest, mildest-winter edge.

ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: Pears are a poor fit for the California desert. Winters are too mild to give enough chill, and summers are brutally hot. A tree may live but will rarely fruit.
ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: Asian pear is essentially out of range in the low California desert: winter chill is too short for even the lowest-chill cultivars in most years, and extreme summer heat plus fire-blight pressure compound it. Trees may survive and bloom in mild years but do not set a dependable crop.
ca_desert.chill_basis_seasoned: Low-desert winters (Coachella, Imperial) bank only about 100 to 400 chill hours, below the requirement of even low-chill Asian pears in most years; intense summer heat further stresses any crop.
ca_desert.chill_basis_beginner: Desert winters are too short and mild to give pears the cold they need, so they rarely fruit here.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Dependable Asian pear country. Cold-enough winters and hot, dry summers suit the full roster, and the dry air keeps fire blight lighter than in the humid East.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Pears fruit well in these higher, drier areas, where the dry air keeps disease down. Water steadily and guard against late frosts.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Late spring frost at elevation can damage early bloom; favor mid to late bloom groups and avoid frost pockets.

warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: Pears grow well in these higher, drier areas, where the dry air keeps disease down. Watch for late spring frosts, water regularly, and protect young trees from strong sun.
warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: Elevation gives this arid region enough chill for a solid variety list, and the dry air keeps fire blight and Fabraea low, a genuinely good pear climate (much of New Mexico, west Texas, the inland intermountain west). The key risks are late spring frost on early bloom and intense sun on young bark; irrigation is essential.
warm_arid.chill_basis_seasoned: High-desert and inland arid winters bank roughly 450 to 850 chill hours, more than the low deserts because of elevation, enough for mid-chill varieties alongside low-chill types.
warm_arid.chill_basis_beginner: Higher, drier areas get a fair amount of winter cold, enough for many pear varieties. A late frost in spring is the thing to watch.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Low-desert winters bank only about 100 to 400 chill hours, below even low-chill Asian pears in most years, and extreme summer heat plus fire blight finish the case. Trees may survive but rarely crop; choose low-chill apples or other fruit instead.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Pears rarely fruit in the Arizona low desert, winters are too mild for the chill they need and summers are too hot.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Heat and sunburn, not frost, are the hazards, but too little chill is the binding limit on fruit.

low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: Pears are a poor choice for the Arizona low desert. Winters are too mild to give enough chill and summers are too hot, so trees rarely fruit.
low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: Asian pear does not fruit dependably in the Arizona low desert: winter chill (around 100 to 400 hours) falls below even low-chill pear needs in most years, and extreme summer heat plus fire blight finish the case. Trees may survive but rarely crop; the desert is far better suited to low-chill apples or other fruit.
low_desert_az.chill_basis_seasoned: Arizona low-desert winters (Phoenix, Tucson) average about 100 to 400 chill hours, below the requirement of even low-chill Asian pears in most years.
low_desert_az.chill_basis_beginner: Desert winters here give too little cold for Asian pears to fruit reliably.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: Central-peninsula winters bank only about 50 to 150 chill hours, below the roughly 200-hour floor of even the lowest-chill Asian pears in most years. A tree may survive but does not fruit dependably, so no growing calendar is shown.
10.suitability_note_beginner: A pear tree might survive here, but it will not fruit. Winters are too warm to wake the tree properly. North Florida, outside this zone, can grow a few low-chill pears.

11.suitability_note_seasoned: The southern peninsula banks essentially no winter chill. Asian pears cannot complete dormancy or set fruit here.
11.suitability_note_beginner: Pears do not grow on the southern Florida peninsula. There is no winter chill to wake the tree.

fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: Pears are not a good fit for the Florida peninsula. The winters are too warm for the tree to fruit. North Florida can grow a few low-chill pears, but the peninsula proper cannot.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: Outside Asian pear's range. UF/IFAS limits pear growing to north and north-central Florida (with low-chill, blight-resistant selections); the central-to-southern peninsula does not bank enough winter chill for dependable bloom or fruit set, and the southern tip none at all.
fl_peninsula.chill_basis_seasoned: The Florida peninsula banks well under 150 chill hours, dropping to near zero in the south, below the requirement of even low-chill Asian pears.
fl_peninsula.chill_basis_beginner: Winters on the Florida peninsula are too mild for pears, even the lowest-chill kinds need more cold than this region provides.

11.suitability_note_seasoned: No appreciable winter chill at reachable elevations. Asian pears cannot break dormancy here, so the tree neither blooms reliably nor fruits.
11.suitability_note_beginner: Pears will not fruit in Hawaii. There is no cold winter to wake the tree.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: Pears are not suited to Hawaii. The climate never gets cold enough in winter for the tree to fruit. Tropical fruits are the right choice here.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: Outside Asian pear's range. With no meaningful winter chill at reachable elevations, pears cannot complete dormancy or set fruit. The verdict below is honest rather than a fabricated planting window; tropical fruits are the right choice here.
hawaii_tropical.chill_basis_seasoned: Hawaii's tropical lowlands bank essentially no winter chill. Pears require a cold dormant period to bloom, which this climate does not supply at any reachable elevation.
hawaii_tropical.chill_basis_beginner: Hawaii does not get cold enough in winter for pears. They need a real cold season to fruit, and this climate stays warm year round.

crops.description_seasoned: A long-lived deciduous fruit tree (Pyrus pyrifolia) grown for round, crisp, apple-shaped fruit, also called the apple pear, sand pear, or nashi. Asian pear is a cross-pollination crop: nearly all cultivars are self-unfruitful, so you plant two different, bloom-overlapping varieties and rely on bees to move pollen between them (a couple, like Shinseiki and 20th Century, are partially self-fruitful but still crop far better with a pollinizer). The signature difference from the European pear is at harvest: Asian pears RIPEN ON THE TREE and are eaten crisp and juicy like an apple. You pick them tree-ripe and sweet, not firm-and-green to finish indoors, and a fruit picked too early stays hard and bland. The trees set very heavily and must be thinned hard for decent fruit size. Fire blight is the major disease, worst in warm, humid regions, so cultivar and rootstock choice matter. Chill requirement is moderate and variety-set (roughly 250 to 600 hours), and rootstock choice sets mature size and how soon the tree bears.
crops.description_beginner: Asian pear is a fruit tree that lives for decades, grown for round, crisp fruit that looks and eats like a juicy apple (people call it the apple pear or nashi). Two things make it special. First, almost every Asian pear needs a second, different Asian pear variety nearby that blooms at the same time, with bees to carry the pollen, or it makes little fruit. Second, and this is the opposite of a European pear: you let Asian pears ripen ON the tree and pick them ready to eat, crisp and sweet. A pear picked too early stays hard and flavorless, because it will not sweeten on the counter. The trees make a huge number of little fruit, so you have to thin a lot of them off to get good-sized pears. The main disease to know is fire blight, worst in warm, damp places, so choosing a resistant variety helps a lot.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Asian pears ripen ON the tree and are picked tree-ripe, the opposite of European pears: the fruit sweetens only on the branch and does not finish ripening off it. Pick when the skin has turned full varietal color (green to yellow on smooth types like 20th Century and Shinseiki, green to golden-brown or bronze on russet types like Hosui, Chojuro, and Shinko), the fruit parts easily from the spur on a gentle upward twist, and a taste test is sweet, crisp, and juicy. Taste is the surest guide, so sample a couple of test fruit before stripping the tree. Asian pears hold on the tree for a few weeks and are eaten firm and crisp like an apple. First meaningful crop typically comes around year 3 to 5, rootstock-dependent.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: An Asian pear is ready to pick when it is ready to EAT, because it ripens on the tree, not off it (the reverse of a European pear). Look for the skin to reach full color: green turning yellow on the smooth kinds, or green turning golden-brown on the russet kinds. Then taste one, it should be sweet, crisp, and juicy, like a very juicy apple. If it is hard and bland, leave the rest on the tree to finish, because they will not sweeten indoors. Handle them gently so they do not bruise. Do not expect a real crop until about the third to fifth year after planting.
crops.bloom_time_seasoned: Asian pears bloom in early spring once their chill requirement is met, generally around the same time as European pears and a few days before apples, which leaves the open bloom exposed to late frost. Cultivars are staggered from early to late over roughly two weeks; bloom timing governs cross-pollination, since only varieties whose windows overlap can pollinate each other. Note that the Chinese-type pears (Ya Li, Tsu Li) bloom very early and reliably cross each other but often finish before the Japanese types open, so pair like with like.
crops.bloom_time_beginner: Asian pears flower in early spring, about the same time as other pears and a bit before apples, so a late frost can catch the open blossoms. Different varieties bloom a few days apart over about two weeks, and two trees can only pollinate each other if they bloom at the same time. One tip: the Chinese kinds (Ya Li, Tsu Li) bloom very early and pollinate each other, but often finish before the Japanese kinds open, so match them up carefully.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Asian pear (Pyrus pyrifolia) is reliably cold-hardy through USDA zone 5, roughly one zone less hardy than European pear, and this guide's roster fruits dependably in zones 5 through 9. At the zone-4 edge the tree survives in favorable, sheltered sites and blooms on ample chill, but winter cold and late frost on the early bloom make a dependable crop unlikely (it survives, without reliable fruit); zone 3 is too cold. At the warm end, low-chill cultivars (Shinseiki, Ya Li) fruit in the mild-winter South and across interior and coastal California, while the frost-free low desert and tropics bank too little chill for any Asian pear. Through the humid Southeast, fire blight, not cold, is the binding constraint, so lean on the more resistant cultivars (Shinko, Chojuro).
crops.hardiness_notes_beginner: Asian pears handle cold winters down to about zone 5, a little less tough than European pears, and the varieties here give reliable fruit in zones 5 through 9. In colder zone 4 a tree can survive and flower in a protected spot but rarely crops well, and zone 3 is too cold. In warm-winter areas, choose a low-chill kind like Shinseiki or Ya Li. The frost-free deep South and tropics simply do not get cold enough. In hot, humid regions, fire blight is the real challenge, so pick a more resistant variety like Shinko or Chojuro.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Chill hours are the accumulated hours between about 32 and 45°F during winter dormancy that a tree must bank before it flowers normally in spring. Asian pear's requirement is moderate and set by the cultivar: this guide's roster runs from about 250 hours (low-chill Shinseiki) to roughly 500 to 600 hours for the late russet types. As a group Asian pears need somewhat LESS chill than European pears and tolerate heat better, which is why they succeed across the warm-winter South and much of California. Match the variety's chill need to what your winters reliably deliver: too little chill gives delayed, straggly bloom and poor fruit set.
crops.chill_hours_note_beginner: Pear trees need a stretch of winter cold before they flower well, measured in chill hours (hours between about 32 and 45°F). Asian pears need a moderate amount, from about 250 hours for a low-chill kind like Shinseiki up to 500 to 600 for the late-ripening types. They need a bit less winter cold than European pears and take heat better, so they do well in warm-winter areas. Pick a variety whose chill need matches your winters; in a mild-winter area, choose a low-chill variety or the tree will bloom poorly and set little fruit.
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Asian pear is only partially self-fruitful: a lone tree, or a single-variety block, sets a light, unreliable crop. Plant two different, compatible Asian pear varieties whose bloom overlaps, within about 50 feet, with bees to move pollen between them. A few cultivars (Shinseiki, 20th Century) are PARTIALLY self-fruitful and set a light crop alone, but even they yield far more with a pollinizer. Two pairing rules: the very-early Chinese pears (Ya Li, Tsu Li) bloom too early to cross the Japanese types, so pair them with each other; and a European pear (Bartlett) can pollinate Japanese Asian pears where their bloom genuinely overlaps. Because the trees also set very heavily once pollinated, plan to thin hard.
crops.pollinator_notes_beginner: This is the most important thing about growing Asian pears: one tree alone makes only a small, unreliable crop. The flowers need pollen from a DIFFERENT Asian pear variety, carried by bees, so plant two different kinds within about 50 feet that bloom at the same time. A couple of varieties (Shinseiki, 20th Century) can set a small crop on their own, but they do much better with a partner. Two tips: the Chinese kinds (Ya Li, Tsu Li) bloom too early to pollinate the Japanese kinds, so pair them together; and a Bartlett (European) pear can pollinate Asian pears if it blooms at the same time. Once they do set fruit, expect a lot of it, so be ready to thin heavily.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: In the planting year, prioritize root and scaffold establishment over fruit. Remove any blossoms that open the first spring so the tree spends its energy on roots and framework. Keep the young tree evenly watered through its first summer and stake it if it is on a size-controlling rootstock. Prune lightly and only in dry weather, fresh cuts on an Asian pear are an entry point for fire blight, and go easy on nitrogen for the same reason. Expect no crop in year 1; a first meaningful harvest comes around year 3 to 5, a bit earlier than a European pear.
crops.year_one_notes_beginner: Do not let your Asian pear fruit in its first year. If flowers open that first spring, pinch them off, so the young tree puts its energy into roots and branches. Water it steadily through the first summer, and stake it if it is a small tree. Prune only a little, and only when the weather is dry, because cuts in damp weather invite fire blight. Go easy on fertilizer too. You will not get pears the first year, and that is normal; your first real crop is usually around the third to fifth year.

pollination.notes_seasoned: Asian pear is only partially self-fruitful: a lone tree, or a single-variety block, sets a light, unreliable crop. Plant two different, compatible Asian pear varieties whose bloom overlaps, within about 50 feet, with bees to move pollen between them. A few cultivars (Shinseiki, 20th Century) are PARTIALLY self-fruitful and set a light crop alone, but even they yield far more with a pollinizer. Two pairing rules: the very-early Chinese pears (Ya Li, Tsu Li) bloom too early to cross the Japanese types, so pair them with each other; and a European pear (Bartlett) can pollinate Japanese Asian pears where their bloom genuinely overlaps. Because the trees also set very heavily once pollinated, plan to thin hard.
pollination.notes_beginner: This is the most important thing about growing Asian pears: one tree alone makes only a small, unreliable crop. The flowers need pollen from a DIFFERENT Asian pear variety, carried by bees, so plant two different kinds within about 50 feet that bloom at the same time. A couple of varieties (Shinseiki, 20th Century) can set a small crop on their own, but they do much better with a partner. Two tips: the Chinese kinds (Ya Li, Tsu Li) bloom too early to pollinate the Japanese kinds, so pair them together; and a Bartlett (European) pear can pollinate Asian pears if it blooms at the same time. Once they do set fruit, expect a lot of it, so be ready to thin heavily.

crops.establishment_note: Roughly the first three years are establishment: the tree builds roots and a scaffold of main branches before it carries a real crop. Remove first-year blossoms, train the framework with light annual dormant pruning (Asian pear is prone to fire blight, so prune conservatively and only in dry weather), and do not expect meaningful yield until bearing begins (around year 3 to 5, rootstock-dependent, a bit earlier than a European pear). Once bearing starts, the trees set very heavily and must be thinned hard for good fruit size.
crops.recommended_rootstock_note: OHxF 87 (semi-dwarf) is a strong backyard pick for Asian pear: it makes a manageable tree, bears reasonably young, and is one of the most productive of the fire-blight-tolerant Old Home x Farmingdale series, which also resists pear decline. Many Asian pears are sold on the vigorous Pyrus betulifolia (betulaefolia) or Pyrus calleryana seedling stocks, which make large, adaptable, disease-tolerant trees that tolerate heavy or wet soil but take longer to bear and need more room; for a smaller yard or a container choose OHxF 333. Note that quince, the dwarfing stock used for some European pears, is graft-incompatible with most Asian pears, so it is not an option here.

rootstock_options.name: Pyrus betulifolia (Betulaefolia)
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask which rootstock the tree is on; betulifolia makes a large, vigorous standard tree (usually not staked).
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: Pyrus betulifolia (betulaefolia) is the classic commercial Asian pear seedling stock: vigorous, deeply anchored, and highly adaptable, tolerating heavy, wet, or dry soils and resisting pear decline. It makes a large standard tree, so it is the choice for a full-size, low-maintenance landscape pear where ultimate size is acceptable; keep it in bounds with summer pruning.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: Betulaefolia is the usual big-tree rootstock for Asian pears. It is tough and easygoing, handling heavy or wet ground, and it lives a long time. The catch is size: it makes a large tree, so give it room, or keep it smaller with regular pruning.

rootstock_options.name: Pyrus calleryana
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask which rootstock the tree is on and whether it tolerates your soil (calleryana handles wet ground well).
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: Pyrus calleryana is a semi-vigorous to vigorous seedling stock, a touch smaller than betulifolia, that tolerates wet soils and carries good fire-blight and pear-decline tolerance. Widely adaptable and productive; a solid standard-tree choice in the South and on heavy ground.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: Calleryana makes a large tree, a little smaller than betulaefolia, and copes well with wet soil and heat. It resists fire blight and pear decline, which makes it a good pick in warm, humid regions. Like betulaefolia, plan for a big tree.

rootstock_options.name: OHxF 97
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask which rootstock the tree is on and whether it needs staking.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: OHxF 97 is a larger, semi-vigorous to near-standard Old Home x Farmingdale stock, hardy and cold-resilient, with strong resistance to fire blight and pear decline, but less precocious than OHxF 87. A durable choice for a bigger in-ground tree, especially in colder regions.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: OHxF 97 makes a larger tree, about 16 to 22 ft, and is tough and cold-hardy with good disease resistance. It is slower to start fruiting than OHxF 87, but a solid pick if you have the room, especially up North.

rootstock_options.name: OHxF 87
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask which rootstock the tree is on and whether it needs staking.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: OHxF 87 is the workhorse backyard pear rootstock: semi-dwarf, precocious for the series, and one of its best producers, with strong fire-blight and pear-decline resistance. The common default for a home Asian pear that stays a manageable size.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: OHxF 87 makes a medium tree, the usual backyard choice. It fruits fairly young for a pear, produces well, and resists fire blight and pear decline. A reliable all-rounder that stays a reasonable size.

rootstock_options.name: OHxF 333
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask which rootstock the tree is on and whether it needs staking (size-controlled stocks usually do).
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: OHxF 333 is a semi-dwarfing Old Home x Farmingdale stock, about half to two-thirds standard size, with strong resistance to fire blight, collar rot, and pear decline. Productivity runs a touch lower than OHxF 87, but it is the best size-controlled, disease-tolerant choice for a small yard and works in a large container.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: OHxF 333 makes the smallest of these trees, about 10 to 14 ft, and resists fire blight and pear decline. It fruits a bit lighter than OHxF 87 but is a great disease-tolerant pick for a smaller yard or a big pot.

pet_safe.note: The flesh is fine, but the seeds contain the same cyanide compounds as apple seeds and are best kept from cats, dogs, and horses.

crops.name: Lime

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Limes care about drainage more than soil type. They grow well in sandy and even rocky ground as long as water never sits around the roots, since soggy soil brings on the foot rot in the disease notes. Deep, loose loam is ideal. On heavy clay, plant the tree high on a raised mound so water drains away. (Sources: UF/IFAS CH092, UF/IFAS CH093.)
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Limes are well adapted to a wide range of soils, including the deep sands and shallow calcareous rocklands of south Florida, but sharp drainage is non-negotiable: they do not tolerate flooded conditions, and wet feet drive Phytophthora foot rot. Deep, well-drained loam or sandy loam is ideal; slightly acidic is preferred, though limes tolerate high-pH calcareous soils if minor-element deficiencies are managed. Plant high on a raised mound on heavy or poorly drained ground. (Sources: UF/IFAS CH092, UF/IFAS CH093.)

ph.note_beginner: Limes like slightly acidic soil (about pH 6.0 to 6.5) but grow in a wide range as long as drainage is good. In high-pH (alkaline) soil, plan to add iron and zinc so the leaves stay green.
ph.note_seasoned: Limes prefer a slightly acidic soil around pH 6.0 to 6.5 but tolerate a broad range (roughly 5.5 to 8.0), including the alkaline calcareous soils of the Florida Keys and rockland. On high-pH ground, expect iron, manganese, and zinc to become less available and plan on nutritional foliar sprays and chelated iron rather than trying to acidify the whole site. (Sources: UF/IFAS CH092, UF/IFAS CH093.)

fertilizer.frequency: light, frequent doses through the growing season
fertilizer.timing: late winter or early spring through summer; taper by late summer
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Feed in light, frequent doses from late winter or early spring through summer, then taper by late summer so late flushes harden before any cold; feeding too late pushes tender growth into frost season, which a lime can least afford. Young trees take small amounts several times a year, building from a fraction of a pound to a few pounds annually as the tree matures. On the calcareous soils where limes are often grown, add nutritional sprays and chelated iron to head off minor-element deficiency. Keep fertilizer off the trunk and water it in.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Feed from early spring through summer in small, regular doses, then stop by late summer. Feeding late in the year pushes out soft new growth that frost can damage, and limes are the citrus most easily hurt by cold. If your soil is alkaline, the tree will also need iron and zinc so its leaves stay green. Keep fertilizer off the trunk and water it in.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: Nitrogen-forward; use a fertilizer formulated for citrus. Young citrus trees take a balanced citrus grade with part of the nitrogen from organic sources; bearing trees shift toward higher potassium and lower phosphorus. On alkaline or calcareous soils, supplement with chelated iron and nutritional sprays of manganese and zinc, and avoid phosphorus-heavy formulas, which worsen iron lockout.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a citrus fertilizer or one with plenty of nitrogen (the first number on the label). In alkaline (high-pH) soil, the tree also needs iron and zinc, often sold as chelated micronutrients, to keep the leaves green. Skip fertilizers heavy in phosphorus (the middle number).
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: Scale the annual nitrogen to tree age and size, splitting it into several light applications rather than one heavy dose. UF/IFAS suggests roughly a quarter pound of a young-tree fertilizer at planting, working up to a few pounds per tree annually over the first several years. Spread feed evenly under the canopy and keep it off the trunk.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Give smaller amounts several times a year rather than one big feeding, and feed more as the tree grows. The simplest path is a citrus fertilizer at the label rate for the tree's age. Scatter it under the branches, not against the trunk.

companions.note_seasoned: For a tree, companions really means root-zone management, not vegetable pairing. Keep lawn grass and weeds cleared out to the drip line: turf competes hard for water and nitrogen and slows a young lime, and string trimmers used to fight grass at the trunk nick the tender bark. Keep organic mulch pulled back at least a foot from the trunk to reduce Phytophthora foot-rot risk. Limes are self-fruitful, so no second tree is needed for pollination. UF/IFAS also cautions against heavy lawn fertilization and herbicide drift near citrus. Low, shallow-rooted plantings well outside the drip line are harmless; anything crowding the trunk or holding moisture against it is not. (Sources: UF/IFAS CH092, Texas A&M AgriLife.)
companions.note_beginner: Keep grass and weeds away from under a lime tree, out to the edge of the branches. They steal water and food the tree needs, and a trimmer used against the trunk can wound the bark. Keep mulch a hand's width back from the trunk. You do not need a second tree for it to fruit.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Lawn grass
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Grass under the tree steals water and food a young lime needs, and trimming it against the trunk can wound the bark. Keep it cleared out to the edge of the branches.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Beginner-register version of the turfgrass-within-drip-line entry; same extension basis (UF/IFAS citrus weed/lawn-competition and trunk-injury cautions). extension_backed/medium.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep lawn grass from growing right up to your lime tree. Grass competes with citrus for water and nutrients, especially while the tree is young, flowering, and flushing. Mowing and trimming close to the trunk can also nick the thin bark. Keep a clear or mulched circle around the base instead.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Weeds at the trunk
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Weeds and damp material crowding the trunk hold moisture against the bark and can rot the base. Keep the area right around the trunk clear and dry.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Beginner-register version of the weed/vegetation-at-trunk concern; same extension basis as the turfgrass entry (UF/IFAS citrus weed competition; foot-rot and rodent-harborage caution). extension_backed/medium.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Pull weeds away from the base of your lime tree. Weeds against the trunk steal water and nutrients, and they give cover to pests and rodents that gnaw the bark. Keep a weed-free or lightly mulched space around the trunk, with any mulch pulled back a little so it does not sit against the bark.

bad_seasoned.name: Turfgrass within the drip line
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Turf competes hard for water and nitrogen in the shallow zone where citrus feeder roots concentrate, and it markedly slows a young lime; UF/IFAS lists lawn competition and mower or trimmer trunk injury among the main causes of poor home-citrus performance. Keep a mulched, grass-free area out to the drip line.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: UF/IFAS home-citrus guidance names lawn/weed competition within the tree row and mechanical trunk injury from mowing/trimming as significant, especially on young trees during bloom and flush. extension_backed/medium: extension-supported competition effect; medium because the quantification is via extension bulletin rather than an opened controlled citrus trial.

bad_seasoned.name: Moisture-holding mulch against the trunk
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Organic mulch piled against the trunk holds moisture on the bark and crown and invites Phytophthora foot rot, to which limes are susceptible. Keep mulch pulled back at least a foot from the trunk.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Persistent moisture held against citrus bark by trunk-piled mulch creates conditions for foot/collar rot (Phytophthora) and harbors bark-gnawing rodents, a sound named mechanism reflected in standard citrus-care guidance to keep mulch off the trunk. mechanistic/medium: clear mechanism, consistently advised, not pinned to an opened controlled trial.

pests.name: Asian citrus psyllid (ACP)
