The catch is Arizona's periodic hard freezes: limes are the most cold-tender citrus and are the first trees lost when a severe freeze hits, so the cell is frost-edge rather than fully reliable.
low_desert_az.cold_basis_beginner: Arizona's low desert is hot, which limes love, and they fruit well most years. But every so often a hard freeze hits, and limes are the first citrus to be damaged, so protect the tree when a freeze is forecast.

10.suitability_note_beginner: Limes fruit reliably in zone 10 Florida, heaviest in summer and scattered year-round. Watch for citrus diseases rather than frost.
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is a minor factor. Zone lows of 35 to 45°F stay at or above the high-20s°F lime-damage point in most years; protect only in an unusual hard freeze.

11.suitability_note_seasoned: Peninsular zone 11 is frost-free and fruits limes heavily, near-continuously in the near-tropical climate with a strong summer peak. Cold is a non-issue; wet-season disease pressure (canker, greasy spot, postbloom fruit drop) is the management focus.
11.suitability_note_beginner: Limes fruit heavily and almost year-round in zone 11 Florida. There is no frost worry, just citrus diseases to watch.
11.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is not a factor here. Lows do not approach the high-20s°F damage point, so no cold protection is needed.

fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: South Florida is one of the best places to grow limes, warm and almost never frosty. Both Key and Persian limes do well, and the main job is managing wet-weather diseases, not cold.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: The Florida peninsula grows limes about as well as anywhere in the country. Zone 11 is frost-free and zone 10 nearly so, and both Key and Persian limes fruit heavily with a summer peak and scattered fruit year-round. The real work here is disease management (canker, greasy spot, postbloom fruit drop) in the humid climate.
fl_peninsula.cold_basis_seasoned: The Florida peninsula is classic lime country, with zone-10 lows of 35-45°F and frost-free zone-11 lows of 40-48°F. Both Key lime (a Keys and south-Florida signature) and Persian lime thrive in the warm, humid climate; cold is a minor-to-nil factor and the management focus shifts to wet-season fungal diseases and citrus canker, to which limes are highly susceptible.
fl_peninsula.cold_basis_beginner: South Florida is prime lime country, warm and barely frosty. Both Key and Persian limes grow well; the main worries are wet-weather diseases rather than cold.

11.suitability_note_seasoned: Frost-free tropical lowland Hawaii fruits limes continuously year-round, with the everbearing habit fully expressed. Cold is a non-issue; disease and pest pressure are the focus.
11.suitability_note_beginner: Limes fruit year-round in tropical Hawaii with no frost worry at all. Just manage pests and diseases.
11.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is not a factor here. Lows do not approach the high-20s°F damage point, so no cold protection is needed.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: Hawaii's warm lowlands are perfect for limes, with fruit all year and no frost. Focus on pests and diseases rather than timing.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: In tropical lowland Hawaii, limes are at home: frost-free, warm, and humid, with continuous year-round bloom and harvest. Both Key and Persian limes thrive. Disease and pest management, not season or cold, drive the calendar here.
hawaii_tropical.cold_basis_seasoned: Lowland Hawaii (zone 11, lows 45-55°F) is frost-free and tropical, an ideal lime climate. Both Key and Persian limes flower and fruit continuously through the year with no cold limitation; the everbearing habit is fully expressed, and management centers on disease and pests rather than season.
hawaii_tropical.cold_basis_beginner: Hawaii's warm lowlands are ideal for limes. There is no frost, and the tree flowers and fruits all year. The main tasks are pests and diseases, not cold.

crops.description_seasoned: Lime (Citrus, chiefly Citrus latifolia and Citrus aurantifolia) is an evergreen subtropical tree grown for its tart, aromatic green fruit and near-continuous productivity in warm climates. Limes are the most cold-tender of the common citrus, more frost-sensitive than lemons, so outside the mildest zones they are grown in containers moved to shelter for winter. The mainstream choice is the seedless Persian (Tahiti) lime; the small, seedy, intensely aromatic Key (Mexican) lime is the tender specialty. Limes are everbearing, mature fruit fast (about 90 to 120 days from bloom), and are picked green, not yellow.
crops.description_beginner: The lime is an evergreen tree that grows in warm climates and gives tart, fragrant green fruit for much of the year. Limes are the citrus most easily hurt by cold, even more than lemons, so in most of the country people grow them in a pot and bring them indoors for winter. The common one is the seedless Persian (Tahiti) lime; the little, seedy Key (Mexican) lime is more aromatic but far more tender. The key thing to remember: pick limes while they are still green, not yellow.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Harvest limes green, at full size, when they feel heavy for their size and juicy. A Persian lime is picked dark to medium-green at about 1.75 inches across; a Key lime is small and, though UF/IFAS notes it matures to a yellow peel, is commonly picked green for kitchen use. This is the reverse of the lemon rule: a yellowing lime is overripe, lower in acid, and near dropping. Clip or twist fruit free. Fruit matures about 90 to 120 days after bloom, with the heaviest crop in summer.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Pick limes while they are still green and full-sized, when they feel heavy and juicy. Unlike lemons, do not wait for them to turn yellow, which means they are overripe. Twist or snip the fruit off. Limes ripen about three to four months after flowering, with the biggest harvest in summer.
crops.bloom_time_seasoned: Limes are everbearing: they flower and set fruit across several flushes through much of the year, with the heaviest bloom from late winter into spring (February to April in Florida) and a summer-weighted harvest. Fruit matures fast, in roughly 90 to 120 days from bloom, much quicker than a lemon's many months, so flowers, green fruit, and ripe fruit are often on the tree together. In tropical climates bloom and harvest run nearly continuously. (Sources: UF/IFAS CH093, UF/IFAS CH092.)
crops.bloom_time_beginner: Limes bloom heaviest in late winter and spring but flower on and off much of the year, so you often see flowers and fruit on the tree at once. Each lime ripens fairly fast, in about three to four months, and the biggest harvest comes in summer.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Limes are among the most frost-tender of the common citrus, with Key (Mexican) lime the tenderest of all: UF/IFAS reports foliage damage at 30°F to 32°F and wood death below 29°F. Persian (Tahiti) lime is somewhat hardier, with foliage damage below about 28°F, wood damage below 26°F, and severe injury or death below 24°F, still less hardy than grapefruit or orange. In the landscape limes fruit dependably only in nearly frost-free zones (roughly 10 to 11), are marginal and need active freeze protection in zone 9, and cannot survive in-ground below about zone 9a. Texas A&M advises potting limes so they can be moved indoors during freezes. (Sources: UF/IFAS CH092, UF/IFAS CH093, Texas A&M AgriLife.)
crops.hardiness_notes_beginner: Limes are among the citrus most easily hurt by frost. Key (Mexican) lime is damaged right around freezing (30°F to 32°F), and even the hardier Persian (Tahiti) lime is hurt in the high 20s°F. Plan on growing one outdoors year-round only in a nearly frost-free spot (roughly zones 10 to 11). Anywhere colder, grow it in a pot you can move indoors when frost is coming.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Limes are subtropical evergreens with essentially no winter chilling requirement (about 0 chill hours). They never go fully dormant, so bloom is triggered by warmth rather than by accumulated winter cold. Chill hours, the limiter for deciduous fruit like peaches and apples, are not what governs where a lime fruits; frost is, and limes have the least frost tolerance of the common citrus. (Sources: UF/IFAS, UC ANR.)
crops.chill_hours_note_beginner: Limes do not need a cold winter to fruit. What they cannot handle is freezing, less than any other citrus. That is the thing to plan around.
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Lime flowers are fragrant and visited by honey bees, but the tree is self-fruitful and Persian lime is parthenocarpic (it sets seedless fruit without pollination), so pollinators improve set rather than being required. The main case where it matters is a tree kept permanently indoors, away from insects, which may set lighter and can be hand-pollinated with a small brush. (Sources: UF/IFAS CH093, UC ANR.)
crops.pollinator_notes_beginner: Bees like lime flowers, but you do not need to do anything. A lime tree sets fruit on its own, and a Persian lime even makes seedless fruit without any pollination.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Limes need well-drained soil above all else: they do not tolerate flooded conditions, and poor drainage invites Phytophthora foot rot. They grow well in sand and in the shallow calcareous rocklands of south Florida, but sharp drainage is the constant. Plant on a raised mound or bed on heavy clay, set the tree so the graft union sits well above grade, and never dig a watering basin that holds water against the trunk. Keep organic mulch at least a foot from the trunk. On alkaline or calcareous soils, plan on nutritional micronutrient sprays and chelated iron. (Sources: UF/IFAS CH092, UF/IFAS CH093.)
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Pick a spot where water never sits after rain; limes grow fine in sandy or rocky soil as long as it drains. On heavy clay, plant on a low mound so the roots stay drained. Keep the knobby graft on the trunk above the soil line, and keep mulch a hand's width back from the trunk. In alkaline soil, plan to add iron and other micronutrients.

pollination.notes_seasoned: Limes are self-fruitful: a single tree sets a full crop with no second variety nearby. Key lime and Persian lime both fruit without cross-pollination, and Persian (Tahiti) lime is parthenocarpic, setting seedless fruit without pollination at all. Flowers are visited by bees, which improve set but are not required. A tree kept permanently indoors may set lighter, so hand-moving pollen with a small brush can help. (Sources: UF/IFAS CH092, UF/IFAS CH093.)
pollination.notes_beginner: You only need one lime tree. It pollinates itself and fruits on its own, and a Persian lime makes seedless fruit with no pollination needed. Bees just help it along.

pruning_window.note_seasoned: Limes need little pruning. Do any shaping or thinning in late winter to early spring before the new flush, never in fall (which pushes tender growth into cold that a tender lime cannot afford) and never a hard dormant-season cut (the tree is never dormant). Remove dead, crossing, or frost-damaged wood, and always strip shoots arising below the graft union, which come from the rootstock. Wait for spring regrowth before cutting freeze-damaged wood, so you can see what survived.
pruning_window.note_beginner: Limes barely need pruning. In late winter or early spring, before new growth starts, snip out any dead or crossing branches and pull off shoots growing from below the graft (the knobby bend low on the trunk). Do not prune in fall, and after a freeze wait for spring growth before cutting off damaged wood so you can see what lived.

crops.establishment_note: A grafted lime usually sets a few fruit in its second year and begins a real crop in about its third year, building toward full production over the following years; air-layered or cutting-grown Key limes can fruit within a year, while seedlings take a year or two longer. (Sources: UF/IFAS CH092, UF/IFAS CH093.)
crops.recommended_rootstock: sour orange (Citrus aurantium), or rough lemon on sandy and calcareous soils
crops.recommended_rootstock_note: At a retail nursery you usually take whatever industry-standard rootstock the tree is grafted on; it is rarely a choice. Where it is, sour orange is a broad default with good fruit quality and foot-rot resistance, though it is susceptible to tristeza in some combinations. On the deep sands and calcareous rocklands where limes are often grown, UF/IFAS favors rough lemon, Volkamer lemon, alemow, or Rangpur lime; on neutral-to-low-pH soils, Swingle citrumelo adds foot-rot and tristeza resistance and some cold tolerance. Key lime is often grown on its own roots from seed, cuttings, or air-layers rather than grafted. Note that scion choice matters less for a lime's cold hardiness than simply avoiding frost.

rootstock_options.name: sour orange (Citrus aurantium)
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Most retail limes are already on a standard industry rootstock; ask whether it is on sour orange, which suits most yard soils.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: A historic broad-adaptation rootstock: tolerant of a wide range of soils including heavier and higher-pH ground, productive, good fruit quality, and resistant to Phytophthora foot rot. Main weakness is susceptibility to severe tristeza virus strains in some scion combinations.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: A good all-rounder that handles most backyard soils.

rootstock_options.name: rough lemon / Volkamer lemon (Citrus jambhiri, C. volkameriana)
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: On deep sandy or calcareous soil, ask whether the tree is on rough lemon or a similar vigorous rootstock suited to those soils.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: Vigorous, drought- and sand-tolerant rootstocks that UF/IFAS recommends for the deep sands and high-pH calcareous soils of Florida; they crop heavily and tolerate alkaline ground. Trade-offs are somewhat lower fruit quality and greater susceptibility to some diseases than sour orange.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: A tough, vigorous rootstock for sandy or rocky, alkaline soils.

rootstock_options.name: Swingle citrumelo (trifoliate hybrid)
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: On neutral to acidic soil, or for disease resistance, ask whether the tree is on Swingle citrumelo or a trifoliate hybrid.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: A trifoliate-orange hybrid with good foot-rot and tristeza resistance and some cold tolerance, widely used in modern nursery production. UF/IFAS recommends it for neutral-to-low-pH soils; it does poorly on high-pH calcareous ground, so match it to soil.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: A common modern rootstock with good disease resistance, best on non-alkaline soil.

pet_safe.note: The fruit is fine, but the peel, leaves, and citrus oils can upset the stomach of cats, dogs, and horses.

crops.name: Orange (Navel)

soil.preferred_texture_seasoned: Deep, well-drained loam to sandy loam
soil.preferred_texture_beginner: Deep, well-draining soil is best, ideally loam or sandy loam.
soil.tolerated_texture_seasoned: Sandy and rocky soils with adequate water and feeding; clay only on a raised mound or berm that guarantees drainage
soil.tolerated_texture_beginner: Sandy and rocky soils are fine as long as you water and feed enough. Clay only works if you plant on a raised mound that keeps the water draining away.
soil.problematic_texture_seasoned: Heavy, poorly drained clay and any site where water stands, which invites Phytophthora foot and root rot
soil.problematic_texture_beginner: Avoid heavy clay that drains poorly, and any spot where water collects and stands. Wet feet can lead to a disease called root rot.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Oranges care most about good drainage. They like deep soil that drains well and stays slightly acidic, kept evenly moist but never soggy. If water sits around the roots, the tree can get a root rot that is the most common way citrus trees die. Heavy clay soil is a problem because it holds water; the fix is to build a low mound or berm and set the tree on top so the crown stays above the slow-draining ground. Keep the knobby graft union above the soil. If your soil is alkaline (high-pH), which is common in the desert and inland West, the tree may not get enough iron and zinc, so use a citrus fertilizer that includes those.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Navel oranges demand sharp drainage above all else. They thrive in deep, well-drained loam or sandy loam, slightly acidic, with steady moisture but no waterlogging. The single most important soil decision is drainage: saturated roots lead to Phytophthora foot and root rot, the disease most likely to kill a citrus tree. On heavy clay, plant high on a raised mound or berm so the root crown drains freely, and set the graft union clear of the soil line. High-pH alkaline soils, common in desert and interior-West regions, are workable but tend to lock up iron and zinc, so a micronutrient-inclusive citrus fertilizer and slow acidification help.

ph.note_beginner: Oranges like soil that is slightly acidic, around pH 6 to 7. The main thing to watch for is alkaline (high-pH) soil, common in the desert and inland West, where the tree cannot take up iron and zinc and the leaves turn yellow with green veins. If that happens, use a citrus fertilizer that includes iron and zinc, and over time you can add sulfur to make the soil a little more acidic.
ph.note_seasoned: Navel oranges prefer a slightly acidic soil, roughly pH 6.0 to 7.0, and tolerate a somewhat wider band. The practical issue is high-pH alkaline soil (common in the desert Southwest and interior West), where iron and zinc become chemically unavailable and the tree shows interveinal chlorosis (yellow leaves with green veins) even though the nutrients are present. Correct with chelated micronutrients and a citrus fertilizer that includes them, and acidify the soil gradually with elemental sulfur for a durable fix.

fertilizer.frequency: split applications through the growing season
fertilizer.type: citrus (nitrogen-forward, with iron, zinc, and manganese)
fertilizer.timing: late winter or early spring through summer; stop by late summer
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Citrus are nitrogen-hungry and respond to a feeding rhythm concentrated in the growing season. Feed a mature navel from late winter or early spring through summer in split applications, and stop by late summer so new growth hardens before winter cold. Young trees get smaller, more frequent doses to build the framework. Alkaline soils chemically lock up iron, zinc, and manganese, so look for a citrus-formulated fertilizer that supplies all three as chelates and water it in well to reach the roots. Over-fertilizing pushes excess tender flush that draws aphids, leafminer, and psyllid.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Oranges are hungry for nitrogen and want most of their food during the growing season. Start feeding a grown tree as the weather warms in late winter or early spring, keep it up through summer in a few split doses, and stop by late summer so the new growth has time to toughen up before cool weather arrives. Feed young trees smaller amounts more often to build the framework. If your soil is alkaline, use a citrus fertilizer that includes iron and zinc so the leaves do not yellow. Do not overfeed, since extra soft growth attracts pests.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A nitrogen-forward citrus formulation (for example a 2-1-1 ratio) with included micronutrients (iron, zinc, manganese), or a product labeled specifically for citrus and avocado
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: A fertilizer made for citrus (look for one labeled citrus or citrus and avocado); these are higher in nitrogen and include the iron and zinc citrus needs
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: Scale nitrogen to tree age and size: a common guideline is roughly 1 to 1.5 pounds of actual nitrogen per mature tree per year, divided across spring-to-summer applications, with proportionally less for young trees. Follow the product label and local extension rates, which vary by region and soil.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Give more as the tree gets bigger, following the amounts on the citrus fertilizer label and splitting it across spring and summer. A small young tree needs only a little; a big grown tree needs more. When in doubt, follow the package directions for the tree's size.

companions.note_beginner: Keep grass and lawn out from under an orange tree, since grass steals the water and food the tree's shallow roots need. A ring of mulch (kept back from the trunk) is better than grass right up to the tree. There is no real benefit to planting other things close around citrus.
companions.note_seasoned: Keep turf and lawn grasses out of the root zone. Grass competes aggressively for water and nutrients in the top soil layer where citrus feeder roots concentrate, and mowing equipment can damage the trunk. A mulched, grass-free area extending to the canopy dripline is the standard recommendation for all citrus. Low-growing nitrogen fixers like white clover or shallow-rooted ground covers planted outside the trunk flare provide living mulch without root competition. Navel oranges are self-fertile and parthenocarpic, so no pollinizer companion is needed. In fact, nearby citrus with fertile pollen may introduce seeds into otherwise seedless fruit.

good_beginner.name: White clover
good_beginner.why_beginner: A low clover outside the trunk area acts as a living mulch and adds a little nitrogen, without stealing water the way lawn grass does.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Clover as a citrus living-mulch/cover crop is extension-supported (UF/IFAS citrus cover-crop program names clovers among legume covers contributing soil N; clover N-fixation nodules pictured in UF/IFAS materials). extension_backed/medium: extension-documented legume-cover benefit; medium because citrus-specific N transfer is site-dependent and clover also competes for water.

good_beginner.name: Nasturtium
good_beginner.why_beginner: An easy flower that covers bare soil and draws in helpful insects. Keep it out from the trunk so it does not crowd the base.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Nasturtium aphid trap-crop + pollinator draw is well documented as a general function and transfers reasonably to citrus aphids; no citrus-specific trial located. traditional/medium (general trap-crop function applied to citrus by sound analogy).

good_beginner.name: Marigold
good_beginner.why_beginner: A simple flower that brings in helpful insects and fills bare ground around the tree. Plant it beyond the trunk, not tight against it.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Marigold nematode-suppression (French marigold vs root-knot nematode) is a real, partly-research-backed mechanism, but its application as a citrus companion is general rather than citrus-trial-specific; pollinator/beneficial draw is sound. traditional/medium (kept traditional because the citrus-specific benefit is by analogy; the nematode mechanism alone could argue mechanistic, flagged).

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Comfrey
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Deep roots pull up nutrients, and the leaves can be cut and dropped as a mulch that feeds the tree. Plant it outside the trunk flare, not right against the tree.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Same basis as apple's comfrey entry: chop-and-drop mulch / non-competing deep taproot / pollinator draw, widely practiced in fruit-tree guilds and partly grounded; dynamic-accumulator mineral claims are permaculture tradition, not peer-reviewed. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Comfrey is a leafy plant that grows well near citrus. Its roots reach deep, so it does not fight the tree for water, and a few times a season you can cut the big leaves and lay them on the soil as a mulch that feeds the tree. Plant it out past the trunk, not right against it, and let its flowers bring in helpful bees.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Yarrow
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A low, shallow-rooted plant that draws beneficial insects and does not compete with the citrus roots when kept outside the dripline.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Yarrow as an insectary/beneficial-attractant + drought-tolerant ground cover is consistently reported and mechanistically plausible (umbel-like flowers recruit predators), but the citrus-specific pest-reduction effect is unquantified. Flowering-cover-crops-recruit-psyllid-predators is noted by UF/IFAS as a general benefit, supporting the direction. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Yarrow is a low, tough plant with flat flower heads that draw in ladybugs, lacewings, and other good bugs that eat aphids and pests off your orange tree. It is shallow-rooted and easygoing, so it does not crowd the citrus roots as long as you keep it out toward the edge of the canopy rather than at the trunk. Let it flower to get the benefit.

good_seasoned.name: Fava bean
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A cool-season nitrogen fixer that can be grown beyond the dripline as a cover, then cut and dropped to feed the soil without crowding the tree.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Legume winter cover crops in citrus are extension-supported for soil N and organic matter (UF/IFAS citrus cover-crop program; California winter legume covers widely used in orchards). Fava is a standard cool-season legume cover. extension_backed/medium: the legume-cover soil-fertility benefit is extension-documented; medium because the citrus-specific N-transfer magnitude is acknowledged by UF/IFAS as not fully quantified in perennial systems and is site/timing dependent.

bad_beginner.name: Turf grass
bad_beginner.why_beginner: Lawn grass under the tree steals the water and food the orange's shallow roots need. A ring of mulch, kept back from the trunk, is better than grass.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Beginner-register version of the citrus-grass-competition concern; same UF/IFAS basis. extension_backed/medium.

bad_beginner.name: Bermuda grass
bad_beginner.why_beginner: A tough, spreading lawn grass that competes hard for water and is difficult to keep out of the root zone. Clear it out to the edge of the branches.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Same citrus-grass-competition basis (UF/IFAS); Bermuda (Cynodon dactylon) is specifically a highly competitive, aggressively spreading turf and appears in the citrus literature as orchard-floor vegetation. extension_backed/medium.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: St. Augustine grass
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A dense, spreading lawn grass that competes aggressively for water and nutrients in the top soil and creeps right up to the trunk. Keep it cleared out to the dripline.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Citrus is extension-documented (UF/IFAS) as highly vulnerable to weed/grass competition within the root zone, especially at bloom/flush; St. Augustine is a notably aggressive spreading turf. extension_backed/medium: extension-supported grass-citrus competition; medium because the specific quantified loss is via extension guidance rather than a St-Augustine-on-citrus controlled trial I opened.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: St. Augustine is a thick, fast-spreading lawn grass, and it is rough on citrus. It soaks up the water and food in the top layer of soil where the tree's roots feed, and it creeps right up to the trunk. Keep a clear or mulched circle around the base of your orange tree and hold the grass back beyond it, since it will keep trying to spread in.

bad_seasoned.name: Pigeon pea
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Pigeon pea is a nitrogen-fixing legume, so it looks like a natural cover crop for citrus, but it carries a specific strike against it. Research testing whether legumes shelter the citrus root weevil (Diaprepes abbreviatus) found that pigeon pea actually supported the weevil's larval development, sustaining a pest whose larvae feed on citrus roots instead of starving it out. The important context for most navel growers: this weevil is established in Florida and the Caribbean, not in the arid citrus regions of California and Arizona, so if you are growing navels in the West, pigeon pea's worst property is not a live threat in your area. The reason to skip it anyway is that the same research also flagged possible chemical interference from pigeon pea on citrus roots, which is not regional, and you give up nothing by choosing a cool-season legume like fava or a clover cover instead. Those deliver the same nitrogen benefit with no root-pest baggage.

provenance.label: research_backed
provenance.reason: Demoted from good_seasoned to bad_seasoned on a measured adverse finding. Lapointe (2003), cited in the peer-reviewed Strauss et al. 2024 HortTechnology review (ASHS), tested whether pigeon pea, pinto peanut, and rattlebox serve as a refuge for Diaprepes abbreviatus and found pigeon pea SUPPORTED weevil larval development (the certified, weight-bearing finding), and noted POTENTIAL allelopathic effects on citrus roots (softer strand, source's own hedge). research_backed/medium: the weevil-refuge effect is a measured experimental result (earns research_backed), confidence medium because (a) the headline practical risk (Diaprepes) is region-specific to FL/Caribbean and absent in arid CA/AZ navel regions, and (b) the allelopathy strand is 'potential', not established. Net: a real, research-backed reason to avoid pigeon pea in citrus, with the regional scope stated honestly in the prose.

pests.name: Asian citrus psyllid
pests.symptoms_seasoned: The psyllid itself is a tiny mottled-brown insect, about an eighth of an inch, that feeds tilted up at a 45-degree angle on new flush, a posture no other citrus pest shares. Its nymphs produce distinctive waxy tubules and curl tender new growth; heavy feeding twists and notches expanding leaves. The insect matters less for its direct damage than for what it carries: it is the vector of Huanglongbing (citrus greening), the most serious citrus disease worldwide. Scout the youngest flush, where it concentrates.
pests.symptoms_beginner: This tiny brown insect has a distinctive resting posture: it perches on new leaves at an angle, with its rear end raised and pointed upward, which is your identification clue. The young ones produce little waxy white threads and cause the new leaf tips to curl. The real danger is not the feeding itself but a fatal disease the psyllid spreads, citrus greening, so it is worth acting on even where the pest is uncommon.
pests.cause_seasoned: Adults lay eggs only on new flush, so populations track flushing cycles and explode in warm weather when trees push tender growth. The pest has spread through most citrus-growing regions of the southern United States; in much of California and the Gulf states it is now established, and any psyllid should be assumed a potential disease carrier.
pests.cause_beginner: The psyllid breeds on fresh new leaves, so it builds up fastest when the tree is putting out tender growth in warm weather. It has spread across the southern states, and any psyllid you find could be carrying the disease.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Buy only certified citrus from a reputable nursery and never move citrus plants or leaves out of a quarantine area, which is the main way the pest and disease jump regions. Inspect each new flush in the warm season. Conserve the natural enemies (a parasitic wasp, Tamarixia, and general predators) that suppress it. Where the disease is present, area-wide psyllid control is the front line.
pests.prevention_beginner: Buy certified citrus from a trusted nursery, and never carry citrus plants or cuttings out of a quarantine zone, because that is how the pest and its disease spread. Check the new leaves often in warm weather. If citrus greening is in your area, follow local guidance on controlling the psyllid.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: On a backyard tree, horticultural oil and insecticidal soap applied to new flush reduce nymphs; thorough coverage of tender growth is key, and repeat as each flush emerges. Do not apply oil above 95°F or to a drought-stressed tree. Most importantly, report suspected psyllids or greening symptoms to your county agricultural office, since this is a regulated pest.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray horticultural oil or insecticidal soap on the new growth to knock back the young psyllids, and repeat each time fresh leaves appear. Hold off on oil when it is hot, above roughly 95°F, or when the tree is short on water, since either condition lets oil burn the leaves. Also report any psyllids or signs of the disease to your local farm advisor or county office, because it is closely tracked.

pests.name: Citrus leafminer
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Silvery, serpentine tunnels winding through new leaves, with a thin dark line of frass down the center of each mine, and leaf margins that curl and pucker around the damage. The larva mines only young, expanding foliage; hardened mature leaves are not attacked. On established trees the injury is cosmetic, but on young trees pushing lots of flush it can slow growth and the curled tissue can shelter other pests.
pests.symptoms_beginner: You will see squiggly silver trails snaking through the new leaves, often with the leaf edge curled up. A tiny caterpillar makes these tunnels inside young leaves only. It looks alarming but rarely hurts an established tree, though it can set back a small young one.
pests.cause_seasoned: A small moth lays eggs on tender new flush, and the larvae mine between the leaf surfaces. Generations cycle quickly in warm weather, so damage peaks on the late-summer and fall flushes rather than the spring growth.
pests.cause_beginner: A tiny moth lays its eggs on the newest leaves, and the larvae tunnel inside them. They breed fast in warm weather, so the worst damage shows up on the late-summer growth.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid pushing excess tender flush with heavy nitrogen or unnecessary summer pruning, since the moth needs young leaves to breed. Tolerate cosmetic mining on bearing trees; resident parasitic wasps usually provide good control if broad-spectrum sprays are avoided.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not over-fertilize or prune a lot in summer, because that creates the tender new leaves the moth needs. On a healthy grown tree, it is best to just live with the trails, since helpful wasps keep it in check.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Chemical control is rarely warranted, and broad-spectrum sprays undermine the parasitic wasps that naturally suppress leafminer populations. For young trees, where the canopy is small enough that leafminer damage slows establishment, a lightweight horticultural oil applied at bud break can discourage adults from laying eggs on the new flush; repeat as each flush emerges because oil breaks down quickly. Follow label heat restrictions and do not spray above 95°F. Leave mined leaves in place, as they continue photosynthesizing.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Usually no treatment is needed, and spraying can kill the good bugs that control it. On a small young tree you want to protect, light horticultural oil on the new leaves discourages the moth. Only spray oil in mild conditions, not in high heat or on a thirsty tree, and leave the tunneled leaves on the tree.

pests.name: Scale insects
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Scale appear as fixed, non-moving bumps clustered on twigs, along the leaf midrib, and beneath the leaves. The armored types form firm gray or brown shells that look almost like raised bark, while the softer types are plumper and somewhat glossy. The soft kinds give themselves away by the honeydew they secrete, which leaves foliage tacky and grows a black sooty film, and you will often find ants patrolling the colony for that sugar. Where numbers run high, expect mottled yellow leaves, premature leaf fall, and dieback at the twig tips.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Scale look like little hard or waxy lumps that sit still on twigs and the undersides of leaves, so it is easy to think they are just part of the branch. The softer kinds make the leaves tacky and a sooty black coating grows on that stickiness. Ants are often crawling around them.
pests.cause_seasoned: A mix of armored and soft scale species tap into the tree and feed on its sap. They get the upper hand on trees that are dusty, crowded, or patrolled by ants, because the ants drive away the lady beetles and parasitic wasps that would otherwise thin the colony.
pests.cause_beginner: Scale are little insects that feed on the tree's sap. They get worst when ants are around, since the ants protect them from the helpful bugs that eat scale.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep the tree vigorous and rinse dust off the canopy, and cut off the ants with a sticky trunk band so the resident beneficial insects can do the work. Look any incoming nursery tree over carefully, because scale frequently hitchhikes in on new stock.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep ants from climbing the tree by wrapping a sticky band around the trunk, which lets the good bugs control the scale, and look over any new tree for lumps before planting it.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: A thorough horticultural oil application, narrow-range petroleum or neem, smothers the scale and is the usual home remedy; the key is wetting every surface, especially twig undersides and leaf backs. Skip oil above roughly 95°F or on a tree that is drought-stressed, since heat plus oil scorches foliage. Plan a follow-up as fresh crawlers hatch.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Coat the lumps with horticultural oil, making sure to reach the backs of leaves and the twigs. Save the spray for cooler, well-watered days, never above roughly 95°F or on a drought-stressed tree, or it can scorch the foliage. Spray again later as new ones appear.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of soft-bodied green, black, or brown aphids on the youngest flush and flower buds, with curled, distorted new leaves and a sticky honeydew coating that draws ants and grows sooty mold. Spring and fall flushes are the targets. One species, the brown citrus aphid, is also a vector of citrus tristeza virus, which raises the stakes where that disease is a concern.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Look for clusters of tiny soft-bodied insects, often green or black, packed onto the newest leaves and flower buds, causing the tips to curl. They secrete a sticky coating that ants follow and that leads to a black sooty film. Navel oranges are most vulnerable during the spring and fall flushes when tender new growth is available.
pests.cause_seasoned: Aphids reproduce explosively on tender new growth in mild weather and are tended by ants for their honeydew. Lush, over-fertilized flush is especially attractive, and ant protection lets colonies outrun their natural enemies.
pests.cause_beginner: Aphids multiply very fast on soft new growth in mild weather, and ants protect them. Too much fertilizer makes extra tender leaves that draw them in.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid forcing excessive tender flush with heavy nitrogen. Control ants so lady beetles, lacewings, and parasitic wasps can suppress colonies. A strong jet of water knocks aphids off new growth and is often all that is needed.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not over-fertilize, which makes the soft growth aphids love, and keep ants out so ladybugs and other helpers can eat them. A blast of water from the hose usually clears them off.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: A forceful water spray, insecticidal soap, or horticultural oil controls aphids; cover the undersides of curled leaves. Repeat as needed. Observe oil heat limits (not above 95°F or on stressed trees). Preserve natural enemies by skipping broad-spectrum insecticides.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray them off with water, or use insecticidal soap or horticultural oil, getting under the curled leaves. Keep oil for mild days only, not in high heat or on a stressed, dry tree, and avoid harsh sprays that kill the good bugs.

pests.name: Citrus red mite
pests.symptoms_seasoned: A fine stippling or silvering on leaves and sometimes fruit rind, with tiny dark-red mites and their cast skins visible on leaf surfaces under a hand lens. Heavy populations bronze the foliage and can cause leaf drop. Mites flare in hot, dusty, dry conditions and after broad-spectrum sprays kill their predators, so outbreaks are often a sign the tree is dust-stressed or was over-sprayed.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Look for leaves that turn a dull, speckled, silvery color, sometimes with tiny red dots moving on them (a hand lens helps). Mites get worse when it is hot, dry, and dusty. A lot of them can bronze the leaves and cause some to drop.
pests.cause_seasoned: Citrus red mite thrives in heat and dust and reproduces rapidly on stressed trees. Dusty roadside or driveway trees and trees sprayed with broad-spectrum insecticides (which remove predatory mites) are the most prone to damaging populations.
pests.cause_beginner: These mites love hot, dusty conditions and build up fast on stressed trees. Dusty trees and trees that have been sprayed with strong insecticides (which kill the helpful mites) get the worst of it.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Hose dust off the canopy in hot, dry spells and keep the tree well watered, since vigorous trees tolerate mites better. Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that destroy the predatory mites providing natural control.
pests.prevention_beginner: Rinse dust off the leaves during hot dry weather and keep the tree watered, because a healthy tree handles mites better. Avoid strong insecticides that kill the good mites.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Damage is usually cosmetic and rarely needs treatment. If populations are heavy on a stressed tree, horticultural oil provides control; observe heat limits strictly, as mite outbreaks coincide with the hot weather when oil is riskiest. Do not apply oil above 95°F or to a drought-stressed tree.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Usually the damage is just cosmetic and needs nothing. If there are a lot of mites, horticultural oil works, but timing is tricky: mites peak in hot weather, which is the riskiest time to oil a tree. Only spray when it has cooled off, never on a hot, dry, stressed tree.

pests.name: Katydids and fruit-surface chewers
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Irregular chewed notches on young leaves and, more conspicuously, smooth shallow gouges or healed scars on the rind of developing fruit, where a katydid or similar chewing insect fed when the fruit was tiny. The damage scars over and grows out as the fruit expands, so it is a cosmetic, surface-only blemish that does not reach the flesh of a navel.
pests.symptoms_beginner: You may find ragged bites out of young leaves, or smooth shallow scars on the skin of the fruit where something chewed it when it was small. On a navel this is only skin-deep: the fruit inside is fine, it just looks marked.
pests.cause_seasoned: Katydids and other occasional chewing insects feed on tender foliage and very young fruit in spring and early summer. Populations are usually low and sporadic in a backyard, and the visible scarring is out of proportion to the actual number of insects.
pests.cause_beginner: Katydids and a few other leaf-chewing insects nibble soft leaves and tiny fruit in spring and early summer. There are usually only a few of them, even though the scars look like a lot.
pests.prevention_seasoned: No action is generally needed on a home tree. Healthy trees outgrow the cosmetic injury, and the chewers are kept in check by birds and general predators. Hand-pick if a particular insect is abundant on a small tree.
pests.prevention_beginner: Caterpillar chewing rarely warrants intervention. An established tree outgrows the leaf notches quickly, and natural predators, including birds and beneficial wasps, keep populations in check on their own. If you spot a caterpillar on a small young tree, you can simply pick it off by hand.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Treatment is rarely justified for cosmetic rind scarring. Hand-picking handles the occasional katydid. Reserve any spray for genuine defoliation of a young tree, and prefer a targeted product over a broad-spectrum insecticide that would disrupt the citrus natural-enemy complex.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spraying is almost never worth it for marks on the skin. Just pick off the bugs by hand. Only consider a spray if a small tree is being stripped of leaves, and then pick a targeted one rather than a harsh insecticide.

diseases.name: Huanglongbing (citrus greening, HLB)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Blotchy, asymmetric yellowing of leaves that does not mirror across the midrib (distinguishing it from a nutrient deficiency, which is usually symmetric), yellow shoots, and corky, enlarged leaf veins. Fruit are small, lopsided, fail to color fully, stay green at the bottom, and taste bitter and salty; seeds often abort. The tree declines over several years and there is no cure. This is the most destructive citrus disease worldwide.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The classic sign is a leaf that is yellow in a blotchy, uneven pattern, with the yellow on one side of the leaf not matching the other (a nutrient problem is usually even on both sides). Fruit stay small, lopsided, green on the bottom, and taste bad. There is no cure, and the tree slowly dies. It is the worst citrus disease there is.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus, the bacterium behind citrus greening, spreads tree to tree via the Asian citrus psyllid feeding on new growth. Inside the tree it clogs the phloem so nutrients cannot reach roots and fruit. No treatment can clear the infection once established, so management is entirely about suppressing the psyllid and removing confirmed trees before they seed the pest further.
diseases.cause_beginner: Bacteria spread by the Asian citrus psyllid as it feeds on new shoots clog the tree's vascular system, blocking the flow of nutrients to roots and fruit. No treatment can reverse the infection; an affected tree is a permanent source of disease spread. The entire management strategy is preventing psyllid feeding and removing any confirmed tree before it extends the outbreak.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant only certified disease-free nursery trees, never move citrus out of quarantine areas, and control the psyllid vector aggressively where it is present. Inspect trees regularly and report suspected greening to your county agricultural commissioner, since coordinated removal of infected trees is the only effective area-wide defense.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Buy only certified clean trees, never move citrus out of a quarantine zone, and control the psyllid that spreads it. Check your tree often, and report anything that looks like greening to your local agricultural office, because removing infected trees quickly is what protects everyone's citrus.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure and no organic remedy for an infected tree. Management is prevention and vector control only: protect trees from the psyllid, and remove and properly dispose of confirmed-infected trees promptly so they cannot serve as a reservoir for further spread.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no treatment that saves an infected tree. Focus entirely on prevention: keep the psyllid off your trees with regular inspection and treatment, and if a tree is diagnosed with citrus greening, remove it promptly to protect your neighbors' trees and the surrounding area. An infected tree left in place becomes an ongoing source of psyllid pressure.

diseases.name: Phytophthora foot rot, root rot, and gummosis
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Watch for gum weeping from the lower trunk and crown (gummosis), and bark at the soil line that turns dark and water-soaked, then later splits and dries as a sunken lesion (foot rot). When the disease works on the feeder roots instead, the tree fades slowly, with leaves yellowing and the canopy thinning out (root rot). The diagnostic clue is foliage that yellows and wilts yet fails to perk up after irrigation, which sets it apart from simple drought, and lesions can climb from the crown onto the lower scaffold limbs.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: This soil water-mold disease shows up as gum oozing low on the trunk, dark mushy bark right at ground level, and a tree that gradually yellows and gets sparse. The big clue: the leaves yellow and wilt but do not bounce back when you water, which means rot rather than thirst.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Phytophthora organisms, which are water molds rather than true fungi, live in the soil and release swimming spores whenever conditions turn wet; those spores splash up onto the trunk or move through saturated ground to the roots. The disease is set up by soggy or poorly draining soil, soil or mulch heaped against the trunk, a graft union buried below grade, and the chronic overwatering that young trees so often receive.
diseases.cause_beginner: It lives in the soil and travels in standing water. It gets going when the ground stays wet, when soil or mulch is mounded up around the trunk, or when the graft union ends up buried. The graft union is that knob low on the trunk, the point where the fruiting variety was joined onto the roots, and it needs to stay above the soil. Watering young trees too much is the usual trigger.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Engineer this one out when you plant, because that is the only reliable defense. The goal is a crown that drains immediately: build a low mound or berm, position the tree so only the uppermost roots are covered, and keep the graft union at least six inches above finished grade per UF/IFAS guidance. Grade the surrounding soil for positive drainage away from the base, hold mulch a foot back from the trunk, and keep drip emitters out of the crown zone. A Phytophthora-tolerant rootstock such as Carrizo, Swingle, or trifoliate provides an additional layer of protection.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Prevention is mostly in the planting. Put the tree up on a small mound, hold the graft union clear of the soil (UF/IFAS says more than six inches above it), make sure water drains off fast, hold mulch a hand's width away from the trunk, and never point water at the base. This is the disease most worth preventing from the start.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Fix the water and drainage problem before anything else, since the tree cannot recover while the roots stay wet. On a fresh trunk lesion you can pare back the dark, dead bark to a rim of healthy green tissue and let the area dry; opening a buried crown to the air sometimes arrests it. Once root rot is advanced on an established tree it is hard to turn around, which is exactly why the planting practices matter so much.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Sort out the drainage or stop the overwatering first, or nothing else will work. For a gummy patch on the trunk, you can gently trim away the dark dead bark down to healthy bark and let it dry out. A serious root case is tough to cure, so getting the planting right up front is what counts.

diseases.name: Citrus canker
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Raised, corky, tan lesions with a water-soaked or oily margin and often a yellow halo, appearing on leaves, twigs, and fruit rind. Unlike many leaf spots, canker lesions erupt through both leaf surfaces and feel rough and raised. Severe infection causes defoliation, twig dieback, and blemished, sometimes dropping fruit. It is a regulated disease in the Gulf states and is far more of a problem in warm, wet, windy climates than in arid ones.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Canker makes raised, rough, tan spots, often ringed with yellow and looking a bit oily at the edges, on leaves, twigs, and the skin of the fruit. The spots come through both sides of the leaf and feel bumpy. Bad cases drop leaves and mark the fruit. It is mostly a problem in warm, wet, windy places like the Gulf Coast.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A bacterium (Xanthomonas citri) that spreads in wind-driven rain and on contaminated tools and hands, entering through natural openings and wounds, including leafminer mines. Warm temperatures, frequent rain, and wind (which wounds tissue and drives the bacteria) make it severe; it is largely absent from dry interior and desert climates.
diseases.cause_beginner: Bacteria spread it through wind-blown rain and on dirty tools and hands. It gets in through tiny wounds, including the tunnels made by leafminers. Warm, rainy, windy weather makes it worse, so it is mainly a humid-climate problem and rarely shows up in dry inland or desert areas.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant certified disease-free stock and choose less-susceptible varieties where canker is established. Avoid working in the canopy when wet, disinfect pruning tools, manage leafminer (whose mines are infection courts) on young trees, and provide good air movement. In regulated areas, follow state guidance, which may include copper programs.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Start with certified clean nursery trees. In regions where canker is established, avoid pruning or working around the tree during or after rain, since the bacteria spread in water, and disinfect your cutting tools between each cut. Controlling leafminer on young trees matters because the feeding tunnels create entry points for the bacteria. Where canker is active in your county, follow your state extension's current guidance.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Copper-based protectant sprays applied before and during the wet season are the primary backyard tool in canker regions; they reduce the rate of new infections without curing what is already present. Once infection establishes in wood, prune out and dispose of heavily affected material and disinfect tools between trees to limit spread. In arid California and the desert Southwest, where the humid conditions canker requires are largely absent, growers rarely encounter this disease.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure, only ways to slow it down. In humid regions, copper sprays during the rainy season help prevent new spots, and you should remove badly infected branches and clean your tools. In dry climates you usually do not need to worry about it.

diseases.name: Greasy spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellow mottling on the upper leaf surface that develops into greasy-looking, blister-like brown-to-black lesions on the underside, giving the leaf a translucent, oily appearance. Affected leaves drop prematurely, often in late winter, thinning the canopy. On fruit a fine black speckling (greasy spot rind blotch) can appear. It is primarily a problem in the humid Southeast and Gulf, driven by warm, wet, humid conditions.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The leaves develop yellow splotches on the upper surface and raised, greasy-looking brown or black blisters on the underside, making the leaf look oily. Affected leaves drop early, usually in late winter, which gradually thins out the tree's canopy. This is mainly a humid-climate disease, concentrated in Florida and along the Gulf Coast, and is rarely seen in the arid West.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Zasmidium citri-griseum, the causal fungus, completes its spore cycle in the layer of decomposing fallen leaves beneath the tree; from that litter, spores are released during warm, humid, wet periods and infect the leaf undersides, with a long latent interval before the characteristic blistering appears. Because the disease regenerates from its own debris, sanitation under the canopy disrupts the cycle.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus causes it, growing on the old fallen leaves under the tree and then infecting new leaves in warm, humid, wet weather. The dead leaves on the ground are where it comes from, so it keeps itself going through the litter.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rake up and remove fallen leaves under the tree to break the disease cycle, the single most useful cultural step. Promote air movement and avoid prolonged leaf wetness where you can. In dry inland and desert climates the disease is essentially absent and no action is needed.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Rake up and get rid of the fallen leaves under the tree, since that is where the fungus lives, and that one step helps the most. Good airflow helps too. In dry inland or desert areas you will probably never see it.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Sanitation (removing leaf litter) is the core organic control. Where pressure is high in humid regions, a horticultural oil or copper spray timed to early summer reduces infection; oil also helps by suppressing the fungus on leaf surfaces. Observe oil heat limits. Most home trees outside the humid Southeast need no treatment.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Cleaning up the fallen leaves is the main organic fix. In humid regions with a lot of it, a horticultural oil or copper spray in early summer helps, but remember not to use oil on very hot days. Most trees outside the humid Southeast do not need anything.

diseases.name: Sooty mold
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Honeydew secreted by sap-sucking insects colonizes leaf surfaces as a black, powdery-sooty layer on leaves, twigs, and fruit; it can be rubbed off, leaving the tissue beneath undamaged. The mold itself does not infect the tree, but heavy deposits shade the leaf and blemish the rind, and the presence of sooty mold is a reliable indicator that aphids, soft scale, mealybugs, or whitefly are active on the tree.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: You will see a black, dusty powder covering the leaves and sometimes the fruit; it wipes off and does not actually damage the tree tissue underneath. This is sooty mold, and it grows on the sticky droppings of sap-sucking insects like aphids, scale, or whitefly feeding above. Finding it is a cue to look for the insect that is producing the honeydew.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Saprophytic fungi colonize the sugary honeydew excreted by aphids, soft scale, mealybugs, or whitefly. The presence of sooty mold is therefore a symptom of an insect infestation, and ants tending those insects make it worse by protecting them from predators.
diseases.cause_beginner: The black mold grows on the sweet honeydew that sap-sucking insects leave behind. So sooty mold really means you have one of those insects feeding on the tree, and ants often make it worse by protecting them.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Control the underlying honeydew producer (aphids, scale, mealybug, or whitefly) and manage ants, and the mold has nothing to grow on. There is no need to treat the mold itself directly.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Get rid of the insect that is making the honeydew (aphids, scale, and so on) and keep ants out, and the mold will have nothing to grow on. You do not need to treat the mold by itself.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Treat the insect, not the mold: horticultural oil or insecticidal soap on the honeydew producer, plus ant control, resolves both. Existing mold can be hosed or wiped off and will weather away once the honeydew stops. Observe oil heat limits.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Treat the insect causing it with horticultural oil or insecticidal soap, and keep ants away. The mold already there can be rinsed or wiped off and will fade once the stickiness stops. Do not use oil on very hot days.

diseases.name: Brown rot of fruit
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: A firm, leathery, light-brown decay on fruit hanging low in the canopy, usually within a few feet of the ground, often with a pungent odor and, in humid weather, a white mold on the surface. It typically appears on the rind of mature fruit during cool, wet fall and winter weather and can continue to rot fruit in storage. The low position on the tree is the giveaway, since the fungus splashes up from the soil.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Brown rot is a firm tan rot on fruit, almost always on the low-hanging fruit near the ground, often with a strong smell. It shows up on ripe fruit in cool, wet fall and winter weather. The clue is that it is the bottom fruit that rots, because the disease splashes up from the soil.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Soil-borne Phytophthora species splash onto low fruit during rain, infecting the rind. Cool, wet weather and fruit or skirt foliage close to the ground create the conditions; the same water molds that cause foot rot are responsible here, attacking fruit instead of trunk.
diseases.cause_beginner: The same kind of soil water-mold that causes trunk rot splashes up onto low fruit when it rains, especially in cool wet weather. Fruit and branches hanging near the ground are the ones that get it.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Skirt-prune the tree so no foliage or fruit hangs within about two feet of the ground, mulch to reduce splash, and harvest low fruit promptly. Good drainage (the same practice that prevents foot rot) reduces the inoculum. In dry-fall climates the disease is uncommon.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Trim the lowest branches so no fruit or leaves hang within about two feet of the ground, add mulch to cut down on splashing, and pick the low fruit early. The same good drainage that prevents trunk rot helps here too. In areas with dry falls it is uncommon.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and dispose of rotted fruit promptly so it does not spread in storage. Where brown rot recurs in wet-winter regions, a copper spray to the lower canopy and fruit before the rainy season is the standard preventive. Skirting and mulching remain the most reliable cultural controls.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick off and throw away any rotted fruit right away so it does not spread to stored fruit. In wet-winter areas where it keeps coming back, a copper spray on the lower fruit before the rains helps. Keeping the low branches trimmed and mulching are the most dependable fixes.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Deep and infrequent. Water established trees thoroughly, then let the top inch or two of soil dry before watering again; the interval stretches in cool weather and shortens in heat. Young trees need more frequent water to establish but still on a soak-and-dry pattern, never kept constantly wet.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water deeply but not too often. Soak the root zone thoroughly, then let the surface dry out, checking with a finger: when the top inch or two feels dry, it is time to water again. Water more often in hot weather and less in cool weather. Young trees dry out faster than established ones, but still let the surface dry between waterings and never keep the soil constantly wet.
watering.amount_seasoned: Each irrigation should push moisture down through the full root depth, which for a mature tree means soaking the soil out to the canopy dripline. Frequent shallow sprinklings develop weak surface roots that dry out quickly and leave the tree drought-prone; they also miss the deep roots that anchor the tree and supply it through summer heat.
watering.amount_beginner: Water enough to soak the soil deeply each time, out as far as the edge of the branches, not just a quick splash at the base. A few quick sprinkles do not reach the deep roots, so a long, thorough soak is better.
watering.method_seasoned: Drip or low-volume emitters around the dripline, or a slow soak from a hose, are ideal. Keep water off the trunk and crown, and never wet the graft union, since a constantly damp crown is a direct route to foot rot. Maintain a mulched, grass-free basin, with mulch pulled back from the trunk.
watering.method_beginner: Use drip emitters or a slow soak from a hose around the outer edge of the branches. Keep water off the trunk and the graft knob, because a wet trunk base can rot. Mulch the area under the tree (but keep the mulch away from the trunk) and keep grass out.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing leaves that wilt but do not recover after watering, leaf drop, mushy or sour-smelling soil, and gumming at the trunk base are signs of overwatering and incipient foot rot. The diagnostic tell is wilting that worsens, not improves, with more water.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Signs of too much water are yellow, wilting leaves that do not perk up when you water, dropping leaves, soggy or bad-smelling soil, and gum oozing at the base of the trunk. The key clue is that watering makes the wilting worse, not better.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Leaves that curl, cup, or dull and gray, wilting that recovers after watering, premature fruit drop, and a hard, dry root zone indicate underwatering. In heat, underwatered trees drop flowers and fruit and sunburn exposed fruit.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Signs of too little water are leaves that curl or look dull and gray, wilting that gets better after you water, fruit dropping early, and dry, hard soil. In hot weather, a thirsty tree drops flowers and fruit and the fruit can sunburn.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Citrus roots are relatively shallow and spreading, concentrated in the top foot or two of soil and extending out to and beyond the dripline. Water the broad root zone, not just the trunk, and adjust the soak-and-dry interval to soil type: sandy soils dry fast and need more frequent water, clay holds longer and needs less.
watering.method_note_beginner: Orange roots are shallow and spread out wide, so water the whole area under and around the branches, not just by the trunk. Sandy soil dries out fast and needs water more often; clay soil holds water longer and needs it less often.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The crucial windows are bloom, fruit sizing through summer, and extreme-heat spells. Even soil moisture through bloom and set prevents flower and fruit drop, and irrigation must be increased during heat waves to prevent drop and rind sunburn. Avoid both drought stress and waterlogging through these periods; consistency matters more than volume.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The most important times to keep up with watering are when the tree is blooming, while the fruit is growing through summer, and during heat waves. Even watering during bloom keeps the flowers and fruit from dropping, and you should water extra during hot spells so fruit does not drop or sunburn. Keep it steady, and avoid both bone-dry soil and soggy soil during these times.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Picked navels keep about one to two weeks at room temperature. Their bigger storage advantage, though, is on the tree: navels hold and continue sweetening on the tree for weeks to months, so the tree itself is the best short-term storage.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Once picked, oranges last about one to two weeks on the counter. But the best way to store them is to leave them on the tree, where they keep and get sweeter for weeks or even months.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerated, navels keep three to four weeks, and up to about six weeks in a crisper drawer. Store them loose or in a perforated bag so they do not sweat; do not seal them airtight.
storage.fridge_beginner: In the fridge, oranges last three to four weeks, up to about six weeks in the crisper drawer. Keep them loose or in a bag with holes so they do not get damp and moldy.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Whole navels do not freeze well, but the juice freezes excellently. Squeeze and freeze juice in airtight containers for up to about six months; segments can also be frozen in syrup. Zest can be frozen for baking.
storage.freezer_beginner: Whole oranges do not freeze well, but the juice does. Squeeze the juice and freeze it in a sealed container for up to about six months. You can also freeze the zest (the colored part of the peel) for cooking.
storage.notes_seasoned: The defining storage feature of navels is the long on-tree hold. Late-maturing selections such as Lane Late extend the harvest and storage season the furthest, holding sound fruit into spring. The exception is hot, dry climates, where fruit left on the tree too long can granulate and dry inside, so in the desert harvest within the prime window rather than relying on the full hold. Handle fruit gently, since rind damage shortens storage life.
storage.notes_beginner: The best thing about navels is that you can leave them on the tree for weeks or months and they keep getting sweeter, so you pick as you need them. Late types like Lane Late hold the longest, into spring. The one exception is hot, dry desert areas, where fruit left on too long can dry out inside, so there you should pick during its best window instead. Handle the fruit gently, since damaged skin spoils faster.

recommended.name: Washington
recommended.subtitle: The original navel, the global standard
recommended.notes_seasoned: The original and most widely planted navel orange worldwide, introduced to the United States from Bahia, Brazil in the 1870s. Seedless, large fruit with excellent fresh-eating quality. Mid-season maturity, typically November through February in California's inland valleys. The benchmark variety against which all other navels are compared.
recommended.recommended_note: Start here. The most reliable and widely available navel for any warm-zone garden.

recommended.name: Cara Cara
recommended.subtitle: Pink-fleshed navel
recommended.notes_seasoned: A bud mutation of Washington navel discovered in Venezuela in 1976. Flesh is deep pink to red due to lycopene, with a flavor slightly lower in acid than Washington. Early to mid-season maturity. Well adapted to California's inland valleys. Most tree and fruit characteristics reflect its Washington ancestry apart from the distinctive flesh color.
recommended.recommended_note: Pick this for the striking pink flesh and slightly sweeter, less acidic flavor.

recommended.name: Lane Late
recommended.subtitle: Extends the navel season
recommended.notes_seasoned: A late-maturing bud sport of Washington navel first selected in Australia. Fruit matures four to six weeks later than Washington and holds well on the tree for several months after reaching maturity. Similar size and shape to Washington with slightly smoother peel and smaller navel. Extends the fresh navel season into late winter and early spring.
recommended.recommended_note: Add this alongside Washington to stretch your harvest into early spring.

recommended.name: Fukumoto
recommended.subtitle: Early-coloring navel
recommended.notes_seasoned: An early-coloring navel selection from Japan. Develops deep rind color weeks before Washington, making it attractive for early-season harvest. Internal quality is similar to Washington. Fruit size tends slightly smaller. Popular in California for extending the harvest window at the early end.
recommended.recommended_note: Choose this for the earliest harvest and rind color in the season.

varieties.note_seasoned: All navel oranges are clonal bud sports or mutations tracing back to the original Washington navel, which was introduced to the United States from Bahia, Brazil in the 1870s. Variety differences are primarily in maturity timing, rind color development, and flesh pigmentation rather than tree habit or hardiness. All are seedless and parthenocarpic. In regions with marginal heat, early-coloring selections like Fukumoto may reach acceptable sugar levels sooner. Late selections like Lane Late extend the harvest window without requiring a second tree.
varieties.note_beginner: All navel oranges make seedless, easy-to-peel fruit and need a lot of summer heat to get sweet. Washington is the classic all-purpose navel. Cara Cara is a navel with pink-red flesh and a sweeter, berry-like taste. Lane Late ripens later and holds on the tree longest, stretching your season. Fukumoto colors up early. Pick based on when you want fruit and whether you would enjoy the pink-fleshed Cara Cara.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: N/A. Hardening off applies to seedlings raised indoors, not to navel oranges. Oranges are bought as grafted nursery trees already acclimated to outdoor conditions, so there is no seedling-hardening step. A containerized nursery tree moved to a much sunnier or hotter spot can be eased into full exposure over a week or two to avoid sunburn, but that is acclimation, not the classic hardening-off of started seedlings.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: N/A for oranges. Hardening off is for seedlings you start indoors, and you do not grow oranges that way. You buy an orange as a young grafted tree from a nursery that is already used to being outdoors. If you move a potted tree into much stronger sun, you can ease it into full sun over a week or two so it does not sunburn, but that is just adjusting it, not the usual hardening-off step.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Plant a grafted nursery tree from a reputable source with certified disease-free stock. Container-grown trees can be planted year-round in frost-free zones; bare-root trees are planted in late winter to early spring. Set the tree at the same soil line as in the nursery container. Do not bury the graft union.
start_method.notes_beginner: Buy a young grafted orange tree from a good nursery, and make sure it is certified disease-free. When you plant it, set it a little high on a small mound and keep that knobby graft union sitting above the soil. If your soil is heavy clay, the mound matters even more so water drains away. You can plant container-grown trees almost any time in frost-free areas; in colder areas plant in spring after frost danger passes.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Use a loose, fast-draining potting mix, ideally one labeled for citrus or cactus. Do not use heavy garden soil in a pot, because it packs down and stays soggy.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in perlite, pumice, or bark chips to help it drain even better. You want a mix that drains fast and never stays soggy, since a potted orange is even more sensitive to wet roots than one planted in the ground.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: Sharp drainage inside the pot is the priority. A mix sold specifically for citrus or cactus works well; so does a quality potting mix lightened with extra perlite or coarse pine bark to keep it from compacting. Never use straight garden soil in a container because it packs tight and holds moisture against the roots.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend in perlite, pumice, or coarse bark to sharpen drainage further. The goal is a mix that drains freely after watering and never stays saturated, since a potted citrus is even less forgiving of wet feet than one in the ground.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out much faster than the ground, especially in heat and wind, so check a potted orange often, maybe every day in summer. Water until it drips out the bottom, then let the top inch dry before watering again. Do not let the pot sit in a saucer full of water.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: A potted orange needs feeding more often than one in the ground, because the frequent watering washes nutrients out of the pot. Use a citrus fertilizer a bit lighter but more often during the growing season, and watch for yellowing leaves (a citrus food with iron and zinc helps prevent that in pots).

overwintering.approach_beginner: If your winters are cold, growing an orange in a pot is the way to do it: keep it on a small (dwarf) tree and move the pot into a garage, sunroom, or by a bright window indoors when frost is coming, then put it back outside when it warms up. This is how people grow oranges in cold places. While it is inside for winter, water it less and stop feeding it.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: For growers outside zones 9-11, a navel on Flying Dragon or another dwarfing rootstock in a large pot is the standard approach to working around the cold limit. When frost threatens, roll or carry the tree into a garage, sunroom, or bright indoor spot, then move it back outside once danger passes. Keep water reduced and hold off on fertilizer while the tree is held cool indoors; this is how navels succeed well north of their in-ground hardiness range.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Oranges are one of the best fruit trees to grow in a pot, especially a dwarf type on Flying Dragon rootstock. That is exactly why a pot is the trick for cold climates: you can move it under cover when frost comes. Use a big pot (bigger is better for a fruiting tree) with plenty of drainage holes and a loose citrus mix, and plan to water and feed more often than a tree in the ground.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Citrus are among the best fruit trees for containers, and a navel on Flying Dragon (a naturally dwarfing trifoliate rootstock) is well suited to a large pot. This makes the navel the cold-climate frost-escape play: a pot you can move under cover. Choose a large container (the bigger the better for a fruiting tree), ensure ample drainage holes, use a coarse citrus mix, and expect to water and feed more often than an in-ground tree. Do not lift peach's container guidance here; unlike peach, citrus genuinely thrives in pots.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Container trees dry out much faster than in-ground ones, particularly in the summer heat that navels need for sweetness. Check the pot daily in hot or windy periods and water before the root zone dries out completely. Good drainage is critical: the saucer should stay empty, not pooling water against the roots. The combination of frequent, deep waterings and a fast-draining mix is what keeps a potted navel healthy. See the container watering note for detail.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Feed more frequently than an in-ground tree at a lighter rate, using a micronutrient-inclusive citrus fertilizer, since pot leaching depletes nutrients and brings on chlorosis quickly. See the container fertilizer note for detail.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering containers are risky for citrus and generally not recommended, because their constantly moist reservoir works against the soak-and-dry cycle citrus needs and raises the foot-rot risk. If used at all, choose one with a true overflow and a coarse mix, let the reservoir empty between fills, and watch closely for overwatering signs.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: Self-watering pots are not a good choice for oranges, because they keep the soil constantly wet, which is the opposite of the soak-and-dry watering citrus likes, and can rot the roots. If you do use one, let the water reservoir run empty between fills and watch for signs of overwatering.
container_notes.container_overwintering_seasoned: Move the pot to a protected spot (garage, sunroom, or indoors by a bright window) before the first frost in cold-winter zones, and return it outdoors after frost danger passes. Hold the tree cool and bright, reduce watering, and stop feeding while it is overwintered. This portability is the whole advantage of growing a navel in a container outside its hardiness range.
container_notes.container_overwintering_beginner: In cold-winter areas, move the pot inside (a garage, sunroom, or by a bright window) before the first frost, and put it back outside once frost is past. Keep it cool and in good light, water it less, and stop feeding while it is inside for winter. Being able to move the pot is the whole point of growing an orange in a container where winters are cold.
