A small young tree needs only a little; a grown mandarin needs more, though still less than a full-size orange tree. When in doubt, follow the package directions for the tree's size.

companions.note_beginner: Keep grass and lawn out from under a mandarin tree, since grass steals the water and food the tree's shallow roots need. A ring of mulch, kept back from the trunk, beats grass growing right up to the tree. There is little real benefit to planting things close around citrus.
companions.note_seasoned: Keep turf and lawn grasses out of the root zone. Grass competes hard for water and nutrients in the shallow layer where citrus feeder roots concentrate, and mowers damage the trunk. A mulched, grass-free basin out to the canopy dripline is the standard recommendation for all citrus, mandarins included. Low, shallow-rooted covers or a cool-season legume kept outside the trunk flare add living mulch without root competition. Mandarins fruit on a single tree, so no pollinizer companion is required; in fact nearby pollen-bearing citrus can put seeds into otherwise seedless fruit.

good_beginner.name: White clover
good_beginner.why_beginner: A low clover outside the trunk area works as a living mulch and adds a little nitrogen, without stealing water the way lawn grass does.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Legume living-mulch / cover crop under citrus is extension-supported for soil nitrogen and organic matter; medium because citrus-specific nitrogen transfer is site-dependent and clover also competes for water.

good_beginner.name: Marigold
good_beginner.why_beginner: A simple flower that brings in helpful insects and fills bare ground around the tree. Plant it beyond the trunk, not tight against it.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Marigold beneficial-insect draw and root-knot nematode suppression are partly grounded as general mechanisms; applied to citrus by analogy, no mandarin-specific trial located.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Yarrow
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A low, shallow-rooted plant that draws beneficial insects and does not compete with citrus roots when kept outside the dripline.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Yarrow is a low, tough plant with flat flower heads that pull in ladybugs, lacewings, and other good bugs that eat aphids. It is shallow-rooted and easygoing, so it does not crowd the tree as long as you keep it out toward the edge of the canopy. Let it flower to get the benefit.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Yarrow as an insectary / drought-tolerant ground cover is consistently reported and mechanistically plausible; the citrus-specific pest reduction is unquantified.

good_seasoned.name: Fava bean
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A cool-season nitrogen fixer grown beyond the dripline as a winter cover, then cut and dropped to feed the soil without crowding the tree.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Cool-season legume cover crops in citrus are extension-supported for soil nitrogen and organic matter; medium because citrus-specific nitrogen-transfer magnitude is site and timing dependent.

bad_beginner.name: Turf grass
bad_beginner.why_beginner: Lawn grass under the tree steals the water and food the mandarin's shallow roots need. A ring of mulch, kept back from the trunk, is better than grass.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Citrus-grass root-zone competition is extension-documented; same basis for mandarins.

bad_beginner.name: Bermuda grass
bad_beginner.why_beginner: A tough, spreading lawn grass that competes hard for water and is difficult to keep out of the root zone. Clear it out to the edge of the branches.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Same citrus-grass-competition basis; Bermuda is a notably aggressive spreading turf in the citrus literature.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: St. Augustine grass
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A dense, spreading lawn grass that competes aggressively for water and nutrients in the topsoil and creeps right up to the trunk. Keep it cleared out to the dripline.
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: St. Augustine is a thick, fast-spreading lawn grass that is rough on citrus. It soaks up water and food in the top layer of soil where the tree's roots feed, and it creeps to the trunk. Keep a clear or mulched circle around the base and hold the grass back beyond it.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Citrus is extension-documented as vulnerable to weed and grass competition in the root zone, especially at bloom and flush; St. Augustine is an aggressive spreading turf.

pests.name: Asian citrus psyllid
pests.symptoms_seasoned: A tiny mottled-brown insect, about an eighth of an inch, that feeds tilted up at a 45-degree angle on new flush, a posture no other citrus pest shares. Nymphs make waxy tubules and curl tender growth. The insect matters less for its feeding than for what it carries: it is the vector of Huanglongbing (citrus greening), the most serious citrus disease worldwide. Scout the youngest flush.
pests.symptoms_beginner: This tiny brown insect rests on new leaves at an angle, rear end raised, which is your clue. The young ones make little waxy white threads and curl the new leaf tips. The real danger is not the feeding but a fatal disease it spreads, citrus greening, so it is worth acting on even where the pest is uncommon.
pests.cause_seasoned: Adults lay eggs only on new flush, so populations track flushing cycles and build fastest in warm weather when the tree pushes tender growth. The pest is established across much of the southern United States, and any psyllid should be treated as a potential disease carrier.
pests.cause_beginner: The psyllid breeds on fresh new leaves, so it builds up fastest when the tree is pushing tender growth in warm weather. It has spread across the southern states, and any psyllid you find could be carrying the disease.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Buy only certified citrus from a reputable nursery and never move citrus plants or leaves out of a quarantine area, the main way the pest and disease jump regions. Inspect each flush in the warm season, and conserve the parasitic wasp Tamarixia and general predators that suppress it.
pests.prevention_beginner: Buy certified citrus from a trusted nursery, and never carry citrus plants or cuttings out of a quarantine zone, since that is how the pest and its disease spread. Check new leaves often in warm weather, and follow local guidance if greening is in your area.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: On a backyard tree, horticultural oil and insecticidal soap on the new flush reduce nymphs; thorough coverage is key, repeated as each flush emerges. Do not apply oil above 95°F or to a drought-stressed tree. Most important, report suspected psyllids or greening symptoms to your county agricultural office, since this is a regulated pest.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray horticultural oil or insecticidal soap on the new growth to knock back the young psyllids, repeating each time fresh leaves appear. Hold off on oil when it is above about 95°F or the tree is short on water, or the oil can burn leaves. Also report any psyllids or signs of the disease to your local farm advisor.

pests.name: Citrus leafminer
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Silvery, serpentine tunnels winding through new leaves, with a thin dark frass line down each mine and leaf margins that curl around the damage. The larva mines only young, expanding foliage; hardened leaves are not attacked. On an established tree the injury is cosmetic, but on a young mandarin pushing lots of flush it can slow growth.
pests.symptoms_beginner: You will see squiggly silver trails snaking through the new leaves, often with the leaf edge curled. A tiny caterpillar makes these tunnels inside young leaves only. It looks alarming but rarely hurts a grown tree, though it can set back a small young one.
pests.cause_seasoned: A small moth lays eggs on tender new flush, and the larvae mine between the leaf surfaces. Generations cycle quickly in warm weather, so damage peaks on the late-summer and fall flushes rather than spring growth.
pests.cause_beginner: A tiny moth lays eggs on the newest leaves, and the larvae tunnel inside them. They breed fast in warm weather, so the worst damage shows on the late-summer growth.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid forcing excess tender flush with heavy nitrogen or unnecessary summer pruning, since the moth needs young leaves to breed. Tolerate cosmetic mining on bearing trees; resident parasitic wasps usually provide good control when broad-spectrum sprays are avoided.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not over-fertilize or prune a lot in summer, because that creates the tender leaves the moth needs. On a healthy grown tree it is best to live with the trails, since helpful wasps keep it in check.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Chemical control is rarely warranted, and broad-spectrum sprays undermine the parasitic wasps. On a young tree where mining slows establishment, a light horticultural oil at bud break discourages egg-laying on the new flush; repeat as each flush emerges. Follow label heat limits and do not spray above 95°F. Leave mined leaves in place.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Usually no treatment is needed, and spraying can kill the good bugs that control it. On a small young tree you want to protect, light horticultural oil on the new leaves discourages the moth. Only spray in mild conditions, not in high heat or on a thirsty tree, and leave the tunneled leaves on.

pests.name: Scale insects
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fixed, non-moving bumps clustered on twigs, along the leaf midrib, and beneath leaves. Armored types form firm gray or brown shells like raised bark; softer types are plumper and glossy and secrete honeydew that leaves foliage tacky and grows black sooty mold, with ants patrolling for the sugar. Heavy numbers bring mottled yellow leaves, early leaf fall, and twig dieback.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Scale look like little hard or waxy lumps that sit still on twigs and leaf undersides, so it is easy to mistake them for part of the branch. The soft kinds make leaves sticky and grow a black sooty coating, and ants are often crawling around them.
pests.cause_seasoned: A mix of armored and soft scale species tap into the tree and feed on sap. They gain the upper hand on trees that are dusty, crowded, or patrolled by ants, since ants drive off the lady beetles and parasitic wasps that would thin the colony.
pests.cause_beginner: Scale are little insects that feed on the tree's sap. They get worst when ants are around, since the ants protect them from the helpful bugs that eat scale.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep the tree vigorous, rinse dust off the canopy, and cut off ants with a sticky trunk band so resident beneficials can work. Inspect any incoming nursery tree, since scale often hitchhikes on new stock.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep ants from climbing the tree with a sticky band around the trunk, which lets the good bugs control the scale, and look over any new tree for lumps before planting it.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: A thorough horticultural oil application, narrow-range petroleum or neem, smothers scale; the key is wetting every surface, especially twig undersides and leaf backs. Skip oil above roughly 95°F or on a drought-stressed tree. Plan a follow-up as fresh crawlers hatch.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Coat the lumps with horticultural oil, reaching the backs of leaves and the twigs. Save the spray for cooler, well-watered days, never above roughly 95°F or on a stressed tree, or it can scorch the foliage. Spray again later as new ones appear.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of soft green, black, or brown aphids on the youngest flush and flower buds, with curled, distorted new leaves and sticky honeydew that draws ants and grows sooty mold. Spring and fall flushes are the targets. The brown citrus aphid is also a vector of citrus tristeza virus, which raises the stakes where that disease is a concern.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Look for clusters of tiny soft-bodied insects, often green or black, packed onto the newest leaves and flower buds, curling the tips. They leave a sticky coating that ants follow and that grows a black sooty film. Mandarins are most vulnerable during the spring and fall flushes.
pests.cause_seasoned: Aphids reproduce explosively on tender new growth in mild weather and are tended by ants for honeydew. Lush, over-fertilized flush is especially attractive, and ant protection lets colonies outrun their natural enemies.
pests.cause_beginner: Aphids multiply very fast on soft new growth in mild weather, and ants protect them. Too much fertilizer makes extra tender leaves that draw them in.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid forcing excess tender flush with heavy nitrogen. Control ants so lady beetles, lacewings, and parasitic wasps can suppress colonies. A strong jet of water knocks aphids off new growth and is often all that is needed.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not over-fertilize, which makes the soft growth aphids love, and keep ants out so ladybugs and other helpers can eat them. A blast of water from the hose usually clears them off.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: A forceful water spray, insecticidal soap, or horticultural oil controls aphids; cover the undersides of curled leaves and repeat as needed. Observe oil heat limits (not above 95°F or on stressed trees), and preserve natural enemies by skipping broad-spectrum insecticides.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray them off with water, or use insecticidal soap or horticultural oil, getting under the curled leaves. Keep oil for mild days only, not in high heat or on a stressed tree, and avoid harsh sprays that kill the good bugs.

pests.name: Citrus red mite
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine stippling or silvering on leaves and sometimes the rind, with tiny dark-red mites and cast skins visible under a hand lens. Heavy populations bronze the foliage and can drop leaves. Mites flare in hot, dusty, dry conditions and after broad-spectrum sprays remove their predators, so an outbreak often signals a dust-stressed or over-sprayed tree.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Look for leaves that turn a dull, speckled, silvery color, sometimes with tiny red dots moving on them (a hand lens helps). Mites get worse when it is hot, dry, and dusty. A lot of them can bronze the leaves and drop some.
pests.cause_seasoned: Citrus red mite thrives in heat and dust and reproduces rapidly on stressed trees. Dusty roadside trees and trees sprayed with broad-spectrum insecticides, which remove predatory mites, are the most prone to damaging populations.
pests.cause_beginner: These mites love hot, dusty conditions and build up fast on stressed trees. Dusty trees and trees sprayed with strong insecticides (which kill the helpful mites) get the worst of it.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Hose dust off the canopy in hot, dry spells and keep the tree well watered, since vigorous trees tolerate mites better. Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that destroy the predatory mites providing natural control.
pests.prevention_beginner: Rinse dust off the leaves during hot, dry weather and keep the tree watered, because a healthy tree handles mites better. Avoid strong insecticides that kill the good mites.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Damage is usually cosmetic and rarely needs treatment. If populations run heavy on a stressed tree, horticultural oil provides control; observe heat limits strictly, as mite outbreaks coincide with the hot weather when oil is riskiest. Do not apply oil above 95°F or to a drought-stressed tree.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Usually the damage is just cosmetic and needs nothing. If there are a lot of mites, horticultural oil works, but timing is tricky: mites peak in hot weather, the riskiest time to oil a tree. Only spray once it has cooled off, never on a hot, dry, stressed tree.

diseases.name: Huanglongbing (citrus greening, HLB)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Blotchy, asymmetric leaf yellowing that does not mirror across the midrib (distinguishing it from a symmetric nutrient deficiency), yellow shoots, and corky, enlarged veins. Fruit are small, lopsided, fail to color fully, stay green at the bottom, and taste bitter and salty; seeds often abort. The tree declines over years and there is no cure. This is the most destructive citrus disease worldwide.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The classic sign is a leaf yellow in a blotchy, uneven pattern, with the yellow on one side not matching the other (a nutrient problem is usually even on both sides). Fruit stay small, lopsided, green on the bottom, and taste bad. There is no cure, and the tree slowly dies. It is the worst citrus disease there is.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus, the bacterium behind greening, spreads tree to tree by the Asian citrus psyllid feeding on new growth, then clogs the phloem so nutrients cannot reach roots and fruit. No treatment clears an established infection, so management is entirely suppressing the psyllid and removing confirmed trees before they seed further spread.
diseases.cause_beginner: Bacteria spread by the Asian citrus psyllid as it feeds on new shoots clog the tree's plumbing, blocking food to roots and fruit. No treatment reverses it; an affected tree is a permanent source of spread. Management is preventing psyllid feeding and removing any confirmed tree.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant only certified disease-free nursery trees, never move citrus out of quarantine areas, and control the psyllid aggressively where it is present. Inspect regularly and report suspected greening to your county agricultural commissioner, since coordinated removal of infected trees is the only effective area-wide defense.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Buy only certified clean trees, never move citrus out of a quarantine zone, and control the psyllid that spreads it. Check your tree often, and report anything that looks like greening to your local agricultural office, because removing infected trees quickly protects everyone's citrus.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure and no organic remedy for an infected tree. Management is prevention and vector control only: protect trees from the psyllid, and remove and properly dispose of confirmed-infected trees promptly so they cannot serve as a reservoir.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no treatment that saves an infected tree. Focus entirely on prevention: keep the psyllid off with regular inspection and treatment, and if a tree is diagnosed with greening, remove it promptly to protect nearby trees. An infected tree left in place becomes an ongoing source of psyllid pressure.

diseases.name: Phytophthora foot rot, root rot, and gummosis
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: A trunk lesion at or near the bud union, appearing first as a drop of gum, then a brown, necrotic, slippery area under the bark that can girdle the trunk. Below ground, dark, rotted feeder roots go with a thinning, yellowing canopy and leaves that wilt but do not recover after watering. It is one of the most serious threats to a citrus tree, and it follows wet feet and a buried graft union.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Look for gum oozing near the base of the trunk and a dark, sunken, slimy patch under the bark, along with a thinning, yellowing canopy. A key clue is leaves that wilt and do not perk up when you water, because the roots are rotting from too much water.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Soil-borne Phytophthora species attack roots and the crown wherever soil stays saturated. A buried or mulch-packed graft union, poor drainage, and overwatering are the drivers; heavy clay and standing water are the classic setups.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soil fungus attacks the roots and trunk base when the soil stays too wet. Poor drainage, overwatering, and burying the graft knob are what let it in.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant high on a mound with the graft union well clear of the soil, guarantee sharp drainage, keep mulch off the trunk, and water with a soak-and-dry rhythm rather than constant moisture. Choose a Phytophthora-resistant rootstock, which most trifoliate and citrumelo stocks provide.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant on a raised mound with the graft knob above the soil, make sure water drains fast, keep mulch off the trunk, and let the soil dry between waterings. Buying a tree on a root-rot-resistant rootstock also helps a lot.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no quick cure once the crown is girdled. Correct the cause: improve drainage, pull soil and mulch back from the crown to let it dry, and cut back irrigation. Minor bark lesions can sometimes be exposed and allowed to callus. Prevention through drainage and planting depth is the real control.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no easy fix once it takes hold. Improve the drainage, clear soil and mulch away from the trunk base so it can dry out, and water less. The best control is preventing it with good drainage and planting the tree high in the first place.

diseases.name: Alternaria brown spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small brown-to-black necrotic spots, often ringed by a yellow halo, on young leaves and shoot tips, plus small, slightly depressed dark spots on young fruit that can cause premature drop. It is a mandarin-and-tangerine-hybrid disease: Dancy tangerine and Minneola tangelo are most severely affected, with Murcott, Orlando, Lee, Nova, and Sunburst often hit. Fruit becomes more resistant as it matures, so mostly young fruit is affected.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small brown or black spots with a yellow ring show up on young leaves and shoot tips, and dark, slightly sunken spots appear on small fruit, which may then drop. This one mainly troubles certain tangerine-type mandarins and tangelos (like Minneola and Murcott); satsuma and clementine are not among the types UF lists as susceptible.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The tangerine pathotype of the fungus Alternaria alternata infects only young, susceptible tissue and spreads on warm, wet, humid weather, so it is most damaging in the humid Southeast and on the susceptible hybrid cultivars. Older, hardened leaves and older fruit are not infected.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus infects the young leaves and small fruit of susceptible mandarin hybrids, spreading in warm, wet, humid weather. It cannot infect older leaves or older fruit.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: The strongest control is variety choice: satsuma and clementine are not among the varieties UF lists as susceptible, so plant those in humid regions rather than a highly susceptible hybrid like Minneola or Murcott. Prune for airflow, avoid overhead wetting, and clear fallen leaves. Copper fungicides on the susceptible flush are the fallback where a prized susceptible variety is grown.
diseases.prevention_beginner: The easiest fix is picking the right variety: satsuma and clementine are not among the susceptible types, so choose those in humid areas instead of a susceptible one like Minneola. Otherwise, prune for good airflow, avoid wetting the leaves, and rake up fallen leaves.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: On a susceptible cultivar, time copper fungicide applications to protect the new flush and small fruit during warm, wet spells, following label rates; there is no rescue for tissue already spotted. On a tolerant variety no treatment is needed.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: If you grow a susceptible type, copper sprays on the new growth during warm, wet weather help protect it, following the label. Spots already there will not heal. On satsuma or clementine you generally do not need to spray at all.

diseases.name: Greasy spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellow mottling on the upper leaf surface with a matching blister-like swelling underneath that collapses into a brown-to-black, greasy-looking spot. Infected leaves drop, mostly in winter and early spring, thinning the canopy. It is a warm, humid-climate disease, most troublesome in Florida and the Gulf where relative humidity is high.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Yellow blotches on top of the leaf with a greasy-looking brown or black blister underneath, followed by leaves dropping, mostly in winter and early spring. It shows up mainly in warm, humid places like Florida and the Gulf Coast.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A fungus infects the underside of leaves during warm, humid, wet weather, with spores building on decaying fallen leaves on the ground. High relative humidity and warm nights are what drive it, so it is a Southeastern and Gulf concern rather than an arid-West one.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus infects the undersides of the leaves in warm, humid weather, and it builds up on old fallen leaves under the tree. It is mainly a problem in humid climates, not dry ones.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rake up and remove fallen leaves to cut the spore source, prune for airflow, and keep the tree vigorous. A summer horticultural-oil or copper application, timed to the main infection period, reduces it where pressure is high.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Rake up and remove the fallen leaves under the tree, since that is where the fungus builds, and keep the canopy open for airflow. In humid areas a summer oil or copper spray helps if it is bad.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Horticultural oil, alone or with copper, applied in early to mid-summer gives good backyard control by smothering the developing infection; sanitation of fallen leaves supports it. In arid regions it rarely warrants treatment.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: A summer spray of horticultural oil (with copper if needed) controls it on a backyard tree, along with cleaning up fallen leaves. In dry climates you usually do not need to do anything.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Picked mandarins keep about one week at room temperature, less than a thick-skinned orange because the loose, thin rind offers little protection. Use them fresh; the whole appeal of a mandarin is eating it soon after picking.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Once picked, mandarins last about a week on the counter, a bit less than an orange because the skin is so thin. They are best eaten fresh and soon.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerated at about 32 to 36°F, mandarins hold two to four weeks. Store them loose or in a perforated bag so they do not sweat, and do not seal them airtight. Unlike a navel, a mandarin does not store well by leaving it on the tree, so the refrigerator, not the branch, is the place to hold the crop.
storage.fridge_beginner: In the fridge, mandarins last two to four weeks. Keep them loose or in a bag with holes so they do not get damp and moldy. Unlike oranges, mandarins do not keep well left on the tree, so the fridge is the way to store them.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Whole mandarins do not freeze well, but the juice freezes excellently. Squeeze and freeze juice in airtight containers for up to about six months, and segments can be frozen in light syrup. Zest freezes for baking.
storage.freezer_beginner: Whole mandarins do not freeze well, but the juice does. Squeeze the juice and freeze it in a sealed container for up to about six months. You can also freeze the zest for cooking.
storage.notes_seasoned: The defining storage difference from a navel is that a mandarin does not hold well on the tree. Satsuma and most early mandarins should be picked promptly at maturity; left on the branch too long the fruit puffs, dries, and loses flavor. Refrigeration is the real storage method. The exceptions are the late holding types, notably Gold Nugget and Pixie, which do keep their quality on the tree for weeks into spring. Handle the thin-skinned fruit gently.
storage.notes_beginner: The big difference from an orange is that a mandarin does not keep well on the tree. Satsumas and most early mandarins should be picked as soon as they are ripe, because left on too long they get puffy and dry inside. Store them in the fridge instead. The exceptions are a few late types like Gold Nugget and Pixie, which do hold on the tree into spring. Handle the thin-skinned fruit gently.

recommended.name: Owari Satsuma
recommended.subtitle: The cold-hardy standard
recommended.notes_seasoned: The most widely planted satsuma in the United States and the benchmark cold-hardy mandarin. A small, spreading, somewhat drooping tree that is the most cold-tolerant of the commonly grown citrus. Fruit is seedless, loose-skinned, easy to peel, with mild, sweet flesh, ripening early (roughly October to December). Its low heat requirement and early maturity let the crop come off before the hardest winter cold, which is why satsuma is the citrus for the cold edge of the range.
recommended.recommended_note: Start here in any cold-edge or Gulf-South garden. The hardiest, earliest, easiest mandarin.

recommended.name: Clementine
recommended.subtitle: The classic easy-peel
recommended.notes_seasoned: The familiar small, deep-orange, loose-skinned clementine ('Algerian' or 'Nules'). Sweet, nearly seedless when grown in isolation, and slightly less cold-hardy than satsuma. It is self-incompatible and facultatively parthenocarpic: on its own it sets seedless fruit, but pollen from another nearby citrus will put seeds into it, so keep it away from pollen-bearing citrus to stay seedless. Ripens early to mid-season, roughly November to January.
recommended.recommended_note: Choose this for the classic easy-peel snack; keep it away from other citrus to keep it seedless.

recommended.name: Gold Nugget
recommended.subtitle: Late, seedless, holds on the tree
recommended.notes_seasoned: A late-ripening, seedless mandarin with a bumpy, dull rind and rich, very sweet flavor. Fruit usually matures by late winter to early spring and holds exceptionally well on the tree, one of the few mandarins that stores on the branch. Strongly alternate-bearing, so thin heavy crops. Well adapted to warm interior and southern-California climates.
recommended.recommended_note: Add this to stretch the season into spring; it holds on the tree unlike most mandarins.

recommended.name: Pixie
recommended.subtitle: Very late, seedless, spring fruit
recommended.notes_seasoned: A very late, seedless mandarin developed at UC Riverside, ripening late winter into spring. Small, sweet, easy to peel, and famously suited to the coastal and inland valleys of southern California (Ojai is the Pixie capital). Notably alternate-bearing, producing a heavy crop one year and a light one the next unless thinned, so plan for and manage the cycle.
recommended.recommended_note: Pick this for a spring-ripening mandarin in a mild-summer California garden; expect and manage alternate bearing.

recommended.name: W. Murcott / Tango
recommended.subtitle: Late, richly flavored
recommended.notes_seasoned: A late-season, richly flavored mandarin (also sold as 'Afourer'). W. Murcott is nearly seedless in isolation but sets seeds readily if cross-pollinated by other citrus; 'Tango' is a seedless selection of it that stays seedless even near pollen. Ripens roughly January into April, extending the mandarin season the furthest at the late end.
recommended.recommended_note: Grow Tango for a seedless late mandarin, or W. Murcott if isolated from other citrus.

seeds.value: seedless alone; W. Murcott seeds if cross-pollinated

varieties.note_seasoned: Mandarins (Citrus reticulata and its hybrids) span a long season by variety. Satsuma is the earliest and hardiest, ripening in fall to early winter; clementine follows in early winter; and late selections such as Gold Nugget, Pixie, and W. Murcott or Tango carry the season into spring. The two recurring themes across the group are seedlessness that can be undone by cross-pollination (isolate seedless types from pollen-bearing citrus) and a strong alternate-bearing tendency that is managed by thinning heavy crops. Satsuma and clementine also shrug off Alternaria brown spot that troubles tangelo and Murcott-type hybrids, a point in their favor in humid regions.
varieties.note_beginner: Mandarins come in many easy-peel, mostly seedless types that ripen from fall through spring depending on variety. Satsuma is the earliest and the toughest in cold. Clementine is the classic snack mandarin. Late types like Gold Nugget, Pixie, and Tango stretch the season into spring. Two things to know: many mandarins are seedless only if kept away from other citrus, and most tend to bear a big crop one year and a small one the next, which you can even out by thinning the heavy year.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: N/A. Hardening off applies to seedlings raised indoors, not to mandarins. Mandarins are bought as grafted nursery trees already acclimated to outdoor conditions, so there is no seedling-hardening step. A containerized tree moved to a much sunnier or hotter spot can be eased into full exposure over a week or two to avoid sunburn, but that is acclimation, not classic hardening off.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: N/A for mandarins. Hardening off is for seedlings you start indoors, and you do not grow mandarins that way. You buy a young grafted tree from a nursery that is already used to being outdoors. If you move a potted tree into much stronger sun, ease it into full sun over a week or two so it does not sunburn, but that is just adjusting it.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Plant a grafted nursery tree from a reputable source with certified disease-free stock. In cold-edge regions choose one on a trifoliate-orange rootstock for maximum cold tolerance. Container-grown trees can be planted year-round in frost-free zones; in cold-winter areas plant in spring after hard-freeze danger passes. Set the tree at the same soil line as in the nursery container, high on a mound, and never bury the graft union.
start_method.notes_beginner: Buy a young grafted mandarin from a good nursery, certified disease-free, and in cold areas ask for one on trifoliate-orange rootstock for the best cold hardiness. Plant it a little high on a small mound with the knobby graft union above the soil. You can plant container-grown trees almost any time in frost-free areas; in colder areas plant in spring after hard freezes are past.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Use a loose, fast-draining potting mix, ideally one labeled for citrus or cactus. Do not use heavy garden soil in a pot, since it packs down and stays soggy.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in perlite, pumice, or bark chips to help it drain even better. You want a mix that drains fast and never stays soggy, since a potted mandarin is even more sensitive to wet roots than one in the ground.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: Sharp drainage inside the pot is the priority. A mix sold for citrus or cactus works well, as does a quality potting mix lightened with extra perlite or coarse pine bark. Never use straight garden soil in a container because it packs tight and holds water against the roots.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend in perlite, pumice, or coarse bark to sharpen drainage. The goal is a mix that drains freely after watering and never stays saturated, since a potted citrus is even less forgiving of wet feet than one in the ground.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out much faster than the ground, especially in heat and wind, so check a potted mandarin often, maybe daily in summer. Water until it drips out the bottom, then let the top inch dry before watering again. Do not let the pot sit in a saucer full of water.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: A potted mandarin needs feeding more often than one in the ground, because frequent watering washes nutrients out of the pot. Use a citrus fertilizer a bit lighter but more often through the growing season, and watch for yellowing leaves, which a citrus food with iron and zinc helps prevent.

overwintering.approach_beginner: If your winters are cold, growing a mandarin in a pot is the way to do it: keep it on a small (dwarf) tree and move the pot into a garage, sunroom, or by a bright window when frost is coming, then put it back outside when it warms. Mandarins, especially satsuma on a dwarfing rootstock, are well suited to this. While it is inside for winter, water it less and stop feeding it.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: For growers north of the in-ground range, a mandarin on Flying Dragon or another dwarfing trifoliate rootstock in a large pot is the standard cold-climate approach, and mandarins are especially well suited to it because the trees are naturally small. When frost threatens, move the tree into a garage, sunroom, or bright indoor spot, then back out once danger passes. Reduce water and hold fertilizer while it is held cool indoors.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Mandarins, especially a dwarf satsuma on Flying Dragon rootstock, are well suited to growing in a pot, because the trees are small to begin with. That also makes a pot the trick for cold climates: you can move it under cover when frost comes. Use a big pot with plenty of drainage holes and a loose citrus mix, and plan to water and feed more often than a tree in the ground.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Mandarins are excellent container citrus: the trees are naturally small, and a satsuma on Flying Dragon (a dwarfing trifoliate rootstock) is well suited to a large pot. This makes the mandarin a strong cold-climate frost-escape play, a pot you can move under cover. Choose a large container with ample drainage holes, use a coarse citrus mix, and expect to water and feed more often than an in-ground tree.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Container trees dry out far faster than in-ground ones, especially in summer heat. Check the pot daily in hot or windy periods and water before the root zone dries out completely. Good drainage is critical: the saucer should stay empty, not pooling water against the roots. Frequent deep waterings plus a fast-draining mix keep a potted mandarin healthy. See the container watering note for detail.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Feed more frequently than an in-ground tree at a lighter rate, using a micronutrient-inclusive citrus fertilizer, since pot leaching depletes nutrients and brings on chlorosis quickly. See the container fertilizer note for detail.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering containers are risky for citrus and generally not recommended, because their constantly moist reservoir works against the soak-and-dry cycle citrus needs and raises foot-rot risk. If used at all, choose one with a true overflow and a coarse mix, let the reservoir empty between fills, and watch for overwatering signs.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: Self-watering pots are not a good choice for mandarins, because they keep the soil constantly wet, which is the opposite of the soak-and-dry watering citrus likes, and can rot the roots. If you do use one, let the reservoir run empty between fills and watch for signs of overwatering.
container_notes.container_overwintering_seasoned: Move the pot to a protected spot (garage, sunroom, or indoors by a bright window) before the first frost in cold-winter zones, and return it outdoors after frost danger passes. Hold the tree cool and bright, reduce watering, and stop feeding while overwintered. This portability is the whole advantage of growing a mandarin in a container outside its hardiness range.
container_notes.container_overwintering_beginner: In cold-winter areas, move the pot inside (a garage, sunroom, or by a bright window) before the first frost, and put it back outside once frost is past. Keep it cool and in good light, water less, and stop feeding while it is inside. Being able to move the pot is the whole point of growing a mandarin in a container where winters are cold.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: N/A. Crop rotation does not apply to a mandarin, which is a permanent tree occupying the same ground for decades rather than an annual replanted each season. There is no rotational sequence to manage.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: N/A for mandarins. Rotation is for vegetables you replant each year. A mandarin tree is permanent and lives in the same spot for many years, so there is nothing to rotate.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotation is not applicable to a permanent tree crop. The one related consideration is citrus replant problems: when removing an old citrus and planting a new one in the same spot, soil-borne issues and residual pathogens can set back the replacement, so replant in fresh ground, rest and improve the old site, or use a tolerant rootstock if replanting in place is unavoidable.
rotation.note_beginner: Rotation does not apply to a permanent tree like a mandarin. The one thing to know: if you remove an old citrus tree, avoid planting a replacement in the identical spot, since the old root zone can harbor pathogens and depleted soil that stress a new tree. Give a replacement a fresh location a few feet away if you can.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Deep and infrequent. Water established trees thoroughly, then let the top inch or two of soil dry before watering again; the interval stretches in cool weather and shortens in heat. Young trees need more frequent water to establish but still on a soak-and-dry pattern, never kept constantly wet.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water deeply but not too often. Soak the root zone, then let the surface dry out, checking with a finger: when the top inch or two feels dry, water again. Water more often in hot weather and less in cool weather. Young trees dry out faster, but still let the surface dry between waterings and never keep the soil constantly wet.
watering.amount_seasoned: Each irrigation should push moisture through the full root depth, which for a bearing tree means soaking the soil out to the canopy dripline. Frequent shallow sprinklings build weak surface roots that dry out fast; a mandarin's smaller root zone still wants a thorough soak, not a splash.
watering.amount_beginner: Water enough to soak the soil deeply each time, out to the edge of the branches, not just a quick splash at the base. A few sprinkles do not reach the deep roots, so a long, thorough soak is better.
watering.method_seasoned: Drip or low-volume emitters around the dripline, or a slow hose soak, are ideal. Keep water off the trunk and crown and never wet the graft union, since a constantly damp crown is a direct route to foot rot. Maintain a mulched, grass-free basin with mulch pulled back from the trunk.
watering.method_beginner: Use drip emitters or a slow hose soak around the outer edge of the branches. Keep water off the trunk and the graft knob, because a wet trunk base can rot. Mulch under the tree, keeping the mulch away from the trunk, and keep grass out.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing leaves that wilt but do not recover after watering, leaf drop, mushy or sour-smelling soil, and gumming at the trunk base are signs of overwatering and incipient foot rot. The tell is wilting that worsens, not improves, with more water.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Signs of too much water are yellow, wilting leaves that do not perk up when you water, dropping leaves, soggy or bad-smelling soil, and gum oozing at the base of the trunk. The key clue is that watering makes the wilting worse, not better.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Leaves that curl, cup, or dull and gray, wilting that recovers after watering, premature fruit drop, and a hard, dry root zone indicate underwatering. In heat, an underwatered mandarin drops flowers and small fruit, and the thin-skinned fruit can shrivel.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Leaves that curl or look dull and gray, wilting that perks back up after you water, dropping fruit, and dry, hard soil mean the tree is too dry. In hot weather a thirsty mandarin drops flowers and little fruit, so keep it evenly watered.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Mandarin roots, like all citrus, are relatively shallow and spreading, concentrated in the top foot or two of soil and reaching out to and beyond the canopy dripline. Water the whole root basin, not just at the trunk, so the feeder roots out under the canopy edge get their share. Keep the trunk and graft union dry, and hold a grass-free, mulched basin so the shallow roots are not competing with turf.
watering.method_note_beginner: Mandarin roots are shallow and spread out wide, so water the whole area under and around the tree, out to the edge of the branches, not just right at the trunk. Keep the water off the trunk base and the graft knob, and keep grass out of that watered area so it does not steal water from the tree's shallow roots.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The bloom and fruit-set period in spring and the summer sizing stretch are the critical windows: uneven moisture then drops flowers and young fruit and can split or shrivel the crop. Keep moisture steady through those months.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The most important times to keep water steady are spring, when the tree flowers and sets fruit, and summer, when the fruit is growing. Uneven watering then makes flowers and fruit drop.

growth_stages.name: Planting and settling in
growth_stages.timing: Set out at planting time, best in early spring once hard-freeze danger passes in cold-winter zones, and any time of year in frost-free zones
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Set the tree high on a mound so the graft union clears the soil and mulch line, backfill with the native soil, and water it in to settle the air pockets, keeping mulch off the trunk. In cold-edge regions plant a tree on trifoliate-orange rootstock for hardiness. Pull off the nursery wrap and stake only if needed.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Plant the tree slightly raised on a low mound with the knobby graft union above the soil. Soak it in well and keep mulch off the trunk. In cold areas, a tree on trifoliate-orange rootstock takes the cold best.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Expect roots to work and a first push of new leaves over the coming weeks once the soil warms, with the canopy staying firm. Watch the mound as it settles so the graft union does not end up buried.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Over the next few weeks you should see new leaves pushing out. Check that the soil has not settled up over the graft union.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Note the planting date, the variety and rootstock, the mound height, and how far the graft union sits above the soil.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Write down the planting date and confirm the graft union is sitting clear of the soil.

growth_stages.name: Establishment years
growth_stages.timing: First two to three years after planting, before the tree carries a real crop; mandarins are precocious and may set a light crop by year two
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Build the tree, not the crop. Remove flowers and fruit the first year so energy goes to roots and framework, even though satsuma is precocious enough to try fruiting early. Water consistently, feed on the citrus nitrogen rhythm, and protect young, frost-tender wood through its first winters, since young trees are far less cold-hardy than an established one.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: For the first couple of years, grow a strong tree rather than a crop. Pinch off the flowers the first year so the tree builds roots. Water it regularly, feed it, and protect it from frost in winter, since young mandarins are much more cold-tender than grown ones.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Steady shoot extension and a filling canopy each warm season, with the trunk thickening and scaffold branches developing. Little to no fruit is the goal here, not a worry.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: You want the tree getting bigger each year, with new branches and a fuller canopy. Do not worry about little or no fruit yet; that is what should happen.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Track shoot growth, canopy fill, any blossom removal, and winter protection each season.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note how much the tree grew this year and that you removed early flowers.

growth_stages.name: Spring bloom
growth_stages.timing: Primarily spring, roughly March through May depending on climate; bloom lasts about three weeks
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Bloom is when the mandarin sets its crop, so any stress now costs fruit. Keep the root zone evenly moist through bloom, avoid fertilizer gaps, and do not let the soil swing dry or saturated, either of which drops flowers. Hold off oil sprays while blooms are open. If you grow a seedless variety, keep it isolated from pollen-bearing citrus so cross-pollination does not seed the fruit.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: When the tree blooms in spring, keep watering even (not too dry, not soggy) and keep feeding, because this is when it sets the fruit. Do not spray oil while it is flowering. If you want seedless fruit, keep the tree away from other citrus so their pollen does not put seeds in it.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fragrant white blossoms opening over a few weeks. Most mandarins set fruit on a single tree without pollination; some natural flower and early-fruit drop is normal self-thinning.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Sweet-smelling white flowers open over a few weeks. Most mandarins make fruit without a second tree or bees. Some flowers and tiny fruit will drop on their own, which is normal.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record bloom start and duration, weather during bloom, and any heavy drop.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when the tree flowered and whether the weather was hot during bloom.

growth_stages.name: Fruit set and summer sizing
growth_stages.timing: From spring set through summer; mandarin fruit develops over roughly seven to ten months, faster than a navel orange
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep irrigation steady through fruit sizing, increasing it in extreme-heat spells to prevent fruit drop and rind sunburn. This is also the year to manage alternate bearing: on a heavy-set on-year, thin fruit in early summer to even out next year's crop, the earlier the better. Mandarins need warmth to sweeten but far less accumulated heat than a navel, and cool nights in fall help color the fruit.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Over the summer the fruit grows and the tree's sugar builds. Keep watering steadily, and water extra during heat waves so fruit does not drop or sunburn. If the tree set a very heavy crop this year, thin some fruit off in early summer so next year is not a bare off-year. Mandarins do not need as much heat as an orange to get sweet.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fruit expanding through summer, with rind color beginning as cooler fall weather arrives. Watch sun-exposed fruit during heat spikes, and note whether this is a heavy on-year or a light off-year.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The fruit gets bigger through summer and starts to color as fall cools. Keep an eye on fruit on the sunny side during heat waves, and notice if this is a big-crop year or a light one.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Track fruit sizing, any heat-spike drop or sunburn, whether you thinned, and the on-year or off-year pattern.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note how the fruit is sizing, whether you thinned a heavy crop, and if it dropped any during a heat wave.

growth_stages.name: Fall and winter ripening
growth_stages.timing: Fall to winter for early types (satsuma from October), winter to spring for late types (Gold Nugget, Pixie into spring)
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest by taste and pick promptly. Mandarins color and sweeten with cool nights, but unlike a navel most types do not hold well on the tree: satsuma and early mandarins puff, dry, and lose flavor if left too long, so pick at maturity and refrigerate. The exceptions are the late holding types (Gold Nugget, Pixie), which do keep on the branch into spring. Early satsuma ripening also gets the crop off before the coldest winter nights.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pick by taste, and do not leave most mandarins on the tree too long. Unlike oranges, satsumas and early mandarins get puffy and dry inside if left on, so pick them when ripe and keep them in the fridge. A few late types like Gold Nugget and Pixie do hold on the tree into spring.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Deepening rind color and sweet, mild flavor on tasting, with the rind loosening from the flesh. In cool-night climates color comes on well; in warm humid climates the rind can stay green-tinged on ripe fruit, so taste rather than color.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The skin colors up and loosens, and the fruit tastes sweet. In warm, humid places the skin can stay a little green even when ripe, so taste one to decide.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record harvest start, taste-test results, how promptly you picked, and any puffing on fruit left too long.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you started picking and whether any fruit left on too long went puffy.

growth_stages.name: Mature bearing
growth_stages.timing: From about the fourth year onward, once the tree carries full crops
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Settle into the annual rhythm: deep, infrequent irrigation adjusted up in heat; nitrogen-forward feeding spring through summer, stopping by late summer; light shaping in spring after harvest plus removal of any below-graft rootstock shoots. The defining mandarin management task is alternate bearing: thin heavy on-year crops early to soften the swing between big and bare years.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Once grown, the tree settles into a yearly routine: water deeply but not too often (more in heat), feed spring through summer and stop by late summer, and prune lightly in spring after harvest. Remove any shoots from below the graft knob, since those are rootstock. The main mandarin job is evening out the big-crop, small-crop cycle by thinning fruit in a heavy year.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Crops that swing between heavy and light years (alternate bearing is strong in mandarins), rootstock suckers below the graft, and any decline that signals a drainage or root issue. Thinning and steady feeding and watering soften the alternate-bearing swing.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A big crop one year and a light one the next is normal for mandarins. Watch for shoots below the graft knob, and for any general decline that could mean a root or drainage problem. Thinning a heavy year evens things out.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Track annual yield, the alternate-bearing pattern, whether you thinned, rootstock suckering, and overall vigor.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note this year's harvest size, whether it was a heavy or light year, and any rootstock shoots below the graft.

notifications.body_seasoned: Your young mandarin is in flower. During the first year, pinch the blossoms off so the tree pours energy into roots and framework rather than fruit, and let it start cropping from its second or third year on.
notifications.body_beginner: Your young mandarin is putting out flowers. In its first year, pull the flowers off so the young tree spends its energy building strong roots. Let it start fruiting in a couple of years.

notifications.body_seasoned: Spring growth is starting. Begin the nitrogen-forward citrus feeding cycle now and continue through summer, stopping by late summer so growth hardens before winter. Scale the amount to a mandarin's smaller canopy, and on high-pH soils use a citrus fertilizer that includes iron and zinc.
notifications.body_beginner: Your mandarin is starting to grow for the season. Start feeding now with a citrus fertilizer and keep feeding through summer, then stop by late summer. A mandarin is a small tree, so it needs less than an orange. If your soil is alkaline, pick a citrus food with iron and zinc so the leaves do not yellow.

notifications.title_seasoned: Thin a heavy crop to fight alternate bearing
notifications.title_beginner: Thin fruit in a big-crop year
notifications.body_seasoned: If your mandarin set a heavy crop this year, thin some fruit off in early summer. Mandarins are strongly alternate-bearing, and removing part of a heavy on-year crop early evens out next year and prevents a bare off-year. The earlier the thinning, the more it helps.
notifications.body_beginner: If your mandarin is loaded with fruit this year, pick some off in early summer. Mandarins tend to make a big crop one year and almost none the next, and thinning a heavy year early helps even that out so you get fruit both years.

notifications.title_beginner: Taste a fruit, then pick it soon
notifications.body_seasoned: Your mandarins are reaching their ripening window. Harvest by taste, and pick promptly once ripe: most mandarins, satsuma especially, puff and dry if left on the tree, so unlike a navel do not hold them on the branch. Refrigerate the crop, or grow a late holding type like Gold Nugget or Pixie if you want fruit to keep on the tree.
notifications.body_beginner: Your mandarins are getting ripe. Taste one, and once it is sweet, pick soon. Most mandarins get puffy and dry if you leave them on the tree, so pick them and keep them in the fridge. A few late types like Gold Nugget and Pixie are the exception and hold on the tree.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Hard freeze coming: protect your mandarin
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hard freeze tonight: cover your mandarin
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Satsuma and other mandarins are the hardiest of the common sweet citrus: a mature, hardened tree withstands brief lows near 15 to 20°F, notably colder than a navel orange. The fruit is more tender than the wood, taking damage around 30°F for a couple of hours, which is why early satsuma is picked before deep winter. Young trees are far more tender than mature ones. On a hard freeze, drape the canopy, mound soil or wrap the graft union, and soak the ground beforehand so it radiates warmth overnight. Bring potted trees under cover.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Mandarins, especially satsuma, take cold better than any other common sweet citrus: a grown, hardened tree can handle a brief dip near 15 to 20°F, colder than an orange. The fruit is more tender than the wood, though, and can be damaged around 30°F, which is why early satsumas are picked before the coldest weather. Cover the tree on a hard freeze night, move a potted one under cover, and watering the ground during the day first gives it a little stored warmth. Young trees need the most protection.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Extreme heat: guard against drop and sunburn
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Heat wave: protect your mandarin
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Mandarins need less heat than a navel to sweeten, but extreme heat spikes into the high 90s°F and above still stress the tree: flowers and young fruit drop, and exposed fruit and bark sunburn. Increase irrigation through the heat event to keep the root zone supplied, and shade young trunks. In the low desert this is a recurring summer concern; satsuma in particular prefers the milder end of the range.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Mandarins do not need as much heat as an orange, but a real heat wave (high 90s°F and up) still stresses the tree, dropping flowers and small fruit and sunburning exposed fruit and bark. Water more during the hot spell, and shade a young trunk so it does not sunburn. In desert areas this comes up all summer.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Hot weather: hold off on horticultural oil
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Too hot to spray oil
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Horticultural and petroleum oil sprays, the backyard standard for scale, mites, and other citrus pests, can burn foliage when applied in high heat or to a drought-stressed tree. Do not spray oil above about 95°F or when the tree is water-stressed. This caution is sharpest in hot climates, where pest pressure and the heat that makes oil risky coincide. Wait for cooler conditions and water the tree first.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Horticultural or petroleum oil sprays are the usual way to deal with scale, mites, and other citrus pests, but they can burn the leaves if you spray in the heat or onto a thirsty, stressed tree. Keep oil for cooler conditions, below about 95°F, and water the tree first. This matters most in hot areas. Wait for the weather to ease before you spray.

planting.text_seasoned: Plant with the graft union standing two to three inches clear of the finished soil and keep mulch off the trunk. A buried or mulch-packed union stays damp and is the classic entry point for citrus foot rot.
planting.text_beginner: Plant so the graft bump sits a couple inches above the soil, and keep mulch off the trunk. A buried, damp union can rot.

planting.text_seasoned: In a cold-edge region, buy a tree grafted on trifoliate orange (Poncirus trifoliata), the standard for maximum cold hardiness. It is the rootstock that lets satsuma push into zone 8.
planting.text_beginner: If your winters are cold, get a mandarin grafted onto trifoliate-orange rootstock, which gives the best cold hardiness and is why satsumas can grow where oranges cannot.

establishment.text_seasoned: Strip the first year's fruit so the tree builds frame before it bears, even though satsuma is precocious enough to try fruiting early. A young tree carrying fruit grows slowly and stays structurally weak.
establishment.text_beginner: For the first year, pick off the fruit so the young tree grows strong first, even if it wants to fruit early.

establishment.text_seasoned: Scout new flush for Asian citrus psyllid while the tree is small and easy to inspect. The psyllid spreads huanglongbing, and tender new growth is where it feeds and lays, so catching it early matters most on a young tree.
establishment.text_beginner: Check the new growth for tiny citrus psyllid insects while the tree is small. They spread a serious citrus disease and go after fresh leaves, so look often.

bloom.text_seasoned: Hold soil moisture steady through the roughly three-week spring bloom; drought stress now drops flowers and the young fruit behind them. Mandarins set their crop from this main flush.
bloom.text_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist during the few weeks the tree flowers in spring. If it dries out, the flowers and tiny fruit drop, and that bloom is the year's crop.

bloom.text_seasoned: Keep a seedless variety isolated from pollen-bearing citrus during bloom. Clementine and W. Murcott are seedless in isolation but set seeds when cross-pollinated, so nearby fertile-pollen citrus can seed an otherwise seedless crop.
bloom.text_beginner: If you want seedless mandarins, keep the tree away from other citrus while it flowers. Types like clementine stay seedless on their own but get seeds if pollen from another citrus reaches them.

fruit_set_development.text_seasoned: On a heavy-set on-year, thin fruit in early summer to blunt alternate bearing. Mandarins swing hard between heavy and light crops, and early thinning of a big crop is the most effective lever, cutting wasted carbohydrate before it suppresses next year's bloom.
fruit_set_development.text_beginner: If the tree is loaded this year, thin some fruit off in early summer. Mandarins tend to make a big crop then almost none the next year, and thinning a heavy year early evens it out.

fruit_set_development.text_seasoned: Water deeply and consistently through summer sizing. Uneven moisture over the fruit-development months shows up as splitting and pre-harvest drop, so a steady rhythm through the heat is the priority.
fruit_set_development.text_beginner: Keep watering deeply and evenly all summer. Uneven watering makes mandarins split or drop, so stay consistent.

ripening_harvest.text_seasoned: Taste before you pick, then pick promptly. Mandarins color before full sweetness in some climates, and unlike a navel most do not hold on the tree: satsuma puffs and dries if left, so pick at maturity and refrigerate.
ripening_harvest.text_beginner: Taste a mandarin before picking, and once ripe do not leave it on the tree long. Most get puffy and dry if left on, so pick them and keep them in the fridge.

ripening_harvest.text_seasoned: For fruit that keeps on the tree into spring, grow a late holding type such as Gold Nugget or Pixie. These are the exception to the pick-promptly rule and store well on the branch.
ripening_harvest.text_beginner: If you want mandarins that hold on the tree into spring, plant a late type like Gold Nugget or Pixie, which keep well on the branch unlike most mandarins.

mature_bearing.text_seasoned: Keep pruning minimal on a bearing mandarin: deadwood, crossing limbs, and rootstock suckers from below the graft. Those suckers are the rootstock, often thorny trifoliate, and left to grow they sap vigor and can overrun the top.
mature_bearing.text_beginner: On a grown tree, prune lightly. Take out dead wood and any shoots from below the graft bump, since those come from the rootstock, not your mandarin.

mature_bearing.text_seasoned: Expect and manage alternate bearing. Mandarins naturally swing between heavy and light years; steady fertility, consistent water, and thinning heavy crops soften the swing, while a sudden unexplained drop instead points to a root, water, or disease problem.
mature_bearing.text_beginner: Mandarin trees often make a big crop one year and a small one the next, which is normal. Steady feeding and watering plus thinning a heavy year help even it out, but a sudden big drop means something is wrong.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A mature standard mandarin yields less than a full-size navel because the tree is smaller, commonly on the order of tens of pounds up to roughly a hundred or more pounds per year under good conditions, varying widely with variety, climate, tree size, and rootstock. Dwarf container trees yield far less but still give a worthwhile home crop.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: A grown mandarin makes a good crop, though less than a big orange tree because the tree is smaller, often tens of pounds up to around a hundred pounds a year in good conditions. It depends on the variety, climate, and tree size. A small dwarf tree in a pot makes much less, but still enough to enjoy.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Trees reach full production around the fourth to seventh year and then bear for decades. Mandarins are strongly alternate-bearing, so expect a marked swing between heavy and light crop years unless heavy years are thinned; this is normal for the group and managed rather than cured.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: A mandarin hits its full crop around four to seven years old and then produces for decades. Mandarins tend to bear a big crop one year and a light one the next, which is normal; thinning the heavy year evens it out.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Strip any flowers that set in the first season so the tree puts its energy into roots and framework rather than fruit, even though mandarins are precocious and may try to bear early. Light bearing typically begins in year two or three, with a full crop building as the tree matures. The early investment pays back in stronger, earlier-peaking production.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Young trees need their first-year energy in roots and branches, not fruit, even though a mandarin may want to fruit early. Snap off any first-season flowers. Fruit will start coming around year two or three, with a real crop as the tree grows. Building up first gets you more fruit in the long run.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No university extension or peer-reviewed source supports timing mandarin planting or care by moon phase. Citrus planting and management are driven by frost timing, soil temperature, and heat accumulation, not lunar cycles, so no moon-phase preference is assigned.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Fruit stays green and tart even though the tree looks healthy
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The mandarins are green and sour even though the tree seems fine
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Mandarins color and sweeten with cool fall nights and adequate warmth in the season. In the warm, humid tropics and on the coolest coastal strips the tree grows and sets fruit but the fruit can stay green-skinned and low in sugar because the climate lacks the diurnal swing (warm days, cool nights) that develops mandarin quality. This is less demanding than a navel's high-heat requirement, but it is still a climate limit, not a care mistake.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Mandarins need cool fall nights and enough warmth to turn sweet and colored. In very warm, humid places (like low-elevation tropics) or the coolest foggy coast, the tree makes fruit but it can stay green and sour because the weather does not have the warm-day, cool-night swing that sweetens it. It is a climate thing, not something you did wrong.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: There is no cultural fix for the missing climate signal. In a marginal-quality area, choose the varieties best suited to it (satsuma tolerates cooler summers; some mandarins fruit at low heat) and a warmer microclimate can help at the margin. In the tropics, cooler uplands give better fruit.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: You cannot fix the climate with watering or feeding. Pick varieties suited to your area (satsuma handles cooler summers well) and a warm, sheltered spot helps a little. In the tropics, cooler hillsides make better fruit.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Fruit is puffy, dry, or loose inside despite looking ripe
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The fruit looks ripe but is puffy and dry inside
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Unlike a navel orange, most mandarins do not hold well on the tree. Satsuma and other early types puff (the rind separating and ballooning away from the flesh) and dry out if left on the branch past maturity, losing juice and flavor. The rind can look fine while the interior declines. This is the mandarin storage reality: pick promptly and refrigerate rather than storing on the tree.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Most mandarins, unlike oranges, do not keep well on the tree. Satsumas and early types get puffy (the skin balloons away from the fruit) and dry inside if left on too long. The skin can still look fine even when the inside has gone dry. The fix is to pick them when ripe and store them in the fridge.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Pick early and mid-season mandarins promptly at maturity and refrigerate them rather than leaving the crop on the tree. If you want fruit that keeps on the branch into spring, grow a late holding type such as Gold Nugget or Pixie, which are the exception.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Pick most mandarins as soon as they are ripe and keep them in the fridge instead of on the tree. If you want fruit that can wait on the tree into spring, plant a late type like Gold Nugget or Pixie.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: A huge crop one year, then almost none the next
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: A big crop one year and hardly any the next
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Alternate bearing (a heavy on-year followed by a light or bare off-year) is a strong, well-known tendency in mandarins, far more pronounced than in sweet oranges. A very heavy crop suppresses the next year's flowering by consuming the tree's carbohydrate and inhibiting the shoot growth that carries next spring's bloom, so the tree swings between extremes. It is normal for the group, not a disease.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Mandarins tend to make a big crop one year and then very little the next. A heavy crop tires the tree and cuts down the growth that would carry next year's flowers, so it swings back and forth. This is normal for mandarins, not a sickness.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Thin heavy on-year crops in early summer, the earlier the better, to even out the cycle; hand thinning or light pruning of a loaded tree reduces the drain and improves next year's bloom. Steady feeding and watering also soften the swing.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: In a big-crop year, pick off some of the fruit in early summer so the tree is not overloaded, which helps it flower and fruit again the next year. Steady feeding and watering help too.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Yellowing leaves with green veins (iron or zinc chlorosis)
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Leaves turning yellow but the veins stay green
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Yellow leaves with a network of green veins, especially on new growth, signal a micronutrient deficiency, most often iron or zinc, common on alkaline, high-pH soils where the nutrients are present but chemically unavailable. This is widespread in desert and interior-West soils. It is distinct from the symmetric overall yellowing of nitrogen shortage and from the blotchy asymmetric yellowing of greening disease.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: When leaves turn yellow but the veins stay green, especially on new growth, the tree is short on a micronutrient, usually iron or zinc. This happens a lot on alkaline (high pH) soils in the desert and inland West, where the nutrient is in the soil but the tree cannot take it up. It looks different from an even all-over yellowing (usually nitrogen) and from the blotchy yellowing of greening.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Correct with a chelated iron or zinc product, applied as a foliar spray for a quick response and to the soil for longer-term supply, and use a citrus fertilizer that includes micronutrients. Lowering soil pH toward slightly acidic over time with sulfur is the durable fix on high-pH ground.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Fix it with a chelated iron or zinc product, sprayed on the leaves for a fast response and added to the soil for the long run, and use a citrus fertilizer that lists micronutrients. Over time, making the soil a little more acidic with sulfur helps the tree use the nutrients already there.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Sudden leaf drop or heavy fruit drop
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The tree is dropping a lot of leaves or fruit
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Several causes look different but end in drop. Cold injury follows a freeze, with leaves wilting, browning, and dropping days later on an evergreen tree that never goes dormant, and fruit can be damaged near 30°F even though the wood is hardier. Overwatering and poor drainage are the other frequent culprit: saturated roots and incipient foot rot cause yellowing and drop, with the tell being leaves that wilt but do not recover after watering. A spring heat spike during or just after bloom also drops flowers and young fruit.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: A few things cause drop. Cold: after a freeze a mandarin (which never goes dormant) can wilt and drop leaves days later, and the fruit can be hurt near 30°F even though the wood is hardier. Too much water or poor drainage rots the roots and drops leaves, and the clue is that watering makes it worse. A hot spell during bloom also drops flowers and little fruit.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Distinguish the cause first. For cold, improve frost protection and wait until spring growth to see what survived before pruning. For overwatering, back off irrigation, confirm sharp drainage, and check the graft union and crown are not buried. For heat-spike drop, keep moisture even and bump irrigation through the hot spell during bloom.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Figure out the cause. If it was frost, protect the tree better next time and wait until spring to trim damaged wood. If it is overwatering, water less, make sure the soil drains fast, and check the graft knob is not buried. If a heat wave hit during bloom, keep the tree well watered through hot spells.

succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Mandarin is a permanent tree planted once and harvested annually for decades. Succession planting does not apply.

crops.recommended_rootstock_note: Trifoliate orange (Poncirus trifoliata) is the preferred rootstock for mandarins, especially satsuma, because it gives the greatest cold hardiness and good fruit quality, which is why satsuma on trifoliate can be grown in the ground in zone 8. For containers and small spaces, Flying Dragon (a dwarfing trifoliate selection) makes a compact tree and is the most cold-hardy of all. In warmer regions, Swingle citrumelo suits wetter soils. Ask the nursery which rootstock the tree is on and match it to your soil, space, and winter cold.

rootstock_options.name: Trifoliate orange (Poncirus trifoliata)
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask for a certified disease-free satsuma or mandarin on trifoliate-orange rootstock (selections such as 'Rubidoux') for maximum cold hardiness. Confirm your soil is not highly alkaline or saline, which trifoliate dislikes.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: The standard cold-hardiness rootstock for mandarins and the reason satsuma can be grown in the ground in the cold-edge zones. Confers the greatest cold tolerance of the common stocks, good Phytophthora and tristeza resistance, and good fruit quality, producing a compact, somewhat slow-growing tree. Not adapted to calcareous, high-pH, or saline soils, where it develops chlorosis.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: Trifoliate orange is the cold-hardiness rootstock, and it is what lets satsumas grow in the ground where oranges cannot. It resists root rot, keeps the tree compact, and gives good fruit. Its weakness is that it dislikes very alkaline or salty soil, so it is less ideal in some desert areas.

rootstock_options.name: Flying Dragon trifoliate
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask specifically for Flying Dragon rootstock (a dwarfing selection of trifoliate orange). The compact size fits containers and small yards and makes frost protection easy.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: A naturally dwarfing mutation of Poncirus trifoliata producing very compact trees ideal for containers and small gardens, and the best cold hardiness of any widely available citrus rootstock. Excellent Phytophthora, nematode, and tristeza resistance. Sensitive to high-pH and saline soils. Fruit quality is good and trees are precocious, though total yield per tree is lower due to the small canopy, which suits a mandarin well.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: Flying Dragon is a dwarfing rootstock that keeps the tree small, perfect for pots and small yards, and it is the key to growing mandarins in cold climates since you can move the pot under cover for winter. It also has the best cold hardiness of the common rootstocks and strongly resists root rot. The tradeoff is a smaller tree with a smaller crop, usually just what a container grower wants.

rootstock_options.name: Swingle citrumelo
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask for Swingle citrumelo rootstock for wetter soils. It handles wet ground better than trifoliate but performs poorly on alkaline or calcareous soils.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: A grapefruit-and-trifoliate hybrid widely used in Florida and the Gulf.
