Excellent Phytophthora resistance, good cold hardiness among standard stocks, and tristeza tolerant, handling wet soils better than most. Produces a good-quality, moderately sized tree. Not well adapted to calcareous or high-pH soils. A strong general-purpose choice for the humid Southeast.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: Swingle citrumelo is a tough rootstock common in Florida and along the Gulf. It strongly resists root rot, handles wet soils better than most, and has decent cold hardiness, making a good tree with good fruit. It is a good pick in humid, wetter regions.

pruning_window.note_seasoned: Citrus needs only light shaping, not the structural pruning of deciduous fruit trees. Remove dead, crossing, or weak wood in spring after harvest, and strip any shoots below the graft union, since these are rootstock (often thorny trifoliate on a mandarin) that will not bear fruit and will sap the tree. The mandarin-specific task is thinning heavy on-year crops in early summer to manage alternate bearing, which is closer to crop-load management than to shaping. Keep the canopy open for light and air; heavy heading cuts are unnecessary and reduce the next crop.
pruning_window.note_beginner: Mandarins need only light pruning, not the heavy shaping peaches and apples get. In spring after harvest, trim out dead, crossing, or weak branches, and pull off any shoots below the graft knob, since those come from the rootstock (often thorny) and will never make mandarins. The one extra job for mandarins is thinning fruit in a heavy year (in early summer) to even out the big-crop, small-crop cycle. Keep the canopy open for light and air, but do not cut it back hard.

crops.establishment_note: Mandarins are precocious and typically begin bearing in the second or third year after planting a grafted nursery tree, a bit earlier than a navel orange. Full production is reached by about year four to seven depending on rootstock and growing conditions.

pollination.notes_seasoned: Most mandarins set a full crop on a single tree and are seedless when grown in isolation. Satsuma is parthenocarpic and reliably seedless. Clementine and W. Murcott are self-incompatible but facultatively parthenocarpic: on their own they set seedless fruit, but pollen from another nearby citrus with fertile pollen will cross-pollinate them and put seeds into the fruit, and pollen can travel a long way, so isolation from pollen-bearing citrus is what preserves seedlessness. A few mandarin hybrids fruit better with a compatible pollinizer, but no pollinizer is required for the common seedless types.
pollination.notes_beginner: Most mandarins make fruit on their own with no second tree needed, and they are seedless when grown away from other citrus. Satsuma is naturally seedless. Clementine and some others are seedless by themselves, but if pollen from another citrus nearby reaches the flowers, the fruit gets seeds, so keep a seedless mandarin away from other pollen-making citrus to keep it seedless.

Windows are generally safe; tighten exact months at the variety-delta / certification pass.

The min_winter_temp_f band edges per region-zone are USDA-zone climate values (reused from the shared citrus zone model), reasoned against documented citrus/satsuma damage thresholds (tree ~15-20°F, fruit ~30°F) rather than a single per-region table. Confirm the numeric edges against sources at cert.

Confirm in review.

Clementine/W. Murcott cross-pollination seediness nuance is authored from UCR variety collection + UC MG Santa Clara ('seedless if grown without a cross-pollinizer') plus general citrus pollination knowledge; the long-distance pollen-transfer specifics came from non-T1 literature and are stated only qualitatively. No self-fruitful claim is fabricated: needs_pollinizer=false reflects that the common seedless types fruit on one tree.

3.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 3 is too cold for an in-ground mandarin. Even satsuma, the hardiest common citrus (mature tree to about 15 to 20°F), is killed by this zone's hard freezes into the low teens°F or below, so there is no dependable crop or establishment window in the ground.
3.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 3 is too cold for a mandarin planted outside. Satsuma is the toughest citrus in cold, but winters here still drop far below what it can take, so it will not survive in the ground.

4.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 4 is too cold for an in-ground mandarin. Even satsuma, the hardiest common citrus (mature tree to about 15 to 20°F), is killed by this zone's hard freezes into the low teens°F or below, so there is no dependable crop or establishment window in the ground.
4.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 4 is too cold for a mandarin planted outside. Satsuma is the toughest citrus in cold, but winters here still drop far below what it can take, so it will not survive in the ground.

5.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 5 is too cold for an in-ground mandarin. Even satsuma, the hardiest common citrus (mature tree to about 15 to 20°F), is killed by this zone's hard freezes into the low teens°F or below, so there is no dependable crop or establishment window in the ground.
5.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 5 is too cold for a mandarin planted outside. Satsuma is the toughest citrus in cold, but winters here still drop far below what it can take, so it will not survive in the ground.

6.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 6 is too cold for an in-ground mandarin. Even satsuma, the hardiest common citrus (mature tree to about 15 to 20°F), is killed by this zone's hard freezes into the low teens°F or below, so there is no dependable crop or establishment window in the ground.
6.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 6 is too cold for a mandarin planted outside. Satsuma is the toughest citrus in cold, but winters here still drop far below what it can take, so it will not survive in the ground.

7.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 7 is too cold for an in-ground mandarin. Even satsuma, the hardiest common citrus (mature tree to about 15 to 20°F), is killed by this zone's hard freezes into the low teens°F or below, so there is no dependable crop or establishment window in the ground.
7.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 7 is too cold for a mandarin planted outside. Satsuma is the toughest citrus in cold, but winters here still drop far below what it can take, so it will not survive in the ground.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: You cannot grow a mandarin in the ground in this region. Satsuma is the toughest citrus for cold, and cold-climate growers grow it in pots, moving them indoors for winter. The newer super-hardy satsuma hybrids reach only about zone 8, not this far north.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In-ground mandarins are not viable in zones 3 through 7. Satsuma is the most cold-hardy common citrus and the type cold-climate growers push furthest, and the newest cold-hardy satsuma hybrids extend only to about zone 8a; north of that, citrus is a container crop moved indoors for winter, a different growing system from this in-ground regional model.
northern_tier.cold_basis_seasoned: Zones 3 through 7 drop into the low teens°F and well below every winter, past even satsuma's roughly 15 to 20°F mature-tree limit, so an unprotected in-ground mandarin does not survive here.
northern_tier.cold_basis_beginner: It gets too cold here for a mandarin to live outside, even a hardy satsuma. Winters drop below what it can take.
northern_tier.heat_basis_seasoned: Heat is moot here: the tree cannot survive the winter, so summer warmth never gets the chance to matter.
northern_tier.heat_basis_beginner: Summer warmth does not matter here, because the tree cannot get through winter in the first place.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 8 is the mandarin's home ground in the Gulf South. Satsuma on trifoliate rootstock is hardy through this zone's winters (mature trees take brief lows near 15 to 20°F), and its early fall-to-winter ripening gets the crop off the tree before the hardest freezes. This is exactly where a navel orange is only marginal, and it is the clearest expression of the mandarin cold-hardiness advantage.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 8 is prime satsuma country in the Gulf South. The tree is hardy here, and because satsuma ripens early (fall to early winter) you usually pick the fruit before the coldest weather arrives. This is where mandarins clearly beat oranges, which are only borderline in zone 8.
8.harvest: Oct - Dec (early satsuma; pick promptly before hard freezes)
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Hard advective freezes into the upper teens°F occur every few years in zone 8; mature satsuma usually survives, but protect young trees and pick ripe fruit ahead of a hard freeze.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 fruits reliably and easily: mild Gulf and Southeastern winters rarely threaten a hardy mandarin, and the heat is ample for good quality. Satsuma, clementine, and late types all do well; cold protection is an occasional need, not routine.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Mandarins do great in zone 9. Winters are mild enough that the tree and crop are safe, and summers are plenty warm for good fruit.
9.harvest: Nov - Jan (satsuma into clementine; a few late types hold longer)
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Zone 9 across the Gulf is mostly safe for mandarins; hard freezes occur in some winters, so keep frost cloth ready for young trees.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: The Gulf South is mandarin country. Satsumas ripen in fall to early winter, before the coldest weather, and they are the toughest citrus for the occasional hard freeze here. This is where mandarins do better than oranges.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: The Gulf South is the mandarin's flagship region. Satsuma on trifoliate rootstock is hardy through zone 8 and its early ripening escapes the hardest freezes, so mandarins fruit reliably here where a navel is only marginal. Harvest runs roughly October (satsuma) into January (clementine and later types).
se_gulf.cold_basis_seasoned: Across the Southeast and Gulf, a mature satsuma is hardy into the mid-to-upper teens°F, well past a navel, and the early fall-to-winter harvest gets fruit off before the worst cold. Hard advective freezes into the upper teens reach the colder, northern edge every few years, at the edge of even satsuma's tolerance for young trees.
se_gulf.cold_basis_beginner: A grown satsuma here handles cold better than any orange, down into the teens°F, and because it ripens early you usually pick before the hardest freezes. Young trees still need protection in a bad freeze.
se_gulf.heat_basis_seasoned: Long, hot, humid Southeastern summers bank ample heat for good mandarin quality; heat is not the limiter. In warm, humid falls the rind can stay green-tinged on ripe fruit, so taste rather than color.
se_gulf.heat_basis_beginner: Summers here are plenty warm for sweet mandarins. In a warm fall the skin can stay a bit green even when the fruit is ripe, which is normal.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 8 in the interior valley has high summer heat and, for a hardy mandarin, tolerable winter cold: satsuma and other mandarins take the valley's radiation frosts better than a navel, and early ripening clears the crop ahead of the coldest nights. Cold protection helps young trees in the colder pockets.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 8 in the valley has plenty of summer heat, and mandarins handle its winter frosts better than oranges do, especially early-ripening satsuma. Protect young trees on the coldest nights.
8.harvest: Nov - Jan (satsuma and clementine; late types into late winter)
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Radiation frosts into the low-20s°F occur in colder zone-8 valley sites; mature mandarins are hardy through this, but protect young trees on the coldest nights.

9.plant_out: Spring ideal; much of the year on the mild valley floor
9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 valley floor is excellent for mandarins: high summer heat for full flavor and color, and winters that only rarely threaten a hardy mandarin. Satsuma, clementine, and late seedless types all fruit reliably; this is major mandarin-growing country.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 9 in the valley is ideal for mandarins. Hot summers make good fruit, and winters are usually mild enough to keep the crop.
9.harvest: Nov - Jan (early types; late selections hold into late winter)
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is an occasional risk on the valley floor; most winters pass without loss, and a hardy mandarin tolerates the usual radiation frosts.

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: The Central Valley is great for mandarins. Summers are hot enough for excellent fruit, and mandarins, especially satsuma, handle the winter frosts better than oranges.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: The interior valley grows premium mandarins: high summer heat for quality, with cold only a minor constraint because mandarins are hardier than navels and ripen earlier. Harvest runs fall into late winter across the variety range.
ca_interior.cold_basis_seasoned: Interior valley winters bring radiation frosts; a mature mandarin, especially satsuma, is hardy into the mid-to-upper teens°F, comfortably past the usual valley lows, so cold rarely limits the crop. Protect young trees in the coldest zone-8 pockets.
ca_interior.cold_basis_beginner: Valley winters can frost, but grown mandarins handle it better than oranges. Only young trees in the coldest spots need much protection.
ca_interior.heat_basis_seasoned: The valley's long, hot summers give mandarins abundant heat for full flavor and color; heat is never the limiter here. Mandarins actually need less heat than a navel, so quality is dependable across the valley.
ca_interior.heat_basis_beginner: Hot valley summers give mandarins all the warmth they need for sweet, colorful fruit.

9.plant_out: Spring ideal; most of the year in this mild, frost-safe climate
9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 on the north coast is frost-safe but cool: a mandarin grows and fruits, and because mandarins need less heat than a navel the fruit is usually more usable than a navel would be here, though cool summers can leave it more tart and slower to color. Satsuma, which tolerates cool summers, is the best bet.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 9 on the north coast is mild and frost-safe. Mandarins grow and fruit here, and they handle the cool summers better than oranges do, though the fruit can be a bit tart and slow to color. Satsuma is the best choice.
9.harvest: Dec - Feb (satsuma best in the cool summers; quality varies by year)
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely a crop factor on the north coast; the limiting factor here is cool summer heat, not winter cold.

10.plant_out: Spring ideal; most of the year in this mild, frost-safe climate
10.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 10 on the north coast is frost-safe but cool: a mandarin grows and fruits, and because mandarins need less heat than a navel the fruit is usually more usable than a navel would be here, though cool summers can leave it more tart and slower to color. Satsuma, which tolerates cool summers, is the best bet.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 10 on the north coast is mild and frost-safe. Mandarins grow and fruit here, and they handle the cool summers better than oranges do, though the fruit can be a bit tart and slow to color. Satsuma is the best choice.
10.harvest: Dec - Feb (satsuma best in the cool summers; quality varies by year)
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely a crop factor on the north coast; the limiting factor here is cool summer heat, not winter cold.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: On the cool north coast a mandarin lives easily and fruits, and it handles the cool summers better than an orange would. Satsuma is the best pick; the fruit can still be a bit tart in the coolest, foggiest spots.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: The north coast is heat-marginal but more forgiving for mandarins than for navels: frost-safe, and mandarins' lower heat requirement means satsuma in particular fruits with usable quality where a navel stays sour. On the coolest immediate coast, quality still slips. This is a quality-margin case, not a cold one.
ca_north_coast.cold_basis_seasoned: The north coast is nearly frost-free; winter lows rarely approach any mandarin cold threshold, so cold does not limit a mandarin here. Heat, not cold, is the constraint.
ca_north_coast.cold_basis_beginner: It barely freezes on the north coast, so cold is not the problem for a mandarin here. Cool summers are.
ca_north_coast.heat_basis_seasoned: Cool, marine north-coast summers bank borderline heat, but mandarins need far less heat than a navel, so satsuma and other cool-tolerant mandarins fruit with reasonable quality here where a navel would stay tart. On the foggiest coast the fruit is more acidic and slower to color.
ca_north_coast.heat_basis_beginner: The north coast is cool, but mandarins need less heat than oranges, so satsuma can make decent fruit here. Right on the foggy coast the fruit is more sour.

9.plant_out: Most of the year (spring ideal) in this frost-free climate
9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 on the south coast is prime mandarin territory: frost-free, with enough warmth for good quality. This is the home of the famous Ojai Pixie and of excellent clementine and Gold Nugget crops. Mandarins do markedly better here than a navel, which is only middling on this coast.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 9 on the south coast is excellent for mandarins. It never freezes and is warm enough for sweet fruit; this is where the famous Ojai Pixie mandarins grow. Mandarins beat oranges here.
9.harvest: Dec - Mar (early satsuma through late Pixie and Gold Nugget)
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely a crop factor on the south coast; a hardy mandarin is well within its cold range here.

10.plant_out: Most of the year (spring ideal) in this frost-free climate
10.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 10 on the south coast is prime mandarin territory: frost-free, with enough warmth for good quality. This is the home of the famous Ojai Pixie and of excellent clementine and Gold Nugget crops. Mandarins do markedly better here than a navel, which is only middling on this coast.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 10 on the south coast is excellent for mandarins. It never freezes and is warm enough for sweet fruit; this is where the famous Ojai Pixie mandarins grow. Mandarins beat oranges here.
10.harvest: Dec - Mar (early satsuma through late Pixie and Gold Nugget)
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely a crop factor on the south coast; a hardy mandarin is well within its cold range here.

ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: The south coast is a top spot for mandarins. It never freezes and is warm enough for sweet fruit, and it is where the well-known Ojai Pixie mandarins grow. Early types ripen in winter and late types like Pixie and Gold Nugget carry into spring.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: The south coast is prime mandarin country and a clear refit up from the navel case: frost-free and warm enough for good quality, home to the Ojai Pixie and to excellent clementine and Gold Nugget crops. Harvest spans early satsuma in winter through the late seedless types into spring.
ca_south_coast.cold_basis_seasoned: The south coast is effectively frost-free; winter lows sit in the 30s°F, well above any mandarin cold threshold, so cold never limits a mandarin here.
ca_south_coast.cold_basis_beginner: The south coast almost never freezes, so cold is no worry for a mandarin here.
ca_south_coast.heat_basis_seasoned: South-coast summers are mild but warm enough for good mandarin quality, since mandarins need much less heat than a navel; this is why the same coast that leaves navels only middling grows superb Pixie and clementine mandarins. Inland of the marine layer, quality rises further.
ca_south_coast.heat_basis_beginner: The south coast is mild but warm enough for sweet mandarins, because mandarins do not need as much heat as oranges. That is why great Pixie and clementine mandarins grow here even though oranges are only so-so.

9.plant_out: Spring; avoid planting into peak summer heat
9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 in the low desert fruits reliably: abundant summer heat and rare winter frost. Clementine and late mandarins such as W. Murcott thrive on the heat; satsuma prefers the milder end and can run softer in flavor in extreme heat. Manage spring fruit-drop with steady irrigation.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 9 in the desert is good for mandarins, with lots of summer heat and little frost. Clementines and late types love the heat; satsuma does better where it is a bit milder. Water well in spring so the tree keeps its fruit.
9.harvest: Nov - Feb (clementine and late mandarins; satsuma earlier)
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Occasional radiation frosts into the upper 20s°F reach colder desert sites; mature mandarins tolerate this, and young trees benefit from protection on the coldest nights.

10.plant_out: Spring; avoid planting into peak summer heat
10.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 10 in the low desert fruits reliably: abundant summer heat and rare winter frost. Clementine and late mandarins such as W. Murcott thrive on the heat; satsuma prefers the milder end and can run softer in flavor in extreme heat. Manage spring fruit-drop with steady irrigation.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 10 in the desert is good for mandarins, with lots of summer heat and little frost. Clementines and late types love the heat; satsuma does better where it is a bit milder. Water well in spring so the tree keeps its fruit.
10.harvest: Nov - Feb (clementine and late mandarins; satsuma earlier)
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Occasional radiation frosts into the upper 20s°F reach colder desert sites; mature mandarins tolerate this, and young trees benefit from protection on the coldest nights.

ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: The desert grows good mandarins, especially clementines and late types that love the heat. Water well in spring so the tree holds its fruit, and frost is rarely an issue.
ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: The low desert is a strong mandarin region on heat: clementine and late hybrids such as W. Murcott ripen richly, while satsuma prefers the milder end of the range. Management centers on spring fruit-drop and steady irrigation rather than cold. Harvest runs late fall into late winter.
ca_desert.cold_basis_seasoned: Low-desert winters bring occasional radiation frosts into the upper 20s to low-30s°F; a mature mandarin is comfortably hardy through this, with any crop risk confined to unusual hard frosts in the colder zone-9 sites.
ca_desert.cold_basis_beginner: The desert can frost on cold nights, but grown mandarins handle it. Cold is only a worry in the coldest spots during a rare hard freeze.
ca_desert.heat_basis_seasoned: Desert summers bank abundant heat; clementine and late mandarins ripen richly and reliably. The flip side of that heat is spring fruit-drop from very hot bloom-time temperatures in the 90s°F, so irrigation matters; satsuma's flavor can soften in the most extreme heat.
ca_desert.heat_basis_beginner: The desert is plenty hot for good mandarins, especially clementines. Very hot spring weather can drop young fruit, so keep the tree well watered.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 8 in the arid inland has adequate summer heat and, for a hardy mandarin, tolerable winter cold: satsuma on trifoliate rootstock takes the zone's lows near the upper teens to mid-20s°F, and early ripening clears the crop before the hardest freezes, so it fruits where a navel is only marginal. Protect young trees on the coldest nights.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 8 here is warm enough in summer for good mandarins, and satsuma is hardy enough to handle the winters, unlike an orange which is borderline. Because satsuma ripens early, you usually pick before the worst cold. Protect young trees on the coldest nights.
8.harvest: Nov - Jan (satsuma; pick promptly before hard freezes)
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Hard freezes into the upper teens°F occur in this zone-8 arid inland; mature satsuma usually survives, but protect young trees and harvest ripe fruit ahead of a hard freeze.

warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: This dry inland region is warm enough for good mandarins, and satsuma is hardy enough for its winters where oranges are borderline. Satsuma ripens early, so you usually pick before the coldest weather.
warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: The warm arid inland grows a reliable satsuma where a navel is only marginal: adequate summer heat, and a mandarin cold-hardiness edge that covers the zone-8 winter lows, with early ripening escaping the hardest freezes. Protect young trees in hard winters.
warm_arid.cold_basis_seasoned: The warm arid inland sits at zone 8, the cold edge for citrus, but satsuma's roughly 15 to 20°F mature hardiness covers the usual upper-teens lows, and early harvest gets fruit off before the worst cold, so a mandarin fruits reliably where a navel does not. Young trees still need protection.
warm_arid.cold_basis_beginner: This inland area gets cold in winter, but satsuma is the hardiest citrus and handles it, and it ripens early enough to pick before the coldest nights. Young trees need protection in a hard freeze.
warm_arid.heat_basis_seasoned: Hot, dry inland summers bank enough heat for good mandarin quality; heat is not the limiter. Quality is good where the tree clears winter, which for a hardy satsuma is most years.
warm_arid.heat_basis_beginner: Summers here are hot and dry, plenty warm for sweet mandarins. Heat is not the problem; winter cold is, and satsuma handles it.

9.plant_out: Spring; avoid planting into peak summer heat
9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 in the Arizona low desert fruits reliably: abundant summer heat and rare frost. Clementine and late mandarins ripen richly; satsuma runs earlier and prefers the milder end. Spring irrigation manages the heat-driven fruit-drop.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 9 in the Arizona desert grows good mandarins, with hot summers and little frost. Clementines love the heat, and satsuma ripens earliest. Water well in spring so the tree holds its fruit.
9.harvest: Nov - Feb (clementine and late types; satsuma earlier)
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Only occasional light frost reaches the Arizona low desert; mature mandarins tolerate it and crop loss to cold is rare.

low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: The Arizona low desert grows good mandarins, ready late fall into late winter. Clementines especially love the heat. Water well in spring, and cold is rarely a problem.
low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: The Arizona low desert is a high-heat mandarin region: clementine and late hybrids ripen richly, satsuma runs earliest, and management centers on spring fruit-drop rather than winter cold. Harvest runs late fall into late winter.
low_desert_az.cold_basis_seasoned: The Arizona low desert at zone 9 brings only occasional light frost; a mature mandarin is comfortably hardy, with crop risk only in an unusual hard frost.
low_desert_az.cold_basis_beginner: The low desert rarely gets a hard frost, so cold is not much of a worry for a grown mandarin here.
low_desert_az.heat_basis_seasoned: Abundant low-desert heat ripens clementine and late mandarins richly. The desert caveat is spring fruit-drop from very hot bloom-time temperatures in the 90s°F, so irrigation matters more than cold; satsuma flavor can soften in the most extreme heat.
low_desert_az.heat_basis_beginner: The Arizona desert is plenty hot for good mandarins, especially clementines. Very hot spring weather can drop young fruit, so keep the tree well watered through spring.

10.plant_out: Most of the year in this frost-free climate
10.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 10 on the Florida peninsula fruits reliably: frost-free winters and hot, humid summers give a mandarin ample warmth. Satsuma is more a north-Florida crop, but clementine and mandarin hybrids fruit well here; expect rind color to lag interior ripeness, so taste rather than color. Favor satsuma or clementine, which are not among the susceptible types, over susceptible tangelos in this humid climate.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 10 in Florida is dependable for mandarins. It does not freeze, and summers are hot enough for sweet fruit. The skin may look greenish even when the fruit is ripe. Satsuma and clementine are good choices; some tangelo-type hybrids get a leaf-and-fruit-spot disease in this humid climate.
10.harvest: Nov - Jan (rind may stay green-tinged when ripe)
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is not a crop factor on the central and southern peninsula; winters are reliably above any mandarin cold threshold.

11.plant_out: Most of the year in this frost-free climate
11.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 11 on the Florida peninsula fruits reliably: frost-free winters and hot, humid summers give a mandarin ample warmth. Satsuma is more a north-Florida crop, but clementine and mandarin hybrids fruit well here; expect rind color to lag interior ripeness, so taste rather than color. Favor satsuma or clementine, which are not among the susceptible types, over susceptible tangelos in this humid climate.
11.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 11 in Florida is dependable for mandarins. It does not freeze, and summers are hot enough for sweet fruit. The skin may look greenish even when the fruit is ripe. Satsuma and clementine are good choices; some tangelo-type hybrids get a leaf-and-fruit-spot disease in this humid climate.
11.harvest: Nov - Jan (rind may stay green-tinged when ripe)
11.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is not a crop factor on the central and southern peninsula; winters are reliably above any mandarin cold threshold.

fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: Central and south Florida grow mandarins easily and never freeze; they are ready in early winter. The skin may stay greenish but the fruit is still sweet. Satsuma and clementine are good picks; some tangelo-type mandarins get a fungal spot in this humid climate.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: The frost-free peninsula fruits dependably, with mandarins ripening roughly November into January. Heat is adequate and cold is a non-factor; the local quirks are humidity-driven rind-greening and the Alternaria brown spot that troubles tangelo and Murcott-type hybrids, so satsuma and clementine are the sound choices here.
fl_peninsula.cold_basis_seasoned: The central and southern peninsula is effectively frost-free; winter lows hold in the upper 30s to upper 40s°F, well above any mandarin cold threshold. Cold does not constrain a mandarin here.
fl_peninsula.cold_basis_beginner: Central and south Florida barely get cold, so a mandarin has nothing to fear from frost here.
fl_peninsula.heat_basis_seasoned: Hot, humid summers bank ample heat for good mandarin quality. The nuance is humidity, not heat shortage: warm nights mean rind color lags interior ripeness, and humid conditions favor Alternaria brown spot on susceptible hybrids, so a green-tinged peel does not signal unripe fruit and variety choice matters.
fl_peninsula.heat_basis_beginner: Central and south Florida are plenty hot for sweet mandarins. The fruit tastes good even when the skin stays a bit green, which is normal in this warm, humid climate.

11.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 11 in Hawaii is frost-free and grows mandarins year-round, but quality is marginal: the warm, humid tropics lack the cool nights that color and sweeten mandarins, so low-elevation fruit tends to stay green-skinned and lower in sugar. Cooler uplands improve quality. This is a diurnal-swing limit, not a cold or heat-shortage one.
11.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 11 in Hawaii grows mandarins all year and never freezes, but the fruit is often less sweet and stays green because the nights do not get cool enough to color it. It is better up in the cooler hills.
11.harvest: Oct - Jan (lower-elevation fruit stays green-tinged and milder)
11.frost_risk_note_seasoned: There is no frost risk in Hawaii; the limiting factor is the lack of cool nights for quality, not cold.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: Mandarins grow all year in Hawaii, but they are often less sweet and stay green because the islands lack the cool nights mandarins need to color and sweeten. Cooler hillsides do better.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: Hawaii grows mandarins year-round but quality is marginal for a counter-intuitive reason: abundant warmth without the cool nights mandarins need to color and drop acid. Lower elevations give greener, milder fruit; cooler uplands do better. This is a quality limit, not a frost or heat-shortage one.
hawaii_tropical.cold_basis_seasoned: Hawaii is frost-free year-round; temperatures never approach any mandarin cold threshold, so cold plays no role here.
hawaii_tropical.cold_basis_beginner: Hawaii never freezes, so cold is simply not a factor for growing mandarins.
hawaii_tropical.heat_basis_seasoned: Hawaii is warm and frost-free, but the humid tropics lack the cool nights a mandarin needs to color and sweeten. At lower elevations fruit can stay acidic and green-skinned even when ripe; cooler uplands give better quality. Warmth is present, but the diurnal swing that develops mandarin quality is not.
hawaii_tropical.heat_basis_beginner: Hawaii is warm and never freezes, but it is missing the cool nights that make mandarins sweet and colored. At low elevations the fruit can stay sour and green; it does better in the cooler hills.

crops.description_seasoned: The mandarin (Citrus reticulata and its hybrids, including satsuma, clementine, and tangerine) is a subtropical evergreen fruit tree grown for small, sweet, loose-skinned, easy-to-peel fruit that is usually seedless. Its defining advantage over other sweet citrus is cold hardiness: satsuma is the most cold-tolerant of the commonly grown citrus, with mature trees withstanding brief lows near 15 to 20°F, notably colder than a navel orange, which lets in-ground mandarins reach zone 8 across the Gulf South and interior valleys. Early ripening (satsuma from fall) also gets the crop off the tree before the hardest winter cold. Mandarins need less summer heat than a navel to sweeten but want cool fall nights to color and drop acid, so they are marginal only in the cool-night tropics and the coolest coasts. Two group traits shape their care: seedless types set seeds if cross-pollinated by other citrus, so isolation preserves seedlessness; and mandarins are strongly alternate-bearing, managed by thinning heavy crops. Unlike a navel, most mandarins do not hold well on the tree and are picked promptly. Trees are small and grafted, usually on trifoliate-orange rootstock for cold hardiness, and productive for decades.
crops.description_beginner: The mandarin is an evergreen citrus tree that makes small, sweet, easy-to-peel fruit that is usually seedless. Its big advantage over other sweet citrus is that it takes cold better: satsuma is the hardiest common citrus, with grown trees handling a brief dip near 15 to 20°F, colder than an orange, so mandarins can be grown in the ground farther north (into zone 8) across the Gulf South and warm valleys. Satsumas also ripen early, so you usually pick the fruit before the coldest weather. Mandarins need less summer heat than an orange to get sweet, but they want cool fall nights to color up, so they struggle mainly in the warm-night tropics. Two things to know: seedless mandarins get seeds if another citrus pollinates them, so keep them apart to stay seedless; and they tend to make a big crop one year and a light one the next, which you even out by thinning. Unlike oranges, most mandarins do not keep well on the tree, so pick them when ripe. The trees are small, grafted (usually on trifoliate-orange rootstock for cold hardiness), and produce for many years.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Harvest mandarins by taste, and pick promptly. The rind loosens and puffs slightly and color deepens as cool fall nights arrive, but in warm, humid climates the rind can stay green-tinged on fully ripe fruit, so taste rather than color decides. Unlike a navel, most mandarins do not hold well on the tree: satsuma and early types puff, dry, and lose flavor if left past maturity, so pick at ripeness and refrigerate. The exceptions are the late holding types, notably Gold Nugget and Pixie, which keep their quality on the tree into spring. Early satsuma ripening also lets the crop come off before the hardest winter cold.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Pick mandarins by taste, not just by color, and do not leave them on the tree too long. The skin loosens and colors as fall nights get cool, but in warm, humid areas it can still look a little green even when the fruit is ripe, so taste one first. Unlike oranges, most mandarins get puffy and dry inside if left on the tree, so pick them when ripe and keep them in the fridge. A few late types like Gold Nugget and Pixie are the exception and do hold on the tree into spring. Early satsumas also let you pick the crop before the coldest weather.
crops.bloom_time_seasoned: Mandarins bloom primarily in spring, typically March through May depending on climate and zone, with fragrant white flowers for about three weeks. Fruit develops over roughly seven to ten months, faster than a navel's ten to twelve, so harvest comes earlier: satsuma ripens from October, clementine in early winter, and late selections such as Gold Nugget, Pixie, and W. Murcott or Tango carry the season into spring. In the low desert satsuma can start earliest; late types hold latest.
crops.bloom_time_beginner: Mandarins bloom in spring, usually March through May depending on where you live, with fragrant white flowers for about three weeks. The fruit then grows for about seven to ten months, a bit faster than an orange, so you harvest earlier: satsumas from fall, clementines in early winter, and late types like Gold Nugget, Pixie, and Tango stretching into spring.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Mandarins are the most cold-hardy of the commonly grown sweet citrus. A mature, hardened satsuma withstands brief lows near 15 to 20°F without serious wood injury, notably colder than a navel orange (about 24 to 26°F) and behind only kumquat among edible citrus. The cold-hardiness order runs roughly satsuma and kumquat, then sour orange and tangerine, then sweet oranges such as navel, then grapefruit, lemon, and lime. The fruit is more tender than the wood, taking damage near 30°F for a couple of hours, but satsuma's early fall ripening usually gets the crop off before the hardest freezes. Trees are evergreen with no dormancy, so growing tissue is always vulnerable, and young trees are far more tender than mature ones. Trifoliate-orange rootstock adds cold hardiness and is standard for cold-edge planting. Beyond cold, mandarins need less summer heat than a navel to sweeten but want cool fall nights to color, so quality, not survival, is the limit in the warm-night tropics. The practical in-ground range is about zones 8 through 11.
crops.hardiness_notes_beginner: Mandarins take cold better than any other common sweet citrus. A grown, hardened satsuma can handle a brief dip near 15 to 20°F without serious damage, colder than an orange (about 24 to 26°F) and beaten only by the kumquat. The fruit is more tender than the wood and can be hurt near 30°F, but satsumas ripen early enough that you usually pick before the worst cold. Because the tree is evergreen and never goes dormant, its leaves and wood can be hurt any time it gets cold enough, and young trees are the most tender. Planting on trifoliate-orange rootstock adds hardiness and is standard in cold areas. Mandarins also need less summer heat than an orange to get sweet, but they want cool fall nights to color up. The usual in-ground range is about zones 8 through 11.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Mandarins require no winter chilling to flower or fruit. They are evergreen and do not enter a chill-triggered dormancy; flowering is driven by spring warming and moisture rather than release from a prior cold period. This distinguishes citrus from deciduous fruit trees such as peaches and apples, which need hundreds of chill hours to break bud dormancy and set a normal crop.
crops.chill_hours_note_beginner: Mandarins do not need any winter chill to flower or fruit. Unlike peaches and apples, which need hundreds of cold hours in winter to wake up and set a crop, citrus is evergreen and is triggered to bloom by spring warmth and moisture instead. So chill hours, which matter a lot for deciduous fruit trees, simply do not apply to mandarins.
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Most mandarins set a full crop on a single tree and are seedless when grown in isolation. Satsuma is parthenocarpic and reliably seedless. Clementine and W. Murcott are self-incompatible but facultatively parthenocarpic: they set seedless fruit on their own, yet fertile pollen from another nearby citrus cross-pollinates them and puts seeds into the fruit, and citrus pollen can travel a long way, so isolation from pollen-bearing citrus is what keeps seedless types seedless. A few mandarin hybrids fruit better with a compatible pollinizer, but the common seedless mandarins need no pollinizer and no bees for a single tree to fruit.
crops.pollinator_notes_beginner: A mandarin makes fruit on its own, with no second tree and no bees needed, and most types are seedless when grown away from other citrus. Satsuma is naturally seedless. Clementine and some others are seedless by themselves, but if pollen from another citrus nearby reaches the flowers, the fruit ends up with seeds, so keeping a seedless mandarin away from other pollen-making citrus is what keeps it seedless.

pet_safe.note: The fruit is fine, but the peel, leaves, and citrus oils can upset the stomach of cats, dogs, and horses.

crops.name: Fig

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Figs are not fussy about soil and grow in a wide range, from sandy to heavier ground, as long as it drains well and does not stay soggy. A loam with some organic matter is ideal, but figs even do fine in poor, rocky soil. The one thing to avoid is sandy soil that is full of root-knot nematodes, tiny soil pests that are the leading killer of figs. Do not make the soil too rich either: too much rich material and feeding pushes soft leafy growth and fewer figs, and that soft growth is more easily hurt by winter cold.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Fig is adaptable across soil textures, from sandy to clay loam, provided drainage is good; it tolerates poor and rocky ground better than most fruit trees. A well-drained loam with moderate organic matter is ideal. The critical avoidance is root-knot-nematode-infested sandy soil, which is the leading cause of fig decline in warm regions, since own-rooted figs carry no resistant rootstock. Keep fertility moderate: over-rich soil and heavy feeding drive vegetative growth at the expense of fruit and produce soft wood that is more prone to winter injury.

ph.note_beginner: Figs do best in slightly acidic soil, around pH 6.0 to 6.5, but they are easygoing and grow well anywhere from about 6.0 up to 7.8 (pH is just a measure of how acidic or alkaline the soil is). Test your soil before planting and only adjust if it is far off: garden lime raises a too-acidic pH and elemental sulfur lowers one that is too alkaline. Mix any amendment in before you plant.
ph.note_seasoned: Fig prefers a slightly acidic soil near pH 6.0 to 6.5 but is tolerant across roughly 6.0 to 7.8, handling near-neutral ground without trouble. Test before planting and correct only a real deficiency: lime raises a too-acidic pH, elemental sulfur lowers an alkaline one. Work amendments in ahead of planting, since pH shifts slowly and is easiest to set before the permanent plant goes in.

fertilizer.timing: early spring as growth resumes, then lightly through early summer; stop by midsummer
fertilizer.example_product: 10-10-10 balanced fertilizer
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Feed lightly. Figs need far less fertilizer than most fruit trees, and over-feeding is a common mistake: excess nitrogen pushes rank leafy growth, delays and reduces fruiting, can cause fruit to split, and produces soft wood that winters poorly. Broadcast a balanced granular evenly around the root zone out toward the drip line, keep it off the stems, and water it in. Halve the rate in colder regions to favor hardiness, and never feed past midsummer, since late nitrogen keeps the plant growing when it should be hardening for winter.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Go easy on the fertilizer. Figs need much less than other fruit trees, and too much does more harm than good: lots of leaves and few figs, split fruit, and soft growth that is easily hurt by winter cold. Scatter a balanced fertilizer around the plant out to where the branches reach, keep it off the stems, and water it in. In colder areas use half as much, and stop feeding by midsummer so the plant can toughen up before winter.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 or 8-8-8 suits figs; they are light feeders and need no high-nitrogen program. Too much nitrogen (N) is counterproductive, driving leaves over fruit and reducing cold hardiness.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: A balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 or 8-8-8 (the three numbers are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium) is all a fig needs. Do not overdo the first number, nitrogen, because too much gives you leaves instead of figs.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A common home rate is about 1/2 pound of 10-10-10 for a young plant and 2 to 4 pounds for a mature one, split into 2 or 3 applications from early spring through early summer; UGA gives a rule of about 1/2 pound per foot of height, up to 5 pounds a year. Do not fertilize at planting; wait until growth begins. Cut these rates in half in northern gardens to keep growth firm for winter.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A simple guide is about 1/2 pound of 10-10-10 for a young fig and 2 to 4 pounds for a big one, spread over 2 or 3 times from early spring to early summer. Do not put fertilizer in the planting hole or feed right at planting; wait until it starts growing. In cold-winter areas, use half as much.

companions.note_seasoned: Fig is parthenocarpic and self-fruitful, so there are no pollination companions to plant: a lone tree fruits with no bees and no fig wasp. The interactions that matter for a fig are at the root zone, not classic vegetable pairings. Keep grass and weeds cleared back and mulch the root area, which competes down weeds and holds moisture, and above all keep the plant out of soil heavily infested with root-knot nematodes, which own-rooted figs cannot resist. A well-mulched, weed-free, nematode-free root zone is the whole companion story.
companions.note_beginner: Figs make fruit on their own with no pollination, so you do not need any companion plants to help them fruit. What matters for a fig is what happens around its roots: keep grass and weeds pulled back and lay down mulch to hold moisture and keep weeds down, and do not plant a fig in soil full of root-knot nematodes (tiny soil pests), because figs cannot fight them off. A mulched, weed-free, pest-free root area is really all a fig asks for.

good_seasoned.name: A mulched, weed-free root zone
good_seasoned.label: traditional

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Orchard-floor mulch/weed-free-ring practice is standard extension guidance for young fruit trees (moisture retention, reduced competition) and is echoed in UMD's fig culture notes, but the specific benefit is general rather than a fig-specific companion effect. traditional/medium.

good_seasoned.why_seasoned: The single most useful thing around a young fig is not another plant but a clear, mulched ring. A layer of organic mulch kept off the stems holds soil moisture (which figs reward with better fruit set), moderates soil temperature at the shallow fig roots, and suppresses the grass and weeds that compete hard with an establishing plant. It also insulates the roots through winter at the cold edge of the fig's range.

bad_seasoned.name: Root-knot-nematode ground (old fig or susceptible-crop soil)
bad_seasoned.label: research_backed

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Root-knot nematode is named by UGA, Clemson, and UF/IFAS as the leading cause of fig decline/death in sandy warm-region soils, and own-rooted figs have no resistant rootstock. Multiple independent extension sources, clear mechanism. extension_backed/high.

bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Do not plant a fig into sandy soil known to carry heavy root-knot nematode populations, or straight into ground where a nematode-declined fig was just removed. Root-knot nematodes are the leading killer of figs in warm sandy regions, and because figs grow on their own roots there is no resistant rootstock to fall back on the way there is for stone fruit. The fix is site selection, not a companion plant: choose the best-drained, least infested ground, or replace a generous volume of soil.

pests.name: Root-knot nematode
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Above ground, a slow, unexplained decline: stunted growth, sparse yellowing leaves, dieback, and poor fruiting that worsens over years. Below ground, the roots carry small knots or galls, and the fine feeder roots are damaged, so the plant cannot take up water and nutrients.
pests.symptoms_beginner: The fig slowly goes downhill for no obvious reason: stunted, with thin yellow leaves, dieback, and fewer figs each year. If you dig up a root, you find small knots or swellings on it. Those knots are the damage from the pest.
pests.cause_seasoned: Root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne species), microscopic soil roundworms that feed inside the roots and form the galls. They build up in warm, sandy soils and are the leading cause of fig decline and death in the Southeast and other warm sandy regions. Own-rooted figs have no resistant rootstock, so there is no cure once a plant is heavily infested.
pests.cause_beginner: Microscopic soil worms called root-knot nematodes that live in the roots and make the knots. They build up in warm, sandy soil and are the number-one killer of figs in warm areas. Because figs grow on their own roots, there is no special root you can buy to resist them and no cure once a plant is badly infested.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no rescue treatment for an infested plant. Manage it by keeping the fig vigorous and well watered so it outgrows light damage, mulching heavily to build soil organic matter and beneficial soil life, and, in the worst sandy sites, growing in a container of clean mix instead. A thick organic mulch is the practical home tool.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Once a plant is badly infested there is no fix. The best you can do is keep the fig strong with steady water and a thick mulch so it can shrug off mild damage, and, in bad sandy soil, grow it in a pot of clean potting mix instead of in the ground.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Prevention is everything: do not plant into known nematode-heavy sandy soil, choose the best-drained ground, mulch heavily, and keep the plant vigorous. Where nematode pressure is high, container culture in clean mix sidesteps the problem entirely.
pests.prevention_beginner: The main thing is to avoid the problem: do not plant in sandy soil known to have these pests, pick well-drained ground, mulch thickly, and keep the fig healthy. Where the soil is bad, growing the fig in a pot of clean mix avoids the pest completely.

pests.name: Dried fruit beetle and fig souring
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Ripening figs ferment and sour from the inside, oozing a scummy or bubbly liquid from the eye and smelling vinegary or yeasty. Small beetles may be seen at the eye of soft fruit. Affected figs are inedible and drop or rot on the plant.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Ripe figs turn sour and mushy inside, with a fizzy or scummy ooze coming out of the little hole at the bottom (the eye) and a vinegary smell. You may see tiny beetles around the soft fruit. The affected figs are ruined.
pests.cause_seasoned: Dried fruit beetles (Carpophilus species) and other sap beetles are drawn to ripe figs and carry souring yeasts and bacteria into the fruit through the open eye. The problem is worst in humid weather and on varieties with a large, open eye, which lets the beetles and moisture in.
pests.cause_beginner: Little beetles called dried fruit beetles are attracted to ripe figs and carry the yeasts that cause souring into the fruit through the open hole at the bottom. It is worst in humid weather and on figs with a big open eye that lets the beetles in.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Pick figs promptly as they ripen and remove any soured or dropped fruit right away so beetles are not drawn in and the yeasts do not build. Choosing varieties with a small or closed eye (such as Celeste) greatly reduces souring. There is no spray that reaches yeasts inside the fruit.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick figs as soon as they are ripe and clean up any soured or fallen fruit right away, so the beetles are not attracted and the souring cannot spread. Growing a variety with a small, tight eye like Celeste helps a lot. No spray fixes souring once it is inside the fig.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep the plant picked clean during ripening, dispose of soured fruit, and favor closed-eye varieties in humid areas. Good airflow and prompt harvest are the durable controls.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep the figs picked and throw away any soured ones, and grow a tight-eye variety like Celeste if your summers are humid. Picking often and keeping the plant open are the best defenses.

pests.name: Birds (and squirrels)
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Ripe and nearly ripe figs are pecked open, half-eaten, or gone entirely, often the best fruit at the top of the plant first. Squirrels strip fruit and can clear a small tree fast. Damage appears exactly as the crop begins to ripen.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Ripe figs get pecked open, half-eaten, or disappear, usually the best ones up high first. Squirrels can strip a small fig fast. It happens right as the figs start to ripen.
pests.cause_seasoned: Birds and squirrels find ripe figs irresistible, and a fig's soft, sweet, unprotected fruit ripening over many weeks is an easy, repeated target. This is one of the most common complaints of home fig growers.
pests.cause_beginner: Birds and squirrels love ripe figs, and because a fig's fruit is soft, sweet, and out in the open for weeks, they come back again and again. It is one of the most common fig problems.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Netting the plant (or key branches) as fruit begins to color is the most effective home control; pick ripe figs promptly and often so less hangs waiting. Reflective tape and scare devices help briefly. A container fig can be moved to a more protected spot.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: The best fix is to drape bird netting over the plant as the figs start to color, and to pick ripe figs often so fewer are left hanging. Shiny tape or scare items help for a while. A potted fig can be moved somewhere more protected.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plan for netting before the crop ripens rather than after the losses start, and keep the plant a manageable size so it can be covered and picked easily.
pests.prevention_beginner: Get the netting ready before the figs ripen, not after the birds find them, and keep the plant small enough to cover and pick easily.

diseases.name: Fig rust
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: In mid to late summer, leaves develop small yellow-orange spots that turn rusty reddish-brown, most on the underside; heavily spotted leaves yellow and drop early, sometimes defoliating the plant well before fall. The current crop usually still ripens, but repeated early defoliation weakens the plant over years.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: In late summer, leaves get small yellow-orange spots that turn rusty brown, mostly underneath, and then yellow and fall early, sometimes stripping the plant before fall. That year's figs usually still ripen, but losing leaves early year after year wears the plant down.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Cerotelium fici. It spreads in warm, humid, wet weather and overwinters on fallen infected leaves, so it is most severe in the humid Southeast and in wet summers, building up where litter is left under the plant.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus called Cerotelium fici. It spreads in warm, wet, humid weather and survives winter on fallen infected leaves, so it is worst in humid areas and wet summers, especially where old leaves pile up under the plant.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Once leaves are spotted there is no cure for that leaf; the goal is to slow the spread and protect next year. Rake up and destroy fallen leaves to remove the overwintering source, and keep the canopy open and dry. Where rust is severe, a neutral copper or Bordeaux fungicide on the new foliage through the growing season is the standard organic option.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Once a leaf is spotted you cannot cure it; the aim is to slow it down and protect next year. Rake up and throw away fallen leaves, and keep the plant open so it dries fast. Where rust is bad, an organic copper spray on the new leaves through the season is the usual treatment.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Sanitation is the backbone: clear fallen leaves each year, prune for airflow, and water at the ground rather than overhead. In rust-prone humid regions, a preventive copper program from spring protects the foliage.
diseases.prevention_beginner: The main prevention is cleanup: rake away fallen leaves every year, prune so air moves through the plant, and water the ground instead of the leaves. In humid areas where rust is common, an organic copper spray starting in spring keeps the leaves protected.

diseases.name: Fig mosaic
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Leaves show scattered yellow, blotchy, or ring-like mottling (a mosaic pattern), sometimes with distorted growth; fruit may be spotted or drop early. Symptoms vary with season and variety and often come and go. The virus does not kill the plant but can reduce vigor and crop.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Leaves get a blotchy, mottled yellow pattern (called a mosaic), and sometimes the fruit is spotted or drops early. It comes and goes with the season and variety. It does not kill the plant, but it can slow it down and cut the crop.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Fig mosaic is a virus complex spread mainly by the tiny fig mite (Aceria ficus) and carried in cuttings taken from infected plants. Once a plant has it, it is systemic and permanent, since there is no cure for a virus in a plant.
diseases.cause_beginner: Fig mosaic is a virus, spread mostly by a tiny mite (the fig mite) and passed along in cuttings from infected plants. Once a plant has it, it is in the plant for good, because there is no cure for a plant virus.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no treatment for a virus in a plant. Manage it by keeping the plant otherwise healthy and vigorous; many infected figs still crop acceptably. Do not propagate cuttings from a mottled plant, and remove a severely stunted, poor-cropping plant.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure for a plant virus. Just keep the fig healthy and well cared for, since many infected plants still fruit alright. Do not take cuttings from a mottled plant to start new ones, and pull out a plant that is badly stunted and barely fruiting.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Prevention is about clean stock and mite control: start with cuttings or plants from healthy, unmottled sources, and keep fig mites in check since they spread the virus. There is no way to cure an infected plant.
diseases.prevention_beginner: The best prevention is starting with a healthy plant and controlling the tiny fig mites that spread it. Buy or take cuttings from plants with clean, un-mottled leaves. There is no way to cure a plant once it is infected.

diseases.name: Fig endosepsis (internal fruit rot)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Ripening fruit rots from the inside near the eye, turning brown and mushy internally while the outside may still look sound; affected figs sour, ooze, and drop. It overlaps with beetle-spread souring and is worst in humid weather on open-eye varieties.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Figs rot from the inside near the little hole at the bottom, going brown and mushy inside even when the outside still looks okay, then souring and dropping. It goes hand in hand with the souring that beetles cause, and is worst in humid weather on figs with a big open eye.
diseases.cause_seasoned: An internal fruit rot caused by fungi (including Fusarium) carried into the fruit through the open eye, often by the same sap beetles that spread souring. Humid conditions and large-eye varieties make it worse.
diseases.cause_beginner: A rot inside the fruit caused by fungi that get in through the open hole at the bottom, often carried by the same little beetles that cause souring. Humid weather and big-eye varieties make it worse.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no in-fruit cure. Control it the same way as souring: pick promptly, remove affected and dropped fruit, and favor small or closed-eye varieties (such as Celeste) in humid areas.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot cure it inside the fruit. Handle it like souring: pick figs promptly, throw away rotten and dropped ones, and grow a tight-eye variety like Celeste if your area is humid.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Choose closed-eye varieties in humid regions, keep fruit picked and the ground clean, and manage the sap beetles that carry the fungi.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Grow a tight-eye variety in humid areas, keep the figs picked and the ground clean, and control the little beetles that carry it.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Water deeply and regularly rather than lightly and often: figure roughly 1 to 1.5 inches of water per week from rain or irrigation through the growing season, more in heat and sandy soil, easing off as fruit finishes and through winter dormancy. A newly planted fig needs the most attention while it roots in; an established fig is fairly drought-tolerant but sizes and sweetens fruit poorly when it runs dry.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water deeply now and then instead of a little every day. Aim for about 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week from rain or the hose during the growing season, more when it is hot or the soil is sandy. A new fig needs steady water while it gets its roots going. An older fig can take some dry spells, but the figs come out small and less sweet if it gets too dry.
watering.amount_seasoned: Water deeply each time so moisture reaches the full root zone rather than wetting only the surface. For an establishing fig, UF/IFAS suggests around 10 gallons per soak two to three times a week in the first season; for a bearing plant, aim for the equivalent of about 1 to 1.5 inches per week through the growing season, more in heat.
watering.amount_beginner: Each time you water, give a deep soak that reaches the roots, not just a splash on top. A new fig wants about 10 gallons per soak, two or three times a week its first summer. An older, fruiting fig wants roughly 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week, and more when it is hot.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the root zone with drip or a soaker hose out toward the drip line, keeping the canopy dry to limit fig rust and fruit souring. Keep moisture especially steady as the fruit sizes and ripens, since a swing from dry to soaked (or heavy rain on ripening figs) causes fruit to split and sour.
watering.method_beginner: Water at the ground around the roots with a drip line or soaker hose, and try to keep the leaves and fruit dry, since wet leaves invite disease. Keep the watering steady while the figs are filling out and ripening, because going from dry to very wet, or a hard rain on ripe figs, makes them split and spoil.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Chronically wet, poorly drained soil shows as yellowing leaves, wilting that persists in wet soil, and general decline as waterlogged roots suffocate. Figs tolerate more moisture than stone fruit but still fail in standing water. Fruit that splits and sours after heavy watering or rain is the other overwatering signal near harvest.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Too much water, or soil that stays soggy, shows up as yellowing leaves, wilting even when the soil is wet, and a plant slowly going downhill, because the roots cannot breathe. Figs handle moisture better than a peach but still cannot sit in waterlogged soil. Figs that split and sour after a lot of water or rain are another sign near harvest.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Underwatering shows as wilting, dull and yellowing leaves, early leaf drop, and, most tellingly, fruit that drops while small or ripens undersized and less sweet. A fig short of water during the summer swell aborts part of its crop, so catch the dry stress before the fruit pays for it.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Too little water shows as wilting, dull yellow leaves, leaves dropping early, and, most clearly, small figs falling off or ripening tiny and less sweet. A fig that gets too dry in summer drops some of its fruit, so try to catch the dryness before the figs suffer.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Through the first season keep the root ball and surrounding soil consistently moist, never waterlogged. Deep soaks of roughly 10 gallons two to three times a week, adjusted for rain and heat, build the root system the plant relies on later.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: While the fig is getting established, keep the soil around the roots evenly moist but not soggy. A deep soak of about 10 gallons two or three times a week, more in heat and less after rain, helps it grow strong roots.

schedule_by_stage.rate: deep soak, ~1 to 1.5 in per week equivalent
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: As the main crop sizes, keep moisture steady, about 1 to 1.5 inches per week as deep soaks. This is the window where even watering translates directly into fuller, sweeter figs and where a dry-then-wet swing causes fruit to split and sour.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: While the figs are filling out, keep the water steady, about 1 to 1.5 inches a week as deep soaks. Even watering now means bigger, sweeter figs, and it keeps the fruit from splitting.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Once the fig is dormant and leafless, water need drops sharply; rely mostly on rainfall and water only in prolonged dry spells so roots do not desiccate. Avoid keeping dormant soil saturated.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: After the leaves drop and the fig is resting for winter, it needs very little water. Let rain do most of the work and only water during long dry stretches. Do not keep the soil soaked in winter.

watering.method_note_seasoned: Water deeply and infrequently at the root zone, ideally by drip or soaker, keeping the canopy dry to limit fig rust and souring. Young figs need consistent moisture through the first season to establish; mature figs are moderately drought-tolerant but drop and undersize fruit under stress, and split when a dry spell breaks in heavy water or rain.
watering.method_note_beginner: Give the fig a deep soak now and then rather than a little every day, and water at the ground instead of over the top, since wet leaves and fruit invite disease. Young figs need steady water the first season. Older figs handle dry spells, but they drop figs when too dry and split them when a dry spell ends in a big soak or rain.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The make-or-break window is the summer fruit swell, when steady moisture sets final size and sweetness and when moisture swings cause splitting and souring. Establishment (the first season) is the other critical period. Ease off through dormancy.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The most important time to keep water steady is summer while the figs are sizing up, when even watering makes them big and sweet and keeps them from splitting. The first season after planting matters too. In winter it needs almost none.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Fill the pot with a good-quality potting mix that drains well. A bark-based mix, or a general potting soil with some extra perlite stirred in, works nicely. Figs are not picky, but avoid a heavy soil dug from the yard, which packs down and drains poorly in a pot.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Keep it simple. Mix in a little compost for fertility and some perlite if the mix seems to hold too much water. Figs take richer mixes better than a peach does, but you still want the pot to drain freely rather than stay wet.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: Use a quality bark-based or peat-based potting mix amended for drainage, not native garden soil, which compacts under container irrigation. Figs tolerate a more moisture-retentive mix than stone fruit but still perform best with free drainage and an air-filled root zone.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend in modest compost for fertility and extra perlite or pumice if the base mix is water-retentive. Figs accept richer container media than most fruit trees, but keep drainage the priority; a top-dress of compost each spring covers most of the plant's needs.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: A fig in a pot dries out much faster than one in the ground. In summer heat, check it daily and water when the top inch or two is dry, until water runs out the bottom. Water more often than a ground fig, but do not leave the pot standing in a saucer of water. In winter, when the plant is resting, give it just enough to keep the root ball from drying out completely.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Frequent watering washes food out of a pot, so feed a little at a time: a diluted balanced liquid feed every few weeks from spring into midsummer, then stop by late summer so the plant does not push tender growth into fall. Do not feed at planting, and stop once it drops its leaves for winter.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Growing a fig in a pot is the easiest way to keep one where winters are too cold for it in the ground, because you can move it somewhere protected. Before hard freezes come, move the pot into an unheated but sheltered spot like an attached garage, shed, or basement that stays cold but does not deep-freeze. The fig is leafless and resting, so it does not need light in there. Water it just once in a while so the roots do not dry out, and bring it back outside when hard frosts are past in spring.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: A container is the standard way to carry a fig through winters colder than its in-ground range. Once the plant is dormant and leafless, move the pot to an unheated but protected space (attached garage, shed, or cool basement) that holds above roughly the mid teens but stays cold enough to keep it dormant. It needs no light while leafless; water sparingly to keep the root ball from drying out. Return it outdoors after hard frosts pass. A container fig still needs its short winter chill, so do not overwinter it in a heated room.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Figs are one of the best fruit trees for a pot, and a pot is the way to grow one if your winters are too cold for a fig in the ground. Use a large container that drains well, keep it watered more often than a ground plant, and move it to a protected spot for winter. A potted fig stays smaller and still gives you a good crop.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Fig is exceptionally well suited to container culture, and a pot is the practical route to fruit in regions colder than its in-ground range, since the plant can be moved to shelter for winter. Use at least a 15-gallon container (20 or more is better) with excellent drainage, water more frequently than an in-ground plant, and overwinter the dormant pot in a protected, unheated space. Expect a smaller plant and a lighter but dependable crop.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: A potted fig dries far faster than one in the ground and has no deep soil to draw on, so check moisture daily in summer heat and water when the top inch or two is dry, until it runs from the drainage holes. Water more often, but never leave the pot standing in a full saucer. Through dormancy the plant needs only enough water to keep the root ball from drying out.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Frequent watering flushes nutrients from a pot, so feed lightly and often: a dilute balanced liquid feed every few weeks through the spring-to-midsummer flush, then stop by late summer so no soft growth is pushed into fall. Do not feed at planting, and ease off entirely once the plant goes dormant.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering or sub-irrigated planter is not the best choice for fig. Figs fruit and firm up best on a wet-then-dry cycle and dislike a root zone held constantly moist by a reservoir, which can invite root problems and, near harvest, split fruit. Figs are more forgiving of moisture than stone fruit, so a self-watering pot is workable in a pinch, but a freely draining pot you water yourself gives better fruit.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot (one with a water tank in the bottom) is not the best choice for a fig. Figs do best when the soil dries out a bit between waterings, and a tank keeps the roots wet all the time, which can cause root trouble and split fruit. Figs handle moisture better than a peach, so it can work if that is what you have, but a regular pot that drains well and that you water yourself grows better figs.
container_notes.container_overwintering_seasoned: Cold protection for a potted fig is mostly about moving it: the exposed pot lets roots freeze several zones colder than in the ground, so shelter the dormant plant in an unheated garage or shed through the coldest months. If it must stay outside in a marginal zone, cluster pots against a wall, wrap them, and bank mulch around them. The goal is a cold, stable dormancy without the deep freezes that kill exposed roots and top growth.
container_notes.container_overwintering_beginner: Protecting a potted fig in winter mostly means moving it somewhere sheltered, because the roots in a pot get much colder than roots in the ground. Put the resting, leafless plant in an unheated garage or shed for the coldest months. If it has to stay outside, push the pots together against a wall, wrap them, and pile mulch around them to keep the roots from freezing.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Figs are highly perishable and do not ripen further once picked, so pick them fully ripe and eat them fast. At room temperature ripe figs hold only about a day, sometimes two, before they begin to spoil, so plan to eat, cook, or refrigerate them the day you pick.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Figs are very perishable and do not ripen after you pick them, so pick them ripe and eat them quickly. On the counter ripe figs last only about a day or two before they go bad, so eat, cook, or refrigerate them the same day you pick.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerate ripe figs unwashed in a single layer and use them within about 2 to 3 days. Cold slows the spoilage but figs are fragile; keep them shallow so they do not crush, and bring them to room temperature before eating for the best flavor.
storage.fridge_beginner: Put ripe figs in the fridge unwashed, in a single layer so they do not crush, and eat them within about 2 to 3 days. Let them warm up to room temperature before eating for the best taste.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Figs freeze well whole or halved. Rinse, dry, and freeze them in a single layer on a tray, then transfer to freezer bags; they keep several months and are best for cooking, baking, and preserves. Figs also dry excellently, the classic way to keep a big crop.
storage.freezer_beginner: Figs freeze nicely whole or cut in half. Rinse and dry them, freeze them on a tray, then pack them into freezer bags. They keep for several months and are great for cooking and jam. Figs also dry very well, which is the traditional way to save a big crop.
storage.notes_seasoned: The key with figs is that they do not ripen off the plant and spoil within a day or two, so ripeness at picking and speed to the table (or fridge, freezer, or drying rack) is everything.
storage.notes_beginner: The main thing to remember is that figs do not ripen after picking and spoil in a day or two, so pick them ripe and use them fast, or refrigerate, freeze, or dry them right away.

recommended.name: Celeste
recommended.recommended_note: Small, sweet, closed-eye fig; cold-hardy and among the most reliable, and its tight eye resists souring in humid areas.

recommended.name: Brown Turkey
recommended.recommended_note: Widely adaptable and forgiving brownish-purple fig; a common, dependable first choice. (Texas Everbearing is a similar strain.)

recommended.name: Chicago Hardy
recommended.recommended_note: One of the most cold-hardy figs; roots survive hard winters and it fruits on new wood after dieback, the pick for zones 6 and the cold edge.

recommended.name: Black Mission
recommended.recommended_note: Rich, dark purple-black classic for mild-winter regions; heavy bearer in California and the warm West.

recommended.name: Kadota
recommended.recommended_note: Light green to amber, closed-eye fig that holds up well; a good canning and drying variety for warm, dry regions.

recommended.name: LSU Purple
recommended.recommended_note: Vigorous, disease-tolerant purple fig bred for the humid South; productive and rust-tolerant.

varieties.note_seasoned: Because all common figs need only about 100 chill hours, choose a variety not by chill (as you would a peach) but by cold-hardiness, disease tolerance, and eye type for your climate. In cold-winter areas favor the hardiest types (Chicago Hardy, Celeste, Marseilles). In humid areas favor a small, closed-eye variety (Celeste) or a rust-tolerant one (LSU Purple) to limit souring and rust. In mild, dry regions almost anything thrives, so pick by flavor and use. All the recommended types are common (parthenocarpic) figs that fruit alone with no pollination.
varieties.note_beginner: All common figs need about the same small amount of winter cold, so you do not pick a fig by chill hours the way you would a peach. Instead, choose by how cold-hardy it is and how well it handles your weather. In cold areas, pick a hardy type like Chicago Hardy or Celeste. In humid areas, pick a small, tight-eye type like Celeste or a rust-tolerant one like LSU Purple to avoid souring and rust. Where it is mild and dry, almost any fig does well, so pick by taste. All of these are common figs that fruit on their own with no pollination.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Hardening off does not apply to fig. It is planted as a dormant, own-rooted bare-root or container plant, not raised from a seedling indoors, so there is no tender transplant to acclimate.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: Hardening off (slowly getting an indoor-grown seedling used to the outdoors) does not apply to fig. You plant it as a dormant bare-root or potted plant, so there is no tender young seedling to ease outside.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Plant a dormant, own-rooted bare-root or container fig in late winter to early spring, once the hardest cold has passed, or in fall to early winter in mild regions.
