Because figs are grown on their own roots there is no graft union to keep above grade; you can even set the plant an inch or two deeper than it grew to encourage a well-anchored, multi-stem bush, the form that best recovers from winter dieback. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots, backfill with native soil, water in well, and mulch, keeping mulch off the stems. Do not fertilize in the hole.
start_method.notes_beginner: Plant a dormant bare-root or potted fig in late winter or early spring after the worst cold, or in fall to early winter where winters are mild. Figs grow on their own roots, so unlike a peach there is no graft joint to keep above the soil; you can even plant it a little deeper to help it grow into a sturdy, multi-stem bush, which bounces back best if winter kills the top. Dig a hole wide enough for the roots, fill it back with the same soil, water it in well, and spread mulch, keeping it off the stems. Do not put fertilizer in the hole.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Annual crop rotation does not apply to a fig, which holds its site for decades. The real site concern is root-knot nematode. Because own-rooted figs have no resistant rootstock, do not plant a fig into sandy ground known to be heavily infested with root-knot nematodes, or where a nematode-declined fig was just removed, without replacing a generous volume of soil.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: You do not rotate a fig the way you rotate vegetables, since it stays put for many years. What matters is root-knot nematode, a tiny soil pest that is the main killer of figs. Do not plant a fig in sandy soil that is known to be full of these pests, or right where a sick fig just came out, unless you dig out and replace a big area of soil first.
rotation.good_after: a well-drained site free of root-knot nematodes, with no recent history of nematode-declined figs
rotation.note_seasoned: If a fig must go where nematodes are a concern, choose a site with the least sandy, best-drained soil available, replace a generous volume of soil, keep the plant vigorous and mulched, and accept that own-rooted figs cannot be rootstock-protected the way stone fruit can.
rotation.note_beginner: If you have to plant where nematodes might be a problem, pick the best-drained, least sandy spot, dig out and replace a big area of soil, and keep the fig healthy and mulched. Remember there is no special root you can buy to protect a fig from these pests.

growth_stages.name: Planting (dormant, own-root)
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Late winter to early spring after the hardest cold, or fall to early winter in mild regions.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Late winter or early spring after the worst cold, or fall to early winter where winters are mild.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A dormant, leafless own-rooted plant (bare-root, or a container plant) with firm stems and healthy roots. Figs are not grafted, so there is no graft union to position.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A leafless dormant plant with firm stems and good roots. Figs are not grafted, so there is no graft joint to worry about.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, spreading the roots in a wide hole. You can set the plant an inch or two deeper than it grew to encourage a sturdy multi-stem bush. Backfill with native soil, water in well, and mulch, keeping mulch off the stems. In cold regions, plant against a warm south-facing wall.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil. You can set it a little deeper than it grew to help it form a bushy plant. Fill the hole with the same soil, water it well, and mulch, keeping mulch off the stems. In cold areas, plant it against a warm south wall.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record the planting date and the variety.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note the day you planted and which fig variety it is.

growth_stages.name: Year-one establishment
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: The first full growing season after planting.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: The first whole growing season after you plant.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Steady new shoot growth and a strengthening root system. A few figs may form the first or second year; that is fine.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Healthy new shoots and a plant settling in. A few figs may come the first or second year, which is fine.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply and regularly through the first season so roots establish, keep a mulched, weed-free ring around the plant, and protect it well its first winter, since a young fig is the most cold-tender it will ever be.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Water deeply and often this first season, keep a mulched, weed-free ring around it, and protect it well its first winter, since a young fig is more cold-tender than an older one.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Log first-season watering and how you protected the plant its first winter.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note your watering and how you protected the young plant its first winter.

growth_stages.name: Formative pruning (years one to three)
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: The first two to three years, while you set the plant's form.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: The first two or three years, while you shape the plant.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Figs are usually trained as an open multi-stem bush (best in cold climates, since it regrows fast after dieback) or as a single-trunk small tree in mild climates. Watch for the framework you want to keep.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Figs are usually grown as an open bush with several stems (best where winters are cold, since it grows back fast after dieback) or as a small single-trunk tree where it is mild. Pick the shape you want.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: For a bush, keep several well-spaced low stems and remove weak, crowded, or crossing growth; for a tree, select one trunk. Figs bear on both old and new wood, so prune lightly to shape rather than heading hard, which would cost the breba crop.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: For a bush, keep several evenly spaced low stems and cut out weak or crowded ones; for a tree, keep one trunk. Figs fruit on both old and new wood, so prune lightly to shape it, not hard, or you lose the early crop.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record your formative pruning and whether you are training a bush or a tree.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note your shaping cuts and whether you are growing a bush or a tree.

growth_stages.name: Winter dormancy
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Roughly December through February, the leafless months.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: About December through February, the bare winter months.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A leafless plant at rest. Figs need only about 100 chill hours, so chill is easily met almost anywhere; the real winter issue is cold injury, not chill.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A bare, resting plant. Figs need very little winter cold (about 100 hours), so that is never the problem; the real worry in winter is cold damage.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: In zones 6 and colder, protect the plant now: wrap the stems, or cut back and bury under mulch and leaves, or move a container to an unheated garage or shed. In zones 7 and warmer, little is needed beyond winter cleanup.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: In zone 6 and colder, protect the plant now: wrap the stems, or cut it back and cover it with mulch and leaves, or move a potted fig into an unheated garage or shed. In zone 7 and warmer, just clean up.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Note the dormant-season protection you applied and any winter lows.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note how you protected the plant and how cold it got.

growth_stages.name: Dormant pruning
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Late winter, after the coldest weather but before growth begins.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Late winter, after the coldest weather but before the plant wakes up.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare stems that show the plant's structure. Any wood killed by winter is now visible and easy to remove.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Bare stems, so you can see the shape and any wood the winter killed.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Prune lightly after the hardest cold has passed: remove dead, frost-killed, weak, and crowded wood, and keep the plant open. Do not head it hard, since figs bear on last year's wood (the breba crop) as well as new wood; heavy pruning trades away the early crop.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Prune lightly after the worst cold: take out dead, frost-killed, weak, and crowded stems, and keep it open. Do not cut it back hard, because figs fruit on last year's wood too, so heavy pruning costs you the early crop.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record the pruning date and how much winter dieback you removed.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you pruned and how much winter-killed wood you took off.

growth_stages.name: Leaf-out and breba set
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Early to mid spring as growth resumes.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Early to mid spring as the plant leafs out.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves unfolding and, on last year's wood, the small breba figs beginning to swell. A fig shows no visible flowers, since its flowers are hidden inside the fruit.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Leaves opening and small early figs (the breba crop) swelling on last year's stems. You will not see any flowers, because a fig's flowers are inside the fruit.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Little to do but watch for a late frost that can nip tender new growth, and remove winter wraps once hard frost is past. Because figs are parthenocarpic, the breba fruit sets on its own with no pollination.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Not much to do but watch for a late frost that can burn the new growth, and take off any winter wraps once hard frosts are done. The early figs set all on their own, with no pollination needed.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Note leaf-out and whether a breba (early) crop set.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when it leafed out and whether early figs formed.

growth_stages.name: Main crop development
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Late spring through summer as new shoots extend.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Late spring through summer as the new shoots grow.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The main crop forming and swelling in the leaf joints of the new growth. Figs need no thinning; the plant carries what it can size. Watch for drought stress, which drops fruit.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The main crop forming and swelling where the leaves meet the new stems. Figs do not need thinning. Watch for dryness, which makes them drop fruit.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep water steady through the swell so fruit does not drop, undersize, or split, and keep feeding light. Watch for fig rust in humid weather and keep the canopy open and dry.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the water steady while the figs fill out so they do not drop or split, and go easy on fertilizer. Watch for rust spots on the leaves in humid weather and keep the plant open.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record watering through the swell and any fruit drop or splitting.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note your watering and any figs dropping or splitting.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Early summer for the breba crop and mid to late summer through fall for the main crop.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Early summer for the first figs and mid to late summer through fall for the main crop.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Ripe figs soften, the neck bends so the fruit droops, color develops fully, and a drop of nectar may show at the eye. Figs ripen a few at a time over many weeks and must ripen on the plant, since they do not ripen after picking.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Ripe figs get soft, droop down as the neck bends, color up fully, and may show a drop of syrup at the bottom. They ripen a few at a time over weeks and must ripen on the plant, since they do not ripen after you pick them.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick figs fully ripe, gently, every day or two as they soften, and eat, refrigerate, freeze, or dry them promptly since they spoil fast. Remove any soured or dropped fruit, and net against birds.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pick figs when fully ripe and soft, gently, every day or two, and eat, refrigerate, freeze, or dry them right away since they spoil fast. Clean up any soured or fallen figs, and net the plant against birds.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record harvest dates and a rough yield.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you picked and roughly how much you got.

notifications.body_seasoned: Plant a dormant own-rooted fig now, after the hardest cold, in full sun on well-drained ground. There is no graft union to fuss over; you can set it slightly deep to build a sturdy multi-stem bush, and in cold areas place it against a warm south-facing wall. Water in well and mulch, keeping mulch off the stems.
notifications.body_beginner: Now is the time to plant a dormant fig, after the worst cold, in a sunny, well-drained spot. Figs grow on their own roots, so there is no graft joint to worry about, and you can plant it a little deep to make a bushy plant. In cold areas plant it against a warm south wall. Water it in and mulch, keeping mulch off the stems.

notifications.body_seasoned: Prune now, in late winter after the hardest cold but before growth begins. Keep it light: remove dead, frost-killed, weak, and crowded wood and open the plant up, but do not head it hard, since figs bear on last year's wood as well as new wood.
notifications.body_beginner: Prune now, in late winter after the worst cold but before the plant wakes up. Keep it light: cut out dead, frost-killed, weak, and crowded stems and open it up, but do not cut it back hard, since figs fruit on last year's wood too.

notifications.body_seasoned: Once hard frosts are past, remove winter wraps, mulch mounds, or bring a container fig back outside. Watch the forecast a while longer, since a late frost can still nip the tender new growth and the swelling breba figs.
notifications.body_beginner: Once hard frosts are done, take off the winter wraps or mulch, or move a potted fig back outside. Keep an eye on the forecast a little longer, since a late frost can still burn the new growth and the early figs.

notifications.body_seasoned: A newly planted fig needs steady moisture through its first season while roots establish. Water deeply at the root zone, roughly 10 gallons two to three times a week in the heat, and keep a mulched, weed-free ring around the plant.
notifications.body_beginner: A new fig needs steady water its first season while its roots grow in. Give it a deep soak at the ground, about 10 gallons two or three times a week in the heat, and keep a mulched, weed-free ring around it.

notifications.body_seasoned: The main crop is ripening now. Pick figs only when fully ripe (soft, drooping on a bent neck, fully colored), since they do not ripen after picking and spoil within a day or two. Pick every day or two, net against birds, and clear any soured or dropped fruit.
notifications.body_beginner: The main crop is ripening. Pick figs only when fully ripe, soft, drooping, and fully colored, since they do not ripen after picking and spoil in a day or two. Pick every day or two, cover the plant against birds, and clean up any soured or fallen figs.

notifications.body_seasoned: Before hard freezes arrive, protect the plant where winters run below the mid teens: wrap the stems, or cut back and bury under mulch and leaves, or move a container to an unheated garage or shed. Dormant fig wood is hardy only to about 15°F to 20°F.
notifications.body_beginner: Before hard freezes come, protect the fig where winters drop below the mid teens: wrap the stems, cut it back and cover it with mulch and leaves, or move a potted fig into an unheated garage or shed. Fig stems are hardy only to about 15°F to 20°F.

notifications.title_seasoned: Anything to log on the fig?
notifications.body_seasoned: It has been a while since your last note. A quick check pays off: note how the plant came through winter and whether it needed to regrow, jot down when it leafed out and started ripening, and watch for early fig rust in humid weather.
notifications.body_beginner: It has been a while since you logged anything. A quick look is worth it: note how the plant came through winter and whether it had to regrow, write down when it leafed out and started ripening, and watch for rust spots on the leaves in humid weather.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Freeze coming, protect your fig
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Cold is the fig's main hazard. Dormant wood is hardy only to about 15°F to 20°F, so if a hard freeze is forecast and the plant is not already protected, wrap the stems, mound mulch, or move a container to shelter. In spring, a late frost on tender new growth nips the leaves and the breba figs, so cover a small plant overnight.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Cold is a fig's biggest danger. The stems are hardy only to about 15°F to 20°F, so if a hard freeze is coming and the plant is not protected, wrap the stems, pile on mulch, or move a potted fig to shelter. In spring, a late frost can burn the new leaves and early figs, so cover a small plant overnight.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Heavy rain, watch ripe figs
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A hard rain on ripening figs, especially after a dry spell, makes them swell fast and split, and the open cracks let in souring. After a soaking rain, check ripening fruit and pick anything ready rather than leaving it to crack and sour.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: A hard rain on ripening figs, especially after a dry stretch, makes them swell fast and split, and the cracks let in rot. After a heavy rain, check the ripe figs and pick any that are ready instead of leaving them to split and spoil.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Humid spell, fig-rust and souring weather
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Muggy weather, watch for rust and souring
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Warm, humid weather drives fig rust on the leaves and beetle-spread souring in the fruit. Keep the canopy open and dry, water only at the root zone, pick ripe figs promptly, and remove any soured fruit so it does not seed more.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Warm, muggy weather brings on rust spots on the leaves and souring in the fruit. Keep the plant open and the leaves dry, water only at the ground, pick ripe figs promptly, and throw away any soured ones so they do not spread.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Dry stretch, keep up deep watering
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Dry spell, do not let the fig run dry
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Drought stress is the main cause of a fig dropping its crop and ripening small, less-sweet fruit. During a dry stretch, water deeply at the root zone, a young plant establishing and a bearing plant during the summer swell most of all, and keep the surface mulched to hold moisture.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: A fig that gets too dry drops its figs and ripens small, less-sweet ones. In a dry spell, give it a deep soak at the ground, especially a young plant and a fruiting plant while the figs are sizing, and keep it mulched to hold moisture.

planting.text_seasoned: Figs are grown on their own roots, so there is no graft union to keep above grade; you can even plant an inch or two deeper to encourage a sturdy, multi-stem bush.
planting.text_beginner: Figs grow on their own roots, so there is no graft joint to worry about. You can plant a fig a little deeper than it grew to help it form a bushy, well-anchored plant.
planting.author: claude_code_gs_arc

planting.text_seasoned: Plant in full sun on well-drained ground, and at the cold edge of the range against a warm, south-facing wall, which banks heat and buys the plant several degrees of winter protection.
planting.text_beginner: Plant where it gets full sun and the soil drains well. In cold areas, plant it against a warm south-facing wall, which holds heat and helps protect it in winter.
planting.author: claude_code_gs_arc

establishment.text_seasoned: A young fig is the most cold-tender it will ever be; protect it well its first winter even in a zone where an established plant would shrug off the cold.
establishment.text_beginner: A young fig is more easily hurt by cold than an older one, so protect it well its first winter, even where a bigger plant would be fine.
establishment.author: claude_code_gs_arc

formative_pruning.text_seasoned: In cold climates train the plant as an open multi-stem bush rather than a single trunk: if a hard winter kills the top, a bush regrows from several low stems and ripens a main crop far faster than a single-trunk tree.
formative_pruning.text_beginner: Where winters are cold, grow the fig as a bush with several low stems, not one trunk. If a hard winter kills the top, a bush grows back fast from the low stems and fruits again much sooner.
formative_pruning.author: claude_code_gs_arc

dormancy.text_seasoned: Figs need only about 100 chill hours, met almost anywhere, so chill is never the limiter; the winter job is cold protection, since dormant wood is hardy only to about 15°F to 20°F.
dormancy.text_beginner: Figs need very little winter cold (about 100 hours), so that is never a problem. The winter job is protecting the plant from hard freezes, since the stems are hardy only to about 15°F to 20°F.
dormancy.author: claude_code_gs_arc

dormancy.text_seasoned: In zone 6, the reliable cold-climate options are to wrap the stems, or cut back and bury the plant under mulch and leaves, or grow it in a container moved to an unheated garage.
dormancy.text_beginner: In zone 6, the ways to get a fig through winter are to wrap the stems, cut it back and cover it with mulch and leaves, or grow it in a pot you move into an unheated garage.
dormancy.author: claude_code_gs_arc

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Prune figs lightly and only after the hardest cold has passed: they bear on last year's wood (the breba crop) as well as new wood, so heavy heading trades away the early crop.
dormant_prune.text_beginner: Prune figs lightly, and wait until the worst cold is over. They fruit on last year's wood too, so cutting hard costs you the early crop.
dormant_prune.author: claude_code_gs_arc

leaf_out.text_seasoned: A fig never shows a visible bloom, since its flowers are inside the fruit; because common figs are parthenocarpic, the breba figs set and ripen with no pollination at all.
leaf_out.text_beginner: A fig never shows flowers, because they are hidden inside the fruit. Common figs make their early crop all on their own, with no pollination needed.
leaf_out.author: claude_code_gs_arc

fruit_development.text_seasoned: Figs need no thinning, but they do need steady water through the summer swell: a dry spell drops fruit, and a swing from dry to soaked (or hard rain on ripening figs) splits and sours it.
fruit_development.text_beginner: Figs do not need thinning, but they do need steady water in summer. If they get too dry they drop figs, and if a dry spell ends in a big soak or rain, the figs split and spoil.
fruit_development.author: claude_code_gs_arc

harvest.text_seasoned: Pick figs only when fully ripe, when they soften and droop on a bent neck, since figs do not ripen after picking; they spoil within a day or two, so eat, chill, freeze, or dry them promptly.
harvest.text_beginner: Pick figs only when fully ripe, soft, and drooping, because they do not ripen after you pick them. They spoil in a day or two, so eat, chill, freeze, or dry them right away.
harvest.author: claude_code_gs_arc

harvest.text_seasoned: Net the plant against birds as fruit begins to color, and remove soured or dropped fruit as you go so beetles and souring yeasts do not build.
harvest.text_beginner: Cover the plant with bird netting as the figs start to color, and clean up any soured or fallen figs so beetles and rot do not build up.
harvest.author: claude_code_gs_arc

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A mature fig (roughly year 4 and up) commonly yields on the order of 20 to 50+ pounds of fruit a year in a good climate, spread over many weeks of picking rather than one flush; a large old plant in a warm region can bear far more. Yield swings widely with winter dieback, water, and variety, and a top-killed plant that regrows carries a lighter, later crop that year.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: A grown fig (about year 4 and up) often gives roughly 20 to 50 pounds of fruit a year in a good climate, picked a few at a time over many weeks rather than all at once, and a big old plant can give much more. How much you get swings with winter cold, water, and variety, and a plant that had to regrow after a hard winter gives a lighter, later crop that year.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Figs reach full bearing quickly for a fruit tree, around years 3 to 5, and stay productive for decades where winters allow, given steady water and light annual pruning. In cold-edge zones, peak yield is capped by how much dieback the plant suffers each winter.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Figs reach full production fast for a fruit tree, around years 3 to 5, and keep bearing for decades where winters allow, as long as you water them and prune lightly each year. In cold areas, the size of the crop depends on how much the winter kills back each year.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Expect little to no fruit the planting year, though a few figs may form in year 1 or 2. The first meaningful crop typically comes by year 2 or 3, with full bearing by years 3 to 5. Focus the early years on establishment and winter protection, not fruit.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Do not expect much fruit the first year, though a few figs may form in year 1 or 2. Your first real crop usually comes by year 2 or 3, with full crops by years 3 to 5. In the early years, focus on getting the plant established and protected in winter, not on fruit.
factors_seasoned: variety and cold-hardiness
winter dieback and protection
summer water during fruit swell
moderate feeding (excess nitrogen cuts fruit)
full sun and heat
root-knot nematode pressure
bird and beetle losses at harvest

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No moon-phase planting preference is asserted. Extension sources do not support timing fig planting or care by lunar phase; site warmth, winter protection, and steady water govern outcomes.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Stems died back or the plant was killed over winter
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The fig died back or died over the winter
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The top growth was killed by winter cold. This is the single most common fig problem outside the warmest zones: dormant fig wood is hardy only to about 15°F to 20°F, and sustained lows below that injure or kill the stems. The good news is that the roots are hardier and usually resprout, so a top-killed fig is rarely dead, just set back a year. The fixes are all about cold: protect the plant over winter, choose a cold-hardy variety, train it as a bush so it regrows fast, or grow it in a container you can shelter.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The winter cold killed the top of the plant. This is the most common fig problem outside the warmest areas, because fig stems are hardy only to about 15°F to 20°F. The good news is the roots are tougher and usually grow back, so a top-killed fig is rarely truly dead, just a year behind. The fixes are about cold: protect the plant in winter, pick a cold-hardy variety, grow it as a bush so it regrows fast, or grow it in a pot you can move to shelter.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Protect the plant next winter (wrap, or cut back and bury under mulch and leaves, or shelter a container), plant a cold-hardy variety like Chicago Hardy or Celeste, and train it as a multi-stem bush for fast recovery.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Protect the plant next winter (wrap it, cover it with mulch and leaves, or shelter a pot), grow a cold-hardy variety like Chicago Hardy or Celeste, and train it as a bush so it grows back fast.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Figs drop while small, or ripe figs split and sour
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Figs fall off small, or ripe ones split and go sour
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Small figs dropping usually means water stress: a fig short of water in summer aborts part of its crop. Ripe figs splitting and souring usually means a moisture swing (a dry spell broken by heavy watering or rain) that makes the fruit swell and crack, letting in the beetles and yeasts that sour it. It is easy to blame the variety, but the real levers are steady water and prompt picking. Over-fertilizing also worsens splitting.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Small figs falling off is usually a sign the plant got too dry in summer, so it drops some of its crop. Ripe figs splitting and souring is usually from a swing in water, a dry spell ended by a big soak or rain, which makes them swell and crack, letting in the pests and rot that sour them. It is easy to blame the variety, but the real fixes are steady water and picking often. Too much fertilizer makes splitting worse too.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Keep water steady through the summer swell and mulch to buffer moisture, pick ripe figs promptly, do not over-fertilize, and in humid areas grow a small, closed-eye variety like Celeste that resists souring.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep the water steady while the figs size up and mulch to hold moisture, pick ripe figs promptly, go easy on fertilizer, and in humid areas grow a tight-eye variety like Celeste that resists souring.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Lots of leaves but few or no figs
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Lots of leaves but hardly any figs
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: A vigorous, leafy fig with little fruit usually has one of three causes: too much nitrogen (rich soil or heavy feeding pushes leaves over fruit), a plant still too young (figs often need a year or two, sometimes three, to settle into cropping), or too much shade. A less common cause is the wrong type of fig entirely: a Smyrna or San Pedro variety cannot fruit without its fig wasp and simply drops everything. Common (parthenocarpic) types fruit on their own in full sun.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: A leafy fig with few figs usually comes from one of three things: too much fertilizer or rich soil (which makes leaves instead of figs), a plant that is still too young (figs often take a year or two to start cropping well), or too much shade. Less often, it is the wrong kind of fig: a Smyrna or San Pedro type needs a special wasp to fruit and just drops everything. Common types fruit on their own in full sun.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Cut back on nitrogen, make sure the plant gets full sun, give a young plant another season, and confirm you are growing a common (parthenocarpic) variety rather than a Smyrna or San Pedro type.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Use less fertilizer, make sure it gets full sun, give a young plant another year, and check that you have a common fig variety, not a Smyrna or San Pedro type that needs a special wasp.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Leaves get rusty spots and drop early in late summer
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Leaves get rusty spots and fall early in late summer
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Yellow-orange spots that turn rusty brown, mostly on the leaf undersides, followed by early yellowing and leaf drop in mid to late summer, are fig rust, a fungus that thrives in warm, humid, wet weather. It overwinters on fallen leaves. The current crop usually still ripens, but repeated early defoliation weakens the plant over years, so the goal is to break the cycle rather than cure this year's leaves.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Yellow-orange spots that turn rusty brown, mostly under the leaves, then early yellowing and leaf drop in late summer, are fig rust, a fungus that likes warm, wet, humid weather. It survives winter on fallen leaves. That year's figs usually still ripen, but losing leaves early year after year wears the plant down, so the aim is to stop the cycle rather than fix this year's leaves.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Rake up and destroy fallen leaves each year to remove the overwintering source, prune for airflow, water at the ground, and where rust is severe apply a copper or Bordeaux fungicide on the new foliage through the season.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Rake up and throw away fallen leaves each year, prune so air moves through the plant, water the ground not the leaves, and where rust is bad use an organic copper spray on the new leaves through the season.

succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Succession planting does not apply to fig. It is a permanent plant that occupies its site for decades and bears over a long ripening season each year, so there is no staggered re-sowing to schedule the way there is for a short-season annual crop.

open_findings.summary: the SECONDARY fig-mosaic-virus claim is textbook-correct (fig mite Aceria fici vectors it, systemic, no cure) but neither cited page (UF/IFAS MG214, UC ANR) names the disease; UC ANR names only the vector mite. Re-anchor at the citation sweep or accept as modeled. Signature disease (fig rust, Cerotelium fici) is fully BACKED on MG214.
chill_hours_range upper (300) is a modeled conservative ceiling; UF/IFAS MG214 backs the ~100h requirement verbatim (low end). Fig is low-chill; chill is rarely the limiter.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: Wave-2 pome/other-tree cert (2026-07-02): parallel per-crop source-truth review (CC agents, WebFetch of cited T1 pages). fig parthenocarpy + Smyrna/San Pedro split verbatim on UF/IFAS MG214; persimmon Asian-self/parthenocarpic vs American-dioecious split BACKED both halves on Clemson/UGA/NCSU; pomegranate self-fruitful verbatim on UGA. Pollination pinned to its cited page under A38; modeled/secondary-citation items recorded as open_findings.

3.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 3 winters (lows to -40°F) kill a fig outright, top and root. Not an in-ground fig zone; grow a container fig overwintered indoors.
3.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 3 is far too cold for a fig in the ground. If you want to try one, grow it in a pot and bring it inside for winter.

4.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 4 winters kill an in-ground fig, roots included in a hard year. Not an in-ground fig zone; grow a container fig moved to an unheated garage or basement for winter.
4.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 4 is too cold for a fig in the ground. Grow it in a pot and move it into an unheated garage or basement for winter instead.

5.suitability_note_seasoned: Very marginal in the ground. Even the hardiest varieties (Chicago Hardy, Celeste) have their tops killed most winters and must regrow, so a light main crop ripens on new wood only in a warm year and only with heavy winter protection. A container fig wintered indoors is far more dependable here.
5.suitability_note_beginner: This is a tough zone for a fig in the ground. Even the hardiest kinds usually get killed to the ground each winter and have to grow back, so you only get a small late crop in a warm year, and only with heavy winter protection. Growing it in a pot you bring inside is much more reliable.
5.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Late spring frosts nip the new growth and any early figs, and winters below the mid teens kill the top back, so treat a main crop as the reward of a warm year on a well-protected, cold-hardy plant.

6.suitability_note_seasoned: The classic protected-fig zone. With heavy winter protection (wrapping, or cutting back and burying under mulch and leaves) and a cold-hardy variety, the plant comes through or regrows and ripens a main crop on new wood most years. Bush training and a warm south wall help. Chicago Hardy and Celeste are the safe picks.
6.suitability_note_beginner: This is the zone where figs fruit with protection. Wrap the plant or cut it back and bury it under mulch and leaves for winter, grow a hardy variety like Chicago Hardy or Celeste, and you can get a main crop most years. Growing it as a bush against a warm south wall helps.
6.frost_risk_note_seasoned: A hard winter kills the top back and a late spring frost can nip new growth; with heavy protection and a cold-hardy variety the plant regrows and ripens a main crop most years.

7.suitability_note_seasoned: The cool edge of reliable in-ground figs. Hardy varieties crop dependably here, occasionally losing some top growth in a severe winter but regrowing quickly. A warm, sheltered site and light protection in cold snaps keep both the breba and main crops coming.
7.suitability_note_beginner: The cool edge where figs grow reliably in the ground. Hardy varieties fruit dependably, now and then losing some top growth in a hard winter but growing back fast. A warm, sheltered spot and a little protection in cold snaps keep the figs coming.
7.frost_risk_note_seasoned: An occasional hard freeze can kill some top growth in a severe winter, and a late frost can nip early growth; light protection in cold snaps and a hardy variety keep cropping reliable.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the north, how well a fig does comes down to winter cold. Figs grow in the ground reliably from about zone 7. Zone 6 fruits only with heavy winter protection and a hardy variety, and zones 3 to 5 are really pot-only, bringing the plant into an unheated garage or shed for winter. Even if the top dies, a fig usually grows back from the roots.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Across the northern tier, fig success is set entirely by winter cold, not chill. Reliable in-ground cropping starts around zone 7. Zone 6 fruits only with heavy winter protection and a cold-hardy variety, and zones 3 to 5 are container territory, where the plant winters in an unheated garage or shed. Even where the top dies back, a fig usually resprouts from the roots.
northern_tier.chill_basis_seasoned: Northern-tier winters bank far more than a fig's ~100-hour chill need, so chill is never the limiter here. The limit is cold injury: dormant fig wood is hardy only to about 15°F to 20°F, so deep winter lows kill the top back and set the whole in-ground map.
northern_tier.chill_basis_beginner: Winters here are far colder than a fig needs, so chill is never the issue. The issue is freeze damage: fig stems are hardy only to about 15°F to 20°F, so deep winter cold kills the top and decides where a fig can grow in the ground.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Reliable fig country. Winters are mild enough to grow figs in tree form, and the long season ripens both a breba and a full main crop. Choose small-eye, rust-tolerant varieties (Celeste, LSU Purple) and a well-drained, nematode-free site.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Great for figs. Winters are mild enough to grow them as a tree, and the long season ripens an early and a main crop. Pick a tight-eye, rust-tolerant variety like Celeste or LSU Purple and a well-drained spot free of nematodes.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Excellent, nearly frost-free fig country with a long ripening season. Figs crop heavily; the main management is humid-weather rust and souring and, in sandy soil, root-knot nematodes. Favor closed-eye, rust-tolerant varieties.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Excellent, almost frost-free fig country with a long season. Figs bear heavily here; the main jobs are managing rust and souring in humid weather and nematodes in sandy soil. Grow a tight-eye, rust-tolerant variety.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: The Southeast is great fig country: mild winters, long hot summers, and figs' small need for winter cold make them one of the easiest backyard fruits here. The two things to watch are humid-weather problems (rust on the leaves and souring in the fruit) and root-knot nematodes in sandy soil, so pick a tight-eye, rust-tolerant variety and a pest-free spot.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: The Southeast is fig country: warm winters, long hot summers, and a fig's tiny chill need make figs one of the most dependable backyard fruits here. The two watch-outs are humid-weather diseases (fig rust, and beetle-spread souring) and root-knot nematodes in sandy soil, so favor small-eye and rust-tolerant varieties and a nematode-free site.
se_gulf.chill_basis_seasoned: Gulf-South winters easily meet a fig's ~100-hour chill need, so chill is never the limiter. Warmth and humidity, not cold, define fig growing here.
se_gulf.chill_basis_beginner: Winters here easily give figs the little cold they need, so chill is never a problem. Heat and humidity, not cold, shape fig growing here.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Prime fig country. Long, hot, dry summers ripen full, sweet crops with low disease pressure, and mild winters let figs grow as sizable trees. Both crops ripen; keep water steady through the summer swell.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Prime fig country. Long, hot, dry summers ripen big, sweet crops with little disease, and mild winters let figs grow into good-sized trees. Both crops ripen here; just keep the water steady while the figs size up.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Excellent fig climate with a long, hot season and mild, nearly frost-free winters. Heavy, high-quality crops with low disease; the main input is steady summer water. Almost any common variety thrives.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Excellent for figs, with a long hot season and mild, almost frost-free winters. Big, high-quality crops with little disease; the main thing is steady summer water. Almost any common variety does well.

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: California's hot, dry inland valleys are about the best fig climate anywhere: lots of heat for sweet fruit, dry air that keeps disease down, and mild winters that let figs grow as full trees. You get both the early and the main crop. Just keep the summer water steady and watch for nematodes in sandy soil.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: California's hot, dry interior valleys are arguably the best fig climate in the country: abundant heat ripens rich, sweet fruit, dry air keeps rust and souring low, and mild winters let figs grow as full trees. Both breba and main crops ripen well. Watch summer water and, in sandy ground, root-knot nematodes.
ca_interior.chill_basis_seasoned: Interior-valley winters easily meet a fig's small ~100-hour chill need, so chill never limits fruiting; abundant summer heat is the asset here.
ca_interior.chill_basis_beginner: Inland winters easily give figs the little cold they need, so chill is never a problem; the big summer heat is what makes figs so good here.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Figs fruit reliably but cool, foggy summers push the main crop later into fall and keep it a bit less sweet than inland. The early breba crop is valued here. Choose a cool-coast variety and the sunniest, most sheltered spot.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Figs fruit reliably here, but the cool, foggy summers ripen the main crop later in fall and a bit less sweet than inland, so the early crop matters more. Pick a coast-friendly variety and the sunniest, most sheltered spot you have.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: The milder, slightly warmer edge of the north coast still fruits figs reliably, with a late main crop shaped by coastal cool. A warm, sun-trapped site improves ripening and sweetness. Cool-coast varieties perform best.
10.suitability_note_beginner: The milder, slightly warmer part of the north coast still fruits figs reliably, with a late main crop shaped by the cool coast. A warm, sunny, sheltered spot ripens them better. Coast-friendly varieties do best.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: Figs grow well on the cooler Northern California coast, but the cool, foggy summers ripen the main crop later and a little less sweet than inland, so the early crop counts for more. Coast-friendly varieties like Osborne Prolific or Desert King do best. Winters are mild and no cold worry.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: Figs grow well on the cooler Northern California coast, but cool, foggy summers ripen the main crop later and a touch less sweet than inland, and the breba crop matters more here. Varieties bred for cool coasts (Osborne Prolific, Desert King) perform best. Winters are mild and pose no cold threat.
ca_north_coast.chill_basis_seasoned: Coastal winters easily meet a fig's small ~100-hour chill need; here the limit is summer warmth for ripening, not chill or cold.
ca_north_coast.chill_basis_beginner: Mild coastal winters easily give figs the little cold they need; here the limit is having enough summer warmth to ripen the fruit, not cold.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Reliable fig country with a long, sunny, low-disease season. Both the breba and main crops ripen well, and winters pose no cold risk. Keep summer water steady and net against birds.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Reliable fig country, with a long, sunny season and little disease. Both crops ripen well, and winters are no cold worry. Keep the summer water steady and net against birds.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: Warm, frost-free, and sunny: excellent for figs, with a long season that ripens full, sweet crops and low disease pressure. Almost any common variety thrives; keep water steady and net against birds.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Warm, frost-free, and sunny: excellent for figs, with a long season that ripens big, sweet crops and little disease. Almost any common variety does well; keep water steady and net against birds.

ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: The mild, sunny Southern California coast is good fig country: enough heat for sweet fruit, a long frost-free season, and little disease in the dry air. Both crops ripen well. Winters are no cold worry, so just keep summer water steady and net against birds.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: The mild, sunny Southern California coast is fine fig country: enough heat to ripen sweet fruit, a long frost-free season, and low disease pressure in the dry air. Both crops ripen well. Winters pose no cold threat, so the focus is steady summer water and netting against birds.
ca_south_coast.chill_basis_seasoned: South-coast winters easily meet a fig's small chill need, so chill never limits fruiting; the mild, sunny climate suits figs well.
ca_south_coast.chill_basis_beginner: Mild coastal winters easily give figs the little cold they need, so chill is never a problem; the sunny climate suits figs well.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Superb fig country. Intense heat and dry air ripen rich, sweet crops with very low disease, and the mild winter easily meets a fig's small chill need. Deep, steady summer water is the whole job; both crops ripen well.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Superb for figs. Strong heat and dry air ripen rich, sweet crops with very little disease, and the mild winter easily gives figs the little cold they need. Deep, steady summer water is the main job; both crops ripen well.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: Excellent, nearly frost-free desert fig country. This is exactly where a fig's low chill need pays off: heavy, high-quality crops in heat that defeats high-chill trees. Keep deep summer water going and net against birds.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Excellent, almost frost-free desert fig country. This is just where figs' low need for cold pays off: big, high-quality crops in heat that beats high-chill trees. Keep the deep summer water going and net against birds.

ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: The low desert is a superb fig climate, and the opposite of high-chill trees: figs need almost no winter cold and love intense heat, so where a cherry or a high-chill peach fails for lack of cold, figs bear heavily. The dry air keeps disease very low. The one thing that matters is deep, steady summer water.
ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: The low desert is a superb fig climate, and a striking contrast with high-chill trees: figs need almost no winter chill and thrive on intense heat, so where a cherry or a high-chill peach fails for lack of cold, figs bear heavily. Dry air keeps disease very low. The one input that matters is deep, steady summer water.
ca_desert.chill_basis_seasoned: Desert winters deliver only modest chill, but a fig's ~100-hour need is easily met, so figs fruit heavily where high-chill trees cannot. Chill is a non-issue and heat is the asset.
ca_desert.chill_basis_beginner: Desert winters are not very cold, but figs need so little winter cold that they fruit heavily where high-chill trees like cherry cannot. Chill is a non-issue here, and the heat is a plus.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Reliable, low-disease fig country. Heat and dry air ripen sweet crops, and mild winters easily meet the chill need. Keep deep summer water going, and choose a well-drained, nematode-free site in sandy ground.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Reliable fig country with little disease. Heat and dry air ripen sweet crops, and mild winters easily give figs the cold they need. Keep the deep summer water going, and pick a well-drained, pest-free spot in sandy soil.

warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: Warm, dry inland areas suit figs very well: plenty of heat for sweet fruit, dry air that keeps disease down, and mild winters that give figs the little cold they need. Deep, steady summer water is the main job, and nematodes are the thing to watch in sandy soil.
warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: Warm, dry inland regions suit figs very well: ample heat ripens sweet fruit, dry air keeps rust and souring low, and mild winters meet the fig's small chill need. Deep, steady summer water is the main input, and root-knot nematodes are the site concern in sandy soil.
warm_arid.chill_basis_seasoned: Warm-arid winters easily meet a fig's ~100-hour chill need, so chill never limits fruiting; heat and dry air are the assets.
warm_arid.chill_basis_beginner: Winters here easily give figs the little cold they need, so chill is never a problem; the heat and dry air are what make figs do well.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Excellent low-desert fig country: intense heat and a long season ripen heavy crops, and the mild winter easily meets the small chill need. Deep, frequent summer water is essential; both crops ripen well and disease is low.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Excellent low-desert fig country: intense heat and a long season ripen big crops, and the mild winter easily gives figs the little cold they need. Deep, frequent summer water is a must; both crops ripen well and disease is low.

low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: The Arizona low desert is excellent for figs. Figs love the intense heat and, unlike high-chill trees, need almost no winter cold, so they bear heavily. Both crops ripen, often the early one in late spring and the main one through summer into fall. Deep, frequent summer water is a must in the extreme heat.
low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: The Arizona low desert is excellent fig country. Figs love the intense heat and, unlike high-chill trees, need essentially no winter chill, so they bear heavily. Both crops ripen, often with the breba in late spring and the main crop through summer into fall. Deep, frequent summer water is essential in the extreme heat.
low_desert_az.chill_basis_seasoned: Low-desert winters are mild, but a fig's ~100-hour chill need is easily met, so figs crop heavily where high-chill trees cannot. Chill is a non-issue and heat is the asset, given enough water.
low_desert_az.chill_basis_beginner: Low-desert winters are mild, but figs need so little winter cold that they crop heavily where high-chill trees cannot. Chill is a non-issue here, and the heat is a plus as long as you water enough.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: Figs fruit dependably here with attention to humid-weather disease and nematodes. Favor small-eye, rust-tolerant varieties (Celeste, LSU Purple), plant in well-drained, nematode-free ground or a container, and pick promptly to limit souring.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Figs fruit dependably here if you manage humid-weather disease and nematodes. Grow a tight-eye, rust-tolerant variety like Celeste or LSU Purple, plant in well-drained, pest-free soil or a pot, and pick promptly to limit souring.

11.suitability_note_seasoned: Marginal in the deep-tropical south. Figs grow and set fruit, but near-absent winter dormancy plus intense humidity, fig rust, souring, and heavy nematode pressure make cropping erratic and short-lived. Best grown in a container of clean mix with a rust-tolerant, small-eye variety.
11.suitability_note_beginner: Marginal in the deep-tropical south. Figs grow and set fruit, but with almost no winter rest and heavy humidity, rust, souring, and nematodes, the crop is unreliable. Best grown in a pot of clean mix with a rust-tolerant, tight-eye variety.

fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: Figs grow and fruit in peninsular Florida, but the warm, very humid climate brings more rust and souring, and sandy soils bring heavy nematode pressure, so figs are less carefree here than in the dry West. Pick a tight-eye, rust-tolerant variety, a pest-free or container spot, and pick often. In the far south, weak winter rest and disease make figs marginal.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: Figs grow and fruit in peninsular Florida, but the warm, very humid climate raises fig rust and beetle-spread souring, and sandy soils bring heavy root-knot nematode pressure, so cropping is less carefree than in the dry West. Favor small-eye, rust-tolerant varieties, a nematode-free or container site, and prompt picking. In the far south, weak dormancy and disease make figs marginal.
fl_peninsula.chill_basis_seasoned: Florida winters easily meet a fig's tiny chill need, so chill never limits fruiting; here the challenge is heat-and-humidity disease and nematodes, not cold.
fl_peninsula.chill_basis_beginner: Florida winters easily give figs the little cold they need, so chill is never a problem; here the challenge is disease from the heat and humidity, and nematodes, not cold.

11.suitability_note_seasoned: Marginal for dependable cropping. Figs grow and set fruit, but near-absent dormancy plus high humidity, fig rust, souring, and nematodes make yields erratic and quality variable. Grow in a container of clean mix, choose a rust-tolerant small-eye variety, and keep up sanitation.
11.suitability_note_beginner: Marginal for a dependable crop. Figs grow and set fruit, but with almost no winter rest and lots of humidity, rust, souring, and nematodes, the crop is up and down. Grow it in a pot of clean mix, pick a rust-tolerant tight-eye variety, and keep the plant and ground clean.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: Figs will grow and fruit in tropical Hawaii, but it is marginal for a dependable home crop: almost no winter cold or rest, high humidity that brings rust and souring, and nematode pressure make the crop unreliable. A pot of clean mix, a rust-tolerant tight-eye variety, and good cleanup give the best chance.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: Figs will grow and fruit in tropical Hawaii, but it is marginal for dependable home cropping: essentially no winter chill or dormancy, high humidity that drives fig rust and fruit souring, and root-knot nematode pressure make cropping erratic. A container of clean mix, a rust-tolerant small-eye variety, and diligent sanitation give the best odds.
hawaii_tropical.chill_basis_seasoned: Tropical winters deliver almost no chill, but a fig's need is so low it is technically met; the real limits are humidity-driven disease and the lack of a real dormancy, not chill.
hawaii_tropical.chill_basis_beginner: The tropics give almost no winter cold, but figs need so little that it is technically enough; the real problems are disease from the humidity and the lack of a real winter rest, not chill.

crops.description_seasoned: Fig (Ficus carica) is a deciduous, Mediterranean fruit tree grown on its own roots from cuttings, prized for soft, honey-sweet fruit that must ripen on the plant and does not survive shipping, so a backyard fig gives you something no store can match. It is one of the easiest fruit trees to grow where winters are mild: it is self-fruitful and parthenocarpic (it sets fruit with no pollination at all), needs very little winter chill (about 100 hours), and thrives on heat, which makes warm regions its home, the opposite of a high-chill tree like cherry. The one real limit is cold. Fully dormant wood is hardy only to about 15°F to 20°F, so fig is grown in the ground in zones 7 to 10, given heavy winter protection in zone 6, and kept in a container that overwinters indoors where winters are colder. Many figs carry two crops: a light early-summer breba crop on last year's wood and a larger late-summer to fall main crop on the new growth.
crops.description_beginner: A fig (Ficus carica) is a fruit tree that drops its leaves each winter and gives you soft, very sweet fruit that has to ripen on the plant and does not keep, which is why a homegrown fig is so much better than a store one. Where winters are mild, figs are one of the easiest fruit trees to grow: one plant makes fruit all by itself with no pollination needed, it needs very little winter cold, and it loves heat, so warm areas suit it perfectly. The one real limit is cold: the stems are hardy only to about 15°F to 20°F. So figs grow in the ground in zones 7 to 10, need heavy winter protection in zone 6, and are best grown in a pot you bring into shelter for winter where it is colder. Many figs give two crops: a few early figs in summer on last year's stems, and a bigger crop in late summer and fall on the new growth.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: A fig is ripe when it softens fully, its neck bends so the fruit droops rather than standing out from the stem, it colors up to its full variety color, and a drop of nectar may appear at the eye. Ripe figs feel soft to a gentle squeeze and detach with the barest tug. Color alone is not ripeness; a fig can be fully colored and still firm and unready. Because figs do not ripen after picking, wait for full softness and droop, and pick every day or two, since a plant ripens a few at a time over many weeks.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: A fig is ripe when it turns soft, droops down instead of sticking straight out (the neck bends), colors up fully, and maybe shows a drop of syrup at the bottom. A ripe fig gives easily to a gentle squeeze and comes off with the lightest pull. Color by itself does not mean ripe; a fig can be fully colored but still hard and not ready. Since figs do not ripen after you pick them, wait for them to go soft and droop, and pick every day or two, because a plant ripens just a few at a time over many weeks.
crops.bloom_time_seasoned: A fig has no showy bloom. Its flowers are tiny and hidden inside the young fruit (the fig you eat is essentially an inside-out cluster of flowers), so there is nothing to see the way a peach or apple flowers. What you watch for instead is leaf-out in early spring and the swelling of the small breba figs on last year's wood. Because common figs are parthenocarpic, that fruit forms and ripens with no pollination at all. The main crop then sets on the new shoots as they extend through late spring and summer.
crops.bloom_time_beginner: A fig never shows flowers, because they are hidden inside the fruit (the fig you eat is really a bundle of flowers turned inside out). Instead of a bloom, you watch for the leaves opening in early spring and the small early figs (the breba crop) swelling on last year's stems. Common figs make that fruit on their own, with no pollination. The main crop then forms on the new shoots as they grow through late spring and summer.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Cold is the one thing a fig cannot shrug off, so lead your planning with it. Fully dormant wood is hardy only to about 15°F to 20°F; sustained lows below that injure or kill the above-ground stems, though the roots are hardier and usually resprout. That sets a clear map: figs grow in the ground with little fuss in zones 7 to 10, need heavy winter protection (wrapping, or cutting back and burying under mulch and leaves) to fruit in zone 6, and are best grown in a container that winters in an unheated garage or shed where winters are colder still. A top-killed fig usually regrows from the base and can ripen a late main crop on the new wood, so a hard winter is rarely the end of the plant, just the end of that year's early fruit. Choose a cold-hardy variety (Chicago Hardy, Celeste, Marseilles) at the cold edge of the range. Winter chill is never the limiter, since a fig's small chill need is met almost everywhere.
crops.hardiness_notes_beginner: Cold is the one thing a fig cannot handle, so plan around it first. The stems are hardy only to about 15°F to 20°F, and sustained cold below that kills the top of the plant, though the roots are tougher and usually grow back. That gives a simple map: figs grow in the ground easily in zones 7 to 10, need heavy winter protection to fruit in zone 6, and are best grown in a pot you move into an unheated garage or shed where it is colder. Even a fig killed to the ground usually grows back from the roots and can ripen a late crop on the new stems, so a hard winter rarely kills the whole plant. Pick a cold-hardy variety like Chicago Hardy or Celeste at the cold edge. Winter chill is never the problem, since figs need so little.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Figs need very little winter cold, only about 100 hours below 45°F, which nearly every region that can grow them meets easily. That is why chill is almost never the limiting factor for a fig, and why figs do so well in mild, warm-winter areas that are too warm for high-chill trees like cherry. What actually limits a fig is the opposite end of the thermometer: not too little cold, but too much. Hard winter freezes below about 15°F to 20°F kill the top growth, so cold hardiness, not chill, is the number to match to your area.
crops.chill_hours_note_beginner: Figs need only a little winter cold, about 100 hours below 45°F, which almost any area that can grow them gets easily. So chill is hardly ever the problem for a fig, and figs do great in mild, warm-winter places that are too warm for high-chill trees like cherry. What actually limits a fig is the other extreme: not too little cold, but too much. Hard freezes below about 15°F to 20°F kill the top of the plant, so the number to match to your area is cold-hardiness, not chill.
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Common home figs are parthenocarpic: they set and ripen fruit with no pollination whatsoever, so a single plant fruits alone with no partner, no bees, and no fig wasp. The flowers are hidden inside the fruit, which is why a fig never shows a visible bloom. The Smyrna and San Pedro types sold in some catalogs are the exception, needing a specific fig wasp (Blastophaga psenes) that is absent across most of the country, so they drop their fruit and are not recommended for home gardens. Stick to the common types (Celeste, Brown Turkey, Chicago Hardy, Black Mission, Kadota) and pollination is simply a non-issue.
crops.pollinator_notes_beginner: Common figs make and ripen fruit with no pollination at all, so one plant is all you need, with no second tree, no bees, and no special wasp. The flowers are inside the fruit, which is why a fig never shows a bloom. A few unusual types (Smyrna and San Pedro) do need a special fig wasp, and that wasp is not around in most of the country, so they just drop their fruit and are not worth planting. Choose a common type like Celeste, Brown Turkey, or Chicago Hardy and you never have to think about pollination.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: In the planting year, prioritize establishment and winter survival over fruit. Plant a dormant own-rooted fig in late winter or early spring after the hardest cold, in full sun on well-drained ground, and against a warm wall at the cold edge of the range. Water consistently through the first season, keep a mulched, weed-free ring around the plant, and protect it especially well its first winter, since a young fig is the most cold-tender it will ever be. Hold fertilizer until growth begins and keep it light. A few figs may form; enjoy them, but do not count on a crop yet.
crops.year_one_notes_beginner: The first year is about helping the plant get established and through winter, not about fruit. Plant a dormant fig in late winter or early spring after the worst cold, in full sun in well-drained soil, and against a warm wall in cold areas. Water it steadily the first season, keep a mulched, weed-free ring around it, and protect it especially well its first winter, since a young fig is more easily hurt by cold than an older one. Wait to fertilize until it starts growing, and go easy. A few figs may form, which is a nice bonus, but do not count on a crop yet.

pollination.notes_seasoned: Common home figs are parthenocarpic: they set and ripen fruit with no pollination at all, so a single tree fruits alone with no partner, no bees, and no fig wasp. The flowers are tiny and hidden inside the young fig, so a fig never shows a visible bloom. The Smyrna and San Pedro types are the exception, requiring a specific fig wasp (Blastophaga psenes) that is absent across most of the country, so they drop their fruit and are not recommended; stick to the common types.
pollination.notes_beginner: Common figs make fruit all by themselves, with no pollination needed at all. One plant is all you need, and there is nothing to see when it flowers because the flowers are inside the fig. Only a few unusual types (Smyrna and San Pedro) need a special wasp to fruit, and that wasp is not around in most places, so just choose a common variety and you never have to think about pollination.

crops.establishment_note: Most figs begin bearing 1 to 2 years after planting, with fuller crops by years 3 to 4.
crops.recommended_rootstock_note: Figs are grown on their own roots from cuttings, not grafted, so there is no rootstock to choose and no graft union to keep above the soil.

rootstock_options.name: Own-root (from cuttings)
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask for a named common (parthenocarpic) variety on its own roots, as a rooted cutting or container plant; figs are not sold grafted.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: Figs are propagated from dormant hardwood cuttings and grown on their own roots, so unlike stone and pome fruit there is no rootstock system: no grafting, no graft union, and no rootstock-driven size control or disease resistance to select. Size is managed by pruning, by variety, and by growing in a container. The one soil-pest caveat is root-knot nematode, which own-rooted figs have no resistant rootstock to fall back on, so a nematode-free, well-drained site is the real substitute for rootstock choice.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: Figs grow on their own roots from cuttings, so there is no rootstock to pick the way there is for a peach or apple. You control the size by how you prune it, by the variety, and by growing it in a pot. Because there is no special root to resist soil pests, the main thing is to plant it in well-drained ground that is free of root-knot nematodes.

pet_safe.note: The fruit is fine, but the milky sap and leaves can irritate the skin and stomach of cats, dogs, and horses.

crops.name: Pomegranate

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Pomegranate is famously easy about soil. It grows best in a deep loam but will handle sandy soils and even heavy clay, as long as water drains away and does not sit around the roots. It also shrugs off alkaline (high-pH) and mildly salty soils that bother most fruit. The one thing it will not take is soggy ground: constantly wet roots bring on root rot. If your soil is heavy or drainage is poor, plant on a raised mound or bed so the roots stay above the wet.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Pomegranate is one of the most soil-adaptable fruits: it prefers a deep loam but tolerates sandy soils, heavy clay, alkaline pH, and mild salinity that would stunt most fruit trees. Drainage is the one firm requirement, since waterlogged soil invites root rot (including Armillaria on wet, heavy ground). On clay or low sites, plant on a raised berm or bed to lift the crown above standing water. It needs little organic matter and thrives on lean ground.

ph.note_beginner: Pomegranate grows well in a wide pH range, about 5.5 to 7.0, and tolerates up to around 7.2 (pH just measures how acidic or alkaline the soil is). It is unusually easygoing about alkaline soil, so most gardeners never need to adjust pH for it. Test your soil before planting, and only correct if it is far outside that range.
ph.note_seasoned: Pomegranate does well across a broad pH band, roughly 5.5 to 7.0, and tolerates up to about 7.2. It is notably alkaline-tolerant, so pH is seldom a limiting factor and rarely needs amending. Test before planting and correct only if the soil is well outside the tolerated range.

fertilizer.timing: late winter to early spring before growth; optional light second feeding in late spring
fertilizer.example_product: 10-10-10 balanced fertilizer
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Pomegranate is a light feeder. Broadcast a modest amount of balanced fertilizer around the root zone in late winter to early spring as growth begins, and water it in. Avoid heavy nitrogen: excess N drives vegetative growth and suckering at the expense of flowers and fruit, and can worsen soft, split-prone fruit. On lean or sandy soils a light second feeding in late spring helps young plants; established plants often need little or none.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Pomegranate does not need much feeding. In late winter or early spring, scatter a small amount of balanced fertilizer around the plant and water it in. Do not overdo nitrogen (the first number on the bag), because too much grows leaves and base shoots instead of fruit. On poor or sandy soil, a light second feeding in late spring helps a young plant, but an established one usually needs very little.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 suits pomegranate; it is a light feeder and draws modestly on all three nutrients. Keep nitrogen restrained, since excess pushes suckers and soft growth over flowering and fruit set.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: A balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 (the three numbers are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium) is plenty for a pomegranate. Go light, and especially do not overdo the first number, nitrogen, which grows leaves and shoots instead of fruit.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A light hand is the rule. A common home approach is about 1 to 2 ounces of actual nitrogen per year of plant age in the early years (for example, a modest handful of 10-10-10 per foot of height), capped for a mature plant, applied in late winter. Skip feeding at planting; wait until growth begins. If growth is already vigorous and green, feed less or not at all.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Feed lightly. A simple approach is a small handful of 10-10-10 for each foot of the plant's height, spread around the plant in late winter, and no more than that for a full-grown one. Do not fertilize right when you plant; wait until it starts growing. If the plant is already growing strongly with deep green leaves, feed less or skip it.

companions.note_beginner: Pomegranate is self-fruitful, so one plant makes fruit on its own and you do not need a second plant to pollinate it (though a second pomegranate nearby can improve fruit set a little). For a shrub like this, the things that help are not the usual vegetable-garden pairings but the space around it: keep grass and weeds pulled back from the base so they do not compete with a young plant, and give it an open, sunny, breezy spot, because crowded, still, humid air at bloom makes flowers drop instead of setting fruit. Flowering plants nearby that draw bees can help set, and they bring in helpful insects that keep aphids and whiteflies down.
companions.note_seasoned: Pomegranate is self-fruitful, so a single plant sets a crop on its own (a second plant nearby can modestly improve set). The interactions that matter for this shrub are about air, light, and the root zone, not classic vegetable companions: keep turf and weeds cleared from the base so they do not compete with a young plant, and site it in open, sunny, breezy ground, since crowded, humid, still air at bloom causes flowers to abort. Nearby pollinator plantings aid set and recruit the beneficials that hold aphids, whiteflies, and mealybugs in check.

good_seasoned.name: Flowering / pollinator and insectary plants
good_seasoned.label: likely

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Pomegranate is self-fruitful, so the pollinator draw is a help, not a requirement; but insect visitation improves set (a documented benefit), and an insectary planting recruits the predators/parasitoids that suppress aphids, whiteflies, and mealybugs. Mechanistic and extension-aligned, but the pomegranate-specific magnitude is modest and unquantified.

good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A skirt of flowering, pollinator- and beneficial-friendly plants around a pomegranate supports fruit set and pest balance. Pomegranate self-pollinates, so this is help rather than a requirement, but better bee activity improves set, and the same flowers recruit the lacewings, hoverflies, and parasitic wasps that keep aphids, whiteflies, and mealybugs in check. Keep them out toward the drip line rather than crowding the base, so air still moves freely through the canopy.

bad_seasoned.name: Crowding and shade that block air movement
bad_seasoned.label: extension_backed

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: UGA Extension is explicit that air circulation is important, especially at bloom: flowers may not set or will abort if conditions are too humid, and open, breezy, sunny sites are advised. Crowding a pomegranate with dense plantings or shade traps humid, still air, suppressing set and raising fruit-disease pressure. Clear extension guidance with a defined mechanism.

bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Do not crowd a pomegranate against a wall of dense plantings or into shade. It needs full sun and moving air, especially at bloom: humid, still air causes flowers to abort and sets up the fruit diseases (Cercospora spot, gray mold, black heart) that plague pomegranate in muggy conditions. Give it an open, sunny, breezy site with room around the canopy so the foliage and fruit dry quickly after rain or dew.

pests.name: Leaf-footed bug
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Often no external mark on the fruit at all; the damage is inside. Cut a fed-on fruit and you find brown spots on the inner rind where the insect's needlelike mouthpart pierced, and arils that have darkened, withered, or turned corky. Late-season feeding as fruit ripens is the worst, and it opens the door to internal fungal rots.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Usually you see nothing wrong on the outside of the fruit, because the damage is inside. If you cut a fruit open, you find brown spots on the inner skin and seeds (arils) that have gone dark, shriveled, or corky. It is worst late in the season as the fruit ripens, and it can let rot start inside.
pests.cause_seasoned: The leaf-footed bug (Leptoglossus species), a large brown true bug with flattened, leaf-like flares on its hind legs. Adults and nymphs pierce fruit to feed; on pomegranate their feeding can introduce yeasts and fungal spores that discolor and rot the arils. They overwinter as adults in sheltered aggregations and move onto fruit as it develops.
pests.cause_beginner: A big brown bug called the leaf-footed bug, named for the little leaf-shaped flares on its back legs. It and its young pierce the fruit to feed, and that can carry in yeasts and fungi that discolor and rot the seeds inside. The adults spend winter hidden in sheltered groups, then move onto the fruit as it forms.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no easy rescue spray for a backyard plant. The practical controls are physical: hand-pick or knock adults and nymphs into soapy water in the cool early morning when they are sluggish, clear the weedy and sheltered spots where they overwinter and aggregate, and bag developing fruit clusters in mesh where feasible. Encourage the natural egg parasites and general predators by keeping insectary flowers nearby.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: For a backyard plant, the best fixes are hands-on: in the cool early morning, knock the bugs into a bucket of soapy water, and clean up the weedy, sheltered places where they spend the winter and gather. Where you can, cover fruit clusters with fine mesh bags. Flowers nearby that bring in helpful insects also keep numbers down.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Monitor from fruit set onward, since the internal damage is invisible until you cut the fruit. Keep the area weed-free to remove overwintering and breeding habitat, and watch for the adults congregating in spring. Early detection and hand-removal before populations build is the most effective home strategy.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep an eye out from the time fruit forms, because you cannot see the damage from outside until you cut a fruit open. Keep weeds cleared to take away the places the bugs hide and breed, and look for the adults gathering in spring. Catching and removing them early, before there are many, works best.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of small soft-bodied insects on new shoots, leaf undersides, and flower stems, with sticky honeydew, sooty black mold on leaves and fruit, curled or distorted new growth, and attending ants.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Groups of tiny soft insects on new shoots and the undersides of leaves, leaving a sticky coating (honeydew) that turns into black sooty mold, plus curled new leaves and ants running up and down the plant.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several aphid species colonize tender pomegranate growth in spring, multiplying fast in warm weather. Their honeydew supports sooty mold and draws ants, which protect the aphids from predators.
pests.cause_beginner: Aphids, tiny sap-sucking insects that build up on soft new growth in spring. They multiply quickly, and the sticky honeydew they leave grows black mold and attracts ants that guard them.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: A strong jet of water knocks aphids off and is often enough on an established plant. Preserve natural enemies (lady beetles, lacewings, syrphid larvae) by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays; insecticidal soap or horticultural oil handles heavier infestations. Control ants, which farm aphids, to let predators work.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spraying the plant with a strong stream of water knocks most aphids off and is often all an established plant needs. Let the good bugs (lady beetles, lacewings) do their job by avoiding harsh sprays; insecticidal soap helps if there are a lot. Keeping ants off the plant lets the helpful insects control them.
