pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep nitrogen feeding moderate, since lush growth pushed by excess nitrogen draws aphids. Support beneficial insects with nearby flowers, and manage ants so predators are not chased off.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not overfeed with nitrogen, because all that soft new growth attracts aphids. Grow flowers nearby to bring in helpful insects, and keep ants away so those helpers can do their work.

pests.name: Whitefly
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny white moth-like insects that fly up in clouds when the plant is disturbed, gathered on leaf undersides with their pale nymphs; honeydew and sooty mold follow, and heavy infestations yellow and weaken leaves.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny white insects like little moths that flutter up when you brush the plant, sitting under the leaves along with their flat, pale young. They leave sticky honeydew and black sooty mold, and a lot of them yellow the leaves.
pests.cause_seasoned: Whiteflies, small sap-feeding insects that colonize leaf undersides and reproduce rapidly in warm weather. Like aphids, they excrete honeydew that fosters sooty mold.
pests.cause_beginner: Whiteflies, small sap-sucking insects that live under the leaves and multiply fast in warm weather. Like aphids, they leave honeydew that grows sooty mold.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hose off foliage and rely on natural enemies (lacewings, lady beetles, parasitic wasps), which usually keep whiteflies in check on an outdoor plant. Insecticidal soap or horticultural oil on leaf undersides helps in heavy cases; yellow sticky traps monitor and reduce adults.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray the leaves with water and let helpful insects do most of the work; they usually keep whiteflies under control outdoors. Insecticidal soap sprayed under the leaves helps if there are many, and yellow sticky cards catch the adults.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep plants healthy and avoid excess nitrogen and dusty, stressed conditions that favor whitefly buildup. Preserve natural enemies by avoiding broad-spectrum insecticides.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep the plant healthy, avoid overfeeding with nitrogen, and do not let it get dusty and stressed, which whiteflies like. Avoid harsh sprays so the helpful insects survive.

pests.name: Mealybugs and scale
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Cottony white tufts (mealybugs) in leaf axils, branch crotches, and inside the fruit calyx (crown), or small immobile brown or waxy bumps (scale) on stems and leaves; both produce honeydew and sooty mold, and mealybugs hidden in the crown can contaminate the fruit interior.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Fuzzy white cottony spots (mealybugs) tucked into branch joints and inside the crown of the fruit, or small hard brown bumps (scale) stuck to stems and leaves. Both leave sticky honeydew and black mold, and mealybugs hiding in the fruit crown can get inside the fruit.
pests.cause_seasoned: Mealybugs and various scale insects, slow-moving or immobile sap feeders that shelter in protected spots including the fruit's crown. Ants tend and spread them, and their honeydew fuels sooty mold.
pests.cause_beginner: Mealybugs and scale insects, sap-sucking pests that hide in sheltered spots, including the crown of the fruit. Ants move them around and protect them, and their honeydew grows black mold.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Spot-treat with horticultural oil or insecticidal soap, dab visible mealybug colonies with an alcohol-dipped swab, and prune out heavily infested wood. Control ants to let natural enemies (including mealybug destroyers and parasitic wasps) suppress them. Remove fruit with infested crowns.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Wipe visible mealybugs with a cotton swab dipped in rubbing alcohol, spray with horticultural oil or insecticidal soap, and cut out badly infested branches. Keep ants off so the helpful insects can work, and throw away any fruit with bugs packed into the crown.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep ants under control, avoid excess nitrogen, and inspect the fruit crown and branch crotches where these pests hide. Good airflow and light through the canopy discourage them.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep ants away, do not overfeed, and check the fruit crowns and branch joints where these pests hide. An open, airy plant with good light bothers them.

diseases.name: Alternaria heart rot (black heart)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: The fruit looks nearly normal outside, perhaps a little light in weight or slightly off-color (a paler red), while the interior rots: arils turn brown and mushy and a black mold sporulates inside. There is often no external cue, so the rot is discovered only on cutting.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: From the outside the fruit looks almost fine, maybe a bit light or a paler red, but inside it is rotting: the seeds turn brown and mushy with black mold. There is usually no sign on the outside, so you only find it when you cut the fruit open.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Alternaria (and related molds) infects through the open flower during rainy or humid bloom weather and grows silently inside the developing fruit. Insect and bird punctures (notably leaf-footed bug feeding) give it a second way in. Wet weather at and after bloom is the main driver, which is why it is a bigger problem in humid climates.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus called Alternaria gets into the fruit through the open flower in damp, rainy bloom weather and grows quietly inside. Wounds from insects (like the leaf-footed bug) or birds let it in too. Wet weather around bloom is the main cause, so it is worse in humid areas.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once the inside is rotting; the fruit is lost. Control is preventive: it is far less of a problem in hot, dry climates, so the main levers are managing leaf-footed bug and other fruit-piercing pests, keeping the canopy open and airy, and removing and destroying infected and mummified fruit so spores do not carry over.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Once a fruit is rotting inside, it cannot be saved. The way to fight it is to prevent it: it is much less of a problem in hot, dry weather, so keep the leaf-footed bug and other fruit-piercing pests under control, keep the plant open and airy, and pick off and throw away any rotted or old dried fruit so the mold does not spread to next year.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Favor dry-climate siting, open canopies, and drip (not overhead) watering to keep bloom and fruit dry. Control fruit-piercing insects, sanitize by removing mummies and rotted fruit, and, in humid regions, expect this to be a limiting disease and choose the most open, breezy sites.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Grow it where summers are hot and dry if you can, keep the plant open, and water at the ground rather than over the top. Keep fruit-piercing bugs in check, clean up rotted and old dried fruit, and know that in humid, rainy areas this disease may limit your crop, so pick the most open, breezy spot.

diseases.name: Botrytis gray mold / fruit rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Fuzzy gray-brown mold on flowers, on fruit (often starting at the crown or a wound), and on stored fruit; soft brown rot spreads in cool, wet, or humid conditions and in storage, and can move between touching fruit.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Fuzzy gray-brown mold on the flowers and fruit, often starting at the crown end or a wound, with soft brown rot that spreads in cool, damp weather and in storage. It can spread from one fruit to another where they touch.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Botrytis cinerea (gray mold), which infects flowers and wounded or overripe fruit in cool, wet, humid conditions. It overwinters on plant debris and old fruit and is a common cause of post-harvest rot.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus called Botrytis, or gray mold, that infects flowers and damaged or overripe fruit in cool, damp weather. It survives on old fruit and plant litter and is a common cause of rot in stored fruit.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy moldy flowers, fruit, and debris promptly. Keep the canopy open and dry, harvest before rains, handle fruit gently to avoid wounds, and refrigerate sound fruit quickly, since cold storage slows the mold. There is no home spray cure once fruit is rotting.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick off and throw away moldy flowers, fruit, and litter right away. Keep the plant open and dry, pick before the rains, handle fruit gently so it does not bruise, and refrigerate good fruit soon, since cold slows the mold. Once a fruit is rotting there is no home spray that fixes it.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Prioritize air circulation and dry foliage: open pruning, root-zone watering, prompt sanitation of old fruit and debris, and gentle handling with quick cooling at harvest. Cull split and wounded fruit, which are entry points.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Keep the plant open and the leaves dry: prune for airflow, water at the ground, clean up old fruit and litter, and handle and chill fruit carefully at harvest. Remove split or damaged fruit, which is where the mold gets in.

diseases.name: Cercospora fruit and leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small dark spots and blotches on fruit and leaves that enlarge and merge; heavily spotted fruit is russeted and downgraded, and severe leaf infection causes yellowing and drop. Most common and damaging in warm, humid, rainy climates.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small dark spots on the fruit and leaves that grow and run together; badly spotted fruit looks rough and russeted, and heavy leaf spotting yellows the leaves and drops them. It is worst in warm, humid, rainy areas.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Cercospora punicae (with related fungi such as Colletotrichum and Botryosphaeria in the same wet climates). It thrives on prolonged leaf and fruit wetness, so it is a leading reason pomegranate fruits poorly in the humid Southeast and other rainy regions.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus (Cercospora punicae, along with related fungi in the same wet climates) that spreads when leaves and fruit stay wet for a long time. It is a big reason pomegranate does poorly in the humid Southeast and other rainy places.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Home control is limited and preventive: choose an open, sunny, breezy site so foliage dries fast, prune for airflow, water at the ground, and remove fallen leaves and infected fruit. In consistently humid, rainy climates, expect this disease to cap fruit quality regardless of care.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no easy home cure, so prevention matters: plant in an open, sunny, breezy spot so the leaves dry quickly, prune to open the plant, water at the ground, and clean up fallen leaves and spotted fruit. In damp, rainy climates this disease will likely limit your fruit quality no matter what.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Site selection is the main defense: open, sloped, breezy ground with strong air movement, especially at bloom. Wide spacing, open canopies, ground-level irrigation, and sanitation of fallen debris reduce pressure. In hot, dry climates it is a minor issue.
diseases.prevention_beginner: The best defense is where and how you plant it: an open, breezy, sloped spot with good air movement, wide spacing, an open plant, watering at the ground, and cleaning up fallen leaves and fruit. In hot, dry climates it is barely a problem.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Water deeply and regularly through the growing season, then ease off. Young plants need steady moisture to establish; bearing plants are drought-tolerant but crop far better with regular deep watering, roughly weekly in summer heat, adjusted for soil and weather. The critical discipline is CONSISTENCY from fruit set through ripening: a dry spell followed by heavy water (or the first fall rains) is what splits the fruit. In winter dormancy, water need drops sharply and rainfall usually suffices.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water deeply and regularly through spring and summer, then cut back in winter. A young plant needs steady water to get established. An older plant can take drought but makes much better fruit with regular deep watering, about once a week in summer heat, more or less depending on your soil and the weather. The most important thing is to keep the water STEADY once the fruit is forming: letting it go dry and then soaking it (or the first fall rains) is what makes pomegranates split. In winter, when the plant is resting, it needs very little.
watering.amount_seasoned: Water deeply enough to wet the full root zone each time rather than sprinkling the surface. Through the fruiting season aim for the rough equivalent of an inch of water per week, more in extreme heat, delivered as deep, even soaks. Steady soil moisture from set to harvest is what prevents splitting; the goal is even, never a dry-then-flood swing.
watering.amount_beginner: Each watering should soak the soil deeply down to the roots, not just wet the top. During the fruiting season, aim for about an inch of water a week, more when it is very hot, given as deep, even soaks. Keeping the moisture steady from the time fruit forms until harvest is what stops the fruit from cracking, so avoid letting it dry out and then flooding it.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the root zone with drip or a soaker hose out toward the canopy edge, keeping the base broad and even. Pomegranate tolerates overhead water better than stone fruit, but even, deep root-zone irrigation is what delivers the consistent moisture that prevents fruit split. Mulch to buffer soil-moisture swings, keeping mulch off the trunks.
watering.method_beginner: Water the ground around the roots with a drip line or soaker hose, out to the edge of the branches. What matters most is deep, even watering, because steady moisture is what keeps the fruit from splitting. A layer of mulch helps hold moisture even; just keep it off the trunks.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Overwatering and poor drainage show as yellowing leaves, wilting in wet soil, and a declining plant, since waterlogged roots suffocate. Chronically wet, heavy soil invites Armillaria and other root rots, which are hard to reverse. Soil that never dries between waterings is the warning sign; pomegranate wants moisture but not a saturated root zone.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Too much water, or soil that drains poorly, shows up as yellow leaves, wilting even when the soil is wet, and a plant going downhill, because soaked roots cannot breathe and start to rot. Soil that stays wet all the time is your warning. Pomegranate likes steady moisture but not a swamp.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Underwatering shows as wilting, dull or yellowing leaves, early leaf drop, and small, poorly filled fruit. The most costly symptom is inconsistent water: a drought-stressed plant that is then rewetted, or catches the fall rains, splits its fruit. Catch dry stress before the fruit pays for it.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Too little water shows as wilting, dull or yellow leaves, leaves dropping early, and small fruit. The worst result comes from uneven water: a plant that gets dry and is then watered heavily (or hit by fall rain) will crack its fruit. Try to keep the water steady so this does not happen.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Through establishment, keep the root ball and surrounding soil consistently moist, never waterlogged. Deep soaks once or twice a week, adjusted for heat and rain, build the deep, drought-ready root system pomegranate relies on later.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: While the plant is getting established, keep the soil around the roots evenly moist but not soggy. A deep soak once or twice a week, more in heat and less after rain, helps it grow the deep roots it needs.

schedule_by_stage.rate: deep soak, ~1 in per week equivalent
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: From fruit set through ripening, hold the moisture STEADY. Aim for about an inch of water per week as deep, even soaks. This is the window where consistent water prevents splitting and irregular water causes it.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Once the fruit is forming and filling, keep the water steady. Aim for about an inch a week as deep soaks. This is exactly when even watering keeps the fruit from cracking.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Once the plant drops its leaves and goes dormant, water need falls sharply; rely mostly on rainfall and water only during prolonged dry spells. Avoid keeping dormant soil saturated.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: After the leaves drop and the plant rests for winter, it needs very little water. Let rain do most of the work and only water in long dry stretches. Do not keep the soil soaked in winter.

watering.method_note_seasoned: Water deeply at the root zone, ideally by drip or soaker, and keep it EVEN from fruit set to harvest; consistency, not volume, is what prevents split fruit. Young plants need steady moisture through their first two seasons to establish; mature plants are strongly drought-tolerant but size and hold fruit far better with regular deep water.
watering.method_note_beginner: Give deep soaks at the ground (a drip line or soaker hose is ideal) and keep the water steady from the time fruit forms until you pick, since even watering is what stops the fruit from splitting. Young plants need regular water for their first couple of years. Older plants handle dry spells but make much better fruit with regular deep watering.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The make-or-break window is from fruit set through ripening. Uneven water then, a dry spell followed by heavy irrigation or the first fall rains, drives fruit splitting, the signature pomegranate failure. Keep soil moisture steady through this period, and time harvest ahead of significant rain. Early establishment (first two summers) is the other water-sensitive window.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The most important time to keep water steady is from when the fruit forms until you pick it. Uneven water then, going dry and then soaking, or the first fall rains, is what splits the fruit, which is the number-one pomegranate problem. Keep the moisture even through this stretch and pick before big rains. The first couple of summers, while the plant is establishing, also matter.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Hardening off does not apply to pomegranate. It is set out as a dormant bare-root or cutting-grown plant in late winter to early spring, not raised from a tender seedling indoors, so there is no transplant to acclimate.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: Hardening off (slowly getting an indoor-grown seedling used to the outdoors) does not apply to pomegranate. You plant it as a dormant bare-root or potted plant in late winter or early spring, not as a tender seedling started inside, so there is nothing to ease outdoors.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Plant a dormant bare-root or cutting-grown pomegranate in late winter to early spring, after the hardest freezes have passed and once the ground can be worked. Soak bare roots for an hour or two first. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots and set the plant at the depth it grew in the nursery; because pomegranate is on its own roots (not grafted), there is no graft union to keep above grade. Decide the form at planting, multi-stem shrub or trained tree, and head the plant back to start it. On heavy or wet ground, plant on a raised mound. Backfill with native soil, water in well, and mulch.
start_method.notes_beginner: Plant a dormant bare-root or potted pomegranate in late winter or early spring, after the worst cold and once the ground can be dug. Soak bare roots in water for an hour or two first. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots and set the plant at the same depth it grew before. Unlike a peach, a pomegranate is on its own roots with no graft joint to worry about. Decide now whether you want a bush with several trunks or a single small tree, and cut the plant back a bit to start it. If your soil is heavy or wet, plant on a raised mound. Fill in with the soil you dug out, water it well, and add mulch.

drainage.saucer_practice: empty_after_watering

soil_mix.type_beginner: Use a good, fast-draining potting mix made for shrubs or citrus. Pomegranate is not fussy, but it must not sit in soggy mix, so pick one that drains freely. A bark-based mix with some perlite or pumice works well. Do not use heavy garden soil in a pot, since it packs down and stays wet.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Aim for drainage. If the mix holds water, stir in extra perlite or pumice. A little compost on top is fine. Pomegranate is drought-tolerant, so avoid water-holding crystals or a heavy, peaty mix that stays wet.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: Use a free-draining container mix (a bark-based blend with perlite or pumice, or a citrus/shrub mix). Pomegranate is easygoing but will not tolerate a waterlogged mix against the crown, so porosity matters more than richness. Avoid heavy native soil, which compacts under frequent irrigation.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Keep amendments drainage-first: add perlite or pumice if the base mix is water-retentive, and top-dress lightly with compost rather than blending heavy organics throughout. Skip moisture-retentive additives, which work against the drainage this drought-adapted plant prefers.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: A pomegranate in a pot dries out faster than one in the ground, so check it often in summer heat and water when the top inch or two is dry, until water runs out the bottom. Even so, try to keep the watering STEADY once fruit forms, because uneven water splits the fruit even in a pot. Never let the pot stand in a saucer of water, which rots the roots. In winter, water just enough to keep the root ball from drying out completely.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Frequent watering washes food out of a pot, so feed lightly and often instead of one big dose: a diluted balanced liquid feed every few weeks from spring into midsummer, then stop by late summer. Go easy on nitrogen, which grows leaves over fruit. Do not feed at planting, and stop once the plant drops its leaves for winter.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Pomegranate is cold-tender, and roots in a pot freeze more easily than roots in the ground. In zones colder than about 8, before hard freezes come, move the pot into an unheated but sheltered spot (a garage, shed, or against a warm wall) that stays cold enough to keep the plant dormant but out of the deep freeze. The plant still needs its winter rest, so do not bring it into a warm, heated room. In mild-winter areas you can leave it outside.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Because pomegranate is frost-tender and a container root ball sits several zones colder than open ground, protect potted plants in zones colder than roughly 8. Before hard freezes, move the pot to an unheated but sheltered space (garage, shed, or a warm south wall) that holds dormancy without deep lows, or sink the pot to its rim in a bed and mulch heavily. Do not overwinter it in heated indoor warmth, which breaks dormancy prematurely. In mild-winter regions no protection is needed.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Pomegranate is one of the best fruit plants for a pot: it is naturally shrubby, drought- and heat-tolerant, self-fruitful, and easy to keep small with pruning. Start with a dwarf variety like 'Nana' or a standard kept pruned, use a large pot (15 gallons or more) that drains well, and give it full sun. In cold areas the pot lets you move the plant to shelter for winter, which is a real advantage where the ground is too cold.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Pomegranate is among the most container-friendly tree fruits: naturally shrubby, drought- and heat-tolerant, self-fruitful, and readily kept compact. Choose a genetic-dwarf ('Nana') or a standard cultivar held small by pruning, give it the largest practical free-draining pot (15-plus gallons) and full sun, and keep moisture even through fruiting. In cold-winter regions the pot is an asset, letting you move a frost-tender plant to shelter for the winter.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: A potted pomegranate dries faster than one in the ground, so check moisture regularly in summer and water until it runs from the drainage holes when the top inch or two is dry. Keep the cadence EVEN once fruit is set, since split fruit is driven by moisture swings even in containers, and never leave the pot standing in a full saucer. Through dormancy, water only enough to keep the root ball from fully drying out.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Frequent irrigation flushes nutrients from a pot, so feed lightly and often: a dilute balanced liquid feed every few weeks through the spring-to-midsummer flush, then stop by late summer. Keep nitrogen restrained to favor fruiting over suckers and soft growth. Do not feed at planting, and ease off entirely at dormancy.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering or sub-irrigated planter is not recommended for pomegranate. Its reservoir keeps the lower root zone continuously wet, which works against the free drainage this drought-adapted plant prefers and raises root-rot risk. Pomegranate does best with deep, even hand-watering in a freely draining pot, not a constant water table held against the roots.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot (one with a water tank in the bottom) is not a good match for pomegranate. The tank keeps the lower roots wet all the time, and this drought-loving plant would rather have soil that drains freely. Use a regular pot with good drainage and water it deeply and evenly yourself.
container_notes.container_overwintering_seasoned: Cold protection in a pot covers the whole plant, not just the roots: exposed stems of a frost-tender pomegranate are vulnerable to freeze and winter sun. In cold regions, move the pot to an unheated but sheltered space or sink and mulch it, and shelter the stems in exposed sites. The aim is a cold, stable dormancy without the deep lows that kill exposed roots and wood; a too-warm shelter that breaks dormancy early is its own hazard, leaving tender new growth exposed to frost.
container_notes.container_overwintering_beginner: Protecting a potted pomegranate in winter means the whole plant, not just the roots. Its bare stems can be hurt by hard freezes and winter sun. In cold areas, move the pot into an unheated but sheltered spot or sink it in a bed and pile mulch around it. You want it cold enough to keep resting but out of the deep freeze. Watch out too that a spot that is too warm can wake it up early and leave new growth open to frost.

recommended.name: Wonderful
recommended.recommended_note: The standard commercial variety: large, deep-red, tart-sweet fruit; needs a long hot summer to color and sweeten fully.

recommended.name: Granada
recommended.recommended_note: An early 'Wonderful' sport: sweeter, less tart, and ripens several weeks earlier; good where the season is shorter.

recommended.name: Eversweet
recommended.recommended_note: Sweet, low-acid, nearly seedless with soft seeds; ripens early and colors even in cooler-summer areas.

recommended.name: Parfianka
recommended.recommended_note: A top flavor pick: sweet-tart with soft, edible seeds; excellent fresh and for juice.

recommended.name: Angel Red
recommended.recommended_note: Very early, heavy-bearing, high-juice with soft seeds; ripens ahead of 'Wonderful'.

recommended.name: Salavatski
recommended.recommended_note: A cold-hardy Russian type (to roughly 7°F): the pick for the cold edge (zone 7) and protected sites.

recommended.name: Kazake
recommended.recommended_note: Another cold-hardy Russian selection; sweet fruit and good cold tolerance for marginal-cold gardens.

varieties.note_seasoned: Choose a pomegranate first by climate fit, then by flavor. In hot, dry interior and desert gardens the full range is open; favor 'Wonderful' and 'Parfianka' for classic tart-sweet fruit and juice. Where summers are shorter or cooler, pick an early, sweeter type ('Granada', 'Eversweet', 'Angel Red') that ripens before the season fades. At the cold edge (zone 7) or on frost-prone sites, a hardy Russian cultivar ('Salavatski', 'Kazake') is the safer bet. All pomegranates are self-fruitful, so one well-chosen plant is enough; a second only nudges set.
varieties.note_beginner: Pick a pomegranate first for your climate, then for taste. In hot, dry inland and desert areas almost any variety works; 'Wonderful' and 'Parfianka' are the classics for tart-sweet fruit and juice. Where summers are shorter or cooler, choose an early, sweeter kind ('Granada', 'Eversweet', or 'Angel Red') that ripens sooner. If your winters are cold (zone 7) or frosty, go with a tough Russian variety like 'Salavatski' or 'Kazake'. Every pomegranate makes fruit on its own, so one good plant is enough; a second only helps a little.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Whole pomegranates keep remarkably well at cool room temperature, out of direct sun, for several weeks; the leathery rind protects the arils. They do not ripen further off the plant, so store them as-is. A cool pantry or garage extends counter life; discard any fruit that is split or shows soft, moldy spots, which spread.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Whole pomegranates last a long time at cool room temperature, out of the sun, often several weeks, because the tough skin protects the seeds inside. They do not ripen more after picking, so just store them as they are. A cool pantry or garage helps them keep. Toss any that are split or have soft, moldy spots, since those spread.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerated whole, pomegranates keep for one to two months, and often longer, in a plastic bag in the crisper. Loose arils (seeds) keep about 5 to 7 days refrigerated in a sealed container. Pomegranate is not prone to chilling injury the way peaches are, so cold storage is the best way to hold the crop.
storage.fridge_beginner: Kept whole in the fridge, pomegranates last one to two months, sometimes longer, in a bag in the crisper drawer. Once you take the seeds out, they keep about 5 to 7 days in a sealed container in the fridge. Unlike peaches, pomegranates do not mind the cold, so the fridge is the best place to store them.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Pomegranate arils freeze excellently. Separate the seeds from the rind and membrane, spread them in a single layer on a tray to freeze, then transfer to freezer bags; they keep their quality for several months and thaw ready to use. Juice also freezes well. Freezing whole fruit is not recommended.
storage.freezer_beginner: The seeds (arils) freeze really well. Take the seeds out of the fruit, spread them on a tray to freeze, then pack them into freezer bags. They keep for several months and are ready to use when thawed. The juice freezes well too. Do not freeze the whole fruit.
storage.notes_seasoned: Pomegranate is one of the best-storing fruits: a tough rind and no chilling sensitivity mean whole fruit holds for weeks to months. The main storage enemy is split or wounded fruit, which molds, so cull those and store only sound fruit.
storage.notes_beginner: Pomegranates store better than almost any fruit: the tough skin and their tolerance of cold mean whole fruit keeps for weeks or months. The thing that spoils in storage is split or damaged fruit, which molds, so keep only the sound ones.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Annual crop rotation does not apply to a pomegranate, which holds its site for decades. Pomegranate has no strong replant-disease complex like stone fruit, so it is not fussy about the previous crop. The one real site concern is Armillaria (oak root fungus): avoid planting where oaks or other woody plants were recently removed on heavy, wet ground, and always choose a well-drained spot.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: You do not rotate a pomegranate the way you rotate vegetables, because it stays in one spot for many years. Unlike a peach, it does not have a strong replant problem, so what grew there before matters little. The main thing to avoid is a wet, poorly drained spot, especially where oaks or other trees were just removed, because a root fungus called Armillaria can live there.
rotation.good_after: any well-drained, sunny site; pomegranate has no stone-fruit-style replant-disease history and is easygoing about the previous crop
rotation.note_seasoned: Pomegranate's site rules are about drainage and light, not rotation: give it full sun and soil that drains, avoid low wet ground and recently cleared oak sites (Armillaria), and it will hold that spot productively for decades.
rotation.note_beginner: For a pomegranate, the site rules are about sun and drainage, not rotation: pick a sunny, well-drained spot, stay away from soggy ground and places where oaks were just removed, and it will grow there for many years.

growth_stages.name: Planting (bare-root or cutting-grown, dormant)
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Late winter to early spring, while dormant, after the hardest freezes and once the soil can be worked.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Late winter or early spring, while the plant is still bare and resting, after the worst cold and once the ground can be dug.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A dormant bare-root or potted plant with firm buds and healthy roots. Because pomegranate is on its own roots, there is no graft union to set above the soil line.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A leafless young plant with firm buds and healthy roots. Unlike a peach, there is no graft joint to keep above the soil, because a pomegranate grows on its own roots.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Set the plant at nursery depth in a wide hole (on a raised mound if the soil is heavy or wet), decide its form (multi-stem shrub or single tree), head it back to start it, backfill with native soil, water in well, and mulch.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Plant at the same depth it grew before, in a wide hole (on a raised mound if your soil is heavy or wet). Decide whether you want a bush or a small tree, cut it back a bit to start it, fill in with the soil you dug, water well, and mulch.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record the planting date and the cultivar you set.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note the day you planted and which variety it is.

growth_stages.name: Year-one establishment
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: The first full growing season after planting.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: The first whole growing season after you plant it.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Steady new shoot growth, vigorous base suckers, and a strengthening root system. Remove any flowers or fruit that form so energy goes to roots and framework.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Healthy new shoots, lots of shoots from the base (suckers), and a plant settling in. Pick off any flowers or fruit this first year so it can focus on roots and branches.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply and regularly through the first summer (the most water-sensitive period), keep a weed-free mulched circle around the base, manage suckers toward your chosen form, and remove first-year fruit.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Water deeply and often this first summer, since a new plant needs steady water to root in. Keep a mulched, weed-free circle around the base, pull the extra base shoots to shape it, and remove any fruit.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Log first-season watering and the date you removed first-year fruit.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note your watering and the day you removed the first-year fruit.

growth_stages.name: Framework and sucker management (years one to three)
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: The first three years, while you build the plant's form before reliable bearing.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: The first three years, while you shape the plant and before it fruits much.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Pomegranate is grown either as a multi-stem shrub (three to six strong trunks) or a single-trunk tree. It suckers freely from the base, and the main early task is choosing which shoots to keep and removing the rest to build an open framework.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Pomegranate is grown as a bush with several trunks or as a single small tree. It sends up lots of shoots from the base (suckers), and the main early job is picking which shoots to keep and pulling the rest to make an open, well-lit plant.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Each year select and keep the best-placed trunks or the single leader, remove competing suckers and crossing, inward, and low growth, and keep the center open so light and air reach the fruiting wood. Pomegranate fruits on spurs on two-plus-year-old wood and at the tips of new growth, so avoid heavy heading.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Each year keep the best trunks (or the single main stem) and cut away the extra base shoots and any branches that cross, crowd, or grow inward, keeping the middle open for light and air. Pomegranate fruits on older wood and shoot tips, so do not shear it back hard all over.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record each year's framework pruning and the trunks or leader retained.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you prune each year and which trunks or main stem you kept.

growth_stages.name: Winter dormancy
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Roughly December through February, the leafless months.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: About December through February, the leafless winter months.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A leafless plant at rest. Pomegranate needs only a short winter chill to break dormancy, so cold is rarely the limiter, but it is frost-tender: hard freezes can damage wood, especially before it is fully dormant or after buds swell.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A bare, resting plant. Pomegranate needs only a little winter cold to wake up properly, so cold is seldom the problem, but it is frost-tender: hard freezes can hurt the wood, especially in late fall and early spring.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Little is required. In cold-edge zones, protect young plants and container plants from hard freezes. Clear fallen leaves, mummified fruit, and debris that harbor disease. Established plants need minimal water now.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Not much to do. In cold areas, protect young or potted plants from hard freezes. Clean up fallen leaves and any old dried fruit that carry disease. An established plant needs very little water now.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Note any winter freeze protection and winter cleanup.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note any winter freeze protection and cleanup you did.

growth_stages.name: Dormant pruning
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Late dormancy, roughly February into March, just before growth resumes.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Late winter, around February into March, just before the plant wakes up.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare branches that show the plant's structure clearly. This is the time to maintain the open framework, thin crowded wood, and remove suckers before growth resumes.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Bare branches, so you can see the whole shape. This is the time to keep the plant open, thin crowded branches, and pull suckers before it starts growing.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Prune lightly to moderately in late dormancy: maintain the open shrub or tree form, remove dead, weak, crossing, and inward wood, thin to let in light, and clear base suckers. Avoid heavy heading, since much fruiting wood is on spurs on older wood and shoot tips. Make clean cuts.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Prune lightly in late winter: keep the open bush or tree shape, cut out dead, weak, crossing, or inward branches, thin to let light in, and remove the shoots from the base. Do not cut it back hard all over, because a lot of the fruit forms on older wood and shoot tips. Make clean cuts.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record the dormant pruning date and how heavily you cut.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note the day you pruned and how much you took off.

growth_stages.name: Bloom
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Late spring into early summer, roughly April through June, later than most deciduous fruit.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Late spring into early summer, about April through June, later than most fruit trees.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Showy orange-red flowers opening in successive flushes over several weeks. Pomegranate is self-fruitful, so a single plant sets fruit. Because bloom is late, spring frost is rarely a threat; humid, still air is the bigger risk to set.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Bright orange-red flowers opening a few at a time over several weeks. One plant makes fruit by itself. Because it blooms late, frost is rarely a problem; damp, still air is what hurts fruit set.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Little intervention is needed. Ensure good air movement and pollinator activity, and keep moisture steady as fruit begins to set. In humid climates, an open, breezy canopy reduces flower abortion and disease.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Not much to do. Make sure air moves through the plant and bees are active, and keep the water steady as fruit starts to form. In humid areas, an open, airy plant helps flowers set and cuts down disease.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record the bloom start date.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when bloom started.

growth_stages.name: Fruit set and even watering
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Late spring through summer, after bloom, as young fruit forms and sizes.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Late spring through summer, after the flowers, as small fruit forms and grows.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small round fruit developing from the flowers, with a persistent crown (the calyx) at the tip. This is when steady soil moisture becomes critical: uneven water from here to harvest is what splits the fruit.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Small round fruit forming from the flowers, with a little crown at the end. This is when steady watering really matters: uneven water from now until harvest is what cracks the fruit.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep soil moisture EVEN through fruit development, the single biggest lever against splitting. Thin lightly only if a young plant is overloaded. Monitor for leaf-footed bug, whose feeding damages the arils invisibly from inside.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist through the summer, which is the main way to stop the fruit from splitting. Thin a little only if a young plant has set too much. Watch for the leaf-footed bug, which damages the seeds inside without showing on the outside.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record fruit set and your watering pattern through summer.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when fruit set and how you watered through summer.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Late summer through late fall, roughly late August through November, varying by variety and region.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Late summer through late fall, about late August through November, depending on the variety and where you live.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fruit at full varietal color that feels heavy, sounds metallic when tapped, and has flattened to a slightly ridged shape. Pomegranate does not ripen further off the plant, and fruit left into the fall rains splits.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Fruit at full color that feels heavy, makes a light metallic sound when tapped, and has flattened into a more six-sided shape. Pomegranates do not ripen more after picking, and fruit left on into the fall rains cracks open.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick at full color, cutting (not pulling) with a short stem. Harvest ahead of significant rain to avoid splitting. Fruit stores for weeks to months; cull any split or moldy fruit as you go.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pick at full color, cutting the fruit off with clippers instead of pulling, leaving a little stem. Pick before big rains so it does not split. The fruit keeps for weeks or months; toss any split or moldy ones as you go.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record harvest dates and a rough yield.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you picked and roughly how much you got.

notifications.body_seasoned: Set a dormant bare-root or cutting-grown pomegranate now, after the hardest freezes, in a full-sun, well-drained spot (a raised mound on heavy or wet soil). It is on its own roots, so plant at nursery depth; there is no graft union to keep high. Decide its form now, multi-stem shrub or single tree, and head it back to start it.
notifications.body_beginner: Now is the time to plant a dormant pomegranate, after the worst cold, in a sunny spot with good drainage (a raised mound if your soil is heavy or wet). It grows on its own roots, so just plant it at the depth it grew before. Decide now whether you want a bush or a small tree, and cut it back a little to start it.

notifications.body_seasoned: Prune now, in late dormancy before growth resumes. Keep it light: maintain the open shrub or tree form, remove dead and crossing wood, thin for light and air, and clear base suckers. Avoid heavy heading, since much of the fruiting wood is on spurs on older wood and shoot tips.
notifications.body_beginner: Prune now, in late winter before it wakes up. Keep it light: hold the open bush or tree shape, cut out dead and crossing branches, thin so light gets in, and pull the shoots from the base. Do not cut it back hard all over, because a lot of the fruit grows on older wood and shoot tips.

notifications.body_seasoned: Your plant is opening its orange-red flowers, and it blooms over several weeks. Pomegranate is self-fruitful, so no second plant is needed. Because it blooms late, frost is rarely a threat; the risk to set is humid, still air, so keep the canopy open and airy, and keep soil moisture steady as fruit begins to form.
notifications.body_beginner: Your pomegranate is opening its orange-red flowers, a few at a time over several weeks. It makes fruit on its own, so you do not need a second plant. Because it blooms late, frost is rarely a problem; damp, still air is what hurts set, so keep the plant open and airy and the water steady as fruit starts to form.

notifications.title_beginner: Water evenly now to prevent splitting
notifications.body_seasoned: Fruit is sizing, and this is the window that decides whether it splits. Keep soil moisture EVEN from now to harvest: deep, regular soaks, no dry-then-flood swings. Uneven water, and the first fall rains, are what crack pomegranates. Watch too for leaf-footed bug, whose feeding damages the arils invisibly from inside.
notifications.body_beginner: The fruit is filling out, and this is when splitting is decided. Keep the soil evenly moist from now until harvest: deep, regular watering, and avoid letting it go dry and then soaking it. Uneven water, and the first fall rains, are what crack pomegranates. Also watch for the leaf-footed bug, which damages the seeds inside without showing on the outside.

notifications.body_seasoned: Through its first two summers a pomegranate is at its most water-sensitive while roots establish; it becomes drought-tolerant only afterward. Water deeply and regularly at the root zone, keep a mulched, weed-free circle around the base, and manage the freely produced suckers toward your chosen shrub or tree form.
notifications.body_beginner: For its first couple of summers, a young pomegranate needs steady water while its roots get going; it only becomes drought-tough later. Give it a deep soak regularly, keep a mulched, weed-free ring around the base, and pull the extra base shoots to shape it into a bush or a tree.

notifications.body_seasoned: Harvest is near. Pomegranate does not ripen off the plant, so pick at full varietal color: the rind goes matte, the fruit feels heavy, sounds metallic when tapped, and flattens to a ridged shape. Pick ahead of significant rain, because fruit left through the rains splits. Cut, do not pull, leaving a short stem.
notifications.body_beginner: Harvest is close. Pomegranates do not ripen after picking, so pick at full color: the skin turns dull, the fruit feels heavy, sounds metallic when tapped, and flattens into a six-sided shape. Pick before big rains, because fruit left out through the rain will crack. Cut it off with clippers, leaving a little stem, instead of pulling.

notifications.body_seasoned: As the plant drops its leaves, clear any split, rotted, or mummified fruit from the plant and ground and rake fallen debris. These carry over black heart, gray mold, and fruit spot to next season, so this cleanup is your cheapest disease control. In cold-edge zones, plan freeze protection for young and container plants.
notifications.body_beginner: As the leaves drop, pick off any split, rotted, or dried-up fruit from the plant and ground and rake up the litter. That old fruit carries diseases into next year, so clearing it is the easiest way to prevent them. In cold areas, get ready to protect young and potted plants from hard freezes.

notifications.title_seasoned: Anything to log on the pomegranate?
notifications.body_seasoned: It has been a while since your last note. A quick check pays off: scan for leaf-footed bug and sucking pests, confirm suckers are managed, and note where bloom and harvest landed this year so you can compare next season.
notifications.body_beginner: It has been a while since you logged anything. A quick look is worth it: check for leaf-footed bug and other pests, make sure the base shoots are pulled, and jot down when the plant bloomed and when you picked so you can compare next year.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Heavy rain, watch ripe fruit
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Rain on ripening pomegranates, especially after a dry spell, is the classic cause of splitting: the rind cannot keep up as the arils take up water fast. After a soaking rain, check ripening fruit and pick anything at full color rather than leaving it to crack. Keeping soil moisture even all season, so the rain is not a sudden change, is the best defense.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Rain on ripening pomegranates, especially after a dry stretch, is the classic cause of splitting: the skin cannot keep up as the seeds soak up water fast. After a heavy rain, check the ripening fruit and pick anything at full color instead of leaving it to crack. Keeping the water steady all season, so the rain is not a sudden change, is the best protection.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost warning, protect the plant
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Pomegranate is frost-tender, and it is most vulnerable before full dormancy in late fall and after buds swell in early spring. If a hard freeze is forecast, protect young plants and container plants: cover them, move pots to shelter, and water the soil beforehand, since moist ground holds heat. A severe freeze may kill the top, but an established plant usually resprouts from its own roots.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Pomegranate is frost-tender, and it is most at risk in late fall before it goes fully dormant and in early spring after the buds swell. If a hard freeze is coming, protect young and potted plants: cover them, move pots to shelter, and water the soil first, since damp ground stays warmer. A hard freeze may kill the top, but an established plant usually grows back from its roots.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Humid spell, watch set and fruit disease
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Muggy weather, watch flowers and fruit
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Warm, humid, still conditions hurt pomegranate two ways: flowers may fail to set or abort at bloom, and fruit diseases (Alternaria black heart, gray mold, Cercospora spot) build up. There is no spraying it away mid-spell: keep the canopy open and airy, water at the root zone, remove any rotting fruit, and manage fruit-piercing pests that open the door to internal rot.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Warm, muggy, still weather hurts pomegranate two ways: flowers may not set or may drop at bloom, and fruit diseases build up. You cannot spray it away once it is muggy, so keep the plant open and airy, water at the ground, pick off any rotting fruit, and control the bugs that pierce the fruit and let rot start inside.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Dry spell, keep the water steady
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Pomegranate is drought-tolerant once established, but two windows still need water: a young plant putting down roots, and fruit development, when EVEN moisture prevents splitting. In a dry stretch, soak deeply and regularly so the soil never swings from bone-dry to wet; it is the swing, more than the dryness, that cracks the fruit.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Pomegranate handles drought once established, but two times still need water: a young plant getting its roots down, and while the fruit is filling, when steady moisture keeps it from splitting. In a dry spell, water deeply and regularly so the soil does not swing from bone-dry to soaked; it is the swing, more than the dryness, that cracks the fruit.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Very hot spell, shade exposed fruit
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Pomegranate thrives in heat, and heat is what ripens sweet, well-colored fruit, but during an extreme heat spell fruit on the sun-exposed side can sunburn, showing as bleached, tan, or blistered patches that later rot. Keep the plant well watered so heat and drought stress do not stack, and leave enough canopy to shade the fruit when you prune.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Pomegranate loves heat, and heat is what makes the fruit sweet and colorful, but in an extreme hot spell the fruit on the sunny side can sunburn, showing as pale, tan, or blistered patches that may rot later. Keep the plant watered so heat and dryness do not hit at once, and when you prune, leave enough leaves to shade the fruit.

planting.text_seasoned: Pomegranate is on its own roots (cutting-grown), not grafted, so there is no graft union to keep above the soil. Set it at the depth it grew in the nursery.
planting.text_beginner: A pomegranate grows on its own roots, not grafted like a peach, so there is no graft joint to worry about. Just plant it at the same depth it was already growing.
planting.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

planting.text_seasoned: Plant in full sun on well-drained ground; on heavy or wet soil, plant on a raised mound. Waterlogged roots are the one thing pomegranate will not tolerate.
planting.text_beginner: Plant where it gets full sun and the soil drains. If your soil is heavy or wet, plant on a raised mound. Soggy roots are the one thing a pomegranate cannot handle.
planting.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

establishment.text_seasoned: Keep a young pomegranate evenly watered through its first summer to establish roots; it becomes drought-tolerant only once established.
establishment.text_beginner: Water a young pomegranate deeply and often through its first summer so the roots get going. It only becomes drought-tough after it is established.
establishment.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

establishment.text_seasoned: Decide the form early, multi-stem shrub or single tree, and manage the freely produced base suckers accordingly from year one.
establishment.text_beginner: Decide early whether you want a bush or a small tree, and from the first year pull the extra shoots that pop up from the base to shape it.
establishment.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

shrub_formation.text_seasoned: Pomegranate fruits on spurs on older wood and on shoot tips, so prune to shape and open the plant rather than heading it back hard, which removes fruiting wood.
shrub_formation.text_beginner: Pomegranate makes fruit on older wood and on the tips of new shoots, so prune to shape and open it up rather than cutting it back hard all over, which cuts off the fruiting wood.
shrub_formation.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

dormancy.text_seasoned: Pomegranate is frost-tender: protect young and container plants from hard freezes, and expect that a plant frozen back will often resprout true-to-type from its own roots.
dormancy.text_beginner: Pomegranate can be hurt by hard freezes: protect young and potted plants in cold snaps. If a plant does freeze back, it usually grows again from the base as the same variety, because it is on its own roots.
dormancy.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Prune in late dormancy: thin for light and air, remove dead and crossing wood, and clear base suckers. Keep it light, and make clean cuts.
dormant_prune.text_beginner: Prune in late winter: thin the plant so light and air get in, cut out dead and crossing branches, and remove the base shoots. Keep it light and make clean cuts.
dormant_prune.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

bloom.text_seasoned: Pomegranate is self-fruitful and blooms late over several weeks, so it largely dodges spring frost. Humid, still air at bloom, not frost, is the main threat to fruit set.
bloom.text_beginner: Pomegranate makes fruit on its own and blooms late over several weeks, so it usually avoids spring frost. Damp, still air during bloom, not frost, is the main thing that hurts fruit set.
bloom.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Keep soil moisture EVEN from fruit set to harvest. A dry spell followed by heavy water or rain is what splits pomegranates, the single most common failure.
fruit_set.text_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist from the time fruit forms until harvest. Going dry and then soaking (or a big rain) is what splits pomegranates, the most common problem there is.
fruit_set.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Scout for leaf-footed bug from fruit set on. Its feeding leaves no external mark but darkens and withers the arils inside and opens the fruit to internal rot.
fruit_set.text_beginner: Watch for the leaf-footed bug once fruit forms. Its feeding leaves no mark outside but darkens and shrivels the seeds inside and lets rot start in the fruit.
fruit_set.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest ahead of the fall rains. Pomegranate does not ripen off the plant, so pick at full color; fruit left through rain splits.
harvest.text_beginner: Pick before the fall rains. Pomegranates do not ripen after picking, so wait for full color, but fruit left out through the rain will crack.
harvest.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

harvest.text_seasoned: Cut, do not pull, the fruit, leaving a short stem. Whole pomegranates then store for weeks to months, and unlike peaches they are not chill-sensitive, so refrigerate freely.
harvest.text_beginner: Cut the fruit off with clippers instead of pulling, leaving a little stem. Whole pomegranates keep for weeks or months, and unlike peaches they do not mind the cold, so the fridge is fine.
harvest.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A mature pomegranate (roughly years 5 and up) commonly yields about 50 to 100-plus fruit per plant, on the order of 30 to 60 pounds, depending on cultivar, size, pruning, and climate fit. Hot, dry sites with even watering produce the heaviest, best-colored crops; cool or humid sites yield less and lower quality.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: A grown pomegranate (about year 5 onward) usually gives roughly 50 to over 100 fruit a year, something like 30 to 60 pounds, depending on the variety, its size, pruning, and how well your climate suits it. Hot, dry gardens with steady watering give the biggest, best crops; cool or humid gardens give less and lower quality.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Plants reach full bearing around years 5 to 6 and stay productive for decades, often well beyond 30 years, given full sun, even moisture, and annual pruning to keep the canopy open and renew fruiting wood.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: A pomegranate hits full production around years 5 to 6 and keeps producing for decades, often much longer than 30 years, as long as it gets full sun, steady water, and yearly pruning to keep it open and growing fresh fruiting wood.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Expect no crop in the planting year and little in year 2. Remove any early fruit so the plant builds roots and framework; the first meaningful harvest typically comes around years 2 to 3, with full bearing by years 5 to 6.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Do not expect fruit the first year, or much the second. If a few fruit form early, pick them off so the plant can grow strong roots and branches. Your first real harvest usually comes around years 2 to 3, with full crops by years 5 to 6.
factors_seasoned: cultivar and climate fit
summer heat accumulation (color and sweetness)
even moisture from set to harvest (split prevention)
annual pruning and sucker management
fruit and root disease pressure (humid climates)
leaf-footed bug and other fruit-piercing pests
plant age and establishment

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No moon-phase planting preference is asserted. Extension sources do not support timing pomegranate planting or care by lunar phase; climate fit, even watering, and harvest timing ahead of rain govern outcomes.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: The fruit split open on the plant
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The fruit cracked open on the plant
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Ripening or ripe fruit cracked, often exposing the arils. This is the signature pomegranate failure, and it is a water problem, not a disease: the rind splits when the arils take up water faster than the skin can stretch, which happens when moisture swings from dry to wet, after a heavy irrigation or the first fall rains following a dry spell. It is tempting to blame the variety, but the fix is watering and timing: keep soil moisture EVEN from fruit set through harvest, and pick ahead of significant rain rather than leaving fruit on the plant.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Ripe or nearly ripe fruit cracked open, sometimes showing the seeds. This is the number-one pomegranate problem, and it is about water, not disease: the skin splits when the seeds soak up water faster than the skin can stretch, which happens when the watering swings from dry to wet, after a big watering or the first fall rains following a dry stretch. It is easy to blame the variety, but the fix is how you water and when you pick: keep the soil evenly moist from the time fruit forms until harvest, and pick before big rains instead of leaving fruit out.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Keep soil moisture even all through fruit development (deep, regular watering, no dry-then-flood swings), mulch to buffer the soil, and harvest at full color ahead of the fall rains.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Water evenly all summer while the fruit fills (deep, regular soaks, no going dry and then soaking), mulch to steady the soil, and pick at full color before the fall rains come.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: The plant flowered but set little or no fruit
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: It flowered but I got almost no fruit
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The plant bloomed but few or no fruit formed. On pomegranate the usual causes are a young plant (it takes 2 to 3 years to begin bearing and 5 to 6 for full crops), humid or cool, still weather at bloom that causes flowers to abort, or excess nitrogen driving leaves and suckers over flowers. People often assume it needs a pollinator partner, but pomegranate is self-fruitful and a lone plant should set. The real levers are patience, an open sunny breezy site, and restrained feeding.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The plant flowered but barely fruited. On pomegranate the usual reasons are a young plant (it takes 2 to 3 years to start fruiting and 5 to 6 for full crops), damp or cool, still weather during bloom that makes the flowers drop, or too much nitrogen growing leaves and shoots instead of flowers. People often think it needs a partner plant, but pomegranate makes fruit on its own. The real fixes are patience, an open, sunny, breezy spot, and going easy on fertilizer.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Give a young plant time, site it in open, sunny, breezy ground so bloom-time air is not humid and still, and keep nitrogen feeding light so the plant favors fruit over leafy growth.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Give a young plant a few years, plant it in an open, sunny, breezy spot so the bloom-time air is not damp and still, and go easy on nitrogen so it makes fruit instead of leaves.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: The fruit looked fine but was rotten inside
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The fruit looked okay but was rotten inside
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: A fruit that looked nearly normal outside was brown and moldy inside when cut. This is Alternaria heart rot (black heart): the fungus infects through the flower in wet or humid bloom weather, or enters through insect punctures (notably leaf-footed bug), and rots the interior with little or no external sign. There is no cure once it is inside. It is far less of a problem in hot, dry climates, so the controls are climate, pest management, and sanitation, not a spray.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: A fruit that looked almost fine on the outside was brown and moldy inside when you cut it. This is Alternaria heart rot, or black heart: a fungus gets in through the flower in damp bloom weather, or through insect holes (especially from the leaf-footed bug), and rots the inside with little sign outside. There is no cure once it is inside. It is much less of a problem in hot, dry weather, so the fixes are climate, pest control, and cleanup, not a spray.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Favor hot, dry-summer siting and open, airy canopies, control leaf-footed bug and other fruit-piercing pests, water at the ground rather than overhead, and remove infected and mummified fruit so spores do not carry over.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Grow it in a hot, dry, open, airy spot if you can, control the leaf-footed bug and other fruit-piercing pests, water at the ground instead of over the top, and clean up any rotted or old dried fruit so it does not spread.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: The fruit was pale, sour, or small
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The fruit was pale, sour, or small
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The fruit ripened but was poorly colored, bland or sour, or undersized. The most common cause is not enough summer heat: pomegranate needs a long, hot season (roughly temperatures above 85°F for 120-plus days) to build color and sugar, so cool coastal or short-summer sites give lower-quality fruit even on a healthy plant. Over-watering late, under-thinning on a young plant, or picking underripe (pomegranate does not ripen off the plant) also dull quality. The fix is climate fit, variety choice, and picking at full color.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The fruit ripened but was pale, bland or sour, or small. The most common reason is not enough summer heat: pomegranate needs a long, hot summer to build color and sweetness, so cool coastal or short-summer spots give lower-quality fruit even on a healthy plant. Watering too much late, letting a young plant carry too much fruit, or picking too early (it does not ripen after picking) also hurt quality. The fix is matching the climate, choosing the right variety, and picking at full color.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: In cooler or shorter-summer areas, choose an early, sweeter variety (Granada, Eversweet, Angel Red), give it the hottest, sunniest spot you have, keep water even, and pick only at full color.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: In cooler or shorter-summer areas, pick an early, sweeter variety (Granada, Eversweet, Angel Red), give it the hottest, sunniest spot you have, keep the water steady, and only pick when it is at full color.

succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Succession planting does not apply to pomegranate. It is a permanent shrub or small tree that occupies its site for decades and bears one crop each season as the fruit ripens in fall, so there is no staggered re-sowing to schedule the way there is for a short-season annual crop.

open_findings.summary: self-fruitful is BACKED (UGA verbatim); the finer nuances (bears perfect + functionally-male flowers, bee/wind pollinated, a second plant modestly improves set) are correct but not on a cited T1 page -- accepted as general horticultural fact / modeled.

chill_hours_range [100,250] is modeled/corroborated: UGA states most cultivars need essentially no chill (qualitative); the band is bracketed by TAMU (~100-200) + UC MG (~200-300), not lifted from a single cited page.

3.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 3 winter lows (to -40°F) are far below any pomegranate's survival threshold; the plant is killed outright. Not a pomegranate zone.
3.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 3 is far too cold for pomegranate to survive. This is not a pomegranate zone.

4.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 4 lows (-20 to -30°F) kill even the hardiest pomegranate cultivars. Not a pomegranate zone.
4.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 4 is too cold for pomegranate. This is not a pomegranate zone.

5.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 5 lows (-10 to -20°F) are below the survival threshold of even cold-hardy pomegranates. Not a pomegranate zone.
5.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 5 is too cold for pomegranate to survive. This is not a pomegranate zone.

6.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 6 lows (-10 to 0°F) exceed what even hardy cultivars endure; the plant is killed or frozen to the ground and does not fruit. Effectively unsuitable outside rare protected microclimates.
6.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 6 (down to about -10°F) is too cold for dependable pomegranate; the plant is killed or frozen back and does not fruit. Treat it as too cold except in unusually warm, sheltered spots.

7.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 7 (0 to 10°F) is the cold edge for pomegranate. Cold-hardy Russian cultivars (Salavatski, Kazake) survive here on warm, protected, hot-summer sites and crop in good years; standard cultivars are unreliable, and a hard freeze can take a season or kill the top. A plant frozen back usually resprouts from its own roots.
7.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 7 (down to about 0 to 10°F) is the cold edge for pomegranate. Tough Russian varieties like Salavatski survive here in warm, sheltered spots and fruit in good years, but common varieties are unreliable and a hard freeze can cost a crop. If it freezes back, it usually grows again from the base.
7.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Late fall and early spring frosts are the main risk here: protect young plants, and expect a crop only in years that escape hard freezes. Choose a cold-hardy cultivar and the warmest, most protected site.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the north, pomegranate is at the edge of what it can take. Zones 3 through 6 are generally too cold, freezing the plant back. Only zone 7 gives a marginal crop, and only with a tough Russian variety in a warm, sheltered, hot-summer spot. Expect some frost damage and off years even then.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Across the northern tier, pomegranate is at its cold limit. It is generally too cold-tender for the colder zones (3 to 6), where hard winters kill it back; only zone 7 offers a marginal crop, and only with a cold-hardy Russian cultivar on a warm, protected, hot-summer site. Even there, expect frost setbacks and off years.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 8 Gulf is warm with ample heat and adequate chill, but humid, rainy conditions cause uneven fruit set and fruit diseases, and wet spells split ripening fruit. Marginal for quality: the plant thrives, the fruit is the challenge. Open, breezy, well-drained sites do best.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 8 on the Gulf is warm with plenty of heat, but the humidity and rain make fruit set uneven and bring fruit diseases, and wet spells split the fruit. The plant does great; the fruit is the hard part. Open, breezy, well-drained spots work best.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 Gulf has abundant heat and a long season but the region's humidity and rainfall still cap fruit quality through disease and splitting. Marginal: reliable growth, unreliable clean fruit. Choose open, airy, well-drained ground.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 9 on the Gulf has lots of heat and a long season, but the humidity and rain still limit fruit quality through disease and splitting. Marginal: the plant grows well, the fruit is iffy. Choose an open, airy, well-drained spot.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: The humid Gulf Southeast is warm enough for pomegranate but only so-so for good fruit. There is plenty of heat and enough winter cold, but the humidity and rain cause poor fruit set and fruit diseases, and wet spells split the fruit. The plants grow and flower fine; getting clean, dependable fruit is the hard part. Pick the most open, breezy, well-drained spot you can.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: The humid Gulf Southeast is warm enough for pomegranate but marginal for quality. Ample warmth and low chill are met, but high humidity and rain drive poor fruit set and fruit diseases (Cercospora spot, black heart, gray mold) and split-inducing wet spells. Plants grow and flower well; dependable, clean fruit is the hard part. Favor the most open, breezy, well-drained sites.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 8 interior is prime: hot, dry summers and ample chill ripen top-quality fruit across the full variety range. Keep summer moisture even to prevent splitting; disease pressure is low in the dry air.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 8 in the interior valleys is ideal: hot, dry summers and plenty of winter cold ripen excellent fruit, and almost any variety works. Keep the summer watering even to prevent splitting; disease is low in the dry air.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 interior is prime pomegranate country: long, hot, dry summers and adequate chill produce reliable, well-colored, sweet fruit. Full variety range; even summer watering is the main task.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 9 in the interior valleys is prime pomegranate country: long, hot, dry summers and enough winter cold give reliable, sweet, colorful fruit. Almost any variety works; even summer watering is the main job.

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: California's hot, dry interior valleys are the BEST place for pomegranate, and where most of the commercial crop grows. Long, hot, dry summers make deeply colored, sweet fruit, the winters give enough cold, and the dry air keeps fruit diseases down. Almost any variety works. Steady summer watering to prevent splitting is the main job.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: California's hot, dry interior valleys are PRIME pomegranate country, the heart of commercial production. Long, hot, dry summers ripen deeply colored, sweet fruit; low chill is easily met; and the dry air keeps fruit disease minimal. The whole variety range is open. Steady summer watering to prevent split is the main task.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 North Coast is frost-safe but heat-limited: cool, foggy summers give lower color and sweetness than the interior. Fruit sets and ripens but is second-tier. Favor the warmest inland sites and an early, sweeter cultivar.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 9 on the North Coast is safe from frost but short on heat: cool, foggy summers give less color and sweetness than inland. The fruit sets and ripens but is not top quality. Choose the warmest inland spot and an early, sweeter variety.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 10 North Coast is mild and frost-free but summer heat is marginal for full ripening, so fruit quality trails the interior. It fruits on the warmest sites; expect paler, more tart fruit than in hot inland gardens.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 10 on the North Coast is mild and frost-free, but the summer heat is marginal for fully ripening the fruit, so quality trails inland gardens. It fruits in the warmest spots; expect paler, more tart fruit.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: The cool, foggy North Coast is marginal for pomegranate. Winters are mild, so frost is not the problem; the issue is summer heat. Cool, overcast summers do not give the heat pomegranate needs to fully color and sweeten, so the fruit tends to be paler and more sour. It fruits, but not as well as inland. Pick the warmest inland pocket and an early, sweeter variety.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: The cool, foggy North Coast is marginal for pomegranate. Winters are mild and frost is not the issue; the limiter is summer heat. Cool, overcast summers do not bank the heat pomegranate needs to color and sweeten fully, so fruit tends to be paler and more sour. It fruits, but quality lags the interior. Choose the warmest inland pocket and an early, sweeter cultivar.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 South Coast (warm inland Southern California) ripens pomegranate reliably: warm, fairly dry summers and mild winters produce good, well-colored fruit across most varieties. Keep summer moisture even to prevent splitting.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 9 on the warm inland South Coast ripens pomegranate dependably: warm, fairly dry summers and mild winters give good, colorful fruit from most varieties. Keep summer watering even to prevent splitting.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 10 South Coast is frost-free and warm but the immediate coast's cooler, moister summers make it marginal for peak quality. It fruits well on the warmest, sunniest sites; quality is best inland from the fog.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 10 on the South Coast is frost-free and warm, but the cooler, damper air right at the coast makes it only okay for top-quality fruit. It fruits well in the warmest, sunniest spots; the best fruit is inland from the fog.

ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: The warmer South Coast grows pomegranate well inland and okay right at the coast. Warm, fairly dry summers and mild winters suit it; inland areas (zone 9) ripen good fruit dependably, while the cooler, foggier coast (zone 10) is fine but lower quality. It is a common, easy backyard fruit here.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: The warmer South Coast fruits pomegranate well inland and marginally at the immediate coast. Warm, fairly dry summers and mild winters suit it; inland valleys (zone 9) ripen good fruit reliably, while the cooler coastal fog belt (zone 10) is adequate but lower quality. A common, easy dooryard fruit here.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 desert is prime: intense heat and dry air ripen richly colored, sweet fruit with little disease, and chill is met. Even irrigation from set to harvest is the key task in the desert's dry extremes.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 9 in the desert is prime: intense heat and dry air ripen deep-colored, sweet fruit with little disease, and there is enough winter cold. Even, steady watering from fruit set to harvest is the main task in the dry desert.
