10.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 10 desert is the hottest, earliest-ripening pomegranate ground: superb color and sweetness, minimal disease, low chill easily met. Prioritize even, deep irrigation to prevent split in the extreme heat.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 10 in the desert is the hottest, earliest-ripening spot: superb color and sweetness, little disease, and plenty of the low winter cold it needs. Focus on even, deep watering to prevent splitting in the extreme heat.

ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: The California low desert is a PRIME spot for pomegranate: intense summer heat and very dry air make deeply colored, sweet fruit with little disease, and the low chill need is easily met. The fruit ripens early. The one thing to watch is watering, since the desert's extremes make even, steady watering (and preventing splits) important.
ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: The California low desert is PRIME for pomegranate: intense summer heat and very dry air produce deeply colored, sweet fruit with minimal disease, and low chill is easily met. Ripening runs early. The one discipline is irrigation, since the desert's extremes make even watering (and split prevention) essential.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 8 warm-arid fruits pomegranate reliably: hot, dry summers and ample chill ripen quality fruit with low disease. A cold-hardy cultivar is a safe pick where winters run cold. Keep summer moisture even.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 8 in the warm, dry inland Southwest fruits pomegranate dependably: hot, dry summers and plenty of winter cold ripen good fruit with little disease. A hardy variety is a safe choice where winters get cold. Keep summer watering even.

warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: The warm, dry inland Southwest is excellent for pomegranate: hot, dry summers ripen sweet, colorful fruit with little disease, and there is plenty of winter cold. Winters can be cold enough that a hardy variety is wise at the edges, but zone 8 fruits dependably. Even summer watering prevents splitting.
warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: The warm, arid inland Southwest is excellent pomegranate country: hot, dry summers ripen sweet, well-colored fruit with low disease pressure, and chill is amply met. Winters are cold enough to demand a cold-hardy cultivar at the colder margins, but zone 8 fruits reliably. Even summer watering prevents split.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 Arizona low desert is prime: intense heat and dry air ripen deeply colored, sweet fruit early with minimal disease, and chill is met. Even, deep irrigation to prevent split is the main discipline.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 9 in the Arizona low desert is prime: intense heat and dry air ripen deep-colored, sweet fruit early with little disease, and there is enough winter cold. Even, deep watering to prevent splitting is the main task.

low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: The Arizona low desert (Phoenix, Tucson) is a PRIME spot for pomegranate: extreme summer heat and very dry air give excellent color and sweetness with little fruit disease, and the low winter cold need is easily met. It is a classic desert-yard fruit here. It ripens early; even, deep watering prevents splitting.
low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: The Arizona low desert (Phoenix, Tucson) is PRIME pomegranate country: extreme summer heat and very dry air produce excellent color and sweetness with minimal fruit disease, and low chill is easily met. It is a classic desert-landscape fruit here. Ripening is early; even, deep irrigation prevents split.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 10 Florida is warm and frost-free with marginally adequate chill, but humidity, rain, and disease pressure cap fruit quality and cause splitting. Marginal: the plant grows and sets some fruit in drier spells, but clean, reliable fruit is difficult.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 10 Florida is warm and frost-free with just barely enough winter cold, but humidity, rain, and disease limit fruit quality and cause splitting. Marginal: the plant grows and sets some fruit in drier spells, but clean, dependable fruit is hard to get.

11.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 11 Florida is frost-free but banks too little winter chill (near zero) and is too humid for dependable fruiting: the plant survives and may flower, but does not set a reliable crop. Treat it as an ornamental here.
11.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 11 Florida is frost-free but gets almost no winter cold and is too humid for dependable fruit: the plant lives and may flower but does not reliably fruit. Treat it as an ornamental here.

fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: The Florida peninsula is warm and frost-free but a poor fit for pomegranate: high humidity and frequent rain cause poor fruit set, fruit diseases, and splitting, and the far south gets little winter cold. The plants grow and flower, but getting clean, dependable fruit is hard, and it gets worse toward the humid, nearly chill-free tip.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: The Florida peninsula is warm and frost-free but poorly suited to pomegranate: high humidity and frequent rain drive poor fruit set, fruit diseases (fruit spot, black heart, rot), and splitting, and the far south banks little winter chill. Plants grow and flower, but clean, dependable fruit is difficult, declining toward the humid, near-chill-free tip.

11.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 11 Hawaii is frost-free but banks essentially no winter chill and is humid, so pomegranate does not go dormant properly and does not fruit reliably. The plant survives and may flower but should be treated as an ornamental.
11.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 11 Hawaii is frost-free but gets almost no winter cold and is humid, so pomegranate does not rest properly and does not reliably fruit. The plant lives and may flower but is best treated as an ornamental.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: Tropical Hawaii is frost-free but a poor fit for pomegranate: almost no winter cold and humid, wet weather mean the plant does not rest properly and fruits poorly at best, with lots of fruit disease. It grows and may flower, but do not count on a dependable crop except maybe in the driest, sunniest leeward spots.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: Tropical Hawaii is frost-free but poorly suited to pomegranate: near-zero winter chill and humid, wet conditions mean the plant does not go properly dormant and fruits erratically at best, with heavy fruit disease. It grows as an ornamental and may flower, but a dependable crop should not be expected outside the driest, sunniest leeward pockets.

crops.description_seasoned: Pomegranate (Punica granatum) is a deciduous, multi-stemmed fruiting shrub, easily trained to a small tree, that thrives on exactly the hot, dry summers most fruit dreads. It is self-fruitful, so a single plant bears, and it is one of the most forgiving fruits a warm-climate gardener can grow: drought-tolerant once established, tolerant of alkaline and heavy soils given drainage, and needing only a short winter chill. The catch is climate fit. Pomegranate wants a long, hot, dry season to ripen sweet, well-colored fruit, so it is superb in California's interior valleys and the low deserts and merely marginal in cool-summer coastal or humid southeastern gardens, where poor set and fruit disease follow the humidity. Its signature failure is splitting: fruit cracks when water swings from dry to wet near ripening, so steady moisture and picking ahead of the fall rains are the two habits that make or break a crop.
crops.description_beginner: A pomegranate is a leafy shrub, easily trained into a small tree, that loves hot, dry summers, the kind of weather that gives most fruit trouble. One plant makes fruit on its own, so you do not need a second one. It is one of the easiest fruits to grow in a warm climate: once it is established it handles drought, poor and salty soils (as long as they drain), and it needs only a little winter cold. The main thing is where you live. Pomegranate needs a long, hot, dry summer to ripen sweet, richly colored fruit, so it is wonderful in hot inland and desert gardens and only so-so in cool foggy coastal spots or humid, rainy areas, where the fruit sets poorly and gets diseases. Its big weak spot is splitting: the fruit cracks open when the watering swings from dry to wet near ripening, so keep the water steady and pick before the fall rains.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: A pomegranate is ready when the rind takes on full varietal color (deep red for 'Wonderful'), shifts from glossy to a slightly matte finish, and the fruit's round shape flattens to a faintly hexagonal, ridged profile as the arils swell and press outward. A ripe fruit feels heavy for its size and makes a metallic, tinny sound when tapped. Pomegranate does not ripen further once picked, so pick at full color; but pick a touch early rather than late, because fruit left on the tree into the fall rains splits. Cut, do not pull, the fruit, leaving a short stem so you do not tear the rind.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: A pomegranate is ripe when the skin turns its full color (deep red for 'Wonderful'), goes from shiny to a little dull, and the round fruit flattens into more of a six-sided shape as the seeds inside swell. A ripe one feels heavy and makes a light metallic, tinny sound when you tap it. Pomegranates do not get sweeter after you pick them, so wait for full color, but do not leave them too long, because fruit left on the tree once the fall rains start will crack open. Cut the fruit off with clippers instead of pulling, and leave a little stem so you do not tear the skin.
crops.bloom_time_seasoned: Pomegranate leafs out late and blooms late, opening its showy orange-red flowers from mid-spring into early summer (roughly April through June depending on region and heat). Unlike early-blooming stone fruit, its late, extended bloom largely sidesteps spring frost; flowers open in successive flushes over several weeks, and only a fraction set fruit. High humidity or still air at bloom is the real enemy of set, so hot, dry, breezy bloom weather is what a good crop wants.
crops.bloom_time_beginner: Pomegranates leaf out late and flower late, opening bright orange-red blooms from the middle of spring into early summer (about April through June depending on where you live). Because it blooms late, it usually escapes the spring frosts that ruin early fruit like peaches. The flowers open a few at a time over several weeks, and only some of them turn into fruit. Damp, humid, still weather at bloom is the biggest problem for fruit set, so hot, dry, breezy weather during flowering gives the best crop.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Pomegranate is the cold-tender member of this group: it survives winters across roughly zones 7 to 11 but is damaged by hard freezes. Standard cultivars like 'Wonderful' tolerate winter lows to about 10 to 15°F; the cold-hardy Russian types (Salavatski and kin) push to around 7°F, and a plant cut back by a severe freeze often resprouts from the base. It is also frost-sensitive in the shoulder seasons, before it is fully dormant in late fall and after buds swell in early spring. Surviving is only half the story: RELIABLE, well-colored fruit needs a long hot summer (roughly temperatures above 85°F for 120-plus days), so the dependable-fruit band is the hot-summer heart of zones 8 to 10. Zone 7 is the cold edge for hardy cultivars on protected sites, and the frost-free tropics (zone 11) are limited by humidity and too little chill or dry heat, not by cold.
crops.hardiness_notes_beginner: Pomegranate is the least cold-hardy fruit in this group. It lives through winters in about zones 7 through 11, but hard freezes hurt it. Common varieties like 'Wonderful' take winter lows down to around 10 to 15°F; tough Russian varieties handle closer to 7°F, and a plant frozen back hard will often grow again from the base. It is also touchy about frost in late fall before it goes fully dormant and in early spring after the buds swell. But just living is not enough for good fruit: pomegranate needs a long, hot summer to ripen sweet, colorful fruit, so you get the most dependable crops in the hot parts of zones 8, 9, and 10. Zone 7 is the cold edge, best with a hardy variety in a warm, sheltered spot, and the frost-free tropics fall short because of humidity and too little cold, not because of frost.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Pomegranate needs only a short winter chill, on the order of 100 to 250 chill hours (hours between 32 and 45°F) depending on cultivar, far less than peach or apple. That low requirement is met almost everywhere it is grown, including the low deserts, so chill is rarely the limiter; the frost-free tropics are the only places that may fall short. The real climate driver for pomegranate is the opposite end of the season: it needs a long stretch of summer heat to ripen sweet, well-colored fruit, which is why hot interior and desert sites outperform cool coastal ones regardless of chill.
crops.chill_hours_note_beginner: Pomegranate needs only a little winter cold, about 100 to 250 chill hours (hours between 32 and 45°F), which is much less than a peach or apple. Almost everywhere it is grown gets enough, even the low deserts, so cold in winter is hardly ever the problem. What pomegranate really needs is the other side of the year: a long, hot summer to make the fruit sweet and deeply colored. That is why it does so much better in hot inland and desert gardens than in cool, foggy coastal ones.
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Pomegranate is self-fruitful: a single plant sets a crop on its own, with no pollinizer partner required. It carries both perfect (fruit-forming) and functionally male flowers on the same plant, and it is pollinated by insects (chiefly bees) and by wind. Because self-pollination works, a lone plant fruits, but planting a second pomegranate nearby, or simply supporting bee activity at bloom, can improve fruit set. Poor set is far more often a weather problem (humid, still, or cool bloom conditions cause flowers to abort) than a pollination-partner problem.
crops.pollinator_notes_beginner: Pomegranate is self-fruitful, which means one plant makes fruit by itself with no second plant needed. Bees and wind do the pollinating. A single plant will fruit, but adding a second pomegranate nearby, or just keeping bees active during bloom, can bump up how much fruit sets. If a pomegranate flowers but sets little fruit, the cause is usually the weather (damp, still, or cool weather at bloom makes the flowers drop) rather than a missing partner plant.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: In the planting year, build the plant, not a crop. Set a dormant bare-root or cutting-grown plant in late winter to early spring after the hardest cold, water it in, and decide its form early: a natural multi-stem shrub (keep three to six strong trunks) or a single-trunk tree (remove suckers and low shoots). Pomegranate suckers freely from the base, so managing suckers is the main year-one training task. Keep the young plant evenly watered through its first summer to establish the roots, and remove any fruit that sets so energy goes into framework. Feed lightly if at all; avoid heavy nitrogen, which pushes soft growth over fruiting.
crops.year_one_notes_beginner: The first year is about growing a strong plant, not getting fruit. Plant a bare-root or potted young plant in late winter or early spring after the worst cold has passed, water it in, and decide the shape early: a natural bush with several trunks (keep three to six strong ones) or a single small tree (rub off the shoots that pop up from the base). Pomegranates send up lots of these base shoots (suckers), so pulling the extras is the main job the first year. Keep the young plant watered steadily through its first summer so the roots get going, and pick off any fruit that forms so the plant can focus on growing. Go easy on fertilizer, and avoid a lot of nitrogen, which grows leaves instead of fruit.

pollination.notes_seasoned: Self-fruitful: a single plant fruits without a pollinizer. It bears both perfect and functionally male flowers and is pollinated by bees and wind. A second plant is optional, not required, and can modestly improve fruit set; supporting bloom-time bee activity helps a lone plant set well.
pollination.notes_beginner: Self-fruitful means one plant makes fruit on its own, with no second plant needed. Bees and wind do the pollinating. A second pomegranate nearby is optional and can improve fruit set a little, but it is never required.

crops.establishment_note: Most pomegranates begin bearing about 2 to 3 years after planting, with full production by years 5 to 6.
crops.recommended_rootstock_note: Pomegranate is grown on its OWN ROOTS, not grafted onto a rootstock. Plants are propagated from hardwood cuttings, so there is no rootstock to choose; you select a CULTIVAR for flavor, ripening season, and cold-hardiness instead. A practical upside of own-root growth: if a hard freeze kills the top, the plant resprouts true-to-type from the base rather than reverting to a rootstock.

rootstock_options.name: Own roots (cutting-grown)
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask for the CULTIVAR you want (e.g. Wonderful, Parfianka, or a cold-hardy Salavatski); pomegranate is sold on its own roots, so there is no rootstock to specify.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: Pomegranate is not grafted; nursery plants are rooted hardwood cuttings on their own roots. There is no size-controlling or pest-resistant rootstock system as with stone fruit, so mature size is managed by pruning and cultivar choice rather than rootstock. Own-root growth means a freeze-killed plant regrows true-to-type from the base, and it is what makes pomegranate an easy, reliable plant to propagate and to keep container-sized.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: Pomegranates are grown from cuttings on their own roots, not grafted onto a special root system like peaches are. So there is no rootstock to pick; you just choose the variety you want. Because it is on its own roots, a plant frozen to the ground grows back as the same variety, and it stays easy to keep small in a pot.

crops.name: Raspberry

soil.preferred_texture_seasoned: Deep, well-drained sandy loam to loam rich in organic matter, slightly acidic to neutral (about pH 5.5 to 7.0). Raspberries have shallow, perennial roots that spread wide and sucker freely, and they will not tolerate wet feet, so sharp drainage is the single most important soil trait.
soil.preferred_texture_beginner: Raspberries do best in loose, well-drained soil with plenty of compost worked in. Their roots are shallow and spreading, and they hate sitting in water, so good drainage matters more than anything. A pH from about 5.5 to 7.0 is fine, much less fussy than a blueberry.
soil.tolerated_texture_seasoned: Heavier loams work if you build in generous compost and plant on a raised berm or ridge so the crown sits above any standing water. Raised rows are standard practice on marginal ground because raspberry roots rot quickly in saturated soil.
soil.tolerated_texture_beginner: Heavier soils can work if you mix in lots of compost and plant on a raised mound or row so the roots stay up out of soggy ground. Raised rows are a common trick for keeping raspberries happy on less-than-perfect soil.
soil.problematic_texture_seasoned: Heavy, poorly drained clay is the worst case: it holds water around the shallow roots and invites Phytophthora root rot, which is the quickest way to lose a planting. If clay is all you have, grow on tall raised beds of amended soil or in large containers.
soil.problematic_texture_beginner: Heavy, wet clay is the hardest soil for raspberries. It stays soggy around the roots and causes root rot, which kills plants fast. If clay is all you have, grow them in a tall raised bed of good soil, or in a big pot.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Raspberries want loose, well-drained soil rich in organic matter, anywhere from slightly acidic to neutral. Their shallow roots rot in soggy ground, so drainage is everything. Mixing in compost and planting on a slightly raised row before planting helps a lot.

ph.note_seasoned: Raspberries prefer a slightly acidic to neutral soil, roughly pH 5.6 to 6.5, and tolerate 5.5 to 7.0. This is far less demanding than a blueberry and close to what most vegetable gardens already have, so no special acidification is needed. In very alkaline soils above about 7.5 the plants can develop iron chlorosis (yellowing between the veins), corrected with chelated iron and added organic matter rather than by drastic pH change.
ph.note_beginner: Raspberries like soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, about pH 5.6 to 6.5, which is what most gardens already have. Unlike blueberries, they need no special acidic soil. If your soil is very alkaline and the leaves yellow between the veins, work in compost and use a chelated-iron product.

fertilizer.timing: early spring as growth begins, with an optional second feeding after fruit set
fertilizer.example_product: a balanced 10-10-10, or composted manure worked in along the row
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Raspberries are moderate feeders. Apply a balanced fertilizer or well-rotted manure in early spring as new growth begins, banded along the row rather than against the crowns. Nitrogen drives the primocane growth that carries next year's (or this fall's) crop, but too much late in the season produces soft, disease-prone canes, so feed early and stop by midsummer. A soil test guides the rate.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Feed raspberries lightly in early spring when growth starts, using a balanced fertilizer or some composted manure spread along the row. That spring feeding fuels the new canes. Avoid feeding late in the season, which makes weak, floppy canes that get diseased.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced complete fertilizer with enough nitrogen to drive primocane growth; roughly a 10-10-10 or composted manure.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer such as 10-10-10, or composted manure.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: About 4 to 5 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 feet of row, split between early spring and just after bloom; less on rich or recently manured ground.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A light scattering along the row in spring, following the package rate for berries, plus an optional second feeding after the flowers fade.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Garlic and onions
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Alliums like garlic and onions are a traditional raspberry neighbor, thought to help mask the planting from some pests, and they take up little room along the row.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: A long-standing companion-planting tradition (alliums as a general pest-confuser); not an extension-tested raspberry yield benefit, so labeled traditional/low.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Garlic and onions are a traditional companion along a raspberry row, valued by many growers for pungent foliage thought to confuse or deter some browsing and sucking pests. The benefit is folk practice rather than a measured yield gain, but alliums are shallow, undemanding, and easy to tuck along the planting edge without competing with the brambles, so there is little downside to trying them.

good_seasoned.name: Garlic and onions
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional edge companion: their pungent foliage is held to deter some pests, and as shallow-rooted alliums they take little from the raspberry row. Folk practice rather than a tested productivity gain.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Allium pest-deterrence is a widely held companion tradition, not an extension-documented raspberry pairing benefit.

good_seasoned.name: Clover or low legume cover
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A low living mulch of clover in the row middles fixes a little nitrogen, holds soil, and suppresses the weeds that otherwise compete with shallow raspberry roots. Keep it mowed and out of the crop row so it does not invade the crowns.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Legume row-middle cover for soil and weed benefit is mechanistically sound and commonly recommended for brambles, but the specific raspberry yield effect is not pair-tested.

bad_seasoned.name: Tomatoes, potatoes, peppers, eggplant, and strawberries
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Keep raspberries away from current or recent plantings of tomato, potato, pepper, eggplant, and strawberry. All host Verticillium wilt, a soil fungus that also kills raspberries; planting brambles on ground that grew nightshades or strawberries within the last few years carries the disease into the new planting.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: The Verticillium-host avoidance (do not follow tomato/potato/pepper/eggplant/strawberry) is a standard extension siting rule for raspberries.

bad_seasoned.name: Wild brambles and old raspberry or blackberry plantings
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Remove nearby wild raspberries, blackberries, and abandoned brambles before planting. They harbor the aphid-spread mosaic viruses, crown gall, and spotted-wing drosophila that move straight into a new planting; wild Rubus is the single biggest reservoir for the diseases that shorten a raspberry patch's life.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Removing nearby wild Rubus to break virus and SWD reservoirs is standard extension guidance for new raspberry sites.

companions.note_seasoned: Raspberry is not a heavy-companion crop; the siting rules that matter most are about what to keep it away from. Do not plant it where tomatoes, potatoes, peppers, eggplant, or strawberries have grown in the last few years, because all share Verticillium wilt, and clear out nearby wild brambles that carry viruses and spotted-wing drosophila. Good neighbors are modest: traditional allium edges and a mowed legume cover in the row middles for soil and weeds. The bigger gains come from spacing, drainage, and a clean start, not from companions.
companions.note_beginner: Raspberries do not need companion plants to do well. The important rules are what to avoid: do not plant them where tomatoes, potatoes, peppers, eggplant, or strawberries grew recently (they share a soil disease called Verticillium wilt), and pull out any wild brambles nearby, which spread viruses. If you want neighbors, garlic along the edge and clover between rows are easy, low-risk choices.

pests.name: Spotted-wing drosophila (SWD)
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small white maggots inside ripe and ripening berries; fruit softens, collapses, and leaks when squeezed. The adult is a tiny vinegar-fly-like insect, the male with a dark spot near each wingtip. Fall-bearing and late crops are hit hardest.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny maggots inside ripe berries, with the fruit going soft and mushy. The adult is a small fly with a spot on each wing.
pests.cause_seasoned: Spotted-wing drosophila (Drosophila suzukii), an invasive vinegar fly whose females cut into healthy ripe fruit to lay eggs, unlike common fruit flies that use only rotting fruit. It is the major modern raspberry pest.
pests.cause_beginner: An invasive fruit fly that lays eggs in good, ripe berries (not just rotten ones), and the maggots feed inside.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Harvest completely and often, every one to two days, so no ripe fruit is left on the cane, and remove and destroy overripe or fallen berries (bag them, do not compost). Open the canopy by pruning to reduce the cool, humid shelter the fly favors. Fine exclusion netting under 1 mm mesh and apple-cider-vinegar monitoring traps help.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick ripe berries every day or two and clean up any fallen or overripe ones (seal them in a bag, do not compost). Keep the planting open and airy. A cup of apple cider vinegar makes a simple monitoring trap.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Choose early-ripening cultivars to dodge peak fly pressure, keep the planting narrow and open, and harvest on a tight schedule. Remove nearby wild brambles that host the fly.
pests.prevention_beginner: Grow earlier varieties when you can, keep the row narrow and clean, and pick often. Clear out wild brambles nearby.

pests.name: Raspberry cane borer
pests.symptoms_seasoned: The tip of a primocane suddenly wilts and the top 6 inches droop, with two rings of punctures girdling the cane about an inch apart just below the wilted tip. A small long-horned beetle does the girdling; its larva tunnels down inside the cane.
pests.symptoms_beginner: The tip of a new cane wilts and bends over, with two rings of tiny punctures just below it. A small beetle causes it.
pests.cause_seasoned: Raspberry cane borer (Oberea species), a slender black-and-yellow long-horned beetle. The female girdles the cane tip with two rows of punctures and lays an egg between them; the larva bores downward through the cane.
pests.cause_beginner: A small beetle that girdles new cane tips and lays an egg there; the grub then tunnels down inside the cane.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Cut and destroy each wilted tip a few inches below the lower ring of punctures as soon as you see it, removing the egg or young larva before it tunnels deep. Hand-pick the adult beetles. No spray is usually needed in a home planting.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: As soon as a tip wilts, snip it off a few inches below the puncture rings and throw it away to remove the grub. Pick off any beetles you see.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Scout primocane tips through early summer and prune out wilted tips promptly; clean up wild brambles that harbor the beetle.
pests.prevention_beginner: Check new cane tips in early summer and cut off any that wilt. Remove wild brambles nearby.

pests.name: Raspberry crown borer
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Whole canes weaken, leaves redden and wilt, and canes break off easily at the base; the crown and lower cane show tunneling and sawdust-like frass. Plants decline over two seasons and can die. A clearwing moth that mimics a yellowjacket is the adult.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Canes weaken, the leaves redden and wilt, and canes snap off at the base. The crown is tunneled inside. Plants slowly die.
pests.cause_seasoned: Raspberry crown borer (Pennisetia marginata), a clearwing moth whose larvae bore into the crown and lower canes over a two-year life cycle, destroying the base of the plant.
pests.cause_beginner: A wasp-mimic moth whose grubs tunnel into the crown and base of the canes over two years, killing the plant from below.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Dig and destroy infested crowns, since the larvae are protected inside and hard to reach. Starting with clean nursery stock on a fresh site is the most effective control; keep plants vigorous so they outgrow light injury.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Dig out and destroy badly infested plants, because the grubs are hidden inside the crown. Start new plantings with healthy plants on clean ground.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant certified, borer-free stock on ground without a recent bramble history, remove wild brambles nearby, and remove and destroy infested crowns to break the two-year cycle.
pests.prevention_beginner: Buy healthy plants, choose a spot with no old brambles, and dig out any plants that get infested.

pests.name: Japanese beetle
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Leaves skeletonized to a lace of veins, and ripening berries chewed, often by clusters of metallic green-and-copper beetles feeding in the open on warm days from early to midsummer.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Leaves chewed down to lace and berries nibbled, by shiny green-and-copper beetles that feed in groups on warm days.
pests.cause_seasoned: Japanese beetle (Popillia japonica), an introduced scarab whose adults feed on raspberry foliage and fruit; grubs develop in nearby turf.
pests.cause_beginner: An introduced beetle whose adults eat the leaves and berries; its grubs live in lawns nearby.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick beetles into soapy water in the cool morning when they are sluggish, the most effective home control. Skip pheromone traps, which draw in more beetles than they catch. Protect ripening fruit with netting.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Knock the beetles into a jar of soapy water in the morning while they are slow. Do not use the bag traps, which attract even more. Net the fruit as it ripens.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep plants vigorous, hand-pick consistently during the flight, and manage grubs in adjacent lawn areas if pressure is high.
pests.prevention_beginner: Pick beetles off regularly while they are active, and keep plants healthy so they shrug off the damage.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small soft-bodied insects clustered on shoot tips and leaf undersides, sometimes curling new growth and leaving sticky honeydew. Their real danger is spreading raspberry mosaic and leaf-curl viruses, not the feeding itself.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny soft bugs on new shoots and under leaves, sometimes with sticky residue. The bigger risk is the viruses they spread.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several aphid species feed on raspberry sap; the large raspberry aphid in particular transmits the mosaic virus complex that causes incurable, crop-shortening decline.
pests.cause_beginner: Small sap-sucking insects whose main threat is carrying plant viruses from one raspberry to another.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Knock light infestations off with a strong spray of water, support lady beetles and other natural enemies, and use insecticidal soap if needed. Avoid heavy nitrogen, which fuels the soft growth aphids prefer.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray them off with water, let ladybugs help, or use insecticidal soap if there are many. Do not over-fertilize.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Start with certified virus-free plants, remove nearby wild brambles and any virus-symptomatic plants, support beneficial insects, and avoid excess nitrogen.
pests.prevention_beginner: Buy certified virus-free plants, pull out wild brambles and any sickly plants nearby, and encourage helpful bugs.

diseases.name: Phytophthora root rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Canes are weak and stunted, leaves yellow or scorch and wilt, and whole canes collapse, worst in low or poorly drained spots. Dug roots are brown to black and rotted, with a reddish-brown discoloration into the crown.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Canes are weak, leaves yellow and wilt, and plants die in soggy spots. The roots are brown and rotten.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Soilborne Phytophthora water molds that attack roots in wet, poorly drained soil; the most damaging and common cause of raspberry decline, especially red raspberries on heavy ground.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soil disease that rots the roots when the soil stays too wet; the most common reason raspberry plantings fail.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once roots rot, so the response is drainage. Plant on tall raised beds or ridges, divert surface water, and replace dead plants with clean stock on a better-drained site.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot fix rotted roots, so it is all about drainage: plant on raised rows, keep water moving away, and replace dead plants on a drier spot.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant only on well-drained ground or raised beds, choose more tolerant cultivars, never let raspberries sit in saturated soil, and start with disease-free plants.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant on raised rows with good drainage, never let the soil stay soggy, and buy healthy plants.

diseases.name: Anthracnose
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small purplish spots on young canes that enlarge into gray-centered, purple-bordered pits; spots also appear on leaves and can crack the bark. Severe infections weaken canes and reduce yield, worst in wet springs.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small purple spots on the canes that grow into gray, sunken pits with purple edges, plus spots on the leaves.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Elsinoe veneta (anthracnose), which overwinters on old canes and infects new growth during wet weather; black raspberries are especially susceptible.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that lives on old canes and infects new growth in wet weather, leaving sunken spots, worst on black raspberries.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Prune out and destroy old fruited canes and the most spotted primocanes, open the canopy for air movement, and avoid overhead watering. A dormant lime-sulfur application before bud break helps in bad cases.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Cut out old and badly spotted canes, keep the planting open and airy, and water at the base, not over the leaves.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Start with clean plants, keep rows narrow and open, prune out spent canes each year, and avoid wetting the foliage. Resistant cultivars reduce pressure.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Use healthy plants, keep the row open, remove old canes yearly, and water low. Pick resistant varieties.

diseases.name: Cane blight and spur blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Cane blight: dark brown to purple cankers spread from pruning wounds, and canes wilt or die back above them, often snapping at the canker. Spur blight: brown-to-purple blotches at the leaf nodes of red raspberry that girdle the buds, so fruiting laterals are weak or fail next year.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Dark cankers on the canes that make them wilt or snap, and brown patches at the leaf joints that weaken next year's fruiting side shoots.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Fungal canker pathogens (Leptosphaeria for cane blight, Didymella for spur blight) that enter through wounds and injured or crowded wood; both are worse in dense, wet, over-fertilized plantings.
diseases.cause_beginner: Fungi that get into the canes through wounds and crowded growth, causing cankers and weak side shoots.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Prune out and destroy infected canes well below the canker, disinfecting tools between cuts, and thin canes for air movement. Avoid wounding canes and do not over-fertilize with nitrogen.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Cut out cankered canes well below the damage, clean your pruners between cuts, and thin the canes so air moves through.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Keep rows narrow and open, thin to the recommended cane density, prune only in dry weather, avoid excess nitrogen, and remove spent floricanes promptly after harvest.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Keep the row thin and airy, prune in dry weather, go easy on fertilizer, and remove old fruited canes right after harvest.

diseases.name: Orange rust
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: In spring, new shoots are spindly, pale, and bunchy, and the undersides of the leaves are covered with bright orange, powdery pustules. Affected plants never recover; the fungus is systemic in the whole plant.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Weak, spindly new shoots in spring with bright orange powder coating the undersides of the leaves. The whole plant is infected for good.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A systemic rust fungus (Arthuriomyces or Gymnoconia) that permanently infects the entire plant, most serious on black and purple raspberries and wild brambles.
diseases.cause_beginner: A rust fungus that infects the whole plant for life, worst on black and purple raspberries and wild brambles.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure: dig out and destroy infected plants, roots and all, as soon as the orange pustules appear, before they shed spores onto healthy plants. Remove nearby wild brambles that carry it.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no fixing it. Dig up and destroy any plant showing the orange powder, roots and all, before it spreads. Pull out wild brambles nearby.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Start with clean nursery stock, inspect new shoots each spring and rogue out any with orange rust immediately, remove wild brambles, and favor red raspberries (more resistant) over black where rust is common.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Buy healthy plants, check new shoots each spring and remove any infected ones right away, and clear out wild brambles.

diseases.name: Raspberry mosaic virus complex
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Leaves are mottled light and dark green, sometimes puckered or curled, and plants gradually stunt; berries become small, seedy, and crumbly, falling apart at picking. Decline worsens year over year with no recovery.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Mottled, puckered leaves and a slow loss of vigor, with small crumbly berries that fall apart when you pick them. Plants only get worse.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A complex of aphid-transmitted viruses (raspberry mosaic) that permanently infect the plant; spread by the large raspberry aphid and carried in infected planting stock and wild brambles.
diseases.cause_beginner: A group of viruses spread by aphids that infect the plant for good, carried in by aphids, infected plants, and wild brambles.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure. Remove and destroy symptomatic plants promptly so they do not seed the aphids that spread it, and manage aphids and wild brambles around the planting.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no fixing a virused plant. Pull out and destroy any plant with mottled leaves and crumbly fruit, and keep aphids and wild brambles in check.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: The whole defense is prevention: plant certified virus-free stock, site new plantings away from old or wild brambles, control aphids, and replace a declining patch on fresh ground rather than from your own suckers.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Start with certified virus-free plants, keep them away from wild brambles, control aphids, and replace an old declining patch with new plants on fresh ground.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Keep the soil consistently moist, about 1 to 2 inches of water per week, more in heat. The most water-sensitive window runs from bloom through harvest, when the developing berries need steady moisture.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist but never soggy, roughly 1 to 2 inches a week, and more during hot, dry spells.
watering.amount_seasoned: 1 to 2 inches per week, adjusted for rainfall, heat, and soil drainage; twice-weekly watering may be needed in summer heat.
watering.amount_beginner: About 1 to 2 inches a week, including rain, and more often in the heat.
watering.method_seasoned: Drip or soaker irrigation keeps the shallow root zone evenly moist without wetting the canes and fruit, which reduces fruit rot and cane disease. Mulch along the row to hold moisture and keep roots cool.
watering.method_beginner: A soaker hose or drip line at the base works best and keeps the leaves and berries dry. A mulch layer along the row holds moisture between waterings.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing, wilting despite wet soil, and collapsing canes point to overwatering or poor drainage; raspberries will not tolerate saturated soil and quickly develop root rot.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If the leaves yellow and wilt while the soil stays wet and heavy, the roots may be drowning. Raspberries hate soggy soil.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Drought stress shows as small, seedy, crumbly berries and scorched leaf margins; berry size and number suffer most during the bloom-to-harvest window.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Small, dry, crumbly berries and crispy leaf edges mean the plant is too dry, especially while the fruit is forming.

schedule_by_stage.rate: 1 to 2 inches of water per week including rain
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Through spring, keep the shallow root zone evenly moist as primocanes and floricanes push growth. Steady moisture now builds the cane vigor that carries the crop; avoid both drought and standing water.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: While the canes are growing in spring, keep the soil damp but not soggy. Raspberry roots are shallow, so check often and water enough to keep the top few inches moist.

schedule_by_stage.rate: 1 to 2 inches per week, more in heat
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Bloom through harvest is the most water-sensitive window. As berries size, consistent moisture drives plump, juicy fruit and prevents the small, seedy, crumbly berries that follow drought; do not let the row dry out now.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: When the berries are forming and ripening, do not let the soil dry out. This is when steady watering matters most for full, juicy fruit.

schedule_by_stage.rate: rainfall in most regions; occasional water in dry winters
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Dormant, leafless canes in a cold-winter region need little to no supplemental water; rainfall usually suffices. Avoid waterlogging dormant roots, which invites root rot.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: In winter, dormant raspberries need little water and usually get enough from rain. Just do not let them sit in soggy soil.

watering.method_note_seasoned: Water at the base, not overhead. Wet fruit and foliage encourage fruit rot, cane diseases, and spotted-wing drosophila, so drip or soaker lines are strongly preferred over sprinklers.
watering.method_note_beginner: Water low, at the soil, rather than over the plants. Keeping the berries and leaves dry helps prevent rot and bugs.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Bloom through harvest is the most water-sensitive window; the first season after planting is also critical while the new plants build roots and canes.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Keep up the water while the berries are forming and ripening, and through the whole first year after planting.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Not applicable. Raspberries are set out as dormant bare-root canes or established nursery plants, not raised from seed, so there is no seedling hardening-off step. Tissue-cultured plug plants, if used, are hardened like any transplant and set out after frost.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: Not applicable. You plant raspberries from dormant bare-root canes or young potted plants, so there is no need to harden off seedlings.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Start from dormant bare-root canes or a potted nursery plant, not from seed. Bare-root canes are the common, economical choice and go in while dormant in late winter or early spring; potted plants can be set out a little later. Buy certified virus-free stock, set the crown so the roots are 1 to 2 inches below the surface, cut the handle cane back to a few inches after planting, and space plants along a prepared row with support in place. Raspberries are own-root plants that sucker freely, so there is no rootstock or grafting.
start_method.notes_beginner: Buy raspberries as dormant bare-root canes or young potted plants from a nursery rather than growing from seed. Plant bare-root canes in late winter or early spring while they are still dormant. Buy certified virus-free plants, set them so the roots are an inch or two deep, and cut the old cane back to a few inches after planting. Put your support or trellis in before or right after planting.

drainage.saucer_practice: Do not let the pot stand in a full saucer; raspberries will not tolerate waterlogged roots.

soil_mix.type_beginner: A good-quality potting mix with compost blended in.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in compost for richness and a little coarse material for drainage.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: A free-draining, compost-rich potting mix; avoid heavy garden soil, which compacts and stays wet in a pot.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Compost for fertility plus perlite or coarse bark to keep the mix open and fast-draining.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out faster than the ground, so check often and water whenever the top inch feels dry, sometimes daily in summer.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Feed lightly through the growing season, since nutrients wash out of pots faster than out of garden soil.

overwintering.approach_beginner: In cold-winter areas, roots in a pot are more exposed than in the ground. Move the container against a sheltered wall, into an unheated garage, or heel it into the ground and mulch heavily for winter.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Potted root zones are far less insulated than ground soil. In cold zones, sink the pot, cluster and mulch containers, or move them to an unheated shelter; the goal is to protect roots from hard freezes while still delivering the winter chill and dormancy the canes need.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Raspberries can be grown in a large pot, which is a good way to control a spreading, suckering plant. Use a big container, at least 10 gallons, fill it with a rich, well-draining mix, and choose a compact or fall-bearing variety. Give it sun, steady water, and a small support, and remember pots dry out fast.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Containers are a practical way to grow raspberries where space is tight or where you want to contain their aggressive suckering. Use a 10-to-15-gallon pot of free-draining, compost-rich mix, choose a compact or fall-bearing cultivar so you can cut canes to the ground each winter, and stake the canes. Keep the mix evenly moist, feed lightly and regularly, and protect the roots over winter while still meeting the plant's chilling and dormancy needs.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Container mixes dry quickly; expect to water more often than in-ground, sometimes daily in summer heat, while never letting the pot stand waterlogged.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Nutrients leach faster from containers; feed lightly but more frequently with a balanced fertilizer through the growing season.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering (sub-irrigated) container can suit raspberries well, since the reservoir wicks steady moisture to the shallow, drought-sensitive roots and smooths out the drying swings that stress pot-grown canes. The one caution is drainage: keep the reservoir from saturating the mix, because raspberries will not tolerate waterlogged roots, and make sure the pot can overflow in heavy rain.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot can help, because it keeps water in a tank at the bottom so the soil stays evenly damp and dries out less. Just make sure it can drain in heavy rain, since raspberries hate soggy roots.
container_notes.container_overwintering_seasoned: Potted root zones are far less insulated than ground soil, so in cold-winter regions a container raspberry needs winter root protection while still going dormant and getting its chill. Sink the pot in the ground, cluster pots together and mulch heavily, or move them to an unheated garage; the goal is to buffer the roots from hard freezes without keeping the plant warm enough to skip dormancy.
container_notes.container_overwintering_beginner: Roots in a pot are more exposed to cold than roots in the ground. In cold-winter areas, protect a potted raspberry over winter: move it against a sheltered wall or into an unheated garage, or bunch pots together and pile mulch around them. You still want it cold enough to go dormant, just not frozen solid.

recommended.name: Boyne
recommended.hardiness_note: One of the hardiest red raspberries, reliable to zone 3.
recommended.note: An extremely cold-hardy summer-bearing red, one of the standards for the far north; suckers freely, with medium, slightly soft, flavorful berries.

recommended.name: Nova
recommended.hardiness_note: Extremely cold-tolerant, hardy to zone 3.
recommended.note: A vigorous, very hardy summer-bearing red with firm, bright fruit and good disease resistance; a dependable cold-climate choice.

recommended.name: Latham
recommended.note: An old, widely adapted summer-bearing red; very hardy and forgiving, with medium, slightly crumbly berries. A classic beginner variety.

recommended.name: Killarney
recommended.hardiness_note: Very cold-hardy, suited to zones 3 to 4.
recommended.note: A hardy summer-bearing red similar to Boyne, with bright, flavorful medium fruit; suckers heavily and tolerates tough winters.

recommended.name: Tulameen
recommended.hardiness_note: Best in mild-winter, cool-summer zones 6 to 8; not for the coldest areas.
recommended.note: A premium late summer-bearing red for milder, longer-season regions such as the Pacific coast; large, firm, exceptionally sweet berries on a long picking window. Less hardy than the prairie reds.

recommended.name: Jewel
recommended.hardiness_note: Hardy to about zone 5; blacks are less cold-hardy than reds.
recommended.note: The standard black raspberry: vigorous, productive, and the most disease-resistant black, with firm, glossy, sweet-rich fruit. Black raspberries do not sucker and are tip-propagated.

recommended.name: Bristol
recommended.note: A heavy-bearing black raspberry with large, firm, flavorful fruit; like all blacks it is more disease- and heat-sensitive than red raspberry and needs a clean, airy site.

recommended.name: Royalty
recommended.hardiness_note: Hardy to about zone 4.
recommended.note: A large, productive purple raspberry (a red-by-black cross) with sweet, full-flavored fruit; vigorous and hardy, picked red-purple for fresh use or fully purple for cooking.

recommended.name: Heritage
recommended.hardiness_note: Widely adapted and hardy to about zone 4.
recommended.note: The classic fall-bearing (primocane) red and possibly the easiest, heaviest producer: mow all canes to the ground each winter for one reliable fall crop, or leave them for a lighter summer crop too. Firm, good-flavored medium berries.

recommended.name: Caroline
recommended.hardiness_note: Hardy to about zone 4.
recommended.note: A vigorous fall-bearing red with large, richly flavored berries and good disease resistance; ripens a little earlier than Heritage, useful for dodging the worst spotted-wing drosophila pressure.

recommended.name: Autumn Bliss
recommended.hardiness_note: Hardy to about zone 4.
recommended.note: An early fall-bearing red that starts ripening weeks ahead of Heritage, helping northern growers finish a crop before frost and beat peak SWD; sturdy, nearly self-supporting canes.

recommended.name: Anne
recommended.hardiness_note: Hardy to about zone 5; give winter protection at the cold edge.
recommended.note: A pale-gold fall-bearing raspberry with large, sweet, mild berries prized for fresh eating; gold types are mutations of red raspberry grown the same way.

recommended.name: Dorman Red
recommended.hardiness_note: Heat-tolerant, low-chill; suited to zones 7 to 9 where standard reds fail.
recommended.note: The one raspberry adapted to the hot, humid Deep South: a heat- and disease-tolerant, low-chill trailing type (part Rubus parvifolius) developed by Mississippi State. It needs a trellis like a trailing blackberry, fruits in early summer, and has fair fresh flavor best suited to cooking.

recommended.name: Bababerry
recommended.hardiness_note: Low-chill; for mild-winter, hot-summer regions, not the cold north.
recommended.note: A low-chill, heat-tolerant fall-bearing red often recommended for hot interior California; grow it with afternoon shade and ample water, since even the heat-tolerant types resent intense sun and dry air.

varieties.note_seasoned: Choose first by cane type, then by hardiness and season. Summer-bearing (floricane) reds give one big early-summer crop on second-year canes and include the hardiest varieties for cold regions; everbearing (primocane) types fruit on first-year canes in late summer or fall and can be mowed to the ground each winter for the simplest pruning and a clean, single fall crop. Black and purple raspberries are summer-bearing, do not sucker, and are less hardy and more disease-prone than reds. In the hot, humid South, standard raspberries fail, and only heat-tolerant low-chill types such as Dorman Red are worth trying. Always start with certified virus-free stock.
varieties.note_beginner: Pick by type first. Summer-bearing red raspberries give one big crop in early summer and include the toughest, most cold-hardy varieties. Everbearing (fall-bearing) types fruit in late summer or fall on new canes, and you can just mow all the canes down each winter, which makes pruning easy. Black and purple raspberries are sweeter and grown a bit differently but are less hardy. In the hot South, only special heat-tolerant kinds like Dorman Red will grow. Whatever you pick, buy certified virus-free plants.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Raspberries are among the most perishable of all fruits; their soft, hollow structure bruises and molds within a day at room temperature. Hold them out only briefly for serving and refrigerate the rest at once. They do not ripen further after picking, so warmth buys nothing.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Raspberries do not last on the counter; they are extremely delicate and mold fast. Leave them out only while you are eating them and refrigerate the rest right away. They will not get sweeter sitting out.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerated, well-handled raspberries keep only about 3 to 5 days. Store them dry and unwashed in a shallow, vented container so they are not crushed, refrigerate immediately after picking, and sort out any soft or moldy berries that spread decay fast. Wash only just before eating.
storage.fridge_beginner: In the fridge, raspberries keep just a few days, about 3 to 5. Leave them unwashed and dry in a shallow vented container, chill them right after picking, and pick out any mushy ones. Rinse only just before eating.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Raspberries freeze well and are easy to put up. Dry-pack them whole without washing: spread on a tray, freeze until solid, then bag and seal with the air pressed out. Freezing loose keeps them from clumping. Texture softens on thawing, so use thawed berries in baking, smoothies, jam, and sauces; they keep good quality for about a year.
storage.freezer_beginner: Raspberries freeze beautifully. Spread them on a tray (do not wash first), freeze until hard, then pour into a freezer bag. They get soft once thawed, so use frozen berries in baking, smoothies, or jam. They keep about a year.
storage.notes_seasoned: Handle as little as possible; raspberries crush easily and a bruised berry molds within hours. Pick fully ripe berries that pull free of the core into a shallow container no more than a few inches deep so the weight does not crush the bottom layer, harvest in the cool morning after dew dries, keep fruit out of the sun, and refrigerate promptly.
storage.notes_beginner: Be gentle, because raspberries crush and mold fast. Pick berries that slip off the plant easily into a shallow container so they do not squash each other. Pick in the cool morning once the dew dries, keep them out of the sun, and get them into the fridge quickly.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Do not plant raspberries where tomato, potato, pepper, eggplant, or strawberry has grown in the last three to five years. All host Verticillium wilt, a soil fungus that also kills raspberries, and the disease persists in the soil. Choose a fresh site with no recent nightshade, strawberry, or bramble history.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Do not plant raspberries where tomatoes, potatoes, peppers, eggplant, or strawberries grew in the last few years. They share a soil disease (Verticillium wilt) that can kill raspberries. Pick a fresh spot instead.
rotation.note_seasoned: Crop rotation in the annual sense does not apply, since a raspberry planting stays in place for a decade or more. But site history matters at planting: avoid ground that recently grew Verticillium hosts (tomato, potato, pepper, eggplant, strawberry) or old or wild brambles, which leave behind soil disease and virus reservoirs. When a planting declines, start the new one on fresh ground rather than replanting the same spot.
rotation.note_beginner: You do not rotate raspberries each year like vegetables, because a patch lives for many years. What matters is the starting spot: do not plant where tomatoes, potatoes, peppers, eggplant, or strawberries grew recently, and avoid old bramble patches. When a patch wears out, plant the new one somewhere fresh.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Dormant bare-root canes or a potted nursery plant going into a prepared, well-drained row with support in place. In most regions this is late winter to early spring, while the plant is dormant.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Your new raspberry canes going into the ground in early spring, in loose, well-drained soil with a trellis or stake ready.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Set the crown so the roots are 1 to 2 inches deep, space plants along the row, cut the old handle cane back to a few inches, water in, and mulch. Put the trellis or support up now. Use certified virus-free stock on ground with no recent nightshade, strawberry, or bramble history.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Plant the canes 1 to 2 inches deep along your row, cut the old cane back to a few inches, water well, and mulch. Set up a stake or trellis. Buy certified virus-free plants.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record planting date, type and cultivar, and the site's recent crop history.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Write down when you planted, which kind of raspberry it is, and what grew there before.

growth_stages.name: Establishment (year 1)
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: First-year canes (primocanes) growing up from the crown and from spreading root suckers. A summer-bearing planting makes little or no fruit this year; a fall-bearing one can ripen a small crop on the new canes this very fall.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: In the first year the new canes grow tall but a summer type makes no real crop yet. A fall-bearing type may give you a few berries this fall.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Let primocanes grow and train them to the support. Keep the row narrow, no wider than about 12 to 18 inches, by removing suckers that wander out of bounds. Water steadily, mulch, and feed lightly in spring. On a fall-bearing type, you can enjoy the first fall crop.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Let the new canes grow and tie them to the support. Pull up any suckers that pop up outside the row to keep it from spreading. Water and mulch. A fall-bearing type may fruit this fall.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Log primocane growth, suckering and how you contained it, watering, and any first fall crop.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note how the canes grew, where suckers came up, and any first berries in fall.

growth_stages.name: Spring growth and budbreak
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Each spring, overwintered floricanes leaf out and push fruiting laterals, while new primocanes emerge from the crown and from root suckers. Growth is fast now. This is the spring feeding window.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: In spring the overwintered canes leaf out and grow side shoots that will fruit, while brand-new canes push up from the ground.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Apply the spring feeding as growth begins. Train floricanes to the trellis, thin crowded or weak new primocanes, and keep the row narrow. Keep soil evenly moist as growth accelerates.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Feed in early spring as growth starts. Tie the fruiting canes to the support, pull out crowded or weak new shoots, and keep the soil damp.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record budbreak, the spring feeding, cane thinning, and trellis training.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when growth started, when you fed, and any thinning or tying up you did.

growth_stages.name: Bloom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small white five-petaled flowers open on the fruiting laterals: in late spring on the floricanes of summer-bearing types, in mid to late summer on the primocane tips of fall-bearing types. Raspberries are self-fertile, but bees boost fruit set.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Small white flowers open on the canes, in late spring for summer types and later in summer for fall types. Bees visit them, but raspberries can pollinate themselves.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Let pollinators work the flowers; no second variety is needed since raspberries are self-fertile. If a late frost threatens open bloom on an early type, cover the planting overnight.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Let the bees do their work. You do not need a second variety. If a frosty night is coming while the early flowers are open, cover the plants that evening.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Log first bloom, full bloom, pollinator activity, and any frost during bloom.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when the flowers opened and any frosty nights while they were open.

growth_stages.name: Fruit set and sizing
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Pollinated flowers set small green druplets that swell into the familiar aggregate berry over a few weeks. This is the most water-sensitive window. Net for birds and begin scouting for spotted-wing drosophila as fruit nears color.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The flowers turn into tiny green berries that grow and color up over the next few weeks. Net for birds and start watching for fruit flies.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture steady and consistent while berries size; drought now means small, seedy, crumbly fruit. Put up bird netting before berries color, and start spotted-wing drosophila monitoring with vinegar traps.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil evenly damp while the berries grow, or they will be small and crumbly. Net the plants before the berries turn color and set out a vinegar trap to watch for fruit flies.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record fruit set, netting installed, watering, and any SWD trap catches.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when green berries appeared, when you put up netting, and any fruit flies you trap.

growth_stages.name: Ripening and harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Berries color fully and slip free of the white central core (receptacle), leaving the hollow, thimble-shaped fruit. They ripen a few at a time over a window of two to several weeks, picked over every two to three days. Frequent, complete picking is the front line against spotted-wing drosophila.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Ripe berries pull off easily, leaving a hollow center. They ripen a few at a time over a couple of weeks, so you pick every two or three days. Picking often also fights the fruit-fly maggots.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick berries that detach with a gentle tug, every two to three days, in the cool morning after dew dries. Remove and destroy overripe and culled fruit. Refrigerate promptly; raspberries are extremely perishable. Keep netting on through the season.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pick berries that come off easily into a shallow container, every two or three days, in the morning. Throw away any overripe ones (sealed in a bag). Refrigerate right away. Keep the netting on.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Log first ripe date, each harvest and rough amount, culls removed, and final pick.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note your first ripe berries, each picking and roughly how much, and the last pick.

growth_stages.name: Post-harvest and spent-cane removal
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Floricanes that fruited now die; their leaves brown and the canes turn brittle. Meanwhile this year's primocanes keep growing to carry next year's crop. On a fall-bearing planting managed for one crop, the canes will be mowed off later in dormancy.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The canes that just fruited die after harvest, while this year's new canes keep growing for next year. Fall-bearing types get cut to the ground later in winter.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: On summer-bearing types, cut the spent fruited floricanes to the ground right after harvest and remove them to reduce disease, leaving the new primocanes. Keep watering and managing suckers; stop feeding by late summer so canes harden before winter.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: On summer types, cut out the canes that just fruited (they are dying) right after harvest, leaving the fresh new canes. Keep watering, and stop feeding by late summer.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record spent-cane removal, primocane condition, and late-summer watering.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you removed the old fruited canes and how the new canes look.

growth_stages.name: Winter dormancy and chilling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Canes drop their leaves and go fully dormant, banking the winter chill the plant needs to break bud and fruit normally. Raspberries are very cold-hardy, but open floral buds and tender primocane tips can be injured by hard late or early freezes.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: In winter the canes lose their leaves and rest, soaking up the cold they need to fruit well next year. Raspberries handle hard winters, but late or early freezes can nip the buds.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Little is needed: avoid waterlogging dormant roots and keep mulch in place. In the coldest regions, a layer of mulch or snow cover protects the canes; container plants need root protection while still getting their chill.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Not much to do in winter. Keep mulch on, do not let the roots sit in soggy soil, and protect potted plants from deep freezes.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Log leaf drop, mulch condition, and any winter protection applied.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when the leaves dropped and any winter protection you added.

growth_stages.name: Dormant-season pruning and training
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Late in the dormant season, the annual pruning that defines a raspberry's productivity: on summer-bearing types remove any remaining spent floricanes and thin the surviving canes to 4 to 6 per foot of row; on fall-bearing types managed for a single crop, mow every cane to the ground. Then narrow the row and tie the kept canes to the trellis.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: In late winter you do the key pruning. For summer types, thin the canes to a few strong ones per foot. For fall types, just mow every cane to the ground. Then tie the kept canes to the support.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Prune in late winter before growth starts. Summer-bearing: remove dead and spent canes, thin to 4 to 6 sturdy canes per foot of row, narrow the row to about a foot wide, and top the canes. Fall-bearing for a single fall crop: cut all canes to the ground. Tie the remaining canes to the trellis.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: In late winter, for summer types cut out dead and old canes and leave 4 to 6 strong ones per foot, then tie them up. For fall types, just cut every cane to the ground. Keep the row about a foot wide.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record pruning date, type of pruning done, canes kept per foot, and trellis work.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you pruned, what you cut, and how you tied up the canes.

notifications.title_seasoned: Set up support before or at planting
notifications.title_beginner: Put up a trellis or stake when you plant
notifications.body_seasoned: Raspberry canes flop and break under a fruit load and in wind, so install a trellis, T-post and wire, or sturdy stakes before or right after planting. Putting it in first avoids disturbing the shallow roots later, and it sets the row width that keeps the planting open and healthy.
notifications.body_beginner: Raspberry canes need support or they bend over and snap. Put in a stake or simple trellis when you plant, before the roots fill in, so you are not disturbing them later.

notifications.title_seasoned: Feed in early spring as growth begins
notifications.title_beginner: Feed your raspberries in early spring
notifications.body_seasoned: As new growth starts in spring, apply a balanced fertilizer or composted manure banded along the row, not against the crowns. This early nitrogen drives the primocane growth that carries the crop. Feed early and stop by midsummer so canes harden before winter.
notifications.body_beginner: When growth starts in spring, scatter a balanced fertilizer or some composted manure along the row. Do not feed late in the season.

notifications.title_seasoned: Keep the row narrow and contain suckers
notifications.title_beginner: Pull suckers to keep the row from spreading
notifications.body_seasoned: Red and yellow raspberries sucker aggressively from their roots and will march out into the lawn and beds if left alone. Through the season, remove or mow suckers that come up outside the intended row, keeping it no wider than about 12 to 18 inches for light, air, and easy picking.
notifications.body_beginner: Raspberries send up new shoots from their roots and spread fast. Pull or mow any that come up outside your row to keep the patch about a foot wide and under control.

notifications.title_seasoned: Net for birds and start watching for SWD
notifications.title_beginner: Net the plants and watch for fruit flies
notifications.body_seasoned: Before berries begin to color, drape bird netting over the planting and start monitoring for spotted-wing drosophila with apple-cider-vinegar traps. Both birds and SWD hit ripening fruit, and SWD is the major modern raspberry pest, so begin a tight harvest schedule as fruit colors.
notifications.body_beginner: Before the berries turn color, cover the plants with bird netting and set out a cup of apple cider vinegar to catch fruit flies. Then plan to pick often as the berries ripen.

notifications.title_seasoned: Pick ripe berries every two to three days
notifications.title_beginner: Pick ripe berries every couple of days
notifications.body_seasoned: Berries ripen a few at a time, so pick over the planting every two to three days, taking only fully colored berries that slip free of the core. Picking completely and often is the front-line defense against spotted-wing drosophila. Pick in the cool morning and refrigerate promptly.
notifications.body_beginner: Berries ripen a few at a time. Pick every two or three days, taking the ones that pull off easily, and clear off any overripe ones. Picking often also helps fight the fruit-fly maggots. Refrigerate right away.

notifications.title_seasoned: Remove the spent fruited canes after harvest
notifications.title_beginner: Cut out the canes that just fruited
notifications.body_seasoned: On summer-bearing raspberries, the floricanes that fruited are now dying. Cut them to the ground and remove them right after harvest to open the row, cut disease pressure, and steer the plant's energy into the new primocanes that will fruit next year. Leave fall-bearing canes for the dormant-season decision.
notifications.body_beginner: On summer-bearing types, the canes that just fruited are dying. Cut them off at the ground after harvest and clear them out, leaving the fresh green canes for next year.

notifications.title_seasoned: Prune by type in late winter
notifications.title_beginner: Prune the canes in late winter
notifications.body_seasoned: In late winter, do the annual pruning that decides the crop. Summer-bearing: remove dead and spent canes and thin the rest to 4 to 6 sturdy canes per foot of row, then narrow the row and tie canes up. Fall-bearing managed for one crop: mow every cane to the ground. Getting the type right is the most common raspberry mistake.
notifications.body_beginner: In late winter, prune. For summer types, cut out old and dead canes and keep 4 to 6 strong ones per foot, then tie them up. For fall types, simply cut every cane to the ground. Cutting the wrong type at the wrong time is the most common raspberry mistake.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost warning during bloom
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A frost is forecast while your raspberries are blooming. Open flowers are frost-tender and a hard frost can destroy the developing crop, a real risk for early-blooming types and in the warm South. Cover the planting overnight and uncover it in the morning.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Frost is coming while your raspberries are flowering. Cover the plants tonight to protect the flowers, and uncover them in the morning.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot, dry spell while berries ripen
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A hot, dry stretch is forecast as berries ripen. Heat above roughly 85 to 90°F scorches fruit, makes berries small and crumbly, and stresses the shallow roots. Keep the soil evenly moist, harvest in the cool morning, and provide afternoon shade in hot-summer regions.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: It is going to be hot and dry while your berries ripen. Keep the soil damp, pick in the cool morning, and give the plants some afternoon shade if you can.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Lots of rain and soggy soil
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Extended heavy rain can waterlog raspberry roots and trigger Phytophthora root rot, especially on heavy ground. Make sure water drains away from the row; raised beds or ridges are the durable protection against wet-soil collapse.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Long heavy rain can leave the soil too soggy, which rots raspberry roots. Make sure water drains away from the plants; raised rows help a lot.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Rain coming before you pick
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Rain is forecast as berries ripen. Wet, warm conditions rot soft raspberries fast and fuel spotted-wing drosophila and gray mold. Let berries dry before picking, harvest promptly and completely once they do, remove any mushy fruit, and refrigerate immediately.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Rain is coming as your berries ripen. Let them dry before you pick, then pick soon and completely, throw away any mushy ones, and refrigerate right away.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Strong wind on the canes
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Strong wind can whip and snap tall, fruit-laden raspberry canes, especially primocanes not yet tied in. Make sure canes are secured to the trellis ahead of a windy stretch, and tip back overly long primocanes that catch the most wind.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Strong wind can snap tall raspberry canes. Tie loose canes to the support before a windy spell, and trim back any extra-long new canes.

planting.text_seasoned: Start with certified virus-free canes on ground that has not grown raspberries, blackberries, or nightshades recently. A clean start is the single biggest factor in how long the planting lives.
planting.text_beginner: Buy certified virus-free plants and pick a spot that has not grown raspberries, blackberries, tomatoes, or potatoes recently. A clean start matters more than anything.
planting.author: plant_team

planting.text_seasoned: Plant on a slightly raised row in well-drained soil and set up the trellis before or right after planting; raspberries rot in wet ground and flop without support.
planting.text_beginner: Plant on a slightly raised row with good drainage, and put up a stake or trellis right away. Raspberries hate soggy soil and fall over without support.
planting.author: plant_team

establishment.text_seasoned: Expect little fruit the first year from a summer-bearing planting; a fall-bearing one can give a small crop this fall. Either way, let the new canes build the framework.
