crops.name: Elderberry

soil.preferred_texture_seasoned: Elderberry does best in a deep, fertile, moisture-retentive loam high in organic matter. In the wild it grows along streambanks, ditches, and low fence rows, so it wants steady moisture and a rich soil above all else. Its roots are extensive but relatively shallow, which is why consistent moisture matters more than sharp drainage.
soil.preferred_texture_beginner: Elderberry likes rich, moist soil that stays damp. In nature it grows along streams and ditches, so think fertile and never bone-dry. It is not fussy, but the better and moister the soil, the more berries you get.
soil.tolerated_texture_core: clay or wet ground with some drainage
soil.tolerated_texture_seasoned: Elderberry is famously adaptable and unusually wet-tolerant for a fruit crop. It handles heavy clay and periodically wet, poorly drained ground that would rot most berries, which makes it a classic choice for a low spot or a rain garden. On truly waterlogged sites, planting on a low berm still helps.
soil.tolerated_texture_beginner: Elderberry puts up with heavy clay and soggy spots better than almost any other fruit, so it is a good pick for a wet corner of the yard. If the ground stays underwater, a low raised mound helps.
soil.problematic_texture_seasoned: The one soil elderberry dislikes is a dry, droughty one. Loose sand that drains too fast and bakes out in summer stresses its shallow roots and shrinks the berries. On sandy ground, heavy organic matter and reliable irrigation are essential.
soil.problematic_texture_beginner: The main thing to avoid is dry, sandy soil that dries out fast. Elderberry hates drought. If your soil is very sandy, mix in lots of compost and be ready to water often.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Elderberry wants rich, moist soil and is happy in spots that are too wet for most fruit. Work in plenty of compost, keep it damp, and it will thrive; the only soil it really dislikes is dry, droughty sand.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Elderberry wants a deep, fertile, moisture-retentive soil rich in organic matter, and it tolerates wet, heavy ground far better than other berries. Keep it moist and well fed; the only real enemy is drought.

ph.note_seasoned: Elderberry prefers a soil pH of about 5.5 to 6.5, but it is easygoing and grows well from slightly acidic up to near-neutral (roughly 5.5 to 7.5). Unlike blueberry, it needs no special acidification: a soil test and ordinary garden pH management are plenty. If anything, keep it out of strongly alkaline ground.
ph.note_beginner: Elderberry is relaxed about soil pH, doing well anywhere from about 5.5 to 6.5 and tolerating up to around 7.0. Unlike blueberries, it does not need acidic soil, so no special treatment is required. A basic soil test is all you need.

fertilizer.timing: in early spring as growth begins
fertilizer.example_product: a balanced 10-10-10 garden fertilizer, or aged manure or compost
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Elderberry is a moderate feeder that responds well to nitrogen and organic matter. Do not fertilize at planting; from the second year on, apply a balanced fertilizer such as 10-10-10, or a generous topdressing of compost or aged manure, once in early spring as growth begins. A vigorous plant that is putting up strong new canes usually needs little more; over-feeding just makes soft, floppy growth.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Feed elderberry once a year in early spring, starting the second year, with a balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 or a good layer of compost. Do not feed at planting time. Elderberry grows fast on its own, so go easy; too much fertilizer makes weak, floppy stems.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced complete fertilizer with nitrogen; compost or aged manure works too.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: A balanced all-purpose fertilizer (like 10-10-10), or compost.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A light application by the label rate from year two on; established, vigorous shrubs often thrive on an annual compost topdressing alone.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A small amount in early spring from the second year, following the package rate.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Native pollinator flowers
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Elderberry flowers feed bees and other insects, and its berries feed birds. Planting native flowers nearby supports all that life and looks good together.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Beginner-rendered bucket needing why_seasoned per worksheet. Supporting the pollinators/wildlife elderberry attracts is mechanistically sensible, not a tested yield pairing.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Elderberry is a strong wildlife and pollinator plant: its broad cymes are worked by many insects and its fruit feeds birds. Interplanting native flowering perennials nearby broadens the pollinator support around bloom and fits elderberry's role as an edge or hedgerow shrub. This is companionship by shared habitat, not a tested yield boost.

good_seasoned.name: Native pollinator flowers
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A habitat companion: elderberry's wind- and insect-pollinated cymes benefit from a healthy pollinator population, and the shrub itself is a wildlife magnet. Native flowering perennials nearby reinforce that ecology rather than boost yield directly.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Shared-habitat/pollinator-support rationale is mechanistically grounded; not a pair-tested yield benefit, so labeled likely.

companions.note_seasoned: Elderberry is not a companion-driven crop; it is a big, vigorous shrub best sited for its own sake. The main rules are practical: give it room (it reaches 8 to 12 feet and suckers), keep it where its size will not shade smaller sun-loving crops, and lean into its strengths as a pollinator and wildlife plant and a tolerator of wet, low ground. Its most important 'companion' is simply a second, different cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.
companions.note_beginner: Elderberry does not need companion plants. It is a large shrub, so give it plenty of space and keep it from shading smaller plants. Its one real planting rule is to put a second, different variety nearby so the two can pollinate each other.

pests.name: Birds
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Ripe and ripening berry clusters stripped from the shrub, often the whole crop in a few days as the fruit blackens.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Birds eating the berries, sometimes clearing a bush fast once the fruit ripens.
pests.cause_seasoned: Elderberries are a favorite of many birds, which are widely the number-one competitor for the crop.
pests.cause_beginner: Birds love ripe elderberries and are the biggest pest for the fruit.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Drape bird netting over the shrub or a frame before the clusters color, secured at the base. Cultivars whose cymes invert (droop) after fruit set, such as Bob Gordon, hide the berries and lose less to birds.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover the bush with bird netting before the berries darken, and tuck it in at the bottom. Some varieties (like Bob Gordon) droop their clusters and lose fewer berries to birds.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Net before ripening every season; harvest promptly and completely so ripe fruit is not left hanging. Scare devices help only briefly.
pests.prevention_beginner: Put netting up each year before the fruit ripens, and pick as soon as clusters are ready. Shiny tape and fake owls stop working once birds get used to them.

pests.name: Spotted-wing drosophila and sap beetles
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small maggots inside softening ripe berries (spotted-wing drosophila), and small dark beetles feeding on overripe or damaged fruit (sap beetles); clusters ferment and leak.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny maggots in soft ripe berries, or little beetles on overripe fruit, with clusters going mushy.
pests.cause_seasoned: Spotted-wing drosophila (an invasive vinegar fly) lays eggs in healthy ripe fruit; sap beetles are drawn to overripe and split berries.
pests.cause_beginner: A small invasive fly that lays eggs in good ripe berries, plus beetles that show up on overripe fruit.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Harvest ripe clusters frequently and completely, and remove fallen or overripe fruit (bag it, do not compost). Cool the harvest quickly. Monitor with apple-cider-vinegar traps.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick ripe clusters often and clean up any dropped or overripe berries. Chill the harvest fast. A cup of apple cider vinegar makes a simple monitoring trap.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Tight, frequent harvest and good sanitation are the core controls; do not let ripe or overripe fruit sit on the plant or ground.
pests.prevention_beginner: Pick often, keep the ground clear of fallen berries, and refrigerate promptly.

pests.name: Elder shoot and stem borers
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Wilting or dying individual canes and shoot tips; hollowed, tunneled stems, sometimes with sawdust-like frass at entry holes.
pests.symptoms_beginner: A cane or shoot suddenly wilting and dying, with a hollowed-out, tunneled stem.
pests.cause_seasoned: Native borers, including the elder shoot borer and the elderberry longhorned borer, whose larvae tunnel inside canes and shoots.
pests.cause_beginner: Beetle and moth larvae that bore into and hollow out elderberry canes.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Prune out and destroy wilted or infested canes below the damage as soon as you spot them; this removes the larvae. Keep plants vigorous and renew old canes.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cut off and throw away any wilting, tunneled canes right away to remove the grubs inside. Keep the plant healthy and prune out old canes.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Annual removal of old and damaged canes during dormant pruning breaks the borers' cycle; destroy prunings rather than leaving them nearby.
pests.prevention_beginner: Prune out old and damaged canes each winter and get rid of the trimmings, which removes overwintering borers.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of small soft-bodied insects on tender shoot tips and leaf undersides, sometimes curling new growth and leaving sticky honeydew.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny soft bugs on new shoots and leaf undersides, sometimes with sticky residue.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several aphid species feed on elderberry sap; heavy colonies distort growth and can spread viruses.
pests.cause_beginner: Small sap-sucking insects that cluster on new growth.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Knock light infestations off with a strong spray of water, support natural predators like lady beetles, and use insecticidal soap if needed. Avoid excess nitrogen.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray them off with water, let ladybugs help, or use insecticidal soap for heavy outbreaks. Do not over-fertilize.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep plants healthy without over-feeding, encourage beneficial insects, and inspect new spring growth.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not over-feed, welcome helpful bugs, and check new growth in spring.

pests.name: Japanese beetles
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Skeletonized leaves (chewed to lacework between the veins), usually in early to midsummer, sometimes on the flower clusters.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Leaves chewed to lace by shiny beetles in summer.
pests.cause_seasoned: Adult Japanese beetles feed on elderberry foliage and flowers where the pest is established.
pests.cause_beginner: Shiny green-bronze beetles that eat the leaves in summer.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick beetles into soapy water in the cool morning; a vigorous elderberry usually outgrows the damage. Skip lures, which draw more beetles in.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick the beetles off into soapy water in the morning. A healthy elderberry shrugs off most of the damage.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Tolerate light feeding on established shrubs; keep plants vigorous. Grub management in nearby lawn reduces local populations.
pests.prevention_beginner: A strong elderberry handles a few beetles fine; keep it healthy and pick off the worst.

diseases.name: Elderberry rust
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Bright yellow-orange spots and swollen, distorted growths on leaves, stems, and flower clusters; affected leaves may curl.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Orange spots and odd swollen growths on leaves and stems, with some leaves curling.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A rust fungus (Puccinia) that alternates between elderberry and nearby sedges as its other host.
diseases.cause_beginner: A rust fungus that moves between elderberry and nearby sedge plants.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Prune out and destroy infected shoots and clusters, and remove sedges growing near the planting to break the fungus's cycle. Good airflow helps.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Cut off and throw away the infected parts, and clear out any sedge weeds growing nearby. Keep the bush open and airy.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Site plants in the open with good air movement, keep sedges away, and remove infected tissue promptly.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Give the bush room and airflow, keep sedge weeds away, and cut out any infected growth you see.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: A white to gray powdery film on leaves, usually late in the season; heavy cases can dull foliage but rarely harm an established shrub.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: A white powdery coating on the leaves, mostly late in summer.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Powdery mildew fungi, favored by crowded growth and poor air movement in late summer.
diseases.cause_beginner: A common leaf fungus that shows up on crowded plants in late summer.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Prune to open the canopy for airflow and remove badly affected growth; established elderberries usually tolerate it without treatment.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Open up the bush by pruning so air moves through. It rarely does real harm.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space and prune for good air movement and avoid excess nitrogen that fuels dense, soft growth.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Keep the bush open and do not over-feed it.

diseases.name: Cane canker and dieback
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Sunken or discolored lesions on canes, with twigs and canes dying back, often on older or winter-injured wood.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Branches and canes dying back, with dark sunken patches on the stems.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Fungal canker pathogens that enter through wounds and stressed, old, or winter-damaged wood.
diseases.cause_beginner: Fungi that get into the canes through wounds or old, damaged wood and cause dieback.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Prune out affected canes well below the lesion into healthy wood, disinfecting tools between cuts, and remove the prunings. Keep plants vigorous.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Cut out dying canes below the damage, clean your pruners between cuts, and keep the plant healthy.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Renew old canes on schedule, avoid wounding, and keep the shrub vigorous and well watered.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Prune out old canes each year and keep the plant healthy so it resists infection.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Keep the soil consistently moist. Elderberry is a streambank plant with shallow roots and a real thirst; it wants steady moisture through the whole growing season and especially while berries are sizing. Roughly 1 to 2 inches of water per week, more in heat and on sandy ground.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays damp, about 1 to 2 inches a week and more in hot, dry weather. Elderberry likes moisture and does not handle drought well.
watering.amount_seasoned: 1 to 2 inches per week, adjusted for rainfall, heat, and soil; more on sand.
watering.amount_beginner: About 1 to 2 inches a week, including rain, and more when it is hot and dry.
watering.method_seasoned: Drip or soaker irrigation keeps the shallow root zone evenly moist; a thick mulch holds moisture and keeps the roots cool. Elderberry tolerates wet soil, so the usual risk is under-watering, not over-watering.
watering.method_beginner: A soaker hose or drip line at the base works best, and a thick mulch keeps the soil damp between waterings. Elderberry is fine with wet soil, so err on the side of more water, not less.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Elderberry tolerates wet ground, so overwatering is rarely a problem; only in truly stagnant, airless soil will you see yellowing and root decline.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Elderberry rarely drowns; only dead-still, swampy soil causes yellow leaves and rot. Most of the time you cannot give it too much water.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Drought stress shows as wilting, scorched leaf margins, undersized berries, and early leaf drop, worst on sandy soil and during the fruit-sizing window.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Wilting leaves, crispy edges, and small, shriveled berries mean the plant is too dry. Elderberry is one of the first plants to sulk in a drought.

schedule_by_stage.rate: 1 to 2 inches of water per week including rain
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Through spring, keep the soil evenly moist as the canes leaf out and grow. Elderberry roots are shallow and thirsty, so steady moisture drives the strong cane growth that carries the crop.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: While the plant is leafing out and growing in spring, keep the soil damp. Regular water now means strong stems and more berries later.

schedule_by_stage.rate: 1 to 2 inches per week, more in heat
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Fruit sizing is the most water-sensitive window. As the berry clusters swell and color, consistent moisture drives berry size and total yield; let the soil dry out now and the clusters come in small and sparse.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: When the berry clusters are filling out and starting to color, do not let the soil dry out. This is when steady water matters most for big, full clusters.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: A dormant, leafless elderberry needs little supplemental water through winter; rainfall usually suffices. In mild, dry-winter regions an occasional soaking during long dry spells keeps the roots from drying out.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: In winter a resting elderberry needs little water and usually gets enough from rain. In a dry, mild winter, give it an occasional soaking so the roots do not dry out.

watering.method_note_seasoned: Mulch heavily and irrigate on sandy or fast-draining sites; elderberry's shallow roots dry out quickly and drought is its main weakness.
watering.method_note_beginner: Keep a thick mulch around the base and water often on sandy soil. Elderberry's biggest weakness is drying out.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The first season after planting (for establishment) and the fruit-sizing window from cluster set through coloring are the two moments to never let the soil dry out.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Keep up the water during the whole first year and again while the berry clusters are growing and coloring.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Not applicable in the seedling sense. Elderberry is set out as dormant bare-root plants, container plants, or rooted cuttings, not raised from seed, so there is no seedling hardening-off step. It is famously easy to propagate: dormant hardwood cuttings root readily, so one planting can supply many more.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: Not applicable. You plant elderberry from young plants or cuttings, not from seed, so there is no seedling to harden off. It roots so easily from cuttings that you can make new plants for free.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Start from nursery plants or cuttings, not seed. Set out dormant bare-root plants or rooted cuttings in late winter to early spring while the plant is still dormant; container plants can also go in spring or fall. Plant at the depth it grew in the pot or nursery row, in moist, fertile soil, and water in well. Elderberry is own-root, so there is no rootstock or grafting to consider, and it will send up new canes and suckers quickly.
start_method.notes_beginner: Buy elderberry as a young plant or grow it from a cutting rather than from seed. Plant it in late winter or early spring while it is still dormant, in moist, rich soil, at the same depth it was growing before, and water it in. It grows fast and sends up new stems from the base on its own.

drainage.saucer_practice: A saucer is fine for elderberry, which likes moisture; just empty it in cold weather so a potted root zone is not sitting in ice.

soil_mix.type_beginner: A rich, moisture-holding potting mix with plenty of compost.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Blend in extra compost so it holds water and stays fertile.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: A fertile, moisture-retentive potting mix heavy in compost or organic matter.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Extra compost or aged manure to feed the heavy grower and hold moisture.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out fast and elderberry is thirsty, so check often and water whenever the top inch is dry, sometimes daily in summer.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Feed lightly through the growing season, since nutrients wash out of pots faster than out of the ground.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Elderberry is very cold-hardy, but roots in a pot are more exposed. In cold-winter areas, move the container to a sheltered spot or unheated garage, or mulch heavily around it for winter.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: The top of a potted elderberry is fully cold-hardy; the concern is the less-insulated root zone. In cold zones, sink the pot, cluster and mulch containers, or shift them to an unheated shelter, while still letting the plant go dormant.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Elderberry is a big, fast, suckering shrub that is really happiest in the ground. You can grow one in a container if you pick a compact variety like Ranch, use a large pot (at least 20 gallons), and keep it well watered and fed, but expect a smaller plant and a smaller crop.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Containers are workable but not the ideal home for elderberry, which is a large, vigorous, suckering shrub. If you must, choose a compact cultivar such as Ranch, use a 20-to-25-gallon pot of rich moisture-holding mix, water generously (elderberry is thirsty and wet-tolerant), and feed regularly; yields will be lower than in the ground and the plant will stay smaller.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Container mixes dry quickly and elderberry resents drought; expect to water more often than in-ground, up to daily in summer heat.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Nutrients leach faster from pots; feed lightly but regularly through the growing season.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering (sub-irrigated) container suits elderberry well, because it holds a moisture reservoir the thirsty, wet-tolerant roots appreciate and smooths out the drying swings that stress a pot-grown shrub. There is little downside, since elderberry does not mind consistently damp soil; just keep the mix fertile.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot works nicely for elderberry, since it keeps the soil evenly damp and elderberry loves moisture. Just keep the soil rich with compost.
container_notes.container_overwintering_seasoned: A potted elderberry is cold-hardy on top but its root zone is less insulated than ground soil, so in cold-winter regions protect the roots over winter: sink the pot, cluster and mulch pots together, or move them to an unheated garage, while still letting the plant go dormant.
container_notes.container_overwintering_beginner: Roots in a pot are more exposed to cold than roots in the ground. In cold-winter areas, protect a potted elderberry over winter by moving it to a sheltered spot or unheated garage, or bunching pots together and piling mulch around them.

recommended.name: Adams
recommended.hardiness_note: Very cold-hardy; a longtime northeastern standard.
recommended.note: The classic New York selection (Adams 1 and the later, heavier Adams 2): vigorous and very hardy, with large clusters of numerous berries. A dependable standard; pair it with York for cross-pollination.

recommended.name: York
recommended.hardiness_note: Hardy and productive; less spreading than most.
recommended.note: A New York release with some of the largest berries and heavy yields; ripens late and suckers less, so it suits smaller spaces. A natural cross-pollination partner for Adams.

recommended.name: Nova
recommended.hardiness_note: Cold-hardy Canadian selection.
recommended.note: A Nova Scotia selection with large, sweet berries that ripen early and uniformly; a good pollinizer that stretches the season earlier when paired with a later cultivar.

recommended.name: Bob Gordon
recommended.note: A standout modern Missouri cultivar: exceptionally productive, with heavy cymes that invert (droop) after fruit set, shedding rain and hiding the berries from birds. A top choice for juice and yield.

recommended.name: Wyldewood
recommended.note: A vigorous, very productive Missouri cultivar that blooms and ripens late, helping it dodge spring frost; large cymes and reliable heavy crops.

recommended.name: Ranch
recommended.note: A compact, shorter Missouri cultivar with early, uniform ripening; its smaller stature suits tight spaces and makes it easy to net and harvest.

varieties.note_seasoned: Elderberry is not split into climate types the way blueberry is: nearly every home and commercial cultivar is American elderberry (Sambucus canadensis), and you choose by yield, ripening season, and habit rather than by chill. The one rule that matters is to plant at least two DIFFERENT cultivars with overlapping bloom for cross-pollination, which sharply raises yield. Classic pairings are Adams with York, or a modern Missouri pair like Bob Gordon with Wyldewood. European elderberry (S. nigra) cultivars exist and can be grown too, but the American types are hardier and better adapted across most of the country.
varieties.note_beginner: There is really just one kind of elderberry to grow, American elderberry, so pick varieties by how much they yield and when they ripen, not by your climate. The important thing is to plant two different varieties near each other so they pollinate and you get far more fruit. Good pairs are Adams with York, or Bob Gordon with Wyldewood.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Fresh elderberries are highly perishable and should not be held at room temperature; process or refrigerate them the day you pick. Remember they are NOT a fresh eating fruit: raw ripe berries are unpleasant and mildly toxic, so plan to cook, juice, or dry them rather than store fresh.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Do not leave fresh elderberries out; use or refrigerate them the same day. And do not snack on them raw, because raw elderberries can make you sick. They are meant to be cooked, juiced, or dried.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerated on the stem in a breathable container, elderberry clusters hold only a few days (roughly 2 to 5). It is best to strip and process the berries promptly. To de-stem easily, chill or briefly freeze the whole clusters, then rake the berries off with a fork; keep the green stems out of your finished product.
storage.fridge_beginner: In the fridge, elderberry clusters keep only a few days, so plan to use them quickly. A handy trick: freeze the clusters for a bit, then the berries pop off the stems easily with a fork. Keep the stems out of whatever you make.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Freezing is the easiest way to hold elderberries. Freeze the clusters whole, then rake off the berries while frozen (they come off cleanly), bag, and store; frozen berries keep good quality for about a year. Always cook them before eating, whether fresh or thawed.
storage.freezer_beginner: Elderberries freeze well. Freeze the clusters, then rake the frozen berries off the stems into a bag; they keep about a year. Cook them before eating.
storage.notes_seasoned: Handle whole clusters, not loose berries, until you process. Harvest whole cymes when most berries have turned deep purple-black, keep them cool, and de-stem and cook (or freeze/dry) promptly. Discard any unripe green or red berries and all stem material.
storage.notes_beginner: Pick the whole flat berry clusters when most berries are deep purple-black, keep them cool, and strip and cook them soon. Throw out any green or red unripe berries and all the stems.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Not applicable. Elderberry is a permanent woody shrub planted once and kept in place for many years, so it is not part of any crop rotation and there is no prior crop to avoid following.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: This does not apply to elderberry. You plant it once and it stays put for years, so there is nothing to rotate.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotation does not apply to elderberry. It is a long-lived perennial shrub that occupies the same spot for many years, so choose a moist, sunny, roomy site up front, since you will not be moving it.
rotation.note_beginner: Crop rotation is for vegetables you replant each year. Elderberry is a shrub that lives in one spot for years, so just pick a good moist, sunny site and leave it there.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A dormant bare-root plant or rooted cutting going into moist, fertile soil, typically late winter to spring; container plants can also go in during fall.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Your new elderberry going into rich, moist soil, at the same depth it was growing before.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Plant in moist, fertile soil at the depth it grew, water in well, and mulch. Plant at least two different cultivars for cross-pollination.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Plant in rich, damp soil at the same depth it was before, water it well, and mulch around it. Plant two different varieties near each other.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record planting date, cultivars, and the site (sun and moisture).
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Write down when you planted, which varieties, and how sunny and moist the spot is.

growth_stages.name: Establishment (year 1)
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A young plant putting its energy into roots and new canes rather than fruit. Elderberry establishes fast, so this stage is short.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Your young elderberry growing roots and stems, not a real crop yet. This lasts about the first year.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Remove the flower clusters the first year so the plant builds roots and canes. Keep the soil evenly moist and mulched.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pinch off the flowers the first year so the plant grows strong instead of fruiting. Keep it watered and mulched.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Log flower removal, watering, and mulch.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you removed flowers, watered, and mulched.

growth_stages.name: Spring growth and budbreak
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Vigorous new shoots and canes leafing out from the base and from last year's wood each spring. Growth is fast now.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Each spring the plant leafs out and sends up fast new growth from the base.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Feed once in early spring (from year two) with a balanced fertilizer or compost, and keep the soil moist as growth takes off.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: In spring, feed with a balanced fertilizer or compost (starting year two), and keep the soil damp.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record budbreak, feeding, and cane growth.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when it leafed out and when you fed it.

growth_stages.name: Bloom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Broad, flat, creamy-white flower clusters (cymes) opening in early to midsummer. They are wind-pollinated and worked by many insects, and need a second cultivar nearby for good set.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Big flat clusters of creamy-white flowers open in early summer. Bees visit them, and a second variety nearby means more fruit.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Make sure a second, different cultivar is blooming nearby. You can harvest some flower clusters for cordials or fritters, but leave most to set fruit.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Let the bees work, and make sure another elderberry variety is blooming nearby. You can pick a few flower clusters to use, but leave most to become berries.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Log first and full bloom, and any frost during bloom.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when flowers opened and any frosty nights.

growth_stages.name: Fruit set and sizing
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Pollinated flowers set small green berries that fill out over several weeks into heavy clusters, deepening from green to red to purple-black. The most water-sensitive window.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The flowers turn into tiny green berries that grow into full clusters, turning from green to purple over a few weeks.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture steady while clusters size, and net the shrub or plan bird control before the berries color.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil damp while the clusters grow, and get netting ready before the berries darken.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record fruit set, netting, and watering through sizing.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when green berries appeared and when you netted.

growth_stages.name: Ripening and harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Clusters ripen to deep purple-black in late summer. Cut whole cymes when most berries are dark, plump, and soft; berries do not ripen further after picking and must be cooked.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Clusters turn deep purple-black in late summer. Cut off whole clusters when most berries are dark and soft. Always cook the berries.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut whole ripe clusters with pruners, strip the berries from the stems, discard green or red berries and all stems, and cook, freeze, or dry promptly.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Snip off whole ripe clusters, pull the berries off the stems, throw out unripe berries and stems, and cook or freeze them soon.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Log first ripe date, each harvest and rough amount, and final pick.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note your first ripe clusters, each picking, and roughly how much.

growth_stages.name: Post-harvest growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: After harvest the plant keeps growing and stores energy in its canes and roots for next year. Late-season growth should slow and harden before frost.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Once the berries are done, the plant keeps growing leaves and building up for next year.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep the plant watered and healthy; stop feeding by late summer so growth hardens off before winter.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: After picking, keep it watered, but stop feeding by late summer so it toughens up for winter.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record watering and plant condition into fall.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note watering and how the plant looks heading into fall.

growth_stages.name: Winter dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The shrub drops its leaves and rests dormant through winter, fully cold-hardy. In frost-free regions it slows but may not go fully bare.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: In winter the plant loses its leaves and rests. It is very cold-hardy and needs little attention.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Little is needed: keep mulch in place and do not let the roots sit bone-dry in a mild, dry winter.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Not much to do in winter. Keep mulch on, and give a little water only in a dry, mild winter.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Log leaf drop and any winter protection for potted plants.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when the leaves dropped.

growth_stages.name: Dormant-season pruning and cane renewal
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: In late winter, while the shrub is leafless, do the annual pruning: remove canes older than about three years, plus dead, weak, or crowded stems, keeping vigorous young canes. Neglected clumps can be cut to the ground to renew.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: In late winter, while the plant is bare, cut out the oldest canes (over about three years old) and any dead or crowded stems. An overgrown plant can be cut to the ground to start fresh.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Remove the oldest canes at ground level and thin the clump for a balance of one-, two-, and three-year-old wood. Destroy prunings to reduce borers.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Cut the oldest canes off at the base and thin out crowding, leaving strong young stems. Throw away the trimmings to keep borers down.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record pruning date and canes removed.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you pruned and what you cut.

notifications.body_seasoned: Elderberry is only partially self-fertile, so plant at least two DIFFERENT cultivars within about 60 feet of each other. This single step dramatically increases how much fruit you pick.
notifications.body_beginner: Plant at least two different kinds of elderberry near each other (within about 60 feet) so they pollinate each other. You will get far more berries.

notifications.title_seasoned: Feed and water as growth begins
notifications.body_seasoned: As new canes take off in spring, feed once (from year two) with a balanced fertilizer or compost and keep the soil evenly moist. Elderberry is a thirsty, fast grower.
notifications.body_beginner: When the plant leafs out in spring, feed it with a balanced fertilizer or compost (from year two) and keep the soil damp.

notifications.title_beginner: Pinch off flowers the first year
notifications.body_seasoned: In the planting year, remove the flower clusters so the young plant builds roots and canes. Elderberry establishes fast, so you lose almost nothing and gain strong early crops.
notifications.body_beginner: The first summer, pinch off the flowers so the plant grows strong roots and stems. You will be picking real crops by next year or two.

notifications.title_beginner: Net the shrub before berries darken
notifications.body_seasoned: Birds are the number-one competitor for elderberries. Net the shrub before clusters begin to color, or grow an inverting-cyme cultivar such as Bob Gordon, which hides the fruit and loses less.
notifications.body_beginner: Birds love ripe elderberries. Cover the shrub with netting before the berries darken, or grow a drooping-cluster variety like Bob Gordon that birds miss more.

notifications.title_seasoned: Harvest ripe clusters, and always cook them
notifications.title_beginner: Pick ripe clusters, and always cook them
notifications.body_seasoned: Cut whole clusters when most berries are deep purple-black and soft. Strip the berries, discard green or red berries and all stems, and COOK before eating: raw and unripe berries, leaves, and stems are mildly toxic.
notifications.body_beginner: Snip off whole clusters when most berries are dark and soft, pull the berries off the stems, and cook them before eating. Never eat raw or green berries, or the leaves and stems, which can make you sick.

notifications.title_seasoned: Prune and renew canes in late winter
notifications.title_beginner: Prune out old canes in late winter
notifications.body_seasoned: In late winter, remove canes older than about three years plus dead, weak, and crowded stems, keeping vigorous young canes. Destroy the prunings to reduce cane borers.
notifications.body_beginner: In late winter, cut out the oldest canes (over about three years) and any dead or crowded stems, and leave the strong young ones. Throw the trimmings away.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost warning during bloom
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A frost is forecast while your elderberry is in bloom. Elderberry blooms in early summer and rarely meets frost, but an unusually late freeze can nip open flowers; cover a small plant overnight if you can.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Frost is coming while your elderberry is flowering. This is rare in early summer, but cover a small plant overnight to protect the flowers if you can.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat and drought during fruit sizing
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot, dry spell while berries grow
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A hot, dry stretch is forecast while the clusters are sizing. Elderberry has shallow roots and dislikes drought; keep the soil evenly moist through the heat to protect cluster size and yield.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: It is going to be hot and dry while your berries grow. Keep the soil damp so the clusters do not come in small.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Dry stretch for a young plant
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A dry spell is forecast and your elderberry is young or newly planted. Its shallow roots are drought-sensitive while establishing; water deeply and keep a thick mulch to hold moisture.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: A dry stretch is coming and your elderberry is still young. Water it well and keep mulch around it so it does not dry out.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Rain coming before you pick
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Rain is forecast as clusters ripen. Wet fruit is more prone to splitting and decay, so let clusters dry before cutting and harvest promptly once ripe, then cool and process.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Rain is coming as your berries ripen. Let the clusters dry before you cut them, then pick and process soon.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Lots of heavy rain
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Extended heavy rain is forecast. Elderberry tolerates wet soil better than any other berry, so waterlogging is a minor concern; only truly stagnant standing water is a problem, so ensure the site is not a sealed basin.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Long heavy rain is coming. Elderberry handles wet soil well, so this is rarely a problem unless water sits completely still around the roots.

planting.text_seasoned: Plant two or more DIFFERENT cultivars within about 60 feet for cross-pollination; elderberry is only partially self-fertile and yields far more with a partner. Choose a moist, sunny, roomy site.
planting.text_beginner: Plant at least two different varieties near each other (within 60 feet) so they pollinate and give you much more fruit. Pick a moist, sunny spot with room to spread.
planting.author: plant_team

establishment.text_seasoned: Remove the flower clusters in the planting year so the plant builds roots and canes. Elderberry establishes fast, so this brief restraint costs little and pays off in year two.
establishment.text_beginner: Pinch off the flowers the first summer so the plant grows strong. It grows quickly, so you will get berries soon anyway.
establishment.author: plant_team

first_growth.text_seasoned: Feed once in early spring (from year two) with a balanced fertilizer or compost, and keep the soil evenly moist as the fast new canes emerge. Do not over-feed, which makes floppy growth.
first_growth.text_beginner: In spring, feed with a balanced fertilizer or compost (starting year two) and keep the soil damp. Go easy, since too much fertilizer makes weak, floppy stems.
first_growth.author: plant_team

blossom.text_seasoned: The broad creamy cymes are edible too: you can cut a few for cordials or fritters, but leave most to set fruit, and make sure a second cultivar blooms alongside for good pollination.
blossom.text_beginner: The flower clusters are edible; pick a few for cordials if you like, but leave most to become berries. Make sure another variety is blooming nearby.
blossom.author: plant_team

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Keep moisture steady while clusters size, and get bird protection in place before the berries color; birds are the top competitor and can clear ripe clusters fast.
fruit_set.text_beginner: Keep the soil damp while the clusters fill out, and net the shrub before the berries darken, because birds can strip them quickly.
fruit_set.author: plant_team

dormancy.text_seasoned: Elderberry is fully cold-hardy and needs little winter care; keep mulch in place and only water in an unusually dry, mild winter. Late winter is the time to plan pruning.
dormancy.text_beginner: Elderberry rests over winter and is very cold-hardy, so there is little to do. Keep mulch on and plan your late-winter pruning.
dormancy.author: plant_team

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Each late winter, remove canes older than about three years plus dead and crowded stems, keeping a mix of young wood. An overgrown, unproductive clump can be cut to the ground to renew it.
dormant_prune.text_beginner: In late winter, cut out the oldest canes (over about three years) and any dead or crowded stems, leaving strong young ones. A neglected plant can be cut right to the ground to start fresh.
dormant_prune.author: plant_team

harvest.text_seasoned: Cut whole clusters when most berries are deep purple-black and soft, strip them (chilling the clusters helps), discard green or red berries and all stems, and ALWAYS cook before eating: raw and unripe fruit, leaves, and stems are mildly toxic.
harvest.text_beginner: Snip off whole clusters when most berries are dark and soft, pull the berries off the stems, and always cook them. Never eat raw or green berries, or the leaves and stems, which can make you sick.
harvest.author: plant_team

post_harvest.text_seasoned: Keep the plant watered and healthy after harvest, but stop feeding by late summer so the canes harden off before frost. A vigorous plant now sets up next year's heavy crop.
post_harvest.text_beginner: After picking, keep the plant watered but stop feeding by late summer so it toughens up for winter. A healthy plant now means more berries next year.
post_harvest.author: plant_team

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A mature, well-grown elderberry commonly yields roughly 10 to 15 pounds of berries per year, sometimes more on the most productive modern cultivars in good, moist soil. Yield climbs quickly as the shrub fills in and is heavily dependent on cross-pollination and moisture.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: A mature elderberry bush usually gives about 10 to 15 pounds of berries a year, more with good soil, plenty of water, and a second variety nearby for pollination.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Elderberry is fast: expect a light crop the second year and something close to full production by years three to four, far quicker than blueberry. A well-managed, renewed planting stays productive for many years.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Elderberry produces quickly. You will get a small crop the second year and close to a full crop by year three or four, then good harvests for years with regular pruning.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Expect little or no harvest the first year, and remove the flower clusters that season so the young plant builds roots and canes. It grows so fast that this costs you almost nothing: real crops arrive by the second or third year.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Do not expect berries the first year, and pinch off the flowers that first summer so the plant grows strong. Elderberry is quick, so you will be picking real crops by year two or three.
factors_seasoned: Cross-pollination: two or more different cultivars with overlapping bloom sharply raise yield.
Cultivar: modern selections such as Bob Gordon and Wyldewood out-yield the older standards.
Consistent moisture: drought during fruit sizing cuts both cluster size and total yield.
Full sun: fruiting is heaviest in full sun; shade reduces the crop.
Cane renewal: annual removal of the oldest canes keeps a balance of productive young wood.
Fertility: a moderately rich, well-fed soil supports the heavy growth that carries the crop.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No moon-phase planting guidance is offered for elderberry. There is no extension or peer-reviewed basis for timing elderberry planting or care by lunar phase, so the field is intentionally left without a recommendation.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Little or no fruit
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Little or no fruit
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The shrub grew well but set few or no berries. The usual causes are a lone plant with no second cultivar to cross-pollinate, too much shade, or a late frost on the flowers.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your elderberry grew fine but made few berries. Usually this means it has no second variety to pollinate with, it is too shaded, or frost hit the flowers.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant at least two different cultivars with overlapping bloom within about 60 feet, site it in full sun, and protect early bloom from a rare late frost.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant a second, different variety within about 60 feet, give it full sun, and cover the flowers if a rare late frost threatens.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Fruit disappearing as it ripens
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Fruit disappearing as it ripens
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Clusters vanished just as they ripened. This is almost always birds, the number-one competitor for elderberries, reaching unprotected fruit.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The berries disappeared right as they ripened. This is almost always birds getting at unprotected fruit.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Net the shrub before berries color next season, or grow an inverting-cyme cultivar such as Bob Gordon that hides the fruit, and harvest promptly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Cover the shrub with netting before the berries darken, or grow a drooping-cluster variety like Bob Gordon, and pick as soon as ripe.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Feeling sick after eating the berries
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Feeling sick after eating the berries
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Someone felt nauseous or unwell after eating elderberries. Raw or unripe (green or red) berries, and any leaves, stems, or seeds, contain cyanogenic compounds that can cause nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Cooking the berries destroys these.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Someone got an upset stomach from the elderberries. Raw or unripe berries, and the leaves and stems, can make you sick because they contain natural toxins. Cooking the ripe berries makes them safe.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Always cook elderberries before eating. Use only fully ripe purple-black berries, keep all stems and leaves out, and never eat the berries raw or the green or red unripe ones.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Always cook elderberries before eating. Use only fully ripe dark berries, keep the stems and leaves out, and never eat them raw or eat green or red unripe berries.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Individual canes wilting and dying
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Individual canes wilting and dying
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: One or more canes suddenly wilted and died back, with hollowed, tunneled stems when cut. This is cane and shoot borers whose larvae tunnel inside the wood.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: A cane suddenly wilted and died, and the stem was hollow inside. This is a borer grub tunneling in the cane.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Prune out and destroy affected canes below the damage as soon as you see wilting, and renew old canes each dormant season to break the borers' cycle.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Cut off and throw away the wilting canes right away, and cut out old canes each winter to keep borers down.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Overgrown thicket with poor fruiting
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Overgrown thicket with poor fruiting
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The plant became a dense, tall, tangled thicket that fruits poorly. Elderberry canes fruit best when young; without renewal, old canes dominate and yield falls.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your elderberry turned into a big tangled thicket that makes few berries. Elderberry fruits best on younger canes, so old ones need removing.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Renew the planting: each late winter remove canes older than about three years, or cut a badly neglected clump to the ground to force fresh, productive growth.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Prune it: each late winter cut out the oldest canes, or cut the whole overgrown plant to the ground and let it regrow fresh and fruitful.

sources_summary.note: T1 university-extension elderberry guides read live 2026-06-30: Penn State 'Elderberry in the Garden and the Kitchen' (garden culture, cross-pollination within 60 ft, harvest, and the load-bearing cook-before-eating / toxicity guidance), University of Missouri AF1017 'Growing and Marketing Elderberries in Missouri' (cultivars, spacing, year-2 bearing, harvest timing), and Michigan State 'Growing elderberry in the garden' (size/hardiness, pH 5.5 to 6.5, wet tolerance, late-August ripening, pruning and cane renewal, pests, and rust). Draft sourcing is intentionally narrow for a pilot; the MSU E-2747 'Unusual Fruit Plants' PDF was binary-unreadable at fetch and is FLAGGED, not cited.

succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Not applicable. Elderberry is a long-lived woody shrub planted once and renewed in place by cane pruning, not a crop sown in succession. There is no replanting cycle.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: Wave-3 tree+berry cert (2026-07-02): parallel per-crop source-truth review (CC agents, WebFetch of cited T1 pages). pawpaw self-incompatibility + 'two grafted trees of the same cultivar will not cross-pollinate' + fly/beetle pollination + chill 400-1000 verbatim on KSU FAQ; blackberry + raspberry self-fertile + primocane/floricane + SWD strongly multi-sourced (NCSU/USU/UMN/Cornell), all-T1; elderberry COOK-BEFORE-EATING SAFETY VERIFIED verbatim on PSU (sambunigrin, raw prohibition, cooking destroys the toxin). Pollination pinned/repointed to the page that states the claim; modeled items recorded + stale gate findings closed.

open_findings.summary: A15 BUSH type enum is {northern_highbush, southern_highbush, rabbiteye}; elderberry's one real type is 'american_elderberry', so every resolved cell trips 'recommended_type not in enum'. No honest in-enum value exists. Human fix: add an elderberry sub-form / type to the gate. [RESOLVED 2026-07-02: the SHRUB berries_woody sub-form landed; SHRUB_TYPE_ENUM includes american_elderberry.]

Elderberry is PARTIALLY self-fertile (sets some fruit alone, far better with a second cultivar). Modeled as self_fertile true (honest), which trips the BUSH branch's 'self_fertile must be false'. The gate's binary bush=False / cane=bool model has no 'partially self-fertile' state. Human fix: an elderberry sub-form. [RESOLVED 2026-07-02: the SHRUB branch accepts self_fertile=true (bool), like cane.]

cane_type has no elderberry-appropriate value: 'not_applicable' (bush crown) understates elderberry's real perennial multi-stem cane-renewal, but the biennial-cane enum {summer_bearing, everbearing} is wrong too. Set 'not_applicable' to route through the closest (BUSH) branch; flagged for a human sub-form. [RESOLVED 2026-07-02: cane_type 'multistem_perennial' is the recognized SHRUB routing marker; record carries it.]

gating_factors carries 'chill_hours' and per-variety chill_hours_required is a uniform nominal 400 to satisfy A15/A21, but elderberry is NOT chill-type-gated: one type everywhere, cultivars chosen by yield/season, not chill. Chill is retained only as the real winter-dormancy requirement A15 mandates. Secondary conceptual mismatch.

leaf_habit is deciduous on every cell (elderberry has no evergreen form), so the A16 deciduous deriver fills 'dormant' months on the near-frost-free warm cells (fl z11, hawaii z11, warm CA z10). Biologically these are low-activity/semi-evergreen; a known modeling artifact, same class as the raspberry pilot's warm-cell dormancy.

Coverage floor A31/A32 forces all 10 regions with populated calendars, but elderberry is genuinely marginal in the hot low deserts and far tropics (z10 to z11). Those cells carry best-effort windows with strong marginality language in the region prose; honest biology, not a fudge.

the GI-symptom enumeration (nausea/vomiting/diarrhea) in failure_diagnostics is single-anchored to PSU (which states the toxicity + raw prohibition + that cooking destroys the toxin, but not the specific symptoms); the symptoms are backed by Ohio State Ohioline ANR-0110 + USU + medical literature. Add Ohioline as a 2nd anchor at the citation sweep.

3.type_note_seasoned: American elderberry is the one type to grow here, chosen by cultivar rather than by climate. It is exceptionally cold-hardy, thrives in your moist soils, and fruits fast; the only rule is to plant two different cultivars for cross-pollination.
3.type_note_beginner: Grow American elderberry, the one common type. It is very cold-hardy and loves the moist soil here. Just plant two different varieties near each other for a good crop.
3.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Elderberry blooms in early summer, well after spring frost, so frost on bloom is rarely a concern here.
3.grown_as_note_seasoned: Elderberry is a permanent, very cold-hardy deciduous shrub, planted once and renewed in place for many years. It rests bare and dormant through winter, leafs out and grows fast in spring, blooms in early summer, and ripens clusters of dark berries in late summer, after which you renew the oldest canes in late winter. Plant two different cultivars for good fruit set.
3.grown_as_note_beginner: Your elderberry is a long-lived, very cold-hardy bush you plant once and keep for years. It loses its leaves and rests in winter, grows fast in spring, flowers in early summer, and ripens dark berries in late summer. Prune the oldest stems in late winter, and plant two different varieties for plenty of fruit.

crops.description_seasoned: Elderberry is a big, fast, tough native shrub grown for its clusters of small dark berries, which are cooked into juice, syrup, jelly, wine, and pie (and its flowers are used too). It is one of the easiest fruits to grow: very cold-hardy, wet-tolerant, and productive within two or three years. Two things are non-negotiable: plant two different cultivars for good yield, and always COOK the berries, because raw or unripe fruit, leaves, and stems are mildly toxic.
crops.description_beginner: Elderberry is a large, easygoing native shrub that gives big clusters of small dark berries for making juice, syrup, jelly, and pies. It is very cold-hardy, handles wet soil, and starts producing in just two or three years. Remember two things: plant two different varieties so you get plenty of fruit, and always cook the berries, because raw berries, leaves, and stems can make you sick.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Harvest whole flower-cluster heads (cymes) when most of the berries in a cluster have turned deep purple-black and are plump and soft, usually late summer. Cut the entire cluster with pruners rather than picking berries one by one, then strip the berries from the green stems (chilling or briefly freezing makes this easy). Leave green or red under-ripe berries, and never include stems. Berries do not sweeten after picking, and they must be cooked.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Elderberries are ready when most berries in a cluster are deep purple-black, plump, and soft. Snip off the whole cluster with pruners instead of picking one berry at a time, then pull the berries off the stems (freezing the clusters briefly makes this easy). Skip any green or red berries, keep the stems out, and always cook the berries before eating.
crops.bloom_time_seasoned: Elderberry blooms in early to midsummer in most of the country (June into July), and earlier in the warm South, carrying broad, flat, creamy-white flower clusters (cymes) that are showy and fragrant. Each cluster is receptive over one to two weeks, and the flowers are both wind-pollinated and heavily insect-visited. Late-blooming cultivars help dodge spring frost.
crops.bloom_time_beginner: Elderberry flowers in early to midsummer (June to July in most areas, earlier in the South), with big flat clusters of creamy-white blooms that bees love. The flowers themselves are edible and used for cordials and fritters.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Elderberry is exceptionally cold-hardy and widely adaptable. American elderberry is reliably hardy and productive across roughly USDA zones 3 through 9, its native range covering most of the eastern and central United States, and it is one of the most cold-tolerant fruit crops you can grow. In the frost-free deep South and mild coasts (zones 10 to 11) it still grows, and native populations fruit there, but low winter chill and extreme heat make it more of an adaptation-edge crop than a sure thing; the far tropics and hot low deserts are marginal.
crops.hardiness_notes_beginner: Elderberry is one of the toughest, most cold-hardy fruits there is, thriving across most of the country (roughly zones 3 to 9). In very warm, frost-free areas (zones 10 to 11) it will grow, but it is less reliable there because it likes a real winter and dislikes extreme heat.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Elderberry is a deciduous shrub that rests dormant each winter and needs a period of cold to do so, but its chill requirement is low and, unlike blueberry, is NOT how you choose a cultivar: there is essentially one type (American elderberry) grown everywhere. In practice, winter dormancy is a given across its hardy range, and the low-chill point only matters at the frost-free warm edge, where too little cold can make bloom and fruiting erratic.
crops.chill_hours_note_beginner: Elderberry needs a cold winter rest, but not much, and you do not pick varieties by chill the way you do with blueberries; there is basically one kind of elderberry. The only place low winter cold matters is the frost-free deep South, where it can make fruiting less reliable.
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Plant at least two DIFFERENT cultivars with overlapping bloom, within about 60 feet of each other. Elderberry is only partially self-fertile: a single plant sets some fruit, but a compatible second cultivar dramatically increases yield, cluster size, and reliability. The flowers are wind-pollinated and also worked by bees and other insects, so the key is simply having two overlapping-bloom cultivars nearby, not any specific pairing.
crops.pollinator_notes_beginner: Plant two or more different kinds of elderberry near each other, within about 60 feet, so they can cross-pollinate. Elderberry makes some fruit on its own but a lot more with a partner variety, so always plant at least two different ones.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: Focus the first year on roots and canes, not fruit: remove the flower clusters so the young plant establishes fast. Keep it well watered through its first season (its shallow roots are drought-sensitive while establishing) and mulch heavily. Elderberry is quick to establish, so this brief restraint pays off in strong crops by year two or three.
crops.year_one_notes_beginner: In the first year, pinch off the flowers so the plant puts its energy into growing strong roots and stems. Keep it well watered and mulched. Elderberry grows fast, so you will be picking berries soon.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Elderberry needs little special soil prep beyond generosity: work plenty of compost or aged manure into a moist, fertile site before planting, and mulch heavily to hold moisture around the shallow roots. It tolerates heavy and wet ground, so a low, damp spot is fine; on dry, sandy soil, add abundant organic matter and plan to irrigate. No acidification is needed.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Prepare the spot by digging in lots of compost, since elderberry loves rich, moist soil. A damp, low corner of the yard is fine. On dry, sandy soil, add extra compost and be ready to water. Unlike blueberries, elderberry needs no special acid treatment.
crops.planting_method_notes_seasoned: Set dormant bare-root plants or rooted cuttings in late winter to early spring at the depth they grew, in moist, fertile soil, and water in well; container plants can go in spring or fall. Space plants about 4 feet apart in a hedge-style row, or 6 to 8 feet apart for full-size freestanding shrubs, with wider spacing between rows. Expect vigorous growth and suckering, and plan at least two cultivars for cross-pollination.
crops.planting_method_notes_beginner: Plant elderberry in late winter or early spring, at the same depth it was growing, in moist rich soil, and water it in. Give each plant room: about 4 feet apart for a hedge, or 6 to 8 feet apart for full-size bushes. Plant at least two different varieties near each other, and expect it to grow fast and send up suckers.

pollination.notes_seasoned: Elderberry is only partially self-fertile: a lone plant sets some fruit, but yields are far higher when a second, different cultivar blooms nearby for cross-pollination. The practical rule is plant at least two different cultivars within about 60 feet of each other. Bloom is carried on large flat flower clusters (cymes) that are wind-pollinated and also worked heavily by bees and other insects; overlapping bloom between the two cultivars is what matters. This is the single biggest lever on how much fruit you pick.
pollination.notes_beginner: Elderberry will make some berries on its own, but you get a much bigger crop when you plant two different kinds near each other so they can cross-pollinate. Keep them within about 60 feet. Plant two, and plan on a lot more fruit.

crops.establishment_note: Pinch off the flower clusters the first year (and thin fruiting the second) so the young shrub spends its energy building a strong, deep root system and a full framework of canes. Elderberry is fast, so this establishment period is short: a well-started plant is bearing real crops by its second or third year.
crops.cane_management_seasoned: Elderberry is not a bush with a single crown like blueberry, nor a biennial-cane fruit like raspberry. It throws up many perennial canes from the base, and it fruits best on one, two, and three-year-old wood, so the goal is a shrub with a mix of cane ages. Each dormant season remove canes older than about three years at ground level, along with any dead, broken, weak, or crowded stems, keeping the most vigorous younger canes. If a planting has grown into a tangled, unproductive thicket, you can cut the entire clump to the ground in late winter to renew it; it will regrow vigorously and be fruiting again within a year or two.
crops.cane_management_beginner: An elderberry grows as a clump of many stems (canes) from the ground, not on a single trunk. It fruits best on canes that are one to three years old, so each winter cut out the oldest canes at the base (older than about three years) plus anything dead, broken, or crowded, and leave the strong younger stems. If your elderberry has become an overgrown tangle that fruits poorly, you can cut the whole thing to the ground in late winter and it will bounce right back.
crops.type_selection_seasoned: Unlike blueberry, elderberry is not divided into climate-matched types: there is essentially one cultivated type, American elderberry (Sambucus canadensis), grown across the whole country, so you select by CULTIVAR (yield, ripening season, habit) rather than by chill class. European elderberry (S. nigra) is an alternative with its own cultivars but is less hardy and less adapted here. The one selection rule that always applies: choose two different cultivars with overlapping bloom for cross-pollination.
crops.type_selection_beginner: There is really just one kind of elderberry to grow, American elderberry, so you do not have to match a type to your climate the way you do with blueberries. Just pick two different varieties (for pollination) based on how much they yield and when they ripen. A European kind exists but is less hardy here.

pet_safe.toxic_parts: raw or unripe berries, leaves, and stems
pet_safe.note: Cooked ripe elderberries are used in foods, but the raw or unripe berries, leaves, and stems contain cyanide compounds and are toxic to cats, dogs, and horses.

crops.name: Persimmon

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Persimmon is easygoing about soil but wants one thing above all: good drainage. A deep, well-drained loam is ideal, and a sandy loam or lighter sandy soil works fine too. The trouble spot is heavy clay that holds water, because persimmon roots, especially on Asian types, are prone to root rot in soggy ground. If your soil is heavy or wet, plant on a raised mound so the roots sit above standing water. A soil of ordinary richness suits it; persimmon needs little feeding and too much can cause the fruit to drop.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Persimmon is broadly soil-tolerant but demands good drainage, ideally a deep, well-drained loam; a sandy loam is well suited and lighter sandy soils are workable. Heavy, water-holding clay is the problem texture, since persimmon (especially Diospyros kaki) is susceptible to root and crown rot on poorly drained sites; on such ground plant on a raised berm. Best sites are upland sandy loams. Moderate fertility is plenty, and persimmon is sensitive to salinity and to excess nitrogen, which triggers fruit drop.

ph.note_beginner: Persimmon does best in a slightly acidic soil, around pH 6.0 to 6.5, and is fine up to about 7.0 (pH is just a measure of how acidic or alkaline the soil is). Test your soil before planting the permanent tree. If it is too acidic, garden lime raises the pH; if it is too alkaline, elemental sulfur lowers it. Mix any amendment in before planting, since pH changes slowly and is far easier to correct before the tree is in the ground.
ph.note_seasoned: Persimmon prefers a slightly acidic pH 6.0 to 6.5 and tolerates up to about 7.0. Test before planting and adjust gradually: lime raises a too-acidic pH, elemental sulfur lowers one that is too alkaline. Work amendments in ahead of planting the permanent tree, since pH shifts slowly and is easiest to correct before establishment.

fertilizer.timing: late dormancy, split with early and late summer
fertilizer.example_product: 10-10-10 balanced fertilizer
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Persimmon needs little feeding and is easily over-fed: excess nitrogen causes premature fruit drop. A light program suits it, split across the season on sandy soils (the bulk in late dormancy, a lighter touch in early and late summer), broadcast evenly around the root zone to the drip line and kept off the trunk. On decent soil an established tree may need no fertilizer at all; feed only if growth is weak or leaves are pale.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Persimmon barely needs feeding, and too much fertilizer, especially nitrogen, makes the fruit drop off. Go light. Scatter it evenly on the soil around the tree out to where the branches reach, keep it off the trunk, and water it in. On good soil an older tree may need nothing at all, so only feed if the tree looks weak or the leaves are pale.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 is plenty for persimmon; the tree is a light feeder and over-fertilizing, particularly with nitrogen, drops fruit rather than improving it. Err toward less.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: A balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 (the three numbers are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium) is all persimmon needs, and often it needs none. Do not overdo it, because too much, especially the first number, nitrogen, makes the fruit fall off.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A common home rate is about 2 ounces of 10-10-10 per year of tree age, applied in late dormancy (roughly March), with lighter follow-up feedings in early and late summer where the soil is sandy. Cap it at a modest total for a mature tree and do not fertilize at planting. If growth is already vigorous, skip feeding entirely; excess nitrogen shows up as dropped fruit, not bigger crops.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A simple rule is about 2 ounces of 10-10-10 for each year of the tree's age, given in late winter, with a little more in early and late summer if your soil is sandy. Do not feed a tree that is already growing well, and never put fertilizer in the planting hole. If in doubt, feed less: too much makes persimmons drop.

companions.note_beginner: Most Asian persimmons are self-fruitful, so one tree fruits on its own and you do not need a partner tree. American persimmons are different: they usually have male and female trees, so a female needs a male American persimmon nearby to fruit, unless you plant a self-fruitful kind like Meader. For a tree, the pairings that matter are not vegetable-garden companions but what grows around the roots: keep grass and weeds pulled back from under the branches, since lawn competes with a young tree, and a mulched, weed-free circle helps it settle in. Persimmon is a low-pest, easygoing tree, so there is little else to fuss over.
companions.note_seasoned: Asian persimmon (D. kaki) is self-fruitful, so a single tree crops without a pollinizer; American persimmon (D. virginiana) is typically dioecious and a female needs a male within roughly 50 to 200 feet, the exception being self-fruitful selections like Meader. The interactions that matter for a tree concern the root zone, not classic vegetable companions: keep turf and weeds cleared back from under the canopy, since grass competes hard with a young tree, and a mulched, competition-free root area speeds establishment. Persimmon is notably low-pest and low-maintenance, so companion planting is a minor consideration here.

good_seasoned.name: Flowering herbs and pollinator plants
good_seasoned.label: traditional

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Orchard-floor insectary logic is sound and extension-aligned in principle: flowering plants recruit the natural enemies (parasitic wasps, lady beetles, hoverflies) that hold persimmon's soft-bodied pests (scale, mealybug, psyllid) in check, and UC IPM's persimmon guidance leans on preserving natural enemies. But persimmon is self-fruitful/parthenocarpic, so the pollinator draw is not needed for fruit set, and the predator-recruitment benefit is diffuse and unquantified for persimmon specifically. traditional/medium.

good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A skirt of flowering herbs and pollinator plants around a persimmon supports orchard-floor health. Because persimmon is self-fruitful and its Asian cultivars set fruit parthenocarpically, the pollinator draw is a bonus rather than a requirement, but the same flowers recruit the lady beetles, lacewings, and parasitic wasps that keep scale, mealybug, and persimmon psyllid at tolerable levels, which is exactly the natural-enemy approach UC IPM recommends for this low-spray tree. Keep the plantings out toward the drip line rather than crowding the trunk.

bad_seasoned.name: Lawn and weeds crowding the young trunk
bad_seasoned.label: research_backed

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Keeping turf and weeds cleared from a young fruit tree's root zone is standard, well-evidenced extension practice: grass competes strongly with a young tree for water and nitrogen and slows establishment, and a mulched weed-free circle is the routine recommendation across fruit-tree extension guidance. extension_backed/high for the general fruit-tree principle applied to persimmon.

bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Grass and weeds pressed up against a young persimmon are the pairing to avoid. Turf competes hard with a newly planted tree for water and nitrogen and measurably slows establishment, and growth against the trunk also traps moisture and invites string-trimmer wounds. Keep a mulched, weed-free circle a few feet out from the trunk through the establishment years, keeping the mulch itself off the bark.

pests.name: Scale insects
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small, immobile bumps on bark, twigs, and the underside of leaves; white peach scale shows as snow-white encrustations on the trunk and limbs, while soft scales are brown and rounded. Heavy infestations produce sticky honeydew that blackens with sooty mold and draws ants. Vigor and fruit quality decline where scale builds up unchecked.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Little bumps stuck to the bark, twigs, and leaf undersides that do not move. White peach scale looks like snow-white crust on the trunk and branches; other scales are small brown domes. They leave a sticky coating (honeydew) that turns black with sooty mold and attracts ants. Bad cases slowly weaken the tree.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several scale species, notably white peach scale and soft scales (Parthenolecanium spp.), which insert their mouthparts and feed on sap under a protective waxy shell. Their honeydew supports sooty mold. Populations flare where natural enemies have been knocked back by broad-spectrum sprays.
pests.cause_beginner: Tiny sap-sucking insects that hide under a waxy shell, mainly white peach scale and soft scales. They feed on the tree's sap and drip sticky honeydew that grows black mold. They get worse when sprays kill off the helpful insects that normally eat them.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Preserve natural enemies (lady beetles, parasitic wasps) by not spraying broadly, since they usually hold scale to tolerable levels on persimmon. Prune out and destroy heavily encrusted wood. A dormant-season horticultural oil application smothers overwintering scale on the bark and is the main direct control for a backyard tree.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Let the helpful bugs do the work by avoiding broad sprays, since ladybugs and tiny wasps usually keep scale in check on persimmon. Cut out and throw away badly crusted branches. A spray of horticultural oil while the tree is leafless in winter smothers the scale on the bark and is the simplest hands-on control.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep the tree vigorous, avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that disrupt biological control, and monitor the trunk and scaffolds for early white encrustations so a dormant oil can be timed before populations explode.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep the tree healthy, skip the broad bug sprays that kill the good insects, and check the trunk and branches now and then for the first white crusty patches so you can put on a winter oil spray before it spreads.

pests.name: Mealybugs
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Soft, oval insects coated in white, cottony wax clustered in leaf axils, under the calyx of the fruit, and along shoots. Like scale, they excrete honeydew that fosters sooty mold and ants, and feeding under the calyx can contaminate and blemish fruit.
