blossom.text_seasoned: A single named mulberry fruits on its own. It is self-fruitful and wind-pollinated, and many cultivars set fruit parthenocarpically, so no second tree or pollinator is needed.
blossom.text_beginner: One named mulberry fruits by itself. It is self-fruitful and pollinated by wind, and many types even set fruit without any pollination, so you do not need a second tree.
blossom.author: claude_code_gs_arc

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Do not thin mulberry; the tree ripens its whole crop over weeks. Get bird netting ready for a small tree as the first berries color.
fruit_set.text_beginner: Do not thin a mulberry; it ripens all its fruit over several weeks. Have bird netting ready for a small tree as the first berries start to color.
fruit_set.author: claude_code_gs_arc

harvest.text_seasoned: Ripe mulberries are extremely perishable and detach at a touch. Pick every day or two, or shake the branches onto a sheet, and refrigerate or freeze promptly.
harvest.text_beginner: Ripe mulberries spoil fast and fall at a touch. Pick every day or two, or shake the branches onto a sheet, and chill or freeze them right away.
harvest.author: claude_code_gs_arc

harvest.text_seasoned: Expect to share with birds and to manage the drop. A mature tree yields more than a household can use, so freeze the surplus and clear fallen fruit so it does not stain or draw pests.
harvest.text_beginner: Plan on sharing with birds and dealing with the drop. A grown tree makes more than you can eat, so freeze the extra and clean up fallen fruit so it does not stain the ground or draw pests.
harvest.author: claude_code_gs_arc

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A mature standard mulberry is an extraordinarily heavy bearer, commonly yielding many gallons of fruit, on the order of tens of pounds and often far more than a household can use, ripening over several weeks. Yield is limited mainly by tree size and birds, not by feeding or thinning; the practical constraint is picking and using the crop, not growing it.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: A grown mulberry produces a huge amount of fruit, easily many gallons over several weeks, usually far more than one family can eat. How much you get depends mostly on the size of the tree and how much the birds take, not on feeding or thinning. The hard part is picking and using it all, not growing it.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Trees reach heavy bearing within a few years and stay productive for decades, given only light annual pruning. A named everbearing cultivar spreads its crop over a long window; a standard tree simply overwhelms with fruit at peak.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: A mulberry reaches heavy production within a few years and keeps bearing for decades with only light pruning. Everbearing types spread the fruit over a long stretch; a full-size tree just gives you an overwhelming amount at peak.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Expect little to no fruit in the first year or two while the tree establishes. Some named everbearing cultivars set a light crop early, sometimes even the first year, but real production begins around years 2 to 3 and builds from there.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Do not expect much fruit the first year or two while the tree settles in. Some everbearing varieties give a little early, sometimes even the first year, but real crops start around years 2 to 3 and grow from there.
factors_seasoned: cultivar and mature size
tree age and establishment
bird pressure
water during fruit fill
site sun and drainage
regional season length

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No moon-phase planting preference is asserted. Extension sources do not support timing mulberry planting or care by lunar phase; site, drainage, and cultivar choice govern outcomes.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Tree grows well but sets no fruit
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The tree is healthy but gives no fruit
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The tree is vigorous but never fruits. The usual causes are a young tree not yet of bearing age (mulberry typically starts around years 2 to 3), a fruitless ornamental mulberry (some are sold specifically as non-fruiting shade trees), or, less commonly, a single-sex seedling, since a few wild mulberries are dioecious with male and female flowers on separate trees. Named fruiting cultivars are self-fruitful and often parthenocarpic, so a lone one fruits on its own. The fix is the plant, not the care: buy a named FRUITING cultivar (not a fruitless ornamental), and give a young tree a couple more seasons.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The tree grows fine but never fruits. Usually it is just young (mulberry starts fruiting around years 2 to 3), or it is a fruitless ornamental mulberry sold as a no-fruit shade tree, or, less often, a wild seedling that happens to be male, since a few mulberries have separate male and female trees. Named fruiting varieties fruit on their own. The fix is the plant, not how you care for it: buy a named FRUITING variety, and give a young tree another year or two.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Buy a named self-fruitful FRUITING cultivar (Illinois Everbearing, Dwarf Everbearing, and similar), avoid fruitless ornamentals, and be patient with a young tree.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Buy a named self-fruitful FRUITING variety like Illinois Everbearing or Dwarf Everbearing, avoid the fruitless ornamental kinds, and give a young tree time.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Berries swell into hard, greenish popcorn-like lumps
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Berries turn into hard popcorn-like lumps
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Some berries swell abnormally, with segments enlarging and staying hard and greenish so the fruit looks like popcorn, and they never ripen. This is popcorn disease, the fungus Ciboria carunculoides, most common in the South and on white mulberries and their hybrids. There is no home spray; it is managed by sanitation. Remove and destroy affected fruit and clear the fallen fruit and debris beneath the tree, since that is where the fungus overwinters.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Some berries puff up hard and greenish like popcorn and never ripen. This is popcorn disease, a fungus (Ciboria carunculoides) most common in the South and on white mulberries and hybrids. No spray fixes it; you manage it by cleanup. Pick off and throw away the affected berries and clear the fallen fruit and debris under the tree, because that is where the fungus waits out the winter.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Clear all fallen and affected fruit each season to break the cycle, and where popcorn disease is common, favor a red mulberry or a more resistant hybrid over the most susceptible white types.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Clean up all the fallen and affected fruit each year to stop it spreading, and where the disease is common, pick a red mulberry or a tougher hybrid instead of the most susceptible white types.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Purple stains on pavement, decking, and cars
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Purple stains all over paths and cars
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The ground, pavement, decking, or vehicles under the tree are stained deep purple, and the stains track indoors. This is not a disease; it is the normal, heavy fruit drop of a productive mulberry, made worse by birds. It is almost always a siting problem. The corrective action is placement: a mature tree cannot be stopped from dropping fruit, so plant future trees, and manage this one, well away from any hard surface, and consider a weeping or dwarf form that is easier to net and harvest.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The ground, pavement, deck, or cars under the tree are stained deep purple, and it gets tracked inside. This is not a disease; it is just the normal heavy fruit drop of a productive mulberry, made worse by birds. It is really a placement problem. You cannot stop a big tree from dropping fruit, so plant future trees, and work around this one, well away from any hard surface, and think about a weeping or dwarf type that is easier to net and pick.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site mulberries away from walkways, patios, drives, and parking; for a small space choose a dwarf or weeping cultivar you can net and pick clean.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant mulberries away from paths, patios, driveways, and parking; for a small yard pick a dwarf or weeping variety you can net and pick clean.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Mulberry seedlings coming up everywhere
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Baby mulberries sprouting all over
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Young mulberry seedlings appear across the yard and in beds, spread by birds eating the fruit. White mulberry in particular self-seeds readily and is considered weedy or invasive in some regions (a noxious weed in a few states). The fix is routine: pull seedlings while small, and where invasiveness is a concern choose a named, less weedy cultivar (and note that some fruitless ornamental selections were, ironically, planted to avoid exactly this).
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Little mulberry seedlings keep popping up around the yard and in beds, spread by birds eating the fruit. White mulberry especially self-seeds a lot and is considered weedy or invasive in some areas. The fix is simple: pull the seedlings while they are small, and if invasiveness is a worry where you live, choose a named, less weedy variety.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Pull seedlings while small, keep fruit cleaned up, and where invasiveness is a local concern choose a named cultivar rather than a wild seedling.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Pull the seedlings while small, keep the fallen fruit cleaned up, and if invasiveness is a concern where you live, plant a named variety rather than a wild seedling.

succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Succession planting does not apply to mulberry. It is a permanent tree that occupies its site for decades and bears once each year, ripening its crop over an extended window, so there is no staggered re-sowing to schedule the way there is for a short-season annual.

open_findings.summary: mulberry pollination is a TYPE-SPLIT (like plum/persimmon): named fruiting cultivars are typically self-fruitful/female (the home-garden default, so self_fertile=true), but the SPECIES is variably monoecious/dioecious and wild red mulberry is usually dioecious (needs both sexes). The strong self-fruitful/parthenocarpic claim is horticultural consensus + a hedged UMD Ask-Extension answer, not a peer-reviewed T1 pub; the pollination prose was REFRAMED (Wave-3b) to lead with the T1-backed wind-pollination + dioecious variability (UF/IFAS Marvelous Mulberries + NCSU), keeping the named-cultivar self-fruitfulness as a hedged practical note. Refine at variety-pass.
chill_hours_range [100,500] is a horticultural-consensus estimate; no cited T1 page publishes a numeric mulberry chill figure (self-disclosed in chill_hours_note). Refine at variety-pass.

popcorn disease (Ciboria carunculoides) is rated 'medium' severity for a fruiting-tree audience, a notch above the cited TAMU handbook's 'of little importance' (which is ornamental-framed). Defensible; OSU co-source (ok_state_ext) returned 403 at review.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: Wave-3b mulberry citation repair + cert (2026-07-02): the absolute 'self-fruitful + parthenocarpic' pollination headline was NOT citable at strong T1 (only a hedged UMD Ask-Extension Q&A), and the cited pages affirmatively state a monoecious-OR-dioecious variability (wild red mulberry usually dioecious). REFRAMED the pollination to lead with the T1-backed wind-pollination + dioecious variability (UF/IFAS 'Marvelous Mulberries' verbatim: wind pollination + monoecious/dioecious; NCSU morus-rubra: usually dioecious), keeping named-cultivar self-fruitfulness as a hedged practical note. self_fertile=true retained as the named-cultivar home-garden default (type-split modeling, cf. plum/persimmon). Pollination pinned under A38.

3.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 3 winter lows (to -30°F and below) exceed the survival threshold of even the hardiest mulberries. Not a mulberry zone.
3.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 3 is too cold for mulberry to survive reliably. This is not a mulberry-growing zone.

4.plant_out: Late winter to early spring (dormant, bare-root)
4.suitability_note_seasoned: The cold edge. Hardy hybrids (Illinois Everbearing, Silk Hope) and white mulberry survive and fruit here, to about -20°F; tender black and low-chill types do not. Expect a slightly later, shorter season and occasional winter dieback of less-hardy wood in severe years.
4.suitability_note_beginner: The cold edge for mulberry. Hardy varieties like Illinois Everbearing survive and fruit here, but tender black and low-chill kinds do not. The season is a bit later and shorter, and a very hard winter may nip some wood.
4.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Late frost is a minor risk: mulberry leafs out later than stone fruit and recovers if the new growth is nipped, so a hard late freeze rarely costs the crop.

5.plant_out: Late winter to early spring (dormant, bare-root)
5.suitability_note_seasoned: Reliable mulberry country for hardy hybrids and white mulberry, with a long summer harvest. Chill is abundant. Choose a cold-hardy cultivar and expect dependable crops.
5.suitability_note_beginner: Hardy mulberries fruit dependably here, with a long summer harvest. Just choose a cold-hardy variety.
5.frost_risk_note_seasoned: An occasional late frost may nip early growth, but mulberry's later leaf-out and quick recovery make crop loss uncommon.

6.plant_out: Late winter to early spring (dormant, bare-root)
6.suitability_note_seasoned: Excellent mulberry country: hardy hybrids fruit heavily over a long summer, and lower-chill types become workable too. Ample chill, a long season.
6.suitability_note_beginner: Great for mulberry: hardy varieties bear heavily over a long summer, and you have more choices here. Plenty of winter cold and a long season.
6.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Late frost risk is low; mulberry's late bloom keeps it out of most spring freezes.

7.plant_out: Late winter to early spring (dormant, bare-root)
7.suitability_note_seasoned: Prime mulberry country across the variety range, from hardy hybrids to warmer, lower-chill types. Long season, ample chill, minimal frost risk.
7.suitability_note_beginner: Prime mulberry country, with almost any variety a good option. Long season, plenty of cold, little frost risk.
7.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Late-frost loss is rare, since mulberry blooms after most spring freezes have passed.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the north, plant a hardy variety like Illinois Everbearing. These fruit well from about zone 5 up and survive in zone 4; only the very coldest zone 3 is too cold. The tender black and low-chill kinds will not make it here. Mulberry blooms late, so frost is not much of a worry.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Across the northern tier, grow a hardy hybrid such as Illinois Everbearing or Silk Hope. These fruit reliably from about zone 5 up and survive to zone 4; only the coldest zone 3 is out of reach. The tender black and low-chill types are not hardy here. Mulberry blooms later than stone fruit, so late frost is a minor concern.
northern_tier.chill_basis_seasoned: Northern-tier winters bank far more chill than any mulberry needs, so chill is never the limiter here; cold hardiness of the cultivar is what matters. Choose a hardy hybrid and cold is not a problem down to about zone 4.
northern_tier.chill_basis_beginner: Winters here are plenty cold for any mulberry. The only thing that matters is picking a cold-hardy variety, and then even zone 4 is fine.

8.plant_out: Late winter to early spring (dormant, bare-root)
8.suitability_note_seasoned: Reliable mulberry country with early bloom and an early-summer harvest. Red, white, and hybrid types all crop well; watch susceptible white types for popcorn disease and keep fallen fruit cleaned up.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Dependable for mulberry, with early bloom and an early-summer harvest. Red, white, and hybrid types all do well; keep an eye on white types for popcorn disease and clean up fallen fruit.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Mulberry blooms with leaf-out in March; a late-March frost rarely troubles it, since new growth recovers.

9.plant_out: Late winter to early spring (dormant, bare-root)
9.suitability_note_seasoned: The warm, lower-chill Gulf edge. Favor lower-chill and red mulberry types; these fruit early and heavily. Popcorn disease pressure is highest on white types in this humid warmth, so sanitation matters.
9.suitability_note_beginner: The warm, lower-chill edge near the Gulf. Choose lower-chill or red mulberry types, which fruit early and heavily. Popcorn disease is most likely on white types in this humid warmth, so keep things clean.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Bloom is early here, but mulberry's later leaf-out and quick recovery keep frost from being a real threat.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: The Southeast grows mulberries beautifully. Red mulberry is native here, and white and hybrid types do great; near the warm coast, choose a lower-chill variety. Fruit comes early, from late spring. The one thing to watch is popcorn disease on white types.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: The Southeast is outstanding mulberry country. Red mulberry is native here, and white and hybrid types thrive; the warm zone 9 edge favors lower-chill cultivars. Harvest comes early, from late spring, and popcorn disease is the one regional watch-out on susceptible white types.
se_gulf.chill_basis_seasoned: Southeastern winters bank enough chill for most mulberries inland, tapering toward the Gulf; low-chill types cover the warm coastal edge. Chill is rarely the limiter for this low-chill fruit.
se_gulf.chill_basis_beginner: Winters here give most mulberries enough cold, and near the coast a low-chill variety covers it. Chill is rarely a problem for a low-chill fruit like mulberry.

8.plant_out: Late winter to early spring (dormant, bare-root)
8.suitability_note_seasoned: Prime mulberry country with hot summers and a long harvest. The full range of white and hybrid types crops reliably; water through fruit fill in the dry heat for best size.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Excellent for mulberry, with hot summers and a long harvest. White and hybrid types crop reliably; water while the fruit fills in the dry heat for the best berries.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Late frost is uncommon and mulberry blooms late enough to dodge most of it; cold valley pockets are the only mild risk.

9.plant_out: Late winter to early spring (dormant, bare-root)
9.suitability_note_seasoned: Warm lower-elevation interior with early bloom and a long, hot harvest season. White, hybrid, and lower-chill types all fruit reliably with irrigation through fruit fill.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Warm lower interior with early bloom and a long, hot picking season. White, hybrid, and lower-chill types all fruit reliably if you water while the fruit fills.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Early bloom rarely meets frost here; mulberry's late leaf-out and recovery keep the crop safe.

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: Interior California is great for mulberry: hot, long summers ripen a big crop, and white and hybrid types do very well and handle drought once established. Both zones fruit reliably, with early bloom and a long harvest.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: Interior California is excellent for mulberry: hot, long summers ripen a heavy crop, and white and hybrid types thrive with good drought tolerance once established. Both zones fruit reliably with early bloom and a long harvest.
ca_interior.chill_basis_seasoned: Interior California banks enough winter chill for most mulberries in a typical year; in the warmest winters a lower-chill cultivar is the safe choice. Chill is rarely limiting for this low-chill fruit.
ca_interior.chill_basis_beginner: The interior usually gets enough winter cold for most mulberries; in a mild winter a lower-chill variety is safest. Chill is rarely a problem for a low-chill fruit like mulberry.

9.plant_out: Late winter to early spring (dormant, bare-root)
9.suitability_note_seasoned: Reliable coastal mulberry country with a mild, slightly later early-summer harvest. White and hybrid types crop well; the cool summers make for a longer, gentler ripening.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Dependable coastal mulberry country with a mild, slightly later early-summer harvest. White and hybrid types do well, and the cool summers give a longer, gentler ripening.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is a minor concern on this mild coast, and mulberry's late bloom keeps it largely out of harm.

10.plant_out: Late winter to early spring (dormant, bare-root)
10.suitability_note_seasoned: The mildest coastal zone still fruits mulberry reliably with lower-chill types, with early bloom and a long, cool harvest. Chill is adequate for the low-chill cultivars grown here.
10.suitability_note_beginner: The mildest coastal zone still fruits mulberry reliably with lower-chill types, with early bloom and a long, cool harvest. There is enough winter cool for the low-chill varieties used here.
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rare here; mulberry fruits without frost concern in this mild coastal climate.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: The cooler California coast grows mulberry well, with a milder, slightly later season. White and hybrid types fruit reliably, mild winters suit lower-chill varieties, and mulberry's drought tolerance helps in the dry summers.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: The cooler California coast grows mulberry well, with a milder, slightly later season. White and hybrid types fruit reliably; the mild winters suit lower-chill cultivars, and drought tolerance is a real asset in the dry summers.
ca_north_coast.chill_basis_seasoned: Coastal winters are mild but usually deliver enough chill for the lower-chill mulberries suited here; chill is rarely the limiter for this fruit.
ca_north_coast.chill_basis_beginner: The coast has mild winters, but they usually give the lower-chill mulberries grown here enough cold. Chill is rarely a problem for mulberry.

9.plant_out: Late winter to early spring (dormant, bare-root)
9.suitability_note_seasoned: Reliable for lower-chill and black mulberry types, with early bloom and an early-summer harvest. The mild climate and long season suit warm-adapted cultivars.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Dependable for lower-chill and black mulberry types, with early bloom and an early-summer harvest. The mild climate and long season suit warm varieties.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is minor on this mild coast; mulberry fruits with little frost concern.

10.plant_out: Late winter to early spring (dormant, bare-root)
10.suitability_note_seasoned: The warm, low-chill edge. Lower-chill and black mulberries fruit here, but the mildest winters bank little chill, so favor genuinely low-chill cultivars (Pakistan, Black Beauty, dwarf types); higher-chill hybrids may bloom and fruit erratically.
10.suitability_note_beginner: The warm, low-chill edge. Lower-chill and black mulberries fruit here, but the mildest winters give little cold, so choose truly low-chill types like Pakistan, Black Beauty, or a dwarf; higher-chill hybrids can fruit unevenly.
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is essentially a non-issue in this mild zone.

ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: The mild Southern California coast grows mulberry well with lower-chill and black types, which fruit early and over a long season. Winters are mild and low in chill, so choose a lower-chill variety, especially in the warmest zone 10 areas.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: The mild Southern California coast is good mulberry country for lower-chill and black types, which fruit early and over a long season. Winters are mild and low in chill, so cultivar choice (a lower-chill type) matters at the warm zone 10 edge.
ca_south_coast.chill_basis_seasoned: South-coast winters are mild and lower in chill; the lower-chill mulberries suited here still get enough, though the warmest zone 10 sites are the low-chill edge where cultivar choice matters most.
ca_south_coast.chill_basis_beginner: The south coast has mild winters with less chill, but the lower-chill mulberries grown here get enough. In the warmest zone 10 spots, choosing a low-chill variety matters most.

9.plant_out: Late winter to early spring (dormant, bare-root)
9.suitability_note_seasoned: Reliable with irrigation and a lower-chill cultivar, fruiting early in the desert heat. Mulberry's heat and drought tolerance make it one of the easier fruit trees here; water deeply through fruit fill.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Dependable with watering and a lower-chill variety, fruiting early in the desert heat. Mulberry handles heat and drought, so it is one of the easier fruit trees here; water deeply while the fruit fills.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is a minor early-season concern; mulberry's late leaf-out keeps it largely clear.

10.plant_out: Late winter to early spring (dormant, bare-root)
10.suitability_note_seasoned: The hottest, lowest-chill desert edge. Low-chill and black mulberries fruit early with irrigation, but the mildest winters bank little chill, so stick to genuinely low-chill cultivars and expect a very early, heat-driven harvest.
10.suitability_note_beginner: The hottest, lowest-chill desert edge. Low-chill and black mulberries fruit early if watered, but winters give little cold, so stick to truly low-chill varieties and expect a very early, heat-driven harvest.
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is essentially a non-issue in this warm zone.

ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: The California desert grows mulberry well if you water it: mulberry loves heat and handles drought, and it fruits early in the strong warmth. Choose lower-chill varieties, since desert winters give limited cold, and water while the fruit fills.
ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: The California desert grows mulberry well with irrigation: it is heat- and drought-tolerant and fruits early in the intense warmth. Choose lower-chill cultivars, since desert winters bank limited chill, and water through fruit fill.
ca_desert.chill_basis_seasoned: Desert winters deliver only modest chill, so lower-chill cultivars are the rule; for those, chill is adequate. Heat and water, not chill, define success here.
ca_desert.chill_basis_beginner: Desert winters give only a little cold, so choose lower-chill varieties, which get enough. Heat and watering, not chill, are what matter here.

8.plant_out: Late winter to early spring (dormant, bare-root)
8.suitability_note_seasoned: Reliable mulberry country across most cultivars, fruiting early and heavily. In Texas the berries green in April and ripen black by late May into June. Heat- and drought-tolerant with occasional deep watering.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Dependable mulberry country for most varieties, fruiting early and heavily. In Texas the berries are green in April and ripen black by late May into June. It handles heat and drought with an occasional deep soak.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Mulberry blooms with leaf-out in spring and its later, recoverable growth keeps late frost from being a real threat.

warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: The warm, dry interior (inland Texas and the Southwest) grows mulberry well: heat- and drought-tough white and hybrid types fruit early and heavily with a little watering. Winters give moderate cold, so most varieties work.
warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: The warm arid interior (inland Texas and the Southwest) is good mulberry country: heat- and drought-tolerant white and hybrid types fruit early and heavily with occasional irrigation. Winters bank moderate chill, so most cultivars work.
warm_arid.chill_basis_seasoned: Warm-arid winters bank moderate chill, enough for most mulberries; only the highest-chill hybrids might want a colder winter. Heat and drought tolerance are the tree's advantage here.
warm_arid.chill_basis_beginner: Winters here give moderate cold, enough for most mulberries. Mulberry's love of heat and tolerance of drought are its big advantages in this dry country.

9.plant_out: Late winter to early spring (dormant, bare-root)
9.suitability_note_seasoned: Fruits very early with irrigation and a low-chill cultivar. The extreme heat and low chill make this a low-chill-only zone; well-watered low-chill and black types crop well, but higher-chill hybrids fruit erratically.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Fruits very early with watering and a low-chill variety. The extreme heat and low chill make this a low-chill-only zone; well-watered low-chill and black types do well, but higher-chill hybrids fruit unevenly.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is a minor early concern; mulberry's late leaf-out keeps it largely clear.

low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: The Arizona low desert grows mulberry if you water it: it loves heat and handles drought, and it fruits very early in the strong warmth. Choose low-chill varieties for the mild winters, and water deeply while it establishes and while the fruit fills.
low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: The Arizona low desert grows mulberry with irrigation: heat-loving and drought-tolerant, it fruits very early in the intense warmth. Choose low-chill cultivars for the mild, low-chill winters, and water deeply through establishment and fruit fill.
low_desert_az.chill_basis_seasoned: Low-desert winters bank little chill, so low-chill cultivars are essential; for those, chill is adequate. Heat and water govern success, not chill.
low_desert_az.chill_basis_beginner: The low desert has mild winters with little cold, so you need low-chill varieties, which get enough. Heat and watering, not chill, decide how it does.

10.plant_out: Late winter to early spring (dormant, bare-root)
10.suitability_note_seasoned: Low-chill mulberries fruit reliably and early here, from spring into early summer. Red, white, and black types all work; keep susceptible white types clean of popcorn disease, and net small trees against heavy bird pressure.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Low-chill mulberries fruit reliably and early here, from spring into early summer. Red, white, and black types all work; keep white types clean of popcorn disease, and net small trees against the many birds.
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is essentially a non-issue in this subtropical zone.

11.plant_out: Late winter to early spring (dormant, bare-root)
11.suitability_note_seasoned: The tropical southern tip banks almost no chill, so only genuinely low-chill and black types fruit, coming in very early. In this warmth the deciduous rhythm blurs and everbearing types may crop intermittently through the year rather than in one clean flush; treat it as a low-chill, warm-adapted planting.
11.suitability_note_beginner: The tropical far south gets almost no winter cold, so only truly low-chill and black types fruit, and very early. In this warmth the tree barely goes dormant, and everbearing types may fruit on and off through the year instead of all at once. Treat it as a low-chill, warm-climate planting.

fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: The Florida peninsula grows mulberry well with low-chill varieties: red, white, and black types all fruit, coming in early from spring, and some everbearing types fruit on and off through much of the warm year. Watch for popcorn disease and birds, and keep the tree away from pavement, since the fruit drop stains.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: The Florida peninsula grows mulberry well with low-chill cultivars: red, white, and black types all fruit, coming in early from spring, and some everbearing types crop intermittently through much of the warm year. Popcorn disease and birds are the main watch-outs, and siting away from pavement is essential given the humid, staining fruit drop.
fl_peninsula.chill_basis_seasoned: Peninsular winters bank very little chill, so low-chill cultivars are essential; for those, the mild winters are enough, and everbearing types can fruit over a long, warm window. Chill, not heat, is the only limiter, and low-chill types solve it.
fl_peninsula.chill_basis_beginner: Florida winters give very little cold, so you need low-chill varieties, and those do fine, sometimes fruiting on and off through much of the year. The only limit is winter cold, and low-chill types handle it.

11.plant_out: Late winter to early spring (dormant, bare-root)
11.suitability_note_seasoned: Low-chill and white mulberries fruit in the tropical warmth, with a long or intermittent harvest rather than a single flush, since the tree barely goes dormant. Treat it as a warm-climate, low-chill planting; birds and the staining drop are the main management issues.
11.suitability_note_beginner: Low-chill and white mulberries fruit in the tropical warmth, over a long or on-and-off season rather than all at once, since the tree barely rests. Treat it as a warm-climate, low-chill planting; birds and the staining fruit drop are the main things to manage.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: Hawaii grows mulberry as a low-chill, warm-climate tree: white and low-chill types fruit, and in the tropical warmth it tends to fruit over a long or on-and-off season rather than all at once. Keep it away from pavement and paths because the fruit stains, and expect a lot of bird interest.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: Hawaii grows mulberry as a low-chill, warm-climate tree: white and low-chill types fruit, and in the tropical warmth the tree tends toward an extended or intermittent harvest rather than a single clean flush. Site away from pavement and paths given the staining drop, and expect strong bird interest.
hawaii_tropical.chill_basis_seasoned: Tropical Hawaii banks essentially no chill, so only low-chill mulberries fruit; for those, the warmth is ample and the deciduous rhythm is muted, giving a long or intermittent harvest. Chill, not heat, is the only limiter, met by low-chill types.
hawaii_tropical.chill_basis_beginner: Hawaii gets essentially no winter cold, so only low-chill mulberries fruit; for those, the warmth is plenty and the tree barely goes dormant, giving a long or on-and-off harvest. The only limit is chill, handled by low-chill types.

crops.description_seasoned: Mulberry (Morus) is a fast-growing, exceptionally easy deciduous fruit tree that ripens sweet, blackberry-like berries over a long early-summer window, picked dead ripe off the tree, which is why they are almost never sold in stores. Nearly all named cultivars are self-fruitful, and many set fruit parthenocarpically (without pollination), so a single tree bears heavily on its own. It is vigorous and broadly adaptable, tolerating poor soil, drought, heat, and a wide pH range, with few serious pests (birds are the main competitor). The trade-offs are size and mess: a standard tree grows large and drops abundant staining fruit, so siting well away from paths, patios, and drives, or choosing a dwarf or weeping cultivar, is the key decision. Given a sunny, well-drained spot with room, a mulberry needs little more than light winter pruning and rewards you for decades.
crops.description_beginner: A mulberry is a fast, very easy fruit tree that gives you sweet, blackberry-like berries over several weeks in early summer. You pick them dead ripe off the tree, which is why you almost never see them in a store. Almost all named mulberries fruit on their own (many even set fruit without any pollination), so one tree is all you need. It is tough and adaptable, handling poor soil, drought, heat, and most pests, and birds are really its only serious competition. The catch is that a standard tree gets big and drops a lot of staining fruit, so the main decision is where to put it (well away from paths, patios, and driveways) or to choose a small dwarf or weeping type. Give it sun, soil that drains, and room, and it asks for little more than a light winter pruning and keeps bearing for decades.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: A mulberry is ready when the berry reaches full deep purple-black (or the ripe color of its cultivar, some are white or pink), turns soft, tastes sweet, and detaches at the gentlest touch. Ripe fruit will practically fall into your hand or drop when the branch is shaken. Unlike stone fruit, there is no firm-pick-and-ripen stage: a mulberry is picked dead ripe and is extremely perishable, so harvest into shallow containers and refrigerate or freeze the same day.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: A mulberry is ripe when the berry turns fully dark purple-black (or the ripe color of your variety, some are white or pink), goes soft, tastes sweet, and comes off at the lightest touch. Ripe fruit almost falls into your hand or drops when you shake the branch. There is no picking firm and ripening later like a peach: you pick mulberries dead ripe, and they spoil fast, so pick into shallow containers and chill or freeze them the same day.
crops.bloom_time_seasoned: Mulberry blooms in spring as it leafs out, the timing shifting by region from late winter in the warm South and mild California to spring in the North. The flowers are inconspicuous greenish catkins rather than showy blossoms, and pollination is by wind. Because named cultivars are self-fruitful and often parthenocarpic, bloom is largely uneventful for the grower; unlike stone fruit, early bloom is not a major frost liability, since mulberry leafs out later and recovers readily.
crops.bloom_time_beginner: Mulberry flowers in spring as its leaves come out, earlier in warm areas and later in cold ones. The flowers are small greenish catkins, not showy blooms, and the wind does the pollinating. Because named mulberries fruit on their own (often without any pollination at all), there is really nothing to do at bloom. Unlike a peach, early flowers are not a big frost worry, since mulberry leafs out later and bounces back easily.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Mulberry as a group spans a very wide climate range because three species and their hybrids cover it: white mulberry (Morus alba) and the hardy hybrids (Illinois Everbearing, Silk Hope) are cold-hardy to about zones 4 to 5 and up; red mulberry (Morus rubra), the native, runs roughly zones 4 to 9; and black mulberry (Morus nigra) and low-chill types are tender, warm-climate trees for about zones 7 to 10 and into the subtropics. The practical result is that some mulberry fruits well across nearly the whole country: choose a hardy hybrid for cold winters and a low-chill or black type for mild and warm regions. Zone 3 is the cold limit for reliable survival; the warm and tropical edge is limited less by heat than by whether enough winter chill accrues for the chosen cultivar, which is why low-chill types are used there.
crops.hardiness_notes_beginner: Mulberry as a whole grows across a huge range of climates, because there are several kinds. The hardy white mulberry and hybrids (like Illinois Everbearing) take cold winters down to about zones 4 to 5, the native red mulberry covers roughly zones 4 to 9, and the tender black and low-chill types are warm-climate trees for about zones 7 to 10 and warmer. So almost everyone can grow some kind of mulberry: pick a hardy hybrid for cold winters and a low-chill or black type for warm areas. Only the very coldest spots (zone 3) are too cold, and in the warmest areas you just need a low-chill variety so it gets enough winter cool to fruit.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Mulberry has a modest winter-chill requirement, low compared with stone fruit, which is why it fruits across so wide a range including mild-winter and subtropical areas. Requirements are cultivar-driven and roughly span about 100 chill hours (low-chill dwarf and Pakistan types) to around 400 to 500 (the hardy northern hybrids). In most of the country chill is never the limiting factor; only in the warmest, nearly chill-free zones does it matter, and there a low-chill cultivar solves it. Note: extension literature rarely publishes numeric mulberry chill figures, so the values here are a horticultural-consensus estimate rather than a single sourced number (see the notes).
crops.chill_hours_note_beginner: Mulberry needs only a modest amount of winter cold, much less than a peach, which is why it fruits in so many places, including mild and even subtropical areas. Different varieties need different amounts, from very little (dwarf and Pakistan types) up to a few hundred hours for the hardy northern kinds. For most gardeners, winter chill is never a problem; only in the very warmest, nearly frost-free areas does it matter, and there you just pick a low-chill variety. (Exact chill-hour numbers for mulberry are hard to find in extension sources, so these are best estimates.)
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Mulberries are wind-pollinated, not insect-pollinated, so pollinators are not needed for fruit set. At the species level they are variable: an individual tree is either monoecious, with male and female flowers together, or dioecious, with the sexes on separate trees, and wild red mulberry is usually dioecious, so an unnamed seedling can turn out to be a non-fruiting male. The practical rule is to buy a named fruiting cultivar, which is typically female and bears a full crop on its own, with many reported to set fruit with little or no pollination. This is the opposite situation from many apples, which require a second, compatible variety to cross-pollinate.
crops.pollinator_notes_beginner: The wind does the pollinating for mulberries, so you do not need bees or, usually, a second tree. The one thing to know: mulberry trees vary, and some kinds have separate male and female trees. A wild, unnamed seedling might turn out to be a male that never fruits, so buy a named fruiting variety instead, which usually makes a full crop on its own. This is the reverse of many apples, which need a second variety nearby to make fruit.

pollination.notes_seasoned: Mulberries are wind-pollinated, so no bees or insects are needed for fruit. Trees are variable: some are monoecious, with both flower sexes on one tree, and some are dioecious, with separate male and female trees, and wild red mulberry is usually dioecious. For a home garden the reliable choice is a named fruiting cultivar, which is typically female and bears a good crop on its own; an unnamed or dioecious seedling can turn out to be a non-fruiting male or need a male tree nearby. This is the opposite of many apples, which require a second, compatible variety to cross-pollinate.
pollination.notes_beginner: The wind pollinates mulberries, so you do not need bees. Mulberry trees vary: some have both male and female flowers on one tree, and some have separate male and female trees. The safe bet is to buy a named fruiting variety, which usually makes fruit on its own. An unnamed seedling can turn out to be a male that never fruits, or need a male tree nearby.

crops.establishment_note: Most mulberries begin bearing about 2 to 3 years after planting, and some named everbearing cultivars set a little fruit even sooner.
crops.recommended_rootstock_note: Unlike stone fruit, mulberry has no size-controlling or pest-resistance rootstock system; choose by the CULTIVAR (and its natural size or a dwarf/weeping form), not the rootstock. Mulberries root readily from hardwood cuttings, so many are grown own-root; named cultivars are also grafted or budded onto seedling Morus alba or rubra, mainly for propagation, not to dwarf the tree.

rootstock_options.name: Own-root (from hardwood cutting)
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask whether the tree is own-rooted (grown from a cutting) or grafted.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: Most common form for mulberry. The tree grows on its own roots, propagated from a hardwood cutting, so there is no graft union to worry about and any suckers are true to type. Full-size and vigorous; choose the cultivar for the size you want.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: The usual way mulberries are grown: the tree is on its own roots, started from a cutting, so there is no graft to keep above the soil and any suckers are the same variety. It grows full-size, so pick the variety for the size you want.

rootstock_options.name: Morus seedling (alba or rubra)
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask which seedling rootstock a grafted tree is on, and keep the graft union above soil.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: Named cultivars are sometimes grafted or budded onto vigorous Morus alba or rubra seedlings, chiefly for propagation rather than size control. It does not dwarf the tree; keep the graft union above the soil line and remove rootstock suckers, which will be the seedling type, not the cultivar.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: Some named mulberries are grafted onto a seedling mulberry root, mainly to propagate them, not to make them smaller. It does not shrink the tree. Keep the graft bump above the soil and pull off any suckers from below it, since those are the rootstock, not your variety.

rootstock_options.name: Genetic dwarf (e.g. Dwarf Everbearing)
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask for a genuine genetic-dwarf cultivar for a small space or container.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: Not a rootstock but a naturally small cultivar, the practical route to a small or container mulberry. Stays compact, fruits young (often the first year and in a pot), and is easy to net against birds. The right choice for patios and small yards.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: This is not really a rootstock but a naturally small variety, and it is the easy way to grow a mulberry in a small yard or pot. It stays little, fruits young (often the first year, even in a pot), and is easy to cover against birds.

crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: In the planting year, prioritize establishment over fruit. Plant a dormant bare-root tree in late winter (or a container tree in the growing season), water consistently through the first season while the roots establish, and keep a weed-free, mulched circle around the trunk. Begin only the lightest formative shaping, and reduce height early if you want an easy-to-pick tree. Mulberry is undemanding: hold off on fertilizer unless growth is weak, and never feed late in the season. Any light first-year fruit on an everbearing cultivar is a bonus, not the goal.
crops.year_one_notes_beginner: The first year is about helping the tree settle in, not getting fruit. Plant a bare-root tree in late winter (or a potted one during the growing season), water it steadily through the first season while the roots get going, and keep a mulched, weed-free ring around the trunk. Do only the lightest shaping, and shorten the tree early if you want it easy to pick. Mulberry is easy: skip fertilizer unless it looks weak, and never feed late in the year. A little fruit the first year on an everbearing type is a nice bonus, not the point.

crops.name: Pawpaw
crops.sunlight: full sun (part shade the first year or two)

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Pawpaw wants a deep, rich, moist soil that still drains well, on the slightly acid side (around pH 5.5 to 7.0). In the wild it grows in bottomland woods with fertile, damp ground, so it likes steady moisture and plenty of organic matter, yet it will not tolerate soil that stays waterlogged. A deep loam with compost worked in is ideal. Heavy clay that holds water is the trouble spot and can rot the roots, so if your soil is heavy, plant on a raised mound and mix in compost to open it up. The one rule you cannot bend is drainage: moist is good, soggy is not.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Pawpaw wants a deep, fertile, moisture-retentive loam that still drains freely, slightly acid at roughly pH 5.5 to 7.0. Its native haunts are bottomland woods with rich, damp soil, so it favors consistent moisture and high organic matter but will not thrive in heavy or waterlogged ground. Work in generous compost before planting. On heavy clay, plant on a raised berm to lift the roots above standing water and amend for aeration. Moisture with drainage is the balance to strike: pawpaw likes it damp but never soggy.

ph.note_beginner: Pawpaw grows best in slightly acidic soil, about pH 5.5 to 7.0 (pH is just a measure of how acidic or alkaline the soil is). Test your soil before planting and adjust slowly if you need to: garden lime raises the pH if the soil is too acidic, and elemental sulfur lowers it if the soil is too alkaline. Mix any of this in before you plant, because pH changes slowly and is much easier to fix before a permanent tree goes in. Pawpaw dislikes very alkaline, chalky soils.
ph.note_seasoned: Pawpaw does best in a slightly acidic soil, roughly pH 5.5 to 7.0. Test the soil before planting and adjust gradually if needed: lime raises a too-acidic pH, while elemental sulfur lowers one that is too alkaline. Work amendments in ahead of planting, since pH shifts slowly and is far easier to correct before the permanent tree is in the ground. Pawpaw performs poorly on high-pH, calcareous soils.

fertilizer.frequency: 2-4x in the first half of the season while young; 1x per year once established
fertilizer.timing: spring as growth begins, through early summer
fertilizer.example_product: 10-10-10 balanced fertilizer
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Pawpaw is a light feeder. Spread a balanced fertilizer evenly around the root zone out to the drip line, keep it off the trunk, and water it in. Young trees respond well to a little fed often, so a light balanced feeding every few weeks through the first half of the season speeds establishment; an established tree needs only a single spring application, if any, on decent soil. Stop feeding by midsummer so no soft late growth is pushed into fall. A ring of organic mulch supplies much of what the tree needs.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Pawpaw does not need heavy feeding. Scatter a balanced fertilizer evenly on the soil around the tree out to where the branches reach, keep it off the trunk, and water it in. Young trees do best with a little food given often, so feed lightly every few weeks through the first half of the season while the tree is getting going. An older tree needs just one spring feeding, or none at all if the soil is good. Stop by midsummer so the tree is not pushed into soft growth that winter can damage. A layer of mulch does a lot of the work.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 suits pawpaw; on fertile, organic-rich ground it may need no feeding at all. Kentucky State recommends a balanced feed (a 20-20-20 is often cited) applied lightly and often to young trees during the first half of the season. Avoid heavy nitrogen, which pushes soft growth at the expense of a sturdy framework.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: A balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 (the three numbers are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium) works well for pawpaw, and on rich soil it may need none. For young trees, a balanced feed given lightly every few weeks in the first half of the season helps them settle in. Do not overdo the nitrogen, the first number, because too much pushes leafy growth instead of a strong frame.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: For a young tree, a light balanced feed (for example a dilute 20-20-20, or about a handful of 10-10-10 scattered over the root zone) every few weeks from bud break through midsummer supports establishment. For a bearing tree, roughly 1 cup of 10-10-10 per inch of trunk diameter, applied once in spring, is ample. Do not fertilize at planting or place fertilizer in the hole; wait until growth begins, and do not feed after midsummer.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: For a young tree, a light balanced feeding (a weak liquid feed, or about a handful of 10-10-10 spread over the roots) every few weeks from when growth starts until midsummer helps it establish. For an older, fruiting tree, about 1 cup of 10-10-10 for each inch of trunk thickness, given once in spring, is plenty. Do not put fertilizer in the planting hole or feed right at planting; wait until the tree starts growing, and stop feeding after midsummer.

companions.note_beginner: The most important companion for a pawpaw is another pawpaw. Pawpaw cannot pollinate itself, so a single tree, or a group of trees that are all the same variety or all suckers from one plant, will flower but set little or no fruit. Plant at least two genetically different pawpaws (two different named varieties, or two or more seedlings) close together so their flowers can cross-pollinate. Beyond that second tree, what matters most is the root zone: keep grass and weeds pulled back from under a young tree, since lawn competes hard for water, and remember pawpaw is a woodland tree that wants shade over its roots and its young leaves for the first year or two.
companions.note_seasoned: The companion that decides whether a pawpaw fruits is a second, genetically distinct pawpaw. The species is self-incompatible, so a lone tree, or a block of one clone (a named variety and its own root suckers are genetically identical), blooms but sets almost nothing. Plant two or more different cultivars or seedlings within a short distance so the fly and beetle pollinators can move pollen between distinct trees. Past that, pawpaw's interactions are about the root zone, not classic vegetable pairings: clear turf from under a young tree, which competes for moisture, and honor its woodland nature by shading the roots and the sun-sensitive young foliage through establishment.

good_seasoned.name: A second, genetically distinct pawpaw
good_seasoned.label: research_backed

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Kentucky State University's pawpaw program and multiple extension sources are explicit that pawpaw is self-incompatible and requires cross-pollination from a genetically different tree; planting at least two different cultivars or seedlings is the standard recommendation for fruit set. extension_backed/HIGH.

good_seasoned.why_seasoned: This is the single most consequential planting decision for pawpaw. Because the species is self-incompatible, a second tree of a different genetic identity is not optional for reliable fruit, it is the prerequisite. Two named cultivars, or two or more seedlings, planted near each other give the fly and beetle pollinators distinct pollen sources to shuttle between. Keep them close, within about 30 feet, since these pollinators do not range far, and be aware that suckers from one tree do not count as a second tree.

bad_seasoned.name: A single tree or an all-one-clone pawpaw patch
bad_seasoned.label: research_backed

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Self-incompatibility means a lone tree or a genetically uniform stand (a named cultivar plus its root suckers, all one genotype) cannot cross-pollinate. KSU documents that wild pawpaw patches are frequently a single clone spread by root suckers, which is why isolated patches often bear little fruit. extension_backed/HIGH.

bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Relying on one tree, or on a thicket that is really one clone spread by root suckers, is the classic reason a healthy, heavy-blooming pawpaw sets almost no fruit. Every flower in a single-genotype stand is incompatible with every other, so no amount of pollinator activity helps. Wild pawpaw patches are often exactly this, one plant colonizing an area, which is why they can flower profusely yet fruit poorly. The fix is genetic diversity: interplant a different cultivar or seedling, and do not mistake a tree's own suckers for a pollen partner.

pests.name: Pawpaw peduncle borer
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Open flowers wilt, blacken, and drop just as they should be setting fruit. Splitting a dropped flower reveals a small pale caterpillar tunneling in the fleshy flower stalk (the peduncle) and floral tissue. In a bad year the borer can destroy the majority of a tree's blossoms, so a heavy bloom yields almost no fruit.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Flowers wilt, turn black, and fall off right when they should be turning into fruit. If you open a fallen flower you may find a tiny pale caterpillar tunneling inside the flower stalk. In a bad year it can ruin most of the flowers, so a tree that bloomed heavily still gives you very few pawpaws.
pests.cause_seasoned: Larvae of the pawpaw peduncle borer (Talponia plummeriana), a small moth. The larva, only about 5 millimeters long, bores into the fleshy tissues of the flower, causing it to wither and drop before it can set fruit. Populations vary sharply year to year.
pests.cause_beginner: The caterpillar of a small moth called the pawpaw peduncle borer. It burrows into the soft tissue of the flower, which makes the flower die and fall. How bad it is changes a lot from one year to the next.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no practical spray for a backyard tree once larvae are inside the flowers. The workable response is sanitation: gather and destroy dropped, infested flowers to reduce the local population, and lean on hand pollination of the healthy flowers to secure a crop despite the losses. Damage is rarely fatal to the tree and often eases the following year.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no easy spray for this on a home tree once the caterpillars are inside the flowers. The best thing you can do is pick up and throw away the fallen, damaged flowers to lower their numbers, and hand-pollinate the healthy flowers so you still get fruit. It does not hurt the tree itself, and it is usually less of a problem the next year.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep the ground under the tree clear of fallen flowers and debris where the borer can complete its cycle. A tree with two genetic partners and hand pollination will still set a crop from the flowers the borer misses, so protecting fruit set is more about pollination insurance than eradication.
pests.prevention_beginner: Rake up and remove fallen flowers so the borer cannot keep its cycle going under the tree. Because pawpaw already sets fruit unreliably, the best insurance is to hand-pollinate the good flowers so you get fruit from the ones the borer does not reach.

pests.name: Zebra swallowtail caterpillars
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Chewed young leaves, usually only a few at a time, with a green-and-black banded caterpillar feeding on the foliage. Damage is almost always light and cosmetic; the caterpillars never appear in numbers large enough to defoliate a tree.
pests.symptoms_beginner: A few young leaves chewed here and there, with a striped green-and-black caterpillar on them. The damage is minor and just cosmetic; there are never enough of them to strip a tree.
pests.cause_seasoned: Larvae of the zebra swallowtail butterfly (Protographium marcellus), for which pawpaw is the sole larval host plant. The caterpillars feed only on young pawpaw foliage and never in great numbers, so they are far more a delight than a threat: the striking adult butterfly depends entirely on pawpaw.
pests.cause_beginner: The caterpillar of the zebra swallowtail butterfly, which can only grow on pawpaw leaves. It feeds on the young leaves but never in big numbers. This is really a bonus, not a pest problem: the beautiful butterfly needs pawpaw to survive.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: No treatment is warranted. The feeding is negligible, and controlling it would remove the caterpillars of a native butterfly that has no other host. Simply leave them be.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Do nothing. The leaf nibbling is harmless, and these are the caterpillars of a lovely native butterfly that has nowhere else to live. Just enjoy them.
pests.prevention_seasoned: None needed or advised. A healthy pawpaw shrugs off the light feeding, and the butterfly is a welcome part of having the tree.
pests.prevention_beginner: None needed. A healthy pawpaw is not bothered by them, and the butterfly is one of the nicest reasons to grow the tree.

pests.name: Fruit-raiding wildlife (raccoons, opossums, squirrels)
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Ripe and nearly ripe fruit disappears from the tree or is found half-eaten on the ground, often overnight, right as it softens. Because pawpaw ripens over a short window and soft fruit is highly aromatic, animals frequently harvest it before the gardener does.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Ripe or almost-ripe fruit vanishes from the tree or turns up chewed on the ground, usually overnight, just as it gets soft. The strong ripe smell draws animals, and they often get to the fruit before you do.
pests.cause_seasoned: Raccoons, opossums, squirrels, and other wildlife are strongly attracted to the intense aroma of ripening pawpaw. Deer, by contrast, avoid the foliage and fruit, so the competition here is from fruit-eating mammals, not browsers.
pests.cause_beginner: Raccoons, opossums, squirrels, and other animals love the strong smell of ripening pawpaw and will help themselves. Deer are the exception: they avoid pawpaw leaves and fruit, so it is the fruit-eaters you are competing with.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Beat the animals to the fruit: pick pawpaws firm but full-sized as they begin to soften and finish ripening indoors, rather than leaving tree-ripe fruit hanging overnight. Check the tree daily through the harvest window. Netting or trunk baffles help where pressure is heavy.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Get to the fruit first. Pick pawpaws when they are full-sized and just beginning to soften, then let them finish ripening indoors instead of leaving soft fruit on the tree overnight. Check the tree every day while it is ripening. Netting or a baffle on the trunk can help if animals are a big problem.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Harvest promptly and do not let ripe fruit accumulate on the tree or ground. Since pawpaw is so perishable anyway, picking at the first give and ripening indoors both protects the crop from wildlife and gives you better control over the fruit.
pests.prevention_beginner: Pick fruit promptly and do not let ripe pawpaws pile up on the tree or the ground. Since the fruit does not keep long anyway, picking it as soon as it starts to soften and ripening it indoors both saves it from animals and lets you manage it better.

diseases.name: Phyllosticta leaf and fruit spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small tan-to-brown spots on the leaves and, at times, superficial dark blotches on the fruit skin. The spotting is cosmetic: it does not defoliate a healthy tree or spoil the flesh, and the fruit inside remains sound. Worst in warm, wet, humid summers with crowded, poorly ventilated foliage.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small tan or brown spots on the leaves, and sometimes dark surface blotches on the fruit skin. It looks worse than it is: the spots are just on the surface, do not harm the tree, and the fruit inside is fine. It shows up most in warm, wet, muggy summers.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Fungi in the Phyllosticta group (and similar leaf-spot fungi). Spores spread in warm, humid, wet weather, and infection is favored by dense canopies that stay wet. Pawpaw is otherwise notably free of serious disease.
diseases.cause_beginner: A leaf-spot fungus that spreads in warm, damp weather, especially where leaves stay wet and crowded. Apart from this minor spotting, pawpaw has very few disease problems.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No fungicide is warranted for what is a cosmetic issue. Improve airflow by not crowding trees, rake and remove fallen spotted leaves at season's end to reduce carryover, and keep the tree vigorous. The fruit is unaffected inside and fully edible.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: No spray is needed for what is only a cosmetic problem. Give trees room for air to move, rake up and remove the spotted fallen leaves in autumn, and keep the tree healthy. The fruit itself is fine to eat.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space and site trees for good air movement, avoid overhead wetting of the foliage, and clear fallen leaves in autumn. These reduce the minor spotting; no routine spray program is needed for pawpaw.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Give trees enough space for air to move, avoid wetting the leaves when you water, and clean up fallen leaves in fall. That keeps the minor spotting down. Pawpaw does not need a regular spray schedule.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Pawpaw wants consistent soil moisture, so water deeply and regularly rather than sparingly, and never let a young tree dry out. Plan on a deep soak once or twice a week through the first two seasons while roots establish, easing toward weekly for a bearing tree in summer heat, always adjusted for rain and soil. It is more moisture-loving than most fruit trees, but it still will not tolerate standing water, so keep the soil damp, not soggy. Through winter dormancy the need drops and rainfall usually suffices.
watering.frequency_beginner: Pawpaw likes steady moisture, so water deeply and regularly, and never let a young tree go dry. For the first two years, plan on a deep soak once or twice a week, easing to about once a week for an older tree in summer heat, adjusting for rain and your soil. It likes more water than most fruit trees, but it still cannot sit in soggy soil, so aim for damp, not waterlogged. In winter, when the tree is resting, it needs much less and rain usually covers it.
watering.amount_seasoned: Water deeply each time so moisture reaches the full root depth rather than wetting only the surface. For an establishing tree, that is on the order of 5 gallons per soak; for a bearing tree, aim for roughly the equivalent of an inch of water per week through the growing season, more in heat. A thick organic mulch over the root zone is especially valuable on pawpaw, holding the even moisture it prefers and keeping the shallow feeder roots cool.
watering.amount_beginner: Each time you water, give a deep soak that reaches all the way down to the roots, not just a splash on top. A young tree wants about 5 gallons per soak. An older, fruiting tree wants roughly an inch of water a week through the growing season, and more when it is hot. A thick layer of mulch over the roots really helps pawpaw, holding in the steady moisture it likes and keeping the roots cool.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the root zone with drip or a soaker hose, out toward the drip line rather than only at the trunk. Overhead watering that wets the foliage is best avoided, since it favors the minor leaf spotting pawpaw can get; deliver water to the soil. Because the young feeder roots run shallow under the natural leaf litter, a wide, mulched, evenly moist root area serves the tree better than a narrow deep well at the trunk.
watering.method_beginner: Water at the ground around the roots with a drip line or soaker hose, spreading it out to the edge of the branches rather than just at the trunk. Try not to spray water over the leaves, since wet foliage can bring on minor leaf spots; put the water on the soil. The feeder roots run shallow, so a wide, mulched, evenly damp area around the tree suits it better than soaking only right at the trunk.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Waterlogged, poorly drained soil shows as yellowing leaves, wilting that persists even in wet ground, and a generally declining tree, since pawpaw roots suffocate and rot when the soil stays saturated. Soggy soil that never dries between waterings is the warning to act on: pawpaw wants steady moisture, but not standing water.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Soil that stays too wet, or drains poorly, shows up as yellowing leaves, wilting that does not go away even when the soil is wet, and a tree slowly going downhill, because the roots cannot breathe and start to rot. Soil that never dries out between waterings is your warning. Pawpaw likes steady moisture, but not water sitting around the roots.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Underwatering shows as wilting and drooping, dull leaves, browning or scorched leaf margins (worse in sun and wind), and early leaf drop in a dry spell. A young pawpaw is especially unforgiving of drought, and the fruit sizes poorly if the tree runs short of water while the crop is filling. Catch the dry stress early, since a stressed young tree can be lost outright.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Too little water shows as wilting and drooping, dull leaves, brown or scorched leaf edges (worse in sun and wind), and leaves dropping early in a dry stretch. A young pawpaw is very sensitive to drying out, and the fruit stays small if the tree gets too dry while the pawpaws are filling out. Catch it early, because a dried-out young tree can die.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Through the first two seasons, keep the root ball and surrounding soil consistently moist, never dry and never waterlogged. Deep soaks of about 5 gallons once or twice a week, adjusted for rain and heat, plus a thick mulch, carry a young pawpaw through its most vulnerable period. Do not let it dry out.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: For the first two years, keep the soil around the roots evenly moist, never bone dry and never soggy. A deep soak of about 5 gallons once or twice a week, more in heat and less after rain, plus a thick mulch, helps a young pawpaw through the time it is most easily lost. Do not let it dry out.

schedule_by_stage.rate: deep soak, ~1 in per week equivalent
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: While the fruit sizes through summer, keep moisture steady. Aim for the equivalent of about an inch of water per week, more in heat, as deep soaks. Even moisture now translates directly into larger, better-filled fruit and prevents the drop that dry stress can trigger.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: While the pawpaws are sizing up over summer, keep the water steady. Aim for about an inch of water a week, more when it is hot, given as deep soaks. Steady watering now means bigger, better fruit and keeps the tree from dropping fruit under stress.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Once the tree is dormant and leafless, water need drops sharply; rely mostly on rainfall and water only during a prolonged dry spell to keep roots from desiccating. Avoid keeping dormant soil saturated.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: After the leaves drop and the tree is resting for winter, it needs very little water. Let rain do most of the work and only water during a long dry stretch so the roots do not dry out. Do not keep the soil soaked in winter.

watering.method_note_seasoned: Water deeply and regularly at the root zone, ideally by drip or soaker under a generous mulch, to hold the even moisture pawpaw prefers; avoid wetting the canopy. Young trees are drought-sensitive and need consistent moisture through at least their first two seasons to establish; a mature tree tolerates short dry spells but sizes fruit poorly under stress and is less drought-hardy than a peach or apple.
watering.method_note_beginner: Give the tree a deep soak now and then rather than a little every day, water at the ground (a drip line or soaker hose under a thick mulch is ideal) instead of spraying the leaves, and keep the soil evenly moist. Young trees are sensitive to drying out and need steady water for at least their first two years. An older tree can handle a short dry spell, but the fruit comes out small if it gets too dry, and pawpaw is thirstier than most fruit trees.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Two windows are make-or-break: the first two seasons after planting, when a young pawpaw can be lost outright to drought, and the summer fruit-filling period, when water stress causes small fruit and premature drop. Keep moisture steady through both. Pawpaw has no equivalent of a mid-season easy-off, since it wants consistent moisture whenever it is in leaf.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The two most important times to keep the tree watered are the first two years after planting, when a young pawpaw can die if it dries out, and midsummer while the fruit is filling, when dryness leads to small fruit and fruit drop. Keep the water steady through both. Unlike some fruit trees, pawpaw wants even moisture the whole time it has leaves.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Conventional hardening off does not apply, but shade acclimation does. Pawpaw is best set out in spring from a container, and its young foliage is genuinely sun-sensitive, so a nursery-grown tree that was shaded needs a shaded or part-shade position for its first year or two before it is exposed to full sun. Ease it into brighter light gradually rather than planting a shade-grown seedling straight into an open, sunny site.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: Hardening off (slowly getting a plant used to the outdoors) works a little differently for pawpaw. You plant it in spring from a pot, and its young leaves burn easily in strong sun, so for the first year or two give it a shady or part-shade spot and let it get used to brighter light slowly. Do not move a shade-grown young pawpaw straight into a hot, open, sunny place.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Plant in spring, as new growth is starting or just after, from a container rather than bare-root. Pawpaw has a deep, brittle taproot and resents disturbance, so a potted tree transplants far more reliably than a field-dug or bare-root one. Dig a hole as wide as the root ball and no deeper, disturb the roots as little as possible, set the tree at the same depth it grew in the pot, backfill with the native soil enriched with compost, water in well, and mulch. Shade the young tree for its first season or two and keep it consistently moist.
start_method.notes_beginner: Plant in spring, as the tree is starting to grow or soon after, and use a potted tree, not a bare-root one. Pawpaw has a deep, easily broken taproot and does not like having its roots disturbed, so a tree grown in a pot moves much more successfully than one dug from a field. Dig a hole as wide as the pot and no deeper, keep the root ball intact, set the tree at the same depth it was in the pot, fill back in with the soil you dug out mixed with compost, water it in well, and mulch. Shade the young tree for its first year or two and keep the soil evenly moist.

soil_mix.type_beginner: If you must grow a young pawpaw in a pot for a while, use a deep container and a rich but free-draining mix, ideally a good bark-based potting mix with extra compost stirred in for fertility and moisture holding. Avoid a dense, water-logging mix, and do not use soil dug from the yard in a pot, because it packs down and drains badly. Because pawpaw sends down a deep taproot, the pot needs to be tall rather than shallow.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in compost for fertility and steady moisture, and add some perlite or pumice if the mix feels heavy, so it drains while still holding water. Pawpaw likes a richer, moister mix than a peach would, but it still cannot sit in soggy soil. Skip water-holding crystals; a good compost-enriched bark mix in a deep pot is the target.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: For the temporary container phase of a young tree, use a deep pot and a fertile, moisture-retentive yet free-draining medium, such as a quality bark-based mix amended with compost. Depth matters more than width because of the taproot; a tall container delays the point at which the root deforms. Avoid dense, waterlogging media and native garden soil, which compacts under regular irrigation.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend in compost for fertility and moisture retention, with perlite or pumice if the base mix is heavy, to keep it draining while still damp. Pawpaw wants a richer, moister rooting medium than most tree-fruit but no standing water at the roots. Avoid moisture-retentive crystals; a deep pot with a compost-enriched bark mix is the right compromise for the container phase.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: A pawpaw in a pot dries out much faster than one in the ground and is very unforgiving of drying out, so check it often, at least daily in summer heat, and water whenever the top inch or two feels dry, until water runs out the bottom. Keep it evenly moist. Never let it sit in a saucer of water, though, because constantly wet roots rot. In winter, when the tree is resting, give it just enough to keep the root ball from drying out completely.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Frequent watering washes food out of a pot, so feed a little at a time with a diluted balanced liquid fertilizer every couple of weeks from spring into midsummer, then stop by late summer so the tree does not push soft growth into fall. Do not feed at planting, and stop once the tree drops its leaves for winter.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Roots in a pot get much colder than roots in the ground, because cold reaches the soil from every side, so even a hardy pawpaw can have its roots freeze in a container. Pawpaw is cold-hardy, but before hard freezes, either sink the pot to its rim in a garden bed or move it to an unheated but sheltered spot like an attached garage or shed that stays cold but not deep-freezing. It still needs the winter cold to rest, so do not bring it into a warm, heated room.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: A potted root ball sits several zones colder than the same roots in open ground, so a pawpaw that is fully hardy in your yard can still lose its roots in a container. Before hard freezes, sink the pot to its rim in a bed or shift it to an unheated but sheltered space (an attached garage or shed) that holds dormancy without the deep lows that kill exposed roots. The tree still needs its winter chill to break dormancy, so do not overwinter it in a heated room.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Pawpaw is really a ground tree, and a pot is at best a short-term holding spot for a young plant, not a long-term home. Its deep taproot wants to go down, not circle in a pot, and a container pawpaw is hard to keep evenly moist and rarely fruits well. If you have no ground space, use the deepest large pot you can, keep it in part shade, water it very attentively, and plan to plant it out as soon as you can. For fruit, two genetically different trees in the ground is the real answer.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Pawpaw is fundamentally a ground tree, and a container is at best a temporary holding measure for a young plant, not a durable growing method. The deep taproot resists confinement, even moisture is hard to maintain in a pot, and a containerized pawpaw seldom crops well. Where ground space is truly lacking, use the deepest large pot available, hold it in part shade, water meticulously, and plan to plant out. Reliable fruit comes from two genetically distinct trees in open ground, not from a container.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: A potted pawpaw dries far faster than one in the ground and is intolerant of drying out, so check moisture at least daily in summer heat and water whenever the top inch or two is dry, until it runs from the drainage holes, keeping it evenly moist. Never leave the pot standing in a full saucer, since continuously wet roots rot. Through dormancy the tree needs only enough water to keep the root ball from drying out completely.
