hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: Honest heads-up: parsnips are not a good fit for lowland Hawaii. They need a long cool season and frost to turn sweet, and the warm lowlands give neither. If you want to experiment, try the coolest months (sow in fall, dig in late winter) and use fresh seed, but expect poor, starchy roots. Cooler upland gardens have a better chance. Most take about 100 to 120 days where the weather is cool enough.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: Parsnip is not suited to tropical-lowland Hawaii: it requires a long cool season and near-freezing weather to convert root starch to sugar, and the warm lowlands provide neither. No CTAHR parsnip source was found, and the nominal cool-months window here is a flagged model for roster completeness, not a recommendation. (Clemson HGIC, cool-season principle) Cooler upland elevations would perform better. Use fresh seed each year. This region's calendar is modeled, not sourced to a Hawaii parsnip reference.

crops.description_seasoned: Parsnip (Pastinaca sativa) is a long-season, cool-climate root crop in the carrot family, grown for its sweet, ivory taproot. It is direct-sown only, and the single most important rule is fresh seed: parsnip seed loses viability within a year, so old seed is the leading cause of failure. Germination is notoriously slow and erratic, often 2 to 3 weeks and sometimes far longer, and the fine seedlings cannot push through a crusted surface, so the seedbed must stay evenly moist for weeks. The crop needs deep, loose, stone-free soil for its long root (commonly 8 to 12 inches) and grows for roughly 100 to 120 days, longer for a late crop. Parsnip is a biennial grown as an annual for the root: it stores energy the first year and bolts to flower the second, so overwintered roots are dug before spring regrowth. Its defining trait is cold-sweetening: frost converts root starch to sugar, so parsnips are harvested after hard frost and are famously left in the ground over winter, dug as needed and growing sweeter the longer they wait. Where summers are hot, parsnip is a fall-sown, winter-harvested crop. One handling note: the foliage and sap can cause a skin rash in sunlight, so gloves are worn when working among the plants on bright days.
crops.description_beginner: Parsnips are a long-season, cool-weather root vegetable in the carrot family. The part you eat is one long, sweet, cream-colored root. Always plant the seeds right where they will grow, and use fresh seed every single year, because parsnip seed goes bad fast and old seed is the main reason parsnips fail. Be patient: the seeds are very slow, often 2 to 3 weeks or more to come up, and they will not break through a dry crust, so keep the surface damp. Parsnips need deep, loose, rock-free soil for their long root (often 8 to 12 inches) and take a long time, about 100 to 120 days. They are a biennial, which means if you leave them past their first winter they shoot up a flower and the root turns woody, so dig overwintered ones before spring. The best thing about parsnips is that frost makes them sweet: the cold turns starch into sugar, so you harvest them after frost and can leave them in the ground all winter, digging them as you need them, sweeter every week. In hot-summer areas, grow them in fall for a winter harvest. One safety note: the leaves and juice can give some people a skin rash in sunlight, so wear gloves on sunny days.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Parsnips are ready when the roots have sized up, often 1 1/2 to 2 inches across at the shoulder and 8 to 12 inches long, with the tops beginning to die back in fall, usually around 100 to 120 days from sowing. But the real cue is cold, not the calendar: flavor sweetens markedly after the roots sit through several frosts as starch converts to sugar, so there is no rush to lift them. In mild soil they hold for weeks, and in cold regions a heavy straw mulch lets them overwinter for pull-as-needed harvest through winter and into early spring, growing sweeter the longer they wait. Loosen the soil beside the row with a spading fork before pulling, because the long roots snap easily. Lift any overwintered roots before they regrow in spring, since once the plant bolts the root turns woody. Wear gloves and long sleeves when handling the foliage in bright sun, as the sap can cause a skin rash.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Parsnips are ready when the roots are full sized, often 1 1/2 to 2 inches across at the top and 8 to 12 inches long, with the leafy tops dying down in fall, usually about 100 to 120 days after planting. But the real signal is cold weather, not a date: parsnips get much sweeter after a few frosts, as the cold turns starch into sugar, so there is no rush. They keep right in the ground, and in cold areas you can pile straw over the row and dig them through winter and into early spring, and they taste sweeter the longer they wait. Loosen the soil next to the row with a garden fork before pulling, because the long roots break easily. Dig any you left in over winter before they start growing again in spring, or the root turns woody. Wear gloves and long sleeves when handling the leaves on a sunny day, since the sap can give some people a rash.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Parsnip quality is set in the seedbed more than anywhere else, because the root runs long, commonly 8 to 12 inches, and any obstruction forks or stunts it. Work the bed deep and fine, loosening and removing stones, clods, and debris to at least 12 inches. A loose sandy loam gives the straightest, longest roots; heavy clay and compacted ground produce short, forked roots and are best improved with compost or worked into deep raised beds. Avoid fresh manure and heavy nitrogen, which drive forked, hairy roots and lush tops at the expense of the root; use only well-finished compost and a low-nitrogen balanced feeding such as 5-10-10. Rake the surface smooth and fine, since the small, slow seeds need close contact and an even, crust-free surface to emerge over their long germination. Aim for a slightly acidic to neutral pH, about 6.0 to 7.0, liming ahead of sowing if a soil test calls for it.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: With parsnips, getting the bed right before you plant matters more than almost anything else, because the root grows very long (8 to 12 inches) and anything it hits makes it fork or come out stubby. Dig and loosen the soil at least 12 inches down and pull out rocks, hard clumps, and roots. Loose, sandy soil grows the straightest parsnips; heavy clay grows short, twisted ones, so mix in compost or use a deep raised bed. Do not add fresh manure or a lot of high-nitrogen fertilizer, which grows leafy tops and forked, hairy roots; use finished compost and a low-nitrogen blend like 5-10-10. Rake the top smooth and fine so the small, slow seeds sit snug against the soil, and aim for a soil pH around 6.0 to 7.0, adding lime ahead of time only if a soil test says so.

pet_safe.note: All parts contain furanocoumarins that can make skin sun-sensitive in cats, dogs, and horses.

crops.name: Kohlrabi

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Kohlrabi grows best in fertile, loose, well-drained soil with plenty of compost mixed in, and it likes steady, even moisture. The bulb stays tender and mild when the plant grows quickly without a check, so soil that holds moisture but drains well is ideal. Soil that dries out or stays soggy stresses the plant and makes the stem tough and woody.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Kohlrabi does best in a fertile, well-drained loam high in organic matter held at even moisture, like the other cole crops. The whole game is fast, uninterrupted growth: a tender, mild swollen stem forms when the plant never checks, while drought, heat, or a stop-start water supply turns it woody, fibrous, and bitter and can crack it. Work in compost before planting and keep the bed evenly moist. Clubroot, the key brassica soil disease, is far more likely in acidic, poorly drained ground, so keep drainage good and the pH up where it is a concern.

ph.note_beginner: Kohlrabi grows best in soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, about 6.0 to 7.0. A simple soil test tells you where you stand. If you have had clubroot, a brassica soil disease, keeping the soil closer to neutral helps hold it back.
ph.note_seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0 (Iowa State gives 6 to 7; Minnesota and Utah State put the workable range at about 6.0 to 7.5). Kohlrabi tolerates roughly 5.5 to 7.5. Clubroot, the major brassica soil disease, is favored by acidic soil below about 6.5, so where it is a concern lime acidic ground well ahead of planting and hold the pH toward neutral.

fertilizer.timing: work a balanced fertilizer in before planting, then side-dress about 3 to 4 weeks later
fertilizer.example_product: 10-10-10 worked in before planting, then 21-0-0 or blood meal as a side-dress
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Kohlrabi is a moderate feeder that wants steady, even growth rather than a late surge. Work a balanced fertilizer such as 10-10-10 into the bed before planting (Iowa State: 1 to 2 pounds per 100 square feet), then side-dress with nitrogen about 3 to 4 weeks after planting or thinning, when the plants are roughly 4 inches tall (Utah State: about half a cup of 21-0-0 per 10 feet of row). Keep nitrogen and water even through bulbing, since both a stall and a late flush hurt texture; avoid heavy late nitrogen, which can grow leaves at the expense of a clean bulb.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Kohlrabi needs decent soil and a little feeding, but not a lot. Mix a balanced fertilizer into the soil before planting, then give one feeding of a nitrogen fertilizer a few weeks later when the plants are a few inches tall. Keep the watering and feeding steady so the bulbs grow smoothly and stay tender.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time to side-dress your kohlrabi with nitrogen as the plants establish.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Time to feed your kohlrabi.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced base feed for steady growth: work a 10-10-10 into the bed before planting, then a single nitrogen side-dress such as 21-0-0 or blood meal about 3 to 4 weeks after planting. Keep it modest and even, since pushing the plant late grows leaves over a clean, tender bulb.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 at planting, then one feeding of a nitrogen fertilizer a few weeks later as the plants take off.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: Work in about 1 to 2 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet before planting, then side-dress with about half a cup of 21-0-0 per 10 feet of row roughly 3 to 4 weeks after planting, banded beside the row and watered in.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Follow the label rate for a balanced vegetable fertilizer at planting, then a light nitrogen feed beside the plants a few weeks later.

companions.note_beginner: Kohlrabi gets along with most vegetables. It does well next to aromatic herbs, onions and other alliums, beets, and quick leafy greens like lettuce that finish before the kohlrabi fills out. The main thing is to keep it away from its own cabbage-family relatives, which share its pests and diseases.
companions.note_seasoned: Most kohlrabi companion pairings are traditional rather than trial-tested. The ones worth acting on are practical: aromatic herbs and alliums as scent-based deterrents for cabbage-family pests, low quick crops like lettuce that use the open ground while the kohlrabi sizes up, and beets sharing the cool-season bed. The well-grounded caution is to separate kohlrabi from other brassicas, which share clubroot and the whole cabbage-family pest complex, a rotation and disease principle more than a tested adjacency effect. As University of Minnesota stresses, treat most companion claims as a starting point and watch your own results.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Onions and other alliums
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Onions, garlic, and chives grow tall and narrow with shallow roots, so they tuck between kohlrabi without crowding it, and their strong smell is widely used to help confuse cabbage-family pests.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Allium scent-masking of brassica pests is a long-standing companion tradition with partial mechanistic support; not trial-isolated for kohlrabi, so low.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Alliums are a traditional brassica companion, their pungent scent thought to mask the crop from the cabbage pests that hunt partly by smell. Shallow-rooted and undemanding, they tuck around kohlrabi without competing for much. Treat it as a low-risk, scent-based aid rather than a proven control.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Lettuce and other leafy greens
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Lettuce grows fast and low, so you can tuck it between young kohlrabi plants to use the space and shade the soil, and it is harvested long before the kohlrabi fills in. Both like the same cool weather.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Pairing fast, shallow cool-season greens with a slower-bulbing brassica is the standard complementary space-and-timing rationale; sound and widely taught but a space benefit rather than a measured kohlrabi-specific effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Lettuce and kohlrabi interplant well on structure and timing: lettuce is shallow and quick, kohlrabi a little slower, so the lettuce uses the open ground and light between young plants and is pulled before the kohlrabi canopies. It is an efficient cool-season space pairing, not a pest effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Beets
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Beets are another cool-season crop that shares the bed easily with kohlrabi without competing for the same space, since beets put their energy down into the root while kohlrabi swells just above the soil.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: A common cool-season bedfellow pairing based on complementary growth and season; not a trial-isolated kohlrabi effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Beets are a traditional, low-risk cool-season neighbor for kohlrabi. They share the same season and undemanding habit, and the beet works the soil below while the kohlrabi swells at the surface, so the two coexist without much competition. A space-and-season pairing rather than a documented benefit.

good_seasoned.name: Onions and other alliums
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional brassica companion whose scent is thought to deter cabbage pests; shallow-rooted and low-competition. A plausible, low-risk pairing rather than a documented effect.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Allium scent-masking lore for brassicas; not trial-isolated.

good_seasoned.name: Lettuce and other leafy greens
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A quick, shallow cool-season crop that uses the open ground and light between young kohlrabi plants and is harvested long before they fill in. Space-driven and traditional, not a documented growth effect; the two share no serious pest.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Space-use intercropping lore; no T1 source documents a lettuce-kohlrabi benefit.

good_seasoned.name: Beets
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A cool-season bedfellow that works the soil below while kohlrabi swells at the surface, so the two share space without much competition. Traditional and low-risk rather than a documented benefit.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Complementary cool-season root-vs-surface pairing; not trial-isolated.

good_seasoned.name: Dill
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Aromatic umbels like dill draw parasitoid wasps and hoverflies that attack the aphids and cabbage caterpillars kohlrabi shares with the cole crops, and the scent is traditionally said to deter cabbage pests. Let some flower, and keep it from shading the plants.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Umbel beneficial-insect attraction is extension-noted for the cole crops; the specific dill-kohlrabi pairing is not trial-isolated.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Other brassicas
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep kohlrabi away from other cabbage-family plants like cabbage, broccoli, kale, and turnips. They share the same pests and diseases, so grouping them together makes problems worse.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Same-family crops share pests and pathogens, so clustering raises pest/disease pressure, and successive brassica planting builds soil-borne clubroot. A sound epidemiological/rotation mechanism rather than a measured antagonism.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Planting kohlrabi shoulder to shoulder with its brassica relatives, cabbage, broccoli, kale, turnip, radish, concentrates the family's shared pests (cabbageworms, loopers, flea beetles, cabbage aphids, root maggots) and shared diseases in one spot, and repeated same-family planting lets soil-borne clubroot build up. Spread brassicas out and rotate where they grow each year.

bad_seasoned.name: Other brassicas
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Cabbage, broccoli, kale, turnip, and the other cole crops share kohlrabi's clubroot and cabbage-family pests, so grouping them concentrates disease and pest pressure. A real rotation and disease principle rather than a tested adjacency effect; the practical rule is to spread brassicas out and rotate them.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Shared clubroot and shared cabbage-family pests are extension-documented; the bad-adjacency claim is a known agronomic principle, not formally pair-tested.

bad_seasoned.name: Pole beans
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional caution pairs the cabbage family with pole beans as poor neighbors. There is no documented mechanism or T1 support; it persists as folklore, and the two also want different seasons.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Folk anti-companion claim with no pattern match or T1 support.

pests.name: Cabbageworms, loopers, and diamondback moths
pests.symptoms_beginner: You'll see ragged holes chewed in the leaves, green caterpillars on the plant, and dark droppings. The leaves are part of why you grow kohlrabi well, and the caterpillars can also chew the bulb.
pests.cause_beginner: These are caterpillars that hatch from eggs laid by white butterflies and small moths. They love cabbage-family plants like kohlrabi and chew the leaves.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray Bt, which is safe and targets only caterpillars, or spinosad, and pick caterpillars and eggs off by hand from under the leaves. Spray again after rain.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover plants with a light fabric row cover after planting to keep the butterflies and moths from laying eggs, clear away old cabbage-family plants, and watch for the first white butterflies.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Ragged holes chewed in the leaves with green caterpillars and dark frass; heavy feeding sets young plants back and the larvae can score the bulb. Imported cabbageworms are velvety green, loopers move in a looping arch, and diamondback larvae are small and wriggle when disturbed.
pests.cause_seasoned: The larvae of the imported cabbageworm, cabbage looper, and diamondback moth feed on brassica foliage; the adults are white or brownish butterflies and moths that lay eggs on the leaves. Kohlrabi is a primary host.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Spray Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki) or spinosad, which target caterpillars and spare beneficials, and hand-pick larvae and eggs from leaf undersides. Repeat after rain, since Bt breaks down.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Use floating row cover or fine mesh from planting to exclude the egg-laying adults, clean up brassica debris that shelters pupae, and scout for the first white butterflies as a spray cue.

pests.name: Cabbage aphids
pests.symptoms_beginner: You'll see clusters of small gray-green insects with a dusty, waxy coating on the new growth and tucked into the folds of the leaves. Leaves may curl and there can be a sticky film.
pests.cause_beginner: Cabbage aphids are tiny insects that suck the plant's juices and breed fast. They love cabbage-family plants like kohlrabi and hide in the leaf folds.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Knock colonies off with a strong spray of water and hit the undersides of leaves with insecticidal soap or neem oil, repeating every few days. Welcome ladybugs and lacewings.
pests.prevention_beginner: Check the growing tips and leaf folds often and act early. Go easy on nitrogen, since soft growth draws them, and clear away old cabbage-family plants after harvest.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: The gray-green, waxy-coated cabbage aphid forms dense colonies on growing tips and leaf undersides and in the leaf axils, curling and distorting the foliage and weakening young plants; heavy colonies foul the crop with honeydew.
pests.cause_seasoned: Brevicoryne brassicae, a brassica-specialist aphid, sucks sap and reproduces rapidly; winged forms move in from cruciferous weeds and other brassica crops. The turnip aphid can also occur.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Dislodge colonies with a strong jet of water and spray insecticidal soap, neem, or horticultural oil with thorough coverage of leaf undersides; repeat every few days. Conserve natural enemies (parasitoid wasps, hoverflies, lady beetles).
pests.prevention_seasoned: Scout growing tips and leaf axils weekly and catch infestations early. Avoid excess nitrogen, use row cover on young plants, and destroy crop debris that carries them over.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms_beginner: Lots of tiny round holes in the leaves of young plants, made by small dark beetles that jump away like fleas when you get close. Bad damage can stunt seedlings.
pests.cause_beginner: Flea beetles are small jumping beetles that chew on young cabbage-family leaves. They hurt seedlings most, because a tiny plant can't grow fast enough to recover.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover young plants with a row cover, and if there are a lot of beetles, use a spray such as spinosad or a kaolin clay coating. The main goal is to get the seedlings big enough to handle it.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover seedlings with row cover from the start, keep them strong with steady water and food so they grow past the damage, and pull nearby weeds in the cabbage family.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny round shot-hole pits chewed in the leaves of young plants; the small dark beetles jump like fleas when disturbed. Heavy feeding stunts seedlings and slows establishment, the costly stage for a fast crop.
pests.cause_seasoned: The crucifer and striped flea beetles chew the foliage of young brassicas; they overwinter in debris and field edges and are most damaging at the seedling stage and in spring, easing as the season warms, so fall crops face less of them.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Protect seedlings with row cover and spray spinosad or apply kaolin clay if pressure is high; the goal is getting plants past the vulnerable seedling stage.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Use row cover from sowing or transplanting, keep seedlings vigorous with even water and feeding so they grow through the damage, clean up weedy brassica relatives, and favor fall plantings, which see lighter pressure.

pests.name: Cabbage root maggot
pests.symptoms_beginner: New transplants and seedlings wilt and grow badly or fall over. If you pull one up, you'll find small white maggots eating the roots. It is worst in cool, wet soil.
pests.cause_beginner: A small fly lays eggs at the base of the plant, and the maggots that hatch burrow down and eat the roots. The fly is most active in cool, damp spring weather.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Once the maggots are in the roots you can't save that plant, so pull and throw away the badly damaged ones. Put your effort into protecting the rest from new eggs.
pests.prevention_beginner: Put a small collar or disk around the base of each transplant to stop the fly from laying eggs there, or use a row cover. Avoid planting into cold, soggy soil, and rotate away from where cabbage-family plants grew.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Plants wilt, grow poorly, and may collapse; pulling a plant reveals small white maggots tunneling in the roots and lower stem. Damage is worst in cool, wet soil at spring establishment.
pests.cause_seasoned: The larvae of the cabbage root fly (Delia radicum) tunnel into brassica roots; the adult lays eggs at the stem base, and the maggots feed below, sometimes killing young plants and opening the door to rots.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no effective rescue once maggots are in the roots; remove and destroy badly affected plants and protect the rest from further egg-laying.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Place a collar or disk around the stem base at transplanting to block egg-laying, or use row cover; avoid planting into cold, wet soil and rotate away from where brassicas grew.

pests.name: Harlequin bug
pests.symptoms_beginner: Shield-shaped black-and-orange (or black-and-red) bugs on the leaves, which develop white or yellow spots, then brown and look tattered. It is mostly a warm-region problem and loves cabbage-family plants.
pests.cause_beginner: The harlequin bug is a colorful stink-bug relative that pierces the leaves and sucks the juices, leaving pale blotches. It strongly prefers cabbage-family plants, especially in the South.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Search out and crush the bugs, their barrel-shaped striped eggs, and the young ones by hand. Use a row cover to keep them off, pull badly infested plants, and clear away weeds and old plants where they hide.
pests.prevention_beginner: Clean up garden debris and cabbage-family weeds where the adults overwinter, use row cover, and consider a trap crop of mustard to lure them away, then destroy it.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Shield-shaped bugs up to about 3/8 inch, brightly black-and-yellow or black-and-red, feeding with piercing-sucking mouthparts that leave white stipples; affected leaves brown and look tattered, and heavy feeding wilts plants. A warm-region brassica specialist.
pests.cause_seasoned: The harlequin bug (Murgantia histrionica) is a true bug that specializes on cole crops, most damaging in the southern United States, where it completes several generations a year and overwinters as an adult in debris and weeds.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick and crush adults, nymphs, and the barrel-shaped egg rows; exclude with floating row cover; remove heavily infested plants. Insecticidal soap, pyrethrum, or neem help where pressure is severe.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Eliminate overwintering sites by removing crop debris and crucifer weeds, use row cover, and deploy an early trap crop of mustard to divert overwintering adults, then destroy it before the main crop is set out.

diseases.name: Clubroot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Plants wilt in the afternoon, stay small and yellowish, and don't bounce back. If you dig one up, the roots are swollen into lumpy, club-shaped knobs.
diseases.cause_beginner: A germ that lives in the soil infects the roots of cabbage-family plants and makes them swell, which stops the plant from taking up water and food. It stays in the soil for years.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There's no cure once a plant has it, so pull and destroy infected plants. Keeping the soil closer to neutral helps hold it back, and growing cabbage-family plants only rarely in that spot starves the germ out.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Don't grow kohlrabi or other cabbage-family plants in the same spot more than once every few years, longer if you've had clubroot. Keep the soil from being too acidic, improve drainage, and clean soil off your tools.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Plants wilt in the heat of the day, grow stunted and yellowed, and recover poorly; roots are swollen into distorted clubs and galls instead of normal fine roots, which later rot.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A soilborne organism (Plasmodiophora brassicae) infects brassica roots and forms the galls, which block water and nutrient uptake. It persists in soil for many years, spreads in contaminated soil and water, and is favored by acidic soils below about pH 6.5.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once plants are infected; remove and destroy them. Raising soil pH toward neutral with lime suppresses the disease, and long rotations starve it out over time.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate brassicas out of affected ground on a long cycle (up to 7 years where clubroot is known), keep soil pH up, improve drainage, and avoid moving infested soil on tools and boots.

diseases.name: Black rot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Yellow patches shaped like the letter V appear at the leaf edges, pointing inward, with black veins inside them. It can spread through the plant and rot it.
diseases.cause_beginner: A bacteria that often comes in on infected seeds or transplants. It gets into the leaves and travels through the plant's veins, spreading fastest in warm, wet weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There's no real cure, so remove and destroy infected plants to keep it from spreading. Don't handle or brush against the plants while they're wet.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Begin with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants, don't plant where cabbage-family crops grew recently, space plants for airflow, and avoid overhead watering.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellow, V-shaped lesions spread inward from the leaf margins, with the veins inside the V turning black; the disease moves through the vascular system and can blacken and kill the plant. Often the most serious brassica disease in warm, wet weather.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A seedborne bacterium (Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris) that enters through leaf pores and wounds and moves through the veins; it spreads in warm, wet conditions and on infected seed or transplants.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no effective cure; remove and destroy infected plants. Avoid working among plants when foliage is wet, since that moves the bacteria.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Start with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants, rotate 2 to 3 years away from brassicas, give plants room for airflow, and avoid overhead watering and handling wet foliage.

diseases.name: Alternaria leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small, round, dark spots on the leaves, each with a yellow ring and faint target-like circles inside, that grow and run together in wet weather and turn sooty in the center.
diseases.cause_beginner: Alternaria fungi that can travel on seed and survive on old plant debris, spreading in splashing water and needing wet leaves to take hold. Warm, humid weather brings it on.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick off the worst leaves, water at the soil in the morning so leaves dry quickly, and clean up debris. Clean seed and airflow handle most of it; a copper fungicide can help in a wet spell if started early.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Use clean seed, water at the base instead of overhead, give plants room so the leaves dry, and rotate crucifers and clear debris between plantings.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small, circular, dark spots with a yellow halo and concentric rings that darken to a sooty center as spores build, enlarging and merging in wet weather. A foliar disease that weakens the plant.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Alternaria fungi (chiefly Alternaria brassicae), which are seedborne and survive on crop debris, spreading in splashing water and needing leaf wetness to infect; warm, wet weather drives it.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove badly spotted leaves, water at the base in the morning so foliage dries, and clear debris. Clean seed and airflow are the main home levers; a copper fungicide can help in a persistently wet season if started early.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Use clean seed, avoid overhead watering, space for airflow, and rotate crucifers and clear debris that carry the fungi between seasons.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Pale yellow blotches on top of the leaves, with fuzzy grayish growth on the underside, mostly in cool, damp weather. Bad cases discolor the leaves.
diseases.cause_beginner: A mold-like disease that loves cool, wet, humid weather and spreads through the air and water. Wet leaves and crowded plants make it worse.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Open up the airflow so leaves can dry, remove the worst leaves, and use a copper spray if it's spreading. It's hard to stop once the weather stays damp.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Space plants so air moves between them, water at the soil instead of from above, and pick resistant varieties if downy mildew is common where you live.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Pale yellow patches on the upper leaf surface with a fuzzy gray-white growth underneath, mainly in cool, damp weather; severe infection discolors and kills foliage. Kohlrabi's cool, humid season overlaps the weather it likes.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A fungus-like organism (Hyaloperonospora parasitica) that thrives in cool, wet, humid conditions and spreads by spores in water and air; long leaf wetness and crowded plantings favor it.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Improve airflow and let foliage dry, remove badly affected leaves, and apply a copper-based fungicide if pressure is high; the disease is hard to stop once humidity stays high.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants for good air movement, water at the soil line rather than overhead, and choose resistant varieties where downy mildew is common.

diseases.name: Blackleg
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Pale, sunken spots dotted with tiny black specks appear on the stem and leaves, and the base of the stem darkens and rots, so the plant may topple. It often arrives on infected seed.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that comes in on infected seed or plants and attacks the stem and leaves of cabbage-family crops. It spreads in wet weather and lingers in old plant debris.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There's no cure, so pull and destroy infected plants. The real fix is prevention: clean seed, rotation, and clearing away old cabbage-family debris.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Start with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants, rotate away from cabbage-family crops for a few years, and clear away old brassica plants where the fungus survives.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Pale, sunken lesions peppered with small black fruiting bodies (pycnidia) on stems and leaves, and a dark, girdling canker at the stem base that can rot the crown and lodge the plant.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Phoma lingam (Leptosphaeria maculans) is chiefly seedborne and survives in brassica debris; it spreads in cool, wet weather by splashing water and infects through wounds and pores.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no effective cure; remove and destroy infected plants. Management is preventive, since the pathogen is carried on seed and in residue.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Use clean, certified, hot-water-treated seed and disease-free transplants, rotate 3 years away from brassicas, and bury or remove crop debris that carries the fungus over.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Give about 1 to 1.5 inches weekly, kept as even as possible; steady moisture is what keeps the bulb tender, and a dry-then-wet swing makes it woody or cracks it.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly 1 to 1.5 inches a week. Try to keep it steady, not dry-then-soaked.
watering.amount_seasoned: About 1 to 1.5 inches per week including rain (Iowa State and Minnesota: roughly 1 inch a week; Utah State up to 1 to 2 inches in heat or sandy soil), with the most attention while the stem is swelling.
watering.amount_beginner: Aim for roughly 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week, a bit more in hot, dry weather.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose where possible to keep foliage dry and discourage the leaf diseases kohlrabi shares with the cole crops.
watering.method_beginner: Water at the base of the plant rather than over the leaves.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves and limp growth; kohlrabi dislikes waterlogged soil, which invites root maggots, clubroot, and rots in cold, wet ground.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Lower leaves yellow and the plant looks soggy and limp.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting and stalled growth, then woody, fibrous, strong-flavored stems; the classic kohlrabi fault is letting the bed dry out, which toughens the bulb, and a heavy soak after a dry spell can split it.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Wilting leaves and a tough, woody bulb. Letting the soil dry out is the main thing that makes kohlrabi woody, and a sudden soaking after a dry spell can crack it.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Even, steady moisture is the whole game with kohlrabi: it keeps the swollen stem crisp, mild, and tender, and prevents the woodiness and cracking that a dry-then-wet cycle causes.
watering.method_note_beginner: Keep the water steady so the bulbs grow crisp and tender. Big swings from dry to wet are what make kohlrabi woody and cracked.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Even moisture matters most while the stem is swelling toward harvest; this is when drought stress turns it woody and a sudden change in watering cracks it.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Water steadily while the bulb is swelling. Do not let it dry out and then suddenly soak it.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Kohlrabi is grown both ways. Direct sowing is simple and common since the crop is fast: sow 1/4 to 1/2 inch deep once the soil is workable and thin to 6 to 9 inches apart. For an earlier or more uniform crop, start transplants indoors about 4 to 5 weeks before set-out and plant them out 1 to 2 weeks before the last frost, since young plants take light frost. Avoid exposing young plants to a long cold spell (more than about a week of nights below roughly 45 to 50°F), which can trigger bolting. Sow the fall crop in mid-summer. Harden transplants off over 7 to 10 days.
start_method.notes_beginner: You can sow kohlrabi seeds right in the garden or start with young plants. For direct sowing, plant the seeds about a quarter to half an inch deep once the soil can be worked, then thin the seedlings to about 6 to 9 inches apart. For transplants, start seeds indoors about a month before planting out, and set them in the garden a week or two before the last frost. Let homegrown seedlings get used to the outdoors over a week before planting. Sow again in mid-summer for a fall crop.

drainage.saucer_practice_seasoned: Do not let the pot stand in a saucer of water. Kohlrabi needs even moisture for a tender bulb, but waterlogged mix causes rot and favors clubroot; empty the saucer within an hour of watering.
drainage.saucer_practice_beginner: Do not let the pot sit in a saucer of water. Kohlrabi needs steady, even moisture, but soil that stays soggy will rot the roots, so empty the saucer within an hour of watering.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Use a bag of loose potting mix made for containers. Garden soil packs down hard in a pot and can bring in clubroot.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in a little compost to help the soil hold water evenly, which keeps kohlrabi tender.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: container_potting_mix
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Use a light, loose potting mix with a handful of compost for even moisture-holding. Avoid garden soil, which compacts in a pot and can introduce the soilborne clubroot pathogen.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out much faster than the ground, so check daily in warm weather. Kohlrabi turns woody if it dries out, so keep the moisture steady.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Feed a bit more often than in the ground, since watering washes nutrients out of pots.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Not applicable. Kohlrabi finishes its cycle in one season and is not overwintered in a pot.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Not applicable. Kohlrabi is grown as a single-season annual and is not held over winter in a container.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Kohlrabi is a great container crop because it is small and shallow-rooted. Use a pot at least 8 inches deep that holds 3 to 5 gallons, with drainage holes, and space the plants about 6 inches apart. Keep it watered evenly and harvest the bulbs young.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Kohlrabi suits containers well: it is compact, shallow-rooted, and quick, so a pot 8 inches or more deep holding 3 to 5 gallons grows several plants spaced about 6 inches apart. Width matters as much as depth, since you want room for several bulbs. Keep the mix evenly moist, because pots dry fast and a checked plant turns woody, and feed lightly. Provide drainage holes and a loose potting mix.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry faster than beds; check moisture daily in heat and water before the mix dries out, since drying out toughens the bulb.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Container kohlrabi needs slightly more frequent feeding than in-ground plants because watering leaches nutrients from the mix.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering container suits kohlrabi well, since it smooths out the steady moisture the crop needs to keep the bulb tender.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match because it keeps the water steady, which keeps kohlrabi from turning woody.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: Kohlrabi is a small, shallow-rooted plant, so a wide, fairly shallow container suits it better than a deep narrow one. Choose a pot at least 8 inches deep holding 3 to 5 gallons, and favor width so you can grow several plants spaced about 6 inches apart. Provide drainage holes and keep the mix evenly moist.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Kohlrabi has shallow roots, so a wide pot works better than a deep, narrow one. Use a container at least 8 inches deep that holds a few gallons, with drainage holes, and give each plant about 6 inches of space.

recommended.name: Early White Vienna
recommended.note: The classic pale-green heirloom and the standard early type; quick, dependable, and best picked young at tennis-ball size.

recommended.name: Early Purple Vienna
recommended.note: The purple-skinned counterpart to White Vienna, with the same creamy white flesh; the skin color is a handsome garden feature and does not affect flavor.

recommended.name: Grand Duke
recommended.note: An award-winning green hybrid that is uniform, slow to turn woody, and a reliable all-around choice.

recommended.name: Kolibri
recommended.note: A vigorous purple hybrid with crisp white flesh, good bolt resistance, and a wide harvest window; popular for both spring and fall.

recommended.name: Quickstar
recommended.note: One of the fastest types, a green hybrid bred for tender early bulbs, good for tight succession sowings.

recommended.name: Kossak
recommended.note: A giant storage type whose large green bulbs stay crisp and tender, with little of the woodiness that oversized standard kohlrabi develops; good for fall and winter keeping.

recommended.name: Superschmelz
recommended.note: An heirloom giant that can reach 8 to 10 inches across and still stay sweet and tender, an exception to the pick-it-small rule; a long-season fall crop.

varieties.note_seasoned: Match the type to the slot. Fast green or purple Vienna types and hybrids like Quickstar, Grand Duke, and Kolibri are the workhorses for spring and fall, picked young at 2 to 3 inches. The purple types (Purple Vienna, Kolibri) differ from the green only in skin color, not flavor. The giant storage cultivars (Kossak, Superschmelz, Gigante) are the exception to harvest-it-small: they hold tender flesh at a much larger size and suit fall and winter storage. Where clubroot is a concern, choose resistant cultivars.
varieties.note_beginner: For most gardens, pick a fast standard variety like White Vienna, Purple Vienna, Grand Duke, or Kolibri, and harvest the bulbs young, about the size of a tennis ball. Purple and green types taste the same; the purple is just prettier. If you want big bulbs, grow a giant type like Kossak or Superschmelz, which stay tender even when large.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Other brassicas (cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kale, Brussels sprouts, collards, turnip, radish), which share clubroot and the cabbage-family pests.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Other cabbage-family crops like cabbage, broccoli, kale, turnips, and radishes.
rotation.good_after: Legumes such as beans and peas, or unrelated crops like tomatoes, squash, or onions.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate so brassicas do not follow brassicas for at least 3 years, and longer where clubroot is known, since the clubroot organism persists in soil for years. Keeping soil pH up also helps suppress it.
rotation.note_beginner: Do not plant kohlrabi or other cabbage-family crops in the same spot year after year. Waiting a few years between them helps avoid soil diseases like clubroot.

bolting.triggers: A cold spell on young plants (more than about a week of nights below roughly 45 to 50°F), which vernalizes them and triggers flowering, plus prolonged summer heat and long days.
bolting.prevention_seasoned: Do not rush transplants out into a long cold snap, since young kohlrabi chilled below about 45 to 50°F for a week or more is vernalized and bolts. Time the spring crop so it sizes up before summer heat, grow the fall crop into cooling weather, and choose bolt-resistant varieties such as Kolibri. Keep plants growing steadily without a check.
bolting.prevention_beginner: Plant kohlrabi so it grows in steady cool weather, not through a long cold snap or into summer heat. Setting young plants out into a hard cold spell can make them flower instead of forming a bulb, so wait for settled weather and pick bolt-resistant varieties.
bolting.note_seasoned: Kohlrabi bolting is mainly a vernalization response: a young plant exposed to a stretch of cold runs to flower instead of swelling a stem, which is why an early spring set-out into a cold snap is the classic cause. Summer heat and long days also push it. A bolted plant will not form a usable bulb, so the fix is timing and steady growth.
bolting.note_beginner: If young kohlrabi gets too cold for too long, or too hot, it flowers early and never makes a good bulb. Steady cool weather and good timing are the main fixes.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Kohlrabi keeps a day or two at room temperature but softens and loses crispness, so refrigerate it soon after harvest. Twist or cut off the leafy tops first, since they pull moisture from the bulb.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Kohlrabi does not keep well on the counter. Cut off the leaves and put the bulb in the fridge soon after picking.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Remove the leaf stems and store the unwashed bulb in a perforated or loose plastic bag in the crisper, where it keeps well for about 2 to 3 weeks (Utah State and Iowa State). The leaves keep only a few days and are best used fresh.
storage.fridge_beginner: Trim off the leaves and store the unwashed bulb in a loose plastic bag in the fridge crisper, where it stays good for about 2 to 3 weeks. Use the leaves within a few days.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Kohlrabi freezes well once peeled, diced, and blanched about 2 to 3 minutes, then cooled in ice water, drained, and frozen. Blanching halts the enzymes that would otherwise cause off-flavors and texture loss in storage.
storage.freezer_beginner: To freeze kohlrabi, peel and dice it, boil the pieces about 2 to 3 minutes, cool them quickly in ice water, drain, and freeze. The quick boil keeps the flavor and texture.
storage.notes_seasoned: Kohlrabi stores noticeably better than most cole crops: a firm bulb holds 2 to 3 weeks refrigerated, and the giant storage types (Kossak) keep for months in cold, humid conditions near 32°F. Quality is still highest fresh, and the leaves are perishable.
storage.notes_beginner: Kohlrabi keeps longer than most cabbage-family vegetables, a few weeks in the fridge, and the big storage types keep for months somewhere cold. Use the leaves quickly, though.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: In about 5 to 10 days, your seeds sprout and push up their first two little leaves, called seed leaves.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil damp and warm. Once you see the first real kohlrabi leaves after the seed leaves, thin out crowded seedlings.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your seeds come up yet?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seeds sprout in about 5 to 10 days at soil temperatures of roughly 60 to 75°F, pushing up two seed leaves (cotyledons).
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep the seedbed or starting mix evenly moist and warm; thin or pot up once the first true leaves appear.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Did your kohlrabi seeds sprout?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The seedlings grow their real leaves and a stronger stem. Direct-sown plants are thinned now; transplants are ready to move outside at about 4 to 5 weeks old.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Thin direct-sown seedlings to about 6 to 9 inches apart. Before planting transplants outside, harden them off over about a week, and avoid setting them out into a long cold snap.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How many real leaves do your seedlings have?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Young plants develop true leaves and a sturdy stem; transplants are ready at about 4 to 5 weeks, and direct-sown stands are thinned to spacing.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin to 6 to 9 inches; harden off transplants over 7 to 10 days and avoid exposing young plants to a prolonged cold spell, which vernalizes them and triggers bolting.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have you thinned or hardened off your kohlrabi?

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant puts on a rosette of broad leaves on a short stem for a few weeks. This leafy growth comes before the bulb swells.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Feed the plant a little nitrogen as it grows and keep it evenly watered. Check the leaves for caterpillars, aphids, and flea-beetle holes.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Is your plant growing lots of healthy leaves?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The plant builds a leafy rosette over several weeks before the stem base begins to swell.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Side-dress with nitrogen as the plant establishes, keep moisture even, and watch for cabbageworms, aphids, and flea beetles.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Is your kohlrabi putting on healthy leafy growth?

growth_stages.name: Stem swelling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The base of the stem, just above the soil, swells into a round, pale-green or purple bulb. This is the part you eat.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the water steady so the bulb stays tender, and watch its size. It is ready when it reaches about 2 to 3 inches across, the size of a tennis ball. Do not let it keep growing past that or it turns woody.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Can you see the bulb swelling at the base?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The stem base swells into the round, above-ground bulb. Even moisture and steady growth here decide whether it is crisp and mild or woody and fibrous.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture even and check size daily as it approaches 2 to 3 inches; a growth check from drought or heat now is what turns the stem woody and bitter.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Has the stem started to swell into a bulb?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The bulb is about 2 to 3 inches across, the size of a tennis ball, firm and smooth. This is the moment to cut it, before it gets bigger and tougher.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Cut the whole bulb off at the base with a knife while it is still young and tender. Standard types get woody if you wait too long, so do not let them grow large. Harvest in the cool morning if you can.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you harvested your kohlrabi yet?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The bulb reaches about 2 to 3 inches in diameter (larger for the giant storage types), firm and smooth, before it turns woody.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut the bulb at the base while young; standard varieties grow tough, woody, and bitter past about 3 inches, so harvest on time. Giant types (Kossak, Superschmelz) hold tender at larger size. Trim the tops and chill promptly.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Did you harvest your kohlrabi?

notifications.body_seasoned: Your kohlrabi bulb should be about 2 to 3 inches across now. Cut it at the base while it is firm and young, before it turns woody and bitter; standard types do not improve by waiting.
notifications.body_beginner: Your kohlrabi should be about the size of a tennis ball now. Cut the bulb off at the base while it is young and tender, before it gets tough.

notifications.body_seasoned: Your kohlrabi is established. Side-dress with nitrogen now to keep growth steady and the bulb tender, placing the feed beside the row and watering it in.
notifications.body_beginner: Feed your kohlrabi a little nitrogen now to keep it growing steadily. Put the fertilizer near the plants and water it in.

notifications.title_seasoned: Heat watch: keep the bulb tender
notifications.title_beginner: Hot weather warning for your kohlrabi
notifications.body_seasoned: A hot spell is coming while your kohlrabi is sizing up. Heat above roughly 75°F turns the stem woody and bitter and can trigger bolting. Keep moisture even and harvest promptly if bulbs are near size.
notifications.body_beginner: Hot weather is on the way while your kohlrabi is forming its bulb. Heat can make it woody and bitter. Keep the soil evenly watered, and pick any bulbs that are nearly ready.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Heat warning while bulbing
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Days well above roughly 75°F while the stem is swelling push fast, fibrous growth that leaves kohlrabi woody and bitter and can trigger bolting. Keep moisture even and harvest any near-size bulbs promptly.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Hot weather while the bulb is forming can make kohlrabi tough and bitter. Water evenly and pick any bulbs that are nearly ready.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hard freeze coming
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Kohlrabi takes light frost in stride, but a hard freeze can damage the bulbs. Cover plants or harvest mature bulbs before a hard freeze.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Kohlrabi handles a light frost fine, but a hard freeze can damage the bulbs. Cover the plants or pick any ready bulbs before a hard freeze hits.

germination.text_seasoned: Sow about 1/4 to 1/2 inch deep into a moist seedbed or starting mix; kohlrabi germinates fast and reliably across a wide soil-temperature range as long as moisture stays even.
germination.text_beginner: Plant the seeds about a quarter to half an inch deep in damp soil, and keep it evenly moist while they sprout.

germination.text_seasoned: Because kohlrabi is so quick, direct sowing works well; start transplants only when you want an earlier or more uniform stand.
germination.text_beginner: Kohlrabi grows fast, so you can plant the seeds right in the garden. Starting indoors is only needed if you want an earlier crop.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin to 6 to 9 inches apart; crowded plants make small, misshapen bulbs and compete for moisture.
seedling.text_beginner: Thin the seedlings to about 6 to 9 inches apart so each one has room to form a good bulb.

seedling.text_seasoned: Avoid setting young transplants out into a prolonged cold snap (over about a week below roughly 45 to 50°F), the classic vernalization trigger for bolting.
seedling.text_beginner: Do not plant young kohlrabi out into a long cold spell, which can make it flower early instead of forming a bulb. Wait for settled weather.

established.text_seasoned: Side-dress nitrogen about 3 to 4 weeks after planting when plants are roughly 4 inches tall, and keep moisture even; steady growth is what keeps the coming bulb tender.
established.text_beginner: Feed the plants a little nitrogen a few weeks after planting and water steadily so they keep growing without a stall.

established.text_seasoned: Scout for flea beetles on young plants and cabbage aphids in the leaf axils; a vigorous, well-watered stand outgrows light flea-beetle feeding.
established.text_beginner: Check young plants for tiny flea-beetle holes and for aphids tucked into the leaves, and keep the plants growing strong.

bulbing.text_seasoned: Keep water even at roughly 1 to 1.5 inches per week as the stem swells; a drought-then-soak swing is what makes kohlrabi woody and splits it.
bulbing.text_beginner: Water steadily while the bulb is swelling. Letting it dry out and then soaking it is what makes kohlrabi tough and cracked.

bulbing.text_seasoned: Watch the bulb size daily as it nears 2 to 3 inches; standard types pass their window quickly and turn woody, so do not let them oversize.
bulbing.text_beginner: Check the bulb every day as it gets close to tennis-ball size. Standard kohlrabi turns woody fast if it grows too big.

harvest.text_seasoned: Cut the bulb at the base at 2 to 3 inches for standard types; harvest on time, since a woody, over-mature kohlrabi will not soften.
harvest.text_beginner: Cut the bulb off at the base when it reaches tennis-ball size. If you wait too long it gets woody and will not get tender again.

harvest.text_seasoned: Trim the leafy tops and chill promptly; the bulb keeps 2 to 3 weeks refrigerated, far longer for the giant storage types.
harvest.text_beginner: Cut off the leaves and get the bulb into the fridge, where it keeps for a couple of weeks.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Each plant yields one swollen-stem bulb, typically 2 to 3 inches across and a few ounces to about half a pound for standard types, harvested once. Giant storage cultivars (Kossak, Superschmelz) yield a single much larger bulb of a pound or more. There are no side shoots, so total yield is set by plant spacing and succession sowings.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Each kohlrabi plant gives you one bulb, picked once. Standard types are about the size of a tennis ball; giant types can be much bigger. To get a steady supply, plant a few seeds every couple of weeks.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Because each plant produces a single bulb harvested at once, there is no extended peak; the way to a steady supply is succession sowing every 2 to 3 weeks across the spring and fall windows. The fast 45 to 60 day cycle makes tight succession practical.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Kohlrabi makes one bulb per plant, so for a steady harvest, sow a small batch every couple of weeks instead of all at once. The crop is fast, so you do not wait long.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: The single most common first-year mistake is letting the bulb grow too big: standard kohlrabi turns woody, fibrous, and bitter past about 3 inches and does not recover, so harvest young rather than waiting for a bigger bulb. New growers also under-water, which toughens the stem.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: The big thing to learn with kohlrabi is to pick it young, at tennis-ball size. If you leave it to get bigger, it turns woody and tough and will not get better. Keeping the water steady also keeps it tender.
factors_seasoned: Harvest timing: standard types must be cut at 2 to 3 inches before they turn woody; a late harvest ruins the bulb.
Even moisture: a steady water supply keeps the stem crisp and mild, while drought or a dry-then-wet swing makes it woody and can crack it.
Temperature: cool, steady growth gives tender bulbs; heat above about 75°F drives fibrous growth and bolting.
Variety: giant storage types (Kossak, Superschmelz) hold tender flesh at a large size, while standard types must be picked small.
Spacing and succession: yield over the season comes from spacing at 6 to 9 inches and sowing in small batches every 2 to 3 weeks.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No reliable extension or peer-reviewed evidence supports timing kohlrabi planting or harvest by moon phase. Plant by soil temperature, frost dates, and the seasonal windows instead.

failure_diagnostics.label: Woody, tough, fibrous bulb
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Letting the bulb grow too big, or growth stress from dry soil or heat.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: You cut the bulb and it was tough, woody, and stringy instead of crisp and tender. This usually means it grew too large, since standard kohlrabi turns woody past about 3 inches, or that the plant got stressed by dry soil or heat and grew fibrous. It is tempting to leave kohlrabi to get bigger like a turnip, but with standard types that backfires. Next time, harvest at tennis-ball size, keep the water steady, and try a giant type like Kossak if you want big tender bulbs.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Pick standard kohlrabi young, at 2 to 3 inches, keep the soil evenly moist, and grow a giant variety if you want larger bulbs.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The bulb was woody, fibrous, and strong-flavored rather than crisp and mild. The usual causes are over-maturity (standard types lignify past about 3 inches) and growth checks from drought or heat that drive fibrous tissue. Growers often leave kohlrabi to size up like a root crop, which ruins standard cultivars. Next time harvest standard types at 2 to 3 inches, hold even moisture, and use a giant storage cultivar (Kossak, Superschmelz) where a large tender bulb is wanted.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Over-maturity in standard types, or growth checks from drought or heat.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Harvest standard types at 2 to 3 inches, keep moisture even, and switch to a giant non-woody cultivar for larger bulbs.

failure_diagnostics.label: Bolting (flowering before a bulb forms)
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: A long cold spell on young plants, or summer heat and long days.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The plant sent up a flower stalk instead of making a bulb. Kohlrabi flowers early when young plants get chilled for a stretch (more than about a week of cold nights) or when summer heat and long days push it, and once it bolts no good bulb forms. A common mistake is planting too early into a cold snap. Next time, wait for settled weather to plant, grow a bolt-resistant variety, and time the crop for steady cool growth.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant into settled weather, not a cold snap or into summer heat, and choose a bolt-resistant variety like Kolibri.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The plant ran to flower instead of swelling a stem. Kohlrabi bolting is largely a vernalization response, a young plant chilled below roughly 45 to 50°F for a week or more is triggered to flower, and summer heat and long days add to it. The classic cause is an early spring set-out into a cold spell. Next time avoid exposing transplants to a prolonged cold snap, time the crop for steady cool growth, and use bolt-resistant cultivars.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Vernalization of young plants by a prolonged cold spell, plus heat and long days.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Avoid a prolonged cold spell on young plants, time for steady cool growth, and choose bolt-resistant varieties.

failure_diagnostics.label: Cracked or split bulb
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Uneven watering, especially a heavy soak after a dry spell.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The bulb cracked open. This comes from uneven watering: when the soil goes dry and then gets a big drink or a heavy rain, the bulb takes up water fast and splits. Next time, keep the watering steady so the soil never swings from bone dry to soaked, and harvest on time rather than letting bulbs sit oversized.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist and avoid a sudden soaking after a dry spell.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The bulb split from uneven moisture: a rapid water uptake after drought stress ruptures the swollen stem. Next time hold steady moisture through bulbing and avoid the dry-then-flood cycle, and harvest on time so bulbs are not standing past size when a rain comes.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Uneven moisture, a fast water uptake after drought stress.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Hold steady moisture through bulbing and harvest on time to avoid the dry-then-flood split.

failure_diagnostics.label: No bulb, just leaves
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Crowding, too much shade, or too much nitrogen late.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The plant grew plenty of leaves but never formed a real bulb. This usually comes from plants set too close together, too much shade, or a lot of nitrogen late on, all of which push leafy growth over the bulb. Next time, thin to 6 to 9 inches, grow in full sun, and keep feeding modest and even.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Thin to 6 to 9 inches, grow in full sun, and go easy on nitrogen late in the crop.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The plant made foliage but no usable swollen stem. The usual causes are crowding, insufficient light, or excess late nitrogen, each favoring leaves over the bulb. Next time thin to 6 to 9 inches, site in full sun, and keep nitrogen modest and front-loaded so the plant transitions to bulbing.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Crowding, low light, or excess late nitrogen pushing foliage over the bulb.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Thin to spacing, give full sun, and keep late nitrogen modest so the plant bulbs up.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Kohlrabi is fast (about 45 to 60 days) and each plant makes a single bulb, so the way to a steady supply is small, frequent sowings rather than one big planting. Sow in batches every 2 to 3 weeks across the spring window and again in late summer for fall, skipping the high heat of summer, when the stem turns woody and bitter. The fall crop, sizing in cooling weather, is often the most dependable.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: Plant kohlrabi in small batches every couple of weeks instead of all at once, since each plant gives one bulb. Grow it in spring and again in late summer for fall, and skip the hottest part of summer.

crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Kohlrabi is ready when the swollen stem reaches about 2 to 3 inches in diameter for standard types, the size of a tennis ball, firm and smooth. Cut the bulb off at the base while it is young; past about 3 inches standard cultivars turn tough, woody, and bitter and do not recover. Giant storage types (Kossak, Superschmelz) stay tender at a much larger size. Trim the leafy tops and refrigerate promptly.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Kohlrabi is ready when the bulb is about the size of a tennis ball, 2 to 3 inches across, firm and smooth. Cut it off at the base while it is young and tender. Do not wait for it to get bigger, since standard kohlrabi turns woody and tough. Giant types are the exception and stay tender when large.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Work plenty of compost into a loose, fertile, well-drained bed before planting, and mix in a balanced fertilizer such as 10-10-10. Loosen any compaction, since kohlrabi wants steady, unchecked growth for a tender bulb, and aim the pH at about 6.0 to 7.0, liming acidic ground where clubroot is a concern.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Before planting, mix a few inches of compost and a balanced fertilizer into loose, well-drained soil. Kohlrabi grows best in rich, evenly moist ground, which keeps the bulbs tender.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: kohlrabi_author_fresh_pilot 2026-06-29 (Claude Code author-bot; FILLED the shell, modeled structurally on the certified broccoli template). Refit to kohlrabi (Brassica oleracea Gongylodes): swollen above-ground edible STEM (no head, no side shoots), single harvest at 2 to 3 in / tennis-ball size, woody/tough/bitter if oversized or stressed, fast 45 to 60 day cycle, cool-season spring + fall, heat threshold ~75°F (USU). Biology sourced from readable T1 kohlrabi pages: UMN, USU, Iowa State, Wisconsin Horticulture; pests/diseases corroborated by Clemson cole-crop factsheets. Region MONTH calendars + frost dates + summer heat gaps are a cool-season-brassica climate function shared with broccoli (legitimately the same months for two B. oleracea cool crops in the same climates); harvest timing + heat physiology are kohlrabi-specific. successions_realized CC-DERIVED (interval_weeks=2). NOT certified: queued for the daily biology-fidelity review + per-crop source-truth sample.

open_findings.summary: The 10-region planting/harvest MONTH calendars (plant windows, frost dates, summer heat gaps, second_planting windows, succession dates) are modeled on the cool-season-brassica climate scaffold shared with the certified broccoli record: for two Brassica oleracea cool-season crops in the same climates the month-level windows are the same climate function, and kohlrabi's faster maturity (45 to 60 vs 55 to 75 days) shifts harvest by days, not months. The kohlrabi-specific refits (single-stem harvest, ~75°F heat threshold, succession cadence) live in the crop-level fields. Several regional sources are scanned/image PDFs not re-parsed at authoring (uga_ext_c963_chart, tamu_agrilife_fall_veg, nmsu_ext_cr457b, uariz_ext_az1005, uhawaii_ctahr_b91); the windows are corroborated by readable T1 (umn_ext, iastate_ext, usu_ext + UGA C943 calendar + UF VH021). A human should re-verify the regional windows against a readable kohlrabi-specific calendar at display-readiness.
open_findings.basis: Plant windows + frost dates are climate facts valid for any cool-season brassica; the readable kohlrabi T1 (UMN spring + fall mid-summer; USU 1 to 2 weeks before last frost; Iowa State early-mid April + mid-July to mid-August) match the temperate windows. No fabricated source; PDF-only regional charts flagged rather than extracted.

open_findings.summary: Each hot-region heat_pause REUSES the regional summer no-grow months from the brassica climate scaffold (a climate fact: the same months are too hot for any cool-season cole crop), while the basis prose is kohlrabi-specific physiology (the swollen stem turns woody and bitter and plants bolt above roughly 75°F, USU). The ~75°F threshold is lower than broccoli's 86/77°F heading ceiling, so if anything kohlrabi's hot-region exclusion is conservative.
open_findings.basis: USU Extension: kohlrabi grows best where temperatures do not exceed 75°F; stems turn tough and woody in heat. Cool northern zones 3 to 4 carry no heat gap (run through), matching the scaffold.

open_findings.summary: Kohlrabi is a genuinely good container crop (compact, shallow-rooted, fast); the specific pot dimensions (3 to 5 gallons, 8 in deep, 6 in spacing) are conventional small-brassica container guidance cited to the Wisconsin Extension containers article rather than a kohlrabi-specific container source.
open_findings.basis: Wisconsin Horticulture growing-vegetables-in-containers (the broccoli container precedent); kohlrabi's small size makes it lower-demand than broccoli, so the dimensions are conservative.

open_findings.summary: Clemson HGIC has no dedicated kohlrabi factsheet readable at authoring (the /factsheet/kohlrabi/ URL 404s); the Clemson cole-crop INSECT-PESTS and DISEASES factsheets, which explicitly cover 'cabbage, broccoli and other cole crops' (kohlrabi included), are cited for the pest/disease set, corroborated by the UMN and Iowa State kohlrabi pages.
open_findings.basis: The shared cabbage-family pest and disease complex (cabbageworm/looper/diamondback, cabbage aphid, flea beetle, root maggot, harlequin bug; clubroot, black rot, Alternaria, downy mildew, blackleg) is documented at the cole-crop family level by Clemson and named for kohlrabi by UMN/USU/Wisconsin.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer gap is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: kohlrabi is a cool-season brassica whose swollen stem turns woody, tough, and bitter when growth is pushed by summer heat above roughly 75°F, and plants stressed by heat run to flower. The leafy tops tolerate warmth, but a tender, mild bulb will not form, so the calendar splits into a spring crop sized before the heat and a fall crop sized as it breaks. (Utah State Extension; University of Minnesota Extension)
