northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In cold-winter areas, grow kohlrabi in spring and again in late summer for fall. Plant in cool weather and pick the bulbs young, about the size of a tennis ball, before they turn woody. The fall crop is usually the easiest.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Across the cold northern zones kohlrabi is a classic two-crop cool-season vegetable: a spring planting set out a couple of weeks before the last frost and sized before summer heat, and a more dependable fall planting sown in mid-summer to mature in cool weather. Cold zones 3 and 4 run no summer heat gap, while milder zones 5 to 7 take a short midsummer pause when growth turns the stem woody and bitter. Harvest at tennis-ball size, about 2 to 3 inches across, before the bulb gets tough.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Mid-summer heat well above roughly 75°F drives fast, fibrous growth that leaves the kohlrabi stem woody and bitter and pushes stressed plants to bolt, so no crop is grown between the spring and fall windows. (Utah State Extension; UGA Extension)

Mid-summer heat well above roughly 75°F drives fast, fibrous growth that leaves the kohlrabi stem woody and bitter and pushes stressed plants to bolt, so no crop is grown between the spring and fall windows. (Utah State Extension; UGA Extension)

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: On the Gulf coast, grow kohlrabi in the cooler months, not in the heat of summer. Plant in fall and again in late winter, and harvest the bulbs while they are still young and tender.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: Along the Gulf and coastal plain kohlrabi is a fall-through-spring crop grown around the hot middle of the year. Plant in the cool months for harvests in spring and again in late fall, and skip high summer, when heat above roughly 75°F makes the stem woody and bitter and pushes plants to bolt. Its fast 50 to 60 day cycle fits tight succession sowings through the long mild season.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Spring and summer heat above roughly 75°F leaves kohlrabi stems woody and bitter, so no crop is grown between the spring harvest and the late-summer fall sowing. (Utah State Extension; UC Master Gardener Program)

Spring and summer heat above roughly 75°F leaves kohlrabi stems woody and bitter, so no crop is grown between the spring harvest and the late-summer fall sowing. (Utah State Extension; UC Master Gardener Program)

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In the inland valleys, grow kohlrabi in the cool months. Plant from late fall through winter for spring, and again in late summer for fall. Avoid the hottest part of summer, and harvest the bulbs young.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: In California's interior valleys kohlrabi is a winter-into-spring crop, planted through the cool months for spring harvests, with a separate fall planting in mid-to-late summer. High spring and summer heat above roughly 75°F is the limit, turning the stem woody and bitter, so the calendar works around it. Pick young for the best texture.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: Along the cool northern California coast you can grow kohlrabi most of the year. Plant a few seeds every couple of weeks for a steady supply, and harvest the bulbs while they are young and tender.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: The mild, cool-summer North Coast is excellent kohlrabi country: the crop grows nearly year-round, with no real summer heat gap, so successive sowings every couple of weeks keep tender bulbs coming through most of the year. Pick at 2 to 3 inches across before the stem toughens.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer heat above roughly 75°F leaves kohlrabi tough and bitter, so no crop is grown between the spring and fall windows. (Utah State Extension; UC Master Gardener Program)
Summer heat above roughly 75°F leaves kohlrabi tough and bitter, so no crop is grown between the spring and fall windows. (Utah State Extension; UC Master Gardener Program)

ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: On the southern California coast, grow kohlrabi in the cooler parts of the year. Plant in winter and again in early summer, and pick the bulbs young.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: On the mild South Coast kohlrabi grows through the cool seasons with only a brief late-summer heat gap. Plant in winter for spring and again in early summer for a fall crop, harvesting young before the stem turns woody. The frost-free winters let the crop run late into the year.

ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: In the desert, grow kohlrabi only in the cool season. Plant in early fall and harvest through the winter. It is too hot the rest of the year.
ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: In the low California desert kohlrabi is strictly a cool-season crop: plant in early fall for winter harvests, since the long hot months are far too warm for a tender bulb. Harvest through winter and into early spring, picking young before any spring heat toughens the stem.

warm_arid.region_label: Warm Arid: Southern New Mexico & West Texas

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: High desert-edge summer heat well above roughly 75°F leaves the kohlrabi stem woody and bitter and pushes plants to bolt, so no crop is grown between the spring and fall windows. (Utah State Extension; Texas A&M AgriLife Extension)

warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: In the dry Southwest, grow kohlrabi in spring and fall, not summer. Plant after the last frost and again in late summer, and harvest the bulbs young before they toughen.
warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: In the warm arid Southwest kohlrabi is grown in spring and fall around a hot summer. Set plants out after the last frost for a spring crop, and sow again in late summer for fall, skipping the high-heat months when the stem turns woody and bitter. Its quick cycle suits the short cool windows.

low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: In the low desert of Arizona, grow kohlrabi in the cool season, planting from late summer through winter. Harvest the bulbs young, and skip the hot summer.
low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: In the Arizona low desert kohlrabi is a fall-to-spring crop planted across the long cool season, from late summer through midwinter, for harvests from fall into spring. The summer is far too hot. Its fast cycle and the long mild window allow many successive sowings.

fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: In peninsular Florida, grow kohlrabi in the cool months from fall into spring. Plant in fall and winter, harvest young, and skip the hot summer.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: On the Florida peninsula kohlrabi is a cool-season crop grown from fall through early spring. Plant from early fall into winter for harvests through the cool months, and avoid the hot, humid summer, which makes the stem woody and invites disease. The long mild window supports repeated sowings of this fast crop.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In Hawaii, grow kohlrabi in the cooler months, especially at higher elevations. Plant late in the year for a winter harvest, and pick the bulbs young.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: In Hawaii's warm lowlands kohlrabi is best grown as a cool-season crop in the milder months, planted late in the year for winter harvests; at higher, cooler elevations the window is wider. Lowland summer heat leaves the stem tough and bitter, so the planting is kept to the coolest part of the year.

crops.description_seasoned: Kohlrabi (Brassica oleracea, Gongylodes group) is a cool-season cole crop grown not for a head or a root but for its swollen above-ground STEM, a round, pale-green or purple bulb that sits on the soil surface topped by a rosette of leaves. It is one of the fastest brassicas, ready in about 45 to 60 days, and is grown like a quick cabbage in the cool shoulders of spring and fall. The whole craft is steady, unchecked growth and timely harvest: a tender, mild, crisp bulb forms when the plant never stalls, while drought, heat above roughly 75°F, or a stop-start water supply, or simply letting it grow too large, turns standard types woody, fibrous, and bitter. Harvest young at 2 to 3 inches, tennis-ball size; giant storage cultivars (Kossak, Superschmelz) are the exception and hold tender flesh at a much larger size. Cold-hardy and frost-tolerant, kohlrabi shares the full cabbage-family pest and disease complex.
crops.description_beginner: Kohlrabi is a cool-season cabbage-family vegetable grown for its odd, tasty swollen stem, a round bulb, green or purple, that sits right on top of the soil with leaves sprouting from it. It is one of the fastest crops in the garden, ready in about 45 to 60 days, and grows best in the cool weather of spring and fall. The trick is simple: keep it growing steadily with even water, and pick the bulb young, about the size of a tennis ball. If you let standard kohlrabi get too big, or let it dry out or cook in summer heat, it turns woody and tough. It handles frost well, and like its cabbage cousins it gets the usual cabbage-family bugs and diseases. The bulb is crisp and mild, good raw or cooked.

thinning.tip_seasoned: Thin direct-sown kohlrabi to 6 to 9 inches apart once seedlings have 2 to 3 true leaves, snipping rather than pulling to avoid disturbing the keepers. Crowded plants compete for moisture and make small, misshapen bulbs, and crowding stress can also push them woody.
thinning.tip_beginner: When the seedlings have a few real leaves, thin them so each plant has about 6 to 9 inches of room. Snip the extras off at the soil instead of pulling, so you don't disturb the ones you keep. Crowded kohlrabi makes small, poor bulbs.

crops.name: Honeydew Melon

soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Honeydew wants a deep, light, well-drained soil in full sun, with sandy loams and loamy sands the classic choice because they warm quickly in spring and drain freely, which this heat-loving, long-season melon rewards. Work a few inches of compost into the bed before planting, but go easier on nitrogen-rich amendments than you would for leafy crops, since excess nitrogen pushes vine at the expense of fruit and sugar. Many growers plant on low, wide hills or raised mounds, which warm faster, drain better, and lift the developing fruit off wet ground. Heavy clay holds water and stays cold, slowing a crop that already needs the longest, warmest season of the common melons and inviting Fusarium wilt and fruit rot, so amend it generously and build mounds, or grow on sandier ground.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Plant honeydew in light, well-drained soil that warms up fast, like a sandy loam, with some compost mixed in. Do not overdo rich, high-nitrogen material, because that gives you lots of leaves and vine but less fruit. Many gardeners plant on low hills or raised mounds, which warm up and drain better and keep the fruit off soggy ground. Honeydew needs a long, hot season, so if your soil is heavy clay, it stays cold and wet and slows the crop, so mix in compost and build the soil into mounds, or pick the sandiest, best-draining spot you have.

ph.note_seasoned: Honeydew grows best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, around pH 6.0 to 6.8, and tolerates a wider band of roughly 5.5 to 7.5. Like other melons it is a little more forgiving of mildly acidic ground than many vegetables, but strongly acidic or strongly alkaline soil tightens nutrient uptake. Test before planting and lime or add sulfur only on the test's advice rather than by guess.
ph.note_beginner: Honeydew likes soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, about pH 6.0 to 6.8, and most garden soil is already close. An inexpensive soil test tells you where you stand and whether you need to adjust it before planting.

fertilizer.frequency: At planting, then side-dress once or twice
fertilizer.type: lower-nitrogen at planting, then nitrogen side-dress
fertilizer.timing: Work into the bed before planting, then side-dress when vines begin to run and again at flowering
fertilizer.example_product: 5-10-10 at planting, then a nitrogen source such as calcium nitrate or blood meal
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Honeydew is a moderate feeder that wants more phosphorus and potassium than nitrogen, since excess nitrogen drives leafy vine at the expense of fruit set and sugar. Work a lower-nitrogen complete fertilizer such as 5-10-10 into the bed before planting (Clemson suggests about 30 pounds per 1,000 square feet), then side-dress with a nitrogen source as the vines begin to run, and again lightly at flowering. Ease off nitrogen once fruit has set so the plant pours its energy into sizing and sweetening the melons rather than growing more vine. Because honeydew hangs on the vine longer than cantaloupe, pair feeding with steady, even moisture, since the nutrients only help a plant that is not also drought-stressed.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Honeydew does not need a lot of nitrogen, and too much gives you big leafy vines but fewer, less sweet melons. Mix a fertilizer that is lower in nitrogen, like a 5-10-10, into the soil before planting, then give the plants a little nitrogen when the vines start to run and again when flowers appear. Once the melons start to form, stop pushing nitrogen so the plant puts its energy into growing sweet fruit instead of more leaves.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Your honeydew vines are running, time to side-dress with a little nitrogen. Then keep feeding light and ease off nitrogen once fruit sets, so the plant builds sweet melons rather than vine.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Your honeydew vines are spreading. Give them a light feeding of nitrogen now.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A lower-nitrogen complete fertilizer such as 5-10-10 worked in at planting, then a nitrogen side-dress as the vines run and again lightly at flowering, easing off nitrogen once fruit sets. Too much nitrogen gives vine and leaf at the expense of fruit and sweetness.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a lower-nitrogen fertilizer like 5-10-10 at planting, then a little nitrogen as the vines spread. Do not overdo the nitrogen once melons form, or you get leaves instead of fruit.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A common approach is a lower-nitrogen complete fertilizer such as 5-10-10 worked into the bed before planting (Clemson cites about 30 pounds per 1,000 square feet), then a nitrogen side-dress about three to four weeks after planting as vines run, placed a few inches out from the plants and watered in, repeated lightly at flowering.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Mix a lower-nitrogen fertilizer or a few inches of compost into the soil before planting. Then feed with a little nitrogen about three to four weeks later, scratched into the soil a few inches away from the plants, and once more when flowers appear.

companions.note_seasoned: Most honeydew companion pairings are traditional rather than trial-tested, and the ones worth acting on serve two practical ends: pollination and pest pressure. Because honeydew fruit set is strongly pollinator-limited, flowering insectary plants like borage near the patch are a genuine help. A trap planting of nasturtium can divert cucumber beetles, which matters more here than for watermelon because those beetles spread bacterial wilt and melons are very susceptible to it. Bush beans fix a little nitrogen the crop can use without the heavy feeding that would grow vine over fruit. The firmest rule is a rotation one: keep honeydew away from other cucurbits, which share its pest and disease complex, including the soilborne Fusarium wilt and the foliar gummy stem blight that build up where melons follow melons.
companions.note_beginner: The most useful honeydew companions are flowers that bring in bees, since honeydew needs lots of bee visits to set fruit. Nasturtiums can lure cucumber beetles away, which is helpful because those beetles spread a wilt disease that melons catch easily. Bush beans add a little nitrogen. The one rule that really matters is to keep honeydew away from other melons, cucumbers, and squash, which all share the same pests and diseases.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Borage
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Borage flowers are loved by bees, and honeydew needs lots of bee visits to set fruit, so a few borage plants nearby can help with pollination.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A strong bee magnet whose flowers recruit the pollinators honeydew fruit set depends on, since each female flower needs many bee visits to set and size a melon. Pollinator-habitat value is well grounded; the specific borage-honeydew pairing is traditional rather than trial-tested.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Honeydew fruit set is pollinator-limited; flowering insectary plants like borage draw bees. Pairing is habitat-based, not pair-isolated.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Bush beans
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Beans pull nitrogen from the air into the soil, which honeydew can use, and they do not share honeydew's pests. A good, traditional neighbor.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Bush beans fix nitrogen that lightly benefits the crop without the heavy nitrogen that would push vine over fruit, and they share none of the cucurbit pests. A traditional, mechanistically plausible pairing rather than a trial-isolated one.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Legume nitrogen fixation is documented; the bean-melon adjacency benefit is traditional, not pair-isolated.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Nasturtium
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Nasturtiums are grown near melons to lure cucumber beetles away, which is extra useful for honeydew because those beetles spread a wilt disease melons catch easily. Their flowers also bring in bees.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Often planted near cucurbits as a trap and deterrent for cucumber beetles, which matters more for honeydew than for watermelon because the beetles transmit bacterial wilt, to which melons are very susceptible. Its flowers also draw the bees honeydew needs for fruit set. Trap cropping is a documented principle, but the specific nasturtium-honeydew effect is not formally isolated, so treat it as a plausible aid.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Trap-cropping for cucurbit beetles is documented in principle; the beetles vector bacterial wilt on melons; the nasturtium-honeydew pairing is not trial-isolated.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Corn
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Corn is the traditional Three Sisters partner that gives sprawling vines something to grow among. With honeydew it is more tradition than a proven boost, and honeydew's full-sun need means you should not let corn shade it.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: The classic Three Sisters partner, though the fit is looser for honeydew than for shade-tolerant squash: tall corn can give the trailing vines structure, but honeydew wants full sun and heat to sweeten, so keep corn from shading the patch. A long-standing intercropping tradition with a space rationale, not a measured yield effect for this pair.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Three Sisters intercropping is documented; the corn-melon benefit is spatial, not trial-isolated, and honeydew's full-sun need weakens the shade rationale.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Other cucurbits
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep honeydew away from other melons, cucumbers, and squash. They share most of the same pests and diseases, so planting them together makes those problems worse.
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Cucumber, cantaloupe, squash, and pumpkin share honeydew's pest and disease complex, including cucumber beetle and the bacterial wilt it carries, aphid-spread mosaic viruses, the mildews, and the soilborne Fusarium wilt and foliar gummy stem blight that build up where cucurbits repeat. Grouping them concentrates that pressure. A real epidemiology and rotation principle rather than a tested adjacency effect: spread cucurbits out and rotate them on a long cycle.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Shared cucurbit pests/pathogens (cucumber beetle plus its bacterial wilt, Fusarium wilt, gummy stem blight, mildews) are extension-documented; the bad-adjacency claim is a sound epidemiological principle, not pair-tested.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Potatoes
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Some gardeners keep potatoes and melons apart, since both are hungry plants and potatoes can bring their own diseases. This is more tradition than a proven rule.
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional caution that potatoes and cucurbits compete heavily and that potatoes can harbor disease and attract pests near melons. There is no strong T1 mechanism for the specific pairing, so it persists mostly as garden lore.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: A folk anti-companion caution; competition is plausible but there is no T1 source isolating a potato-melon antagonism.
