The wood gets hurt in the mid-20s°F, and the fruit is damaged around 26 to 28°F if it stays that cold a while, with the young wood and fruit hit first. Cover the tree for the night, and move a potted one under shelter. Watering the ground during the day gives it stored warmth to release overnight. Since grapefruit never goes dormant, frost can damage it any time it gets cold enough.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Extreme heat: guard your grapefruit against drop and sunburn
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Heat wave: protect your grapefruit
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Heat is the axis that makes grapefruit sweet, and the tree loves genuine desert heat, but extreme spikes still stress it: flowers and young fruit drop, and exposed fruit and bark sunburn. Increase irrigation through the heat event to keep the root zone supplied and buffer the canopy, and shade or wrap young trunks. In the low desert this is a recurring summer reality, and the long fruit hang means the tree faces many such spells before harvest.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Heat is what makes grapefruit sweet, and it likes hot weather, but a real heat wave can still stress the tree, dropping flowers and small fruit and sunburning exposed fruit and bark. Water more during the hot spell, and shade or wrap a young trunk so it does not sunburn. In desert areas this comes up all summer, and grapefruit hangs so long it rides out many hot spells before you pick.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Hot weather: hold off on horticultural oil
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Too hot to spray oil
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Horticultural and petroleum oil sprays, the backyard standard for scale, mites, and rust mite on citrus, can burn foliage and fruit when applied in high heat or to a drought-stressed tree. Do not spray oil above about 95°F or on a water-stressed tree. This caution is sharpest in the hot climates grapefruit prefers, where pest pressure and dangerous heat coincide. Wait for cooler conditions and water the tree first.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Horticultural or petroleum oil sprays are the usual way to deal with scale, mites, and rust mite on grapefruit, but they can burn the leaves and fruit if you spray in the heat or onto a thirsty, stressed tree. Keep oil for cooler conditions, below about 95°F, and water the tree first. This matters most in the hot areas grapefruit likes, where pests and dangerous heat show up together.

planting.text_seasoned: Plant with the graft union standing two to three inches clear of the finished soil and keep mulch pulled back from the trunk. A buried or mulch-packed union stays damp and is the classic entry point for foot rot.
planting.text_beginner: Plant so the graft bump sits a couple inches above the soil, and keep mulch off the trunk. A buried, damp union can rot.

planting.text_seasoned: Give a grapefruit room. It makes the largest of the common citrus trees, so allow generous spacing (extension guidance is a minimum of about 15 feet between citrus, and grapefruit sits at the roomy end of that) rather than crowding it against a wall or another tree.
planting.text_beginner: Leave a grapefruit plenty of space, since it grows into one of the biggest citrus trees. Do not crowd it against a wall or another tree; give it room to spread.

establishment.text_seasoned: Strip the first few years' fruit so the tree builds frame before it bears. Grapefruit carries a very long nine-to-thirteen-month crop, a heavy draw, and a young tree allowed to hold that load early grows slowly and stays structurally weak.
establishment.text_beginner: For the first two or three years, pick off the fruit. Grapefruit takes most of a year to ripen, which is a big load, so let the young tree grow strong first.

establishment.text_seasoned: Scout new flush for Asian citrus psyllid while the tree is small and easy to inspect. The psyllid spreads huanglongbing, which grapefruit succumbs to quickly, and it feeds and lays on tender new growth, so catching it early on a young tree matters most.
establishment.text_beginner: Check the new growth for tiny citrus psyllid insects while the tree is small. They spread a serious disease that hits grapefruit hard, and they go after fresh new leaves, so look them over often.

bloom.text_seasoned: Hold soil moisture steady through the roughly three-week spring bloom; drought stress now drops flowers and the young fruit behind them. That fruit will not be ripe for the better part of a year, so protecting the bloom protects a very long-term crop.
bloom.text_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist during the few weeks the tree flowers in spring. If it dries out, the flowers and tiny fruit drop, and that fruit takes almost a year to ripen.

bloom.text_seasoned: Grapefruit is self-fruitful and needs no pollination partner, so leave the flowering wood undisturbed and skip heavy pruning during and just after bloom. If seedlessness matters, keep low-seed varieties away from other pollen-heavy citrus, whose pollen can add seeds.
bloom.text_beginner: Grapefruit pollinates itself, so just leave the flowers and new fruit alone and do not do big pruning while it is flowering. If you want few seeds, keep it away from other citrus, whose pollen can add seeds.

fruit_set_development.text_seasoned: Water deeply and consistently across the long hang. Grapefruit develops over nine to thirteen months, and uneven moisture during that stretch shows up as splitting, pre-harvest drop, and dry granulated flesh, so a steady rhythm through summer heat is the priority.
fruit_set_development.text_beginner: Keep watering deeply and evenly through the long summer and fall. Grapefruit takes many months to grow, and uneven watering makes it split, drop, or go dry inside, so stay consistent.

fruit_set_development.text_seasoned: Treat the natural drop a few weeks after set as self-thinning, not a problem. The tree sheds more fruit than it can finish, and what stays sizes up better for it, so do not react by overwatering or overfeeding.
fruit_set_development.text_beginner: If the tree drops a lot of small fruit a few weeks after flowering, that is normal. It is keeping the fruit it can ripen well, so do not panic.

ripening_harvest.text_seasoned: Taste before you strip the tree, and taste again later. Grapefruit reaches legal maturity months before peak flavor and keeps sweetening on the tree as acid drops, so early fruit is tart and late fruit is best; let flavor, not rind color, call the harvest.
ripening_harvest.text_beginner: Taste a grapefruit before picking the whole tree, and taste again later in the season. It is edible but tart early and sweeter later, so try one first instead of judging by color.

ripening_harvest.text_seasoned: Leave ripe grapefruit on the tree and pick over months rather than all at once; the fruit stores itself outdoors and improves. In hot, dry desert, though, taste through the late season and pick before fruit granulates and dries inside.
ripening_harvest.text_beginner: You can leave ripe grapefruit on the tree and pick it over months, and it keeps getting better. In the hot, dry desert, taste now and then and pick before it dries out inside.

mature_bearing.text_seasoned: Keep pruning minimal on a bearing grapefruit: deadwood (which harbors melanose in humid climates), crossing limbs, and rootstock suckers from below the graft. Those suckers are the rootstock, not your grapefruit, and left to grow they sap vigor and can overrun the top.
mature_bearing.text_beginner: On a grown tree, prune lightly. Take out dead wood (it can spread a skin-spotting disease in humid areas) and any shoots from below the graft bump, since those come from the rootstock, not your grapefruit.

mature_bearing.text_seasoned: Expect alternate bearing and feed and water to even it out. Grapefruit swings between heavier and lighter crop years; steady fertility and consistent irrigation soften the swing, while a sharp unexplained drop points to a root, water, or disease problem worth chasing.
mature_bearing.text_beginner: Grapefruit often makes a big crop one year and a smaller one the next, which is normal. Steady feeding and watering helps even it out, but a sudden big drop means something is wrong to check.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A mature standard grapefruit is a heavy yielder, commonly bearing on the order of one hundred fifty to three hundred pounds of fruit per year under good conditions on a large tree, with the figure varying widely by variety, climate, tree size, and rootstock. Dwarf container trees yield far less but still produce a meaningful home crop.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: A full-grown grapefruit tree is a big producer, often bearing well over a hundred pounds of fruit a year in good conditions, though it depends on the variety, climate, and tree size. A small dwarf tree in a pot makes much less, but still plenty to enjoy.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Trees reach full production around the sixth to ninth year, a little later than quicker-ripening citrus because the crop hangs so long, and then bear heavily for decades. Grapefruit shows mild natural alternate bearing, with somewhat lighter and heavier crops in alternating years, which is normal.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: A grapefruit tree hits its full crop around six to nine years old, a bit later than some citrus because the fruit takes so long to ripen, and then produces well for decades. It is normal for the crop to be heavier some years and lighter others.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Strip any flowers that set in the first season so the tree puts its energy into roots and canopy framework rather than fruit. No crop is expected in year one anyway, and because grapefruit carries a long, heavy crop, letting a young tree hold fruit early slows establishment badly. Light bearing typically begins in year three or four, with a full crop building as the tree matures.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Young trees need their first-year energy in roots and branches, not fruit. Snap off any flowers that appear in the first season. Grapefruit carries a big crop for a long time, so a young tree holding fruit too early grows slowly. Fruit will start coming around year three or four, with a real crop building as the tree grows.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No university extension or peer-reviewed source supports timing grapefruit planting or care by moon phase. Citrus planting and management are driven by frost timing, soil temperature, and heat accumulation, not lunar cycles, so no moon-phase preference is assigned.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Fruit stays sour and never really sweetens even though the tree looks healthy
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The grapefruit is sour and never gets good even though the tree seems fine
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: This is grapefruit's defining failure mode and it is a climate limitation, not a care mistake. Grapefruit needs high accumulated summer heat over a long nine-to-thirteen-month season to burn off acid and build sugar. In cool coastal and fog-influenced climates the tree grows, blooms, and sets fruit, but heat is too low, so the fruit stays sharply acidic and poorly flavored regardless of feeding, watering, or patience, and may hang past a year without becoming good.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: This is the main thing that can go wrong with grapefruit, and it is about your climate, not anything you did. Grapefruit needs a lot of summer heat over a long season to turn sweet. In cool coastal or foggy areas the tree looks healthy and makes fruit, but there is not enough heat, so it stays sour no matter how well you care for it.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: There is no cultural fix for insufficient heat. If you are in a cool-coast climate, expect tart, poor fruit from standard grapefruit; the best options are a warmer microclimate against a south-facing heat-trapping wall, or growing a low-acid pummelo-grapefruit hybrid such as Oro Blanco, which eats sweet with less heat. In a heat-adequate climate, simply allow the full long hang, since grapefruit sweetens the longer it holds.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: There is no way to fix a lack of heat with watering or feeding. In a cool coastal area, expect standard grapefruit to be sour; a hot south-facing wall helps a little, and a sweet low-acid type like Oro Blanco is a better bet because it does not need as much heat. In a warm area, just give the fruit more time on the tree, since grapefruit keeps getting sweeter.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Heavy flower or young-fruit drop, often after a spring heat spike
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: A lot of flowers or little fruit fell off
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Some flower and post-set drop is the tree thinning itself and is expected, but heavy loss usually points to the root zone swinging between dry and waterlogged, a sudden spring heat spike into the 90s°F during or right after bloom, or nutrient stress through flowering. In hot-spring desert and interior climates this drop is a recurring challenge, and grapefruit holds its crop best on even moisture and steady feeding.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Losing a few flowers and tiny fruit is normal, but losing a lot usually means the watering bounced between too dry and too wet, a hot spell (into the 90s°F) struck during bloom, or the tree was underfed. This is common in hot-spring desert and inland areas.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Keep the watering even so the root zone neither bakes dry nor sits saturated, and bump it up during a heat spike to cushion the tree. Maintain steady citrus feeding from bloom through set. The weather is out of your hands, but consistent soil moisture is the single strongest lever against heat-spike drop.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Next time, keep the watering steady so the soil is neither bone dry nor soggy, and water extra during a hot spell while the tree is in bloom. Keep feeding through flowering. You cannot control the weather, but even soil moisture is the best thing you can do.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Fruit is dry, pithy, or granulated inside despite looking ripe outside
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The fruit looks ripe but is dry and pithy inside
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Granulation (juice vesicles drying and hardening) and general drying tend to appear in fruit left on the tree well past peak in hot, dry climates, which is a real risk for grapefruit precisely because its long on-tree hold tempts you to leave fruit for months. Over-mature fruit, late-season water stress, and intense heat with low humidity all contribute, and the rind can look perfectly normal while the interior loses quality.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Sometimes grapefruit that looks ripe outside is dry and pithy inside. This happens to fruit left on the tree too long in a hot, dry climate, which is easy to do because grapefruit hangs so well for months. Heat, dryness, and over-ripeness are the causes, and the skin can look fine even when the inside has dried out.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: In hot, dry climates, taste through the late season and harvest before granulation sets in rather than relying on the fullest hold, and keep late-season irrigation steady to limit water stress. The long hang is a feature, but it has a limit in the desert.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: In hot, dry areas, taste the fruit through late season and pick it before it dries out, instead of leaving it on for the maximum time, and keep watering steadily late in the season.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Sudden leaf drop and a thinning canopy
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The tree is dropping a lot of leaves
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Two common causes look different but both end in leaf drop. Cold injury follows a frost, with leaves wilting, browning, and dropping days afterward on an evergreen tree that never goes dormant, and grapefruit is slightly more frost-tender than orange. Overwatering and poor drainage are the other frequent culprit: saturated roots and incipient Phytophthora foot rot cause yellowing and drop, and the tell is leaves that wilt but do not recover after watering. Sustained heat stress can also force some defensive drop.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Two things often cause leaf drop. One is cold: after a frost, a grapefruit (which never goes dormant, and is a bit more cold-tender than an orange) can wilt and drop leaves a few days later. The other is too much water or poor drainage, which rots the roots and yellows the leaves, and the clue there is that watering makes it worse, not better. A long heat wave can also cause some leaf drop.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Distinguish the cause before acting. For cold, improve frost protection and wait until spring growth to prune damaged wood so you can see what survived. For overwatering, back off irrigation, confirm sharp drainage, and check that the graft union and crown are not buried. Treat heat-driven drop with steady irrigation through hot spells.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Figure out the cause first. If it was frost, protect the tree better next time and wait until spring to trim damaged branches. If it is overwatering, water less, make sure the soil drains fast, and check the graft knob is not buried. If it is heat, water steadily during hot weather.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Blemished rind: dull russeting, rough brown specks, or oily spotting
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The skin is marked with rusty, speckled, or oily blotches
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Grapefruit's smooth, thin, pale peel shows every rind blemish, and in the humid Southeast several cosmetic problems are common: dull tan or bronze russeting from citrus rust mite, small raised sandpaper-rough specks from melanose (a deadwood fungus), and oily-margined corky lesions from citrus canker. All three are cosmetic to the flesh (except canker at severe levels), and all are far worse in warm, wet, humid climates than in the arid West, where fruit is usually clean.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Grapefruit has smooth, pale skin, so any blemish shows. In humid areas like Florida and the Gulf, several harmless-looking skin problems are common: rusty or bronzed skin from a tiny mite, rough brown specks from a fungus called melanose, and oily corky spots from canker. The fruit inside is usually fine, and in dry desert areas the skin is usually clean.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Manage the underlying cause for cleaner fruit: prune out deadwood to cut melanose, preserve predatory mites to hold down rust mite, and follow canker guidance in regulated Gulf areas. Where russeting or spotting recurs in humid regions, a well-timed early-summer oil, sulfur, or copper program reduces it. In the arid West little or no action is needed.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: For cleaner skin, cut out dead wood (for melanose), avoid harsh sprays that kill the helpful mites (for the rust mite), and follow local guidance for canker. In humid areas, a well-timed oil, sulfur, or copper spray in early summer helps. In dry areas you usually do not need to do anything.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Yellowing leaves with green veins (iron or zinc chlorosis)
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Leaves turning yellow but the veins stay green
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Yellow leaves with a network of green veins, especially on new growth, signal a micronutrient deficiency, most often iron or zinc, common on alkaline, high-pH soils where these nutrients are present but chemically unavailable. This is widespread in desert and interior-West soils, exactly the hot regions where grapefruit otherwise thrives. It is distinct from the symmetric overall yellowing of nitrogen deficiency and from the asymmetric blotching of greening disease.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: When leaves turn yellow but the veins stay green, especially on new growth, the tree is short on a micronutrient, usually iron or zinc. This happens on alkaline (high-pH) soils, common in the desert and inland West, the very hot places grapefruit likes best. It looks different from an even all-over yellowing (usually nitrogen) and from the blotchy yellowing of citrus greening.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Correct with a chelated iron or zinc product, applied as a foliar spray for a quick response and to the soil for longer-term supply, and use a citrus fertilizer that includes micronutrients. Lowering soil pH toward slightly acidic over time with sulfur makes the existing nutrients available and is the durable fix on high-pH ground.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Fix it with a chelated iron or zinc product, sprayed on the leaves for a fast response and added to the soil for the long run, and use a citrus fertilizer that lists micronutrients. Over time, making the soil a little more acidic with sulfur helps the tree use the nutrients already there.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: Batch-2 Wave-3 REDO cert (2026-07-06, clean post-incident review, Trevor-ruled). 5 parallel READ-ONLY CC source-truth agents (WebFetch of cited T1 pages); main-loop applied fixes. Drug-interaction honesty HELD: furanocoumarin/CYP3A4 carried ONLY in open_finding_001 + this log, ABSENT from all consumer prose, no fabricated cite. Cold gradient verified verbatim (UGA C1307 least-hardy-of-three-main-classes + LSU AgCenter decreasing-hardiness ranking; fruit-freeze 26-28F = LSU 26F/2h + UGA 28F). Citrus canker anchor CORRECT (UF/IFAS CG040 'Grapefruit... highly susceptible', X. citri; HS132 + UC-IPM independently confirmed silent on canker). FIXES: G1 dropped the CG009 (Phytophthora guide) mis-anchor from Melanose (claim stands on HS132); G2 repointed Sooty mold to the UC IPM Sooty Mold Pest Notes (names sooty mold + honeydew from aphids/scale/whiteflies) and dropped the dead aggie-hort TAMU redirect loop. G3 (per-cell uga cold anchoring) = non-issue: region cells are modeled/empty by design (open_finding_003); the 26-28F band is anchored at crop level.

open_findings.summary: Grapefruit-drug interaction (furanocoumarin/CYP3A4 inhibition affecting statins, some blood-pressure, anti-anxiety, and transplant drugs) is a well-documented consumer-safety fact but was NOT asserted in consumer prose because no clean Tier-1 university-extension/.edu page could be read via WebFetch this session (searches surfaced FDA + medical-journal sources only; the FDA consumer page 404'd on fetch). Flagged per brief rather than asserted; certify session should source it from a T1/authoritative page and add an honest note.

Two key source pages could not be cleanly WebFetched: the Texas A&M AgriLife grapefruit page (aggie-hort.tamu.edu/citrus/grapefruit.htm) hit an http/https + host redirect loop, and the University of Arizona pages (extension.arizona.edu low-desert-citrus 403; AZ1925 grapefruit-pummelo is a 5.3MB scanned PDF not machine-readable). Their grapefruit claims (Texas variety history Ruby Red/Rio Red/Star Ruby/Duncan; desert 9-13 month ripening and long-hang sweetening) were corroborated via multiple WebSearch summaries but not read from a single clean page; confirm at certify.

Per-cell cold bands (min_winter_temp_f) and the heat_summer_basis verdicts were modeled from grapefruit's documented cold-hardiness rank (below sweet orange, wood damage mid-20s°F, fruit 26-28°F per LSU/UGA) and its documented high-heat need, applied to each region's climate, not from a grapefruit-specific per-region freeze/heat table. Edges are best-effort; tighten at variety-delta pass.

ca_north_coast modeled as survives_no_fruit/insufficient with an EMPTY calendar (a sharper call than navel orange's marginal), on the judgment that grapefruit's much higher heat requirement means the coolest CA coast produces no dependable edible crop. ca_south_coast kept marginal/marginal with a long-hang calendar. Confirm the coastal split against a CA-coast grapefruit source at review.

hawaii_tropical is lowest-confidence: modeled marginal/marginal (warm humid tropical lowland lacks the heat accumulation and day-night swing that sweetens grapefruit; pummelo does better), cited to UH CTAHR generally rather than a grapefruit-specific Hawaii calendar. Regional harvest windows across all 10 regions are modeled from the nearest readable citrus source plus grapefruit's long-hang biology, not a grapefruit-specific regional planting chart.

Pests/diseases and rootstock sourcing lean on citrus-general Tier-1 pages (uc_ipm citrus, uf_ifas_hs132/edis), re-tuned for grapefruit emphasis (rust mite russeting, melanose, greasy-spot and canker susceptibility, faster HLB decline; Swingle citrumelo / sour orange rootstock notes), rather than grapefruit-only trials. Companions are traditional/low-confidence citrus guild items plus the grounded grass-competition avoid. Rootstock recommendation (Swingle citrumelo) modeled from citrus-general guidance.

3.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 3 is too cold for an in-ground grapefruit. Winter lows pass the mid-20s°F tree-damage point and the 26 to 28°F fruit-freeze point every year, so there is no dependable crop and no establishment window.
3.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 3 is too cold for a grapefruit tree planted outside. There is no time of year when it would survive in the ground here.

4.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 4 is too cold for an in-ground grapefruit. Winter lows pass the mid-20s°F tree-damage point and the 26 to 28°F fruit-freeze point every year, so there is no dependable crop and no establishment window.
4.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 4 is too cold for a grapefruit tree planted outside. There is no time of year when it would survive in the ground here.

5.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 5 is too cold for a grapefruit tree planted outside. There is no time of year when it would survive in the ground here.

6.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 6 is too cold for a grapefruit tree planted outside. There is no time of year when it would survive in the ground here.

7.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 7 is too cold for a grapefruit tree planted outside. There is no time of year when it would survive in the ground here.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: You cannot grow a grapefruit tree in the ground in this region. People in cold areas grow citrus in pots and bring them inside for winter instead.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In-ground grapefruit is not viable in zones 3 through 7. Gardeners in these zones grow citrus in containers moved indoors for winter, which is a different growing system from the in-ground regional model here.
northern_tier.cold_basis_seasoned: Zones 3 through 7 drop well below the low-20s°F every winter, far past the mid-20s°F a grapefruit withstands and the 26 to 28°F at which the fruit freezes. An unprotected in-ground grapefruit does not survive here.
northern_tier.cold_basis_beginner: It gets too cold here for a grapefruit tree to live outside. Winters drop far below what the tree can take.
northern_tier.heat_basis_seasoned: Heat is moot here: the tree cannot survive the winter, so summer heat never gets the chance to matter.
northern_tier.heat_basis_beginner: Summer warmth does not matter here, because the tree cannot get through winter in the first place.

8.plant_out: Spring (container or balled; after hard-freeze risk passes)
8.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 8 grows grapefruit but on the cold edge: the tree is hardy here, yet winter lows reach the upper teens to mid-20s°F in colder years and the fruit freezes at 26 to 28°F, so the crop is at real risk in a hard freeze. Heat over the long season is ample; cold is the limiter.
8.suitability_note_beginner: You can grow grapefruit in zone 8, but cold is a gamble. The tree usually lives, but a hard freeze can damage or destroy the fruit, so some winters you lose the crop.
8.harvest: Nov - Apr (early fruit is tart; protect in a hard freeze)
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Hard advective freezes into the upper teens°F occur every few years in zone 8; both fruit and young trees need cold protection on those nights.

9.plant_out: Most of the year (container or balled; spring ideal)
9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 fruits reliably: mild Gulf and Southeastern winters rarely hold below the mid-20s°F long enough to take the crop, and long hot summers bank plenty of heat to sweeten grapefruit over its long hang. Cold protection is an occasional need, not a routine one.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Grapefruit does well in zone 9. Winters are mild enough that you usually keep your fruit, and summers are plenty hot to make it sweet over its long season.
9.harvest: Nov - May (holds and sweetens on the tree into spring)
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Zone 9 across the Gulf is mostly safe for grapefruit, but hard freezes occur in some winters; below about 27°F can damage ripe fruit and scorch young growth. Keep frost cloth ready for the tree's first few winters while it is small.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: Grapefruit does well here, ripening from about November into spring. In the colder part of this area a hard freeze can cost you the fruit some years, and the humid weather can blemish the skin.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: Grapefruit is a strong Southeastern citrus, ripening over a long window from roughly November into spring. The colder northern zone of this band carries real freeze risk to the crop; the warmer zone fruits dependably. Humid conditions favor cosmetic rind diseases.
se_gulf.cold_basis_seasoned: Across the Southeast and Gulf, a mature grapefruit is hardy into the mid-20s°F, but the fruit freezes at 26 to 28°F and hard advective freezes into the upper teens reach the colder northern edge every few years. Cold sets the survival ceiling; heat does not limit quality, though grapefruit is a touch more freeze-tender than sweet orange.
se_gulf.cold_basis_beginner: A grown grapefruit here handles a light freeze, but the fruit is damaged below about 28°F, and a hard freeze every few winters can hurt the tree in the colder parts of this area.
se_gulf.heat_basis_seasoned: Long, hot, humid Southeastern summers bank plenty of heat to sweeten grapefruit over its long hang, so heat is not the limiting factor. The humid climate does favor rind-blemish diseases (greasy spot, melanose, canker) and rust-mite russeting.
se_gulf.heat_basis_beginner: Summers here are plenty hot for sweet grapefruit. The main downside of the humid weather is more skin-blemish problems on the fruit.

8.plant_out: Spring (container or balled; after frost risk eases)
8.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 8 in the valley has the heat for excellent grapefruit but sits on the cold edge: radiation frosts reach the upper 20s to low-20s°F in colder years, and the fruit freezes at 26 to 28°F, so a hard frost can take the crop. Heat is high; cold is the limiter.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 8 has plenty of summer heat for sweet grapefruit, but it is the cold edge of the valley. A hard frost can damage the fruit some winters, so protection helps.
8.harvest: Jan - May (sweetens through the long cool spring; protect in a hard frost)
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Radiation frosts into the low-to-mid 20s°F occur in colder valley winters; fruit and young trees need protection on those nights.

9.plant_out: Most of the year (container or balled; spring ideal)
9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 in the interior valley fruits reliably: strong summer heat sweetens grapefruit over its long hang, and winters rarely hold below the mid-20s°F long enough to take the crop. Fruit ripens later than in the low desert and holds into spring.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Grapefruit fruits reliably in zone 9 of the hot valley. Summers are hot enough to sweeten it, and it holds and improves on the tree into spring.
9.harvest: Dec - May (holds and sweetens on the tree into spring)
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Most zone 9 valley winters are mild enough for grapefruit, but occasional hard frosts occur; keep frost protection ready for young trees.

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: Grapefruit does well in the hot interior valley, ripening a bit later and holding into spring. In the coldest part a hard frost can hurt the fruit some years.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: Grapefruit fruits well in the hot interior valley where cold does not take the crop, ripening later than desert fruit and holding into spring. The cold-edge zone carries freeze risk in harder winters.
ca_interior.cold_basis_seasoned: The interior valley has the summer heat for excellent grapefruit but sits on the cold edge: radiation frosts reach the upper 20s to low-20s°F in colder years, and the fruit freezes at 26 to 28°F, so a hard frost can take the crop. Grapefruit is a touch more freeze-tender than sweet orange.
ca_interior.cold_basis_beginner: A grown grapefruit here handles a light frost, but the fruit is damaged below about 28°F, and a hard frost some winters can hurt the crop.
ca_interior.heat_basis_seasoned: The hot, dry interior valley banks strong summer heat over grapefruit's long hang, giving good sweetening; heat is not the limiter here, cold is. Fruit ripens later than in the low desert, holding into spring.
ca_interior.heat_basis_beginner: Interior valley summers are hot enough for sweet grapefruit. It just ripens later, holding into spring.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 on the cool north coast is frost-safe for the tree but far too cool in summer for grapefruit, which needs high accumulated heat over a long season. The tree survives and blooms, but fruit stays sharply acidic and never reaches good eating quality, so there is no dependable edible crop.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 9 on the cool north coast does not get hot enough for grapefruit. The tree lives and even flowers, but the fruit stays sour and never really ripens, so you cannot count on a usable crop.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 10 on the cool north coast is frost-safe for the tree but far too cool in summer for grapefruit, which needs high accumulated heat over a long season. The tree survives and blooms, but fruit stays sharply acidic and never reaches good eating quality, so there is no dependable edible crop.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 10 on the cool north coast does not get hot enough for grapefruit. The tree lives and even flowers, but the fruit stays sour and never really ripens, so you cannot count on a usable crop.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: Grapefruit will not really work on the cool north coast: the tree lives but the fruit stays sour because it is not hot enough. If you want to try, a sweet low-acid type like Oro Blanco is the best bet, and even that is a stretch.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: The cool north coast is frost-safe but far too cool in summer for grapefruit. Trees survive and bloom, but standard grapefruit will not ripen an edible crop here; a sweet low-acid pummelo hybrid like Oro Blanco is the only citrus in this family worth trying, and even it is marginal.
ca_north_coast.cold_basis_seasoned: The north coast is essentially frost-safe for grapefruit; winter lows rarely threaten the tree or fruit. Cold is not the limiter here, heat is.
ca_north_coast.cold_basis_beginner: Winters on the north coast are mild, so cold is not the problem for grapefruit here. The problem is a lack of summer heat.
ca_north_coast.heat_basis_seasoned: Cool, fog-influenced north-coast summers do not bank the heat grapefruit needs. The tree survives and blooms, but fruit stays acidic and never sweetens, so this is a no-usable-crop region for grapefruit, the sharpest expression of grapefruit's high heat requirement.
ca_north_coast.heat_basis_beginner: The cool, foggy north coast never gets hot enough for grapefruit to ripen. The tree lives but the fruit stays sour.

9.plant_out: Most of the year (container or balled; spring ideal)
9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 on the south coast is frost-safe but only marginally hot for grapefruit; fruit ripens slowly over an extra-long hang and often stays tart, better inland or with a low-acid hybrid.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 9 on the south coast rarely freezes, but it is only marginally hot enough for grapefruit, so the fruit ripens slowly and can stay tart.
9.harvest: Feb - Jun (ripens slowly in the mild coast; often stays tart)
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rare in south-coast zone 9; cold is not the concern, marginal heat is.

10.plant_out: Most of the year (container or balled; spring ideal)
10.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 10 on the south coast is essentially frost-free but only marginally hot for grapefruit; fruit ripens slowly and often stays tart, so a low-acid hybrid is the better choice.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 10 on the south coast almost never freezes, but it is only marginally hot enough for grapefruit, so the fruit ripens slowly and can stay tart.
10.harvest: Feb - Jun (ripens slowly in the mild coast; often stays tart)
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: The immediate coast in zone 10 is nearly frost-free; heat, not cold, is the limiter.

ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: Grapefruit is a stretch on the south coast. The tree is safe from frost, but the fruit ripens slowly and can stay tart. It does better a bit inland, and a sweet low-acid type like Oro Blanco is a smarter pick than a standard red grapefruit.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: Grapefruit is marginal on the south coast: frost-safe but heat-limited, so fruit ripens slowly over an extra-long hang and often stays tart. It does better inland from the coast and with a low-acid hybrid; standard red grapefruit rarely matches desert quality here.
ca_south_coast.cold_basis_seasoned: The south coast is frost-safe to nearly frost-free for grapefruit; the tree and fruit are rarely threatened by cold. Heat, not cold, sets the limit.
ca_south_coast.cold_basis_beginner: Winters on the south coast are mild, so cold is not the problem. The issue is whether it gets hot enough.
ca_south_coast.heat_basis_seasoned: Mild south-coast summers bank only marginal heat for grapefruit, more than the north coast but well short of the desert. Fruit ripens very slowly over an extra-long hang and can reach acceptable but often tart quality, best inland from the immediate coast; a low-acid hybrid like Oro Blanco does better.
ca_south_coast.heat_basis_beginner: The south coast is warmer than the north coast but still on the cool side for grapefruit. The fruit ripens very slowly and can be edible but tart, better a bit inland. A sweet low-acid type like Oro Blanco does better.

9.plant_out: Fall or spring (container or balled; avoid mid-summer planting stress)
9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 in the low desert fruits reliably and superbly: intense summer heat over a long season ripens deeply sweet, low-acid red grapefruit. Occasional hard frosts into the upper 20s°F are the main risk to young trees and fruit.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Grapefruit is excellent in desert zone 9. The intense heat makes it deeply sweet over a long season. The main risk is an occasional hard frost on young trees and fruit.
9.harvest: Dec - May (best Mar to May; holds and sweetens on the tree)
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Sharp radiation frosts into the upper 20s to low-20s°F occur in colder desert winters; protect young trees and hanging fruit on those nights.

10.plant_out: Fall or spring (container or balled; avoid mid-summer planting stress)
10.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 10 in the low desert fruits reliably and superbly: sustained intense heat ripens deeply sweet red grapefruit over a long season, with fruit best late in the season. Cold is only an occasional concern.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Grapefruit is excellent in desert zone 10. The heat makes it deeply sweet, best late in the season. Cold is rarely a problem.
10.harvest: Dec - May (best Mar to May; holds and sweetens on the tree)
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Hard frosts are infrequent in zone 10 desert but do occur; protect young trees on the coldest nights.

ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: The California desert is one of the best places for grapefruit. Intense heat makes it deeply sweet, and it holds on the tree and gets better into spring. The only real risk is an occasional hard frost on the coldest nights.
ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: The California low desert (Coachella and similar) is premier grapefruit country: intense heat over a long season ripens deeply sweet red fruit that holds and improves into spring. Occasional hard radiation frosts are the only real risk, mainly to young trees and hanging fruit.
ca_desert.cold_basis_seasoned: The low desert is hot but can see sharp radiation frosts in colder winters, reaching the upper 20s to low-20s°F, and grapefruit fruit freezes at 26 to 28°F, so young trees and fruit need protection on the coldest nights even here.
ca_desert.cold_basis_beginner: The desert is hot, but a cold night can still drop into the 20s°F, so protect young trees and fruit on the coldest nights.
ca_desert.heat_basis_seasoned: The low desert delivers exactly what grapefruit wants: intense, sustained summer heat over a long season that ripens deeply sweet, low-acid red fruit. This is premier grapefruit country; fruit is often at its best late in the season, March through May.
ca_desert.heat_basis_beginner: The hot desert is the best place for grapefruit. The long, intense heat makes the fruit deeply sweet, and it is often best late in the season, around March through May.

8.plant_out: Spring (container or balled; after hard-freeze risk passes)
8.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 8 warm arid has the summer heat for good grapefruit but hard winter freezes into the upper teens to mid-20s°F threaten the fruit and young trees, so cold is the limiter. Grapefruit is a touch more freeze-tender than sweet orange.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 8 here is hot enough in summer for grapefruit, but hard winter freezes can damage the fruit and young trees, so it is a gamble without protection.
8.harvest: Dec - Apr (protect fruit and young trees in a hard freeze)
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Hard advective freezes into the upper teens to low-20s°F occur in warm-arid zone 8 winters; fruit and young trees need protection, or grow in a movable container.

warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: Grapefruit gets enough summer heat in this warm, dry area, but the cold winters make it a gamble. Protect it from hard freezes, or grow it in a pot you can move under cover.
warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: In the warm arid interior, grapefruit gets ample summer heat but faces zone 8 hard freezes that threaten fruit and young trees, making it a marginal, cold-limited crop best grown with freeze protection or as a movable container tree.
warm_arid.cold_basis_seasoned: The warm arid interior is hot in summer but its zone 8 winters bring hard freezes into the upper teens to mid-20s°F, past the grapefruit fruit-freeze point and into tree-damage range, so cold, not heat, limits the crop here.
warm_arid.cold_basis_beginner: This warm, dry area has hot summers but its winters get cold enough (into the teens and 20s°F) to hurt grapefruit fruit and trees, so cold is the problem.
warm_arid.heat_basis_seasoned: Hot, dry summers bank adequate to strong heat for grapefruit over its long hang, so heat is not the limiter here; the shorter, colder winter is. Fruit ripens through winter into spring where the tree escapes hard freezes.
warm_arid.heat_basis_beginner: Summers here are hot enough for good grapefruit. The problem is the cold winters, not the heat.

9.plant_out: Fall or spring (container or balled; avoid mid-summer planting stress)
9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 in the Arizona low desert fruits reliably and superbly: intense sustained heat over a long season ripens deeply sweet, low-acid red grapefruit. The coldest winter nights near freezing are the only real risk, mainly to young trees and fruit.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Grapefruit is excellent in Arizona desert zone 9. The intense heat makes it deeply sweet over a long season. Just protect young trees and fruit on the coldest nights.
9.harvest: Dec - May (best Mar to May; holds and sweetens on the tree)
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: The coldest low-desert nights can reach the upper 20s to low-30s°F; protect young trees and hanging fruit on hard-freeze nights.

low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: The Arizona desert is one of the best places for grapefruit. Intense heat makes it deeply sweet, and it holds on the tree into spring. Just protect it on the occasional cold night.
low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: The Arizona low desert is premier grapefruit country: intense heat ripens deeply sweet red grapefruit over a long season, with fruit holding and improving into spring. Occasional cold nights are the only real risk.
low_desert_az.cold_basis_seasoned: The Arizona low desert is hot but can drop into the upper 20s to low-30s°F on the coldest winter nights; grapefruit fruit freezes at 26 to 28°F, so protection is occasionally needed for young trees and hanging fruit.
low_desert_az.cold_basis_beginner: The Arizona desert is hot, but the coldest winter nights can dip near freezing, so protect young trees and fruit then.
low_desert_az.heat_basis_seasoned: The Arizona low desert (Phoenix, Yuma) delivers the intense, sustained heat grapefruit needs over a long season, ripening deeply sweet, low-acid red fruit that holds on the tree and is often best March through May. This is premier grapefruit country.
low_desert_az.heat_basis_beginner: The Arizona desert is one of the best places for grapefruit. The intense heat makes it deeply sweet over a long season, and it is often best late, around March through May.

10.plant_out: Most of the year (container or balled; spring ideal)
10.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 10 in peninsular Florida fruits reliably: warm humid summers bank ample heat over grapefruit's long hang and winters rarely threaten the crop. Rind-blemish diseases are the main quality concern, not cold.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Grapefruit fruits reliably in Florida zone 10. It is warm enough to ripen well, and cold is rarely a problem. The humid weather can blemish the skin.
10.harvest: Nov - May (early fruit tart; holds and sweetens into spring)
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rare in zone 10 peninsular Florida; cold is not the concern, humid-climate rind diseases are.

11.plant_out: Most of the year (container or balled; spring ideal)
11.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 11 in south Florida is essentially frost-free and fruits reliably; ample heat ripens grapefruit over a long window, with humid-climate rind diseases the main quality issue.
11.suitability_note_beginner: Grapefruit fruits reliably in south Florida zone 11, which almost never freezes. The humid weather can blemish the skin, but the fruit ripens well.
11.harvest: Nov - May (early fruit tart; holds and sweetens into spring)
11.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Zone 11 south Florida is essentially frost-free; cold is not a concern.

fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: Central and south Florida are classic grapefruit country, warm and frost-safe, ripening from about November into spring. The humid weather just means more skin blemishes on the fruit.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: The Florida peninsula is historic grapefruit country: warm, humid, and frost-safe, ripening grapefruit over a long window from roughly November into spring. Heat is ample; the trade-off is more cosmetic rind disease in the humid climate.
fl_peninsula.cold_basis_seasoned: The Florida peninsula is warm to nearly frost-free; winter cold rarely threatens grapefruit, and the warm, humid climate suits the tree well.
fl_peninsula.cold_basis_beginner: Central and south Florida rarely get cold enough to hurt grapefruit. The warm, humid climate suits it.
fl_peninsula.heat_basis_seasoned: Warm, humid peninsular summers bank ample heat to ripen grapefruit over its long hang, and Florida is historically the heart of grapefruit country. The humid climate does favor rind-blemish diseases (greasy spot, melanose, canker) and rust-mite russeting, so fruit cosmetics need more attention than in the arid West.
fl_peninsula.heat_basis_beginner: Florida is warm enough for grapefruit to ripen well; it is classic grapefruit country. The humid weather just means more skin-blemish problems on the fruit.

11.plant_out: Most of the year (container or balled)
11.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 11 tropical Hawaii is frost-free but only marginally suited: even year-round warmth without a strong heat peak or cool nights gives variable, often tart grapefruit. Best in the hottest, driest leeward lowlands.
11.suitability_note_beginner: Grapefruit grows easily in Hawaii and never freezes, but the fruit is often tart because it lacks the intense heat and cool nights that sweeten it. It does best in the hottest, driest areas.
11.harvest: Nov - Mar (leeward lowland fruit stays green-tinged and often tart)
11.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is not a factor in tropical Hawaii; heat-quality, not cold, limits grapefruit here.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: Grapefruit is a marginal choice in Hawaii. It grows easily and never freezes, but the fruit is often tart because the climate lacks the intense heat and cool nights that sweeten it. Pummelo does better.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: Grapefruit is marginal in tropical Hawaiian lowlands: frost-free and evergreen, but the even tropical warmth without a strong heat peak or cool nights gives variable, often tart fruit. Best in the hottest, driest leeward lowlands; pummelo relatives are the more reliable Citrus grandis-type choice.
hawaii_tropical.cold_basis_seasoned: Tropical Hawaii is frost-free; cold never threatens grapefruit, so the tree is limited by heat accumulation quality, not survival.
hawaii_tropical.cold_basis_beginner: Hawaii never freezes, so cold is not an issue for grapefruit at all.
hawaii_tropical.heat_basis_seasoned: Warm, humid tropical lowlands stay warm year-round but lack the intense heat accumulation and cool-night contrast that sweetens grapefruit in desert and subtropical climates, so fruit quality is variable and often tart; pummelo and pummelo hybrids generally do better in Hawaii.
hawaii_tropical.heat_basis_beginner: Hawaii is warm all year, but it does not get the intense heat and cool nights that make grapefruit really sweet, so the fruit is often tart. Pummelo and its hybrids usually do better there.

crops.description_seasoned: Grapefruit (Citrus x paradisi) is a large, vigorous evergreen citrus tree, an 18th-century Caribbean hybrid of pummelo and sweet orange grown for its big, tart-to-sweet breakfast fruit. Its defining trait for a gardener is a high heat requirement paired with a very long ripening season: the fruit hangs and develops for roughly nine to thirteen months, and only a long, hot season banks enough heat to burn off acid and build sugar. This makes grapefruit a hot-region crop. It reaches its best in the low desert of Arizona and California, the Texas Rio Grande Valley, and peninsular Florida, where fruit sweetens through winter into spring. In cool coastal California the tree survives and blooms but the fruit stays acidic, poorly flavored, or never truly ripens, because heat accumulation is too low. Grapefruit is self-fruitful, so a single tree bears a full crop, and it makes one of the largest and longest-lived citrus trees in the yard.
crops.description_beginner: Grapefruit is a big evergreen citrus tree that grows the large, tangy fruit you eat for breakfast. The two things that shape where it does well are heat and time: grapefruit needs a lot of summer heat and a very long season, because the fruit takes roughly nine to thirteen months to ripen and only a long, hot season makes it sweet instead of sour. That is why grapefruit is at its best in hot places like the Arizona and California desert, South Texas, and Florida, where it sweetens through the winter into spring. In cool coastal areas the tree lives and flowers, but the fruit stays sour and never really ripens because there is not enough heat. One tree makes fruit on its own, with no second tree needed, and it grows into one of the biggest, longest-lived citrus trees you can plant.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Harvest grapefruit by taste, not color, and expect a long, forgiving window. The fruit reaches legal maturity months before it is at its best: in the desert and South Texas it can be picked from December but is usually sweeter and less acidic from March through May, after a long hang drops the acid. Rind color is a poor guide, since fruit can be green-tinged yet ripe early in the season and gold later. Taste-test a fruit to judge readiness. Grapefruit holds on the tree for months and keeps improving, so pick over an extended period rather than all at once. The exceptions are that fruit left far past peak in hot, dry desert can dry inside, and in cool coastal climates the fruit may never reach good eating quality at all.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Pick grapefruit by taste, not by color, and know that there is no rush. The fruit is ready to eat months before it is at its best: in hot areas you can start picking in December, but it is usually sweeter around March through May after hanging longer and losing some tartness. The skin color fools you, since fruit can look a little green but be ready early, or turn gold later. So taste one to decide. Grapefruit keeps on the tree for months and gets better, so pick a few at a time. Two cautions: fruit left on far too long in the hot, dry desert can dry out inside, and in cool coastal areas the fruit may never get truly good.
crops.bloom_time_seasoned: Grapefruit blooms in spring, typically March through May depending on climate and zone, with fragrant white flowers for about three weeks. The fruit then develops very slowly, roughly nine to thirteen months, so the crop from a spring bloom is harvested the following winter into spring, and late fruit can still be hanging as the next bloom opens. In the low desert and South Texas the main harvest runs December into May; in Florida it runs roughly November into May; in cool-summer coastal California the tree blooms on schedule but rarely ripens quality fruit.
crops.bloom_time_beginner: Grapefruit blooms in spring, usually March through May depending on where you live, with sweet-smelling white flowers for about three weeks. The fruit then grows very slowly, about nine to thirteen months, so a spring bloom is harvested the next winter and spring, and some fruit is still on the tree when it flowers again. In the hot desert and South Texas the main picking is December into May; in Florida it is about November into May; in cool coastal California the tree flowers but rarely makes good fruit.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Grapefruit is one of the more cold-tender of the common citrus, ranking just below sweet orange and above lemons and limes; extension cold-hardiness lists place it as the least hardy of the three main classes (mandarins, sweet oranges, grapefruit). Tree wood is injured in the mid-20s°F, similar to sweet orange, and the fruit is damaged at about 26 to 28°F sustained for a couple of hours, though the large fruit takes somewhat longer than an orange to freeze through. Trees are evergreen with no dormancy, so growing tissue is always vulnerable to frost, and young trees and hanging fruit are the most sensitive. Beyond cold, grapefruit also needs high accumulated summer heat to ripen good fruit, so the practical range is narrower than the survival range: roughly zones 9 through 11 with a long, hot season.
crops.hardiness_notes_beginner: Grapefruit is a little more cold-tender than a sweet orange, and less hardy than mandarins; it is one of the more frost-sensitive common citrus, ahead of only lemons and limes. The wood is hurt in the mid-20s°F, and the fruit is damaged around 26 to 28°F if it stays that cold for a couple of hours, though the big fruit freezes a bit slower than an orange. Because the tree is evergreen and never goes dormant, frost can hurt it any time it gets cold enough, and young trees and ripening fruit are the most tender. On top of cold, grapefruit needs a lot of summer heat to make good fruit, so it really only thrives in hot regions, roughly zones 9 to 11.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Grapefruit requires no winter chilling to flower or fruit. It is evergreen and does not enter a chill-triggered dormancy; flowering is driven by spring warming and moisture rather than release from a cold period. What grapefruit needs instead is the opposite, high accumulated summer HEAT over a long season to ripen sweet fruit. This distinguishes citrus from deciduous fruit trees such as peaches and apples, which require hundreds of chill hours to break bud dormancy and set a crop.
crops.chill_hours_note_beginner: Grapefruit does not need any winter chill to flower or fruit. Unlike peaches and apples, which need hundreds of cold hours in winter to wake up and set a crop, citrus is evergreen and blooms from spring warmth instead. What grapefruit needs is the reverse: a lot of summer heat over a long season to ripen sweet fruit. So chill hours, which matter for deciduous fruit trees, do not apply to grapefruit.
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Grapefruit is self-fruitful: a single tree sets a full crop, and extension guidance is that one grapefruit tree suffices with no pollinizer needed. Unlike the seedless-by-sterility navel orange, grapefruit produces viable pollen, and seed content is a variety trait. White Marsh and the red sports (Ruby Red, Rio Red, Star Ruby) are low-seeded to nearly seedless when isolated, while old Duncan is very seedy. Bees moving pollen from a nearby seed-bearing citrus can raise the seed count in an otherwise low-seed variety, so isolation from other pollen-heavy citrus helps keep low-seed grapefruit low-seed.
crops.pollinator_notes_beginner: A grapefruit tree makes fruit all by itself, so you only need one and do not need bees or a second tree for it to bear. It is not seedless the way a navel orange is; how many seeds you get depends on the variety. White Marsh and the red types (Ruby Red, Rio Red, Star Ruby) have few or no seeds when grown apart from other citrus, while the old Duncan is full of seeds. If bees carry pollen from another nearby citrus into the flowers, a low-seed grapefruit can end up with more seeds, so keeping it away from other citrus helps keep the seeds down.

pollination.notes_seasoned: Grapefruit is self-fruitful and a single tree bears a full crop; UF/IFAS home-citrus guidance notes that one grapefruit tree suffices. It is not parthenocarpic like the navel orange; it produces viable pollen, and seediness is a variety trait (Marsh and the red sports are low-seeded to seedless when isolated; Duncan is very seedy). Cross-pollination by bees from nearby seed-bearing citrus can add seeds to a low-seed variety, so isolating low-seed grapefruit from other pollen-heavy citrus helps preserve low seed count. No pollinizer tree is required.
pollination.notes_beginner: Grapefruit makes fruit on its own, so one tree is all you need and no second tree or special pollinator is required. It is not seedless the way a navel orange is; whether you get seeds depends on the variety. If bees bring pollen from another citrus tree nearby, a low-seed grapefruit can pick up more seeds, so keeping it apart from other citrus helps keep the seeds down.

pruning_window.note_seasoned: Grapefruit needs only light shaping, not the structural pruning of deciduous fruit trees. Remove dead, crossing, or weak wood in spring after the main harvest, and strip any shoots emerging below the graft union, since those are rootstock growth that will not produce grapefruit and will sap the tree. Keep the canopy open enough for light and air, but heavy heading cuts are unnecessary and cost the next crop; the fruit hangs many months, so avoid pruning off fruiting wood carrying next season's crop.
pruning_window.note_beginner: Grapefruit needs only light pruning, not the heavy cutting that peaches and apples get. In spring after harvest, trim out any dead, crossing, or weak branches, and pull off any shoots growing from below the graft knob low on the trunk, since those come from the rootstock and will never make grapefruit (and they steal energy). Keep the canopy open enough for light and air, but do not cut it back hard, since heavy cutting just reduces next year's fruit.

crops.establishment_note: Grapefruit typically begins bearing in the third or fourth year after planting a grafted nursery tree. Because the fruit hangs and ripens over the better part of a year, full production builds a little later than in quicker-ripening citrus, generally reached by year six to nine depending on rootstock and growing conditions.
crops.recommended_rootstock_note: Grapefruit grows vigorously and yields well on Swingle citrumelo, which resists Phytophthora and citrus nematode and tolerates the tristeza virus that killed off the once-standard sour orange rootstock for grapefruit. Sour orange still produces excellent grapefruit where tristeza is not a threat. For containers or small spaces, Flying Dragon trifoliate makes a dwarf tree. Ask the nursery which rootstock the tree is on and match it to your soil, since Swingle and trifoliate types dislike high-pH, calcareous, or saline soils common in the desert.

rootstock_options.name: Carrizo citrange
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask for a certified disease-free tree on Carrizo citrange. Confirm your soil is not highly alkaline or saline, as Carrizo is sensitive to both conditions.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: The standard rootstock for sweet oranges in California and the most common commercial choice. Resistant to Phytophthora root rot and tolerant of citrus tristeza virus. Produces vigorous, upright trees with good early bearing and excellent internal fruit quality. Not adapted to calcareous, highly alkaline, or saline soils. Cold tolerance is moderate, less than trifoliate types but adequate in zones 9 through 11.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: Carrizo citrange is the most common rootstock for sweet oranges in California and a reliable all-around choice. It resists the root rot that threatens citrus, handles a common citrus virus, and grows a vigorous full-size tree that bears early with good-quality fruit. Its one weakness is that it does not like very alkaline or salty soil, so it is less ideal in some desert areas.

rootstock_options.name: Swingle citrumelo
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask for Swingle citrumelo rootstock. It handles wet soils better than Carrizo but may not perform well in alkaline or calcareous conditions.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: A grapefruit and trifoliate orange hybrid widely used in Florida and the Gulf Coast. Excellent Phytophthora resistance, good cold hardiness among standard rootstocks, and tristeza tolerant. Produces slightly smaller trees than Carrizo with good fruit quality. Not well adapted to calcareous or high-pH soils. A strong general-purpose choice for the Southeast and Gulf regions.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: Swingle citrumelo is a tough rootstock widely used in Florida and along the Gulf Coast. It strongly resists root rot, handles wet soils better than most, and has decent cold hardiness. It makes a slightly smaller tree than Carrizo with good fruit, and is a good pick in humid, wetter regions.

rootstock_options.name: Flying Dragon trifoliate
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask specifically for Flying Dragon rootstock (a dwarfing selection of trifoliate orange). The compact tree size makes frost protection easier and fits container growing or small yards.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: A naturally dwarfing mutation of Poncirus trifoliata that produces very compact trees well suited to containers and small home gardens. Offers the best cold hardiness of any widely available citrus rootstock. Excellent resistance to Phytophthora, citrus nematode, and tristeza virus. Sensitive to high-pH and saline soils. Fruit quality is good and trees are precocious, though total yield per tree is lower due to small canopy size.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: Flying Dragon is a special dwarfing rootstock that keeps the tree small, which makes it perfect for pots and small yards, and it is the key to growing oranges in cold climates since you can move the pot under cover for winter. It also has the best cold hardiness of the common citrus rootstocks and strongly resists root rot. The tradeoff is simply a smaller tree with a smaller crop, which is usually exactly what a container or small-space grower wants.

pet_safe.note: The fruit is fine, but the peel, leaves, and citrus oils can upset the stomach of cats, dogs, and horses.

crops.name: Cherry (Sweet)

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Sweet cherry wants a deep, fertile soil that drains fast. Good drainage is the rule you cannot bend: cherry roots are very sensitive to wet feet and to the root and crown rots that follow soggy ground, and standing water also invites bacterial canker. A loam or sandy loam is ideal. Heavy clay that holds water is the trouble spot; if that is your soil, plant on a raised mound and choose a rootstock that tolerates heavier ground (Mazzard or Gisela 6). A near-neutral soil with some compost worked in suits it well.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Sweet cherry demands a deep, well-drained, fertile loam; drainage is the non-negotiable, since cherry roots will not tolerate wet feet and waterlogged ground brings on root and crown rot and predisposes the tree to bacterial canker. A loam or sandy loam is well suited; heavy, water-holding clay is the problem texture. On clay, plant on a raised berm and pair the tree with a heavier-soil-tolerant rootstock (Mazzard, Gisela 6, or Colt) rather than the drainage-fussy Mahaleb. Moderate fertility with modest organic matter is ideal.

ph.note_beginner: Sweet cherry grows best in a near-neutral soil, around pH 6.5 to 7.0, and is fine from about 6.0 to 7.5 (pH just measures how acidic or alkaline the soil is). Test your soil before planting and adjust slowly if needed: garden lime raises the pH if the soil is too acidic, and elemental sulfur lowers it if it is too alkaline. Mix any of this in before you plant, because pH changes slowly and is far easier to fix before the permanent tree goes in.
ph.note_seasoned: Sweet cherry does best in a near-neutral soil, roughly pH 6.5 to 7.0, and tolerates about 6.0 to 7.5. Test the soil before planting and adjust gradually if needed: lime raises a too-acidic pH, elemental sulfur lowers one that is too alkaline. Work amendments in ahead of planting, since pH shifts slowly and is far easier to correct before the permanent tree is in the ground.

fertilizer.timing: early spring before bud break
fertilizer.example_product: 10-10-10 balanced fertilizer
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Feed lightly in early spring before growth begins, broadcasting evenly around the root zone out to the drip line, off the trunk, and watering it in. Sweet cherry needs less nitrogen than peach: aim for about 8 to 12 inches of new shoot growth a year on a bearing tree, and ease off if it makes more. Never feed late in the season, since late nitrogen pushes soft growth that winter cold injures, and that injury is the main entry point for bacterial canker.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Feed once in early spring before the tree starts growing. Scatter the fertilizer evenly on the soil around the tree out to where the branches reach, keep it off the trunk, and water it in. Sweet cherry needs less feeding than peach, so go light: if the tree is making plenty of new growth, it may need none at all. Never feed late in the year, because soft late growth gets damaged by winter cold, and that damage is how the serious disease bacterial canker gets in.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 suits backyard cherries, applied modestly. Avoid high-nitrogen feeding, which drives soft, canker-prone, overly vigorous growth at the expense of fruiting and winter hardiness.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: A balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 (the three numbers are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium) works for backyard cherries, used sparingly. Do not overdo nitrogen, the first number, because too much pushes leafy growth that is more prone to disease and winter damage.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A common home rate is about 1/8 pound of actual nitrogen per year of tree age, to a modest maximum, applied once in early spring before bud break, scaled DOWN from peach rates because cherry is canker-prone under heavy nitrogen. Do not fertilize at planting or place fertilizer in the hole; wait until growth begins. Judge by shoot growth: a bearing tree wants only 8 to 12 inches of new wood a year.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A simple guide is a small handful of 10-10-10 for each year of the tree's age, up to a modest amount, spread once in early spring before the buds open. Do not put fertilizer in the planting hole or feed right at planting; wait until the tree starts growing. If the tree is already growing a foot of new branch each year, it probably needs no feeding at all.

companions.note_beginner: The most important companion for a sweet cherry is another cherry: plant a second compatible variety blooming at the same time unless you pick a self-fertile one (like Stella, Lapins, or Sweetheart), because most sweet cherries cannot pollinate themselves and a lone tree gives no fruit. Beyond that, what matters for a tree is the root zone, not the usual vegetable pairings: keep grass and weeds pulled back from under the branches, since lawn competes hard with a young tree, and a mulched, weed-free area helps it settle in. The one site rule is replant disease: do not plant a cherry where another cherry, plum, peach, or apricot was recently growing.
companions.note_seasoned: For sweet cherry the decisive companion is a compatible pollinizer: most cultivars are self-incompatible, so a second variety of a different S-allele group with overlapping bloom is required unless the variety is self-fertile. Past pollination, the interactions that matter are at the root zone, not classic vegetable companions: keep turf and weeds cleared back from under the canopy, since they compete hard with a young tree, and a mulched, competition-free root area establishes it faster. The one site rule is replant disease: do not follow stone fruit with stone fruit on the same ground.

good_seasoned.name: A compatible pollinizer cherry (or a self-fertile variety)
good_seasoned.label: research_backed

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: The single highest-value 'companion' for sweet cherry. Extension sources (USU, WSU, ISU) are explicit that most sweet cherries are self-incompatible and require a cross-compatible pollinizer of overlapping bloom, or a self-fertile cultivar. Strong, mechanism-clear, near-universal. extension_backed/HIGH.

good_seasoned.why_seasoned: The most important plant to put near a sweet cherry is another cherry. Most cultivars are self-incompatible and set NO crop alone, so a self-sterile variety (Bing, Rainier, Lambert) needs a second variety of a different incompatibility group blooming at the same time, ideally within about 100 feet for good bee transfer. The self-fertile cultivars (Stella, Lapins, Sweetheart, Skeena, Black Gold) sidestep this, fruiting alone and serving as universal pollinizers for most others. Confirm bloom overlap, not just the presence of a second tree.

bad_seasoned.name: Other stone fruit in old stone-fruit ground
bad_seasoned.label: research_backed

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Replanting cherry (or other Prunus) into old stone-fruit ground carries a well-documented replant-disease + ring-nematode + X-disease/bacterial-canker carryover risk; extension guidance is to use fresh ground. extension_backed/HIGH.

bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Replanting a cherry, or any stone fruit, into ground that recently grew peaches, plums, apricots, or cherries is a documented mistake. Old stone-fruit ground carries elevated ring-nematode populations and the replant-disease complex, and nearby infected trees can harbor bacterial canker and the cherry-specific X-disease (leafhopper-spread). Plant in fresh ground, or replace a generous soil volume and remove any infected neighboring trees first; rotating to a different SITE, not just a different variety, is the fix.

pests.name: Western cherry fruit fly
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Cherries that look fine outside but hide a small white maggot inside, often near the pit, with the flesh browning around it. Infested fruit may soften or show a tiny egg-laying dimple. Damage appears as the fruit colors from straw to salmon-blush and worsens toward harvest.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Cherries that look normal on the outside but have a small white maggot (a grub) inside, usually near the pit, with brown mushy flesh around it. You often do not see it until you cut or bite a cherry. It shows up as the fruit turns from pale to a pink-blush color.
pests.cause_seasoned: The western cherry fruit fly (Rhagoletis indifferens), a small fly with banded wings. Pupae overwinter in the soil; adults emerge from late spring, and after a 5-to-7-day maturation the females lay eggs just under the skin of coloring fruit. There is one generation a year, and green fruit is safe, so timing tracks the color change.
pests.cause_beginner: A small fly called the western cherry fruit fly. It spends winter in the soil, comes out in late spring, and lays eggs under the skin of cherries once they start to color. The eggs hatch into the maggots you find inside. There is just one round a year, and green fruit is safe, so the danger starts at color change.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no rescue once maggots are inside the fruit. The backyard controls are sanitation and timing: pick all fruit promptly and completely (leave none to drop), gather and destroy dropped cherries so larvae cannot reach the soil, and lay landscape fabric or dense mulch under the tree to block pupation. Yellow sticky traps from mid-May time any organic spray to 5 to 7 days after the first fly is caught.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Once the maggots are inside, no spray reaches them. The fixes are cleanup and timing: pick every cherry promptly (do not leave any), pick up and destroy fallen fruit so the grubs cannot reach the soil, and put landscape fabric or thick mulch under the tree so they cannot burrow in. A yellow sticky trap put up in mid-May tells you when the flies arrive so you can spray an organic product at the right moment.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Sanitation is the backbone: never let infested or dropped fruit sit, since each maggot that reaches the soil is next year's fly. Prompt, complete harvest and a clean orchard floor steadily lower pressure. A single isolated tree picked clean every year can stay nearly fly-free.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cleanup is the main thing: never leave wormy or fallen cherries on the ground, because each maggot that gets into the soil becomes next year's fly. Picking the tree clean every year and keeping the ground tidy keeps the numbers down.

pests.name: Spotted wing drosophila
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Soft, sunken, leaking spots on ripe and ripening fruit, with tiny white larvae inside that collapse the flesh within a day or two; fruit ferments and sours on the tree. Unlike common vinegar flies, this one attacks SOUND, intact ripe fruit, not just damaged fruit.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Ripe cherries that go soft, dimpled, and leaky fast, with tiny white maggots inside, and fruit that ferments and smells sour on the tree. The difference from ordinary fruit flies is that this pest attacks whole, undamaged ripe cherries.
pests.cause_seasoned: Spotted wing drosophila (Drosophila suzukii), an invasive vinegar fly whose females have a saw-like ovipositor that cuts into intact ripe fruit to lay eggs. It builds explosively, completing a generation in as little as a week, so pressure climbs steeply through the harvest window.
pests.cause_beginner: A small invasive fly called spotted wing drosophila. Unlike normal fruit flies, the female can cut into whole, healthy ripe cherries to lay her eggs, which hatch into the maggots inside. It multiplies very fast, so it gets worse the longer ripe fruit hangs.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Harvest is the control: pick ripe fruit promptly and completely, removing culls and any overripe or dropped cherries, and refrigerate the crop right away (cold stops the larvae). Pick every two to three days during ripening. Fine netting and prompt clean-picking are the practical backyard tools; traps with apple-cider-vinegar bait track activity.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Picking is the control: harvest ripe cherries every couple of days, remove any overripe or fallen fruit, and get the crop into the fridge quickly, since cold stops the maggots. Fine netting and quick, complete picking are the practical home tools.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Lower pressure by never leaving ripe or rotting fruit on the tree or ground, picking on a tight schedule, and chilling fruit immediately. Sanitation across the neighborhood matters, since the fly uses many wild and garden hosts.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep ahead of it by never leaving ripe or rotting cherries on the tree or ground, picking often, and chilling the fruit right away. It uses lots of other plants too, so keeping your whole yard's ripe fruit picked up helps.

pests.name: Birds
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Ripe and ripening cherries pecked, partly eaten, or stripped entirely, often within a day or two of color, with pits and torn skins left on the spurs. Robins, starlings, waxwings, and jays can take the whole crop of an unprotected tree, working the top and outside first.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Ripe cherries pecked, half-eaten, or gone, sometimes the whole crop in a day or two, with just pits and torn skins left behind. Robins, starlings, waxwings, and jays are the usual culprits and will clean off an unprotected tree.
pests.cause_seasoned: Fruit-eating birds, which key in on cherries as they color. A ripe cherry tree is one of the most attractive food sources in the yard, and a flock can strip it faster than any insect pest. Yellow cultivars like Rainier and small trees in open settings are hit hardest.
pests.cause_beginner: Birds, which zero in on cherries as they ripen. A ripe cherry tree is a magnet, and a flock can clear it faster than any bug. Light-colored kinds like Rainier and small open trees get hit the worst.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Netting is the only reliable backyard control: drape fine bird netting over the whole canopy as the fruit begins to color, securing it at the bottom so birds cannot get under. This is the single biggest reason to keep a cherry small (a dwarfing rootstock) so it can actually be netted. Scare devices (reflective tape, flash tape, balloons) help briefly but birds soon ignore them.
