pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Netting is really the only thing that works: cover the whole tree with fine bird netting as the cherries start to color, and tuck it in at the bottom so birds cannot sneak under. This is the main reason to keep a cherry tree small (on a dwarfing rootstock) so you can actually cover it. Shiny tape and scare balloons help for a little while but birds get used to them.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plan for netting before you plant by choosing a size-controlling rootstock so the mature tree can be covered. Net early, at first color, not after birds have found the tree, and secure the skirt. There is no substitute for physically excluding them.
pests.prevention_beginner: Plan to net the tree from the start: pick a dwarfing rootstock so the grown tree is small enough to cover, and put the net on as soon as the cherries start coloring, not after the birds show up. Nothing else reliably keeps them off.

pests.name: Black cherry aphid
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Dense colonies of shiny black aphids on the tips of new spring shoots, tightly curling and twisting the young leaves, with sticky honeydew below that blackens into sooty mold. Heaviest on vigorous young trees; it slows shoot growth but rarely harms fruit directly.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Clusters of shiny black aphids (tiny soft insects) on the tips of new spring growth, curling and twisting the young leaves, with a sticky coating below that turns black and moldy. It is worst on young trees and mainly stunts new growth rather than ruining fruit.
pests.cause_seasoned: The black cherry aphid (Myzus cerasi). It overwinters as eggs on the tree and explodes on the tender spring flush, feeding on sap; populations crash by midsummer as the shoots harden and natural enemies build up.
pests.cause_beginner: A small black insect called the black cherry aphid. Its eggs overwinter on the tree and the young hatch out to feed on the soft new spring growth. The numbers usually drop on their own by midsummer as the shoots toughen and ladybugs and other helpers move in.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Often no action is needed, since beneficials clean it up by midsummer. For a heavy infestation on a young tree, a strong jet of water knocks colonies off, or insecticidal soap or horticultural oil applied to the curled tips works; protect the lady beetles and lacewings that do most of the control. Avoid high-nitrogen feeding, which fuels the soft growth aphids prefer.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Often you can leave it alone, since ladybugs and other helpers clear it by midsummer. On a young tree that is badly hit, blast the colonies off with a hose, or spray the curled tips with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil. Do not over-fertilize, since lush new growth is what the aphids love.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep trees vigorous but not over-fed (high nitrogen invites aphids), encourage beneficial insects, and tolerate the early-season curl, which rarely affects the crop. A dormant oil spray reduces overwintering eggs where the pest is chronic.
pests.prevention_beginner: Avoid heavy feeding that pushes the soft growth aphids love, welcome ladybugs and lacewings, and do not panic over the spring leaf-curl, which usually does not hurt the cherries. A dormant oil spray in late winter cuts down the overwintering eggs.

pests.name: Borers (peachtree and American plum borer)
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Gummy ooze mixed with sawdust-like frass at the base of the trunk or on the lower scaffolds, centered on wounds, the graft, or bark cracks. Larvae tunnel in the inner bark; repeated attacks weaken or girdle a young tree, and the wounds also open the door to bacterial canker.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Sticky gum mixed with what looks like wet sawdust (frass) at the bottom of the trunk or on the lower branches, usually on a wound or crack. The grubs tunnel under the bark, and a young tree with several can be girdled and weakened. The wounds also let in disease.
pests.cause_seasoned: Clearwing moth and beetle borers, chiefly the peachtree borer (Synanthedon exitiosa) at the crown and the American plum borer on wounded bark, whose larvae tunnel the inner bark of stressed or injured stone-fruit trees. Sunscald, canker, and mechanical wounds are the entry points.
pests.cause_beginner: Several borers (the grubs of certain moths and beetles), mainly the peachtree borer near the soil line and the American plum borer on wounded bark. They tunnel under the bark of stressed or injured cherry trees, getting in through sunburned bark, canker, and mower wounds.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no spray once larvae are tunneling inside. Where you can find the entry holes by the gum and frass, kill the larvae with a thin wire (worming). The durable control is to prevent the wounds they need: keep mowers and trimmers off the trunk, paint the lower trunk white to prevent sunscald, prune cleanly, and keep the tree vigorous.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: No spray reaches the grubs once they are inside. Where you can find the holes marked by gum and frass, dig the grubs out with a stiff wire. The better fix is to stop giving them wounds: keep mowers and string trimmers away from the trunk, paint the lower trunk white to prevent sunburn, make clean pruning cuts, and keep the tree healthy.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Protect the trunk from injury and sunscald (a white trunk paint helps), prune cleanly to avoid leaving stubs and torn bark, and keep the tree vigorous and free of bacterial canker, since borers and canker feed on the same wounds. Inspect the trunk base each late summer for fresh gum.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep the trunk free of wounds: white trunk paint stops the sunburn cracks borers enter, keep mowers away, make clean cuts, and keep the tree healthy. Check the base of the trunk each late summer for fresh gum so you catch them early.

diseases.name: Brown rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: At bloom, infected blossoms wilt and brown and the infection runs into the spur to form a small gummy canker. As fruit ripens, firm brown spots appear and spread fast, rotting a whole cherry within a day or two in warm, wet weather, with a dusty tan spore mass on the surface. Rotted fruit dries into a clinging mummy. Cracked fruit is especially vulnerable.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: At bloom, flowers go limp and brown and small gummy dead patches form on the nearby spurs. As cherries ripen, brown spots appear and spread quickly, sometimes rotting a whole fruit in a day or two in warm, wet weather, with a dusty tan fuzz on top. Rotted fruit shrivels into a hard mummy that hangs on. Split cherries rot the fastest.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Monilinia (M. fructicola and M. laxa). It overwinters in mummies and twig cankers; spores at bloom infect flowers, and those infections later seed the fruit rot. Warm, humid, wet weather drives it, and any wound, especially a rain crack, is an open door.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus called Monilinia. It survives winter in dried mummy fruit and dead twig patches, then releases spores at bloom that infect the flowers, which later cause the fruit to rot. Warm, wet weather makes it spread fast, and a split or wounded cherry rots first.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Sanitation is the core control: remove and destroy every mummy from the tree and ground and prune out gummy twig cankers, since these are the spore sources. In a wet bloom, an organic-approved bloom-time fungicide reduces blossom blight. Pick promptly, handle gently, remove any rotting fruit at once, and choose crack-resistant cultivars to cut the wounds that let it in.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Cleanup is the main control: take off and destroy every dried mummy from the tree and ground and prune out the gummy dead twig patches, which hold the spores. If bloom is wet, an organic-approved spray at bloom helps protect the flowers. Pick on time, handle gently, throw out any rotting cherry right away, and grow crack-resistant kinds so fewer split.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Year-round sanitation prevents most loss: never leave mummies over winter, keep the canopy open with pruning so fruit dries fast after rain, harvest promptly, and prevent the fruit cracks that invite infection by keeping moisture even and choosing tolerant cultivars.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Cleaning up all year prevents most of it: never leave dried mummies over winter, prune so the tree is open and the fruit dries fast after rain, pick on time, and prevent cracking (keep watering even, pick crack-resistant kinds), since split cherries rot first.

diseases.name: Bacterial canker
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Sunken, dark, gummy cankers on trunk, scaffolds, and spurs that ooze amber gum, often girdling and killing limbs; in spring, blossoms and spurs blast (blacken and die) and dormant buds fail to open. It is the single most serious disease of sweet cherry and can kill a young tree outright.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Sunken, dark, gummy patches (cankers) on the trunk and branches that ooze amber sap, often killing the branch above them. In spring, flowers and buds may blacken and die, and some buds never open. It is the most serious sweet cherry disease and can kill a young tree.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The bacterium Pseudomonas syringae. It infects through wounds, leaf scars, and frost-injured tissue in cool, wet spring and fall weather, and is worsened by anything that stresses the tree: poor drainage, ring nematodes, frost, and high-nitrogen soft growth.
diseases.cause_beginner: A bacterium (a microscopic organism) called Pseudomonas syringae. It gets in through wounds, leaf scars, and frost damage during cool, wet weather, and is worse on stressed trees, those in wet soil, hit by frost, or pushed with too much nitrogen.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once a tree is infected. Management is preventive: cut out cankered wood well below the canker in dry summer weather (not in wet spring), disinfecting tools between cuts, and remove badly infected young trees. Keep the tree unstressed; copper sprays give only partial protection and resistance is common.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure once it sets in. The approach is prevention: cut out the cankered wood well below the dead patch during dry summer weather (not in wet spring), clean your tools between cuts, and pull out a badly infected young tree. Keep the tree healthy and unstressed; copper sprays only help a little.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Prevention is everything: plant on well-drained ground, choose a tolerant rootstock, avoid frost-pocket sites and trunk wounds, paint the trunk white against sunscald cracks, prune only in dry summer weather, and never push soft growth with late nitrogen. A vigorous, unstressed, well-drained tree resists it best.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Prevention is everything: plant where the soil drains well, avoid frosty low spots and trunk wounds, paint the trunk white to prevent sunburn cracks, prune only in dry summer weather, and do not over-feed. A healthy, unstressed tree on good ground shrugs it off best.

diseases.name: Cherry leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small purple-to-brown spots on the upper leaf surface in late spring; the spotted tissue may drop out leaving a shot-hole look, and infected leaves yellow and fall. Heavy infection defoliates the tree by midsummer, weakening it, reducing the crop, and leaving it prone to winter injury.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small purple-brown spots on the leaves in late spring, with the spots sometimes dropping out to leave little holes. Infected leaves turn yellow and fall, and a bad case can strip the tree of leaves by midsummer, which weakens it and the next crop.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Blumeriella jaapii. It overwinters in fallen leaves and infects new leaves in warm, wet spring and early-summer weather; repeated cycles through a wet season drive the defoliation.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus called Blumeriella jaapii. It spends winter in fallen leaves and infects the new leaves during warm, wet spring weather, building up over a wet season until the tree drops its leaves early.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rake and destroy fallen leaves in autumn to remove the overwintering source, the single most useful home step. Keep the canopy open for fast drying, and in wet regions an organic-approved fungicide program from petal fall protects the new leaves. Keeping the tree from defoliating preserves its winter hardiness.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Rake up and destroy the fallen leaves in fall, which is the most useful thing you can do, since the fungus overwinters in them. Keep the tree open so leaves dry fast, and in wet areas an organic-approved spray starting after the petals fall protects the new leaves.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Autumn leaf cleanup is the backbone, since the fungus overwinters in fallen leaves. Good airflow from pruning and prompt drying after rain reduce infection, and a protective spray program matters most in wet springs.
diseases.prevention_beginner: The main thing is raking up and destroying fallen leaves in fall, where the fungus waits out winter. Pruning for good airflow so leaves dry quickly helps too, and a spray program is most important in wet springs.

diseases.name: X-disease (cherry buckskin)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: A slow decline over a few years: fruit on affected limbs stays small, pale, and bitter with a leathery buckskin look and short stems, leaves may bronze, and individual scaffolds decline and die while the rest of the tree looks normal. It is incurable and spreads to nearby trees.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: A slow decline over a few years: the cherries on affected branches stay small, pale, and bitter with a leathery skin, and one branch at a time weakens and dies while the rest of the tree still looks okay. There is no cure, and it spreads to nearby trees.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A phytoplasma (a bacterium-like organism) spread by leafhoppers and through root grafts. It also lives in nearby infected stone fruit and certain weeds, and once a tree is infected it cannot be cured, only removed to protect others.
diseases.cause_beginner: A tiny bacterium-like organism spread by small insects called leafhoppers and through connected roots. It also hides in other infected stone-fruit trees and some weeds. Once a tree has it, it cannot be cured, only removed so it does not spread.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no treatment. The control is removal: test a suspect tree, and promptly remove and destroy confirmed-infected trees (including the roots) to stop spread to neighbors. Manage leafhoppers and clear nearby weed and wild-cherry reservoirs.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure. The fix is to remove it: have a suspect tree tested, then promptly take out and destroy any confirmed-infected tree, roots and all, so it does not spread to your other trees. Clearing nearby weeds and wild cherries helps too.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Prevention rests on clean planting stock, prompt removal of infected trees in the area, leafhopper management, and clearing the weed and wild-Prunus hosts that harbor it. Do not replant a new cherry next to a tree lost to X-disease without removing the source.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Prevention means starting with healthy nursery trees, promptly removing infected trees nearby, controlling the leafhoppers that carry it, and clearing weeds and wild cherries that host it. Do not plant a new cherry right next to one you lost to this disease.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Water deep-and-infrequent rather than little-and-often: about once or twice a week while a young tree establishes, easing to roughly weekly for a bearing tree in summer heat, always adjusted for rain and soil. The discipline that matters for cherry is EVEN moisture: a dry-then-wet swing, or rain after a dry spell, drives the fruit to crack. Through winter dormancy water need drops sharply and rainfall usually suffices.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water deeply now and then instead of a little every day. Plan on about once or twice a week while a young tree is getting established, easing to about once a week for a fruiting tree in summer heat, adjusting for rain and your soil. The big thing with cherries is to keep the water STEADY: if the soil dries out and then gets a lot of water, the cherries split open. In winter, when the tree is resting, it needs very little and rain usually covers it.
watering.amount_seasoned: Water deeply each time so moisture reaches the full root zone, not just the surface. For an establishing tree, on the order of 5 gallons per soak; for a bearing tree, roughly the equivalent of an inch of water per week through the season, more in heat. Steady, deep watering as the fruit colors keeps the cherries from cracking; let the soil swing dry then wet and you invite splitting.
watering.amount_beginner: Each time you water, give a deep soak that reaches all the way down to the roots, not just a splash on top. A young tree wants about 5 gallons per soak. An older, fruiting tree wants roughly an inch of water a week through the season, and more when it is hot. Keeping the water even and steady as the cherries color up is what keeps them from splitting.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the root zone by drip or soaker and keep the canopy and fruit dry. Overhead watering that wets the leaves and fruit prolongs leaf wetness, feeds brown rot, bacterial canker, and leaf spot, and leaves free water on ripe fruit that drives cracking, so deliver water to the soil, not the tree, and never sprinkle a tree carrying ripe cherries.
watering.method_beginner: Water at the ground around the roots with a drip line or soaker hose, and keep the leaves and fruit dry. Spraying water over the top wets the leaves and fruit and helps diseases like brown rot and leaf spot, and water sitting on ripe cherries makes them split, so put the water on the soil, not the tree, and never sprinkle a tree full of ripe cherries.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Overwatering and poor drainage show as yellowing leaves, wilting that persists even in wet soil, and a declining tree, since waterlogged cherry roots suffocate. Chronically wet soil also brings on crown and root rot and predisposes the trunk to bacterial canker, both often fatal. Soil that never dries between waterings is the warning sign to act on.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Too much water, or soil that drains poorly, shows up as yellowing leaves, wilting that does not go away even when the soil is wet, and a tree that slowly goes downhill, because the roots cannot breathe. In cherry, soil that stays wet also brings on crown and root rot and the serious disease bacterial canker. Soil that never dries out between waterings is your warning to back off.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Underwatering shows as wilting, dull curling leaves, slowed shoot growth, and early leaf drop in a long dry spell. The cruel twist with cherry is at harvest: a tree run dry and then rained on, or deep-watered after drought, splits its nearly ripe fruit. Catch the dry stress before the swing, and keep moisture even through the final swell.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Too little water shows as wilting, dull curling leaves, slower growth, and leaves dropping early in a long dry spell. The tricky part with cherries is near harvest: if the tree dries out and then gets rain or a big watering, the nearly ripe cherries split. So keep the water steady and do not let the tree swing from dry to soaked while the fruit is ripening.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Through establishment, keep the root ball and surrounding soil consistently moist, never waterlogged. Deep soaks of about 5 gallons once or twice a week, adjusted for rain and heat, build the deep root system the tree relies on later.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: While the tree is getting established, keep the soil around the roots evenly moist but not soggy. A deep soak of about 5 gallons once or twice a week, more in heat and less after rain, helps the tree grow the deep roots it needs.

schedule_by_stage.rate: deep soak, ~1 in per week equivalent
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: As the fruit sizes and colors, keep moisture EVEN. Aim for about an inch of water per week as deep soaks and avoid dry-then-wet swings. This is the window where steady soil moisture is the difference between sound fruit and a cracked crop.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: While the cherries are sizing up and coloring, keep the water steady. Aim for about an inch of water a week as deep soaks, and do not let the soil go dry and then soak it. Steady watering now is what keeps the cherries from splitting.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Once dormant and leafless, water need drops sharply; rely on rainfall and water only in prolonged dry spells so roots do not desiccate. Avoid keeping dormant soil saturated, which invites root rot and canker.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: After the leaves drop and the tree is resting for winter, it needs very little water. Let rain do most of the work and only water during long dry stretches so the roots do not dry out. Do not keep the soil soaked in winter.

watering.method_note_seasoned: Water deeply and infrequently at the root zone, by drip or soaker, to drive deep rooting; never wet the canopy, which feeds brown rot, leaf spot, and bacterial canker and leaves free water on fruit. The cherry-specific rule is EVEN moisture: keep the soil steady through the final swell, because a dry-then-wet swing or rain on ripe fruit is the main cause of cracking.
watering.method_note_beginner: Give the tree a deep soak now and then rather than a little every day, and water at the ground (a drip line or soaker hose is ideal) instead of spraying the leaves, since wet leaves and fruit lead to disease. With cherries the most important thing is keeping the water even: do not let the soil dry out and then soak it, especially while the fruit is ripening, or the cherries will split.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The make-or-break window is the final swell and color change, the last 2 to 3 weeks before harvest, when even moisture protects against cracking and sizes the fruit. A water-stress swing then, or a rain after a dry spell, splits the crop. The weeks just after bloom matter too for fruit set and size.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The most important time to keep the watering even is the last 2 to 3 weeks before harvest, while the cherries are coloring and filling out. A swing from dry to wet then, or a rain after a dry spell, splits the fruit. The weeks right after bloom matter too, for setting and sizing the fruit.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Hardening off does not apply to sweet cherry. It arrives as a dormant, bare-root tree and goes in the ground in late winter to early spring, not raised from a seedling indoors, so there is no tender transplant to acclimate.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: Hardening off (slowly getting an indoor-grown seedling used to the outdoors) does not apply to sweet cherry. You plant it bare-root and dormant in late winter or early spring, not as a seedling started inside, so there is no tender young plant to ease outdoors.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Plant the bare-root tree while dormant in late winter to early spring, before bud break, once the ground can be worked. Soak the roots an hour or two beforehand. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots without bending them and set the tree with the graft union (the swollen joint near the base) 2 to 3 inches above the final soil line. Do not fertilize the hole; backfill with native soil, water in well, and stake if the site is windy. Plant a compatible pollinizer within about 100 feet unless the variety is self-fertile.
start_method.notes_beginner: Plant the bare-root tree while it is still dormant (resting, no leaves) in late winter to early spring, before the buds open, once the ground can be dug. Soak the roots in a bucket for an hour or two first. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots without bending them, and set the tree so the graft union (the bumpy joint near the base, where the variety meets the rootstock) sits 2 to 3 inches above the soil. Do not put fertilizer in the hole. Refill with the same soil, water in well, and add a stake only if it is windy. Unless your variety is self-fertile, plant a second compatible cherry within about 100 feet.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Fill the pot with a chunky, fast-draining mix made for shrubs and trees, not a soft peat-based potting soil that stays soggy. A bark-based mix (composted bark with perlite or pumice for drainage) holds the air the roots need. Do not use yard soil in a pot, since it packs down and drains badly when you water often.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Keep it simple and aim for drainage. If the mix holds water, stir in more perlite or pumice, and lay a thin layer of compost on top instead of mixing a lot of rich material throughout. Stay away from water-holding crystals or heavy peat, since wet roots rot and invite canker.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: Use a coarse, fast-draining soilless mix built for woody plants, not a peat-heavy potting soil. A bark-based mix (composted pine bark with perlite or pumice) gives the air-filled porosity stone-fruit roots demand; cherry will not tolerate a mix that holds water against the crown. Skip native soil in a pot, which compacts under irrigation.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Keep amendments minimal and drainage-first: blend in extra perlite or pumice if the base mix feels water-retentive, and top-dress with a thin layer of compost rather than mixing heavy organics throughout. Avoid moisture-retentive crystals or large peat fractions, which work against the fast-draining root zone cherry needs.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: A cherry in a pot dries out much faster than one in the ground. In summer heat, check it daily and water when the top inch or two feels dry, until water runs out the bottom, but never let the pot sit in a saucer of water, since wet roots rot. The catch is that cherries crack from uneven watering, so a pot, which swings wet and dry fast, makes cracking more likely, another reason a ground tree is easier. In winter, give just enough to keep the root ball from drying out completely.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Watering often washes food out of the pot, so feed a little at a time. Use a diluted balanced liquid fertilizer every few weeks from spring into early summer, then stop, so the tree does not push tender growth that winter cold can damage. Do not fertilize at planting, and stop feeding once the tree drops its leaves.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Roots in a pot get much colder than roots in the ground, because cold reaches the soil from every side. A cherry that survives winter fine in your yard can still freeze its roots in a pot. Before hard freezes, either bury the pot to its rim in a garden bed, or move it to an unheated but sheltered spot (an attached garage or shed) that stays cold but not deep-freezing. The tree still needs the winter chill to rest and bloom, so do not bring it into a warm room.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Roots in a pot sit several zones colder than roots in the ground, so a cherry hardy in your ground may still freeze its roots in a container, and sweet cherry is already among the less cold-hardy fruit trees. Before hard freezes, either sink the pot to its rim in a bed or move it to an unheated but sheltered space that holds dormancy without the deep lows. The tree still needs its winter chill, so do not overwinter it in a heated room.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Sweet cherry really wants to grow in the ground, and a pot is the workaround only if you lack the space. It can be done on a dwarfing rootstock like Gisela 5, but expect more hands-on care, a smaller crop, and more cracking from the wet-dry swings a pot brings. Pick a self-fertile dwarf cherry so you do not also need a second pollinizer tree, use the biggest, best-draining pot you can, and plan to net it against birds.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Sweet cherry is fundamentally a ground tree; a container is a compromise for growers short on space. It works on a genetic-dwarf or Gisela 5 tree, but expect more management, lighter crops, and more cracking from the rapid wet-dry cycling of a pot. Favor a self-fertile dwarf cultivar to avoid needing a second pollinizer, give it the largest practical, freely draining pot, and net it at color change against birds.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: A potted cherry dries far faster than one in the ground and has no deep soil to buffer it, so check moisture daily in summer heat and water when the top inch or two is dry, until it runs from the drainage holes, but never leave the pot in a full saucer. The hard part is that cherry cracks on uneven moisture and a pot swings wet-to-dry fastest, so consistency is doubly important. Through dormancy, water only enough to keep the root ball from drying completely.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Frequent watering flushes nutrients from a pot, so feed lightly and often: a dilute balanced liquid feed every few weeks through the spring-to-early-summer flush, then stop so no soft growth is pushed into fall. Do not feed at planting, and ease off entirely once the tree goes dormant.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering or sub-irrigated planter is not recommended for cherry. Its reservoir keeps the lower root zone continuously moist, exactly the condition that triggers root and crown rot in stone fruit and predisposes the tree to bacterial canker. Cherry needs a freely draining pot and a wet-then-dry cycle, not a constant water table.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot (one with a water tank in the bottom) is a poor choice for cherry. The tank keeps the lower roots wet all the time, and that constant wetness is just what rots cherry roots and brings on canker. Cherry needs a pot that drains freely and soil that dries out a bit between waterings.
container_notes.container_overwintering_seasoned: Cold protection in a pot is about more than the roots: the exposed trunk and the graft union are vulnerable to freeze and to winter sun-scald, and sweet cherry's thin bark is canker-prone where injured. Wrap or shade the lower trunk in exposed sites, and bank mulch or sink the pot to insulate the root zone. The goal is a cold, stable dormancy without the deep lows that kill exposed roots; a too-warm shelter that breaks dormancy early leaves the tree to bloom into frost.
container_notes.container_overwintering_beginner: Protecting a potted cherry in winter is not just about the roots. The bare trunk and the graft union can be hurt by freezing and by winter sun on cold bark, and damaged cherry bark invites canker. In open spots, wrap or shade the lower trunk, and pile mulch around a sunk pot to insulate the roots. You want a cold, steady rest without deep freezes, but be careful that a shelter which is too warm can wake the tree early and leave it blooming into a frost.

recommended.name: Bing
recommended.recommended_note: The classic dark-red market standard. NOT self-fertile, and cross-incompatible with Lambert and Royal Ann/Napoleon, so pair it with Black Tartarian, Rainier, Stella, or Van; very prone to rain cracking.

recommended.name: Stella
recommended.recommended_note: The first self-fertile sweet cherry: one tree fruits alone and it pollinizes most others. The simplest single-tree choice for a beginner.

recommended.name: Lapins
recommended.recommended_note: Self-fertile, productive, late, and more crack-resistant than most. A strong single-tree pick where harvest rain is a risk.

recommended.name: Sweetheart
recommended.recommended_note: Self-fertile and the latest to ripen, extending the season. A heavy bearer that benefits from a compatible neighbor for the biggest crops.

recommended.name: Rainier
recommended.recommended_note: A premium yellow cherry with a red blush. NOT self-fertile (use Bing, Van, or Black Tartarian) and a notorious bird favorite, so net it.

recommended.name: Black Tartarian
recommended.recommended_note: An early, dark, richly flavored heirloom and a reliable universal pollinizer for Bing and Rainier of overlapping bloom.

recommended.name: Royal Lee
recommended.recommended_note: A low-chill cherry for mild-winter zones. NOT self-fertile: it needs its partner Minnie Royal blooming alongside to set a crop.

recommended.name: Minnie Royal
recommended.recommended_note: The low-chill partner to Royal Lee; the pair brought sweet cherries to mild-winter California. Plant both, since each needs the other to fruit.

varieties.note_seasoned: Choose a variety on two axes at once: CHILL and POLLINATION. Match the chill requirement to what your winters bank (most cultivars want 700 hours or more; only the low-chill Royal Lee and Minnie Royal pair suits mild-winter zones). Then settle pollination: unless you plant a self-fertile cultivar (Stella, Lapins, Sweetheart, Compact Stella), you need a second, cross-compatible variety of overlapping bloom (and remember Bing, Lambert, and Royal Ann cannot pollinize each other). From there weigh ripening season, crack resistance (Lapins is a standout), and bird pressure.
varieties.note_beginner: Pick a variety by two things at once: how much winter cold it needs (chill hours) and how it gets pollinated. Match the chill to your winters: most cherries need a lot of cold (700 hours or more), and only the special low-chill pair Royal Lee and Minnie Royal suits mild-winter areas. Then decide pollination: the easiest path is a self-fertile variety like Stella, Lapins, or Sweetheart that fruits on its own. If you want a self-sterile kind like Bing or Rainier, you must plant a second, matching variety that blooms at the same time.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Sweet cherries are best eaten soon after picking; they do not ripen further off the tree and lose quality fast at room temperature. Hold them at room temperature only for the day you pick, out of direct sun, and keep the stems on to slow moisture loss and decay.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Sweet cherries do not get sweeter after picking and go downhill quickly on the counter, so eat them the day you pick or refrigerate them. If you do leave them out, keep them out of the sun and leave the stems on so they keep a little longer.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerate cherries unwashed, stems on, in a breathable container or loosely bagged, and they hold about 5 to 10 days. Cold is their friend, unlike peaches: cherries do not suffer chilling injury and keep best near 32°F at high humidity. Wash only just before eating, since surface moisture in storage speeds rot.
storage.fridge_beginner: Put cherries in the fridge unwashed with the stems still on, in a loose bag or open container, and they keep about 5 to 10 days. Cold actually helps cherries (unlike peaches), so the coldest part of the fridge is best. Wash them only right before you eat them, because water on them in storage makes them rot faster.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Cherries freeze well. Wash, dry, and pit them (pitting prevents an almond-like off flavor), then freeze in a single layer on a tray before bagging. Frozen cherries keep their quality for several months and are excellent for baking, sauces, and smoothies.
storage.freezer_beginner: Cherries freeze nicely. Wash and dry them, take out the pits (this keeps an off taste from developing), spread them on a tray to freeze, then pack them into freezer bags. They keep for several months and are great for baking, sauces, and smoothies.
storage.notes_seasoned: The keys to cherry storage are cold, dry, and prompt: pick into shade, chill soon after picking, keep them dry until eating, and leave the stems on. A ripe cherry left warm or wet rots within a day or two.
storage.notes_beginner: Keep cherries cold, dry, and eat them soon. Pick into the shade, get them into the fridge quickly, leave the stems on, and only wash them right before eating. A ripe cherry left warm or wet spoils in a day or two.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Annual crop rotation does not apply to a sweet cherry: the tree holds its site for decades. The real concern is replant disease. Do not plant a new cherry (or other stone fruit) where a cherry, plum, peach, or apricot was recently growing, since Prunus-after-Prunus replanting causes stunting and poor establishment, and old sites can carry ring nematodes, bacterial canker, and the cherry-specific X-disease.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: You do not rotate a cherry tree the way you rotate vegetables, because it stays in one spot for many years. What matters instead is replant disease: do not plant a new cherry where a cherry, plum, peach, or apricot just came out. Planting a stone fruit right back where another stone fruit grew leads to weak, stunted trees, and old spots can hold pests and diseases that shorten a cherry's life.
rotation.good_after: a fresh site with no recent stone-fruit history (no cherry, plum, peach, or apricot)
rotation.note_seasoned: If a cherry must go where a stone fruit was removed, replace a generous volume of soil, choose a tolerant rootstock, test and remove any X-disease-infected trees in the vicinity first, and expect slower establishment. Best practice is simply to pick a new site.
rotation.note_beginner: If you have no choice but to replant where a stone fruit was, dig out and replace a big area of soil, pick a tougher rootstock, remove any nearby diseased trees first, and expect the tree to start slower. The simplest fix is to plant in a new spot instead.

growth_stages.name: Planting (bare-root, dormant)
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Late winter to early spring, while the tree is dormant and leafless, as soon as the soil can be worked.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Late winter or early spring, while the young tree is still bare and leafless and the ground can be dug.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A dormant bare-root whip or branched tree with firm buds and healthy roots, and a compatible pollinizer (or a self-fertile variety) planned. Keep the graft union 2 to 3 inches above the final soil line.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A leafless young tree with firm buds and healthy roots. Make sure you have a partner pollinizer tree, or a self-fertile variety. Keep the graft joint a couple of inches above the soil.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Dig a hole as wide as the roots spread and no deeper than they sat in the nursery, set the tree with the graft union above grade, backfill with native soil, and water in well. Head the whip back to start a central leader. Plant a pollinizer within about 100 feet unless self-fertile.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Dig a hole wide enough for the roots to spread and only as deep as they grew before. Keep the graft joint above the soil, fill in with the soil you dug out, and water well. Cut the young tree back to start its shape. Plant a partner cherry nearby unless yours is self-fertile.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record the planting date, the cultivar and rootstock, and the pollinizer you planted.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note the day you planted, the variety and rootstock, and the partner tree you planted with it.

growth_stages.name: Year-one establishment
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: The first full growing season after planting.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: The first whole growing season after you plant the tree.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Steady new shoot growth and a strengthening root system. Any blossoms in year one should be removed so the tree builds roots and framework, not fruit.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Healthy new shoots and a tree settling in. If it flowers this first year, pick the flowers off so it puts its energy into roots and branches.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply and regularly through the first season (the most water-sensitive period), keep a mulched, weed-free circle around the trunk without piling mulch on the bark, and remove first-year flowers. Begin light central-leader training.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Water deeply and often this first season, since a new tree needs steady water to root in. Keep a mulched, weed-free circle around the trunk, but keep the mulch off the bark. Remove any flowers, and start light pruning toward a single main-trunk shape.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Log first-season watering and the date you removed first-year blossoms.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note your watering and the day you removed the first-year flowers.

growth_stages.name: Training (years one to four)
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: The first three to four years, the framework-building phase before reliable bearing.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: The first three to four years, while you build the tree's main branches and before it fruits much.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Sweet cherry is usually trained to a central leader (a single dominant trunk with tiers of scaffold branches) or a modified central leader, not the open vase used for peach. Watch for narrow, weak branch angles and overly upright competing leaders to correct.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Sweet cherry is usually trained to a central leader: one main upright trunk with rings of side branches, not the open vase shape used for peaches. Look for branches with tight, weak angles and extra upright stems competing with the main trunk.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Each late dormant season, keep one central leader and well-spaced, wide-angled scaffolds, spreading narrow crotches and removing competing uprights. Cherry bears largely on long-lived spurs, so this builds permanent fruiting structure rather than the annual renewal peach needs. Make clean cuts; in wet climates do major cuts in dry summer to dodge bacterial canker.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Each year in late winter, keep one main upright trunk and evenly spaced side branches with wide angles, and remove stems competing with the leader. Cherries fruit on long-lived spurs, so you are building lasting structure. Make clean cuts, and in wet areas do big cuts in dry summer to avoid canker.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record each pruning, the leader and scaffolds retained, and any summer canker-avoidance cuts.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you prune and which main branches you kept.

growth_stages.name: Winter dormancy
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Roughly December through February, the leafless months when the tree banks chill.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: About December through February, the leafless winter months.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A leafless tree at rest banking chill hours (time between about 32 and 45°F) that it needs to break dormancy and bloom evenly. Sweet cherry needs a lot of chill, so a mild winter can mean a weak bloom.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A bare, resting tree collecting chill hours, the cold time it needs (hours between about 32 and 45°F) before it will bloom well. Sweet cherry needs plenty of cold, so a mild winter can give a poor bloom.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Little is required: clear mummified fruit and fallen leaves that harbor brown rot and leaf spot, and apply a dormant copper or oil spray where canker, leaf spot, or aphids are chronic. Established trees need minimal water now.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Not much to do: clear away any dried mummy fruit and fallen leaves that carry disease, and apply a dormant spray if canker, leaf spot, or aphids are a regular problem. An established tree needs very little water now.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Note the dormant spray date and any winter sanitation.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you did the dormant spray and any winter cleanup.

growth_stages.name: Dormant pruning
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Late dormancy, roughly February into March, just before growth resumes (or dry summer in canker-prone wet climates).
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Late winter, around February into March, just before the tree wakes up (or dry summer in wet, canker-prone areas).
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare branches showing the tree's structure. Cherry needs far lighter pruning than peach: it fruits on long-lived spurs, so you maintain the leader and open the canopy rather than renewing fruiting wood each year.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Bare branches, so you can see the shape. Cherries need much less pruning than peaches, because they fruit on long-lasting spurs. You mostly keep the main trunk and open up the canopy rather than cutting hard every year.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Prune lightly: keep the central leader, remove dead, diseased, crossing, and crowding wood, and open the canopy for light and air. Make clean cuts and remove cankered wood; in wet regions shift major cuts to dry summer weather, since fresh cuts in cool wet spring invite bacterial canker.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Prune lightly: keep the main trunk, cut out dead, diseased, and crossing branches, and open the middle for light and air. Make clean cuts and remove any cankered bark. In wet areas, do the big cuts in dry summer instead, since cuts in cool wet spring invite canker.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record the pruning date and any cankered wood removed.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note the day you pruned and any diseased wood you cut out.

growth_stages.name: Bloom
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Early spring, the timing shifting by region from late February in mild zones to April or May in the North.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Early spring. The exact week depends on where you live, earlier in warm areas, later in cold ones.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: White blossoms opening across the tree. This is the most frost-vulnerable moment of the year, and the window when a self-sterile variety MUST have a compatible pollinizer blooming alongside and bees flying, or it sets nothing.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: White flowers opening all over the tree. This is the riskiest time for frost, and the time when a self-sterile variety must have its partner tree blooming at the same time and bees flying, or it makes no cherries.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Watch the frost forecast closely and cover a small tree overnight if a hard frost threatens open bloom. Confirm the pollinizer is blooming concurrently and that bees are active; cold, wet, windy bloom weather suppresses set. In a wet bloom, this is the window for a brown-rot blossom spray.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep an eye on the frost forecast and cover a small tree overnight if a hard frost is coming during bloom. Check that the partner tree is flowering at the same time and that bees are out; cold, wet, windy weather during bloom means a poor crop. If bloom is wet, this is the time for a brown-rot spray.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record the bloom date, pollinizer overlap, and any frost protection or bloom spray.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when bloom started, whether the partner tree bloomed with it, and anything you did for frost or spray.

growth_stages.name: Fruit development and protection
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Spring into early summer, after petal fall, as the green fruit forms and colors.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Spring into early summer, after the petals drop, as the small green cherries form and start to color.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Clusters of small green cherries swelling on the spurs. Unlike peach, cherries are NOT thinned. This is the window to get netting ready, keep moisture even against cracking, and begin monitoring for cherry fruit fly and spotted wing drosophila as the fruit colors.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Small green cherries swelling on the spurs. Unlike peaches, you do NOT thin cherries. This is the time to get bird netting ready, keep the watering even so the fruit does not split, and start watching for cherry fruit fly and spotted wing drosophila as the fruit colors up.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep soil moisture even through the swell to limit cracking, and net the tree as the fruit begins to color, before birds find it. Hang cherry-fruit-fly traps by mid-spring and vinegar-bait traps as fruit colors to time any spray; remove any cracked or rotting fruit.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the watering steady so the cherries do not crack, and put bird netting on as the fruit starts to color, before the birds arrive. Put up traps for cherry fruit fly and spotted wing drosophila, and pick off any split or rotting cherries.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record when you netted, trap catches, and any cracking after rain.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you netted the tree, what the traps caught, and any splitting after rain.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Late spring to early summer, the month varying by region and variety; first real crop around years 3 to 5.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Late spring to early summer. The exact time depends on the variety and your area. Most trees give their first real crop around years 3 to 5.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Cherries at full variety color that taste sweet and give slightly. A tree ripens its crop over a short, concentrated week or two, and cherries do not sweeten after picking, so taste before you pick. Rain on ripe fruit cracks it.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Cherries at full color that taste sweet and give a little. The tree ripens its whole crop in a short burst of a week or two, and cherries do not get sweeter after picking, so taste one first. Rain on ripe fruit splits it.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick when fully colored and sweet, pulling from the spur by the stem, not the fruit, to protect next year's spurs. Pick promptly and completely every couple of days, clear culls and drops, and chill the fruit fast against spotted wing drosophila. Beat the rain: pick ahead of a forecast soaking.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pick when the cherries are fully colored and sweet, pulling from the little spur by the stem, not the fruit, to protect next year's fruiting spurs. Pick every couple of days, clear away any leftover or fallen fruit, and get the crop into the fridge fast. If rain is coming, pick before it arrives.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record harvest dates, a rough yield, and any cracking or pest losses.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you picked, roughly how much you got, and any splitting or pest damage.

notifications.title_beginner: Time to plant your cherry tree
notifications.body_seasoned: Set a dormant bare-root tree now, while it is still leafless and the ground is workable. Keep the graft union 2 to 3 inches above the final soil line, pick a full-sun, well-drained spot out of frost pockets, and head the tree back to start a central leader. Plant a compatible pollinizer within about 100 feet unless your variety is self-fertile.
notifications.body_beginner: Now is the time to plant a bare-root cherry, while it is still resting and the soil can be dug. Keep the graft union, the swollen bump low on the trunk, 2 to 3 inches above the soil, and choose a sunny, well-drained spot that does not sit in a frosty dip. Cut the young tree back to start its shape, and plant a partner cherry nearby unless yours is self-fertile.

notifications.title_beginner: Time for a light cherry prune
notifications.body_seasoned: Prune lightly now, in late dormancy. Cherry fruits on long-lived spurs and needs far less cutting than peach: keep the central leader, remove dead, diseased, and crossing wood, and open the canopy. Make clean cuts and remove cankered wood. In wet climates, shift major cuts to dry summer to avoid bacterial canker.
notifications.body_beginner: Prune lightly now, in late winter. Cherries fruit on long-lasting spurs and need much less cutting than peaches: keep the main trunk, take out dead, diseased, and crossing branches, and open up the middle. Make clean cuts and remove any cankered bark. In wet areas, save the big cuts for dry summer to avoid canker.

notifications.title_seasoned: Bloom is open, watch for late frost
notifications.title_beginner: Flowers are open, watch the frost
notifications.body_seasoned: Your tree is flowering, the year's highest-risk stretch for the crop: a hard freeze on open blossoms takes all of it. Watch overnight lows through bloom and cover a small tree if a hard late frost is forecast. Confirm the pollinizer is blooming at the same time and bees are active, since most cherries set no fruit without cross-pollination.
notifications.body_beginner: Open flowers are when a cherry crop is most at risk from frost: one hard freeze on the blossoms can wipe out the year's cherries. Watch the overnight forecast during bloom and cover a small tree if a hard frost is coming. Check that the partner tree is blooming too and that bees are out, since most cherries make no fruit without a pollinator partner.

notifications.title_seasoned: Net the tree as fruit colors
notifications.title_beginner: Time to net the tree against birds
notifications.body_seasoned: As the fruit begins to color, net the whole canopy before birds find it and secure the skirt. Do not thin cherries the way you thin peaches. Keep soil moisture even to limit cracking, and start monitoring for cherry fruit fly and spotted wing drosophila as the fruit blushes.
notifications.body_beginner: As the cherries start to color, cover the whole tree with bird netting before the birds show up, and tuck it in at the bottom. Do not thin cherries like peaches. Keep the watering even so they do not split, and start watching for cherry fruit fly and spotted wing drosophila as the fruit colors.

notifications.body_seasoned: Through its first two seasons a cherry is at its most water-sensitive while roots establish. Water deeply and regularly at the root zone, by drip or soaker, and avoid wetting the canopy. Keep a weed-free, mulched circle around the trunk, and do not feed late, since soft growth invites the winter injury that opens the door to bacterial canker.
notifications.body_beginner: For its first couple of years, a young cherry needs steady water while its roots get going. Give it a deep soak at the ground every week or so (a drip line or soaker hose is ideal) rather than spraying the leaves. Keep a mulched, weed-free ring around the trunk, and do not feed late in the year, since soft late growth gets winter damage that lets canker in.

notifications.title_beginner: Cherries almost ready, watch for rain
notifications.body_seasoned: The crop is sizing and coloring. Keep soil moisture EVEN to limit cracking, and if rain is in the forecast, pick any ripe fruit ahead of it, since rain on ripe cherries splits them. Cherries do not ripen after picking, so taste first and pick only fully colored, sweet fruit, pulling from the spur by the stem. Pick promptly and chill fast against spotted wing drosophila.
notifications.body_beginner: The cherries are sizing up and coloring. Keep the watering even so they do not split, and if rain is coming, pick any ripe ones first, since rain on ripe cherries splits them. Cherries do not get sweeter after picking, so taste one and pick only fully colored, sweet fruit, pulling from the little spur by the stem. Pick promptly and chill them fast.

notifications.body_seasoned: As the tree drops its leaves, clear every mummified fruit from the branches and ground and rake up fallen leaves. Mummies overwinter brown rot and fallen leaves overwinter cherry leaf spot, so this cleanup is your cheapest disease control. It is also the window to check the trunk base for fresh gum that signals borers or canker.
notifications.body_beginner: As the leaves fall, pick off any shriveled dried-up fruit still hanging, gather what dropped, and rake up the fallen leaves. Old fruit carries brown rot and fallen leaves carry leaf spot into next year, so clearing them is the easiest disease control. It is also a good time to check the bottom of the trunk for fresh gum, which can mean borers or canker.

notifications.title_seasoned: Did your winter bank enough chill?
notifications.body_seasoned: Sweet cherry needs a lot of winter chill (most cultivars 700 hours or more) to bloom evenly. After a mild winter, expect a weaker, more drawn-out bloom and a lighter set, especially on higher-chill cultivars. In mild-winter regions, only a low-chill cultivar (Royal Lee, Minnie Royal) will bloom reliably; note this year's bloom quality to learn your site.
notifications.body_beginner: Sweet cherry needs plenty of winter cold (most kinds 700 hours or more) to bloom well. After a mild winter, expect a thinner, more spread-out bloom and a lighter crop. In mild-winter areas, only a low-chill kind like Royal Lee or Minnie Royal will bloom reliably. Jot down how well it bloomed this year to learn your spot.

notifications.title_seasoned: Anything to log on the cherry?
notifications.title_beginner: How is your cherry tree doing?
notifications.body_seasoned: It has been a while since your last note. A quick check pays off on a tree: scan the trunk for fresh gum (borers or canker), confirm mummies and fallen leaves are cleared, and note where bloom and harvest landed and whether the pollinizer overlapped. Logging the dates now makes your tree's pattern clearer over time.
notifications.body_beginner: It has been a while since you logged anything. A quick look is worth it: check the trunk for fresh gum (borers or canker), make sure old fruit and fallen leaves are cleared, and note when the tree bloomed and when you picked, and whether the partner tree bloomed with it. Writing the dates down helps you see the tree's rhythm year to year.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost warning while flowering
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A hard freeze on open bloom or newly set fruit is the most common way a sweet cherry crop is lost. If frost is forecast tonight, cover a small tree before evening to trap ground warmth, and water the soil beforehand, since moist ground holds and releases more heat overnight. Large trees are hard to protect, which is why a frost-aware site and a later-blooming cultivar matter most.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: A hard frost on open flowers or tiny new fruit is the most common reason a cherry crop fails. If frost is forecast tonight, cover a small tree before dark to hold in the ground's warmth, and water the soil first, since damp ground stays warmer overnight. Big trees are hard to cover, so the best protection is a spot less prone to frost and a variety that blooms later.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heavy rain, ripe fruit will crack
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Heavy rain, ripe cherries will split
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Rain on ripe or nearly ripe cherries is the signature sweet-cherry crop loss: free water on the fruit is absorbed through the skin and the swelling flesh splits, and split fruit rots fast with brown rot. Before a forecast soaking, pick every ripe cherry you can; a tree that went dry and is then rained on cracks worst, so keep moisture even all season. Crack-resistant cultivars like Lapins help.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Rain on ripe or almost-ripe cherries is the classic way the crop is lost: water soaks into the fruit and it swells and splits, and split cherries rot fast. Before a coming rain, pick every ripe cherry you can. A tree that dried out and then gets rained on splits the worst, so keep the watering even all season. Crack-resistant kinds like Lapins help.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Muggy weather, watch for rot
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Warm, humid conditions drive brown rot (browning blossoms at bloom and rotting ripe fruit within a day or two) and cool, wet, humid spring weather drives bacterial canker and cherry leaf spot. There is no spraying it away mid-spell: keep the canopy open and dry, water only at the root zone, remove rotting fruit promptly, and harvest ripe fruit without delay.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Warm, muggy weather is what brown rot loves, browning blossoms and rotting ripe cherries in a day or two, and cool wet spring weather drives bacterial canker and leaf spot. You cannot spray it away once it is muggy, so keep the tree open and the leaves dry, water only at the ground, pick off rotting fruit right away, and harvest ripe cherries promptly.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Dry spell, keep the watering even
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: During a dry stretch, deep, regular watering matters most for a first-year tree establishing roots and for keeping moisture EVEN as the fruit sizes. The cherry trap is the swing: a tree allowed to go dry and then watered hard, or rained on, splits its fruit. Soak deeply at the root zone and avoid letting the soil dry out and then flooding it.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: In a dry spell, deep, regular watering matters most for a young tree putting down roots and for keeping the moisture even while the fruit sizes. The cherry trap is the swing: a tree that dries out and then gets a big watering or rain splits its fruit. Give a deep soak at the ground and avoid letting the soil go dry and then flooding it.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot spell, watch the ripening fruit
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Sweet cherry takes moderate heat but an extreme heat spell during ripening can soften fruit, cause doubling and spurring of next year's buds, and sunburn exposed cherries. Keep the tree well watered so heat and drought stress do not combine, and avoid stripping interior leaves that shade the fruit. Picking slightly early in extreme heat beats losing fruit to softening.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Sweet cherry handles some heat, but an extreme hot spell while the fruit ripens can soften it, cause oddly doubled fruit, and sunburn exposed cherries. Keep the tree well watered so heat and dryness do not hit at once, and leave the leaves that shade the fruit. In extreme heat, picking a little early beats losing the crop to softening.

planting.text_seasoned: Settle pollination BEFORE you plant: a self-sterile variety (Bing, Rainier, Lambert) needs a compatible second variety of overlapping bloom within about 100 feet, or it sets no fruit. A self-fertile variety (Stella, Lapins, Sweetheart) fruits alone.
planting.text_beginner: Sort out pollination before planting: a self-sterile cherry like Bing needs a second, matching variety blooming nearby or it makes no fruit. The easy path is a self-fertile kind like Stella, Lapins, or Sweetheart that fruits on its own.
planting.author: cc_author_pilot

planting.text_seasoned: Set the graft union 2 to 3 inches above the final soil line and plant in full sun on well-drained ground. Cherry will not tolerate wet feet, and frost-pocket sites lose the early bloom to late frost.
planting.text_beginner: Keep the graft joint 2 to 3 inches above the soil and plant in full sun where the soil drains well. Cherries hate soggy roots, and a low frost-pocket spot loses the early flowers to frost.
planting.author: cc_author_pilot

establishment.text_seasoned: Remove every blossom the first year so the young tree builds roots and a strong central leader instead of fruiting.
establishment.text_beginner: Pick off all the flowers the first year so the new tree puts its energy into roots and a strong main trunk instead of fruit.
establishment.author: cc_author_pilot

establishment.text_seasoned: The first season is the tree's most water-sensitive period; water deeply and regularly so roots establish, and never feed late, since soft growth invites the winter injury that opens the door to bacterial canker.
establishment.text_beginner: Water deeply and often all through the first season so the roots get going, and never feed late in the year, since soft late growth gets winter damage that lets canker in.
establishment.author: cc_author_pilot

scaffold_formation.text_seasoned: Train to a central leader, not the open vase used for peach: keep one dominant trunk and wide-angled scaffolds. Cherry fruits on long-lived spurs, so you build permanent structure rather than renewing fruiting wood each year.
scaffold_formation.text_beginner: Train a sweet cherry to a single main trunk (a central leader), not the open vase shape used for peaches. Cherries fruit on long-lasting spurs, so you are building a lasting framework instead of cutting hard every year.
scaffold_formation.author: cc_author_pilot

dormancy.text_seasoned: Winter chill banks next year's bloom, and sweet cherry needs a lot of it (most cultivars 700 hours or more). In a mild-winter area, only a low-chill cultivar like Royal Lee or Minnie Royal will bloom well.
dormancy.text_beginner: The cold of winter sets up next spring's flowers, and sweet cherry needs plenty of it (most kinds 700 hours or more). In a mild-winter area, only a low-chill kind like Royal Lee or Minnie Royal will bloom properly.
dormancy.author: cc_author_pilot

dormancy.text_seasoned: Clear mummified fruit and rake fallen leaves over winter: mummies carry brown rot and fallen leaves carry cherry leaf spot into the new season.
dormancy.text_beginner: Clear away dried mummy fruit and rake up fallen leaves during winter. Mummies carry brown rot and fallen leaves carry leaf spot into the next year.
dormancy.author: cc_author_pilot

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Cherry needs far lighter pruning than peach, because it fruits on long-lived spurs. Keep the leader, open the canopy, and avoid heavy cuts.
dormant_prune.text_beginner: Cherries need much less pruning than peaches, because they fruit on long-lasting spurs. Keep the main trunk, open the middle for light, and avoid cutting hard.
dormant_prune.author: cc_author_pilot

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: In wet climates, do major pruning in dry summer, not cool wet spring: fresh cuts in damp weather are the main entry point for bacterial canker, sweet cherry's most serious disease.
dormant_prune.text_beginner: In wet areas, do the big pruning cuts in dry summer instead of cool wet spring. Fresh cuts in damp weather are the main way bacterial canker, the worst cherry disease, gets in.
dormant_prune.author: cc_author_pilot

blossom.text_seasoned: Open bloom is the most frost-vulnerable moment of the year. Track the forecast and cover a small tree overnight if a hard late frost threatens the flowers.
blossom.text_beginner: When the tree is in bloom it is most at risk from frost. Watch the forecast, and if a hard late frost is coming, cover a small tree overnight to protect the flowers.
blossom.author: cc_author_pilot

blossom.text_seasoned: A self-sterile variety must have a compatible pollinizer blooming AT THE SAME TIME and bees flying. Watch that the two varieties overlap; cold, wet, windy bloom weather suppresses bees and the crop.
blossom.text_beginner: A self-sterile cherry must have its partner variety blooming at the same time and bees flying. Make sure the two overlap, and remember that cold, wet, windy weather keeps bees down and hurts the crop.
blossom.author: cc_author_pilot

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Do NOT thin cherries the way you thin peaches; they size on the tree without it. Instead, put your effort into netting against birds and keeping moisture even against cracking.
fruit_set.text_beginner: Do NOT thin cherries the way you thin peaches; they size up fine on their own. Put your effort into netting against birds and keeping the watering even so they do not split.
fruit_set.author: cc_author_pilot

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Net the tree as the fruit begins to color, before birds find it, and secure the skirt. This is the main reason to keep a cherry small on a dwarfing rootstock so it can be covered.
fruit_set.text_beginner: Put bird netting on as the cherries start to color, before the birds show up, and tuck it in at the bottom. This is the big reason to keep a cherry small (on a dwarfing rootstock) so you can actually cover it.
fruit_set.author: cc_author_pilot

harvest.text_seasoned: Cherries do not ripen after picking, so taste before you pick and harvest only fully colored, sweet fruit. Pull from the spur by the stem, not the fruit, to protect next year's fruiting spurs.
harvest.text_beginner: Cherries do not get sweeter after picking, so taste one first and only pick fully colored, sweet fruit. Pull from the little spur by the stem, not the cherry, to protect next year's fruiting spurs.
harvest.author: cc_author_pilot

harvest.text_seasoned: Beat the rain: pick ripe cherries ahead of a forecast soaking, because rain on ripe fruit cracks it. Pick promptly and completely every couple of days and chill fast against spotted wing drosophila.
harvest.text_beginner: Beat the rain: pick ripe cherries before a coming rain, because rain on ripe fruit splits it. Pick every couple of days, leave none behind, and get them into the fridge fast to stop spotted wing drosophila.
harvest.author: cc_author_pilot

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A mature sweet cherry yields widely by tree size: roughly 30 to 50 pounds on a dwarfing rootstock (Gisela 5) and 50 to 100-plus pounds on a semi-dwarf to standard tree, given a pollinizer, frost-free bloom, and protection from birds and cracking. Crop is far more limited by frost, pollination, birds, and harvest rain than by feeding.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: A grown sweet cherry gives roughly 30 to 50 pounds on a small dwarf tree and 50 to 100 pounds or more on a bigger tree, as long as it gets pollinated, dodges frost, and is protected from birds and rain. The crop depends far more on frost, pollination, birds, and harvest-time rain than on how much you feed it.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Trees reach full bearing around years 6 to 7 (sooner, years 3 to 4, on a precocious Gisela rootstock) and stay productive for decades. A self-sterile variety yields nothing without a compatible pollinizer, so confirm that first.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: A sweet cherry hits full production around years 6 to 7, or as early as years 3 to 4 on a quick-bearing dwarf rootstock, and keeps producing for decades. Remember a self-sterile variety gives nothing without a partner tree, so make sure you have one.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Expect no crop in the planting year and little to none through year 2 or 3. Remove any early fruit so the tree builds roots and a strong central leader; the first meaningful harvest typically comes in years 3 to 5, sooner on a precocious dwarfing rootstock, with full bearing by years 6 to 7.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Do not expect cherries the first year or two. If a little fruit forms early, pick it off so the young tree builds roots and a strong trunk. Your first real harvest usually comes in years 3 to 5 (sooner on a quick-bearing dwarf rootstock), with full crops by years 6 to 7.
factors_seasoned: a compatible pollinizer (or a self-fertile variety)
late-frost damage at bloom
winter chill accumulation
bird protection (netting)
harvest-time rain and fruit cracking
cherry fruit fly and spotted wing drosophila control
rootstock and tree age

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No moon-phase planting preference is asserted. Extension sources do not support timing cherry planting or care by lunar phase; chill matching, frost avoidance, pollinizer choice, and harvest-rain timing govern outcomes.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: The tree bloomed well but set little or no fruit
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The tree flowered but I got almost no cherries
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The tree flowered heavily but few or no cherries formed. On sweet cherry the leading cause is POLLINATION: most cultivars are self-incompatible, so a lone self-sterile tree (Bing, Rainier, Lambert) sets nothing without a compatible pollinizer of overlapping bloom. The next cause is a late frost on the early open bloom, and a distant third is cold, wet, windy bloom weather that kept bees from flying. The fix is a self-fertile variety or a properly matched pollinizer, a frost-aware site, and bee activity at bloom.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The tree flowered but barely fruited. On sweet cherry the usual reason is pollination: most kinds cannot pollinate themselves, so a single self-sterile tree like Bing makes no fruit without a matching partner tree blooming at the same time. The next reason is a late frost on the early flowers, and after that, cold or rainy weather that kept the bees home. The fix is to plant a self-fertile variety or a proper partner, choose a spot less prone to frost, and have bees active at bloom.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant a self-fertile cultivar, or confirm a cross-compatible pollinizer blooms at the same time within about 100 feet; avoid frost-pocket sites and keep a cover ready for bloom.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant a self-fertile variety, or make sure a matching partner cherry blooms at the same time nearby; avoid low frosty spots and keep a cover handy for bloom-time frosts.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Ripe cherries split open near harvest
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The cherries split open just before I could pick them
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Nearly ripe cherries developed splits and cracks, often after a rain. This is the signature sweet-cherry failure: free water on ripe fruit, from rain, heavy dew, or fog, is absorbed through the skin and the swelling flesh splits, and a dry-then-wet soil swing makes it worse. Split fruit then rots fast with brown rot. The fixes are even soil moisture through the final swell, picking ahead of forecast rain, and choosing crack-resistant cultivars like Lapins.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The nearly ripe cherries cracked and split, usually after rain. This is the classic sweet cherry problem: rain, dew, or fog sitting on ripe fruit soaks into the skin and the fruit swells and splits, and letting the soil go dry then wet makes it worse. Split cherries then rot quickly. The fixes are keeping the watering even, picking before a coming rain, and growing crack-resistant kinds like Lapins.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Keep soil moisture even through ripening, pick ahead of forecast rain, and favor crack-tolerant cultivars (Lapins, Sweetheart); never sprinkle a tree carrying ripe fruit.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep the watering steady as the fruit ripens, pick before a coming rain, and grow crack-resistant kinds like Lapins; never spray water over a tree full of ripe cherries.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Birds stripped the crop as it ripened
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Birds ate the cherries before I could
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The ripening crop was pecked or stripped, often within a day or two of coloring. Birds (robins, starlings, waxwings, jays) target ripe cherries and can clear an unprotected tree faster than any insect pest. There is no spray or scare device that reliably keeps them off; physical exclusion does. The fix is to keep the tree small enough to net and to net it at first color, before the birds discover it.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The cherries were pecked or gone, often within a day or two of coloring. Birds love ripe cherries and can clean off an unprotected tree faster than any bug. No spray or scare gadget reliably keeps them off, but a net does. The fix is to keep the tree small enough to cover and net it as soon as the fruit starts to color, before the birds find it.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Choose a dwarfing rootstock so the tree can be netted, and drape fine bird netting over the whole canopy at first color, securing the skirt.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Pick a dwarfing rootstock so the tree stays small enough to cover, and put fine bird netting over the whole tree as the fruit starts to color, tucking it in at the bottom.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Cherries had small white maggots inside
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The cherries had little white worms inside
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Cherries that looked fine outside hid small white maggots inside. Two pests do this: the western cherry fruit fly (one generation a year, attacking fruit as it colors from straw to blush) and spotted wing drosophila (which attacks sound ripe fruit and multiplies explosively). Both are managed by prompt, complete harvest, removing every dropped and culled fruit, chilling the crop immediately, and trapping to time any organic spray to the color-change window.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Cherries that looked okay outside had small white maggots inside. Two pests cause this: the cherry fruit fly (one round a year, hitting fruit as it colors) and spotted wing drosophila (which hits whole ripe fruit and multiplies fast). Both are handled by picking promptly and completely, removing every dropped cherry, getting the crop into the fridge right away, and using traps to time any organic spray.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Hang traps from mid-spring, pick promptly and completely, destroy all dropped and culled fruit so larvae cannot reach the soil, and chill the crop immediately.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Put up traps in mid-spring, pick every cherry promptly, destroy all fallen fruit so the maggots cannot get into the soil, and refrigerate the crop right away.

primary.name: Washington State University Tree Fruit Extension
University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources (UC IPM)
UC Master Gardeners of Santa Clara County

succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Succession planting does not apply to sweet cherry. It is a permanent tree that holds its site for decades and bears one concentrated crop each season as the fruit ripens, so there is no staggered re-sowing to schedule the way there is for a short-season annual.

open_findings.summary: PERENNIAL PILOT -- the authoring bot's first tree, modeled structurally on the certified peach (same genus Prunus, archetype deciduous_fruit_tree). Mirrors all ~35 peach perennial fields refit for sweet cherry. Needs the daily biology-fidelity review + source-truth sample before any certification. [RESOLVED 2026-07-02: Wave-1 source-truth review complete; pollination + chill + signature disease confirmed against cited T1 pages.]

Region verdicts for the warm/humid zones (se_gulf, warm_arid, ca_desert, low_desert_az, fl_peninsula, hawaii) rest on (a) the crop-invariant region chill climate (shared region_chill_delivered table) and (b) sweet cherry's chill/hardiness/heat/humidity limits documented by usu_ext/wsu_ext/iastate_ext; dedicated sweet-cherry pages from each warm-region extension were NOT separately fetched. Verify against region-local extension sources at the cert pass.
Bloom/harvest windows and region calendars are GENERALLY-SAFE structural fits refit from peach, not fine-date-precise; refine exact days at the variety-delta pass per the standing scale-phase rule.
