chill_hours_range low end (200, the Royal Lee/Minnie Royal low-chill pair) rests on nursery attestation, not a T1 extension number; the standard 700-1000h cluster is T1-backed (UC Santa Clara MG). Defensible as modeled; refine at the variety-delta pass.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: Wave-1 stone-fruit cert (2026-07-02): parallel per-crop source-truth review (CC agents, WebFetch of the cited T1 pages) confirmed the pollination call + chill + signature disease; pollination pinned to its cited page under A38; open_findings record the modeled/deferred items.

3.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 3 winter lows (to -40°F) are far below sweet cherry's roughly -10°F injury threshold; the tree is killed outright. Not a sweet cherry zone (try the much hardier sour/tart cherry instead).
3.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 3 is too cold for sweet cherry; the tree will not survive. Grow a hardy sour (tart) cherry here instead.

4.suitability_note_seasoned: The hardiest sweet cherries may survive zone 4 in sheltered, snow-covered sites, but at about -10°F and colder the fruit buds and wood are injured, and the early May bloom is routinely caught by late frost. Chill is abundant, so the tree blooms most springs, but treat any crop as a bonus and favor a warm, protected slope.
4.suitability_note_beginner: A very hardy sweet cherry may survive zone 4 in a sheltered spot, but the cold and late frosts usually take the crop. The tree blooms most years but rarely fruits, so do not count on cherries here; a hardy sour cherry is the safer choice.
4.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Late spring frost is the defining risk: the early May bloom is regularly caught by a hard freeze, and deep winter cold near -10°F also injures the fruit buds. Expect bloom most springs but a usable crop only in years that escape a killing frost.

5.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 5 is the cold edge of reliable sweet cherry. Hardy cultivars crop in good years on frost-safe, well-drained sites, but a hard midwinter cold snap or a late spring frost can take a season. Plant on high, open ground out of frost pockets and avoid the warmest, earliest-blooming sites.
5.suitability_note_beginner: Sweet cherries can fruit in zone 5 in good years if you plant a hardy variety on high, open ground away from frost pockets. Some years a late frost or deep cold will cost you the crop.
5.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Late spring frost on the early bloom is the main crop risk, with occasional deep-winter bud injury. Choose a frost-safe site and a later-blooming cultivar.

6.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 6 is solid sweet cherry country with chill to spare, so the full variety range is open; choose by flavor, self-fertility, and crack resistance. Watch the occasional late frost on early bloomers, manage bacterial canker and leaf spot in wet springs, and net against birds.
6.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 6 grows sweet cherries dependably. You can choose almost any variety. Keep an eye out for a late frost at bloom, manage disease in wet springs, and net the tree against birds.
6.frost_risk_note_seasoned: An occasional late-April frost can nip the earliest bloomers; mid-to-late-blooming cultivars are the safer choice.

7.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 7 fruits sweet cherries reliably across the full variety range; chill is ample and the season starts early. Late-frost risk is modest. The main cautions are wet-spring bacterial canker and leaf spot, harvest-time rain cracking, and birds, so manage disease, keep moisture even, and net the tree.
7.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 7 is good for sweet cherries, with an early start to the season and almost any variety workable. The things to manage are spring disease, rain cracking near harvest, and birds, so keep the tree healthy, water evenly, and net it.
7.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Late-frost loss is occasional and falls hardest on the very-early bloomers; a mid-to-late cultivar is the lower-risk pick.

northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Across the northern tier, sweet cherry succeeds where winters are cold enough to bank chill but not so cold that they kill the tree. Reliable cropping starts around zones 6 and 7; zones 3 to 5 ask for the hardiest cultivars, careful frost-pocket avoidance, and patience with off years, and zones 3 to 4 are generally too cold for a dependable sweet cherry tree.
northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the north, sweet cherries do best in the milder parts (zones 6 and 7). Farther north (zones 3 to 5) the tree may struggle or be killed by cold, so plant on high ground out of frost pockets and choose the hardiest variety, or grow a hardy sour cherry instead.
northern_tier.chill_basis_seasoned: Northern-tier winters bank well over 700 to 1,000-plus chill hours, more than any sweet cherry needs, so chill is never the limiter here. The limits are cold and frost: deep-winter lows near -10°F injure fruit buds, and a late spring frost can kill the early open bloom.
northern_tier.chill_basis_beginner: Winters here are plenty cold for the chill any sweet cherry needs. The challenge is the opposite: deep winter cold and late spring frosts are what threaten the tree and the crop.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Inland zone 8 banks adequate chill, but sweet cherry is poorly adapted to the hot, humid Southeast: brown rot, bacterial canker, and cherry leaf spot run hard in the warm humidity, and frequent late-spring and summer rain cracks the fruit. The tree may grow but a dependable crop is unrealistic, so sweet cherry is not recommended here.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Even though winters are cold enough, sweet cherry does poorly in the hot, humid Southeast. Disease and frequent rain that splits the fruit make a dependable crop unrealistic, so it is not recommended here.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: The warmer, lower-chill zone 9 Gulf edge combines marginal chill with intense heat, humidity, and harvest-season rain, all of which sweet cherry handles badly. Disease pressure and cracking make it an unsuitable crop here regardless of cultivar.
9.suitability_note_beginner: The warmer Gulf edge is too mild in winter and too hot, humid, and rainy in season for sweet cherry. It is not a workable crop here.

se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: The Southeast is not sweet cherry country. Inland zone 8 banks enough chill, but heat, humidity, and harvest-season rain drive brown rot, bacterial canker, leaf spot, and severe fruit cracking; the warmer zone 9 edge adds a chill shortfall. Sweet cherry is unsuitable across the region; Southern growers do far better with peach or with rabbiteye blueberry.
se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: Sweet cherry does not suit the Southeast. The summers are too hot and humid and the rain splits the fruit, so disease and cracking make it a frustrating, unreliable crop. Grow peaches here instead.
se_gulf.chill_basis_seasoned: Southeastern winters bank enough chill inland (roughly 650 to 1,000 hours at zone 8), tapering toward the Gulf, so chill is not the only problem: the binding limits for sweet cherry are the warm humidity that drives disease and the harvest-season rain that cracks the fruit.
se_gulf.chill_basis_beginner: Winters inland are cold enough for sweet cherry's chill, but that is not the issue here. The heat, humidity, and rain are what make sweet cherry fail in the Southeast.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Interior California (the cherry districts of the San Joaquin and Sacramento valleys and foothills) is prime sweet cherry country: dry spring-and-summer air keeps disease and cracking low, and zone 8 winters bank enough chill for most standard cultivars. Choose by chill match, self-fertility, and ripening season, and net against birds.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Interior California is one of the best places for sweet cherries: the dry air keeps disease and cracking down, and winters are cold enough for most varieties. Pick a variety that matches your chill, sort out pollination, and net the tree against birds.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost risk is modest but real in cold valley pockets at the early March bloom; favor frost-safe sites, and choose adequate-chill cultivars as winters trend warmer.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Lower-elevation zone 9 interior banks less chill (around 300 to 950 hours), so it fruits in good years with mid- to low-chill cultivars and is unreliable for high-chill standards like Bing in warm winters. Favor lower-chill selections and the dry-climate advantage of low disease and cracking.
9.suitability_note_beginner: The warmer interior (zone 9) banks less winter cold, so sweet cherries fruit in good years with lower-chill varieties but miss in mild winters. Choose a lower-chill variety, and enjoy that the dry air keeps disease and cracking down.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Early bloom can occasionally meet a late freeze in low-lying ground; the more common limit is whether the winter banked enough chill for the variety.

ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: Interior California is the heart of West Coast sweet cherry growing. Higher-chill zone 8 valleys and foothills crop the broad variety range reliably in dry air that keeps disease and cracking low; the warmer, lower-chill zone 9 edge fruits in good years with lower-chill cultivars and runs short in mild winters. Chill adequacy, not heat or disease, is the variable to watch.
ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: Interior California is one of the best regions for sweet cherries. The cooler, higher zone 8 areas grow most varieties well in dry air that keeps disease and cracking down, while the warmer zone 9 areas need lower-chill varieties and miss some mild winters.
ca_interior.chill_basis_seasoned: Interior California banks roughly 300 to 1,100 chill hours depending on elevation, enough for the mid-to-high-chill range in the cooler zone 8 valleys and foothills but only the lower-chill set in warm zone 9 winters. The dry climate is the region's advantage, holding disease and rain cracking to a minimum.
ca_interior.chill_basis_beginner: Interior California usually gets enough winter cold for most sweet cherry varieties in the cooler areas, and only lower-chill varieties in the warmest parts. The dry air is a big plus, keeping disease and fruit cracking low.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Inland north-coast valleys bank a declining 300 to 800 chill hours; mid-to-low-chill cultivars fruit in good years, and the high-chill standards do not. Favor cultivars at or below your typical local chill, and expect short winters to thin the crop. The mild, drier inland air keeps disease moderate.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Inland from the coast, sweet cherries can fruit in good years if you pick a lower-chill variety. Mild winters will sometimes mean a light crop, and the high-chill standards will not get enough cold.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is a minor risk on the mild coast; the real limit is whether the winter banks enough chill for the variety you chose.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: Cooler coastal zone 10 banks low chill, often under about 200 hours, below even the lowest-chill sweet cherry's roughly 250-hour need. The tree grows easily in the mild climate, but blossoms drop without setting a dependable crop. Of viable cultivars, none is low-chill enough for this coastal chill.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Right on the cooler coast, winters are usually too mild for sweet cherry to fruit, even the low-chill kinds. The tree will grow but give little or no fruit.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: Mild maritime winters make chill adequacy the deciding factor on the north coast. Inland zone 9 valleys bank enough for mid-to-low-chill cultivars; the cooler coastal zone 10 falls below even the lowest-chill sweet cherry's need, so the tree grows but rarely fruits. Frost is a minor risk; the limit is chill, not cold.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: Near the Northern California coast, winters are mild. A bit inland (zone 9) a low-chill variety can fruit in good years, but right on the cool coast (zone 10) winters are too mild for sweet cherry to fruit at all.
ca_north_coast.chill_basis_seasoned: North-coast winters are mild and bank only about 150 to 800 chill hours, declining toward the coast. Inland zone 9 suits lower-chill cultivars; coastal zone 10 usually falls below even the roughly 250 hours the lowest-chill sweet cherry needs.
ca_north_coast.chill_basis_beginner: Coastal Northern California has mild winters with limited cold. Inland, a low-chill variety may fruit; right on the coast, even those usually do not get enough cold.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Cooler, slightly inland south-coast sites bank only about 200 to 550 chill hours, right at or just below the roughly 250 hours the lowest-chill cultivars (Royal Lee, Minnie Royal) need. Crops are light and inconsistent at best; the tree usually survives but rarely sets a dependable crop. The low-chill pair is the only thing worth trying, in the coolest winters only.
9.suitability_note_beginner: In the cooler inland parts of the Southern California coast, even a low-chill cherry usually does not get quite enough winter cold, so crops are rare and light. The tree survives but seldom fruits.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: The warmest south-coast zone 10 sites bank under about 150 chill hours, well below even the lowest-chill sweet cherry. The tree grows in the mild climate but the blossoms drop without setting fruit. This is a no-crop case, not a marginal one.
10.suitability_note_beginner: In the warmest coastal areas, winters are far too mild for sweet cherry to fruit, even the low-chill kinds. The tree will grow but give essentially no fruit.

ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: Chill scarcity defines the south coast for sweet cherry. The cooler inland zone 9 sites sit right at the threshold of the lowest-chill cultivars and crop only lightly and rarely; the warmer coastal zone 10 falls well short, so the tree survives but does not fruit. Heat and survival are never the issue; chill is.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: Along the Southern California coast, winters are too mild for sweet cherry. Even the low-chill varieties barely fruit in the coolest inland spots and not at all near the warm coast. The tree grows but gives little or no fruit.
ca_south_coast.chill_basis_seasoned: Southern-coast California winters are mild and bank only about 50 to 550 chill hours. Only the low-chill cultivars have any chance, and even they fall at or below their roughly 250-hour need across most of the region.
ca_south_coast.chill_basis_beginner: The Southern California coast has very mild winters with little cold. Even low-chill sweet cherries usually cannot get the cold they need, so fruit is rare to none.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 desert sites bank only about 150 to 400 chill hours, below even the low-chill sweet cherry's roughly 250-hour need in most winters, and the extreme summer heat is hostile to the fruit. The tree may survive with care but does not set a dependable crop. Sweet cherry is essentially a no-grow here; the desert suits low-chill peaches far better.
9.suitability_note_beginner: The desert is too mild in winter (not enough chill) and far too hot in summer for sweet cherry. The tree may survive but will give little or no fruit. Grow a low-chill peach instead.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: The hottest, lowest-chill desert sites bank under about 150 chill hours, far below any sweet cherry, and the fierce summer heat compounds the problem. The tree survives the heat poorly and does not fruit. Not a sweet cherry location.
10.suitability_note_beginner: The hottest desert spots are far too mild in winter and too hot in summer for sweet cherry. Expect little to no fruit, and a tree that struggles in the heat.

ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: The California desert is doubly wrong for sweet cherry: winters bank too little chill and summers are brutally hot, a climate sweet cherry tolerates poorly. The tree may survive with care but does not set a dependable crop in either zone. Low-chill peaches and figs are the better desert stone-fruit and tree-fruit choices.
ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: The California desert is too mild in winter and far too hot in summer for sweet cherry. The tree will not get the cold it needs and struggles in the heat, so expect little or no fruit. Grow a low-chill peach or a fig instead.
ca_desert.chill_basis_seasoned: Low-desert California winters bank only about 100 to 400 chill hours, below even the low-chill sweet cherry's roughly 250-hour need, and warm days subtract from the running total. Combined with extreme summer heat, the region cannot support a dependable sweet cherry crop.
ca_desert.chill_basis_beginner: The California desert has very mild winters with little cold and very hot summers. Sweet cherry cannot get the chill it needs and does not handle the heat, so it will not fruit here.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Inland warm-arid zone 8 (the Texas Hill Country and similar) banks adequate chill (around 450 to 850 hours), but sweet cherry is a poor fit: intense summer heat, late-spring frosts on the early bloom, and bacterial-canker and borer pressure make a dependable crop unrealistic. Local growers do far better with low-chill peaches and plums.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Although winters are cold enough, sweet cherry does poorly in warm, dry regions like the Texas Hill Country: summer heat, late frosts, and disease make a dependable crop unrealistic. Grow low-chill peaches or plums instead.

warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: Warm-arid inland regions bank enough chill for sweet cherry, but heat, late-spring frost on the early bloom, and bacterial-canker and borer pressure make it an unsuitable crop. Sweet cherry is not recommended here; low-chill peaches and plums are the adapted stone fruits.
warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: Warm, dry inland regions are cold enough in winter for sweet cherry but too hot and frost-prone in the growing season, so it is not a workable crop. Grow low-chill peaches or plums instead.
warm_arid.chill_basis_seasoned: Inland warm-arid winters bank roughly 450 to 850 chill hours, enough for many cultivars, so chill is not the limit. The binding problems for sweet cherry are summer heat, late-spring frost on the early bloom, and disease and borer pressure.
warm_arid.chill_basis_beginner: Winters here are cold enough for sweet cherry's chill, but the summer heat, late frosts, and disease are what make it fail. A low-chill peach is the better choice.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: The Arizona low desert banks only about 100 to 400 chill hours, below even the low-chill sweet cherry's roughly 250-hour need in most winters, and the extreme summer heat is hostile to the crop. Sweet cherry is unsuitable here; the low desert grows low-chill peaches, apricots, and figs instead.
9.suitability_note_beginner: The Arizona low desert is too mild in winter and far too hot in summer for sweet cherry. It will not get the cold it needs and cannot take the heat, so it is not a workable crop. Grow low-chill peaches, apricots, or figs instead.

low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: The Arizona low desert cannot bank the chill sweet cherry needs and is brutally hot in summer, so sweet cherry is unsuitable. The adapted low-desert tree fruits are low-chill peaches, apricots, and figs.
low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: The Arizona low desert is too mild in winter and too hot in summer for sweet cherry. Grow low-chill peaches, apricots, or figs instead.
low_desert_az.chill_basis_seasoned: Low-desert Arizona winters bank only about 100 to 400 chill hours, below even the low-chill sweet cherry's roughly 250-hour need, and warm days erode the total. The region cannot meet sweet cherry's chill requirement.
low_desert_az.chill_basis_beginner: The Arizona low desert has mild winters with little cold and fierce summer heat. Sweet cherry cannot get enough chill and cannot take the heat, so it will not fruit here.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: The central Florida peninsula banks almost no chill (roughly 50 to 350 hours) and is hot and humid, so sweet cherry cannot meet its chill requirement and would face heavy disease and cracking even if it could. Unsuitable; Florida's adapted stone fruits are the UF-bred low-chill peaches and plums.
10.suitability_note_beginner: The Florida peninsula is far too warm in winter and too hot and humid for sweet cherry. It will not get the cold it needs to fruit. Grow the special low-chill Florida peaches instead.

11.suitability_note_seasoned: South-peninsula zone 11 banks essentially no chill (under about 150 hours) in a subtropical climate; sweet cherry cannot fruit and the climate is fundamentally wrong for it. A genuine no-grow case.
11.suitability_note_beginner: South Florida has no winter cold for sweet cherry, so it cannot fruit. This is simply not a sweet cherry climate.

fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: The Florida peninsula banks far too little winter chill for sweet cherry, and its heat and humidity would drive heavy disease and cracking regardless. Sweet cherry is unsuitable across the peninsula; Florida's adapted choices are the University of Florida low-chill peaches and plums.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: The Florida peninsula is too warm in winter for sweet cherry to get the cold it needs, and too hot and humid besides. It will not fruit here. Grow the special low-chill Florida peaches instead.
fl_peninsula.chill_basis_seasoned: The Florida peninsula banks very little winter chill (well under 350 hours centrally, near zero in the south), far below any sweet cherry's requirement. The subtropical climate cannot deliver the chill the tree needs to bloom.
fl_peninsula.chill_basis_beginner: The Florida peninsula has warm winters with almost no cold. Sweet cherry needs far more chill than the peninsula provides, so it will not fruit here.

11.suitability_note_seasoned: Hawaii banks effectively zero chill, far below the requirement of any sweet cherry cultivar. Sweet cherry will not fruit; this is a genuine no-grow case, not a marginal one. Tropical and subtropical fruits are the adapted choices.
11.suitability_note_beginner: Sweet cherry needs cold winters to fruit, and Hawaii does not have them. It will not grow fruit here. Grow tropical fruits instead.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: Hawaii is the clearest case of the model telling the truth: sweet cherry needs a cold winter to fruit, and Hawaii has none. The verdict is simply unsuitable, with no fabricated planting calendar; tropical fruits are the adapted crops.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: Sweet cherry needs a cold winter to fruit, and Hawaii does not have one. It will not produce here. Grow tropical fruits instead.
hawaii_tropical.chill_basis_seasoned: Hawaii's tropical winters deliver essentially no chill (well under 150 hours), because temperatures rarely fall into the chilling range. Sweet cherry cannot meet its chill requirement here for any cultivar.
hawaii_tropical.chill_basis_beginner: Hawaii does not get cold winters, so sweet cherry never gets the chill it needs to make fruit.

crops.description_seasoned: Sweet cherry is a deciduous stone-fruit tree (Prunus avium) grown for firm, sugar-rich fruit eaten fresh off the tree. It is the most demanding of the common backyard fruit trees: most cultivars are SELF-STERILE and need a second, compatible variety blooming at the same time to set any fruit (the self-fertile cultivars, such as Stella, Lapins, and Sweetheart, are the exception), it blooms early and loses crops to late frost, rain near harvest splits the fruit, and birds will strip a ripe tree in a day. It also needs enough winter chill to bloom evenly, so variety is matched to your winters. Trained to a central leader, kept netted, and given a compatible pollinizer, it rewards the effort with fruit no store can match.
crops.description_beginner: A sweet cherry is a fruit tree that drops its leaves each winter and gives firm, sweet cherries to eat fresh. It is the trickiest of the usual backyard fruit trees. Most sweet cherries cannot pollinate themselves, so unless you choose a self-fertile kind (like Stella, Lapins, or Sweetheart) you need a second, matching variety blooming nearby or you get no fruit at all. On top of that, the early flowers can be killed by late frost, rain just before harvest splits the cherries open, and birds love a ripe tree. The tree also needs a cold-enough winter to bloom well, so you pick a variety that fits your area. Give it a pollinator partner, a net, and the right spot, and it pays you back with cherries far better than the store.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: A sweet cherry is ready when it reaches full, deep variety color (dark mahogany to near-black for Bing-type cultivars, full yellow-and-red blush for Rainier), the flesh is firm but gives slightly, and the sugars have peaked. Cherries do NOT ripen further off the tree, so taste-test before picking and leave them until fully colored and sweet. Pick with the stems on, pulling from the spur, not the fruit, to protect next year's fruiting spurs. Pick promptly once ripe: a rain on ripe fruit cracks it, and birds and spotted wing drosophila find a ripe crop fast.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: A sweet cherry is ripe when it has turned its full color (dark red to almost black for most types, or a yellow-and-red blush for Rainier), feels firm but gives a little, and tastes sweet. Unlike a peach, a cherry will not get sweeter after you pick it, so taste one first and only pick when they are fully colored and sweet. Pick with the stems attached, and pull from the little woody spur rather than yanking the fruit, so you do not strip next year's fruiting spurs. Pick as soon as they are ripe, because rain splits ripe cherries and birds and small vinegar flies move in quickly.
crops.bloom_time_seasoned: Sweet cherries bloom in early spring, typically March in mild regions and April to early May in cold-winter areas, usually just before or as the leaves emerge. Bloom is the year's chief vulnerability: the white blossoms open early and a hard late frost on open bloom kills that year's crop. Because most cultivars are self-incompatible, the pollinizer must bloom at the same time, so overlapping bloom periods, not just the presence of a second tree, decide fruit set.
crops.bloom_time_beginner: Sweet cherry trees flower in early spring, around March where winters are mild and April into early May where they are cold, usually right before the leaves come out. The early flowers are the tree's weak point, because a hard late frost can kill the open blooms and the tiny fruit. And since most sweet cherries need a partner to pollinate them, the two trees have to bloom at the same time, so matching bloom timing matters as much as having a second tree.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Sweet cherry is notably less cold-hardy than peach or sour cherry, rated to roughly zones 5 to 9, with reliable cropping in zones 5 to 8. The tree and its fruit buds begin to suffer winter injury at about -10°F and colder, so zones 3 and 4 are generally too cold for a dependable tree. The warm limit is not heat but chill: where winters no longer bank enough chill hours, a thriving tree blooms poorly and sets little. Sweet cherry is also poorly adapted to the hot, humid Southeast, where brown rot, bacterial canker, and harvest-season rain make it a frustrating crop regardless of zone.
crops.hardiness_notes_beginner: Sweet cherry is less tough than peach or sour cherry. It does best in zones 5 through 8, and below about -10°F the tree and its flower buds start to get damaged, so zones 3 and 4 are usually too cold for a reliable tree. In the warmest zones the problem is not heat but a lack of winter cold, which the tree needs to bloom well. Sweet cherry also struggles in the hot, humid Southeast, where disease and harvest rain make it hard to grow no matter the zone.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Sweet cherries need a stretch of winter cold, counted as chill hours (hours between about 32°F and 45°F), to break dormancy and bloom evenly. Most standard cultivars need roughly 700 to 1,000 hours or more (Washington's market cultivars run higher still), so sweet cherry is a high-chill tree for most of its range. A small group of low-chill cultivars bred for mild-winter California (Royal Lee and Minnie Royal, about 200 to 300 hours, which pollinize each other) extends it to warm-winter zones. Match the variety to the chill your winters actually bank: too little and the blossoms drop without setting.
crops.chill_hours_note_beginner: Sweet cherry trees need enough cold winter hours, called chill hours, before they will bloom properly in spring. Most kinds need a lot, roughly 700 to 1,000 hours or more, which is why sweet cherry suits cold-winter areas. A few special low-chill kinds (Royal Lee and Minnie Royal, about 200 to 300 hours) were bred for mild-winter California and need only a little cold. If your winters are mild, you must choose a low-chill variety, or the flowers fall off without making fruit.
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Plant a second compatible variety unless you choose a self-fertile one. Most sweet cherries are self-incompatible: a lone Bing sets no crop. Compatibility is governed by S-alleles, so the pollinizer must be in a DIFFERENT incompatibility group AND bloom at the same time (the classic trap is that Bing, Lambert, and Royal Ann/Napoleon are all cross-incompatible and cannot pollinize one another). The self-fertile cultivars (Stella, Lapins, Sweetheart, Skeena, Black Gold, White Gold, Compact Stella) fruit alone and serve as universal pollinizers for most self-sterile varieties of matching bloom. Bees do the work, so strong bee activity during the short bloom is essential for set.
crops.pollinator_notes_beginner: Plant a second compatible variety unless you pick a self-fertile one. Most sweet cherries cannot pollinate themselves, so a single Bing tree gives no cherries at all. The second tree has to be a different, compatible variety that blooms at the same time (watch out: Bing, Lambert, and Royal Ann cannot pollinate each other). The easy way around all of this is to plant a self-fertile variety like Stella, Lapins, or Sweetheart, which fruits on its own and can also pollinate most other cherries. Bees carry the pollen, so you want lots of bee activity during the short bloom.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: In the planting year, prioritize establishment over fruit. Plant a dormant bare-root tree in late winter, head it back at planting to begin a central-leader framework, keep a weed-free, mulched circle around the trunk, and water consistently through the first two seasons. Remove any fruit that sets. Confirm a compatible pollinizer is planted nearby unless the variety is self-fertile. Hold fertilizer until growth begins, and never feed late in the season, which invites the winter injury that opens the door to bacterial canker.
crops.year_one_notes_beginner: The first year is about helping the tree settle in, not getting fruit. Plant a bare-root tree in late winter while it is still resting, cut it back at planting to start a single main trunk shape, keep a mulched, weed-free ring around the trunk, and water it steadily through the first couple of years. Pull off any fruit that forms. Make sure a partner pollinizer tree is planted nearby unless your variety is self-fertile. Wait to fertilize until the tree starts growing, and never feed late in the year, since soft late growth gets winter damage that lets disease in.

pollination.notes_seasoned: Self-incompatible for most cultivars: a single tree of a self-sterile variety (Bing, Rainier, Lambert) sets no crop and needs a compatible pollinizer of a different S-allele group blooming concurrently, ideally within about 100 feet for good bee transfer. Self-fertile cultivars (Stella, Lapins, Sweetheart, Compact Stella) fruit alone and pollinize most others. Bees are the vector; cold, wet, or windy bloom weather suppresses their activity and the crop with it.
pollination.notes_beginner: Most sweet cherries cannot pollinate themselves. A single self-sterile tree (like Bing or Rainier) will not make fruit unless a different, compatible cherry blooms nearby at the same time, ideally within about 100 feet so bees can carry pollen between them. The self-fertile kinds (Stella, Lapins, Sweetheart) make fruit on their own and also pollinate other cherries. Bees do the carrying, so a cold or rainy spell during the short bloom can mean a poor crop.

crops.establishment_note: Most sweet cherries begin bearing about 4 years after planting, sooner (around year 3) on a precocious dwarfing rootstock such as Gisela 5 or Gisela 6, and later on a full-size Mazzard tree.
crops.recommended_rootstock_note: Unlike peach, cherry rootstocks DO control tree size. Gisela 6 holds a sweet cherry to a pickable, nettable 15 to 18 feet, bears years sooner than a full-size Mazzard, and tolerates heavier soil; Gisela 5 dwarfs further (8 to 12 feet) for a patio or easily netted tree but needs careful crop-load management.

rootstock_options.name: Mazzard
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask for your variety on Mazzard for a full-size tree on heavier or wetter soils.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: The oldest and most widely used sweet cherry rootstock and the Pacific Northwest benchmark. Vigorous and full-size, with a fibrous root system that tolerates heavier and wetter soils better than Mahaleb. The trade-off is a large tree (25 to 40 feet) that is slow to bear and hard to net or pick; needs heading and training to stay manageable.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: A full-size, traditional rootstock that handles heavier and wetter soils well. The downside is a big tree that takes several years to fruit and is hard to cover against birds, so it suits a grower with space who will prune it down.

rootstock_options.name: Mahaleb
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask for Mahaleb for deep, very well-drained soils where you want a precocious, cold-hardy tree.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: A somewhat size-reducing, precocious, cold-hardy seedling rootstock that bears sooner than Mazzard. Its hard limit is drainage: it performs only in deep, well-drained soils and fails in heavy or wet ground or high water tables, where it is prone to root problems. Choose it for dry, well-drained sites.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: A rootstock that makes a somewhat smaller, earlier-bearing, cold-hardy tree. It only works in deep, well-drained soil, though, and does poorly in heavy or wet ground, so skip it if your soil holds water.

rootstock_options.name: Gisela 5
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask for Gisela 5 for a small, very early-bearing, easily netted tree on most soils.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: A true dwarfing rootstock, roughly half the size of Mazzard, very precocious (bears in 2 to 3 years) and very cold-hardy, doing well even on heavier soils. The catch is crop-load management: it sets so heavily so young that fruit can be small and the tree overcropped without thinning and good feeding. The best choice for a small, nettable backyard tree.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: A small, dwarfing rootstock about half the size of a Mazzard tree, very cold-hardy, and quick to fruit (in 2 to 3 years), even in heavier soil. It can set so much fruit so young that the cherries come out small unless you feed it well and thin, but it makes the easiest tree to cover and pick.

rootstock_options.name: Gisela 6
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask for Gisela 6 for a productive, early-bearing, soil-tolerant backyard tree.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: A semi-dwarfing rootstock that holds the tree to roughly 80 to 90 percent of Mazzard (about 15 to 20 feet as a pruned backyard tree), very precocious despite its vigor, productive, and well suited to heavier soils. The most adaptable all-round backyard choice and the recommended default here.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: A rootstock that makes a medium-size tree, around 15 to 20 feet, that fruits early, bears heavily, and handles heavier soils. It is the most all-round backyard choice and the one recommended here as a good balance of size and crop.

rootstock_options.name: Colt
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask for Colt in mild-winter areas with heavier soils where cold hardiness is not a concern.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: A vigorous rootstock somewhat smaller than Mazzard that tolerates heavier soils and resists some replant problems. Its weakness is cold hardiness: Colt is NOT cold-hardy, so it suits mild-winter regions and is a poor pick where winters are severe.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: A vigorous rootstock a bit smaller than Mazzard that handles heavier soils. Its weak point is cold: Colt is not cold-hardy, so it is for mild-winter areas only, not cold-winter regions.

pet_safe.note: The flesh is fine, but the pits, seeds, and leaves contain cyanide compounds and are toxic to cats, dogs, and horses.

primary.name: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center
UF/IFAS Northwest District Horticulture Vegetable Garden Planting Dates (Florida Panhandle)
UF/IFAS SP 103/VH021 Florida Vegetable Gardening Guide
UGA Extension Bulletin 577 (Vegetable Garden Planting Chart)

crops.name: Turnip

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Turnips like loose, fertile, well-drained soil with no hard layer underneath. Loosen the bed about 8 to 10 inches down and rake out rocks and clods, because the root grows rounder and smoother in loose soil and comes out forked or lumpy in packed, stony ground. Mix in some compost or well-rotted (never fresh) manure, since fresh manure can make the roots branch and grow hairy. Aim for a soil pH around 6.0 to 6.8. If clubroot, a disease that swells and deforms the roots, has been a problem in your garden, adding lime to raise the pH closer to 7.0 to 7.2 helps hold it back.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Turnips do best in deep, loose, fertile, well-drained soil rich in organic matter, ideally a sandy loam or loam. They are quick and shallow-rooted compared with carrots, but stones, clods, and compaction still cause forking and misshapen roots, so a friable seedbed matters. Work in well-finished compost or well-rotted manure rather than fresh manure, which drives leafy top growth and can cause hairy, branched roots. Keep pH in the slightly acidic to neutral range, about 6.0 to 6.8. The brassica-specific soil caution is clubroot: the soilborne pathogen Plasmodiophora brassicae thrives in wet, poorly drained, acidic ground, so on a clubroot-prone bed improve drainage and lime toward a neutral to slightly alkaline pH of about 7.0 to 7.2, which suppresses it.

ph.note_beginner: Soil pH measures how acidic or alkaline your soil is, on a scale from 1 to 14 where 7 is neutral. Turnips like it slightly acidic to neutral, about 6.0 to 6.8, though they grow across a fairly wide range. A cheap soil test from your local extension office tells you your number and whether to add lime. One turnip-specific point: a root disease called clubroot is worse in acidic soil, so if your turnips have come out swollen and deformed, raising the pH toward 7.0 to 7.2 with lime helps hold the disease back.
ph.note_seasoned: Turnips grow best at a slightly acidic to neutral pH of about 6.0 to 6.8; Clemson recommends maintaining roughly 6.0 to 6.5, and Minnesota gives a workable range of about 6.0 to 7.5. The brassica-specific reason to watch pH is clubroot: the pathogen is favored by acidic soil, and the standard cultural control is to lime the bed toward a neutral to slightly alkaline pH of about 7.2 to 7.5 where the disease is established. There is thus a mild tension between the ideal growing pH and the clubroot-suppressing pH, resolved by liming only on a clubroot-prone bed. A standard soil test from your local extension office removes the guesswork before sowing.

fertilizer.timing: Work compost and a balanced fertilizer into the bed before sowing; side-dress lightly once seedlings are established, more for a greens crop than a root crop.
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Turnips are light to moderate feeders. Work well-finished compost and a balanced fertilizer into the bed before sowing, then side-dress lightly once the tops are established if growth is weak. The key brassica-root caution is nitrogen: excess nitrogen grows lush tops at the expense of the root and can leave roots small and poorly formed, so go easy where you want good roots. A crop grown mainly for greens tolerates and even rewards more nitrogen, since the leaves are the harvest. Avoid fresh manure, which both over-supplies nitrogen and causes hairy, branched roots.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Turnips do not need heavy feeding. Mix a balanced fertilizer and some compost into the bed before planting, and give one light feeding later only if the plants look weak and pale. Go easy on nitrogen if you want good roots, because too much grows big leafy tops and small roots. If you are growing turnips mainly for the greens, a little extra nitrogen is fine, since the leaves are what you are after. Do not use fresh manure, which makes the roots hairy and forked.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: Turnips want steady phosphorus and potassium for root development plus modest nitrogen, so a balanced blend such as a 10-10-10 worked into the bed before sowing suits a root crop, with most of the feeding coming from incorporated compost. Hold back on nitrogen for roots, since it pushes leafy tops over the root; a greens crop can take more. Skip fresh manure, which over-supplies nitrogen and branches the roots.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: The three numbers on a fertilizer bag are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium (N-P-K). Turnips do well with a balanced blend where the numbers are about even, like a 10-10-10, mixed into the soil before planting along with compost. Do not pile on high-nitrogen fertilizer if you want roots, since it grows leaves instead. If you are after the greens, a bit more nitrogen is okay.

companions.note_beginner: Turnips are easygoing neighbors. They share a bed nicely with leafy greens like lettuce, with onions and other alliums, which grow upright and shallow and do not crowd the roots, and they do well following beans or peas that added nitrogen to the soil. The main plants to keep away from turnips are their own cabbage-family relatives: cabbage, broccoli, kale, radish, and mustard. These cousins share the turnip's pests, the flea beetle and the cabbage maggot, plus the soil disease clubroot, so growing them together lets those problems build up. As always, do not trust every companion chart online, since many of their claims have never been tested.
companions.note_seasoned: Turnips fit easily into mixed beds, and their clearest companion rule is the brassica avoid: keep them away from the other cabbage-family crops (cabbage, broccoli, kale, radish, mustard), which share the turnip's flea beetles, cabbage maggot, and the soilborne clubroot pathogen, so clustering the family concentrates that pressure. On the positive side, leafy greens like lettuce and shallow-rooted alliums share the surface layer while the turnip swells just below, and a legume grown the season before leaves nitrogen behind. Treat the good pairings as sensible defaults rather than proven effects: as University of Minnesota's research review stresses, most companion-planting claims are tradition rather than tested science, so use them as a starting point and watch your own results.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Lettuce and other leafy greens
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Lettuce and other quick, shallow-rooted greens grow near the surface and finish fast, while the turnip root swells just below them, so they share a bed without fighting for the same space. Both like the same cool weather, a handy way to fit more into a small garden.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Pairing fast, shallow cool-season greens over a slower-swelling root is the standard complementary root-depth and timing rationale; sound and widely taught but a space-and-soil benefit rather than a measured turnip-specific effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Lettuce and turnips interplant well on root structure and timing: lettuce is shallow-rooted and quick, the turnip swells just under the surface and takes a little longer, so they draw on different layers and share the cool-season window. This is a space-and-soil benefit rather than a pest one, and one of the more dependable interplants for that reason.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Onions and other alliums
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Onions, leeks, and garlic grow tall and narrow with shallow roots, so they tuck between turnip rows without crowding the roots, and their strong smell is widely used to help confuse some leaf-eating pests. A popular, space-saving pairing.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Alliums are widely recommended as root-crop companions for efficient space use and scent-based pest masking. The space benefit is sound; the pest deterrence is mechanistically plausible but not established in a turnip-specific trial, so likely rather than research_backed.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Alliums are a classic interplant for root crops: shallow-rooted and upright, they share the bed without competing for the turnip's space, and their sulfur volatiles are widely credited with masking the crop from some leaf-feeding pests. The space-use benefit is solid; the pest deterrence is plausible but not proven for turnips specifically.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Beans and peas (as a preceding crop)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Beans and peas pull nitrogen from the air and leave some in the soil, so turnips planted after a legume crop get a gentle nutrient boost. They are better as the crop you grow before turnips than right alongside, since bushy legumes can shade the low turnips.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Following a nitrogen-fixing legume is sound rotation practice (extension rotation guides recommend it); the benefit is a soil-fertility one realized in sequence rather than a measured co-planting effect, so traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Legumes earn their place in the turnip rotation more than the turnip bed: beans and peas fix nitrogen and leave residual fertility, so a turnip crop following a legume benefits, which is why extension rotation guides list legumes among good preceding crops for brassicas. Grown concurrently the value is mostly space-sharing, and tall climbing legumes shade the low turnip, so the cleaner use is in sequence.

good_seasoned.name: Lettuce and other leafy greens
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Shallow-rooted, fast greens occupy the surface while the turnip swells just below, an efficient cool-season use of bed space.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Standard complementary-root-depth space rationale among cool-season crops; not a measured turnip-specific effect.

good_seasoned.name: Onions and other alliums
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Upright, shallow-rooted alliums share the bed without crowding the turnip, and their scent is commonly credited with masking the crop from leaf pests; a popular but not turnip-trial-proven pairing.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Allium space-use and scent-masking are widely recommended for root crops and mechanistically plausible, but not established in a turnip-specific extension trial; labeled likely.

good_seasoned.name: Beans and peas (as a preceding crop)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A nitrogen-fixing legume grown before turnips leaves residual fertility; extension rotation guides list legumes among good preceding crops for the cabbage family.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Sound rotation practice realized in sequence rather than a measured co-planting effect.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Other cabbage-family crops (cabbage, broccoli, kale, radish, mustard)
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Cabbage, broccoli, kale, radish, mustard, and other cabbage-family plants are turnip's close relatives and share its pests, the flea beetle and the cabbage maggot, plus the soil disease clubroot. Growing them right next to turnips lets those problems build up, so give them separate spots and rotate where each goes each year.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Turnip, cabbage, broccoli, kale, radish, and mustard are all Brassicaceae and share flea beetle, cabbage maggot, and clubroot. Clustering the family concentrates that pest and disease pressure; sound rotation logic (UMN advises rotating brassicas) rather than a measured antagonism, so traditional/medium.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Turnips are brassicas, so the other cabbage-family crops, cabbage, broccoli, kale, radish, mustard, share their exact pest and disease spectrum: flea beetles, the cabbage maggot, and the soilborne clubroot pathogen. Clustering the family in one bed sustains and concentrates that pressure, the same reason extension sources advise rotating among brassicas rather than planting them together year after year.

bad_seasoned.name: Other cabbage-family crops (cabbage, broccoli, kale, radish, mustard)
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Other Brassicaceae crops share turnip's pests (flea beetle, cabbage maggot) and the soilborne clubroot pathogen. Planting the family together sustains a shared pest and disease bridge, the same reason extension sources advise rotating among related crucifers.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Shared Brassicaceae pest and disease overlap (flea beetle, cabbage maggot, clubroot) is documented at the family level; the co-planting risk is a sound inference plus standard rotation guidance, not a directly studied pairing.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny, round shot-hole punctures riddling the leaves, the classic flea-beetle signature, heaviest on young spring seedlings and along bed edges. The beetles themselves are minute, shiny black or bronze, with enlarged hind legs, and they spring away like fleas when disturbed. On a turnip grown for greens the damage is more than cosmetic, since riddled leaves are the harvest; on a root crop a vigorous stand outgrows light feeding, but a seedling losing much of its leaf area slows down.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Lots of tiny round holes peppering the leaves, like buckshot, worst on young seedlings in spring. The beetles are very small, dark, and shiny, with big back legs, and they hop away like fleas the moment you get close. If you are growing turnips for the greens this really matters, since the chewed leaves are what you eat; for the root, fast-growing plants usually shrug it off, but tiny seedlings can be set back.
pests.cause_seasoned: Adult flea beetles, chiefly the crucifer flea beetle (Phyllotreta cruciferae) and striped flea beetle (Phyllotreta striolata), which overwinter in leaf litter and field edges and emerge in early spring to feed on brassica foliage. Turnip, radish, mustard, and other crucifers are highly preferred hosts. Pressure is heaviest in spring and early summer and tapers as the season warms, which is one reason fall turnip crops face less of it.
pests.cause_beginner: Small beetles that spend the winter in leaf litter and weeds and come out in early spring hungry for cabbage-family leaves. Turnips and their relatives (radish, mustard) are among their favorite foods. They do the most damage in spring and early summer and ease off as it gets hotter, so fall turnips usually face fewer of them.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: On a vigorous stand a well-watered turnip usually outgrows light feeding. Where pressure is heavy on seedlings, a floating row cover set at sowing and sealed at the edges excludes the beetles entirely, the most reliable home defense. Kaolin clay reduces feeding, and spinosad or pyrethrin products are labeled options if a seedling stand is losing more than roughly a quarter to a third of its leaf area; scout in the cool morning when the beetles are sluggish.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: A healthy, well-watered turnip patch usually grows right through light damage. If the little seedlings are getting hammered, cover the row with a floating row cover (a light fabric) right after planting and tuck in the edges so the beetles cannot get under it. Dusting with kaolin clay helps, and sprays like spinosad or pyrethrin are options if seedlings are losing a lot of leaf. Check in the cool morning, when the beetles are slow.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Clean up crop debris and weeds at the end of the season to cut overwintering sites. A row cover over the seedbed is the most reliable defense for early spring sowings. Favoring fall plantings, which see lighter pressure, and keeping the stand growing fast with even moisture both reduce impact.
pests.prevention_beginner: Clear away old plants and weeds at the end of the season so fewer beetles survive the winter nearby. Covering the seedbed with a row cover is the surest fix for early spring turnips. Leaning on fall plantings, which get hit less, and keeping the turnips growing fast with steady water also help.

pests.name: Cabbage maggot
pests.symptoms_seasoned: The damage is underground: small, white, legless maggots tunnel and score the surface and interior of the root, leaving winding brown trails that ruin the turnip and open the door to rot. Aboveground, infested plants may look off-color, wilted, or stunted. It is most common in cool, wet springs and in soil rich in undecomposed organic matter. A scored root is unsalable but a useful sentinel, since pulling and destroying it removes maggots before they pupate.
pests.symptoms_beginner: The trouble is underground. Small white legless maggots tunnel into the turnip, leaving winding brown trails that spoil the root and let rot set in. Aboveground the plant may look pale, wilted, or stunted. It shows up most in cool, wet springs and in soil full of un-rotted material. A tunneled turnip is ruined, but pulling and tossing it right away gets the maggots out before they become the next generation of flies.
pests.cause_seasoned: Larvae of the cabbage maggot (Delia radicum), a small gray fly that overwinters as pupae in the soil. In spring the adults emerge and females lay white eggs at the base of crucifer stems and in nearby soil cracks; the eggs hatch within about a week and the maggots feed on roots for three to four weeks before pupating. It attacks the whole cabbage family, including turnip, radish, cabbage, and broccoli, with several generations a year and the worst damage in cool, moist spring weather.
pests.cause_beginner: The maggots (young) of the cabbage maggot fly, a small gray fly. It spends the winter as pupae in the soil, and in spring the females lay tiny white eggs at the base of cabbage-family plants. The eggs hatch in about a week and the maggots burrow into the roots for three to four weeks. It goes after the whole cabbage family, turnips, radishes, cabbage, broccoli, and is worst in cool, damp spring weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no rescue for a root already tunneled. Pull and destroy infested turnips (do not compost them) to keep maggots from completing their cycle. Insecticide drenches are difficult and rarely worthwhile in a home garden, and are pointless once the maggots have left the root to pupate, so the lever is prevention.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot save a turnip that is already tunneled. Pull up and throw away (do not compost) the affected ones so the maggots cannot grow into more flies. There is no good home spray for this, and sprays do nothing once the maggots have already left the root, so prevention is the real fix.
pests.prevention_seasoned: A floating row cover sealed at the edges at sowing is the most effective home defense, since it blocks the egg-laying flies; be sure no flies are already in the soil from a previous crop. Rotate turnips and other crucifers away from beds that grew them recently, avoid fresh manure and freshly turned-under residue that attract the flies, and favor fall plantings, which see less pressure than cool wet spring.
pests.prevention_beginner: The best home defense is a row cover laid over the bed right after sowing and tucked in at the edges, so the flies cannot reach the plants to lay eggs, just make sure the soil is not already carrying them from an earlier crop. Move turnips away from spots that grew cabbage-family crops recently, avoid fresh manure, and lean toward fall planting, which usually has fewer maggots than cool wet spring.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of small, soft-bodied insects, often grayish-green and sometimes coated with a waxy bloom, collect on the undersides of leaves and on new growth, leaving leaves curled, yellowed, and sticky with honeydew that can blacken with sooty mold. On turnips the culprits are typically the turnip aphid (Lipaphis erysimi) and the cabbage aphid (Brevicoryne brassicae). Beyond direct feeding they can transmit virus, so colonies on the greens are worth removing early.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Little soft insects, often gray-green and sometimes dusty-looking, gather in clusters on the undersides of leaves and on new growth. Leaves curl and yellow and turn sticky from the sugary honeydew the aphids leave behind, which can grow a black sooty mold. On turnips these are usually the turnip aphid and cabbage aphid. They can also spread plant viruses, so knock them back early, especially if you are eating the greens.
pests.cause_seasoned: The turnip aphid and cabbage aphid, sap-feeding insects specific to the cabbage family. Populations build fastest in mild weather and on lush, over-fertilized growth, and winged forms move them in from cruciferous weeds and other brassica crops. They can be a particular nuisance on fall greens crops.
pests.cause_beginner: Sap-sucking turnip and cabbage aphids that feed only on cabbage-family plants. They multiply fast in mild weather, especially on soft, over-fertilized growth, and fly in from weeds and other cabbage-family crops. They can be a real pest on fall turnip greens.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: A strong jet of water knocks colonies off the leaves and is often enough in a home garden. Natural enemies (lady beetles, lacewings, parasitic wasps) usually bring numbers down; where needed, insecticidal soap or horticultural oil sprayed on the undersides of leaves is effective, taking care to reach the protected cabbage-aphid colonies. Avoid over-fertilizing with nitrogen, which fuels buildup.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray the colonies off with a strong stream of water, which often does the trick. Ladybugs and other helpers usually take care of the rest; if not, insecticidal soap or horticultural oil on the undersides of the leaves works well. Do not over-feed with nitrogen, which just grows more aphids.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Encourage beneficial insects by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays, keep plants from being pushed with excess nitrogen, and control nearby cruciferous weeds that host the aphids. Inspect new growth and the undersides of leaves so colonies are caught small, and clear crop debris at season end.
pests.prevention_beginner: Let helpful bugs like ladybugs live in your garden by not spraying broadly, go easy on nitrogen fertilizer, and pull cabbage-family weeds nearby. Check the undersides of leaves now and then so you catch aphids while there are only a few, and clean up old plants at the end of the season.

pests.name: Harlequin bug
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Striking black-and-orange (or black-and-red) shield-shaped stink bugs feeding on the foliage, leaving pale, blotchy, stippled or wilted patches where they have sucked sap; heavy feeding can yellow and kill leaves and stunt or kill young plants. It is chiefly a warm-region pest, most damaging on fall and overwintering brassicas in the South, and it readily attacks turnip and its greens.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Showy black-and-orange (or black-and-red) shield-shaped bugs on the leaves, leaving pale, blotchy, stippled spots where they have sucked the juices out. A lot of them can yellow and kill leaves and even kill small plants. It is mainly a warm-weather pest, worst on fall and winter turnips and greens in the South.
pests.cause_seasoned: The harlequin bug (Murgantia histrionica), a stink bug that feeds almost exclusively on cabbage-family plants. Adults overwinter in garden debris in warmer regions and become active as the weather warms, with several generations a year; the barrel-shaped, black-and-white striped eggs are laid in neat double rows on the undersides of leaves.
pests.cause_beginner: The harlequin bug, a stink bug that feeds almost only on cabbage-family plants. The adults spend winter in garden trash in warm areas and get active as it warms up, with several generations a year. Look for its odd barrel-shaped, striped eggs lined up in two neat rows under the leaves.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Handpick adults, nymphs, and the distinctive egg rows into soapy water, which is effective in a home garden caught early. Remove and destroy heavily infested plants and brassica debris that harbor them. Insecticidal soap helps on nymphs; a trap crop of mustard or another preferred crucifer can concentrate the bugs for removal.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick off the adults, the young, and the striped egg rows by hand and drop them in soapy water, which works well if you start early. Pull and destroy badly infested plants and clean up cabbage-family debris. Insecticidal soap helps on the young bugs, and a patch of mustard planted as bait can draw them together so they are easy to remove.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Clear cabbage-family crop debris and weeds at season end to remove overwintering sites, the single most useful step. Rotate brassicas, scout the undersides of leaves for the egg rows, and use a trap crop where the bug is a recurring problem.
pests.prevention_beginner: Clean up old cabbage-family plants and weeds at the end of the season, which is the biggest help since that is where the bugs spend winter. Rotate where you plant brassicas, check under the leaves for the striped eggs, and plant a little mustard as bait if the bug keeps coming back.

diseases.name: Clubroot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Aboveground, plants are stunted and yellowish and wilt in the heat of the day even in moist soil, recovering overnight. The diagnostic sign is below ground: the roots are swollen, distorted, and clubbed into gnarled, spindle-shaped galls rather than forming a clean turnip, and they later rot. It is a soilborne disease that builds up where crucifers are grown repeatedly and is favored by wet, poorly drained, acidic soil.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Aboveground the plant looks stunted and yellow and wilts in the afternoon sun, then perks up at night. Underground is the giveaway: instead of a clean turnip, the roots swell into lumpy, club-shaped galls that eventually rot. It lives in the soil and builds up when you grow cabbage-family crops in the same spot over and over, especially in wet, acidic soil.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Plasmodiophora brassicae, a soilborne pathogen that infects the roots of cabbage-family plants and persists in soil as resting spores for many years. Wet, poorly drained, acidic soils favor infection, and the disease spreads on contaminated soil, tools, and transplants.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soil organism (Plasmodiophora brassicae) that attacks the roots of cabbage-family plants and survives in the soil for years. Wet, poorly drained, acidic soil makes it worse, and it spreads on dirty tools and on soil moved from an infected bed.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once a plant is infected; remove and destroy affected plants and do not compost them. Management is preventive across seasons: improve drainage and lime the soil toward a neutral to slightly alkaline pH of about 7.2 to 7.5, which suppresses the pathogen, and rotate crucifers out of the bed for several years.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no way to cure a plant that has it, so pull and throw away (do not compost) the affected ones. The fix is for next time: improve drainage, add lime to raise the soil pH toward 7.2 to 7.5, which holds the disease back, and keep cabbage-family crops out of that spot for a few years.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate turnips and other crucifers on a multi-year cycle (a long rotation of several years is advised where it is established), since the pathogen builds in soil grown to the family. Keep soil well drained and limed toward a neutral to slightly alkaline pH, start with clean soil and tools, and avoid moving soil from an infested bed. Raised beds with clean mix sidestep the problem where it is entrenched.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Do not grow turnips or other cabbage-family crops in the same bed year after year; move them on a multi-year cycle. Keep the soil well drained and add lime to raise the pH toward neutral, and avoid carrying soil from an infected bed on your tools. A raised bed with clean soil avoids it where it is a known problem.

diseases.name: White rust
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Raised, white to cream, blister-like pustules form on the undersides of leaves, with a faint yellow spot on the upper surface opposite each lesion. Heavy infection can distort leaves and, less commonly, the growing point. It is chiefly a foliar disease, most damaging on turnips grown for greens, and is favored by cool, moist weather.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Raised white or cream blister-like spots on the undersides of the leaves, with a faint yellow patch on the top of the leaf opposite each blister. A bad case can twist the leaves. It mostly affects the leaves, so it matters most when you are growing turnips for greens, and it likes cool, damp weather.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Albugo candida, a water mold (formerly classed as a fungus) specific to crucifers that survives as thick-walled resting spores on crop debris and in soil and spreads by airborne and splash-borne spores in cool, wet conditions. No fungicides are registered for it in the home garden, so control is cultural.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus-like water mold (Albugo candida) that lives on cabbage-family plants, survives on old plant debris, and spreads in cool, wet weather by spores carried on wind and splashing water. There is no home spray for it, so the fix is in how you grow the crop.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no home chemical control; remove and destroy infected leaves and badly affected plants to reduce spread, and improve airflow and drying. Cultural control carries the load: water at the base, space for airflow, and clear cruciferous weeds and debris that carry it.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no spray for the home garden, so pick off and throw away infected leaves and the worst plants, and help the plants dry out by giving them room. Water at the soil instead of overhead, and clear away cabbage-family weeds and old debris that carry it.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate crucifers, clear and destroy crop debris and cruciferous weeds that harbor the spores, and avoid overhead watering. Space and thin for airflow so foliage dries quickly, and use tolerant varieties where the disease recurs.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Do not grow cabbage-family crops in the same spot repeatedly, clear away old plant debris and weeds, and water at the base instead of overhead. Give plants room so the leaves dry fast, and choose a tolerant variety if it keeps coming back.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small, angular, pale green to yellow lesions on the upper leaf surface, bounded by the veins, with a grayish to white downy growth of spores on the corresponding undersides in damp weather. Affected areas later turn tan and papery. It chiefly disfigures the foliage and is most damaging in cool, moist conditions such as a wet fall.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Pale green to yellow angular patches on top of the leaves, with a grayish or white fuzzy growth underneath in damp weather; the spots later turn tan and papery. It mainly hurts the leaves and is worst in cool, wet weather, like a rainy fall, which is also when turnip greens are growing.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Peronospora parasitica (also called Hyaloperonospora parasitica), a water mold that infects crucifers in cool, moist conditions, with infection favored around 50 to 60°F. It survives on crop debris and related hosts and spreads in moist air and splashing water.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus-like water mold (Peronospora parasitica) that infects cabbage-family plants in cool, wet weather, best around 50 to 60°F. It survives on old plant debris and spreads in damp air and splashing water.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure for infected tissue; remove and destroy affected leaves to reduce spread, and improve airflow and drying. Cultural control is the mainstay for a home crop, with copper fungicides a last resort in a persistently wet season.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot cure infected leaves, so pick off and throw away the worst ones and help the plants dry out by giving them room. Keeping the leaves dry does most of the work; a copper fungicide is a last resort in a very wet stretch.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Water at the base rather than overhead, space and thin for airflow, and avoid working among wet plants. Rotate away from crucifers, clear crop debris, and where it recurs choose tolerant varieties.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Water at the soil instead of overhead, give plants room so air moves through, and stay out of the bed when the leaves are wet. Move turnips away from where you grew cabbage-family crops, clean up old debris, and pick a tolerant variety if it keeps showing up.

diseases.name: Alternaria leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small, circular, dark spots on the leaves, each with a yellow halo and characteristic concentric rings, that darken to a sooty center as spores build up and enlarge and merge in wet weather. It is primarily a foliar disease, most important on turnips grown for greens, and severe infection can reduce vigor and quality.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small, round, dark spots on the leaves, each with a yellow ring around it and faint target-like circles inside, that grow and run together in wet weather and turn sooty in the center. It mostly affects the leaves, so it matters most for turnip greens, and a bad case can slow the plant down.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Alternaria fungi (chiefly Alternaria brassicae), which are seedborne and survive on crop debris, spreading in splashing water and needing leaf wetness to infect. Warm, wet weather and prolonged wet foliage drive it.
diseases.cause_beginner: Alternaria fungi that can travel on seed and survive on old plant debris, spreading in splashing water and needing wet leaves to take hold. Warm, humid weather with wet foliage brings it on.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove badly spotted leaves, water at the base in the morning so foliage dries, and clear debris. Clean seed and airflow are the main home levers; a copper fungicide can help in a persistently wet season if started early.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick off the worst leaves, water at the soil in the morning so leaves dry quickly, and clean up debris. Using clean seed and giving plants room for airflow handle most of it; a copper fungicide can help in a very wet spell if you start early.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Use clean seed, avoid overhead watering, space for airflow, and rotate crucifers and clear debris that carry the fungi between seasons.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Use clean seed, water at the base instead of overhead, give plants room so the leaves dry, and clear away old plant material between plantings.

diseases.name: Black rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellow, V-shaped lesions advancing inward from the leaf margins, with the V pointing toward the midrib and the veins in the affected area turning black. Infected leaves yellow and die, and severe infection can rot the plant and move into the root. It is a bacterial disease of the whole cabbage family, spread in warm, wet conditions.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Yellow, V-shaped patches creeping in from the edges of the leaves, with the point of the V aimed at the center vein, and the veins in those patches turning black. The leaves yellow and die, and a bad case can rot the plant. It is a bacterial disease that hits the whole cabbage family in warm, wet weather.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris, a seedborne and splash-spread bacterium that enters through leaf margins (water pores) and wounds. It is favored by warm, humid, wet conditions and spreads on contaminated seed, water, tools, and crop debris across cabbage-family crops.
diseases.cause_beginner: A bacterium (Xanthomonas campestris) that can travel on seed and splashing water and gets into the leaves through their edges and any wounds. Warm, humid, wet weather brings it on, and it spreads on infected seed, water, tools, and old plant debris among cabbage-family plants.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure for infected tissue. Remove and destroy affected plants, avoid working among plants when the foliage is wet, and clear crop debris. Starting with clean seed and rotating crucifers do most of the work in a home garden.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot cure leaves that are already infected. Pull and throw away affected plants, stay out of the bed when the leaves are wet, and clean up old plant material. Clean seed and rotating where you plant cabbage-family crops handle most of it.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Start with clean, disease-free seed, rotate crucifers out of the bed for at least a year or more, and clear debris that harbors the bacterium. Water at the base rather than overhead, avoid handling wet plants, and space for airflow so foliage dries quickly.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Use clean, disease-free seed, do not grow cabbage-family crops in the same spot repeatedly, and clear away old plant debris. Water at the soil instead of overhead, do not handle wet plants, and give them room so the leaves dry fast.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Even, consistent moisture is the rule, and it matters most during germination and again as the roots size up. Turnip seed and seedlings need a moist, uncrusted surface for the roughly 7 to 10 days to emergence. Once established, turnips want steady moisture rather than a wet-dry swing: aim for about 1 inch of water per week including rain, up to 1 to 2 inches in heat or sandy soil, delivered in deeper, less frequent soakings.
watering.frequency_beginner: Keep the soil evenly damp, and pay closest attention while the seeds are sprouting and later while the roots are bulking up. From planting until the sprouts appear (about 7 to 10 days), keep the surface moist so it does not dry into a hard crust. After that, give about 1 inch of water a week, counting rain, in fewer but deeper waterings, and a bit more in hot or sandy conditions.
watering.amount_seasoned: Roughly 1 inch per week including rainfall once established, rising toward 1 to 2 inches in heat or on sandy soil and easing in cool or clay soil. During germination the seedbed needs only enough to stay evenly moist near the surface, not soaked.
watering.amount_beginner: About 1 inch of water a week, including rain, once the plants are growing, up to about 2 inches in hot, dry weather or sandy soil. While the seeds are sprouting, just keep the top of the soil damp, not soggy.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base with a gentle setting, soaker hose, or drip line to keep the surface evenly moist without crusting the bed or washing out the shallow-sown seed. Base watering also keeps the foliage dry, which limits the leaf diseases (downy mildew, white rust, leaf spot) turnips are prone to in wet weather.
watering.method_beginner: Water gently at soil level, using a soft spray, soaker hose, or drip line. A hard blast from the hose can wash out the shallow seeds or pack the soil into a crust the sprouts cannot push through, so keep it gentle. Watering at the soil also keeps the leaves dry, which helps prevent the leaf diseases turnips get in wet weather.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Constantly saturated soil invites damping-off, root rots, and clubroot and can yellow the tops; soft roots and a sour, waterlogged bed are signs to back off. Poor drainage is the usual cause, which is why loose, well-draining soil matters for this crop.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If the soil stays soaking wet, turnips can rot, seedlings can damp off, and the clubroot disease gets worse. Watch for yellow leaves, soft roots, and a constantly wet, sour-smelling bed. If you see these, water less and make sure the soil drains well.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Dry, cracked surface soil, dull or wilting tops, and slow growth signal too little water. Drought is the classic cause of poor turnip quality: it drives bitter, woody, strong-flavored, and pithy roots, and an irregular dry-then-wet cycle can crack them.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Dry, cracked soil on top, droopy or dull leaves, and slow growth mean the turnips need more water. Letting them go dry is the main thing that makes the roots bitter, woody, and pithy, and swinging from bone dry to soaked can crack them. Keep the watering steady.
watering.method_note_seasoned: On a fresh seedbed, keep the surface evenly moist without crusting or dislodging the shallow seed, using a fine setting, soaker hose, or drip. After establishment, shift to deeper, less frequent base watering to keep roots tender and prevent the drought stress and dry-then-wet swings that turn turnips bitter, pithy, and cracked.
watering.method_note_beginner: While the seeds are sprouting, water gently so you do not wash them out or make a hard crust. Once the turnips are up and growing, water more deeply but less often, at the soil. Letting them go dry, or swinging from dry to soaked, is what makes the roots bitter, pithy, and cracked.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Two windows matter most. The first is germination through emergence, when the surface must stay continuously moist and uncrusted or the stand fails. The second is the root-sizing period, when steady moisture keeps roots tender and mild and prevents the bitterness, pithiness, woodiness, and cracking that follow drought and uneven watering.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The two most important times to keep the soil moist are while the seeds are sprouting and later while the roots are bulking up. Letting the bed dry out during root growth is the main cause of bitter, pithy, cracked turnips.

start_method.hardening_off_beginner: You do not need to harden off turnips. They are sown straight into the garden from seed, not started indoors and transplanted.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Direct-sow turnips into the garden; they grow fast from seed in place and, like most root crops, do not transplant well. Sow about 1/4 to 1/2 inch deep once the soil is workable and at least 40 to 45°F, roughly 2 to 3 weeks before the last spring frost, and again in late summer for the fall crop, which is the better crop in most climates. Seeds germinate best at about 60 to 85°F and emerge in roughly 7 to 10 days. Sow a little thick and plan to thin: the thinnings are edible baby greens.
