Keep the surface moist and uncrusted until the seedlings emerge.
start_method.notes_beginner: Plant turnip seeds right in the garden where they will grow, since turnips do not like being moved. Sow them about 1/4 to 1/2 inch deep once the soil is no longer frozen or soggy (about 40 to 45°F), roughly 2 to 3 weeks before your last spring frost, and again in late summer for a fall crop, which is usually the best crop. They sprout in about 7 to 10 days. Plant a little thick and plan to thin them later; the little plants you pull out are tasty baby greens. Keep the soil surface damp until the sprouts appear.

container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: Turnips suit containers well and need less depth than carrots because the root is round and sits near the surface. A pot 8 inches or deeper with adequate width works well; a 5-gallon bucket or a window box at least 8 to 10 inches deep holds a good crop, and a wider, shallower tub is ideal for a cut-and-come-again greens crop. Width matters as much as depth, since you want several roots thinned to 3 to 4 inches apart. Provide drainage holes and a loose potting mix.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Turnips grow well in pots and do not need as deep a container as carrots, because the round root sits near the top of the soil. A pot at least 8 inches deep with some width works well, like a 5-gallon bucket or a deep window box, and a wide, shallow tub is great if you just want greens. Make sure it has drainage holes and use loose potting mix. Width helps too, since you want room to thin the turnips to about 3 to 4 inches apart.

drainage.saucer_practice_seasoned: Do not let the pot stand in a saucer of water. Turnips need even moisture for tender, mild roots, but waterlogged mix causes rot and favors clubroot; empty the saucer within an hour of watering.
drainage.saucer_practice_beginner: Do not let the pot sit in a saucer of water. Turnips need steady, even moisture, but soil that stays soggy will rot the roots, so empty the saucer within an hour of watering.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Use a bag of loose potting mix made for containers. Garden soil packs down hard in a pot and makes for misshapen roots, and it can also bring in clubroot.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in a little compost to help the soil hold water evenly, which keeps turnips tender and from turning bitter.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: container_potting_mix
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Use a light, loose potting mix; a handful of compost improves moisture-holding. Avoid garden soil, which compacts in a pot and can introduce the soilborne clubroot pathogen.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out much faster than the ground, so check daily in warm weather. Turnips need steady moisture, if the soil keeps drying out the roots turn bitter and pithy. Keep it evenly damp but not waterlogged.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Mix a little balanced slow-release fertilizer into the potting mix at planting. Too much fertilizer, especially high-nitrogen kinds, grows big leafy tops and small roots, though that is fine if you are growing for greens.
container_notes.notes_beginner: Turnips are a good container crop, even better than carrots for shallow pots, because the root sits near the surface. Use a pot at least 8 inches deep with drainage holes and loose potting mix, keep the soil evenly moist, and thin the seedlings to about 3 to 4 inches apart. A wide, shallow tub also makes a nice greens-only crop you can snip and let regrow.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Turnips suit containers well and tolerate shallower pots than carrots since the round root swells near the surface. Use a container at least 8 inches deep with drainage holes and a loose potting mix, keep moisture even to keep roots tender and mild, and thin to a final 3 to 4 inches apart. A wide, shallow tub is also well suited to a cut-and-come-again greens crop, and a loose soilless mix avoids introducing clubroot.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry far faster than garden beds, and uneven moisture turns turnip roots bitter, pithy, and cracked. Check the top inch or two daily in warm weather and water before the mix dries out; aim for consistently moist but never soggy.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Turnips are light feeders for roots. Mix a balanced slow-release fertilizer into the potting mix at sowing, or apply a half-strength liquid feed once the tops are a few inches tall. Excess nitrogen drives leafy tops at the expense of roots, which is acceptable for a greens crop.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering container suits turnips once they are growing, because steady sub-irrigation delivers the even moisture that keeps roots tender and mild. It does not help germination, though: the seed sits at the dry surface above the wicking zone, so keep the top inch moist by hand until the stand is up.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot works well for turnips once they are growing, because it keeps the water steady, and steady water means tender, mild roots. It will not keep the seeds moist while they sprout, though, since they sit up at the dry top, so water the surface gently by hand until the seedlings come up.

recommended: Purple Top White Globe: the classic all-purpose turnip, round with a purple-and-white root and good greens, about 50 to 55 days
Hakurei: a sweet, mild white salad turnip (F1) eaten raw or cooked, fast at about 38 days, with tender greens
Tokyo Cross and other Tokyo types: quick, uniform white hybrids good for baby and salad turnips
Shogoin: a Japanese type grown for abundant, mild greens as well as a white root
Seven Top: a greens-only turnip grown for the leaves, with no usable root
Golden Ball (Golden Globe): an heirloom with sweet, mild yellow flesh
Scarlet Queen: a red-skinned, white-fleshed round type with a crisp, mild flavor
White Lady and Just Right: smooth white hybrids, dual-purpose for roots and greens
varieties.note_seasoned: Turnip variety choice splits by purpose and speed. Purple Top White Globe is the dependable all-rounder for roots and greens, maturing in about 50 to 55 days; for a sweet, mild root eaten raw, the fast white salad types (Hakurei, Tokyo Cross) are ready in roughly 35 to 40 days. Greens growers choose leafy types such as Shogoin or the rootless Seven Top, which put their energy into abundant tops. For color and flavor, Golden Ball offers sweet yellow flesh and Scarlet Queen a red skin. Sow salad and greens types thicker and harvest young; let main-crop and storage types size to about 2 to 3 inches. Full-size storage roots can take 60 to 80 days.
varieties.note_beginner: There are turnips for different uses. Purple Top White Globe is the dependable classic for both roots and greens, ready in about 50 to 55 days. For sweet, mild turnips you can eat raw, look for fast salad types like Hakurei or Tokyo, ready in about 35 to 40 days. If you mainly want the leafy greens, grow Shogoin or Seven Top (which makes greens but no real root). Golden Ball has sweet yellow flesh and Scarlet Queen has red skin. Plant salad and greens kinds a bit thicker and pick them young; let regular turnips grow to about 2 to 3 inches across.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Do not plant turnips where another cabbage-family crop (Brassicaceae) grew the previous seasons, including turnip, rutabaga, radish, cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kale, collards, Brussels sprouts, kohlrabi, and mustard, since they share soilborne clubroot and root pests (cabbage maggot, flea beetle) that build up where the family is grown repeatedly. University of Minnesota advises against following any of these crops for the past four years, and longer rotations are recommended where clubroot is established. Avoid beds heavily manured for the previous crop, because the readily available nitrogen drives leafy top growth and branches the roots.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Do not grow turnips where you grew turnips, radish, cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kale, collards, or mustard in recent years. These are all in the same cabbage family and share the same soil pests (cabbage maggot, flea beetle) and a root disease called clubroot, which build up over time. Minnesota suggests waiting four years before any of them go back in the same bed, and longer where clubroot is a known problem. Also avoid beds that got a lot of manure for the last crop, since the extra nitrogen grows leafy tops and makes the roots branch.
good_after: Legumes such as beans and peas that have added nitrogen
Fruiting crops such as tomatoes and squash
Alliums such as onions and garlic
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate turnips on a multi-year cycle, keeping them and all other cabbage-family crops out of a bed for several seasons after they are grown there; Minnesota recommends a four-year gap, and a longer one where clubroot is present. This breaks the buildup of the soilborne clubroot pathogen and the root pests the family shares. Following a legume that has added nitrogen, or another nitrogen-depleting crop, suits turnips well; avoid following a heavily manured crop, whose residual nitrogen pushes tops over roots and branches them.
rotation.note_beginner: Move your turnips to a different spot each year, and do not put them, or their relatives like cabbage, broccoli, radish, and kale, back in the same bed for several years (Minnesota says about four). This keeps the cabbage maggot, flea beetle, and clubroot disease from piling up. Turnips do well following beans or peas, which add nitrogen, but not right after a bed that got heavy manure, since leftover nitrogen grows leaves instead of roots.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Poor for more than a few days. At room temperature turnip roots lose moisture and soften quickly, and the greens wilt within a day; cut the tops from the roots and refrigerate both. Counter storage is only for what you will use within a couple of days.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Not good for more than a few days. Left out, turnip roots go soft and the leaves wilt fast. Cut the tops off, keep out only what you will eat soon, and refrigerate the rest.
storage.fridge_seasoned: The best everyday option. Cut off the green tops first, since the leaves pull moisture from the root; store the greens separately in a bag and use them within a few days. Keep the unwashed roots in a perforated or loosely closed plastic bag in the crisper drawer, where high humidity and cold hold them for one to several weeks. Small salad turnips are most perishable; main-crop roots keep best.
storage.fridge_beginner: This is the best way for everyday storage. First cut off the leafy tops, because the leaves draw water out of the root. Keep the greens in a separate bag and eat them within a few days. Put the unwashed roots in a loosely closed or vented plastic bag in the crisper drawer, where they stay firm for one to several weeks. Little salad turnips do not keep as long as bigger main-crop ones.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Workable after cooking. Turnip roots are best frozen cooked rather than raw: peel, dice, boil or steam until just tender, cool, and freeze, or freeze as a mash. The greens freeze like spinach after a brief blanch. Quality holds for roughly 8 to 12 months.
storage.freezer_beginner: You can freeze turnips, but cook them first. Peel, dice, and boil or steam them until just tender, cool, and freeze, or freeze them mashed. The greens freeze like spinach after a quick dip in boiling water. They keep well for about 8 to 12 months.
storage.notes_seasoned: For larger harvests, main-crop turnips are fair keepers. In cold climates they can be left in the ground under a thick straw mulch and pulled until the soil freezes hard, or packed unwashed in damp sand in a box in a root cellar or unheated garage held near 32 to 40°F at high humidity, where they hold for two to four months. Store roots only; use the greens fresh.
storage.notes_beginner: If you grow a lot, regular turnips store for a while. In cold areas you can cover the row with thick straw and dig them until the ground freezes solid, or pack unwashed roots in damp sand in a box kept somewhere cold like an unheated garage, around 32 to 40°F, where they last two to four months. Store just the roots; eat the leafy greens fresh.

thinning.when: Once seedlings stand 2 to 4 inches high, while still small enough to use as baby greens.
thinning.to_spacing: 2 to 4 inches (3 to 4 for full-size roots, closer for salad turnips and greens)
thinning.method: Snip or pinch the extra seedlings off at the soil line rather than pulling, to avoid disturbing the keepers' roots.
thinning.tip_seasoned: Turnips are sown a little thick and must be thinned, or the crowded roots stay small and misshapen. Thin to a final 2 to 4 inches apart once seedlings reach 2 to 4 inches tall, closer for salad turnips and greens and wider (3 to 4 inches) for full-size roots, snipping the extras at the soil line rather than pulling so you do not disturb the ones you keep. Do not waste the thinnings: the young leaves are tender baby turnip greens, so thinning is also a first small harvest.
thinning.tip_beginner: Turnips are planted a bit thick, so you need to thin them, or the crowded roots stay small and lumpy. Thin them to about 2 to 4 inches apart once they are 2 to 4 inches tall, closer together if you just want greens or small salad turnips, snipping the extra ones off at the soil line with scissors instead of pulling. Do not toss the thinnings, the little leaves are tasty baby turnip greens, so thinning is really your first harvest.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare soil for about 7 to 10 days, then a quick, even flush of seedlings, since turnip seed germinates fast and uniformly. The first leaves are narrow seed leaves; emergence stalls if the surface dries or crusts.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Bare soil for about a week to ten days, then a quick, even crop of seedlings, because turnip seed sprouts fast. They will not come up well if the surface dries out or forms a hard crust.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep the surface consistently moist until emergence, watering lightly in warm or windy weather, and never let a crust form. Turnips need little help here beyond even moisture.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the top of the soil damp until the seedlings appear, watering gently in warm or windy weather so it never dries into a crust.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have your turnips germinated? Note the emergence date to track days to maturity from a real sowing.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your turnip seedlings come up yet? Jot down the date they appeared.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seedlings putting out true leaves, sown a little thick so the stand is too dense for good roots until thinned. Watch for flea-beetle shot-holes on the young leaves, which hit seedlings hardest.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Little seedlings growing their first true leaves, planted a bit thick so they are too crowded to make good roots until you thin them. Look for tiny round holes from flea beetles, which go after young plants.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin to a final 2 to 4 inches apart once seedlings reach 2 to 4 inches, snipping the extras at the soil line; the thinnings are edible baby greens. Keep the bed weed-free and evenly moist, and cover with row fabric if flea beetles are heavy.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Thin the seedlings to about 2 to 4 inches apart once they are 2 to 4 inches tall, snipping the extras at the soil line. Eat the thinnings as baby greens. Keep weeds out and the soil evenly damp, and use a row cover if flea beetles are bad.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have you thinned your turnips to final spacing?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you thinned your turnips so they have room to grow?

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Steady leaf growth as the plants build the swelling root below; the shoulders of the roots begin to show at the soil surface. Outer leaves can be taken sparingly for greens without checking root growth.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Leafy tops growing while the turnip root swells underground; you may see the tops of the roots poking up at the soil line. You can pick a few outer leaves for greens without hurting the root.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Maintain even moisture, about 1 inch per week, to keep roots tender and mild and prevent bitterness and pithiness. Go easy on nitrogen for a root crop. Watch for aphids on the greens and leaf diseases in wet weather.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the watering steady, about 1 inch a week, so the roots stay tender and mild and do not get bitter. Do not over-feed with nitrogen if you want good roots. Watch for aphids on the leaves and leaf spots in wet weather.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How do your turnip tops look? Note any exposed shoulders or leaf damage.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How are your turnip tops looking? Note if any root tops are showing or the leaves look chewed.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Roots sizing to about 2 to 3 inches across, the sweet, tender, mild stage; check by brushing a shoulder rather than by the calendar. Most main-crop varieties reach this near 50 to 60 days, salad types sooner. Flavor is milder and sweeter in cool weather, sharper and pithier in heat.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Roots grown to about 2 to 3 inches across, the best size for sweet, tender turnips. Check by brushing the soil off a shoulder rather than counting days. Most are ready around 50 to 60 days, salad kinds sooner, and they taste milder and sweeter in cool weather.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pull a test turnip to check size before harvesting in earnest. Do not let roots oversize or sit in heat, which turns them woody, pithy, and strong-flavored. Keep picking the greens, and in cold regions mulch to hold roots in the ground; frost sweetens them.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pull one turnip to check the size before digging the rest. Do not leave them to get too big or sit through hot weather, which makes them woody and strong. Keep picking the greens, and in cold areas pile straw over the row to keep digging; frost makes them sweeter.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have you harvested your first turnips? Log the date and how they sized up.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you pulled your first turnips? Note the date and how they turned out.

notifications.body_seasoned: Direct-sow turnips about 2 to 3 weeks before your last frost, once the soil is workable and at least 40 to 45°F. Sow 1/4 to 1/2 inch deep, a little thick, and plan to thin. The fall crop, sown in late summer, is often the better one.
notifications.body_beginner: Plant turnip seeds right in the garden about 2 to 3 weeks before your last frost, once the ground is no longer frozen or soggy. Plant them 1/4 to 1/2 inch deep and a bit thick, and plan to thin. The fall crop, planted in late summer, is often the best one.

notifications.body_seasoned: Once seedlings stand 2 to 4 inches, thin to a final 2 to 4 inches apart, snipping at the soil line. The thinnings are edible baby greens. Crowded turnips stay small and misshapen.
notifications.body_beginner: Once the seedlings are 2 to 4 inches tall, thin them to 2 to 4 inches apart, snipping the extras at the soil line. Eat the thinnings as baby greens. Crowded turnips stay small.

notifications.title_seasoned: Watch young turnips for flea beetles
notifications.title_beginner: Check turnip seedlings for flea beetles
notifications.body_seasoned: Flea beetles pepper young turnip leaves with tiny shot-holes and hit seedlings hardest in spring. A floating row cover at sowing is the best defense; a vigorous stand outgrows light feeding.
notifications.body_beginner: Flea beetles make tiny round holes in young turnip leaves and are worst on spring seedlings. A row cover laid over the bed is the best fix; healthy, fast-growing plants usually outgrow light damage.

notifications.body_seasoned: As roots size up, hold even moisture (about 1 inch per week). Drought and a dry-then-soaked cycle turn turnips bitter, pithy, and cracked; keep nitrogen modest for good roots.
notifications.body_beginner: As the roots grow, water evenly, about 1 inch a week. Letting the soil dry out makes turnips bitter and pithy. Go easy on nitrogen if you want good roots.

notifications.title_beginner: Check if your turnips are ready
notifications.body_seasoned: Around 50 to 60 days, check by size: a root about 2 to 3 inches across is the sweet, tender stage. Pull a test turnip. Do not let them oversize or sit in heat, which turns them woody and pithy.
notifications.body_beginner: Around 50 to 60 days, check by size: a turnip about 2 to 3 inches across is at its best. Pull one to test. Do not leave them to get too big or sit through hot weather, which makes them woody.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat turns turnips pithy and triggers bolting
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot weather hurts turnips
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Sustained heat above about 75°F turns roots woody, pithy, and sharp-flavored and can prompt bolting, especially as days lengthen. Harvest mature roots promptly, keep moisture even, and mulch or shade if you can; lean on the fall crop where summers are hot.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: When it stays above about 75°F, turnips get woody, pithy, and strong-tasting, and plants can bolt (run to flower). Harvest any that are ready, keep watering steady, and add mulch or shade if you can. In hot places, grow turnips in fall instead of summer.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Dry weather, keep turnips watered
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: During germination the seedbed must not dry out or crust. Once established, keep moisture even (about 1 inch per week); drought is the classic cause of bitter, woody, pithy turnips.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: While seeds are sprouting, do not let the surface dry out or crust over. Once growing, water evenly (about 1 inch a week); letting turnips go dry makes them bitter and woody.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Light frost is fine, and sweetens turnips
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost is okay for turnips
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Turnips tolerate frost and sweeten in cool weather, and the roots hold in the ground. Before a hard freeze, harvest or pile on a thick straw mulch to keep digging; the greens take light frost too.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Turnips handle frost and get sweeter in cool weather, and the roots keep in the ground. Before a hard freeze, harvest them or pile on thick straw so you can keep digging. The greens take a light frost too.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Damp weather favors turnip leaf diseases
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Damp weather can bring leaf disease
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Cool, wet weather favors downy mildew and white rust, and warm, wet spells favor Alternaria leaf spot and black rot on the foliage. Water at the base, keep plants thinned for airflow, and remove badly affected leaves.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Cool, wet weather can bring downy mildew and white rust, and warm, wet spells bring leaf spots, on the leaves. Water at the soil, keep plants thinned so air moves through, and pick off badly affected leaves.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heavy rain after dry soil may crack roots
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Heavy rain can crack turnips
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A heavy soaking after dry soil makes roots take up water fast and crack. If turnips are near maturity, consider harvesting before a big rain, and keep beds well drained to limit clubroot.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: A heavy rain after dry soil makes turnips drink fast and crack. If your turnips are near ready, think about harvesting before a big storm, and keep the bed draining well.

germination.text_seasoned: Turnip seed germinates fast and evenly, usually in 7 to 10 days at 60 to 85°F, so emergence is rarely the problem. Keep the surface evenly moist and uncrusted until the seedlings appear, and sow shallowly, about 1/4 to 1/2 inch deep.
germination.text_beginner: Turnip seeds sprout quickly, usually in 7 to 10 days, so they are easy to start. Just keep the soil surface damp and free of a hard crust until they come up, and plant them shallow, about 1/4 to 1/2 inch deep.
germination.author: plant

germination.text_seasoned: Sow turnips a little thick and plan to thin, since not every seed comes up and a fuller stand lets you thin for baby greens. Sow closer for a salad or greens crop, wider for full-size roots.
germination.text_beginner: Plant turnip seeds a bit thick and plan to thin them later, since not every seed sprouts and the extras make good baby greens. Plant closer together for greens or small salad turnips, wider apart for big roots.
germination.author: plant

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin to a final 2 to 4 inches once seedlings reach 2 to 4 inches, snipping at the soil line rather than pulling to spare the keepers' roots. Crowded turnips stay small and misshapen; closer spacing suits salad and greens types.
seedling.text_beginner: Thin the turnips to about 2 to 4 inches apart once they are 2 to 4 inches tall, snipping the extras at the soil line instead of pulling, so you do not disturb the ones you keep. Crowded turnips stay small. Plant closer if you just want greens.
seedling.author: plant

seedling.text_seasoned: Flea beetles riddle young turnip leaves with shot-holes and hit spring seedlings hardest. A floating row cover laid at sowing and sealed at the edges is the most reliable defense; a vigorous, well-watered stand outgrows light feeding, and fall crops face less pressure.
seedling.text_beginner: Flea beetles make tiny holes in young turnip leaves and are worst on spring seedlings. The best fix is a row cover (a light fabric) laid over the bed when you plant. Healthy, well-watered plants usually grow past light damage, and fall turnips get hit less.
seedling.author: plant

established.text_seasoned: Hold even moisture, roughly 1 inch per week including rain, in deeper, less frequent soakings. Drought and a dry-then-flooded cycle are the main causes of bitter, woody, pithy, and cracked turnips, so steadiness matters more than volume.
established.text_beginner: Keep the water steady, about 1 inch a week counting rain, in fewer but deeper waterings. Letting the soil dry out, or swinging from dry to soaked, is what makes turnips bitter, woody, and cracked. Being steady matters more than giving a lot at once.
established.author: plant

established.text_seasoned: Go easy on nitrogen for a root crop: excess nitrogen and fresh manure grow lush tops at the expense of the root and can branch it. A crop grown for greens is the exception and rewards more nitrogen, since the leaves are the harvest.
established.text_beginner: Do not over-feed turnips with nitrogen if you want good roots, since too much (and fresh manure) grows big leafy tops and small, branched roots. If you are growing turnips for the greens, a little more nitrogen is fine, because the leaves are what you want.
established.author: plant

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest by size, not the calendar: a root about 2 to 3 inches across is the sweet, tender, mild stage, which most main-crop turnips reach near 50 to 60 days and salad types sooner. Roots left to oversize or sit in heat turn woody, pithy, and strong.
harvest.text_beginner: Harvest by size, not a set date: a turnip about 2 to 3 inches across is at its best. Most reach this around 50 to 60 days, salad kinds sooner. Turnips left to get too big or sit in hot weather turn woody and strong-tasting.
harvest.author: plant

harvest.text_seasoned: Do not forget the greens: pick a few young outer leaves through the season and cook the rest like spinach or collards at harvest. Mature roots are in no rush in cool weather, since flavor sweetens after light frost and roots hold in the ground under a straw mulch.
harvest.text_beginner: Do not forget the leaves: pick a few young outer ones as you go and cook the rest like spinach or collards. There is no rush to dig mature turnips in cool weather, since they get sweeter after a light frost and keep in the ground under a layer of straw.
harvest.author: plant

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: One root per plant, plus a flush of edible leaves along the way. Yield is best thought of by row length: at a 2 to 4 inch final spacing, a 10-foot row yields roughly 5 to 10 pounds of roots depending on size at harvest, alongside greens taken as outer leaves and thinnings. A greens-only crop yields more leaf per foot of row.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Each plant gives you one turnip root, plus leaves you can eat as it grows. It helps to think by row length: a 10-foot row gives roughly 5 to 10 pounds of turnips depending on size, plus greens picked as outer leaves and thinnings.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: There is no repeat root harvest; a sowing matures over a short window roughly 50 to 60 days after planting and is pulled over a couple of weeks. The greens give a longer, light pick-as-you-go harvest. Continuous supply comes from succession sowing every 3 to 4 weeks through the cool-season window.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Turnips do not regrow a new root after you pull them, since each plant makes one root. A planting is ready about 50 to 60 days after sowing and you harvest it over a couple of weeks, while the leaves give a longer, light harvest. For a steady supply, plant a new short row every 3 to 4 weeks.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Turnips are an annual grown fresh from seed every season, so there is no first-year-versus-later distinction as with perennials; the first sowing performs as well as any, provided the soil is loose, the stand is thinned, and moisture stays even.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Turnips are grown fresh from seed each year, so your very first planting can do just as well as any later one. The main things that decide your results are loose soil, thinning the seedlings, and keeping the bed evenly damp.
factors_seasoned: Thinning: a crowded, unthinned stand yields small, misshapen roots.
Even moisture: drought or dry-then-wet cycles turn roots bitter, pithy, and cracked.
Temperature at finish: roots maturing in sustained heat above about 75°F turn woody, pithy, and strong, and plants may bolt.
Nitrogen balance: excess nitrogen or fresh manure grows tops at the expense of roots.
Soil looseness: stones and compaction cause forked, misshapen roots.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting assigns root crops like turnips to the waning moon, the period after the full moon, on the folk principle that the changing lunar pull favors root growth. This is long-standing gardening folklore with no controlled scientific evidence of an effect on turnip germination or yield. Plant turnips by soil temperature and your cool-season window, not the moon; this is recorded only for growers who follow the tradition.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Plants bolt (run to seed)
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Turnips flower instead of making roots
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The plant sent up a flower stalk instead of sizing a root. Turnip bolting is driven by heat and lengthening days, and by a cold spell on young plants (vernalization) followed by long spring days. Once it bolts, the root stays small, woody, and strong, so spring crops sown too late or carried into early summer heat are most at risk.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The turnip sent up a tall flower stalk instead of growing a good root. This usually happens with heat and long days, or when young plants get a cold snap followed by the long days of late spring. Once it flowers, the root stays small and tough.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sow the spring crop early enough to mature before summer heat and long days, and lean on the fall crop, which dodges the long-day trigger. Avoid sowing too late in spring, keep moisture even, and choose bolt-resistant varieties for spring sowings.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant the spring crop early enough to finish before the summer heat and long days, and rely on the fall crop, which avoids the long days that cause flowering. Do not plant too late in spring, keep the watering steady, and pick bolt-resistant varieties for spring.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Woody, pithy, strong-flavored roots
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Tough, spongy, strong turnips
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Roots grew coarse, fibrous, spongy in the center (pithy), and sharp-tasting. The usual causes are maturing in sustained heat above about 75°F, over-maturity from being left in the ground too long, or drought and uneven moisture. Pithiness and strong flavor are the classic signs of turnips grown or held through hot, dry weather.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The turnips came out tough, spongy in the middle, and strong-tasting. This usually comes from growing in heat above about 75°F, leaving them in the ground too long, or letting them get too dry.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Time the crop so roots mature in cool weather, leaning on the fall crop and sowing spring crops early; harvest at 2 to 3 inches rather than letting roots oversize, and keep moisture even. Frost-finished turnips are the sweetest and mildest.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plan the crop so the turnips finish in cool weather: rely on the fall planting and sow spring crops early. Harvest them at 2 to 3 inches instead of letting them get big, and keep the watering steady. Turnips that finish after a frost are the sweetest.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Swollen, clubbed, distorted roots
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Lumpy, club-shaped roots
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Instead of clean turnips, the roots are swollen, distorted, and clubbed, with the plants stunted and yellow and wilting by day. This is clubroot, a soilborne disease of the cabbage family favored by wet, poorly drained, acidic soil that builds up where crucifers are grown repeatedly.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Instead of clean turnips, the roots came out swollen, lumpy, and club-shaped, and the plants looked stunted and yellow and wilted in the afternoon. This is clubroot, a soil disease of the cabbage family that gets worse in wet, acidic soil and in beds where you grow cabbage-family crops over and over.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Rotate crucifers out of the bed for several years, improve drainage, and lime toward a neutral to slightly alkaline pH of about 7.2 to 7.5, which suppresses the pathogen. Remove and destroy affected plants (do not compost), and avoid moving soil from the infested bed on tools.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep cabbage-family crops out of that bed for a few years, improve drainage, and add lime to raise the pH toward 7.2 to 7.5, which holds the disease back. Pull and throw away affected plants (do not compost), and do not carry soil from that bed on your tools.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Forked, hairy, or misshapen roots
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Forked or hairy turnips
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Roots grew forked, twisted, hairy, or lumpy because they met an obstruction, a stone, clod, or compacted layer, because the stand was left unthinned and crowded, or because of fresh manure or excess nitrogen, which causes branching and hairy roots.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The turnips came out forked, twisted, hairy, or lumpy because they hit something hard as they grew, like a rock or packed soil, because they were too crowded, or because of fresh manure or too much nitrogen, which makes roots branch and grow hairy.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Work the bed loose and remove stones before sowing, thin to 2 to 4 inches so roots are not crowded, and avoid fresh manure and heavy nitrogen. On heavy or rocky ground, use a raised bed or a deep, loose container.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Loosen the bed and pull out rocks before planting, thin the turnips to 2 to 4 inches so they are not crowded, and skip fresh manure and heavy nitrogen feeding. On rocky or heavy soil, use a raised bed or a deep, loose container.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Leaves riddled with shot-holes
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Leaves full of tiny holes
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The leaves are peppered with tiny round shot-holes, heaviest on young spring seedlings, the work of flea beetles. On a turnip grown for greens this ruins the harvest; on a root crop it mostly slows seedlings, but a heavily fed-on stand sizes up poorly.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The leaves are covered in tiny round holes, worst on young spring plants. This is flea beetle damage. If you are growing turnips for greens it spoils the leaves; for the root it mostly just slows down the young plants.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Cover the seedbed with a floating row cover at sowing to exclude the beetles, clean up debris where they overwinter, and favor fall crops, which face less pressure. Keep seedlings growing fast with even moisture so they outgrow light feeding.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Cover the seedbed with a row cover when you plant to keep the beetles off, clean up old plant debris where they spend winter, and lean on fall crops, which get hit less. Keep seedlings growing fast with steady water so they outgrow light damage.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Poor or patchy germination
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Seeds did not come up well
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Few or uneven seedlings emerged. Turnip seed normally germinates fast, so most failures trace to a seedbed that dried or crusted during the roughly week-long germination, old seed, sowing too deep, or cold wet soil that slows emergence and invites damping-off.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Few seedlings came up, or they came up patchy. Turnip seed usually sprouts fast, so most failures come from the soil surface drying out or crusting while sprouting, old seed, planting too deep, or cold soggy soil.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Keep the surface evenly moist from sowing to emergence, sow shallowly (about 1/4 to 1/2 inch) with fresh seed, and wait for the soil to warm to at least 40 to 45°F before sowing.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep the soil surface damp from sowing until the seedlings appear, plant shallow (about 1/4 to 1/2 inch) with fresh seed, and wait until the soil warms to at least 40 to 45°F before planting.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Turnips succession well: sow a short row every 3 to 4 weeks through the cool-season window rather than one large planting, so roots mature in sequence. In cold-summer climates that means spring through early summer, then a late-summer sowing for the main fall crop; in hot-summer climates it means fall through early spring, skipping the heat. Stop spring sowings before sustained heat, since turnips maturing in hot soil turn woody, pithy, and strong and tend to bolt. The fall crop is the prime one in most regions.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: Instead of planting all your turnips at once, sow a short row every 3 to 4 weeks. That way they are ready a few at a time over several weeks. In places with cool summers, start in spring and keep going into early summer, then sow again in late summer for the main fall crop. In hot-summer places, grow them in fall, winter, and early spring and skip the summer heat. The fall crop is usually the best one.

crops.description_seasoned: Turnip (Brassica rapa) is a fast, cool-season, dual-purpose crop in the cabbage family (Brassicaceae), grown for both its swollen root and its edible leaves, the turnip greens cooked like collards or spinach. It is direct-sown and quick: seed germinates in about 7 to 10 days, and most varieties size a usable root in roughly 40 to 60 days, with fast salad types ready in about 35 days and greens harvestable sooner. Roots are sweetest, mildest, and most tender pulled at about 2 to 3 inches across; sustained heat above about 75°F turns them woody, pithy, and sharp, and long days plus heat push the plant to bolt, so the fall crop is the prime one in most climates. Turnips tolerate frost and sweeten in cool weather. As a brassica, turnip's pests and diseases are the cabbage-family set, flea beetle, cabbage maggot, aphids, and harlequin bug, with clubroot, white rust, downy mildew, Alternaria leaf spot, and black rot, so it is rotated and grouped with the cole crops, not with carrots. The planting season inverts by climate: spring and fall where summers are cool, and fall through early spring where summers are hot.
crops.description_beginner: Turnips are a fast cool-weather crop in the cabbage family that you grow for two foods at once: the round root and the leafy greens, which you cook like collards or spinach. You plant the seeds right in the garden, and they are quick: they sprout in about a week to ten days, and most are ready in roughly 40 to 60 days, with fast salad kinds ready in about 35 days and greens sooner. Roots taste best pulled small, about 2 to 3 inches across; in heat above about 75°F they turn woody and strong-tasting, and hot, long days make the plant flower (bolt), so the fall crop is usually the best one. Turnips handle frost and get sweeter in cool weather. Because turnips are a cabbage-family plant, their bugs and diseases are the cabbage-family ones (flea beetle, cabbage maggot, aphids, harlequin bug, plus clubroot and some leaf diseases), so you rotate and group them with cabbage and kale, not with carrots. When you plant depends on your climate: spring and fall where summers are cool, and fall through early spring where summers are hot.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Turnips are a dual harvest. The leaves can be picked young throughout, taking a few outer leaves per plant so the root keeps sizing; the thinnings at the seedling stage are the first baby greens, and greens-type varieties are cut and allowed to regrow. The roots are ready by size rather than the calendar: brush soil from a shoulder and pull when it is about 2 to 3 inches across, the sweet, tender, mild stage, which for most main-crop varieties lands near 50 to 60 days and for salad types sooner. Do not let roots oversize or sit in heat, which turns them woody, pithy, and strong. There is no rush in cool weather: flavor sweetens after light frost, and roots hold in the ground. In cold regions a heavy straw mulch lets you dig through early winter until the ground freezes hard. Lift by hand, or loosen with a fork in heavier soil, and cut off the tops, keeping the greens for the kitchen and storing the roots separately.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Turnips give you two harvests. You can pick the leaves young all along, taking a few outer ones per plant so the root keeps growing, and the seedlings you thin out are your first baby greens. The roots are ready by size, not a set date: brush the soil off a shoulder and pull when the turnip is about 2 to 3 inches across, the sweet, tender stage, usually around 50 to 60 days, sooner for salad kinds. Do not let them get too big or sit through hot weather, which makes them woody and strong. There is no rush in cool weather: they get sweeter after a light frost and hold in the ground. In cold areas, pile straw over the row and dig them into early winter until the ground freezes. Pull by hand, or loosen with a fork in heavy soil, and cut off the tops, keeping the greens to cook and storing the roots separately.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Turnips reward a loose, fertile, well-drained seedbed worked fine before sowing. Loosen the bed about 8 to 10 inches deep, less than carrots need since the root swells near the surface, and remove stones and clods that fork the roots. Rake the surface smooth and fine for the small seed, and work in well-finished compost or well-rotted (not fresh) manure, since fresh manure branches the roots and over-supplies nitrogen. Aim for a slightly acidic to neutral pH of about 6.0 to 6.8. The brassica-specific concern is clubroot: it thrives in wet, poorly drained, acidic soil, so on a clubroot-prone bed improve drainage and lime toward a neutral to slightly alkaline pH of about 7.2 to 7.5, which suppresses it. On heavy clay, work in compost or use a raised bed for the drainage and loose texture turnips prefer.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Turnips do best in loose, rich, well-drained soil raked smooth before you plant. Loosen the bed about 8 to 10 inches down, a bit less than carrots need since turnip roots sit near the surface, and pull out rocks and hard clumps that make roots fork. Rake the top fine and smooth for the small seeds, and mix in compost or well-rotted (never fresh) manure, since fresh manure makes the roots hairy and branched. Aim for a soil pH around 6.0 to 6.8. One cabbage-family note: a root disease called clubroot is worse in wet, acidic soil, so if it has been a problem, improve drainage and add lime to raise the pH toward 7.2 to 7.5. If your soil is heavy clay, mix in compost or use a raised bed for the loose, well-drained soil turnips like.

open_findings.summary: days_to_maturity is set to [40, 60] (mid 50) to span the home-garden usable-root window: fast salad types (Hakurei, Tokyo) at roughly 35 to 40 days, the classic Purple Top White Globe at about 50 to 55, and greens harvestable sooner. Clemson and USU give 60 to 80 days for full tennis-ball-size roots, and UGA gives 50 to 60; the chosen range favors the harvest-at-usable-size norm and is noted in prose. The spread, not a single number, is the honest figure.
