crops.name: Leek

soil.preferred_texture_seasoned: Deep, loose, fertile loam or sandy loam high in organic matter grows the longest, cleanest shanks and lets you draw soil up easily to blanch.
soil.tolerated_texture_seasoned: Tolerates silt loam and sandier ground if it is kept fertile and evenly moist; sandy soils need more frequent watering and feeding.
soil.problematic_texture_seasoned: Heavy, tight clay and soils that crust or stay waterlogged are poor: they make for short, dirty shanks, are hard to earth up, and the constant wet around the base invites rot.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Leeks like deep, loose, rich soil with lots of compost worked in. Loose soil matters because you grow the long white part of a leek by pulling soil up around the stem, and that is much easier in soft, crumbly ground than in heavy clay. Keep the soil evenly moist all season.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Work in generous compost or rotted manure before planting and aim for a deep, loose, fertile, well-drained bed. Leeks are long-season, moderately heavy feeders with a shallow root system, so the soil must hold both moisture and nutrients near the surface across many months; loose ground also makes the repeated earthing-up that blanches the shank far easier.

ph.note_beginner: Leeks grow best in soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, about 6.0 to 7.0. A simple soil test takes out the guesswork. If your test comes back below about 6.0, adding garden lime brings it up.
ph.note_seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0 (UMN gives 6.0 to 7.0; UF/IFAS lists 6.5 to 7.0 for Florida). Leeks tolerate a wider 5.5 to 7.5 band but dislike strongly acid ground; below about 6.0 a liming amendment helps. Confirm with a soil test before adjusting.

fertilizer.frequency: Side-dress once or twice during the long season
fertilizer.timing: Work a balanced feed into the bed at planting, then side-dress with nitrogen through summer
fertilizer.example_product: 10-10-10 at planting, then ammonium sulfate (21-0-0) or another nitrogen source to side-dress
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Leeks are long-season, moderately heavy feeders. Work a balanced fertilizer such as 10-10-10 into the bed before planting (UMN suggests about one cup per 10 feet of row mid-season), then side-dress with nitrogen once or twice while the shafts are lengthening. USU gives a quarter pound of ammonium sulfate (21-0-0) per 100 square feet in the middle of May and again in late June. Keep nitrogen steady through summer for thick shanks, but avoid heavy late feeding, which together with crowding and wet leaves worsens leek rust.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Leeks grow for a long time and are fairly hungry plants. Mix a balanced fertilizer into the soil before planting, then feed once or twice with a nitrogen fertilizer through the summer while the stems are growing. Steady feeding builds thick stems. Do not pile on a lot of fertilizer late in the season, since soft, crowded, well-fed plants get rust more easily.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time to side-dress your leeks with nitrogen to push shaft growth.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Feed your leeks some nitrogen now to grow thicker stems.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced base such as 10-10-10 at planting, then nitrogen side-dressings (for example ammonium sulfate, 21-0-0) through summer to build long, thick shanks.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 at planting, then feed with a nitrogen fertilizer once or twice during summer.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: About a quarter pound of ammonium sulfate (21-0-0) per 100 square feet at each side-dressing (USU), or roughly one cup of 10-10-10 per 10 feet of row mid-season (UMN), or the label rate of a balanced fertilizer.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: About a quarter pound of a nitrogen fertilizer such as ammonium sulfate for every 100 square feet each time you feed, or follow the package directions.

pests.name: Onion thrips
pests.identification_seasoned: Tiny slender insects rasping silvery streaks and flecks into the leaf folds and the tight neck of the shaft; heavy feeding in hot, dry spells weakens plants and slows shaft growth.
pests.identification_beginner: Very small insects that leave silvery streaks and specks on the leaves, often down where the leaves fold together. They are worst in hot, dry weather.
pests.cause_seasoned: Onion thrips (Thrips tabaci) build through warm, dry weather and shelter deep in the leaf folds where sprays miss them; weak, drought-stressed leeks are hit hardest.
pests.cause_beginner: A tiny insect called onion thrips. It multiplies fast in hot, dry weather and hides in the tight folds of the leaves, and it bothers stressed plants the most.
pests.management_seasoned: Keep plants vigorous and evenly watered, hose off light infestations, and rotate away from alliums; treat persistent outbreaks per local extension guidance.
pests.management_beginner: Keep the plants healthy and well watered, spray them off with water if thrips are light, and do not plant leeks where you grew onions or leeks last year. For heavy infestations, ask your local extension office what to use.

pests.name: Leek moth
pests.identification_seasoned: Pale, papery window-pane patches where caterpillars have eaten the inner leaf tissue, then tunnels bored down into the shaft; two generations feed roughly May to June and August to October.
pests.identification_beginner: Whitish, see-through papery patches on the leaves where small caterpillars have eaten the inside, and later tunnels down into the stem. There are two waves, in late spring and again in late summer.
pests.cause_seasoned: Larvae of the leek moth (Acrolepiopsis assectella), a small brown moth; young caterpillars mine the foliage and older ones bore into the stems, then pupate in net-like silk cocoons spun on the leaves.
pests.cause_beginner: The caterpillars of a small brown moth. The young ones eat the inside of the leaves and the older ones tunnel into the stem, then spin little net-like cocoons on the plant.
pests.management_seasoned: Cover the crop with insect-proof mesh through the flight periods, rotate alliums, and find and crush the white net-like cocoons on the foliage.
pests.management_beginner: Cover the plants with fine insect netting during late spring and late summer when the moths are active, move leeks to a new spot each year, and squash any little net-like cocoons you find on the leaves.

pests.name: Onion maggot
pests.identification_seasoned: Wilting, yellowing young plants and rotting at the base riddled by small white larvae; stand loss is worst in cool, wet conditions early in the season.
pests.identification_beginner: Young plants wilt and yellow, and the base rots with small white grubs inside. It is worst in cool, wet weather.
pests.cause_seasoned: Larvae of the onion maggot fly (Delia antiqua), whose eggs are laid at the plant base; populations carry over in allium residue left in the ground.
pests.cause_beginner: The larvae (maggots) of a small fly that lays eggs at the base of the plant. They survive in leftover allium debris.
pests.management_seasoned: Rotate away from alliums, remove cull plants and crop residue, and use floating row cover at establishment to block egg-laying.
pests.management_beginner: Do not plant leeks where alliums grew recently, clean up old plant debris, and cover young plants with row-cover fabric so the fly cannot lay eggs on them.

pests.name: Allium leaf miner
pests.identification_seasoned: Neat rows of white dots punched in the leaves by the egg-laying flies, then white legless maggots and small brown pupae tunneling in leaves and shafts; the autumn generation is usually the most damaging.
pests.identification_beginner: Lines of small white dots on the leaves, then white maggots and little brown pupae tunneling inside the leaves and stem. The fall wave does the most damage.
pests.cause_seasoned: The allium leaf miner (Phytomyza gymnostoma), an increasingly widespread fly with two generations a year, active roughly March to April and again September to November; secondary rots often follow the tunneling.
pests.cause_beginner: A fly called the allium leaf miner. It is active in spring and again in fall, and its maggots tunnel inside, often letting rot set in afterward.
pests.management_seasoned: Cover the crop with insect-proof mesh during the two flight periods (about March to April and September to November) and rotate alliums, since the flies emerge from pupae in the soil.
pests.management_beginner: Cover the plants with fine insect netting in spring and again in fall when the flies are active, and move leeks to a new spot each year.

diseases.name: Leek rust
diseases.identification_seasoned: Bright orange pustules scattered on both leaf surfaces that break open to a dusty spore powder; severe infection shrivels leaves early and saps vigor, common from mid-summer into late autumn.
diseases.identification_beginner: Bright orange spots and dusty pustules on the leaves, mostly from mid-summer into fall. Bad cases brown and shrivel the leaves.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Puccinia porri (formerly P. allii); it is worse on crowded plants, in humid weather, and on nitrogen-rich, low-potassium soils.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that causes orange rust. It spreads in damp, humid weather and is worse when plants are crowded or pushed with too much nitrogen.
diseases.management_seasoned: Space plants for airflow, avoid excess nitrogen, balance feeding, remove and destroy badly infected leaves and post-harvest debris, and choose more rust-tolerant varieties where available.
diseases.management_beginner: Give plants room so air moves between them, do not over-feed with nitrogen, pull off and bin badly spotted leaves, and clear away old leaves after harvest. Pick rust-tolerant varieties if you can.

diseases.name: White rot
diseases.identification_seasoned: Yellowing, dieback, and wilting starting at the leaf base, with a fluffy white mold and tiny poppy-seed-like black sclerotia at the base and roots; affected plants pull up easily.
diseases.identification_beginner: Leaves yellow and wilt from the bottom, and the base and roots grow a fluffy white mold dotted with tiny black specks. Sick plants lift right out of the ground.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The soilborne fungus Stromatinia cepivora (Sclerotium cepivorum), whose sclerotia survive in soil for over 20 years and germinate in response to allium roots; even a few sclerotia per soil sample can start the disease.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soil fungus that attacks onions, garlic, and leeks. Its tiny resting bodies can live in the soil for more than 20 years and wake up when allium roots are near.
diseases.management_seasoned: There is no cure once plants are infected; remove and destroy them. Plant only clean stock, practice strict sanitation to avoid moving infested soil, and note that rotation alone will not control it because the sclerotia persist so long.
diseases.management_beginner: There is no cure, so pull and destroy infected plants. Start with clean plants, keep infested soil off your tools and boots, and do not rely on rotation alone, because this fungus lives in the soil for decades.

diseases.name: Pink root
diseases.identification_seasoned: Roots turn pink, then red, and shrivel, stunting plants and shortening shafts; most common where alliums are grown repeatedly and in warm soils.
diseases.identification_beginner: The roots turn pink, then red, then shrivel. Plants stay small with short stems. It is common when alliums are grown in the same spot often.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A soilborne fungus that builds up in continuous allium ground and is favored by warm soil; stressed plants show it worst.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soil fungus that builds up when onions and their relatives are grown in the same ground year after year, especially in warm soil.
diseases.management_seasoned: Rotate away from alliums for several years, start with clean transplants, and keep plants unstressed and evenly watered.
diseases.management_beginner: Rotate where you plant leeks, start with clean healthy transplants, and keep the plants well cared for so they are not stressed.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Keep the soil consistently moist across the whole long season; leeks are shallow-rooted and any drought check shortens and toughens the shaft. They do not need a dry-down at the end the way bulb onions do.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water leeks regularly so the soil stays evenly moist the whole time they grow. Their roots are shallow, so dry spells make the stems shorter and tougher. Unlike onions, you do not stop watering at the end.
watering.amount_seasoned: Aim for about an inch of water per week from rain plus irrigation (USU advises moistening the soil to a depth of about 18 inches every seven days), more in heat or sandy soil, delivered steadily.
watering.amount_beginner: About an inch of water a week is a good target, and more during hot, dry weather. Steady is better than a flood one week and nothing the next.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base with drip or a soaker to keep the foliage dry; lingering leaf wetness and humidity feed leek rust.
watering.method_beginner: Water the soil at the base of the plants, not over the leaves. Keeping the tops dry helps prevent rust.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Waterlogged soil with yellowing, mushy bases signals overwatering; standing moisture around the shaft encourages basal and white rots.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If the soil stays soggy and the bottoms of the plants turn yellow and soft, that is too much water. Sitting in wet soil makes leeks rot.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Bluish, wilting, or tip-burned leaves and stalled growth mean the plants are short of water; under-watered leeks make thin, short, fibrous shanks.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Wilting, bluish, or brown-tipped leaves mean the leeks are too dry. Leeks that do not get enough water make thin, short, tough stems.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Base or drip watering keeps the foliage dry, which matters for leeks because lingering leaf wetness and humidity are exactly what leek rust needs.
watering.method_note_beginner: Watering at the base instead of over the leaves keeps the tops dry, and dry tops are less likely to get rust.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Shaft lengthening through summer and early fall is the most water-sensitive phase; never let the bed dry out while the stems are bulking.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The most important time to keep leeks watered is through summer and early fall while the stems are growing. Do not let them dry out then.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Harden off greenhouse or windowsill seedlings with about a week of gradual outdoor exposure before set-out. Transplant when seedlings are pencil-thick and roughly 8 inches tall; trimming the tops and roots back slightly at planting is a traditional aid that is optional.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: If you grew your own seedlings indoors, set them outside for a few hours a day for about a week before planting so they get used to sun and wind. Plant them when they are about as thick as a pencil and around 8 inches tall.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Two entry points: start seed indoors about 10 weeks before set-out for transplants (the usual approach, since leeks are slow and long-season), or direct-sow in mild, long-season areas. Transplant into a deep dibble hole about 6 inches deep and water gently so soil washes in around the seedling without filling the hole; this sets the seedling deep and starts the blanched shank. Drop the transplant in and do not pack soil around it.
start_method.notes_beginner: Most gardeners start leeks from seed indoors about 10 weeks before planting out, because they grow slowly and need a long season. In mild areas you can also sow seeds straight in the garden. To plant a seedling, make a hole about 6 inches deep with a dibber, drop the seedling in, and just water it; the soil washes in on its own. Planting deep like this starts the long white stem.

drainage.saucer_practice_seasoned: Empty the saucer after each watering; leeks must never sit in standing water, which saturates the shaft base and invites rot.
drainage.saucer_practice_beginner: After you water, pour out any water that collects in the saucer under the pot. Leeks should never sit in standing water, because soggy soil around the base leads to rot.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Use a bag of potting mix with some compost stirred in.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in compost, and a slow-release balanced fertilizer at planting.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: A deep, free-draining potting mix blended with compost.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Work in compost for fertility and a slow-release balanced feed at planting; container leeks feed steadily over a long season.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Water container leeks more often than garden leeks. The soil in a pot dries out fast, and dry spells make the stems short and tough.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Because you water pots often, the food washes out faster. Give container leeks a little balanced fertilizer regularly through the season.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Leeks are very cold-hardy, so a deep pot of leeks can sit out and be harvested into winter in mild areas. Where freezes are hard, move the pot to a sheltered spot or mulch around it, since roots in a container get colder than roots in the ground.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Leeks are cold-hardy enough to stand in a deep container and be harvested through winter in mild-winter zones. In colder zones, group pots against a wall or mulch them, since a container root zone chills faster than open ground.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Leeks grow in pots if the pot is deep, because the long white stem needs depth. Use a container at least 12 inches deep with drainage holes, and space plants about 4 to 6 inches apart. Pots dry out fast, so check the soil often and keep it evenly moist, or the stems stay short.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Leeks suit a deep, well-drained container at least 12 inches deep so the shaft has room to lengthen, spaced about 4 to 6 inches apart. Containers dry fast and the crop is long, so water before the surface crusts and feed steadily; interrupted growth makes thin, short shanks. You can mound mix up the stems in the pot to blanch them just as in the ground.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Expect to water more frequently than in-ground; the shallow root zone in a pot dries quickly and any drought check shortens the shaft.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Frequent watering leaches nutrients, so feed container leeks lightly but regularly across the long season.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering containers suit leeks well, smoothing out the steady moisture they need; keep the mix free-draining so the shaft base never stays saturated.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: Self-watering pots work nicely for leeks because they keep the soil evenly moist. Just use a mix that drains well so the base is not sitting in water.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Avoid following leeks or other alliums (onions, garlic, shallots) in the same ground; several allium diseases, including pink root and especially white rot, persist in soil, white rot for over 20 years. A home garden can target at least 3 to 4 years between allium crops.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Do not plant leeks where you grew onions, garlic, or other leeks recently. Some allium diseases live in the soil and build up, and white rot can last over 20 years. Wait at least 3 to 4 years before growing alliums in the same spot again.
rotation.good_after: leafy greens or legumes
rotation.note_seasoned: Leeks follow well after a leafy or legume crop. Like other alliums, they are traditionally kept away from beans and peas, which alliums are thought to inhibit.
rotation.note_beginner: Leeks do well planted after leafy greens or beans and peas. Just do not plant beans or peas right next to leeks, since alliums can slow them down.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Leeks are not a long-keeping crop and do not store at room temperature. The best storage is to leave them standing in the garden and harvest as needed; lifted leeks soften quickly in a warm room.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Leeks do not keep at room temperature. The best way to store them is to leave them growing in the garden and dig them up as you need them.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Trimmed leeks keep about one to two weeks in the refrigerator, ideally wrapped to hold moisture; USU notes they hold best in cold (32 to 40°F), humid conditions.
storage.fridge_beginner: In the refrigerator, trimmed leeks last about one to two weeks, best wrapped so they do not dry out. They keep best cold and humid.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Leeks freeze well sliced; texture softens, so use frozen leek in cooked dishes such as soups and stews rather than raw.
storage.freezer_beginner: You can slice leeks and freeze them. They go soft after thawing, so use frozen leeks in cooked food like soups, not in salads.
storage.notes_seasoned: The classic way to store leeks is in the ground: they are cold-hardy and stand through frost, so in much of the country you simply leave them and harvest into winter. In the coldest zones, mulch heavily over them or lift and heel them into damp sand or soil in a cold, sheltered spot.
storage.notes_beginner: The simplest way to keep leeks is to leave them in the garden, because they handle frost and stand through winter. In very cold areas, pile mulch over them or dig them up and tuck them into damp sand or soil somewhere cold and sheltered.

recommended.name: King Richard
recommended.recommended_note: A fast, tall early leek that sizes up in roughly 75 to 100 days, good for a late-summer and fall harvest. Less cold-hardy than the winter types, so use it before hard freezes.

recommended.name: Lancelot
recommended.recommended_note: A reliable, vigorous mid-season leek for fall harvest, widely adapted and a good first choice if you are unsure.

recommended.name: Large American Flag
recommended.recommended_note: Also sold as Broad London, a dependable open-pollinated standard for fall harvest with thick shanks. The USU-listed classic for home gardens.

recommended.name: Tadorna
recommended.recommended_note: A hardy, uniform leek that stands well into cold weather, bridging the fall and overwintering windows.

recommended.name: Bandit
recommended.recommended_note: A very cold-hardy, blue-green overwintering leek (the Blauwgroene Winter type) that stands through winter into spring in milder zones. Slow and late, but the most weather-tough choice.

recommended.name: Giant Musselburgh
recommended.recommended_note: A hardy old Scottish heirloom with broad, mild shanks that stands cold well, a traditional pick for a winter standing crop.

varieties.note_seasoned: Choose by season first. Early or summer types (King Richard) are fast and tall but less hardy, for late-summer and fall use. Maincrop types (Lancelot, Large American Flag, Tadorna) carry the main fall harvest. Overwintering types (Bandit, Giant Musselburgh) are slower, shorter, and blue-green but the most cold-hardy, bred to stand in the ground through winter into spring. Matching variety to how late you want to harvest matters far more for leeks than for onions, since leeks have no day-length requirement.
varieties.note_beginner: Pick a leek by when you want to harvest. Early types like King Richard grow fast for late summer and fall but are less hardy. Maincrop types like Lancelot or American Flag give the main fall crop. Overwintering types like Bandit or Giant Musselburgh are tougher and slower, made to stand in the garden through winter so you can dig them up fresh in the cold months. Unlike onions, leeks do not care about day length, so just match the type to your season.

companions.note_beginner: Leeks are easygoing neighbors. Their strong allium smell is traditionally said to help hide carrots from the carrot rust fly, and they tuck in nicely beside celery, beets, and lettuce. The main thing to avoid is planting them next to beans or peas, which alliums can slow down. These are helpful traditions, not sure things.
companions.note_seasoned: Leeks earn their companion reputation mostly through scent, traditionally credited with masking carrots from the carrot rust fly, so the classic leek-and-carrot pairing is the best known. They also share a long cool-season bed comfortably with celery, beets, and lettuce. The firm caution is the legume conflict: alliums are widely held to inhibit beans and peas, so keep leeks away from them. Most of these claims are traditional rather than trial-proven; treat them as low-risk suggestions.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Carrots
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Leeks and carrots are a classic pair. The strong onion-family smell of leeks is said to help hide carrots from the carrot rust fly, and the two do not crowd each other.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: The allium-scent masking of carrot rust fly is the best-known companion mechanism in the onion family and is widely repeated for leeks; specific leek-carrot field trials are thin, so traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Leeks and carrots are the textbook allium-and-umbellifer pairing. The leek's sulfur scent is traditionally credited with masking carrots from the carrot rust fly, and the two have complementary upright forms that share a bed without crowding. Treat the pest benefit as a plausible tradition rather than a proven effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Celery
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Celery and leeks both like the same rich, moist soil and long cool season, so they make easy, undemanding neighbors.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: A long-standing kitchen-garden pairing based on shared rich-soil, long-season culture rather than a measured effect; traditional/low.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Celery and leeks are a traditional bed pairing built on shared culture: both want deep, rich, evenly moist soil and a long cool season, and both are often trenched or earthed up, so they fit the same management. The benefit is compatibility and efficient use of a rich bed, not a documented pest or growth effect.

good_seasoned.name: Carrots
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: The pungent foliage of leeks is traditionally cited as masking the scent cues carrot rust fly uses to find carrots, and the two have complementary upright habits. Intuitive and long-standing, but not cleanly demonstrated at the bed scale.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Long-standing interplanting tradition with a plausible scent-masking mechanism; specific leek-carrot field evidence is thin.

good_seasoned.name: Celery
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional companion sharing leeks' need for deep, rich, moist soil and a long cool season; the two use the same well-fed bed efficiently without a documented pest effect.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Shared rich-soil long-season culture; a conventional pairing rather than a research-demonstrated benefit.

good_seasoned.name: Beets
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Beets share leeks' cool-season culture and a non-competing form, making them an easy neighbor that uses space efficiently; mostly a good-neighbor pairing with a modest traditional allium pest-repel bonus.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Compatible culture and spacing plus the general allium pest-repel reputation; no leek-specific measured effect.

good_seasoned.name: Lettuce
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Quick, shallow-rooted lettuce fills the row between slow upright leeks and shares the cool season, a space-efficient and traditional intercrop harvested long before the leeks fill in.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Spacing- and season-compatible intercrop; conventional companion advice without pair-specific trial evidence.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Beans and peas
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep leeks away from beans and peas. Onions and their relatives, including leeks, are thought to slow the growth of these legumes.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: The allium-inhibits-legume claim is a long-standing and widely repeated companion tradition across the onion family; mechanism is debated, so traditional/medium.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Alliums, including leeks, are traditionally held to inhibit beans and peas, so the long-standing advice is to keep them apart. The mechanism is debated and the effect is not firmly demonstrated, but it is a consistent enough tradition across the onion family to respect as a low-cost precaution.

bad_seasoned.name: Beans and peas
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Alliums, including leeks, are widely held to inhibit legumes, so the traditional rule is to keep leeks away from beans and peas. The claim is consistent across the onion family but not cleanly demonstrated; treat it as a low-cost precaution.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Long-standing allium-inhibits-legume tradition across the onion family; mechanism debated, not pair-trial-proven.

growth_stages.name: Germination & Emergence
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A single looped seed leaf pushes up bent like a hairpin, then straightens into the first slender grass-like blade. Leeks germinate slowly and unevenly over cool to moderate soil, so stands come up over a week or two.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Look for thin, grass-like shoots, each starting bent over in a little loop like a hairpin, then standing up. Leeks sprout slowly, so do not worry if they come up over a week or two rather than all at once.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep the surface evenly moist so the fine seed never dries mid-germination, and keep seedlings weed-free; young leeks compete poorly. If you set transplants, this stage is already behind you.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the top of the soil damp so the tiny seeds do not dry out, and pull weeds early. If you planted young plants instead of seeds, you can skip this stage.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Note your sowing date and first emergence; the gap tells you your soil's germination pace for next season.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Write down when you planted and when the first shoots appeared. That tells you how fast your soil sprouts leeks next time.

growth_stages.name: Seedling Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Slow, thin, upright seedlings build toward pencil thickness and about 8 inches tall over roughly 8 to 10 weeks, usually indoors or in a nursery bed. This is a patient stage; leeks are deliberate growers.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The seedlings grow slowly into thin, upright plants, getting to about pencil thickness and 8 inches tall over a couple of months, usually indoors. Be patient, this is just how leeks grow.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep seedlings in good light, evenly moist, and lightly fed. Grow them to pencil thickness before transplanting; a stronger seedling makes a thicker shaft later.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the seedlings in bright light, water them evenly, and feed a little. Grow them until they are about as thick as a pencil before planting out.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Track sowing-to-transplant time; leeks reward a full, unhurried seedling stage with bigger plants.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note how long the seedlings took to reach planting size. It helps you time your indoor start next year.

growth_stages.name: Transplant & Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: After set-out into a deep dibble hole, the transplant roots in and resumes upright growth. Early leaves green up and the base sits deep in its hole, the start of the blanched shank.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: After you plant the seedling deep in its hole, it settles in and starts growing upright again. The base is sunk deep in the soil, which is what starts the long white stem.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Plant into a 6-inch dibble hole and water without filling it, so soil washes in gradually. Keep the bed weed-free and evenly moist while plants take hold.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Plant each seedling in a deep hole and just water it, letting the soil wash in on its own. Keep weeds out and the soil moist while the plants settle.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Note your transplant date and spacing; it anchors the long run to harvest.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Write down when you planted out and how far apart. It helps you plan next year.

growth_stages.name: Shaft Lengthening & Blanching
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Through summer and early fall the plant stacks leaves and the white shaft lengthens and thickens. This is the main growth phase, driven by steady moisture, feeding, and repeated earthing up to blanch the stem.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Through summer and early fall the plant grows lots of leaves and the white stem gets longer and thicker. This is the main growing time, helped by steady water, feeding, and pulling soil up around the stems to keep them white.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Feed and water steadily, and earth up the stems a couple of times, drawing loose soil up around them (never more than an inch at a time, and not over the leaf joint) to lengthen the blanched white shank.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep watering and feeding, and two or three times pull loose soil up around the stems to grow a longer white part. Add only an inch of soil at a time and keep it below where the leaves split.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Log feeding and earthing-up dates against final shaft length; it tunes your blanching routine.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you fed and hilled the soil up. Comparing that to how long the white part got helps next year.

growth_stages.name: Maturity, Harvest & Standing
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Shanks reach about an inch or more across and the leeks are ready. Because they are cold-hardy, they hold their quality standing in the ground through frost, so harvest runs from fall into winter as needed rather than all at once.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The white stems reach about an inch or more across and the leeks are ready. Leeks handle frost, so you can leave them in the ground and dig them up fresh from fall into winter instead of all at once.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest by loosening with a fork and lifting (do not just pull), starting when shanks are big enough. Leave the rest standing and harvest as needed; in the coldest zones mulch heavily so you can dig through frozen ground.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Harvest by loosening the soil with a fork and lifting the leek out, not yanking. Pick the biggest first and leave the rest growing. In very cold places, pile mulch over them so you can still dig them up.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record first and last harvest dates and how late they stood; it sets your overwintering plan.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Write down when you started and stopped harvesting and how late they lasted. It helps you plan next winter.

notifications.title_beginner: Time to start leek seeds inside
notifications.body_seasoned: Sow leek seed indoors now, roughly 10 to 12 weeks before set-out. Leeks are slow growers, so the long lead lets seedlings reach pencil thickness before they go out. Direct-sowing in a mild, long-season area? Skip this one.
notifications.body_beginner: If you are growing leeks from seed, plant them in trays indoors now, about 10 to 12 weeks before they go outside. Leeks grow slowly and need this head start. In mild areas you can sow straight in the garden instead.

notifications.body_seasoned: Plant pencil-thick seedlings into 6-inch dibble holes once the soil is workable; leeks are cold-hardy and go out around the last frost. Drop each into its hole and water it in without filling the hole.
notifications.body_beginner: Plant your young leeks now, once the soil can be worked, around your last frost. Make a deep hole for each, drop the seedling in, and just water it so the soil washes in. Leeks handle cool weather, so you do not wait for warm soil.

notifications.title_seasoned: Earth up your leeks to blanch
notifications.title_beginner: Pull soil up around your leeks
notifications.body_seasoned: Begin earthing up: draw loose soil up around the shanks to blanch them, no more than an inch at a time and kept below the leaf joint. Repeat a few times through the season for a longer white stem.
notifications.body_beginner: Start pulling loose soil up around the stems to grow a longer white part. Add only about an inch of soil at a time and keep it below where the leaves split. Do this a few times over the season.

notifications.title_seasoned: Feed leeks to build the shafts
notifications.body_seasoned: Side-dress nitrogen during summer to drive shaft growth, repeating once or twice. Keep feeding steady but not excessive, since lush, crowded, well-fed leeks are more prone to rust.
notifications.body_beginner: Give your leeks a nitrogen feed now and again during summer to grow thicker stems. Do not overdo it, though, since heavily fed, crowded plants get rust more easily.

notifications.body_seasoned: Once shanks reach about an inch across, lift leeks as needed by loosening with a fork. They hold standing in the ground through frost, so harvest into winter rather than all at once.
notifications.body_beginner: When the white stems are about an inch across, start digging leeks as you need them, loosening the soil with a fork first. They keep growing and standing through frost, so you can harvest all the way into winter.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Hard freeze on a standing crop
weather_triggers.title_beginner: A hard freeze with leeks still in the ground
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Leeks themselves shrug off frost and even sweeten with it, but a hard freeze can lock them into frozen ground. Mulch heavily over the row before the freeze so you can still dig leeks through the cold.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Leeks handle frost fine and even taste better for it, but the ground can freeze solid around them. Pile mulch over the row before a hard freeze so you can still dig them up.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat and dry stress while shafts size
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot, dry weather while the stems grow
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Hot, dry spells check shaft growth, since leeks are shallow-rooted and any drought interruption shortens and toughens the stem. Water deeply and evenly through a heat spell; mulch helps hold moisture.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Hot, dry weather while the stems are growing makes them shorter and tougher, because leeks have shallow roots and do not like to dry out. Water deeply and evenly during heat, and mulch helps keep the soil moist.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Damp, humid weather and rust
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Long leaf wetness and humidity from mid-summer on are exactly what leek rust needs. Space plants for airflow, water at the base, ease off heavy nitrogen, and remove badly spotted leaves to slow it.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Damp, humid weather from mid-summer on brings on orange leek rust. Give plants room so air moves between them, water at the base, do not over-feed, and pull off the worst spotted leaves.

germination_emergence.text_seasoned: Sow into cool-to-moderate, evenly moist soil and be patient: leek seed germinates slowly and unevenly. Keep the surface from drying while the fine seed comes up.
germination_emergence.text_beginner: Plant leek seeds in moist soil and wait. They sprout slowly and not all at once, so keep the soil surface damp until the little shoots appear.

seedling_growth.text_seasoned: Grow seedlings to pencil thickness and about 8 inches tall before set-out; a fuller seedling stage builds a thicker final shaft. Keep them in strong light so they do not stretch.
seedling_growth.text_beginner: Let the seedlings grow until they are about as thick as a pencil and 8 inches tall before planting out. Strong seedlings make bigger leeks. Keep them in bright light so they do not get leggy.

establishment.text_seasoned: Transplant deep: set seedlings into a 6-inch dibble hole and just water them in, letting soil wash around the stem rather than packing it. Deep setting starts the blanched shank.
establishment.text_beginner: Plant each seedling in a deep hole made with a dibber and just water it, so the soil washes in on its own. Planting deep like this is what starts the long white stem.

shaft_lengthening.text_seasoned: Earth up two or three times as the plants grow, drawing loose soil up around the shanks no more than an inch at a time and never above the leaf joint, to lengthen the white shaft and avoid stem rot.
shaft_lengthening.text_beginner: Two or three times during the season, pull loose soil up around the stems to grow a longer white part. Add only about an inch at a time and keep it below where the leaves split, or the stem can rot.

shaft_lengthening.text_seasoned: Keep moisture and feeding steady through summer; an unbroken growth run is what builds long, thick shanks, while drought checks and crowding make them thin and short.
shaft_lengthening.text_beginner: Keep watering and feeding steadily through summer. Leeks grow best without interruption, so do not let them dry out or get crowded, or the stems stay thin and short.

maturity_harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest by loosening with a fork and lifting once shanks are about an inch across; leave the rest standing. Leeks are cold-hardy and hold quality through frost, so harvest from fall into winter as needed.
maturity_harvest.text_beginner: When the stems are about an inch across, loosen the soil with a fork and lift the leeks out, do not yank them. Leave the rest growing. Leeks handle frost, so dig them fresh from fall into winter as you need them.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: One leek per plant. At 4-to-6-inch spacing, a 10-foot row yields roughly 20 to 30 leeks, harvested over a long fall-to-winter window rather than all at once.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Each plant makes one leek. A 10-foot row gives you roughly 20 to 30 leeks, and you dig them over a long stretch from fall into winter, not all at the same time.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Because leeks stand in the ground and are harvested as needed, there is no single flush: the harvest spreads across fall and winter, and mixing early and overwintering types stretches it further.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Leeks do not all finish at once. Because they stand in the garden, you harvest them gradually through fall and winter, and growing both early and late types spreads it out even more.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: The biggest first-year lever is a long, unbroken growing season: start seed early enough, keep moisture and feeding steady, and earth up for the white shank. Rushed or stop-start leeks make thin, short stems.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: The most important thing your first year is giving leeks a long, steady season: start the seeds early, keep them watered and fed, and hill soil up for the white part. Leeks that are rushed or stressed stay thin and short.
factors_seasoned: long unbroken growing season
consistent moisture
steady but not excessive nitrogen
earthing up for shaft length
spacing for airflow against rust

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No verified evidence ties leek growth or yield to moon phase; growth is driven by temperature, moisture, and feeding. Planting timing follows soil readiness and the long season, not lunar phase.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Thin, short, or tough shanks instead of fat tender stems.
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: The leeks stay thin and short, or are tough, instead of growing into fat tender stems.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Almost always a growth check: too short a season, drought, crowding, weed competition, or thin feeding. Leeks need a long, steady, well-fed run to bulk the shaft.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Usually the plants got stressed or did not have enough time: a dry spell, crowding, weeds, or too little food. Leeks need a long, steady season to grow thick.
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Start seed earlier for a longer season, thin or space to 4 to 6 inches, keep moisture and nitrogen steady through summer, and earth up to lengthen the white shank.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Start the seeds earlier, give plants room (about 4 to 6 inches apart), keep them watered and fed all summer, and pull soil up around the stems to grow a longer white part.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Bright orange pustules and dusty spots on the leaves.
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Bright orange spots and dusty patches on the leaves, mostly from mid-summer into fall.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Leek rust (Puccinia porri), favored by humidity, crowding, and nitrogen-rich, low-potassium soils; spores spread in damp weather.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: A fungus called leek rust. It spreads in damp, humid weather and is worse when plants are crowded or pushed with too much nitrogen.
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Space plants for airflow, water at the base, ease off heavy nitrogen and balance feeding, remove badly infected leaves and post-harvest debris, and choose more tolerant varieties. Plants can usually still be harvested and eaten.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Give plants more room, water at the base not over the leaves, do not over-feed with nitrogen, and pull off the worst leaves. You can usually still eat lightly rusted leeks.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: A hard round flower stalk shoots up from the center (bolting).
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: A tall, hard flower stalk shoots up from the middle of the leek.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Bolting in leeks is triggered by stress, especially a spell of cold on an over-large or overwintered plant, then warmth. Once a woody flower stalk forms, the shank toughens and stops sizing.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Bolting happens when a leek is stressed, often by cold weather on a big or overwintered plant followed by warmth. Once the hard flower stalk forms, the stem turns woody and stops growing.
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Use appropriately sized transplants, avoid very early exposure of large plants to prolonged cold, and for overwintering choose bolt-resistant winter varieties. Harvest any bolters promptly while still usable.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Plant the right-sized seedlings, avoid letting big plants sit through a long cold spell too early, and use winter varieties for overwintering. Use up any that bolt while they are still good.

succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Leeks are a single, long-season standing crop, not a successioned one. One main planting matures over many months and then holds in the ground to be harvested gradually through fall and winter, so staggered sowings do not yield a staggered, faster turnover the way a quick salad crop does. The way to stretch the leek harvest is to mix early and overwintering varieties in one planting, not to plant in repeated successions.

3.zone_notes: Coldest northern zone: a single long-season crop. Start seed indoors in late winter, transplant in May once soil is workable, and harvest from early fall. Leeks stand through frost, so dig into late fall and, under deep mulch, beyond. Lean on faster early varieties so shafts size up before the ground locks.

4.zone_notes: Start seed indoors in late winter, transplant mid-April into May, and harvest from early fall. Cold-hardy leeks stand through frost into November; mulch heavily to keep harvesting as the ground hardens.

5.zone_notes: Start seed indoors in late winter, transplant in April, and harvest from early fall. Leeks are very cold-hardy and stand into late fall; deep mulch extends harvest toward winter.

6.zone_notes: A long runway: start seed indoors in winter, transplant from mid-March, and harvest standing leeks from early fall well into December under mulch. Overwintering varieties push the harvest furthest.

7.zone_notes: Warm edge of the northern tier: start seed indoors in winter, transplant in March, and harvest a standing crop from early fall through the winter with overwintering varieties and a little mulch.

northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In the cold-winter North, leeks are a single long-season crop and a standout fall and early-winter vegetable. Start seed indoors in late winter, since leeks are slow, then set pencil-thick transplants into deep dibble holes around the last frost; leeks are cold-hardy and do not wait for warm soil. Grow them on through summer with steady water and feeding, earthing soil up around the stems to blanch the white shank, and begin harvesting in early fall. The best part is that leeks stand through hard frost, sweetening with cold, so you dig them fresh into late fall and, under deep mulch, into winter. Lean on early varieties in the coldest zones and overwintering types where winters are milder.
northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: If you live in the colder northern states (zones 3 to 7), leeks are a one-time, long-season crop that really shines in fall and early winter. Start seeds indoors in late winter because leeks grow slowly, then plant the young leeks into deep holes around your last frost; they handle cold, so you do not wait for warm weather. Grow them all summer with steady water and food, pulling soil up around the stems to make the long white part, and start harvesting in early fall. The great thing about leeks is that they stand right through frost and even taste sweeter for it, so you can dig them fresh into late fall and, with a thick mulch, into winter.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Leek windows for this region are authored from the cited leek and regional extension sources; leeks are transplanted (or direct-sown in mild areas) and grown as a long-season standing crop, earthed up to blanch, then harvested gradually.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The standing crop holds through fall and winter in this region, so the harvest tail runs long.

8.zone_notes: In the Southeast and Gulf, leeks are a cool-season crop. Start seed in late summer, set transplants fall into early winter, and harvest winter into spring. Summer is too hot, so the bed turns over to other crops then.

9.zone_notes: Mild Gulf and coastal Southeast: set fall transplants and harvest through winter into spring before summer heat. Use the cool months; leeks do not size up in the southern summer.

se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: In the Southeast and along the Gulf, leeks are a cool-season crop grown through the mild fall, winter, and spring. Start seed in late summer, set transplants from fall into early winter, and harvest from winter into spring. The region's hot, humid summer is too much for leeks, so the bed turns over to warm-season crops then, and you replant leeks the following fall. Watch for leek rust in the humid weather: space plants, water at the base, and go easy on nitrogen.
se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast and along the Gulf (zones 8 to 9), leeks grow in the cool months. Start seeds in late summer, plant young leeks from fall into early winter, and harvest from winter into spring. Summer is too hot and humid, so you grow other things then and plant leeks again the next fall. Orange rust likes the damp weather, so give plants room, water at the base, and do not over-feed.

8.zone_notes: California interior valleys: hot, dry summers push leeks into the cool half of the year. Start seed in late summer, transplant in fall, and harvest winter into spring. The mild winter lets leeks stand and be dug as needed.

9.zone_notes: Warm interior valley: a fall-planted, winter-to-spring leek crop. Hot summers are skipped; the mild winter lets the standing crop be harvested gradually.

ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: In California's interior valleys, hot, dry summers push leeks into the cool half of the year. Start seed in late summer, transplant in fall, and harvest from winter into spring; the mild winter lets the standing crop be dug as needed. Earth up for the white shank and keep moisture steady. The regional planting window is modeled on UC allium timing, since UC's planting tables give onions rather than leeks directly.

The mild winter means you can leave them standing and dig them as you need them. Pull soil up for the white part and keep them watered.

crops.description_seasoned: Leek (Allium ampeloprasum) is the mild, sweet allium grown not for a bulb but for its long, thick, blanched white stem, or shank. It is a patient, long-season crop, usually started indoors in late winter and transplanted deep so soil can be earthed up around the stem to blanch it. Its great virtue is cold-hardiness: leeks stand in the garden through hard frost, sweetening with the cold, and are dug fresh from fall into winter rather than harvested all at once. There is no bulbing and no day-length requirement, so unlike onions you simply match the variety, early or overwintering, to how late you want to harvest.
crops.description_beginner: A leek is a mild, sweet relative of the onion, but instead of a bulb you grow and eat the long white stem. Leeks take a long time, so most gardeners start them indoors in late winter and plant them deep, then pull soil up around the stems to keep the bottom part white and tender. The best thing about leeks is that they handle cold: they stand right in the garden through frost and even taste sweeter for it, so you can dig them up fresh from fall into winter instead of all at one time.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Leeks are ready once the white shank is about an inch or more across and several inches long; there is no need to wait for a set size, and you can begin earlier for slim leeks. Lift by loosening with a fork rather than pulling. Because they are cold-hardy, leave the rest standing and harvest from fall into winter as needed.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Leeks are ready when the white stem is about an inch or more thick. You do not have to wait for an exact size, and smaller ones are fine too. Loosen the soil with a fork and lift them out gently. Since leeks handle frost, leave the others in the ground and dig them up fresh from fall into winter as you need them.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: leek_author_fresh_pilot (Claude Code lane authoring, 2026-06-29). Authored by FILLING the leek shell, modeled STRUCTURALLY on the certified onion allium template, with biology RE-DERIVED for leek from live T1 extension sources (UMN, USU, UMD, and UF/IFAS HS1388 for core growing biology, pH, spacing, days to maturity, blanching, fertilizer, watering, harvest and overwintering; RHS for sowing/transplant timing, overwintering varieties, leek moth, leek rust, and allium leaf miner; UC IPM for allium white rot). KEY LEEK-VS-ONION REFITS: leek is grown for the blanched STEM and does NOT bulb, so it carries NO photoperiod machinery (gating_factors=[], no day_length typing on varieties or cells); it is a LONG-SEASON crop started indoors in late winter and transplanted deep, BLANCHED by earthing up/trenching; and it is VERY COLD-HARDY, standing through frost as a fall-into-winter standing crop (the headline) rather than cured and stored like onions. Per-region calendars: northern_tier (spring-transplant, fall-into-winter standing) from UMN/USU/UMD; se_gulf, ca_desert, low_desert_az, fl_peninsula and the CA Mediterranean regions modeled as cool-season fall-plant/winter-spring crops with summer season_over (UF/IFAS gives the Florida leek calendar directly; the others are modeled on the cool-season allium pattern and FLAGGED). DRAFT for review, not certified: launch flags false.

The range is consistent with onion's [48, 90] narrowed to the cooler leek preference.

open_findings.summary: days_to_maturity [90, 150] spans early types (King Richard ~90 to 100) to slow overwintering types (~150). Sourced figures cluster at 100 to 120 (UMN/USU), 70 to 120 (UMD), and 100 to 130 (UF/IFAS); the upper tail to 150 is a modeled allowance for overwintering varieties.

No readable T1 leek calendar was found for NM/AZ high-and-low desert, the CA UC planting tables (which list onions, not leeks), or Hawaii CTAHR. UF/IFAS HS1388 gives the Florida leek calendar directly (fl_peninsula, and informs se_gulf), and UMN/USU/UMD anchor the northern_tier spring-to-fall standing crop.

Leek is a UK staple, so RHS is authoritative on leek biology and pests; US planting MONTHS were taken from the US extension sources, not RHS.

crops.name: Brussels Sprouts

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Brussels sprouts like rich, fertile soil with plenty of compost worked in, and they do best in firm, settled ground rather than loose, fluffy soil. Loose soil tends to give loose, open sprouts, so firm the bed before planting and keep it evenly moist but never waterlogged.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Brussels sprouts are heavy feeders that reward a fertile, well-drained loam high in organic matter, but they have one quirk worth honoring: they sprout most tightly in firm, settled soil. Loose, recently dug ground encourages loose, blowy sprouts and lodging of the tall, top-heavy stalk, so work in compost ahead of time and let the bed firm up before planting. Keep moisture even through the long season; the plant needs steady water but resents waterlogged ground.

ph.note_beginner: Brussels sprouts grow best in soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, about 6.0 to 7.0. A simple soil test tells you where you stand. If you have had clubroot, keeping the soil closer to neutral helps hold it back.
ph.note_seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0; the plant still does fine across a wider 5.5 to 7.5 band. Clubroot, the key brassica soil disease, is far more likely below pH 6.5, so where it is a concern hold the soil toward the neutral end and lime acidic ground well ahead of planting.

fertilizer.timing: starter at transplanting, then side-dress about 4 and 8 weeks later
fertilizer.example_product: Blood meal, 21-0-0, or a balanced 10-10-10 vegetable fertilizer
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Brussels sprouts are long-season heavy feeders that need steady nitrogen to build the tall, leafy stalk that carries the crop. Work a balanced fertilizer such as 10-10-10 into the bed before planting, then side-dress with nitrogen about 4 and 8 weeks after transplanting. Ease off heavy nitrogen once sprouts begin forming, since late, lush growth encourages loose, leafy sprouts and draws aphids.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Brussels sprouts grow for a long time and need regular feeding. Mix a balanced fertilizer into the soil before planting, then feed with a nitrogen fertilizer about a month and again two months after planting. Once the little sprouts start forming, go easier on the nitrogen, because too much makes loose, leafy sprouts and brings aphids.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time to side-dress your brussels sprouts with nitrogen.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Time to feed your brussels sprouts.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: High N to build the stalk and leaves; a 10-10-10 starter worked in before planting, then a nitrogen side-dress such as 21-0-0 at about 4 and 8 weeks. Ease off N as sprouts set.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 at planting, then a nitrogen feed a month or two later.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: Side-dress about half a cup of 21-0-0 per 10 feet of row at roughly 4 and 8 weeks after transplanting, watered in alongside the plants.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Follow the label rate for a nitrogen-rich vegetable fertilizer, applied beside the plants.

companions.note_beginner: Brussels sprouts do well next to aromatic herbs, onions, and quick cool-season crops you can tuck in while the plants are small. The most important rule is to keep them away from other cabbage-family plants, which share the same pests and diseases.
companions.note_seasoned: Most brussels sprouts companion pairings are traditional rather than trial-tested. The ones worth acting on are practical: aromatic herbs and alliums as scent-based deterrents for cabbage pests, small flowering plants such as sweet alyssum and dill to draw the parasitic wasps and hoverflies that attack aphids and caterpillars (a habitat tactic Clemson recommends for cole crops), and quick crops like lettuce that use the open ground while the slow brussels plants fill in. The well-grounded caution is to separate brussels sprouts from other brassicas, which share clubroot and the whole cabbage-family pest complex, a rotation and disease principle more than a tested adjacency effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Sweet alyssum
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Sweet alyssum makes lots of tiny flowers that bring in helpful insects which eat aphids, a major brussels pest.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Clemson recommends planting small flowers like sweet alyssum and dill near cole crops to attract beneficial parasites and predators; the specific alyssum-brussels pairing is not trial-isolated, so medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Sweet alyssum is one of the better-supported brussels companions because aphids are this crop's signature pest. Its low mats of tiny flowers are a classic insectary plant, drawing the hoverflies, lacewings, and parasitic wasps that prey on cabbage aphids and caterpillars, and Clemson specifically advises small flowers like alyssum near cole crops for biological control. Let it self-sow along the bed edge.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Dill
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Dill's flowers attract helpful insects that hunt the aphids and caterpillars that bother brussels sprouts.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Clemson names dill among the small flowers that attract beneficial parasites to cole crops; aromatic umbels are widely extension-noted for recruiting parasitoid wasps and hoverflies. Brussels-dill not trial-isolated, so medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Dill works for brussels sprouts mainly through beneficial insects. Its umbel flowers draw the parasitoid wasps and hoverflies that attack cabbage aphids and the cabbage-family caterpillars, and Clemson lists dill among the flowers to plant near cole crops for natural control. Let some flower, and keep it off to the side so it does not crowd the big plants.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Onions
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Onions are a traditional neighbor for cabbage-family plants; their strong smell is said to help confuse and deter cabbage pests.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Allium scent-masking of brassica pests is a long-standing companion tradition with partial mechanistic support; not trial-isolated for brussels, so low.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Alliums are a traditional brassica companion, their pungent scent thought to mask the crop from the cabbage pests that hunt partly by smell. Shallow-rooted and undemanding, onions tuck around young brussels plants without competing for much. Treat it as a low-risk, scent-based aid rather than a proven control.

good_seasoned.name: Sweet alyssum
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A classic insectary plant whose tiny flowers recruit hoverflies, lacewings, and parasitic wasps against cabbage aphids, the brussels crop's worst pest. Clemson recommends small flowers like alyssum near cole crops for biological control.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Clemson advises alyssum/dill near cole crops to attract beneficial parasites; not isolated for brussels.

good_seasoned.name: Dill
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Aromatic umbels like dill draw parasitoid wasps and hoverflies that attack brussels aphids and caterpillars; Clemson lists dill among the flowers to plant near cole crops. Let some flower, and keep it from crowding the plants.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Clemson cole-crop beneficial-habitat recommendation; specific dill-brussels pairing not trial-isolated.

good_seasoned.name: Onions
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional brassica companion whose scent is thought to deter cabbage pests; shallow-rooted and low-competition. A plausible, low-risk pairing rather than a documented effect.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Allium scent-masking lore for brassicas; not trial-isolated.

good_seasoned.name: Lettuce
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A quick, shallow cool-season crop that uses the open ground and light between young brussels plants and is harvested long before they fill in. Space-driven and traditional, not a documented growth effect; the two share no serious pest.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Space-use intercropping lore; no T1 source documents a lettuce-brussels benefit.

good_seasoned.name: Nasturtiums
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Often planted as a trap crop for cabbage aphids near brassicas. Trap cropping is a documented principle but is not a tested brussels-nasturtium pairing, so treat it as a plausible aid rather than a proven control.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Trap cropping for aphids is a documented mechanism; the specific nasturtium-brussels pairing is not formally tested.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Other brassicas
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep brussels sprouts away from other cabbage-family plants like broccoli, cabbage, kale, and cauliflower. They share the same pests and diseases, so grouping them makes problems worse.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Same-family crops share pests and pathogens, so clustering raises pest/disease pressure, and successive brassica planting builds soil-borne clubroot. A sound epidemiological/rotation mechanism rather than a measured antagonism.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Planting brussels sprouts shoulder to shoulder with their brassica relatives, broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, kale, collards, concentrates the family's shared pests (cabbage aphids, cabbageworms, loopers, harlequin bugs, root maggots) and shared diseases in one spot, and repeated same-family planting lets soil-borne clubroot build up. Spread brassicas out and rotate where they grow each year.

bad_seasoned.name: Other brassicas
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, kale, and the other cole crops share brussels sprouts' clubroot and cabbage-family pests, so grouping them concentrates disease and pest pressure. A real rotation and disease principle rather than a tested adjacency effect; the practical rule is to spread brassicas out and rotate them.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Shared clubroot and shared cabbage-family pests are extension-documented; the bad-adjacency claim is a known agronomic principle, not formally pair-tested.

bad_seasoned.name: Strawberries
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional caution that brassicas and strawberries inhibit each other. There is no documented mechanism or T1 support; it persists as folklore.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Folk anti-companion claim with no pattern match or T1 support.

pests.name: Cabbage aphids
pests.symptoms_beginner: You'll see clusters of small gray-green insects with a dusty, waxy coating on the new growth and, worst of all, packed down inside the developing sprouts where they are very hard to wash out. Leaves may curl and there can be a sticky film.
pests.cause_beginner: Cabbage aphids are tiny insects that suck the plant's juices and breed fast, especially on the long-season fall crop. They love brussels sprouts and hide right inside the little sprouts, which is the part you eat.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Knock colonies off with a strong spray of water and hit the undersides of leaves and into the sprouts with insecticidal soap or neem oil, repeating every few days. Welcome ladybugs and lacewings, which eat aphids.
pests.prevention_beginner: Check the growing tips and sprouts often and act early, before the aphids get down into the sprouts. Go easy on nitrogen fertilizer once sprouts form, since soft growth draws them, and clear away old cabbage-family plants after harvest.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: The gray-green, waxy-coated cabbage aphid is the signature brussels sprouts pest. Colonies build on growing tips and leaf undersides and then lodge deep inside the developing sprouts, where they contaminate the marketable buds with insects and honeydew and are extremely hard to clean at harvest. Populations explode on the long-season late-summer and fall crop.
pests.cause_seasoned: Brevicoryne brassicae, a brassica-specialist aphid, sucks sap and reproduces rapidly; on brussels sprouts it feeds in the upper leaves, flower buds, and especially within the forming sprouts. Contamination of the harvested sprouts with aphids and sticky honeydew is usually the real problem rather than plant stunting.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Dislodge colonies with a strong jet of water and spray insecticidal soap, neem, or horticultural oil with thorough coverage of leaf undersides and into the sprouts; repeat every few days. Conserve natural enemies (the parasitoid Diaeretiella rapae, hoverflies, lady beetles) that suppress this aphid.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Scout growing tips and the leaf axils weekly and catch infestations before aphids colonize the sprouts. Avoid excess nitrogen once sprouts set (soft growth favors them), use reflective mulch or row cover on young plants, and destroy crop debris that carries them over.

pests.name: Cabbageworms and cabbage loopers
pests.symptoms_beginner: You'll see ragged holes chewed in the leaves, green caterpillars on the plant, and dark droppings, and later the caterpillars may bore into the sprouts. Some loop up in the middle as they crawl.
pests.cause_beginner: These are caterpillars that hatch from eggs laid by white butterflies and small moths. They love cabbage-family plants and chew the leaves, and they can tunnel into the sprouts you want to eat.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray Bt, which is safe and targets only caterpillars, or spinosad, and pick caterpillars and eggs off by hand from under the leaves. Spray again after rain, since it washes off.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover plants with a light fabric row cover after planting to keep the butterflies and moths from laying eggs, clear away old cabbage-family plants, and watch for the first white butterflies as your signal to act.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Ragged holes chewed in the leaves with green caterpillars and dark frass; as the season goes on, larvae also bore into the sprouts and foul them. Imported cabbageworms are velvety green; cabbage loopers move in a looping arch; diamondback larvae are small and wriggle when disturbed; the cross-striped cabbageworm shows black and white bands.
pests.cause_seasoned: The larvae of the imported cabbageworm, cabbage looper, and diamondback moth (Clemson rates the diamondback the most numerous in home gardens) feed on brassica foliage and contaminate the sprouts; the adults are white or brownish butterflies and moths that lay eggs on the leaves.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Spray Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki) or spinosad, which target caterpillars and spare beneficials, and hand-pick larvae and eggs from leaf undersides. Repeat after rain, since Bt breaks down.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Use floating row cover or fine mesh from transplanting to exclude the egg-laying adults, clean up brassica debris that shelters pupae, and scout for the first white butterflies as a spray cue. Tighten control once sprouts begin forming, since damage to the buds is the costly kind.

pests.name: Harlequin bug
pests.symptoms_beginner: Shield-shaped black-and-orange (or black-and-red) bugs on the leaves, which develop white or yellow spots, then brown and look tattered. It is mostly a warm-region problem and loves cabbage-family plants.
pests.cause_beginner: The harlequin bug is a colorful stink-bug relative that pierces the leaves and sucks the juices, leaving pale blotches. It strongly prefers cabbage-family plants, especially in the South.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Search out and crush the bugs, their barrel-shaped eggs laid in rows, and the young ones by hand. Use a row cover to keep them off, pull badly infested plants, and clear away weeds and old plants where they hide over winter.
pests.prevention_beginner: Clean up garden debris and cabbage-family weeds where the adults overwinter, use row cover, and consider a trap crop of cleome or mustard to lure them away from the main crop, then destroy it.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Shield-shaped bugs up to about 3/8 inch, brightly black-and-yellow or black-and-red, feeding with piercing-sucking mouthparts that leave white stipples; affected leaves brown and look tattered, and heavy feeding wilts and deforms plants. A warm-region brassica specialist.
pests.cause_seasoned: The harlequin bug (Murgantia histrionica) is a true bug that specializes on cole crops, most damaging in the southern United States, where it completes two to three generations a year and overwinters as an adult in debris and weeds.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick and crush adults, nymphs, and the barrel-shaped egg rows; exclude with floating row cover; remove heavily infested plants. Insecticidal soap, pyrethrum, or neem help where pressure is severe.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Eliminate overwintering sites by removing crop debris and crucifer weeds, use row cover, and deploy an early trap crop of cleome or mustard to divert overwintering adults, then destroy it before the main crop is set out.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms_beginner: Lots of tiny round holes in the leaves of young plants, made by small dark beetles that jump away like fleas when you get close. Bad damage can stunt seedlings.
pests.cause_beginner: Flea beetles are small jumping beetles that chew on young cabbage-family leaves. They hurt seedlings most, because a tiny plant can't grow fast enough to recover.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover young plants with a row cover, and if there are a lot of beetles, use a spray such as spinosad. The main goal is to get the seedlings big enough to handle the damage.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover seedlings with row cover from the start, keep them strong with steady water and food so they grow past the damage, and pull nearby weeds in the cabbage family.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny round shot-hole pits chewed in the leaves of young plants; the small dark beetles jump like fleas when disturbed. Heavy feeding stunts or kills seedlings and slows establishment of the long-season crop.
pests.cause_seasoned: Flea beetles chew the foliage of young brassicas and are most damaging at the seedling stage; a vigorous transplant generally outgrows them, but a stalled seedling can be set back badly.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Protect seedlings with row cover and spray spinosad if pressure is high; the goal is getting plants past the vulnerable seedling stage.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Use row cover from transplanting, keep seedlings vigorous with even water and feeding so they grow through the damage, and clean up weedy brassica relatives nearby.

pests.name: Cabbage root maggot
pests.symptoms_beginner: New transplants wilt and grow badly or fall over. If you pull one up, you'll find small white maggots eating the roots. It is worst in cool, wet soil.
pests.cause_beginner: A small fly lays eggs at the base of the plant, and the maggots that hatch burrow down and eat the roots. The fly is most active in cool, damp weather.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Once the maggots are in the roots you can't save that plant, so pull and throw away the badly damaged ones. Put your effort into protecting the rest from new eggs.
pests.prevention_beginner: Put a small collar or disk around the base of each transplant to stop the fly from laying eggs there, or use a row cover. Avoid planting into cold, soggy soil, and rotate away from where cabbage-family plants grew.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Transplants wilt, grow poorly, and may collapse; pulling a plant reveals small white maggots tunneling in the roots and lower stem. Damage is worst in cool, wet soil at establishment.
pests.cause_seasoned: The larvae of the cabbage root fly tunnel into brassica roots; the adult lays eggs at the stem base, and the maggots feed below, sometimes killing young plants.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no effective rescue once maggots are in the roots; remove and destroy badly affected plants and protect the rest from further egg-laying.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Place a collar or disk around the stem base at transplanting to block egg-laying, or use row cover; avoid planting into cold, wet soil and rotate away from where brassicas grew.

diseases.name: Clubroot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Plants wilt in the afternoon, stay small and yellowish, and don't bounce back. If you dig one up, the roots are swollen into lumpy, club-shaped knobs.
diseases.cause_beginner: A germ that lives in the soil infects the roots of cabbage-family plants and makes them swell, which stops the plant from taking up water and food. It stays in the soil for years.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There's no cure once a plant has it, so pull and destroy infected plants. Keeping the soil from being too acidic (closer to neutral) helps hold it back, and growing cabbage-family plants only rarely in that spot starves the germ out.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Don't grow brussels sprouts or other cabbage-family plants in the same spot more than once every few years, longer if you've had clubroot. Keep the soil from being too acidic, improve drainage, and clean soil off your tools.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Plants wilt in the heat of the day, grow stunted and yellowed, and recover poorly; roots are swollen into distorted clubs and galls instead of normal fine roots.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A soilborne organism (Plasmodiophora brassicae) infects brassica roots and forms the galls, which block water and nutrient uptake. It persists in soil for many years, spreads in contaminated soil and water, and infects most readily in acidic soils below pH 6.5.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once plants are infected; remove and destroy them. Raising soil pH toward neutral with lime suppresses the disease, and long rotations starve it out over time.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate brassicas out of affected ground on a long cycle (UMN advises 5 to 7 years where clubroot is known), keep soil pH up, improve drainage, and avoid moving infested soil on tools and boots.

diseases.name: Black rot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Yellow patches shaped like the letter V appear at the leaf edges, pointing inward, with black veins inside them. It can spread through the plant and rot the leaves and sprouts.
