diseases.cause_beginner: A bacteria that often comes in on infected seeds or transplants. It gets into the leaves and travels through the plant's veins, spreading fastest in warm, wet weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There's no real cure, so remove and destroy infected plants to keep it from spreading. Don't handle or brush against the plants while they're wet, because that spreads the bacteria.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Begin with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants, don't plant where cabbage-family crops grew recently, space plants for good airflow, and avoid overhead watering.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellow, V-shaped lesions spread inward from the leaf margins, with the veins inside the V turning black; the disease moves through the vascular system and can blacken and rot foliage and sprouts.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A seedborne bacterium (Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris) that enters through leaf pores and wounds and moves through the veins; it spreads in warm, wet conditions and on infected seed or transplants.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no effective cure; remove and destroy infected plants. Avoid working among plants when foliage is wet, since that moves the bacteria.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Start with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants (a hot-water seed treatment helps), rotate 2 to 3 years away from brassicas, give plants room for airflow, and avoid overhead watering and handling wet foliage.

diseases.name: Alternaria leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small dark spots on the leaves that grow into round patches with rings inside them, like a tiny target. Bad cases yellow the leaves and can spot the sprouts.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that spreads in warm, wet weather and infects the leaves, leaving target-like spots. It is worse on crowded, damp plantings and can come in on infected seed.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove and destroy badly spotted leaves, improve airflow so leaves dry quickly, and use a copper spray if it spreads. Avoid wetting the leaves when you water.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Start with clean seed, rotate away from brassicas, space plants for airflow, water at the soil line, and clear away old plant debris.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark lesions enlarge into circular spots with characteristic concentric rings (a target-spot look) and a yellow halo; severe spotting downgrades the leaves and can blemish the sprouts. Favored by warm, wet conditions.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Fungi in the genus Alternaria (chiefly A. brassicicola) infect brassica foliage, spreading by spores in wind and splashing water; infected seed, crop debris, and long leaf wetness drive it.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy spotted leaves and debris, improve airflow, avoid overhead watering, and apply a copper-based fungicide if pressure is high.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Use clean, disease-free seed (a hot-water treatment helps), rotate about 3 years away from brassicas, space for airflow, water at the soil line, and clear crop debris that harbors spores.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Pale yellow blotches on top of the leaves, with fuzzy grayish growth on the underside, mostly in cool, damp weather. Bad cases discolor the leaves and can spot the sprouts.
diseases.cause_beginner: A mold-like disease that loves cool, wet, humid weather and spreads through the air and water. Wet leaves and crowded plants make it worse.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Open up the airflow so leaves can dry, remove the worst leaves, and use a copper spray if it's spreading. It's hard to stop once the weather stays damp.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Space plants so air moves between them, water at the soil instead of from above, and pick resistant varieties if downy mildew is common where you live.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Pale yellow patches form on the upper leaf surface with a fuzzy gray growth underneath, mainly in cool, damp weather; severe infection discolors leaves and can blemish the sprouts. Brussels sprouts' cool, humid season overlaps the weather it likes.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A fungus-like organism (Hyaloperonospora brassicae) that thrives in cool, wet, humid conditions and spreads by spores in water and air; long leaf wetness and crowded plantings favor it.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Improve airflow and let foliage dry, remove badly affected leaves, and apply a copper-based fungicide if pressure is high; the disease is hard to stop once humidity stays high.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants for good air movement, water at the soil line rather than overhead, and choose resistant varieties where downy mildew is common.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Give about 1 to 1.5 inches weekly, kept even through the long season.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly 1 to 1.5 inches a week.
watering.amount_seasoned: About 1 to 1.5 inches per week, a little more in hot, dry spells while the plant is sizing up.
watering.amount_beginner: Aim for roughly 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose where possible.
watering.method_beginner: Water at the base of the plant rather than over the leaves.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves and limp growth; brussels sprouts dislike waterlogged soil and can rot at the crown or fall prey to root maggots in cold, wet ground.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Lower leaves yellow and the plant looks soggy and limp.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting, stalled growth, and loose, bitter sprouts; drought stress during sprout formation directly hurts sprout quality.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Wilting leaves and small, loose, bitter sprouts.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Even moisture across the long season keeps the plant growing steadily and the sprouts firm; dry spells stall the plant and give loose, bitter sprouts.
watering.method_note_beginner: Keep the water steady so the plant grows without stalling and the sprouts stay firm.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Even moisture matters most while the plant is building its frame and again as the sprouts form and fill.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Water steadily while the plant is growing big and while the sprouts are forming.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Brussels sprouts are almost always transplanted because of their long season. Start seeds indoors about 5 to 6 weeks before set-out. In cold regions, sow in spring and transplant in late spring or early summer to mature in the cool fall; in warm regions, sow in mid to late summer and transplant in late summer or fall for a winter crop. Set out sturdy young plants with about 4 to 6 true leaves and harden them off over 7 to 10 days.
start_method.notes_beginner: Brussels sprouts take a long time to grow, so it is easiest to start them as transplants. Sow seeds indoors about 5 to 6 weeks before you plant out. In cold areas, plant out in late spring or early summer so they mature in fall. In warm areas, plant in late summer or fall for a winter crop. Let homegrown seedlings get used to the outdoors over a week before planting.

drainage.saucer_practice: Empty the saucer after watering so roots never sit in water; brussels sprouts resent waterlogged soil.

soil_mix.type_beginner: A good-quality potting mix, not garden soil.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in compost and a slow-release fertilizer for the long season.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: A rich, well-drained commercial potting mix high in organic matter.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend in compost and a slow-release balanced fertilizer; container plants feed for months and exhaust a small soil volume.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out faster than the ground, so check daily in warm weather; a tall plant in a pot is thirsty.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Feed a bit more often than in the ground, since watering washes nutrients out of pots.

overwintering.approach_beginner: In mild-winter areas, a brussels plant in a big pot keeps standing and producing through the cold; just move it to a sheltered, sunny spot and keep picking. In cold areas, the small soil volume freezes hard, so pull the pot against the house during deep freezes or harvest the whole stalk before the worst cold.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Brussels sprouts are cold-hardy enough to stand through winter in a container in mild zones, holding their sprouts in a sheltered, sunny spot. In colder zones the limited root volume freezes harder than open ground, so move containers against a wall during hard freezes, or treat the potted crop as a single fall-into-early-winter planting and cut the stalk before deep cold.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Brussels sprouts can grow in a large pot, but they are tall, top-heavy, long-season plants, so they are not the easiest container crop. Use a deep pot of at least 5 gallons, one plant per pot, stake it so it does not topple, and keep it well watered and fed. Pick sprouts from the bottom up.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Brussels sprouts are a marginal container crop: they are large, top-heavy, and occupy the pot for months, so the gains of a container (mobility, soil control) come with real demands. Use a deep, heavy container of at least 5 gallons (10 is better), one plant per pot, stake the stalk against toppling, and keep moisture and feeding steady since a small soil volume runs out over a long season. The general container-vegetable guidance applies; brussels-specific container figures are modeled, not separately sourced.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry faster than beds; check moisture daily in heat and water before the mix dries, since drought stress loosens the sprouts.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Container plants need more frequent feeding than in-ground ones because watering leaches nutrients over the long season.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering container suits brussels sprouts well, since it smooths out the steady moisture that keeps the plant growing and the sprouts firm over a long season.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match because it keeps the water steady, which the long-season plant needs.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: Brussels sprouts grow into a tall, top-heavy stalk with a substantial root system, so choose a deep, wide-based container of at least 5 gallons and 12 inches deep for stability, and stake the plant. A broad, heavy pot resists toppling and buffers the fast drying a narrow pot suffers.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Brussels sprouts get tall and top-heavy, so give one plant a deep, heavy pot that holds at least 5 gallons and is about 12 inches deep, and stake it so it does not tip over. A wide, sturdy pot is better than a tall skinny one.

recommended.name: Long Island Improved
recommended.note: A dependable open-pollinated heirloom (about 90 days) with good production, eating quality, and storage; compact and a longtime garden standard. Seed-saveable, unlike the hybrids.

recommended.name: Jade Cross / Jade Cross E
recommended.note: An early, productive AAS-winning hybrid (about 100 days) on a shorter, wind-firm plant; the 'E' strain carries some Botrytis resistance. A reliable first choice.

recommended.name: Diablo
recommended.note: A late, heavy-yielding hybrid (about 110 days) of high quality that holds well in cold; a strong pick for a full fall-into-winter harvest.

recommended.name: Hestia
recommended.note: A uniform, upright hybrid bred for tidy, even sprouts and good standing ability; widely grown for fall. Days to maturity approximate.

recommended.name: Nautic
recommended.note: A hybrid with a notably broad disease-resistance package (black rot, Fusarium yellows, powdery mildew, white rust per Cornell), useful where brassica disease is chronic. Days to maturity approximate.

recommended.name: Redarling / Ruby (red types)
recommended.note: Purple-red sprouts that hold their color when cooked; ornamental as well as edible. Red types tend to be later (about 140 days) and a touch less productive, so give them a long season.

varieties.note_seasoned: Match the variety to the season length. Where the season is short, lean on early types (Jade Cross, Long Island Improved) that finish before deep cold; where it is long and cool, late heavy-yielders like Diablo reward the wait. Hybrids (Jade Cross, Hestia, Nautic, Diablo) give more uniform sprouts and firmer standing than the open-pollinated Long Island Improved, which in turn is the one to grow for saving seed. Where brassica disease is chronic, choose a resistant hybrid such as Nautic. Red types are slower and more ornamental than productive.
varieties.note_beginner: Jade Cross and Long Island Improved are easy, dependable choices, and Long Island Improved lets you save seed. Diablo is a later, heavy producer for a long cool season. Hestia gives neat, even sprouts, and red types like Redarling are pretty but slower. If brassica diseases are a problem where you live, look for a disease-resistant variety such as Nautic.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Other brassicas (broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, kale, collards, kohlrabi, turnip, radish, mustard), which share clubroot and the cabbage-family pests.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Other cabbage-family crops like broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, kale, and turnips.
rotation.good_after: Legumes such as beans and peas, or unrelated crops like tomatoes, squash, or onions.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate so brussels sprouts and their brassica relatives do not return to the same ground for at least 3 years, and longer where clubroot is present; the University of Minnesota advises against growing cole crops where they grew in the past four years, and clubroot warrants a 5-to-7-year break. Holding soil pH near neutral also helps suppress clubroot.
rotation.note_beginner: Don't plant brussels sprouts or other cabbage-family crops in the same spot year after year. Waiting at least 3 years between them, and longer if you have had clubroot, helps avoid soil diseases.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Sprouts soften and yellow at room temperature within a day or two, so refrigerate promptly after picking. A key brussels advantage is that the plant itself is the best storage: sprouts hold firm on the standing stalk for weeks in cold weather, so harvest close to use.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Don't leave brussels sprouts out on the counter; they soften and yellow fast. Refrigerate them soon after picking, and remember the plant keeps them best of all, holding the sprouts on the stalk in cold weather.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerate unwashed in a perforated bag in the crisper; sprouts hold their quality for roughly 3 to 5 weeks, and up to several months near 32°F at high humidity. Keep them away from ethylene-producing fruit, which yellows them faster.
storage.fridge_beginner: Store brussels sprouts unwashed in a perforated bag in the fridge's crisper drawer, where they stay good for about 3 to 5 weeks. Keep them away from apples and other ripening fruit, which make them go off sooner.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Brussels sprouts freeze well once blanched: trim and wash, blanch about 3 to 5 minutes depending on size, cool quickly in ice water, drain, and freeze. Blanching halts the enzymes that otherwise cause off-flavors and loss of color, and frozen sprouts keep up to about a year.
storage.freezer_beginner: Brussels sprouts freeze well if you blanch them first. Trim and wash them, boil 3 to 5 minutes, cool right away in ice water, drain, and freeze. They keep up to about a year.
storage.notes_seasoned: Quality is highest straight from the garden, and the standing plant is its own cold store: a whole stalk can be cut and kept upright in a cool cellar, or left in the garden to harvest as needed while temperatures stay above about 20°F. The sprouts sweeten in the cold, so there is little reason to stockpile; chill promptly whatever you pick.
storage.notes_beginner: Brussels sprouts are best right after picking, and the plant is its own best storage: in cold weather the sprouts hold on the stalk for weeks and even get sweeter after frost. You can also cut the whole stalk and stand it in a cool spot. Pick what you need when you need it, and chill it quickly.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: In about 5 to 10 days, your seeds sprout and push up their first two little leaves (the seed leaves).
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the starting mix damp. Once the first real leaves appear, give the seedlings strong light so they do not get leggy.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your seeds come up yet?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seeds sprout in about 5 to 10 days, pushing up two seed leaves (cotyledons). Brussels sprouts are started indoors for transplanting because of their long season.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep the starting mix evenly moist and give bright light from emergence to avoid stretch; thin or pot up once the first true leaves appear.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Did your brussels sprouts seeds sprout?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The seedlings grow their real leaves and a stronger stem. They are ready to plant out at about 5 to 6 weeks old, with several true leaves.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Harden the seedlings off over about a week before planting out. Watch for flea beetle holes on the young leaves.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How many real leaves do your seedlings have?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Young plants build true leaves and a sturdy stem; transplants are ready at about 4 to 6 true leaves, roughly 5 to 6 weeks from sowing. Set out sturdy young plants rather than oversized ones.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harden off over 7 to 10 days before setting out at the wider 18-to-24-inch spacing; protect seedlings from flea beetles and cabbage root maggot with row cover and collars.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are your transplants ready to go out?

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant grows into a tall, leafy stalk over the summer (in cool regions) or fall (in warm regions). This is when it builds the frame that will carry the sprouts.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Feed with nitrogen and keep it evenly watered so it grows steadily. Firm the soil around the base and stake tall plants. Check for aphids and caterpillars.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Is your plant growing into a tall, leafy stalk?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The plant builds a tall, leafy stalk over several weeks, laying down the frame whose leaf axils will later carry the sprouts. Steady growth now sets the yield; the stalk does not form sprouts until cool weather arrives.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Side-dress with nitrogen, keep moisture even, firm and hill the soil at the base, and stake the top-heavy stalk. Scout for cabbage aphids, caterpillars, and harlequin bugs as the frame fills out.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Is your stalk putting on steady leafy growth?

growth_stages.name: Sprout formation
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: As the weather cools, small buds like tiny cabbages start to form where each leaf joins the stalk, beginning at the bottom and working up. This is the crop forming.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Many gardeners snap off the lowest leaves as the sprouts swell. When the bottom sprouts are about an inch across, you can cut off the very top of the plant (top it) to push the upper sprouts to size up more evenly. Ease off heavy nitrogen now.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have little sprouts started forming along the stalk?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Sprouts form in the leaf axils up the stalk as cool weather sets in, maturing from the bottom upward. Heat here gives loose, leafy, bitter sprouts, so the plant should be timed to reach this stage in cool fall or winter weather.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Remove lower leaves as the sprouts swell to give them room. Optionally top the plant (cut out the growing point) when the lowest sprouts are about 1 inch across, less than 60 days before harvest, to even up and hasten the upper sprouts; ease off nitrogen so sprouts stay firm rather than blowy.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are sprouts forming and firming from the base up?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The lowest sprouts firm up to about 1 inch across, tight and deep green. They keep ripening up the stalk over several weeks, and they taste best after a frost.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Twist or snap off the firm sprouts from the bottom up, taking the leaf below each, and leave the smaller ones up top to keep growing. Keep picking up the stalk through fall and into the cold.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you started picking sprouts from the bottom?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Sprouts reach harvest size (about 1 to 1.5 inches, firm, tight, deep green) from the bottom of the stalk upward, beginning roughly 90 days from transplanting and continuing for weeks. Frost sweetens them; mature plants hold while temperatures stay above about 20°F.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Snap or twist the lowest mature sprouts and strip the leaf below each, working up the stalk over several weeks; harvest the best sprouts after a frost or two. In the coldest zones, cut the whole stalk before a hard freeze and store it cool.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are you harvesting sprouts up the stalk?

notifications.title_beginner: You can top your brussels sprouts now
notifications.body_seasoned: If you want to even up and hasten the upper sprouts, cut out the growing point at the top of the stalk now that the lowest sprouts are about an inch across. Top less than 60 days before your intended harvest, and ease off heavy nitrogen so sprouts stay firm.
notifications.body_beginner: Once the bottom sprouts are about an inch across, you can snip off the very top of the plant. This pushes the rest of the sprouts to grow bigger and more evenly. It is optional, but many gardeners do it.

notifications.title_seasoned: Start picking from the bottom up
notifications.title_beginner: Time to start picking brussels sprouts
notifications.body_seasoned: The lowest sprouts should be firm and about 1 to 1.5 inches across. Snap or twist them off from the bottom of the stalk upward, taking the leaf below each, and leave the upper sprouts to keep sizing up. They are sweetest after a frost.
notifications.body_beginner: Your lowest sprouts should be firm and about an inch across. Twist them off starting at the bottom of the stalk and work your way up over the next few weeks. They taste sweeter after a frost.

notifications.title_seasoned: Frost is coming: expect sweeter sprouts
notifications.title_beginner: Frost ahead, your sprouts will sweeten
notifications.body_seasoned: A frost is on the way, which is good news: brussels sprouts take frost in stride and the cold actually sweetens them. Mature plants hold while temperatures stay above about 20°F, so keep harvesting; in the coldest spots, cut whole stalks before a hard freeze.
notifications.body_beginner: Frost is coming, but that is good for brussels sprouts: the cold makes them sweeter. The plants handle frost fine down to about 20°F, so keep picking. In very cold areas, cut the whole stalk before a hard freeze.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot weather warning for your brussels sprouts
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Brussels sprouts form firm sprouts only in cool weather; sustained heat above about 75°F to 80°F gives loose, leafy, bitter sprouts or stalls sprouting entirely. Keep moisture even, and recognize that in hot regions this is a fall and winter crop timed to mature after the heat breaks.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Hot weather makes brussels sprouts grow loose, leafy, and bitter instead of forming tight little sprouts. Keep them watered, and remember they are really a fall and winter crop in warm areas. There is not much to do but wait for cool weather.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hard freeze coming
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Brussels sprouts are among the most cold-hardy garden vegetables and a freeze sweetens the sprouts; mature plants tolerate hard frost and hold while temperatures stay above about 20°F. Below that, the sprouts can be damaged, so in the coldest zones cut whole stalks before a deep freeze; for most freezes, simply keep harvesting.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Brussels sprouts handle hard freezes well, and the cold makes them taste sweeter, so you usually do not need to do anything. They are fine down to about 20°F. In very cold weather below that, cut the whole stalk and store it, since a deep freeze can damage the sprouts.

germination.text_seasoned: Start seeds indoors about 5 to 6 weeks before set-out; brussels sprouts are transplanted, not direct sown, because of their long season.
germination.text_beginner: Start seeds indoors about 5 to 6 weeks before you plan to plant them out.

germination.text_seasoned: Sow about 0.25 to 0.5 inch deep into a moist starting mix and give bright light from emergence to keep seedlings stocky.
germination.text_beginner: Plant the seeds about a quarter to half an inch deep, keep them damp, and give them strong light so they do not get leggy.

seedling.text_seasoned: Transplant sturdy young plants with 4 to 6 true leaves at 18 to 24 inches apart in rows 24 to 36 inches apart; harden off over 7 to 10 days first.
seedling.text_beginner: Space plants about 18 to 24 inches apart, with wide rows, since they get big. Harden the seedlings off over about a week before planting out.

seedling.text_seasoned: Protect transplants from flea beetles with row cover and from cabbage root maggot with stem collars, especially in cool, wet soil.
seedling.text_beginner: Cover young plants with a row cover to stop flea beetles, and put a collar around the stem to keep root maggots out.

established.text_seasoned: Side-dress nitrogen as the stalk builds and keep moisture even at about 1 to 1.5 inches per week; firm and hill the soil at the base and stake the top-heavy plant against lodging.
established.text_beginner: Feed with nitrogen and water steadily while the stalk grows tall, and stake it so it does not blow over. Firm the soil around the base.

established.text_seasoned: Scout the growing tips and leaf axils for cabbage aphids and the undersides for caterpillars; getting ahead of aphids now keeps them out of the sprouts later.
established.text_beginner: Check the new growth for aphids and under the leaves for green caterpillars, and deal with them early before the sprouts form.

sprout_formation.text_seasoned: Strip the lower leaves as sprouts swell to give them room, and optionally top the plant (remove the growing point) when the lowest sprouts are about 1 inch across to even up and hasten the upper sprouts.
sprout_formation.text_beginner: Pull off the lower leaves as the sprouts grow, and when the bottom sprouts are about an inch across you can cut off the very top of the plant to push the rest to size up evenly.

sprout_formation.text_seasoned: Ease off heavy nitrogen once sprouts set; late lush growth gives loose, blowy sprouts and draws aphids. Even moisture keeps them firm.
sprout_formation.text_beginner: Once the sprouts start forming, go easy on the nitrogen, because too much makes loose, leafy sprouts and brings aphids.

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest from the bottom up: snap or twist the lowest firm, tight sprouts (about 1 to 1.5 inches) and strip the leaf below each, leaving the upper sprouts to keep sizing up over several weeks.
harvest.text_beginner: Pick from the bottom of the stalk up. Twist off the firm, tight sprouts about an inch across and take the leaf under each, leaving the smaller ones up top to keep growing.

harvest.text_seasoned: Sprouts are sweetest after a frost or two; mature plants hold while temperatures stay above about 20°F, and a whole stalk can be cut and stored cool before a hard freeze.
harvest.text_beginner: Brussels sprouts taste best after frost, and the plant keeps them well in cold weather. Before a really hard freeze, cut the whole stalk and store it somewhere cool.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A single stalk yields roughly 50 to 100 sprouts, about 0.75 to 2 pounds per plant, harvested progressively up the stalk over several weeks rather than all at once. Extension row yields run about 4 to 10 pounds per 10 feet of row depending on variety and season length.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Each plant gives you a stalk of about 50 to 100 sprouts, picked a few at a time over several weeks, often a pound or two per plant. How much you get depends on the variety and how long and cool your season is.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Sprouts mature from the bottom up over weeks, peaking in the cool weather of late fall and, in mild zones, winter. Production stalls or fails in heat (loose sprouts), and ends when a deep freeze below about 20°F damages the plant or when warmth in spring makes overwintered plants bolt.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: The sprouts ripen up the stalk over several weeks, with the best picking in cool late fall and, in mild areas, winter. They do poorly in heat and stop once a hard freeze or spring warmth ends the plant.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: The two keys to a good crop are timing and patience: time the plant to reach sprout formation in cool weather (heat gives loose, bitter sprouts), and then harvest progressively from the bottom rather than waiting for the whole stalk. New growers often plant too late, pick too early (before the sprouts firm up and a frost sweetens them), or give up on a plant that simply has not reached cool weather yet.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Here is the trick: brussels sprouts need cool weather to form good sprouts, so plant them to mature in fall, not summer. Then pick from the bottom up as the sprouts firm, a few at a time, instead of waiting for the whole plant. Be patient, the best sprouts come after frost.
factors_seasoned: Timing and temperature: sprouts form firm and sweet only in cool weather; reaching sprout formation in heat gives loose, bitter, leafy sprouts or none at all.
Season length: brussels sprouts need roughly 90 to 180 days, so a short season or a late planting limits how far up the stalk the crop ripens before deep cold.
Nitrogen and even moisture: steady feeding builds the stalk, but excess nitrogen late and drought stress both loosen the sprouts.
Topping and lower-leaf removal: topping the plant and stripping lower leaves even up and hasten the sprouts, raising usable yield in a short season.
Variety: early types finish in short seasons; late heavy-yielders need a long cool window; red types are slower and less productive.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No reliable extension or peer-reviewed evidence supports timing brussels sprouts planting or harvest by moon phase. Plant by the season and frost dates and harvest by sprout firmness instead.

failure_diagnostics.label: Loose, open, blowy sprouts
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Warm weather while the sprouts were forming, loose soil, or too much nitrogen late in the season.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Instead of tight little cabbages, your sprouts are loose, open, and leafy. This usually means the plant was forming sprouts in weather that was too warm, or it was growing too fast and soft from rich soil or extra nitrogen, or the ground was too loose. People often blame the variety, but timing and conditions are almost always the cause. Next time, plant so the sprouts form in cool fall weather, firm the soil before planting, and ease off nitrogen once sprouts start.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Aim for sprouts to form in cool weather, firm the soil before planting, and go easy on late nitrogen.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Sprouts are loose and leafy rather than firm and tight. The usual drivers are heat during sprout formation, excess late nitrogen, loose or recently dug soil, and drought stress; brussels sprouts set tightly only in cool, settled conditions. Next time time the crop so sprout formation lands in cool fall or winter weather, plant into firm soil, taper nitrogen as sprouts set, and keep moisture even.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Heat during sprout formation, excess late nitrogen, loose soil, or drought stress.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Time sprout formation for cool weather, plant into firm soil, taper late nitrogen, and hold even moisture.

failure_diagnostics.label: Tall leafy stalk but no sprouts
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Planted too late or in too much heat, or fed too much nitrogen, so the plant grew leaves instead of sprouts.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your plant grew into a big leafy stalk but never made sprouts, or only tiny ones. Brussels sprouts need a long, cool stretch to form sprouts, so this usually means they were planted too late, ran into heat, or got so much nitrogen that they kept making leaves. Next time, start them earlier so they have a long season, plan for the sprouts to form in cool fall weather, and ease off the nitrogen once the stalk is built.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Start earlier for a long season, aim for cool-weather sprouting, and go easy on nitrogen later on.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The plant built a tall vegetative stalk but set few or no sprouts. The causes are an insufficient cool window (planted too late, or heat persisted), or excess nitrogen keeping the plant vegetative. Brussels sprouts need roughly 90 to 180 days and cool weather to fill the stalk. Next time start 5 to 6 weeks ahead under cover, set out on time so sprout formation reaches cool weather, taper nitrogen after the frame is built, and consider topping to push the sprouts.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Too short a cool window (late planting or persistent heat) or excess nitrogen keeping the plant vegetative.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Lengthen the season with an earlier start, time sprouting for cool weather, taper nitrogen, and top to push sprout set.

failure_diagnostics.label: Aphids packed into the sprouts
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Cabbage aphids settling into the forming sprouts, often worse on soft, over-fed fall plants.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: You found dense clusters of small gray-green insects tucked down inside the sprouts, hard to wash out. Cabbage aphids love brussels sprouts and hide right in the sprouts, and they breed fastest on soft growth from too much nitrogen on the long fall crop. People often miss them until harvest. Next time, scout the growing tips and leaf axils weekly, knock colonies off early, avoid overfeeding nitrogen, and welcome ladybugs and lacewings.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Scout weekly, knock off colonies early, go easy on nitrogen, and encourage beneficial insects.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Dense cabbage-aphid colonies lodged inside the sprouts, contaminating the harvested buds and very hard to clean. The waxy gray-green cabbage aphid specializes on brassicas, explodes on the long-season fall crop, and favors the soft growth excess nitrogen produces. Next time scout tips and axils weekly, dislodge colonies early with a water jet or insecticidal soap into the axils, taper nitrogen as sprouts set, and conserve natural enemies; once aphids are inside the sprouts they are nearly impossible to remove.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Cabbage aphids colonizing the leaf axils and sprouts, worsened by soft, over-fertilized fall growth.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Scout weekly, dislodge colonies early into the axils, taper nitrogen, conserve beneficials, and act before aphids reach the sprouts.

failure_diagnostics.label: Stunted, yellow plants with clubbed roots
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Clubroot, a soil disease of cabbage-family plants, or planting brassicas in the same spot too often.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your plants stayed small and yellowish, wilted in the afternoon, and when you dug one up the roots were swollen into lumps. That is clubroot, a soil disease that infects cabbage-family roots and lasts for years in the soil. It builds up when brassicas are grown in the same spot repeatedly and in acidic soil. Next time, rotate so cabbage-family crops do not return to that bed for several years, keep the soil pH near neutral, and improve drainage.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Rotate brassicas out of that bed for several years, keep soil pH near neutral, and improve drainage.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Plants were stunted and chlorotic, wilted by day, and showed galled, clubbed roots, the signature of clubroot (Plasmodiophora brassicae). The soilborne organism persists for years and builds under repeated brassica cropping and acidic, poorly drained soil. Next time rotate cole crops out for at least 3 years (5 to 7 where clubroot is known), lime toward a neutral pH, and improve drainage; there is no in-season cure.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Clubroot building in soil cropped to brassicas too frequently, favored by acidic, wet soil.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Use a long brassica rotation, raise pH toward neutral, improve drainage, and remove and destroy infected plants.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start indoors about 5 to 6 weeks before set-out and transplant in late spring or early summer to mature in the cool fall.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: First sprouts firm at the base of the stalk about 90 to 110 days after transplanting, as fall cools.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest continues up the stalk through the fall frosts that sweeten the sprouts, then deep winter ends it.

3.zone_notes: In the coldest zone, start indoors and transplant by early June; the plant grows through summer and the sprouts ripen with the first fall frosts. Deep winter ends the crop, so it is a single fall harvest.

4.zone_notes: Transplant in early summer to mature in fall; harvest runs from the first frosts into November, sweetening in the cold, until a deep freeze ends it.

5.zone_notes: A single long-season crop: transplant in June, grow through summer, and harvest from October through the fall frosts that sweeten the sprouts.

6.zone_notes: Transplant in early-to-mid summer for a fall-into-early-winter harvest; the plant stands and the sprouts hold and sweeten while temperatures stay above about 20°F.

7.zone_notes: In the mild end of the cold tier, transplant in midsummer for a late-fall and winter harvest; sprouts sweeten with frost and the plant often holds into January.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In cold regions, brussels sprouts are a single long-season crop. Start seeds indoors in spring, plant them out in late spring or early summer, and let them grow all summer; the sprouts form as fall cools and taste best after frost. Harvest from the bottom of the stalk up through fall and into early winter. Deep winter cold eventually ends the crop.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Across the cold northern tier brussels sprouts are grown as one long-season crop, not a spring-and-fall double crop. Start transplants under cover about 5 to 6 weeks ahead, set them out in late spring to midsummer (earlier in the shortest-season zones), and let the stalk build through summer; there is no summer heat pause because the plant grows vegetatively through the warm months and only sets sprouts as fall cools. Harvest progressively up the stalk from the first frosts, which sweeten the sprouts, into early winter while temperatures hold above about 20°F. In the milder z7 the harvest often runs into January.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Seed indoors in early-to-mid summer and transplant from late summer into fall for a winter crop.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Sprouts firm from the base about 90 to 120 days after transplanting, through late fall and winter.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest continues through winter into early spring until rising heat turns the sprouts bitter.

8.zone_notes: In the upstate and inland Southeast, seed indoors in early July and transplant in late summer for a winter harvest; high summer is too hot for sprouts, so the planting calendar leaves it out.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: brussels sprouts are a cool-season brassica that builds a leafy stalk in mild weather but sets firm, tight sprouts only when temperatures cool, roughly into the 60°F to 65°F range. Through the hot months the plant either stalls or makes loose, leafy, bitter sprouts, and cabbage aphid pressure peaks, so the crop is grown to mature in the cool season and the hottest months are left out of the planting calendar. In the inland Southeast the late-spring heat builds toward a hot, humid summer that gives loose, buggy sprouts, so brussels sprouts are grown as a fall-through-spring crop and summer is excluded. (Clemson Cooperative Extension; University of Georgia Extension)

9.zone_notes: Along the warm coastal plain, transplant in early-to-mid fall once the worst heat breaks and harvest through the mild winter into spring; summer is the off-season.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: brussels sprouts are a cool-season brassica that builds a leafy stalk in mild weather but sets firm, tight sprouts only when temperatures cool, roughly into the 60°F to 65°F range. Through the hot months the plant either stalls or makes loose, leafy, bitter sprouts, and cabbage aphid pressure peaks, so the crop is grown to mature in the cool season and the hottest months are left out of the planting calendar. Along the Gulf and lower coastal plain the long, hot, humid summer makes poor, aphid-prone sprouts, so brussels sprouts are strictly a fall-through-spring crop. (Clemson Cooperative Extension; LSU AgCenter)

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast, brussels sprouts are a fall and winter crop, not a summer one. Start seeds indoors in mid-summer and set transplants out in late summer or early fall once the worst heat eases. Harvest through the mild winter into spring; frost makes the sprouts sweeter. Skip the hot summer, when the plants grow poorly and aphids are bad. Note that brussels sprouts are a minor, somewhat challenging crop in the Deep South because the cool window is short.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: Across the Southeast brussels sprouts are a fall-through-spring crop, and a somewhat marginal one: the cool window is short and summer heat excludes the crop. Seed indoors in early-to-mid July and transplant from about mid-August (Upstate) to mid-October (Coastal Plain), harvest progressively through a mild winter into spring, and expect frost to sweeten the sprouts. The hot, humid summer is left out of the calendar, and growers lean on quick-maturing varieties and clean culture to dodge the aphid and caterpillar pressure the region is known for.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start transplants about 6 weeks ahead and set them out in mid-to-late summer (UC IPM: interior valleys July to August).

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Sprouts firm from the base through fall into winter, about 90 to 150 days from transplanting.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest continues through the cool winter; spring warmth ends quality.

8.zone_notes: UC IPM places interior-valley transplanting in July to August; the plant establishes in late summer and the sprouts form and are harvested through the cool fall and winter. Harvest months are derived from the planting window and maturity.

9.zone_notes: Transplant in mid-to-late summer per UC IPM and harvest through fall and winter; the hottest part of summer is the limiting period rather than a calendar pause, since planting is timed into late summer. Harvest months are derived.

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In California's hot interior valleys, set out brussels sprouts transplants in mid-to-late summer so they mature in the cool fall and winter. Keep them watered through the late-summer heat while they get established, then harvest from the bottom of the stalk up through the cool months. Summer heat is the enemy of good sprouts, so do not plant for a summer harvest.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: In the interior valleys brussels sprouts are set out in mid-to-late summer (UC IPM gives July to August) to establish through the heat and mature in the cool fall and winter. There is no separate summer planting pause here because planting is timed into late summer; the off-season is the post-harvest spring stretch. Keep transplants watered through establishment, harvest progressively through the cool months, and expect the best sprouts after the first frosts. Harvest months are derived from the sourced planting window plus the crop's maturity.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: In the cool, foggy coast, transplant across late winter to late spring (UC IPM: North Coast February to May).

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Sprouts firm through summer into fall, about 90 to 150 days from transplanting in the mild coastal climate.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The cool maritime climate gives a long harvest from summer through fall and into winter.

9.zone_notes: The cool, foggy coast is prime brussels country: transplant from late winter through spring and harvest over a long summer-through-winter season with no summer heat exclusion. Harvest months are derived from the planting window and maturity.

10.zone_notes: In the mildest fog-belt zone brussels sprouts crop nearly year-round from late-winter and spring sets; the marine layer keeps summer cool enough to avoid a heat pause. Harvest months are derived.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: The cool, foggy California coast is some of the best brussels sprouts country there is. Plant transplants from late winter through spring, and the mild, foggy summers let the plants keep forming sprouts for a long harvest from summer into winter. There is no need to stop for summer heat here.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: The cool, fog-cooled north and central coast is ideal brussels sprouts country (the foggy California coast is the heart of US production). Transplant from late winter through spring (UC IPM gives February to May for the North Coast); the marine layer holds summer mild enough that there is no heat pause, and plants crop over a long season from summer through fall and into winter. Harvest months are derived from the sourced planting window plus maturity.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Transplant in fall (San Diego Master Gardeners give September to November; a late-winter set is also possible).

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Sprouts firm from the base about 90 to 100 days after a fall set, through winter into spring.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The mild coast gives a long winter-into-spring harvest; summer heat ends it.

9.zone_notes: On the south coast, transplant in fall and harvest through the mild winter into spring; midsummer is excluded as too warm for firm sprouts.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: brussels sprouts are a cool-season brassica that builds a leafy stalk in mild weather but sets firm, tight sprouts only when temperatures cool, roughly into the 60°F to 65°F range. Through the hot months the plant either stalls or makes loose, leafy, bitter sprouts, and cabbage aphid pressure peaks, so the crop is grown to mature in the cool season and the hottest months are left out of the planting calendar. On the southern California coast the mild winter is the growing season and midsummer is too warm for firm sprouts, so brussels sprouts are planted in fall for a winter-into-spring harvest and the hottest months are excluded. (UC Master Gardeners San Diego County; UC IPM)

10.zone_notes: In the mildest south-coast zone brussels sprouts crop through winter and well into spring from a fall set; only the hottest midsummer weeks are excluded.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: brussels sprouts are a cool-season brassica that builds a leafy stalk in mild weather but sets firm, tight sprouts only when temperatures cool, roughly into the 60°F to 65°F range. Through the hot months the plant either stalls or makes loose, leafy, bitter sprouts, and cabbage aphid pressure peaks, so the crop is grown to mature in the cool season and the hottest months are left out of the planting calendar. On the southern California coast the mild winter is the growing season and midsummer is too warm for firm sprouts, so brussels sprouts are planted in fall for a winter-into-spring harvest and the hottest months are excluded. (UC Master Gardeners San Diego County; UC IPM)

ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: On the southern California coast, plant brussels sprouts transplants in fall for a harvest through the mild winter and into spring. The winter is the growing season here. Skip midsummer, which is too warm for the plants to form tight sprouts.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: On the south coast brussels sprouts are a fall-planted, winter-into-spring crop: transplant from about September to November (San Diego Master Gardeners), harvest progressively through the mild winter and into spring, and exclude the warm midsummer when sprouts will not firm. A late-winter set is also workable in the mildest spots. Harvest months are derived from the sourced planting window plus maturity.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set transplants in early fall once the worst desert heat breaks (UC IPM lists the desert valleys among brussels-growing regions).

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Sprouts firm through the cool desert winter, about 90 to 130 days from transplanting.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest runs through the short cool winter; heat returns early and ends it.

9.zone_notes: In the low desert brussels sprouts are a short winter crop: transplant in early fall after the heat breaks and harvest through the cool winter. The long hot season leaves no crop in the ground from spring through summer. Harvest months are derived.

10.zone_notes: A short cool-season window only: transplant in early fall and harvest in winter; spring and summer are the off-season. Harvest months are derived from the planting window and maturity.

ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: In the low desert of California, brussels sprouts are a short winter crop. Set transplants out in early fall once the brutal heat eases, and harvest through the cool winter. There is no crop from spring through summer because it is far too hot.
ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: In the California low desert brussels sprouts are a short winter crop set out in early fall as the heat breaks and harvested through the cool months; the long hot season means nothing is in the ground from spring through summer. UC IPM lists the desert valleys among brussels regions, but no desert-specific brussels planting-month table was readable, so the window is modeled on the region's cole-crop fall-set pattern and the harvest months are derived from maturity.

warm_arid.region_label: Warm Arid: El Paso & High Desert

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Grow as a fall crop: start transplants in summer and set out in late summer (NMSU lists brussels sprouts as a transplanted fall crop of about 93 days).

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Sprouts firm from the base through late fall into winter.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest through late fall and winter; hard cold and then spring heat end it.

8.zone_notes: In the high desert and El Paso area brussels sprouts are a fall crop: transplant in late summer and harvest late fall into winter. Summer is excluded as too hot; the planting window is modeled on cole-crop fall guidance.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: brussels sprouts are a cool-season brassica that builds a leafy stalk in mild weather but sets firm, tight sprouts only when temperatures cool, roughly into the 60°F to 65°F range. Through the hot months the plant either stalls or makes loose, leafy, bitter sprouts, and cabbage aphid pressure peaks, so the crop is grown to mature in the cool season and the hottest months are left out of the planting calendar. In the hot, arid Southwest the late-spring and early-summer heat excludes brussels sprouts, which are grown as a fall transplant crop for a late-fall and winter harvest. (NMSU Cooperative Extension)

warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: In the warm, dry Southwest around El Paso, grow brussels sprouts as a fall crop. Start transplants in summer and set them out in late summer, then harvest through late fall and winter. Summer is too hot for them.
warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: In the warm-arid high desert (El Paso and similar zone-8 areas) brussels sprouts are a fall transplant crop: set out in late summer for a late-fall and winter harvest, with summer excluded by heat. NMSU lists brussels sprouts as a roughly 93-day transplanted crop, but its zone-8 planting-month table was not readable and the Texas A&M fall guide did not parse, so the planting window is modeled on the region's cole-crop fall-set guidance and the harvest months are derived.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Sow or set transplants from late summer into fall (University of Arizona Maricopa calendar: seed about August to mid-October).

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Sprouts firm through the cool desert winter, about 130 to 150 days from sowing.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest through the cool winter into early spring; heat returns and ends it.

9.zone_notes: In the Arizona low desert brussels sprouts are a winter crop: the University of Arizona Maricopa calendar lists sowing from about August to mid-October, with transplants set in early fall, for a harvest through the cool winter into early spring. Summer is the long off-season.

low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: In the Arizona low desert (Phoenix and Yuma), brussels sprouts are a winter crop. Start them from late summer into fall, set transplants in early fall, and harvest through the cool winter into early spring. The long hot season means no crop from spring through summer.
low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: In the Arizona low desert brussels sprouts are a long-season winter crop. The University of Arizona Maricopa County calendar lists sowing from about August to mid-October; set transplants in early fall and harvest through the cool winter into early spring, when returning heat ends the crop. The off-season runs spring through summer. Harvest months are derived from the sourced planting window plus the crop's long maturity.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set transplants in fall and early winter (UF/IFAS lists brussels for the cooler months: central Florida about September to February, south Florida October to January).

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Sprouts firm through the short cool peninsular winter.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest through the cool winter; rising heat quickly ends it.

10.zone_notes: In central peninsular Florida brussels sprouts are a marginal winter crop: transplant in fall and early winter and harvest in the coolest months. The long warm season leaves no crop from spring through summer, and lowland heat often impairs sprout formation.

11.zone_notes: In south Florida brussels sprouts are at the warm edge of their range: a brief winter window only, transplanting late fall for a short cool-season harvest, often with loose or poorly formed sprouts. Marginal crop.

fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: In peninsular Florida, brussels sprouts are a winter-only crop, and a tricky one. Set transplants out in fall, harvest in the coolest months of winter, and accept that the warm climate often gives loose, poorly formed sprouts. They are not a reliable Florida crop, especially in the south.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: In peninsular Florida brussels sprouts are a marginal winter crop. UF/IFAS lists them only for the cool months (central Florida about September to February, south Florida October to January), and the short, warm winter often impairs firm sprout formation, especially in the south. Transplant in fall and harvest through the coolest weeks; nothing grows from spring through summer. The marginal performance is a sourced caveat, and harvest months are derived from the planting window.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Modeled on CTAHR cole-crop guidance: a cool-season planting at low elevation (about October to November), with cooler uplands giving a wider window.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Sprouts firm through the coolest months at low elevation; uplands are more reliable.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest in the coolest months; lowland warmth limits sprout formation.

11.zone_notes: Brussels sprouts are marginal in lowland tropical Hawaii: a cool-season window only, with firmer sprouts at cooler elevations. The window is modeled on CTAHR cole-crop guidance because the cited bulletin (B-91) is a 1943 scanned PDF that did not parse and does not table brussels months directly.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: Brussels sprouts are a hard crop in Hawaii because it is usually too warm for them to form tight sprouts. At low elevation, try them only in the coolest months; cooler upland areas do better. Expect loose sprouts in the warm lowlands.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: Brussels sprouts are marginal in tropical Hawaii: the lowlands rarely cool enough for firm sprouts, and cooler higher elevations are more reliable. The cool-season window is modeled on CTAHR cole-crop and leafy-green guidance, since the cited CTAHR Bulletin B-91 is a 1943 scanned PDF that did not parse and does not list brussels sprouts months directly. Treat the window and the derived harvest as a modeled estimate pending a parseable modern CTAHR source.

crops.description_seasoned: Brussels sprouts are a cool-season brassica grown for the small, cabbage-like buds that form in the leaf axils along a tall central stalk, harvested progressively from the bottom up. A long-season crop needing roughly 90 to 180 days, it is timed to mature in cool fall and winter weather: heat gives loose, bitter sprouts, while frost actually sweetens them, so the best sprouts come after the first hard frosts. It is one of the most cold-hardy garden vegetables, standing in the garden into early winter while temperatures hold above about 20°F.
crops.description_beginner: Brussels sprouts grow as small cabbage-like buds along a tall stalk, and you pick them a few at a time from the bottom up. They take a long time, about 3 to 6 months, and taste best when they mature in cool fall weather. Frost makes them sweeter, so the best sprouts come after the cold sets in. Summer heat makes them loose and bitter, so they are really a fall and winter crop.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Pick sprouts from the bottom of the stalk upward once they are firm, tight, and about 1 to 1.5 inches across, deep green, before they loosen or yellow. Snap or twist off the lowest mature sprouts and strip the leaf below each as you go; the upper sprouts keep sizing up for weeks. Flavor is best after a frost or two.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Start picking at the bottom of the stalk when the lowest sprouts are firm and about 1 inch across, like tiny cabbages, and still tight and green. Twist them off and pull the leaf under them, then work up the stalk over the following weeks. They taste sweetest after a frost.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Work plenty of compost into a fertile, well-drained bed before planting and confirm pH is near 6.0 to 7.0. Then let the bed firm up: brussels sprouts set tighter sprouts in settled soil, and loose ground gives blowy sprouts and a lodging-prone stalk. Because clubroot and other brassica diseases build in the soil, choose a bed where no cole crop has grown for at least 3 years.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Before planting, mix plenty of compost into a rich, well-drained bed and let it settle so it is firm rather than fluffy, which helps the sprouts grow tight. Try not to plant where you grew other cabbage-family crops in the last few years, since that spreads soil diseases.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Brussels sprouts are largely a single long-season planting rather than a true succession crop: each plant holds the bed for months and is harvested progressively up the stalk. In short-season regions, set out one crop and let it ride. In long, mild regions such as the cool coast you can stagger a couple of sowings about a month apart to spread the harvest. Time plantings so the sprouts form in cool weather; in hot regions skip summer and plant for a fall and winter crop.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: Brussels sprouts grow for a long time, so most gardeners plant just one crop and pick from it for weeks, rather than planting in batches. In mild areas with a long cool season you can stagger a couple of plantings a month apart. The key is to plant so the sprouts form in cool fall weather; in hot areas, skip summer and grow them for fall and winter.

crops.name: Okra

soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Okra performs best in deep, fertile, well-drained sandy loam to loam that is high in organic matter and warms quickly in spring. It is widely adaptable and grows across most soil types, but drainage is what matters: heavy, compacted, or poorly drained clay holds cold water that rots seed and stalls the warmth-loving roots. Work 2 to 3 inches of compost into the bed before planting, both to feed this long-season plant and to lighten a heavy soil. A sandy loam that warms early suits the earliest sowings; amend or build raised rows on clay so the soil drains and warms.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Okra likes rich, well-drained soil with plenty of compost worked in, and it grows in most kinds of soil as long as water drains away. The one thing it will not tolerate is cold, soggy ground, which rots the seed and holds the plant back. Mix a few inches of compost into the bed before planting. If your soil is heavy clay or stays wet, build up rows or raised beds so it drains and warms faster, because okra is a warm-weather plant that wants warm soil.

ph.note_seasoned: Okra grows well in slightly acidic to neutral soil, roughly pH 6.0 to 6.8, and tolerates a wider band from about 5.5 to 7.5, including the mildly alkaline soils common across the South and interior West. It is more forgiving of pH than many garden crops, so the practical step is a soil test before planting and lime only if the test shows the soil running below about 6.0. Strongly acidic soil is the one to correct, since it ties up the phosphorus and calcium this heavy-fruiting plant draws on.
ph.note_beginner: Okra is not fussy about soil pH and does well in slightly acidic to neutral soil, about 6.0 to 6.8, which is where most garden soil already sits. An inexpensive soil test tells you where you stand. The main thing to fix is very acidic soil, which a little garden lime corrects before planting.

fertilizer.frequency: At planting, then side-dress after first pods
fertilizer.type: balanced at planting, then a light side-dress once pods begin
fertilizer.timing: Work into the bed before planting, then side-dress once the first pods are picked, and again a few weeks later
fertilizer.example_product: balanced 10-10-10 at planting, then calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0) or 10-10-10 to side-dress
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Okra is a moderate, steady feeder over a long season, and the classic mistake is too much nitrogen, which gives a tall leafy plant with few pods. Work a complete fertilizer such as 10-10-10 into the bed before planting (about 2 pounds per 100 square feet), then side-dress lightly once the first pods are harvested and again two to three weeks later, with 10-10-10 or a nitrogen source like calcium nitrate. Pair feeding with steady moisture, since the nutrients only help a plant that is not also drought-stressed at pod set.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Okra needs only modest feeding, and too much nitrogen makes a big leafy plant with few pods. Mix a balanced fertilizer such as 10-10-10 into the soil before planting, then give a light feeding once the first pods come in and again a few weeks later. Water it in, and keep the granules off the stems and leaves.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Your okra is setting its first pods, time for a light side-dress. Keep nitrogen modest so the plant builds pods, not just leaves.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Your okra is starting to make pods. Give it a light feeding now.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A complete fertilizer such as 10-10-10 worked in before planting, then a light nitrogen side-dress (10-10-10 or calcium nitrate 15.5-0-0) once pods begin and again a few weeks later. Go easy on nitrogen, which trades pods for leaf.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 at planting, then a little extra once pods begin. Do not overdo the nitrogen, or you get leaves instead of pods.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A common rate is about 2 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet worked into the bed before planting, then a side-dress of roughly 3 ounces of 10-10-10 per 100 feet of row (or a comparable nitrogen source such as calcium nitrate) once the first pods are picked, repeated two to three weeks later, scratched in a few inches out from the plants and watered in.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Mix a balanced fertilizer or a few inches of compost into the soil before planting. Then, once the first pods come in, feed lightly with a balanced fertilizer scratched into the soil a few inches away from the plants, and once more a few weeks later.

companions.note_seasoned: Okra companion pairings are largely traditional rather than trial-tested, and the useful ones fall into a few practical roles. As a tall, late, heat-loving Malvaceae, okra does not share the disease load of tomatoes and other nightshades, so it makes a good rotational and bed neighbor for them rather than a competitor for the same soil pests. Southern peas and other legumes are a long-standing Southern partner, fixing nitrogen and, in the case of cowpeas, acting as a trap that pulls stink bugs and leaf-footed bugs off the pods. Quick crops like lettuce and radish use the open ground while young okra is small, and flowering insectary plants draw the bees and beneficial insects that help. The firmest rule is a rotation one: keep okra away from cotton, hibiscus, and other mallows, which share its root-knot nematode and fusarium problems.
companions.note_beginner: Most okra companion advice is garden tradition, but a few pairings genuinely help. Okra is tall and does not catch the same diseases as tomatoes, so it is a fine neighbor for them. Southern peas and beans add nitrogen and can lure stink bugs away from the pods, and quick crops like lettuce or radish fill the space while the okra is still small. The one rule that really matters is to keep okra away from cotton and other mallow-family plants, which share its soil pests.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Southern peas (cowpeas)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Southern peas are a classic okra partner in the South. They add nitrogen to the soil, and they pull stink bugs and leaf-footed bugs toward themselves and away from the okra pods. A traditional pairing with a sound reason behind it.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Cowpeas fix nitrogen for the long-season okra crop and serve as a documented trap crop for stink bugs and leaf-footed bugs, which prefer the peas to the okra pods. A traditional Southern intercrop with a mechanistically sound basis rather than a trial-isolated yield effect.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Legume nitrogen fixation and cowpea trap-cropping for stink bugs are documented mechanisms; the okra-cowpea adjacency benefit is traditional, not pair-isolated.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Basil and aromatic herbs
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Basil and other strong-smelling herbs are often planted near okra to confuse or deter pests. There is no hard proof for this exact pair, but it is widely done and harmless.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Aromatic herbs are a traditional pest-confusion interplant; the volatile-oil deterrence is broadly claimed but not extension-documented for okra specifically. Low risk, widely practiced.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Aromatic-herb pest deterrence is classic companion-planting lore, not T1-documented for okra.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Lettuce and radish
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Quick crops like lettuce and radish grow and finish fast while the okra is still small, so they use the open ground before the okra towers over them. A practical space-sharing pairing.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Fast cool-season crops occupy the inter-row space and finish before young okra closes the canopy, an efficient succession-in-place use of the bed rather than a measured biological interaction.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Space-and-time intercropping is a sound cultural practice; the specific okra pairing is practical, not trial-isolated.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Sunflowers and flowering insectary plants
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Flowers like sunflowers nearby bring in bees and other helpful insects. Okra flowers are mostly self-pollinating, but the extra bee visits and the predators that flowers attract are a low-risk help.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Insectary flowers recruit pollinators and natural enemies near the patch. Okra is largely self-pollinating, so the benefit is habitat and beneficial-insect support rather than essential pollination, and the pairing is habitat-based rather than pair-tested.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Cotton, hibiscus, and other mallows
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep okra away from cotton, hibiscus, hollyhock, and other mallow-family plants. They are okra's close relatives and share the same root-knot nematodes, wilt, and leaf pests, so growing them together builds those problems up in the soil.
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Okra is a Malvaceae, so cotton, ornamental hibiscus, hollyhock, and other mallows share its root-knot nematode, fusarium wilt, and several leaf pests. Clustering or rotating mallow to mallow concentrates that pressure and lets soilborne problems persist. A sound epidemiology and rotation principle rather than a tested adjacency effect.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Shared Malvaceae host range for root-knot nematode and fusarium is extension-documented; the bad-adjacency claim is a sound rotation principle, not pair-tested.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Sprawling vine crops over young okra
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Vigorous sprawling crops like sweet potatoes or winter squash can run over and shade out young okra before it gets tall. Give okra a clear start, or keep the sprawlers a row away.
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Aggressive ground-running crops can smother and shade slow-starting okra seedlings during establishment; this is a competition-for-light caution rather than a documented antagonism. Spacing resolves it once okra gains height.
