rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Annual crop rotation does not apply to a sour cherry: the tree holds its site for decades. The real concern is replant disease. Do not plant a new cherry (or other stone fruit) where a cherry, plum, peach, or apricot was recently growing, since Prunus-after-Prunus replanting causes stunting and poor establishment, and old sites can carry ring nematodes and bacterial canker.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: You do not rotate a cherry tree the way you rotate vegetables, because it stays in one spot for many years. What matters instead is replant disease: do not plant a new cherry where a cherry, plum, peach, or apricot just came out. Planting a stone fruit right back where another stone fruit grew leads to weak, stunted trees, and old spots can hold pests and diseases that shorten a cherry's life.
rotation.good_after: a fresh site with no recent stone-fruit history (no cherry, plum, peach, or apricot)
rotation.note_seasoned: If a cherry must go where a stone fruit was removed, replace a generous volume of soil, choose a tolerant rootstock, remove any diseased or infected neighboring trees first, and expect slower establishment. Best practice is simply to pick a new site.
rotation.note_beginner: If you have no choice but to replant where a stone fruit was, dig out and replace a big area of soil, pick a tougher rootstock, remove any nearby diseased trees first, and expect the tree to start slower. The simplest fix is to plant in a new spot instead.

growth_stages.name: Planting (bare-root, dormant)
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Late winter to early spring, while the tree is dormant and leafless, as soon as the soil can be worked.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Late winter or early spring, while the young tree is still bare and leafless and the ground can be dug.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A dormant bare-root whip or branched tree with firm buds and healthy roots. Sour cherry is self-fruitful, so a single tree is all you need. Keep the graft union (if the tree is grafted) 2 to 3 inches above the final soil line.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A leafless young tree with firm buds and healthy roots. You only need one tree, since sour cherry fruits on its own. Keep the graft joint (if the tree has one) a couple of inches above the soil.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Dig a hole as wide as the roots spread and no deeper than they sat in the nursery, set the tree with the graft union above grade, backfill with native soil, and water in well. Head the whip back to begin the framework. One self-fruitful tree is all you plant.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Dig a hole wide enough for the roots to spread and only as deep as they grew before. Keep the graft joint above the soil, fill in with the soil you dug out, and water well. Cut the young tree back to start its shape. You only need one tree, since it fruits on its own.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record the planting date, and the cultivar and rootstock.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note the day you planted, and the variety and rootstock.

growth_stages.name: Year-one establishment
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: The first full growing season after planting.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: The first whole growing season after you plant the tree.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Steady new shoot growth and a strengthening root system. Any blossoms in year one should be removed so the tree builds roots and framework, not fruit.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Healthy new shoots and a tree settling in. If it flowers this first year, pick the flowers off so it puts its energy into roots and branches.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply and regularly through the first season (the most water-sensitive period), keep a mulched, weed-free circle around the trunk without piling mulch on the bark, and remove first-year flowers. Begin light central-leader training.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Water deeply and often this first season, since a new tree needs steady water to root in. Keep a mulched, weed-free circle around the trunk, but keep the mulch off the bark. Remove any flowers, and start light pruning toward a single main-trunk shape.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Log first-season watering and the date you removed first-year blossoms.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note your watering and the day you removed the first-year flowers.

growth_stages.name: Training (years one to four)
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: The first three to four years, the framework-building phase before reliable bearing.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: The first three to four years, while you build the tree's main branches and before it fruits much.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Sour cherry is usually trained to a central leader (a single dominant trunk with tiers of scaffold branches) or a modified central leader, not the open vase used for peach. Watch for narrow, weak branch angles and overly upright competing leaders to correct.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Sour cherry is usually trained to a central leader: one main upright trunk with rings of side branches, not the open vase shape used for peaches. Look for branches with tight, weak angles and extra upright stems competing with the main trunk.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Each late dormant season, keep one central leader and well-spaced, wide-angled scaffolds, spreading narrow crotches and removing competing uprights. Cherry bears largely on long-lived spurs, so this builds permanent fruiting structure rather than the annual renewal peach needs. Make clean cuts; in wet climates do major cuts in dry summer to dodge bacterial canker.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Each year in late winter, keep one main upright trunk and evenly spaced side branches with wide angles, and remove stems competing with the leader. Cherries fruit on long-lived spurs, so you are building lasting structure. Make clean cuts, and in wet areas do big cuts in dry summer to avoid canker.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record each pruning, the leader and scaffolds retained, and any summer canker-avoidance cuts.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you prune and which main branches you kept.

growth_stages.name: Winter dormancy
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Roughly December through February, the leafless months when the tree banks chill.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: About December through February, the leafless winter months.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A leafless tree at rest banking chill hours (time between about 32 and 45°F) that it needs to break dormancy and bloom evenly. Sour cherry needs a lot of chill, so a mild winter can mean a weak bloom.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A bare, resting tree collecting chill hours, the cold time it needs (hours between about 32 and 45°F) before it will bloom well. Sour cherry needs plenty of cold, so a mild winter can give a poor bloom.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Little is required: clear mummified fruit and fallen leaves that harbor brown rot and leaf spot, and apply a dormant copper or oil spray where canker, leaf spot, or aphids are chronic. Established trees need minimal water now.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Not much to do: clear away any dried mummy fruit and fallen leaves that carry disease, and apply a dormant spray if canker, leaf spot, or aphids are a regular problem. An established tree needs very little water now.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Note the dormant spray date and any winter sanitation.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you did the dormant spray and any winter cleanup.

growth_stages.name: Dormant pruning
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Late dormancy, roughly February into March, just before growth resumes (or dry summer in canker-prone wet climates).
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Late winter, around February into March, just before the tree wakes up (or dry summer in wet, canker-prone areas).
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare branches showing the tree's structure. Cherry needs far lighter pruning than peach: it fruits on long-lived spurs, so you maintain the leader and open the canopy rather than renewing fruiting wood each year.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Bare branches, so you can see the shape. Cherries need much less pruning than peaches, because they fruit on long-lasting spurs. You mostly keep the main trunk and open up the canopy rather than cutting hard every year.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Prune lightly: keep the central leader, remove dead, diseased, crossing, and crowding wood, and open the canopy for light and air. Make clean cuts and remove cankered wood; in wet regions shift major cuts to dry summer weather, since fresh cuts in cool wet spring invite bacterial canker.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Prune lightly: keep the main trunk, cut out dead, diseased, and crossing branches, and open the middle for light and air. Make clean cuts and remove any cankered bark. In wet areas, do the big cuts in dry summer instead, since cuts in cool wet spring invite canker.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record the pruning date and any cankered wood removed.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note the day you pruned and any diseased wood you cut out.

growth_stages.name: Bloom
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Early spring, the timing shifting by region from late February in mild zones to April or May in the North.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Early spring. The exact week depends on where you live, earlier in warm areas, later in cold ones.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: White blossoms opening across the tree. This is the most frost-vulnerable moment of the year. Because sour cherry is self-fruitful, no pollinizer is needed, so the only bloom-time concerns are a hard late frost on open bloom and enough bee activity to work the flowers.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: White flowers opening all over the tree. This is the riskiest time for frost. A sour cherry fruits on its own, so you do not need a second tree; the only things to watch are a hard late frost and having bees out to work the flowers.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Watch the frost forecast closely and cover a small tree overnight if a hard frost threatens open bloom. Sour cherry sets on its own, so there is no pollinizer to confirm; just make sure bees are active, since cold, wet, windy bloom weather suppresses set. In a wet bloom, this is the window for a brown-rot blossom spray.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep an eye on the frost forecast and cover a small tree overnight if a hard frost is coming during bloom. The tree pollinates itself, so there is no partner tree to check; just hope for bees to be out, since cold, wet, windy weather during bloom means a lighter crop. If bloom is wet, this is the time for a brown-rot spray.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record the bloom date, bee activity, and any frost protection or bloom spray.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when bloom started, whether bees were active, and anything you did for frost or spray.

growth_stages.name: Fruit development and protection
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Spring into early summer, after petal fall, as the green fruit forms and colors.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Spring into early summer, after the petals drop, as the small green cherries form and start to color.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Clusters of small green cherries swelling on the spurs. Unlike peach, cherries are NOT thinned. This is the window to get netting ready, keep moisture even against cracking, and begin monitoring for cherry fruit fly and spotted wing drosophila as the fruit colors.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Small green cherries swelling on the spurs. Unlike peaches, you do NOT thin cherries. This is the time to get bird netting ready, keep the watering even so the fruit does not split, and start watching for cherry fruit fly and spotted wing drosophila as the fruit colors up.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep soil moisture even through the swell to limit cracking, and net the tree as the fruit begins to color, before birds find it. Hang cherry-fruit-fly traps by mid-spring and vinegar-bait traps as fruit colors to time any spray; remove any cracked or rotting fruit.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the watering steady so the cherries do not crack, and put bird netting on as the fruit starts to color, before the birds arrive. Put up traps for cherry fruit fly and spotted wing drosophila, and pick off any split or rotting cherries.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record when you netted, trap catches, and any cracking after rain.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you netted the tree, what the traps caught, and any splitting after rain.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Late spring to early summer, the month varying by region and variety; first real crop around years 3 to 5.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Late spring to early summer. The exact time depends on the variety and your area. Most trees give their first real crop around years 3 to 5.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Cherries at full, deep red color, soft and juicy. Sour cherry stays tart even when ripe, so go by color and richness, not sweetness. A tree ripens its crop over a short, concentrated week or two, and the fruit does not improve after picking, so taste before you pick. Rain on ripe fruit cracks it.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Cherries at full deep-red color, soft and juicy. Sour cherries stay tart even when ripe, so judge by color and juiciness rather than sweetness. The tree ripens its whole crop in a short burst of a week or two, and the fruit does not improve after picking, so taste one first. Rain on ripe fruit splits it.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick when fully colored, soft, and richly flavored, pulling by the stem, or letting a dead-ripe fruit part from the stem for processing. Pick promptly and completely every couple of days, clear culls and drops, and chill the fruit fast against spotted wing drosophila. Beat the rain: pick ahead of a forecast soaking.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pick when the cherries are fully colored, soft, and full-flavored, pulling by the stem (a dead-ripe sour cherry may slip off the stem, which is fine for pies). Pick every couple of days, clear away any leftover or fallen fruit, and get the crop into the fridge fast. If rain is coming, pick before it arrives.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record harvest dates, a rough yield, and any cracking or pest losses.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you picked, roughly how much you got, and any splitting or pest damage.

notifications.title_beginner: Time to plant your cherry tree
notifications.body_seasoned: Set a dormant bare-root tree now, while it is still leafless and the ground is workable. Keep the graft union 2 to 3 inches above the final soil line, pick a full-sun, well-drained spot out of frost pockets, and head the tree back to start its framework. Sour cherry is self-fruitful, so a single tree is all you plant.
notifications.body_beginner: Now is the time to plant a bare-root cherry, while it is still resting and the soil can be dug. Keep the graft union, the swollen bump low on the trunk, 2 to 3 inches above the soil, and choose a sunny, well-drained spot that does not sit in a frosty dip. Cut the young tree back to start its shape. You only need one tree, since sour cherry fruits on its own.

notifications.title_beginner: Time for a light cherry prune
notifications.body_seasoned: Prune lightly now, in late dormancy. Cherry fruits on long-lived spurs and needs far less cutting than peach: keep the central leader, remove dead, diseased, and crossing wood, and open the canopy. Make clean cuts and remove cankered wood. In wet climates, shift major cuts to dry summer to avoid bacterial canker.
notifications.body_beginner: Prune lightly now, in late winter. Cherries fruit on long-lasting spurs and need much less cutting than peaches: keep the main trunk, take out dead, diseased, and crossing branches, and open up the middle. Make clean cuts and remove any cankered bark. In wet areas, save the big cuts for dry summer to avoid canker.

notifications.title_seasoned: Bloom is open, watch for late frost
notifications.title_beginner: Flowers are open, watch the frost
notifications.body_seasoned: Your tree is flowering, the year's highest-risk stretch for the crop: a hard freeze on open blossoms takes all of it. Watch overnight lows through bloom and cover a small tree if a hard late frost is forecast. Sour cherry is self-fruitful, so there is no pollinizer to coordinate; just make sure bees are active, since cold, wet bloom weather thins the set.
notifications.body_beginner: Open flowers are when a cherry crop is most at risk from frost: one hard freeze on the blossoms can wipe out the year's cherries. Watch the overnight forecast during bloom and cover a small tree if a hard frost is coming. The tree pollinates itself, so there is no partner tree to worry about; just hope for bees to be out, since cold, wet weather at bloom means fewer cherries.

notifications.title_seasoned: Net the tree as fruit colors
notifications.title_beginner: Time to net the tree against birds
notifications.body_seasoned: As the fruit begins to color, net the whole canopy before birds find it and secure the skirt. Do not thin cherries the way you thin peaches. Keep soil moisture even to limit cracking, and start monitoring for cherry fruit fly and spotted wing drosophila as the fruit blushes.
notifications.body_beginner: As the cherries start to color, cover the whole tree with bird netting before the birds show up, and tuck it in at the bottom. Do not thin cherries like peaches. Keep the watering even so they do not split, and start watching for cherry fruit fly and spotted wing drosophila as the fruit colors.

notifications.body_seasoned: Through its first two seasons a cherry is at its most water-sensitive while roots establish. Water deeply and regularly at the root zone, by drip or soaker, and avoid wetting the canopy. Keep a weed-free, mulched circle around the trunk, and do not feed late, since soft growth invites the winter injury that opens the door to bacterial canker.
notifications.body_beginner: For its first couple of years, a young cherry needs steady water while its roots get going. Give it a deep soak at the ground every week or so (a drip line or soaker hose is ideal) rather than spraying the leaves. Keep a mulched, weed-free ring around the trunk, and do not feed late in the year, since soft late growth gets winter damage that lets canker in.

notifications.title_beginner: Cherries almost ready, watch for rain
notifications.body_seasoned: The crop is sizing and coloring. Keep soil moisture EVEN to limit cracking, and if rain is in the forecast, pick any ripe fruit ahead of it, since rain on ripe cherries splits them. Cherries do not ripen after picking, so taste first and pick only fully colored, ripe fruit, pulling from the spur by the stem. Pick promptly and chill fast against spotted wing drosophila.
notifications.body_beginner: The cherries are sizing up and coloring. Keep the watering even so they do not split, and if rain is coming, pick any ripe ones first, since rain on ripe cherries splits them. Cherries do not get sweeter after picking, so taste one and pick only fully colored, ripe fruit, pulling from the little spur by the stem. Pick promptly and chill them fast.

notifications.body_seasoned: As the tree drops its leaves, clear every mummified fruit from the branches and ground and rake up fallen leaves. Mummies overwinter brown rot and fallen leaves overwinter cherry leaf spot, so this cleanup is your cheapest disease control. It is also the window to check the trunk base for fresh gum that signals bacterial canker.
notifications.body_beginner: As the leaves fall, pick off any shriveled dried-up fruit still hanging, gather what dropped, and rake up the fallen leaves. Old fruit carries brown rot and fallen leaves carry leaf spot into next year, so clearing them is the easiest disease control. It is also a good time to check the bottom of the trunk for fresh gum, which can mean bacterial canker.

notifications.title_seasoned: Did your winter bank enough chill?
notifications.body_seasoned: Sour cherry needs a lot of winter chill (most cultivars 700 hours or more) to bloom evenly, and there is no low-chill option, so it is fundamentally a cold-climate tree. After a mild winter, expect a weaker, more drawn-out bloom and a lighter set. In a truly mild-winter region it will not bloom reliably at all; note this year's bloom quality to learn your site.
notifications.body_beginner: Sour cherry needs plenty of winter cold (most kinds 700 hours or more) to bloom well, with no low-chill version, so it is really a cold-climate tree. After a mild winter, expect a thinner, more spread-out bloom and a lighter crop. Where winters are mild it will not bloom reliably at all. Jot down how well it bloomed this year to learn your spot.

notifications.title_seasoned: Anything to log on the cherry?
notifications.title_beginner: How is your cherry tree doing?
notifications.body_seasoned: It has been a while since your last note. A quick check pays off on a tree: scan the trunk for fresh gum (bacterial canker), confirm mummies and fallen leaves are cleared, and note where bloom and harvest landed and how well it set. Logging the dates now makes your tree's pattern clearer over time.
notifications.body_beginner: It has been a while since you logged anything. A quick look is worth it: check the trunk for fresh gum (bacterial canker), make sure old fruit and fallen leaves are cleared, and note when the tree bloomed and when you picked, and how well it set. Writing the dates down helps you see the tree's rhythm year to year.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost warning while flowering
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A hard freeze on open bloom or newly set fruit is the most common way a sour cherry crop is lost. If frost is forecast tonight, cover a small tree before evening to trap ground warmth, and water the soil beforehand, since moist ground holds and releases more heat overnight. Large trees are hard to protect, which is why a frost-aware site and a later-blooming cultivar matter most.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: A hard frost on open flowers or tiny new fruit is the most common reason a cherry crop fails. If frost is forecast tonight, cover a small tree before dark to hold in the ground's warmth, and water the soil first, since damp ground stays warmer overnight. Big trees are hard to cover, so the best protection is a spot less prone to frost and a variety that blooms later.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heavy rain, ripe fruit will crack
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Heavy rain, ripe cherries will split
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Rain on ripe or nearly ripe cherries is a classic cherry crop loss: free water on the fruit is absorbed through the skin and the swelling flesh splits, and split fruit rots fast with brown rot. Before a forecast soaking, pick every ripe cherry you can; a tree that went dry and is then rained on cracks worst, so keep moisture even all season. Sour cherry cracks less than sweet cherry and much of the crop is processed, but a hard rain at ripening still splits fruit, so pick ahead of it.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Rain on ripe or almost-ripe cherries is the classic way the crop is lost: water soaks into the fruit and it swells and splits, and split cherries rot fast. Before a coming rain, pick every ripe cherry you can. A tree that dried out and then gets rained on splits the worst, so keep the watering even all season. Sour cherry splits a bit less than sweet cherry and is often cooked anyway, but a hard rain at ripening still splits fruit, so pick before it.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Muggy weather, watch for rot
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Warm, humid conditions drive brown rot (browning blossoms at bloom and rotting ripe fruit within a day or two) and cool, wet, humid spring weather drives bacterial canker and cherry leaf spot. There is no spraying it away mid-spell: keep the canopy open and dry, water only at the root zone, remove rotting fruit promptly, and harvest ripe fruit without delay.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Warm, muggy weather is what brown rot loves, browning blossoms and rotting ripe cherries in a day or two, and cool wet spring weather drives bacterial canker and leaf spot. You cannot spray it away once it is muggy, so keep the tree open and the leaves dry, water only at the ground, pick off rotting fruit right away, and harvest ripe cherries promptly.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Dry spell, keep the watering even
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: During a dry stretch, deep, regular watering matters most for a first-year tree establishing roots and for keeping moisture EVEN as the fruit sizes. The cherry trap is the swing: a tree allowed to go dry and then watered hard, or rained on, splits its fruit. Soak deeply at the root zone and avoid letting the soil dry out and then flooding it.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: In a dry spell, deep, regular watering matters most for a young tree putting down roots and for keeping the moisture even while the fruit sizes. The cherry trap is the swing: a tree that dries out and then gets a big watering or rain splits its fruit. Give a deep soak at the ground and avoid letting the soil go dry and then flooding it.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot spell, watch the ripening fruit
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Sour cherry takes moderate heat but an extreme heat spell during ripening can soften fruit, cause doubling and spurring of next year's buds, and sunburn exposed cherries. Keep the tree well watered so heat and drought stress do not combine, and avoid stripping interior leaves that shade the fruit. Picking slightly early in extreme heat beats losing fruit to softening.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Sour cherry handles some heat, but an extreme hot spell while the fruit ripens can soften it, cause oddly doubled fruit, and sunburn exposed cherries. Keep the tree well watered so heat and dryness do not hit at once, and leave the leaves that shade the fruit. In extreme heat, picking a little early beats losing the crop to softening.

planting.text_seasoned: Sour cherry is self-fruitful, so pollination needs no planning: one tree sets a full crop on its own, unlike most sweet cherries. Choose the variety and tree size you want, such as Montmorency for pies or the naturally dwarf North Star for a small, easily netted tree.
planting.text_beginner: A sour cherry pollinates itself, so you do not need to plan pollination at all: one tree makes a full crop on its own, unlike most sweet cherries. Just pick the variety you want, like Montmorency for pies or the small, easy-to-net North Star.
planting.author: cc_author_pilot

planting.text_seasoned: Set the graft union 2 to 3 inches above the final soil line and plant in full sun on well-drained ground. Cherry will not tolerate wet feet, and frost-pocket sites lose the early bloom to late frost.
planting.text_beginner: Keep the graft joint 2 to 3 inches above the soil and plant in full sun where the soil drains well. Cherries hate soggy roots, and a low frost-pocket spot loses the early flowers to frost.
planting.author: cc_author_pilot

establishment.text_seasoned: Remove every blossom the first year so the young tree builds roots and a strong central leader instead of fruiting.
establishment.text_beginner: Pick off all the flowers the first year so the new tree puts its energy into roots and a strong main trunk instead of fruit.
establishment.author: cc_author_pilot

establishment.text_seasoned: The first season is the tree's most water-sensitive period; water deeply and regularly so roots establish, and never feed late, since soft growth invites the winter injury that opens the door to bacterial canker.
establishment.text_beginner: Water deeply and often all through the first season so the roots get going, and never feed late in the year, since soft late growth gets winter damage that lets canker in.
establishment.author: cc_author_pilot

scaffold_formation.text_seasoned: Train to a central leader, not the open vase used for peach: keep one dominant trunk and wide-angled scaffolds. Cherry fruits on long-lived spurs, so you build permanent structure rather than renewing fruiting wood each year.
scaffold_formation.text_beginner: Train a sour cherry to a single main trunk (a central leader), not the open vase shape used for peaches. Cherries fruit on long-lasting spurs, so you are building a lasting framework instead of cutting hard every year.
scaffold_formation.author: cc_author_pilot

dormancy.text_seasoned: Winter chill banks next year's bloom, and sour cherry needs a lot of it (most cultivars 700 hours or more), with no low-chill option. It is a cold-climate tree, so a truly mild-winter area cannot bloom it well.
dormancy.text_beginner: The cold of winter sets up next spring's flowers, and sour cherry needs plenty of it (most kinds 700 hours or more), with no low-chill version. It is a cold-climate tree, so it will not bloom well where winters are mild.
dormancy.author: cc_author_pilot

dormancy.text_seasoned: Clear mummified fruit and rake fallen leaves over winter: mummies carry brown rot and fallen leaves carry cherry leaf spot into the new season.
dormancy.text_beginner: Clear away dried mummy fruit and rake up fallen leaves during winter. Mummies carry brown rot and fallen leaves carry leaf spot into the next year.
dormancy.author: cc_author_pilot

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Cherry needs far lighter pruning than peach, because it fruits on long-lived spurs. Keep the leader, open the canopy, and avoid heavy cuts.
dormant_prune.text_beginner: Cherries need much less pruning than peaches, because they fruit on long-lasting spurs. Keep the main trunk, open the middle for light, and avoid cutting hard.
dormant_prune.author: cc_author_pilot

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: In wet climates, do major pruning in dry summer, not cool wet spring: fresh cuts in damp weather are the main entry point for bacterial canker, sour cherry's most serious disease.
dormant_prune.text_beginner: In wet areas, do the big pruning cuts in dry summer instead of cool wet spring. Fresh cuts in damp weather are the main way bacterial canker, the worst cherry disease, gets in.
dormant_prune.author: cc_author_pilot

blossom.text_seasoned: Open bloom is the most frost-vulnerable moment of the year. Track the forecast and cover a small tree overnight if a hard late frost threatens the flowers.
blossom.text_beginner: When the tree is in bloom it is most at risk from frost. Watch the forecast, and if a hard late frost is coming, cover a small tree overnight to protect the flowers.
blossom.author: cc_author_pilot

blossom.text_seasoned: Sour cherry is self-fruitful, so a single tree sets its own crop with no pollinizer, unlike sweet cherry. At bloom, just watch for frost and hope for bees; cold, wet, windy weather that grounds the bees is the main thing that thins the set.
blossom.text_beginner: A sour cherry fruits on its own, so one tree sets a crop with no partner, unlike a sweet cherry. At bloom, just watch for frost and for bees to be active; cold, wet, windy weather that keeps bees home is what thins the crop.
blossom.author: cc_author_pilot

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Do NOT thin cherries the way you thin peaches; they size on the tree without it. Instead, put your effort into netting against birds and keeping moisture even against cracking.
fruit_set.text_beginner: Do NOT thin cherries the way you thin peaches; they size up fine on their own. Put your effort into netting against birds and keeping the watering even so they do not split.
fruit_set.author: cc_author_pilot

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Net the tree as the fruit begins to color, before birds find it, and secure the skirt. This is the main reason to keep a cherry small on a dwarfing rootstock so it can be covered.
fruit_set.text_beginner: Put bird netting on as the cherries start to color, before the birds show up, and tuck it in at the bottom. This is the big reason to keep a cherry small (on a dwarfing rootstock) so you can actually cover it.
fruit_set.author: cc_author_pilot

harvest.text_seasoned: Sour cherries do not improve after picking and stay tart even when ripe, so go by full deep-red color and juiciness, not sweetness. Pull by the stem; a dead-ripe fruit may slip off the stem, which is fine for pies.
harvest.text_beginner: Sour cherries do not get better after picking and stay tart even when ripe, so judge by full deep-red color and juiciness, not sweetness. Pull by the stem; a dead-ripe one may come off the stem, which is fine for cooking.
harvest.author: cc_author_pilot

harvest.text_seasoned: Beat the rain: pick ripe cherries ahead of a forecast soaking, because rain on ripe fruit cracks it. Pick promptly and completely every couple of days and chill fast against spotted wing drosophila.
harvest.text_beginner: Beat the rain: pick ripe cherries before a coming rain, because rain on ripe fruit splits it. Pick every couple of days, leave none behind, and get them into the fridge fast to stop spotted wing drosophila.
harvest.author: cc_author_pilot

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A mature sour cherry yields by tree size: roughly 15 to 30 pounds on a genetic dwarf (North Star), 20 to 40 on a semi-dwarf (Meteor), and 30 to 60-plus pounds on a full-size Montmorency, given a frost-free bloom, leaf-spot control, and protection from birds. Because the tree is self-fruitful, crop is limited by frost, leaf spot, and birds rather than by pollination.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: A grown sour cherry gives roughly 15 to 30 pounds on a small dwarf like North Star and 30 to 60 pounds or more on a full-size Montmorency, as long as it dodges frost, keeps its leaves, and is protected from birds. Since one tree fruits on its own, the crop depends on frost, disease, and birds far more than on pollination or feeding.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Trees reach full bearing around years 4 to 6 and stay productive for 20 to 25 years. A self-fruitful tree needs no pollinizer, so the levers on yield are frost avoidance, cherry leaf spot control, and bird netting.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: A sour cherry hits full production around years 4 to 6 and keeps bearing for 20 to 25 years. One tree is all you need, so the things that decide your crop are avoiding frost, controlling cherry leaf spot, and netting against birds.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Expect no crop in the planting year and little to none through year 2. Remove any early fruit so the tree builds roots and a strong framework; the first meaningful harvest typically comes in years 3 to 4, sooner on a precocious dwarf, with full bearing by years 4 to 6.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Do not expect cherries the first year or two. If a little fruit forms early, pick it off so the young tree builds roots and strong branches. Your first real harvest usually comes in years 3 to 4 (sooner on a small dwarf tree), with full crops by years 4 to 6.
factors_seasoned: late-frost damage at bloom
cherry leaf spot and early defoliation
winter chill accumulation
bird protection (netting)
cherry fruit fly and spotted wing drosophila control
rootstock and tree age

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No moon-phase planting preference is asserted. Extension sources do not support timing sour cherry planting or care by lunar phase; chill matching, frost avoidance, and cherry leaf spot control govern outcomes.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: The tree bloomed well but set little or no fruit
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The tree flowered but I got almost no cherries
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The tree flowered heavily but few or no cherries formed. Because sour cherry is self-fruitful, this is almost never a pollination problem, so do not go looking for a partner tree. On sour cherry the leading cause is a late frost on the open bloom or tiny set fruit, and a distant second is a mild winter that banked too little chill for an even bloom. Cold, wet, windy bloom weather that grounds the bees can also thin the set. The fixes are a frost-aware site, frost cover at bloom, and making sure your winters actually deliver the chill this cold-climate tree needs.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The tree flowered but barely fruited. Since a sour cherry pollinates itself, this is almost never about needing a second tree. The usual reason is a late frost on the flowers or the tiny new fruit, and sometimes a winter too mild to give the tree the cold it needs to bloom evenly. Cold or rainy weather that keeps bees home can also cost you fruit. The fixes are planting away from frost pockets, covering the tree during a bloom-time frost, and growing it only where winters are truly cold.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant on a frost-aware site out of low pockets, keep a cover ready for a bloom-time frost, and confirm your region banks enough winter chill; a pollinizer is not the answer for a self-fruitful sour cherry.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant away from low frosty spots, keep a cover handy for a bloom-time frost, and make sure your winters are cold enough. You do not need a second tree, since sour cherry fruits on its own.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: The tree dropped its leaves by midsummer
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The leaves turned yellow and fell off in summer
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The tree yellowed and shed its leaves well before fall, often with small purple-brown spots on them first. This is cherry leaf spot, the signature disease of sour cherry, and Montmorency is especially prone, dropping leaves after only a few lesions. It is easy to dismiss as a watering or feeding problem, but the cause is a fungus overwintering in last year's fallen leaves that reinfects in warm, wet spring weather. Early defoliation weakens the tree, leaves the fruit poorly ripened, and cuts next year's crop, so it is worth taking seriously.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The tree turned yellow and lost its leaves in the middle of summer, often with small purple-brown spots first. This is cherry leaf spot, the main disease of sour cherry, and Montmorency catches it badly, dropping leaves after just a few spots. It looks like a watering or feeding issue but it is a fungus that lives over winter in fallen leaves and reinfects in wet spring weather. Losing the leaves early weakens the tree and next year's cherries.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Rake up and destroy every fallen leaf this autumn, keep the canopy open for fast drying, and in wet regions run an organic-approved fungicide program from petal fall, especially on a susceptible Montmorency.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Rake up and destroy all the fallen leaves this fall (that is where the fungus hides), keep the tree open so leaves dry fast, and in wet areas spray an organic-approved fungicide starting after the petals fall, especially on Montmorency.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Ripe cherries split open near harvest
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The cherries split open just before I could pick them
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Nearly ripe cherries developed splits and cracks, usually after a rain. Free water on ripe fruit is absorbed through the skin and the swelling flesh splits, and a dry-then-wet soil swing makes it worse; split fruit then rots fast with brown rot. Sour cherry cracks less obsessively than sweet cherry and much of the crop is processed anyway, but a soaking rain right at harvest can still cost you fruit. The fixes are even soil moisture through ripening and picking ahead of a forecast rain.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The nearly ripe cherries cracked and split, usually after rain. Water sitting on ripe fruit soaks in and the fruit swells and splits, and letting the soil go dry then wet makes it worse; split cherries rot quickly. Sour cherry cracks a bit less than sweet cherry, and a lot of it gets cooked anyway, but a hard rain right at harvest can still cost you fruit. Keep the watering even and pick before a coming rain.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Keep soil moisture even through ripening and pick ahead of forecast rain; a fast-ripening sour cherry is easy to bring in before a soaking.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep the watering steady as the fruit ripens and pick before a coming rain; sour cherry ripens fast, so it is easy to pick before a soaking.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Cherries had small white maggots inside
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The cherries had little white worms inside
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Cherries that looked fine outside hid small white maggots inside. Two pests do this: the cherry fruit fly (one generation a year, attacking fruit as it colors) and spotted wing drosophila (which attacks sound ripe fruit and multiplies explosively). Both are managed by prompt, complete harvest, removing every dropped and culled fruit, chilling the crop immediately, and trapping to time any organic spray to the color-change window.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Cherries that looked okay outside had small white maggots inside. Two pests cause this: the cherry fruit fly (one round a year, hitting fruit as it colors) and spotted wing drosophila (which hits whole ripe fruit and multiplies fast). Both are handled by picking promptly and completely, removing every dropped cherry, getting the crop into the fridge right away, and using traps to time any organic spray.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Hang traps from mid-spring, pick promptly and completely, destroy all dropped and culled fruit so larvae cannot reach the soil, and chill the crop immediately.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Put up traps in mid-spring, pick every cherry promptly, destroy all fallen fruit so the maggots cannot get into the soil, and refrigerate the crop right away.

succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Succession planting does not apply to sour cherry. It is a permanent tree that holds its site for two decades or more and bears one concentrated crop each season as the fruit ripens, so there is no staggered re-sowing to schedule the way there is for a short-season annual.

3.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 3 is the cold frontier for sour cherry, but this is the hardiest of the common tree fruits: the genetic-dwarf cultivars North Star, Meteor, and Mesabi survive winters near -30°F and crop in most years on sheltered, snow-covered sites. Chill is abundant; the risks are a hard midwinter freeze and a late spring frost on the bloom. Plant the hardiest cultivar on a protected slope out of frost pockets.
3.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 3 is the coldest edge for sour cherry, but it is the toughest of the usual fruit trees. The hardiest kinds (North Star, Meteor, Mesabi) survive very cold winters and fruit in most years in a sheltered, snowy spot. The risks are deep winter cold and a late spring frost. Plant the hardiest variety in a protected place out of frost pockets.
3.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Deep winter cold and a late spring frost on the bloom are the crop risks; the hardiest cultivars and a sheltered, snow-holding site are the answer.

4.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 4 is solid sour cherry country. Chill is ample and the tree is fully hardy here, so Montmorency and the hardy dwarfs crop reliably. Watch for a late spring frost on the bloom, and plan on cherry leaf spot control and bird netting.
4.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 4 grows sour cherries dependably. It is plenty cold and the tree is fully hardy, so Montmorency and the hardy dwarfs fruit well. Watch for a late frost at bloom, control cherry leaf spot, and net against birds.
4.frost_risk_note_seasoned: An occasional late frost can nip the bloom; otherwise the main jobs are leaf spot control and bird netting.

5.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 5 is prime sour cherry country, the heart of the Great Lakes tart-cherry belt, with ample chill and full hardiness. The full cultivar range crops reliably; the season's work is cherry leaf spot control in wet springs, harvest-time bird netting, and watching an occasional late frost.
5.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 5 is excellent for sour cherries, the heart of the Great Lakes pie-cherry belt. It is plenty cold and fully hardy, so any variety works. The main jobs are controlling cherry leaf spot in wet springs, netting against birds, and watching for a late frost.
5.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Late-frost loss is occasional; leaf spot and birds are the steadier concerns.

6.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 6 fruits sour cherries reliably, with ample chill and an earlier start. The full variety range is open. The cautions are cherry leaf spot and brown rot in warm, wet springs, harvest-time rain, and birds, so manage disease, keep moisture even, and net the tree.
6.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 6 grows sour cherries well, with plenty of cold and an earlier season. Almost any variety works. Watch for cherry leaf spot and brown rot in warm wet springs, rain near harvest, and birds, so manage disease, water evenly, and net the tree.
6.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Late-frost risk is modest; warm-spring disease and birds are the main concerns.

7.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 7 is the warm edge for sour cherry: winters bank only marginal chill for the higher-chill cultivars, and warmer, more humid springs drive cherry leaf spot and brown rot hard. It fruits in good years, best with the lower-chill hardy cultivars and a disciplined leaf-spot program, but it is less dependable than the colder zones.
7.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 7 is the warm edge for sour cherry. Winters give only just enough cold for the higher-chill kinds, and the warmer, wetter springs bring more cherry leaf spot and brown rot. It fruits in good years, best with a lower-chill hardy variety and steady disease control, but it is less reliable than colder zones.
7.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Chill shortfall in warm winters and spring disease pressure, not frost, are the limits here.

northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: The northern tier is sour cherry's home ground. Winters bank far more chill than the tree needs, and it is hardy across the whole range, so zones 4 to 6 crop reliably (the Great Lakes tart-cherry belt sits here). Zone 3 asks for the hardiest dwarf cultivars and patience with off years, and zone 7 is the warm edge where chill runs short and spring disease bites. The steady work everywhere is cherry leaf spot control and bird netting.
northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: The northern tier is the best region for sour cherries. Winters are more than cold enough and the tree is hardy throughout, so zones 4 to 6 fruit dependably (this is the Great Lakes pie-cherry belt). Zone 3 needs the hardiest small varieties and some patience, and zone 7 is the warm edge where cold runs short and disease is worse. Everywhere, the main jobs are controlling cherry leaf spot and netting against birds.
northern_tier.chill_basis_seasoned: Northern-tier winters bank well over 700 to 1,000-plus chill hours, more than any sour cherry needs, so chill is never the limiter here. The limits are the opposite: deep-winter cold at the zone 3 edge and, toward zone 7, warm-spring disease pressure.
northern_tier.chill_basis_beginner: Winters here are plenty cold for the chill any sour cherry needs. The challenges are the opposite: very deep cold at the coldest edge and, in the warmest part, more spring disease.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Inland zone 8 banks marginal chill, but sour cherry is a cold-climate tree poorly suited to the hot, humid Southeast: it rarely gets the winter cold it needs, and cherry leaf spot, brown rot, and harvest-season rain run hard in the warmth. Sour cherry is not recommended here.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Even inland, the Southeast is too mild in winter and too hot and humid for sour cherry, a cold-climate tree. It rarely gets the cold it needs, and disease and rain make it fail. It is not recommended here.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: The warmer, lower-chill zone 9 Gulf edge cannot bank the winter chill sour cherry needs, and the heat, humidity, and harvest rain drive disease and cracking. Unsuitable regardless of cultivar.
9.suitability_note_beginner: The warmer Gulf edge is far too mild in winter and too hot and humid for sour cherry. It will not fruit here.

se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: The Southeast is not sour cherry country. Winters are too mild to give this cold-climate tree its chill, and heat, humidity, and harvest rain drive cherry leaf spot, brown rot, and cracking. Southern growers do far better with peach or rabbiteye blueberry.
se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: Sour cherry does not suit the Southeast. Winters are too mild for the cold it needs, and the heat, humidity, and rain bring disease. Grow peaches or rabbiteye blueberries instead.
se_gulf.chill_basis_seasoned: Southeastern winters bank only marginal chill inland (roughly 650 to 1,000 hours at zone 8) and less toward the Gulf, short of what sour cherry needs, and the warm humidity that drives disease seals the verdict.
se_gulf.chill_basis_beginner: Winters here do not get cold enough for the chill sour cherry needs, and the heat and humidity bring disease on top of that. It is not a workable crop.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Interior California grows sweet cherries well but is a poor fit for sour cherry: the mild Mediterranean winters bank only about 500 to 1,100 chill hours, short and unreliable for a tree that wants a real cold winter, so it survives and grows but rarely banks enough chill to bloom and set a dependable crop. There is no low-chill sour cherry to fall back on.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Interior California is great for sweet cherries but not for sour cherry, which needs a real cold winter. The mild winters here usually do not give it enough cold, so the tree grows but rarely fruits well. Unlike peaches, there is no low-chill sour cherry to plant instead.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Lower-elevation zone 9 interior banks even less chill (around 300 to 950 hours), well below what sour cherry needs, so the tree survives but does not fruit dependably. Grow low-chill stone fruit or a sweet cherry here instead.
9.suitability_note_beginner: The warmer interior (zone 9) is even milder in winter, too mild for sour cherry to fruit reliably. The tree survives but rarely crops. Grow low-chill fruit or a sweet cherry instead.

ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: Interior California, the heart of West Coast sweet cherry growing, is a poor fit for sour cherry. The mild winters do not reliably bank the high chill a tart cherry needs, and there is no low-chill sour cherry, so the tree survives but seldom fruits well. This is a sweet-cherry and low-chill-stone-fruit region, not a sour-cherry one.
ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: Interior California is famous for sweet cherries but is a poor choice for sour cherry. The mild winters do not give it the deep cold it needs, and there is no low-chill version, so the tree lives but rarely fruits. Grow sweet cherries or low-chill fruit here instead.
ca_interior.chill_basis_seasoned: Interior California banks roughly 300 to 1,100 chill hours depending on elevation, enough for many sweet cherries but short and unreliable for the higher-chill sour cherry, which has no low-chill cultivar to fall back on.
ca_interior.chill_basis_beginner: Interior California usually does not get cold enough in winter for a sour cherry, which needs a lot of chill and has no low-chill version. Sweet cherries do far better here.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: The mild zone 9 inland edge of the North Coast banks only about 300 to 800 chill hours, short of what sour cherry needs, so the tree survives but rarely fruits. A cold-climate tart cherry is out of place on the mild California coast.
9.suitability_note_beginner: The milder inland part of the North Coast does not get cold enough for sour cherry, so the tree survives but rarely fruits. It is a cold-climate tree that does not suit the mild California coast.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: The cool coastal zone 10 banks very little winter chill (roughly 150 to 600 hours), far too little for sour cherry to bloom and set. The tree survives but does not fruit here.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Right on the cool coast (zone 10) there is far too little winter cold for sour cherry. The tree survives but will not fruit.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: The North Coast's mild maritime winters do not bank the chill sour cherry needs, so the tree survives but does not fruit dependably anywhere in the region. It is a cold-climate crop out of place here.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: The mild coastal winters of the North Coast do not give sour cherry the cold it needs, so it survives but does not fruit. It is a cold-climate tree that does not belong here.
ca_north_coast.chill_basis_seasoned: The North Coast banks only about 150 to 800 chill hours, well below the high chill sour cherry requires, and there is no low-chill tart cherry, so the crop cannot be relied on.
ca_north_coast.chill_basis_beginner: The mild coast does not get cold enough for sour cherry's high chill needs, and there is no low-chill version, so it will not fruit.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: The mild South Coast inland (zone 9) banks only about 200 to 550 chill hours, far below sour cherry's need, so the tree survives but does not fruit. This is a mild-winter region unsuitable for a cold-climate tart cherry.
9.suitability_note_beginner: The milder inland part of the South Coast is far too warm in winter for sour cherry. The tree survives but will not fruit.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: The cool South Coast (zone 10) banks almost no winter chill (roughly 50 to 350 hours), so sour cherry cannot bloom or set. It will not fruit anywhere on the mild Southern California coast.
10.suitability_note_beginner: The Southern California coast (zone 10) has almost no winter cold, so sour cherry will not fruit at all.

ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: The South Coast's mild winters are far too warm for sour cherry, which needs a real cold winter. The tree survives but does not fruit anywhere in the region.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: The mild winters of the South Coast are much too warm for sour cherry. It survives but will not fruit here.
ca_south_coast.chill_basis_seasoned: The South Coast banks only roughly 50 to 550 chill hours, far short of what sour cherry needs, with no low-chill tart cherry available, so the crop fails.
ca_south_coast.chill_basis_beginner: The mild South Coast does not get nearly cold enough in winter for sour cherry, so it will not fruit.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: The California desert banks almost no winter chill (about 150 to 400 hours at zone 9) and bakes in summer heat, both hostile to a cold-climate sour cherry. Unsuitable; grow low-chill stone fruit or figs.
9.suitability_note_beginner: The California desert is far too mild in winter and far too hot in summer for sour cherry. It will not work here. Grow low-chill peaches or figs instead.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: The hottest desert (zone 10) banks essentially no chill (roughly 100 to 300 hours) and its extreme summer heat compounds the problem. Sour cherry is unsuitable.
10.suitability_note_beginner: The hottest desert has almost no winter cold and brutal summer heat, so sour cherry cannot grow here.

ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: The California desert is doubly wrong for sour cherry: far too little winter chill and far too much summer heat. It is unsuitable across the region; grow low-chill stone fruit, figs, or pomegranate.
ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: The California desert is too mild in winter and too hot in summer for sour cherry. Grow low-chill peaches, figs, or pomegranates instead.
ca_desert.chill_basis_seasoned: The desert banks only about 100 to 400 chill hours, nowhere near what sour cherry needs, and the extreme summer heat seals it.
ca_desert.chill_basis_beginner: The desert does not get nearly cold enough in winter for sour cherry, and the summer heat is too much besides.

8.suitability_note_beginner: Warm, dry inland areas (zone 8) do not get cold enough in winter for sour cherry, and the growing season is hot and frost-prone. The tree may live but rarely fruits, so it is not a workable crop.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: The Arizona low desert banks essentially no winter chill (about 100 to 400 hours) and endures extreme summer heat, both hostile to a cold-climate sour cherry. Unsuitable; grow low-chill stone fruit or figs.
9.suitability_note_beginner: The Arizona low desert is far too mild in winter and far too hot in summer for sour cherry. It will not grow here. Grow low-chill peaches or figs.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: The Florida peninsula banks almost no winter chill (roughly 50 to 350 hours at zone 10) and is hot and humid year-round, so sour cherry, a cold-climate tree, cannot get the cold it needs and would face relentless disease. Unsuitable.

11.suitability_note_beginner: South Florida never gets cold, so sour cherry cannot fruit here at all. Grow tropical fruit instead.

11.suitability_note_seasoned: Hawaii has no winter chill to speak of (about 0 to 150 hours) and no cold season, so a cold-climate sour cherry cannot break dormancy, bloom, or fruit. Unsuitable; grow tropical fruit.
11.suitability_note_beginner: Hawaii does not have a cold winter, so sour cherry cannot bloom or fruit here at all. Grow tropical fruit instead.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: Sour cherry needs a cold winter to fruit, and Hawaii does not have one. Grow tropical fruit instead.
