crops.description_seasoned: Sour cherry, also called tart or pie cherry, is a deciduous stone-fruit tree (Prunus cerasus) grown for bright, tart fruit destined for pies, preserves, juice, and the freezer rather than fresh dessert eating. It is far easier than sweet cherry on the two counts that matter most: it is SELF-FRUITFUL, so a single tree crops with no pollinizer, and it is markedly more cold-hardy, thriving in cold-winter zones 4 to 6 where sweet cherry struggles. It is also naturally small, a large bush or compact tree easy to net against birds. It still needs a real cold winter to bloom, and it still faces brown rot, birds, and above all cherry leaf spot, which will defoliate an unsprayed Montmorency. Montmorency is the classic; North Star and Meteor are compact and very hardy.
crops.description_beginner: A sour cherry (also called a tart or pie cherry) is a hardy fruit tree that drops its leaves each winter and gives tart fruit best used for pies, jam, juice, and freezing rather than eating fresh. It is much easier to grow than a sweet cherry for two big reasons: ONE tree makes fruit on its own (no second tree needed), and it is far tougher in cold winters, doing well in zones 4 to 6. It is also naturally small, so it is easy to cover against birds. It still needs a cold winter to bloom, and it still gets brown rot, birds, and especially cherry leaf spot, a disease that will strip the leaves off an unsprayed tree. Montmorency is the classic variety; North Star and Meteor stay small and are very hardy.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: A sour cherry is ready when it reaches full, deep red color, hangs soft and juicy, and pulls free easily. Unlike sweet cherry, sour cherry is picked at full softness for processing, and a dead-ripe Montmorency will often part from its stem, which is fine for pies and juice. Taste is the guide: the fruit stays tart even ripe, but sugars and juice peak in the last few days, so let it hang until fully colored and richly flavored. Pick promptly and completely once ripe, because rain cracks ripe fruit and birds and spotted wing drosophila move in fast; a whole tree often ripens within a week or two.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: A sour cherry is ripe when it turns full deep red, feels soft and juicy, and comes off easily. Unlike a sweet cherry, you pick a sour cherry fully soft for cooking, and a dead-ripe one may even pull off the stem, which is fine for pies and juice. It stays tart even when ripe, so go by color and juiciness rather than sweetness, and let it hang until fully red and full-flavored. Pick it all promptly once ripe, since rain splits ripe fruit and birds and small vinegar flies show up quickly; the whole tree usually ripens within a week or two.
crops.bloom_time_seasoned: Sour cherries bloom in early to mid spring, typically April to early May across their cold-winter range, usually just before or as the leaves emerge. Sour cherry blooms a little later than sweet cherry, which helps it dodge some late frosts, but a hard freeze on open bloom still takes the crop. Because the tree is self-fruitful, bloom timing is not a pollination puzzle the way it is for sweet cherry; the only bloom-time concern is frost and enough bee activity to work the flowers.
crops.bloom_time_beginner: Sour cherry trees flower in early to mid spring, usually April into early May, right around when the leaves come out. They bloom a bit later than sweet cherries, which helps them escape some late frosts, but a hard frost on the open flowers can still kill the crop. Because a sour cherry fruits on its own, you do not have to match bloom times with a partner tree; the only things to watch at bloom are frost and having bees active.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Sour cherry is among the most cold-hardy of the common tree fruits, notably tougher than sweet cherry: it fruits reliably in zones 4 to 6, survives into zone 3 with the hardiest cultivars (North Star, Meteor, Mesabi), and shrugs off winters near -25°F. Its limit is warmth, not cold. Toward zone 7 and warmer the winters no longer bank enough chill and summer heat and humidity drive cherry leaf spot and brown rot, so the crop turns marginal, then unsuitable through the low-chill South, warm coasts, and deserts. Sour cherry is fundamentally a northern, cold-winter crop.
crops.hardiness_notes_beginner: Sour cherry is one of the toughest fruit trees in the cold, much hardier than sweet cherry. It fruits dependably in zones 4 to 6 and, with the hardiest varieties like North Star or Meteor, can survive into zone 3 and winters near -25°F. Its weak spot is the opposite of cold: in zone 7 and warmer the winters are too mild to give it the cold rest it needs, and the heat and humidity bring disease, so it becomes unreliable and then will not fruit at all in the warm South, mild coasts, and deserts. It is really a cold-climate crop.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Sour cherry needs a solid stretch of winter cold, counted as chill hours (hours between about 32°F and 45°F), to break dormancy and bloom evenly. Most cultivars want a substantial chill, roughly 700 to 1,000 hours or more (Montmorency near 1,000), with the cold-hardy North Star and Meteor at the lower end and the tart Morello types similar. There is no low-chill sour cherry the way there is for peach, so it stays a cold-winter tree throughout its range. Where winters no longer bank that chill, the tree blooms weakly and sets little, which is why the mild South and West coasts are off the table.
crops.chill_hours_note_beginner: Sour cherry trees need plenty of cold winter hours, called chill hours, before they will bloom well in spring. Most kinds need a lot, roughly 700 to 1,000 hours or more, so sour cherry only suits cold-winter areas. Unlike peaches, there is no low-chill sour cherry for mild climates. If your winters are mild, the tree will bloom poorly and make little or no fruit, which is why it is not grown in the warm South or along the mild coasts.
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Sour cherry is self-fruitful, so a single tree sets a full crop with no pollinizer partner, the reverse of most sweet cherries. Montmorency, North Star, Meteor, and English Morello all fruit alone. A second sour cherry can raise set slightly but is never required. The tree is insect-pollinated, mainly by bees, so supporting bee activity during the short bloom helps a lone tree fill out its crop.
crops.pollinator_notes_beginner: A sour cherry pollinates itself, so one tree makes a full crop with no second tree needed. This is the easy difference from most sweet cherries, which must have a partner. Montmorency and the other common sour cherries all fruit on their own. Bees still carry the pollen from flower to flower, so lots of bee activity during the short bloom helps a single tree set well.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: In the planting year, prioritize establishment over fruit. Plant a dormant bare-root tree in early spring, head it back at planting to begin a modified central-leader or open-center framework, keep a weed-free, mulched circle around the trunk, and water consistently through the first two seasons. Remove any fruit that sets. No pollinizer planning is needed, since the tree is self-fruitful. Hold fertilizer until growth begins and never feed late, which invites the winter injury that opens the door to bacterial canker.
crops.year_one_notes_beginner: The first year is about helping the tree settle in, not getting fruit. Plant a bare-root tree in early spring while it is still resting, cut it back at planting to start its shape, keep a mulched, weed-free ring around the trunk, and water it steadily through the first couple of years. Pull off any fruit that forms. You do not need a second tree, since sour cherry fruits on its own. Wait to fertilize until it starts growing, and never feed late in the year, since soft late growth gets winter damage that lets disease in.

pollination.notes_seasoned: Sour cherry is SELF-FRUITFUL: a single tree sets a full crop on its own with no second variety required, the opposite of most sweet cherries. Montmorency, the dominant cultivar, is reliably self-fertile, as are North Star, Meteor, and English Morello. A second sour cherry blooming nearby can nudge set a little higher but is never necessary. Bees are still the vector, so cold, wet, or windy weather during the short bloom can thin a crop even on a self-fertile tree.
pollination.notes_beginner: Sour cherry pollinates itself, so ONE tree makes a full crop with no partner needed. This is the big, easy difference from most sweet cherries, which need a second, matching variety to fruit. Montmorency and the other common sour cherries (North Star, Meteor) all fruit on their own. Bees still do the work of moving pollen within the tree, so a cold or rainy spell during the short bloom can still cost you some fruit.

crops.establishment_note: Most sour cherries begin bearing about 3 to 4 years after planting, a little sooner on a naturally dwarf cultivar such as North Star and later on a full-size tree.
crops.recommended_rootstock_note: Sour cherry is naturally a small tree or large bush (often 12 to 18 feet, less on a dwarf), so rootstock is more about soil fit and precocity than size. Mahaleb is the traditional sour cherry rootstock: precocious and cold-hardy, but only on deep, well-drained ground. Choose Mazzard for heavier or wetter soils, a Gisela for a smaller, easily netted tree, and remember the genetic-dwarf cultivars (North Star, Meteor) stay small on their own without any dwarfing rootstock.

rootstock_options.name: Mahaleb
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask for your sour cherry on Mahaleb for deep, very well-drained soil where you want a precocious, cold-hardy tree.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: The classic sour cherry rootstock: precocious, cold-hardy, and somewhat size-controlling, bearing sooner than Mazzard. Its hard limit is drainage; it performs only in deep, well-drained soil and fails in heavy or wet ground, where it is prone to root rots. The traditional default on dry, well-drained sites.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: The traditional sour cherry rootstock. It makes an earlier-bearing, cold-hardy tree, but it only works in deep, well-drained soil and does poorly where the ground holds water, so skip it if your soil stays wet.

rootstock_options.name: Mazzard
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask for Mazzard for heavier or wetter soils where Mahaleb would struggle.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: A vigorous, full-size seedling rootstock with a fibrous root system that tolerates heavier and wetter soils far better than Mahaleb. The trade-off is a larger, later-bearing tree that is harder to net and pick; a good pick where drainage is imperfect.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: A full-size rootstock that handles heavier and wetter soils better than Mahaleb. The downside is a bigger tree that fruits a bit later and is harder to cover against birds.

rootstock_options.name: Gisela 5
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask for Gisela 5 for a small, very early-bearing, easily netted tree, even in a large pot.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: A true dwarfing rootstock, roughly half standard size, very precocious and very cold-hardy, doing well even on heavier soils. It sets so heavily so young that fruit can run small without good feeding and crop thinning; the best choice for a small, nettable, or containerized tree.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: A small dwarfing rootstock about half the usual size, very cold-hardy, and quick to fruit (in 2 to 3 years), even in heavier soil. It can overset when young, so feed it well; it makes the easiest tree to net and pick.

rootstock_options.name: Gisela 6
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask for Gisela 6 for a productive, early-bearing, soil-tolerant backyard tree.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: A semi-dwarfing rootstock holding the tree to a compact backyard size, very precocious despite its vigor, productive, and well suited to heavier soils. The most adaptable all-round backyard choice where a naturally-dwarf cultivar is not used.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: A rootstock that makes a compact tree that fruits early, bears well, and handles heavier soils. A good all-round backyard choice.

rootstock_options.name: Own-root / genetic dwarf (North Star, Meteor)
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask for North Star or Meteor, which are naturally small and often sold on their own roots.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: Several of the best backyard sour cherries (North Star at 8 to 10 feet, Meteor at 10 to 14 feet) are genetic dwarfs that stay small without any dwarfing rootstock and are frequently grown on their own roots. Very cold-hardy and easy to net; the simplest small-tree route.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: Some sour cherries, like North Star and Meteor, are naturally small trees (8 to 14 feet) and need no special dwarfing rootstock. They are very cold-hardy and easy to cover against birds, the simplest way to get a small tree.

pet_safe.note: The flesh is fine, but the pits, seeds, and leaves contain cyanide compounds and are toxic to cats, dogs, and horses.

crops.name: Microgreens Mix
crops.sunlight: bright indirect light or a grow light
crops.water: keep the medium evenly moist; bottom-water once greened to keep leaves dry

soil.preferred_texture_seasoned: A fine, moisture-holding soilless medium: seed-starting mix, coconut coir, or a hydroponic fiber mat (hemp, jute, or similar).
soil.preferred_texture_beginner: Use a fine, soil-free growing medium that holds moisture well, such as seed-starting mix, coconut coir, or a growing mat made from hemp or jute fiber.
soil.tolerated_texture_seasoned: Peat-based mixes and inert mats both work; the choice trades water-holding against cleanliness at harvest.
soil.tolerated_texture_beginner: Both peat-based mixes and fiber mats work well. Mixes hold more water, while mats stay cleaner at harvest, so pick whichever suits you.
soil.problematic_texture_seasoned: Garden soil and heavy potting mixes are too coarse and carry pathogen and pest risk for a raw, densely sown crop.
soil.problematic_texture_beginner: Skip garden soil and regular potting mix. They are too coarse, and they can carry pests and germs that are risky for a crowded crop you eat raw.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Use a light seed-starting mix, coconut coir, or a special growing mat made for microgreens. Do not use garden soil.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: A clean, fine, moisture-retentive soilless medium gives even germination and a clean cut; coir and fiber mats keep grit off the harvest.

ph.note_seasoned: pH is not a practical lever for a single short indoor cycle on a soilless medium; standard seed-starting mixes and coir sit in a workable range and need no adjustment.
ph.note_beginner: You do not need to worry about soil pH for microgreens. The mixes and mats sold for them are already fine as is.

fertilizer.timing: not applicable
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Microgreens are harvested before they exhaust the seed's own reserves, so no fertilizer is needed for a single cycle on an inert medium or seed-starting mix. Added nutrients mainly raise the risk of algae and off-flavors.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: You do not need to feed microgreens. The seed carries enough food to get the plant to harvest, and adding fertilizer just invites algae and odd flavors.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: None.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: None needed.

companions.note_seasoned: Not applicable. Microgreens are grown as dense single-type indoor trays, so there is no interplanting or companion relationship. Grow each type in its own tray and combine after harvest.
companions.note_beginner: Not applicable. Microgreens grow as one type per tray indoors, so there are no companion plants. If you want a mix, just combine different trays after cutting.

pests.description_seasoned: Small dark flies whose larvae live in persistently wet medium and feed on organic matter and tender roots. They are the main indoor microgreen pest and a symptom of an over-wet tray rather than a primary threat.
pests.description_beginner: Tiny dark flies that show up around constantly damp soil. Their larvae live in the wet mix. They are the main bug you might see indoors, and they usually mean the tray is staying too wet.
pests.management_seasoned: Let the surface dry between waterings where the crop allows, bottom-water, and keep airflow up. Because the cycle is so short, most trays are harvested before gnats build to a real problem; sanitized trays and fresh medium between cycles break the cycle.
pests.management_beginner: Keep the surface from staying soaking wet, water from the bottom, and keep air moving. Since microgreens are harvested so fast, gnats rarely get bad before you cut. Clean trays and fresh mix between batches keep them away.

diseases.description_seasoned: Soil-borne fungi (Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and others) rot seedlings at the soil line under wet, crowded, still conditions, often alongside fuzzy white or gray surface mold. It is the number-one microgreen failure.
diseases.description_beginner: The most common microgreen problem. In wet, crowded, stuffy conditions, tiny fungi rot the baby plants right at the base, and you often see fuzzy white or gray mold on the surface too.
diseases.management_seasoned: Prevention is the whole game: wrung-sponge moisture, bottom-watering once greened, constant gentle airflow, a sensible seeding rate, and sanitized trays between cycles. There is no rescue spray for a raw cut crop; a badly affected tray is composted and restarted clean.
diseases.management_beginner: You cannot spray this away on a crop you eat raw, so the fix is prevention: keep the mix just damp (not soggy), water from the bottom once the leaves are up, keep a small fan running, do not sow too thickly, and clean your trays between batches. If a tray molds badly, toss it and start over with clean equipment.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Mist once or twice daily through germination and blackout to hold even surface moisture; once greened, bottom-water as the tray dries.
watering.frequency_beginner: While the seeds are sprouting, lightly mist the surface once or twice a day so it stays damp. After you move the tray into the light, water from the bottom whenever it starts to dry out.
watering.amount_seasoned: Enough to keep the medium at wrung-sponge moisture, never saturated; pour off any standing water after bottom-watering.
watering.amount_beginner: Just enough to keep the soil damp like a wrung-out sponge, never soggy. After bottom-watering, tip out any water left sitting in the tray.
watering.method_seasoned: Mist during germination and blackout; switch to bottom-watering once the canopy is up so foliage stays dry.
watering.method_beginner: Mist the top while the seeds are sprouting, then water from the bottom once the leaves are up so the leaves stay dry.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Standing water, a sour smell, fuzzy white growth on the medium or stems, and collapsed seedlings all signal overwatering and the damping-off that follows it.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Water sitting in the tray, a bad smell, fuzzy white mold, or seedlings flopping over mean it is too wet. Cut back on water and improve airflow.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Curling, limp cotyledons and a medium that has pulled away from the tray edges indicate the canopy has dried too far between waterings.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Limp, curling leaves and soil that has shrunk away from the sides mean it got too dry. Water from the bottom right away.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Wet foliage in a dense, still canopy is the main driver of mold and damping-off, so the cycle moves deliberately from misting to bottom-watering and pairs it with constant gentle airflow.
watering.method_note_beginner: Wet leaves packed close together with no air movement is what causes mold. That is why you switch to watering from the bottom once the leaves are up, and keep a gentle fan going.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The blackout-to-light transition is the highest-risk window: the canopy is dense, humidity under the cover is high, and a single overwatering here can seed damping-off across the whole tray.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The riskiest time is right when you uncover the tray and move it into the light. The plants are crowded and damp, so do not overwater, and make sure air is moving.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Do not hold cut microgreens at room temperature; they wilt and spoil within hours. Refrigerate immediately after cutting.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Do not leave cut microgreens out on the counter. They go limp fast, so put them in the fridge right after cutting.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerate dry in a vented container lined with a paper towel; most types keep about 5 to 7 days, and sturdier ones (pea, sunflower, radish) can hold close to 2 weeks. Harvest only what you will use soon.
storage.fridge_beginner: Keep cut microgreens in the fridge in a container with a paper towel to absorb extra moisture. Most last about 5 to 7 days; tougher ones like pea, sunflower, and radish can last closer to 2 weeks.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Not recommended. Freezing collapses the delicate cells and ruins the texture. Microgreens are a fresh, cut-and-eat crop.
storage.freezer_beginner: Do not freeze microgreens. Freezing turns them mushy. They are meant to be eaten fresh.
storage.notes_seasoned: Cut clean and dry: harvest with sanitized scissors into a clean container, keep the foliage dry, and chill promptly. Because they are eaten raw, the same clean-water and sanitized-surface rules that govern growing also govern handling.
storage.notes_beginner: Because you eat microgreens raw, keep everything clean: cut them with clean scissors into a clean, dry container and refrigerate right away.

recommended.name: Radish
recommended.note: Fast brassica, 8 to 12 days; spicy. A reliable backbone of most mixes; no presoak.

recommended.name: Broccoli
recommended.note: Fast brassica, 8 to 12 days; mild. Popular for flavor and nutrition; no presoak.

recommended.name: Kale
recommended.note: Fast brassica, 8 to 12 days; nutty, strong. No presoak.

recommended.name: Arugula
recommended.note: Fastest in the mix, 6 to 8 days; peppery. No presoak; mist, do not soak.

recommended.name: Mustard / cabbage
recommended.note: Fast brassicas, about 8 to 12 days; pungent to mild. No presoak.

recommended.name: Pea shoots
recommended.note: Large seed: presoak about 6 hours; 8 to 10 days; sweet, tender. Sow heavily (about 150 g per tray).

recommended.name: Sunflower
recommended.note: Large seed: presoak about 12 hours; 9 to 10 days; nutty, crunchy. Hull may need a gentle rinse off the canopy.

recommended.name: Cilantro
recommended.note: Slow, 21 to 28 days; distinctive flavor. No presoak; patience and clean conditions matter.

recommended.name: Basil
recommended.note: Slow, 12 to 16 days; intense flavor. Mucilaginous seed: mist, do not soak.

varieties.note_seasoned: A balanced mix pairs fast brassicas (radish, broccoli, kale, arugula, mustard) for quick bulk and color with a sweet large-seed type (pea or sunflower, presoaked) and, if you want complexity, a slower aromatic (basil, cilantro). The practical splits are: presoak the large seeds only; mist (never soak) the mucilaginous ones (basil, cilantro, cress, chia); and either sow a pre-blended mix or grow types separately and combine at harvest, since blackout times and finish dates differ. Never use seed from solanaceous crops (tomato, pepper, eggplant), because their seedlings carry alkaloids and are not safe to eat raw.
varieties.note_beginner: A good mix combines fast, easy types like radish, broccoli, and arugula with something sweet like pea or sunflower. A couple of rules make it work: soak only the big seeds (pea, sunflower) before sowing, and just mist the sticky ones like basil and cilantro instead of soaking. Different types finish at different times, so many people grow them in separate trays and combine after cutting. Important: never grow microgreens from tomato, pepper, or eggplant seed, as those baby plants are not safe to eat.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Not applicable. Microgreens are never moved outdoors or transplanted; the whole cycle is indoors.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: Not applicable. Microgreens stay indoors from seed to harvest, so there is no hardening off.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Sow densely and evenly across pre-moistened medium (rates run from about 10 g for arugula to 150 g of pea per 1020 tray). Presoak only the large seeds (pea about 6 hours, sunflower about 12); brassicas and small seeds go on dry. Do not bury the seed; press it into contact, then cover for blackout. Dense, even contact is what gives a uniform stand and a clean single cut.
start_method.notes_beginner: Scatter the seeds thickly and evenly over damp growing medium. Big seeds like pea and sunflower do better after a soak (pea about 6 hours, sunflower about 12); small seeds like radish and broccoli go on dry. Do not bury the seeds, just press them down so they touch the surface, then cover the tray to keep them dark for a few days.

drainage.saucer_practice_seasoned: Nest the drilled tray inside a solid, hole-free tray. The outer tray catches runoff, lets you bottom-water, and is poured off so the crop never sits in standing water.
drainage.saucer_practice_beginner: Set the tray with holes inside a second solid tray with no holes. The bottom tray lets you water from below and catch extra water, which you then pour out so the roots are not sitting in water.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Seed-starting mix, coconut coir, or a microgreen growing mat.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: None needed.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: Seed-starting mix, coir, or an inert fiber mat; about 1 to 2 inches deep.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: None; the medium is a substrate, not a nutrient source, for a single cycle.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Water from the bottom by setting the tray in a little water, then pour off what is left.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: No fertilizer needed.

overwintering.approach_seasoned: Not applicable. Microgreens are an indoor year-round cycle crop, harvested in days, with no dormant or overwintered phase.
overwintering.approach_beginner: Not applicable. Microgreens grow indoors all year and are harvested within a couple of weeks, so there is nothing to overwinter.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: The tray is the entire growing system: shallow, drained, nested over a solid tray for bottom-watering, sanitized between cycles. A clean, reused, food-grade tray beats a single-use clamshell for both food safety and consistent results.
container_notes.notes_beginner: For microgreens, the tray is the whole setup. Use a shallow tray with drainage holes sitting inside a solid tray so you can water from the bottom. Wash and sanitize trays between batches.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Bottom-water from the nesting tray; never leave the tray standing in water.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: None for a single cycle.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering reservoirs keep the medium too wet for a dense raw crop and raise the damping-off risk; bottom-water by hand and pour off the excess instead.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: Skip self-watering pots for microgreens. They keep things too wet, which causes mold. Water from the bottom by hand and tip out the extra.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: A shallow flat tray works best: a 1020-style tray or any shallow food-safe container, with about 1 to 2 inches of medium. Depth beyond that wastes mix without helping a crop that is cut in days.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Use a shallow, wide tray, like a standard 1020 tray or any clean food-safe container. About 1 to 2 inches of growing mix is plenty. You do not need anything deep.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Not applicable. Microgreens grow on fresh or sanitized medium each cycle with no soil-borne carryover, so crop rotation does not apply.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Not applicable. You use fresh growing medium and clean trays each time, so there is nothing to rotate.
rotation.note_seasoned: Sanitation between cycles, not rotation, is the disease control for microgreens: compost the spent medium, then wash and sanitize the tray before the next sow.
rotation.note_beginner: Instead of rotating crops, just keep things clean: toss the used medium and wash and sanitize the tray before starting again.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Dense even broadcast on pre-moistened medium; large seeds presoaked.
growth_stages.description_beginner: Scatter seeds thickly on damp medium; soak only big seeds first.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Seeds imbibe and split under a weighted cover at about 74 °F.
growth_stages.description_beginner: Seeds sprout under a covered, warm tray.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Dark period (about 1 to 4 days by type) that stretches stems and evens the stand before light.
growth_stages.description_beginner: A few days in the dark that make the stems stretch evenly.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Uncovered into 18 hours of light at 68 to 72 °F; cotyledons green and the first true leaf may form.
growth_stages.description_beginner: Uncovered into bright light so the leaves turn green.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Single cut at cotyledon to first-true-leaf; eaten fresh.
growth_stages.description_beginner: Snip and eat when the little leaves are open.

notifications.message_seasoned: Check whether the canopy has lifted. It may be time to end blackout and move into light.
notifications.message_beginner: Time to check your tray: if the sprouts are up, uncover it and give it light.

notifications.message_seasoned: Switch from misting to bottom-watering now that the canopy is up, and make sure a fan is running.
notifications.message_beginner: Now that the leaves are up, water from the bottom and keep a fan going.

notifications.message_seasoned: Most mixes are at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage now, so cut and refrigerate promptly.
notifications.message_beginner: Your microgreens are likely ready to snip. Cut them and put them in the fridge.

notifications.message_seasoned: Start your next tray to keep the staggered supply going.
notifications.message_beginner: Start a new tray so you always have microgreens coming.

sow.text_seasoned: Pre-moisten the medium to wrung-sponge feel, then broadcast seed densely and evenly. Presoak only large seeds (pea about 6 hours, sunflower about 12); sow brassicas and small seeds dry. Press seed into contact but do not bury it; buried seed greens poorly and traps moisture against the stems.
sow.text_beginner: Dampen the growing medium so it feels like a wrung-out sponge, then scatter seeds thickly and evenly. Soak only big seeds (pea, sunflower) first; small seeds go on dry. Press the seeds down so they touch the surface, but do not cover them with soil.

germination.text_seasoned: Cover the tray and keep it warm (about 74 °F) and dark. Mist to hold even surface moisture, never soggy. A light weight on the cover keeps seed in firm contact so roots drive down rather than lifting the seed.
germination.text_beginner: Put the cover on and keep the tray warm (around 74 °F) and dark. Mist lightly so the surface stays damp but not wet. A small weight on the cover helps the roots push down.

blackout.text_seasoned: Hold the weighted cover in the dark for roughly the first half of the dark period (about 1 to 4 days by type), then flip the cover off the canopy so it shades without touching. The dark stretch lengthens and evens the stems before greening.
blackout.text_beginner: Keep the covered tray in the dark for a few days (1 to 4, depending on the type). The darkness makes the stems grow taller and more even before you give them light.

light.text_seasoned: Uncover into 18 hours of bright light at 68 to 72 °F and switch from misting to bottom-watering so foliage stays dry. Run a gentle fan; the dense canopy plus high humidity is the damping-off window. Harvest at cotyledon to first true leaf.
light.text_beginner: Uncover the tray into bright light for about 18 hours a day at 68 to 72 °F, and start watering from the bottom so the leaves stay dry. Keep a gentle fan going to prevent mold. Cut when the first little leaves are open.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Yield is measured per tray, not per plant: a well-sown 1020 tray returns roughly 6 to 12 ounces of cut microgreens depending on type and seeding rate.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: You measure microgreens by the tray, not by each plant. A full tray usually gives you a few good handfuls (about 6 to 12 ounces).
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Every tray is a single harvest at peak; continuous supply comes from staggered sowings, not from regrowth.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Each tray gives one harvest at its best. To keep a steady supply, start new trays every few days.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: There is no establishment year; the first tray performs the same as any later tray. Expect to dial in seeding rate and watering over the first few cycles.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: There is no waiting period with microgreens. Your very first tray works just like the rest; you will just get a feel for how much to sow and water after a few tries.
factors_seasoned: seeding density (too sparse wastes the tray; too dense traps moisture and invites mold)
even moisture and the mist-to-bottom-water transition
constant gentle airflow
seed type and freshness
light intensity and the full 18-hour daily duration

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Not applicable. Microgreens are an indoor, light-controlled, seedling-stage crop with no lunar or seasonal timing.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Fuzzy white or gray growth on the medium, stems, or seed; seedlings collapsing at the base
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Fuzzy white or gray mold, or baby plants flopping over at the bottom
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Damping-off and mold from overwatering, a saturated medium, dense sowing, and poor airflow; the number-one microgreen failure
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Too much water plus crowded plants and no air movement, which leads to mold. This is the most common microgreen problem.
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Switch to bottom-watering, pour off standing water, run a gentle fan, thin your seeding rate next time, and sanitize trays between cycles. Do not bury seed at sowing.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Water from the bottom, tip out extra water, keep a small fan going, sow a little less thickly next time, and clean your trays between batches.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_seasoned: Wrung-sponge moisture, constant airflow, dry foliage, and sanitized trays prevent it.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_beginner: Keep the soil just damp, the air moving, the leaves dry, and the trays clean.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Tall, pale, weak stems that fall over
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Long, thin, pale stems that flop
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Too little light, or light introduced too late after blackout
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Not enough light, or leaving the tray covered too long
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Uncover on time and give bright light for the full 18 hours; move closer to the grow light or a brighter window.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Uncover the tray on schedule and give it bright light for about 18 hours a day, closer to the light.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_seasoned: End blackout once the canopy lifts and provide adequate light intensity and duration.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_beginner: Take the cover off as soon as the sprouts are up and give them plenty of light.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Patchy, uneven germination across the tray
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Some spots sprout, others stay bare
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Uneven sowing, uneven moisture, no weighted cover, or old seed
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Seeds spread unevenly, dry spots, no weight on the cover, or old seed
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Sow evenly on pre-moistened medium, use a weighted cover for even seed-to-medium contact, and use fresh microgreen-grade seed.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Spread seeds evenly on damp medium, put a light weight on the cover, and use fresh seed made for microgreens.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_seasoned: Even sow, even moisture, weighted blackout cover, fresh seed.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_beginner: Even seeds, even moisture, a weighted cover, and fresh seed.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Seed hulls clinging to the canopy at harvest (common on sunflower)
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Seed shells stuck on the leaves, especially sunflower
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Hulls not shed during germination; insufficient weight or moisture during blackout
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: The seed shells did not fall off while sprouting
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Use adequate blackout weight and moisture; mist and gently brush or rinse hulls off the canopy before harvest.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Use enough weight and moisture during the dark phase, then gently mist and brush or rinse the shells off before cutting.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_seasoned: Proper weighted blackout and consistent moisture help hulls release.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_beginner: Keep the cover weighted and the tray evenly moist so the shells come off on their own.

indoor_cycle.tip_seasoned: The cycle is sow -> blackout -> light -> harvest. Germinate at about 74 °F under a weighted cover in the dark (1 to 4 days by type), uncover into 18 hours of light at about 68 to 72 °F to green up, then cut at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage. Most types finish in 7 to 21 days; a typical mix runs about 10 to 14.
indoor_cycle.tip_beginner: Microgreens follow the same four steps every time: plant, keep dark, give light, then harvest. Keep the covered tray warm (around 74 °F) and dark for a few days while the seeds sprout, then uncover it into bright light (about 68 to 72 °F) for roughly 18 hours a day until the leaves green up. Most are ready in 1 to 3 weeks.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: For a steady supply, stagger sowings: start a fresh tray every 3 to 5 days rather than one big tray at once. Indoors there is no season, so the cadence is limited only by your tray count and counter space.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: To always have microgreens ready, start a new tray every few days instead of one big batch. Because they grow indoors, you can keep this going all year.
succession_policy.notes: successions and max_successions_per_season are intentionally null: microgreens run continuously year-round indoors, so there is no season length to cap against. The practical limit is tray count and counter space, not climate (window_type: continuous_indoor).

crops.description_seasoned: Microgreens are the young seedlings of vegetables and herbs, harvested at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage roughly 1 to 3 weeks after sowing. They are grown indoors year-round in a short repeatable cycle: a dense even sow on a shallow tray of mix or a fiber mat, a brief dark blackout to drive even germination and stem stretch, then light to green up, then cut. A mix blends several types (fast brassicas, larger soaked seeds, and slower greens) for a range of color and flavor in one tray. Because there is no frost, season, or hardiness zone involved, the same tray grows identically on a windowsill anywhere.
crops.description_beginner: Microgreens are baby vegetable and herb plants that you harvest very young, about 1 to 3 weeks after planting, when they are just a couple of inches tall. You grow them indoors all year on a shallow tray of seed-starting mix or a special growing mat. The steps are always the same: scatter seeds thickly, cover the tray to keep it dark for a few days while they sprout, then move it into the light to green up, then snip and eat. A mix is just several kinds grown together for variety. There is no outdoor season or weather to worry about, so they grow the same way no matter where you live.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Cut at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage, typically 7 to 21 days from sowing depending on the type (the mix runs about 10 to 14). Snip just above the medium with clean scissors; the stand will not regrow, so the tray is a single cut.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Your microgreens are ready when the first little seed-leaves are open and, for many types, the first true leaf is just showing, usually 1 to 2 weeks after sowing. Snip them just above the soil with clean scissors and eat them fresh. They do not grow back, so you start a new tray each time.

crops.name: Sunflower Sprouts
crops.sunlight: bright light: a sunny window or a grow light on about 18 hours a day after the dark phase
crops.water: keep the medium evenly moist; mist through germination, then bottom-water once greened so the leaves stay dry

soil.preferred_texture_seasoned: A fine, moisture-holding soilless medium: seed-starting mix or pre-moistened coconut coir gives an even stand and a clean cut at the base.
soil.preferred_texture_beginner: Use a fine, soil-free growing medium that holds moisture, such as seed-starting mix or coconut coir. It gives an even stand and a clean cut.
soil.tolerated_texture_seasoned: Peat-based mixes and clean fiber mats both work; sunflower's vigorous roots grip a mat well, though a shallow layer of coir or mix holds moisture more forgivingly under the weighted blackout.
soil.tolerated_texture_beginner: Both peat mixes and growing mats work. A shallow layer of coir or mix holds water a little more forgivingly, which helps under the weighted cover.
soil.problematic_texture_seasoned: Garden soil and heavy potting mixes are too coarse and carry pathogen and pest risk for a dense crop eaten raw.
soil.problematic_texture_beginner: Skip garden soil and regular potting mix. They are too coarse and can carry pests and germs that are risky for a crowded crop you eat raw.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Use a light seed-starting mix or coconut coir about 1 to 2 inches deep. Do not use garden soil.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: A clean, fine, moisture-retentive soilless medium about 1 to 2 inches deep gives even germination and a clean cut; coir keeps grit off the harvest.

ph.note_seasoned: pH is not a practical lever for a single short indoor cycle on a soilless medium; seed-starting mix and coir sit in a workable range and need no adjustment.
ph.note_beginner: You do not need to worry about soil pH for sunflower shoots. The mixes and coir sold for growing them are already fine as is.

fertilizer.timing: not applicable
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Sunflower shoots are cut long before they exhaust the seed's own reserves, so no fertilizer is needed for a single cycle on coir or seed-starting mix. Added nutrients mainly raise the risk of algae, off-flavors, and mold in the dense mat.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: You do not need to feed sunflower shoots. The large seed carries plenty of food to get to harvest, and adding fertilizer just invites algae, odd flavors, and mold.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: None.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: None needed.

companions.note_seasoned: Not applicable. Sunflower shoots are grown as a dense single-species indoor tray, so there is no interplanting or companion relationship. If you want variety, grow other shoots in their own trays and combine after cutting.
companions.note_beginner: Not applicable. Sunflower shoots grow as one crop per tray indoors, so there are no companion plants. For a mix, just combine different trays after cutting.

pests.description_seasoned: Small dark flies whose larvae live in persistently wet medium and feed on organic matter and tender roots. They are a symptom of an over-wet tray rather than a primary threat, and the dense sunflower mat holds moisture readily.
pests.description_beginner: Tiny dark flies that show up around constantly damp medium. Their larvae live in the wet mix. They usually mean the tray is staying too wet, which the thick sunflower mat can do easily.
pests.management_seasoned: Let the surface dry between waterings once the canopy is up, bottom-water, and keep airflow moving. Because the cycle is only 8 to 14 days, most trays are cut before gnats build; sanitized trays and fresh medium between cycles break the cycle.
pests.management_beginner: Keep the surface from staying soaking wet, water from the bottom, and keep air moving. Since sunflower shoots are cut so fast, gnats rarely get bad first. Clean trays and fresh medium between batches keep them away.

diseases.name_seasoned: Damping-off and mold in the seed mat
diseases.description_seasoned: Soil-borne fungi (Rhizoctonia, Botrytis, and others) rot seedlings at the base under wet, crowded, still conditions, often alongside fuzzy white or gray mold on the medium, on the dense mat, or on seed hulls that failed to shed. It is the number-one sunflower-shoot failure and is favored by warm, humid, over-wet trays.
diseases.description_beginner: The most common problem. In wet, crowded, stuffy conditions, tiny fungi rot the baby plants at the base, and you often see fuzzy white or gray mold on the surface, on the thick mat, or on leftover seed shells.
diseases.management_seasoned: Prevention is the whole game: wrung-sponge moisture, bottom-watering once greened, constant gentle airflow, a sensible seeding rate, and sanitized trays between cycles. Do not confuse the normal fuzzy white root hairs at germination with mold. There is no rescue spray for a raw cut crop; a badly affected tray is composted and restarted clean.
diseases.management_beginner: You cannot spray this away on a crop you eat raw, so the fix is prevention: keep the mix just damp (not soggy), water from the bottom once the leaves are up, keep a small fan running, do not sow too thickly, and clean your trays between batches. The fuzzy white fuzz right at the roots when they sprout is normal root hairs, not mold. If a tray molds badly, toss it and start over clean.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Mist once or twice daily through germination and blackout to hold even surface moisture; once greened, bottom-water as the tray dries.
watering.frequency_beginner: While the seeds are sprouting under the cover, mist the surface once or twice a day so it stays damp. After you uncover the tray into light, water from the bottom whenever it starts to dry out.
watering.amount_seasoned: Enough to keep the medium at wrung-sponge moisture, never saturated; pour off any standing water after bottom-watering.
watering.amount_beginner: Just enough to keep the medium damp like a wrung-out sponge, never soggy. After bottom-watering, tip out any water left sitting in the tray.
watering.method_seasoned: Mist during germination and blackout; switch to bottom-watering once the canopy is up so the foliage and any clinging hulls stay dry.
watering.method_beginner: Mist the top while the seeds are sprouting, then water from the bottom once the leaves are up so the leaves and any leftover shells stay dry.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Standing water, a sour smell, fuzzy growth on the medium or the seed mat, and collapsed seedlings all signal overwatering and the damping-off that follows it.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Water sitting in the tray, a bad smell, fuzzy mold on the mat, or seedlings flopping over mean it is too wet. Cut back on water and improve airflow.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting, limp cotyledons and a medium that has pulled away from the tray edges indicate the canopy has dried too far between waterings.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Limp, drooping leaves and medium that has shrunk away from the sides mean it got too dry. Water from the bottom right away.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Wet foliage in a dense, still canopy is the main driver of mold and damping-off, so the cycle moves deliberately from misting to bottom-watering and pairs it with constant gentle airflow.
watering.method_note_beginner: Wet leaves packed close together with no air movement is what causes mold. That is why you switch to watering from the bottom once the leaves are up, and keep a gentle fan going.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The blackout-to-light transition is the highest-risk window: the canopy is dense, humidity under the weighted cover is high, and a single overwatering here can seed damping-off across the whole tray.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The riskiest time is right when you uncover the tray and move it into the light. The plants are crowded and damp, so do not overwater, and make sure air is moving.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Do not hold cut sunflower shoots at room temperature; they wilt within hours. Refrigerate immediately after cutting.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Do not leave cut sunflower shoots out on the counter. They go limp fast, so put them in the fridge right after cutting.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerate dry in a vented container lined with a paper towel; sunflower shoots are sturdy and keep about 7 to 14 days, longer than most microgreens. Because they are eaten raw, avoid washing before storage: post-harvest washing is largely ineffective and can raise contamination risk.
storage.fridge_beginner: Keep cut sunflower shoots in the fridge in a container with a paper towel to absorb extra moisture. They are tough and last about 1 to 2 weeks, longer than most microgreens. Do not wash them before storing; wash just before you eat.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Not recommended. Freezing collapses the crisp cells and ruins the signature crunch. Sunflower shoots are a fresh, cut-and-eat crop.
storage.freezer_beginner: Do not freeze sunflower shoots. Freezing turns them mushy and kills the crunch. Eat them fresh.
storage.notes_seasoned: Cut clean and dry: harvest with sanitized scissors into a clean container, keep the foliage dry, and chill promptly. Because they are eaten raw, the same clean-water and sanitized-surface rules that govern growing also govern handling.
storage.notes_beginner: Because you eat sunflower shoots raw, keep everything clean: cut them with clean scissors into a clean, dry container and refrigerate right away.

recommended.name: Black oil sunflower
recommended.note: The standard shoot seed. Thin black hulls, high germination, nutty flavor; presoak about 8 to 12 hours, finishes about 9 to 12 days.

recommended.name: Striped (confection) sunflower
recommended.note: Larger, thicker-hulled seed that sheds its shell less readily; usable but hullier and slower than black oil, so black oil is preferred.

varieties.note_seasoned: Grow from raw black oil sunflower seed sold for sprouting or growing, not roasted, salted, or seasoned snack seed and not treated field seed. Black oil is the standard because the thin hull, high germination, and vigorous shoot make for a reliable, nutty, crunchy stand. Presoak 8 to 12 hours, then germinate under weight; the weighted blackout is what drives even rooting and helps the clinging hulls release. Cut at the plump-cotyledon stage before the first true leaves expand.
varieties.note_beginner: Use raw black oil sunflower seed sold for sprouting or growing, not the roasted or salted kind and not treated bird or field seed. Black oil is the go-to because it sprouts well and makes a nutty, crunchy shoot. Soak the seed 8 to 12 hours, then grow it under a weight, which helps the black shells fall off. Cut when the seed leaves are full and before the first true leaves appear.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Not applicable. Sunflower shoots are never moved outdoors or transplanted; the whole cycle is indoors.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: Not applicable. Sunflower shoots stay indoors from seed to harvest, so there is no hardening off.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Presoak the seed 8 to 12 hours, then broadcast it densely and evenly (about 48 grams, roughly 1.5 ounces, per standard 1020 tray) across pre-moistened medium so the seeds touch but do not stack. Do not bury the seed; press it into contact, then cover and add a flat weight of about 2 to 5 pounds. The weight keeps the seed in firm contact so roots drive down rather than lifting the seed, and it is what helps the black hulls split off the cotyledons instead of riding up on them.
start_method.notes_beginner: Soak the seed 8 to 12 hours first, then scatter it thickly and evenly (about 48 grams, or 1.5 ounces, per standard 1020 tray) over damp growing medium so the seeds touch but are not piled up. Do not bury the seeds, just press them down, then cover the tray and set a flat weight of about 2 to 5 pounds on top. The weight keeps the seeds in good contact and helps the black shells pop off the leaves instead of getting stuck on them.

drainage.saucer_practice_seasoned: Nest the drilled tray inside a solid, hole-free tray. The outer tray catches runoff, lets you bottom-water, and is poured off so the crop never sits in standing water.
drainage.saucer_practice_beginner: Set the tray with holes inside a second solid tray with no holes. The bottom tray lets you water from below and catch extra water, which you then pour out so the roots are not sitting in water.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Seed-starting mix or coconut coir, about 1 to 2 inches deep.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: None needed.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: Seed-starting mix or pre-moistened coir; about 1 to 2 inches deep.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: None; the medium is a substrate, not a nutrient source, for a single cycle.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Water from the bottom by setting the tray in a little water, then pour off what is left.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: No fertilizer needed.

overwintering.approach_seasoned: Not applicable. Sunflower shoots are an indoor year-round cycle crop, harvested in days, with no dormant or overwintered phase.
overwintering.approach_beginner: Not applicable. Sunflower shoots grow indoors all year and are harvested within a couple of weeks, so there is nothing to overwinter.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: The tray is the entire growing system: shallow, drained, nested over a solid tray for bottom-watering, and topped with a weighted second tray for the blackout. Sanitize between cycles; a clean, reused, food-grade tray beats a single-use clamshell for both food safety and consistent results.
container_notes.notes_beginner: For sunflower shoots, the tray is the whole setup. Use a shallow tray with drainage holes sitting inside a solid tray so you can water from the bottom, plus a second tray on top with a weight for the dark phase. Wash and sanitize trays between batches.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Bottom-water from the nesting tray; never leave the tray standing in water.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: None for a single cycle.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering reservoirs keep the dense sunflower mat too wet and raise the damping-off risk; bottom-water by hand and pour off the excess instead.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: Skip self-watering pots for sunflower shoots. They keep the thick mat too wet, which causes mold. Water from the bottom by hand and tip out the extra.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: A shallow flat tray works best: a 1020-style tray or any shallow food-safe container, with about 1 to 2 inches of medium, plus a matching second tray to weight the blackout. Depth beyond that wastes medium without helping a crop cut in days.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Use a shallow, wide tray, like a standard 1020 tray or any clean food-safe container, with about 1 to 2 inches of medium. A second matching tray on top holds the weight during the dark phase. You do not need anything deep.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Not applicable. Sunflower shoots grow on fresh or sanitized medium each cycle with no soil-borne carryover, so crop rotation does not apply.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Not applicable. You use fresh growing medium and clean trays each time, so there is nothing to rotate.
rotation.note_seasoned: Sanitation between cycles, not rotation, is the disease control for sunflower shoots: compost the spent medium and hulls, then wash and sanitize the tray before the next sow.
rotation.note_beginner: Instead of rotating crops, just keep things clean: toss the used medium and shells and wash and sanitize the tray before starting again.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Presoak seed 8 to 12 hours, then broadcast densely and evenly on pre-moistened medium; do not bury.
growth_stages.description_beginner: Soak the seed 8 to 12 hours, then scatter it thickly on damp medium; do not cover with soil.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Seeds imbibe and root under a covered, weighted tray at about 74 °F.
growth_stages.description_beginner: Seeds sprout under a covered, weighted, warm tray.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: About 3 to 4 dark days under 2 to 5 pounds of weight that stretch the stems evenly and help the hulls split off the cotyledons.
growth_stages.description_beginner: About 3 to 4 days in the dark under a weight, which makes the stems stretch evenly and helps the shells come off.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Uncovered into about 18 hours of light at about 72 °F; cotyledons green and plump, and any clinging hulls are rubbed or rinsed off.
growth_stages.description_beginner: Uncovered into bright light so the seed leaves turn green; brush off any leftover shells.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Single cut at the base at the plump-cotyledon stage, before the first true leaves expand; eaten fresh.
growth_stages.description_beginner: Snip at the base when the seed leaves are full and before true leaves form; eat fresh.

notifications.message_seasoned: Check whether the canopy has lifted the weighted tray. It may be time to end blackout and move into light.
notifications.message_beginner: Time to check your tray: if the sprouts have pushed up the cover, uncover it and give it light.

notifications.message_seasoned: Switch from misting to bottom-watering now that the canopy is up, run a fan, and start rubbing off any clinging hulls.
notifications.message_beginner: Now that the leaves are up, water from the bottom, keep a fan going, and gently brush off any stuck shells.

notifications.message_seasoned: Sunflower shoots are near the plump-cotyledon stage now. Cut before the first true leaves expand, then refrigerate promptly.
notifications.message_beginner: Your sunflower shoots are likely ready. Cut them before the first true leaves appear, then put them in the fridge.

notifications.message_seasoned: Presoak seed and start your next tray to keep the staggered supply going.
notifications.message_beginner: Soak seed and start a new tray so you always have sunflower shoots coming.

sow.text_seasoned: Presoak the seed 8 to 12 hours in clean water, then broadcast it densely and evenly (about 48 grams per 1020 tray) on wrung-sponge-moist medium. Press the seed into contact but do not bury it; buried seed greens poorly and traps moisture against the stems. Use raw sprouting-grade or growing-grade black oil seed, never roasted or treated seed.
sow.text_beginner: Soak the seed 8 to 12 hours in clean water, then scatter it thickly and evenly (about 48 grams, or 1.5 ounces, per 1020 tray) over damp medium. Press it down so it touches the surface, but do not cover it with soil. Use raw black oil sunflower seed sold for sprouting or growing, not roasted or treated seed.

germination.text_seasoned: Cover the tray, add a flat 2 to 5 pound weight, and keep it warm (about 74 °F) and dark. Mist to hold even surface moisture, never soggy. The weight keeps seed in firm contact so roots drive down, and it is what pries the clinging black hulls off the cotyledons.
germination.text_beginner: Put the cover on, set a flat weight of about 2 to 5 pounds on top, and keep the tray warm (around 74 °F) and dark. Mist lightly so the surface stays damp but not wet. The weight helps the roots push down and helps the black shells come off the leaves.

blackout.text_seasoned: Hold the weighted cover in the dark for about 3 to 4 days. The dark stretch lengthens and evens the stems, and the pressure keeps working the hulls loose before greening. If the canopy lifts the weight early, that is your cue the stand is ready for light.
blackout.text_beginner: Keep the covered, weighted tray in the dark for about 3 to 4 days. The darkness makes the stems grow taller and even, and the weight keeps loosening the shells. When the sprouts push the weight up, they are ready for light.

light.text_seasoned: Uncover into about 18 hours of bright light at about 72 °F and switch from misting to bottom-watering so foliage stays dry. Run a gentle fan; the dense canopy plus high humidity is the damping-off window. Rub the canopy lightly by hand or rinse to shed remaining hulls, and harvest at the plump-cotyledon stage before the first true leaves expand.
light.text_beginner: Uncover the tray into bright light for about 18 hours a day at about 72 °F, and start watering from the bottom so the leaves stay dry. Keep a gentle fan going to prevent mold. Gently rub or rinse off any stuck shells, and cut when the seed leaves are full, before the first true leaves show.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Yield is measured per tray, not per plant: sunflower shoots are among the heavier-yielding microgreens because the seedlings are large and substantial, so a well-sown 1020 tray returns a generous single cut.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: You measure sunflower shoots by the tray, not by each plant. Because the seedlings are big and hearty, a full tray gives a generous handful, more than most microgreens.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Every tray is a single harvest at peak; continuous supply comes from staggered sowings, not from regrowth.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Each tray gives one harvest at its best. To keep a steady supply, start new trays every few days.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: There is no establishment year; the first tray performs the same as any later tray. Expect to dial in the presoak, seeding rate, and blackout weight over the first few cycles.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: There is no waiting period. Your very first tray works just like the rest; you will just get a feel for the soak, how much to sow, and how much weight to use after a few tries.
factors_seasoned: seeding density (too sparse wastes the tray; too dense traps moisture and invites mold in the mat)
presoak length and even moisture through germination
enough weight during blackout to root evenly and shed hulls
constant gentle airflow once uncovered
cutting at the plump-cotyledon stage before the shoots toughen

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Not applicable. Sunflower shoots are an indoor, light-controlled, seedling-stage crop with no lunar or seasonal timing.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Fuzzy white or gray growth on the medium, the seed mat, or clinging hulls; seedlings collapsing at the base
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Fuzzy white or gray mold on the mat or shells, or baby plants flopping over at the bottom
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Damping-off and mold from overwatering, a saturated medium, dense sowing, and poor airflow; the number-one sunflower-shoot failure. Do not mistake the normal fuzzy white root hairs at germination for mold.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Too much water plus crowded plants and no air movement, which leads to mold. This is the most common problem. Note the fuzzy white fuzz right at the roots when they first sprout is normal, not mold.
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Switch to bottom-watering, pour off standing water, run a gentle fan, thin your seeding rate next time, and sanitize trays between cycles. Do not bury seed at sowing.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Water from the bottom, tip out extra water, keep a small fan going, sow a little less thickly next time, and clean your trays between batches.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_seasoned: Wrung-sponge moisture, constant airflow, dry foliage, and sanitized trays prevent it.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_beginner: Keep the medium just damp, the air moving, the leaves dry, and the trays clean.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Black seed hulls still clinging to the cotyledons at harvest
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Black seed shells stuck on the leaves at cutting time
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Hulls did not shed during germination: too little weight or uneven moisture under the blackout cover, or the tray was uncovered too early.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: The shells did not come off while sprouting, usually from too little weight, dry spots, or uncovering too soon.
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Mist the canopy to soften the hulls, then gently rub by hand or rinse them off; most fall away. A brief dunk-and-swish in a bowl of water at harvest floats the rest off.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Mist the leaves to soften the shells, then gently rub them off with your hand or rinse them; most fall off. Swishing the cut shoots in a bowl of water floats the rest away.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_seasoned: Use adequate blackout weight (about 2 to 5 pounds) and even moisture, and hold blackout the full 3 to 4 days so hulls release on their own.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_beginner: Use enough weight (about 2 to 5 pounds) and even moisture, and keep the tray covered the full 3 to 4 days so the shells come off by themselves.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Tall, pale, weak stems that fall over
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Long, thin, pale stems that flop
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Too little light, or light introduced too late after blackout
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Not enough light, or leaving the tray covered too long
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Uncover on time and give bright light for the full 18 hours; move closer to the grow light or a brighter window.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Uncover the tray on schedule and give it bright light for about 18 hours a day, closer to the light.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_seasoned: End blackout once the canopy lifts the weight and provide adequate light intensity and duration.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_beginner: Take the cover off as soon as the sprouts push up the weight and give them plenty of light.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Tough, fibrous, or bitter shoots
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Chewy or bitter shoots
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Harvested too late, once the first true leaves began to expand and the stems started to fiber up.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Cut too late, after the first true leaves started to grow.
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Cut earlier next cycle, at the plump-cotyledon stage, typically around 9 to 12 days.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Cut earlier next time, when the seed leaves are full and before true leaves show, usually around 9 to 12 days.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_seasoned: Harvest at the plump-cotyledon stage before true leaves expand; sunflower shoots are best young and crisp.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_beginner: Harvest while the seed leaves are full and before true leaves form; they are best young and crunchy.

indoor_cycle.tip_seasoned: The cycle is soak -> sow -> weighted blackout -> light -> harvest. Presoak the seed 8 to 12 hours, germinate at about 74 °F under a covered, weighted (2 to 5 pound) tray in the dark for about 3 to 4 days, uncover into about 18 hours of light at about 72 °F to green up, rub or rinse off the clinging hulls, then cut at the plump-cotyledon stage. Most trays finish in about 8 to 14 days.
indoor_cycle.tip_beginner: Sunflower shoots follow the same steps every time: soak, plant, keep dark under a weight, give light, then harvest. Soak the seed 8 to 12 hours, keep the covered, weighted tray warm (around 74 °F) and dark for about 3 to 4 days, then uncover it into bright light (about 72 °F) for roughly 18 hours a day until the leaves green up. Brush off the leftover black shells, then cut when the seed leaves are full. Most are ready in about 8 to 14 days.

primary.name: Utah State University Extension -- Grow Your Own Microgreens
Penn State Extension -- The ABCs of Microgreens
University of Nevada, Reno Extension -- Microgreens and Produce Safety (PubID 3468)

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: For a steady supply, stagger sowings: presoak and start a fresh tray every 4 to 7 days rather than one big tray at once. Indoors there is no season, so the cadence is limited only by your tray count and counter space.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: To always have sunflower shoots ready, soak and start a new tray every few days instead of one big batch. Because they grow indoors, you can keep this going all year.
succession_policy.notes: successions and max_successions_per_season are intentionally null: sunflower shoots run continuously year-round indoors, so there is no season length to cap against. The practical limit is tray count and counter space, not climate (window_type: continuous_indoor).

Species correct; NO health/nutrition over-claim (flavor/texture only -- 'nutty, crunchy shoot'); hull-removal covered (unshed hulls flagged the #1 failure); sprout-vs-shoot framing correct. Reviewed in the MAIN LOOP (the dispatched review agent returned corrupted output, 0 tool calls). FIXES: fungus-gnat pest -> UC IPM Pest Notes pn7448; damping-off de-named 'Pythium' -> 'Rhizoctonia, Botrytis, and others' + trimmed to psu_microgreens; storage dropped the shelf-life-less usu + added psu; UNR food-safety URL -> live naes.unr.edu/dfi.

open_findings.summary: Clinging-hull behavior and hull-removal method are modeled on the weighted-blackout technique. The weighted (2 to 5 lb) cover is sourced to usu_ext, which documents the weighted top tray; the specific claim that the weight helps the hulls detach and that clinging hulls are rubbed or rinsed off at harvest is grower-documented and is stated by OSU Extension's microgreens publication, which returned HTTP 403 and was not fetchable this session, so it is flagged and anchored to the nearest fetched T1 source (usu_ext).

Harvest stage (cotyledon to just before first true leaf) is cited to usu_ext (9 to 10 day sunflower window) and psu_ext (harvest when cotyledons developed, before/as true leaves emerge). The refinement that shoots turn tough, fibrous, or bitter once true leaves expand is grower-reported and not pinned to a fetched T1 page; flagged as modeled.

The guidance to use raw black oil sunflower seed sold for sprouting or growing (not roasted, salted, striped confection, or treated field/bird seed) is framed as grower practice plus food safety: unr_ext establishes seed as a pathogen source and the need for safe, appropriately sourced seed for a raw crop, but does not name black oil specifically. The black-oil-versus-confection preference is traditional grower knowledge, not a single-page citation.

Seeding rate (~48 g per 1020 tray) and the 9 to 10 day finish are usu_ext's sunflower-specific figures; broader Tier-1 microgreen guidance (psu_microgreens 7 to 21 days, Colorado State 12 to 14 days) runs longer, so days_to_maturity [8,14] with mid 11 and germination_temp_f [68,75] are modeled to span type and condition variation. Commercial growers often sow heavier than 48 g. Tighten the exact rate and window at the variety-delta pass.

crops.description_seasoned: Sunflower sprouts, better called sunflower shoots, are the young seedlings of Helianthus annuus grown indoors from black oil sunflower seed and cut at the plump-cotyledon stage, roughly 8 to 14 days after sowing. The cycle is a short, repeatable indoor one: presoak the seed 8 to 12 hours, sow it densely on a shallow tray of coir or seed-starting mix, germinate under a covered, weighted tray in the dark for about 3 to 4 days, then uncover into light to green up and cut. Two things set sunflower apart from leafier microgreens: the large seed must be soaked, and the black hulls cling to the cotyledons, so growers weight the tray to help them shed and rub or rinse the stragglers off before harvest. The payoff is a nutty, crunchy, substantial shoot that many growers keep for texture alone. Because there is no frost, season, or hardiness zone involved, the same tray grows identically on a windowsill anywhere.
crops.description_beginner: Sunflower sprouts, usually called sunflower shoots, are baby sunflower plants you grow indoors from black oil sunflower seed and cut young, about 8 to 14 days after planting. The steps are always the same: soak the seed for 8 to 12 hours, scatter it thickly on a shallow tray of coconut coir or seed-starting mix, cover the tray with a weight to keep it dark for a few days while it sprouts, then uncover it into bright light to green up, then snip and eat. Sunflower has two quirks compared with leafy microgreens: the big seed needs a soak, and the black shells stick to the leaves, so you press the tray with a weight to help them fall off and rub or rinse off any that remain. In return you get a nutty, crunchy, filling shoot that is a favorite for its texture. There is no outdoor season or weather to worry about, so they grow the same way no matter where you live.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Cut at the plump-cotyledon stage, typically about 9 to 12 days from sowing (the workable window runs 8 to 14), before the first true leaves expand and the stems fiber up. Snip at the base with clean scissors; the stand will not regrow, so the tray is a single cut. Rub or rinse off any clinging black hulls first.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Your sunflower shoots are ready when the seed leaves are full and open and before the first true leaves start to show, usually about 9 to 12 days after planting. Brush or rinse off any leftover black shells, then snip the shoots at the base with clean scissors and eat them fresh. They do not grow back, so start a new tray each time.

crops.name: Pea Shoots
crops.sunlight: bright indirect light or a grow light
crops.water: keep the medium evenly moist; bottom-water once greened and never let the heavy seed mat stay waterlogged

soil.preferred_texture_seasoned: A fine, moisture-holding soilless medium: seed-starting mix, coconut coir, or a hydroponic fiber mat (hemp, jute, or similar). Peas root aggressively, so a slightly deeper mix or a thick mat, about 1 to 2 inches, anchors the heavy seed better than a thin pad.
soil.preferred_texture_beginner: Use a fine, soil-free growing medium that holds moisture well, such as seed-starting mix, coconut coir, or a growing mat made from hemp or jute fiber. Peas send down strong roots, so about 1 to 2 inches of mix, or a thick mat, works better than a thin one.
soil.tolerated_texture_seasoned: Peat-based mixes and inert mats both work; the choice trades water-holding against a clean cut. A denser pea mat sheds water slowly, so lean toward the better-draining option.
soil.tolerated_texture_beginner: Both peat-based mixes and fiber mats work well. Mixes hold more water, while mats stay cleaner at harvest. Because a thick pea planting holds a lot of water, pick whichever drains better for you.
soil.problematic_texture_seasoned: Garden soil and heavy potting mixes are too coarse and carry pathogen and pest risk for a dense, raw, soaked-seed crop.
soil.problematic_texture_beginner: Skip garden soil and regular potting mix. They are too coarse, and they can carry pests and germs that are risky for a crowded crop you eat raw.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Use a light seed-starting mix, coconut coir, or a growing mat made for microgreens, about 1 to 2 inches deep. Do not use garden soil.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: A clean, fine, moisture-retentive soilless medium gives even germination and a clean cut; a slightly deeper bed helps the vigorous pea roots hold the heavy seed in place.

ph.note_seasoned: pH is not a practical lever for a single short indoor cycle on a soilless medium; standard seed-starting mixes and coir sit in a workable range and need no adjustment for pea shoots.
ph.note_beginner: You do not need to worry about soil pH for pea shoots. The mixes and mats sold for microgreens are already fine as is.

fertilizer.timing: not applicable
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Pea shoots are harvested while still living on the large seed's own food reserves, so no fertilizer is needed for a single cycle on an inert medium or seed-starting mix. Added nutrients mainly raise the risk of algae and off-flavors on a dense, wet planting.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: You do not need to feed pea shoots. The big pea seed carries plenty of food to reach harvest, and adding fertilizer just invites algae and odd flavors.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: None.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: None needed.

companions.note_seasoned: Not applicable. Pea shoots are grown as a dense single-type indoor tray, so there is no interplanting or companion relationship. Grow them in their own tray and combine with other greens after harvest.
companions.note_beginner: Not applicable. Pea shoots grow as one crop per tray indoors, so there are no companion plants. If you want a salad mix, just combine them with other greens after cutting.

pests.description_seasoned: Small dark flies whose larvae live in persistently wet medium and feed on organic matter and tender roots. They are the main indoor pea-shoot pest and a symptom of an over-wet tray rather than a primary threat; the heavy soaked-seed mat holds a lot of water and is especially inviting.
pests.description_beginner: Tiny dark flies that show up around constantly damp soil. Their larvae live in the wet mix. They are the main bug you might see indoors, and they usually mean the tray is staying too wet, which is easy to do with a thick, soaked pea planting.
pests.management_seasoned: Let the surface dry between waterings where the crop allows, bottom-water, and keep airflow up. Because the cycle is so short, most trays are harvested before gnats build to a real problem; sanitized trays and fresh medium between cycles break the cycle.
pests.management_beginner: Keep the surface from staying soaking wet, water from the bottom, and keep air moving. Since pea shoots are harvested so fast, gnats rarely get bad before you cut. Clean trays and fresh mix between batches keep them away.

diseases.description_seasoned: Soil-borne fungi (Rhizoctonia, Botrytis, and others) rot seedlings at the soil line under wet, crowded, still conditions, often alongside fuzzy white or gray surface mold. It is the number-one pea-shoot failure, and the dense mat of large soaked seeds is unusually prone: it traps moisture, stays humid, and mats down airflow.
diseases.description_beginner: The most common pea-shoot problem. In wet, crowded, stuffy conditions, tiny fungi rot the baby plants at the base, and you often see fuzzy white or gray mold on the surface. A thick layer of soaked pea seeds holds a lot of water, so it molds easily if the air is still.
