diseases.management_seasoned: Prevention is the whole game: drain the soaked seed well before sowing, keep the medium at wrung-sponge moisture, bottom-water once greened, run constant gentle airflow, sow a sensible (not overwhelming) rate, and sanitize trays between cycles. There is no rescue spray for a raw cut crop; a badly affected tray is composted and restarted clean.
diseases.management_beginner: You cannot spray this away on a crop you eat raw, so the fix is prevention: drain the soaked seed well, keep the mix just damp (not soggy), water from the bottom once the leaves are up, keep a small fan running, do not pile the seed on too thick, and clean your trays between batches. If a tray molds badly, toss it and start over with clean equipment.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Mist once or twice daily through germination and blackout to hold even surface moisture; once greened, bottom-water as the tray dries. The dense pea canopy hides a lot of wet medium, so check that it is drying between waterings.
watering.frequency_beginner: While the seeds are sprouting, lightly mist the surface once or twice a day so it stays damp. After you move the tray into the light, water from the bottom whenever it starts to dry out. Peas grow thick, so make sure the mix is drying a little between waterings.
watering.amount_seasoned: Enough to keep the medium at wrung-sponge moisture, never saturated; pour off any standing water after bottom-watering. The soaked seed already carries a lot of water, so err on the drier side early.
watering.amount_beginner: Just enough to keep the soil damp like a wrung-out sponge, never soggy. After bottom-watering, tip out any water left sitting in the tray. Since the seeds were soaked, go easy on water at first.
watering.method_seasoned: Mist during germination and blackout; switch to bottom-watering once the canopy is up so foliage stays dry.
watering.method_beginner: Mist the top while the seeds are sprouting, then water from the bottom once the leaves are up so the leaves stay dry.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Standing water, a sour smell, fuzzy white growth on the seed mat or stems, and collapsed seedlings all signal overwatering and the damping-off that follows it.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Water sitting in the tray, a bad smell, fuzzy white mold, or seedlings flopping over mean it is too wet. Cut back on water and improve airflow.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting tips, limp tendrils, and a medium that has pulled away from the tray edges indicate the canopy has dried too far between waterings.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Wilting, limp shoots and soil that has shrunk away from the sides mean it got too dry. Water from the bottom right away.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Wet foliage in a dense, still canopy is the main driver of mold and damping-off, and a thick pea planting is the worst offender, so the cycle moves deliberately from misting to bottom-watering and pairs it with constant gentle airflow.
watering.method_note_beginner: Wet leaves packed close together with no air movement is what causes mold, and a thick pea tray is especially prone. That is why you switch to watering from the bottom once the leaves are up, and keep a gentle fan going.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The blackout-to-light transition is the highest-risk window: the canopy is dense, humidity under the cover is high, and a single overwatering of the already-soaked seed mat here can seed damping-off across the whole tray.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The riskiest time is right when you uncover the tray and move it into the light. The plants are crowded and damp, so do not overwater, and make sure air is moving.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Do not hold cut pea shoots at room temperature; they wilt within hours. Refrigerate promptly after cutting.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Do not leave cut pea shoots out on the counter. They go limp fast, so put them in the fridge right after cutting.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerate dry in a vented container lined with a paper towel. Pea shoots are among the sturdier microgreens and hold roughly 1 to 2 weeks when kept cool and dry. Harvest only what you will use soon.
storage.fridge_beginner: Keep cut pea shoots in the fridge in a container with a paper towel to absorb extra moisture. They are one of the tougher microgreens and can last about 1 to 2 weeks.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Not recommended. Freezing collapses the delicate cells and ruins the texture. Pea shoots are a fresh, cut-and-eat crop.
storage.freezer_beginner: Do not freeze pea shoots. Freezing turns them mushy. They are meant to be eaten fresh.
storage.notes_seasoned: Cut clean and dry: harvest with sanitized scissors into a clean container, keep the foliage dry, and chill promptly. Because they are eaten raw, the same clean-water and sanitized-surface rules that govern growing also govern handling, and post-harvest washing is discouraged because it damages tissue and invites spoilage.
storage.notes_beginner: Because you eat pea shoots raw, keep everything clean: cut them with clean scissors into a clean, dry container and refrigerate right away. Do not wash them after cutting; washing bruises the leaves and makes them spoil faster.

recommended.name: Dun (field) pea
recommended.note: The workhorse for shoots: an inexpensive brown field pea, sweet and tender. Presoak about 8 to 12 hours; sow heavily. Much cheaper than shelling-pea seed.

recommended.name: Speckled pea
recommended.note: A speckled field/forage pea, similar in flavor and price to dun pea; vigorous and reliable for a dense tray. Presoak about 8 to 12 hours.

recommended.name: Green field pea
recommended.note: A green-cotyledon field pea (Canadian or spring types); slightly sweeter look, same handling. Presoak about 8 to 12 hours; sow heavily.

recommended.name: Dwarf types (Green Arrow and similar)
recommended.note: Standard shelling and dwarf garden peas grow fine as shoots but cost more per pound; use them if that is the seed you have. Presoak about 8 to 12 hours.

recommended.name: Snow / snap pea types
recommended.note: Edible-pod varieties also make good, sweet shoots; more expensive as microgreen seed. Presoak about 8 to 12 hours.

varieties.note_seasoned: For pea shoots, buy inexpensive whole (not split) dun, speckled, or green field pea seed rather than pricey shelling-pea seed; all taste sweet and grow the same way. Whatever the type, the two rules are: presoak the large seed about 8 to 12 hours (overnight) before sowing, and use fresh, untreated, food-grade seed. Always confirm seed is untreated and sold for sprouting or food, since some agricultural pea seed is treated with fungicide and is not safe to eat.
varieties.note_beginner: The cheapest and easiest choice for pea shoots is whole (not split) dried field peas, sold as dun, speckled, or green peas; they taste sweet and grow just like the pricier garden-pea seed. Two things matter most: soak the seeds for about 8 to 12 hours (overnight) before planting, and use fresh seed sold for sprouting or eating. Do not use farm seed treated with fungicide, which is colored and not safe to eat.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Not applicable. Pea shoots are never moved outdoors or transplanted; the whole cycle is indoors.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: Not applicable. Pea shoots stay indoors from seed to harvest, so there is no hardening off.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Presoak the large pea seed about 8 to 12 hours (overnight), rinsing once or twice to wash and aerate it; some guides use as little as 6 hours. Drain it well, then sow densely and evenly across pre-moistened medium, roughly 150 grams per standard 1020 tray, a heavy rate that reflects the big seed. Do not bury the seed; press it into firm contact, then cover for blackout with a weighted lid, since the large pea seed needs weight to stay put and root down.
start_method.notes_beginner: Soak the peas in water for about 8 to 12 hours (overnight) before planting, rinsing them once or twice. Drain them, then scatter them thickly and evenly over damp growing medium, close to a full single layer. Do not bury the seeds, just press them down so they touch the surface, then cover the tray, with a little weight on the lid, to keep them dark for a few days.

drainage.saucer_practice_seasoned: Nest the drilled tray inside a solid, hole-free tray. The outer tray catches runoff, lets you bottom-water, and is poured off so the crop never sits in standing water.
drainage.saucer_practice_beginner: Set the tray with holes inside a second solid tray with no holes. The bottom tray lets you water from below and catch extra water, which you then pour out so the roots are not sitting in water.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Seed-starting mix, coconut coir, or a microgreen growing mat.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: None needed.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: Seed-starting mix, coir, or an inert fiber mat; about 1 to 2 inches deep to anchor the heavy seed.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: None; the medium is a substrate, not a nutrient source, for a single cycle.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Water from the bottom by setting the tray in a little water, then pour off what is left.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: No fertilizer needed.

overwintering.approach_seasoned: Not applicable. Pea shoots are an indoor year-round cycle crop, harvested in days, with no dormant or overwintered phase.
overwintering.approach_beginner: Not applicable. Pea shoots grow indoors all year and are harvested within a couple of weeks, so there is nothing to overwinter.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: The tray is the entire growing system: shallow, drained, nested over a solid tray for bottom-watering, sanitized between cycles. A clean, reused, food-grade tray beats a single-use clamshell for both food safety and consistent results. Give peas a touch more depth than tiny brassica seeds so the roots can anchor.
container_notes.notes_beginner: For pea shoots, the tray is the whole setup. Use a shallow tray with drainage holes sitting inside a solid tray so you can water from the bottom, with about 1 to 2 inches of mix. Wash and sanitize trays between batches.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Bottom-water from the nesting tray; never leave the tray standing in water.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: None for a single cycle.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering reservoirs keep the medium too wet for a dense raw crop and raise the damping-off risk, which is already high for a thick pea mat; bottom-water by hand and pour off the excess instead.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: Skip self-watering pots for pea shoots. They keep things too wet, which causes mold, and a thick pea tray is already prone to it. Water from the bottom by hand and tip out the extra.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: A shallow flat tray works best: a 1020-style tray or any shallow food-safe container, with about 1 to 2 inches of medium. Depth beyond that wastes mix without helping a crop that is cut in days.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Use a shallow, wide tray, like a standard 1020 tray or any clean food-safe container. About 1 to 2 inches of growing mix is plenty. You do not need anything deep.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Not applicable. Pea shoots grow on fresh or sanitized medium each cycle with no soil-borne carryover, so crop rotation does not apply.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Not applicable. You use fresh growing medium and clean trays each time, so there is nothing to rotate.
rotation.note_seasoned: Sanitation between cycles, not rotation, is the disease control for pea shoots: compost the spent seed mat, then wash and sanitize the tray before the next sow.
rotation.note_beginner: Instead of rotating crops, just keep things clean: toss the used seed mat and wash and sanitize the tray before starting again.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Soak the large seed about 8 to 12 hours, drain, then broadcast densely on pre-moistened medium.
growth_stages.description_beginner: Soak the peas overnight, drain, then scatter them thickly on damp medium.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Seeds imbibe and split under a weighted cover at about 70 °F.
growth_stages.description_beginner: Seeds sprout under a covered, warm tray.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Dark period of about 3 days that stretches the stems and evens the stand before light.
growth_stages.description_beginner: About three days in the dark that make the shoots stretch evenly.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Uncovered into 18 hours of light at 68 to 72 °F; the shoots green and put out tendrils.
growth_stages.description_beginner: Uncovered into bright light so the shoots turn green.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Cut at about 4 to 6 inches, when tendrils and the first true leaves show; eaten fresh.
growth_stages.description_beginner: Snip and eat when the shoots are a few inches tall with little curling tendrils.

notifications.message_seasoned: Start soaking your pea seed tonight, about 8 to 12 hours before you plan to sow.
notifications.message_beginner: Soak your peas in water tonight, about 8 to 12 hours before planting tomorrow.

notifications.message_seasoned: Check whether the canopy has lifted. It may be time to end blackout and move into light.
notifications.message_beginner: Time to check your tray: if the shoots are up, uncover it and give it light.

notifications.message_seasoned: Switch from misting to bottom-watering now that the canopy is up, and make sure a fan is running.
notifications.message_beginner: Now that the shoots are up, water from the bottom and keep a fan going.

notifications.message_seasoned: Pea shoots are usually at 4 to 6 inches with tendrils now, so cut and refrigerate promptly.
notifications.message_beginner: Your pea shoots are likely ready to snip. Cut them and put them in the fridge.

notifications.message_seasoned: Start soaking seed for your next tray to keep the staggered supply going.
notifications.message_beginner: Soak seed for a new tray so you always have pea shoots coming.

sow.text_seasoned: Presoak the large pea seed about 8 to 12 hours (overnight), rinsing once or twice to wash and aerate it, then drain it well. Broadcast densely on pre-moistened medium (about 150 grams per 1020 tray). Press the seed into contact but do not bury it; buried seed greens poorly and traps moisture against the stems.
sow.text_beginner: Soak the peas in water for about 8 to 12 hours (overnight), rinse them once or twice, then drain. Scatter them thickly and evenly over damp growing medium, close to a full single layer. Press the seeds down so they touch the surface, but do not cover them with soil.

germination.text_seasoned: Cover the tray and keep it warm (about 70 °F) and dark. Mist to hold even surface moisture, never soggy, and remember the soaked seed is already water-laden. A weight on the cover keeps the large seed in firm contact so roots drive down rather than lifting the seed.
germination.text_beginner: Put the cover on and keep the tray warm (around 70 °F) and dark. Mist lightly so the surface stays damp but not wet. A weight on the cover helps the big pea seeds stay put and push their roots down.

blackout.text_seasoned: Hold the weighted cover in the dark for about 3 days, then flip the cover off the canopy so it shades without touching. The dark stretch lengthens and evens the stems before greening; peas need the weight longer than small seeds to shed their seed coats and stand up.
blackout.text_beginner: Keep the covered tray in the dark for about three days. The darkness makes the shoots grow taller and more even before you give them light. Peas do better with a weight on top for that time.

light.text_seasoned: Uncover into about 18 hours of bright light at 68 to 72 °F and switch from misting to bottom-watering so foliage stays dry. Run a gentle fan; the dense canopy plus high humidity is the damping-off window, and a thick pea mat is the worst offender. Harvest at about 4 to 6 inches when tendrils and the first true leaves show.
light.text_beginner: Uncover the tray into bright light for about 18 hours a day at 68 to 72 °F, and start watering from the bottom so the leaves stay dry. Keep a gentle fan going to prevent mold. Cut when the shoots are about 4 to 6 inches tall with little curling tendrils.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Yield is measured per tray, not per plant: a well-sown 1020 tray of pea shoots returns roughly 8 to 16 ounces, on the higher end for microgreens thanks to the large seed and taller shoots.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: You measure pea shoots by the tray, not by each plant. A full tray usually gives you several good handfuls (roughly 8 to 16 ounces), more than most tiny microgreens.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Treat each tray as a single main harvest at peak. Pea shoots can sometimes push a lighter second cut, but continuous supply comes from staggered sowings, not from regrowth.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Plan on one main harvest per tray. Peas may give a smaller second cutting, but the reliable way to keep a steady supply is to start new trays every few days.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: There is no establishment year; the first tray performs the same as any later tray. Expect to dial in soak time, drainage, and seeding rate over the first few cycles.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: There is no waiting period with pea shoots. Your very first tray works just like the rest; you will just get a feel for soaking, watering, and how much to sow after a few tries.
factors_seasoned: seed type and freshness (inexpensive whole field peas work as well as garden-pea seed)
a full 8 to 12 hour presoak and good drainage of the soaked seed
seeding density (heavy, but not so piled that airflow is choked)
constant gentle airflow to prevent mold on the dense mat
light intensity and the full 18-hour daily duration

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Not applicable. Pea shoots are an indoor, light-controlled, seedling-stage crop with no lunar or seasonal timing.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Fuzzy white or gray growth on the seed mat, stems, or seed; seedlings collapsing at the base
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Fuzzy white or gray mold, or baby plants flopping over at the bottom
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Damping-off and mold from overwatering, a saturated mat of soaked seed, dense sowing, and poor airflow; the number-one pea-shoot failure
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Too much water plus crowded seed and no air movement, which leads to mold. This is the most common pea-shoot problem.
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Drain the soaked seed better next time, switch to bottom-watering, pour off standing water, run a gentle fan, and sanitize trays between cycles. Do not pile the seed on or bury it at sowing.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Next time drain the soaked seed well, water from the bottom, tip out extra water, keep a small fan going, and clean your trays between batches. Do not pile the seeds on too thick.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_seasoned: Well-drained soaked seed, wrung-sponge moisture, constant airflow, dry foliage, and sanitized trays prevent it.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_beginner: Drain the soaked seed, keep the soil just damp, the air moving, the leaves dry, and the trays clean.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Tall, pale, weak stems that fall over
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Long, thin, pale stems that flop
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Too little light, or light introduced too late after blackout
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Not enough light, or leaving the tray covered too long
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Uncover on time and give bright light for about 18 hours; move closer to the grow light or a brighter window.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Uncover the tray on schedule and give it bright light for about 18 hours a day, closer to the light.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_seasoned: End blackout once the canopy lifts and provide adequate light intensity and duration.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_beginner: Take the cover off as soon as the shoots are up and give them plenty of light.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Many hard seeds that never sprout, or very uneven germination
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Lots of peas that just sit there and never sprout
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Too short a soak, old or split seed, uneven moisture, or no weighted cover
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: The peas were not soaked long enough, or the seed was old or split
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Give a full 8 to 12 hour presoak, use fresh whole (not split) seed, sow on evenly pre-moistened medium, and use a weighted cover for even seed-to-medium contact.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Soak the peas the full 8 to 12 hours, use fresh whole peas (not split ones), spread them on evenly damp medium, and put a weight on the cover.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_seasoned: Full presoak, fresh whole seed, even moisture, and a weighted blackout cover.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_beginner: A full soak, fresh whole peas, even moisture, and a weighted cover.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Shoots turn tough, stringy, or bitter
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: The shoots get chewy or bitter instead of sweet
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Harvested too late; past about 6 inches and into fibrous stems, the sweetness fades and texture toughens
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Left too long before cutting. Older, taller pea shoots get stringy and lose their sweet flavor.
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Cut at about 4 to 6 inches while tender; if a tray is overdue, harvest the tender tips and compost the tough lower stems.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Cut them at about 4 to 6 inches while they are tender. If a tray got away from you, just snip the soft tops.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_seasoned: Harvest in the 4 to 6 inch window; stagger sowings so no tray sits past its prime.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_beginner: Cut in the 4 to 6 inch window, and start trays a few days apart so none get overgrown.

indoor_cycle.tip_seasoned: The cycle is presoak, sow, blackout, light, harvest. Soak the large seed about 8 to 12 hours, then germinate at about 70 °F under a weighted cover in the dark for roughly 3 days, uncover into about 18 hours of light at 68 to 72 °F to green up, then cut at about 4 to 6 inches when tendrils and the first true leaves show. Most trays finish in 10 to 16 days, a bit later than small brassica microgreens; a shorter cotyledon-stage cut can be taken nearer 8 to 10 days. Cutting above the lowest node can yield a lighter, coarser second flush a week or so later.
indoor_cycle.tip_beginner: Pea shoots follow five steps: soak, plant, keep dark, give light, then harvest. Soak the peas overnight (about 8 to 12 hours), keep the covered tray warm (around 70 °F) and dark for about three days while they sprout, then uncover into bright light (about 68 to 72 °F) for roughly 18 hours a day until they green up. They are usually ready in 10 to 16 days, a little later than tiny microgreens like radish. If you cut above the lowest little leaf, you may get a smaller second cutting about a week later.

primary.name: Utah State University Extension - Grow Your Own Microgreens
Penn State Extension - A Step-By-Step Guide for Growing Microgreens at Home
University of Nevada, Reno Extension - Microgreens and Produce Safety (PubID 3468)

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: For a steady supply, stagger sowings: start a fresh tray every 5 to 7 days rather than one big tray at once. Indoors there is no season, so the cadence is limited only by your tray count and counter space. Remember to start the presoak the night before each sow.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: To always have pea shoots ready, start a new tray every week or so instead of one big batch. Because they grow indoors, you can keep this going all year. Just remember to soak the next batch of peas the night before you plant.
succession_policy.notes: successions and max_successions_per_season are intentionally null: pea shoots run continuously year-round indoors, so there is no season length to cap against. The practical limit is tray count and counter space, not climate (window_type: continuous_indoor).

verification_status.verification_log_ref: Batch-2 Wave-5 cert (2026-07-06, Trevor-ruled). microgreen (pea shoots). SPECIES SAFETY VERIFIED: garden pea Pisum sativum throughout (Fabaceae), NO confusion with the toxic ornamental sweet pea (Lathyrus) -- the 'sweet pea flavor' wording is USU's own Table-1 flavor descriptor for pea microgreens, not the ornamental. NUTRITION/HEALTH over-claim CLEAN. Growing claims verified on USU (6-hour presoak; harvest at first true leaves ~8-10d cotyledon / 10-16d for the 4-6in shoot cut); HONEST on regrowth (yield comes from staggered sowings, NOT cut-and-come-again). Reviewed in the MAIN LOOP (the dispatched agent returned corrupted output, 0 tool calls; species + nutrition + growing claims re-verified directly). FIXES: fungus-gnat pest -> UC IPM pn7448; damping-off de-named 'Pythium' -> 'Rhizoctonia, Botrytis, and others' + trimmed to psu_microgreens; storage dropped usu + added psu; UNR URL updated.

open_findings.summary: Cut-and-come-again second harvest is hedged and modeled. Catalog T1 microgreen sources (usu_ext, psu_microgreens) treat a tray as a single cut, and other extension microgreen guidance states microgreens do not regrow; the pea exception (branching from stem nodes for a lighter, coarser second flush) rests on pea-shoot field-culture sources (WSU PNW567 by Carol Miles; U Delaware Weekly Crop Update) that were PDF-unreadable or not in the source catalog this session. Presented as a hedged possibility, not a promise; cited to the nearest catalog anchor. Confirm at the variety/source-truth pass.

Variety/type list (dun, speckled, green field pea, dwarf/Green Arrow, snow/snap) and the 'whole field peas are cheaper than shelling-pea seed' guidance are modeled from general pea-shoot horticulture (WSU / U Delaware pea-shoot materials, PDF-unreadable/uncatalogued this session) rather than a readable catalog T1 microgreen page that names pea shoot cultivars. Cited to the nearest anchor usu_ext (which lists 'Pea' with sweet-pea flavor). The untreated-seed food-safety caveat is standard and corroborated by unr_ext. Confirm cultivar specifics at the variety pass.

Judgment calls. Presoak authored as 8 to 12 hours (psu_ext step-by-step) while usu_ext Table 1 lists 6 hours; the longer overnight soak is the safer default for the large seed and both are cited. days_to_maturity 10 to 16 (and indoor_cycle days_to_harvest 10 to 16) reflect the taller pea SHOOT vs usu_ext's 8 to 10 for a shorter cotyledon-stage pea microgreen; the upper bound 16 and harvest height 4 to 6 inches (psu_ext observed ~4 to 5) are modeled. germination_temp_f 65 to 75 is modeled as comfortable room temperature (usu_ext germinates at ~74 F) reflecting the cool-season tolerance of peas. harvest_urgency set to medium (pea shoots store and hold better than tender brassica microgreens).

crops.description_seasoned: Pea shoots are the young seedlings of the garden pea (Pisum sativum), grown indoors as a tall, sweet microgreen and cut at about 4 to 6 inches when the tendrils and first true leaves appear, roughly 10 to 16 days after sowing. The large seed is the whole story: it must be presoaked about 8 to 12 hours before a heavy, dense sow, it carries enough food to reach harvest without fertilizer, and its bulk gives shoots that are taller, sweeter, and sturdier than tiny brassica microgreens. The cycle is presoak, then a dense sow on a shallow tray of mix or a fiber mat, a short dark blackout under a weight to even the stand and shed seed coats, then light to green up, then cut. Because there is no frost, season, or hardiness zone involved, the same tray grows identically on a windowsill anywhere.
crops.description_beginner: Pea shoots are baby pea plants that you grow indoors and harvest young, about 10 to 16 days after planting, when they are a few inches tall with curling tendrils. They taste sweet and fresh, like a snap pea, and are more tender and a little taller than tiny microgreens like radish. The big pea seed makes them easy but has one special step: you soak the peas overnight (about 8 to 12 hours) before planting them thickly on a shallow tray of seed-starting mix or a growing mat. Then you cover the tray to keep it dark for a few days while they sprout, move it into the light to green up, and snip them off. There is no outdoor season or weather to worry about, so they grow the same way no matter where you live.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Cut at about 4 to 6 inches, when the tendrils and first true leaves have appeared, typically 10 to 16 days from sowing (a shorter cotyledon-stage cut can be taken nearer 8 to 10 days). Snip just above the medium with clean scissors. Cutting instead just above the lowest node or leaf can leave the plant to push a lighter, coarser second flush about a week later, but the main tray is best treated as a single cut.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Your pea shoots are ready when they are about 4 to 6 inches tall with little curling tendrils and the first true leaves, usually 10 to 16 days after planting. Snip them just above the soil with clean scissors and eat them fresh. If you instead cut a bit higher, above the lowest little leaf, the plants may grow a smaller second batch about a week later, though it will not be as nice as the first.

crops.name: Celery

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Celery is a marsh plant at heart, so it wants soil that stays damp and rich. Give it a loam or silt loam with lots of compost or rotted manure mixed in, the kind of soil that holds water without turning to swamp. Light, sandy soil is the hardest place to grow celery, because it dries out fast and celery hates drying out: that is what gives you stringy, bitter stalks. If your soil is sandy, dig in plenty of compost first, or grow celery in a raised bed or a big container with a moisture-holding mix. Celery is a heavy feeder, so a rich soil to start with makes the whole season easier.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Celery descends from a wild marshland plant and performs best in deep, rich, moisture-retentive soil high in organic matter, classically the muck and peat soils of commercial districts but in the home garden a well-amended loam or silt loam. Work in generous compost or well-rotted manure before planting, both to feed this heavy feeder and to hold the steady moisture celery demands. The texture priority is the opposite of its relative the carrot: where carrot wants a light, open, stone-free channel, celery wants water-holding capacity, since brief drying is what turns the petioles stringy, pithy, and bitter. Light sandy soils are the most difficult, drying too fast for celery's shallow roots; amend them heavily or switch to a raised bed. Reasonable drainage still matters, because waterlogged ground invites the pink rot and damping-off that plague this crop.

ph.note_beginner: Soil pH measures how acidic or alkaline your soil is, on a scale from 1 to 14 where 7 is neutral. Celery likes it slightly acidic to near neutral, roughly 6.0 to 6.8. It is not extremely fussy, but very acidic soil can lock up calcium, and celery already struggles with calcium, that is what causes the black, dead centers called blackheart. A cheap soil test from your local extension office tells you your number and whether to add lime before planting.
ph.note_seasoned: Celery grows best in slightly acidic to near neutral soil, roughly pH 6.0 to 6.8, and tolerates a band of about 5.8 to 7.0. Holding pH toward the upper end of that range matters more for celery than for most vegetables, because adequate calcium availability is central to preventing blackheart (the calcium-related death of the growing tip), and strongly acidic soil reduces calcium uptake. A standard extension soil test removes the guesswork and tells you whether lime is warranted before transplanting.

fertilizer.timing: Mix compost and a balanced fertilizer into the bed before transplanting, then side-dress with nitrogen every 3 to 4 weeks through the season.
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Celery is a heavy feeder with a high nitrogen demand, the opposite of its low-nitrogen relative the carrot. Work plenty of compost or rotted manure plus a balanced fertilizer into the bed before transplanting, then side-dress with nitrogen every 3 to 4 weeks through the season, on the order of a quarter cup of a high-nitrogen source such as 21-0-0 per 10 feet of row each application. Steady feeding and steady water together drive the fast, uninterrupted growth that produces tender stalks; any check from hunger or drought shows up as tough, stringy, bitter petioles.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Celery is a hungry plant, the opposite of carrots. Mix lots of compost and a balanced fertilizer into the soil before you plant, then feed it again with a nitrogen fertilizer about every 3 to 4 weeks all season. The goal is to keep celery growing fast and without a pause. If it runs short of food or water, even for a while, the stalks turn tough, stringy, and bitter instead of crisp.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: Celery is nitrogen-hungry and benefits from rich, steadily fed soil. Start with a balanced blend such as 10-10-10 worked in with compost at transplanting, then carry the crop with regular nitrogen side-dressings. Unlike root crops, celery will not fork or run to leaf from generous feeding: with celery the risk runs the other way, since underfeeding is a direct cause of stringy, bitter stalks. Keep calcium adequate as well, because calcium shortage, often triggered by uneven watering rather than truly low soil calcium, causes blackheart.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: The three numbers on a fertilizer bag are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium (N-P-K). Celery wants plenty of all three to start, like a 10-10-10, plus extra nitrogen (the first number) fed through the season. Mix compost in too. With celery you cannot easily overfeed the way you can with carrots: too little food is the bigger danger, because hungry celery grows tough and bitter.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: Work a balanced fertilizer such as 10-10-10 into the bed at transplanting along with generous compost, then side-dress nitrogen every 3 to 4 weeks, about a quarter cup of 21-0-0 per 10 feet of row each time (Utah State University Extension). Celery removes a lot of nitrogen over its long season, so err toward steady, repeated feeding rather than one heavy dose.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Mix a balanced vegetable fertilizer into the bed when you plant, with lots of compost, then feed again with a little nitrogen fertilizer every 3 to 4 weeks. A small handful of a high-nitrogen feed per few feet of row each time is plenty. Steady small feedings beat one big one.

companions.note_beginner: Celery is an easygoing neighbor that fits well among cabbage-family crops, bush beans, and onions or leeks, which many gardeners pair with it by tradition. The clearest plants to keep apart from celery are its own carrot-family relatives, carrot, parsnip, parsley, dill, and fennel, because they share the same pests and diseases. As always, treat most companion-planting charts with some skepticism, since many of their claims have not held up when tested.
companions.note_seasoned: Celery slots easily into a mixed cool-season bed. The traditional pairings are with brassicas (cabbage, broccoli), bush beans, and alliums (onion, leek), all long-standing companion-planting lore rather than tested relationships, useful but not guaranteed. The best-grounded avoids are celery's own family, the Apiaceae: carrot, parsnip, parsley, dill, and fennel share its pest and disease spectrum (carrot rust fly, leaf blights, aster yellows), so clustering them concentrates that pressure. As with carrot, most companion-chart claims for celery rest on tradition rather than extension trials, so weight them accordingly.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Cabbage-family crops (cabbage, broccoli)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Celery and cabbage-family plants are a classic old-time pairing. They like the same cool weather and rich, moist soil, so they make easy bed-mates. This is traditional garden wisdom rather than a tested rule, but it is harmless and convenient.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Celery-with-brassicas is a long-standing companion-planting tradition. Both are heavy-feeding, moisture-loving cool-season crops with compatible culture, so they co-exist well, but there is no measured pest or yield effect in extension trials. Traditional/medium: widely taught, mechanistically harmless, not proven.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Celery and the cabbage family share a culture, cool weather, rich soil, and steady moisture, so they make compatible neighbors, and the pairing is a fixture of traditional companion-planting guides. Treat the benefit as cultural compatibility and efficient bed use rather than a measured pest effect, since the relationship has not been demonstrated in controlled trials.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Bush beans
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Bush beans are a traditional celery companion. Beans add some nitrogen to the soil, which suits hungry celery, and the two do not compete for the same space. A popular pairing, though more tradition than proven fact.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Beans-with-celery is traditional companion lore resting on the general legume nitrogen-contribution rationale. The nitrogen benefit to a neighboring crop in one season is modest and not celery-specific in any trial. Traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: The bean-celery pairing rests on the familiar legume rationale: beans fix nitrogen and are thought to share some with neighbors, which suits a nitrogen-hungry crop like celery. The in-season transfer is modest and not celery-specific in any controlled work, so treat this as traditional companion lore rather than a measured boost.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Onions and leeks
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Onions, leeks, and other alliums are a traditional companion for celery, valued for their strong scent that some gardeners believe helps confuse pests. The evidence is thin, but they share a bed without trouble.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Allium-with-celery is traditional aromatic-confusion lore, the same family of claims that is mechanistically plausible for carrot rust fly but not demonstrated for celery. Traditional/low: commonly repeated, evidence thin.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Alliums are a traditional aromatic companion, credited with masking the scent of neighboring crops from pests. The mechanism is the same one cited for the carrot-onion pairing and is plausible against the shared carrot rust fly, but it is not demonstrated for celery specifically. A harmless, space-sharing pairing best treated as tradition.

good_seasoned.name: Cabbage-family crops (cabbage, broccoli)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Brassicas and celery share cool-season timing, rich soil, and high moisture needs, so they co-exist well in a mixed bed. A traditional pairing valued for cultural compatibility rather than a measured pest or yield effect.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Long-standing companion tradition; compatible culture, no extension-trial pest/yield effect.

good_seasoned.name: Bush beans
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Legumes are traditionally paired with heavy feeders like celery for their nitrogen contribution. The in-season benefit is modest and not celery-specific, so this is companion tradition rather than a documented effect.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Legume nitrogen-sharing rationale, traditional, not celery-specific in trials.

good_seasoned.name: Onions and leeks
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Alliums are a traditional aromatic companion credited with masking neighboring crops from pests; plausible against the shared carrot rust fly but unproven for celery. Treat as tradition.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Aromatic-confusion lore, thin evidence, not demonstrated for celery.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Carrots, parsnips, and parsley
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: These are all celery's close cousins in the carrot family, and they catch the same pests and diseases, like the carrot rust fly and leaf blights. Growing them right next to celery lets those problems build up, so spread them around the garden instead.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Shared-Apiaceae pest and disease overlap (carrot rust fly, leaf blights, aster yellows) is documented at the family level; the co-planting caution is a sound inference plus standard rotation logic, consistently repeated. Traditional/medium.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Carrot, parsnip, and parsley are fellow Apiaceae and share celery's pests and diseases, including carrot rust fly, the leaf blights, and aster yellows. Clustering the family concentrates that pressure, the same reason extension sources advise rotating related crops apart. Give each its own area rather than running them side by side.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Dill and fennel
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Dill and fennel are also carrot-family relatives and share celery's pests. Fennel in particular is a poor neighbor to most vegetables, so keep both well away from your celery.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Same Apiaceae shared-pest logic as carrot/parsley, plus fennel's near-universal bad-companion tradition (allelopathy reputation). Traditional/medium, consistent with the carrot record's fennel ruling.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Dill and fennel are carrot-family relatives that share celery's pest spectrum, and fennel additionally carries a near-universal reputation as a poor companion to most garden crops, attributed to root compounds that suppress neighbors. The lab work behind fennel's allelopathy targets weeds rather than celery, but between the shared pests and the tradition, the simple handling is to keep both well away from the celery bed.

bad_seasoned.name: Carrots, parsnips, and parsley
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Fellow Apiaceae that share celery's pests and diseases (carrot rust fly, leaf blights, aster yellows); clustering the family sustains a shared pest and disease bridge, the reason extension guidance rotates related crops apart.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Family-level shared pest/disease overlap, documented; co-planting caution is sound rotation inference.

bad_seasoned.name: Fennel
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: An Apiaceae relative with the same pest spectrum and a long-standing reputation for releasing compounds that inhibit nearby plants. Traditional lore treats fennel as antagonistic to most crops; for celery the concern is shared pests plus that reputation.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Fennel's broad antagonism is companion-planting tradition with limited controlled support; shared-family pest overlap is the plausible mechanism.

pests.name: Celery leafminer
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Pale, winding, snakelike tunnels (mines) trace through the leaf tissue, and heavier infestations leave leaves blotched, blistered, and partly dried. The damage is the larvae feeding between the upper and lower leaf surfaces; pinprick stippling on the foliage marks where adult females punctured leaves to feed and lay eggs. Light mining is cosmetic, but a heavy attack reduces the plant's vigor and the eating quality of the leafy tops.
pests.symptoms_beginner: You will see pale, squiggly trails winding through the leaves, like someone drew on them with a white pen. Those are tunnels made by tiny maggots feeding inside the leaf. Badly hit leaves look blotchy and dried out. A little is just cosmetic, but a lot weakens the plant.
pests.cause_seasoned: Larvae of leafminer flies in the genus Liriomyza (notably Liriomyza trifolii and L. huidobrensis), small flies whose maggots mine within the leaf. Populations build in warm weather and can run through several overlapping generations; the pest also attacks many other vegetables and ornamentals, and natural enemies usually hold it in check unless broad-spectrum insecticides flare it up.
pests.cause_beginner: The young (larvae) of small leafminer flies (Liriomyza). The adult fly lays eggs in the leaf, and the maggots that hatch tunnel around inside it. They like warm weather and attack lots of different plants. Tiny wasps usually keep them down on their own, unless heavy spraying kills off those helpers.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Pick off and destroy heavily mined leaves to remove the larvae inside, and protect the natural enemies (parasitic wasps) that normally control leafminers by avoiding broad-spectrum insecticides, which commonly make leafminer outbreaks worse. Floating row cover over young plants excludes the egg-laying adults.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick off and throw away the worst-tunneled leaves, since the maggots are inside them. Avoid spraying broad insecticides, which kill the tiny helpful wasps that normally keep leafminers in check and can make the problem worse. A row cover over young plants keeps the flies off.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Cover young plants with floating row cover to exclude egg-laying adults, keep plants vigorous, and rely on conservation of natural enemies rather than spraying. Remove crop debris that can harbor pupae, and scout the leaves for the first stippling and mines so light infestations can be hand-removed before they build.
pests.prevention_beginner: Lay a light row cover over young celery to keep the flies from laying eggs, keep the plants growing strongly, and let the natural helper insects do their job by not spraying. Check the leaves often, and pull off the first tunneled ones before they multiply.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of small soft-bodied insects, often green or gray, gather on the youngest growth and in the leaf and stalk crevices, leaving the plant sticky with honeydew that may turn black with sooty mold. Beyond direct feeding, aphids are the main concern as a vector: they transmit celery mosaic virus, which yellows, mottles, twists, and stunts the foliage with no cure.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Little soft insects, usually green or gray, clustered on the newest leaves and in the crevices of the stalks, often leaving a sticky film. The bigger worry is that aphids spread a virus (celery mosaic) that yellows, mottles, and twists the leaves, which cannot be cured.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several aphid species colonize celery, including the bean aphid and foxglove aphid. They reproduce rapidly in mild weather and are spread further when winged forms move between plants; their role in moving celery mosaic virus from infected weeds and old celery makes even modest populations worth watching.
pests.cause_beginner: Several kinds of aphids (small sap-sucking insects) feed on celery and multiply fast in mild weather. The main reason to care is that they carry a virus from plant to plant, so even a few can do harm beyond their feeding.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Dislodge colonies with a strong jet of water, and conserve the lady beetles, lacewings, and parasitic wasps that suppress aphids by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays. Insecticidal soap or horticultural oil controls heavy infestations. Promptly remove any plant showing mosaic symptoms, since it is a reservoir the aphids will spread from.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Knock aphids off with a hard spray of water, and protect the ladybugs and other helpers that eat them by not using harsh sprays. Insecticidal soap handles bad cases. If a plant shows yellow, mottled, twisted leaves (the virus), pull it out so aphids cannot spread it.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Control nearby weeds and remove old celery and carrot-family volunteers that host both aphids and the virus, use reflective mulch to deter colonizers where mosaic is a problem, and keep natural enemies active by minimizing insecticide use. Row cover protects young plants.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep weeds down and clear out old celery and carrot-family plants nearby, since they shelter aphids and the virus. Encourage natural helpers by not spraying harshly, and use a row cover on young plants. Reflective (silver) mulch helps keep aphids away where the virus is common.

pests.name: Carrot rust fly
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Rusty-brown tunnels and scarring in the lower stalk bases and roots, sometimes with a rusty residue, and aboveground stunting or off-color foliage in heavier attacks. As a shared carrot-family pest, the same fly that mines carrots will work celery's crown and root zone where its populations are active.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Rusty-brown tunnels and scars low on the stalks and roots, and weak or off-color plants when it is bad. It is the same pest that tunnels carrots, and it goes after celery too where it is common.
pests.cause_seasoned: Larvae of the carrot rust fly (Psila rosae), whose females are drawn to the scent of carrot-family foliage and lay eggs near the crown; the maggots burrow into the lower stalks and roots. It is most damaging in cool, humid, maritime regions and far less of a problem in hot-summer areas.
pests.cause_beginner: The maggots of the carrot rust fly, a small fly that attacks the whole carrot family, including celery. The female lays eggs near the base of the plant and the maggots tunnel into the lower stalks and roots. It is mainly a problem in cool, damp, coastal areas.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no rescue for tissue already mined; trim damaged portions. Limit further loss by removing and not composting infested plants and clearing wild or volunteer carrot-family plants nearby that sustain the fly.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot fix tunnels that are already there, just cut away the damaged parts. Pull and throw away (do not compost) badly hit plants, and clear out any wild carrot-family weeds nearby that keep the fly going.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Floating row cover sealed at the edges at planting is the most reliable home defense, since the low-flying females cannot reach the crowns. Rotate celery away from where carrot-family crops grew last year, and avoid planting it next to carrots or parsnips.
pests.prevention_beginner: A row cover laid over the bed and tucked in at the edges is the best defense, because the low-flying fly cannot reach the plants to lay eggs. Also keep celery away from where you grew carrots or parsnips last year, and do not plant it right next to them.

diseases.name: Early blight (Cercospora leaf spot)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small yellow spots appear on both surfaces of the leaves and enlarge into gray, roughly circular lesions about 1/4 to 3/4 inch across; as they multiply the tissue between them turns papery and often splits and cracks, and severe spotting blights the foliage. In contrast to late blight, the petioles often stay relatively clean even when the leaves are heavily spotted. Badly blighted plants size up poorly.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small yellow spots show up on both sides of the leaves, then grow into gray, round patches about a quarter inch to three quarters of an inch wide. As they spread the leaf turns papery and cracks. Unlike late blight, the stalks often stay fairly clean even when leaves are spotty. A badly blighted plant grows poorly.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Cercospora apii, which is seedborne and also survives on celery debris in the field. It is favored by warm conditions, roughly 60 to 86°F, with leaf wetness from rain, dew, fog, or overhead irrigation; spores spread on wind and splashing water.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus (Cercospora apii) that can ride in on the seed and survive on old celery debris. It likes warm weather, about 60 to 86°F, together with wet leaves from rain, dew, fog, or overhead watering. The spores spread in wind and splashing water.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure for infected tissue; management slows spread. Remove badly spotted leaves, space and avoid overhead watering so foliage dries quickly, and in a wet season a copper-based fungicide labeled for vegetables can suppress spread if started early. The same protectant fungicides that control late blight also help with this disease.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot cure leaves that are already spotted, only slow it down. Pick off the worst leaves, water at the soil so the leaves stay dry, and give plants room. In a wet year a copper fungicide labeled for vegetables, started early, can help.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Start with disease-indexed (Cercospora-tested) seed and disease-free transplants, rotate celery and other carrot-family crops out of the bed for at least a year, clear crop debris, water at the base in the morning, and space plants for airflow. Avoid working among plants while the foliage is wet.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Use clean, tested seed and healthy transplants, do not grow celery (or its relatives) in the same spot two years running, clear away old debris, water at the soil in the morning, and give plants room so leaves dry fast. Stay out of the bed when the plants are wet.

diseases.name: Late blight (Septoria leaf spot)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small, discrete yellow spots appear on leaves and petioles and enlarge, often coalescing, then turn tan and dry to a papery texture; tiny dark fruiting bodies (pycnidia) speckle the lesions, the diagnostic sign that separates it from early blight. Unlike early blight, late blight readily lesions the stalks themselves, downgrading the harvest. It is usually the more damaging of the two celery blights.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small yellow spots on the leaves and stalks that enlarge, run together, and turn tan and papery, speckled with tiny dark dots (the telltale sign). Unlike early blight, this one spots the stalks too, which ruins the part you eat. It is usually the worse of the two blights.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Septoria apiicola (unrelated to the potato and tomato late blight). It is seedborne, the primary inoculum source, and survives on infected debris. Development stops below about 55°F and is favored above 70°F with leaf wetness from rain, heavy dew, fog, or sprinkler irrigation; splashing water disperses the spores.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus (Septoria apiicola, not the same as potato or tomato late blight). It usually arrives on the seed and survives on old debris. It needs wet leaves and stops growing below about 55°F, getting worse above 70°F with rain, dew, fog, or overhead watering, which splash the spores around.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No treatment cures infected tissue. Remove infected leaves, avoid overhead irrigation once plants are established, keep foliage as dry as possible, and apply a protectant fungicide (copper is acceptable for organic growers) at first symptoms if wet weather continues.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot cure leaves or stalks that are already infected. Pull off the worst leaves, stop watering from overhead, keep the plants as dry as you can, and if wet weather keeps up, a copper fungicide started at the first spots can slow it.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: The single most important step is Septoria-indexed (tested) seed, since seed is the main source; plant only disease-free transplants, avoid overhead sprinkling, rotate out of celery for at least a year, plow under or remove infected residue, and stay out of the bed when foliage is wet.
diseases.prevention_beginner: The most important thing is to start with tested, clean seed, because the disease usually comes in on the seed. Use healthy transplants, water at the soil instead of overhead, do not grow celery in the same place two years in a row, clear away infected leftovers, and keep out of the bed when the plants are wet.

diseases.name: Pink rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Brown, water-soaked lesions develop on the petioles at or near the soil line and expand into soft, watery, decayed areas; in humid conditions a white cottony mold grows over them, later bearing hard black resting bodies (sclerotia) the size of small seeds. Plants weakened by calcium deficiency are especially susceptible. It is a rot of the dense, moist plant base rather than a leaf disease.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Brown, water-soaked spots low on the stalks near the soil that turn into soft, mushy, rotted areas, sometimes covered in fluffy white mold with hard black specks in it. It rots the base of the plant, and plants short on calcium are hit hardest.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The soilborne fungus Sclerotinia sclerotiorum, which survives in soil as long-lived sclerotia and attacks many crops. It is favored by cool, wet conditions, prolonged leaf wetness, fog, dense canopies that stay damp, and overhead irrigation, which is why crowded, constantly wet celery is at greatest risk.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soil fungus (Sclerotinia) that lives for years in the ground and attacks many plants. It thrives in cool, wet, crowded conditions where the base of the plant stays damp, so over-tight planting and overhead watering make it worse.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no effective home cure once plants are infected; remove and destroy affected plants rather than composting them. Management is cultural: improve air movement and drying at the plant base.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no home cure once a plant has it, so pull and throw away infected plants (do not compost them). The real fix is in how you grow it, keeping the base of the plants drier and less crowded.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate away from celery and other susceptible crops to lower soil inoculum, space plants and rows for good airflow so the canopy and plant bases dry, use drip rather than sprinkler irrigation, avoid late-season overhead watering, and ensure adequate calcium and even moisture to keep plants from being predisposed.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Move celery to a fresh spot each year, give plants enough room so air moves through and the bases dry out, water at the soil with drip instead of overhead, and keep calcium and watering steady so the plants are not weakened and easy to infect.

diseases.name: Blackheart (calcium deficiency)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: The young leaves and growing point in the center of the plant turn brown to black and die, while the outer stalks may still look healthy, so the damage is hidden until the plant is cut open. Secondary soft-rot bacteria often invade the dead tissue, producing a slimy, foul interior. It is a physiological disorder, not an infection, though it opens the door to one.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The inside center of the plant, the youngest leaves and the growing tip, turns brown or black and dies, while the outer stalks can still look fine, so you often do not see it until you cut the plant open. Rot bacteria then move into the dead part and make it slimy and smelly.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A localized calcium deficiency in the fastest-growing tissue. It is usually not caused by truly calcium-poor soil but by anything that interrupts calcium delivery to the growing point: uneven or insufficient watering, rapid growth surges, high salts, or strongly acidic soil that limits calcium uptake. Celery's heavy water demand and shallow roots make it particularly prone.
diseases.cause_beginner: The growing center runs short of calcium. Usually the soil has enough, but the plant cannot move calcium to its fast-growing tip when watering is uneven, growth is too rushed, or the soil is too acidic. Celery is especially prone because it is shallow-rooted and needs so much water.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Damaged tissue does not recover; trim it away and use the sound outer stalks. The disorder is prevented, not cured: focus on the cultural causes for the next planting.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: The blackened center will not come back, so cut it out and use the good outer stalks. You cannot cure it once it happens; the answer is to prevent it next time.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: The core prevention is even, uninterrupted moisture, since erratic watering is the usual trigger; keep soil pH in the recommended slightly acidic to neutral range so calcium stays available, avoid forcing soft, rapid growth with excessive nitrogen, and maintain adequate soil calcium where tests show it is low. Some growers find a calcium foliar spray to the developing heart helps under risky conditions.
diseases.prevention_beginner: The main fix is steady, even watering, never letting the soil swing from dry to soaked, because uneven water is what usually triggers it. Keep the soil pH in the right range so calcium stays available, do not push soft growth with too much nitrogen, and add calcium (like lime) only if a soil test shows you need it.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Celery is the thirstiest of the common garden vegetables and the least forgiving of a dry spell. It is shallow-rooted and descends from a marsh plant, so it wants the soil kept evenly and constantly moist, never swinging from dry to wet. Plan on at least 1 to 2 inches of water per week from rain or irrigation, and more in heat or on light soil, delivered often enough that the surface root zone never dries.
watering.frequency_beginner: Celery needs more water, more steadily, than almost anything else in the garden. Keep the soil evenly damp all the time and never let it dry out. Give it at least 1 to 2 inches of water a week, counting rain, and more in hot weather or sandy soil. With celery, steady is the whole game.
watering.amount_seasoned: A minimum of 1 to 2 inches per week, increased in heat, wind, or fast-draining soil, applied frequently enough to avoid any dry-down. Mulch helps hold moisture and moderate soil temperature for the shallow roots.
watering.amount_beginner: At least 1 to 2 inches a week, and more when it is hot or your soil is sandy. It is better to water a bit more often than to soak it once and let it dry out. A layer of mulch helps keep the soil damp.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base with drip or a soaker hose to keep the root zone constantly moist while keeping the foliage and the dense plant base dry, since wet leaves and a damp crown favor the leaf blights and pink rot. Avoid overhead sprinkling, especially late in the day and late in the season.
watering.method_beginner: Water at the soil with a drip line or soaker hose so the roots stay damp but the leaves and the crowded base of the plant stay dry. Wet leaves bring on the leaf-spot diseases and stalk rot, so avoid spraying the plants from overhead, especially in the evening.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Constantly saturated, poorly drained soil invites pink rot and damping-off and yellows the foliage. The goal is steady moisture in well-amended, draining soil, not standing water; a sour, waterlogged bed and soft rotting stalk bases are the warning signs.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Soil that stays soaking wet, not just damp, can rot the base of the plant and turn the leaves yellow. You want steady moisture in rich soil that still drains, not a swamp. Mushy stalk bases and a sour, wet bed mean ease off.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Even brief drought is the classic celery failure: the petioles turn stringy, tough, pithy or hollow, and bitter, and the plant may bolt under combined heat and water stress. Wilting, dull foliage and slow growth signal that the crop has already been checked, and the quality loss from a dry spell is not reversible.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Letting celery go dry, even once, is the most common mistake. It makes the stalks stringy, tough, hollow, and bitter, and the damage does not undo itself. Droopy, dull leaves and stalled growth mean you waited too long, so keep the water steady rather than catching up after the fact.
watering.method_note_seasoned: The whole craft of growing good celery is steady water at the roots with a dry canopy. Use drip or a soaker hose and mulch to hold even moisture for the shallow roots, and keep overhead wetting off the foliage and crown to limit blight and pink rot. Any interruption shows up directly in the eating quality, so consistency matters more than volume.
watering.method_note_beginner: Good celery comes down to keeping the roots evenly wet while keeping the leaves dry. Use a drip line or soaker hose and some mulch to hold the moisture, and avoid spraying the plants from above. Letting it dry out, even briefly, is what makes celery stringy and bitter, so do not rely on catching up later.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Celery needs even moisture for its entire life, but two windows are most punishing to miss: the long establishment and bulking-up period when the stalks are forming, when any dry-down produces stringy, bitter petioles, and any heat-plus-drought stretch, which can trigger bolting. There is no slack period where celery tolerates drying.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Celery needs steady water its whole life, with no real break. The most important stretch is the long stretch while the stalks are filling out, when drying out makes them tough and bitter. Hot, dry spells are also dangerous because they can make celery bolt (run to seed). Basically, never let it get dry.

start_method.hardening_off_beginner: Yes, harden celery off before transplanting, but do it by gradually reducing water rather than by exposing the plants to cold. Celery is unusual here: chilling the seedlings to toughen them can backfire and make them bolt later, so ease them outdoors over 7 to 10 days into mild, not cold, conditions.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Always start celery as a transplant; it is too slow and too long-season to direct sow in most of the country. Sow seed indoors about 8 to 10 weeks before the target transplant date, barely covering the fine seed (it needs light and warmth, ideally about 70°F, to germinate, and is slow, often 2 to 3 weeks). Grow the seedlings on and transplant out when they have several true leaves and, critically, only after the danger of a hard frost or a prolonged cold snap has passed: young celery exposed to roughly two or more weeks of temperatures near or below 50°F can vernalize and bolt later instead of forming usable stalks. Harden off over 7 to 10 days by easing water, not by chilling.
start_method.notes_beginner: Start celery indoors from seed, or buy young plants, because it is too slow to plant straight in the garden in most areas. Sow the seed about 8 to 10 weeks before you plan to set plants out. Barely cover the tiny seeds, since they need light and warmth (around 70°F) to sprout, and be patient, they can take 2 to 3 weeks. Plant out only after the risk of hard frost and long cold spells is over: cold-shocked young celery often bolts (runs to seed) later instead of making good stalks. Harden the plants off over a week or so by watering a little less, not by putting them out in the cold.

container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: Celery is shallow-rooted, so depth is less critical than steady moisture and volume: a container at least 8 inches deep holds the roots, but a wider, larger pot (5 gallons or more) is far easier to keep evenly moist, which is the whole challenge. Group several plants in a roomy trough or half-barrel rather than single small pots, which dry too fast.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Celery does not need a deep pot because its roots are shallow, but it does need a pot big enough to stay damp. A container at least 8 inches deep works, but a bigger one (5 gallons or more) is much easier, because small pots dry out fast and celery hates drying out. A wide trough holding several plants is ideal.

drainage.saucer_practice_seasoned: A saucer can actually help here, because celery wants constant moisture: leaving a little water in the saucer between waterings buffers the pot against drying. Do not let it stand permanently full, though, since a constantly waterlogged mix invites pink rot and root rot.
drainage.saucer_practice_beginner: Unlike most plants, celery likes it damp, so a little water left in the saucer between waterings can help keep it from drying out. Just do not let it sit full all the time, or the roots can rot.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Use a quality potting mix and stir in plenty of compost so it holds water well. Celery wants a rich, moisture-holding mix, not a fast-draining one.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in compost and even a little extra of a water-holding material; the goal is a mix that stays damp between waterings. A slow-release fertilizer mixed in gives the heavy feeder a steady start.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: container_potting_mix
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend in generous compost to raise moisture-holding capacity; celery wants a rich, water-retentive mix rather than the light, fast-draining blend most container crops prefer. Incorporate a slow-release balanced fertilizer at potting to start the heavy feeder off well.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out much faster than the ground, and celery is the least forgiving plant about drying out, so check daily and often twice a day in heat. Keep the mix evenly damp at all times. This is the single hardest part of growing celery in a container.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Celery is a heavy feeder and a container has limited food, so feed every 1 to 2 weeks with a balanced liquid fertilizer once the plants are growing, in addition to mixing slow-release fertilizer in at planting.
container_notes.notes_beginner: Celery can be grown in a container, but it is demanding: the main job is never letting the pot dry out. Use a big, wide pot (5 gallons or more) with a rich, moisture-holding mix, keep it evenly damp (often watering daily), feed regularly, and place it in full sun to light afternoon shade. A self-watering container suits celery especially well.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Celery grows acceptably in containers if you can meet its moisture demand, which is the limiting factor. Use a large, wide container (5 gallons or more) with a rich, water-retentive mix, keep it constantly and evenly moist (often daily watering, twice daily in heat), and feed regularly since pot volume limits available nutrients. A self-watering or sub-irrigated container is genuinely well matched to celery's appetite for steady moisture.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry far faster than beds, and celery is the least drought-tolerant common vegetable, so moisture management is the whole task: check at least daily, twice daily in heat or wind, and keep the mix evenly moist. Letting a potted celery dry even once produces stringy, bitter stalks.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: With limited pot volume, supplement the slow-release fertilizer mixed in at potting with a balanced liquid feed every 1 to 2 weeks once growth is underway; celery's long season and heavy nitrogen demand exhaust container nutrients quickly.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering (sub-irrigated) container is one of the best ways to grow celery, because the constant wicking delivers exactly the even, uninterrupted moisture celery needs and that hand-watering struggles to maintain. Choose a large reservoir and a rich, wicking mix, and keep the reservoir topped up; this setup directly targets celery's single greatest weakness.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot is a great choice for celery, maybe the easiest way to grow it, because it keeps the soil steadily damp on its own, which is exactly what celery needs and what is hard to do by hand. Use a big one, keep the water reservoir filled, and use a rich mix that wicks moisture up well.

recommended: Tall Utah 52-70 and its strains: the standard green, self-blanching home and market type, crisp and stringless when grown well
Tango: vigorous, relatively fast and more forgiving than most, a good first choice
Conquistador: more tolerant of heat and less-than-ideal conditions, easier than classic types
Golden Self-Blanching: a compact, pale-stalked self-blanching type that needs little or no manual blanching
Giant Pascal and other Pascal types: traditional green trench-blanched celery, larger but more demanding
varieties.note_seasoned: Celery varieties split into two broad styles. Green, self-blanching types (the Utah and Pascal lineages, plus Tango and Conquistador) keep their green color and are the standard for most home gardens; the so-called self-blanching trait means they need less manual blanching than old trench types, not none. Golden or yellow self-blanching types naturally produce paler, milder stalks with minimal effort. For a first crop, choose a forgiving green type such as Tango or the heat-tolerant Conquistador over the larger, fussier Pascal types. There is also leaf celery (cutting celery) and celeriac (root celery), which are grown differently and are not covered here.
varieties.note_beginner: Celery comes in two main styles. Green types (like Tall Utah, Tango, and Conquistador) stay green and are what most people grow. Golden or self-blanching types make paler, milder stalks with less fuss. For your first try, pick an easier green variety like Tango or the more heat-tolerant Conquistador rather than the big old Pascal types, which are harder to grow well. (Leaf celery and celeriac are relatives grown differently and not covered here.)

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Do not plant celery where another carrot-family crop (Apiaceae) grew the previous season, including celery, carrot, parsnip, parsley, dill, or fennel, since they share soilborne diseases and pests, including the leaf blights, aster yellows, and carrot rust fly. Also avoid beds with a recent history of Sclerotinia (pink rot, white mold), which has a wide host range and persists in soil. A three-year gap before celery or its relatives return to a bed is the standard guideline.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Do not grow celery where you grew celery, carrot, parsnip, parsley, dill, or fennel last year, because they are all in the same family and share the same soil pests and diseases. Also avoid spots where white mold (pink rot) has been a problem, since it lingers in the soil and attacks many crops. Wait about three years before celery or its relatives go back in the same bed.
good_after: Legumes such as beans and peas, which leave nitrogen for this heavy feeder
Brassicas such as cabbage and broccoli
Alliums such as onions and garlic
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate celery on a three-year cycle, keeping it and all other carrot-family crops out of a bed for two seasons after celery grows there, to break the buildup of the shared leaf blights, aster yellows, and root pests. Because the blights are also seedborne, rotation works alongside clean seed rather than replacing it. Following a nitrogen-leaving legume crop suits celery's heavy appetite; avoid following crops that left a Sclerotinia (white mold) problem in the soil.
rotation.note_beginner: Move celery to a new spot each year and keep it and its relatives (carrot, parsley, dill) out of the same bed for about three years, to stop shared diseases and pests from piling up. Planting celery after beans or peas is ideal, since they leave nitrogen behind for this hungry crop. Avoid beds where white mold has been a problem.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Poor. At room temperature celery wilts and goes limp and rubbery within a day or two as it loses moisture, fastest if the stalks are cut. Keep only what you will use within a day on the counter and refrigerate the rest.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Not good. Left out, celery goes limp and bendy in a day or two as it dries out. Keep out only what you will use right away and refrigerate the rest.
storage.fridge_seasoned: The best everyday option, and celery keeps unusually well cold. Store whole heads or stalks in the crisper, ideally wrapped to hold humidity; many growers find wrapping celery in aluminum foil keeps it crisp markedly longer than a plastic bag, since the foil lets the plant's natural ethylene escape while holding moisture. At high humidity near 32°F celery holds two weeks to a month or more.
storage.fridge_beginner: This is the best way, and celery stores well cold. Keep it in the crisper drawer, wrapped to hold moisture. A popular trick many gardeners swear by is to wrap celery in aluminum foil instead of a plastic bag, which keeps it crisp longer. It will last from two weeks to a month or more.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Workable for cooking use only, after blanching. Frozen celery loses its crunch and is best reserved for soups, stocks, and stews. Chop, blanch in boiling water about 3 minutes, cool quickly in ice water, drain, and freeze; quality holds for several months. Raw-frozen celery turns limp and watery on thawing.
storage.freezer_beginner: You can freeze celery, but only for cooking, not for eating raw, since it goes limp once thawed. Chop it, dip it in boiling water for about 3 minutes, cool it fast in ice water, drain, and freeze. Use it in soups and stews. It keeps for several months.
storage.notes_seasoned: For a larger harvest, celery holds in the ground in mild weather and tolerates light frost, often sweetening slightly, but a hard freeze damages it, so lift before the ground freezes hard. Whole plants can be dug with roots and heeled into damp sand in a cold cellar or unheated garage near 32 to 40°F at high humidity, where they keep for one to two months. Store unwashed and trim just before use.
storage.notes_beginner: If you grow a lot, celery keeps in the ground in mild weather and takes a light frost, but a hard freeze ruins it, so harvest before the ground freezes solid. You can also dig whole plants with their roots and set them in damp sand in a cold spot like an unheated garage, around 32 to 40°F, where they last a month or two.

thinning.when: Not applicable: celery is set out at final spacing as transplants.
thinning.method: Not applicable. Celery is transplanted at its final spacing, so there is nothing to thin.
thinning.tip_seasoned: Celery is not thinned, because it is grown from transplants set directly at their final spacing of 6 to 10 inches rather than from a thickly sown row. Closer spacing (toward 6 inches, especially for self-blanching types planted in blocks) gives higher yield but more slender stalks, while wider spacing gives stockier plants; choose your spacing at transplanting rather than thinning later.
thinning.tip_beginner: You do not thin celery, because you plant it as young transplants spaced where they will grow, 6 to 10 inches apart, instead of sowing a crowded row. Planting on the closer side gives more but slimmer stalks; a bit farther apart gives stockier plants. You set the spacing when you plant, so there is nothing to pull out later.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare flats for a long time, then tiny, thread-fine seedlings with two narrow seed leaves.
