Celery germinates slowly and unevenly, often 2 to 3 weeks, needs light and warmth (about 70°F) and a surface that never dries, so patchy or no emergence usually traces to drying out, burying the fine seed too deep, or cold.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Empty seed trays for a while, then very small, thin seedlings with two narrow first leaves. Celery is slow to come up, often 2 to 3 weeks, and needs warmth, light, and a surface that never dries out. If little comes up, the seed was probably buried too deep, dried out, or was too cold.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Sow on the surface or barely covered, keep the medium constantly moist and around 70°F, and provide light. Bottom heat and a humidity dome help. Do not let the surface dry during the long germination window.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Sow the seeds on top of the mix or barely cover them, keep them warm (around 70°F), give them light, and never let the surface dry out. A clear cover and a warm spot help. Be patient, since they are slow.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Has your celery germinated? Note the emergence date to track the long season from a real sowing.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your celery seedlings come up yet? Jot down the date they appeared.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Slow-growing seedlings developing true, divided celery leaves over many weeks indoors. Growth is gradual; celery spends roughly 8 to 10 weeks reaching transplant size with several true leaves and a developing root system.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Small plants slowly growing their real, divided celery leaves over many weeks indoors. Celery takes its time, about 8 to 10 weeks, to reach a size big enough to plant out.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep seedlings evenly moist, warm, and well lit, and feed lightly once true leaves appear. Hold them above roughly 50°F, since prolonged chilling of seedlings can vernalize and later bolt them. Harden off over 7 to 10 days by easing water, not by chilling, before transplanting after hard-frost danger passes.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the seedlings damp, warm, and in good light, and give a weak feeding once they have real leaves. Keep them above about 50°F, because cold seedlings often bolt later. Before planting out, harden them off over a week by watering a little less, and wait until hard frosts are past.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are your celery seedlings near transplant size (several true leaves)?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are your celery plants big enough to plant outside yet?

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: After transplanting, steady leafy growth and a thickening cluster of upright stalks. This long bulking-up period is when even moisture and steady feeding matter most: any check from drought or hunger here sets in stringiness and bitterness that will not reverse.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: After planting out, the plants put on leaves and the bundle of stalks thickens and stands up. This long stretch is when steady water and feeding matter most, because going dry or hungry now makes the stalks tough and bitter for good.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Maintain constant even moisture (1 to 2 inches per week or more) and side-dress nitrogen every 3 to 4 weeks. Mulch to hold moisture. Watch for leaf blights in wet weather and keep foliage dry by watering at the base. Begin blanching self-blanching or green types in the last 2 weeks before harvest if you want milder, paler stalks.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist all the time and feed with nitrogen every 3 to 4 weeks; mulch helps. Water at the soil so the leaves stay dry, which limits leaf-spot diseases. If you want milder, paler stalks, blanch (block the light) in the last couple of weeks before harvest.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How is your celery sizing up? Note watering consistency and any leaf spotting.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How is your celery growing? Note if you have kept the water steady and seen any leaf spots.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Plants reaching usable size, roughly 3 inches or more across the base with stalks 6 to 8 inches or taller, generally 80 to 120 days after transplanting. Stalks should be firm and crisp; cracking, pithiness, or seed-stalk formation (bolting) signal it is past prime or stressed.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Plants that have grown to a good size, about 3 inches or more across the base with stalks at least 6 to 8 inches tall, usually 80 to 120 days after planting out. The stalks should be firm and crisp. Cracking, hollow centers, or a flower stalk shooting up mean it is past its best.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest whole plants by cutting at the base, or take outer stalks as needed and let the center keep growing. Harvest before a hard freeze; light frost is tolerated and can sweeten the stalks. Do not leave mature plants in hot soil, which coarsens them and risks bolting.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Cut the whole plant off at the base, or just snap off the outer stalks as you need them and let the middle keep growing. Pick before a hard freeze (a light frost is fine and can sweeten it). Do not leave grown celery sitting in hot weather, which makes it tough.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have you harvested celery? Log the date, the size, and the eating quality (crisp vs stringy).
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you cut your first celery? Note the date and how it turned out.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to start celery seed indoors
notifications.title_beginner: Time to start celery seeds inside
notifications.body_seasoned: Start celery indoors about 8 to 10 weeks before your transplant date. Surface-sow the fine seed, keep it warm (about 70°F), moist, and lit, and expect slow germination over 2 to 3 weeks.
notifications.body_beginner: Start celery seeds indoors about 8 to 10 weeks before you plan to plant out. Barely cover the tiny seeds, keep them warm and damp with light, and be patient, they take 2 to 3 weeks to sprout.

notifications.title_seasoned: Transplant celery once cold snaps are past
notifications.body_seasoned: Set celery out only after the danger of hard frost and prolonged cold has passed, since chilled young plants bolt. Space 6 to 10 inches apart in rich, moist soil, and harden off first by easing water, not by chilling.
notifications.body_beginner: Plant celery outside only after hard frosts are over, because cold young plants often bolt later. Space them 6 to 10 inches apart in rich, damp soil, and harden them off first by watering a little less.

notifications.body_seasoned: Hold even moisture, at least 1 to 2 inches per week and more in heat. Any dry-down makes celery stringy and bitter and can trigger bolting. Water at the base and mulch to hold moisture.
notifications.body_beginner: Keep the soil evenly damp, at least 1 to 2 inches of water a week, more when hot. Letting celery dry out, even once, makes it stringy and bitter. Water at the soil and mulch to hold the moisture.

notifications.body_seasoned: Celery is a heavy feeder. Side-dress nitrogen every 3 to 4 weeks through the season to keep growth fast and the stalks tender; underfeeding produces tough, stringy celery.
notifications.body_beginner: Celery is a hungry plant. Feed it with a nitrogen fertilizer every 3 to 4 weeks all season to keep it growing fast and tender. Underfed celery turns tough and stringy.

notifications.title_beginner: Check if your celery is ready
notifications.body_seasoned: From about 80 days after transplant, check size: a base roughly 3 inches across with firm, crisp stalks 6 to 8 inches or taller is ready. Take outer stalks as needed or cut the whole plant; harvest before a hard freeze.
notifications.body_beginner: Starting around 80 days after planting out, check the size: a base about 3 inches across with firm, crisp stalks at least 6 to 8 inches tall is ready. Snap off outer stalks as needed or cut the whole plant, and pick before a hard freeze.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Dry weather, water celery now
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Celery has no drought tolerance: even a brief dry-down turns stalks stringy, hollow, and bitter and can trigger bolting. Water deeply and keep the soil constantly moist; mulch to buffer the shallow roots.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Celery cannot handle dry soil at all. Even a short dry spell makes the stalks stringy, hollow, and bitter and can make it bolt. Water it well and keep the soil damp, and add mulch to help hold moisture.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot weather hurts celery
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Sustained heat above about 75°F coarsens stalks, turns them bitter, and combined with drought can trigger bolting. Keep moisture even, mulch, provide afternoon shade if possible, and harvest before a long hot stretch.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: When it stays hotter than about 75°F, celery gets tough and bitter and may bolt (run to seed), especially if it also gets dry. Keep it well watered, mulch it, give it afternoon shade if you can, and harvest before a long hot spell.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: A cold snap can make young celery bolt
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Cold can make young celery bolt
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Young celery exposed to roughly two or more weeks near or below 50°F can vernalize and later bolt instead of forming stalks. Protect recent transplants from prolonged cold with row cover; mature plants are far less sensitive.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Young celery that sits through a couple of weeks of cold (near or below 50°F) often bolts later instead of making good stalks. Cover recently planted celery during long cold spells. Older, bigger plants are much less at risk.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Light frost is fine; harvest before a hard freeze
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Light frost is okay; pick before a hard freeze
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Celery tolerates light frost, which can mildly sweeten it, but a hard freeze damages the stalks. Before a hard freeze, harvest, or dig and store whole plants, or protect them with cover.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: A light frost does not hurt celery and can make it a bit sweeter, but a hard freeze ruins the stalks. Before a hard freeze, harvest it, or dig up whole plants to store, or cover them.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Wet, humid weather favors celery blight
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Damp weather can bring leaf spots
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Warm, wet foliage favors the early and late blights (Cercospora and Septoria) and pink rot. Water at the base only, keep leaves dry, space for airflow, and remove badly spotted leaves.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Warm, wet weather with wet leaves brings on celery's leaf-spot diseases and stalk rot. Water only at the soil, keep the leaves dry, give plants room for air to move, and pick off badly spotted leaves.

germination.text_seasoned: Celery seed is fine and needs light to germinate, so surface-sow it or barely cover it, and hold the medium warm (about 70°F) and constantly moist. Germination is slow and erratic, often 2 to 3 weeks, so do not give up early or let the surface dry.
germination.text_beginner: Celery seeds are tiny and need light to sprout, so sow them on top of the mix or barely cover them. Keep them warm (around 70°F) and never let the surface dry out. They are slow, often 2 to 3 weeks, so be patient.
germination.author: plant

germination.text_seasoned: Because celery needs roughly 8 to 10 weeks indoors before transplant and a long season after, start seed early, on the order of 10 to 12 weeks before your intended set-out date, to make the most of the cool growing window.
germination.text_beginner: Celery takes about 8 to 10 weeks to grow big enough to plant out, plus a long season after that, so start the seeds early, around 10 to 12 weeks before you plan to plant outside.
germination.author: plant

seedling.text_seasoned: Do not chill celery seedlings to harden them, and do not rush them outdoors during cold weather: roughly two or more weeks near or below 50°F can vernalize young plants and make them bolt later. Hold seedlings above 50°F and harden off by easing water, not temperature.
seedling.text_beginner: Do not toughen up celery seedlings by making them cold, and do not put them out while it is still cold. About two weeks near or below 50°F can make young celery bolt (run to seed) later. Keep them warmer than 50°F and harden them off by watering less, not by chilling them.
seedling.author: plant

seedling.text_seasoned: Keep seedlings evenly moist, well lit, and lightly fed once true leaves appear, so they grow on steadily; a stalled, hardened seedling transplants poorly and is more prone to bolting.
seedling.text_beginner: Keep the seedlings damp, in good light, and give a weak feeding once they have real leaves so they keep growing. A stunted, stressed seedling does not transplant well.
seedling.author: plant

established.text_seasoned: Even, uninterrupted moisture is the heart of growing good celery: at least 1 to 2 inches per week and more in heat, with no dry-down. A check from drought sets in the stringiness and bitterness that cannot be reversed, so water at the base and mulch the shallow roots.
established.text_beginner: Steady water is the single most important thing for good celery: at least 1 to 2 inches a week, more in heat, and never let it dry out. A dry spell makes it stringy and bitter for good, so water at the soil and mulch around the plants.
established.author: plant

established.text_seasoned: Celery is a heavy feeder: side-dress nitrogen every 3 to 4 weeks to keep growth fast and the stalks tender. Underfeeding, like underwatering, produces tough, bitter celery, so do not skimp.
established.text_beginner: Celery is a hungry plant. Feed it with a nitrogen fertilizer every 3 to 4 weeks to keep it growing fast and tender. Not feeding it enough, like not watering it enough, makes it tough and bitter.
established.author: plant

established.text_seasoned: Guard against blackheart (the death of the growing center) by keeping moisture even and pH and calcium adequate, since the disorder is triggered mostly by interrupted calcium delivery rather than truly low soil calcium. Even watering is the main lever.
established.text_beginner: To prevent blackheart (when the inside center turns black and dead), keep the water steady and the soil pH and calcium in a good range. Usually the soil has enough calcium, but uneven watering stops the plant from using it, so steady water is the main fix.
established.author: plant

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest by size and need rather than a strict date: a base roughly 3 inches across with firm, crisp stalks is ready, generally 80 to 120 days after transplant. Take outer stalks as you need them and let the center keep growing, or cut the whole plant at the base.
harvest.text_beginner: Harvest by size, not a set date: a base about 3 inches across with firm, crisp stalks is ready, usually 80 to 120 days after planting out. You can snap off the outer stalks as you need them and let the middle keep growing, or cut the whole plant at the base.
harvest.author: plant

harvest.text_seasoned: Celery tolerates light frost (which can mildly sweeten it) but is damaged by a hard freeze, so harvest or protect plants before one. For storage, keep it cold and humid; wrapping in foil is a well-regarded trick for holding crispness longer than a plastic bag.
harvest.text_beginner: Celery handles a light frost, and it can taste a little sweeter after, but a hard freeze ruins it, so pick or cover it before one. To store, keep it cold and damp; many gardeners find wrapping it in aluminum foil keeps it crisp longer than a plastic bag.
harvest.author: plant

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: One head per plant, typically harvested whole, though you can also take outer stalks over time and let the center keep growing. A well-grown plant yields a bunch of perhaps 10 to 20 usable stalks; expect less from stressed or under-watered plants.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Each plant gives you one head of celery, which you usually cut whole. You can also snap off the outer stalks a few at a time and let the middle keep growing. A good plant gives a bunch of maybe 10 to 20 usable stalks; stressed plants give less.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: There is no repeat harvest from a single planting beyond taking outer stalks; a planting matures over a window and is cut over a few weeks. Continuous supply comes from a spring and a fall planting (and successive batches a couple of weeks apart) rather than one long-bearing crop.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: A celery planting is ready over a few weeks and then it is done, apart from picking outer stalks. For a steady supply, plant a spring crop and a fall crop, and stagger a couple of batches a week or two apart, instead of one big planting.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Celery is grown fresh from seed each season as an annual crop (it is botanically a biennial, flowering in its second year, which is why a cold snap that mimics winter makes it bolt), so there is no first-year-versus-later distinction; the first planting performs as well as any when moisture and feeding stay steady.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: You grow celery fresh from seed every year, so your first planting can do just as well as any later one. (Celery is naturally a two-year plant that flowers in its second year, which is why a cold spell that feels like winter to a young plant makes it bolt.) The keys to success are steady water and feeding.
factors_seasoned: Even moisture: any dry-down makes stalks stringy, bitter, and pithy, the single biggest factor in celery quality.
Steady feeding: celery is a heavy nitrogen feeder, and underfeeding directly toughens the stalks.
Temperature window: prolonged cold on young plants causes bolting, while sustained heat above about 75°F coarsens and bitters the stalks.
Calcium and pH: interrupted calcium delivery, often from uneven water, causes blackheart in the growing center.
Season length: celery needs a long, mild stretch (about 80 to 120 days from transplant plus the indoor start), so timing the crop to the cool window is essential.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting assigns aboveground leafy and stalk crops like celery to the waxing moon, the period from new moon to full, on the folk principle that rising lunar influence favors leafy top growth. This is long-standing gardening folklore with no controlled scientific evidence of an effect on celery. Time celery by your cool-season window and soil warmth, not the moon; this is recorded only for growers who follow the tradition.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Stringy, tough, bitter stalks
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Stringy, tough, bitter celery
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The petioles came out fibrous, tough, and strong or bitter in flavor. The dominant cause is a growth check, almost always a dry spell, but also underfeeding, heat, or simply slow growth from cold or crowding. Celery must grow fast and without interruption to stay tender; once stringiness sets in it does not reverse.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The stalks turned tough, stringy, and bitter. This almost always comes from the plant going dry at some point, or from not enough food, too much heat, or just slow growth. Celery has to grow fast and steady to stay crisp, and once it goes stringy it stays that way.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Keep moisture constant (1 to 2 inches per week or more, never a dry-down), feed nitrogen every 3 to 4 weeks, grow in the cool season so heat does not coarsen the crop, and choose a more forgiving variety such as Tango or Conquistador. Mulch to steady soil moisture.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Never let it dry out (1 to 2 inches of water a week, more in heat), feed it every 3 to 4 weeks, grow it in cool weather, and pick an easier variety like Tango or Conquistador. Mulch helps keep the soil evenly damp.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Bolting (premature seed stalk)
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Celery bolted (sent up a flower stalk)
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The plant sent up a tall flowering stalk instead of forming a usable head, and the stalks turned tough and bitter. The usual trigger is vernalization: young transplants exposed to roughly two or more weeks near or below 50°F read it as winter and flower. Heat-plus-drought stress can also push stressed plants to bolt.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The plant shot up a tall flower stalk instead of making a good head, and the stalks went tough and bitter. The usual cause is cold: young plants that sat through a couple of weeks of cold weather (near or below 50°F) think winter has passed and try to flower. Hot, dry stress can also cause it.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Transplant only after hard-frost danger and prolonged cold are past, protect early transplants from cold snaps with row cover, do not chill seedlings to harden them, and keep moisture even in heat. Choose bolt-resistant varieties where spring is cold.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant out only after the cold is truly past, cover young plants during cold snaps, do not toughen seedlings by making them cold, and keep them well watered in heat. Pick a bolt-resistant variety if your spring is cold.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Blackheart (blackened center)
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Black, dead center (blackheart)
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The young leaves and growing point in the center died and turned brown to black while the outer stalks looked fine, often followed by a slimy secondary soft rot. It is a localized calcium deficiency in the fast-growing tissue, usually caused by interrupted calcium delivery (uneven watering, growth surges, high salts, or acidic soil) rather than genuinely low soil calcium.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The inside center of the plant turned brown or black and died, even though the outer stalks looked okay, and it may have gone slimy. It is caused by the growing tip running short of calcium, usually because watering was uneven, not because the soil truly lacked calcium.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Keep moisture even above all, hold soil pH in the slightly acidic to neutral range so calcium stays available, avoid forcing soft growth with excess nitrogen, and add calcium only where a soil test shows a real shortfall. Some growers foliar-feed calcium to the heart under risky conditions.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Most of all, keep watering steady. Keep the soil pH in the right range so calcium is available, do not push soft growth with too much nitrogen, and only add calcium (lime) if a soil test says you need it.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Cracked or hollow, pithy stalks
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Cracked or hollow stalks
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Stalks split lengthwise or came out hollow and pithy inside. Hollow, pithy petioles trace to uneven growth from inconsistent water or nutrition and to over-maturity; boron deficiency can also cause cracked, brittle stalks. As with stringiness, the root issue is usually an interrupted, uneven growth pattern.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The stalks split open or came out hollow and spongy inside. This usually comes from uneven growth, the plant speeding up and slowing down because water or food was not steady, or from leaving it too long. A shortage of the nutrient boron can also cause cracking.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Keep water and feeding steady to maintain even growth, harvest at maturity rather than holding plants too long, and where cracking recurs have soil tested for boron, correcting only on a confirmed deficiency since excess boron is toxic.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep water and feeding steady so the plant grows evenly, harvest on time instead of leaving it too long, and if cracking keeps happening, have your soil tested for boron and add it only if a test says to (too much is harmful).

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Leaf and stalk spotting (blight)
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Spotty leaves and stalks (blight)
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Yellow then gray or tan spots spread across the leaves, and in the case of late blight onto the stalks, sometimes speckled with tiny dark fruiting bodies. These are the early (Cercospora) and late (Septoria) blights, both often seedborne and spread by wet foliage. Heavy infection blights the foliage and downgrades the stalks.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Yellow then gray or tan spots spread over the leaves, and with late blight onto the stalks too, sometimes with tiny dark dots. These are celery's leaf-spot diseases (early and late blight). They often come in on the seed and spread when the leaves stay wet.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Start with disease-indexed (tested) seed and clean transplants, rotate out of celery and its relatives for at least a year, water at the base to keep foliage dry, space for airflow, remove infected leaves, and stay out of the bed when plants are wet.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Use clean, tested seed and healthy plants, do not grow celery (or carrots and parsley) in the same spot two years running, water at the soil so leaves stay dry, give plants room, pull off spotted leaves, and keep out of the bed when it is wet.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Celery is a long-season crop, so it does not succession-sow rapidly the way salad crops do, but you can stagger transplants a couple of weeks apart within a window and grow both a spring and a fall crop in milder climates. In cold-summer regions that usually means a single main crop transplanted after frost and grown through summer; in warm regions it means a fall and a late-winter or spring crop bracketing the summer heat. Time each window so the long crop matures in cool, not hot, weather and never goes short of water.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: Celery takes a long time to grow, so you do not replant it every couple of weeks like lettuce. Instead, set out plants a week or two apart within a planting window, and in milder areas grow a spring crop and a fall crop. In cold-summer areas you usually get one main summer crop; in hot areas you grow it in fall, winter, and early spring to dodge the heat. Aim for the crop to finish in cool weather, and never let it dry out.

heat_threshold_temp_f.basis_seasoned: Air-temperature ceiling for celery quality. Extension sources put celery's optimum near 60 to 70°F (UC Master Gardeners of Santa Clara County give 60 to 65°F best, tolerating 45 to 75°F; Utah State gives an ideal of 55 to 65°F). Sustained air above roughly 75°F coarsens and bitters the stalks and, combined with drought, can trigger bolting, so the planting calendar in warm regions excludes the hottest months.

crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Celery is ready when the plant has reached usable size, judged by feel rather than a strict date: a base roughly 3 inches or more across, with firm, crisp, upright stalks generally 6 to 8 inches or taller, usually 80 to 120 days after transplanting. Harvest the whole plant by cutting at the soil line, or take outer stalks as needed and let the center keep growing. Harvest before a hard freeze; light frost is tolerated and can sweeten the stalks, but stalks that are cracking, going hollow or pithy, or sending up a seed stalk are past their best.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Celery is ready when it has grown to a good size: a base about 3 inches or more across, with firm, crisp stalks at least 6 to 8 inches tall, usually 80 to 120 days after you planted it out. Cut the whole plant off at the base, or just snap off the outer stalks as you need them and let the middle keep growing. Pick before a hard freeze (a light frost is fine and can sweeten it). Stalks that are cracking, hollow, or shooting up a flower stalk are past their best.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Celery quality is set by moisture and fertility more than by tilth, so prepare a rich, water-retentive bed. Work in generous compost or well-rotted manure to feed this heavy feeder and to build the water-holding capacity celery's shallow roots depend on, and add a balanced fertilizer at planting. On light sandy soil, amend heavily or build a raised bed with a moisture-holding mix; on the heaviest soils, ensure the bed still drains enough to avoid the pink rot that thrives in waterlogged ground. Aim for a slightly acidic to neutral pH (about 6.0 to 6.8) so calcium stays available and blackheart is less likely.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Good celery starts with rich, damp soil, so prepare the bed by digging in lots of compost or rotted manure. This feeds the hungry plant and helps the soil hold the steady moisture celery must have. Mix in a balanced fertilizer at planting too. If your soil is sandy and dries fast, add extra compost or use a raised bed with a moisture-holding mix. Aim for a soil pH around 6.0 to 6.8 so the plant can get the calcium it needs.
crops.description_seasoned: Celery (Apium graveolens) is a cool-season member of the carrot family grown for its crisp leaf stalks, and it has a reputation as one of the more demanding vegetables for good reason. Descended from a wild marsh plant, it wants what few crops want all at once: a long, mild growing season of roughly 80 to 120 days from transplant, constant and even moisture, rich heavily fed soil, and freedom from both hard cold and summer heat. It is started indoors 8 to 10 weeks ahead and transplanted out only after hard-frost danger passes, because young plants chilled for a couple of weeks near 50°F will bolt. The through-line of celery culture is steadiness: any check from drought, hunger, heat, or cold shows up directly as stringy, bitter, hollow, or cracked stalks, and calcium starved by uneven watering blackens the growing heart. Grown with that steadiness, in the cool shoulders of the year, it rewards the effort with tender, flavorful stalks far better than the store offers.
crops.description_beginner: Celery is a cool-weather vegetable in the carrot family, grown for its crisp stalks, and it is honestly one of the trickier crops to grow well. It came from a wild marsh plant, so it wants steady dampness, rich soil, lots of food, and mild weather, all at the same time, over a long season (about 80 to 120 days after you plant it out). You start it indoors 8 to 10 weeks early and plant it outside only after hard frosts are over, because young celery that gets too cold will bolt (run to seed). The big secret is to keep it growing steadily and never let it get dry, hungry, too hot, or too cold. Any of those makes the stalks stringy, bitter, hollow, or cracked. Get the steady care right, grow it in the cooler parts of the year, and homegrown celery is far more tender and flavorful than what you buy.

open_findings.summary: Regional planting windows are modeled from the nearest readable T1 source (MSU upper-midwest, USU intermountain, TAMU south, UC coastal, UF/IFAS Florida, UH Hawaii) plus celery's biology, NOT a region-specific celery planting chart for each of the 10 regions; the UGA b577 and several state planting-date PDFs that would tighten exact months are scanned PDFs that could not be read this session. Windows are generally-safe but the exact months should be tightened in the variety-delta pass.

hawaii_tropical is the lowest-confidence cell: celery is a marginal tropical-lowland crop grown mainly in cool uplands or the cool season, modeled as a cool-season winter window with a warm-month heat_pause and cited to UH CTAHR generally rather than a celery-specific Hawaii source. Confirm against a CTAHR vegetable calendar in review.

Companion pairings are authored as TRADITIONAL/low-to-medium confidence only; no celery-specific companion trial was found in a readable T1 source. The carrot-family avoids rest on documented shared-pest overlap; the goods (brassicas, beans, alliums) are companion lore.

Judgment calls: pH preferred set to 6.0-6.8 (sources cluster 5.8-6.8, tolerating to ~7.0); category set to 'Leafy Greens' (no stalk/petiole category exists in the taxonomy; UGA groups celery with leafy petiole vegetables). days_to_maturity 80-120 from transplant per MSU (some sources give 98-130 from seed).

The self-blanching / trench-or-wrap-to-reduce-bitterness-and-greening claim in varieties carries no citation (varieties.sources=None, anchoring_urls=None) and was not on the two T1 pages read this session (USU, MSU home-garden); it is standard, correct horticulture. tamu_agrilife (a record source) is currently in an http/https cross-host redirect loop and was UNREACHABLE this session -> flagged for the post-123 URL-liveness sweep. Attach a T1 blanching anchor (TAMU once reachable, or UMN/PSU) at the variety pass.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: Wave-6 cert (2026-07-02): CC source-truth review. Blackheart-as-localized-calcium-deficiency-from-uneven-watering backed (USU + MSU); long-cool-season + steady water + DTM 80-120-from-transplant backed (MSU verbatim '80 to 120 days from transplants'; USU/UC-MG cool-season + 1-2 in/week water); Cercospora apii early blight backed VERBATIM (UC IPM: lesion 0.25-0.75 in, temp 60-86F, seedborne, petioles stay symptomless). transplant.label: primary
transplant.synthesis_note_seasoned: Celery in this region is transplanted into the windows resolved below and modeled from the nearest readable Tier-1 source plus celery's cool-season biology. In cold-winter regions celery is grown as a single main crop: start seed indoors in late winter, transplant after the danger of hard frost and prolonged cold has passed (chilled young plants bolt), and grow through the relatively mild northern summer for a late-summer to fall harvest before hard freezes. Constant moisture and steady feeding through the long season are the limiting factors, not heat.

harvest_start.label: primary

harvest_end.label: primary

The cool, mild California coast is celery's ideal climate, with a long growing window. Sow indoors in late fall to winter and transplant from late winter through spring (and again in midsummer in the mildest spots) for a long harvest from late spring into fall.
