crops.name: Shallot

soil.preferred_texture_seasoned: Loose, fertile loam or sandy loam with steady moisture-holding capacity grows the cleanest, fullest clumps.
soil.preferred_texture_beginner: Shallots grow the best clumps in loose, rich soil that holds moisture well. Loam or sandy loam is ideal.
soil.tolerated_texture_seasoned: Tolerates a range of soils, including silt loam and sandier ground, as long as drainage and fertility are good.
soil.tolerated_texture_beginner: Shallots handle a range of soils, including silty and sandier ones, as long as the soil drains well and is rich enough to feed the plants.
soil.problematic_texture_seasoned: Avoid heavy, tight clay and soils that crust or cap; the shallow allium roots and the dividing bulbs struggle in them, and poor internal drainage invites bulb rots.
soil.problematic_texture_beginner: Avoid heavy, tight clay and soil that forms a hard crust on top. Shallots have shallow roots and dividing bulbs that struggle in those conditions, and soil that drains poorly can rot the bulbs.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Shallots like loose, rich, well-drained soil. Mix in compost before you plant. They do poorly in heavy clay or in soil that forms a hard surface crust, because their roots stay shallow and the multiplying clump needs air and steady moisture right near the surface.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Work generous organic matter into the bed before planting and aim for a loose, fertile, well-drained spot; shallots are heavy feeders with small root systems, so the soil has to carry both water and nutrients close to the surface where the clump divides.

ph.note_beginner: Shallots like soil close to neutral, about pH 6.0 to 7.0, and will tolerate roughly 5.5 to 7.5. They do not like sour (acidic) soil. A simple soil test takes the guesswork out, and garden lime helps if the test comes back too low.
ph.note_seasoned: Shallots grow best near neutral, roughly pH 6.0 to 7.0, tolerating about 5.5 to 7.5. They dislike strongly acid soil; below about pH 6.0 a liming amendment helps. Confirm with a soil test before adjusting.

fertilizer.timing: Side-dress during leaf growth, then taper off as the clump divides and bulbs form
fertilizer.example_product: ammonium sulfate or a balanced vegetable fertilizer
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Shallots are heavy feeders. Drive leaf growth early with nitrogen, side-dressing at about 30 and 60 days after planting, because the leaf canopy built before bulbing sets the size and number of bulbs in the clump. Then stop: hold off on nitrogen after about mid-July. Late, excess nitrogen delays maturity and produces thick necks and soft bulbs that store poorly.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Shallots are hungry plants. Feed them nitrogen while the leaves are growing, because strong leaves now mean a fuller clump of bulbs later. Feed about a month after planting and again a month after that, then stop feeding by about mid-July. Feeding late makes thick necks and soft shallots that do not keep well.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time to side-dress your shallots with nitrogen to push leaf growth before the clump bulbs up.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Feed your shallots some nitrogen now to grow plenty of leaves before the bulbs form.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: Higher first-number (N) feeds early; ease off nitrogen as the clump starts to bulb.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a feed higher in the first number (nitrogen) early on, then stop the nitrogen once the bulbs start forming.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: About half a pound of ammonium sulfate (21-0-0) per 100 square feet at each of the two side-dressings, or the label rate of a balanced fertilizer.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: About half a pound of a nitrogen fertilizer such as ammonium sulfate for every 100 square feet each time you feed, or follow the package directions.

pests.name: Onion thrips
pests.identification_seasoned: Tiny slender insects rasping silvery streaks and flecks into the leaf necks and folds; heavy feeding reduces clump size and invites disease.
pests.identification_beginner: Very small insects that leave silvery streaks and specks on the leaves, often down in the crease where leaves meet. Bad infestations shrink the bulbs.
pests.cause_seasoned: Onion thrips (Thrips tabaci) build through warm, dry spells, sheltering in the leaf axils where sprays miss them.
pests.cause_beginner: A tiny insect called onion thrips. It multiplies fast in warm, dry weather and hides in the tight folds of the leaves.
pests.management_seasoned: Keep plants vigorous and watered, hose off light infestations, use reflective mulch, and rotate away from alliums; treat persistent outbreaks per local extension guidance.
pests.management_beginner: Keep the plants healthy and watered, spray them off with water if thrips are light, and do not plant shallots in the same spot every year. For heavy infestations, ask your local extension office what to use.

pests.name: Onion maggot
pests.identification_seasoned: Wilting, yellowing plants and rotting bulbs riddled by small white larvae; stand loss is worst in cool, wet springs.
pests.identification_beginner: Young plants wilt and yellow, and bulbs rot with small white grubs inside. Worst in cool, wet spring weather.
pests.cause_seasoned: Larvae of the onion maggot fly (Delia antiqua), whose eggs are laid at the plant base; populations carry over in allium residue.
pests.cause_beginner: The larvae (maggots) of a small fly that lays eggs at the base of allium plants. They survive in leftover onion and shallot debris.
pests.management_seasoned: Rotate away from alliums, remove cull bulbs and crop residue, and use floating row cover at emergence to block egg-laying.
pests.management_beginner: Do not plant shallots in the same place each year, clean up old allium scraps, and cover young plants with row-cover fabric so the fly cannot lay eggs on them.

pests.name: Allium leafminer
pests.identification_seasoned: Rows of white dots punched down a leaf edge (egg-laying scars), then twisted, distorted leaves; cream-colored larvae mine the leaves and tunnel down into the bulb, where their pupae overwinter.
pests.identification_beginner: Look for a neat line of small white dots along the leaves, then leaves that twist and curl. Tiny pale grubs tunnel inside the leaves and down into the bulb.
pests.cause_seasoned: The allium leafminer (Phytomyza gymnostoma), an invasive fly that attacks alliums including shallot; adults fly and lay eggs in a spring generation (about March into May) and again in fall (September into October).
pests.cause_beginner: A small invasive fly that attacks onions, shallots, garlic, and leeks. The adults come out and lay eggs in spring and again in fall, and the grubs tunnel into the plants.
pests.management_seasoned: Floating row cover or insect netting installed before each flight and sealed at the edges gives close to full control; time it to the spring and fall adult emergence, rotate away from alliums, and use spinosad if covers are not practical.
pests.management_beginner: Cover the plants with row-cover fabric or fine netting before the flies appear in spring and again in fall, sealing the edges so none get in. Rotating where you plant alliums helps too. A spinosad spray is an option if you cannot use covers.

diseases.name: White rot
diseases.identification_seasoned: Yellowing, wilting, dying-back leaves, then a fluffy white mat of mycelium at the base and on the bulb studded with tiny black, poppyseed-like sclerotia; clumps collapse and rot.
diseases.identification_beginner: Leaves turn yellow and wilt, and the base of the plant grows a fluffy white mold dotted with tiny black specks. The bulbs rot.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A soilborne fungus (Sclerotium cepivorum) that attacks only alliums and favors cool, moist soil. Its sclerotia survive in the ground for 20 to 30 years, so once a bed is infested it stays infested.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soil fungus that attacks only onions, shallots, garlic, and leeks. It likes cool, damp soil, and its survival specks last in the ground for decades, so an infected bed stays a problem for years.
diseases.management_seasoned: There is no rescue once it appears. Avoid introducing it on infested sets or soil, remove and dispose of infected clumps (do not compost), and rotate alliums out of the bed for as long as possible; the disease is essentially permanent in infested ground.
diseases.management_beginner: There is no cure once it shows up, so the goal is to keep it out. Buy clean sets, pull and throw away (do not compost) any infected plants, and do not grow alliums in that spot again for many years.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.identification_seasoned: Pale, elongated patches on the leaves carrying a fuzzy gray-violet sporulation in humid mornings; affected leaves yellow and collapse, cutting bulb size.
diseases.identification_beginner: Pale patches on the leaves with a fuzzy gray-purple coating in damp weather. The leaves yellow and flop, and the bulbs end up smaller.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus-like pathogen Peronospora destructor, favored by cool, wet, humid conditions and lingering leaf wetness; it spreads fast in crowded, poorly aired plantings.
diseases.cause_beginner: A mildew that spreads in cool, wet, humid weather, especially when the leaves stay wet and the plants are crowded.
diseases.management_seasoned: Space for airflow, water at the base to keep foliage dry, rotate away from alliums, and remove infected debris; choose tolerant varieties where downy mildew is a recurring problem.
diseases.management_beginner: Give the plants room for air to move, water at the base so the leaves stay dry, rotate where you plant, and clear away sick leaves. Pick tolerant varieties if this is a regular problem for you.

diseases.name: Botrytis neck rot
diseases.identification_seasoned: A soft, sunken rot starting at the neck in storage, often with gray mold; immature or poorly cured clumps are most susceptible.
diseases.identification_beginner: Shallots go soft and rotten at the neck after harvest, sometimes with gray mold. It mostly hits bulbs that were not dried well.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Botrytis infection of immature or insufficiently cured necks; excess late nitrogen and bent-over green tops worsen it.
diseases.cause_beginner: A mold that gets into the neck of shallots that were harvested too green or not dried properly. Too much late fertilizer and bending the tops down make it worse.
diseases.management_seasoned: Let tops mature naturally, do not knock down green tops to force bulbing, cure thoroughly until necks are tight, and store cool and dry.
diseases.management_beginner: Let the tops fall on their own, do not bend them over, dry (cure) the shallots well until the necks are tight, and store them somewhere cool and dry.

diseases.name: Pink root
diseases.identification_seasoned: Roots turn pink then red and shrivel, stunting plants and shrinking the clump; common where alliums are grown repeatedly and in warm soils.
diseases.identification_beginner: The roots turn pink, then red, then shrivel up. Plants stay small and make small clumps. Common when alliums are grown in the same place often.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A soilborne fungus (Setophoma terrestris) that builds in continuous allium ground; stressed plants show it worst.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soil fungus that builds up when shallots and their relatives are grown in the same ground year after year. Stressed plants get it worst.
diseases.management_seasoned: Rotate away from alliums for several years, start with clean, disease-free sets, and keep plants unstressed.
diseases.management_beginner: Rotate where you plant shallots, start with clean, healthy sets, and keep the plants well cared for so they are not stressed.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Keep the soil consistently moist through leaf growth and bulb division; shallots have small, shallow root systems, and any drought check directly reduces clump size and bulb count. Then stop watering once the tops begin to fall, to start the bulbs curing.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water shallots regularly so the soil stays evenly moist while they grow. Their roots are shallow, so dry spells make smaller clumps. Stop watering when the tops start to flop over, so the bulbs can begin to dry.
watering.amount_seasoned: Aim for roughly an inch of water per week from rain plus irrigation, more in heat or sandy soil, keeping moisture near field capacity in the top 8 to 12 inches where the roots feed.
watering.amount_beginner: About an inch of water a week is a good target, and more during hot, dry weather. Steady moisture is better than a flood one week and nothing the next.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base with drip or a soaker to keep the foliage dry; wet tops invite the leaf and neck diseases that spoil bulbs in storage.
watering.method_beginner: Water the soil at the base of the plants, not over the leaves. Keeping the tops dry helps prevent disease.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Waterlogged soil and yellowing, mushy bases signal overwatering; standing moisture around the clump encourages basal and neck rots.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If the soil stays soggy and the bottoms of the plants turn yellow and soft, that is too much water. Sitting in wet soil makes shallots rot.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Bluish, wilting, or tip-burned leaves and stalled growth indicate the clump is short of water; under-watered shallots stay small and turn more pungent.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Wilting, bluish, or brown-tipped leaves mean the shallots are too dry. Shallots that do not get enough water stay small and taste sharper.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Base or drip watering keeps the foliage dry, which matters for shallots because lingering leaf wetness feeds the neck and downy mildew diseases that spoil bulbs in storage.
watering.method_note_beginner: Watering at the base instead of over the leaves keeps the tops dry, and dry tops are less likely to get the diseases that make shallots rot later.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Bulb division and enlargement is the most water-sensitive phase; never let the bed dry out between leaf growth and the time the clump sizes up.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The most important time to keep shallots watered is while the clump is splitting and the bulbs are getting bigger. Do not let them dry out then.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Sets need no hardening; push them into workable soil directly. If you raise seedlings indoors instead, give them a week of gradual outdoor exposure and keep them pencil-thick or smaller at set-out.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: Sets (small dried bulbs) go straight into the ground, no hardening needed. If you grew your own seedlings indoors, set them outside for a few hours a day for a week first so they get used to sun and wind.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Sets are the classic and easiest route: each one divides into a clump of 6 to 12 bulbs. Push sets root-end down with the tip just at or above the surface, 1 to 2 inches deep, at final spacing, since shallots are not thinned. Choose firm, healthy sets; oversized or already-sprouted sets are primed to bolt rather than divide cleanly. Seed is the other path and gives single, uniform bulbs from modern hybrids, started about 8 to 10 weeks before set-out for the largest plants.
start_method.notes_beginner: The easy way to grow shallots is from sets, which are small bulbs you buy and plant. Each set splits into a clump of several bulbs. Push each set in pointy-end up so the tip just shows at the soil surface, and space them at their final distance because shallots are not thinned. Pick firm sets and avoid big or already-sprouting ones, which tend to flower instead of dividing. You can also grow shallots from seed, started indoors about 8 to 10 weeks early, which gives single bulbs rather than clumps.

drainage.saucer_practice_seasoned: Empty the saucer after each watering; shallots must never sit in standing water, which saturates the shallow clump zone and invites rot.
drainage.saucer_practice_beginner: After you water, pour out any water that collects in the saucer under the pot. Shallots should never sit in standing water, because soggy soil around the clump leads to rot.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Use a bag of potting mix with some compost stirred in.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in compost, and a slow-release fertilizer at planting helps.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: A free-draining potting mix blended with compost.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Work in compost for fertility and a slow-release balanced feed at planting.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Water container shallots more often than garden ones. The soil in a pot dries out fast, and dry spells make the clumps small.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Because you water pots often, the food washes out faster. Give container shallots a little fertilizer regularly while the leaves are growing, then ease off once the clump starts to bulb.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Where winters are mild, you can plant shallot sets in pots in fall and let them grow over winter for a spring harvest. Move or cover the pots during hard freezes, because roots in a container get colder than roots in the ground.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: In mild-winter zones, fall-set container shallots overwinter for a spring clump; protect pots from hard freezes since roots in a container chill faster than in open ground.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Shallots grow well in pots because their roots stay shallow. Use a wide container at least 10 inches deep with drainage holes, and space the sets 6 inches apart. Pots dry out faster than garden beds, so check the soil often and do not let it stay dry, or the clumps will be small.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Shallots are shallow-rooted and container-friendly. A wide, well-drained pot at least 10 inches deep, roughly 5 gallons or more, holds a few sets spaced 6 inches apart, each dividing into its own clump. Containers dry fast, so water before the surface crusts and feed a touch more often than in the ground; interrupted growth shrinks the clumps.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Expect to water more frequently than in-ground; the shallow root zone in a pot dries quickly and any drought check reduces final clump size.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Frequent watering leaches nutrients, so feed container shallots lightly but regularly through leaf growth, tapering as the clump bulbs up.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering containers suit shallots well, smoothing out the steady moisture they need; keep the mix free-draining so the clump zone never stays saturated.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: Self-watering pots work nicely for shallots because they keep the soil evenly moist. Just use a mix that drains well so the bulbs are not sitting in water.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Avoid following shallots or other alliums (onions, garlic, leeks) in the same ground; several allium diseases, including white rot and pink root, persist in soil for years. White rot sclerotia can survive decades, so commercial guidance runs 5 to 7 years between allium crops; a home garden can target at least 3 to 4.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Do not plant shallots where you grew shallots, onions, garlic, or leeks recently. Some allium diseases live in the soil and build up, and white rot in particular lingers for years. Wait at least 3 to 4 years before growing alliums in the same spot again.
rotation.good_after: leafy greens or legumes
rotation.note_seasoned: Shallots follow well after a leafy or legume crop and pair poorly before beans and peas, which alliums tend to inhibit.
rotation.note_beginner: Shallots do well planted after leafy greens or beans and peas. Just do not plant beans or peas right next to shallots, since alliums can slow them down.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: After curing, store cured clumps, broken into individual bulbs, in a cool, dry, well-ventilated spot near 32 to 40°F; warmer than about 40°F encourages sprouting. Good storage types hold for many months, often longer than onions.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Once the shallots are cured (dried), split the clumps into single bulbs and keep them somewhere cool, dry, and airy. They keep best just above freezing; a warm spot makes them sprout. Good storage kinds last many months.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Whole cured shallots do not need refrigeration and can sweat in the crisper. Fresh green shallots are the exception, keeping a week or two chilled.
storage.fridge_beginner: You do not need to refrigerate whole cured shallots, and the fridge can make them damp. Fresh green shallots are the exception and keep a week or two in the fridge.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Shallots freeze well chopped for cooking; texture softens, so use frozen shallot in cooked dishes rather than raw.
storage.freezer_beginner: You can chop shallots and freeze them for cooking. They go soft after thawing, so use frozen shallots in cooked food, not in salads.
storage.notes_seasoned: Storage life tracks type: Dutch yellow and red storage shallots keep for many months, while the gray and French types are thinner-skinned and best used within a few months. Thorough curing is the single biggest lever on how long any shallot keeps; use thick-necked bulbs first.
storage.notes_beginner: How long a shallot keeps depends on its type. Dutch yellow and red kinds last many months; the gray and French kinds are best eaten within a few months. Drying (curing) them well is the most important thing for good storage, and any thick-necked bulbs should be used first.

recommended.name: Conservor
recommended.recommended_note: A modern seed-grown hybrid for northern gardens, single-bulbed and very uniform, with excellent storage life. A good choice where long-day adaptation and long keeping matter.

recommended.name: Ambition
recommended.recommended_note: A popular seed-grown hybrid producing round, coppery bulbs that store well; widely grown across the North as a reliable long-day type.

recommended.name: Dutch Yellow
recommended.recommended_note: The common golden-brown set shallot, a dependable, widely adaptable keeper with a stronger, more onion-like flavor; one of the best for long storage.

recommended.name: French Red
recommended.recommended_note: The familiar reddish-brown French shallot grown from sets, the most common dry shallot, prized in the kitchen; a good all-around home-garden choice.

recommended.name: Zebrune
recommended.recommended_note: A long, torpedo-shaped "banana" shallot with pink-brown skin and a mild, refined flavor; easy to peel and slice, adaptable across the central latitudes.

recommended.name: Gray Griselle
recommended.recommended_note: The gray or true French shallot, widely considered the best-flavored; harder to find and a poor keeper (two to three months), so grow it to eat fresh, not to store.

recommended.name: Southern multiplier
recommended.recommended_note: The traditional Southern multiplier or green shallot, grown from sets through the mild-winter South for fresh green shallots and small bulbs; short-day adapted to the lower latitudes.

varieties.note_seasoned: Choose by how you will use them, then by what suits your latitude. Set-grown traditional shallots (Dutch Yellow, French Red, Gray Griselle, Southern multiplier) divide into clumps and are forgiving about day length; modern seed hybrids (Conservor, Ambition) give single, uniform bulbs and are typed long-day for the North. As a rule, the Dutch yellow and red types store longest while the gray and French types are best eaten within a few months.
varieties.note_beginner: Pick a shallot by how you want to use it and where you live. The traditional kinds grown from sets, like Dutch Yellow, French Red, and the gourmet Gray, split into clumps and are easy about day length. The newer kinds grown from seed, like Conservor and Ambition, make single bulbs and suit the North. Dutch yellow and red shallots keep the longest; gray and French ones are best eaten within a few months.

companions.note_beginner: Shallots are good neighbors for carrots, beets, lettuce, and cabbage-family plants, mostly because their strong allium smell is thought to keep some pests away. The main thing to avoid is planting them next to beans or peas, since alliums can slow those down. These are helpful traditions, not sure things, so do not worry if your garden does a little differently.
companions.note_seasoned: Shallots earn their companion reputation mostly through allium scent, which is traditionally credited with deterring aphids and the carrot rust fly, so they pair well with carrots, beets, lettuce, and brassicas. The one firm caution is the legume conflict: alliums are widely held to inhibit beans and peas, so keep shallots away from them. Most of these claims are traditional rather than trial-proven; treat them as low-risk suggestions, not guarantees.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Carrots
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Shallots and carrots are a classic garden pair. The strong allium smell is said to help hide carrots from the carrot rust fly, and the two plants do not crowd each other's roots.

provenance.label: research_backed
provenance.reason: Same allium/carrot call as the certified carrot and onion entries: scent-masking against carrot rust fly is the best-evidenced companion mechanism, with classic intercropping trials showing substantial fly-damage reduction at small scale. Applies to shallot as an allium; medium because the small-scale effect is hard to scale and no single quantified figure was opened to a T1 source for shallot specifically.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Carrots and alliums are the textbook reciprocal pairing. Shallots' sulfur scent helps mask carrots from the carrot rust fly, and the two have complementary root habits. Intercropping trials have measured real reductions in carrot fly where alliums and carrots grow together. Plant in alternating rows with enough shallot density for the scent-masking to register; the strongest results come from small mixed plantings rather than large solid blocks.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Beets
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Beets and shallots grow well side by side. They like the same cool weather and stay out of each other's way.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Rests on the general allium pest-repel reputation plus non-competition (different root and canopy profiles). Widely recommended and sound on space grounds, but no beet-specific measured effect. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Beets and shallots share a bed comfortably. The allium pungency helps deter pests that bother beets, and because shallots bulb shallowly with sparse upright foliage while beets put their energy into a single root, the two do not crowd each other above or below ground. Mostly a good-neighbor, efficient-space pairing with a modest pest-repel bonus.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Lettuce
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Fast little lettuce plants fit nicely in the gaps between shallots and like the same cool season, so you get two crops from one spot.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Complementary root and canopy space efficiency (extension-endorsed interplant logic) plus a modest allium aphid-repel bonus. Sound and widely taught but a space/timing benefit rather than a measured lettuce-specific effect. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Lettuce and shallots interplant efficiently. Lettuce is shallow-rooted and quick while shallots send narrow clumps down with little leafy spread, so they occupy different space and the lettuce fills in between rows. The allium scent offers a little aphid deterrence over the lettuce as a bonus. Treat it as a space-and-timing pairing first, mild pest help second.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Brassicas (cabbage, broccoli)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Cabbage and broccoli like the same cool weather as shallots, and the strong allium smell is thought to bother some of their pests.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Mirrors the certified broccoli<-onion call: extension trial work including alliums in a mix reduced cabbage looper and imported cabbageworm in brassicas. extension_backed/medium because alliums were used within a multi-species mix rather than isolated, and shallot specifically was not the trialed allium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Shallots are a well-supported brassica companion through the allium family effect. Their sulfur scent helps mask the cabbage family and deter its signature pests, and extension trial work with alliums in a mix showed reduced caterpillar damage. Alliums are shallow and undemanding, so they tuck between brassicas without competing for the heavy feeding those crops want.

good_seasoned.name: Carrots
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: The pungent allium foliage is widely cited as masking the scent cues carrot rust fly uses to find carrots, and the two have complementary root habits. The pairing is traditional and intuitive, with small-scale trial support, though not cleanly demonstrated at the bed scale for shallot specifically.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Long-standing allium interplanting tradition with a plausible scent-masking mechanism; specific-pair field evidence is at small scale.

good_seasoned.name: Beets
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional bed companion: similar cool-season culture and shallow, non-competing form make beets an easy neighbor that uses space efficiently alongside shallots.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Compatible culture and spacing; a conventional pairing rather than a research-demonstrated benefit.

good_seasoned.name: Lettuce
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Quick, shallow-rooted lettuce fills the row between slow upright shallots and shares their cool-season window, a space-efficient and traditional intercrop.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Spacing- and season-compatible intercrop; conventional companion advice without pair-specific trial evidence.

good_seasoned.name: Brassicas (cabbage, broccoli)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Cabbage-family crops share shallots' cool-season timing, and the strong allium scent is traditionally credited with discouraging some brassica pests, with extension mix-trial support for alliums generally.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Shared season plus an allium pest-deterrence claim supported for alliums in mixes; not verified for shallot specifically.

growth_stages.name: Sprouting & Emergence
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: From sets, a green shoot pushes up within a week or two as the bulb roots down; from seed, a single looped seed leaf emerges bent like a hairpin, then straightens into a slender tube. Stands from seed are sparse and uneven; sets are quicker and surer.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: If you planted sets, look for green shoots coming up within a week or two. If you planted seeds, look for thin grass-like shoots that start bent in a little loop, then stand up. Sets come up faster and more reliably than seed.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep the surface evenly moist so sets root in and seed never dries mid-germination, and keep the bed weed-free from the start; allium seedlings are weak competitors. Set sets at final spacing, since shallots are not thinned.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the top of the soil damp so the sets root in well and any seeds do not dry out, and pull weeds early, because young shallots lose out to weeds easily. Space sets at their final distance, since you do not thin shallots.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Note your planting date and first emergence; the gap tells you your soil's pace for next season.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Write down when you planted and when the first shoots appeared. That tells you how fast your soil starts shallots next time.

growth_stages.name: Leaf & Canopy Building
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Each set sends up a fan of upright tubular leaves and begins to split at the base into multiple growing points. This is the stage that decides clump size: the leaf canopy built now sets how many bulbs the clump can make and how large they get. You want vigorous, uninterrupted leaf growth, not a check from drought, weeds, or cold.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Each plant grows a fan of upright leaves and starts to divide at the base into several shoots. This stage matters most for how full your clump gets, so you want steady, unbroken growth.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Push leaf growth: side-dress nitrogen, hold moisture steady, and stay ruthless about weeds. Front-load the feeding so the canopy is built before day length triggers bulbing; nitrogen applied late goes to soft necks instead of bulbs.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Help the plants grow lots of healthy leaves now. Feed with nitrogen, keep the soil evenly moist, and keep weeds out. Do most of the feeding early, because feeding too late leads to soft necks that do not store well.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Track feeding dates and how many shoots each clump throws; that previews how full the clump will be.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you fed the plants and how many shoots each one makes. More shoots now means a fuller clump later.

growth_stages.name: Clump Division & Bulb Initiation
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Once day length crosses the cultivar threshold, the plant stops adding leaves and each growing point swells into its own bulb, so a single set becomes a cluster of 6 to 12. This is the photoperiod switch: the trigger is day length, set by your latitude and the season, not the calendar. The clump bulbs up on whatever leaf count it reached, which is why the leaf stage mattered.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: When the days reach the right length, the plant stops making new leaves and each shoot swells into its own bulb, turning one planted set into a clump of several. This switch is set by how long the days are where you live, not by the calendar, so you cannot speed it up.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: There is no action that moves this trigger; the work was done in the leaf stage. Keep moisture steady so the swell starts without a check, and confirm you planted a type suited to your latitude.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: You cannot make this happen faster, so just keep watering steadily as the clump starts to fill out. If nothing swells, or it swells when the plants are still tiny, you may have the wrong type for your area, which is the thing to fix next year.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Note the date division visibly began and how many bulbs each clump sets; over seasons this confirms whether your variety fits your site.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Write down when the clumps started to split and how many bulbs each makes. Over time this shows whether your shallot type suits where you live.

growth_stages.name: Bulb Sizing
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tops stay green and upright while the bulbs in the clump swell and shoulders begin to show at the soil surface. This is the fast-fill window; steady, even moisture now translates directly into size, while any drought check costs final weight.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The leaves stay green and standing while the bulbs in the clump get bigger below them and start to show at the soil surface. This is when shallots put on most of their size, so keep the watering steady.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Hold even moisture through the swell and taper nitrogen off; late nitrogen now thickens necks and works against storage. Do not bend the tops to force them, an old trick that backfires because the standing leaves are still feeding the bulbs.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep watering evenly and stop adding nitrogen, because feeding now leads to thick necks that do not store. Do not bend the green tops down to hurry them, an old trick that actually makes shallots smaller, since those leaves are still feeding the bulbs.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Log when you stopped feeding and any dry spells; matching those against final size tells you how tight your moisture needs to be.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you stopped feeding and any times the bed dried out. Comparing that to your harvest size shows how steady the watering needs to be.

growth_stages.name: Maturity & Curing
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The necks soften and the tops fall over on their own; most tops down is the harvest cue. After lifting the whole clump, the bulbs are not storage-ready until cured: outer scales turn papery and the necks dry tight, which seals each bulb against rot.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The necks get soft and the green tops flop over by themselves. When most have fallen, it is time to harvest. After you lift the clumps, the bulbs still are not ready to store until they have dried: the skins turn papery and the necks dry shut.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Loosen and lift whole clumps on a dry day, handling gently to avoid the bruises that seed storage rot. Cure one to two weeks in a warm, airy, shaded spot until scales rustle and necks are tight, then break the clump into bulbs and store cool and dry.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: On a dry day, loosen the soil and lift each clump, handling them carefully so they do not bruise. Then dry (cure) them for one to two weeks somewhere warm, shaded, and breezy until the skins go papery and the necks dry shut. Split the clumps into single bulbs and keep them cool and dry.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record the lift date, curing length, and how the bulbs stored; curing time versus storage life is the feedback that pays off all season.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Write down when you harvested, how long you dried the shallots, and how well they kept. That tells you next year how long to dry them.

notifications.body_seasoned: Push sets into workable soil as soon as it can be worked in spring, or in fall in mild-winter zones. Set them tip-up with the point just at the surface, at final 6 to 8 inch spacing, since shallots are not thinned. Firm, modestly sized sets resist bolting.
notifications.body_beginner: Plant your shallot sets now, once the soil can be worked in spring (or in fall where winters are mild). Push each one in pointy-end up so the tip just shows, spaced 6 to 8 inches apart. Use firm, not-too-big sets so they do not bolt.

notifications.body_seasoned: Side-dress nitrogen now and again about a month later to drive leaf growth before bulbing; stop feeding by about mid-July. The canopy built now sets how full the clump becomes.
notifications.body_beginner: Feed your shallots a nitrogen fertilizer now and again about a month later to grow plenty of leaves before the bulbs form. Stop feeding by about mid-July. More leaves now means a fuller clump later.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: A cold spell could make shallots bolt
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A warm stretch followed by several weeks below about 50°F can vernalize young plants: they misread the swing into and out of cold as a completed winter and switch to flowering rather than dividing. Cover young plants through an unseasonable cold spell, especially oversized or sprouted sets, which are already primed to bolt.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Shallots can bolt (send up a flower stalk instead of making a clump) when warm weather is followed by a few weeks of cold and then warmth again, because the plant thinks a winter has passed. If a cold spell is coming, cover young plants, especially if you used big or sprouting sets, which bolt the easiest.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Cover young fall-planted shallots
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Established shallots are cold-hardy, but young fall-set plantings in the South want protection through a hard freeze. Cover them with row cover or mulch when a hard freeze threatens.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Grown shallots handle cold well, but young fall-planted ones in the South should be covered during a hard freeze. Use row-cover fabric or mulch when a hard freeze is coming.

germination_emergence.text_seasoned: Push sets in root-end down with the tip just at the surface, 1 to 2 inches deep, at final 6 to 8 inch spacing, since shallots are not thinned. Plant shallow; burying the bulb or hilling soil over it damages the shallow roots and shrinks the clump.
germination_emergence.text_beginner: Push each set in pointy-end up so the tip just shows, about 1 to 2 inches deep, spaced 6 to 8 inches apart, since you do not thin shallots. Plant them shallow and do not pile soil over the bulbs, because the roots are shallow and that hurts them.

leaf_canopy_building.text_seasoned: Push leaf growth now: the canopy each plant builds before day length flips it to bulbing sets how full the clump becomes. Side-dress nitrogen at about 30 and 60 days, keep moisture steady, and stay ruthless about weeds, which shallots compete with poorly.
leaf_canopy_building.text_beginner: Focus on growing lots of healthy leaves now, because the leaves built early decide how full your clump gets. Feed with nitrogen about a month after planting and again a month later, keep the soil moist, and pull weeds, since shallots do not compete with weeds well.

bulb_initiation.text_seasoned: Clump division is triggered by day length crossing the cultivar threshold, not by anything you do, so there is no action that moves it; the leaf count reached before the switch sets how many bulbs form and how large. Keep moisture steady so the swell starts without a check, and confirm you planted a type suited to your latitude.
bulb_initiation.text_beginner: When the days reach the right length, the plant stops making leaves and each shoot swells into its own bulb. You cannot speed this up, so just keep watering steadily as the clump fills out. If nothing swells, or it swells while plants are tiny, you likely have the wrong type for your area, which is the thing to fix next year.

bulb_sizing.text_seasoned: As the clump swells, taper off nitrogen and let the necks mature; do not bend or break the green tops to force bulbing, since the leaves are still feeding the bulbs and knocking them down reduces final size.
bulb_sizing.text_beginner: When the bulbs start to swell, stop adding nitrogen. Do not bend over the green tops to hurry things along, an old trick that backfires, because the leaves are still feeding the bulbs and breaking them makes the shallots smaller.

maturity_curing.text_seasoned: Harvest when most tops have naturally fallen and necks have softened. Loosen and lift whole clumps on a dry day; careful handling avoids the bruises that seed storage rot.
maturity_curing.text_beginner: Harvest when most of the tops have flopped over on their own and the necks feel soft. Lift the whole clumps gently on a dry day, and try not to bruise them, since bruises lead to rot in storage.

maturity_curing.text_seasoned: Cure in a warm, airy, shaded spot for one to two weeks until outer scales are papery and the neck is tight and dry, then break the clump into bulbs and trim tops about an inch above each bulb. Poor curing is the main cause of storage loss.
maturity_curing.text_beginner: Dry (cure) the shallots in a warm, airy, shaded place for one to two weeks until the skins are papery and the necks are tight. Then split the clumps into single bulbs and cut the tops about an inch above each. Shallots that are not dried well are the ones that rot in storage.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: One set yields a clump of about 6 to 12 bulbs; wider spacing makes larger clumps, denser spacing makes fewer, bigger single bulbs. A 10-foot row at 6-inch spacing returns roughly several pounds of cured shallots in a good season.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Each set you plant gives you a clump of about 6 to 12 shallots. Spacing them wider makes bigger clumps; planting close makes fewer, larger single bulbs. A 10-foot row gives several pounds in a good year.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: All clumps of a variety size up and mature together as day length triggers bulbing, so the harvest comes in one main flush rather than over a long window.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Shallots of the same kind all finish around the same time, so you harvest most of them together rather than a few at a time.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Matching variety type to your latitude and giving each clump room are the biggest first-year yield levers; crowded clumps make many tiny bulbs, and a mismatched type bulbs too early or barely divides.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: The biggest things for a good first harvest are picking a type suited to where you live and giving each set room to make a full clump. Crowding gives lots of tiny bulbs.
factors_seasoned: variety type matched to latitude
spacing for clump room
leaf count at bulb initiation
consistent moisture
early nitrogen then taper
freedom from bolting

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No verified evidence ties shallot bulbing or yield to moon phase; bulbing is driven by day length and temperature. Planting timing follows soil readiness and the cold-snap window, not lunar phase.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Plants send up a hollow flower stalk (bolt) instead of dividing into a clump.
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: A shallot shoots up a tall round flower stalk instead of making a good clump.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Bolting is vernalization, not day length: a young plant that experiences several weeks below about 50°F and then warms reads the cold-then-warm sequence as a passed winter and switches to flowering. Oversized or already-sprouted sets are part-vernalized and bolt readily; planting too early into cold soil does the same. Once a stalk forms, the clump stops dividing and stores poorly.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: This is called bolting, triggered by cold, not by day length. If young plants sit through a few weeks of cold and then it warms, they think a winter passed and try to make seeds. Big or sprouting sets and planting too early into cold soil are the usual causes. A bolted shallot stops making its clump and will not keep.
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Prevention is the only fix. Use firm, modestly sized sets, avoid already-sprouted ones, and wait until soil has warmed past the cold window for spring plantings. If a few bolt, pull and use them soon; removing the stalk does not restore the clump.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: You cannot reverse bolting, so prevent it: plant firm, not-too-big sets, avoid sprouting ones, and do not plant too early into cold soil in spring. If a few bolt anyway, pull them and use them right away, because they will not store.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Tops grow well but the clump barely divides or bulbs stay small.
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Lots of green leaves, but the clump stays small or the bulbs do not size up.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: A day-length mismatch is a common cause: a long-day type grown too far south never reaches its trigger, while a short-day type grown too far north bulbs almost immediately on few leaves. Crowding, late nitrogen, and weed competition also cap clump size.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Often the wrong type for your area, plus crowding. A northern (long-day) shallot grown in the South may never bulb well, and a southern (short-day) one grown in the North bulbs too soon. Planting too close, feeding too late, and weeds also keep clumps small.
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Match the variety to your latitude, give each set 6 to 8 inches, front-load nitrogen so the canopy is built before bulbing, and keep the bed weed-free.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Choose a type suited to where you live, give each set room, feed early so the plant makes plenty of leaves first, and keep weeds out.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Bulbs rot at the neck or base in storage.
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Shallots rot at the top or bottom after you store them.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Harvesting too green, poor curing, excess late nitrogen, and bruising all drive storage rots (neck rot, basal rot). Thick necks never seal properly.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Picking shallots too early, not drying them enough, too much late fertilizer, and bruising all cause storage rot. Thick-necked bulbs never seal up.
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Let most tops fall before harvest, cure one to two weeks until necks are tight and scales rustle, handle gently, taper nitrogen at bulbing, and store cool and dry.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Wait until most tops have flopped, then dry the shallots one to two weeks until the necks are tight, handle them gently, stop fertilizing once bulbs form, and store them cool and dry.

succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Shallots are a single main planting per season. Bulbing is gated by day length, so every plant of a given variety reaches its trigger and matures on roughly the same schedule regardless of when within the planting window it went in; staggered plantings do not yield a staggered clump harvest. The successioned allium is the green onion or scallion, which is a separate crop.

open_findings.summary: Spacing 6 to 8 inches: USU gives 3 to 6 inches for sets and UF/IFAS about 6 inches; the 8-inch upper end is modeled to give each multiplying clump room (wider spacing yields fuller clumps per USU's density note).

open_findings.summary: Regional calendars are set-planting adaptations of onion's frost + photoperiod windows (same species, Allium cepa): the indoor seed-start tokens are dropped and sets are planted directly, so 14 of 20 cells differ token-for-token from onion. Six cells (ca_north_coast z9/z10, ca_south_coast z9/z10, fl_peninsula z10/z11) are byte-identical to onion because those mild and frost-free cells carry no indoor-start token to drop, so the set-planting strip coincides with onion's.

The six identical cells are a legitimate convergence, not a copy. Review item: spot-check the southern fall windows against a shallot-specific regional source.

plant_out.label: main
plant_out.source_quote: Plant a bulb set in early spring as soon as the ground can be worked, or in autumn after the first frost
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Shallots are cold-hardy: sets go into workable spring soil about two weeks before the last frost, as soon as the ground can be worked. The early window banks leaf growth before long summer days trigger the clump to divide. No fall arm in the cold North, where hard winters would kill overwintered sets.

harvest_start.label: main

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Clumps size up across early-to-mid summer as days reach 14 to 16 hours, then mature when most tops fall over. At a 90 to 120 day maturity from a spring set, the first clumps pull in mid-to-late summer; the date is back-derived from the plant-out window plus the fast end of maturity.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The pull window closes at the slow end of maturity, after which whole clumps are lifted and cured one to two weeks before storage. Curing folds into the tail of the harvest window rather than extending the calendar.

3.day_length_note_seasoned: This latitude calls for long-day shallots, which bulb at 14 to 16 hours of daylight. Northern summer days are long enough to trigger the clump to divide on a well-built canopy. Modern seed hybrids are typed long-day; traditional set types are more forgiving here.
3.day_length_note_beginner: Go with long-day shallots, like the seed hybrids, or any reliable set type. They wait for long summer days before forming bulbs, which suits the long days where you live.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the colder northern states (zones 3 to 7), shallots are a one-time spring crop grown from sets. Plant the little bulbs as soon as the ground can be worked, pointy-end up, 6 to 8 inches apart. Each set splits into a clump of several shallots that you dig in mid-to-late summer once the tops flop over. Long-day or any reliable set type works here. Winters are too hard for fall planting in the open ground.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In the cold-winter North (zones 3 to 7), shallot is a single spring-planted crop from sets. Push sets into workable soil about two weeks before the last frost, 6 to 8 inches apart, tip at the surface. The clump divides and sizes up as summer days reach 14 to 16 hours, then matures when most tops fall, roughly 90 to 120 days out. Long-day seed hybrids and traditional set types both perform; fall planting is not viable in the open ground here.

crops.description_seasoned: Shallot (Allium cepa, Aggregatum group) is a cool-season allium grown for the small, fine-grained bulbs prized for their mild, sweet, faintly garlicky flavor. Its signature is multiplication: plant one set and it divides underground into a cluster of 6 to 12 bulbs, so you lift a whole clump where an onion gives a single bulb. Like the bulb onion it shares a species with, shallot is photoperiodic, a cluster sizes up only once day length crosses a cultivar threshold, which is why the right type tracks your latitude. Traditional set-grown shallots are more forgiving about day length than seed onions, but matching the type to your region still pays off. Grow it like an onion otherwise: a heavy-feeding, shallow-rooted plant in loose, fertile soil, kept evenly moist while the clump fills, then eased off water as the tops fall to begin curing. Well-cured shallots store for months, often longer than onions.
crops.description_beginner: A shallot is a small, mild onion relative that grows in a cluster. Here is the fun part: you plant one little bulb (called a set) and it splits underground into a bunch of 6 to 12 bulbs, so you dig up a whole clump from each one you planted. Shallots taste sweeter and gentler than regular onions, with a hint of garlic, and they keep for many months once dried. They are the same species as the onion, so like onions they start making bulbs based on how long the days are, not on the calendar. The traditional kinds grown from sets are easygoing about this, but it still helps to pick a type suited to where you live. Give them rich, loose soil and full sun, water them steadily, and they are one of the easiest alliums to grow.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: A shallot clump is ready when most of the tops have yellowed and fallen over on their own and the necks have started to soften and dry, usually 90 to 120 days from a spring set. Lift the whole cluster on a dry day, brush off loose soil, and cure before storing. You can also pull green shallots early, at 50 to 60 days, for fresh use like scallions.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Your shallots are ready to dig when most of the leafy tops have flopped over and turned yellow and the necks feel soft, usually about 3 to 4 months after planting sets in spring. Dig up the whole clump on a dry day, then dry (cure) the bulbs before storing. If you want fresh green shallots sooner, you can pull a few young plants at around 50 to 60 days and use them like green onions.

photoperiod.explainer_seasoned: Shallot is the same species as the bulb onion (Allium cepa), so it is photoperiodic: the clump stops adding leaves and starts dividing into bulbs only once day length crosses a cultivar threshold. Types fall into the same classes by latitude, long-day at 14 to 16 hours, intermediate-day at 12 to 14 hours, and short-day at 10 to 12 hours. Long-day types fit northern latitudes, short-day types fit the South where they are fall or winter planted, and intermediate types span the middle. One important nuance: traditional set-grown shallots are widely reported as more day-length forgiving, closer to day-neutral, than seed onions, while modern seed-grown hybrids behave like day-length-typed onions. Matching the type to your latitude still gives the fullest clumps. Day length triggers bulbing only; it never moves your planting date, which stays anchored to frost and soil temperature.
photoperiod.explainer_beginner: Shallots are the same species as onions, so like onions they decide to start making bulbs based on how long the days are, not on a date. The types are sorted the same way: long-day kinds suit the North, short-day kinds suit the South (where they are planted in fall or winter), and intermediate kinds suit the middle of the country. One nice thing: the traditional shallots grown from sets are more easygoing about day length than seed onions, so they are forgiving for beginners. Still, picking a type that matches where you live gives you the fullest clumps. Day length decides when the bulbs form, but it does not change when you plant, which still depends on frost and soil temperature.

crops.name: Lemongrass

soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Lemongrass grows best in a moist, rich, well-drained loam with high organic content. As a fast-growing grass it is a heavy user of both nutrients and water, so a fertile soil amended generously with compost supports the vigorous clump growth that produces thick, harvestable stalks. Good drainage matters despite the high water demand: soils that stay waterlogged invite root rot. The plant tolerates a range of soil types, so the practical goal is a soil that holds moisture and feeds well while still draining freely.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Give lemongrass rich, moist soil that has been improved with plenty of compost. It is a hungry, thirsty grass, so the better the soil, the bigger the clump. Make sure the spot still drains, because soil that stays soggy can rot the roots.

ph.note_seasoned: Lemongrass is not fussy about pH and tolerates a wide range of soils. A preferred range of 6.0 to 7.5 keeps the full spectrum of nutrients available to this fast-growing, nutrient-hungry grass, and it will grow acceptably in mildly acidic through mildly alkaline ground. No specific pH figure is published in the Tier-1 extension guides consulted, so this range is modeled from the plant's documented tolerance of varied soils and from general practice for culinary grasses.
ph.note_beginner: Lemongrass is easygoing about soil pH. Aim for roughly 6.0 to 7.5, which is ordinary garden soil, and you will not need to make any special adjustment.

fertilizer.timing: Weekly to every other week through the active summer growing season; ease off as fall approaches
fertilizer.example_product: balanced soluble fertilizer at half strength (as recommended for lemongrass), or a nitrogen-forward all-purpose liquid
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Like other grasses, lemongrass is a heavy nitrogen feeder, and steady feeding drives the vigorous leaf and stalk growth that makes a productive clump. Utah State Extension recommends feeding weekly with a half-strength solution of a balanced soluble fertilizer from June through September; a nitrogen-forward all-purpose liquid every one to two weeks works similarly. Container plants need more frequent feeding than in-ground clumps because nutrients leach with each watering. Taper feeding as fall approaches so growth is not pushed into cold weather.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Lemongrass is a hungry grass and grows fastest when fed often. Use a liquid fertilizer at about half strength every week or two through the summer. If it is in a pot, feed a bit more often, since watering washes nutrients out. Stop feeding as fall nears.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time to feed your lemongrass. Grasses are heavy nitrogen users; apply a balanced soluble fertilizer at half strength, or a nitrogen-forward all-purpose liquid, every one to two weeks through the summer growing season. Feed container plants a little more often.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Your lemongrass could use a feed. Mix a liquid fertilizer to about half the label strength and water it in at the base. Do this every week or two through summer, a bit more often for pots.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: Nitrogen-forward; a balanced soluble at half strength or a higher-first-number all-purpose liquid keeps this fast-growing grass in vigorous leaf
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a general-purpose feed higher in the first number (nitrogen)
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: Half-strength soluble fertilizer weekly through summer; more frequent for containers as nutrients leach
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Half the label strength, every week or two through summer

pests.name: Generally pest-resistant (aromatic-oil deterrence)
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Healthy in-ground lemongrass rarely shows insect damage. Extension guides describe it as essentially free of pest problems when grown well, an effect attributed to the citral-rich essential oils in its foliage that repel many insects. Scattered chewing or a few sap-feeders may appear on stressed or crowded plants but seldom rise to a real infestation outdoors.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Lemongrass is one of the least pest-troubled herbs you can grow. Its own lemony oils keep most bugs away, so outdoor plants usually look clean.
pests.cause_seasoned: The plant's aromatic oils (notably citral) are used in insect-repellent products. Robust, well-watered clumps in full sun are the least attractive to pests; stress and crowding are what invite occasional trouble.
pests.cause_beginner: Lemongrass makes lemony oils that many insects dislike, so it is naturally left alone. Keeping it healthy and unstressed keeps it that way.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rarely needed outdoors. For the occasional sap-feeder, a strong jet of water or an insecticidal soap spray is sufficient. Remove and destroy badly damaged outer leaves. Improving airflow and vigor usually resolves minor issues without any product.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: You will seldom need to treat lemongrass. If you do see a few bugs, blast them off with water or use an insecticidal soap. Trim off any damaged leaves.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Grow in full sun with rich soil and steady water to keep clumps vigorous, and divide crowded clumps so air moves through them. Vigorous plants are the best defense.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep lemongrass healthy with sun, rich soil, and plenty of water, and divide it when it gets crowded. A strong plant rarely has pest trouble.

pests.name: Spider mites (indoor and hot, dry conditions)
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine stippling or a dusty, faded look on the leaf blades, sometimes with delicate webbing where the leaf meets the stem, most often on plants overwintered indoors or grown in hot, dry, stagnant air. Heavy feeding bronzes and dries the foliage.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny specks and a faded, dusty look on the leaves, sometimes with fine webbing. This shows up mostly on plants kept indoors over winter.
pests.cause_seasoned: Spider mites (Tetranychidae) thrive in the warm, dry, low-airflow conditions of a heated indoor room, which is exactly where potted lemongrass spends the winter. They are far less of a problem on well-watered outdoor clumps.
pests.cause_beginner: Spider mites are tiny pests that love warm, dry indoor air. They tend to appear on lemongrass that is overwintering inside.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rinse the foliage with a strong spray of water, raise humidity around indoor plants, and treat persistent infestations with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil, covering the leaf undersides. Cutting the plant back hard before bringing it indoors reduces the mite population it carries in.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray the leaves with water to knock mites off and raise the humidity around indoor plants. For stubborn cases, use insecticidal soap. Cutting the plant back before bringing it inside helps a lot.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Before overwintering, cut the plant back and inspect it, and keep indoor humidity up with misting or a nearby water tray. Avoid hot, dry, stagnant spots for indoor pots.
pests.prevention_beginner: Before bringing lemongrass indoors, trim it back and check it over. Keep the indoor air from getting too hot and dry by misting now and then.

diseases.name: Lemongrass rust
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small chlorotic (yellow) flecks appear on both leaf surfaces and enlarge into reddish to crimson streaks; on the leaf underside these rupture into powdery orange-brown pustules. Severe infection produces large patches of tan to purplish dead tissue and dries the leaves, cutting yield and quality. It is favored by warm, humid weather and crowded, poorly ventilated plantings.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Yellow flecks that turn into reddish streaks, plus orange-brown powdery spots on the undersides of the leaves. Bad cases dry the leaves out. It shows up most in warm, humid, crowded conditions.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Rust caused by the fungus Puccinia nakanishikii, the most notable disease of lemongrass in humid tropical and subtropical areas; the University of Hawaii CTAHR documents it, and it has been reported on Florida lemongrass. Spores spread on wind and splashing water, and dense, wet, still canopies favor infection.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus called rust, spread by wind and splashing water. It is most common where it is warm, humid, and the plants are packed close together.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy heavily infected leaves to reduce spore load, and open the clump up by dividing and thinning to improve airflow. Water at the base rather than overhead so leaves dry quickly. Copper-based fungicides can be used preventively where rust pressure is high; culture is the primary control.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Cut off and throw away badly spotted leaves, and thin or divide crowded clumps so air moves through. Water at the base, not over the leaves. A copper fungicide can help if rust is a recurring problem.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space and divide clumps for good air movement, water at the soil line to keep foliage dry, and avoid overhead irrigation in humid weather. Vigorous, uncrowded plants in full sun resist rust best.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Give plants room, divide crowded clumps, and water at the base so the leaves stay dry. Good airflow and full sun are the best prevention.

diseases.name: Leaf blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Brown, elongated lesions develop along the leaf blades in warm, wet weather and can spread quickly through dense plantings, browning and drying the foliage from the tips and margins inward.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Brown streaks and dead patches on the leaves during warm, wet spells. In crowded plants it can spread fast.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A foliar leaf-blight fungus that is favored by prolonged leaf wetness, high humidity, and crowding. As with rust, still, wet canopies drive it, and it is the second disease of note for lemongrass grown in humid regions.
diseases.cause_beginner: A leaf fungus that thrives when leaves stay wet and plants are packed together in warm, humid weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves, thin or divide crowded clumps, and switch to base watering to shorten leaf-wetness periods. Copper-based products can be used preventively under heavy pressure.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Trim off the blighted leaves, thin crowded clumps, and water at the base instead of over the top. A copper spray can help in bad cases.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Prioritize airflow (wide spacing, regular division) and dry foliage (base watering, morning irrigation). Avoid working in or harvesting from wet plants, which spreads spores.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Keep plants spaced and divided so air moves through, and water at the base so leaves dry fast. Try not to handle the plants while they are wet.

diseases.name: Root rot (overwatering in poor drainage)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellowing, wilting, and collapse of stalks despite wet soil, with soft, dark, decayed roots and stalk bases. It appears when a thirsty plant is grown in soil that stays waterlogged, especially in containers with poor drainage.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The plant yellows, wilts, and rots at the base even though the soil is wet. The roots turn soft and dark. This comes from soil that stays soggy.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Although lemongrass demands abundant water, its roots rot in soil that is chronically waterlogged. Soil-borne rot organisms take hold when drainage is poor or a pot sits in standing water, so drainage is as important as watering volume.
diseases.cause_beginner: Lemongrass loves water but hates sitting in it. If the soil or pot does not drain, the roots rot.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once roots are extensively rotted; remove affected plants. Improve drainage, repot into a free-draining mix, empty saucers after watering, and water generously but allow excess to drain freely.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot save a badly rotted plant, so remove it. Fix the drainage, repot into fresh mix if it is in a container, and never let the pot sit in standing water.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant in well-drained, organically rich soil; in containers use a free-draining mix and pots with ample holes, and empty the saucer after each watering. Water deeply and often, but let the excess escape.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Grow lemongrass in soil or a pot that drains well. Water it a lot, but make sure the extra water can run out and the pot never sits in a full saucer.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Frequently through the warm season; in-ground clumps deeply 2-3 times per week in heat, containers often daily
watering.frequency_beginner: Water often. In the ground, water deeply a few times a week in hot weather; in a pot, check daily and do not let it dry out.
watering.amount_seasoned: Keep the root zone consistently moist; this is a high-water-demand grass, so err toward generous, deep watering while ensuring drainage
watering.amount_beginner: Keep the soil consistently moist, never bone dry. Lemongrass drinks a lot.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base by hand or flood irrigation rather than overhead sprinklers; keeping the foliage dry limits rust and leaf blight, and base watering suits this thirsty grass. In containers, water until it drains from the bottom and empty the saucer.
watering.method_beginner: Water at the base of the plant, not over the leaves, to help prevent leaf diseases. In a pot, water until it runs out the bottom, then empty the saucer.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing and wilting despite wet soil, soft dark stalk bases, and a soured, waterlogged root zone signal root rot from poor drainage rather than too little water.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Yellow, wilting leaves and a soft, dark base even though the soil is wet mean the roots are sitting in water. Improve the drainage.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Leaf tips and margins browning and curling, slowed clump expansion, and thin, slow-forming stalks indicate the plant is not getting enough water, especially during hot, dry spells.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Browning, curling leaf tips and slow growth mean it is thirsty. Lemongrass wilts and browns quickly when it runs short of water.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: A newly set-out division or rooted start needs consistently moist soil to establish its roots; do not let it dry out during the first few weeks.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep a new plant's soil moist while it settles in. Do not let it dry out.

schedule_by_stage.frequency: 2-3 times per week in-ground; daily for containers in heat
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: This is the main growth phase, when heat and water drive rapid clump expansion. Water deeply and often, ensuring drainage.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: During the hot growing months, water deeply and often. This is when the clump bulks up.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Maintain generous, consistent moisture as stalks thicken to harvestable size; water stress thins the stalks.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep watering well as the stalks fatten up. Dry spells make thin stalks.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Keep moisture steady through the harvest period to sustain continued stalk production from the clump.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep watering as you harvest so the clump keeps making new stalks.

watering.method_note_seasoned: Lemongrass has an unusually high water demand for an herb, yet it still needs sharp drainage. The reconciling rule is to water deeply and frequently while never letting the root zone stagnate. Watering at the base or by flood irrigation, rather than overhead, both suits the plant and keeps foliage dry to limit rust and leaf blight.
watering.method_note_beginner: Lemongrass drinks more than most herbs but hates soggy roots. Water it deeply and often, at the base, and make sure the extra water drains away.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The first few weeks after planting (root establishment) and the peak heat of summer, when a fast-growing clump can dry out quickly, are the moments water stress does the most damage.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Water most carefully right after planting and during the hottest part of summer, when the plant dries out fastest.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Lemongrass is almost always started from a division of an existing clump, from a nursery transplant, or by rooting a fresh grocery-store stalk (leaves and roots removed) in a glass of water, where roots form in about two to three weeks. Seed is possible but slow and rarely used. Start or pot up divisions indoors roughly 8 weeks before the last frost to have a well-rooted plant ready to set out. Transplant outdoors only after all frost danger has passed and the soil has warmed, and harden plants off over several days first. It grows slowly until summer heat arrives, then bulks up dramatically.
start_method.notes_beginner: The easiest way to start lemongrass is from a division or a nursery plant, or by standing a fresh grocery-store stalk in a glass of water until it grows roots (about two to three weeks), then potting it up. Get it going indoors about 8 weeks before your last frost, then set it outside once frost is past and the soil is warm. Ease it into the outdoors over a few days first. It stays small until summer heat kicks in, then takes off.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Whole fresh stalks keep for several days to about a week at cool room temperature. For anything longer, refrigerate or freeze. The tough stalks are far more durable than tender leafy herbs.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Fresh stalks last a few days to a week on the counter. For longer storage, use the fridge or freezer.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Wrapped loosely or sealed in a bag, fresh stalks keep 2 to 3 weeks in the refrigerator. Unlike basil, lemongrass has no chilling-injury problem and refrigerates well.
storage.fridge_beginner: Lemongrass keeps well in the fridge, about 2 to 3 weeks, wrapped or in a bag. Cold does not hurt it the way it does basil.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Lemongrass freezes excellently and is the best way to keep a large harvest. Freeze whole trimmed stalks, or slice or mince the tender bases and freeze in bags or portioned in ice cube trays; frozen stalks keep their flavor for many months. Leaves can be dried for tea.
storage.freezer_beginner: Lemongrass freezes very well. Freeze whole stalks or chop the tender part and freeze it in bags. It keeps its flavor for months. Dry the leaves for tea.
storage.notes_seasoned: Lemongrass stores far more easily than delicate leafy herbs: the stalks are fibrous and sturdy, refrigerate for weeks, and freeze for months with little flavor loss. Trim the leafy tops and peel tough outer layers before storing the tender stalk base you cook with. The cut leaves dry well for tea.
storage.notes_beginner: Lemongrass is easy to store. Keep stalks in the fridge for a couple of weeks or freeze them for months. Trim the tops and peel the tough outer layers off the part you cook with. Dry the leaves for tea.

recommended: West Indian lemongrass (Cymbopogon citratus): the common culinary lemongrass, of Malaysian origin, grown for its thick, tender edible stalks; this is the type sold as grocery-store lemongrass and the one to grow for cooking

East Indian lemongrass (Cymbopogon flexuosus, also called Cochin or Malabar grass): native to India, Sri Lanka, Burma, and Thailand; also culinary and a major source of lemongrass essential oil, with somewhat more slender stalks

Citronella grass (Cymbopogon nardus / C. winterianus): a related but non-culinary species grown for citronella oil and as an ornamental insect-repellent plant; do not confuse it with edible lemongrass for cooking
varieties.note_seasoned: For cooking, grow West Indian lemongrass (Cymbopogon citratus), the species with the plump, tender stalk bases used in kitchens and the one usually sold fresh in stores. East Indian lemongrass (C. flexuosus) is also edible and is the main oil-crop species, with more slender stalks. The genus Cymbopogon holds dozens of species, and it is worth knowing that citronella grass (C. nardus and C. winterianus), the source of citronella oil, is a close relative that looks similar but is grown for repellent oil and ornament, not for eating. When buying a plant or a rooting stalk for the kitchen, confirm it is C. citratus.
varieties.note_beginner: For cooking, choose West Indian lemongrass (Cymbopogon citratus), the kind sold in grocery stores with the thick, tender stalks. There is also East Indian lemongrass (C. flexuosus), which is edible too and used for oil. Watch out for citronella grass, a lookalike relative grown to make citronella oil and to repel bugs, not for eating. If you want to cook with it, make sure you are getting C. citratus.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Tomatoes
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Lemongrass shares tomatoes' love of heat, full sun, and steady water, and its strong citrus oils are a traditional insect deterrent, so gardeners often tuck a clump at the corner of a warm-season bed. Give it room, since a mature clump is large.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Lemongrass essential oils (citral, geraniol) are well documented as insect repellents, and it is a common companion-planting recommendation for warm-season vegetable beds, but I found no Tier-1 extension trial measuring a lemongrass companion effect on tomato. Labeled traditional/low: sound shared-conditions rationale plus a real repellent mechanism, but no crop-specific measurement on this pairing.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Lemongrass and tomatoes both want heat, sun, and regular water, so they make easy neighbors. Lemongrass's strong lemony scent is a traditional way to help keep some insects away. Just give the grass its own space, because it grows into a big clump.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Peppers
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Peppers want the same heat, sun, and moisture as lemongrass and mature on a similar warm-season schedule, so they share a bed comfortably. The grass's aromatic oils are a traditional pest deterrent for the planting.

provenance.label: traditional
