crops.name: Marigold
crops.flower_type: single to fully double, daisy- to carnation- and pompon-form
crops.description_seasoned: Marigold (Tagetes species) is a warm-season, frost-tender annual in the Asteraceae family, native to Mexico and Central America. It is grown for showy blooms and as the classic companion plant, in three main types: compact French marigolds (Tagetes patula), tall large-pompon African or American marigolds (Tagetes erecta), and petite, lacy, edible-flowered Signet marigolds (Tagetes tenuifolia). Sown into warm soil after frost, it reaches first bloom in roughly 7 to 9 weeks and flowers continuously from summer until the first fall frost. It thrives in heat, full sun, and even poor soil, and is notably drought-tolerant once established. Its best-supported pest function is nematode suppression: French marigolds grown as a dense cover stand and incorporated lower root-knot nematode populations for the following crop.
crops.description_beginner: Marigolds are easy, cheerful flowers and the classic companion plant, grown for blooms rather than food. They love heat and full sun, handle poor soil and dry spells, and bloom from summer until the first fall frost. There are three main kinds: small bushy French marigolds, tall big-flowered African (or American) marigolds, and tiny lacy Signet marigolds with edible petals. Plant the seeds outside after your last frost once the soil is warm, and you get flowers in about two months. Keep snipping off faded blooms to get more. Their most proven garden trick is fighting soil nematodes: grow a thick patch of French marigolds and dig them in before planting vegetables that nematodes attack.

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Marigolds are not fussy and grow in most ordinary garden soil as long as water drains away and does not pool. Soil that is moderately fertile and well drained is ideal; very rich soil grows lots of leaves and fewer flowers. Avoid soggy ground, which rots the roots. If your soil is very acidic, the leaves can speckle bronze, so a normal garden range works best.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Marigolds want moderately fertile, well-drained soil and tolerate a wide range of textures, including poorer ground; the consistent failure is wet, poorly drained soil that rots roots and crowns. They are light feeders, so over-rich soil pushes foliage at the expense of bloom. On strongly acidic soil (below about pH 5.5), foliage can show a bronze speckling from manganese or iron toxicity, so a near-neutral range is preferred.

ph.note_beginner: Marigolds are not picky about soil pH (how acidic or alkaline the soil is). A normal garden range around 6.0 to 7.0 is ideal, and you usually do not need to change anything. Only very acidic soil, below about 5.5, can cause speckled, bronze-looking leaves.
ph.note_seasoned: Marigolds perform best across roughly 6.0 to 7.0 and tolerate a little outside that. No pH adjustment is typically warranted, but strongly acidic soil (below about 5.5) can trigger manganese or iron toxicity that bronze-speckles the foliage, so favor a near-neutral bed.

crops.tip_seasoned: Soil warmth, not the calendar, is the real germination trigger: direct-sow into soil near 65 to 70 °F after frost and seedlings break ground in 5 to 8 days. Go light on nitrogen and avoid overwatering, both of which give leaves at the expense of bloom; deadhead or cut for the vase to sustain flowering to frost. For root-knot nematode pressure, grow French types (Tagetes patula) as a dense, solid cover stand for two months before the susceptible crop, then turn them under, rather than scattering a few among the vegetables.
crops.tip_beginner: Wait until the soil is warm (about 65 to 70 °F) before planting marigold seeds outside; they sprout in under a week in warm soil. Go easy on fertilizer and do not overwater, since both give you lots of leaves but fewer flowers. Snip off faded blooms (deadheading) to keep more coming. If you have a nematode problem in a vegetable bed, the trick that actually works is to plant a thick patch of French marigolds there for a couple of months first, then dig them in, not just dotting a few among your vegetables.

fertilizer.timing: At planting, then sparingly
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Marigolds are light feeders; a modest balanced dose worked into the soil at planting is usually all they need. Excess nitrogen pushes soft, leafy growth and suppresses bloom, so favor a balanced or slightly lower-nitrogen feed over a high-nitrogen one, and skip routine feeding once established.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Marigolds do not need much feeding. Mix a little balanced fertilizer or compost into the soil before planting and that is usually plenty. Too much fertilizer, especially the high-nitrogen kind, gives you leaves instead of flowers, so go light.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time for an optional light feed. Marigolds are light feeders, so one modest dose of a balanced fertilizer supports steady bloom; skip it entirely if you mixed compost or fertilizer into the bed at planting.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: It is a good time to give your marigolds a little feed if you want. They do not need much, so one light dose of a balanced fertilizer is plenty, and you can skip it if you already worked some into the soil at planting.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 worked in at planting suits marigolds better than a high-nitrogen lawn-type feed, which favors foliage over flowers.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: The three numbers on fertilizer (N-P-K) are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. For marigolds, pick a balanced one like 10-10-10 rather than a high first-number (nitrogen) lawn feed, which gives leaves instead of flowers.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A single light application at planting is usually sufficient; if supplementing, use a balanced fertilizer at about half the label rate for annual flowers. Avoid repeated high-nitrogen feeding, which favors foliage over bloom.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A little goes a long way. One light feeding when you plant is usually enough. If you do feed again, use about half the amount the package suggests, and avoid high-nitrogen feeds.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.note_beginner: Very tiny pests that thrive in hot, dry, dusty conditions and cause fine speckling and webbing on leaves. Marigolds are especially prone to them in midsummer. Spray plants with water and keep them watered to discourage mites.
pests.note_seasoned: Marigold's most characteristic pest: stippling and fine webbing under hot, dry, dusty conditions, worst in midsummer and on stressed or container plants. Raise humidity around foliage with base watering and dislodge with water sprays; insecticidal soap or miticide for heavy infestations.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.note_beginner: Tiny soft insects that cluster on new growth and buds. A strong spray of water or insecticidal soap usually handles them, and the flowers draw ladybugs and hoverflies that eat them.
pests.note_seasoned: Soft-bodied sap-feeders on tender growth and buds; usually held in check by the beneficials marigold flowers attract. Hose off or treat with insecticidal soap if populations build.

pests.name: Slugs and snails
pests.note_beginner: These chew ragged holes in leaves and young plants, especially in damp weather and on tender seedlings. Hand-pick at night, remove hiding spots, or use iron-phosphate bait.
pests.note_seasoned: Ragged feeding on young plants and lower foliage in damp conditions; marigold seedlings are a frequent target. Reduce mulch harborage, hand-pick at night, or use iron-phosphate bait.

pests.name: Japanese beetles
pests.note_beginner: Shiny copper-and-green beetles that chew flowers and leaves in early-to-midsummer. Hand-pick them into soapy water in the morning when they are sluggish.
pests.note_seasoned: Metallic beetles that feed on blooms and skeletonize foliage in early-to-midsummer. Hand-pick at dawn into soapy water; avoid pheromone traps, which concentrate beetles.

diseases.name: Botrytis blight (gray mold)
diseases.note_beginner: A fuzzy gray mold that rots flowers and buds in cool, damp, crowded conditions, especially on the big double African types whose dense blooms trap moisture. Space plants for airflow, water at the soil, and remove rotted flowers.
diseases.note_seasoned: The signature wet-weather disease of marigold (Botrytis cinerea), favored by humidity, crowding, and overhead wetness; the dense double African blooms are especially prone to rotting from the center. Manage culturally: full sun, generous spacing, base watering, and prompt removal of spent or rotted heads. Do not compost infected debris.

diseases.name: Leaf spots and powdery mildew
diseases.note_beginner: Brown or dark spots, or a white powdery film on leaves, more common in damp, humid weather and crowded plantings. Keep foliage dry, space plants out, and remove badly affected leaves.
diseases.note_seasoned: Foliar spotting and occasional powdery mildew under humidity and crowding, spread by overhead wetness and splash. Manage with base watering, spacing for airflow, morning irrigation if overhead is unavoidable, and sanitation of infected debris.

diseases.name: Root, stem, and crown rot (damping-off)
diseases.note_beginner: Wet, poorly drained soil rots roots and stem bases, and young seedlings can collapse at the soil line. Plant in well-drained soil, do not overwater, and wait for warm soil before sowing.
diseases.note_seasoned: Soilborne rots and seedling damping-off driven by overwatering, poor drainage, and cold wet soil at sowing; dwarf French types are prone to rotting if kept too wet. Prevent with well-drained soil, warm-soil sowing, and restrained watering rather than treatment.

diseases.name: Aster yellows
diseases.note_beginner: A disease spread by leafhoppers that distorts and yellows growth and turns flowers green or deformed. There is no cure; remove and discard affected plants so it does not spread.
diseases.note_seasoned: A leafhopper-vectored phytoplasma causing chlorosis, distortion, and virescent (greened) blooms across the aster family. No cure; rogue out symptomatic plants promptly and manage leafhoppers and nearby weed reservoirs.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Keep soil evenly moist through germination and establishment, then water deeply but less often; established marigolds are notably drought-tolerant, and over-frequent shallow watering invites root rot and foliar disease.
watering.frequency_beginner: Keep the soil damp while seeds sprout and plants get going. After that, water deeply but less often. Grown marigolds handle dry spells well, so you do not need to water every day, and soggy soil does more harm than dryness.
watering.amount_seasoned: Aim for roughly one inch of water per week from rain plus irrigation during active growth, applied deeply and less often rather than in frequent shallow doses; let the soil dry somewhat between waterings. Established and especially African and Signet plantings tolerate less.
watering.amount_beginner: Marigolds like about one inch of water a week, counting rain. Water deeply once or twice a week instead of a little every day, and let the soil dry out a bit between waterings. Once established, they handle dry spells well.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base with drip or a soaker hose and avoid overhead wetting; on the tall African types in particular, overhead watering breaks stems and leaves the dense blooms wet, which invites gray mold. If you must use a sprinkler, water in the morning so foliage dries fast.
watering.method_beginner: Water the ground around the plant, not the leaves. A soaker hose or watering can at the base works best. Tall marigolds especially can flop or rot if you spray water over the top, so keep the flowers dry; if leaves get wet, water in the morning so they dry by midday.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting despite wet soil, and soft, rotting stems or crowns signal overwatering or poor drainage; persistently wet, dense blooms also raise gray-mold pressure. Dwarf French types rot readily if kept saturated.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If lower leaves turn yellow, the plant wilts even though the soil is wet, or the base looks soft and mushy, you are likely overwatering or the soil drains poorly. Wet flowers also turn moldy.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting in the heat of the day that recovers by evening, dulling leaf color, and reduced flower size at bud point indicate underwatering, most critically during establishment and at first bloom; established plants are forgiving of short dry spells.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Marigolds that are too dry wilt in the afternoon heat, look dull, and make smaller flowers. They are thirstiest right after planting and when the first buds form, but established plants bounce back from short dry spells.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Water at the base with drip or a soaker hose and keep water off the foliage and blooms; dry, well-spaced plants are the main cultural lever against gray mold and leaf spot. Avoid overhead sprinkling on tall African types, whose heavy wet heads snap stems.
watering.method_note_beginner: Water the soil around the plant, not the leaves or flowers. A soaker hose or a watering can at the base works best, because dry, airy plants resist mold. Avoid spraying water over the top of tall marigolds, which can break their stems.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The critical moisture windows are germination and seedling establishment and the onset of flowering; drought stress at first bud reduces flower size and count, while excess moisture any time risks root rot.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The most important times to keep the soil moist are right after planting while seeds sprout, and when the first flower buds form. Letting plants get too dry then means fewer, smaller flowers, but never keep them soggy.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Not applicable: marigold is grown for blooms and as a companion plant, not stored as food. Cut-flower vase guidance lives in the notes below; Signet petals are an edible garnish but are used fresh, not stored.
storage.room_temp_beginner: This does not apply. Marigolds are flowers, not food to store. See the vase-life tips in the notes. The small Signet types have edible petals, but you use those fresh.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Not applicable: marigold is a cut flower, not a refrigerated edible. See vase life in the notes.
storage.fridge_beginner: This does not apply. There is nothing to refrigerate; marigolds are flowers, not food. See the notes for keeping cut blooms fresh.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Not applicable: marigold is a cut flower and is not frozen for storage. See vase life in the notes.
storage.freezer_beginner: This does not apply. You do not freeze marigolds; they are flowers, not food. See the notes for vase life.
storage.notes_seasoned: Marigold is grown for bloom and companion value, not as a stored edible, so the refrigerate and freeze fields do not apply. For cut flowers, recut stems and strip the strongly scented lower leaves below the waterline (they foul vase water fast), use clean water with floral preservative, and keep blooms out of direct sun. Vase life is several days to about a week. The Signet types have edible, spicy-tarragon petals used fresh as a garnish.
storage.notes_beginner: Marigolds are flowers for the garden and the vase, not food to store, so there is nothing to refrigerate or freeze. To make cut flowers last, trim the stems, pull off the smelly lower leaves that would sit underwater, and use a clean vase with fresh water. They usually stay nice for several days to a week. The small Signet marigolds have edible petals with a spicy, tarragon-like flavor, used fresh.

recommended: Bonanza / Durango (French, Tagetes patula; compact double bedding types, early and uniform)
Janie series (French, dwarf, very early, container and edging)
Single Gold / 'Nema-Gold' (French, single-flowered; the cultivar trialed for root-knot nematode suppression)
Queen Sophia / Sophia series (French, large crested double blooms, bicolor)
Crackerjack / Inca II (African, Tagetes erecta; tall, large pompon cut-flower blooms)
Antigua series (African, compact large-flowered, uniform bedding)
Lemon Gem / Tangerine Gem (Signet, Tagetes tenuifolia; lacy foliage, masses of small edible single flowers)
varieties.note_seasoned: Choose by type and purpose. French marigolds (Tagetes patula) are the compact, bushy, long-blooming bedding and edging workhorses and the type to use for root-knot nematode cover plantings (cultivars such as 'Single Gold' and 'Tangerine' are the trialed performers). African or American marigolds (Tagetes erecta) are the tall, large-pompon types for the back of the border and for cutting; they benefit most from deadheading and staking. Signet marigolds (Tagetes tenuifolia) are the petite, lacy, heat- and drought-tough edgers, smothered in small single flowers whose petals are edible. Single, open-faced flowers serve pollinators better than the densest doubles.
varieties.note_beginner: Pick the type for your spot. French marigolds are small, bushy, and bloom for a long time, perfect for beds, pots, and edging, and they are the type that suppresses soil nematodes when planted thickly. African marigolds are the tall ones with big round pompon flowers, good at the back of a bed and for cutting. Signet marigolds are tiny, lacy plants covered in small flowers, very tough in heat and drought, with petals you can eat. Open, single flowers are best for bees and butterflies.

companions.note_beginner: Marigolds are the classic companion plant, grown to help the rest of the garden more than for themselves. The one pest benefit that research actually supports is against root-knot nematodes (tiny soil worms that damage roots): if you grow a thick, solid patch of French marigolds in a problem bed for about two months and then dig them in, before planting a crop that nematodes attack, they can lower the nematode numbers. Just dotting a few marigolds among your vegetables has not been shown to do this. The old idea that their strong smell drives away insects, rabbits, and deer is traditional belief, sometimes helpful but not reliable. What marigolds clearly do is bring in bees and helpful insects, so they are a cheerful, useful edge or border plant almost anywhere. There is no plant you must keep them away from; just give them room and sun.
companions.note_seasoned: Marigold inverts the usual companion framing: it is the plant you place to benefit others. Its one research-supported pest function is nematode suppression, and only in a specific form: French marigolds (Tagetes patula) grown as a dense, weed-free solid stand for about two months in the target bed and then incorporated, ahead of a susceptible crop, can reduce root-knot and lesion nematode populations via root-released alpha-terthienyl. UF/IFAS is explicit that simply interplanting a few marigolds among vegetables has not been shown to reduce nematodes, and the African types are less effective than French for this. The broader reputation, that marigold scent repels insects, rabbits, and deer, is traditional companion lore: sometimes borne out, not reliably documented. What is solid is that marigold is a strong pollinator and beneficial-insect draw, so it earns its place as an insectary edge or border. There is no biologically antagonistic companion to avoid; site for sun and airflow.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Vegetable beds with a nematode problem (French marigold as a cover crop)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: If a bed has root-knot nematodes, grow a thick patch of French marigolds there for about two months, then dig them in, before planting vegetables that nematodes attack. This is the marigold trick that research actually backs.

provenance.label: research_backed
provenance.reason: UF/IFAS ENY-056, Clemson, Iowa State, and LSU AgCenter all document that French marigold (T. patula) grown as a dense solid cover stand for ~2 months and then turned under suppresses root-knot and lesion nematodes via root-released alpha-terthienyl. The key qualifier (cover/preceding planting, not interplanting) is stated by the same sources.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: This is marigold's evidence-based pest function. French marigolds planted as a dense, weed-free solid stand for about two months and then incorporated, ahead of the susceptible crop, reduce root-knot and lesion nematode populations through root-released alpha-terthienyl. It is a sequential, whole-bed treatment, not a concurrent interplant: keep the stand free of grass and weeds (so nematodes cannot feed on other roots) and follow with the vegetable crop the next season. African types are less effective than French.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Tomatoes and peppers
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Marigolds are traditionally planted with tomatoes and peppers, and they do draw in bees and helpful predator insects. The idea that their smell repels pests is folklore, so enjoy the flowers and beneficial bugs and do not count on them as bug spray.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: The marigold-with-tomatoes pairing is a classic companion tradition. The reliable benefit is beneficial-insect recruitment (aster-family flowers support aphid predators and parasitic wasps); the scent-repellent and the casual-interplant nematode claims are NOT supported (UF/IFAS), so framed traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional pairing whose real, defensible benefit is beneficial-insect habitat rather than pest repellence. Marigold nectar and pollen draw hoverflies, lacewings, lady beetles, and parasitic wasps whose larvae prey on aphids and other soft-bodied pests of tomatoes and peppers. Note the honest limits: the popular claims that marigold scent repels pests, and that interplanting a few marigolds controls the nematodes that bother tomatoes, are not supported by extension trials. Plant them as an insectary edge for predator support and color, not as a substitute for pest control.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Cucurbits (squash, melon, cucumber)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Squash, melons, and cucumbers need insects to move pollen to set fruit. Marigolds bloom a long time and bring in the bees that do that job.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Cucurbits require insect pollination for good fruit set, and marigold is a documented long-season pollinator draw, so improved visitation plausibly helps. likely (not research_backed) because the marigold-to-cucurbit-yield link is inferred from the two solid facts, not directly trialed.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A well-grounded pollinator pairing. Cucurbits depend on insect pollination, with several bee visits needed per flower for proper fruit set, and marigold is a reliable, long-blooming pollinator magnet across the cucurbit fruiting window. More pollinator traffic plausibly means better set and fewer aborted fruits. Plant marigolds in nearby rows so the pollinators they draw spill onto the crop; this is a visitation benefit, not a pest-control one.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Brassicas and beans
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Marigolds add color and bring in helpful bugs alongside cabbage-family crops and beans without crowding them for food. Traditionally they are also planted to deter pests, though that part is folklore.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Companion tradition pairs marigold with brassicas and beans for pest deterrence; the defensible mechanism is beneficial-insect habitat and low nutrient competition. The deterrent claim is unverified for these crops, so traditional/low, flagged as the softest pairing.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A habitat-level pairing. Marigold adds beneficial-insect and pollinator habitat alongside cabbage-family crops and beans with low nutrient competition, and the flowers support parasitic wasps and predators that help manage aphids and caterpillars. The traditional claim that marigold scent deters cabbage pests and bean beetles is not extension-verified; treat it as a loose, garden-ecosystem pairing, kept to the edges so it does not shade lower crops.

good_seasoned.name: Vegetable beds with a nematode problem (French marigold cover crop)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: French marigolds (T. patula) grown as a dense, weed-free solid stand for about two months and turned under ahead of a susceptible crop suppress root-knot and lesion nematodes via root-released alpha-terthienyl. A sequential whole-bed treatment, not a concurrent interplant; African types are less effective.

provenance.label: research_backed
provenance.reason: UF/IFAS ENY-056, Clemson root-knot nematode factsheet, Iowa State, and LSU AgCenter document the cover-crop method and species effectiveness; the same sources state interplanting is ineffective.

good_seasoned.name: Tomatoes and peppers
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Interplanted marigolds raise beneficial-predator and pollinator visitation (hoverflies, lacewings, lady beetles, parasitic wasps), supporting aphid and caterpillar suppression. The scent-repellent and casual-interplant nematode claims are not extension-supported; value them for beneficials and color.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Classic companion tradition; the defensible benefit is beneficial-insect recruitment (extension-aligned in principle), while the repellent/interplant-nematode claims are not supported (UF/IFAS).

good_seasoned.name: Cucurbits (squash, melon, cucumber)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Cucurbits depend on insect pollination for fruit set; marigold's long bloom draws bees into the planting so more flowers set fruit. A visitation benefit, not a pest-control one.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Cucurbit fruit set is insect-pollination-dependent and marigold is a documented pollinator draw; the yield link is inferred, not directly trialed.

good_seasoned.name: Brassicas and beans
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Adds pollinator and beneficial-insect habitat with low nutrient competition; the traditional pest-deterrent claim is not extension-verified for these crops.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Long-standing companion tradition; habitat benefit is defensible, the deterrent claim is not verified for marigold specifically.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Indoor-started transplants need 7 to 10 days of hardening off, increasing outdoor exposure gradually, before transplanting after all frost danger has passed.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: If you started plants indoors, harden them off first: set them outside for a little longer each day over about a week so they get used to sun and wind before you plant them out.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Marigolds direct-sow readily into warm soil (about 65 to 70 °F) at 1/4 in depth and germinate in 5 to 8 days, the simplest method in long-season areas. To gain weeks or for the slow-developing tall African types, start indoors 4 to 6 weeks before last frost (up to 8 weeks for African) and transplant after frost. Pinch tall African types once to encourage branching; French and Signet types need no pinching.
start_method.notes_beginner: The easiest way is to sow marigold seeds straight into warm garden soil (about 65 to 70 °F) after your last frost, a quarter inch deep; they sprout in under a week. For a head start, or for the tall African types, start them indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost (about 8 weeks for African) and move them outside afterward. You can pinch the tops of tall types once to make them bushier.

soil_mix.type_beginner: regular potting mix that drains well
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Use a potting mix that drains well. If it stays soggy, mix in some perlite or coarse sand. A little compost helps with food. Skip heavy mixes that hold too much water, since marigolds rot in wet soil.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: general-purpose well-draining potting mix
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: A free-draining mix is the priority; blend in perlite or coarse sand if the base mix holds too much water, and a modest amount of compost for fertility. Avoid heavy, water-retentive mixes that keep the root zone saturated, since dwarf French types rot readily.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out faster than the garden, so check them in hot weather. Water when the top inch of soil feels dry, and let the extra drain out the bottom. Do not let the pot stay soggy, and try not to wet the leaves.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Watering pots often washes out their food, so feed potted marigolds lightly every few weeks during bloom with a balanced fertilizer, and go easy on it to keep flowers coming.

overwintering.approach_beginner: This does not apply. Marigolds are one-season flowers that die at the first frost, so there is nothing to overwinter. Just plant new seeds or transplants next year.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Not applicable: marigold is a frost-tender annual grown for a single season and killed by the first frost; it is not overwintered. Re-sow or replant each year.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Compact French and Signet marigolds are excellent in pots, window boxes, and on balconies. Use a pot with drainage holes, a well-draining potting mix, and full sun. Tall African types need a larger, deeper pot. Do not let pots stay soggy, since marigolds rot in wet soil.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Dwarf and compact French and Signet series are the container performers, thriving in window boxes, edging pots, and balcony containers; full sun and a free-draining mix are essential, since marigolds rot in saturated pots. Tall African types are workable in large, deep containers but want room and may need staking.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry faster than ground beds, so check in heat and water when the top inch is dry, letting excess drain freely; never let the mix stay constantly wet, which rots roots. Water at the base to keep foliage dry.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Frequent watering leaches nutrients from containers, so a light feeding every few weeks with a balanced fertilizer through the bloom season suits potted marigolds; keep nitrogen modest to favor flowers over foliage.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering containers work for marigolds only if the surface dries between top-ups; keep the wick reservoir from saturating the root zone, since constant moisture undercuts their drought-adapted roots and rots dwarf types.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot can work for marigolds, but only if the top of the soil dries out between waterings. Marigolds do not like soil that is wet all the time and will rot in it.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: As an aster-family (Asteraceae) annual, avoid following marigold immediately with other susceptible asters where soilborne or foliar disease has built up; rotate the bed to an unrelated family for a season if gray mold or leaf spot was heavy. Note the inverse: a French marigold stand is itself a beneficial rotation tool, lowering root-knot nematode pressure for the crop that follows.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Marigolds are in the daisy family (Asteraceae). If they had a lot of disease, do not plant them, or other daisy-family flowers, in the same spot the very next season. On the flip side, a thick planting of French marigolds is actually a good thing to grow before nematode-prone vegetables, because it lowers the nematodes in that soil.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotation matters less for a fast-growing ornamental annual than for heavy-feeding vegetables, but moving marigolds to a fresh bed each year and clearing infected debris at season end limits carryover of gray-mold and leaf-spot inoculum. Used deliberately, a two-month French marigold cover stand turned under is a documented preceding-crop treatment for root-knot nematodes.
rotation.note_beginner: Rotating marigolds is not as important as it is for vegetables, but it still helps. Plant them in a different spot each year if you can, and clean up old, diseased leaves at the end of the season. Used on purpose, a thick patch of French marigolds grown for a couple of months and then dug in is a real way to cut down soil nematodes before you plant vegetables there.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seed leaves (cotyledons) emerge from warm soil within roughly 5 to 8 days.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The first little leaves push up through the soil in under a week.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep soil warm (near 70 °F) and evenly moist; do not let it crust or dry out during emergence.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil warm and damp until the seedlings come up.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Seedlings emerged?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your seeds sprouted?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: First true, finely divided leaves develop; the plant is small and establishing roots.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Real, ferny leaves appear and the little plant starts to settle in.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin or space French and Signet to 8 to 10 in, African to 12 to 16 in; water at the base to keep foliage dry and watch for slugs.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Space plants out (small types 8 to 10 inches, tall types about a foot) and water the soil, not the leaves.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Thinned and spaced?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you spaced out your seedlings?

growth_stages.name: Established / vegetative
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Plant grows bushier with several leaf sets and begins branching; tall African types gain height.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant gets bigger and bushier with more leaves.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pinch tall African types once to force branching; French and Signet branch naturally and need no pinching. Maintain spacing and airflow.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: For tall types, pinch off the top once to make them branch out; small types do this on their own.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Plants established and pinched (if tall)?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are your plants filling in?

growth_stages.name: Budding
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flower buds form at stem tips; stems lengthen toward bloom.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Flower buds start to form at the tops of the stems.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture even at bud point; begin scouting for spider mites and, in damp weather, gray mold.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist and start checking for tiny mites and mold.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: First buds visible?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Do you see flower buds yet?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Blooms open and continue; first bloom is roughly 7 to 9 weeks from sowing (French sooner, African later) and continues to first frost.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Flowers open, about two months after planting, and keep coming until frost.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Deadhead spent blooms, or cut for the vase, to sustain bloom; water at the base and keep heads dry.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Snip off faded flowers (or cut some for a vase) to get more blooms.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: First bloom open?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Has your first flower opened?

growth_stages.name: Seed saving (optional)
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Selected heads left on the plant dry to brown and set viable seed.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A few flowers left on the plant dry out and form seeds.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Leave chosen heads to dry fully before collecting seed; expect hybrids (most bedding series) not to come true.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Let a few flowers dry out fully on the plant before collecting their seeds.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Seed heads drying?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are you saving any seeds?

notifications.body_seasoned: Soil should be warm enough now. Direct-sow at about 65 to 70 °F, a quarter inch deep, after frost danger has passed, or set out transplants.
notifications.body_beginner: Your last frost has passed, so you can plant marigold seeds or transplants outside once the soil feels warm, about a quarter inch deep for seeds.

notifications.body_seasoned: Tall African types branch and bloom better if pinched once now; French and Signet types need no pinching.
notifications.body_beginner: If you are growing the tall type of marigold, pinch off the top once now so it grows bushier. The small types do not need this.

notifications.body_seasoned: First blooms are opening. Deadhead spent flowers, or cut for the vase, regularly to sustain bloom through to first frost.
notifications.body_beginner: Your first flowers are opening. Snip off faded ones (or cut some for a vase) to keep more blooms coming all season.

notifications.body_seasoned: A first fall frost is forecast within a few days and will end the marigold season. Cut remaining blooms to enjoy indoors.
notifications.body_beginner: Frost is expected in a few days, which will end your marigolds. Cut the flowers that are left and bring them inside.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost warning
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Marigolds cannot survive frost. Cover them or cut the flowers before a frosty night, in spring or fall.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Marigolds cannot handle frost. Cover them or cut the flowers before a cold, frosty night, in spring or fall.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Damp weather warning
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Damp, still, humid weather drives gray mold and leaf spot, especially on dense double blooms. Improve airflow, water at the base, and remove rotted heads.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Wet, still, humid weather can make flowers and leaves moldy, especially on the big double types. Give plants room for air, water at the soil, and pick off any rotted blooms.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot weather ahead
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Good news: marigolds thrive in heat and full sun, and summer is their peak rather than a stress period. Maintain even moisture and water at the base.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Good news: marigolds love hot, sunny weather, and summer is their best season. Just keep them watered at the base, especially in pots.

germination.text_seasoned: Direct-sow once soil is near 65 to 70 °F; warmth, not the calendar date, is the germination trigger, and seed sown into cold, wet soil rots or damps off. In warm soil, marigolds sprout in 5 to 8 days.
germination.text_beginner: Plant seeds outside only once the soil is warm, around 65 to 70 °F. Cold, wet soil makes seeds rot instead of sprout. In warm soil they come up in under a week.

germination.text_seasoned: Sow at about 1/4 in depth; marigolds germinate quickly and reliably in warm soil, which makes direct sowing the simplest method in long-season areas.
germination.text_beginner: Plant the seeds about a quarter inch deep. In warm soil they sprout fast, so planting straight in the ground works well.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin or space seedlings by type once they have a few true leaves: French and Signet to 8 to 10 in, tall African to 12 to 16 in. Generous spacing for airflow is a primary cultural defense against gray mold and leaf spot.
seedling.text_beginner: Once seedlings have a few real leaves, space them out: small types about 8 to 10 inches apart, tall types about a foot. Room for air to move helps prevent mold.

seedling.text_seasoned: Watch young marigolds for slugs and snails in damp weather; seedlings are a frequent target. Reduce mulch harborage, hand-pick at night, or use iron-phosphate bait, and water at the base.
seedling.text_beginner: Keep an eye on young marigolds for slugs and snails, which chew tender seedlings in damp weather. Hand-pick them at night or use a pet-safe iron-phosphate bait.

established.text_seasoned: Pinch the growing tip of tall African types once to force branching and more, sturdier stems; French and Signet types branch naturally and need no pinching. Keep nitrogen modest so plants flower rather than run to foliage.
established.text_beginner: If you are growing tall marigolds, pinch off the top once to make them bushier with more flowers. Small types do this by themselves. Go easy on fertilizer so you get flowers, not just leaves.

established.text_seasoned: Maintain airflow and water at the base as plants fill in; full sun, spacing, and dry foliage keep gray mold and leaf spot in check, sharpest where humidity is high.
established.text_beginner: As plants grow, keep air moving between them and water the soil, not the leaves. Full sun, space, and dry leaves are what keep mold away, especially in humid areas.

budding.text_seasoned: Keep moisture even as the first buds form; drought stress at bud point reduces flower size and count, but never let the soil stay wet, which rots roots and buds.
budding.text_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist when the first flower buds appear, but not soggy. Too dry means smaller flowers; too wet rots the plant.

budding.text_seasoned: Scout for spider mites in hot, dry spells (marigold's most characteristic pest) and for gray mold on dense buds in damp weather; addressing crowding and dryness early limits both.
budding.text_beginner: As buds form, check for tiny spider mites in hot, dry weather and for gray mold on the buds in damp weather. Catching crowding and watering problems early keeps both down.

flowering.text_seasoned: Deadhead spent blooms back to the next leaf node, or cut for the vase, to redirect energy from seed set into new flowers and sustain bloom to first frost. French types rebloom well even without deadheading; African types benefit most from it.
flowering.text_beginner: Snip off faded flowers back to the next set of leaves (or cut fresh ones for a vase) to get more blooms until the first fall frost. The small French types keep blooming on their own, but the big types flower more if you deadhead.

flowering.text_seasoned: For a documented nematode benefit, treat French marigolds as a cover crop, not a casual interplant: grow a dense, weed-free solid stand for about two months in the target bed, then incorporate it, ahead of the susceptible crop. Interplanting a few among vegetables has not been shown to reduce nematodes.
flowering.text_beginner: If you want marigolds to fight soil nematodes, the method that works is to grow a thick patch of French marigolds in the problem bed for about two months, then dig them in, before planting vegetables there. Just scattering a few among your crops does not do it.

seed_saving.text_seasoned: To save seed, leave some heads on the plant to dry fully to brown before collecting; most modern bedding marigolds are hybrids, so their seed will not come true to type.
seed_saving.text_beginner: To save seeds, leave a few flowers on the plant and let them dry and turn brown before picking them. Note that seeds from hybrid marigolds will not grow into the same flower next year.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A single marigold blooms profusely over a season; French and Signet types carry dozens of small to medium flowers continuously, while the tall African types produce fewer but much larger pompon blooms well suited to cutting. Deadheading or cutting sustains production to frost.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: One marigold gives you lots of flowers over the summer. The small French and Signet types make many small blooms at once, while the tall African types make fewer but big, showy flowers good for cutting. Keep picking faded flowers and they keep coming until frost.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Marigolds bloom the first season from seed, roughly 7 to 9 weeks after sowing (French sooner, African later), so there is no establishment year; a spring sowing flowers from early summer to first frost.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Marigolds flower the same year you plant them, usually about two months after sowing. There is no waiting year. Plant in spring and you will have flowers from summer until the first frost.
factors_seasoned: Type: French and Signet types yield many small flowers for color and edging; tall African types yield fewer, larger blooms for cutting.
Deadheading and cutting cadence: regular deadheading or cutting sustains bloom; neglected African plants set seed and slow, though French types rebloom well on their own.
Pinching: pinching tall African types produces more, sturdier flowering stems.
Spacing and airflow: adequate spacing sustains healthy foliage and longer productive life by limiting gray mold and leaf spot.
Season length: a longer frost-free season and successive sowings extend total bloom into fall.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No T1 evidence supports a moon-phase planting preference for marigold; left unset.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Flowers and buds rotting with gray fuzz (gray mold)
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Flowers turned mushy with gray fuzz
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Botrytis gray mold took hold, favored by humidity, crowding, and overhead wetness; the dense double African blooms rot from the center.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: A mold called gray mold (Botrytis) rotted the flowers, usually because the air was humid, plants were crowded, or the blooms stayed wet.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Space plants for airflow, water at the base, site in full sun, and remove spent or rotted heads promptly; favor single-flowered or French types in humid sites.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Give plants more room next time, water the soil instead of the flowers, plant in full sun, and pick off faded blooms before they rot.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Tall, leafy plants with few blooms
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Plants grew tall and leafy with few flowers
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Too much nitrogen or too much shade drove leafy growth at the expense of bloom; unpinched tall types also grow tall and sparse.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The plants got too much high-nitrogen feed or too much shade, so they grew leafy instead of flowery.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Keep nitrogen modest, grow in full sun, and pinch tall African types once to force branching.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Next time, go easy on fertilizer, plant in full sun, and pinch the tops of tall types to make them bushy.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Seedlings collapsed or plants rotted at the base
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Young plants fell over, or the base rotted
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Damping-off and root or stem rot struck plants in cold, wet soil or kept too wet; dwarf French types are especially prone in saturated soil.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: A rot at the base, from cold or soggy soil, killed the plants. Overwatering is the usual cause.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait for warm soil (about 65 to 70 °F) before sowing, ensure good drainage, and water less, letting the soil dry between waterings.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Wait until the soil is warm before planting, make sure it drains well, and do not keep it soggy.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Plants blackened by frost
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Frost killed or damaged the plants
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Marigold is frost-tender; frost at either end of the season, planting out too early in spring or the first frost in fall, kills or damages plants.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Marigolds cannot handle frost. A late spring frost or the first fall frost will damage or kill them.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Direct-sow or transplant only after all frost danger has passed, and expect plants to end with the first fall frost.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant only after your last frost in spring, and know that the first frost in fall ends the marigold season.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Speckled, dusty-looking leaves with fine webbing (spider mites)
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Leaves looked speckled and dusty with fine webs
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Spider mites built up in hot, dry, dusty conditions, marigold's most characteristic pest, stippling leaves and webbing the foliage in midsummer.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Tiny spider mites, which love hot and dry weather, speckled the leaves and spun fine webs. Marigolds get them easily in midsummer.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Keep plants watered, raise humidity around foliage with base watering, and dislodge mites with water sprays; use insecticidal soap or a miticide for heavy infestations.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep plants watered and spray the leaves with water to knock mites off. For bad cases, use insecticidal soap.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Seeds failed to come up
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Few or no seeds sprouted
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Cold soil is the usual cause; seed sown before soil reaches about 65 to 70 °F germinates slowly, erratically, or rots.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Cold soil is usually why marigold seeds do not sprout well. Planted too early in cool soil, they come up poorly or rot.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait for warm soil (about 65 to 70 °F), sow at 1/4 in, and keep evenly moist during emergence.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Wait for warm soil, plant a quarter inch deep, and keep it damp until they sprout.

primary.name: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center
UC Statewide IPM Program (UC ANR)
primary.publisher: UC Statewide Integrated Pest Management Program

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Sow successively every 2 to 3 weeks from after last frost through midsummer to keep fresh, vigorous plants coming; older plantings tire as the season wears on. There is no heat pause: marigolds thrive through peak summer.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: For flowers all season, plant a new small batch of seeds every 2 to 3 weeks from after the last frost into midsummer. Fresh young plants give the best flowers late in the season. Unlike cool-season crops, marigolds love the heat, so you do not stop for summer.
succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Successive sowing offsets the gradual decline of older plantings, sustaining bloom volume and plant vigor into fall.

crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Marigold is grown for garden display, companion value, and cutting; cut blooms for the vase when flowers are fully open and the stem is firm just below the head, in the cool of the morning into clean water. Strip the strongly scented lower leaves below the waterline. Deadhead spent blooms throughout the season to sustain flowering to frost.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Marigolds are mostly for garden color and helping the garden, but you can cut them for a vase when the flowers are fully open and the stem feels firm. Cut in the morning and put them straight into clean water, pulling off the smelly lower leaves first. Snip off faded flowers through the season to keep more coming.

open_findings.summary: Per-region planting DATES for the California regions (ca_interior, ca_north_coast, ca_south_coast, ca_desert), warm_arid, and low_desert_az are MODELED on the warm-season-annual frost-bracketed pattern and the certified structural twin zinnia, because the catalogued marigold pages (UC IPM, Clemson, UF/IFAS, UMN) give culture but not region-specific dated planting tables for marigold. Marigold shares zinnia's identical warm-season frost-bracketed lifecycle (plant after last frost, bloom through summer heat to first frost, no heat pause), so the windows are well-grounded climate carryovers; a marigold-specific regional planting-date source would tighten them.

hawaii_tropical year_round:true rests on a CLIMATE DERIVATION (frost-free zone 11 + heat-loving annual + pause_in_heat:false), mirroring the certified zinnia hawaii treatment, not a marigold-specific Hawaii continuity table. CTAHR documents marigold cultivation and marigold-nematode cover cropping in Hawaii, but the specific CTAHR marigold-nematode publication (pd-35) is a scanned PDF and was NOT fetched per the source-or-flag rule; the year-round Hawaii calendar is therefore a sound climate inference, upgradeable if a readable HI-specific marigold source surfaces.

The regional numeric calendar skeleton (per-zone frost dates, planting-window offsets, the 12-token monthly calendars, and the derived successions_realized counts) is carried from the certified warm-season-annual twin zinnia, because marigold occupies the identical frost-bracketed warm-season niche. All consumer prose, biology, sources, and bloom timing were refit to marigold. First-bloom timing differs by type (French ~7 weeks, tall African ~9 to 13 weeks); a representative days_to_maturity of 50 to 70 (mid 60) was used, consistent with the carried harvest offsets. Region-specific marigold confirmation is the daily-review follow-up.

FRAMING (not a sourcing gap): root-knot nematode SUPPRESSION by French marigold (Tagetes patula) is framed as research-supported ONLY for a dense, weed-free solid COVER/preceding stand grown ~2 months then incorporated (UF/IFAS ENY-056, Clemson root-knot nematode factsheet, Iowa State, LSU AgCenter); UF/IFAS explicitly states casual interplanting among vegetables has NOT been shown to reduce nematodes, and African types are less effective than French. The broader insect/rabbit/deer scent-repellent companion reputation is framed as TRADITIONAL belief throughout, not extension-verified. This honesty boundary is load-bearing for the companion and tip prose.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: Author-fresh gold-standard DRAFT (companion_and_ornamental_flower archetype), modeled structurally on certified zinnia. Biology fully refit to marigold (Tagetes) from T1 sources: Clemson HGIC marigold factsheet, UMN Extension marigolds, UF/IFAS Gardening Solutions marigolds, NC State Extension Tagetes toolbox, Penn State marigolds folklore, Iowa State marigolds, UF/IFAS ENY-056 (NG045) marigolds for nematode management, Clemson root-knot nematode factsheet (via the nematode framing), LSU AgCenter marigolds-and-nematodes, and UC IPM marigold. Frost-anchored warm-season regional skeleton carried from the zinnia twin (see findings 001-003). Expect a Claude Code correction loop + daily biology-fidelity review per the pilot workflow.

crops.deadheading_seasoned: Deadhead spent blooms back to the next leaf node through the season to redirect energy from seed set into new flowers and sustain bloom to first frost; cutting for the vase serves the same function. French and Signet types rebloom well even with little deadheading, while the tall African doubles benefit most from it. Pinch tall African types once when young to force branching and more, sturdier stems.
crops.deadheading_beginner: Deadheading means snipping off flowers once they fade. Do it regularly: cut the old bloom back to the next set of leaves, and the plant makes more flowers instead of going to seed. Cutting fresh flowers for a vase does the same job. The small French and Signet marigolds keep blooming even if you skip it, but the big African types flower a lot more if you deadhead. Pinch the tops of tall types once when young to make them bushier.

direct_sow.label: primary

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the northern tier, marigolds grow in one summer window. Wait until a week or two after your last frost, when the soil has warmed, then plant seeds or transplants; the flowers come from summer until the first fall frost. Marigolds bloom fast, so even short northern summers give plenty of flowers, and starting plants indoors helps. You never stop for heat here; cold is the only limit, at both ends of the season.

Wait until the soil is warm (about 65 to 70 °F) and frost danger has passed, then direct-sow or set out transplants; plants bloom from summer to the first fall frost. Marigold's fast development, first bloom in about 7 to 9 weeks for French and Signet types, leaves plenty of flowering time even in the coldest zones, and starting indoors buys a head start where the season is short. There is no heat pause here; the limit is frost on both ends. Sow every two to three weeks where the longer zones allow.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast and Gulf, marigolds love the heat. Plant after your last spring frost once the soil is warm, and they flower all summer right up to the first frost in fall. You do not stop for hot weather here, because hot weather is when marigolds are happiest. The main things to watch are gray mold and leaf spots in the humidity, so give plants space for air, water at the soil, and pick off rotted blooms. In a bed with soil nematodes, a thick patch of French marigolds grown first and dug in can help.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: Across the Southeast and Gulf, marigold is a warm-season bedding workhorse: direct-sow after the last spring frost once soil is warm, and it blooms straight through the region's hot, humid summer until the first fall frost. There is no midsummer heat pause; heat is when marigold performs best. The real regional pressure is gray mold and leaf spot in the humidity, so give plants room, water at the base rather than overhead, and remove rotted heads promptly. Sow every two to three weeks into midsummer to keep fresh plants coming, and consider a French marigold cover stand to lower root-knot nematodes ahead of vegetables.

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In California's inland valleys, marigolds thrive through the hot, dry summer. Plant after the last frost once the soil is warm, and they bloom into fall until the first frost. They handle the heat and dry spells well, so water deeply but let the soil dry out between waterings. Plant a new batch every few weeks for continuous flowers.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: In California's interior valleys, marigold is a long-season warm-weather bedding and edging plant: sow or transplant after the last frost into warm soil, and it blooms through the hot, dry summer to the first fall frost. Heat and sun are ideal, not stressful. Water deeply but let the soil dry between waterings, since the dry-summer climate suits marigold's drought tolerance and overwatering rots roots. Sow successively for a steady supply, and use a French marigold cover stand where root-knot nematodes are a problem.

fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: In Florida, marigolds grow as a warm-season flower, best in the cooler, drier parts of the year and through summer where they can take the heat and humidity. The small French types bloom nearly all year, while the big African types do best in spring. Humidity brings gray mold, so give plants room, water at the soil, and pick off rotted blooms. A thick patch of French marigolds dug into the soil helps with Florida's common root-knot nematodes.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: In the Florida peninsula, marigold is a warm-season bedding plant grown mainly in the cooler, drier parts of the year and through summer where heat and humidity allow; French types excel nearly year round while the large African types do best in spring. Heat and humidity drive gray mold, so space for airflow, water at the base, and remove rotted heads. French marigold cover plantings are a documented tool against root-knot nematodes, a common Florida soil problem.

No frost + no heat pause + a heat-loving tolerant annual = no season-closing factor, so continuous. This is a CLIMATE DERIVATION from sourced inputs, NOT a CTAHR year-round continuity quote (none exists).

harvest_end.label: primary

harvest_end.label: succession
