11.calendar_basis: Frost-free z11 + T1 pause_in_heat:false (UC IPM, no heat stall) + zinnia documented in CTAHR Hawaii home-garden grow-lists = no season-closing factor, so continuous year-round bloom. Climate-DERIVED, not a CTAHR year-round continuity quote (none exists; searched, outcome C). The wet/rainy months raise powdery-mildew pressure but do not stop the crop.
11.planting_note: Sow or transplant after the last frost once soil is warm (about 65 to 70 °F); first blooms in roughly 7 to 9 weeks, then continuous bloom through summer to the first fall frost. Deadhead, or cut for the vase, to keep flowers coming. Sow again every 2 to 3 weeks through midsummer for a steady supply.
11.zone_notes: Frost-free and warm year round, so marigolds bloom continuously here with no seasonal gap; this heat-loving annual simply keeps going, kept fresh by replacing tired plants.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In Hawaii and other frost-free tropical areas, marigolds bloom all year, loving the warmth and sun; just replace tired plants now and then. The humidity can bring gray mold on the big double flowers, so give them room for air and water at the soil. Marigolds are also grown in Hawaii as a cover crop to fight root-knot nematodes in the soil.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: In Hawaii and similar frost-free tropics, marigold blooms year round with no seasonal gap, thriving in the warmth and full sun; replace tired plants to keep color fresh. Humidity raises gray-mold pressure on dense blooms, so favor airflow, base watering, and single or French types. Marigold is also grown in Hawaii as a cover crop against root-knot nematodes, a significant local soil pest.

crops.name: Nasturtium
crops.description_seasoned: Nasturtium (Tropaeolum majus) is an easy, fast-growing, frost-tender annual in the Tropaeolaceae family, native to the Andes of South America. It comes in two habits: trailing or climbing types that scramble several feet across the ground, up low trellises, or out of hanging baskets, and compact bush or mounding types that hold to about a foot. It is grown for three things at once: cheerful long-spurred flowers in warm yellows, oranges, and reds; an entirely edible plant with a peppery, watercress-like bite in its leaves, flowers, and seed pods; and a well-known companion role as an aphid trap crop. A counterintuitive key to flowering: nasturtium blooms best in lean, poor soil, and rich soil or extra fertilizer drives lush leaves at the expense of flowers. It is a cool-preference plant that flowers most freely in spring and fall, slows or stops in extreme summer heat, and is killed by the first frost.
crops.description_beginner: Nasturtiums are some of the easiest flowers to grow, and the whole plant is edible with a peppery, watercress-like taste: the round leaves, the bright flowers, and even the green seed pods, which you can pickle like capers. They come in two styles: trailing kinds that spill from baskets and climb low supports, and bushy kinds that stay about a foot tall. The big surprise with nasturtiums is that they flower best in poor soil. Rich soil or fertilizer gives you lots of leaves but few flowers, so do not feed them. They also make a famous companion plant: aphids love nasturtiums, so gardeners use them as a sacrificial trap to pull aphids away from beans, cabbage-family crops, and squash. Sow the big seeds right where they will grow, since nasturtiums do not like being moved. They love cool weather, slow down in extreme summer heat, and die at the first frost.

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Nasturtiums are happiest in poor, lean, well-drained soil. This is the opposite of most flowers: rich, fertile soil or added fertilizer makes them grow lots of leaves and very few flowers. Ordinary or even sandy, sandy-loam soil that drains well is ideal, and you do not need to add compost or feed. Just make sure water drains away and does not pool, since soggy soil rots the roots.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Nasturtium wants lean, well-drained soil and is one of the few garden plants that flowers better in poor ground: high fertility and nitrogen push vigorous foliage and delay or suppress bloom. Sandy to sandy-loam soils are ideal, and the plant tolerates a wide pH and even neglect, but the consistent failure is wet, poorly drained soil that rots the roots. Skip compost and fertilizer at planting; reserve any feeding for genuinely impoverished soil, and even then keep it light and low-nitrogen.

ph.note_beginner: Nasturtiums are not picky about soil pH (how acidic or alkaline the soil is). A normal garden range, roughly 6.0 to 7.5, is fine, and they tolerate a bit outside it. You usually do not need to change anything.
ph.note_seasoned: Nasturtium performs across a broad pH band and is essentially unfussy; roughly 6.0 to 7.5 is ideal, and it tolerates mildly acidic to mildly alkaline soil. No pH adjustment is typically warranted. Soil fertility and drainage matter far more to flowering than pH does.

crops.tip_seasoned: The single most useful nasturtium rule is counterintuitive: do not feed them. Lean, poor soil gives the most flowers, while rich soil or nitrogen gives all leaves and few blooms. Direct-sow the large seeds where they are to grow, about 1/2 in deep, after frost once soil is near 55 to 65 °F; they resent transplanting, so if you must start indoors use biodegradable pots. Soak seeds overnight to speed germination. As an aphid trap crop, plant a sacrificial stand a few feet away from beans, brassicas, or squash, then pull and destroy it once aphids load up. Pick leaves, flowers, and young green seed pods for the kitchen as they come.
crops.tip_beginner: The most important nasturtium tip is surprising: do not fertilize them. Poor soil gives you lots of flowers, while rich soil or feeding gives you lots of leaves and hardly any flowers. Plant the big seeds right where you want them to grow, about half an inch deep, after your last frost, because nasturtiums do not like having their roots disturbed. Soaking the seeds overnight helps them sprout. If you want to use them against aphids, plant a patch a few feet away from your beans, cabbage, or squash as a trap, and pull it out once it is covered in aphids. Pick the peppery leaves, flowers, and young green seed pods to eat.

fertilizer.timing: Generally not needed
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Nasturtium is the rare flower that should not be fed: it blooms best in lean soil, and added nitrogen or fertilizer drives leafy growth at the expense of flowers. On genuinely poor or sandy soil, at most one light, low-nitrogen feeding can help, but in average soil skip fertilizer entirely. Over-feeding is the most common reason a healthy-looking nasturtium refuses to bloom.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Do not fertilize nasturtiums. They flower best in poor soil, and feeding them, especially with nitrogen, gives you a big leafy plant with few flowers. Only if your soil is very poor and sandy might one light feeding help. In normal garden soil, give them nothing.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Reminder: nasturtiums usually need no feeding at all. Skip fertilizer unless the soil is genuinely impoverished, and even then keep it light and low-nitrogen, since feeding favors foliage over flowers.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: A reminder that nasturtiums do best with no fertilizer. Feeding them usually means more leaves and fewer flowers, so you can skip it unless your soil is very poor.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: Nasturtium generally wants no supplemental feeding; if soil is genuinely impoverished, a single light, low-nitrogen application is the most it needs. High-nitrogen feeds favor foliage over bloom.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: The three numbers on fertilizer (N-P-K) are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. For nasturtiums the best choice is usually none at all. A high first number (nitrogen) is the worst thing for them, giving leaves instead of flowers.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: Typically zero. Reserve feeding for genuinely poor soil, and then use a single light, low-nitrogen application at roughly half the label rate for annual flowers; do not feed routinely.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Usually none. If your soil is very poor, you can give one small, light feeding, but otherwise do not feed them at all.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.note_beginner: Tiny soft insects that cluster on stems and new growth. Aphids love nasturtiums, which is exactly why gardeners use the plant as a trap to lure them away from vegetables. On a plant you are keeping, hose them off or use insecticidal soap; the flowers also draw ladybugs and hoverflies that eat them.
pests.note_seasoned: Expected, and by design: aphids strongly prefer nasturtium, which is the basis of its trap-crop use. On a trap stand, monitor and pull or destroy the planting once it is heavily loaded. On an ornamental or edible planting, dislodge with water sprays or insecticidal soap; resident hoverflies, lacewings, and lady beetles the flowers attract usually keep numbers in check.

pests.name: Cabbage white caterpillars (imported cabbageworm)
pests.note_beginner: Green caterpillars, the larvae of the white cabbage butterfly, that chew holes in nasturtium leaves. Pick them off by hand, or use the natural spray Bt if they get bad.
pests.note_seasoned: Larvae of the imported cabbage white (Pieris rapae) feed on nasturtium foliage, which shares the mustard-oil chemistry of brassicas. Hand-pick, exclude with row cover where practical, or treat with Bt for heavy pressure. Caterpillar holes on edible leaves are cosmetic; harvest clean young leaves.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.note_beginner: Tiny black beetles that hop and chew small round holes in the leaves. Nasturtiums actually draw flea beetles, so like aphids they can be used to pull these pests off more valuable crops.
pests.note_seasoned: Small jumping beetles that pit the foliage with shot-holes; nasturtium is among the plants flea beetles favor, so it doubles as a flea-beetle trap. Damage is mostly cosmetic on an established plant. Floating row cover protects young plantings; pick young leaves from below the worst feeding for the kitchen.

pests.name: Slugs and snails
pests.note_beginner: These chew ragged holes in leaves and young plants in damp weather, and tender nasturtium seedlings are a favorite. Hand-pick at night, remove hiding spots, or use iron-phosphate bait.
pests.note_seasoned: Ragged feeding on seedlings and low, sprawling foliage in damp conditions; the trailing mat of a vigorous nasturtium offers harborage. Reduce mulch and debris, hand-pick at night, or use iron-phosphate bait.

pests.name: Whiteflies and spider mites
pests.note_beginner: Tiny insects on the undersides of leaves: whiteflies fly up in a cloud when disturbed, and spider mites cause fine speckling in hot, dry spells. Spray with water or insecticidal soap if they build up.
pests.note_seasoned: Whiteflies and, in hot dry conditions, spider mites colonize leaf undersides on stressed or sheltered plants. Hose foliage, raise humidity with base watering, and use insecticidal soap for persistent infestations; both are secondary pests rarely needing intervention outdoors.

diseases.name: Mosaic and aphid-borne viruses
diseases.note_beginner: Viruses spread by aphids can mottle, streak, or distort the leaves. There is no cure, so pull and discard badly affected plants and keep aphids in check.
diseases.note_seasoned: Several viruses, mostly aphid-vectored, cause mosaic mottling, ringspots, and leaf distortion. There is no treatment; rogue out symptomatic plants and manage aphid vectors. Because nasturtium concentrates aphids, it can also serve as a virus reservoir, a reason to keep a trap stand at a distance from susceptible crops.

diseases.name: Bacterial wilt
diseases.note_beginner: In hot, humid regions a soilborne bacterial wilt can cause plants to suddenly droop and collapse. There is no cure; remove affected plants and avoid replanting in the same spot.
diseases.note_seasoned: Southern bacterial wilt (Ralstonia) can collapse plants in hot, humid soils, most relevant in the Deep South. No chemical control; remove infected plants and rotate away from the site. Uncommon outside warm humid regions.

diseases.name: Aster yellows
diseases.note_beginner: A disease spread by leafhoppers that yellows and distorts growth and can turn flowers green. There is no cure; remove and discard affected plants so it does not spread.
diseases.note_seasoned: A leafhopper-vectored phytoplasma causing chlorosis, distortion, and virescent blooms. No cure; rogue out symptomatic plants and manage leafhoppers and nearby weed reservoirs. Overall, nasturtium is bothered by few diseases.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Keep soil evenly moist through germination and establishment, then water moderately; established nasturtiums tolerate some drought and even neglect, but bloom and leaf quality suffer if they dry out badly. In heat, watering becomes more important, not less, and keeps plants flowering longer.
watering.frequency_beginner: Keep the soil damp while seeds sprout and plants get going. After that, water when the top inch of soil is dry. Grown nasturtiums handle short dry spells, but they flower and taste better with steady moisture, especially in hot weather.
watering.amount_seasoned: Roughly one inch of water per week from rain plus irrigation during active growth, applied deeply; let the surface dry slightly between waterings. Raise frequency during hot, dry spells, when consistent moisture sustains bloom and keeps the edible parts tender rather than bitter.
watering.amount_beginner: About one inch of water a week, counting rain. Water deeply rather than a little every day, and let the top of the soil dry a bit between waterings. Water more in hot, dry weather to keep flowers and leaves coming.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base with a can, drip, or soaker hose and keep water off the foliage where practical; the dense trailing mat of a vigorous plant stays wet and invites slugs and leaf problems. Morning watering lets any wet foliage dry quickly.
watering.method_beginner: Water the soil around the plant, not the leaves. A watering can or soaker hose at the base works best. If the leaves get wet, water in the morning so they dry by midday.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting despite wet soil, and soft, rotting stems signal overwatering or poor drainage; nasturtium rots readily in saturated soil. Lush, dark, flowerless foliage usually points to over-rich soil rather than water.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If lower leaves turn yellow, the plant wilts even though the soil is wet, or the base looks soft and mushy, you are overwatering or the soil drains poorly. A big leafy plant with no flowers usually means the soil is too rich, not too wet.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting in the heat of the day, dulling leaf color, and smaller, sparser flowers indicate underwatering; bitter, tough leaves and a flowering pause in heat are also relieved by deeper, more frequent watering.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Nasturtiums that are too dry wilt in the afternoon, look dull, and make fewer, smaller flowers, and the leaves can taste sharp and tough. A good deep watering usually perks them up.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Water at the base and keep the sprawling foliage as dry as practical; well-spaced, base-watered plants resist slugs and foliar problems. In heat, water more often to hold bloom and keep edible leaves and flowers tender.
watering.method_note_beginner: Water the soil, not the leaves, and water more often in hot weather. Keeping the big leafy plant from staying wet helps avoid slugs and leaf spots.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The critical moisture windows are germination and establishment and any stretch of summer heat; drought stress in heat stalls bloom and turns the edible parts bitter, while saturated soil any time risks root rot.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The most important times to keep the soil moist are right after planting while seeds sprout, and during hot summer weather. Letting plants dry out in the heat means fewer flowers and sharper-tasting leaves, but never keep them soggy.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Nasturtium leaves and flowers are best used the day they are picked; they wilt quickly at room temperature. Harvest in the cool of the morning and use promptly. Green seed pods for pickling can sit briefly at room temperature before processing.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Use nasturtium leaves and flowers the same day you pick them, since they wilt fast. Pick them in the morning and use them soon. Green seed pods for pickling can wait a little while before you process them.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerate flowers and leaves gently: wash, pat dry, and store in a loose bag or a container lined with damp paper towel, ideally using within a day or two. The delicate flowers bruise easily, so handle minimally and refrigerate only briefly.
storage.fridge_beginner: Keep nasturtium leaves and flowers in the fridge in a loose bag or on a damp paper towel, and use them within a day or two. The flowers are delicate, so handle them gently.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Fresh leaves and flowers do not freeze well for later use, though flowers can be frozen into ice cubes for decoration. The durable storage form is the pickled green seed pods, which keep for months refrigerated.
storage.freezer_beginner: You cannot really freeze the fresh leaves or flowers to use later, but you can freeze flowers in ice cubes to look pretty in drinks. To keep nasturtiums long-term, pickle the green seed pods.
storage.notes_seasoned: The whole plant is edible with a peppery, watercress-like bite. Use leaves and flowers fresh in salads, as a garnish, or stuffed; younger leaves are milder, while stressed or older leaves and hot-weather growth turn sharper. The standout keeper is the green, immature seed pod: harvested young and pickled in spiced vinegar, it becomes poor man's capers and stores for months. Remove interior flower parts and the bitter white petal base before eating the flowers.
storage.notes_beginner: You can eat the whole nasturtium plant, and it tastes peppery like watercress. Use the leaves and flowers fresh in salads or as a garnish; younger leaves are milder. The best part to store is the green seed pod: pick it young and pickle it in vinegar to make poor man's capers, which keep for months. When eating the flowers, pull out the inner parts and the white base of the petals, which can taste bitter.

recommended: Jewel series (bush, Tagetes... Tropaeolum majus; compact mounding ~12 in, semi-double flowers held above the leaves, classic bedding and container type)
Alaska series (bush; cream-and-green variegated leaves, single flowers, very ornamental foliage)
Empress of India (bush; deep blue-green leaves and rich crimson-scarlet single flowers, heirloom)
Tip Top / Whirlybird (bush; upward-facing flowers on compact plants, easy for cutting and eating)
Climbing or Tall Trailing mix / 'Tall Single Mixed' (trailing-climbing; vigorous 6 to 10 ft stems for trellises, fences, and hanging baskets)
Phoenix or Bloody Mary (novelty bush; split, fringed petals and bicolor flowers)
varieties.note_seasoned: Choose by habit and use. Bush or mounding types (Jewel, Tip Top, Whirlybird, Alaska) stay near a foot and suit beds, edging, containers, and the kitchen, with flowers often held up above the foliage for easy picking. Trailing and climbing types (Tall Trailing / Climbing mixes) run 6 to 10 ft and are the choice for trellises, fences, spilling baskets, and quick screening, and they make the most generous trap-crop stands. Foliage-feature types such as Alaska (variegated) and Empress of India (dark leaves) earn their place even between flushes of bloom. All parts of all types are edible.
varieties.note_beginner: Pick the type for your spot. Bushy types like Jewel and Tip Top stay about a foot tall and are great in pots, beds, and edging, with flowers that sit up where you can pick them. Trailing or climbing types grow several feet and are perfect for hanging baskets, fences, and trellises, and they make the biggest patches for trapping aphids. Some types, like Alaska with its variegated leaves, look good even without flowers. Every kind is edible.

companions.note_beginner: Nasturtiums are a famous companion plant, mostly because aphids love them. The trick that actually works is to use nasturtium as a trap crop: plant a patch a few feet away from beans, cabbage-family crops, or squash, let the aphids gather on the nasturtiums instead of your vegetables, then pull and destroy the patch once it is covered in them. Plant the trap a little distance off, not right next to your crops, or the pests just hop over. Nasturtiums also bring in hoverflies and ladybugs that eat aphids. The old idea that their smell drives squash bugs and cucumber beetles away from squash and cucumbers is traditional garden lore, sometimes helpful but not proven. There is no plant you must keep nasturtiums away from, but remember that as a trap they draw pests, so site the trap stand thoughtfully.
companions.note_seasoned: Nasturtium's companion value rests on one well-supported function and several traditional ones. The supported function is as an aphid trap crop: aphids strongly prefer nasturtium, and extension sources report it reduces pest pressure when planted near brassicas, beans, and cucurbits, so it is used as a sacrificial decoy that is monitored and destroyed once loaded. Effective use is sequential and spatial, a stand set a few feet off from the protected crop, not a casual interplant right among it, because a trap concentrates pests (and aphid-borne viruses) where it sits. Nasturtium also recruits aphid predators (hoverflies, lacewings, lady beetles) as an insectary plant. The broader reputation, that nasturtium scent repels squash bugs and cucumber beetles from cucurbits, is traditional companion lore: occasionally borne out, not reliably documented. There is no biologically antagonistic companion to avoid; the main caution is trap placement.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Brassicas and cucurbits (nasturtium as an aphid trap crop)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Aphids love nasturtiums more than they love your vegetables. Plant a patch of nasturtiums a few feet away from cabbage-family crops or squash so the aphids gather there instead, then pull and destroy the patch once it is loaded. This is the nasturtium trick that research actually supports.

provenance.label: research_backed
provenance.reason: University extension (UMN, UC ANR) documents nasturtium as an aphid trap crop that reduces pest pressure near brassicas, squash, and pumpkin, because aphids prefer it. Efficacy depends on placement (a stand set at a distance, monitored, and removed when infested), which the same sources state. Labeled research_backed/medium: the trap function is documented, the magnitude is placement-dependent.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: This is nasturtium's evidence-based pest function. Aphids strongly prefer nasturtium, so a stand grown as a sacrificial trap a few feet from brassicas or cucurbits pulls aphids off the protected crop; extension sources report reduced pest pressure with this use. It is a monitored, sequential treatment: site the trap at a distance (too close and pests simply move onto the crop), scout it, and pull and destroy the planting once it is heavily infested so it does not become a pest and virus reservoir.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Aphid predators and pollinators (insectary value)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Nasturtium flowers bring in hoverflies, ladybugs, and lacewings, whose young eat aphids, plus bees. So even beyond the trap-crop trick, a few nasturtiums help the good bugs in your garden.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Nasturtium is a documented draw for hoverflies and other aphid predators and for pollinators; the resulting pest-suppression benefit to neighbors is well-grounded but inferred rather than directly trialed for nasturtium specifically. Labeled likely/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Beyond the trap function, nasturtium acts as an insectary plant: its open, nectar-rich flowers recruit hoverflies, lacewings, and lady beetles whose larvae prey on aphids, alongside bees. Interplanted at the garden edge, it supports the beneficial community that helps manage soft-bodied pests on neighboring crops. A habitat benefit, well-grounded but inferred rather than directly measured for nasturtium.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Squash and cucumbers (traditional pest deterrence)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Gardeners have long planted nasturtiums with squash and cucumbers in the hope of keeping squash bugs and cucumber beetles away. This is traditional advice and not proven, so enjoy the flowers and the beneficial bugs, but do not rely on nasturtiums as a bug repellent.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: The nasturtium-deters-squash-bugs/cucumber-beetles pairing is long-standing companion tradition, not extension-verified. The defensible benefits (trap-cropping aphids, beneficial-insect habitat) are kept separate; the scent-repellent deterrence claim is labeled traditional/low.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional cucurbit pairing whose repellent claim is not extension-verified. Nasturtium is widely interplanted with squash and cucumbers on the belief that its scent deters squash bugs and cucumber beetles; this is companion lore, occasionally reported, not documented in trials. The honest, defensible benefits in a cucurbit bed are aphid trap-cropping and beneficial-insect habitat, not repellence. Treat the deterrent reputation as a bonus, not a control method.

good_seasoned.name: Brassicas and cucurbits (aphid trap crop)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Aphids prefer nasturtium, so a sacrificial stand set a few feet from brassicas or cucurbits draws aphids off the crop; extension sources report reduced pest pressure. Monitor and destroy the stand once heavily infested, since a trap concentrates pests and aphid-borne viruses where it sits.

provenance.label: research_backed
provenance.reason: UMN and UC ANR document nasturtium as an aphid trap crop reducing pressure near brassicas and cucurbits; efficacy is placement-dependent (distance, monitoring, removal).

good_seasoned.name: Aphid predators and pollinators (insectary)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Nasturtium's open, nectar-rich flowers recruit hoverflies, lacewings, lady beetles, and bees; the aphid predators it draws help manage soft-bodied pests on neighboring crops. A habitat benefit, well-grounded but inferred for nasturtium specifically.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Documented draw for hoverflies and other aphid predators and pollinators; neighbor benefit inferred, not directly trialed.

good_seasoned.name: Squash and cucumbers (traditional deterrence)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Traditionally interplanted with cucurbits to deter squash bugs and cucumber beetles; this repellent claim is companion lore, not extension-verified. The defensible cucurbit-bed benefits are aphid trap-cropping and beneficial-insect habitat.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Long-standing companion tradition; deterrence unverified for nasturtium, separated from the supported trap/habitat benefits.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: If started indoors, harden off transplants over 7 to 10 days before setting out after frost; nasturtium resents root disturbance, so move the whole biodegradable pot without breaking the root ball.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: If you started plants indoors, harden them off first: set them outside for a little longer each day over about a week before planting them out, and move them in their biodegradable pots so you do not disturb the roots.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Direct sowing is strongly preferred: nasturtium has a sensitive root system and resents transplanting, so sow the large seeds in place, about 1/2 in deep, after frost once soil is near 55 to 65 °F. Soaking seeds overnight speeds germination, which takes roughly 7 to 12 days. In very short-season areas you can gain a few weeks by starting indoors about 4 weeks before last frost, but only in biodegradable pots set out intact to avoid root shock.
start_method.notes_beginner: The best way to grow nasturtiums is to plant the big seeds right where they will grow, about half an inch deep, after your last frost. They do not like having their roots disturbed, so direct sowing works best. Soaking the seeds overnight helps them sprout, usually in one to two weeks. If your season is very short, you can start them indoors about a month early, but use biodegradable pots and plant the whole pot so the roots are not disturbed.

soil_mix.type_beginner: plain, lean potting mix that drains well
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Use a basic potting mix that drains well, and do not enrich it. Nasturtiums flower best in lean soil, so skip the compost and slow-release fertilizer that come in many mixes if you can. If the mix stays soggy, add perlite or coarse sand.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: lean, free-draining potting mix (skip enriched or fertilizer-charged blends)
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Favor a plain, free-draining mix over a rich or fertilizer-charged one, since high fertility suppresses bloom; blend in perlite or coarse sand if drainage is poor. Avoid water-retentive, heavily amended mixes that keep the root zone wet and push foliage over flowers.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out faster than the ground, so check them in hot weather and water when the top inch is dry, letting the extra drain out the bottom. Trailing types in baskets dry out especially fast.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Do not feed potted nasturtiums, or feed only very lightly. Even in pots, fertilizer usually means more leaves and fewer flowers.

overwintering.approach_beginner: This does not apply. Nasturtiums are one-season plants that die at the first frost, so there is nothing to overwinter. Plant new seeds next year, or let them self-sow.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Not applicable: nasturtium is a frost-tender annual grown for a single season and killed by frost; it is not overwintered. Re-sow each year, or rely on self-seeding in mild-winter areas.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Nasturtiums are excellent in pots and hanging baskets. Trailing types spill beautifully over the sides of a basket, and bush types suit pots and window boxes. Use a pot with drainage holes and a plain potting mix, give them sun, and do not fertilize. They are a great edible, colorful container plant.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Nasturtium is a strong container and basket subject: trailing types cascade from hanging baskets and raised pots, while bush types fill window boxes and patio pots. Use a free-draining, unenriched mix and full sun, and withhold fertilizer to favor bloom over foliage. Containers dry faster, so the watering, not the feeding, is the variable to manage.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers, and especially hanging baskets of trailing types, dry quickly; check in heat and water when the top inch is dry, letting excess drain freely. Never let the mix stay saturated, which rots the roots.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Keep feeding minimal to none even in containers; the leaching argument that drives feeding most potted annuals is outweighed here by nasturtium's bloom-suppressing response to nitrogen. At most, a single very light low-nitrogen feed if growth is genuinely starved.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering containers are a poor match for nasturtium: their constantly moist reservoir works against the lean, dry-leaning conditions that drive flowering and risks root rot. Use a conventional free-draining pot and let the surface dry between waterings.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: Self-watering pots are not a good choice for nasturtiums, which do not like soil that is wet all the time and can rot in it. Use a regular pot with drainage holes and let the top of the soil dry out between waterings.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Nasturtium is in its own family (Tropaeolaceae), unrelated to the common vegetable families, so it fits almost anywhere in a rotation and shares few soilborne problems with vegetables. The main caution is the inverse of a benefit: because it concentrates aphids and aphid-borne viruses, do not site a trap stand where it will seed a virus problem into a susceptible following crop, and clear heavily infested plantings at season end.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Nasturtiums are in their own plant family, not related to the usual vegetables, so you can plant them almost anywhere and they will not pass on vegetable diseases. The one thing to watch is that, because they attract aphids, a heavily infested trap patch should be cleared away at the end of the season rather than left to spread aphids or virus.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotation is low-stakes for a fast annual in its own botanical family; nasturtium can follow almost any crop and is a useful filler and edge plant. Used deliberately, it doubles as a trap crop, so plan its placement around the aphid-magnet role rather than around disease carryover, and remove spent infested stands promptly.
rotation.note_beginner: You do not need to worry much about rotating nasturtiums, since they are in their own plant family and can follow almost anything. Just remember they pull in aphids on purpose when used as a trap, so clear away a heavily bug-covered patch at the end of the season.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seed leaves emerge from warm soil within roughly 7 to 12 days; soaked seed comes up faster.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The first leaves push up through the soil in one to two weeks.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Direct-sow 1/2 in deep into soil near 55 to 65 °F; soak seed overnight first and keep soil evenly moist until emergence. Do not disturb the roots later.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Plant the soaked seeds half an inch deep right where they will grow, and keep the soil damp until they sprout.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Seedlings emerged?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your seeds sprouted?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Rounded, long-stemmed true leaves develop; the young plant begins to mound or run.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Round, lily-pad-like leaves appear and the little plant starts to spread.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin or space to 10 to 12 in. Do NOT fertilize. Watch for slugs and for the first aphids, especially on a trap stand.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Space plants about 10 to 12 inches apart and do not feed them. Watch for slugs and aphids.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Thinned and spaced?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you spaced out your seedlings?

growth_stages.name: Established / vegetative
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Plant fills in; bush types mound, trailing types extend running stems. Lush, dark, flowerless growth signals soil that is too rich.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant gets bigger, either mounding up or trailing out. Lots of leaves but no flowers means the soil is too rich.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep withholding fertilizer; let lean soil drive flowering. Direct trailing stems to supports or let them spill. Begin harvesting young leaves.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Still do not fertilize. Guide trailing stems onto a support or let them hang, and start picking a few young leaves to eat.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Plants established and unfed?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are your plants filling in?

growth_stages.name: Budding
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Long-spurred flower buds form on slender stalks above or among the foliage.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Flower buds with a little tail (spur) start to form.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture even at bud point; in heat, water more and consider light afternoon shade to sustain flowering.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist as buds form, and water more in hot weather to keep flowers coming.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: First buds visible?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Do you see flower buds yet?

growth_stages.name: Flowering and harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Open flowers from roughly 5 to 8 weeks after sowing, continuing through the season; bloom is heaviest in cool spring and fall and slows in peak heat.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Flowers open about six to eight weeks after planting and keep coming, best in cooler weather.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick flowers and young leaves regularly for the kitchen, which also keeps plants tidy and blooming; deadhead spent flowers. Watch for young green seed pods to harvest for pickling.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pick flowers and young leaves to eat, snip off faded flowers, and watch for the green seed pods to pickle.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: First bloom open?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Has your first flower opened?

growth_stages.name: Seed saving and pods (optional)
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Green seed pods follow the flowers; left on the plant they ripen, dry to tan, and drop. Most older types come true from saved seed.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Round green seed pods form where flowers were. Left alone they dry out and fall, and you can save them to plant next year.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest young green pods for pickling, or leave some to dry on the plant and collect the large seeds; expect open-pollinated types to come true, hybrids less so.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pick young green pods to pickle as capers, or let a few dry on the plant to save the big seeds for next year.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Pods forming?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are you saving seeds or pods?

notifications.body_seasoned: Frost danger has passed. Direct-sow the large seeds 1/2 in deep into soil near 55 to 65 °F; soak overnight first, and do not enrich the soil.
notifications.body_beginner: Your last frost has passed, so you can plant nasturtium seeds outside, about half an inch deep, right where they will grow. Soak them overnight first and do not add fertilizer.

notifications.body_seasoned: As plants fill in, resist feeding. Nasturtium blooms best in lean soil; nitrogen gives foliage instead of flowers. Lush, flowerless growth means the soil is already too rich.
notifications.body_beginner: Now that your plants are growing, remember not to fertilize them. Feeding gives you leaves instead of flowers. A big leafy plant with no flowers means the soil is too rich.

notifications.body_seasoned: Flowers are opening. Pick young leaves and open flowers regularly for salads and garnish, watch for green seed pods to pickle, and deadhead to sustain bloom.
notifications.body_beginner: Your flowers are opening. Start picking the peppery leaves and flowers to eat, and watch for green seed pods to pickle as capers.

notifications.body_seasoned: A first fall frost is forecast within a few days and will end the nasturtium season. Harvest remaining leaves, flowers, and green pods.
notifications.body_beginner: Frost is expected in a few days, which will kill your nasturtiums. Pick the last of the leaves, flowers, and green pods to use.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost warning
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Nasturtiums cannot survive frost. Harvest what you can before a frosty night, in spring or fall; there is no protecting them long-term.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Nasturtiums cannot handle frost. Pick the leaves and flowers before a cold, frosty night, since frost will kill the plants.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot weather warning
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Nasturtium is a cool-preference plant: in extreme heat it can slow or stop flowering and the leaves turn sharper. Water more deeply, and light afternoon shade helps it hold bloom and quality.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Nasturtiums like cool weather and can stop flowering in extreme heat. Water them more in a heat wave, and a little afternoon shade helps keep the flowers and leaves coming.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Watch for aphids
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Aphids favor nasturtium. On a trap stand this is the point, so monitor and remove it once loaded; on a plant you are keeping, hose them off or use insecticidal soap.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Aphids love nasturtiums. If yours is a trap plant, that is the idea, so pull it once it is covered in them. Otherwise, spray them off with water or insecticidal soap.

germination.text_seasoned: Direct-sow where plants are to grow: nasturtium resents root disturbance, so seeding in place avoids transplant shock. Sow 1/2 in deep after frost into soil near 55 to 65 °F; soaking seed overnight speeds the 7 to 12 day germination.
germination.text_beginner: Plant the seeds right where you want the plants, about half an inch deep, after your last frost. Nasturtiums do not like being moved, so do not start them in trays unless you use biodegradable pots. Soaking the seeds overnight helps them sprout.

germination.text_seasoned: Sow into lean, unenriched soil. Resist the urge to amend with compost or fertilizer at planting; rich soil sets the plant up to grow leaves instead of flowers from the start.
germination.text_beginner: Plant in plain, poor soil and do not add compost or fertilizer. Rich soil makes nasturtiums grow leaves instead of flowers.

seedling.text_seasoned: Do not fertilize, even now. The most common cause of an all-leaves, no-flowers nasturtium is rich soil or feeding; lean conditions are what trigger bloom. Space plants 10 to 12 in for airflow and to limit slugs.
seedling.text_beginner: Do not feed your nasturtium seedlings. The number one reason nasturtiums make leaves but no flowers is too much food. Space them about 10 to 12 inches apart.

seedling.text_seasoned: Watch young plants for slugs and snails in damp weather and for the first aphids; tender seedlings and a sprawling habit invite both. Hand-pick slugs at night or use iron-phosphate bait.
seedling.text_beginner: Keep an eye on young nasturtiums for slugs and snails in damp weather, and for aphids. Hand-pick slugs at night or use a pet-safe iron-phosphate bait.

established.text_seasoned: Keep starving them, in the good sense: withholding fertilizer and keeping soil lean is the single biggest lever for flowering. If a plant is lush, dark, and flowerless, the soil is too rich, so stop feeding and wait it out.
established.text_beginner: Keep not feeding your nasturtiums. Lean, hungry soil is what makes them flower. If a plant is big and leafy with no flowers, the soil is too rich, so do not add anything and be patient.

established.text_seasoned: To use nasturtium against aphids, treat it as a trap crop: grow a stand a few feet off from beans, brassicas, or cucurbits, monitor it, and pull and destroy it once aphids load up. Set too close, the trap just funnels pests onto the crop.
established.text_beginner: If you want nasturtiums to fight aphids, use them as a trap: plant a patch a few feet away from your beans, cabbage, or squash, watch it, and pull it out once it is covered in aphids. Do not plant it right next to your crops.

budding.text_seasoned: Keep moisture even as buds form, and step watering up in heat: nasturtium is cool-preference and stalls in extreme heat, so deep watering and light afternoon shade help it keep setting flowers.
budding.text_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist as buds form, and water more in hot weather. Nasturtiums like it cool and can stop flowering in extreme heat, so a little afternoon shade and more water help.

flowering.text_seasoned: Harvest by eating: pick young leaves, open flowers, and tender green seed pods regularly. Frequent picking and deadheading keep the plant tidy and blooming, and the young growth is the mildest and best on the plate.
flowering.text_beginner: Pick and eat your nasturtiums: the young leaves, the flowers, and the green seed pods. Picking often keeps more flowers coming, and the youngest leaves and flowers taste the best.

flowering.text_seasoned: For poor man's capers, harvest the immature green seed pods while still soft, ideally in trios behind spent flowers, and pickle them in spiced vinegar; older pods toughen and dry. Leave a few pods to dry on the plant if you want to save seed.
flowering.text_beginner: To make poor man's capers, pick the green seed pods while they are still young and soft, then pickle them in vinegar. Older pods get tough. Leave a few to dry on the plant if you want seeds for next year.

seed_saving.text_seasoned: To save seed, leave some pods on the plant to ripen and dry to tan, then collect the large seeds; open-pollinated and heirloom types come true, while hybrids may not. Nasturtium often self-sows where winters are mild.
seed_saving.text_beginner: To save seeds, leave some pods on the plant until they dry and turn tan, then collect the big seeds. Heirloom types grow true to the parent; hybrids may not. In mild areas, nasturtiums often reseed themselves.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A single nasturtium yields steadily over the season: a continuous supply of edible round leaves, a long run of flowers (heaviest in cool spring and fall), and successive flushes of green seed pods for pickling. Trailing and climbing types cover far more ground and produce more total foliage and bloom than compact bush types, and also make the most generous trap-crop stands.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: One nasturtium gives you a steady supply of peppery leaves, lots of flowers (most in cool weather), and green seed pods to pickle, all season until frost. The trailing, climbing types grow much bigger and give you more than the small bushy types.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Nasturtium produces fully in its single season from seed, reaching first bloom in roughly 5 to 8 weeks; there is no establishment year. A spring sowing yields leaves within weeks and flowers from early summer to frost, with cooler regions and fall enjoying the heaviest bloom.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Nasturtiums produce the same year you plant them. You can pick leaves within a few weeks and flowers in under two months, right up until frost. There is no waiting year.
factors_seasoned: Soil fertility: lean soil gives the most flowers; rich soil or fertilizer shifts the plant to abundant foliage with few blooms.
Habit: trailing and climbing types yield far more total leaf, flower, and pod than compact bush types.
Season and heat: bloom peaks in cool spring and fall and slows in extreme summer heat; cooler regions flower most freely.
Harvest cadence: regular picking of leaves and flowers, plus deadheading, sustains tender new growth and bloom.
Water: steady moisture, especially in heat, keeps leaves tender and flowers coming; drought stress turns leaves bitter and curbs bloom.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No T1 evidence supports a moon-phase planting preference for nasturtium; left unset.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Lush, leafy plant with few or no flowers
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Big leafy plant but hardly any flowers
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The classic nasturtium failure: soil too rich or fertilizer applied. High fertility and nitrogen drive vegetative growth and suppress bloom; too much shade compounds it.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The soil was too rich or the plant was fed. Nasturtiums make leaves instead of flowers when they get fertilizer or grow in rich soil. Too much shade can add to it.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Grow in lean, unamended soil, withhold all fertilizer, and give full sun. If a plant is already leafy, stop feeding and wait; lean conditions eventually trigger bloom.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Next time, plant in poor soil, do not fertilize at all, and give full sun. If it is already too leafy, just stop feeding and wait for flowers.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Plant covered in aphids
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Plant covered in aphids
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Expected: aphids strongly prefer nasturtium, which is why it works as a trap crop. A problem only if the plant is one you meant to keep or eat, or if it sits too close to a susceptible crop.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: This is normal. Aphids love nasturtiums, which is why people use them to trap aphids. It is only a problem if you wanted to eat the plant or it is right next to your vegetables.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Use it on purpose as a trap a few feet from the protected crop and remove it when loaded; on edible or ornamental plants, hose off aphids or use insecticidal soap and rely on the predators the flowers attract.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Use nasturtiums as a trap plant a few feet from your vegetables and pull them when covered in aphids. On a plant you want to keep, spray the aphids off with water or insecticidal soap.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Flowering stopped and leaves turned sharp in midsummer heat
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Plant stopped flowering in the summer heat
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Nasturtium is cool-preference; sustained extreme heat slows or halts bloom and intensifies leaf pungency. In the hottest regions it is best grown as a cool-season crop in spring and fall.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Nasturtiums like cool weather. In a hot summer they often stop flowering for a while and the leaves get sharper-tasting. In hot places, grow them in spring and fall instead of midsummer.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water deeply in heat, give light afternoon shade, and in hot-summer regions time plantings for the cool shoulders; bloom usually resumes as temperatures fall.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Water more in heat and give afternoon shade. In hot areas, plant for spring and fall instead of midsummer, and the flowers usually come back when it cools.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Plants blackened by frost
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Frost killed or damaged the plants
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Nasturtium is frost-tender; frost at either end of the season, planting out too early in spring or the first frost in fall, kills or damages plants.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Nasturtiums cannot handle frost. A late spring frost or the first fall frost will damage or kill them.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Direct-sow only after all frost danger has passed, and expect plants to end with the first fall frost; let them self-sow in mild-winter areas.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant only after your last frost in spring, and know the first fall frost ends the season. In mild areas they often reseed themselves.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Seeds failed to come up
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Few or no seeds sprouted
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Usually cold or dry soil, sowing too shallow (nasturtium needs darkness to germinate), or unsoaked hard seed; germination is slow and erratic below about 55 °F.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Usually the soil was too cold or dry, the seeds were too shallow, or they were not soaked. Nasturtium seeds need to be covered (they sprout in the dark) and like a soak first.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Soak seed overnight, sow 1/2 in deep into warm (55 to 65 °F), evenly moist soil after frost, and keep it from drying during emergence.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Soak the seeds overnight, plant them half an inch deep in warm, damp soil after frost, and keep the soil moist until they come up.

primary.name: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources
UC Statewide IPM Program (UC ANR)
primary.publisher: UC Statewide Integrated Pest Management Program

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Sow successively every 2 to 3 weeks through the cool growing windows to keep fresh, vigorous plants coming; older plantings tire and grow leggy. Unlike heat-loving annuals, nasturtium favors cool weather, so in hot-summer regions concentrate sowings in spring and fall and pause through peak heat.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: For a steady supply, plant a new small batch of seeds every 2 to 3 weeks during the cool parts of the season. Fresh young plants give the best leaves and flowers. In hot-summer areas, plant in spring and again in fall and skip the hottest part of summer.
succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Successive sowing offsets the decline of older, leggier plantings; because nasturtium is cool-preference, the realized windows cluster in spring and fall and contract or pause through summer heat in hot regions.

crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Nasturtium is harvested continuously and eaten fresh. Pick young leaves and fully open flowers in the cool of the morning, using them the same day; younger growth is the mildest. Harvest the immature green seed pods while still soft to pickle as poor man's capers. Regular picking and deadheading keep plants tidy and blooming to frost.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Nasturtiums are ready to pick a little at a time all season. Snip young leaves and open flowers in the morning and use them the same day, and pick the green seed pods while they are still soft to pickle as capers. Keep picking and the plant keeps making more, right up to frost.

open_findings.summary: The frost-anchored warm-season regional skeleton for the SIX non-heat-paused regions (northern_tier, ca_north_coast, ca_south_coast, se_gulf, fl_peninsula, hawaii_tropical), namely the per-zone frost dates, planting-window offsets, the 12-token monthly calendars, and the optional indoor arm, is carried from the certified structural twin zinnia, because nasturtium shares the same frost-bracketed niche there (plant after last frost, grow to first frost; frost dates are region+zone climate data, not crop-specific). ALL consumer prose, biology, sources, edible/companion framing, and bloom timing were refit to nasturtium. The optional indoor arm is retained because nasturtium can be started indoors in biodegradable pots in short-season areas, though direct sowing is strongly preferred (it resents root disturbance). A nasturtium-specific regional planting-date source would tighten these windows.

The summer heat_pause in the FOUR hot regions (ca_interior z8/z9, warm_arid z8 use a conservative Jul-Aug gap; ca_desert z9/z10 and low_desert_az z9 use a long May-Sep gap with nasturtium grown as a fall-through-spring cool-season crop) is HAND-AUTHORED, not carried from zinnia (which is heat-loving and has zero heat_pause). The THERMAL FACT is sourced: nasturtium is a cool-preference annual that blooms best in spring and fall, slows or stops in extreme heat, and needs deeper watering and afternoon shade in heat (University of Maryland Extension; UC ANR; UF/IFAS). The PRECISE per-region heat_pause months are MODELED on that documented cool-preference plus each region's summer climate; the catalogued T1 nasturtium pages do not publish region-specific dated summer-exclusion tables, so the exact month placement is a climate-informed model pending region-specific confirmation. NOTE the deliberate boundary: fl_peninsula and se_gulf were left WITHOUT a hard heat_pause because UF/IFAS states nasturtium is grown spring through fall throughout Florida and year-round in South Florida; a hard summer exclusion there would contradict the catalogued source.

COMPANION FRAMING (not a sourcing gap): the APHID TRAP CROP function is framed as research/extension-supported (UMN reports nasturtium reduces pest pressure planted near brassicas, beans, squash, and pumpkin because aphids prefer it; UC ANR documents the trap-crop/sacrificial use), with the load-bearing qualifier that efficacy is placement-dependent (a stand set a few feet off, monitored, and destroyed once infested). Nasturtium also drawing flea beetles is framed as part of the same trap dynamic. The broader claim that nasturtium scent DETERS squash bugs and cucumber beetles from cucurbits is framed throughout as TRADITIONAL companion lore, not extension-verified. Beneficial-insect/pollinator recruitment is labeled likely. This honesty boundary (supported aphid-trap vs traditional deterrence) is load-bearing for the companion, tip, and pest prose.

days_to_maturity is set to 35 to 60 days (mid 50) as days to first edible harvest and bloom: catalogued T1 pages do not publish a single days-to-flower figure, but consistently describe nasturtium as fast/rapid-growing with young edible leaves in weeks and first bloom in roughly 5 to 8 weeks (UF/IFAS notes seed pods develop about 4 months after seeding, a separate, later stage used for the days_to_maturity_mid sanity, not the harvest figure). germination_temp_f 55 to 65 and the 7 to 12 day germination reflect nasturtium's cool-germinating habit (Wisconsin Horticulture). These representative numbers are flagged for daily-review confirmation against a region-specific source.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: Author-fresh gold-standard DRAFT (companion_and_ornamental_flower archetype), modeled structurally on certified zinnia. Biology fully refit to nasturtium (Tropaeolum majus) from catalogued T1 sources, all WebFetch-verified live 2026-06-29: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox (Tropaeolum majus), Wisconsin Horticulture Extension nasturtium, UMN Extension nasturtiums article + UMN Extension edible flowers, UC ANR nasturtiums article, UF/IFAS Gardening Solutions nasturtiums, University of Maryland Extension nasturtium, and UC IPM nasturtium. Three headline refits vs zinnia: edible whole plant (peppery leaves/flowers + pickled seed pods = poor man's capers); aphid trap crop (supported) vs traditional squash-bug/cucumber-beetle deterrence (hedged); thrives in poor soil, do not over-feed. Cool-preference heat_pause hand-authored in the 4 hot regions; frost-anchored warm-season skeleton for the 6 non-heat regions carried from the zinnia twin (see findings 001-004). Expect a Claude Code correction loop + daily biology-fidelity review per the pilot workflow.

crops.deadheading_seasoned: Deadheading overlaps with harvest for nasturtium: picking flowers and young leaves for the kitchen, and snipping spent blooms, keeps the plant tidy, redirects energy from seed set into new flowers and growth, and sustains bloom through the season. Shear back leggy, tired trailing stems midseason to force fresh growth. Leave a few seed pods to mature only if you want to save seed or harvest them late; for capers, pick the pods young and green.
crops.deadheading_beginner: For nasturtiums, deadheading and harvesting are the same thing: keep picking the flowers and young leaves to eat, and snip off faded flowers, and the plant keeps making more instead of going to seed. If trailing stems get long and tired, cut them back to spark fresh growth. Leave a few pods to ripen only if you want to save seeds, but pick them young and green if you want capers.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note: Nasturtium direct-sows in place after the last spring frost once soil is near 55 to 65 °F; it resents root disturbance, so seeding where plants are to grow is the hero method. Germinates in 7 to 12 days, faster from soaked seed.

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.synthesis_note: Optional, short-season-only transplant arm: start about 4 weeks before last frost in biodegradable pots and set out intact after frost, to avoid the root disturbance nasturtium dislikes.

plant_out.label: primary

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the northern tier, nasturtiums are easy summer flowers that actually like the cooler weather here. Wait until after your last frost when the soil is warm, then plant the big seeds right where you want them, since they do not like being moved. You get peppery leaves within weeks and flowers from early summer until the first fall frost. Do not fertilize them, or you will get leaves and few flowers. Plant a patch a few feet from your vegetables to trap aphids, and pick the leaves, flowers, and green seed pods to eat.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In the northern tier, nasturtium is an easy single-season summer crop and is well suited to the cooler northern climate, which it prefers. Wait until the soil has warmed and frost danger has passed, then direct-sow the large seeds where they are to grow; they resent transplanting. Plants give edible leaves within weeks and flower from early summer to the first fall frost, with little summer heat to slow them. Grow them lean: do not fertilize, since rich soil gives leaves instead of flowers. Use a sacrificial stand as an aphid trap a few feet from beans, brassicas, or squash, and pick leaves, flowers, and green pods through the season.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast and Gulf, nasturtiums do best in the cooler spring and fall. In the hot, humid Gulf summer they keep going rather than quitting if you give them afternoon or partial shade and steady water. Plant after your last spring frost in poor, well-drained soil, and do not fertilize. Use them as a trap to pull aphids off your vegetables, and pick the peppery leaves, flowers, and green seed pods to eat.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: Across the Southeast and Gulf, nasturtium is grown mainly in the milder shoulder seasons, spring and fall, and it keeps going through summer where it is given some shade; it is cool-preference and blooms most freely before and after peak summer. Direct-sow after the last spring frost into lean, well-drained soil. In the hot, humid Gulf summer nasturtium is not paused: it carries on if you give it afternoon or partial shade and steady water, which help hold bloom through the heat. Do not fertilize. Humidity can bring leaf problems and, rarely, bacterial wilt, so favor airflow and base watering. Use nasturtium as an aphid trap crop near brassicas and cucurbits, and harvest the edible leaves, flowers, and green pods.

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In California's inland valleys, nasturtiums grow best in the cooler spring and fall, taking a break in the hottest part of summer (July and August), when the heat stops them flowering. Use them to trap aphids away from your vegetables, and pick the leaves, flowers, and green pods to eat.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: On California's cool, foggy coast, nasturtiums are right at home and often naturalize. Plant after the last frost in poor, well-drained soil, and they flower from spring through fall with little trouble from heat, sometimes nearly all year in mild spots. Do not fertilize them, especially in rich coastal soil, or you get leaves instead of flowers. Watch for slugs and aphids in the damp air, and use the aphids to your advantage by trapping them away from your vegetables. Pick the leaves, flowers, and green pods to eat.

Do not fertilize, since the rich coastal soils especially can drive all leaves and few flowers. Cool, damp air can favor slugs and aphids; the aphids make it a ready trap crop near beans and brassicas. Harvest leaves, flowers, and green pods all season.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: May through September is excluded by extreme low-desert heat: nasturtium is a cool-preference annual that blooms best in spring and fall and stalls, scorches, and stops flowering once sustained daytime temperatures climb into the 100s °F, so in the low desert it is grown as a fall-through-spring crop and paused through the intense summer, resuming as the heat breaks. Not a frost gap but a summer heat exclusion. (University of Maryland Extension; UC ANR; UF/IFAS)

low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: In the Arizona low desert, plant nasturtiums only in the cool season: sow in fall when it cools for flowers from late fall through spring, and skip the extreme summer (about May through September), when the heat is far too intense. Plant in poor, well-drained soil, do not fertilize, and water through the mild winter. Use them to trap aphids off your winter vegetables, and pick the leaves, flowers, and green pods to eat.
low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: In the Arizona low desert, nasturtium is grown only in the cool season: sow in fall as temperatures drop for bloom from late fall through spring, and pause through the extreme summer (roughly May through September), when low-desert heat well into the 100s °F excludes it entirely. Grow it lean and unfertilized in well-drained soil and water consistently through the mild winter. It is an easy, rewarding cool-season flower and edible here. Use a stand as an aphid trap near winter vegetables, and harvest leaves, flowers, and green pods through the season.

11.zone_notes: This frost-free zone has essentially no killing frost, so nasturtium runs through the cool season into the warm months; plant from late winter for the longest show and replace plants as they tire, easing off through the hottest weather.

fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: In Florida, nasturtiums grow spring through fall, and all year in the frost-free south, doing best in the cooler, drier months. They slow in the worst summer heat and humidity but keep going if you give them afternoon or partial shade and steady water. Plant in poor, well-drained soil, do not fertilize, and keep them watered. Use them to trap aphids off your vegetables, and pick the leaves, flowers, and green seed pods to eat.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: In the Florida peninsula, nasturtium is grown spring through fall, and year round in the warmest, frost-free south, doing best in the cooler, drier stretches. It eases in peak summer heat and humidity but is not paused here: given afternoon or partial shade and steady water, it keeps going through the Florida summer, in line with UF/IFAS guidance that it grows spring through fall throughout Florida. Direct-sow into lean, well-drained soil, do not fertilize, and keep it watered. Humidity can bring leaf problems and rarely bacterial wilt, so favor airflow. Use it as an aphid trap near vegetables, and harvest the edible leaves, flowers, and green pods.
