crops.description_seasoned: Lavender is a woody Mediterranean perennial sub-shrub in the mint family, grown for its fragrant summer flower spikes and silvery, aromatic foliage. It thrives on neglect in full sun and lean, sharply drained soil, and its defining care act is an annual hard cut-back after bloom that keeps it compact and prevents it from going woody and splitting open. English lavender is both the hardiest type and the one used in cooking, while the showy Spanish and French types are tender and ornamental.
crops.description_beginner: Lavender is a small woody shrub with silvery leaves and fragrant purple flower spikes in summer. It comes from the dry Mediterranean, so it wants full sun, poor dry soil, and very little water, and it actually does worse if you pamper it. The one job that matters is trimming it back every year after it flowers so it stays bushy instead of turning into bare woody sticks. English lavender is the hardy, cook-with-it kind; the frillier Spanish and French types are mainly for looks and are not cold-hardy.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Cut for fresh bouquets when about half the buds on a spike have opened; cut for drying or culinary use a little earlier, when only the first one or two buds on the spike have opened, so the buds hold their color and oils. Harvest in the morning after the dew dries but before the heat, when the fragrance is most concentrated.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: For a fresh vase, cut the stems when about half the little buds on the spike have opened. For drying or cooking, cut a bit sooner, when just the first couple of buds have opened. Cut in the morning once the dew has dried, when lavender smells strongest.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: English lavender (Lavandula angustifolia) is the hardiest type, reliably perennial in roughly zones 5 to 9 and surviving zone 4 with good drainage and winter protection. Lavandins are nearly as hardy. Spanish and French lavenders are tender (about zone 7 to 8 and warmer) and are grown as container plants brought in for winter in colder regions. Good drainage matters as much as cold: lavender rots in wet winter soil before cold alone kills it.
crops.hardiness_notes_beginner: English lavender is the toughest and comes back year after year in most of the country (about zones 5 to 9, and zone 4 if you protect it). The showy Spanish and French types are not cold-hardy, so in cold areas grow them in pots you bring inside for winter. Just as important as cold: lavender hates wet feet in winter and will rot in soggy soil.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: In the first year, focus on root establishment: water regularly until the plant is settled, then taper off. Pinch or lightly clip flowers and shape the young plant to encourage bushy lateral growth rather than letting it flower heavily; it will reach full size in about three years and live well over a decade with the right lean, dry conditions.
crops.year_one_notes_beginner: The first year is about getting the roots going. Water it fairly regularly until it is established, then cut back. It helps to trim it lightly and not let it flower too hard the first season, so it grows bushy. It takes about three years to reach full size and can live for more than ten.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Choose the sunniest, best-draining spot you have. Work an inch of coarse compost into the top several inches of soil, and on heavy clay improve drainage with a raised bed or mound rather than by digging in sand, which can worsen drainage in clay. Aim for lean, gritty, near-neutral to slightly alkaline ground.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Pick the sunniest spot with the best drainage. Mix a little coarse compost into the top of the soil. If your ground is heavy clay, plant lavender in a raised bed or mound instead, because that drains better. The goal is poor, gritty soil, not rich soil.
crops.bloom_time_beginner: Lavender flowers in summer. Some kinds (English types) bloom in early summer and may flower again later; the big hybrid types bloom once, a little later. When yours blooms depends on where you live.
crops.bloom_time_seasoned: Lavender blooms in summer; English types often flower in late spring to early summer and may rebloom later in the season, while lavandins bloom once, later in summer. Exact timing shifts with your region and is set per zone.

dormancy_window.note_seasoned: In zones with freezing winters, lavender goes dormant. Hold off on watering and feeding, leave any hard pruning for spring, and protect tender Spanish or French types or move container plants under cover. A dormant plant needs almost no water, and it is wet soil or a fresh fall cut, not the cold itself, that usually rots or kills it over winter.
dormancy_window.note_beginner: Where winters freeze, lavender rests through the cold months. Stop watering and feeding it, save any big trim for spring, and in cold areas shelter the tender types or bring potted plants somewhere protected. A resting plant barely needs water, and it is usually soggy soil or a late-season haircut, not the cold, that kills lavender over winter.

pollination.notes_seasoned: Lavender is self-fertile and needs no pollinizer partner; it is grown for its flowers, not fruit, so no cross-pollination planning is required. Its blooms are highly attractive to bees and other pollinators.
pollination.notes_beginner: You only need one lavender plant for it to flower well; it does not need a partner plant. Bees love the flowers, but that is a bonus for your garden, not something the plant needs to bloom.

pruning_window.note_seasoned: After the flowers fade, shear the whole plant back by about a third, cutting into soft green growth only and never into the bare woody base, which will not resprout. This yearly cut is what keeps lavender compact and long-lived; without it the plant turns leggy, splits open at the center, and declines within a few years.
pruning_window.note_beginner: Once it finishes flowering, trim about a third off the plant, cutting only into the soft green parts and never down into the hard, woody stems, because those will not grow back. Do this every year and your lavender stays round and bushy. Skip it and the plant gets tall and woody, flops open in the middle, and slowly dies off.

pet_safe.note: Its essential oils (linalool) can cause mild stomach upset in cats, dogs, and horses if eaten.

crops.name: Sunflower
crops.flower_type: single-stem to branching, daisy-form single, semi-double, and double, dwarf to giant
crops.description_seasoned: Sunflower (Helianthus annuus) is a fast, warm-season, frost-tender annual in the Asteraceae family, native to North America and grown both as an ornamental and for its edible, wildlife-valuable seed. Cultivars range enormously: from single-stem giants that top 10 feet with one massive head, to multi-branching types that carry many smaller blooms, to dwarf forms under 2 feet for pots and edging, in oilseed, confection, and pollen-free cut-flower classes. It is direct-sown into warm soil after frost (the big taproot resents transplanting), thrives in heat, full sun, and even lean soil, and is notably drought-tolerant once established. Young plants are heliotropic, tracking the sun east to west by day, while mature heads settle facing east. The flowers are a major pollinator and beneficial-insect draw, and the ripening seed heads are a magnet for birds and squirrels. Note its mild allelopathy: roots and decomposing residue release compounds that can suppress some neighboring plants, so it is best sited at a bed edge.
crops.description_beginner: Sunflowers are easy, fast, cheerful flowers grown both for their blooms and for edible seeds that people and birds love. They come in a huge range: towering giants over 10 feet tall with one big head, bushy branching types with lots of smaller flowers, and little dwarf kinds under 2 feet for pots. Plant the large seeds straight into warm soil after your last frost, because sunflowers have a deep taproot and do not like being moved. They love heat and full sun and handle dry spells well. Young plants turn to follow the sun across the sky, and the open flowers bring in bees and butterflies. Watch out: birds and squirrels will raid the ripening seed heads, so cover them if you want to save the seeds. One thing to know is that sunflowers can hold back a few nearby plants with natural chemicals from their roots and old stalks, so it is smart to plant them along an edge.

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Sunflowers are not fussy and grow in most ordinary garden soil as long as water drains away and does not pool. A deep, loose, well-drained soil suits their long taproot best. They tolerate sandy, clay loam, and silty soils, but soggy, heavy clay that stays wet can rot the roots. Mixing in some compost helps, especially for the big branching and large-flowered types, which are hungrier feeders.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Sunflowers do best in deep, loose, well-drained soil that lets the taproot run, and they tolerate a wide range of textures including clay loam, silty clay loam, and sandy loam; the consistent failure is wet, poorly drained ground that rots roots and invites stalk rot. They are moderate to heavy feeders, especially the multi-branching and large single-flowered types, so soil enriched with composted organic matter plus a slow-release fertilizer supports the biggest plants and heads. Excess nitrogen, however, gives soft, leafy, weak-stalked growth prone to lodging, so favor balanced fertility over a high-nitrogen push.

ph.note_beginner: Sunflowers are easygoing about soil pH (how acidic or alkaline the soil is). A range around 6.0 to 7.5 is ideal, and most garden soil is already fine, so you usually do not need to change anything. They even tolerate slightly alkaline soil.
ph.note_seasoned: Sunflowers perform best across roughly 6.0 to 7.5 and are tolerant of soils a little outside that, including mildly alkaline ground up to about 8.0. pH adjustment is rarely warranted; focus instead on drainage and depth for the taproot rather than on fine-tuning acidity.

crops.tip_seasoned: Soil warmth, not the calendar, is the germination trigger: direct-sow about 1 inch deep once soil is past 50 °F and warming (ideally 70 to 85 °F) after frost, and seedlings emerge in 7 to 10 days. Direct sowing is strongly preferred because the taproot resents disturbance; if you must start indoors, use biodegradable pots and transplant young, before the taproot develops. Match spacing to type: roughly 6 inches for small cut-flower singles, 12 inches for mid-size, and 18 to 24 inches for branching and giant types. Stake tall single-stem giants against wind, and as seed heads ripen, bag them in paper or cheesecloth to beat the birds if you want the seed.
crops.tip_beginner: Wait until the soil is warm before planting sunflower seeds outside, about a week after your last frost; plant them an inch deep and they sprout in 7 to 10 days. Plant the seeds right where they will grow, because sunflowers have a deep root and do not like being moved. Space small types about 6 inches apart, medium ones about a foot, and the big branching or giant ones 18 to 24 inches apart. Tie tall sunflowers to a stake so wind does not topple them. When the seed heads start to ripen, cover them with a paper bag or cheesecloth if you want to keep the seeds, or the birds will get them first.

fertilizer.timing: At planting, with optional light feeding during growth
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Sunflowers, especially the multi-branching and large single-flowered types, are moderate to heavy feeders. Work compost and a balanced, slow-release fertilizer into the bed at planting, and supplement lightly through the season if growth is pale or the soil is lean. Avoid heavy nitrogen, which drives soft, leafy, weak-stalked growth that lodges in wind and delays bloom; a balanced ratio favoring steady stalk and head development is the goal.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Sunflowers, especially the big branching and large-flowered kinds, are fairly hungry plants. Mix compost and a balanced fertilizer into the soil before planting, and you can feed lightly again during the season if the leaves look pale. Do not overdo the high-nitrogen kind, though: too much makes tall, floppy, leafy plants with weaker stems and fewer flowers.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time for an optional feed. Sunflowers are moderate to heavy feeders, so a balanced fertilizer now supports strong stalks and big heads; skip it if you worked compost and slow-release fertilizer into the bed at planting and growth looks vigorous.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: It is a good time to feed your sunflowers if they need it. A balanced fertilizer now helps them grow strong stems and big flowers. You can skip it if you already mixed compost into the soil and the plants look healthy and green.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 worked in at planting, with phosphorus and potassium to back flower and seed development, suits sunflowers better than a high-nitrogen lawn-type feed, which favors weak, leafy growth.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: The three numbers on fertilizer (N-P-K) are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. For sunflowers, a balanced one like 10-10-10 works well. Avoid a high first-number (nitrogen) lawn feed, which gives leaves and floppy stems instead of strong flowers.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: Incorporate compost plus a balanced slow-release fertilizer at the label rate for annual flowers at planting; one optional light side-dressing during rapid growth is plenty for most home plantings. Lean-soil or large single-stem plantings may want a second light feeding, but keep nitrogen modest.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Mix compost and a balanced fertilizer into the soil when you plant, following the package amount. One more light feeding while the plants are growing fast is usually plenty. Go easy, and avoid high-nitrogen feeds.

pests.name: Birds and squirrels
pests.note_beginner: Birds and squirrels love sunflower seeds and will strip a ripening seed head fast, sometimes in a day or two. If you want to save the seeds, cover the heads with a paper bag, cheesecloth, or netting once the petals fade. If you are growing sunflowers just for the flowers or to feed wildlife, this is a feature, not a problem.
pests.note_seasoned: The signature sunflower pest at seed stage: birds (finches, jays, blackbirds) and squirrels raid ripening heads and can clear a head quickly. To save seed, cover heads with a paper sack, cheesecloth, or nylon netting secured with a band once the bright petals begin to brown. The same trait makes standing heads valuable as natural bird feeders if seed saving is not the goal, so manage it by intent rather than as pure loss.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.note_beginner: Tiny soft insects that cluster on new growth, buds, and the backs of leaves. A strong spray of water or insecticidal soap usually handles them, and sunflowers draw ladybugs and other helpers that eat them.
pests.note_seasoned: Soft-bodied sap-feeders on tender growth, buds, and leaf undersides; rarely damaging on vigorous plants and usually checked by the beneficials sunflowers attract. Hose off or treat with insecticidal soap only if populations build on young plants.

pests.name: Sunflower moth and head-clipping weevil
pests.note_beginner: These two pests attack the flower head. Sunflower moth caterpillars tunnel into the developing head and eat the seeds, often leaving webbing. The head-clipping weevil chops the stalk an inch or two below the head, so the whole head droops or drops. Cleaning up old stalks at season end and not planting sunflowers in the same spot every year both help.
pests.note_seasoned: The classic head-infesting pair. Sunflower moth (a small buff-gray moth) lays eggs as heads open; larvae tunnel into the seeds, web the face of the head, and can predispose it to Rhizopus head rot. The sunflower head-clipping weevil (metallic black, long snout) girdles the stalk 1 to 2 inches below the head, dropping it to the ground. Both are managed culturally in the garden: sanitation (destroy spent stalks and dropped heads), crop rotation away from continuous sunflower, and tolerance, since home-scale damage is usually limited.

pests.name: Cutworms
pests.note_beginner: Fat gray or brown caterpillars that hide in the soil and cut off young seedlings at the soil line overnight, leaving them toppled. A cardboard or foil collar around the stem of a new seedling protects it, and clearing weeds before planting helps.
pests.note_seasoned: Stout, smooth gray-to-black caterpillars that sever seedlings at or just below the soil line at night, leaving gaps in the stand. Reduce weedy harborage before sowing, use stem collars on transplants or thinned seedlings, and scout new plantings; damage is a seedling-stage concern that established plants outgrow.

pests.name: Leaf-feeding caterpillars and beetles
pests.note_beginner: Several caterpillars and beetles chew or skeletonize sunflower leaves but rarely do enough damage to need spraying on a healthy plant. Hand-pick if numbers are high.
pests.note_seasoned: A guild of defoliators (thistle caterpillar, woollybears, beet armyworm, sunflower beetle) chew or skeletonize foliage, mostly cosmetic on vigorous garden plants. Hand-pick or spot-treat only at high densities; the plants tolerate substantial leaf loss before bloom is affected.

diseases.name: Sclerotinia (white mold) head and stalk rot
diseases.note_beginner: A fungus that causes a soft, watery rot of the stalk base or the flower head, often with white cottony mold and hard black lumps inside. It thrives in cool, wet conditions and lives in the soil for years, so it is hard to cure. Avoid planting sunflowers where this rot has occurred, give plants room and good drainage, and remove and discard infected plants.
diseases.note_seasoned: Caused by Sclerotinia sclerotiorum, which produces basal stalk rot/wilt, mid-stem rot, and head rot, the most serious sunflower disease. The soilborne sclerotia persist for years and fungicides are largely ineffective, so management is preventive: avoid beds with a white-mold history or recent susceptible broadleaf crops, ensure drainage and airflow, space generously, and remove and destroy infected plants and heads rather than composting them.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.note_beginner: A disease that stunts young plants, yellows the leaves with pale blotches on top and white mold underneath, and can kill seedlings in cool, wet soil. Plant in well-drained soil, do not overwater seedlings, and pull out badly affected plants. Some seed is sold as mildew-resistant.
diseases.note_seasoned: Caused by Plasmopara halstedii, favored by cool temperatures, high humidity, and waterlogged soil; symptoms include stunting, leaf chlorosis with white downy sporulation on the undersides, and seedling death. It survives in soil for years, so prevention centers on well-drained soil, restrained watering at the seedling stage, resistant hybrids where available, and roguing infected plants; there is no effective rescue treatment once infection takes hold.

diseases.name: Rust
diseases.note_beginner: Small cinnamon-brown spots or bumps on the leaves, usually the undersides, that can spread in warm, wet weather and yellow the foliage. Space plants for airflow, water at the base, and remove badly rusted leaves; it rarely kills a healthy garden plant.
diseases.note_seasoned: Caused by Puccinia helianthi, producing cinnamon-brown uredinial pustules chiefly on lower leaf surfaces, spreading by wind in warm, humid conditions and defoliating heavily in bad years. Manage with spacing and base watering for faster leaf drying, sanitation of infected debris, and resistant cultivars; fungicides exist for severe pressure but are seldom needed in the home garden.

diseases.name: Septoria leaf spot and powdery mildew
diseases.note_beginner: Two common leaf problems: Septoria makes brown, angular spots on the leaves, and powdery mildew leaves a white powdery film, both worse in humid, crowded plantings. Give plants room, water the soil rather than the leaves, and clean up fallen debris.
diseases.note_seasoned: Septoria helianthi causes angular brown leaf spots, while powdery mildew lays a white film on foliage in humid, crowded sites; both are foliar and rarely fatal but reduce vigor late in the season. Manage culturally with generous spacing, base watering, morning irrigation if overhead is unavoidable, and removal of infected debris; rotation away from continuous sunflower limits Septoria carryover.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Keep soil evenly moist through germination and establishment, then water deeply but less often; established sunflowers are notably drought-tolerant thanks to a deep taproot, but the roughly 20 days before and after flowering are the critical window when steady moisture builds the head and fills the seed.
watering.frequency_beginner: Keep the soil damp while seeds sprout and young plants get going. After that, water deeply but less often, since grown sunflowers handle dry spells well. The most important time to water is the few weeks right before and after the flower opens, when the plant is building its head and seeds.
watering.amount_seasoned: Aim for roughly 1 inch of water per week from rain plus irrigation during active growth, applied deeply to reach the taproot rather than in frequent shallow doses; increase around flowering and seed fill, and let the soil dry somewhat between waterings otherwise.
watering.amount_beginner: Sunflowers like about 1 inch of water a week, counting rain. Water deeply once or twice a week instead of a little every day, so the water reaches the deep root, and let the soil dry a bit in between. Water a little more when they are flowering and making seeds.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base with drip or a soaker hose to keep foliage dry, which limits rust, Septoria, and powdery mildew; deep, infrequent watering also encourages the taproot down. If you must use a sprinkler, water in the morning so leaves dry quickly.
watering.method_beginner: Water the ground around the plant, not the leaves, using a soaker hose or watering can at the base. Dry leaves get less disease. Water deeply so it soaks down to the deep root. If leaves do get wet, water in the morning so they dry by midday.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting despite wet soil, and soft, discolored stalk bases signal overwatering or poor drainage, which also invites Sclerotinia and downy mildew; seedlings in cold, wet soil damp off.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If lower leaves turn yellow, the plant wilts even though the soil is wet, or the base of the stalk looks soft and dark, you are likely overwatering or the soil drains poorly. Cold, soggy soil also rots seedlings.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting in the heat of the day that recovers by evening, dulling foliage, and a smaller head or poorly filled seeds indicate underwatering, most critically in the weeks around flowering; established plants are otherwise forgiving of short dry spells.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Sunflowers that are too dry wilt in the afternoon heat, look dull, and make a smaller flower or fewer good seeds, especially if they go dry around bloom time. Once established, they bounce back from short dry spells.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Water at the base with drip or a soaker hose and keep water off the foliage; dry leaves are the main cultural lever against rust, Septoria, and powdery mildew. Deep, less frequent watering suits the taproot and the plant's drought adaptation.
watering.method_note_beginner: Water the soil around the plant, not the leaves, with a soaker hose or at the base. Dry leaves resist disease. Water deeply and less often, which suits the deep root and the plant's love of the heat.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The critical moisture windows are germination and seedling establishment and roughly the 20 days before and after flowering, when water shortage cuts head size and seed fill; excess moisture in cold soil at sowing risks damping-off and rot.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The most important times to keep the soil moist are right after planting while seeds sprout, and the few weeks before and after the flower opens. Going dry then means a smaller flower and fewer seeds, but never keep the soil soggy.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Sunflower seed is a real, storable harvest, unlike a pure cut flower. Once heads are cured until the backs are brown and dry and the seeds part easily, thoroughly dried seed keeps for several months at cool room temperature in an airtight container, away from light and humidity; check periodically for any sign of moisture, mold, or insects. Heads cut for the vase are enjoyed fresh, not stored.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Sunflower seeds are something you can actually store, unlike most cut flowers. After you dry the heads until the backs are brown and the seeds come off easily, keep the dried seeds in an airtight jar somewhere cool and dark. They last several months at room temperature. Check now and then that they are still dry and not mouldy. Flowers cut for a vase are just enjoyed fresh.
storage.fridge_seasoned: For longer keeping, hold thoroughly dried seed (in-hull or hulled) in a sealed container in the refrigerator, where it stays fresh for up to a year; the cold slows the seed oils from going rancid. This suits both eating seed and seed saved for next year.
storage.fridge_beginner: To keep sunflower seeds longer, put the well-dried seeds in a sealed container in the fridge, where they stay good for up to a year. The cold keeps the oils in the seed from going stale. This works for seeds to eat and seeds to plant next year.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Fully dried sunflower seed freezes well in an airtight container for long-term storage of a year or more, useful for saved planting seed or eating seed; thaw it still sealed so condensation does not form on the seed.
storage.freezer_beginner: For the longest storage, freeze well-dried sunflower seeds in a sealed container, where they keep for a year or more, whether you are saving them to plant or to eat. Let them warm up still sealed so water does not collect on them.
storage.notes_seasoned: Sunflower is grown both for ornament and for an edible, wildlife-valuable seed crop, so it does have a harvest to store. The key to good storage is full drying: cure cut heads in a warm, dry, airy, rodent-free spot until the seeds rattle loose, then store dry as above. For cut flowers, cut when the bloom is just opening, recut the stem, strip lower leaves below the waterline, and use clean water; vase life is roughly a week, longer for pollen-free types. If you are growing for seed, protect ripening heads from birds and squirrels, which strip them fast.
storage.notes_beginner: Sunflowers give you both flowers and edible seeds, so unlike most cut flowers there is a harvest to store. The main thing is to dry the seeds completely: hang cut heads in a warm, dry, airy place safe from mice until the seeds come off easily, then store them dry. For flowers in a vase, cut when the bloom is just opening, trim the stem, pull off the lower leaves, and use clean water; they last about a week. If you want the seeds, cover the ripening heads so birds and squirrels do not eat them first.

recommended: 'Mammoth' / 'Mammoth Russian' (giant single-stem, 9 to 12 ft, one huge head, classic edible seed type)
'Sunzilla' / 'American Giant' (giant single-stem, 12+ ft, large heads for seed and show)
'Autumn Beauty' (branching, multi-head, warm bicolor mix, long cutting display)
'Lemon Queen' (branching, soft-yellow, strong pollinator favorite)
ProCut series (single-stem, pollen-free, fast cut-flower standard, uniform)
'Teddy Bear' (dwarf, fully double fluffy blooms, about 2 to 3 ft, containers)
'Sunspot' / 'Music Box' (dwarf to compact, big flowers on short plants for pots and edging)
'Italian White' (branching, creamy pale petals, smaller pollen-free blooms for cutting)
varieties.note_seasoned: Choose by purpose and size. For edible or bird seed, the giant single-stem types ('Mammoth', 'Sunzilla', 'American Giant') deliver one large head of plump seed but need staking and 18 to 24 inches of space. For cutting, single-stem pollen-free types (ProCut series, 'Italian White') give clean, uniform, mess-free stems and succession-sow well, while branching types ('Autumn Beauty', 'Lemon Queen') carry many smaller blooms over a long window and are the best pollinator and color choice. For pots, edging, and small spaces, dwarf types ('Teddy Bear', 'Sunspot', 'Music Box') stay under 2 to 3 feet. Open, single, pollen-bearing flowers feed pollinators best; pollen-free cut-flower types trade that for vase tidiness.
varieties.note_beginner: Pick the type for your goal. For big edible or bird seeds, grow the giant kinds like 'Mammoth', which make one huge head but need a stake and lots of room. For cutting flowers for a vase, pollen-free single-stem types like the ProCut series are clean and tidy, while branching types like 'Autumn Beauty' and 'Lemon Queen' make lots of smaller flowers over a long time and are best for bees. For pots and small spaces, dwarf types like 'Teddy Bear' stay short. Open, single flowers with pollen are the best ones for bees and butterflies.

companions.note_beginner: Sunflowers are mainly grown for their own flowers and seeds, but they are a strong pollinator and beneficial-insect plant, so they help the wider garden too. Their open heads, made of hundreds of tiny flowers, bring in bees, butterflies, and helpful predator insects, and the ripening seeds feed birds. Tall, sturdy types can act as a natural trellis or windbreak for vining crops like cucumbers, squash, and melons, which also benefit from the extra pollinators. The honest catch is allelopathy: sunflower roots and old stalks release natural chemicals that can hold back some plants, especially potatoes and pole beans, and the hulls can stop seeds from sprouting. So plant sunflowers along an edge rather than in the middle of sensitive crops, and clean up the stalks and dropped hulls at season end.
companions.note_seasoned: Sunflower is grown chiefly for itself, but it earns a place in the wider garden as a pollinator and beneficial-insect powerhouse: the composite heads supply abundant nectar and pollen to bees (including specialist sunflower bees), butterflies, and predatory and parasitic insects, and the seed heads are a documented wildlife and bird food. Sturdy tall types double as a living trellis or windbreak for cucurbits, which tolerate sunflower's allelopathy and gain from the pollinator traffic. The load-bearing honest caveat is that allelopathy: Helianthus annuus is a recognized allelopathic species (roots, residue, and seed hulls release growth-inhibiting compounds), best documented as a weed-suppressing cover-crop trait but also capable of stunting sensitive neighbors. Site sunflowers at a bed edge, not amid sensitive crops, keep potatoes and pole beans clear, and remove residue and spilled hulls at season end. There is no concurrent pairing that is broadly antagonistic to the sunflower itself; the antagonism runs the other way, from sunflower to certain neighbors.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Bees, butterflies, and beneficial insects (pollinator planting)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: A sunflower head is hundreds of tiny flowers, so it brings in lots of bees and butterflies, plus helpful bugs that eat pests. Planting sunflowers along the edge of a vegetable garden is a great way to support pollinators.

provenance.label: research_backed
provenance.reason: Extension sources (NC State plant toolbox, Clemson HGIC) document sunflower as a major nectar and pollen source supporting bees, specialist sunflower bees, butterflies including monarchs, and beneficial insects; Texas A&M notes pollinators improve sunflower seed set, confirming the strong floral-resource value.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Sunflower's best-supported companion function. The composite head offers abundant, accessible nectar and pollen across a long bloom, drawing honey bees, native and specialist sunflower bees, butterflies (a noted late-season nectar source for monarchs), and predatory and parasitic insects that help manage aphids and caterpillars elsewhere in the garden. Single, pollen-bearing types serve pollinators far better than pollen-free cut-flower selections. Plant as an insectary edge or border near the vegetable garden.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Cucumbers, squash, and melons (living trellis and pollinator support)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Tall, strong sunflowers can act like a living pole for vining cucumbers, squash, and melons to climb, and they pull in the bees these crops need to set fruit. These vine crops handle sunflowers nearby better than most.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Cucurbits depend on insect pollination for fruit set and tolerate sunflower allelopathy comparatively well (vs potatoes/beans); sunflower is a documented long-bloom pollinator draw and a sturdy support. The pairing is inferred from these solid facts plus traditional trellis use, hence likely rather than research_backed.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A well-grounded structural and pollinator pairing. Cucurbits need many bee visits per flower for proper set, and sunflower is a reliable, long-blooming pollinator magnet; the sturdy stalks of tall single-stem types also serve as a living trellis or windbreak. Cucurbits, corn, and squash are noted to tolerate sunflower allelopathy comparatively well, unlike potatoes and pole beans. Site sunflowers on the windward or northern edge so they support rather than shade the crop, a visitation-and-structure benefit, not a pest-control one.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Birds and wildlife (seed-head food source)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Left to ripen and dry on the plant, sunflower heads become a natural bird feeder that finches and other birds love through fall and winter. This is wonderful for wildlife, but it is the opposite of what you want if you are trying to save the seeds for yourself.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: NC State and Clemson document sunflower seed heads as a valued wildlife and bird food (leave standing dead heads as natural bird feeders). Framed traditional/high as a deliberate wildlife-gardening use rather than a crop-yield interaction.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A deliberate wildlife-gardening use rather than a crop interaction. Standing heads left to ripen are a documented food source for finches, jays, and other seed-eating birds (and small mammals) into fall and winter, so dead heads left on the plant function as natural bird feeders. The tension is direct: this is mutually exclusive with saving seed for yourself, which requires bagging the heads. Choose the use per planting.

good_seasoned.name: Bees, butterflies, and beneficial insects (pollinator planting)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: The composite head supplies abundant nectar and pollen over a long bloom, drawing honey bees, native and specialist sunflower bees, butterflies (a late-season monarch nectar source), and predatory and parasitic insects useful elsewhere in the garden. Single, pollen-bearing types serve pollinators best.

provenance.label: research_backed
provenance.reason: NC State plant toolbox and Clemson HGIC document the nectar/pollen and specialist-bee value; Texas A&M notes pollinators raise sunflower seed set and oil yield.

good_seasoned.name: Cucumbers, squash, and melons (living trellis and pollinator support)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Cucurbits depend on insect pollination for fruit set and tolerate sunflower allelopathy comparatively well; sunflower's long bloom draws bees, and tall single-stem types double as a living trellis or windbreak. Site on the windward or northern edge to avoid shading the crop.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Cucurbit set is pollination-dependent and sunflower is a documented pollinator draw and sturdy support; cucurbits tolerate sunflower allelopathy better than potatoes/beans. Yield link inferred, not directly trialed.

good_seasoned.name: Birds and wildlife (seed-head food source)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Standing heads left to ripen feed finches, jays, and other birds and small mammals into fall and winter, functioning as natural bird feeders. Mutually exclusive with saving seed, which requires bagging the heads; choose by intent per planting.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: NC State and Clemson document the wildlife/bird-food value of standing seed heads; framed as a deliberate wildlife use.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Potatoes
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Sunflowers can hold back potatoes growing right next to them, because of natural chemicals from the sunflower's roots and old stalks. Keep potatoes out of the sunflower bed, and plant sunflowers along an edge instead.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Sunflower is a recognized allelopathic species (NC State tags H. annuus allelopathic; Penn State lists sunflowers among allelopathic garden plants). Potatoes are commonly cited as sensitive; the species-level allelopathy is documented, the potato-specific sensitivity is widely reported but not pinned to a single extension trial, so likely/medium.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Sunflower allelopathy in action. Helianthus annuus releases growth-inhibiting compounds from roots and decomposing residue, and potatoes are among the crops commonly reported as sensitive, showing stunting near sunflowers or in soil where they grew. The species-level allelopathy is documented by extension sources; the potato-specific call is well-reported tradition rather than a single trial, so keep potatoes out of the sunflower bed, avoid following sunflower with potatoes in the same soil, and clear residue and hulls.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Pole and runner beans
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Pole beans are another crop that sunflowers can slow down when planted close, so do not use a sunflower as a bean pole. Grow beans elsewhere and use cucumbers or squash near sunflowers instead.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Pole/runner beans are traditionally listed among plants sensitive to sunflower allelopathy. The species allelopathy is documented; the bean-specific claim is companion-planting tradition, and some sources note beans tolerate it, so framed traditional/low and the softest pairing.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A hedged allelopathy caution. Pole and runner beans are traditionally listed among crops sensitive to sunflower's allelochemicals, so despite the tempting idea of using a sunflower stalk as a bean trellis, the pairing is commonly discouraged. Note the honest uncertainty: reports conflict, and some sources hold that beans tolerate sunflower better than potatoes do. Treat it as a cautious, traditional avoidance, favor cucurbits for the living-trellis role, and keep beans in a separate bed.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Tender seedlings under bird-feeder hull drop
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: The hulls that drop from sunflower seeds (including under bird feeders) carry chemicals that can stop other seeds from sprouting and stunt small plants. Do not start a seedbed right under sunflowers or a feeder, and rake up fallen hulls.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Sunflower seed hulls are widely documented as allelopathic (the classic bare patch under bird feeders); extension sources recognize sunflower allelopathy and the role of residue. Effect on a specific seedbed is inferred, so likely/medium.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: The residue side of sunflower allelopathy. Seed hulls are the most-cited source of the inhibitory compounds, the reason a bare, weed-free patch often forms under a sunflower-seed bird feeder. Avoid sowing a fresh seedbed directly beneath sunflowers or a feeder, rake up accumulated hulls, and do not mulch sensitive beds with sunflower residue. This is a residue-management caution rather than a living-plant antagonism, and it is part of why sunflower works as a weed-suppressing cover crop.

bad_seasoned.name: Potatoes
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Helianthus annuus releases growth-inhibiting allelochemicals from roots and residue; potatoes are commonly reported as sensitive, stunting near sunflowers or in their old soil. Keep potatoes out of the sunflower bed and out of the following rotation, and clear residue and hulls.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Species-level allelopathy documented (NC State, Penn State); potato sensitivity widely reported but not a single trial.

bad_seasoned.name: Pole and runner beans
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Traditionally listed among crops sensitive to sunflower allelochemicals, so a sunflower stalk is a poor bean trellis despite the temptation; reports conflict and some hold beans tolerate it, so a cautious, hedged avoidance. Favor cucurbits for the living-trellis role.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Companion-planting tradition; species allelopathy documented, bean-specific claim is hedged and contested.

bad_seasoned.name: Tender seedlings under bird-feeder hull drop
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Seed hulls are the most-cited source of sunflower's inhibitory compounds, the reason a bare patch forms under a sunflower-seed feeder. Do not sow a seedbed directly under sunflowers or a feeder, rake accumulated hulls, and do not mulch sensitive beds with sunflower residue.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Hull allelopathy widely documented (bird-feeder bare patch); extension recognizes sunflower allelopathy and residue role. Seedbed effect inferred.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Any indoor-started transplants need 7 to 10 days of hardening off, increasing outdoor exposure gradually, before setting out after all frost danger has passed; handle the rootball gently, since sunflowers resent root disturbance.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: If you started plants indoors, harden them off first: set them outside for a little longer each day over about a week so they get used to sun and wind before planting them out, and be gentle with the roots.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Direct sowing is the strongly preferred method: sunflowers form a deep taproot early and resent transplanting, so sow seed about 1 inch deep into warmed soil (past 50 °F, ideally 70 to 85 °F) after frost, and they germinate in 7 to 10 days. To gain a couple of weeks in short seasons, start indoors only 2 to 3 weeks before last frost in biodegradable pots and transplant before the taproot circles, disturbing roots minimally. Thin to type-appropriate spacing once seedlings are up. Stake tall single-stem giants early so the support is in place before the head gets top-heavy.
start_method.notes_beginner: The best way is to sow sunflower seeds straight into warm garden soil (about 1 inch deep) after your last frost; they sprout in 7 to 10 days. Sunflowers have a deep root and do not like being moved, so plant them where they will grow. If your season is short, you can start a few indoors 2 to 3 weeks before the last frost in biodegradable pots and move them out gently, pot and all. Put a stake in for tall types early, before the big flower makes them top-heavy.

soil_mix.type_beginner: regular potting mix that drains well
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Use a deep pot and a potting mix that drains well. Mix in a little compost for food, since sunflowers are hungry, and add perlite if the mix stays too wet. Sunflowers have a deep root, so depth matters more than width.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: general-purpose well-draining potting mix with added compost
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Prioritize depth for the taproot and free drainage; blend compost into a quality potting mix for the heavier feeding these plants want, and add perlite if the base mix holds too much water. Choose dwarf or compact cultivars for containers.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out faster than the garden, so check them often in hot weather and water when the top inch of soil feels dry, letting the extra drain out the bottom. Do not let the pot stay soggy.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Watering pots washes out their food, so feed potted sunflowers every couple of weeks with a balanced fertilizer through the growing season, going easy on high-nitrogen feeds so stems stay strong.

overwintering.approach_beginner: This does not apply. Sunflowers are one-season flowers that die at the first frost, so there is nothing to overwinter. Just plant new seeds next year, or save some seeds from this year's heads.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Not applicable: sunflower is a frost-tender annual grown for a single season and killed by the first frost; it is not overwintered. Re-sow each year, optionally from saved seed of open-pollinated types.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Dwarf sunflowers like 'Teddy Bear' and 'Sunspot' grow well in pots, window boxes, and on balconies. Use a deep pot with drainage holes (depth matters for the root), a well-draining mix with some compost, and full sun. The giant types are not suited to containers because they get far too big and top-heavy.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Containers suit dwarf and compact cultivars only; giants are unworkable in pots given their size and top-heaviness. Provide depth for the taproot (a deep pot matters more than a wide one), free drainage, compost-enriched mix for the heavier feeding, and full sun. Water and feed more often than in the ground, since pots dry and leach faster.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry faster than ground beds, so check in heat and water when the top inch is dry, letting excess drain freely; the deep root still wants a deep, thorough soak rather than frequent sips, and never a constantly wet pot.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Frequent watering leaches nutrients from containers, so feed potted sunflowers every couple of weeks with a balanced fertilizer through active growth; keep nitrogen moderate to maintain sturdy stems on the compact types.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering containers can work for dwarf sunflowers if the surface dries between top-ups; keep the reservoir from saturating the root zone, since constant moisture undercuts the drought-adapted taproot and invites basal rot.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot can work for dwarf sunflowers, but only if the top of the soil dries out between waterings. Sunflowers do not like soil that is wet all the time and can rot at the base in it.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: As an aster-family (Asteraceae) annual, avoid following sunflower immediately with itself or other susceptible asters where soilborne disease has built up, especially Sclerotinia (white mold), which persists in soil for years; rotate to an unrelated family for a season or more. Because of allelopathy, also avoid following sunflower with sensitive crops such as potatoes in the same soil, and clear residue and hulls before replanting.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Sunflowers are in the daisy family (Asteraceae). Do not plant sunflowers, or other daisy-family plants, in the same spot the next year, especially if there was any stalk or head rot, since that fungus stays in the soil. Because sunflowers leave behind chemicals that can slow some plants, also avoid planting potatoes right where sunflowers grew, and rake up old stalks and hulls first.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotation matters more for sunflower than for many ornamentals because its key diseases are soilborne and persistent. Avoid planting sunflower on the same ground in back-to-back years, particularly where Sclerotinia, downy mildew, or rust appeared, and clear infected debris at season end. Used deliberately, sunflower is also a recognized weed-suppressing cover crop thanks to the same allelopathy that cautions against following it with sensitive vegetables.
rotation.note_beginner: Rotating sunflowers helps more than it does for many flowers, because their main diseases live in the soil. Try not to grow sunflowers in the same spot two years running, especially if you saw any rot, mildew, or rust, and clean up old stalks and leaves at the end of the season. On the useful side, sunflowers are sometimes grown on purpose as a cover crop to hold down weeds, using the same natural chemicals that mean you should not follow them with touchy crops like potatoes.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seed leaves (cotyledons) push up from warm soil within roughly 7 to 10 days; the large seed gives a strong, fast emergence.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The first two seed leaves push up through the soil in about 7 to 10 days.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep soil warm (ideally 70 to 85 °F) and evenly moist; protect emerging seedlings from birds, slugs, and cutworms, which target the big sprouting seed.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil warm and damp until the seedlings come up, and watch for birds and cutworms that go after the new sprouts.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Seedlings emerged?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your seeds sprouted?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: First true leaves develop and the taproot drives down; the seedling establishes quickly and starts to gain height.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Real leaves appear and the little plant starts growing fast.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin to type-appropriate spacing (about 6 in for small cut-flower singles, 12 in for mid-size, 18 to 24 in for branching and giant types); guard against cutworms and water at the base.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Thin the seedlings to the right spacing for your type (small ones about 6 inches apart, big ones 18 to 24 inches), and protect them from cutworms.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Thinned and spaced?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you spaced out your seedlings?

growth_stages.name: Established / vegetative
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Rapid stem elongation; single-stem types shoot up toward full height, branching types put out side stems. Young plants visibly track the sun east to west during the day.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant grows tall fast. Young sunflowers turn to follow the sun across the sky during the day.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Stake tall single-stem giants now, before the head adds weight; keep moisture steady and feed lightly if soil is lean. Branching types need no pinching.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Put a stake in for tall types now, before the heavy flower forms. Keep the soil watered and feed lightly if the leaves look pale.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Plants established and staked (if tall)?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are your plants growing tall?

growth_stages.name: Budding
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A flower bud forms at the stem tip (or several on branching types); the bud tracks the sun by day before bloom.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A flower bud forms at the top of the stem and faces the sun as it moves.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture even as the head forms; begin the critical-water window. Scout for aphids and for sunflower moth as buds open.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist as the bud forms, and start checking for aphids and head pests.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: First bud visible?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Do you see a flower bud yet?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The head opens; first bloom is roughly 60 to 100 days from sowing depending on type. The mature head stiffens and settles facing east, and pollinators work the disk flowers.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The flower opens, about 2 to 3 months after planting. The grown flower settles facing east, and bees work the center.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep water steady through bloom (the critical window); cut single-stem and branching cut-flower types just as the head opens, and deadhead branching types to prolong display. Leave heads on if you want seed.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep watering through flowering. Cut flowers for a vase just as they open, and snip faded blooms off branching types for more. Leave heads on the plant if you want seeds.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: First bloom open?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Has your sunflower opened?

growth_stages.name: Seed ripening and harvest (optional)
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: After bloom, petals drop and the head matures over about 30 to 45 days: the back of the head turns from green to yellow then brown, the central florets dry, and the seeds plump and firm.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: After the petals fall, the head slowly dries: the back turns yellow then brown and the seeds get plump and firm. This takes about a month.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: To save seed, cover ripening heads with paper sacks or cheesecloth once petals brown to beat birds and squirrels; cut heads when backs are brown and cure in a warm, dry, airy, rodent-free spot until seeds release, then store dry.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: If you want the seeds, cover the heads with a paper bag or cheesecloth once the petals turn brown so birds do not get them. Cut the heads when the backs are brown, hang them somewhere warm and dry to finish, then rub the seeds off and store them dry.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Seed heads ripening or bagged?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are you saving seeds?

notifications.body_seasoned: Frost danger has passed and soil should be warming. Direct-sow about 1 inch deep once soil is past 50 °F (ideally 70 to 85 °F); sunflowers resent transplanting, so sow where they will grow.
notifications.body_beginner: Your last frost has passed, so you can plant sunflower seeds outside about an inch deep once the soil feels warm. Plant them right where they will grow, because they do not like being moved.

notifications.body_seasoned: Tall single-stem and giant types grow fast now. Set a sturdy stake before the head adds weight, so wind does not snap or lodge the stalk later.
notifications.body_beginner: If you are growing a tall sunflower, put a strong stake in now, before the big flower forms and makes it top-heavy in the wind.

notifications.body_seasoned: Heads are opening. Cut single-stem and branching cut-flower types just as the head opens for the longest vase life, and deadhead branching types to prolong the display.
notifications.body_beginner: Your sunflowers are opening. Cut some for a vase just as they open, and snip faded flowers off the branching types to get more blooms.

notifications.body_seasoned: Petals are browning and seeds are filling. If you want the seed, bag the heads in paper or cheesecloth now to beat birds and squirrels, then cut and cure once the backs turn brown.
notifications.body_beginner: The petals are turning brown and the seeds are filling. If you want to keep the seeds, cover the heads with a paper bag or cheesecloth now so birds do not eat them, then cut and dry the heads when the backs are brown.

notifications.body_seasoned: A first fall frost is forecast within a few days and will end the sunflower season. Cut remaining blooms for the vase, and harvest or bag any heads you are saving for seed.
notifications.body_beginner: Frost is expected in a few days, which will end your sunflowers. Cut the flowers that are left for a vase, and bring in or cover any heads you are saving for seeds.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost warning
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Sunflowers cannot survive frost. Cover young plants or cut the flowers before a frosty night, in spring or fall.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Sunflowers cannot handle frost. Cover young plants or cut the flowers before a cold, frosty night, in spring or fall.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Strong wind warning
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Tall single-stem and giant sunflowers are top-heavy and lodge or snap in storms. Make sure stakes are secure ahead of strong wind, especially once heads have filled.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Tall sunflowers can blow over or snap in strong wind, especially with a heavy flower on top. Check that your stakes are tied firmly before a windy storm.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot weather ahead
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Good news: sunflowers thrive in heat and full sun, and summer is their peak rather than a stress period. Water deeply at the base, especially around flowering.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Good news: sunflowers love hot, sunny weather, and summer is their best season. Just water deeply at the base, especially when they are flowering.

germination.text_seasoned: Direct-sow once soil is past 50 °F and warming (ideally 70 to 85 °F) after frost; warmth, not the date, is the trigger, and the big seed emerges strongly in 7 to 10 days. Sow where plants will grow, since the taproot resents transplanting.
germination.text_beginner: Plant seeds outside once the soil is warm, after your last frost. The large seeds come up well in 7 to 10 days. Plant them where they will grow, because sunflowers do not like being moved.

germination.text_seasoned: Sow about 1 inch deep, deeper than most flowers, to anchor the taproot; protect the sprouting seed and seedlings from birds and cutworms, which target the large, oil-rich sprouts.
germination.text_beginner: Plant the seeds about an inch deep. Keep an eye out for birds and cutworms, which like to eat the big sprouting seeds.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin to type once seedlings have true leaves: about 6 in for small cut-flower singles, 12 in for mid-size, and 18 to 24 in for branching and giant types. Spacing for airflow limits rust, Septoria, and powdery mildew later.
seedling.text_beginner: Once seedlings have real leaves, thin them to the right spacing: small types about 6 inches apart, medium ones about a foot, and the big branching or giant ones 18 to 24 inches. Room for air helps prevent leaf diseases.

seedling.text_seasoned: Cutworms sever young sunflowers at the soil line overnight; use stem collars on thinned seedlings or transplants and clear weedy harborage before sowing. Damage is a seedling-stage concern that vigorous plants outgrow.
seedling.text_beginner: Cutworms can cut down young sunflowers at night. Put a little collar of cardboard or foil around the stem of a new seedling, and clear weeds before planting. Bigger plants are not bothered.

established.text_seasoned: Stake tall single-stem and giant types early, before the head adds weight, so wind does not lodge or snap the stalk; branching types are self-supporting and need no pinching. Keep nitrogen modest so stalks stay sturdy.
established.text_beginner: Put a stake in for tall sunflowers early, before the heavy flower forms, so wind does not topple them. Branching types hold themselves up. Go easy on high-nitrogen fertilizer so the stems stay strong.

established.text_seasoned: Young plants and buds are heliotropic, tracking the sun east to west by day and resetting east overnight; as heads mature and stems stiffen they settle facing east, which warms them at sunrise and draws more morning pollinators. This is normal, not a problem.
established.text_beginner: Young sunflowers turn to follow the sun across the sky during the day, then face east again by morning. As they get older, the flowers settle facing east for good. This is normal and even helps bring in bees.

budding.text_seasoned: Keep moisture even as the head forms; the roughly 20 days before and after flowering are the critical water window, when shortage cuts head size and seed fill. Water deeply to the taproot, never to saturation.
budding.text_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist as the bud forms. The weeks just before and after flowering are the most important time to water, or you get a smaller flower and fewer seeds. Water deeply, but do not make the soil soggy.

budding.text_seasoned: Scout opening heads for sunflower moth (webbing and tunneled seeds) and the head-clipping weevil (a girdle 1 to 2 inches below the head that drops it). Garden management is sanitation and rotation, not routine spraying.
budding.text_beginner: As the flower opens, check for head pests: sunflower moth caterpillars web and tunnel the head, and the head-clipping weevil chops the stalk just below the flower. The best fixes are cleaning up old stalks and not planting sunflowers in the same spot each year.

flowering.text_seasoned: For the vase, cut just as the head opens and the back is still greenish, recut the stem, and strip lower leaves; pollen-free types stay tidy longest. Deadhead branching types to prolong bloom. Leave heads on the plant if seed is the goal.
flowering.text_beginner: For a vase, cut sunflowers just as they open, trim the stem, and pull off the lower leaves; pollen-free kinds stay neatest. Snip faded flowers off branching types for more blooms. Leave the flowers on the plant if you want seeds instead.

flowering.text_seasoned: Open, pollen-bearing flowers are a major nectar and pollen source for honey bees, native and specialist sunflower bees, and butterflies; pollinator visitation also improves the plant's own seed set. Pollen-free cut-flower types trade this away for vase tidiness.
flowering.text_beginner: Open sunflowers with pollen are great for bees and butterflies, and the visiting bees also help the plant make more seeds. The pollen-free types meant for vases do not feed bees, so grow some regular ones too if you want to help pollinators.

seed_ripening.text_seasoned: To save seed, bag ripening heads in paper sacks or cheesecloth once petals brown; birds and squirrels otherwise strip a head fast. The same standing heads make excellent natural bird feeders if you would rather feed wildlife.
seed_ripening.text_beginner: If you want the seeds, cover the heads with a paper bag or cheesecloth once the petals turn brown, or birds and squirrels will get them first. If you would rather feed the birds, just leave the heads standing as a natural bird feeder.

seed_ripening.text_seasoned: Harvest when the back of the head is brown and the seeds part easily: cut the head with a length of stalk and cure it in a warm, dry, airy, rodent-free place until the seeds release, then rub them off and store fully dried. Saved open-pollinated seed comes true; hybrid seed will not.
seed_ripening.text_beginner: Harvest seeds when the back of the head is brown and the seeds come off easily. Cut the head with some stem, hang it somewhere warm and dry and safe from mice until the seeds loosen, then rub them off and store them dry. Seeds from regular (open-pollinated) sunflowers will grow true; seeds from hybrids will not.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Yield depends entirely on type. A single-stem giant produces one large head (often 8 to 14 inches or more across) yielding a substantial crop of seed; branching types produce many smaller heads over a longer window, ideal for cut flowers and pollinators but smaller individual seed heads; dwarf types give modest blooms for color. A well-grown large head can hold many hundreds to over a thousand seeds.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: How much you get depends on the type. A giant sunflower makes one big head full of seeds, sometimes over a foot wide. Branching types make lots of smaller flowers over a longer time, great for cutting and for bees but with smaller seed heads. Dwarf types are mostly just for pretty flowers. One big head can hold many hundreds of seeds.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Sunflowers bloom the first season from seed, roughly 60 to 100 days after sowing depending on type (fast cut-flower singles sooner, giants later), so there is no establishment year; a spring sowing flowers in summer, with seed ripening over the following month.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Sunflowers flower the same year you plant them, usually 2 to 3 months after sowing. There is no waiting year. Plant in spring and you get flowers in summer, with seeds ripening about a month after that.
factors_seasoned: Type: single-stem giants give one large seed head; branching types give many smaller heads and more cut flowers; dwarf types give modest blooms.
Spacing and airflow: adequate spacing builds sturdier plants and limits rust, Septoria, and powdery mildew.
Water around bloom: steady moisture in the roughly 20 days before and after flowering drives head size and seed fill.
Staking: staking tall types prevents wind lodging that can cost the whole head.
Bird and squirrel protection: bagging ripening heads is the difference between a full seed harvest and a stripped one.
Pollination: pollinator visitation improves seed set, so pollen-bearing types and nearby pollinator habitat raise seed yield.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No T1 evidence supports a moon-phase planting preference for sunflower; left unset.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Seed head stripped or empty before harvest
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Birds or squirrels ate all the seeds
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Birds and squirrels reached the ripening head first; sunflower seed is a prime target and an unprotected head can be cleared in a day or two.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Birds or squirrels got to the seed head before you did. They love sunflower seeds and can clear a head fast.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Bag ripening heads in paper sacks or cheesecloth once petals brown, and harvest promptly when backs turn brown rather than leaving heads standing, unless feeding wildlife is the goal.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Next time, cover the heads with a paper bag or cheesecloth once the petals brown, and harvest as soon as the backs turn brown instead of waiting.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Plant leaned, snapped, or blew over
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The sunflower fell over or snapped
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: A tall, top-heavy single-stem type lodged in wind, often worsened by an unstaked stalk, a shallow root from transplanting, or soft growth from excess nitrogen.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: A tall sunflower got top-heavy and blew over in the wind, usually because it was not staked, or it grew too soft from too much fertilizer.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Stake tall and giant types early, direct-sow for a deep anchoring taproot, and keep nitrogen modest so stalks stay sturdy.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Next time, stake tall types early, plant the seeds in place so the root grows deep, and go easy on high-nitrogen fertilizer.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Tall, leafy plant, weak stalk, late or small bloom
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Tall and leafy with a weak stem and small flower
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Excess nitrogen or too much shade drove soft, leafy growth at the expense of a strong stalk and head; sunflowers need full sun and balanced, not high-nitrogen, feeding.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The plant got too much high-nitrogen feed or too much shade, so it grew leafy and floppy with a small flower.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Grow in full sun, keep nitrogen modest and balanced, and favor phosphorus and potassium for head and seed development.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Next time, plant in full sun and go easy on fertilizer, especially the high-nitrogen kind.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Soft rot of the stalk base or head with white mold
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The stem base or flower rotted with white mold
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Sclerotinia (white mold) caused basal stalk rot or head rot, favored by cool, wet conditions and poorly drained soil; the soilborne fungus persists for years and is hard to cure.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: A soil fungus called white mold (Sclerotinia) rotted the stem base or flower, usually in cool, wet, poorly drained conditions. It is hard to fix once it starts.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Improve drainage, space and rotate (avoid beds with a white-mold or recent broadleaf-crop history), remove and destroy infected plants, and do not compost them.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Next time, plant in well-drained soil with more space, move sunflowers to a new spot, and pull and throw away (do not compost) any rotted plants.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Rusty, spotted, or mildewed leaves
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Leaves got rusty, spotted, or powdery
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Rust (cinnamon pustules), Septoria leaf spot (angular brown spots), or powdery mildew (white film) built up in humid, crowded, overhead-wet conditions; foliar and rarely fatal but weakening late season.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Leaf diseases like rust, leaf spot, or powdery mildew showed up, usually because plants were crowded, humid, or watered overhead. They hurt the leaves but rarely kill the plant.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Space for airflow, water at the base, irrigate in the morning if overhead is unavoidable, remove infected debris, and rotate away from continuous sunflower.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Next time, give plants more room, water the soil instead of the leaves, clean up sick leaves, and grow sunflowers in a different spot.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Seeds failed to come up
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Few or no seeds sprouted
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Usually cold, wet soil or seed eaten by birds, cutworms, or wireworms; seed sown before soil reaches about 50 to 70 °F germinates slowly, erratically, or rots.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Usually cold, wet soil, or birds and soil pests eating the seed. Planted too early in cold soil, sunflower seeds come up poorly or rot.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait for warm soil (ideally 70 to 85 °F), sow about 1 inch deep, keep evenly moist during emergence, and protect the seed from birds and cutworms.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Wait for warm soil, plant about an inch deep, keep it damp until they sprout, and protect the seeds from birds and cutworms.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Single-stem cut-flower types in particular reward succession sowing: sow every 1 to 3 weeks from after last frost through midsummer for a continuous run of fresh blooms, since each single-stem plant flowers once. Branching types bloom over a longer window from one sowing, and giants are a single grand plant. There is no heat pause: sunflowers thrive through peak summer.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: For sunflowers all summer, plant a new small batch of seeds every 1 to 3 weeks from after the last frost into midsummer, especially the single-stem cutting types, since each one flowers just once. Branching types bloom for a long time from one planting, and giant types are a one-and-done show. Sunflowers love the heat, so you do not stop for summer.
succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Single-stem sunflowers flower once, so staggered sowings are how cut-flower growers keep a steady supply; branching and giant types are less succession-dependent.

crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Sunflower has two harvests. For cut flowers, cut when the bloom is just opening and the back of the head is still greenish, in the cool of the morning into clean water, stripping lower leaves; pollen-free types stay tidiest and vase life runs about a week. For seed, let heads ripen on the plant until the back turns from yellow to brown, the florets dry, and the seeds plump and firm (about 30 to 45 days after bloom); bag ripening heads in paper or cheesecloth to beat birds and squirrels, then cut and cure the head in a warm, dry, airy, rodent-free spot until the seeds release.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Sunflowers give you two harvests. For a vase, cut the flowers just as they open, in the morning, into clean water, and pull off the lower leaves; pollen-free types stay neatest. For seeds, leave the heads on the plant until the back turns brown and the seeds are plump and firm, about a month after the flower opens. Cover the ripening heads with a paper bag or cheesecloth so birds and squirrels do not get them, then cut the head and dry it somewhere warm and airy until the seeds come loose.

open_findings.summary: Per-region planting DATES for the California regions (ca_interior, ca_north_coast, ca_south_coast, ca_desert), warm_arid, and low_desert_az are MODELED on the warm-season-annual frost-bracketed pattern and the certified structural twin zinnia, because the catalogued sunflower pages (UMN, Clemson, MU, UF/IFAS, NCSU, Illinois, Purdue) give culture but not region-specific dated planting tables for sunflower. Sunflower shares zinnia's warm-season frost-bracketed lifecycle (direct-sow after last frost, bloom through summer heat to first frost, no heat pause), so the windows are well-grounded climate carryovers; a sunflower-specific regional planting-date source would tighten them. UF/IFAS does give Florida-specific timing (late winter to early spring seeding, with decline in late-spring heat), reflected in the fl_peninsula prose.

hawaii_tropical year_round:true rests on a CLIMATE DERIVATION (frost-free zone 11 + heat-loving annual + pause_in_heat:false), mirroring the certified zinnia hawaii treatment, not a sunflower-specific Hawaii continuity table. No catalogued readable Hawaii-specific sunflower planting source was found; the year-round Hawaii calendar is a sound climate inference, upgradeable if a readable HI-specific sunflower source surfaces. No PDF was shelled out per the source-or-flag rule.

The regional numeric calendar skeleton (per-zone frost dates, planting-window offsets, the 12-token monthly calendars, and the derived successions_realized counts) is carried from the certified warm-season-annual twin zinnia, because sunflower occupies the identical frost-bracketed warm-season niche. All consumer prose, biology, sources, varieties, pests/diseases, and bloom timing were refit to sunflower. The carried calendar represents the BLOOM/ornamental cycle (first bloom roughly 60 to 100 days from sowing by type, per MU's 70 to 120 days to bloom); SEED harvest ripens about 30 to 45 days AFTER bloom and is handled in prose and the seed_ripening growth stage, not as separate calendar tokens. release_verify's Step-5.5 note will correctly flag the calendars as value-identical to zinnia: attest as climate-derived, not pasted. This is the daily-review item.

ALLELOPATHY FRAMING (load-bearing honesty boundary, not a sourcing gap): Helianthus annuus is documented as an allelopathic species at the species level (NC State plant toolbox tags H. annuus #allelopathic; Penn State 'Allelopathy in the Home Garden' lists sunflowers among allelopathic plants; UF/IFAS recognizes the phenomenon), and seed hulls are widely documented as the classic inhibitory residue (the bare patch under bird feeders). The SPECIFIC sensitive-neighbor list (potatoes, pole/runner beans) is well-reported companion-planting tradition rather than a single extension trial, and reports conflict (some hold beans tolerate it; cucurbits/corn/squash tolerate it comparatively well). The companion 'bad' entries are therefore labeled likely/medium (potatoes, hull residue) and traditional/low (pole beans), with the species-level allelopathy verified_against_sources:true and the crop-specific calls hedged. The extension sources name the phenomenon but do not enumerate the garden-crop sensitivity list, so the specific pairings are the reviewer's confirm item.

DETAILED PEST/DISEASE specifics are sourced to readable T1 HTML pages: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension Entomology 'Managing Insect Pests of Texas Sunflowers' (sunflower moth, head-clipping weevil, cutworms, seed/stem weevils, defoliators) and the NDSU Extension 'Sunflower Disease Diagnostic Series' INDEX page (readable HTML naming Sclerotinia head/stalk rot, downy mildew, rust, Septoria leaf blight, powdery mildew, etc.), plus Clemson and Illinois for downy/powdery mildew. The per-disease NDSU detail pages and the SDSU 'Diseases of Sunflower' chapter are PDFs and were NOT fetched per the source-or-flag rule; management specifics are framed from the readable summaries. The TAMU guide is field/production-scaled (economic thresholds), adapted to home-garden cultural management (sanitation, rotation, tolerance) in the prose. Severities are home-garden calls: birds/squirrels high (the signature seed-stage pest), Sclerotinia high, others medium/low.

DAYS_TO_MATURITY [60,100] (mid 80) and start_method represent type-spanning judgment calls. Sunflower bloom timing ranges widely by type: fast single-stem cut-flower types bloom in ~55 to 65 days while giants take 100 to 120+ days (MU Extension states 70 to 120 days to bloom); [60,100] mid 80 is a representative central range consistent with the carried zinnia harvest offsets, with the full spread described in prose. start_method.start is set to 'both' (not 'direct') because UMN, Illinois, Clemson, and MU all document indoor starting as a real option, but the DIRECT-SOW preference and taproot transplant-sensitivity are the dominant framing throughout (weeks_before shortened to 3, biodegradable-pot caveat) per the task's direct-sow emphasis. category retained as the shell's 'Edible & Harvest' (not zinnia's 'Companion & Pollinator') to honor sunflower's genuine seed-harvest use, which also drives the real (non-'not applicable') storage and harvest fields.
