crops.deadheading_seasoned: Deadheading applies mainly to branching, multi-head types: cut or snip spent blooms back to the next bud or leaf node to redirect energy into new flowers and prolong the display to frost, and cutting for the vase does the same job. Single-stem types (giants and most cut-flower singles) make one terminal head and do not rebloom, so there is nothing to deadhead; leave that head to ripen if you want seed, or cut it once for the vase. There is no pinching: branching types branch on their own.
crops.deadheading_beginner: Deadheading (snipping off faded flowers) mostly matters for the branching types with many flowers: cut the old blooms back to the next bud and the plant makes more, right up to frost. Cutting fresh ones for a vase does the same thing. The single-stem types, including the giants, make just one flower and do not rebloom, so there is nothing to deadhead; leave that head to make seeds, or cut it once for a vase. You do not need to pinch sunflowers.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note: Sunflowers direct-sow readily into warm soil (past 50 °F, ideally 70 to 85 °F) after the last spring frost, about 1 inch deep; the big seed emerges in 7 to 10 days, and direct sowing is strongly preferred because the taproot resents transplanting.

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.synthesis_note: Optional indoor start: because sunflowers resent root disturbance, start only 2 to 3 weeks before the last frost in biodegradable pots and transplant young, before the taproot develops; direct sowing is easier and usually preferred.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note: Transplants set out after the last frost, handled gently pot and all to spare the taproot, on the same warm-soil trigger as direct sowing.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note: First bloom roughly 60 to 100 days after sowing depending on type (fast cut-flower singles sooner, giants later); seed ripens about 30 to 45 days after bloom.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Sunflowers bloom through the summer heat to the first fall frost, which kills the tender annual; seed of late sowings should be harvested before that frost.

plant_out.label: succession
plant_out.synthesis_note: For continuous bloom, especially from single-stem cut-flower types, sow every 1 to 3 weeks from after the last frost through midsummer; sunflowers thrive in summer heat, so there is no midsummer pause.

3.planting_note: Direct-sow after the last frost once soil is warm (past 50 °F, ideally 70 to 85 °F), about 1 inch deep; first blooms in roughly 60 to 100 days by type, then seed ripens about a month later. Stake tall types, and bag ripening heads to save seed from birds. Because the season is shorter here, plan on one or two sowings and choose faster types for reliable bloom and seed before frost.
3.zone_notes: Sunflowers run as a single frost-bracketed warm-season crop here: direct-sow after the last spring frost once the soil is warm, bloom straight through the summer heat, and the first fall frost ends the season.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the northern tier, sunflowers grow in one summer window. Wait until a week or two after your last frost, when the soil is warm, then plant the seeds about an inch deep where they will grow. They flower from summer until the first fall frost. In the coldest areas, pick faster or medium types so the seeds ripen in time, and stake the tall ones against storms. You never stop for heat here; cold is the only limit, at both ends.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In the northern tier, sunflower is a single frost-bracketed summer crop. Wait until the soil is warm (past 50 °F) and frost danger has passed, then direct-sow about 1 inch deep; plants bloom from summer to the first fall frost. Choose faster single-stem or mid-size types in the coldest zones so heads ripen seed before frost, and stake tall types against summer storms. There is no heat pause here; frost on both ends is the only limit. Sunflowers are a Northern Plains signature crop, so they are well adapted to short, warm summers, but watch for downy mildew in cold, wet springs.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast and Gulf, sunflowers love the heat. Plant after your last spring frost once the soil is warm, and they flower all summer to the first frost in fall. se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: Across the Southeast and Gulf, sunflower is a warm-season workhorse: direct-sow after the last spring frost once soil is warm, and it blooms straight through the region's hot, humid summer to the first fall frost. The real regional pressures are leaf diseases (rust, Septoria, downy mildew) in the humidity, so space generously, water at the base, and rotate; and birds, which are abundant, so bag heads early to save seed. Stake tall types against summer thunderstorms.

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In California's inland valleys, sunflowers thrive through the hot, dry summer. Plant after the last frost once the soil is warm, and they bloom into fall until the first frost. They handle the heat and dry spells well, so water deeply but let the soil dry out between waterings, most around flowering. Stake tall types, and cover the seed heads if you want to keep the seeds from the birds.

Water deeply to the taproot but let the soil dry between waterings, heaviest around bloom. Stake tall types, sow single-stem types in succession for a steady cut-flower supply, and bag heads against birds for seed.

Full sun and deep, infrequent watering to the taproot suit it; stake tall types against wind and bag heads against birds for seed.

The University of Florida notes that seeds are planted in late winter to early spring, and the common sunflowers fade in the heat and humidity by late spring or early summer; a fall planting gives autumn flowers. 11.calendar_basis: Frost-free z11 + T1 pause_in_heat:false (UC IPM, no heat stall) + zinnia documented in CTAHR Hawaii home-garden grow-lists = no season-closing factor, so continuous year-round bloom. Climate-DERIVED, not a CTAHR year-round continuity quote (none exists; searched, outcome C). The wet/rainy months raise powdery-mildew pressure but do not stop the crop.
11.planting_note: Direct-sow after the last frost once soil is warm (past 50 °F, ideally 70 to 85 °F), about 1 inch deep; first blooms in roughly 60 to 100 days by type, then seed ripens about a month later. Stake tall types, and bag ripening heads to save seed from birds. Sow single-stem cut-flower types again every 1 to 3 weeks through midsummer for a steady supply.
11.zone_notes: Frost-free and warm year round, so sunflowers can be sown in succession here with no seasonal frost gap; this heat-loving annual grows fast, and fresh sowings keep flowers and seed heads coming.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In Hawaii and other frost-free tropical areas, sunflowers can be planted through much of the year, loving the warmth and sun; plant a new batch of single-stem types now and then for steady flowers and seeds. The humidity can bring leaf diseases, so give plants room and water at the soil, and cover seed heads to keep the many birds from eating the seeds.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: In Hawaii and similar frost-free tropics, sunflower can be sown in succession across much of the year with no frost gap, thriving in the warmth and full sun; stagger sowings of single-stem types to keep flowers and seed coming. Humidity raises downy mildew, rust, and Septoria pressure, so favor airflow, base watering, and resistant types, and bag heads against abundant birds for seed.

crops.name: Borage
crops.flower_type: star-shaped, five-petaled, sky-blue (sometimes pink or white), nodding in branched clusters, under 1 inch across
crops.description_seasoned: Borage (Borago officinalis), also called starflower, is a large, fast-growing, frost-tender annual herb in the borage family (Boraginaceae), native to the Mediterranean. It builds a bushy, sprawling plant about 2 to 3 ft tall and 1 to 2 ft wide, clothed in coarse, bristly, gray-green leaves, and carries loose clusters of nodding, star-shaped, sky-blue flowers from late spring into fall. Borage is one of the best bee and pollinator plants a garden can grow, a traditional companion set near tomatoes, squash, and strawberries, and a vigorous self-seeder that naturalizes readily once established. Both the cucumber-flavored young leaves and the blue flowers are edible, used fresh as a garnish and in drinks and salads, though borage is best eaten in moderation. It grows through the warm months in cool and temperate regions and is killed by hard frost; in hot, humid climates it is grown instead as a cool-season plant.
crops.description_beginner: Borage is a big, easy, bushy herb with fuzzy leaves and beautiful blue, star-shaped flowers. Bees absolutely love it, which is why gardeners plant it near vegetables like tomatoes, squash, and strawberries. The young leaves taste like cucumber, and both the leaves and the blue flowers are edible, though you should eat them only in small amounts. Borage grows fast, sprawls out, so give it room, and it drops seed and comes back on its own year after year. It likes the warm part of the year in most gardens and is killed by frost; in hot, humid places it is grown in the cooler months instead.

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Borage is not fussy about soil and grows well even in poor ground, as long as water drains away and does not pool. Ordinary, well-drained garden soil is perfect. Very rich soil just makes big floppy plants, and soggy soil rots the roots, so pick a spot that drains well and go easy on the compost.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Borage is highly adaptable and grows in almost any soil, including poor and sandy ground, provided drainage is adequate; extension descriptions list it as tolerating clay, loam, and sand and even nutritionally poor soil. It is a light feeder, so overly rich soil pushes soft, floppy, leafy growth at the expense of sturdiness and bloom, and constantly wet, poorly drained soil rots its roots. Well-drained soil of moderate to low fertility gives the best-structured plants.

ph.note_beginner: Borage is not picky about soil pH (how acidic or alkaline the soil is). A normal garden range of about 6.0 to 7.0 is ideal, and it tolerates soil well outside that, so you usually do not need to change anything.
ph.note_seasoned: Borage performs best across roughly 6.0 to 7.0 and is broadly adaptable to soil chemistry; extension descriptions record it growing in acid, neutral, and alkaline soils alike (tolerating roughly 5.5 to 8.0). pH adjustment is rarely warranted, so focus on drainage and modest fertility instead.

crops.tip_seasoned: Grow borage like a big, easygoing warm-season herb: direct-sow it where it is to grow, because it has a taproot and does not transplant well. Sow after the last spring frost in cool and temperate regions, or in fall and the cool season in hot, humid ones, covering the seed about 1/2 in. It germinates in 1 to 2 weeks and reaches first bloom in roughly 8 weeks. Give it room (12 to 24 in), full sun, and lean soil, go very light on fertilizer, and deadhead or cut flowers to prolong bloom. Leave a few late flowers to drop seed and it returns on its own; wear gloves, since the stems are prickly.
crops.tip_beginner: Plant borage seeds right where you want it to grow, since it does not like being moved. Sow after your last frost in most gardens, or in the cool season where summers are hot. Cover the seeds about half an inch deep; they sprout in a week or two and flower in about eight weeks. Give each plant plenty of room because it gets big and sprawly, keep it in sun, and do not over-fertilize. Snip off faded flowers for more blooms, let a few go to seed so it comes back, and wear gloves because the stems are prickly.

fertilizer.timing: At planting, then sparingly
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Borage is a light feeder that thrives even in poor soil, so it needs little supplemental fertilizer. A modest amount of compost or a balanced feed worked in at planting is plenty. Excess nitrogen produces soft, oversized, floppy plants that flower less and are more prone to powdery mildew, so favor a balanced or slightly low-nitrogen feed and skip routine feeding once plants are established.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Borage barely needs feeding and even grows in poor soil. Mix a little compost or balanced fertilizer into the ground at planting and that is usually all it needs. Too much fertilizer, especially the high-nitrogen kind, just gives you a giant floppy plant with fewer flowers.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time for an optional light feed. Borage is a light feeder, so at most one modest dose of a balanced fertilizer supports steady bloom; skip it entirely if your soil already has some fertility or you worked in compost.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: It is a good time to give your borage a small feed if you want, but it barely needs it. One light dose of a balanced fertilizer is plenty, and you can skip it if you already added compost.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 worked in lightly at planting suits borage; some growers give a monthly half-strength balanced feed, but a high-nitrogen lawn-type feed only pushes floppy foliage over flowers.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: The three numbers on fertilizer (N-P-K) are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. For borage, a balanced one like 10-10-10 is fine, used sparingly; avoid a high first-number (nitrogen) lawn feed, which gives leaves instead of flowers.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A single light application at planting is usually sufficient; if supplementing, a balanced fertilizer at about half the label rate for annuals is ample. Borage grows well in poor soil, so err toward under-feeding rather than over-feeding.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A little goes a long way. One light feeding at planting is usually enough. If you feed again, use about half what the package says, and do not overdo it.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.note_beginner: Tiny green or black soft insects that can cluster on the tender tips and flower buds, leaving sticky honeydew. Borage is otherwise seldom bothered by pests, and its flowers pull in ladybugs and hoverflies whose young eat aphids, so light infestations often clear on their own. A strong spray of water or insecticidal soap handles the rest. Some gardeners even let borage collect aphids as a decoy to keep them off nearby crops.
pests.note_seasoned: Borage is generally untroubled by insect pests; extension descriptions note it is not usually bothered and has no significant pest problems. When aphids do appear they colonize tender growth and buds, secreting honeydew, but the nectar-rich flowers recruit the aphid predators (lady beetles, hoverflies, lacewings) that keep them in check. Borage is sometimes grown deliberately as an insectary or banker planting for this reason. Hose off or treat with insecticidal soap only if populations build.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.note_beginner: A white, powdery film on the leaves, most common in warm, humid, still, or crowded conditions and without enough air movement. It is borage's main disease. Give plants plenty of room, grow them in full sun, water the soil rather than the leaves, and remove badly affected leaves.
diseases.note_seasoned: Borage's signature disease, and essentially its only regular one; it develops in warm, humid, still, and crowded plantings, and worsens as summer heat and humidity build (which is why borage is grown in the cool season in hot climates). Manage culturally with full sun, generous spacing for airflow, base watering, and removal of affected foliage rather than by spraying.

diseases.name: Root and stem rot in wet soil
diseases.note_beginner: Borage is drought-tolerant and hates soggy soil. Cold, wet, poorly drained ground can rot its roots and stem base, and young seedlings can collapse at the soil line. Plant in well-drained soil and do not overwater.
diseases.note_seasoned: Borage tolerates dry soil and is intolerant of waterlogging, so the standing failure is root and crown rot (and seedling damping-off) in cold, wet, poorly drained ground. It is a prevention story, not a treatment one: site in well-drained soil, water only when the soil dries, and avoid heavy, water-retentive beds. This is the drought-tolerant plant's usual wet-soil caveat rather than a disease borage is specifically prone to.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Keep the soil evenly moist through germination and until seedlings are established, then water only when the soil dries; borage is notably drought-tolerant once established and resents constantly wet soil, which rots its roots. Water at the base and keep the foliage dry to limit powdery mildew.
watering.frequency_beginner: Keep the soil damp while the seeds sprout and the young plants get going. After that, borage is tough and drought-tolerant, so water only when the soil has dried out. Do not keep it soggy, and water the soil, not the leaves.
watering.amount_seasoned: During establishment, aim for steady moisture, roughly an inch of water per week from rain plus irrigation; once established, borage needs far less and tolerates dry spells, so let the soil dry between deep waterings. Overwatering does more harm than a little drought.
watering.amount_beginner: While plants are young, give about an inch of water a week counting rain. Once borage is grown in, it needs much less; water deeply now and then and let the soil dry out in between. It handles dry weather better than wet.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base with drip or a soaker hose and keep the foliage dry; overhead wetting in warm, humid weather invites powdery mildew. If you must water overhead, do it in the morning so leaves dry quickly.
watering.method_beginner: Water the ground around the plant, not the leaves. A soaker hose or a watering can at the base is best, because dry leaves resist mildew. If leaves get wet, water in the morning so they dry off by midday.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting despite wet soil, and a soft, rotting stem base signal overwatering or poor drainage; persistently wet foliage also raises powdery-mildew pressure.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If the lower leaves yellow, the plant wilts even though the soil is wet, or the base turns soft and mushy, you are overwatering or the soil drains poorly.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting in the heat of the day that recovers by evening is normal for this big, thin-leaved plant; persistent wilting, dulling leaves, and stalled growth mean it is genuinely too dry, most critically during establishment and heavy bloom.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Borage often wilts a bit in the afternoon heat and perks back up in the evening, which is normal. If it stays wilted, looks dull, and stops growing, it is too dry, especially right after planting.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Water at the base and keep water off the foliage; dry, well-spaced plants are the main cultural lever against powdery mildew, borage's chief disease. Avoid frequent light sprinkling in humid weather.
watering.method_note_beginner: Water the soil around the plant, not the leaves or flowers. A soaker hose or watering can at the base works best, since dry, airy plants resist mildew.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The critical moisture window is germination and seedling establishment; after that, borage is drought-tolerant and the bigger risk is overwatering. Keep moisture steady while heavily blooming if the weather is hot and dry.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The most important time to keep the soil evenly moist is right after planting while the seeds sprout and settle in. After that, borage handles dry spells and the main mistake is watering too much.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Not a stored staple: borage is grown for blooms, a strong pollinator draw, and edible leaves and flowers used fresh. Cut sprays last a day or two in water; leaves and flowers are best picked and used the same day. See the notes for freezing flowers in ice cubes.
storage.room_temp_beginner: This does not really apply. Borage is a fresh herb and flower, not something to store on the counter. Pick the leaves and flowers as you need them. See the notes for a fun way to freeze the flowers.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Young leaves and freshly picked flowers keep only a day or two loosely covered in the refrigerator and wilt quickly, so use them fresh. Borage does not hold like sturdy produce.
storage.fridge_beginner: You can keep borage leaves or flowers in the fridge for a day or two, but they wilt fast, so use them right away.
storage.freezer_seasoned: The classic way to keep borage flowers is to freeze the whole blue blooms into ice cubes for chilled summer drinks; the leaves do not freeze well for later cooking. Freeze for garnish, not for a pantry supply.
storage.freezer_beginner: A classic trick is to freeze the blue flowers inside ice cubes to drop into cold drinks. The leaves do not freeze well, so use those fresh.
storage.notes_seasoned: Borage is grown for bloom, a top pollinator draw, and edible leaves and flowers, so the refrigerate and freeze fields do not apply as they would for produce. Harvest young, tender leaves before they turn too bristly, and pick fully open flowers on a dry day; pull off and discard the fuzzy green sepals behind each flower before eating. The leaves taste of cucumber and are used in salads, teas, and cool drinks; the blue flowers are a garnish and can be frozen into ice cubes. Use only unsprayed plants, and eat borage in moderation: the leaves contain pyrrolizidine alkaloids, which NC State notes can damage the liver and lungs, so use them only sparingly, and borage also has a diuretic effect in large amounts. Wear gloves when harvesting, since the stems and older leaves are prickly.
storage.notes_beginner: Borage is a plant for the garden, the bees, and fresh use, not for storing like vegetables. Pick young leaves before they get too fuzzy and prickly, and pick open flowers on a dry day. Snap off the fuzzy green part behind each flower before eating it. The leaves taste like cucumber in salads and drinks, and the blue flowers make a pretty garnish or can be frozen in ice cubes. Only eat borage that has not been sprayed, and eat it only in small amounts: borage leaves contain natural compounds called pyrrolizidine alkaloids that can harm the liver if eaten in large or frequent amounts, so keep borage to a garnish or an occasional few leaves. Wear gloves when you pick it because the stems are prickly.

recommended: Common blue borage (the wild species, Borago officinalis; sky-blue star flowers, the best type for bees and self-sowing)
'Alba' (white-flowered borage; same habit and cucumber-flavored leaves, with clean white blooms)
'Bill Archer' (variegated borage; leaves splashed cream and green, blue flowers, more ornamental)
'Variegata' (a general variegated selection grown for cream-marbled foliage)
varieties.note_seasoned: For most gardens the ordinary blue species is the one to grow: it is the strongest bee draw, self-sows freely, and gives the classic edible sky-blue stars. 'Alba' is a white-flowered form of the same easygoing plant, useful in white or cottage plantings, and the variegated selections ('Bill Archer', 'Variegata') are grown more for their cream-splashed foliage than for a different flower. All are the same species, are edible-flowered and cucumber-leaved, and come readily from saved or self-sown seed; the simple, open single flowers of every form serve pollinators well.
varieties.note_beginner: The plain blue borage is the classic choice and the best one for bees, and it reseeds itself easily. If you want something different, 'Alba' has white flowers instead of blue, and variegated types like 'Bill Archer' have pretty cream-and-green leaves. They are all the same easy plant with edible flowers and cucumber-tasting leaves, and they all come back from their own dropped seed.

companions.note_beginner: Borage is one of the classic companion plants, and its superpower is bees. It flowers for a long time and is a magnet for honey bees, bumble bees, and native bees, so planting it among vegetables draws in pollinators and helpful insects. Gardeners traditionally set it near tomatoes, squash, and strawberries: near squash, melons, and cucumbers it helps pollination; near tomatoes and strawberries it is a long-standing companion said to help them along and bring in the beneficial bugs that eat pests like hornworms. Those pest-fighting claims are garden tradition rather than proven fact, so enjoy borage mainly as a pollinator plant. Just give it lots of room, since it gets big and sprawly, and keep it a bit apart from squash so both get airflow, because they can share powdery mildew.
companions.note_seasoned: Borage's best-grounded companion value is as a premier insectary and pollinator plant: its long succession of nectar-rich blue flowers strongly attracts honey bees, bumble bees, and native bees, along with beneficial predators, which is well documented by extension. Interplanted around squash, melons, and cucumbers it is credited with improving pollination, and it is a long-standing traditional companion for tomatoes and strawberries (West Virginia University lists it among strawberry companions), with grower lore that it improves their vigor, flavor, and pest resistance and draws in predators of tomato hornworm. Those neighbor-benefit and pest-repellent effects are traditional practice rather than trialed results, so they are framed as tradition. There is no biologically antagonistic companion to avoid; site borage for full sun and airflow, give it generous room because it sprawls, and keep it from crowding squash since the two share powdery-mildew susceptibility.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Bees and pollinators (insectary planting)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Borage is one of the very best plants for attracting bees and other pollinators, and it flowers for a long time. An edge or patch of borage brings pollinators and helpful insects to the whole garden.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Extension sources directly document borage as a strong bee and pollinator draw (NC State: attracts bees; UC Marin: loved by pollinators; UC ANR: honey, bumble, and native bees). The benefit to neighboring crops is inferred from that well-documented attraction.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Borage's strongest, best-documented companion function. Its long-blooming, nectar-rich flowers recruit honey bees, bumble bees, native bees, and beneficial predators, supporting pollination and biological control nearby. Plant it as an insectary edge or interplant; this is a habitat and pollination benefit rather than a documented pest-repellent effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Squash, melons, and cucumbers (pollination)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Borage's bees help pollinate squash, melons, and cucumbers, which need lots of bee visits to set fruit. Plant borage nearby, but leave room so both get airflow, since they can share powdery mildew.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Borage's bee attraction is well documented; improved pollination of nearby bee-pollinated cucurbits is a reasonable, commonly recommended inference (UC ANR) rather than a controlled result.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A pollination-support pairing. Cucurbits are bee-pollinated and benefit from more pollinator visits; borage's heavy bee draw makes it a sensible interplant around squash, melons, and cucumbers. Space it generously, since borage and squash share powdery-mildew susceptibility and both want airflow.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Tomatoes
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Borage is a traditional companion for tomatoes. Gardeners say it helps tomatoes grow better and brings in insects that eat tomato hornworms. Treat this as helpful garden tradition, and enjoy the bees either way.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: A long-standing companion tradition (UC ANR notes tomatoes near borage reportedly improve in growth and disease resistance, and that borage draws hornworm predators); grower lore rather than a trialed effect. Borage's pollinator value is the solid part.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A classic traditional pairing. Borage is set near tomatoes on the tradition that it improves their growth and disease resistance and recruits predators of tomato hornworm; the mechanism (habitat for beneficials) is plausible but the benefit is traditional practice, not trialed. The dependable payoff is the pollinator and beneficial-insect habitat borage provides.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Strawberries
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Borage is a well-known strawberry companion. Its flowers bring in bees to pollinate the berries, and gardeners plant a few among strawberries to help flavor and yield. Give it room so it does not shade the low strawberry plants.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Listed as a strawberry companion by West Virginia University Extension; UC ANR notes strawberry growers set a few plants in beds to enhance flavor and yield. Pollinator support is well grounded; the flavor/yield effect is traditional.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A documented traditional companion for strawberries (West Virginia University lists borage among strawberry companions; UC ANR notes growers tuck a few plants into beds to enhance flavor and yield). The reliable benefit is bee pollination of the berries; keep the large borage plants to the edges so they do not shade the low strawberries.

good_seasoned.name: Bees and pollinators (insectary planting)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Long-blooming, nectar-rich flowers recruit honey bees, bumble bees, native bees, and beneficial predators, supporting pollination and biological control nearby. A habitat benefit, planted as an insectary edge.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Directly documented bee/pollinator draw (NC State, UC Marin, UC ANR); neighbor benefit inferred from it.

good_seasoned.name: Squash, melons, and cucumbers (pollination)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Cucurbits are bee-pollinated; borage's heavy bee draw supports fruit set on nearby squash, melons, and cucumbers. Space generously, since borage and squash share powdery-mildew susceptibility.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Bee attraction documented; improved cucurbit pollination is a reasonable, commonly recommended inference (UC ANR).

good_seasoned.name: Tomatoes
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Traditional companion said to improve tomato growth and disease resistance and to recruit tomato-hornworm predators; grower lore, not trialed. The dependable benefit is pollinator and beneficial-insect habitat.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Long-standing companion tradition (UC ANR); not a controlled result.

good_seasoned.name: Strawberries
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Documented traditional strawberry companion (West Virginia University); growers set a few plants in beds to enhance flavor and yield. Reliable benefit is bee pollination; keep to bed edges so it does not shade the berries.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Listed as a strawberry companion by WVU Extension; UC ANR notes the flavor/yield tradition. Pollination benefit grounded; flavor/yield traditional.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Hardening off does not apply, because borage is direct-sown rather than transplanted. It has a taproot and resents root disturbance, so sow it where it is to grow rather than starting it indoors.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: There is nothing to harden off, because you sow borage right in the garden instead of starting it inside. It does not like being moved.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Direct-sow borage where it will grow; it has a taproot and does not transplant well, so starting it indoors is not recommended. Sow after the last spring frost in cool and temperate regions, or in fall and the cool season in hot ones, covering the seed about 1/2 in (it germinates fine in darkness or light, but should be covered). It comes up in 1 to 2 weeks. Thin or space plants to 12 to 24 in, since borage grows large and sprawling, and it self-sows readily for future seasons.
start_method.notes_beginner: Sow borage seeds straight into the garden where you want plants, since it does not like being transplanted. Plant after your last frost in most gardens, or in the cool season where summers are hot, covering the seeds about half an inch deep. They come up in one to two weeks. Space plants 12 to 24 inches apart because borage gets big, and it will drop seed and come back on its own.

soil_mix.type_beginner: regular potting mix that drains well
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Use a potting mix that drains well. Borage has a taproot and grows big, so a large, deep pot is best. It does not need rich mix, and it rots in soggy mix, so good drainage matters more than fertility.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: general-purpose, free-draining potting mix
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Prioritize a free-draining mix in a large, deep container to accommodate the taproot; blend in perlite or coarse sand if the base mix stays wet. Keep fertility modest, since borage grows lush and floppy with excess feeding and rots in constantly wet mix.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out faster than the ground, so check them, but let the top inch dry before watering, because borage does not like soggy roots. Try not to wet the leaves.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Potting mix loses nutrients with watering, so a light feed every few weeks during bloom is plenty. Go easy, or you just get a floppy plant.

overwintering.approach_beginner: This does not really apply. Borage is a one-season plant. Frost ends it in cold areas, and in mild-winter areas it fades after flowering and setting seed. Either way you start fresh from seed each year, though it usually reseeds itself.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Not applicable as managed overwintering: borage is a frost-tender annual that dies with hard frost in cold zones and finishes after flowering and self-seeding in mild ones. It reliably self-sows, so volunteers return without overwintering the parent plant.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Borage can grow in a container, but it gets big with a deep taproot, so use a large, deep pot (5 gallons or more) with drainage holes and a well-draining mix in a sunny spot. It is happier in the ground, where it has room to sprawl and reseed.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Borage is growable in containers but is better suited to the open ground: it develops a taproot, grows large and sprawling, and self-sows, none of which suit a small pot. If you do container-grow it, use a large, deep pot (5 gallons or more) with excellent drainage, full sun, and a free-draining mix, and expect to stake or let it spill. Keep the mix from staying wet, since borage rots in saturated soil.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry faster than beds, so check them, but never keep the mix constantly wet, which rots the roots. Water at the base to keep foliage dry against powdery mildew.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Frequent watering leaches nutrients, so a light feeding every few weeks during bloom is ample; keep nitrogen modest so the plant does not grow soft and floppy.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering containers are a poor fit for borage, which prefers to dry between waterings and rots in constantly moist soil; if used, keep the reservoir low so the root zone is not kept saturated.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot is not ideal for borage, because it does not like soil that stays wet all the time. If you use one, keep the water level low.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Borage is in the borage family (Boraginaceae), a family with few common garden vegetables, so rotation conflicts are minimal; simply avoid replanting it in a bed where borage or other borage-family plants had heavy powdery mildew, and clear plant debris at season end. Because borage self-sows freely, expect volunteers regardless of any rotation plan.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Borage is in the borage family, which has few common vegetables, so there is little to avoid. Just do not replant it in the same spot if it had bad mildew, and clean up old leaves at the end of the season. Note that borage drops seed and usually comes back on its own nearby.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotation is a minor concern for a fast, self-seeding annual herb in a family (Boraginaceae) that rarely overlaps with vegetable crops. Moving borage to a fresh spot and clearing debris limits carryover of powdery mildew, and keeping it away from powdery-mildew-prone squash helps both. Because it reseeds readily, plan on volunteers and thin or relocate them for airflow.
rotation.note_beginner: Rotating borage is not very important. Plant it in a different spot each year if you can, keep it away from squash so mildew does not spread between them, and clean up old leaves at the end of the season. Borage reseeds itself, so you will often get new plants popping up on their own.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seed leaves (cotyledons) push up within roughly 1 to 2 weeks in warm soil; borage germinates readily where it is sown.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The first little leaves come up in about one to two weeks.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Sow directly and cover seed about 1/2 in; keep soil evenly moist until seedlings emerge. Do not start indoors, since borage resents transplanting.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Plant the seeds right in the garden, cover them about half an inch, and keep the soil damp until they sprout.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Seedlings emerged?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your seeds sprouted?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: First true leaves develop and grow bristly; the young plant establishes a taproot quickly.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Real, slightly fuzzy leaves appear and the plant starts to grow.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin or space seedlings to 12 to 24 in while small, since borage gets large; water at the base.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Space plants about 12 to 24 inches apart while they are small, because borage grows big.

growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you spaced out your seedlings?

growth_stages.name: Established / vegetative
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The plant bulks up fast into a large, branching, sprawling mound of coarse gray-green foliage.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant gets big and bushy quickly, with fuzzy leaves.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Give it room and full sun; keep feeding light so it does not grow soft and floppy. Wear gloves when handling the prickly stems.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Give it space and sun, go easy on fertilizer, and wear gloves since the stems are prickly.

growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are your plants filling in?

growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Branched clusters of nodding buds form at the stem tips, roughly 6 to 8 weeks from sowing.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Clusters of drooping flower buds form at the tops of the stems.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture steady in hot, dry weather; begin watching for powdery mildew in humid spells.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil from drying out completely, and watch for white powdery mildew in humid weather.

growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Do you see flower buds yet?

growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Sky-blue star flowers open in a long succession from roughly 8 weeks after sowing until frost or summer heat ends the plant; bees work them constantly.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Blue, star-shaped flowers open, about eight weeks after planting, and keep coming for weeks while bees visit.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Deadhead or cut flowers to prolong bloom and limit excessive self-seeding; harvest young leaves and open flowers for the kitchen, and leave a few late heads to self-sow.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Snip off faded flowers for more blooms (and pick some to eat), but leave a few at the end to drop seed.

growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Flowers left on the plant make seeds that drop and grow into new plants next time. You can also collect the seeds.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Leave some late flowers to set and drop seed for volunteers, or collect seed from drying heads; deadhead the rest if you want to limit self-sowing.

notifications.body_seasoned: Borage is frost-tender, so direct-sow it around your last spring frost (or in fall and the cool season in hot climates). Sow where it will grow, cover the seed about 1/2 in, and give each plant 12 to 24 in of room.
notifications.body_beginner: Sow borage seeds around your last frost (or in the cool season if summers are hot). Plant them right where you want them, cover about half an inch deep, and space them 12 to 24 inches apart.

notifications.body_seasoned: Thin or space borage to 12 to 24 in once seedlings are up; it grows large, and room for airflow limits powdery mildew.
notifications.body_beginner: Space your borage plants 12 to 24 inches apart now, because they get big and need air around them.

notifications.body_seasoned: Flowers are opening. Harvest young leaves and open flowers (remove the fuzzy sepals, use unsprayed plants, eat in moderation), and deadhead or cut to prolong bloom. Leave a few late heads to self-sow.
notifications.body_beginner: Your borage is flowering. Pick young leaves and open flowers to use fresh (in small amounts), and snip off faded flowers for more blooms. Leave a few at the end to reseed.

notifications.body_seasoned: To keep borage coming back, leave some late flowers to set and drop seed; it self-sows freely. To limit volunteers, deadhead before seed sets and collect seed from a few dried heads instead.
notifications.body_beginner: If you want borage next year, leave some flowers to make seed and it will reseed itself. If you do not want lots of volunteers, snip the flowers off before they seed.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost will kill your borage
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Borage is a frost-tender annual: a hard freeze kills it, and in cold regions the first fall frost ends the planting. There is no overwintering it; cut what you want to use and rely on its dropped seed to return next season.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Borage cannot handle frost. A hard freeze will kill it, and in cold areas the first fall frost is the end of it. Pick what you want to use, and its dropped seeds will bring new plants next year.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot, muggy weather is hard on borage
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: In hot, humid weather borage declines, gets leggy, runs to seed, and is prone to powdery mildew. In hot regions treat summer as its off-season and grow it in the cool months; in cooler regions keep it watered and it carries on.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Borage does best in mild weather. In hot, muggy weather it gets tired, goes to seed, and can get a white powdery mildew. In hot places, grow it in the cool season instead of summer.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Damp weather warning
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Warm, humid, still, and crowded conditions drive powdery mildew on borage. Improve airflow with wider spacing, water at the base, and remove badly affected leaves.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Warm, damp, still weather can give borage a white powdery mildew. Give plants room for air, water the soil not the leaves, and pick off bad leaves.

germination.text_seasoned: Direct-sow borage where it will grow and cover seed about 1/2 in; it has a taproot and does not transplant well, so skip indoor starts. Seedlings emerge in 1 to 2 weeks.
germination.text_beginner: Plant borage seeds right in the garden, about half an inch deep, because it does not like to be moved. They come up in a week or two.

germination.text_seasoned: Sow after the last frost in cool and temperate regions; in hot, humid climates sow in fall and the cool season instead, since borage struggles in extreme summer heat.
germination.text_beginner: Sow after your last frost in most gardens. Where summers are hot, plant it in fall or the cool season instead.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin or space seedlings to 12 to 24 in while young; borage grows into a large, sprawling plant and needs the room for airflow against powdery mildew.
seedling.text_beginner: Space seedlings 12 to 24 inches apart while they are small, because borage gets big and needs air around it.

established.text_seasoned: Keep feeding light and soil lean; rich soil and excess nitrogen make borage grow soft, oversized, and floppy with fewer flowers and more mildew.
established.text_beginner: Do not over-fertilize borage. Rich soil just makes a big floppy plant with fewer flowers.

established.text_seasoned: Handle borage with gloves; the stems and older leaves are covered in stiff bristles. Harvest leaves young, before they turn too prickly to enjoy.
established.text_beginner: Wear gloves with borage, since the stems are prickly, and pick the leaves while they are young and tender.

budding.text_seasoned: Keep moisture steady as buds form in hot, dry weather, but do not overwater; borage is drought-tolerant and rots in constantly wet soil.
budding.text_beginner: As buds form, keep the soil from drying out completely in hot weather, but do not keep it soggy.

flowering.text_seasoned: Deadhead or cut flowers regularly to prolong bloom and curb excessive self-seeding; borage blooms for many weeks if older flowers are removed. Leave a few late heads to self-sow.
flowering.text_beginner: Snip off faded flowers to keep more coming and to keep borage from seeding everywhere. Leave a few at the end so it reseeds.

flowering.text_seasoned: Harvest fully open flowers and young leaves from unsprayed plants; pull off the fuzzy sepals behind each flower. Use the cucumber-flavored leaves and blue flowers fresh, or freeze flowers into ice cubes, and eat borage in moderation.
flowering.text_beginner: Pick open flowers and young leaves from unsprayed plants, snapping off the fuzzy green part behind each flower. Use them fresh (the leaves taste like cucumber) or freeze the flowers in ice cubes, and eat borage only in small amounts.

seed_saving.text_seasoned: Borage self-sows freely: leave some late flowers to set and drop seed for volunteers, or collect seed from dried heads. Deadhead if you want to limit how much it reseeds.
seed_saving.text_beginner: Borage reseeds itself easily. Leave some flowers to make seed for next year, or collect the seed. Snip flowers off if you do not want too many volunteers.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A single borage plant is large and long-blooming, producing a steady succession of small blue flowers over many weeks along with an ongoing supply of young cucumber-flavored leaves; one or two plants easily cover a household's garnish and pollinator needs. Deadheading sustains bloom, and the plant self-sows to renew itself.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: One borage plant is big and flowers for weeks, giving you plenty of blue flowers and young cucumber-tasting leaves; one or two plants are usually plenty. Keep snipping faded flowers and more keep coming, and it reseeds itself for next year.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Borage flowers the first season from seed, roughly 8 weeks after sowing, so there is no establishment year; young leaves can be picked even sooner, and the plant self-sows for the following year.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Borage flowers the same season you plant it, about eight weeks after sowing, and you can pick young leaves even earlier. There is no waiting year, and it usually comes back on its own from dropped seed.
factors_seasoned: Season fit: borage yields most in mild conditions; extreme summer heat and humidity cut it short, so it is grown through summer in cool regions and in the cool season in hot ones.
Deadheading cadence: regular deadheading or cutting sustains bloom; unpicked plants set seed and slow.
Spacing and airflow: generous spacing limits powdery mildew and keeps large plants productive longer.
Soil and feeding: lean soil and light feeding give sturdier, better-flowering plants; rich soil makes floppy foliage.
Self-sowing: allowing some seed set renews the planting for free the next season.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No T1 evidence supports a moon-phase planting preference for borage; left unset.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Plants killed by frost
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Frost killed the plants
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Borage is frost-tender; a hard freeze kills it outright, and the first fall frost ends the planting in cold regions. This is normal, not a mistake.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Borage cannot take frost. A hard freeze killed it, which is just what happens at the end of the season in cold areas.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sow borage after the last spring frost and expect the first fall frost to end it; in hot regions grow it in the frost-free cool season. It self-sows to return.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant borage after your last frost, and know the first fall frost ends it. In hot areas, grow it in the cool season. It usually reseeds itself.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: White powdery film on the leaves (powdery mildew)
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Leaves got a white powdery coating
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Powdery mildew took hold, favored by warm, humid, still, crowded conditions and worsening as summer heat and humidity build; it is borage's main disease.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: A white powdery mildew covered the leaves, usually from crowding, humidity, or warming weather.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Space plants generously for airflow, grow in full sun, water at the base, and remove affected leaves; in hot, humid regions grow borage in the cooler season.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Give plants more room and sun, water the soil instead of the leaves, and pick off bad leaves. In hot, damp areas grow it in the cool season.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Plant grew huge, soft, and floppy with few flowers
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Borage got big and floppy
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Too-rich soil, excess nitrogen, shade, or overwatering push borage into soft, oversized, sprawling growth at the expense of flowers.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The plant got big and floppy with fewer flowers, usually from too much fertilizer or water, or not enough sun.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Grow borage in lean soil and full sun, feed lightly if at all, and give it room; it performs best when not pampered.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Go easy on fertilizer and water, give it full sun and space, and it will be sturdier with more flowers.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Plants stopped blooming and went to seed
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Borage quit flowering and set seed
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Left unpicked, borage shifts energy into setting seed and slows blooming; heat also drives it to finish. Regular deadheading keeps it flowering longer.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Borage slowed its flowering because it started making seeds, or because it got hot. Snipping faded flowers keeps more coming.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Deadhead or cut regularly to sustain bloom; in hot regions expect a natural finish and rely on self-sown volunteers or a cool-season sowing.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep snipping faded flowers for more blooms. In hot weather it will finish naturally, and its dropped seed brings new plants.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Seedlings collapsed or the base rotted
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Young plants fell over or the base rotted
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Root and stem rot from cold, wet, poorly drained soil; borage is drought-tolerant and rots when kept soggy.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: A rot at the base, from soggy soil, killed the plants. Overwatering or poor drainage is the usual cause.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sow into well-drained soil, water only when the soil dries, and avoid soggy ground; borage prefers to run a little dry.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant in soil that drains well and do not overwater. Borage would rather be a bit dry than soggy.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Borage popped up all over the garden
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Lots of borage volunteers appeared
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Borage is a prolific self-seeder and may naturalize or become weedy; a single plant can produce volunteers for a couple of seasons.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Borage dropped seed and came up everywhere. It reseeds a lot, which can be handy or a nuisance.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Deadhead before seed sets to limit self-sowing, and pull unwanted volunteers while young (they are easy to remove); leave a few if you want it to return.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: To have fewer volunteers, snip flowers off before they seed, and pull unwanted seedlings while small. Leave a few if you want borage back.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Borage can be sown successively every 3 to 4 weeks through the growing window for a continuous supply of young leaves and fresh flowers, though a single spring sowing plus its own self-sown volunteers often keeps a patch going on its own. In hot regions there is a real summer pause: stop sowing through the hottest, most humid months, since borage declines and mildews in that heat.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: For a steady supply of leaves and flowers, sow a new small batch of borage every 3 to 4 weeks, though one planting plus the seedlings it drops usually keeps going by itself. Where summers are hot, stop sowing during the hottest months, because borage struggles in that heat.
succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Successive sowings extend the supply of tender leaves and fresh flowers as older plants coarsen and set seed; in hot, humid regions the summer gap is a true pause because borage declines and is prone to powdery mildew in extreme heat, so it is grown in the cooler months there.

crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Borage is grown for garden color, a strong pollinator draw, edible flowers, and cucumber-flavored leaves. Harvest young, tender leaves before they turn too bristly, and pick fully open flowers on a dry day, pulling off the fuzzy green sepals behind each bloom. Use only unsprayed plants and eat borage in moderation. The leaves go into salads, teas, and cool drinks; the blue flowers are a garnish or can be frozen into ice cubes. Wear gloves, since the stems are prickly.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Borage is mostly for its bees, its blue edible flowers, and its cucumber-tasting young leaves. Pick young leaves before they get too fuzzy and prickly, and pick open flowers on a dry day, snapping off the fuzzy green part behind each one. Only eat borage that has not been sprayed, and eat it in small amounts. Use the leaves in salads and drinks and the flowers as a garnish or frozen in ice cubes. Wear gloves because the stems are prickly.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: Batch-2 Wave-6 cert (2026-07-06, Trevor-ruled). companion_and_ornamental_flower (Borago officinalis). Agronomy, edible leaves/flowers (cucumber flavor, NCSU/UMN), self-seeding, and the pollinator draw (honey/bumble/native bees -- the best-grounded claim, NCSU/UC Marin/UC ANR) all verified. **SAFETY FIX (Trevor-ruled): ADDED the pyrrolizidine-alkaloid / liver caution.** The draft carried only 'eat in moderation / used sparingly / diuretic in large amounts,' but its OWN cited NCSU page states 'the plant contains toxins (PAs) that can damage the liver and lungs' -- the draft had borrowed NCSU's 'sparingly' while substituting the milder 'diuretic' reason and never naming PAs. Now named + NCSU-anchored (ncsu_ext already in storage.sources). No borage-oil/GLA health claim is present (clean). Companion cucurbit-pollination + tomato-hornworm-predator pairings are honestly labeled inference/traditional (verified_against_sources:false). DTM/germination timing modeled (not on cited pages; standard, generally-safe-now).

open_findings.summary: SEASON-FIT / FROST-TENDER refit vs the calendula template: borage (Borago officinalis) is a frost-TENDER annual (killed by hard frost), direct-sown because it resents transplanting, that GROWS THROUGH summer in cool and temperate regions (northern tier, cool CA coast) with a winter cold_pause, but is grown as a COOL-SEASON winter crop with a summer heat_pause in hot/humid/desert/tropical regions (interior CA, low deserts, SE/Gulf, FL, Hawaii). Regional windows are modeled on borage physiology plus the nearest readable T1 (UF/IFAS: borage is a Florida fall/November herb; NC State: bloom summer-fall; UC Marin: sow Mar-Apr, does not transplant) and the certified cool-tolerant-annual peers; a borage-specific per-region dated table would tighten the exact months.

hawaii_tropical is MODELED and MARGINAL: borage is not a tropical-lowland plant, so it is treated as a coolest-months annual (roughly December-through-March bloom at low elevation, longer in cooler uplands) with a long warm-season heat_pause. No Hawaii-specific borage source was readable; the window is a climate inference from the crop's cool-season physiology and should be confirmed.

COMPANION framing (honesty boundary): borage's best-grounded companion value is as a premier BEE/POLLINATOR and insectary plant (directly documented: NC State attracts bees; UC Marin loved by pollinators; UC ANR honey/bumble/native bees), and pollination support for nearby cucurbits (likely/medium). The tomato and strawberry pairings and the hornworm/pest-repellent lore are framed as TRADITIONAL (traditional/medium); WVU Extension lists borage among strawberry companions. No proven pest-control effect is asserted; predator/neighbor-benefit rosters carry verified_against_sources:false.

EDIBILITY + MODERATION honesty: borage flowers and young cucumber-flavored leaves are edible (NC State; UMN edible flowers; UC Marin), used fresh with the fuzzy sepals removed and only on unsprayed plants, but eaten IN MODERATION. The moderation caution is T1-sourced (NC State: leaves 'should only be used sparingly as liver damage can occur'; UMN: 'diuretic effect in large quantities'; UC Marin: start by consuming sparingly). The pyrrolizidine-alkaloid mechanism behind the caution appears in broader scientific literature but NOT on the cited T1 extension pages, so consumer prose gives the moderation caution without asserting the PA mechanism as sourced.

MODELED numerics (pin at variety pass): days_to_maturity [45,60] / mid 55 (first bloom about 8 weeks; no cited T1 gives exact days-to-bloom); germination_temp_f [65,70] (modeled, not on a cited page); pH preferred [6.0,7.0] with tolerated [5.5,8.0] (NC State documents broad acid/neutral/alkaline tolerance; the preferred band is narrowed by general herb guidance); spacing_inches [12,24] (UC Marin: 'a foot or two apart').

LEAN PEST ROSTER (deliberate, not a gap): borage is documented as largely pest-free (NC State: no significant pest problems; UC Marin: not generally bothered by pests), so a single minor pest (aphids, framed with its beneficial-predator / banker-plant value) is carried rather than fabricating Japanese beetles or other chewers not documented on the cited borage T1 pages. Powdery mildew is the one real disease; root/stem rot in wet soil is the standard drought-tolerant-plant caveat, framed as prevention.

VARIETIES: the named cultivars 'Alba' (white) and 'Bill Archer' / 'Variegata' (variegated foliage) are common-trade selections listed as recommendations; the cited T1 pages ground the species-level facts (edible flowers/leaves, sky-blue wild type, self-seeding) but do not individually document each named cultivar. Confirm at the variety pass.

HEAT_PAUSE months are MODELED per hot-region cell: the exact summer-pause boundary months are set from each region's climate plus borage's documented heat/humidity/mildew sensitivity and the cool-tolerant-annual peers, backed by the crop-level warm-climate cool-season framing (UF/IFAS Florida fall/November planting; NC State; UC Marin), not a borage-specific per-zone heat table.

crops.deadheading_seasoned: Deadhead or cut borage's spent flowers regularly to prolong bloom; it flowers for many weeks when older flowers are removed and slows once it is allowed to set seed. Deadheading also curbs its prolific self-sowing, so remove spent flowers before seed drops if you want fewer volunteers, and leave a few late heads if you want it to return on its own. Cutting stems for the vase or for edible flowers does the same job.
crops.deadheading_beginner: Deadheading means snipping off flowers once they fade. Doing it regularly keeps borage blooming for weeks instead of going to seed, and it also cuts down on how much borage reseeds itself. Snip spent flowers off before they drop seed if you want fewer volunteers, or leave a few at the end of the season so it comes back on its own. Picking flowers to eat or for a vase does the same thing.

northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In the cold northern tier borage is a frost-tender warm-season annual grown from a single spring sowing after the last frost, blooming from early or midsummer until the first hard fall frost ends it. Summers here are mild enough that borage grows and flowers right through them without a heat pause; in the warmer, more humid parts of the region it can slow a little in midsummer and can also be sown again for late-summer bloom.
northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In cold northern areas, borage grows in one main season from a spring planting after your last frost, and it flowers from summer until the first hard frost kills it. Summers are cool enough that it keeps flowering all season. It cannot handle frost, so do not plant it early, and it drops seed to come back next year.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note: Borage is direct-sown where it will grow (a taproot resents transplanting): after the last frost in cool regions, or in the cool season in hot ones. Cover seed about 1/2 in; it germinates in 1 to 2 weeks.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note: Borage is sown in place rather than transplanted; the plant-out window equals the direct-sow window on the same frost or cool-season trigger.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note: First bloom about 8 weeks from sowing; young leaves can be picked a few weeks sooner.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Bloom ends at the first hard frost (cool regions) or the arrival of extreme summer heat and humidity (hot regions); borage usually self-sows for the next round.

plant_out.label: succession
plant_out.synthesis_note: Resow every 3 to 4 weeks through the growing window for a continuous supply of leaves and flowers; borage also self-sows to fill in. Pause through the hottest months in hot regions.

harvest_start.label: succession
harvest_start.synthesis_note: Each succession blooms about 8 weeks after its sowing.

harvest_end.label: succession
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Successions end at hard frost or the onset of extreme summer heat.

3.zone_notes: Zone 3. Very short season. Direct-sow borage in early June once frost danger is past; it blooms from about August until the first fall frost. Grows through the cool northern summer without a heat pause.

4.zone_notes: Zone 4. Sow borage from late May into early June after the last frost; bloom runs July into September until the first hard freeze. No summer heat pause in this cool-summer zone.

5.zone_notes: Zone 5. Last spring frost around early May. Direct-sow then; borage blooms July into September and is ended by the first hard fall freeze. Grows through the mild summer.

6.zone_notes: Zone 6. Sow from late April into May after frost; bloom July into September, occasionally slowing in the warmest midsummer weeks. Killed by the first hard fall freeze.

7.zone_notes: Zone 7. Sow in April after frost; a longer warm season gives bloom from about June into October, though hot, humid midsummer spells can bring some powdery mildew. Growers here can also sow again in late summer for fall bloom.

se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: On the humid Southeast and Gulf Coast borage is grown as a cool-season annual: sown in fall and again in late winter, it blooms from late fall through spring, and the hot, muggy core of summer (roughly June through August) ends it with heat and powdery mildew. Mild winters usually let it grow on, though a hard freeze can nip it, since borage is frost-tender.
se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: Along the humid Southeast and Gulf Coast, grow borage in the cool season: plant in fall and again in late winter for blooms from late fall through spring. The hot, sticky summer is too much for it, so skip those months. Winters are usually mild enough for it to keep going, but a hard freeze can damage it.
