crops.name: Calendula
crops.flower_type: single to double, daisy-form, in gold, orange, yellow, and apricot
crops.description_seasoned: Calendula (Calendula officinalis), commonly called pot marigold, is a cool-season, frost-tolerant annual in the Asteraceae family, native to the Mediterranean. Despite the name, it is not a true marigold (those are Tagetes); it is a separate genus grown for single to double daisy-form blooms in gold, orange, yellow, and apricot. It thrives in the cool shoulders of the year, blooming almost continuously from spring or fall sowings, and through winter in mild and Mediterranean zones, but it languishes and stops flowering once sustained summer heat above roughly 85°F sets in. Plants tolerate frost to about 25°F, self-seed readily, and rebloom well with deadheading. The petals are edible, lending a saffron-like color to food, and calendula has a long traditional use in skin salves.
crops.description_beginner: Calendula, also called pot marigold, is an easy, cheerful flower for cool weather. It is not the same plant as the marigolds you may know (those are a different plant called Tagetes). Calendula handles light frost, blooms in the cool parts of the year, spring and fall, and right through winter in mild-winter areas, but it fades and stops flowering in hot summer weather. The gold and orange petals are edible and add color to food, and the flowers have long been used in skin creams and salves. Plant the seeds in cool weather, snip off faded blooms to get more, and it will often drop seed and come back on its own.

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Calendula is easygoing and grows in most ordinary garden soil as long as water drains away and does not pool. Moderately fertile, well-drained soil is ideal. It handles poorer soil too, but soggy ground rots the roots, so pick a spot that drains well and add a little compost if your soil is thin.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Calendula wants well-drained, moderately fertile loam but is highly adaptable to a wide range of soil textures, from sand to clay, provided drainage is adequate. The consistent failure is wet, poorly drained soil, which rots roots and crowns, especially in the cool, damp conditions calendula otherwise favors. It is a light feeder, so very rich soil pushes soft foliage at the expense of bloom and invites disease.

ph.note_beginner: Calendula is not picky about soil pH (how acidic or alkaline the soil is). A normal garden range around 6.0 to 7.0 is ideal, and you usually do not need to change anything.
ph.note_seasoned: Calendula performs best across roughly 6.0 to 7.0 and tolerates a little outside that range. It is broadly adaptable to soil chemistry, so pH adjustment is rarely warranted; focus on drainage and moderate fertility instead.

crops.tip_seasoned: Treat calendula like a cool-season crop, the way you would spinach or lettuce: direct-sow into cool soil near 60°F, in early spring and again in late summer or fall, and through winter in mild and Mediterranean zones. It germinates in 1 to 2 weeks and reaches first bloom in about 6 to 8 weeks. Go light on nitrogen, deadhead or cut for the vase to sustain bloom, and expect it to fade once sustained heat above about 85°F arrives. Leave a few heads to drop seed and it returns on its own.
crops.tip_beginner: Plant calendula in cool weather, not summer heat. Sow the seeds in early spring and again in late summer or fall (and through winter where winters are mild). They sprout in a week or two and flower in about 6 to 8 weeks. Go easy on fertilizer, snip off faded flowers to keep more coming, and know that hot summer weather will slow or stop the blooms. Let a few flowers go to seed and calendula often replants itself.

fertilizer.timing: At planting, then sparingly
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Calendula is a light feeder and needs little supplemental fertilizer. A modest balanced dose worked into the soil at planting is usually enough. Excess nitrogen pushes soft, leafy growth that flowers poorly and is more prone to powdery mildew and aphids, so favor a balanced or slightly lower-nitrogen feed and skip routine feeding once established.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Calendula does not need much feeding. Mix a little balanced fertilizer or compost into the soil before planting and that is usually plenty. Too much fertilizer, especially the high-nitrogen kind, gives you leaves instead of flowers and more pest and mildew trouble.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time for an optional light feed. Calendula is a light feeder, so one modest dose of a balanced fertilizer supports steady bloom; skip it if you mixed compost into the bed at planting.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: It is a good time to give your calendula a little feed if you want. It does not need much, so one light dose of a balanced fertilizer is plenty, and you can skip it if you already worked some compost into the soil.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 worked in at planting suits calendula better than a high-nitrogen lawn-type feed, which favors foliage over flowers.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: The three numbers on fertilizer (N-P-K) are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. For calendula, pick a balanced one like 10-10-10 rather than a high first-number (nitrogen) lawn feed, which gives leaves instead of flowers.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A single light application at planting is usually sufficient; if supplementing, use a balanced fertilizer at about half the label rate for annual flowers. Avoid repeated high-nitrogen feeding, which favors foliage over bloom.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A little goes a long way. One light feeding when you plant is usually enough. If you do feed again, use about half the amount the package suggests, and avoid high-nitrogen feeds.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.note_beginner: Tiny green or black soft insects that cluster on new growth, buds, and the undersides of leaves, leaving sticky honeydew and curled leaves. Calendula is a known aphid magnet. A strong spray of water or insecticidal soap usually handles them, and the flowers also draw in ladybugs and hoverflies that eat them.
pests.note_seasoned: Calendula is notably attractive to aphids and is sometimes grown as a deliberate trap or banker plant. Soft-bodied sap-feeders colonize tender growth and buds, secreting honeydew and occasionally vectoring viruses. Usually held in check by the beneficial predators the flowers recruit; hose off or treat with insecticidal soap if populations build.

pests.name: Whiteflies
pests.note_beginner: Small white flying insects that hide and feed on the undersides of leaves and fly up in a cloud when disturbed. Knock them back with a hard stream of water or insecticidal soap, and check leaf undersides regularly.
pests.note_seasoned: Tiny white sap-feeders that congregate on lower leaf surfaces, producing honeydew and sooty mold; calendula is a frequent host. Manage with strong water sprays, insecticidal soap, and removal of heavily infested lower leaves; yellow sticky cards help monitor.

pests.name: Slugs and snails
pests.note_beginner: These chew ragged holes in leaves and young plants, especially in the cool, damp weather calendula likes and on tender seedlings. Hand-pick at night, remove hiding spots, or use iron-phosphate bait.
pests.note_seasoned: Ragged feeding on seedlings and lower foliage in the cool, moist conditions calendula favors; young plantings are a frequent target. Reduce mulch harborage, hand-pick at night, or use iron-phosphate bait, and avoid overhead watering late in the day.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.note_beginner: A white, powdery film on leaves, most common in warm, humid weather, crowded plantings, and as summer heat arrives. It is calendula's main disease and a sign the season is turning too warm for it. Space plants for airflow, water at the soil, plant in full sun, and remove badly affected leaves.
diseases.note_seasoned: Calendula's signature disease, worsening as warm, humid weather and summer heat set in, which is also when the cool-season plant naturally declines. Favored by crowding, shade, and overhead wetness. Manage culturally with full sun, generous spacing, base watering, and sanitation; in mild and Mediterranean zones it is least troublesome in the cool months and worst in the warm shoulder.

diseases.name: Damping-off and root or stem rot
diseases.note_beginner: Wet, poorly drained soil rots roots and stem bases, and young seedlings can collapse at the soil line, especially in cold, soggy soil. Plant in well-drained soil, do not overwater, and avoid sowing into cold, waterlogged ground.
diseases.note_seasoned: Soilborne rots and seedling damping-off driven by cold, wet, poorly drained soil, the standing risk for a cool-season plant grown through damp weather. Prevent with well-drained soil, restrained watering, and good airflow rather than treatment; do not sow into waterlogged ground.

diseases.name: Cucumber mosaic and aster yellows
diseases.note_beginner: Less common problems spread by insects: a mosaic virus carried by aphids that mottles and distorts leaves, and aster yellows, spread by leafhoppers, which yellows and deforms growth. There is no cure; remove and discard affected plants and manage the insects that spread them.
diseases.note_seasoned: Occasional insect-vectored problems: cucumber mosaic virus (aphid-transmitted, causing mottling and distortion) and aster yellows phytoplasma (leafhopper-vectored, causing chlorosis and virescent, greened blooms across the aster family). No cure; rogue out symptomatic plants and manage aphids, leafhoppers, and nearby weed reservoirs.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Keep soil evenly moist through germination and establishment, then water regularly but moderately; calendula prefers consistent moisture in cool weather but resents waterlogged soil, which rots roots and feeds disease. Water at the base and avoid wetting foliage to limit powdery mildew.
watering.frequency_beginner: Keep the soil damp while seeds sprout and plants get going, then water regularly but do not keep it soggy. Calendula likes steady moisture in cool weather, but wet, mucky soil rots it. Water the soil, not the leaves.
watering.amount_seasoned: Aim for roughly one inch of water per week from rain plus irrigation during active growth, applied at the base; let the surface dry slightly between waterings. Needs are lower in the cool, short days of winter bloom and higher as plants size up in spring.
watering.amount_beginner: Calendula likes about one inch of water a week, counting rain. Water the soil deeply a couple of times a week rather than a little every day, and let the top of the soil dry a bit between waterings. It needs less in cool winter weather.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base with drip or a soaker hose and keep foliage dry; overhead wetting in the cool, humid conditions calendula favors invites powdery mildew and crown rot. If you must use a sprinkler, water in the morning so leaves dry fast.
watering.method_beginner: Water the ground around the plant, not the leaves. A soaker hose or watering can at the base works best, because dry leaves resist mildew. If leaves do get wet, water in the morning so they dry by midday.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting despite wet soil, and soft, rotting stems or crowns signal overwatering or poor drainage; persistently wet foliage also raises powdery-mildew and damping-off pressure.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If lower leaves turn yellow, the plant wilts even though the soil is wet, or the base looks soft and mushy, you are likely overwatering or the soil drains poorly.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting in the warmth of the day, dulling leaf color, and smaller flowers at bud point indicate underwatering, most critically during establishment and at first bloom; chronic drought hastens the heat-driven decline of the planting.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Calendula that is too dry wilts in the warmth of the day, looks dull, and makes smaller flowers. It is thirstiest right after planting and when the first buds form.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Water at the base with drip or a soaker hose and keep water off the foliage; dry, well-spaced plants are the main cultural lever against powdery mildew, calendula's chief disease. Avoid overhead sprinkling in cool, humid weather.
watering.method_note_beginner: Water the soil around the plant, not the leaves or flowers. A soaker hose or a watering can at the base works best, because dry, airy plants resist mildew.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The critical moisture windows are germination and seedling establishment and the onset of flowering; drought stress at first bud reduces flower size and count, while excess moisture any time risks crown rot and mildew.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The most important times to keep the soil evenly moist are right after planting while seeds sprout, and when the first flower buds form. Never let it get soggy, though.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Not a stored staple: calendula is grown for blooms, an edible-petal garnish, and traditional herbal use. Cut flowers last several days in a vase; fresh petals are used the day they are picked. See the notes for drying petals for longer storage.
storage.room_temp_beginner: This does not really apply. Calendula is a flower, not food to store on the counter. You use the petals fresh, or dry them. See the notes for how to keep cut flowers and dry petals.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Fresh-picked petals keep a few days loosely covered in the refrigerator, but are best used fresh. The flowers themselves are a cut flower, not a refrigerated edible. See the notes.
storage.fridge_beginner: You can keep fresh petals in the fridge for a few days, but they are best used right away. See the notes for drying them to store longer.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Calendula is not frozen for storage. To keep petals long term, dry them rather than freeze. See the notes.
storage.freezer_beginner: Do not freeze calendula. To store the petals, dry them instead. See the notes.
storage.notes_seasoned: Calendula is grown for bloom, a pollinator draw, an edible petal garnish, and traditional herbal use, so the refrigerate and freeze fields do not apply as for produce. For cut flowers, cut in the cool of the morning into clean water and expect several days of vase life. The ray petals are edible: pull them from the flower head, discard the bitter green base, and use fresh as a slightly bitter, saffron-like color for soups, rice, salads, and butters, or dry them on a screen out of direct sun and store airtight for tea, color, and salve-making. Use only unsprayed flowers.
storage.notes_beginner: Calendula is a flower for the garden and the vase, not food to store like vegetables. To make cut flowers last, cut them in the morning and put them in clean water. The orange and gold petals are edible: pull them off the flower, skip the bitter green base, and sprinkle them fresh on food for color (a cheap stand-in for saffron), or dry them on a screen and keep them in a sealed jar for tea or homemade salve. Only eat flowers that have not been sprayed.

recommended: Pacific Beauty (tall, long-stemmed mix in cream to deep orange; a classic cut-flower strain)
Bon Bon (dwarf, very early, compact double blooms for beds, edging, and containers)
Resina (pale lemon, high-resin selection favored for herbal and salve use)
Indian Prince (deep orange with a bronze-red petal reverse, tall and weather-tough)
Snow Princess / Ivory Princess (soft cream to pale yellow doubles)
Calypso (compact, dark-centered doubles in orange and yellow)
Greenheart Orange (novelty orange with a green center)
varieties.note_seasoned: Choose by height and purpose. Tall strains such as Pacific Beauty and Indian Prince give long, cuttable stems for the vase and the back of a bed; dwarf, early types such as Bon Bon and Calypso suit edging, the front of a border, and containers. For herbal and salve use, growers favor high-resin selections such as Resina (often grown as single or semi-double flowers that are easy to pick). Most calendula are open-pollinated and come reasonably true from saved seed, and all are edible-petaled; single and semi-double forms serve pollinators best.
varieties.note_beginner: Pick the type for your spot. Tall kinds like Pacific Beauty and Indian Prince give long stems good for cutting; short, early kinds like Bon Bon and Calypso are great for the front of a bed or in pots. If you want calendula for skin salves or tea, look for Resina, a type grown for that. All calendula have edible petals, and the simpler, more open flowers are best for bees. Most come true from seed you save yourself.

companions.note_beginner: Calendula is a classic, cheerful companion plant grown to help the rest of the garden. Unlike true marigolds (Tagetes), it is not a proven soil-nematode fighter, so do not expect that from it. What it does well is bring in bees and helpful insects like hoverflies and ladybugs, whose young eat aphids. Gardeners also plant it as a trap or decoy because aphids love it, drawing them off nearby crops, and it traditionally goes near vegetables for color and pollinators. There is no plant you must keep it away from; just give it sun and room, and remember it likes cool weather, so pair it with other cool-season crops.
companions.note_seasoned: Calendula's companion value is pollinator and beneficial-insect support, not the nematode suppression documented for true marigolds (Tagetes); pot marigold is a separate genus and should not be assumed to share that effect. Its open, nectar-rich flowers draw bees, hoverflies, lacewings, and lady beetles whose larvae prey on aphids, so it earns its place as an insectary edge. Because aphids are strongly attracted to calendula, it is also used traditionally as a trap or banker plant to pull aphids off a main crop, a tactic with a plausible mechanism but limited formal trialing. As a cool-season annual it pairs naturally with other cool-season vegetables and flowers. There is no biologically antagonistic companion to avoid; site for sun and airflow.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Bees and beneficial insects (insectary planting)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Calendula flowers for a long time and bring in bees and helpful bugs like ladybugs and hoverflies. Their young eat aphids, so a calendula edge or border helps the whole garden.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Calendula is widely documented by extension as a pollinator and beneficial-insect draw (NC State lists it as attracting pollinators); the predator-recruitment benefit to neighbors is well-grounded but inferred rather than directly trialed, so likely/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Calendula's best-grounded companion function. Its open, long-blooming flowers recruit bees and aphid-predators (hoverflies, lacewings, lady beetles, parasitic wasps), supporting biological control nearby. Plant it as an insectary edge or interplant for predator support and color; this is a habitat benefit, not a documented pest-repellent effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Aphid-prone crops (as a trap or decoy plant)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Aphids love calendula, so some gardeners plant it near aphid-prone crops to lure the aphids onto the calendula instead. Watch the calendula and wash off or remove the aphids there.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Calendula's strong attractiveness to aphids is documented (it is a known aphid host), and trap-cropping is a recognized tactic, so the pairing is plausible; the decoy benefit is traditional garden practice rather than trial-verified, so traditional/low.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional trap-crop pairing. Calendula is strongly attractive to aphids, so it is planted near aphid-prone crops as a decoy to concentrate aphids on the calendula, where they can be hosed off, removed, or left for predators. The mechanism (a preferred host pulling pests off the cash crop) is sound, but the protective effect is traditional practice, not formally trialed; monitor and manage the aphids on the trap so it does not become a reservoir.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Cool-season vegetables (lettuce, brassicas, peas)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Calendula grows in the same cool weather as lettuce, cabbage-family crops, and peas, so it makes an easy, colorful companion in the cool-season garden, adding flowers and pollinators without crowding them for food.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Calendula shares the cool-season niche of these crops and adds beneficial-insect and pollinator habitat with low nutrient competition; a long-standing, sensible companion tradition rather than a trial-backed yield effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A cool-season habitat pairing. Calendula occupies the same cool shoulders as lettuce, brassicas, and peas, adding pollinator and beneficial-insect habitat and color with low nutrient competition. The benefit is ecosystem support and aphid-predator recruitment; keep it to edges and ends of rows so it does not shade lower crops.

good_seasoned.name: Bees and beneficial insects (insectary planting)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Open, long-blooming flowers recruit bees and aphid-predators (hoverflies, lacewings, lady beetles, parasitic wasps), supporting biological control nearby. A habitat benefit, planted as an insectary edge.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Extension documents calendula as a pollinator and beneficial-insect draw; the neighbor benefit is inferred from that, not directly trialed.

good_seasoned.name: Aphid-prone crops (as a trap or decoy plant)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Calendula is strongly attractive to aphids, so it is used as a decoy to concentrate aphids on it and off the cash crop; a sound mechanism but a traditional, not trial-verified, tactic. Manage the aphids on the trap.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Calendula is a documented aphid magnet and trap-cropping is recognized; the protective benefit is traditional practice, not formally trialed.

good_seasoned.name: Cool-season vegetables (lettuce, brassicas, peas)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Shares the cool-season niche of these crops, adding pollinator and beneficial-insect habitat and color with low nutrient competition; keep to edges so it does not shade lower crops.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: A sensible cool-season companion tradition; habitat and pollinator benefit is defensible, the yield effect is not trialed.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Indoor-started transplants need about a week of hardening off, increasing outdoor exposure gradually, before transplanting. Because calendula is frost-tolerant to about 25°F, transplants can go out a couple of weeks before the last spring frost.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: If you started plants indoors, harden them off first: set them outside for a little longer each day over about a week before planting them out. Calendula handles light frost, so it can go out a couple of weeks before your last frost.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Calendula direct-sows readily into cool soil (about 60°F) at 1/4 to 1/2 in depth; cover the seed, because light inhibits germination. It germinates in 1 to 2 weeks and is the simplest method in the cool shoulders. To gain time in short-season areas, start indoors about 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost and transplant; calendula resents heavy root disturbance, so use cells or pots and transplant while young. Pinch once when young for bushier plants.
start_method.notes_beginner: The easiest way is to sow calendula seeds straight into cool garden soil (about 60°F), a quarter to half an inch deep, and cover them well because the seeds need darkness to sprout. They come up in one to two weeks. For a head start, sow indoors about 6 to 8 weeks before your last frost and move the young plants outside. You can pinch the tops once to make plants bushier.

soil_mix.type_beginner: regular potting mix that drains well
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Use a potting mix that drains well. If it stays soggy, mix in some perlite or coarse sand. A little compost helps with food. Calendula rots in cold, wet potting mix, so good drainage matters.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: general-purpose well-draining potting mix
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: A free-draining mix is the priority; blend in perlite or coarse sand if the base mix holds too much water, plus a modest amount of compost for fertility. Avoid heavy, water-retentive mixes that keep the cool root zone saturated.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out faster than the garden, so check them, but do not let calendula sit soggy. Water when the top inch of soil feels dry and let the extra drain out the bottom. Try not to wet the leaves.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Watering pots washes out their food, so feed potted calendula lightly every few weeks during bloom with a balanced fertilizer, and go easy to keep flowers coming.

overwintering.approach_beginner: This does not really apply. Calendula is a one-season flower. In cold areas the first hard freeze ends it; in mild-winter areas it blooms through winter and then fades in summer heat. Either way you start new seed each season, though it often reseeds itself.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Not applicable as a managed overwintering: calendula is a cool-season annual. In cold zones a hard freeze ends the planting; in mild and Mediterranean zones it grows and blooms through winter as the main season and declines in summer heat. It frequently self-sows, so volunteers appear without overwintering the parent plant.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Compact, dwarf calendula like Bon Bon and Calypso are excellent in pots, window boxes, and on balconies for cool-season color. Use a pot with drainage holes, a well-draining mix, and a sunny spot. Keep pots from staying soggy, and move or plant them for the cool seasons rather than the heat of summer.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Dwarf and compact strains are the container performers for cool-season displays, thriving in window boxes, edging pots, and balcony containers; full sun to part shade and a free-draining mix are essential, since calendula rots in cold, saturated pots. Containers are useful for placing calendula in its cool seasons and pulling it forward in the cool shoulders rather than the heat of midsummer.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry faster than ground beds, so check them, but never let the mix stay constantly wet, which rots cool-season roots. Water at the base to keep foliage dry against powdery mildew.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Frequent watering leaches nutrients from containers, so a light feeding every few weeks with a balanced fertilizer through the bloom season suits potted calendula; keep nitrogen modest to favor flowers over foliage.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering containers work for calendula only if the surface dries between top-ups; keep the wick reservoir from saturating the root zone, since constant cool moisture invites crown rot and mildew.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot can work for calendula, but only if the top of the soil dries out between waterings. Calendula does not like soil that is wet all the time.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: As an aster-family (Asteraceae) annual, avoid following calendula immediately with other susceptible asters where powdery mildew or aster yellows built up; rotate the bed to an unrelated family for a season if disease was heavy, and clear infected debris at season end. Calendula self-sows freely, so volunteers may appear regardless of rotation.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Calendula is in the daisy family (Asteraceae). If it had a lot of mildew or virus, do not plant it, or other daisy-family flowers, in the same spot the very next season, and clean up the old leaves. Note that calendula drops seed and often comes back on its own.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotation matters less for a fast cool-season ornamental annual than for heavy-feeding vegetables, but moving calendula to a fresh bed and clearing infected debris limits carryover of powdery mildew and aphid-vectored virus. Because it readily self-seeds, expect volunteers, and thin or relocate them to keep airflow.
rotation.note_beginner: Rotating calendula is not as important as it is for vegetables, but it helps. Plant it in a different spot each year if you can, and clean up old, diseased leaves at the end of the season. Calendula reseeds itself, so you will often get new plants popping up nearby on their own.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seed leaves (cotyledons) emerge from cool soil within roughly 1 to 2 weeks; the seeds need darkness, so they must be covered.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The first little leaves push up through the soil in one to two weeks. The seeds need to be covered to sprout.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep soil cool and evenly moist near 60°F; cover seed about 1/4 to 1/2 in, since light inhibits germination.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil damp and cover the seeds well, because they need darkness to sprout.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Seedlings emerged?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your seeds sprouted?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: First true leaves develop on a low rosette; the plant is small and establishing roots in cool weather.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Real leaves appear and the little plant starts to settle in.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin or space plants to 8 to 12 in; water at the base and watch for slugs and aphids in damp weather.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Space plants about 8 to 12 inches apart and water the soil, not the leaves.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Thinned and spaced?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you spaced out your seedlings?

growth_stages.name: Established / vegetative
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Plant grows bushier with several leaf sets and begins branching; a quick grower in cool conditions.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant gets bigger and bushier with more leaves.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pinch the growing tip once for bushier plants; keep nitrogen modest so plants flower rather than run to leaf.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pinch off the top once to make the plant branch out, and go easy on fertilizer.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Plants established and pinched?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are your plants filling in?

growth_stages.name: Budding
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flower buds form at stem tips; stems lengthen toward bloom, roughly 6 to 8 weeks from sowing.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Flower buds start to form at the tops of the stems.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture even at bud point; begin scouting for aphids and, in warm humid weather, powdery mildew.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist and start checking for aphids and white powdery mildew.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: First buds visible?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Do you see flower buds yet?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Blooms open and continue; first bloom is roughly 6 to 8 weeks from sowing and continues through the cool season until hard frost or summer heat ends it.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Flowers open, about six to eight weeks after planting, and keep coming through the cool weather.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Deadhead spent blooms, or cut for the vase, to sustain bloom; harvest petals on a dry morning; water at the base.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Snip off faded flowers (or cut some for a vase, or pick petals to eat) to get more blooms.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: First bloom open?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Has your first flower opened?

growth_stages.name: Seed saving (optional)
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Selected heads left on the plant dry to brown and set viable, curved seed; most calendula come reasonably true from seed.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A few flowers left on the plant dry out and form curved seeds you can save.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Leave chosen heads to dry fully before collecting; open-pollinated types come fairly true, and calendula self-sows readily.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Let a few flowers dry out fully on the plant before collecting their seeds. Calendula also reseeds itself.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Seed heads drying?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are you saving any seeds?

notifications.body_seasoned: Calendula is frost-tolerant, so you can direct-sow into cool soil near 60°F a couple of weeks before the last frost, or sow in late summer and fall, and through winter in mild zones. Cover the seed.
notifications.body_beginner: You can plant calendula seeds in cool weather, even a couple of weeks before your last frost, since it handles light frost. Sow about a quarter inch deep and cover them well.

notifications.body_seasoned: Thin or space calendula to 8 to 12 in once seedlings have a few true leaves; airflow limits powdery mildew.
notifications.body_beginner: Space your calendula plants about 8 to 12 inches apart now so air can move between them.

notifications.body_seasoned: First blooms are opening. Deadhead spent flowers, or cut for the vase, regularly to sustain bloom through the cool season; pick petals on a dry morning for fresh use or drying.
notifications.body_beginner: Your first flowers are opening. Snip off faded ones (or cut some for a vase, or pick petals to eat) to keep more blooms coming.

notifications.body_seasoned: As sustained heat above about 85°F arrives, calendula slows, stops blooming, and is prone to powdery mildew. In hot regions treat the planting as ending for summer and resow in fall; in cool-summer regions it carries on.
notifications.body_beginner: Calendula likes cool weather. When real summer heat arrives, it will slow down and stop flowering. In hot areas, let it finish and plant again in fall. In cool-summer areas it keeps going.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot weather will slow your calendula
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Calendula is a cool-season flower that stops blooming and declines once sustained heat above about 85°F arrives, often with powdery mildew. In hot regions, let the planting finish and resow for fall; in cool-summer regions, keep it watered and it carries on.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Calendula does not like heat. When it gets hot, it will slow down, stop flowering, and may get a white powdery mildew. In hot places, plan to replant in fall. In cool-summer places, just keep it watered.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Damp weather warning
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Warm, humid, still weather drives powdery mildew on calendula, especially as the season warms. Improve airflow, water at the base, and remove badly affected leaves.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Warm, damp, still weather can give calendula a white powdery mildew on the leaves. Give plants room for air, water at the soil, and pick off bad leaves.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost warning
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Calendula tolerates light frost to about 25°F and often blooms through it; a hard freeze below that will damage or kill it. In cold zones, expect the first hard freeze to end the season; cut remaining blooms to enjoy indoors.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Calendula handles light frost and keeps blooming, but a hard, deep freeze will kill it. In cold areas, the first hard freeze ends the season, so cut the last flowers and bring them inside.

germination.text_seasoned: Cover calendula seed about 1/4 to 1/2 in; light inhibits germination, so darkness and cool soil near 60°F are the triggers. Seedlings emerge in 1 to 2 weeks.
germination.text_beginner: Cover the seeds well, about a quarter to half an inch deep, because calendula needs darkness to sprout. In cool soil they come up in one to two weeks.

germination.text_seasoned: Sow into cool soil, the way you would spinach: direct-sow in early spring and again in late summer or fall, and through winter in mild and Mediterranean zones. Calendula germinates poorly in hot soil.
germination.text_beginner: Plant calendula in cool weather, not summer heat. Sow in early spring and again in late summer or fall (and in winter where winters are mild). Hot soil keeps the seeds from sprouting well.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin or space seedlings to 8 to 12 in once they have a few true leaves; generous spacing for airflow is the main cultural defense against powdery mildew.
seedling.text_beginner: Once seedlings have a few real leaves, space them about 8 to 12 inches apart. Room for air to move helps prevent the white mildew.

seedling.text_seasoned: Scout young calendula for aphids and slugs in cool, damp weather; calendula is an aphid magnet. Hose off aphids or use insecticidal soap, and the beneficials the flowers draw will help later.
seedling.text_beginner: Watch young calendula for aphids and slugs in cool, damp weather; aphids really like calendula. Spray them off with water or use insecticidal soap.

established.text_seasoned: Pinch the growing tip once on young plants to force branching and more flowering stems; keep nitrogen modest so plants flower rather than run to soft, mildew-prone foliage.
established.text_beginner: Pinch off the top once when the plant is young to make it bushier with more flowers. Go easy on fertilizer so you get flowers, not just leaves.

established.text_seasoned: Maintain full sun and airflow and water at the base; dry, well-spaced foliage is what keeps powdery mildew in check, sharpest as the weather warms.
established.text_beginner: Keep calendula in sun with room around it and water the soil, not the leaves. Dry, airy plants are what keep the white mildew away, especially as it warms up.

budding.text_seasoned: Keep moisture even as the first buds form; drought stress at bud point reduces flower size and count, but never let the soil stay wet, which rots crowns and feeds mildew.
budding.text_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist when the first flower buds appear, but not soggy. Too dry means smaller flowers; too wet rots the plant.

budding.text_seasoned: Scout for aphids on buds and for powdery mildew as warm, humid weather arrives; addressing crowding and overhead wetness early limits both.
budding.text_beginner: As buds form, check for aphids on them and for white powdery mildew in warm, damp weather. Catching crowding and wet leaves early keeps both down.

flowering.text_seasoned: Deadhead spent blooms back to the next leaf, or cut for the vase, to redirect energy from seed set into new flowers and sustain bloom through the cool season. Leave a few late heads to self-sow.
flowering.text_beginner: Snip off faded flowers back to the next leaves (or cut fresh ones for a vase) to get more blooms through the cool weather. Leave a few at the end to drop seed for next time.

flowering.text_seasoned: Harvest petals on a dry morning from fully open, unsprayed flowers; pull the ray petals and discard the bitter green base. Use fresh as a saffron-like color, or dry on a screen out of sun and store airtight for tea, color, and traditional salve.
flowering.text_beginner: Pick petals from fully open flowers on a dry morning, using only unsprayed plants. Pull off the colorful petals and skip the bitter green base. Use them fresh on food for color, or dry them and keep in a jar for tea or homemade skin salve.

seed_saving.text_seasoned: To save seed, leave some heads to dry fully to brown before collecting the curved seeds; most calendula are open-pollinated and come reasonably true, and the plant self-sows freely.
seed_saving.text_beginner: To save seeds, leave a few flowers on the plant until they dry and turn brown, then collect the curved seeds. Calendula usually grows true from saved seed and also reseeds itself.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A single calendula blooms generously over the cool season, carrying a steady succession of 2 to 3 in daisy flowers; dwarf types make many smaller blooms for color and edging, while tall strains give fewer, longer-stemmed flowers for cutting and petal harvest. Deadheading or cutting sustains production until heat or hard frost ends it.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: One calendula gives you lots of flowers over the cool season. Short types make many small blooms; tall types make fewer, bigger flowers on long stems good for cutting or for picking petals. Keep snipping faded flowers and more keep coming until it gets too hot or freezes hard.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Calendula blooms the first season from seed, roughly 6 to 8 weeks after sowing, so there is no establishment year; a cool-season sowing flowers through the cool months and self-sows for the next.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Calendula flowers the same season you plant it, about six to eight weeks after sowing. There is no waiting year, and it often drops seed and comes back on its own.
factors_seasoned: Season fit: calendula yields most in cool weather and stops blooming in sustained heat above about 85°F, so a long cool shoulder or mild winter maximizes total bloom.
Type: dwarf types yield many small flowers for color and edging; tall strains yield fewer, longer-stemmed blooms for cutting and petals.
Deadheading and cutting cadence: regular deadheading or cutting sustains bloom; neglected plants set seed and slow.
Pinching: pinching young plants once produces more, sturdier flowering stems.
Spacing and airflow: adequate spacing limits powdery mildew and sustains a longer productive life.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No T1 evidence supports a moon-phase planting preference for calendula; left unset.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Plants stopped blooming and got leggy in summer heat
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Calendula quit flowering when it got hot
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Calendula is a cool-season annual; sustained heat above about 85°F stops flowering and makes plants leggy and mildew-prone. This is normal, not a mistake.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Calendula does not like heat. When summer warmed up, it stopped flowering and got tall and tired. That is just how this cool-season plant behaves.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Grow calendula in the cool shoulders and mild winters; sow in early spring and again in fall, and treat summer as its off-season in hot regions.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant calendula in the cool parts of the year, spring and fall, and skip the hot months. In mild-winter areas, grow it right through winter.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: White powdery film on the leaves (powdery mildew)
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Leaves got a white powdery coating
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Powdery mildew took hold, favored by warm, humid, crowded, shaded conditions, and it worsens as the season warms past calendula's cool comfort range.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: A white powdery mildew covered the leaves, usually because plants were crowded or shaded, the air was humid, or it was warming up.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Space plants for airflow, grow in full sun, water at the base, and remove affected leaves; grow in the cooler part of the season.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Give plants more room and sun, water the soil instead of the leaves, and pick off bad leaves. Growing in cooler weather helps most.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Seedlings collapsed or plants rotted at the base
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Young plants fell over, or the base rotted
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Damping-off and root or stem rot struck plants in cold, wet, poorly drained soil; calendula rots if kept saturated in cool weather.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: A rot at the base, from cold, soggy soil, killed the plants. Overwatering or poor drainage is the usual cause.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sow into well-drained soil, do not overwater, and ensure airflow; avoid sowing into cold waterlogged ground.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant in soil that drains well, do not keep it soggy, and give plants room for air.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Plants killed by a hard freeze
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: A hard freeze killed the plants
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Calendula tolerates light frost to about 25°F but a hard freeze below that damages or kills it; in cold zones the first hard freeze ends the season.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Calendula handles light frost but not a hard, deep freeze. A hard freeze ended the plants.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Expect cold-zone plantings to end at the first hard freeze; in mild zones calendula blooms through the winter.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: In cold areas, know the first hard freeze ends calendula. In mild-winter areas it keeps going through winter.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Sticky, curled growth crawling with aphids
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Tiny bugs and sticky leaves (aphids)
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Aphids colonized the plant; calendula is strongly attractive to them, clustering on buds and new growth, leaving honeydew and sometimes vectoring virus.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Aphids, which love calendula, covered the new growth and buds and left everything sticky.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Hose off aphids or use insecticidal soap, encourage the beneficials the flowers draw, and use calendula deliberately as a trap plant if helpful.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Spray aphids off with water or use insecticidal soap. The flowers also bring in ladybugs that eat them.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Seeds failed to come up
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Few or no seeds sprouted
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Usual causes are uncovered seed (light inhibits germination) or hot soil; calendula germinates best covered, in cool soil near 60°F.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Calendula seeds did not sprout, usually because they were not covered (they need darkness) or the soil was too warm.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Cover seed 1/4 to 1/2 in, sow into cool soil near 60°F, and keep evenly moist during emergence.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Cover the seeds well so they are in the dark, plant in cool soil, and keep it damp until they sprout.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Sow successively every 3 to 4 weeks through the cool windows, early spring and again late summer into fall, and through winter in mild and Mediterranean zones, to keep fresh, vigorous plants in bloom. There IS a heat pause: stop sowing through the hot months, since calendula germinates and blooms poorly in summer heat.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: For flowers all through the cool season, sow a new small batch of seeds every 3 to 4 weeks in spring and again in late summer and fall (and through winter where winters are mild). Stop during the hot months: calendula does not do well sown into summer heat.
succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Successive cool-season sowings offset the decline of older plantings and bridge the cool shoulders; the summer heat gap is a true pause because calendula germinates and flowers poorly above about 85°F.

crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Calendula is grown for garden color, pollinators, cutting, edible petals, and traditional herbal use. Cut blooms for the vase when flowers are fully open and the stem is firm, in the cool of the morning into clean water; expect several days of vase life. Harvest petals from fully open, unsprayed flowers on a dry morning, pulling the rays and discarding the bitter green base. Deadhead spent blooms through the cool season to sustain flowering.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Calendula is mostly for cool-season color, pollinators, and its edible petals. Cut flowers for a vase when fully open and the stem feels firm, in the morning into clean water. To eat the petals, pick fully open, unsprayed flowers on a dry morning, pull off the colorful petals, and skip the bitter green base. Snip off faded flowers through the season to keep more coming.

open_findings.summary: COOL-SEASON REFIT vs the warm-season zinnia/marigold structural twins: calendula (Calendula officinalis) is a frost-tolerant (to about 25°F) cool-season annual that blooms in the cool shoulders and mild winters and STOPS blooming in sustained summer heat above about 85°F, the opposite of zinnia and the true marigolds (Tagetes). The regional calendars are therefore modeled on the certified cool-season annuals lettuce-leaf and carrot (fall and late-winter sowings, summer heat_pause in hot regions, winter bloom in mild and Mediterranean zones, cold-bracketed in cold zones), NOT on zinnia's warm-season skeleton. Per-region planting windows are modeled on those cool-season peers plus the UF/IFAS FP087 calendula zone table; a calendula-specific dated regional table per region would tighten them.

hawaii_tropical is MODELED and flagged MARGINAL: calendula is heat-intolerant and tropical lowland Hawaii is warm year-round, so it is treated as a cool, dry-season annual (roughly December-through-March bloom at low elevation, longer in cooler uplands) with a long warm-season heat_pause. No Hawaii-specific calendula source was readable (CTAHR was not used for this crop); the window is a climate inference from the crop's cool-season physiology and should be confirmed or refined.

COMPANION FRAMING (not a sourcing gap, a load-bearing honesty boundary): calendula is the pot marigold, NOT a true marigold (Tagetes), and is NOT claimed to suppress root-knot nematodes (the documented Tagetes effect). Its companion value is framed as pollinator and beneficial-insect (aphid-predator) support (likely/medium), a traditional aphid trap or decoy crop (traditional/low, sound mechanism but not formally trialed), and a cool-season habitat companion (traditional/medium). The edible-petal and traditional skin-salve uses are framed honestly as culinary garnish (a saffron-color substitute, per UMN edible flowers) and long-standing traditional herbal use.

The heat_pause months per warm-region cell are aligned to the certified cool-season peers (lettuce-leaf, carrot) at the same region and zone and backed by the crop-level heat physiology sources (USU Extension: prefers below about 85°F, stops blooming in extreme heat; UW Extension: languishes in prolonged hot summer; UF/IFAS: cool-season annual). The exact summer-pause boundary months are modeled to the peers rather than to a calendula-specific per-zone heat table.

DTM [45,60] is a modeled cool-season-annual estimate; no cited T1 source publishes calendula days-to-first-bloom (UW gives only germination 5-15 days). Not contradicted by any source; pin or hedge at the variety pass.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: Wave-6 cert (2026-07-02): CC source-truth review, WebFetch of the 4 cited T1 pages. The pot-marigold-vs-Tagetes honesty boundary HELD -- calendula is distinguished from true marigold (Tagetes) verbatim on UW-Madison, and the record affirmatively DISCLAIMS the Tagetes root-knot-nematode effect ('NOT a proven soil-nematode fighter') rather than claiming it. Edible petals + pesticide-free caveat backed (UMN edible-flowers); cool-season / 85F heat-fade + frost-to-25F backed verbatim (USU). Companion value honestly graded (pollinator likely/medium, aphid trap-crop traditional/low; predator roster labeled verified_against_sources:false). Only gap: DTM [45,60] modeled -> open_finding.

crops.deadheading_seasoned: Deadhead spent blooms back to the next leaf through the cool season to redirect energy from seed set into new flowers and sustain bloom; cutting for the vase or harvesting petals serves the same function. Calendula reblooms well with regular deadheading and slows when it is allowed to set seed, though it self-sows freely if you leave the last heads. Pinch young plants once to force branching and more flowering stems.
crops.deadheading_beginner: Deadheading means snipping off flowers once they fade. Do it regularly: cut the old bloom back to the next set of leaves and the plant makes more flowers instead of going to seed. Cutting flowers for a vase or picking petals does the same job. Leave a few flowers at the end of the season to drop seed, and calendula often comes back on its own. Pinch young plants once to make them bushier.

northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In the northern tier, calendula is a frost-tolerant cool-season annual grown from a spring sowing for bloom from early summer to the first hard freeze. It handles light frost to about 25°F, so it can be direct-sown a couple of weeks before the last frost or started indoors for an earlier start. The far-northern zones (3 to 5) have cool enough summers that calendula blooms steadily through the warm months; in the warmer, more humid zones 6 and 7 it can slow in midsummer heat and is also grown as a fall crop.
northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the cold northern states, calendula grows in one main season from a spring planting and blooms from early summer until a hard freeze. It handles light frost, so you can sow it a couple of weeks before your last frost. In the coldest areas summers are cool enough that it flowers all summer; in warmer zones it may slow in midsummer heat, and you can also plant it again for fall.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note: Calendula direct-sows into cool soil near 60°F; cover the seed (light inhibits germination). It germinates in 1 to 2 weeks. Sow in the cool windows, spring and fall, and through winter in mild and Mediterranean zones.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note: Transplants set out into cool soil on the same trigger; calendula tolerates light frost to about 25°F, so it can go out a couple of weeks before the last spring frost.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note: First bloom about 6 to 8 weeks after sowing; bloom continues through the cool season.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Bloom ends when sustained heat above about 85°F arrives (hot regions) or a hard freeze below about 25°F kills the plant (cold regions).

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.synthesis_note: Optional transplant arm: start indoors about 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost and set out after hardening; transplant while young, since calendula resents heavy root disturbance.

plant_out.label: succession
plant_out.synthesis_note: Resow every 3 to 4 weeks through the cool windows to keep fresh plants in bloom; pause through the hot months.

harvest_end.label: succession
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Successions end at summer heat or hard frost.

3.zone_notes: Cold short-season zone (USDA 3). Last spring frost around late May, first fall frost around mid-September. Calendula is sown after the soil works in spring (or started indoors in April) for a summer bloom that ends at the first hard freeze; summers are cool enough that no heat gap is needed.

4.zone_notes: Cold zone (USDA 4). Last spring frost around mid-May. Spring sowing or an indoor start in March gives bloom from June to the first fall freeze; cool summers let calendula flower continuously with no heat gap.

5.zone_notes: Zone 5. Last spring frost around late April. Calendula blooms from June into October, tolerating the light early frosts; summers are mild enough for continuous bloom without a heat gap.

6.zone_notes: Zone 6. Last spring frost around mid-April. A spring sowing gives a long bloom from May into October; calendula generally flowers through the moderate summer, slowing only in the hottest, most humid spells.

7.zone_notes: Zone 7 (upper South / mid-Atlantic). Hot, humid midsummer (July to August) stalls calendula, which is grown as a spring and a fall crop bracketing the heat; winters are cold enough that a hard freeze ends the fall planting.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Jul, Aug is excluded by summer heat: calendula is a cool-season annual that flowers best below about 85°F and stops blooming, grows leggy, and is prone to powdery mildew once sustained heat arrives, so in the upper South, it is grown in the cool shoulders and mild winter and skipped through the hottest months. (Utah State University Extension; University of Wisconsin Extension)

se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: Across the Southeast and Gulf, calendula is a cool-season annual grown from fall and late-winter sowings for bloom through fall, winter, and spring; it tolerates the mild winters and light frosts. The hot, humid summer (roughly May through August) ends the season with heat and powdery mildew, so calendula is skipped in midsummer and resown for fall.
se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast and Gulf, plant calendula in fall and again in late winter for flowers through the cool months. It handles the mild winters and light frosts here. Skip the hot, humid summer, when it stops blooming and gets mildew, and plant again when things cool off in fall.

ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: In California's interior valleys, calendula is a classic cool-season annual: sown in fall and again in late winter, it blooms from late fall through spring in the mild, frost-light winters. The hot, dry interior summer (roughly May through August) stops bloom, so it is a cool-shoulder and winter crop here.
ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In California's hot inland valleys, plant calendula in fall and late winter for flowers from late fall through spring. Winters are mild, so it blooms right through them. Summer is too hot, so it takes the summer off.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: On California's cool, foggy north coast, calendula thrives nearly year-round: mild winters and cool, maritime summers suit this cool-season annual, so it blooms from spring through fall and often through the mild winter. Summer heat rarely builds enough to force a hard pause, though it can slow in the warmest inland pockets.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: On California's cool, foggy north coast, calendula does wonderfully and blooms most of the year. The mild winters and cool summers are just what this cool-season flower likes, so plant it any time from late winter through summer.

ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: On California's mild south coast, calendula is at its best as a winter and cool-shoulder annual: sown late summer through spring, it blooms from fall through early summer in the frost-free Mediterranean climate. The warmest summer weeks (roughly June through August) slow and stop bloom, softer than in the interior but still a real pause.

Plant it from late summer through spring and it blooms from fall into early summer; winters here barely frost. The warmest weeks of summer (about June to August) slow it down, so that is its rest period.

ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: In California's low desert valleys, calendula is strictly a cool-season and winter annual: sown in fall, it blooms from late fall through spring in the warm, frost-light winters. The extreme desert summer (roughly May through September) is far too hot, ending bloom entirely until fall.
ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: In the California low desert, calendula is a winter flower only. Plant it in fall for blooms from late fall through spring, when the weather is pleasant. The brutal desert summer (about May through September) is way too hot, so it is finished until fall.
