crops.name: Zinnia
crops.flower_type: single to fully double, daisy- to dahlia-form

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Zinnias grow in most ordinary garden soil as long as water drains away and does not pool. Mixing in a little compost helps. The main thing to avoid is soggy, waterlogged ground.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Zinnias want well-drained soil with moderate organic matter and tolerate a wide range of textures; the one consistent failure is wet, poorly drained ground. They are not heavy feeders, so fertility matters less than drainage and airflow.

ph.note_beginner: Zinnias are not picky about soil pH (how acidic or alkaline the soil is). A normal garden range around 6.0 to 7.0 is fine, and you usually do not need to change anything.
ph.note_seasoned: Zinnias are not pH-fussy and perform across roughly 6.0 to 7.0, tolerating slightly outside that. No pH adjustment is typically warranted for them specifically.

crops.tip_seasoned: Soil temperature, not the calendar, is the real germination trigger: wait for soil at 70 °F before direct-sowing. Space for airflow and water at the base to keep powdery mildew off the foliage, and choose interspecific hybrid series (Profusion, Zahara) where mildew pressure is high.
crops.tip_beginner: Wait until the soil is warm (about 70 °F) before planting zinnia seeds outside; planting too early in cold soil makes them rot. Give plants space so air moves between them, and water the soil, not the leaves, to avoid a white powder on the foliage called powdery mildew. In humid areas, look for Profusion or Zahara types, which resist it.

fertilizer.timing: At planting, then sparingly
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Zinnias are light feeders; rich organic soil plus a modest dose at planting is usually enough. Excess nitrogen pushes soft leafy growth at the expense of bloom and worsens mildew susceptibility, so favor a balanced or slightly phosphorus-leaning feed over a high-nitrogen one.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Zinnias do not need much feeding. Mix some compost into the soil before planting and that is often plenty. Too much fertilizer, especially the high-nitrogen kind, gives you lots of leaves but fewer flowers, so go light.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time for a light feed. Zinnias are light feeders, so a single modest dose of a balanced fertilizer now supports steady bloom; skip it if you worked compost into the bed at planting.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: It is a good time to feed your zinnias a little. They do not need much, so one light dose of a balanced fertilizer is plenty. If you already mixed compost into the soil when planting, you can skip this.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10, or a bloom-oriented lower-nitrogen blend, suits zinnias better than a high-nitrogen lawn-type feed.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: The three numbers on fertilizer (N-P-K) are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. For zinnias, pick a balanced one like 10-10-10 rather than a high first-number (nitrogen) lawn feed.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A single light application at planting is usually sufficient; if supplementing, use a balanced fertilizer at about half the label rate for annual flowers. Avoid repeated high-nitrogen feeding, which favors foliage over bloom and increases mildew susceptibility.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A little goes a long way. One light feeding when you plant is usually enough. If you do feed again, use about half the amount the package suggests. Too much, especially high-nitrogen feed, gives you leaves instead of flowers.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.note_beginner: Tiny soft insects that cluster on new growth and flower buds. A strong spray of water or insecticidal soap usually handles them, and zinnias often draw ladybugs and hoverflies that eat them.
pests.note_seasoned: Soft-bodied sap-feeders on tender growth and buds; usually held in check by the beneficials zinnias attract (lady beetles, hoverfly larvae). Hose off or treat with insecticidal soap if populations build.

pests.name: Japanese beetles
pests.note_beginner: Shiny copper-and-green beetles that chew flowers and leaves, especially in early-to-midsummer. Hand-pick them into soapy water in the morning when they are sluggish.
pests.note_seasoned: Metallic beetles that skeletonize foliage and feed on blooms in early-to-midsummer; zinnias are a known preferred host, which is part of their trap-crop value. Hand-pick at dawn into soapy water; avoid pheromone traps, which concentrate beetles.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.note_beginner: Very tiny pests that show up in hot, dry, dusty conditions and cause fine speckling on leaves. Spraying leaves with water and keeping plants watered helps.
pests.note_seasoned: Stippling and fine webbing under hot, dry, dusty conditions; raise humidity around foliage with base watering and dislodge with water sprays. Watch container plants in particular.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.note_beginner: A white, powdery coating on leaves, common in humid weather and crowded plantings. Prevent it by spacing plants for good airflow, watering the soil not the leaves, and choosing resistant types like Profusion and Zahara.
diseases.note_seasoned: The signature zinnia foliar disease (Golovinomyces / Erysiphe spp.), favored by humidity, cool nights, and crowding. Management is cultural and varietal: full sun, generous spacing for airflow, base watering, and the interspecific resistant hybrids (Profusion, Zahara). Do not compost infected debris.

diseases.name: Alternaria and bacterial leaf spot
diseases.note_beginner: Brown or dark spots on leaves and petals, worse when leaves stay wet. Keep foliage dry, space plants out, and remove badly spotted leaves.
diseases.note_seasoned: Foliar/flower spotting (Alternaria zinniae; Xanthomonas) spread by overhead wetness and splash; manage with base watering, spacing, morning irrigation if overhead is unavoidable, and sanitation of infected debris.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Keep soil evenly moist through germination and establishment, then water deeply but less often; established plants are notably drought-tolerant and over-frequent shallow watering invites foliar disease.
watering.frequency_beginner: Keep the soil damp while seeds sprout and plants get going. After that, water deeply but less often. Grown-up zinnias handle dry spells well, so you do not need to water every day.
watering.amount_seasoned: Aim for roughly one inch of water per week from rain plus irrigation during active growth, applied deeply and less often rather than in frequent shallow doses; established plantings tolerate less. Deep, infrequent watering encourages deeper roots and keeps foliage dry.
watering.amount_beginner: Zinnias like about one inch of water a week, counting rain. Water deeply once or twice a week instead of a little every day. Once they are established, they handle dry spells well.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base with drip or a soaker hose and avoid overhead wetting; if you must use a sprinkler, water in the morning so foliage dries fast. Dry leaves are the single biggest lever against powdery mildew.
watering.method_beginner: Water the ground around the plant, not the leaves. A soaker hose or watering can at the base works best. If leaves do get wet, water in the morning so they dry by midday. Dry leaves help prevent disease.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting despite wet soil, and root or crown rot signal overwatering or poor drainage; persistently wet foliage also raises powdery mildew and leaf-spot pressure.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If lower leaves turn yellow, the plant wilts even though the soil is wet, or the base looks mushy, you are likely overwatering or the soil drains poorly. Wet leaves also invite disease.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting in the heat of the day that recovers by evening, dulling leaf color, and shortened stems or reduced flower size at bud point to underwatering, most critically during establishment and at first bloom.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Zinnias that are too dry wilt in the afternoon heat, look dull, and make shorter stems or smaller flowers. They are thirstiest right after planting and when the first buds form.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Water at the base with drip or a soaker hose and keep water off the foliage; dry leaves are the single biggest cultural lever against powdery mildew and leaf spot. If overhead watering is unavoidable, do it early so leaves dry quickly.
watering.method_note_beginner: Water the soil around the plant, not the leaves. A soaker hose or a watering can at the base works best, because dry leaves help prevent the white powdery mildew zinnias are prone to. If you must use a sprinkler, water in the morning so leaves dry fast.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The critical moisture windows are germination/seedling establishment and the onset of flowering; drought stress at first bud can shorten stems and reduce bloom count.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The most important times to keep the soil moist are right after planting while seeds sprout, and when the first flower buds form. Letting plants get too dry then means fewer and shorter flowers.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Not applicable: zinnia is grown for cut blooms, not stored as food. Vase-life guidance lives in the notes below.
storage.room_temp_beginner: This does not apply. Zinnias are flowers for a vase, not food to store. See the vase-life tips in the notes.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Not applicable: zinnia is a cut flower, not a refrigerated edible. See vase life in the notes.
storage.fridge_beginner: This does not apply. There is nothing to refrigerate; zinnias are cut flowers, not food. See the notes for keeping blooms fresh.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Not applicable: zinnia is a cut flower and is not frozen for storage. See vase life in the notes.
storage.freezer_beginner: This does not apply. You do not freeze zinnias; they are flowers, not food. See the notes for vase life.
storage.notes_seasoned: Zinnia is a cut flower, not a stored edible, so the refrigerate and freeze fields do not apply. For vase life, recut stems on arrival, strip leaves below the waterline, use clean water with floral preservative, and keep blooms out of direct sun and away from ripening fruit. Expect one week or more.
storage.notes_beginner: Zinnias are flowers for a vase, not food to store, so there is nothing to refrigerate or freeze. To make cut flowers last, trim the stem ends, pull off any leaves that would sit under the water, and use a clean vase with fresh water. Keep them out of hot sun. They usually stay nice for a week or more.

recommended: Benary's Giant (tall, large fully double dahlia-form, premier cut flower)
State Fair Mix (tall, large blooms, vigorous)
Queen Lime / Queen series (tall, muted designer tones, cut flower)
Oklahoma series (tall, smaller flor-quality double blooms, strong stems)
Profusion series (interspecific Zinnia x marylandica, powdery-mildew and leaf-spot resistant, compact)
Zahara series (interspecific Zinnia x marylandica, disease-resistant, compact, low-maintenance)
Cactus-flowered / Giant Cactus (quilled, shaggy petals)
Thumbelina (dwarf bedding, container and edging)
varieties.note_seasoned: Variety choice is the highest-leverage disease decision: the interspecific hybrid series Profusion and Zahara (Zinnia x marylandica) are bred for powdery-mildew and leaf-spot resistance and hold up in hot, humid conditions where tall Zinnia elegans types mildew. For cutting, the tall fully double elegans types (Benary's Giant, State Fair, Queen, Oklahoma) give the best stems and vase performance; for beds, borders, and containers, the compact resistant hybrids are the low-maintenance pick. Single and semi-double, wide-faced blooms with prominent centers serve pollinators best.
varieties.note_beginner: If powdery mildew (a white coating on leaves) is common where you garden, the most important choice is the variety: Profusion and Zahara types resist it and stay healthy in heat and humidity. For tall flowers to cut and put in a vase, pick double-flowered types like Benary's Giant or State Fair. For pots and small spaces, the compact Profusion and Zahara types are easiest. Flat, open, single flowers with an obvious center are the best for feeding bees and butterflies.

companions.note_beginner: Zinnias are mostly planted to help other crops. They are one of the best flowers for attracting bees and butterflies, so gardeners plant them next to or around vegetables (like tomatoes, squash, and beans) to bring in pollinators and helpful bugs that eat pests. Open, flat, single flowers feed pollinators best. There is no plant you need to keep zinnias away from. The only thing to watch is crowding: packing them tightly against bushy, disease-prone plants traps damp air and makes powdery mildew (a white coating on leaves) more likely, so give them room for air to move.
companions.note_seasoned: Zinnia's companion role inverts the usual framing: it is the crop you place to benefit others. As one of the best annual pollinator magnets, especially for butterflies, it is interplanted between vegetable rows or as a border to pull bees, hoverflies, and predatory insects toward fruiting and cucurbit crops, and it doubles as a trap crop that can draw Japanese beetles and aphids off more delicate plants. Tall, single, wide-faced blooms with prominent disc florets serve pollinators better than dense doubles. There is no biologically antagonistic companion to avoid; the only caution is spacing. Crowding zinnias against dense, disease-prone neighbors traps humidity and raises shared powdery-mildew pressure, so site for airflow rather than avoiding any particular plant.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Tomatoes
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Zinnias draw bees and helpful predator insects that improve tomato pollination and pest control when planted nearby.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Tomatoes self-pollinate, so zinnia's pollinator-attraction (its strongest function) does little for the tomato itself; the real benefit is recruiting aphid predators (hoverfly/lacewing/parasitic-wasp), which aster-family flowers do (HGTV names aster-family flowers for supporting aphid predators). traditional/medium: beneficial-recruitment is real and extension-aligned in principle, but the tomato-specific benefit is indirect and unquantified.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: With tomatoes, zinnia's contribution is mostly beneficial insects rather than pollination, since tomatoes self-pollinate. Zinnia's nectar draws hoverflies, lacewings, and parasitic wasps whose larvae prey on aphids and other soft-bodied pests that bother tomatoes, and the bold blooms can pull some pests onto the zinnias instead. Site them at the bed edge as an insectary strip; expect predator support and color, not a direct pollination boost.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Cucurbits (squash, melon, cucumber)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Squash, melons, and cucumbers need insects to move pollen to make fruit. Zinnias bring in the bees that do that job.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: The mechanism is well grounded: cucurbits require insect pollination (multiple bee visits per fruit for good set), and zinnia is a documented strong, long-season pollinator attractant, so improved pollinator visitation plausibly improves cucurbit fruit set. likely rather than research_backed because, while each link is solid, I located no controlled trial measuring zinnia-interplanting -> cucurbit yield specifically; the inference is strong but not directly trialed. This is the best-grounded of zinnia's pairings.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: This is zinnia's strongest vegetable pairing, because cucurbits depend on insect pollination, squash and melon flowers need several bee visits to set fruit properly, and zinnia is a reliable, long-blooming bee and butterfly magnet right through the cucurbit fruiting window. More pollinator traffic means better fruit set and fewer aborted or misshapen fruits. As a bonus, zinnias can also draw cucumber beetles and aphids onto themselves. Plant them in nearby rows so the pollinators they pull in spill over onto the crop.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Beans
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Zinnias bring in bees and helpful bugs without crowding beans for food, since beans make their own nitrogen.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Beans are largely self-pollinating, so the benefit is beneficial-predator recruitment (parasitic wasps for bean beetles, aphid predators) - aster-family flowers support these. traditional/medium: real and extension-aligned in principle, indirect and unquantified for beans specifically.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Beans gain mostly from the beneficial insects zinnia brings in. The nectar supports parasitic wasps and predators that help manage bean beetles and aphids, and the flowers add pollinator traffic and structural diversity to the planting. Beans are largely self-pollinating, so the value here is predator recruitment and habitat rather than pollination. Keep zinnias to the edges so they do not shade lower bush beans.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Corn
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: A traditional pairing: zinnias planted near corn draw in pollinators and helpful insects.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Corn is wind-pollinated, so zinnia's headline pollinator benefit does not apply; the only plausible benefit is general beneficial-insect/predator support, which is diffuse for corn specifically. traditional/low: the weakest-grounded of zinnia's four pairings - real at the garden-ecosystem level but with little corn-specific basis. Flagging as the softest call in the zinnia set.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Corn benefits the least directly of zinnia's partners, since corn is wind-pollinated and gets nothing from added bee traffic. What zinnia offers is general garden-ecosystem support, drawing predators and parasitoids that prey on aphids and caterpillars, including corn pests like corn earworm to a degree, plus color and diversity. Treat this as a loose, habitat-level pairing rather than a targeted one.

good_seasoned.name: Tomatoes
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Interplanted zinnias raise pollinator and beneficial-predator visitation (bees, hoverflies, predatory wasps), supporting fruit set and aphid and hornworm suppression. Site taller single-flowered types with open disc florets where insects can reach the blooms.

provenance.label: research_backed
provenance.reason: Penn State and UF/IFAS name zinnia among the best annuals for drawing pollinators and beneficial insects to interplanted vegetables.

good_seasoned.name: Cucurbits (squash, melon, cucumber)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Cucurbits depend on insect pollination for fruit set; zinnia's nectar draw pulls bees into the planting so more flowers set fruit. Taller, single, wide-faced blooms give pollinators the easiest access.

provenance.label: research_backed
provenance.reason: Penn State and UF/IFAS identify zinnia as a top pollinator-attracting annual for interplanting with vegetables; cucurbit fruit set is insect-pollination-dependent.

good_seasoned.name: Beans
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Zinnias add pollinator and beneficial-insect habitat alongside beans with low nutrient competition; legumes fix their own nitrogen, so avoid over-feeding the pairing.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Mechanistic (beneficial-insect habitat plus low competition), not a trial result.

good_seasoned.name: Corn
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A classic interplant for pollinator and beneficial draw at the field edge or between rows.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Long-standing companion-planting tradition; not extension-trial-verified for zinnia specifically.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Indoor-started transplants need 7 to 10 days of hardening off, increasing outdoor exposure gradually, before transplanting after all frost danger has passed.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: If you started plants indoors, harden them off first: set them outside for a little longer each day over about a week so they get used to sun and wind before you plant them out.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Zinnias direct-sow readily into warm soil (70 °F) at 1/4 in depth and are the simplest, strongest method that way, since they resent root disturbance; transplant shock can cause double varieties to throw single blooms for a spell. To gain weeks in short seasons, start indoors 4 to 6 weeks before last frost in cells, disturb roots minimally, and transplant after frost. Pinch at four leaf sets.
start_method.notes_beginner: The easiest way is to sow zinnia seeds straight into warm garden soil (about 70 °F) after your last frost, a quarter inch deep. They do not like having their roots disturbed, so direct sowing usually works best. If your season is short, you can start them indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost and move them outside afterward, handling the roots gently.

soil_mix.type_beginner: regular potting mix that drains well
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Use a potting mix that drains well. If it stays soggy, mix in some perlite or coarse sand. A little compost helps with food. Skip heavy mixes that hold too much water.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: general-purpose well-draining potting mix
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: A free-draining mix is the priority; blend in perlite or coarse sand if the base mix holds too much water, and a modest amount of compost for fertility. Avoid heavy, water-retentive mixes that keep the root zone saturated.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out faster than the garden, so check them every day when it is hot. Water when the top inch of soil feels dry, and let the extra drain out the bottom. Try not to wet the leaves.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Watering pots often washes out their food, so feed potted zinnias lightly every few weeks during bloom, rather than just once. Use a balanced fertilizer and go easy on it.

overwintering.approach_beginner: This does not apply. Zinnias are one-season flowers that die at the first frost, so there is nothing to overwinter. Just plant new seeds next year.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Not applicable: zinnia is a frost-tender annual grown for a single season and killed by the first frost; it is not overwintered. Re-sow each year.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Smaller zinnia types like Thumbelina, Profusion, or Zahara are great in pots and on balconies. Use a pot with drainage holes, a well-draining potting mix, and full sun. Do not cram too many plants into one pot, so air can move and leaves stay healthy.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Dwarf and compact series (for example Thumbelina, Profusion, Zahara) are the container performers; full sun, free-draining mix, and not crowding multiple plants per pot keep airflow up and mildew down. Taller cut-flower types are workable in large containers but want depth and staking-free spacing.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry faster than ground beds, so check daily in heat and water when the top inch is dry, letting excess drain freely; do not let the mix stay constantly wet. Water at the base to keep foliage dry.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Frequent watering leaches nutrients from containers, so a light feeding every few weeks with a balanced fertilizer through the bloom season suits potted zinnias better than the single ground-bed dose; keep nitrogen modest.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering containers work for zinnias provided the surface dries between top-ups; keep the wick reservoir from saturating the root zone, since constant moisture undercuts their drought-adapted roots and raises disease risk.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot is fine for zinnias as long as the top of the soil dries out a bit between waterings. Zinnias do not like soil that is wet all the time.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: As an aster-family (Asteraceae) annual, avoid following zinnia immediately with other susceptible asters where soilborne or foliar disease has built up; rotate the bed to an unrelated family for a season if powdery mildew or leaf spot was heavy.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Zinnias are in the daisy family (Asteraceae). If they had a lot of disease, do not plant them, or other daisy-family flowers, in the same spot the very next season. Give the bed a year with a different kind of plant.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotation matters less for a fast-growing ornamental annual than for heavy-feeding vegetables, but moving zinnias to a fresh bed each year and clearing infected debris at season end limits carryover of powdery mildew and leaf-spot inoculum.
rotation.note_beginner: Rotating zinnias is not as important as it is for vegetables, but it still helps. Plant them in a different spot each year if you can, and clean up old, diseased leaves at the end of the season so problems do not carry over.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seed leaves (cotyledons) emerge from warm soil within roughly 5 to 7 days.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The first little leaves push up through the soil in about a week.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep soil warm and evenly moist; do not let it crust or dry out during emergence.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil warm and damp until the seedlings come up.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Seedlings emerged?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your seeds sprouted?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: First true leaves develop; the plant is small and establishing roots.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Real leaves appear and the little plant starts to settle in.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin or space to 9 to 12 in; water at the base to keep foliage dry.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Space plants about 9 to 12 inches apart and water the soil, not the leaves.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Thinned and spaced?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you spaced out your seedlings?

growth_stages.name: Established / vegetative
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Plant grows bushier with several true-leaf sets and begins branching.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant gets bigger and bushier with more leaves.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pinch above the fourth leaf set to force branching; maintain spacing and airflow.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pinch off the top above the fourth set of leaves to make it branch out.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Plants pinched?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you pinched your zinnias?

growth_stages.name: Budding
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flower buds form at stem tips; stems lengthen toward bloom.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Flower buds start to form at the tops of the stems.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture even at bud point; begin scouting for mildew and pests.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist and start checking for mildew and bugs.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: First buds visible?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Do you see flower buds yet?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Blooms open fully and continuously; first bloom is roughly 60 to 70 days from sowing and continues to first frost.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Flowers open, about two months after planting, and keep coming until frost.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut and deadhead regularly to drive continuous bloom; water at the base.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep cutting flowers and removing faded ones to get more blooms.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: First bloom open?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Has your first flower opened?

growth_stages.name: Seed saving (optional)
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Selected heads left on the plant dry to brown and set viable seed.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A few flowers left on the plant dry out and form seeds.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Leave chosen heads to dry fully before collecting seed; expect hybrids not to come true.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Let a few flowers dry out fully on the plant before collecting their seeds.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Seed heads drying?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are you saving any seeds?

notifications.body_seasoned: Soil should be warm enough now. Direct-sow at about 70 °F, a quarter inch deep, after frost danger has passed.
notifications.body_beginner: Your last frost has passed, so you can plant zinnia seeds outside once the soil feels warm, about a quarter inch deep.

notifications.body_seasoned: Plants should have about four true-leaf sets. Pinch the growing tips to force branching and more stems.
notifications.body_beginner: Your zinnias should have about four sets of leaves now. Pinch off the tops so they grow bushier with more flowers.

notifications.body_seasoned: First blooms are opening. Cut and deadhead regularly to drive continuous cut-and-come-again bloom.
notifications.body_beginner: Your first flowers are opening. Keep cutting them and snipping off faded ones to get more blooms all season.

notifications.body_seasoned: A first fall frost is forecast within a few days and will end the zinnia season. Cut remaining blooms to enjoy indoors.
notifications.body_beginner: Frost is expected in a few days, which will end your zinnias. Cut the flowers that are left and bring them inside.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Zinnia is frost-tender at both ends of the season. Frost will damage or kill plants; protect or harvest blooms before a frost event.
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Zinnias cannot survive frost. Cover them or cut the flowers before a frosty night, in spring or fall.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: clemson_hgic_1149

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Humid, still conditions with wet foliage and cool nights drive powdery mildew and leaf spot. Improve airflow, water at the base, and scout closely.
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Damp, still, humid weather makes the white powdery mildew more likely. Keep leaves dry, give plants room for air, and check them often.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: clemson_hgic_1149

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Zinnias thrive in heat and full sun; summer is their peak, not a stress period. Maintain even moisture and keep watering at the base.
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Good news: zinnias love hot, sunny weather. Summer is their best season. Just keep them watered at the base.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: uf_ifas_zinnia

germination.text_seasoned: Wait for soil at about 70 °F before direct-sowing; soil temperature, not the calendar date, is the real germination trigger, and seed sown into cold, wet soil rots or damps off.
germination.text_beginner: Plant seeds outside only once the soil is warm, around 70 °F. Cold, wet soil makes the seeds rot instead of sprout, so warmth matters more than the date on the calendar.

germination.text_seasoned: Sow at about 1/4 in depth; zinnias germinate in roughly 5 to 7 days in warm soil and resent root disturbance, which is why direct sowing is the strongest method.
germination.text_beginner: Plant the seeds about a quarter inch deep. In warm soil they usually sprout in about a week. Zinnias do not like their roots disturbed, so planting straight in the ground works best.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin or space seedlings to 9 to 12 in once they have a few true leaves; generous spacing for airflow is a primary cultural defense against powdery mildew later.
seedling.text_beginner: Once seedlings have a few real leaves, thin them so plants stand about 9 to 12 inches apart. Giving them room for air to move helps prevent the white powdery mildew zinnias often get.

seedling.text_seasoned: Keep the soil evenly moist while seedlings establish, watering at the base; this is one of the two critical moisture windows, and overhead wetting at this stage invites early disease.
seedling.text_beginner: Keep the soil damp while young plants get going, and water at the base, not on the leaves. This is one of the times zinnias most need steady moisture.

established.text_seasoned: Pinch the growing tip above about the fourth set of true leaves to force basal branching; pinched plants produce more numerous, longer, sturdier stems than unpinched ones.
established.text_beginner: When plants have about four sets of leaves, pinch off the very top. This makes the plant branch out and grow bushier, giving you more and longer flower stems.

established.text_seasoned: Maintain airflow and water at the base as plants fill in; full sun, spacing, and dry foliage together keep powdery mildew and leaf spot in check, sharpest where humidity is high.
established.text_beginner: As plants grow, keep air moving between them and keep watering the soil, not the leaves. Full sun, space, and dry leaves are what keep that white powdery mildew away, especially in humid areas.

budding.text_seasoned: Sustain even moisture as the first buds form; drought stress at bud point shortens stems and reduces bloom size, so this is the second critical moisture window after establishment.
budding.text_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist when the first flower buds appear. Letting plants get too dry now means shorter stems and smaller flowers.

budding.text_seasoned: Scout for early powdery mildew and leaf spot as the canopy closes and for Japanese beetles in early to midsummer; addressing crowding and removing affected leaves early limits spread.
budding.text_beginner: As plants get bushy, check for the white powdery mildew or dark leaf spots, and for Japanese beetles in early summer. Removing affected leaves and easing crowding early keeps problems from spreading.

flowering.text_seasoned: Cut and deadhead continuously: removing spent and cut blooms back to the next leaf node redirects energy from seed set into new flowers, driving cut-and-come-again bloom from summer to first frost.
flowering.text_beginner: Keep cutting flowers and snipping off faded ones, cutting back to the next set of leaves. This tells the plant to make more flowers instead of seeds, so you get blooms all the way to the first fall frost.

flowering.text_seasoned: Harvest stems when blooms are fully open and the stem is firm just below the flower (the wiggle test); zinnias do not open much after cutting, so cutting too early shortens vase life.
flowering.text_beginner: Cut zinnias when the flower is fully open and the stem just under it feels firm, not floppy. Zinnias do not keep opening in the vase, so picking them too early gives shorter-lived flowers.

seed_saving.text_seasoned: To save seed, let some heads stay on the plant and dry fully to brown before collecting; zinnias are open-pollinated insect-pollinated, so seed from hybrids will not come true to type.
seed_saving.text_beginner: To save seeds, leave a few flowers on the plant and let them dry out and turn brown before you pick them. Note that seeds from hybrid zinnias will not grow into the same flower next year.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A single cut-flower zinnia, pinched and cut regularly, yields dozens of stems over a season, often a stem or more per week per plant at peak; dwarf bedding types produce more, smaller blooms for color rather than cutting.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: One cut-flower zinnia can give you dozens of flowers over the summer if you keep cutting, often a stem or more each week at its peak. The small bedding types make lots of little flowers for color rather than for cutting.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Zinnias bloom the first season from seed, typically about 60 to 70 days after sowing, so there is no establishment year; a spring sowing flowers from summer to first frost.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Zinnias flower the same year you plant them, usually about two months after sowing. There is no waiting year. Plant in spring and you will have flowers from summer until the first frost.
factors_seasoned: Cultivar type: tall cut-flower varieties yield long stems for the vase; dwarf bedding types yield more, smaller blooms for color.
Cutting and deadheading cadence: frequent cutting drives cut-and-come-again production; neglected plants set seed and slow.
Pinching: pinched plants branch and yield more, sturdier stems than unpinched single-stem plants.
Spacing and airflow: adequate spacing sustains healthy foliage and longer productive life by limiting powdery mildew.
Season length: a longer frost-free season and successive sowings extend total stem yield into fall.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No T1 evidence supports a moon-phase planting preference for zinnia; left unset.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: White powdery coating on leaves (powdery mildew)
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Leaves got a white, powdery coating
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Powdery mildew took hold, favored by humidity, cool nights, crowding, and wet foliage. It is the signature zinnia foliar disease.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: A fungus called powdery mildew spread on the leaves. It thrives when plants are crowded, the air is humid, and leaves stay wet.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Space plants generously for airflow, water at the base, site in full sun, and choose interspecific resistant series such as Profusion or Zahara where mildew pressure is high.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Give plants more room next time so air moves between them, water the soil instead of the leaves, and try resistant types like Profusion or Zahara.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Tall, leggy plants with few blooms
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Plants grew tall and spindly with few flowers
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Unpinched plants and too much nitrogen drive single-stem, leafy growth at the expense of branching and bloom; low light also reduces flowering.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The plants were not pinched, or got too much high-nitrogen feed, so they grew tall and leafy instead of full and flowery.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Pinch above the fourth leaf set to force branching, keep nitrogen modest, and grow in full sun.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Next time, pinch the tops when plants are young to make them bushy, go easy on fertilizer, and plant in full sun.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Seedlings collapsed at the soil line (damping-off)
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Young seedlings fell over and died
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Damping-off, a fungal collapse at the stem base, struck seedlings sown into cold, wet soil or kept too wet.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: A fungus rotted the seedlings at the base, usually because the soil was too cold and wet when they were planted.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait for soil at about 70 °F before sowing, avoid overwatering, and ensure good drainage.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Wait until the soil is warm, around 70 °F, before planting, and do not keep the soil soggy.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Plants blackened by frost
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Frost killed or damaged the plants
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Zinnia is frost-tender; frost at either end of the season, planting out too early in spring or the first frost in fall, kills or damages plants.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Zinnias cannot handle frost. A late spring frost or the first fall frost will damage or kill them.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Direct-sow or transplant only after all frost danger has passed, and expect plants to end with the first fall frost.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant only after your last frost in spring, and know that the first frost in fall ends the zinnia season.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Seeds failed to come up
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Few or no seeds sprouted
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Cold soil is the usual cause of poor zinnia germination; seed sown before soil reaches about 70 °F germinates slowly, erratically, or rots.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Cold soil is usually why zinnia seeds do not sprout well. Planted too early in cool soil, they come up poorly or rot.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait for warm soil (about 70 °F), sow at 1/4 in, and keep evenly moist during emergence.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Wait for warm soil around 70 °F, plant a quarter inch deep, and keep it damp until they sprout.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Flowers and leaves chewed (Japanese beetles)
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Bugs chewed the flowers and leaves
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Japanese beetles, which favor zinnia as a host, skeletonize foliage and feed on blooms in early to midsummer; aphids and spider mites can also build up.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Japanese beetles, which love zinnias, chewed the flowers and leaves in early summer. Aphids and tiny spider mites can also show up.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Hand-pick beetles at dawn into soapy water and avoid pheromone traps, which concentrate them; hose off or use insecticidal soap for aphids and mites.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Pick beetles off in the early morning and drop them in soapy water; do not use beetle traps, which draw more in. Spray aphids and mites off with water or insecticidal soap.

primary.name: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Sow successively every 2 to 3 weeks from after last frost through midsummer to keep a steady supply of fresh, vigorous stems; older plantings decline as the season wears on even with deadheading, so younger successions carry late-summer quality. There is no heat pause: zinnias thrive through peak summer.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: For flowers all season, plant a new small batch of seeds every 2 to 3 weeks from after the last frost into midsummer. Fresh young plants give the best flowers late in the season. Unlike cool-season crops, zinnias love the heat, so you do not stop for summer.
succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Successive sowing offsets the gradual decline of older plantings and disease accumulation, sustaining stem quality and bloom volume into fall.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note: UMN Extension direct-seeds zinnia once soil is at least 70 degrees F (transplants once soil reaches 60 degrees F), which in the northern tier falls a week or two after the last frost. Cold-zone gardeners lean on the transplant arm and the fast first-bloom for a head start.

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.synthesis_note: Start indoors about 4 to 6 weeks before last frost for a head start; transplant after frost once soil warms.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note: Transplants set out on the same warm-soil/after-frost trigger as direct sowing.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note: First bloom 8 to 12 weeks after sowing (Clemson HGIC 1149).

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Blooms from summer to the first fall frost (UC IPM: zinnia blooms summer and fall); the tender annual is killed by frost, which ends the season. Fast first-bloom means months of bloom even in the coldest zones.

plant_out.label: succession
plant_out.synthesis_note: Where the season is long enough (zones 6 to 7), sow every 2 weeks through early summer; the coldest zones (3 to 4) get a single sowing because the frost-bracketed window is short.

harvest_start.label: succession
harvest_start.synthesis_note: Each succession reaches first bloom 8 to 12 weeks after its sow date.

harvest_end.label: succession
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Successions bloom to the first fall frost.

3.planting_note: Sow once the soil warms to about 70 °F, roughly a week or two after the last frost; transplants can go out a bit earlier once soil hits 60 °F. First blooms about 8 to 12 weeks later, then bloom right up to the first fall frost. Because the season is short here, start indoors for a head start and plan on a single sowing.
3.zone_notes: Zone 3 runs a single frost-bracketed summer bloom: plant after the last frost once soil is warm, and zinnia's fast first-bloom still leaves weeks of flowers before the first fall frost ends the season. Winter is simply too cold for the tender annual, so the calendar rests then.

4.planting_note: Sow once the soil warms to about 70 °F, roughly a week or two after the last frost; transplants can go out a bit earlier once soil hits 60 °F. First blooms about 8 to 12 weeks later, then bloom right up to the first fall frost. Because the season is short here, start indoors for a head start and plan on a single sowing.
4.zone_notes: Zone 4 runs a single frost-bracketed summer bloom: plant after the last frost once soil is warm, and zinnia's fast first-bloom still leaves weeks of flowers before the first fall frost ends the season. Winter is simply too cold for the tender annual, so the calendar rests then.

5.planting_note: Sow once the soil warms to about 70 °F, roughly a week or two after the last frost; transplants can go out a bit earlier once soil hits 60 °F. First blooms about 8 to 12 weeks later, then bloom right up to the first fall frost. Sow every 2 weeks through early summer for a steady cutting supply.
5.zone_notes: Zone 5 runs a single frost-bracketed summer bloom: plant after the last frost once soil is warm, and zinnia's fast first-bloom still leaves months of flowers before the first fall frost ends the season. Winter is simply too cold for the tender annual, so the calendar rests then.

6.planting_note: Sow once the soil warms to about 70 °F, roughly a week or two after the last frost; transplants can go out a bit earlier once soil hits 60 °F. First blooms about 8 to 12 weeks later, then bloom right up to the first fall frost. Sow every 2 weeks through early summer for a steady cutting supply.
6.zone_notes: Zone 6 runs a single frost-bracketed summer bloom: plant after the last frost once soil is warm, and zinnia's fast first-bloom still leaves months of flowers before the first fall frost ends the season. Winter is simply too cold for the tender annual, so the calendar rests then.

7.planting_note: Sow once the soil warms to about 70 °F, roughly a week or two after the last frost; transplants can go out a bit earlier once soil hits 60 °F. First blooms about 8 to 12 weeks later, then bloom right up to the first fall frost. Sow every 2 weeks through early summer for a steady cutting supply.
7.zone_notes: Zone 7 runs a single frost-bracketed summer bloom: plant after the last frost once soil is warm, and zinnia's fast first-bloom still leaves months of flowers before the first fall frost ends the season. Winter is simply too cold for the tender annual, so the calendar rests then.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the northern tier, zinnia grows in one summer window. Wait until a week or two after your last frost, when the soil has warmed to about 70 °F for seeds (or 60 °F if you are setting out transplants), then plant; the flowers come from summer until the first fall frost. Zinnia blooms fast, in about 8 to 12 weeks, so even short northern summers give you plenty of flowers, and starting plants indoors gives you a head start. You never stop for heat here; cold is the only limit, at both ends of the season. In the milder zones you can sow again every couple of weeks for more flowers.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In the northern tier, zinnia is a single frost-bracketed summer crop. Wait until a week or two after the last frost, once soil reaches about 70 °F for direct sowing (or 60 °F for transplants, per UMN Extension), then sow; the plants bloom from summer to the first fall frost. Zinnia's fast first-bloom, about 8 to 12 weeks, leaves plenty of flowering time even in the coldest zones, and the transplant arm buys a head start where the season is short. There is no heat pause here; the limit is frost on both ends. Sow every two weeks where zones 6 to 7 allow.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note: Across the Southeast and Gulf, zinnias are direct-sown after the last spring frost once soil is reliably near 70 degrees F; Clemson HGIC 1149 sets sowing after frost danger at ~70 degrees F soil, and UF/IFAS notes spring planting throughout the region. Hero method is direct sowing (zinnias resent root disturbance).

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.synthesis_note: Optional early-color transplant arm: start indoors about 4 to 5 weeks before last frost and set out after frost, handling roots minimally. Direct sowing is preferred in this long-season region; the transplant arm only buys earliest color.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note: Transplants set out after the last frost, the same trigger as direct sowing; no advantage to planting into cool soil.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note: First bloom 8 to 12 weeks after direct sowing per Clemson HGIC 1149; the 60-day mark is the early edge of that window, sooner from transplants.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Healthy plants bloom through the hot Southeast summer, often until the first frost, which kills the tender annual; UF/IFAS confirms heat-through-summer bloom and frost as the season end.

plant_out.label: succession
plant_out.synthesis_note: For continuous cut-and-come-again bloom, sow successively every 2 weeks from after last frost through midsummer; the last sow is bounded so the final flush reaches first bloom (8 to 12 weeks) well before first frost. Zinnias bloom through summer heat, so there is no midsummer pause.

harvest_start.label: succession
harvest_start.synthesis_note: Each succession reaches first bloom 8 to 12 weeks after its sow date.

harvest_end.label: succession
harvest_end.synthesis_note: All successions bloom until the first fall frost ends the season.

8.planting_note: Direct-sow after the last frost once soil is near 70 °F; first blooms about 8 to 12 weeks later, carrying through summer to the first fall frost. Sow every 2 weeks into midsummer for a steady cutting supply.
8.zone_notes: Zone 8 has a real winter frost period, so zinnias run as a single long warm-season bloom crop here: plant after the spring frost, enjoy bloom straight through the hot summer, and expect the first fall frost to end the season.

9.planting_note: Direct-sow after the last frost into warm soil near 70 °F; the warmer zone 9 season is longer than zone 8, with first blooms in roughly 8 to 12 weeks and cut-and-come-again bloom through summer until the first fall frost. Sow every 2 weeks for continuous stems.
9.zone_notes: Zone 9's longer warm season gives an earlier spring sow and a later first frost than zone 8, so the bloom window stretches several weeks further on both ends. It is still a single frost-bracketed warm-season crop, not a separate fall cycle.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast and Gulf, zinnia loves the heat. Wait until your last spring frost has passed and the soil feels warm, then sow seeds straight into the bed; the plants will flower all summer long, right up to the first frost in fall. You do not stop for hot weather here, because hot weather is exactly when zinnia is happiest. The main thing to watch is powdery mildew, a white powder on the leaves that the humidity encourages, so give plants space for air to move, water at the soil and try to keep the leaves dry, and pick mildew-resistant types like Profusion or Zahara if you can. Plant a few new seeds every couple of weeks through midsummer and you will always have fresh flowers to cut.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: Across the Southeast and Gulf, zinnia is a warm-season bedding workhorse: direct-sow after the last spring frost once soil reaches roughly 70 °F, and it will bloom straight through the region's hot, humid summer until the first fall frost. There is no midsummer heat pause; heat is when zinnia performs best. The real regional pressure is powdery mildew and foliar leaf spot in the humidity, so give plants room (space rows about a foot apart), water at the base rather than overhead, and favor mildew-resistant series such as Profusion and Zahara. Sow every two weeks into midsummer to keep fresh, vigorous cutting stems coming as older plantings tire.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note: UC MG Santa Clara cut-flower chart direct-sows zinnia April through June (zones 8b/9a/9b); the Central Valley interior plants after the last frost into warm soil. Direct sowing is the hero method.

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.synthesis_note: Optional early-color transplant arm; direct sowing preferred (zinnias resent root disturbance).

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note: Transplants set out on the same warm-soil/after-frost trigger as direct sowing.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note: First bloom 8 to 12 weeks after sowing (Clemson HGIC 1149).

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Blooms through the hot Central Valley summer (UC IPM: zinnia thrives in hot weather, blooms summer and fall) to the first fall frost.

plant_out.label: succession
plant_out.synthesis_note: Sow successively every 2 weeks through the spring and early-summer window for continuous cutting; UC IPM confirms bloom through summer with no heat pause.

harvest_end.label: succession

8.planting_note: Direct-sow from April into June once the last frost has passed and soil is warm; first blooms about 8 to 12 weeks later, carrying through the hot Central Valley summer to the first fall frost. Sow every 2 weeks for a steady cutting supply.
8.zone_notes: Zone 8 in the interior valleys runs a single long warm-season bloom: plant after the spring frost, bloom straight through the hot, dry summer (zinnia thrives in the heat here), and finish at the first fall frost.

9.planting_note: Direct-sow from spring once frost has passed and soil is warm; the longer zone 9 season gives an earlier start and later first frost than zone 8, with first blooms in about 8 to 12 weeks and bloom through summer to fall. Sow every 2 weeks for continuous stems.
9.zone_notes: Zone 9's longer warm season stretches the single bloom window on both ends versus zone 8. It stays a single frost-bracketed warm-season crop, with zinnia blooming hard through the hot, dry interior summer.

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In the Central Valley, zinnia loves the long hot summer. Plant seeds after your last spring frost once the soil is warm, anytime from April into June, and the plants will flower all the way through summer until the first fall frost. You do not need to stop for the heat, because heat is exactly what zinnia wants. Our dry summers mean less powdery mildew than in humid places, but still space plants out and water at the soil, not over the leaves. Sow a few new seeds every couple of weeks for nonstop flowers to cut.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: In California's interior valleys, zinnia is a single long warm-season crop. Direct-sow from April into June once the last frost has passed and soil is warm (the UC Master Gardener cut-flower chart sows zinnia April through June), and it blooms straight through the hot, dry Central Valley summer to the first fall frost. Heat is no obstacle here; zinnia thrives in it, so there is no midsummer pause. Summers are dry, so powdery mildew pressure is lower than in humid regions, but still give plants room for airflow and water at the base. Sow every two weeks for a steady cutting supply.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note: Cool maritime soil delays the warm-season start: UC Marin sets the warm-season soil trigger at 60 to 65 degrees F, reached on the north coast around late April to May. Direct-sow once soil warms; cool nights slow early growth.

start_indoors.label: primary

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note: Transplants set out on the same warm-soil/after-frost trigger as direct sowing.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note: First bloom 8 to 12 weeks after sowing (Clemson HGIC 1149); cool coastal nights can push it later.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Blooms through the mild maritime summer (UC IPM: thrives in heat, blooms summer and fall) to the first fall frost. Frost-limited, not heat-limited.

plant_out.label: succession
plant_out.synthesis_note: Where the cool-coast season allows, sow every 2 weeks after soil passes 60 to 65 degrees F; the shorter front-end season bounds how many successions fit.

harvest_end.label: succession

9.planting_note: Wait for the cool maritime soil to reach 60 to 65 °F, generally May, then direct-sow; cool nights slow early growth so first blooms come a little later, then carry through the mild summer to the first fall frost. The limit here is cool soil and frost, not heat.
9.zone_notes: Zone 9 on the north coast is frost-limited and slowed by cool summer nights, not by heat. Zinnia goes in later than in the interior, once soil warms, and disease pressure is lower than in humid regions because coastal summers are dry. Give airflow anyway.

10.planting_note: Sow once the mild-coast soil reaches 60 to 65 °F, generally mid-spring, into a long mild season; first blooms about 8 to 12 weeks later, carrying through summer to the first fall frost. Cool nights, not heat, set the pace.
10.zone_notes: Zone 10 on the north coast has a longer mild season than zone 9 but the same cool-night, frost-limited character. Dry coastal summers keep powdery mildew pressure lower than in humid regions.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: On the cool north coast, the thing zinnia is waiting for is warm soil, not warm air. Use a soil thermometer and hold off sowing until the soil hits about 60 to 65 °F, usually around May. Cool nights make the plants start a little slowly, but once going they flower through the mild summer until the first fall frost. Coastal summers are dry, so powdery mildew is less of a problem here than in humid places, but still pick resistant types and leave room for air to move. Sow a few more seeds every couple of weeks if your season is long enough.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: On the cool north coast, zinnia is frost-limited and slowed by cool nights, not by heat. The key is soil temperature: wait until it reaches 60 to 65 °F (UC Marin's warm-season threshold), generally around May, before sowing. Cool maritime nights push the bloom start later, but the plants then flower through the mild summer to the first fall frost. Dry coastal summers keep powdery mildew pressure lower than in humid regions; choose mildew-resistant types and give airflow as a sensible precaution. Sow every two weeks where the shorter season allows.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note: Mild-winter coastal SoCal: sow once soil reaches the 60 to 65 degrees F warm-season trigger (UC Marin, coastal CA), generally April to May. A long mild season follows.

start_indoors.label: primary

plant_out.label: primary

harvest_start.synthesis_note: First bloom 8 to 12 weeks after sowing (Clemson HGIC 1149).

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Blooms through the dry warm summer well into fall (UC IPM: thrives in heat, blooms summer and fall); the cool-season slowdown and any rare frost end the season. Not a year-round crop.

9.zone_notes: Zone 9 on the south coast offers a long mild season: a spring sow blooms through the dry warm summer into fall. It is mild but still seasonal, not a year-round crop; the cool-season slowdown ends the run.

10.planting_note: Sow once soil warms to 60 to 65 °F in early to mid spring, into a long mild coastal season; first blooms about 8 to 12 weeks later, carrying through summer into late fall. Sow every 2 weeks for continuous cutting.
10.zone_notes: Zone 10 on the south coast has the longest mild season of the California coast, but zinnia is still a seasonal warm-season annual here, not year-round: the cool-season slowdown, not frost, winds the season down.

ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: On the mild south coast, zinnia gets a long season. Wait for the soil to warm to about 60 to 65 °F in spring, then sow; the plants flower through the warm dry summer and into fall. It is mild here, but zinnia is still a warm-season flower, not a year-round one, so it winds down as the cool season arrives. You do not stop for heat, and dry summers mean powdery mildew is only a moderate worry. Sow a few new seeds every couple of weeks for flowers all season.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: On the mild south coast, zinnia runs a long single warm-season window. Sow once soil reaches 60 to 65 °F in spring (UC Marin's warm-season threshold), and the plants bloom through the dry warm summer well into fall. It is mild here but still seasonal, not a year-round crop; the cool-season slowdown ends the run. Heat is no obstacle, so there is no midsummer pause, and dry summers keep powdery mildew pressure moderate. Sow every two weeks across the long season for continuous cutting stems.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note: Low desert: sow after the mild last frost in spring once soil is warm. UC ANR notes low-desert annual timing differs from other regions; new sowings are held out of the brutal midsummer peak, but zinnia (a heat-lover, unlike the cool-season annuals the desert limits) is sown spring into early summer.

9.zone_notes: Zone 9 low desert has a mild winter and an intense summer. Zinnia is a heat-lover, so unlike cool-season annuals it blooms through the summer; the practical limit is on starting new sowings in peak heat, not on flowering. There is no heat pause.

10.planting_note: Sow in late winter to early spring ahead of the summer peak; first blooms about 8 to 12 weeks later, then bloom through the intense summer to the first fall frost. New sowings are held out of peak heat, but established plants keep flowering, so there is no heat pause.
10.zone_notes: Zone 10 low desert is hotter and milder-wintered than zone 9, with an even longer frost-free run. Zinnia blooms through the desert summer; only the starting of new sowings pauses for peak heat. Mildew pressure is low in the dry air.

ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: In the low desert, zinnia actually likes the heat, so you do not stop it for hot weather; you just pick the right time to plant. Sow after your mild last frost in late winter or spring, before the most brutal heat arrives, and the plants will keep flowering all through the desert summer to the first fall frost. The hottest months are a bad time to start new seeds, but plants already growing keep blooming, so there is no real pause. The dry air means powdery mildew is rarely a problem. Sow a few new seeds every couple of weeks while the weather allows.
ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: In the low desert, zinnia is a heat-lover that blooms through the intense summer, so the rhythm is set by when to start sowings, not by any bloom pause. Sow after the mild last frost in late winter to spring, ahead of the brutal peak; established plants then flower right through the desert summer to the first fall frost. Unlike the cool-season annuals the desert heat limits, zinnia keeps going in the heat, so there is no heat pause; simply hold new sowings out of the hottest months. Dry desert air keeps powdery mildew pressure low. Sow every two weeks within the plantable windows for continuous stems.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note: South Florida spring sow: UF/IFAS EP452 lists zinnia among heat-tolerant annuals to plant in spring (March in the south-FL calendar) that last into fall. Direct sowing is the hero method; soil is well past 70 degrees F by the spring planting window.

direct_sow.label: secondary
direct_sow.synthesis_note: South Florida fall sow: UF/IFAS Gardening Solutions documents zinnia is also planted in the fall in South Florida. A second sowing in early fall (offset back from the late/absent first frost) gives cool-dry-season bloom. This is the fall window the se_gulf region deferred; it lives here on fl_peninsula's own T1.

start_indoors.label: primary

plant_out.label: secondary
plant_out.synthesis_note: Fall transplants set out in early fall for the second south-FL window.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note: First bloom 8 to 12 weeks after sowing (Clemson HGIC 1149); 60 days is the early edge.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Bloom is continuous through the south-FL summer (UF/IFAS: zinnias handle hot summers and bloom through them); the season runs to the first frost at the z10 edge, longer at frost-free z11. No midsummer bloom gap, so no pause token.

plant_out.label: succession
plant_out.synthesis_note: For continuous cutting stems, sow successively every 2 weeks within the spring window and again within the fall window. New successions are not started into the peak summer rainy season (UF/IFAS EP452 drops zinnia from the May to August planting lists), though established plants keep blooming through summer.
