10.planting_note: Two sowing windows: a spring sow around February to March and a second sow in early fall, the south-Florida fall window. Direct-sow into warm soil past 70 °F; first blooms about 8 to 12 weeks later. Plants bloom right through the hot, wet summer between the windows, so the gap is in sowing, not in bloom. Hold new sowings out of the peak rainy months and sow every 2 weeks within each window for steady stems.
10.zone_notes: Zone 10 gets two zinnia sowing windows, spring and fall, with bloom carrying through the summer in between. Only a rare, brief frost limits the very edges of the season; the real summer pressure is heat plus heavy rain and the powdery mildew and leaf spot that humidity brings.

11.planting_note: At the frost-free tip, zinnia still runs on two sowing windows, spring and fall, rather than year-round planting: a spring sow around February to March and a fall sow in October. Direct-sow into warm soil; first blooms about 8 to 12 weeks later, carrying through the summer. The season is bounded by the summer wet and disease peak and the cool-season slowdown, not by frost. Sow every 2 weeks within each window for continuous cutting.
11.zone_notes: Zone 11 has no killing frost, but zinnia is still planted in two windows here, spring and fall, not as a year-round crop: the summer wet season and its disease pressure, not cold, set the rhythm. Favor mildew-resistant types and give plants generous spacing for airflow.

fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: In south Florida you get two good times to plant zinnia: once in spring, around February or March, and again in early fall. In between, your plants keep flowering right through the hot summer, so you are not waiting on blooms, just holding off on planting new seeds during the wettest, stickiest part of summer. The big thing to watch here is powdery mildew, a white powder on the leaves, because Florida's humidity and rain make it worse than in drier places. Give plants plenty of room so air can move through, water at the soil instead of over the leaves, and choose mildew-resistant types like Profusion or Zahara when you can. Plant a few new seeds every couple of weeks in each window and you will always have fresh flowers to cut.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: In south Florida, zinnia runs on two sowing windows rather than one long season: a spring sow (around February to March per the UF/IFAS south-Florida calendar) and a second sow in early fall, the fall window the rest of the Southeast does not get. Between them the plants bloom straight through the hot, humid summer, so the break is in sowing, not in flowering. There is no heat pause. The defining regional pressure is disease: the humidity and summer rains make powdery mildew and leaf spot sharper here than anywhere else, so space plants generously for airflow, water at the base, keep new sowings out of the wettest peak months, and lean on mildew-resistant series like Profusion and Zahara. Sow every 2 weeks within each window for a steady cutting supply.

plantings.label: main
plantings.year_round_basis: frost_free_climate_derived: z11 is frost-free (no frost to bracket the normally frost-anchored season); pause_in_heat:false is T1-confirmed (UC IPM, no heat stall); zinnia is documented grown in Hawaii via CTAHR/Honolulu home-garden grow-lists. No frost + no heat pause + a heat-loving tolerant annual = no season-closing factor, so continuous. This is a CLIMATE DERIVATION from sourced inputs, NOT a CTAHR year-round continuity quote (none exists).

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note: No zinnia-specific CTAHR year-round continuity statement exists (searched, outcome C); year_round is DERIVED from frost-free z11 + T1 pause_in_heat:false (UC IPM: zinnia thrives in hot weather, blooms summer and fall) + zinnia's presence in CTAHR Hawaii home-garden grow-lists. Climate-derived, not a sourced continuity quote. The rainy/wet months raise leaf-wetness and powdery-mildew pressure but do not stop the crop (basil precedent).

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note: First bloom about 8 to 12 weeks after sowing (Clemson HGIC 1149); year-round continuous bloom once established.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Year-round cell: no seasonal end. Continuous cut-and-come-again; start new plants any time of year.

plant_out.label: succession
plant_out.synthesis_note: Sow every 2 weeks year-round for continuous cutting stems; no seasonal gap in frost-free z11 (climate-derived, see main arm basis). Hold new sowings out of the wettest stretch where powdery mildew pressure peaks, though established plants keep blooming.

harvest_start.label: succession
harvest_start.synthesis_note: Each succession reaches first bloom 8 to 12 weeks after its sow date.

harvest_end.label: succession
harvest_end.synthesis_note: No seasonal end; continuous year-round.

11.calendar_basis: Frost-free z11 + T1 pause_in_heat:false (UC IPM, no heat stall) + zinnia documented in CTAHR Hawaii home-garden grow-lists = no season-closing factor, so continuous year-round bloom. Climate-DERIVED, not a CTAHR year-round continuity quote (none exists; searched, outcome C). The wet/rainy months raise powdery-mildew pressure but do not stop the crop.
11.planting_note: In frost-free low-elevation Hawaii, zinnia can be planted and bloomed year round; there is no frost season to bracket it and no midsummer heat pause. Sow any time, with first blooms about 8 to 12 weeks later, and keep sowing every 2 weeks for continuous cutting. The wet, rainy months raise powdery-mildew pressure, so favor resistant types, space for airflow, and water at the base; established plants keep blooming through the wet stretch.
11.zone_notes: Zone 11 is frost-free, so zinnia has no cold season to stop it and, as a heat-lover, no summer pause either; it runs continuously. The year-round call here is derived from the frost-free climate plus zinnia's heat tolerance and its documented presence in Hawaii home gardens, rather than a single Hawaii planting-date source. The practical limit is the wet-season powdery-mildew and leaf-spot pressure, not temperature.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In Hawaii's frost-free lowlands, you can plant zinnia any time of year and enjoy flowers all year, because there is no frost to stop it and it loves the heat. Sow seeds whenever you like, expect first blooms in about 8 to 12 weeks, and plant a few more every couple of weeks for a steady supply to cut. The main thing to watch is powdery mildew, a white powder on the leaves that the rainy, humid weather encourages, so give plants room for air to move, water at the soil rather than over the leaves, and choose mildew-resistant types like Profusion or Zahara when you can. Your plants will keep flowering right through the wet season.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: In frost-free low-elevation Hawaii, zinnia grows continuously year round: there is no frost season to bound it, and as a heat-lover it takes no midsummer pause. Sow at any time, with first blooms about 8 to 12 weeks later, and succession every 2 weeks keeps young, vigorous cutting stems coming. Be clear that this year-round call is climate-derived, from the frost-free zone plus zinnia's T1-confirmed heat tolerance and its presence in CTAHR Hawaii home-garden lists, rather than a single Hawaii planting-date publication. The defining pressure is disease: the rainy, humid months sharpen powdery mildew and leaf spot, so favor resistant series such as Profusion and Zahara, space generously for airflow, and water at the base. Established plants bloom through the wet stretch.

crops.description_seasoned: Zinnia (Zinnia elegans and related species) is a warm-season, frost-tender annual in the Asteraceae family, native to Mexico. It is grown for showy blooms, not food, across a wide size range from dwarf bedding types near 6 in to cut-flower types reaching 3 to 4 ft. Sown into warm soil after frost, it reaches first bloom in roughly 60 to 70 days and flowers continuously from summer until the first fall frost. It loves heat and full sun, so summer is its peak rather than a stress period. The defining care moves are cutting and deadheading, which drive cut-and-come-again bloom, and spacing for airflow to limit powdery mildew.
crops.description_beginner: Zinnias are easy, cheerful flowers you grow for blooms, not for eating. They love heat and full sun, so summer is their best season. You plant the seeds outside after your last frost, once the soil is warm, and you get your first flowers in about two months. They keep blooming until the first frost in fall. The more you cut the flowers, the more the plant makes, so cutting and removing faded blooms (called deadheading, snipping off spent flowers) keeps them going. Give plants room to breathe so the leaves stay dry and healthy.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Harvest for the vase when the bloom is nearly but not fully open and the stem is firm from the cut point to just below the flower head; a stem that stays rigid when gently shaken is ready, a floppy one is not. For longest vase life, cut before the small true flowers (the disc florets) emerge at the center. Cut in the cool of morning into clean water. Typical vase life is one week or more.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Cut zinnias for a vase when the flower is almost fully open. Test the stem first: hold it and give a gentle shake. If it stands up straight and stiff, it is ready to cut. If the flower flops over, wait a day or two. Cut in the morning and put the stems straight into clean water. Cut flowers usually last a week or longer indoors.
crops.deadheading_seasoned: Deadhead spent blooms back to the next leaf node throughout the season to redirect energy from seed set into new flower production and sustain cut-and-come-again bloom. Cutting for the vase serves the same function, so a working cutting garden is effectively self-deadheading. Pinch young plants at about four true-leaf sets to force basal branching and longer, more numerous stems.
crops.deadheading_beginner: Deadheading means snipping off flowers once they fade. Do it regularly: cut the old bloom back to the next set of leaves, and the plant will make more flowers instead of going to seed. Cutting fresh flowers for a vase does the same job. When plants are young, pinch out the top above the fourth set of leaves to make them branch out bushier with more stems.

crops.name: Cosmos

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Cosmos grows in almost any soil that drains well, and it actually flowers best in poor, un-fed soil. You do not need to add compost or fertilizer. The main thing to avoid is rich, soggy ground: too much richness gives leaves instead of flowers, and wet soil can rot the roots.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Cosmos wants well-drained soil that is on the lean side; low fertility is a feature, not a problem. It tolerates a wide range of textures, from sand to clay, and a wide pH range. The one thing to avoid is rich, heavily amended, or wet ground: excess fertility, especially nitrogen, drives tall leafy growth with few flowers, and soggy soil invites root and stem rots.

ph.note_beginner: Cosmos is not picky about soil pH (how acidic or alkaline the soil is). A normal garden range around 6.0 to 7.0 is fine, and it tolerates soils quite a bit more acidic or alkaline, so you usually do not need to change anything.
ph.note_seasoned: Cosmos is not pH-fussy and performs across roughly 6.0 to 7.0, tolerating both mildly acidic and alkaline soils well outside that band. No pH adjustment is normally warranted.

crops.tip_seasoned: Grow cosmos hard: full sun and lean, unimproved soil are the whole trick. Rich ground and fertilizer push soft, tall, floppy foliage with few flowers, so skip the feed and go easy on water. Direct sow after the last frost once the soil reaches about 65 °F, deadhead or cut for continuous bloom, stake or plant the tall types close together, and let a few heads drop seed to renew the stand.
crops.tip_beginner: Cosmos likes to be left alone. Give it full sun and poor soil, and do not fertilize; rich soil and feeding give you tall leafy plants with hardly any flowers. Plant the seeds outside after your last frost once the soil is warm, keep cutting the flowers to get more, and give the tall types something to lean on. A few dropped seeds will come back on their own next year.

fertilizer.type: None to very low; usually unnecessary
fertilizer.timing: Skip; feed only very lean soils lightly, if at all
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Do not fertilize cosmos. It flowers best in lean soil, and feeding, especially nitrogen, pushes soft foliage and stem elongation at the expense of bloom and makes tall types flop. If the soil is truly impoverished sand, a single light dose of a low-nitrogen, bloom-leaning fertilizer at planting is the most you should give.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Do not feed cosmos. It flowers best in poor soil, and fertilizer, especially the high-nitrogen kind, gives you lots of leaves and few flowers, plus tall floppy plants. Only if your soil is very poor sand should you give one small dose of a low-nitrogen flower fertilizer when you plant.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Cosmos rarely needs feeding. Skip fertilizer unless your soil is very poor; if you feed at all, use a small dose of a low-nitrogen, bloom-oriented blend, since extra nitrogen costs you flowers.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Good news: cosmos usually needs no fertilizer at all. Only feed if your soil is very poor, and then just a little of a low-nitrogen flower food. Too much feeding means fewer flowers.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: If you feed at all, a low-nitrogen, phosphorus-leaning ratio such as 5-10-10 suits cosmos; avoid balanced or high-nitrogen lawn-type feeds, which drive foliage over bloom.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: The three numbers on fertilizer (N-P-K) are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. If you feed cosmos at all, pick one low in the first number (nitrogen), like 5-10-10, not a high-nitrogen lawn feed.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: None is the right amount for most soils. At most, one light application of a low-nitrogen fertilizer at planting on very poor ground; never feed repeatedly, which favors foliage and lodging over bloom.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: For most gardens, none. At most, one small feeding of a low-nitrogen fertilizer when you plant, and only if the soil is very poor. More than that gives you leaves instead of flowers.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.note_seasoned: Soft-bodied sap-feeders cluster on tender growth and buds and can spread viruses; usually held in check by the beneficial insects cosmos attracts. Hose off or treat with insecticidal soap if populations build.
pests.note_beginner: Tiny soft insects that cluster on new growth and buds. A strong spray of water or insecticidal soap usually handles them, and cosmos draws beneficial insects that eat them.

pests.name: Aster leafhoppers
pests.note_seasoned: Small wedge-shaped hoppers that feed on sap; they matter chiefly as the vector that spreads aster yellows to cosmos and other asters. Control nearby weed hosts, tolerate low numbers, and promptly remove any aster-yellows plants.
pests.note_beginner: Little wedge-shaped hopping insects. On their own they do minor feeding damage, but they spread a serious incurable disease called aster yellows, so keep weeds down nearby and pull out any plants that get it.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.note_seasoned: Fine stippling and bronzing under hot, dry, dusty conditions; raise humidity around foliage with base watering and dislodge with water sprays. Watch container plants in particular.
pests.note_beginner: Very tiny pests that show up in hot, dry, dusty conditions and cause fine pale speckling on leaves. Spraying the leaves with water and keeping plants watered helps.

diseases.name: Aster yellows
diseases.note_seasoned: The signature cosmos disease: a phytoplasma spread by leafhoppers that yellows foliage, stunts and distorts growth, and turns flowers into small, greenish, leaf-like structures, often with witches broom. Cosmos is a named host. There is no cure; remove and destroy infected plants, control leafhoppers, and clear weed hosts.
diseases.note_beginner: A disease spread by leafhoppers that turns leaves yellow, stunts the plant, and makes deformed greenish flowers. It cannot be cured. Pull out and throw away (do not compost) any affected plants, and keep weeds down nearby.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.note_seasoned: A white, powdery coating on foliage, favored by humidity, crowding, and shade. Management is cultural: full sun, generous spacing for airflow, and base watering. Do not compost infected debris.
diseases.note_beginner: A white, powdery coating on the leaves, common in humid weather and crowded plantings. Prevent it with full sun, space between plants for airflow, and watering the soil, not the leaves.

diseases.name: Gray mold (Botrytis)
diseases.note_seasoned: Fuzzy gray mold on faded blooms and foliage in damp, humid, crowded conditions. Deadhead spent flowers, improve airflow, avoid overhead watering, and remove affected tissue.
diseases.note_beginner: A fuzzy gray mold that grows on old flowers and leaves in damp, crowded conditions. Snip off faded blooms, give plants room for air, and keep the leaves dry.

diseases.name: Stem canker
diseases.note_seasoned: Occasional problems: sunken stem lesions (canker) or sudden wilting (bacterial wilt), worse in wet, dense plantings. Remove and destroy affected plants, avoid overwatering and crowding, and rotate the bed.
diseases.note_beginner: Now and then cosmos gets a stem canker (a sunken sore on the stem) or a sudden wilt. Pull and throw away affected plants, avoid overwatering and crowding, and plant somewhere different next year.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Keep soil evenly moist through germination and establishment, then water sparingly; established cosmos is markedly drought-tolerant and resents wet feet. Overwatering, like overfeeding, favors foliage over flower.
watering.frequency_beginner: Keep the soil damp while seeds sprout and young plants get going. After that, water only when the soil is dry, because grown cosmos handles dry spells well and does not like constantly wet soil.
watering.amount_seasoned: A modest amount of water is plenty; roughly half an inch to an inch per week from rain plus irrigation during active growth, less once established. Deep, infrequent watering suits its drought-adapted roots; constant moisture reduces bloom and raises disease risk.
watering.amount_beginner: Cosmos needs only a moderate amount of water, about half an inch to an inch a week counting rain, and less once it is established. Water deeply now and then rather than a little every day.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base and avoid keeping foliage wet; if overhead watering is unavoidable, do it early so leaves dry fast. Dry foliage limits powdery mildew and gray mold.
watering.method_beginner: Water the ground around the plant, not the leaves. If you do get the leaves wet, water in the morning so they dry by midday, which helps prevent disease.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting in wet soil, soft stems, and root or stem rot signal overwatering or poor drainage; lush, dark, flowerless growth also points to too much water and fertility.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If lower leaves yellow, the plant wilts even though the soil is wet, or the base gets soft and mushy, it is getting too much water or the soil drains poorly. Lots of leaves but few flowers is another sign of too much water and food.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Afternoon wilting that recovers by evening and dulling foliage indicate underwatering, most critically during establishment and at first bud; established plants tolerate real drought.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Cosmos that is too dry wilts in the afternoon heat and looks dull. It is thirstiest right after planting and when the first buds form; once established it handles dry spells well.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Water at the base and keep foliage dry; dry leaves are the main cultural lever against powdery mildew and gray mold. Water only when the soil dries, since cosmos is drought-adapted and overwatering reduces bloom.
watering.method_note_beginner: Water the soil, not the leaves, and let the soil dry between waterings. Cosmos likes it on the dry side once established, and dry leaves help prevent disease.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The critical moisture windows are germination and seedling establishment and the onset of budding; after that, ease off, since established cosmos flowers best kept lean and on the dry side.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Keep the soil moist while seeds sprout and when the first buds form. After that, cosmos prefers to be kept on the drier side.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Not applicable: cosmos is grown for cut blooms, not stored as food. Vase-life guidance lives in the notes below.
storage.room_temp_beginner: This does not apply. Cosmos are flowers for a vase, not food to store. See the vase-life tips in the notes.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Not applicable: cosmos is a cut flower, not a refrigerated edible. See vase life in the notes.
storage.fridge_beginner: This does not apply. There is nothing to refrigerate; cosmos are cut flowers, not food. See the notes for keeping blooms fresh.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Not applicable: cosmos is a cut flower and is not frozen for storage. See vase life in the notes.
storage.freezer_beginner: This does not apply. You do not freeze cosmos; they are flowers, not food. See the notes for vase life.
storage.notes_seasoned: Cosmos is a cut flower, not a stored edible, so the refrigerate and freeze fields do not apply. For vase life, cut when buds are just opening, recut stems, strip leaves below the waterline, use clean water, and keep blooms out of direct sun. Expect a fairly short vase life of about 4 to 6 days.
storage.notes_beginner: Cosmos are flowers for a vase, not food to store, so there is nothing to refrigerate or freeze. To keep cut cosmos fresh, cut when the buds are just opening, trim the stem ends, remove any leaves that would sit under water, and use a clean vase. They usually last about 4 to 6 days.

recommended: Sensation series (Cosmos bipinnatus, tall 3 to 4 ft, large single pink, rose, and white blooms; classic cut flower)
Sonata series (Cosmos bipinnatus, dwarf and compact near 18 to 24 in, early, good for beds and containers)
Seashells Mix (Cosmos bipinnatus, fluted, rolled tubular ray petals in pink, rose, and white)
Purity (Cosmos bipinnatus, pure white; a florist and cut-flower staple)
Versailles series (Cosmos bipinnatus, strong straight stems bred for cut-flower production)
Picotee (Cosmos bipinnatus, white petals edged in crimson)
Cosmic series (Cosmos sulphureus, compact 12 to 18 in, semi-double orange, gold, and red; heat-tolerant)
Bright Lights Mix (Cosmos sulphureus, semi-double orange, gold, and scarlet, heat- and humidity-tolerant)
Sunny / Lemon series (Cosmos sulphureus, compact clear yellow to red)
varieties.note_seasoned: The most important choice is species. Garden cosmos (Cosmos bipinnatus) is the tall, airy, feathery-foliage plant with pastel pink, white, and lavender daisies, and it supplies the premier cut-flower series (Sensation, Versailles, Purity, Seashells). Sulphur or orange cosmos (Cosmos sulphureus) is usually shorter and coarser, in hot orange, gold, and red, and takes heat and humidity notably better, so it is the stronger pick for the Deep South and low desert (Cosmic, Bright Lights, Sunny). Dwarf series such as Sonata and Cosmic suit beds and containers; tall types want support and are the best for cutting. Single, open-faced blooms serve pollinators better than dense doubles.
varieties.note_beginner: There are two kinds of cosmos. Garden cosmos is tall with feathery leaves and pink, white, or lavender flowers, and it is the best for cutting (look for Sensation, Purity, or Versailles). Orange cosmos is shorter with orange, gold, and red flowers and handles heat and humidity better, so choose it in hot, humid areas (Cosmic, Bright Lights). For pots and edges pick a dwarf like Sonata or Cosmic. Flat, open, single flowers feed bees and butterflies best.

companions.note_beginner: Cosmos is mostly grown to help the rest of the garden. It is one of the best flowers for bringing in bees, butterflies, and helpful bugs that eat pests, so plant it near vegetables like tomatoes, squash, and beans. One important tip: cosmos blooms best in poor soil, so do not plant it in a rich, well-fed vegetable bed, or you will get tall leafy plants with few flowers. Put it along a leaner edge instead. It also drops seed and comes back on its own, so pull extra seedlings if you do not want more. There is no plant you need to keep it away from.
companions.note_seasoned: Cosmos, like other insectary annuals, is planted to benefit its neighbors rather than the other way around. Both species are strong nectar sources that draw bees, butterflies, and other beneficial insects, and birds feed on the seed heads; sulphur cosmos is an especially noted beneficial-insect plant. Interplant it as a border or insectary strip near fruiting and cucurbit crops to lift pollinator visitation and natural pest control. One cosmos-specific caution: it flowers best in lean soil, so do not plant it inside a richly fertilized vegetable bed, where the extra nitrogen makes it tall, leafy, and flowerless; site it at the drier, leaner edge. It also self-seeds freely, so deadhead or thin volunteers where you do not want a stand. No plant is biologically antagonistic to it.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Tomatoes
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Cosmos draws bees and helpful predator insects that improve pest control near tomatoes.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Tomatoes self-pollinate, so cosmos's pollinator draw does little for the tomato itself; the real benefit is recruiting aphid and hornworm predators (hoverflies, lacewings, parasitic wasps), which nectar-rich aster-family flowers support. likely/medium: mechanism is sound and extension-aligned but not trialed for this specific pairing.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: With tomatoes, cosmos's contribution is beneficial insects rather than pollination, since tomatoes self-pollinate. Its nectar draws hoverflies, lacewings, and parasitic wasps whose larvae prey on aphids and hornworm eggs. Site it at the bed edge as an insectary strip, in leaner soil, and expect predator support and color rather than a direct pollination boost.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Cucurbits (squash, melon, cucumber)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Squash, melons, and cucumbers need insects to move pollen to set fruit, and cosmos brings in the bees that do it.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Cucurbits require insect pollination and cosmos is a documented long-season bee and butterfly magnet, so improved visitation plausibly improves fruit set. likely rather than research_backed because no controlled cosmos-interplant yield trial was located; this is the best-grounded of cosmos's pairings.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: This is cosmos's strongest vegetable pairing: cucurbits depend on insect pollination, their flowers need several bee visits to set well, and cosmos is a reliable, long-blooming pollinator magnet through the fruiting window. More pollinator traffic means better fruit set. Plant it in nearby rows so the bees it pulls in spill onto the crop.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Beans
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Cosmos brings in bees and helpful bugs without competing for food, since beans make their own nitrogen.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Beans are largely self-pollinating, so the benefit is beneficial-predator recruitment; aster-family flowers support these. traditional/medium: real and extension-aligned in principle, indirect and unquantified for beans specifically.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Beans gain mostly from the beneficial insects cosmos brings in. Its nectar supports predators and parasitoids that help manage bean beetles and aphids, and it adds pollinator traffic and habitat with little nutrient competition, since legumes fix their own nitrogen. Keep cosmos to the edges so tall plants do not shade low bush beans.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Corn
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: A traditional pairing: cosmos near corn draws in pollinators and helpful insects.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Corn is wind-pollinated, so cosmos's pollinator benefit does not apply; the only plausible benefit is general beneficial-insect support, which is diffuse for corn. traditional/low: the weakest-grounded of cosmos's pairings.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Corn benefits the least directly, since it is wind-pollinated and gains nothing from added bee traffic. What cosmos offers is general garden-ecosystem support, drawing predators and parasitoids that prey on aphids and caterpillars, plus height and color at the field edge. Treat this as a loose, habitat-level pairing.

good_seasoned.name: Tomatoes
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Interplanted cosmos raises pollinator and beneficial-predator visitation; tomatoes self-pollinate, so the value is aphid and hornworm predator support rather than pollination.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Mechanistic pollinator or beneficial-insect draw grounded in UF/IFAS and UC IPM (cosmos attracts bees and butterflies); not a cosmos-specific interplant yield trial.

good_seasoned.name: Cucurbits (squash, melon, cucumber)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Cucurbits depend on insect pollination for fruit set; cosmos's long-season nectar draws bees into the planting so more flowers set fruit.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Mechanistic pollinator or beneficial-insect draw grounded in UF/IFAS and UC IPM (cosmos attracts bees and butterflies); not a cosmos-specific interplant yield trial.

good_seasoned.name: Beans
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Cosmos adds pollinator and beneficial-insect habitat with low nutrient competition; legumes fix their own nitrogen, so do not over-feed the pairing.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Mechanistic pollinator or beneficial-insect draw grounded in UF/IFAS and UC IPM (cosmos attracts bees and butterflies); not a cosmos-specific interplant yield trial.

good_seasoned.name: Corn
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A classic interplant for pollinator and beneficial draw at the field edge or between rows.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Mechanistic pollinator or beneficial-insect draw grounded in UF/IFAS and UC IPM (cosmos attracts bees and butterflies); not a cosmos-specific interplant yield trial.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Indoor-started transplants need 7 to 10 days of hardening off, with gradually increasing outdoor exposure, before setting out after all frost danger has passed.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: If you started plants indoors, harden them off first: set them outside for a little longer each day over about a week before planting them out.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Cosmos direct-sows readily into warm soil (about 65 °F) at roughly 1/4 in depth and is very successful sown straight into the garden, so direct sowing is the simplest, strongest method. To gain time in short seasons, start indoors about 4 weeks before last frost and transplant after frost. Sow into lean soil in full sun, and pinch young plants at three to four leaf sets to encourage branching.
start_method.notes_beginner: The easiest way is to sow cosmos seeds straight into warm garden soil (about 65 °F) after your last frost, about a quarter inch deep. If your season is short, you can start them indoors about 4 weeks before the last frost and move them outside afterward. Remember to use poor soil, not rich, and pinch the young tops to make them branch.

soil_mix.type_beginner: a potting mix that drains well; nothing rich
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Use a potting mix that drains well, and do not make it rich. If it stays soggy, mix in perlite or coarse sand. Skip heavy, water-holding mixes and added fertilizer.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: free-draining, low-fertility potting mix
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Use a free-draining mix and keep it lean; blend in perlite or coarse sand if it holds too much water. Avoid rich, compost-heavy or moisture-retentive mixes and slow-release feed, which drive foliage over bloom.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out faster than the garden, so check them, but let the top of the soil dry out between waterings. Cosmos does not like soil that stays wet.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Go very easy on fertilizer in pots, or skip it. Too much feeding gives you leaves instead of flowers.

overwintering.approach_beginner: This does not apply. Cosmos is a one-season flower that dies at the first frost, so there is nothing to overwinter. Plant new seeds next year, or let it drop its own.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Not applicable: cosmos is a frost-tender annual grown for a single season and killed by the first frost; it is not overwintered. Re-sow each year, or let it self-seed.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Choose the shorter cosmos types like Sonata, Cosmic, or Sunny for pots. Use a pot with drainage holes, a well-draining mix, full sun, and go easy on water and food. Tall cosmos can be grown in a big deep pot but will need staking and can tip over.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Dwarf and compact series (for example Sonata, Cosmic, Sunny) are the container performers; full sun, a lean free-draining mix, and restrained watering and feeding keep them compact and flowering. Tall garden cosmos is workable in large deep containers but needs support and can get top-heavy.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry faster than beds, so check them, but let the top of the mix dry between waterings; cosmos dislikes constantly wet roots. Water at the base.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Skip or minimize feeding even in containers; if the mix is exhausted, a single very light low-nitrogen feed is plenty. Overfeeding pots gives leaves, not flowers.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering containers are a poor fit for cosmos, which prefers to dry between waterings; if used, keep the reservoir low so the root zone is never constantly wet.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: Self-watering pots are not ideal for cosmos, which likes to dry out a bit between waterings. If you use one, keep the water level low so the soil does not stay wet.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: As an aster-family (Asteraceae) annual, avoid following cosmos immediately with other susceptible asters where aster yellows or foliar disease has built up; rotate the bed to an unrelated family for a season if aster yellows, powdery mildew, or gray mold was heavy.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Cosmos is in the daisy family (Asteraceae). If it had a lot of disease, do not plant it, or other daisy-family flowers, in the same spot the next season. Give the bed a year with a different kind of plant.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotation matters less for a fast, self-seeding ornamental annual than for heavy-feeding vegetables, but clearing infected debris at season end and moving the planting limits carryover of aster yellows host material, powdery mildew, and gray mold. Pull and destroy any aster-yellows plants rather than composting them.
rotation.note_beginner: Rotating cosmos is not as important as it is for vegetables, but it still helps. Clean up old, diseased leaves at the end of the season, and pull and throw away (do not compost) any plants with aster yellows so the problem does not carry over.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seed leaves emerge from warm soil, usually in about 1 to 2 weeks (7 to 21 days).
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The first little leaves push up through the soil in about one to two weeks.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep soil warm (about 65 °F) and evenly moist during emergence; sow shallow, about 1/4 in.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil warm and damp until the seedlings come up.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Seedlings emerged?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your seeds sprouted?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: First true, feathery leaves develop; the plant is small and establishing roots.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Real feathery leaves appear and the little plant starts to settle in.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin or space to 12 to 18 in; do not enrich or fertilize the soil, and water at the base.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Space plants about 12 to 18 inches apart, do not add fertilizer, and water the soil, not the leaves.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Thinned and spaced?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you spaced out your seedlings?

growth_stages.name: Established / vegetative
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Plant grows taller and branches; tall types begin to need support.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant gets bigger and bushier and starts to branch out.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pinch above the third or fourth leaf set to force branching; stake or plant tall types close together.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pinch off the top above the third or fourth set of leaves to make it branch, and give tall plants support.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Plants pinched?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you pinched your cosmos?

growth_stages.name: Budding
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flower buds form at stem tips; stems lengthen toward bloom.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Flower buds start to form at the tops of the stems.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture even at bud point, then ease off; begin scouting for aster leafhoppers, aphids, and mildew.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist as buds form, then water less, and start checking for bugs and mildew.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: First buds visible?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Do you see flower buds yet?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Blooms open continuously; first bloom is roughly 60 to 70 days from sowing and continues to first frost.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Flowers open, about two months after planting, and keep coming until frost.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut and deadhead regularly to drive continuous bloom; cut leggy plants back to 12 to 18 in to force rebloom.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep cutting flowers and removing faded ones; cut tall floppy plants back to get more blooms.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: First bloom open?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Has your first flower opened?

growth_stages.name: Seed saving (optional)
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Selected heads left on the plant dry to brown and set viable seed; cosmos self-seeds readily.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A few flowers left on the plant dry out and form seeds, and cosmos drops seed on its own.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Leave chosen heads to dry fully before collecting; deadhead the rest if you do not want volunteers. Hybrids do not come true.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Let a few flowers dry out fully on the plant before collecting seeds; snip off the others if you do not want them reseeding.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Seed heads drying?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are you saving any seeds?

notifications.body_seasoned: Frost danger has passed. Direct-sow into warm soil (about 65 °F), a quarter inch deep, in a lean, full-sun spot.
notifications.body_beginner: Your last frost has passed, so you can plant cosmos seeds outside once the soil is warm, about a quarter inch deep, in poor soil and full sun.

notifications.body_seasoned: Plants should have three to four leaf sets. Pinch the growing tips to force branching, and stake or plant tall types close.
notifications.body_beginner: Your cosmos should have three to four sets of leaves now. Pinch off the tops so they grow bushier, and support the tall ones.

notifications.body_seasoned: First blooms are opening. Cut and deadhead regularly to drive continuous bloom to first frost.
notifications.body_beginner: Your first flowers are opening. Keep cutting them and snipping off faded ones to get more blooms all season.

notifications.body_seasoned: A first fall frost is forecast within a few days and will end the cosmos season. Cut remaining blooms to enjoy indoors.
notifications.body_beginner: Frost is expected in a few days, which will end your cosmos. Cut the flowers that are left and bring them inside.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost warning
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Cosmos is frost-tender at both ends of the season. Frost will damage or kill plants; cover them or cut blooms before a frost event.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Cosmos cannot survive frost. Cover the plants or cut the flowers before a frosty night, in spring or fall.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Humid, still weather
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Damp, still, humid, crowded conditions drive powdery mildew and gray mold; leafhopper activity spreads aster yellows. Improve airflow, water at the base, and scout closely.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Damp, still, humid weather makes powdery mildew and gray mold more likely, and leafhoppers can spread disease. Keep leaves dry, give plants room for air, and check them often.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot, dry weather ahead
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Cosmos thrives in heat and full sun and tolerates drought; summer is its peak, not a stress period. Keep it lean and on the dry side and avoid the urge to overwater or feed.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Good news: cosmos loves hot, sunny, dry weather. Summer is its best season. Do not overwater or feed it; keep it lean and let it shine.

germination.text_seasoned: Sow after the last frost once soil reaches about 65 °F; cosmos is very successful direct-sown, germinating in about 1 to 2 weeks. Cold, wet soil rots seed.
germination.text_beginner: Plant seeds outside after your last frost, once the soil is warm (about 65 °F). Cosmos grows easily from seed sown right in the ground and sprouts in one to two weeks.

germination.text_seasoned: Sow at about 1/4 in into lean, unimproved soil in full sun; do not amend or fertilize the bed, since richness costs you flowers.
germination.text_beginner: Plant the seeds about a quarter inch deep in poor soil and full sun. Do not add compost or fertilizer, because rich soil gives leaves instead of flowers.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin or space seedlings to 12 to 18 in once they have a few true leaves; airflow limits powdery mildew and gray mold later.
seedling.text_beginner: Once seedlings have a few real leaves, thin them to about 12 to 18 inches apart. Room for air to move helps prevent mildew and mold.

seedling.text_seasoned: Keep soil evenly moist while seedlings establish, watering at the base, then ease off; cosmos is drought-adapted and dislikes constant moisture.
seedling.text_beginner: Keep the soil damp while young plants get going, watering at the base, then let it dry more. Cosmos likes it on the dry side once established.

established.text_seasoned: Pinch the growing tip above about the third or fourth leaf set to force branching; pinched plants make more, sturdier stems.
established.text_beginner: When plants have three to four sets of leaves, pinch off the very top. This makes the plant branch out with more flower stems.

established.text_seasoned: Stake tall garden-cosmos types or plant them close so they support one another; thin, weak stems flop in wind and rain, worse in rich soil.
established.text_beginner: Give tall cosmos support, or plant them close together so they hold each other up. Their thin stems flop over in wind, especially in rich soil.

budding.text_seasoned: Resist feeding and overwatering as buds form; excess nitrogen and moisture push foliage and lodging over bloom. Lean and dry is the rule.
budding.text_beginner: Do not feed or overwater when buds form. Too much food or water gives you leaves and floppy plants instead of flowers.

budding.text_seasoned: Scout for aster leafhoppers and aphids and for early powdery mildew as the canopy closes; promptly remove any aster-yellows plants to protect the rest.
budding.text_beginner: As plants fill in, check for aphids and leafhoppers and for white powdery mildew. Pull out any plant with yellow, distorted growth (aster yellows) right away.

flowering.text_seasoned: Cut and deadhead continuously back to the next leaf or bud to redirect energy from seed set into new flowers, driving bloom from summer to first frost.
flowering.text_beginner: Keep cutting flowers and snipping off faded ones, back to the next set of leaves. This tells the plant to make more flowers instead of seeds, right up to the first frost.

flowering.text_seasoned: If plants grow tall, leggy, and sparse, cut them back to about 12 to 18 in to force a fresh flush of branching and rebloom in roughly a month.
flowering.text_beginner: If plants get tall and floppy with few flowers, cut them back to about 12 to 18 inches. They will bush out and rebloom in about a month.

seed_saving.text_seasoned: Cosmos self-seeds freely; leave some heads to dry fully to brown before collecting seed, and deadhead the rest if you do not want volunteers. Hybrids will not come true.
seed_saving.text_beginner: Cosmos drops seed and comes back on its own. To save seeds, leave a few flowers to dry and turn brown before picking them, and snip the others off if you do not want more plants. Seeds from hybrids will not match the parent.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A single cut-flower cosmos, pinched and cut regularly, yields many airy stems over a season; dwarf bedding types produce more, smaller blooms for color rather than cutting. Vase life is short, so value is in volume and continuous bloom.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: One cutting-type cosmos can give you lots of flowers over the summer if you keep cutting. The short, dwarf types make plenty of small flowers for color rather than for the vase.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Cosmos blooms the first season from seed, typically about 60 to 70 days after sowing, so there is no establishment year; a spring sowing flowers from summer to first frost.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Cosmos flowers the same year you plant it, usually about two months after sowing. There is no waiting year. Plant in spring for flowers from summer until the first frost.
factors_seasoned: Species and cultivar: tall Cosmos bipinnatus supplies long cut stems; Cosmos sulphureus is shorter and more heat-tolerant; dwarf types yield more, smaller blooms.
Soil fertility: lean soil maximizes bloom; rich soil and fertilizer shift yield to foliage.
Cutting and deadheading cadence: frequent cutting drives continuous production; neglected plants set seed and slow.
Pinching and support: pinched, staked plants branch and yield more, sturdier stems than unpinched, unsupported ones.
Season length: a longer frost-free season and successive sowings extend total stem yield into fall.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No T1 evidence supports a moon-phase planting preference for cosmos; left unset.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Tall, leafy plants with few or no flowers
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Plants grew tall and leafy with hardly any flowers
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The classic cosmos failure: soil too rich or too much fertilizer, especially nitrogen, plus overwatering or too much shade, drove foliage at the expense of bloom.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The soil was too rich or fed too much (especially high-nitrogen fertilizer), or the plants got too much water or shade, so they made leaves instead of flowers.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Grow cosmos hard next time: full sun, lean unimproved soil, no fertilizer, and only modest water.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Next time give cosmos full sun and poor soil, do not fertilize, and go easy on water.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Tall plants flopped over
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The plants fell over
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Tall garden-cosmos stems are thin and weak; rich soil, no support, and wind and rain caused lodging.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Tall cosmos has thin, weak stems. Rich soil and no support, plus wind or rain, made them flop over.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Keep soil lean, stake or plant tall types close together for mutual support, or choose dwarf series like Sonata or Cosmic.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Next time use poor soil, give tall plants support or plant them close together, or grow a short type like Sonata or Cosmic.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Yellow, stunted plants with deformed greenish flowers (aster yellows)
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Leaves yellowed and flowers came out deformed and greenish
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Aster yellows, a leafhopper-spread phytoplasma, infected the plants, causing yellowing, stunting, and distorted, leaf-like green flowers, often with witches broom. There is no cure.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: A disease called aster yellows, spread by leafhoppers, infected the plants. It turns leaves yellow, stunts growth, and makes deformed greenish flowers. It cannot be cured.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Remove and destroy infected plants promptly (do not compost), control leafhoppers, and clear nearby weed hosts.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Pull out and throw away any affected plants right away (do not compost), keep weeds down, and watch for leafhoppers.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: White powdery coating on leaves (powdery mildew)
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Leaves got a white, powdery coating
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Powdery mildew took hold, favored by humidity, crowding, and shade.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: A fungus called powdery mildew spread on the leaves. It thrives when plants are crowded, humid, or shaded.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Give plants full sun and generous spacing for airflow, and water at the base rather than overhead.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Next time give plants more room and full sun, and water the soil instead of the leaves.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Plants blackened by frost
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Frost killed or damaged the plants
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Cosmos is frost-tender; frost at either end of the season, planting out too early in spring or the first fall frost, kills or damages plants.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Cosmos cannot handle frost. A late spring frost or the first fall frost will damage or kill it.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sow or transplant only after all frost danger has passed, and expect the season to end with the first fall frost.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant only after your last frost in spring, and know that the first frost in fall ends the cosmos season.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Seeds failed to come up
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Few or no seeds sprouted
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Poor germination usually traces to cold, wet soil, sowing too deep, or the seedbed drying out during emergence.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Cosmos seeds usually fail because the soil was too cold and wet, planted too deep, or dried out before sprouting.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait for warm soil (about 65 °F), sow shallow at about 1/4 in, and keep evenly moist for the first week or two.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Wait for warm soil around 65 °F, plant only about a quarter inch deep, and keep it damp until they sprout.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Sow successively every 2 to 3 weeks from after last frost through midsummer to keep fresh, vigorous stems coming; older plantings decline as the season wears on even with deadheading. There is no heat pause: cosmos thrives through peak summer. Letting a few plants self-seed also renews the stand.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: For flowers all season, plant a new small batch of seeds every 2 to 3 weeks from after the last frost into midsummer. Fresh young plants give the best flowers late in the season, and cosmos loves the heat, so you do not stop for summer.
succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Successive sowing offsets the gradual decline and disease accumulation of older plantings, sustaining stem quality and bloom volume into fall.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: Batch-2 Wave-6 cert (2026-07-06, Trevor-ruled). companion_and_ornamental_flower (Cosmos bipinnatus / sulphureus, annuals -- verified). Agronomy (poor-soil/low-fertility, self-seeding, deadheading, drought) all T1-verified; companion/pollinator honesty EXEMPLARY (provenance-labeled; corn self-flagged as the weakest pairing because it is wind-pollinated); edibility correctly declined (cut flower, not a stored edible). FIXES: softened the beneficial-insect prose -- dropped the specific 'lady beetles / hoverfly larvae / lacewings / parasitic wasps' stated beyond what UF/IFAS + UC IPM support -> 'beneficial insects'; kept the T1-verified bees/butterflies and re-framed the seed-head 'finches' as 'birds' (NCSU-backed); dropped the 'Japanese beetles' pest (on no cited cosmos page); dropped 'bacterial wilt' from the stem-canker disease (unsupported; stem canker kept, NCSU). Companion-provenance blocks left as honestly-labeled inference (verified_against_sources:false).

open_findings.summary: Regional planting windows are modeled from cosmos biology (direct-sow after last frost at soil about 65 F; bloom summer to first fall frost) applied to each zone's frost dates plus the nearest regional T1 anchor; no cosmos-specific regional planting chart was located, so the frost-anchored windows mirror the certified warm-season-annual template (zinnia). Windows are generally safe; tighten at variety-delta pass.
hawaii_tropical year-round is a climate derivation (frost-free zone 11 plus cosmos heat tolerance), not a Hawaii-specific cosmos continuity source; cited to UH CTAHR generally plus UC IPM cosmos.

days_to_maturity [60,90] and first-bloom 60 to 70 days modeled from UF/IFAS ('2 to 3 months after planting') and NCSU; the range spans the two species (C. sulphureus faster, roughly 7 weeks; C. bipinnatus slower). spacing_inches [12,18] modeled toward the low end of NCSU's 12 in to 3 ft width; germination_temp_f [65,75] from NCSU (at least 65 F) and UF/IFAS (70 to 75 F optimal).

Companions are mechanistic/traditional (pollinator plus beneficial-insect draw), not a cosmos-vegetable interplant yield trial; cucurbits is the best-grounded pairing. The cosmos-specific caution (site in lean soil so bed fertility does not cause all-foliage) and the self-seeding note are grounded in the fertility sources.

The overwatering-specifically-reduces-bloom detail is corroborated by University of Illinois Extension (read via WebFetch, not admitted to source_catalog this session); the record cites catalog-present UC IPM ('well drained and not too rich'), NCSU ('poor-soil-tolerant; tolerates drought'), and UF/IFAS ('do not fertilize cosmos, as this can prevent them from producing flowers') for the lean-soil, low-water refit.

Cited source ids are catalog PARENT ids (ncsu_ext, uf_ifas, uc_ipm, umn_ext, and regional anchors) carrying the exact cosmos page URL in anchoring_urls, following the certified-zinnia uc_ipm precedent. Cosmos-topical sub-ids (e.g. ncsu_ext_cosmos_bipinnatus, ncsu_ext_cosmos_sulphureus, uf_ifas_cosmos, uc_ipm_cosmos, uc_ipm_aster_yellows, umn_ext_cosmos) should be minted into source_catalog at certification.

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.synthesis_note: For a head start, cosmos can be started indoors about 4 weeks before the last frost and set out after frost, though direct sowing is usually easier and just as fast.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note: Set transplants or thinned direct-sown plants out after the last frost once soil is warm; space for airflow and support the tall types.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note: First blooms open roughly 60 to 70 days after sowing and continue as plants are cut and deadheaded.

harvest_end.label: primary

3.planting_note: Sow after the last frost once soil is about 65 °F. First blooms open in about 60 to 70 days, then flower until the first fall frost. 3.zone_notes: Zone 3 runs a single frost-bracketed season: plant after the last frost once soil is warm, and cosmos's fast first-bloom leaves weeks to months of flowers before the first fall frost ends the season. Winter is too cold for the tender annual, so the calendar rests then.

northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In the cold northern tier, cosmos is a reliable single-summer annual: its fast first-bloom fits the short frost-bracketed season.
