crops.description_seasoned: Cosmos (Cosmos bipinnatus and Cosmos sulphureus, Asteraceae) is a warm-season, frost-tender annual grown for airy, daisy-like blooms on tall, branching, fine-foliage plants, not for food. Garden cosmos (C. bipinnatus) reaches roughly 3 to 6 ft with pink, white, rose, and lavender flowers; sulphur or orange cosmos (C. sulphureus) is usually shorter, 1 to 3 ft, in hot orange, gold, and red, and takes heat and humidity better. Sown into warm soil after frost, cosmos reaches first bloom in about 60 to 70 days and flowers from summer to the first fall frost. Its defining trait is that it thrives on neglect: lean, low-fertility soil and full sun give the most flowers, while rich soil and fertilizer give lush leaves and few blooms. It is a top pollinator and beneficial-insect plant, a good cut flower, and it self-seeds freely.
crops.description_beginner: Cosmos are easy, airy flowers you grow for blooms, not for eating. There are two kinds: tall garden cosmos with feathery leaves and pink, white, or lavender flowers, and shorter orange cosmos in bright orange, gold, and red that handle heat better. They love full sun and, unusually, they bloom best in poor soil with no fertilizer. Plant the seeds outside after your last frost, once the soil is warm, and you get flowers in about two months that keep coming until the first fall frost. Bees and butterflies love them, they make good cut flowers, and they drop seed and come back on their own.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Cut cosmos for the vase when the buds are just cracking open and showing color, since the flowers continue to open in water. Cut in the cool of the morning into clean water and strip the lower leaves. Cosmos has a fairly short vase life, roughly 4 to 6 days, so cut often and keep the plants deadheaded to drive fresh stems.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Cut cosmos flowers when the buds are just starting to open and show their color; they keep opening in the vase. Cut in the morning, put the stems straight into clean water, and pull off the lower leaves. Cosmos does not last as long as some cut flowers, about 4 to 6 days, so cut them often.
crops.deadheading_seasoned: Deadhead spent blooms back to the next leaf or side bud through the season to redirect energy from seed set into new flowers and sustain bloom to frost. Cutting for the vase does the same job. When plants grow tall and leggy, cut them back to about 12 to 18 in to force a fresh flush of branching and rebloom in roughly a month. Pinch young plants at three to four leaf sets to encourage bushier, better-branched growth.
crops.deadheading_beginner: Deadheading means snipping off flowers once they fade. Do it regularly, cutting the old bloom back to the next set of leaves, and the plant makes more flowers instead of going to seed. Cutting flowers for a vase does the same thing. If plants get tall and floppy with few flowers, cut them back to about 12 to 18 inches and they will bush out and rebloom in about a month.

crops.name: Chamomile
crops.flower_type: single daisy-form, small white rays around a domed golden-yellow center, apple-scented
crops.description_seasoned: Chamomile most often means German chamomile (Matricaria chamomilla, also sold as Matricaria recutita), an easy, quick-growing annual in the Asteraceae family grown for the small white-and-gold daisy flowers used to make a mild, apple-scented tea. It forms erect, branching stems to about 2 ft with fine, ferny foliage, blooms from early to midsummer, and self-seeds so freely that it often returns on its own. It prefers cool conditions and well-drained soil, tolerates poor ground and light frost, and asks for little fertilizer; the open flowers draw bees, hoverflies, and other beneficial insects. A distinct plant, Roman chamomile (Chamaemelum nobile), is a low, mat-forming perennial groundcover used for aromatic chamomile lawns rather than as an upright cutting herb, so choose German chamomile for tea flowers and Roman chamomile for a perennial carpet.
crops.description_beginner: Chamomile is an easy, cheerful herb grown for the little white daisy flowers you dry to make a soft, apple-scented tea. The common garden kind, called German chamomile, is a fast annual that grows about 2 ft tall with feathery leaves, flowers in early to midsummer, and drops seed so it often comes back on its own. It likes cool weather and well-drained soil, does not need rich soil or much fertilizer, and its flowers bring in bees and helpful insects. There is a second, different plant also called chamomile: Roman chamomile, a low, spreading perennial used as a fragrant ground cover or lawn. For tea flowers, grow German chamomile; for a carpet you can walk on, grow Roman chamomile.

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Chamomile is easygoing and grows in most ordinary garden soil as long as water drains away and does not pool. Light, well-drained soil is ideal, and it even does well in poor, sandy ground. Heavy, soggy clay is the one thing to avoid, since wet soil rots the roots, so pick a spot that drains well and only add a little compost if your soil is very thin.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: German chamomile wants well-drained soil and actually thrives in poor, light ground, so it is one of the few flowers that flowers better lean than rich. It grows in sandy to loamy soils and even tolerates clay if drainage is good, but heavy, wet, poorly drained soil is the consistent failure, rotting shallow roots and feeding botrytis and damping-off. Because it is a light feeder that thrives on minimal fertility, skip heavy amendment; the priority is drainage, not richness.

ph.note_beginner: Chamomile is not picky about soil pH (how acidic or alkaline the soil is). Anywhere from about 6.0 to 7.5 is fine, and it even takes slightly alkaline soil, so you usually do not need to change anything.
ph.note_seasoned: Chamomile is broadly adaptable to soil chemistry and performs well across roughly 6.0 to 7.5, leaning if anything toward the neutral-to-slightly-alkaline end (UC Master Gardeners note a slightly alkaline soil is preferred). pH adjustment is rarely warranted; focus on drainage and lean fertility instead.

crops.tip_seasoned: Grow chamomile like an easy cool-season herb: surface-sow the tiny seed and press it in without covering, because light aids germination, into soil around 55°F in early spring (or in fall, and through winter in mild and Mediterranean zones). It sprouts in about 1 to 2 weeks and reaches first bloom in roughly 8 to 10 weeks. Keep fertilizer minimal, water only moderately, and pick the flowers every few days at full open for the best tea. Leave a few late heads to drop seed and it reseeds itself readily.
crops.tip_beginner: Plant chamomile in cool weather. Scatter the tiny seeds on top of the soil and just press them in without covering, because they need light to sprout, in early spring (or fall where winters are mild). They come up in one to two weeks and flower in about eight to ten weeks. Go easy on fertilizer and water, and pick the little daisy flowers every few days when they are fully open to dry for tea. Leave a few flowers at the end to drop seed and it usually comes back on its own.

fertilizer.timing: Little to none; lean soil is fine
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Chamomile is a light feeder that thrives in poor soil and needs little or no supplemental fertilizer. If the ground is very thin, a modest amount of compost at planting is plenty. Excess nitrogen pushes soft, floppy foliage at the expense of flowers and invites aphids and mildew, so favor lean conditions and skip routine feeding.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Chamomile hardly needs feeding and actually does better in poor soil. Mix a little compost in before planting only if your soil is very thin, and otherwise leave it alone. Too much fertilizer, especially the high-nitrogen kind, gives you leaves instead of flowers and more bug and mildew trouble.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Optional: chamomile rarely needs feeding. Only if plants look pale and starved in genuinely poor soil, give one light dose of a balanced fertilizer; otherwise skip it, since lean soil gives the best flowers.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: You can usually skip feeding chamomile. Only if the plants look pale and hungry in poor soil, give one small dose of a balanced fertilizer. Lean soil actually gives you more flowers.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: If you feed at all, a balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 at a light rate is enough; a high-nitrogen lawn-type feed favors foliage over flowers and is the wrong choice for a lean-loving herb like chamomile.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: The three numbers on fertilizer (N-P-K) are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. Chamomile barely needs any, but if you feed, pick a balanced one like 10-10-10 rather than a high first-number (nitrogen) lawn feed, which gives leaves instead of flowers.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: At most a single light application, or a little compost worked in at planting, is sufficient for the season. Avoid repeated feeding; chamomile flowers best on lean soil and gets floppy and pest-prone when overfed.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A little goes a long way, and often none is needed. If you do feed, one light feeding at planting is plenty, and avoid high-nitrogen feeds.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.note_beginner: Tiny green or black soft insects that cluster on new growth and buds, leaving sticky honeydew and curled leaves. Chamomile is otherwise nearly pest-free, and the flowers themselves bring in ladybugs and hoverflies whose young eat aphids. A strong spray of water or insecticidal soap handles a bad patch.
pests.note_seasoned: The one pest chamomile draws with any regularity. Soft-bodied sap-feeders colonize tender tips and buds, secreting honeydew; soft, overfed growth is the most susceptible. Usually held in check by the beneficial predators the flowers recruit, so hose off or treat with insecticidal soap only if populations build, and keep nitrogen low to reduce the lush growth aphids prefer.

pests.name: Thrips
pests.note_beginner: Very slender insects that rasp at flowers and leaves and can leave silvery flecks or distorted blooms, mostly in hot, dry spells. They are a minor issue on chamomile. Keep plants healthy, and a blast of water or insecticidal soap knocks back a heavy patch.
pests.note_seasoned: A minor, occasional pest of the flowers in hot, dry weather, causing stippling and some petal distortion. Rarely damaging enough to treat on a trouble-free herb like chamomile; monitor blooms, and use water sprays or insecticidal soap only if numbers climb. Not specifically documented on the chamomile extension pages, so treated as a general garden-flower pest.

pests.name: Mealybugs
pests.note_beginner: Small, soft, white cottony insects that cluster on stems and leaf joints, mostly on indoor or container plants, leaving sticky honeydew. Uncommon on chamomile outdoors. Dab them off with a cotton swab or treat with insecticidal soap.
pests.note_seasoned: An occasional problem chiefly on container-grown or indoor chamomile, appearing as white, waxy clusters at stem nodes with honeydew and sooty mold. Rare on healthy garden plants; spot-treat with alcohol on a swab or insecticidal soap. Not specifically documented on the chamomile extension pages, so treated as a general container-plant pest.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.note_beginner: A white, powdery film on leaves, most common in crowded plantings and warm, humid, still weather. Chamomile is usually trouble-free, so this shows up mainly when plants are packed together or the air is stagnant. Space plants for airflow, grow in full sun, water at the soil, and remove badly affected growth.
diseases.note_seasoned: The most likely foliar disease on chamomile, favored by crowding, shade, humidity, and overhead wetness, and sharpest as warm, muggy weather sets in. Chamomile is generally disease-free, so cultural control carries it: full sun, generous spacing, base watering, and sanitation. It is worst in the humid heat of a hot-region summer, one reason chamomile is grown in the cooler part of the year there.

diseases.name: Botrytis (gray mold)
diseases.note_beginner: A fuzzy gray mold that rots flowers and stems in cool, damp, crowded conditions, and it can spoil flowers as they dry if they are packed together while still moist. Give plants room for air, water at the base, and dry picked flowers spread out in a single layer.
diseases.note_seasoned: Gray mold, favored by prolonged moisture, dense plantings, and poor airflow, which can blight flowers on the plant and also spoil harvested heads that are piled damp. Manage with spacing, base watering, and prompt, single-layer drying of picked flowers; excess moisture is the driver, so lean, well-drained, airy plantings rarely see it.

diseases.name: Damping-off (seedlings)
diseases.note_beginner: Young seedlings collapse at the soil line and die, caused by cold, wet, poorly drained soil or sowing too thickly. Sow into well-drained soil that is not soggy, do not overwater seedlings, and thin crowded ones so air can move.
diseases.note_seasoned: Seedling collapse from soilborne fungi in cold, wet, poorly drained, or overcrowded conditions, the standing risk when surface-sown chamomile is kept too wet. Prevent rather than treat: well-drained soil, restrained watering, thin stands, and good airflow. Do not sow into cold, waterlogged ground.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Keep soil evenly moist through germination and seedling establishment, then water only moderately; established chamomile is fairly drought-tolerant and prefers to run on the dry side rather than sit wet. Water at the base and avoid wetting foliage and flowers to limit powdery mildew and botrytis.
watering.frequency_beginner: Keep the soil damp while seeds sprout and plants get going, then water only when the top inch is dry. Grown-up chamomile handles dry spells well and hates soggy soil, so err on the dry side. Water the soil, not the leaves.
watering.amount_seasoned: Aim for light, regular watering during establishment, then taper to only what keeps plants from wilting; roughly half to one inch per week from rain plus irrigation is usually ample, and less in cool weather. Let the surface dry between waterings.
watering.amount_beginner: Chamomile needs less water than most flowers. Water seedlings to keep them going, then give established plants a deep drink only when the soil has dried out on top. About half an inch to an inch a week, counting rain, is plenty.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base with drip or a soaker hose and keep foliage and flowers dry; overhead wetting in warm, humid weather invites powdery mildew and botrytis. If you must sprinkle, do it in the morning so plants dry fast.
watering.method_beginner: Water the ground around the plant, not the leaves or flowers. A soaker hose or a watering can at the base works best, since dry leaves resist mildew. If leaves get wet, water in the morning so they dry by midday.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting despite wet soil, soft rotting stems, and gray mold on flowers signal overwatering or poor drainage; persistently wet foliage also raises powdery-mildew and damping-off pressure.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If lower leaves yellow, the plant wilts even though the soil is wet, or the base and flowers look soft or moldy, you are likely overwatering or the soil drains poorly.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting in the day's warmth, dull, grayish foliage, and fewer, smaller flowers indicate underwatering, most critically during germination and establishment; mature plants tolerate short dry spells well.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Chamomile that is too dry wilts in the warmth of the day, looks dull, and makes fewer flowers. It is thirstiest while seeds sprout and plants are young; older plants shrug off short dry spells.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Water at the base and keep water off the foliage and flowers; dry, well-spaced plants are the main cultural lever against powdery mildew and botrytis. Avoid overhead sprinkling in warm, humid weather.
watering.method_note_beginner: Water the soil around the plant, not the leaves or flowers. A soaker hose or a can at the base works best, because dry, airy plants resist mildew and mold.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The critical moisture window is germination and seedling establishment; surface-sown seed must not dry out while sprouting. Once established, chamomile needs little water and resents excess, which risks rot and mildew.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The most important time to keep the soil evenly moist is while the seeds sprout and the seedlings are young. After that, chamomile needs little water, and too much causes rot and mildew.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Not a stored staple: chamomile is grown for its flowers, which are dried for tea. Fresh-picked heads are best used or dried the day they are picked; they do not hold at room temperature. See the notes for drying flowers for long-term storage.
storage.room_temp_beginner: This does not really apply. Chamomile is a flower you dry, not food to store on the counter. Use the flowers fresh or dry them right after picking. See the notes for how to dry them.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Fresh flowers keep only a day or two loosely covered in the refrigerator and are best dried promptly instead. See the notes for drying.
storage.fridge_beginner: You can hold fresh flowers in the fridge for a day or two, but they are best dried right away. See the notes.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Chamomile is not frozen for storage. To keep flowers long term, dry them rather than freeze. See the notes.
storage.freezer_beginner: Do not freeze chamomile. To store the flowers, dry them instead. See the notes.
storage.notes_seasoned: Chamomile is grown for tea flowers, a pollinator draw, and a traditional companion, so the refrigerate and freeze fields do not apply as for produce. Pick the flowers when they are just fully open, ideally on a dry morning, snipping or stripping only the heads. Dry them promptly, spread in a single layer on a screen out of direct sun with good airflow, and handle gently so they do not discolor or heat; a few days of air-drying is usual. Store the dried flowers airtight, away from light, for tea. Use only unsprayed flowers. A safety note: chamomile is in the daisy (Asteraceae) family, and NC State cautions it can cause allergic skin reactions or oral swelling in people who are allergic to ragweed and related plants, so anyone with a ragweed or daisy allergy should be cautious with chamomile.
storage.notes_beginner: Chamomile is a flower you dry for tea, not a vegetable to store. Pick the little daisy flowers when they are fully open, best on a dry morning, taking just the flower heads. Spread them out in a single layer on a screen or tray in an airy, shaded spot and let them air-dry for a few days, then keep the dried flowers in a sealed jar out of the light. Only use flowers that have not been sprayed. One safety note: chamomile is a daisy-family plant, and people who are allergic to ragweed or daisies can react to it, so be careful with chamomile tea if you have those allergies.

recommended: German chamomile (Matricaria chamomilla / recutita): the common annual tea chamomile; erect to about 2 ft, self-seeding
'Bodegold' (German): an upright strain that blooms a few weeks earlier and heavier, with larger flowers, good for tea and easy picking
'Bona' (German): a productive strain grown for tea flowers
Roman chamomile (Chamaemelum nobile): a distinct low, mat-forming perennial groundcover, not an upright tea annual
'Treneague' (Roman): a non-flowering perennial selection grown as a fragrant chamomile lawn
'Flore Pleno' (Roman): a perennial with showy double, cream-white flowers
varieties.note_seasoned: The most important variety choice is which species you want. For tea flowers, grow German chamomile (Matricaria chamomilla), the erect, self-seeding annual; named strains such as 'Bodegold' (upright, earlier and heavier bloom, easy to pick) and 'Bona' (bred for oil content) are selections of it. Roman chamomile (Chamaemelum nobile) is a separate low-growing perennial used as a fragrant groundcover or lawn, not as a cutting herb: 'Treneague' is a non-flowering clone grown for chamomile lawns, and 'Flore Pleno' bears double cream flowers. German chamomile comes readily from seed and self-sows; Roman selections are usually set from plants or divisions.
varieties.note_beginner: First decide which chamomile you want. For tea, grow German chamomile, the tall annual with lots of little daisy flowers; 'Bodegold' is a popular type that flowers early and heavily and is easy to pick. Roman chamomile is a different, low, spreading perennial used as a scented ground cover or lawn, not for cutting: 'Treneague' makes a no-mow chamomile lawn because it barely flowers, and 'Flore Pleno' has pretty double cream flowers. German chamomile grows easily from seed and reseeds itself; the Roman kinds are usually bought as small plants.

companions.note_beginner: Chamomile is a classic, easygoing companion flower. Its open flowers bring in bees, hoverflies, and other helpful insects, and gardeners have long planted it near cabbage-family crops, onions, and herbs, where tradition says it improves their vigor and flavor (a nice old belief, though not something studies have proven). It asks for little, self-sows, and there is no plant you must keep it away from; just give it sun and room, and pair it with other cool-season crops. Do not let it reseed into beds where you do not want volunteers.
companions.note_seasoned: Chamomile's best-grounded companion value is pollinator and beneficial-insect support: its open, apple-scented flowers draw bees, hoverflies, and other predators of aphids, so it earns a place as an insectary planting. It also carries a deep well of traditional companion lore, especially as a good neighbor to brassicas, onions, and other herbs and as a general garden tonic (the old name 'the plant's physician'); that tradition is worth passing along but is not formally trialed. As an easy, self-seeding annual it slots naturally among cool-season vegetables and herbs. There is no biologically antagonistic companion to avoid; the main caution is its prolific self-seeding, so site it where volunteers are welcome.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Bees and beneficial insects (insectary planting)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Chamomile flowers a long time and brings in bees and helpful bugs like hoverflies and ladybugs. Their young eat aphids, so a patch or border of chamomile helps the whole garden.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Extension sources document chamomile's open flowers as attractive to bees and butterflies and note the beneficial insects it draws; the benefit to neighboring crops is well-grounded but inferred rather than directly trialed.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Chamomile's best-grounded companion function. Its open, apple-scented flowers recruit bees and aphid predators (hoverflies, lacewings, lady beetles), supporting biological control nearby. Plant it as an insectary edge or interplant; this is a habitat benefit, not a documented pest-repellent effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Brassicas, onions, and herbs (traditional companion)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Gardeners have long planted chamomile next to cabbage-family crops, onions, and other herbs, saying it helps them grow better and taste better. It is a lovely old tradition, not something proven, but chamomile is a harmless, pretty neighbor that also feeds pollinators.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: A long-standing companion tradition (chamomile as a tonic for brassicas, onions, and herbs) with a plausible pollinator and beneficial-insect mechanism but no formal trial support; framed as tradition.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional companion pairing. Folk practice places chamomile beside brassicas, onions, and herbs as a vigor-and-flavor tonic (the 'plant's physician' lore). The defensible part is the pollinator and beneficial-insect habitat it adds; the direct vigor claim is traditional, not trialed, so grow it for habitat and color rather than a promised yield effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Cool-season vegetables and herbs (habitat companion)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Chamomile grows in the same cool weather as many vegetables and herbs, so it makes an easy, colorful companion that adds flowers and pollinators without crowding them. Keep it to edges so its reseeding does not take over.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Chamomile shares the cool-season niche and adds beneficial-insect and pollinator habitat with low competition; a sensible companion tradition rather than a trial-backed yield effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A cool-season habitat pairing. Chamomile occupies the same mild-weather window as many vegetables and herbs, adding pollinator and beneficial-insect habitat and color with low nutrient competition on lean soil. Keep it to edges and manage its self-seeding so volunteers do not crowd the crop.

good_seasoned.name: Bees and beneficial insects (insectary planting)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Open, apple-scented flowers recruit bees and aphid predators (hoverflies, lacewings, lady beetles), supporting biological control nearby. A habitat benefit, planted as an insectary edge.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Extension documents chamomile flowers as attractive to bees and butterflies; the neighbor benefit is inferred from that, not directly trialed.

good_seasoned.name: Brassicas, onions, and herbs (traditional companion)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Folk practice places chamomile beside brassicas, onions, and herbs as a vigor-and-flavor tonic; the defensible part is the pollinator and beneficial-insect habitat it adds. A sound habitat mechanism but a traditional, not trialed, tactic.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: A recognized companion tradition with a plausible pollinator mechanism; the direct vigor benefit is traditional practice, not formally trialed.

good_seasoned.name: Cool-season vegetables and herbs (habitat companion)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Shares the cool-season niche of many vegetables and herbs, adding pollinator and beneficial-insect habitat and color with low competition on lean soil; keep to edges and manage self-seeding.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: A sensible cool-season companion tradition; the habitat and pollinator benefit is defensible, the yield effect is not trialed.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Indoor-started transplants need about a week of hardening off before setting out. Move chamomile out young: it resents transplanting once it is more than a couple of inches tall, so set out small plants. Seedlings tolerate light frost, so they can go out around the last spring frost.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: If you started plants indoors, harden them off first: set them outside for a little longer each day over about a week. Move chamomile out while it is still small (under a couple of inches), because bigger plants do not transplant well. It handles light frost, so it can go out around your last frost.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Chamomile is easiest direct-sown: scatter the fine seed on the surface of cool soil (around 55°F) and press it in without covering, since light aids germination. It sprouts in about 1 to 2 weeks and self-thins little, so thin to 8 to 12 in. To gain time in short-season areas, start indoors about 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant while seedlings are small, because larger plants transplant poorly. Sowing in fall lets it overwinter and reseed in mild zones.
start_method.notes_beginner: The easiest way is to scatter chamomile seeds right on top of cool garden soil (about 55°F) and just press them in, without covering, because the seeds need light to sprout. They come up in one to two weeks. For a head start, sow indoors about 4 to 6 weeks before your last frost and move the young plants out while they are still small, since big plants do not transplant well.

soil_mix.type_beginner: regular potting mix that drains well
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Use a potting mix that drains freely. If it stays soggy, mix in perlite or coarse sand. Chamomile likes lean soil, so you do not need much compost. Good drainage matters more than richness.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: free-draining, low-fertility potting mix
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: A free-draining mix is the priority; blend in perlite or coarse sand if the base mix holds too much water. Keep fertility low, since chamomile flowers best lean and gets floppy in rich mix. Avoid heavy, water-retentive mixes that keep roots wet.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out faster than the garden, so check them, but let chamomile dry out a bit between waterings and never sit soggy. Water when the top inch feels dry and let the extra drain away. Try not to wet the leaves.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Potting mix has little food, so a very light feeding once or twice during bloom is plenty for potted chamomile. Go easy, since too much fertilizer gives leaves instead of flowers.

overwintering.approach_beginner: This does not really apply. German chamomile is a one-season annual. In cold areas the first hard freeze ends it; in mild-winter areas a fall sowing can grow through winter. Either way it usually drops seed and reseeds itself, so new plants appear on their own.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Not applicable as a managed overwintering: German chamomile is an annual. In cold zones a hard freeze ends the planting; in mild and Mediterranean zones a fall sowing overwinters and blooms in the cool season. It self-sows freely, so volunteers appear without overwintering the parent. (Roman chamomile, a separate perennial, does overwinter, but it is a different plant.)

container_notes.notes_beginner: Chamomile grows fine in a roomy pot with drainage holes, a well-draining mix, and full sun, though its airy, upright form is a bit loose for tidy containers. Keep pots from staying soggy, feed lightly, and grow it for the cool seasons rather than the peak of summer heat.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Chamomile is container-workable but not a natural container specimen: the erect, branching habit is loose, so give it a wide pot, full sun, and a free-draining, low-fertility mix. It rots in cold, saturated pots, so let the mix dry between waterings. Containers are useful for keeping the fine-seeded plant where you can watch it and for growing it in the cool shoulders rather than midsummer heat.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry faster than ground beds, so check them, but let the mix dry between waterings; chamomile resents constant wetness, which rots roots and feeds mold. Water at the base to keep foliage dry.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Potting mixes carry little fertility, but chamomile needs little; a single light feeding through the bloom season is enough. Keep nitrogen modest to favor flowers over floppy foliage.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering containers are a poor fit for chamomile, which wants to dry between waterings; a constantly moist reservoir keeps the root zone too wet and invites rot and mildew. A free-draining pot you water by hand is better.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: Self-watering pots are not ideal for chamomile, because it likes to dry out a little between waterings. A regular pot with drainage holes that you water yourself works better.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: As an aster-family (Asteraceae) annual, avoid following chamomile immediately with other susceptible asters in the same bed where powdery mildew or botrytis built up; rotate to an unrelated family for a season if disease was heavy, and clear infected debris at season end. Chamomile self-sows freely, so volunteers may appear regardless of rotation.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Chamomile is in the daisy family (Asteraceae). If it had a lot of mildew or mold, do not plant it, or other daisy-family flowers, in the same spot the very next season, and clean up the old plants. Note that chamomile drops seed and often comes back on its own.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotation matters less for a fast, lean-loving annual herb than for heavy-feeding vegetables, but moving chamomile to a fresh bed and clearing infected debris limits carryover of powdery mildew and botrytis. Because it self-seeds so readily, expect volunteers, and thin or relocate them to keep airflow and to stop it colonizing beds you want for other crops.
rotation.note_beginner: Rotating chamomile is not as important as it is for vegetables, but it helps. Plant it in a different spot each year if you can, and clean up old, diseased plants at the end of the season. Chamomile reseeds itself heavily, so you will often get new plants popping up on their own.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tiny seed leaves emerge from cool soil within roughly 1 to 2 weeks; the fine seed is surface-sown, because light aids germination, so it must not be buried.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The first tiny leaves appear in one to two weeks. The seeds sit on the soil surface, since they need light to sprout.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Surface-sow onto soil near 55°F and press in without covering; keep the surface evenly moist until seedlings appear.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Scatter the seeds on top of the soil, press them in, and do not cover them. Keep the surface damp until they sprout.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Seedlings emerged?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your seeds sprouted?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fine, ferny true leaves develop on a small plant that establishes quickly in cool weather.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Feathery real leaves appear and the little plant starts to settle in.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin to 8 to 12 in for airflow; water at the base and watch for aphids and damping-off in damp weather.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Thin plants to about 8 to 12 inches apart and water the soil, not the leaves.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Thinned and spaced?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you thinned your seedlings?

growth_stages.name: Established / vegetative
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Plant grows bushier and branches into erect stems to about 2 ft; a quick grower in cool conditions.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant gets taller and bushier, branching into upright stems.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pinch the growing tip once for bushier plants; keep fertilizer minimal so plants stay sturdy rather than soft and floppy.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pinch off the top once to make the plant branch out, and go easy on fertilizer.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Plants established and pinched?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are your plants filling in?

growth_stages.name: Budding
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small flower buds form at stem tips; first bloom is roughly 8 to 10 weeks from sowing.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Little flower buds start to form at the tops of the stems.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture even but not wet; begin scouting for aphids and, in humid weather, powdery mildew.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil lightly moist and start checking for aphids and any white powdery mildew.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: First buds visible?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Do you see flower buds yet?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small white-and-gold daisies open in a long, prolific flush from early to midsummer; harvest heads at full open and pick every few days.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Lots of little white daisy flowers open, from early to midsummer, and keep coming.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick flowers when just fully open, ideally on a dry morning, snipping only the heads; frequent picking sustains bloom and holds down self-seeding.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pick the flowers when they are fully open (every few days) to dry for tea. Frequent picking keeps more coming.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: First flowers open?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your first flowers opened?

growth_stages.name: Seed saving / self-sow (optional)
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Heads left on the plant dry and shed abundant fine seed; German chamomile self-sows freely and can become weedy if never picked.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A few flowers left on the plant dry out and drop lots of tiny seeds.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Leave some late heads to dry and self-sow, or collect the fine seed; remove all heads if you want to prevent volunteers.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Leave a few flowers to dry and drop seed for next year, or pick them all if you do not want it spreading.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Seed heads drying?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are you letting some go to seed?

notifications.body_seasoned: Chamomile seedlings tolerate light frost, so you can surface-sow into cool soil around 55°F near the last frost, or sow in fall in mild zones. Press the seed in but do not cover it, since light aids germination.
notifications.body_beginner: You can plant chamomile seeds in cool weather, around your last frost, since the seedlings handle light frost. Scatter the tiny seeds on top and press them in, but do not cover them, because they need light to sprout.

notifications.body_seasoned: Thin chamomile to 8 to 12 in once seedlings have a few true leaves; airflow limits powdery mildew and botrytis.
notifications.body_beginner: Thin your chamomile to about 8 to 12 inches apart now so air can move between the plants.

notifications.body_seasoned: First flowers are opening. Pick heads at full open on a dry morning and dry them for tea; pick every few days to sustain bloom and limit self-seeding.
notifications.body_beginner: Your first flowers are opening. Pick them when fully open, every few days, and dry them for tea. Frequent picking keeps more coming.

notifications.title_seasoned: Summer heat and humidity will slow bloom
notifications.body_seasoned: Chamomile prefers cool conditions; in the heat and humidity of a hot-region summer it declines and is prone to powdery mildew and botrytis. In hot regions treat the planting as finishing for summer and resow in fall; in cool-summer regions it carries on to frost.
notifications.body_beginner: Chamomile likes cool weather. In hot, muggy summer areas it slows down and can get mildew or mold. In hot places, let it finish and plant again in fall. In cool-summer places it keeps going until frost.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat and humidity will slow bloom
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot, muggy weather will slow your chamomile
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Chamomile prefers cool conditions and declines in the heat and humidity of a hot-region summer, often with powdery mildew or botrytis. In hot regions, let the planting finish and resow for fall; in cool-summer regions, it runs on to frost with little trouble.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Chamomile likes cool weather. In hot, humid summers it slows down, stops flowering well, and may get mildew or mold. In hot places, plan to replant in fall. In cool-summer places, it keeps going.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Damp weather warning
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Warm, humid, still, or wet weather drives powdery mildew and botrytis on chamomile, especially in crowded stands. Improve airflow, water at the base, and remove badly affected growth; dry picked flowers in a single layer.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Warm, damp, still weather can give chamomile a white powdery mildew or a gray mold. Give plants room for air, water at the soil, and pick off bad growth. Dry picked flowers spread out, not piled up.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost warning
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Chamomile seedlings and plants tolerate light frost, so a light frost is usually no cause for concern; a hard freeze will kill the annual. In cold zones, expect the first hard freeze to end the season.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Chamomile handles light frost fine, so a light frost is usually okay. A hard, deep freeze will kill it. In cold areas, the first hard freeze ends the season.

germination.text_seasoned: Surface-sow chamomile and press the fine seed in without covering; light aids germination, so do not bury it. In cool soil near 55°F seedlings emerge in about 1 to 2 weeks.
germination.text_beginner: Scatter the tiny seeds on top of the soil and press them in, but do not cover them, because chamomile needs light to sprout. In cool soil they come up in one to two weeks.

germination.text_seasoned: Sow into cool soil in early spring (or fall in mild zones); chamomile prefers cool conditions and does not need warm soil to start. Keep the surface evenly moist while the fine seed germinates.
germination.text_beginner: Plant chamomile in cool weather, in early spring (or fall where winters are mild). It does not need warm soil. Just keep the surface damp until the little seeds sprout.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin seedlings to 8 to 12 in once they have a few true leaves; spacing for airflow is the main defense against powdery mildew, botrytis, and damping-off on a stand of fine-seeded chamomile.
seedling.text_beginner: Once seedlings have a few real leaves, thin them to about 8 to 12 inches apart. Room for air to move helps prevent mildew and mold.

seedling.text_seasoned: Do not let surface-sown seedlings dry out, but avoid keeping them soggy; cold, wet, crowded soil causes damping-off. Water at the base and thin promptly.
seedling.text_beginner: Keep young chamomile from drying out, but not soggy, since cold wet soil rots seedlings. Water the soil, not the leaves, and thin crowded ones.

established.text_seasoned: Keep chamomile lean: it thrives in poor soil and flowers best with little or no fertilizer, while rich soil and excess nitrogen make soft, floppy, aphid- and mildew-prone growth.
established.text_beginner: Go easy on food and water. Chamomile actually does better in poor soil, and too much fertilizer gives you floppy leaves and more bugs instead of flowers.

established.text_seasoned: Pinch the growing tip once on young plants to encourage branching and more flowering stems; it also makes the airy, upright plant a little sturdier.
established.text_beginner: Pinch off the top once when the plant is young to make it branch out with more flowering stems.

budding.text_seasoned: As buds form, keep plants in full sun with airflow and water at the base; dry, well-spaced foliage is what keeps powdery mildew and botrytis in check as the weather warms and humidifies.
budding.text_beginner: As buds form, keep chamomile in sun with room around it and water the soil, not the leaves. Dry, airy plants resist mildew and mold.

budding.text_seasoned: Scout buds and tips for aphids and, in warm humid weather, for early powdery mildew; addressing crowding and overhead wetness early limits both on an otherwise trouble-free herb.
budding.text_beginner: As buds form, check the tips for aphids and for any white mildew in warm, damp weather. Catching crowding and wet leaves early keeps both down.

flowering.text_seasoned: Pick heads when just fully open, before the white rays reflex and dry, ideally on a dry morning, snipping only the flower. Picking every few days sustains bloom and, by removing heads, holds down self-seeding.
flowering.text_beginner: Pick the flowers when they are fully open, before the petals start to droop and dry, best on a dry morning. Take just the flower heads, and pick every few days to keep more coming.

flowering.text_seasoned: Dry picked flowers promptly in a single layer on a screen, out of direct sun with good airflow, handling gently to avoid discoloration or heating; store airtight, away from light, for tea. Use only unsprayed flowers.
flowering.text_beginner: Dry the flowers right after picking: spread them in one layer on a screen or tray in an airy, shaded spot for a few days, then keep them in a sealed jar out of the light. Only use flowers you have not sprayed.

seed_saving.text_seasoned: To let chamomile return, leave some late heads to dry and shed seed; it self-sows freely and can become weedy. To prevent volunteers, pick or remove all heads before they mature.
seed_saving.text_beginner: To get chamomile back next year, leave a few flowers on the plant to dry and drop seed. It reseeds itself easily, so pick all the flowers if you do not want it spreading.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A single chamomile plant carries a long, prolific flush of small daisy flowers from early to midsummer, yielding a steady, repeated harvest of tea heads picked every few days. A short row supplies plenty of flowers for home tea; picking often extends the bloom and self-seeding keeps the patch going.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: One chamomile plant makes lots of little flowers over several weeks, and you pick a handful every few days. A short row gives you plenty of flowers to dry for tea, and it keeps blooming the more you pick.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Chamomile blooms the first season from seed, roughly 8 to 10 weeks after sowing, so there is no establishment year; a cool-season sowing flowers through the season and self-sows for the next.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Chamomile flowers the same season you plant it, about eight to ten weeks after sowing. There is no waiting year, and it usually drops seed and comes back on its own.
factors_seasoned: Season fit: chamomile yields most in cool-to-mild weather and declines in the heat and humidity of a hot-region summer, so a long cool shoulder or mild winter maximizes total bloom.
Picking cadence: picking flowers every few days at full open sustains bloom; neglected plants set seed and slow.
Soil fertility: lean soil gives sturdy, floriferous plants, while rich, high-nitrogen soil pushes floppy foliage over flowers.
Spacing and airflow: adequate spacing limits powdery mildew and botrytis and sustains a longer productive life.
Variety: strains such as 'Bodegold' bloom earlier and heavier than the wild type.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No T1 evidence supports a moon-phase planting preference for chamomile; left unset.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Plants declined and stopped flowering in summer heat and humidity
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Chamomile faded when it got hot and muggy
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Chamomile prefers cool conditions; in the heat and humidity of a hot-region summer it declines, stops flowering well, and is prone to powdery mildew and botrytis. This is normal for the annual in a hot climate, not a mistake.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Chamomile likes cool weather. When summer got hot and muggy, it faded and stopped flowering well. That is just how this cool-preferring annual behaves in the heat.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: In hot regions grow chamomile in the cool season, from fall and late-winter sowings, and treat summer as its off-season; in cool-summer regions it runs on to frost.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: In hot areas, plant chamomile in the cool season, fall and late winter, and skip the hot months. In cool-summer areas it keeps going until frost.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: White powdery film or gray mold on leaves and flowers
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Leaves got a white coating or the flowers went moldy
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Powdery mildew or botrytis took hold, favored by crowding, shade, humidity, and overhead or excess moisture; both worsen in warm, muggy weather and on packed stands.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: A white powdery mildew or a gray mold set in, usually because plants were crowded or shaded, the air was humid, or the leaves and flowers stayed wet.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Space plants for airflow, grow in full sun, water at the base, keep soil lean and not soggy, and dry picked flowers in a single layer; grow in the cooler part of the season in hot regions.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Give plants more room and sun, water the soil not the leaves, do not overwater, and dry picked flowers spread out. In hot areas, grow chamomile in cooler weather.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Seedlings collapsed at the soil line
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Young seedlings fell over and died
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Damping-off struck seedlings in cold, wet, poorly drained, or overcrowded soil; surface-sown chamomile kept too wet is the standing risk.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: A rot at the soil line, from cold, soggy, or crowded conditions, killed the young seedlings. Overwatering and thick sowing are the usual causes.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sow into well-drained soil, do not overwater, thin promptly for airflow, and avoid sowing into cold, waterlogged ground.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Sow into soil that drains well, do not keep it soggy, and thin crowded seedlings so air can move.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Plants killed by a hard freeze
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: A hard freeze killed the plants
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Chamomile tolerates light frost but a hard freeze kills the annual; in cold zones the first hard freeze ends the season.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Chamomile handles light frost but not a hard, deep freeze. A hard freeze ended the plants.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Expect cold-zone plantings to end at the first hard freeze; in mild zones a fall sowing can grow through winter, and it usually reseeds.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: In cold areas, know the first hard freeze ends chamomile. In mild-winter areas a fall planting can grow through winter, and it often reseeds.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Sticky, curled tips crawling with aphids
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Tiny bugs and sticky leaves (aphids)
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Aphids colonized soft growth and buds, leaving honeydew; lush, overfed plants are the most susceptible on an otherwise nearly pest-free herb.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Aphids clustered on the new growth and buds and left everything sticky. Soft, overfed plants attract them most.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Hose off aphids or use insecticidal soap, keep nitrogen low to avoid soft growth, and let the beneficials the flowers draw help.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Spray aphids off with water or use insecticidal soap, and go easy on fertilizer. The flowers also bring in ladybugs that eat them.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Seeds failed to come up
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Few or no seeds sprouted
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Usual causes are seed buried too deep (light aids germination, so it must be surface-sown) or the surface drying out; chamomile germinates best pressed into moist soil in the open.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Chamomile seeds did not sprout, usually because they were buried (they need light) or the surface dried out before they came up.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Surface-sow and press in without covering, keep the surface evenly moist during emergence, and sow into cool soil.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Scatter the seeds on top and press them in without covering, keep the surface damp until they sprout, and plant in cool soil.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Chamomile blooms a long time from one sowing and self-sows, so heavy succession is optional, but a fresh sowing every 4 weeks through the cool windows keeps young, vigorous plants coming into flower. There IS a heat pause in hot regions: stop sowing through the hottest, most humid months, when chamomile declines and molds.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: One chamomile sowing flowers for weeks, and it reseeds itself, so you do not have to resow often. If you want a steady supply, sow a small new batch every 4 weeks through the cool season. In hot areas, stop during the hottest months, when chamomile struggles.
succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Successive cool-season sowings keep fresh plants coming into bloom, though chamomile's long single flush and prolific self-seeding make it less succession-dependent than cut-and-come flowers; the hot-region summer gap is a true pause because chamomile declines and molds in heat and humidity.

crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Chamomile is grown for tea flowers, a pollinator draw, and a traditional companion. Harvest the small white-and-gold heads when they are just fully open, before the rays reflex and dry, ideally on a dry morning, snipping or stripping only the flowers. Pick every few days through the bloom to keep flowers coming and to limit self-seeding. Dry the flowers promptly in a single layer for tea, and use only unsprayed blooms.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Chamomile is grown for its little daisy flowers, which you dry for tea. Pick the flowers when they are fully open, before the petals droop and dry, best on a dry morning, taking just the flower heads. Pick every few days to keep more coming. Then dry them spread out in a single layer. Only use flowers that have not been sprayed.
crops.deadheading_seasoned: For chamomile, picking the flowers is the deadheading: removing open heads for tea keeps the plant flowering instead of setting seed and slowing. Pick every few days through the bloom. Leave a few late heads if you want it to self-sow for next year, but remove them if you want to prevent weedy volunteers. Pinch young plants once to force branching and more flowering stems.
crops.deadheading_beginner: Deadheading chamomile just means picking the flowers. Taking the open flowers for tea keeps the plant making more instead of going to seed, so pick every few days. Leave a few flowers at the end if you want it to drop seed and come back, or pick them all if you do not want it spreading. Pinch young plants once to make them bushier.

northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In the northern tier, German chamomile is an easy, frost-tolerant annual sown in spring for bloom from early to midsummer until the first hard freeze. Seedlings tolerate light frost, so it can be surface-sown around the last frost or started indoors and set out young. The cool northern summers suit it well, so it flowers through the warm months in the coldest zones; in the warmer, more humid zones 6 and 7 it can slow in the muggiest midsummer spells and is also grown as a fall crop. It self-sows freely.
northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the cold northern states, chamomile grows in one main season from a spring sowing and flowers from early or midsummer until a hard freeze. It handles light frost, so you can sow it around your last frost. The cool summers suit it, so it flowers all summer in the coldest areas; in warmer zones it may slow in the muggiest heat, and you can also plant it again for fall. It drops seed and often comes back on its own.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note: German chamomile is surface-sown onto cool soil near 55°F and pressed in without covering, because light aids germination. It sprouts in about 1 to 2 weeks. Sow in the cool windows, spring and fall, and through winter in mild and Mediterranean zones.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note: Transplants are set out young into cool soil on the same trigger; chamomile seedlings tolerate light frost, so they can go out around the last spring frost, but move them while small, since larger plants transplant poorly.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note: First bloom about 8 to 10 weeks after sowing; flowers are picked at full open every few days through the bloom.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Bloom ends at the first hard freeze in cold regions, or as the heat and humidity of high summer bring on decline and disease in hot regions.

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.synthesis_note: Optional transplant arm: start indoors about 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost and set out while seedlings are small, since larger chamomile transplants poorly.

plant_out.label: succession
plant_out.synthesis_note: Resow every 4 weeks through the cool windows to keep fresh plants coming into bloom; pause through the hottest months in hot regions.

harvest_start.label: succession
harvest_start.synthesis_note: Each succession blooms about 8 to 10 weeks after its sowing.

harvest_end.label: succession
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Successions end at hard frost or the decline of high summer.

3.zone_notes: Cold short-season zone (USDA 3). Last spring frost around late May, first fall frost around mid-September. Chamomile is surface-sown once soil works in spring, or started indoors in April, for a midsummer bloom that ends at the first hard freeze; the cool summers need no heat gap.

4.zone_notes: Cold zone (USDA 4). Last spring frost around mid-May. A spring sowing or indoor start gives bloom from early summer to the first fall freeze; cool summers let chamomile flower continuously with no heat gap.

5.zone_notes: Zone 5. Last spring frost around late April. Chamomile blooms from early summer into October, taking the light early frosts; summers are mild enough for continuous bloom without a heat gap. It reseeds itself.

6.zone_notes: Zone 6. Last spring frost around mid-April. A spring sowing gives a long bloom from early summer into October; chamomile generally flowers through the moderate summer, slowing only in the hottest, most humid spells.

7.zone_notes: Zone 7 (upper South / mid-Atlantic). Hot, humid midsummer (July to August) slows chamomile, which is grown as a spring and a fall crop bracketing the heat; winters are cold enough that a hard freeze ends the fall planting.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Jul, Aug is skipped for summer heat: German chamomile is a cool-preferring annual that flowers best in the mild parts of the year and declines in the heat and humidity of a hot-region summer, when powdery mildew and botrytis take hold, so in the upper South it is grown in the cool season and skipped through the hottest months. (Montana State University; University of Wisconsin Extension)

se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: Across the Southeast and Gulf, German chamomile is a cool-season annual grown from fall and late-winter sowings for bloom through fall, winter, and spring; it takes the mild winters and light frosts. The hot, humid summer (roughly May through August) ends the season with heat, powdery mildew, and botrytis, so chamomile is skipped in midsummer and resown for fall. It self-sows readily.
se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast and Gulf, plant chamomile in fall and again in late winter for flowers through the cool months. It handles the mild winters and light frosts here. Skip the hot, humid summer, when it fades and gets mildew or mold, and plant again when it cools off in fall.

ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: In California's interior valleys, German chamomile is a cool-season annual: sown in fall and again in late winter, it blooms from late fall through spring in the mild, frost-light winters. ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: On California's cool north coast, mild, foggy summers and frost-light winters give German chamomile a long season: sown from late winter through summer, it blooms from spring into late fall with no real heat gap. It self-sows freely in this gentle climate.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: On California's cool, foggy north coast, chamomile has a long, easy season. Plant from late winter through summer for flowers from spring into late fall. The mild summers mean no real summer break. It often reseeds itself.
