verification_status.verification_log_ref: Batch-2 Wave-6 cert (2026-07-06, Trevor-ruled). companion_and_ornamental_flower. Species correct + verified: German chamomile (Matricaria chamomilla / recutita, annual, the tea type) vs Roman (Chamaemelum nobile, perennial groundcover). Tea use (dried flowers) is T1-sourced (Wisconsin/NCSU/UC MG/Montana/Texas MG); NO calming/sleep/digestive health claim -- the tea is described sensorially only ('mild, apple-scented'), conservative. **SAFETY FIX (Trevor-ruled): ADDED the Asteraceae/ragweed-daisy ALLERGY caution.** The draft carried NO allergy note; its cited NCSU page states chamomile 'can cause allergic skin reactions or oral swelling to those with ragweed allergies' (NCCIH corroborates ragweed/daisy cross-reactivity). Now added to the safety note + NCSU-anchored (ncsu_ext added to storage.sources). FIX: dropped the unsourced 'Bona selected for high essential-oil content' -> 'grown for tea flowers' (Montana only says the cultivar was grown). DTM [60,75] + numeric pH modeled (not on cited pages; disclosed); generic disease entries (powdery mildew/botrytis/damping-off) left as low-severity general herb diseases.

open_findings.summary: GERMINATION REFIT (load-bearing, opposite of the calendula template): German chamomile seed needs LIGHT to germinate and is surface-sown and pressed in without covering (NC State 'seeds need light to germinate, so surface sow and press into the soil'; UW-Madison), whereas the calendula template requires darkness and covering. Every germination-related field (start_method, germination stage, tips, notifications, failure_diagnostics, region direct_sow synthesis) was re-authored to surface-sow. Sowing trigger changed to soil_temp_55f (UC Master Gardeners: plant when soil is above 55 deg).

PER-REGION WINDOWS MODELED: the 10-region / per-zone planting and harvest windows and the summer heat_pause months are modeled on the certified cool-season peers (lettuce-leaf, carrot) and the calendula sibling calendar (same cool-tolerant annual-flower niche), adjusted for chamomile's physiology (cool-preferring but somewhat more heat-tolerant; blooms through northern summers to frost; frost-hardy seedlings; fall-sown cool-season crop in hot regions). No chamomile-specific dated per-region planting chart was available for all 10 regions. Windows are generally safe; tighten exact months at the variety-delta pass.

HEAT_PAUSE basis MODELED to peers: chamomile is more heat-tolerant than calendula, so the warm-region summer heat_pause is placed to match the certified cool-season peers rather than a chamomile-specific per-zone heat table, and its basis leads with chamomile's documented cool preference (Montana State: 'prefers cooler climates') plus heat/humidity disease pressure (powdery mildew, botrytis), not a hard temperature threshold. The pause is retained in the genuinely hot regions to satisfy the cool-season timing guardrail; a chamomile-specific heat boundary would refine the exact pause months.

DTM and pH MODELED: days_to_maturity [60,75] (mid 68, ~8 to 10 weeks to first bloom) is a modeled estimate consistent with Montana State's field note (mid-May transplant flowered early-to-mid July) and NC State/UW 'early to midsummer' bloom, but no cited T1 page publishes a chamomile days-to-first-bloom number. pH preferred [6.0,7.5] / tolerated [5.5,8.0] is modeled from UC Master Gardeners ('slightly alkaline preferred') plus general herb tolerance; no numeric T1 range was found. Neither is contradicted by any source; pin at the variety pass.

SECONDARY PESTS + ROMAN CULTIVARS partly modeled: aphids are documented on chamomile (NC State, UW-Madison); thrips and mealybugs are included as general garden/container-flower pests, NOT specifically documented on the chamomile extension pages read (flagged in-entry). Powdery mildew, botrytis, and seedling damping-off are standard for a moisture-stressed Asteraceae and framed with the T1 cultural guidance, but the specific disease list is horticulturally standard rather than each named on a single read T1 chamomile page. Roman chamomile is confirmed a DISTINCT perennial and the record cites that to uwi_hort (the UW-Madison German-chamomile page explicitly contrasts Roman as a perennial); the NC State Chamaemelum nobile page was read as corroboration but is folded under ncsu_ext. The specific Roman cultivar attributes of 'Treneague' (non-flowering lawn) and 'Flore Pleno' (double) are widely-documented horticultural knowledge, not pinned verbatim to a single read T1 page.

hawaii_tropical is MODELED and flagged MARGINAL: chamomile is heat-limited and tropical lowland Hawaii is warm year-round, so it is treated as a cool, drier-season annual (roughly December-through-March bloom at low elevation, longer in cooler uplands) with a long warm-season heat_pause. No Hawaii-specific chamomile source was readable; the window is a climate inference from the crop's cool-preferring physiology and should be confirmed or refined. SOURCE-ID NOTE: Montana State WARC content is filed under the catalogued id msu_bozeman (Montana State University), anchored to the MSU Western Agricultural Research Center chamomile page; the 'Bodegold' cultivar and warm-climate bloom timing are filed under the catalogued id tamu_agrilife, anchored to the Texas A&M AgriLife Master Gardener 'Bodegold' plant-library page (a Master Gardener source, treated as supporting T1-extension, not load-bearing).

pet_safe.note: German chamomile is a mild irritant that can cause contact dermatitis or oral swelling; the related Roman chamomile is listed by the ASPCA as toxic to cats, dogs, and horses.

crops.name: Sweet Alyssum
crops.flower_type: tiny four-petaled, honey-scented, borne in dense clusters (racemes)

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Sweet alyssum is not fussy about soil as long as it drains well. Average garden soil is fine, and it even tolerates poor, sandy, or gritty ground. What it cannot take is heavy, soggy soil that stays wet, which leads to the stem and root rots that are the main way this plant is lost. Do not overdo the compost or fertilizer, because very rich soil gives you leaves instead of flowers.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Sweet alyssum grows in average, well-drained soil and tolerates poor, sandy, or rocky ground, a nod to its Mediterranean coastal origins. Sharp drainage is the priority: poorly drained, consistently wet soil drives the stem and crown rots that are its chief weakness, and plants decline outright in soggy beds. Avoid over-enriching, since overly fertile soil promotes foliage at the expense of flowers.

ph.note_beginner: Sweet alyssum grows across a wide range of soil pH and does not need special adjustment. A near-neutral soil, roughly 6.0 to 7.0 on the pH scale (a measure of how acidic or alkaline soil is), suits it well, and it tolerates soil somewhat more acidic or more alkaline than that. Getting the drainage right matters far more than the exact pH.
ph.note_seasoned: Sweet alyssum is adaptable on pH, growing in acid, neutral, or mildly alkaline soils; a near-neutral 6.0 to 7.0 is a safe target, with tolerance to either side. No narrow optimum is published for it, so drainage and moderate fertility are the levers that matter, not pH correction.

crops.tip_seasoned: Treat sweet alyssum as a fast, cool-season carpet: surface-sow the seed and barely cover it, since it needs light to germinate, or set out transplants around your last frost. It flowers in 6 to 8 weeks and blooms hardest in the cool of spring and fall, stalling in summer heat. Do not over-fertilize, since rich soil pushes leaves at the expense of flowers, and give it well-drained soil to head off the stem and root rots that are its main weakness. When it looks ragged in the heat, shear it back by a third to a half and it reflushes as the weather cools. Interplant it among vegetables to draw in the hoverflies and parasitic wasps that prey on aphids.
crops.tip_beginner: Sweet alyssum is quick and easy. Scatter the seed on the surface and barely cover it, because it needs light to sprout, or plant small transplants around your last frost. It blooms in about 6 to 8 weeks and flowers best in cool spring and fall weather, slowing down when it gets hot. Do not feed it much, because too much fertilizer gives you leaves instead of flowers, and plant it in soil that drains well so it does not rot. If it gets scraggly in summer, cut it back by about a third and it will flower again once it cools off. Plant some right in your vegetable bed to bring in the good bugs that eat aphids.

fertilizer.timing: Lightly at planting; a light feed to aid recovery after a summer shear
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Sweet alyssum is a light feeder, and overly fertile soil promotes leafy growth at the expense of flowers. A modest dose of a balanced or low-nitrogen fertilizer at planting is plenty; in containers, feed lightly through the season since frequent watering leaches nutrients. A light feeding together with a shearing and water helps heat-stalled plants recover and reflush as it cools.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Sweet alyssum does not need much food, and too much gives you leaves instead of flowers. Mix a little balanced or low-nitrogen fertilizer into the soil at planting. In pots, feed lightly now and then, because watering washes food out. If plants look tired after summer heat, a light feed along with a trim and a good watering helps them flower again as it cools.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time for a light feed. A modest dose of a balanced or low-nitrogen fertilizer supports bloom; skip it if the soil is already rich, since excess feeding pushes foliage over flowers.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: It is a good time to feed your sweet alyssum a little. One light dose of a balanced or low-nitrogen fertilizer is plenty. If your soil is already rich, you can skip it, because too much food means fewer flowers.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: Lean toward a light, balanced or low-nitrogen ratio such as 5-10-5; a high-nitrogen feed drives leafy growth and suppresses the bloom that makes sweet alyssum useful as both an edging and an insectary plant.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: The three numbers on fertilizer (N-P-K) are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. For sweet alyssum, choose a low first-number blend like 5-10-5 rather than a high-nitrogen lawn feed, which would give you leaves instead of flowers.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A light dose worked in at planting is usually all it needs in the ground. If supplementing, use a balanced fertilizer at about half the label rate for annual flowers, and keep nitrogen modest.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A little at planting is usually enough in a garden bed. If you feed again, use about half the amount the package suggests and keep it low-nitrogen.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.note_beginner: Small soft insects that cluster on new growth. Ironically, sweet alyssum is best known for attracting the hoverflies and tiny wasps whose young eat aphids, so light infestations often take care of themselves. A strong spray of water or insecticidal soap handles heavier ones.
pests.note_seasoned: Soft-bodied sap-feeders on tender growth; usually minor on sweet alyssum, whose own draw of syrphid flies and parasitoids tends to suppress them. Hose off or treat with insecticidal soap only if colonies build, and conserve the natural enemies the plant attracts.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.note_beginner: Tiny dark beetles that jump when disturbed and chew small round holes in leaves. Because sweet alyssum is in the cabbage family, it can attract them, especially near cole crops. Floating row cover on seedlings and healthy, vigorous plants usually keep damage cosmetic.
pests.note_seasoned: As a Brassicaceae member, sweet alyssum can host flea beetles, which shot-hole the foliage; damage is usually cosmetic on an established carpet. Protect seedlings with row cover where pressure is high, and note the shared-pest overlap when interplanting near cole crops.

pests.name: Cabbage-family caterpillars
pests.note_beginner: Caterpillars such as cabbage white larvae sometimes chew the leaves. Pick them off, or use a targeted Bt product if there are many.
pests.note_seasoned: Larvae of cabbage whites and related brassica-feeding caterpillars occasionally graze the foliage; usually cosmetic on sweet alyssum. Hand-pick or apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) where populations warrant, and monitor when it is interplanted with cole crops.

pests.name: Slugs and snails
pests.note_beginner: In cool, damp weather these chew ragged holes in the low foliage, mostly at night. Hand-pick after dark, set traps, or use iron-phosphate bait, and clear damp hiding spots near the plants.
pests.note_seasoned: Slugs and snails rasp holes in the low, dense canopy under damp, mild conditions. Reduce harborage, hand-pick at night, and use traps or iron-phosphate baits; pressure is highest in shaded, mulched, irrigated plantings.

diseases.name: Stem, crown, and root rot
diseases.note_beginner: The most common way sweet alyssum is lost. Plants wilt, yellow, and collapse from the base, usually because the soil stayed wet or drained poorly. Plant in well-drained soil, do not overwater, and do not crowd plants into soggy beds.
diseases.note_seasoned: Sweet alyssum's signature weakness: stem and crown/root rots favored by wet, poorly drained soil, which collapse the plant at the base and cause outright decline in soggy beds. Management is cultural, excellent drainage, restrained watering, and airflow; very good drainage is essential for good performance.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.note_beginner: A disease that shows as yellowing above and a grayish fuzz on the underside of leaves, worst in cool, wet, crowded conditions. Space plants for airflow and keep the foliage dry.
diseases.note_seasoned: Cool, wet, crowded conditions favor downy mildew, with yellowing above and sporulation beneath. Manage with spacing for airflow, base watering in the morning, and sanitation of infected debris.

diseases.name: Damping-off
diseases.note_beginner: Seedlings sometimes rot at the soil line and topple over soon after sprouting, usually in cold, wet, overplanted conditions. Sow into a clean, well-draining mix, do not overwater, and give seedlings light and air.
diseases.note_seasoned: A seedling-stage collapse at the soil line driven by cold, saturated, overcrowded conditions and soilborne fungi. Sow thinly into a clean, free-draining medium, avoid overwatering, and provide light and airflow; the same drainage discipline that limits the crown rots limits this.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Keep soil moderately and evenly moist during establishment and active bloom; sweet alyssum is shallow-rooted and does best with consistent moisture, though it tolerates short dry spells once established. Let the surface dry slightly between waterings and avoid keeping the soil saturated, which drives the stem and root rots that are its main weakness.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water to keep the soil evenly moist, but not soggy, while plants are getting started and blooming. Sweet alyssum has shallow roots and likes steady moisture, but it can handle a short dry stretch once it is established. Let the top of the soil dry a little between waterings, and never leave it sitting wet, or it can rot.
watering.amount_seasoned: Aim for roughly one inch of water per week from rain plus irrigation during active growth, enough to keep the root zone moist but never waterlogged. In heat, a little extra water alongside a shearing helps stalled plants push a fresh flush as the weather cools.
watering.amount_beginner: About one inch of water a week, counting rain, is a good target while it is growing and blooming. In hot weather, watering a bit more along with a trim helps it recover and flower again once it cools off.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base in the morning so foliage dries quickly, which limits the downy mildew and rots this crop is prone to in damp, crowded plantings. Drip or a soaker hose is ideal for a dense carpet.
watering.method_beginner: Water the soil in the morning rather than the leaves, so the foliage dries fast. This helps prevent the mildew and rot that can trouble a dense patch of sweet alyssum. A soaker hose or watering at the base works best.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing, wilting despite wet soil, and soft, collapsing stems at the base signal overwatering or poor drainage and the onset of stem and root rot, sweet alyssum's chief weakness.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If the plants yellow, wilt even though the soil is wet, or turn soft and mushy at the base, you are overwatering or the soil drains poorly. That is the start of rot.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting between waterings, dull gray-green foliage, and reduced, short-lived bloom point to underwatering; the shallow root system shows drought stress quickly in wind and warming weather.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Sweet alyssum that is too dry wilts between waterings, looks dull, and makes fewer flowers. Its shallow roots dry out fast, so check it often in wind or as it warms up.
watering.drought_tolerance: Moderate; tolerates short dry spells once established
watering.method_note_seasoned: Water at the base in the morning and keep water off the dense foliage; morning base watering plus good drainage are the main cultural levers against the mildew and rots of a crowded carpet.
watering.method_note_beginner: Water the soil in the morning, not the leaves. Dry foliage and well-drained soil are what keep a thick patch of sweet alyssum healthy. A soaker hose or base watering is best.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The critical moisture windows are germination and establishment of the shallow-rooted seedlings and the recovery flush after a summer shearing; keep moisture steady but never saturated throughout.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The most important times to keep the soil evenly moist are when seeds are sprouting and seedlings are getting started, and right after you cut plants back in summer. Even then, do not let the soil stay soggy.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Not applicable: sweet alyssum is grown for garden effect and for the beneficial insects it draws, not as a stored edible. It can be cut as tiny fragrant sprigs; short cut-flower guidance lives in the notes below.
storage.room_temp_beginner: This does not really apply. Sweet alyssum is a garden flower, not food to store. You can snip tiny fragrant sprigs for a small posy; see the notes for keeping them fresh.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Not applicable as a stored food. Cut sprigs hold a few days if kept cool in water; see the notes for vase-life tips.
storage.fridge_beginner: There is nothing to refrigerate as food. Cut sprigs last a few days in water kept cool. See the notes for keeping them fresh.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Not applicable: sweet alyssum is not frozen or stored as food.
storage.freezer_beginner: This does not apply. You do not freeze or store sweet alyssum as food.
storage.notes_seasoned: Sweet alyssum is a bedding and insectary flower, not a stored crop, so the refrigerate and freeze fields do not apply. The honey-scented sprigs are short-stemmed and suit tiny nosegays; cut in the cool of the morning into clean water, keep them cool and out of direct sun, and expect only a few days of vase life. The plant's real value stays in the garden, where its long bloom feeds hoverflies, tiny wasps, and bees.
storage.notes_beginner: Sweet alyssum is a garden flower, not something you store as food, so there is nothing to refrigerate or freeze. Its little sweet-smelling sprigs are very short, so they make tiny posies rather than tall cut flowers. Cut them in the morning into clean water and keep them cool; they only last a few days. It is most useful left in the garden, where its flowers feed helpful insects.

recommended: Carpet of Snow (classic low white, 3 to 4 in, spreading carpet)
Royal Carpet (1953 All-America Selections, violet-purple, very low at about 3 in)
Snow Crystals (tetraploid, vigorous large white flowers, improved heat tolerance)
Clear Crystal series (large fragrant flowers in white, purple, or lavender-shades, about 6 in)
Easter Bonnet series (early, compact mixed colors, 4 to 10 in)
Aphrodite series (compact, unusual apricot, salmon, lemon, and purple shades)
Snow Princess (sterile vegetative hybrid, very heat-tolerant, blooms through summer, does not self-seed)
Rosie O'Day (1961 All-America Selections, rose-pink, compact)
varieties.note_seasoned: Variety choice mostly trades flower color and heat tolerance. Seed-grown types (Carpet of Snow, Royal Carpet, Rosie O'Day, Easter Bonnet, Clear Crystal) give a low spreading carpet and reseed, but bloom declines in summer heat. The tetraploid Snow Crystals is more vigorous and somewhat more heat- and drought-tolerant. For unbroken bloom through summer, choose sterile vegetative hybrids such as Snow Princess, which are bred for heat and cold tolerance and, being sterile, put all their energy into flowers rather than seed and do not self-sow.
varieties.note_beginner: The main differences between types are color and how well they handle heat. Seed-grown kinds like Carpet of Snow (white) and Royal Carpet (purple) give a low, spreading carpet and reseed themselves, but they slow down in summer heat. If you want flowers all summer long, look for a sterile hybrid like Snow Princess, which is bred to keep blooming in heat and cold. Because it makes no seed, it flowers nonstop but will not come back on its own from dropped seed.

companions.note_beginner: Sweet alyssum is one of the best companion flowers for a vegetable garden. Its sweet, honey-scented flowers pull in helpful insects, hoverflies (also called flower flies), tiny parasitic wasps, lady beetles, and lacewings, whose young feed on aphids and other pests. Planting it as an edging or in strips right among your vegetables, especially aphid-prone crops like lettuce, brassicas, and peppers, gives those good bugs food and a home base so they stick around. It is also a magnet for bees. One thing to know: sweet alyssum is in the cabbage (mustard) family, so it can share a few pests with cabbage-family crops, like flea beetles and cabbage caterpillars; usually its benefits far outweigh that. There is no plant you must keep it away from. Just do not crowd it into soggy soil, where it tends to rot.
companions.note_seasoned: Sweet alyssum's headline role is as an insectary, or companion, plant. Its honey-scented, easily accessible flowers supply nectar and pollen to natural enemies of aphids, syrphid (hover) flies, parasitic wasps, lady beetles, and lacewings, over a long bloom period, and their larvae or broods then prey on pest aphids. This is well documented in commercial agriculture: sweet alyssum is planted in insectary strips in California organic lettuce and broccoli fields to draw syrphid flies for aphid control, and extension and university trials report increased hoverfly and parasitoid abundance and reduced aphid numbers where it is interplanted (the field-level effect is real but context-dependent, so it is best framed as habitat support rather than a guaranteed control). Interplant it as edging or strips among aphid-prone crops. A caveat: as a Brassicaceae member it can host some brassica pests (flea beetles, cabbage caterpillars, aphids), so monitor when interplanting near cole crops. There is no biologically antagonistic companion to avoid; the meaningful caution is siting, since wet, poorly drained beds raise its rot pressure.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Aphid-prone vegetables (lettuce, brassicas, peppers)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Planted as an edging or strip among these crops, sweet alyssum draws in hoverflies and tiny wasps whose young eat aphids, helping keep the pests off your vegetables.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Sweet alyssum is documented in extension and commercial IPM guidance as an insectary plant used in California organic lettuce and broccoli to attract syrphid flies for aphid control. likely/medium: the beneficial-attraction and commercial use are well established, but the home-garden pest-reduction effect is context-dependent rather than guaranteed.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Interplanting sweet alyssum among aphid-prone vegetables provides nectar and pollen that sustain syrphid flies and parasitic wasps whose offspring prey on aphids. Documented in California organic lettuce and broccoli insectary strips; treat as habitat support that tilts the odds, not a guaranteed control.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Fruiting crops and tunnels (strawberry, cucurbits, tomatoes)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Sweet alyssum planted alongside fruiting crops brings in the same helpful insects; in one university trial, strawberries grown with it had far fewer aphids.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: A Purdue high-tunnel trial reported more parasitoid wasps and syrphid flies and lower strawberry aphid numbers where sweet alyssum was interplanted, while noting causation could not be proven. likely/low: promising and university-sourced, but a single-setting observation.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: In a Purdue high-tunnel study, interplanted sweet alyssum increased parasitoid wasp and syrphid fly abundance and coincided with markedly lower aphid populations on strawberry, though the authors note causation was not established. A supportive, context-limited pairing.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Bees, butterflies, and general pollinators
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: The honey-scented flowers bloom over a long season and are a favorite of bees and butterflies, adding pollinator traffic to the whole garden.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Multiple extension sources describe the honey-scented flowers as very attractive to bees, flower flies, small wasps, and butterflies. likely/medium: the pollinator attraction is well documented; the garden-wide benefit is diffuse.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Sweet alyssum's honey-scented flowers are described across extension sources as very attractive to bees, flower flies, stingless wasps, and butterflies over a long bloom period, making it a broad pollinator and beneficial-insect nectary. Habitat and ecosystem support rather than a targeted companion effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Cool-season bedding partners (snapdragons, dianthus, calendula, cool greens)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: These all like the same cool weather and low, tidy habit, so they make an easy, good-looking edging or bed together.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: A shared-culture bedding and edging combination for cool-season color. traditional/low: a sound and common design pairing, not a measured biological one.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Snapdragons, dianthus, calendula, and cool-season greens share sweet alyssum's cool-season culture and low, front-of-bed habit, making them natural bedding and edging partners. The pairing is cultural and aesthetic; site all of them for drainage and airflow.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Indoor-grown or purchased transplants need about 7 to 10 days of hardening off before setting out. Sweet alyssum tolerates cool weather and light frost well, so hardening is mainly about adjusting seedlings to wind and direct sun.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: If you started or bought plants grown under cover, harden them off first: set them outside for a little longer each day over about a week. Sweet alyssum handles cool weather and light frost, so this is mostly to get it used to wind and full sun.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Sweet alyssum is easily direct-sown and is often the simplest path: surface-sow and barely cover the seed, since it needs light to germinate, on cool, moist soil around the last frost, and it flowers in roughly 6 to 8 weeks. For a head start, sow indoors about 5 to 6 weeks before set-out, pressing seed onto the surface under light, and transplant around the last frost. In mild-winter regions, sow in fall for winter and spring bloom. Do not bury the seed. Deadhead or shear rather than pinch, and leave a few plants to self-sow.
start_method.notes_beginner: The easiest way is to sow sweet alyssum right where you want it: scatter the seed on cool, moist soil and barely cover it, because it needs light to sprout, around your last frost. It flowers in about 6 to 8 weeks. To get a jump on the season, start seed indoors about 5 to 6 weeks early, pressing it onto the surface so light reaches it, and plant out around the last frost. In mild areas, sow in fall for winter and spring flowers. Do not bury the seed, and leave a few plants to drop seed for next year.

soil_mix.type_beginner: regular potting mix that drains well
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Use a potting mix that drains well. Do not add a lot of extra fertilizer, because rich mix gives you leaves instead of flowers. If the mix stays soggy, add perlite or coarse sand.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: general-purpose, free-draining potting mix
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: A free-draining mix is the priority given sweet alyssum's rot susceptibility; blend in perlite or coarse sand if the base mix holds water. Keep added fertility modest, since overly rich mix favors foliage over bloom.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots, window boxes, and baskets dry out faster than the ground, especially in wind, so check them often. Water when the top inch feels dry and let the extra drain out the bottom; do not let the pot stay soggy.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Frequent watering washes food out of pots, so feed potted sweet alyssum lightly every few weeks during bloom rather than heavily, using a low-nitrogen fertilizer.

overwintering.approach_beginner: In mild-winter areas, sweet alyssum planted in fall keeps blooming through winter and into spring, so containers can carry it over with a sheltered spot during cold snaps. In cold-winter areas, frost eventually kills the plants, but they often drop seed and come back on their own, and you can simply resow.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: In mild-winter zones sweet alyssum is grown as a fall-planted winter annual and containers hold through the cool season; give pots a sheltered spot in hard cold. In cold zones a hard freeze ends the planting, but self-sown seedlings and easy reseeding carry it forward rather than overwintered crowns.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Sweet alyssum is excellent in pots, window boxes, and hanging baskets, where it spills over the edge in a fragrant sheet of bloom right at nose height. Use a container with drainage holes and a well-draining mix, set it in sun with some afternoon shade in hot areas, and do not overcrowd, so air can move and the foliage stays healthy.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Sweet alyssum is a first-rate container, window-box, and basket plant, spilling over the rim as a fragrant carpet. Use free-draining mix and pots with drainage holes, site for sun with afternoon shade in hot climates, and avoid crowding to keep airflow up. Containers dry faster than beds, so check often, and shear heat-tired plants to reflush as it cools.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry faster than ground beds, so check daily in wind or warmth and water when the top inch is dry, letting excess drain freely. Do not let the mix stay saturated; the shallow root system rots in standing wet.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Frequent watering leaches nutrients from containers, so a light feeding every few weeks through the bloom season suits potted sweet alyssum better than a heavy dose, which would push foliage over flowers.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering containers can work only if the surface dries between top-ups; keep the reservoir from saturating the shallow root zone, since constant moisture drives the stem and root rots that are sweet alyssum's main weakness.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot is risky for sweet alyssum unless the top of the soil dries out between waterings. It rots in soil that stays wet all the time, so do not let the reservoir keep the roots soggy.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: As a mustard-family (Brassicaceae) plant, sweet alyssum can share soilborne problems with cole crops, so avoid massing it into beds where brassica clubroot or persistent stem and root rots have built up. Improve drainage and rotate seasonal-color beds before returning it.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Sweet alyssum is in the cabbage family, so avoid planting it where cabbage-family crops had disease problems like clubroot or where soil stayed wet and rotted plants. Fix the drainage and plant something unrelated there first.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotation matters less for a short-season, reseeding cool-season flower than for heavy feeders, but because sweet alyssum is a Brassicaceae member, it is worth keeping it out of beds with a history of brassica clubroot and improving drainage to limit the stem and root rots that are its main disease risk.
rotation.note_beginner: Rotating sweet alyssum is not as important as for vegetables, but since it is a cabbage-family plant, do not put it where cabbage-family crops had disease trouble, and give it well-drained soil. Clean up old, diseased plants so problems do not carry over.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seed leaves (cotyledons) emerge in roughly 7 to 14 days in cool, moist soil (about 60 to 70 °F); seed must sit at or just under the surface, since light aids germination.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The first little leaves appear in about one to two weeks in cool, moist soil, as long as the seed is on or barely under the surface where light can reach it.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Surface-sow and barely cover; keep the surface evenly moist and do not bury the seed, which suppresses germination.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Scatter the seed on the surface and barely cover it, and keep it damp. Do not bury it, or it will not sprout well.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Seedlings emerged?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your seeds sprouted?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: First true leaves develop on small, shallow-rooted seedlings that begin to branch low and spread.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Real leaves appear and the little plants start to branch and spread out low to the ground.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin or space to about 4 to 8 in, water at the base, and watch for damping-off in cold, wet, crowded conditions.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Space plants about 4 to 8 inches apart, water the soil rather than the leaves, and do not keep seedlings soggy, which can rot them.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Thinned and spaced?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you spaced out your seedlings?

growth_stages.name: Established / vegetative
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Plants knit into a low, spreading mound or carpet and begin setting buds as cool weather settles in.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plants fill in into a low carpet and start forming flower buds.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture even and fertility modest (rich soil favors foliage over bloom); no pinching is needed, as it branches on its own.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist and do not over-fertilize, or you get leaves instead of flowers. You do not need to pinch it.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Plants mounding and budding?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Is your alyssum filling in?

growth_stages.name: Budding
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Dense clusters of buds form across the canopy; bloom is imminent, roughly 6 to 8 weeks from sowing.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Lots of tiny buds appear all over and the first flowers are about to open, around 6 to 8 weeks from seed.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture even; scout for slugs and, near cole crops, flea beetles, and watch for soft, rotting stems in wet spells.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist and check for slugs and any soft, rotting stems, plus flea beetles if it is near cabbage-family crops.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: First buds visible?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Do you see flower buds yet?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The plant covers itself in honey-scented bloom through the cool season, drawing hoverflies, small wasps, and bees; flowering slows and plants look ragged in summer heat and revive as it cools.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant covers itself in sweet-smelling flowers all through the cool season and buzzes with helpful insects. It slows down and looks scraggly in summer heat, then bounces back when it cools.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Deadhead or lightly shear to sustain bloom; when heat-tired, shear by a third to a half with water and a light feed to force a reflush; leave a few plants to self-sow.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Trim off old flowers or give the plant a light haircut to keep it blooming. When summer heat wears it out, cut it back by a third to a half, water, and feed lightly to get fresh flowers. Leave a few plants to reseed.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: First bloom open?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Has your first flower opened?

growth_stages.name: Self-seeding (optional)
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Left unsheared late in the season, plants set small seedpods that dry and drop seed; volunteer seedlings appear the following season.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: If you leave some plants alone late in the season, they form little seedpods and drop seed, and new seedlings pop up on their own next year.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Leave a few plants to set and shed seed; note that seed-grown named varieties often revert toward taller, white-flowered plants, and sterile hybrids (Snow Princess) will not self-sow.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Leave a few plants unsheared to drop seed if you want volunteers. The seedlings may not match a fancy variety and often come back white, and sterile hybrids like Snow Princess will not reseed.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Seedpods drying?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are you letting some plants reseed?

notifications.body_seasoned: Sweet alyssum tolerates cool weather and light frost. Surface-sow (barely covering the seed) or set out transplants around your last spring frost in cold zones, or in fall as the heat breaks in mild zones.
notifications.body_beginner: Sweet alyssum likes cool weather and handles light frost. Scatter seed on the surface and barely cover it, or plant transplants, around your last spring frost in cold areas, or in fall once summer heat eases in mild areas.

notifications.title_beginner: Give it a light trim to keep flowers coming
notifications.body_seasoned: Blooming has begun. Deadhead or lightly shear spent flowers to sustain bloom through the cool season; a whole-plant haircut is the easiest way to deadhead such a dense carpet.
notifications.body_beginner: Your sweet alyssum is flowering. Snip off old flowers, or just give the whole plant a light haircut, to keep it blooming through the cool season.

notifications.body_seasoned: The carpet is coming into flower and starting to draw hoverflies, small wasps, and bees. Snip short fragrant sprigs in the cool morning if you want a small posy.
notifications.body_beginner: The flowers are opening and starting to attract helpful insects and bees. Cut short sweet-smelling sprigs in the morning if you want a tiny bouquet.

notifications.body_seasoned: In hot weather sweet alyssum slows, looks ragged, and may stop flowering. Shear plants back by a third to a half with water and a light feed to force a reflush as it cools, or grow a sterile heat-tolerant hybrid for summer bloom.
notifications.body_beginner: As it gets hot, sweet alyssum slows down and looks scraggly. Cut it back by a third to a half, water it, and feed lightly, and it will flower again once it cools. For flowers all summer, grow a heat-tolerant type like Snow Princess.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot weather will stall your sweet alyssum
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Sweet alyssum is a cool-season plant: growth and flowering slow and plants look ragged in summer heat. Give afternoon shade and steady moisture, and shear heat-tired plants to reflush as it cools, or grow a sterile heat-tolerant hybrid.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Sweet alyssum does not like heat. In hot weather it slows down, gets scraggly, and flowers less. Give it afternoon shade and steady water, and trim it back so it flowers again when it cools. Heat-tolerant types like Snow Princess keep going in summer.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Soggy soil can rot sweet alyssum
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Wet, poorly drained soil drives the stem and root rots that are sweet alyssum's chief weakness. Improve drainage, ease off watering, and water only in the morning at the base.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: When the soil stays wet, sweet alyssum can rot at the base. Make sure water drains away, water less, and water in the morning at the soil, not the leaves.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Sweet alyssum handles light frost
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Sweet alyssum tolerates cool weather and light frost and blooms through the cool season; a hard freeze eventually kills the topgrowth, but plants often self-sow and return. No protection is needed for light frosts.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Good news: sweet alyssum takes cool weather and light frost in stride and keeps blooming. A hard freeze will eventually kill it, but it usually drops seed and comes back. You do not need to protect it from light frost.

germination.text_seasoned: Surface-sow sweet alyssum and barely cover the seed, since it needs light to germinate; keep the surface evenly moist at about 60 to 70 °F and expect emergence in 7 to 14 days. Burying the seed is the most common reason it fails to come up.
germination.text_beginner: Scatter sweet alyssum seed on the surface and barely cover it, because it needs light to sprout. Keep the surface damp and it comes up in one to two weeks. Burying the seed too deep is the usual reason it does not sprout.

seedling.text_seasoned: Space seedlings about 4 to 8 in and grow them on cool in a free-draining medium; cold, saturated, crowded conditions invite damping-off, and airflow plus dry foliage are the main defense.
seedling.text_beginner: Give seedlings about 4 to 8 inches of room and keep them in soil that drains well. Cold, soggy, crowded seedlings can rot and topple (damping-off), so do not overwater and let air move between them.

established.text_seasoned: Go easy on fertilizer: overly fertile soil pushes sweet alyssum toward foliage instead of flowers. Put your effort into sharp drainage instead, since wet soil is what triggers the stem and root rots that kill it.
established.text_beginner: Do not over-feed sweet alyssum; rich soil gives you leaves, not flowers. Focus on good drainage instead, because wet soil is what rots it.

budding.text_seasoned: As buds form, scout for slugs in the damp canopy and, if it is interplanted near cole crops, for flea beetles and cabbage caterpillars; because sweet alyssum is a Brassicaceae member it can share these pests, though damage is usually cosmetic.
budding.text_beginner: When buds form, check for slugs in the damp leaves, and for flea beetles or caterpillars if it is next to cabbage-family crops. Sweet alyssum is in the cabbage family, so it can share those pests, but the damage is usually minor.

flowering.text_seasoned: Deadhead or lightly shear through bloom, and when plants stall in heat cut them back by a third to a half with water and a light feed: this is the single biggest lever on a long show, forcing a fresh, compact reflush once nights cool.
flowering.text_beginner: Keep trimming off old flowers, or give the whole plant a light haircut. When summer heat stalls it, cut it back by a third to a half, water, and feed lightly, and it will flower again once nights cool. This is the best way to get a long bloom.

flowering.text_seasoned: Keep some sweet alyssum in continuous bloom right among aphid-prone vegetables: the honey-scented flowers feed syrphid flies and parasitic wasps whose larvae and broods prey on aphids, the same tactic used in California organic lettuce and broccoli insectary strips.
flowering.text_beginner: Keep some sweet alyssum flowering right in your vegetable bed. Its sweet flowers feed hoverflies and tiny wasps whose young eat aphids, the same trick big organic lettuce and broccoli growers use to control pests.

seed_saving.text_seasoned: Leave a few plants unsheared late in the season to set and drop seed, and sweet alyssum reseeds and returns freely, though seed-grown named varieties tend to revert toward taller white forms; sterile hybrids such as Snow Princess make no seed and will not self-sow.
seed_saving.text_beginner: Leave a few plants untrimmed at the end of the season and sweet alyssum will drop seed and come back on its own. The volunteers may be taller and white rather than matching a fancy variety, and sterile types like Snow Princess will not reseed.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A single sweet alyssum plant spreads into a low mat that can carry hundreds of tiny flowers at once over a long cool season, and a few plants quickly knit into a fragrant carpet. Its practical yield is bloom and beneficial-insect habitat rather than a harvest; sterile hybrids bloom longest and heaviest.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: One sweet alyssum plant spreads into a low mat covered in tiny flowers, and a few plants soon form a fragrant carpet. You are growing it for the flowers and the helpful insects they bring, not for a harvest. Heat-tolerant hybrids flower the longest.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Sweet alyssum blooms the first season, roughly 6 to 8 weeks from sowing, so there is no establishment year; a fall sowing in mild zones flowers from fall through spring.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Sweet alyssum flowers the same season you plant it, about 6 to 8 weeks from seed, with no waiting year. A fall sowing in a mild area blooms from fall through spring.
factors_seasoned: Type: sterile heat-tolerant hybrids (Snow Princess) bloom longest and heaviest; seed-grown types are cheaper and reseed but slow in heat.
Deadheading and shearing: a light haircut when plants tire drives a fresh flush and sustains long bloom.
Season length and climate: cool-summer regions bloom spring to frost; hot-summer regions bloom spring and fall around a summer pause; mild-winter regions bloom fall through spring.
Heat: sustained summer heat slows and stalls bloom on seed-grown types until cooler weather returns.
Drainage and fertility: sharp drainage prevents the stem and root rots, and modest fertility favors flowers over foliage.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No T1 evidence supports a moon-phase planting preference for sweet alyssum; left unset.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Plants wilted and collapsed from the base (stem/root rot)
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Plants wilted and rotted at the base
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Stem and root rot, sweet alyssum's most common cause of loss, took hold in wet, poorly drained soil, collapsing the plant at the base.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The plant rotted at the base, usually because the soil stayed too wet or did not drain well.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant in well-drained soil, water in the morning at the base, avoid overwatering and crowding, and improve drainage before replanting.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Next time use well-drained soil, water in the morning at the soil, do not overwater or crowd the plants, and fix soggy spots first.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Plants looked ragged and stopped flowering in summer
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Plants got scraggly and stopped flowering in the heat
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Heat is sweet alyssum's limit: growth and flowering slow and seed-grown plants look ragged in summer, recovering as the weather cools.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: It got too hot. Sweet alyssum slows down and looks scraggly in summer heat, then perks back up when it cools.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Shear heat-tired plants by a third to a half with water and a light feed to force a reflush, give afternoon shade in hot regions, and grow a sterile heat-tolerant hybrid for summer bloom.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Cut heat-tired plants back by a third to a half, water and feed lightly, and give them afternoon shade in hot areas. For flowers all summer, grow a heat-tolerant type like Snow Princess.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Seeds failed to come up
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Few or no seeds sprouted
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Burying the seed is the usual cause: sweet alyssum needs light to germinate, so seed sown too deep, or left to dry out, comes up poorly.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The seed was probably buried too deep or dried out. Sweet alyssum seed needs light and even moisture to sprout.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Surface-sow and barely cover the seed, keep the surface evenly moist at about 60 to 70 °F, and do not let it dry out during germination.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Scatter seed on the surface and barely cover it, keep it damp, and do not bury it. It needs light to sprout.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Lush foliage but few flowers
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Lots of leaves but not many flowers
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Overly fertile soil or heavy feeding, especially high nitrogen, drove leafy growth at the expense of bloom.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Too much fertilizer, especially high-nitrogen feed, gave you leaves instead of flowers.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Feed lightly with a balanced or low-nitrogen fertilizer and avoid over-enriching the soil; sweet alyssum flowers best on modest fertility in full sun.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Feed only a little, with a low-nitrogen fertilizer, and do not over-enrich the soil. Sweet alyssum flowers best with modest food and plenty of sun.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Low foliage chewed full of holes (slugs/snails)
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Something chewed ragged holes in the low leaves
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Slugs and snails rasped holes in the low, dense canopy at night under damp, mild conditions.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Slugs and snails ate the low leaves at night. They thrive in the cool, damp conditions of a dense patch.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Reduce damp harborage, hand-pick at night, and use traps or iron-phosphate baits; press hardest in shaded, mulched, irrigated plantings.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Clear damp hiding spots, pick them off after dark, and use traps or iron-phosphate bait, especially in shady, mulched, watered beds.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Yellow blotches with gray fuzz beneath the leaves (downy mildew)
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Yellow patches with gray fuzz under the leaves
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Downy mildew took hold in cool, wet, crowded conditions, yellowing leaves above with sporulation beneath.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: A disease called downy mildew spread in cool, wet, crowded conditions, making yellow patches with gray fuzz underneath.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Space for airflow, water at the base in the morning, and remove and discard infected foliage.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Give plants more room, water the soil in the morning, and remove leaves that are infected.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Sweet alyssum is fast and reseeding, so it is often a one- or two-window bedding planting rather than a continuously sown crop, but you can stagger sowings every 2 to 3 weeks through the cool season for unbroken fresh bloom and to replace tired or rotted patches. In mild zones that window is fall through spring with a summer heat pause; in cold zones it is spring and again in late summer around a midsummer pause. Anchor sowings to the cool side of the season, since bloom stalls above summer heat.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: Sweet alyssum grows fast and reseeds itself, so many gardeners just plant it once or twice. For nonstop flowers, you can sow a fresh batch every couple of weeks during the cool season. In mild areas that means fall through spring, pausing for summer heat; in cold areas, spring and again in late summer, skipping the hottest part. Keep sowings on the cool side of the year, since it stalls in heat.
succession_policy.count_note_seasoned: Season total is not a fixed cap; it is the per-zone count of staggered sowings the cool-season window supports at a 2-to-3-week cadence, bounded by the summer heat pause and, in cold zones, the winter cold pause. Derived per zone, not sourced.
succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Staggered sowing offsets the decline of heat- and age-tired patches and losses to rot, sustaining fresh bloom and insectary habitat across a long cool season.

open_findings.summary: Per-region planting/bloom windows and the 12-token calendars are modeled on the cool-season frost-bracketed pattern (region+zone frost dates from the shared climate table; summer heat-pause months aligned to certified cool-season peers per the timing guardrail), re-derived for sweet alyssum's direct-sow, fast 6-to-8-week bloom, frost tolerance, and summer heat stall. No crop-specific dated regional alyssum charts were read; held to the generally-safe-now bar. Tighten at the variety pass.

pH preferred set to a modeled near-neutral 6.0 to 7.0 (tolerated 5.5 to 7.8). NCSU documents broad tolerance across acid/neutral/alkaline soils and no source read gives a narrow published optimum, so this is a judgment call; drainage and modest fertility are the real levers.

germination_temp_f [60,70] modeled from the general horticultural range; the extension pages read (Clemson, Wisconsin, UF) emphasize the light requirement and surface sowing but do not all state a temperature. Nearest-source cited; refine if a T1 alyssum germination-temperature figure is found.

fertilizer.npk_ratio 5-10-5 is modeled. Sources (Wisconsin, UF/IFAS) say feed lightly and not heavily, since rich soil favors foliage over flowers, but publish no specific ratio; a light, low-nitrogen blend is the honest reading.

Brassica-family pests (flea beetles, cabbage-family caterpillars) are family-modeled: the T1 pages read describe sweet alyssum as generally trouble-free and beneficial-insect-friendly (UF: 'generally pest free'; NCSU names downy mildew and stem/crown rots), so these entries rest on its Brassicaceae membership rather than an alyssum-specific pest report. Kept low-severity and framed as shared-pest overlap when interplanted near cole crops.

Insectary companion claims are hedged: the syrphid-fly/parasitoid aphid-control role is well documented in extension and commercial IPM guidance (UC ANR, Wisconsin, Purdue high-tunnel trial, Illinois), but the home-garden pest-reduction effect is context-dependent, so companions are labeled likely (low-to-medium confidence) and framed as habitat support rather than guaranteed control.

hawaii_tropical near-year-round bloom assumes cool high-elevation (upcountry) culture; sweet alyssum is a cool-season plant poorly suited to warm tropical lowlands. Modeled as a cool-upland year-round bloomer with two sowing pulses; flagged for the reviewer.

days_to_maturity [45,60] (mid 55) is an approximate seed-to-first-bloom estimate from the widely stated '6 to 8 weeks from sowing' (Wisconsin, Clemson, UF); not a single published DTM. Spacing [4,8] in reflects a carpet planting derived from published width of roughly 6 to 12 in. Refine at the variety-delta pass.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer heat gap (July) in Northern Tier (Cold Zones): sustained summer heat slows and stalls sweet alyssum bloom and the seed-grown plants look ragged, so the crop is not carried through this stretch; growth resumes and plants reflush from a shearing as the weather cools. Warm soil also works against the cool germination this crop needs. Not a frost gap but a summer heat exclusion. (Wisconsin Horticulture; NC State Extension)

northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In the Northern Tier, sweet alyssum is a fast cool-season carpet: sow around the last frost and it flowers in 6 to 8 weeks, blooming from late spring to first frost in the cooler zones and around a short midsummer heat pause in the warmer ones. It tolerates light frost, and while a hard freeze ends the planting, it self-sows and returns. Interplant it among cool-season vegetables to draw hoverflies and parasitic wasps for aphid control.
northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: Up north, sweet alyssum is a quick cool-weather flower. Plant it around your last frost and it blooms in about 6 to 8 weeks, flowering from late spring until the first hard freeze in cool areas, with a short break in midsummer heat in warmer spots. It shrugs off light frost, and even though a hard freeze finishes it, it usually drops seed and comes back. Tuck it in with your vegetables to bring in good bugs that eat aphids.

Plant it in fall or late winter, trim it now and then to freshen it, and keep some flowering near your vegetables all year to bring in helpful insects. It reseeds itself easily.
