description_seasoned: Bee balm (Monarda didyma and the native wild bergamot M. fistulosa) is a hardy herbaceous perennial in the mint family (Lamiaceae), native to North America and grown as a top pollinator and hummingbird plant. Clump-forming and spreading by rhizomes, it sends up 2 to 4 foot, square, aromatic stems topped with shaggy, whorled heads of tubular flowers in red, pink, or lavender through mid to late summer. It is cold-hardy (roughly zones 3 to 9), a premier nectar source for bumblebees, long-tongued bees, butterflies, and ruby-throated hummingbirds, and its minty leaves make Oswego tea. Its defining problem is powdery mildew, so the core care is full sun, airflow through spacing and division, even moisture, and mildew-resistant cultivars.
crops.description_beginner: Bee balm is a hardy perennial flower, meaning it comes back every year, grown mostly to bring bees, butterflies, and especially hummingbirds to your garden. It has shaggy, colorful flower heads in red, pink, or purple on tall stems, and minty-smelling leaves you can dry for tea. It blooms in mid to late summer and is very cold-hardy. It spreads by underground roots, so give it room or grow it in a pot. Its one big problem is powdery mildew, a white powder on the leaves, so plant it in full sun, leave space between plants for air, keep the soil moist, and pick mildew-resistant types.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: For the vase, cut stems when the flowerheads are mostly open, in the cool of the morning, into clean water; deadheading and cutting both prolong bloom. For tea, harvest the aromatic leaves at their best just before the plant blooms, or use the edible flowers, and air-dry them out of direct sun until crisp. Leave a share of blooms uncut for the pollinators and hummingbirds that make bee balm worth growing.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: To cut flowers for a vase, snip stems when most of the little flowers on the head are open, in the morning, and put them straight into clean water. To make tea, pick the minty leaves (best just before the plant flowers) or use the flowers, and dry them out of the sun until crisp. Leave some flowers on the plant for the bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds.
crops.deadheading_seasoned: Deadhead spent flowerheads back to the next leaf node through the bloom season to prolong flowering and limit self-seeding; cutting stems for the vase serves the same purpose. Pinch stem tips once in late spring to force branching for a fuller, more floriferous plant, and cut the whole plant back after bloom and frost for winter.
crops.deadheading_beginner: Deadheading means snipping off flowers once they fade. Do it through the summer, cutting the old bloom back to the next set of leaves, and the plant makes more flowers instead of seeding all over. Cutting flowers for a vase does the same job. Early on, pinch the stem tips once in late spring so the plant grows bushier, and cut the whole plant back after it finishes and frost hits.

crops.name: Viola
crops.flower_type: single five-petaled, flat-faced (pansy and viola form)

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Violas like rich, moist soil that still drains well, with plenty of compost mixed in. The thing to avoid is heavy, soggy ground that stays wet, because wet feet lead to root rot, the most common way these plants are lost.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Violas want a humus-rich, consistently moist but well-drained soil; work in compost before planting. Drainage is the make-or-break factor, since warm, wet, poorly drained soil drives the crown and root rots that are viola's chief weakness. They favor a slightly acidic soil and resent high-alkaline ground.

ph.note_beginner: Violas do best in slightly acidic soil, around 5.4 to 5.8 on the pH scale (a measure of how acidic or alkaline soil is). They dislike high-alkaline soil, where leaves yellow and root rot becomes more likely, so avoid liming the bed for them.
ph.note_seasoned: Viola is happiest in a slightly acidic soil of about 5.4 to 5.8 and tolerates a bit either side of that. High pH is the real risk: alkaline soil triggers iron deficiency and favors black root rot, so do not lime a viola bed and correct genuinely alkaline ground before planting.

crops.tip_seasoned: Treat viola as a cool-season flower: set out frost-tolerant transplants as the heat breaks in fall (mild zones) or in early spring (cold zones), since heat above roughly 75 °F, not cold, is its limit. Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil and water at the base in the morning to head off the crown and root rots that are its main weakness, and deadhead regularly to drive a long bloom. The flowers are edible from pesticide-free plants.
crops.tip_beginner: Violas love cool weather, so plant them when it is cool: in fall once summer heat eases, or in early spring. Heat, not cold, is what stops them. Give them well-drained soil, water in the morning at the soil rather than the leaves so they do not rot, and keep snipping off faded flowers to get more. The flowers are edible if you grow them without bug sprays.

fertilizer.timing: At planting, then in early spring
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Violas are light feeders. Mix a slow-release granular fertilizer into the bed at planting and feed again in early spring; a low-nitrogen, phosphorus-leaning blend such as 5-10-10 suits them. Avoid high-nitrogen fertilizer, which forces soft, leggy growth at the expense of bloom and, in cold weather, stretches the plants.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Violas do not need much food. Mix a slow-release granular fertilizer into the soil when you plant, and feed once more in early spring. Pick a low-nitrogen type like 5-10-10. Too much nitrogen (a high first number) gives you tall, floppy plants with fewer flowers.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time for a light feed. A modest dose of a balanced or low-nitrogen fertilizer now supports steady cool-season bloom; skip it if you mixed slow-release granules into the bed at planting.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: It is a good time to feed your violas a little. One light dose of a balanced or low-nitrogen fertilizer is plenty. If you already mixed slow-release food into the soil when planting, you can skip this.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A low-nitrogen, bloom-leaning ratio such as 5-10-10 suits violas better than a high-nitrogen feed, which stretches them in the cool weather they grow in.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: The three numbers on fertilizer (N-P-K) are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. For violas, choose a low first-number blend like 5-10-10 rather than a high-nitrogen lawn feed.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A slow-release dose worked into the bed at planting plus a second feeding in early spring is usually enough; if supplementing, use a balanced fertilizer at about half the label rate for annual flowers. Keep nitrogen modest to avoid cold-weather stretch.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A little goes a long way. Mix slow-release food in when you plant, then feed once more in early spring. If you feed again, use about half the amount the package suggests, and keep it low-nitrogen.

pests.name: Slugs and snails
pests.note_beginner: Slugs and snails chew ragged holes in viola leaves and flowers, mostly at night and in the cool, damp weather violas love. Hand-pick after dark, set out traps, or use iron-phosphate bait, and clear damp hiding spots near the plants.
pests.note_seasoned: The characteristic cool-season viola pest: slugs and snails rasp holes in foliage and bloom under the damp, mild conditions violas thrive in. Reduce harborage, hand-pick at night, and use traps or iron-phosphate baits; pressure is highest in shaded, mulched, irrigated beds.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.note_beginner: Tiny soft insects that cluster on new growth and buds and can spread viruses. A strong spray of water or insecticidal soap usually handles them.
pests.note_seasoned: Soft-bodied sap-feeders on tender growth and buds; cool-season colonies can build quickly and vector viruses. Hose off or treat with insecticidal soap, and conserve the lady beetles and hoverflies that feed on them.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.note_beginner: Very tiny pests that show up in hot, dry conditions late in the viola season and cause fine speckling on leaves. Spraying leaves with water and keeping plants watered helps.
pests.note_seasoned: Stippling and fine webbing under hot, dry conditions as the season warms; a late-season problem that coincides with the heat decline. Raise humidity with base watering and dislodge with water sprays; rarely worth treating on a fading planting.

pests.name: Foliage-feeding caterpillars
pests.note_beginner: Caterpillars sometimes chew viola leaves and flowers. Pick them off, or use a targeted Bt product if there are many.
pests.note_seasoned: Various caterpillars, including fritillary larvae that favor violets, chew foliage and bloom; usually cosmetic. Hand-pick, or apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) where populations warrant, leaving native fritillary larvae where butterflies are wanted.

diseases.name: Crown and root rot
diseases.note_beginner: The most common way violas are lost. The plant wilts, yellows, and collapses from the base, usually because the soil stayed warm and wet or did not drain well. Plant in well-drained soil, do not overwater, and start with healthy plants.
diseases.note_seasoned: Viola's signature killer: crown and root rots (black root rot from Thielaviopsis, plus Pythium and Phytophthora) favored by warm, wet, poorly drained soil and high pH. Plants wilt and collapse at the base. Management is cultural: excellent drainage, restrained watering, slightly acidic soil, healthy transplants, and rotating beds where rot has built up.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.note_beginner: A disease that shows as yellow blotches on top of leaves with a grayish fuzz underneath, worst in cool, wet weather. Space plants for airflow and keep the leaves dry.
diseases.note_seasoned: Cool, wet conditions favor downy mildew: angular yellow lesions above with sporulation beneath. Manage with spacing for airflow, base watering, morning irrigation, and sanitation of infected debris.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.note_beginner: A white, powdery coating on leaves, more common in crowded plantings. Give plants room for air to move and water the soil, not the leaves.
diseases.note_seasoned: A white fungal coating favored by crowding and moderate temperatures; cosmetic to moderate. Manage with spacing, airflow, and base watering rather than overhead wetting.

diseases.name: Leaf spots and anthracnose
diseases.note_beginner: Brown or dark spots on leaves, worse when leaves stay wet. Keep foliage dry, space plants out, and remove badly spotted leaves.
diseases.note_seasoned: Foliar spotting (including pansy leaf spot and anthracnose) spread by overhead wetness and splash; manage with base watering, spacing, morning irrigation, and sanitation of infected debris.

diseases.name: Gray mold (Botrytis blight)
diseases.note_beginner: A gray, fuzzy mold on faded flowers and damaged leaves in cool, damp weather. Remove spent blooms and dead leaves promptly.
diseases.note_seasoned: Botrytis blight grays and rots spent blooms and senescing tissue under cool, humid, still conditions. Deadhead promptly, improve airflow, and clear debris; it follows neglect of spent flowers.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Keep soil evenly moist; violas have shallow roots and dislike both drought and waterlogging. Water through fall and winter whenever less than about an inch of rain falls in a week, but let the surface dry slightly between waterings to keep the crown rots at bay.
watering.frequency_beginner: Keep the soil evenly damp but never soggy. Violas have shallow roots, so they dry out faster than you might expect, yet they rot if kept wet. Water when the top of the soil starts to dry, and through fall and winter water any week it does not rain much.
watering.amount_seasoned: Aim for roughly one inch of water per week from rain plus irrigation during active growth, applied so the root zone is moist but never saturated. The shallow root system needs steadier moisture than a deep-rooted annual, but standing wet is the rot risk.
watering.amount_beginner: Violas like about one inch of water a week, counting rain. Because their roots are shallow, do not let them bake dry, but do not keep them swimming either. Moist, not soggy, is the goal.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base in the morning so foliage dries by midday; never water in the late afternoon or evening, which leaves foliage and crowns wet overnight and invites disease. Drip or a soaker hose is ideal.
watering.method_beginner: Water the soil around the plant in the morning, not the leaves, and never in the evening. Wet leaves and crowns overnight lead to disease. A soaker hose or watering can at the base works best.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting despite wet soil, and a soft, collapsing crown signal overwatering or poor drainage and the onset of root and crown rot, viola's chief weakness.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If lower leaves yellow, the plant wilts even though the soil is wet, or the base turns soft and mushy, you are overwatering or the soil drains poorly. That is the start of root rot.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting between waterings, dull foliage, and small, short-stemmed blooms point to underwatering; the shallow root system shows drought stress quickly, especially in wind and warming weather.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Violas that are too dry wilt between waterings, look dull, and make small flowers. Their shallow roots dry out fast, so check them often in wind or as it warms up.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Water at the base in the morning and keep water off the foliage and crowns; morning watering and good drainage are the main cultural levers against viola's crown and root rots. Never water in the evening.
watering.method_note_beginner: Water the soil in the morning, not the leaves, and never at night. Dry leaves and well-drained soil are what keep violas from rotting. A soaker hose or base watering is best.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The critical moisture windows are establishment after transplanting and the cool peak-bloom stretch; let the surface dry slightly between waterings throughout to protect the crown.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The most important times to keep the soil evenly moist are right after planting while roots establish and during peak bloom. Even then, let the surface dry a bit between waterings so the base does not rot.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Use viola flowers the day they are picked for the best look and flavor; at room temperature cut blooms wilt within hours. Pick in the cool morning and keep them shaded until use.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Use viola flowers the same day you pick them. Left out at room temperature they wilt within hours, so pick in the morning and keep them in the shade until you need them.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerate freshly picked blooms briefly in a single layer in an airtight container on a slightly damp paper towel; they hold a few days. Wash gently just before use and harvest the day of use for edible purposes.
storage.fridge_beginner: To keep viola flowers a few days, lay them in one layer in a sealed container on a slightly damp paper towel in the fridge. Rinse them gently right before you use them.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Whole blooms freeze well suspended in ice cubes for drinks; candied flowers (brushed with egg white, dusted with fine sugar, air-dried) keep for weeks in an airtight container. Violas are not frozen as a bulk food.
storage.freezer_beginner: You can freeze whole viola flowers inside ice cubes to dress up drinks. You can also candy them: paint with egg white, sprinkle with fine sugar, and let them dry. Candied flowers keep for weeks in a sealed container.
storage.notes_seasoned: Viola, pansy, and Johnny-jump-up flowers are edible, with a mild grassy, faintly wintergreen flavor, and serve as garnish on salads, desserts, and cakes. Eat only flowers grown without pesticides (nursery plants are often treated), harvest the day of use, wash gently, and remove the bitter white heel at the petal base. Dark blooms can briefly tint the tongue.
storage.notes_beginner: Viola and pansy flowers are edible and have a mild, slightly green flavor. They look lovely on salads, cakes, and desserts. Only eat flowers you grew without bug sprays, pick them the day you use them, rinse gently, and pinch off the little white base of the petals, which can taste bitter. Dark flowers may color your tongue for a bit, which is harmless.

recommended: Majestic Giant (large 3 to 4 in pansy blooms, improved heat and cold tolerance)
Matrix / Delta series (large-flowered pansies, uniform, weather-tough bedding)
Sorbet series (Viola cornuta, small abundant blooms, very cold-hardy and longer into warmth)
Cool Wave (trailing/spreading pansy for baskets and overwintering beds)
Icicle pansies (bred for cold, fall-planted to overwinter and rebloom in spring)
Helen Mount / Johnny-jump-up (Viola tricolor, tricolor blooms, freely self-seeds, most heat-tolerant)
Penny series (Viola cornuta, compact, early and weather-resilient)
Panola (pansy x viola, mid-size blooms blending pansy color with viola toughness)
varieties.note_seasoned: Variety choice trades flower size against weather toughness. Large-flowered garden pansies (Majestic Giant, Matrix, Delta) give the biggest blooms but are the least heat-tolerant; violas (Viola cornuta: Sorbet, Penny) carry smaller, more numerous flowers and push later into warmth and harder into cold; Johnny-jump-ups (Viola tricolor) are the toughest and most heat-tolerant and self-seed freely. For overwintering in cold zones, choose cold-bred series such as Icicle or the trailing Cool Wave. Panolas split the difference between pansy size and viola resilience.
varieties.note_beginner: Bigger flowers usually mean less toughness. Large garden pansies (Majestic Giant, Matrix, Delta) have the showiest blooms but fade fastest in heat. Violas (Sorbet, Penny) have smaller, more numerous flowers and handle both cold and early warmth better. Johnny-jump-ups are the hardiest and most heat-tolerant and reseed themselves. If you want flowers to survive winter, look for cold-bred types like Icicle or the trailing Cool Wave.

companions.note_beginner: Violas are mostly grown for cool-season color and edible flowers, and they mix happily with almost anything that likes the same cool weather. Gardeners tuck them under spring bulbs like tulips and daffodils, among cool-season greens such as lettuce and kale, and beside other cool-weather annuals. They also feed early bees when little else is blooming. There is no plant you must keep violas away from. The only real caution is wet soil: do not crowd them into soggy, poorly drained beds, where the crown and root rot that troubles violas spreads.
companions.note_seasoned: Viola's companion role is the cool-season color-and-edible layer rather than a pest-management partner. It underplants spring bulbs for layered early color, interplants among cool-season greens and other cool-weather annuals that share its culture, and offers early-season nectar and pollen plus larval forage for fritillary butterflies. There is no biologically antagonistic companion to avoid; the meaningful caution is siting. Crowding violas into wet, poorly drained, or rot-prone beds raises shared crown and root-rot pressure, so favor drainage and airflow and rotate away from beds where rot has built up.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Spring-flowering bulbs (tulips, daffodils, crocus)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Violas planted over spring bulbs fill the bare ground with color while the bulbs are coming up, then bloom alongside them.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: A long-standing ornamental design pairing (underplanting bulbs with violas for layered cool-season color), not a biological interaction. traditional/low: real and widely practiced, but a look-and-timing benefit, not a measured horticultural one.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Underplanting spring bulbs with violas is a classic layered-color pairing: the violas carpet the bed through fall and winter and bloom with the bulbs in spring. The benefit is ornamental and phenological, not biological, and the two share the same cool-season, well-drained culture.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Cool-season greens (lettuce, kale, spinach)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Violas add edible flowers and color to a bed of cool-season greens, and both grow in the same cool weather and come out when it heats up.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: An edible-bed interplant: violas and cool greens share cool-season culture and harvest windows, and violas add modest early-pollinator forage. likely/low: the shared-culture and dual-edible benefit is real, but no controlled trial measures a yield or pest effect on the greens.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Interplanting violas among cool-season greens pairs two crops on the same cool-season clock: both are set out as the heat breaks and both finish at summer's onset, and the viola flowers are edible alongside the greens. Expect shared culture and a little early-pollinator traffic rather than a documented pest or yield effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Cool-weather annuals (snapdragon, dianthus, sweet alyssum, ornamental kale)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: These all like the same cool weather as violas, so they make an easy, good-looking fall-to-spring bed together.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: A shared-culture bedding combination for fall, winter, and early-spring color. traditional/low: a sound and common design pairing, not a biological one.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Snapdragons, dianthus, sweet alyssum, and ornamental kale share viola's cool-season culture and frost tolerance, making them natural cool-weather bedding partners. The pairing is cultural and aesthetic; site all of them for drainage and airflow.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Early pollinators and butterflies
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Violas bloom early when few other flowers are open, giving bees an early meal, and some butterflies lay eggs on violets.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Violas provide early-season nectar and pollen and Viola species are documented larval host plants for fritillary butterflies. likely/medium: the host-plant relationship and early forage are real and well-established botanically, though the garden-level benefit is diffuse rather than a measured companion effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: As one of the earliest and latest things in bloom, viola supplies nectar and pollen to early-emerging bees, and Viola species are the obligate larval host for fritillary butterflies. Treat this as habitat and ecosystem support: leave some self-sown Johnny-jump-ups where fritillaries are wanted.

good_seasoned.name: Spring-flowering bulbs (tulips, daffodils, crocus)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Violas carpet the bed over dormant and emerging spring bulbs, blooming through the cool months and alongside the bulbs in spring; a layered-color, shared-culture pairing rather than a biological one.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Ornamental underplanting tradition, not a measured interaction.

good_seasoned.name: Cool-season greens (lettuce, kale, spinach)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Shares the cool-season clock with leafy greens (set out as heat breaks, finished by summer) and adds edible flowers plus early-pollinator forage to the bed; cultural pairing, not a documented pest or yield effect.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Shared cool-season culture plus dual-edible bed; mechanistic, not trialed.

good_seasoned.name: Cool-weather annuals (snapdragon, dianthus, sweet alyssum, ornamental kale)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Frost-tolerant, cool-season bedding partners on viola's culture and schedule; an aesthetic and cultural pairing. Site all for drainage and airflow.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Shared-culture cool-season bedding combination.

good_seasoned.name: Early pollinators and butterflies
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Supplies early-season nectar and pollen to bees and is the larval host for fritillary butterflies; habitat support rather than a targeted companion effect.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Early forage plus the documented Viola-fritillary host relationship; botanically established, garden-level benefit diffuse.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Indoor-grown or purchased transplants need 7 to 10 days of hardening off before setting out, though viola transplants tolerate cool and light frost well, so the process is mainly about adjusting to wind and direct sun.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: If you started or bought plants grown under cover, harden them off first: set them outside for a little longer each day over about a week. Violas handle cold easily, so this is mostly to get them used to wind and full sun.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Viola is most often set out as transplants, since seed-to-bloom runs roughly 10 to 14 weeks and the seed needs cool, dark conditions (about 65 to 75 °F) that summer soil cannot give. Start indoors 6 to 8 weeks ahead in cells, kept cool and covered to exclude light, then transplant once the weather is cool: late summer for fall and winter bloom in mild zones, early spring for spring bloom in cold ones. Direct sowing works in mild climates when soil is cool. Do not pinch; deadhead instead to drive bloom.
start_method.notes_beginner: The easiest path is to buy or start transplants, because viola seed takes 10 to 14 weeks to bloom and needs cool, dark soil to sprout, which summer cannot provide. Start seed indoors 6 to 8 weeks ahead, kept cool and covered so it is dark, then plant out when the weather is cool: late summer in mild areas for fall and winter flowers, or early spring in cold areas. You can sow straight in the ground where the soil is cool. Do not pinch the tops; just remove old flowers to keep them blooming.

soil_mix.type_beginner: regular potting mix that drains well
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Use a potting mix that drains well, with a little compost mixed in. If it stays soggy, add perlite or coarse sand. Avoid heavy mixes that hold water, since violas rot in wet soil.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: general-purpose, free-draining potting mix
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: A free-draining mix is the priority given viola's rot susceptibility; blend in perlite or coarse sand if the base mix holds water, plus modest compost for fertility. Avoid heavy, water-retentive mixes.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots and window boxes dry out faster than the ground, especially in wind, so check them often. Water when the top inch feels dry and let the extra drain out the bottom; do not let the pot stay soggy.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Frequent watering washes food out of pots, so feed potted violas lightly every few weeks during bloom with a low-nitrogen fertilizer rather than once.

overwintering.approach_beginner: In mild areas, violas planted in fall keep going through winter and bloom again in spring, which is their whole appeal. Mulch beds with straw or evergreen boughs, and move or protect containers when a hard freeze below about 25 °F is coming. Watering plants before a freeze helps them come through it.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Viola is overwintered on purpose in mild zones: fall-planted beds, mulched with straw or evergreen boughs, hold through winter and rebloom in spring. Containers are more exposed and want protection below about 25 °F; hydrating plants before a hard freeze improves survival. In the coldest zones, snow cover and the hardier violas and Johnny-jump-ups are what carry crowns through winter.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Violas are excellent in pots, window boxes, and hanging baskets, where their cool-season color sits right at eye level. Use a container with drainage holes and a well-draining mix, set it where it gets morning sun, and do not cram too many plants in, so air can move and the leaves stay healthy.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Violas are first-rate container, window-box, and basket plants; trailing types such as Cool Wave spill nicely. Use free-draining mix and pots with drainage holes, site for morning sun, and avoid crowding to keep airflow up and the crown rots down. Containers dry and freeze faster than beds, so adjust watering and protect them in hard freezes.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry faster than ground beds, so check daily in wind or warmth and water when the top inch is dry, letting excess drain freely. Do not let the mix stay saturated; the shallow viola root system rots in standing wet.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Frequent watering leaches nutrients from containers, so a light feeding every few weeks with a low-nitrogen fertilizer through the bloom season suits potted violas better than a single dose.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering containers can work for violas only if the surface dries between top-ups; keep the reservoir from saturating the shallow root zone, since constant moisture drives the crown and root rots that are viola's main weakness.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot is risky for violas unless the top of the soil dries out between waterings. Violas rot in soil that stays wet all the time, so do not let the reservoir keep the roots soggy.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Avoid replanting violas into a bed where crown or root rot (black root rot, Pythium, Phytophthora) built up the previous season, since these soilborne rots persist. Rotate seasonal-color beds to an unrelated planting and improve drainage before returning violas.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Do not put violas back in the same spot if they rotted there last season. The fungi that cause root rot stay in the soil, so plant something different there, fix the drainage, and come back to violas later.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotation matters less for a short-season cool-weather flower than for heavy feeders, but moving violas to a fresh, well-drained bed and clearing infected debris limits carryover of the crown and root rots that are their main disease risk.
rotation.note_beginner: Rotating violas is not as important as for vegetables, but it still helps. Plant them in a different, well-drained spot if rot was a problem, and clean up old, diseased leaves at the end of the season so it does not carry over.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seed leaves (cotyledons) emerge in roughly 10 to 14 days in cool soil (about 65 to 75 °F); seed must be covered to exclude light.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The first little leaves push up in about a week and a half, as long as the soil is cool and the seed is covered to keep it dark.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep the medium cool, evenly moist, and dark until emergence; warm soil inhibits germination.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil cool, damp, and covered until the seedlings come up. Warm soil keeps the seeds from sprouting.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Seedlings emerged?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your seeds sprouted?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: First true leaves develop; the plant is small and establishing a shallow root system.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Real leaves appear and the little plant starts to settle in.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Grow on cool; thin or space to 6 to 10 in and water at the base to keep foliage and crown dry.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep them cool, space plants about 6 to 10 inches apart, and water the soil, not the leaves.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Thinned and spaced?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you spaced out your seedlings?

growth_stages.name: Established / vegetative
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Plant fills out into a low mound and begins setting buds as cool weather settles in.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant gets bushier and starts forming flower buds.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Maintain even moisture and airflow; do not pinch (violas branch on their own). Begin deadheading as bloom starts.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist with room for air to move. You do not need to pinch violas. Start removing faded flowers as they bloom.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Plants mounding and budding?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are your violas filling out?

growth_stages.name: Budding
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flower buds form on short stems; bloom is imminent in cool weather.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Flower buds appear and the first flowers are about to open.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture even; scout for slugs and aphids and for crown rot in wet, warm spells.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist and check for slugs, aphids, and any soft, rotting stems.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: First buds visible?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Do you see flower buds yet?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Blooms open continuously through the cool season, slowing only in hard cold and ending when sustained heat above roughly 75 °F arrives.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Flowers open and keep coming all through the cool weather, stopping only when it gets hot.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Deadhead regularly to extend bloom; shear leggy plants by a third in warming weather; pick edible flowers the day of use.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep removing faded flowers to get more. Cut back floppy plants by a third as it warms. Pick flowers to eat the same day you use them.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: First bloom open?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Has your first flower opened?

growth_stages.name: Seed saving (optional)
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Capsules left on the plant dry and split, ejecting seed; Johnny-jump-ups self-sow freely from these.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Seed pods dry out and pop open. Johnny-jump-ups drop their own seed and come back on their own.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Leave a few capsules to dry and collect before they shatter; expect hybrids not to come true, while Johnny-jump-ups reseed reliably.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Leave a few seed pods to dry and gather the seed before they burst. Fancy hybrids will not look the same next year, but Johnny-jump-ups reseed true enough.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Seed capsules drying?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are you saving any seeds?

notifications.body_seasoned: Violas tolerate frost, so set transplants out in cool weather: about three weeks before the last spring frost in cold zones, or as summer heat breaks in fall for mild zones.
notifications.body_beginner: Violas handle frost, so you can plant them in cool weather: a few weeks before your last spring frost in cold areas, or in fall once the summer heat eases in mild areas.

notifications.body_seasoned: Blooming has begun. Remove faded flowers before they set seed to extend the bloom period through the cool season.
notifications.body_beginner: Your violas are flowering. Pinch off the old, faded flowers before they make seeds, and the plants will keep blooming much longer.

notifications.body_seasoned: Pick blooms in the cool morning for the vase or the plate; for edible use, harvest the day of use and only from pesticide-free plants.
notifications.body_beginner: Pick flowers in the morning. If you want to eat them, pick them the same day and only use violas grown without bug sprays.

notifications.body_seasoned: Sustained heat above roughly 75 °F fades and stretches violas. Give afternoon shade and steady moisture to stretch the show, or pull and replace tired plants as the cool season ends.
notifications.body_beginner: As it warms up, violas fade and get leggy. Give them afternoon shade and keep them watered to keep them going a bit longer, or pull them out and plant something for summer.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot weather will stress your violas
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Unlike summer flowers, violas decline in heat: sustained temperatures above roughly 75 °F fade blooms and stretch plants. Provide afternoon shade and steady moisture, or expect the cool-season show to end.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Violas do not like heat. When it gets warm, they get pale and floppy and stop flowering. Give them afternoon shade and keep the soil moist, or know the cool-season show is ending.

weather_triggers.action: Warm, wet soil raises rot risk
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Warm, soggy soil can rot violas
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Warm, wet, poorly drained soil drives the crown and root rots that are viola's chief weakness. Improve drainage, ease off watering, and water only in the morning at the base.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: When the soil is warm and stays wet, violas can rot at the base. Make sure water drains away, water less, and water in the morning at the soil, not the leaves.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Violas handle frost and light snow
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Good news: violas are frost-hardy and bloom any time it is above freezing, shrugging off frost and light snow. Hydrate plants before a hard freeze below about 25 °F, and mulch beds.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Good news: violas love the cold. They keep blooming above freezing and bounce back from frost and light snow. Just water them before a hard freeze and mulch the bed.

germination.text_seasoned: Sow into cool soil (about 65 to 75 °F) and cover the seed to exclude light; warm soil and light both inhibit viola germination, which is why seed is started in late summer under cover rather than direct-sown into warm beds.
germination.text_beginner: Plant viola seed in cool soil, around 65 to 75 °F, and cover it so it stays dark. Warm soil and light both keep the seeds from sprouting, so they are usually started indoors in late summer.

seedling.text_seasoned: Grow seedlings on cool and space them 6 to 10 in for airflow; cool, airy conditions and dry foliage are the main defense against the leaf diseases and crown rots violas are prone to.
seedling.text_beginner: Keep young plants cool and give them 6 to 10 inches of space so air moves between them. Cool, airy conditions and dry leaves help prevent the rots and leaf diseases violas can get.

established.text_seasoned: Do not pinch violas; they branch and mound on their own. Focus instead on drainage and morning base watering, since warm, wet soil is what triggers the crown and root rot that kills them.
established.text_beginner: You do not need to pinch violas; they fill out by themselves. Put your effort into good drainage and watering in the morning at the soil, because wet soil is what rots them.

budding.text_seasoned: As buds form, scout for slugs and snails in the cool, damp canopy and for soft, collapsing crowns in any warm, wet spell; catching both early prevents the two most common viola losses.
budding.text_beginner: When buds form, check for slugs and snails in the damp leaves and for any soft, rotting stems at the base, especially in warm wet weather. Catching them early saves the plants.

flowering.text_seasoned: Deadhead continuously: removing spent flowers before they set seed redirects energy into new bloom and is the single biggest lever on a long cool-season show, from fall through winter and spring in mild zones.
flowering.text_beginner: Keep snipping off faded flowers before they make seeds. This tells the plant to make more flowers and is the best way to get a long bloom, all through fall, winter, and spring in mild areas.

flowering.text_seasoned: For edible blooms, pick the day of use from pesticide-free plants, wash gently, and remove the bitter white heel at the petal base; the mild grassy flavor suits salads, desserts, candying, and ice cubes.
flowering.text_beginner: To eat the flowers, pick them the day you use them from plants grown without bug sprays, rinse gently, and pinch off the little white base. They have a mild flavor and look great on salads, cakes, and in ice cubes.

seed_saving.text_seasoned: Let a few capsules dry on Johnny-jump-ups (Viola tricolor) and they will reseed and naturalize freely; collect seed before the capsules shatter if you want to sow it deliberately, and expect hybrid pansies not to come true.
seed_saving.text_beginner: Leave a few seed pods on Johnny-jump-ups and they will drop seed and come back on their own. Gather seed before the pods pop if you want to plant it yourself. Fancy hybrid pansies will not grow back the same.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A single viola or pansy, deadheaded through the cool season, yields a steady succession of blooms over months; smaller-flowered violas and Johnny-jump-ups produce the most flowers, while large-flowered pansies give fewer, bigger blooms.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: One viola or pansy plant gives you flowers steadily for months if you keep removing the faded ones. The small-flowered violas and Johnny-jump-ups make the most flowers; the big pansies make fewer, larger ones.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Violas bloom the first season from seed or transplant, roughly 10 to 14 weeks from sowing, so there is no establishment year; a fall planting flowers from fall through spring in mild zones.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Violas flower the same season you plant them, about 10 to 14 weeks from seed, with no waiting year. A fall planting in a mild area blooms from fall right through spring.
factors_seasoned: Type: small-flowered violas and Johnny-jump-ups yield the most blooms; large pansies yield fewer, bigger flowers.
Deadheading cadence: frequent removal of spent flowers drives continuous bloom; neglected plants set seed and slow.
Season length and climate: mild zones bloom fall through spring, cold zones flower spring and fall around a summer pause.
Heat: sustained warmth above roughly 75 °F fades blooms and ends the productive season.
Drainage and watering: well-drained soil and morning base watering keep plants healthy and productive by avoiding crown and root rot.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No T1 evidence supports a moon-phase planting preference for viola; left unset.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Plants wilted and collapsed from the base (crown/root rot)
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Plants wilted and rotted at the base
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Crown and root rot, viola's most common cause of loss, took hold in warm, wet, poorly drained soil (often with high pH), collapsing the plant at the base.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The plant rotted at the base, usually because the soil was warm and stayed too wet or did not drain well.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil, water in the morning at the base, avoid overwatering, start with healthy plants, and rotate beds where rot built up.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Next time use well-drained soil, water in the morning at the soil, do not overwater, and do not replant violas where they rotted before.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Plants stretched leggy and pale with few blooms
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Plants got tall, pale, and stopped flowering
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Heat is viola's limit: temperatures above roughly 75 °F, or planting too early into lingering warmth, make plants leggy and pale with few flowers and invite disease.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: It got too warm. Violas stretch out, lose color, and stop flowering in heat, or when planted too early while it is still hot.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant as the heat breaks rather than early, give afternoon shade in warm regions, keep nitrogen modest, and treat them as a cool-season flower.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant once it has cooled off, not while it is still hot, give them some afternoon shade in warm areas, and go easy on fertilizer.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Seeds failed to come up
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Few or no seeds sprouted
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Warm soil and light are the usual causes: viola seed needs cool (about 65 to 75 °F), dark conditions, and germinates poorly in warm summer soil or when left uncovered.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The soil was too warm or the seed was not covered. Viola seed needs cool, dark soil to sprout.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Start seed in cool conditions, cover it to exclude light, and keep evenly moist; start indoors in late summer rather than direct-sowing into warm beds.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Sow in cool soil, cover the seed so it is dark, and keep it damp. Starting indoors in late summer works better than planting outside in warm soil.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Leaves and flowers chewed full of holes (slugs/snails)
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Something chewed ragged holes in the leaves and flowers
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Slugs and snails, the characteristic cool-season viola pest, rasped holes in foliage and bloom at night under the damp, mild conditions violas favor.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Slugs and snails ate the leaves and flowers at night. They thrive in the cool, damp weather violas like.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Reduce damp harborage, hand-pick at night, and use traps or iron-phosphate baits; press hardest in shaded, mulched, irrigated beds.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Clear damp hiding spots, pick them off after dark, and use traps or iron-phosphate bait, especially in shady, mulched, watered beds.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Bloom slowed and plants set seed
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Flowering slowed down
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Without regular deadheading, plants put energy into seed rather than new flowers, so bloom volume fell off through the season.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The old flowers were left on, so the plant made seeds instead of more flowers and slowed down.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Deadhead spent flowers regularly before they set seed, and shear leggy plants by a third to force a fresh flush.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep snipping off faded flowers before they form seeds, and cut floppy plants back by a third to get fresh growth.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Yellow blotches with gray fuzz beneath the leaves (downy mildew)
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Yellow patches with gray fuzz under the leaves
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Downy mildew took hold in cool, wet, crowded conditions, yellowing leaf tops with sporulation beneath.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: A disease called downy mildew spread in cool, wet, crowded conditions, making yellow patches with gray fuzz underneath.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Space for airflow, water at the base in the morning, and remove and discard infected foliage.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Give plants more room, water the soil in the morning, and remove leaves that are infected.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Stagger transplant sets every 2 to 3 weeks through your cool-season window for continuous, fresh bloom and to replace plants lost to slugs or rot. In mild zones that window is fall through spring with a summer heat pause; in cold zones it is early spring and again in late summer, around a midsummer pause. Violas fade above roughly 75 °F, so anchor plantings to the cool side of the season.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: For nonstop flowers, plant a fresh batch every couple of weeks during the cool season rather than all at once. In mild areas that means fall through spring, pausing for summer heat; in cold areas, early spring and again in late summer, skipping the hottest part. Violas fade once it gets hot, so keep your plantings on the cool side of the year.
succession_policy.count_note_seasoned: Season total is not a fixed cap; it is the per-zone count of staggered plantings the cool-season window supports at a 2-to-3-week cadence, bounded by the summer heat pause and, in cold zones, the winter cold pause. Derived per zone, not sourced.
succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Staggered planting offsets losses to slugs and rot and the gradual decline of older plants, sustaining fresh bloom across a long cool season.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: Wave-6 cert (2026-07-02): CC source-truth review, all cited URLs sampled. Edible petals + pesticide-free caveat backed (UMN edible-flowers; NCSU corroborates), handled conservatively (remove bitter white heel, harvest day-of, nursery plants often treated). Cool-season fade backed multi-source (Clemson/UF-IFAS/NCSU); crown/root-rot complex backed (Clemson). FIX: dropped clemson_hgic from the 2 edibility anchors (that page has no edibility content; UMN alone backs it). DTM [70,90] honestly flagged as accepted_inference. Disease-anchor upgrade (dedicated Clemson pansy-diseases factsheet) recorded as an open_finding for the variety pass, keeping viola consistent with the zinnia/marigold flower archetype.

open_findings.note: The cold end of the roster (zones 3 to 5) rests on the hardier members of the genus: Johnny-jump-up (Viola tricolor, NCSU zones 2 to 9) and viola (Viola cornuta), plus snow cover, rather than garden pansies proper (Viola x wittrockiana, NCSU zones 6 to 10). Modeled at the genus level, as the slug 'viola' spans pansies/violas/Johnny-jump-ups; review whether cold-zone copy should foreground the hardier species.

Per-region planting/bloom windows and the 12-token calendars are modeled on the cool-season frost-bracketed pattern: region+zone frost dates carried from the shared climate table, summer heat-pause months aligned to the certified cool-season peers (lettuce, carrot) per the cool-season timing guardrail. Crop-specific dated regional viola tables would tighten exact windows; held to the generally-safe-now bar.

hawaii_tropical near-year-round bloom assumes COOL high-elevation culture (upcountry); pansies and violas are cool-season plants not suited to warm lowland tropics. Modeled as a cool-upland year-round bloomer with two planting pulses; flagged for the reviewer.

days_to_maturity [70, 90] is an approximate seed-to-bloom estimate. Sources give 'start indoors 6 to 8 weeks before transplant' (Clemson) plus cool-weather bloom thereafter and 10 to 14 day germination, not a single published DTM. Refine at the variety-delta pass.

preferred pH 5.4 to 5.8 follows the pansy-specific Clemson HGIC and UF/IFAS optimum (tied to avoiding black root rot and iron chlorosis at higher pH). NCSU notes broader tolerance toward neutral; tolerated_range set to 5.2 to 6.5.

succession_policy.suitable kept True (mirroring the zinnia template) and framed as staggered transplant sets across the cool-season window; viola is more often a one- or two-window bedding planting than a continuously sown succession crop. successions_realized is derived per zone from the window length split on heat/cold pauses. Reviewer may prefer suitable=False.

open_findings.summary: Wave-6: dropped clemson_hgic from the two edibility anchors (storage + tips_by_stage.flowering[1]); the cited Clemson pansies-and-johnny-jump-ups page carries no edibility content. umn_ext_edible_flowers fully backs the edible-petals + pesticide-free + harvest-day-of + remove-bitter-white-heel claims (NCSU corroborates the pesticide caveat elsewhere).

Disease entries follow the flower archetype (crop-level sourcing, like zinnia/marigold -- no per-entry anchors). At the variety pass, anchor crown/root rot, leaf spots/anthracnose, and gray mold to Clemson's dedicated pansy-diseases-insect-pests factsheet (https://hgic.clemson.edu/factsheet/pansy-diseases-insect-pests/), which names Thielaviopsis/Phytophthora/Pythium/Colletotrichum/Botrytis verbatim; anchor downy + powdery mildew to uf_ifas / uc_ipm (the Clemson disease sheet does not name those two).

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In this region, violas are a cool-weather flower: they love the cold and bloom above freezing, and heat is what stops them. Plant in early spring and again in late summer, skipping the hottest weeks; the hardy little violas can survive winter under snow.
