crops.description_seasoned: Viola is the classic cool-season bedding flower: garden pansies (Viola x wittrockiana), violas or horned violets (Viola cornuta), and Johnny-jump-ups (Viola tricolor) are short-lived perennials almost always grown as cool-season annuals. They are very frost-hardy, blooming any time the temperature is above freezing and shrugging off light snow, which makes them the workhorse of fall, winter, and early-spring color in mild zones and the first and last color of the season in cold ones. Their one hard limit is heat: blooms fade, stems stretch, and plants turn ragged once sustained warmth above roughly 75 °F arrives, so in most regions they pause or are pulled through summer and return in fall. The flowers are edible, and Johnny-jump-ups self-seed and naturalize.
crops.description_beginner: Violas, pansies, and Johnny-jump-ups are cheerful flowers for cool weather. Unlike most flowers, they love the cold: they keep blooming through fall, winter, and early spring in mild areas and bounce back from frost and light snow. What they cannot take is heat. Once summer warmth arrives, they get leggy, pale, and stop flowering well, so in hot areas they are grown as a fall-to-spring flower and replaced when it heats up. The flowers are edible and pretty on a salad or cake, and the little Johnny-jump-up type reseeds itself and pops up on its own year after year.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Pick blooms when they are fully open and freshly colored, cutting in the cool of the morning. For edible use, harvest the same day you plan to use them and use only flowers grown without pesticides. For bedding color there is no single harvest: the plant blooms continuously through the cool season, and regular picking and deadheading drive more flowers.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Pick viola flowers when they are open and bright, ideally in the morning. If you are going to eat them, pick them the same day and only use flowers you grew yourself without bug sprays. For garden color there is nothing to harvest all at once: the plant keeps making flowers all through the cool season, and picking or snipping off old blooms makes it flower even more.
crops.deadheading_seasoned: Remove faded flowers before they set seed to extend the bloom period; this is the single most effective way to keep violas flowering through a long cool season. If plants stretch and grow leggy in late-spring warmth, shear them back by about a third to force fresh, compact growth and a late flush before heat ends the season.
crops.deadheading_beginner: Snip off old, faded flowers before they form seeds. This simple step keeps violas blooming much longer. If the plants get tall and floppy as the weather warms, cut them back by about a third and they will green up and flower again before summer heat finishes them off.

crops.name: Sweet Pea
crops.flower_type: pea-like (papilionaceous): a large upright standard with flared wings and a keel; plain or ruffled (Spencer)
crops.description_seasoned: Sweet pea (Lathyrus odoratus) is a cool-season annual climber in the legume family (Fabaceae), grown for intensely fragrant, pea-like flowers in white, pink, lavender, blue, and crimson. Climbing types scramble 5 to 8 ft up a trellis, netting, or strings by curling leaf tendrils, while dwarf and bush types stay under 2 to 3 ft and need no support. It is sown very early: as soon as the soil can be worked in late winter or early spring in most of the country, or in fall in mild-winter regions, because young plants tolerate frost and the plant flowers best in cool weather and fades fast once summer heat sets in. Despite its name and pea-like pods, sweet pea is strictly ornamental: its seeds and pods are poisonous, it is not the edible garden pea (Pisum sativum), and it should not be planted where the pods could be mistaken for food. It is prized above all as a cut flower, with the strongest scent from heirloom and Grandiflora types.
crops.description_beginner: Sweet peas are climbing flowers loved for their sweet, strong perfume and their soft, ruffly blooms in white, pink, purple, blue, and red. Most kinds climb 5 to 8 ft up a trellis, netting, or strings, holding on with curly tendrils, though there are short bushy types that need no support. They like cool weather, so you plant them very early, as soon as the ground can be worked in late winter or early spring, or in fall where winters are mild. Young plants shrug off frost, but the plants tire out and stop blooming once hot summer weather arrives. One important safety note: sweet peas are only for looks. The seeds and pods are poisonous, and this is not the edible pea you cook with, so never eat any part and keep it away from your vegetable peas. They make wonderful, fragrant cut flowers for a vase.

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Sweet peas like deep, rich, well-drained soil with plenty of compost or organic matter mixed in, because they grow a deep root system and are hungry, thirsty plants. Dig the bed over and work in compost before planting. A pH that is neutral to slightly alkaline is ideal; if your soil is acidic, a little garden lime helps. The one thing to avoid is soil that stays soggy, which rots the roots.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Sweet pea wants a deep, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil rich in organic matter: it develops a substantial root system and roots best in ground dug over and amended with compost, the opposite of a lean flower like nasturtium. Loam and sandy loam are ideal; heavy clay works if it drains and is lightened with organic matter. Aim for a neutral to slightly alkaline pH and lime an acid soil. The consistent failures are waterlogged ground, which invites root rot, and thin dry soil that cannot hold the steady moisture the plant needs through bloom.

ph.note_beginner: Sweet peas prefer soil that is neutral to slightly alkaline, roughly 6.5 to 7.5. Unlike most flowers they tolerate a touch of lime, so if your soil is quite acidic, mixing in a little garden lime before planting helps. You usually do not need to make it more acidic.
ph.note_seasoned: Sweet pea favors a near-neutral to slightly alkaline soil, about 6.5 to 7.5, and tolerates a mildly acidic to mildly alkaline band. It is one of the flowers that responds to a light liming of acid soils. pH matters less than depth, fertility, and steady moisture, but a very acidic soil is worth correcting before sowing.

crops.tip_seasoned: Sweet pea is all about cool-season timing and support. Sow very early, as soon as the soil is workable in late winter or spring, or in fall in mild-winter zones, into deep, rich, well-drained soil near neutral to slightly alkaline pH. Soak the hard seeds overnight and, for stubborn dark-coated seed, nick the coat opposite the eye to speed the 10 to 21 day germination. Give climbers a 5 to 6 ft trellis, netting, or strings from the start. Pinch seedlings above the second or third leaf pair at about 4 to 6 in to force branching, keep the soil evenly moist, and feed moderately. Cut flowers often and deadhead: once pods set, blooming slows and stops. Expect the show to wind down as summer heat arrives.
crops.tip_beginner: The two secrets to sweet peas are planting early and giving them something to climb. Plant them in cool weather, as soon as you can work the soil in late winter or early spring, or in fall if your winters are mild. Soak the hard seeds in water overnight before planting to help them sprout, and set up a trellis, netting, or strings 5 to 6 ft tall for them to climb. Keep the soil rich and evenly moist, and feed them lightly now and then. When plants are a few inches tall, pinch out the growing tip to make them bushier. Pick the flowers often for the vase: the more you cut, the more they bloom, and if you let seed pods form the plant stops flowering. Remember, the seeds and pods are poisonous, so grow them just for their beauty and scent.

fertilizer.type: Balanced, then bloom-oriented (moderate, avoid excess nitrogen)
fertilizer.timing: Compost at planting, then feed every 3 to 4 weeks in active growth
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Sweet pea is a moderate feeder grown in rich soil, not a lean-soil flower. Work compost or well-rotted manure into the bed before sowing, then feed roughly every 3 to 4 weeks through active growth and bloom. Because it is a legume that fixes some of its own nitrogen, go easy on high-nitrogen feeds: excess nitrogen pushes leafy vines at the expense of flowers. A balanced feed early shifting to one higher in phosphorus and potassium as buds form supports the longest, strongest flush of bloom.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Sweet peas grow in rich soil and like regular, gentle feeding, unlike some flowers that prefer poor soil. Mix compost into the bed before planting, then feed every few weeks while they are growing and flowering. Do not overdo nitrogen (the first number on the label), because too much gives you lots of leaves and few flowers. A general flower food, or one aimed at blooms, works well.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Reminder: feed sweet peas moderately every 3 to 4 weeks in active growth, favoring phosphorus and potassium over nitrogen once buds form. They grow in rich soil but too much nitrogen trades flowers for foliage.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Time to feed your sweet peas. Give them a gentle dose of flower food every few weeks while they grow and bloom, and go light on high-nitrogen feeds so you get flowers, not just leaves.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: Compost-enriched soil plus a balanced feed early, shifting to a lower-nitrogen, higher phosphorus and potassium feed at budding. Avoid heavy nitrogen: as a legume, sweet pea needs little added N and over-feeding it suppresses bloom.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: The three numbers on fertilizer (N-P-K) are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. For sweet peas, avoid a high first number (nitrogen), which gives leaves instead of flowers. A balanced or bloom-type food, with compost worked in at planting, is ideal.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A generous compost amendment at planting, then a balanced liquid or granular feed at label rate every 3 to 4 weeks, easing off nitrogen and favoring bloom-type feeds once flowering begins.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Mix a few inches of compost into the soil before planting, then feed with a normal-strength flower food about once a month while they grow and bloom.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.note_beginner: Small soft insects that cluster on new shoots, buds, and leaf undersides, sucking sap and, more importantly, spreading virus diseases. Hose them off, use insecticidal soap, and encourage ladybugs and hoverflies.
pests.note_seasoned: The key pest of sweet pea: several species (pea aphid, potato aphid, others) colonize shoots and buds, and as vectors of enation mosaic and pea mosaic viruses they matter far beyond their direct feeding. Manage early with strong water sprays, insecticidal soap, or horticultural oil, and support natural enemies; heavy aphid pressure plus virus is a common cause of ruined plantings.

pests.name: Thrips (including western flower thrips)
pests.note_beginner: Tiny slivers that rasp leaves and flowers, leaving silvery flecks and distorted growth, and they spread spotted-wilt virus. Remove badly affected growth and treat with insecticidal soap or spinosad if numbers build.
pests.note_seasoned: Thrips scar foliage and blooms with silvery stippling and black specks and, as vectors of tomato spotted wilt and impatiens necrotic spot virus, seed serious virus problems. Monitor with the flowers, treat build-ups with insecticidal soap or spinosad, and rogue virus-symptomatic plants.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.note_beginner: Tiny mites that cause fine pale speckling and webbing on leaves in hot, dry weather. Spray plants with water and use insecticidal soap or horticultural oil if they build up.
pests.note_seasoned: Hot, dry, dusty conditions late in the season favor spider mites, which stipple and bronze the foliage and spin fine webbing. Base watering, raising humidity, and insecticidal soap or oil check them; they often coincide with the plant's heat decline.

pests.name: Slugs and snails
pests.note_beginner: These chew ragged holes in leaves and can devour tender seedlings overnight in damp weather. Hand-pick at night, remove hiding places, or use iron-phosphate bait.
pests.note_seasoned: Slugs and snails are a real threat to young sweet peas, capable of stripping seedlings in a night during cool, damp spring weather. Reduce debris, hand-pick after dark, and use iron-phosphate bait around emerging or newly set plants.

pests.name: Caterpillars and leafminers
pests.note_beginner: Various caterpillars chew leaves and buds, and leafminers make pale winding trails inside the leaves. Pick off caterpillars or use Bt, and remove mined leaves.
pests.note_seasoned: Foliage-feeding caterpillars (including corn earworm) and vegetable leafminers occasionally damage sweet pea leaves, buds, and flowers. Hand-pick or treat caterpillars with Bt or spinosad, and remove mined foliage; damage is usually cosmetic on a vigorous plant.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.note_beginner: A white, powdery coating on leaves and stems, worst in warm weather and crowded, dry-rooted plantings, that yellows and shrivels foliage. Improve airflow, water at the base, and remove affected leaves.
diseases.note_seasoned: Powdery mildew (Microsphaera / Erysiphe spp.) is the common late-season foliar disease, coating leaves with white growth and hastening decline as the weather warms. Manage culturally: space and support for airflow, keep roots moist but foliage dry, water early, and remove affected leaves; it often marks the end of the cool-season run.

diseases.name: Root, stem, and crown rots
diseases.note_beginner: Soilborne rots (in wet or reused soil) cause wilting, browning at the base, and collapse. There is no cure once established; avoid waterlogged soil, do not bury the crown, and rotate to fresh ground.
diseases.note_seasoned: Rhizoctonia, Pythium, and Fusarium cause damping-off of seedlings and root, stem, and crown rot of older plants, with wilting, basal browning, and collapse, favored by wet, poorly drained, or legume-cropped soil. There is no rescue treatment: ensure drainage, avoid overwatering and burying the crown, use clean soil, and rotate off recent pea, bean, or sweet pea ground.

diseases.name: Mosaic and spotted-wilt viruses
diseases.note_beginner: Aphids and thrips spread viruses that mottle, streak, ring-spot, and distort leaves and flowers. There is no cure; control the insects and pull and destroy affected plants.
diseases.note_seasoned: Aphid-borne mosaics (pea enation mosaic, pea mosaic) and thrip-borne spotted wilt (TSWV, INSV) cause mottling, ringspots, streaking, and distortion with no treatment. Management is vector control (aphids, thrips) plus prompt roguing of symptomatic plants; keeping sweet pea away from edible peas limits shared virus reservoirs.

diseases.name: Anthracnose and leaf spots
diseases.note_beginner: Fungal spotting diseases cause whitish or dark lesions on leaves, shoots, and flower stalks, worse in wet weather. Use healthy seed and clean soil, improve airflow, and remove affected parts.
diseases.note_seasoned: Anthracnose and several leaf-spot fungi lesion leaves, shoots, and flower stalks, spreading in wet conditions and sometimes carried on seed. Favor clean seed and soil, airflow, and base watering, and remove affected tissue; usually secondary to mildew and the rots on sweet pea.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.note_beginner: Grayish moldy growth on the undersides of leaves in cool, wet, humid spells, with yellowing above. Improve airflow, keep foliage dry, and remove affected leaves.
diseases.note_seasoned: Downy mildew (Peronospora) produces grayish sporulation on leaf undersides with yellow blotching above under cool, damp, humid conditions. Cultural control (airflow, dry foliage, sanitation) is the mainstay; it is a minor, weather-driven problem relative to powdery mildew and the rots.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Keep the soil consistently, evenly moist: sweet pea has high water needs and does not tolerate drying out, which stalls growth, shortens stems, and cuts bloom. Water deeply and regularly through establishment and the whole flowering period, increasing frequency as the weather warms. Do not let the bed swing between bone-dry and saturated.
watering.frequency_beginner: Sweet peas like steady moisture and do not like to dry out. Keep the soil damp (not soggy) all through their growing and flowering season, watering deeply and regularly, and more often as the weather warms up. Letting them get dry means shorter stems and fewer flowers.
watering.amount_seasoned: Aim for at least one inch of water per week from rain plus irrigation during growth, more in heat or fast-draining soil, applied deeply to reach the deep root system. Consistency matters more than volume: frequent shallow sips are worse than a deep soak that keeps the whole root zone moist.
watering.amount_beginner: Give them about an inch of water a week, and more in hot or dry spells. Water deeply so it soaks down to the roots, rather than a light sprinkle every day. The goal is soil that stays evenly damp.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base with a can, drip line, or soaker hose and keep water off the foliage where practical; wet leaves in crowded plantings invite powdery mildew and other leaf diseases. Water early in the day so any splashed foliage dries quickly, and mulch to hold moisture and keep the roots cool.
watering.method_beginner: Water the soil at the base of the plants, not over the leaves, using a watering can or soaker hose. Watering in the morning and keeping the leaves dry helps prevent mildew. A layer of mulch keeps the soil moist and the roots cool.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting despite wet soil, and soft, browning stems at the base signal overwatering or poor drainage; sweet pea roots and crowns rot readily in saturated ground. Standing water and heavy, airless soil are the usual causes.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If the lower leaves yellow, the plant wilts even though the soil is wet, or the base of the stems looks soft and brown, the soil is too wet or drains poorly. Sweet peas rot in soggy ground, so ease off and improve drainage.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting in the heat of the day, stalled growth, shorter flower stems, and early bud drop point to underwatering; dry stress is quickly punished with poor bloom and hastens the plant's summer decline.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Sweet peas that are too dry wilt in the afternoon, stop growing well, and make short stems with few flowers, and buds may drop off before opening. A deep, regular watering usually turns this around.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Base-water deeply and consistently, keep foliage dry, and mulch: steady moisture at the root zone with good airflow above is the balance that sustains long stems and bloom while holding down mildew.
watering.method_note_beginner: Water deeply and often at the base, keep the leaves dry, and mulch the soil. Steady moisture below with dry, airy leaves above gives you the best flowers and the least disease.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The critical moisture windows are germination and establishment and the entire budding-to-bloom period; any drought stress in spring shortens stems and drops buds, and dryness in warming weather accelerates the end of the season.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The most important times to keep the soil moist are while seeds sprout and settle in, and all through budding and flowering. Letting them dry out then means fewer, shorter-stemmed flowers and a faster finish when it warms up.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Sweet pea is a short-lived cut flower with a vase life of about 5 days at room temperature. Cut in the cool of the morning, condition the stems in cool water, and keep the vase out of direct sun, heat, and drafts. Change the water and recut stems to stretch the display.
storage.room_temp_beginner: As a cut flower, sweet peas last only about 5 days in a vase at room temperature. Pick them in the cool morning, put them straight in water, and keep the vase out of hot sun and drafts. Fresh water and a fresh snip on the stems helps them last.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Sweet pea stems hold best cool: store cut stems in water in a cool spot or a refrigerator around 40 °F to slow aging and prolong vase life, and refrigerate briefly to firm blooms before arranging. They are highly perishable, so use them promptly.
storage.fridge_beginner: Sweet peas keep better cool. Standing in water in the fridge or a cold room (about 40 °F) helps them last a little longer. They fade fast, so enjoy them soon after cutting.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Sweet pea flowers cannot be frozen or dried for later use as fresh flowers; they are strictly a fresh-cut bloom. The only thing worth keeping to the end of season is dried seed for resowing, and those seeds are poisonous and must never be eaten.
storage.freezer_beginner: You cannot freeze or dry sweet pea flowers to use later; they are only good fresh in a vase. At the end of the season you can let a few pods dry to save seeds for next year, but remember those seeds are poisonous and are only for planting.
storage.notes_seasoned: Handle sweet pea as the delicate, fragrant cut flower it is: cut young, condition cool, and expect only about 5 days in the vase. There is no edible or preserved form; every part is inedible and the seeds and pods are poisonous. Save dried seed only for planting, clearly labeled and kept away from food and children.
storage.notes_beginner: Sweet peas are a fresh cut flower and nothing more: pick them young, keep them cool, and enjoy the scent for their few days in the vase. No part is edible, and the seeds and pods are poisonous. If you save seeds to replant, label them and keep them well away from food and children.

recommended: Spencer types (climbing; large, ruffled, long-stemmed flowers on 6 to 8 ft vines, the classic exhibition and cut-flower sweet pea, fragrance variable)
Grandiflora / old-fashioned heirlooms including 'Old Spice' (climbing; smaller plainer flowers but the strongest fragrance and the best heat tolerance, good where summers warm early)
'Cupani' / 'Matucana' (climbing; the original 1600s bicolor with maroon and violet flowers and intense scent, very heirloom)
'Mars', 'Memories', 'Oban Bay' (climbing; named cultivars noted for fragrance and long stems)
Dwarf and bush types 'Bijou', 'Little Sweetheart', 'Cupid' (mounding 8 in to 3 ft, self-supporting, for containers, edging, and baskets, no trellis needed)
varieties.note_seasoned: Choose by habit, fragrance, and heat timing. Spencer types give the largest, most ruffled, longest-stemmed flowers and are the florist and show standard, but fragrance varies by cultivar. For scent and for gardens where heat comes early, the Grandiflora and old-fashioned heirlooms (notably 'Old Spice', and the original 'Cupani' / 'Matucana') carry the strongest perfume and better heat tolerance, trading some flower size. Dwarf and bush selections ('Bijou', 'Little Sweetheart', 'Cupid') stay compact and self-supporting for pots and edging, needing no trellis. All are ornamental only, with poisonous seeds and pods.
varieties.note_beginner: Pick a type for your goal. For big, ruffly, long-stemmed cut flowers, choose Spencer types, but check that the variety is described as fragrant, since scent varies. For the strongest perfume, and for hot-summer gardens, choose old-fashioned or heirloom kinds like 'Old Spice' or the original 'Cupani', which smell wonderful and take heat a bit better. If you do not want to put up a trellis, grow dwarf or bush types like 'Bijou' or 'Little Sweetheart' in a pot or along an edge. All types are for looks only, and the seeds and pods are poisonous.

companions.note_beginner: Sweet peas are grown for their flowers and scent, not as a companion or pest-control plant, so there is not much proven companion science here. Their open, nectar-rich flowers do draw bees and other pollinators to the garden, and as a legume they fix a little nitrogen in the soil. The most useful and best-supported rule is a keep-away one: do not plant sweet peas next to your edible garden peas. They share pests and diseases such as aphids, viruses, and root rots, and because sweet pea pods are poisonous, keeping the two apart avoids any dangerous mix-up. Grow sweet peas up their own trellis, fence, or obelisk where the scent can be enjoyed.
companions.note_seasoned: Sweet pea's garden value is ornamental (fragrance and cut flowers) plus modest pollinator draw and light nitrogen fixation as a legume; it is not a documented trap or repellent companion, so its pairings are best framed honestly rather than as pest control. The one well-grounded, load-bearing guidance is separation from edible peas (Pisum sativum): the two share aphids, aphid-borne viruses, and soilborne root rots, and sweet pea's poisonous pods should never be grown intermingled where they could be confused with an edible crop. Site it on its own support, and rotate it away from ground that recently grew peas, beans, or sweet pea to limit soilborne carryover.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Pollinators (bees and other flower visitors)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Sweet pea's fragrant, nectar-rich flowers bring bees and other pollinators into the garden, which helps everything nearby that needs pollinating. This is a nice side benefit, not a pest-control trick.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Sweet pea is an open, nectar-bearing flower that draws pollinators; the general benefit to a garden is well grounded but not the subject of a sweet-pea-specific companion trial. Labeled likely/low.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: As an open, scented, nectar-rich legume flower, sweet pea recruits bees and other pollinators, a general habitat benefit to a mixed planting. This is a reasonable inference from its floral biology rather than a documented companion effect, so it is offered as a modest, honest benefit, not a pest-management claim.

good_seasoned.name: Pollinators (insectary / habitat)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Sweet pea's fragrant, nectar-rich flowers draw bees and other pollinators, a general habitat benefit. Inferred from floral biology, not from a sweet-pea-specific trial.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Pollinator draw is well grounded for an open nectar flower; neighbor benefit inferred, not directly trialed for sweet pea.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Edible garden peas (Pisum sativum)
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep sweet peas away from your edible peas. They catch the same pests and diseases (aphids, viruses, root rots), and because sweet pea seeds and pods are poisonous, growing them tangled together risks a dangerous mix-up at harvest. Give sweet peas their own spot and trellis.

provenance.label: research_backed
provenance.reason: Sweet pea and edible pea share aphids, aphid-borne viruses, and soilborne root rots (UC IPM; extension), and NC State states sweet peas are poisonous and should not be planted near edible peas. Both the disease-sharing and the toxicity-confusion rationale are sourced. Labeled research_backed/medium.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Do not interplant sweet pea with edible peas. The two share aphids, aphid-borne viruses (enation mosaic, pea mosaic), and soilborne root rots, so proximity concentrates shared problems; and because sweet pea's seeds and pods are poisonous, extension guidance is explicit that it should not be grown near edible peas where the pods could be confused for food. Separate the plantings and rotate sweet pea off recent pea or bean ground.

bad_seasoned.name: Edible garden peas (Pisum sativum)
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Shared aphids, aphid-borne viruses, and soilborne root rots make co-planting a liability, and sweet pea's poisonous pods should not be grown intermingled with an edible pea crop. Extension states plainly that sweet peas should not be planted near edible peas.

provenance.label: research_backed
provenance.reason: Shared pest/disease pressure (UC IPM) plus NC State's explicit statement that sweet peas are poisonous and should not be planted near edible peas.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: If started indoors, harden off over 7 to 10 days before setting out; sweet pea seedlings are cold-tolerant, so they can go out early, even before the last frost, once hardened. Transplant while young with minimal root disturbance, ideally from deep root-trainers or biodegradable pots, because the plant makes a long taproot that resents being cramped or broken.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: If you started plants indoors, harden them off by setting them outside for longer each day over about a week before planting out. Sweet pea seedlings handle cold, so they can go out early. Move them while small and try not to disturb the roots, since they grow a long taproot; deep pots or biodegradable pots help.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Both methods work. Direct-sow as soon as the soil is workable in late winter or early spring (fall in mild-winter zones), or start indoors about 6 weeks earlier in deep cells or root-trainers for an earlier, stronger start. Soak the hard seed overnight; for dark, hard-coated seed that has not swelled, nick the coat opposite the eye with a knife or file to speed the 10 to 21 day germination near 60 °F. Sow about 1 in deep, and pinch seedlings above the second or third leaf pair to force basal branching. Provide the climbing support at or before planting.
start_method.notes_beginner: You can plant seeds straight in the ground or start them indoors. Direct-sow as soon as you can work the soil in late winter or spring (or in fall where winters are mild), or start seeds indoors about 6 weeks earlier in deep pots. Soak the hard seeds overnight first; if any have not swelled, carefully nick the hard coat with a file to help them sprout, which takes 10 to 21 days. Plant about 1 in deep, and when seedlings are a few inches tall pinch out the tip to make them bushier. Put the trellis up when you plant.

container_notes.shape_requirements: Deep pot for the long taproot; climbing types need a tall support anchored in the pot

soil_mix.type_beginner: rich, well-drained potting mix with added compost
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Use a good-quality potting mix and blend in some compost, since sweet peas are hungry and thirsty. Make sure the pot drains well, and add a little lime if your mix is very acidic. Pick a deep pot so the long roots have room.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: rich, moisture-retentive but free-draining mix, compost-amended, neutral to slightly alkaline
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Favor a fertile, moisture-retentive yet free-draining mix enriched with compost; sweet pea is a deep-rooted, moderate feeder that dries out fast in pots. A deep container (at least 10 in) suits the taproot, and a light liming corrects an acidic mix. Avoid shallow pots and lean, fast-drying blends.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out much faster than the ground, and sweet peas hate drying out, so check daily in warm weather and keep the mix evenly moist. Deep pots and a mulch on top help hold moisture.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Container sweet peas need regular feeding since watering washes nutrients out. Feed with a flower food every couple of weeks while they grow and bloom, going easy on high-nitrogen types.

overwintering.approach_beginner: This does not really apply: sweet peas are one-season plants that finish when summer heat arrives. In mild-winter areas you plant them in fall to grow over winter and bloom in spring, then replace them; you do not carry a plant over for years.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Not applicable as a perennial: sweet pea is an annual that ends with summer heat. In mild-winter regions it is fall-sown to overwinter as a young plant and bloom in late winter to spring, but it is replaced each year rather than overwintered as an established plant.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Sweet peas grow well in a large, deep pot, especially the dwarf and bush types that do not need a trellis. For climbing types, use a big pot with a tall support pushed firmly into the soil. Keep the mix rich and evenly moist, feed regularly, and give them sun. The main challenge in pots is keeping up with watering.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Sweet pea containers well if the pot is deep and never allowed to dry out. Dwarf and bush selections ('Bijou', 'Little Sweetheart', 'Cupid') are the natural fit for pots and baskets, needing no support; climbing types require a tall, well-anchored trellis or obelisk set in a large, deep container. Use a rich, moisture-retentive mix, feed regularly, and site in full sun with steady water. The limiting factor is moisture: pots dry fast, and sweet pea punishes drought with short stems and bud drop.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry quickly and sweet pea will not tolerate it; check daily in warm spells and keep the mix evenly moist, letting excess drain freely. Mulching the surface and using a deep pot buffer the swings that cause bud drop.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Feed potted plants more regularly than in-ground, since frequent watering leaches nutrients; a balanced feed every 2 weeks, easing nitrogen at bloom, sustains flowering without forcing foliage.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering container can suit sweet pea's high, steady moisture demand, but only with a genuinely free-draining mix: a constantly saturated reservoir against the crown invites root and crown rot. Keep the wick zone moist, not waterlogged.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: Self-watering pots can help because sweet peas like steady moisture, but do not let the soil stay soggy, which rots the roots. Use a well-draining mix and keep it damp, not wet.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Sweet pea is a legume (Fabaceae), so rotate it off ground that recently grew peas, beans, or sweet pea itself: the family shares soilborne root rots (Rhizoctonia, Pythium, Fusarium) and the same aphids and viruses, which build up with repeated legume cropping. Extension guidance is to avoid planting sweet pea in the same spot in consecutive years; a 3 year gap on a given bed is prudent, especially if root rot has appeared.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Sweet peas are in the pea and bean family, so do not plant them where peas, beans, or sweet peas grew in the last few years. Those crops share the same soil diseases and pests, which build up over time. Move sweet peas to a fresh spot each year, and give a bed about 3 years before growing them there again.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate sweet pea like the legume it is: follow non-legumes such as leafy greens, brassicas, or alliums, and avoid replanting it after peas, beans, or sweet pea to limit soilborne root rot and virus carryover. Because it is grown ornamentally, siting is also about the support structure and where the fragrance is enjoyed, but the disease-driven rotation away from recent legume ground is the substantive rule.
rotation.note_beginner: Because sweet peas are related to peas and beans, plant them after non-legume crops like leafy greens, cabbage-family plants, or onions, and not right after peas or beans. This helps avoid the soil diseases that legumes share. Each year, give them a fresh spot, and their own trellis where you can enjoy the scent.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seedlings emerge in roughly 10 to 21 days from cool soil near 60 °F; soaked or nicked seed comes up faster and more evenly.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The first shoots push up in about two to three weeks.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Soak seed overnight (nick hard-coated seed), sow about 1 in deep into workable soil in late winter or early spring, or in fall in mild zones, and keep evenly moist.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Soak the seeds overnight, plant them about 1 in deep, and keep the soil damp until they sprout.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Seedlings emerged?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your seeds sprouted?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Paired leaflets and the first clasping tendrils develop; growth is slow and hardy in cool weather.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Small climbing plants with curling tendrils appear and slowly get taller.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pinch above the second or third leaf pair at 4 to 6 in to force basal branching, set up the trellis or netting, and protect from slugs and birds.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: When plants are a few inches tall, pinch out the tip to make them bushier, put up the trellis, and watch for slugs and birds.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Pinched and supported?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you pinched and added support?

growth_stages.name: Established / vine growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Vines lengthen and grab the support with tendrils; rich soil and steady moisture drive strong, leafy, upward growth.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant climbs quickly up its support and fills in with leaves.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Train new growth onto the support, keep soil evenly moist, and feed moderately; go easy on nitrogen so the plant sets buds rather than only foliage.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Guide the climbing stems onto the trellis, keep the soil moist, and feed lightly.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Vines climbing and fed?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are your vines climbing well?

growth_stages.name: Budding
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flower stems (peduncles) rise from the leaf axils bearing several buds; long, strong stems come from cool weather, moisture, and steady feeding.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Flower stems with buds start to rise up among the leaves.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture and feeding steady as buds form; support long stems and watch for aphids and thrips that can distort buds or spread virus.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep watering and feeding as buds appear, and watch for aphids and thrips.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: First buds visible?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Do you see flower buds yet?

growth_stages.name: Flowering and cutting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fragrant flowers open from the base of each stem upward, roughly 10 to 14 weeks after sowing; bloom is heaviest in cool weather and slows as heat builds.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Sweet-smelling flowers open along the stems, best in cool weather.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut stems for the vase as the lowest florets open and remove all developing pods, which is what keeps bloom going; water deeply in warming weather and use light afternoon shade to extend the season.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Cut flowers often for the vase and pull off any seed pods, and water well as it warms up.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: First bloom open?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Has your first flower opened?

growth_stages.name: Heat decline and seed saving (optional)
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: As sustained heat arrives, flowering slows, stems shorten, and plants yellow and fade; pods left to mature signal the end and can be dried for seed.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: In hot weather the plant slows down, makes fewer flowers, and starts to yellow and finish.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Let a few pods dry on the plant only if saving seed (label and store the poisonous seed away from food), then pull spent plants; in mild zones sow a fresh fall crop later.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: To save seeds, let a few pods dry on the plant, keep them away from food since they are poisonous, then remove the finished plants.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Plants finishing or seed saved?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are your plants finishing for the season?

notifications.body_seasoned: Sweet peas are sown early. As soon as the soil is workable, direct-sow soaked seed about 1 in deep, or set out hardened, indoor-started plants; the cold-tolerant seedlings can go out well before the last frost.
notifications.body_beginner: You can plant sweet peas now, as soon as the ground can be worked. Soak the seeds overnight, plant them about 1 in deep, and set up a trellis. The young plants handle cold, so early is good.

notifications.body_seasoned: At 4 to 6 in, pinch above the second or third leaf pair to force branching, and have the 5 to 6 ft support in place for the tendrils to grab.
notifications.body_beginner: When your seedlings are a few inches tall, pinch out the top to make them bushier, and make sure a trellis or netting is ready for them to climb.

notifications.title_beginner: Time to cut your sweet peas
notifications.body_seasoned: Flowers are opening. Cut stems as the lowest florets open and remove every developing pod; frequent cutting and no seed set is what keeps sweet peas blooming.
notifications.body_beginner: Your flowers are opening. Start cutting them for the vase and pull off any seed pods you see. The more you pick, the more flowers you get.

notifications.body_seasoned: As sustained heat arrives, expect bloom to slow and stems to shorten. Water deeply and use light afternoon shade to stretch the season; in hot regions the plant will soon finish.
notifications.body_beginner: When it turns hot, sweet peas slow down and stop blooming. Water them well and give some afternoon shade to keep them going a bit longer, but they will finish as summer sets in.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot weather warning
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Sweet pea is a cool-season plant that declines rapidly in heat: flowering slows, stems shorten, and plants yellow. Water deeply, mulch to cool the roots, and give light afternoon shade; in the hottest regions the season is ending.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Sweet peas do not like heat and slow down or stop flowering when it gets hot. Water them well, mulch the soil, and give afternoon shade to help, but hot weather means the season is winding down.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hard freeze warning
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Young sweet pea plants tolerate frost and light freezes, but a hard freeze below about 25 °F can damage them. Protect fall-sown or early plants with row cover during a severe cold snap.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Sweet peas handle frost, but a hard freeze (below about 25 °F) can hurt young plants. Cover them with a frost cloth if a severe cold night is coming.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Watch for aphids and thrips
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Aphids and thrips build on sweet pea in warm spells and spread mosaic and spotted-wilt viruses. Hose off aphids or use insecticidal soap, and remove virus-symptomatic plants promptly.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Aphids and thrips like sweet peas and can spread virus diseases. Spray aphids off with water or insecticidal soap, and pull any plants with streaked or distorted leaves.

germination.text_seasoned: Sow early into cool soil: sweet pea germinates near 60 °F and seedlings are frost-hardy, so late-winter or early-spring sowing (fall in mild zones) gives the long cool run the plant needs before heat.
germination.text_beginner: Plant sweet peas early, in cool weather. The seeds sprout in cool soil and young plants handle frost, so late winter or early spring (or fall where winters are mild) is the right time.

germination.text_seasoned: Soak the hard seed overnight; dark, hard-coated seed that stays hard can be nicked opposite the eye to let water in and even up the 10 to 21 day germination.
germination.text_beginner: Soak the seeds in water overnight before planting. If any seeds are dark and stay hard, carefully nick the hard shell with a file so water can get in.

seedling.text_seasoned: Pinch seedlings above the second or third leaf pair at 4 to 6 in: removing the growing tip forces multiple basal shoots and a bushier, more productive plant.
seedling.text_beginner: When seedlings are a few inches tall, pinch off the very top. This makes the plant send up several stems from the base instead of one, so you get more flowers.

seedling.text_seasoned: Get the support up early: climbing types need a 5 to 6 ft trellis, netting, or strings from the start, since the tendrils grab as they grow and a late support means tangled vines.
seedling.text_beginner: Put the trellis or netting up right away for climbing types. Sweet peas grab on as they grow, so having 5 to 6 ft of support ready keeps them tidy.

seedling.text_seasoned: Protect tender seedlings from slugs, snails, and birds, which can strip young sweet peas overnight; hand-pick or bait for slugs and net against birds where they are a problem.
seedling.text_beginner: Watch young sweet peas for slugs, snails, and birds, which love the tender shoots. Use slug bait or hand-pick at night, and net the plants if birds are a problem.

established.text_seasoned: Keep the soil evenly moist and feed moderately as vines climb; sweet pea is a deep-rooted, thirsty legume, but ease off nitrogen so growth turns to buds rather than all foliage.
established.text_beginner: As the vines climb, keep the soil evenly moist and feed lightly. Do not overdo nitrogen fertilizer, or you get lots of leaves and few flowers.

established.text_seasoned: Mulch the root zone to keep it cool and moist: sweet pea roots resent heat and drying, and a mulch buffers the swings that shorten stems and drop buds as the weather warms.
established.text_beginner: Spread a mulch over the soil to keep the roots cool and damp. This helps sweet peas keep making long-stemmed flowers as it warms up.

budding.text_seasoned: Scout for aphids and thrips as buds form: both distort buds and spread mosaic and spotted-wilt viruses. Control aphids early and rogue out any mottled, streaked, or ringspotted plants.
budding.text_beginner: As buds form, check for aphids and thrips. They can twist the buds and spread virus. Wash aphids off, and pull out any plants with streaky or mottled leaves.

flowering.text_seasoned: Cut daily at the peak: harvest each stem as its lowest one or two florets open, and never let pods set. Frequent cutting with no seed development is the single strongest driver of continued bloom.
flowering.text_beginner: Cut sweet peas often, as soon as the bottom flowers on a stem open, and pull off any seed pods. Picking a lot and stopping seeds is what keeps them blooming.

flowering.text_seasoned: Manage powdery mildew in warm, crowded, or dry-rooted plantings: space and support for airflow, water at the base early in the day, and remove affected leaves; mildew often marks the plant's late-season decline.
flowering.text_beginner: In warm weather sweet peas can get powdery mildew, a white dust on the leaves. Space plants for airflow, water at the base in the morning, and remove badly affected leaves.

decline_seed.text_seasoned: To save seed, leave a few pods to ripen and dry to tan on a spent plant, then collect and label the seed for planting only: sweet pea seed is poisonous and must be kept from food and children. Open-pollinated and heirloom types come reasonably true.
decline_seed.text_beginner: If you want seeds for next year, let a few pods dry on the plant until tan, then collect them. Label them for planting only and keep them away from food and children, because they are poisonous. Heirloom types grow fairly true from saved seed.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A well-grown climbing sweet pea yields many fragrant, cuttable stems over a concentrated cool-season run, heaviest in spring or the mild months, tapering as heat arrives. Kept cut and pod-free, a plant produces for several weeks; let it set seed or hit heat and production falls off quickly. Dwarf and bush types give a shorter, lower flush suited to containers and edging rather than steady cutting.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: A healthy climbing sweet pea gives you lots of sweet-smelling flowers for cutting over several weeks in the cool part of the season, then slows and stops in the heat. Keep cutting and remove seed pods for the most flowers. Dwarf and bush types make fewer flowers over a shorter time, but are great in pots.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Sweet pea flowers in its single season from seed, reaching first bloom in roughly 10 to 14 weeks and cutting for several weeks after; there is no establishment year. A very early or fall sowing that builds a strong root system in cool weather gives the earliest and most abundant bloom.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Sweet peas flower the same year you plant them, usually about three months after sowing, with no waiting year. Planting early, while it is cool, gives you more and earlier flowers.
factors_seasoned: Timing: an early or fall sowing that roots in cool weather gives longer stems and far more bloom than a late sowing caught by heat.
Support and pinching: pinched, well-supported climbers branch and yield more than unpinched, sprawling plants.
Cutting and deadheading: constant cutting with no seed set is the strongest driver of continued flowering.
Moisture and feeding: steady moisture and moderate feeding sustain long stems; drought and excess nitrogen both cut bloom.
Heat: sustained warmth ends the season; cool-summer and coastal regions flower far longer than hot-summer ones.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No T1 evidence supports a moon-phase planting preference for sweet pea; left unset.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Flowering stopped and plants yellowed in early summer
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Plants quit blooming and yellowed when it got hot
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Normal end-of-season for a cool-season plant: sustained heat slows and stops bloom, shortens stems, and yellows the vines. In hot regions this comes early, which is why sweet pea is grown as a fall-to-spring or very-early-spring crop there.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: This is normal. Sweet peas like cool weather and finish when summer heat arrives, slowing down and turning yellow. In hot places, that happens early, so they are grown mainly over the cool months.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sow as early as possible (or in fall in mild zones) to bank cool-season growth before heat, choose heat-tolerant heirlooms, and give afternoon shade, deep water, and mulch as it warms.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant as early as you can (or in fall where winters are mild), pick heat-tolerant heirloom types, and use afternoon shade, deep watering, and mulch to stretch the season.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Lush vines with few flowers
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Big leafy vines but hardly any flowers
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Usually too much nitrogen or too little light: as a legume in rich, over-fed soil, sweet pea runs to foliage. Letting pods set, or not cutting, also shuts down bloom.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Usually too much nitrogen fertilizer or not enough sun makes leafy vines with few flowers. Letting seed pods form, or not picking flowers, also stops blooming.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Ease off nitrogen and favor phosphorus and potassium at budding, give full sun, and cut flowers constantly while removing every pod.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Cut back on nitrogen feed, give full sun, and keep cutting the flowers while removing seed pods.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Seeds failed to come up
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Few or no seeds sprouted
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Commonly hard, unsoaked seed, warm or dry soil, or rot in cold wet ground. Sweet pea has a hard coat and germinates best in cool, moist, workable soil near 60 °F.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Usually the seeds were not soaked, or the soil was too warm, too dry, or cold and soggy. Sweet pea seeds are hard-coated and sprout best in cool, moist soil.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Soak overnight and nick hard seed, sow about 1 in deep into cool, evenly moist, workable soil in late winter or spring, and avoid cold waterlogged beds.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Soak seeds overnight (nick very hard ones), plant about 1 in deep in cool, damp soil in late winter or spring, and avoid cold soggy ground.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Buds dropped before opening
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Flower buds fell off without opening
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Bud drop follows stress: dryness or erratic watering, a sudden warm spell, low light, or over-feeding. Sweet pea sheds buds when moisture or temperature swings.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Buds drop when the plant is stressed, usually from dry or uneven watering, a sudden hot spell, too much shade, or too much fertilizer.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Keep moisture steady, mulch, feed moderately, and site in full sun with afternoon relief in warm areas; consistency prevents most bud drop.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist, mulch, feed gently, and give full sun with some afternoon shade where it is hot. Steady care stops most bud drop.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: White dusty leaves or mottled, distorted growth
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: White powder on leaves, or streaked, twisted leaves
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: White dust is powdery mildew, common in warm, crowded, or dry-rooted plantings late in the season. Mottling, streaking, and distortion are aphid- and thrip-borne viruses (mosaic, spotted wilt) with no cure.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: A white dusty coating is powdery mildew, common late in the season. Streaked, mottled, or twisted leaves are virus diseases spread by aphids and thrips, which cannot be cured.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: For mildew, improve airflow, water at the base early, and remove affected leaves. For virus, control aphids and thrips and rogue out symptomatic plants promptly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: For mildew, space plants for airflow, water in the morning at the base, and remove bad leaves. For virus, control aphids and thrips and pull out affected plants.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Sweet pea is largely a single-cohort crop, but a couple of successive sowings across the cool window (early plus late in the sowing season) stretch the cut-flower supply, since the plant is undone by heat rather than tired plantings. In mild-winter regions the two real windows are fall and late winter; in cold regions, one early-spring sowing (optionally split by a few weeks) is the practical maximum before summer heat closes the season.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: You can sow sweet peas a couple of times a few weeks apart during the cool planting window to spread out the flowers, but there is no long succession like lettuce, because summer heat ends them. In mild-winter areas, plant once in fall and again in late winter; in cold areas, one early-spring sowing is usually it.
succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Realized sowings are few and clustered in the cool shoulders: sweet pea flowers on a concentrated spring or winter-to-spring run and is ended by heat, so successive sowings extend cutting modestly rather than delivering many staggered crops.

crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Sweet pea is harvested as a cut flower, not a food. Cut stems in the cool of the morning when the lowest one or two florets on the stem have just opened and the upper buds still show color; stems are typically 10 to 14 in long. Plunge them straight into water and expect a vase life of about 5 days. Cut daily at peak: frequent cutting, plus removing any seed pods, is what keeps the plant producing. Every part is inedible and the seeds and pods are poisonous, so this is a vase crop only.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Sweet peas are picked for their flowers and scent, not to eat. Cut the stems in the morning when the bottom one or two flowers on the stem have just opened. They last about 5 days in a vase. The more you cut, the more the plant blooms, so pick often and pull off any seed pods you find. Never eat any part of the plant: the seeds and pods are poisonous.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: Batch-2 Wave-7 cert (2026-07-06, Trevor-ruled) -- FINAL WAVE. companion_and_ornamental_flower (Lathyrus odoratus, annual climber, Fabaceae). SAFETY WATCH-ITEM EXEMPLARY -- the toxic-seed handling is the best in the batch: 'seeds and pods are poisonous / no part is edible / ornamental only / vase crop only', explicitly distinguished from the edible garden pea (Pisum sativum), saved seed 'labeled and kept away from food and children', all NCSU-anchored; it even turns the toxicity into an honest safety-driven companion rule (keep sweet peas away from edible peas to avoid a dangerous harvest mix-up). Agronomy/pests/diseases verified vs NCSU/UC IPM/Cornell (climbing support, deadhead-to-prolong-bloom, cool-season, powdery+downy mildew, aphid/thrips virus vectors). FIXES (minor): softened the beginner 'they actually like a touch of lime' -> 'tolerate a touch of lime' (the pH range 6.5-7.5 sits within NCSU's stated 6-8); de-named the unverified anthracnose binomial 'Glomerella cingulata' -> 'Anthracnose'. Spacing 3-6in (vs Cornell ~8in) kept as legit intensive cut-flower spacing. Reviewed by agent + main-loop self-verify of the toxicity section (the agent's WebFetch was network-blocked; verified via search).

open_findings.summary: Regional planting/harvest windows and the fall-vs-early-spring sowing split are MODELED from sweet pea's documented cool-season biology (NC State: cool-weather annual, challenging in hot humid summers; UC IPM: in warm-winter areas plant early for early spring bloom; Cornell: sow mid-late March in Zone 5, thrives cool, seedlings tolerate cold) plus each region's frost climatology (frost dates carried from the certified frost-anchored roster). The catalogued T1 sweet-pea pages do not publish region-by-region dated planting charts, so exact months are a climate-informed model to tighten at variety-pass.

The summer heat_pause months in every warm region are HAND-AUTHORED, not carried from nasturtium (which is warm-season and paused far less). The THERMAL FACT is sourced (sweet pea is cool-season and declines rapidly in heat: NC State, UC IPM). The precise per-region heat_pause months (e.g. desert Apr-Sep, se_gulf/ca_interior May-Sep, FL May-Oct, south-coast Jun-Sep, warm northern zones Jul-Aug) are MODELED on that documented cool-preference plus each region's summer climate and the certified cool-season peer lettuce-leaf's heat_pause pattern; no T1 sweet-pea page publishes dated summer-exclusion tables. Note the deliberate boundary: the cool CA north coast carries only a light late-summer (Aug-Sep) decline, and cold northern zones 3-5 carry NO heat_pause at all (cool summers let bloom run to frost).

pH preferred 6.5 to 7.5 (tolerated 6.0 to 7.8, neutral to slightly alkaline, lime-responsive) reflects widely stated horticultural consensus and NC State's high-organic-matter soil guidance, but none of the four catalogued T1 pages I read stated an explicit numeric pH range for sweet pea; the range is modeled and cited to the nearest source (NC State soil). Confirm against a pH-stating extension source at variety-pass.

days_to_maturity 65 to 100 (mid 85) as days from sowing to first bloom, germination_temp_f 55 to 65, germination 10 to 21 days, and spacing 3 to 6 in are representative values: Cornell gives germination near 60 F in 10 to 21 days, 2 to 4 plants per foot on a trellis, and a mid-late-March sowing blooming mid-late June in Zone 5 (roughly 12 to 14 weeks); NC State gives bloom May-July. No single T1 page prints one days-to-bloom figure, so the range is synthesized from these and flagged.

hawaii_tropical is lowest-confidence: sweet pea is a cool-season plant that is genuinely marginal in the tropical lowlands and is best at cooler elevations or in the coolest winter months. The single z11 cell is modeled as a late-fall-sown winter attempt with a long warm-month heat_pause (Apr-Oct), cited to NC State and UC IPM cool-season/heat-decline guidance rather than a Hawaii-specific sweet-pea calendar. Confirm or drop in review.

In cold zones 6-7 within the northern tier, the single spring cohort is modeled as ending with a midsummer heat_pause (Jul-Aug) rather than resuming (sweet pea cannot be re-sown for a fall bloom in a short season), while cooler zones 3-5 carry continuous cool-summer bloom to frost with no heat_pause. This split, and the succession_policy (suitable but with a low realized count clustered in the cool shoulders, since heat and not plant age ends the crop), are modeled judgment calls consistent with the cool-season peer and sweet pea's single-flush biology.

crops.deadheading_seasoned: For sweet pea, cutting and deadheading are the same job and the single biggest lever on bloom length. Harvest flowers for the vase while the lowest one or two blooms on a stem are just opening, and remove any developing seed pods promptly: once the plant sets seed it reads the season as finished and stops flowering. Keep every stem picked and no pods maturing, and a healthy plant flowers for weeks longer before summer heat ends it. Leave a few pods to ripen and dry only if you deliberately want to save seed at the end of the season.
crops.deadheading_beginner: With sweet peas, picking the flowers is how you keep them blooming. Cut stems often for the vase, and snip off any little seed pods you see forming. If the plant is allowed to make seeds, it thinks its job is done and quits flowering. So the trick is simple: keep cutting the flowers and never let pods develop, and the plant keeps making more blooms until summer heat stops it. Only leave a few pods to dry at the very end if you want to collect seeds for next year.

3.planting_note: Sweet pea is a cool-season flower here: start seed indoors about 6 weeks early or direct-sow as soon as the soil is workable, since the young plants tolerate frost. Cut flowers often and remove pods; bloom runs through the cool summer, ending with heat or the first hard frost.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: July and August are a summer heat gap: sweet pea is a cool-season annual that stops flowering and yellows once sustained warmth arrives, and in these warmer northern zones midsummer heat ends the single spring cohort (no second crop is sown before winter). Not a frost gap but a summer heat exclusion. (NC State Extension; UC IPM)

northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In the northern tier, sweet pea thrives in the cool climate. Start seed indoors about 6 weeks before setting out, or direct-sow as soon as the ground is workable in early spring, since the young plants tolerate frost; a 5 to 6 ft trellis, deep rich soil, and steady moisture do the rest. Plants flower through the cool summer and, in the coolest zones, well into fall, ending with heat or the first hard frost. Grow it lean on nitrogen, cut constantly, and remove pods to keep bloom coming. Keep it away from edible peas, and remember the seeds and pods are poisonous.
northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: Sweet peas love the cool weather of the northern tier. Start seeds indoors about six weeks early, or plant them right in the ground as soon as it can be worked in spring, because young plants handle frost. Give them a 5 to 6 ft trellis, rich soil, and steady water. They bloom through the cooler summer, ending at the first hard frost. Cut flowers often and pull off seed pods to keep more coming. Do not plant them near your edible peas, and remember the seeds and pods are poisonous.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: The cool, foggy north coast is ideal sweet pea country: fall or late-winter sowings into rich, well-drained soil give a long run of fragrant, long-stemmed cut flowers from late winter through spring and into summer, easing only as late summer arrives. Give a 5 to 6 ft trellis, keep evenly moist, feed moderately, pinch to branch, and cut constantly while removing pods. Watch for aphids, thrips, and powdery mildew. Keep it away from edible peas; the seeds and pods are poisonous.

crops.name: Radish Microgreens
crops.sunlight: bright indirect light or a grow light
crops.water: keep the medium evenly moist; mist during blackout, then bottom-water once greened to keep leaves dry

soil.preferred_texture_seasoned: A fine, moisture-holding soilless medium: seed-starting mix, coconut coir, or a hydroponic fiber mat. Radish is a large brassica seed, so a firm even surface it can press into gives the most uniform stand.
soil.preferred_texture_beginner: Use a fine, soil-free growing medium that holds moisture well, such as seed-starting mix, coconut coir, or a growing mat. Radish seed is large and sprouts strongly, so it does well on any of these.
soil.tolerated_texture_seasoned: Peat-based mixes and inert mats both work; the choice trades water-holding against a cleaner cut, and radish is forgiving on either.
soil.tolerated_texture_beginner: Both peat-based mixes and fiber mats work well. Mixes hold more water, while mats stay cleaner at harvest, so pick whichever suits you.
soil.problematic_texture_seasoned: Garden soil and heavy potting mixes are too coarse and carry pathogen and pest risk for a raw, densely sown crop.
soil.problematic_texture_beginner: Skip garden soil and regular potting mix. They are too coarse, and they can carry pests and germs that are risky for a crowded crop you eat raw.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Use a light seed-starting mix, coconut coir, or a growing mat made for microgreens. Do not use garden soil.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: A clean, fine, moisture-retentive soilless medium gives even germination and a clean cut; coir and fiber mats keep grit off the harvest.

ph.note_seasoned: pH is not a practical lever for a single short indoor radish cycle on a soilless medium; standard seed-starting mixes and coir sit in a workable range and need no adjustment.
ph.note_beginner: You do not need to worry about soil pH for radish microgreens. The mixes and mats sold for microgreens are already fine as is.

fertilizer.timing: not applicable
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Radish microgreens are cut long before they exhaust the seed's own reserves, so no fertilizer is needed for a single cycle on an inert medium or seed-starting mix. Added nutrients mainly raise the risk of algae and off-flavors.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: You do not need to feed radish microgreens. The seed carries enough food to reach harvest, and adding fertilizer just invites algae and odd flavors.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: None.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: None needed.

companions.note_seasoned: Not applicable. Radish microgreens are grown as a dense single-type indoor tray, so there is no interplanting or companion relationship. Grow the tray on its own and combine with other greens after harvest.
companions.note_beginner: Not applicable. Radish microgreens grow as one type per tray indoors, so there are no companion plants. If you want a mix, just combine trays after cutting.

pests.description_seasoned: Small dark flies whose larvae live in persistently wet medium and feed on organic matter and tender roots. They are the main indoor microgreen pest and a symptom of an over-wet tray rather than a primary threat; radish's short, vigorous cycle usually finishes before they build up.
pests.description_beginner: Tiny dark flies that show up around constantly damp medium. Their larvae live in the wet mix. They are the main bug you might see, and they usually mean the tray is staying too wet. Radish grows so fast you often cut before they matter.
pests.management_seasoned: Let the surface dry between waterings where the crop allows, bottom-water, and keep airflow up. Because the radish cycle is so short, most trays are harvested before gnats become a real problem; sanitized trays and fresh medium between cycles break the cycle.
pests.management_beginner: Keep the surface from staying soaking wet, water from the bottom, and keep air moving. Since radish microgreens are harvested so fast, gnats rarely get bad before you cut. Clean trays and fresh mix between batches keep them away.

diseases.description_seasoned: Soil-borne fungi (Rhizoctonia, Botrytis, and others) rot seedlings at the base under wet, crowded, still conditions, often alongside fuzzy white or gray surface mold favored by warm, humid air. Radish is one of the least trouble-prone microgreens, so this shows up mainly when a tray is overwatered or sown too thickly.
diseases.description_beginner: In wet, crowded, stuffy conditions, tiny fungi rot the baby plants at the base, and you often see fuzzy white or gray mold too. Radish is one of the easiest, least problem-prone microgreens, so this usually only happens if the tray is too wet or sown too thickly.
diseases.management_seasoned: Prevention is the whole game: wrung-sponge moisture, bottom-watering once greened, constant gentle airflow, a sensible seeding rate, and sanitized trays between cycles. There is no rescue spray for a raw cut crop; a badly affected tray is composted and restarted clean. Note that radish's abundant fine white root hairs are often mistaken for mold; a light mist flattens root hairs and they rebound as they dry, while mold stays matted and spreads.
diseases.management_beginner: You cannot spray this away on a crop you eat raw, so the fix is prevention: keep the mix just damp (not soggy), water from the bottom once the leaves are up, keep a small fan running, do not sow too thickly, and clean trays between batches. One radish quirk: the fine white fuzz at the base is usually harmless root hairs, not mold. A quick mist flattens root hairs, while real mold stays matted and smells musty.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Mist once or twice daily through germination and the brief blackout to hold even surface moisture; once greened, bottom-water as the tray dries.
watering.frequency_beginner: While the seeds are sprouting, lightly mist the surface once or twice a day so it stays damp. After you move the tray into the light, water from the bottom whenever it starts to dry out.
watering.amount_seasoned: Enough to keep the medium at wrung-sponge moisture, never saturated; pour off any standing water after bottom-watering.
watering.amount_beginner: Just enough to keep the medium damp like a wrung-out sponge, never soggy. After bottom-watering, tip out any water left sitting in the tray.
watering.method_seasoned: Mist during germination and blackout; switch to bottom-watering once the canopy is up so foliage stays dry.
watering.method_beginner: Mist the top while the seeds are sprouting, then water from the bottom once the leaves are up so the leaves stay dry.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Standing water, a sour smell, fuzzy matted growth on the medium or stems, and collapsed seedlings all signal overwatering and the damping-off that follows it.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Water sitting in the tray, a bad smell, fuzzy matted mold, or seedlings flopping over mean it is too wet. Cut back on water and improve airflow.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Curling, limp cotyledons and a medium that has pulled away from the tray edges indicate the canopy has dried too far between waterings.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Limp, curling leaves and medium that has shrunk away from the sides mean it got too dry. Water from the bottom right away.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Wet foliage in a dense, still canopy is the main driver of mold and damping-off, so the cycle moves deliberately from misting to bottom-watering and pairs it with constant gentle airflow.
watering.method_note_beginner: Wet leaves packed close together with no air movement is what causes mold. That is why you switch to watering from the bottom once the leaves are up, and keep a gentle fan going.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The blackout-to-light transition is the highest-risk window: the canopy is dense, humidity under the cover is high, and a single overwatering here can seed damping-off across the whole tray.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The riskiest time is right when you uncover the tray and move it into the light. The plants are crowded and damp, so do not overwater, and make sure air is moving.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Do not hold cut radish microgreens at room temperature; they wilt and spoil within hours. Refrigerate immediately after cutting.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Do not leave cut radish microgreens out on the counter. They go limp fast, so put them in the fridge right after cutting.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerate dry in a vented container lined with a paper towel. Radish is one of the sturdier types and often holds close to 2 weeks, longer than tender greens that keep about 5 to 7 days. Do not wash before storing; surface moisture shortens shelf life.
storage.fridge_beginner: Keep cut radish microgreens in the fridge in a container with a paper towel to soak up extra moisture. Radish is one of the longer-keeping types and can last close to 2 weeks. Do not wash them before storing, since extra water makes them spoil faster.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Not recommended. Freezing collapses the delicate cells and ruins the texture. Radish microgreens are a fresh, cut-and-eat crop.
storage.freezer_beginner: Do not freeze radish microgreens. Freezing turns them mushy. They are meant to be eaten fresh.
storage.notes_seasoned: Cut clean and dry: harvest with sanitized scissors into a clean container, keep the foliage dry, and chill promptly. Because they are eaten raw, extension food-safety guidance is not to wash them after harvest, since post-harvest washing can bruise tissue and invite contamination; the same clean-tool, clean-surface rules that govern growing govern handling.
storage.notes_beginner: Because you eat radish microgreens raw, keep everything clean: cut them with clean scissors into a clean, dry container and refrigerate right away. It is better not to rinse them after cutting, since washing bruises them and makes them spoil faster.

recommended.name: Daikon
recommended.note: White stems, green leaves; peppery with a strong radish bite. Fast and vigorous; no presoak.

recommended.name: China Rose
recommended.note: Bright pink stems; milder, slightly sweet spice. Popular for color; no presoak.

recommended.name: Rambo
recommended.note: Deep purple stems and leaves; mildly spicy. Grown mostly for its color; no presoak.

recommended.name: Sango
recommended.note: Purple-stemmed type similar to Rambo; peppery and colorful. No presoak.

recommended.name: Red Arrow
recommended.note: Bright pink stems, light green leaves; fast and flavorful. No presoak.

varieties.note_seasoned: Radish is among the fastest, most vigorous, and most beginner-proof microgreens: the large seed germinates strongly with no presoak, needs only a short blackout, and finishes in roughly a week. The signature flavor is the peppery, pungent bite radish is known for, and it is described in extension trials as nutty and spicy. Named types differ mostly in stem color rather than growing method: white-stemmed Daikon runs strongest in spice, pink-stemmed China Rose and Red Arrow are milder and colorful, and purple Rambo or Sango are grown chiefly for their deep color. All are handled identically. Never grow microgreens from solanaceous seed (tomato, pepper, eggplant), whose seedlings carry alkaloids and are not safe to eat raw.
varieties.note_beginner: Radish is one of the easiest and fastest microgreens to grow, which makes it a great first crop. The big seeds sprout strongly without soaking, need only a couple of dark days, and are usually ready in about a week. They taste peppery, like a spicy radish. The named kinds mostly just differ in color: Daikon has white stems and the most bite, China Rose and Red Arrow have pink stems and milder flavor, and Rambo and Sango have striking purple stems. You grow them all the same way. One safety rule for any microgreen: never grow them from tomato, pepper, or eggplant seed, as those baby plants are not safe to eat.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Not applicable. Radish microgreens are never moved outdoors or transplanted; the whole cycle is indoors.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: Not applicable. Radish microgreens stay indoors from seed to harvest, so there is no hardening off.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Sow densely and evenly across pre-moistened medium, roughly 40 grams of seed per standard 1020 tray. Radish is a large brassica seed that germinates strongly, so it needs no presoak: sow it dry. Do not bury the seed; press it into firm contact, then cover for a short blackout of about 1 to 3 days under a light weight. Even seed-to-medium contact is what gives a uniform stand and a clean single cut.
start_method.notes_beginner: Scatter the seeds thickly and evenly over damp growing medium, about 40 grams for a standard tray. Radish seed is large and sprouts easily, so you do not need to soak it first; just sow it dry. Do not bury the seeds, press them down so they touch the surface, then cover the tray to keep it dark for a day to a few days.

drainage.saucer_practice_seasoned: Nest the drilled tray inside a solid, hole-free tray. The outer tray catches runoff, lets you bottom-water, and is poured off so the crop never sits in standing water.
drainage.saucer_practice_beginner: Set the tray with holes inside a second solid tray with no holes. The bottom tray lets you water from below and catch extra water, which you then pour out so the roots are not sitting in water.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Seed-starting mix, coconut coir, or a microgreen growing mat.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: None needed.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: Seed-starting mix, coir, or an inert fiber mat; about 1 to 2 inches deep.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: None; the medium is a substrate, not a nutrient source, for a single cycle.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Water from the bottom by setting the tray in a little water, then pour off what is left.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: No fertilizer needed.

overwintering.approach_seasoned: Not applicable. Radish microgreens are an indoor year-round cycle crop, harvested in days, with no dormant or overwintered phase.
overwintering.approach_beginner: Not applicable. Radish microgreens grow indoors all year and are harvested within a couple of weeks, so there is nothing to overwinter.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: The tray is the entire growing system: shallow, drained, nested over a solid tray for bottom-watering, sanitized between cycles. A clean, reused, food-grade tray beats a single-use clamshell for both food safety and consistent results.
container_notes.notes_beginner: For radish microgreens, the tray is the whole setup. Use a shallow tray with drainage holes sitting inside a solid tray so you can water from the bottom. Wash and sanitize trays between batches.
