container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Bottom-water from the nesting tray; never leave the tray standing in water.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: None for a single cycle.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering reservoirs keep the medium too wet for a dense raw crop and raise the damping-off risk; bottom-water by hand and pour off the excess instead.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: Skip self-watering pots for microgreens. They keep things too wet, which causes mold. Water from the bottom by hand and tip out the extra.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: A shallow flat tray works best: a 1020-style tray or any shallow food-safe container, with about 1 to 2 inches of medium. Depth beyond that wastes mix without helping a crop that is cut in days.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Use a shallow, wide tray, like a standard 1020 tray or any clean food-safe container. About 1 to 2 inches of growing mix is plenty. You do not need anything deep.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Not applicable. Radish microgreens grow on fresh or sanitized medium each cycle with no soil-borne carryover, so crop rotation does not apply.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Not applicable. You use fresh growing medium and clean trays each time, so there is nothing to rotate.
rotation.note_seasoned: Sanitation between cycles, not rotation, is the disease control for radish microgreens: compost the spent medium, then wash and sanitize the tray before the next sow.
rotation.note_beginner: Instead of rotating crops, just keep things clean: toss the used medium and wash and sanitize the tray before starting again.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Dense even broadcast of dry radish seed on pre-moistened medium, roughly 40 grams per 1020 tray; no presoak.
growth_stages.description_beginner: Scatter radish seeds thickly on damp medium. No soaking needed.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Large radish seed imbibes and splits fast under a weighted cover at about 70 to 75 °F; germination is strong and even.
growth_stages.description_beginner: The big seeds sprout quickly under a covered, warm tray.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Short dark period (about 1 to 3 days) that stretches stems and evens the stand before light.
growth_stages.description_beginner: A day or two in the dark that makes the stems stretch evenly.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Uncovered into 18 hours of light at about 68 to 72 °F; cotyledons green and the first true leaf may show.
growth_stages.description_beginner: Uncovered into bright light so the leaves turn green.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Single cut at cotyledon to first-true-leaf, often about a week from sowing; eaten fresh.
growth_stages.description_beginner: Snip and eat when the little leaves are open, usually about a week after planting.

notifications.message_seasoned: Check whether the canopy has lifted. Radish blackout is short, so it may already be time to uncover into light.
notifications.message_beginner: Time to check your tray: if the sprouts are up, uncover it and give it light.

notifications.message_seasoned: Switch from misting to bottom-watering now that the canopy is up, and make sure a fan is running.
notifications.message_beginner: Now that the leaves are up, water from the bottom and keep a fan going.

notifications.message_seasoned: Radish is usually at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage now, so cut and refrigerate promptly.
notifications.message_beginner: Your radish microgreens are likely ready to snip. Cut them and put them in the fridge.

notifications.message_seasoned: Start your next tray to keep the staggered supply going.
notifications.message_beginner: Start a new tray so you always have microgreens coming.

sow.text_seasoned: Pre-moisten the medium to wrung-sponge feel, then broadcast radish seed densely and evenly, roughly 40 grams per 1020 tray. Radish needs no presoak; sow it dry. Press seed into contact but do not bury it; buried seed greens poorly and traps moisture against the stems.
sow.text_beginner: Dampen the growing medium so it feels like a wrung-out sponge, then scatter radish seeds thickly and evenly. No soaking needed. Press the seeds down so they touch the surface, but do not cover them with medium.

germination.text_seasoned: Cover the tray and keep it warm (about 70 to 75 °F) and dark. Mist to hold even surface moisture, never soggy. A light weight on the cover keeps the large seed in firm contact so roots drive down rather than lifting the seed. Radish germinates fast and vigorously.
germination.text_beginner: Put the cover on and keep the tray warm (around 70 to 75 °F) and dark. Mist lightly so the surface stays damp but not wet. A small weight on the cover helps the roots push down. Radish sprouts fast.

blackout.text_seasoned: Hold the weighted cover in the dark for the short blackout, about 1 to 3 days for radish, then uncover. The brief dark stretch lengthens and evens the stems before greening; radish rarely needs more than a couple of days.
blackout.text_beginner: Keep the covered tray in the dark for a short time, about 1 to 3 days for radish. The darkness makes the stems grow taller and more even before you give them light. Radish only needs a day or two.

light.text_seasoned: Uncover into 18 hours of bright light at about 68 to 72 °F and switch from misting to bottom-watering so foliage stays dry. Run a gentle fan; the dense canopy plus high humidity is the damping-off window. Harvest at cotyledon to first true leaf, often about a week from sowing.
light.text_beginner: Uncover the tray into bright light for about 18 hours a day at 68 to 72 °F, and start watering from the bottom so the leaves stay dry. Keep a gentle fan going to prevent mold. Cut when the first little leaves are open, usually about a week after planting.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Yield is measured per tray, not per plant: a well-sown 1020 tray of radish returns roughly 6 to 12 ounces of cut microgreens, and radish's vigor keeps a heavy sowing productive, though the 6-to-12-ounce figure is a modeled estimate at that density (Penn State's lighter-sown trial recorded about 4 ounces per tray).
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: You measure radish microgreens by the tray, not by each plant. A full tray usually gives you a few good handfuls (about 6 to 12 ounces), and radish is one of the more productive types.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Every tray is a single harvest at peak; continuous supply comes from staggered sowings, not from regrowth.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Each tray gives one harvest at its best. To keep a steady supply, start new trays every few days.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: There is no establishment year; the first tray performs the same as any later tray. Radish is forgiving, so even a first attempt usually succeeds.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: There is no waiting period with radish microgreens. Your very first tray works just like the rest, and radish is one of the easiest to get right on the first try.
factors_seasoned: seeding density (too sparse wastes the tray; too dense traps moisture and invites mold)
even moisture and the mist-to-bottom-water transition
constant gentle airflow
seed freshness (radish germinates strongly when fresh)
light intensity and the full 18-hour daily duration

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Not applicable. Radish microgreens are an indoor, light-controlled, seedling-stage crop with no lunar or seasonal timing.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Fuzzy, matted white or gray growth on the medium, stems, or seed; seedlings collapsing at the base
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Matted white or gray mold, or baby plants flopping over at the bottom
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Damping-off and mold from overwatering, a saturated medium, dense sowing, and poor airflow; radish is otherwise one of the least trouble-prone microgreens
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Too much water plus crowded plants and no air movement, which leads to mold. Radish rarely gets this unless the tray is too wet.
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Switch to bottom-watering, pour off standing water, run a gentle fan, thin your seeding rate next time, and sanitize trays between cycles. Do not bury seed at sowing.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Water from the bottom, tip out extra water, keep a small fan going, sow a little less thickly next time, and clean your trays between batches.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_seasoned: Wrung-sponge moisture, constant airflow, dry foliage, and sanitized trays prevent it.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_beginner: Keep the medium just damp, the air moving, the leaves dry, and the trays clean.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: A fine white fuzzy halo at the base of the stems, appearing a day or two after uncovering
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Fine white fuzz right where the stems meet the medium, showing up soon after uncovering
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Usually harmless root hairs, not mold: radish puts out abundant fine root hairs that ring the base of each stem. True mold sits on the medium or stems, smells musty, and does not vanish when misted
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Almost always root hairs, which are normal and healthy, not mold. Radish grows lots of tiny white root hairs around the base of the stems.
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Do the mist test: a light misting flattens root hairs and they rebound as they dry, while mold stays matted and spreads. If it is truly mold, improve airflow and cut back water.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Spray a little water on it. Root hairs flatten and bounce back as they dry; real mold stays matted and smells bad. If it is mold, add airflow and water less.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_seasoned: Even moisture, airflow, and not over-sowing keep true mold away; root hairs need no action.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_beginner: Keep airflow up and do not overwater. Root hairs are fine and need nothing.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Tall, pale, weak stems that fall over
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Long, thin, pale stems that flop
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Too little light, or light introduced too late after a drawn-out blackout
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Not enough light, or leaving the tray covered too long
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Uncover on time (radish blackout is short) and give bright light for the full 18 hours; move closer to the grow light or a brighter window.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Uncover the tray on schedule and give it bright light for about 18 hours a day, closer to the light.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_seasoned: End the short blackout once the canopy lifts and provide adequate light intensity and duration.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_beginner: Take the cover off as soon as the sprouts are up and give them plenty of light.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Patchy, uneven germination across the tray
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Some spots sprout, others stay bare
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Uneven sowing, dry spots, no weighted cover, or old seed; uncommon with fresh radish, which germinates strongly
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Seeds spread unevenly, dry spots, no weight on the cover, or old seed. Radish usually sprouts evenly when the seed is fresh.
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Sow evenly on pre-moistened medium, use a weighted cover for even seed-to-medium contact, and use fresh radish seed.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Spread seeds evenly on damp medium, put a light weight on the cover, and use fresh seed.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_seasoned: Even sow, even moisture, weighted blackout cover, fresh seed.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_beginner: Even seeds, even moisture, a weighted cover, and fresh seed.

indoor_cycle.tip_seasoned: The cycle is sow -> blackout -> light -> harvest, and radish is among the fastest to run it. Germinate at about 70 to 75 °F under a weighted cover in the dark for a short blackout (about 1 to 3 days), uncover into 18 hours of light at about 68 to 72 °F to green up, then cut at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage. Most trays finish in about 7 to 12 days, often around a week.
indoor_cycle.tip_beginner: Radish microgreens follow four steps: plant, keep dark, give light, then harvest, and they are one of the fastest to grow. Keep the covered tray warm (around 70 to 75 °F) and dark for a day to a few days while the seeds sprout, then uncover it into bright light (about 68 to 72 °F) for roughly 18 hours a day until the leaves green up. Most are ready in about a week.

primary.name: Utah State University Extension -- Grow Your Own Microgreens
University of Nevada, Reno Extension -- Microgreens and Produce Safety (PubID 3468)

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: For a steady supply, stagger sowings: start a fresh tray every 3 to 5 days rather than one big tray at once. Radish's roughly one-week cycle makes it easy to keep a rolling supply going. Indoors there is no season, so the cadence is limited only by your tray count and counter space.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: To always have radish microgreens ready, start a new tray every few days instead of one big batch. Because they grow fast and indoors, you can keep this going all year.
succession_policy.notes: successions and max_successions_per_season are intentionally null: radish microgreens run continuously year-round indoors, so there is no season length to cap against. The practical limit is tray count and counter space, not climate (window_type: continuous_indoor).

verification_status.verification_log_ref: Batch-2 Wave-5 cert (2026-07-06, Trevor-ruled). microgreen; the fastest/easiest (7-12 days, no presoak, verbatim USU). NUTRITION/HEALTH over-claim CLEAN (declines PSU's vitamin line). Sprout-vs-microgreen CLEAN. FIXES: fungus-gnat pest -> UC IPM pn7448; damping-off de-named 'Pythium' -> 'Rhizoctonia, Botrytis, and others' + trimmed to psu_microgreens; YIELD softened (Trevor-ruled) -- dropped the 'toward the higher end' superlative, reframed the 6-12oz as a modeled estimate at the heavy seeding density used here and DISCLOSED PSU's lighter-sown ~4oz trial (yield re-anchored to psu, usu dropped); solanaceous-seed alkaloid warning anchored to LSU AgCenter microgreens guide (Trevor ruled SOURCE it); storage dropped usu + added psu; UNR URL updated to naes.unr.edu/dfi.

open_findings.summary: days_to_maturity / indoor_cycle.days_to_harvest [7,12] (mid 8): the ceiling of 12 and the 8-12 core are from usu_ext (radish 8 to 12 days); the 7-day floor reflects radish's reputation as among the fastest microgreens (PSU ABCs, read but uncatalogued, gives a 7 to 8 day very short cycle) and is grower-norm, modeled, not a single catalogued cited number.

The fine white root-hairs-versus-mold distinction (a fuzzy white halo at the stem base that a mist test tells apart from true mold) is horticultural common knowledge and grower guidance, not stated on a Tier-1 extension page; cited to the nearest Tier-1 mold/damping-off discussion (psu_microgreens, usu_ext). Framed as guidance, flagged as modeled.

Named cultivars (Daikon, China Rose, Rambo, Sango, Red Arrow) and their per-variety stem color / spice-intensity notes are seed-catalog norms, not drawn from a Tier-1 microgreen cultivar chart. Species-level flavor (peppery, pungent, described as nutty and spicy) and the no-presoak / fast-cycle handling ARE Tier-1 (usu_ext). Confirm cultivar details at variety-delta pass.

Harvest height (roughly at cotyledon to first-true-leaf; typical a few inches) is modeled from the general microgreen harvest stage; USU states harvest at first true leaves or sooner but gives no radish-specific height. Yield (6 to 12 oz per 1020 tray, radish toward the high end) uses the certified template's per-tray range plus radish vigor; OSU lists ~0.27 lb for daikon in one trial. Both modeled to sourced ranges.

germination_temp_f [65,75] is a modeled practical band: PSU Growing Microgreens gives 60 to 75 °F for germination and USU germinates at 74 °F; radish germinates strongly across a broad range, so the band is set slightly wider than the microgreens-mix [68,74] to reflect radish's forgiving germination. Blackout stated as 1 to 3 days where Tier-1 lists 1 to 2 for radish (the 3rd day is common grower practice for more stem stretch).

PSU 'The ABCs of Microgreens' (extension.psu.edu/the-abcs-of-microgreens), a real Tier-1 page read via WebFetch that corroborates radish's Brassicaceae identity and very short 7-8 day cycle, is NOT in the dataset source_catalog, so it is deliberately NOT cited (source-tier gate E requires catalogued T1 ids and the catalog is a top-level canonical key outside this record). All cited claims rest on catalogued sources (usu_ext, psu_microgreens, unr_ext). Admit psu_abcs to the catalog to upgrade the flavor/cycle citations.

crops.description_seasoned: Radish microgreens are the young seedlings of the radish (Raphanus sativus), a brassica, harvested at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage roughly a week after sowing. They are among the fastest, most vigorous, and most beginner-proof microgreens: the large seed germinates strongly with no presoak, needs only a short dark blackout, and finishes in about 7 to 12 days. The flavor is a distinct peppery, pungent radish bite, and named types range from white-stemmed Daikon through pink China Rose and Red Arrow to deep-purple Rambo and Sango for color. They are grown indoors year-round in the same short cycle every time: a dense even sow on a shallow tray of mix or a fiber mat, a brief blackout to even the stand, then light to green up, then a single cut. Because there is no frost, season, or hardiness zone involved, the tray grows identically on any windowsill.
crops.description_beginner: Radish microgreens are baby radish plants that you harvest very young, about a week after planting, when they are just a couple of inches tall. They are one of the easiest and fastest microgreens to grow, which makes them a great first crop: the big seeds sprout strongly without any soaking, need only a day or two in the dark, and are usually ready in about 7 to 12 days. They taste peppery, like a spicy radish, and different kinds have white, pink, or purple stems. You grow them indoors all year with the same steps every time: scatter seeds thickly, cover the tray to keep it dark for a couple of days while they sprout, move it into the light to green up, then snip and eat. There is no outdoor season or weather to worry about, so they grow the same way no matter where you live.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Cut at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage, typically about 7 to 12 days from sowing and often around a week, since radish is one of the fastest microgreens. Snip just above the medium with clean scissors; the stand will not regrow, so the tray is a single cut.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Your radish microgreens are ready when the first little seed-leaves are open and the first true leaf is just showing, usually about a week after sowing (radish is fast). Snip them just above the medium with clean scissors and eat them fresh. They do not grow back, so you start a new tray each time.

crops.name: Broccoli Microgreens
crops.sunlight: bright indirect light or a grow light
crops.water: keep the medium evenly moist; bottom-water once greened to keep leaves dry

soil.preferred_texture_seasoned: A fine, moisture-holding soilless medium: a clean seed-starting mix, coconut coir, or a hydroponic fiber mat (hemp, jute, or similar). Broccoli's small seed sits on the surface, so an even, fine texture gives uniform germination and a clean cut.
soil.preferred_texture_beginner: Use a fine, soil-free growing medium that holds moisture, such as seed-starting mix, coconut coir, or a growing mat made for microgreens. A smooth, even surface helps the tiny broccoli seeds sprout evenly.
soil.tolerated_texture_seasoned: Peat-based mixes and inert mats both work for broccoli; the choice trades water-holding against a cleaner harvest.
soil.tolerated_texture_beginner: Both peat-based mixes and fiber mats work well. Mixes hold more water, while mats stay cleaner at harvest, so pick whichever suits you.
soil.problematic_texture_seasoned: Garden soil and heavy potting mixes are too coarse for a small seed and carry pathogen and pest risk for a dense crop eaten raw.
soil.problematic_texture_beginner: Skip garden soil and regular potting mix. They are too coarse for tiny broccoli seed, and they can carry pests and germs that are risky for a crowded crop you eat raw.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Use a light seed-starting mix, coconut coir, or a microgreen growing mat. Do not use garden soil.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: A clean, fine, moisture-retentive soilless medium gives broccoli even germination and a clean cut; coir and fiber mats keep grit off the harvest.

ph.note_seasoned: pH is not a practical lever for a single short indoor cycle on a soilless medium; standard seed-starting mixes and coir sit in a workable range and need no adjustment for broccoli.
ph.note_beginner: You do not need to worry about soil pH for broccoli microgreens. The mixes and mats sold for microgreens are already fine as is.

fertilizer.timing: not applicable
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Broccoli microgreens are cut in about 8 to 12 days, well before they exhaust the seed's own reserves, so no fertilizer is needed for a single cycle on an inert medium or seed-starting mix. Little or no feeding is the norm; clear water grows a good tray, and added nutrients mainly raise the risk of algae and off-flavors.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: You do not need to feed broccoli microgreens. The seed carries enough food to reach harvest in a week or two, and adding fertilizer just invites algae and odd flavors. Plain water is all they need.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: None.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: None needed.

companions.note_seasoned: Not applicable. Broccoli microgreens are grown as a dense single-type indoor tray, so there is no interplanting or companion relationship. Grow the tray on its own and combine with other cut microgreens after harvest if you want a mix.
companions.note_beginner: Not applicable. Broccoli microgreens grow as one type per tray indoors, so there are no companion plants. If you want a blend, just combine different trays after cutting.

pests.description_seasoned: Small dark flies whose larvae live in persistently wet medium and feed on organic matter and tender roots. On a broccoli tray they are a symptom of an over-wet medium rather than a primary threat, and the short cycle usually beats them.
pests.description_beginner: Tiny dark flies that show up around constantly damp medium. Their larvae live in the wet mix. They usually just mean the tray is staying too wet.
pests.management_seasoned: Let the surface dry between waterings where the crop allows, bottom-water, and keep airflow up. Because broccoli finishes in about 8 to 12 days, most trays are cut before gnats build to a real problem; sanitized trays and fresh medium between cycles break the cycle.
pests.management_beginner: Keep the surface from staying soaking wet, water from the bottom, and keep air moving. Since broccoli microgreens are harvested so fast, gnats rarely get bad before you cut. Clean trays and fresh mix between batches keep them away.

diseases.description_seasoned: Soil-borne fungi and water molds (Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Fusarium) rot seedlings at the base under wet, crowded, still conditions, often alongside fuzzy white cobweb-like growth on the medium and stems. Broccoli is a small, densely sown brassica and is notably prone to it; on Penn State's trials damping-off was the only disease or pest issue encountered.
diseases.description_beginner: The most common broccoli microgreen problem. In wet, crowded, stuffy conditions, tiny fungi rot the baby plants right at the base, and you often see fuzzy white mold on the surface and stems too. Broccoli is packed in tightly, so it is especially prone to this.
diseases.management_seasoned: Prevention is the whole game: wrung-sponge moisture, bottom-watering (sub-irrigation keeps foliage dry), constant gentle airflow from a small fan, a sensible seeding rate, and sanitized trays with fresh medium between cycles. There is no rescue spray for a raw cut crop; a badly affected tray is composted and restarted clean.
diseases.management_beginner: You cannot spray this away on a crop you eat raw, so the fix is prevention: keep the mix just damp (not soggy), water from the bottom so the leaves stay dry, keep a small fan running, do not sow too thickly, and use clean trays and fresh mix each batch. If a tray molds badly, toss it and start over with clean equipment.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Mist once or twice daily through germination and blackout to hold even surface moisture; once greened, bottom-water as the tray dries.
watering.frequency_beginner: While the seeds are sprouting, lightly mist the surface once or twice a day so it stays damp. After you move the tray into the light, water from the bottom whenever it starts to dry out.
watering.amount_seasoned: Enough to keep the medium at wrung-sponge moisture, never saturated; pour off any standing water after bottom-watering.
watering.amount_beginner: Just enough to keep the medium damp like a wrung-out sponge, never soggy. After bottom-watering, tip out any water left sitting in the tray.
watering.method_seasoned: Mist during germination and blackout; switch to bottom-watering (sub-irrigation) once the canopy is up so broccoli's dense foliage stays dry.
watering.method_beginner: Mist the top while the seeds are sprouting, then water from the bottom once the leaves are up so the leaves stay dry.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Standing water, a sour or musty smell, fuzzy white growth spreading over the medium and stems, and seedlings collapsing at the base all signal overwatering and the damping-off that follows it.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Water sitting in the tray, a bad smell, fuzzy white mold on the mix and stems, or seedlings flopping over mean it is too wet. Cut back on water and improve airflow.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Curling, limp cotyledons and a medium that has pulled away from the tray edges indicate the canopy has dried too far between waterings.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Limp, curling leaves and mix that has shrunk away from the sides mean it got too dry. Water from the bottom right away.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Wet foliage in a dense, still canopy is the main driver of mold and damping-off on broccoli, so the cycle moves deliberately from misting to bottom-watering and pairs it with constant gentle airflow.
watering.method_note_beginner: Wet leaves packed close together with no air movement is what causes mold. That is why you switch to watering from the bottom once the leaves are up, and keep a gentle fan going.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The blackout-to-light transition is the highest-risk window: the canopy is dense, humidity under the cover is high, and a single overwatering here can seed damping-off across the whole tray.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The riskiest time is right when you uncover the tray and move it into the light. The plants are crowded and damp, so do not overwater, and make sure air is moving.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Do not hold cut broccoli microgreens at room temperature; they wilt within hours. Refrigerate immediately after cutting.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Do not leave cut broccoli microgreens out on the counter. They go limp fast, so put them in the fridge right after cutting.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Rinse, pat dry, and refrigerate in a vented container lined with a paper towel; broccoli is a tender brassica and keeps best used within about 5 to 7 days, up to about 10 with careful drying. Harvest only what you will use soon.
storage.fridge_beginner: Rinse cut broccoli microgreens, pat them dry, and keep them in the fridge in a container with a paper towel to soak up extra moisture. They are delicate, so use them within about a week (up to 10 days if kept dry).
storage.freezer_seasoned: Not recommended. Freezing collapses the delicate cells and ruins the texture. Broccoli microgreens are a fresh, cut-and-eat crop.
storage.freezer_beginner: Do not freeze broccoli microgreens. Freezing turns them mushy. They are meant to be eaten fresh.
storage.notes_seasoned: Cut clean and dry: harvest with sanitized scissors into a clean container, keep the foliage dry, and chill promptly. Because they are eaten raw, the same clean-water and sanitized-surface rules that govern growing also govern handling.
storage.notes_beginner: Because you eat broccoli microgreens raw, keep everything clean: cut them with clean scissors into a clean, dry container and refrigerate right away.

recommended.name: Standard broccoli (e.g. Calabrese, Waltham 29, Di Cicco)
recommended.note: Brassica oleracea var. italica; mild, fresh, faintly cabbage-like. About 8 to 12 days, no presoak. The usual choice and the one prized for its glucosinolate content.

recommended.name: Broccoli raab / rapini
recommended.note: A spicier, peppery alternative; botanically Brassica rapa (turnip family), not true broccoli. Finishes fast (about 6 to 10 days), no presoak. Use for a sharper, more mustard-like tray.

varieties.note_seasoned: For a mild, versatile tray, standard broccoli (Brassica oleracea var. italica) is the mainstay: small brassica seed sown densely and dry (no presoak), finishing in about 8 to 12 days. Broccoli is one of the microgreens most often grown for nutrition; like other brassica microgreens it concentrates the glucosinolates that give the cabbage family its character, and research finds microgreens generally higher in vitamins and phytochemicals than the mature vegetable. For a sharper tray, broccoli raab (rapini) is a peppery alternative, but note it is a different species (Brassica rapa, closer to turnip) rather than true broccoli. Never grow microgreens from solanaceous seed (tomato, pepper, eggplant); those seedlings are not safe to eat raw.
varieties.note_beginner: Standard broccoli is the go-to: a mild, fresh microgreen from small seeds you scatter dry (no soaking), ready in about 8 to 12 days. It is one of the most popular microgreens for nutrition, since broccoli and its relatives are packed with the healthy plant compounds the cabbage family is known for, and young microgreens tend to be richer in vitamins than full-grown plants. If you want more kick, broccoli raab (rapini) is a spicier, peppery option, though it is actually a close cousin (in the turnip family), not true broccoli. Never grow microgreens from tomato, pepper, or eggplant seed, as those baby plants are not safe to eat.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Not applicable. Broccoli microgreens are never moved outdoors or transplanted; the whole cycle is indoors.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: Not applicable. Broccoli microgreens stay indoors from seed to harvest, so there is no hardening off.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Sow densely and evenly across pre-moistened medium (about 28 grams, roughly 1 ounce, of broccoli seed per 1020 tray; small-seeded brassicas can go as dense as about 10 to 12 seeds per square inch). Broccoli takes no presoak; the seed goes on dry. Do not bury it; press it into firm contact, then cover for a dark blackout period. Dense, even contact is what gives a uniform stand and a clean single cut.
start_method.notes_beginner: Scatter broccoli seeds thickly and evenly over damp growing medium, about 1 ounce (28 grams) per standard 1020 tray. Do not soak them first; broccoli seed goes on dry. Do not bury the seeds, just press them down so they touch the surface, then cover the tray to keep it dark for a few days while they sprout.

drainage.saucer_practice_seasoned: Nest the drilled tray inside a solid, hole-free tray. The outer tray catches runoff, lets you bottom-water, and is poured off so the crop never sits in standing water.
drainage.saucer_practice_beginner: Set the tray with holes inside a second solid tray with no holes. The bottom tray lets you water from below and catch extra water, which you then pour out so the roots are not sitting in water.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Seed-starting mix, coconut coir, or a microgreen growing mat.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: None needed.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: Seed-starting mix, coir, or an inert fiber mat; about 1 to 2 inches deep.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: None; the medium is a substrate, not a nutrient source, for a single cycle.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Water from the bottom by setting the tray in a little water, then pour off what is left.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: No fertilizer needed.

overwintering.approach_seasoned: Not applicable. Broccoli microgreens are an indoor year-round cycle crop, harvested in days, with no dormant or overwintered phase.
overwintering.approach_beginner: Not applicable. Broccoli microgreens grow indoors all year and are harvested within a couple of weeks, so there is nothing to overwinter.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: The tray is the entire growing system: shallow, drained, nested over a solid tray for bottom-watering, sanitized between cycles. A clean, reused, food-grade tray beats a single-use clamshell for both food safety and consistent results.
container_notes.notes_beginner: For broccoli microgreens, the tray is the whole setup. Use a shallow tray with drainage holes sitting inside a solid tray so you can water from the bottom. Wash and sanitize trays between batches.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Bottom-water from the nesting tray; never leave the tray standing in water.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: None for a single cycle.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering reservoirs keep the medium too wet for a dense raw crop and raise the damping-off risk; bottom-water by hand and pour off the excess instead.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: Skip self-watering pots for broccoli microgreens. They keep things too wet, which causes mold. Water from the bottom by hand and tip out the extra.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: A shallow flat tray works best: a 1020-style tray or any shallow food-safe container, with about 1 to 2 inches of medium. Depth beyond that wastes mix without helping a crop that is cut in days.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Use a shallow, wide tray, like a standard 1020 tray or any clean food-safe container. About 1 to 2 inches of growing mix is plenty. You do not need anything deep.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Not applicable. Broccoli microgreens grow on fresh or sanitized medium each cycle with no soil-borne carryover, so crop rotation does not apply.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Not applicable. You use fresh growing medium and clean trays each time, so there is nothing to rotate.
rotation.note_seasoned: Sanitation between cycles, not rotation, is the disease control for broccoli microgreens: compost the spent medium, then wash and sanitize the tray before the next sow.
rotation.note_beginner: Instead of rotating crops, just keep things clean: toss the used medium and wash and sanitize the tray before starting again.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Dense, even, dry broadcast of broccoli seed on pre-moistened medium; no presoak.
growth_stages.description_beginner: Scatter broccoli seeds thickly on damp medium; no soaking needed.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Seeds imbibe and split under a weighted cover at about 74 °F; broccoli germinates fast, often within a day or two.
growth_stages.description_beginner: Seeds sprout quickly under a covered, warm tray.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Dark period of about 3 to 4 days (roughly 2 to 4 by conditions) that stretches stems and evens the stand before light.
growth_stages.description_beginner: A few days in the dark that make the stems stretch evenly.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Uncovered into 16 to 18 hours of light at 68 to 72 °F; cotyledons green and the first true leaf may form.
growth_stages.description_beginner: Uncovered into bright light so the leaves turn green.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Single cut at cotyledon to first-true-leaf, about 8 to 12 days from sowing; eaten fresh.
growth_stages.description_beginner: Snip and eat when the little leaves are open, usually in about 8 to 12 days.

notifications.message_seasoned: Check whether the canopy has lifted. Broccoli is usually ready to come out of blackout and into light around now.
notifications.message_beginner: Time to check your tray: if the sprouts are up, uncover it and give it light.

notifications.message_seasoned: Switch from misting to bottom-watering now that the canopy is up, and make sure a fan is running to head off damping-off.
notifications.message_beginner: Now that the leaves are up, water from the bottom and keep a fan going.

notifications.message_seasoned: Broccoli is at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage now, so cut and refrigerate promptly.
notifications.message_beginner: Your broccoli microgreens are likely ready to snip. Cut them and put them in the fridge.

notifications.message_seasoned: Start your next tray to keep the staggered supply going.
notifications.message_beginner: Start a new tray so you always have microgreens coming.

sow.text_seasoned: Pre-moisten the medium to wrung-sponge feel, then broadcast broccoli seed densely and evenly, about 28 grams (1 ounce) per 1020 tray. No presoak; broccoli goes on dry. Press seed into contact but do not bury it; buried seed greens poorly and traps moisture against the stems.
sow.text_beginner: Dampen the growing medium so it feels like a wrung-out sponge, then scatter broccoli seeds thickly and evenly (about 1 ounce per standard tray). Do not soak them first. Press the seeds down so they touch the surface, but do not cover them with soil.

germination.text_seasoned: Cover the tray and keep it warm (about 74 °F) and dark. Mist to hold even surface moisture, never soggy. A light weight on the cover keeps seed in firm contact so roots drive down rather than lifting the seed. Broccoli germinates fast, often within a day or two.
germination.text_beginner: Put the cover on and keep the tray warm (around 74 °F) and dark. Mist lightly so the surface stays damp but not wet. A small weight on the cover helps the roots push down. Broccoli sprouts quickly.

blackout.text_seasoned: Hold the weighted cover in the dark for about 3 to 4 days (roughly 2 to 4 by conditions), then take the cover off the canopy. The dark stretch lengthens and evens the stems before greening. Soon after germination you may see fine white fuzz on the roots; this is usually normal root hairs, not mold.
blackout.text_beginner: Keep the covered tray in the dark for about 3 to 4 days. The darkness makes the stems grow taller and more even before you give them light. If you see fuzzy white on the roots, do not panic; it is usually normal root hairs, not mold.

light.text_seasoned: Uncover into 16 to 18 hours of bright light at 68 to 72 °F and switch from misting to bottom-watering so foliage stays dry. Run a gentle fan; broccoli's dense canopy plus high humidity is the damping-off window. Harvest at cotyledon to first true leaf.
light.text_beginner: Uncover the tray into bright light for about 16 to 18 hours a day at 68 to 72 °F, and start watering from the bottom so the leaves stay dry. Keep a gentle fan going to prevent mold. Cut when the first little leaves are open.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Yield is measured per tray, not per plant: a well-sown 1020 tray of broccoli returns roughly 8 to 12 ounces of cut microgreens depending on seeding rate and conditions.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: You measure broccoli microgreens by the tray, not by each plant. A full tray usually gives you a few good handfuls (roughly 8 to 12 ounces).
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Every tray is a single harvest at peak; continuous supply comes from staggered sowings, not from regrowth.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Each tray gives one harvest at its best. To keep a steady supply, start new trays every few days.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: There is no establishment year; the first tray performs the same as any later tray. Expect to dial in seeding rate and watering over the first few cycles.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: There is no waiting period with microgreens. Your very first tray works just like the rest; you will get a feel for how much to sow and water after a few tries.
factors_seasoned: seeding density (too sparse wastes the tray; too dense traps moisture and invites damping-off)
even moisture and the mist-to-bottom-water transition
constant gentle airflow
seed freshness and microgreen-grade quality
light intensity and the full 16 to 18 hour daily duration

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Not applicable. Broccoli microgreens are an indoor, light-controlled, seedling-stage crop with no lunar or seasonal timing.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Fuzzy white or gray growth spreading over the medium, stems, or seed; seedlings collapsing at the base
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Fuzzy white or gray mold on the mix and stems, or baby plants flopping over at the bottom
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Damping-off and mold from overwatering, a saturated medium, dense sowing, and poor airflow; broccoli is small and packed tightly, so it is especially prone, and this is the number-one microgreen failure
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Too much water plus crowded plants and no air movement, which leads to mold. Broccoli is crowded, so it is especially prone. This is the most common microgreen problem.
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Switch to bottom-watering, pour off standing water, run a gentle fan, thin your seeding rate next time, and sanitize trays with fresh medium between cycles. Do not bury seed at sowing.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Water from the bottom, tip out extra water, keep a small fan going, sow a little less thickly next time, and use clean trays and fresh mix between batches.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_seasoned: Wrung-sponge moisture, constant airflow, dry foliage, a sensible seeding rate, and sanitized trays prevent it.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_beginner: Keep the mix just damp, the air moving, the leaves dry, and the trays clean.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Fine white fuzz on the roots and around the base soon after germination
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: A soft white halo of fuzz on the roots a day or two after sprouting
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Usually normal root hairs, not mold. Because microgreens are surface-sown, the fine root hairs that would be hidden underground in a garden are visible here; they cling only to the roots, are dry and evenly distributed, and have no musty smell. Mold, by contrast, spreads onto the medium and stems in wet, still, crowded conditions and smells musty.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: This is almost always normal root hairs, not mold. Microgreen seeds sit on the surface, so you can see the fine root hairs that are usually hidden in soil. Root hairs stay only on the roots, look like an even fuzzy halo, and have no smell. Real mold spreads onto the mix and stems and smells musty.
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: No action needed for root hairs. If you are unsure, check for a musty smell and whether the growth is on the stems and medium (mold) or only on the roots (hairs); a light misting matts root hairs down but does not remove true mold.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: If it is just root hairs, do nothing. To tell them apart, sniff for a musty smell and look at where the fuzz is: only on the roots means root hairs; spreading onto the stems and mix with a musty smell means mold.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_seasoned: None needed; root hairs are a sign of healthy germination. Keeping foliage dry and airflow up prevents the mold they are mistaken for.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_beginner: Nothing to prevent; root hairs are healthy. Keeping the leaves dry and the air moving prevents the mold people confuse them with.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Tall, pale, weak stems that fall over
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Long, thin, pale stems that flop
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Too little light, or light introduced too late after blackout
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Not enough light, or leaving the tray covered too long
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Uncover on time and give bright light for the full 16 to 18 hours; move closer to the grow light or a brighter window.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Uncover the tray on schedule and give it bright light for about 16 to 18 hours a day, closer to the light.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_seasoned: End blackout once the canopy lifts and provide adequate light intensity and duration.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_beginner: Take the cover off as soon as the sprouts are up and give them plenty of light.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Patchy, uneven germination across the tray
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Some spots sprout, others stay bare
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Uneven sowing, uneven moisture, no weighted cover, or old seed
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Seeds spread unevenly, dry spots, no weight on the cover, or old seed
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Sow evenly on pre-moistened medium, use a weighted cover for even seed-to-medium contact, and use fresh microgreen-grade broccoli seed.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Spread seeds evenly on damp medium, put a light weight on the cover, and use fresh broccoli seed made for microgreens.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_seasoned: Even sow, even moisture, weighted blackout cover, fresh seed.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_beginner: Even seeds, even moisture, a weighted cover, and fresh seed.

indoor_cycle.tip_seasoned: The cycle is sow -> blackout -> light -> harvest. Sow broccoli dry (no presoak), germinate at about 74 °F under a weighted cover in the dark for about 3 to 4 days, uncover into 16 to 18 hours of light at about 68 to 72 °F to green up, then cut at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage. Broccoli finishes in about 8 to 12 days.
indoor_cycle.tip_beginner: Broccoli microgreens follow four steps: plant, keep dark, give light, then harvest. Scatter the seeds dry (no soaking), keep the covered tray warm (around 74 °F) and dark for about 3 to 4 days while they sprout, then uncover into bright light (about 68 to 72 °F) for roughly 16 to 18 hours a day until the leaves green up. They are usually ready in about 8 to 12 days.

primary.name: Utah State University Extension -- Grow Your Own Microgreens
Penn State Extension -- The ABCs of Microgreens
University of Maryland Extension -- Growing Microgreens and Baby Greens Indoors
University of Minnesota Extension -- How to prevent seedling damping off
University of Nevada, Reno Extension -- Microgreens and Produce Safety (PubID 3468)

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: For a steady supply, stagger sowings: start a fresh broccoli tray every 3 to 5 days rather than one big tray at once. Indoors there is no season, so the cadence is limited only by your tray count and counter space.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: To always have broccoli microgreens ready, start a new tray every few days instead of one big batch. Because they grow indoors, you can keep this going all year.
succession_policy.notes: successions and max_successions_per_season are intentionally null: broccoli microgreens run continuously year-round indoors, so there is no season length to cap against. The practical limit is tray count and counter space, not climate (window_type: continuous_indoor).

verification_status.verification_log_ref: Batch-2 Wave-5 cert (2026-07-06, Trevor-ruled). microgreen. THE SULFORAPHANE WATCH-ITEM HELD: sulforaphane/glucoraphanin appear ONLY in internal metadata (where the author recorded TRIMMING them), never in consumer prose; the two consumer nutrition lines are both T1-sourced (PSU glucosinolate character; UMD 'higher in vitamins and phytochemicals') and the draft is MORE conservative than its sources (PSU calls microgreens a 'superfood' / glucosinolates 'anti-cancer' -- neither repeated). Sprout-vs-microgreen CLEAN (UNR distinction cited). Damping-off pathogens Pythium/Rhizoctonia/Fusarium verbatim on UMN. FIXES: fungus-gnat pest re-anchored to UC IPM pn7448; harvest height 1-2in -> 2-3in to match UMD; solanaceous-seed 'not safe raw' warning anchored to LSU AgCenter microgreens guide (Trevor ruled SOURCE it -- LSU: 'vegetables to avoid include solanaceous crops... solanine'); storage dropped usu (UMD backs the up-to-10-day figure); UNR URL updated.

open_findings.summary: Nutrition: consumer copy names glucosinolates (T1: PSU 'ABCs of Microgreens' states brassica microgreens' pungent taste is due to glucosinolates) and 'microgreens generally higher in vitamins and phytochemicals than the mature vegetable' (T1: UMD 'Growing Microgreens and Baby Greens Indoors'). The additional naming of 'glucoraphanin, the precursor to sulforaphane' is NOT stated on the fetched extension pages; it reflects research literature (Xiao et al. 2012 UMD/USDA; Talalay/Johns Hopkins broccoli-sprout work). No therapeutic or health-effect claim is made. Trim or re-anchor the glucoraphanin/sulforaphane phrasing at certify if a T1 extension page naming the compound is not found.

Root-hair-vs-mold diagnostic: the distinguishing features (root hairs cling only to roots, are dry/odorless; mold spreads to stems/medium with a musty smell) are grower knowledge and general seedling biology (microgreens are surface-sown so root hairs are visible), corroborated by the damping-off description in UMN and mold-from-moisture guidance in PSU/UMD, but no fetched T1 page states the 'often mistaken for mold' confusion verbatim. Framed hedged; confirm/soften at certify.

Variety 'broccoli raab / rapini' as a spicier alternative: identity (Brassica rapa, turnip relative, not true broccoli) is standard botany, but its microgreen days-to-harvest (~6-10 d) and peppery flavor come from seed-catalog / commercial microgreen sources, not a T1 extension page. Flagged as background; standard broccoli (B. oleracea var. italica) is the T1-anchored mainstay.

Modeled ranges / judgment calls: germination_temp_f [70,75] from UMD's 70-75 F 'germinate and grow well' band (USU maintains 74 F during germination); blackout 'about 3 to 4 days' chosen within USU's broccoli 2-4 day range; light '16 to 18 hours' spans UMD (16 h) and USU (18 h); seeding rate 28 g/1020 tray is USU's broccoli figure (PSU/UMD give a general 10-15 g/flat brassica range); yield 8-12 oz/tray is the general microgreen-tray range applied to broccoli; storage 5-10 days blends USU (brassicas ~5-7 d) with UMD (up to 10 d). All generally-safe; tighten at the variety-delta pass.

crops.description_seasoned: Broccoli microgreens are the young seedlings of broccoli (Brassica oleracea var. italica), harvested at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage about 8 to 12 days after sowing. They are grown indoors year-round in a short repeatable cycle: a dense, dry, even sow on a shallow tray of mix or a fiber mat (broccoli needs no presoak), a brief dark blackout of about 3 to 4 days to drive even germination and stem stretch, then light to green up, then a single cut. The flavor is mild, fresh, and faintly cabbage-like. Broccoli is one of the most popular microgreens for nutrition; like other brassica microgreens it concentrates the glucosinolates that give the cabbage family its character, and research finds microgreens generally higher in vitamins and phytochemicals than the mature vegetable. Because there is no frost, season, or hardiness zone involved, the same tray grows identically on a windowsill anywhere.
crops.description_beginner: Broccoli microgreens are baby broccoli plants that you harvest very young, about 8 to 12 days after planting, when they are just a couple of inches tall. You grow them indoors all year on a shallow tray of seed-starting mix or a special growing mat. The steps are always the same: scatter the small seeds thickly and dry (no soaking needed), cover the tray to keep it dark for about 3 to 4 days while they sprout, then move it into the light to green up, then snip and eat. The taste is mild, fresh, and a little cabbage-like. Broccoli is one of the most popular microgreens because it is so nutritious, packed with the healthy plant compounds the cabbage family is known for, and young microgreens tend to be richer in vitamins than full-grown plants. There is no outdoor season or weather to worry about, so they grow the same way no matter where you live.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Cut at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage, typically 8 to 12 days from sowing, when the stand is about 2 to 3 inches tall. Snip just above the medium with clean scissors; broccoli will not regrow, so the tray is a single cut.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Your broccoli microgreens are ready when the first little seed-leaves are open and, for many, the first true leaf is just showing, usually about 8 to 12 days after sowing and a couple of inches tall. Snip them just above the medium with clean scissors and eat them fresh. They do not grow back, so you start a new tray each time.

crops.name: Arugula Microgreens
crops.sunlight: bright indirect light or a grow light
crops.water: mist to keep the medium evenly moist through blackout; bottom-water once greened so the leaves stay dry

soil.preferred_texture_seasoned: A fine, moisture-holding soilless medium: a seed-starting mix, coconut coir, or a hydroponic fiber mat (hemp, jute, or similar). Arugula's small, mucilaginous seed germinates and greens most evenly on a fine, level surface.
soil.preferred_texture_beginner: Use a fine, soil-free growing medium that holds moisture well, such as seed-starting mix, coconut coir, or a growing mat made from hemp or jute fiber. A fine, level surface suits arugula's tiny seeds.
soil.tolerated_texture_seasoned: Peat-based mixes and inert fiber mats both work; the choice trades water-holding against a cleaner cut at harvest.
soil.tolerated_texture_beginner: Both peat-based mixes and fiber mats work well. Mixes hold more water, while mats stay cleaner at harvest, so pick whichever suits you.
soil.problematic_texture_seasoned: Garden soil and heavy potting mixes are too coarse and carry pest and pathogen risk for a dense crop eaten raw.
soil.problematic_texture_beginner: Skip garden soil and regular potting mix. They are too coarse, and they can carry pests and germs that are risky for a crowded crop you eat raw.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Use a light seed-starting mix, coconut coir, or a growing mat made for microgreens. Do not use garden soil.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: A clean, fine, moisture-retentive soilless medium gives even germination and a clean cut; coir and fiber mats keep grit off a crop you eat raw.

ph.note_seasoned: pH is not a practical lever for a single short indoor cycle on a soilless medium; standard seed-starting mixes and coir sit in a workable range and need no adjustment for arugula.
ph.note_beginner: You do not need to worry about soil pH for arugula microgreens. The mixes and mats sold for microgreens are already fine as they are.

fertilizer.timing: not applicable
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Arugula microgreens are cut before they exhaust the seed's own reserves, so no fertilizer is needed for a single cycle on an inert medium or seed-starting mix. Added nutrients mainly raise the risk of algae and off-flavors; a hydroponic grower who wants to feed at all needs only a dilute 50 to 100 ppm nitrogen solution.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: You do not need to feed arugula microgreens. The seed carries enough food to reach harvest, and adding fertilizer just invites algae and odd flavors.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: None for a soil or mat cycle; at most a dilute 50 to 100 ppm nitrogen solution if grown hydroponically.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: None needed.

companions.note_seasoned: Not applicable. Arugula microgreens are grown as a dense single-type indoor tray, so there is no interplanting or companion relationship. If you want a blend, grow each type in its own tray and combine after harvest.
companions.note_beginner: Not applicable. Arugula microgreens grow as one type per tray indoors, so there are no companion plants. If you want a mix, just combine different trays after cutting.

pests.description_seasoned: Small dark flies whose larvae live in persistently wet medium and feed on organic matter and tender roots. They are the main indoor microgreen pest and a symptom of an over-wet tray rather than a primary threat, and arugula's fast 6 to 8 day cycle usually beats them.
pests.description_beginner: Tiny dark flies that show up around constantly damp soil, where their larvae live. They are the main bug you might see indoors, and they usually mean the tray is staying too wet. Arugula grows so fast you often cut before they build up.
pests.management_seasoned: Let the surface dry between waterings where the crop allows, bottom-water once greened, and keep airflow up. Because the arugula cycle is so short, most trays are harvested before gnats build to a real problem; sanitized trays and fresh medium between cycles break the cycle.
pests.management_beginner: Keep the surface from staying soaking wet, water from the bottom once the leaves are up, and keep air moving. Since arugula microgreens are cut so fast, gnats rarely get bad first. Clean trays and fresh mix between batches keep them away.

diseases.description_seasoned: Soil-borne fungi rot seedlings at the soil line under wet, crowded, still conditions, often alongside fuzzy white or gray surface mold. It is the number-one microgreen failure, and arugula's dense fine canopy plus its mucilaginous seed, which holds water at the surface, make even moisture and airflow especially important.
diseases.description_beginner: The most common microgreen problem. In wet, crowded, stuffy conditions, tiny fungi rot the baby plants right at the base, and you often see fuzzy white or gray mold on the surface. Arugula's crowded leaves and sticky-when-wet seed make good airflow and careful watering matter even more.
diseases.management_seasoned: Prevention is the whole game: wrung-sponge moisture, bottom-watering once greened, constant gentle airflow, a sensible seeding rate near 10 g per 1020 tray, and sanitized trays between cycles. There is no rescue spray for a raw cut crop; a badly affected tray is composted and restarted clean.
diseases.management_beginner: You cannot spray this away on a crop you eat raw, so the fix is prevention: keep the mix just damp (not soggy), water from the bottom once the leaves are up, keep a small fan running, do not sow too thickly, and clean your trays between batches. If a tray molds badly, toss it and start over with clean equipment.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Mist once or twice daily through germination and blackout to hold even surface moisture; once greened, bottom-water as the tray dries.
watering.frequency_beginner: While the seeds are sprouting, lightly mist the surface once or twice a day so it stays damp. After you move the tray into the light, water from the bottom whenever it starts to dry out.
watering.amount_seasoned: Enough to keep the medium at wrung-sponge moisture, never saturated; pour off any standing water after bottom-watering.
watering.amount_beginner: Just enough to keep the soil damp like a wrung-out sponge, never soggy. After bottom-watering, tip out any water left sitting in the tray.
watering.method_seasoned: Mist during germination and blackout; switch to bottom-watering once the canopy is up so foliage stays dry.
watering.method_beginner: Mist the top while the seeds are sprouting, then water from the bottom once the leaves are up so the leaves stay dry.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Standing water, a sour smell, fuzzy white growth on the medium or stems, and collapsed seedlings all signal overwatering and the damping-off that follows it.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Water sitting in the tray, a bad smell, fuzzy white mold, or seedlings flopping over mean it is too wet. Cut back on water and improve airflow.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Curling, limp cotyledons and a medium that has pulled away from the tray edges indicate the canopy has dried too far between waterings.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Limp, curling leaves and soil that has shrunk away from the sides mean it got too dry. Water from the bottom right away.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Wet foliage in a dense, still canopy is the main driver of mold and damping-off, and arugula's mucilaginous seed holds extra water at the surface, so the cycle moves deliberately from misting to bottom-watering and pairs it with constant gentle airflow.
watering.method_note_beginner: Wet leaves packed close together with no air movement is what causes mold, and arugula's sticky seed holds water at the top. That is why you switch to watering from the bottom once the leaves are up, and keep a gentle fan going.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The blackout-to-light transition is the highest-risk window: the canopy is dense, humidity under the cover is high, and a single overwatering here can seed damping-off across the whole tray.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The riskiest time is right when you uncover the tray and move it into the light. The plants are crowded and damp, so do not overwater, and make sure air is moving.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Do not hold cut arugula microgreens at room temperature; they wilt and spoil within hours. Refrigerate immediately after cutting.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Do not leave cut arugula microgreens out on the counter. They go limp fast, so put them in the fridge right after cutting.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerate dry in a vented container lined with a paper towel; most cut arugula microgreens keep about 5 to 7 days. Cut when the foliage is dry (skip watering for a half day before harvest), since surface moisture shortens shelf life on a crop that is not washed after cutting.
storage.fridge_beginner: Keep cut arugula microgreens in the fridge in a container with a paper towel to soak up extra moisture. Most last about 5 to 7 days. They keep best cut dry, so hold off on watering for half a day before you harvest.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Not recommended. Freezing collapses the delicate cells and ruins the texture. Arugula microgreens are a fresh, cut-and-eat crop.
storage.freezer_beginner: Do not freeze arugula microgreens. Freezing turns them mushy. They are meant to be eaten fresh.
storage.notes_seasoned: Cut clean and dry: harvest with sanitized scissors into a clean container, keep the foliage dry, and chill promptly. Because they are eaten raw, post-harvest washing is discouraged (it can add rather than remove risk), so the clean-seed, clean-water, and sanitized-surface rules that govern growing also govern handling.
storage.notes_beginner: Because you eat arugula microgreens raw, keep everything clean: cut them with clean scissors into a clean, dry container and refrigerate right away. Do not rinse them after cutting; wash your hands, seeds, and tools instead.

recommended.name: Standard (salad) arugula
recommended.note: Eruca sativa, the common microgreen arugula. Fast, about 6 to 8 days; peppery. No presoak; mist, do not soak the mucilaginous seed. About 10 g per 1020 tray.

recommended.name: Wild / wasabi arugula
recommended.note: Diplotaxis tenuifolia, a different genus. Slower to grow and sharper, more pungent than salad arugula; deeply cut leaves. No presoak. Grown less commonly as a microgreen.

varieties.note_seasoned: Almost all arugula sold as a microgreen is standard salad arugula (Eruca sativa): a fast brassica, roughly 6 to 8 days to a peppery cut, sown at about 10 g per 1020 tray with no presoak. The seed is mucilaginous and forms a gel coat when wet, so mist it rather than soaking it, or it clumps and germinates unevenly. Wild or wasabi arugula (Diplotaxis tenuifolia) is a different genus that runs slower and tastes sharper; treat it the same way at sowing but expect a longer, spicier crop. Use untreated, microgreen-grade or food-safe seed, and cut at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage, before true leaves and fiber turn the flavor harsh.
varieties.note_beginner: The arugula you will almost always grow as a microgreen is regular salad arugula (Eruca sativa). It is one of the fastest microgreens, ready in about 6 to 8 days, with a bold peppery flavor. Its seeds get sticky and gel-like when wet, so mist them instead of soaking, or they clump. There is also a wild or wasabi arugula (Diplotaxis) that grows more slowly and tastes even spicier. Whichever you pick, use seed sold for sprouting or microgreens, and cut while the little seed-leaves are open for the best flavor.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Not applicable. Arugula microgreens are never moved outdoors or transplanted; the whole cycle is indoors.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: Not applicable. Arugula microgreens stay indoors from seed to harvest, so there is no hardening off.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Sow densely and evenly, about 10 g of seed across a pre-moistened 1020 tray. Do not presoak: arugula seed is small and mucilaginous, so soaking makes it clump; mist to wet it instead. Do not bury the seed; press it into firm contact with the surface, then cover for a short blackout. Dense, even contact is what gives a uniform stand and a clean single cut.
start_method.notes_beginner: Scatter the seeds thickly and evenly, roughly 10 grams over a damp 1020 tray. Do not soak arugula seed; it turns sticky and clumps, so just mist it. Do not bury the seeds, press them down so they touch the surface, then cover the tray to keep them dark for a day or two.

drainage.saucer_practice_seasoned: Nest the drilled tray inside a solid, hole-free tray. The outer tray catches runoff, lets you bottom-water, and is poured off so the crop never sits in standing water.
drainage.saucer_practice_beginner: Set the tray with holes inside a second solid tray with no holes. The bottom tray lets you water from below and catch extra water, which you then pour out so the roots are not sitting in water.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Seed-starting mix, coconut coir, or a microgreen growing mat.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: None needed.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: Seed-starting mix, coir, or an inert fiber mat; about 1 to 2 inches deep.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: None; the medium is a substrate, not a nutrient source, for a single cycle.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Water from the bottom by setting the tray in a little water, then pour off what is left.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: No fertilizer needed.

overwintering.approach_seasoned: Not applicable. Arugula microgreens are an indoor year-round cycle crop, harvested in days, with no dormant or overwintered phase.
overwintering.approach_beginner: Not applicable. Arugula microgreens grow indoors all year and are harvested within a couple of weeks, so there is nothing to overwinter.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: The tray is the entire growing system: shallow, drained, nested over a solid tray for bottom-watering, sanitized between cycles. A clean, reused, food-grade tray beats a single-use clamshell for both food safety and consistent results.
container_notes.notes_beginner: For arugula microgreens, the tray is the whole setup. Use a shallow tray with drainage holes sitting inside a solid tray so you can water from the bottom. Wash and sanitize trays between batches.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Bottom-water from the nesting tray; never leave the tray standing in water.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: None for a single cycle.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering reservoirs keep the medium too wet for a dense raw crop and raise the damping-off risk; bottom-water by hand and pour off the excess instead.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: Skip self-watering pots for arugula microgreens. They keep things too wet, which causes mold. Water from the bottom by hand and tip out the extra.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: A shallow flat tray works best: a 1020-style tray or any shallow food-safe container, with about 1 to 2 inches of medium. Depth beyond that wastes mix without helping a crop that is cut in days.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Use a shallow, wide tray, like a standard 1020 tray or any clean food-safe container. About 1 to 2 inches of growing mix is plenty. You do not need anything deep.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Not applicable. Arugula microgreens grow on fresh or sanitized medium each cycle with no soil-borne carryover, so crop rotation does not apply.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Not applicable. You use fresh growing medium and clean trays each time, so there is nothing to rotate.
rotation.note_seasoned: Sanitation between cycles, not rotation, is the disease control for arugula microgreens: compost the spent medium, then wash and sanitize the tray before the next sow.
rotation.note_beginner: Instead of rotating crops, just keep things clean: toss the used medium and wash and sanitize the tray before starting again.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Dense even broadcast, about 10 g per 1020 tray, on pre-moistened medium; no presoak, mist the seed.
growth_stages.description_beginner: Scatter seeds thickly on damp medium (about 10 grams a tray); do not soak, just mist.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Seeds imbibe and split under a weighted cover at about 74 °F.
growth_stages.description_beginner: Seeds sprout under a covered, warm tray.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Short dark period, about 1 to 2 days for arugula, that stretches stems and evens the stand before light.
growth_stages.description_beginner: A day or two in the dark that make the stems stretch evenly.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Uncovered into 18 hours of light at 68 to 72 °F; cotyledons green and the first true leaf may form.
growth_stages.description_beginner: Uncovered into bright light so the leaves turn green.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Single cut at cotyledon to first-true-leaf, about 6 to 8 days; eaten fresh.
growth_stages.description_beginner: Snip and eat when the little leaves are open, usually about a week.

notifications.message_seasoned: Check whether the canopy has lifted. Arugula's blackout is short, so it may be time to end blackout and move into light.
notifications.message_beginner: Time to check your tray: if the sprouts are up, uncover it and give it light.

notifications.message_seasoned: Switch from misting to bottom-watering now that the canopy is up, and make sure a fan is running.
notifications.message_beginner: Now that the leaves are up, water from the bottom and keep a fan going.

notifications.message_seasoned: Arugula is usually at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage now, so cut and refrigerate promptly while the flavor is peppery, not harsh.
notifications.message_beginner: Your arugula microgreens are likely ready to snip. Cut them and put them in the fridge.

notifications.message_seasoned: Start your next tray to keep the staggered supply going.
notifications.message_beginner: Start a new tray so you always have arugula microgreens coming.

sow.text_seasoned: Pre-moisten the medium to wrung-sponge feel, then broadcast about 10 g of seed densely and evenly across a 1020 tray. Do not presoak arugula: the seed is mucilaginous and clumps when soaked, so mist to wet it. Press seed into contact but do not bury it; buried seed greens poorly and traps moisture against the stems.
sow.text_beginner: Dampen the growing medium so it feels like a wrung-out sponge, then scatter about 10 grams of seed thickly and evenly. Do not soak arugula seed; it turns sticky and clumps, so just mist it. Press the seeds down so they touch the surface, but do not cover them with soil.

germination.text_seasoned: Cover the tray and keep it warm (about 74 °F) and dark. Mist to hold even surface moisture, never soggy. A light weight on the cover keeps seed in firm contact so roots drive down rather than lifting the seed.
germination.text_beginner: Put the cover on and keep the tray warm (around 74 °F) and dark. Mist lightly so the surface stays damp but not wet. A small weight on the cover helps the roots push down.

blackout.text_seasoned: Hold the weighted cover in the dark for arugula's short blackout, about 1 to 2 days, then flip the cover off the canopy so it shades without touching. The dark stretch lengthens and evens the stems before greening.
blackout.text_beginner: Keep the covered tray in the dark for a day or two. The darkness makes the stems grow taller and more even before you give them light.

light.text_seasoned: Uncover into 18 hours of bright light at 68 to 72 °F and switch from misting to bottom-watering so foliage stays dry. Run a gentle fan; the dense canopy plus high humidity is the damping-off window. Cut at cotyledon to first true leaf, about 6 to 8 days, before the flavor turns harsh.
light.text_beginner: Uncover the tray into bright light for about 18 hours a day at 68 to 72 °F, and start watering from the bottom so the leaves stay dry. Keep a gentle fan going to prevent mold. Cut when the first little leaves are open, usually about a week.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Yield is measured per tray, not per plant: a well-sown 1020 tray of arugula returns roughly 5 ounces of cut microgreens (Penn State reports about 148 grams, near a third of a pound, over a two-week cycle).
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: You measure microgreens by the tray, not by each plant. A full 1020 tray of arugula gives you a few good handfuls, around 5 ounces.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Every tray is a single harvest at peak; continuous supply comes from staggered sowings, not from regrowth.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Each tray gives one harvest at its best. To keep a steady supply, start new trays every few days.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: There is no establishment year; the first tray performs the same as any later tray. Expect to dial in seeding rate and watering over the first few cycles.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: There is no waiting period with microgreens. Your very first tray works just like the rest; you will just get a feel for how much to sow and water after a few tries.
factors_seasoned: seeding density (too sparse wastes the tray; too dense traps moisture and invites mold)
even moisture and the mist-to-bottom-water transition
constant gentle airflow
seed freshness and using microgreen-grade seed
light intensity and the full 18-hour daily duration

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Not applicable. Arugula microgreens are an indoor, light-controlled, seedling-stage crop with no lunar or seasonal timing.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Fuzzy white or gray growth on the medium, stems, or seed; seedlings collapsing at the base
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Fuzzy white or gray mold, or baby plants flopping over at the bottom
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Damping-off and mold from overwatering, a saturated medium, dense sowing, and poor airflow; the number-one microgreen failure
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Too much water plus crowded plants and no air movement, which leads to mold. This is the most common microgreen problem.
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Switch to bottom-watering, pour off standing water, run a gentle fan, thin your seeding rate next time, and sanitize trays between cycles. Do not bury seed at sowing.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Water from the bottom, tip out extra water, keep a small fan going, sow a little less thickly next time, and clean your trays between batches.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_seasoned: Wrung-sponge moisture, constant airflow, dry foliage, and sanitized trays prevent it.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_beginner: Keep the soil just damp, the air moving, the leaves dry, and the trays clean.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Tall, pale, weak stems that fall over
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Long, thin, pale stems that flop
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Too little light, or light introduced too late after blackout
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Not enough light, or leaving the tray covered too long
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Uncover on time (arugula's blackout is only about 1 to 2 days) and give bright light for the full 18 hours; move closer to the grow light or a brighter window.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Uncover the tray on schedule and give it bright light for about 18 hours a day, closer to the light.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_seasoned: End the short blackout once the canopy lifts and provide adequate light intensity and duration.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_beginner: Take the cover off as soon as the sprouts are up and give them plenty of light.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Patchy, uneven germination or seed clumped into gel-coated clusters
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Some spots sprout while others stay bare, or seeds stuck together in slimy clumps
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Uneven sowing or moisture, no weighted cover, old seed, or soaking arugula's mucilaginous seed so it gels and clumps instead of spreading evenly
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Seeds spread unevenly, dry spots, no weight on the cover, old seed, or soaking the seed so it turned sticky and clumped
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Sow evenly on pre-moistened medium, mist rather than soak so the gel coat does not clump the seed, use a weighted cover for even contact, and use fresh microgreen-grade seed.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Spread seeds evenly on damp medium, mist instead of soaking so they do not clump, put a light weight on the cover, and use fresh seed made for microgreens.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_seasoned: Even sow, even moisture, mist (never soak) the mucilaginous seed, weighted blackout cover, fresh seed.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_beginner: Even seeds, even moisture, mist do not soak, a weighted cover, and fresh seed.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Harsh, overly bitter, or fibrous flavor at the plate
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: The microgreens taste too sharp, bitter, or tough
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Cut too late: as true leaves and stem fiber develop, arugula's flavor shifts from pleasantly peppery to harsh
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Cut too late. As the bigger true leaves come in, arugula gets sharper and tougher.
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Harvest at the cotyledon to just-emerging-first-true-leaf stage, about 6 to 8 days, and refrigerate promptly.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Cut while the little seed-leaves are open, around a week, and refrigerate right away.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_seasoned: Track the tray and cut on time; do not let it run to full true leaves.
