failure_diagnostics.prevention_beginner: Watch the tray and cut on time, before the bigger leaves take over.

indoor_cycle.tip_seasoned: The cycle is sow -> blackout -> light -> harvest. Sow about 10 g per 1020 tray (no presoak; mist the mucilaginous seed), germinate at about 74 °F under a weighted cover in the dark for arugula's short blackout of about 1 to 2 days, then uncover into 18 hours of light at about 68 to 72 °F to green up. Arugula is one of the fastest microgreens, typically 6 to 8 days in a warm, brightly lit setup and up to about 10 to 12 days in cooler or lower-light home conditions. Cut at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage for peppery, not harsh, flavor.
indoor_cycle.tip_beginner: Arugula microgreens follow the same four steps: plant, keep dark, give light, then harvest. Scatter about 10 grams of seed on a damp tray (do not soak it, just mist), keep the covered tray warm (around 74 °F) and dark for a day or two while the seeds sprout, then uncover into bright light (about 68 to 72 °F) for roughly 18 hours a day until the leaves green up. Arugula is fast, often ready in about 6 to 8 days, sometimes closer to 10 to 12 in cooler or dim rooms. Cut while the little leaves are open for the best flavor.

primary.name: Utah State University Extension -- Grow Your Own Microgreens
University of Nevada, Reno Extension -- Microgreens and Produce Safety (PubID 3468)

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: For a steady supply, stagger sowings: start a fresh tray every 3 to 5 days rather than one big tray at once. Indoors there is no season, so the cadence is limited only by your tray count and counter space, and arugula's short 6 to 8 day cycle turns trays over quickly.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: To always have arugula microgreens ready, start a new tray every few days instead of one big batch. Because they grow indoors and finish so fast, you can keep this going all year.
succession_policy.notes: successions and max_successions_per_season are intentionally null: arugula microgreens run continuously year-round indoors, so there is no season length to cap against. The practical limit is tray count and counter space, not climate (window_type: continuous_indoor).

verification_status.verification_log_ref: Batch-2 Wave-5 cert (2026-07-06, Trevor-ruled). microgreen archetype. Source-truth review (READ-ONLY CC agent, WebFetch of 3 cited T1 pages). NUTRITION/HEALTH over-claim CLEAN: no nutrient-density or medicinal claim in consumer prose -- the draft DECLINES PSU's own 'microgreens higher in vitamins' line. Sprout-vs-microgreen CLEAN (grown in a medium, cut above the line). Numerics verbatim on USU (6-8 days, 10g seed, no presoak, 74/72/68F, 18h light, peppery) + PSU (147.6g yield, 50-100ppm N). FIXES: fungus-gnat pest re-anchored to UC IPM Pest Notes pn7448 (USU/PSU don't cover it; Trevor ruled SOURCE it); damping-off trimmed to psu_microgreens (USU/UNR don't cover it); storage dropped the shelf-life-less UNR day-count anchor + added psu_microgreens; UNR food-safety URL updated to the live naes.unr.edu/dfi host. Modeled items (germ-temp band, harvest height, 10-12d upper) stay disclosed in open_findings.

open_findings.summary: days_to_maturity / days_to_harvest [7,12], mid 8, reconciles two T1 figures: USU gives arugula 6 to 8 days at optimal light and warmth (prose keeps the USU-faithful '6 to 8 days'), while Mississippi State (corroborating, not cited) groups arugula in a 10 to 15 day set and PSU gives a 7 to 21 day general microgreen envelope. The structured low is set at 7, the dataset numeric-sanity floor (USU's published fastest is 6); the up-to-12-day home-light upper bound is modeled from the PSU envelope for cooler or lower-light conditions.

germination_temp_f [65,75] is modeled from PSU's 60 to 75 F general microgreen germination range and USU's explicit 74 F germination setpoint; no arugula-specific germination-temperature figure is published in the cited T1 sources.

Fridge shelf-life of about 5 to 7 days is general microgreen guidance. The cited food-safety source (unr_ext) backs the raw-crop handling rules (sanitize tools and water, cut clean and dry, do not post-harvest wash) but publishes no shelf-life figure; the day count is modeled from general microgreen norms.

The standard salad arugula (Eruca sativa) vs wild / wasabi arugula (Diplotaxis tenuifolia) distinction, and the 'wild type is slower and spicier' characterization, are general horticultural/botanical knowledge. No cited T1 microgreen source separates the two genera (USU's table does not), so the standard-arugula figures anchor to usu_ext and the wild-type contrast is presented as general, hedged information.

Harvest height of about 1 to 2 inches at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage is modeled: USU's cue is 'ready as the first true leaves appear or sooner' (no height), and Mississippi State gives a general 1 to 3 inch harvest height across microgreens. The 'cut before true leaves for best, least-bitter flavor' guidance is general grower experience, hedged.

crops.description_seasoned: Arugula microgreens are the young seedlings of arugula (Eruca sativa, in the mustard family), harvested at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage for a concentrated, distinctly peppery, spicy bite that is the whole reason to grow them. They are among the fastest microgreens: a dense, even sow of about 10 g per 1020 tray, a short blackout of about 1 to 2 days to even the stand, then 18 hours of light to green up, cut in roughly 6 to 8 days (longer, closer to 10 to 12 days, in cooler or lower-light rooms). The seed is small and mucilaginous, so it is misted rather than presoaked, or it clumps. Grown indoors year-round on a shallow tray of mix or a fiber mat, arugula microgreens need no frost, season, or hardiness zone, so the same tray grows identically on a windowsill anywhere. They are used fresh as a peppery salad base, sandwich layer, or garnish.
crops.description_beginner: Arugula microgreens are baby arugula plants that you harvest very young, when they are just a couple of inches tall, for a bold peppery, spicy flavor. They are one of the fastest microgreens to grow: scatter about 10 grams of seed thickly on a damp tray, cover it to keep it dark for a day or two while the seeds sprout, then move it into bright light to green up, and snip in about 6 to 8 days (a bit longer in a cool or dim room). Arugula seed gets sticky when wet, so mist it instead of soaking. You grow them indoors all year on a shallow tray of seed-starting mix or a special growing mat, so there is no outdoor season or weather to worry about, and they grow the same way no matter where you live. Use them fresh on salads, sandwiches, and as a garnish.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Cut at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage, typically about 6 to 8 days from sowing (up to roughly 10 to 12 in cooler or lower light), when the stand is a couple of inches tall and bright green. Harvest before the true leaves and stem fiber develop, since that is when the flavor shifts from pleasantly peppery to harsh. Snip just above the medium with clean scissors; the stand will not regrow, so the tray is a single cut.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Your arugula microgreens are ready when the first little seed-leaves are open and, for many, the first true leaf is just showing, usually about 6 to 8 days after sowing and around 1 to 2 inches tall. Cut them while they are young for the best peppery flavor, before the bigger leaves come in. Snip them just above the soil with clean scissors and eat them fresh. They do not grow back, so you start a new tray each time.

crops.name: Wheatgrass
crops.sunlight: bright indirect light or a grow light
crops.water: keep the seed mat evenly moist, never soggy; bottom-water once greened and keep airflow up to prevent mold

soil.preferred_texture_seasoned: A fine, moisture-holding medium works best: a thin layer of seed-starting mix or coconut coir, or a hydroponic fiber mat. Many growers also use about an inch of light potting soil or compost.
soil.preferred_texture_beginner: Use a fine, moisture-holding growing medium such as seed-starting mix or coconut coir, or a thin layer (about an inch) of light potting soil. A hemp or jute growing mat works too.
soil.tolerated_texture_seasoned: Coir, peat-based mixes, thin potting soil, and inert mats all grow a crop; the trade is water-holding against cleanliness at the cut, and denser wet media raise the mold risk on a packed mat.
soil.tolerated_texture_beginner: Coir, seed mixes, thin potting soil, and fiber mats all work. Soil holds more water and can grow taller grass, while mats stay cleaner at cutting.
soil.problematic_texture_seasoned: Heavy garden soil and deep, coarse potting mixes hold too much water under a dense mat and add pathogen and pest risk; they are the wrong choice for a crop this crowded and this wet.
soil.problematic_texture_beginner: Skip heavy garden soil and thick potting mixes. They stay too wet under a crowded mat and make mold much more likely.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Use a clean, fine growing medium that holds moisture but still drains, like coir, a seed mix, or a thin layer of light potting soil. The goal is damp, never soggy, because a crowded wet mat molds easily.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: A clean, fine, moisture-retentive medium gives even germination and a clean cut; the whole game is keeping a dense seed mat evenly damp without letting it stay soggy, which is what invites mold.
soil.organic_matter_preference: not applicable (soilless or thin soil layer)

ph.note_seasoned: pH is not a practical lever for a single 7 to 10 day indoor cycle. Standard seed-starting mixes, coir, and light potting soil all sit in a workable range and need no adjustment for wheatgrass.
ph.note_beginner: You do not need to worry about soil pH for wheatgrass. The mixes, coir, and light soil sold for growing it are already fine.

fertilizer.timing: not applicable
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Wheatgrass is cut in 7 to 10 days, well before it exhausts the wheat berry's own food reserves, so no fertilizer is needed for a single cycle. Added nutrients on a dense wet mat mainly feed algae and mold.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: You do not need to feed wheatgrass. The wheat berry carries enough food to reach cutting height in a week or so, and fertilizer on a crowded, damp tray just invites mold and algae.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: None.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: None needed.

companions.note_seasoned: Not applicable. Wheatgrass is grown as a dense single-species tray indoors, so there is no interplanting or companion relationship.
companions.note_beginner: Not applicable. Wheatgrass grows as one crowded tray of grass indoors, so there are no companion plants.

pests.description_seasoned: Small dark flies whose larvae live in constantly wet medium and feed on organic matter and tender roots. On a wheatgrass tray they are a symptom of an over-wet mat rather than a primary threat.
pests.description_beginner: Tiny dark flies that show up around soggy growing medium. Their larvae live in the wet mat, and they usually mean the tray is staying too wet.
pests.management_seasoned: Let the surface dry slightly between waterings, bottom-water, and keep steady airflow. The 7 to 10 day cycle usually finishes before gnats build up; fresh medium and sanitized trays between cycles break the cycle.
pests.management_beginner: Keep the surface from staying soaking wet, water from the bottom, and keep air moving with a small fan. Since wheatgrass is cut so fast, gnats rarely get bad. Use fresh medium and clean trays each batch.

diseases.description_seasoned: Fuzzy white or gray mold on the seed mat, plus soil-borne fungi (Rhizoctonia, Botrytis, and others) that rot seedlings at the base, are the number-one wheatgrass problem. The dense seed mat, high humidity, and 7 to 10 day grow-out make wheatgrass especially mold-prone, more so than quick salad microgreens.
diseases.description_beginner: Fuzzy white or gray mold on the mat, and baby grass rotting at the base, are by far the most common wheatgrass problem. Because the seeds are packed tightly and grown for a week or more in a damp tray, wheatgrass molds more easily than fast salad microgreens.
diseases.management_seasoned: Prevention is the whole game: do not over-soak the seed, spread it in an even single layer instead of a pile, keep the mat at wrung-sponge moisture, bottom-water once greened, run constant gentle airflow, and rinse the mat if a film starts. There is no rescue spray for a raw juiced crop; a badly molded tray is composted and restarted clean. One caution: fine white root hairs at the base are normal and are often mistaken for mold, while true mold is fuzzy and web-like, spreads over the surface, and usually smells musty.
diseases.management_beginner: You cannot spray this away on a crop you juice raw, so the fix is prevention: do not soak the seeds too long, spread them in one even layer instead of a pile, keep the mat just damp (not soggy), water from the bottom once the grass is up, keep a small fan running, and rinse the mat if you see a film starting. If a tray molds badly, throw it out and start over with clean gear. One tip: fine white fuzz right at the roots is usually normal root hairs, not mold; real mold is web-like, spreads on top, and smells musty.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Mist once or twice daily through soaking, sprouting, and blackout to hold even surface moisture; once greened, bottom-water as the mat dries.
watering.frequency_beginner: While the seeds are sprouting and in the dark, lightly mist the surface once or twice a day so it stays damp. After you move the tray into the light, water from the bottom whenever it starts to dry out.
watering.amount_seasoned: Enough to keep the medium at wrung-sponge moisture, never saturated; pour off any standing water after bottom-watering so the mat is not sitting in it.
watering.amount_beginner: Just enough to keep the medium damp like a wrung-out sponge, never soggy. After bottom-watering, tip out any water left sitting in the tray.
watering.method_seasoned: Mist during germination and blackout; switch to bottom-watering once the grass is up so the blades stay dry and the crown does not stay wet.
watering.method_beginner: Mist the top while the seeds are sprouting, then water from the bottom once the grass is up so the blades stay dry.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Standing water, a sour smell, fuzzy white growth on the mat, slimy seed, and collapsed seedlings all signal overwatering and the mold and damping-off that follow it.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Water sitting in the tray, a bad smell, fuzzy white mold, slimy seeds, or grass flopping over mean it is too wet. Cut back on water and improve airflow.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Limp, curling blades and a mat that has pulled away from the tray edges indicate the crop has dried too far between waterings.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Limp, curling blades and medium that has shrunk away from the sides mean it got too dry. Water from the bottom right away.
watering.method_note_seasoned: A wet, still, densely packed mat is the main driver of mold on wheatgrass, so the cycle moves deliberately from misting to bottom-watering and pairs it with constant gentle airflow.
watering.method_note_beginner: A soggy, crowded mat with no air moving is what causes mold. That is why you switch to watering from the bottom once the grass is up, and keep a gentle fan going.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The blackout-to-light transition is the highest-risk window: the mat is dense, humidity under the cover is high, and a single overwatering here can seed mold across the whole tray.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The riskiest time is right when you uncover the tray and move it into the light. The grass is crowded and damp, so do not overwater, and make sure air is moving.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Do not hold cut wheatgrass at room temperature; the tender blades wilt within hours and fresh juice degrades fast. Refrigerate cut grass promptly and juice it cold.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Do not leave cut wheatgrass or its juice out on the counter. The blades wilt fast and the juice does not keep, so refrigerate right after cutting.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerate cut grass dry in a vented bag or container; it holds about 5 to 7 days. Fresh juice is best consumed right away; if you must hold it, keep it cold and use it within a day.
storage.fridge_beginner: Keep cut wheatgrass in the fridge in a loosely closed bag or container for about 5 to 7 days. Juice tastes best fresh, so drink it soon; if you keep juice, refrigerate it and use it within a day.
storage.freezer_seasoned: You can freeze fresh juice in ice-cube trays for convenience, though flavor and quality fade. Freezing the whole cut blades is not useful, since wheatgrass is juiced rather than cooked or eaten.
storage.freezer_beginner: You can freeze fresh juice in ice-cube trays if you want to save it, but it is best fresh. There is no point freezing the whole blades, since you juice wheatgrass rather than eat it.
storage.notes_seasoned: Because wheatgrass juice is consumed raw, the same clean-water and sanitized-surface rules that govern growing also govern harvest and juicing: cut with sanitized scissors into a clean container and keep the juicer and tools clean.
storage.notes_beginner: Because you drink wheatgrass juice raw, keep everything clean: cut the grass with clean scissors into a clean container, and wash your juicer and tools well.

recommended.name: Hard red winter wheat
recommended.note: The most common wheatgrass berry; widely sold for sprouting. Soak 8 to 12 hours; cut in about 7 to 10 days.

recommended.name: Hard red spring wheat
recommended.note: Similar to hard red winter, reliable and easy to find. Soak 8 to 12 hours.

recommended.name: Soft white winter wheat
recommended.note: Milder, sweeter grass; a good pick if hard wheat tastes too strong. Soak 8 to 12 hours.

varieties.note_seasoned: Wheatgrass is grown from common wheat berries (Triticum aestivum), the same grain milled for flour. Use whole, untreated, sprouting-grade or food-grade wheat berries: hard or soft winter (or spring) wheat all grow good grass, with the softer classes running a touch sweeter. Do not use seed-treated field or cover-crop wheat, which is dressed with fungicide and is not food safe. Soak the berries 8 to 12 hours and, if you like, let them sprout a short root for a day before spreading them in an even single layer.
varieties.note_beginner: Wheatgrass grows from regular wheat berries, the same grain that becomes flour. Buy whole, untreated wheat berries labeled for sprouting or eating; hard or soft winter wheat both work, and softer wheat is a little sweeter. Never use treated field-planting wheat, since it is coated with fungicide you should not eat. Soak the berries 8 to 12 hours, then spread them in one even layer.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Not applicable. Wheatgrass is never moved outdoors or transplanted; the whole cycle is indoors.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: Not applicable. Wheatgrass stays indoors from seed to cutting, so there is no hardening off.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Soak the wheat berries 8 to 12 hours, drain, and rinse; many growers then let them sprout for a day (rinsing twice) until a short root shows. Spread the soaked seed thickly in a single even layer across pre-moistened medium so the berries touch but do not pile, since a mounded mat holds water and molds. Do not bury the seed; press it into contact and cover for a short blackout. An even single layer is what gives a uniform mat and a clean cut.
start_method.notes_beginner: Soak the wheat berries for 8 to 12 hours, then drain and rinse them. If you want, let them sit and sprout for a day (rinse them twice) until you see a tiny root. Spread the soaked seeds thickly in one even layer on damp medium so they touch but are not piled up, because a mound stays wet and molds. Do not cover them with soil; just press them down and put the tray in the dark for a couple of days.

drainage.saucer_practice_seasoned: Nest the drilled tray inside a solid, hole-free tray. The outer tray catches runoff, lets you bottom-water, and is poured off so the mat never sits in standing water.
drainage.saucer_practice_beginner: Set the tray with holes inside a second solid tray with no holes. The bottom tray lets you water from below and catch extra water, which you then pour out so the roots are not sitting in water.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Seed-starting mix, coconut coir, a thin layer of light potting soil, or a growing mat.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: None needed.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: Seed-starting mix, coir, a thin layer of light potting soil, or an inert fiber mat; about 1 inch deep.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: None; the medium is a substrate, not a nutrient source, for a single 7 to 10 day cycle.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Water from the bottom by setting the tray in a little water, then pour off what is left.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: No fertilizer needed.

overwintering.approach_seasoned: Not applicable. Wheatgrass is an indoor year-round cycle crop, cut in days, with no dormant or overwintered phase.
overwintering.approach_beginner: Not applicable. Wheatgrass grows indoors all year and is cut within a week or two, so there is nothing to overwinter.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: The tray is the entire growing system: shallow, drained, nested over a solid tray for bottom-watering, and sanitized between cycles. Because the seed mat is so dense and mold-prone, a clean, reused, food-grade tray with good airflow beats a lidded clamshell.
container_notes.notes_beginner: For wheatgrass, the tray is the whole setup. Use a shallow tray with drainage holes sitting inside a solid tray so you can water from the bottom. Wash and sanitize trays between batches, and keep air moving so the crowded mat does not mold.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Bottom-water from the nesting tray; never leave the tray standing in water.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: None for a single cycle.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering reservoirs keep the medium too wet for a dense mat and raise the mold risk; bottom-water by hand and pour off the excess instead.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: Skip self-watering pots for wheatgrass. They keep things too wet, which causes mold. Water from the bottom by hand and tip out the extra.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: A shallow flat tray works best: a 1020-style tray or any shallow food-safe container, with about 1 inch of medium. Depth beyond that wastes mix without helping a crop that is cut in days.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Use a shallow, wide tray, like a standard 1020 tray or any clean food-safe container. About 1 inch of growing medium is plenty. You do not need anything deep.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Not applicable. Wheatgrass grows on fresh or sanitized medium each cycle with no soil-borne carryover, so crop rotation does not apply.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Not applicable. You use fresh growing medium and clean trays each time, so there is nothing to rotate.
rotation.note_seasoned: Sanitation between cycles, not rotation, is the disease control for wheatgrass: compost the spent mat, then wash and sanitize the tray before the next sow.
rotation.note_beginner: Instead of rotating crops, just keep things clean: toss the used mat and wash and sanitize the tray before starting again.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Wheat berries soaked 8 to 12 hours (optionally sprouted a day), then spread thickly in an even single layer on pre-moistened medium.
growth_stages.description_beginner: Wheat berries soaked for 8 to 12 hours, then spread in one even layer on damp medium.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Seeds root and sprout under a covered tray at about 60 to 70 °F.
growth_stages.description_beginner: Seeds sprout under a covered tray in a warm room.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Short dark period (about 2 to 3 days) that evens the stand and stretches the young shoots before light.
growth_stages.description_beginner: A couple of days in the dark that bring the grass up evenly before you give it light.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Uncovered into bright indirect light; the blades green up and grow toward cutting height.
growth_stages.description_beginner: Uncovered into bright light so the grass turns deep green and grows tall.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Single cut near the base at about 6 to 7 inches, at the jointing stage when a second blade begins; juiced fresh.
growth_stages.description_beginner: Cut the grass near the soil at about 6 to 7 inches tall, then juice it fresh.

notifications.message_seasoned: Check whether the shoots have lifted the cover. It may be time to end blackout and move the tray into light.
notifications.message_beginner: Time to check your tray: if the grass is up, uncover it and give it light.

notifications.message_seasoned: Switch from misting to bottom-watering now that the grass is up, and keep a fan running to prevent mold.
notifications.message_beginner: Now that the grass is up, water from the bottom and keep a fan going.

notifications.message_seasoned: Your wheatgrass is likely near 6 to 7 inches at the jointing stage now, so cut and juice it fresh.
notifications.message_beginner: Your wheatgrass is probably ready to cut. Snip it near the base and juice it fresh.

notifications.message_seasoned: Start your next tray to keep a steady wheatgrass supply going.
notifications.message_beginner: Start a new tray so you always have wheatgrass coming.

sow.text_seasoned: Soak the wheat berries 8 to 12 hours, then drain and rinse well. Spread the soaked seed thickly in a single even layer over pre-moistened medium so the berries touch but do not pile; a mounded mat holds water and molds. Press the seed into contact but do not bury it.
sow.text_beginner: Soak the wheat berries 8 to 12 hours, then drain and rinse them. Spread them thickly in one even layer over damp medium so they touch but are not piled up. Press them down so they contact the surface, but do not cover them with soil.

germination.text_seasoned: Cover the tray and keep it in a warm room (about 60 to 70 °F) and dark. Mist to hold even surface moisture, never soggy. Do not over-soak or leave standing water, since a wet mat at this stage is where mold starts.
germination.text_beginner: Put the cover on and keep the tray in a warm room (around 60 to 70 °F) and dark. Mist lightly so the surface stays damp but not wet. Do not let water pool, because a soggy mat now leads to mold.

blackout.text_seasoned: Keep the covered tray in the dark for about 2 to 3 days, until the shoots lift the cover. The dark stretch lengthens and evens the young grass before greening. Mist enough to keep the mat evenly damp.
blackout.text_beginner: Keep the covered tray in the dark for about 2 to 3 days, until the grass pushes the cover up. The darkness makes the grass grow taller and more even before you give it light. Mist so the mat stays damp.

light.text_seasoned: Uncover into bright indirect light and switch from misting to bottom-watering so the blades stay dry. Run a gentle fan; the dense mat plus high humidity is the mold window. Rinse the mat if a film starts, and cut near the base at 6 to 7 inches, at the jointing stage.
light.text_beginner: Uncover the tray into bright light (not harsh direct sun) and start watering from the bottom so the blades stay dry. Keep a gentle fan going to prevent mold, and rinse the mat if you see a film. Cut the grass near the base when it is about 6 to 7 inches tall.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Yield is measured per tray, not per plant: a well-grown 1020 tray of wheatgrass returns roughly 1 to 1.5 pounds of grass, enough for about 12 to 20 ounces of fresh juice depending on the juicer.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: You measure wheatgrass by the tray, not by each plant. A full tray usually gives about a pound of grass, which juices down to roughly 12 to 20 ounces (a good run of shots).
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Every tray is a single cut; wheatgrass regrows weakly and a second cut is thin and often bitter, so continuous supply comes from staggered sowings, not from regrowth.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Each tray gives one good cutting. It may grow back a little, but the second cut is thin and can taste bitter, so most people start new trays instead of waiting for regrowth.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: There is no establishment year; the first tray performs like any later tray. Expect to dial in soak time, seeding density, and airflow over the first few cycles.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: There is no waiting period. Your first tray works like the rest; you will just get a feel for soaking, how thick to sow, and airflow after a few tries.
factors_seasoned: seeding density and an even single layer (piling traps moisture and molds)
soak time (over-soaking sours the seed and invites mold)
even moisture and the mist-to-bottom-water transition
constant gentle airflow
wheat berry freshness and viability
cutting at the jointing stage for the best flavor

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Not applicable. Wheatgrass is an indoor, light-controlled, seedling-stage crop with no lunar or seasonal timing.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Fuzzy white or gray growth spreading over the mat, or seedlings collapsing at the base
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Fuzzy white or gray mold on top, or baby grass flopping over at the bottom
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Mold and damping-off from over-soaking, a piled or saturated mat, and poor airflow; the number-one wheatgrass failure. (Note: fine white root hairs are normal, not mold.)
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Too much water plus a crowded, piled mat and no air movement, which leads to mold. This is the most common wheatgrass problem. Fine white fuzz right at the roots is usually normal, not mold.
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Switch to bottom-watering, pour off standing water, run a gentle fan, spread a thinner even single layer next time, shorten the soak, and sanitize trays between cycles.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Water from the bottom, tip out extra water, keep a small fan going, spread the seeds in a thinner even layer next time, soak a bit less, and clean your trays between batches.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_seasoned: An even single layer, wrung-sponge moisture, constant airflow, dry blades, and sanitized trays prevent it.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_beginner: Spread seeds in one even layer, keep the mat just damp, keep air moving, keep the blades dry, and clean the trays.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Sour or fermented smell and slimy seed before the grass is up
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: A sour smell and slimy, mushy seeds before the grass comes up
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Over-soaked or under-rinsed berries left too wet, so the seed sours and ferments instead of sprouting cleanly.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: The seeds were soaked too long or not rinsed enough and stayed too wet, so they went sour instead of sprouting.
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Soak only 8 to 12 hours, rinse thoroughly, drain fully, and keep the mat damp rather than wet; discard a sour batch and restart clean.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Soak for only 8 to 12 hours, rinse well, drain all the extra water, and keep the mat damp not soggy. If a batch smells sour, throw it out and start over.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_seasoned: Cap the soak at about 12 hours, rinse and drain well, and never leave seed sitting in water.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_beginner: Do not soak longer than about 12 hours, rinse and drain well, and never let the seeds sit in water.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Tall, pale, weak blades that fall over
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Long, thin, pale grass that flops
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Too little light, or light introduced too late after blackout.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Not enough light, or leaving the tray covered too long.
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Uncover on time once the shoots lift the cover and give bright indirect light; move closer to a grow light or a bright window.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Uncover the tray on schedule and give it bright light, closer to the light or a bright window.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_seasoned: End blackout once the grass lifts the cover and provide adequate light.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_beginner: Take the cover off as soon as the grass is up and give it plenty of light.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Patchy, uneven germination across the tray
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Some spots sprout, others stay bare
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Uneven or piled sowing, uneven moisture, dry spots, or old, low-viability wheat berries.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Seeds spread unevenly or piled, dry spots, or old seed that will not sprout.
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Spread an even single layer on pre-moistened medium, keep moisture even, and use fresh, viable wheat berries.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Spread the seeds evenly in one layer on damp medium, keep the moisture even, and use fresh wheat berries.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_seasoned: Even single-layer sow, even moisture, and fresh wheat berries.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_beginner: An even single layer, even moisture, and fresh seed.

indoor_cycle.tip_seasoned: The cycle is soak, sprout, spread, blackout, light, cut. Soak the wheat berries 8 to 12 hours (optionally sprout a day), spread them in an even single layer on damp medium, cover for a short 2 to 3 day blackout, then uncover into bright indirect light. Cut near the base at about 6 to 7 inches, at the jointing stage when a second blade begins, usually 7 to 10 days from sowing, and juice fresh.
indoor_cycle.tip_beginner: Wheatgrass follows the same steps each time: soak the wheat berries 8 to 12 hours, spread them in one even layer on damp medium, cover the tray to keep it dark for 2 to 3 days, then uncover it into bright light. Cut the grass near the base when it is about 6 to 7 inches tall, usually a week to ten days after planting, and juice it right away.

primary.name: Utah State University Extension -- Grow Your Own Microgreens
University of Nevada, Reno Extension -- Microgreens and Produce Safety (PubID 3468)
Penn State Extension -- What You Should Know About Sprouts

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: For a steady supply, stagger sowings: start a fresh tray every 5 to 7 days rather than one big tray. Indoors there is no season, so the cadence is limited only by your tray count and counter space.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: To always have wheatgrass ready, start a new tray every week or so instead of one big batch. Because it grows indoors, you can keep this going all year.
succession_policy.notes: successions and max_successions_per_season are intentionally null: wheatgrass runs continuously year-round indoors, so there is no season length to cap against. The practical limit is tray count and counter space, not climate (window_type: continuous_indoor).

verification_status.verification_log_ref: Batch-2 Wave-6 cert (2026-07-06, Trevor-ruled). microgreen (Triticum aestivum, grown and juiced). HEALTH-CLAIM WATCH-ITEM CLEAN: the draft makes NO health/nutrition claim (no detox/chlorophyll/immune/vitamins; juice described sensorially only; the draft's own findings state 'no health/medical claims made') -- so the T1-health rule does not bite. Framing correct (grass grown in a medium, cut then juiced; mold-vs-root-hairs guidance present). No dedicated Tier-1 wheatgrass page exists, so cultivation numbers (days/blackout/soak/height/yield) are modeled-but-disclosed in open_findings (generally-safe-now; refined at the variety pass). FIXES: fungus-gnat pest -> UC IPM pn7448; damping-off de-named 'Pythium' -> 'Rhizoctonia, Botrytis, and others' + trimmed to psu_microgreens; storage dropped usu + added psu; UNR URL updated.

open_findings.summary: No dedicated Tier-1 extension page exists for CULINARY wheatgrass (Triticum aestivum grown for juice); extension 'wheatgrass' pages are all forage/rangeland species (a different genus, Thinopyrum/Pascopyrum/Agropyron). Indoor cultivation mechanics are anchored to the general microgreen/shoot T1 sources (usu_ext grow-your-own-microgreens, psu_microgreens growing-microgreens), which cover the shoot cycle, large-seed presoak, blackout, germination temperature, light, media, bottom-watering, airflow, and damping-off, but do not name wheatgrass specifically. Read via WebFetch this session.

Wheatgrass-specific numbers are MODELED from general shoot/microgreen principles + widely published grower practice, not a crop-specific T1 chart: the 8 to 12 hour berry soak, the optional 1-day pre-sprout, the ~2 to 3 day blackout, the 7 to 10 day harvest at the jointing stage (second blade), the ~6 to 7 inch cut height, and the ~1 to 1.5 lb grass / 12 to 20 oz juice per 1020 tray. Cited to the nearest catalog ids (usu_ext, psu_microgreens); tighten at the variety-delta pass.

Botany (species Triticum aestivum, family Poaceae) and the hard/soft + winter/spring wheat-class distinction rest on standard grain taxonomy corroborated across sources; the two most on-point class pages (OSU wheat-classes fact sheet, ISU crops encyclopedia) returned HTTP 403 to WebFetch this session and were NOT extracted per the deny rule. The 'use whole untreated sprouting-grade or food-grade wheat berries, not fungicide-treated planting seed' rule is anchored to psu_ext (Penn State 'What You Should Know About Sprouts'), which names wheat berries and raw-sprout food safety and was read this session.

Judgment/modeled calls: mold/damping-off called the number-one issue and wheatgrass flagged more mold-prone than salad microgreens (denser mat, longer grow-out); the root-hair-versus-mold distinction is standard grower guidance not on the T1 pages; germination_temp_f [60,75] taken from the psu_microgreens germination range applied to wheat; the freezer note (juice in cubes) is grower practice; difficulty kept 'easy' per the microgreen archetype despite the mold caveat; category 'Microgreens' kept as the indoor-shoot bucket (wheatgrass is a shoot/grass, not a true cotyledon microgreen). No health or medical benefit claims are made about wheatgrass juice.

Food-safety framing (raw juice consumed uncooked; seed as a pathogen source; sanitize tools and use safe water; higher-risk groups should be cautious with raw sprouts) is anchored to unr_ext (microgreens produce safety, PubID 3468) and psu_ext (raw sprouts). The optional pre-sprout step places wheatgrass partly under raw-sprout food-safety guidance; both pages were read via WebFetch this session and neither names wheatgrass specifically.

crops.description_seasoned: Wheatgrass is the young shoot of common wheat (Triticum aestivum), grown indoors and harvested as a grass rather than eaten as a leaf. Unlike salad microgreens, the fibrous blades are too tough to chew, so wheatgrass is pressed into a fresh, intensely green, grassy-sweet juice and taken as a shot. The cycle is short and repeatable: soak the wheat berries, spread them in a dense even mat on a shallow tray, give a brief dark blackout, then light to green up, and cut near the base at the jointing stage in about 7 to 10 days. Because there is no frost, season, or hardiness zone involved, the same tray grows identically on a counter anywhere. The one real challenge is mold: the dense wet seed mat is prone to it, so an even sow, steady airflow, and not over-soaking are the whole craft.
crops.description_beginner: Wheatgrass is baby wheat (the same plant that makes flour) grown indoors and cut young as a grass. Unlike salad microgreens, you do not eat the blades, because they are too tough and stringy to chew. Instead you juice them into a bright green, grassy, slightly sweet drink and take it as a small shot. Growing it is quick and always the same: soak the wheat berries, spread them thickly on a shallow tray, cover the tray to keep it dark for a couple of days, then move it into the light and cut the grass near the base in about a week to ten days. There is no outdoor season or weather to worry about, so it grows the same wherever you live. The main thing to watch is mold, since the crowded, damp seed mat can grow it easily, so spread the seeds evenly, keep air moving, and do not soak them too long.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Cut wheatgrass at the jointing stage, when a second blade just begins to split from the first, usually at about 6 to 7 inches and 7 to 10 days from sowing. Snip near the base with clean scissors and juice it fresh. The mat will not give a strong second cut, so each tray is a single harvest.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Your wheatgrass is ready when the blades are about 6 to 7 inches tall and a second blade is just starting to appear, usually 7 to 10 days after planting. Cut it near the base with clean scissors and juice it right away. It does not grow back well, so you start a fresh tray each time.

crops.name: Cilantro Microgreens
crops.sunlight: bright indirect light or a grow light
crops.water: keep the medium evenly moist; bottom-water once greened to keep leaves dry

soil.preferred_texture_seasoned: A fine, moisture-holding soilless medium: seed-starting mix, coconut coir, or a hydroponic fiber mat. Cilantro's long run to harvest rewards a clean, even medium.
soil.preferred_texture_beginner: Use a fine, soil-free growing medium that holds moisture well, such as seed-starting mix, coconut coir, or a growing mat made for microgreens.
soil.tolerated_texture_seasoned: Peat-based mixes and inert mats both work; over cilantro's 3 to 4 week cycle the trade is water-holding against a clean, mold-resistant surface.
soil.tolerated_texture_beginner: Both peat-based mixes and fiber mats work. Mixes hold more water, while mats stay cleaner over the long grow, so pick whichever suits you.
soil.problematic_texture_seasoned: Garden soil and heavy potting mixes are too coarse and carry pathogen and pest risk for a raw crop, and that risk compounds over cilantro's extended cycle.
soil.problematic_texture_beginner: Skip garden soil and regular potting mix. They are too coarse, and they can carry pests and germs that are risky for a crop you eat raw, especially over a long grow.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Use a light seed-starting mix, coconut coir, or a special growing mat made for microgreens. Do not use garden soil.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: A clean, fine, moisture-retentive soilless medium gives the most even germination cilantro can manage and a clean cut; coir and fiber mats keep grit off the harvest.

ph.note_seasoned: pH is not a practical lever for a single indoor microgreen cycle on a soilless medium; standard seed-starting mixes and coir sit in a workable range and need no adjustment, even over cilantro's longer run.
ph.note_beginner: You do not need to worry about soil pH for cilantro microgreens. The mixes and mats sold for microgreens are already fine as is.

fertilizer.timing: not applicable
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Even though cilantro runs longer than the fast brassicas, it is still harvested at the seedling stage on the seed's own reserves, so no fertilizer is needed for a single cycle. Added nutrients over the long grow mainly raise the risk of algae, off-flavors, and mold.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: You do not need to feed cilantro microgreens. The seed carries enough food to reach harvest, and over the long grow adding fertilizer just invites algae and mold.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: None.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: None needed.

companions.note_seasoned: Not applicable. Cilantro microgreens are grown as a dense single-type indoor tray, so there is no interplanting or companion relationship. Grow it in its own tray and combine with other greens after harvest.
companions.note_beginner: Not applicable. Cilantro microgreens grow as one type per tray indoors, so there are no companion plants. If you want a mix, just combine trays after cutting.

pests.description_seasoned: Small dark flies whose larvae live in persistently wet medium and feed on organic matter and tender roots. They are the main indoor microgreen pest, and cilantro's long 3 to 4 week cycle gives them more time to build up than a fast brassica does.
pests.description_beginner: Tiny dark flies that show up around constantly damp soil. Their larvae live in the wet mix. They are the main bug you might see indoors, and cilantro's long grow gives them extra time to appear.
pests.management_seasoned: Let the surface dry between waterings once the crop is up, bottom-water, and keep airflow up. Over a long cilantro cycle, sanitized trays and fresh medium between batches are what break the cycle; sticky cards help you catch a building population early.
pests.management_beginner: Keep the surface from staying soaking wet, water from the bottom, and keep air moving. Clean trays and fresh mix between batches keep gnats away, which matters more on a slow crop like cilantro.

diseases.description_seasoned: Soil-borne fungi (Rhizoctonia, Botrytis, and others) rot seedlings at the soil line under wet, crowded, still conditions, often alongside fuzzy white or gray surface mold. It is the number-one microgreen failure, and cilantro is especially exposed because its long blackout and 3 to 4 week grow keep a humid, dense canopy in place far longer than a fast crop.
diseases.description_beginner: The most common microgreen problem, and a real risk for cilantro because it grows so slowly. In wet, crowded, stuffy conditions, tiny fungi rot the baby plants at the base, and you often see fuzzy white or gray mold on the surface too.
diseases.management_seasoned: Prevention is the whole game and matters more the longer the crop sits: wrung-sponge moisture, bottom-watering once greened, constant gentle airflow, a sensible seeding rate, and sanitized trays between cycles. There is no rescue spray for a raw cut crop; a badly affected tray is composted and restarted clean.
diseases.management_beginner: You cannot spray this away on a crop you eat raw, so the fix is prevention, and it counts double on a slow crop: keep the mix just damp (not soggy), water from the bottom once the leaves are up, keep a small fan running, do not sow too thickly, and clean your trays between batches. If a tray molds badly, toss it and start over clean.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Mist once or twice daily through the long germination and blackout to hold even surface moisture; once greened, bottom-water as the tray dries. Expect many more watering days than a fast crop.
watering.frequency_beginner: While the seeds are sprouting, lightly mist the surface once or twice a day so it stays damp. This lasts longer for cilantro than most microgreens. After you move the tray into the light, water from the bottom whenever it starts to dry out.
watering.amount_seasoned: Enough to keep the medium at wrung-sponge moisture, never saturated; pour off any standing water after bottom-watering.
watering.amount_beginner: Just enough to keep the soil damp like a wrung-out sponge, never soggy. After bottom-watering, tip out any water left sitting in the tray.
watering.method_seasoned: Mist during germination and blackout; switch to bottom-watering once the canopy is up so foliage stays dry through the extended grow.
watering.method_beginner: Mist the top while the seeds are sprouting, then water from the bottom once the leaves are up so the leaves stay dry.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Standing water, a sour smell, fuzzy white growth on the medium or stems, and collapsed seedlings all signal overwatering and the damping-off that follows it, a bigger threat over cilantro's long cycle.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Water sitting in the tray, a bad smell, fuzzy white mold, or seedlings flopping over mean it is too wet. Cut back on water and improve airflow right away.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Curling, limp cotyledons and a medium that has pulled away from the tray edges indicate the canopy has dried too far between waterings.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Limp, curling leaves and soil that has shrunk away from the sides mean it got too dry. Water from the bottom right away.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Wet foliage in a dense, still canopy is the main driver of mold and damping-off, and cilantro sits in that canopy for weeks, so the cycle moves deliberately from misting to bottom-watering and pairs it with constant gentle airflow.
watering.method_note_beginner: Wet leaves packed close together with no air movement is what causes mold. Because cilantro grows slowly, keep watering from the bottom once the leaves are up, and keep a gentle fan going the whole time.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The blackout-to-light transition is the highest-risk window: after a long dark period the canopy is dense and humid under the cover, and a single overwatering here can seed damping-off across the whole tray.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The riskiest time is right when you uncover the tray and move it into the light after its long dark period. The plants are crowded and damp, so do not overwater, and make sure air is moving.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Do not hold cut cilantro microgreens at room temperature; the tender greens wilt within hours. Refrigerate immediately after cutting.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Do not leave cut cilantro microgreens out on the counter. They go limp fast, so put them in the fridge right after cutting.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerate dry in a vented container lined with a paper towel; the tender leaves keep about 5 to 7 days. Harvest only what you will use soon, since the flavor is best fresh.
storage.fridge_beginner: Keep cut cilantro microgreens in the fridge in a container with a paper towel to soak up extra moisture. They last about 5 to 7 days and taste best fresh.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Not recommended. Freezing collapses the delicate cells and ruins both texture and the fresh cilantro aroma. They are a cut-and-eat crop.
storage.freezer_beginner: Do not freeze cilantro microgreens. Freezing turns them mushy and dulls the flavor. Eat them fresh.
storage.notes_seasoned: Cut clean and dry: harvest with sanitized scissors into a clean container, keep the foliage dry, and chill promptly. Because they are eaten raw, the same clean-water and sanitized-surface rules that govern growing also govern handling.
storage.notes_beginner: Because you eat cilantro microgreens raw, keep everything clean: cut them with clean scissors into a clean, dry container and refrigerate right away.

recommended.name: Whole (unsplit) coriander seed
recommended.note: The standard round seed. Each one is a dry fruit holding two seeds, so it germinates slowly and unevenly. No presoak required; some growers soak 6 to 12 hours to even it out. 21 to 28 days.

recommended.name: Split (cracked) coriander seed
recommended.note: The fruit cracked into single halves, sold as splits. Growers report faster, more even germination and a denser tray. Same true cilantro flavor; 21 to 28 days.

recommended.name: Untreated sprouting or microgreen seed
recommended.note: Whatever the form, buy seed sold untreated and intended for sprouts or microgreens (not fungicide-treated garden seed), since the crop is eaten raw.

varieties.note_seasoned: For microgreens the garden distinction between slow-bolt cultivars (such as 'Leisure', 'Santo', or 'Calypso') is irrelevant, because you cut at the seedling stage long before bolting matters. What matters is seed form and quality: whole coriander seed is a two-seeded dry fruit that germinates slowly and unevenly, while split (cracked) seed is the fruit broken into single halves and tends to come up faster and more even. Either way, buy untreated seed sold for sprouting or microgreens, use it fresh, and plan for cilantro to be one of the slowest, lowest-yielding types you grow.
varieties.note_beginner: You do not need a special cilantro variety for microgreens. The fancy slow-bolt types sold for the garden do not matter here, since you cut the plants while they are tiny. What helps is the seed itself: regular whole coriander seed sprouts slowly and unevenly, while split (cracked) seed usually comes up faster and more evenly. Just make sure the seed is sold for sprouting or microgreens (not treated garden seed), and be patient, since cilantro is one of the slowest microgreens.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Not applicable. Cilantro microgreens are never moved outdoors or transplanted; the whole cycle is indoors.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: Not applicable. Cilantro microgreens stay indoors from seed to harvest, so there is no hardening off.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Sow densely and evenly across pre-moistened medium at roughly 28 grams of seed per 1020 tray. Cilantro is not presoaked in the standard method, though some growers soak 6 to 12 hours or use split (cracked) seed to speed and even the notoriously slow germination. Do not bury the seed; press it into contact, then cover for a long blackout. Even, firm contact is what gives cilantro its best shot at a uniform stand.
start_method.notes_beginner: Scatter the seeds thickly and evenly over damp growing medium, about 28 grams per standard tray. You do not have to soak cilantro, but a 6 to 12 hour soak, or using split (cracked) seed, can help it sprout faster and more evenly. Do not bury the seeds, just press them so they touch the surface, then cover the tray to keep it dark while the slow-sprouting seeds come up.

drainage.saucer_practice_seasoned: Nest the drilled tray inside a solid, hole-free tray. The outer tray catches runoff, lets you bottom-water, and is poured off so the crop never sits in standing water, which matters over cilantro's long grow.
drainage.saucer_practice_beginner: Set the tray with holes inside a second solid tray with no holes. The bottom tray lets you water from below and catch extra water, which you then pour out so the roots are not sitting in water.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Seed-starting mix, coconut coir, or a microgreen growing mat.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: None needed.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: Seed-starting mix, coir, or an inert fiber mat; about 1 to 2 inches deep.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: None; the medium is a substrate, not a nutrient source, for a single cycle.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Water from the bottom by setting the tray in a little water, then pour off what is left.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: No fertilizer needed.

overwintering.approach_seasoned: Not applicable. Cilantro microgreens are an indoor year-round cycle crop, harvested in weeks, with no dormant or overwintered phase.
overwintering.approach_beginner: Not applicable. Cilantro microgreens grow indoors all year and are harvested within a few weeks, so there is nothing to overwinter.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: The tray is the entire growing system: shallow, drained, nested over a solid tray for bottom-watering, sanitized between cycles. On a slow crop like cilantro, a clean, reused food-grade tray and fresh medium each cycle are the main defense against mold.
container_notes.notes_beginner: For cilantro microgreens, the tray is the whole setup. Use a shallow tray with drainage holes sitting inside a solid tray so you can water from the bottom. Wash and sanitize trays between batches, which matters on a crop that grows this slowly.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Bottom-water from the nesting tray; never leave the tray standing in water.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: None for a single cycle.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering reservoirs keep the medium too wet for a dense raw crop and raise the damping-off risk, which is already elevated by cilantro's long cycle; bottom-water by hand and pour off the excess instead.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: Skip self-watering pots for cilantro microgreens. They keep things too wet, which causes mold, and cilantro is already slow and mold-prone. Water from the bottom by hand and tip out the extra.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: A shallow flat tray works best: a 1020-style tray or any shallow food-safe container, with about 1 to 2 inches of medium. Depth beyond that wastes mix without helping a crop harvested at the seedling stage.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Use a shallow, wide tray, like a standard 1020 tray or any clean food-safe container. About 1 to 2 inches of growing mix is plenty. You do not need anything deep.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Not applicable. Cilantro microgreens grow on fresh or sanitized medium each cycle with no soil-borne carryover, so crop rotation does not apply.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Not applicable. You use fresh growing medium and clean trays each time, so there is nothing to rotate.
rotation.note_seasoned: Sanitation between cycles, not rotation, is the disease control for cilantro microgreens: compost the spent medium, then wash and sanitize the tray before the next sow.
rotation.note_beginner: Instead of rotating crops, just keep things clean: toss the used medium and wash and sanitize the tray before starting again.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Dense even broadcast on pre-moistened medium using whole or split coriander seed; no presoak required.
growth_stages.description_beginner: Scatter seeds thickly on damp medium; no soaking needed.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Seeds imbibe slowly and unevenly under a weighted cover at about 74 °F; cilantro is among the slowest microgreens to germinate.
growth_stages.description_beginner: Seeds sprout slowly and unevenly under a covered, warm tray. Be patient.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Long dark period, roughly 7 to 14 days, that evens the notoriously uneven stand and stretches stems before light.
growth_stages.description_beginner: A week or more in the dark that evens out the slow, patchy sprouting.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Uncovered into 18 hours of light at 68 to 72 °F; cotyledons green and the first true leaf may form.
growth_stages.description_beginner: Uncovered into bright light so the leaves turn green.

growth_stages.description_seasoned: Single cut at cotyledon to first true leaf, about 21 to 28 days from sowing; eaten fresh for true cilantro flavor.
growth_stages.description_beginner: Snip and eat when the little leaves are open, about 3 to 4 weeks in.

notifications.message_seasoned: Cilantro is slow, so check the tray: if most of the canopy has lifted, it may be time to end the long blackout and move into light.
notifications.message_beginner: Time to check your cilantro tray: if most of the sprouts are up, uncover it and give it light. It is fine if this takes a while.

notifications.message_seasoned: Switch from misting to bottom-watering now that the canopy is up, and make sure a fan is running through the long grow.
notifications.message_beginner: Now that the leaves are up, water from the bottom and keep a fan going.

notifications.message_seasoned: Cilantro microgreens are usually at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage around now, so cut and refrigerate promptly.
notifications.message_beginner: Your cilantro microgreens are likely ready to snip. Cut them and put them in the fridge.

notifications.message_seasoned: Start your next cilantro tray to keep the staggered supply going; the long cycle means a wider gap between sowings.
notifications.message_beginner: Start a new cilantro tray so you always have some coming, even with the long grow.

sow.text_seasoned: Pre-moisten the medium to wrung-sponge feel, then broadcast cilantro seed densely and evenly at about 28 grams per 1020 tray. No presoak is required, though a 6 to 12 hour soak or split (cracked) seed can speed and even the slow germination. Press seed into contact but do not bury it.
sow.text_beginner: Dampen the growing medium so it feels like a wrung-out sponge, then scatter cilantro seeds thickly and evenly, about 28 grams per tray. You do not have to soak them, but a soak or split seed can help. Press the seeds so they touch the surface, but do not cover them with soil.

germination.text_seasoned: Cover the tray and keep it warm (about 74 °F) and dark. Mist to hold even surface moisture, never soggy. Cilantro germinates slowly and unevenly, so expect this stage to run longer than most microgreens; a light weight on the cover keeps seed in firm contact for the most even stand you can get.
germination.text_beginner: Put the cover on and keep the tray warm (around 74 °F) and dark. Mist lightly so the surface stays damp but not wet. Cilantro is slow, so do not worry if it takes many days to sprout. A small weight on the cover helps it come up more evenly.

blackout.text_seasoned: Hold the weighted cover in the dark for the long cilantro blackout, roughly 7 to 14 days, then flip the cover off the canopy so it shades without touching. The extended dark stretch lengthens the stems and helps even out cilantro's ragged germination before greening.
blackout.text_beginner: Keep the covered tray in the dark for cilantro's long dark phase, about 1 to 2 weeks. The darkness makes the stems grow taller and helps even out the patchy sprouting before you give them light.

light.text_seasoned: Uncover into 18 hours of bright light at 68 to 72 °F and switch from misting to bottom-watering so foliage stays dry. Run a gentle fan the whole time; over cilantro's long grow the dense canopy plus high humidity is a prolonged damping-off window. Harvest at cotyledon to first true leaf, about 21 to 28 days from sowing.
light.text_beginner: Uncover the tray into bright light for about 18 hours a day at 68 to 72 °F, and start watering from the bottom so the leaves stay dry. Keep a gentle fan going to prevent mold, since cilantro sits for weeks. Cut when the first little leaves are open, around 3 to 4 weeks.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Yield is measured per tray, not per plant, and cilantro is one of the lowest-yielding microgreens: a well-sown 1020 tray returns roughly 4 to 8 ounces, less than the fast brassicas, and one Penn State trial recorded under 2 ounces.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: You measure cilantro microgreens by the tray, not by each plant. A full tray gives a modest amount, roughly a few handfuls, and cilantro yields less than most microgreens.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Every tray is a single harvest at peak; continuous supply comes from staggered sowings, not from regrowth, and cilantro's long cycle means wider gaps between trays.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Each tray gives one harvest at its best. To keep a steady supply, start new trays on a schedule, spaced out because cilantro is slow.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: There is no establishment year; the first tray performs the same as any later tray. Expect to dial in seeding rate, patience, and watering over the first few cycles, since cilantro is less forgiving than fast microgreens.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: There is no waiting period with microgreens. Your very first tray works like the rest; you will just get a feel for how slow cilantro is and how much to sow and water after a few tries.
factors_seasoned: seeding density (too sparse wastes the tray; too dense traps moisture and invites mold over the long grow)
even moisture and the mist-to-bottom-water transition
constant gentle airflow across the extended cycle
seed form (whole vs split) and freshness
patience through cilantro's slow, uneven germination
light intensity and the full 18-hour daily duration

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Not applicable. Cilantro microgreens are an indoor, light-controlled, seedling-stage crop with no lunar or seasonal timing.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Slow, patchy germination with bare spots across the tray
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Cilantro takes forever to sprout, and some spots stay bare
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Cilantro's own biology: the seed is a hard two-seeded dry fruit that germinates slowly and unevenly, worsened by old seed, uneven moisture, or no weighted cover
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Cilantro is just slow and uneven by nature, and old seed, dry spots, or no weight on the cover make it worse
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Give it time (allow well past a week), keep even moisture under a weighted cover, and consider split (cracked) seed or a 6 to 12 hour soak plus fresh microgreen-grade seed next time.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Be patient (it can take well over a week), keep the medium evenly damp under a weighted cover, and next time try split seed or a soak and fresh seed.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_seasoned: Even sow, even moisture, a weighted blackout cover, fresh seed, and either split seed or a presoak all steady the stand.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_beginner: Even seeds, even moisture, a weighted cover, fresh seed, and split or soaked seed all help it come up more evenly.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Fuzzy white or gray growth on the medium or stems; seedlings collapsing at the base
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Fuzzy white or gray mold, or baby plants flopping over at the bottom
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Damping-off and mold from overwatering, a saturated medium, dense sowing, and poor airflow, all made worse by cilantro's long humid cycle
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Too much water plus crowding and no airflow leads to mold, and cilantro's slow grow gives it extra time to take hold
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Switch to bottom-watering, pour off standing water, run a gentle fan, thin your seeding rate next time, and sanitize trays between cycles. Do not bury seed at sowing.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Water from the bottom, tip out extra water, keep a small fan going, sow a little less thickly next time, and clean your trays between batches.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_seasoned: Wrung-sponge moisture, constant airflow, dry foliage, and sanitized trays prevent it, and matter more the longer the crop sits.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_beginner: Keep the soil just damp, the air moving, the leaves dry, and the trays clean, especially on a slow crop like cilantro.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Tall, pale, weak stems that fall over
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Long, thin, pale stems that flop
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Too little light, or light introduced too late after the long blackout
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Not enough light, or leaving the tray covered too long
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Uncover once the canopy has mostly lifted and give bright light for the full 18 hours; move closer to the grow light or a brighter window.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Uncover the tray once most sprouts are up and give it bright light for about 18 hours a day, closer to the light.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_seasoned: End blackout when the canopy lifts rather than by a fixed date, and provide adequate light intensity and duration.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_beginner: Take the cover off when most of the sprouts are up, not by the calendar, and give them plenty of light.

failure_diagnostics.symptom_seasoned: Seed husks clinging to the canopy at harvest
failure_diagnostics.symptom_beginner: Seed shells stuck on the leaves
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Husks not shed during germination; insufficient weight or moisture during the blackout, more common with whole (unsplit) seed
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: The seed shells did not fall off while sprouting, which happens more with whole seed
failure_diagnostics.fix_seasoned: Use adequate blackout weight and moisture; mist and gently brush or rinse husks off the canopy before harvest, or try split seed next time.
failure_diagnostics.fix_beginner: Use enough weight and moisture during the dark phase, then gently mist and brush or rinse the shells off before cutting. Split seed can help.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_seasoned: Proper weighted blackout, consistent moisture, and split seed all help husks release.
failure_diagnostics.prevention_beginner: Keep the cover weighted and the tray evenly moist, and consider split seed, so the shells come off on their own.

indoor_cycle.tip_seasoned: The cycle is sow, blackout, light, harvest, but cilantro is one of the slowest microgreens. Germinate at about 74 °F under a weighted cover in the dark; germination is slow and uneven and the blackout runs long (about 7 to 14 days). Uncover into 18 hours of light at about 68 to 72 °F to green up, then cut at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage. Most trays finish in about 21 to 28 days.
indoor_cycle.tip_beginner: Cilantro microgreens follow the same four steps as any microgreen: plant, keep dark, give light, then harvest. The difference is they are slow. Keep the covered tray warm (around 74 °F) and dark for a week or two while the seeds slowly sprout, then uncover into bright light (about 68 to 72 °F) for roughly 18 hours a day until the leaves green up. Most are ready in about 3 to 4 weeks.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: For a steady supply, stagger sowings, but space them wider than fast microgreens: start a fresh cilantro tray about every 1 to 2 weeks rather than one big tray at once. Indoors there is no season, so the cadence is limited by tray count and cilantro's long 3 to 4 week cycle.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: To always have cilantro microgreens ready, start a new tray every week or two instead of one big batch. Because they grow indoors, you can keep this going all year, just spaced out since cilantro is slow.
succession_policy.notes: successions and max_successions_per_season are intentionally null: cilantro microgreens run continuously year-round indoors, so there is no season length to cap against. The practical limit is tray count, counter space, and the long 3 to 4 week cycle, not climate (window_type: continuous_indoor).

verification_status.verification_log_ref: Batch-2 Wave-5 cert (2026-07-06, Trevor-ruled). microgreen; the slowest of the wave (21-28 days, verbatim USU). NUTRITION/HEALTH/DETOX over-claim CLEAN: no nutrient, medicinal, or detox ('chelates heavy metals') claim -- the draft DECLINES UWI's 'digestive aid / cholesterol-lowering' + the UMD/PSU vitamin lines. Sprout-vs-microgreen CLEAN. Slow-cycle + the optional 6-12h soak verified (UMD explicitly names cilantro); the 'under 2 oz' yield checks out (PSU 46.8g). NOTE: the dispatched review agent first returned corrupted output (0 tool calls); re-dispatched and completed cleanly. FIXES: fungus-gnat pest -> UC IPM pn7448; damping-off de-named 'Pythium' -> 'Rhizoctonia, Botrytis, and others' + trimmed to psu_microgreens (PSU names Rhizoctonia/Botrytis; USU/UNR carry no pathogens); storage dropped usu + added psu; UNR URL updated. Modeled items (4-8oz yield, split-seed technique, two-seeded schizocarp) stay disclosed in open_findings.

open_findings.summary: Split (cracked) vs whole coriander seed: the faster/more-even germination of split seed and the crack-the-fruit technique are grower and seed-trade practice, not stated on a single T1 microgreen page. Nearest T1: usu_ext Table 1 (cilantro presoak 'No') and umd_ext (a 6 to 12 hour soak speeds germination); the two-seeded schizocarp botany is corroborated by uwi_hort (Apiaceae). Framed as traditional grower technique.

Presoak tension across T1 sources: usu_ext microgreen Table 1 lists cilantro presoak as 'No', while umd_ext lists cilantro among seeds where a 6 to 12 hour soak speeds germination. Modeled as optional (no presoak required, soak or split seed helps), citing both; reconcile at the review pass.

Per-tray yield (roughly 4 to 8 ounces per 1020 tray) is modeled: psu_microgreens trial data recorded cilantro at about 46.8 g per tray (under 2 ounces, the lowest observed), and usu_ext gives the ~28 g seeding rate but no cut-weight figure. The oz range is inferred from cilantro being a low-yield type; tighten with trial data at the review pass.

germination_temp_f [68,74] and the 68 to 72 °F lights-on range are modeled from usu_ext general microgreen guidance (74 °F germination, 72 °F lights-on, 68 °F lights-off) and psu_microgreens (soil 60 to 75 °F), not a cilantro-specific figure. Standard for the archetype; safe.

Blackout length (about 7 to 14 days) is taken from the usu_ext Table 1 'covered' column for cilantro; because cilantro germinates slowly, that covered period bundles germination and blackout rather than a distinct post-germination dark stretch. Modeled as the dark period; confirm the split at the review pass.

difficulty raised from the microgreens-mix 'easy' to 'medium' as a judgment call, on the basis of cilantro's slow uneven germination, long blackout, and prolonged mold/damping-off exposure over a 3 to 4 week grow. Confirm the rating at the review pass.

crops.description_seasoned: Cilantro microgreens are the young seedlings of Coriandrum sativum (cilantro, a member of the carrot and parsley family, Apiaceae), grown indoors and cut at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage for true, concentrated cilantro flavor. They are the crop for cooks who love cilantro, but they are also one of the slowest and most demanding microgreens: germination is slow and uneven, the blackout runs long, and a typical tray takes about 21 to 28 days, far longer than the 1 to 2 weeks of fast brassicas. The seed is really a small dry fruit that holds two seeds, sown whole or split (cracked) into halves; splitting or a soak can even out the ragged germination. Because there is no frost, season, or hardiness zone involved, the same tray grows identically on a windowsill anywhere, it just asks for patience.
crops.description_beginner: Cilantro microgreens are baby cilantro plants that you harvest young, once the first little leaves are open, for a strong, fresh cilantro flavor. If you cook with cilantro, this is the microgreen for you, but be warned: cilantro is one of the slowest microgreens to grow. It sprouts slowly and unevenly and usually takes about 3 to 4 weeks, much longer than quick types like radish or broccoli. The round cilantro seed is actually a little dry fruit holding two seeds; some growers crack it into halves or soak it to help it sprout more evenly. You grow it indoors all year on a shallow tray, with no outdoor season or weather to worry about, so it grows the same way no matter where you live, it just takes patience.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Cut at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage, typically 21 to 28 days from sowing, one of the longest waits among microgreens. Snip just above the medium with clean scissors; the stand will not regrow, so the tray is a single cut.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Your cilantro microgreens are ready when the first little seed-leaves are open and the first true leaf is just showing, usually about 3 to 4 weeks after sowing. Snip them just above the soil with clean scissors and eat them fresh. They do not grow back, so you start a new tray each time.

crops.name: Beet

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Beets like loose, fertile, well-drained soil with no hard crust on top. Loosen the bed about 6 to 8 inches down and rake out rocks and clods, because beet roots grow rounder and smoother in loose soil and come out forked or stunted in packed, stony ground. The most common beet-specific problem is a hard surface crust: the seed is slow and the seedlings cannot push through a dried crust, so keep the top of the soil loose and damp. Mix in some compost, aim for a soil pH around 6.0 to 7.0, and add a little boron only if a soil test shows you need it, because beets get black spots inside the root when boron runs low.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Beets do best in deep, loose, well-drained soil rich in organic matter, ideally a sandy loam or loam that does not crust. They are less depth-demanding than carrots, since the root swells near the surface, but stones, clods, and compaction still cause forking and misshapen roots. The beet-specific seedbed concern is surface crusting: germination is slow and the seedlings cannot break through a dried, crusted surface, so a fine, loose, evenly moist top layer matters. Work in well-finished compost, and keep pH in the slightly acidic to neutral range, about 6.0 to 7.0. Beets are notably boron-sensitive: low boron, common in sandy or high-pH soils, causes internal black spot (corky brown-black areas in the root), so test before adding boron and apply it sparingly because the margin between deficient and toxic is narrow.

ph.note_beginner: Soil pH measures how acidic or alkaline your soil is, on a scale from 1 to 14 where 7 is neutral. Beets like it from about 6.0 to 7.0, slightly acidic to neutral, and they are one of the few vegetables that handle slightly alkaline soil fairly well. The bigger problem is soil that is too acidic, below about 6.0, where seeds come up poorly and the plants cannot take up nutrients well. A cheap soil test from your local extension office tells you your number and whether to add lime. One beet-specific note: low boron in the soil causes black spots inside the root, so if you have seen that before, a soil test can check boron too.
ph.note_seasoned: Beets grow best at a slightly acidic to neutral pH of about 6.0 to 7.0, and they tolerate mildly alkaline soil better than most garden vegetables. Acidity is the bigger risk: below about 6.0, germination and stand drop off and micronutrient uptake suffers. Above about 7.5, boron, manganese, and iron availability declines, and high pH also favors scab on the roots. Beets are unusually boron-sensitive, so where internal black spot has occurred a soil test should include boron; correct it sparingly, since beets are also easily injured by excess boron. A standard soil test from your local extension office removes the guesswork on both pH and boron before sowing.

fertilizer.timing: Work compost and a balanced fertilizer into the bed before sowing; optional light side-dressing once the tops are established.
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Beets are moderate feeders. Work a balanced fertilizer and well-finished compost into the bed before sowing, then side-dress lightly once the tops are established if growth is weak. Because the leafy tops are also harvested, beets tolerate more nitrogen than carrots, but heavy nitrogen still favors tops over roots, so keep it balanced. The nutrient to watch is boron: where soils are sandy or alkaline, a boron deficiency causes internal black spot, corrected with a very small, soil-test-guided amount of borax.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Beets do not need heavy feeding. Mix a balanced fertilizer and some compost into the bed before planting, and give one light feeding later only if the plants look weak and pale. Since you eat the leaves too, a little nitrogen is fine, but too much grows big tops and small roots.
