crops.name: Cucumber

soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Cucumbers do best in a moisture-retentive yet well-drained loam or sandy loam enriched with plenty of organic matter. Work several inches of compost or well-rotted manure into the bed before planting, since these are fast, thirsty plants with shallow roots that resent both drought and waterlogging. Many growers plant in low hills or mounds, which warm faster in spring and drain well, and a trellis keeps the fruit straight and off wet ground. Sandy loams warm early and suit the first sowings, while heavy clay holds water and invites root and fruit rot, so amend it generously or build raised mounds.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Plant cucumbers in rich, well-drained soil with plenty of compost mixed in. They grow fast and have shallow roots, so they like soil that stays evenly moist but never soggy. Many gardeners plant them on low hills or mounds, which warm up quicker and drain better, and growing them up a trellis keeps the fruit clean and straight. If your soil is heavy or stays wet, build up mounds or use raised beds so the roots do not sit in water.

ph.note_seasoned: Cucumbers do best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, around pH 6.0 to 6.5. They still grow across a wider band, roughly 5.5 to 7.0, but uptake of some nutrients tightens as the soil turns alkaline. Test before planting and lime or add sulfur only on the test's advice rather than by guess.
ph.note_beginner: Cucumbers like soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, about pH 6.0 to 6.5, and most garden soil is already close. An inexpensive soil test tells you where you stand and whether you need to adjust it before planting.

fertilizer.frequency: At planting, then side-dress once or twice
fertilizer.type: balanced at planting, then nitrogen side-dress
fertilizer.timing: Work into the bed before planting, then side-dress about a week after flowering begins and again 3 weeks later
fertilizer.example_product: balanced 10-10-10 at planting, then a nitrogen source such as blood meal
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Cucumbers are moderate feeders over a short, fast season. Work a balanced fertilizer or several inches of compost into the bed before planting, then side-dress with a little nitrogen about a week after flowering starts and again roughly three weeks later if the plants look pale. The main pitfall is too much nitrogen, which drives lush vines and leaf at the expense of fruit and draws aphids and disease. Pair feeding with steady, even moisture, because the nutrients only help a plant that is not also drought-stressed, and drought stress is what turns cucumbers bitter.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Cucumbers grow fast and need a moderate amount of feeding, not a lot. Mix a balanced fertilizer or compost into the soil before planting, then feed with a little nitrogen about a week after the flowers start, and again a few weeks later if the plants look pale. Do not overdo the nitrogen, since too much makes leafy vines instead of cucumbers. Keep the plants evenly watered too, because feeding only helps a well-watered plant.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Your cucumbers are flowering, time for a light nitrogen side-dressing. Keep nitrogen moderate so the plant sets fruit instead of running to leaf, and keep the water steady.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Your cucumbers are starting to flower. Give them a light feeding of nitrogen now.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 worked in at planting suits cucumbers, followed by a light nitrogen side-dress once they flower. Avoid high-nitrogen lawn-type fertilizers, which push foliage at the expense of fruit.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer with equal numbers, like 10-10-10, at planting, then a little nitrogen once flowers appear. Avoid high-nitrogen lawn fertilizer.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: Work a balanced fertilizer or 1 to 2 inches of compost into the bed before planting. Then side-dress lightly with nitrogen about a week after flowering begins, placed a few inches out from the plants and watered in, repeating about three weeks later if needed. A common rate is roughly 1 tablespoon of 10-10-10 per plant, or a comparable scoop of compost or balanced organic fertilizer.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Mix some compost or a balanced fertilizer into the soil before planting. Then feed once with a little nitrogen about a week after flowers appear, scratched into the soil a few inches from the stem and watered in, and again a few weeks later if the plants look pale.

companions.note_seasoned: Cucumber companions earn their place by drawing pests away, bringing in bees, or feeding the soil, rather than by crowding the bed. Give vining plants room or a trellis, and use companions as a border or light interplanting. The signature cucumber pest is the cucumber beetle, which also vectors bacterial wilt, so radish and nasturtium are traditionally interplanted to lure or deter beetles, and a row of sunflowers or corn can serve as a living trellis and windbreak. Because cucumbers are insect-pollinated, pollinator flowers like borage and dill keep bees working the blooms and improve fruit set. Beans fix nitrogen for the moderately hungry vines. Most of these pairings are traditional or mechanistic rather than trial-proven, and are labeled accordingly. The firmest rule is a rotation one: keep cucumbers away from other cucurbits, which share the whole pest and disease complex.
companions.note_beginner: The most useful cucumber companions are flowers that bring in bees, since cucumbers need bee visits to set fruit, plants like radish and nasturtium that lure pest beetles away, and beans that feed the soil. Sunflowers or corn can act as a natural trellis. The one rule that really matters is to keep cucumbers away from other squash, melons, and pumpkins, which all share the same pests and diseases.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Radish
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Radishes are often planted among cucumbers to lure cucumber beetles, the cucumber's worst pest, away from the vines. They grow fast and are pulled before they crowd anything. A popular, low-risk traditional pairing.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A long-standing trap and deterrent planting for cucumber beetles, the pest that also spreads bacterial wilt to highly susceptible cucumbers. Radishes are quick, cheap, and out of the bed before they compete, which makes them an easy interplant even though the beetle-reduction effect is traditional rather than trial-isolated.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Radish-as-cucumber-beetle-deterrent is a widely repeated traditional interplant; no T1 trial isolates the effect on cucumber.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Nasturtium
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Nasturtiums lure cucumber beetles and aphids away from cucumbers and their flowers bring in bees. An easy, edible-flowered neighbor.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Often planted near cucurbits as a trap and deterrent for cucumber beetles and aphids, and its flowers draw the bees cucumbers depend on for fruit set. Trap cropping is a documented principle, but the specific nasturtium-cucumber effect is not formally isolated, so treat it as a plausible aid.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Trap-cropping for cucurbit beetles/aphids is documented in principle; the nasturtium-cucumber pairing is not trial-isolated.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Beans
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Beans pull nitrogen from the air into the soil, which the fast-growing cucumber appreciates, and they do not share its pests. A good, traditional neighbor.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Pole or bush beans fix nitrogen that benefits the moderately heavy-feeding cucumber, and they share none of the cucurbit pests. The nitrogen benefit largely reaches neighbors after the beans break down, so treat it as season-long soil-building rather than an instant feed, but the mechanism is sound.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Legume nitrogen fixation via Rhizobium is established biology; the same-season transfer to an adjacent cucumber is modest, so mechanistic/medium rather than research_backed.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Sunflower
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: A row of sunflowers gives cucumber vines something to climb and a bit of shade, and the blooms bring in bees. A practical, traditional support plant.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Tall sunflowers can serve cucumbers as a living trellis and light windbreak, lifting the vines off the ground for cleaner, straighter fruit and better airflow, while their flowers recruit pollinators. The structural benefit is real and practical; the pairing is traditional rather than a measured yield effect.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Sunflower-as-trellis is a structural intercropping practice; the cucumber benefit is space-and-support, not a trial-isolated pair effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Borage
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Borage flowers are loved by bees, and cucumbers need bee visits to set fruit, so a few borage plants nearby can help with pollination. Mainly grown to bring in bees.
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A strong bee magnet whose flowers recruit the pollinators cucumber fruit set depends on, since the female flowers need repeated bee visits to size a fruit. Pollinator-habitat value is well grounded; the specific borage-cucumber pairing is traditional rather than trial-tested.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Cucumber fruit set is pollinator-dependent; flowering insectary plants like borage draw bees. Pairing is habitat-based, not pair-isolated.

good_seasoned.name: Dill
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Dill flowers draw hoverflies, lacewings, and parasitic wasps that prey on aphids, and it is the classic kitchen partner for pickling cucumbers. The beneficial-insect draw is mechanistically sound; the specific cucumber pairing is traditional. Let some plants flower for the benefit.

provenance.reason: Umbel flowers like dill are documented insectary plants for aphid predators; the cucumber-specific benefit is traditional, not pair-isolated.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Other cucurbits
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep cucumbers away from other squash, melons, and pumpkins. They all get the same pests and diseases, so planting them together makes those problems worse.
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Summer and winter squash, melon, and pumpkin share cucumber's whole pest and disease complex, including cucumber beetle with the bacterial wilt it spreads (to which cucumber is especially susceptible), squash bug, powdery and downy mildew, and angular leaf spot. Grouping them concentrates that pressure and lets problems build. A real epidemiology and rotation principle rather than a tested adjacency effect: spread cucurbits out and rotate them.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Shared cucurbit pests/pathogens and cucumber-beetle wilt vectoring are extension-documented; the bad-adjacency claim is a sound epidemiological principle, not pair-tested.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Potatoes
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Some gardeners keep potatoes and cucumbers apart, since both are hungry plants and potatoes can bring their own diseases. This is more tradition than a proven rule.
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional caution that potatoes and cucumbers compete for the same nutrients and that potatoes can harbor blight and attract pests near the vines. There is no strong T1 mechanism for the specific pairing, so it persists mostly as garden lore.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: A folk anti-companion caution; competition is plausible but no T1 source isolates a potato-cucumber antagonism.

bad_seasoned.name: Other cucurbits
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Summer and winter squash, melon, and pumpkin share cucumber's whole pest and disease complex, including cucumber beetle with the bacterial wilt it spreads (to which cucumber is especially susceptible), squash bug, powdery and downy mildew, and angular leaf spot. Grouping them concentrates that pressure and lets problems build. A real epidemiology and rotation principle rather than a tested adjacency effect: spread cucurbits out and rotate them.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Shared cucurbit pests/pathogens and cucumber-beetle wilt vectoring are extension-documented; the bad-adjacency claim is a sound epidemiological principle, not pair-tested.

bad_seasoned.name: Potatoes
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional caution that potatoes and cucumbers compete for the same nutrients and that potatoes can harbor blight and attract pests near the vines. There is no strong T1 mechanism for the specific pairing, so it persists mostly as garden lore.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: A folk anti-companion caution; competition is plausible but no T1 source isolates a potato-cucumber antagonism.

pests.name: Cucumber beetles
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small yellow beetles, striped (three black stripes) or spotted (eleven black spots), chew young leaves, stems, flowers, and fruit. The bigger threat is indirect: both kinds transmit bacterial wilt, to which cucumbers are highly susceptible, so beetle feeding on seedlings can be followed weeks later by sudden, runaway vine wilt and collapse.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Small yellow beetles with stripes or spots chew the leaves and flowers, especially on young plants. Worse, they spread bacterial wilt, a disease that makes cucumber vines suddenly wilt and die.
pests.cause_seasoned: Striped and spotted cucumber beetles feed on cucurbits and carry the bacterium that causes bacterial wilt in their gut, infecting plants as they feed. Cucumber is more susceptible to the wilt than squash or pumpkin, so even light beetle pressure on seedlings can be costly. Bitter-fruited varieties attract more beetles.
pests.cause_beginner: Cucumber beetles feed on the plants and carry the germ that causes bacterial wilt, infecting cucumbers as they chew. Young seedlings are most at risk, and cucumbers catch the wilt easily.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Protect seedlings with row cover removed at flowering, hand-pick beetles in the cool morning, and use yellow sticky traps to monitor and reduce numbers. Where bacterial wilt is a known problem, controlling the beetles is the only effective control of the disease, since there is no cure once a plant is infected.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover young plants with row cover (remove it when flowers open so bees can get in), pick the beetles off in the morning when they are slow, and use yellow sticky traps. Keeping the beetles down is the best way to avoid the wilt disease they spread.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Exclude beetles from seedlings with row cover, keep young plants vigorous so they grow past the vulnerable stage, choose non-bitter varieties that attract fewer beetles, clear weeds and debris, and rotate away from where cucurbits grew. Aim control at the early-season colonizers that vector wilt.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover seedlings until they flower, keep them growing strong, clear away weeds and old plants, and do not plant where squash-family crops grew last year.

pests.name: Squash bug
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Leaves develop yellow specks that brown and wilt, and heavily fed vines wilt rapidly and turn brittle. Flat bronze to brick-red egg clusters appear on leaf undersides along the veins, and gray-brown adults and pale nymphs cluster near the crown and under debris.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Leaves get yellow spots, then brown and wilt, and you find clusters of shield-shaped gray-brown bugs and their bronze eggs on the undersides of leaves near the base of the plant.
pests.cause_seasoned: The squash bug, a true bug that feeds with piercing-sucking mouthparts on cucurbit foliage and stems, injecting saliva that wilts and browns the vines. Populations build through the season and are hardest to control once nymphs are large; the bugs overwinter as adults in garden debris.
pests.cause_beginner: Squash bugs pierce the leaves and stems and suck out the juices, which makes the vines wilt. They breed through the summer and hide in plant debris over winter.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick adults, crush the egg masses on leaf undersides, and trap bugs by laying a board near the plants overnight, then lifting it in the morning and destroying the cluster underneath. Target young nymphs with insecticidal soap, since large nymphs and adults are tough to kill.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick the bugs off by hand and scrape off the egg clusters under the leaves. A board laid on the ground overnight draws them underneath, then lift it in the morning and destroy them. Treat the young bugs with insecticidal soap.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Use row cover on young plants until flowering, clean up vines and debris at season's end to cut overwintering sites, and rotate cucurbits. Scout leaf undersides for the bronze egg clusters from early in the season and act before nymphs mature.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover young plants until they flower, check under the leaves for eggs early in the season, and clean up old vines after harvest so the bugs have nowhere to overwinter.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Colonies of small soft-bodied insects, often melon aphids, cluster on leaf undersides and growing tips, causing leaves to curl, pucker, and yellow, with sticky honeydew and sooty mold following. Beyond direct feeding, melon aphids transmit cucumber mosaic and other viruses that mottle and distort the foliage and fruit.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny soft insects gather on the undersides of leaves and on new growth, making leaves curl and turn yellow, often with a sticky film. They can also spread viruses to your cucumbers.
pests.cause_seasoned: Melon and other aphids suck sap and reproduce rapidly in warm weather, building up quickly on stressed or over-fertilized plants. The honeydew they excrete fosters sooty mold, and several aphid species spread cucumber mosaic virus.
pests.cause_beginner: Aphids are small insects that suck the plant's juices and multiply fast, especially on soft, over-fed growth. The sticky honeydew they leave behind grows black mold.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong jet of water and spray insecticidal soap or horticultural oil with thorough coverage of leaf undersides, repeating every few days. Conserve lady beetles, lacewings, and parasitic wasps, which usually bring aphids under control. Reflective or aluminum-foil mulch deters them from young plants.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water and treat the undersides of the leaves with insecticidal soap, repeating every few days. Ladybugs and other helpful insects eat aphids, so welcome them.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen, which drives the soft growth aphids favor, scout leaf undersides and growing tips, and support natural enemies rather than spraying broadly. Reflective mulch deters aphids from young plants.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen, check the undersides of leaves regularly, and let helpful insects do their work instead of spraying everything.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine pale yellow and reddish-brown stippling on the upper leaf surface, often with faint webbing on the undersides, in hot, dry weather. Damage can develop very quickly: leaves bronze, dry, and drop, and a heavy infestation can kill a plant.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny specks and a dusty, stippled look on the leaves, sometimes with fine webbing underneath, mostly in hot, dry weather. The leaves can dry out and die fast.
pests.cause_seasoned: Two-spotted spider mites feed on the contents of individual leaf cells, and they multiply explosively in hot, dry, dusty conditions, especially on water-stressed plants. They are not insects, so many insecticides do not touch them.
pests.cause_beginner: Spider mites are tiny relatives of spiders that suck the juice from leaf cells. They love hot, dry, dusty conditions and breed very fast.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Knock mites off with a strong spray of water to the leaf undersides, and treat with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil twice, about five days apart, covering the undersides well. Conserve predatory mites, lady beetles, and minute pirate bugs, which are the main natural controls.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray the undersides of the leaves with a strong jet of water, and treat with insecticidal soap, repeating in about five days. Keeping the plants watered and the area free of dust helps a lot.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep plants well watered and avoid drought stress, since mites flare on dry, dusty plants. Hose down foliage in hot spells, avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that kill the mites' natural enemies, and scout leaf undersides in hot weather.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep cucumbers well watered, since dry, dusty plants attract mites. Rinse the leaves in hot weather and avoid spraying broad insecticides that kill the helpful bugs.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: White, powdery patches appear on the upper and lower leaf surfaces and stems, spreading until leaves yellow, brown, and die back ahead of schedule. Early defoliation cuts the season short, reduces yield, and exposes fruit to sunscald.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: A white, powdery coating spreads over the leaves until they turn yellow and brown and die. The plant fades early and the cucumbers may not size up well.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Powdery mildew fungi that thrive between about 50 and 90°F in dry weather with high humidity, and unlike most leaf diseases they do not need leaf wetness to infect. Crowded plantings, poor airflow, and shade worsen it, and it is one of the most common late-season cucumber diseases.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that spreads on warm days with high humidity, especially where plants are crowded and air does not move well. It does not need wet leaves to take hold.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Treat at the first spots, before it spreads, with a labeled fungicide such as sulfur, potassium bicarbonate, neem, or horticultural oil, covering both leaf surfaces, and remove the worst leaves. Avoid overhead watering. Once it is widespread, control is mostly damage limitation.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Treat early, at the first white spots, with a labeled fungicide like sulfur or horticultural oil, and remove badly affected leaves. Water the soil, not the leaves. Once it covers the plant it is hard to stop.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Choose resistant varieties, space plants generously for airflow, plant in full sun, and avoid excess nitrogen and overhead watering. Scout from midsummer and treat at the first sign, since prevention and early action beat rescue.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Pick resistant varieties, give plants plenty of room so air moves between them, plant in full sun, and water at the base. Start checking in midsummer and act at the first white spots.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Angular yellow blotches, bounded by the leaf veins, appear on the upper leaf surface, with a grayish or purplish fuzzy growth on the underside in humid weather. Spots brown and run together, and severe infection rapidly defoliates the vines. Cucumber is one of the most susceptible cucurbits.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Yellow patches show on top of the leaves, often boxed in by the veins, with fuzzy gray growth underneath in damp weather. The spots brown and spread until the leaves die. Cucumbers catch it easily.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A fungus-like water mold (Pseudoperonospora cubensis) that spreads on wind-borne spores and needs leaf wetness and humidity to infect, so it flares in wet, humid spells and dewy conditions. It moves fast once established and is favored by crowding and prolonged leaf wetness.
diseases.cause_beginner: A mold-like disease that spreads in wet, humid weather and needs wet leaves to infect. It can move through a planting very quickly, and cucumbers are especially prone to it.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Improve airflow, let foliage dry, remove badly affected leaves, and apply a labeled fungicide such as copper or chlorothalonil, covering leaf undersides, when conditions favor the disease. Avoid overhead irrigation, which keeps leaves wet and feeds the infection.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Open up the planting so leaves dry faster, remove the worst leaves, and use a labeled fungicide when wet weather sets in. Do not water over the leaves.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space for airflow, water at the soil line rather than overhead, choose resistant varieties where available, and avoid working among wet vines. Scout closely in humid weather, when the disease can appear and spread quickly.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Give plants room so air moves between them, water at the base, and watch closely in humid weather. Choose resistant varieties if downy mildew is common where you live.

diseases.name: Bacterial wilt
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Individual leaves, then whole vines, wilt and collapse even though the soil is moist, often spreading until the plant dies. A field test helps confirm it: cut a wilted stem and slowly draw the cut ends apart, and infected sap pulls into thin, sticky white strands. Cucumber is especially susceptible.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Vines wilt and die even though the soil is wet. If you cut a wilted stem and pull the two ends apart slowly, infected sap stretches into sticky white strings. Cucumbers get this disease easily.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A bacterium (Erwinia tracheiphila) spread by striped and spotted cucumber beetles, which carry it in their gut and infect plants as they feed. It clogs the water-conducting tissue, so the plant wilts despite adequate water. Cucumber and muskmelon are far more susceptible than squash and pumpkin.
diseases.cause_beginner: A germ spread by cucumber beetles as they feed. It blocks the plant's water pipes, so the vine wilts even when watered. Cucumbers are very prone to it.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once a plant is infected; remove and destroy wilting plants to limit spread. Control is really beetle control, so management aims at keeping cucumber beetle numbers down, especially early in the season.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure once a plant has it, so pull and destroy infected plants. The real fix is keeping cucumber beetles down, since they spread it.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Manage cucumber beetles from seedling stage with row cover removed at flowering, keep young plants vigorous, choose less-bitter varieties that attract fewer beetles, and remove infected plants promptly. Controlling the beetle vector is the only effective control of the disease.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Keep cucumber beetles under control, since they spread the disease. Cover young plants until they flower, and pull any plant that wilts and tests positive with the sap-string check.

diseases.name: Angular leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small, water-soaked spots on the leaves expand until they are boxed in by the larger veins, giving them an angular shape. In humid weather a milky bacterial ooze dries to a thin white crust on the underside, and as the spots dry they tear away, leaving ragged holes. Fruit can develop small, sunken, water-soaked spots.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small water-soaked spots on the leaves, bounded by the veins so they look angular. In damp weather a white crust forms underneath, and the dried spots tear out, leaving ragged holes in the leaves.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A seedborne bacterium (Pseudomonas syringae pv. lachrymans) that is spread by splashing water, rain, and handling wet plants, and overwinters in crop residue. It is most damaging in warm, wet weather, roughly 75 to 82°F with frequent rain.
diseases.cause_beginner: A bacterial disease carried on seed and spread by splashing water and wet hands. It is worst in warm, rainy weather and survives the winter in old plant debris.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no rescue spray that cures it; remove badly affected leaves, avoid working among wet plants, and apply a labeled copper bactericide at the first sign to slow spread. Water at the base to keep foliage dry.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure, so remove the worst leaves, stay out of the patch when the plants are wet, and use a labeled copper spray early if it is spreading. Water the soil, not the leaves.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant certified disease-free seed and resistant varieties, do not work among wet vines, water at the soil line rather than overhead, rotate cucurbits on a three to four year cycle, and remove crop debris after harvest.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Buy clean seed and resistant varieties, water at the base, stay out of the patch when it is wet, and clean up old vines at the end of the season. Move cucumbers to a new spot each year.

diseases.name: Anthracnose
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellowish or water-soaked leaf spots that turn brown to black and may drop out, giving a shot-hole look, plus elongated tan lesions on stems and dark, circular, sunken cankers on the fruit. In wet weather the fruit cankers ooze a pinkish spore mass and rot.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Brown or black spots on the leaves that can fall out and leave holes, and dark, sunken, circular spots on the cucumbers themselves that rot in wet weather.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A fungus (Colletotrichum orbiculare) that needs several days of rainy, warm weather to infect and spreads in splashing water. It survives on old cucurbit residue and on infected seed.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that spreads in warm, rainy weather and splashing water, and survives on old plant debris and infected seed.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove infected leaves and fruit, avoid overhead watering, and apply a labeled fungicide such as chlorothalonil preventatively in wet spells. Do not save seed from infected plants.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove infected leaves and fruit, water at the base, and use a labeled fungicide in long wet spells. Do not save seed from sick plants.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Use disease-free seed and resistant varieties, rotate out of cucurbits for three years, remove and destroy old vines and residue after harvest, and water at the soil line to keep foliage dry.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Start with clean seed, rotate cucumbers to a new spot for a few years, clean up old vines after harvest, and water the soil rather than the leaves.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Aim for about 1 inch of water per week, more in heat or sandy soil, delivered deeply and less often rather than in light daily sprinkles. Even, steady moisture is what keeps cucumbers from turning bitter and misshapen.
watering.frequency_beginner: Give cucumbers about 1 inch of water a week, more when it is hot and dry. Water deeply rather than a little every day, and try to keep it steady so the fruit does not turn bitter.
watering.amount_seasoned: Around 1 inch per week is the working range, leaning higher during flowering and fruit sizing and through hot, dry spells. Cucumbers are over 95 percent water and have shallow roots, so they show drought stress fast: uneven or inadequate water gives bitter, pinched, or curled fruit.
watering.amount_beginner: About 1 inch of water a week is a good target, more while the plant is flowering and the cucumbers are growing. Cucumbers are mostly water, so do not let them dry out.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base of the plant with drip or a soaker hose, keeping the foliage as dry as possible, since wet leaves invite powdery and downy mildew and angular leaf spot on an already disease-prone crop. A 2 to 3 inch mulch holds soil moisture even, which directly reduces bitterness, and keeps soil from splashing onto the leaves.
watering.method_beginner: Water the soil, not the leaves, using a soaker hose or watering wand at the base. Keeping the leaves dry helps prevent the leaf diseases cucumbers are prone to, and a layer of mulch keeps the soil evenly moist so the fruit stays sweet.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting even when the soil is wet, and soft, rotting stems at the base point to overwatering or poor drainage. Saturated soil invites root and fruit rot, especially on heavy ground.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If lower leaves yellow, the plant wilts even though the soil is wet, or the base gets soft and mushy, it is getting too much water or the soil drains poorly.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Midday wilting that recovers overnight is normal in heat, but leaves that stay limp and dull signal real drought. The clearest fruit-stage tell is bitter, pinched, or curled cucumbers, which trace directly to inadequate or uneven water during sizing.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Some midday wilting in hot weather is normal and passes by evening. Leaves that stay wilted mean the plant is too dry, and drought while fruit is forming gives bitter, misshapen cucumbers.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Base watering is the most useful habit for cucumbers, because the same plant that wants steady moisture is also disease-prone and turns bitter under stress. Keep water on the soil, air moving through the leaves, and the moisture even, and mulch to buffer the swings.
watering.method_note_beginner: Watering the soil instead of the leaves is the best thing you can do for cucumbers. It keeps them hydrated without encouraging leaf disease, and steady moisture keeps them from going bitter.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The water-critical stretch is flowering through fruit set and sizing. Steady moisture here drives well-formed, sweet fruit; uneven or short water gives bitter, pinched, curled cucumbers even with good pollination.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The most important time to keep cucumbers watered is when they are flowering and the fruit is growing. Even watering then gives you sweet, well-shaped cucumbers.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Harden off indoor-started cucumbers over 7 to 10 days, easing them into direct sun and wind before transplanting. Handle the rootball gently, because cucurbits resent root disturbance and a checked seedling sulks for weeks; use larger cells or peat pots and set plants out young, before the roots circle the pot.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: If you started seedlings indoors, set them outside for a little longer each day over about a week so they get used to sun and wind. Be gentle with the roots when you plant, since cucumbers do not like having their roots disturbed. Peat pots you can plant whole help a lot.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Because cucurbits resent root disturbance, direct sowing once the soil is reliably warm (at least 70°F at 2 inches; seed will not germinate below about 50°F) is the simplest, most reliable method, and direct-sown plants quickly catch up. Sow several seeds about 1 inch deep per hill or station and thin to the strongest. Start seeds indoors only to gain two to three weeks in a short season, sowing in peat pots three to four weeks before planting out and setting them out before they outgrow the pot.
start_method.notes_beginner: The easiest way to grow cucumbers is to sow seeds right where they will grow, once the soil is warm (about 70°F). Plant a few seeds 1 inch deep in each spot and keep the strongest. Start seeds indoors only if your season is short, about three weeks before planting out, ideally in peat pots you can plant whole, and move them outside while they are still small.

drainage.saucer_practice: If you use a saucer, empty it after watering. Cucumbers will not tolerate sitting in standing water, which invites root and stem rot.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Use a good bagged potting mix, not garden soil, which packs down too hard in a pot.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in compost and a slow-release fertilizer at planting. Pots need feeding more often than beds because watering washes nutrients out.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: Use a rich, free-draining peat- or coir-based potting mix, not garden soil, which compacts and drains poorly in a container.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend in about a third compost plus a slow-release balanced fertilizer at planting. Because frequent watering flushes nutrients, plan to feed a container cucumber more regularly than one in the ground.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out much faster than garden beds. In summer a potted cucumber may need water every day, sometimes twice. Check daily and water until it drains from the bottom, since drying out makes cucumbers bitter.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Feed a potted cucumber more often than a garden plant, with a balanced liquid feed every couple of weeks once it is growing strongly.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Not applicable. Cucumbers live for one season and die with the first frost, so there is nothing to overwinter. Plant new seeds next year.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Not applicable. Cucumber is a frost-tender annual that completes its life in a single season and is killed by the first hard frost, so there is nothing to overwinter. Pull spent vines at season's end and start fresh from seed the following year.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Cucumbers grow well in a container if you pick a compact or bush variety and give it a big enough pot, at least 5 gallons and 12 inches deep, with a small trellis or cage for the vines. Put it in full sun, keep it well watered (pots dry out fast, and dry cucumbers turn bitter), and feed it regularly. Water the soil, not the leaves, to help avoid mildew.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Cucumbers are one of the better container cucurbits, especially compact or bush types such as Spacemaster, Bush Champion, Salad Bush, or Patio Snacker, and the parthenocarpic types that fruit without pollinators suit a balcony well. They still want a real pot: at least 5 gallons and 12 inches deep, larger is better, with a trellis or cage so the vines climb and the fruit hangs straight. Give it full sun, water at the base daily in heat (a dry pot makes bitter fruit), and feed regularly, since a small soil volume dries and depletes fast over the short, fast season. The container figures here follow general container-vegetable guidance; cucumber-specific container numbers are modeled.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry far faster than beds, and a cucumber in a pot can need water once or even twice a day in summer heat. Check daily by feeling the top inch of mix, and water until it runs from the drainage holes; even moisture prevents the bitter, misshapen fruit that water swings cause.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Feed container cucumbers more often than in-ground ones, since steady watering leaches nutrients. After the slow-release charge at planting, add a balanced liquid feed every 2 to 3 weeks, keeping nitrogen moderate once fruit sets.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering container suits a potted cucumber well, smoothing the moisture swings this thirsty, bitterness-prone plant dislikes. Keep the reservoir topped up in heat, still water from below to keep foliage dry, and use a large enough planter that the roots are not constantly waterlogged.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match because it keeps the water steady, which cucumbers like and which keeps them from going bitter. Keep the reservoir filled, especially in hot weather, and use a big pot.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: A container cucumber needs a deep, sturdy pot, at least 12 inches deep and 5 gallons or more, with a trellis or cage so the vines climb rather than sprawl over the rim. Trellising in a pot keeps the fruit straight and the foliage open against mildew. Choose compact, bush, or parthenocarpic types for containers rather than long sprawling vining kinds.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Give a container cucumber a deep, sturdy pot, at least 12 inches deep and 5 gallons or more, and add a small trellis or cage for the vines to climb. Climbing keeps the cucumbers straight and the leaves healthier. Pick a compact or bush variety for a pot, not the big sprawling kinds.

recommended.name: Marketmore 76
recommended.recommended_note: The standard open-pollinated slicing cucumber: long, dark-green, 8 to 9 inch fruit on disease-tolerant vines. Dependable and widely adapted, with resistance to several common diseases.

recommended.name: Straight Eight
recommended.recommended_note: Classic heirloom slicer with straight, smooth 8 inch fruit; an All-America Selections winner and a reliable garden standard.

recommended.name: Boston Pickling
recommended.recommended_note: Old open-pollinated pickling type with prolific, blocky, bumpy 3 to 6 inch fruit; excellent for pickles and seed-saveable.

recommended.name: National Pickling
recommended.recommended_note: Productive pickling cucumber bred for uniform small fruit; good for whole pickles when picked young.

recommended.name: Suyo Long
recommended.recommended_note: Asian burpless heirloom with long, ribbed, mild, thin-skinned fruit that is gentle on digestion; best trellised so the fruit hangs straight.

recommended.name: Diva
recommended.recommended_note: Award-winning parthenocarpic (seedless, burpless) slicer that sets fruit without pollination; tender, bitter-free, thin skin. Excellent under cover or in containers.

recommended.name: Lemon
recommended.recommended_note: Round, pale-yellow heirloom the size of a lemon; mild, never bitter, and very productive. A fun, easy garden novelty.

recommended.name: Spacemaster
recommended.recommended_note: Compact bush slicer on short vines; one of the best choices for containers and small beds while still yielding full-size fruit.

varieties.note_seasoned: Choose a cucumber by use and space. For fresh eating, slicing types like Marketmore 76 (disease-tolerant and reliable) or Straight Eight are the standards; for pickles, the blocky, bumpy pickling types like Boston Pickling or National Pickling, picked small. Burpless and parthenocarpic types such as Suyo Long and Diva are bred to be mild, thin-skinned, and easy to digest, and the seedless parthenocarpic kinds set fruit without bees, which suits container and covered growing. Compact bush types like Spacemaster fit small beds and pots. Where disease pressure is high, lead with mildew- and wilt-tolerant varieties, and remember that less-bitter varieties also attract fewer cucumber beetles.
varieties.note_beginner: Pick a cucumber for how you will use it. Slicing types like Marketmore 76 or Straight Eight are best for fresh eating, pickling types like Boston Pickling are best for pickles and picked small, and burpless or seedless types like Suyo Long or Diva are mild and easy to digest. If you only have a pot or a small bed, choose a compact bush type like Spacemaster. Disease-resistant varieties are worth seeking out, and milder, less-bitter kinds also attract fewer pest beetles.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Avoid planting cucumbers where another cucurbit grew in the last few years, including squash, melon, pumpkin, and other cucumbers. They share cucumber beetle with the bacterial wilt it spreads, squash bug, powdery and downy mildew, angular leaf spot, and anthracnose, all of which build up in the soil and on debris.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Do not plant cucumbers where you grew squash, melons, pumpkins, or other cucumbers in the last few years. They get the same pests and diseases, which build up in the soil.
rotation.good_after: Legumes such as beans and peas, sweet corn, leafy greens, or alliums like onions and garlic make good preceding crops, since they do not share the cucurbit pest and disease complex, and a legume leaves nitrogen behind for the moderately hungry cucumber.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate cucurbits on a 3 year cycle, and a 3 to 4 year break where angular leaf spot or anthracnose has been a problem, since both persist on residue. The point is to break the buildup of cucumber beetle, beetle-vectored wilt, and soilborne and seedborne disease. Clear and remove spent vines at season's end rather than tilling them in, which removes overwintering pest and disease sites and makes rotation more effective.
rotation.note_beginner: Try not to grow cucumbers or their relatives in the same spot more than once every 3 years or so. Moving them around the garden each year helps avoid a buildup of pests and disease. Clean up old vines at the end of the season too.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Cucumbers are tender and short-lived off the vine. At room temperature they keep only a day or two before softening, so use them quickly or refrigerate, with the caveat that cucumbers are chilling-sensitive and do not love a very cold fridge either.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Cucumbers do not keep long at room temperature, just a day or two. Use them soon or put them in the fridge, but not the coldest part.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Stored in the warmest part of the refrigerator, ideally around 45 to 50°F at high humidity, cucumbers keep about a week. They are chilling-sensitive below about 50°F, where prolonged cold causes pitting, water-soaked spots, and faster breakdown, so they store neither as long nor as cold as hardy vegetables. Keep them away from apples, tomatoes, and other ethylene producers, which hasten yellowing.
storage.fridge_beginner: Keep cucumbers in the fridge for about a week, in the warmer crisper drawer rather than the coldest spot, since too-cold storage causes soft, pitted spots. Keep them away from apples and tomatoes, which make them go bad faster.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Cucumbers do not freeze well for fresh use, turning limp and watery because of their high water content. The practical way to keep a glut is to pickle it; freezing is only worth it for blended uses like soups or smoothies.
storage.freezer_beginner: Cucumbers do not freeze well, since they are mostly water and turn mushy. The best way to keep extra cucumbers is to make pickles.
storage.notes_seasoned: Treat cucumbers as a use-it-soon vegetable rather than a keeper. The answer to a glut is not long storage but eating, sharing, and above all pickling, which is exactly why pickling varieties exist. Keep fruit cool but not cold, around 45 to 50°F at high humidity, and use within a week.
storage.notes_beginner: Cucumbers are best used fresh and soon after picking. If you have too many, the best options are to eat them, share them, or turn them into pickles. Keep them cool but not too cold, and use them within about a week.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seeds sprout in about 4 to 10 days in warm soil (70 to 95°F is ideal); cold soil below about 50°F rots seed rather than germinating it.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: In warm soil, seeds sprout in about a week. Two seed leaves push up first. If the soil is cold, seeds rot instead of sprouting.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Sow 1 inch deep in warm soil. Keep evenly moist, not soggy. If you sowed several seeds per spot, thin to the strongest seedling once true leaves appear.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Plant seeds 1 inch deep once the soil is warm. Keep the soil damp until they sprout. If several come up together, keep the strongest one.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Did your cucumber seeds germinate, and how many days did it take?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your seeds sprouted yet?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Cotyledons followed by the first true leaves; growth is fast once warm. Watch for cucumber beetles, which target young plants and can transmit bacterial wilt, to which cucumbers are very susceptible.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: After the first two rounded leaves, true leaves appear and the plant grows quickly. Watch for striped or spotted beetles chewing the young leaves.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Protect from cucumber beetles, with row cover if needed (remove it at flowering for pollination). Provide a trellis early if growing vining types. Keep evenly watered and free of weeds.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep an eye out for beetles on young plants. Set up a trellis now if your cucumbers climb. Water regularly and keep weeds down. A light row cover protects seedlings, but remove it once flowers form.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How are your seedlings developing? Any sign of beetle damage?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How do your young plants look?

growth_stages.name: Established and vining
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Rapid leafy growth and lengthening vines that begin to throw tendrils and climb. This is the window to side-dress and to get the trellis in place before the vines sprawl, and to keep scouting for beetles and aphids.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant grows fast, sending out vines and curling tendrils that grab onto a trellis. This is when you feed it and make sure it has something to climb.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Side-dress lightly with nitrogen as flowering nears. Train vines onto the trellis. Mulch to hold even moisture (which prevents bitterness). Keep scouting for cucumber beetles and aphids.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Give the plant a light feeding of nitrogen now. Guide the vines onto their trellis. Add mulch to keep the soil evenly moist, which keeps the fruit from going bitter.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have your cucumbers been side-dressed and trained up? Any pests on the leaves?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are your plants climbing and growing well?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Yellow flowers open. Most cucumbers are monoecious, so male flowers (on thin stalks) usually open first and drop, which is normal; female flowers carry a tiny cucumber behind the bloom. Gynoecious and parthenocarpic types behave differently.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Yellow flowers open. The first flowers are usually male and fall off, which is normal. Female flowers have a tiny cucumber at their base.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Encourage pollinators and avoid spraying open blooms, since fruit set depends on repeated bee visits. If small fruit yellow and shrivel, pollination is poor; hand-pollinate in the morning. Keep moisture steady now to avoid bitterness.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Let the bees do their work and do not spray the flowers. If tiny cucumbers turn yellow and shrivel, the flowers were not pollinated, and you can hand-pollinate with a small brush. Keep watering steadily.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are you seeing female flowers and fruit set? Any small fruit aborting?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Is your plant flowering? Are any little cucumbers forming?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Glossy, firm fruit reaching pickable size for the type (2 to 4 inches for pickling, 6 to 8 for slicing), sizing up fast, often noticeably bigger day to day at peak.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Shiny, firm cucumbers reaching the size you want. They grow fast, so they are ready before you expect.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick every 1 to 2 days, cutting or clipping the stem. Harvest young for tenderness and to keep the plant producing; remove any oversized or yellowed fruit you missed, since they shut down new set and can turn bitter.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Check every day or two and pick the cucumbers while they are firm and shiny. Cut the stem rather than pulling. Picking often keeps more coming, and remove any big yellow ones you missed.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How much are you harvesting, and how often are you picking?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you started picking cucumbers?

growth_stages.name: End of season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Declining production, increasing powdery or downy mildew, or sudden wilting from bacterial wilt. The first frost kills the plant outright.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant slows down and the leaves may get powdery and white or yellow and spotted, or it wilts suddenly from disease. Frost kills it.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pull and remove spent vines rather than tilling them in, to cut overwintering pest and disease sites. A summer-sown succession often crops cleanly after the first planting fades to mildew or wilt.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pull out finished plants and clear them away at the end of the season. This helps prevent pests and disease next year. A second planting made in summer often keeps producing after the first one is done.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Is this planting winding down? Did you remove the spent vines?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Is your plant finished for the season?

notifications.body_seasoned: Your cucumber seedlings are up, which is when cucumber beetles colonize and can infect highly susceptible plants with bacterial wilt. Scout daily and protect young plants with row cover until flowering.
notifications.body_beginner: Your young cucumbers are up. Check for small striped or spotted yellow beetles, which spread a wilt disease cucumbers catch easily, and cover the plants until they flower.

notifications.body_seasoned: Time to sow a succession planting. A fresh sowing now, counted back from your first fall frost, often outproduces the spring crop on cleaner plants once beetles and mildew wear the first planting down.
notifications.body_beginner: Now is a good time to plant a second cucumber as a backup. Pests and mildew often wear out the first plants by late summer, so a fresh planting keeps cucumbers coming.

notifications.title_seasoned: Check your cucumbers, they size up fast
notifications.body_seasoned: Your cucumbers are fruiting. At peak they size up fast, so check every 1 to 2 days and pick young. Frequent picking keeps the plant producing; a fruit left to oversize turns bitter and stops new set.
notifications.body_beginner: Your cucumbers are making fruit. Check every day or two and pick them while firm and shiny, they grow fast.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost is coming, cucumbers will not survive it
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost warning for your cucumbers
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A frost is forecast. Cucumber is frost-tender and the first frost ends the plant, so pick everything usable now. There is no reliable way to carry a cucumber vine through a freeze.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Frost is coming, and it will kill your cucumbers. Pick all the cucumbers you can use before it hits.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat and dry soil can turn cucumbers bitter
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot spell may make cucumbers bitter
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A stretch of extreme heat is forecast. Heat over about 90°F plus dry soil drives the stress that makes cucumbers bitter and can stall fruit set. Keep moisture steady and mulched; quality recovers as the heat eases.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Very hot weather is coming. Heat and dry soil can make cucumbers taste bitter and slow them down. Keep them well watered and mulched, and they usually recover when it cools.

germination.text_seasoned: Soil temperature, not the calendar, governs cucumber germination. Wait until soil is at least 70°F at 2 inches; seed sown in cold ground below about 50°F rots before it sprouts.
germination.text_beginner: Wait for warm soil before sowing. Cucumber seeds rot in cold ground but sprout fast once it warms up.

seedling.text_seasoned: Cucumber beetles swarm young plants and spread bacterial wilt, which cucumbers catch easily. A floating row cover protects seedlings, but pull it off at flowering so bees can pollinate.
seedling.text_beginner: Protect young plants from beetles. A light cover helps, but take it off once flowers appear so bees can reach them.

established.text_seasoned: Get the trellis in early. Cucumbers grown up a trellis make straighter fruit, stay cleaner and drier, suffer less disease, and are far easier to pick than sprawling vines.
established.text_beginner: Give your cucumbers something to climb. Grown up a trellis, the fruit is straighter and cleaner and the plant gets less disease.

established.text_seasoned: Even moisture is the anti-bitterness habit. Mulch and water steadily; the drought and heat swings that stress the plant are exactly what drive the bitter compound into the fruit, worst at the stem end and skin.
established.text_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist and mulched. Letting cucumbers dry out, then soaking them, is what makes them taste bitter.

flowering.text_seasoned: Early male flowers opening and dropping with no fruit is normal; females, each with a tiny cucumber behind the bloom, come a little later. Judge pollination by whether small fruit size up or yellow and shrivel.
flowering.text_beginner: The first flowers often fall off without making cucumbers, that is normal. Real trouble is when tiny cucumbers turn yellow and shrivel, which means poor pollination.

flowering.text_seasoned: If set is poor in cool or pollinator-scarce conditions, hand-pollinate in the morning: pick a male flower, strip the petals, and dab pollen onto the center of each open female. Parthenocarpic types skip this entirely.
flowering.text_beginner: If cucumbers are not forming, you can hand-pollinate. In the morning, pick a male flower, peel off the petals, and gently touch it to the center of a female flower.

harvest.text_seasoned: Pick young and pick often. At peak, fruit sizes up fast, so check every 1 to 2 days; harvesting promptly keeps the plant setting new fruit instead of slowing down, and young fruit is the most tender.
harvest.text_beginner: Pick cucumbers while firm and shiny and check every day or two, they grow fast. Picking often keeps more cucumbers coming.

harvest.text_seasoned: Missed one and it turned yellow and seedy? Cut it off and compost it; leaving mature, seedy fruit on the vine tells the plant to stop setting, and over-ripe cucumbers turn bitter anyway.
harvest.text_beginner: If a cucumber got big and yellow, pick it off anyway. Leaving over-ripe fruit on the plant makes it stop producing.

end_of_season.text_seasoned: Pull spent vines and remove them rather than tilling them under, which buries overwintering beetles and disease residue. Clean beds now mean fewer pests and less angular leaf spot and anthracnose next season.
end_of_season.text_beginner: At the end of the season, pull up old vines and clear them away. This cuts down on pests and disease next year.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A healthy plant yields heavily over its short season, commonly 10 or more slicing cucumbers per vine and many more from pickling types picked small, often 5 pounds or more in a long, warm climate. A few plants are plenty for fresh eating; a pickling project wants a block of them.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: One cucumber plant produces a lot over the season, often a dozen or more slicing cucumbers. Two or three plants are plenty for fresh eating, while pickling takes more.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: At peak in warm weather a plant sets fruit quickly, and cucumbers size up so fast that picking every 1 to 2 days is essential. Frequent harvest at this stage actually keeps the plant producing; leaving a mature, seedy fruit on the vine signals it to slow down or stop.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: At its peak, a cucumber plant makes fruit fast. Pick every day or two, since picking often actually keeps more cucumbers coming.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Cucumber is forgiving and productive even for a first-time grower; the usual first-year surprises are bitterness from letting the plants dry out, and a sudden mid-season collapse from beetle-spread bacterial wilt. Steady water and early beetle control head off both.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Cucumber is one of the easier crops for beginners. The two things that catch people out are bitter fruit from letting the plants get dry, and plants suddenly wilting from a beetle-spread disease. Water steadily and watch for beetles early.
factors_seasoned: Even moisture: steady water through fruit set drives sweet, well-formed fruit; drought and heat swings cause bitterness and misshapen cucumbers.
Harvest frequency: picking young and often keeps a plant productive; letting fruit oversize and seed-up slows or stops new set.
Pollination: poor pollination in cool or pollinator-scarce conditions causes small fruit to abort; parthenocarpic types are exempt.
Pest and disease pressure: cucumber beetle and the bacterial wilt it vectors, plus powdery and downy mildew, commonly end the first planting.
Season length and heat: warm seasons extend the productive window, but extreme heat stalls set and drives bitterness; a frost ends it.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No T1 source supports timing cucumber planting by moon phase. We do not make a recommendation here; sow by soil temperature and frost dates instead.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Cucumbers tasted bitter
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The cucumbers were bitter
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Stress, usually heat or uneven water, drove up the plant's natural bitter compound (cucurbitacin), which concentrates in the skin and at the stem end. Wide temperature swings, drought, and poor nutrition all bring it on, and some varieties are inherently more bitter than others.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The plant got stressed, usually by hot, dry, or uneven conditions, which makes cucumbers bitter. The bitterness sits mostly in the skin and the stem end.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Heat, drought, irregular watering, or temperature swings stressing the plant; bitter-prone varieties make it worse.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Hot, dry, or uneven growing conditions, sometimes plus a naturally bitter variety.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water steadily and mulch to keep soil moisture even, harvest before fruit oversizes, and grow non-bitter or burpless varieties. Peeling and cutting off the stem end removes most of the bitterness from a fruit you have already picked.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep the plants evenly watered and mulched so they do not dry out, pick the cucumbers young, and try a burpless or non-bitter variety. Peeling and cutting off the stem end takes most of the bitterness out.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Small fruit yellowed and shriveled instead of sizing up
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Tiny cucumbers turned yellow and shriveled
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Poor pollination. Each female cucumber flower needs several bee visits to set; without enough pollen the young fruit aborts, yellowing and shriveling at the tip rather than sizing up. Common in cool, wet, or pollinator-scarce conditions and early in the season.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The flower was not pollinated well, so the little cucumber died instead of growing. This often happens in cool or rainy weather, or when there are few bees.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Inadequate transfer of pollen to the female flower, often compounded by early-season timing before pollinator activity peaks.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Not enough pollination of the flower.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant flowers to draw pollinators, avoid spraying open blooms, and hand-pollinate in the morning if early set is poor. Parthenocarpic varieties set fruit without pollination and sidestep the problem entirely.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Grow some flowers nearby for the bees, and hand-pollinate early cucumbers if needed. It usually gets better as more flowers open and bees get active, or grow a seedless variety that does not need bees.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Healthy vine wilted and collapsed in midsummer
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Plant suddenly wilted and died
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Most likely bacterial wilt, to which cucumbers are highly susceptible: cucumber beetles infected the plant, and the bacterium clogged its water-conducting tissue, collapsing a previously vigorous vine. The sap-string test confirms it. Squash bug feeding can cause similar wilting.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Usually bacterial wilt, a disease cucumber beetles spread that cucumbers catch easily. It clogs the plant's water pipes so the vine wilts even when watered. Cut a wilted stem and pull it apart slowly to see sticky white strings.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Bacterial wilt (Erwinia tracheiphila) introduced by cucumber beetles, clogging the water-conducting tissue; or heavy squash bug feeding.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: A beetle-spread disease, or heavy feeding by squash bugs.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Control cucumber beetles from the seedling stage with row cover until flowering, keep young plants vigorous, grow less-bitter varieties that draw fewer beetles, and remove infected plants promptly. There is no cure once a plant is infected.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep cucumber beetles down, since they spread the disease there is no cure for. Cover young plants until they flower, and pull any plant that wilts and shows the sticky-string sign.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Leaves turned white and powdery, then the plant faded early
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Leaves got white and powdery and the plant died back
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Powdery mildew defoliated the plant ahead of schedule. The white fungal coating spread across the leaves until they browned and died, cutting the productive season short and exposing fruit to sunscald. Downy mildew (yellow vein-bounded blotches with gray underside) does the same in humid weather.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Powdery mildew, a white coating on the leaves, spread until the leaves died and the plant stopped early. Downy mildew, with yellow patches and fuzzy gray undersides, does similar damage in damp weather.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Powdery or downy mildew fungus, worsened by crowding, poor airflow, and high humidity around the foliage; downy needs leaf wetness, powdery does not.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: A mildew fungus, made worse by crowded plants and poor air flow.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Choose resistant varieties, space and trellis plants for airflow, water at the base, and treat at the first spots. A summer-sown succession can carry harvest past the worst of it.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Pick resistant varieties, give plants room and a trellis for air flow, water the soil not the leaves, and treat early spots. A second planting helps too.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Cucumbers crop hard for a few weeks and then tire, so succession sowing keeps the supply steady instead of feast-then-famine. A first sowing after your last frost, then a second about three weeks later, spreads the harvest and keeps vigorous plants coming as the originals fade. The real payoff is late season: cucumber beetle, bacterial wilt, and powdery and downy mildew often take down the first planting by midsummer, so a replacement sown in early to midsummer, counting back from your first fall frost so it has time to mature, frequently outproduces the spring crop on cleaner, less stressed plants.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: Cucumbers produce heavily for a few weeks, then slow down, so plant a few seeds now and a few more about three weeks later for a steadier supply. A second planting in summer is a smart backup, since pests and mildew often wear out the first plants by late summer.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: cucumber_author_fresh_pilot 2026-06-29 (Claude Code lane, web access). Structurally mirrored on certified zucchini-courgette (warm_season_fruiting, Cucurbitaceae, continuous-immature-harvest twin), every value re-derived for Cucumis sativus. Core biology source-verified by live WebFetch: UMN Growing cucumbers (pH 6.0-6.5, soil >=70F, 1 in/week water, harvest often, bitterness from stress, cucumber beetle/bacterial wilt/powdery mildew/anthracnose/angular leaf spot); UMD Growing cucumbers (DTM 50-65, 12 in spacing / hills / trellis 9-12 in, full sun 6-10h, succession ~July 1, moderate fertilizer side-dress after flowering, pickling 2-4in / slicing 5-8in, trellis benefits, storage 45-50F 95% RH); Clemson cucumber + cucurbit insect-pest + cucurbit-disease factsheets (sandy-loam-to-clay-loam, soil 70F won't germinate <50F, slicing/pickling/burpless-seedless types + named varieties, downy/powdery/bacterial-wilt/anthracnose/CMV, squash bug/melon aphid/spider mite/pickleworm); UMN angular leaf spot. Cucumber-vs-zucchini refits: CLIMBING/trellis emphasis (straighter fruit, less disease), slicing vs PICKLING vs burpless/parthenocarpic types, BITTER-from-stress as a first-class note across watering/tips/diagnostics, cucumber HIGH susceptibility to beetle-vectored bacterial wilt, spider mites in heat. whole_crop_gate target PASS (0). NOT launch-ready: author_fresh_pilot pending biology-fidelity review + per-zone calendar source verification.

open_findings.summary: Per-zone resolved_by_zone planting/harvest windows are MODELED on the certified summer-squash twin schedule (cucumber and summer squash are direct-sown after frost on the same dates and share DTM 50-65, so extension charts list them together) plus the shared frost anchors. Individual per-zone dates are not each source-verified against a live cucumber-specific regional planting calendar.
open_findings.basis: Warm-season frost-anchored windows are physiologically identical to summer squash; calendars are internally coherent (A5/A24/A28 PASS) and anchored to each region's planting chart. Daily biology review + a per-region source-truth sample should confirm the cucumber dates before flip.

open_findings.summary: hawaii_tropical z11 authored bounded-continuous (NOT year_round); CTAHR B-91 is a scanned/image PDF that did not parse at the cert fetch (the same unparseable-PDF case as zucchini and blueberry). Corroborate against a parseable CTAHR cucumber source at the display-readiness pass.
open_findings.basis: z11 frost-free alone is insufficient for year_round (the onion/zinnia rule); the cited B-91 PDF is unparseable, so the honest bounded-continuous default stands rather than an unsupported year_round upgrade. No fabricated source.

open_findings.summary: Container figures (min_pot_gallons 5, recommended 10, depth 12 in) follow general container-vegetable guidance (UW-Madison Horticulture) rather than a cucumber-specific container source. Cucumber is a well-documented good container crop with a trellis, so the numbers are reasonable but modeled.
open_findings.basis: General container-vegetable guidance; cucumber-specific container gallonage is not separately T1-sourced. Flagged for the display-readiness pass.

open_findings.summary: ph.tolerated_range [5.5,7.0] is the general cucurbit tolerance band; the preferred [6.0,6.5] is T1 (UMN, Clemson). The tolerated endpoints are not each sole-anchored to a cucumber-specific statement.
open_findings.basis: Preferred range is source-exact; the wider tolerated band is standard, uncontroversial cucurbit guidance. Re-anchor at display-readiness.

northern_tier.plantings_provenance: Cucumber regional windows modeled on the certified summer-squash twin (zucchini-courgette): cucumber and summer squash are direct-sown after frost on the same schedule and share days-to-maturity (50-65), so extension planting charts list them on the same dates. Windows anchored to the region's planting chart plus the shared frost anchors; succession geometry and successions_realized are CC-derived, not authored. Region-specific per A5; spot-verify per-region at the daily review.
northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In the colder northern states (zones 3 to 7), cucumber is a summer crop. Plant after your last frost once the soil is warm, and in the coldest areas start a few seedlings indoors about three weeks early for a head start. Plant a second batch about three weeks after the first so the harvest keeps coming, since the first plants tire by late summer.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Across the northern tier (zones 3 to 7) cucumber is a single warm-season crop. Direct-sow after the last frost once the soil reaches 70°F, or set out transplants started about three weeks earlier in the shortest-season zones to gain time. One continuous summer window runs until the fall-frost runway closes, and a second sowing about three weeks after the first spreads the harvest and replaces the first planting as beetles and mildew wear it down. The exact dates shift later toward the colder northern edge and earlier in the milder south of the region.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer sowing gap is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: in deep-summer heat cucumber flowering and fruit set falter and the fruit turns bitter. When daytime highs run in the 90s°F and higher with warm nights, heat injures the flowers and pollen so plants set poorly or drop young fruit, and heat-plus-drought stress drives the bitter compound (cucurbitacin) into what fruit does form. Set and quality recover as temperatures ease, which is why these hot regions split into a spring and a fall crop rather than running through summer. (regional extension planting chart; UMN Extension growing cucumbers)

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast and Gulf, cucumber grows in two seasons, spring and fall, with a break in the hottest part of summer. Plant in spring once frost has passed, then plant again in late summer for a fall crop. Skip the peak of summer, when heat and pests make cucumbers struggle and turn bitter.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: In the Southeast and Gulf (zones 8 to 9) cucumber is a true spring-and-fall crop with a hot midsummer gap. Sow in spring from about April, making a second sowing two to three weeks later, then stop: heat, humidity, beetle-vectored wilt, and mildew curtail production and turn fruit bitter through the worst of summer. Sow again for fall by mid to late August so plants establish before cooling weather. The exact dates shift earlier in spring and later in fall toward the Gulf, and the reverse toward the cooler northern edge. The midsummer stretch is a deliberate no-plant gap, not a growing month.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer sowing gap is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: in deep-summer heat cucumber flowering and fruit set falter and the fruit turns bitter. When daytime highs run in the 90s°F and higher with warm nights, heat injures the flowers and pollen so plants set poorly or drop young fruit, and heat-plus-drought stress drives the bitter compound (cucurbitacin) into what fruit does form. Set and quality recover as temperatures ease, which is why these hot regions split into a spring and a fall crop rather than running through summer. (regional extension planting chart; UMN Extension growing cucumbers)
