crops.description_seasoned: Cucumber is a fast warm-season cucurbit grown for its tender, immature fruit, picked young while the skin is still glossy and the seeds are soft. Plants are vigorous and tendrilled, either long-vining or compact bush types, and they crop heavily over a short window once the heat arrives. Like summer squash, cucumber is a continuous-harvest crop: pick every day or two and the plant keeps setting, but let a fruit oversize and it turns seedy and yellow and the plant slows down. Growers choose among slicing types for fresh eating, blocky pickling types, and burpless or seedless (parthenocarpic) types bred to be mild and easy to digest. Cucumbers want warm soil, full sun, and steady, even moisture; uneven water and heat or drought stress are what turn the fruit bitter and misshapen.
crops.description_beginner: Cucumber is an easy, fast warm-season vegetable grown for its crisp, immature fruit, picked while small and shiny. The plants grow as long vines or compact bushes and produce a lot in a short time. Like zucchini, you pick cucumbers often, every day or two, while they are still young; if you leave one on too long it gets fat, seedy, and yellow, and the plant stops making new ones. You can grow slicing cucumbers for fresh eating, small pickling cucumbers, or burpless and seedless types that are mild and gentle on the stomach. Cucumbers like warm soil, full sun, and steady watering. Letting them get too hot or too dry is what makes them taste bitter.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Harvest cucumbers young and often, while the skin is glossy and firm and the seeds are still soft. Pick pickling types at about 2 to 4 inches, slicing types at about 6 to 8 inches, and burpless types per their variety length; the exact size is your preference, but earlier is more tender. Cut or clip the stem rather than pulling, to avoid tearing the brittle vine. At peak, check every 1 to 2 days, because a fruit left on the vine quickly turns yellow, seedy, and bitter, and a single oversized cucumber signals the plant to stop setting new ones. Remove any oversized or yellowed fruit you missed to keep the plant producing.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Pick cucumbers while they are young, firm, and shiny, before the skin dulls or yellows. Pickling cucumbers are usually picked small, around 2 to 4 inches, and slicing cucumbers around 6 to 8 inches, but the size is up to you. Cut or clip the stem instead of pulling, so you do not damage the vine. Check every day or two, because cucumbers grow fast and an over-ripe one turns yellow, seedy, and bitter, and leaving big fruit on the plant makes it stop producing. Pull off any you missed to keep more coming.
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Most cucumbers are monoecious: each plant carries separate male and female flowers, so a single plant sets fruit with no second variety needed. The flowers are insect-pollinated, mostly by bees, and each female needs several bee visits to size a fruit. Poor pollination, common in cool, wet, or pollinator-scarce conditions, shows up as small fruit that yellow and shrivel, and early-season male flowers often open and drop before the first females appear, which is normal. Two variety types behave differently: gynoecious (nearly all-female) hybrids set heavily but usually need a pollenizer plant in the mix, and parthenocarpic types set seedless fruit without any pollination at all, which is why they suit greenhouses, row covers, and containers. Plant flowers nearby and avoid spraying open blooms to keep pollinators working, and hand-pollinate with a small brush if set stalls.
crops.pollinator_notes_beginner: Most cucumber plants have both male and female flowers, so you only need one plant to get fruit. Bees move the pollen between the flowers, and each cucumber needs several bee visits, so anything that brings bees to your garden helps. If your early cucumbers stay small and shrivel, the flowers usually were not pollinated well, often in cool or rainy weather. Some special varieties, called seedless or parthenocarpic, make cucumbers without any bees at all, which is handy for pots and covered beds.

crops.name: Collards (Collard Greens)

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Collards like rich, loose soil that holds moisture but still drains well. Mix in plenty of compost before planting, since these big leafy plants are hungry feeders. They grow in most garden soils, but do best when the soil is fertile and never bone dry or waterlogged.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Collards are not fussy about soil texture and grow across a wide range, but they perform best in a fertile, well-drained loam or sandy loam high in organic matter. Because they are leafy heavy feeders held in the ground for months, work in plenty of compost before planting and keep moisture even. Tough, stringy leaves and stalled growth follow soil that either ponds water or bakes dry, so steady drainage and steady moisture both matter.

ph.note_beginner: Collards grow best in soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, around 6.0 to 6.8. A simple soil test tells you where you stand. If you have had clubroot, keeping the soil closer to neutral helps hold it back.
ph.note_seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 6.8; collards still grow across a wider 5.5 to 7.5 band. Holding the soil toward neutral, roughly 6.8 to 7.2, also helps suppress clubroot, a key brassica soil disease, so a grower with clubroot history should lean to the high end.

fertilizer.timing: balanced feed at planting, then side-dress with nitrogen 3 to 4 weeks later and after heavy cutting
fertilizer.example_product: 10-10-10 at planting, then calcium nitrate, blood meal, or 27-3-3 to side-dress
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Collards are leafy and N-hungry, and steady nitrogen drives the deep green color and tender growth that make the crop. Work a balanced fertilizer into the bed at planting, then side-dress with nitrogen about 3 to 4 weeks later, and feed again after a heavy cutting to push new leaves. Extension guides commonly cite a nitrogen side-dressing such as calcium nitrate or 27-3-3 along the row; on long-held plants a feed every 3 to 4 weeks keeps them productive. Avoid overdoing nitrogen, which softens growth and draws aphids.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Collards grow a lot of leaves, so they need regular feeding to stay deep green and tender. Mix some fertilizer into the soil when you plant, feed again about 3 to 4 weeks later, and give a light feed after a big harvest so it grows fresh leaves. Do not overdo it, since too much fertilizer makes soft growth that bugs love.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time to side-dress your collards with nitrogen.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Time to feed your collards.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced feed such as 10-10-10 at planting, then nitrogen side-dressings (calcium nitrate, blood meal, or 27-3-3) 3 to 4 weeks later and after heavy cutting to keep tender leaves coming.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a balanced vegetable fertilizer at planting, then a nitrogen-rich feed like blood meal as the plant grows.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: About 1.5 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 feet of row at planting, then side-dress roughly half a cup of calcium nitrate (or the label rate of a nitrogen source) per 25 feet of row every 3 to 4 weeks on long-held plants.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Follow the label rate for a balanced fertilizer at planting and a nitrogen-rich feed as it grows.

companions.note_beginner: Collards do well next to aromatic herbs, onions, and quick cool-season crops like lettuce and beets. The main thing is to keep them away from other cabbage-family plants, which share their pests and diseases, so planting them together makes problems worse.
companions.note_seasoned: Most collard companion pairings are traditional rather than research-tested. The ones worth acting on are practical: aromatic herbs and alliums as scent-based deterrents against the cabbage-family pests that hammer collards in the South, and quick cool-season crops like lettuce and beets as interplants that use space while the collards are small. The well-grounded caution is to separate collards from other brassicas, which share clubroot and the whole cole-crop pest complex, a rotation and disease principle more than a tested adjacency effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Onions
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Onions are a traditional neighbor for collards; their strong smell is said to help confuse and deter cabbage pests.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: A UMN-cited Iowa study found a thyme/onion/nasturtium mix reduced cabbage looper and imported cabbageworm damage in brassicas, and aromatic alliums are widely advised as scent-based deterrents for cole crops. extension_backed/medium: the trial used onion within a multi-species mix on broccoli rather than onion alone on collards, so the effect is supported but not cleanly isolated.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Onions are one of the better-supported brassica companions. Their pungent allium scent helps mask the collards from cabbage-family pests, loopers, cabbageworms, and root maggots, that hunt partly by smell, and extension trial work including onion in a mix with cole crops showed reduced caterpillar damage. Alliums are shallow-rooted and undemanding, so they tuck around collards without competing for much.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Dill
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Dill is a classic friend for cabbage-family plants. Its strong smell is said to put off pests, and its flowers bring in helpful insects.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Umbel/aromatic plantings are extension-noted for attracting parasitoid wasps and predators that prey on brassica caterpillars and aphids; the specific dill-collard pairing is not trial-tested, so medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Dill works for collards mainly through beneficial insects. Its umbel flowers attract parasitoid wasps and predators like hoverflies and lady beetles that prey on the aphids and cabbage caterpillars collards draw, and extension work pairing aromatic umbels with brassicas has shown reduced caterpillar damage. Let some dill flower for the benefit, and site it nearby rather than crowding the collards.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Lettuce
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Lettuce grows fast and low, so you can tuck it between young collard plants to use the space while the collards fill in.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Rests on the complementary-root-depth / succession interplant logic extensions endorse generally (a quick short crop under a slower one). Sound and widely taught, but a space/timing benefit rather than a measured collard-specific effect.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Lettuce and collards interplant well on structure and timing rather than chemistry. Lettuce is shallow-rooted and quick, collards taller and slower, so the lettuce uses the open ground and light between young collard plants and is harvested before the collards spread. Expect an efficient use of the bed in the cool shoulder season, not pest protection.

good_seasoned.name: Onions
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Alliums are a traditional companion for brassicas, their scent thought to deter cabbage pests, and an extension-cited trial including onion in a mix with cole crops showed reduced caterpillar damage. A practical, low-risk pairing that shares no major pest with collards.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: UMN-cited Iowa study included onion in a mix that reduced cabbage looper/imported cabbageworm on brassicas; isolated onion-on-collard effect not cleanly quantified.

good_seasoned.name: Dill
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Aromatic umbels like dill draw parasitoid wasps and predators that attack brassica caterpillars and aphids; extension work pairing umbels with cole crops has shown reduced damage. Let some flower, and keep it from crowding the collards.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Umbel/aromatic predator-recruitment for brassicas is extension-supported; specific dill-collard pairing not trial-tested.

good_seasoned.name: Lettuce
good_seasoned.timing: interplant along edges in cool weather
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A shallow, quick cool-season crop that shares collards' spring and fall windows and tucks along the bed edge, using space and light while the collards are still small. Space-driven and traditional, not a documented growth effect, and the two share no serious pest.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Space-use intercropping lore; no T1 source documents a lettuce-collard benefit.

good_seasoned.name: Beets
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A cool-season root that shares collards' window and works the lower soil while collards feed higher up. A traditional, space-efficient pairing rather than a tested effect.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Cool-season interplant lore; no T1 source documents a beet-collard benefit.

good_seasoned.name: Nasturtiums
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Often planted as a trap crop for cabbage aphids near brassicas. Trap cropping is a documented principle but works best for moderately mobile pests and is not a tested collard-nasturtium pairing, so treat it as a plausible aid rather than a proven control.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Trap cropping for aphids is a documented mechanism, but the specific nasturtium-collard pairing is not formally tested.

good_seasoned.name: Aromatic herbs (thyme, mint, sage)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Strongly scented herbs are a long-standing brassica companion, thought to mask the crop from cabbage moths and aphids that locate hosts by smell. Folk practice with partial mechanistic support rather than a measured collard-specific benefit.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Aromatic-herb pest confusion is well-documented companion tradition for brassicas; no collard-specific T1 trial.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Other brassicas
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep collards away from other cabbage-family plants like broccoli, cabbage, kale, and cauliflower. They share the same pests and diseases, so planting them together makes problems worse.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Same-family crops share pests and pathogens, so clustering raises pest/disease pressure, and successive brassica planting builds soil-borne clubroot. A sound epidemiological/rotation mechanism rather than a measured antagonism.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Planting collards cheek-by-jowl with their brassica relatives, broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, kale, Brussels sprouts, concentrates the whole family's shared pests (cabbage worms, loopers, flea beetles, harlequin bugs, root maggots) and shared diseases in one spot, and repeated same-family planting lets soil-borne clubroot build up. Spread brassicas out and rotate where they grow each year.

bad_seasoned.name: Other brassicas
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, kale, and the other cole crops share collards' clubroot and cabbage-family pests, so grouping them concentrates disease and pest pressure. A real rotation and disease principle rather than a tested adjacency effect; the practical rule is to spread brassicas out and rotate them.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Shared clubroot and shared cabbage-family pests are extension-documented; the bad-adjacency claim is a known agronomic principle, not formally pair-tested.

bad_seasoned.name: Strawberries
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional caution that brassicas and strawberries inhibit each other. There is no documented mechanism or T1 support; it persists as folklore.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Folk anti-companion claim with no pattern match or T1 support.

pests.name: Cabbageworms and cabbage loopers
pests.symptoms_beginner: You'll see ragged holes eaten in the big leaves, green caterpillars on the plant, and little dark droppings. Some caterpillars loop up in the middle as they crawl.
pests.cause_beginner: These are caterpillars that hatch from eggs laid by white butterflies and small moths. They love cabbage-family plants like collards and chew the leaves, which are the part you eat.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray a product called Bt, which is safe and targets only caterpillars, or pick the caterpillars and eggs off by hand from under the leaves. Spray again after rain, since it washes off.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover plants with a light fabric row cover right after planting to keep the butterflies and moths from laying eggs. Clear away old cabbage-family plants, and watch for the first white butterflies as your signal to act.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Ragged holes chewed through the leaves, with green caterpillars and dark frass on the foliage. Imported cabbageworms are velvety green; cabbage loopers move in a looping arch; diamondback larvae are small and wriggle when disturbed. Because collards are sold and eaten as whole leaves, even modest feeding scars the crop.
pests.cause_seasoned: The larvae of the imported cabbageworm, cabbage looper, and diamondback moth feed on brassica foliage; the adults are white or brownish butterflies and moths that lay eggs on the leaves. Caterpillar pressure runs especially long on collards in the warm South, where the crop is in the ground most of the year.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Spray Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) or spinosad, which target caterpillars, and hand-pick larvae and eggs from leaf undersides. Repeat after rain, since Bt breaks down.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Use floating row cover from transplanting to exclude the egg-laying adults, clean up brassica debris that shelters pupae, and scout for the first white butterflies as a spray cue.

pests.name: Harlequin bug
pests.symptoms_beginner: Shield-shaped black-and-orange (or black-and-red) bugs on the leaves, which develop white or yellow spots, then brown and look tattered. It is mostly a warm-region problem and loves collards.
pests.cause_beginner: The harlequin bug is a colorful stink-bug relative that pierces the leaves and sucks the juices, leaving pale blotches. It strongly prefers cabbage-family plants like collards, mustard, and kale, especially in the South.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Search out and crush the bugs, their eggs (little barrel-shaped eggs in rows), and young ones by hand. Use a row cover to keep them off, pull out badly infested plants, and clear away weeds and old plants where they hide over winter.
pests.prevention_beginner: Clean up garden debris and cabbage-family weeds where the adults overwinter, use row cover, and consider a trap crop of mustard or an early collard planting to lure them away from the main crop, then destroy it.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Shield-shaped bugs up to about 3/8 inch, brightly black-and-yellow or black-and-red, feeding with piercing-sucking mouthparts that leave white stipples; affected leaves brown and look tattered, and heavy feeding wilts and deforms plants. A warm-region pest that prefers collards, mustard, and kale over other cole crops, and a leading reason summer collards in the Deep South get buggy.
pests.cause_seasoned: The harlequin bug (Murgantia histrionica) is a brassica-specialist stink bug, most damaging in the southern United States, where it completes two to four generations a year and overwinters as an adult in debris and weeds.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick and crush adults, nymphs, and the barrel-shaped egg rows; exclude with floating row cover; remove heavily infested plants. Pyrethrins are permitted in organic production if pressure is severe.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Eliminate overwintering sites by removing crop debris and crucifer weeds, use row cover, and deploy an early trap crop of mustard, collards, or rapeseed to divert overwintering adults, then destroy it before the main crop is set out.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_beginner: You'll see clusters of tiny soft insects on the new growth and tucked into the leaf folds, often a waxy gray-green kind. Leaves curl and pucker, and there may be a sticky coating.
pests.cause_beginner: Aphids are tiny insects that suck juice from the plant. They breed fast and hide deep in the leaf folds and growing tip, where they are hard to wash out.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water, or use insecticidal soap or neem oil, making sure to hit under the leaves and into the folds where they hide. Repeat every few days.
pests.prevention_beginner: Welcome helpful bugs like ladybugs and lacewings that eat aphids, don't overdo the nitrogen fertilizer (lush growth attracts them), and check the new growth often.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of small soft-bodied insects on growing tips and leaf undersides; the waxy gray-green cabbage aphid is especially troublesome because it lodges in the crown and leaf folds and is hard to wash out at harvest.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several aphid species, notably the cabbage aphid, suck sap from collards; they multiply quickly and their feeding distorts growth and contaminates the harvested leaves. Populations explode in warm weather, so summer collards need close scouting.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong jet of water, or spray insecticidal soap or neem, covering leaf undersides and the crown; repeat every few days. Catch infestations early before they lodge in the growing point.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Encourage natural enemies like lady beetles and lacewings, avoid overfeeding nitrogen (which spurs the soft growth aphids favor), and inspect growing tips early so colonies do not lodge in the crown.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms_beginner: Lots of tiny round holes in the leaves of young plants, made by small dark beetles that jump away like fleas when you get close. Bad damage can stunt seedlings.
pests.cause_beginner: Flea beetles are small jumping beetles that chew on young cabbage-family leaves. They hurt seedlings most, because a tiny plant can't grow fast enough to recover.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover young plants with a row cover, and if there are a lot of beetles, use a spray such as spinosad or a kaolin clay coating. The main goal is to get the seedlings big enough to handle it.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover seedlings with row cover from the start, keep them strong with steady water and food so they grow past the damage, and pull nearby weeds in the cabbage family.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny round shot-hole pits chewed in the leaves of young plants; the small dark beetles jump like fleas when disturbed. Heavy feeding stunts or kills seedlings and scars the leaves of a leaf crop.
pests.cause_seasoned: Flea beetles chew the foliage of young brassicas and are most damaging at the seedling stage; on collards they also leave cosmetic shot-holes in the harvested leaves.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Protect seedlings with row cover, and spray spinosad or apply kaolin clay if pressure is high; the goal is getting plants past the vulnerable seedling stage.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Use row cover from sowing or transplanting, keep seedlings vigorous with even water and feeding so they grow through the damage, and clean up weedy brassica relatives nearby.

pests.name: Cabbage root maggot
pests.symptoms_beginner: New transplants wilt and grow badly or fall over. If you pull one up, you'll find small white maggots eating the roots. It's worst in cool, wet spring soil.
pests.cause_beginner: A small fly lays eggs at the base of the plant, and the maggots that hatch burrow down and eat the roots. The fly is most active in cool spring weather.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Once the maggots are in the roots you can't save that plant, so pull and throw away the badly damaged ones. Put your effort into protecting the rest from new eggs.
pests.prevention_beginner: Put a small collar or disk around the base of each transplant to stop the fly from laying eggs there, or use a row cover. Don't plant into cold, soggy soil, and avoid spots where you grew cabbage-family plants last year.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Transplants wilt, grow poorly, and may collapse; pulling a plant reveals small white maggots tunneling in the roots and lower stem. Damage is worst in cool, wet spring soil, so it bites the early spring planting more than the fall one.
pests.cause_seasoned: The larvae of the cabbage root fly tunnel into brassica roots; the adult lays eggs at the stem base, and the maggots feed on the roots below, sometimes killing young plants.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no effective rescue once maggots are in the roots; remove and destroy badly affected plants and protect the rest from further egg-laying.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Place a collar or disk around the stem base at transplanting to block egg-laying, or use row cover; avoid planting into cold, wet soil and rotate away from where brassicas grew.

diseases.name: Clubroot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Plants wilt in the afternoon, stay small and yellowish, and don't bounce back. If you dig one up, the roots are swollen into lumpy, club-shaped knobs.
diseases.cause_beginner: A germ that lives in the soil infects the roots of cabbage-family plants and makes them swell, which stops the plant from taking up water and food. It stays in the soil for years.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There's no cure once a plant has it, so pull and destroy infected plants. Adding lime to make the soil less acidic (closer to neutral) helps hold it back, and growing cabbage-family plants only rarely in that spot starves the germ out.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Don't grow collards or their cabbage-family relatives in the same spot more than once every 3 years, or longer if you've had clubroot. Keep the soil from being too acidic, improve drainage, and clean soil off your tools.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Plants wilt in the heat of the day, grow stunted and yellowed, and recover poorly; roots are swollen into distorted clubs and galls instead of normal fine roots.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A soilborne organism (Plasmodiophora brassicae) infects brassica roots and causes the galls, which block water and nutrient uptake. It persists in soil for many years and spreads in contaminated soil and water.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once plants are infected; remove and destroy them. Raising soil pH toward 7.0 or above with lime can suppress the disease, and long rotations starve it out over time.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate brassicas on a cycle of at least 3 years, and longer where clubroot is known; keep soil pH up, improve drainage, and avoid moving infested soil on tools and boots.

diseases.name: Black rot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Yellow patches shaped like the letter V appear at the leaf edges, pointing inward, with black veins inside them. It can spread through the plant and rot the leaves you want to eat.
diseases.cause_beginner: A bacteria that often comes in on infected seeds or transplants. It gets into the leaves and travels through the plant's veins, spreading fastest in warm, wet weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There's no real cure, so remove and destroy infected plants to keep it from spreading. Don't handle or brush against the plants while they're wet, because that spreads the bacteria.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Begin with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants, don't plant where cabbage-family crops grew recently, space plants for good airflow, and avoid overhead watering.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellow, V-shaped lesions spread inward from the leaf margins, with the veins inside the V turning black; the disease moves through the vascular system and can blacken and rot the harvested leaves. Warm, wet Southern weather drives it hard.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A seedborne bacterium (Xanthomonas campestris) that enters through leaf pores and wounds and moves through the plant's veins; it spreads in warm, wet conditions and on infected seed or transplants.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no effective cure; remove and destroy infected plants. Avoid working among plants when foliage is wet, since that moves the bacteria.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Start with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants, rotate away from brassicas, give plants room for airflow, and avoid overhead watering and handling wet foliage.

diseases.name: Alternaria leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small dark spots on the leaves that grow into round patches with concentric rings, like a tiny target. Bad cases make the leaves yellow and unusable.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that spreads in warm, wet weather and infects the leaves, leaving target-like spots. It's worse on stressed plants and in crowded, damp plantings.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove and destroy badly spotted leaves, improve airflow so leaves dry quickly, and use a copper spray if it spreads. Avoid wetting the leaves when you water.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Start with clean seed, rotate away from brassicas, space plants for airflow, water at the soil line, and keep plants healthy so they resist infection.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small dark lesions enlarge into circular spots with characteristic concentric rings (a target-spot look) and a yellow halo; because the leaves are the crop, even moderate spotting reduces the harvest. Favored by warm, wet conditions.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Fungi in the genus Alternaria (with Cercospora causing a similar leaf spot) infect brassica foliage, spreading by spores in wind and splashing water; infected seed, crop debris, and long leaf wetness drive it.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy spotted leaves and debris, improve airflow, avoid overhead watering, and apply a copper-based fungicide if pressure is high.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Use clean, disease-free seed, rotate away from brassicas, space for airflow, water at the soil line, and clear crop debris that harbors spores.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Pale yellow blotches on top of the leaves, with fuzzy grayish growth on the underside, mostly in cool, damp weather. Bad cases discolor the leaves.
diseases.cause_beginner: A mold-like disease that loves cool, wet, humid weather and spreads through the air and water. Wet leaves and crowded plants make it worse.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Open up the airflow so leaves can dry, remove the worst leaves, and use a copper spray if it's spreading. It's hard to stop once the weather stays damp.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Space plants so air moves between them, water at the soil instead of from above, and pick resistant varieties if downy mildew is common where you live.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Pale yellow patches form on the upper leaf surface with a fuzzy gray-white growth underneath, mainly in cool, damp weather; severe infection discolors and downgrades the leaves.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A fungus-like organism that thrives in cool, wet, humid conditions and spreads by spores in water and air; long leaf wetness and crowded plantings favor it. Collards' cool-season window overlaps the weather it likes.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Improve airflow and let foliage dry, remove badly affected leaves, and apply a copper-based fungicide if pressure is high; the disease is hard to stop once humidity stays high.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants for good air movement, water at the soil line rather than overhead, and choose resistant varieties where downy mildew is common.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Give about 1 to 1.5 inches weekly, kept even through the season, and more in hot, dry spells.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly 1 to 1.5 inches a week.
watering.amount_seasoned: About 1 to 1.5 inches per week, leaning to the high end during summer heat in the South.
watering.amount_beginner: Aim for roughly 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week, more when it is hot.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose where possible.
watering.method_beginner: Water at the base of the plant rather than over the leaves.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves and limp, soft growth; collards dislike waterlogged soil and can rot at the crown.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Lower leaves yellow and the plant looks soggy and limp.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting, slowed growth, and tough, stringy, bitter leaves; drought stress is the main cause of poor leaf quality, especially in summer heat.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Wilting leaves that turn tough and bitter, especially in hot weather.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Even moisture is the key to tender, mild collard leaves; the crop holds through summer heat far better when it never dries out, since dry spells make the leaves tough and bitter.
watering.method_note_beginner: Keep the water steady so the leaves stay tender, not tough, and water more in hot weather.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Steady moisture through the main leaf-production weeks, and especially during summer heat in warm regions, matters most for tender, mild leaves.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Water steadily while the plant is making lots of leaves, and keep it up through summer heat.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Collards can be direct sown or transplanted, and in the South direct sowing is the norm. For a spring crop, start seeds indoors about 4 to 5 weeks before set-out and transplant around 3 to 4 weeks before the last frost, or direct sow as soon as the soil is workable; collards tolerate frost. For a fall and winter crop, sow in mid to late summer so plants size up before cold, then harvest through fall and, in mild zones, winter. Harden transplants off over 7 to 10 days. Thin or set plants 18 to 24 inches apart for full-size plants.
start_method.notes_beginner: You can sow collard seeds right in the garden or start them indoors. For spring, start seeds about a month before planting out, and set plants in the garden a few weeks before your last frost, or just sow seeds once the soil can be worked. For a fall crop, sow in mid to late summer so it is ready before winter. Space full-size plants 18 to 24 inches apart. If you grow your own transplants, let them get used to the outdoors over a week before planting.

drainage.saucer_practice: Empty the saucer after watering so roots never sit in water; collards dislike waterlogged soil.

soil_mix.type_beginner: A good-quality potting mix, not garden soil.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in some compost for a steady supply of nutrients.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: A light, well-drained commercial potting mix high in organic matter.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend in compost and a slow-release nitrogen source; container collards still feed steadily.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out faster than the ground, so check daily in warm weather.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Feed a bit more often than in the ground, since watering washes nutrients out of pots.

overwintering.approach_beginner: In mild-winter areas, a potted collard keeps going through winter; just move it to a sheltered, sunny spot. In cold areas, pull the pot against the house or into an unheated garage during hard freezes, or grow a fast variety and enjoy it before deep winter.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Collards are very cold-hardy and overwinter in a container in mild zones, where they keep producing through winter in a sheltered, sunny spot. In colder zones the limited root volume of a pot freezes harder than open ground, so move containers against a wall or into an unheated structure during hard freezes, or treat the potted crop as a single fall-into-winter planting.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Collards grow into big plants, so give each one a pot of at least 5 gallons that is 12 inches or more deep, one plant per pot. Keep it watered and fed, and pick the lower leaves as you need them. In hot areas, give it some afternoon shade.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Collards make a good container crop, but they get large, so size up: use a container of at least 5 gallons and 12 inches deep, one plant per pot, and keep moisture even since pots dry quickly. Crop the lower leaves and leave the growing point, and in warm regions give afternoon shade and avoid heat-absorbing dark pots.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry faster than beds; check moisture daily in heat and water before the mix dries out.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Container collards need more frequent feeding than in-ground plants because watering leaches nutrients.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering container suits collards well, since it smooths out the steady moisture that keeps the leaves tender and mild.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match because it keeps the water steady, which keeps collard leaves tender.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: Collards build a tall stem and a heavy rosette of large leaves over a long season, so choose a container at least 5 gallons and 12 inches deep, one plant per pot. A broad, sturdy pot keeps the top-heavy plant from tipping and buffers the fast drying that narrow pots suffer.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Collards get tall and leafy, so give each one a roomy pot that holds at least 5 gallons and is about 12 inches deep. A wide, heavy pot is better than a tall skinny one because it holds moisture and keeps the big plant from tipping over.

recommended.name: Georgia (Georgia Southern)
recommended.note: Large, crumpled blue-green leaves on a tall plant; a classic Southern heirloom prized for tolerance of both heat and poor soil, and dependable yields. Slower to bolt and forgiving for beginners.

recommended.name: Vates
recommended.note: Compact, non-heading plant with large dark green leaves that hold color in cold; bolt-resistant and very cold-hardy, a dependable garden standard.

recommended.name: Champion
recommended.note: An improved Vates type, compact and slow to bolt, with good cold tolerance; a reliable choice for fall and overwintering.

recommended.name: Morris Heading (Carolina Improved Heading)
recommended.note: A Southern heading type that forms a loose head of tender leaves; a traditional favorite where a milder, cabbage-like collard is wanted.

recommended.name: Top Bunch
recommended.note: A fast, vigorous hybrid with tender, slightly savoyed leaves and good bolt resistance; quick to a first cutting and good for repeated harvest.

recommended.name: Blue Max
recommended.note: A productive hybrid with smooth blue-green leaves and uniform, vigorous growth; widely grown for high yields of tender leaves.

varieties.note_seasoned: Match the variety to the slot. Georgia (Georgia Southern) is the heat- and stress-tolerant Southern heirloom for summer-into-fall production; Vates and Champion are compact, bolt-resistant, very cold-hardy types that shine in fall and overwintering. Top Bunch and Blue Max are fast, uniform hybrids for quick, repeated cutting. Morris Heading is the traditional heading collard for a milder, more tender leaf. Where clubroot or other brassica diseases are a concern, look for resistant cultivars.
varieties.note_beginner: Georgia is an easy, tough heirloom that takes heat and poor soil, great for beginners. Vates and Champion are compact and very cold-hardy, perfect for a fall or winter crop. Top Bunch and Blue Max are fast hybrids if you want tender leaves sooner. Morris Heading makes a softer, cabbage-like collard.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Other brassicas (broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, kale, Brussels sprouts, kohlrabi, turnip, radish, mustard), which share clubroot and cabbage-family pests.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Other cabbage-family crops like broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, kale, and turnips.
rotation.good_after: Legumes such as beans and peas, or unrelated crops like tomatoes, squash, or onions.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate so collards and their brassica relatives do not return to the same ground for at least 3 years, and longer where clubroot is present, since the clubroot organism persists in soil for years. Keeping soil pH near neutral also helps suppress clubroot. In the South, where collards are grown nearly year-round, planning that rotation across beds takes extra thought.
rotation.note_beginner: Do not plant collards or other cabbage-family crops in the same spot year after year. Waiting at least 3 years between them, and longer if you have had clubroot, helps avoid soil diseases.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Collards wilt and toughen at room temperature and lose quality within a day or two, so do not leave them out. Refrigerate as soon as possible after cutting; if they must sit briefly, stand the stems in water like cut flowers.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Do not leave collards out on the counter. They wilt fast in the warmth, so get them into the fridge soon after picking.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerate unwashed in a loose or perforated bag in the crisper; collards hold their quality for roughly 1 week, and up to about 10 to 14 days held near 32°F at high humidity, a bit longer than tender greens because the leaves are sturdier. Washing before storage traps moisture and speeds spoilage.
storage.fridge_beginner: Store collards unwashed in a loose bag in the fridge's crisper drawer, where they stay good for about a week, sometimes up to 2 weeks if very cold. Wait to wash them until you are ready to cook.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Collards freeze well once blanched: strip the leaves from the tough stems, blanch about 3 minutes in boiling water, cool quickly in ice water, drain, and freeze. Blanching halts the enzymes that otherwise cause off-flavors and loss of color in storage.
storage.freezer_beginner: Collards freeze well if you blanch them first. Strip the leaves off the tough stems, boil them for about 3 minutes, cool them right away in ice water, drain, and freeze.
storage.notes_seasoned: Quality is highest straight from the garden, and a key collard advantage is that the plant itself is the best storage: leaves keep on the plant for weeks in cool weather and sweeten after frost, so harvest close to when you will use them rather than stockpiling. Chilling promptly after cutting keeps the leaves crisp and mild.
storage.notes_beginner: Collards are best right after you pick them, and the plant is its own best storage: in cool weather the leaves keep on the plant for weeks and even get sweeter after frost. So pick what you need when you need it, and chill it quickly after cutting.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: In about 5 to 10 days, your seeds sprout and push up their first two little leaves (the seed leaves).
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the soil damp. Once the first real collard leaves appear after the seed leaves, thin crowded seedlings.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have your seeds come up yet?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seeds sprout in about 5 to 10 days at soil temperatures of roughly 45 to 85°F, pushing up two seed leaves (cotyledons).
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep the seedbed or starting mix evenly moist; thin or pot up once the first true leaves appear.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Did your collard seeds sprout?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The seedlings grow their real, smooth leaves and a stronger stem. They are ready to move outside at about 4 to 5 weeks old.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: If you grew transplants, harden them off over about a week before planting out. Watch for flea beetle shot-holes on the young leaves.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How many real leaves do your seedlings have?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Young plants develop true leaves and a sturdy stem; collard transplants are ready at about 4 to 5 weeks. Flea beetles are the main seedling threat.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harden off over 7 to 10 days before setting out; thin or set plants 18 to 24 inches apart and protect seedlings from flea beetles with row cover.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How many true leaves does your seedling have?

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant grows into a tall stem with a bunch of big leaves on top. This is when it builds the frame that you will harvest from for months.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Feed with nitrogen and keep it evenly watered so the leaves stay tender. Check for aphids in the growing tip and caterpillars and harlequin bugs on the leaves.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Is your plant growing lots of healthy leaves?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The plant builds an upright stem topped with a rosette of large leaves over several weeks, laying down the productive frame.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Side-dress with nitrogen, keep moisture even for tender leaves, and scout for aphids, cabbageworms, and harlequin bugs while the frame fills out.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are your collards putting on healthy leafy growth?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Once the lower leaves are about 8 to 10 inches, start picking. Take the lowest, outside leaves and leave the center to keep growing, so the plant gives leaves for months. Or cut the whole young plant.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pick the outer leaves regularly, never stripping more than about a third at once. Feed lightly after a big harvest. The leaves taste sweeter after frost.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Have you started picking outer leaves?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Lower leaves reach usable size (8 to 10 inches) at about 55 to 75 days; harvest cut-and-come-again, taking the lowest leaves and leaving the growing bud, or cut whole young plants at 6 to 10 inches.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Crop the outer leaves regularly to keep new growth coming, side-dress lightly after heavy picking, and expect the best flavor after a frost.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are you harvesting outer leaves?

growth_stages.name: Overwintering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: As cold sets in, collards keep going. They are the most cold-hardy cabbage-family plant: in mild areas you harvest right through winter; in cold areas the plant may rest under cover and regrow, then send up a flower stalk (bolt) in spring.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: In mild zones, keep picking through winter. In cold zones, protect plants with a row cover or low tunnel. When spring warmth makes the plant bolt, harvest what is left, since the leaves turn bitter once it flowers.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Are your collards still producing in the cold?
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Collards are the hardiest of the cole crops: mature plants shrug off hard frost and freezes into the low-to-mid 20s°F and below, sweetening as starch converts to sugar. In mild zones they crop through winter; in cold zones they overwinter under cover and resume, then bolt as spring warms and days lengthen.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest through winter in mild zones; use row cover or low tunnels in cold zones. Once the plant bolts in spring, harvest remaining leaves promptly, as flavor turns bitter, and pull it to make room.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are your collards overwintering or starting to bolt?

notifications.title_beginner: Time to start picking collard leaves
notifications.body_seasoned: Your collards' lower leaves should be about 8 to 10 inches now. Begin cropping the lowest, outermost leaves and leave the central bud so the plant keeps producing for months.
notifications.body_beginner: Your collards' outside leaves should be big enough to pick. Take the lowest, outer ones and leave the middle growing, so it keeps making more.

notifications.body_seasoned: Collards need steady nitrogen for tender leaves. Side-dress now and again after heavy cuttings, placing the feed near the plant and watering it in.
notifications.body_beginner: Collards like regular feeding. Give them some nitrogen now, and again after big harvests, to keep tender leaves coming.

notifications.title_seasoned: Frost is coming: expect sweeter collards
notifications.title_beginner: Frost ahead, your collards will sweeten
notifications.body_seasoned: A frost is on the way. Collards are the most cold-hardy cole crop and the cold actually sweetens the leaves, so there is no need to cover them for a normal frost; just keep harvesting.
notifications.body_beginner: Frost is coming, but that is good news for collards: the cold makes the leaves sweeter. You do not need to cover them for a normal frost. Keep picking.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot weather note for your collards
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Collards are the most heat-tolerant cole crop and usually run right through summer, but sustained heat above about 90°F can toughen the leaves and speed pest pressure. Keep moisture even, harvest in the cool morning, and in hot regions give afternoon shade. Only in genuinely extreme heat (desert valleys, peak Florida and Hawaii summers) is collards a true off-season crop.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Collards handle heat better than other greens and usually keep growing through summer. In a hot spell, water evenly, pick in the cool morning, and give some afternoon shade so the leaves stay tender. Only in the very hottest places is summer really off-season for collards.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hard freeze coming
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Collards are the most cold-hardy cole crop and a freeze sweetens the leaves; mature plants tolerate hard frost and freezes into the low-to-mid 20s°F and below. In the coldest zones a deep freeze may damage exposed leaves, so a row cover or low tunnel extends the harvest, but for most freezes simply keep picking.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Collards handle hard freezes better than almost any vegetable, and the cold makes them taste sweeter, so you usually do not need to do anything. In very cold areas, a row cover or low tunnel helps them keep going through the worst cold.

germination.text_seasoned: Sow about 0.25 to 0.5 inch deep into a moist seedbed or starting mix; collards germinate reliably across 45 to 85°F in about 5 to 10 days.
germination.text_beginner: Plant the seeds about a quarter to half an inch deep in damp soil, and keep it evenly moist while they sprout in 5 to 10 days.

germination.text_seasoned: For a spring crop start indoors about 4 to 5 weeks before set-out, or direct sow as soon as the soil is workable; for a fall crop sow in mid to late summer.
germination.text_beginner: Start seeds indoors about a month before planting out, sow them in the garden once the soil can be worked, or sow in late summer for a fall crop.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin or transplant to about 18 to 24 inches apart for full-size plants, or closer (10 to 15 inches) if you will cut them young; harden transplants off over 7 to 10 days.
seedling.text_beginner: Space plants about 18 to 24 inches apart for big plants, or closer together if you plan to cut them while young.

seedling.text_seasoned: Protect seedlings from flea beetles with row cover; a vigorous, well-watered seedling outgrows light feeding damage.
seedling.text_beginner: Cover young plants with a light row cover to stop flea beetles from peppering the leaves with holes.

established.text_seasoned: Side-dress nitrogen as the plant builds and keep moisture even at roughly 1 to 1.5 inches per week; drought stress is the top cause of tough, stringy leaves, especially in heat.
established.text_beginner: Feed with nitrogen and water steadily, about 1 to 1.5 inches a week, so the leaves stay tender and mild.

established.text_seasoned: Scout the growing tip and crown for cabbage aphids, the leaves for cabbageworms, and, in the South, for harlequin bugs; catching them early keeps the harvested leaves clean.
established.text_beginner: Check the growing tip for aphids and the leaves for caterpillars and shield-shaped harlequin bugs, and deal with them early.

harvest.text_seasoned: Crop the lower leaves once they reach 8 to 10 inches, taking no more than about a third of the plant so the growing bud keeps producing for months; or cut whole young plants and let them regrow.
harvest.text_beginner: Pick the lowest leaves when they are about hand-sized or bigger, and leave the center growing, so the same plant keeps making leaves. Or cut the whole young plant and let it grow back.

harvest.text_seasoned: Leaves are sweetest after a frost or two; in cool weather you can keep harvesting straight from the garden even after the foliage has frozen.
harvest.text_beginner: Collards taste sweeter after frost, and you can keep picking even after the leaves have frozen in cool weather.

overwintering.text_seasoned: In mild zones keep cropping through winter; in cold zones a low tunnel or row cover extends the harvest, and collards take more cold than any other cole crop.
overwintering.text_beginner: In mild areas keep picking all winter. In cold areas, cover the plants to keep harvesting longer; collards handle cold better than any other cabbage-family plant.

overwintering.text_seasoned: Watch for spring bolting as warmth and long days return: harvest remaining leaves before the flower stalk elongates, since the leaves turn bitter once the plant flowers.
overwintering.text_beginner: In spring, collards that lived through winter will send up a flower stalk and turn bitter, so pick the last good leaves before that happens.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A single collard plant yields a steady run of large outer leaves over a long season rather than one harvest, roughly 1 to 2 pounds or more per plant depending on variety, season length, and how often you crop it. Extension yields run about 8 to 15 pounds per 10 feet of row.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: Each collard plant gives you a steady supply of big leaves over months, not one big harvest. How much you get depends on the variety and how long your season is, but a few plants keep producing for a long time.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Production climbs as the plant sizes up and then holds for weeks to months as you crop the lower leaves, peaking in the cool weeks of fall and, in mild zones, through winter. Collards keep producing through summer in much of the South, slowing only in genuinely extreme heat, and the crop ends when the plant bolts in spring.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Collards produce the most once the plant is full-sized, and they keep going strongest in cool fall weather and, in mild areas, through winter. Unlike most greens they also keep going through summer in the South, and they stop once they flower in spring.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: The key to total yield is cropping the lower leaves regularly while leaving the central growing bud: frequent, moderate picking keeps a plant productive for months, whereas stripping a plant bare or letting old leaves toughen on the stem checks it. New growers often pick too timidly or take the bud, which stalls the plant.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Here is the trick: pick the lower leaves often, but always leave the small center bud to keep growing. Regular picking keeps a plant making leaves for months. Do not take the middle of the plant, and do not let old leaves toughen on the stem.
factors_seasoned: Harvest method: regular cut-and-come-again cropping of lower leaves (leaving the bud) sustains months of production; taking the bud or stripping the plant ends it.
Temperature: cool weather through fall and mild winters gives the highest-quality, sweetest leaves; collards also produce through Southern summers but the leaves are milder in cool weather.
Variety: Georgia and the Vates types crop longest; fast hybrids like Top Bunch reach a first cutting sooner.
Nitrogen and even moisture: steady nitrogen and consistent water keep new leaves tender; stress makes them tough, stringy, and aphid-prone.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No reliable extension or peer-reviewed evidence supports timing collard planting or harvest by moon phase. Plant by soil temperature, frost dates, and the seasonal windows instead.

failure_diagnostics.label: Bolting (flower stalk and bitter leaves)
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: A plant that lived through winter and is now flowering in spring, or summer heat and long days on a stressed plant.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your collards shot up a tall stalk with buds or yellow flowers and the leaves turned bitter. Collards are biennials that bolt (run to flower) mostly in their second spring after a cold winter, and sometimes from heat and long days on a stressed plant. Once they bolt the leaves go bitter and tough. People often blame the plant, but it is just its life cycle. Next time, treat an overwintered plant as a spring bonus you harvest before it flowers, and pick bolt-resistant types like Vates or Champion.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Harvest overwintered plants before they bolt in spring, grow bolt-resistant varieties, and keep plants unstressed with steady water.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The plant elongated a flowering stalk and the leaves turned bitter and tough. Bolting is driven mainly by vernalization (a cold winter) flowering the biennial in its second spring, and secondarily by heat and long days on stressed plants; once it bolts, leaf quality is lost. Next time crop overwintered plants out before the stalk elongates, choose bolt-resistant cultivars (Vates, Champion, Top Bunch), and avoid drought stress.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Vernalization flowering the biennial in spring, or heat and long days on a stressed plant.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Crop overwintered collards before they bolt, favor bolt-resistant varieties, and hold even moisture to avoid stress-triggered bolting.

failure_diagnostics.label: Tough, stringy, bitter leaves
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Drought stress, leaves left on the plant too long, or extreme heat.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your collard leaves are tough, leathery, and bitter instead of tender. This usually comes from the plant drying out, from leaving leaves on too long so they age, or from very hot weather. It is tempting to think the variety is bad, but conditions are almost always the cause. Next time, keep the soil evenly moist, pick leaves while they are young to medium-sized, and remember that frost actually sweetens them.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep moisture steady, pick leaves young, give afternoon shade in extreme heat, and enjoy the post-frost sweetening.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Leaves are tough and stringy rather than tender. Drought stress, over-mature leaves, and extreme heat are the usual causes; collards tolerate heat but their leaf quality still suffers when they dry out, and flavor is best in cool weather and sweetened by frost. Next time hold even moisture, crop leaves at a young-to-medium size, shade them in genuinely extreme heat, and lean on the cool shoulders and fall window for the sweetest leaves.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Drought stress, over-mature leaves, or genuinely extreme heat.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Hold even moisture, crop leaves young, shade in extreme heat, and use the cool fall and winter window for the sweetest leaves.

failure_diagnostics.label: Bugs all over summer collards
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Warm-season pests, especially harlequin bugs, cabbageworms, and aphids, which build up on collards left in the ground through Southern summers.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your summer collards got covered in shield-shaped harlequin bugs, green caterpillars, or clusters of aphids, and the leaves are stippled and chewed. Collards keep growing in summer heat, but so do their pests, and pressure is worst in the warm South. People often stop scouting once the plants are big. Next time, scout weekly, use row cover, hand-pick harlequin bugs and their barrel-shaped eggs, spray Bt for caterpillars, and clean up old plants and weeds where pests overwinter.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Scout weekly in warm weather, use row cover, hand-pick harlequin bugs, spray Bt for caterpillars, and clear old plants and weeds.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Summer collards drew heavy harlequin bug, caterpillar, and cabbage-aphid pressure, with stippled, chewed, and contaminated leaves. The crop's summer persistence is also its pest liability in the South, where harlequin bugs run several generations a year. Next time scout weekly, exclude with row cover, hand-pick harlequin adults and egg rows, use Bt or spinosad for caterpillars, knock down aphid colonies early, and remove crucifer weeds and debris that harbor overwintering adults.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Warm-season brassica pests (harlequin bug, cabbageworms, cabbage aphid) building on long-held summer collards, worst in the South.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Scout weekly, exclude with row cover, hand-pick harlequin bugs and egg rows, treat caterpillars with Bt, and sanitize overwintering sites.

failure_diagnostics.label: Stunted, yellow plants with clubbed roots
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Clubroot, a soil disease of cabbage-family plants, or planting brassicas in the same spot too often.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your collards stayed small and yellowish, wilted in the afternoon, and when you dug them up the roots were swollen into lumps. That is clubroot, a soil disease that infects cabbage-family roots and lasts for years in the soil. It usually builds up when brassicas are grown in the same spot repeatedly, which is easy to do with a near-year-round crop. Next time, rotate so cabbage-family crops do not return to that bed for at least 3 years, keep the soil pH near neutral, and improve drainage.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Rotate brassicas out of that bed for at least 3 years, keep soil pH near neutral, and improve drainage.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Plants were stunted and chlorotic, wilted by day, and showed galled, clubbed roots, the signature of clubroot (Plasmodiophora brassicae). The soilborne organism persists for years and builds under repeated brassica cropping and acidic, poorly drained soil, a real risk where collards are grown nearly year-round. Next time rotate cabbage-family crops out for at least 3 years (longer where known), lime toward a neutral-to-slightly-alkaline pH, and improve drainage; there is no in-season cure.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Clubroot building in soil cropped to brassicas too frequently, favored by acidic, wet soil.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Use a 3-year-plus brassica rotation, raise pH toward neutral, and improve drainage; remove and destroy infected plants.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Collards crop over a long window, so rather than one big planting, sow small batches every 2 to 3 weeks through the cool stretches of spring and again from late summer for a fall and winter crop. Because each plant is cropped over many weeks, you need fewer sowings than for a fast crop, but staggering keeps tender young leaves coming. In the South you can plant across most of the year; only in genuinely extreme heat (deserts, peak Florida and Hawaii summers) do you skip the peak and plant for fall and winter instead.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: Plant collards in small batches a couple of weeks apart, in spring and again in late summer for fall, rather than all at once. Each plant keeps giving leaves for a long time, so you do not need many. In hot-desert and tropical areas, skip the peak summer and plant for fall and winter.

verification_status.verification_log_ref: collards_author_fresh_pilot (Claude Code lane authoring, 2026-06-29). Authored as a NEW gold-standard record modeled STRUCTURALLY on the certified broccoli template, with kale (same species, Acephala group) as the closest content analog and swiss-chard as the heat-tolerance calendar pattern. All collard biology re-derived from live T1 extension sources: UGA CAES Cultivating Collards, UMN growing-collards-and-kale, NC State collard-greens, UMD leafy greens, Clemson cole-crop pests/greens for biology and pests/diseases; per-region planting calendars from UC ANR/UC MG, UF/IFAS VH021 + FL calendars, UGA C943, LSU/MSU State/TAMU, UArizona/NMSU, CTAHR, plus Cornell/Iowa State/UMaine/UNH/MSU for the northern tier. DRAFT for review, not certified: launch flags false. Key collards-vs-broccoli refits: loose-leaf NON-HEADING green (no head_forming/side_shoots stages; cut-and-come-again lower leaves or whole-plant harvest; added overwintering stage); the MOST cold-hardy cole crop (frost-sweetened, holds through hard freezes into the low-to-mid 20s F and below) AND the MOST heat-tolerant (runs through Southern summers). Heat model sits BETWEEN kale and swiss-chard: collards RUN THROUGH the humid Deep South (se_gulf), the mild CA coasts (ca_north_coast, ca_south_coast), and the high desert (warm_arid, with a winter cold_pause), and reserve heat_pause for the genuine extremes only, the hot interior valley peak (ca_interior Jul-Aug), the deserts (ca_desert, low_desert_az), and the peak Florida and Hawaii summers, each backed at the cell. days_to_maturity 55-75, spacing 18-24 in, pH 6.0-6.8; Brassicaceae rotation; harlequin bug + caterpillars emphasized as the Southern collard pests. successions_realized NOT hand-authored (CC deriver fills it). See collards_NOTES.md for flags and modeled values.

open_findings.summary: Heat_pause footprint is a modeled judgment call positioning collards BETWEEN kale (8 heat_pause regions) and swiss-chard (4): heat_pause is placed only in ca_interior (Jul-Aug peak), ca_desert, low_desert_az, fl_peninsula, and hawaii_tropical; collards RUN THROUGH se_gulf, ca_north_coast, ca_south_coast, and warm_arid summers. ca_interior gets a summer pause while warm_arid runs through summer (with a winter cold_pause) because their limiting seasons differ (interior valley-floor heat vs high-desert winter cold).
open_findings.basis: Supported by collards' documented heat tolerance (UGA: grows in summer with moisture, 'tolerant to heat and cold'; UF VH021: 'cold and heat tolerant'), the swiss-chard precedent (runs through the same merely-warm regions), and the UC cole-crop interior-valley planting window being fall-only. The exact per-region run-through-vs-pause line is the load-bearing biology call for the daily review.

open_findings.summary: germination_temp_f [45, 85] is the standard cole-crop germination envelope; the collard-specific T1 pages state 5 to 10 day germination but not an explicit min/max soil temperature, so the range is modeled on the brassica germination envelope (shared with kale/broccoli).
open_findings.basis: Consistent with broccoli/kale germination_temp_f and the 5 to 10 day germination the collard sources report.

open_findings.summary: Variety days_to_maturity are sourced for Georgia (75) and Vates (75) from UGA; Champion (75), Morris Heading (85), Top Bunch (55), and Blue Max (68) are modeled from typical seed-trade figures (catalog/T2) rather than a T1 page, since the T1 collard sources do not table per-cultivar DTM.
open_findings.basis: DTMs are within the collard 55-85 day band the T1 sources give; flagged for a source-truth pass against a T1 variety table at review.

open_findings.summary: hawaii_tropical z11 uses a bounded low-elevation winter window with a summer heat_pause and notes high-elevation year-round; CTAHR B-91 is a 1943 scanned PDF that did not parse via WebFetch and does not table collards' planting months directly (inferred from its cole-crop / leafy-green guidance, corroborated by NC State). Corroborate against a parseable modern CTAHR source at review.
open_findings.basis: Same systemic Hawaii-PDF convention Trevor blessed for kale/broccoli; only the PDF parse and bulletin age are gaps.
