plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set collards out around the last frost, or direct sow when the soil is workable; sow again in midsummer for fall.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Collards crop cut-and-come-again from about 55 to 75 days after sowing.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest continues for months and through frosts, sweetening in the cold.

3.zone_notes: In the coldest zone, collards crop from summer through the fall frosts that sweeten them; deep winter ends the unprotected crop, so it is a single long season.

4.zone_notes: Plant in spring once the soil is workable and again in midsummer for fall; harvest runs through the fall frosts, then deep winter ends it.

5.zone_notes: A long season from spring through the fall frosts; under a low tunnel or row cover harvest can extend into winter, since collards are very cold-hardy.

6.zone_notes: Plant in early spring and midsummer; collards hold later into winter than most greens, often into December before hard cold ends the crop.

7.zone_notes: In the mild end of the cold tier collards run nearly year-round: a spring and a fall planting, harvest through the warm summer (collards tolerate it) and through winter, with the leaves sweetest after frost.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In cold areas, collards are mostly a spring-through-fall crop, with a late-summer planting for fall. They handle frost better than almost any vegetable and get sweeter after it, so you can keep picking well past the first freezes. In the very coldest zones, winter eventually ends them unless you cover them.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: In the cold zones collards are one long cool-season crop. Direct sow or set transplants out around the last frost (collards take cold well), with a midsummer sowing for a fall crop that runs through the frosts, which sweeten the leaves. Collards are the hardiest cole crop, so harvest stretches later than most greens; under a low tunnel it can reach into winter, but deep cold eventually ends the open-ground crop.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: In the Deep South plant late winter and again late summer; collards run nearly year-round, slowing only in the hottest, buggiest weeks of midsummer.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Collards crop cut-and-come-again from about 55 to 75 days after sowing.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest continues for months and through frosts, sweetening in the cold.

8.zone_notes: Nearly year-round: a late-winter and a late-summer planting carry harvest across all four seasons. Collards run through the humid summer where cool-season peers cannot, though midsummer leaves toughen and pest pressure peaks.

9.zone_notes: In the warm coastal zone collards grow nearly year-round; the fall planting carries the main cool-season crop and a late-winter sowing extends into summer. Even moisture keeps the leaves tender through the heat.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: Along the Gulf Coast, collards are the classic green grown almost all year. Plant in late winter and again in late summer, and they keep going through the hot summer when other greens quit. Summer leaves can be a bit tougher and buggier, so the spring and fall crops are the tastiest.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: The Gulf and coastal plain are collard country, where the crop grows nearly year-round. Plant in late winter for a spring-into-summer crop and again in late summer for a fall-and-winter crop; collards keep producing right through the hot, humid summer with even moisture, where lettuce and most brassicas cannot. Midsummer leaves are a touch tougher and pest pressure (harlequin bugs, caterpillars, aphids) peaks, so quality is best in the cool shoulders.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Plant late winter and again late summer; the July to August valley-floor peak is too hot even for collards.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Collards crop cut-and-come-again from about 55 to 75 days after sowing.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest continues for months and through frosts, sweetening in the cold.

8.zone_notes: A spring crop and a fall crop bracket a short July to August heat break; collards hold the June and September shoulders that stop lettuce and broccoli.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Collards are the most heat-tolerant cole crop and run through the warm shoulders of the interior valleys, but the genuinely extreme valley-floor summer, with sustained highs around 100 to 105°F in July and August, pushes even collards past good leaf production and concentrates harlequin bug and aphid pressure, so the peak is left out of the planting calendar and the crop resumes in fall. The June and September shoulders can often be pushed with afternoon shade and steady water, which collards tolerate better than lettuce or broccoli.

9.zone_notes: In the hottest interior valleys the July to August peak is excluded, but collards run the long cool shoulders on either side, planted late winter and late summer.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Collards are the most heat-tolerant cole crop and run through the warm shoulders of the interior valleys, but the genuinely extreme valley-floor summer, with sustained highs around 100 to 105°F in July and August, pushes even collards past good leaf production and concentrates harlequin bug and aphid pressure, so the peak is left out of the planting calendar and the crop resumes in fall. The June and September shoulders can often be pushed with afternoon shade and steady water, which collards tolerate better than lettuce or broccoli.

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In California's hot inland valleys, grow collards in spring and again from late summer into winter. They take more heat than most greens and hold the edges of summer, but the hottest part of July and August is too much even for collards, so skip it.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: In the hot interior valleys collards are a long cool-season crop with a genuine summer break. Plant in late winter for a spring crop and in late summer (when the worst heat eases) for a fall-and-winter crop. Collards out-tolerate lettuce and broccoli and hold the June and September shoulders, but the July and August valley-floor peak, around 100 to 105°F, is left out.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Plant late winter and early fall; the mild coast carries collards nearly year-round.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Collards crop cut-and-come-again from about 55 to 75 days after sowing.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest continues for months and through frosts, sweetening in the cold.

9.zone_notes: The cool coastal climate grows collards nearly year-round; mild summers mean no heat break and mild winters no cold break, so one planting runs for many months.

10.zone_notes: Frost-free coastal pockets grow collards year-round; plant late winter and early fall and crop the lower leaves continuously.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: Along California's cool north coast, collards grow almost all year. The mild weather means you can plant in late winter and again in early fall and keep picking for months, with no real summer or winter break.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: On the cool north coast collards grow nearly year-round. Mild summers and mild winters let one planting run for many months; plant in late winter and again in early fall, and crop the lower leaves continuously. Neither heat nor cold interrupts the crop here.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Plant late winter and early fall; the mild south coast carries collards nearly year-round.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Collards crop cut-and-come-again from about 55 to 75 days after sowing.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest continues for months and through frosts, sweetening in the cold.

9.zone_notes: The mild south coast grows collards nearly year-round; collards run through the moderate coastal summer that bolts lettuce, with even moisture and a little afternoon shade inland.

10.zone_notes: Frost-light south-coast zones grow collards year-round; plant late winter and early fall and crop the lower leaves continuously.

ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: Along California's mild south coast, collards grow almost all year. The warm but moderate summers do not stop them the way they stop lettuce, and winters are gentle, so plant in late winter and early fall and keep picking.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: On the mild south coast collards run nearly year-round. Summers are warm but moderate near the coast, and collards out-tolerate lettuce here, producing right through them with even moisture; winters are frost-light. Plant late winter and early fall and crop continuously.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Plant October to November and again in late winter; the extreme summer is excluded.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Collards crop cut-and-come-again from about 55 to 75 days after sowing.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest continues for months and through frosts, sweetening in the cold.

9.zone_notes: A fall-through-spring crop: plant October to November (and a late-winter sowing), harvest December into May; the June to September peak above 105°F is excluded.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Collards tolerate more heat than any other cole crop, but the desert valleys are a genuine extreme: sustained summer highs around and above 105 to 115°F, with germination failing above about 85°F, scorch and stall even collards, so the peak summer is left out of the planting calendar and the crop runs as a fall-through-spring green. The shoulder months can sometimes be pushed with heavy afternoon shade, mulch, and steady water.

10.zone_notes: In the hottest desert valleys collards run as a cool-season green from fall to late spring; the extreme June to September summer is the off-season.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Collards tolerate more heat than any other cole crop, but the desert valleys are a genuine extreme: sustained summer highs around and above 105 to 115°F, with germination failing above about 85°F, scorch and stall even collards, so the peak summer is left out of the planting calendar and the crop runs as a fall-through-spring green. The shoulder months can sometimes be pushed with heavy afternoon shade, mulch, and steady water.

ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: In the low desert, grow collards from fall into spring. Plant in October and pick through winter and spring. The summer here is too extreme even for collards, so June through September is the off-season.
ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: In the desert valleys collards are a fall-through-spring crop. Plant from October and harvest into spring; even this heat-tolerant green cannot hold the genuinely extreme summer, around and above 105 to 115°F, so June through September is excluded. A late-winter sowing extends the spring crop.

warm_arid.region_label: Warm Arid: Southern New Mexico & West Texas

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Plant late winter and late summer; collards run through the dry summer but hard winter freezes end the open-ground crop.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Collards crop cut-and-come-again from about 55 to 75 days after sowing.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest continues for months and through frosts, sweetening in the cold.

8.zone_notes: Collards run through the hot, dry summer here with steady water and afternoon shade, unlike in the lower-elevation deserts; the limiting season is winter, when hard December and January freezes end the open-ground crop, though their strong hardiness and row cover extend it.

warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: In the high desert, collards handle the hot dry summer with steady water and some shade, and they are tough enough to take a lot of winter cold. Plant in late winter and late summer; the hardest winter freezes in December and January usually end the crop unless you cover it.
warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: In the high desert of southern New Mexico and West Texas collards face hot, dry summers and genuinely cold winters. Plant late winter and late summer; collards run through the dry summer with even moisture and afternoon shade (drier heat is easier on them than humid heat), and the hard winter freezes of December and January end the open-ground crop, though row cover and their strong hardiness push it.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Plant October to December and again in late winter; the extreme low-desert summer is excluded.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Collards crop cut-and-come-again from about 55 to 75 days after sowing.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest continues for months and through frosts, sweetening in the cold.

9.zone_notes: A long cool-season crop: plant October through December (and a late-winter sowing), harvest into spring; the June to September desert summer is the off-season.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Collards tolerate more heat than any other cole crop, but the desert valleys are a genuine extreme: sustained summer highs around and above 105 to 115°F, with germination failing above about 85°F, scorch and stall even collards, so the peak summer is left out of the planting calendar and the crop runs as a fall-through-spring green. The shoulder months can sometimes be pushed with heavy afternoon shade, mulch, and steady water.

low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: In the Arizona low desert, grow collards from fall into spring. Plant October through December and pick through winter and spring. Summer here is far too hot, so June through September is off.
low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: In Arizona's low desert collards are a fall-through-spring crop. Plant from October through December and harvest into spring; the 105 to 115°F summer, June through September, is the off-season even for this heat-tolerant green. A late-winter sowing extends the harvest.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Plant September onward and harvest through the cool season; the hot, wet summer is excluded.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Collards crop cut-and-come-again from about 55 to 75 days after sowing.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest continues for months and through frosts, sweetening in the cold.

10.zone_notes: A fall-planted cool-season crop harvested December through May; the hot, humid, disease-prone June to August summer is the off-season.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Even this heat-tolerant green is left out of the Florida peninsula's peak summer: June through August brings sustained heat in the low-to-mid 90s°F with high humidity, heavy rain, and intense disease and pest pressure, so UF and the Florida calendars treat collards as a fall-through-spring crop. It resumes with the fall planting.

11.zone_notes: In the warmest south-Florida zone collards run as a fall-through-spring green; the June to August peak of heat, humidity, and pest pressure is excluded.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Even this heat-tolerant green is left out of the Florida peninsula's peak summer: June through August brings sustained heat in the low-to-mid 90s°F with high humidity, heavy rain, and intense disease and pest pressure, so UF and the Florida calendars treat collards as a fall-through-spring crop. It resumes with the fall planting.

fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: In peninsular Florida, grow collards from fall through spring. Plant starting in September and pick through the cool months. The hot, wet summer brings too many bugs and diseases, so June through August is off, even though collards take heat well.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: On the Florida peninsula collards are a fall-through-spring crop. UF and the Florida calendars plant from September and harvest through the cool months; the hot, humid, rainy summer (June through August) brings heavy disease and pest pressure that even this heat-tolerant green sits out. South Florida extends the planting window into winter.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Plant in fall and harvest through the cooler months; low-elevation summer is excluded, high elevation grows year-round.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Collards crop cut-and-come-again from about 55 to 75 days after sowing.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest continues for months and through frosts, sweetening in the cold.

11.zone_notes: Low-elevation Hawaii grows collards as a cool-season crop, fall-planted and harvested into spring; the warm, wet June to September summer is excluded, while high-elevation areas grow it year-round.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: At low elevation in Hawaii the summer is too warm and wet for good collard quality, so the planting calendar centers on the cooler months and excludes roughly June through September; at higher elevations collards can be grown year-round. The bounded window is inferred from CTAHR cole-crop guidance and corroborated by NC State, pending a parseable modern source.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In low-elevation Hawaii, grow collards in the cooler months, planting in fall and picking through winter and spring; the warm, wet summer is off-season. Up in the cooler highlands, collards can grow all year.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: At low elevation in Hawaii collards are a cooler-season crop, planted in fall and harvested through the milder months; the warm, wet summer (roughly June through September) is too much for good leaf quality. At higher elevations the milder year-round climate lets collards grow continuously.

crops.description_seasoned: Collards (Brassica oleracea, Acephala group) are a loose-leaf, non-heading cabbage relative grown for their large, smooth blue-green leaves, the same species as kale and the classic green of Southern gardens. Their signature is unusual tolerance of BOTH cold and heat: collards are the most cold-hardy of the cole crops, sweetening after frost and holding through hard freezes, yet they are also the most heat-tolerant, producing right through Southern summers where lettuce and most brassicas have long since bolted. A collard plant builds a stout upright stem topped with a rosette of broad leaves, and you crop the lower leaves over a long run or cut the whole young plant. In much of the South they grow nearly year-round; everywhere else they shine in the long cool shoulders of spring and fall.
crops.description_beginner: Collards are a leafy cousin of kale and cabbage, grown for their big, smooth green leaves. They are the famous green of Southern cooking, and they are tough: they handle cold better than almost any other vegetable and get sweeter after frost, but they also keep growing in summer heat that stops other greens. The plant grows tall with a bunch of large leaves at the top. You pick the lower leaves a few at a time for months, or cut the whole young plant. In warm areas collards grow almost all year; in cooler areas they do best in spring and fall.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Start cropping outer leaves once they reach about 8 to 10 inches, taking the lowest, oldest leaves first and leaving the central bud and upper rosette to keep producing. Leaves are most tender picked young to medium-sized; old leaves turn tough and stringy. Alternatively cut the whole young plant near the soil line at 6 to 10 inches and let it regrow, or harvest the tender inner rosette. Flavor is mildest and sweetest in cool weather and after a frost.
crops.harvest_ready_beginner: Begin picking when the lower leaves are about the size of your hand or bigger, around 8 to 10 inches. Take the lowest, outside leaves and leave the middle growing, so the plant keeps making more for months. You can also cut the whole young plant off near the ground and let it grow back. The leaves taste best picked while still tender, and they get sweeter after a frost.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Collards are leafy heavy feeders that reward a fertile, well-drained loam worked deeply and enriched with compost or aged manure before planting. Loosen the bed 8 to 12 inches, mix in organic matter for steady moisture and nitrogen, and aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 6.8. Where clubroot has appeared, lime toward the high end of that band. Good drainage matters as much as fertility: collards make their best leaves in soil that stays evenly moist but never waterlogged.
crops.soil_prep_beginner: Collards like rich, loose soil with lots of compost mixed in. Dig the bed over and work in compost or aged manure before planting, since collards are hungry plants that grow a lot of leaves. Aim for a soil pH around 6.0 to 6.8, and make sure water drains away well. Keep the soil moist but not soggy and the plants will reward you with big, tender leaves.

versioning_note: Two version fields. `version` tracks crop content (planting dates, sources, biological data) and bumps when data inside `crops` changes. `schema_version` tracks the shape of the dataset (rule structure, sub-object schemas, top-level fields) and bumps when structure changes. They are independent. As of schema_version 2.8, deployed structure includes: symmetric `_seasoned`/`_beginner` register suffixing on prose fields (Phase 0); the three-array companions register-by-membership model (`*_beginner`/`*_beginner_seasoned`/`*_seasoned`); the additive `regions{}` sibling with `northern_tier` lifted and warm regions scaffolded PENDING (Phase A/B); and the calendar-model scaffolding (session 4c): a `track` field (`beginner`/`succession`/`second_planting`) on each `plantings[]` entry, a crop-level `calendar_basis` (`frost_anchored`/`non_seasonal_indoor`/`generic_placeholder`) with the relaxed validator `plantings` length >= 1 UNLESS `calendar_basis` explains it, and the extended `calendar[]` vocabulary adding `cold_pause`/`heat_pause`/`season_over` (reserved; populated per-crop in gold-standard arcs, not bulk-applied). As of schema_version 2.9, the perennial/tree extension is scaffolded (null-by-archetype): chill_hours_*, bloom_*, pollination, rootstock_options, dormancy_window/pruning_window, cane_management, renovation, establishment_years on woody/perennial archetypes; plus universal watering_method + schedule_by_stage + drought_tolerance + critical_periods + fertilizer.amount + container self-watering, and sources/anchoring_urls plumbing on watering/fertilizer/thinning/varieties. Values authored per anchor; this bump is additive scaffolding only.

weatherkit.name: Apple WeatherKit
weatherkit.note: WeatherKit is the resolution-layer data source for bolt-threshold and heat-pause anchors. Underlying service: Apple Weather. Data products used: current conditions, hourly forecast (10-day, up to 240 hours), and daily forecast (10 days). Coverage: global, with US coordinate-level resolution adequate for gardener microclimate purposes; updates hourly to sub-hourly. WeatherKit is a forecast service, not a historical-validation dataset; its role in this dataset is resolution at notification time, not validation. Known limitation: 10-day forecast horizon constrains sustain-window math for bolt thresholds in cool-season crops where the relevant window can exceed 10 days; the methodology page documents the resolution approach for that case. Per Apple's WeatherKit attribution requirements, apps that display Apple Weather data must include the Apple Weather trademark and a link to additional data sources.
weatherkit.citable_for: Apple WeatherKit API for weather forecast and current-conditions data. Citable for forecast-driven app behavior. Not citable for biological-mechanism claims; not a research source.

usu_ext_english_lavender.citable_for: USU Extension peer-reviewed fact sheet on English lavender (Lavandula angustifolia): pH 6.5-7.5, zones 5-10 (hardy z5, z4 with mulch/south wall), spacing 18-24 inches, 1-2 ft tall/wide and 3 years to full size, 10-15 year lifespan, propagated from cuttings (seed not recommended, 100-200 days seed-to-transplant), low fertility needs and over-fertilizing reduces flowers, deep-infrequent watering, prune yearly after flowering, harvest as flowers begin to open, dry hung upside down, Munstead/Hidcote recommended, companion low-water perennials.
